text: The iteration count l equals the number of nodes whose estimated total is below the goal's estimated total, and is usually smaller than the node count n.
A* can be understood as a low-fill version of Dijkstra.
A simple A* with a good heuristic can plan across tens of thousands of nodes in one frame, but worlds of hundreds of thousands or millions of locations need hierarchical planning and other remedies.
A* cannot run on raw level geometry and needs the level represented as a directed, non-negative weighted graph.
when: Applying A* to a game level
why: A* relies on nodes and weighted connections to measure route cost

text: Ignoring data-structure overhead, A* takes O(lm) time, with l iterations and m the mean count of outgoing edges per node.
why: Iterations count nodes whose estimated total cost is below the goal's, and each iteration's inner loop scans about m outgoing connections, as in Dijkstra.

text: A* peak memory use is O(lm), because the open list ends with O(lm) entries.
A simple A* pathfinder suits a shooter level with 5 to 50 characters, but would likely struggle with 1000 characters across a continent-sized world.
why: The challenge is scale: large character counts on a far bigger world need a different implementation.

text: Big-O order alone can mislead about real A* speed; priority queue, graph, and heuristic costs determine actual performance.
why: The heuristic runs roughly once per loop step, and its processing can dominate execution time.

text: Use the general A* version when node counts vary, such as with streamed level sections, or when memory is too tight for specialized versions.
Use distance for plain shortest paths and time when speed matters; use blended costs when a character has tactical concerns.
why: Time-based costs can diverge from distance, and blended costs sum many concerns so the least dangerous route wins.

text: Underestimating heuristic suits when accuracy outweighs speed or heuristic is not consistently near-perfect; overestimating suits when small suboptimality is acceptable and speed matters.
why: Overestimating rapidly degrades A*'s performance, while underestimating still returns the correct answer.

text: Branch and bound is a backtracking search over a tree of partial solutions that keeps the best solution found so far and prunes any branch whose bound cannot beat it.
Exhaustive search iterates through every possible configuration of the search space.
Backtracking solves a problem by trying steps toward a solution, recording each one, and undoing those that reach a dead end.
The eight queens problem asks for placement of eight queens on a chessboard so that no queen attacks another.
Checking every assignment of characters to slots grows far too fast to be practical; for 20 characters and 20 slots the count is roughly 2500 trillion.
Eight queens has 92 solutions when mirror and rotated placements are counted separately, but only 12 are essentially different.
The search tree often grows exponentially with a problem parameter, so search effort grows at a similar rate.
Exhaustive breadth-first simulation is practical only for small levels with a restricted move set, and is impractical at the scale of large open-world games.
when: when considering exhaustive simulation for mechanic testing
why: The state space grows too fast for large levels.

text: Backtracking splits a problem into partial tasks that form a search tree, which the search builds and prunes as it proceeds.
Three Boolean arrays track occupancy: eight rows, 15 diagonals indexed by row plus column, and 15 diagonals indexed by row minus column shifted by 7.
when: Eight by eight board with coordinates running from 1 to 8.
why: Every field on one diagonal shares a constant coordinate sum or difference, so one flag tracks that whole diagonal.

text: Handling easy items first can use up valid slots, leaving the hard items with no valid option.
why: Placing easy items first spreads them across the slots the hard item needs, leaving it no place to go.

text: Users do not control artifacts directly, so selecting a favourite does not tell the computer how to interpret that choice.

1) For each character, collect valid slots below the cost limit, storing cost and slot number, and add one divided by one plus cost to its ease. 2) Mark all slots open. 3) Sort characters by ease, least easy first. 4) Sort each candidate list by cost. 5) Give each character its first open candidate and mark that slot filled.
when: Assigning characters to formation slots
why: Constrained characters are placed before flexible ones, and this works in most cases.

text: 1) Keep the best selection and its value in global variables. 2) At each leaf, instead of printing, replace them only when the current value is larger.
1) Select the first candidate for the next step. 2) While candidates remain and the current one cannot be completed, select the next candidate.
when: building an incomplete solution
why: Steps toward a total solution are recorded tentatively and erased when found to lead into a dead end.

text: 1) Record the move. 2) Call Try on the extended partial solution. 3) If the attempt failed, erase the record. 4) Return whether the attempt succeeded.
why: A recorded move is undone when the recursive attempt fails, so dead-end steps are not kept.

text: 1) Place a queen in the next column on a safe row. 2) If every column is filled, record and print the placement. 3) Otherwise recurse to the next column. 4) Remove the queen and try the next safe row.
when: Enumerating every solution of a placement problem.
why: Safety of a square reduces to checking its row and two diagonals, which the three flags answer directly.

text: 1) Pair the next man with the first untried woman in his preference list. 2) Keep the pairing only if the partial assignment stays stable. 3) If no woman fits, undo the last pairing and try his next choice. 4) Report each complete assignment as a solution.
when: finding all stable pairings by backtracking over men in a fixed order
why: The search follows the same schema as the all-queens enumeration, reusing its record-and-cancel structure.

text: Measure a character's flexibility per actual slot, not per role; a restricted character is still flexible if many matching slots exist.
when: Computing ease of assignment
why: Costs are summed over actual slots, so a role with many open slots raises a restricted character's rating.

text: Handle a degenerate or complete case with a conditional around the whole procedure body, so callers need no extra checks.
why: The guard sits inside the procedure, so the degenerate full-board case is handled correctly, much as arithmetic handles zero.

text: Pass the search state as parameters rather than reading it from global variables, where possible.
when: When the needed search state is already known at the moment the procedure is called.
why: Global variables hold the whole construction state, but only the last position is needed, which parameters carry more simply.

text: To find every solution, put the recursive call and the undo inside the loop body, not in the loop guard, so scanning continues after each success.
when: When every solution to a problem is wanted instead of just one.
why: Scanning must continue after a success to reach the remaining candidates.

text: Place exactly one queen in each column, so the choice at each step is only the row of the queen in that column, among eight rows.
when: Eight queens on an eight by eight board.
why: Queens attack along their column, row and diagonals, so two queens in one column would check each other.

text: An opening book stores move sequences from the game's start, usually as a hash table keyed by board position; entries list candidate moves and each line's estimated average outcome.
Human players and successful computer programs both rely on pattern recognition drawn from past games or a database rather than calculating the optimal move each time.
Unlike a transposition table, one opening book position may have several recommended moves, because openings branch like a tree.
Sophisticated pattern recognition has been tried for set plays, especially in Go and Chess, but no dominant general method has emerged for board games.
Most commercial board game programs use the opponent's thinking time by searching during it and storing results in a transposition table.
Many developers stop as soon as the goal is seen, because the first route found is often the shortest or close to it.
why: Alternative routes that are shorter differ by very little, so stopping early loses little.

text: Late in games like chess, backgammon and checkers, simplified boards can again be handled with stored lookups similar to opening books.
when: remaining material is small enough

text: On an open grid, central squares have higher hit probability than edge squares because more placements of a piece cover them.
when: no prior hits and no obstacles on the board
why: more legal placements pass through central squares

text: With a plain list, each expert scanning the board costs time proportional to the number of entries; a hash keyed on semantic identifiers reduces lookup to near-constant time.
when: When many experts or a large linear blackboard are involved.
why: Keying a hash by data meaning lets an expert check cheaply whether a relevant entry exists instead of scanning.

text: 1) Start from an initial opening library. 2) Record the program's statistical results for each line. 3) Lower the score of any line that keeps losing for this program, so it is avoided later.
when: When a program that uses an opening book keeps losing with a line marked as good.
why: Database scores reflect broad expert play, while each AI has its own characteristics that may differ.

text: 1) Search all states with breadth-first simulation over the available moves. 2) Check whether the goal is reached. Use this when no heuristics exist for the unknown effects of arbitrary code.
when: when the effects of generated code on the game state are unknown
why: Without domain heuristics, only exhaustive search can verify reachability.

text: When importing opening sequences, record at each intermediate position which line it belongs to and how strong that line is.
why: Positions can sit in many opening lines, so per-position records let lookups handle transpositions automatically.

text: Avoid full collision detection in targeting simulations by stopping early, for example when the projectile is well below the target's height.
when: Running targeting simulations
why: Full collision testing takes too long across many simulated shots, so a cheap height cutoff is used.

text: Brute force enumeration gives an exact probability but grows with outcome count, while Monte Carlo runs are cheap at scale but approximate and change on every recalculation.
when: Choosing a method to find a probability.
why: Monte Carlo averages random trials, so each estimate is itself random and shifts between runs.

text: Replacing ten by a base B in both conversion routines yields conversion routines for base B.
Present a technique as a sequence of increasingly efficient versions, starting with simpler stepping stones, so the final design's structure is easy to understand.
when: Explaining or documenting a non-obvious algorithm
why: Simpler stages show why the final design looks as it does

text: Compare expected and worst-case performance when they differ; some algorithms have improbable worst cases that can often be ignored in practice.
when: When an algorithm's worst case needs deliberately contrived, highly improbable inputs.
why: Ordinary use rarely produces those engineered inputs, so typical runs perform much better.

text: Interchanging the two branch tests in binary search slightly improves efficiency, because equality occurs only once.
why: The equality outcome is the one that ends the search, so it is the branch to test second.

text: Algorithm performance uses O() notation with n usually a problem component, like characters in an area; approximate time or memory replaces O() when it is too involved.
when: When a full O() derivation is too involved for the algorithm.
why: Full derivations are not practical for implementation work, so a rough indication is more useful.

text: 1) Scan the program text to find all procedure definitions. 2) Find every procedure call inside each definition. 3) Order the subroutines topologically using the call relation.
Looping over cells adds overhead, but short per-cell unit lists cut pair checks enough to offset it.
why: Each unit is checked only against units in its own cell, not against every unit in the battle.

text: Game data means every number that defines a game object, such as hit points, damage per hit, hits per turn, or armor class.
A game object is a single item in one of a game's systems, such as a card, weapon, unit, equipment, tech, or character.
Four characteristic points can represent a fuzzy set: minimum and maximum values where membership is 1, their average, and the bisector that splits the area under the curve in half.
when: Choosing an output point for a fuzzy set
why: These points give distinct ways to locate a representative output.

text: A corrected formula can still leave one outlier far off the curve, so manual tuning of individual values remains necessary.
RPGs typically expose hit points, damage, accuracy, and the numbers deciding whether an attack hits and what effect it has.
A balance formula that works for typical values can still fail at extremes, and if it is correct in most cases, the general formula may not need changing.
when: Balance math being checked at edge conditions.
why: Extreme values expose limits that typical values do not reach.

text: Root-mean-square error is computed by squaring each player's rating error, taking the mean, then taking the square root.
when: when measuring rating accuracy in simulation

text: A polynomial trendline of degree n fits a sum of powers of x up to xⁿ, so degree 2 includes x squared and degree 3 includes x cubed.
when: Choosing a polynomial trendline for curved data.

text: R-squared runs from 0 for the worst fit to 1 when the curve passes exactly through every point. Values near 1 indicate a strong fit.
when: Judging how well a trendline matches the data.

text: At 30 fps, frame latency is about 100 to 133 ms plus display lag; at 60 fps it is about 50 to 67 ms plus display lag.
when: Excluding display delay.
why: The delay is set by about four frames of latency at the chosen frame rate.

text: No fixed R-squared cutoff separates good from bad fits. A low value is a sign to try a different trendline type rather than accept the curve.
when: Evaluating a trendline's R-squared value.
why: The acceptable level depends on the data and the curve type chosen.

text: A rounded decimal standing in for an exact matrix value can slightly distort the computed probabilities.
when: When spreadsheet matrix inversion returns an error because the matrix has no inverse.

text: Fractional values are harder for players to process, so avoid them when the game allows.
when: Game allows whole-number values
why: Players struggle to compare fractions quickly.

text: A curve can fit existing data well yet mislead when extended; early exponential and sigmoid fits look alike, and real player counts must level off.
when: When extrapolating a fitted curve beyond the current data set.
why: Domain limits, such as a finite player base, rule out extrapolations that a good fit alone would support.

text: 1) Open the chart's customize options. 2) Open the series settings. 3) Tick the Trendline checkbox and choose a trendline type.
when: A chart's points do not match a formula you already know.
why: Each trendline type bends a chosen curve family toward the points by shrinking the gap between the curve and each point.

text: 1) Plot paired values as a scatter chart. 2) Add a linear trendline. 3) Display R-squared. 4) Compare it with the correlation coefficient computed from the same data.
when: Checking whether a fitted trend reflects real relationship or chance.

text: 1) Fit a formula relating price to expected damage per second using the first few known weapon rows. 2) Use it to fill in the remaining rows. 3) Check that all weapons fall on one curve.
when: a data set of items should follow one value curve
why: Gold cost is assumed to be tied to expected damage per second, so all weapons must share one relationship.

text: 1) Repeatedly multiply the start vector by the transition matrix. 2) Record the chance of having reached the finish state after each turn. 3) Median is the first turn where that cumulative chance exceeds 0.5. 4) Finishing probability on a turn is the difference from the previous turn. 5) Mean is the sum of turn times finishing probability, stopped once it converges.
when: measuring a single-player race game's length distribution
why: the final-state probability curve gives the full length distribution

text: Bicubic interpolation costs more computation than bilinear interpolation, though still cheap, in exchange for smooth rounded terrain.
when: Terrain in games where sharp peaks and valleys would cause collision problems
why: Sharp peaks and valleys from bilinear interpolation make collision detection unreliable and let characters get stuck.

text: A bidirectional (doubly linked) list links each node to its successor and predecessor, removing a unit in constant time by adjusting only neighbors' pointers; it can carry a header node.
A scene graph node holds a local transform, an optional mesh pointer (null for grouping-only nodes), and a list of child nodes.
An array is a homogeneous, random-access structure whose components share one base type and are selected by an integer index, which may be any expression evaluated at run time.
A cross-reference index stores each word of a text in a search tree, where each node heads a list of the line numbers in which the word occurs.
In a circular list the last node points back to the first node instead of to NIL.
Integer node numbers enable very fast optimizations of A*.
Incremental hash updates are much faster than full recalculation when many pieces are on the board.
Deciding which fields are hot and which are cold is often unclear, since some fields matter only in certain entity modes or level regions.
An array of n components is declared ARRAY n OF T with indices 0 to n-1, and a component is selected as x[i]. Components can be updated individually.
Array element offsets are linear, equal to index times element size, while records have no uniform offset rule and select fields by fixed identifiers.
Fundamental structures such as arrays, records and sets have a fixed storage pattern set by their declaration, while dynamic structures change in value and shape during computation.
Separation uses constant memory and time linear in the number of candidate neighbors checked.
Condensation needs a waypoint list supporting sorting by value, nearby queries, sequential next, and removal between next calls, with each waypoint storing a position and a value.
The signal store is a hash set supporting set and check operations, and it should be cleared of stale identifiers from time to time.
when: Implementing a central signal store
why: Stale identifiers accumulate and can cause false results

text: A dummy header node removes the special case of an empty list.
Key transformation uses only a static array with no dynamic allocation, but its fixed size makes it unsuitable when item count is unknown or varies strongly.
Add a separate object collection when the game frequently processes every object regardless of position, since it lets the game visit all objects directly.
when: Live objects that need per-frame processing and must all be visited regardless of position
why: A direct list makes traversal faster than going through the spatial structure; the trade is keeping both in sync.

text: The more inactive objects there are, the more a separate active-object collection is worth its extra memory and sync cost.
Use fine-grained dirty flags when changes are sparse and sending unchanged data is costly; use coarse-grained flags when changes cluster within groups and per-chunk overhead matters.
when: Changes are sparse or clustered within groups.
why: Sparse changes make unchanged data expensive to resend, while clustered changes make coarse groups efficient.

text: When derived data is easy to maintain incrementally, prefer a running total updated on each change over a dirty flag that triggers a full recomputation.
when: Derived data can be adjusted incrementally with each change.
why: Incremental updates avoid the full recomputation a dirty flag would trigger.

text: Low-level representation decisions can be left to hardware designers, who know current technology best.
when: When the detailed encoding depends on current hardware technology.
why: Hardware specialists know the technology best.

text: Skip a spatial partition when the object count is small, since the extra effort is not worth it.
when: When the number of objects is small
why: A partition's benefit grows with object count, while its bookkeeping and position updates cost effort.

text: Let the sorting method adapt to its data structure; a weak structure used cleverly can still give strong performance.
when: When sorting data held on tape or disk while a larger random-access primary store exists
why: Leaving available random-access memory unused is unjustified; an array sort on initial runs makes runs near the store size.

text: Choose the data representation around the most frequent operation, such as the safety test, rather than around the most natural picture of the data.
why: A natural matrix makes availability checks cumbersome, and the most frequently executed operation should be the simplest to perform.

text: Inserting observers at the front of a linked list makes the most recently added observer notified first, so notification runs in reverse registration order.
when: when observers are added to the front of an intrusive list
why: each insertion becomes the new head

text: Creating from a linear-scan pool takes O(n) time, so a large, mostly full pool slows creation.
when: When the pool is huge and mostly occupied.
why: Creation scans through the pool until it finds an open slot, which can mean examining the whole collection.

text: The cardinality of an array type is card(T) = card(T0)^n, where n is the array size and T0 its base type.
Component j of an array lives at address i0 + j*s, where i0 is the start of component 0 and s is the component size in words.
why: A linear mapping keeps address computation simple and efficient, so whole-number component sizes are preferred.

text: Signal and wait take constant time and memory, while a hash-set check costs O(n/b) for n signals and b buckets; a lone wait returns in constant time per frame.
when: Analyzing signal store performance
why: Hash-set buckets spread the check cost across the store

text: Scanning a queue for duplicates costs linear time, while a hash table keyed on the sound id checks for duplicates in constant time.
when: Queues of pending requests grow large.
why: Lookup cost depends on the data structure.

text: Empirically, deletion needs about one rotation per five deletions, against one per two insertions; overall, deletion is about as complex as insertion.
A pathfinding graph interface has one operation, returning the connections leaving a node. A connection interface has three: cost, start node and end node.
why: Algorithms such as A* and Dijkstra need the outgoing connections of a node and each connection's cost and destination.

text: Each record holds a pointer to its first offspring and a pointer to its next sibling, which lets a multiway tree be read as a binary tree.
Software bugs can make some collected data simply wrong, so numbers cannot be trusted without checking.
why: Collection code may silently skew results, so hand-counted spot checks are needed to verify it.

text: The efficiency of the open and closed list structures in map flooding depends on non-trivial implementation choices.
Hard-coding a character's real name into code is risky because names may change late in development; internal codenames are safer.
when: Naming identifiers for characters or assets.
why: Late renames then require widespread code edits.

text: Using an index outside the declared array range is a common mistake, so good systems should warn about such access.
when: When an array index is computed by an expression rather than written as a constant
why: Computed indices can easily land outside the declared range, which is one of the most frequent programming mistakes.

text: Putting the inner comparison in a separate match function hides the inner loop, adds call overhead, and blocks the outer index from skipping ahead more than one.
when: In a potentially long inner loop of a basic operation such as string search
why: Each step's procedure call adds cost, and a separate inner loop cannot supply information for skipping ahead in the outer loop.

text: Densely packed node records make flag access costly, which can change the performance comparison between tree variants.
when: Nodes store flags in tight memory layouts
why: Extra bit-level access work adds cost per node visited

text: A fixed hash table size can cause poor storage use or overflow when the item count is misjudged, so treating hashing as universal is a mistake.
when: When an a priori estimate of the item count is needed for a fixed-size table
why: The table size is fixed and cannot adapt to actual demand, so a poor estimate wastes storage or overflows.

text: 1) Separate fields read every frame from fields used rarely. 2) Keep hot fields in the main component. 3) Move cold fields into a separate object referenced by one pointer.
when: When a few fields dominate per-frame traversal and others are touched only once.
why: Per-frame loops then load less unused data into the cache.

text: 1) Sort all waypoints by decreasing value. 2) Take the next waypoint as current. 3) Get nearby waypoints sorted by increasing value. 4) Check neighbors in order, stopping at the first more valuable one. 5) Skip neighbors the character cannot easily reach. 6) If the squared value difference exceeds the weighted distance term, remove the lower-valued waypoint from both lists.
why: Stopping at a more valuable neighbor is safe because that pair was already checked when that neighbor was the current waypoint.

text: 1) Multiply each matrix entry by the matching state entry. 2) Sum all products with one formula. 3) Enter it as an array formula, using Ctrl+Shift+Enter in a spreadsheet program or the ArrayFormula function in a web spreadsheet. 4) Fill it down and across.
when: matrices too large to type each product by hand
why: Hand-typed products become error-prone as the matrix grows

text: 1) For a sum, start at zero and add each element for indices 0 to N-1. 2) For a maximum, start with the first element at index 0, then for indices 1 to N-1 update the maximum and its index whenever the current element exceeds it.

1) Scan the text, printing each line with its number, and insert each word with its line number into the search tree. 2) Print the table with an inorder traversal, writing each word followed by its line numbers.
Give callers one query interface that hides caching details, so the caching can be optimized later without rewriting AI code.
why: The caller never needs to know whether a value was cached or recomputed, so caching logic can change behind the interface.

text: When keeping two collections, update both on every object creation or destruction so they stay in sync.
when: partition plus separate object collection

text: Implement a FIFO queue as a linked list with insert, extract and empty-test operations, and reuse the storage of extracted nodes to save memory.
Appending at the end of a singly linked list needs a second pointer to the last element, and the first element must be handled as a special case.
when: When new elements must be added at the tail so insertion order is preserved.
why: Scanning to find the end costs effort that a second pointer avoids.

text: Using the partition as the only object store saves memory and complexity over keeping two collections; choose it when location queries are the main need and storage must stay minimal.
when: When the partition alone holds objects, with no separate object collection.
why: Storing objects once avoids the memory overhead and sync work of maintaining two collections.

text: Array and SIMD layouts trade flexibility for speed, so they suit networks whose structure rarely changes, while simple per-neuron code suits experimentation.
when: Choosing an implementation for a neural network.
why: Optimized layouts are harder to modify and reshape.

text: An intrusive observer list is cheap, but each observer can watch only one subject at a time because the observer holds a single next pointer.
when: when choosing an intrusive list for observers
why: one next pointer links an observer into only one list

text: In an intrusive list the data contains the node, which is less flexible but more efficient than an ordinary list where the node contains the data.
when: when choosing a linked list layout
why: embedding the link avoids separate allocations at the cost of flexibility

text: A fixed array with an update method suits batch processing, but asynchronous processing that pulls one request while others remain needs a true queue.
when: Choosing between batch processing and asynchronous pulls.
why: A batch clears all pending requests at once, which cannot leave some behind.

text: Looking up sibling components by entity ID is slower than direct access, but it matters because components often interact during update.
when: When finding a component of an entity requires mapping an ID to an object.
why: Sibling components interact during update, so the lookup happens often and is performance-critical.

text: Sequential slot assignment is O(n) time and O(1) memory and simple, but it causes behavioral problems that advanced assignment methods fix, and reassigning only changed characters would be an optimization.
when: Choosing a slot assignment method
why: Simplicity versus behavior quality

text: A time of day is stored as a fraction of a day, where 0 is midnight and values approach 1 near the end of the day.
WEEKNUM(date) returns the week number within the year, from 1 to 53, since a year runs slightly longer than 52 weeks.
YEAR(date) returns the year as an integer, and MONTH(date) returns the month as an integer from 1 for January to 12 for December.
In weight-limited selection, each object has a weight and a value, and the goal is maximal total value with total weight kept within a limit.
TODAY() takes no parameters and returns the current date.
The validity properties of a division scheme strongly constrain which character movement algorithms can be used.
when: Selecting movement algorithms for a graph.
why: Movement algorithms assume the graph's validity guarantees.

text: Uniform random values from 0 to 1 have a mean of 0.5 and a theoretical standard deviation of about 0.2887.
Because input counts are not strictly equal, a balanced multiway merge must handle any number of active inputs.
Test a streak formula on known sequences, such as all identical results or alternating results, before trusting it on the full enumeration.
Check solver results against the inverse-based solution; the two sets of probabilities should be similar.
why: Independent methods catch arithmetic or logic errors

text: Weighting child entropy by each child's share of examples favors balanced splits, because unbalanced splits leave high-entropy children.
when: choosing a split attribute

text: The centroid index is the sum of each node's position times its access weight, divided by the total weight W, rounded to the nearest integer.
why: The centroid is the weighted center of gravity of access frequencies, a heuristic approximation rather than the exact optimum.

text: Use time-of-day fractions for time offsets such as differences or added seconds; adding a whole number to a date-time shifts it by days, not time.
when: doing time arithmetic on a current date-time
why: A date-time value's whole-number part is read as days, so whole-number additions shift the date.

text: A clock built on NOW() looks stale between recalculations, so finer-grained live timing needs a workaround.
when: When a spreadsheet clock uses NOW() and recalculates manually or only at minute or hour intervals.
why: NOW() and TODAY() refresh only when data changes or a recalculation is forced, and automatic settings cannot go finer than a minute.

text: TODAY() by itself does little, and only becomes useful once arithmetic or comparisons are applied to it.
when: When TODAY() is combined with date arithmetic or comparisons.

text: Matching WEEKNUM values alone can mislead across years, so dates should be checked with YEAR() as well to confirm they fall in the same week.
when: Grouping dates by week across multiple years
why: Week numbers repeat each year, so equal numbers do not guarantee the same week.

text: Unmatched partners must be excluded from stability comparisons, or the test compares against assignments that do not exist.
when: When testing whether an assignment in a stable-marriage style matching is unstable.

text: 1) Start the weight limit at a step size. 2) Run the search for that limit. 3) Increase the limit by the step and repeat until a given upper limit is reached.
when: Solving the selection problem for a range of weight limits.

text: Use WEEKNUM() when organizing tasks by week, and MONTH() when organizing them by month.
Verify LLM output before trusting it, since plausible answers may be false.
when: When using an LLM to produce facts, references, or calculations.

text: When one run is exhausted in a two-way natural merge, copy the rest of the other run to the output instead of selecting its least keys.
when: two-way natural merge reaching the end of one run
why: The remaining keys are already in order and all follow the output written so far.

text: A weighted sum of objectives lets some objectives dominate while others suffer; multiobjective methods such as NSGA-II instead return the set of nondominated individuals.
when: When one number cannot capture an artefact's several quality aspects

text: In event passing, a central checking system detects interesting changes and notifies every character that might care about them.
A coroutine is a process that pauses at breakpoints and resumes at the same place when called again.
An event manager treats the event code as an opaque value, so it needs no knowledge of what each code means in the game.
Event passing is not faster in principle than polling, since checks still have to be made and the mechanism adds messaging work.
Events have different delivery deadlines: a siren notice can be delayed a couple of seconds, while a 'you have been shot' event must be delivered instantly because an animation may depend on it.
Event types carry the data listeners need, such as the participants and time of a collision or the enemy location in a sighting report.
why: Responding to an event takes more than knowing it occurred; listeners act on its specifics.

text: With n queued events and m registered listeners, event dispatch time grows as n times m and memory grows as n plus m.
Event passing adds bookkeeping: the manager must match events to interested characters, and each character holds an event until the code that needs it runs.
when: When there is no way to share checking work among characters
why: The event manager still performs the same checks as polling, plus added message-passing overhead.

text: An event manager has four elements: an optional checking engine, an event queue, a registry of (interest code, listener) pairs, and a dispatcher that notifies matching listeners each run.
1) While the event queue is not empty, pop the next event. 2) Notify every listener whose registered code matches the event's code. 3) Repeat until the queue is empty.
1) Create a registration record holding the listener and its interest code. 2) Add the record to the registration list. A listener needing several codes registers once per code.

1) Make the polyphase sort the main program. 2) Write the run distribution as a coroutine. 3) Treat each run switch as a breakpoint. 4) Replace end-of-file tests with a test whether the coroutine has finished.
why: Each coroutine call resumes where it last stopped, so switches are marked as resumption points.

text: A listener needing several codes can instead use codes that are powers of two, combined as a bit mask, so one registration covers all of them.
when: when a listener needs several codes and fewer registrations are wanted

text: Listeners implement an event listener interface so they can register with the manager and be notified correctly.
In interactive evolution the computer proposes artifacts and the human's ratings serve as fitness, selecting which individuals reproduce and die out; for tracks this improves quality and interest.
A blind watchmaker interface steers generated results by having the user pick among generated options rather than set parameters directly.
First-improvement hill descent accepts the first neighbour with a lower score instead of scanning all neighbours for the best.

Evolutionary algorithms are stochastic searches modelled loosely on natural selection: a population is scored each generation, the fittest reproduce, and offspring vary through crossover and mutation.
Gaussian mutation adds small Gaussian-distributed random values to every number in a real-valued vector.
A BNF grammar is defined by non-terminals, terminals, production rules, and a start symbol.

Grammatical evolution is an evolutionary algorithm that uses linear integer genomes and a context-free grammar to map genomes to phenotypes, so it can generate any output describable by production rules.
Optimality is defined by a positive-valued function applied to each solution.
Search-based PCG with evolutionary algorithms has two main challenges: designing the evaluation function and choosing the content representation.
Grammars and their rules can themselves be produced by search methods such as evolution, enabling automatic grammar design.
Angelina evolves rules, maps, and initial placement as separate entities through cooperative co-evolution, and judges each element partly in isolation.
when: when generating full games automatically with separately evolved components
why: Separate evolution lets each component be scored on its own qualities before combination.

text: Genetic algorithms rely more on recombination and use different selection mechanisms than other evolutionary variants.
The whole μ+λ algorithm can be written in 10 to 20 lines, and even its 1+1 version can work well.
Grammatical evolution can generate mathematical formulas, program code, game levels, and physical or architectural designs.
Human evaluation in interactive evolution takes one of three forms: a numerical score proportional to preference, an ordering by preference, or selecting favourites to breed more from.

Interactive evolution has been applied to 2D art from L-systems, mathematical expressions, neural networks, 3D art, animation, typography, graphic design, rhythm and melody, industrial design, image retrieval and robot motion.
Highly unequal run distribution in natural merge is statistically unlikely, so accepting it costs little efficiency in practice.
when: Evaluating a merge-side fix for unequal run counts.

text: A faster but more intricate stable matching algorithm also handles sets of unequal size.
A stable marriage instance can have several stable pairings, ranging from one best for men to one best for women.
A large population and enough rooms per chromosome let selection find connected negative-representation dungeons.
when: evolving negative room encodings
why: Selection pressure gradually favours connected layouts.

text: Heuristic design is largely empirical; visualise fill in-game or through statistics rather than relying on intuition.
why: Fill can differ sharply between indoor and outdoor layouts, so performance depends on the level.

text: Adaptive step sizes tend to give useful gains, while momentum rarely gave reliable gains.
Start hill climbing from several initial values spread across the landscape and keep the best result, since a poor start can lead to a smaller peak.
when: When the initial guess may not lie on the slope toward the best value
why: a single start may converge to a lower peak

text: For short real-valued vectors, CMA-ES is particularly effective.
when: low-dimensional real-valued representations

text: Use a multiobjective algorithm when no single number captures content quality.
when: When one number cannot capture an artefact's several quality aspects
why: Weighted sums can let some functions dominate, sacrificing the rest.

text: Use μ+λ as a straightforward baseline when mutation is the main source of variation; match the mutation operator to the representation and fitness landscape.
Use interactive evolution when fitness is hard to write as a formula but a human can judge quality, such as for subjective beauty or deceptive measures.
when: When designing a fitness function is difficult, e.g. subjective beauty or deceptive problems
why: On deceptive problems, a crude numeric measure can do more damage than good.

text: Evolving content during play with player behaviour as fitness makes the whole game a distributed evolutionary algorithm, shaping future content without any explicit selection step.
why: Usage frequency serves as fitness, so often-used weapons are more likely to evolve.

text: A genetic algorithm can generate building designs procedurally, producing candidate structures from rules that a user then selects among.
Grammatical evolution can generate platformer levels by placing structural and enemy chunks on a 2D array, with a context-free design grammar bounding positions and sizes.
why: Context-free grammars restrict which solutions are reachable, so a simple grammar is preferred.

text: Crossover and mutation applied to sparse starting populations can reach good levels relatively easily.
when: When random level generation would rarely produce connected layouts, as with high wall or fill probabilities.
why: Sparse starts make nearly all initial levels connected, leaving the search operators to find good levels.

text: The random range plays the role of temperature: it starts large and is reduced over the run.
when: When annealing by adding random noise to neighbour evaluations during hill climbing.
why: A large range lets the best neighbour be overridden often; narrowing it later makes the choice nearly greedy.

text: Adding a proportion of the last improvement to the score for continuing in the same direction lets a climber overshoot sub-peaks, notice the decline, and reverse, escaping them at the cost of slower convergence.
when: landscape contains a small local maximum before the global one
why: momentum carries the climber past small local maxima

text: NEAT evolves neural networks by starting from small networks and growing their topology over generations, so complexity increases gradually.
A level generator can be encoded as a genome of 14 to 24 agents that move concurrently and affect each other only through the content they generate.
when: evolving Mario-style level generators
why: Independent agents make generators compositional and searchable.

text: The μ+λ evolution strategy keeps the best μ individuals as an elite, creates λ offspring by copying and mutating them, and repeats until a stopping condition is met.
When check results cannot be shared, event passing can be significantly slower, taking as long as each character checking for itself plus messaging overhead.
when: check results cannot be shared between characters
why: each character still performs its own check and the messaging adds cost

text: If the genome runs out before mapping finishes, the individual must be penalised as invalid or the codons must wrap around and be reused.
when: Grammatical mapping with a fixed-length genome
why: Otherwise the mapping cannot complete

text: A representation whose mutations cause large, unpredictable changes makes evolution perform poorly.

1) Keep a population of rule sets ranked by fitness. 2) Select two fairly fit parents. 3) Combine them with crossover and mutation into a child. 4) Check the child for correctness, playability, performance and similarity to the population. 5) Name a child that passes all checks, measure its fitness and add it to the population.

1) Define a design grammar mapping the genotype to a level with specified element types and properties. 2) Add player experience model output to fitness, scoring each level by its predicted emotional state for the player.
when: when generating levels personalised to a player
why: Ranking content by the experience it evokes in one player lets the search target that player's predicted emotional response.

text: 1) At each step, add a random value to every neighbour's evaluation. 2) Choose the neighbour with the best adjusted score.
why: Bounded random noise usually leaves the best neighbour as the winner but occasionally lets a large draw override it.

text: 1) Initialise μ+λ individuals randomly, by hand, or from earlier runs. 2) Evaluate each, combining several evaluation functions into one fitness if needed. 3) Sort by fitness and remove the λ worst. 4) Replace them with copies of the μ survivors. 5) Mutate the copies. 6) Stop if good enough or at the maximum generation; otherwise repeat from step 2.

1) Start from the grammar's start symbol. 2) At each choice point, read the next integer codon and take it modulo the number of alternatives. 3) Select that production and expand the leftmost non-terminal. 4) Symbols with one option expand without reading a codon. 5) Repeat until no non-terminals remain.
when: Mapping an integer genome to a phenotype through a grammar

text: 1) Initialise a population of random variable-length integer vectors. 2) Evaluate each individual's fitness. 3) Apply genetic operators to produce the next generation. 4) Repeat.
When a genetic algorithm solves a constrained production problem, encode the domain rules into its representation so it cannot propose invalid solutions.
when: genetic algorithm applied to constrained scheduling or production
why: Otherwise it may suggest illegal schedules.

text: Use the direct annealing method for simple parameter learning where a simpler method is not enough.
when: simple parameter learning
why: Adding a random number to each neighbour's score avoids computing an exponential acceptance term, making it simpler to implement.

text: Do not automate life-or-death or important decisions with predictive AI without human oversight.
when: When predictive AI makes important decisions about someone's life, such as hiring or loan approval, without oversight.
why: Predictions learned from past data carry human biases, and automating them can entrench injustice and discrimination.

text: Use recursion when the problem, function or data structure is itself defined recursively and the depth of recursion stays small.
when: When the underlying problem or data is itself defined in recursive terms.

text: Write simple recurrences such as factorial and Fibonacci iteratively rather than recursively.
when: When a routine's only recursive call sits at the very start or end of its body.

text: Genetic programming evolves tree structures, while grammatical evolution evolves linear integer genomes that a grammar maps to outputs.
when: Choosing between tree-based and grammar-based evolution

text: An unstable equilibrium is balanced so that any small disturbance sends the character away; its basin of attraction has zero size.
Connections that loop from a later layer back to an earlier one create a recurrent network, and some networks have no designated inputs or outputs.
The same action in the same state can lead to different results because other characters and the player are also acting.
A main strength of reinforcement learning is handling uncertainty, which lets designers expose simpler states to the algorithm.
Designers often cannot predict which actions are good, because action quality may depend on player behaviour or on randomly generated maps.
Adding uncertainty to mimic the difficulty of guessing others' thoughts did not look more believable and greatly slowed learning.
when: Designing observational learning for believability.

text: Predictive AI can work well for recommendations and spam filtering, though false positives still occur.
A shallower iteration's best move is usually a good candidate to examine first in the deeper search.
when: iterative deepening
why: the shallow result gives a good estimate of the best move

text: Predictive AI assumes the future resembles the past, so it works best when nothing changes or when change is modeled.
when: When predicting people's behavior or situations that may shift.
why: Predictions assume past data still holds, but people and situations change, including in response to predictions.

text: Ordering rules by combination offset lets a single conclusion array, indexed by offset, replace the stored identifier lists in each rule.
when: When every possible combination of input states has a rule present in the rule block.
why: Each combination's offset identifies its rule, so stored lists of input state identifiers are unnecessary.

text: A prediction can change the decisions that produce the predicted outcome, so the forecast itself alters what happens.
when: When predictions are used to guide choices by people or organizations.
why: Acting on a forecast alters the conditions the forecast was built on, so past patterns stop holding.

text: Random starting individuals still work, because some are less bad than others, and a carefully designed fitness function detects that gap.
when: When the initial generation is random and all individuals are very unfit.
why: Selection lets the less unfit individuals reproduce, so the next generation tends to be better on average.

text: Q-learning time grows linearly with iterations, and array memory grows with actions times states.
when: When the game lets the AI revisit every state and action several times across learning
why: Storing Q-values in arrays indexed by state and action costs memory proportional to the product of actions and states, while hash lookups only pay off when most combinations go unvisited.

text: A prediction-based AI at full competence can be effectively unbeatable, since it counters every sequence it anticipates.
when: In combo-based melee games where the player performs timed move sequences
why: A predictor that anticipates a player's sequence can select a counter each time, so at full competence it wins every exchange unless its skill is deliberately reduced.

text: Visibility pruning does not remove false connections that span a gap with no navigable region in between, such as a large vertical drop.
when: When two regions are separated by a large vertical gap with no navigable region between them
why: Line-of-sight tests only confirm visibility, not traversability, and the post-processing fix needs an intermediate navigable region to catch the false link.

text: 1) Keep only the most likely moves at each turn. 2) Extend those move sequences well beyond the base depth. 3) Ideally pair with iterative deepening, extending just the strongest candidates carried over from the prior pass.
when: When branching is too high for full search and the horizon effect is noticeable
why: Searches the few promising lines much deeper than a full search could.

text: 1) Give each attack a priority based on its utility, set to zero when it is on cooldown. 2) Trigger the attack whose priority equals the maximum of all priorities. 3) Put that attack into cooldown.
when: Several abilities compete for use each second
why: A priority of zero prevents selection, so cooling-down attacks are skipped.

text: Use action prediction when the player makes repeated choices from a small set of options.
when: When the player repeatedly picks from a small set of options such as passages, weapons, tactics or cover points
why: People cannot randomize their choices reliably, so their past selections reveal patterns a learner can exploit to anticipate the next one.

text: Abandon a rule as soon as its running minimum falls below the current best degree for its output, since it cannot become that output's maximum.
when: When evaluating fuzzy rules that combine clauses with AND and take the maximum over rules for one output
why: Once a rule's running minimum drops below the best output degree found so far, it cannot become the maximum, so its remaining evaluation is wasted.

text: Avoid restarting a multiple-start climb during online play, because the AI may suddenly appear to perform worse when it restarts.
when: online play with the player watching the AI
why: a restart from a poor value makes the AI look like it has degraded

text: A good genotype representation should map to valid phenotypes, small mutations should cause small phenotypic changes, and crossover should blend parent phenotypes.
when: Designing a representation for evolutionary search
why: These properties make evolution behave predictably

text: Recurrent networks can show very complex and unstable behavior and are much harder to control than feedforward networks.
when: Choosing a network structure.
why: Feedback loops let activity circulate and change over time.

text: For a character with radius, shift each inflection point outward from its vertex rather than modelling true arcs, which gives believable paths.
when: Adjusting visibility graph nodes for character size
why: The offset approximates the arcs a wide character would follow around corners

text: A queued manager can run as an anytime algorithm, sending events only when the AI has processing budget left.
when: When events must be spread across frames because many events go to many characters and the AI has limited budget
why: Queuing events lets the manager dispatch them only while processing time remains, avoiding frames with a far greater AI load than others.

text: Each activation gets its own local variables and parameters, and name lookup uses the most recently created set, so repeated names do not conflict.
why: Each recursive activation creates a fresh set of bound variables and parameters, and scope rules make names resolve to the newest set, so the copies do not interfere.

text: The arbiter uses no extra memory and runs in time linear in the number of experts.
why: The arbiter only keeps a running maximum over the experts' insistence values in one pass, so it needs no extra storage beyond the single best expert.

text: The number of block-format rules equals the product of the state counts of all inputs; inputs with 2, 3 and 3 states give 18 rules.
when: When every input's fuzzy states cover all possible values and every combination of states has a rule
why: The rule count is the product of the state counts across inputs, so each added input multiplies the number of rules needed.

text: Block-format decision memory is O(n+m) for the input and output degree arrays, where n is the input state count and m the output state count, plus rule storage.
when: When the rule block is fully enumerated with every input state combination present
why: Because all combinations exist, conclusions can sit in one array indexed by combination offsets, so the rules need not store input state identifiers.

text: Block-format decision time is proportional to the rule count times the number of clauses per rule, because each clause is evaluated.
when: When rules are fully enumerated with one clause per input and all combined by AND
why: Each clause must be evaluated for every rule, so total work grows with the number of rules times the clauses in each rule.

text: Plans on tile graphs look blocky, and characters following them move strangely unless the path is smoothed.
when: Moving characters along tile-graph routes.
why: Routes are restricted to grid steps.

text: Unlike pathfinding, a closed location may be updated during map flooding, because the strength function is arbitrary.
when: When the influence strength function is arbitrary rather than a shortest-path cost
why: An arbitrary strength function means a node already marked closed may later receive a better value, so it must be removed from the closed list and reprocessed.

text: 1) Make one cell show a marker when the attack is the next action and blank otherwise. 2) Make a second cell hold the remaining cooldown, decreasing by 1 each second while above zero. 3) When cooldown reaches zero, reset it to the cooldown length if the attack is ready, otherwise keep it at zero.
when: Modeling a timed ability with cooldown using iterative calculation

text: Keep character-specific movement cost modifiers in character data; a heavy unit might pay tenfold the slope cost of a light unit.
when: When a unit type's movement cost differs from others, such as a heavy unit versus a light one on slopes
why: Movement cost modifiers belong to each character's data because a single terrain-based cost cannot capture how differently unit types are slowed by the same ground.

text: Test attacks with a distance check against the attack range, not an exact position match.
when: When attacks have a range so units in neighboring cells may interact
why: Exact position matching only suits grid games like checkers or chess, while range-based attacks can reach across cell boundaries and need a distance test.

text: In zero-sum games the final scores of all players add to zero, while in non-zero-sum games each score reflects only that player's outcome.

1) Generate random choices for two players with RANDBETWEEN(1,3). 2) Map each number to Rock, Paper or Scissors with nested IF(). 3) Decide the winner with nested IF(), returning 1, 2 or 0 for a tie. 4) Use a self-incrementing timer and log each game's winner over 30 games.
when: Comparing iterative and non-iterative simulations of a randomized game

text: 1) Generate random choices for each player in their own columns. 2) Map choices to symbols and determine the winner on each row. 3) Number each game on its row and fill the rows down for the full run.
when: Comparing against the iterative version of a randomized game simulation

text: Dijkstra's algorithm finds a minimum-cost path between a start and a goal in a directed weighted graph with non-negative costs.
Each Dijkstra node record stores the node, the connection that reached it, and its cost-so-far.
A knight's tour is a sequence of legal knight moves that visits every square of an n by n board exactly once.
A word is any sequence of letters and digits that begins with a letter.
when: when building a word index

text: Unsuccessful searches are modeled by weights on the gaps between consecutive keys, which correspond to external nodes of the tree.
Dijkstra usually suffers heavy fill in point-to-point searches, exploring most of a level including areas far from the final path; only occasionally is its fill small.
Textbook analyses give O(n²) for Dijkstra, matching graphs so densely connected that m equals n.
Dijkstra was designed to find shortest routes from one start node to all other nodes, so a single point-to-point search wastes effort.
Dijkstra is a simpler version of A*, and it can be adapted to a single goal but remains inefficient for that purpose.
A reached node's cost-so-far equals its current node's cost-so-far plus the connection cost; the start node has cost zero, so the same code handles every iteration.
A dedicated Dijkstra implementation can skip the comparison for closed nodes because no better route will be found, but A* cannot skip it.
Full Dijkstra stops only when the open list is empty and every reachable node is closed; a pathfinding search can stop earlier.
In linear search, no element before the current index equals the search argument at any step of the scan.
Linear search finds the first occurrence because the match returned is the one with the least index.
Linear search always terminates, because the index grows each step and reaches N after at most N steps.
A complete knight's tour on an n by n board contains n squared minus one moves from its starting square.
A knight has up to eight candidate destinations, found by adding fixed row and column offset pairs to its current square.
Use linear search when the data are unordered or no other information about them is available.
when: When the data are unordered or no other information about them is available
why: Without ordering or other information, the only way to rule out a match is to scan the array element by element until the target is found or the end is reached.

text: Within a page, use binary search when it holds many keys and sequential search when it holds few.
when: Within a page of a multi-key disk-based tree, when the page holds many keys
why: Binary search needs far fewer comparisons than a sequential scan when the page holds many keys, while a sequential scan suffices for small pages.

text: Dijkstra expands outward from the start, recording for each reached node its cost-so-far and the connection used to reach it, processing the cheapest open node each iteration.
why: Controlled spreading keeps every recorded link pointing back toward the origin along a least-cost path.

text: The shortest-path method in question runs in O(nm) time, where n is the count of nodes nearer than the goal and m is the mean number of edges leaving each node.
when: When the pathfinding list operations are ignored
why: Work comes from visiting each closer node and looping over its outgoing connections.

text: Dijkstra's worst-case memory is O(nm), since the closed list holds n nodes and the open list holds at most nm entries.
why: Memory is the combined size of the open and closed lists at termination.

text: Dijkstra performs about nm additions and finds, and about n extractions and smallest-element searches.
why: Additions and finds happen per connection, while extractions occur once per processed node.

text: Knuth-Morris-Pratt search needs on the order of M+N character comparisons even in the worst case, for pattern length M and text length N.
why: Precomputed pattern information from partial matches avoids re-comparing characters already examined.

text: If additions or finds cost more than O(m), or extractions and smallest-element searches cost more than O(1), Dijkstra runs slower than O(nm).
why: Those operations run nm or n times, so their per-call cost multiplies into total run time.

text: Starting an enumeration index at 1 still produces every combination, but the outcomes come out out of order and are harder to read.
why: With a remainder operation, a 0-based count yields a clean repeating sequence, while a 1-based count shifts it.

text: Looking up items by key during input is a linear list search, so input cost grows with the number of items.
when: Building the leader list from ordering pairs
why: Each lookup scans the list rather than using a faster index

text: Dijkstra uses three structures: a simple list for the final path, a pathfinding list holding open and closed nodes, and a graph giving outgoing connections.

1) Create a record for the start with zero cost and no connection; put it on open and leave closed empty. 2) While open is not empty, take its smallest element as current; stop if it is the goal. 3) For each outgoing connection of current, compute the candidate cost to the end node; skip it if the end node is closed, or if it is open with cost less than or equal to the candidate. 4) Otherwise store the candidate cost and connection, and add the end node to open if absent. 5) After all connections, move current from open to closed. 6) If the goal was not reached, return no solution; otherwise walk back from goal to start collecting connections and reverse them.
Stop a Dijkstra pathfinding search only when the goal is the cheapest node on the open list.
when: single start-to-goal pathfinding
why: Until then, routes through unprocessed nodes may still be cheaper, so only this stop guarantees the optimal route.

text: Avoid plain Dijkstra for single start-to-goal searches in games; prefer A*.
when: single start-to-goal searches
why: Dijkstra expands in all directions, so most of its work never contributes to the final route.

text: Speed-ups for Dijkstra often use more than O(nm) memory because they make key operations fast.
why: Faster key operations are the aim, so implementations are picked that use more memory.

text: Dijkstra gives costs to many or all nodes, useful for tactical analysis, but its fill is heavy for one goal, which A* avoids.
when: When the search needs a route between only two points
why: It expands nodes without regard to the goal, so much of its work is wasted.

text: Dijkstra needs no heuristic to tune, but its search fill slows large levels; A* is typical there because it uses a heuristic.
when: large levels
why: Dijkstra is simple to program and needs no heuristic tuning, which keeps many developers using it.

text: A severely unbalanced decision or priority search tree degrades traversal from logarithmic to linear time, losing logarithmic bounds on search, insertion and deletion, with poor average behaviour.
why: Logarithmic cost holds only under the assumption that the tree stays balanced.

text: Portal graphs with visibility-style connections give very smooth paths, while tile graphs tend to produce erratic paths.
when: Choosing a graph representation for smooth movement
why: Visibility connections allow straight segments across open space

text: A weighted graph attaches a numeric cost, often representing time or distance, to each connection.
when: Modelling traversable connections for pathfinding.
why: Costs let search compare routes.

text: A wildcard node, marked with an asterisk, matches any node and leaves the matched node unchanged on the right-hand side.
The graph is usually a lookup table indexed by node number, where each entry holds an array of connections, and the lookup is called in the inner loop so it must be cheap.
A division scheme is valid if every point in one region can reach every point in a connected region.
when: Assessing a pathfinding graph's division scheme.
why: Invalid connections can produce plans the character cannot execute.

text: Placing nodes geometrically is extremely difficult, so graph reduction is the only semi-practical approach.
Deleting the rightmost node of a Fibonacci tree is the worst case, since it may require a rotation at every level on the search path.
Use an optimal static search tree only for fixed key sets with reliable access statistics, such as compiler keyword lookup.
when: When the set of keys is fixed and the lookup probability of each key is known
why: Such trees are a special case rather than the usual choice.

text: Use paged tree storage when the tree exceeds primary store or keeping it there is too costly, and insertions and deletions still occur.
when: Choosing a storage layout for a search tree
why: Paging trades a little structure overhead for far fewer slow accesses

text: Without smell, the graph-based sense manager resembles the region manager but finds candidate sensors faster and stops sound passing through walls.
when: smell is not simulated
why: The graph links let candidate sensors be gathered directly, while the earlier method mishandled cases such as signals passing through walls.

text: Math texts call nodes vertices, connections edges and costs weights, but in game code vertex usually means a geometry point, so pick one vocabulary and keep it.
when: In game development contexts, where vertices usually mean geometry points
why: Vertices and arcs already carry other meanings in game graphics, so the terms are ambiguous there.

text: Visibility graphs from complex geometry can grow very large, since most points see most others, and a cavern may yield hundreds of inflection points.
when: Generating visibility graphs from detailed geometry
why: Dense line-of-sight connections multiply with the number of points

text: When nodes are quantized into Dirichlet domains, two connected nodes may fail to reach each other, making the graph invalid.
when: Quantizing visibility graph nodes
why: Domain boundaries can separate points that the visibility connection assumed were reachable

text: Every elimination and closure of a merge source must update the index map consistently, or selection will use wrong files.
why: The index map is the only record of which sequences remain available, so selection depends on it.

text: 1) If the node belongs to a building instance, delegate to that instance. 2) Otherwise query the main graph and add zero-cost entrance connections, treating building exits and world nodes as the same point.
when: When a path enters or exits a building instance from the main world graph
why: The distance between buildings is hard to measure.

text: Compute connection costs when converting the level into a graph, an offline step independent of the pathfinder.
why: Connection methods only return stored values, so costs must be prepared ahead of the search.

text: 1) Place nodes at the inflection points of simplified geometry. 2) Cast a ray between each pair of nodes. 3) Connect the pair when the ray hits no other geometry.
when: Generating a graph from level geometry
why: Connections represent unobstructed straight moves between points

text: 1) Put nodes on a grid, e.g. one every half meter, discarding those inside walls or unreachable from the ground; in portal engines, build one section at a time. 2) Link the dense graph and assign costs. 3) Reduce it to a few thousand nodes while keeping the level's overall structure.
when: automatic node placement
why: A full grid is enormous and dense, with tens of millions of nodes, so it must be reduced to a manageable size.

text: 1) Consider each connection in turn. 2) If its route passes through other nodes, remove the connection. 3) Keep the remaining connections as the pathfinding graph.
when: after building a point-of-visibility graph
why: A character must pass through the intermediate nodes anyway, so a direct connection is redundant.

text: 1) Define walkable space with overlapping volumes. 2) Use the volumes as the pathfinding graph. 3) Treat action waypoints only as goals for the pathfinder.

1) Find a subgraph matching the left-hand side and mark its nodes. 2) Remove edges between marked nodes. 3) Transform marked nodes to right-hand side counterparts, add unmatched right-hand nodes, and remove marked nodes with no counterpart. 4) Copy right-hand edges. 5) Clear all marks.
when: Applying a graph grammar rule to a host graph
why: Node identifiers let each matched node be paired with its specific right-hand counterpart.

text: If movement is possible in both directions, store two separate connections, one for each direction.
when: a link can be traversed both ways
why: Each direction can differ in reachability and in cost.

text: Connect two groups if any low-level node in one links to any low-level node in the other. Set their cost by hand or compute it from the low-level links between them.
why: Higher-level links must mirror whether a character can cross between groups.

text: A hierarchical graph must report its number of levels, switch the active level, and convert a node between levels. Going up is a lookup; going down uses a stored representative node, such as one near the group centre.
why: A single upper-level node can correspond to many lower-level nodes, so one representative must be picked.

text: Automatic visibility graph generation needs heavy hand cleanup, so polygonal meshes suit automatic generation better, while regular Dirichlet domains suit manual placement.
when: Choosing a graph generation method
why: Visibility graphs produce many nodes that must be cleaned up, though some developers use them successfully

text: Linking triangles that share only one vertex smooths jagged movement across dense meshes, but lets characters clip corners.
when: Characters pathing across a dense triangle mesh
why: Diagonal-vertex links smooth the zigzag path of a character crossing a dense mesh.

text: Diamond-square is a fast, common fractal terrain method that alternates diamond and square steps over a grid, reducing random offset magnitude at each level.
A grid is a persistent bucket sort: its buckets are kept and updated over time.
Diamond-square output approximates fractional Brownian motion terrain.
Even with smooth visuals, many games keep a grid beneath the surface: a uniform table of elevation values known as a height field, which the pathfinder also uses.
Use diamond-square when a fast, simple fractal terrain is enough and fine control over the result is not required.
why: Cheap to code and fast to run, it approximates fractional Brownian motion without simulating random walks.

text: On height-field grids, connection cost can combine distance and elevation change so that downhill moves cost less than uphill moves.
when: Outdoor terrain tile graphs.
why: Climbing takes more effort than descending over the same distance.

text: A height-reduced flag is set when a node is removed or when rebalancing shrinks a subtree, and rebalancing is considered only while the flag is set.
With linear falloff and a threshold influence, a unit's radius is its base influence divided by the threshold, minus one; it contributes only to locations inside that radius.
Limiting each unit's contribution to its radius reduces time to O(nr), where n is the number of units and r is the typical count of locations inside one radius.
when: When a threshold influence defines each unit's radius of influence
why: Only locations inside each unit's radius are updated, and that count is far below the total map size.

text: A diamond-square generator takes three parameters: seed sets the initial corner values, iterations sets the number of passes, and roughness sets the magnitude of random offsets.
An order-i Hilbert curve is four half-size order-(i-1) curves, suitably rotated, joined by three connecting lines, with order 0 empty.
Diamond-square gives limited control over the result, so specific features such as a required ridge are hard to enforce.
A limited radius stops small influences from accumulating over long distances, so a group of weak units may have no influence on a location they surround.
when: When influence is cut off at a fixed radius
why: Contributions beyond the radius are discarded, so weak units spread around a location never combine.

text: 1) Seed the four corners of a heightmap. 2) Diamond step: set each square's centre to the corners' average plus a random value. 3) Square step: set each side midpoint to the average of its two corner neighbours and the centre, plus a random value. 4) Split into four smaller squares, reduce roughness, and repeat for the set number of iterations.
1) Divide each coordinate by the cell size and truncate to an integer per axis. 2) Push the unit onto the front of that cell's list.
when: adding a unit to a grid

text: 1) Record the new position. 2) If old and new cells match, return early. 3) Otherwise unlink from the old cell's list, fixing neighbor and head pointers. 4) Insert into the new cell.
when: a unit moves
why: Units moving within a cell cost almost nothing.

text: 1) Loop over every grid cell and pass its unit list to a per-cell handler. 2) In each cell, compare each unit only with units after it in the list. 3) For cross-cell attacks, check four of the eight neighboring cells.
when: resolving melee or attack range in a grid
why: Each unit pair is then considered exactly once.

text: A good hash function spreads keys evenly over the index range and is cheap to compute; ideally its output looks random.
Key transformation maps each item's key to an array index with a hash function, so retrieval computes the index and checks the entry there.
On a hash clash, a new state can instead be searched without being stored in the table.
The bucket index is the hash value modulo the number of buckets, and there are almost always fewer buckets than possible keys.
Because the key space is far larger than the array, a hash function maps many keys to the same index, so collisions are unavoidable.
The load factor a is the ratio of occupied locations to total locations, ranging from 0 for an empty table to near 1 for a full one.
Aim for as many buckets as possible to hold exactly one entry; full buckets slow lookup and suggest more buckets, while empty ones suggest fewer.
why: Too-full buckets slow lookup because each entry in a bucket must be checked.

text: Choose a prime table size for hashing letter-sequence keys, because power-of-two sizes give very uneven index distribution for similar words.
when: keys are sequences of letters or structured identifiers
why: similar keys map to the same index under a power-of-two modulus

text: Linear probing advances one slot at a time, wrapping around circularly; it is simple but causes entries to cluster heavily around their primary index.
when: Using open addressing with a simple probe step
why: Occupied runs grow, so later keys hit longer collision chains

text: When the computed slot holds a different key, a deterministic secondary index sequence is generated to find another slot.
when: lookup or insertion hits an occupied slot
why: the table has one slot per index, so a second candidate is needed

text: Expected hash probes depend only on load factor, not table size, and stay small even when the table is nearly full, though linear probing costs more than uniform probing.
when: a hash table's occupancy is kept below a chosen threshold
why: probe cost is a function of how full the table is, not how large it is

text: With prime table size N, quadratic probing visits at least half the slots; with non-prime N it may miss free slots and not examine every entry.
when: Sizing a quadratically probed table
why: Prime size keeps the probe sequence spread across the table; non-prime size lets probe sequences repeat before covering all slots.

text: Comparing full game states is slow because a state can hold hundreds of items, so a hash value is used for the table lookup instead.
when: When a search must tell whether a board position was already evaluated
why: Full state comparison costs time proportional to state size.

text: Quadratic probing uses slot (h0 + i squared) mod N, and can be computed without multiplication by adding an odd increment that grows by 2 at each step.
when: Implementing quadratic probing in open addressing
why: Successive odd increments sum to the squares, so no multiplication is needed

text: Under linear probing, the expected probes for insertion or retrieval equal (1 − a/2)/(1 − a), where a is the load factor.
when: estimating linear probing lookup cost

text: A general hash table holds an array of buckets, each a list of entries; the hash value selects a bucket, and the entries inside are checked for a match.
Positions act like hash keys that change unexpectedly, which makes a position-organized structure tricky to maintain.
when: When the objects being partitioned by position change location
why: Re-filing a moved object into a new spot costs extra code and processing time.

text: Worst-case hash retrieval is poor, since a probe sequence may visit only occupied slots before finding an empty one or the key.
