Deleting entries from an open-addressed hash table is cumbersome; chaining into a separate overflow area makes deletion easier.
1) Find the highest assigned slot number. 2) Add one to get the slot count.
when: A pattern derives its slot count from current assignments
why: Slot numbers act as indices, so converting the highest index into a total requires adding one.

text: 1) Compute h = H(k) for the search key k. 2) Read entry T[h]. 3) If its key equals k, the item is found; otherwise apply the collision sequence.
when: searching a fixed-size hash array
why: The slot at the computed index may hold a different key, so the stored key must be compared before accepting the entry.

text: 1) Estimate the expected item count. 2) Make the table about 10% larger than that count. 3) Keep the fixed size, since it cannot grow.
when: a hash table with a known upper bound on item count
why: a fixed table with a margin keeps occupancy and probe cost low

text: Compute simple hash ORD(k) MOD N, N the array size (prime); avoid bit masks and exclusive-or, which spread keys unevenly despite being faster.
when: Building or choosing a hash function for a fixed-size table
why: A full modulus by a prime spreads keys more evenly than bit-level masking; fast bit operations can lose the even spread a good hash needs.

text: On a hash clash, replace the stored entry only when the new state uses fewer actions, so the shallower state is kept.
when: Two different states share a hash slot
why: Keeping the shallower repeat avoids more duplicated search work

text: Probing loops need a termination guard, such as aborting with an overflow error when the probe increment reaches the table size N.
when: Writing any open addressing probe loop
why: Without a guard, a full or badly sized table makes the loop run forever

text: Hashing gives about one step plus key check but needs fixed size, suiting data with known upper bound; trees adapt to unknown, variable or decreasing volume.
when: Choosing between hashing and tree structures for lookup
why: Fixed-size arrays or tables cannot grow and waste space or overflow when item count is misjudged, whereas trees grow dynamically.

text: Buckets keep more entries but lookups must scan lists; one entry per bucket gives fast lookup but loses colliding entries.
when: When searching for moves, where lookup speed matters more than retaining every stored entry.
why: Too-full buckets slow lookup because entries must be scanned, so the aim is to keep buckets near one entry.

text: Chaining links colliding entries into lists, costing pointer space and maintenance; open addressing keeps no links and instead probes other table slots.
when: Resolving hash collisions
why: Links cost memory, while probing costs extra table scans

text: Linear probing is simplest but clusters entries; quadratic probing avoids primary clustering at a cost close to linear probing.
when: Choosing a probe sequence for open addressing
why: Non-linear probe steps spread entries without much extra work

text: A priority search tree combines search-tree order on one coordinate with heap order on the other, so each node carries two keys acting as plane coordinates.
Typical operations on a radix priority search tree include enumeration of points in a rectangle, finding the least or largest x or y within limits, and deleting a point.
Use a radix priority search tree for points in a bounded two-dimensional space, especially for rectangle queries with integer coordinates.
Radix priority search tree: midpoint-split x-intervals halve per level, height ≤ log of coordinate range (word length for integers); fixed dividing lines confine updates to one spine.
when: When no two nodes share an x-value, a property the tree's invariant guarantees.
why: Search behaves like bisection or radix search over the coordinate range, giving logarithmic operation bounds.

text: Enumerating points with x0 ≤ x < x1 and y ≤ y1 in a radix priority search tree takes O(log N + s) operations, with N the x-space size and s the points reported.
when: When the query rectangle's bottom edge lies on the x-axis, so the lower y bound is zero.

text: A priority heap is an array-based tree where node i has children 2i and 2i+1; the smallest element is at the head, and insertion and removal take O(log n).
why: The compact array layout is what lets heap-sort exploit the tree structure to keep elements ordered.

text: Priority-based, deadline-driven event queues are complex to design and build.
when: When an event manager queues events and dispatches them later instead of immediately.
why: A simple dispatch-immediately design avoids storage and queue management code, which queued designs need.

text: Partial-order planning search space grows exponentially with plan length, so POP is rarely used in large practical applications.
when: Planning long plans
why: Each unresolved ordering and binding multiplies the number of partial plans to consider.

text: Inserting a point that must lie above and between existing nodes forces a large restructuring of a priority search tree.
when: When the new node's coordinates force it to sit above and between existing nodes.
why: Node positions are largely dictated by the ordering invariants, leaving little freedom to absorb a new point locally.

text: 1) Descend from the root. 2) If the position is empty, place a new node. 3) If the x-value exists, stop; x-values stay distinct, so duplicates are not inserted. 4) If the new y is smaller, swap and continue the displaced point downward. 5) Go left if x is below the midpoint, else right.
Keep the open-list priority queue separate from node records rather than linking records together.
when: Implementing A* node storage
why: Linked records waste memory, complicate code and cause poor cache behaviour

text: In a priority search tree, a left child has a smaller x than its parent and a right child has a larger x, while both children have a y not smaller than the parent's.
why: Dividing lines with fixed x values do not move when nodes are inserted, so upkeep stays on one spine.

text: A heuristic is an approximate rule that usually works but not always.
Overestimating heuristics are called inadmissible, and they can still be used.
In STRIPS, a state is a set of ground, function-free literals, either propositional (true or false propositions) or first-order (relations over objects).
A STRIPS operator has a name, parameters, a precondition conjunction, and an effect conjunction.
Three heuristics recur across AI and software and serve as good starting points when approaching a new problem.
when: when first approaching an unfamiliar problem

text: Heuristics appear in everyday reasoning and are embedded in many algorithms, though many are never stated explicitly.
The heuristic is called about O(lm) times; a typical heuristic takes constant time, so it does not change the complexity order.
A* with a zero heuristic behaves identically to Dijkstra.
A heuristic that underestimates everywhere makes A* return an optimal path, the same one Dijkstra would find.
Slight overestimates often still yield the optimal path.
SMA* is a lossy search that discards information, so the path it returns is not guaranteed to be optimal.
when: Evaluating whether SMA* fits a task.
why: Discarded nodes may have been on the best route.

text: Momentum handles a landscape with a sub-peak before the main peak, but all three hill climbing extensions fail on near-random landscapes.
when: landscape is near-random

text: In one dimension two neighbors are tried; in two dimensions four samples are used, and more samples around a circle improve results at extra evaluation cost.
With an alphabet of about 128 symbols, a mismatch usually occurs after one or two comparisons, so straight search is fast in practice.
SMA* suits tasks where memory is limited, a near-optimal path is acceptable, and the heuristic is well-behaved.
when: Choosing a search algorithm under memory limits.
why: Bounded memory is its purpose, and optimality is traded away.

text: Use momentum, adaptive resolution and multiple trials when the landscape has some local maxima but is not overwhelmed by sub-optima.
when: landscape has some local maxima but few sub-optima
why: Near-random landscapes leave no correlation for any systematic search to exploit.

text: More problem-specific knowledge in a heuristic reduces search; a perfect heuristic needs no search at all.
why: Knowledge about the problem lets the estimate direct the search, so less exploration is needed.

text: An underestimating heuristic biases the search toward cost-so-far, so A* explores nodes near the start more, which is slower.
An operator can run only when its preconditions hold; running it deletes the conditions its effects negate and adds its positive effects.
why: Conditions not listed are assumed false, so preconditions and effects must be stated as explicit positive or negative literals.

text: Multiplying the Euclidean heuristic by 0.5 restored use of good positions in a strongly negative-weighted case, at the price of slightly more search work.
when: large negative tactic weights make search miss good positions
why: Scaling down keeps the heuristic from overestimating.

text: Each hill climbing step costs O(n) time for n parameters and O(1) memory; total steps are capped by a steps parameter.
Under uniform hashing, the expected probes for insertion or retrieval equal -ln(1 − a)/a, where a is the load factor.
when: estimating hash table lookup cost
why: It averages per-key probe counts over all stored keys, approximating the harmonic sum with a logarithm.

text: In state-space search, nodes are world states and arcs are operator applications. Forward progression starts at the initial state; backward regression starts at the goal. It produces total-order plans.
why: Operators define transitions between states, so each arc in the search tree is one operator application.

text: Assuming a heuristic change helps without measuring fill can produce inferior results.
why: Heuristic quality is hard to predict by intuition, so only observing the search's fill reveals whether it helps.

text: While a pathfinder is paused, the character keeps moving, so the stored plan's start point can become stale.
when: planning spans several frames while the character moves
why: the start node no longer matches the character's position

text: SMA* results depend heavily on the heuristic, since a strongly underestimating heuristic lets useless nodes push out important ones.
when: Using SMA* with a poor heuristic.
why: Misleading estimates decide which nodes are kept in the bounded list.

text: 1) Cap the open list at a fixed size. 2) When a new node's total cost is not lower than every node in the full list, discard it. 3) Otherwise add it and remove the node with the largest total.
when: Running a memory-bounded search.
why: Bounding the list limits memory at the cost of possibly discarding useful nodes.

text: 1) Start from a guessed parameter set and evaluate its score. 2) For each parameter, with others fixed, try one step up and one step down. 3) Apply only the best improving tweak. 4) Repeat until no tweak improves the score or a step limit is reached.
why: The technique is very simple and fast to run, often giving very good results.

text: Engineer tactic weights so additions outweigh subtractions for most connections, keeping the Euclidean heuristic valid.
when: When tactical pathfinding subtracts quality from connection costs.
why: Subtraction can push a connection's cost below its straight-line distance, which breaks the estimate's validity.

text: With few actions and all sequences reachable, use a flat array indexed by window and action; the largest value in a row gives the predicted action.
when: small action sets where most sequences occur
why: A flat array avoids the overhead of hash tables.

text: Use iterative deepening when the program cannot know in advance how long it may think, such as timed chess or games where the player controls the pace.
when: time for a move is unknown
why: A fixed-depth search may not finish before a move is due; a usable answer is always available at each depth reached.

text: Use matrix inversion when the payoff matrix is invertible; use a solver or other methods when it is not.
why: Inversion gives an exact answer only when an inverse exists; a solver can approach a target when it does not.

text: Underestimates keep A* optimal but slower; overestimates speed the search but may silently return suboptimal paths without any error message.
when: When in-game believability matters more than finding the optimal path.
why: Overestimates shrink the weight of cost-so-far, so the search heads for the goal sooner and can miss the cheapest route.

text: A sorted open list gives the best node immediately but costs more on insertion; since A* adds far more nodes than it removes, cheap insertion often wins.
why: Sorting pays off only if removals roughly match insertions; with far more insertions, the cost of sorted insertion dominates.

text: Small open-list limits make SMA* wander toward the target and give poor routes, while large limits reduce that risk but lose the memory benefit.
when: Setting the open-list limit for SMA*.
why: A small list discards alternatives too early, and a large list approaches unbounded A*.

text: Hill climbing is fast and often gives good results on a mostly smooth landscape, but it can get stuck on local maxima.
when: landscape is mostly smooth with few sub-peaks

text: STRIPS is efficient for modelling world states with simple descriptions, but its simplicity limits complex planning problems, which motivates extensions such as ADL.
when: Choosing a planning representation
why: Only positive literals describe states, and the closed-world assumption treats everything unlisted as false.

text: Combining the large mismatch shift with a second shift adds table and logic cost; the gain was judged not worth the complexity.
why: Matches are rarer than mismatches, so large shifts on mismatch are most valuable.

text: If valid slots grow in proportion to total slots, slot assignment time becomes O(kn).
when: Valid slots scale with total slots

text: Further speed-ups from specializing A* depend on the cost structure and other assumptions about the graph.
Threshold splitting becomes more accurate as more examples arrive, since more data refines the chosen boundary.
when: When more training examples are available for a continuous attribute.
why: The cutoff is placed midway between boundary values in the current set, so it shifts as the data changes.

text: A procedure that makes only one recursive call, placed at its start or end, can be rewritten as a loop without recursion.
when: the procedure has one recursive call and no branching
why: a single chain of calls carries no branching that a loop cannot reproduce

text: Slot assignment runs in roughly O(k a log a) steps, with a denoting the mean count of valid slots per character. Memory, O(kn), is often the real constraint.
why: Time depends on the average number of valid slots per character, which is usually far below the total slot count.

text: A technique description covers seven parts: problem, general method, pseudo-code, data structure needs, implementation notes, performance analysis, and weaknesses.
why: Readers need these parts to build and adjust each method.

text: 1) Select a cell involved in the loop. 2) Use Trace Precedents and Trace Dependents to draw arrows showing which cells reference which. 3) Follow the arrows to find the circular reference.
when: Diagnosing circular reference errors in a spreadsheet
why: Arrows display reference relationships between cells, so the loop becomes visible.

text: Set the cutoff midway between the top value of group A and the bottom value of group B, so unseen values get classified sensibly.
why: The split that gains the most information lies in the gap between the two groups' values.

text: Finding which building owns a node needs a binary search over offsets, O(log n) for n buildings, with caching making it nearly O(1) in practice. Exit and entrance checks are hash lookups, near O(1) with a well-balanced hash.
when: When node values are numeric, so a reasonably sized hash table cannot map them.
why: Entrance and exit checks run in the innermost pathfinding loop, so lookup speed is critical.

text: Generic building designs share one pathfinding graph per type. Each placed instance wraps that graph in a translator that offsets node values and adds exit connections, and a world graph routes lookups to the right place.
when: large worlds reuse building designs
why: one stored graph serves hundreds of placed copies

text: 1) Start the first instance's offset at the main graph's node count. 2) Add the previous instance's node count to each later offset. 3) Keep node values unique across all instances and types.
when: numeric node values in a shared world graph
why: prevents node collisions between instances

text: 1) Translate the requested node into building-graph values. 2) Query the building graph for connections. 3) Translate results back. 4) For exit nodes, add zero-cost connections to the world.
why: Exit and entry points are assumed co-located, so the connection adds no distance.

text: Use instancing for massive worlds with reused buildings only together with hierarchical pathfinding, treating each building instance as one higher-level node. The speed cost is then negligible.
when: massive worlds with reused buildings
why: the hierarchy hides the translation overhead

text: Instancing added enough per-step cost to halve execution speed in one test, so it is not worth it when one master graph fits in memory.
when: a single master graph fits in memory
why: the translation overhead in the hot loop costs speed

text: Iterative deepening analyzes a move at a shallow depth first and revisits it at greater depth later.
Google Sheets does not support iterative calculation, so time simulation there requires a row-by-row method.
IDA* stores only the path under test, with no open or closed list; it is simple, often under 50 lines, but re-plans the same nodes each iteration, sometimes slower than Dijkstra.
when: When memory is the tightest limit, such as on handheld hardware.
why: restarting from scratch each cutoff costs more time than A*

text: At maximum iterations 100, a self-referencing cell like A1 =A1+1 rises by 100 per recalculation; at 1 it rises by 1, so keep 1 for step-by-step time simulation.
when: Iterative calculation is enabled
why: Each recalculation runs the loop once per allowed iteration.

text: A level parameter that decreases by one per call bounds recursion depth by its starting value, which guarantees termination.
why: Recursion only proceeds while the level stays above zero, so each call moves toward a base case.

text: The two-variable iterative Fibonacci computes its result in a number of steps linear in n, avoiding recomputation of values.
why: Naive recursion branches into two calls per step and redoes work; keeping the last two values avoids repeating it.

text: Minimal height-balanced trees of this family satisfy N_0 = 0, N_1 = 1, and N_h = N_(h-1) + 1 + N_(h-2); the sequence also goes by a second name.

1) Set the cutoff to the start node's heuristic value. 2) Recursively extend paths whose cost so far plus heuristic is below the cutoff. 3) When all such paths are exhausted, raise the cutoff to the smallest total that exceeded it. 4) Restart and repeat until the goal is found.
when: memory is the main limit, such as handheld devices
why: stores only the current path

text: 1) Search one ply deep, then two plies, and so on, increasing depth. 2) After each completed depth, check whether time has run out. 3) If time runs out mid-search, use the result of the last completed depth.
when: the time available for a move is uncertain
why: a finished shallower result is always available as a fallback

text: 1) Keep the current value and its predecessor in two variables. 2) Advance the pair until the index reaches n. 3) Update the pair with two assignments and no temporary variable.
why: Recursive evaluation re-derives the same values through exponentially many calls; carrying the last two values forward computes each one only once.

text: Begin iterative deepening at depth two, since a one-ply search gives little useful information, but still run the one-ply search when branching is large or time is short.
when: When the branching factor is high or the clock is tight.
why: a one-ply result carries little information on its own

text: Turn on iterative calculation only when a value should deliberately advance step by step, such as a turn or time counter.
why: Accidental circular references are usually errors, so the default warning helps catch them.

text: A singly linked list node holds a key, a successor pointer and other data, and the list is accessed through a pointer to its first node.
Repeated head insertion produces a list whose elements appear in reverse order of their insertion.
A list is a degenerate tree where every node holds no more than a single subtree.
Linked lists suit small, varying collections whose access frequencies are unknown, such as a compiler symbol table with entries added and removed.
when: Collections of relatively few elements (under about 50) that change in size and have unknown access frequencies

text: Reuse a node's next field to build a new chain once the old chain is no longer needed, avoiding extra storage.
when: Rearranging linked nodes during a sort
why: The old link is free after the chain has been consumed

text: Removed nodes are not explicitly freed; they are reclaimed only if a garbage collector exists to reclaim unreferenced nodes.
why: Reclaiming depends on detecting that no remaining variable refers to a node, which is the job of an implementation-level collector rather than the language.

text: Deleting a node itself moves its successor's value into it and deletes the successor; this needs a successor and no other pointer to the deleted node.
when: When the designated node has a successor and no other pointer refers to the node
why: A singly linked list cannot reach a node's predecessor, so removing the node directly is impossible; copying the successor forward avoids that.

text: Passing the subtree link by value loses a newly allocated node, because the new pointer never reaches the parent's field.
when: Recursive insertion into a tree
why: The parent's pointer is not updated when only a copy of it is passed

text: 1) Allocate a new node. 2) Link its successor to the current head. 3) Move the head pointer to the new node. The order of these steps matters.
1) Link the new node to the designated node's old successor. 2) Link the designated node to the new node.
Insert a new node after the designated node, copy the designated node's contents into it, then store the new key in the designated node.
when: Predecessor links are not available.
why: A singly linked chain offers no route back to predecessors, so the new element goes after the designated one and the values are swapped instead.

text: 1) Test whether the pointer is NIL and stop if it is. 2) Apply the operation to the current element. 3) Move to the successor and repeat.
when: When an operation must be applied to every element of a linked list
why: The loop stops at the end marker and follows each link once, so the operation touches every element and nothing else.

text: 1) Walk one pointer ahead through the list. 2) Keep a second pointer one step behind it. 3) Insert the new node at the position the trailing pointer marks.
when: When elements must be kept in key order as they are added to a linked list
why: Linked insertion can happen cheaply at any position, which arrays and sequences do not allow, so ordering comes at nearly no extra cost.

text: Preallocating all node records gives fast lookup but wastes memory when most nodes are never considered, while an array of null pointers creates records only when needed.
when: Choosing node storage for A* on large graphs or memory-limited consoles
why: Preallocation trades memory for speed; lazy creation trades lookup simplicity for memory

text: String search finds the first occurrence of a pattern of M items within a text of N items, where 0 < M < N.
Two strings are equal when all their characters match. One string is less than another when, at the first position where they differ, its character is smaller.
The shift depends only on the pattern, so it is precomputed as a table before searching, and computing that table is itself a KMP-style search over the pattern.
During straight search, no match begins before the current start, and the first j pattern characters match at the current start.
Straight search ends with no match once the start passes N minus M, or with a match once the pattern index reaches M.
String search is basic to every text processing system, so efficient string search algorithms matter.
Three string search methods are straight search, Knuth-Morris-Pratt and Boyer-Moore, and Boyer-Moore is the most efficient of the three.
A linked list has no index, so search must proceed sequentially and stops at a matching key or at the end of the list.
Use linear search for short strings, under about 30 characters, and binary search for a large sorted table of strings.
when: searching strings in a table

text: Sequential search of a linked list is acceptable when the list is short.
why: Elements can only be reached by following links one after another, with no direct indexing as arrays allow.

text: A one-dimensional spatial lookup sorts units by position and uses binary search, lowering total cost to O(n log n); spatial partitions extend this to more dimensions.
when: units arranged along one line
why: The engine must repeatedly answer which objects are near a location, and storing objects by position makes that lookup efficient.

text: If a player knows the seeding method and RNG algorithm, a few observed results reveal their exact position in the sequence, after which all future results are predictable.
when: When a player has correctly guessed the seed method and the generator algorithm
why: The sequence is fixed by seed and algorithm, so a few observed outputs pin down the current place in it.

text: A string comparison loop advances while characters are equal and not the terminator. The terminator acts as a sentinel that stops the loop without a separate bounds check.
when: When strings end in a terminating character used as the stop marker
why: Reaching the terminator ends the scan automatically, so the length need not be tested inside the loop.

text: In the worst case straight string search takes on the order of N times M comparisons, when each start matches nearly the whole pattern before failing.
when: Text made mostly of one repeated character, with a late mismatch against a similar pattern

text: 1) For each start i from 0 to N-M, set the pattern index j to 0. 2) While text[i+j] equals pattern[j], increment j. 3) If j reaches M, report a match at i. 4) On mismatch, try the next start position.
1) Run a separate routine that checks for events every few frames. 2) Send any detected hit to the event manager. 3) The manager handles it as usual.
1) Run a binary search over the sorted table, using string comparison as the key test. 2) Compare the bounding entry with the search string to confirm a match.
when: Searching a large table of strings that is alphabetically ordered

text: Use a terminator that never occurs in the text, typically 0X, as the least character in the set; otherwise string ordering comparisons give wrong results.
when: Marking string length with an appended terminator instead of a stored length

text: At each node check only one bound: alpha where the opponent minimizes, and beta where the player maximizes.
when: implementing alpha-beta search with minimax nodes
why: Each node can only be cut off by the bound its side is trying to improve.

text: When a string comparison loop ends, strings that end together are equal. Otherwise the first differing characters determine their order.
when: Comparing strings stored as fixed-size character arrays
why: A match requires every position to agree, so the comparison hunts for any disagreeing pair.

text: Replace separate find-first and find-next procedures with one loop that tests each candidate in an IF, which keeps the all-solutions version simpler.
when: Enumerating all solutions to a constraint problem, such as placing eight queens
why: Once the candidate test sits in the loop body, no logical result needs returning.

text: Store all word characters in one shared buffer, keep only each word's starting index in its tree node, and truncate words to a fixed maximum length.
when: Storing words of widely different lengths in a word-indexing tree
why: words of different lengths then share one structure

text: Precomputing the shift table adds complexity, but it pays off when the same pattern is searched repeatedly or the text is much longer than the pattern.
when: choosing between simple and table-driven string search
why: The shift values depend only on the pattern, not the text, so they can be computed once and reused.

text: A sentinel removes the NIL test from the search loop, but a failed lookup returns the sentinel, so the caller must check for it and the structure is no longer a strict tree.
why: The loop's termination test is complex, so a shared end marker is sought to simplify it.

text: Binary search on a sorted array finds the insertion point faster than walking a linked list.
The comparison count of binary insertion is nearly independent of input order: reverse-ordered input needs the fewest comparisons and already-ordered input the most.
Binary insertion does not reduce item moves, which remain of order n², since each insertion still shifts many items.
Use binary insertion only where key comparisons are much more expensive than item moves, which is rarely the case.
why: Moving items is usually costlier than comparing keys, so saving comparisons yields little.

text: Using non-strict comparisons makes the comparand act as a sentinel for both scans, so the scans need no explicit bounds checks.
when: Implementing the quicksort partition scans.
why: The comparand itself stops each scan at the array ends.

text: In an ordered list, a search for a missing key stops at the first larger key, which is exactly where the new key must be inserted.
when: Inserting a new key into a linked list kept ordered by increasing keys

text: The gain from move-to-front grows with both the degree of clustering in the input and the length of the list.
when: Comparing self-organizing lists with static lists
why: Stronger clustering and longer lists make cheap repeat accesses more valuable

text: Binary search halves the remaining range per comparison, needing at most log2 N steps rounded up, versus about N/2 comparisons on average for linear search.
when: The array is sorted in non-decreasing order.
why: Halving the remaining range at each step.

text: Bisection targeting uses constant memory, and its time depends on simulation sampling resolution and the accuracy threshold.
Binary insertion makes about n·(log(n) - log(e)) key comparisons in total, with a bias of up to ±0.5 per search from truncated division.
why: Integer truncation when bisecting the search interval can add one extra comparison per search.

text: On average, a search of an ordered list for a new word scans only half of the list.
when: Inserting a new word into a lexicographically ordered word list
why: The scan stops at the insertion position, which lies on average midway through the list.

text: Binary insertion gives only a marginal gain over straight insertion and can be slower than straight insertion with sequential search on already sorted input.
when: input already sorted
why: The binary search cuts only comparisons, while item moves, which cost more, remain of order n squared.

text: Multi-level bucket schemes add considerable complexity and are generally not worth building.
why: Tuning the bucket parameters takes time and is rarely needed.

text: Changing binary insertion's loop test to less-or-equal, or simplifying its lower-bound assignment, can break the sort, so verify the altered version on crafted inputs.
Without clustering in the input, reordering a list by access gives little or no gain over a static list.
when: Input keys are spread evenly with no repeats in short runs
why: Reordering only helps when recent keys predict future ones

text: 1) Convert the dragless firing solution's vertical component to an elevation angle as the first guess. 2) Simulate and measure the signed miss distance. 3) If overshot, set the upper bound to the guess and the lower bound to -90 degrees; if undershot, set the lower bound to the guess and the upper bound to 45 degrees. 4) If the upper bound still undershoots, no solution exists. 5) Repeatedly take the midpoint angle, simulate, and replace the bound on the side the sign indicates until the miss is within margin.
when: Closed-form firing solution is impractical, such as with drag
why: Constant memory search converging on the target

text: 1) Keep bounds L and R around the candidate section. 2) While L is less than R, set the middle to the mean of L and R. 3) Move L past the middle or R onto it, depending on the comparison. 4) When L equals R, test the element at R for equality unless R equals N.
when: Searching an array whose elements are in non-decreasing order
why: Simpler termination condition; finds the match with least index.

text: 1) Take the sorted prefix as the search interval. 2) Sample the middle item and keep the half containing the insertion point. 3) Stop when the interval has length 1. 4) Shift items from that position right by one and insert the new item.
when: When inserting each item into an already ordered destination prefix during sorting
why: The prefix is already ordered, which allows locating the insertion point by bisection.

text: 1) Search the list while keeping a pointer to the predecessor of each candidate. 2) On a match, unlink the found element from its position. 3) Insert it at the top of the list.
when: Each successful search on a self-organizing list
why: Recently found elements move forward so repeat accesses are cheap

text: 1) Compute h = H(k). 2) Compare the key at h; stop if it matches or the slot is free. 3) Otherwise advance to the next probe index using a function G of the probe count i, and repeat from step 2.
when: Looking up or inserting a key in an open addressing table
why: Probing visits a fixed sequence of slots until the key or a free slot is found

text: When a search for an absent key fails in a move-to-front list, insert the new key at the top of the list.
when: Search misses in a self-organizing list
why: A key searched once is likely to be searched again soon

text: Linked lists allow only sequential search, while arrays allow direct indexing and sorted arrays allow binary search.
when: Searching for an element by key in a linked list

text: LLM errors are fabricated misinformation rather than false perceptions, so the term fabrication describes them better than hallucination.
LLMs give answers that are plausible rather than necessarily accurate, and they can cite nonexistent sources and perform poorly on math.
Each payoff equation can be written as one matrix row, with opponent probabilities in the left columns and the payoff in the rightmost column.
Multiplying a matrix by a column vector gives a new column vector, where each output entry is the sum of one matrix row multiplied piece by piece by the vector.

1) Write the payoff matrix M and a column p of ones. 2) Compute c as M inverse times p. 3) Divide each entry of c by the sum of all entries so the probabilities total 1. In a spreadsheet, use MMULT with MINVERSE as an array formula.
when: the payoff matrix is invertible
why: Normalizing by the sum converts raw solutions into valid probabilities

text: 1) If a diagonal entry is zero, swap in a row with a non-zero leading value. 2) Add scaled multiples of the top row to clear entries below the top diagonal. 3) Clear the bottom-left entry the same way. 4) If the middle pivot is zero and the bottom row's middle entry is not, swap those rows. 5) Clear the bottom row's center entry. 6) Solve the triangular system by substitution.
when: solving a 3 by 3 payoff matrix without inversion
why: Triangular form lets values be found one at a time by substitution

text: Display an error when no non-zero pivot can be found during a row swap, or when the bottom row is all zeros, since then no single solution exists.
when: When a row operation cannot find a non-zero pivot, or the bottom row becomes all zeros

text: A matrix is in triangular form when every entry below the diagonal is zero and every diagonal entry is non-zero; entries above the diagonal may be anything.
A trendline is a best-fit line or curve drawn through chart data when no known formula matches the points, so an approximate equation can be used.
A slope function s(x) gives how far up the slope a point sits, x of the way between lattice points; for bilinear interpolation s(x) equals x.
Two independent random columns can show apparent correlation, and small samples produce much larger apparent correlations than large ones.
Use squared distances in condensation comparisons so square roots are avoided.
why: The weight is only ever used in squared form, so squaring it once beforehand suffices.

text: Where subtractions dominate, the pathfinder avoids the area, so characters underuse very good tactical positions, an effect players rarely notice.
why: The areas are likely exceptionally good, so treating them as merely very good is usually hidden from the player.

text: Steady-state rating error always exists, because a player at their true rating still gains or loses points after each game.
when: when running a rating simulation over many games
why: Each game shifts a player's rating even when it already matches their true skill, so the estimate keeps drifting away from the truth.

text: A tree reflects only the examples provided, so an attribute that looks irrelevant in a small set may matter once more data arrives.
when: learning from a small example set

text: A small example set may not cover the situations a game produces, so the network will fail on the test set or in play.
when: Training data is limited.

text: MINVERSE returns an error when a matrix has no inverse; if a small change to one value clears the error, use an approximation or another method.
why: Some matrices have no inverse at all, so the function has no exact result to return.

text: A predictive model can learn patterns caused by how people were treated, mistaking the effect of care for a causal benefit.
when: When care or intervention depends on the same factors the model predicts.
why: Prioritized patients receive treatment that changes the observed outcome.

text: 1) Work column by column from the top left. 2) If a diagonal entry is zero, swap rows. 3) To cancel an entry, multiply one row by a whole number, then add rows. 4) Solve the bottom equation first and substitute upward. 5) Apply the sum-to-one rule to find remaining values.
why: The diagonal pivot must be nonzero before the entries below it can be cleared, and the swap also places a zero there.

text: Miss distance must be signed, positive for overshoot and negative for undershoot, because a plain distance is always positive and cannot indicate which side was missed.
when: Iterative shot targeting
why: A plain distance test only yields positive values, so the sign must be set separately to tell overshoot from undershoot.

text: Use the equation label option when you plan to extrapolate a trendline beyond the data, since it displays the formula you can then apply.
when: Extrapolating a fitted curve past the charted range.
why: The displayed equation lets you compute values outside the original points.

text: If all nodes have equal weight, the centroid is exactly the optimal root; otherwise the optimal root usually lies close to the centroid.
The chance that the optimal root lies very close to the centroid increases with the number of nodes n.
A balanced tree is generally not optimal when access is skewed; the optimal shape can be degenerate, with the most frequent key at the root.

1) Place all genuine and special nodes on a line, weighted by access frequency. 2) Take the weighted centroid as the root candidate. 3) Search a limited range around it for the best local root. 4) Apply the same steps to each subtree, using exact dynamic programming once subtrees are small.
when: when building a large search tree
why: runs in O(n log n) time with O(n) storage

text: The centroid method gives a nearly optimal tree in O(n log n) time and O(n) storage, while the exact method needs quadratic storage but yields the true optimum.
when: choosing a search-tree construction method
why: It aims for near-optimality rather than the true optimum, which allows a heuristic construction method.

text: SMS-EMOA is a multiobjective evolutionary algorithm; it can combine two or three objectives while other objectives act as constraints.
The starting parameter guess can be random, set by programmer intuition, or taken from the result of a previous run.
Swarm methods such as particle swarm and ant colony optimisation can serve the same search purpose but are not strictly evolutionary.
Lowering the temperature over the run shrinks randomness, so the search gradually accepts fewer worse moves.
why: Temperature sets the amount of randomness, and worse moves are accepted with probability proportional to e to the minus energy over temperature.

text: Tuning momentum, step size, and temperature together is largely trial and error and hard to balance.
Use an array of per-parameter step sizes when parameters differ in scale, rather than one constant step.
when: parameters differ in scale
why: A single constant fixes every tweak to one size, so a per-parameter array lets each parameter take its own step.

text: A binary heap is an array in which each element is less than both children; the children of index i sit at 2i+1 and 2i+2.
A bucketed queue sorts buckets by value range, leaves contents unsorted, appends insertions, and removes from the first non-empty bucket; bucket count tunes the balance.
Bucketed queues are more cache-friendly for very large graphs; for a few thousand to tens of thousands of nodes, a heap is often enough.
when: For enormous route searches involving nodes numbering in the millions.
why: Bucketed queues fit the processor's memory cache better, which makes them much faster at that scale.

text: A balanced priority search tree gives logarithmic bounds but makes insertion and deletion complicated, so it trades implementation simplicity for guaranteed performance.
why: Balancing secures guaranteed logarithmic bounds, but the scheme is intricate enough that it is hardly used in practice.

text: 1) Simulate the game or test many times with random inputs. 2) Record the result of each trial and count the outcomes of interest. 3) Divide the count of the target result by the total number of trials to estimate its probability.
when: when the math for a probability is too hard
why: Repeated trials estimate odds without complex calculation. Estimates probabilities that are hard to compute exactly.

text: Some transitions are one-way, such as a drop that cannot be climbed back, so a node pair may connect in one direction only.
Repeating one transition matrix forms a Markov chain whose stable final values are an eigenvector of that matrix, if one exists.
Games often apply several different transition matrices for different events, so stable final values matter less in practice.
In Monte Carlo tallies, use COUNTIF instead of a per-row IF helper column plus AVERAGE when only a success rate is needed.
when: only a success rate is needed
why: COUNTIF tallies all matching rows in a single step, so no per-row flag column is needed.

text: The median number of transitions to reach a final state is the first transition where the cumulative probability of being in that state exceeds 0.5.
when: the chain has a final state
why: The cumulative chance of having reached the final state is the distribution, so crossing 0.5 splits games into equal halves.

text: The most likely entry route is the transition that has the highest chance of first reaching the final state, found by MAX() then locating that column with MATCH().
why: MAX returns only the highest value, not its position, so MATCH is needed to locate the transition.

text: Much Markov literature assumes the total is 1, so its methods may not carry over to game values with other totals.
why: Markov processes concern distributions of random variables, so the literature assumes totals of 1.

text: 1) Write formulas that compute one roll per row. 2) Flag rows in the target range with IF and AVERAGE the flags for an estimate. 3) Recalculate several times to see the spread. 4) List every unique outcome, one per row. 5) Apply the same flag count to those rows for the exact probability. 6) Compare.
when: Estimating a probability and checking the estimate against an exact count.
why: Enumerating every unique outcome gives an exact probability to check the simulated estimate against.

text: 1) Create one worksheet per game state. 2) Place each state's calculations in row 1 of its sheet. 3) Link each sheet to the one before it.
when: Row-by-row simulation becomes hard to read on one sheet

text: 1) Store the transition matrix with origin states in columns and destination states in rows. 2) Enter the starting state as a column vector. 3) Multiply the matrix by the current vector to get the next state. 4) Repeat for each transition.
when: simulating a Markov chain in a spreadsheet

text: A ring buffer is a fixed array with head and tail indices that wrap around modulo the capacity, giving a queue with no dynamic allocation.
One cell stays unused as a gap between head and tail, which keeps full and empty states distinguishable.
If a ring buffer fills up, the tail collides with the head and overwrites pending items, so an assertion should detect the full state.
when: When the queue reaches its capacity of pending requests.
why: The unused gap between tail and head exists only below capacity, so a full queue removes it and the tail meets the head.

text: 1) Enqueue: write at the tail, then advance the tail by one modulo the array size. 2) Dequeue: read the item at the head, then advance the head by one modulo the array size. 3) The queue is empty when head equals tail.
when: Implementing a fixed-size queue.
why: Wrapping indices let the buffer run indefinitely without shifting elements.

text: Queue events when broadcasting many events to many characters within a limited per-frame budget, and spread the queued events over several frames to smooth processor use.
when: many events go to many characters with a limited per-frame budget
why: events cannot all be handled in one frame

text: RANDBETWEEN(low, high) returns a random integer including both bounds, spread evenly, so RANDBETWEEN(1,6) simulates a die; each cell gets a new value on recalculation.
A pseudorandom number generator (RNG) repeatedly applies an erratic math function, feeding each output back in to produce the next number.
The seed is the starting value of an RNG, normally set once when the game starts.
RAND() returns a decimal from 0 up to but not including 1, so it can return 0 but never 1.
Computers can run millions of trials in minutes, making simulation practical for systems too complex to solve by hand.
A riffle shuffle preserves the relative order of cards within each half, so some deck orders cannot occur after a single shuffle.
After a riffle shuffle, cards near the top and bottom of the deck stay near those positions.
Automated card shufflers can be less random than human shuffles, and card-by-card stacking algorithms have their own flaws.
RAND() can in principle produce identical values, which would break the one-to-52 ranking, but the chance is negligible for simulation.
Use a seeded RNG in virtually all video games, since it is usually the only practical option.
when: video games
why: Outsourcing true randomness is rarely workable for routine game needs.

text: Shuffling the population before selection can help escape loss-of-gradient situations.
Using milliseconds elapsed since midnight as a seed gives about 86.4 million possible seeds per day.
A 64-bit integer has about 1.8×10^19 distinct values, so a 64-bit seed space is roughly 2^64.
why: A 64-bit machine integer can hold only 64 bits' worth of distinct values, bounding the seed count.

text: A 52-card deck has 52! (about 8×10^67) possible orders.
why: Each card placed has one fewer remaining slot choice, so the counts multiply down to one.

text: A 256-bit seed is needed to reach every 52-card shuffle, and it still falls short for 60-card decks.
why: The number of possible deck orders exceeds the number of distinct seeds, so most orders are unreachable.

text: Multiplying RAND() by the width of a range and adding the lower bound gives a decimal from the lower bound up to, not including, the upper bound.
when: Generating values in an arbitrary range.
why: RAND() returns values from 0 up to but never reaching 1, so scaling keeps the upper end open.

text: The cubic slope function s(x) = 3x² − 2x³ is simple and fast; it weights neighbouring points by 1 − s(x) and s(x).
when: Bicubic terrain interpolation
why: Linear weights rise too evenly; an S-shaped curve keeps values near lattice points flatter.

text: Good sorting algorithms need on the order of n·log(n) comparisons, while simple straight methods need on the order of n² comparisons.
Random-swap shuffling is very inefficient and never fully unbiased: each card stays slightly likelier in its original position, and more swaps only shrink this bias.
why: Cards that are never picked stay where they started.

text: Reusing a predictable seed in every session lets anyone who knows it replay the same results.
when: When players can save and reload after a random roll.
why: Repeating a failed roll lets a player keep retrying until a win, breaking the balance of random outcomes.

text: Seeding from only fractional milliseconds (0 to 999) gives just 1000 seeds, so repeated play looks suspiciously identical.
why: The seed space is small enough that repeated outcomes eventually recur in visible play.

text: In competitive play, a determined opponent can study early results, identify the seed, and predict every later result.
when: competitive play
why: Early outputs narrow the small set of possible seeds until only one matches.

text: Even with 86.4 million seeds, a player who starts at about the same time each day may eventually receive a repeated seed.
when: When a player starts play around the same time each day.
why: The finite seed pool means the same clock-derived seed can come back on a later day.

text: A seed taken from milliseconds since midnight leaves about 86 million candidates, which a modern computer can search in seconds.
when: When the seed-generation method has been guessed.
why: A few seconds of computation is enough to test every candidate millisecond seed.

text: Rounding RAND() straight to an integer is wrong: rounding down always gives 0, and rounding to nearest gives only 0 or 1.
why: RAND() returns values from 0 up to but never reaching 1, so rounding can only ever yield 0 or 1.

text: 1) Start with an unshuffled deck. 2) Pick two random positions and swap the cards there. 3) Repeat the random swaps many times, such as a few thousand for 52 cards.

1) Research the RNG algorithm and how its seed is generated. 2) Narrow the seed candidates to a few million or fewer. 3) Generate and store each candidate's output sequence. 4) Match observed outputs, adding more until the match is unique. 5) Verify the remaining outputs.
when: When observed outputs come from a seeded pseudorandom generator, such as a spreadsheet RAND-based coin flip
why: Storing every possible output sequence at once is infeasible, so the candidate seed space must be narrowed first.

text: 1) Open File > Options > Formulas. 2) Check Enable Iterative Calculation. 3) Set the maximum number of iterations.
when: Excel workbook needs a deliberate loop, such as a time counter
why: Circular references normally error because dependent cells have no defined update order; iteration lets Excel settle them within a set limit.

text: Before MOD when extracting a digit, take the integer part of the division with FLOOR(a/b) or QUOTIENT(a,b), since MOD on a fractional value does not isolate the correct digit.
when: When a column must cycle through values several times slower than another column.
why: Removing the fraction lets the following MOD pick the right digit.

text: Players cycle between active play and rest periods to reset their rating deviation.
when: in pure Glicko systems
why: going inactive lets deviation rise again

text: Showing a player near the bottom of a friends list may encourage spending to catch up.
when: when a friends list shows a player trailing peers
why: visible gaps to peers motivate catch-up behavior

text: Glicko extends Elo with a per-player RD uncertainty value that changes over time, so effective K varies between players. Its formulas are more complicated than Elo's.
Rank is an ordinal standing showing no gap size, only that no one sits between neighbors. Rating is an approximate absolute measure, usually of skill, whose numerical differences are meaningful.
Harkness is an early tournament method that sets a new rating from opponents' average rating and event score alone, ignoring the prior rating.
RANK(value, range) returns a value's position in a range, where 1 is the highest number, 2 the second highest, and so on.
Rating inflation is a rising average rating over time and deflation is a falling average, both caused by points entering or leaving a zero-sum rating system.
K-factor is the number of new players each player brings in, borrowed from viral marketing, and a high value sharply lowers acquisition cost.
A ranking system determines and updates each player's rank, while a rating system assigns and updates each player's rating; Elo is the best-known rating system.

Ranking systems serve several purposes: progression if ranks reset often, rewards (one-time if permanent, ongoing if reset), dominance against friends or worldwide, and clarifying or mystifying ratings.
A learning algorithm should save implementation work overall, but learners usually need hand-holding such as correct data presentation, result validation and testing.
why: Learners need extra support, so total effort can exceed hand coding.

text: Player star ratings, typically 1 to 5 in app stores, differ from professional reviewer scores, which aggregator sites average.
Across many trials, unlikely streaks still occur, but aggregate results converge toward predicted values, and convergence strengthens as the trial count grows.
Use Glicko to find a player's true rating quickly under frequent play, especially when uncertainty should grow during inactivity.
when: When finding each player's true rating quickly matters and players play frequently.
why: Rating deviation shrinks with each game, so every result narrows the rating estimate faster.

text: A player's RD falls after each game and rises slowly during inactivity, so a long break makes the player's next rating less certain.
when: When a player has been inactive for some time.
why: Skill may drift during a break, so the system widens the uncertainty to let the rating adjust.

text: In a rating-based league, everyone starts with the same provisional rating, and the highest-rated player at the end is the winner.
when: When a league is run with a rating system instead of a tournament format.

text: Negative feedback makes the power difference between players swing back and forth rather than grow steadily.
why: Trailing players gain power faster, so each lead is pulled back and the gap oscillates.

text: A rating floor is positive sum: a floor-rated player who loses gains nothing, but the opponent still gains points, which inflates the system.
when: a rating floor exists
why: The floor-rated loser keeps their points while the winner still gains, so total points in the system rise.

text: A low learning gain makes weight updates small, giving slow but stable learning that accumulates repeated errors while ignoring one-off errors.
when: Gain is set low relative to the weight update step.
why: Small steps average out isolated examples, so only consistently seen errors shift the weights much.

text: Rewarding rank gains with currency rewards play without charging per game, and players feel they earned it because they wanted to rank up.
when: when a monthly rank reset is used
why: Players see the currency as earned because ranking up is something they wanted anyway, not a per-game payment.

text: A Glicko rating is often shown as R ± 2RD, a range expected to contain the true rating about 95% of the time.
when: When a Glicko rating is displayed to players instead of a single number.

text: A minimum RD of about 30 is suggested so that every game still moves ratings a little.
when: When implementing Glicko in practice with frequent play.
why: Very low deviation barely shifts ratings, making outcomes seem meaningless, so a floor keeps each game mattering.

text: Under a rating system that moves a player's rating by 10 points for each percentage point away from 50%, results stay within 500 points of the opponents' average.
Each game puts max(1, 10 − floor(D/20)) points at risk, where D is the rating difference: 10 under 20, then one less per additional 20 points, minimum 1.
when: when a point scheme scales stakes by rating gap
why: Developers want players to face closely rated opponents, so stakes shrink as the rating gap grows.

text: With frequent play, RD falls toward zero in pure Glicko. Without a minimum RD, ratings barely move and players may feel results no longer matter.
when: When a player plays frequently under a pure Glicko implementation.
why: low deviation makes ratings change little

text: Because prior rating is ignored, these ratings can swing widely when a player's performance is inconsistent between events.
when: When a player's performance varies a lot between events.
why: The new rating depends only on this event's results and opponents' ratings, ignoring the prior rating.

text: 1) Compute R, the average rating of the opponents. 2) Convert the event score to a percentage. 3) If exactly 50%, the new rating is R. 4) If above 50%, add 10 points per percentage point above 50; if below, subtract 10 per point below 50.
1) Modify the Elo rating change formula so the outcome is weighted 90% skill and 10% luck. 2) Verify that rating updates reflect that split.
when: when a game is mostly skill with a meaningful luck component

text: 1) Create thousands of simulated players with hidden true ratings. 2) Pair them with the matchmaking system. 3) Compute each match's win probability from the true rating gap. 4) Draw a random result and update system ratings. 5) Measure error against true ratings.
when: when comparing or testing a rating system
why: Real players' true skill is unknown, so hidden true ratings let the system's error be measured.

text: 1) Fill C1 to C52 with =RAND(). 2) In D1 enter =RANK(C1,$C$1:$C$52). 3) Fill D1 down to D52. Column D then holds 1 through 52 in random order.
when: you need a random ordering of a numbered set
why: Ranking random values gives each position exactly once, producing a random ordering of 1 through 52.

text: 1) Read each response from the file. 2) Count mentions per hit, drop hits never mentioned, and sort the rest by count. 3) For each category, list respondents whose first choice is a top-three hit of that category.
when: ranked-choice survey split into categories

text: 1) Ignore draws so neither player gains or loses rating. 2) If the stronger player still wins sometimes, score draws separately, based on the expected draw-to-win ratio at that rating gap. 3) Or change rules to prevent drawing exploits.
when: When a draw should not count as half a win.
why: Draws can distort ratings if scored as half wins.

text: Compare the win probabilities implied by point gains with observed win rates; a rating system is consistent when they match.
why: The predicted win chance is the points gained divided by the gain plus the loss, so the opponent's predicted chance sums to one.

text: Build rank tables once from the preference lists, so that looking up a partner's rank becomes a single operation during repeated stability tests.
when: stability must be checked many times during a search
why: searching a preference list on every test is slow

text: Use rank to show relative standing when the exact gap does not matter; use rating when you need to know how far apart two players are, such as in matchmaking.
why: Rank records only ordering, so the size of the gap between neighboring players is not recorded.

text: Tying rank to rating makes it hard to reset rank without also resetting ratings, which reduces the value of matchmaking.
when: when deciding whether rank should be derived from rating
why: Since rank follows rating, resetting rank also means resetting ratings, which weakens matchmaking's ability to pair evenly matched opponents.

text: Overall ratings as a tiebreaker give highly rated players an edge from outside the event and may look unfair, since they reward advantages existing before the tournament.
when: when choosing a round robin tiebreaker

text: Factorial n! is the product of integers 1 through n, defined by initial value and recurrence: each term equals the next index times the previous term.
A Fibonacci number of order p is the sum of the preceding p+1 terms; order 1 gives the ordinary Fibonacci numbers.
Fibonacci numbers start with 0 and 1, and each later term is the sum of the two preceding terms.
A recursive definition refers to itself, so a finite statement can describe infinitely many objects or computations.
A procedure is directly recursive when it calls itself, and indirectly recursive when it calls another procedure that eventually calls it back.
A recursive program is a composition of ordinary statements with one call to itself, and a procedure gives that composition a name.
A Fibonacci tree of height h has a root with a Fibonacci tree of height h-1 on one side and one of height h-2 on the other; the empty tree and a single node are base cases.
A tree traversal is a short recursion that does nothing on an empty subtree and applies a chosen operation to every node it visits.
A tree is either empty or a node with a finite number of disjoint subtrees.
Natural numbers, binary trees and the factorial function are recursively defined, so their definitions refer to themselves.
A recursive AVL insertion can return a flag saying whether the subtree grew, which the caller uses to update its own balance factor.
On an expression tree, preorder gives prefix notation, postorder gives postfix notation, and inorder gives infix notation without the parentheses needed for precedence.
When a balanced tree is built from input, values are read in preorder: the root first, then the left subtree, then the right subtree.
Prefer a loop over recursion when values follow a simple recurrence and each step needs only the previous result.
when: When the values to compute come from a simple recurrence.
why: With only one call at the start or end, the recursion is plain repetition that can be written as a loop.

text: Naive recursive Fibonacci makes two self-calls for each call with an argument above 1, so the number of calls grows exponentially with n.
when: When Fibonacci is coded as a direct transcription of its recurrence.

text: In the basic eight queens program, the safety test runs about 161 times per solution, averaged over all 92 solutions.
when: Plain backtracking without symmetry reduction, all solutions enumerated.
why: The program does not detect symmetric duplicates, so the average runs over all 92 solutions.

text: Each recursion level stores its state on the system stack, such as local variables and parameters in quicksort, so deep recursion costs storage even when the program is correct.
when: When recursion depth can grow large, as in quicksort's worst case.
why: Each activation needs room for its variables plus the recorded state of the computation, so total storage grows with depth.

text: The belief that recursion is inefficient largely comes from naturally iterative problems being written recursively.
when: When recursion is taught through examples better solved iteratively.
why: Recursive definitions of a problem do not make recursion the best solution, so poorly chosen examples mislead.

text: 1) Number each state uniquely from its variables. 2) Work backward, deriving each state from its predecessor states. 3) Fill the table in a spreadsheet to avoid enumeration errors.
when: a state machine has many states that are easier to compute with a table than by hand
why: backward recursion lists every path without missing cases

text: 1) Deduce the recursion scheme that relates each order of the figure to smaller orders. 2) Encode that scheme as a recursive drawing procedure.
when: Drawing self-similar curves such as superimposed W-curves.

text: 1) Study a non-recursive program for a similar task. 2) Use it as a guideline to build an iterative version of the recursive one. 3) Derive general conversion rules from the result.
when: Converting a recursive program to iteration.

text: 1) Initialize the variables that the recursive levels would carry. 2) While the base-case condition is false, perform one level's work per iteration. 3) Return the accumulated result.
when: converting a single-call recursive procedure into a loop

text: A square is safe for a queen exactly when its row and both of its diagonals are unoccupied.
when: Column conflicts are already excluded by one queen per column.
why: Tracking rows and diagonals directly makes the most frequently executed check a simple lookup.

text: Describe a stack of disks recursively as its top disk plus the rest, and move the rest out of the way using the auxiliary rod.
when: Towers of Hanoi style problems with an auxiliary peg.

text: Guard each recursive call with a condition that eventually becomes false, such as recursing with n-1 only while n is greater than 0.
why: Without such a guard the recursive calls never end; the guard is the recursive analogue of a loop variant.

text: Pass the index as a parameter and return the computed value from the function instead of updating a shared result variable.
when: a recursive or iterative computation produces a single result
why: a returned value removes the need for shared state between levels

text: Row-by-row simulation works without iteration but uses more sheet space and more copy-and-paste work than the iterative approach.
when: When the spreadsheet program lacks support for iteration.
why: Without iteration, each time step needs its own row referring to the previous row, costing extra space and copying.

text: Keeping a naturally recursive algorithm recursive preserves its structure, whereas converting it to pure iteration needs an explicit stack that often obscures the structure.
why: Simulating recursion iteratively means managing a stack by hand, which hides what the program does.

text: Repeatedly halving a decimal digit array with nested loops produces negative powers of two, such as 0.5, 0.25 and 0.0009765625 for 2^-10.
In repeated-squaring exponentiation, the invariant is that the original power equals the current x raised to i, times y.
Repeated-squaring exponentiation makes about as many passes as the exponent has binary digits.
A tree of recursive calls can repeat the same subcomputations many times, so the cost is the total call count rather than the depth.
why: Separate branches recompute identical values, which an iterative scheme avoids by keeping intermediate values in variables.

text: 1) Set y to 1.0 and copy the exponent into i. 2) While i is positive, multiply y by x when i is odd, square x, and halve i with integer division. 3) Result is y.
when: raising a real number to a non-negative integer power without an exponent operator

text: Common partitioning schemes for pathfinding graphs include Dirichlet domains, grid tiles, visibility points, and polygon meshes.
when: Choosing how to divide a level into graph regions.
why: Each scheme turns continuous space into regions and connections.

text: Spread items evenly during balancing, so later neighbour fetches are postponed, since fetching a page is a costly transfer.
when: When a B-tree page underflows and items must be borrowed from a neighbouring page
why: Pulling the adjacent page into main memory is expensive, so it pays to move several items per retrieval.

text: Fill, the number of nodes a search examines, is the main measure of heuristic quality.
why: Accurate heuristics steer the search straight toward the answer, so fewer nodes get examined.

text: Converting a number to or from decimal text takes time proportional to its number of digits.
when: When numbers must be exchanged with a human through readable text
why: Readable output needs an extra conversion from binary values into decimal notation beyond the raw transfer.

text: Giving the user more control over selection can match their wishes better, but it raises cognitive effort and fatigue.
when: In interactive evolution, where a human picks, ranks or scores artifacts
why: Greater control widens the human's cognitive load, which leads to tiredness.

text: Backward chaining is rarely used in typical game AI, though it may suit contrived goal-driven game situations.
when: Deciding between chaining approaches for game AI
why: Typical game rule systems are driven by state changes rather than goal queries.

text: Backward chaining starts from a goal and checks rule conclusions that could produce it, recursively establishing each rule's conditions until they are all found in the database.
when: Solving goal-directed problems such as theorem proving or planning
why: Working back from a goal finds only the rules relevant to reaching it.

text: Under the closed-world assumption, any condition not stated is false, so initial states, goals, and preconditions use only positive literals, while effects may negate conditions.
when: Writing STRIPS problems
why: Unstated conditions default to false, so state descriptions only need the true facts.

text: Variable-depth search lets different branches stop at different depths, using conditions that decide when to stop each branch; alpha-beta pruning is one example.
Some games, like chess, can last nearly unlimited turns, with competition move-limit rules imposing a cap.
Some events need no checking: a game object can enqueue an event directly, such as a 'ready-for-battle' signal sent to squad members.
Skipping already-visited pairs halves the comparisons but still leaves growth at O(n²).
When selecting from n objects, each object is either included or excluded, so the unpruned search covers 2^n sets.
when: When choosing a subset from n objects with include-or-exclude decisions and no pruning
why: Each object has two outcomes, so n independent decisions multiply into 2^n combinations.

text: Without an underlying order, finding nearby units requires scanning the entire array.
when: units stored without spatial order
why: With no ordering, finding units near a point forces examining every entry.

text: Without bounding criteria that cut the search drastically, the 2^n growth makes exhaustive search impractical.
why: Each added object doubles the candidate sets, so only strong pruning keeps exhaustive search workable.

text: A sentinel is a copy of the search key past the last element of an array or list, so scans always stop at a match without an end-of-list test.
Place a sentinel node at the start of a linked list so that search needs no separate end-of-list test, which simplifies the code.
when: Implementing a linked list search
why: The sentinel guarantees the search always stops

text: Alpha and beta form a search window that narrows as the search proceeds, so more branches fall outside it and get pruned.
why: Moves outside the window can never be chosen by either side, so exploring them is wasted.

text: A sentinel requires one extra array slot beyond the N items.
why: The extra slot holds a guaranteed match at the end, so the bounds test can be dropped from the loop.

text: Moving boundary checks out of the procedure forces every call site to repeat them, so postpone such optimization until the algorithm is correct.
when: While an algorithm is still being built and not yet shown correct
why: Each caller would need its own check or a justification for omitting it, adding room for error.

text: Testing the key before the end-of-list condition in a combined search loop reads a field of a nonexistent NIL node.
when: A search loop combines two termination conditions.

text: 1) Enlarge the array to N+1 slots. 2) Store the search key in slot N. 3) Scan from index 0, testing only for a match. 4) If the index equals N afterward, the key is absent.
when: unordered data where one loop test per step is wanted

text: 1) Point every empty branch to one shared sentinel node. 2) Store the target key in the sentinel before searching. 3) Loop with only the key comparison. 4) A failed lookup returns the sentinel, which the caller must test.
why: Sharing one terminal node removes the separate end-of-branch test that a nil check would need.

text: Judge a search variant by stating its loop invariant, then check that it ends with the element equal to the argument if one exists, or with no match otherwise.
when: comparing or correcting binary search variants
why: A variant is correct only if its invariant holds throughout and its final state reports the right result.

text: A sort is stable if items with equal keys keep their original relative order in the output.
A run is a maximal ordered subsequence: it cannot be extended at either end without breaking the order.
Quicksort sorts by exchanging items over large distances, using a partition step that splits the array around a chosen comparand.
Sorting permutes a set of items so that their ordering values are non-decreasing, which makes later searching easier.
The key is the explicit field whose value determines an item's position in the ordering.
Bubblesort is weak among straight sorting methods, with little beyond simplicity to recommend it; in reported measurements it was the slowest method overall.
In-place sorting methods fall into three principal categories: sorting by insertion, sorting by selection, and sorting by exchange.
Bubblesort's exchanges are of order n², ranging from zero for sorted input up to a worst case of order n².
The early-stop and last-exchange improvements remove redundant comparisons but do not reduce the number of exchanges.
In external sorting, array-based sorts are useful mainly in the distribution phase, since later merge passes handle runs longer than main store.
Heapsort keeps its binary heap inside the array being sorted.
Building a heap from input in reverse order needs no moves.
Heapsort beats Shellsort at large sizes.
when: large n

text: In measured times, the array version of straight merge sort beats heapsort and loses to quicksort.
With N sequences, polyphase merge performs an (N-1)-way merge, while balanced merging performs an N/2-way merge, so polyphase needs fewer passes.
when: Comparing polyphase and balanced merge with the same number of sequences.
why: A higher merge degree reduces the number of passes.

text: For the improved bubblesort, the average pass count is about n minus a constant times the square root of n, and average comparisons are about (n² - n(k + ln n))/2, with k a constant.
when: average case

text: The first version of this method assumes the item count is a power of two, and a later refinement removes that restriction.
Any type with a total ordering relation can be sorted by the same methods once each item is reduced to its key.
An array gives direct access to every item, while a sequential file exposes only its front item, so the two need different methods.
In the reported measurements, Quicksort ran two to three times faster than Heapsort.
Quicksort sorts reverse-ordered input about as fast as sorted input.
Straight insertion is stable, since equal keys are never passed over.
Straight merging on sequential storage needs three tapes.
The expected comparisons and moves of Quicksort on random permutations can be derived by adapting the analysis of random binary search tree insertion.
Sort after compiling candidate lists using an in-place sort such as quicksort. With linked lists, sorting during insertion may be faster.
when: Choosing sort timing for candidate lists
why: Linked lists allow very quick inserts, so sorting as items arrive is cheap; arrays suit a final in-place sort.

text: Plot the probabilities of each maximum run length to see how the distribution is shaped.
why: The graph reveals the distribution's shape and how often each streak length appears.

text: Straight sorting methods are learned first because they clarify the main sorting principles, have short programs, and are fast for small inputs.
why: Sophisticated methods need fewer operations, but each is more intricate, so simple methods win for small inputs.

text: For sizes that are not powers of two, keep merging full groups while enough items remain, and let the final short groups finish the pass.
The best cutoff m for a quicksort-plus-simple-sort hybrid is expected to be small.
Use a quickselect-style partition method for medians and other quantiles of large sets; it's not worth it for sets of about 10 elements or fewer.
when: When the median or k-th smallest item is needed rather than a full ordering
why: Partitioning narrows toward the target rank, avoiding the cost of fully sorting all items.

text: Heapsort is very efficient for large n and its advantage grows with n, but it is not recommended for small inputs.
when: Sorting a large number of items; small numbers of items are not recommended.

text: Polyphase planning only needs to track run counts per sequence, not keys, because merging n runs always produces exactly n runs.
when: Planning a polyphase merge schedule.
why: The number of runs evolves predictably regardless of key values.

text: Before adopting quicksort, judge how much performance would be lost if unlucky input causes worst-case behavior.
when: Choosing a sorting method for uncertain input.
why: Quicksort's average speed comes with a quadratic worst case.

text: Prefer this method when moving items dominates the cost, as on peripheral storage.
when: Sorting with peripheral storage devices, where item moves dominate the cost.
why: Moving items on peripheral devices costs far more than comparing keys, so moves drive the total effort.

text: Use a stable sort when items are already ordered by a secondary property that must survive the sort.
when: items with a secondary order
why: A stable method leaves items with equal primary keys in their existing order, so an earlier secondary ordering survives.

text: Straight insertion suits small inputs and nearly sorted data, where it can beat straight selection.
when: small or nearly sorted input

text: Use straight merge sort when data sits on sequential external storage too large for main memory.
