when: Data too large for main memory, stored on sequential storage such as tape or disk.
why: Only one component is directly accessible at a time, so array-style sorting fails and merging becomes the main technique.

text: When men are paired in a fixed order, track availability only for women, since each man's status follows from the index being processed.
when: When men are paired in a fixed order, so each man's status depends on the index being processed.
why: A man's marital status is fully determined by the current index, so a separate array for men is unnecessary.

text: Changing a behaviour's phase shifts when it runs without changing its frequency, so behaviours sharing a frequency can be spread over consecutive frames.
why: Three behaviours at frequency 3 with phases 0, 1 and 2 run on consecutive frames.

text: When a merge source reaches end of file, it is eliminated, the active count and live count drop, and the index map is rearranged.
When a merge source reaches end of run, it is excluded from selection until the current output run is complete, then becomes available again.
when: When the next key on a source is less than the current key, ending the run.

text: Merging r runs distributed over N files leaves about r/N runs per pass, so after k passes about r/N^k runs remain.
when: When runs are equally distributed over N files.
why: Each pass cuts the run count by a factor of N, so the number of passes becomes log base N of n.

text: Sifting a new element at the top moves it down along the path of the smaller child, and each smaller child rises one level.
when: When a new element is added on top of an existing heap.

text: Merging two sequences of n runs each yields exactly n runs, so the number of runs halves with each merge pass.
when: Natural merge sort performing successive passes.
why: Each pair of corresponding runs combines into one run.

text: Polyphase merge always combines runs from two sources into a third. When a source is exhausted, it becomes the next destination, so no fixed pass structure is needed.
when: Merging runs across several sequences.
why: Abandoning rigid strict passes lets each sequence be reused as soon as it empties, rather than waiting for a pass boundary.

text: If the largest value is always chosen as comparand, each partition leaves only one item on one side, needing about n splits and order n^2 comparisons.
when: Quicksort on inputs that defeat the comparand choice.
why: Splits are maximally unbalanced.

text: Straight selection costs about n^2/2 comparisons because each scan keeps only the minimum and discards the outcome of every other comparison.
when: Analyzing straight selection sort.
why: Each scan keeps only the single least item, so the outcome of other comparisons is discarded and later scans repeat work.

text: A sift ends when an element with a smaller key is found or the left end of the ordered prefix is reached.
Sorting efficiency is measured by C, the number of key comparisons, and M, the number of item moves (transpositions). Both are functions of n.
why: Efficiency means economy of time, so counting key comparisons and item moves captures the work a sort performs.

text: The basic bubblesort always makes (n² - n)/2 key comparisons, regardless of input order.
The partition-based selection method averages about 2n comparisons, giving linear average cost in n.
when: If on average each split halves the partition that holds the desired quantile.
why: Each split halves the remaining partition, so the comparison counts form a geometric series summing to about 2n.

text: With six sequences and a heap of 100 items, about 165 million initial runs can be sorted in ten partial passes.
when: With six sequences and a heap of 100 items.

text: On random keys, expected run length from heap run generation is about twice the heap size, rather than the heap size.
when: When the keys in the input sequence are randomly distributed.

text: Heapsort's worst-case total moves are of order n log n, from about n/2 sifts to build the heap and n-1 sifts to sort.
why: Each sift is bounded by a logarithm of the heap size and there are linearly many sifts, so the total moves grow as n log n.

text: Heapsort's average number of moves is about (n/2) log n.
why: The sifting phase dominates: each of the n-1 sifts moves items down a heap of roughly log n levels, so the total stays on the order of n log n.

text: The number of polyphase passes is roughly the logarithm of the number of runs n, taken to the base of the merge degree.
when: Estimating passes for a polyphase merge.
why: Each pass with N sequences reduces the run count by a factor of about N-1, so the number of passes is the log of the run count in that base.

text: Quicksort partitioning averages about n/6 exchanges per partition over all comparand positions; the exact value is (n - 1/n)/6.
when: Estimating quicksort exchange counts.
why: Each element left of the bound is exchanged only if it previously sat in the right partition, and averaging the probability over all bounds yields the value.

text: With a median split at every level, quicksort needs about n log n comparisons and about n log n / 6 exchanges.
when: Estimating quicksort cost in the best case.
why: Balanced splits give about log n levels of n work each.

text: A sift makes at least 1 and at most i-1 comparisons, and about i/2 on average over all permutations.
Straight insertion makes about n-1 comparisons and 2(n-1) moves on sorted input, about n²/2 of each in reverse order, and about n²/4 of each on average.
why: Sorted input means each insertion stops immediately, while reversed input forces every new item to shift past all earlier ones; random input averages halfway.

text: Naive QuickSort can recurse to depth n in the worst case, while a refined partitioning limits the depth to about log(n).
why: Naive composition recurses on both partitions regardless of size, so a bad split can nest n levels deep; the refined version recurses only into the smaller partition.

text: An array-based merge uses one array of double length, so it needs storage for twice the item count: its two ends act as destinations and its two halves as sources.
The balanced variant uses 2N files: N inputs and N outputs that swap roles after each pass.
why: Alternating input and output files lets each pass feed the next, so only a fixed set of 2N files is needed regardless of how many passes run.

text: Sorting methods divide into internal sorting, on arrays in fast random-access store, and external sorting, on sequential files on disks and tapes.
why: Arrays live in fast random-access memory while files sit on slower sequential devices, so the access pattern of each class demands different algorithms.

text: Distribution alternates runs across output files without checking whether two runs on one file could merge, so consecutive runs there can silently change the run count.
when: When distributing runs across several output files in a multiway merge sort without checking run boundaries.
why: Two consecutive runs landing on the same file merge automatically, so the actual run counts on each file can differ from what the distribution assumed.

text: Index handling for direction and destination in an array merge adds considerable administrative overhead.
why: Tracking which end is the destination and flipping roles each pass requires extra index bookkeeping that a single doubled array must still manage.

text: A heavy item out of place sinks to its position in one pass, but a light item out of place rises only one step per pass.
when: When a single misplaced item sits out of place in an otherwise sorted array during bubble passes.
why: the pass direction moves items at different speeds

text: Exchanges cost more than comparisons, so bubblesort's improvements help less than intuition suggests.
why: Bubblesort improvements only cut redundant comparisons, while exchanges, which dominate cost, stay unchanged, so the gains are smaller than expected.

text: Sorted or nearly sorted input tends toward quicksort's worst-case behavior, so test it deliberately.
Hoare's Find has order n-squared worst-case comparisons, because each partition may remove only one candidate.
why: Each partition step removes only one candidate when the split is maximally unbalanced, so the work sums to a quadratic total.

text: Combining heap run generation with polyphase merging is awkward, because both need routines called from several places.
when: When integrating heap run generation with polyphase merging.
why: Both routines are invoked from several places in each program, so combining them forces awkward restructuring of the control flow.

text: Judging heapsort on small examples misleads, since large items are sifted toward the front before reaching the far right.
why: Large items first sift toward the front before reaching the far end, which looks wasteful on small inputs but pays off as n grows.

text: Finding run ends costs extra comparisons, and sequential files expose only one element at a time, so run boundaries must be detected with a look-ahead.
when: Implementing natural merge on sequential files.
why: Sequential files expose only one element at a time, so deciding where a run ends requires comparing the current key with the next one.

text: Strict comparisons cause many needless swaps when keys are equal: a run of n identical keys causes about n/2 swaps.
when: Partitioning arrays containing many duplicate keys.
why: Strict scans stop on equal keys and swap them.

text: Choosing the first or last element as comparand makes an already sorted array the worst case, while the middle element makes it the best case.
when: Choosing a fixed comparand position in quicksort.
why: Sorted input then always splits unevenly or evenly, respectively.

text: Pushing the right partition and continuing with the left lets the stack grow to n entries on worst-case input.
when: Iterative quicksort with a stack of pending ranges.
why: Each partition leaves one element on one side, so pending work accumulates.

text: Straight insertion is unsuitable for large n, and each insertion shifts a run of items, so its move count stays quadratic.
why: Each insertion shifts all larger items one place, and across n insertions these shifts accumulate to a quadratic total.

text: Split phases only copy items and move none into order, yet they make up half the copying in a straight merge sort.
why: Splitting only redistributes items without reordering them, so its copying work contributes nothing to sortedness while still costing as much as merging.

text: Inserting keys in strictly ascending or descending order turns a plain search tree into a linked list.
why: Every new key lands as the child of the previous extreme key, so each insertion extends one chain instead of splitting the tree.

text: 1) Use a 2n-element array, a direction flag, run length 1, and a destination pointer. 2) While run length is below n, merge adjacent run pairs into the other half. 3) When one run is exhausted, copy the other's tail. 4) Double run length. 5) If the result is in the upper half, copy it down.

1) Distribute initial runs cyclically over N output files and count the runs. 2) Each pass uses L inputs if fewer than N runs remain, else N; former outputs become inputs and outputs are emptied. 3) Merge one run from each active input into the current output by repeatedly copying the smallest front key. 4) Repeat passes until a single run remains.
1) Scan from the right end toward the front, comparing each adjacent pair. 2) Swap any pair that is out of order. 3) Repeat passes until no further pass is needed.
Record whether any exchange happened in a pass, and stop when a pass makes none.
why: Passes over an already ordered array make no swaps, so a pass with no exchanges signals that sorting is finished.

text: Remember the index of the last exchange, and let later passes stop there, since everything below that index is already in order.
1) Run quicksort until partitions are shorter than a cutoff m. 2) Finish each short partition with a simple sort such as bubble sort.
when: when short segments are cheap to finish with a simple sort

text: 1) Partition the segment. 2) Handle the shorter partition with an iterative loop. 3) Handle the longer partition with a recursive call, so only one recursive call remains.
when: writing recursive quicksort

text: 1) Merge five sequences onto a sixth until the fifth is empty. 2) Merge four sequences onto the fifth, then three onto the fourth, then two onto the third. 3) Copy the first sequence onto the second.
when: cascade merge starting from a perfect distribution on five sequences

text: 1) Count comparisons and moves for each sort. 2) Measure each sort's real running time on your machine. 3) Fit coefficients that turn the counts into estimated time.
when: comparing straight sorts by running time
why: Counts of comparisons and moves must be multiplied by fitted per-operation coefficients to become estimates of real running time.

text: 1) Partition around x = a[k], giving indices i > j with items left of j at most x and items right of i at least x. 2) If j < k < i, a[k] is the answer. 3) If j < k, repeat on the upper part; if i > k, on the lower part. 4) Stop at one item.
when: finding the k-th smallest item
why: A partition places smaller values left and larger values right, so only the side holding index k needs further work.

text: 1) Write the top item to the current run. 2) Read the next input item into the top position. 3) Sift it down.
when: heap run generation
why: Each item passes through the heap like through a funnel, so the least key leaves each time.

text: 1) Fill the upper half of the heap without ordering. 2) Fill the lower half and build the heap. 3) Pass remaining input through, starting a new run when a key cannot continue the current run. 4) At end of input, flush the lower part and relocate the upper part. 5) Flush remaining items as the last run.
why: Items that cannot extend the current run are parked in the upper heap, so the lower heap can keep feeding the current run.

text: 1) Build the heap in place: from the middle index back to index 0, sift each element into place. 2) Swap the top element with the last heap element, shrink the heap by one, and sift the new top down. Repeat until one element remains.
why: Storing each extracted top element in the slot freed by the shrinking heap lets the full sort run in place.

text: 1) Call select to choose a destination. 2) Copy the next run there. 3) Repeat until the source is exhausted.

1) Each source with a positive dummy count decrements it and is skipped. 2) If no sources remain active, output a dummy run. 3) Otherwise merge one real run from the active sources, selecting the smallest front key and removing exhausted sources.
when: Each merge step of a polyphase merge at the current level.
why: Dummy counts stand in for runs that do not physically exist.

text: 1) Make the output the newest source. 2) Make the old first sequence the new output. 3) Shift the dummy counts with the sequences. 4) Recompute the coefficients one level down.
when: After finishing one level of a polyphase merge.
why: Rotation lets each finished level feed the next as a new source.

text: 1) Fix the desired final state, with all data on one sequence. 2) Work backward through the merge steps to derive the initial run count on each sequence.
when: Choosing the initial run distribution for a polyphase merge.
why: Arbitrary initial distributions can waste passes or stall the merge.

text: 1) Choose a comparand x. 2) Scan from the left for an item not less than x and from the right for an item not greater than x. 3) Swap them and continue until the scans meet.
when: Partitioning an array in quicksort.
why: Each stop-and-swap moves a misplaced item from each side to the other, so both halves end up correctly bounded.

text: 1) Partition the range around a comparand. 2) Recursively sort the left side if it has more than one element. 3) Recursively sort the right side likewise.
when: Implementing quicksort recursively.

text: 1) Write the current item to the destination. 2) Read the next key from the source. 3) Set the end-of-run flag if the source is exhausted or its next key is smaller than the item just written.
when: Copying items from a run-aware source to a destination.
why: A smaller next key means the current run has ended.

text: 1) For each i from 1 to n-1, take x = a[i]. 2) While the element left of x is larger than x, shift that element one place right. 3) Place x in the vacated position.
1) Merge single items into ordered pairs. 2) Merge pairs into ordered quadruples, then quadruples into octets. 3) Keep doubling run length until the whole sequence is ordered.
why: Merging is a simpler operation than sorting, so building order from merges of ordered pieces is easier to implement.

text: 1) For pass i, scan a[i] through a[n-1] to find the index k of the smallest key. 2) Swap a[i] with a[k]. 3) Repeat for the next i.
why: Each pass examines all remaining items, so the least key is known before it is placed, fixing one position at a time.

text: 1) Split the task for m elements into m subtasks. 2) In each subtask, swap one element into the last position. 3) Generate the permutations of the remaining m-1 elements. 4) Pass each complete permutation to a parameter procedure.
when: Generating all n! permutations without an extra array.

text: 1) Sort a linked list into increasing order by an integer key. 2) Reverse the sorted list with a separate procedure that reverses its node order.
Take the simpler flat partition option when it is adequate.
why: Simpler structures take less effort to understand and build, and memory stays fixed because adding objects never requires creating new partitions.

text: Keep the scanning pointer forward-only when the data come from buffered secondary storage.
when: When the text is streamed from external storage, where rewinding is expensive
why: Backing up the pointer would disturb sequential access to buffered data.

text: To compare structured keys, search for the first pair of unequal components. If no such pair exists, the keys are equal.
when: When the keys are composite values such as character arrays
why: A match needs every component to agree, so the comparison reduces to finding one component that disagrees.

text: When sorting arrays, permute items in place. Methods that copy items into a second result array are of minor interest, since storage economy is the predominant requirement.
when: sorting arrays
why: Storage economy is the main requirement for array sorts, so methods that copy items into a second array matter little.

text: Swap the two destination ends after each merged group, so that output fills both ends evenly.
when: merging into an array in both directions
why: Alternating the destination keeps both output sequences equally loaded.

text: Choose the hybrid cutoff m by timing the hybrid for several values and keeping the one with the least total time.
Let a bubble sort finishing a segment of length m sweep exactly m-1 times instead of testing for a final sorted pass.
when: bubble sort as the finishing step of a hybrid
why: Since the optimal cutoff is small, a separate final pass that only confirms sortedness is likely not worth its cost.

text: Test quicksort on constructed worst-case and best-case permutations of the keys 1 to n to see how it behaves at the extremes.
State the invariant that holds after each repetition of a straight sort, and use it to reason about correctness.
Track run boundaries during heap run generation so the output switches to a new run at the right time.

why: The heap starts empty, is partly filled near the end, and finally empties.

when: Writing the control loop of a polyphase merge.
why: Further merges may still involve dummy runs on a sequence that already reached end of file.

text: Push the longer partition onto the stack and continue directly with the shorter one; the stack depth is then at most about log n.
when: Implementing iterative quicksort with an explicit stack.
why: Work on the smaller side is finished quickly and the pending stack stays shallow.

text: A run-aware file reader should track the next key and an end-of-run flag alongside the end-of-file indicator.
when: Designing file access for natural merge sort.
why: Merge code can then handle runs without low-level buffering details.

text: Keeping follow-on counts sorted speeds prediction but slows registration; leave them unsorted because registration happens far more often.
why: Registration runs on every action, while prediction runs less often.

text: Straight sorting methods have short programs and are faster for small n, but must not be used for large n. Advanced methods need fewer operations, but each operation is more complex.
when: choosing a sorting method by input size
why: Advanced methods' operations are more intricate in detail, which offsets their smaller operation count when n is small.

text: Cascade merge can beat polyphase despite leaving sequences idle and using plain copy steps.
when: very large files with six or more sequences

text: Heap run generation with polyphase merging handles huge run counts, but its program is far more complex than simple array sorts of the same task.
why: A heap of size m lengthens the initial runs by an expected factor of m, so few passes can cover a huge number of runs.

text: Fusing the split and merge phases of straight merging halves the copying, at the cost of a fourth tape.
why: Splitting only copies items without permuting them, so merging straight into the redistribution removes that work.

text: Straight selection does the same number of comparisons on easy and hard inputs, so it adapts to input order far less than insertion.
why: its comparison count depends only on n

text: A dummy run is a hypothetical empty run that fills the gap when real run counts do not form a perfect sum.
when: polyphase distribution with imperfect run counts

text: The median is the item that is no larger than half the items and no smaller than the other half.
Natural merge sort ignores fixed run lengths and merges the ordered subsequences already present in the input, called runs, so it exploits partial order.
An iterative quicksort replaces recursion with an explicit stack of pending index pairs (low and high), useful where recursion is unavailable.
when: Implementing quicksort in a language without recursion.

text: Shakersort is an improved bubblesort that alternates the direction of successive passes, carrying heavy items right and light items left.
Shellsort runs insertion sort over chains of elements a fixed gap apart, then repeats with smaller gaps until the gap is 1.
Merging combines two or more ordered sequences into one ordered sequence by repeatedly choosing among the currently accessible front items.
A pass is the smallest repeated subprocess of a merge sort and consists of a split phase and a merge phase, each one operation over all the data.
The best Shellsort gap sequence is unknown, and its analysis is mathematically hard, so many cost questions remain open.
A pigeonhole sort could reduce the total cost of position-sorted lookup further, to O(n).
Straight merge sort makes fewer key comparisons than item moves, because copying a run's tail needs no comparisons.
Picking the exact median is rare, with probability 1/n, but a random comparand is only a factor 2 ln 2 worse than the ideal on average.
when: Choosing a comparand for quicksort.

text: Alternating pass direction does not reduce the number of exchanges a bubble-type sort performs.
Almost-sorted input is rare in practice.
Shellsort was introduced in 1959 as a refinement of straight insertion.
In the worst case, the final gap-1 pass does all the sorting work.
A sequence that is already k-sorted stays k-sorted after an i-sort, so earlier ordering is preserved.
At large n, quadratic methods such as straight insertion fall far behind n·log(n) methods on reverse-ordered input.
when: large n, reverse-ordered input

text: After pass i, the front of the array holds the i+1 smallest items in sorted order.
Avoid straight merge sort for data in main store: it needs room for 2n items and carries high index overhead, so it is rarely used on arrays there.
when: data in main store
why: It needs storage for twice as many items and carries heavy index bookkeeping, which makes it poor for data already in main memory.

text: Choose gap increments that are not multiples of each other, so chains interact as often as possible; shared factors keep chains independent and waste passes.
why: Shared factors make a pass merge chains that never interacted before; avoiding them lets chains interact more often.

text: Use shakersort only for nearly sorted items; on most inputs it is slower than straight insertion and selection, except already sorted arrays.
when: nearly sorted items
why: Exchanges cost more than key comparisons, so cutting redundant checks gains little against insertion and selection.

text: A plain linear search for the smallest front key is sufficient when the number of files is small, because selection is the most frequently executed step.
when: number of merge files is modest
why: selection dominates run time

text: Use multiway merging when more files are available, because it needs fewer passes.
Spread dummy runs as evenly as possible over the N-1 sequences, so that as many merges as possible involve real runs.
Natural merge is worth using when the input is already partly ordered, because it needs fewer passes than straight merging.
when: Choosing a merge sort variant for partly sorted input.
why: Existing runs reduce the number of passes required.

text: Shellsort is reasonable for moderate n, while better algorithms exist for large inputs.
when: moderate n

text: Ordered insertion pays off only when many distinct words occur compared to their total number of occurrences.
why: On insertion of a new word, an ordered list is searched only halfway on average.

text: Use tree sort when the same structure must support both searching and sorting; for ordering alone, faster dedicated sorting methods exist.
when: Choosing a sorting method
why: A search tree serves lookups and ordering at once, but pure sorting has better methods

text: Each step needs a predecessor-free item; if none exists, a loop exists, no linear order is valid, so the sort must detect it, not emit a wrong order.
why: Acyclicity, guaranteed by partial-order axioms, is exactly what makes a linear arrangement possible.

text: A merge ignores any source holding a dummy run; if every source holds a dummy, the output receives a dummy run.
A look-ahead buffer holds the next unread element of a sequential file, letting a program peek at the upcoming key to detect run boundaries.
when: Merging or scanning runs from a sequential file.
why: Sequential files expose only one element at a time.

text: Alternating pass direction removes the asymmetry of plain bubblesort, so a single misplaced light item no longer needs one pass per step to reach its place.
when: When a single misplaced item lies in the light end of an otherwise sorted array.
why: Plain passes sweep one way, so a light item crawls one step per pass while a heavy one sifts far.

text: Earlier passes with larger gaps leave the data partly ordered, so later passes with smaller gaps merge already sorted chains and finish quickly.
why: Every chain sort is either small or runs on nearly sorted data, so little rearranging remains.

text: Merge output alternates between two destinations that serve directly as the sources of the next pass, so no separate split phase is needed.
why: Split phases never permute items and account for half the copying, so folding them into the merge removes that wasted work.

text: In a selection pass the running minimum changes with probability 1/i, so the expected number of assignments is the harmonic number H(n-1).
why: Each element becomes the new running minimum only if it is smaller than all earlier ones, which has chance 1/i.

text: Tree sort avoids shifting elements as insertion sort does, because inserting into a search tree only changes links.
when: Comparing tree sort with array insertion sort
why: Links are rewired locally instead of moving stored components

text: Straight methods grow quadratically; selection and exchange sorts make exactly (n²-n)/2 comparisons, whatever the initial order.
why: The selection scan inspects every remaining element on each pass, whatever the data order.

text: Distributing runs over N files and merging N ways needs about log base N of n passes, since each pass divides the number of runs by N.
Each pass copies all n items, so the worst-case total is n·log base N of n copy operations.
why: A pass by definition copies the whole data set, so total effort scales with the number of passes.

text: Straight merge sort needs about log n passes, since run length doubles each pass until it exceeds n.
why: Each pass doubles the subsequence length, and sorting stops once that length exceeds n.

text: Straight merge sort makes about n log n item moves, because each pass copies all n items once.
Natural merge sort needs at most about n log n moves in the worst case, and fewer on average; comparisons increase because run ends require consecutive key comparisons.
when: Estimating natural merge sort cost on n items.
why: Finding run boundaries requires comparing each key with its successor.

text: Partitioning n items makes exactly n comparisons.
when: When partitioning uses two inward scans that exchange items until they meet.
why: Each item is compared once during the two scans.

text: Each extraction from a selection tree takes about log n comparisons, so the selection phase costs about n log n.
when: Estimating tree sort cost.
why: Only the path from the root to the removed key is recomputed.

text: Shakersort makes n-1 comparisons in its best case.
when: input already sorted

text: The gap sequence 1, 4, 13, 40, 121, where each gap is three times the next plus one, is considered reasonable.
why: Increments that are not multiples of each other let chains interact in every pass, rather than combining chains that never interacted.

text: The gap sequence 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, where each gap is twice the next plus one, gives effort proportional to n^1.2.
Shellsort's operation count is about c·n^1.2, while Heapsort and Quicksort are about c·n·log(n), with c a system-dependent constant.
Straight selection makes at least 3(n-1) moves on ordered input and at most n²/4 + 3(n-1) on reverse-ordered input.
For large n, expected assignments in straight selection come to about n*(ln(n) + 0.577), where 0.577 is a fixed mathematical constant (about 0.5772).
when: large n
why: Each element is the new minimum with probability 1/k, so a pass's expected assignments sum to a harmonic number, which for large n approximates a logarithm plus the same fixed 0.577 constant.

text: Merging two pages that are both at minimum size yields 2n-1 items, which reverses a split.
when: When the sibling page is already at minimum size, so no item can be borrowed from it.
why: Balancing is impossible then, so the combined items plus the ancestor's middle key form one page, the exact inverse of a split.

text: A well-coded tree sort can nearly match the speed of the best array sorting methods.
when: Comparing sorting implementations
why: Using a tree instead of an array removes the need to shift the components above the insertion point.

text: Moves usually cost far more than key comparisons, so saving comparisons yields modest gain; on peripheral storage moves outweigh comparisons by several orders of magnitude, so comparison counts mislead.
when: When data is moved on peripheral storage devices.
why: Moving keys along with their attached data is generally much more expensive than comparing keys, so saving comparisons helps only modestly.

text: Plain minimax on merging branches searches the same subtree once per merge, duplicating work and wasting time.
when: Without a transposition table.
why: Merged paths reach identical positions that get searched again.

text: A multiway merge program is not a small generalization of a two-way merge program; its structure differs throughout, including tracking which inputs remain active.
when: When merging several inputs whose run counts need not be equal.
why: Exhausting one input no longer ends the merge, so the set of still-active inputs must be tracked.

text: A partition routine that takes the middle element as pivot can fail on particular inputs.
Alternately distributing runs to two files can accidentally join two runs when the next run's first key exceeds the current run's last key, which changes the run counts per file.
when: Natural merge sort distributes runs alternately onto two auxiliary files.
why: A joined run reduces the count on one file, so counts become unequal.

text: Straight selection remains quadratic in comparisons, so it is practical only for small n.
why: The comparison count is fixed at n(n-1)/2 whatever the input order, since the algorithm always scans the remaining array.

text: 1) Merge runs from both inputs while both have data. 2) When one input is exhausted, copy all remaining items of the other input to the output in one pass; stopping early loses that tail.
when: Natural merge where input run counts may be unequal.
why: Copying the whole tail, not at most one run, prevents data loss and keeps worst-case performance unchanged.

text: 1) Distribute runs alternately from the main file to two auxiliary files. 2) Merge corresponding runs from the two auxiliary files back into the main file. 3) Repeat until the main file holds a single run.
when: Running natural merge sort on a sequential file.

text: 1) Generate pseudo-random integer input. 2) Write the result as text with run boundaries marked. 3) Report the item and run counts to verify the merge.
when: Testing a natural merge implementation.
why: Visible boundaries and counts reveal lost or joined runs.

text: 1) Compare keys in pairs. 2) Compare the winners in pairs, and repeat until one winner remains. The root then holds the least key, using n-1 comparisons in total.
when: Building a selection tree to find the minimum.
why: Retaining comparison outcomes avoids rescanning all keys.

text: 1) Follow the path from the root to the least key and remove it. 2) Refill each vacated slot with the winner of the alternative branch, or leave a hole at the bottom. 3) The next minimum then appears at the root.
when: Extracting keys in order from a selection tree.
why: Each extraction only retraces one path of about log(n) levels, so n extractions cost roughly n log(n).

text: 1) Run a right-to-left pass that bubbles the least item leftward, then set the left bound just past the last exchange. 2) Run a left-to-right pass that bubbles the largest item rightward, then set the right bound just before the last exchange. 3) Repeat rounds until the left bound exceeds the right bound.
1) Choose a decreasing sequence of gaps whose last value is 1. 2) For each gap h, insertion-sort each chain of elements h positions apart. 3) Finish with gap 1.
why: The final gap-1 pass alone can finish whatever order the earlier passes left, so it guarantees a sorted result.

text: 1) After each pass, swap the source and destination roles by flipping a direction flag. 2) Double the run length. 3) Start the next pass.
why: Since both sides share one doubled array, a flag is needed to record which end currently serves as the source.

text: 1) Insert all items into a search tree. 2) Scan the tree in order, emitting items as they are visited.
when: Sorting items with a binary search tree
why: In-order traversal of a search tree yields keys in sorted order

text: Within a merge, while both sources have items, compare their current heads, copy the smaller item, and advance that source and the destination.
Stop the outer loop when run length is at least n, rather than testing for equality.
why: sizes that are not powers of two never hit run length exactly n

text: Build a natural merge that reads runs from both ends of a double-length array inward, then compare its speed with the sequence-based natural merge.
Any correctness argument for a merge over runs must hold for arbitrary run counts per input, not only for equal counts.
when: Proving or testing a natural merge sort.
why: Run counts can become unequal after distribution.

text: An output file should remember the last item written, so distribution can detect when writing would unintentionally join two runs.
when: Distributing runs to output files during natural merge.
why: Joining runs silently changes run counts.

text: Any decreasing gap sequence ending in 1 produces a correct Shellsort.
why: The final unit-gap pass alone can finish whatever order the earlier passes left, so it guarantees a sorted result.

text: Switch the destination after each completed run, where run length starts at one and doubles before each pass, so both destinations fill evenly.
why: Alternating the destination after each run spreads merged items evenly across both destination sequences.

text: Represent the chosen objects as a set of indices, and carry the current total weight and the value still achievable as recursion parameters.
When a set is not partially ordered, a topological sort should report a loop of elements instead of only a failure message.
when: When the input pairs contain a cycle, so the set is not partially ordered.
why: A bare failure message is often unhelpful, while a loop of elements shows exactly where the cycle lies.

text: Count leaders during input and decrement the count on each output; if any remain at the end, the ordering relation is not a partial order.
when: Finishing a topological sort
why: Leftover items cannot be placed without a predecessor cycle

text: Send equal keys down the same branch as greater keys, so equal items keep their insertion order in an in-order scan.
when: Sorting with duplicate keys in a search tree
why: Consistent handling of equal keys preserves their original relative order

text: When a tree is used for sorting, items with duplicate keys must still be inserted, not merely counted, or they will be lost from the output.
when: Sorting data with repeated keys via a search tree
why: Sorting must output every item, not one entry per key

text: As the finishing step of a hybrid, selection sort costs more index handling than bubble sort, which sweeps the whole segment.
why: Selection cannot sweep across the whole array in one pass, so it does more index bookkeeping than a bubble sweep.

text: Sorting the whole list and selecting the k-th element costs roughly n log n, whereas partition-based selection averages linear time yet degrades to quadratic in the worst case.
when: Finding a median or another quantile without sorting all the candidates first
why: Each partition step roughly halves the set holding the target, so total comparisons sum to about 2n.

text: Natural merge can either correct the distribution so run counts differ by at most one, or accept unequal counts and fix the merge to handle them. Each choice has a cost.
when: Fixing a natural merge bug caused by unequal run distribution.
why: Correcting distribution keeps the merge simple; fixing the merge tolerates arbitrary counts.

text: A naive selection tree for n items needs 2n-1 storage units, and holes left by extractions cause needless comparisons; the goal is n items in n units without holes.
when: Choosing between tree-based selection sorts.
why: Extra storage and holes both add cost; heapsort meets both goals.

text: Straight selection makes far fewer moves than straight insertion, but insertion is faster on sorted or nearly sorted input.
Sierpinski curves are closed and free of crossovers, so their base is a non-empty open curve whose four outer corner links are drawn explicitly.
Four pattern procedures differ only by 90-degree rotation; each combines four smaller patterns with explicit connecting lines, some drawn at double length.
why: The connecting lines lie outside the recursion pattern itself, so they must be added explicitly.

text: 1) For each order from 1 to n, halve the unit length. 2) Move the starting point to the middle of the smaller square. 3) Draw that order's curve, superimposed on the previous ones.
when: Drawing orders 1 through n on one figure.

text: 1) Set the starting coordinates. 2) Compute the unit length from the size of the plane. 3) Invoke the base pattern.
Pairwise checks are fastest for small groups, but checking every unit against all others each frame scales with the square of the count; use spatial structures once hundreds clash.
when: large numbers of characters or units needing neighbor queries, such as large battles with frequent collisions
why: Pairwise cost grows quadratically with object count.

text: Identifiers in programs and words in text tend to cluster, so a key just accessed is likely to be requested again soon.
when: Input data shows clustering of repeated keys
why: Accesses are correlated in time rather than spread evenly over the keys

text: A collision detector takes a start position and movement amount, returning the first collision along that move with its position and surface normal, ignoring anything beyond the movement amount.
Adaptive partitions such as BSPs and k-d trees choose split planes so each side holds about the same number of objects.
A bounding volume hierarchy is an adaptive partition tuned to a specific set of objects.
An octree is the three-dimensional version of a quadtree, splitting a volume into eight cubes.
A spatial partition keeps objects arranged by position, letting the game locate objects at or near a point quickly.
A location query asks which objects are at or near a given position.
Locality means a small change to a genotype causes, on average, a small change in the phenotype and in fitness.
Most tactical analysis implementations use tile grids, a convention inherited from real-time strategy games.
In tile-based worlds, stored per-radius tile patterns laid over the character's tile can quickly list the tiles to check for waypoints.
when: Worlds built on a tile grid
why: Precomputed patterns avoid computing distances for every tile

text: Predicting collisions for AI queries is hard when geometry is processed on dedicated graphics hardware.
With good pruning, a binary space partition tree can reduce neighbor search to logarithmic time in the number of potential targets.
when: Good pruning is achieved

text: Connection costs between regions are measured between representative points, usually region centres, so adjacent regions can still have a sizeable connection cost.
when: Graphs built from divided regions.
why: A large room or long corridor makes centre-to-centre distance large.

text: Units in adjacent cells can still be within attack range, so neighboring cells must be checked as well as the unit's own cell.
when: attack range is involved

text: Quadtree split boundaries always fall at the halfway points of the square being divided.
Spatial partitions cut linear or quadratic searches down, and their payoff grows as object counts rise.
Spatial partitions are common for moving objects and for static art and geometry; large games often run several partitions for different content types.
The common spatial structures are the grid, quadtree, BSP, k-d tree, and bounding volume hierarchy.
Quadtrees and octrees are tries.
After partitioning, keys left of the split are at most x and keys right of it are at least x, with a possibly empty middle zone of keys equal to x.
Use flat partitions or fixed grids when objects are spread fairly evenly and simplicity or fixed memory footprint matters; choose hierarchical when space is largely empty or objects clump together.
Use fixed partitions when objects are added and moved constantly; use adaptive partitions when the set is mostly static and consistent performance matters.
when: When units cluster in one area, so a fixed grid puts most of them in a single cell
why: Building adaptive partitions from a complete object set is more efficient.

text: Manual division often gives the best results because it can be tuned per level, and automatic techniques are needed when the graph must be built without hand work.
when: Choosing between hand-built and generated pathfinding graphs.
why: Hand tuning captures level-specific detail that automation misses.

text: Use a spatial partition when object counts are large and location queries are frequent enough to hurt performance.
why: The structure exists to cut linear or quadratic location work down to something cheaper.

text: Knowing the one-dimensional relative of a spatial structure helps judge whether it fits a problem.
why: Each spatial structure extends a familiar one-dimensional structure into more dimensions.

text: Clustered objects overload a few fixed partitions, wasting memory on empty areas and degrading searches back toward O(n²) behavior.
when: objects unevenly distributed in space
why: Fixed boundaries do not adjust to where objects are.

text: Regular tile connections can be computed when the pathfinder requests neighbours instead of being stored in advance, and blocked tiles return no connections.
when: Generating tile graphs at run time.
why: Regular adjacency is predictable, so it need not be stored.

text: Moving one object in an adaptive partition can shift boundaries and force many other objects to change partitions, similar to rebalancing a tree.
when: When partition boundaries depend on the set of objects
why: Shifting boundaries cascade, much like balanced search trees where one insertion forces many nodes to move.

text: Removing an object can collapse subdivisions once the parent's total count falls below the threshold.
Clustered objects stay balanced in a quadtree because no square holds more than the fixed maximum count.
when: When objects are heavily clustered together
why: Each square is capped at a fixed maximum, so no partition grows overfull.

text: Without locality, every search method performs no better than random search.
when: When a representation has no locality
why: Search depends on small genotype changes causing small fitness changes to guide it.

text: When tree nodes sit on disk, each pointer step can cost a disk access, so search cost is driven by the number of accesses rather than by comparisons.
when: Tree is stored on secondary storage
why: Disk access latency is far larger than the cost of an in-memory comparison

text: Multi-resolution tile maps, quadtrees and octrees, and binary space partition trees are spatial structures that find nearby waypoints or objects quickly; graphics and physics engines use them.
when: When a level has a few hundred characters rather than a small number
why: Storing objects spatially makes nearby-object queries relatively easy.

text: A fixed grid overlays the play area with equal square cells and stores each unit in the cell containing its position, with each cell heading a doubly linked list of its units.
why: Splits the battlefield into smaller independent groups so units only check neighbors in the same cell.

text: A quadtree begins as a single square spanning the whole space, then divides any overfull square into four equal quadrants, recursively.
why: Only overcrowded squares are subdivided further, so the partitioning adapts to where objects are.

text: A spatial partition has three parts: a position for each object, a spatial structure that stores objects, and an update step when positions change.
A partially blocked tile can make the graph invalid depending on the shape of the blockage, while fully blocked or fully empty tiles are safe.
when: Marking obstacles on a tile graph.
why: Partial blockage may leave some points in the tile unreachable from neighbours.

text: Very small cells make the outer loop over all cells expensive, cancelling the gain from short per-cell lists.
when: cells made very small
why: The savings from shorter inner lists must outweigh the outer loop over cells, which grows as cells shrink.

text: Scanning a sparse grid for its few occupied cells wastes time; a separate object collection avoids that scan.
when: grid mostly empty
why: Walking every empty cell to find the occupied ones wastes time; a separate object list avoids that.

text: 1) Start with long jumps. 2) While improvement continues, grow jump length somewhat. 3) When improvement stops, assume overshoot and reduce jump length. Can be combined with momentum or used alone.
when: When fixed-size steps are large enough that the search may keep overshooting the best value.
why: Large steps can leap over the optimum repeatedly, so shrinking them later is what lets the search actually land on it.

text: 1) Give each game state a fixed block of rows, such as four rows per state. 2) Have each cell refer to the matching cells in the block directly above. 3) Separate blocks with a horizontal border.
when: A single time step's state is too wide for one row
why: Blocks make successive game states easy to compare and read.

text: 1) Find the square containing the object and insert it there. 2) If its count exceeds the maximum, split it into four equal squares. 3) Move its objects into the matching squares. 4) Repeat step 2 for any overfull child square.
why: Only overfull squares are split, so the partitioning adapts to where objects cluster while its boundaries stay fixed.

text: 1) Remove the object from its current square. 2) Add it at its new position. Both steps are quick, so moving an object is cheap.
why: Adding one object triggers at most one subdivision, so the work per move stays bounded by the maximum count.

text: 1) Count the access frequency of each key. 2) Reinsert the keys in decreasing order of access count. 3) Compare the resulting average path length with that of an optimal tree.
when: When the tree is reorganized at set time intervals from measured access counts.

text: Limit nearest-point search with spatial partitioning such as quad-tree, octree, BSP, or multiresolution map; test only nearby waypoint pairs supplied by the structure or grid for a large speed-up.
when: large numbers of domains
why: Searching only nearby points avoids checking every domain.

text: When an object moves, update the spatial structure so it can still be found by location; otherwise it stays in a stale cell and nearby objects stop finding it.
Characters must switch to the new room's event manager each time they change rooms.
when: characters change rooms
why: alerts arrive solely from the manager of the room they occupy

text: Use the standard collections of your language instead of raw linked lists in production grid code.
Check four of the eight neighboring cells so every adjacent pair of units is considered exactly once.
why: Checking all eight neighbours would register the attack between each adjacent pair twice, once from each side.

text: One ring of neighboring cells suffices only when the attack distance is smaller than a cell; longer ranges require several rings.
when: attack ranges relative to cell size

text: Interpolate terrain heights with a nonlinear slope function rather than linear weights, to get rounded peaks and gradual slopes instead of sharp straight ones.
when: Smoothing terrain between lattice points
why: Mountains commonly rise in an S-curve, starting gently, steepening, then levelling off, which linear weighting cannot produce.

text: Exclude an object only if the value still achievable without it exceeds the best value found so far; otherwise prune that branch.
when: When deciding whether to exclude an object from a weight-limited value selection.

text: To make a dynamic tree disk-resident, change only its pointers so they hold disk addresses instead of main-store addresses.
when: Converting an in-memory tree to secondary storage
why: Pointers are the only part that refers to node location

text: Fixed (flat) partitions give constant, predictable memory and cheap insertion and movement; adaptive (hierarchical) partitions balance clustered or empty space better but need several layers updated when objects move.
when: When large parts of the play space are empty.
why: Adding objects in a flat layout creates no new partitions, so its memory can be fixed in advance.

text: Spatial partitions add update cost, code complexity, and memory overhead, which must be outweighed by search savings; moving objects must be reorganized inside the structure.
when: When location queries are frequent enough that search performance suffers.
why: Organizing objects by position means each move must re-index them, much like a hash table whose keys keep changing.

text: Small clusters give accurate estimates but produce a large table and long preprocessing; large clusters give little gain over a simpler heuristic.
when: When choosing cluster size for a cluster-based pathfinding heuristic.

text: Restricting lower searches to high-level groups is much faster but can miss the best route. Incremental planning avoids this and costs nothing for sections never needed.
when: choosing between full-plan exclusion and section-by-section planning
why: exclusion never examines nodes outside the chosen groups

text: A pairing of n men with n women is stable when no unmatched man and woman would each rather be with the other than with their current partner.
Generating candidates in a fixed systematic order makes each candidate appear once, so every node of the search tree is visited exactly once.
Plain backtracking reports mirror and rotated placements as separate solutions; symmetry removal must be added explicitly, as the search does not recognize symmetry.
when: Counting distinct solutions of a board placement problem.
why: The search does not recognize board symmetries.

text: 1) Restrict the search for the first column to about half of its rows. 2) Compute reflections and the centre-point image of each solution. 3) Keep only one representative of each symmetry class.
when: Counting essentially different solutions of a symmetric board problem.
why: Reflected and centre-point images of a valid placement are also valid, so counting them separately duplicates the same arrangement.

text: 1) Assume the tentative pairing is stable. 2) Scan the women the man ranks above his candidate, checking whether any prefers him to her current partner. 3) Scan the men the candidate ranks above her partner, checking whether any prefers her to his current partner. 4) Any success means instability.
when: checking whether a tentative pairing keeps a stable matching
why: A preferred woman who was still single would already have accepted him, so only married candidates can reveal instability.

text: To judge a sort's stability, check whether any step can move one item past another item with an equal key.
Simulated annealing is named after metal cooling: slow cooling settles into a low-energy state, while rapid cooling leaves defects.
Cascading elitism is a multistage selection scheme resembling a mu+lambda evolution strategy, with a separate selection stage per objective so each receives suitable selection pressure.
Use a lower alpha when transitions are highly random, where rewards or resulting states vary widely each time.
when: Transitions are noisy.
why: A low alpha averages out random variation instead of overwriting stored values.

text: Use a higher alpha when only a few iterations are allowed, so values change enough to be useful.
when: Training budget is small.
why: Few updates leave little time for values to converge at a low rate.

text: Annealing adds a shrinking random term to hill descent, so early search accepts poor moves while later search becomes predictable.
why: Gradually lowering randomness lets the search settle into a low-energy state, much as slow cooling lets metal reach its lowest energy setup.

text: A worse neighbour is accepted with probability proportional to e^(-E/T), where E is the score increase and T is the current temperature.
when: When a neighbouring value has a worse score than the current one.
why: T stands for the simulation's randomness level, so the chance of accepting a worse move depends on how much randomness is allowed.

text: Each annealing step costs O(n) time and O(1) memory, where n is the number of parameters.

1) Record the starting score. 2) For each parameter, try an up and a down tweak. 3) Accept any improvement. 4) Otherwise accept a worse value probabilistically. 5) Reset rejected parameters. 6) Return the originals if nothing was accepted.
why: The temperature-scaled random term added to each trial score lets a worse value sometimes come out ahead.

text: 1) Begin alpha near 0.7 so values change quickly while little is known. 2) Reduce alpha gradually toward about 0.1 so values gained later are protected.
when: Training Q-learning over many iterations.
why: Early learning needs fast change, while later learning needs stability.

text: The alignment of a pattern in the text is the text index minus the pattern index.
In Knuth-Morris-Pratt search, a shift value of minus one means the pattern moves entirely past the current text position.
A pattern matches at start position i when pattern element j equals text element i+j for every j in the pattern.
The outer hash table is keyed by window, and each entry holds a follow-on count table plus the total count of times that window was seen.
Transforming each element of a character sequence transforms the whole text, so per-element routines can work on full text.
when: When a data set can be treated as a string of characters
why: Applying one identical function to each element yields the sequence of results, so per-element routines handle the whole text.

text: Each successive column cycles through its values more slowly than the one before, so combined columns enumerate every combination.
when: Building outcome columns from a single row index.

text: A hierarchical N-gram costs O(n) memory and O(n) time, where n is the highest N-gram size used.
With well-filled hash tables, registering an action takes constant time, while predicting takes time linear in the number of possible actions.
when: When the hash tables are not full
why: Hash assignment and retrieval then take constant time, so each registration is a single step.

text: Memory use for an N-gram predictor grows with the product of the window length N and the number of possible actions.
Boyer-Moore needs about N/M comparisons in its luckiest case and substantially fewer than N in nearly all other cases, for text length N and pattern length M.
when: When every final pattern character meets an unequal text character right away

text: 1) Repeatedly take the remainder after dividing by ten and divide by ten, pushing each remainder into a temporary array. 2) Pop the digits from the array and write them in that order.
when: When writing a number out as decimal digits
why: Remainders yield the least significant digit first, so writing digits directly as they are generated emits them in reverse order; the stack reverses them back.

text: 1) Start a streak counter at 1 for the first result. 2) For each later result, add 1 to the previous counter if it matches the prior result, otherwise reset it to 1. 3) Take the maximum counter in the row.
when: finding the longest run of identical results in a sequence

text: 1) Compare the pattern from its right end against the text. 2) On a mismatch, shift the pattern by the table value of the aligned text character. 3) A match is found when the pattern index reaches zero; failure occurs when the text index passes the end.

1) For each character, record the distance from the pattern end to its rightmost occurrence, excluding the last position. 2) Give characters absent from the pattern a shift equal to the full pattern length.
when: Precomputing the shift table for string search.

text: 1) Set the value to zero. 2) While the next character is a digit, multiply the value by ten and add that digit. 3) Stop at the first non-digit.
when: When a sequence of decimal digits is read and converted to a numeric value
why: Each digit read multiplies the running value by ten and adds it, so the number builds up from its leading digit.

text: 1) Search the list for the word. 2) If found, increment its count. 3) If not found, insert the word.
when: When the text has been tokenized and each word encoded as an integer

text: During string search, never move the text pointer backward; after a mismatch, shift only the pattern.
when: searching a text with a precomputed shift table
why: Previous comparisons already reveal the text characters, so moving back would discard that information.

text: On a mismatch, choose the largest shift that keeps the matched part consistent and makes the next compared pattern character differ from the one that just mismatched.
when: after a partial match fails
why: The largest consistent shift skips the most positions, and a differing character avoids a guaranteed failing comparison.

text: Keep a pointer to the last item of each occurrence list and append there, so line numbers stay in ascending order during scanning.
when: When line numbers must print sorted low to high in the cross-reference index.
why: avoids sorting each list separately

text: Attributes with more than two distinct regions, such as hurt versus almost dead, can be split by several thresholds, but game trees usually reach the same effect through repeated binary splits on one attribute.
A split threshold is local to a node, so the same attribute may split at different values in different branches.
when: When a continuous attribute is split into two categories by a threshold
why: deeper nodes have smaller example sets

text: Running one pass per frame while reusing values from earlier frames is common, but fast-moving units can leave stale blur behind.
when: When fast-moving characters move across the map

text: Generalizations of binary search trees to higher dimensions include BSP trees, k-d trees and bounding volume hierarchies.
An AVL tree is a binary search tree in which, at every node, the heights of the two subtrees differ by at most one.
A node's balance factor equals its right subtree's height minus its left subtree's height, and is always -1, 0 or +1.
In a B-tree of order n, each page except the root holds between n and 2n items.
Underflow occurs when a page holds fewer than n items after a removal.
A binary B-tree, also called a 2-3 tree, is an order-1 B-tree kept entirely in main store, whose nodes hold one or two items.
Preorder visits root, left, then right; inorder visits left, root, then right; postorder visits left, right, then root.
A multiway tree is a tree whose nodes may have any number of children.
An optimal search tree minimizes weighted path length among all search trees over a fixed key set, given known access frequencies.
A tree is perfectly balanced when, for every node, the counts of nodes in its two child subtrees are within one of each other.
In a binary search tree, every key in a node's left subtree is less than the node's key, and every key in its right subtree is greater.
A symmetric binary B-tree allows horizontal pointers on both left and right sides, with no two horizontal pointers consecutive on any search path.
why: Removes the left and right asymmetry of earlier binary B-trees

text: The root is at level 0, a child lies one level below its parent, and the height or depth of a tree is the maximum level of any element.
A leaf has no descendants, while an interior node has at least one; a node's degree is its number of direct descendants.
An ordered binary tree has a left and a right subtree at each node, and either subtree may be empty.
A tree whose degree is above 2 is called a multiway tree.
Child nodes can be stored as a first-child, next-sibling binary tree, allowing any number of children without variable-size arrays.
The slot assignment problem is NP-complete, so exact optimal assignment is not feasible in reasonable time and a heuristic is used.
Any logarithm base gives the same ordering of gains, so the base can be dropped when only comparing attributes.
when: only comparing gains
why: only ordering matters

text: When two structures exist, each can be optimized for its own use case.
The left-to-right horizontal distribution rule is not known to be optimal, but it works well in practice.
Locating, inserting and deleting a node in an AVL tree each cost O(log n) operations, even in the worst case.
why: the balance criterion bounds the height

text: The tallest AVL trees for a given number of nodes are built from Fibonacci trees.
A node's balance factor needs only two bits, and the speed of reading and updating these factors often decides implementation efficiency.
why: nodes are usually densely packed in memory

text: Only two imbalance configurations need separate handling: insertion into the outer subtree of the heavy child, and insertion into its inner subtree; the others follow by symmetry.
AVL rotations restore balance using only pointer changes and balance-factor updates.
All leaf pages of a B-tree lie at the same level.
A non-leaf B-tree page with m keys has m+1 children.
Reading all keys of a B-tree from left to right yields them in increasing order.
A B-tree decreases in height only when its empty root is deleted.
In the reference implementation, the main program handles a root split separately and allocates the new root.
The best page size depends on the storage and computing system, and it has been analysed theoretically.
Other proposed B-tree improvements give only marginal gains over the standard scheme.
A B-tree increases in height only when the root splits into a new root holding one item, so it grows upward from the leaves.
A node with one or two items has two or three descendants, which gives the 2-3 tree its name.
The rightmost node of a left subtree has at most one child, so it is easy to unlink; the leftmost node of the right subtree works equally well.
An inorder traversal of a binary search tree visits its keys in sorted order.
The order in which keys are inserted, rather than their values, determines the shape of an unbalanced search tree.
Removing a node's successor works by cyclically exchanging three pointers, and the removed node can be reused at the head of another list.
Binary trees suffice for pedigree relations, since no person has more than two parents.
Every subtree of an optimal search tree is itself optimal, which allows optimal trees to be built bottom-up.
Each node of a symmetric binary B-tree stores one key and two flags, one for the left pointer and one for the right pointer, marking each as horizontal or vertical.
Insertion reports each subtree as unchanged, having gained a sibling, or grown in height, and these three states drive rebalancing.
when: Inserting into a symmetric binary B-tree

text: SBB-tree insertion uses four rebalancing cases: single rotations for left-left and right-right, and double rotations for left-right and right-left.
when: Restoring the SBB-tree rule after insertion

text: Every AVL tree is also a symmetric binary B-tree, so SBB-trees form a larger class of trees.
Binary B-trees correspond canonically to red-black trees, linking the two structures.
Search trees of this kind are used in compilers and databases to organize stored objects.
Prefer repeated binary threshold splits over explicit multi-split algorithms in typical game applications, since deeper nodes place thresholds at new positions in smaller example sets.
when: Building a decision tree for game behavior.
why: Repeated splits on one attribute approximate multiple regions cheaply.

text: Use the AVL criterion when the rebalancing rule must stay simple but search paths must stay close to the perfect height.
why: A simple balance rule keeps rebalancing manageable while average search paths stay short.

text: B-trees suit large ordered indexes that need insertions and deletions when the full tree does not fit in primary storage.
when: When page accesses dominate the total search effort
why: Page-based nodes keep worst-case lookups to logarithmically many page reads and keep pages at least half full.

text: Before splitting a full page, first try balancing it with a neighbouring page; this known variation delays splitting.
Tree reorganization is more worthwhile when the ratio of accesses to insertions is high and the node count is large.
why: Random trees improve their average search path by at most about 39%, which caps worthwhile reorganization effort.

text: Use a search tree when items are retrieved by a unique key and a tree fits better than a linear list.
why: Searching follows one path from the root down to the target, so lookup is a simple loop.

text: AVL trees suit workloads where retrieval far outnumbers insertions, while SBB-trees suit moderate retrieval-to-insertion ratios.
when: Selecting a balanced search tree for a workload
why: Rebalancing cost matters more when insertions are frequent

text: Use binary trees for data with two-way branching, such as family trees, tournament histories, and arithmetic expressions with binary operators.
when: Modeling hierarchical data
why: Two children per node matches data that splits into two choices at each step

text: Changing the root decision discards the entire subtree, because every lower split was chosen on the old root's partition.
when: the best attribute at the root changes

text: Finding several thresholds at once requires computing gain for a number of scenarios that grows exponentially with the number of splits.
when: Using explicit multi-split algorithms.

text: Balanced partitions give consistent query time, which helps keep frame rate stable.
when: When steady frame timing matters more than peak query speed

text: Each real run replaces a dummy taken from the piles in a left-to-right pattern, which evens out the remaining dummies quickly.
why: Taking dummies in horizontal layers from the left shrinks piles evenly, so leftovers even out fastest.

text: At a leaf the achieved value equals the achievable value, so the current selection replaces the stored optimum only if its value is larger.
when: After all objects have been decided, at a search leaf
why: Once every object is decided, the achievable value is exact, so it can be compared with the stored best.

text: When the left subtree grows, a factor of +1 becomes 0 and growth stops, 0 becomes -1 and growth continues, and -1 triggers rebalancing; the right side is mirrored.
A purely sequential update of the whole database fetches each page exactly once.
when: When an entire B-tree database is updated in pure sequential order

text: Inserting a key into a leaf that holds fewer than 2n items changes only that page, and no split is needed.
why: Only insertion into a full page affects the tree structure; a page with room absorbs the item alone.

text: If the parent overflows after a split, it is split the same way, and this can repeat up to the root.
why: The middle key moves into the ancestor, which can overflow in turn; this upward push is the only route to extra height.

text: Recursive insertion returns a flag and any item that must move up, so each caller either absorbs that item or splits its own page.
Binary B-tree insertion has four cases, set by whether the left or right subtree grew and whether the affected key already has a sibling.
When the right subtree grows under a lone key, the key gains a sibling; when the key already has a sibling, the node splits and its middle node moves up.
why: A lone key can absorb a grown right child by turning its link horizontal; a second sibling would create a three-node page needing a split.

text: Left-subtree growth under a lone key requires a pointer rotation, because the left pointer cannot be horizontal.

Grouping subtrees into pages that are read as one unit replaces many node accesses with one page access. With 100 nodes per page, a million-item search needs about 3 page accesses instead of about 20.
when: Tree is stored on disk
why: One page read fetches many nodes at once, so the access count falls to the logarithm of N in base page size

text: A new node is placed in the empty subtree where the search ended, so the search path and the insertion point are the same.
when: Inserting into a binary search tree
why: An unsuccessful search always ends at a missing child

text: The shape of a binary search tree built by insertion depends on the order of arrival, so the same keys can produce a very different tree than a balanced one.
when: Building a search tree from a key sequence
why: Each key is placed relative to earlier keys only

text: In the worst case, finding one of N keys in a B-tree of order n needs about log base n of N page accesses, where n is the page capacity parameter.
why: Each page holds between n and 2n items, so the tree height is about log base n of N.

text: With constant-time tests and a balanced tree, the decision tree walk takes logarithmic time, O(log2 n), in the number of decision nodes.
why: Cost grows with the number of nodes visited, and a balanced tree keeps that path short.

text: Threshold splitting costs time and memory linear in the number of examples, per attribute.
For N sequences, a perfect initial distribution uses sums of N-1 down to 1 consecutive Fibonacci numbers of order N-2; for six sequences the order is four.
when: polyphase sort with N sequences

text: Distribution starts at level one; each level's dummy goal is the difference between its Fibonacci row and the previous row.
when: horizontal distribution of initial runs

text: An AVL tree with n nodes has height h satisfying log(n+1) < h < 1.4404 * log(n+2) - 0.328.
why: Balance rules keep the height within about 45 percent of a perfectly balanced tree, whatever the node count.

text: A tree reaches the perfect height exactly when its node count has the form 2^k - 1.
Empirical tests suggest AVL height stays near log n plus about 0.25; the exact expected height for random insertion orders is an unproven open problem.
when: When all permutations of the keys are equally likely to be the insertion order.

text: Rebalancing is needed on average once per two insertions, with single and double rotations about equally likely (empirical).
Because every page except the root is at least half full, B-tree storage utilization is at least 50 percent.
The maximum search path length in a binary B-tree is 2 log N.
Storage of a tree node is measured as its key words plus one word per pointer, assuming one-word pointers.
Tree cost equals the sum of each key's success frequency times its level, plus the sum of each gap's unsuccessful frequency times its external level.
why: It measures the expected searching effort, averaging over the access probabilities of keys and gaps.

text: Subtree weight w_ij equals w_i,j-1 plus a_j plus b_j, where a_j is the key's success frequency and b_j the gap's unsuccessful frequency.
Naive search over all roots costs about n cubed over six; Knuth's root bound reduces the work to order n squared.
A perfectly balanced tree of n nodes has a search depth of about log n, since every level except the lowest is filled completely.
Averaged over all insertion orders, a random binary search tree of n keys has average path length about 2 ln n, roughly 1.386 times that of a perfectly balanced tree.
when: all keys are equally likely to be looked up
why: The random tree's path grows like 2 ln n while the perfect tree grows like log₂ n, so their ratio tends to a constant.

text: The average path length of a random binary search tree equals 2((n+1)/n · H_n − 1), where H_n is the nth harmonic number, approximately 2(ln n − 0.423) for large n.
why: A recurrence on subtree sizes solves to a harmonic sum, and a classical series expansion of that sum gives the logarithmic form.

text: The average path length of a perfectly balanced tree is about log n minus 1.
Perfect balance can improve average search path length of a random binary search tree by at most about 39 percent.
when: all keys are equally likely to be looked up
why: the ratio 2 ln 2 bounds the gain from perfect balance

text: In a perfectly balanced binary search tree of n items, about log n comparisons suffice for a lookup.
why: n items can be arranged with height as small as log n, and each comparison descends one level.

text: In a symmetric binary B-tree, all terminal nodes lie at one level, the longest search path is at most twice the tree height, and the height is at most log N.
when: Analyzing SBB-tree search cost
why: Balanced terminal depth and the no-consecutive-horizontal rule bound the path length

text: The average path length of a tree is its internal path length divided by its number of nodes.
when: Comparing the shapes of trees with different sizes
why: Normalizing by node count makes trees of different sizes comparable

text: Adding special nodes so every node has the tree's full degree d requires (d-1) times n plus 1 special nodes for n original nodes.
when: Computing external path length
why: Each missing subtree slot needs one special node

text: A tree of height h and degree d holds at most the sum of d to the power i for i from 0 to h-1 nodes; for binary trees this is 2 to the power h, minus 1.
when: Bounding node capacity for a given height
why: Each level can hold up to d times as many nodes as the level above

text: A binary B-tree node has left and right pointers plus a Boolean flag; only the right pointer may be horizontal, marking a sibling link rather than a descendant link.
when: When each page's items form a linked list of one or two entries.
why: merging descendant and sibling pointers into one binary node

text: Each B-tree page stores an item count, a leftmost child pointer, and an array of 2n entries, each with a key, a child pointer, and optional extra data.
A red-black tree stores one flag on each incoming pointer: vertical pointers mark black nodes, horizontal pointers mark red nodes, and no two reds are adjacent on a path.
when: When node records are densely packed, so field access needs part-word selection.
why: Uses one bit per node instead of two pointer flags

text: A leader holds a key, a predecessor count, a trailer list, and a next link; a trailer holds a reference to a leader and a next link.
when: When the number of elements is not known in advance.
why: Separates the node set from the successor relations

text: An object-tree interpreter can be clear and simple to read yet far too slow and memory-hungry at runtime.
when: Choosing an execution model for performance-sensitive behavior
why: Readability and runtime cost are independent, so a clean design can still perform poorly.

text: Overwriting a node's record without comparing costs can discard a better route already found.
when: When a search reaches a node that is already on the open or closed list.
why: A later arrival usually costs more, so an unconditional overwrite throws away the earlier, cheaper route.

text: Attributes with many values create wide, wasteful branching in a decision tree.
A naive update walks a new example to a leaf and splits it on a conflicting action, which only appends branches and can create long sequential chains.
when: When a decision-tree update meets a terminal node whose stored action conflicts with the new example
why: Appending splits at the end of the tree only grows it with sequential branches, so flatter trees are preferred instead.

text: String search scans two arrays together, with indices coordinated by the data, which makes the loops hard to write correctly.
