why: Coordinating two indices over two arrays by data makes loops error-prone, so a dedicated loop construct is used to handle them correctly.

text: Copying a merge tail needs no comparisons, but each copied item still counts as a move.
why: On peripheral storage the cost of moves dominates the cost of comparisons by orders of magnitude, so comparison counts matter little.

text: When sequences rotate, dummy counts and coefficients must rotate with the sequence map, or the merge schedule becomes wrong.
when: Implementing polyphase tape rotation.
why: Dummy counts and coefficients are tied to tape positions, so rotating the sequence map requires rotating them consistently.

text: The balance criterion bounds only height, not shape: an AVL tree can be up to about 45 percent taller than a perfectly balanced tree.
why: The balance criterion guarantees a bound on height relative to a perfectly balanced tree, not that the shape is perfectly balanced.

text: Unlike insertion, which causes at most one rotation, AVL deletion can cascade rotations up the search path.
why: Deleting a node can reduce subtree height at every level along the search path, whereas insertion only causes a single local rotation.

text: Moving a page from secondary to primary storage dominates search cost, so optimizing in-page comparisons misses the real cost; count page accesses instead.
why: Fetching a page from secondary store takes far longer than searching in main store, so the page transfer dominates total search time.

text: Order-1 B-trees are poor for large data on secondary storage, because about half of their pages hold a single item.
when: when data lives on secondary storage
why: About half of the pages in such a tree hold only one item, wasting storage and page fetches.

text: Binary B-tree insertion treats left and right growth asymmetrically, which looks artificial and motivates a symmetric variant.
why: The asymmetric treatment of left and right growth seems unnatural, so a symmetric variant removes this asymmetry.

text: In a first-child next-sibling structure the two pointers have different meanings, so a sibling must not be treated as an offspring in data definitions.
why: The two pointers have different meanings, so treating a sibling as an offspring is incorrect even though the structure looks like a binary tree.

text: Individual random search trees may be far worse than the average, up to a linear degenerate shape, so the 39 percent figure describes averages only.
why: The 39 percent improvement is an average over equally probable lookups, so individual trees can deviate widely from it.

text: A disk-resident tree grown in random insertion order can reach worst cases near 10^4 page accesses, erasing the paging advantage.
when: Insertions and deletions are interleaved on a paged tree
why: Unbalanced growth produces long search paths

text: 1) Scan or binary-search the current page for the key. 2) If found, stop. 3) If the key falls between two keys, follow the child pointer between them and repeat at each level. 4) A missing child means the key is absent from the tree.
when: searching a B-tree
why: Keys in each page are ordered, so the child pointer between two bracketing keys is the only place the key can be.

text: 1) Define the target rebalancing cases, such as LL, LR, RR and RL for AVL insertion or every case of a symmetric binary B-tree. 2) Search for a short key sequence that triggers each case at least once. 3) Determine its minimal length.
when: when testing rebalancing code
why: Each rebalancing case must be exercised at least once, so a key sequence that triggers all cases is needed to test them.

text: 1) Detect which split type suits each attribute. 2) Compile the result into a multi-decision, float-decision, or integer threshold node.
when: Building a decision tree learner.
why: Each attribute may suit a different split type, so the right splitting routine must be chosen per attribute before compiling the node.

text: 1) If the node is terminal or has one subtree, remove it as in ordinary tree deletion. 2) If it has two subtrees, replace it with the rightmost node of its left subtree, then remove that node.
when: deleting a node from an AVL tree
why: A node with two subtrees cannot be unlinked with a single pointer, so it is replaced by a neighbouring node with at most one subtree.

text: 1) Follow the search path to confirm the key is absent. 2) Insert the new node and set its balance factor. 3) Retreat along the path, checking and rebalancing each node.
when: inserting a key into an AVL tree
why: Balance factors are checked on the way back up, so rebalancing is only needed at nodes whose height has changed.

text: 1) Descend along rightmost pointers from the inner key's position to a leaf. 2) Copy that leaf's rightmost item into the place of the deleted key. 3) Remove that item from the leaf.
when: deleting a key stored on an inner page
why: An inner key has no direct removal, so it is replaced by an adjacent key that sits on a leaf page and can be removed easily.

text: 1) When the target page already holds 2n items, gather its 2n+1 keys including the new one. 2) Divide them equally between the old page and a newly allocated page. 3) Move the middle key up into the parent page.
when: when inserting into a full page
why: Splitting the full page's keys evenly keeps both new pages at least half full, preserving the B-tree occupancy bounds.

text: 1) If the key is absent, stop. 2) If its node has at most one child, link its parent to that child, or to nothing. 3) If it has two children, overwrite its key and count with those of the rightmost node of its left subtree, then unlink that node by replacing it with its left child.
why: A node with two children cannot be removed by a single pointer change, so its key is replaced by a neighbour that has at most one child.

text: 1) Insert keys in a fixed order into an empty tree, noting which keys cause splits and height increases. 2) Delete the same keys in the same order under each underflow scheme, noting merges and height decreases. 3) Compare the schemes.
when: when comparing B-tree underflow strategies
why: Running the same insertion and deletion sequence under each scheme makes split, merge and height changes directly comparable.

text: 1) Set weights and path lengths for empty subtrees and single keys. 2) For increasing subtree widths, compute each subtree's weight and minimal path length over all candidate roots. 3) Read the optimal tree from the full key range.
when: When keys have known access probabilities and total search steps should be minimized over many trials.
why: Counting the root at level 1 charges the first comparison, and weighting nodes by access probability makes the sum reflect expected search cost.

text: 1) Use the next input value as the root. 2) Build the left subtree from nl = n DIV 2 values. 3) Build the right subtree from nr = n - nl - 1 values. Apply recursively.
when: all input values are known in advance
why: splitting counts evenly at each node yields minimal height

text: 1) Print the left subtree. 2) Print the node preceded by one tab per level. 3) Print the right subtree. This in-order traversal yields an indented view of the tree.
1) Start at the root. 2) Compare the target key with the node's key. 3) Stop if equal, else go left or right. 4) Repeat until found or an empty branch is reached.
1) Start with an empty search tree. 2) For each word, search the tree. 3) If found, increment its count. 4) If not found, insert it with count 1.
when: Counting occurrences of keys in a growing set
why: One pass builds the frequency table without a prior key list

text: 1) Point the root at a sentinel node. 2) Set the sentinel's key to the search value before every search. 3) On a match, increment that node's count. 4) On reaching the sentinel, allocate a node whose two children both point to the sentinel.
when: Implementing insertion with a sentinel
why: The sentinel removes the empty-subtree test from the search loop

text: Keep a full search path plus room for splits in main store during insertion, and keep the root there permanently, since splits need the ancestor pages.
when: when the tree is stored on secondary storage
why: searches fetch about log n of N pages and splits need the ancestor pages

text: When gains tie during incremental tree updates, keep the current attribute to avoid unnecessary rebuilding.
when: When several attributes give the same information gain during an incremental tree update.
why: Switching attributes would invalidate the whole subtree below the decision, so keeping the current one avoids a costly rebuild.

text: A node can only be removed if all its connections go to marked nodes, so rules must be designed around this constraint.
Use horizontal distribution when the initial run count must be tracked exactly, as polyphase sort requires.
when: When polyphase sorting must keep exact counts of runs on each tape.
why: Two consecutive runs sent to the same tape may merge, so run counts assumed in advance can be wrong.

text: Handle a height shrink in the left branch and in the right branch with two mirror-image rebalancing procedures.
when: When a deletion reduces the height of a subtree in a balanced tree.
why: The two operations are symmetric but must be invoked from several points in the deletion algorithm.

text: Use a single rotation (LL or RR) when the heavy child leans the same way as its parent; use a double rotation (LR or RL) when it leans the other way.
when: rebalancing an AVL node after insertion

text: Deleting a key that lies on a leaf page means removing it directly from that page.
when: When the item to be deleted lies on a leaf page of a B-tree.
why: Removing from a leaf needs no replacement step, whereas interior items must first be swapped with an adjacent leaf item.

text: Repair an underfull page by balancing with a sibling or merging with it, choosing according to the page's position in its parent.
when: after a deletion leaves a page below its minimum
why: Merging is needed when the sibling page has no spare items to lend because it is already at minimum size.

text: Remove a node with two children by overwriting its contents with a neighbour's rather than relinking it.
when: When the node being deleted has two child subtrees.
why: one parent pointer cannot lead to both child subtrees

text: Use a tree traversal when an algorithm must process nodes in a defined sequence, such as printing a tree or evaluating an expression tree.
when: When an operation must be applied to every node of a tree in a fixed order.
why: Ordering the visits lets an algorithm refer to the next element, which simplifies its description.

text: Pass a subtree reference to a traversal by value, so the callee cannot change the caller's pointer.
when: When writing recursive tree traversal procedures that receive a node pointer as a parameter.
why: a variable parameter would let the callee redirect the caller's pointer

text: To construct the tallest balanced tree for a given node count, search for the insertion order that forces maximal height under AVL insertion.
when: When a maximum-height balanced tree with a given number of nodes is wanted.

text: To exercise every AVL deletion rebalancing routine, find a permutation of a balanced tree's keys that triggers each routine at least once.
Balanced trees pay off when retrievals far outnumber insertions; plain tree insertion wins when records must be tightly packed or insertions are frequent.
when: When lookups vastly outnumber inserts.
why: Rebalancing operations are complex, so balanced trees justify their cost only when retrievals dominate the workload.

text: Storing children in a fixed array per node wastes space when child counts vary strongly; a linked list of children avoids this waste.
when: When the number of children varies strongly among nodes.
why: A fixed array per node leaves much storage unused when child counts differ widely.

text: Exact dynamic programming needs quadratic storage, impractical for very large n. For unsuccessful searches only, the optimal alphabetic binary tree algorithm needs linear storage and n log n work.
when: When the number of keys n is very large.
why: Required storage grows as n squared, which becomes unacceptable for large n.

text: Building a perfectly balanced tree suits fixed key sets, but restoring perfect balance after random insertions is expensive, so the construction is poor for trees that receive later insertions.
when: insertions follow the initial build
why: perfect balance is defined by node counts that change with each insertion

text: SBB-trees have longer average search paths than AVL trees but need rebalancing less often.
when: Choosing between SBB-trees and AVL trees
why: Looser balance rules allow more shape flexibility, which reduces restructuring work

text: A circular reference is a loop where a cell depends on itself, directly or through other cells, such as A1 =A2+1 with A2 =A1+1.
A checking engine often calls other services, such as a physics or collision detector, to determine whether an event has occurred.
Checks differ in kind: a siren is a single on/off value, collisions need geometric prediction, and speech recognition scans voice input for commands.
Use event passing when many agents need the same result, or when checks can be done for all agents at once rather than agent by agent.
when: many agents share a check result
why: shared checks are done once for everyone

text: The checking engine decides whether something has happened that a listener may want, and it can check everything or use listeners' interests to narrow its work.
Spreadsheets normally flag circular references because they cannot determine which cell should update first.
when: Under normal spreadsheet recalculation, when a chain of formulas loops back on itself.
why: All cells recalculate simultaneously, so there is no order that resolves a mutual dependency.

text: Test that a candidate lies on the board before checking its visited state, because an out-of-range index is an invalid matrix lookup.
why: A visited-state value exists only for in-range indices, so the bounds conditions must be checked before it.

text: Looping menu music behind lobby or pause screens is interactive, because players can stop it at any moment to enter or leave the game.
when: Music plays during menus or pause screens.
why: Players can exit at any time.

text: Musical motifs that appear unexpectedly stand out in memory more than music that closely tracks each scene.
why: Music that tracks its scene too closely is argued to be forgotten, while unexpected placement gets noticed.

text: Vertical recombination layers musical parts that fit together harmonically, so any subset of parts played at once still sounds coherent.
Music transitions can switch immediately, crossfade, wait for the end of the current cue, or switch at the next measure, beat, or beat-aligned position.
Vertical layering keeps several aligned tracks, called stems, playing together and changes intensity by raising or lowering their mix instead of switching between separate pieces.
A stem can be a single track or a group of tracks, and the term comes from film post-production where soundtracks are grouped into dialogue, music and effects.
Rhythm in music depends on the number and type of notes within a bar.
Most action-adventure games use a unique chime or tune to signal victory.
Place a dramatic sound event such as dialogue, an alarm or an explosion at a music switch point, since listener attention goes to it and hides the join.
when: A switch between two music pieces is needed and a dramatic event naturally falls at the switch point or the story provides one.
why: A simple swap between pieces can sound clumsy.

text: Use a consistent, explicit link between game state and music when players need that information to play well; avoid it when you want players to be less predictable.
when: when choosing how predictable a music response should be
why: Music can carry information that nothing else in the game provides, so players must hear it to play well.

text: Replace a looping music bed with a beat counter that restarts the music at the bed's length in beats to limit timing drift.
when: Music must stay synchronised with beat-timed events over long play
why: Looping sound drifts relative to the beat over time

text: Crossfades work best with music lacking strong directional melody or phrasing, since the player can interrupt any arc at any time.
when: Choosing crossfades for game music
why: Directional music loses its arc when the player can break it at any moment.

text: Raise a boss's music intensity as its health falls, and add short stingers on each hit.
when: when a boss fight is underway
why: Music's power comes from signalling that something is special, and constant music wears that signal down.

text: Decide whether music scores what is happening now, what has already happened, or what is about to happen.
when: when planning a music response to a scene
why: Music is well suited to suggesting tension, release, and conflict, so what it tracks should follow the intended effect.

text: Transition cues ease intensity changes by leading down, building up, or managing tempo, and can also act as stingers that highlight an action.
when: When a direct switch between two main cues sounds unsatisfactory.

text: Use sudden volume changes, break expectations by varying repeated sounds, place sources to unnerve, move sources, and add low-frequency sound for threat.
when: When designing unsettling mood
why: Repeating a sound with a changed pattern breaks listener expectations, so the same cue can startle the player.

text: Announce-then-recede layering applies to many sound elements beyond weapons and helps thin busy mixes.
when: When many simultaneous sounds in a confined area blur into one mass.
why: Once an onset signals an event, continued repetition adds little new information and can be turned down.

text: Scaling the distance to an enemy into a fade level raises bass and bell stems as the player approaches, making tension rise continuously.
when: Layered music reacting to enemy proximity
why: Stem volume follows a continuous scaled value rather than switching on and off.

text: Knowing the music's position and time to its next transition point lets the game start a change immediately or hold it until a more musical moment.
when: when the game controls when a music change happens
why: timing information lets the game choose between instant and musically aligned changes

text: A cue change made on a beat resets the measure counter, so the next measure restarts at beat one.
when: when a cue changes on a beat rather than a bar
why: the bar count must align with the new cue

text: Muting and unmuting stems from a gameplay timer makes the mix respond to how much time the player has left.
when: when a timer is a gameplay variable

text: Checking a state variable at fixed intervals and unmuting the stem whose range contains its value lets interactive music change intensity while stems stay time-aligned.
when: stems are kept aligned in time and played together
why: aligned stems sound correct when unmuted partway through

text: Muting all but one track of a set of aligned stems yields an ambient version of the piece, while playing all tracks yields the most intense state.
when: When one piece of music must cover many different game circumstances.

text: Crossfading between sound cues across ranges of a game variable, such as speed, makes the sound follow that variable.
when: When a sound has a complex relationship with an in-game variable such as speed.

text: Music built from two-, four-, or eight-bar segments that fit together in any order can be chained at random for variety from few assets.
when: limited music assets
why: Random order multiplies combinations

text: When failed inputs alter playback, the track plays incorrectly, so the player effectively controls the background music.
when: rhythm games where failed inputs change the track
why: playback depends on the player's timing

text: Plan for roughly double the usual sound design effort for a VR game, since object interactions need believable sound.
when: Scoping audio work for a VR project
why: Each object interaction needs believable sound

text: Bar-line time equals beats per bar multiplied by 60 divided by tempo, applied cumulatively; at 120 bpm and 4 beats per bar each bar lasts 2 seconds.
when: Steady tempo.
why: A constant tempo makes bar boundary times calculable from the tempo alone.

text: A half-beat pulse interval equals 60 divided by tempo, divided by 2; a 0.2 second delay imitates 150 bpm.
when: Generating rhythmic pulses from a delay node.
why: Each pulse drives the sequencer's next step, so the delay interval sets the rhythm's timing.

text: Allowing any of seven main cues to move to any other yields 127 possible transitions, most of which would not make musical sense.
when: When any cue might need to move to any other cue.
why: Many cue pairs have no musically or logically valid path, such as a stealth cue jumping straight to an end cue.

text: Each game state has a loop. A combat intro leads into an action cue, and an end cue returns to the state's loop.
when: when structuring adaptive music across game states

text: A music change request carries a cue index and a timing choice. The timing choice selects which pulse lets the request reach the cue switch.
when: when routing music change requests through a timed switch
why: The switch only emits on an input pulse, and the timing choice decides which pulse passes its gate.

text: Music can sync to a scene in four ways: hitting the action, playing the emotion, playing the meta-emotion, or counterpoint against the emotion.
when: when deciding how music responds to on-screen events

text: A transition cue can be an end cue for the outgoing piece, an intro for the incoming piece, or both in sequence, such as CueA, EndCueA, IntroCueB, CueB.
when: When a direct move between two main cues sounds unsatisfactory.

text: A mix that visibly shifts draws attention to itself, so ducking should be subtle enough to go unnoticed.
Leitmotifs that start at unaligned times produce a messy combined result, so their timing must be planned.
why: Unaligned musical parts clash, so keeping them synchronised and varying their volume avoids the mess.

text: Allowing a direct jump from a calm loop to an end cue skips the combat that should sit between them. Transition rules must block such shortcuts.
when: when defining transitions between music states
why: Many pairings of cues are nonsensical, such as jumping from a quiet stealth loop straight to an ending, so most transitions must be excluded.

text: A cue change request waits for its chosen boundary, so it does not take effect instantly even though it was sent.
when: when a music change is requested between boundaries

text: Too little reaction in music misses chances to heighten emotion.
when: when music ignores changes in the scene

text: An abrupt switch from ambient to combat music sounds unmusical. It works only for shock value, so most moments need smoother transitions.
when: when switching between contrasting music states
why: The jolt of a sudden cut is the only thing that can justify skipping a smoother join.

text: Changes in stem selection are heard only when a part is retriggered, so a one-minute part can delay an arrangement change by up to a minute.
when: When the layered parts used for arrangement changes are long rather than short.
why: A playing sound's volume is fixed when it starts, so mix changes wait for the next retrigger.

text: The legacy play-music-track node has no fade-out on stop and cannot be stopped once started.
when: When choosing between the legacy music-track node and the standard sound playback node for music.
why: The standard playback node fades out when stopped, but the legacy node gives no trigger for fading or stopping.

text: In some engine builds, crossing a distance crossfade boundary incorrectly retriggers the sound, so test by moving through boundaries carefully.
when: When a sound uses distance-based crossfade in an affected engine build.

text: Treating the whole queue as a live structure means lag between request and processing can visibly change how sounds behave.
when: Sound requests wait in a queue before playing.
why: Delay between request and playback alters perceived behavior.

text: 1) Start the first cue at its timing point. 2) Trigger each next sound from the previous one's Finished output or a remote event sent when it ends. 3) Edit tracks so starts and ends line up. 4) Let play-once tracks stop at natural ends.
when: when chaining music tracks so a second cue follows a first without gaps
why: Play-once cues mark a natural musical conclusion, so they should simply run to their end and halt.

text: 1) Compute beat length in seconds as 60 divided by tempo in BPM. 2) Convert it to a float. 3) Send a beat pulse from a delay into a gate. 4) Open the gate on the trigger event so the next beat plays the stinger, then close it.
when: Playing a stinger on the next musical beat after a game event
why: Musical events land on the beat instead of at an arbitrary time

text: 1) Record save point positions and how often players restart a level. 2) Ask whether music should repeat exactly each time. 3) Monitor each player's playing style over time. 4) Let the adaptive system respond to that style.
when: When tuning adaptive music for a level.
why: Restart and save data show where music timing matters, and style tracking lets the system adapt per player.

text: 1) Discuss with designers the roles music should play and the emotion or goal of each scenario. 2) Identify the events that need music and their start and end points. 3) Map the music to gameplay variables such as player health or enemy health. 4) Obtain access to the gameplay data needed to turn values into emotional meaning.
when: When deciding where and how music appears in a game
why: Game composers often work from text design documents, so spotting requires active discussion.

text: 1) Place a touch trigger that fires a sound-playing action aimed at the player. 2) Create a cue with a Random node of sounds, an Attenuation node and a Speaker node. 3) Attach it to that sound-playing action and preview.
when: Building an event-driven randomized sound
why: Triggers play variety on each event

text: 1) Place an ambient sound at the source. 2) Crossfade several sound layers over distance with a distance crossfade node. 3) Set each layer's fade-in start and end so all are at full volume at the source. 4) Match the attenuation to the farthest layer.
when: Building a large source whose detail should appear as the listener approaches.
why: Layers that fade in at different distances reproduce how real large sources sound.

text: 1) Start a delay when a quiet music state begins. 2) If the delay expires, switch to a faded version of the track. 3) Gate it so the faded version plays once and ends.
when: A player may stay in a quiet state unnaturally long
why: Fading out after a timeout restores impact when the state lasts too long.

text: 1) Place triggers at each area boundary. 2) On touch, play the area's music. 3) Stop the other area's music through its stop input.
when: Simple switching between location music
why: Triggers start and stop pieces without any musical timing.

text: 1) Define music states such as ambient, action, triumph and death. 2) Trigger each state through events like pickup, hit or goal. 3) Test each death or failure state directly with a debug command.
when: Testing interactive music states
why: Direct state triggers let designers verify each transition.

text: 1) Work out how the existing system routes its cues. 2) Add your music cues to the existing sound playback objects. 3) Set tempo and beats-per-measure variables to match your music. 4) Create triggers that call a track at the next beat or next measure.
when: Extending a transition music system with new cues
why: Matching tempo and timing to the music keeps cue changes on the beat.

text: 1) Compose several parts that fit together. 2) Mute and unmute parts to preview combinations. 3) Mix parts with random selectors to produce varied combinations. 4) Weight the selectors so some combinations are more or less likely.
when: Building a long-duration background score that avoids obvious repetition
why: Random combinations of vertically compatible parts keep a long background from grating through repetition.

text: 1) Start on the ambient track. 2) Switch to the action track when the player approaches a point of interest. 3) Play a win track or a death track when the outcome occurs. 4) Optionally return to ambient when the win track finishes.
when: Music reacts to proximity and fight outcome

text: Start a music playback from a level startup event, a switch, or a trigger, depending on when the source should begin playing.
1) Start a looping background track from a level startup event or a trigger. 2) Fire stingers from the gameplay event that confirms the successful action.
when: When the background bed is purely rhythmic rather than melodic or harmonic.
why: Without pitched content, any melody or harmony in a stinger has nothing in the bed to clash with.

text: 1) Count beats with a counter that resets at the bar length. 2) Feed each reset into a looping switch that sets a bar number. 3) Compare the bar number to pick the matching stinger. 4) Pass beat and measure events through a remote event to keep the logic tidy.
when: When a looping bed's harmony changes between halves and stingers must match the current half.
why: Routing beat and measure pulses through remote events keeps the visual scripting graph from becoming cluttered.

text: 1) Start every part together at level startup. 2) Make all parts the same length. 3) Fade each part's volume by its distance to its source.
when: Several sources of music are mixed according to player distance
why: Distant sources can all sound at once, so the parts must blend musically together.

text: 1) When the gameplay event happens, open a gate for the new cue. 2) Keep the current cue running until the next bar pulse. 3) On that pulse, start the new cue and stop the old one.
when: when a cue change must land on a bar line

text: 1) Start the music on a trigger. 2) Chain delays whose total equals the intended length. 3) Use a counter compared with a target to open or close gates for events. 4) On target reached, close the active gate, open the finale gate and remove the blocker.
when: a timed challenge with music and objectives

text: 1) List all main cues. 2) For each pair, record whether a move is allowed and its switch timing. 3) Build this matrix before composing so required links and their handling are known.
when: interactive music with several main cues
why: unrestricted transitions produce many musically nonsensical moves

text: 1) Play each track with a finished output. 2) Route state-change triggers through the finished output. 3) Only the ambient track may be interrupted unmusically, so reaction to spotting stays instant.
when: switching music states in a stealth or combat setting
why: changes then land on musical points and any piece length works

text: 1) Choose a looping ambient base track. 2) Assign each action or zone a short musical phrase. 3) Layer those phrases over the loop as the player acts.
when: building music that responds to player actions
why: Layering keeps a steady base while player input adds musical variety.

text: Cancel or drop secondary feedback when a more important event occurs, such as cancelling a reload animation when the player starts moving.
when: When a more important event happens while lower-priority feedback such as an animation or dialog is still playing.
why: Too many simultaneous signals overwhelm players' working memory, so less important ones must give way.

text: After a faded-out track ends, music should restart only when a state change selects a different track.
when: Designing music that has faded out due to inactivity
why: Prevents the faded track from restarting without a meaningful change.

text: Compose tracks that end cleanly on a bar, and switch between them only at bar ends instead of crossfading.
Set a fade in and fade out length for every music playback so that transitions between states are smooth.
why: Players can undermine flowing or rhythmic music at any moment, so a short overlap suits music written in a flexible style.

text: Write a separate melodic stinger for each harmony, and choose among them by tracking the current position in the music.
when: When stingers are pitch-based rather than percussive and the underlying harmony keeps changing.
why: A pitched stinger sounds dissonant over harmonies it was not written for, so it must match the current chord.

text: Store switch markers as metadata in the file header rather than chopping the audio file into pieces.
when: Making a commercial track interactive.
why: The full file stays intact, so the programmer can still apply a fade-out envelope.

text: Fade out menu and pause music rather than cutting it off abruptly; a short fade is the minimum acceptable treatment.
when: Music stops when the player leaves a menu or pause state.
why: An abrupt cut is jarring and seen as a serious lapse.

text: Make death and idle cues reachable from every music state, so they can interrupt any section.
when: when designing music state transitions

text: End a boss fight with a triumph cue that replaces the combat music.
when: when the main threat is defeated

text: Set each music transition's timing point to the next beat, the next bar, or the end of the current cue when mapping gameplay triggers to cues.
when: when mapping gameplay triggers to music cues
why: Timing must respond quickly enough to gameplay yet keep the music flowing, trading responsiveness against continuity.

text: Start all stems together, and retrigger them all when the first stem finishes, so the layers stay in sync.
when: when playing several looping stems as one piece
why: separate sounds drift apart without a shared restart

text: Stop in-world music when the player leaves its room, so it does not carry into the next area.
when: when the player exits the room

text: Decide with the designer what each game variable means emotionally before mapping it to music.
when: when choosing which game variables drive music
why: Game variables only make emotional sense in combination, which needs the designer's input before they are mapped to music.

text: Pitch-shift interface sounds into the key of the menu music, or choose tones that suit the background music.
when: When menu music plays while the game is in menu mode
why: Mismatched pitch against playing music sounds harsh, so matching the key or tones avoids an abrasive clash.

text: Lead into a big audio event with a quiet section where possible, since the contrast gives the event more impact than a preduck.
when: Designing the timing of a loud sound event.
why: Contrast from silence or low level is the strongest route to impact.

text: Immediate or at-beat switches respond quickly to game events but may clash with the beat; waiting for a bar or beat-aligned point keeps music correct, with a short delay.
when: when choosing a switch point for a music change triggered by a gameplay event
why: Responsiveness and musical continuity pull in opposite directions.

text: Phrase-based concatenation builds sentences from opening, middle and end phrases and works best for relaxed, low-intensity speech.
Merging duplicates at enqueue time saves queue slots and is simpler, while merging inside update moves the cost to the processor.
when: Choosing where to aggregate duplicate sound requests.
why: Each placement trades queue space against processing time.

text: Even a simple room tone can strongly affect the mood of a space.
An ambient zone is a reverb-volume setting that tells the audio system how sound is attenuated and filtered depending on whether the listener is inside or outside the volume.
Ambient zone settings are interior volume, exterior volume, interior low-pass filter and exterior low-pass filter, each with a transition time between the inside and outside states.
A rain environment can use six types: general rain, rain on trees, rain on water, rain on a metal roof, rain on hollow metal barrels, and rain on plants.
Real buildings and spaceships usually have constant or repeating electrical or mechanical sources, which looping sound files can reproduce.
Movers have six sound slots: Close (start of closing), Closed (end of closing), Closing (loop), Open (start of opening), Opened (end of opening), and Opening (loop).
Moving sound sources make a space feel more realistic whether or not the source is visible.
Crowd audio is not music, so its layers do not need to align in time, unlike interactive music layers.
In dungeon-crawling levels, object sounds can signal events happening elsewhere in the level.
Let a lift or platform start when a character stands on it, not only from a switch, when players should ride it directly.
why: A Mover Event output fires when a player or NPC is attached to the platform, so it can start the movement without a switch.

text: For distant ambiences, attach individual channels to invisible objects so the sounds move as the player rotates.
when: When good multichannel recordings of a distant ambience are available
why: Channels locked to speakers don't pan, so tying each channel to an object makes it move as the player rotates.

text: Area-based sources sound less directional with a large minimum radius and a linear or logarithmic-reverse curve, so they pan less.
when: the source comes from an area rather than a point
why: Sounds spread across a wide area have no single origin, so a large minimum radius and gentle curve reduce panning.

text: When isolating sounds with ambient zones, decide for each sound whether to attenuate, filter, or both.
Let an ambient sound set the mood on entry, then fade it to a lower level, making its point and then receding.
when: When the player enters an area

text: For surround ambience, mix it in a digital audio workstation as a multichannel source and import it into the engine.
when: When stereo playback cannot create spatial effects
why: Rear and hard-to-locate sounds raise tension, and that effect is only audible on surround setups.

text: Use a sudden stop of a constant room tone to make the player expect something, rather than for constant scares.
when: When building anticipation
why: Stopping a sound is rarer than a sudden sound, so it is more effective.

text: Ambient sound effects tied to the game's activities build the atmosphere of a setting.
Overlapping copies of the same sound roughly double the perceived volume, so their radius minimum and maximum values must be adjusted.
when: multiple overlapping ambient sound sources
why: summed sources add up in level

text: Non-looping ambient sounds played at random delays avoid long loops in memory and vary how often and when each sound appears.
when: building natural ambience from individual elements
why: random timing hides repetition

text: When the listener passes from one ambient zone into another, the exterior effects of the outer zone stack with the interior effects of the inner one, so sound is attenuated further, as in real space.
when: Listener moves between nested or adjacent zoned spaces
why: Physical sound passes through each barrier and loses energy cumulatively

text: Controlling each crowd sound's volume during playback lets it fade up or down with game variables, so crowd response tracks game state.
when: Complex blending of sourced crowd recordings

text: Eerie light and chanting with no visible threat can sustain tension during a quiet moment.
when: during low-action moments
why: Cues without visible sources keep tension alive.

text: Changing ambient sound from natural noises to steady drums and unsettling tones raises tension as the player collects objectives.
why: Changing ambient noise communicates how far the player has progressed in the game state.

text: Moving a sound's origin away from its object to stop overlap through walls is not a satisfactory fix.
when: a source leaks into a neighbouring room
why: The inside sound needs its current falloff to stay natural, and walls don't automatically block sound in the engine.

text: A hard switch has no midpoint, so a player standing in a doorway flickers constantly between the two sound states.
Fixed ambient zones do not change when the player opens a door or window or breaks a wall, so the audio stops matching the situation.
when: Environments the player can alter.
why: Zones configured in advance cannot react to changed barriers.

text: 1) Select a sound in the asset browser. 2) Right-click the floor in the 3D view and choose Add Actor, then add a simple ambient sound actor using that sound. 3) Play from that floor point to test.
when: quick placement of a room tone in an empty room
why: An empty room with no ambient sound sounds lifeless and unreal, so it needs a room tone.

text: 1) Open the Content Browser's Actor Classes tab. 2) Expand Sounds, then the ambient sound category. 3) Select the simple ambient sound actor and right-click the Perspective viewport to add it. 4) If no sound was selected, assign one with the green arrow in its properties.
when: when an actor type is not in the right-click menu
why: Some actor types are missing from the viewport's right-click menu, so they must be picked from the Actor Classes browser instead.

text: 1) Place ambient sound actors for machinery using existing or imported sounds. 2) Balance the mix by setting each sound's Volume Scale, with 1.0 as the maximum.
when: When a room contains machinery that should be brought to life with sound
why: Individual sounds usually need level adjustment to blend into an effective mix, and volume cannot be pushed past 1.0.

text: 1) Select a sound in the Content Browser. 2) Open the ambient sound actor's properties. 3) In the Wave slot, click the green arrow to assign the selected sound. 4) Reselect the sound if the arrow does nothing.
when: When the green arrow does nothing after the sound is selected

text: 1) Place inside and outside toggleable ambient sounds. 2) Create a Touch event on the trigger volume. 3) Use Touched and Untouched outputs to toggle the inside and outside sounds.
when: moving between indoor and outdoor areas
why: Switching whole area ambiences creates the impression of a changed environment, sidestepping the cost of many small sounds.

text: 1) Set a minimum and maximum delay between sounds. 2) Set each sound's weight to control its relative chance. 3) Enable modulation to randomize volume and pitch on each play.
when: configuring randomized ambience
why: delay range sets frequency, weight sets selection, and modulation adds variation

text: 1) Start with the complete object. 2) Play its movement sequence in reverse. 3) Its open and close sounds also play in reverse, so the object appears to assemble itself.
when: an object is built up rather than taken down

text: 1) Convert the static mesh into an animated actor. 2) Key its movement in a sequence. 3) Add its sounds to the actor's properties or as sound tracks in the sequence.
when: When a static mesh such as a door or elevator must move and produce sound
why: Doors and elevators make sound while they move, and a static mesh has to become an animated actor before it can move at all.

text: 1) Select the animated actor. 2) Create a mover event from it. 3) Its output fires when a pawn is attached to it. 4) Edit the movement sequence the event generates.
when: When a moving platform should start automatically once the player stands on it

text: 1) Attach a trigger volume to each note panel. 2) Set it to detect projectiles by touch, blocking complex collisions and ignoring zero-extent queries. 3) Link each hit to a sound playback.
when: Building projectile-activated musical panels
why: Trigger volumes detect projectile contact and route each hit to its note.

text: 1) Attach triggers to moving objects. 2) Offset them so they sit on the floor, not at the object's origin. 3) Keep a central trigger fixed to add a stable base value.
when: Triggers that follow moving lights or actors
why: Attached triggers move with their actor, so offset keeps them at ground contact.

text: Never leave an environment completely silent unless silence is an explicit aesthetic choice, and even then it is discouraged.
when: designing any space
why: real spaces rarely are silent

text: Use one large ambient zone around a building for a sound that covers the whole level, instead of placing many emitters around each building's geometry.
when: A broad environmental sound such as rain spans the level
why: Engines often do not know where walls are, so zones supply that geometry

text: In multi-floor buildings, separate floors horizontally with ambient zones so that sound does not bleed between floors.
when: Building with several stacked floors
why: Sound from one floor would otherwise leak into the floor above or below

text: Base movement sounds on how the character moves, the surface underfoot, and the situation, giving each situation its own sound set.
why: Limbs move together, so a step is part of whole-body motion rather than an isolated footfall.

text: Moveable ambient sounds always loop their sound cue, even when the cue itself is not set to loop.
In intense moments, turn off quiet ambience when frequent loud events would mask it, freeing digital headroom and simplifying the mix.
when: when many loud events occur
why: Loud, frequent events mask quiet ambience anyway.

text: Ambient zones cannot overlap, so each must fit its room exactly; yet overlapping toggleable reverb volumes switched by door state can muffle an outer ambience to simulate occlusion.
when: Placing zones in a level with several rooms holds the no-overlap rule; simulating occlusion from doors or walls in an interior layout uses toggled overlapping volumes.
why: Zones without exact boundaries leak sound between rooms, while each toggled volume changes the reverb and filter applied to sounds inside it.

text: Placing several smaller sounds around geometry fakes occlusion, but costs time and voices and can cause phasing.
why: Shaping separate sounds around the geometry lets them avoid overlapping walls, which is what fakes the occlusion.

text: Ducking lowers music or effects while speech plays; real ducking drives a compressor's side-chain with the speech signal.
An exception sound class sits outside the parent and child class tree, so a sound mode targeting the tree does not change it.
Assigning sounds to importance categories and ducking lower-importance sounds when higher-importance ones play keeps critical audio audible; very high importance sounds are not ducked.
when: when a higher-importance sound plays
why: Lower-importance sounds turn down, medium a little and low a lot, so priority sounds stand out.

text: An expander reduces audio below a threshold, and at extreme settings it acts as a noise gate.
A ducking mode can set the effects and music classes, with their children, to 0.2 while leaving the dialogue class unaffected.
when: When dialogue during a cut-scene must stay audible over other audio
why: Players need to focus on the dialogue, so competing classes are turned down while it plays.

text: 1) Identify the category of each sound to be lowered. 2) Create a mix-state preset with a category volume effect per category at reduced volume. 3) Leave the target sound's category out. 4) End the preset after a short duration, or with a second action that restores the default mix.
when: Making one sound stand out while other sounds duck
why: Ducking chosen classes isolates the target sound without changing its own volume.

text: Use volume ducking to lower competing sounds, such as music and effects, during dialogue so players can make out each line.
when: when dialogue must always be heard over music and effects
why: Competing sounds are reduced so the dialogue remains intelligible when the environment is busy.

text: Use exception classes for sounds that should ignore the usual mix rules.
when: when sounds should ignore the usual mix rules
why: An exception class sits outside the hierarchy the sound mode targets, so the mode does not change it.

text: Concatenation plays audio segments end to end, each after the previous finishes, forming new sequences; a sound cue's concatenator node does this.
when: Building varied sounds from short segments
why: Reordering segments creates new variations from stored material

text: Lossless compression keeps every attribute of a sound intact, while lossy compression alters the sound to reduce its data size.
when: Choosing an audio compression method
why: Lossy methods trade fidelity for smaller files

text: Sound files must be 16-bit wav, mono or stereo, at any sample rate.
Film can use nearly unlimited channels and top-quality sounds, whereas games must fit instantly playable sounds into a fixed memory budget that may be very small on portable consoles.
when: Comparing audio constraints of games and film
why: Games have a fixed RAM limit at playback time

text: Console-specific audio formats such as XMA and Vorbis are designed for games and can reach up to 10:1 compression.
when: Compressing game audio for consoles
why: Formats are built for fast game playback

text: Some engines let markers inside a WAV file define multiple start points, so one sample can play from different positions and give variety without chopping the file.
when: The audio engine supports WAV cue markers
why: Markers are stored in the WAV header

text: Recording a separate sound for every interaction multiplies sample counts quickly; one desk pen with 13 sound types across 15 surfaces needs 195 samples.
when: Planning interaction sounds for many objects and surfaces
why: Combinatorial growth of object actions times surfaces exceeds RAM and recording time

text: CD-quality audio uses about 176 kB per second, so roughly 10 seconds fit in about 1.8 MB of older console sound memory.
when: Estimating sample memory cost
why: Stereo 16-bit 44.1 kHz data rate

text: Suggested sample rates by category: 44 kHz for key high-frequency sounds, 22 kHz for player weapons, 18 kHz for dialogue, 11 kHz for distant ambience or room tones.
when: Starting sample rate assignments
why: Rough tiers balancing quality against memory

text: Wavetable synthesis plays a stored waveform cycle at varying rates to produce pitched tones, a technique closely related to playing one sample at multiple pitches.
Channel suffixes name speakers: _fl front left, _fr front right, _fc front centre, _lf low frequency, _sl and _sr side left and right, _bl and _br back left and right.
A playback object that sets a fade level and fade time while a sound plays enables analogue-style volume changes.
when: Adjusting volume of an already playing sound

text: Some sequencers offer a capture-effects-tail export option that reduces the effort of producing decay samples.
when: Producing decay samples from a sequencer

text: DownLoadable Sound packages custom sample banks with MIDI scores so music sounds as the composer intended on any playback device.
why: General MIDI alone depended on each sound card's instrument set.

text: Games can last from ten hours to hundreds of hours, far longer than films, which makes writing and storing enough music a problem.
16-bit audio has limited dynamic range, so the system must control which sounds play and how many to prevent clipping.
Loops convey continuous sources such as engines or turbines and repeat regardless of interactions.
Set sample rate by how important a sound is and how often players hear it, not by frequency content alone, since usage determines audible impact.
when: Assigning sample rates across a project
why: Frequently heard or key sounds deserve higher quality than rare, distant ones; choosing from frequency content alone can waste or starve memory.

text: Trim leading and trailing silence from sounds before import, e.g. dialogue lines, since silent samples still use memory; in one example this nearly halved file size with no audible change.
when: Preparing sound files for import
why: Silent samples still consume bytes; silence can make up a large share of a file

text: Choose a sample rate from where a sound's energy lies, not from a fixed rule. Sounds concentrated at low frequencies tolerate lower rates than bright sounds.
when: Deciding the sample rate for a game sound
why: Frequency content determines which rates remove audible detail

text: Talk to programmers early to learn how audio playback and memory work on the target platform.
when: Starting audio planning for any platform
why: Hardware details may be under non-disclosure and vary by system

text: An odd number of bars in a loop gives more variation when layered with other loops.
when: When layering several loops that share a tempo but differ in length
why: Loops of mismatched lengths combine into a long pattern before repeating, producing nonrepetitive texture.

text: Downsampling a bright sound such as crickets removes its high frequencies and audibly degrades it, while a low-frequency rumble keeps its quality at lower rates.
when: Sound energy extends into high frequencies
why: Frequencies above the new rate's limit are lost

text: Recombining N heel parts with N toe parts yields N times N distinct footsteps, so four heels and four toes give 16 variants.
when: Building variation from separable sound segments
why: Each heel-toe pairing is a distinct combination

text: Storing a transient at full rate and a tail at a lower rate can cut file size by more than half with little audible change.
when: A sound's transient is bright while its tail is dull
why: Only the transient needs the high sample rate

text: Generating a sound from many short reordered segments can replace dozens of stored sounds with a small total file size.
when: Many similar short sounds are needed
why: Runtime reordering reuses the same segments

text: A gated loop keeps restarting while its gate is open, so a newly opened gate takes effect only when the current cue finishes.
why: Triggers are only handled when each track reaches its Finished output, so a gate change waits for the current cue to end.

text: Halving sample rate halves file size (369 kB at 44 kHz to 186 kB at 22 kHz), so lower rates fit proportionally more seconds in a memory budget.
when: Reducing a sample's rate by half or fitting sounds into a fixed budget
why: File size scales with samples per second; storage per second falls in proportion to sample rate

text: A segment with no content above 7.5 kHz can be resampled to 15 kHz without audible change.
when: Choosing a lower rate for a low-frequency tail
why: Sampling at twice the highest content frequency preserves it

text: At 16-bit depth, 44 kHz audio uses 88.2 kB per second, 22 kHz uses 44.1 kB, 11 kHz uses 22.05 kB, and 8 kHz uses 16 kB.
when: Estimating mono sample storage at 16-bit depth
why: Storage is sample rate times bytes per sample

text: Four loops of 4, 6, 9 and 11 bars realign only after 2,376 bars, requiring 594, 396, 264 and 216 repetitions respectively.
why: Full resynchronisation happens at the lowest common multiple of the loop lengths, which sets each loop's repeat count.

text: A four-sentence branching exchange needs 25 separate sound files to cover all permutations, so file count grows quickly with branching.
when: When dialogue branches by player response and characters may vary
why: Each speaker variant and each branch needs its own recorded line, multiplying the file count.

text: Estimate final audio file size from each line's duration and sample rate, using the prototype's updated duration.
when: when planning storage or asset budgets
why: Prototype dialogue gives a rough indication of the final assets' size, so its duration and sample rate predict them.

text: iXMF (Interactive eXtensible Music Format), from the IASIG, is an open cross-platform standard that holds both implementation instructions and audio data for interactive music.
Timing in the editor's quick play window is unreliable, so verify beat-synced audio in a full standalone launch.
when: Testing rhythm-aligned sound effects during development
why: Editor playback timing is inaccurate and differs from the shipped game

text: Inaccurate loop edits make the pulse drift out of time, and the error grows with every repetition.
when: Layering loops over long play sessions

text: Editing music at arbitrary points in a wav file produces audible clicks.
when: Cutting or joining music at points not aligned to the waveform or musical structure.

text: A long loop cycle does not by itself guarantee interesting listening.
when: Relying on phasing for variety.

text: Check duration figures derived from loop length and repetition counts before quoting them, since they can fail to reconcile.
when: Stating how long a loop set plays.

text: The legacy music track and arrangement tools in an older engine are limited and partly broken, so simple one-shot playback nodes are the better choice for most music work.
why: Few features, and its fade-down cannot be triggered and playback cannot be stopped, unlike the one-shot node's fade-out.

text: A loop that does not join smoothly produces an audible seam, which becomes obvious at high firing rates.
when: Looping weapon sound retriggered at very high fire rates, such as miniguns.
why: The seam repeats many times per second.

text: 1) Cut the initial transient into its own file. 2) Loop the sustained section while the trigger is held. 3) Fade the loop in over about 0.2 seconds on fire and out on release. 4) Play a tail on release.
when: Very high fire rates on a looped weapon
why: Retriggering one long sample exhausts voices at high rates; a loop avoids that.

text: 1) Create a new package in the Custom Levels Packages folder. 2) Click Import at the bottom of the Content Browser. 3) Browse to the wav folder and choose the file. 4) Save the package.
when: When importing your own sounds rather than using the supplied sample library.

text: 1) Put two or more loops of different lengths in one ambient sound source. 2) Let them play together. The result drifts out of time and takes a long time to repeat.
when: a single loop sounds unnatural or repetitive
why: loops of different lengths drift apart, producing new combinations

text: 1) Examine frequency over time to find where high-frequency content ends. 2) Split the sound into a transient and a tail. 3) Keep the transient at full rate and resample the tail to a lower rate.
when: Saving memory on a sound whose frequency content changes over time
why: Each segment is stored only at the rate its content requires

text: 1) Add markers in the audio editor at chosen points. 2) Confirm with the audio programmer which marker format the engine reads. 3) Trigger playback from each marker.
when: Using multiple start points in one WAV
why: The engine must read the marker format correctly

text: 1) Stream stereo music, speech, stereo ambience and anticipated big moments from disk. 2) Keep short, frequently used sounds in RAM. 3) Free RAM for interaction sounds.
when: RAM is limited and many sounds are needed
why: Long stereo assets are the costliest to hold in memory

text: 1) Right-click the source sound asset in the content browser and open it in the sound previewer. 2) Wait for the previewer to convert the variants. 3) Double-click a quality setting to audition it. 4) Confirm to apply the chosen setting to the sound.
when: Choosing a Vorbis quality level for a sound that will ship with Vorbis compression
why: Audition before committing so the smallest acceptable quality is picked

text: Give each music layer a short fade-in and a longer fade-out so intensity changes blend in rather than cutting.
when: Playing layered ambient music in response to game state
why: Fades soften changes between layers.

text: 1) Copy the sequence so it repeats. 2) Export the result and trim it to keep the second half, which contains the decay. OR 1) Export with empty bars after the loop. 2) Mix-paste the decay portion back into the start.
when: Exporting a looping music section whose notes ring past the loop point
why: Exporting only the loop cuts off sustained tails, so the decay must be folded back in.

text: 1) Keep the sentence structure fixed. 2) Record only the variable words, such as team names or home and away. 3) Stitch recorded pieces together in playback.
when: Sentences with few changing words
why: Avoids recording every full combination

text: Remove clicks and pops by zooming into the waveform and editing them, or with a click/pop eliminator in the editor's noise reduction menu.
when: Pops still slip through despite using a pop shield during recording.

text: Audition compressed sounds in the game, since lossy compression can produce unpredictable artifacts and default Vorbis quality 40 can be audibly lossy.
when: After applying lossy compression or shipping Vorbis at default settings
why: Artifacts may not show in editing tools; default quality is a generic starting point, not tuned per sound

text: Cut looping sounds into a loop section and tail, and edit the loop point so the join is smooth, since the seam between end and restart is audible.
when: Preparing a sound to loop
why: The join between end and start is audible

text: A loop sound cue must contain an explicit Loop node to repeat; without one, the system's default looping applies, so check loop behaviour during setup.
when: Setting up looped sounds, such as weapon fire

text: Export two files for a loop with folded decay: a first-play version and a looping version, since the looping version on first play gives decays with no notes behind them.
when: Looping music whose decay wraps to the start
why: The folded decay plays wrong on the first playing, before its notes have sounded.

text: Sound filenames must not contain spaces; replace spaces with underscores.
Lower the sample rate only when the sound has no content near its top frequency, since otherwise high frequencies are lost audibly.
when: Deciding whether downsampling is safe
why: Content above half the new rate cannot be represented

text: Stream sounds into and out of memory per game area so only the sounds needed nearby occupy RAM.
when: Large levels with memory limits
why: Limits resident audio to the current area

text: Do not change the sound class of existing engine or tutorial assets, since this can cause unintended effects later.
when: Modifying shipped or provided sound assets
why: Other content may depend on their current class

text: For fast retriggered weapons, use a short fire sample that retriggers and add a longer tail on trigger release.
when: fast retriggered weapons
why: Retriggering long samples exhausts voices and causes phasing.

text: Give the composer control over audio file size so creative choices come first, while removing assets only when necessary.
when: managing audio budgets for constrained distribution
why: Creative decisions lose quality when size limits are imposed without input.

text: Under tight memory budgets, discarding some high-frequency content by lowering the sample rate is often an acceptable cost.
when: Memory is tightly constrained
why: Saved memory can outweigh the loss of top-end detail

text: Game audio trades how much interactivity sound can express against how much memory can be spent storing it.
when: Planning how reactive sound should be
why: More expressive sound requires more stored or generated material

text: A gate can start open or closed and can close after a set number of messages, controlling when events pass through.
when: Designing event flow for sound and alerts.
why: Initial state and message count determine which events reach their target.

text: Converting loops from stereo 44.1 kHz to mono 22 kHz cuts their memory size by roughly a factor of four or more.
when: Storing many loops in limited memory.
why: Lower sample rate and channel count reduce file size.

text: Crossfading is harder with loops, because all elements must stay in sync while they crossfade.
when: When crossfading weapon sound layers by distance in a looping weapon sound.

text: A Continuous Modulator varies pitch or volume from game variables, such as vehicle velocity.
when: Sound should track a changing game value
why: Ties audio response to gameplay state

text: A pawn sound group is a class that holds a character's cues for movement, impacts, pain, death and gibbing.
FMOD and Wwise are common audio middleware that handle parameter-driven mixing with real-time parameter controllers (RTPCs).
Audio middleware is often a friendlier environment for sound designers than built-in engine tools.
A synchronous playSound call scattered across game systems blocks the caller, handles requests one at a time, and runs on whichever thread calls it.
why: These three problems motivate decoupling sound requests with a queue.

text: Back up a script file before editing it so the original can be restored if something breaks.
when: Modifying engine or sound group scripts.
why: A broken script edit can stop the whole game from compiling or running.

text: Audio trackers work best when visuals are hidden by fog or darkness, because the sound heightens tension.
when: When visuals are deliberately obscured by fog or darkness.
why: Obscured visuals push players to rely on sound, and not knowing where a threat is adds tension.

text: Either volume or pitch alone can convey proximity, so the two need not both change.
Placing sounds on an animation timeline with notifies is easier than scripting for people who are not scripters.
when: When sound timing should follow an animation
why: Notifies attach a sound to chosen animation time points, so no script needs writing.

text: Pointing many placed objects at one shared sound asset means adjusting that single asset updates every instance.
when: Many objects need identical sound behaviour and tuning
why: Instances share the asset rather than duplicating it.

text: Switching cues cuts off the old cue's note decays, and crossfading keeps some decay but also keeps all the old cue's other notes.
when: Transitioning between music cues
why: A hard switch ends sounding notes, while a crossfade preserves them along with unwanted material.

text: Summing several on/off states into one counter lets every combination map onto a smaller set of music levels, such as rising danger.
when: When several switches each add to a shared danger level.

text: Audio calls run on the caller's thread, so rendering, AI and other threads hit the API concurrently without synchronization while the dedicated audio thread sits idle.
when: When engine systems run on separate threads across multi-core hardware and the audio API is synchronous.
why: Callers invoke the API on their own threads instead of routing through the audio thread.

text: The volume multiplier can be 1.4 minus the scaled distance, and the pitch multiplier can be (1.6 minus the scaled distance) divided by 2.
when: In an enemy tracker whose beep scales with player-to-enemy distance.
why: Subtracting the scaled distance means smaller distances give larger volume and pitch multipliers.

text: A switch variable can be treated as an array in which each index holds a separate volume value for one music layer.
when: When stem volumes should be set explicitly instead of via engine distribution curves.

text: Players who cross doorways quickly may notice the switching, which breaks immersion.
when: When players quickly enter and exit rooms that use doorway switching.

text: Most script compile errors come from spelling mistakes.
when: When compiling scripts after editing them and errors appear.

text: Scripted audio needs careful planning of triggers and events, which makes the level labor-intensive to build.
1) Link the Touch output to a sound-playing action. 2) Choose New Action, Sound, then the play-sound action.
1) Enable real-time audio playback in the editor. 2) Enable real-time mode for the perspective viewport. 3) Select the ambient actor and open its properties to check the assigned sound.
when: When an ambient looping sound cannot be heard in the editor.

text: 1) Fade out the current state's track over a short time. 2) Fade in the next state's track over the same time. 3) Ensure the two overlap so the change is smooth.
when: Switching between music states
why: Simultaneous fades avoid an abrupt cut between tracks.

text: 1) Give each switch its own trigger. 2) Have each trigger add to or subtract from one shared variable. 3) Map ranges of that variable to music levels with compare nodes. 4) Tune fade in and fade out lengths until the crossfades sound smooth.
when: Music must respond to any combination of several on/off states
why: Ambiguous music in tonality and rhythm makes the necessary transitions between intensity layers appear less clumsy.

text: Any edited script must be recompiled before the change appears in the game.
when: Editing a script, such as a footstep sound group script after adding a surface type.
why: The engine loads compiled script code, not the edited text.

text: Set a trigger's max trigger count to 0 to allow unlimited retriggers.
when: Event sounds should replay each time the player enters
why: Zero removes the trigger count limit

text: Use a parent multiplier with a child correction when one child must ignore a broad change.
when: A broad mix change should exclude one child class.
why: Correcting the child with the inverse multiplier restores its level without naming the other children.

text: Adjust a parent class when one change should cover all its sounds, and a child class when only one kind of sound needs its own level.
when: Choosing where to set a volume or pitch adjustment in the class tree.
why: Settings applied to a parent class propagate to every child sound class beneath it.

text: Replace the referenced cues in a pawn sound group with your own, then recompile the scripts.
Write audio scripts as gameplay descriptions that map each step to the dialogue it triggers, rather than as actor scripts.
why: Mapping steps to lines helps developers align audio with play.

text: The root cause is that playSound tells the engine to play immediately, yet callers invoke it whenever convenient; the fix is to decouple receiving a request from processing it.
Testers without good headphones, or who play their own music, give unreliable feedback on game audio.
when: When running audio playtests.
why: Poor playback or competing sound hides how the game's music actually sounds and feels.

text: 1) Check radii in the Top viewport. 2) Use volume and radii together. 3) Test with Play from here.
why: Radii limit a sound to be heard only around its object instead of across the whole area.

text: 1) Set the volume modulation minimum output near 1.0. 2) Play the sound cue. 3) Move the pitch minimum output up and down to hear the velocity-to-pitch relation.
why: The cue scales the 0 to 5,000 velocity input to 0 to 1, so the minimum output controls the mapping.

text: Having fewer counters or pieces in mid-game can give control of initiative, so the evaluation must encode such preferences rather than just counting material.
when: Mid-game in games like Reversi where the final winner has the most counters
why: Initiative can outweigh a temporary material deficit

text: Games place objects farther apart than real life, so characters take more footsteps over the same distance.
In multiplayer, footsteps can reveal where other characters are and what type of character they are.
Change footsteps with player state, such as heavier steps at low health, to give subtle feedback beyond the health bar.
Limit how many NPC footsteps play at once; keep the nearest or watched one at full volume and attenuate the rest.
when: many NPCs share one sound cue in a small area
why: shared cues in a small area make repetition obvious

text: Background breathing audio that quickens as the player succeeds can convey progress without visual UI.
when: Conveying progress through sound.

text: 1) Examine the footfall. 2) Move it to the nearest suitable location. 3) Adjust the rest of the animation to match, using inverse kinematics.
when: When characters walk up stairs, cross platforms, or must avoid ground obstacles like twigs.

text: Sort materials into sound-blocking and sound-transmitting groups, treating transmitting materials like air.
when: game code for sound propagation
why: Real materials carry sound at different speeds

text: Local footfall correction is practical, while lookahead planning across animations can reach distant goals but needs huge graphs.
Iterative sound spreads slowly, a few nodes per run, which needs shared timestamp bookkeeping; instant spread was found equally believable.
when: When sound travels slowly enough and exact wavefront accuracy is not required.
why: The timestamp already used for smell can be reused to update sound.

text: Diegetic sound sources can draw players toward a location or warn them that other people are nearby.
when: when a diegetic sound source plays in a space

text: Diegetic UI shows information inside the game world, such as an ammo count on the weapon itself; it can strengthen narrative and physical presence but is harder to make usable.

Diegetic music comes from sources within the game world, such as radios, televisions, tannoys, loudspeakers, or characters singing or playing instruments, so players hear it as part of the environment.
Use diegetic information when it is clear and comfortable for players; keep a HUD element when players need stable or additional information the world display cannot give.
why: Removing the HUD entirely adds friction and memory load and can break immersion.

text: When camera cuts are frequent and sound panning becomes distracting, use a separate cinematic sound track with its own continuity instead of following the camera.
when: Cut-scenes with frequent cuts.
why: Decoupling sound from the camera removes sudden directional jumps.

text: Use diegetic music for sources that exist in the world, and non-diegetic music for score-like emotional support.
when: Choosing music source for a scene
why: Source placement determines whether music feels part of the world or outside it.

text: Changing a sequence's play rate scales its motion speed, where 1.0 is normal, and sound tracks placed in it follow that speed without separate files.
why: Samples are triggered individually from the sequence rather than played as one long file, so timing follows playback speed.

text: Making an in-world interface that matches the game's setting while staying clear and easy to perceive is hard.
Built-in open and close sounds fire only at a sequence's start and end, so they cannot mark starting or stopping midway.
when: When a moving object must start or stop partway through its sequence.

text: Sound events fire at sequence timing, so an end marker placed after the final key delays the end sound past the moment motion stops.
when: When the sequence end marker is placed after the final key of the movement.
why: sounds are triggered by the sequence timeline

text: 1) Pause gameplay while the response overlay is shown. 2) Present response choices as UI buttons. 3) Resolve the chosen branch before resuming play.
when: Player chooses a dialogue response

text: 1) Mute camera-relative game audio with a Set Sound Mode action triggered from a Matinee event. 2) Place sound cues on Sound Tracks along the timeline to rebuild the scene. 3) Control overall sequence level with an Audio Master track and fade it with the curve editor.
when: Building a cut-scene whose mix matters more than the camera position.
why: Muting the default mix stops automatic 3D sound from interfering with the authored cinematic mix.

text: 1) Add a sound track to a group in the sequence. 2) Assign a sound cue. 3) Place it on the timeline. 4) Edit its keys to change volume or pitch over time.
when: When a sequence can be played back at different speeds
why: Individually triggered samples follow the sequence's playback speed, unlike one long sample.

text: Prefer diegetic UI in VR when presence is a priority and the information can be shown in the world.
when: In VR, when the information shown is part of the game world
why: Overlays force the eyes to refocus on close elements, causing visual fatigue.

text: Use a brief static burst between tracks when a diegetic radio changes station.
when: when the player switches a diegetic radio

text: Diegetic health systems can increase presence but are harder to get right for usability.
Players respond to audible stealth feedback by choosing silenced weapons, avoiding noisy surfaces, walking rather than running, closing doors, and deliberately making noise to distract enemies.
when: Stealth games where enemies react to sound.
why: Sound becomes a tactical resource the player can control.

text: A movable static mesh that uses the physics engine to collide with level geometry and other such objects reports collisions, and its impact velocity can drive sound logic.
when: Physics objects that should trigger sounds on collision.

text: Real weapons often change character as the clip empties, so a state-dependent fire sound can mirror that behavior.
A player character's bullet impact cue is set in its own pawn sound group.
Player hits play together with hit, crushed or gibbed sounds.
Bullets travel faster than sound, so a player can be hit before hearing the shot, and a bullet whizz-by is the sound of a near miss.
A retriggered weapon restarts its fire sound on each shot while the fire button is held; this suits mechanical weapons at moderate rates of fire.
when: moderate rates of fire

text: Give collision trigger volumes a retrigger delay so a collision sound does not repeat rapidly in quick succession.
when: A player stays in contact or bounces against an object.
why: Without a delay the same impact sound fires many times in a row.

text: Loop a beeping sound until the player uses an available special state, so the player keeps noticing that it is ready.
when: A special ability is ready but unused
why: A repeating cue keeps an unused ability in the player's attention.

text: Frequent machine gun impacts repeat quickly, so modulate pitch and volume and randomly recombine samples.
when: frequent automatic weapon impacts

text: Sounds placed behind the player raise perceived threat, because hearing warns of threats that are out of view, hidden or far away.
when: When the listener hears through a 5.1 or higher surround setup
why: Hearing covers off-screen threats.

text: Bystanders reacting with sound and animation to an entity can reveal that the entity is a nuisance, even if it looks harmless.
when: When nearby townspeople react to an entity approaching them

text: Sound that does not fade with distance makes a threat seem omnipresent and keeps its location ambiguous.
when: When the soundscape is 2D, so sound does not fade with distance
why: A sound without distance falloff suggests both distance and closeness at once.

text: If an enemy reacts to each hit with a sound, and that sound quickens as the enemy closes distance during lulls in fire, its approach builds tension.
when: brief lulls in the player's attacks
why: a faster rhythm signals proximity

text: Relying only on sudden shock sounds weakens horror, because stopping a sound is rarer and more effective at building tension.
