Play informational lines 2D, center-channel-only or radio-processed so they stay audible at any distance; spatialize character lines whose meaning lies in emotion.
when: Choosing playback treatment for a dialogue line; informational lines must be understood more than spatialized
why: Distance attenuation can push a needed line below audibility; routing speech to the center keeps it intelligible, while emotional lines work best in place.

text: Barks often signal a change in AI state, such as hearing something, so players read them as information about what the character perceives.
when: NPC reacts to a stimulus

text: Players notice when a line plays back identically, even hours later, and this can pull them out of the game.
when: A short line repeats across a play session
why: Identical audio is easy to recognize and breaks the illusion of a living world

text: Each escalating line paired with a matching sound effect conveys the character's anxiety.
when: when a character's emotional state changes in play

text: Players can listen to voiceover while fighting, but reading text does not combine well with combat, so voiceover suits action moments.
when: during combat
why: Reading competes with shooting for attention, while listening can happen alongside it.

text: ADR (automated or automatic dialogue replacement, also called looping) re-records dialogue that has unusable quality, with actors syncing to their original performance on screen.
Combat barks, also called soundsets, are short callouts directly tied to combat, and may carry variables controlling how often and when they play.
Subtext is an unspoken feeling conveyed through indirect words, which the audience understands but the character does not state.
Recording game dialogue is very labor-intensive, with scripts of tens of thousands of lines, hundreds of thousands of processed lines, and many takes per line.

Dialogue affects several departments beyond narrative design, including editing, localization and translation, and audio when the game has voiced lines, so writers should keep them in mind while drafting.
why: Each department shapes how the final words reach the player

text: Ambient chatter establishes location or situation, so its atmosphere matters more than the information in its words.
Nonspeech vocals such as pain, dying and screaming are unpleasant to edit, a practical cost to plan for.
Game squads usually get international or clearly localized accents even though a real platoon might share one region.
Adding player counts and events such as passes, tackles and fouls multiplies recording combinations further, and large rosters create the same problem.
Full-motion video dialogue is handled like linear film, usually panned to the center speaker, though some panning may suit the scene.
Dialogue varies widely in dynamic range from whisper to shout, so its levels need processing.

Sound cues are stored in packages separate from their wav files, and each language version of the wav package takes a three-letter language code suffix that the game selects from its language setting.
when: Organizing localized audio in a game engine
why: Separate packages let the engine load the correct language version at runtime

text: Non-word vocals such as screams and pain sounds may not need replacing in localization, though preferences vary by region.
when: Deciding which audio needs localized versions
why: Non-verbal sounds carry little language meaning

text: Face animation to dialogue is normally the animation department's job, and facial animation assets can be created from a skeletal mesh.
A table read is even better when it includes the actors, the VO director, or the audio designers, because it makes the voice actors' work easier.
Written forms such as graffiti can replace dialogue or cutscenes, and narrative designers are often pressured to use as little text as possible.
Text dialogue lacks voice, accent, inflection and emotion, so writers must convey emotion and personality through context and formatting.
Games played on phones and in group settings can feature spoken roles, player decisions and rich narratives, yet compact displays restrict available text space.
Prototype dialogue before final recordings exist using self-recording, the built-in speech synthesizer, or downloadable text-to-speech programs.
when: before final voice recordings exist
why: Getting dialogue in quickly supports testing, and TTS lines hint at final file sizes.

text: Cast voices that are distinctive and easy to tell apart, since characters often speak off screen; a supporting voice too like the lead confuses listeners.
when: When characters frequently speak off screen

text: Use a professional director when possible; if directing yourself, know what you want, communicate it clearly and keep the actor relaxed.
when: When you direct the session yourself rather than hiring a professional
why: Post-production cannot rescue a flat performance, and performance matters more than equipment.

text: Frequently triggered barks need the most variants; coordinate with programmers to learn how often each cue fires, or leave slots empty where cues are not called.
when: Designing NPC barks or voice lines that play often
why: Frequent repetition of few variants becomes obvious to players

text: Sometimes breaths are part of the performance, so leave them alone and adjust the expander threshold instead.
when: Breaths carry performance meaning
why: Breaths keep an intimate feel, while removing them sounds more formal.

text: Use the English recordings as a timing template so local actors can match the original pacing; actors experienced in dubbing film match rhythm to visuals well.
when: Recording localized dialogue for fixed visuals
why: Matching the original rhythm keeps lip movements and cuts aligned

text: After the first mention, refer to a player by pronoun and reintroduce the name later.
when: Writing repeated commentary references to a player
why: Natural speech avoids repeating names and sounds less mechanical

text: Use a second mic placed further away to capture lines meant to sound distant.
when: when a line needs a distant-sounding delivery

text: Spoken dialogue is written more sparsely than on-screen text, and narrative designers must plan for that difference.
Each line of dialogue should express one or more character traits, rather than only conveying situation information.
when: When writing character dialogue
why: Lines that express traits reveal the speakers, not only the plot.

text: In games, answer how and what questions in plain text, and answer why questions, such as motivation and feeling, with subtext.
when: Writing dialogue that must also convey information.
why: Clarity usually outranks expressive quality in games.

text: More game conditions tracked allow more specific dialogue lines to be chosen.
Letting the player pick a character at the start multiplies the number of lines needed across the game, such as doubling it for a male or female choice.
when: Scoping dialogue production for a game with selectable characters
why: Each selectable speaker needs its own version of every line

text: A voiceover keeps playing when enemies return mid-speech, so the player can keep fighting without gameplay being interrupted.
when: Action games where players stay focused on combat while story is delivered
why: Narration stays audible while attention remains on fights, unlike text that demands reading.

text: A good dialogue editor should match a recording rate of 50 to 100 lines per hour.
A 20-team league with home and away games gives 38 games per team, so an opening sentence needs 760 versions to cover every match.
when: Recording sentences with variable names
why: Spoken names fixed into the line multiply the combinations, so each pairing needs its own take to cover the season.

text: Speech such as radio dialogue carries most of its power between about 500 Hz and 4,000 Hz, so the notch is placed in that range.
when: Notching a mode for speech
why: Carving the dialogue's frequency band out of other sounds lets speech stand through the mix more naturally than ducking volume.

text: Informational dialogue conveys what the player must do and is clear, articulate and complete. Character dialogue conveys thoughts and emotion and sounds naturalistic, with emphasis on how words feel.
when: Classifying a line before deciding how to record and play it back
why: The two kinds have different goals, so they need different delivery and playback treatment

text: Sports commentary has two types: play-by-play reflects the specific action as it happens, and color commentary offers background, analysis or opinion, usually during lulls.
when: Designing commentary systems for live sports
why: Each type serves different moments of play and needs different timing

text: Verb-driven story choices are structurally a dialogue tree, with fixed options and responses, differing only in how the choice is expressed.
why: Designers author both sides of each exchange in advance, so nothing needs simulating.

text: Stitching separately recorded words or fragments produces audible seams, tonal jumps and unnatural sound, because pitch flow and word spacing vary between takes, worst in fast or excited speech.
when: Assembling sentences from separately recorded words or name fragments
why: Speech joins depend on phonetic and prosodic continuity that separate takes rarely share

text: Dialogue that contradicts the situation, such as calm chatter during a pitched battle or ignoring a nearby crash, makes the AI look stupid and breaks believability.
why: Dialogue reveals the AI's state to the player

text: A naturalistic informational line can be missed at a distance because it lacks the clarity needed to be understood.
when: Delivering instructions through casual or conversational speech
why: Natural speech is less articulate and attenuates faster than clear, deliberate delivery

text: A translation longer than the English delivery will not fit existing animation without careful adjustment, and close-up faces make sync harder.
when: Localizing lines for close-up or fast-paced sequences
why: Extra syllables must fit a fixed visual timing window

text: Relying heavily on dialogue to instruct the player can make the speech sound less realistic.
when: Games where speech is the main way of guiding players, openly or through hints

text: When voices are recorded after characters are modeled and animated, actors imitate visible motion rather than expressing the character's feelings, losing emotional power.
when: Production order places voice recording at the end
why: Actors must fit lines to pre-made animation instead of driving the performance

text: Dialogue that refers to a game state, such as an empty weapon, fails when no animation or interface exists for that state.
why: Planned visuals or interface for that state were never built, so the line contradicts what players see.

text: Token-filled lines may grow longer in languages that mark gender in word forms, and can then exceed character limits.
when: Localizing token-based dialogue.
why: Grammatical gender adds words that English does not need.

text: Stale voice-over notes left on changed lines confuse actors and directors and can ruin a performance.
when: When a line is revised after its actor notes were written
why: Actors and directors shape delivery from those notes, so outdated ones misdirect the performance.

text: 1) Learn which animators will work on the scene. 2) Confirm they will invest time, assets and effort in any needed visual or spectacle. 3) Keep continuous dialogue between narrative design and the cutscene team.
when: When a cutscene's narrative point depends on visuals the animation team must build
why: The story is only realized as intended through continuous coordination

text: 1) Write a cutscene for your own game. 2) Use an existing sample script as a reference. 3) Format it to match your team's tools or the traditional screenplay layout.
when: practicing script writing for your own game
why: Matching the reference and team format makes the script readable and usable by others.

text: 1) Record stage dialogue even if it may be unusable. 2) Play back the scratch track for actors. 3) Use it to recall the performance and sync any ADR re-recording.
when: recording dialogue on a motion-capture stage
why: the scratch track helps actors recall and sync their performance

text: Reduce overemphasized sibilant consonants such as s and z with a de-esser, which is a compressor that responds only to sibilant frequencies.
when: Recorded dialogue has harsh sibilance
why: Recording can unnaturally emphasize these consonants, so a targeted fix is needed.

text: 1) Record the opening phrase, the item or name variants, and the joining words as separate sound cues. 2) Combine them at runtime from variables that select each variant. 3) Check that each stitched line sounds smooth when joined.
when: Building a recap line from recorded fragments such as shot targets and scores
why: Stitched fragments can sound disjointed unless each piece is recorded and checked as part of the full line

text: 1) Have actors project as if outdoors, not in a studio voice. 2) Lower the actor's own voice in headphones or play wind ambience they must shout over. 3) Avoid proximity effect and experiment with mic distance and angle in an acoustically dead, treated room.
when: Recording dialogue meant to sound outdoors
why: Studio rooms and close mics remove the acoustic space and projection that outdoor speech carries

text: 1) Connect a delay to a set sound mode action that lowers effects and ambience but leaves dialogue alone. 2) After the dialogue finishes, return the mix to default.
when: When key spoken instructions must be heard over a noisy background
why: Ducking background sound keeps critical spoken instructions audible in a noisy space.

text: 1) Trigger a short attention-drawing line as the player approaches a quest giver. 2) On interaction, play a voiceover explaining the situation instead of text. 3) Accept the quest on click, with no confirmation, and update the journal.
when: when the game should avoid interactive dialogue
why: Narration explains the situation without pausing play, since listeners can keep their attention on other tasks.

text: Localized audio files must match the exact length of the English assets, since length differences change the total asset size.
when: Producing foreign-language versions of existing audio
why: Size and timing of each file are tied to the asset budget

text: Use interactive dialogue when the design needs player-responsive dialogue or dialogue that must set variables affecting future events, alignment or approval scores.
when: Games where players choose what their character says
why: Choices set conditionals that the game later recognizes, so future events and reactions depend on them.

text: Do not begin dialogue production until the story, characters and mission details are complete and signed off by all parties.
why: Dialogue is mostly asset management, so starting before content is fixed invites costly mistakes.

text: Keep pitch variation subtle for natural ambience, and avoid pitch modulation on voices.
when: randomizing pitch of ambient sounds
why: audible pitch shifts on voices sound unnatural

text: Have a programmer call sound cues from a database rather than wiring each branch by hand in visual scripting.
when: Large branching dialogue systems
why: Hand-wired branches become unmanageable

text: Foreign-language lines for cut scenes and FMVs must sync to the existing English animation, since reanimating for new timing costs too much.
when: Localizing dialogue tied to animated or filmed sequences
why: Re-animating for different line timing is expensive

text: Record several takes of frequently used lines, and give each character who may speak a line its own version; record at least two versions of every line.
when: Planning how many recordings a game's dialogue needs
why: Common situations recur and identical playback is noticed

text: Assign priorities and expiry times to queued commentary lines; drop a line when a newer event has overtaken it or it has waited too long.
when: Queuing commentary lines for fast-moving game events
why: Fast play makes queued lines stale and misleading

text: Urgent events should override color commentary, and each interruption point needs a recovery line to resume the topic naturally.
when: A commentary line is interrupted by an urgent event
why: Human commentators return to topics with fresh phrasing, and a game needs equivalent recovery lines

text: Batch-convert script lines into separate audio files so you can prototype them and estimate the likely size of final assets.
when: When dialogue is needed in-game quickly for testing before final recording
why: Duration and sample rate of the generated files reveal the likely size of final assets.

text: Place the script on a stand just below head height so the actor projects forward instead of bowing the head.
why: Bowing the head reduces forward projection.

text: Process indirect dialogue, such as overheard comments and radio lines, to match its playback medium before playing it.
when: When speech is heard as overheard comments or radio transmissions

text: Balance the levels of every sound source in a room so that dialogue in it stands out.
when: You control all sound sources in the room
why: Instructional dialogue carries information the player needs, so it has to be heard over other sources.

text: During busy moments such as battle, route dialogue cues into a dedicated speech audio group that boosts them above the mix.
when: Busy action where speech must cut through
why: Busy battle mixes can mask speech, so boosting its class helps it stand out.

text: Record actors for good performances, then process the speech files to suit the game.
Raise vocal pitch with jump height so the audio rises with the motion, which feels subconsciously satisfying to players.
when: jump and fall states with vocal feedback
why: Matching audio to motion reinforces the jump.

text: Suppress tutorial lines once the player has already performed the action, so experienced players do not hear instruction they have mastered.
when: When the player performs a tutorial action before its line would play
why: Experienced players would find instruction for skills they already have redundant.

text: When one box is too full, split information across sequential boxes: the first introduces the scenario and characters, the next lists objectives and rewards.
Leave room in character limits for translation, since some languages expand lines considerably.
when: When text will be translated into languages that mark gender in word forms
why: Gendered word forms in those languages can push translated lines past the character limit.

text: Outside speech scenes, keep dialogue terse and action-oriented; a speech can work if trimmed to a few opening or closing lines.
when: Outside speech scenes
why: Ambient or interactive dialogue can carry story, so cutscene time should feature spectacle the rest of the game lacks.

text: Give actors notes covering pronunciations of foreign or fantasy words, meanings they may not know, and plot facts that shape delivery.
when: writing voice-over comments
why: Actors record lines out of order and often without seeing the game.

text: Make each voice-over comment mean one clear thing and describe the specific tone, rather than using a vague label like sarcastic.
when: In games with large cinematic voice-over budgets
why: Vague labels can be read as anything from cruel to affectionate.

text: Synthesized speech is cheap and needs no storage, but it makes characters sound robotic and undermines seriousness. Subtitles can work better because players imagine a richer voice.
when: When deciding how to deliver spoken dialogue
why: Players' imagined voices usually exceed what synthesis can produce

text: Keeping breaths makes dialogue feel more intimate, while removing them makes it sound more formal or official.
when: Editing dialogue breaths
why: Some breaths are part of the actor's performance and should stay in.

text: Boosting a speech class lets dialogue cut through a busy mix, while balancing levels alone is enough when you control every source in the room.
when: Choosing how to keep dialogue audible
why: Dialogue gets buried under many competing sources, and a class boost raises it in the center channel.

text: Writing many variants of a line is tedious, while hearing one line repeated constantly costs players patience and annoys them.
when: Deciding how many variants a bark set needs.
why: Identical repeated lines quickly wear on players, so bark frequency needs monitoring.

text: A tracker beep that speeds up, rises in pitch and grows louder as the player approaches conveys proximity without visuals.
when: When fog or darkness hides the visuals on purpose
why: It forces reliance on audio and builds tension from knowing something is nearby but unseen.

text: A harsh game-over sound can prompt players to restart quickly rather than linger, so sound choices shape how players respond to failure.
when: designing failure feedback
why: Audio cues influence the emotional reaction and pacing after failure.

text: Interactive sound is tied to events, so the same action should always trigger the same response, giving players dependable feedback.
Start a warning state, such as low health, by adding a heartbeat, a visual filter and reverb together when a variable crosses a threshold.
when: A state the player must notice
why: Layering sound with visual effects reinforces the feeling of danger.

text: Switch a weapon to a distinct warning sound when its ammo falls below a set threshold, giving the player audible feedback on ammo status.
when: Ammo runs low during firing

text: A low-ammo warning can trigger when remaining ammo drops below a threshold such as 25 rounds.
when: Example value; choose a threshold per weapon

text: 1) Use three or more music layers. 2) Set a master timer sound that retriggers all layers so they loop constantly. 3) Compare the health value to a start threshold per layer. 4) When health is below the threshold, raise that layer's volume multiplier.
when: Building music layers that enter and leave with player health
why: A constant loop keeps layers in sync, while thresholds bring them in as health falls.

text: Use sound effects to give feedback on scoring and to mark the start and end of levels.
Instantaneous sound is common in games, while modelling travel delay adds realism at the cost of extra work.
Sound tracks suit repeated discrete events, while a continuous sound needs its own speed variations to follow a changing speed.
Distinct enemy vocalizations heard before enemies are visible let players locate an attack's direction and change their priorities.
when: Enemies approach from directions the player cannot yet see
why: Sound reveals direction and threat before sight does.

text: A distinctive alert sound that signals imminent danger triggers emotional and behavioral responses in players through conditioning.
when: a sound repeatedly precedes danger
why: the sound has been paired with threat

text: Stingers are short motifs or cues played over existing music to highlight or acknowledge specific game events without changing the whole score.
Audio rewards are not rewards in themselves; they enhance other rewards or guide the emotion of a rewarding scene.
Audio feedback feels more visceral than visual feedback and makes touch easier to simulate.
Music can warn players that an enemy is approaching or has spotted them.
Enemy speech and dying gasps indicate enemy health, and symbolic sounds can also convey enemy status.
A bot's pawn sound group covers dodge, double jump, land, default footstep, dying, small, medium and large pain, falling-damage landing, gib, crushed, body explosion and instant gib cues.
Game audio can use motifs and themes as metaphors for characters, mark transitions, and give direct or indirect feedback on progress, as film does.
when: designing music and sound for narrative and progress
why: Recurring musical material links sound to meaning and state.

text: Some sounds signal danger or disrupt play, while others guide players toward destinations.
Use stingers for actions too brief to justify a full change in intensity.
when: when an event is brief
why: Too brief an event does not merit rewriting the score's energy, so a short cue layered over the music fits.

text: Build a stinger from several short variants and choose one at random each time it plays.
when: when a stinger plays repeatedly

text: Stingers work over purely rhythmic background music, since no melody or harmony clashes with them.
when: when the background music has no melody or harmony
why: no pitched content can clash with the stinger

text: Music written for scenarios with a fixed duration can build naturally to a climax, since the timing is known in advance.
when: the scenario has a set length
why: The end time is known in advance, so the music's build can land on the climax.

text: Use sound to confirm player input or announce that something new is about to happen, but not to convey precise information.
when: designing feedback channels
why: Sound signals events well but conveys exact values poorly.

text: A timer-expiry sound jolts players out of a trance-like focus and back to awareness that the game is ending.
when: designing timer or time-limit feedback
why: Sudden audio breaks absorbed attention and restores awareness of time pressure.

text: Hidden audio sources that reward collection turn listening into an optional side exploration activity.
why: Rewards for finding hidden sources give the listening its own goal, separate from the main path.

text: 1) Decide how the interface should feel if it were a real physical object. 2) Choose sounds that create that feeling.
when: When designing sound for a virtual interface that gives little touch feedback
why: Touch is central to feedback when manipulating things, and the mind maps sound to touch, so sound can stand in for it.

text: 1) Start from one short triangle wave as the sole source. 2) Create several sound cues that reference it. 3) Shift each cue's pitch with an oscillator to produce a distinct alarm.
when: building varied alarms from one sound source
why: pitch modulation changes a single tone into distinct alarms

text: 1) Route an alert message through a gate. 2) Set the gate closed when the line of sound is blocked, such as a closed door. 3) Open the gate when the path is clear, so the listener only reacts to audible alerts.
when: Faking a guard's hearing of a noise event.
why: A gate that blocks the message stops the enemy from reacting to a sound it could not hear.

text: 1) Route a damage event to a randomized cue with at least 10 lines expressing uncertainty. 2) Delay the response. 3) Play a give-up line after the delay. 4) Count events in a counter; at a threshold of two rapid hits, trigger the alert.
when: Designing AI reaction to player noise
why: A timed hold keeps the guard alert for a while before it decides the threat is gone.

text: 1) Recheck the distance on a looping delay, at a short interval of 0.1 to 0.5 seconds. 2) Divide the raw distance to bring it to a usable scale. 3) Map the scaled distance to the beep's delay, volume and pitch.
when: When the player holds a device whose beep speeds up and gets louder near an enemy.
why: Raw distance values are too large to use directly as a delay or multiplier, so they need scaling.

text: A distinct sound or visual cue attached to a reward can make players anticipate that reward before they see it.
when: Designing chests, pickups or other reward objects.
why: Players learn the cue-reward pairing and respond to the cue with heightened awareness and anticipation.

text: Attach a short musical stinger to each event that confirms a successful player action, so every success is musically acknowledged.
when: Rewarding precise actions such as jumping onto a moving platform
why: Rhythm-only background leaves no pitched content for an overlaid stinger to conflict with.

text: Stop the adaptive music system when a terminal cue such as victory or death plays, so nothing else follows.
when: when a victory or death cue plays

text: Fire stingers from gameplay events such as hits, playing them as a separate sound over the background music.
when: when a gameplay event needs acknowledgment
why: Rhythm-only background leaves no pitched content for an overlaid stinger to conflict with.

text: Over melodic or harmonic music, track the music's playback position before layering pitched stingers, to avoid clashes.
when: when the background music has melody or harmony
why: Pitched stingers may not suit whatever harmony is currently playing, so they can clash.

text: Give clear, specific direction; avoid reading a line for the actor to imitate, using that only as a last resort.
when: Directing a voice actor
why: Most actors dislike imitation

text: Run a countdown threat on a delay that the player's correct action cancels, so that action also stops the ticking.
when: when a timed threat must be defusable

text: Give each beneficial or harmful pickup type a clearly distinct sound so players can tell them apart by ear.
when: Multiple pickup types with different effects exist.
why: Distinct sounds let players identify the effect without looking.

text: Match audio to the rhythm of the player's clicks and keystrokes, since audio can either support or disrupt that input rhythm.
when: designing audio for digital input-driven play
why: Sound timed against input reinforces the player's pace; mistimed sound breaks it.

text: When paths look identical, give each option a distinct sound so players can listen to find the one that leads forward.
when: visually ambiguous choices
why: Pleasant major-key notes on the correct path let players tell routes apart by listening.

text: Use audio to warn that a hidden threat is nearby, so players can turn away instead of dying unfairly.
when: a threat is hidden from view but the player must act on it
why: Unseen threats otherwise cause unfair deaths.

text: Celebratory sounds like jingles and fanfares can mark solved puzzles, gained items, and victories.
when: after puzzles, item gains, or victories
why: sound marks success for the player

text: Syncing an enemy's death to a musical hit satisfies the music more than exact hit counting, at the cost of slight mismatch with hit counts and collapse timing.
when: Enemy deaths timed to music
why: Players rarely count hits precisely, and a slight delay in collapse often feels realistic.

text: 1) Add a footstep notify to the character animation, marking left or right foot, so footsteps play in sync with foot contact. 2) A script reads the physical material under the foot and selects the mapped sound cue, so each surface is audible.
when: Adding footsteps to a new character
why: Footsteps must be timed to animated foot contact

text: Footfall planning selects a sequence of animations so a character's feet land only at suitable positions, for stairs, platforms and obstacles.
Footstep repetition (sometimes called FRM) is the audible sameness of repeated footsteps, reduced by treating them as movement sounds with variation.
Running, jumping, sliding, tripping and different speeds each produce distinct sounds, since running makes a single impact rather than a heel-toe rhythm.
Collision sound classes: a light plastic thud, a metal crash or crumple, a metal-rending tier with long aftereffects, and a separate most-violent class when a part breaks off.
Limit footfall lookahead to the next couple of animations, treating it as a third pathfinding level.
why: Planning footfalls across a long series of animations produces very large search graphs.

text: Add start and slowing-down sounds, or crossfade by velocity, because characters do not reach full speed at once.
when: walk and run animations are used
why: Real movement ramps up gradually, so sounds should follow the build-up in speed.

text: Choose from several footstep wavs at random, with slight pitch and volume variation, keeping pitch changes small.
why: Identical repeats are what make footsteps feel repetitive, so variation hides the repeated sample.

text: Use slightly different samples for each foot in a left-right rhythm, since people lean more on one side.
why: Uneven weight on each side makes alternating footsteps naturally differ.

text: Playing one impact sound per collision fails when many objects collide at once, because too many voices are used, causing phasing that sounds wrong.
when: Many physics collisions occur in a short burst
why: Simultaneous identical impacts overlap and interfere

text: A jump sound that rises with height gained reinforces that holding the button yields a higher jump.
when: When holding the jump button yields a variable-height jump.
why: The rising pitch matches the height gained, reinforcing the feel of holding for more height.

text: Three grapple sounds carry the claw's physicality: a rising extend tone, a two-part connection impact, and a dull thud when the claw hits an unconnectable surface; no sound plays when it connects to nothing.
when: Grapple extends and contacts a surface
why: Distinct sounds for connection and failed contact make the claw feel metallic and surfaces feel stony.

text: A threshold of more than four collisions within 0.3 seconds switches from individual rock impacts to a single multiple-collision sound.
when: Tuning a dense debris collision trigger
why: Threshold and window values set when the switch happens

text: 1) Obtain separate heel and toe samples, since most footsteps have a heel-contact part and a toe or flat-foot part. 2) Concatenate them into one footstep so each step has a heel-then-toe shape.
when: Creating footstep variation from recorded samples
why: Independent parts multiply the number of distinct combinations

text: 1) Duplicate an existing impact entry. 2) Increase its array index. 3) Set the material type and its sound cue. Custom surface types can be defined and linked to their own impact cues.
when: adding a new surface type
why: Impact sounds are chosen from the material type that the hit surface reports.

text: 1) Count collision events in a short rolling time window. 2) When the count exceeds a set threshold, stop playing individual impacts. 3) Play one prerecorded multiple-collision sound instead.
when: Physics events arrive in dense bursts, such as debris or shattering
why: A single composite sound avoids voice use and interference from many impacts

text: 1) Create a physical material with a new type name and set its parent to the default physical material. 2) Apply it to a material. 3) Add an array entry in the footstep sound group script pointing to your sound cue. 4) Recompile the scripts.
when: Giving a surface its own footstep sound.
why: The default parent makes unmatched surfaces fall back to default footsteps, and script changes only take effect after recompiling.

text: 1) Restrict the key input to an area with a trigger volume. 2) A key press starts the movement sequence. 3) Releasing the key stops it. 4) Play a looping sound only while the sequence reports motion.
when: movement must stop midway
why: built-in open and close sounds fire only at sequence start and end

text: 1) Open the animation set editor for the weapon. 2) Open the animation sequence tab. 3) Add a sound notify at a time point. 4) Reference a sound cue, which plays each time that animation runs.
why: Attaching the sound to the animation makes it fire whenever that animation plays.

text: 1) Use a short looping sound for prolonged contact. 2) Modulate it slightly so it varies as the load on the contact changes.
when: Sustained contact such as grinding
why: Variation tracks the changing weight on the contact point.

text: Leave out, or give a low selection weight to, any footstep that sounds too distinctive, since it stands out and makes the set feel repetitive.
why: A distinctive sample stands out and makes the whole set feel more repetitive.

text: Use animation notifies to synchronise sound with complex reload and firing animations.
when: When reload or firing animations are complex and need precise timing.
why: Triggering the sound from within the animation locks its timing to the motion itself.

text: Group collision sounds into tiers by impact velocity so that harder impacts sound more forceful.
when: When collisions range from light taps to violent crashes.
why: Scaling sound with speed conveys the increasing power of each collision.

text: Editing existing sound cues changes default sounds for everyone using that copy, whereas extending the script with new physical material types leaves existing materials unchanged.
when: Choosing how to customise footsteps.
why: Extending the script isolates changes to new material types, while editing cues alters shared defaults.

text: A key-held sequence can stop midway, while a reversed sequence suits objects that are built up rather than taken down.
when: When a moving object is driven by holding a key.

text: Above a set NPC count, one group sound cue replaces individual footsteps; this saves voices, but players may then struggle to locate individuals by sound.
when: When more than a set number of NPCs share an area.
why: People perceive more than two things as a group, and a single group cue saves voices.

text: Performative music is music the player directly controls, as in rhythm-action games.
Multimodal game music appeals to hearing, sight, and action-oriented touch at the same time, so one musical experience spans several senses.
Note-level interaction usually requires MIDI and sample-based playback, or an advanced stem muting and unmuting system.
Add a global control that changes several intensity layers together over a fixed cycle of pulses to give random textures an overall shape.
when: Generative music sounds predictable or lacks direction.
why: Random textures alone can become monotonous.

text: Use generative methods when a piece must last an indeterminate time without becoming repetitive.
when: Games whose play time can run to hundreds or thousands of hours, such as large online worlds
why: Long play needs variation to avoid repetition, and writing and storing that much fixed music is impractical within console memory.

text: Mapping sound effects to player movement across grid zones lets the player unknowingly compose a score, as each action adds a musical phrase over an ambient loop.
when: designing interactive or generative music
why: Action-linked musical phrases make play itself produce the soundtrack.

text: Recorded everyday sounds, such as doors and household objects, can be turned into tracks that build tension.
why: Sounds that echo genre tropes, such as distant battles or movement inside buildings, heighten tension and signal the actions players must take.

text: Changing a volume multiplier affects a sound only when it is next triggered, not while it is already playing.
when: Driving generative music intensity with volume variables.
why: Short sampled elements make the change sound almost instant.

text: 1) Start a looping delay at the shortest pulse length or regular half-beats. 2) Create a looping switch with one link per pulse, stepping outputs as a sequencer. 3) Attach a random sample from a set to each hit. 4) Add random selectors with empty outputs so some pulses stay silent, and random gates for extra hits on selected pulses.
when: Building generative textures or percussion from short samples in real time.
why: Long non-repeating patterns are produced at low memory cost.

text: Rendering music to a wav file is simple and consistent but big, costly in memory and inflexible, while MIDI with sample banks stays small and allows tempo and controller changes at almost no size cost.
when: Choosing a music format for interactive play.
why: Wav fixes a single performance; MIDI keeps the performance editable.

text: Vary impact sounds by surface material: a coin on wood sounds very different from one on glass, so use a distinct sound per surface, not one generic loop.
when: Designing impact sounds for virtual objects, or sounds that vary with the surface they hit, such as rain
why: Surface changes how the sound reads; rain sounds differently on each surface.

text: When a virtual object makes no sound on impact, the player is reminded the world is fake.
when: A virtual object is dropped or hits a surface silently
why: Silence where a physical response is expected breaks that expectation and reminds the player the world is pretend, destroying presence.

text: Sliding, scraping and rolling sounds are usually driven by velocity mapped to both volume and pitch, though the exact relationship depends on how robust the physics engine is.
The standard physical material set comprises Wood, Water_Shallow, Water, Sand, Metal, Liquid, Glass, Foliage, Energy, Dirt and Default.
The same weapon sound techniques apply to melee weapons such as axes and swords, and to magic spells.
Impact sounds come in three tiers: low is high-pitched and click-like, medium has more bass like a drum, and hard is an exaggerated rubbery twang.
Assign physical materials inside the material itself rather than per object, so every use of the material behaves consistently.
when: Setting up surfaces used across many objects.
why: A single material assignment applies to all its instances.

text: Use many distinct surface types that change often, rather than extra recordings of one surface, because repetition is most audible on continuous surfaces, which are rare in reality.
when: When spacing between game objects forces many footsteps, so one surface type repeats often
why: What counts is how many surface kinds exist and how frequently they switch, more than the footstep sounds themselves; real ground rarely stays uniform.

text: Source impact and collision sounds from recordings of real collisions to ground them in physical reality.
why: Real recordings sound physically credible

text: Layering a few explosion and debris samples in any combination yields many variants; four explosions and three debris sounds give 127 combinations, and it suits melee impacts too.
when: A repeated event needs many distinct variants, such as explosions or hit and punch sounds in combat games
why: Each non-empty subset of layers forms a distinct combination; layering works for any repetitive impact event.

text: A trigger volume shaped around an object can fire a collision sound when the player touches it, so the impact seems to come from that object.
when: Adding impact sounds to objects in a level without physics-based collision audio.
why: Trigger volumes detect overlap and can start a sound event at the object's location.

text: Footstep sounds change with surface type. Each surface's material references a physical material, which selects the footstep sound cue to play.
when: Surfaces built as BSP, static mesh or terrain
why: Footsteps are routed through the surface's material chain, so the surface type determines the sound.

text: An explosion can trigger a temporary mix mode that muffles high frequencies and adds a whine, then resets to default after a few seconds, simulating temporary deafness.
when: A single event should cause a short altered hearing state.
why: Filtering the top end and adding a tone mimics the perceptual effect of a blast on hearing.

text: Hitting a living target gives a heavy organic thud that gets louder and more emphatic as impact speed rises.
when: When a vehicle hits a living creature at high collision speed
why: Layered organic thud sounds that grow with force convey the power of each collision and add sensitivity to it.

text: Playing twenty individual impact sounds for twenty falling rocks produces wave interference and fails.
when: Large numbers of simultaneous small impacts
why: Overlapping identical samples phase against each other

text: Trigger-based collision sounds must be set up separately for each object, and the method cannot cover footsteps.
when: Covering many collisions across a game.
why: Per-object setup is laborious and does not scale to the whole game.

text: Changing a shared material alters every object that uses it, so test changes on a spare or dedicated material instance.
when: Assigning a new physical material to a surface.
why: Materials are shared assets, so one edit propagates to all instances.

text: Impact sound slots on physical materials are blank and hard-coded in the player script, so filling them has no effect.
when: Assigning impact sounds to physical materials
why: The player's script, not the physical material, supplies those sounds.

text: 1) Select a floor surface and find its material in the content browser. 2) Open the material editor and assign a suitable physical material. 3) Save and play the level to check each surface produces its own footstep.
when: Making surfaces in a level sound distinct when stepped on.
why: Without physical materials, all surfaces use the same default footstep sound.

text: 1) Read the hit surface's material type in the attachment script. 2) Look up the impact sound cue assigned to that type. 3) Play that cue at the hit point.
when: instant-hit weapon impacts
why: Looking up the cue by material type lets each surface sound different, mirroring the footstep system.

text: Add echo to large spaces, rustling to grass and thick sloshing to swamps, so players sense how a space would feel to occupy.
why: Sound conveys the texture of a world players cannot touch.

text: Weight memorable impact sounds low inside a random container so they play less often.
when: random containers of impact sounds
why: A distinctive sound stands out on every hit, so it should be weighted to appear less often to avoid being noticed.

text: Give a projectile that misses a wall a different sound from one that hits an enemy, so players can tell outcomes apart.
Music can encourage six player states: searching for hidden things, destroying quickly, realizing a wrong direction, moving carefully, worrying about bystanders, and fast travel without looking back.
when: Choosing music for a scene or section
why: Music works at a deep level, changing moods and actions that players do not consciously notice.

text: Game music usually shifts intensity in response to gameplay variables rather than tightly synchronising to movement, since game action timing is not fixed.
when: Scoring interactive gameplay.
why: Player-driven action cannot be predicted like fixed cartoon timing.

text: Players react to the same track differently, so one track can annoy one player and stimulate another.
why: Music reactions are subjective.

text: Mickey Mousing means music that imitates on-screen action so closely it works almost like a sound effect.
Reactive music changes in response to player actions or game state and only receives commands from the engine. It can use linear sections, horizontal transitions or vertical layering.
Interactive music feeds its current playback position and time until its next transition point back to the game, creating a feedback loop.
Interactive music makes player input part of the music, either by prompting timed button presses along a track or by letting player actions generate the soundtrack.
Game engines such as UDK are limited in communicating with some external music interfaces, so dedicated audio tools like Max or Pure Data may be needed for advanced interactive music.
when: Building advanced interactive music beyond engine tools
why: Engine music tooling does not connect to all desired interfaces.

text: Percussive stingers fit any harmony, whereas melodic stingers can clash with chords they were not written for.
Motifs can belong to individuals, to broad groups such as heroes and villains, or to races or social groups.
Most game music in current games is reactive rather than interactive.
Some games, such as MMOs, can exceed 1,000 hours of play, so original music for the full duration is unrealistic to write and store.
Game music is usually 2D, played over a scene rather than coming from a source.
Linear music suits some designs; demanding games need interactive models where music state feeds game decisions. Simple playback can be enough; choose by time, resources and game needs.
when: Choosing a music model for a game
why: Demanding games need the music state available as an input to their decisions.

text: Any game variable, such as enemy count, ammo, health or hunger, can drive stem volume the same way as distance.
when: Designing adaptive stem mixing
why: The fade mechanism depends only on a numeric value.

text: Keep the current music through non-threatening tasks, and switch only when a new threat appears.
when: when the player performs a task without danger

text: Switch to a driving riff when an enemy appears, so tension rises during fights in confined spaces.
when: enemy encounters in confined spaces
why: a driving riff adds tension

text: In music-based games, correct input plays the music as intended, while incorrect input plays a wrong note or error sound.
when: Player input controls which musical elements sound.
why: Playback is tied to note-level input.

text: Music signals safety or imminent danger, so switching music between exploration and enemy-attack modes changes how threatened players feel.
when: In action games switching between exploration and imminent enemy attack
why: Emotional arousal spreads to the whole situation rather than only its cause, so the music's signal shapes how threatened players feel.

text: Musical notes that speed up as the player gains power and speed link the score to the player's progress.
when: When gameplay actions themselves produce musical sounds

text: Game music falls into three categories: reactive, interactive and performative. They differ in what information passes between the game and the music.
why: Reactive music only receives commands from the engine, while interactive music implies a feedback cycle between game and music.

text: Interactive game music raises two core problems: transitions between musical states when events do not land on musical points, and variation enough to fill play that can last hundreds of hours.
when: When game events can occur at any moment rather than on musical beats
why: Music needs predetermined lengths to stay coherent, which clashes with events that arrive at any time.

text: Switching music by location with simple triggers ignores musical position and entry points, causing brusque, clunky transitions, especially between different keys.
when: Switching music when the player crosses a location boundary
why: A player can cross a boundary at any moment, not at a musical point.

text: Pitch-shifting a stinger to fit a harmony also changes its playback speed, so it is not a clean fix.
why: Changing a sample's pitch multiplier also changes how fast it plays back, so pitch and speed cannot be set independently.

text: Reacting to every game variable makes the link to game systems too obvious, and players feel they're performing the soundtrack instead of playing the game.
when: when music responds to many game variables
why: When players feel they control the score rather than the game, their immersion in the game world breaks.

text: Drive game music intensity and layer selection from variables such as enemy presence, nearby enemy count, player and enemy health, weapon condition, ammo, distance to a save point or target, and pickups, so the score tracks combat state as it changes.
when: Designing reactive music intensity.
why: State changes map naturally to musical intensity.

text: 1) Build in-game examples of the music using middleware such as FMOD or Wwise. 2) Demonstrate them in gameplay to the team. 3) Iterate with designers so the music integrates into the design.
when: When proving the value of interactive music early
why: In-game demonstrations persuade more effectively than describing how music will respond to variables.

text: Establish how reactive adaptive music should be only through thorough testing with several different people, and test the system yourself too.
when: When designing adaptive or interactive music.
why: The right degree of reactivity cannot be guessed; feedback from varied listeners reveals it.

text: Give each character a specific motif, and vary its arrangement, tempo or articulation to convey that character's emotion.
why: Manipulating a character's motif reveals the character's nature and what they feel at any moment, and its appearance signals their presence.

text: Score trailers, cutscenes and credits to a fixed length and to specific visual moments, as in film.
when: Content plays linearly with a set duration.
why: A fixed running length means the music can be timed to known picture moments in advance, as in film.

text: Expose music changes to level designers as preset named events, keeping timing logic inside the music system.
when: when level scripts need to change music
why: designers call events without managing timing

text: Let gameplay events read the music's state, so an event such as an enemy's death waits for the next bar line when the music is ready.
when: when a gameplay event should land on a musical moment
why: the game uses music state as an input

text: Use a game event such as an enemy spotting the player as a music switch input, with the same structure as switching on location.
when: when music should change on a gameplay event

text: Play a distinct announcement and sound when a special state starts, and another when it ends, so the player notices the change.
Grunts are wordless sounds in four kinds: screams of fear, joy or rage; effort sounds scaled to action difficulty; surprise sounds like a sharp breath; and laughter or giggles.
Layer randomised cloth rustle and equipment jangles over footsteps; equipment such as armour can vary the sound and give the player feedback.
why: Movement involves more than the feet, so cloth and equipment sounds are needed alongside footsteps.

text: Record two or three inflection variants of stitched phrases and choose among them by game intensity, so short routine actions and tense late moments sound appropriately different.
when: A line is reused across situations with different emotional weight
why: A single inflection cannot fit every context in which the line plays

text: Layer sounds over events to accentuate an emotion or to contrast it.
when: designing audio feedback for game events
why: Listeners process sound emotionally even without consciously attending to it.

text: Layering N stored sounds in random combinations yields 2^N minus 1 distinct non-silent sounds; 3 sounds give 7, 5 give 31, 7 give 127, 10 give 1,023.
when: Estimating variety from stored layers
why: Each sound can play alone, in any subset, excluding silence

text: 1) Place several sounds in a mixer and set relative volumes. 2) Delay secondary layers by a randomized amount. 3) Add modulators for slight pitch and volume variation. 4) Add attenuation for distance.
when: Building a complex event sound from several layers
why: Each step adds controlled variety and realism

text: 1) Loop a steady, randomized ambient layer of general crowd noise. 2) Layer specific crowd reactions over it. 3) Add variable fade-ins and fade-outs to each layer so it blends naturally.
when: Building sports or event crowd audio
why: Real sports crowds already consist of a constant murmur with reactions on top, so the layering mirrors them.

text: When time is short, blend fragments of existing film or game soundtracks to test a sound direction quickly.
when: when time is short
why: Audible rough mockups show whether a direction works, since people struggle to describe sound in words.

text: Layer sounds on a visual object when you want a new character but the object must still seem to produce the sound.
when: when the object must still seem to produce the sound
why: Seeing and hearing an object together makes the brain fuse them into one event, so layered sounds still read as its own.

text: Layer several recordings together to build the sound of a scene or level.
Randomized fade envelopes create many varied versions from one file, trading playback logic complexity for memory savings.
when: Memory is limited and many varied versions are needed
why: Stored audio stays small while the system generates variety

text: Players judge loudness relative to preceding sounds: a quiet sound feels loud after quiet surroundings, and a loud event's impact depends on its level change from the passage before.
when: Any game with varying ambient and event audio; when a loud sound follows a quieter passage
why: Loudness is perceived comparatively; hearing is sensitive to changes in volume rather than absolute loudness

text: Adding fine detail layers only near a source can keep the mix cleaner when many sources are active at once.
when: Several enemies or sources are audible at the same time.
why: Distant sources contribute only their low-detail layers, reducing clutter.

text: Quiet sounds that matter in calm scenes are masked by louder events during action and go unheard.
when: when loud events play nearby
why: Louder sounds mask quieter ones.

text: Many PC players set their volume by the loudness of a notification sound, such as a new-mail alert, which can be very loud on older systems.
when: On PC, when players set their default volume for a game.
why: Players calibrate their default volume to a system alert they hear, so that alert becomes the reference.

text: Additive mixing brings in new sounds or raises existing ones in response to game variables, in order to signal a state.
Normalization measures a file's peak sample and scales its gain so that peak reaches a chosen target value.
Arrangement is the number of simultaneous sound sources, set by the activity map, voice limiting and occlusion.
Headphones and portable speakers often have limited frequency response, so very high sample rates may add no audible benefit.
when: Choosing sample rates for portable or consumer playback
why: Output hardware cannot reproduce frequencies beyond its range

text: The engine's interactive mixing tools are less transparent than desired and have limits, so simple systems can still be used creatively.
Game mixing resembles music production more than film mixing, because many elements sound at once and the player may listen selectively.
Triggered mixing is also called active mixing, while predetermined and automated mixing are called passive mixing.
A mix can be intentionally busy or intentionally sparse, depending on what the moment needs.
Use an 'Only' sound mode, which silences other classes, to find which part of the mix causes a problem.
when: When troubleshooting a mix problem
why: Silencing all other groups leaves one group audible, so you can hear which part is at fault.

text: Switch sound modes in response to gameplay events, such as when a cut-scene starts, to change the mix.
why: Control over the volume of separate sound groups lets the mix shift with gameplay.

text: A timed mix mode with a recharge period, guarded by a gate, cannot be retriggered while active, keeping its effect predictable.
A class's volume multiplied by a center-channel adjuster gives its center volume, for example 0.2 times 10 equals 2.0.
when: When critical dialogue must be highlighted on a multichannel speaker setup.

text: Starting volumes per category are roughly: dialogue 1.4, weapons 1.1, music 0.75, ambience 0.5. These assume raw files are already at similar loudness.
when: Setting initial volume multipliers for an engine mix, after raw assets are normalized.
why: Perceived loudness is subjective and frequency-dependent, so these are only starting points to tune by ear.

text: What the player hears depends on source volume, source count, timbre, spatial format (3D, stereo, multichannel), distance attenuation, reverberation, occlusion, and global, group or bus volume controls.
why: Control over the mix is needed for the player to make sense of many simultaneous sounds.

text: Six concerns shape a game soundscape mix: arrangement, panning, volume, compression and limiting, EQ, and reverb.
why: Games must convey information through many simultaneous elements, so mixing resembles music production more than film.

text: Perceived loudness depends on frequency content, not only sound level, so averaging decibel values or matching peak levels can make sounds seem wrong or unequal.
A playing sound's volume cannot be changed by a volume multiplier set on playback; the multiplier only applies when the sound starts.
Ducking the whole volume of many sounds can sound artificial; a subtler method called notching may suit better where it fits.
Interrupting a mix mode loses the prior state unless it is tracked explicitly, so the system does not resume it afterward.
when: When a different mode interrupts an active mode and that interrupting mode later ends
why: The system does not record the mode that was active before the interruption, so it falls back to the default instead of resuming it.

text: Editing the shared sound classes and modes package changes every later call to that mode across the game, so back up the original before changing it.

1) Divide the game into contained windows such as save-point segments, levels, or exploration and conflict sections. 2) Plan loud and quiet passages within each window. 3) Balance intense sections with quiet or tense ones.
when: Planning the dynamic shape of game audio
why: Players return at different times and volumes, so a single film-style climax cannot be relied on

text: 1) Scale the game variable into a useful volume range. 2) Send a fade trigger each time the value changes. 3) Move the volume to the new level over a short fixed time.
when: Driving music volume from a changing game value
why: Short fades keep changes smooth while tracking the value.

text: 1) Attach a trigger to the player so it moves with them. 2) Give it a radius of about 900 units. 3) Count enemies entering the radius. 4) When more than two are inside, stop one playing sound and toggle off two toggleable ambient sound actors.
when: When more than two enemies are inside a radius around the player
why: Quiet ambient sounds would be masked by the louder nearby events anyway, so removing them cleans the mix and frees headroom.

text: 1) Play the console startup sound and dashboard sounds. 2) Set your playback so these are comfortable. 3) Mix the game against that level, which approximates typical player listening volume.
when: No professional mixing room is available
why: Players rarely want to adjust volume during play, and platform startup sounds already reflect a level people set for their own systems.

text: 1) Activate the altered mix mode when the event occurs. 2) Play the event sound and any tone. 3) After a fixed duration, reset the mode to default.
when: A short, single-event altered audio state.
why: A timed reset returns the mix without manual intervention.

text: Keep quiet sounds and music quiet so that loud sounds stand out, and avoid making everything loud.
when: Mixing game audio across all content
why: Without quiet reference points, players lower the volume and loud moments lose their impact

text: Play movement sounds louder briefly when the surface changes, then let them fade, since they compete for headroom and voices in firefights.
when: during combat
why: movement sounds crowd out voices and weapons

text: Set predetermined preamp levels for normal, whispered and shouted lines to get the best signal-to-noise ratio for each delivery.
Reset a sound mode manually when its end is tied to an event, such as an explosion, so the event's audio is unaffected by the mode.
when: when the mode's end is tied to a scene event
why: A fixed timer could work, but a manual reset is considered safer, and resetting when the scene event fires keeps that event's audio unaffected.

text: Mix so players never need to touch the volume control to hear the game.
why: Players listen through very different devices and setups, and they should not have to reach for the volume control.

text: Normalize assets to full scale where possible, since in-engine mixing reduces gain rather than boosting it.
when: Preparing source files for a game mix.
why: Mixing can only lower levels cleanly, so headroom must be preserved at the source.

text: Manual leveling by an experienced engineer gives the best result, but is rarely practical at around 350,000 lines, while automatic averaging of wav volume rarely works.
when: Leveling large dialogue volumes
why: Hand-riding faders across that many lines takes too long, and automatic averaging fails because perceived loudness depends on more than the average level of the file.

text: Directional microphones artificially boost bass when the speaker is very close, a phenomenon called the proximity effect; voices within about three inches are likely affected.
when: Positioning a speaker relative to a directional microphone
why: Directional mics respond to close sources with extra low-frequency gain

text: A correctly positioned pop shield keeps an enthusiastic speaker at a safe distance from the microphone.
when: Recording energetic or close-speaking actors
why: The shield physically limits how near the actor can get

text: Off-axis frequency response differs from on-axis response, and combined with projected performance it can suggest outdoor space.
when: Choosing mic angle for an open-environment effect
why: Off-axis pickup changes timbre and reverberant balance

text: Very early in the morning is often quiet, which makes it a good time for field recording.
Use close mic placement for dramatic, boomy voices and avoid it for normal dialogue; a normal distance is roughly 8 to 18 inches.
when: Choosing mic distance for a recording session
why: Proximity boost enriches lows for dramatic effect but colors ordinary speech

text: Avoid compression and EQ during recording so that processing choices stay flexible later.
Position the mic above the actor's head, angled toward the mouth, with a pop shield to reduce popping from plosive consonants.
why: Placing the mic above the head keeps it clear of the script stand, and the angle plus a pop shield reduces the air bursts from plosive consonants.

text: Carry a portable recorder so unexpected interesting sounds can be captured when they occur.
Non-diegetic music is score-style music that characters in the game world cannot hear, similar to a film score.
Ducking means temporarily lowering the volume of playing music, for example under important dialogue.
Notching cuts a frequency band in a sound mode's EQ where competing sound sits, so a sound comes through without lowering overall volume.
Predetermined elements are set before run time, automated elements are processed at run time, and triggered elements respond to events or variables at run time.
Routing sounds into a shared group lets one control adjust many sounds at once, like a drum group controlling a whole kit.
A mixer snapshot stores the volume of each group plus settings such as EQ or effects, and is called a sound mode in UDK.
Music targeted at the player plays to the player's ears without panning, which suits non-diegetic music.
Mix design balances two demands: giving players information and giving them emotion.
The default audio class hierarchy has three top-level parents, Music, Voice and SFX, and other classes such as Weapon sit beneath them as children.
Each sound group has volume and pitch that act as a master control for every cue assigned to it.
Adding LFE bleed on a system that already uses bass management can cause comb filtering, since low frequencies are routed to the subwoofer twice.
Dedicated speakers for impact sounds, placed so their blasts can be felt physically, reinforce a sense of place.
why: Sound arriving from many directions, including dedicated speakers for the blasts, gives the impression of being out on the water.

text: Prefer unique sounds sent to the LFE channel over LFE bleed where the system allows it.
when: Low frequencies need to reach the subwoofer on a multichannel system.
why: Dedicated sub content avoids the comb filtering of double-routed bass.

text: Soundmode changes are cumulative: a child class's change stacks on its parent's, and the audible level is the combination of both.
Only one primary snapshot can be live at once; activating a new one replaces the current, while modifier mixes scale sound group values on top without replacing it.
when: Designing a mix system with several overlapping mix states.
why: Separating a base state from temporary adjustments avoids one state overwriting another.

text: SoundClasses form a parent/child tree that works like a mix bus group, so changing a parent adjusts all its children, letting one setting control a whole family of sounds.
when: Organizing sound effects, music and voice in a game mix.
why: Hierarchical grouping lets a single adjustment cover related sounds.

text: Music that closely matches its scene and sound effects tends to fade into audio obscurity.
when: When music closely mirrors the mood of the scene and its sound effects
why: Expected, matching music blends into the scene and is forgotten, whereas an unexpected musical motif stands out in memory.

text: 1) Assign frequency bands to sound groups that often play together. 2) Set ballpark volume per category. 3) Normalize each asset folder in the DAW. 4) Finish these decisions before the formal mixing stage.
when: Preparing audio assets before the mix stage on a game.
why: Planning frequency and level in advance keeps overlapping sounds from masking each other at runtime.

text: 1) Schedule the loud event's sound with a short delay. 2) Just before the event, briefly lower all other sounds. 3) Let the event play at full level while the rest of the mix is ducked.
when: A loud event needs impact but no quiet lead-in is possible.
why: The sudden contrast between ducked and full-level sound makes the event hit harder.

text: 1) Select the cue in the editor. 2) Set its sound group in the properties panel. 3) Verify the group in the list view.
when: Assigning audio cues to mix groups in the engine's editor.

text: A sound played via a cue must belong to the ambient class for ambient zones to influence it; sounds linked straight to ambient actors need no such class.
when: Using sound cues in ambient or scripted playback; ambient zones appear to do nothing to a cue.
why: Zones only affect ambient-class sounds; the mismatch produces no error, while other classes simply pass through untouched.

text: Mix for how people listen, not for what microphones record; treating an accurate recording of a scene as the goal is a mistake.
when: When many sounds overlap in a busy scene, as at a crowded party
why: Microphones hear objectively, people listen subjectively.

text: Edits to a shared sound mode package affect the whole game, so restore the original settings when finished.
Draw mix ideas from film, literature and other art forms, not only from other games.
why: Other media such as film and literature hold a long tradition of subjective, emotional mixing that games can draw on.

text: Give sounds that will often play simultaneously distinct frequency ranges, such as music in one band and effects in another, so each keeps some room.
when: Many sounds and music share the same area.
why: Sounds competing in the same frequency range mask each other.

text: Ambient sound actors that play without an assigned cue are placed in the Ambient class automatically.
when: Ambient actors play sound without a cue.

text: Abstract projectile music is a musical space with no goals or rules where player-fired bouncing projectiles hit note-tuned panels, so the player builds a piece by layering bounces.
Aleatoric methods leave some aspects of musical output to chance while the composer controls the range of possibilities.
Anempathetic music expresses an emotion different from the on-screen action, sometimes the opposite of it.
Designer music is composed to shape listeners' feelings in targeted ways, and it resembles modern game scores.
Some game music works more as a soundscape than a melody, shaping atmosphere rather than carrying a tune.
Consider alternative instrument palettes before defaulting to a large orchestra, since orchestral scores fit genre expectations but provoke milder reactions.
when: Starting a new score.
why: Most listeners already know the orchestral sound.

text: A composer-friendly authoring tool for interactive music is the missing link between composers and interactive music systems.
Writing music in short blocks and allowing state changes only at block ends keeps musical continuity while still reacting quickly.
when: When game events need to change the music quickly
why: A transition that sounds musically wrong also loses emotional impact, so limiting changes to block ends keeps the music coherent.

text: Nonlinear music with dissonance can evoke fear.
Familiar cultural music styles paired with dread-filled scenes create unease through contrast with their usual cheerful associations.
Somber music played during an intense fight can sharpen a tragic moment by contrasting with the action.
when: When the music should express an emotion that differs from, or opposes, the on-screen action

text: Judging interactive music as concert music skews the verdict, because many listeners' tastes come from linear film scores.
when: When listeners evaluate interactive music without gameplay
why: Linear film listening habits do not match how music functions in games.

text: Aleatoric textures suit ambient music but can sound samey or noodly, so they need added variation or dramatic control.
when: When producing ambient music that should not feel too repetitive
why: Randomness is itself predictable, so random textures can become monotonous and lack dynamic change.

text: 1) Propose a new, bolder musical idea the producers may not have considered. 2) Prepare a predictable version alongside it. 3) Use the predictable version as a fallback if the new idea fails.
when: When presenting music concepts to producers
why: A fallback reduces the risk of trying unconventional ideas.

text: Engage early in design as an advocate for music where it helps and as an advocate for silence where it is not needed.
when: When participating in early design discussions about sound
why: Composers often work from only a text design document with no finished footage, so early input matters.

text: Use anempathetic music when a moment should feel surprising or emotionally sharp.
New age music raised relaxation and lowered hostility and tension, but it also lowered mental clarity and vigor, trading alertness for calm.
Tying music or sound tempo to game speed, such as enemy movement speed, gives players an audio cue that danger is increasing.
when: When enemies speed up during play
why: A heartbeat-like sound that quickens with the enemies has a very visceral effect on the player.

text: Blend music with sound effects and world sounds, using environmental and creature noises as instruments, so effects and loops are heard as one integrated piece.
when: composing game audio
why: Separate-sounding effects break immersion; blended audio strengthens immersion.

text: Reserve music for emotionally important moments and fade out persistent states, since constant music loses its signalling power.
when: Deciding how often music plays or when music signals important events.
why: Constant music stops signalling anything; contrast with silence makes situations stand out.

text: Instrument choice evokes a time, place and culture faster than melody, harmony or rhythm.
when: Choosing an instrument palette.
why: Instrumentation is the most immediately evocative musical element.

text: Music acts continuously and largely unnoticed; the unconscious mind converts it into a steady current of feeling.
when: during play or film with background music
why: conscious attention skips music while the unconscious keeps processing it

text: Sounds that echo genre tropes, such as distant battles or running out of ammunition, quickly signal the situations players expect.
why: The sounds reuse familiar genre conventions, which adds tension to each level.

text: Empathetic music supplies the emotion a moment expects, like a climactic theme for a large battle, completing it rather than repeating what is on screen.
A leitmotif is a musical motif tied to a character, group or entity, so that hearing it signals that subject's presence or state.
A score can express the feeling that underlies what a player does in the game.
Artwork and sound can convey a physical state such as cold, such as visible breath, shivering, or wind whistling, without real conditions matching.

Genre music norms: casual/puzzle games use simple loops; platformers use retro synth; racing uses licensed pop; sports/simulation use menu-only or licensed radio music; strategy/RPG/MMO use location music; action/shooter are cinematic.
Music explicitly tied to game variables becomes an informational device that can convey information players cannot get elsewhere.
The same melody can feel lonely on a solo flute and ready for battle on brass and drums, so instrumentation shapes its emotional meaning.
Streaming large recorded files from CD, DVD and Blu-ray made rendered audio practical and it became the mainstream choice over MIDI.
why: Storage capacity removed the file-size constraint.

text: In-world music sources help establish a game's time, place and culture.

Streamed audio gives consistent playback, arguably better sound quality, and recorded musicians, which MIDI with DLS cannot match. MIDI with DLS suits memory- or bandwidth-limited platforms or note-level control.
Unlike music, most game audio originates with things and creatures inside the game's environment.
Music is universal across humans and can trigger visceral responses.
Music can modulate activity in limbic structures involved in emotion, including the amygdala, hypothalamus and hippocampus.
The brain is drawn to certain repetition, and music's tendency toward repetition makes it inherently pleasurable.
Nonmusical sounds carry strong emotion: grinding metal evokes tension, a pulse evokes anticipation, rain evokes calm, whistles evoke silliness, and squelching evokes disgust.
Compose each character's motif to fit with the others, writing them over the same harmonic structure and defining locations through accompaniment instrumentation.
when: Many motifs and locations may sound together.
why: Shared harmony keeps melodic clashes manageable.

text: Music can act as a theme that channels the design; if part of the game clashes with the music, that part should change.
why: Music chosen early already settles many subconscious decisions about the game's feel and atmosphere.

text: Writing layers over a static harmony, such as a single chord or drone, makes vertical combinations easier and reduces the repetition a chord cycle creates.
when: When writing for a generative system that recombines layers through controlled randomness
why: With no harmonic change, motifs never need to be checked against a moving chord, and a single drone avoids a cyclical chord feel.

text: Positive meanings often rise in pitch and negative meanings often fall, a rule of thumb borrowed from speech.
when: Designing positive and negative feedback sounds
why: Speech conveys positive meaning with rising pitch and negative meaning with falling pitch.

text: Fast tempo with large pitch variation tends to express joy, and melodies in minor keys are often perceived as sad.
