Music that departs from a genre's conventional instrument palette can help a game feel distinct from its peers.
Fast songs aid mental clarity, smoother songs aid relaxation or concentration, and slow music with oppressive riffs lowers mood.
Slow, melodic music with faint echo can make a space feel ethereal.
why: Players cannot physically touch game spaces, so sound such as echo supplies the sense of material texture.

text: Accompany the gain of a new weapon or ability with a heroic tune.
when: When players gain access to a new weapon or ability
why: Pairing a sound with a specific, repeatable event closely links them and reinforces the player's sense of agency.

text: In reward vaults or vistas, use a relaxing melody that contrasts with the intense rhythms of the challenge before it.
when: after intense challenges
why: contrast marks relief and reward

text: A piece of music that suits the intended play makes many subconscious decisions about the game's feel and atmosphere.
when: When choosing music at the very start of development, before the game's details are settled
why: Music that fits how the game should feel already embodies many decisions about its atmosphere.

text: Sudden sounds shock, but stopping a sound that has been present since the start creates anticipation, which builds tension.
Sparse melodic instruments and a constant ambient wind can produce relaxation and happiness.
Pleasant major-key tones can mark forward paths, while harsh minor-key tones mark paths that return players to the start.
when: When players must pick between visually identical paths
why: Sound cues let players tell apart paths that look the same, so they can choose by ear.

text: With n independent on/off music variables there are 2^n combinations; ten variables give 1,023 non-empty combinations.
when: Planning how many distinct musical states a game can produce
why: Each independent on/off variable doubles the mix count, so few sources can yield many combinations.

text: A tempo-matched pulse can emit a beat event on every beat and a measure event on the first beat of each bar, to drive timed music changes.
when: when music changes must align to the beat or bar
why: Transitions must land on the beat or bar line, so the pulse signals let switches wait for those points.

text: 1) Listen to game music and describe the emotions it evokes. 2) Watch the levels the music accompanies. 3) Note whether the music matches the action or contrasts with it.

1) Give each threat a rating. 2) Have overlapping threat areas add their ratings, capped at a maximum. 3) Compare the total against thresholds, playing the matching intensity layer and stopping the others.
when: Mapping overlapping scare sources onto music intensity levels
why: A central variable summing triggers lets the music reflect how many threats are near.

text: 1) Play the soundtrack alone, away from the game. 2) Judge whether it recalls much of the feeling of play. Strong recall means music carries much of the emotion.
when: judging how much emotion music contributes
why: Music is processed unconsciously into a continuous feeling and separates easily from the rest of the experience.

text: Choose music early, possibly before the game is fully defined, since it shapes the game's feel.
why: A piece that already feels right gives an early target for how the game should play.

text: Use genre music conventions as a starting point, and depart from them deliberately when the design calls for it.
Use a legacy music-track node only when one piece must play unchanged across a whole level.
why: It offers no way to stop it once started or to trigger a fade out, unlike other sound nodes.

text: Let mix and music chart the emotional landscape of a game, shaping how it feels across its moments.
Fast tempo suits action and slow tempo suits relaxation, and rhythm that follows natural body beats feels natural.
when: Choosing music tempo
why: Tempo is tied to the body's own rhythms, so pace maps onto arousal.

text: Occlusion simulated for player audio has little effect on whether an AI character learns of a sound.
when: When deciding whether an AI character becomes aware of a sound
why: AI hearing uses only distance attenuation, while occlusion matters only for what the player hears.

text: Obstruction is when an obstacle blocks the direct sound path while reflections from the room still reach the listener.
Exclusion is when direct sound reaches the listener through a gap such as a doorway, while reflections hit the obstacle.
Occlusion is when a wall, object or surface blocks the path between listener and source, muffling both direct and reflected sound.
The Max low-pass radius setting defines the distance where the low-pass filter is fully applied, fading toward the Min radius setting.
when: Configuring distance-based filtering on an ambient sound
why: Filter strength is interpolated between the two radii

text: The volume and frequency content lost to occlusion depends on the material, and brick has a strong muffling effect.
Some engines need the level geometry defined for them before they can trace occlusion.
Exact real-time occlusion exceeds the processing budget usually given to audio, so developers fake it.
Modern engines trace a simple path from each emitter to the listener; if geometry interrupts it, a filtered version plays, filtered live or prerendered.
A point-source ambient sound is heard clearly through walls because the engine does not block it at walls, and attenuation must stay wide enough to fill the room.
when: a sound source sits inside a small room near walls
why: the engine does not occlude sound at walls

text: 1) Place an ambient zone for each blocking wall. 2) Filter or attenuate exterior sounds inside the wall zones. 3) Keep the listener's room sounds and any doorway or gap outside all zones unfiltered.
when: When a sound and listener line up through a doorway
why: Leaving the doorway unattenuated is a cheap imitation of sound passing through a gap without full modelling.

text: 1) Identify where the listener and source are separated by an opening or barrier. 2) Place a zone that only filters at openings. 3) Place a zone that filters and attenuates at solid walls.
when: Engine lacks native occlusion for a barrier
why: Specific zones approximate occlusion where automatic systems are unavailable

text: A zone that only filters keeps the volume of a sound heard through an opening like a window, while a zone that also attenuates reduces it, as a wall would.
when: Simulating sound passing through windows versus walls
why: Openings transmit high frequencies less than full volume loss

text: In air, sound pressure falls with the square of distance, so volume roughly halves, about 6 dB, each time distance doubles.
Driving pitch and volume with separate oscillators makes them modulate independently, rather than following a single cycle, producing a more organic looping sound.
when: Creating looping sounds such as insect buzz
why: Independent cycles prevent pitch and volume from moving in lockstep

text: Using a scaled game value as an index into a lookup array of volume values produces non-linear volume curves that are easy to edit.
when: mixing layers from a game variable such as distance
why: The default mapping is linear, so an array lets the designer define custom volume curves.

text: An example modulator range keeps pitch between 0.4 and 1.05 and volume between 0.1 and 1.0 of full volume.
when: Setting a starting range for pitch and volume modulation
why: Ranges are a starting point to tune per sound

text: In the sound mode EQ, frequency is set in Hz, gain runs from 0.0 to 1.0, and mid bandwidth runs from 0.1 to 2.0.
why: Bandwidth numbers are not intuitive, so measuring the output of white noise reveals the effect.

text: Linear velocity-to-volume mapping can feel wrong, because a small change in velocity may not sound like a proportional change in loudness.
1) Poll the health value at short intervals. 2) Normalize it to a 0 to 1 range by dividing by its maximum. 3) Subtract from 1.0 to get volume for a layer or sound that should rise as health falls.
when: a music layer or sound should grow louder as health drops
why: Inverting the normalized health makes low health correspond to high volume.

text: 1) Enable rigid body collision notification on the physics object. 2) Route the impact velocity through a divider to bring it into a usable range. 3) Feed the result into the sound's volume multiplier. 4) Set the sound origin to the physics object. 5) Tune the divider value by ear.
when: Making a physics collision sound louder for harder impacts.
why: Raw impact velocities are far outside a usable volume range, so scaling is needed.

text: 1) Create a movement track in a sequence editor for the moving sound. 2) Place keys by moving the actor to each position and adding a key on the timeline. 3) Set red markers for the sequence start and end and green markers for the looping section. 4) Start the sequence at level startup and enable looping.
when: Making a sound travel a path, such as birds or insects moving through an area.
why: Keyframed paths let a sound pass by or circle the listener.

text: 1) Add music layers to the scenario. 2) Change float values with Set Variable. 3) Listen to how each layer's volume responds to each change.
when: Testing how music layers should respond to game variables

text: Scale effort sounds to the difficulty of the action, so a small jump and a large climb sound distinctly different.
when: A character performs a physical action with variable difficulty.

text: Phasing loops are intentionally layered loops of different lengths, distinct from the phasing artifact, which is a problem to avoid.
Sounds with more high-frequency content are more affected by phasing, so avoid overlapping them.
when: choosing sounds that will overlap
why: Copies of one sound offset by only a few milliseconds make their waveforms interfere, producing an audible artifact.

text: Phasing is a comb-like artifact when the same sound overlaps itself or several copies play together, a few to 35 ms out of time; subtle pitch variation reduces it.
when: the same sound overlaps itself or several copies play together
why: the offset waveforms interfere

text: Loops of different lengths at the same tempo drift against each other and realign only after their lowest common multiple of bars, producing long non-repeating combinations.
when: Layering rhythmic loops of different bar lengths.
why: Each restart meets a different section of the other loop.

text: Two loops of 3 and 4 bars realign after 12 bars; 6 and 8 bars after 24; 7 and 9 bars after 63.
when: When layering two looping parts whose bar lengths differ.
why: Each loop must finish whole cycles before both start points coincide again, so the combined pattern only recurs then.

text: If overlap cannot be avoided, detune the copies slightly using the pitch property of the ambient sound source.
when: same sound must overlap
why: slight detuning breaks up the interference

text: Phasing loops work best with rhythmic elements; harmonic combinations are often too complex to avoid clashes predictably.
when: Choosing material for loop layering.
why: Harmonic parts combine in too many ways for clashes to be foreseen and avoided.

text: Players rate identical graphics higher when the game has high-quality audio than when it has low-quality audio.
when: comparing versions with the same visuals
why: Sound conveys bodily, touch-like feedback more readily than sight, so audio quality affects how the visuals are judged.

text: Audio details that go unnoticed on screens add a great deal to presence in VR.
To reproduce a frequency accurately, sample at twice that frequency, so content up to 12 kHz requires a 24 kHz sample rate.
when: Choosing a sample rate for a sound
why: Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem

text: Sound memory budgets vary widely: early-2000s console-class systems had about 2 MB for sound, handhelds up to about 500 kB, and current-generation consoles about 15 to 25 MB.
when: Estimating memory for a target platform
why: Values are ballpark and depend on hardware and project sharing

text: Cinema mixes play at a known reference level in theaters, while games are a home medium with setups from mono TV to 7.1 surround.
Modern titles occupy hundreds of megabytes, and art and audio now far outweigh code in size.
Perceptual lossy codecs discard audio listeners are unlikely to notice, like high frequencies or sounds hidden beneath louder simultaneous sounds.
when: Compressing audio with perceptual codecs
why: Removed content is chosen by what listeners are unlikely to notice

text: Consumer formats such as MP3 decode slowly, so they are generally unsuitable for sounds that must start instantly in games.
when: Choosing a playback format for instant sounds
why: Decoding needs processing time and power

text: Cross-platform projects are often built to the lowest specification among their platforms, so the weakest memory budget constrains everything.
when: Shipping on several platforms
why: One shared asset set must fit the smallest target

text: 1) Inspect the sound's frequency display to find where its energy lies. 2) Play white noise through the target platform's speakers to hear its real range. 3) Choose the lowest rate that keeps the needed content.
when: Before fixing a sample rate for a target platform
why: Displays and listening reveal the true content and playback limits

text: 1) Raise the sound one octave in an audio editor, which halves its file size. 2) Import it. 3) Play it one octave down in the engine to restore the original pitch.
when: Memory is critical, such as portable consoles or smartphone downloads
why: Halving the sample rate by pitch-up stores half the samples

text: Avoid depending on platform limiters, which stop distortion but act unpredictably; design the mix so they are rarely needed.
why: Built-in limiters act crudely and in ways that are hard to predict.

text: Larger or longer sources produce deeper pitches, so pitch-shifting one recording can represent differently sized versions of an object, conveying size without extra visuals.
when: Several objects share one basic sound source and differ mainly in size, or when designing sound effects for objects of varying size
why: Pitch relates to the size of the sound source; low pitch suggests mass and power, so consistent pitch communicates size

text: A continuous modulator scales its input range to 0 to 1, and its minimum output values set the lowest level for volume and pitch.
Per-element modulators or separate cues for each layer give finer control than a single shared modulator.
when: Layered cues need individual control over their elements
why: Each element can vary independently

text: Keep modulation ranges moderate so that varied sounds still remain believable.
when: Setting pitch or volume random ranges
why: Extreme variation makes a sound sound unnatural

text: Random pitch modulation in a fire cue only partly reduces retriggering problems.
when: When a long fire sample is retriggered frequently.
why: Subtle pitch changes soften waveform interference between overlapping retriggers, but only to some extent.

text: Modulation adds variation to a sound without storing extra samples, saving memory.
when: Memory is limited and variety is needed
why: Variation comes from runtime parameter changes

text: Large pitch shifts can change a sound's character, so one recording can serve different sources, such as a chicken call reused as rats.
when: Reusing a sample for a different object
why: Strong pitch changes alter timbre as well as pitch

text: Active modifier mixes combine by multiplying their values, so two modifiers on the same sound group compound their effect.
when: Several modifiers scale the same sound group at once.
why: Multiplying scale factors makes independent modifiers stack without naming each other.

text: A parent class multiplier applies to all its children, and a child can be corrected with its own multiplier, so the two combine as a product.
when: A broad change should apply to a family but one child must keep its level.
why: Multipliers multiply down the class tree, so a child value of 2.0 cancels a parent value of 0.5.

text: Pitch multiplier = target frequency / source frequency. For a source at 220 Hz, A4 (440 Hz) is 2.0 and C3 (130.81 Hz) is about 0.595.
when: Retuning a looped single-cycle sample to other notes
why: Playback rate scales pitch linearly with the ratio of frequencies

text: 1) Set minimum and maximum pitch values on the modulator. 2) Set minimum and maximum volume values. 3) Each time the cue plays, the modulator picks random values within those ranges.
when: Adding variation to a sound without new samples
why: Random values within ranges produce varied playback

text: Storing a sound an octave higher halves its size but can lose high-frequency content at the top of the range; downsampling loses more.
when: Choosing how to shrink a sound file
why: Octave-up storage keeps more quality than plain downsampling at the same size

text: Reflection pattern signals space: distinct echoes suggest distant outdoor surfaces, many quick reflections a confined tunnel, sparse long reflections a large room; muffled or absent reverb suggests open outdoors or no reflection.
when: Choosing reverb character or designing ambient sound for a location
why: Listeners judge room size, shape and enclosure from how reflections and reverb arrive over time.

text: A quiet repeating sound buried in ambience is hard to locate, so a temporary sense-boost mode can help players find it.
when: when a quiet repeating cue is buried in ambience
why: Temporarily focusing on one source pulls attention to it, so it can be picked out of surrounding sound.

text: Reverb is a dense cloud of reflections, while an echo is a single distinct repeat of a sound.
Acoustic properties such as reverb and off-screen placement characterize an environment as much as the objects in it.
Close listening to real-world sounds is the key skill for building detailed, believable sound worlds, even when the environment is simple.
when: designing ambient sound
why: detail comes from careful observation

text: Looping sounds feel false when heard repeatedly, so reserve long loops for the sounds that matter most.
when: designing ambient soundscapes
why: repetition of a loop is noticeable

text: Give weapon sounds prebaked layers and different tail samples for each reverberant environment where they will be heard.
when: Weapons fired in varied acoustic spaces

text: Convincing ambience is built from many layers of sound at different distances, such as distant, middle distance, and close, rather than a single sound.
when: When building background ambience to make a game world feel alive.
why: layers at varied distances give depth, as an oil painting is built from many layers

text: Dry studio dialogue placed in a reverberant scene sounds unnatural unless processed with the scene's reverb first.

1) Make separate inside and outside sound sets. 2) Place a trigger volume around the interior, such as a doorway. 3) On entering, switch off outside sounds and switch on inside sounds; reverse on leaving. 4) Fade between sets over about one second.
when: sound differs inside and outside a room; faking occlusion cheaply at a doorway
why: avoids overlap between the two sound sets

text: Use an imitation reverb system: 1) Keep the dry fire sound in the weapon script. 2) Send a console event on each shot. 3) Play extra reverb layers from that event. 4) Set each trigger volume's multiplier so position controls which layers are audible.
when: weapon sound must vary by location; built-in reverbs do not suit the weapon
why: built-in reverbs can be too blunt for a weapon

text: Fill a room with several smaller ambient sound sources instead of one point source, so the sound comes from across the room.
when: a single point source does not fill the room
why: one point source sounds localized rather than spread through the space

text: 1) Use one recorded hissing sample. 2) Vary its filtering and pitch to suggest different sources. 3) Check the variations in context.
when: Creating varied ambience from a single source sample
why: Filtering and pitch change perceived source character

text: 1) Add a Looping node and a Delay node to a cue. 2) Set Delay min and max equal to the desired interval. 3) Place an ambient sound actor with auto play on.
when: Building repeating ambience at fixed intervals
why: Looping plus delay produces a regular repeat

text: 1) Place looping outdoor ambience and indoor room tone as ambient sounds. 2) Create a reverb volume enclosing the interior. 3) Set interior and exterior volumes and apply some filtering. 4) Rebuild level geometry so the zone takes effect.
when: Switching between outdoor sounds and an enclosed space
why: Zone attenuation only applies after geometry is rebuilt and volumes are set

text: 1) Size a builder brush around the area. 2) Convert it to a reverb volume. 3) Pick a reverb preset type. 4) Set a fade time for room transitions and a volume strength. Ambient sounds inside the volume receive its reverb.
when: Adding reverb to a room or area in a level editor.
why: Abrupt reverb changes between adjacent rooms sound jarring, so a fade time eases the transition.

text: 1) Import a still concept image into a simple video editor. 2) Stretch the image along the timeline. 3) Add about one minute of environment ambience.
when: When early concept visuals are available before the game is built.
why: Sound is hard to describe in words, so a working demonstration communicates an idea better than documents.

text: Add a looping mechanical room tone inside an enclosed hangar as an ambient sound so the interior has its own character.
when: Designing an enclosed industrial space

text: Switching gives either inside or outside sound rather than a blend; it is acceptable where noise levels would mask the difference anyway.
when: When noise levels or occlusion mean the other sound set would not be heard anyway.
why: Without separately filtered versions of each set, switching cannot produce a realistic muffled blend.

text: Modelling reflections accurately in real time needs a lot of computing power, so games normally use precalculated reverb presets instead.
when: Choosing how to produce reverb in a real-time game.
why: Full reflection modelling costs more processing than a game budget usually allows.

text: A long hall reverb suits a location, but a battle may need reverb removed or a different wet/dry balance, so reverb choice depends on the situation.
when: When game design brings a battle into a location otherwise suited to long reverb.
why: A location's realism alone does not settle the mix; situational demands change the appropriate reverb and wet/dry balance.

text: Listeners first hear a meter introduce itself, then come to form an expected schedule from its repetition.
when: while listening to a metered piece
why: repetition builds expectation

text: Music-based games make performing music the core mechanic, judging the player mainly on input timing and, with a microphone, on pitch accuracy.
Meter is the set of repeated elements across a piece of music.
Faster music speeds up people's actions, while slower music makes them linger longer and consider extra purchases or options.
when: Music is used during play or in venues where pacing matters
why: The music's tempo sets the pace of actions, and people do not notice this influence.

text: In rhythm games, a warning light sequence precedes each note, and a trigger volume around the note detects the player's shot.
when: Building a note-timing rhythm mechanic.
why: Warnings give the player time to hit the note accurately.

text: Heavily rhythmic or strongly directional music is hard to make work in games because the player can interrupt it at any point.
when: Choosing music style for interactive play
why: Interruptions break rhythmic and directional structure.

text: 1) Send each note through a gate that opens only at the correct moment. 2) Log a good note when the player's input meets the open gate. 3) Log a dead note otherwise. 4) Add or subtract score values for each event.
when: Scoring a timed note-hit mechanic.
why: Gates separate valid and invalid hits by timing.

text: 1) Place the music on the timeline and play it. 2) Tap a key at musical points to create target events. 3) Enter tempo and beats per bar so targets reach the hit area one bar after they are triggered. 4) Shift the music one bar later so events line up with the first beat. 5) Connect hit and miss sounds to scoring.
when: when building a simple rhythm action prototype
why: Tempo and beat count set target speed so each one arrives at the aim area a bar after it is triggered.

text: Two sound cues can reference the same wave with different count limits, and the game can switch between them as circumstances change.
More than two similar sounds are heard as a group, so decide whether instances must sync precisely or use a grouped sound file.
why: Listeners perceive more than two similar sounds as one group.

text: Variation effort should target sounds that vary in the real world; mechanical sounds like weapon fire are similar each time and can repeat without loss of realism.
when: Deciding which sounds need multiple variants
why: Real-world variation is what players expect; mechanical repetition is believable

text: Vary other DSP such as envelope or filter on each repetition where the engine allows it.
when: When the engine allows envelope or filter changes on each repetition.
why: Footstep repetition irritates players more than most game audio, so each repeat needs variation.

text: Vary each part's volume with a modulator so that repeated combinations do not sound identical.
when: When background music plays for long stretches in areas players may stay for hours.
why: Long stays make exact repetition of the same background music wearing on players.

text: For fast looping, choose sounds that are not heavy or booming; high-frequency elements loop well at high rates.
when: fast-firing looped weapons

text: Random selection without replacement excludes recently played sounds until all have played, then resets the pool, so repeats are spaced out. With two inputs it alternates between them, so the same sample never repeats back to back.
when: Choosing among several variants that should not repeat back to back
why: Prevents the same sound from playing consecutively and spreads repeats evenly

text: Randomly combining aligned tracks inside a sound cue yields a different mix each time, and varies layers within one tension level.
when: When the goal is variation inside one tension level rather than moving between tension levels

text: Making symbolic sounds too varied makes them feel like they belong to a different game and weakens their learned meaning.
when: For symbolic feedback sounds whose meaning comes from the information they convey
why: Listeners respond to what the sound signals rather than its texture, so the same sample can repeat, but each sound must stay distinct.

text: Excessive sound gimmicks turn corny and may backfire, producing the reverse of the feeling intended.

1) Put all variants or lines in a single Random node, optionally weighted. 2) Enable randomization without replacement. 3) Track which item has played and pick randomly from the remaining ones, so each returns after the longest possible gap.
when: Building a sound container with several variants or lines that repeat often
why: Reduces repetition in short succession

text: 1) Create a range of variants for each frequently played interaction sound, per sound tier. 2) Choose one at random for each instance. Hearing the same sound repeatedly becomes annoying and distracting.
when: Interaction sounds or sound tiers that play often
why: Varied sounds avoid repetition that draws attention away from play and fatigues the listener

text: 1) Pick a random heel segment. 2) Pick a random toe segment. 3) Play them in sequence each time the cue is called.
when: Playing a footstep or similar two-part sound at runtime
why: Random pairing gives varied output from few samples

text: 1) Surface the fade durations of each sound-playing node. 2) Attach a random float to these durations. 3) Retrigger the sounds so each play uses new random values.
when: Making looping ambient layers less static
why: Changing envelopes each playback adds movement

text: 1) Use one source recording for all objects of the type. 2) Set a pitch scale per object, higher for smaller and lower for larger. 3) Verify each variant sounds right.
when: Multiple sizes of the same sound-producing object
why: Avoids storing a separate recording per size

text: 1) Play a sound with randomized fade-in length. 2) Stop it after the fade-in delay so it fades out. 3) Pick a new random fade-out length and restart after it plus a short gap.
when: Generating many varied wave-like loops from one sample
why: Changing envelope lengths reshapes one file into many waves without silence

text: Maintain a healthy variety of each ambient sound type so no single line dominates.
when: For combat barks and other vocal sounds that crop up frequently during play

text: Random gating of extra hits adds unpredictability, with a lower chance on rarer pulses and a higher chance on common ones.
when: Adding variation to generated rhythms.
why: Always playing the extra hit would be predictable, so a random gate keeps it unexpected.

text: Unrestricted random layer combinations maximize variety, while weighted and limited combinations reduce variety but give more musical results.
when: choosing how to combine random music layers
why: unrestricted randomness can produce unmusical combinations

text: Subtractive mixing removes or filters out non-essential sounds during a special state so the remaining sounds dominate and the state feels focused.
A SoundMode is a snapshot mix that sets volume, pitch or EQ for selected sound classes and is triggered from scripting or the console.
Automated volume ducking can be overridden at run time, so it counts as a triggered mix behavior rather than a fixed one.
Sound mode values are multipliers applied to the class tree, not absolute levels, so changes stack down the tree.
Snapshot transitions may take effect instantly or be spread across a transition window.
Fire shell shock automatically when an explosion occurs within a set radius of the player, not only by manual trigger.
when: Building a shell shock effect for real gameplay.
why: Automatic triggers keep the effect tied to the player's actual proximity to the blast.

text: Snapshots can be keyed to states like in-game or menu, places, or occurrences such as a power-up or shellshock.
why: Each snapshot stores group volumes and other mix settings, so switching states adjusts the whole mix together.

text: A Set Sound Mode that targets a sound class silences every sound outside that class, including ambience.
when: Switching to a dedicated cinematic mix.
why: Only sounds in the chosen sound class remain audible under the mode.

text: A mode's initial delay sets when its change starts, fade-in time sets how long it takes to apply, and fade-out time sets how long it takes to undo. A duration of 1 lasts until the next mode change.
A sound mode's EQ has three bands: a high shelf, a low shelf, and a parametric mid band.
why: A parametric mid band can notch the frequency range where the dialogue's energy sits, so it cuts through without ducking everything else.

text: A sound mode with a limited duration can end before the event it supports, such as a line of dialogue, so choose an infinite mode or lengthen it to cover the event.
when: When a line of dialogue runs longer than the sound mode's set duration
why: The mode switches itself off when its duration expires, restoring the mix before the event has finished.

text: New or edited sound modes may not appear until the engine editor is restarted.
1) Store the current mix mode in a variable when it changes. 2) Before reverting to default, check that variable. 3) Restore the stored mode if it is still wanted.
when: A temporary mix mode must return to the prior state when it ends.
why: Explicit tracking preserves the previous state that the snapshot system does not keep.

text: Priority snapshots restore the previous primary snapshot automatically when a higher one switches off, but a single snapshot slot loses the prior state unless tracked separately.
when: Primary snapshots with priorities are tracked, or two mix states must coexist, such as a shell shock during an altered-hearing mode.
why: Tracking the loaded snapshot lets the system restore the prior state automatically, while only one active state can occupy a single slot.

text: A SoundCue is a node-based playback system that can choose, modify and spatialize sounds, not a single wav file.
when: Setting up interactive sounds
why: Most interactive sounds need selection and variation logic

text: The speaker node in an audio cue graph sets global volume and pitch multipliers, maximum simultaneous playback count, and facial animation data for the cue.
when: Setting overall cue volume, pitch or polyphony
why: Global settings govern every sound the cue triggers.

text: Cue graphs are built from nodes such as Speaker, Attenuation, Concatenator, Delay, Distance Crossfade, Looping, Mixer, Modulator, Continuous Modulator, Oscillator, Randomized, SoundNodeWaveParam and Sound Node Mature.
when: Designing a cue graph
why: Each node performs one playback or variation job, and chaining them builds variety

text: The musical aesthetic producers want may differ from what the composer expected, so concepting should happen before much music is written.
when: At the start of music production

text: Audio sketches set a prototype's tone and help bring animatics and other prototypes to life.
In game audio, creation and implementation cannot be separated, so composers need to understand the systems that govern their music.
Audio mockups make people quickly voice dislikes, influence other departments such as animation, form early sound associations, and prompt team discussion.
Sound effects are often revised to reduce perceived violence, as seen with film age ratings.
Game sound makes flat images feel substantial, sets mood, describes off-screen space, and gives feedback on actions and status.
Sound design work is often grouped into atmospheres, weapons, creatures and spells.
Game sound design follows the Foley process used in film, with the added requirement that sounds be repeatable in play.
why: Repeated playback makes identical sounds stale, so the design must support variation.

text: A sound designer may be asked for effects and music late in production, or may lay out the full audio plan early so sound supports gameplay.
Sound is a major part of how players understand a gamespace, alongside visuals, mechanics, and problem-solving.
Build a quick audio mockup and play it for the team instead of describing the sound idea in a design document, since most people lack vocabulary for sound.
when: When people struggle to describe audio or a sound idea
why: People react well to a concrete example even when they cannot put a sound idea into words.

text: Use other games, earlier entries in the same series, and films as musical references, since established cues act as emotional shorthand.
when: When discussing music style with producers
why: Shared references convey emotional tone quickly.

text: Extract maximum variety from minimal source material, and grasp your tools thoroughly to exploit their full potential.
when: Designing game audio under memory limits
why: Interactivity must be balanced against the memory available to store sounds

text: Use subjective or interpretive audio that reflects the character's state rather than strict realism when it better serves the moment.
when: The character's state matters more than a literal sound source.
why: Audio shaped by the character's perception strengthens immersion from their point of view.

text: Use ducking and EQ changes in the mix to focus attention and model altered physical or psychological states, which deepens immersion.
when: When a character's altered physical or psychological state should be conveyed
why: Shifting the mix toward subjective sounds lets the player hear the world through the character's point of view.

text: Re-creating existing soundtracks in video quickly reveals whether a sound designer has a good ear.
when: When assembling a sound design demo reel
why: Recreating an existing soundtrack directly exposes how fine a listener's ear is for detail.

text: Train listening by tapping, rubbing and scraping everyday objects, and by stopping to notice sounds in the street.
Sound need not be realistic to be satisfying; exaggerated, stylized sounds can give more satisfaction than realistic ones.
Use simple effects that share one consistent relationship, such as pitch and size, rather than many splashy effects with no common logic.
when: when choosing how much polish to add to sound and visuals
why: Consistency conveys physical properties more clearly than lavish effects

text: When visuals become more realistic, replace playful effect sounds with ones that match the physical interaction so actions seem logical.
when: Raising visual realism in a stylized game
why: Mismatched sounds break believability

text: Sound effects repeatedly paired with threats, failures or successes become conditioned cues that trigger matching emotions when heard again.
why: conditioning links a sound to the outcome it accompanies

text: Sound creates rhythms that players learn to expect, which can change their speed and support layered challenges.
Adding music and sound only at the very end of development is a common mistake.
A stat fix can go unnoticed when sound is poor, and a sound fix can seem like a balance fix.
when: Evaluating weapon changes
why: Players judge weapons by how they sound as well as their numbers.

text: 1) Edit existing music against the game's graphics or illustrations. 2) Present the edits to producers as references. 3) Use the reactions to find the desired style before writing full music.
when: When establishing a music aesthetic early in production
why: Producers often lack musical vocabulary, so real examples communicate style better than words.

text: 1) Identify separate peaks with gaps in a waveform. 2) Mark and save each peak as its own file. 3) Concatenate the files in random order inside a cue.
when: Working with sounds made of distinct peaks, such as beeps
why: Separate events can be reordered into new sequences

text: 1) Pitch the recording up in an audio editor. 2) Import it. 3) Play it back at the inverse pitch scale in the engine to restore its original pitch.
when: A needed pitch shift exceeds the engine's range or the file must shrink
why: Compensates for the engine's limited pitch range

text: 1) Mark the musical in and out points of each section of a commercial track. 2) Calculate bar-line times from tempo and beats per bar. 3) Store markers as file metadata. 4) Call markers at bar lines during play.
when: The track has a steady tempo and its sections map clearly to intensity levels.
why: Markers allow interactive switching without cutting the audio file.

text: Talk through the character and context with the actor before recording, and stay open to an original angle the actor brings.
when: Before a voice recording session
why: Actors become upset when the director seems unsure, so talking through the character builds their comfort and confidence.

text: 1) Build a normal version of a scene. 2) Build a second version with a changed theme. 3) Compare the two to see how sound shifts mood.
1) Pause at each branching point. 2) Listen for whether the guiding sound gets louder or softer. 3) Choose the direction where it grows louder.
when: a sound marks the correct branch
why: A difficult maze of four-exit rooms makes a loudness shift at each exit a usable route signal.

text: Judge interactive game music inside the game, in the context where players will hear it, rather than as standalone concert listening.
when: When reviewing or approving game music
why: Music's job is to improve the game, and players experience it in context.

text: Before recording, multiply interaction sound types by surfaces to test whether the planned set fits the memory budget and recording time.
when: Planning a set of interaction sounds
why: Hearing repeated samples breaks immersion, but full coverage can exceed RAM, disk and time

text: Record all equipment and actor-relative mic and script positions with photos and measurements, stored in the session, so later lines still match.
when: when lines may be recorded in different studios or months apart
why: Lines recorded later in other rooms can stand out as sounding different unless the original setup is reproduced.

text: Keep rejected sound concepts, since they are often wanted and approved months later.
when: When a producer later asks for new sounds after earlier ideas were turned down.

text: Capture location and studio recordings cleanly, so they remain usable as source material for later processing and layering.
Game audio balances good quality, large variation and small memory footprint; a project can usually satisfy only two of the three.
when: Deciding which quality to sacrifice for a sound
why: Each pair of goals costs the third

text: Spatialized sound makes sounds seem to come from a particular place, and it is important and powerful in VR.
Attenuation makes a sound quieter with distance, because games cannot reproduce real-world volume and physics and must approximate them.
A directional sound cone gives a source a front: full volume inside the inner cone, a set reduced level between inner and outer cones, and a reduced, low-pass filtered level outside the outer cone.
when: Modelling sources that are louder and clearer in one direction.
why: Directional falloff mimics how a speaker sounds from behind compared with in front.

text: 2D sound plays over a scene regardless of how far the source is from the viewpoint, establishing setting and atmosphere.
3D sound grows louder as the player nears its source, marking specific locations and making areas feel more or less spacious.
Many engines ignore walls and lack accurate sound propagation, since full propagation exceeds console processing power, so occlusion needs deliberate workarounds.
Sound is carried as compression waves in any medium, and its intensity falls with distance from spreading and friction.
In air, sound moves at roughly 345 meters per second.
In first-person games, sound comes from the player's head, which is the camera; in 2D, third-person or fixed isometric games, sound may come from the character or a point offset from it.
Directional sound cones were not available in UDK at the time of writing, so other engines may be needed for this effect.
when: Choosing an engine for directional audio.

text: Keeping versions of a sound with different filter settings allows variation for conditions such as hot sun or dense fog.
when: Designing atmospheric audio across environmental conditions.

text: Stereo files, ambient sound simple actors and any sound cue without an attenuation object are usually not spatialised.
when: Checking which sounds pan or attenuate.

text: Spatialisation gives direction information, which matters most for weapon fire, footsteps and dialogue.
when: Deciding which sounds to spatialise.
why: Direction helps players locate threats and understand speech.

text: A copied animated actor that already has movement sounds keeps them, so each duplicated segment moves with its own sound.
Multichannel files play to fixed speakers and do not pan, so they suit explosions, surround music and quad or surround ambiences.
Layouts such as 5.1, 6.1 and 7.1 each use a different subset of the channel suffixes.
Files with matching channel suffixes import as one combined sound wave.

Sound travels from a source as waves and reaches the listener directly (dry) or after reflection or passage through materials (wet), and the balance between them tells listeners about their surroundings.
Stereo sound files do not pan in UDK, so the spatialize option has no effect on them, though they still attenuate when played from an object.
when: Engine sound playback with stereo files.

text: Standard spatialization applies a low-pass filter over distance, which may not suit weapon sounds.
In third-person or isometric games, camera-based audio can reveal sources the character cannot see; keep camera-based spatialisation where the player's view and hearing should match.
when: Designing listener position for third-person, isometric or aligned-perspective sequences
why: Camera sees more than the character, so its audio can reveal unseen sources; matching sound direction to view reinforces spatial awareness.

text: Spatialised music or score pans oddly and distracts the player, so lay it as non-spatialised stereo or move only part of its reverb into the surrounds.
when: Adding music or score to gameplay or cut-scenes.
why: Spatialising score makes it pan oddly and distracts from the action.

text: Real-world sound falloff is not copied directly in games, because playback dynamic range is limited, game distances differ from real ones, and very large radii keep many quiet sounds playing.
when: Setting attenuation radii for game sounds
why: Recording and playback cannot match physical dynamic range, and wide radii consume voices

text: Pair a non-spatialised stereo ambience bed with locally spatialised spot effects, since obvious panning across a stereo ambience sounds odd.
when: Building environmental ambience.
why: The bed stays stable while localised sources give direction.

text: Distance bands can switch between sounds using comparison logic, so each range plays its own cue.
Mono files spatialise to the object playing them and pan between speakers as the player moves; stereo files play directly to the listener without spatialising or localising.
when: Choosing file channel format for world sources
why: Spatialization needs a single source position, which stereo files lack.

text: A sound plays at full volume inside its Radius Min sphere and fades to silence at its Radius Max sphere.
why: Real-world volume falloff cannot be reproduced in games, so a radius-based fade is used instead.

text: Spatialized copies pan as the listener moves, so several copies can make one source sound like many. Disabling spatialization stops this panning.
when: multiple spatialized ambient copies
why: each copy's stereo position changes with listener movement

text: Applying a low-pass filter whose strength depends on distance makes one stored sound sound duller in the centre and brighter at the edges, letting one sample serve several places.
when: One sample must appear in several locations with different tonal character
why: High frequencies are removed more as distance decreases

text: Air absorbs high frequencies over distance, so sounds get duller as they travel; a distance-based low-pass filter can approximate this, brightening as the listener approaches.
when: Simulating realistic distance attenuation of distant sounds.
why: High frequencies are absorbed more than low frequencies as sound travels through air.

text: Smaller, high-frequency detail layers are added as the listener approaches a source, so close-up sounds reveal more fine detail.
when: A complex sound source with several components.
why: Distance attenuates high frequencies and small components first, so they appear only up close.

text: A cue outside its attenuation's maximum radius is not played, so when it enters the radius it starts late and falls out of alignment with other parts.
when: When layered musical parts are gated by distance so they only sound near a listener.
why: Playback is skipped for cues the listener cannot hear, so a late-entering cue never lines up with the rest.

text: A system that monitors sound levels at the player's location can cull masked quiet sounds, cleaning frequency content and creating headroom for important sounds.
when: When many sounds overlap, such as during battle, and quieter ones are masked.
why: Masked sounds add nothing audible, so dropping them avoids clipping and muddy frequency buildup.

text: Distance algorithm and min/max radius settings in attenuation determine how clearly a sound's direction and distance can be heard.
when: When off-screen enemies approach and their vocalizations must indicate direction before they are seen.

text: Inside a cue's minimum radius a sound plays normally, while outside it the sound is heard as a personal radio with center speaker routing, radio effects and no distance attenuation.
when: A cue uses the radio filter setting.
why: The radio filter replaces spatial playback beyond the radius.

text: Muffled, distant sounds heighten the sense of how near and far things are.
when: When landscaping sound to suggest the distance of a feature such as a waterfall.
why: Muffling marks a source as far away, so it contrasts with nearer sounds.

text: Delaying sound so it moves near 100 meters per second feels noticeably realistic in third- and first-person titles.
when: When the game chooses to model a delayed speed of sound instead of instant travel.
why: Many games let sound travel instantly, and real sound speed is too fast to notice, so the delay must be slowed to be perceptible.

text: Common distance attenuation curves are linear, logarithmic, inverse, log reverse and natural sound. Linear suits looping room tone; logarithmic suits short-range sounds; inverse suits loud distant sources; log reverse suits sounds stopped by walls.
when: Choosing a falloff curve for a point source
why: Each curve shape matches a different listening situation

text: Center channel, bleed, rear and spatial effects need a 5.1 or higher multichannel speaker system; expecting them on stereo playback will fail.
when: When the mix is heard on a stereo system rather than surround hardware.
why: They are only clearly audible on surround hardware.

text: Overly large attenuation radii fill the mix with quiet sounds, consuming headroom and voices.
when: Setting max radius for many point sources
why: Every audible source takes a voice even when it is quiet

text: Sound that pans with a turret or camera rather than the driver's position can feel wrong to the player.
when: Vehicle sounds tied to a rotating turret or camera
why: Panning that disagrees with the player's viewpoint breaks immersion

text: Getting attached to early sound ideas is a pitfall, because they will change several times.
when: When early audio concept tracks are being shared with producers for feedback.
why: Listeners struggle to describe audio but reject examples quickly, so early concepts mainly reveal what people don't want.

text: Using raw distances, which run into the thousands, directly as delay times produces delays of around 1,000 seconds.
when: When a game-unit distance value is fed straight into a delay or timing object.
why: Game distances run into the thousands, far beyond a useful time range, so they must be scaled down.

text: Curve-based vehicle tuning is hard for non-programmers to reach, so designers often need custom vehicle versions.
when: When vehicle engine pitch is driven by velocity-to-RPM and torque curves in the engine.

text: 1) Put 2D and 3D audio cues in a map. 2) Watch how players react to the 3D cue. 3) Check whether the 2D sound changes how players view the map.

1) Select the sound actor and open its properties (F4). 2) Under the simple ambient sound settings, open Attenuation and set Radius Min and Radius Max. 3) Or select the actor, press space to cycle to Scale, and drag the square handles to change the Max radius.
Use several instances of the ambient sound to fill the room without spilling past the walls, in engines lacking occlusion.
when: a source must fill a room but not leak
why: multiple sources keep the sound inside the space

text: 1) Render a filtered version of a sound in an audio editor. 2) Crossfade between the dry and filtered files by listener distance using a distance crossfade node. 3) Set the closest input to full level near the source.
when: The engine lacks a filter-over-distance setting.
why: Prerendered filtering can capture complex frequency changes that a simple low-pass filter misses.

text: 1) Copy the sound cue and re-reference the playing sound. 2) Enable spatialization, attenuation and attenuate-with-low-pass-filter. 3) Adjust the low-pass filter radius maximum and minimum until the distance falloff sounds right.
when: Making a distant sound darken with distance.
why: The low-pass radius values set where filtering begins and ends.

text: 1) Import channel files with suffixes to get one combined multichannel sound. 2) Loop it in a sound cue. 3) Re-import the channels without suffixes. 4) Place a note per speaker position and target each with a sound cue and playback.
why: Suffixed channel files merge automatically on import, so stripping suffixes keeps each channel separate for per-speaker playback.

text: 1) Count NPCs within a radius of the player. 2) When the count passes a set number, swap their footsteps to tighter attenuation curves. 3) Use separate curves for single-player and multiplayer.
when: When many NPCs reference the same cue within a confined area.

text: 1) Create an object variable for the sound target in the scripting graph. 2) Assign any actor, including an invisible note actor, as the source. 3) Use a tag display option to locate the source in the editor.
when: Playing a sound from a position that has no visible mesh.
why: The note actor appears in the editor so it can be placed and selected, yet it stays hidden during play.

text: 1) Split the stereo file into left and right channels. 2) Play each channel through a point source at its own position.
when: Spatializing a stereo music source in the world
why: Separate point sources give a stereo file a localized position.

text: 1) Attach a dynamic trigger to the player actor. 2) Set an offset behind and above the player. 3) Play the sound through that trigger.
Play a sound through the in-world object it comes from so it appears to originate there and attenuates with distance as the listener moves away.
when: Sounds that should appear to originate from a location or in-world object
why: Distance attenuation makes the sound fade as the listener moves away from the object.

text: Match echo to the room, since echo in a small room differs from echo in a large one.
when: Designing ambience for virtual spaces
why: Believable echo depends on the space's size

text: Size each sound's radii so it covers its own area and does not spill into neighbouring rooms.
when: level layouts with several adjacent rooms
why: Radii set how far each sound is heard.

text: When attenuation is set inside a shared sound asset, instances cannot adjust the falloff radius per placement in the level.
when: Placing many instances of a shared sound asset
why: Attenuation is stored in the asset, not per actor

text: Spatialise mono sound sources that come from a physical point, such as a radio or television, so they pan through the speakers as the player turns.
when: Placing in-world sources.
why: Panning a point source gives direction, which helps the player locate it.

text: Play music not tied to a specific object as 2D to the player, so its stereo image stays fixed while the player turns.
when: Music or distant stereo ambience without a source location.
why: A 2D sound is not positioned in the world, so it does not pan or attenuate with the listener.

text: Stop a diegetic sound when its source is destroyed, and play an effect at the source to show it.
when: when the source object is destroyed

text: Check that a voice actor can play several distinct characters, ideally at least four and often many more.
when: Hiring voice talent
why: Characters often speak off screen, so players need voices they can tell apart by ear alone.

text: Use 2D sound to establish the vastness of a space or for important sounds that must always be heard.
why: The sound has one volume that does not change with the player's distance from any source.

text: Use 3D sound to guide players, mark paths, or flag secrets, and 2D sound for atmosphere that covers the whole space.
why: Its loudness rises as the player nears the source, which conveys how close the player is to that spot.

text: Prerendered crossfaded filter versions give finer control over distance-based tone than a simple low-pass filter, at the cost of extra audio files to produce and store.
when: Choosing between runtime low-pass filtering and prerendered variants.
why: Real frequency changes with distance are more complex than a single low-pass cutoff.

text: Visually identical objects feel different when given different sounds; weapon sound shapes the player's sense of power and can change play style.
when: when identical-looking objects receive different audio
why: Sound changes how a visual is perceived, so the audio attached to an object sets how it reads.

text: Sound conveys material qualities that players cannot physically touch, reinforcing the world's narrative state through echoes, rustling, sloshing, and music.
Sound gives players gameplay information and describes space beyond the screen.
Common symbolic danger sounds include dogs barking, glass breaking, forbidden acts, whispers, reversed reverb, people in pain, low-frequency bangs or rumbles, and a baby crying.
Sound timbre conveys material: a stretched-rubber collision sound reads as bouncy, a breaking sound as crumbling stone, even on limited hardware.
Pickup sounds act as learned signals, so the player associates each sound with a reward or punishment and seeks or avoids it.
when: Games with collectibles or pickups that help or harm.
why: Players learn a fixed sound's meaning through repeated pairing with an outcome.

text: Keep symbolic sounds that convey game information, such as pickups or power-ups, consistent rather than varied, since variation distracts players or hides meaning.
when: Designing feedback sounds that signal game state; sounds act as earcons with a fixed learned meaning
why: Players must recognize the meaning quickly; variation breaks recognition and makes players attend to the sample instead of its meaning, while consistent sounds are processed automatically

text: Use symbolic or stylized sound effects, such as small abstract rumbles, when visuals are stylized, instead of realistic recordings.
when: when the art style is iconic or cartoonish
why: Realistic sound on stylized visuals reads as inconsistent

text: Tie sound timing and pitch to motion and collisions so audio gives players clues about the physical world.
why: Sound timing and pitch are among the few clues players use to infer how the physical world behaves.

text: A realistic engine simulation models the engine, induction system, exhaust and wheels, using crossfades, granular sources and DSP effects.
Heavy but sharp percussion can evoke the material of an enemy, such as crunching armor or bone.
Treat realism as a tool, not a target: once the world is convincingly real and consistent, decide deliberately when to move beyond realism to serve gameplay or narrative.
when: Designing the overall sound approach of a game.
why: Strict realism is not always the goal; emotional use of sound opens more creative options.

text: Modulating the volume of looping noise with a slow sine-shaped oscillator makes the sound swell and fade, adding movement such as wind without extra samples.
when: Adding natural movement to a looping sound such as wind or waves
why: Level changes over time read as motion, and modulated level also shifts perceived tone

text: Pleasant tones for successful actions act as positive reinforcement, while jagged buzzers for failures act as punishment, shaping what players repeat.
why: Sound tied to an action signals whether the player's act was good or bad, so it encourages or discourages that act.

text: Start oscillator frequencies at 0.2, then 0.1, then 0.05, giving three distinct pitch modulations for alarm cues.
when: creating three alarm cues from one tone

text: An oscillator in a sound cue has amplitude, center, frequency and offset ranges. Modulation values are a center plus or minus amplitude; frequency is twice the sine rate in Hertz; offset is the phase multiplied by 2π.
when: Configuring an oscillator node in a sound cue

text: Two identical tones at the same pitch blend into one longer tone, hiding the second event.
when: Repeated feedback sounds overlap in time
why: With no pitch difference, the ear has no cue that a second tone has started.

text: Missing hit and footstep sounds leave the world feeling less physical, and with a limited sound palette the remaining sounds must carry the feel.
when: Sound palette is limited and hit or footstep sounds are absent
why: Without impact and locomotion sounds, the world reads as less solid.

text: A new material must reference an existing default physical material or a new physical material to produce the correct footstep sound.
when: Creating new surface materials
why: Footstep sound selection depends on the physical material the material references.

text: Choose musical tones so any combination sounds consonant, letting players layer sequences freely without dissonance.
when: Designing interactive musical sound sets
why: Free combination by the player must not produce dissonance.

text: In UDK, pitch scale ranges from 2.0 (one octave up) to about 0.4 (a little under half speed), limiting in-engine shifts.
when: Setting pitch scale on sound actors
why: Shifts beyond this range need pre-shifting in an audio editor

text: Any sound class not named in a sound mode keeps its volume at 1.0.
Typical priority groups are player weapons, NPC weapons, explosions, mission dialogue, dialogue chatter and ambience.
Switch off spatialisation on ambient sounds and sound cues, even mono files, to keep distance fade without panning; use this for large objects with no clear point of origin.
when: Non-point sound sources such as large machinery or waterfalls that lack one clear origin.
why: Panning would suggest one origin point, so keeping only distance fade avoids that false direction.

text: Make wall ambient zones slightly narrower than the walls, since sound only attenuates and filters gradually around a corner.
when: When an ambient zone behind a wall stands in for an obstruction effect.
why: Sound bends around corners, so attenuation and filtering build up gradually rather than abruptly.

text: Use notching when a sound must stand out without an obvious duck in volume, especially over dense music or battle ambience.
when: When important dialogue must stay audible over dense battle ambience or music.
why: Lowering all sounds' volume sounds artificial, while cutting only the dialogue's frequency band lets it stand out.

text: Each sound request is handled independently, so the engine cannot aggregate or prioritize them; identical simultaneous sounds sum into one sound that is too loud, and excess sounds exceed channel limits and get cut off.
when: Many sounds are requested in the same frame.
why: Independent handling leaves the engine no chance to combine or rank requests.

text: Actors differ: looping ones repeat waves; toggleable ones switch via scripting; non-looping ones play random sounds at random times; collision ones play a cue once; moveable ones attach to cinematics.
when: Choosing a sound actor for a level sound
why: Each actor suits a different playback pattern

text: If a sound's source sits where the player never reaches the minimum filter distance, the unfiltered version is never heard there.
when: Placing a filtered ambient sound source
why: The player stays beyond the minimum radius

text: The meaning of mid bandwidth values is not documented, so setting them requires trial and error.
why: The meaning of the bandwidth numbers is not explained to non-developers, so values must be found by testing.

text: Calling a synchronous audio API from several threads without locking can break things.
when: When a synchronous audio call is made from several game systems running on different threads.
why: The call runs on whichever thread invokes it, so concurrent callers reach the same API simultaneously.

text: 1) Create a white noise cue. 2) Apply the sound mode. 3) Record the output. 4) Check the frequency spectrum for the notch.
when: When precise EQ results from a sound mode are needed.
why: A frequency spectrum of the recorded output shows how the EQ reshaped the sound.

text: 1) Trigger a sound mode from a Set Sound Mode action in the visual scripting system. 2) Or type the setsoundmode console command followed by the mode name.
Rotation can be keyed in a sequence the same way as position, so swinging movers are animated and sounded like sliding ones.
A real car engine is many sound sources, each reacting differently to driver input and physics states.
Built-in engine tools are limited for convincing car simulation but cover the basic principles.
A vehicle content script can reference an engine loop, collision, enter, exit, scrape, jump, duck and explosion sounds.
A velocity-driven engine sound can use four layers: idle, low, medium and high engine.
Vehicle driving audio can use two layers: an engine revving noise and a tire noise of crumbling gravel.
Set exact times on keys so that paired movers finish their motion together.
when: two doors or movers must end at the same moment

text: Driver-linked sound principles apply to any moving object, such as skateboards or jet skis, whose sound relates to game variables.
when: moving objects with sound tied to game variables

text: Crossfade several engine recordings made at different speeds instead of pitching one sample across a wide range, which keeps engine timbre realistic.
when: Designing engine sound for a vehicle that changes speed
why: Large pitch shifts alter a sample's timbre

text: A sliding whoosh is among the most important sounds for conveying physical contact with the ground.
why: Paired with footsteps, these cues make the player feel the character is part of a lawful, physical setting.

text: Scale crash sound loudness and intensity with collision velocity so impacts feel proportionate to how hard they were.
when: Vehicle collisions with environment objects such as trees that abruptly remove momentum
why: Sound can convey impact severity when visuals are limited

text: Sending a scaled vehicle velocity or engine RPM value to a named parameter on a sound cue links it to a continuous modulator that scales engine loop volume and pitch.
why: The modulator rescales the incoming value to 0 to 1 inside the cue, so one input drives both volume and pitch.

text: Looping one short waveform cycle and playing it at different pitch multipliers yields different notes, so a melody can be built from a tiny sample. Multiplier equals target frequency divided by the source frequency.
when: Creating melodic or tonal sound from minimal sample memory
why: Playback rate sets pitch, so one stored cycle can cover many notes

text: A scaled physics impact velocity can select between several sound variants, not just set volume, by checking which value range it falls within.
when: One physics value should choose among distinct impact sounds such as hard, medium and soft.
why: Range checks on one value pick the variant that matches the event's intensity.

text: Reading velocity through a controllable curve, such as square root or squared, decouples the audio response from the raw physics value.
when: A linear velocity-to-sound response sounds unnatural for a material or motion.
why: Curves let designers tune how loudness and pitch respond without changing the physics.

text: Sharp drops in an RPM curve make engine pitch step up in stages, which suggests gear changes.
why: The non-linear RPM-to-pitch mapping produces uneven pitch changes that suggest the vehicle is shifting through gears.

text: A steep acceleration curve reaches its final range quickly, so the vehicle spends most of its time creeping toward top speed.
why: The torque curve speeds through the early gear-like changes, leaving most of the run in the slow final section.

text: Rounds per minute equals 60 divided by the fire interval in seconds, so a 0.3 second interval gives 200 rounds per minute.
A car-like engine sound setup can map RPM from about 500 up to 5,000.
The idle engine layer falls from full volume at velocity 0 to silent at velocity 500.
when: Example values for one vehicle; tune per vehicle

text: The low engine layer rises from silent at velocity 100 to full volume at velocity 300.
when: Example values for one vehicle; tune per vehicle

text: The medium engine layer rises from silent at velocity 800 to full at 1500, then falls back to silent by velocity 2000.
when: Example values for one vehicle; tune per vehicle

text: The high engine layer rises from silent at velocity 1100 to full volume at velocity 2000.
when: Example values for one vehicle; tune per vehicle

text: Scaling incoming pitch values can map the low engine cue onto a pitch range from 0.9 to 1.5.
when: Example values for one vehicle

text: Vehicle acceleration comes from a torque-versus-speed curve, and engine RPM comes from an RPM-versus-speed curve.
why: Non-linear point-based curves let acceleration and RPM change unevenly across the speed range.

text: Without a cap on scaled impact velocity, rare extreme physics values can produce disproportionately loud sounds.
when: Mapping physics impact velocity to sound volume.
why: Physics engines occasionally produce unpredictable extreme values.

text: Recording separate decay samples for each block is possible but laborious, so schedule enough production time for it.
when: Planning music production with decay samples
why: Per-block decay recording multiplies the export and integration work.

text: 1) Store the current play rate. 2) Add or subtract a fixed step, such as 0.2. 3) Write the result back to the sequence's play rate.
when: speed should change in discrete steps under player control
why: Separate sound layers can follow playback speed, so no separate file is needed for each speed.

text: 1) Record a separate decay sample for each music block. 2) Overlap it with the start of the new cue. 3) Play the previous cue's decay sample only on the first playing of the new cue.
when: Preserving natural decay at cue transitions
why: A dedicated decay sample lets the old cue ring out without carrying its other notes.

text: 1) Attach a trigger that switches on all engine sound cues, starting them silent. 2) Poll vehicle velocity every 0.1 seconds. 3) Map velocity to layer volumes and pitch.
when: Building a speed-responsive engine sound
why: Crossfading between recordings preserves the timbre when pitch shifting alone would not sound realistic.

text: Modulate engine and tire pitch with turn angle, tire friction and speed; rising pitch in turns makes tire squeal and gravel crunch audible, reinforcing carving.
when: vehicle sounds in a driving game
why: Pitch changes make motion readable by ear

text: Add movement sounds and vocalizations to a still or a series of images to imagine how a character or creature will interact.
when: Only a still concept image is available for a character or creature.
why: People are poor at describing sound, so a quick mockup communicates the idea better than talking about it.

text: A wild line is dialogue recorded without picture or existing audio, with animation and lip sync built to match it afterward.
The human voice affects listeners at a deep subconscious level, making voice a powerful storytelling tool in games and film.
A voice center channel volume sends dialogue to the center speaker in 5.1 and 7.1 setups, making speech easier to understand than spatialized sound.
Give voices accents and personality types such as serious, joker or rookie to individualize them, and make main characters especially distinct from the rest of the cast.
when: When characters often speak off screen
why: Distinctive voices let players tell speakers apart without seeing them.

text: Record whisper and shout lines with the scene context, distance and environment noted, and agree on a fixed preamp setting for them.
when: Recording lines whose loudness is part of their meaning
why: Without the scene, a whispered line may be inaudible in play

text: Voices are a finite resource: each playing sound copy uses one, and engines limit simultaneous voices from 48 to a theoretical 512, forcing priority decisions.
why: Limited channels force priority choices, and each copy of a sound takes its own channel.

text: Apply a high-pass filter around 100-150 Hz for male voices and 150-200 Hz for female voices to cut rumble while keeping natural tone.
when: Dialogue has low rumble from mic handling
why: Filtering these lows cuts the rumble without significantly changing the natural timbre of the voice.

text: A play-sound node finishes after the placeholder's original length, not the spoken length, so add a delay of about the line's length afterward.
when: when triggering prototype dialogue in a sequence
why: The node marks itself finished using the imported placeholder's length, and the updated spoken-length duration does not change that.

text: Overlapping retriggered sounds use up voices quickly when several weapons fire in one area.
when: busy areas with several weapons firing
why: Each retrigger overlaps earlier instances, so several voices stay occupied at once.

text: 1) State character sex. 2) State wanted voice age, which may differ from actor age. 3) State accent. 4) Describe pitch, timbre, intonation and personality. 5) Reference example voices.
when: Briefing a voice actor

text: 1) Import a very short placeholder sound wave into a sound cue. 2) Enable the text-to-speech option. 3) Type the dialogue into the spoken text field. 4) The node duration updates to the spoken length; the placeholder itself is not played.
when: When dialogue must be added fast for testing and prototyping.
why: It lets prototype lines play right away and gives a rough estimate of the final asset size.

text: 1) Group sound cues into categories. 2) Assign each category a voice count based on its importance.
1) Tag each sound group by relative importance. 2) When voices run out, cull lower-priority sounds and keep high-priority ones playing.
Ambient chatter and nonspeech vocals such as pain, dying, and screaming should be spatialized so they seem to come from their characters in the game world.
why: Such chatter sets the scene while its words matter less, so it should come from the speaker's position.

text: The window for collapsing duplicate sound requests is only as large as the queue: a fast processor leaves little to batch, while a backed-up queue offers more merge opportunities.
when: Requests arrive faster than they are processed.
why: Merge chances depend on how many requests wait together.

text: A sound class option called Always Play prioritizes assigned sounds when the voice count is limited, as a simple approximation of priority.
Use a one, two, many approach to switch sound from single events to a group sound as event count rises, the same idea used for footsteps.
when: Scaling sound for repeated events
why: Few events read as individual sounds, while many read as one texture

text: Per-sound concurrency limits are usually enough on current platforms, and with more voices available the question becomes whether to play everything at all.
when: When the number of available voices has expanded on modern platforms.
why: Current platform capacity makes simple per-sound caps typically sufficient.

text: Game events determine the density and nature of sound at any moment, so audio mixing begins in game design.
when: Deciding how audio should peak and rest over play
why: Event pacing drives how many sounds play and how intense they are

text: Wide attenuation radii let distant sounds play, so footsteps heard from far away can produce many concurrent instances.
when: When footsteps should be audible from a significant distance.

text: A synchronous playSound call does not return until the audio engine finishes processing it, so loading a sound from disk can freeze the game for several frames.
when: When the sound file must first be loaded from disk.
why: The caller waits for the full engine work to complete.

text: A sound cue's Max Concurrent Play Count caps its simultaneous instances and defaults to 16; lower it for sounds that stack.
when: When many NPCs share a confined area and their footsteps stack.

text: Concurrent voices from retriggering are roughly sample length in seconds multiplied by shots per second.
when: retriggered weapon fire sounds
why: Long samples at high rates exhaust the voice pool quickly.

text: Without a full spatial sound field, players cannot filter sounds, so playing every sound at once produces an undecipherable mix.
why: Spatial cues let listeners pick out one source; without them, all sources blur into one indistinct mix.

text: Long ricochet sounds add to voice count.
why: Their long duration keeps each instance occupying a voice for longer.

text: 1) Increment a counter when each event's tone starts. 2) Decrement it when that tone finishes. 3) While the count is above 1, play a raised-pitch variant instead of the single tone.
when: Overlapping event sounds must stay distinct
why: Two tones at the same pitch blend into one, so the second event's feedback is lost.

text: 1) Reduce the attenuation maximum radius of the sound. 2) Or lower the concurrent play count on footstep cues to cut overlapping voices.
when: In a crowded space

text: 1) Scan pending requests from head to tail, wrapping the ring. 2) If an entry has the same sound id, set its volume to the larger of the two and skip enqueuing. 3) Otherwise enqueue the request.
when: Identical sound requests may arrive together and should collapse into one.
why: Duplicates would otherwise sum into an overly loud sound.

text: Decide which sounds the listener most needs to hear at each moment, and why, before setting any volume levels; selecting what stands out is the sound designer's job.
why: Playing every sound at once produces an indecipherable mix, so priorities must be chosen first.

text: Multiple ambient copies fill a space but cost voices, cause volume doubling, and can introduce phasing and panning changes.
when: deciding whether to use several copies of one sound
why: the fill benefit comes with resource and sound-quality costs

text: Real-time frequency analysis and multiband compression can cull masked sounds automatically on modern hardware, while simple scripted event logic can be enough.
why: Loud event sounds mask quiet ambience, so a count-based trigger can handle masking without analysing the signal.

text: A gunshot's high-frequency content is concentrated in its first few hundred milliseconds, while its tail is mostly low frequency.
when: Analysing how a percussive sound's spectrum changes over time
why: Transients carry bright energy that decays faster than the tail

text: A weapon's fire interval is the time in seconds between shots; a smaller interval means faster fire.
Very high rate weapons, up to about 6,000 rounds per minute, are usually vehicle mounted.
A weapon with an alternate fire mode keeps a separate fire interval for each mode.
Default engine weapons often lack elaborate reload animations.
