Mechanical weapons vary little from shot to shot, so a very subtle pitch change is often enough to avoid identical repeats.
when: mechanical weapon fire sounds
why: Weapons built on a repeating mechanical process sound nearly identical from shot to shot.

text: Sci-fi beam weapons are often built on a constant loop instead of retriggered shots.
when: sci-fi beam weapons
why: A beam-like quality needs a continuous sound rather than repeated transients.

text: In a shooter, combine weapon sound systems with whatever real-time acoustic processing the engine provides.
when: Shooter games

text: A retriggered weapon restarts its fire sound every fire interval while the trigger is held, until ammo runs out.
when: trigger held on a retriggered weapon
why: Each fire interval triggers another shot, so the sound replays without stopping until the ammo is spent.

text: Releasing the breath-hold key during the delay restarts the sway animation early.
when: breath-hold delay is running

text: A held beam sound has three parts: a start sound at press, a loop played while held, and an end sound on release.
While the forced end-fire call stops refiring, changing the fire interval has no audible effect.
when: single-shot weapons using the forced end-fire call
why: The forced end-fire call overrides the interval.

text: Long samples retriggered often can phase.
when: A long sample that retriggers frequently.
why: Overlapping copies of the sound interfere with one another's waveforms.

text: Machine-gun rates of 600 to 1,200 rounds per minute cause problems with simple retriggering.
when: simple retriggering at machine-gun rates

text: Pitch-shifting one engine sample across a large range changes its timbre unnaturally, so pitch shifting alone does not make engine sound realistic.
when: Pitch-shifting a single recording by a significant amount.
why: Large pitch changes alter the timbre of the recording, so it stops sounding natural.

text: 1) Play a loud start sound on each shot to announce it. 2) Play the retriggered body at the same moment at a lower level. 3) Play a tail when the trigger is released.
when: rapid retriggered weapons, especially busy firefights
why: Keeps busy firefights from turning into a muddy wall of sound

text: Consider crossfading weapon sounds as listener distance changes. 1) Create several versions of the fire sound at different distances. 2) Set the boundaries of each version in a distance crossfade node. 3) Play one sound cue that crossfades between versions by distance.
when: Deciding how a weapon's character should change over distance, given game type and simultaneous weapons.

text: 1) Keep a dry retriggered fire sound unchanged. 2) Hold a separate tail sample for each space. 3) Use trigger volumes to set each tail's volume. 4) Play the outside tail at full volume when no zone is entered.
when: retriggered weapons in large spaces where tails must change with location
why: Long samples are hard to use with retriggering

text: 1) Record or select several short samples. 2) Reorder them randomly at runtime. 3) Add slight pitch modulation to some segments.
when: Creating continuous textures such as fire or crackle
why: Random ordering and pitch variation avoid obvious repetition

text: 1) Place a Take Damage event on the object. 2) Connect it to play the sound cue. The setup matches a Touch event on a trigger volume.
when: Playing a sound when an object is hit or destroyed
why: Damage events fire on player actions

text: 1) On zoom in, start the sway animation and breathing loops. 2) On the breath-hold key, play a breath-hold cue and stop the sway. 3) After a short delay, around three seconds, resume the loops. 4) On zoom out, close the gates and end the zoom.
when: scoped weapon with breathing sway
why: Sway makes aim drift, and holding breath steadies the sights.

text: 1) Back up the unedited script in a separate folder. 2) Remove read-only protection from the working copy and open it in a text editor. 3) Copy the sound cue's full name from the content browser. 4) Paste it over the existing cue reference. 5) Save, close the editor and compile scripts. 6) Test in the exercise room.
when: replacing a weapon sound
why: Keeping an untouched copy lets the original script be restored later.

text: 1) Place a weapons locker from the actor classes. 2) Open its properties. 3) Add the weapon class to its list.
when: adding a weapon to your own level

text: To make a weapon fire exactly one shot per trigger press, play its fire cue in an overridden firing function, then call the engine's end-fire stop function.
when: single-shot weapons
why: The end-fire stop function prevents the weapon from refiring.

text: When extending a complex weapon script, replace only the cues you need and leave the rest intact.
when: weapon scripts with many cue references

text: When a beam touches a surface or pawn, layer an impact loop chosen by target: a flesh loop for an enemy pawn, a surface loop otherwise.
when: beam hits a surface or pawn

text: Looped weapon sounds need sample-accurate sync between the dry loop and any extra reverb layers.
when: looped weapon with extra reverb layers

text: When a weapon has its own reload animations, call sound cues directly from the animation rather than adding script hooks.
when: Weapons with custom reload animations
why: Avoids scripting for each sound

text: In one-on-one combat, a point of attack bonus raises hit chance by the same amount that a point of armor class lowers the opponent's hit chance.
when: both sides need the same number of hits to win
why: the outcome then depends only on relative hit chances

text: Against N attackers, one point of armor class is worth about N points of attack bonus, because the character is attacked N times for each attack it makes.
when: each enemy attacks once per round and the character attacks once per round

text: Magical attacks that ignore armor bypass the armor reduction in the damage formula.
HP, Attack, and Defense are not fully equivalent, so conversions between them are approximations.
when: using anchor conversions for balance
why: Real combat effects depend on context beyond a single conversion rate.

text: Treating attack bonus and armor class as interchangeable ignores encounter structure, so their true relative value can differ between fights.
when: When one side's stat is far above or below the opponent's.
why: Once a hit chance reaches 100% or 0%, extra bonuses add nothing, so each stat's value depends on the matchup.

text: Symmetric design means all players start with the same state, rules, and goals; cosmetic differences such as piece colors do not count, so any difference comes from the players.
Symmetry is a spectrum: small details, such as who moves first or who starts with the ball, break symmetry, so a mostly symmetric game can be asymmetric through one element.
Use symmetry when the design allows: symmetric PvP games are fair without balancing effort and easier to balance, since unequal starts or resources can give one side an unfair advantage.
why: Equal starting positions remove one source of unfair advantage that would otherwise need tuning.

text: Symmetric games start balanced, but symmetry alone does not guarantee balance: resources, strategies, pacing, skill gaps, or moving first (large advantage or disadvantage) can still tilt it.
why: Balance also depends on resources, strategies, and turn order, which symmetry does not equalize.

text: Arrange three or more competing options in a circle so each beats one and loses to another, so each has a clear answer and none is universally best.
when: Designing three or more competing options.
why: Keeps all options balanced.

text: Board games and most sports are symmetric, so skill and strategy decide; most games overall are asymmetric through characters, first movers, or factions.
when: Choosing between symmetric and asymmetric starts.
why: Symmetry removes unequal starting advantages.

text: In competitive shooters, challenge arrives immediately because duels resolve quickly, while mastery builds across many matches.
when: competitive shooter play
why: Duels end in seconds, so skill develops over repeated sessions.

text: In well-balanced asymmetrical games, each side has roughly equal winning chances when both sides are played skillfully.
when: Designing asymmetrical sides
why: Multiplayer balance often comes down to how resources and powers are distributed at the start.

text: When every player starts with a different advantage, the outcome depends mainly on skill because each side is advantaged.
when: asymmetric starting conditions
why: Balanced compensation across asymmetric starts shifts the decider to skill.

text: A weaker player with a strong pre-game choice, such as a deck or character, can beat a stronger player with a weak choice.
when: Predicting match outcomes in games with pre-match builds or loadouts.
why: Pre-game choices can outweigh player skill differences.

text: Symmetric design gives all players the same abilities and paths, while asymmetric design gives players different starting advantages or resources.
why: The choice determines whether outcomes depend on skill or on the starting setup.

text: A handicap is the PvP equivalent of a difficulty setting: one player starts in an advantaged position or gains an ongoing advantage.
Popularity is how many times a character is chosen; in a mirror match, the character counts twice.
PvE progression usually rises in absolute terms against a fixed yardstick, while PvP tracks power relative to opponents, leaving more options since no fixed yardstick exists.
Some degenerate strategies in a genre become so widely used that they turn into standard features of that genre.
In symmetrical games, all players start with the same units, resources, and information, so fairness mainly concerns who moves first.
Comparing an asymmetric starting state with a symmetric one shows how starting conditions shape play.
PvP games must keep providing stronger opponents, and the pool of human players is effectively unlimited.
In PvP, gains and losses are measured relative to opponents, so the game becomes a tug-of-war in which each player tries to reach the goal first.
PvP victory may be direct, such as eliminating all other players, or indirect, such as scoring points that power makes possible; some games win by exhausting opponents' power.
In plain Rock-Paper-Scissors, the symmetric optimal mix is one-third each throw, and any other ratio gives the opponent a counter that wins more often than it loses.
In a symmetric game, the solution is identical for both players; each strategy in use earns equal payoff, and in a symmetric zero-sum game every such payoff is zero.
when: Applying symmetric zero-sum analysis to an intransitive game

text: Without a special win rule, the symmetric three-player game has an equilibrium of 1:1:1 across the three throws.
when: no special win rule applies
why: the game is symmetric

text: The first-move advantage in chess disappears at lower skill levels.
when: lower-skill play

text: In many PvP games, power grows late through stronger attacks, larger unit counts, more resources, or higher levels, and this pattern appears across card, board, strategy and online games.

In PvE the designer controls encounters and their generation rules, so encounter probabilities can be estimated and expected-value calculations are fairly easy, even for procedurally generated content.
when: Designing PvE encounters or generated content with known rules
why: The designer knows the generator and the typical encounter

text: In PvP, opponents vary strategy and the metagame shifts, so expected value is unstable and playtesting and analytics are the main ways to find typical use.
when: Balancing games where players face other players
why: Opponent behavior is unknown and changes over time

text: Balance each object against a few archetype baselines instead of all pairings; this quickly reaches a reasonable ballpark for large-roster games like fighting games, MOBAs, and card games.
when: Large rosters of characters, items or units.
why: Pairwise testing grows combinatorially while baseline comparisons grow linearly, giving reasonable starting balance with little effort.

text: A design can begin from any element, but letting story dictate every choice is a common mistake.
why: Fixing the story early forces the other elements to bend around an inflexible premise.

text: When player versus player combat is not central to a game, question why it exists, since it creates an easy opening for griefers.
why: Removing the system avoids having to police griefing later, which is messy to enforce.

text: Small differences in range, geometry, and attack rate can turn a dull unit into one that generates many tactics, at similar implementation cost.
when: comparing units with similar roles
why: Two units sharing a role differ only slightly in attack shape and damage, and that small gap yields the more elegant design.

text: Co-op games often aim to make players feel skilled and powerful, so balance is weighted toward the player, slightly or greatly.
when: Balancing multiplayer co-op PvE encounters
why: Players should feel they fought a strong opponent, even when they ultimately win or lose by a designed margin.

text: Unit counts can reverse basic counter relationships: enough cheap units beat a few counters before contact, and a large group of one type can beat a few units that normally counter it.
when: evaluating army compositions
why: Quantity changes the outcome of individual matchups.

text: Track the average rating of active players over time to detect rating inflation or deflation.
when: Rating systems that are mostly zero-sum, where points transfer between players.

text: In PvE games, score benefits positively and costs or flaws negatively, summing to a worth such as a gold price or monster difficulty.
when: PvE games where objects carry costs, such as purchasable or found weapons.

text: In PvP with resource costs, the balance curve is the identity (y = x): benefit points minus cost points equals zero for a balanced item, negative below the curve, and positive above it.
when: Balancing PvP items with resource costs
why: A common reference line makes items directly comparable

text: Archetype balance does not guarantee pairwise balance; a unit balanced in theory may still have favorable matchups against most others, creating an unbalanced metagame.
when: After archetype-based balancing.
why: Baseline comparisons miss specific matchup advantages.

text: Premade characters that differ sharply in abilities invite close scrutiny, so any balance gap between them is easy for players to spot.
when: balancing fixed character options
why: Players compare fixed options directly.

text: Asymmetric designs carry no promise of fairness and demand careful balancing so that players perceive them as fair enough.
why: Asymmetric games lack the shared starting conditions and rules that make symmetric games fair automatically.

text: 1) Identify the source of asymmetry: starting positions, resources, goals, or core rules. 2) Balance asymmetric elements on the same cost curve and stat math. 3) Where numbers cannot compare sides, add intransitive counters so no single strategy dominates.
when: Balancing PvP factions or sides.
why: Shared stats allow numeric analysis; counters prevent one dominant strategy.

text: 1) Decide whether the game should be symmetrical or asymmetrical. 2) Record the reasons for that choice. 3) Check whether the goal reliably measures skill or offers everyone an interesting challenge.

1) Confirm the game is symmetric with no dominance. 2) Set all payoffs to zero and probabilities to sum to 1. 3) Solve the equations. An odd number of options that each beat half the others yields an equal mix.
when: Solving symmetric zero-sum games where each option beats and loses to equally many others
why: A strategy paying less than the rest would be dropped, and one paying more would be chosen exclusively, so viable strategies must tie.

text: 1) Balance one character and compute its benefits minus costs. 2) Balance every other character to that same positive total.
when: PvP games without item costs
why: Characters should feel useful and powerful, so a positive constant suits better than zero.

text: Sort like objects by their computed worth and plot them in a spreadsheet to reveal the progression.
when: PvE games with computer-controlled enemies
why: Objects of equal value would give no sense of advancement, while sorted worth exposes a rising progression.

text: 1) Pair players of nearly equal rating. 2) Widen the allowed rating gap for each second a player waits. Closer matches cost longer waits.
when: Rated games.
why: Automation prevents self-selection while keeping queues moving.

text: 1) Set value per HP. 2) Set an improvement rate between successive weapons. 3) Give weapons with critical-hit chance a cost premium. 4) Compute each cost from averaged damage plus benefits. 5) Plot costs in list order so they trace the expected progression. 6) Investigate any point off the progression.
when: Building a PvE weapon list from formulas
why: Plotting exposes outliers that need checking

text: 1) Give each person a random unit. 2) Pair players randomly. 3) Rotate opponents across rounds. 4) Record each player's win-loss record, each unit's win-loss record, and final remaining health totals.
when: running a balance test tournament
why: Random assignment means players do not run their own character, and close matches signal balance.

text: In balanced PvP, players of equal skill should each have a reasonable, roughly equal chance to win, and outcomes should not be predetermined or outside players' control.
when: Designing or balancing competitive player-versus-player games.
why: Initial conditions that differ between players create built-in bias, so the result tilts before play begins.

text: Handle disruptive players in competitive deathmatch with bans, since every other player is an opponent and each match stands alone.
when: competitive deathmatch rules

text: Choose a PvP game length based on audience and mechanical depth, then tune progression so players reach the end at a good pace.
why: Once the result seems certain, players see no point in playing it out.

text: Evaluate balance separately for each skill tier, since the strategies available to novices and experts differ.
when: Strategy games where some openings are easy to execute but hard to stop at low skill.
why: Such openings succeed against novices, while experts know how to defend them, so the balance shifts with skill.

text: Symmetry narrows the possibility space and keeps comparisons clear; asymmetry widens it and creates richer interactions but can overwhelm players with decisions.
why: Far-asymmetric designs force many hard decisions at once, which can overwhelm players.

text: Players may bid to keep a strong item from a rival, or push prices up so a rival pays more than planned.
when: Rivals compete for the same item
why: An item too powerful in a rival's hands can justify paying more than it is worth to oneself.

text: A peak is a manually added item that falls outside the procedural growth range, adding surprise and variety.
In an open auction, any player may bid at any time by exceeding the current high bid, running in real time without turns until no one raises. The most recent high bid wins.
A circle auction is turn-based: each player in turn either bids above the previous bid or passes.
In a silent auction, all bidders secretly bid at once and then reveal; the highest bid wins.
In a Dutch auction, the price starts high and drops at a fixed rate; the first bidder to stop the counter pays the current price.
Each bidder's maximum is the core quantity an auction reveals, and bidding is how that maximum is determined.
An unpurchased property goes to auction, which is not limited by its printed face value.
Circle auctions are common in analog games and rare in digital games, while open auctions are the most common format in online markets.
Other auction payment variants include paying the gap to the next lower bid, having the top bidder pay fully while losers pay extra, and having only the top and bottom bidders pay.
when: Designing a non-standard payment rule
why: Each variant shapes whether players bid high, low, or moderately

text: Auctions move resources that bidders pay for with their own resources; items the game itself offers are production, not trade.
Winner-pays is safest for single-item auctions since players pay only when receiving; choose it when bidding should feel safe, and all-pay or partial-pay rules for tension or extreme bids.
when: Choosing a payment rule for an auction
why: When all bidders must pay something, losers bear a cost, so low bids no longer feel safe.

text: Auction items that have different, situational value to each player, such as an item worth more to one character class; this makes players reveal and weigh their willingness to pay.
when: Deciding whether an item should be auctioned or designing an item for auction
why: Each player has a maximum price they will pay, and an auction brings that figure out.

text: Make the winner pay a price for a strategic position, which raises tension and gives losers a chance to recover.
when: Designing advantage positions
why: Without a price, a strong player keeps compounding advantage from one success until the game ends early.

text: Keep ample choice in all areas, and make sure nothing limits options as the game progresses.
when: Designing strategic options
why: Once a strategy dominates, players abandon the rest, so a small edge can shrink choice a lot.

text: Components that are weak alone can jointly produce a strong effect, so price the set together rather than each piece in isolation.
In a draft, weaker teams pick first from available players, so talent spreads across teams and weak competitors regain strength.
when: Ordered drafting of available players each season.
why: Picking order is inverse to performance, so good players reach weaker teams.

text: A reserve price means no one wins if the top bid is below it. Hidden reserves push bidders to open higher to avoid a wasted bid, especially when bidding costs something or is limited.
when: An auction has a minimum acceptable price
why: Bidders fear losing a bid that does not win

text: A buyout price lets any bidder end the auction and win immediately; depending on timing rules it either gives everyone a chance or lets early bidders deny the item to later ones.
when: An auction includes an instant-win price

text: In a negative auction, players bid to avoid a harmful item. Winning too often can trigger a feedback penalty or a bonus for non-winners, and such a penalty is usually unnecessary unless won items help win future auctions.
when: Items are harmful and players bid to avoid them
why: The resources already spent on winning act as the deterrent, so extra penalties are rarely needed unless winning yields resources that improve later bids.

text: Hidden auction contents turn bidding into a probability problem, and players without privileged information may copy the bids of informed bidders.
when: Item contents are hidden from some bidders
why: Uninformed bidders can read the informed players' bids as a signal of value and bid in step with them.

text: In single-item auctions, bidders may wait out high prices or snipe items they see as bargains. With unknown future items, players take more calculated risks than when future items are known.
when: Items are auctioned one at a time in sequence
why: Known future items let players plan ahead; surprises change plans

text: Bundling items into a lot raises stakes and can attract more players when different items suit different players.
when: Several items are bid on together and go to the top bidder
why: Mixing items that suit different players gives more bidders a reason to join the auction.

text: In an open auction, the sale happens as soon as the bid passes the second-highest willingness to pay.
when: Bidders raise in real time

text: In a multi-round circle auction, bidding continues until everyone passes, which slightly favors earlier bidders. Ties go to whoever first bid that amount.
when: Circle auction runs until all but one pass

text: In an all-pay auction, every bidder pays their bid whether or not they win, so players hesitate unless the item is important and bids can be very high or very low.
when: Everyone pays their bid regardless of outcome
why: When only one item can be won, players dislike spending resources on a bid that fails to win.

text: When the top two bidders pay, middling bids become dangerous: players bid zero if others bid high, bid small if others bid zero, and bid high if others bid small.
when: The top bidder wins and the second-highest also pays
why: The runner-up pays without receiving anything, so any moderate bid that fails to win is a pure loss.

text: In an open auction where the top two bidders pay, a low-value item can escalate indefinitely, because the second bidder would rather lose a small amount than a larger one.
when: Open auction with top-two payment
why: Each top bidder would rather pay one more step to outbid the rival than lose the amount already committed.

text: In a second-price auction, the winner pays the second-highest bid, and in a silent auction bidding one's true maximum is the best strategy.
when: Silent auction where the winner pays the second-highest bid

text: Paying auction proceeds to the bank removes currency from the economy, which causes deflation.
when: Auction proceeds go to the bank

text: Paying auction proceeds to other players, usually the sellers, keeps the auction zero-sum for the economy.
when: Auction proceeds go to players rather than the bank
why: Money moves between players instead of leaving the game, so the total amount of currency stays the same.

text: When an auction item is given away to a known recipient, others have reason to bid a nominal amount to block that player; with a random recipient, players may hold off bidding in hope of luck.
when: An auction item is given to a winner chosen by the designer
why: Rivals would rather pay a nominal amount than let that player take the item for free.

text: Turn-based Dutch auctions can lower costs each time a player declines, and some designs let the seller raise, hold, or lower the price.
when: Designing a Dutch auction variant
why: The turn-based version avoids needing special equipment to run the falling price.

text: With imperfect information, the winning price usually lands well below the highest maximum, often near the second-highest maximum, since bidders cannot bid just above rivals.
when: Bidders do not know rivals' maximums
why: Bidders underbid when they lack full information

text: Each object's data can be split into costs (price and drawbacks) and benefits (usefulness that creates desire); balance is judged on the totals per object, not on any single attribute.
when: Balancing items with multiple attributes
why: Individual attributes can mislead; the totals determine fairness

text: 1) Top bidder picks an item. 2) Second-highest bidder picks next. 3) Continue in bid order until all items are taken. 4) If items equal players, the lowest bidder gets the leftover item, tempting zero bids; with fewer items than players, disinterested players bid a nominal amount.
when: Items are distributed by bid order rather than sold (item draft auction)
why: The last pick is forced onto the lowest bidder

text: Unclaimed items can be discarded, removing them so the game continues as if the auction never happened; they can also be kept for the next auction or handed out over several passes of the draft.
when: A draft or auction leaves unclaimed items

text: Price an item by cost per point of its effect, then add fixed bonuses for special conditions on top of the base price.
when: pricing damage or healing items with linear value
why: A linear base keeps prices proportional, and bonuses handle special cases.

text: 1) Bid goes around the table once. 2) Last player either bids higher or lets the current high bidder win, effectively buying at a fixed price.
when: Running a single-round circle auction
why: The last bidder effectively faces a fixed price, which gives them an edge.

text: 1) If no bids arrive before the time limit, return the item to the owner. 2) Owner may relist at the same or lower price. 3) Alternatively, add items or incentives to the pool and repeat the auction until someone bids.
when: An auction ends with no bids

text: 1) Use a tiebreaker such as a coin flip, turn order, or highest unique bid. 2) If the tiebreak also ties, all bids are lost.
when: Two or more silent bids are equal
why: Equal top bids are possible in silent auctions, so a resolution rule must exist.

text: Apply cost-curve analysis to digital games by gathering online item lists and, for thousands of objects, using spreadsheet formulas to finish in reasonable time.
when: Analyzing a digital game with thousands of game objects
why: Digital data sets are larger, so working backward is slower and manual analysis becomes impractical.

text: A seller bidding on their own item usually is a poor move, but it can keep the item cheaply if others bid low.
when: The seller may bid on their own auction
why: Seller bids are paid to the bank

text: Large, persistent choices change scope for many departments and can affect sequels, so they should be funded only when content and testing budgets allow.
when: Considering a large persistent choice
why: Permanent branches multiply the work and budget across many departments and may extend into sequels.

text: Judgment players perceive as unfair will be resented rather than motivating, so feelings of unfairness should be avoided as much as possible because they generate negative emotion.
why: Emotion guides behavior and can impair reasoning, and people resent judgment they see as unfair rather than being driven by it.

text: An unbalanced game usually has several interacting problems rather than one resource that is too high or too low.
why: Balance elements react to one another, so a single fault spreads into several off-kilter elements rather than one number.

text: When a second player may answer after a first player's wrong guess, the second player gains an advantage because they have already seen the first guess.
when: Games where players respond in sequence to the same question
why: Information from earlier answers is available to later players.

text: An overpowered item usually matters less than expected: players only pull ahead until the content catches up with their ability.
when: an item is well above the curve in a progression game
why: later content scales up to match the player's growing strength

text: Overpowered rare cards in head-to-head card games are resented and can create a pay-to-win perception.
when: Competitive card games with rarity-based power.
why: Power tied to rarity or money feels unfair to opponents.

text: Players may not read a pricing formula, but they can still feel whether a weapon seems balanced.
when: Designing numeric item pricing
why: Perceived fairness depends on play experience, not on visible math

text: Games resolve uncertainty into an unequal outcome, so they are not designed to prove that everyone is equal.
In rock-paper-scissors structures, each move beats one other and loses to one, so no configuration leaves a player content; this is the simplest symmetrical structure without equilibrium.
when: Symmetrical games where both players share the same moves.

text: Mathematical balance covers numerical elements such as level curves, item costs, hit points, and object rarity, where rarity itself is often derived from math.
why: Most balance questions reduce to numerical relationships.

text: Perfect imbalance is the term for games that improve when small, deliberate imbalances are added to strategies.
Asymmetry can faithfully simulate a real situation that was itself unequal, such as a historical conflict between opposing forces.
Some games have only one path to victory, where the winner is the player who executes the core strategy best.
Two games can demand similar skill yet differ greatly in luck, depending only on whether random item or power-up effects are present.
Most real interactions have unequal payoffs, such as fighting-game block, jab, and throw, where each option beats another by a different amount.
Balancing a game for all skill levels at once is nearly impossible because the strategies multiply, so designers must choose a target skill level.
Leave most balancing to designers, since player-set values tend to drift toward overpowered settings where fun is brief and returning to normal balance feels dull and restrictive.
when: Considering letting players choose balance values
why: Players want both challenge and easy wins, and overpowered settings remove challenge.

text: When offering two options, give them similar benefit levels so that the choice between them is interesting.
When the allowed trade size falls during a round, down to single cards, players can read that the round is nearing its end.
when: Rounds where trade size decreases as play progresses.
why: Trades move toward single cards as players consolidate on a preferred resource, so everyone sees how near the others are to finishing sets.

text: If every playtester takes or avoids a stat, that points to an imbalance.
when: Playtesting a system with stat choices.
why: A god or dump stat makes the choice non-meaningful, since skipping a necessary stat weakens the character.

text: The nature and balance of roles is a critical design consideration, especially when roles differ or players define them.
when: When roles differ between players or players define their own roles

text: Each failure trap needs a custom solution based on how and why it emerges, since no single fix covers all traps.
when: When addressing a failure trap.
why: Traps have different causes and mechanics.

text: Designers who understand what players find fair can affect profitability more than financial analysts can.
when: setting prices or monetization features
why: Perceived fairness drives purchase decisions

text: Keep deviations from the cost curve small; large ones make items feel broken, such as a weapon that carries the player with no challenge or an enemy that traps the player for long.
when: Placing items or enemies off the curve
why: Small deviations give surprise, while large ones harm the experience

text: Pick a row-per-object balance layout when you need to contrast many same-kind items, such as enemies, weapons, cards, or character classes.
Tie moral choices to gameplay only after testing whether gameplay rewards pull against the narrative.
when: Before linking moral choices to mechanics
why: Punitive gameplay tied to non-standard moral paths can make the game unappealing to those players.

text: Temporarily removing a player's powers is a gentler penalty than permanent loss of progress.
when: When a penalty is needed but must stay recoverable
why: Recoverable penalties keep failure consequential without ending investment

text: Deliberately unfair asymmetric powers generate wild stories and funny interactions that strict fairness tends to suppress.
when: When the goal is stories and humor rather than honest competition

text: Players who build and test decks shape final balance partly through the metaeconomy, so balance is not set by the designer alone.
when: Collectible card games with deck building
why: Deck choices and trading respond to play and spread through the market.

text: Multiplayer balance requires fair starts and no single dominant strategy; single player balance requires skill to match the target audience.
A balance sheet lists each game object in its own row and each attribute in its own column, ending with a formula that places every object on its cost/power curve.
A defensible set of numbers can still feel unfair, because player perception, not the numbers alone, determines balance; check balance against how players perceive prices and power.
when: When evaluating whether a balance tuning is successful
why: Balance is judged by players' perception, which can differ from the math.

text: Without balancing relationships, a game can resolve too quickly.
why: Positive feedback reinforces one player's lead, and only negative feedback counters it to keep the two players balanced.

text: Judging a stat within a single build hides whether it is a god stat or a dump stat.
Labeling a game as entirely skill or entirely luck ignores that the answer can depend on whether the observer is a participant or outsider.
when: Classifying a game's luck or skill
why: The role of the observer changes which uncertainty matters.

text: An optimal opening strategy for equal health does not carry over once health totals become uneven, since some moves can end the match outright and become equally useful.
when: Analyzing a fighting game across different health states
why: Lethal thresholds change which moves are useful

text: A deliberately unfair game loses competitive legitimacy, so it cannot support a fair contest between players.
when: When asymmetry is deliberately made unfair instead of balanced

text: Degenerate strategies can give unfair advantages to some players and spoil the experience for those playing by the rules.
A cost formula that omits the damage an item will face from the opponent makes every item look above the curve.
why: Damage may fail to get through against stronger opponents, so leaving that out overstates each item's expected value.

text: Abilities on cards sitting above or below the curve can skew estimates, so check values against known game behavior before trusting one.
Balancing only for one extreme alienates either casual players or expert players.
when: When balancing end-game content, where viable and optimal builds diverge over time
why: Balancing to the optimal build makes the game too hard for most players, and that gap widens over time.

text: Each fix can cause new problems elsewhere, so tuning one problem at a time does not converge.
when: When the same mechanic or tool is used in many other places in the game
why: Tuning a mechanic alters every strategy it touches, not only the one being fixed.

text: 1) Identify a character, unit, or ability that is overpowered. 2) Reduce its strength (nerf). 3) Verify the change through extensive playtesting.
when: When a character or ability is overpowered relative to other options
why: Overpowered elements dominate play and reduce the value of other choices.

text: Set player expectations through title or packaging when imbalance is intentional or unavoidable.
why: Players who choose to play an obviously unfair game have already accepted its imbalance, so the title shields it from being judged as unbalanced.

text: Avoid strategy interactions with exactly one pure equilibrium, because players always settle into that choice and the decision disappears.
why: With a single equilibrium every player knows the one viable move and needn't predict others, so the decision loses its meaning.

text: A game object is balanced when its overall profile, including stats, cost, rarity, strengths, and weaknesses, is comparable to other objects, and when it has some situation in which a player would choose it.
when: When evaluating or tuning individual game objects
why: Objects are judged in aggregate, and each needs a reason to be used.

text: Balance a tool through non-essential properties such as price, weight, vulnerability, or new mechanics, rather than changing its essential property.
when: When the tool's essential properties are already locked at their extremes
why: Changing essential traits would blur each tool's role and clash with the game's fiction.

text: Breaking conventions can create immersion that fair design cannot, but unfair design without fail-safes can wear down careless players until they quit.
when: When an unfair design has no fail-safe mechanisms
why: Harsh threats that match the grim fiction honestly feel more immersive than softened ones.

text: No single balance method suits every project and no fixed percentage split applies; methods apply broadly, and some combine well while others contradict.
why: Designers must experiment to find the methods that suit them.

text: 1) Form a speculative model of how elements relate, built as spreadsheet models from tuning experience. 2) Change the game to match it. 3) Playtest and compare observed play against predictions. 4) If play contradicts the model or testers favor unpredicted strategies, revise, rebalance, and test again.
when: balance modeling, especially during alpha
why: Observed play exposes gaps in the model.

text: An anchor is a fixed reference value or unit against which other game values are scaled, such as currency cost or damage per hit.
An economic anchor can be replaced by another resource, such as time, when that resource becomes more valuable to people than the currency.
A choice between two effects is worth at least as much as the better effect, because the player can always pick that one.
A starting balanced object is balanced only because the designer declares it so; objects shaped to it end up roughly equal in power to each other.
Two equations with two unknowns usually have a unique solution.
Cloning, reusing another game's data and numbers, is one of five balance methods, though the term is often used derisively.
Most games have an anchor resource, usually the win or loss stat, such as HP in RPGs or victory points in board games.
Common balancing methods include doubling and halving, guessing exact values to train intuition, documenting and tuning a model, planning for balance in advance, and avoiding player-driven balancing.
Objects that can be balance-tested include trading cards, units in miniatures or strategy games, and items, classes or feats in tabletop RPGs.
Hit points and currency can be the same resource when currency buys healing through spells or health packs.
when: Currency can purchase healing

text: Balance is a method for reaching goals rather than a goal itself, and it can serve fiction, clarity, simplicity, and elegance as well as fairness and depth.
Change whichever of cost or benefit is easier to adjust: an interesting card may need only a cost change; an item weak even when free needs more power.
when: When an object sits off the power curve and must be corrected
why: Keeping whichever value the designer is unwilling to change fixed leaves only the other one to adjust.

text: Locking essential properties at extremes yields distinct tools that span a broad space of possibility.
when: When tools have essential properties that define their role and fiction
why: Extreme settings make each tool's role unmistakable, widening the strategies players can explore.

text: Buffing a weak option raises its value to players, while nerfing a dominant option reduces its share of play in the metagame.
when: When issuing post-launch balance patches to fix old, egregious content

text: When someone pulls ahead, the rest coordinate against the frontrunner, forming a self-reinforcing loop that a tipping mechanism can interrupt.
when: Multiplayer games with competitive leads

text: A loop that balances rewards with penalties can trap players, as when profits go entirely to debt payments in a business simulation.
why: Each reward is cancelled by a penalty within the loop, so extra play never leads to real progress.

text: Removing aim assist from a powerful weapon in one mode, such as unzoomed use, weakens its close-range use without the player noticing, steering it toward its intended role.
when: A weapon's strength spills into a role meant for another weapon
why: Hidden difficulty discourages the overlapping use while the weapon's stated accuracy stays the same.

text: A balance value is a weighted total where benefits raise and costs or limitations lower it, placing objects on the cost/power curve: zero on it, negative below, positive above.
when: costs are subtracted from benefits on an identity curve
why: Higher scores mean more power and distance from zero shows how far off balance an object is, so the score is easy to read.

text: Benefits are worth 1 per point of power or toughness and 1 for most keywords.
when: Cards with power, toughness, and keywords.
why: Most keyword abilities on existing cards appear to be worth 1, so that value is assumed for new keywords.

text: Judge balance with three dials: difficulty (too easy, too hard, just right), quantity (too little, too much, enough), and timing (too early, too late, on time).
when: When the tuned dials are in line with the game's target audience
why: Balance is recognized by feel, so the three dials turn that feeling into concrete questions a designer can check.

text: Judge balance against three modifiers: target audience, designer's intent, and purpose.
why: The modifiers pin down what the game is for, which sets what counts as balanced.

text: Supporting math converts every stat, special effect, and limitation into one anchor unit, such as gold, so all pieces can be summed and compared.
when: pricing or checking items
why: A common unit makes different effects directly comparable.

text: Many equations containing conflicting data may have no consistent solution unless some values are guessed.
when: When many equations exceed the unknowns and some disagree
why: Surplus equations that conflict leave no single answer, so values must be guessed, unlike a matched count of equations and unknowns.

text: A worked damage-per-second calculation can contradict its own stated result when a rate such as seconds per attack is wrong, so verify the arithmetic and units.
when: checking a worked example before using it as a reference
why: A wrong rate value silently changes the final result.

text: Most game-balance math breaks down at extreme values, so test edge cases in playtesting and treat live games with caution when changing them.
why: Expected-value math ignores factors like the value of players' time, so actual experience can contradict what the numbers predict.

text: 1) List every resource and map how each relates to the others. 2) Choose as anchor the one all others convert into or connect to, often hit points or currency. 3) Set the anchor's value and derive the rest from it. 4) Tune individual items or stats only after this step.
when: three or more resources interact and no pairwise comparison captures them, when choosing an anchor for an existing game, or when starting any balance pass
why: Converting every resource to one anchor gives a consistent basis; a resource all others link to can organize the economy; a fixed base number gives every value a reference point.

text: Show a second measure such as accuracy next to total score, so that different play styles are both credited.
when: a scoring screen rewards one measure
why: a second measure rewards a different style

text: Objects intended to be exactly balanced should land close to zero on the curve; if they do not, the math needs correction.
why: Extreme-ranked objects should match observed play, so mismatches expose faulty formulas.

text: Show a benefits-minus-costs balance column as three tiers (too weak, balanced, too strong), optionally with a close-enough threshold, or as a gradient with set minimum and maximum.
when: Spreadsheets comparing benefits and costs.
why: Visual tiers make off-curve objects stand out.

text: Replace reinforcing loops with balancing ones, such as passing the turn after scoring, so power is checked.
when: Designing competitive feedback
why: A reinforcing loop rewards the leader repeatedly, so the game ends early with the stronger player winning.

text: Pick an anchor, a value set first and used to balance all others, because player and enemy power depend heavily on each other.
when: When balancing player and enemy power
why: Interdependence means one value must be fixed to balance the rest

text: Balance every new unit against one fixed baseline unit, so all units are judged on the same scale.
when: tuning a set of units

text: Once mechanics will not change, build formula-based spreadsheets that show relationships between mechanics so they can serve as balancing tools.
when: after core mechanics are fixed
why: Building the models now saves redoing them, because later mechanic changes won't invalidate the formulas.

text: Alternate options that players choose between must have equal expected benefit, meaning benefit multiplied by probability of use should match across alternates.
when: designing free alternates limited to one main and one alternate
why: unequal expected values make one choice dominate the other

text: To change an object's expected value, adjust its raw benefit, the game-wide frequency of its situations, or how often those situations occur where the item is found.
why: Expected value weights each situation's benefit by how often it occurs, so changing either term moves the total.

text: Balance the strategies available in a specific situation against a specific opponent, rather than comparing tools on an abstract power measure.
why: Tool usefulness shifts with the situation and with the other tools in play, so comparisons stripped of that context carry no meaning.

text: A fixed challenge breaks flow at either end of the skill range; as players improve during a playthrough, it becomes too easy and causes boredom, common in long PvE games.
when: Long PvE games where a single run gives players time to become noticeably more capable.
why: Players improve during a single playthrough.

text: Fixing one problem can create another, including in experiences no tester has reached, so check each fix against the whole system before accepting it.
when: When a change is made to fix a problem caused by interacting system elements.

text: Build a system-level model from many varied playtests before balance decisions; one or two tests, self-play, or a handful of samples can mislead by chance.
when: tuning by few trials or tests
why: Few stories or samples confuse anecdote with system behavior and yield confident wrong answers.

text: Build tunable values so they can change while the game runs: in prototypes so effects show immediately, and after release through a content management system to keep balancing.
when: prototyping
why: Changing values at runtime and after shipping speeds up tuning and extends the balancing loop beyond launch.

text: Award extra lives at regular milestones, such as every 10,000 points or every hundred collected items; regular milestones make each life feel earned and raise the chance of completing all levels.
why: Regular milestones make each extra life feel earned.

text: Racers that slow after a player's crash and speed up as the player closes in aid catch-up, yet AI advantages players cannot use break mutual opportunity and are disliked.
when: Racing against computer cars; designing AI assistance or catch-up mechanics.
why: Players perceive asymmetric advantages as unfair.

text: Nongamers can complete a tutorial and understand basics, yet still be overrun in combat and fail to enjoy the game, when the game is aimed beyond its original audience.
when: testing a game with nongamer players
why: Basic understanding does not guarantee enjoyment.

text: Early development usually contains many dominant strategies, and finding and removing them is progress even when it feels like confusion.
when: Balancing a game in early development
why: Discovering dominant options is part of iterating toward balance

text: A player who pulls ahead early and keeps a narrow lead may be deliberately controlling the opponent's experience, which signals skill.
when: Tracking in-match play patterns to infer skill.
why: Maintaining control without a crushing margin requires skill.

text: Players expect occasional difficulty spikes; a boss only slightly harder than its predecessor produces boredom.
when: a boss is only slightly harder than the previous boss
why: players expect occasional spikes and read small steps as no change

text: Players first find an exploitable enemy comical, then grow bored when repeating the same exploit, and most players who find an exploit adopt it.
when: Players discover a dominant, repetitive tactic
why: A helpless opponent is amusing briefly, but repetition removes challenge and interest.

text: When players choose difficulty, many pick a challenge slightly harder than even odds, struggle, and give up unless matchmaking or dynamic difficulty adjustment intervenes.
when: player-selected difficulty without automatic balancing
why: With no hard numbers to check against, people inflate their odds and ability, so they choose a harder option than a fair match.

text: A player far behind in a competitive game must go through the motions of a game they cannot win, which feels excruciating when it lasts a long time.
when: When a player or team falls far behind in a competitive match or race.
why: The outcome is decided but play continues.

text: A character's popularity and win rate can rise steadily with no update as players copy a strong strategy.
when: Observing a steady rise in a character's metrics between patches.
why: Strategies spread through imitation among players.

text: Each parameter setting is a location on a landscape with an associated score; one parameter is a point on a line, two form a point on a plane.
Chicken motivators are nonserious, nonexplicit, occasional symbolic signals that influence behavior without harming team climate.
A PvP game is balanced on initial conditions when every participant has roughly equal odds of winning at the start, given equal skill.
when: competitive PvP games

text: Game balance is a feeling players get across a whole game; it emerges from play rather than being added like a feature.
Game balance is a sub-field of game design focused on the numbers and formulas that underlie a game.
A tuning game asks the player to play a mechanic while rebalancing its parameters against one another, so each goal may need a different tuning.
The Goldilocks zone is the middle band of challenge between frustration and boredom, where flow is sparked, and it differs from player to player.
Game AI relies on many numeric parameters, including steering constants, pathfinding costs, tactical blend weights, and decision probabilities.
Isolating which objects, properties, behaviors or relationships cause a problem is one of the hardest parts of tuning.
Balance is an ongoing process: experience improves the first guess, but player preferences shift over time.
Making one change at a time lets a marginally working game be tuned without losing earlier work.
Balancing a deep interaction system can take years of development and tuning before the game is ready.
Meaningful games are often too long and variable for a class period, and they let each player proceed at their own speed, while teachers must keep one pace.
when: adopting games in a classroom
why: Class schedules and shared pacing conflict with game structure

text: Many educators did not grow up with video games, and building a game that delivers a complete, assessable, engaging lesson is very hard.
when: adopting games in a classroom
why: Limited familiarity with games and difficult design slow adoption

text: Games that keep developing after release, such as MMOs, online trading card games, and free-to-play mobile titles, add expansions and new content over time.
By the post-launch stage the team understands the game's balance far better, so its starting information is richer than in earlier phases.
Teams often keep working after release, watching player feedback and shipping small online patches to fix important problems.
why: Most players are online and can download small updates.

text: Initial-condition bias can come from random turn order, starting position, or the chosen character, class, or faction.
Variety can come from visuals, size, speed, movement mode, cover-seeking, ranged versus close-range attacks, hit points, and AI behavior.
Modeling time, money, skill and luck together needs four dimensions, which is harder to chart than the two-axis skill-luck plot.
A game played for thousands of years can still have its exact balance and first-turn value unknown.
Balance patches can continue for years after release, because a large player base finds imbalances that a much smaller beta group misses.
Initial numbers are usually wrong, so never treat a first prototype's starting values as final; repeated guessing and revision builds design intuition.
when: Once balancing begins in earnest on a first playable prototype built from initial guesses.
why: An initial version may be highly unbalanced and need iteration.

text: Negative feedback and random mechanics that favor the player who is behind can give less skilled players a real chance to win.
when: when designing PvP for mixed skill levels
why: Advantages for the trailing player offset skill gaps.

text: No designer balances a game perfectly by hand on the first try; build a playable version first, then let real players reveal the problems.
when: When a playable build is first put in front of real players, especially first-time ones.
why: Balance problems become visible only when the game runs with real players.

text: Balance intuition is built mainly by making many games.
Designers often assume their numbers are off by less than they really are, so test a doubling or halving to check.
when: reviewing tuned values
why: Initial estimates tend to underestimate how far values are from balance.

text: Adjusting numerical values is usually easier than rewriting story sections when difficulty and story pacing conflict.
when: Fixing mismatches between difficulty and narrative
why: Numbers can be tuned quickly, while narrative rewrites are costly.

text: Turn-based games convert easily to paper prototypes, while real-time games can sometimes be converted to turn-based play or run in real time with human helpers.
when: when building a paper prototype
why: Board games are quick to build and can reproduce the core play, so flaws surface earlier.

text: Prefer relatively simple systems with enough content to analyze; avoid games with dozens of stats or giant manuals.
when: choosing a game to analyze and expand
why: Too many stats and rules make analysis slow and overwhelming.

text: Personal experience can be supplemented with strategy articles and player or developer forums when judging balance.
when: When the judge is not deeply familiar with the game being assessed.
why: Community write-ups show which items players have already flagged at the extremes.

text: Assume any existing design is imperfect; if it seems perfect, look harder for flaws.
when: Starting a balance review of a game.
why: Unexamined assumptions of perfection hide real problems.

text: Announcing regular balance changes during beta can build player excitement.
when: During beta, once the studio has told the community that balance will change regularly.

text: Before mechanics are stable, focus on building tools rather than active balancing, unless playtesters strongly report a problem that blocks progress.
when: Early development, while the analytics hooks for later balancing are being planned.
why: Recording data costs programmer time and bandwidth, so what gets collected has to be chosen early.

text: Expose a few key parameters of a mechanic as editable fields so players or students can tune it without programming.
when: Teaching or testing game balance.
why: Players who never program can still learn how adjusting values reshapes how a mechanic feels.

text: Be cautious when criticizing a released game, since the production context and constraints behind its design are usually unknown.
when: when judging a game after release
why: Criticism is easy from outside, but the production context is often missing.

text: Use follow-up schedules as a guide, since over-eager contact can wear on a publisher.
when: following up after a pitch
why: Agreeing a response date at the meeting sets shared expectations about when a follow-up is expected.

text: Balancing less interesting tasks with interesting ones, and interacting positively with others, is a major professional asset.
when: Team production where preferred tasks cannot always be chosen
why: Story reaches its potential only when integrated into production, which requires knowing what teammates need and enjoy.

text: Compare expressive range charts during development as a debugging tool, not only after the system is finished.
when: When changing a generator's input parameters or adding a grammar rule during development.
why: Some parameter changes that look minor produce very different content spaces, which charts expose.

text: Telling players a game is not balanced but fun tends to improve their experience.
when: Games knowingly unbalanced but narratively engaging.
why: Sets expectations so imbalance is read as part of the experience.

text: A strong online game needs both a strong game and strong community support, since a dull game leaves nothing to discuss and weak support lets players drift away.
why: Players who cannot find the people they want to talk to quickly leave.

text: A saw-tooth difficulty pattern gives variance and expresses mastery better than a steady climb in difficulty.
Track a limit as a static attribute and its current value as a dynamic attribute, so fixed and changing parts stay separate.
when: when an object has a maximum such as speed or capacity
why: The limit changes only on rare events like upgrades, while the current value changes constantly during play.

text: As a final check, ask whether the game feels right and why or why not, to catch balancing problems that detailed checks missed.
when: After applying detailed balancing reviews
why: Stepping back to the whole experience reveals issues that focused checks overlook

text: Feel emerges from how parameters interact, so when tuning one value, check the values it partners with.
Control of many objects can use a cursor whose influence falls off with distance from its center, giving full control near the center and partial control farther away.
when: Controlling large groups of objects at once.
why: Player control stays binary, so a falloff cursor would let influence vary smoothly and partially across a group.

text: Caution players at least three times before any catastrophic event.
when: scheduling warnings for catastrophic events
why: Repeated warnings make the threat fair and expected.

text: Scale warnings to impact: strong warnings for high-consequence events, small or no warnings for minor ones, which players learn to expect through experience.
when: deciding how much warning an event needs
why: Proportional warnings keep minor events from feeling punitive.

text: Design a flexible system that stays simple, so different players can find the experience they prefer.
Use deliberate unfairness when exploration, history, or humor matters more than honest competition.
Fixed ratio schedules are weak standalone motivators; pair them with other schedules that cover the gaps between rewards.
why: Long gaps let players stop and walk away

text: If no strong core can be found, or the built core is poor, consider restarting with a different concept.
when: If no strong core can be found, or the built core is poor.

text: Expect a mechanic's timing or radius to need tuning; a shorter or smaller planned value may work better than the first estimate.
Variety can come from changing the enemy formations or arrangements that players see when a mission starts.
If weapon growth feels too slow, increase per-level gain, the damage ceiling, or both.
when: Weapon progression feels flat

text: Bosses and unique items are often variants of a common entity, and a prototype reference can express them directly without an abstract base.
when: when authoring variants of an existing entry
why: the simplest existing entry can serve as the prototype

text: Labeled difficulty levels can prime expectations, so an easy mode that helps the player and a hard mode that helps the AI may be accepted.
when: Designing difficulty modes
why: Labels set player expectations about what kind of help is fair.

text: Harder features impose more cognitive load, which leaves room for fewer other features taught at the same time.
when: sequencing onboarding
why: Cognitive capacity is limited, so load adds up across simultaneously taught features.

text: As enemies are destroyed, the survivors speed up and get harder to hit, so difficulty rises within each wave.
Each new wave restarts with slow, easy enemies, so difficulty resets easier even though waves get harder overall.
A new, much harder activity after main progression, often with different mechanics, gives veterans fresh challenge but eventually runs out of appeal.
Restricting lawless attacks to specific zones, enforced by guards that hunt flagged characters, splits a world into areas with and without player attacks.
A team wave awards a bonus to every player who survives the level, while a gladiator wave awards the bonus only to the first player to defeat the other.
when: Alternating cooperative and competitive wave types in a two-player arena
why: Bonus rules tie rewards to either shared survival or direct rivalry

text: A slight skew in an opponent's intransitive mix creates a fully dominant counter, so the balanced equilibrium of an intransitive game can be fragile.
Spatial transposition can turn a linear input-to-response curve into an exponential one, or recognize groups of inputs from different controls as one signal.
Fixed damage and hit points make fights fully predictable, so each encounter becomes a counted sequence of hits rather than a decision.
when: combat with deterministic damage
why: Without variance, the outcome is known in advance and engagement drops.

text: Reducing the power of moves that beginners use most and experts use less lowers win rate at low skill while leaving high-skill play largely unchanged.
when: Balancing a character whose strength is concentrated at low skill levels.
why: Changes hit the moves that matter at the affected rating band.

text: An explicit difficulty setting limits the range of hidden adaptation, so each setting shifts within its own band of internal levels.
An old rule of thumb allots about six months of balancing after a working version exists, though the true time depends on the game's type and scope.
Balancing can consume a large share of total development time, around half.
Five layers each at 80% certainty give about 33% survival (0.8 to the fifth power); with each layer at 30% certainty, a design five layers up survives unchanged only about 0.2% of the time.
when: Estimating whether a stacked design will survive playtesting
why: Multiplication of uncertainties makes high-layer designs fragile.

text: With n distinct playable characters, pairings alone yield about n squared matchups, counting order; ten characters give about a hundred.
Progression takes four classes: character, player skill, narrative, and mechanical. A game may use one, several, or none of them.
Creating a character's AI is not just setting parameter values, so a data-driven editor alone is insufficient; decision logic and combining behaviors need a dedicated AI design tool.
why: Different characters need different decision logic and selecting among behaviors at the right time, which data values alone cannot provide.

text: Making AI opponents stronger by boosting raw performance is easy but does not make the content itself interesting; designing good content is the harder problem.
when: When making computer opponents harder by giving them superior car performance
why: Raising opponent performance needs no content design, while crafting an interesting track is a non-trivial creative task.

text: Balancing cannot meaningfully start until the game works, and schedules spent making it functional often leave too little time to balance it, so the release feels unbalanced.
when: When the schedule is consumed before the game is functional
why: Balancing presupposes a fully working version, and its duration grows with the number of new gameplay elements.

text: Trusting the first formula without a common-sense check leaves hidden errors in the cost curve.
when: When objects on a derived cost curve seem to conflict with common sense

text: A paper balance is untested, so its results are provisional until playtesting confirms them.
when: When making a first-run card balance attempt on paper before any playtest

text: A progression chart can only approximate reward timing, because designers cannot control how long players take or the order of challenges in non-linear levels.
when: When plotting reward placement across a PvE game with non-linear levels
why: Designers cannot control how long a level takes a player or the order in which challenges are met.

text: Automatic topological analysis can absorb very large amounts of tuning time, sometimes months.
when: When the topological analysis goes beyond the simplest kind
why: Its complexity is formidable, so manual placement by a level designer ends up easier overall.

text: Designers often misjudge which AI behaviors are difficult and which are easy to add.
A breakable link tuned too fragile or too sturdy is a common error; the right threshold can only be found through playtesting.
Keeping the goals and adjusting numbers until the budget looks reasonable is the most common beginner mistake, and it leads to overpromising and underbudgeting.
when: When beginning developers build the budget for a project plan
why: Overpromising risks lost money, an overworked team, and undelivered promises.

text: Layout tuning can absorb large amounts of time, so set a stopping point rather than endlessly pushing data around.
when: When it is unclear which entity data is hot or cold in a real game
why: Hot and cold data is rarely clear-cut, so it is easy to get drawn into endless rearranging.

text: Balancing by guesswork and self-testing is useful early but too coarse for fine-grained balance.
when: Late-stage balance refinement.
why: Few testers cannot detect small differences.

text: Complaints such as 'too easy', 'impossible', 'unfair', and 'not fun' usually trace back to how hit points are handled.
why: Player challenge rests largely on managing the hit point resource, which depends on pacing.

text: Adding a tool can reduce depth if it creates a degenerate strategy, and extra viable strategies add complexity without necessarily adding decision depth.
when: When a new tool makes one choice obviously best in a given decision
why: Counting options is easy to measure, but the real goal is a richer player thought process.

text: Extreme penalties such as erasing long saved progress or permanently removing hard-earned advancement can make players quit or exploit the system, and are often judged too harsh.
when: When a penalty wipes out large amounts of player investment
why: Losses that are severe and irreversible outweigh the value of the challenge for many players

text: A weak curve starts with disappointment, lacks a hook, peaks only briefly, and falls below the quitting threshold, so later content fails to build and the experience fades.
why: Without a hook, interest keeps sliding after a disappointing start until it falls below the point where the audience disengages.

text: Treating game design as trivial amusement underrates how strongly games shape experiences and thinking.
why: Games create experiences, and life consists of experiences, so their effects on people run deep.

text: A catastrophic event with no prior signs feels arbitrary and makes the player feel cheated.
when: designing sudden major setbacks
why: Players perceive unannounced disasters as unfair.

text: Random balance changes are not perfect imbalance; each change must be deliberate.
when: When deliberately perturbing balance in a game where no player can do everything well
why: A clearly understood balance curve lets changes be made purposefully rather than at random.

text: Trouble arises when players expect a fair contest and only discover the imbalance during play.
when: When players are led to expect a fair contest that turns out unbalanced
why: Violated expectations cause frustration.

text: Early deaths that feel unfair make players quit, especially in free-to-play games where commitment is low.
when: early game
why: Players have little commitment to endure unfair early losses.

text: Tuning a game for expert players can spoil it for the average player.
when: When balancing difficulty for a broad audience
why: Expert preferences often differ from the general player population.

text: Reacting to each playtest problem with a quick knob turn makes the game lurch between imbalances, because strategies are coupled and each fix causes another problem.
when: When a playtest shows something wrong and the designer reacts by turning a knob
why: Strategies are coupled, so each fix for one problem causes another.

text: Beta and live balancing and monetization assume critical UX issues are already fixed, which is often not the case.
when: Beta and live operation
why: Analytics-driven balancing and monetization presume earlier user-research problems were already resolved.

text: An exploitable imbalance can destroy the game's intended play even when no one planned it.
when: When a new tool produces a strategy that is obviously best in a decision
why: With one option always best, the choice is always the same and the decision process disappears.

text: 1) Confirm the rules are internally complete. 2) Only then check fairness and balance. 3) Test for fun and challenge. 4) Keep the whole system in motion throughout.
when: Once the rules are fully consistent and equitable for every participant.
why: A system is only understood when studied in motion as a whole, so playtesting follows defining its elements.

text: 1) Sort all players by rating from highest to lowest. 2) Use the resulting order as the high-granularity rank.
1) Adjust store prices or currency drop rates during alpha or beta testing. 2) Make post-launch price changes when an item proves worth more or less than expected.
when: During alpha or beta testing, or post-launch if an item's worth is judged off from expectations.
why: Scarcity forces tradeoff decisions that make play interesting, while too little currency frustrates players stuck grinding.

text: 1) Add a new mechanic column, blank or zero for every existing row. 2) Enter tentative costing math based on current game knowledge. 3) Document the mechanic and justify its cost in a cell note.

1) Sketch the expected power curve for a short PvP game. 2) Play it or record a session. 3) Track each player's distance from the win condition over time. 4) Compare the real curve with the prediction.
when: A PvP game that is very short, under about five minutes, and that the designer knows well.

text: 1) Take a simple barter game. 2) Add a new layer of complexity to its trading system, such as dynamically changing item values. 3) Playtest the change.
when: Practicing economy design
why: Dynamic values reveal how trade behavior shifts under changing prices.

text: 1) Place every reward on a chart showing its approximate position in the game. 2) Mark gaps where little happens for a long stretch. 3) Size each reward by its intensity: big power gains, major level transitions or permanent world changes, and climaxes or story reversals. 4) Sum intensity over time to graph the player's sense of progress.
when: Early design check for pacing problems before playtests.
why: Shows the general shape of progress as the player experiences it.

text: 1) Test the value at its minimum, maximum and midpoint to learn how the game feels. 2) Tune from there.
when: A number with a known range but unknown right value.
why: Extremes reveal how the value shapes play.

text: 1) Start balance tests with the dev team, close family and friends. 2) Ask testers to try to break systems and find exploits. 3) Record which tester gave each feedback item.
when: Early balance testing.
why: Different testers reveal different problems, and their source matters.

text: 1) Assign sounds to importance categories. 2) Set ducking levels. 3) Playtest and get feedback from players and audio professionals. 4) Repeat trial and error until the balance is right.
when: Tuning sound ducking for interactive audio in games.
why: Finding the right balance requires trial and error.

text: 1) Pick a reasonable best guess for each unknown parameter, such as grid size or spawn count. 2) Play and observe. 3) Revise the values after testing.
when: Early prototype whose parameters, such as grid size or spawn count, are still unknown.
why: The right values can't be known until the game is played, so later revision is expected.

text: 1) Write down the expected relationships between the balanced elements. 2) For each experiment, record whether it improved the game and whether it matched the model. 3) Revise the model when results disagree with it.
when: When balancing several interacting values
why: Written expectations make it easier to see why a change had an effect and to build on past results

text: 1) When a value feels wrong, guess an exact number rather than a round one. 2) Test it. 3) Use the result to refine the next guess, converging on a value that feels right.
when: When repeatedly adjusting one value by feel
why: Exact guesses give intuition precise feedback, while rounded steps stop it from improving

text: 1) While playing or watching a game, judge whether it is balanced, looking for slight imbalances since no game is perfect. 2) For each imbalance, note what it is, its severity, its cause and how you would fix it. 3) Later check the notes with mathematical analysis.
when: Playing or watching existing games to build balance intuition, focusing on clearly over- or underpowered objects.
why: Notes made now can later be checked against mathematical analysis to confirm or disprove the initial intuition.

text: 1) Identify the types of trading in a chosen game. 2) Swap in a different auction mechanic. 3) Predict the effect on play.
when: Evaluating a trade or auction mechanic in an existing game

text: 1) Guess how long a recent game's combat lasts. 2) Time it with a stopwatch. 3) Compare the result with your guess and note whether it felt longer or shorter.
when: calibrating intuition about fight length

text: 1) Choose a game and imagine a remake that keeps core mechanics. 2) Define at least three balance questions analytics could answer. 3) For each question, list needed metrics and collection methods. 4) Plan calculations, visualizations and the patterns that would support each conclusion.
when: Planning an analytics study for an existing game's balance.
why: A structured plan ties each balance question to measurable evidence.

text: 1) Study the design decisions and numbers of games you play. 2) Make your own games. 3) Balance those games and test the results.
when: When you are not currently building an original title or altering an existing one, and want to sharpen balance skills.
why: Studying the numbers behind others' designs reveals how their choices affect play, which builds balance skill.

text: 1) Track each player's strike probability on odd and even turns and their cumulative expected strikes. 2) Find the turn at which a player's chance of losing first passes 50%. 3) Repeat for three, four, five and more players to find turn-order patterns.
