when: checking whether the first player in a multiplayer dice game has an advantage
why: the first player's opening roll differs, so equal-probability assumptions are only approximate

text: 1) Write down an intuitive guess of the optimal mix. 2) Solve the payoff equations. 3) Compare the guess with the solution to calibrate intuition.
when: Solving an intransitive game with altered payoffs
why: Intuition about payoffs is often wrong

text: 1) Disable the character animation. 2) Replay the same movements. 3) Note what feels lost, such as arcs, turns, slides and landings.
when: auditing how much feel comes from presentation
why: Removing one layer reveals how much feel it carries.

text: 1) Make one player or component grossly stronger. 2) Observe how the rest of the game responds.
when: probing how a system reacts to imbalance
why: Locking parameters makes testers exercise one part of the mechanics, so its effects can be seen independently.

text: 1) Create AI agents with different playing characteristics. 2) Use them to playtest many generated levels, since the mechanism needs many levels tested.
when: when a personalisation mechanism needs many playtested levels
why: Testing needs many levels played, so agents with varying styles supply that volume.

text: 1) Observe harmful player behavior in playtests. 2) Remove the reward and any mechanic that enables it. 3) Reward the cooperative behavior you want, such as staying close to others.
when: When playtests show antisocial behavior that the rules allow or reward.
why: Operant conditioning: behaviours that go rewarded or unpunished tend to grow, while punished or unrewarded ones fade.

text: 1) Pick a game and its current emotional tone. 2) Replace its music with a piece evoking a very different feeling. 3) Note whether the result is unsettling, funny or strange.
when: exploring tone options
why: Pairing music with a contrasting emotion to the existing tone can produce an unsettling, richer effect.

text: 1) Create formless color swatches for each scene. 2) Review them in sequence. 3) Judge the visual and emotional progression by color alone.
when: Planning visual and emotional arc across scenes.
why: Color alone reveals mood progression without detail distraction.

text: Tune difficulty and pacing in small, measured steps guided by aggregated metrics rather than large guesses.
when: Mid-project balancing.
why: Coarse guesswork yields erratic progress; precise measurement enables steady improvement.

text: 1) Identify why optimal play stalls the game. 2) Add, remove, or change one rule at a time. 3) Test each change. 4) Repeat until the game is interesting and finishes under optimal play, using the fewest changes.
when: when a competitive game stalls under optimal play
why: Small isolated changes reveal which rule causes the problem.

text: 1) Define key performance indicators with product managers. 2) Let players in and collect play data. 3) Tune the game toward the predefined KPIs, meeting publisher performance criteria before launch.
when: When tuning a live or free-to-play game against performance goals
why: Only live play data collected at scale can show whether the balance is succeeding in such games.

text: 1) Replace one power type with the other type the deck already uses. 2) Swap in power cards by discarding matching action cards from the deck. 3) Drop power cards in favor of duplicates of any action card that exists in the game.
when: when adjusting power cards in a deck of fixed size
why: each option shifts resource supply without changing deck size

text: 1) List the game variables in the prototype. 2) Change one variable and observe its effects on the others. 3) Try to create easy, medium, and hard levels by tweaking variables alone.
when: Tuning a prototype
why: Judging whether variables are viable requires a clear picture of the intended player experience.

text: 1) Edit matrix entries to represent a changed rule. 2) Recompute the length distribution. 3) Compare the new median and mean with the old.
when: testing a proposed rule change to a track game
why: matrix edits give exact effects without playtesting

text: 1) Have players try the opening level, then suggest a setting. 2) Explain each difficulty with concrete examples. 3) Let players adjust difficulty mid-game.
when: When players are unsure which explicit difficulty level to pick.
why: Difficulty names lack a shared meaning, so players need help choosing.

text: Rebalance through repeated testing and give-and-take adjustments after each change, rather than trusting a single pass, until the whole game seems balanced.
Unforgiving difficulty is acceptable only when the game is transparent about how harsh it is and players consent to it; hiding that harshness breaks the consent.
when: Designing unforgiving challenge, especially early in a game or in free-to-play games where players are less engaged.
why: Players who aren't yet deeply engaged may not be prepared for harsh challenges they weren't warned about.

text: Set computer opponents slightly below the top performance a skilled human could reach, so they remain beatable.
when: Racing games with computer opponents that keep pace with the human player.
why: Keeping opponents slightly below perfect human speed keeps the pack tight as long as the human stays close.

text: If the score comes from a differentiable formula, compute the best parameter values directly; otherwise search by trying settings in the game.
when: tuning AI parameters
why: A differentiable formula yields the best values explicitly, while otherwise only trying values in the game reveals how well they perform.

text: Expose the same controls to scripted AI that the player has, such as forward speed, turning and weapon changes, so an AI character can be swapped for a human player.
when: When AI characters are driven by a scripting language
why: Controls given as speed, turning and weapon choices, not target points, let a human stand in for the AI with little effort.

text: Schedule balance passes late, once systems are in place, and start the main balance work after all content is complete.
when: During alpha, once systems are in and before all content is in
why: Like a recipe that cannot be perfected without all its ingredients, balance depends on content that does not yet exist.

text: Test high-skill balance with dedicated players who practice daily and can play intensely for long sessions.
when: tuning skill-based balance
why: Expert-level balance only shows up when testers sustain intense play for long stretches and keep their skills sharp.

text: Mathematics is one of several balance methods, and no single method should be used to the exclusion of the others.
Make parameter evaluation fast, for example by running the game at high speed without rendering or by using heuristics that skip running the game.
when: searching parameter spaces by trial
why: Techniques that need a full game with a real player are unlikely to be practical.

text: Label each stretch of an interest curve with the interest type holding attention there, showing which factor works at each moment.
why: Examining a player's interest is the best measure of experience quality, and labeling each stretch adds detail to that examination.

text: Fix the underlying collection bug rather than only scrubbing its output, so the cleaning does not have to be repeated.
when: Data problems recur across collection periods
why: Repeated scrubbing wastes effort on the same faults

text: After every balance change, recheck the metrics that motivated it to confirm the expected effect.
when: After a balance change made to fix a problem in the past
why: The change may fix the problem, leave it unresolved, or overshoot the target, and only the original metric shows which.

text: Check moves with 100% hit rates before analysis, since they may be designed to be unblockable or unavoidable rather than data errors; confirm with whoever wrote the data collection code.
when: Move hit-rate data shows moves that always connect.
why: Such values usually reflect intended mechanics, not measurement mistakes.

text: An exploit that works but is slower than normal play is not a practical exploit.
Budget extensive tuning time for any car avatar, whatever its art style, since its handling is judged against real driving.
when: building a car avatar
why: Feel expectations are high even for stylized vehicles

text: Look for game elements that are too simple to be interesting.
Decide carefully which post-release problems to patch; often wait, since quick patches to temporary spikes cut off the community's natural adaptation.
when: deciding on post-release balance changes
why: Deciding is hard after release, and waiting lets players adapt.

text: Tune combat pacing to the skill and reaction speed of the intended players; one speed does not suit every audience.
Check each goal for whether it is too hard, too easy, unclear, or hidden from players.
when: fun testing
why: Hearing testers narrate their goals shows whether they pursue the intended goals or wander off to side aims.

text: Pursue high-skill balance when the game's meaning comes from skill-driven challenge; prefer lower-skill balance when meaning comes mainly from story or socializing.
when: A game of skill that aims to support endlessly deep play
why: A skill game that fails under skilled play has no value, so its balance cannot be compromised.

text: When rebalancing costs, change only the quantity of a power, never its type.
when: When adjusting card costs to bring each card near a power curve

text: Make the easiest difficulty really easy, since being too easy is safer than being so hard that some players cannot play at all.
when: When offering several difficulty levels to players of varied skill
why: Overly easy play costs little, while an easy mode that is too hard can shut some players out entirely.

text: Parties of friends can create larger skill gaps, so tracking a separate MMR for solo and group play keeps matchmaking even.
when: when matchmaking includes premade groups
why: Regular teammates coordinate better, so the same player's rating in a group may differ from their solo rating.

text: Building a complete supporting math costs slow trial and error plus playtesting or analytics, but afterward it speeds design and balance considerably.
when: deciding whether to invest in a full balance system
why: Most of the balance work is paid up front and returns benefits later.

text: Rebuilding a failing mission affects gameplay, level design and art, while salvaging it cheaply usually shifts extra work onto the narrative team.
when: A playable mission is not working
why: Each fix spreads cost to different departments

text: Memorized optimal strategies give reliable, measurable skill, but they lack the adaptive, clever decisions that let players turn a loss into a win.
when: When optimal play means following a well-practiced algorithm rather than improvising
why: Executing a known pattern rewards repetition, not improvised choices that rescue a losing position.

text: Tuning enemies for viable builds makes optimal builds trivial, while tuning for optimal builds makes content too hard for most players.
when: tuning late-game content
why: One tuning target cannot serve both build levels.

text: Tuning the probabilities of a fixed random outcome and tuning the effects of each space both reach a target median length, but the two differ in ease and in how they change play.
when: choosing how to hit a target game length
why: changing odds keeps rules intact while changing effects alters what each space does

text: Explicit difficulty selection is simple and reasonably effective, but players may fear choosing wrong because difficulty names have no standard meaning. Adaptive difficulty avoids this by adjusting silently.
when: When choosing how to offer difficulty modification.
why: Explicit choices are transparent but risky to pick; adaptive adjustment is hidden but can be noticed and exploited.

text: A build is the full set of choices a player makes when creating a character, including class, equipment, skills, attributes, and other customization.
The gap between viable and optimal builds widens as characters level, because min-maxing players optimize every level gain.
when: characters progress through levels
why: Optimizers compound small advantages at each level.

text: Builds fall into four levels: optimal (best mathematically extractable), viable (playable throughout), marginally viable (winnable by skilled players), and nonviable (hopeless even for experts).
when: Evaluating character build strength and balancing content
why: Most players rely on viable builds, which should carry a typical player through at normal settings.

text: Test combinations of abilities, not just single abilities, because a model that values abilities separately misses synergy that can make low-rated objects strong.
when: When a game has enough comparable objects to find many similar pairs
why: When many ratings conflict, no unique consistent solution exists and the model must rely on guesses.

text: Keep card power fairly even, since useless cards waste design effort; a standout card is tolerable when its deck's other cards fall below average, because deck strength decides matchups.
when: When the remaining cards in the deck sit below average.
why: In constructed play, players pick freely from the whole pool, so each card is judged against peers at its cost.

text: A property's value rises as a player nears completing a set; the final piece, like a third color-set item, is worth far more to someone holding two.
when: A set of complementary items grants a bonus when completed.
why: The final piece unlocks the full set bonus, which only the holder of the partial set can use.

text: Playtesters tend to build narrow, extreme decks that maximize power, which exposes dominant strategies in the card pool.
when: during playtesting of a card pool
why: Players search for the strongest combinations.

text: A flush is a five-card poker hand whose cards all share one suit; card rank does not matter.
Six-card poker variants can include Three and Three, which holds two three-of-a-kinds, and Four and Two, which holds a four-of-a-kind plus a pair.
If several objects rated too high share one ability, that ability is probably overvalued in the model.
When testing starter decks, look for one starter that wins consistently, or one much weaker that can be forced on an opponent.
when: When balancing the four starter decks during playtesting
why: Testers aim to break the game, so they search for a dominant starter or a weak one to force on opponents.

text: Do not multiply probabilities when rolls add into a shared total, since each result changes the target for the next; count those cases directly.
when: rolls contribute to one running total

text: When one color is the most powerful alone, reduce its self-sufficiency by making its strongest commons rare.
when: When a color on its own can cover a deck's essentials
why: Making the strongest commons rare removes easy access to a color's key effects, so decks must mix colors to get what they need.

text: Adding colors makes colored costs harder to pay early: with three colors, a two-of-one-color card is on average not castable before turn eight.
when: Systems with three or more colors.
why: Once several colors share the land base, lands of each needed color arrive slowly, so only single-color costs are reliably castable early.

text: A deck that drives challengers away pushes its owner to keep improving it.
Drawing from a shuffled deck is dependent, because each card drawn changes which cards remain and therefore the odds of later draws.
When discarded cards are reshuffled into the deck before redrawing, a discarded card can come back, so redraw odds include that chance.
when: a mulligan or redraw returns cards to the same deck
why: the replacement draw samples from a deck that still contains the discards

text: With one land per turn and no mana carryover, available mana on a turn equals the smaller of the turn number and the lands drawn so far.
With one card in three a land, a seven-card opening hand and one draw per turn give expected arrival turns of 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, and 11 for the first six lands.
when: seven-card opening hand, one draw per turn, one card in three is a land

text: Base 1 for existing; 1 per colorless mana; 2 and 3 for first and second colored mana; +1 at five total mana, +1 at six, +2 at seven.
when: Cards with power, toughness, and mana costs.

text: Counting deck orderings as distinct treats identical cards as different and gives a wrong total; divide out every group of duplicate cards for exact counts, since shuffle counts grow rapidly.
why: Lands are interchangeable for this problem, so many distinct orderings produce the same outcome and must be merged.

text: Changing a card's cost changes it in every deck that contains it, so recheck all matchups after each edit.
when: when cards appear in several decks
why: shared cards couple deck matchups

text: Card combinations that repeat an effect can drive games into long stalls where neither side can end the game quickly.
why: Long games lead players to concede.

text: Mechanics that move cards between players can cause unintended behavior that goes beyond what the designer intended.
Raising a fraction to a large power by hand is impractical, so use a calculator for such probability products.
Treating face-down removals as changing the odds is a mistake, since no information is gained and the odds stay the same.
when: When reshuffling a deck that no one has yet seen
why: Reordering cards nobody has seen changes only the sequence, not what remains in the pool, so the probabilities stay the same.

text: Using the original count of matching cards for a later draw ignores cards already drawn; subtract drawn cards from both the success count and the deck size.
when: When a later draw follows earlier revealed cards from the same deck
why: Probabilities are recalculated each time a card is revealed, so counts taken before those reveals go stale.

text: 1) Rank hand types so rarer hands outrank common ones. 2) Count distinct card combinations forming each hand type. 3) Divide each count by total combinations of that size; the lower probability ranks higher.
when: adding new hand types to a ranking
why: rarity reflects how hard a hand is to make

text: 1) Give testers the modified starter decks or individual cards. 2) If testing individual cards, have testers build decks under a copy limit per card. 3) Have every player, including the designer, try to break the game.
when: playtesting modified card game components

text: 1) Do heavy math up front, aligning card costs and benefits on a cost curve. 2) Playtest to refine the supporting math.
when: tabletop card games
why: Tabletop games cannot be tracked in player data the way digital ones can, so the cost math has to be settled before testing begins.

text: 1) Pick four units and balance each against the baseline. 2) Play them against each other until all four are about equal to the baseline and to one another.
when: solo balancing of a small set of units

text: 1) Define the favorable hands, such as five or more cards of one suit. 2) Count them with the choose operator. 3) Divide by the total number of possible hands.
when: computing the probability of a hand pattern from a shuffled deck
why: favorable over total gives the probability

text: When players can build any deck, balance each card against others on the same cost curve, since individual card value matters.
when: In a constructed format where players build decks from any available cards
why: Players can pick any card, so each card's value is judged against others at the same cost level.

text: Only the power costs of Action cards may be changed; power types, card effects, and core rules stay fixed.
when: When balancing constructed cards.

text: Price colored mana above colorless mana; in a two-color setup with an even split, colored mana should cost about double.
when: Two-color systems with an even split of color sources.
why: Finding a land of one specific color takes about two land draws on average.

text: Do not put cards at risk unless players opt in to playing for ante.
why: The hostile behavior that card-risking produced outweighed whatever it added to play.

text: When each mulligan reshuffles and redraws, the chance of failing every attempt is the product of each attempt's failure probability.
when: a player mulligans repeatedly down to smaller hands
why: each redraw is independent of earlier attempts

text: Single-color systems avoid colored and colorless distinctions, but their lack of variety leaves weaknesses that opponents can exploit.
when: Resource systems that use only one color.
why: Each color in this design carries its own strengths and gaps, so a deck limited to one color exposes weaknesses that a rival can spot and target.

text: Making each color able to paralyze or counter everything forces players out of one color, but limiting single-color self-sufficiency makes players combine resources from several sources.
when: when a deck game should require multicolor decks
why: Players could sidestep many design problems by restricting their deck to a single color, which the designer wanted to discourage.

text: Non-digital card games can fix imbalances by restricting or banning cards, which angers owners, or by issuing errata, which is hard to spread and enforce.
when: after a card game is released
why: Unlike an online game that can push a patch, a physical card set cannot be changed after release, so fixes are limited to bans or errata.

text: As the curve moves, previously banned or disallowed options may become viable again.
Judge each option by the roles it serves in each region, since an option can be useless in some regions yet essential in others.
when: When weighing weapons across several regions of a level-based game.

text: Use restrictions to block game-breaking loopholes or imbalances that favor early actions.
why: Gating a strong unit behind a prerequisite stops one player from rushing it while others are still building weaker units.

text: Removing a rarely chosen option based only on telemetry can cut revenue, because that option may be shaping how players choose.
when: When telemetry is used without careful analysis or awareness of data-mining limits.
why: low choice share can hide a comparison effect

text: In real-time games, restrict overly powerful actions so they become a resource the player must manage.
when: In real-time games with actions that are too powerful.

text: Score restrictions such as Defender as a cost of about 1 point, not as a negative benefit.
when: Abilities that limit what a card can do.
why: A restriction takes value away from the card, so it counts against it.

text: COGS (cost of goods sold) is the per-unit cost to actually make the game.
A collectible that protects players from enemies and grants extra lives gains endogenous value, because both help players finish levels.
why: The player's main goal in these levels is simply finishing them, and the item directly helps that goal.

text: A small collectible gains value when it feeds into a long chain of rewards that ends in a major payoff.
when: when designing collectibles or currencies
why: Value is inherited from the rewards the collectible unlocks

text: Chaining unlocks from coin totals to star doors ties collection to the highest rewards, encouraging precise play to gather every coin.
why: Each coin's worth flows through a chain of unlocks to the biggest rewards, so collecting every coin becomes worth the effort.

text: 1) List every cost and benefit in the game. 2) Value resource costs, which may follow any numeric relationship the game needs. 3) Value the most common benefits, those on nearly everything. 4) Work progressively toward rarer, more complex costs and benefits.
when: building a supporting math from scratch

text: 1) Build a column of sequential numbers. 2) Add a column multiplying them by a constant for a linear curve. 3) Add a column where each value is the previous times a fixed ratio for exponential growth. 4) Chart each column alone, then all together.
when: Comparing linear, triangular and exponential growth before choosing a curve for a game value.
why: Graphing each curve separately and then together shows how their shapes differ.

text: Combo-based designs appear as dual-wielding, support classes, card combos, and support towers.
A score multiplier that rises with consecutive successful actions without failure rewards long-term survival and foresight over single large, often lucky, combos.
why: Big plays often depend on luck, while lasting requires planning several moves ahead, so the multiplier ties score to skill.

text: Completing any event adds bonus time to every open combo, regardless of event type, so one success keeps all chains alive.
why: Linked combo systems mean an event in one chain counts toward the others, so the player keeps moving toward the next target.

text: Early game favors negative feedback to keep the match open; late game switches to positive feedback for a final, irreversible win.
why: Negative feedback pulls the leader back toward the center, keeping players close and producing reversals, though too strong a loop can stall the game.

text: 1) Find the total power of the combo as a whole. 2) Price the combo as a whole. 3) Split that price across components according to their standalone usefulness outside the combo.
when: When a game object is useful only in combination with another object.
why: Its combined effect depends on a separate action players must take elsewhere, so that off-object action is the cost to account for.

text: Count the opportunity cost of the setup action a combo needs, and offset the situational benefit by it, since the combo is useless without that action.
when: When a game object is useful only in combination with another object.
why: The combined effect happens only when a separate action is taken elsewhere, and that action is the cost to count.

text: Against an unequal opponent, the weaker player loses power early and falls further over time.
when: when players differ in skill
why: the weaker side's losses compound

text: Temporary dominance of one option is common, and players may need time to find counters before the balance settles.
when: judging a short-term imbalance after release
why: Large post-release player numbers reveal techniques that small beta groups never found, and each new technique spreads as others copy it.

text: Team competitive games balance teams against each other, so numbers still matter even when players do not level up during a match.
Perfectly balancing a trading card game is hard, so slightly stronger cards tend to appear even when designers aim for parity.
when: Designing a TCG

text: Combining tournament entry fees with tournament rewards creates interactions that need careful balancing.
Newcomers often displace entrenched series, since small challengers hold edges that big studios struggle to copy.
When two competitors share a positive-sum setup and feedback reinforces leaders, a slight early advantage grows until the gap becomes large by the finish.
when: In positive-sum PvP games with positive feedback loops.
why: Positive feedback lets the leader convert each advantage into more, so a tiny early lead compounds over time.

text: Transitive systems suit cost-to-benefit balancing, while intransitive systems like rock-paper-scissors need different balancing methods.
why: Equality and inequality chain across comparisons, so one scale of value works; rock-paper-scissors breaks that chain.

text: Hiding matchmaking rating and showing rank gives status without a number that could discourage low-rated players, who still feel competent when winning about half their games.
when: when deciding whether to display matchmaking rating or raw skill numbers
why: players compare outcomes to their own sense of skill, not to a number

text: If a hidden rating drives matchmaking while players chase a visible rank, they may intentionally drop their rating to face weaker opponents.
when: When a hidden rating drives matchmaking but a different visible rank is shown.
why: a lower hidden rating yields easier matches

text: Players may stop playing for a while to raise their RD, an unintended incentive that produces larger rating swings on return.
when: rating systems where RD rises during inactivity
why: a higher RD makes rating changes larger

text: Head-to-head play produces a personal, one-on-one contest that suits focused, competitive players.
when: when two players compete directly
why: The one-on-one structure concentrates attention on the opponent.

text: Your game competes with dozens of similar titles for attention, so competitive context can matter as much as quality.
when: When a game enters a market already crowded with similar titles.
why: Buyers weigh a game against close rivals, so a clear gap it fills can matter as much as its quality.

text: The K factor sets the maximum change from one game and represents the uncertainty in a rating.
In multilateral competition, three or more players compete directly against each other.
The expected scores of the two players in a game always sum to 1.
The divisor 400 is a chosen convention; a 200-point rating gap gives an expected score of about 0.76.
There is no universally accepted K value; each rating implementation chooses its own.
Elo assumes a much more skilled player eventually wins almost every game against a weaker one, so win chance approaches certainty as the skill gap grows.
Elo is designed for two-player games and must be modified to rate three or more players.
Most online ranking systems are objective, based on rating, results, or other performance data.
Give new or provisional players a higher K so their ratings reach their true skill level quickly, then lower K for established players.
why: Their true skill is still largely unknown, so early results should shift the rating more.

text: Some systems lower K above a rating threshold, and top-level tournaments may use a lower K, on the theory that top players' skill changes slowly.
when: Players above a set rating, or in very high-level tournaments.
why: Highly skilled players' ability changes slowly, and a large K would make their ratings too volatile.

text: Use plain Elo for two-player, skill-based games such as chess; avoid it when luck is significant, more than two players compete, or draws do not equal half a win.
when: Two-player games where skill, not chance, decides outcomes.
why: Elo assumes skill-based outcomes and that a draw equals half a win, and both can fail.

text: Online seasons leave few gaps between them, because designers want players to keep returning.
when: With online games.
why: Long breaks risk players leaving and never coming back, so designers keep play continuous.

text: Competitive games usually balance for expert players, since they are played intensely for long periods by skilled players.
when: Competitive games intended for long study by professional players.
why: Balancing across the whole skill range is impossible, so the expert level gets priority.

text: A larger K makes a rating react more strongly to each result, while a smaller K makes it change slowly.
why: K sets the largest swing one game can produce, scaling the rating change.

text: Monthly resets paired with rewards for the previous month's rank let top performers start higher, saving time for skilled players.
why: Rewards for logging in create an incentive to return, and good performers avoid restarting at the bottom.

text: In an open-challenge ladder, any player may challenge any other; a winner moves up one place, swapping with the player immediately above, and the loser stays put.
when: Online games where anyone may issue a challenge to any opponent.

text: Players who leave permanently take their points with them: below-average leavers inflate the system, and above-average leavers deflate it.
why: Exiting removes a player's whole rating from the system, shifting the total away from average.

text: Elo expected score E = 1/(1+10^((R_opp−R_player)/400)), the score a player is expected to earn against an opponent; equivalently, with Q=10^(R/400), E = Q_player/(Q_player+Q_opp).
why: E is a win probability bounded between 0 and 1, based on the rating difference.

text: Elo update: new rating = old rating + K × (A - E), where A is 1 for a win and 0 for a loss, and E is the expected score.
why: The rating moves by how far the result deviated from the prior estimate, scaled by uncertainty.

text: A common scheme uses K = 32 for provisional players and K = 16 after a set number of rated games.
why: Newcomers' skill is largely unknown, so early results should move their ratings more.

text: Half-win scoring for draws is fair only if a draw truly equals half a win; otherwise weaker players who easily force draws gain rating by challenging stronger ones.
when: Games where draws are possible and the weaker side can draw often.
why: Half-win scoring rewards defensive draw-seeking against stronger opponents.

text: Designers hide standings so all players feel they have a chance, but this hides a growing gap; trailing players may not notice until contact ends their game quickly.
when: positive feedback has built a large hidden gap
why: Players cannot see opponents' progress and so misjudge their own position.

text: A simulated rating far outside the spread of opponent ratings usually signals a calculation error, since Elo ratings stay bounded by opponents' ratings.
why: Ratings move only relative to opponents' ratings, so they have practical upper and lower bounds.

text: Elo does not explicitly model luck, so it can misjudge players in games where chance strongly affects outcomes.
when: Games with chance mechanics that let a less skilled player win by luck.
why: Elo's model assumes skill-based games, where the favorite nearly always wins as skill gaps grow.

text: 1) For each game, compute the expected score E from the rating difference. 2) Add the E values across all games. 3) Set A to the total actual score. 4) Add K × (A - summed E) to the old rating, rounding as the system requires.
when: a rating period containing several games
why: Elo can be applied to an entire event, so per-game expectations are summed into one update.

text: 1) Check whether an early leader usually wins the prototype. 2) If so, identify the reinforcing relationship. 3) Change it to a balancing one.
when: Testing competitive balance in a prototype
why: A reinforcing relationship lets early advantages compound, creating imbalance.

text: In Monrad pairing, the first-ranked player plays the second, the third plays the fourth, and so on down the full rankings.
when: In Swiss-system tournaments.

text: Avoid stagnation, because a competition needs an eventual winner.
When spenders become stronger, pair players by skill in matchmaking so the game stays competitive.
when: If a game is balanced so players who spend more become more powerful.
why: Matching by skill rather than spending keeps the game feeling fair and competitive for players.

text: Choosing K trades responsiveness against stability: a low K reacts slowly to real changes in performance, while a high K is dominated by recent games.
why: Too low a K ignores real performance changes; too high lets recent games dominate the rating.

text: Most people avoid barriers and follow the crowd, which eventually means competing in the most crowded space.
why: People feel safer following the crowd, so those who cross a barrier early face few rivals.

text: A creative technique found by players spreads quickly through the community and can force a design response.
when: after release with a large player base
why: A large player population uncovers imbalances that smaller beta tests never revealed, and every opponent meeting the technique sees it.

text: A card game can be intentionally unfair: seating order and a positive feedback loop create its fun, while players accept the obvious unfairness from the start.
why: The unfairness is visible and central to the design, so players accept it.

text: Aim for repetition with variation: uniform escalation feels flat, while too little consistency feels like noise.
when: tuning enemy difficulty
why: Players need consistent rules to learn from, plus variation to stay engaged.

text: Games deliberately create challenge through friction built into the design.
why: Players need a difficulty that is neither so easy it bores them nor so hard it stresses them.

text: Conflicting card values can result from deliberate placement above or below the curve, colors that are not truly equivalent, or metagame factors such as rarity or synergy.

Use intentional imbalance only when no player can do everything well, the balance curve is understood intuitively and mathematically, and enough options exist that counters exist without hard counters.
when: Deciding whether a deliberate imbalance is justified.
why: These conditions keep imbalance purposeful rather than damaging.

text: Virtual challenge is enemy power such as health, attack, or speed, or sheer numbers, and it forces the player to sustain strategy longer or with more precision.
why: Stronger or more numerous enemies raise required effort.

text: The appropriate failure rate depends on the audience and game goals; there is no single universal target for difficulty.
when: Setting difficulty for a PvE game
why: Different audiences and genres have different expectations for how often players fail.

text: Solving hard technical problems, such as special algorithms, a distinct look and feel, or multiplayer server technology, is a barrier because rivals cannot easily replicate it.
Doubling virtual skill, such as health or damage, improves win odds even for an unskilled player.
when: power-based progression
why: Power adds to outcomes independent of player decisions.

text: If difficulty is not adjusted for players, complaints that the game is too hard follow.
why: Designers who master a game before release judge its difficulty by their own skill, not by players' skill.

text: Choose a target skill level for balance and accept that other levels may have degenerate strategies.
when: When a skill-driven game must suit players across many skill levels
why: Balancing one skill level is manageable, but covering all levels multiplies the strategies to consider.

text: When an expansion adds mechanics, focus balance work on those new mechanics and on how they interact with existing ones.
why: The base balance is already understood from earlier phases, so effort can go to the new parts.

text: If new expansion cards are balanced against an older power curve, most fall behind the strongest past cards, and the trend continues indefinitely.
when: Designing new expansion sets
why: New cards are compared to the wrong baseline.

text: 1) Analyze a game's released content and derive a model relating cost to power and effect. 2) Create a new mechanic and estimate its cost from the model and intuition. 3) Design five to ten objects showcasing it. 4) Balance the objects with the model, playtest, and adjust both.
when: designing an expansion for an existing game

text: Expansions drive purchases, but needing to keep buying to stay competitive can push away veteran players.
when: Selling card expansions
why: Forced spending erodes loyalty among experienced players.

text: Expected value is the sum of each result's value times its probability; it is the long-run average per trial, which observed averages over many trials approach.
when: Evaluating an action with uncertain outcomes; comparing the worth of player actions
why: It gives the long-run average payoff.

text: Gamma controls how much an action's Q-value depends on the value of the state it leads to, determining whether the learner can discover long action sequences.
Expected value is the reward multiplied by the chance of success; for example, 100 points at a 20 percent chance gives 20 points.
when: When comparing risky and safe options
why: It converts different risk levels into a common scale

text: Give hard-to-measure items, such as speed boots or a warp shortcut, a numerical estimate so they can enter the expected value calculation.
when: when an item's value is hard to measure
why: Expected value only accounts for outcomes that have been assigned a number.

text: Estimating the chance of success is the hardest part; treat the estimate as a hypothesis and test it with prototypes, since the model and the prototype inform each other.
when: When building an expected-value model of a risky action
why: Chance estimates are rarely accurate before play testing

text: Use expected value to check that probabilities are balanced, but do not rely on it alone, since player experience may disagree with the numbers.
why: Math breaks down at extremes, and players value their time, so low stakes can feel unworthy despite a positive value.

text: A fair six-sided die has an expected value of 3.5.
Expected profit per play equals the chance of winning times the prize, minus the stake; a positive result means the player has a mathematical edge.
Expected values hide variance; random shuffles and acceleration or card-draw effects can make a single game deviate far from average timing.
why: Random shuffles and draw effects can push one game's timing far from the average used for balancing.

text: Predicting player choices from expected value alone misses how players weigh gains, losses, and regret.

1) Identify situations where the object is better or worse than normal. 2) Estimate each situation's probability and value difference from baseline. 3) Multiply and sum to get expected value. 4) Also check best and worst cases with their opportunity costs.
when: Costing a transitive mechanic whose usefulness depends on the situation, where the player cannot realistically swap the object for another
why: A single average can hide large swings in value.

text: When computing expected value, use perceived probabilities as well as actual ones, since players' perceptions determine how they play.
why: Players estimate event frequencies through trial and error, and those estimates are often wrong.

text: Players seek shortcuts, exploits, and degenerate strategies that bypass intended challenge, and they resent designers who let them break the game yet still search for them.
when: when a system's rules or rewards can be circumvented
why: Players seek the fastest route to a reward or past an obstacle, and they keep hunting for breaks even while resenting them.

text: Following required procedures even when they are less efficient is what distinguishes game behavior from ordinary behavior.
why: Rule-set procedures steer players into interactions that would probably never happen outside the game.

text: Virtual skills give a feeling of power, but when they dominate and real skill matters little, the power feels hollow to players.
when: game progression relies heavily on virtual skills
why: power comes from the character rather than the player's ability

text: Inconsistent or unclear behavior makes players focus on the confusion instead of the fight.
when: Units or enemies behave inconsistently
why: Confusion diverts attention from play.

text: Idle animations that have no effect on gameplay still convey personality and impatience, shaping how players perceive a character.
when: when a character is left without player input
why: expressive idle behavior signals character without changing challenge

text: Players find exploits quickly and share them widely, so item duplication is especially damaging when duplicates are usable or tradable.
why: Exploits spread online quickly, and duplicates that can be used or traded carry real value to players.

text: Players may exploit rating errors by targeting opponents they believe are overrated, and new players entering at median ratings are often weaker than their rating suggests.
when: Open matchmaking with imprecise initial ratings.
why: Rating errors create predictable profitable matchups.

text: A game dark pattern is deliberately built design that harms players' interests, probably without their knowledge or agreement.
Cheats that ship with a game often exist to speed up playtesting and bug hunting.
Game design shapes how players communicate and act, so designers should understand these effects as they can influence the human condition.
why: Games are experiences that change people, not only entertainment.

text: Almost every game has a barrier when you look low enough, such as required hardware, reading ability, or motor coordination.
Publishers favor teams with shipped games over teams with brilliant ideas, because ideas are plentiful and implementation is scarce.
why: Production is expensive and risky, so a proven group lowers the publisher's exposure while ideas are plentiful.

text: Before changing numbers for an overvalued or ignored option, first determine whether the cause is real mathematical imbalance or players misreading information the game failed to communicate.
when: An attribute or skill is consistently overvalued or ignored
why: Buffing or nerfing fixes real imbalance, but misreading is not fixed by number changes.

text: Steer players toward a desired behavior with indirect cues, such as a weapon lowered but still usable, visible characters conversing, or a companion suggesting restraint, rather than clunky prohibitions.
when: A game wants to discourage an action without forbidding it outright.
why: Priming is more elegant than explicit rules.

text: Because mental models can be pushed into situations impossible in reality, imagination can explore options the real world would not allow.
why: Models are not bound by physical constraints.

text: Indirect control can bridge the action gap in the player's mind, making possibilities feel nearly limitless despite a small set of verbs.
why: Games must simulate every action and its effects live, which keeps the verb set small compared to stories.

text: Strategies sitting roughly 10% to 15% off the cost curve can create a game-within-a-game in which players hunt for exploits.
when: Deliberate imbalance between strategies in a multi-strategy game.
why: A small off-curve edge rewards searching, while a perfectly balanced game gives no reason to search.

text: Duplicate accounts used as farms to funnel items to a main account allow trade-based exploitation, a particular problem in social games.
when: In social games where players can gift items to friends through a friend network.
why: Extra accounts widen the gifting network, so surplus items can be routed to the main account.

text: If players know the game eases when they play badly, they may deliberately play badly to get past hard sections, defeating the system's purpose.
when: When difficulty responds to player performance
why: Adaptive systems create an incentive to fail on purpose

text: 1) List each progression type and its rewards. 2) Classify each as fixed or random schedule, noting that a random-seeming schedule may be fixed for an informed player. 3) Check for patterns or emphasis at certain times. 4) Estimate reward frequency and mean time between rewards. 5) Find points where many loops close together and check for closure. 6) Find long stretches with few rewards and note how they feel. 7) Model the system in a spreadsheet or Machinations.

1) Find when saving is allowed. 2) Test seed persistence: reload mid-game, trigger random events, quit, reload the same save, and see if results repeat. 3) Check how easily a save file can be duplicated. 4) List every exploit. 5) Rate each by practicality.
when: Games with chance-based mechanics and save-reload support.

text: 1) Playtest the game. 2) Ask players what they can do with a reward. 3) If they cannot say, the reward is not communicating its value and should be revised.
when: checking reward clarity
why: players who cannot name a reward's use do not perceive it

text: Fixing an exploit can rework a behavior, remove the item behind it, substitute a currency reward, accept the flaw, or postpone the decision; each option carries its own cost.
when: a game exploit needs a response
why: no option is clearly best, so costs must be weighed

text: In a single-player action game, accepting an exploit is viable because perfect balance matters less than it does in competitive play.
when: the game is single-player and not competitive
why: balance errors do not harm other players

text: A slim initial edge can balloon into an advantage too large to overcome by midgame, leaving trailing players feeling powerless.
when: When a positive loop operates in a competitive game.
why: Compounding gains make catching up impossible.

text: A negative feedback loop damps itself: its output reduces its own input, so leaders are burdened, trailing players receive help, and the field stays together.
why: Stabilizing the game keeps players in contention.

text: A reinforcing relationship is a feedback loop where a change to one element moves another in the same direction, pushing the system toward an extreme and amplifying early advantage.
A positive feedback loop is a snowball effect in which a system's output amplifies its own input, rewarding leaders and punishing trailing players.
Zero sum games hold total power constant, so analysis focuses on each player's individual power curve.
The cumulative-advantage effect is the tendency for popular things to attract more popularity, so successful games gain advantages that make later success easier.
Zero-sum transfers such as rent move currency between players without creating or destroying any, so the economy's total amount is unchanged.
Negative loops based on absolute power can force every player to slow near the end, and positive loops based on relative power are also possible.
In racing games, computer opponents may speed up when the player leads and slow down when the player trails, to keep the field bunched.
In a positive-sum game, one player's gain does not require another's loss; for example, when every dice roll pays out resources to all players, everyone benefits.
Pair positive feedback with negative feedback so trailing players can catch up and the game does not feel futile, especially when an early lead should not hold.
when: When a luck-driven early lead feels decisive.
why: Negative feedback counteracts runaway leaders.

text: Protect early experience even while ramping difficulty, because app store ratings depend on how new players first feel about the game.
when: In free-to-play games that are rated on app stores.
why: Players enjoying the early ramp are the ones most likely to leave positive reviews.

text: When new player numbers drop suddenly, check whether the download page broke or changed recently.
Negative loops can be written into rules, arise from how rules interact, or emerge from how players choose to play.
why: Identifying the source tells designers where to adjust the loop.

text: Reinforcing loops make output grow or decline steadily and support risk-reward, so a leader with an advantage tends to extend it.
why: Each gain increases the next gain's likelihood.

text: Reinforcements arriving mid-fight can stretch a combat many times longer than the same encounter without them.
when: strategy or squad combat with arriving units
why: Each new arrival adds fighting time.

text: Options landing slightly above the new curve become the next reference point, so some power inflation is always present.
when: In persistent games that add expansion content over time.
why: New sets are balanced against prior top options, so content slightly above the new curve keeps raising the baseline.

text: With negative feedback, a player's power curve rises faster when behind and falls faster when ahead, so the curve depends on opponents.
With positive feedback, the power curve climbs or drops more sharply over time, with larger swings late in the game, and usually ignores opponents.
In PvP, feedback loops can drastically shift the balance of power and come to dominate multiplayer dynamics.
Negative feedback matters most late in the game, when large power gaps have formed, and can keep outcomes open until the end.
why: It directly counters relative power gaps, which only build up after players have had time to diverge.

text: Randomized items that are weaker for the leader and stronger for trailing players keep competitors bunched together.
Positive feedback applied early in a game has a much larger effect than the same loop applied late in the game.
why: The loop compounds across the remaining game, so starting it earlier gives it more time to amplify.

text: In a system that is positive-sum with negative feedback, every participant's power still rises, but leaders gain less while trailing participants gain faster, so the curves braid together.
In resource-building board games, trading supplies negative feedback when opponents refuse to trade with the leader and bank exchange rates are poor.
why: Bad bank rates push players toward trading with opponents, so opponents hold leverage to refuse or overcharge the leader.

text: In racing games, forward progress toward a goal makes play positive sum, while rubber-banding and weighted item pickups keep players close.
why: A distance victory means progress doesn't subtract from rivals, and rubber-banding keeps everyone feeling in contention.

text: When top seats carry many advantages, players tend to stay there, while those at the bottom struggle to climb, so rankings become self-reinforcing.
when: Ranked games where ranking grants advantages for the next round.
why: Advantages compound each round, so the lead tends to persist.

text: A reinforcing loop that amplifies early advantage lets one player win too early and stagnates competition.
when: Early leader gains compound
why: The strong player keeps being rewarded over and over, so a single success compounds into a runaway lead.

text: A reset can be triggered by players: when enough players in succession perform a costly late-game action, everyone's economy resets.
why: The reset becomes a goal that is unpredictable yet inevitable, which builds excitement as players grow powerful enough.

text: With positive feedback in a negative sum game, the stronger player loses power more slowly, so once a losing slide begins its losses accelerate.
when: in negative sum games
why: the leader's advantage protects its power while the trailing player's losses compound

text: With negative feedback in a negative sum game, stronger players lose power faster, creating a race to the bottom in which power curves braid downward.
why: players with more power are disadvantaged

text: With positive feedback in a zero sum game, an early leader pushes harder and the match concludes quickly, so this pattern suits short games.
why: early advantage compounds

text: With negative feedback in a zero sum game, swings in power drag the leader back toward the middle, causing repeated reversals.
why: losing ground to a leader restores balance

text: In an unregulated metagame, winning brings money and fans, which buys better players, which wins more; this positive feedback loop lets successful players pull further ahead.
when: Metagame systems with no limiting rules, such as free spending on talent.
why: Revenue from success is reinvested into the means of winning.

text: Unlimited resources create a positive feedback loop in which units or workers generate resources that fund more units.
when: Resources can be harvested indefinitely
why: Output reinvested into production compounds over time.

text: In competitive games, trading acts as negative feedback: players who are behind receive better deals, while players who are ahead receive worse deals or none.
when: Competitive games with player-to-player trading
why: Trade terms favor the trailing side, which pulls standings back together

text: Mechanics that link actions to rewards can create positive or negative feedback loops that push play out of balance.
when: When diagramming how actions pay off in a game system.
why: Reward links that compound or cancel can swing the system far from equilibrium.

text: Suspense weakens when the outcome is already locked, because later events no longer change the balance of consequence.
when: When a match or contest is nearly decided.
why: Tension depends on whether the next event can still change the result.

text: Players continuously tune their own challenge by the speed of their advance, with skilled players triggering several enemy groups at once while cautious players clear each group first.
when: When encounters are triggered by player movement.
why: Players control how many challenges they face at once.

text: In good games, changing one variable sets off chains of cause and effect that are nonlinear, emergent, and hard to predict.
when: When a fix for one problem is applied to a mechanic that many strategies and places rely on.
why: Each shared tool is reused in many places, so a fix in one spot propagates to every strategy that uses it.

text: A stat that improves items which raise the same stat can compound exponentially, letting power trivialize carefully crafted challenges.
why: Each boost feeds the crafting that produces the next, so the gains multiply rather than add.

text: Celebrity, news and political effects on a game are nonlinear and can be amplified by sociological snowball effects.
when: a small change in attention affects a game's performance
why: Social amplification makes outcomes disproportionate to the initial cause.

text: Negative feedback has three sources, each shaping perceived fairness differently: player-controlled actions, outside control such as AI or dice, and known physics affecting everyone.
why: Who or what applies the drag determines whether players feel in control, subject to chance, or bound by shared laws.

text: Balance can be pictured as a board whose pieces are linked by rubber bands, move on their own under partly understood rules, and are partly hidden by fog.
why: Changing one linked piece shifts every piece tied to it, so a move's effects are not contained.

text: Rubber-banding can make players feel punished for doing well and rewarded for doing poorly.
when: When computer opponents speed up when behind or slow down when ahead.
why: Visible catch-up assistance undermines the sense that skill determines the result.

text: If negative feedback is too strong in a zero sum game, no player can separate from the pack and the game may stalemate.
why: reversals cancel every lead

text: Streak rewards that grow daily but drop after a missed day can feel punishing and damage intrinsic motivation.
when: When rewards grow with consecutive daily logins and a missed day resets them.
why: Losing a reward that was earned feels punishing, which can undermine intrinsic motivation.

text: 1) Receive the input signal from the device. 2) Interpret and filter it, often into a different value range. 3) Use it to modulate a game parameter. Then ask how each parameter changes over time and how parameters relate.
when: auditing how a game responds to an input

text: 1) Add randomness such as external events or shifting alliances. 2) Or let weaker players group together. 3) Or let them call in a third party.
when: Trailing players need a way back
why: Shifting the balance of power keeps the game from stagnating while still allowing someone to win.

text: 1) Give each resource, ability, or option a number. 2) Sum the values per side. 3) Adjust values or resources until totals match. 4) Start with scores like low=1, medium=2, high=3. 5) After observed play, double the weight of any category that seems to decide outcomes. 6) Test the matched totals in play.
when: opposing sides differ in several resources or powers
why: Assigning numbers to each attribute turns a vague comparison into totals that can be compared directly.

text: 1) Set the starting state from the first turn's score difference. 2) Apply the per-turn difference transitions to get the state distribution after each turn. 3) Sum the probability mass on the winning side of zero after each turn to get win probability by turn.
when: Two players race and each turn's score change is random.
why: Stepping the chain forward turns the random process into a win probability curve over turns.

text: 1) Model each side's progress as a count of random hits. 2) Compute, for each damage target, the probability each side reaches it first. 3) Search targets for the one whose win chance is closest to 50%.
when: Two sides race to a damage target, one dealing steady damage and the other dealing random chunks.
why: Tuning the target to even odds balances a mismatched race.

text: Include the average expected opposing effect in the cost term so that a total of zero marks a balanced item.
why: Leaving out the average incoming damage made every card appear too strong.

text: Give players who return after a break extra progression, instead of making them pay for lost time.
when: Designing progression for lapsed players
why: Rest bonuses are a healthier model that avoids punishing disengagement

text: If streaks are included, pair them with bonuses that raise the chance of continuing a streak, offsetting the higher chance of a miss after a run of hits.
when: designing streak mechanics
why: Streaks are statistically more likely to end after a run of hits

text: Any reward is better than none if it gives clear feedback on the player's actions.
why: feedback connects the reward to the action

text: A negative loop keeps results uncertain and players in contention, preventing early endings; overused, it punishes success, rewards poor play, and lengthens the game.
when: When adding or evaluating catch-up mechanics.
why: It erases early advantages, so late actions matter more and strong play is penalized.

text: Positive feedback can end a game quickly once a lead is clear, but unchecked it makes the leader seem untouchable and trailing players feel futile.
when: When a lead is clear, the leader seems untouchable, or the designer wants fast conclusions.
why: Ending a decided game early means players do not sit through remaining motions, while a trailing player who can never catch up loses motivation.

text: Free-to-play friction is difficulty that outpaces the player after an easy start, deliberately leaving them short of resources to force time-versus-money choices and purchases.
when: games earning revenue from in-game purchases
why: Late-game frustration may be used to push players to pay for progress.

text: Extrinsic rewards can undermine intrinsic motivation for already engaging activities, but help simple, highly repetitive tasks when the rewards are salient and their value rises with effort.
when: Attaching rewards to an already enjoyable activity harms motivation; for simple, repetitive tasks, effort-scaled salient rewards sustain work.
why: External payment can replace the enjoyment that previously sustained the activity; clear, effort-scaled rewards sustain repetitive work.

text: Most players eventually hit a stage where frustration lingers long enough that they quit.
when: difficulty rises steadily through ordered levels
why: Accumulated struggle over long stretches, not a single hard moment, is what pushes players to quit.

text: Rather than becoming frustrated, heavy spenders often spend more to catch up, pushing prices upward like an auction with one bidder.
when: After a paid advantage is cancelled by matchmaking
why: Matchmaking erases the paid edge, and spending more is the way to regain it, as in an auction.

text: Players who self-identify as gamers are often willing to pay high prices for content that matters to them.
Hobby game buyers are mostly men in their teens and twenties who play weekly and may spend hundreds of dollars a year on supplements.
why: The games are very complex, which leads fans to buy many add-on components each year.

text: Grinding games spread quickly among casual players because they are easy to pick up, but players later exhaust the pointless loot and then seek new ideas, friends and experiences.
when: Grind-based loot games over a long time span
why: Easy entry drives rapid spread, while repetitive loot cannot sustain interest once it is exhausted.

text: In the early days of a free-to-play game, players have what they need, so items are neither above nor below the curve.
when: early days of a free-to-play game
why: Early demand is fully met by what players already have, so the items sit on the curve.

text: Players who do not understand what to do and why feel incompetent and may stop playing.
when: Tutorials that leave players unsure of goals
why: Lack of understanding erodes competence and motivation

text: Free-to-play games sometimes raise difficulty at a chosen point so that only paying players stay, letting product managers focus on that group.
when: Free-to-play games with monetization goals.
why: Steep difficulty jumps filter out non-paying players.

text: In free-to-play games, challenge often rises past the player's resources around day three, forcing players to improve, grind, or spend money.
why: Pressure grows while resources stay fixed in price, so the player is pushed past what they can meet.

text: Lowering a vehicle's friction value during an input changes the resulting motion, as with a powerslide, so simulation variables can be the response target.
why: Friction feeds the simulation's force calculations, so changing it reshapes the whole resulting motion.

text: Typical F2P KPIs: average monetization, fixed-interval retention returns, average session length. Early on, Day 1 retention and session length matter most for bringing players back.
Churn is the percent of players lost each month; ideally it is zero, and high churn prompts retention efforts.
why: A larger monthly loss of players signals weaker retention, which triggers requests for ways to keep them engaged.

text: Free-to-play health depends on three areas: acquisition (new players arriving), conversion (free players starting to pay) and retention (players staying and returning).
Players commonly believe earlier independent events, such as previous rolls or a run of losses, influence later ones, so a win feels due.
when: watching sequences of independent random results or after several losses
why: Independence is misread as dependence

text: People cannot randomize accurately: they alternate more than chance and underestimate long runs, so a short history of choices often reveals their next pick.
when: the player makes repeated choices from a small set, or when predicting human randomized choices
why: human attempts at randomness are biased and predictable

text: Players feel futile rather than hopeful when the perceived chance of success seems too low.
when: Setting drop rates for desired items
why: Hope requires a plausible chance of success.

text: Facing a small certain loss versus a large probable loss, people tend to gamble rather than accept the sure loss.
Players feel that spotting false patterns in chance is a real skill, and designers can use that feeling.
why: Humans seek patterns constantly, including where none exist, so chance outcomes seem predictable to them.

text: Occasional accidental-feeling headshots let weaker players score kills, which generally suits play outside top-level competition.
when: Shooter headshots are hard to land reliably at range
why: Small, fast-moving targets make some hits feel lucky, evening the field.

text: Humans are poor at appearing random on purpose, so skill against people lies in detecting their patterns while concealing one's own.
when: Playing intransitive games against human opponents
why: People cannot generate truly random sequences deliberately

text: Regular login bonuses build a habit that leads to other activity, and frequent visitors may later be tempted to spend money.
when: when designing login rewards
why: players who return for a bonus usually stay to do more

text: House edge is expected loss divided by amount wagered, the share of each bet lost; it is the gap between payout and true odds, the house's average profit.
The hot-hand fallacy is the belief that a streak of successes makes further success more likely, the reverse of the gambler's fallacy.
A loot box is a chance-based reward, such as a card pack or chest, bought with in-game currency that yields either a valued item or junk.
Only gambling disorder is recognized as a behavioral addiction in the DSM, while claims about game or social media addiction are complex.
Loot boxes are positively correlated with problem gambling.
Gambling is a special case, because external monetary rewards drive compulsion rather than the intrinsic rewards of play.
when: a game involves money wagers
why: Money rewards are external to play itself

text: Psychological manipulation in monetization raises the same ethical question even when players can afford to pay.
Gacha gives a random item from a list where some items are rarer than others, found in free-to-play games, trading card games, and toy vending.
Some governments have considered legal limits on gacha mechanics.
A bet can win slightly under half of plays yet have negative expected value, because payout sizes and losing odds together set the result.
Under a house edge, even optimal play loses over time, and methods that shift odds toward the player are usually banned by operators.
Belgium bans loot boxes because they may count as gambling at a psychological level.
Simple games with short plays can use a low house edge, because volume makes up the earnings per play.
when: Games that are simple, with brief individual rounds.
why: Low earnings per round are offset because players repeat the game many times.

text: Games with large jackpots or big possible wins can carry a higher house edge, since players tolerate larger expected losses when the potential win is large.
when: Games with a large jackpot or other large possible win.
why: Players accept bigger expected losses when a much larger payout is possible.

text: Random loot tables can determine drops from defeated enemies; tying them to deliberate combat rewards skill, and drop chance can scale with enemy difficulty so stronger foes make good items more likely.
when: Designing loot drops for combat encounters.
why: Ties rewards to player action so the reward feels earned.

text: In gambling games where a single currency is exchanged for cash in either direction, that exchange is the only production source and resources move between players through play.
when: Casino or poker-style games where one currency converts to cash in both directions.

text: When found equipment supplies most of the power, the gap between viable and optimal builds narrows, so enemy balance survives the player's build choices.
why: Items the player does not choose limit how far builds can diverge.

text: A house rake, a percentage of each hand's bets, makes a zero-sum game negative sum for players because table money drops with every hand.
when: when a third party takes a cut from each round
why: The removed money leaves the players' pool permanently.

text: Expected occurrences of a rare event equal trials times per-trial probability: 50,000 attempts at 1/10,000 gives about five; N packs give N times a card's per-pack probability.
when: many attempts, a large player base, or card-pack draws
why: A rare per-attempt chance still recurs often when a large player base generates many attempts.

text: Unlikely outcomes at odds of roughly 3:1 or 4:1 start to feel wrong to players.
when: When a player is favored to win at roughly 75–80% or higher.
why: Players overrate unlikely-but-possible outcomes, expecting wins far more often than the odds allow, so honest results feel unfair.

text: Set the exchange rate between unwanted items or grinding time and one wanted item deliberately, since it governs how the sense of progress feels.
when: Designing conversion of unwanted loot
why: The rate determines how much effort each desired item costs.

text: In a 30-item set with three equal rarity tiers weighted 10%, 30% and 60%, completing the full set takes about 293 random purchases on average.
when: Calculating expected cost of completing a gacha collection
why: Rare items are much less likely, so full collections need many draws.

text: Completing a gacha set grows steeply with set size; a 100-per-rarity set needs over 5,000 purchases.
when: Estimating the cost of large gacha collections
why: Collection cost grows faster than set size because rare items are hard to obtain.

text: A game is fair when its expected value for each player is zero; a positive expected value favors the player and a negative one favors the house.
when: Checking whether a betting or reward game is balanced
why: Zero expected value means no long-run advantage.

text: In a zero-sum rating system, P(win) = Y/(X+Y) where X is points gained for a win and Y points lost for a loss; the opponent's probability is X/(X+Y).
when: In a two-player zero-sum rating system, against one specific opponent.
why: Ratings stay steady at a skill level only if point exchanges match the predicted result.

text: If Y is zero, P(win) is 0 whatever X is; if X is zero, P(win) is 1. If both are zero the probability is undefined.
when: When a loss costs a player zero rating points.
why: A player should never be expected to both win and lose.

text: For a fair wager, the expected gain or loss per play equals the sum over outcomes of each outcome's probability times its payout.
when: When the game is fair, with no rigged outcomes.

text: Multiplayer loot fairness can use guild loot queues, Need vs. Greed requests, auction-house trading, or converting unwanted items into resources, fusion, or equipment upgrades.
when: Designing shared or random loot systems
why: Guild loot requests and need-or-greed rules offset long dry spells, and trading lets players swap unwanted drops for needed items.

text: Hidden probability can remove agency: a small chance effect, such as a 5% critical hit, may never be perceived by players.
when: When a choice's effect comes from a hidden probability, such as a small critical-hit chance.
why: Unless the effect is clearly perceived, choices seem meaningless and players lose their sense of agency.

text: A fixed low price per draw hides how much a full collection costs, leading players to overspend without realizing it.
when: Pricing gacha draws
why: The per-draw price looks small while the expected total is large.

text: A rising revenue metric can hide player harm and erode the trust a studio and the industry will need later.
1) Model the gamble as an infinite state machine with a stop state. 2) Track expected winnings per step with a Markov chain. 3) Compare the chance of ruin against the gain at each stopping point.
when: deciding when to stop an open-ended gamble
why: the chain shows how expected value and ruin risk change with each extra flip

text: When a game has player choices or changing conditions, such as a growing progressive jackpot, use the average value for changing conditions and assume the player makes optimal choices.
when: calculating house edge
why: The house edge is an average expected loss, so varying conditions must be reduced to an expected value.

text: Avoid loot boxes used to drive retention or conversion, especially when they can be bought with real money or earned as in-game currency.
when: When loot boxes are used to drive retention or conversion and can be bought with in-game currency or real money.
why: Mounting evidence shows gambling-like mechanics can harm players, especially children, and correlate with problem gambling.

text: Avoid loot boxes in games that children can access.
when: games accessible to children
why: gambling-like rewards exploit young players

text: Bending probability to reinforce players' wrong beliefs gives them something known to be false, which is dishonest, though it may still deliver the enjoyment players want.
when: designing random outcomes around players' known misconceptions
why: Players leave with false beliefs the designer knows are untrue

text: Designers usually offer several resource generation routes, framed as a trade-off between time spent and money spent.
when: When a resource can be bought, earned by grinding, or accumulated over time.

text: Intransitive counters, such as circular counters in fighting games where each side counters some moves, prevent a single dominant strategy.
when: When players start in radically different situations and numeric comparison between them is not possible

text: Between equal opponents, trades and tempo cause sudden alternating drops in power, which are short-term trade-offs that can be reversed later.
when: when players are evenly matched
why: trades shift power back and forth

text: A character that is hard to play may perform poorly for beginners yet rise to the top in expert hands.
when: Comparing a high-skill-ceiling character across rating bands.
why: Its strength requires mastery that beginners lack.

text: Some attributes can be filed as either cost or benefit, such as a conditional bonus that is a strength against one target and a limitation elsewhere; the classification matters less than the total.
when: Attributes with conditional effects

text: Game masters often put parties at numerical and power disadvantage for drama, which makes defensive stats more powerful in practice.
when: tabletop campaigns where the GM designs encounters
why: sustained disadvantage raises the value of defense relative to attack

text: Measure each ability in isolated comparisons before valuing combinations, so one ability's value is not distorted by others.
when: Before combining abilities into a card's estimate.

text: Good systems do not reveal a dominant strategy at first glance or after repeated play.
when: Designing competitive systems
why: If both sides know the winning move, play becomes a predictable sequence fixed from the start, which is dull for both.

text: Leave gaps between power levels, such as ranges 10 to 100 or 100 to 1000, to allow future expansion.
when: Designing tiered power levels
why: Gaps let later content slot in without rebalancing existing tiers.

text: In a point-buy system, a god stat that most builds max out or a dump stat that builds ignore signals a potential imbalance.
when: reviewing attribute balance
why: Players concentrate points where value is highest and avoid where it is lowest.

text: A cost that grows with lead, such as extra fuel burned by the leader, forces more stops and lets trailers catch up, affecting all players equally while each chooses risk.
why: Trailing racers drafting behind the leader burn less fuel, so they can later take the lead.

text: A multiplying effect on a fragile in-play unit stays balanced when the unit is easy to remove and rarely survives more than a few turns.
when: card games where multiplied units can be removed
why: Short survival limits how long the multiplier's power can accumulate.

text: When spending adds options rather than strength, a complete collection need not yield the strongest build if cards are balanced.
when: In collectible card games where purchases should add variety rather than power

text: Factions can share identical base stats yet differ in mechanics, so each excels in different tactics.
when: Designing asymmetric factions with equal stats
why: Different mechanics let each side win through its own style.
