text: An upgrade that raises movement speed can let a player circle a slow, stationary enemy indefinitely while attacking without taking damage, creating a degenerate strategy.
when: Enemy movement and attack speed are unequal relative to the player's upgraded speed
why: Speed advantage removes the enemy's ability to retaliate, making the fight trivial and repetitive.

text: Balance systems depend on one another, so resizing one element disturbs others; stronger starting characters may require retuning other systems to match.
when: When one element, such as starting character strength, is changed in a tightly tuned game
why: Balance elements depend on one another.

text: Imperfect substitutes are goods that do similar jobs. When one is much cheaper, players tend to buy it instead of the other.
when: Two goods serve similar purposes at different prices
why: Players choose the cheaper option that still fulfills the same role

text: Flat bonuses added per chain step grow linearly, not multiplicatively, so they add less than a multiplier that scales all points.
An action that blocks later options constrains future play, and the size of that constraint depends on how the game's mechanics interlock; it is never zero.
when: When taking an action rules out other actions later, such as adding a new faction to a deck
why: Lost versatility later is paid on top of the immediate resource price, so it is an added hidden cost.

text: A board-wide effect that spares the caster's own units while hitting opposing units can wipe out most enemy forces, making it strong enough to shape the metagame.
when: When the player builds a deck whose own units avoid the effect's targets
why: Sparing one's own units while hitting the rest gives a one-sided result

text: Requiring prerequisite upgrades before powerful units become available prevents players from rushing strong units early and forces all players along a similar resource path.
when: Real-time strategy games with tiered unit access
why: Gating high-tier units behind prerequisites equalizes early progression.

text: Rising budgets against flat prices push publishers toward fewer titles with higher production values and broader appeal, so each title must sell more units.
when: When production budgets rise while the retail price stays fixed

text: A hidden counter that drops after failures and rises after successes can weaken or strengthen enemies, letting challenge track player performance.
when: When implementing adaptive difficulty.
why: Failures signal the player needs easier conditions and successes signal they can handle more.

text: Opponents may foul a poor free-throw shooter every possession, judging a missed free throw cheaper than losing the ball, which distorts play around that player.
when: When an offensive player is weak at free throws.
why: Opponents judged a missed free throw less costly than the ball being taken in normal play.

text: Seven common keyword abilities in a creature card game are each worth about one cost point.
when: Standard keyword valuation in a power-and-toughness card game.
why: Isolating cards that carry a single unknown keyword lets its value be estimated from the rest.

text: A type-specific bonus's first-pass value is its raw extra benefit, as if always active, multiplied by how often that enemy type appears.
when: as a first pass only, before adjusting for context

text: A group buff's expected value equals its percentage times the top attack value it applies to, multiplied by the probability that the buff is used.
when: When a buff targets one ally and the group contains strong attackers who would receive it
why: Groups let the buff go to their best members, so its value follows the top attack.

text: A fighting character's balance is set by reach, speed, damage, priority, jump, combo and stun abilities.
when: In head-to-head fighting games with large character rosters

text: A hard counter that nullifies a single object and does nothing else breaks the counter condition of perfect imbalance.
Stackable multipliers that appear early can end games prematurely and make clear early-game dominant strategies.
when: designing stackable multiplier effects
why: Early multipliers accelerate outcomes before players can respond.

text: Ignoring color requirements makes decks with three or more colors look cheaper than they play, and more colors make the gap larger.
when: Costing decks with three or more colors.

text: A favorite strategy that experts like is not dominant if it lacks effective counters; a balanced game can have a favorite alongside other viable options.
when: Evaluating popular strategies
why: A balanced game gives other players enough counter-choices, so a favorite cannot win every time.

text: Pricing an option with extra abilities the same as a plain option leaves the plain one clearly weaker.
when: When two creatures share a cost but one has extra abilities
why: The version with more abilities wins outright at identical cost, so the plain one has no reason to be chosen.

text: A change players love can still harm the studio if it costs too much revenue.
when: When a change players like removes revenue from a free-to-play game
why: Losing revenue can force the studio to shut down, which harms every player.

text: 1) Rank each mechanic's power from play experience. 2) Decide whether returns scale linearly, polynomially, logarithmically or custom. 3) Set how many generic power equal one specific power. 4) Build a balance sheet with a formula where zero is on the curve. 5) Adjust only cost quantities until each object is near zero.
Three ways to handle the build gap: target one extreme; ship tiers of difficulty; or let found equipment supply most power while attributes and passives add minor bonuses.
when: designing progression balance
why: Shipping difficulty tiers serves players of every skill level; letting found gear carry most power narrows how far the best build outpaces a viable one.

text: 1) Pass units among group members until each unit has had a balance pass. 2) Pair the modified units and balance them against each other.
when: several people balancing a set of units

text: At first playable, check balance only at the macro level by comparing broad strategies, builds, or play styles, and defer finer tuning.
when: first playable stage
why: At this stage testing targets engagement and core mechanics, so fine balance would be premature.

text: Do not use deliberate imbalance to justify horrendously broken or ridiculously underpowered options.
when: When a game offers several strategies and multiple paths to victory.
why: A slight off-curve option lets players hunt for and exploit the edges, creating a game within the game.

text: Classify each game element as deterministic or non-deterministic before balancing, because each kind needs a different approach.
why: designers balance the two kinds differently

text: To hold a continent, reinforce until the defending side keeps at least a 50% advantage.
when: Defending a continent with a bonus in a dice combat game.
why: A defensive edge of at least 50% keeps the continent stable against attacks.

text: Give characters a relatively large health pool when their art is large and detailed, because a one-hit kill contradicts the animation, sound and visual metaphor.
when: when designing fighter health for a game with detailed, well-animated characters
why: Health totals must match the visual and audio impression of the character

text: Effects that take, swap, or reshuffle opponents' cards add nastiness and appeal; when the nastiness outweighs the appeal, cut them.
why: Such effects lead players to sabotage their own pieces so opponents cannot seize them.

text: An even match gives each side an equal chance, while a fair match lets the most skilled player win; handicaps are usually voluntary and players choose them only when they prefer even matches.
when: when deciding whether to offer handicaps
why: Players default to expecting fair matches, so handicaps suit those who want equal odds.

text: High-skill balance requires removing any idea that could yield a degenerate strategy at any skill level, which rules out many worthwhile ideas and is costly to test.
when: When deciding if top-skill balance is worth its cost given how skill-driven the game is.
why: Testing at high skill can take weeks or months, and degenerate strategies often surface after release, requiring long-lived patches.

text: Balancing for lower skill is cheaper: degenerate strategies need only be non-obvious, testing needs no long study, and late discoveries matter little.
why: Only obvious exploits need removing, so no long hunt for optimal strategies is required.

text: Gut feeling, built with experience and not fully teachable from a book, drives much balancing; experienced designers notice imbalance before testers react and spot loopholes or dead ends immediately.
when: In final refinement, after the core build works and is internally complete.
why: Accumulated design experience sharpens intuition.

text: Circular balance gives each option a counter that beats it, so no option is supreme and every option has both strengths and weaknesses.
Balance is fairness as players perceive it: a balanced game follows the expectations it sets from the beginning and does not jerk players around.
Game balance is adjusting a game's elements until they produce the experience the designer wants, mixing simple arithmetic with judgment.
when: When tuning a game's elements
why: Balance determines whether a game feels monotonous, confusing or frustrating even with strong story, art and technology

text: Breadth is the number of distinct options such as classes or weapons; depth is how items, creatures, and effects keep increasing across the game.
Balance means adjusting the relative power of game mechanics, such as the speed, price, mass, health, or damage of tools, units, strategies, or characters.
Fairness requires that nobody holds an advantage when play begins.
Balance spans mathematics, difficulty, progression, initial conditions, multiple strategies, and game objects, with fairness as the shared thread.
why: These dimensions together determine whether a game is fair.

text: A derived cost curve can flag items sitting above or below the original progression.
Fairness-focused balancing ranks among the most basic balance types, so the fairness lens suits any game.
Every game has many interacting factors, so no two balancing problems are exactly alike, and some balance choices follow arithmetic while others rest on designer judgment.
when: When approaching a balance problem
why: Interacting factors make each case distinct

text: The goal of balance is to be just right for the game's purpose, reached through repeated iterative play.
The build gap is most visible in end-game content, where a final boss may fall in one hit or become impossible.
Some balance numbers are chosen by feel, picking values that seem right, rather than by calculation.
Art-focused games may be intentionally unbalanced, relying on designer intuition and small playtests because budgets rarely support large analytics.
when: games balanced for an artistic statement
why: budgets and communities rarely support large-scale analytics

text: A thorough gap analysis considerably strengthens a pitch to money people.
when: When showing investors how the game differs from close competitors.

text: Games earning revenue from sales, expansions or sequels must balance toward fun.
when: Games not built to earn resource-based income after the sale.
why: Players stuck in constant scarcity are unlikely to buy later content.

text: For games too large to solve, estimate balance from designer intuition, expert opinion, tournament statistics, or computer simulation, which improves as computing power grows.
when: Evaluating balance of games like chess or Go.
why: Full solution is infeasible, so indirect evidence is needed.

text: Balance is essential to depth, because a deep game generates decisions where even experts cannot be sure of the best option.
In a skill game that supports endlessly deep play, high-skill balance is nonnegotiable.
A balanced game where every strategy has equal value feels flat, so good games need peaks of effectiveness and troughs of failure.
why: Equal-value strategies leave no reward for skill and nothing worth learning.

text: Recurring patterns of balance are called balance types, and a structured set of questions helps examine each type.
when: When analyzing a game's balance systematically
why: Recurring patterns let designers reuse examination methods across games

text: Treating balance as a scale that weighs quantities against each other misleads; monster difficulty cannot be placed against loot to compare them.
why: Monster difficulty and loot share no common unit, so they cannot be weighed against each other.

text: A game can seem broken to novices while being well balanced at the top of its skill range.
when: When players lack the skill to execute the game's strongest strategies.
why: Novices have not found the strongest strategy or cannot perform it, so the balance stays hidden from them.

text: A change that is fair and strategically interesting can still break the fiction, such as an unrealistically long weapon range.
when: When a change would undermine story consistency, rhythm, ease of use, or readability.
why: The change would not fit the game's fiction, so fairness alone cannot justify it.

text: Changing an expected player ability in one area, such as jump distance, defies player expectation and frustrates them even if the change is otherwise balanced.
when: When the adjustment applies to one level only, not across the game.

text: Making a vehicle painfully slow may be fair, but driving it becomes a chore that undoes the value of the change.
Forcing symmetry onto a game whose premise is inherently asymmetric, such as a required first mover, is not an easy fix for fairness.
why: Symmetric games are fair automatically because both sides share starting positions and rules. Asymmetric games lack that guarantee and need careful balancing to be fair.

text: 1) Declare one object balanced. 2) Shape every other object's costs and benefits to match it. 3) Compare the shaped objects against one another to confirm they are roughly equal in power.
when: When numeric objects such as weapons, creatures or loot must be made meaningful relative to one another.
why: a designer-declared anchor makes the rest of the set comparable

text: 1) Set the game's macro structure. 2) Choose progression curves, often combining several styles such as exponential XP and logarithmic levels. 3) Set an anchor and use it to scale breadth and depth.
when: final step of a first-pass balance after macros and progression
why: The earlier structure and progression choices supply everything a first-pass balance needs.

text: 1) Identify the goal that becomes unreachable over time. 2) Propose rule changes that add money drain or end pressure. 3) Test that match length falls.
when: A goal recedes and games run too long
why: Restoring reachable goals shortens play.

text: 1) Total the item's benefits. 2) Total its costs and drawbacks. 3) Check whether the net value falls on the curve.
when: reviewing a teammate's item or a previous version before an expansion
why: Once the cost curve and its supporting math are correct, every item can be judged against one standard, making balancing straightforward.

text: For general balance testing, instruct testers to play to win so they reveal options that are too strong or too weak.
when: When playtesting to find strategies or objects that are too strong or too weak, rather than bugs.
why: Testers who play to win try degenerate strategies, which exposes options that are overpowered or underpowered.

text: Keep deck sizes, action card effects and the set of action cards fixed; change only the cost amount of an action card, not its types.
when: when rebalancing a card-based game
why: these constraints keep decks comparable

text: A balance change improves the game only if it creates fewer problems than it solves.
when: When a balance problem tempts a quick, reactive change.
why: Existing problems are easy to notice, while the new problems a fix may cause are hard to foresee.

text: Write a clear problem statement before changing any balance values.
when: A game is out of balance
why: Designers who jump to fixes before understanding the real problem make a mess.

text: Prioritize the most impactful and visible parts for balance, since there is never time to fix everything.
when: In the final phase before release, when time for balance fixes is limited.
why: Perception of balance matters to players just as much as actual fairness.

text: Balance the game fairly across good, dark, and neutral paths, and check every ramification of gameplay changes.
when: When moral choices carry gameplay consequences such as gained abilities or powers.
why: Players do not reliably take the moral path, and overly punitive consequences for other paths can make the game unappealing.

text: Check every balance change against fiction, flow and pacing, accessibility, and clarity, not only fairness and depth.
why: Balance affects the whole experience.

text: Gameplay rewards such as new abilities make players care, even non-story-focused ones, but a strong reward can override a story's moral weight so players ignore the intended consequence.
when: Tying moral choices to gameplay rewards

text: Shortening or lowering the accuracy of a stun reduces frustration but can weaken the character's strategy; strengthening other moves adds viable strategies but raises overall power.
when: Choosing a response to a single repeated tactic dominating play.
why: Each fix changes a different axis: play experience versus overall strength and variety.

text: Cloned games often copy another game's economy exactly, changing only names and art.
Reuse a balanced game's numbers only when the new game is systemically the same, since a slight mechanical difference can silently invalidate copied numbers.
when: When the new game is systemically the same as a game already known to have good balance.
why: A minor mechanical difference can make numbers that worked in the original design fail in the new one.

text: Before copying a balanced game's numbers, understand why its elements are balanced, so similar systems are built with intent.
why: Copying without grasping the reasons behind a game's balance can carry over numbers that fail under a different design.

text: Even when cloning, analyze balance with mathematics or other methods so the new game can be fixed if it breaks.
when: When cloning numbers from an existing game.
why: Copying numbers without analyzing them leaves a designer exposed to breaking the game without knowing why.

text: Money or currency is any all-purpose resource traded for other resources, information, or saved time, such as skill points spent on skills; most games use one main currency.
Farmer representatives approach players in-game, offering currency in exchange for cash sent through third-party payment apps.
when: When in-game currency can be farmed and exchanged for real money outside the game.

text: If players can buy goods with real money, they will likely trade those goods for cash, creating a secondary economy.
when: In games with open economies where players can trade items with each other.

text: Players buy time: when grinding is slow, players will pay real money for currency if trading allows it, even when direct paid rush is banned.
when: When currency is tradeable for real money.
why: Trading lets players convert money into the time saved by grinding.

text: Players buy cards they never plan to use, simply to remove annoying or overly powerful cards from circulation.
when: a card threatens their deck or annoys them
why: Removing a card from the pool keeps it from annoying the player or being used against their deck.

text: When players know a bonus recurs at a fixed interval, they will pay to continue after dying to keep reaching it.
when: predictable recurring bonuses
why: players anticipate and value the next bonus

text: A resource is anything a player receives that can be used or traded to acquire something else.
why: A broad definition lets designers audit every exchangeable thing in a game.

text: A resource is an object made valuable by scarcity and usefulness toward the player's goal; designers make resources valuable by making them scarce, so players want them.
In a real-currency economy, some resources are real money, as in gambling games that take money to play or pay real money, and games selling in-game property or exclusive rewards.
A game economy is defined by two meaningful decisions: how the player earns money and how the player spends it.
when: Judging whether a resource system counts as a real economy.
why: If players lack either the earning choice or the spending choice, the system is not an economy.

text: A consumable is a resource the player uses up in acquiring something else, and once used it is gone.
In a fixed economy, all resources come from inside the game, designers set prices before launch, and players cannot affect prices or buy in with real money.
In a player-dynamic economy, resources come from the game but players set prices through trade or auction using in-game currency.
A money sink is a negative-sum mechanic that removes currency from the economy without creating it elsewhere, and positive-sum economies need sinks to stay stable.
In games, inflation is a continual rise in the price of goods or services, driven by a shift in supply or demand that raises market prices.
Resource generation is how players gain resources, by buying them with in-game or real currency, grinding through combat, or accumulating them over time.

Resource conversion turns one resource into another resource or a permanent item, such as through crafting or buying from a store; it creates something new, while consumption changes something that already exists.
Resource trading lets players exchange resources through negotiation, haggling or gifts, giving them a reason to interact, which matters in community-driven games.
Resource consumption is spending resources for an in-game benefit or to remove a barrier; designers control it through demand, quantity, timing and effect.
Total resource supply is either unlimited or capped, and designers control rarity or make items strictly limited.
A closed economy is self-contained, with no route for outside forces, including real currency, to alter its resources; the majority of big-budget and tabletop economies are closed.
An open economy lets outside forces, such as buying currency with real money or rushing production, directly affect in-game money and resources.
An economy is positive sum if players collectively gain value, negative sum if they collectively lose it, and zero sum if gains and losses cancel.
A game economy forms when items can be exchanged among players or between players and the system.
Premium currency is bought with real money, is hard to earn in play, and is often spent on cosmetics or on options that let paying players gain an advantage.
Game-specific resources are items players collect, find, mine, or win, which they can use now or later to improve their game state.
An economic reset takes everyone's wealth away and restarts all players from the same starting point.
Units are used when a player is represented by several objects at once, and they can keep fixed values or upgrade and evolve over time.
Resources are assets that help players reach goals, and they play a role similar to real-world resources.
A rival good can be consumed by only one customer at a time, while a nonrival good, like a game, can be distributed to any number of customers at almost no cost.

Metaeconomies emerge outside the game: players sell characters or items on external auction sites, sometimes for hundreds of dollars, and worldwide card-trading markets can shape play without in-game trading.
Balancing a multiplayer economy requires weighing nine concerns at once: fairness, challenge, choices, chance, cooperation, time, rewards, punishment, and freedom.
when: Large online games where players trade with each other.
why: Trading between players creates many interacting concerns that single-factor fixes cannot address.

text: Resource classes form one interwoven economy of tradeoffs, so changing one resource affects the others.
why: Resources are connected through exchange, not isolated.

text: Common curve shapes: experience points are exponential, experience levels are logarithmic, skill point identity, HP increases are linear with a random value in a range, monster strength is linear, and item values are linear with damage or protection.
Without a common currency, a barter economy with millions of goods implies trillions of possible pairwise exchange rates.
Economic system types are rarely named in the field; mechanics, platform and connectivity usually dictate them, and games can combine several types.
Common money sinks are NPC merchants selling items for gold, consumables that must be rebought, repair costs for weapons and armor, and death penalties that take money or items.
Gold farmers grind in-game currency using bots or hired workers, and at peak one estimate counted over 100,000 people working as full-time gold farmers.
A game whose currency is mostly injected by sources and removed only by involuntary sinks is strongly positive-sum, so players grow richer over time and bankruptcy becomes harder to reach.
why: Net currency creation makes the win condition recede and lengthens play.

text: When at most one resource source arrives per turn and unused resources are lost, a player has at most N resource units on turn N.
Resources can further a player's aims, be combined into new items, and be bought and sold in markets.
Resources may be exchanged directly between players or placed in fixed positions by the designer for players to find and collect.
Resources take many forms, including cards, weapons, ammunition, power-ups, time, units, turns, and terrain; finding and managing them is central to many games.
Currency is among the most powerful resource types because it lets players trade without bartering goods they happen to hold.
Currency does not have to follow a standard banknote system; barter systems can achieve similar trade goals.
A game economy needs tradable goods, participants that trade them, such as players or a central treasury, and channels for trading, like auctions or vendor stalls.
Currency is optional in an economy; when present, it helps facilitate trade.
Persistent online worlds combine a labor market, where players earn gold from menial tasks sold to shopkeepers or other players, with a goods market for weapons, armor, and magic items.
A player-driven trading layer can behave as a small economy, with prices set by valuations and perceived uses.
A single resource can follow different curves with different partner resources, such as identity with one and another shape with a second.
Strictly limiting or forbidding extra purchases gives everyone equal resources, but is rarely practical for games that depend on sales.
when: Tournament-style games, not purchase-driven business models

text: Economic game theory works only on very simple systems, so it rarely helps when designing actual games.
Time, currency, levels, health and purchased items are resources a game may use, and their relationships (time as currency, currency as time, health linked to time) are worth examining.
when: Analyzing a game's resource design.

text: Many free-to-play games pair a regular currency with a second one that is hard to earn through play and is mostly sold for real money.
In competitive games, content is often unlocked by spending in-game currency.
Earning real money from games existed before blockchain games, as shown by gold farming in massively multiplayer online games.
A food cap alone does not stop large armies, since players reach the cap and then rebuild from resource surpluses after losses.
when: limiting army size with a population cap
why: Surplus resources let players refill the cap quickly.

text: Designers can interpret marketing data creatively to address market trends without sacrificing core gameplay.
when: When marketing data reveals buyer trends the designer wants to address.
why: The marketing team is the strongest link to buyer demands, so their data can guide features.

text: Specialized barter currencies tied to in-world goods can suit a world better than a generic universal currency.
when: When a game's fantasy setting would clash with a generic money currency.
why: They make the economy feel native to the world's rules.

text: With all other factors equal, doubling an item's benefit should double its cost.
when: all other factors are equal

text: Revisit the cost curve and its supporting math to find the cause of an imbalance, because the cause may reveal other cards that need changes.
when: after a card or deck is found too strong

text: Use a single all-purpose currency for most games and question any extra resource that does not add meaningful choice.
why: Unneeded resource types add complexity, and an overcomplicated game tends to end poorly.

text: Use a resource-only economy, where collected materials are the main way to become stronger, when gathering itself should drive growth.
why: Gathered materials can be crafted into tools that raise damage, mining speed and durability.

text: Rather than adding currency sinks, designers may cut the positive-sum sources feeding inflation, or wipe the economy clean.
when: Economies showing inflation
why: Surplus entering without matching removal keeps piling up; sinks remove currency without creating new supply.

text: Give players a small budget of points that alter rolls in their favor during risky moments, to balance risk without fixed odds.
when: Risky actions are too rare or too routine
why: Player control over outcomes adjusts risk without changing base odds.

text: When tuning a generated dungeon's health, energy, and reward items, map their links first to see which generator parameters affect each other.
when: Dungeon generation with several interdependent resources.
why: Changing one linked parameter shifts the others.

text: Counter runaway accumulation by offering different rewards, avoiding groupings that reward control, or giving players reasons to spend resources.
when: Each additional unit is more useful and players chase control
why: Spending pressure and varied rewards stop players from monopolizing resources.

text: When resources are unlimited, efficient economic ramp-up matters more than unit deaths, and multiple victory paths keep play from reducing to one route.
when: Resource-rich strategy games
why: Economic speed decides outcomes more than unit trades.

text: Currency can reward playing against human opponents, since such players supply entertainment and challenge to others regardless of payment.
why: Human opponents supply challenge and entertainment to others whether or not they paid.

text: Track several linked resources, such as health, supplies and vehicle condition, so each travel choice carries a cost.
In an economy, spending helps players earn more, which gives more chances to spend, forming a loop that carries players forward.
why: Spending on things that boost earnings gives players more chances to spend, a pattern players find appealing.

text: Left unchecked, a positive loop drives games toward an irreversible conclusion, known as the empire problem.
when: When a leader's advantage compounds without limit.
why: Each gain produces more gains, so the lead becomes unassailable.

text: When players create and sell items with no progression, every item effectively becomes a prestige item.
when: Player-created item economy without progression.
why: With no progression mechanics, items confer no gameplay edge, so their worth is purely status.

text: In a positive-sum economy where currency is added without being removed, average currency per player grows over time, shifting the demand curve so players pay higher prices for the same goods.
when: Monster loot in MMOs or similar sources add currency without removing it.
why: Monster loot enters the economy while nothing is taken from anyone else, so total currency keeps growing.

text: When prices outpace what players can earn, new and returning players find items unattainable, because prices keep rising while they are away.
why: Earning rates are tiny next to item costs, so returning players see gear as out of reach.

text: Very high-priced cosmetic status items can drain large amounts of currency quickly when wealthy players buy them.
when: When currency has grown excessively inflated in a live economy

text: Requiring expensive items for quests pulls currency from all players, acting as a sink.
why: A mandatory purchase forces every player to spend, so the drain hits the whole player base, not only the wealthy.

text: Supply-side inflation occurs when the amount of currency entering a game rises sharply, causing market prices of goods to climb as the oversupply spreads through the player community.
why: Excess currency entering through external sources raises prices for items and services across the economy.

text: Buying currency for cash can make purchased currency a larger source of currency than in-game earnings, inflating the economy.
when: When players can trade real money for in-game currency.
why: Currency miners add more gold than they spend, so bought gold can outweigh what the game itself pays out.

text: Currency-store items are priced to what will monetize; because challenge outpaces item power, spending is pushed.
why: Players lack the resources to meet rising pressure, so they must spend money to succeed.

text: Because each later resource unit arrives later on average, each one is worth more than the last, so costs should rise faster after early units.
why: Each successive unit tends to arrive later in expected turns, so each one is worth more.

text: In property-trading board games, spending income on income-producing assets forms a positive loop that stops a positive-sum game from running forever.
Inflation penalizes newcomers, who have to grind harder to close the gap, whereas deflation penalizes veterans, who must win just to stay even.
when: When rating values are lasting, carried over, and visible to the player base

text: A fixed-rate bank exchange caps how much a resource can be worth in trade, since players can always convert at that rate.
when: A game offers a bank conversion rate alongside player trade
why: Players compare trade offers against the bank rate, limiting inflated prices.

text: A rule forcing players holding too many cards to surrender half their hand discourages hoarding and spreads resources back into play.
when: Resource-collection games with a card-hand limit
why: Losing a large share of a big hand makes accumulation costly.

text: In Battlefield 1942 assault matches, each death drains a ticket count and controlling a required point drains the opponent's tickets, so control shifts the balance.
Resource value changes over a game as better versions appear, so newer materials depreciate older ones.
when: In games where tools or items are upgraded in tiers.
why: Better tiers save more time, making earlier tiers less useful.

text: Free-to-play games make real-money prices hard to compare against in-game currency through irregular bundles and dual currencies, which reduces player scrutiny of costs and can increase spending.
when: games selling in-game currency for real money
why: Players who cannot easily compute the effective unit price tend to question purchases less.

text: When an item is priced in two currencies that can be both bought and earned, with one much rarer, the true cost becomes hard to judge.
when: dual-currency economies with a premium and a common currency
why: Players must convert between currencies with no clear exchange rate.

text: Keeping a price fixed while reducing the currency it buys raises the effective price without changing the list price.
when: When developers want more money without visibly raising prices

text: Money-for-time sells speed along the same progression curve free players follow, so it does not change relative power.
Inventory items are kept scarce through high purchase prices or through the opportunity cost of searching for them.
Special terrain can act as a primary resource in map-based strategy, and terrain can also serve as a resource in less obvious ways, such as scoring squares in word games.
when: In map-based systems such as strategy games

text: Time works as a resource when each player has a limited time budget tracked by a clock, and countdowns add dramatic tension.
why: Players already know the pressure of a deadline, so rationing a time budget carries emotional weight.

text: Renewable units often carry a cost per unit, and whether that cost is balanced is best checked through playtesting.
when: Games where players can build new units over time
why: Cost per unit interacts with the rest of the resource structure in ways that are hard to predict.

text: When points are scarce, players spend them carefully, so each use becomes a spectacular, memorable event.
when: Limited resources tied to dramatic actions
why: Scarcity raises the value of each spend.

text: Funding choices such as budget size or monetization model shape a game's design, so form follows funding.
why: Money is the fuel for the industry, so funding decisions cannot be kept separate from design.

text: Resource limits determine how long a match can last, so they set the game's pace.
when: Designing match length
why: Finite supply caps how long play can continue.

text: In a positive-sum economy where money enters the game without draining, the bankruptcy goal recedes over time and matches can run very long.
when: Money flow is not drained by play
why: Accumulating wealth makes elimination rarer and slower.

text: In many free-to-play games, difficulty above player ability forces grinding or a small payment, so money can stand in for time, skill and luck.
when: In free-to-play games with a difficulty ramp designed to exceed player ability
why: Grinding time can make up for missing skill or luck, and money buys out that time.

text: Reducing a primary damage source pushes players toward costlier or limited alternatives, which may run out before the level ends.
when: When a player's primary attack is weakened
why: Half damage against armored foes can drop to zero, so the primary attack stops working.

text: A gain-rate powerup raises XP gain only from its purchase time onward, so XP earned before the purchase is unchanged.
when: In an idle game where players spend XP on rate-boosting powerups

text: Making a resource run out and replenishing it through a secondary action changes how the resource is used and how the secondary action feels.
when: when designing consumable resources such as ammunition
why: Scarcity gives players a reason to use the resource selectively

text: Upkeep drains gold income in proportion to army size, so large surpluses are prevented and players are encouraged to fight with smaller armies.
when: players can rebuild instantly from resource surpluses after losses
why: The drain removes the benefit of hoarding resources for mass rebuilding.

text: Games are antirival: they become better as more people play, through stronger communities, more play partners, user-made content and word of mouth.
when: a game's player base grows
why: Larger audiences generate value that attracts further players.

text: Economy control methods include limiting how much money the game creates and controlling the ways money is earned and spent.
A typical competitive 60-card deck holds about 20 resource sources, roughly one card in three.
when: As a baseline, ignoring cards that accelerate mana or draw extra cards
why: Competitive decks vary widely in land count, so 20 is taken as a reasonable average starting point.

text: Game resources fall into five classes: time, currency, game-specific objects, hit points or lives, and experience with levels.
when: When listing a game's resources.
why: These classes cover the common exchangeable things players spend and gain.

text: Games commonly fall into five economic system types: fixed, player-dynamic, free-to-play, prestige and real currency, which differ in where resources come from, whether players set prices, and whether real money enters.
In games where items are bought with a resource such as gold, mana, or experience points, that resource cost can serve as the anchor for scaling other item numbers.
when: When a game's values are transitive, so higher cost implies greater strength
why: A shared anchor lets very different elements be compared directly against one another.

text: Open economies, where players can buy advantages, stay fair through three methods: limiting spending, limiting power, and providing competitive gates.
when: In open economies where players can buy in-game resources with real money
why: Outside purchases mean the designer no longer controls resource production, making balance harder.

text: An economy disconnected from other resources may be unnecessary altogether.
when: When a subsystem trades only within itself.
why: Disconnected resources add complexity without contributing to the core tradeoffs.

text: The five economy types leave many edge cases, so they work as shared vocabulary rather than strict categories.
when: When a game has edge cases or features more than one economy type
why: Real systems are shaped by mechanics, platform and connectivity rather than by the labels.

text: Inflation can look harmless because players are richer too, but when it comes from gold farming or pay-to-win it unfairly favors those who pay.
when: When inflation comes from gold farming or pay-to-win spending
why: Players must pay more to keep up, so the scales tip toward those willing to pay.

text: Once farmed currency circulates among players, designers cannot easily remove it, so money sinks only work if they affect all players.
when: When farmed currency is held by some players but not all
why: Gold had passed from farmers through players and sellers, so a sink would only reach some holders.

text: Adding house rules without checking sources and sinks can increase inflation; for example, sending tax money to a free parking pot removes a sink and worsens it.
when: When changing rules that move currency.

text: Deliberate-looking inflation costs player trust even when each increase is small.
Replacing a power-up with currency can disturb the economy if the currency is handed out in amounts that are too large.
when: a power-up is swapped for currency
why: the economy absorbs the extra currency

text: A scarce resource offered as a quest reward is weak if players have not yet felt its scarcity or cannot craft anything interesting with it.
when: Designing scarce resources and rewards
why: A resource gains value only when players recognize its scarcity and use

text: Purchasing power can let one player assemble an unbeatable deck from many purchased decks.
when: In trading card games where players can buy many decks
why: Owning many decks lets a player collect the strongest cards, since players only pick the best.

text: Spreading resource gathering evenly across all resources does not plan ahead to stockpile what later needs, so reserves are not built.
when: In games where AI modules for gathering and construction are largely independent
why: Gathering AI is independent of construction planning, so it never looks ahead to later needs.

text: Offering a power boost when a player is stuck can make them feel like a failure who needs to pay.
when: a player is blocked by an obstacle
why: The offer ties the purchase to a moment of frustration

text: If a unit pays its cost in a resource other than the one that decides most games, matchups can swing wildly.
Assuming a fixed usage frequency for an object is unreliable, because use depends on what else the player owns, acquisition order, and play style.
when: When the game is not entirely linear, so players can acquire objects in different orders
why: Players may also use suboptimal tools

text: Removing scarcity, for example by making ammunition infinite, can remove the reason to use the resource at all, so players use it constantly.
when: when considering whether a consumable should be unlimited
why: Without cost, the resource no longer shapes player choices

text: 1) For each resource type, list games that use it. 2) If none come to mind, research and play several examples.
1) Define the basic function of a resource type. 2) Apply that function in new ways rather than copying familiar games.

1) List every resource in the game state. 2) Find which resources convert into others through core mechanics or special object rules. 3) Draw the flow as boxes for resources and arrows for conversions.
when: analyzing a game's economy before balancing it

text: 1) Fairness: can buying or earning grant unfair edges? 2) Challenge: can purchases trivialize play, or is earning too hard? 3) Choices: enough earn and spend options, and is earning skill or luck based? 4) Cooperation: can players pool funds or collude? 5) Pacing: is earning too slow or fast, and do rewards matter? 6) Autonomy: can players acquire desired goods independently?
when: Reviewing an economy that involves trading between players.
why: Player-to-player trading requires balancing many economy factors at the same time, which makes it hard.

text: 1) Ask how players earn money and whether other earning methods should exist. 2) Ask what players can buy and why. 3) Ask whether money is too easy or too hard to get and how to adjust it. 4) Ask whether earning and spending choices are meaningful. 5) Ask whether one universal currency suits the design or specialized currencies would serve better.
when: After an economy is defined, to check that it is controlled and meaningful.
why: An economy adds depth and a life of its own, yet is hard to keep controlled.

text: 1) Introduce pricier goods. 2) Raise existing prices, which players dislike. 3) Lower the drop rates that add currency.
when: Designer responds to demand-side inflation.
why: Rising currency per player shifts demand right, so players can afford higher prices.

text: 1) Measure average currency per player over time. 2) If it grows or shrinks, adjust sources or sinks. 3) Aim for sinks that remove about as much currency as sources add.
when: Keeping a positive-sum economy stable.
why: Stable currency per player means prices hold their value.

text: 1) Ban accounts linked to currency farming. 2) Build tools that detect and disable bots.
when: When external farmers flood the economy with currency.
why: Removing the sources of illicit currency limits the oversupply.

text: 1) Control availability, so store-sold items rarely sell above store price. 2) Set loot rarity, since rarer items are usually worth more. 3) Place stores so nearby buy or sell options cap prices. 4) Restrict item properties, since class-only items have limited markets.
when: When designers want to influence player-set trade prices.
why: Players selling to a store or NPC will not accept less at auction, so market prices get anchored.

text: 1) Remove auction trading. 2) Or build a performance economy that rewards in-game actions over what players can afford.
when: When real-money currency trading distorts the economy.
why: Players pay real money to skip grinding, and currency bought outside the game floods the economy.

text: 1) Start with a fixed economy. 2) Add a production source. 3) Add a bank exchange cap. 4) Restrict trade timing and partners. 5) Make values fluctuate with supply and demand.
when: Evolving a simple trading card game into a richer economy
why: Each added layer increases complexity while keeping the game playable.

text: 1) Decide whether the economy grows over the game and whether that growth is controlled. 2) Decide how currency supply is controlled. 3) Decide how prices are set. 4) Decide what restricts trade.
when: Designing a game economy from scratch
why: These four decisions determine the economy's growth, inflation, pricing, and trade flow.

text: 1) Start by letting players self-regulate resource recycling. 2) Observe whether players hoard items. 3) If hoarding breaks the economy, switch to designer control of supply.
when: Managing item supply in a persistent online economy
why: Unregulated recycling can let hoarding distort availability.

text: Keep two identity resources separate when one is scarce in some situations, when theme rules out the exchange, or when one is more versatile.
when: deciding whether two equal-value resources should remain distinct
why: Scarcity, theme, and versatility each break a true one-to-one identity in play.

text: 1) Choose a game with several resource types and list as many as possible. 2) Identify how they relate or are exchanged during play. 3) Draw each resource as a box and each relationship, numeric relation or exchange rate as an arrow. 4) Choose the resource best suited as anchor.
when: First analyzing a game's economy, when a balance issue involves several resources, or analyzing a classic game's resource economy.
why: Makes hidden links between resources visible.

text: 1) Map the resource cost to cost points, keeping the curve as identity. 2) Map each benefit to benefit points. 3) Subtract cost points from benefit points to find the item's position relative to the curve. 4) Compare items only after conversion; raw resource units against stat points reverse the apparent balance.
when: Items whose resource costs grow non-linearly, or items whose costs are in raw resource units
why: Converting costs keeps the identity curve valid without changing it; unit mismatch reverses the apparent balance.

text: 1) List every party that receives part of a sale. 2) Note each party's share. 3) Explain why each share is that size. 4) Use the gaps to find the questions to answer.
when: analyzing any business model
why: Following the money reveals how the business really works

text: 1) Identify where a currency comes from, such as starting amount or loot. 2) Identify where it goes, such as shops, NPCs, other players, or event costs.
when: Analyzing a currency's flow through a game economy.
why: Sources and sinks determine whether the currency stays balanced.

text: Include only the resources a game truly needs, and keep testing whether each one is necessary.
when: When designing a game's resource set.
why: Extra resources complicate play and usually end poorly.

text: List the game's resources and how they connect before balancing, both early in design and for games already in production.
when: Early in game design, or when a game in production is already unbalanced.
why: Balance depends on how resources flow between systems, so knowing the pieces is the first step.

text: To fix an unbalanced object, change its costs or benefits, or change surrounding systems, level design, or encounter frequency, while keeping the object itself the same.
when: an object's value is off and the object's design should stay fixed
why: the surrounding context often determines how valuable the object is

text: Cap how many of an essential resource a player can gift to one recipient per day.
when: The gifted resource is essential and the game depends on its sales
why: The cap forces players to build a wider network instead of relying on one friend

text: Sinks must not conflict with the goal of stopping inflation, so designers should check that sources and sinks stay in balance.
when: In a persistent online game, checking whether average currency per player is growing or shrinking.
why: Sinks should remove about as much currency as sources add, so the economy stops growing.

text: Designers who do not want cash trades should design the trading system so it does not allow them.
why: Enforcing a terms-of-service ban on cash trades creates heavy support work and angry, banned players.

text: When a card, combination, or deck is too strong, adjust its cost by hand.
Tie every economic action to the player's objective so that each action advances or hinders progress, and balance resource utility against scarcity.
why: Economic choices only matter when they affect the goal.

text: In live games, taper currency from drops over time, reducing the flow of new money into the economy.
when: In a positive-sum economy where drops add currency without removing any from others.
why: Drops add currency without taking it from anyone, so the money supply and per-player currency inflate.

text: Convert resources that trade into each other (time to points, coins to lives, coins per time unit) using their exchange rate, read from numeric relations.
when: Resources convert into one another

text: A resource needs both utility, meaning it helps reach goals, and scarcity, meaning it is not overly abundant.
Designers plan which resources players can find or earn, so that meeting challenges yields what is needed to advance.
Design currency to reward the activities you want players to do, so that earning it adds value through play rather than through money.
when: When players expect eventual parity with paying players, regardless of spending.

text: Showing market data helps players decide well, whereas concealment leaves the community a shared puzzle to solve.
why: Public figures let players analyze every element, as wikis do; hidden figures turn the economy into a collective puzzle.

text: Closed economies are easier to design and balance because the designer controls all production and consumption, while open economies are harder because players may spend very different amounts and the designer loses control.
when: When players can buy in-game resources with real money or otherwise add resources from outside the system.
why: The designer controls all production and consumption, so no outside inflow disrupts the balance.

text: Designers can forbid cash trades, tolerate them without accepting responsibility for disputes, or formalize them by building cash acceptance and transfer into the game.
when: When deciding whether players may trade in-game goods for real money.
why: Banning cash trades consumes support time and invites backlash from banned players.

text: A simple conversion rate, such as 10 cents per unit, makes costs transparent, whereas a complex rate reduces the number of players who question their purchases.
when: designing real-money currency pricing
why: Transparency aids informed buying; complexity suppresses comparison.

text: Buying the cheapest income upgrade now raises income sooner, while saving for a costlier upgrade with better cost-to-benefit ratio earns less early but more later.
when: idle games with several upgrades and a fixed time horizon

text: Limited resources make unit losses permanent and focus play on preserving units, while unlimited resources let players rebuild losses and care less about any one unit.
when: Designing tactical unit economy
why: Replaceability determines how much each unit matters.

text: Treating spending as the player's free choice serves the business, but accepting measurable harm to players conflicts with entertainment as the product.
when: When a game measurably pushes low-income players to spend beyond what they can afford.
why: The product is meant to be entertainment, yet measurable harm makes players' real lives worse.

text: Reusable items cost more up front but save per use, paying off after upfront cost difference ÷ per-use saving uses; consumables cost less up front but repeat the expense.
when: Choosing between a reusable item and repeated consumable purchases
why: Per-use savings accumulate until they repay the up-front cost

text: Juice does not change game systems, yet players perceive balance through it, so it still shapes the experience.
why: Perceived balance depends on feedback, not only on numbers.

text: Gravity and jump force are counterparts; together they set the feel of a jump, so tuning one changes how the other reads.
When hands are hidden but production is public, attentive players can track much of the game state.
Players can reverse engineer a shipped game's numbers, but cannot recover the designers' route or reasons.
The mathematical structure of most games is now publicly documented, so solving numbers has value, but it works best alongside a target experience.
Community wikis, FAQs, and strategy guides often publish a game's underlying numbers in charts, which are useful for balance analysis.
R-squared measures how closely a trendline follows the data; the trendline with the highest R-squared fits best.
when: comparing trendlines fitted to the same data

text: In a realistic game, numbers stay muted and cluster around average values, with large deviations treated as notable exceptions.
when: When the game aims for a realistic tone rather than an epic one.
why: Large deviations from the norm draw immediate player attention, so they work as notable exceptions.

text: Customer acquisition cost is the average spend needed to get one player to download the game and start playing it.
Publishers typically pay developers an advance against royalties, which the developer uses to pay staff, cover overhead, and subcontract parts of the work.
Specialized media contractors are usually hired for short periods on contract, charging by the hour or by the day.
First-time developers get lower royalty rates because they are riskier, while proven hit makers can negotiate higher rates.

Cultural hits often result from several factors combining, such as cheap social venues, fast infrastructure, economic recession and media coverage, and their individual contributions cannot be disentangled.
when: explaining an unexpected market hit

text: Designing for community matters most when revenue depends on subscription renewals, sequels, or microtransactions, since extended play drives all three.
when: games relying on recurring revenue
why: Longer play directly increases renewals and in-game spending.

text: Design choices drive profitability, so design and management each control the other's outcome.
why: Designers may misjudge profit impacts of their choices, so business staff step in to direct design decisions.

text: In a crowded free market, earning money requires reaching very large audiences, which favors publishers with large marketing budgets.
when: competing in a flooded free-to-play market
why: Monetization depends on scale of players reached

text: Developer royalties are commonly 10 to 15% of net sales, paid after portal revenue is received, negotiable, and higher when the developer delivers a finished product.
when: When the developer delivers a finished product and the publisher only provides distribution.
why: The rate is negotiated based on the developer's track record and how much the publisher funds.

text: After recoupment, a developer typically receives 10% to 18% of the publisher's net sales revenue; at 15%, the publisher keeps 85%.
when: After the publisher has recouped development costs from sales.
why: Milestone payments are advances, so the publisher keeps all revenue until they are recovered.

text: A mainstream game can cost five to ten million dollars or more to develop, with the company carrying all the risk.
why: Companies see little reason to pay outsiders for ideas.

text: Game development is very risky; plan for dry spells and unexpected costs, especially for a studio with only a few titles.
when: For small developers who have produced only one or two games.
why: They lack the financial cushion to absorb a dry spell or unexpected costs.

text: A quest objective is a special item that completes a mission when obtained, traded or handed over, and it may appear as a lasting object or a single-use one.
A franchise license or a partner who trusts only certain people can be a barrier.
The quantity dial applies to resources, players, creatures and other components.
Real idle games have far richer cost and benefit systems than small spreadsheet models of the same genre.
Adding an army to a smaller territory gives a larger gain in attacker win chance than adding the same army to a larger one.
when: Deciding where to place reinforcements in a dice combat game.
why: The marginal effect of an extra army is bigger when the base is smaller.

text: 1) List every square a player can end a turn on. 2) Remove squares that are only ladder bottoms or chute tops, since a turn never rests there. 3) Count the remaining squares as states.
when: building a state machine for a track board with ladders and chutes
why: transit-only squares add states that never hold a player

text: Quantitative design, which tunes games primarily from analytics, can produce dull designs and erode trust in designers' instincts, though handled well it reveals player behavior subtly.
when: When relying on analytics to drive design decisions
why: Metrics can flatten design intent and displace designer judgment.

text: A gift of powerful items to a low-level character can make it too strong; an item restriction such as a high level requirement lets it be held but not used until the character levels up.
when: When players can transfer rich items to low-level characters.

text: Gifting of daily allocations the giver does not own drives retention: reciprocity means giving more tends to bring receiving more, prompting repeat sessions and invites.
when: Free-to-play games with daily gift allowances that reward reciprocity
why: Allocations are not owned, so gifting drives return visits and invites rather than economic exchange; reciprocation creates repeat sessions and retention

text: Unlimited gifting of an essential limited resource lets players supply each other and avoid buying it, reducing monetization.
when: A gifted resource is needed for most progression and is sold in the store
why: Friends can cover each other's needs indefinitely without spending

text: When a gifted resource is rare, players recruit real-world friends to join, and communities post invitation threads, so gifting spreads the game organically.
when: Gifted items that are scarce or valued
why: Scarcity makes players want more senders, which drives invitations

text: Hit points track health and are arguably the most important resource in a game, and the challenge of a game is largely the player's ability to manage them.
Health may be a standalone resource or a property of each life, and it dramatizes how close lives and units come to being lost.
Players trade other resources for hit points, such as money for potions or time spent resting while the character heals.
The ratio of health to damage is arbitrary but sets each enemy's perceived strength and signals which targets are dangerous or impervious.
when: when tuning health and damage values
why: The number of hits gives direct feedback on threat

text: Consumables such as healing potions restore hit points, armor and power-ups slow or prevent their loss, and weapons, magic, and aggressive actions cause loss.
When enemy HP is tuned to the damage weapons deal, HP becomes the anchor that weapon power is balanced against.
when: skill-based games with no item prices
why: Monster HP is calibrated to weapon damage, so HP anchors how weapon power is balanced.

text: Doubling a character's health doubles the value of attack bonus relative to armor class.
If enemies keep full offense until defeated, lethal focused damage is worth more than partial area damage, because removing enemies one at a time cuts enemy output.
when: Enemies deal full damage until they die
why: Each kill removes that enemy's future attacks

text: Until a player earns a health container, one hit is fatal; once one exists, a hit costs a container instead of a life, and a life is lost only with none left.
when: early in a run
why: Containers add a buffer before lives are at risk.

text: HP increases can be linear with a random value in a range, for example a level 5 gain of +25 HP within a 10 percent band.
when: Designing per-level HP gains.

text: Use health as the common unit for valuing cards: one point of Cost removes exactly one point of health.
when: Valuing cards in a cost-paid-in-health duel.
why: Unpreventable health loss means one cost point equals exactly one point of health.

text: A player can hold up to ten health containers, earned by collecting enough small packets that enemies drop.

Action-game health restoration via placed medical kits is very fast but somewhat unrealistic, while role-playing restoration via eating or resting fits the story better but is slow and can frustrate players.
Even games without visible numbers have them, such as damage, range, ammunition, health, and object positions in a shooter.
Designers sometimes set values with no discernible pattern, such as a weapon with very high damage and a very low drop rate.
when: tuning individual items or abilities

text: Large numbers are hard to manage in board games.
Exact combat formulas are often hidden in games, so community wikis, FAQs, and strategy guides are common sources for stats and formulas.
when: analyzing a combat with real game math

text: When an item's cost looks right on paper but feels wrong in play, look for hidden sunk, setup, or opportunity costs; ignoring setup cost makes the item look much cheaper.
when: Cost-curve analysis of items
why: A listed price alone cannot reveal why an item feels off

text: Initial values are guesses, so matched totals can mislead until observed play confirms or revises them.
Combining random values silently reshapes the outcome distribution, so check the resulting distribution rather than assuming it.
why: Designers often add random numbers without realizing how the sum changes the spread.

text: A single long balance formula hides mistakes that separate subtotal columns would make visible.
when: When a spreadsheet balances many mechanics through one complex combined formula
why: Splitting the formula into simpler parts makes it easier to understand and makes errors easier to detect.

text: Handle extreme values either by writing special-case math for the edges or by placing hard caps so players cannot reach them.
when: A general formula is correct for typical values but fails at limits.
why: A general formula can be sound overall yet fail at the edges, so it may not need rewriting.

text: AI typically receives about 5–25% of processor time, and can exceed 50% when graphics work moves to the graphics card.
why: AI shares the frame budget with graphics, physics and other systems.

text: Analog stick and gyroscope responses rarely map linearly to perceived force, so tune the response curve to match what players feel.
when: Designing analog or gyroscope controls
why: Intended movement and perceived intensity relate non-linearly.

text: Push AI time budgets close to the frame limit, and prefer a consistently long component over one whose cost fluctuates.
when: When all processing must finish within a fixed frame time such as 16 ms at 60 Hz
why: Unused frame time is wasted, and a fluctuating component can cause the frame rate to drop.

text: Automating a task can remove tedium but also remove meaningful decisions, so check that the removed input is not a meaningful choice before automating.
when: Before automating a task.
why: Player inputs are how players shape the game state, and indirect control itself forms a challenge.

text: A permanent item is a found, traded or bought object that exists in the world, cannot be consumed or used as material, and persists after the player disposes of it.
An item is on the curve when its total value, from stats and abilities with drawbacks counted, matches its cost.
An effect that hits only a small minority of cards is often dead in typical matchups and becomes useful only when the metagame favors that minority.
when: Removal that targets a card subtype or category
why: Few opposing cards match the target, so the effect rarely has value

text: A unit that has valid targets only in a fraction of rounds has its effective efficiency multiplied by that fraction.
when: enemy types arrive on a fixed schedule
why: Swarm towers deal no damage to non-flying enemies, so they contribute only when flyers appear.

text: Items that become obsolete quickly lose their value, which can make earlier collection feel pointless if the design does not account for it.
A later skill can make earlier ones obsolete, and a branch clearly stronger than others turns the choice into no real choice.
when: Designing skill progression and branches
why: Players pick the dominant option, so the apparent choice has no real alternative.

text: A unit that offers no real choices fails the fun criterion.
why: Without decisions there is nothing for the player to do, so a balanced unit still is not interesting.

text: A versatile option that is never best can make blind choices feel uninteresting unless switching or carrying several items is allowed.
when: The player must choose gear before the situation is known
why: The choice feels like guessing with no clear winner

text: 1) List situations where the option is the only one covering a role. 2) Check whether remaining options cover those situations at acceptable cost. 3) Identify regions left with no viable option.
Leave a blank cell at the end of an optional part column so some random picks add nothing, giving some drops no added part.
why: A blank entry lets a roll add nothing, so some drops receive no extra part.

text: Where total value can grow and corrective feedback pushes back on leaders, late-game gains can be large, players keep overtaking each other, and the ending becomes exciting.
when: late phase of a growing-pie contest with corrective feedback
why: Negative feedback shrinks the leader's gains and speeds trailing players' power growth, so the lead keeps swinging.

text: Mostly negative-sum games can still have late positive-sum events, such as pawn promotion in chess-like games, that pull the game toward a close finish.
when: late in a mostly negative-sum game

text: Very large multipliers are best saved for late game, where they bring a likely-decided game to a satisfying end.
when: designing strong multiplicative effects
why: Late placement speeds a settled endgame and gives players a sense of epic victory.

text: In PvE, a positive power loop can make the late game suddenly easy so players rush through it; changing the loop or adding content can fix this.
why: Positive player-power feedback removes challenge from later content, so the player experiences it as shorter.

text: When bonuses are large, the attacker's advantage grows as the game goes on, which creates a positive feedback loop that pushes the game toward a close finish even under optimal play.
when: Late-game conquest with large continent bonuses and growing armies.
why: Attacker advantage at scale compounds as armies accumulate.

text: Rewards that unlock later in a match are more impactful, because each later event changes the overall game state more.
when: When designing escalating rewards tied to progress such as kill counts.
why: Later events shift the broader state more than early ones.

text: Granularity is the spacing between neighboring numbers in a game's value system.
Enlarging a grid lengthens play and weakens tension when the center stops dominating; the piece count must rise to match the new cell count.
when: Changing board dimensions
why: In a seven-column grid, every horizontal or diagonal four must touch the center column.

text: Multiplying a value range by 10 creates room for many more items between the same minimum and maximum, as sword damage 1 to 10 scaled to 10 to 100 shows.
when: Planning content that will grow over time
why: Larger integer ranges leave gaps for future items without fractional values.

text: Low granularity is especially harmful in expandable games such as trading card games and online RPGs with expansions.
when: Game will receive expansions
why: Expansions need unused numeric space to add new power levels.

text: Joining text parts without spaces makes names run together; add a space at the end or start of each part.
when: When building item names by joining text parts from several spreadsheet columns

text: 1) Compute the current level from total XP. 2) Compute XP still needed for the next level. 3) Show progress as the share of the current level's XP span already earned, so the bar is empty right after leveling and full just before the next.
Make each level gain feel meaningful through gains in HP, stats, skills or spells.
why: Level gains must be felt in tangible stats, so progression stays fun alongside XP rewards from combat and quests.

text: Too little granularity leaves no room to add content except at the high end; too much makes differences meaningless to players.
when: Choosing the scale of numeric values
why: Tight numbers block new items; huge numbers lose perceptual meaning.

text: Treat a situational weakness as a negative value and weight it by its frequency, just like a benefit.
when: The object is worse than baseline in some situations
why: Liabilities affect expected value in the same way as benefits

text: Recognizable licensed brands can sell well regardless of gameplay quality, so licensing reduces publisher risk by relying on existing exposure.
when: When a game integrates recognizable licensed characters, personalities, music or other properties
why: Brand recognition drives purchase independent of how good the game is

text: Licensors raise their prices as a game's profits grow, which can push publishers to invest in original intellectual property instead.
A large licensed title may cost hundreds of thousands of dollars for the licence plus a royalty of 1% to 10% of net revenue to the rights holder.
when: When a publisher uses a licensed property owned by an outside rights holder
why: Products built on familiar brands have sold well regardless of gameplay quality, which lowers publisher risk.

text: A licence may be unavailable or too expensive to justify, a common reason a licensed project gets rejected.
Rewards perceived as controlling are less efficient overall at sustaining motivation.
when: Rewards such as gold or loot are framed as the player being managed rather than as their own choice.

text: A variable deck is one whose composition changes between rounds as players add and remove cards.
Variety means enemies and weapons that force different responses, not simply more enemies or higher damage numbers.
Weapon enhancements can add damage per shot, raise accuracy, or add bullets.
Weapons commonly specialize by range, close-quarters use, or effectiveness against large slow targets, while armor may resist physical or magical attacks, grant evasion, or give stat bonuses.
Randomized spawn timing and randomized loot drops correspond to variable-interval and variable-ratio reward schedules.
Some collectible card games instead make rare cards stronger, rewarding heavier spending.
Test rare random drops with a pseudorandom model before shipping to see how often they appear across playthroughs.
when: When a rare item has a small drop chance, such as a fraction of a percent.
why: Low probabilities are hard to judge by intuition and show their effect only in aggregate.

text: Give even common enemies a chance to drop a reward, so routine encounters stay worth engaging with.
why: Each encounter then carries a possible payoff.

text: Use rarity mainly for intricate or specialized cards, and sometimes to limit cards that are too strong in large numbers.
when: When a card's strength would unbalance the game if many copies existed.
why: Power confined to rare cards would force players to be wealthy or fortunate to build a competent deck.

text: Loot tables that give randomized rewards at set probabilities implement variable ratio reinforcement directly and suit repeated monster fighting or looting.
when: Designing loot for repeated enemy encounters
why: Randomized payoffs at fixed probabilities keep players acting for the next possible reward.

text: A wide skill range is simple to pick up yet difficult to master, while a narrow range is either fully known or not known at all.
why: Once the single good strategy is learned, a narrow-range game stops offering anything new.

text: Lowering the drop rate of rewards forces players to buy more or play longer to obtain the same amount.
why: It adds friction: players who won't pay must grind longer, accept weaker results, or leave.

text: When complete card collections are attainable, rarity mainly helps players who spend more money rather than balancing power.
when: collectible card games where players can buy full sets
why: Rarity was meant to offset power by scarcity and trading, but big spenders could collect every copy, removing that scarcity.

text: In one action-RPG example, roughly one enemy in every hundred killed drops an item that upgrades killing power, a drop rate of about 1 percent.
when: when tuning rare item drops for a repetitive combat loop
why: A rare, unpredictable reward keeps players killing and opening containers despite tedious repetition

text: A specific rarer-tier item can appear more often than an item in a less rare tier when its tier is small or its slot chance is high; verify each item's per-draw probability.
when: when a game picks one random item from a tier
why: tier rank alone does not set each item's frequency

text: A class that plays like another class with a thinner skill tree will be judged underpowered by players, so class balance is the first concern.
when: Games where characters are organized into classes.
why: Players compare classes directly.

text: Relying on rarity to offset power assumes limited spending and limited trading, which may fail when a game becomes very popular.
when: When a card game's popularity lets players spend heavily and collect full sets.
why: Collecting every card in multiples was achievable and strongly unbalancing, and scarcity could not prevent it.

text: A liability that appears rarely can still matter a lot if the player meets it at a bad moment.
when: Rare situations where the object performs poorly
why: The timing of the encounter can make a rare weakness decisive

text: 1) List loot, healing, and experience as connected resources. 2) Verify that changing one shifts the others as intended. 3) Check the economy as a whole rather than each piece alone.
when: When checking a generated dungeon's rewards.
why: Connected resources must be balanced together to avoid unintended shortages or surpluses.

text: 1) List loot items in A1 to A6. 2) In B1 enter =INDIRECT("A"&RANDBETWEEN(1,6)). 3) Fill down for more drops.
when: all items have equal chances
why: A random integer selects a row number, and INDIRECT fetches that cell's entry.

text: 1) Put each part list in its own column. 2) Pick one random entry per column with INDIRECT and RANDBETWEEN. 3) Join the picks with the & operator into one item name.
when: items are built from several parts, such as a weapon's prefix, base and suffix
why: The & operator sticks picks together, so spacing must be added to keep words apart.

text: Place weapon pickups on the grid; a unit standing on one can use that weapon in the following round.
A slow-reloading close-range weapon trades reuse speed for strong damage up close, while a long-range explosive trades safety for distant damage that can also hit its user.
when: In a shooter where weapons have no cost to fire.
