why: Without a resource cost to use, weapons must be balanced through built-in drawbacks such as slow reloads or self-damage.

text: An option with low average value can still appeal to players when it produces sudden large swings.
when: a card or action with rare but dramatic effects
why: Players are drawn to dramatic swings.

text: If a pro-gamer wants to cut a mechanic because it feels unfair, it is probably too random; reduce its randomness rather than removing the mechanic.
why: Pro players resent losing to weaker opponents through luck, so their cut requests flag excessive randomness.

text: Adding randomness to a value is generally easier than authoring many deterministic variants to widen outcomes.
when: When a designer wants more possible outcomes from a single mechanic.
why: One random range yields many outcomes, while each new deterministic variant needs its own authored event.

text: In a long game of summed random rolls, an early lead from luck tends to average out, so a large early advantage can still be overturned.
when: Heavily luck-based games with many accumulating rolls.
why: The law of large numbers reduces the influence of short-term gains.

text: Replacing a damage formula with a wide random roll raises outcome variance, devalues upgrades and resources, and can make mass unit production the only viable strategy.
when: combat damage is randomized over a wide range
why: Once the roll ignores unit and armor stats, upgrades no longer affect who wins.

text: Randomizing a fixed value widens outcomes: a fixed 5 damage made random from 1 to 7 yields seven outcomes instead of one.
why: Each integer in the new range becomes a distinct possible result, so the count of outcomes grows with the range.

text: Adding luck widens the potential audience because weaker players can win some games, but too much luck makes players feel they have no influence on the result.
when: Tuning the luck level of a competitive game
why: Luck lets weaker players win occasionally, while excessive luck removes perceived agency.

text: A likely-loss outcome with a small chance of winning creates underdog tension without overriding the player's choice.
when: Designing combat or contests between mismatched opponents
why: Doubt over a probable result keeps attention engaged.

text: If luck decides N percent of outcomes, expected win probability should stay between N/200 and 1 − N/200 rather than reaching 0 or 1.
when: Games where chance can decide results.
why: Luck lets weaker players win sometimes, so certainty is unrealistic.

text: Expected win probability equals (1 − L) times the skill-based probability plus 0.5 times L, where L is the probability that a game is decided by luck.
when: Rating games that include a luck component.
why: Luck-decided games favor neither player, so they pull results toward 0.5.

text: Goals driven by luck, where the player cannot improve their odds, feel futile and cause frustration when they fail.
when: Designing goals with a large random component
why: Without any means of influence, a loss after a few wins feels out of the player's hands.

text: Generating an entire number table from one random starting value often amuses the designer more than the player.
when: Seeding a progression randomly
why: Players gain little from arbitrary numbers.

text: If the game's result is predictable, players lose interest, so the outcome must remain uncertain.
when: In game systems that end in a winner or measurable result.

text: The game industry is hit-driven: publishers earn most of their money from a few big hits, and roughly the top 20 titles generate about 80% of industry revenue.
Players act unpredictably in trade, so gifting a large amount of currency to a high-level character can make out-of-reach items affordable, and designers should gate items with use requirements.
when: When players can pass currency to other characters, such as through gifts.
why: Use requirements mean that affording an item does not guarantee the player can actually use it.

text: Visible prestige items can sell very quickly after release, even at prices near double a regular subscription.
when: Items that other players can see
why: Their value depends on being seen by others

text: Every business decision is a bet on human psychology, which designers already understand, and financial details can be learned as needed.
Players enjoy debating tier lists, and off-curve items give them hidden gems to find and let less popular choices win in unexpected ways.
when: Games with many comparable items
why: Discoverable outliers sustain discussion and experimentation

Units sold counts purchases, and new pitches often estimate it from the results of similar games.

An industry initiative is working to define shared ethical standards for Western game studios.

Publishers relying on licences and sequels can release few original titles; one large independent's originals were about 16% of output.
Industry coalitions of over 160 companies share best practices for reducing toxic player behavior.

text: Build industry relationships through events and local meetups long before the pitch is ready, since networks take time to form.

text: After the economy stabilizes, prices can be lowered over time to match earlier-game changes.
why: Lowered prices track the economic shifts that happened earlier in the game.

text: Keep the lowest tiers holding only a small share of players, so even weak players avoid feeling at the very bottom.
when: when setting tier population sizes
why: Keeps low-ranked players from feeling they are at the very bottom.

text: Barriers to entry such as regulation, special hardware, expertise, and algorithms can reverse profitability, leaving most protected market participants profitable.
when: a market is protected by barriers
why: Barriers limit the number of competitors

text: A markdown reserve means the publisher covers part of the loss when a title is discounted at retail.
when: a retail price is reduced
why: The publisher pays for part of the discount

text: Producing a large batch at once can lower the cost per unit compared to producing in small amounts.
when: Production scales with batch size
why: Economies of scale spread fixed costs across more units.

text: Growing budgets and team sizes raise sales expectations, pushing publishers toward games with blockbuster potential.
why: Larger teams and longer timelines mean each game must sell very well to justify its cost.

text: A large installed base keeps an older console viable as a release platform for years after its successor launches.
why: A huge owner base gives publishers an audience worth releasing for.

text: Because games are nonrival, one excellent game can take nearly every customer, leaving other good games with none, so the market works like a winner-take-all tournament.
when: many comparable games compete in one market
why: Copying costs almost nothing, so the top title captures the bulk of demand.

text: Worldwide game industry revenue, including hardware, was about $43 billion in 2007.
when: Figures for 2007.

text: Breakeven units equal development and marketing costs divided by price per unit; a $400,000 cost at $5 per unit requires 80,000 units.
Effective per-use cost of a prerequisite-gated item equals (sunk cost + unit cost × uses) ÷ uses, spreading the setup cost over expected uses.
when: An item requires a prerequisite that must be paid first
why: Setup cost is shared across all units the player builds

text: Casual publishers typically fund production budgets of $50,000 to $200,000.
Some aggregators let developers keep 60% of revenues while retaining all intellectual property rights.
Market barriers come in seven kinds: technical, hardware, expertise, sales and distribution, imagination, relationship, and uncertainty.
A profit checklist is a set of questions for testing whether a game can make money; it asks where money goes, what it costs, how much it earns, and what entry barriers exist.
when: while designing a game
why: Profit is what keeps the industry running, so a game's money questions must be answered.

text: Publisher letters of intent, sent when risks and return are acceptable, are not signed deals: a full contract is still needed, and the publisher can cancel for internal reasons.
why: Publishers can still cancel at this stage for internal reasons.

text: A game that requires a license that is unavailable or unaffordable is likely to be rejected.
Ignoring the intended audience makes a well-made game look unbalanced.
when: When evaluating difficulty.
why: Difficulty judged against the wrong target seems wrong even when it fits the intended players.

text: A balanced item curve can still leave free-to-play players under-supplied; the shortfall comes from the pressure curve, not the items.
when: When game pressure rises faster than the store's item costs
why: Pressure grows while items stay priced on the curve, so resources fall short of demand.

text: In some games bulk currency purchases cost more per unit than small ones, so buying more does not always save money.
when: designing currency bundle tiers
why: Players assume larger purchases give better value, and this assumption is exploited.

text: Leaving out intangible value, such as an item's convenience or a shortcut's benefit, misjudges what an outcome is really worth.
when: when valuing items and shortcuts

text: Underestimating how many players a large budget requires leads to unrealistic free-to-play plans.
when: When per-player profit is only about fifty cents
why: Small profit per player means a large budget requires a very large player count.

text: Judging a retailer as greedy without considering its low-margin position leads to a wrong conclusion.
when: evaluating a retailer's share
why: Margin pressure explains much of its share

text: Relying on churn and ROI alone shows business health but reveals neither why players leave nor what to change.

1) Total each labor category from line items. 2) Add benefits to each line item before rollup. 3) Add other direct costs such as software licenses and specialized services. 4) Add overhead. 5) Add production insurance if purchased. 6) Apply markup.
why: Each step feeds the next to reach the final price.

text: Submit the publisher's required legal disclosure forms; skipping them or using your own forms gets a submission discarded.
when: When a company requests a disclosure form during submission
why: Missing the form signals the submitter does not understand the submission procedure.

text: If designers can predict when players usually acquire each item in an overlapping set, price each item for that typical point in the collection.
Introductions through a trusted contact work far better than cold outreach to busy gatekeepers, who ignore emails and cancel meetings.
when: Approaching a busy publisher or executive
why: Listeners trust people they know, so a vouched-for pitch gets a hearing.

text: The casual market is huge but hard to get noticed in unless a game suddenly becomes fashionable, while hardcore players reward deep games that cost more to make but may earn more.
why: Casual players are far more numerous, but hardcore players pay much more for games they care about.

text: Under an affiliate-label arrangement, the studio splits development and marketing expenses to reduce publisher exposure, in return for 65% to 75% royalties.
why: Sharing development and marketing costs lowers the publisher's exposure, which justifies a larger developer revenue share.

text: Each business model imposes different design constraints: arcade games sell quick play, MMOs sell long subscriptions, shrink-wrapped games sell units via reviews, and noncommercial games express ideas.
when: choosing a business model for a game
why: Each model has a different revenue mechanism that drives different design goals.

text: The metagame is everything players do outside actual play that affects their chance of winning, such as studying opponents, building decks, drafting, or negotiating salaries.
Metagame rules such as drafts, salary caps, revenue sharing, and team size limits exist to keep strong competitors from pulling away, and metagame balance strongly shapes game balance.
when: Designing competitive systems that must stay balanced over time.
why: They interrupt the positive feedback loop of success begetting success.

text: A rock-paper-scissors metagame, though better than one dominant strategy, shifts focus from in-match play toward deck choice.
why: A counter-card wastes resources unless the opponent runs the deck it targets, so deck choice carries much of the outcome.

text: A special card that matches only its twin can occupy the second draw and cause failure, pulling match odds slightly below the standard-deck value.
when: a deck with extra cards that match only each other
why: a wasted draw counts as a failure

text: Spreading a unit group protects it from area damage but exposes it to attackers that pick off isolated units, while concentration does the reverse.
when: designing or playing positional unit fights
why: Formation trades one vulnerability for another.

text: Older decks can become non-viable as power rises, which can alienate veteran players.
when: Power curve keeps rising
why: Previously strong cards fall out of competitive use.

text: A nonviable build may be obvious immediately or hidden for a long time, and discovering it late can force a full replay and make players quit.
when: Designing builds that can become nonviable
why: Late discovery wastes player time and damages willingness to continue or recommend the game.

text: A high pick rate can suggest a nerf, but a pick-rate gap may stem from missing visual and sound cues on other options rather than from balance problems.
when: when class or hero pick rates look skewed
why: players cannot choose options whose strengths are not signaled

text: Use a metagame rule only when the imbalance originates in the metagame itself; avoid metagame patches for imbalances that come from cards, units, or mechanics.
when: Choosing where to fix an imbalance.
why: A metagame fix for a game-level imbalance only treats a symptom and leaves the original problem in place.

text: ARPU is revenue over a period, such as the last thirty days, divided by all engaged users (MAU). ARPPU divides by paying users only and is usually much higher.
Players generally view pay-to-win as unfair and expect to reach the same capabilities whether or not they pay.
when: Free-to-play or competitive games with paid advantages.
why: Pay-to-win is perceived negatively, and paid edges tend to level out among paying players, leaving no real advantage.

text: Whales are a small group of heavy spenders, sometimes spending thousands of dollars, whom designers tune the game around; one study found half of revenue came from 0.15% of players.
Problematic monetization is most common in freemium games; free-to-play models raise more ethical concerns than premium upfront-paid games, though it increasingly appears in premium games.
People judge prices against a prior reference: a large first figure makes later items look cheap; a crossed-out higher price makes a discount seem better even when value is unchanged.
when: presenting prices, discounts or offers
why: Anchoring: people use prior information as a reference point when judging new information.

text: A decoy option that steers users toward a pricier choice is a dark pattern: the gain goes to the business while the cost falls on the user.
when: The decoy is designed to push users toward a more expensive purchase they would not otherwise make.
why: The gain goes to the business while the cost falls on the user.

text: Do not expose under-18 players to gambling-like monetization such as loot boxes; they are more vulnerable to psychological pressure and cannot be reliably screened out.
when: The game is likely to be played by under-18s.
why: Young players have weaker impulse control and developers cannot easily verify players' ages.

text: Paid games can tolerate onboarding friction because buyers are committed; free-to-play players drop off with each extra step since they have not paid.
when: Choosing onboarding friction levels by business model; designing tutorials for free-to-play or mobile games.
why: Paying players have invested in the purchase and are more likely to persist; non-payers have less reason to persist through extra steps.

text: Players usually object when a closed game economy is turned open, for example when money can be purchased with real currency.
when: When a closed economy gains purchasable currency.
why: A closed economy is insulated from outside influence; buying currency lets some players change the shared resources from outside.

text: Players with cash often buy rather than work out whether they are spending money or time.
when: players who can pay real money for in-game progress
why: Buying is the quicker option, so the cost in time or money is rarely calculated.

text: Paying an opponent to throw a match can happen regardless of whether the opponent actually delivers the loss.
People paid per output produce more work of lower quality, and they stop when payment ends, while unpaid people keep going on their own.
when: when a reward is tied to output quantity
why: Payment changes the reason for doing the task.

text: Many players feel that buying power in adventure games is cheating, because the purchase seems to sell the answer to an obstacle.
when: paid power is offered as a shortcut past a challenge
why: Buying the solution undermines the sense of earning victory

text: Players tolerate overt pay-to-win design less than they did earlier.
when: modern collectible card games

text: Anchoring can lead people to buy items they care about less, buy several items, or exceed their budget, often without noticing the influence.
when: purchase decisions involving discounts or comparisons
why: Comparisons shape judgment unconsciously, including comparisons with other items on sale.

text: Brand labels can strongly shift stated preference even when blind tests show no clear preference.
when: When comparing products in blind tests versus with visible brand labels
why: A brand cue engages emotion-related brain regions during consumption

text: In free-to-play games the typical design underdelivers on a key resource, often time, or makes keeping up with game speed hard without buying upgrades, pressuring players to spend money.
when: In free-to-play games with paid progression
why: Scarcity of time or speed pushes players toward purchases

text: Players of anywhere venue games are generally unwilling to pay much up front and prefer free games when possible.
when: Choosing a pricing model for short-session games.
why: Habits formed in this venue favor low or no initial cost.

text: Young adults aged 18 to 24 play less than children but keep playing with established tastes, and often have both time and money, making them major game consumers.
when: Designing for young adults aged 18 to 24
why: Growing income and free time combine with established tastes to make them major buyers

text: Players often sense that a free-to-play design deliberately creates moments that push them to pay.
why: Free access is used to hook players, and charges arrive at moments when players need something.

text: In a three-option subscription test, most students chose the expensive bundle when a decoy was present, but most chose the cheap option once the decoy was removed.
when: Three tiers where the middle tier is nearly as costly as the top tier but worth much less.
why: The decoy made the top tier look like the obvious value, which vanished when the decoy was removed.

text: Free-to-play economies offer resources bought with real money or earned through monetizing actions such as watching ads; purchases typically trade money for time, a core hook.
A blockchain is a decentralized, distributed ledger that records transactions across many participants.
Pay-to-win designs gate the top gear behind purchases, so the biggest spenders gain a lasting power edge.
Pay-to-rush lets money buy speed through progression.
Average LTV is the average amount a player spends over their whole play history; many players pay zero while a few pay a lot.
ARPDAU is revenue per daily active user, showing how much players spend each day.
A non-fungible token (NFT) is a unique asset whose ownership and authenticity are recorded on a blockchain.
Non-gameplay factors such as display hardware can shift timing and aim in competitive play.
when: Competitive play where players use different setups.

text: Publishers have announced interconnected economies in which franchise items bought in one place can be used in another game, signalling intent toward interoperability.
Support for players who pay is typically prioritized over support for non-payers, who get minimal attention.
Designers and players often question the ethics of per-player pricing and drop-rate changes.
An economy can shift sharply when a game changes its monetization model, such as moving between pay-to-play and free-to-play.
Many free-to-play games build monetization around selling virtual skills.
Vanity items that change appearance without affecting power are a major monetization method in some popular online games.
why: Players pay to express identity, not to gain advantage.

text: Players still do not find purchase models entirely fair, so a payment system that feels fair while sustaining great games would likely be widely adopted.
Free-to-play games are given away to attract the most players, then charge for extras at moments when players want something.
In an open app store with low barriers, roughly 90 percent of games lose money and about 10 percent are profitable.
when: entry is easy and the market is crowded
why: Low barriers let many competitors enter

text: Platform holders often sell hardware below cost and earn mainly by charging publishers for each title released.
when: a console or platform business model
why: Revenue comes from software licensing rather than hardware sales

text: In one reviewed game, each player may give up to five random gifts per day, and ungiven gifts are wasted.
when: Daily gifting systems with fixed allowances

why: Non-paying players dilute the per-player average.

text: In a variant with pick-dependent switch offers, a player who is offered a switch wins one-half of the time.
when: the switch is offered only sometimes

text: Decoy pricing is common in free-to-play currency offers and is considered ethically questionable.
Business metrics for free-to-play games focus mainly on retention and conversion.
The monetization model shapes game design; a free-to-play game is not designed the same way as a paid-upfront game.
Player-traded cosmetic item economies can become very large; one reported market totaled over $50 million in a single year.
Do not overweight how a player obtained their deck when judging whether a game is fun, since fun does not depend on it.

when: valuing items that combine several bonuses

text: Compare marketing spend with income to judge whether acquisition is paying off.

text: Compare win rate with amount spent to see whether non-paying players are being punished.
When options differ greatly in value, price the object close to the value of the best option.

why: A weak option costs its owner nothing when unused, yet players take it whenever it proves useful, so its price should track that peak use.

text: Even under profitability pressure, monetization should respect players, with extra care when the audience includes minors.
when: small studios with revenue pressure
why: Tactics such as opt-out defaults exploit status-quo bias, so a UX mindset requires weighing their ethics even when revenue is tight.

text: Without consumables levels become hard, with them easy; free boosts ease early play, then players must pay, often at the point of failure, to keep progressing.

why: Levels tuned hard without boosts make paid consumables the easy path, and losses near the finish invite buying them.

text: Gaining wealth or possessions produces a strong rush, and games can trigger it with artificial in-game wealth rather than real money.
when: Games without real-money stakes that build artificial wealth systems and hand players wealth within them.
why: Acquisition is a basic emotional trigger that does not require real-world value.

text: Daily chests can draw players to launch the game even without an intrinsic urge to play, and players may stay to explore new quests or invitations.
when: Free-to-play daily login design
why: Extrinsic rewards pull players in before intrinsic motivation exists

text: Offering players a paid way to avoid a small certain loss exploits their urge to avoid it and can drive spending.
when: a game takes away earned rewards on failure
why: people pay to avoid a sure loss

text: Without a publisher, the developer bears customer acquisition costs; spending $6 per customer on a $7 share would leave only $1.

why: Acquisition spending a publisher would normally cover shifts onto the developer, shrinking the net share.

text: Selling goods through an intermediate currency hides real-money cost per item, because players must convert packs before they can compare value.
when: goods priced in premium virtual currency sold in packs
why: Conversion adds a step between money paid and value received.

text: When in-game currency is tied to real-money purchases, cutting currency income reduces spending on those purchases.
when: Currency gates a paid sink
why: Players with less currency buy fewer gated items and so spend less real money.

text: A paid edge in rated play fades as the buyer's rating rises, until the buyer faces only other paying players and the advantage no longer separates them.
when: competitive games with rating and paid advantages
why: paying players reach the level of other paying players

text: In a time-limited event, early rank gains build a sense of skill, and later drops can prompt purchases to regain position.
when: when a time-limited event ranks players
why: players who rose feel loss when they fall

text: Currency for watching a full advertisement pays the developer directly, making ad viewing a monetized reward activity.
when: when rewarding players for watching ads
why: The developer is paid for each fully watched ad, and in-game currency lets designers reward that viewing.

text: If the chance of being offered a switch depends on whether the first pick was right, switching's advantage can vanish, leaving switching and staying equally good.
when: the host's offer depends on the player's pick
why: the offer rate changes which outcomes lead to a win

text: In progression games, grinding for levels or loot raises character power, so time can substitute for skill or luck in overcoming challenges.
when: RPG-style progression
why: Grinding raises character power (virtual skill), which shifts the odds of surviving a challenge.

text: A combined option is worth only its best single part if players know which part they need, but worth the sum of parts if they cannot learn it in time.
when: each part is needed by a different outcome

text: Adding a clearly inferior, distracting option can make a more expensive option look more attractive than it did without the decoy, shifting choices toward the pricier one.
when: Users choose among several options with prices or values that are easy to compare.
why: A decoy changes the reference point, so the pricier option seems a better deal by comparison.

text: In free-to-play games, a decoy currency package can push players toward a pricier bundle of in-game currency bought with real money.
when: Players buy virtual currency such as coins or gems with real money and see several package sizes.
why: The same decoy effect that shifts subscription choices also shifts the choice of currency package.

text: Profit per player equals average LTV minus customer acquisition cost; an LTV of $5 against a $3 cost leaves about $2 per player.
why: Average spend across all players, including non-payers, is set against the average cost of winning each player.

text: For a modest mobile game with a $500K budget, the figures in the example imply about a million players are needed to break even.
when: When each player nets only about fifty cents of profit.
why: Development cost must be recovered from a small per-player margin, so the number of players needed grows large.

text: Portals typically share 25 to 50% of revenue with publishers.
PvP games without item costs, such as fighting games, treat character costs and benefits as equal and opposite, but aim for a positive total so characters feel useful.
when: PvP games with no purchasable objects, such as fighting games or single-character MMOs with varied character strengths

when: When developers want to change effective price to better fit their target audience
why: A fixed high list price means sales ending or changing won't catch players off guard.

text: Player-reported monetization problems fall into eight domains: spending-driven dynamics, unmet expectations, monetized quality of life, predatory ads, confusing currency, pay-to-win, microtransactions, and other (limited-time offers, battle passes, deceptive UI).
A free scripting language can carry hidden legal exposure, including liability for copyright or patent breaches, and its up-front cost is only part of its total cost.
when: When using free or open source software that no vendor licenses or stands behind
why: Without a licensor taking responsibility, the user cannot know whether copied or patented code is included and may be liable.

text: Paying for brain-unlocking programs based on the ten percent myth wastes money on unsupported claims.
why: Even simple actions such as clenching a fist use more than ten percent of the brain, so the claim is false.

text: Using variable rewards to monetize raises ethical concerns, especially when children are players.
Pay-to-win models can drive away non-paying players.
In pay-to-win games where players buy units for easier gameplay, the purchase unbalances the game for non-paying players while the publisher profits.
when: In mobile pay-to-win games
why: Buying advantage shifts difficulty onto players who do not pay

text: Rising friction can be used to push players toward a choice between paying and leaving, which is a monetization decision rather than a balance one.
when: After a player has used up free boosts that reduce a difficulty spike

text: Studios often copy business models such as seasons or loot boxes without checking whether they are ethical.
when: When a live game's content cadence slows and players may drift away
why: Ethical problems are carried over unexamined

text: If an item requires a secondary resource that is much harder to obtain, players may leave items unfinished without it.
when: Costs require hard-to-get resources
why: Secondary resource scarcity blocks completion.

text: Metrics can reveal that a monetization design extracts the most money from low-income players, who may spend more than they can afford.
when: When a designer finds the game specifically exploits a type of low-income player

text: 1) Study your own and competitors' data to set a starting price. 2) Test in a region that resembles your target but is not the main audience. 3) Revise based on feedback. 4) Test in further regions. 5) Launch worldwide.
when: F2P games setting prices before a broad launch
why: A test market with cheap user acquisition, similar play habits, and strong language fluency gives representative results.

text: 1) Divide each pack's price by its units to get cost per unit. 2) List pack combinations whose units sum exactly to the target. 3) Compare total prices of those combinations and choose the cheapest.
when: packs sold in fixed sizes at different prices

text: Keep customer acquisition spend below LTV per customer; a $5 LTV supports spending $4 per player, while a $3 LTV makes spending $4 unwise.
when: self-publishing
why: Finding the right spend level is among the hardest parts of self-publishing.

text: Ask players how they feel about price points, free-to-play, and premium pricing, and which features make them decide to buy.
when: designing a monetization model
why: Player perception of price and value guides purchases

text: Before committing to a business model for a game meant to reshape its category, determine what audiences are willing to spend money on, and why.
when: For transformational games aiming to become a sustainable business
why: Good intentions alone don't yield a sustainable business; knowing what people will and won't pay for does.

text: Define the key bullet-point features for the box early, so they keep the design on track when ideas arrive from all directions.
when: When many design ideas are arriving from many directions during development

text: The two main levers of free-to-play profit are raising LTV and lowering acquisition cost.
Decide personally where your monetization ethics line lies, since there is no fixed right answer and otherwise someone else will decide.
why: If you don't decide, someone else will, and you bear the job loss if you dislike their choice.

text: Avoid making paid advantages the main path to competitive success, since many players tolerate them poorly.
when: In competitive free-to-play games where content is unlocked by spending currency
why: Paid advantages erode as other paying players catch up, and many players tolerate pay-to-win poorly.

text: Avoid guilt-tripping quitters, charging to keep earned items, FOMO season items, punishing streaks, hidden pay-to-win, paying to skip friction or game over, gambling-like loot boxes, and forced auto-play defaults.
why: these pressure players against their own interests

text: Check a game's business model; free-to-play games with micro-transactions can be problematic for the youngest players.
when: when choosing games for young children

text: In free-to-play competitive games, selling time savings can make results depend on spending rather than skill, so those who spend the most win.
when: Competitive games where progress can be bought.
why: Players who pay gain speed that others cannot match by playing better.

text: Free-to-play resources sold for real money fall into three groups: pay to win, not pay to win, and cases that depend on how they are implemented.
when: Designing or assessing monetization of a free-to-play game.
why: Whether a purchase affects competitive outcome determines fairness perception.

text: PC releases carry no royalty to the operating system or hardware maker, while console releases bring per-unit royalties and the maker's approval control.
when: choosing between PC and console release
why: Console makers charge a per-unit royalty and keep final approval over the game, whereas selling on PC involves paying no such fee to the platform owner.

text: Pinball numbers are the practice of adding zeros to values to make rewards feel more exciting.

when: Designing a game without precedent for its mechanics.

text: Add peaks to item and enemy progression where you want variety or memorable rewards; do not rely on the procedural curve alone.

why: Pure curves feel flat; variation on both sides keeps challenge shifting.

text: The worth of an item or action depends on its net effect on the anchor stat, not on its face value.
when: valuing items in a multi-stat system
why: Converting every effect to the anchor reveals the true value of each option.

text: The highest total output and the highest output per cost can come from different configurations, so both must be checked.
when: When optimizing tower placement under a budget, with both raw total damage and damage per cost as goals

text: Let heavier moves deal more damage and lighter moves less, so the weight of an attack is reflected in the numbers.
when: when assigning damage values to attacks in a combat game
why: Damage that matches attack weight makes the attack feel more substantial

text: Perfectly regular, predictable progression makes the challenge feel constant, so players grow bored; small deviations from the curve create surprise.
when: PvE item and enemy progression
why: Predictable progression removes surprise and memorable moments

text: Applying a level-based multiplier to only one damage source let that character grow faster than the intended progression curve, with the multiplier increasing itself.
when: When adding multipliers tied to growing stats.
why: A scaling bonus that feeds back into its own source creates an unintended positive loop.

text: In digital games, needlessly large numbers make low-end values trivial and therefore worthless.
when: Digital games with large values
why: Small rewards become negligible against huge totals.

text: If most options are mundane and a few are far stronger, the mundane ones become junk.
why: Play concentrates on a handful of options, leaving the rest disregarded and discarded by players.

text: Adjusting unit counts or costs may not change the behavior you target; a new system such as an economic drain may be needed.
when: a behavior persists after numeric tuning
why: Numbers alone may not alter the incentives driving the behavior.

text: Choosing numbers on wildly different scales, such as life in the thousands, makes conversions messy and breaks cross-mechanic relationships.
why: Converting between mismatched quantities needs awkward arithmetic and rounding, which breaks the interplay between systems.

text: 1) Identify nearby resources that are limited and distant ones that are effectively unlimited. 2) Defend supply lines to the distant sources. 3) Attack enemy gatherers while they are exposed.
when: Maps mix limited nearby and unlimited distant resources
why: Early control of the distant supply decides long-term income.

text: State every cost and benefit as a number before comparing objects.
why: Costs and benefits must be numeric so that cost curves and their intersections can reveal how objects relate.

text: Plan for power creep in any game with repeated expansions by building each new curve around the current best options.
when: game receives repeated expansions
why: New content must be viable against prior best options, so each release lands slightly above the curve and the cycle repeats.

text: Whether a game shows its numbers or hides them, those numbers must be designed.
Analyze a game's number progression to determine which curve type it follows.
Decide early whether all options are equally overpowered (still tunable) or none are, since this fixes the range of starting figures.
when: When first setting numbers for a game with no playtest or analytics data yet
why: If everything is uniformly overpowered, the whole set can still be tuned down together and kept comparable.

text: Score partial damage as the damaged percentage of the unit's cost, and score a destroyed unit as its full cost.
when: building payoffs for unit-versus-unit fights with resource costs

text: Apply a maximum velocity to the ship's velocity vector as a catchall against runaway speed, choosing the limit mainly for pragmatic reasons.
when: ship velocity can grow without bound under thrust
why: Without a cap, accumulated thrust can push speed to unplayable levels; very high or low limits slightly change feel.

text: Making actions such as moves, questions, or turns a limited resource forces players to plan so they do not waste potential actions.
when: Turn-based or question-limited games where each action has a budget
why: A finite action budget turns every action into a decision with an opportunity cost.

text: Action point systems charge one, two, or no points per action depending on its complexity, and some games do not use time this way at all.
Abundant resources lose value, and resources without utility become merely curious finds.
When the goal is elimination through zero-sum transfers, a positive sum economy can prolong play, because wealth keeps growing while transfers slowly remove players.
when: when victory requires eliminating opponents from a growing economy
why: Total wealth grows faster than transfers can eliminate players, so the endgame stretches out.

text: A fast-firing weapon can exhaust a fixed ammo supply within seconds, so sustained damage depends on ammo supply rather than peak output.
when: When a weapon's fire rate is high and its ammo supply is limited
why: Rapid fire empties the finite ammo store fast, so peak output cannot be held for long.

text: Adding power cards by removing action cards keeps deck size fixed but reduces the deck's number of action cards.
when: when rebalancing by trading action cards for power cards

text: 1) Find the maximum resource gained per turn from the drop rules. 2) Estimate the share of resource cards in the deck. 3) Compute the expected turn each resource unit arrives. 4) Set costs so later units cost more.
when: deriving a starting cost curve for a resource-based card game
why: units that arrive later on average are worth more

text: Building that spends resources to raise future production is a weak sink long term, since the builds pay for themselves.
why: Such builds boost output enough to recoup their cost, so they stop draining the economy over time.

text: MAU (monthly active users) counts unique or returning users active in a month; it equals DAU if the same people play daily, and high churn makes it much larger.
Retention rate equals 100% minus churn and measures how long players stay engaged; it is a key performance indicator, especially for free-to-play games.
why: Players' self-reported fun is biased and a poor predictor, so retention serves as a measurable proxy for engagement.

text: Most players follow the path of least resistance and leave default settings unchanged; only a minority of power users adjust them.
when: Designing default settings for a game.
why: Players rarely explore menus, so defaults effectively define the experience for most players.

text: Players grow frustrated when they feel no closer to an answer.
when: Puzzles offering only right-or-wrong feedback
why: Lack of perceived progress removes motivation to continue

text: Players retell surprising or interesting game moments to others, and sharing recorded play sessions is a common way they do so.
when: Game events are interesting enough to recount
why: Good games generate sequences of events so interesting that people feel compelled to relay them to others.

text: Anticipation for a sequel comes partly from wanting to re-enter a familiar world, not only from curiosity about its new plot.
why: Players bond with the world itself, which they can revisit and reshape, so excitement attaches to returning there.

text: Players resume play after unknown gaps, and games usually ignore how much time has passed.
when: When a player resumes a game after an unknown break of hours or days

text: If core mechanics hold playtesters' interest, the design is considered solid.
when: When testing a prototype with playtesters.
why: A prototype isolates a few mechanics so their function can be judged without polish or full features.

text: Players of light-story games expect short sessions and rarely become absorbed in a plot, so story and gameplay must be established quickly.
when: the opening of a light-story game
why: Short sessions leave little time for slow story setup to pay off.

text: Revealing hidden information produces the same emotional shift as an actual change in the player's situation.
when: When information is withheld and later disclosed.
why: The unconscious registers a reveal as an equivalent change in value.

text: Certain players never master a demanding mechanic and quit, and others end up puzzled and annoyed.
when: mechanics that demand learning and retrying
why: Understanding a mechanic demands attention spent on instructions, errors and repeated attempts, which some players cannot sustain.

text: Players given the option to refuse objectives or ignore allies still choose a fast, insistent core action when it is more compelling than the alternatives.
when: the core action is fast and insistently presented
why: the action's immediate pull outweighs the freedom to refuse

text: Highly skilled players may sit motionless while their minds search the space of possibilities, and the quality of that search makes the activity engaging.
when: Expert play in a deliberative board game such as high-level chess.
why: The internal decision process, searching possible moves and anticipating responses, carries the emotional engagement even when the body is still.

text: Players may keep playing a game long after they have become bored with it, because motivation mechanisms persist without enjoyment.
when: games with strong motivation loops but weak fulfillment
why: Wanting continues even when liking has faded.

text: Rewards released in increments for consistent play over real time encourage players to return regularly.
when: rewards are tied to regular play over real time
why: each return brings a new increment

text: Scarcity by time or count pressures hesitant buyers into quick decisions.
why: Scarcity creates urgency

text: Well-balanced games can feel unfair to newcomers, since those players lack the skill needed to use the balancing strategies that keep play fair.
when: When the balancing strategies need execution skill that newer players have not yet built.
why: Newcomers see only the surface of the game, lacking the skill to execute the counters that make it balanced.

text: Completion is the satisfaction of finishing a goal, such as collecting all items or clearing a level.
Cycle time is how long a processor takes to receive one input and generate one result.
Incentives can be contingent on engagement, completion, or performance; non-contingent incentives are given regardless of behavior.
Retention indicates whether players appreciate a game, but it is too coarse a measure for most specific UX issues.
Lacking a re-onboarding plan is linked to increased player churn.
Closure can come from a failed session if the episode feels satisfying, but this is hard to design.
Information linked to familiar knowledge, or that is simple, organized, meaningful, or image-based, is retained better than complex, messy, or word-only content.
Completion can be made nearly unattainable on purpose, as with gacha collections.
Paid user acquisition has been costly, at upwards of $2.50 per paying player, so organically acquired players are valuable.
when: Mobile F2P user acquisition at the time of writing

text: Recoverable penalties, such as lost hit points, feel small, while irrecoverable losses, such as lost levels, cost far more play time and feel much larger.
why: Penalties that cannot be restored are perceived as costlier.

text: Stable active player counts can hide high churn when new arrivals replace departing players.
Completing and balancing a game usually adds fun, but the original spark can fade, so refinement must recover it.
when: When a game is already functional, complete and balanced and is being polished.
why: The finishing work can dilute the appeal the core gameplay had at the start, which needs deliberate restoring.

text: Reward players for returning rather than penalizing them for leaving.
when: In free-to-play games that depend on players returning regularly.
why: Rewarding returns secures loyalty without the coercion that penalizing absence introduces.

text: Rewards that vanish after a short deadline or require cumulative login days punish missed days and create fear of missing out.
when: When a reward expires quickly or needs many cumulative login days.
why: Missed rewards push players to feel pressure to return rather than to enjoy play

text: Discomfort accumulates over long sessions, so home play that often runs past an hour needs more comfort work than short sessions.
when: planning VR session length
why: Short timed sessions keep mild motion discomfort tolerable, whereas extended play gives that discomfort time to build.

text: Control feels continuous only when the game responds steadily at about 100 ms or better, because the player's processors run concurrently and can change input roughly every 240 ms.
when: In real-time games where the player expects immediate control response.
why: Gaps in responsiveness break the flow of control even when averages look fine.

text: Meaningful material, repetition across varied contexts, and deeper processing all slow the rate at which memorized information is forgotten.
when: When a game's learning material is meaningful and reinforced by the game itself.
why: Arbitrary material without purpose or memory aids fades fastest, while linking new information to familiar knowledge preserves it.

text: Depth adds complexity and confusion, which can cause frustration, loss of control and autonomy, and churn, while a lack of depth makes a game boring and also loses players.
when: When deciding which features to keep as a game's feature set grows.

text: Too few decisions bring boredom within seconds, while too many overflow the mind and break flow.
when: When tuning moment-to-moment decision pacing rather than overall skill-versus-challenge averages.
why: Each decision holds the mind only briefly, so new decisions must keep arriving at the right rate.

text: Requiring a set number of defeats before a reward drops spreads the payoff across repeated encounters with that enemy.
when: When every enemy can grant a valued reward that needs many defeats.
why: Each encounter moves the player toward a visible prize, turning repeated fights into progress.

text: F2P designers funnel as many players as possible into the game, then steer them toward monetizing.
when: When rising difficulty pushes non-paying players toward paid shortcuts.
why: Players who spend most matter most, so clearing out non-spenders quickly lets designers focus on them.

text: Prestige resets lower virtual skill and power but grant a permanent stacking bonus that speeds later progress.
when: Idle games with prestige systems.
why: Progress slows once rewards run out, so resetting restores fast early gains that the permanent bonus keeps accelerating.

text: A craving for novelty drives game purchases, and game hardware loses value quickly as newer hardware appears.
why: Curiosity favors what is new over proven quality, so novelty outweighs tested worth in what people choose.

text: Losing a life in a level resets that level's coins, enemies and timer, so the player gets another attempt at collecting value.
when: Lives reset progress on failure
why: Resetting the level restores the value pool the player can collect.

text: Fear of loss depends on two factors: the size of the potential loss and its probability.
why: Expected loss combines magnitude and likelihood.

text: Rewards every few minutes make long grinding periods feel shorter, so collect-and-kill loops can hide repetitive effort.
when: quest loops in fast action games
why: Frequent small payoffs keep the player feeling advanced, so the repetition behind them registers less.

text: Frequent reward drops keep players on a continuous high of acquisition, so the rate of rewards strongly shapes how rich the play feels.
when: When designing loot or reward systems with artificial wealth.
why: Rewards arriving often sustain the feeling of getting rich more than narrative or challenge does.

text: Churn is the percentage of players who leave within a time unit and are replaced by new players.
why: Equal active-user counts can hide whether the same people stay or are constantly replaced.

text: Track session length, how often players return, and how long accounts stay active before they stop returning.
Using loss aversion to push engagement feels controlling because it pressures players to play.
why: Pressuring players to engage with loss-aversion hooks is felt as controlling because it requires them to play, which can erode intrinsic motivation.

text: Taking away earned points is rarely used because players feel their earned points have been cheapened.
when: Considering penalties that subtract score.
why: Players value points they have earned, so removing them feels unfair.

text: Ignoring time and money when analyzing a game's challenge is a mistake, since in many games they matter as much as skill and luck.
when: In games that involve character progression, such as RPGs
why: Players can trade time spent grinding or money spent for power, so their survival depends on those as well as skill and luck.

text: 1) Align story, gameplay, and player power so they reach a satisfying conclusion together at the end of the progression.

Test these possible exit causes: 1) a run of consecutive losses 2) season or tournament end dates 3) repeated sightings of the same few characters 4) weak or abrasive teammates 5) a rank or level where play turns rote 6) account age when interest fades.
when: Investigating why players stop returning
why: Each candidate cause is a specific pattern that might push players to leave, and each must be checked against player behavior rather than assumed.

text: Treat player quitting as possible evidence of a design problem, and investigate and iterate the design rather than assuming players are at fault.
why: players owe the designer nothing

text: Closure needs a chance to reflect and an inability to return to earlier phases, which loss or relief can supply.
when: When designing an ending or phase transition
why: Reflection and no return make the player able to leave the game behind

text: Use the forgetting curve as a baseline when estimating how much players will forget between play sessions.
when: planning teaching across sessions
why: Memory of information decays over time, so the curve gives a starting estimate of how much is forgotten between sessions.

text: Shield low-level players by cancelling incentives to attack them, or by establishing protected starting zones.
why: Players who spend more gain power, so without gates higher-level players can exploit newcomers, which removes the incentive to attack the weak.

text: Avoid removing external rewards later, and avoid reducing their value when a player disengages.
why: Removing or shrinking a reward after a missed day makes the loss feel punishing, which can weaken the player's intrinsic motivation to play.

text: Treat a reward as the launch point for the next goal, not as the end of the activity.
why: Rewards are feedback that players use to pursue their goals, so a reward that is treated as an ending stops driving continued play.

text: Check whether rewards are too generous or penalties too harsh, since outcome values should leave player choices interesting.
when: when tuning rewards and penalties

text: Monetization should respect players' time and money, and players who disengage should not be punished.
why: Punishing disengagement and using dark patterns exploit players, so monetization must respect their time and money.

text: For each reward, check whether it is useful, romantic, or tied to the story, and whether its timing encourages continued play.
when: Auditing a prototype's rewards

text: Lives are usually treated as more-is-better with no downside, but too many make the game easy and too few make it hard; lives shape how cautiously players take risks.
when: Setting starting resources such as lives
why: Lives set how costly a failure is, so too many make the game easy and too few make it hard, changing how cautiously players act.

text: Always-rewarded behavior rises quickly but extinguishes quickly, while variable-ratio rewards take longest to establish but best sustain behavior over time.
when: Choosing a reward schedule for a repeated action.
why: Variable-ratio schedules sustain behavior because the random timing of rewards keeps players responding, while always-rewarded behavior stops quickly once rewards end.

text: Scarce lives with no save game raise stakes, but losing all lives restarts the whole game, so a run must finish in one session.
Daily return rewards, such as free-to-play chests, encourage players to come back, but they raise ethical concerns that must be weighed.
Market prices fluctuate because new items enter the market, purchases change supply, and the set of logged-in buyers changes.
when: In player-driven markets where players buy and sell items
why: Supply changes with each listing or purchase, and the pool of logged-in buyers changes over time, so prices shift.

text: In player-driven economies, prices converge quickly on supply-and-demand values, so a rarer item of equal play value trades for more, even without circulation data.
when: Player-driven economies with items of equal play value but different rarity

text: With fixed prices on overlapping items, players must decide how many is enough, so diminishing returns become a deliberate choice.
when: overlapping items keep the same price
why: each extra item adds less value

text: An anchor is a single reference value, such as a currency, that lets every good be priced and compared with one number instead of countless pairwise exchange rates.
In a prestige economy, goods cost real money but do not affect gameplay beyond status, and they are often limited edition.
Market price is the point where supply and demand curves intersect, and any shift in either curve moves it.
A comparative anchor is a number or set of features that makes one choice roughly equal to another when all factors are considered.
when: options should feel fair but need not match exactly

text: A supply curve counts how many sellers will sell at a given price or higher. It rises to the right because more sellers join as price rises.
why: Each seller has a minimum acceptable price

text: A demand curve counts buyers willing to pay at least a given price. It never rises as price rises, because buyers drop out as price increases.
why: Each buyer has a maximum price they will pay

text: In a fixed-price format, the vendor lists an amount and holds it open until a purchaser appears. It is the most common video game auction format.
Sunk costs are setup expenses that must be paid before a desired item or ability becomes available.
A market segment is a cluster of players grouped by hobbies, prior ability, spending level, social background, device access, or geographic region.
Game values such as damage, costs and XP gains only have meaning relative to other values in the economy, and a number strong at one stage can be weak at another.
Cost is not only financial: rarity and other access limits count as costs, so an item rarely found in a typical playthrough is effectively more expensive.
Raising both currency quantity and unit price is a clear price rise, not a hidden one.
Prestige goods rely on visibility, limited quantity, or both, and their prices follow supply and demand.
Prestige virtual goods have reached $10,000 or more, and designers still do not know the upper price limit, though their sense of buyer tolerance has improved.
Exclusive choices lock out options in tech trees, competing quests, faction-limited decks, and faction-specific resource types, where adding a faction makes resources harder to gather.
Portals often let players try a game free for one hour, then charge around $20 by credit card to keep playing.
Mechanics costed similarly can still play very differently, so equal costs should not be assumed correct and the imbalance is expected.
when: Early playtesting of card or mechanic costs.
why: Mechanics with the same cost can differ greatly in power, so equal costs do not guarantee balance.

text: In board games, expect bigger price swings with three players than with six; if stable prices matter, add rules for smaller groups.
when: When designing a board game where stable trade prices matter for small player counts.

text: Benchmark prices against competing and trending games, using bulk currency purchases as the usual comparison; prices often match across many games, especially from one publisher.
when: Setting initial market prices for a free-to-play game
why: Competitors' price points establish a baseline for what the market currently tolerates.

text: Designers aim to shrink the low-spending segment, because big spenders barely react to price.
why: Heavy spenders are largely unaffected by higher prices, so they become the focus rather than low spenders.

text: Cutting a price is simple, whereas increases provoke backlash, especially as public price history spreads through communities.
when: Launching a free-to-play game and deciding its initial price points
why: Price history becomes public among networked players as communities grow, so past increases are visible.

text: Prestige pricing has a window: above it nobody buys, below it so many buyers own the item that it loses prestige.
The skill needed to execute a strategy should match its effectiveness, so players climb toward the most rewarding peaks.
why: Strategies with stronger outcomes demand more skill to execute, so their varying payoffs are kept in balance.

text: Barriers have a huge effect on profitability, so exploit them wherever you can.
when: judging whether a market is worth entering
why: Protected markets are much more profitable

text: A game built for one audience can feel unapproachable to others; this is as designed, not unbalanced, so judge it against its own audience.
when: A game designed for one target demographic's level of challenge and pressure
why: Pressure suited to one demographic is unsuitable for another, so the mismatch follows from the chosen audience.

text: When a target quantity must be hit exactly, the lowest cost-per-unit pack alone may not reach it, so smaller packs can be needed.
when: buyers need an exact amount from fixed pack sizes

text: An option with a lower stat sum can be compensated with a stronger intrinsic stat, extra abilities, a gentler XP curve, or raised stats.
when: a starting option falls below the anchor sum

text: Base costs on the maximum damage in the range; average or minimum damage can be used instead.
when: Pricing damage ranges

text: Compare how similar games price the same kind of extra; a consistent pattern across them is a standard to understand.
when: Pricing new item extras
why: Shared conventions reflect what players expect.

text: Developers may weight team rating changes by each player's contribution, such as activity in a shooter.
when: team games where contribution varies widely
why: A passive player adds less to the team's result than an active one, so equal weighting would misstate contribution.

text: When all options are similar, begin with 1.5× one option's value, then adjust.
when: all options have similar value

text: With partial foreknowledge, price a bundle between the single-part price and the sum of parts, scaled by how certain players can be.
when: Players are only partly sure which component of a bundle they will need
why: Certainty about needing each part determines how much of the combined value a player actually gets.

text: Effects tied to a target's state or composition can be worthless in most contexts and decisive in others, so their cost should reflect the range of their value, not one case.
when: Effects whose usefulness depends on target state, such as healing or count-based damage
why: Value swings from near zero to decisive with circumstances

text: Market price depends on demand and availability: high demand with low supply usually raises price, while low demand with high supply usually lowers it.
when: Comparing demand and supply levels in a market

text: Easy distribution lowers barriers and floods the market with products, driving prices toward free, so easy store access does not mean easy profit.
when: a platform makes publishing or store access very easy
why: Supply rises faster than demand; access lowers barriers and increases competition.

text: Demand for a resource shifts permanently when balance changes, new content, newly found strategies or growing player wealth change how much players want it or can pay.
In player-dynamic economies, players set transaction prices, but supply and demand still bound what is reasonable: items priced too high go unsold, and trades demanding too much are rejected.
when: Player-dynamic economies where players trade or auction items among themselves
why: Auction prices are set by supply and demand rather than fixed by the designer.

text: Fewer players produce larger price swings, because each player controls a bigger share of supply and demand.
when: Player-dynamic economies with a small number of players
why: Each participant's trades weigh more heavily in a small market.

text: Shopkeepers buying at steady prices keep newcomers employed, while high-level item offers are less competitive, pushing trade toward player-to-player exchange.
when: Persistent worlds with a shop and player market
why: Fixed shop prices give a guaranteed income floor that player markets cannot easily undercut at high levels.

text: When currency is sold in bundles at non-round rates, players find it harder to track real spending.
when: When a game sells in-game currency for real money.
why: Unclear exchange rates make the real cost of purchases less visible.

text: A high initial price with fixed-duration percent-off sales keeps the list price constant, so players are not surprised when a sale ends.
when: Testing which price earns the most, using percent-off sales in a free-to-play game
why: Sales have a fixed duration, so players anticipate their end and are motivated to buy before it.

text: Per-player pricing shows different prices to different players: non-spenders may see better offers, while likely buyers, especially for new items without history, may pay more.
when: A free-to-play game aiming to monetize more of its players
why: Likely purchasers buy regardless of cost, so higher prices can be charged to them.

text: Doubling an item's cost while doubling all rewards makes the item look pricier but leaves the real time and effort cost unchanged.
why: Prices are felt relative to the rewards that earn them.

text: A peak's high cost raises its sell-back value where selling is allowed, which is typically half the purchase value.
when: Game allows selling items
why: Sell value scales with purchase cost.

text: When each purchase of the same generator costs more, players are pushed toward a broader mix of generators.
when: Repeated purchases raise cost
why: Escalating cost makes diversifying cheaper than stacking one type.

text: Raising one substitute's price can increase demand and sales for the other, while lowering one substitute's price draws buyers away from the other.
when: A price on one of two substitute goods changes
why: Buyers switch between goods that replace each other

text: Complementary goods have demand that rises and falls together, so owning some pieces raises demand for the rest.
when: Goods are used together, such as matching gear pieces
why: Owning part of a set makes the remaining parts more valuable

text: With unchanged demand and supply, prices stay constant. Lower demand or higher supply lowers prices, while higher demand or lower supply raises them. Opposite-direction shifts have indeterminate effects when both move the same way.
when: Demand or supply curves shift

text: In fixed-price sales, the seller's price choice drives efficiency: a high price lets the top bidder pay their maximum, while a very low price lets even the lowest bidder buy and the seller earns far less.
when: Setting a fixed price for an item
why: A buyer whose maximum willingness to pay exceeds the posted price will buy, so the price itself decides who gets the item.

text: Limitations and drawbacks act as negative costs that discount an item, such as a class restriction reducing value by a percentage or a wielder's elemental weakness.
when: valuing restricted or penalized items
why: Each drawback lowers the price the item should carry.

text: A switching cost reduces the diminishing-return effect in proportion to its size, because overlapping items matter less when switching is costly.
The easier a player can switch between objects, the less value within-object versatility has.
when: The player can swap between objects freely
why: Specialists can be used whenever they fit the situation

text: As a player collects more objects, each new one's value falls: a fully optimizing player covers all targets with a small set, so extra objects have diminishing returns and should cost less.
when: The player collects many objects covering overlapping targets
why: Earlier objects already provide most of the added benefit

text: The payoff of a trade changes with unit cost, replaceability, and location; losing a costly unit near one's base is far worse than losing it mid-map.
when: strategy games with unit trades and base proximity
why: Replacement cost and strategic stakes vary with cost and position.

text: Lucrative niches draw in developers, which heightens rivalry and erodes returns, so the market tends toward a state in which every niche yields roughly equal profit.
when: a segment proves lucrative
why: Competitors are drawn in by visible profit, eroding it over time.

text: Protection from a color is worth 1 point per instance.
Net value equals benefits minus costs: zero means on the curve, positive means above it, and negative means below it.
when: Comparing a card against the cost curve.

text: Expected cost of a deferred purchase equals the chance of guessing right times the single-part price, plus the chance of guessing wrong times the sum of all parts.
when: the buyer can buy the second part after learning the guess was wrong

text: A game card can be modeled as an equation that sets its costs equal to its benefits, with each cost and benefit as an unknown to solve for.
when: When reverse-engineering the original balance of a card from its known costs and benefits.

text: Five levers offset diminishing returns in item sets: repeat-purchase cost changes, fixed costs, rising income, acquisition-based costs, and switching costs; they can be combined.
when: items overlap in coverage and players will likely acquire most of them

text: Market models are simplified attempts to chart a complex system, and most real market factors such as disasters, memes, politics and chance lie outside any model.
when: using a market model to predict game success
why: Real markets are nonlinear and driven by many unmodeled forces.

text: Reducing F2P pricing to a single number ignores the blend of market data, rival analysis, A/B tests, audience targeting, and flexibility it requires.
Treating an exclusive choice as costless because no resource is spent ignores the lost future options, which are a real cost.
when: an action limits later choices
why: A committed choice makes later resource gathering harder, since each added faction or resource type raises the difficulty of getting what's needed.

text: Returns, budget overruns, withheld approvals, and schedule slips can push small publishers out of business.
why: Costs from returned stock and overruns pile up, while the three-to-six-month sales window leaves little time to recover them.

text: Comparing tools by raw power without context is meaningless, because a tool's value depends on the opponent it faces.
why: Each tool's usefulness shifts with the situation and with the other tools held, so no single ranking holds.

text: Assuming the market is permanently fixed ignores the chance that a newcomer will overturn a dominant title.
when: judging a market with a dominant hit

text: Judging the market only by visible successes creates survivorship bias, because the many failed games are hidden from view.
when: estimating a game's odds from published examples
why: Visible winners misrepresent the true failure rate.

text: 1) Describe every stat and effect the item provides. 2) Assign each a value in the anchor currency, such as 10 gold per HP. 3) Cost special abilities such as healing, winning ties or post-elimination effects the same way. 4) Sum all values for the item's price.
when: Setting an item's price in a fixed economy as a starting point, or inventing a new item.
why: Anchoring price to stats gives a consistent baseline that testing can refine.

text: 1) Set a cost per point of damage. 2) Multiply it by the average of the damage range. 3) Apply a multiplier for each extra hit per second above the baseline. 4) Keep one operation consistent: multiply or add the rate value throughout.
when: Pricing melee weapons by damage and attack rate
why: A consistent formula makes items comparable

text: 1) List the prerequisite's immediate benefits. 2) List the later benefits it enables. 3) Price the prerequisite by the sum of both.
when: Pricing a prerequisite in a tech tree or progression chain
why: Prerequisites that look weak alone gain their value from the powerful abilities they unlock later.

text: 1) Choose a price range and step size. 2) List prices in one column. 3) Use formulas in adjacent columns for demand and supply at each price. 4) Fill down the table. 5) Chart both curves against price.
when: Modeling a market where quantity demanded falls and quantity supplied rises with price.
why: Formulas keep every value linked to the curve equations, so changes update the whole table.

text: Price items so that scarcity forces trade-offs; if players can buy everything they want, the game is unbalanced.
If a store or NPC buys an item at a set price, players will not sell it for less on the market, so that price acts as a floor.
why: A guaranteed sale to an NPC gives players an outside option, so they won't accept less from other players.

text: In a balanced in-game economy, more expensive items should also be more powerful and useful.
when: When pricing items in an in-game economy
why: Players expect price to correlate with value.

text: Test different price ranges to learn players' price tolerance and the points where they drop off.
Apply each costing rule uniformly to every matching item, for example adding a flat 10% to the cost of any resurrection effect.
when: Costing items with shared effects.
why: First-pass numbers are expected to be off, so a simple consistent formula serves as a starting point to refine.

text: In adventure-style free-to-play games, charge for access to content such as an adventure, and let power items come as rewards earned in play.
when: deciding what a paid offering should contain
why: Purchases framed as access feel heroic instead of like cheating

text: To survive a red ocean, become the largest player in the market or find a blue ocean to move into.
when: operating in a crowded market
why: Competition erodes profit for small players

text: When players buy many items from one source, let later purchases cost less, optionally framed in the story as a loyalty reward.
Price an either-or object above its most valuable option but below the sum of all options, since the player can use only one.
when: the player picks one effect from several options with known value

text: Base a sunk cost on expected value: how many units or uses a typical game produces once the prerequisite is built.
when: Estimating how many uses to spread a prerequisite cost over
why: Typical play determines how much setup is actually recovered

text: A percentage trade cost discourages large trades because its perceived size grows with the amount, while a flat fee discourages small trades and favors large ones.
For at-least-one events, count the none case instead of summing many hit-count cases, provided it is one simple combination of independent outcomes.
when: counting successes directly would need many separate cases
why: avoids summing several hit-count cases

text: Summing several dice concentrates totals near the middle, while a single die spreads results evenly across its range; with two six-sided dice 7 is common and 12 rare.
when: choosing between dice setups with equal range
why: Combining outcomes produces a bell-like distribution rather than a flat one.

text: The probability that an event does not occur equals 1 minus the probability that it occurs: P(not) = 1 − P(happens).
why: Enumerating outcomes can solve any probability problem, but this shortcut avoids listing every outcome.

text: For independent events that must all succeed, multiply their probabilities; four 10% drops in a row have chance 1/10,000.
when: events are independent, so none affects the others

text: When outcomes are equally likely, probability equals favorable outcomes divided by total possible outcomes, so it always lies between 0 and 1.
when: When the possible outcomes are equally likely
why: This gives the probability directly from counts.

text: Every probability must lie between 0 and 1; a negative or greater-than-1 result signals a calculation error.
why: Probability is a share of all possible outcomes, so it cannot be negative or exceed the whole.

text: For events that can occur together, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B); adding them directly overcounts, or enumerate outcomes.
when: events can happen together
why: Outcomes that belong to both events are counted twice when added, so the overlap must be subtracted.

text: Players and gamblers find odds less intuitive than probabilities, so expressing outcomes as odds can make a game seem fairer than it is.
when: When gambling games present payouts as odds to players

text: A conservative Markov process keeps the sum of its state vector constant, which suits values that represent a distribution or counts of game objects.
Entropy measures how much the actions in a set agree: it is 0 when all actions match and 1 when two actions are evenly split.
A flush has all five cards of one suit; a straight flush has consecutive ranks in one suit, and a royal flush is ten through ace in one suit.
Theoretical probability is the mathematically expected rate, while practical probability is the rate observed across actual trials.
A probability distribution curve plots the chance of each possible outcome, so the shape of a random result can be seen at a glance.
dN denotes a die with N faces; any device giving each integer from 1 to N equal probability counts as a die.
A count before the d means several dice are summed, and a constant after it is added, as in 2d6+1.
Rolls are independent when no past or future event influences a roll, so earlier results never change the odds of the next roll.
Probability is a value from 0 (never happens) to 1 (always happens), expressible as a decimal, fraction, or percentage.
Odds express the ratio of occurrences to non-occurrences, so a 1 on a d4 has odds of 1:3 (or 3:1 against).
The number of ways to choose k items from n distinct items when order does not matter is C(n,k) = n!/(k!(n−k)!), written COMBIN(n,k) in spreadsheets.
The number of ordered arrangements of k items chosen from n distinct items is P(n,k) = n!/(n−k)!, written PERMUT(n,k) in spreadsheets.
Independent events do not influence later outcomes, while in dependent events learning one outcome changes the probabilities of future outcomes.
Card draws are dependent only when cards are drawn without replacement, so the deck changes after each draw.
Theoretical probability equals the number of favorable outcomes divided by the total number of equally likely outcomes.
Random generators have no memory, so a streak does not make the opposite result more likely; believing a streak makes the next result hot or due is wrong.
when: trials are independent
why: each trial is independent of earlier ones

text: The entropy helper returns 0 for an empty set or a set containing a single action.
