Relatively prime frequencies reduce clashes but do not remove them; frequencies 2, 3 and 5 still coincide every 6 and every 30 frames.
When all payoffs are equal, the payoff vector is one repeated value, and since it only scales the probability column, it can be set to 1 in every position.
when: solving equal-payoff matchups

text: A hand-tuned dice outcome function can be neither increasing nor decreasing and still work well, if it creates tension through reversals of fortune.
when: designing dice-result outcomes with uneven values
why: Non-monotonic results make each roll uncertain and engaging.

text: Bingo balls, lottery balls and board game spinners can be biased by uneven paint weight or friction.
Transitive data appears in RPG shop prices and leveling, FPS weapon upgrades, life-simulation purchases, tower upgrades, trading card costs, arcade scoring, and sports salaries.
Six dice showing each face exactly once occur about 1.5% of the time, so such bonuses are rare even though every face is equally likely.
Across very many random trials, results cluster near the expected value, while short series show streaks and uneven results.
Independent rolls can be performed in any order without changing the probability that all succeed.
Standard deviation must be read relative to the mean, since the same spread is minor around a large mean but large around a small one.
Classical logic makes 'a AND b entails c' equivalent to '(a entails c) OR (b entails c)'.
Estimating probabilities is itself a skill; skilled players predict outcomes better by calculating odds.
A single random selection, such as one die roll, gives every outcome an equal chance.
Expected values of independent dice add when summed: three dice each averaging 5/3 together average 5 per roll.
In Blackjack a normal win pays 1:1, while a natural blackjack pays 3:2.
By convention 0! = 1, and factorials grow very quickly.
A full house is very unlikely in a standard five-card draw and becomes more common only when players draw more cards or have wild cards.
Opening a losing option does not change the odds of the player's first choice, so the unopened option holds all the probability the first choice lacks.
when: a host reveals one losing option among three
why: the host always reveals a losing option, so the reveal carries information

text: With three options, one prize, and a host who always reveals a losing option, switching to the remaining option wins two-thirds of the time, staying one-third.
when: the first pick is uniformly random and the host knows the prize location

text: In a shuffled 52-card deck, after one card is drawn, the chance the next card shares its rank is 3 in 51, about 1 in 17.
Five cards can be played in 5 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 120 different orders.
when: each card must be played once in sequence
why: each position in the order has one fewer choice

text: Total expected profit and percentage player advantage measure different things and can move in opposite directions, so a bigger total prize may shrink the relative edge.
Casinos spend heavily to remove equipment bias, since perceived rigging could cost them their gambling license.
Casinos use real-time statistics to tell lucky players from cheats, which is a practical deterrent.
Long-run state shares depend directly on the transition probabilities, so small probability changes can noticeably shift the steady-state mix.
when: tuning transition probabilities in a game system
why: the steady state is a function of the matrix entries

text: With one die left to roll, about four failures usually occur before a 1 appears.
when: a single die is being rerolled until it shows a 1
why: a fixed one-in-six chance per roll makes the expected wait short

text: A five-of-a-kind on the first roll of five six-sided dice is less than one in a thousand.
Going for a five-of-a-kind every turn across 13 scoring categories gives roughly a 46% chance of at least one such result.
when: a player chases the same combination in every scoring category
why: each category gives another chance of success

text: Working out why a designer chose a particular number builds balance skill.
when: When playing games whose underlying numbers are published in wikis or strategy guides

text: The card-equation method works best with many comparable objects; a dozen unrelated objects need other analysis methods.
when: When a game has many similar objects that can be compared in pairs

text: Cap early bets and raise the cap over time, so a lucky early leader cannot dominate while late hands can still be decisive.
when: in betting games with escalating stakes
why: caps stop early runaway leads while allowing a final decisive stage

text: Use the same probability-weighted sum when equally likely outcomes pay out different amounts, such as a rare large prize among small ones.
when: payouts or results differ in value
why: Multiplying each payout by its chance lets a rare large prize count in proportion to how often it occurs.

text: When one more roll could win the game outright, keep rolling despite the risk, since the immediate win chance can outweigh expected points.
when: a single roll can end the game in your favor
why: Equal expected damage can still hide unequal chances of winning outright, so win probability matters beyond the average.

text: Enumeration is practical for small outcome spaces, such as a few dice, but becomes impossible for large ones, so shortcut rules are needed then.
when: Choosing between counting and formulas
why: The number of outcomes grows exponentially with each roll.

text: Reshaping a random element's probability distribution curve can change how it feels, so test curve shapes rather than accepting the default.
when: when tuning a random element
why: The shape of the distribution determines whether randomness feels exciting or hopeless to players.

text: Intuitive estimates of multi-trial odds often differ from computed values, so calculate rather than trust intuition.
when: When estimating the chance of an outcome across many repeated rolls

text: Sum several dice when results should cluster around a middle value; use one die when every outcome should be equally likely.
when: Choosing a random generator for a stat or result
why: A single die gives each face an equal chance, while summed dice make middle totals more likely.

text: Experience with dice and card games already builds much of the intuition needed for game math.
why: The required math is basic arithmetic and simple algebra, and the concepts mirror everyday dice and card play.

text: Moderate streaks are normal over many rolls, but an extreme streak, such as twenty identical results, suggests a biased die.
when: When a streak of identical die results is extremely long, such as twenty in a row
why: A streak of twenty is astronomically unlikely for a fair die, so it points to bias.

text: For unbounded chance outcomes or infinite-state chains, simulation or truncation to the first few hundred cases or states gives an answer close enough.
when: Exact enumeration is impossible and a precise closed form is not needed.
why: Probabilities of large outcomes or far states shrink quickly, so truncation loses little.

text: For at-least-one questions, count the complement, the case where none occurs, and subtract its probability from 1.
when: When asking for the chance of drawing at least one copy of specific cards
why: the complement is often easier to count than the success cases

text: A combo needing two specific cards in a small opening hand succeeds reasonably often only with extra draws or other strategies.
when: a combo depends on two specific cards early
why: small hands rarely contain both specific cards

text: In dice-based combat, rolling more dice always improves a player's chance of winning the battle.
when: Choosing how many dice to roll in a combat exchange.
why: Extra dice give more chances to win each pairwise comparison.

text: Prefer copy-and-fill over hand-written rows for large outcome tables, since no formula is needed and only copying and filling is involved.
when: a probability formula seems too complicated to write directly
why: Each extra die takes the same copy-and-fill effort, so the approach scales to any size.

text: In a short race, a source that deals rare large hits can beat a steady source with the same average damage; as the race lengthens, win rates converge toward even.
when: two attackers have equal expected damage per turn
why: variance decides short races, while averages dominate long ones

text: Under ante, a deck built from many purchased decks risks its best card, and a winner takes a more valuable card, which limits how far purchasing power helps.
when: players play for ante
why: Under ante, a winner takes a more valuable card, so the buyer of many decks gambles the best card.

text: Uncertainty creates surprises, and surprises are a big reason players enjoy games, so chance is central to enjoyment.
Tracking cards already played is a skill, because each revealed card changes the odds of the cards that follow.
when: When revealed cards change the odds of cards still to come, as in blackjack.

text: In blackjack, optimal play depends on whether high or low cards remain in the deck, shifting odds toward the player without guaranteeing a win.
when: Games where hidden information changes the odds of an action.
why: Remaining deck composition alters the probability of each outcome.

text: Removing a card face-down without looking gives no new information, so the probabilities for the remaining cards do not change.
why: Probabilities for unseen cards are computed from what is known, and an unseen removal adds nothing to that knowledge.

text: Each revealed card adds information, which changes the probabilities for the cards still unseen; probabilities depend on what is known rather than only on what is physically removed.
when: When drawn cards are not replaced and each card is seen as it is drawn.
why: Each revealed card changes what is known, and probabilities for unseen cards are calculated from that known information.

text: When every initial deal is equally likely, a player's win chance equals the fraction of all deals in which they win.
when: Deals are dealt uniformly at random and outcomes are fully determined by the deal and play choices
why: Uniform likelihood turns win probability into a simple count over the enumerated deal space.

text: Frequent small losses with occasional modest wins and no large unexpected losses keep players engaged in chance-based games.
why: Players accept minor setbacks readily but react strongly against large unexpected losses.

text: Repeated reload-and-retry turns low-probability outcomes into near-certain ones, undermining carefully balanced odds.
when: When outcomes are re-randomized after every save reload.
why: Every reload grants a fresh attempt, so repeated retries make a rare success close to certain.

text: Extra setbacks such as chutes usually lengthen games, while extra shortcuts such as ladders shorten them; a setback placed just before a large shortcut can instead shorten games.
when: tuning the number and placement of track shortcuts and setbacks
why: each element changes the path to the finish, and placement changes the net effect

text: Additional rerolls raise the chance of reaching a target combination, and with enough rolls the chance of reaching it passes 50%, making that roll count the median.
when: a player chases a combination with repeated rerolls
why: each reroll gives another independent chance to improve the hand

text: When an enemy spreads its attacks evenly over several targets, each target is attacked less often, so its armor class matters proportionally less than attack bonus.
A specific face on a fair n-sided die has probability 1/n; a 1 on a d4 has probability 1/4, or 25%.
when: For a fair die where each face is equally likely.
why: Equal likelihood of each face means the n faces share the total probability evenly.

text: Rolling n dice with s faces, or flipping n coins, gives s^n equally likely ordered results; ten coin flips give 1024.
when: dice are distinguishable

text: Entropy is the sum over actions of minus p_i times log2 p_i, where p_i is the proportion of examples with action i.
The probability of first entering a final state at a given transition equals its cumulative probability minus the previous transition's cumulative probability.
why: Cumulative probability includes earlier entries, so subtracting the previous value isolates entries made on this step.

text: The mean number of transitions to a final state is the sum of each transition number multiplied by its first-entry probability, computed as an array formula.
when: When computing the average number of steps before a final state is reached.
why: Expected value weights each outcome by its probability and sums the results.

text: Probabilities of all distinct, non-overlapping outcomes sum to exactly 1; any other sum signals an arithmetic error.
when: Verifying probability calculations.
why: Complete outcome sets must cover all possibilities once.

text: The chance of rolling no six in five rolls of a die is (5/6)^5, about 40%.
A wager with expected value of -1/18 per dollar loses about 5.6 cents for every dollar wagered.
For a d6 where a 1 wipes a turn total X, one more roll changes expected points by (20 - X)/6.
when: When a roll of 1 erases points accumulated earlier in the same turn.
why: Each of six equally likely faces contributes its gain or loss, and the averages combine into one expected value.

text: A house edge between about 0.25% and 30% is workable; below 0.25% is not profitable enough, and above 30% players will not tolerate it.
when: tuning casino-style rules
why: Below the lower bound the game is unprofitable, and above the upper bound players will reject it.

text: Three six-sided dice produce totals from 3 to 18, with values around 10 and 11 most common and extremes rare.
why: Middle totals can be formed by many dice combinations, while extreme totals can be formed by very few.

text: The expected value of a die equals the sum of all its faces, counting repeats, divided by the number of faces; for a fair d6 this is 3.5.
when: For a fair die where every face has equal chance.
why: With equal chances, the mean is the plain average of the face values.

text: The number of outcomes for several dice equals faces per die raised to the number of dice: five six-sided dice give 7,776 and seven 4-sided dice give 4^7 = 16,384.
when: Judging whether enumeration is practical.
why: Each die can show any face independently, so the number of outcomes multiplies across dice.

text: The probability that n independent attempts all fail equals (1 − p)^n, where p is the success chance per attempt.
A Poker full house occurs in 3,744 of 2,598,960 five-card hands, a probability of about 0.00144.
why: Probability is the number of qualifying hands divided by the total number of hands.

text: With switch-offer chance R after a right first pick and W after a wrong one, staying wins 1/3 and switching wins 2/3 times W plus 1/3 times (1 - R).
when: a host offers a switch with pick-dependent probabilities
why: The player can always keep the first pick, so the offer's value is compared against that fallback.

text: A two-dice sum's expected count in 36 rolls equals 36 times its probability, giving 1 for sums of 2 or 12 and 5 for sums of 6 or 8.
when: two six-sided dice

text: A one-attacker versus one-defender battle is won by the attacker with probability 15/36, and two attackers versus one defender gives about 0.754 for the attacker.
when: Estimating attacker win chance in a one-exchange-at-a-time dice combat.
why: These exact values anchor the recursive odds for larger battles.

text: In a push-your-luck turn, each roll either adds its face value to a turn total or, on a losing face, wipes the whole total; the player may bank it by stopping.
Dice-driven track games can be cast as a Markov chain: one state per reachable square, with each turn applying a transition matrix built from die-roll probabilities.
when: analysing a dice-driven track game
why: the matrix turns the board rules into a Markov chain that can be computed exactly

text: Adding per-attempt chances to estimate the chance of at least one success is a common error that overstates the result and can exceed 100%.
Adding probabilities of events that must all occur, instead of multiplying independent ones, gives impossible totals, and forgetting to subtract overlaps counts them twice.
when: Combining probabilities.
why: Event type determines whether to add or multiply.

text: Requiring an exact combination of distance and turn can make a plan impossible, because available animations rarely match the needed values precisely.
when: Planning with discrete animations
why: Each animation covers fixed amounts, so a needed move may not be exactly achievable

text: Multiplying a single die roll by a number does not simulate several dice, and it removes possible totals such as odd numbers.
why: Multiplying one die's result by a constant keeps only that die's multiples, so totals such as 7 cannot occur.

text: Double-counting is the main trap in enumerating card hands, so each hand must belong to exactly one category.
why: Some hands satisfy two category definitions at once, such as four-of-a-kind also containing two pairs.

text: Checking all eight neighboring cells registers every cross-cell attack twice.
when: When a grid-based combat check scans all eight neighboring cells for each unit.
why: Each adjacent pair is visited from both of its cells.

text: A simple average of outcomes is wrong when outcomes have unequal probabilities; each result must be weighted by its probability.
when: outcomes differ in probability
why: a simple average treats every outcome as equally likely

text: Treat each die as distinguishable when counting arrangements; ignoring which die shows which value miscounts the favorable total.
Probability errors usually come from miscounting favorable or total outcomes, since those counts are not always obvious.
when: Calculating probability by formula
why: A wrong count gives a wrong probability even when the formula is correct.

text: Multiplying probabilities of events that affect each other gives wrong results, so confirm independence before multiplying.
when: when events may influence each other

text: Counting arrangements is error-prone, so verify the arrangement count for each case before multiplying.
Treating averages from revenue diagrams as fixed numbers is a mistake, since actual deals are detailed and vary.
when: using revenue split figures
why: Real contracts differ from typical averages

text: Designers overuse six-sided dice from familiarity, though the d6 is popular mainly because cubes are cheap to manufacture.
why: Novices use it out of familiarity; six does not divide 100 evenly and people do not count in base six.

text: When stating odds, specify whether they are true odds or payout odds, since the two differ.
why: Odds ratios are unintuitive, so they are rarely used for randomness and mostly appear as gambling payouts.

text: Adding separate single-card counts without subtracting draws missing both cards double-counts draws and can produce impossible probability values.
when: When finding the chance of at least one of two specific cards, and both can be drawn together.
why: Draws missing both cards appear in each single-card count, so they are double-counted and must be subtracted once.

text: Marked or tampered cards or tiles break the usual probability calculations, so computed odds no longer match actual outcomes.
when: A random set may be marked or manipulated
why: The calculations rely on equal likelihood, which tampering removes.

text: Double counting in dice outcome tallies is the main risk; repeated arrangements must be divided by their symmetry factor.

1) Describe the remaining deck as a state of counts of each card type. 2) Recurse on the chance of drawing each type next. 3) Stop with the target outcome when the run condition is met. 4) Sum the branch probabilities.
when: computing the chance of a streak in a finite shuffled sequence
why: the state space is too large to enumerate by hand, so a program must fill it automatically

text: 1) Put row indexes 0 to 16383 in column A. 2) In column B use MOD(A,4)+1. 3) For each later column, divide the index by the next power of 4, apply FLOOR, take MOD 4, and add 1. 4) Fill each formula down.
when: Generating every outcome of seven 4-sided dice without copy-and-fill blocks.

text: 1) Put one RANDBETWEEN formula in each cell of a column. 2) Fill the formula down until the column holds one cell per die. 3) Use SUM on that column to get the total.
when: Rolling large numbers of dice, such as 100 six-sided dice.
why: Fill-down of one cell per die is easier than writing many separate calls when the number of dice is large.

text: 1) Define each hand category precisely. 2) Count the card sets in each category with COMBIN or PERMUT.
when: computing hand probabilities from a deck

text: 1) Count rows with each maximum run length using COUNTIF. 2) Divide each count by the total number of outcomes. 3) Check that the probabilities sum to 1.
1) Create a state machine with labeled states and transitions. 2) Mark the initial and final states. 3) Give each transition a probability. 4) Describe in plain language what the machine does.
when: designing a probability-driven game system for analysis
why: explicit states and probabilities make the system solvable

text: Subtract one card's equation from a near-identical card's equation to isolate the value of the single stat that differs between them.
when: two cards differ in only one stat or cost
why: Equations that differ in only one term leave a single unknown after combining, so the difference isolates it.

text: 1) Assign each required result to its own slot. 2) Count the choices left for each slot, shrinking the pool as values are used. 3) Multiply the counts. 4) Divide by the total number of possible outcomes.
when: each die or slot must show a different specified value
why: multiplying choices counts ordered arrangements

text: 1) Write a loop over every combination of die faces. 2) Sum each combination's total. 3) Count totals meeting the target condition. 4) Divide that count by the total number of combinations.
when: too many dice outcomes to count by hand
why: gives an exact answer by brute force

text: 1) For each pack slot, multiply the chance that slot holds a given tier by 1 divided by that tier's size. 2) Sum across slots to get a specific card's average copies per pack.
when: When each pack slot's card is determined independently of the other slots.

text: 1) Find existing games with similar complexity, play time, and maximum win. 2) Look up or calculate their house edges. 3) Tune your rules to land at a similar edge.
when: When a comparable existing casino game has similar complexity, play time, and maximum win.

text: 1) Find the chance of failure on a single attempt. 2) Raise that chance to the power of the number of independent attempts. 3) Subtract the result from 1 to get the chance of at least one success.
when: 'at least one success' questions with repeated independent attempts
why: Multiplying failure chances gives the chance of none, which is simpler than adding overlapping cases.

text: 1) List each possible outcome and its value. 2) Multiply each value by its probability. 3) Sum the products to get the expected value.
when: Comparing actions or checking a game's fairness
why: The sum gives the long-run average payoff.

text: 1) Cap each outcome's value at what the situation can actually use. 2) Multiply the capped value by its probability. 3) Compare the capped expected values to choose an action.
when: Evaluating an action whose benefit depends on the target's state
why: Only usable value shapes the real choice.

text: 1) Write out every possible outcome. 2) Mark the outcomes that meet the condition. 3) Divide the marked count by the total count.
when: The outcome space is small enough to list
why: Direct counting avoids errors in shortcut formulas.

text: 1) Split all outcomes into mutually exclusive cases by the number of successes. 2) Count the arrangements in each case. 3) Multiply each case's single-arrangement probability by its arrangement count. 4) Sum the cases.

1) Plot levels against required XP as a scatter plot. 2) Add linear, polynomial degree 2 and 3, and exponential trendlines. 3) Compare their R-squared values. 4) If the curve has distinct segments, fit each segment separately.
when: choosing a formula for an XP curve from data

text: 1) Count the distinct items needed for a complete set. 2) Compute the probability that repeated independent draws cover every item. 3) Compute the expected number of draws needed to collect all items, which exceeds the minimum number of draws.
when: collecting one of each of several equally likely items

text: 1) Compute the chance of each entry on the first table. 2) For entries that trigger another roll, multiply by the chance of the next table's entry. 3) Repeat through each nested table to get the chance of a specific final item.
when: loot tables where an entry rolls again on another table

text: 1) When ties reroll, discard tie outcomes. 2) Divide the win probability by the sum of win and loss probabilities to get the win chance.
when: contests where ties force a reroll until one side wins
why: Ties just restart the contest, so only decisive win or loss outcomes matter for the final result.

text: 1) Count the favorable shuffles that meet each condition on card positions and multiply the counts. 2) Count all distinct shuffles, treating identical cards as interchangeable. 3) Divide favorable by total.
when: computing the chance of a specific opening hand or draw pattern from a deck
why: Treating identical cards as interchangeable keeps the count correct.

text: 1) Tally favorable outcomes. 2) Divide that tally by the total number of possibilities. 3) Recalculate the total after every reveal, because it shrinks and changes.
when: finding probabilities when earlier results affect later ones
why: Each revealed card removes an option, so the remaining possibilities and their probabilities change.

text: 1) Start from the total orderings of all cards as if distinct. 2) Divide by the factorial of the count of each group of identical cards. 3) Multiply the factorials of the groups, which gives the number of distinct shuffles.
when: decks containing several copies of the same card
why: When only rank matters, cards of the same rank count as equivalent for the problem.

text: 1) Group identical cards by rank, ignoring suits. 2) Choose the ranks for each part of the hand, respecting order between different roles. 3) Choose the required number of cards within each rank group. 4) Multiply the counts and divide by the total number of hands.
when: counting hands where cards are distinguished only by rank

text: 1) List the mutually exclusive categories of the first card. 2) Multiply each category's probability by the second-card match chance given that category. 3) Add the products. 4) Check that all outcomes sum to 1.
when: computing the chance of a matching pair from a deck with special cards
why: conditioning on the first card changes the second-card odds

text: 1) List every equally likely setup. 2) For each strategy, count the setups it wins. 3) Divide by the total number of setups.
when: checking a counterintuitive probability with a small number of cases
why: exhaustive counting gives exact odds

text: 1) Count draws missing card A. 2) Count draws missing card B. 3) Add those counts. 4) Subtract draws missing both. 5) Divide by total draws to get the chance of missing at least one. 6) Subtract from 1 to get the chance of having both.
when: chance that a fixed-size draw contains at least one copy of each of two specific cards
why: subtracting the overlap avoids double-counting draws missing both

text: 1) Compute the chance of success for the initial hand. 2) Account for each redraw from the full deck after reshuffling. 3) Apply any later draw to the remaining deck, updating the counts at each step.
when: computing the chance of holding a key card after mulligans and an extra draw
why: each step changes the deck composition for the next

text: 1) Count distinct hands as unordered sets of cards. 2) Multiply by the number of play orders only if the order changes the outcome.
when: counting initial deals in a card game where hands are dealt face down
why: choosing which cards a hand holds differs from ordering them for play

text: 1) List the probability of each early outcome directly. 2) Multiply the continuation chances along each path. 3) Stop summing once the remaining probability is negligible, or switch to a simulation.
when: A repeated chance event where each continuation has a fixed probability.
why: Path probabilities shrink, so a short prefix already approximates the total.

text: 1) Compare the highest die on each side; the lower roll loses one army, and ties go to the defender. 2) If both sides rolled at least two dice, compare the second-highest pair the same way.
when: Resolving a dice-based combat round where each side rolls several dice.
why: Pairwise comparison of sorted dice decides which army is lost each exchange.

text: 1) List every possible dice roll for both sides. 2) Resolve each roll by pairwise comparison. 3) Sum the probabilities of outcomes that win the battle.
when: Computing exact combat odds for a small battle with a finite set of rolls.
why: Enumeration gives exact odds that can be checked by spreadsheet.

text: 1) Set the one-vs-one win chance as the base case. 2) For any battle, sum over each possible roll result: its probability times the win chance of the smaller battle it leaves. 3) Fill a grid by attacker and defender counts.
when: Computing win odds for battles of any size in a dice-based combat game.
why: Each battle reduces to smaller battles with known odds, so the grid builds up exactly.

text: 1) Model each turn as a state pair of strikes (0 to 5) and dice rolled (1 to 6). 2) Add a single final state for six strikes. 3) Use the resulting Markov chain to find mean, median and mode of total rolls.
when: analyzing the length of a dice game where players are eliminated after a fixed number of strikes
why: a Markov chain captures the probabilistic transitions between strike and dice-count states

text: 1) Frame the process as states that record only the number of dice rolled per turn. 2) Find the steady state and the turns needed to reach it. 3) For each dice-count state, compute the failure probability. 4) Multiply each failure probability by the state's steady-state probability and sum the products.
when: estimating the long-run chance of a strike on any turn in a dice game
why: the steady-state probabilities determine the average outcome, not the starting state

text: 1) Count the arrangements for each outcome category of the roll. 2) Divide by symmetry to remove double counting for repeated arrangements. 3) Check that all category counts sum to the total number of possible rolls.
when: computing exact probabilities for a multi-die roll
why: the sum check reveals double counting when too high and missed cases when too low

text: 1) Define states for no match, pair, three, four, and five of a kind. 2) Set transition probabilities for each reroll count. 3) Multiply the initial state vector by the matrix once per reroll to find the probability of each state.
when: computing the chance of reaching a target combination within a fixed number of rerolls
why: repeated matrix multiplication gives the state distribution after each roll

text: 1) List the faces 1 to n in column A. 2) For each new die, copy the existing rows below themselves until the row count is n times larger. 3) Fill the new column with each face value over its own equal block of rows. 4) Repeat for each die until the row count equals n to the power of the dice.
when: listing every outcome of several n-sided dice in a spreadsheet

text: 1) Shuffle the deck and draw seven opening cards, then one card each turn. 2) Note the first turn with 6 available mana. 3) Repeat the shuffle many times. 4) Average the recorded turns.
when: estimating how soon a deck reaches a mana threshold

text: 1) List items in column B. 2) In column A, enter cumulative lower bounds starting at 0, in ascending order. 3) Use =VLOOKUP(RAND(),A1:B5,2) to pick an item.
when: probabilities are not simple round weights
why: A random number falls into a cumulative band, so one lookup selects an item according to its weight.

text: Roll multiple dice by calling RANDBETWEEN separately for each die and adding the results.
why: Scaling one roll by a multiplier does not produce a sum of independent dice, so separate calls are needed.

text: Check that each column of the transition matrix and the starting state vector sums to 1 using SUM().
when: When building a Markov chain transition matrix in a spreadsheet
why: Probabilities out of each state must total 1 for the chain to be valid

text: Before counting a run placed on a destination, check whether its first key continues the last key written there; if so, count it as replacing a dummy.
when: When distributing runs onto output sequences in a polyphase merge sort
why: Each output sequence must remember its last written key so that a new run can continue it.

text: Limit player losses to the amount wagered; avoid designs where a bad outcome costs more than the bet.
when: Wagering games.
why: Players who bet their last chips cannot pay larger losses, so such rules are hard to enforce.

text: For mutually exclusive events, the chance that either occurs is the sum of their individual probabilities.
when: when events cannot happen together

text: Compute the chance of at least one event as 1 minus the chance that none occurs.
when: When counting all cases of at least one event would require adding many separate possibilities
why: The complement, that none occurs, is often a single easy calculation that avoids those separate cases.

text: Plot standard error bars around each win rate to judge whether differences between characters are likely real.
when: When comparing win rates between characters to judge whether the differences are real
why: Error whiskers show how much a win rate could vary by chance, and they shrink as data grows.

text: Use 'chance' for a qualitative sense of likelihood and 'probability' or odds when a precise figure is needed.
when: When describing likelihood in general terms without giving numbers

text: Use the combination formula or COMBIN when order does not matter, and the permutation formula or PERMUT when each ordering counts as a distinct outcome.
why: Mixing them up gives the wrong count.

text: The basic combination and permutation formulas, including COMBIN and PERMUT, assume every item is distinct, so duplicate items require a separate adjustment.
when: When a deck contains duplicate cards rather than all distinct cards
why: The formulas count each arrangement of distinct items, so identical copies make many arrangements equivalent and get overcounted.

text: Drawing with replacement, or reshuffling after each draw, makes every draw independent and equivalent to rolling a die with that many faces; loot drops work this way.
when: Loot drop systems in most cases where each drop does not depend on earlier drops.
why: Drops are not removed from the pool, unlike cards drawn from a deck.

text: For multi-draw success, first find draws that cannot fail, then count successes only among the cards still in the deck at each draw that can fail.
when: computing a probability over a sequence of draws without replacement
why: removed cards change the remaining deck

text: Model the finishing state as absorbing: its column keeps probability 1 and all other entries in it are zero, so the player stays finished.
when: building a Markov model of a race or track game
why: a finished player must not leave the end state

text: Repeating entries encodes simple round weights but becomes impractical at large sizes; a cumulative threshold table handles any probabilities in a short list.
when: When drop chances are not neat round numbers.
why: A table of millions of repeated rows would use too much memory to be practical.

text: Rules fix the damage range while chance picks the outcome within it, so the mix should be chosen based on the experience wanted.
1) When a value's right size is unknown or clearly off, double or halve it in the needed direction rather than making small tweaks. 2) Once the workable range is found, narrow it with midpoints.
when: tuning a value whose right range is unknown or clearly wrong
why: Large steps reveal the value's influence and the limits of good balance sooner than small changes lost in noise.

text: An identity curve pairs two values one-to-one: 10 food for 10 gold, or a rise of 5 in one matching a rise of 5 in the other.
A cost curve, interchangeably called a power or cost/power curve, relates an item's cost to its power, found by scaling item numbers to a common anchor.
A linear curve, y = mx with fixed multiplier m, gives each added unit the same cost, such as 5 gold per food; identity is m = 1.
A logarithmic curve, the inverse of an exponential (y = log_b x, or x = b^y), needs 4 times as much gold per extra food in food-for-gold trades, showing steep diminishing returns.
A curve is a mathematical function, a graph of how one game resource changes as another changes, rather than an aesthetic one, named after both, such as experience against level.
why: Named curves make progression relationships explicit and comparable.

text: Curves can be straight, gently sloped, or hilly; a learning curve describes how quickly players must learn as challenge rises, and a ramp is an informal term for a curve that climbs.
why: Shared vocabulary lets designers describe and choose progression shapes.

text: An item above the cost curve gives more benefit than its cost predicts; an item below it gives less.
Progression balance is judged on three questions: whether difficulty rises at a good rate, whether player power keeps pace with enemy power, and whether overall difficulty suits the audience.
when: Evaluating PvE progression in single-player, tabletop, or co-op games, where a group progresses as one character would.

text: Progression balance covers how fast players gain power and whether gains arrive steadily or in bursts tied to specific places.
Power progression is the growth of a player's strength through stat gains, levels, abilities, and items.
An exponential curve multiplies the previous result by a fixed base each step; with base 4, 1 to 4 food cost 2, 8, 32, and 128 gold.
An exponential progression multiplies a base by itself a set number of times, so values start modest and then grow faster and faster.
A level curve, also called an XP curve, shows how much experience is needed for a level based on the character's current level.
Velocity is the rate of change in power over time; acceleration is the rate of change in velocity. Together they describe how a progression system's pace behaves.
Power is broad and can include pieces, cards, resources, board position, actions, stats, equipment, or anything that affects standing.
In a cumulative table, each item's lower bound equals the sum of the probabilities of all items listed before it.
A triangular leveling curve is one where each later level needs more XP than the previous one, with cost rising by a steady step per level.
Level curves are often logarithmic relative to XP, while XP is often exponential up to a certain point; RPG XP curves often start exponential and later level out.
when: designing level and XP progression
why: Each level requires more XP than the last, so level grows slowly against XP.

text: Common game curve shapes include identity, linear, exponential, logarithmic, triangular, and custom curves; a curve may be straight, gently sloped, or a series of hills and valleys.

Linear sequences add a fixed step per term, triangular (polynomial) sequences rise gently at first then accelerate steadily, and exponential sequences multiply by a fixed factor, growing fastest over time.
Cost curves and their intersections reveal how weapons, creatures, characters, and loot relate to one another.
Some games grant no power gains at all; strength then comes only from the player's mastery.
Triangular curves are probably the most common increasing-returns formula in game design, and their cost pattern is easy to follow.
Power curves are easier to balance than skill curves because designers directly control both player power and enemy power.
why: Designers set when the player gains power and when enemies rise to counter it.

text: Adding cash jackpots and easing purchase requirements to a board game can raise typical play time from about ninety minutes to three hours or more.
when: When players modify a game's rules to change its pacing
why: Rule modifications that add rewards and loosen constraints can lengthen sessions substantially

text: Progression curves commonly follow five patterns: linear, exponential, fast-early then slowing, repeated tension-and-release, and irregular; none suits every system.
Use a custom curve, or cap or replace exponential and logarithmic curves, when a standard shape produces jumps too large for the experience.
when: designing progression or scaling curves where a standard progression produces jumps that are too large
why: Standard shapes can produce unpleasant extremes that hurt play.

text: Smooth curves are rare for monsters and items, so designers often hand-edit spreadsheets to add peaks and valleys and adjust rarity.
when: When tuning monsters and items with spreadsheet curves.

text: A procedural progression can make each object a fixed percentage stronger than the previous one, such as 5%.
when: When building object progression data from scratch.

text: A derived curve passes the common-sense test when the most-above objects dominate play and the most-below objects are seldom used.
when: When checking a derived balance curve against how objects are used in play.

text: Compare cards with the same effect but different power types, such as specific-only, generic-only or mixed, to check that costs are valued consistently.
when: When cards share an effect but differ in the mix of power types in their costs.

text: Power should arrive in periodic spikes, such as finding a strong weapon or unlocking an ability, rather than ramping smoothly.
For sequels, reuse the previous game's data and tweak it for new play, items, and locations.
when: When designing a sequel that builds on an earlier game.

text: Casual and free-to-play games should balance progression toward the time players expect to gain a level.
when: In casual and free-to-play games where quick visible progress matters.
why: Players expect a level within a certain time, and missing it hurts retention.

text: An identity relationship often suggests a single resource would do, unless the game gives reasons to keep both.
when: two resources that exchange at equal amounts
why: Equal exchange makes one of the two resources redundant.

text: In solo skill-based games, designers usually assume a player is ready for the next level after completing the previous one, while in PvP games rank based on wins or a matchmaking metric signals readiness.
when: When gating progression by player readiness

text: In single-player card games against AI, gaining stronger cards over time meets expectations and matters less for balance.
when: Single-player progression card games.
why: Players expect power growth as the core experience.

text: A fixed XP step feels slower at higher levels, so a logarithmic increase keeps perceived progression pace steady.
when: Designing experience point progression
why: Perceived change shrinks as absolute values grow, per Weber-Fechner.

text: Increase reward value gradually as the player progresses so later rewards still feel good.
why: Growing rewards counter habituation, and players still enjoy them even when they know the scaling is designed.

text: In an epic, over-the-top game, push numbers to extremes with big contrasts, and pull back only when necessary.
when: games aiming for an over-the-top feel
why: The feel the designer wants determines how far numbers should be pushed.

text: A damage bonus against the final or progress-gating enemy can be worth far more than its encounter share suggests, since it removes the last obstacle.
when: When the enemy is the final boss rather than a weak early enemy.
why: It is literally the last obstacle, so extra damage there matters far more.

text: In persistent games with expansions, cost-power rises over time as each new set is balanced against the strongest earlier options, and slight overpowering accumulates across sets.
when: persistent games with expansions or sets released over time
why: Small accidental overpowering compounds across sets.

text: A reward that raises player power eases difficulty briefly, until enemy strength scales up and challenge returns, so the cycle repeats.
When XP needed per level roughly doubles from one level to the next, XP awarded from combat and quests must be tuned to keep pace with it.
when: Character levels use an XP requirement that grows each level.
why: Level pacing must line up with XP from combat and quests to keep the game fun.

text: If power grows too fast, the game becomes trivial once the player finds one dominant weapon; if it grows too slowly, players are forced into tedious grinding.
Under positive feedback both players share the same power-curve shape, but one curve is shifted slightly later, as if that player lost one early turn.
when: In positive-sum games with positive feedback, between competing players.
why: Positive feedback lets an early leader keep extending the gap over time.

text: A power spike may briefly overpower the player until difficulty rises to catch up.
Lowering the base of an XP exponential partway through the curve makes later levels take much less time to reach.
when: a level curve switches from a higher base to a lower base at a set level
why: A smaller base produces smaller increments per level.

text: Exponential effects start slowly and then ramp to extremes, which can unbalance a system or make a level curve drag.
when: systems using exponential growth for stats or requirements
why: Compounding multiplies small differences into very large ones.

text: Many XP values map to one level, while each level maps to a range of XP values, so XP-to-level is many-to-one.
when: reading a level table
why: A level covers a band of XP totals.

text: Ramp-out raises difficulty faster than player skill, so players usually sense strain by day two or three, after which premium currency offers appear.
when: After the opening stages, around the second or third day of play.

text: Player power rises through purchased items, level-ups and drops, while the area's challenge types stay the same.
when: Within one area, such as a single dungeon, level, or play session

text: Winning fights levels the player up and makes later fights easier, but stronger enemies and more victories needed per level offset this, so net power gain stays close to linear.
when: In player-versus-environment games where levelling comes from winning fights against enemies
why: Rising enemy strength and more victories needed per level counteract the gains from each level-up.

text: In an idle run, virtual skill often rises logarithmically, so slowing progress eventually prompts a reset, while maximum virtual skill before each reset may rise exponentially.
when: In idle games where each reset grants permanent stackable multipliers

text: F2P puzzle games start with easy three-star levels, then the same skill earns two stars, then one, then borderline passes, raising friction over time.
when: In free-to-play puzzle games, once players have learned mechanics and become invested

text: Price multiplying with each owned unit makes cost grow geometrically, while each unit adds only a fixed amount of income per second.
when: idle games with compounding unit prices and fixed unit output

text: In many RPGs costs grow faster than stat bonuses, while in many collectible card games benefits grow faster than costs, so late-game cards are powerful.
when: Choosing how costs and benefits scale across a game
why: Earn rates and game length shape which side grows faster

text: Progress rate is roughly the inverse of resistance: the more resistance a system presents, the slower players advance.
Exponential progression arises when early resources generate more resources through positive feedback, so growth accelerates over time.
when: when early gains produce further gains
why: Each gain increases the rate of the next gain.

text: If power is the reward and rises steadily until the end, the game finishes just as players reach their peak, so they never enjoy feeling dominant.
when: when power rises steadily to the game's end
why: No period of dominance remains before the game ends.

text: Because a lifetime points total never decreases, the system is positive-sum and cannot reflect a decline in current skill.
when: When a rating equals total points earned across a player's whole career

text: As income grows with progress, fixed prices feel cheaper later, because less exploring or fighting is needed to afford each item.
when: When player income rises during progression while item prices stay constant

text: A quantity formed by multiplying a linear factor with a triangular factor grows faster than either factor alone.
when: Two growing factors multiply together in a value such as a sell price or profit.
why: Each factor's growth compounds with the other's, so the product accelerates.

text: Idle XP grows linearly with elapsed time, so total time XP equals elapsed seconds multiplied by the gain rate.
when: progression accrues while the player is away or idle

text: If killing ten monsters worth 100 experience each gives a level needing 1000 points, progression works, but if required experience doubles each level with no cap, players may need thousands of kills.
when: When experience requirements grow per level with no cap.
why: Grinding grows when the content supplying experience fails to keep pace with rising level requirements.

text: An XP requirement of 100 × 2^Level starts at 100 and doubles each level, so it reaches 200 and then 400.
when: early character leveling with per-level doubling

text: Next unit cost equals base cost × 1.1^N, where N is units already owned, rounded up to a whole number.
when: idle game units whose price rises with each purchase

text: Experience required for level N can be computed as N times (N minus 1) times a constant K, so the requirement grows quadratically with level.
when: Designing a level progression curve.

text: Gate progression with stackable currency: 100 coins yield one star, unlocking the first gate; three stars open two more levels, and eight stars open the first boss area.
why: Chaining coin collection into unlocks ties every coin to the highest reward tier.

text: Triangular numbers follow y = (x² − x)/2 for each n, growing faster than linear but slower than exponential, rising faster and faster over a long range.
when: modeling a quantity that grows by one more step each level

text: A cost curve ties the numbers of many objects into one progression, so their relative power can be compared directly.
why: Costs and benefits must first be expressed as numbers before objects can be compared.

text: Competitive games with resource-cost items use an identity curve: one point of cost equals one point of benefit, and an item is balanced when totals match.
when: player-versus-player games where items cost resources
why: Comparing total cost against total benefit directly makes balance checks straightforward.

text: Progression curves are commonly classified as identity, linear, exponential, logarithmic, or polynomial, with custom shapes for anything else.
Players who notice ramp-out often object to the precise point where difficulty rises.
when: In free-to-play games, as players grow aware of monetization practices

text: Changing a single rule can have a large, unexpected effect on total play time.
when: When editing one rule of a game with established length
why: Length is influenced by subtle interacting factors

text: If weapons, characters, and enemies all follow the same trajectory, challenge stays constant and the game becomes boring.
when: All content scales identically
why: No variation in difficulty or reward curve.

text: Only the direction of supply and demand curves is fixed; their shapes may be straight, curved, or wavy.
when: Modeling a market with supply and demand curves
why: Assuming a particular curve shape can mislead analysis

text: If every item sits exactly on the curve, choices seem to matter little, because every option has the same value.
when: Designing item sets for player choice
why: Equal values remove meaningful differences between options

text: A single item off the plotted progression is a signal to check it, not proof that it is wrong; the designer may then rarify it, restrict it to a class, or narrow its damage range.
when: Reviewing a plotted item list

text: 1) Choose a guiding growth multiplier, such as 1.5 per area or doubling difficulty per level. 2) Derive all values from that rule. 3) Adjust numbers during play to reach the desired feel.
when: starting a new game's balance or designing a fixed-length progression such as a ten-level RPG
why: A single guiding rule gives a foundation that spares much of the trial and error of tuning each value by hand.

text: 1) Select 30 to 60 comparable objects from a self-contained subset of mechanics. 2) Derive the cost math and list every assumption. 3) Build a spreadsheet showing each object's distance above or below the curve. 4) Apply a common-sense check. 5) Correct the formulas and repeat until results resemble reality.
1) Tune the baseline pace at which power is gained or lost, which sets the balance between zero-sum and positive-sum outcomes. 2) Add, remove, strengthen, or weaken feedback loops.
when: game length is too long or too short
why: Power gain or loss sets how fast the ending condition is reached, so changing that rate changes game length.

text: 1) Set starting and ending stat values. 2) Subtract the start from the end. 3) Divide the difference by the number of level gains to get gain per level. 4) Add random ranges for variety.
when: When planning stat growth across levels.
why: Known start and end values fix the total growth, so the per-level gain follows from the level count.

text: 1) Start the XP curve as an exponential. 2) After a few levels, switch to custom values. 3) Round values down to end in zeros so they are easy to remember.
when: building a level curve that must soften late-game jumps
why: Custom values after the switch reduce extreme level-to-level increases, and round numbers aid player recall.

text: 1) Raise difficulty sharply at a set point. 2) Only players who pay keep pace. 3) Use the paying group's data to focus monetization.
when: free-to-play games that want to monetize a subset of players
why: Players who do not pay fall behind, leaving the paying group as the focus.

text: To get growth between linear and exponential, start with a triangular curve and modify it.
when: needing a growth rate between linear and exponential
why: The triangular form is a simple base that can be adjusted.

text: 1) Plot level on the x-axis and required XP on the y-axis. 2) Classify the overall shape. 3) Check whether the shape changes between early and late levels, and describe each segment.
when: analyzing XP-per-level progression of a game

text: 1) Set an anchor value such as gold per point of damage. 2) Choose a starting damage and an improvement rate. 3) Compute each tier as the previous times the rate. 4) Derive costs from the anchor, rounded to the nearest 5.
when: Generating a weapon progression table
why: A fixed rate yields a predictable curve tied to a common currency.

text: Fix an item above the curve by lowering its benefit or raising its cost or rarity; fix one below it by adding benefit or lowering its cost.
For a shipped game whose balance data is lost, derive its cost curve after the fact so later expansions can reuse its math.
when: original spreadsheets are unavailable
why: future developers need the curve to build consistent new content

text: Balance every new object on the existing cost curve, with supporting math showing each object's place on the curve as closely as practical.
Generate derived values with spreadsheet formulas that reference cost cells, so one formula change fills down to update every affected item.
when: Building item costs in a spreadsheet.
why: A single formula edit propagates to every dependent value, avoiding manual edits across dozens or hundreds of items.

text: In progressive-level games, increase difficulty from level to level, but balance each level individually.
when: Designing sequential difficulty levels

text: Decide how fast players advance and when progression caps, since each choice defines a curve for the progression.
when: designing any progression system
why: Players feel the timing of progression as a recognizable pattern, and those expectations become ingrained in genres.

text: Spending a resource must never reduce a progression level, so progression should track a total that spending does not decrement.
when: designing a currency that players can spend

text: Power creep pushes players to buy new content to stay competitive, but older strategies and items fall behind.
when: Long-running games with a big, highly skilled player community
why: Even tiny advantages get found and adopted by a large, skilled community, so they become the norm.

text: Raising difficulty through power bonuses is cheap, while raising it through AI skill is expensive but can feel like a new game; blocking easy paths to victory forces a harder route to the same goal.
why: Adjusting opponent skill can shift the experience enough that it seems new once the player improves.

text: Exponential leveling is fast early but becomes too slow later, so designers usually impose a level cap before progression grows impractical.
when: designing a level curve with exponential growth
why: Requirements at high levels can grow to millions of points, making progress unreasonably slow.

text: Keep punishment gentle, understandable, and tuned through testing; avoid penalties harsh enough to make players quit, but keep punishment as a threat, which creates tension even when it rarely lands.
when: Designing penalties in a game
why: Harsh penalties make players frustrated or cautious, while mild ones make challenge meaningless; threatened punishment creates tension even when it rarely lands.

text: Economic resets are uncommon and cluster at major milestones, such as the move from alpha to beta or from pre-release testing to full release.
Punishment can make a game more enjoyable by giving resources value, making risk exciting, and raising challenge.
why: A resource only feels valuable when losing it is possible, and success feels sweeter when failure was possible.

text: Common punishment types are shaming, loss of points, shortened play, terminated play, setback, removal of powers, and resource depletion.
Resource depletion, losing money, goods, ammunition, shields, or hit points, is one of the most common forms of punishment.
Ask what each punishment is for, whether players find it fair, whether it could be a reward with equal or better effect, and whether strong punishments are matched by strong rewards.
when: Reviewing punishments in a game
why: Fair, purposeful punishments that are balanced against rewards maintain motivation

text: A reset levels the field for newcomers: someone joining just before it starts has a fair shot.
why: Everyone loses accumulated wealth at once, so earlier accumulation no longer gives an edge.

text: A reset result that sends the score to zero can drop a near-goal score sharply, so states close to the goal are not safe from setbacks.
when: A race-to-target game with a reset outcome on the random spinner.
why: The reset ignores how high the score already is.

text: Even an anticipated reset leaves inflation intact, since the economy remains positive-sum and latecomers stay behind.
why: Resources still enter the economy overall, so accumulation and inflation resume after the reset.

text: Punitive mechanics can drive away even engaged players, who may then stop caring about the story.
Rewards in level design do more than pay players off: they incentivize behavior, entice exploration, build curiosity, and pace the experience.
Most in-game rewards are intrinsic, except real-money-linked currencies, player-driven economies, and esports, where rewards are largely extrinsic.
Multiplicative stat effects are rare in strategy and card games because they can break balance.
when: designing card or strategy effects that multiply stats
why: Compounding multipliers can overwhelm other game elements.

text: Check which rewards exist, whether players enjoy and understand them, whether they arrive too regularly, and whether they grow at the right pace.
when: Auditing a game's reward system
why: Rewards that are misunderstood, predictable or mistimed lose their motivating effect

text: Award points for every meaningful action, including stunts, hits and combinations, so each action the player takes feels valuable.
Rewards are generally more efficient than punishments for shaping player behavior; non-physical punishments are central to conditioning.
why: Behavioral learning works through stimulus-response conditioning, where rewards and non-physical punishments shape behavior.

text: Rewards that help the player win carry more weight, and rewards tied to the story or carrying romantic associations seem more valuable.
when: Designing reward types

text: When rewards in open-ended social games become rarer and then stop, players quit or switch to other play such as decorating.
If a player loses a life while chasing a high-value target, the chase's reward is lost, so the risk can outweigh the points.
when: when a reward is only granted on success and failure costs a life
why: Lost life erases the value the player was pursuing

text: 1) Start from the power-reward schedule. 2) Add location-based and story-based rewards. 3) Locate areas with a surplus or shortage across all reward types. 4) Check whether memorable areas are explained by their rewards. 5) Check whether any reward type dominates and whether that suits the genre.
when: When extending an existing power-reward schedule with location- and story-based rewards

text: Reward actions that fit the fantasy, because rewarding tedious actions that contradict it works against the fantasy.
Treat rewards as feedback that informs players about their performance, and give them the same usability care as other feedback.
why: Players expect rewards in games, and rewards signal how well they are performing.

text: Show players what a reward is worth before they commit to a task.
when: before players accept a task
why: Players need to know the reward's value to commit meaningfully.

text: For creative, teamwork, ethical, or quality-focused tasks, keep extrinsic rewards non-salient, except rewards that highlight progress.
when: the task involves creativity, teamwork, ethics, or quality
why: salient external rewards can undermine intrinsic engagement

text: Ask what purpose each reward serves, especially for progression, and why it is meaningful when received.
when: designing rewards and progression
why: unclear rewards feel arbitrary to players

text: When the story promises a reward, level designers choose what it is and balance its value and power against the rest of the game.
when: Story-driven loot or rewards

text: Do not tie pay or prizes to measured output in creative game development work.
when: Creative design and development roles.
why: Extrinsic rewards cause the problems that follow from conditional payment in creative work.

text: Scale rewards with task difficulty or length: harder or longer content should pay off via rarer drops, more experience points, or achievements, with payoffs proportional to effort.
when: When rewards are set for tasks that differ in difficulty or duration
why: Players judge balance by whether rewards are worth the time spent, and feel shortchanged when small effort yields too much or repetition yields little.

text: Enemies that hide behind cover and take three hits from the basic weapon seem stronger than their health implies.
when: Enemy uses cover and requires several basic shots
why: Cover and extra hits make the enemy feel more durable to the player.

text: Raising a game's speed variable as the score climbs makes difficulty track the player's ability.
when: Games where the score reflects player skill and speed can be scaled.

text: Making each successive failure about 10% less likely than pure probability dictates shortens failure streaks, and sufficiently long streaks become impossible.
Score values that rise steeply with the size of a feat can make the largest achievements dominate the total score.
Shape difficulty as a sinusoidal curve inside the flow zone rather than a linear rise in step with mastery.
when: When tuning how challenge changes as the player's skill grows
why: A linear rise can leave players feeling no growth.

text: Easy, medium, and hard modes help players find their level, but each version must be created and balanced, and players may dispute which version is authentic.
when: When offering players a choice of difficulty settings

text: Making targets easier to hit but worth fewer points creates a risk-reward gradient, so players who take harder shots gain more.
Intrinsic motivation comes from inside the player, for an activity's own sake or pleasure; extrinsic motivation comes from external rewards, payment, or avoiding punishment.

Operant conditioning shapes voluntary actions: an action performed after a stimulus is linked to the reward or punishment that follows it, unlike classical conditioning, which manipulates involuntary responses.
Fixed-interval rewards, given on a set time schedule regardless of action, are poor motivators: players ignore them until return nears, check often, take them, then ignore them again.
why: Motivation rises only as the return time approaches.

text: Classical conditioning links two stimuli through repeated pairing, so one comes to trigger a response associated with the other.
Intermittent or random rewards shape behavior more strongly than fixed or continuous rewards, but rewards should still track the player's real progress.
Rewards or avoided punishment make a behavior more frequent; punishment or going unrewarded makes it less frequent, and withdrawing punishment after a behavior also increases it.
why: Experiments on animals showed these effects, later extended to people.

text: Variable ratio reinforcement, where rewards follow an unpredictable number of actions, sustains more consistent engagement than fixed-interval or fixed-ratio schedules.
when: Designing reward timing for repeated player actions
why: Players cannot predict the reward moment, and unpredictable payoffs sustain repeated behavior more strongly than fixed payoffs.

text: Variable-ratio rewards, granted after a randomized count of actions, hold players longer and sustain activity far better than fixed rewards with identical average value.
when: Choosing between fixed and random payoffs for the same expected reward, or designing rewards for sustained repeated activity.
why: Unpredictable payoffs keep each reward feeling like a surprise, while predictable ones become dull; each action carries a shot at a big payout.

text: Design motivation to satisfy competence, autonomy and relatedness; this intrinsic motivation matters most in educational games and lasts longer than extrinsic rewards.
when: When designing educational games
why: These three needs drive sustained engagement.

text: Flooding players with rewards in short bursts, making each one too intense, or giving a steady stream of small rewards lowers every reward's value until players stop caring.
when: Designing reward schedules
why: Happiness from gains follows diminishing returns, and players quickly learn to expect rewards that arrive regardless of their actions.

text: Rewards that arrive regardless of player action lose their meaning; random rewards not linked to player action break the sense of being rewarded for skill.
why: Players feel rewarded for skill when a random roll still depends on actions they deliberately chose.

text: Praise learners' effort rather than innate intelligence, since praising smartness makes later failure feel like a verdict on ability, and effort praise encourages learning goals.
when: giving feedback on learners' performance
why: Effort praise supports a malleable view of ability.

text: Long stretches without a sense of progress can make players feel they are playing wrong even when they are doing fine.
when: In games centred on advancement systems

text: Acquiring an item that expands how the player can interact with the world creates excitement.
Uncertain rewards are valued less, and risk-averse people discount them more than risk-seekers do.
Non-physical punishment such as a bad grade can cause stress or aggression and can hurt learning and retention.
Variable rewards do not automatically sustain engagement with daily or routine tasks.
when: Chance-based bonuses are attached to repetitive everyday work or chores.
why: Schedule effects seen in animals in specific settings may not carry over to humans in every context.

text: Performance-contingent rewards that require meeting a standard of excellence are often perceived as controlling.
when: when rewards require meeting a standard of excellence
why: Players feel pressure to reach the standard.

text: Players will play token-based gambling only when real money is at stake, because tokens create little internal value.
when: games with tokens and no real stakes
why: Little internal value gives players little reason to play.

text: Players collect items expecting value, then ignore them once they find the items serve no purpose beyond scoring.
when: a collectible that only adds to a score
why: A score with no use does not help players reach their goal.

text: Players rate rewards delivered at random times as more pleasurable than the same rewards delivered on a fixed pattern.
when: when rewards are timed predictably versus unpredictably
why: Surprise makes an experience more enjoyable

text: Players find larger reward numbers more exciting, so 100 gold feels better than 10 gold.
when: Displaying rewards
why: Bigger numbers feel more significant even at equal value ratios.

text: Player demand for an item usually falls as they accumulate more of it, so they buy less of it.
when: Players stockpile a consumable with fixed price
why: Each additional unit adds less value to the player.

text: Tiny penalties invite reckless play, while large penalties invite caution.
when: Games whose failure penalty is tiny versus games whose failure penalty is severe.
why: Players weigh expected loss against the reward for each risk.

text: Players are chiefly driven by gaining ground on rivals, which raises their odds after a strong move, regardless of whether the contest is positive-sum, negative-sum or zero-sum.
why: Standing relative to opponents drives satisfaction in PvP.

text: After a reset, players must replay to regain their former rank, which encourages regular play.
when: after a seasonal reset
why: rank recovery requires continued activity

text: Players attribute random rewards to their own skill, treating a lucky result as the payoff of a calculated risk.
when: random rewards occur
why: attribution bias

text: Beyond a point, much larger prizes feel roughly equal to smaller ones, so raising the prize does little to attract players when win odds stay very low.
when: win odds are very low and prizes are already huge
why: Players judge prize value by feel, not by its numeric size

text: After a lucky streak, players credit their skill, then perform lower when results regress, and feel frustrated by the drop.
when: after an unusually successful run ends
why: Self-serving bias credits success to skill

text: Publicized winners and unseen losers make a gamble seem more likely to pay off than it really is.
when: lotteries and similar gambles with heavily reported jackpots
why: Vivid winners are easily recalled while losers go unnoticed

text: Coins are common enough that running out of health is rare, yet the restore rule still makes players seek coins when health is low.
when: low health
why: Coins restore health directly.

text: Players build an internal scale of relative reward from experience, so a stunt-heavy round can make stunts feel more valuable than captures.
when: scoring has several action types
why: Repeated scoring teaches players how actions compare

text: People persist longer when told they are improving rapidly than when told they are good but not improving.
when: Cognitive training tasks where people receive feedback on their progress.
why: Perceived growth in competence predicts motivated effort more strongly than actual skill level does.

text: People often lose interest in an activity after an external monetary reward, if they first found the activity interesting.
when: the activity was initially interesting and the reward felt external
why: money makes the reason for engaging feel external

text: When a task's meaning is weak, players are less motivated to follow instructions, which weakens attention and memory.
when: when players cannot see why a task matters
why: Low motivation to follow instructions reduces attention given to the task, and attention sets how strongly it is remembered.

text: Many children disengage from traditional curricula, so educational games must excite them to hold their motivation.
when: When designing learning activities for children.
why: Motivation is a key pillar of learning through play.

text: Players enjoy rewards and dislike punishment, so designers often emphasize rewards and limit punishments.
why: Players play to enjoy themselves rather than to endure hardship.

text: Players trained by a convention to expect a behavior learn a new rule best when it subverts that expectation at the point of use.
when: when a convention has trained players to expect a behavior
why: The surprise at the point of use makes the new rule memorable.

text: Players respond to emergent reinforcement schedules as they do to designed ones, so emergent patterns can decide whether a game holds or loses players.
when: Reward timing arising from interacting lower-level mechanics rather than an explicit designer-set schedule.

text: Under fixed ratio schedules players show long low-activity stretches followed by bursts of effort as they push toward the next reward.
when: fixed ratio reward schedules
why: Players work hard when they decide they want the next reward

text: Unpredictable alternation between reward and withholding keeps people pursuing an outcome, the same effect that makes slot machines compelling.
when: Designing any system with intermittent rewards
why: Unpredictability sustains pursuit more strongly than predictable reward timing.

text: When players can see into a building before entering, they weigh the risk of searching longer against the chance of better rewards.
when: when time pressure exists and loot is visible
why: visibility lets players judge whether a trip is worth the risk

text: Players need new content such as characters, maps or events; without it they become bored and leave.
when: When players stop receiving novelties such as new characters, maps or events.

text: Players grow accustomed to rewards, so a reward that felt exciting earlier can seem unimportant later.
when: Rewards stay the same size over a long play session.
why: Repeated exposure reduces the emotional impact of an unchanged reward.

text: Positive means something is added and negative means something is removed, and neither term means good or bad; combined they yield positive reward, positive punishment, negative punishment and negative reward.
The minor gift is an innate ease with some discipline, for example level design, arithmetic, or piano; it does not guarantee enjoyment.
Genuine affection for the craft is a designer's greatest asset: it sustains effort with whatever skills one has and shows in the finished product.
Inherent interest is the attention an event captures by itself, such as a dangerous live act that is hard to look away from.
DRL is a differential rate schedule in which an early attempt restarts the interval, encouraging low, steady rates of activity.
when: designing paced or deliberate actions
why: Rewards go only to players who wait out the interval.

text: DRH is a differential rate schedule that requires a set number of actions within an interval to earn the reward, for example five defeats within one minute.
when: designing timed burst challenges
why: Rewards go only to players who act quickly enough.

text: A fixed ratio schedule gives a reward after a set number of actions, and that ratio stays the same every time.
A fixed interval schedule makes a reward available a set time after it was last taken, rather than after a number of actions.
A variable interval schedule makes a reward available after a randomized amount of time, rather than after a fixed one.
A reinforcement schedule is a set of rules that determines when rewards are given.
An experimental enclosure with levers, lights, and dispensers, wired by hidden logic, is used to test reward schedules on animals.
Positive reinforcement rewards a correct action, while punishment follows a wrong one.
Negative reinforcement strengthens an action because it removes an unpleasant condition.
A set of objects without relationships between them is only a collection; relationships are what turn objects into a system.
A compulsion machine does not seriously try to fulfill players and treats each decision as a way to maximize motivation.

Fixed interval rewards arrive after set time periods, fixed ratio rewards after set numbers of actions, variable interval rewards after unpredictable times, and variable ratio rewards after unpredictable numbers of actions.

Task-contingent rewards depend on engagement, completion, or performance: engagement-contingent rewards reward taking part, completion-contingent rewards reward finishing, performance-contingent rewards reward doing well.
Predictable reward timing lets players anticipate payoffs, a pattern that resembles classical conditioning.
why: expectation sustains continued play

text: Most games use intermittent rewards, while dice and card draws always involve them and chess and Go are rare exceptions.
Push notifications that draw players back while they are not playing come closest to pure extrinsic rewards.
when: Designing re-engagement messaging
why: They motivate return without any play-driven interest

text: Real game motivations are usually mixed, as a player may enjoy a chase while also wanting points.
Intrinsically motivated people tend to perform better than extrinsically motivated people.
Fixed-ratio rewards, given after a set number of actions, work better than fixed-interval rewards for sustaining repeated behavior.
