Real-world rewards that drive motivation include food, money, power, and social status.
The brain does not distinguish real from virtual rewards, so virtual rewards are less intense than real ones but keep some of their power.
why: The brain evolved without games

text: Collecting appeals to many player types, from small sets within one session to long-running collections.
Well-timed weapons and loot in good games come from design that relates thousands of data points.
In PvE progression, rewards arrive most often early and slow over time as the player becomes invested, but the slowdown must not reach the point where players feel no progress.
Trading card games often run seasonal rotations that retire older cards from play at the season's close.
XP bars are fixed ratio in principle, but when XP is earned through random number generation they behave as variable ratio.
when: XP gains depend on random outcomes.

text: Most game rewards are task-contingent feedback tied to what the player does.
Rewards usually change behavior better than punishment.
For complex tasks requiring concentration, investment, or creativity, intrinsic motivation tends to improve performance.
when: the task is complex or creative
why: external rewards crowd out the engagement these tasks need

text: Reward correct use of level elements and let players learn from their earlier mistakes.
why: Reusing earlier encounters in later levels lets prior experience inform later successes.

text: Most games combine several reward types because each one satisfies a different player desire.
when: Designing the reward structure of a game.
why: A single reward type rarely satisfies all players.

text: Strong games are extended sequences of tangible, reachable, satisfying small objectives.
when: designing a long activity
why: Regularly attainable targets keep players engaged.

text: Seasonal resets limit rating drift because ratings do not survive long enough to drift far.
when: When player ratings are reset regularly, as in season play.

text: Fixed interval rewards support player strategy, fixed ratio rewards show growing mastery, and variable rewards make gameplay more exciting.
when: designing reward schedules

text: Judge a reward's value from the player's current situation, since a skill or item feels valuable only once its need is felt, such as a larger backpack only after inventory limits appear.
when: Designing skill trees, rewards, or resource economies
why: Perceived value is subjective and depends on what the player has experienced

text: Tune reward timing through repeated trial and error, accepting a good-enough balance rather than a perfect one.
when: Balancing a reward schedule
why: Reward pacing is discovered through iteration rather than derived in advance

text: Daily quests encourage logging in and playing, and quests that require a featured character or strategy, rotated over time, push players to explore systems they might otherwise miss.
when: when designing daily quests
why: Quests need players to log in and play, so completing them creates a reason to return.

text: Satisfaction from a gain follows diminishing returns, so many small gains spread over time feel better than the same total granted in a short window.
when: When gains are granted in a short window versus spread out gradually over a long time.
why: Each extra gain adds less satisfaction than the one before.

text: When community events are frequent, players keep checking back to learn what is coming up, which sustains return visits.
when: When events occur on a regular schedule
why: Players anticipate upcoming events and check for announcements.

text: When two stimuli repeatedly occur close together, the first comes to trigger the response that normally follows the second, without the learner acting deliberately.
when: When the pairing happens without the learner needing to take any action.
why: Association forms passively and largely implicitly.

text: In operant conditioning, the learner discovers that a particular action changes the likelihood of an outcome, so consequences shape how often the action is repeated.
when: When a learner's own action is followed by a reward or punishment.

text: When a previously rewarded behavior stops being reinforced, it declines, a process called extinction.
A disruptive behavior that goes unpunished or feels rewarded tends to increase over time.
when: Multiplayer behavior is left unchecked
why: Operant conditioning: consequences shape how often a behavior recurs

text: Well-practiced conditioned associations are retrieved almost instantly, faster than facts that must be worked out step by step.
why: conditioning bypasses calculation

text: Each time a memory is reinforced, it is reconsolidated and the forgetting curve becomes less steep.
when: When repetitions of the same information are spaced apart in time.
why: reconsolidation occurs at every repetition

text: Rewards can enhance motivation when they give useful information, confirm competence, or enable something people already wanted.
The four motivation types are not independent; together they shape perception, feelings, cognition, and behavior.
why: The four motivation types shape perception, feelings, cognition, and behavior together, so none operates in isolation; there is no fixed hierarchy among them.

text: Classical conditioning is passive association, while operant conditioning requires the learner to perform an appropriate action to receive a reward.
Operant conditioning, learning an action to gain a reward, is robust but transfers poorly; motivation can stop when rewards stop.
when: When a rewarded activity loses its external payoff or the player stops finding value in the reward
why: Behavior is tied to the reward contingency rather than to the skill itself.

text: Letting players work on several reward-bearing tasks at once superimposes variable ratio schedules on one another.
when: When players can work on several reward-bearing tasks at the same time
why: Each task pays out unpredictably, so overlapping tasks combine into a schedule where rewards arrive at irregular, unforeseeable moments.

text: In a variable interval schedule, checking more often lowers the chance of a reward, so players have less reason to repeat the action quickly.
why: Checking more often lowers the odds of a reward, so the player has less incentive to repeat the action quickly.

text: Attaching money to creative work can displace the intrinsic reasons developers have for it, such as wanting to make something great, gain recognition, progress, and autonomy.
when: When introducing pay or bonuses tied to creative output.
why: Extrinsic incentives can crowd out internal motivation.

text: Regular, visible progress in the work is the main driver of daily motivation, more than social approval or product quality.
when: When organizing creative work over days and weeks.
why: Seeing one's own advancement sustains engagement even when the overall game is still weak.

text: Rewards reinforce correctly executed mechanics, which teaches players how to play.
why: behaviorist reinforcement links rewarded actions to later repetition

text: Granting a bonus only when the player attacked during the turn ties the reward to action, so players who merely hoard resources gain nothing.
when: When the game's balance makes attacking a non-optimal strategy
why: Bonuses conditioned on attacking make passive resource hoarding worthless, so the reward is tied to the action itself.

text: Events that can occur on any action but arrive in bursts after long buildups behave like a variable ratio schedule.
when: When events can occur on any action but arrive in bursts after long buildups
why: Because each action has an unpredictable chance of producing the event, the timing behaves like a variable ratio reward schedule.

text: A variable-ratio schedule, rewarding after an unpredictable 1 to 20 responses, produces higher and steadier responding than rewarding every response.
why: A reward after an unpredictable number of responses keeps the player unsure when payoff comes, so responding stays high and steady.

text: Fixed schedules cause pausing after each reward and fast extinction when rewards stop, ratio schedules beat interval schedules, and variable ratio gives the highest, steadiest response.
why: Players pause after predictable rewards, and when expected rewards stop they quickly give up; unpredictable rewards keep responding steady because the timing is unknown.

text: Many staggered progression loops running at once give a small reward every few turns; each timer is deterministic, yet the combined schedule feels irregular.
when: When many staggered progression loops run concurrently and each rewards on a deterministic timer
why: The overlap of independent deterministic timers produces a combined reward timing that players perceive as irregular.

text: Unlocking newly evolved content as achievement rewards, with a capped set carried at once, ties content novelty to player progress.
when: When newly unlocked content is granted as achievement rewards and a limited set is carried at once

text: Layering several fixed ratio reward schedules keeps at least one close to payoff at any moment, because when one falls into its dip another is near its reward and the player shifts focus.
when: Designing reward loops that must avoid motivation gaps
why: Dips in one schedule are covered by others, so motivation stays high.

text: A monster giving 0 points with two-in-three chance and 30 points with one-in-three chance keeps the same average of 10 points as a fixed 10-point reward.
when: Designing a random payoff with a set average.
why: Matching the expected value preserves balance while changing how the reward feels.

text: A 10% chance of a 10-gold reward per enemy defeat yields a long-run average of 1 gold per kill, yet streaks of three rewards or fifty empty kills both occur.
when: Setting probabilities for randomized rewards
why: Each draw is independent, so streaks in both directions are normal even with a stable average.

text: Operant view: any rewarding operant behavior, such as gaming, drug use, sex, or eating, can become addictive.
why: Any rewarding operant behavior can become addictive, since the same reinforcement process underlies gaming as underlies drug use, sex, or eating.

text: Reward schedules vary on two axes: basis, where time gives an interval schedule and behavior gives a ratio schedule, and predictability, which is fixed or variable.
When an expected reward fails to arrive, it acts like punishment and makes the behavior less likely to be repeated.
when: The game signals a reward that the player then does not receive.
why: The missing reward is experienced as a negative consequence of the action.

text: A reinforcer is not automatically a reward, since the behaviorist vocabulary is easily confused with everyday meanings.
Grouping pleasure seeking and pain avoidance together as one motivation hides differences that matter for design.
why: Pleasure seeking and pain avoidance are separate sets of motivational circuits rather than ends of one continuum, so merging them hides distinct effects.

text: Operant conditioning ignores unobservable processes such as attention and memory, and it can overlook side effects.
why: The paradigm excludes unobservable processes like attention and memory, and its focus on observable behavior lets undesirable side effects go unnoticed.

text: Unintended rewards can spread harmful behavior, because players repeat actions they find rewarding.
when: When a game rewards harmful actions such as trolling, and players are free to experiment with them
why: Players repeat actions they perceive as rewarding, so an unintended reward for a harmful behavior spreads it.

text: When players can predict exactly when the next reward comes, they feel no pull to start a new cycle right after getting one.
why: A fixed ratio schedule's predictability produces long pauses after each reward, because the player waits until they decide to start the next cycle.

text: A token achievement for a very large effort feels underwhelming; match reward size to the time and effort invested.
when: When a large effort is rewarded with only a minor token such as an achievement unlock
why: Rewards inform players about their mastery, so a reward that is small relative to the effort is felt as disappointing.

text: If players can focus on just one reward schedule, they finish it, reach a large motivation gap, and stop; overlapping tasks and rewards spread across the world prevent this.
when: Designing reward schedules that players can complete individually
why: Finishing a lone schedule removes the reason to keep playing until a new one starts.

text: 1) Identify how the task satisfies competence, autonomy, and relatedness. 2) Frame the task around meaning and purpose for the player.
why: players find tasks rewarding when core needs and meaning are satisfied

text: 1) List every way the player grows stronger, such as loot, boss drops, level-up abilities, and exploration finds. 2) Note how often each appears across the game. 3) Build a timeline of sections, such as regions or quest lines. 4) Estimate section times for a reasonable playthrough. 5) Flag sections with many or very strong rewards and sections with few. 6) Model random rewards with a pseudorandom spreadsheet across one or more playthroughs. 7) Compare reward density in each section with how grindy players find it.
when: When checking whether reward pacing matches how players perceive grinding.
why: Mapping rewards over time reveals pacing gaps that are invisible in isolated item lists.

text: Never use physical punishment, which is unethical and harmful.
why: Physical punishment is generally less effective at changing behavior than rewards.

text: Record and display how often each random outcome occurs, so players can check for themselves whether the system is fair.
when: outcomes come from a random process players may doubt

text: Use DRH for quick, bursty activity such as timed combat challenges, and DRL for deliberate, paced activity rather than rushing.
when: choosing a reward schedule for a design goal
why: Each schedule shapes a distinct activity pattern.

text: Use variable intervals when steady low-intensity motivation over long periods is wanted; use fixed intervals when players can be expected to return at a known time.
why: The chance of reward drops with each early check, so players are not pushed to act again quickly.

text: Do not tie variable-ratio rewards to money, directly or via in-game currency indirectly tied to real money; use variable rewards to spice up gameplay instead.
when: Designing chance-based rewards such as loot boxes or card packs.
why: Such mechanics are linked to problem gambling and disordered gaming, and are ethically problematic especially when children are targeted.

text: Let the game world react to achievements, such as NPCs celebrating after a rescue, to reward players.
why: Without a reward signalling mastery, players perceive the lack as a penalty.

text: Deliver rewards close to the actions that earned them, because a reward received hours later is less meaningful.
when: designing reward timing
why: meaning is strongest when the reward is received

text: Variable interval trades intensity for continuity: it sustains motivation steadily but more weakly than a variable ratio schedule.
why: Randomized reappearance times avoid the motivation gaps that fixed timing produces.

text: Designs that only trigger behavior, like virtual Skinner boxes, extract intense behavior and may succeed briefly, but they lose players once the tricks are learned; designs built on fulfillment sustain engagement.
when: Choosing a reward structure for a game
why: Players who learn the reward tricks stop finding the experience worthwhile, while fulfilling experiences keep them playing.

text: Variable rewards are acceptable as engagement but become a dark pattern when used to push spending, as with slot machines and loot boxes.
when: Random rewards are tied to purchases made with real or in-game currency.
why: The reward mechanic shifts from engaging play to encouraging money spent.

text: In a single d6 push-your-luck turn, keep rolling below a turn total of 20 and stop above it; at exactly 20 rolling and stopping are equal.
when: a 1 ends the turn and other faces add their value
why: expected gain from one more roll is positive below 20

text: When behind, accept more risk to catch up; when ahead, prefer steady gains that avoid giving the opponent a run of good luck.
why: Merely keeping pace with a leader usually loses, while a steady lead denies the trailing player chances for lucky streaks.

text: Offer a choice between a safe small reward and a risky large reward, with rewards proportional to risks. Adding even a little of this can turn a monotonous game exciting.
when: Designing decision points where players pick between safety and risk
why: Risk-reward choices create tension and make dull play more engaging

text: Offering a difficulty increase after success, or giving bigger shares of rewards on later missions to successful players, creates an incentive to take on harder challenges.
when: Tying rewards to challenge choice
why: Players are motivated to accept greater risk when the reward grows.

text: A reward gains value when finding it means facing greater risk, so scarce loot tied to danger feels more valuable.
when: Loot located behind dangerous encounters.
why: Risk gives the reward its value.

text: In a format with stakes, a strategy that can hardly lose lets its owner play risk-free, distorting the format's incentives.
when: When each game is played for an ante stake.
why: Even a low win rate recovers wagered cards with a surplus, so losses are cushioned.

text: 1) Estimate each option's chance of success and its reward. 2) Multiply each reward by its chance to get expected values. 3) Adjust rewards so expected values match, so neither option is strictly better. 4) Test the estimates with prototypes.
when: When designing or checking choices that trade speed or safety against reward
why: Equal expected values make the choice a real decision rather than an obvious one; expected value reveals whether risky options are worth taking

text: Give the smallest, hardest-to-hit target the highest point value so that risk and reward pull the player toward it.
when: when assigning point values to targets of different size and danger
why: Higher reward for higher risk creates a meaningful choice between safe and risky targets

text: A SKU (stock keeping unit) is a unique inventory item, and each console release and each language version counts as its own SKU.
Sold in means a retailer bought copies from the publisher, while sold through means a customer bought them.
Existing sales relationships and forces can be a barrier; a product needing a large field sales force can be too costly to sell market by market.
Subscription revenue can weaken over time, pushing a game toward a free-to-play model.
when: a subscription game loses paying subscribers
why: Players may stop paying recurring fees

text: Some user-generated sites award cash prizes to top-rated games each week and month.
Publishers pay the royalty for every manufactured console unit up front, before games are delivered for retail.
On a $10 direct download sale, the developer generally collects about $7 before marketing costs.
why: Going direct removes publisher, retailer and disc-manufacturing layers from the revenue split.

text: Developer royalty rates can step up at unit thresholds, for example 10% up to 60,000 units, 15% up to 120,000, and 20% up to 240,000.
Treating the 70% storefront share as pure profit ignores marketing costs, which are usually substantial and can consume most of the remainder.
when: When a self-published game must spend to reach players.
why: Per-customer acquisition spend can leave very little of the storefront share.

text: Royalties calculated after deductions such as tax, duties, shipping, insurance, and returns invite creative accounting; define deductions narrowly and exclude publisher overhead.
when: When royalties are based on net sales revenue after publisher deductions.
why: Deductions give the publisher room to manipulate the royalty base.

text: When a publisher quotes sales, ask whether the figure is sold in or sold through before accepting it.
when: when a publisher quotes sales
why: Publishers must buy back unsold retail stock, so sold-in and sold-through counts can diverge sharply.

text: Calculate developer royalties on the publisher's share after the portal's cut, not on the full sale price.
Games with extensive public online documentation make their peaks easier to identify through analysis.
Some games ask players for app store reviews before the difficulty ramp takes effect.
Total downloads and app-store rankings by downloads or revenue are related measures of a game's reach.
Most games lose in the market, but reviews and awards spotlight winners while failures disappear from view.
When a press mention brings a download spike, trace where the new players came from so future content suits them.
Reach is worth about half a point, as the defensive half of Flying; since costs are whole numbers, a Reach-only card is rounded slightly above the curve.
when: Cards whose only ability is Reach.
why: Flying combines an offensive and a defensive benefit, and Reach supplies only the defensive one.

text: ROI = (R − C) / C, where R is total revenue and C is total cost including development, maintenance and marketing, expressed as a percentage. Breaking even gives 0%.
Obfuscated pricing depends on players trusting that buying more always saves more, which a bulk price inversion can break.
when: evaluating currency bundle pricing
why: Players who rely on that assumption may overspend.

text: Revenue-driven choices that damage users' interests can crowd out the UX mindset.
why: UX places people ahead of the business, so gains taken at users' expense conflict with it.

text: For an established game, review players' published strategies, tier lists, and derived math, then use them as a starting point or a check on your own analysis.
when: Analyzing balance in a game with a player community.

text: Base revenue on comparable titles, give a range rather than one figure, and ensure the low end of the range still shows a profit.
when: Presenting financial projections
why: A range with a profitable floor shows the project is viable even when results disappoint.

text: Read ARPU and ARPPU together when most players in a free-to-play game pay nothing.
when: Free-to-play game with a large non-paying majority.
why: Each figure alone gives an incomplete picture of spending.

text: Changing point values shifts what play is emphasized but does not change balance; board size and the number of distinct piece types do.
Running counts of random outcomes move toward their expected proportions over time, so displayed counts let players watch fairness emerge.
Sort by a balance value to group objects of similar power, with those far from the curve collecting at the top and bottom of the list.
why: Balance values are signed around zero, so distance from zero signals how far an object sits off the curve.

text: Show scores against the player's own previous score and against others' scores through a high-score list and achievements.
why: Comparison gives each run a reference point

text: When starting lives are few, an extra life is highly valuable, and a steady coin-based extra-life reward gives a low-level, continuous incentive.
when: designing reward systems with limited lives
why: Scarcity makes each life precious, and periodic rewards keep players motivated.

text: Point values for asteroids were 20, 50 and 100 for large, medium and small, and 200 and 1,000 for large and small saucers.
when: when setting point values for a tiered set of enemies
why: Escalating values reward the harder, smaller targets

text: In a two-player dice race, the score difference, which changes by at most the largest per-turn gap, can serve as a finite state machine giving exact win probability instead of a simulation estimate.
when: Two players accumulate scores through random dice rolls with a fixed maximum per turn.
why: Tracking only the difference keeps the reachable state range small and predictable as turns pass.

text: A single scoring metric can silently favor one play style over another, leaving the other style's skill unrewarded.
when: simple scoring based on total points
why: A single total-points number rewarded rapid firing, so players who favored careful aim scored lower, hiding their skill.

text: Expect the first balance models to be inaccurate; each playtest round should revise both the mathematical model and the balance as testing and play data reveal errors.
when: Once core mechanics are largely settled and formula spreadsheets are being started
why: First-pass numbers and formulas are guesses, so playtesting is needed to show whether the model's predictions hold.

text: A Monte Carlo simulation estimates a probability by repeating random trials many times and counting how often the event occurs.
Mathematical tools can analyze a game's systems, reveal relationships between objects, and identify and remove imbalances.
Game balance math needs only basic arithmetic and simple grade-school algebra; more advanced math can be learned just in time.

1) Set up a projectile in an isolated simulation and fire it with the guessed parameters. 2) Advance the physics at coarse intervals, recording positions. 3) Find the nearest point on the recorded piecewise linear path to the target; that distance is the closest approach. 4) Repeat the search with new guesses.
when: Simple force models give poor results and forces such as drag, lift, or wind must be modelled
why: Reuses the engine's own physics, so any modelled force or moving target is handled

text: 1) Build the random formulas. 2) Trigger a forced recalculation without editing. 3) Record the result. 4) Repeat several times and check that results fall in a narrow range.
when: Verifying a simulation estimate is stable.
why: Each edit reruns random cells, so forcing repeated recalculations samples new outcomes to see whether results cluster.

text: 1) Record all state needed at one time step on a single row. 2) Hardcode the initial state in row 1 with no formulas. 3) In each later row, compute the state from the row above. 4) Copy the formulas down to extend the simulation.
when: Spreadsheet programs that lack iterative calculation
why: Without iterative calculation, each row must carry the whole game state so the next row can be computed from it.

text: 1) Write a Monte Carlo simulation of the game. 2) Simplify if needed, such as treating card spaces as blank or applying a fixed buying policy. 3) Define power as cash plus chosen assets. 4) Average power over time across thousands of games. 5) Plot individual games to see single-session variation. 6) Judge sum type, feedback loops, ending speed, phases and length.
when: when assessing a board game's progression with simulation
why: Simulation reveals whether a game's economy and length suit its audience.

text: 1) Write the starting state as a probability vector. 2) Multiply the vector by the transition matrix. 3) Repeat until the vector stops changing. The result is the steady state.
when: finding the long-run share of time in each state
why: repeated multiplication converges to the stationary distribution

text: 1) Simulate many complete games with random outcomes. 2) Record each game's length. 3) Average the lengths to estimate the expected game length.
when: estimating game length for cases too complex to solve exactly
why: sampling approximates the distribution when the exact matrix is impractical

text: Physics-based targeting is costly and needs an engine able to run isolated simulations, so it suits cases where simpler force assumptions visibly fail.
when: Choosing between closed-form, bisection and physics-based targeting
why: Many simulations per shot consume time

text: Playtesting and analytics give the most reliable values but need a built game and real player data, while early in design an estimated first value is the only option.
when: Choosing how to set a situational cost during development
why: Real usage data requires a built game with players, which early design lacks and budgets may not allow, so a first estimate is needed.

text: Prices rise when players suspect a new use for an item, since they fear what rivals will do with it.
when: an item's use is rumored or inferred
why: fear of rivals' plans

text: In a positive-sum game, total power among players grows; in negative-sum it shrinks; in zero-sum it stays constant, with power only shifting between players.

Single-player game length can be modeled as a Markov chain whose states are the current score below the goal plus one absorbing state for finishing, giving the mean, median and mode of turns to finish.
when: A race-to-target game where each turn moves a score by a random spinner result.
why: The chain turns the random sequence of turns into a distribution of finishing times.

text: In single-player RPGs, currency is produced by grinding, trading occurs only between the player and NPCs (a command economy), and most resources are unlimited while some powerful items are scarce.
Well-balanced single-player and cooperative titles usually lean slightly toward the player, and that lean persists as the player's mastery grows.
when: single-player and cooperative games

text: Story-focused games gain too little from deep balance, so they can be left somewhat imbalanced, freeing resources for world and story.
when: Games whose appeal rests on social play, story, or other emotional triggers not tied to skill
why: Their value does not depend on skill, so the cost of high-skill balance is not justified and effort shifts to world and story.

text: When each element has one purpose, a tweak changes one aspect of play, so balancing becomes methodical rather than guesswork.
why: Each tweak then affects a single aspect, so the effect on other systems is predictable.

text: A game can lose stability when its length or late-game trade rules change, so those structural features should be rechecked after any change.
when: Changing game length or late-game trade rules.
why: New content, rule changes, and emerging strategies shift the relative value of existing items, so stability can break unexpectedly.

text: If all but one term of a card's equation is known, the leftover ability can be assigned the value that balances the equation.
when: a card has exactly one unknown ability
why: Once every other term is known, the equation has a single answer, so the missing value can be solved directly.

text: A situational effect is a mechanic whose benefit changes with circumstances. Situational balance is the process of setting a fixed cost for it.
Cost a situational option by its benefit multiplied by its probability of use when the player cannot know the situation in advance.
when: an option is only useful in some game situations and the player cannot foresee which
why: the expected benefit reflects how often the option actually pays off

text: Adjust a component's share of a combo's price for its side benefits and for any drawback that can hurt its own holder.
why: Travel, failure, and replacement costs add to the sticker price, so the true cost is higher than what is paid.

text: The strength of substitution between two goods indicates how efficiently one good replaces the other.
when: Comparing two substitute goods
why: Buyers switch to the cheaper of two near-equivalent options, so how much they switch reveals how close the substitute is.

text: Costing a symmetric effect by its average impact on the population ignores deck construction, which players control and which can make the effect far from even.
when: Symmetric effects in games where players build their own decks
why: Players choose deck contents knowing the effect, so population averages mislead

text: 1) Estimate the probability-weighted expected value of the benefit. 2) For some effects, find the maximum and minimum possible value. 3) Set the fixed cost within that range.
when: Setting a fixed cost for a situational effect before playtest data exists
why: The benefit varies with circumstances, and real usage data is unavailable until the game is built and played.

text: Include shadow costs when pricing options: hidden non-resource drawbacks behind listed prices, such as sunk costs and opportunity costs, or prices will seem arbitrary.
when: pricing options where past investment or unused alternatives matter
why: hidden costs make prices seem arbitrary to designers and players

text: Check whether revenue comes from many small spenders or a few large ones.
In a dice track game the mean game length sits above the median and mode, because a few very long games pull the mean upward while barely moving the median or mode.
when: interpreting average game length
why: long-tail outcomes shift the mean but not the middle of the distribution

text: Where card equations disagree, identify the pattern most cards follow and treat the outliers with suspicion.
when: When reverse-engineering a game's original balance math from its existing card stats

text: The observed rate equals successes divided by trials, and with more trials it moves closer to the theoretical probability.
Unweighted win rate averages mislead when strong characters are picked more; the play-weighted average can sit below 50% even if few exceed it.
1) Test with hardcore players to set the high benchmark. 2) Test with novices to set the low benchmark. 3) Tune the variables to fall in the median between the two.
when: Balancing a single difficulty for a target audience when multiple levels are impractical
why: Balancing to the median serves the largest share of the audience.

text: 1) Store the spinner weights in cells. 2) Make the Markov chain read those weights. 3) Adjust weights by hand or with a solver until the median game length is as close to a target as possible.
when: tuning a random spinner to hit a target game length
why: weights control the spread of outcomes, which sets the median

text: Add occasional enemies with higher or lower hit points or strength so difficulty has peaks and valleys rather than uniform levels.
why: Uniform difficulty feels flat, and outliers break predictability in a useful way.

text: Limit trading to one phase of the active player's turn, to that player only, and to resources only, with at least one resource on each side.
when: Designing a trading system between players
why: Limits on partner, timing, and item type change how often and how easily trades happen.

text: An economic system is a set of rules governing how resources are generated, acquired, traded and spent, broader than the currency players see.
Endogenous value is worth caused by factors inside the system; play money matters only within the game it belongs to.
A bet on an outcome the bettor cannot control is gambling; if the bettor has inside information or can influence the result, it is cheating.
when: Classifying a wager on a contest
why: Gambling depends on lack of control, and influence turns a bet into cheating.

text: A trade moves owned resources between players in exchange for something of value, so the giver owns the resource beforehand and both players gain something usable afterward.
when: Classifying exchanges between players
why: Keeping trade distinct from gifting lets their balance effects be analyzed separately

text: A gift moves allocated resources the giver does not own, and nothing returns to the giver; reciprocation may be suggested but is not required.
when: Classifying free transfers between players in F2P games

text: Most games with economic systems share five mechanics: resource generation, conversion, trading, consumption and limits; a game with only one is usually not considered to have an economic system.
Three phrases for a game's resource framework are often used as synonyms, though players usually mean which currencies are earned and spent, and in what amounts.
Explicit futures enable four kinds of deals: buying on credit, lending resources, favorable deals for later considerations, and short- or long-term pacts.
Trade limits on item type, timing, and partner exist to prolong play, block exploitation, prevent kingmaking, and simplify rules.
A fixed barter economy keeps card values constant, requires trades to match in card count, and allows trading at all times.
Light trade restrictions preserve tension and strategy, while unrestricted trade suits children's and mass-audience games where simple exchange is enough.
why: Trade mechanics turn plain exchange into layered choices and give the designer control over how play unfolds.

text: In a conflict over features, the party holding the money usually prevails, so designers gain influence by explaining features in financial terms.
when: when negotiating features or scope with budget holders
why: Whoever controls the money has the final say, so framing a feature as revenue-generating is more likely to persuade them.

text: A cost attached to each trade removes resources from the economy and reduces trivial trades; use trade costs to control resource flow between players or to remove currency.
why: Money taken out through the fee acts as a sink that stops the currency supply from inflating.

text: When a leader's output snowballs past what they can use, or trading is central and they gain a slight lead, rivals may refuse to deal with them, slowing them.
when: In economic games where production snowballs or trading is central and a player gains a slight lead.
why: Refusing trades denies the leader the means to extend the lead.

text: Equipping a collected reward turns it into an ability the player can use for the rest of the game.
why: Equipped souls turn a long, repeated reward process into a lasting upgrade that makes later interactions more rewarding.

text: Limiting trade partners, timing, or trade counts makes players gather resources more slowly and reduces the role of negotiation.
Holding traded items for a period, set by account security and whether traders are friends, helps block exploitation such as multi-account gifting farms.
Differing valuations create arbitrage: a trader can profit by moving items from players who ignore them to players who prize them.
If a seller must buy or keep an unsold item, a penalty makes sellers offer items that others value.
when: Unsold items are forced back onto the seller
why: Forced buy-back makes a worthless listing costly to the seller, so the seller has to pick items others will bid on.

text: Trading rests on mutual benefit: each side exchanges a resource it values less for one it values more, so both gain from the exchange.
when: Two players hold resources of differing value to them
why: Value differs between holders, creating gains on both sides

text: Designers create the need to trade by giving each player a different assortment of resources and keeping them scarce, so no one has everything when needed.
when: Designing resource distribution that should drive trading
why: Uneven, scarce holdings make each player depend on others

text: Rewards not connected to a meaningful purpose or impact are a common pitfall that undermines motivation.
why: Motivation rests on satisfying players' needs for competence, autonomy and relatedness, which rewards with no purpose cannot meet.

text: Clear rewards for effort can reward mediocrity, so a reward structure may pay out for minimal effort.
why: Simple, legible reward logic ties payouts directly to actions, so collecting them needs little skill or effort.

text: Calling gifts 'trades' blurs the distinction between owned exchanges and allocated transfers, which confuses discussion of their economic effects.
when: Naming player-to-player transfers in F2P games
why: Gifts involve resources not owned beforehand and nothing returned, so naming them trades mislabels the exchange.

text: 1) List how currency and resources are generated. 2) Identify conversions into permanent goods. 3) Note trading rules. 4) List consumption paths. 5) Check finite limits on items and buildings. 6) Identify zero-sum transfers.
when: When analyzing an existing game's economy against the five mechanics.
why: Covering each mechanic reveals where the economy is incomplete or imbalanced.

text: 1) Gather five object types with six of each. 2) Deal them randomly and evenly. 3) Define the goal and which trades are allowed. 4) Decide which information is public or hidden. 5) Ensure no starting advantage, or keep rounds short and repeat them so luck averages out.
when: Designing a trading game with random starting hands
why: Random deals can give unequal starts, so fairness needs either equal starts or averaging over rounds

text: 1) Limit trades per player per day with a time-based cost. 2) Cap the number of open trade postings to stop players from flooding the board with bad offers.
when: When trade exploitation or spam threatens the economy.
why: The per-trade cost acts as a sink that pulls currency out of the economy to prevent inflation.

text: 1) Define the roles: four sellers each hold one identical resource, and four buyers want the lowest price. 2) Decide which side, if any, holds the advantage. 3) Assess whether each mechanic feels interesting, boring, tense, or frustrating to each side.
when: Designing a multi-seller, multi-buyer auction

text: Show full information about traded items; when players cannot misrepresent items, the trading system is hard to abuse.
why: Total information about received items leaves no room to deceive a trade partner, so the system is hard to use for griefing.

text: Forbidding trades during dice rolls and movement avoids ambiguity about when ownership switches mid-action.
when: When a trade could change which player owns something while another player's roll or movement is still resolving.
why: Blocking trades at that moment avoids needing special rules for ownership changing mid-landing.

text: Tie rewards to deliberate player actions that the player understands and can control.
when: Designing achievements, trophies, and goals
why: Rewarding deliberate, controllable actions feels more meaningful than rewarding things the player did not know about or was not trying for.

text: Keep free-to-play onboarding short so players reach the core experience before they get bored.
when: Designing free-to-play games.
why: Players abandon long introductions before experiencing the game.

text: Trade need not be avoided, but designers should watch for the openings it creates in a closed economy.
why: Trade brings unpredictability into an otherwise closed economy, letting players find exploits and trade money for time.

text: Trading rare items for gold makes them attainable but removes the gradual resistance curve toward a goal.
when: Adding trading to a loot economy
why: Coarse exchange gives no granular steps, so progress feels abrupt.

text: Unique, resellable items can add gameplay value, but selling in-ecosystem items instead of the game copy turns play into earning.
when: When the product sold is in-game items rather than the game copy itself.

text: In a transition matrix, columns represent the current state and rows represent the next state, so each entry gives the probability of moving from the column state to the row state.
when: constructing or reading a Markov transition matrix
why: this layout makes each column a distribution over next states

text: A board-game transition matrix over squares is sparse: each state reaches at most six next states with probability 1/6 each for a six-sided die.
when: building a transition matrix for a die-driven track
why: a single die roll limits reachable squares to six

text: Check that each column of a transition matrix sums to 1 before running a Markov chain; a missing entry can be found from the others.
when: validating or building a transition matrix
why: each column is a probability distribution over next states, so a sum other than 1 breaks the chain

text: A first-player or second-player advantage can differ by skill level, so win rates across many games at varied skill levels can reveal it, while optimal play may yield a draw.
when: Judging which seat or side has an edge in a simple game.
why: Novices make mistakes that favor one seat, so results depend on skill.

text: Skipping the starting player's first draw reduces the advantage of going first.
At top tournament level, moving first in chess gives a slight advantage whose cause, tactical, strategic or psychological, is not conclusively settled.
when: top-level competitive play

text: In four-player free-for-alls, plain win rate averages 25%. Define a win as finishing above a chosen opponent or in the top two to restore a 50% average.
when: Multiplayer matches with more than two players
why: Only one of four players wins a plain free-for-all, so the average is low; counting top-two finishes gives two winners per match.

text: In free-for-all games, expected results can be based on average opponent rating, strongest opponent, weakest opponent, or a weighted mix.
when: Free-for-all multiplayer rating.
why: Different reference opponents predict outcomes differently.

text: Real-time fixed-price sales go first-come, first-served, while turn-based versions give the first player the first option.
when: Choosing how a fixed-price sale resolves
why: In turn-based sales the offer passes in turn order, so the first player is offered the item before anyone else.

text: A weapon that destroys objects needing several hits from a weaker weapon feels more powerful.
when: Comparing two weapons that break the same object types
why: Faster destruction is read as higher power, shaping how players perceive weapon strength.

text: A strictly dominated option is worse than another option on every attribute that matters, so it offers no real choice.
Within-object versatility means an object works acceptably across several situations but is never the best choice for any one of them.
A creature whose cost, power and toughness are all unknown needs three independent equations to solve.
when: vanilla creatures with no abilities
why: each unknown needs its own equation

text: Power-ups give a player a temporary boost and are kept scarce through limited number, short duration, or use only in certain states.
Sparklines can show each game object's power level relative to others along a cost curve, one small chart per row.
When unsure of an object's strength, err weak: too-weak objects are rarely used but do little harm, while too-strong ones are always used and crowd out balanced objects.
when: When unsure how strong or costly an object should be.
why: A too-strong object gets picked every time and crowds out balanced options, while a too-weak one only goes unused.

text: Pair each strength with a drawback so objects are comparable and roster members are roughly equal in strength; e.g., a sword dealing more damage might be rarer or pricier.
when: When designing competing items, options or rosters with trade-offs
why: Compensating drawbacks let different objects be worth choosing in different situations; pairing gives roughly equal total value.

text: Unique objects that resist numerical comparison are best balanced through playtesting and analytics that reveal how players use them.
when: game objects with no direct numeric equivalent
why: numbers cannot compare them directly

text: In stats-heavy games, cost-curve analysis gives a first balance estimate before playtesting.
why: Costs and benefits are first lined up along a curve, so playtesting then only has to smooth out the edges.

text: Start by valuing a benefit that works half the time at half the value of an always-on version, then adjust for how much players value predictability and how much control they have over the outcome.
when: Valuing coin-flip or probabilistic effects
why: Expected value gives a baseline; predictability and player control shift it

text: Among units, the one with the lowest average remaining health is the most balanced.
when: When characters are rotated among players across a tournament with varied matchups.
why: Blowouts reveal a dominant character, while narrow wins reveal evenly matched ones, so close outcomes mark balance.

text: Cost specialized units that are only useful in one situation as if that situation arises nearly 100% of the time, and adjust the access cost rather than the unit's power.
when: a unit is built only when a specific situation is expected
why: players who pay to access the unit will use it when it is relevant

text: A temporary damage multiplier can make a normally weak option the best choice while active, so balance must be checked in those states.
Keep small enemy groups always beatable as a reliable gear source, and reserve larger groups to guard the best treasure.
why: Early small groups guarantee gear, while larger guarded groups add risk that makes the big treasures worth pursuing.

text: Assuming uniform 1-5 for Strength and Damage (20% each), each extra Strength point adds 20% to both the chance of eliminating the opponent's card and the chance of surviving.
when: Estimating card values before playtesting
why: Opponent Strength is uniform over 1-5, so each added point covers an equal fifth of outcomes for both winning and surviving.

text: Players facing unknown future challenges favor versatile objects, since versatility's value rises with uncertainty; known situations favor specialists, who win only when predictable.
when: The player must commit to equipment before learning the situation; future challenges are unknown
why: Players do not know what they will face.

text: Giving each unit one numeric value lets the AI sum values to judge which side is ahead and compare value with cost to pick the best unit to build.
when: strategy and board games
why: A single number replaces complex capability calculations, letting the AI sum each side and compare value against cost.

text: When ammo is limited, players switch to weapons that have more ammo available; when ammo is plentiful, they fire freely and use more weapons.
when: Ammo supply varies across a shooter
why: Players optimize for resources they can sustain.

text: A low-damage stun that frequently precedes a high-damage follow-up can make a character frustrating without being overpowered, because opponents spend much of each match disabled.
when: A character's win rate is middling but player complaints about play experience are high.
why: Time spent stunned removes the opponent's agency, even when damage totals look modest.

text: A side dealing steady damage against a side dealing rare large hits: raising the required damage changes which side is favored, so the balanced target is found by search.
when: Comparing a steady attacker against an infrequent high-damage attacker in a race.
why: Larger targets give the high-variance side more chances to hit, shifting the win odds.

text: A common setup makes each weapon 25% stronger than the previous (125% of its damage) and adds 5% cost to weapons with a critical-hit chance.
when: Using a fixed growth rate for PvE weapon progressions

text: Near-identical creature pairs can reveal an exchange rate, where one point of power or toughness may equal one colorless mana.
when: comparing creatures that differ by one stat point

text: Strength's expected benefit is ((Strength-1)/5) × opponent's Damage; with average Damage 3, this is ((Strength-1)/5) × 3.
when: Estimating how much a card's Strength prevents incoming damage.
why: Strength only blocks opponent cards with lower Strength, so its chance of working scales with how many values lie below it.

text: Leaving an overpowered item in place distorts overall game balance, not just its own use, and changes how long players take to finish the game.
Objects fail in two ways: one so weak that no one uses it is unbalanced, and one so strong it is found early and never replaced makes the rest of a long game pointless.
when: When tuning object power across a long game
why: Both extremes remove meaningful choice.

text: Relying on statistics alone misses problems, so designers must also keep an intuitive sense of how the game feels.
when: Balancing with data
why: Numbers do not capture everything about play.

text: Raw expected value overstates high-variance actions when their benefit is capped by the situation, such as damage beyond an enemy's remaining hit points.
when: Comparing attacks against low-health targets
why: Excess benefit is never received.

text: Balancing for one target skill level leaves other players exposed to strategies that dominate for them.
when: When balancing a skill-driven game across more than one skill level.
why: Each added skill level multiplies the strategies to consider, making simultaneous balance across every level close to impossible.

text: 1) Pick two cards identical in cost and stats except for one ability. 2) Compare their costs. 3) Treat the cost difference as that ability's value.
when: Estimating the value of a single keyword ability.
why: Isolating one difference measures each ability separately.

text: 1) Give a unit a special advantage. 2) Pair it with a matching drawback.
when: Balancing a unit or option
why: Each option's advantage is matched by a defined weakness, so no option overwhelms the rest and the set stays balanced.

text: 1) Set starting stats from player expectations for each option. 2) Sum each option's stats. 3) Use the sum of a baseline option as the anchor for designing the others.
when: designing starting characters, races, or classes
why: Summing stats gives one comparable total, so a class that comes in low can be spotted and raised.

text: 1) Identify each extra on the item. 2) Value it as a percent increase on the base cost. 3) Offset that value for drawbacks such as rarity or cooldown.
when: Pricing items with extra properties
why: Consistent percentage valuation keeps extras comparable.

text: 1) Learn the rules by playing the baseline against itself. 2) Play the unit against the baseline until you can call it too weak, too strong, or about right. 3) Make one or two changes to health, resources, one ability, or one roll. 4) Return the unit to rotation and repeat.
when: When a roster is too large to test every character against every other.
why: Testing against one fixed opponent avoids hundreds of pairwise matchups while still judging each character.

text: 1) Place each candidate unit type in every slot of a fixed grid and total the output of each layout. 2) Divide each layout's output by its total cost. 3) Check whether the highest-output and highest-efficiency layouts match. 4) Compute each type's output per cost, crediting support units with the damage they enable. 5) Compare the types' efficiencies.
when: When comparing unit types placed in a fixed grid of slots under a fixed budget.
why: The highest-output layout and the highest-output-per-cost layout can differ, so both must be checked.

text: 1) Compare what the player can already do with what the new object adds that nothing else provides. 2) Multiply that added benefit by the share of time it is useful.
when: The player can carry many objects and swap them freely
why: Without opportunity cost, an object's value is its added benefit over existing options times how often that benefit applies.

text: Judge a damage, cost or reward value against the target's HP, the weapon's maximum damage and the rest of the economy, not in isolation.
why: Challenge and reward come from how numbers relate to each other, so a single figure means little on its own.

text: Tune each unit's values by comparing its benefit against its cost, then verify the balance through playtesting.
why: Power and cost trade-offs only show their real balance once units are prototyped and played.

text: Assign each extra point of attack and each special effect, such as healing or stat bonuses, a fixed value in the anchor unit, chosen by the designers.
when: building a supporting math
why: Each effect needs a number before items can be priced consistently.

text: Check overall balance across top, middle and low tiers, and check whether a specific concern is a real problem.
when: Balancing a roster of characters
why: Uneven tiers are acceptable when each tier has many options and no character is useless or overpowering.

text: Judge a new unit by three questions: is it fun with real choices, is it balanced against the baseline without extreme matchups, and do its mechanics match its theme?
when: designing a new unit
why: Unusual mechanics create very strong or very weak matchups against many other characters, breaking balance beyond the baseline.

text: Judge specialized units, such as ground-only or air-only towers, against all-purpose units across every enemy type rather than a single one.
when: When comparing a unit that works only against some enemy types with an all-purpose unit.

text: Weigh each balance change's benefit against its cost to fiction, pacing, player expectations, and other parts of the experience before adopting it.
why: Fairness and strategic depth are worth nothing if the change breaks narrative coherence, flow, accessibility, or clarity.

text: Solving a problem with a computer begins by choosing an abstraction: the subset of data relevant to the task, keeping properties that matter and ignoring peripheral ones.
A clear problem statement widens the creative space, gives a standard for judging ideas, and aligns team members who might otherwise solve different problems.
Games need not follow physical laws, so designers can distill physical interaction into abstract forms and use rules that manipulate arbitrary relationships between variables to widen expression.
why: Unlike the physical world, a game can link arbitrary variables, so expression and connection are not limited to what physics allows.

text: Changing the abstract relationships between objects can alter the meaning of their spatial relations, giving rules a human meaning beyond challenge.
when: Seeking expressive depth beyond triumph, collection and challenge
why: Spatial meaning comes from the rules linking objects, not only from their positions.

text: Modeling even a seemingly trivial space abstractly can reveal surprising design insights.
when: A game appears to have no space
why: All games hold information or state somewhere, so even a point-like game can be modeled as a space, exposing design insights.

text: Represent elements abstractly to leave room for players' imagination; concrete detail, as in shooters and sports games, rarely supports rich player-spun stories.
when: the goal is for players to generate their own stories
why: distant representation invites players to fill gaps

text: Change how a decision feels by revealing or hiding existing information before reworking systems, since information changes are usually quicker and easier.
why: Adding or removing information changes how a decision is thought through without altering mechanics, so the game itself stays the same.

text: Each yes/no question halves the remaining possibilities, so twenty well-chosen questions can single out one answer among over a million.
when: Turning a guess-only riddle into a puzzle with progress
why: Two to the power of twenty exceeds one million

text: An abstract variable gains meaning only through the goals and relationships a designer defines, such as a collectible that matters because it restores health or counts toward a goal.
when: Designing goals for abstract variables that have no inherent meaning.
why: A value matters only when it links to a measurable step toward an explicit goal, such as unlocking content.

text: Animation actions range from primitive feedback such as particle effects and recoil to large sequences such as cutscenes driven by a camera on a predefined track.
when: Classifying AI actions
why: Animations provide the visual feedback that makes actions readable to players.

text: Action games are real-time games that test reaction time and hand-eye coordination.
Action games can increase visual attention and the number of objects a player can attend to at once.
Build boss fights as choreographed stages tied to a play style that reveal the boss's vulnerabilities, so players learn weaknesses mid-fight; a single boss can take 20 to 30 minutes.
when: designing bosses
why: Scripted phases let players learn the weakness during the fight.

text: Choosing which actions exist is the most fundamental design decision, and small changes to actions can have large ripple effects on emergence or predictability.
why: Without actions nothing happens, and changes to the action set propagate into what emerges or what stays predictable.

text: Long action animations let normal players catch up with perfect play, lowering the skill ceiling, while fast action and precise controls raise it and keep players striving.
why: Delays let ordinary players mentally close the gap with a perfect player, shrinking the difference between them.

text: With a small cap on active shots, projectiles that must cross the screen block new fire, so usable fire rate falls as target distance grows.
when: a cap on simultaneous projectiles
why: New shots cannot fire until an earlier one leaves the screen.

text: The same airborne attack button triggers different moves depending on whether the jump began below or at maximum running speed.
when: When the character's speed at takeoff determines which jump is triggered.

text: Leaving the ground locks facing direction, and air steering becomes lateral and at a reduced rate rather than rotational.
Once upward speed reaches zero, a much stronger gravity pulls the character down quickly, so jumps have little sustain.
why: A higher gravity at the apex returns the character to the ground fast, so there is little hang time.

text: A narrow line-shaped attack is strong when enemies line up and weak when they surround the unit, so its value depends on enemy geometry.
why: A stream strikes everything along its length, so enemies in a line are all hit while surrounding enemies mostly fall outside it.

text: Circular area attacks rarely hit their full area, and they offer fewer situations than directional attacks.
why: Full circular damage needs enemies surrounding the unit, which opponents can easily avoid, so its options stay limited.

text: A slower attack rate allows shoot-and-retreat tactics that frequent attacks make impossible.
why: Between slow shots there is time to reposition, while a frequently attacking unit gives no window to move.

text: Limited ammunition that drops by one per shot, refilling only after a unit spends a full turn on a supply tile, creates a firing-versus-resupply trade-off.

1) Name the intended combat feel. 2) Choose the trigger: every turn, passing another player, or landing on a set space. 3) Define mechanics that support core play. 4) Define outcomes and effects on each participant. 5) Write clear rules that feel native to the game.
when: designing house rules for a game without combat
why: Combat added to a game without one must support the existing core play, or it will feel disconnected from it.

text: Never place a player in a state where death is certain and no response is possible; deaths should trace back to mistakes or unnecessary risks.
why: Players accept death they could foresee and avoid, but an unavoidable death with no response feels unfair.

text: Arcade racing targets a broad audience with accessible handling, while simulator racing targets enthusiasts with realistic driving.
Aesthetics are how a game looks, sounds, smells, tastes and feels, relating most directly to player experience; early prototypes normally leave out its visual and aural dramatic elements.
Ending a hazard's sound and its camera effects when the player leaves the area signals that they are safe.
why: The sound and camera effects are the danger's signal, so removing them when leaving reveals the threat has passed.

text: Levels look cluttered yet feel open when passable platforms act as resources rather than obstacles.
when: When platforms are passable unless flagged as impassable and the swing mechanic already demands focus.
why: Passable platforms can be used to move through, so the space feels open even when visually crowded.

text: Atmosphere is a diffuse emotional haze that permeates a game and is felt when nothing salient is happening, rather than being tied to specific events.
Beauty is not a property of any particular feature; something is beautiful when perceiving it is pleasurable.
Shade is diffused light filtered through screens, curtains, or stained glass.
Shadowspace is an area where the player can move undetected because shadow hides them, making one area read as separate spaces.
A gym level is a test room used to observe game feel, such as how fast players aim and whether they overshoot or fall short of a target.
Atmosphere is usually serene and contemplative, but it can also be negative, such as a sense of dread.
Sound can push players away from hazards as well as draw them toward objects of interest.
Levels communicate mainly through sight and sound, with little use of touch.
Aesthetics layered over a simple model make digesting that model pleasurable, as in computer RPGs built on simple rule systems.
when: when a game's underlying rules are simple
why: Sensory pleasure offsets the effort of learning the model.

text: Once the abstract layout works, apply aesthetics to it, since aesthetics can bias an early view of the space.
when: Shaping a game world
why: A sound structure supports the look built on top of it.

text: Direct beauty toward a specific purpose rather than spreading it over everything.
when: When deciding where to invest visual beauty.
why: Concentrated beauty serves the design more than uniform beauty.

text: Cover a whole area with one large reverb volume, then place smaller volumes inside it and give them higher priority.
when: Designing reverb for an area with distinct sub-spaces
why: A higher priority makes the nested volume's settings win where the two overlap, so the inner space keeps its own sound.

text: Hint at a meditative space with music that fades in as the player approaches, since injured players will head toward the sound for safety.
when: when a meditative space is hard to preview visually
why: players in need of safety are drawn toward soothing sounds

text: Environmental cues such as breezes, placed so players feel them during the relevant action, can reinforce a setting's feel.
Shadow is the absence of light caused by an obstruction; it hides occupants, letting them see without being seen, so moving from dark into light makes the player the watched one.
when: in areas with mixed lighting
why: Lit areas expose players to observers in the dark.

text: Switching a sound set when the player crosses a volume boundary suits sound changes at room thresholds.
when: generating or designing rooms with different sounds
why: sound changes at the boundary match the space the player enters

text: Shadows cast perpendicular to the player's sight line form a repeating rhythm that pulls the player along the main path.
Shadow lines parallel to the player's sight line converge on a vanishing point, which can direct the player toward a destination.
why: Perspective distortion makes lines running into the depth of the scene meet at one point.

text: Hazards such as projectile waves or obstacles timed to musical cues make the player's movement and the soundtrack line up, so play itself feels musical.
when: In constant-runner or rhythm games where hazards arrive in waves synced to music.
why: Repeated exposure teaches players to anticipate the rhythm, so their inputs drift into time with the music.

text: Moving static objects relative to the avatar's movement can create an impression of speed.
Atmosphere emerges from visuals, sound, music and mechanics working together, so each channel should reinforce the others.
Environmental reactions such as dust, debris, spray patterns and chunks breaking off reinforce the perceived force and material of the environment.
when: Impacts on surfaces
why: Each reaction is a visible clue to material and force.

text: Meditative spaces are small, calm areas that give low-intensity moments between combat and platforming, either for enjoying avatar movement or for a restful atmosphere.
when: Between intense combat or platforming sections, where pacing needs relief.
why: Pauses from intense action let players mentally recover and get ready for what comes next.

text: Fancy visuals can make a game's functional space look more complex than it really is, so model the space by which positions matter in play.
when: Games with elaborate visuals over a functionally simple discrete space.
why: Visual detail does not change which positions and moves affect outcomes.

text: If a game's appearance suggests one balance of dexterity and thought but its play delivers another, both audiences may reject it.
when: When a game's visuals signal a genre that its mechanics do not match
why: Players who expect action or puzzles are disappointed when the other demand dominates

text: Beauty clashes with grim themes such as depression, horror, or unease, so applying it there undermines the intended aesthetic.
when: When designing games with dark or unsettling themes.
why: Pleasant beauty works against the feelings the theme aims to produce.

text: Calm views do not reliably preview meditative spaces, so these spaces work best as surprises or refuges rather than advertised destinations.
Tuning movement in an empty space makes jump height and speed hard to judge; add platforms and topology early.
when: While the movement system is being implemented.
why: Surrounding geometry gives motion meaning and a reference point for judging distances like jump height.

text: 1) Describe the game's mood without words. 2) List visual content that could deepen it. 3) List audible content that could deepen it. 4) Check that visuals, sounds, music and mechanics pull toward one mood.
when: the world feels flat or lacks a distinct mood, or during aesthetic review
why: atmosphere surrounds players and makes them part of the game world

text: 1) Use music. 2) Use slow-paced interaction. 3) Apply a fiction to flavor the mood.
when: When building an atmosphere-focused game.
why: These elements together build a background mood that the fiction then colors.

text: 1) Build the volume from a brush sized to the room geometry. 2) Snap it to the room with a mould command. 3) Enlarge it slightly so it is easy to select. 4) Hide BSP geometry if the volume is hard to select.
when: Placing reverb volumes in an editor viewport
why: A volume the same size as its room is hard to select while the room geometry is visible

text: 1) Place the one directional light at the angle each level needs. 2) Tune ambient color. 3) Tune light intensity. 4) Tune light color to vary the conditions.
when: when only one dynamic light is affordable, such as on mobile
why: One sun-like light plus ambient tuning can produce varied moods.

text: Treat aesthetics as a core part of the whole player experience, not as surface decoration added after mechanics are finished.
why: A designer shapes the entire experience, and visuals and sound affect how players engage with it.

text: Every room a generator creates should have room tone, since no space should be silent.
when: procedurally generating rooms
why: silence makes generated spaces feel unreal

text: Check the radii of sound sources placed near walls, since each source can leak into neighbouring rooms.
when: placing sound sources in generated or designed rooms
why: sources leak through walls

text: Use sound triggers for warnings or rewards, and toggleable sounds at objectives for gentle steering.
Treat lighting and weather as part of environment design rather than decoration, and include them from the start of a generated space.
when: when designing or generating a natural environment
why: weather and light make environments more convincing and dynamic

text: Form-follows-function can be broken for gameplay reasons, but the resulting ambiguity must be weighed against the gameplay gain.
when: A gameplay need conflicts with a clear visual signal.
why: Mismatched form costs player understanding.

text: Atmosphere games de-emphasize individual emotional punches and let players sink into a thick mood, while punch-driven games deliver sharper moment-to-moment peaks.
when: When choosing a game's overall emotional approach.
why: Focusing on mood spreads emotion thinly over time rather than concentrating it in peaks.

text: In the early and mid-1990s most game AI was hard-coded, and hard-coding remains common on modest platforms such as handhelds, PDAs, and mobile phones.
Designers' ideas about character behavior are rarely fixed, and some hard-looking features are simple while some simple-looking ones are hard.
Strong guards make player fighting in a settlement far less likely, though determined groups can still take it by killing every guard.
when: Guards are strong and numerous
why: An attacker must defeat all guards before fighting inside

text: A player hiding with two entrances must guess which one the opponent will use, and their choice of watching direction determines whether an entering opponent is killed or gains the first shot.
when: Positional standoffs with multiple entry points.
why: Deadly weapons make the first shot decisive, so the guess made before sight of the opponent settles the duel.

text: Players will look for tricky ways to avoid punishment, so consider how they might dodge a penalty before adding it.
when: When designing a harsh penalty such as permanent data loss
why: Severe loss states give players a strong incentive to find workarounds

text: A simple predator can wander, chase prey when it sees them, and return home when prey is absent.
when: Designing a basic predator's state logic.
why: Each intermediary link makes indirect control harder, so creatures near the top need simple logic.

text: Seek runs in constant time and uses constant memory.
Use the simplest technique supporting the required behavior; simple techniques do most game AI work. Add a specialized technique only when a specific AI-based gameplay effect requires it.
why: Specialized techniques add flavor only in small doses; overusing them can ruin the game.

text: Seek: 1) compute the vector from character to target; 2) normalize it; 3) scale it to maximum acceleration; 4) output as linear acceleration with zero angular component. Flee uses the same calculation with direction reversed.
A casual doodle can sometimes become the central theme of a game.
Symbolic containers such as crates or pots signal expected items, prompting players to search a space.
why: players associate containers with items

text: Style and form carry a game's visual language, communicating with players about the space.
In Western culture, red suggests passion or love, blue suggests sadness or tranquility, and yellow suggests happiness.
Distinctive work often lies in its rhythm, patterns, and style rather than in the specific moves or techniques.
why: The same tricks felt new when performed with a different rhythm and style, so presentation changes how they read.

text: When your visual look is distinctive and attractive, consider building your games around it.
why: A distinct visual style is one of the two routes by which designers become famous.

text: Order, complexity, repetition, and visual rhythm, such as similarly scaled repeated elements, help players sort visual information and make a space easy to categorize.
when: When arranging objects within a scene
why: Consistent patterns reduce the effort needed to read a space

text: Vertical structure can carry symbolic meaning, such as linking earth and heaven or enclosing a sacred interior, and can shape how occupants feel about a space.
when: Designing sacred, monumental or emotionally charged spaces
why: Verticality communicates meaning and mood beyond its practical function.

text: Realistic scenes of animals and conquering armies at an entrance warn visitors of the consequences of defying power before they go in.
why: Architecture was used to convey a ruling power's might and ferocity.

text: Tall pointed arches and vertical linear elements can suggest power and a mythical presence in a level.
Toy boxes need no polished environment art, since players never reach them.
when: Developer test scenes that players cannot reach
why: Their purpose is mostly functional for testing, so they do not need to look finished for players.

text: A limited or dominant color palette can produce a moodier look than full color, and can imitate shade in 2D games.
when: in 2D or retro-style visuals
why: Restricted colors shape atmosphere and suggest shadow.

text: When environmental symbols are distinct and repeated, prefabricated objects become a visual language that players gradually learn to read.
why: Repeated exposure to a unique look lets players learn what the object means.

text: Camouflage depends on material pattern tags that designers must set for every material, so its quality depends on the level's markup.
why: The camouflage check reads the pattern of whatever material lies behind the character, and designers supply those pattern types.

text: 1) Assign a material palette per level or stage. 2) Choose natural, homely materials for safe areas. 3) Choose rough, machine, or hazardous, damaged materials for dangerous areas, so progression is readable at a glance. 4) Apply via tile sets and color maps.
when: When varying generated or authored spaces along a multi-level quest journey
why: Material change signals progression at a glance

text: 1) Find a vista that shows a significant part of a world. 2) Diagram the visual forces that draw the player's eye. 3) Look for environment art assets arranged in triads.
when: When analyzing or designing a wide view in open-world or roleplaying games
why: Visual forces guide attention across a vista

text: Draw everyday objects using measuring and referencing for proportion, varied line weight for depth, and shading or hatching for lighting; finish with a hierarchical drawing that directs attention to key objects.
when: practicing sketch fundamentals

text: A degenerate strategy succeeds in every situation, giving the best payoff for least risk, so it is obviously the best choice and turns the decision into a nondecision.
Non-zero-sum: gains and losses need not cancel, so totals may be above or below zero and all players may win or lose together; each should focus on own winning.
Strategies that beat each other in cycles, such as the triangle, and asymmetrical structures like four-move castle battles lack pure equilibria; none dominates, so optimal play is a probability mix.
If one choice is always optimal over full play, players converge on it, the game plays out identically and feels flat, and the decision carries no meaning.
when: two-choice situations
why: A fixed best answer removes meaningful decisions.

text: Unequal sides with different win conditions provoke debate: novices spend much time testing whether one side has the advantage, while experienced players may judge it balanced.
why: Uncertainty about who holds the advantage keeps players debating fairness, since the right strategy is not obvious.
