text: Novices know simple hard counters, while experts know the minimum force needed against arbitrary mixtures of units.
when: games with blendable army compositions
why: Knowledge of nuanced counters separates skill levels.

text: Degenerate strategies are hacks and loopholes that break a world's reality or give unfair advantages; some become accepted creative play within the rules.
Prefer natural balancing when one well-chosen rule can produce the desired difficulty curve, and be cautious of stacking rules to force a behavior.
when: Tuning difficulty or behavior in a design.
why: Stacked rules make a design harder to understand and control.

text: Options that no build can viably use also signal imbalance.
when: Reviewing a set of choices for balance.
why: A choice where some options are unusable gives the player no real decision.

text: Beyond stat sums, designer judgment about play styles settles the balance, and pure numbers stop being useful at some point.
when: balancing asymmetric options
why: Once stat totals are set, comparing raw numbers runs out, so judgment about playstyles must decide balance.

text: Players call combat unfair when they have no means to counter or protect themselves. Check that every threat has a counter, and do so with a checklist suited to the game's movement model.
when: Playtesters complaining that a fight feels unfair
why: Players perceive unanswerable damage as unfair, so counters preserve a sense of fairness.

text: Multiple equilibria are better than one, since each player must think about what the other will do.
why: A single equilibrium leaves each player one viable option, so the strategic decision and guessing at others disappears.

text: A broad imbalance that stems from core mechanics should be noted for later rather than fixed immediately at first playable.
when: first playable stage
why: At this stage testing targets engagement and core mechanics, so balance is not yet being judged.

text: When testing constructed decks, look for a deck so strong it dominates the format and forces others to copy it or build a counter.
when: Balancing individual cards in a format where players build their own decks
why: Testers are told to break the game, and a deck that dominates exposes overpowered cards.

text: Dominant strategies and overpowered objects beat all alternatives and shrink choice; once known, players stop using weaker options, making play a predictable exchange.
when: When testing a system already judged internally complete for fairness and balance
why: Once one option outclasses the rest, the other options stop offering real choice.

text: Intransitive counters act as an emergency brake: without any counter, a dominant strategy dominates the metagame and ruins balance, while with counters the metagame tends to correct imbalance.
when: When a designer cannot tell whether the game is balanced or which strategies players will find
why: Every dominant option is weak to at least one counter, so it cannot stay on top unchecked.

text: Ignoring a god stat or investing in a dump stat weakens the character, even when the choice is made for role-play reasons.
when: Character builds with stats that are god or dump stats.
why: Game systems score the build regardless of the player's intent.

text: A tiny advantage is amplified across a large skilled player base, and the most common best option comes to be treated as the true curve.
when: Over time, in a large, highly skilled competitive player base
why: Any competitive edge, however small, gets picked up and then taken as the normal cost.

text: Extreme dominant strategies tend to fade as players tire of them and regular opponents refuse to face them.
when: Among a regular group of opponents who can choose not to face a deck
why: Boredom and social pressure remove the strategy from play.

text: A poorly designed game tends to collapse into one dominant tactic, while a well-balanced design supports a large space of strategies.
when: evaluating a game's strategic depth
why: Imbalanced options let one choice outperform all others.

text: The farther a balance value sits from zero, the further the object is from balance in either direction.
when: When costs are subtracted from benefits and scaled to an identity curve
why: Higher values naturally read as stronger, so distance from zero is easy to interpret.

text: Games with several strategies or win paths also need checks on each strategy's use, improvement over time, win rate against others, and internal diversity and challenge.
when: Game has several strategies or paths to victory
why: Analytics aim to ensure the game meets its goals, and comparing strategies reveals whether they are balanced.

text: Strategies that make one combat mode strong can undermine the other, so melee and ranged combat in one game often need balancing against each other.
when: When a game combines melee and ranged combat
why: Each mode's dominant tactics can erase the other

text: Counters that roll over at a maximum value can expose exploits near that cap, so cap values need checking in testing.
If attacking gives no advantage, optimal play never ends an elimination game, and with two players the game can stall entirely.
when: when a competitive game lacks reasons to attack
why: Without benefit to attacking, players avoid conflict and the game stops progressing.

text: Combining systems at very different scales produces two games in one box, because one system's variables are irrelevant to the other.
when: designing a game with systems at different scales
why: Effort spent on one system is wasted during the other's sections.

text: Players lock onto one overpowered option and repeat it whenever possible, which bores the player using it and frustrates opponents.
Doubling or halving a value is a drastic change that can feel counterintuitive, so use it as a diagnostic rather than a final value.
when: tuning with the doubling or halving method
why: Large steps overshoot the eventual target.

text: Copying another game's balance math usually fits your design poorly, and such copying has led to legal disputes.
why: Games differ, so another game's balance math is likely to be wrong for yours.

text: Degenerate strategies are often dull to play with or against, so the cards that enable them should be reduced or removed.
An overpowered unit gets mass-produced and makes the other units irrelevant, so keep unit power proportional to cost.
If one route to a goal is always easier, a dominant strategy emerges and everyone pursues it, collapsing the variety that multiple routes were meant to create.
when: Offering several routes to one goal
why: Players optimize for the easiest path.

text: 1) Collect player-reported symptoms. 2) Trace each symptom back to the underlying systems, resources and their connections. 3) Treat the chain of connected issues as a whole rather than fixing one value in isolation.
when: A game in production feels wrong after launch or in testing.
why: Players describe symptoms, but the designer must diagnose the systems behind them.

text: Fix a nonviable build by changing its content, changing the attribute or skill system so the build works, or blocking the nonviable pick, such as granting essential skills automatically to a class.
when: When characters look viable early in playtests but fail later, or testers still produce nonviable builds.
why: Players lack the information to foresee what a build will do or which challenges it will meet, so their picks are guesses.

text: 1) Write the payoff table for one player. 2) Set each option's expected payoff to the game value X, with probabilities summing to 1. 3) Solve the linear system by triangular reduction or substitution for the opponent's mix. 4) Repeat from the other player's side.
when: finding optimal probability mixes in a zero-sum game
why: An option with a higher payoff would be chosen exclusively and a lower one would be dropped, so every option worth playing must pay the same.

text: If one unit dominates, adjust its cost or power, or adjust the others, then retest.
when: When playtest data shows one unit dominating the others.

text: 1) Identify any dominant strategy that limits player choice. 2) If none exists, list the viable strategies. 3) For each strategy, list the opposing strategies that counter it.
when: Auditing a prototype's strategy space
why: A strategy that fails against some counters cannot be dominant, and a balanced game leaves opponents enough counters.

text: 1) Identify the option that clearly outperforms the rest. 2) Change the rules so other options regain value. 3) Recheck that meaningful choice has returned.
when: A dominant strategy has been found
why: Restoring competing options brings back real decisions

text: Pair invading targets with chaseable targets so both hunters and defenders have a role that fits their play style.
when: combat games with mixed play styles
why: Defensive players need invaders to guard against and offensive players need targets to chase; each play style needs its own kind of target.

text: In games with several paths to victory, each strategy should be viable and competitive against the others when played well.
when: games with several paths to victory
why: a strategy that beats the others while another cannot compete is an imbalance

text: Penalize repeating a purely defensive action in consecutive turns when a safe option can be repeated and cause standstill matches.
when: simultaneous-choice games with a repeatable safe option
why: Defensive loops stop progress and leave matches stalled

text: Cut a concept when it cannot be balanced without breaking its essential properties, especially when aiming for high-skill balance.
when: When high-skill balance is the goal and flaws only surface under testing by skilled players.
why: Patching problems with special-case rules is inelegant, and an unbalanced concept is unusable in play.

text: One-hit kills are acceptable when the player has a way to evade them, such as cover.
when: In grid-based games where the player can block damage, take cover, or back out of an encounter.
why: Evasion turns an instant death into a fair decision instead of an unanswerable loss.

text: When limiting player actions, use simple, obvious limits rather than attempts to disguise them.
why: Players already accept that mechanics have limits, so camouflaged blockers read as contrived.

text: If a degenerate strategy bypasses intended mechanics and blocks meaningful playtesting, apply blunt fixes to the obvious killer problems.
when: early builds too unbalanced to playtest meaningfully
why: Balance problems that stop meaningful testing prevent iteration, so fixes need only make the game testable.

text: Counter cycles: in-game actions close at four layers (dominant, counter, counter-counter reverting to dominant, no further layer); fixed strategies such as custom decks close at three (dominant, counter, counter-counter class).
when: Fixed strategies picked before a match, such as a custom deck brought to a card tournament.
why: Players cannot alter a committed strategy during the game, so they cannot respond to each new layer of counter.

text: Asymmetrical games hand opponents distinct abilities, resources, rules, or goals, creating a significant balancing task while still needing fairness. Asymmetry can model real conflicts; most digital games are asymmetrical.
why: Identical starting forces make many real conflicts implausible.

text: Artificial balancing adds explicit rules until a game behaves as wanted, whereas natural balancing lets the desired effect emerge from interactions among a few simple rules.
A balancing relationship is one where a change moves another element in the opposite direction, pushing the system toward equilibrium.
Asymmetric design means players differ in starting state, paths, rules, or character choices; any unmirrored element breaks symmetry.
Balance means the system has the intended scope and complexity, and its elements work together without undesired results.
Randomness is blind when the player has no clues, hidden when the player is unaware of it, and measured when players know the possible outcomes and their probabilities.
when: Classifying how players encounter random outcomes
why: The three differ in whether players can see or estimate the odds.

text: Changing the narrative rarely breaks a game, while changing the resource economy often does.
Balance is contextual and applies to single cards, classes, units, levels or whole games, meaning different things for single-player, competitive and cooperative play.
A tossed coin tends to land on the side that was face-up when the toss began.
A spun coin is more biased than a tossed one, because uneven weight pulls its heavier side down.
In asymmetric games each player may have a different optimal mix.
A fully certain game with no unknown outcomes is hardly a game, but certainty can still shape a level's pacing.
when: when considering how much outcome predictability a game should have
why: Certain elements are a tool for pacing, not a replacement for uncertainty.

text: In a heavily luck-based game, a little luck early on can dominate play.
Make random elements feel like exercised skill, and make skilled actions feel like risks, to balance chance against skill.
when: when designing the relationship between chance and skill
why: Players who feel control over a chance outcome experience challenge rather than hopelessness.

text: Alternate chance and skill decisions, such as a random draw followed by a player choice, to create a pleasing rhythm of tension and relaxation.
when: Designing turn or action sequences that mix randomness and strategy.
why: Alternation keeps players both relaxed by luck and engaged by decisions.

text: The right mix of skill and chance depends on the audience, since preferences vary with age, gender, and culture.
when: Choosing how much randomness a game should include.
why: Players from different groups prefer different levels of chance.

text: A random-driven game stays skill-based when players can calculate their chance of success for nearly any action.
why: Exposed odds let players weigh choices, and no single unavoidable roll decides outcomes.

text: Use subclassing when variants differ in behavior that needs different code; avoid it when they differ mainly in data.
when: Choosing between subclasses and data for variant types.
why: Data-only differences do not justify a class and a rebuild per variant.

text: Probability is tricky to reason about, since the math is hard and gut feelings are often wrong, so designers should shape chance on purpose.
Concealing luck can make a game feel more skill-based while still letting weaker players win some games.
when: Balancing a game whose audience includes many weaker players
why: Players who feel their skill matters stay engaged even when luck decides some results.

text: Balancing loops keep a game from resolving too quickly by counteracting runaway advantage.
why: A scoring gain that costs the scorer the next turn offsets its own benefit.

text: Giving one roll value a choice between helping yourself or hindering an opponent creates player-to-player interaction.
Chance elements such as dice reduce the first mover's advantage.
when: Symmetrical games with a first-move edge
why: A poor opening roll can be offset by a strong roll from the second player.

text: Giving one player a bonus payoff on one option shifts both players' optimal mixes and gives the bonus holder a positive game value.
when: one side has an extra payoff option

text: Adding a third option that beats one throw and loses to another, with a draw against the third, removes dominance and yields infinitely many optimal mixes rather than a unique solution.
when: Adding an option to a symmetric three-throw game with no dominated option
why: The payoff equations become dependent, so no single solution is determined

text: Adding options to a symmetric intransitive game increases the number of equations but not the difficulty of the method.
when: Extending a symmetric intransitive game to more options

text: When a winning move ends the game regardless of its damage, the payoff of several moves can become equal, so asymmetric health states produce asymmetric payoffs and different optimal strategies per player.
when: Scoring a game where a lethal hit ends the match
why: Any outcome that ends the game pays the same win value

text: Chance can alter relationships, and even removing one element from an ordered sequence can change the dynamics of the whole system.
why: Numbers or suits written on the cards create relationships, so each card becomes part of the system's structure.

text: Casino dice are machined to roughly 10 micrometers, with even paint and tight weight balance, yet tiny deviations still remain.
why: Even precise manufacturing leaves small flaws, but they rarely produce deviations large enough to disturb play.

text: Asymmetric objectives take five forms: ticking clock, protection, combined, individual-objective, and complete asymmetry. Each gives sides different victory conditions while remaining balanced.
why: Each side's differing objective is weighed against the others so the game stays fair.

text: Balancing unequal sides is difficult, and players may argue about their advantages for a long time.
when: When opposing sides have unequal forces and different goals.
why: Unclear which strategies will win leaves players unsure whether the sides are fair.

text: Using balanced, fun, and fair as one word blurs the difference between balance as a method and the goals it serves.
why: Balancing only shifts relative power among mechanics, a means usable toward many different ends.

text: Replace a random value with player choice, provided the options are balanced: 1) Give each player one card per possible result value. 2) Each card is played once. 3) Collect all cards back after use.
when: replacing a random value with player choice

text: 1) Compute the probability that none of the events occur. 2) Subtract that from 1 to get the probability that at least one occurs.
when: Probability of at least one of several independent events.
why: Negation is simpler than summing many cases.

text: 1) Decide how much of the game is physical and how much is mental. 2) Identify the target market's preference. 3) Make the game's appearance signal that balance clearly.

text: 1) Pick a bias or fallacy that makes odds seem favorable to players. 2) Build the rules so the true odds favor the house. 3) Use only standard components. 4) Playtest to see whether intuition misleads players as intended. 5) Revise based on results.

why: Testing confirms whether the intended misperception actually occurs.

text: Multiply probabilities of independent events that must all occur; add probabilities of mutually exclusive outcomes; subtract overlaps when outcomes can happen together.

why: Correct operation avoids impossible totals or double counting.

text: Ban any character or option whose power makes choosing it almost guarantee a win, since that makes competition pointless.

why: A dominant choice removes meaningful decisions.

text: Design weapons so that finding a new one does not make older ones obsolete.
why: Keeps every weapon useful for its own situation.

text: Ban policies punish griefers but require policing and judgment about intent, whereas avoiding systems that griefers can easily exploit prevents the problem at its source.
why: Deciding whether an act was intentional abuse or harmless fooling around is costly.

text: Campaign videos should show a short taste of gameplay; long talking videos are harder to fund.
when: Producing a crowdfunding video

text: Choose consoles when the design targets a broad living-room audience and production values matter.
why: Consoles reach that audience but bring licensing obligations

text: Check business appeal: theme and story attract buyers, the game is explainable at a glance, it stands against genre and rivals, production is affordable, business model makes sense.
why: Designers aiming to sell must fold commercial realities into the design itself.

text: Avoid artificially gating content behind other modes, such as locking multiplayer mini-games behind story mode.

why: Gating frustrates players who want to share content with friends right away.

text: Giving each player a distinct token or piece from a limited set is a simple way to let players express themselves.

text: Common cards should be simple but not necessarily weaker than rares; otherwise only wealthy or lucky players can build a decent deck.
why: Otherwise a good deck depends on owning or drawing rares, favoring wealthy or fortunate players.

text: Counter-cards with other useful effects, or designs where player choices matter more than deck contents, reduce the rock-paper-scissors problem.
why: Otherwise the metagame itself becomes the focus, and strong counters make actually playing feel unnecessary.

text: For each draw point, the player takes the topmost card of their draw pile into hand.
For each discard point, the opponent chooses one card from their hand and discards it.

when: Matching-set trades where players hide exact cards and state only quantity.

text: Drawing turn order one token at a time from a bag lets a player take several turns in a row, early or late in the round.
when: turn order is randomized by drawing tokens
why: the draw does not enforce alternation between players

text: When players know the situation in advance, as with sideboard cards chosen against an opponent, the option is used almost always when relevant, so its cost is mainly opportunity cost and metagame cost.

text: When cards can change game rules in different ways, the game system becomes expandable, since new cards add new rule effects.

text: Adding betting or draw rounds adds real information and decisions, whereas adding more cards to the deck adds variety without new information.
why: More cards enlarge the set of possible hands but add nothing that helps tell those hands apart.

text: A counter-card aimed at one dominant card forms a rock-paper-scissors cycle: the dominant deck beats most decks, the counter beats it, and other competent decks beat the counter.
when: When a competitive scene is saturated with players relying on one dominant card or strategy.
why: The counter is inefficient against decks other than the one it targets.

text: A closely matched collectible card game uses about 7 cards in hand, 20 starting life, 3 to 10 mana per turn, and creature power and toughness of about 1 to 8.
why: Close scaling of numbers across game systems keeps them working together, so one mode's complexity is not left idle.

text: A board of 64 squares has 2,016 pairwise relationships among its squares.

text: Cards with different stats at the same cost can imply conflicting values for the same stat, so their equations cannot all hold at once.
Counter-cards aimed at each popular strategy push players toward narrow decks that refuse opponents holding answers to them.
when: When players can pick their opponent each time instead of being compelled to face varied decks.
why: Players can avoid opponents holding the cards that would beat them, so a narrow deck can dodge its losing matchups.

text: A counter-card is weak when the opponent does not play the card it targets.

text: 1) List every object in the game and its properties. 2) Add each object's behaviors across different game states. 3) Describe relationships between objects and whether each is defined by position, power, value, or another factor.
when: when analyzing a board game's system structure
why: Without relationships among objects there is only a collection of parts, not a system.

text: Write card text precisely so no two players can read it differently; ambiguous text gets read in whatever way favors the player, causing costly disputes.
when: When a card's wording can be understood more than one way by different players.
why: Players favor advantageous interpretations, so ambiguity is a design risk.

text: If a player has no cards left at the start of Select, the player with more health wins, and equal health is a tie.
when: Card duels where a player can run out of cards.

text: When one card's effect prevents what another card's effect does, state explicitly which one applies.
when: two effects on different cards conflict, such as protection versus destruction
why: Otherwise the interaction is open to dispute.

text: Treat each premade deck as one unit and tune matchups so any two decks split wins near evenly between equally skilled players.
when: when balancing a set of starter decks
why: matchup fairness depends on the whole deck

text: In a classless design, labels such as healer or fighter are player descriptions rather than game rules, and any skill is open to any character.

Character progression converts experience points into levels, and levels into skills, abilities and performance gains.
A state is a set of rules describing how a character responds to input, so the same input can yield different responses in different states.
when: designing character movement with multiple modes
why: States explain why identical controls can feel different in different situations.

text: Classic tabletop-style RPG systems use six core scores: charisma, wisdom, intelligence, constitution, dexterity and strength.
Classes usually add attribute bonuses or penalties and class-only skills, with class-specific skills as the main differentiator that steers characters toward roles.
When two elements each serve one purpose and both are needed, combining them into one can save introduction time and budget.
when: time or budget is tight
why: Single-purpose elements consume introduction time and art budget that a very short game cannot spare.

text: 1) Find strange features players talk about with excitement. 2) Identify funny or unique qualities. 3) Keep flaws that players actually like. 4) Check these remain after an elegance pass.
when: After simplifying a design to confirm its memorable qualities survived
why: Cleanup can remove the traits that make a game distinctive

text: 1) Decide the experience you want the player to have. 2) Find how characters can help create that experience while keeping their in-world goals intact.
why: Characters should still fulfill their in-world roles, so the designer steers the experience only indirectly.

text: Check whether a class locks players into one role or supports several play styles.
when: reviewing a class design
why: Meaningful tradeoffs among stats and builds give players reasons to choose differently.

text: Specify each character type as its own object with properties, traits, behavior, and AI. Types include player characters, enemies, friends and allies, neutral characters, and others.
when: When the game involves character types such as player characters, NPCs, and enemies.

text: A class specialized for stealth excels at sneaking but struggles in open fights against many enemies, so each class trades strength in one situation for weakness in another.
when: designing class roles
why: Specialization makes each class strong only in some situations.

text: Single-player dominance in videogames came partly from the novelty of interactive worlds and partly from technical limits of software and hardware.
Automated pairing and partial anonymity between players make collusion harder to organize.
when: In rated competitive games where players enter matches to be paired against others.
why: Top players who know each other and track results could otherwise predict which opponents are overrated.

text: Good games often show the eventual winner trailing for several turns before recovering, a sign of drama that designers aim for.
Catch-up mechanics let trailing players overtake the leader by other means, so attacking the leader is not necessarily the best move.
when: When the game has built-in catch-up opportunities such as negative feedback loops.
why: Catch-up options let trailing players win by other routes, so a costly head-to-head fight with the leader is not their best bet.

text: A competitive game should measure skill fairly, make winning something players want and feel proud of, let novices and experts each compete meaningfully, and ensure experts usually beat novices.
when: Evaluating a competitive game's design
why: Fair measurement and meaningful competition across skill levels sustain motivation to win

text: One caught cheater at a big event erodes players' confidence in the entire rating system.
when: In competitive games with online communities where prizes or prestige are at stake.
why: If a major winner is caught cheating, players lose credibility in the system and may leave if they feel unable to compete fairly.

text: 1) List how players can cheat in the game. 2) For each method, judge whether anyone would notice it. 3) Decide whether players trust the game enough to keep playing.

text: Some advantage is normal; close only loopholes that ruin the experience for others, without removing emergent play.

why: Unintended loopholes leave the game incomplete, but blocking all unusual play would remove emergent play.

text: An equipment slot is a fixed place on a character that accepts only one type of item, so a weapon cannot fit a helmet slot.

Side-scrolling shooters need continuous time and entities such as terrain, enemies, lives and spawn points in their encoding.

text: When players have matched skill, firing position and weapon quality decide duels.
when: competitive shooter with even skill levels

text: Bursts of dense combat decisions should last only about 10 seconds, since longer bursts become exhausting.

why: Repetition without variety becomes tedious.

text: Combat volume can be the whole game, share the stage with exploration and story, or sit alongside other systems such as building.

text: Combat is defined by seven pillars: genre, time, pacing, feel, participants, progression and volume.
when: When planning combat early, and again later when cutting or adding combat elements.
why: Knowing these first guides how combat is shaped and later helps decide what to cut or add.

text: The shoot, look and move core is three actions whose combination underlies many successful games.
why: Few mechanics to implement and learn, yet their interaction yields many distinct experiences.

text: Because shots resolve simultaneously, two players can hit each other in the same round.
Giving enemies many hit points and no counters creates bullet sponges, which leaves no room for mastery.
why: Without counters, the only tool is brute force, so skill has nothing to express.

text: 1) Pick a game where combat is part of the experience. 2) Imagine a version with nearly all combat and one with none. 3) Describe play in each. 4) List the combat and other system changes each would need.
when: testing how central combat is to a design
why: Shows which systems depend on combat.

text: 1) Describe a game's combat pillars: genre, time, pacing, feel, participants, progression and volume. 2) Repeat the breakdown for another title sharing that genre. 3) Compare where the pillars differ and how that changes play.
when: analyzing games in the same genre

text: 1) Set vertical velocity to zero instantly. 2) Add a forward force. 3) On landing, enter a slide state.

when: pacing a game's combat schedule

text: Do not allow a dive attack to follow a triple jump or a long jump.

text: Let a jump press during crawling go straight to a jump, then keep running while the duck button is held, returning to ducking only when it is released.
when: Jumping out of a crawl
why: Crawling is rarely used, and a jumping player would rather return to running than to a crouch.

why: Gives ducked state its own distinct moves

text: Leaving spawn camping as a feature creates a game within the game for competitors, but many players find it frustrating.

text: When players can build and sell objects, user-made content can support subcultures such as reenactments, art exhibitions, and sports.

why: Player-created spaces become attractions, and visiting one another's spaces enables socialization.

text: A virtual skill belongs to the character rather than the player, such as a character's level in a combat skill.

Human play tends to spend more time social than solitary, so games are expected to follow that pattern.
Remote viewing through streamed video is growing, so spectators deserve a place in design considerations.

Keep a constant flow of topics for conversation through shifting content, strategic depth, and events or rule changes over time.

why: Players need topics to discuss to keep relationships going.

text: Include an activity that players find hard to stop once started.

text: Social progression includes influence, ranking, and guilds, where guilds grant rank, responsibility, privilege and prestige inside a group.

Cramming every idea into one level delivers wish fulfillment without a good experience, since wish fulfillment alone does not make a level good.
why: Too many concepts were introduced hastily and challenges became too punishing for players to clear.

text: 1) Make inviting friends easy, such as importing social media contacts. 2) Let players join friends' matches or missions quickly. 3) Show friends' recent missions or rewards in the menu.

text: 1) Find something in the current game the member can love. 2) Or propose a new feature that could take the game somewhere they would enjoy.

text: 1) Ask honestly whether your game helps people, answering yes or no. 2) If yes, name the specific effect it has on players. 3) If no, ask whether the design could change to provide one.

why: Helping people requires enough players to actually play the game, so a game nobody enjoys helps no one.

text: Designers should create regular community events, such as competitions, practice sessions, or goal challenges, because they give players something to anticipate and share, even when players also organize their own.

text: Make customized elements visible, for example by switching to third-person during emotes or adding replays that show the avatar performing combat moves.

text: Targeting an overlooked segment can yield outsized success but cannot be measured reliably, so it suits designers who accept risk and do not need predictable returns.

text: Competition can be direct, as in multiplayer play against other players, or indirect, through leaderboards, rankings and comparison with other players.

text: In player-versus-player play, two players compete directly against each other.

why: Exploits arise from unintended gaps in balance

text: A few simple rules applied equally to all pieces can produce vast ranges of positions; simple underlying rules do not imply simple outcomes, as interacting elements generate sophisticated collective behavior.

text: Simplicity means a virtual setting is less complex than reality, while transcendence means the player holds more power than in real life.

A simple strategy uses one tool to solve one problem, such as placing defenders in front of an attacking unit.
Conway's Game of Life places cells on a grid as on or off. An empty cell with exactly three live neighbors becomes live; a live cell with fewer than two or at least four live neighbors dies.
Perfect information games are easier to analyze, and many turn-based AI techniques assume this property. The best known algorithms target two-player, zero-sum, perfect information games.
Computers take over rule bookkeeping and state tracking that would make a tabletop version of a complex game tedious.
Rule text signals innate complexity through exception words such as unless, except, but, and even if.
Games commonly hold resources such as currency, items, cards, mana, units, structures, upgrades, hit points, experience, and player time.
Very simple objects and procedures can produce extremely complex results, as chess and Go demonstrate.
Dependencies can be circular, such as walls depending on construction while construction depends on walls, and simple layered pictures tend to hide them.
Keep rule count small so rich emergence comes from few rules; many explicit balancing rules can work against design. Balance those few well so the game feels calm.
when: adding innate complexity to balance a game
why: Stacking rules to force a result feels artificial, whereas simple rules interacting can produce the desired difficulty curve on their own.

text: Connect each rule and element to its surroundings so it seems part of them; when all elements do this, the game gains a strong sense of wholeness.
why: Elements that feel woven into their surroundings make the whole game read as living rather than assembled from parts.

text: When unsure which AI technique to use, check what similar genres commonly do, then consider doing it differently to fit your game.
when: Choosing among AI techniques for a new game

text: Aim for a simple ruleset that continually generates balanced surprises, and verify this only by playing and changing the game until surprises appear.
when: When designing a core ruleset
why: Emergent surprises can only be confirmed through extended play

text: Choose a simple world model with a few rules and keep those rules consistent, since players learn a world's rules within minutes.
why: Consistency under exploration matters more than detail.

text: Detect special combined interactions between objects and reward each one as a distinct event.
why: Each distinct interaction is satisfying on its own, which gives onlookers something to notice.

text: Adding complexity to a reward system does not guarantee a better experience.
when: When deciding how many reward types a game needs.
why: Layered rewards can set off unintended positive or negative feedback within the mechanics.

text: Building invests players in a world, while tearing it down offers a different kind of fun; offering both can help.
why: Building makes players invested, while people also enjoy tearing things down, so the two give different kinds of pleasure.

text: When artists condense loosely followed wireframe features, first check whether your design is convoluted before insisting on exact compliance.
why: Artists simplifying a layout can signal that players may also find the design convoluted.

text: A simple, elegant design is often the hardest to implement.
The simpler a game is, the better it serves as a social pretext, because added complexity competes with the conversation.
when: designing games meant to enable conversation
why: A light activity gives people a reason to meet and removes awkwardness, while extra complexity would pull attention away from talking.

text: Elegance lowers a mechanic's learning cost as well as raising its benefit, so aim for designs that can be explained in a few sentences.
why: Complicated mechanics impose a learning burden that can outweigh the gains they bring.

text: A simple, elegant design is the baseline, because easy-to-learn games move players past the skill barrier faster.
when: designing competitive or cooperative games
why: Lower learning barriers shrink skill gaps sooner.

text: Few objects, few properties, a single behavior, and fixed relationships make a system easy to learn and fully solvable, but players lose interest once they learn the optimal move for each situation.
why: Limited, fully predictable possibilities mean the optimal play can be found and exhausted.

text: When the computer handles steering and aiming after a click, the player only sets destinations, so the game falls outside true game feel despite polish and simulation.
when: units or avatars move automatically after player commands
why: the player does not guide the journey

text: Complex objects have many properties that change gradually during play, and objects with more such properties tend to have less predictable relationships with other objects.
why: Many changing, non-binary properties multiply the ways an object can interact with others, making those interactions harder to foresee.

text: A change to one design element forces rework in every element that depends on it, so an upstream change ripples through the whole chain of dependent work.
why: Game-design parts depend on one another, unlike independent tasks such as painting separate houses.

text: Rules produce emergence, with distinct play styles and unique occurrences, so games are more than containers for linear stories.
why: Rules generate varied player-driven outcomes, creating spaces of possibility rather than one fixed sequence.

text: Sandbox designs produce a shallow but wide hierarchy with many direct subclasses, so improvements to the base class benefit many classes at once.
when: Applying subclass sandbox across many behaviors.
why: Wide trees with a central base make base-class changes widely useful, though base-subclass coupling remains real.

text: Possibilities grow exponentially with each added property or option, yet a mathematically more complex system or one with more behaviors is not automatically more enjoyable.
Without clear purposes, a game's rules grow into a tangle that becomes more convoluted as the game evolves.
Innate complexity often earns a bad reputation because it is hard for players to learn.
when: When a game's rules are numerous and full of exceptions
why: Steep learning curves discourage players

text: A toy with no learnable depth pushes players toward self-made goals that quickly become boring, so the design effectively fails.
when: Open-ended software toys where players set their own goals
why: Self-invented goals become the game players actually play, so their shallowness reflects on the design.

text: 1) List the innate complexity in the game, meaning complexity from explicit rules and content. 2) Ask whether any of it could emerge from interactions among simple parts. 3) If emergent complexity does not appear in play, work out why.
when: deciding whether to add a new rule or let the desired behavior emerge from existing interactions
why: Behavior that arises from interactions balances naturally, whereas stacked rules force it artificially.

text: Build a matrix of properties and options to calculate a design's combinatorial complexity mathematically before playtesting.
why: Small changes to a few properties can multiply complexity, so calculating it beforehand shows the effect early.

text: 1) Count how many distinct activities the player wants and what kinds they are. 2) Set the number of choices to match that count.
when: Designing options for a player
why: Matching choices to desires produces a feeling of freedom.

text: Choose any reliable AI technique for a game character regardless of whether it is bottom-up or top-down, instead of enforcing a single architectural philosophy.
why: Top-down and bottom-up methods blur together in practice, so reliability for the task matters more than philosophy.

text: Introduce enemy complexity in waves and layers, so new elements attach to a basic understanding the player already has.
when: When a game's combat options or complications are increasing
why: Players absorb new elements more easily when they build on existing knowledge.

text: A world simpler than reality pairs with a transcendent player power; increasing that power must not remove challenge from the game.
when: after setting the world and the player's power
why: Unchallenged power ends the sense of achievement

text: Obvious rules attract newcomers but offer less depth, while deeper rules with complex interactions reward study but deter beginners.
why: Complex rules raise the entry barrier for newcomers, even when the deeper game is the better one.

text: Simplifying a bloated mechanic may lose some nuance, but it frees player attention for more efficient and explorable options.
why: Less to learn leaves more player attention for other options, and players appreciate what remains.

text: Conflict is the tension between players' objectives and the rules, procedures, or situations that stop them reaching goals directly, forcing them to work around the blockers.
A construction objective requires building, maintaining, or managing objects, in either a direct or indirect competitive setting.
Capture objectives require taking or destroying the opponent's terrain or units while avoiding one's own capture; this objective is found across chess, checkers, shooters, and strategy games.
Chase objectives require catching an opponent or escaping capture; chases may pit a player against the system, against other players, or one-sided, and players may chase and be chased simultaneously.
Pair the experience a game offers with its natural opposing force, so the theme becomes a conflict between the two.
when: When a game's subthemes describe a pleasant experience but lack tension
why: Conflict gives a theme power that subthemes alone lack

text: Let a wider range of clashes emerge organically from the game's systems, instead of relying solely on scripted confrontations.
when: designing rules for a story-generating game
why: Story-machine rules work best when little story is written ahead, so conflict emerges from rules rather than set pieces.

text: Combined objectives pair a protected objective with a timer, and teams swap roles to try to beat the time.
when: Team-based asymmetric maps
why: The displayed time gives the swapping team a benchmark to beat on the same map.

text: In a conflict theme, each side fights with tools that express its nature, so the opposing force uses its own items against the playful side.
when: When designing the opposing sides of a conflict-based game
why: Tools that match each side's nature reinforce the theme

text: Without human opponents, a single-player game must create conflict entirely through designed puzzles and structures.
why: The game system is the only opponent, so tension must be built into its puzzles and structures.

text: Chase outcomes can be decided by speed or dexterity, by stealth and strategy, or by logic and deduction, depending on how the chase is designed.
Construction games often use resource management or trading and are decided by strategic choices rather than chance or dexterity.
When captures compete with a line-completion win, an attack can run out of steam in ladder-like sequences, which shapes the flow of play.
when: When captures compete with a line-completion win.
why: The capture rule and the line-win rule conflict, so the attacker must switch to blocking the opponent's line.

text: A conflict theme can be stated as one force that wants to destroy something, which must survive.
why: A theme alone lacked bite and conflict, so pitting it against a natural opponent supplies the tension.

text: Conflict has three classic sources: obstacles, opponents, and dilemmas.
1) Identify each player's objective. 2) Identify the rules that block it. 3) Note whether players oppose one another. Compare these across games to see how conflict differs.
when: When comparing conflict across several games.
why: Conflict arises from how player goals interact with the rules and procedures that constrain behavior, which players then work to resolve.

text: 1) Identify the conflict in the game. 2) Classify its source as obstacles, opponents, dilemmas, or a combination.
when: when analyzing a game's conflict

text: Context gives immediate spatial meaning to actions, while rules give longer-term, sustainable meaning.
Specific devices are ephemeral, while the places people use them persist and are easy to overlook.
A ship's feel depends on combining its physics with the right spatial and rule context, not on physics alone; earlier attempts with similar physics did not achieve the same feel.
Background elements set the spatial setting, and active threats give meaning to the player's motion.
when: designing the context around a movement-based game
why: Threats make movement purposeful, while the setting frames where it happens.

text: Architectural knowledge and understanding of spatial activity, flow and balance can change how players feel about a space.
when: when designing game environments

text: An input's meaning can depend on the avatar's location, and this dependence can be continuous, such as a response that scales with distance to a point.
Breaking conventions is usually a mistake since players rely on learned expectations; a deliberate break with precise intent can add challenge, while unintended inconsistency only confuses.
when: Considering a mechanic that deliberately violates players' expectations.
why: Unexpected behaviour adds difficulty, but unintended inconsistency only confuses players, and conventions carry learned expectations players rely on.

text: Early VR and AR often copy conventions from console, PC and mobile games, which neglects presence as the new core.
when: When a new medium has just appeared, such as VR and AR.
why: Bodily presence, bringing the body into the simulation, is the new medium's core, and older console, PC and mobile conventions do not address it.

text: Copying a pattern's form without its purpose misses the point, because each pattern exists to solve a specific experience problem.
why: Using only the spatial form skips the problem-solving role the pattern exists to address.

text: Design a game meant for conventions to play quickly with minimal equipment.
when: When the game is intended for play at conventions.
why: Quick, low-equipment play suits convention settings.

text: A departure from a familiar control convention can serve the design but requires players to relearn, so it needs a clear design reason and an expected adjustment period.
when: Considering a non-standard control scheme.
why: Breaking habits costs players time and can frustrate them even when the new scheme is intentional.

text: Options that differ only in name, or that nobody would pick, give players no real choice.
when: Many options exist but outcomes are identical or one dominates
why: Players sense that the decision has no effect

text: Cosmetic choices with identical effects can still carry emotional value.
when: Choices that differ only in appearance.

text: When a board loops, model it as a sequence of discrete points; cosmetic corner size and piece placement within a square carry no meaning.
when: When a board loops back on itself as a line of discrete squares.
why: Each square acts as a point with no spatial extent, so visual size or in-square position does nothing functionally.

text: A decentralized world is run by independent servers and people rather than owned and controlled by a single business.
Decentralized proto-metaverses aim for blockchain interoperability and have their own currencies and content creation and monetization tools, but items made on one cannot yet be used on another.
Items and avatar identities bought or earned on one centralized platform generally cannot be used on another platform yet.
Cross-promotional events between platforms and franchises are not interoperability, which requires items and identities to work across platforms.
Device-to-device data exchange lets players visit one another's towns, trade items, and send gifts.
In decentralized spaces where anyone can create content, hateful content and disruption of others create trust and safety problems.
when: When anyone can create content in a decentralized space.

text: In highly interconnected designs, changing one part ripples into others, e.g. changing jump height can affect level geometry, enemy behavior, animation, sound, and story.
when: When changing a core design value after it has been planned
why: Every system built on the original value must be revisited.

text: A dependency links two design parts so that a change in one forces changes in the other; it does not mean the foundation must fail.
Deep interlock means two elements define each other, so removing one changes what the other is, as a piece's meaning depends only on opposing pieces.
The critical path is the set of missions, narrative and gameplay elements required to finish the game.
In a game, level appearance depends on layout, layout depends on the player's tools, and the tools depend on the basic interface.
A weak element often suggests a useful change in another element, so look across categories for improvements rather than fixing one element in isolation.
when: When a design has a clear weakness.

text: A dependency stack arranges elements in layers, with each element depending on the layers beneath it.
when: When choosing which design elements to build first.
why: Elements cannot function without the ones they rely on, so the stack reveals the build order.

text: 1) Break the game into elements such as mechanics, controls, interfaces, and subsystems. 2) Identify key dependencies among them. 3) Draw the relationships as a layered graph.
when: When the design is a paper plan or is partly implemented and tested.
why: It shows which parts to prioritize now and which to defer.

text: Design systems that generate events rather than authoring the events directly, since mechanics and players together produce the play sequence.
why: Mechanics and players interact during play to generate events, rather than the events being fixed in advance.

text: Unlike passive viewing of a film, a game demands exploration, and that exploration is central to how players perceive game feel.
when: When the player can freely explore the world instead of watching a fixed frame.
why: Players' practiced perception makes any small inconsistency stand out while they explore.

text: An exploration objective asks players to explore areas; it is nearly always paired with a goal that is more competitive.
Experimental designs at the edges of the game definition may point toward new forms of play and interactivity.
when: when exploring new forms of play
why: Existing boundary cases already apply the structural and narrative tools of games to serious subject matter, which widens what interaction can do.

text: Technology can enable previously impossible designs, but many of the greatest designs come from tireless experimentation rather than technical advance alone.
when: When a hardware or software advance makes a previously unattainable feature feasible.

text: 1) Temporarily set aside craft constraints. 2) Ask extreme questions, such as invincibility, very fast movement, or infinite resources. 3) Keep any experiment that reveals a missed opportunity or emotional moment, incorporating its lesson rather than simply reversing it.
when: Design feels flat or over-smoothed
why: Most extreme trials fail, but occasional ones expose overlooked openings or emotional beats that polishing had flattened.

text: 1) Pick an experience from your own life you would want to share. 2) Distill its core feel into a small, concrete element. 3) Draw sources from outside games and your own genre. 4) Shape a tetrad element with the inspiration, from one source or blended sources.
1) List the key moments of the game, checking which ones players would name among their top ten. 2) Make each moment as powerful as possible. 3) Chart the strengthened moments on an interest curve.
when: before drawing an interest curve
why: Interest curves are built from these peaks, and an experience's quality is judged by how well its sequence holds attention.

text: 1) List the game's elements. 2) Remove one element at a time until the game becomes trivial. 3) Restore the last removed element; what remains is the core.
when: Identifying the core of a game you know.
why: Stripping elements stops right before meaningful play disappears, so the last restored piece is the minimum that makes the game function.

text: Encourage learners to explore, discover and experiment, and give immediate feedback about success and failure.
when: When learners can act on their surroundings and receive immediate feedback about outcomes.
why: active experimentation with prompt feedback supports learning

text: Basic actions are the base operations a player can perform directly, forming the fundamental verbs of a game.
Amplification is the sense of a small input commanding a large, complex response, and it is one of the main pleasures of play.
Big games take over public spaces for playful interaction, deliberately breaching the usual boundary between play and everyday life.
Designers first set both the position and the tactical data of each tactical location by hand.
Some official rules began as laws, such as the requirement to announce check in chess, and became part of the written rules over time.
when: Explaining how rules come to be official
why: Repeated clarifications eventually become standard rules.

text: Near transfer occurs between closely related domains, while far transfer to distant domains is rarely found.
Dropping inactive players from global ratings only partly solves the problem, since players then play just enough to keep their place.
Social interaction and physical exercise are enjoyable parts of many games but are not essential; removing problem solving turns a game into just an activity.
Every game is built from four basic elements, and these four form the starting framework for studying game anatomy.
Different designers can proceduralize the same source system differently, emphasizing different aspects of it.
Automatic game design is still exploratory, though prototype systems exist.
Some probability questions have outcomes that can grow without limit, so listing every case and dividing by the total is impossible.
when: A chance process can repeat without a fixed upper bound on its result.
why: An infinite outcome space cannot be enumerated.

text: Some battle sizes cannot arise from a starting battle, because each roll removes at least two armies, so those states can be skipped in the grid.
when: Building a recursive odds table for a dice combat with pairwise losses.
why: Losses come in pairs per roll, so parity constrains reachable army counts.

text: Make every iteration loop count by assessing and mitigating the biggest risks in it.
when: Planning each development iteration
why: Targeting risk ensures each loop yields the most valuable learning

text: Altering rules, such as handicapping a stronger player, can keep play fun for mixed-skill groups.
why: Fun depends on players' attitude, and a game can be ruined when players refuse to adapt its rules in a playful spirit.

text: Designers should sometimes break their own rules, since this expands possibility and rewards players who test the limits of a world.
why: Rule-breaking widens what a world allows and pays off players who probe its edges.

text: Use symmetry when players compete directly and results should reflect skill and strategy alone.
when: When players compete directly and are expected to have roughly equal skill.
why: Equal resources leave skill and strategy as the only differences, so results reveal who is best.

text: Timing often follows from difficulty or quantity, but can be off on its own when pressure arrives too fast or the player progresses too slowly.
when: When the player progresses too slowly or conflict escalates too quickly, even though difficulty and quantity are right.

text: Prefer integers that are simple to handle, compute and contrast; if values are fractional, multiply everything to make them whole.
when: Choosing numeric values
why: Players process whole numbers more easily than fractions and decimals.

text: When players plan around an effect, an unreliable benefit acts as a drawback, so it should be priced below half the value of a fully reliable version.
when: Effects that players must plan around
why: Unpredictability makes planning harder, which costs the player

text: Color-code a balance column with two thresholds, for example one hue under zero and another over zero, to flag outliers quickly.
when: scanning a balance column for values far from balance
why: color makes off-curve values visible without reading every number

text: If quitting a mission through one exit path fires no event, that mission's completion rate may look inflated.
when: when some exit paths are not instrumented
why: abandonments through the uninstrumented path are never counted

text: Weaker players can be attractive targets too, so not everyone must attack the leader.
when: When the current leader is hard to identify or early leads confer only a small advantage.
why: Knocking out an opponent can yield their resources, and the weak are simpler to knock out.

text: Win and lose conditions are the main levers for game length: too short leaves no time for strategy, while too long bores players or discourages them from starting.
when: When tuning how long a game lasts
why: Conditions determine how many turns or moves a session contains

text: Changing a tool to fix one situation also changes every other situation where that tool is used, so tuning for one case alters many others.
when: When the same mechanic is reused across many parts of a game.

text: Combat should present orthogonal dilemmas, each needing a different strategy, rather than contests over damage per second.
when: Designing enemy and weapon sets
why: Distinct enemy traits require distinct responses, pushing players to adjust their plan rather than just dealing more damage.

text: Basic delimitations set physical limits on the game, such as field dimensions, maximum team size, and required positions like a goalkeeper.
when: When a game's rules must be read and enforced by players rather than a machine.

text: Assuming the designer controls the player's perception or hardware leads to misplaced design effort, since both lie outside the designer's reach.
why: Perception is fixed and designers rarely build the hardware, so their real influence lies in the internal game-state steps.

text: A well-built artifact does not guarantee the intended player experience, so problems should be diagnosed as either artifact faults or faults in the experience it produces.
when: Evaluating whether a design works.
why: Designers can only hope players enjoy the experiences their artifacts generate.

text: Borrowing values from other professions without checking their fit to game design's task can be as mistaken as applying military values to scientific work.
why: Each profession's values fit its own task, and game design's task differs.

text: Scenario-based games with random tiles, cards and dice can give one player a lucky or unlucky advantage, and some players may be eliminated early.
when: Games with many scenario variants and random elements.
why: Layered randomness and uneven scenarios compound imbalance.

text: A unit missing the abilities that define its theme fails the theme criterion.
when: When checking whether a character's mechanics match its theme.
why: A name should predict what the unit does, and absent signature abilities break that expectation.

text: Lower bounds in a VLOOKUP threshold table must be in ascending order from the top, since the default match returns the largest bound not exceeding the key.
when: When a weighted loot table would have too many entries to list individually.

text: 1) List the main storyline as ordered sections the player must pass through. 2) Rate each section's difficulty 1-5. 3) Mark memorable high points with an x. 4) Record section name, rating, and x flag in a spreadsheet.
when: Analyzing a game's pacing, using a walkthrough or memory of the game if needed.
why: Turns subjective impressions of slow and fast parts into comparable data.

text: 1) Decide whether the game needs a macro-level or micro-level worldbuilding approach. 2) List the research topics that approach requires. 3) Only then begin research.
when: starting worldbuilding for a game
why: The chosen approach determines which topics to research.

text: 1) Perform a design task by hand, without computer support. 2) Note what was easy, what was hard, and what you wished the computer could do. 3) Note what the computer could not help with. 4) If a tool is available, repeat the task with it and record the differences.
when: When a design tool is available to download and try after a manual run of the task.
why: Doing the task by hand first reveals which needs a computer could actually meet.

text: 1) Subclass the base class. 2) Override the sandbox method. 3) Compose calls to the protected provided operations inside it.
when: A new behavior is needed in a family that uses a sandbox base class.
why: Base-class operations are marked protected to signal that only derived classes are meant to use them.

text: If the spark of fun is missing, decide whether to keep the idea or return to the drawing board.
when: Core idea fails to engage

text: Avoid mechanics that allow pilfering between players, unless the aim is an experience built for griefers that frustrates others.
when: When items give players a lot of power that others could take from them.
why: Being robbed makes victims feel violated, and that feeling is what draws griefers to such a feature.

text: Start design from the activity players perform moment to moment, rather than from content, narrative, or aesthetics alone.
when: early design
why: Games are dynamic systems of action

text: Only a system-level model reveals non-obvious effects of a change, while stories reveal only obvious and immediate ones.
when: When judging a change's effects on a game that has undergone heavy playtesting.
why: Ripple effects across interlinked parts only become visible after a designer models the whole game, not from a few play sessions.

text: Marking every useful location gives good tactical behavior but costs the level designer a lot of time.
when: When a level designer places tactical positions by hand for enemy AI.
why: Very high-quality tactical behavior needs every useful position marked, which multiplies the designer's placement work.

text: Betting on an unproven platform can create a barrier, since early adopters benefit if its sales unexpectedly grow, but it carries risk.
why: A new, patent-protected platform is hard for rivals to copy quickly, which creates the barrier.

text: The brain categorizes objects before they reach conscious attention, so a label replaces the detailed view.
why: Labeling is cheaper than perceiving every detail, so the mind sorts objects early to save effort.

text: Teams can agree on what to do now while the best long-term path is still debated, as captured by the phrase 'disagree and commit'.
when: The best path is still debated but action is needed

text: Essential features are the few traits that make an experience memorable; incidental features are details that could change without losing what made it memorable.
Bottom-up design starts from a robust, general physical simulation and then finds enjoyable play within it, instead of coding only the parameters one mechanic needs.
Good software architecture is judged by how easily the codebase accommodates change; if nobody modifies the code, its design matters little.
Level designers execute gameplay and design individual levels. Systems designers build systems such as combat, crafting and mini-games.
A domain-expert PCG system holds knowledge about games or players and uses it to critique or modify content, often within a tool or designer system.
A judgment call is a decision with no single correct answer, where the same choice can lead to disaster or triumph.
The engineering filter asks how the design will be built; technology limits may block an idea, but the question can also reveal practical new features.
Feeling that something is true from personal experience does not make it true, which is why scientists avoid drawing conclusions from introspection.
A clean game with minimal excess detail encourages players to experiment, while a dirty game with excess detail makes beginners suspect a hidden trap.
One decision can be informed, dramatic, weighted, immediate, and long-term at once, such as spending a scarce resource now that is needed later.
The gameplay section is the largest part of the outline and covers overview, controls, interfaces, rules, scoring and win conditions, modes and features, levels, flowchart, and any editor.
Batch programs take input, run to completion, produce output, and stop, while interactive programs give immediate feedback to a live user.
Letting players write assembly-like programs is rare and suits only games where that programming is the point.
Better authoring tools tend to produce better content, and many well-liked games have strong authoring tools behind them.
Fixed ratio and variable ratio are the two reinforcement schedules most important to game designers.
Everyday objects such as folders, tabs, cars, books, and backpacks are recognized instantly, so they can carry meaning to players quickly.
Trust introspection on how an experience feels and on subjective matters like ethics, drama, and mind, but not on physics or natural history.
when: evaluating experience quality
why: Game design concerns how experiences feel, which introspection judges reliably, unlike objective physical facts.

text: Record the design options you did not choose so you can test them later.
when: Making numeric or design decisions.
why: Early numeric guesses will need revising through playtesting, so recorded alternatives give ready options to try.

text: Keep charts that justified a decision, since they later help you recall why the decision was made.
Check each of the eight pleasures against the game's aesthetics, mechanics, and experience to see which the design actually supports.
when: reviewing a game design
why: Motivation for human actions traces back to pleasure seeking, and each player favors particular kinds of pleasure.

text: Repeat traits across related elements, such as a boss sharing features with its minions, to create pleasing, unifying echoes.
Inner contradictions, where a feature works against the purpose it serves, are a root cause of bad design; remove them rather than excusing them.
Check every use of a stat before calling it a dump stat, since an apparently irrelevant stat may control carrying capacity or access to obstacles.
when: Evaluating whether a stat can be ignored.
why: A stat that looks irrelevant may also govern carrying capacity or access to obstacles, giving it hidden value.

text: In-game value reflects how much players care about succeeding, so it works as a diagnostic of their motivation.
why: A game's success depends on players' willingness to treat its rewards as important, which is what gives in-game value its meaning.

text: Judge working definitions by whether they lead to better game designs, and drop those that give no useful insight.
Keep each technology forecast concrete and give reasons for it, since the reasons matter as much as the guesses.
when: When forecasting how a game technology will develop.
why: Reasons build instinct for how technology fits the human mind.

text: Rapid technological change benefits game designers, because each new technology opens new kinds of games to make.
What a designer does with an idea after it emerges matters more than the idea's source.
Beginners often borrow elements from successful games, which is normal, but the aim should be to break conventions and innovate.
when: early in a designer's career

text: Playing games alone is not enough; analyze each game you play and identify one specific thing to learn from it.
why: Analysis builds game literacy, which lets a designer talk about systems in depth and share ideas through specific examples.

text: Avoid adding an operation to the base class if only one or a few subclasses use it, since it adds complexity for every subclass.
when: Deciding whether an operation belongs in a shared base class.
why: Unused operations bloat the base class and burden all subclasses, though consistency with other provided operations can justify it.

text: Judge a game by whether its systems keep generating intense moments, not by one authored highlight.
why: Experiences arise moment to moment from simple mechanics interacting, so they are not stored in content and keep recurring in new forms.

text: Recording decisions saves the team from solving the same problems again.
why: Decisions fade from memory as their number grows, and writing them down also helps the designer develop ideas.

text: Alignment games are decided either by logic and calculation alone, or by chance combined with calculation.
Over thirty review questions can evaluate artwork rather than mechanics, covering emotion, surprise, curiosity, unification, resonance, challenge, reward, beauty, and physical and virtual interface.
when: when evaluating or improving how a game looks and sounds
why: Lenses built for judging mechanics can be redirected at artwork to refine and unify its aesthetics.

text: General health checks cover engagement (player count, session length, return frequency), progression (improvement, progress or winning, pacing), and diversity and challenge in play.
why: Analytics exists to confirm the game meets its design goals, which for most games means being enjoyable.

text: Alignment objectives take two forms: arranging pieces in a spatial pattern, or creating conceptual matches between categories of pieces.
Adding a new interaction to a puzzle late can require major structural changes to the puzzle.
why: The existing puzzle structure is built around the intended solution path, so an added action forces a rebuild.

text: Builds that seem viable early can become nonviable later, and testers may build strong characters that still prove nonviable.
The words positive and negative are loaded; systems design uses reinforcing and balancing instead.
why: Those labels carry value connotations that can mislead, so some systems theories name the relationships reinforcing and balancing.

text: Without a designer who keeps focus on the vision, gameplay decisions get lost among other production concerns.
when: On highly complex productions where gameplay focus is a full-time job.
why: A dedicated person must focus on gameplay without budgeting, scheduling, and allocation distractions crowding in.

text: Listing outcomes by hand is practical only for small counts, and double-counting or missing similar results is easy.
when: Counting outcomes manually.
why: Long lists invite errors.

text: Design principles stay isolated because designers rarely publish findings and often know little about other fields.
when: Looking for established design principles
why: Knowledge does not circulate across disciplines.

text: Judging a game trivial because it looks simple overlooks that its design determines the experiences players value.
why: Experiences form from play with a design, and the parts players value are set by that design, so simple looks don't make it trivial.

text: Falling in love with a proposed solution narrows the search, and assuming only one kind of solution is valid cuts off alternatives.
why: Starting from the problem rather than a fixed solution opens a wider creative space and avoids ruling out valid approaches.

text: Hoping a team disagreement resolves on its own fails; unresolved differences must be addressed directly.
why: The team must eventually agree on one decision, so a standing objection needs direct work rather than waiting it out.

text: Pursuing flawed notions of realism distracts from entertainment and delight, and simulating reality for its own sake wastes effort.
why: Accurate-looking physics does not guarantee fun, so simulation should be judged by whether it entertains.

text: Shipped game engines often contain excellent subsystem code while the architecture joining them is neglected, leaving heavy coupling and features bolted on wherever they fit.
when: under intense production deadlines
why: Deadline pressure favors fast feature insertion over structural design.

text: Building an entire character or system at once assumes a certainty the design does not yet have.
when: When a design depends on lower-level systems that have not yet been proven.
why: Uncertainty in underlying systems cascades upward, so an untested design built on them will likely fail until its core is iterated.

text: 1) List every assumption about the game, such as where it is played, where the player looks, and how the player touches the device. 2) For each, ask how the design would work if it were false. 3) Pursue any broken assumption that yields a useful insight. Most assumptions still hold, but an occasional broken one can yield a key insight.
why: Most assumptions hold, but testing each one by imagining it false occasionally reveals a useful insight.

text: Ask these questions of each candidate design: 1) Does it feel right? 2) Will the intended audience like it enough? 3) Is it well designed? 4) Is it novel enough? 5) Will it sell? 6) Can it be built? 7) Does it meet social and community goals? 8) Do playtesters enjoy it enough?
why: Many constraints apply at once, so a design is finished only when it clears every one without needing changes.

text: 1) State the game's purpose. 2) State each subsystem's purpose. 3) Find anything that contradicts these purposes. 4) Change it so the contradiction is removed.
when: reviewing a design for qualities that defeat its goal

text: 1) State the experience the player should have. 2) Identify what is essential to that experience. 3) Build that essence into the game, changing the game wherever the experience created differs from the target.
when: Checking whether a game delivers its intended experience.
why: Knowing the essence shows which parts can change safely and which cannot.

text: 1) Hold the four elements and the player experience in view together. 2) Identify which elements make the experience enjoyable and which detract from it. 3) Change elements to improve the experience.
when: When reviewing how a game's structure produces the experience players actually have.
why: Structure and experience must be judged together to see what causes what.

text: 1) Read the problem statement. 2) Identify which tetrad elements (technology, mechanics, story, aesthetics) it already fixes. 3) Build the remaining design from the unfixed elements.
when: when reviewing a problem statement before designing
why: a statement often decides some elements, leaving the rest open

text: 1) Pick a story you want to pursue or a mechanic you want to explore. 2) Treat that choice as the problem statement.
when: when no design constraints exist
why: With total freedom there is no direction, so a chosen story or mechanic supplies the constraints a design needs.

text: 1) List the basic actions. 2) List the strategic actions. 3) Compare the ratio of strategic to basic actions. 4) List actions players wish they had. 5) Enable wished-for actions as basic or strategic actions where feasible.
when: when reviewing a game's action set
why: Actions are what make anything happen in a game, so small changes to them spread into many other parts of play.

text: 1) List the challenges the game contains. 2) Judge each as too easy, too hard, or right. 3) Check it suits a wide range of skill levels. 4) Trace how difficulty rises with success. 5) Confirm enough variety and identify the peak difficulty.
when: Reviewing a game's challenge structure
why: Covers difficulty fit, scaling, variety and ceiling in one pass

text: 1) Name the fantasy your world fulfills. 2) Name who the player imagines being inside it. 3) Name what the player imagines doing there.
when: Choosing the anchor for a world early in design
why: Players carry hidden wishes, and a world only draws them in if it fulfills those wishes.

text: 1) Align everyone on the design as early as possible. 2) Use open, respectful debate to resolve differing visions of the same game.
