when: Passionate members hold different visions of the same game
why: Differing visions are the hardest team problem, and early alignment plus respectful hearing of each idea is what resolves them.

text: 1) Start with a simple bulleted list of ideas. 2) Write down each question the ideas raise. 3) When a question is settled, record the decision and its reason. 4) Let the notes fall into sections over time.
when: Beginning a design document with no formal structure
why: Working on design mostly means answering questions

text: 1) Find close competing games that lack one key component you plan to provide. 2) Compare them with your game to show the gap. 3) Present the gap to money people.
when: when justifying a game's market place
why: Players choose among many rivals, so a clearly missing feature that people want marks a real opening.

text: 1) Describe one game in detail for a newcomer. 2) Describe a very different game the same way. 3) Compare the descriptions, noting differing and similar elements. 4) Focus on underlying mechanics, not surface features.
when: when learning what makes games share common structure
why: Shared underlying mechanics let very different games still be recognized as games.

text: To find essential parts, remove one rule or procedure at a time and check whether the game is still playable.
when: when analyzing a game's structure
why: Formal structure is what makes something a game, so removing a rule exposes which parts are essential.

text: 1) Begin with a start node. 2) Draw lines to each decision or condition, such as 'has key' and 'doesn't have key'. 3) Lead each outcome to the next event or to a node where further outcomes occur.
when: mapping branching player choices

text: 1) Choose the abstraction: decide which data and properties matter to the task. 2) Choose a representation that encodes that data with the facilities available, suited to the operations applied to it.
why: The two steps are rarely separable, and the representation must fit the operations performed on the data.

text: When selecting technologies, judge them by what they add to the experience and favor those leading toward a better world, not merely novel or exciting ones.
when: When selecting technologies for a game
why: Judging technology by excitement leads to poor choices.

text: Record design discussions in lasting media, such as notebooks, email, forums, mailing lists, fileshares, wikis, or printed documents, rather than relying on spoken words.
why: Spoken words are easily forgotten and misunderstood.

text: Keep written records of all publisher approvals and decisions, since they document what was agreed.
when: Whenever a development phase is finished and signed off by the publisher

text: Answer player-type design questions at the concept stage, before layout work, once genre and target player type are known.
when: concept stage of a multiplayer space
why: Questions asked against the chosen mechanics or genre produce guidelines that shape the layout of the space.

text: Ask whether the design meets experience standards for beauty, engagement arcs, a theme that resonates, and balance tuning.
why: Gut feel is not always right, so the other filters offset its blind spots.

text: Check the mix of simplicity and power deliberately, since the combination is easily botched.
A choice must be understood when it is made, and its impact must be perceivable through the environment, AI agents, or audio-visual effects.
why: Players must perceive a choice's impact, since otherwise the choice does not register as meaningful.

text: Do not change a game's feel just to suit the AI markup tool.
Take rules and examples from any creator of experiences, whatever their field.
when: Seeking design principles
why: Principles from one medium often apply to others, since all rest on the human mind.

text: Treat design approaches as tools in a toolbox, open-minded but practical, and judge them by whether they produce better experiences.
when: Evaluating a borrowed design principle
why: The test of a principle is the experience it produces.

text: Test whether indirect control produces the intended behavior and not unintended desires or expectations in players.
when: After adding layout or setup meant to steer players
why: Indirect cues like music can shape player moods and actions without players noticing, so unintended control is possible.

text: Compare your production values with rivals and decide whether you aim to be top-tier or the cheaper option.
why: Rivals shape how players judge a game as much as its raw quality does.

text: Use analytics to confirm the game meets its design goals, which for most games means being fun.
when: After changing a game element, such as enemy strength or enemy count, to alter difficulty or flow.
why: Designers assume a change works, so player data is needed to confirm it had the intended effect.

text: When only one feature or fix is possible, choose by its impact on the player experience as a whole.
when: Deadline allows one change
why: Ranking tasks by their effect on overall player experience gets the most value from a single limited slot.

text: Use single player versus game when the system can supply challenge through puzzles or structure.
why: Without human opponents, this pattern depends on built-in puzzles or structures to generate conflict.

text: A flowchart must show every path through the game, every outcome, how a player wins or is eliminated, and what happens if a connection drops.
Base the gameplay overview on the physical or software prototype, which serves as the model for how the game plays.
Each designer should decide for themselves which values they believe in, rather than adopting a single prescribed set.
why: No one can prescribe the best values for every designer, and each person benefits from reflecting on which standards they hold.

text: A stack ignores the weakest dependencies to focus on the strongest and most dangerous ones, but that omission can hide real risks.
when: When a design has so many interdependent elements that full analysis is impractical for one person.
why: Analyzing every relationship among so many elements is impossible for one person, so reduction is the only workable approach.

text: Turtling means avoiding combat, building defenses, and then swooping in to attack opponents who have been weakened.
An uninformed decision is arbitrary because the player does not know how strong each option is.
Twitch decisions take under a second and need simple conscious reasoning, such as punch or kick; action games are built largely on them.
Tactical decisions take one to five seconds, engage conscious thought and use more information, including past outcomes, such as choosing equipment or units.
Stay with 2.5D for most cases, since its algorithms are simple and fast, and the up vector can stay fixed for orientation.
when: Developing most steering systems.
why: Its algorithms are simple to implement and execute faster than full three-dimensional steering.

text: Use a simple count threshold to decide whether to trust a prediction, unless a measured gain justifies formal confidence calculations.
when: deciding whether an N-gram prediction is reliable
why: A more complex confidence measure gave no measurable prediction improvement, and its mathematics is costly.

text: An element that serves fewer than two purposes is a candidate for cutting, a rule of thumb borrowed from screenwriting.
why: Elements serving only one purpose carry little weight, so combining or removing them often serves the design better than adding more.

text: Giving a weaker option a secondary benefit, such as a chance to heal, turns a simple strongest-pick choice into a judgment about what the player values.
when: When options differ only by a single stat and one option dominates.
why: A clearly dominant option removes meaningful choice.

text: Cutting a tool is often better than weakening it, since a slow, pointless version harms the game more than having no version.
when: A tool's key properties cause imbalance
why: A weakened tool that is unsatisfying and strategically pointless damages play more than simply not having the tool.

text: Most interesting decisions are tradeoffs between resources, such as gold for an item, mana for a spell, real money to speed a unit, or hours for high-level play.
why: A resource's cost only feels acceptable or not relative to the other numbers it sits beside.

text: In turn-based games players control pacing, so designers still must manage decision scope, because the size of each decision drives tedium or stalling.
when: Turn-based games, where players decide how long each of their own turns takes.
why: Players set their own timing, but consequences of decision size remain.

text: When killing an NPC costs almost nothing in resources, the act feels like a mercy rather than a choice that deserves reflection.
when: NPC death carries no resource cost
why: A cheap kill spends almost no resource, so the player never has to pause and reconsider the decision.

text: 1) Ask whether the script can implement an established AI technique. 2) If not, decide whether a dedicated C++ implementation, alongside or instead of scripting, would be more practical.
when: When deciding how to implement a character behavior.
why: Established AI techniques solve behavior problems elegantly, so their value lies in the algorithm rather than in the language used to write it.

text: 1) Anticipate how each disruptive behavior could be rewarded within the game and its ecosystem. 2) Change the rules or rewards so that behavior no longer pays. 3) Recheck the design for new exploits.
when: Designing multiplayer systems
why: Antisocial behavior is permitted by the design, so the design decides what it rewards

text: 1) Do characters need level-scale understanding? 2) Must they act in sequence or timing with each other? 3) Can they decide individually yet produce group behavior, or must some decisions be made for the group?
when: When planning tactical and strategic AI for characters.

text: 1) Identify what the player must understand to play. 2) Decide whether imagination can convey it more easily. 3) List high-quality realistic details to provide. 4) Let imagination fill gaps left by low-quality details. 5) Reuse details that imagination can extend. 6) Keep only details that inspire rather than stifle imagination.
when: Deciding how much detail a game should show versus leave to the player's imagination
why: Well-chosen detail supports understanding while imagination carries the rest

text: Explain each design decision by naming the trade-off it accepted and its effect on player experience.
when: explaining or reviewing a design decision
why: Every design involves trade-offs, and their cost to the player is what determines whether the choice works

text: Use the closed-form drag solution when the model matches and accuracy matters; use an iterative simulation otherwise, and the closed form does not apply when squared-speed drag is present.
when: Choosing a projectile drag solution
why: The closed form only holds for purely linear drag

text: Beauty costs production time and artistic skill, and it may not fit the game's tone.
when: When deciding how much polish to invest in visuals.
why: Beauty demands time and skill and can clash with the intended mood.

text: When a subject is vague in the public mind, audiences bring their own associations, which a designer can build on.
when: Adapting a familiar place, film, or idea that lacks a clear theme
why: Audiences already hold a loose sense of what the subject means

text: Real-time control is one of three components, so a generated level can be fully playable yet lack game feel if avatar movement is not continuous.
when: generating levels for real-time control

text: Use a reference solution to prove by existence that a level is solvable, avoiding a separate search algorithm.
when: When procedurally generating levels that must be playable.
why: The existence of a valid solution inside the map is itself proof that the level can be completed.

text: Decide whether generated spaces use discrete level boundaries or seamless traversal, since this structural choice is separate from level structure.
when: When a world is larger than the screen space available to show it at once.
why: Limited screen space forced designers to split larger environments into smaller screen-sized spaces.

text: Players learn a space's possibilities through its rules and symbols, so any generated layout must make those rules readable.
when: generating layouts that players must navigate and understand
why: Designers communicate a world's rules through gameplay, so players can only grasp a space's possibilities if those rules are legible.

text: Examining why a wrong prediction failed shows what you misjudged and improves later forecasts.
when: after a forecast turns out wrong

text: Test first in monetizing regions similar to the target but outside the core audience, favoring low acquisition cost, similar play patterns, and high language competency.
when: When launching a free-to-play game whose economy must be tested before its main region.
why: Regions that mirror the target without being its main demographic let the team iterate on feedback before wider testing.

text: Test themed restrictions, such as decks limited to one card type, to see whether the card pool supports them at competitive strength.
why: Restrictions reveal gaps in the card pool.

text: Use repeated simulation when the theoretical math is too complicated or when hidden factors may change the results.
why: Running the test repeatedly measures the actual system, so factors the math missed still appear in the results.

text: Leaving cheating loopholes open harms a game even if players rarely exploit them, because the possibility alone creates stress.
when: In multiplayer games where players can cheat against or among each other
why: Players must keep watching for cheating, and when cheating seems possible but undetectable, non-cheaters lose interest and quit.

text: Designers and players often assert answers, especially on forums, but hunches are not evidence; many detailed questions need analytics to answer.
when: When questions concern retention, progression, win rates, or balance across strategies in a player base
why: Hunches and forum opinions can be wrong, so measured play data is needed to answer detailed questions.

text: Assuming what players learn in one part of a game will transfer to another context without testing it.
Reward values set generously for testing can remain in the live game and must be reduced before launch to avoid breaking the economy.
when: Testing with generous rewards
why: Generous testing values inflate player resources after release.

text: Generated content must be playable: a level must be finishable, a staircase climbable, and a weapon usable.
why: Unlike generative art, generated game content must work within rules and interactions, which pure generation ignores.

text: Keep generated gaps no wider than the blocks a player can jump over, and keep pipes no taller than the player can pass.
when: Generating platform levels with random gaps and pipes
why: Ensures a path from start to end exists

text: Filter out rule sets that draw more often than not, favour one player, give a serious first- or second-move advantage, or run too short or too long on average.
when: When screening many candidate rule sets before spending time on deeper quality measurements
why: Outcome-based criteria matched human rankings and gave a robust playability estimate, while intrinsic criteria did not.

text: Write reachability constraints recursively, so that connectivity follows from a base case and a step rule.
when: When generating mazes or levels with a declarative constraint solver
why: Layering simple rules into compound ones lets complex requirements such as connectivity be expressed to a solver.

text: After each human edit, test the level's playability and regenerate the affected parts so the level stays solvable and playable.
when: when a human edits a generated level in a mixed-initiative tool
why: Edits can break solvability, and regeneration restores a valid level.

text: Match a generator's path structure to the intended experience, since labyrinth and maze structures create different gameplay.
why: Branching multi-path structures and single-path structures produce different kinds of gameplay.

text: Show an obscene message only to its sender and filter it for everyone else, so the griefer cannot tell whether the filter worked.
when: In online chat where griefers seek reactions from obscene messages
why: Giving the griefer no feedback about whether the filter worked removes the fun they get from the attempt.

text: When a feature pleases one group of players and frustrates another, offer variants so each group can get a suitable experience.
Raising the required pass proportion removes false links but can greatly increase analysis time.
when: When distant regions get false links through doorways and corners during line-of-sight connection analysis
why: A zero threshold stops at the first passing check, so a stricter threshold forces many more checks per pair.

text: Game design is second-order: designers set rules and context but cannot fully predict or directly control how players behave, including in level design.
why: player behavior emerges from the rules

text: The same design principles and process apply across board, card, dice, party, gambling, arcade, athletic and video games, since a game is a game regardless of medium.
A personal theme is a private purpose behind a designer's work, which the designer identifies by looking inward.
Shared design terms give designers, evaluators and critics a common language for discussing design and critique.
A well-aligned game has a reward structure built around a meaningful core, so good design raises little ethical concern.
A value curve is a graph that rates several games across a set of market values, so overlaps and unique values become visible.
when: When comparing a game against competitors
why: A single curve says little; comparison across games reveals where a design stands.

text: A value reflects an affect-laden decision about the sort of person one aims to become, an ideal worth pursuing though nobody fully realizes it.
Passion also means persistence and determination to ship a strong game regardless of obstacles, which backers need to see before entrusting you with funds.
when: Pitching to funders
why: Backers bet on people who will see the project through.

text: A personal theme often takes one of three forms: a vision that could change someone's life, a wonderful experience to share, or a terrible event to prevent for others.
Game systems leave room for imagination, fantasy, inspiration, and social skill within the game space.
All design principles are ultimately rooted in psychology and anthropology, so connecting principles across fields is a long-term goal.
Games are entered by choice, aimed at goals, built on conflict, governed by rules, and produce outcomes that can be a win or a loss.
Science and creativity are not opposed; games are art, and UX practice can serve artistic vision rather than limit it.
Playing violent games does not by itself cause real-world violence, but studios should still reflect on the content they normalize.
Knowledge and skill alone are not enough for exemplary game design; designers also need values to stay steady through daily turmoil.
Ethical questions are hard; each studio should define its own code rather than assume settled answers.
why: Ethics is a long-debated, complicated topic, so no settled answer should be assumed for a studio.

text: Original games with new mechanics, interfaces, and worlds may need a planning horizon of a day or less.
when: when the design is largely untested
why: Original designs rest on untested foundations and many interlocking uncertainties, so long-range plans are quickly invalidated.

text: Use symmetry when players need obvious comparisons and a feeling that the field is balanced.
why: Symmetric games are balanced by construction since all players start equal, and symmetry makes that balance visible to players.

text: Knowing why a fun part is fun matters as much as identifying it, since the reason shows what to keep, strengthen, or copy.
Concept art does not always need polish, since rough sketches or models are often enough to do the job.
when: When concept art only needs to convey the basic idea rather than the game's true feel
why: Fully polished art takes time, so rough work can often communicate the idea efficiently.

text: Before committing to a feature, mode, event, campaign or sale, ask why the target audience would care and whether it fits the core experience.
when: when proposals come from the team or management
why: unexamined additions dilute the core experience

text: Use challenge where skill tests and mastery are central to the emotional goal, and do not assume it must be present in every design.
when: When choosing emotional triggers for a design.
why: Challenge suits some emotional goals but not all.

text: The value of versatility depends on foreknowledge (how far ahead a player can plan) and switching cost (how hard changing choices is), and foreknowledge's value is inversely proportional to switching cost.
when: evaluating options that let players switch between modes or loadouts
why: low switching cost makes advance knowledge less important, and vice versa

text: Overfocusing on one element (mechanics, gameplay structure, story, technology or aesthetics) neglects the others and the experience, which matters most; judging by one element skews review.
why: All four elements are essential and interconnected, so neglecting any one undermines the whole experience.

text: Designers tend to sand down ideas that seem too good or too bad, which balances the game but flattens it.
why: Extremes of effectiveness pay off for high-skill play, and balance comes from matching skill required to payoff.

text: Use the usability pillars as a checklist and shared vocabulary across design, art, audio and user research.
why: The pillars give the whole studio a shared vocabulary so anyone can take part in improving the UX.

text: 1) At the end of each prototype or sprint, ask whether you are excited about the game. 2) If excitement has faded, try to recover it. 3) If it will not return, consider working on something else.
when: after every prototype and every sprint, alongside risk review and planning
why: Lost passion often signals the subconscious sees a problem, and it often predicts failure.

text: 1) Ask whether the game feels magical. 2) Ask whether people get excited just hearing about it; if not, find out why. 3) Ask whether it advances the state of the art meaningfully. 4) Ask whether it makes the world better.
when: When judging whether a project and its technology choices are heading toward a better world

text: 1) Map the market values your game could offer. 2) Estimate your team's resources. 3) Choose one or two values to be best at, or a single value if the team is small. 4) Cut the rest.
when: When scoping a new game
why: Matching ambition to resources keeps the chance of a clear winning value realistic.

text: Give clients a real creative role without giving up the design vision; this is about shared ownership, not deceiving the client.
when: When a client wants ownership of the creative work
why: Clients who feel they helped create the work tend to defend it when others criticize it.

text: Before other decisions, define the game's experience pillars and target audience.
Offer a virtuous option alongside harmful ones so players can make a moral choice.
Designers must sell the game to teammates, management and investors, using good language skills, a clear vision and a strong presentation.
when: when seeking funding, approval or team buy-in
why: Only a clear, persuasive pitch can gather the team and win the backing needed to keep the project moving.

text: Prefer short words, since they fit more easily in speech bubbles and in actors' mouths, whether the game is voiced or read.
Break conventions only when the fiction's harshness is the core experience and the audience accepts unfairness; otherwise keep conventions.
when: the fiction's harshness is the core experience and the audience accepts unfairness
why: Unfairness only pays off for audiences who accept it

text: Only values that are better than every competitor, or that no competitor offers, are worth pursuing; values offered at a lower level than competitors add little.
when: When choosing which values a game should emphasize
why: Players have alternatives, so being merely comparable gives no reason to choose the game.

text: Each added market value costs development resources, dilutes the emotional purity of the experience, and may clash with other values, so teams must limit how many values they pursue.
when: When deciding how many values a game will pursue
why: Values compete for resources and can be logically incompatible with one another.

text: Designers know their game better than players and cannot experience it as newcomers, so what is fun for them may be too hard or hidden for typical players, such as starvation.
why: Developers' deep expertise makes it hard to picture what a typical player knows, so needed information goes unshared.

text: Constant-only scripts let designers set stats and trigger feedback without writing rules, yet the behavior remains a fixed list of values.
when: Giving designers scripting before adding logic
why: Without conditionals or computation, each script produces the same result every time.

text: The designer acts as a translator between programmers, artists and producers so that everyone works on the same game.
The game designer plans the objectives, rules and procedures that players set in motion, and is responsible for a compelling player experience.
A designer-style PCG system designs parts of a game, or whole games, autonomously; the limit case is a fully autonomous generator, usually within one genre.
Level designers with coding skills can build basic logic, triggers or scripts that control AI.
Most designers build motivation systems mainly through instinct and experimentation rather than detailed knowledge of psychology.
Game designers usually work in relative obscurity and receive little public respect, and publishers often prefer they stay unknown.
why: Fame makes designers more expensive to employ.

text: Studios fall into three categories: standalone outfits, fully held subsidiaries, and part-owned affiliates.
Designers often cannot predict the commercial outcome of an unexplored concept; outcomes may range from very small sales to very large ones.
when: When developing a game in a fully unexplored segment
why: Without references, conventions, or players, the number of buyers is unknowable in advance.

text: Designers answer many questions and eliminate many uncertainties; the hard part is making interrelated mechanics, fiction, art, and technology work as one experience.
A designer's influence over game feel is limited to the computer, game world and output devices; human perception, muscles and input hardware are treated as fixed.

Core designer tasks include brainstorming concepts, creating and playtesting prototypes, writing concept and design documents updated throughout production, communicating the vision, creating or overseeing levels, and advocating for the player.

Game design draws on animation, anthropology, architecture, brainstorming, business, cinematography, communication, creative writing, economics, engineering, games, history, management, mathematics, music, psychology, public speaking, sound design, technical writing, visual arts.
Designers cannot observe player experiences directly because they occur inside another person and cannot be shared, so attentive listening to players is essential.
why: Experience is private and not externally visible.

text: Designers cannot touch experiences directly; they shape the game, and the game is what produces the player's experiences.
Companies exist to make money, so responsibility for making games beneficial rests with the individual designer rather than the company.
Creative people work differently: some generate many ideas, some dig deeply into one, some think alone, and others thrive bouncing ideas off groups.
Designers tend to see everyday situations as systems of goals, obstacles and rules, such as finance, courtship and workplace competition.
Designers can add richer emotional qualities to known games or invent new mechanics for games not yet made.
Acting as a game designer, including saying so aloud, helps build the identity, since people tend to become what they act as.
when: Confidence is low at the start
why: Acting on a role reinforces it.

text: An efficient designer should understand scheduling and budgeting nearly as well as the producer, though not create or track those documents.
when: At the start of any production
why: Without a clear grasp of the full scope, the producer falls back on rough estimates, making schedule and budget inaccurate.

text: Accepting how little you understand is the most basic step toward becoming a skilled game designer.
why: it leads to more testing and fewer overconfident decisions

text: Designers know their game deeply, so a goal that seems obviously valuable to them may not yet feel engaging to new players.
when: Judging the value of goals or rewards
why: Players lack the designer's knowledge of the game

text: The designer is usually the best person to pitch the game, because they know it best and must believe in it to persuade others.
when: When someone must be convinced to fund, publish, or distribute the game

text: Designers need a genuine love of play, and it must be actively kept alive, because repeatedly testing one's own game can turn into work.
when: during long development and repeated self-testing
why: Repeated testing of one's own game can drain enjoyment.

text: Designers forget the player's perspective over time, so projecting into the player's view requires constant attention.
when: Long design processes
why: Familiarity with the design gradually replaces the player's viewpoint

text: Holding to creative purity at the audience's expense leads to catering to an audience of one.
why: Enjoyment hinges on the audience understanding the work, which requires seeing it from their viewpoint and taking outside feedback.

text: 1) Work in an isolated space. 2) Control distractors such as notifications. 3) Prevent interruptions during focused work.
when: When a task requires deep focus
why: Messages, notifications, and ambient noise divide attention, so controlling those distractions protects focused work.

text: 1) Choose a game you find unfun. 2) List what you dislike. 3) Identify what its designers missed. 4) Propose concrete improvements.

Designers should learn at least one programming language, via a beginner book, class, or questions to programmers, even without plans to become programmers, to judge feasibility and speak engineers' language.
when: When designing digital games
why: Shared vocabulary makes collaboration with engineers easier.

text: A good designer advocates for the player, judging each decision by what players will experience.
Ensure someone can focus on gameplay without too many other duties.
when: Staffing game design
why: Budget and schedule duties pull against gameplay advocacy, so the gameplay role needs freedom from them.

text: Designers cannot force a specific trade or outcome; they can only make it possible and tempting.
why: Designers shape rules rather than the player experience itself, so they can only open up possibilities that players may or may not take.

text: Designers share responsibility for making games that fit into balanced lives.
when: designing engaging games
why: Engagement can harm players when it crowds out other life areas

text: Design around predictable perception errors rather than blaming players for them.
why: Players' flawed intuitions about probability make a fair game feel wrong, so the fault lies in predictable biases rather than in the players.

text: Designers decide which behaviors are possible, rewarded, or punished, and are responsible for those choices.
why: Rules limit what a player can do even in freer games, so which behaviors exist reflects design decisions.

text: Accept that players know outside information and design systems that still create the intended experience, using fair, gamelike threats and explicit, attainable goals.
when: When players bring outside knowledge about the game's interface, platform, and purpose
why: Fear of threats the player knows cannot happen weakens tension.

text: Too little challenge bores players; too much causes anxiety and frustration, which can drive them away toward a more rewarding activity.
why: Attention holds only in a narrow band between boredom and frustration, so challenge outside that band pushes players to disengage.

text: Dynamic difficulty adjustment is a negative feedback loop that changes challenge in real time based on estimated player performance or payment model, instead of a fixed setting.
Raise challenge and probabilities gradually with skill; sudden spikes or sharp drops within a short span usually signal imbalance unless there is good reason.
when: When designing difficulty progression.
why: Smooth scaling keeps challenge matched to growing skill; sudden deviations break players' expectations of the curve.

text: Scale challenge with player skill to keep play in the flow zone, neither too easy nor too hard; too easy becomes boring and too hard becomes stressful.
why: Players persist longer when they perceive rapid improvement, so a sense of growing competence drives motivated effort.

text: Dynamic difficulty adjustment raises difficulty when the player does well and lowers it when they struggle; as negative feedback, it punishes success and can make the game feel unfair.
Opening that kills players while they learn controls, or packs every mechanism in too fast with punishing challenges, frustrates players and disrupts learning, so playtesters cannot finish.
Use zigzag curves alternating hard fun with easy fun, such as a relaxed phase after a main challenge; they prevent excessive frustration and are more interesting than a straight climb.
when: Sequencing challenge and relief; designing difficulty progression.
why: Continuous difficulty can cause excessive frustration.

text: In long PvE games, raise difficulty with player skill through play, offering new strategies rather than more obstacles in less time; this rising challenge is a difficulty curve.
when: In any long PvE game where players improve within one playthrough, when designing challenge progression.
why: Repeating the same challenge faster stops producing fiero.

text: Disclosing dynamic difficulty makes its punishment of success an expected rule, but aware players may game it or see events as artificial, so hidden adaptation can work better.
when: When considering dynamic difficulty adjustment in a game.
why: Undisclosed adjustment makes players resent it, while awareness invites exploitation and undermines trust in events.

text: In a low-skill idle game where power rises steadily, perceived challenge falls as the player improves, so the game must add new difficulty to keep the player challenged.
when: games where power grows without new skill demands
why: Rising power and learned skill both reduce perceived challenge.

text: Evenly matched players tend to produce the most exciting games because the outcome stays uncertain.
when: PvP matches between players of similar skill
why: Uncertainty keeps players engaged through the match.

text: Learners who improved most rated the training as challenging but not too challenging.
when: when training games are tuned for learning gains
why: Difficulty in a productive middle range supports engagement and improvement.

text: Players will retry a hard challenge hundreds of times when each attempt might end in a win.
when: challenges with an uncertain chance of success per attempt
why: Each attempt carries a chance of reward

text: The relationships between control parameters shape the overall feel of control more than any single mapping does.
when: Tuning movement and control systems
why: Players perceive feel through how parameters relate, such as speed against turning radius

text: Several unusually long completion times can mean players were sandboxing the level, or were confused by a core mechanic yet kept playing instead of quitting.
when: several sessions far longer than typical
why: Confusion does not always cause players to quit.

text: Players usually run toward the next action, so pacing can be shaped subtly through narrative cues in the path and rewards for exploration.
when: when pacing a level
why: players head for the next goal unless drawn elsewhere

text: In level-based F2P games, players often lose when they are close to finishing a level.
Players who fail just before a regularly scheduled bonus are motivated to keep spending to reach it.
when: a bonus appears after a fixed run of stages
why: anticipation of the bonus outweighs the setback

text: A positive feedback loop amplifies its own effect, usually favoring the player already ahead; 'positive' means additive, not good, so reading it as good misidentifies the effect.
when: When analyzing designs or bug reports.
why: Positive refers to amplification, which can be harmful.

text: Challenge is not difficulty alone; a task is challenging only relative to a particular player's ability, so the same task can bore experts and overwhelm novices.
Perceived difficulty comes from four elements: player skill, virtual skill (power), virtual challenge (enemy power or numbers), and skill challenge (new ways of playing).
why: Each element contributes separately to how hard a challenge feels.

text: Balance is the subjective sense of fairness; progression should feel earned through choices and every player should believe they can win through skill or luck.
Hard Fun is enjoyment of mastering a challenge; Easy Fun is exploration, curiosity, and joy of interaction.
Challenge is a core pleasure because every game poses a problem to solve, though some players need more than challenge alone.
A challenge consists of two parts: goals and constraints.
Depth is the maximum skill at which a game stays interesting, while accessibility concerns the minimum skill at which it becomes playable.
A deliberately unfair game is an asymmetric design that accepts unfairness on purpose, as a third option beyond symmetry and balanced asymmetry.
A difficulty curve describes how challenge changes across a game; balance means the player is challenged at their current ability relative to the designer's intent and target audience.
why: Balance is judged against what the game is meant to do for its players.

text: Practicing interest curve drawing can give designers insights that others miss.
Balance matters mainly because it makes a game feel fair, and fun is only one possible goal; some games aim at other experiences such as art.
when: Deciding how much balance matters.
why: Balance serves the experience the game intends.

text: A balanced game is not necessarily fun, and a fun game is not necessarily balanced.
when: Judging balance and enjoyment.
why: The two qualities vary independently.

text: In the 1970s and 1980s games were harder and longer because players were assumed to improve, so designers filled the game space and characters often died for trivial mistakes.
why: Designers assumed players would get better over time

text: By the mid-1990s difficulty levels became common to cover a range of ability and taste, and expert-level modes were seen either as a badge of honor or as a frustration.
why: Players of varied ability needed options

text: In the mid-2000s player-created modes such as permadeath became common, restarting the game from scratch on death.
In the 2010s designers combined accessibility options with optional challenge, giving players both easier assist features and harder opt-in modes within one game.
Each difficulty level is a different balance of the same system variables, not a separate game.
when: Designing multiple skill levels

text: The interest-curve approach applies to any entertainment experience, including rides, films, and games.
No game can stretch one simple skill across a broad range, because players eventually exhaust aiming, movement, or map knowledge.
Fairness and depth are the goals balancing achieves most directly, so they stand above the other goals it can serve.
why: Balancing is the key method for reaching them.

text: Courses become harder through sharper and more frequent turns and through more obstacles.
One experience can be built from several physical forms, such as a window, a hole in a surface, or a gap in foliage.
Some games intend repeated deaths followed by eventual progress, while games for very young children skew so far toward the player that losing is nearly impossible.
when: When judging whether a difficulty level is appropriate.
why: Acceptable difficulty depends on the intended experience and audience.

text: Average game difficulty has generally eased over time, so older hard games were often aimed at average audiences of their era.
when: When comparing difficulty across release eras.
why: Player expectations and design norms changed across decades.

text: Difficulty curve can mean learning curve, monster strength relative to the player, or competitive level between PvP arenas.
when: When reading design documents that use the term.
why: The same phrase refers to different measures in different contexts.

text: Games commonly offer several difficulty levels, where higher levels give the AI power bonuses or reduce the player's power; this is relatively cheap to design and build.
The difficulty dial applies at every scale, from a single encounter to the whole game.
Deliberately punishing games set high difficulty by design, while meditative games keep pressure very low by design.
Difficulty tiers can be easy (little resistance), normal (tuned for typical builds), hard (challenging for typical builds), and hardest (challenging even for optimal builds).
Balancing a fighting roster by hand is hard, since each character has many numbers and players cannot customize move sets.
Frequent checkpoints let a large open world work without rooms, since losing a challenge is a minor setback; long gaps make failure serious and undermine learning through repeated failure.
when: Large freely explorable worlds full of difficult challenges
why: A light tone softens failure.

text: Keep failure gentle while a mechanic is new, and apply strong challenge once players understand the basics and are engaged.
when: early learning; especially in free-to-play games
why: Challenging players to master a game is more engaging than challenging them mainly to learn it.

text: Offer difficulty settings or skill brackets when players differ widely in their ability to manage hit points.
why: Difficulty choices and skill brackets give players outside-the-game options for handling the hit-point resource.

text: An action is challenge if its result is predictable, its goal is clear and its feedback immediate; otherwise it is interference.
Not every successful experience follows the exact ideal curve, but most successful ones share some of its elements.
When players can set enemy number and hostility, still provide defaults that give a good first play experience.
when: games with adjustable enemy settings

text: An added option may be ignored by some optimal strategies, so its value as a balance addition should be checked, not assumed.
when: Evaluating a new option that creates infinitely many optimal mixes
why: Some optimal solutions drop the option entirely

text: Depth can be shaped by tuning both the input-to-response mapping and the challenges the player faces.
why: Designers control challenges as well as input mapping, and the challenges define the skills players develop.

text: Prioritize mechanics-first design when a perfectly balanced, clear challenge matters most.
when: the core goal is a balanced, clear challenge
why: mechanics-first design produces balance and clarity

text: Use the hardest standard setting from a fresh start as a difficulty benchmark; a level the designer cannot beat that way is likely too difficult.
Offering many activities and spaces suited to different play styles encourages unplanned play, especially in multiplayer games with many character types.
when: a game has many play styles or character types
why: varied options let players choose their own paths

text: Check difficulty, especially in early levels; avoid sudden spikes by moving the challenge later or adding easier levels before it.
when: observing a playtest of early levels
why: sudden jumps frustrate new players

text: Widen jumps and chain them in quick succession as levels progress.
when: Platformers where difficulty ramps up across successive levels

text: Difficulty should rise mostly in step with skill and power, with occasional deliberate spikes on top; a well-balanced curve need not be a perfect progression.
why: Occasional spikes keep play interesting and unpredictable, while moderate steps alone leave players bored.

text: Limited hardware can still produce meaningful, rewarding play when designers find unique uses for its constraints.
when: Designing within tight technical limits
why: Constraints can focus designers on distinctive, rewarding solutions.

text: Lives and scoring that reward improved skill motivate players to get better in anticipation of greater rewards.
when: designing the rules that frame player progress
why: Anticipated rewards tied to skill give players a reason to improve.

text: Expect difficulty pitching a truly original design aimed at a niche audience in a market that favors fewer, bigger titles.
why: Rising development costs force each title to sell more units, so its appeal must be broad.

text: Layering explicit and adaptive difficulty lets a game serve novices while staying honest for experts, widening its skill range.
when: Games with both an explicit difficulty selection and adaptive difficulty
why: Adaptive difficulty can be manipulated by experts, so a locked top mode gives them an honest challenge.

text: Narrative games usually balance for middle or bottom skill levels because they are not played as intensely.
when: Narrative-driven games, as opposed to competitive strategy games

text: Facing a more skilled opponent causes anxiety; flow returns by building skill, and lowering the challenge is harder once the player has noticed it.
when: A player who meets a more practiced opponent than their current skill

text: A goal with a constraint, such as a time limit, puts an implicit question in the player's mind about whether they can achieve it.
Struggling against a skill test produces a pleasurable state of focus, and passing it brings energy, capability, and dominance.
when: When a game is built around skill tests.
why: Effort on a test followed by success generates focus and then mastery feelings.

text: When some strategies are obviously easy and others obviously hard, players self-select the difficulty that matches their skill, without any settings menu.
when: When designing strategy options of differing difficulty.
why: Players pick the option that fits their ability.

text: Raising challenge as the game progresses can build a rising sense of tension.
why: Challenge acts as conflict the player must resolve, and that struggle produces tension.

text: Players usually need progressively more experience points for each successive level.
when: When designing experience levels.

text: A persistent bonus for the leader makes the leader more robust, which can turn late play into one-against-many.
Permadeath erases a character on death, so one loss can wipe out a run that may exceed 50 hours.
when: long roguelike runs

text: A power-up loses value when it duplicates an effect the player already holds.
when: power-ups overlap in their effects
why: Redundant effects add nothing new, so players lose incentive to collect them.

text: A power-up that makes the character pass through enemies reduces the challenge to timing jumps alone.
when: an invulnerability power-up is granted
why: Removing the threat of enemy contact leaves only the remaining obstacles as challenge.

text: Competition makes the effective skill ceiling unlimited, since a player can only become better than others and never reach completion.
A mild conditional penalty for a failure state can correct drift in play by encouraging careful behavior without punishing the player harshly.
when: Single-player games where a checkpoint return is the failure consequence
why: A small cost for failure steers players back toward careful play.

text: Pass/fail challenges suit only players whose skill falls in a narrow band; weaker players always fail and stronger players find no challenge.
Softer failure outcomes such as a slowed recovery or an incapacitated ally let the game continue, keeping players out of frustrating dead ends.
when: When a failed challenge would otherwise end play outright.
why: Continuing play spares players who fail from frustration while still making failure costly.

text: Elastic fallbacks such as a weak infinite-ammo weapon or a regenerating minimum health pull a stuck player back to a state where challenges are hard but doable.
when: When a player falls into a state where progress is near impossible.
why: Restoring a minimum capability prevents permanent dead ends.

text: Combining horizontal and vertical trajectories makes landings on specific platforms hard; consistent spacing makes that skill learnable.
Level sets built by designers of different skill can show a noticeable difficulty jump, which harms balance, pacing and enjoyment.
when: When a stage set from a moderately skilled author is followed by one from an expert author.

text: Low starting health and stamina make early exploration risky, which reinforces a limited lesson plan.
when: In an early tutorial area, before the character gains more health or stamina.
why: Being fragile against foes and hazards restricts how far the character can roam.

text: Optional challenge modifiers, such as more damage or exploding enemies, let players switch between levels for extra money and experience, keeping the default accessible.
when: When designing optional challenge modifiers for players who vary widely in taste and skill.
why: Players who want challenge opt in for rewards, while others keep the easier default.

text: Giving trailing racers the strongest items and leaders weaker ones keeps the field close and nudges racers toward the middle of the flow channel.
when: Racing games where skilled and novice players race together.
why: strong items let trailing racers catch up

text: Within one area, difficulty jumps when the player enters a new space after mastering the previous one.
when: Player has mastered the previous space and enters a new one in the same area.
why: The area's challenge types stay the same while player power grows, so entering a new space feels like a sudden step.

text: A boss at the end of an area causes a brief difficulty spike, followed by a power bump from boss loot or the next area's upgrades.
when: When a stage concludes with a boss fight or final test.

text: Under Elo with luck, players seek much stronger opponents for big gains; under masterpoint-style scoring, they seek weak opponents, since wins earn equal points.
when: Choosing opponents under each scoring system.
why: Point payoffs differ by opponent strength depending on scoring rules.

text: Enemies that speed up as the player destroys more of them tie rising tension directly to player progress.
when: When a fixed set of enemies must be cleared.
why: Progress itself raises the stakes.

text: Dynamic difficulty adjustment changes challenge on the fly to fit player skill, but it can break the sense that opponents are fixed challenges to master.
when: When considering automatic difficulty scaling
why: Players who know enemy strength depends on their skill stop treating opponents as fixed obstacles

text: Adaptive difficulty lowers a hidden difficulty level after each failure and raises it after each success, within fixed minimum and maximum bounds.
when: Titles where the audience is not meant to attain expert-level mastery.

text: Raising horde frequency as players master an area, and lowering it when they struggle, keeps the challenge matched to their skill.
when: Shooters where a director system rates how the group is doing and spawns foes to match.

text: Death count can indicate challenge, and when graphed over time for a long game it can resemble an interest curve.
when: Very long experiences, such as multiplayer games played for hundreds of hours.
why: Deaths signal challenge, and challenge is linked to how interesting the experience feels.

text: Challenge far below skill produces boredom, challenge far above skill produces frustration, and high-stakes danger produces anxiety; flow lies between these.
when: Judging whether difficulty suits a player's current level.
why: Balance between challenge and skill determines the emotional state.

text: Each challenge has an interesting introduction followed by stepped challenges that rise in difficulty.
A good interest curve has labeled parts: prior expectation, an early hook, rising interest with small rests, a climax, and a resolution leaving the player satisfied.
why: A hook previews what lies ahead and offers an interest spike that sustains focus over the slow opening.

text: The classic pacing curve starts slow, rises through several cycles of tension and calm, reaches a climax, and then falls.
A middle path estimates player performance like dynamic difficulty adjustment but lets the player choose the difficulty level.
when: Designing difficulty systems
why: Players keep agency over challenge while the system still supports them.

text: A challenge is won when character power from time spent, plus player skill, plus combat luck, exceeds its difficulty.
when: Games where character power grows with time spent grinding.
why: Time, skill and luck can substitute for one another, so their combined total decides whether the challenge is beaten.

text: Challenge is only one emotional trigger; treating it as necessary for every game narrows the emotions a design can reach, since many games create strong emotion without a predefined objective.
when: When defining what a game must contain.
why: Restricting design to challenge excludes other emotional triggers.

text: Direct questions about difficulty tend to produce requests for easier play.
When players must prepare for future challenges they cannot foresee, such as during character creation, they default to the most familiar option.
when: Character creation before players know the challenges
why: Unfamiliar options offer no basis for prediction, so players pick the known choice

text: A goal that seems impossible makes players give up, because they stop believing they have a real chance.
when: Setting goal difficulty
why: Belief in success drives continued effort.

text: Lowering difficulty after repeated defeats can feel insulting and disappointing to players, because it removes the satisfaction of mastering a challenge through practice.
when: When a game makes enemies easier after the player keeps losing
why: Players who improve through practice want their mastery to be earned against the same challenge

text: Setting challenge too high early in a game produces frustration and can drive players away.
when: Early in a game, when the player's ability is still low.

text: Setting challenge at the right moment is hard, and developers tend to overestimate what is needed.
Novice designers often confuse real and virtual skill, so keep the two clearly distinct in design.
why: Virtual skill can climb through repeated input even when real skill stays flat, and too much of it feels hollow.

text: Adding player power in a way that removes challenge destroys the wish fulfillment the pairing was meant to create.
when: increasing player power

text: Treating skill and luck as a single slider hides games with high amounts of both, or little of either.
why: Skill and luck are often inversely related but not always, so a single axis cannot capture how much of each a game has.

text: Including every version of a challenge in one level leaves players stuck; spread the variations across the game.
when: designing levels with a challenge type
why: too many variants at once overwhelm learning

text: Do not let difficulty and stress rise together, since the harder the game gets, the harder it feels, which seems unfair.
when: When a long play session accumulates player fatigue
why: Breathing spaces let attention recover, while rising difficulty combined with constant pressure can make the game feel unfair.

text: Making late levels so hard that most players quit causes frustration and abandonment, even though extra difficulty can extend play.
why: Many rival games compete for the same time, so frustrated players leave instead of pushing through.

text: A game that claims to be fair while secretly manipulating numbers will frustrate players who discover it.
why: Players expect a fair opponent that is only more skilled, so discovering a hidden advantage breaks that expectation.

text: Irregular speed changes from poor balance can look like intentional variety but are usually a defect.
when: When progression speeds up and slows down at several points without following a single formula
why: Unplanned spikes and drops in pace are typically caused by balancing errors rather than design choices.

text: 1) Alternate demanding challenges with easier moments, where players feel powerful against weaker enemies. 2) Let players meet lower-level enemies now and then, ideally ones they once found hard. 3) Make progress visible, for example by tracking defeated foes.
why: Players relax and feel dominant in easier stretches, which expresses mastery; alternating intense challenge with feeling powerful is especially compelling.

text: 1) Decide in advance what percentage of players should complete the game. 2) Design the difficulty curve so that target share of players can finish. 3) Keep the first one or two levels simple.
when: Planning difficulty for a game with a completion goal.
why: Early success builds confidence, and confident players persist.

text: 1) Compare the model's ranking with tier lists, popular high-profile deck lists and market prices relative to rarity. 2) Check that objects rated above the curve top the lists and those rated below are rarely played. 3) Investigate each mismatch.
when: When the game is established and has an active player community publishing tier lists and deck lists
why: Real-world play, rankings and prices show whether the model's over- or under-rated items hold up in practice.

text: 1) Ramp difficulty numerically in a spreadsheet. 2) Add difficulty spikes by hand on top of the ramp.
why: Players need occasional difficulty spikes to stay interested, since a merely moderate step up bores them.

text: 1) Draw the curve of the experience's interest. 2) Check for a hook, rising interest with rests, and a grand finale. 3) Revise the weak parts. 4) Compare with a curve drawn by playtesters.
why: Individual tastes differ, but the patterns of pleasurable captivation are remarkably similar across people.

text: 1) Write a sentence or paragraph stating the object's purpose. 2) List its design knobs, the numbers that may change. 3) List the numbers and constraints that must not change to keep the object's identity.
when: Before balancing in earnest, when the balance is likely to be far off
why: Notes on purpose and fixed constraints steer changes so the object keeps its identity.

text: 1) Estimate the performance of a theoretically perfect player. 2) Compare it with the most skilled possible human. 3) If they match, the game has a reachable ceiling; if perfect play beats every human, the game is limitlessly deep.
why: Matching a perfect player against the best human shows whether any skill gap remains for players to learn.

text: 1) Set all payoffs to zero and probabilities to sum to 1. 2) Eliminate variables until two equations remain. 3) Express the other probabilities in one free variable. 4) Keep every probability between 0 and 1 to find the valid range.
when: Solving a symmetric zero-sum game with infinitely many solutions
why: Symmetry forces equal payoffs, and two equal numbers that sum to zero must both be zero.

text: To move a game from chance toward skill, replace random elements with player choices, such as letting players pick cards, starting points, or equipment instead of generating them randomly.
when: adjusting a game's position on the play matrix
why: Player-chosen variables shift the experience toward skill, the quadrant that the target audience enjoys.

text: 1) Offer hints when the player is stuck. 2) Secretly adjust difficulty. 3) Provide alternative challenges that the player can take instead.
when: When a single-player player cannot pass a challenge.
why: Each option lets the player keep progressing without fully blocking play.

text: 1) Decide early which areas should challenge players. 2) Reduce navigational load in the remaining areas.
why: Players have limited attention, so cues that reduce navigation in non-challenge areas free attention for core challenges.

text: 1) Scale difficulty by adding more monsters, tougher monsters, harder terrain and fewer health packs. 2) Let the player's skill growth stand in for character growth.
when: Game has no character levels, as in most first-person shooters.
why: Individual weapons stay as strong over time, so difficulty must rise through enemies and terrain to match the player's growing skill.

text: 1) Set the maximum enemy count for a location. 2) Play the encounter at maximum spawn with the expected damage range. 3) Confirm the player can still survive consistently.
when: varying enemy spawn counts
why: Random spawn ranges must stay survivable at their upper bound.

text: 1) List the challenges in a sequence. 2) Estimate each challenge's virtual challenge, skill challenge, virtual skill, and player skill. 3) Compute perceived challenge for each. 4) Plot the values to check whether difficulty rises too fast or too slow.
when: checking a difficulty progression
why: Plotting the sequence reveals spikes and flat stretches before players reach them.

text: Plan difficulty curves that rise with player skill rather than staying flat, since flat or falling challenge may convince players they have already conquered it and leave.
when: Designing progression for any game.
why: Flat challenge bores players once mastered.

text: Early on, choose intentionally which spots should test players and which should not, so future feedback has benchmarks to measure against.
when: When drafting a UX strategy's opening phase.
why: Defined goals reveal which pain points deserve priority and which can be ignored.

text: Let players choose difficulty from a wide spectrum of activities and difficulties, since perceived difficulty is subjective and changes with the player's state.
when: Designing difficulty options.
why: A fixed difficulty suits some players and frustrates others.

text: Balance challenge so players stay engaged, avoiding both frustration and boredom.
why: Conflict creates tension that players must work to resolve, which lets them connect emotionally with the game.

text: Offer variable difficulty levels with descriptive, non-judgmental labels, such as story mode rather than easy.
when: When players differ in expertise, so their flow zones differ
why: Different players need different challenge levels, so offering choices lets each find their own flow zone.

text: Offer customizable handicaps so players of different levels can compete at challenges they both enjoy.
when: When opponents have very different skill levels, such as computer-controlled ones

text: Offer two or more related puzzles at once where one blocked challenge could halt all progress.
when: When players can get stuck on one puzzle and might quit
why: Switching to another puzzle gives a break from the blocked one, so players return with fresh energy.

text: Balance a game so several strategies complement one another, with foreground and background both meaningful and interlocked.
Stop ongoing harm with real penalties such as ranking or points deductions, or brief bans.
when: when a violation causes ongoing harm

text: Check whether concentrating points in one or two attributes beats spreading them out, and whether any attribute is strong only for certain character types.
when: balancing a point-buy attribute system

text: Compare skill demands of games only within the same kind of skill, such as tactical depth against tactical depth.
when: Comparing two games' skill requirements
why: Different skill kinds are not measured on a common scale.

text: Challenge should test strategic decisions, such as choosing which item to use in a situation, not rote memorization of arbitrary details like recipes.
when: deciding what players must memorize
why: The limited mental workload should go to core challenges, since spending it on menus or arbitrary recall wastes it.

text: Do not place players in demanding multitasking situations unless multitasking is the challenge, especially while they are learning.
when: learning phases or when multitasking is not the challenge
why: demanding dual tasks overload working memory

text: Use elastic challenges with several success levels so one challenge gives achievable but demanding goals to a wide range of skill.
why: Several graded rewards let most players score something while experts still have a target.

text: Make each level harder than the last so that built skill is tested again, pairing this with a release-and-tension pattern.
why: Escalating difficulty keeps players between frustration from too much challenge and boredom from too little.

text: Avoid challenges before players are ready, and provide healing when it is needed.
why: The main challenge depends on managing the health resource, which depends on the designer pacing the game.

text: Combine mechanics only after each has been learned separately, when players need to use them together.
Use player personality types to inform multiplayer gamespace decisions.
Overall difficulty should suit the target audience so the game is neither too hard nor too easy for the people playing it.
Use catch-up item systems only where keeping the field close is part of the intended experience, not as a universal rule.
In casual games, losing may not be possible; the design focus shifts to how fast or slow progress is.
when: Designing a casual game

text: Balance risks from player skill just as carefully as chance elements such as drawn cards or die rolls.
when: In games often seen as purely skill-based, such as chess or baseball
why: Players make expected-value choices about playing safe or taking big risks, so each risk must be balanced.

text: Offer player choice over balance mainly through difficulty levels.
when: Deciding where players may adjust balance
why: Difficulty levels let players pick challenge without breaking the designed balance

text: Guarantee a minimum score for any round, for example a 50-point bonus when the score would otherwise be zero, so no attempt ends at zero.
when: score-based games
why: A floor keeps effort visibly rewarded

text: Offer a locked top-difficulty mode that disables adaptation, so experts who would otherwise manipulate it get an honest challenge.
when: When expert players can manipulate an adaptive difficulty system
why: Adaptation serves novices, while a locked mode gives experts an unmanipulated challenge.

text: Use adaptive difficulty only for games whose players will not reach very high skill, because expert players decode and exploit it, so expert-facing games need more honest difficulty.
when: Choosing between adaptive and honest difficulty.
why: Experts detect and exploit hidden adjustments.

text: Closing the gulf of execution removes challenge, while some friction is necessary because challenge requires the possibility of failure; the design task is distinguishing meaningful challenge from usability problems.
when: When friction between intent and action is meant as gameplay challenge rather than a usability problem.
why: Games depend on overcoming obstacles between intent and action to create mastery.

text: A medium or low skill ceiling can cause skill play to become dull once reached, but a game can stay excellent by offering art, exploration, and narrative beyond skill.
when: When players quickly reach the top of the skill range and performance cannot improve further.
why: Players stop improving once they reach the ceiling.

text: When one special option triggers a hazard that the other option can avoid, each option carries a different cost.
why: Each choice creates a dilemma, since moving one piece can leave others exposed to the hazard.

text: Ruthless games (high probability, high penalty) produce extreme caution, masocore games (high probability, low penalty) encourage repeated attempts, punishing games (low probability, high penalty) produce disproportionate caution, and casual games (low on both) remove anxiety.
when: choosing failure penalty and frequency
why: The combination of loss probability and size determines the play style.

text: Sophisticated clue systems cost much to build, while simpler fixes such as a prompt or environmental cue can be enough.
when: When players are stuck at an obstacle and need help to continue.
why: Building sophisticated clue intelligence is costly and time consuming.

text: Making a game both deep and accessible is difficult, because gentle ramps suit learners while limitless depth can make early lessons unclear and opponents exploit mistakes.
when: When designing a game meant for both novices and experts.
why: Accessible ramps and deep competitive play pull in different directions.

text: Hard turn or time limits fix game length directly and can be compelling, but they may signal too little playtesting; tuning progression addresses length at its source.
when: When a game must end at a set point

text: Dynamic difficulty adjustment adapts to player skill and performance automatically, but it is harder to implement and tune than player-selected difficulty levels.
Designers can either make a game harder than the market average or give players tools to adjust difficulty themselves. The right choice depends on genre, era and business model.
when: When deciding how hard a game should be relative to peers
why: Average difficulty varies by genre, era and business model, so the target must be set against them

text: Offering a difficulty change after repeated deaths removes the excuse for dying again, but some players find it patronizing.
when: Designing difficulty prompts after failure
why: The prompt helps stuck players but can feel condescending.

text: Some starvation is easy to fix by increasing sight radius or revealing more information, such as more cards.
when: When information starvation is obvious and visibly caused by hidden elements

text: When players see too little hidden state, play degrades into reactive thrashing, low skill, and mostly random choice, such as when they see only their own hidden cards and current bets.
when: Players cannot see enough of the game state
why: Without enough information to plan, decisions lose meaning and the skill ceiling drops toward chance.

text: Sparse save points force long stretches of play between saves, which makes optimizing every action impractical.
why: Reloading far-back saves costs lots of redone play, which discourages save-scumming for optimization.

text: To fix a slow opening, temporarily add positive sum rules, start players at a higher power level, or offer more engaging early choices.
when: when the opening feels slow
why: more power or meaningful choices make the opening engaging

text: Use a time or turn limit that declares the leader at that point the winner to stop a negative feedback stalemate.
when: when negative feedback can stall the game
why: it forces a result without a decisive finish

text: Make early failures survivable, show clearly that an action failed, and let players retry at once, rather than punishing them with unfair deaths.
when: Players are still learning a mechanic
why: Unfair deaths during learning feel unfair and drive players away

text: Detect when a player is stuck, then give just enough help to pass the obstacle without destroying its challenge.
when: When players repeatedly fail at the same obstacle
why: Prolonged stuck states make players quit in frustration and never return.

text: Use small setbacks such as lost resources, a lost ally, missed content, or lost information, so the game continues along a new path.
when: When failure should cost something without stopping play.
why: Setbacks keep play moving.

text: Reduce cue salience or add lookalike decoys when uncertainty is part of the challenge; decoys that resemble enemies create false alarms.
when: uncertainty is intended as challenge
why: Lookalikes raise uncertainty but can cause players to attack innocent objects.

text: Digital games often leave the resolving action to the system rather than stating it as a player action, because the program adjudicates the end of play.
when: Comparing board and digital game procedure lists
why: Players in digital games do not perform the closing action themselves.

text: Digital games are not automatically more complex than nondigital games; complexity depends on design choices rather than the medium.
Digital games consist of three technical parts: input, output, and AI. Controls form the input part.
Digital games have no set boundaries in virtual space but hard boundaries in physical reality.
Tune a digital multiplayer game to produce the social interaction of a three-to-six person board game.
why: Generations of board game tuning have settled on three-to-six players as an ideal group size for social play.

text: An elder game is a post-progression activity that keeps veteran players engaged after a leveling game stops offering new discoveries.
Give experienced players a meaningful role, such as hiding or creating challenges for others; they take pride in it and enjoy the status it brings.
Elder games take five forms: a harder game, governance privileges, the joy of creation, guild management tools, and a chance to teach.
Elder game forms vary by genre: artistic expression in sim and social games, raids, PvP, guild leadership and new content in MMOs, and ending a campaign satisfyingly in tabletop RPGs.
when: Designing post-progression content

text: Endless games, including tabletop RPGs, MMOs and some free-to-play titles, can be modeled with a final elder game phase whose start depends on progression length.
when: When a game has no end point, like ongoing RPG campaigns or persistent online worlds

text: Granting elders too much control, such as governance privileges, carries risk.
If players quit at the elder game, soften the transition with expansions that raise the level cap, multiple replayable builds, or an elder game that appeals to progression-oriented players.
when: when subscribers churn at the elder game transition
why: an abrupt transition ends engagement early

text: Emergence is complex, unpredictable collective behavior arising when simple rules or unique components interact, producing results that no single rule or element specifies or possesses.
when: Once a game system is running
why: Elements are interrelated and take on new dimensions in motion.

text: Players find meaning in a game through experiences that emerge when they interact with its design.
when: When players interact with a game's systems.
why: Experiences arise from interaction, so meaning comes from design.

text: Players build stories from randomized dialogue and simple combat rules, even when the game models no meaning behind the events.
when: observing autonomous fights between characters
why: players interpret ambiguous events as meaningful

text: Actual play concentrates on equilibrium configurations, so most of a game's possible combinations never occur in practice.
why: Players in equilibrium have no incentive to deviate, while off-equilibrium states push someone to switch.

text: Systems balanced separately can interact in unplanned ways that often surface only at alpha.
when: Multiple systems combine in play
why: Each system is tuned alone, so combined effects go unseen.

text: Emergent movement techniques that require mastery tend to add to competitive play.
when: Players discover unplanned techniques
why: Skill-based techniques reward practice and create depth.

text: Local symmetry means many small internal symmetries within parts of a design, appearing in rooms, rule systems and balance, rather than one overall mirror image.
Innate complexity comes from many rules and exceptions, often from simulating a complex situation or adding rules to tune balance.
when: When a ruleset has many special cases
why: Complexity located in the rules themselves, rather than in their interaction

text: Emergent complexity arises when simple rules produce intricate situations, as in Go, whose very simple rules create billions of complex positions.
when: When evaluating how rich a game's play can become from few rules
why: Interaction of simple rules generates varied situations

text: An emergent reinforcement schedule is a reward pattern arising from the interaction of basic game mechanics, not from an explicit designer-set rule.
Different starting patterns in the Game of Life evolve in very different ways, and some produce moving structures that cycle through shapes across the grid.
Most strategic actions are not written in the rules; they emerge as players combine basic actions during play.
Interpretation and simulation are the two primary routes by which game feel will evolve, and processing power allows richer input parsing across time, space and state.
Before a game is played, its elements form a latent potential that becomes a working system only when played.
Memorable moments can emerge from physics, gravity, weapon tuning, map layout and multiplayer interacting, without being authored.
Judge unintended strategies by impact: if an action is not game-breaking, it may become a secret worth keeping.
when: players discover an unplanned strategy
why: harmless discoveries can enrich play

text: Fast action games may cap useful counter layers at two or three, since players cannot process more in time.
when: Real-time or fast action games.
why: Reaction time limits how many layers players can act on.

text: A herding ecosystem should have about two predator levels above the herded creatures, plus possibly one level below, so predators can be countered by other predators.
when: Designing a food chain where the player protects a vulnerable herded group.
why: Two levels let predators be countered by other predators; more levels risk the helpful predator being absent when needed.

text: Many interacting subjects with different roles make coordination and sacrifice possible; a game where all pieces follow identical rules tends to feel dull.
when: Choosing how many distinct entities a game uses
