why: Varied subjects create varied strategic options.

text: High counts of verbs, objects per verb, goal routes and controlled subjects tend to produce emergent play, while low counts tend to produce predictable play.
when: when reviewing a game's action and goal counts

text: A single rule that makes invaders move faster as fewer remain produces both a slow start that speeds up as the player succeeds and targets that get harder to hit, without coding either property directly.
when: When a wanted outcome emerges from rule interactions instead of added special cases
why: Both properties emerge from the one rule's interaction with play.

text: When a divergent goal stays close to the official goal, as killing usually helps capture an objective, the game is harmed but not broken.
when: In multiplayer, when one player's off-goal play affects the whole group
why: The divergent action still advances the official goal, so teammates' roles still hold together.

text: Giving each player a unique power produces new interactions from combinations, so a modular game stays surprising across hundreds of plays.
why: Each combination of unique abilities creates interactions the designer may not have anticipated, so repeated plays stay new.

text: Rule exceptions that differ between movement and capture can unlock emergent structures that simpler rules would never produce.
when: Movement and capture rules differ

text: Deep games sustain themselves by wrapping games inside games, revealing a deeper layer each time one is mastered.
why: A single skill like aiming has limited depth to master, so new layers are needed to keep the skill range broad.

text: In emergent systems, climaxes can recur at random, and predefined pacing cannot fully control them because decisions are generated on the fly.
when: In systems-based games where decisions are generated on the fly
why: Mechanics generate decisions on the fly, so the designer cannot schedule them in advance to follow a pacing curve.

text: Balanced complex strategies add depth because even very skilled players cannot execute all their contingencies perfectly.
why: Each choice ends up weighing more interacting variables, which enriches the play experience.

text: Changing the lower-level mechanics that produce an emergent schedule changes the reward rhythm, even when no schedule rule is edited.
when: when adjusting mechanics that generate rewards, such as in a generated dungeon
why: Emergent schedules are products of rule interactions

text: Designers cannot control what players do, but they control the rules of the systems players use; rich mechanics, objects and spaces that suit different play styles let emergent narrative grow.
why: Rich systems of mechanics, objects, and spaces give players the opportunity to create their own stories.

text: Free interaction with a limited asset set produces emergent play, and linear introductions teach players how to use the assets first.
why: A limited asset set helps players learn the symbolic system, and freedom to act with those assets is what creates emergence.

text: Customization can be layered across the community, the avatar, and the home, letting players shape each scope.
when: Games whose primary mechanic is socialization between players
why: Letting others visit customized spaces enables socialization between players.

text: Assuming that designing a game and seeing what emerges will reliably produce the intended feeling.
when: When a specific feeling, such as coldness, is important to the game
why: Sound effects and game rules can be chosen deliberately to deliver that feeling to players.

text: A long stretch of unchanging play means gameplay progression has failed.
Reading edges or folds differently can make several solutions valid, so a puzzle may have more than one answer unless its rules constrain interpretation.
when: When the game is a puzzle rather than an action game
why: A puzzle needs a precisely defined solution, so ambiguous readings of its elements must be constrained.

text: Stacking many exotic AI techniques in one design is a sign the team lacks focus, and tends to hurt the result.
when: When a design combines several unusual AI techniques together
why: Simple techniques do most of the AI work, so one or two advanced techniques can serve specific effects.

text: Rapid mass predation can melt down a level of an ecosystem, so unintended consequences must be checked during design.
when: Tuning predator-prey rates.
why: Unintended effects spread through connected species, so structural guidelines such as food chain depth are needed to prevent a rapid collapse.

text: Unplanned movement techniques can let players cross levels in ways not intended, altering level flow.
when: Movement techniques skip designed routes
why: Players reach areas the level layout did not anticipate.

text: Solving a payoff table that still contains dominated options can produce invalid probabilities below 0 or above 1.
Copying mechanics directly from a traditional or competitor's game makes a submission feel familiar and unoriginal.
when: When a game is submitted to a publisher for acceptance
why: Reviewers see many submissions, and a copied design reads as something they have already played.

text: Dynamics react unpredictably to rule changes, so a mechanic that removes one dynamic may let other dynamics emerge.
when: Adding a mechanic to fix an unwanted dynamic
why: Systems respond to rule changes in ways that are hard to predict

text: Quick, local patches to a connected mechanic can break its relationships with other mechanics.
when: When the mechanic is connected to many others rather than limited to one target
why: A change to one connected mechanic ripples into all the others it touches.

text: The most dangerous failure traps emerge from unplanned interactions between design elements, so they are hard to predict during design.
when: When systems interact in ways nobody anticipated.
why: Unforeseen combinations, such as running out of ammo at a checkpoint, can make a challenge impossible.

text: Players who lack the cultural background for a convention may fail to read it, and may get stuck and quit.
when: A convention relies on knowledge the player has not acquired.
why: Conventions only communicate to players who share the priming.

text: Without clear limits, a world's possibilities can grow too large for players to understand.
why: Clear boundaries, overviews, and consistent abstraction keep a world's possibilities manageable and believable.

text: 1) Count the player verbs. 2) Count how many objects each verb acts on. 3) Count the routes to each goal. 4) Count the subjects players control. 5) Check how actions change constraints as side effects.
when: when judging whether a game leans toward emergence

text: Control an unwanted emergent dynamic indirectly by changing the mechanics that produce it, not by steering the dynamic itself.
when: A player pattern emerging from systems is undesirable
why: Dynamics cannot be controlled directly, only shaped through the rules that drive them

text: Test for emergent interactions among tools and mechanics, not only obvious ones, because degenerate strategies are often hidden from designers.
when: When many tools and mechanics can interact with one another in a game
why: A degenerate strategy removes the decisions that give a game its depth.

text: Innate complexity suits faithful simulation or fine balance tuning but is hard to learn; emergent complexity keeps rules simple while producing rich play.
when: When deciding how complex a ruleset should be
why: Rule-heavy designs cost learnability, while simple rules can still yield depth

text: When difficulty adjusts subtly, players feel success comes from their own skill, while novices keep a real chance to win.
when: Games with adaptive difficulty or rubber-band opponents.

text: Players attribute emotions like fear or boredom to simple game pieces even when the rules define no such states.
when: pieces behave in ways that look like choices
why: apophenia projects feelings onto behavior that looks purposeful

text: When players can communicate and negotiate in a dilemma, they can both deceive and cooperate, unlike in fixed-rule versions.
when: dilemmas with communication
why: Negotiation opens room for trust and deceit

text: Fiero is the feeling of personal triumph over adversity, arising from frustration followed by a sharp shift to feeling very good.
Emotion drives player engagement, and designers can add it through narrative and NPC relationships.
Emotion-focused design can inspire the team, widen the audience, and give a competitive edge.
The games industry usually addresses emotion through visual aesthetics, music, and narrative, while game feel is often overlooked.
Games produce fiero directly through the player's own choices, which films cannot do.
why: Fiero comes from overcoming obstacles the player struggled against, which requires frustration before success.

text: More compelling games generate more internal value, so players care about outcomes without needing external stakes.
why: Endogenous meaning is internally generated, so value comes from inside the game rather than outside it.

text: Players use games for five emotional purposes: venting frustration, cheering up, gaining perspective, building confidence, and relaxing.
why: Games give people a way to regulate their emotional state.

text: The emotion pillar comprises game feel, presence, and surprises.
Placing two clashing emotions side by side can cancel both out rather than producing a blended or interesting effect.
when: When designing juxtaposed emotional moments.
why: Juxtaposition and antagonism lie on a fine line, and an attempt can annihilate both feelings.

text: Aim for a broad picture of emotional response that serves design goals rather than trying to separate exactly which effects come from emotion and which from cognition.
when: Designing for player emotion.

text: Identify the essential features of a memorable experience and build them into the game, leaving out incidental details.
when: recreating a real-world experience in a game
why: players respond to the essential features, not incidental ones

text: Apply the same care to players that you would put into a gift, so they feel someone considered how the game will make them feel.
Build emotions on purpose: fear needs time and space to grow, and planning needs information and a place to plan.
when: When a designer wants players to feel a specific emotion such as fear or planning.
why: Emotions like fear or planning need time, space, and material to develop; without them the intended feeling does not form.

text: Show progression clearly, through skill growth, levels or progress bars, so players feel their competence grow.
when: When an activity requires sustained effort to learn or improve at.
why: competence is a core intrinsic motivation need

text: A game that is easy to use but boring will not be played, so engagement matters as much as usability.
why: Games are autotelic, played for the pleasure of playing rather than an external end.

text: Engageability, the second game UX pillar, has three overlapping parts: motivation, emotion, and game flow.
why: Games are played for their own sake, so a usable game still fails if it does not engage players.

text: Engageability is whether a game holds player interest, covering fun, engagement, emotion, motivation, flow, and how players remember the experience. It fails when the game is too easy, too hard, or its goals stop exciting players.
Engaging players means making them feel mentally immersed in the game.
An interest curve plots a player's interest across an experience over time, showing where interest rises, dips, and peaks.
An interesting choice has upsides and downsides, often framed as risk versus reward, and changes the player's chance of winning.
Player experience can be annotated by self-reports (free response during play or forced questionnaire data) or by third-person experts and external observers.
Games are interactive, have challenge (too little or too much makes them bad), and create their own internal value.
Many commercial games fail to engage or retain players even with large budgets, and educational games usually have smaller budgets, making engagement harder.
Engage-ability is harder to define than usability, because player motivations are not fully understood and no solid guidelines exist yet.
Engagement is preferred over fun or immersion as a term, because it can be broken down more objectively.
why: Fun means different things to different people.

text: Leave players wanting more: ending activities while players still want to continue makes timing feel right.
when: Setting the length of play sessions or rounds
why: Players return to a game that ends before they tire of it.

text: Inherent interest rises with risk over safety, fancy over plain, and the unusual over the ordinary.
Inherent interest can appeal to base instincts and to higher instincts; check which of each an experience reaches and whether it could reach more.
Decide whether an event's appeal comes from its content, its arrangement, or its presentation.
Check whether the rules produce stories with good interest curves, rising tension and payoff, rather than flat sequences of events.
when: tuning rules for story output
why: Games act as machines that produce stories during play, so the rules shape the story output players experience.

text: Consider how a game will affect people in the future, not only how it plays today.
why: Games shape lasting fantasies and ideals that people carry through their lives.

text: Confusing the player with the interface can be acceptable when the confusion is part of the intended game experience.
why: Interface friction unrelated to play produces frustration with no link to the core experience.

text: Physical action alone does not engage the mind; engagement needs expectation, uncertainty, consequence and decision together.
why: Engagement comes from the mind's internal decision process; a game full of motion without meaningful choices leaves players disengaged.

text: Engagement in educational games can be measured with questionnaires built around game flow.

Players engage with games at three levels: spectator, participant, and transformational. Spectators watch others play with minimal risk, participants are actively involved, and transformational play can change how a player thinks or lives.
Interest can be broken into three factors; the first, inherent interest, is a property of events on their own.
Prototypes described as not fun often lack meaningful choice between safe and risky options.
when: Diagnosing why a prototype feels dull.
why: Without a real decision, players only repeat the same action.

text: 1) List the questions the game puts in the player's mind. 2) Find what makes players care about each question. 3) Add elements that make players invent further questions.
when: reviewing a game's curiosity hooks
why: Players' underlying motives sit behind stated goals, so questions only hold attention when those motives are addressed.

text: 1) Identify what players value in the game. 2) Find ways to make that value greater for them. 3) Examine how in-game value relates to players' motivations.
when: reviewing a game's valued items
why: In-game value tracks players' investment in winning, so it points to where the design can improve.

text: 1) Identify which parts of the game are fun and why. 2) Identify which parts need more fun. 3) Find weak parts where sections fail to give the same pleasure or surprise.
when: reviewing a game for fun

text: Recommendations for children should rest on evidence specific enough to guide concrete action.
why: The video game category is not homogeneous and play context matters, so broad claims cannot guide specific action.

text: When the late stage feels rote, introduce mechanics reserved for that stage.
when: when the end game feels repetitive
why: late-only mechanics give the final phase its own identity

text: Leave room for free play inside the rigid game structure rather than fixing every action.
why: Play is free movement inside a rigid structure, so locking every action removes the play itself.

text: Age-rating systems inform parents about content and suggest appropriate player ages; use them for games with violent content so parents can make informed choices.
when: games with violent content

text: Geopolitical review (GeoPS) checks a game's deep localization, covering regional dialects, cultures, taboos and how context changes the meaning of content.
Technological progress is accelerating: a thousand years ago people could guess daily life a century ahead, while today even life ten years ahead is hard to predict.
Foul language is a matter of appropriateness rather than safety, so it is not the core safety concern.
In June 2020, a diabetes self-management title became the first game cleared by a US regulator to treat a medical condition, childhood ADHD.
Many multiplayer games use codes of conduct and temporary bans to manage antisocial behavior.
Unethical content does not prove a real-life harmful impact, but it still deserves ethical reflection.
If a game rewards meanness, players will exploit it, so test specifically for incentives that make players treat each other badly.
why: Players optimize toward whatever the game rewards, and a rewarded mean strategy can drain fun from opponents' play.

text: Understanding ethical challenges protects players and helps studios avoid fines and lawsuits.
when: When a game is aimed at or played by children
why: Regulators have recently increased fines and class actions against studios, including for child privacy violations and dark patterns.

text: In protection objectives, one side guards an object while the other tries to capture it.
when: Asymmetric objectives

text: Removing easy griefing opportunities reduces the need for bans and policing.
Protecting the early ranks from star loss lets evenly matched players advance over time.
If designers exclude a harmful action, such as harming bystanders, players cannot choose it, so the design determines whether that choice exists at all.
Reputation systems let players police one another, keeping order without separating player groups.
why: Spread-out worlds with loose interaction rules invite antisocial play, and reputation that keeps offenders out of shared areas counters it.

text: A push mechanic can be used against inactive players, who get shoved into danger while away from their controls.
Blaming players for not following the intended design does not remove a degenerate strategy; designers must respond with restrictions or affordances.
when: When players do not play the way the designer intended
why: The designer must push players toward fun play, and a degenerate strategy can be more fun than the intended one, so it may need to become core.

text: Releasing a game far ahead of what players can accept has caused many game failures.
why: Every successful game mixes novelty with familiarity, and novelty alone lacks the staying power to keep players.

text: Focusing on profanity filters while missing predatory contact risk leaves the most serious danger unaddressed.
when: When a game involves strangers talking to each other
why: Anonymity lets dangerous people exploit innocents, while foul language has nothing to do with safety.

text: Blockchain networks have an environmental impact, which the choice of consensus method affects.
why: Proof-of-work is high energy-consuming, while proof-of-stake is more sustainable.

text: 1) Avoid dark patterns. 2) Avoid the attention economy. 3) Consider the moral values the game conveys. 4) Adopt a code of ethics to resolve grey areas.
why: Games are influential and part of culture, so studios carry responsibility for what they expose players to.

text: Check every in-game gesture against each target region, since the same gesture can mean something positive, rude or obscene elsewhere.
when: A game uses gestures and ships to multiple regions.
why: A gesture can mean something rude in another region, which alienates players or triggers scandal after release.

text: Do not add frustration to push players toward purchases, because doing so is unethical.
when: For young players
why: Children's self-control is still developing, so they resist manipulative psychological pressure less easily than adults.

text: Binding promises need reporting and dispute-resolution mechanisms.
when: When players often make complex ongoing deals
why: Binding trades make players more willing to make future offers, so disputes over those deals need resolving.

text: A game that exploits a cognitive bias should also reveal that bias to players so they learn to recognize it, and it must still be fun.
when: designing around a bias or fallacy
why: awareness reduces later susceptibility to the bias

text: Protect young players from disruptive behavior and shady monetization practices.
when: The audience includes players under 18
why: Children are more vulnerable to psychological pressure

text: Give players ways to block people they do not want to meet again and ways to flag inappropriate behavior.
when: When disruptive behavior is directed at strangers in the game
why: Unwanted behavior from strangers is perceived as harassment or unfairness, which is not motivating for players.

text: Explain to offenders why their behavior is unacceptable and give them a chance to make amends.
when: for a first or minor violation
why: Without consequences, disruptive behaviors are tolerated and proliferate.

text: Once a report is verified, tell the victim that their voice was heard and that action was taken.
Do not make gambling-style mechanics easily accessible to minors, since this crosses an evidence-based ethical line.
why: Gambling-like mechanics show growing evidence of harm, especially to children, and correlate with problem gambling, a fully recognized addiction.

text: Make players protected by default and let them voluntarily opt into being attackable, rather than forcing risk on everyone.
when: In multiplayer games where players can attack other players
why: Forced player-versus-player risk drove away law-abiding players, while opt-in attackability still satisfies those who want combat.

text: Apply the griefing review early, before players find the weak points.
when: during design

text: Consider ethics throughout development rather than afterwards, because design choices always affect players.
Advocate for story across all disciplines: convey the narrative focus and make sure each discipline is invested in it.
Content is unethical when unethical actions are rewarded and their moral opposites are impossible; allowing both keeps a design out of that category.
when: Evaluating whether a game's moral content is problematic.
why: Removing the moral alternative removes the player's ability to choose the ethical path.

text: When business goals conflict with players, prioritize accessibility, inclusion, ethics and early player-safety consideration, keeping profit from costing players; otherwise balance player interests against business goals.
why: Players are the top priority because UX aims at improving people's lives through games, so ethics outweighs business interests.

text: Ethical responsibility: companies must follow law but bear none, only individuals do; or studios should accept responsibility for game effects now, without waiting for an industry code.
why: Only individuals can hold ethical responsibility, since corporations are legal entities with no capacity for ethics.

text: Players keep retrying after failure when they attribute it to correctable personal mistakes and sense a real chance of success.
when: When players fail a challenge.
why: Self-attributed failure implies the challenge is fair, and a perceived real chance keeps players willing to retry.

text: Entertaining failure reduces frustration and eases learning. Players enjoy failure with escalating, humorous consequences that open new states, and may deliberately trigger failures for amusement.
when: When players fail repeatedly, or when failure leads to dramatic or humorous outcomes rather than dead ends.
why: Fun failure makes repeated attempts less frustrating, and interesting new states make failure rewarding in itself.

text: In modern games failure is usually temporary and followed by retrying; limited lives and restarts feel frustrating, while in school failure can make children feel not smart enough.
why: Games frame failure as a step toward winning rather than a judgment.

text: Gameplay, not graphics, story or new features, keeps players staying, so aim for an experience that holds attention as long and as intensely as possible.
why: Players who praise visuals or plot still drop off unless core play engages them.

text: Let players fail and be penalized only by events they can understand and prevent, so they can improve next time; random, unstoppable penalties feel unfair and drive players away.
when: When designing penalties for failure.
why: Losing all sense of control makes the game feel unfair, and players seldom return.

text: Failure that costs resources but keeps the player in a new situation, rather than restarting, keeps play moving and avoids repetition.
when: When a failed attempt would otherwise restart the same situation.
why: A changed situation gives the player a new approach to try.

text: A dead end occurs when a player cannot reach the objective no matter what they do.
Failure can come in degrees rather than as a binary end of play, so a mistake can slow progress without stopping the game.
why: Degrees of failure stretch the success-failure spectrum in both directions.

text: A failure trap is a long stretch of play in which failure is guaranteed and the player cannot escape it.
Dead ends appear as missing items in adventure games, depleted forces in strategy games, and inescapable spaces in FPS games.
Online identities and social networks raise questions about what happens when players die, such as online memorials or avatars passed to descendants.
Grinding known skills takes time without adding difficulty, so friction and difficulty do not map one to one.
why: Time investment adds friction that is not difficulty.

text: Some failure traps are so deeply built into a design that they cannot be solved cleanly, as racing and sports games have not fully solved the dead-man-walking trap.
A penalty that players find a nuisance can be reframed as a benefit, such as a need that instead grants a temporary boost when satisfied.
when: A realistic survival mechanic is disliked because it only punishes neglect.
why: Players respond much better to rewards for upkeep than to penalties for forgetting it.

text: Show players something new, or let them do something new, to capture their interest immediately.
when: when judging whether events are interesting on their own

text: Failure states deserve design effort because players spend a large share of their time in them.
Mechanics that stun the player can frustrate, so their design uncertainty is high.
Begin a physical game with a hard break from everyday reality, and end it with a structured off-boarding.
Because losing the avatar halts play, designers can tap survival instincts as a motivator.
Forcing a card draw and a play every turn, with passing disallowed, makes most cards harm opponents, which pushes players to attack soon.
when: in card games that disallow passing
why: harmful cards make inaction impossible to sustain

text: A stated play time can hide long stretches of repetitive grinding, so the value delivered is smaller than the claim suggests.
when: in story-heavy RPGs
why: padding does not count as real content

text: A demanding activity requirement alienates casual players whose schedules rarely allow frequent sessions.
Emotional benefits can backfire if the game is as frustrating as real life.
when: a game causes repeated frustration
why: The game then repeats the stress it was meant to relieve

text: A hook without good gameplay yields only a gimmick.
Forcing players to repeat content after each failure turns punishment into a petty waste of their time.
why: Setbacks that let play continue keep the player in an ongoing situation instead of restarting the challenge.

text: Judge fairness by viewing the game from each player's position and confirming each has a winning chance that feels fair for their skill.
Make hit zones and collision forgiving, for example smaller than the visible model, and use coyote time and air control in platformers.
when: Designing character collision and platforming controls.
why: Forgiving physics prevents errors that come from imprecise input rather than poor skill.

text: In systems terms, feedback is a direct link where an output changes another element of the system, unlike the everyday sense of any information returned to a player.
Feedback calls such as playing a sound or spawning particles do not change game rules but strongly increase how intense an effect feels.
when: Designing scripted effects
why: Presentation calls shape player perception without altering state.

text: Metaphors built on systems players already know, such as Newtonian physics, electricity, or fire, need almost no learning burden.
when: When the system being imitated is one people already understand
why: Players bring prior knowledge of these systems.

text: Play is a continuous cycle in which information flows from player to game and back, and this cycle generates the player's experience.
why: Returned information shapes what the player does next, so feedback quality governs understanding and enjoyment.

text: Systems are fractal: a subsystem can be as small as one resource and one mechanic, while the whole game economy is the largest system, so analysis can target any scale.
when: Choosing the scope of analysis.
why: Shared resources are how one system affects others, so analysis can target any nested scale.

text: Elegance is efficiency: a simple-to-learn system yielding rich emergent complexity, strong emotional impact and wide play variety, with low player comprehension demand and developer effort.
A game is a self-contained, rule-bound system that draws players into structured conflict and ends in an unequal result. It is recognized once its formal elements are combined and set in motion.
Easy but deep means a game takes minutes to learn and a lifetime to master. Making it easy to learn is the easier half of design; creating depth is harder.
Game anatomy is the internal structure of a game: how its pieces fit together and produce its behavior.
Formal elements are the structural parts of a game; without them, a game stops being a game.
Formal-element question themes include the objective and its clarity, the choices made, the winning strategy, loopholes, and interaction with others.
An elegant game allows few basic actions but many strategic ones.
why: Basic actions that interact well with one another create strategic depth, while many poorly interacting actions bloat the game and confuse players.

text: Make each element of a game as beautiful as it can be, since individually fine elements can still leave the whole feeling flat.
when: when reviewing presentation quality
why: Some elements are beautiful only in combination with others, so the overall feel depends on how the parts are composed together.

text: Elegance comes from removing excess, as a sculptor carves away material, rather than from adding more features.
why: Each mechanic costs design effort, computing resources, and player attention, so extra features make the game harder to understand.

text: Elegant designs often look plain, because their strength lies in the possibility space that emerges in play rather than in flashy features.
why: A simple design can generate far more challenges, tactics, and situations in play than a flashier design of similar mechanical complexity.

text: The best way to widen a skill range is an elegant system with depth squeezed from each simple mechanic.
why: Simple systems are easy to learn and hard to master.

text: Choosing one tetrad element constrains the others: mechanics need supporting technology, aesthetics that show them clearly, and a story that makes them sensible.
when: When a designer picks mechanics to drive the game's play
why: Mechanics define what a game is, so the technology, aesthetics, and story must be chosen to support and show them.

text: Many different combinations of formal elements are possible, and each combination can produce a different play experience.
Every game is built from four equally essential elements: mechanics, story, aesthetics and technology. None outranks the others, and each can be shaped to support the others.
The essential formal elements of games are participants, goal, methods, constraints, assets, opposition, limits, and outcome.
why: Stripping out the objective or the rules stops the activity from being a game at all.

text: A game's underlying system is formed by how its formal and dramatic elements interact, and this interaction strongly shapes the player experience.
why: Games create a structured conflict that players resolve through an entertaining process, so how the elements interact defines the game.

text: 1) List every purpose a single game element serves. 2) Count those purposes; an element serving more purposes indicates a more elegant design.
when: judging whether an element earns its place in the design
why: Elements serving many purposes keep a system simple to learn while still producing rich emergent complexity.

text: 1) List which of the four element categories the design uses. 2) Assess each element on its own for strengths and weaknesses. 3) Assess all four together for harmony and a shared theme.
when: When reviewing a whole game design.
why: Judging from one element alone produces a skewed review.

text: 1) List all game elements. 2) For each, count its purposes. 3) Combine or remove elements serving only one or two purposes. 4) Extend elements serving several purposes to take on more.
when: A game feels cluttered or several elements do similar jobs
why: Reducing redundant elements makes the design cleaner and more coherent

text: 1) Identify players: number, requirements, roles and special knowledge. 2) Identify objective, procedures, rules, conflict, boundaries and possible outcomes. 3) Note dramatic elements: challenge, play, premise, character and story.
when: when analyzing a game's formal and dramatic elements

text: 1) Define the conflict. 2) State the rules and procedures. 3) Define each player's goal and win condition. 4) Identify the most important player action and how it works. 5) Map a typical turn, ideally as a flowchart. 6) Define player count and interaction. 7) Record the working title, audience, platform, and restrictions. 8) Include only the most critical rules at this stage.
when: After choosing a concept and before prototyping
why: Outlining the formal system pins down mechanics before detailed work begins.

text: Let form signal function: give different functions different forms, so an armored enemy with a weak back signals slowness and a weak point.
when: Adding items, weapons or interface elements that differ in behaviour from existing ones.
why: Similar-looking elements with different meanings lead players to mistakes.

text: Make deliberate decisions about all four elements for every game, because each requires conscious design choices.
when: when planning or reviewing a game's design
why: Each element powerfully influences the others, so every one forces important decisions regardless of the game.

text: Elegance must be balanced against character: an over-honed design becomes elegant but boring, and over-cleaning strips memorable qualities, so keep purposeless oddities that can make a game memorable.
when: When simplifying or optimizing a design solely for clean structure.
why: Over-cleaning strips qualities players remember and enjoy; memorable qualities often lie outside pure function.

text: Fun is a goal in nearly every game, yet resists analysis because it is subjective and its sources are not always easy to explain.
Four fun types double as playstyles: challenge-driven, effortless, meaning-driven, and social; each unlocks a distinct set of emotions.
why: Designers cannot create play experiences directly, so each playstyle is a set of mechanics that unlocks a particular emotion.

text: Fun is partly a state of mind, so turning a tedious task into a game can make it enjoyable.
why: Fun is subjective, so a problem that feels tedious to one person can feel like a delightful puzzle to another.

text: Players tend to seek minimal workload, so motivation must be deliberately designed rather than assumed.
why: the brain prefers low-effort paths

text: Fatigue in interactive evolution comes from many selections, slow feedback, too much content on screen, or requests for very specific input.
when: In interactive evolution, where human input drives the search
why: The listed factors cause cognitive overload in the user.

text: Clashing tones placed close together, such as tragedy followed by a bravado line, can produce unintended amusement.
when: When an emotional beat is followed by a tonally mismatched beat.
why: The collision of incompatible feelings can strike players as funny.

text: A humorous tone makes logical absurdities produced by emergence feel funny rather than wrong, so players accept them more readily.
when: emergent events produce unrealistic results
why: humor reframes incongruity as entertainment

text: Fun is pleasure combined with surprise, a working definition that can be revised; a fun interface should provide both.
Fun is mostly emotional and dramatic appeal, which draws players in, keeps them trying, and keeps them playing.
Humor arises when two unrelated things are abruptly linked by a paradigm shift, often producing a bark-like laugh.
Fun includes sad or emotional experiences, not only laughter.
Interactive evaluation scores content from a human's interaction with it, so a player is in the loop; feedback is either explicit, asked for, or implicit, inferred from behaviour.
Depth measures the amount of material a game offers to learn; deep games keep revealing new lessons for years, while shallow ones are exhausted once their trick is known.
Fun has been defined as a mix of challenge, competition and interaction, as learning, and as a personal experience that varies by individual, and sources disagree.
Games are voluntary, so a game without emotional appeal loses players or never gets them.
Fun is subjective and contextual, so no single taste defines it.
Play can take serious, aggressive, or fantastical forms, depending on the game and its players.
Many people who dismiss games as meaningless can name one that matters deeply to them, which shows games can carry real meaning.
No fun meter exists, so absolute interest is hard to quantify; designers judge relative changes in interest instead.
Successful games typically combine three of the four fun keys.

Fun is widely targeted but poorly defined; studies measure it as a function of player behaviour, as self-reported experience, or as predefined alternating challenge patterns that assume challenge drives fun.
No widely accepted, predictive theory of fun exists, and many enjoyment and flow frameworks are hard to unify or lack empirical validation.
Games are an interactive art form and a major entertainment source, and their impact is usually more modest than publicized and can be positive or negative depending on the game and how it is played.
Gameplay progression is balanced when interest is mostly sustained, because players vary in how much novelty they want.
why: interest varies between players

text: Most jobs contain an element of fun that workers can find.
when: when looking for ways to make routine work engaging
why: Whether an activity is fun depends on one's attitude toward it, not on whether it is classed as work or play.

text: Prefer generated games that a learner can improve at over time, not trivially won or unwinnable ones, since much of fun comes from getting better.
when: when selecting generated games for players
why: playing is a form of learning

text: Engaging a loop costs cognitive load, time, sometimes resources, and opportunity cost; these costs become sunk investment that players weigh against expected payout and alternatives.
when: when deciding whether to keep engaging a loop
why: Accumulated investment makes players reluctant to abandon a loop even when its payoff falls.

text: Interest in an experience comes from three factors: inherent interest in the events, poetry of presentation, and projection by the guest.
when: When the events themselves are not inherently interesting
why: Poetry of presentation then has to carry the experience and sustain interest.

text: Pleasure classification lists have gaps and can miss subtle pleasures such as destruction and nurturing.
when: When such pleasure taxonomies are used as a complete description of player desire.
why: Simple category schemes cannot cover the full complexity of what people want from play.

text: Limiting design goals to fun hides the wide range of emotions a designer can target.
when: When design discussions default to fun as the only goal vocabulary.
why: fun became the default vocabulary, not a real limit

text: Keep eliminated players engaged: let them become NPCs or monsters that harass others, see all information in social deduction games, or keep doing tasks and chatting.
when: When players are eliminated before a game ends.
why: Eliminated players otherwise wait idle through the rest of the game.

text: Submission is entering the magic circle of a new set of rules and meaning, where disbelief is suspended easily; a game's success depends on players' willingness to pretend its goals matter.
Spontaneity often marks play but is not always present; a planned game of softball is still play.
Stereoscopic 3D images date back to 1838, so 3D imagery alone is not what makes VR new.
Beyond challenge, games have further sources of fun: play, fantasy, social interaction, exploration, collection, stimulation, self-expression, and construction or destruction.
Games can offer beauty through detailed characters, graceful motion, and well-chosen color compositions.
Favor preserving the spirit of play over trying to gamify every activity.
when: When the goal is education or lasting behavior change.
why: Most gamification frameworks lack empirical validation, so they are hard to rely on for success.

text: Watching a game can create social connection without everyone playing, and a compelling spectacle can win over non-players in a shared room.
when: when some people in a group would rather watch than play
why: Social connection can form through watching, so non-players still gain from the experience.

text: Defining play as aimless release of surplus energy is outdated and wrongly claims that play has no goals.
why: The surplus energy theory no longer explains play

text: 1) Ask whether the game is interesting to watch and why. 2) Identify changes that would make it more interesting to watch.
when: when spectators matter, such as onlookers in a room or remote viewers of streamed play
why: Spectators have long watched play, but only stay for games that are worth seeing.

text: To perceive more detail, suspend label-making and let detail-oriented perception take over.
when: looking at an object to draw or design it
why: Low-level categorization for efficiency means labels replace the detail of what is seen.

text: Spectacle is cheap to make, since a large blast suffices, while learning, social and character triggers need interrelated mechanics or characters.
when: choosing emotional triggers
why: Spectacle needs no interlocking systems, whereas other emotional sources depend on interrelated mechanics or characters.

text: Sandbox games offer more player agency, but it is still bounded by what designers planned, so some actions are possible while their moral opposites are not.
when: Designing open-world or sandbox games with morally charged actions.
why: Designers choose which actions exist, which limits how players can express their values.

text: Scripting separates behavior design from the engine so designers can change behaviors without programmer involvement, and also supports modding, level logic, interface code, and rapid AI prototyping.
Scripts can be handled as data files, and a language simple enough lets level designers or technical artists write behaviors.
Subclass Sandbox suits a base class with many derived classes whose shared behavior should be reused, when the base can supply every operation they need.
when: Many subclasses share behavior and coupling to the rest of the program should be minimal.
why: Without the needed operations in the base, subclasses cannot compose their behavior.

text: When a game system changes, only the base class may need edits, not every subclass, because coupling is confined to the base.
when: An engine subsystem's interface changes.
why: Subclasses depend on the base's operations rather than on the engine directly.

text: In Subclass Sandbox the composing method lives in the derived class and primitive operations live in the base class; in Template Method the base class holds the method and derived classes implement the primitives.
when: Comparing the two patterns that both build behavior from primitive operations.
why: The placement of the method is the only structural difference between the two patterns.

text: 1) Make the needed operations protected methods of the base class. 2) Add an abstract protected virtual sandbox method that subclasses must override. 3) For each new subclass, inherit from the base, override the sandbox method, and compose calls to the provided operations.
when: Building a base class whose subclasses assemble behavior from shared operations.
why: Subclasses then need no engine headers, and engine coupling stays inside the base class while subclasses define only the composition.

text: 1) List the system's parts and their dependencies. 2) Rate each part's uncertainty. 3) Identify the core parts. 4) Iterate the core a few times before adding any backlog ideas.
when: A character or system is too large to analyze at once.
why: Parts depend on lower-level systems, so the whole design is unlikely to work as planned.

text: Store shared attributes in the type object and per-instance state in the typed object.
when: Designing typed objects that share a type.
why: Shared values need one copy per type, while current state varies per object.

text: Boundaries separate what happens inside a game from everything outside it, both formally and emotionally.
Game clichés are conventions reinforced across many games, arbitrary in form but useful for systems that have no real-world counterpart.
Games can differ in medium, cost, real-time versus turn-based play, and how their rules are stored, yet all still count as games.
The difference between games and puzzles lies mainly in goal structure rather than mechanics, so many puzzles can become games and vice versa.
ESRB and PEGI ratings flag inappropriate content rather than a target age, so a rating does not mean a game is made for a specific age.
Ask whether non-game human activities could benefit from good game design principles.
why: Games generate experiences, and all of life is built from experiences.

text: Game boundaries are either physical, enforced by space and code such as level architecture, or conceptual, sustained by social agreement among players.
Games are classified by three properties: the number of players, the goals of those players, and the information each player has.
Games lie on a spectrum from well-aligned fulfilling play to pure compulsion, with three parts: well-aligned, mixed, and compulsion machines.

1) Estimate a game's typical length from memory. 2) Look up its published play time, or check several rules sites for folk games. 3) Compare the listed time with your estimate. 4) Decide whether that length suits the game and propose changes that lengthen or shorten it while keeping core play.
when: when evaluating a tabletop game's length
why: perceived length often differs from listed length

text: Voice chat is harder to filter than text, though voice recognition is making automated voice filtering possible.
Turn-based games where clock time does not affect mechanics are often recorded as simple lists of moves with no timing.
An update method often doubles as a sandbox method.
Independent design parts can be built in any order, while interdependent parts must be built in dependency order.
Unusual edits to a prototype often reveal the most about its mechanics.
Prefer rewording a card over adding long exception text to the rules.
why: Long rule additions to fix each ambiguity make the game harder to learn.

text: Use the Update Method for many live, mostly independent entities that must be simulated over time; it fits poorly to abstract turn-based games like chess.
when: When a collection of independent objects must each run their behavior once per frame.
why: Each entity encapsulating its own behavior keeps the game loop uncluttered and makes adding or removing entities easy.

text: Wide inheritance trees are easier to work with than deep ones.
when: Choosing an inheritance shape for a family of classes.
why: Shallow hierarchies avoid long chains of overrides and dependencies.

text: Use Type Object when many kinds are needed, when the types are not known up front, or when designers must add types without code changes.
when: Choosing a type system for a game with many or unknown kinds.
why: Hard-coded language types are too rigid for open-ended or data-authored content.

text: Automated chat filters based on forbidden or allowed word lists can be circumvented, since human pattern recognition finds workarounds faster than machines.
when: When relying on automated chat filtering to stop offensive language.
why: Humans detect patterns better than machines, so players find workarounds to word-based filters.

text: Games are problem-solving pursued with a playful mindset, and that mindset is what separates them from work.
A game system is a designer-made group of mechanics and resources that controls a related set of gameplay behaviors toward a specific outcome, and can be understood mostly in isolation.
A game is a voluntary control system: a contest between powers, confined by rules, that produces a disequilibrial outcome.
A game is an interactive system whose meaning comes from within, asking players to strive toward an objective.
A game is a system whose purpose is entertainment; it structures conflict and gives players an engaging process for resolving it.
Each game generator is a runnable miniature theory of game design, usually simplified or exaggerated.
Games are engineered systems that produce experiences: designers build mechanics, wrap them in fiction, and play yields events triggering emotions that fuse into one integrated experience.
Early board games served religious, military and cultural purposes as well as entertainment.
Game terms evolve as technology changes, so definitions must be revised continually and no dictionary can be final.
Claims that a young medium is too primitive for depth tend to fade as its technology matures, as happened with early film.
A technology is foundational only if the whole design is built around it; added later to an existing design, it is decorational.
Online persistent worlds and life simulations sit at the edges of the working definition of a game.
Frame an item's purpose as a situation the player faces, such as being hurt and needing to heal, rather than as a bare function like regenerating health.
when: Introducing items or systems
why: A situational reason gives the element value in the player's context

text: When comparing control across games, the output envelope is sufficient; the underlying simulation matters mainly for craft, not for measurement.
when: comparing control across games
why: For measurement, players only perceive the output, so the simulation is mostly irrelevant.

text: Stories and movies are weak metaphors for games because they lack dynamic interaction between mechanics; think of a game as an engine of experience instead.
when: When picking a metaphor to think with while designing games.
why: Stories and films have no dynamic interaction between parts.

text: A game is not one-way communication: the designer prepares the setting, and the experience is realized only when players arrive and act.
Five domains of play are novelty, challenge, stimulation, harmony, and threat.
Defining a game as a problem-solving activity is too broad, because work also involves problem solving, such as cutting production costs.
why: Problem solving alone does not separate games from work

text: Let players speak to each other freely, since designs relying on nonverbal play to build bonds have failed to form communities.
when: When the game is meant to foster an online community among its players.
why: Friendship needs a channel for talk, and nonverbal play alone has repeatedly failed to produce bonded groups.

text: Copying a reference game's surface reproduces technique but not the feeling behind it, so the copy looks flat; ask what questions its designers answered instead.
when: studying reference games
why: Borrowing finished techniques without the reasoning behind them produces work that does not stand out.

text: Skin is the player's experience of a game; skeleton is the set of elements that make the game up. Designers need both views.
A system is a tool for analysis and discussion rather than a fixed object, so its boundaries are chosen by the analyst.
Games engage players in structured conflict shaped by formal and dramatic elements; challenge can come from the system, other players, or both.
A system is an integrated set of interacting elements that together form a whole with a shared goal or purpose.
The four basic system elements are objects, properties, behaviors, and relationships.
A system's behavior arises from how its elements are arranged and interact, so studying each element alone does not reveal it.
A game combines interacting mechanics, hardware built from billions of transistors, foundational technologies, human players, and culture and markets, so no one fully understands it.
why: each layer interacts with the others

text: Strategy games can be split into combat, magic, and resource management subsystems, each part of the whole game.
CD-ROM storage made photographic-quality imagery possible, far beyond what pixel art allowed.
Systems well suited to simulation include the circulatory system, city traffic, a nuclear reactor, a cell's workings, endangered species ecology, and atmospheric heating and cooling.
Do not treat system boundaries as rigid: a resource can belong to one system yet appear in another, like hit points in character and combat systems, hiding cross-system effects.
when: Classifying resources into systems.
why: Rigid categories hide cross-system effects.

text: Test whether a game's objective is clear by stating it in one sentence.
when: reviewing a design's goals

text: Well-structured performance programs add inherent interest, while music evoking another place or empathy for the performer adds projection.
Study how hits in your market and demographic succeeded, to learn what players reward.
when: preparing a design or pitch
why: Shared knowledge of hits builds credibility with funders

text: For truly original concepts, look at the world rather than only at other games.
when: when seeking original concepts
why: Ideas drawn from existing games stay derivative, while everyday systems offer untapped potential for play.

text: Teams with fewer resources should focus on one or two values, because being best at one thing beats being mediocre at many.
when: When team size or budget is limited
why: Only a focused design has a realistic chance of being superior on at least one value.

text: Single-screen display limits forced designers to adapt tabletop and sports rules, simplifying them to fit the view.
when: When the hardware can display only a small game area at one time.
why: A side-on display could not show court lines, so rules depending on them had to be dropped.

text: The six numbered mechanics are space, time, objects, actions, rules, and skill.
1) Pick an activity from everyday life. 2) Sketch a plausible core game structure for it.
why: Breaking everyday systems into objects and relationships builds designer skill and reveals new possibilities for games.

text: 1) List elements with no clear purpose. 2) Remove the least important element and test whether the game still functions. 3) Check whether it stays complete and balanced. 4) Repeat removal until the game stops functioning. 5) Ask whether extraneous elements remain.
when: When reviewing an original game prototype for extraneous elements.
why: Keeping each element's purpose clear means tweaking one element changes only one aspect of play, keeping balancing manageable.

text: 1) List the objects in the system. 2) List its behaviors. 3) List its relationships. 4) Work out exactly how each element interacts with the others.
when: when analyzing any system for design ideas
why: Mapping how each part interacts with the others reveals the dynamics a game can be built on.

text: 1) Sketch the core actions on paper or a whiteboard. 2) Connect each action to its meters and rewards. 3) Spot features disconnected from the main loop. 4) Redesign to integrate them.
when: During early design, before formal modeling.
why: Rough sketches expose balance and feedback problems early and reveal features that do not connect to the main mechanics.

text: Explain the reasons behind anything players must do or learn, and pair those reasons with clear signs and feedback.
when: Introducing actions, systems, or items
why: Players perceive an element as intended when its purpose is clear

text: Direct players' mental effort toward the core experience and intended challenges, and remove unintended friction such as confusing controls, menus or icons.
when: designing game workload
why: Cognitive load is limited and no precise measure exists, so the balance is approximate.

text: Study classic games first to learn design craft, then try to improve on them.
Synchronized loops that conclude together produce total completion and a drop in ongoing cognitive load, and placed regularly they give natural breakpoints; staggered loops keep players hooked.
when: When choosing how progression loops end
why: Synchronization ends engagement cycles, while staggering sustains it

text: A small-scope RPG keeps its focus on stats, sheets and inventory in a tiny space, but gains market traction only with a large explorable world behind the story.
when: When a role-playing game is designed around a very small confined space.
why: Roleplaying players traditionally expect a vast realm to explore, which a large world provides.

text: Hobbies such as trading collectibles, drafting teams from statistics, or a designer's childhood collecting can supply structural ideas for collectible card games or core concepts adapted to interactive media.
Players generalise from similar forms, expecting similar things to behave alike; once they learn a rule, they apply it to new items that look alike.
when: Introducing new items, weapons or mechanics.
why: Players rely on visual resemblance to predict function, so learned rules transfer to look-alike elements.

text: Good shape is a pleasing form, found in visuals and level layouts; a well-shaped level feels solid and has a graceful curve.
Gradients are qualities that change gradually, such as a challenge curve that rises slowly or smoothly shaped probability curves.
High-level rules set broad goals and govern systems such as health and damage.
An idea is a loose concept stated verbally or in a short description, while a design is a detailed execution of that idea.
Modes on separate input channels can overlap and switch independently without conflict, such as movement on a thumbstick and spells on a button.
Finite state machines have a limited number of states, but the idea extends to infinitely many states, as in a spell whose damage grows through a chain of states.
General system theory, developed in the 1940s, studies how interacting elements behave across many disciplines.
A mechanic used only once is a gimmick; it may be worthwhile but cannot be elegant.
Attach experience rewards to encounters in game data and track faction or rank levels separately from character levels.
when: When generating content with a progression system.
why: Separate tracks keep each kind of growth independent.

text: Making predictions forces you to study historical trends, which often yields correct insights about the future.
Short handle phrases that summarize a game, such as a genre blend in a few words, help listeners remember and repeat it.
when: Naming and describing a game
why: Compact phrases travel easily between people.

text: Complex imperative behavior is harder to express as data, so it favors code-based subclasses over a data-driven approach.
when: Deciding how to define behaviors with branching logic.
why: Arbitrary control flow is awkward to capture in data definitions.

text: Economic, political, biological, or psychological systems can be used as metaphors if players already understand them, such as supply and demand or forming relationships.
when: When players already understand the real-world system being imitated.
why: Familiar systems carry almost no learning burden, whereas invented rules such as altered physics would be hard to grasp.

text: Listeners judge ideas by how useful they are to them right now, not by overall merit, so good ideas can be rejected for timing.
when: When pitching an idea to a listener.
why: A pitch is a negotiation in which the listener weighs how the idea helps them get what they want.

text: Implementing a generator exposes the affordances and constraints of a design problem, and better generators and better design understanding reinforce each other.
why: Writing a working program forces a designer to confront how the manual content process really works.

text: Most games are sets of interrelated subsystems rather than a single system, so they can be broken into discrete functional units.
why: Discrete units make it visible how mechanics interrelate, so changes can be made without disturbing working parts.

text: Designs that depend on imagination to solve a problem fail when imagination cannot actually solve it, so designers must know its limits.
when: when a design relies on players imagining a solution
why: Imagination cannot solve every problem.

text: A consistent system the player cannot understand is no more predictable than a random one, and its threats and opportunities stay hidden.
why: Foreseeing outcomes requires understanding the cause-and-effect rules, as intuitive physics lets people anticipate what a dropped object will do.

text: Players trained to value progression can find the shift to the elder game jarring, and some never reach it because they lack patience for the grind.
when: Players approach the end of progression
why: Long grinding stages filter out players who value progression rather than the later goals.

text: Players who reach an ending often suspect it is not the real one, and then stop experiencing the story to wonder what they should have done.
when: a game offers multiple endings
why: Uncertainty about the correct path breaks immersion

text: Players forgive choices that are not honored when the story order is free, though designers should still offer choices.
when: In open narratives with free ordering.
why: The order is free, so players accept the design.

text: Dying world: very old and ending, unlike the hopelessly struggling fallen world; heroes may save its people but cannot delay its end.
why: Confusing dying and fallen worlds leads to the wrong tone and conflict.

text: The ending is the moment play completely resolves, not the moment the player dies.
A destroyed world is annihilated or beyond recognition, and its story focuses on rebuilding or moving on.
A fallen (dystopian) world has lost all hope, with suffering and war as the usual state of life.
PvE games with no defined end, such as MMOs, life simulators, tabletop campaigns and idle games, rely on progression mainly as a reward and teaching structure.
when: Designing games with no fixed ending

text: Game endings must satisfy gameplay, cinematic, and narrative needs at once, often requiring new mechanics, trailer-worthy cutscenes, memorable boss fights, and a satisfying conclusion.
why: Endings are hard because several departments need different things from them.

text: Senior leadership sometimes sets the ending before much of the game is built, which can limit narrative designers' influence over it.
If novices have very short games and feel frustrated, add a grace period during which the player cannot lose.
when: Early prototypes end too quickly for new players.
why: A protected opening gives players time to learn before real risk begins.

text: Being eliminated from play leaves a long idle gap until the next round, whereas surviving keeps decisions arriving at least once per second in a short intense fight.
when: round-based competitive play with elimination
why: Eliminated players make no decisions until the round resets

text: When one enemy remains it moves very fast, and any enemy reaching the bottom ends the game regardless of lives left.
when: In an arcade-style wave shooter where aliens descend toward the bottom of the screen.
why: Survivors speed up as their numbers fall, so late-wave difficulty climbs and a single breach ends the game regardless of lives.

text: Map layout, weapon tuning, and matchmaking together shape the pattern of end-of-match rewards such as kill counts.
when: in competitive multiplayer modes
why: Kill counts are rewards that emerge from combat design rather than a set algorithm, so layout, tuning and matchmaking shape their pattern.

text: When a story advances only after a level succeeds, failure replays the level until success and the plot stays frozen in place.
when: story is gated behind level completion
why: Story outcomes are resolved by players rather than an author, which makes traditional narrative methods hard to fit into gameplay.

text: A fail/good/better/best outcome scale can mask linear structure, since success levels alter the enemy count in the subsequent mission and their equipment quality.
when: Linear missions should feel responsive without branching
why: Players need to feel influence even when outcomes do not change the story, so graded success hides the fixed path.

text: A hazard trapped in a state that changes in a later level foreshadows its release when that state changes.
If any drop ends the match, large team games often never reach a result.
when: in large team games
why: Ending on any disconnect means the game often never finishes, while continuing penalizes the teammates of the dropped player.

text: 1) Conclude play once one participant drops out. 2) Award victory to the participant in the best standing at that point. 3) For a gentler variant, grant remaining participants a few turns or a short time before finishing.
why: If players can help each other, a first-elimination end creates tense alliances, as the leader pushes to finish the weakened player.

text: 1) Watch for stalemate, where players avoid each other. 2) Add a timed trigger that forces a conclusion. 3) Move survivors into a space where the match resolves quickly. 4) Guarantee a single winner within a fixed time.
when: A competitive match risks becoming boring through avoidance.
why: Forced endings prevent endless stalling and keep the game length bounded.

text: Competitive strategy games should offer a surrender mechanism so that a hopeless player can end the match and reach the next game sooner.
when: When a match is clearly lost.
why: Ending a hopeless match escapes a failure trap.

text: Give endings the same care as the rest of the game, since the journey is often what players remember when they do not reach the end.
Harmony means each element's response, context and polish agree with one cohesive promised perception of a unique physical reality; it does not mean emulating real-world physics.
when: when judging whether an element's feel fits its design
why: Consistency with promised behavior matters more than realism

text: Games let players manipulate time in ways impossible in real life, including stopping, speeding, and rewinding it.
Start with stark, uniform boundaries and let them gradually break down during play to pull the audience into a mystery.
when: when a space-based experience needs to build curiosity
why: The contrast between order and disorder draws players in.

text: Introduce choice gradually: limit options early, then expand the play space as the player learns the systems.
when: When a game offers a large system of choices to players.
why: Limited early options help players get used to a large set of possibilities before the scope expands.

text: Phases can shift gradually with no explicit rule change as the power balance drifts; each side then tries to stretch or shrink phases, which creates strategy.
when: when rules stay fixed but the balance of play shifts
why: players compete over when phases start and end

text: Immediate feedback in games helps players adjust or keep their actions, which supports learning through play.
why: Feedback on whether an action is appropriate lets players adjust or keep it during play, which builds the skills society expects.

text: A design that cuts across traditional categories can draw a very large audience, combining newcomers seeking a low-pressure creative experience with hardcore players wanting a break.
when: When a game does not fit one established genre or player type
why: Crossing categories opens two audiences that existing games do not serve together.

text: A creature-collecting RPG follows traditional RPG structure but lets players capture the opposing creatures they defeat and add them to their own team.
The metaverse is a fully immersive shared 3D world where users socialize, work, shop, and play through embodied avatars.
Alternate reality games combine real-world and online interaction to create gameplay.
Adventure games emphasise exploration, item collection, and puzzle solving, with the player cast as a character on a quest or mission.
Action-strategy hybrids combine physical dexterity with strategic decisions in one game.
A mixed game alternates compulsive grinding with fulfilling moments, a pattern often caused by craft mistakes that better alignment could fix.
Mode-first design builds one strong central gameplay mode and creates variety by changing the board conditions each time the mode is entered.
A metroidvania is an action game with a continuous, persistent space, platform-jumping movement, and items that expand the avatar's moveset.
Genres where gameplay centers on influencing character minds through AI, rather than physical action, have very few high-selling examples.
Online MOBA and MMO genres have remained in workbench spaces rather than moving to the hearth.
Some games switch into a separate mode with completely different rules and interface, almost like a separate game.
Most action video games and most sports run in continuous time.
Genre is usually settled before combat design begins; combat may be the whole game in one genre and one component in another.
Open-source platforms where anyone can run an instance are decentralized, unlike centralized, closed-source services.
Centralized platforms owned and controlled by one business, which allow user-generated content, are considered early proto-metaverses.
Whether an edge-case experience counts as a game is disputed, so categorization of such designs is contested.
Alternate reality games can send players to real-world locations and devices to find further instructions.
Early strategy games were turn-based; real-time strategy became popular in the 1990s.
A publisher's output can be concentrated in a few genres, with action, sports, and racing making up about 54% of one publisher's titles.
Each genre has standard concrete representations, such as a capture shown as removing a piece or hidden information shown by face-down cards.
Game experiences are always emotionally mixed, with several feelings occurring at once, such as hope and worry during a close match.
Strategy games, building games, economic simulations, and pen-and-paper roleplaying games usually represent elements through statistics and symbols.
Some critics also require RPG progression or 2D, but the style can be treated as a level design approach rather than a game genre.
A card game meant to be played in under an hour with a basic deck and expandable booster sets lets players buy and trade cards to improve their decks.
when: In a collectible card game where a basic deck holds only part of the card pool.
why: Players are pushed to buy boosters and trade cards, since a basic deck is only a fraction of the system.

text: Follow the default control mapping shared by genre peers for common actions; departing from it makes learning harder and can drive players to quit.
when: Designing controls for action games with aim, shoot, sprint, jump, crouch and reload.
why: Players carry learned mappings across games, so unfamiliar layouts raise the learning cost.

text: Blending genres and modes within one design can produce distinctive games that stand out and last.
when: when seeking to differentiate a game

text: Established genres are largely solved; unless you can ask new questions of a genre, pursue new gameplay territory instead.
when: When an idea does not fit an existing genre
why: Genre designers have already worked out many core gameplay issues.

text: Combat-focused campaigns commonly run 10 or more hours, RPGs often 30 or more, and older RPGs 50 or more.
when: estimating target game length

text: Play types ordered from most to least interactive: games, puzzles, toys, and stories. Games are rule-based systems where opposing players respond to each other; puzzles are rule-based with a solution goal rather than an opponent.
Recreating an existing game within the same genre gives players little reason to choose yours, so differentiation is required.
when: When working within an existing, well-defined genre.
why: Players bring expectations from earlier games in the genre, so the design must offer something distinct to attract them.

text: Genre pressure can steer designers toward tried-and-true gameplay, limiting originality.
1) Identify the non-negotiable mechanics of the genre. 2) Identify common mechanics you may change. 3) List what else must change to support each change.
when: designing within an established genre
why: Changing a common mechanic shifts which parts of play stand out, and other elements must change to support it.

text: Keep the number of modes as low as possible, since every added mode must be learned by the player.
why: Each added mode is something players must learn, and unnoticed mode changes can confuse them.

text: Do not let genre labels drive core design; treat them as commercial tools, not creative limits.
when: During the design process, as opposed to business planning.
why: Genres help with business decisions but tend to restrict creativity and steer designers toward familiar solutions.

text: Mechanics are procedures and rules defining a game's goal, player options and outcomes, and make a game a game; rulebook or code forms define them equally.
A core mechanic is the basic action, or set of actions, a player repeats throughout the designed game.
Micromanagement arises when a task splits into many small, tedious decisions; with many nearly meaningless tokens to move, handling takes longer than thinking.
why: Interaction becomes a physical chore that displaces the mental decision-making players came for.

text: Shooters often use ragdoll physics decoratively, so a struck enemy's body flies and lands in a way that adds visual impact.
when: a hit enemy in a shooter

text: The core mechanic is the central activity of the game, and it should be understood before production begins.
Some rules define objects and concepts, such as a deck, draw pile, or weapon, and the rest of the design depends on these building blocks.
Medium-level rules give immediate meaning to specific objects, such as the flag in a capture-the-flag game.
Core pillars are the things players must learn and master in a game, and they indicate where players should be challenged.
A core mechanic summary names the repeated action the player performs and the goal that action drives toward.
when: When describing a game's core gameplay.
why: Naming both the repeated action and the goal captures what drives play.

text: Mechanics are the rules players can act on, defining what they can do. Dynamics are the ways players use those mechanics to optimize their play and maximize their chance to win.
A multirole mechanic serves several distinct roles, such as offense, defense, scouting, or deception, so one tool creates more choices.
Core gameplay is the minimal set of mechanics at the bottom of a game's dependency stack that still makes the game worthwhile.
A single game element can serve several roles at once, such as short-term and long-term goals, risk pacing, score, and rewards.
The four action-card mechanics are costed similarly, yet their effects in play differ greatly.
Small rule variables such as grid size or win length can shift both game length and how interesting the game feels.
No universally agreed taxonomy of game mechanics exists, because even simple games have tangled mechanics.
A wall kick needs horizontal speed above a threshold, airborne state, wall contact within 20 ms, a quick stick pull away from the wall, and a jump press.
Micromanagement matters only when it affects the player's experience; it is not a problem in itself.
Mechanic roles include harasser, scout, disabler, and deceiver, and in fighting games punch, block, block breaker, and ranged harassment.
Strategy arises when basic actions interact with each other, objects and space; judge verbs by strategic yield, since one well-interacting verb beats several mediocre ones.
when: Adding basic actions to a game or deciding whether to add a verb
why: Interactions, not raw verb count, generate strategy; strategic yield per verb matters more than quantity.

text: Start game design from the verbs players perform, since each verb's basic action can become a core mechanic; common examples include jumping, exploring, rolling and flinging.
when: When designing a game around its core mechanic, starting from the player's basic verbs.
why: The repeated verb a player performs is the foundation that shapes what each game feels like.

text: When building objects around a mechanic, not every object must use it; some can interact with it or act as soft counters that stay useful on their own.
when: building a mini-expansion around a costed mechanic

text: Use the game feel loop to locate where a design might be improved, and as a foundation for building game feel from scratch.
why: Designers only shape the computer-side steps, since player perception and input hardware are fixed.

text: Use cooldowns on powerful actions that would be overused without a waiting period.
