why: A waiting period stops a strong action from being used constantly.

text: Every single restriction buys a small near-term payoff, yet a pile of them may suffocate the game.
when: When a mechanic change alters a shared parameter that many existing levels depend on.
why: Each added rule forces existing content to be rebuilt, and the cost surfaces only later.

text: A competitive game can keep its players for over a decade when balance, pace, skill and decisions sustain play, rather than its setting.
why: Setting alone is shared by many military games with mixed results, so mechanics must explain lasting play.

text: Depth in a multiplayer shooter comes from many interacting variables such as grenades, stealth, noise, teammate communication, clock pressure and player fatigue, not from the number of options alone.
when: In shooters where a single shot can be decisive, so hidden positions matter.
why: Hidden information lets deception matter; without it, play reduces to aim and dodge.

text: Jump height depends on how long the jump button is held: the initial impulse is fixed, but holding longer raises the peak up to a maximum.
why: Gives players fine control over the jump through timing.

text: An emergency teleport that sets position to a random location gives the player an escape that carries unpredictable risk.
when: when designing a panic escape for a player craft
why: Randomness makes the escape useful but risky

text: Changing a system variable directly changes play, and only playtesting shows how much.
why: Effects on strategy, balance and social dynamics only show up once people actually play it.

text: For each damage point, the opponent sends the topmost card of their draw pile to the discard pile.
Letting one verb act on many kinds of objects multiplies its meaningful strategic uses, even though the verb itself stays the same.
when: Designing an action such as shooting
why: Each new valid target creates new decisions for the player.

text: A mechanic causes certain dynamics, and those dynamics can carry story and involve the player.
when: Designing rules that players will act on
why: Designers control mechanics directly, but dynamics are players' own applications of the rules and cannot be directly controlled.

text: In an elegant design, mechanics interact tightly, so changing one mechanic ripples into many others.
why: Interlocking mechanics multiply into many possibilities, so a fix to one shifts the others too.

text: Adding exceptions that hide targets from a clear detection signal turns that signal into a judgment, since players must keep estimating what the signal misses.
when: When a detection signal has exceptions that let some targets stay hidden.
why: Players must keep weighing what the signal may miss, which turns reading it into a judgment.

text: Mechanics such as who can be shot and who appears on the radar signal which characters the game values.
Four properties with three options each give 81 cards; removing a property with three options leaves 27; adding a three-option property multiplies the deck size by three.
After wall contact, players have about a fifth of a second to pull away from the wall and press jump.
A tool that turns high-level behavior definitions into stack bytecode bridges a low-level VM and non-programmer designers.
when: Designers need to author behavior without writing low-level code
why: A raw VM is harder to use than C++, so a translator is needed.

text: The MDA framework treats games as systems with Mechanics, Dynamics and Aesthetics, where interaction between them builds player behavior.
why: Framing games as interacting systems makes design choices easier to reason about.

text: Core mechanics form the road of a game, the defining path. Content added to the game should decorate the road and never block or hinder core mechanics.
when: Adding story or other content to a game
why: Blocking the core damages the game's feel and idea

text: Mechanical criteria for judging a generated experience are accessibility, clarity of the interface, and depth.
when: When judging an experience as generated by mechanics rather than as an emergent story.
why: It focuses on the system the designer controls, rather than on the story players get.

text: Designers who understand internal mechanics so well that they forget how players experience them can lose sight of what players feel.
Adding many verbs, especially ones that interact poorly with the rest, makes a game bloated and confusing.
when: Expanding a game's action set
why: Poorly interacting verbs add complexity without adding strategy.

text: Players can reject a mechanic because of its name or presentation even when its effects are sound; a neutral name can carry the same dynamic.
when: naming or presenting a new mechanic
why: Players respond to how a mechanic is framed as well as to what it does.

text: 1) Strip away the surface features of two similar games. 2) List the rules they share. 3) Translate those shared rules into a playable paper format.
when: When comparing two similar games from the same genre, such as real-time strategy games.
why: Shared rules are the core mechanics of the genre.

text: 1) Pick two or three known games. 2) Write a short core gameplay description for each. 3) Sketch how their activities interrelate. 4) Repeat for your own concept, guessing where unsure.
when: When learning to model core gameplay or starting a new concept.
why: Diagramming trains the designer to see how activities connect, and guesses improve through prototyping.

text: Scripts that watch fast-changing events should restart from the beginning each frame rather than resume, to avoid acting on stale information.
when: the script reacts to rapidly changing events
why: Resuming a paused run could leave it acting on information that has gone out of date.

text: Broadcast spell effects through the sense manager so that affected characters are notified, removing the need for spell-specific detection tests.
Give rotation a slight attack, a short ramp to full turn speed, because without it rotation feels stiff and robotic.
when: when tuning how quickly a turning input reaches full rotation speed
why: A small ramp softens the start of a turn and removes the robotic feel

text: Visualize the game's mechanics in a flowchart that defines the relationship and purpose of each mechanic.
why: Mapping each mechanic's relationships and purpose early keeps rule sets from becoming tangled as the game evolves.

text: Derive operational rules from the foundational structure so that player actions match how game state actually changes.
why: Operational pieces such as boards and chips only track the underlying game state, so they follow from it.

text: State the specific change a game should produce and the method that causes it, such as a practice task, rather than vague goals like teaching math.
when: at the start of designing a transformational game
why: A solution cannot be designed until the needed change is clearly stated.

text: Enemies that need several stomps to defeat can add a layer to their difficulty, with each stage removing a distinct part.
when: designing an enemy with multiple parts
why: Staged defeats extend an encounter and communicate structure.

text: Let the core experience set priorities, since a feature that suits one game type, such as PvP, may not benefit a game built around teamplay.
when: Choosing features
why: Every design choice is a tradeoff, so a clear target experience shows which features to pursue and which to skip.

text: Let mechanics grow out of the core idea, and learn from existing mechanics without copying them.
Label every button in the control scheme and mark unused ones as nonfunctional.
when: documenting a digital control scheme

text: Add a new mechanic only if it fills a role not already covered, and prefer mechanics that open strategies that did not exist before.
when: When a proposed mechanic would overlap the role of an existing mechanic in the game.
why: Variations on existing interactions add content without adding new choices.

text: Vary decision scope across a sequence, mixing compressed twitch runs, profound decisions and several tactical decisions rather than repeating one scope.
Alternate decisions of similar scope but different subject matter, since similar-scope choices such as moving an army and placing a building still feel different.
why: Holding one decision type for long stretches grows dull, while switching between two kinds keeps interest.

text: A mechanic may distort the story or muddy the marketing message.
why: Every mechanic carries costs in design effort, computing resources, and player attention.

text: A game's objective is a clear goal players work toward; it is a key structural element, and without it the experience loses much of its shape.
A game keeps its result uncertain until the end, then resolves it into a measurable, unequal outcome such as a single winner.
Game mechanics are the rule-based interactions that remain once aesthetics, technology and story are stripped away.
Foundational rules are the abstract formal structure of a game: a mathematical representation of its state and of how and when that state changes.
A game state is everything describing a game in progress at one instant, including whose turn it is; it is what would be saved to resume the game later.
A game rule is an arbitrary, designed relationship between abstracted variables: arbitrary because no higher order dictates it, and designed because a designer creates it deliberately.
A forbidden-act objective makes players try to get competitors to break a rule, such as by laughing, talking, letting go, or making a wrong move.
Game objects are abstractions defined by rules, such as a poker straight or a chess king, and exist only within the game's system rather than as real-world things.
Game objects can be physical, abstract, or both, and include playing pieces, players, avatars, terrain, and in-game concepts such as a bank.
Every alteration to the available controls creates a new game state; a game where you steer a vehicle, pilot an aircraft, or pedal a bicycle has three states.
A game object is a visual representation paired with scripted behavior, and repeated pairing lets players read the object as a symbol of its mechanic.
when: when objects are consistently linked to the same behavior
why: Players learn the association through repeated use, so the look comes to signal the function.

text: Final states have no outgoing transitions, and a state machine may have none.
Forbidden-act games often have a physical component involving stamina, flexibility, or chance, and they are rare in digital games.
why: Digital games have limited direct competition and fair play is hard to monitor.

text: PvP games often split into three stages: opening, middle and final. Designers can identify, design, measure and adjust these stages to fix dull or dragging sections.
when: When a PvP game has well-defined transitions between distinct game phases.
why: Measurable player power over time lets designers tune game length by trial-and-error adjustment of the numbers.

text: Isolating and abstracting subsystems with defined inputs and outputs supports functional independence, so changes elsewhere can be traced, much like object-oriented programming.
when: Designing large-scale systems
why: Subsystems with defined inputs and outputs let a change's effects on other parts be traced.

text: Define every game object, concept, and behavior, and describe how they relate to one another.
Some games are pure mechanics with abstract representations, such as poker, soccer and tile-swapping puzzles, yet still create tension, doubt and triumph.
Designing decisions is the purest form of game design, since story, visuals and sound are not required for a game to exist.
Good goals are concrete, achievable, and rewarding: players must understand them, believe they can reach them, and find the reward satisfying at the right challenge level.
when: Designing player goals
why: Each quality keeps players motivated to attempt and complete the goal.

text: Counting purposes is only a rough guide to elegance, because part of elegance resists measurement.
Asking players to practice a skill with no threat or target makes the instruction meaningless.
why: Without a threat or target, players have less motivation to follow the instruction, so they pay less attention and remember the task less well.

text: Purity of purpose: each game component should be clearly defined, have a reason to exist, and have a single mission, doing only one job.
why: Tweaking one element then changes only one aspect of gameplay, keeping balancing methodical and rules from becoming tangled.

text: Pursuing purity can strip out depth, while adding depth without clarity confuses players; balance the two.
why: Depth of experience matters too, especially in games, so purity alone can strip out something the player values.

text: Internal completeness means the rules address loopholes arising in play; gaps create dead ends, let players sidestep the intended conflict, or spark rule arguments.
Levels of scale means structures nested at several sizes, such as short, midterm and long-term goals that chain together.
Level design crafts a specific puzzle configuration within fixed rules, aiming for drama, coherence, and chosen difficulty. Rule design invents the overall rules, goal, and format.
Other rules limit player behavior and govern reactions to situations, such as requiring a player to give up every card of a requested rank.
Operational rules are the rules players use to play the game; knowing them is enough to play.
Low-level rules set the physical traits of single objects, like how much damage is needed to destroy an enemy.
Interoperability means content and identity work across platforms, similar to how email works across different providers.
A predictable system needs two properties: consistency, meaning it acts the same across situations so lessons carry over, and comprehensibility, meaning the player can grasp it.
How the high, medium and low levels of game rules interact with one another remains under-explored in many games.
Keys are not inherently bad design; access rewards can go beyond lock-and-key mechanisms.
when: When choosing an access mechanism
why: Other gate types can serve the same progression purpose

text: Every operational rule corresponds to a foundational rule that updates some game state.
Free-form games such as tag work with loosely defined boundaries without harming the experience.
Rescue or escape objectives are often combined with partial objectives that add puzzle-like goals on top of the overall goal.
The interaction set holds most operational rules, specifying what happens when two sprite types collide, such as death, teleportation, or score change.
A tower defense game's core needs a map, something to protect, towers, and enemies advancing toward that target.
Each stack element can hide several pages of interlocking design detail, so changing one interface can force redesign of a seemingly separate feature.
Use reinforcing loops to create risk-reward and let choices drive unequal outcomes; use balancing loops to counter runaway advantage and extend play.
when: Designing pace and outcome spread
why: A reinforcing loop magnifies whichever side is already ahead, while a balancing loop pushes the outcome back toward parity.

text: Creatures higher in a food chain should have simpler behavior, and by the top of the chain behaviors should be very simple.
when: Designing predators the player influences only indirectly.
why: The player's control weakens with each intermediate level, so higher creatures need simpler logic.

text: Designers usually think in operational rules and shift to foundational rules when they want to change or improve the game.
when: when a designer wants to change a game

text: Catch-up mechanics, hidden information, or an earlier end condition can keep a PvP outcome open when one player is pulling ahead.
when: when a PvP outcome is becoming certain
why: These options restore uncertainty about who will win.

text: Organise character behaviour by state to achieve the target feel, keeping relationships between values intact matters more than internal structure.
when: implementing a character with several movement states
why: Consistent value relationships produce the intended feel regardless of code layout.

text: Apply game theory at the level of individual interactions such as a single exchange of attacks, blocks or throws, since it cannot analyze a whole match.
when: When analyzing one brief exchange of opposing actions rather than a whole match or round.
why: Designers often dismiss it as too abstract, but it works at this local scale.

text: Objects referencing the same type object behave as that type, so new types need only type-object data, not new classes; a large subclass family signals this fit.
when: A family of subclasses grows into dozens or hundreds, or a type system is built from data instead of a class hierarchy.
why: Behavior follows from the shared type data rather than a language-level class; data-driven designs handle many variants without a class for each one.

text: Distinct movement rules for pieces on a shared grid give each piece a different role in play.
why: Each piece's own movement pattern lets the shared board combine pieces into many different strategies.

text: When objects are packed tightly, steering around them becomes demanding, and speed and turning radius matter much more.
why: An empty space offers nothing to steer around or measure skill against, so crowding is what makes handling matter.

text: A periodic hazard that removes pieces from the board forces each move to be weighed against the safety of a player's other pieces.
A rule that temporarily gives a specific object high importance, such as a health pack at low health, changes how players read a space and move through it.
when: when a game needs a level's layout to drive player decisions in real time
why: Placement alone is not enough; the rule adds meaning on top of position

text: Layered rules at high, medium and low levels can reinforce one another to convey solidity and mass in a fighting game.
when: when a game needs its characters or attacks to feel solid and heavy
why: Each level supports the same impression, so the combined effect is stronger than any single rule

text: The first player to reach ten kills wins the match.
when: when kill scoring is used

text: Type Object replaces a rigid class hierarchy with one typed-object class and one type-object class, where each type object is a data-defined type that typed objects reference.
when: When a game needs many breeds of similar entities, with several instances of each breed.

text: When rule sets grow so intricate that players can't sketch a basic mental model of operation, overwhelm follows.
why: Players cannot hold that many rules and tracked states in mind, so the experience turns confusing.

text: Two modes that share one input channel can conflict, because one button or thumbstick ends up doing two jobs.
when: When a new mode would reuse a button or thumbstick already assigned to another mode.
why: Each input channel can carry only one instruction at a time, so overlapping modes conflict.

text: Treating combat purely as a math problem misses the uncertain space created by players, weapons, enemies and the possibilities between them.
Distant targets slow the firing rate and demand more precise aim, which can make shooting feel sluggish.
when: When a limit on simultaneous on-screen shots applies and shots persist until they leave the screen.
why: Shots occupy the limit until they travel off-screen, so distant targets tie up the firing slots for a long time.

text: When roles overlap, the design pays for two mechanics to do one mechanic's work, making the redundant one dead weight.
when: When a new mechanic would fill a role that an existing mechanic already covers.
why: The extra mechanic adds design cost and complexity without enabling any play the first one could not already deliver.

text: Hard invisible blocks that the player can detect cheat within the game's own rules and undermine trust in the entire mechanical system.
why: players start thinking about what the designer wants rather than what the mechanics allow

text: 1) List possible partners for a proposed mechanic: other mechanics, allies, multiple opponents, environment, morality, narrative, and player stats. 2) Count the realistic interactions with each. 3) Favor mechanics with many. Mechanics touching many systems tend to be elegant; those touching only one or two probably are not.
when: before building or testing a mechanic
why: Designers can judge elegance on paper before costly testing.

text: 1) Identify each tool's essential properties. 2) Push them to an extreme and lock them. 3) Balance using only the non-essential properties.
when: Balancing a tool whose role can be stated as a few essential properties
why: Keeps tool roles distinct and consistent with the fiction

text: 1) Identify which parts of the game are so primal that an animal could play them. 2) Identify which parts could be made more primal.
when: when aiming for intuitive, powerful play
why: Actions so old that animals already perform them feel intuitive without any teaching.

text: 1) For each interaction pattern, list games you enjoy. 2) For any pattern with none, research and play several examples.
when: when studying interaction patterns

text: Two units cannot occupy the same cell.
when: When resolving the move step for units on a shared grid.

text: Explore the less-mapped areas of games as seriously as the well-structured ones.
Give terrain and board areas the same design attention as playing pieces, because they interact with other objects in the same way.
Identify the core mechanic first, meaning the actions a player repeats most while pursuing the goal, and build outward from it rather than designing the whole game at once.
when: Before building any prototype.
why: Focusing on the repeated action loop keeps the design coherent.

text: Test a done flag in the main loop condition so the game can exit cleanly.
when: Writing a game loop that must end
why: Without a quit condition the loop runs forever.

text: Isolated mechanics are easy to tune with no side effects but rarely produce much variety; connected mechanics create many play situations but resist simple fixes.
when: choosing between one-off effects and systems of relationships
why: Isolation makes tuning easy only because it limits how the mechanic interacts.

text: Replacing conventional failure with a late, dramatic consequence breaks genre convention; a designer may accept that cost when the theme matters more than convention.
when: When the theme requires that the player character not die in the conventional way.
why: A sudden mid-game death would undo the dramatic build-up the theme depends on, and the theme outweighs genre convention.

text: Using different counts per object type (four to eight each) makes some objects rarer and builds in inequality that the design must then balance.
when: Trading games where object scarcity should differ

text: One input driving both thrust and rotation is integrated control; separate inputs for each keep the dimensions independent.
Isolated starting areas allow slow gearing up, while busy areas offer better upgrades but more rivals.
when: In multiplayer games where players choose where they spawn
why: Skydiving gives an overview of the map, so players can judge the risk of each landing spot before choosing.

text: An event is any occurrence during play, like one piece taking another or a character hitting a wall and rebounding off it.
Exceptions added to movement rules, such as a two-square first move or diagonal-only captures, make the rules complex but balanced and interesting.
Engine distance units are roughly 2 cm each, but game distances differ from real ones, so reference sizes matter more than the nominal conversion.
Most games are not event-driven in the GUI sense, so an event loop is not the default game structure.
Engine and scripting limits such as rendering distance, NPC animation triggers and quest branching can constrain what a world design can include.
When errors cannot be prevented, provide recovery through undo, retry from a nearby checkpoint, or resetting decisions.
when: Designing systems where players may make regrettable choices.
why: Recovery options relieve players and reduce frustration from mistakes.

text: Charging extra costs for acting early offsets the benefit of a random early turn, so players weigh a tempo gain against its price.
when: designing a turn-order system with random streaks
why: costs keep early and late turns from being uniformly advantaged

text: Perfect information means players know every game state element at all times and the outcome of every possible move from the start. Chess, Draughts, Go and Reversi are examples.

1) List one player's options as rows and the opponent's as columns. 2) Assign +1 for a win, -1 for a loss, and 0 for a tie or draw. 3) Treat the opponent's choices as probabilities and your options as payoffs equal to the probability-weighted sum of outcomes.
when: Modeling a simultaneous-choice game as a payoff table or analyzing matchups between options
why: The opponent's choice is hidden and not under the player's control, so it is modeled as a probability distribution.

text: Because no pure equilibrium exists, a matching-pennies-style interaction stays interesting across many repeated games.
why: Without a stable choice, each player keeps gaining by predicting or deceiving the opponent.

text: In complex games payoffs are not given as numbers, so players must evaluate them in real time from costs, context, positioning, unit proportions, and skill.
when: strategy games with unit or resource trades
why: Unlike fixed-prize games, the payoff of each choice is hidden and must be inferred.

text: A stable strategy profile is one where no player can improve their result by changing only their own strategy.
A dilemma is a choice where every option gains something and loses something, so no option is clearly best.
A loophole is a flaw players exploit for an unfair or unintended advantage, and it blocks a game from being complete.
A ply is one player's turn, while a move is one round in which all players have taken a turn.
In imperfect information games, hidden randomness such as a dice roll determines which moves are legal, so players cannot know their options in advance. Backgammon is an example.
A disequilibrial outcome starts out even, and then one side wins and the other loses.
Incomplete information means players know which elements are unknown and their possible values; imperfect information means players hold some data that may be wrong.
when: Designing hidden game state
why: The two differ in whether players know what they do not know.

text: Skill in a game with a known optimal policy means executing a memorized, well-practiced strategy, not making adaptive decisions.
Game value is the expected net gain per game under optimal mixed play, so a value of 1/12 means one extra win per 12 games.
A dominated option is one that is never better than another option across all of the opponent's choices.
Dilemmas are choices whose good or bad consequences are uncertain.
The Prisoner's Dilemma is a non-zero-sum game in which each player's individually rational choice leaves both players worse off than mutual cooperation would.
Negative sum games shrink the total power in play over time.
Game theory is an abstract mathematical study of idealized games; its terminology is used in turn-based AI, but it applies only weakly to real-time games.
In perfect information games, choosing a move is still uncertain because the opponent's choice is unknown, but every option the opponent could take is fully known.
A balanced ratio is a long-term trend; the options need not be exactly equal at every moment.
when: Evaluating random choices over many repetitions.

text: Game theory also covers sequential choice, negotiation and cooperation, which are outside the intransitive method described here.
With the double-Rock win rule, the three-player equilibrium is about 3:4:3, closer to 1:1:1 than the two-player equilibrium.
when: double-Rock win rule is applied

text: Dilemmas can drive both single-player and multiplayer games.
In a room with two doors, a defender wants to cover the door the attacker chooses while the attacker wants the other door, forming matching pennies.
A game can be positive sum overall while containing zero-sum parts, such as limited spaces or unique bonuses that only one player can hold at a time.
Poker is zero sum: whatever one player wins from the pot equals what the other players collectively lost.
When both units die in a fight, the net payoff is zero for both sides.
when: fights between units of the same type

text: Check whether any single strategy dominates: a dominant strategy is clearly superior to all others, solves the puzzle, and removes meaningful decisions.
when: Auditing a game's decision space where options differ greatly in value
why: A dominant strategy makes other options pointless

text: Several effective counter-strategies are more fun than one. Alternatively, use many enemy types, each with one unique but strong counter-strategy.
when: When designing enemy tactics
why: Multiple answers keep play varied and interesting

text: With more than two players, the best strategy may be to gang up on the strongest opponent rather than to make every opponent lose.
when: more than two players
why: Removing the strongest rival first makes the weaker opponents easier to pick off later.

text: Judge a challenge's replay value by whether it has a dominant strategy; do not fault a game for that when finding the strategy is its purpose.
when: Evaluating whether a challenge stays interesting across repeated play
why: A solved dominant strategy ends the challenge for most players

text: Rock-paper-scissors counter relationships are a legitimate way to create variety, especially in RTS games where unit strengths are easy to read.
when: Designing unit counters where strengths are easy to read
why: Readable counters let each unit be strong against some units and weak against others, which leaves room for mastery.

text: When some strategies beat random play, an equal mix over all options is usually not optimal.
when: a strategy beats random play more often than it loses
why: Options that beat random play earn more than random mixing does, so weighting them more heavily pays off.

text: If a payoff system has more equations than unknowns and yields contradictions, dominated options are likely present and should be removed.
when: solving a payoff table that gives inconsistent results

text: A randomized mix that deviates from equilibrium proportions can be exploited by an opponent who always plays the countermove to the overused option.
why: The opponent gains an advantage from the predictable bias.

text: Equilibria are self-reinforcing because players have no reason to switch, while non-equilibrium configurations are unstable because someone gains by changing alone.
when: In real multiplayer games with many possible strategy combinations

text: When players knowingly take risks, repeated rolls make a bad outcome eventually likely, even if each risk was reasonable.
Changing the value of one outcome shifts the optimal frequencies of all options, not only the changed one; making a winning throw riskier makes opponents use it less, so its counter is played more.
when: Adjusting payoffs in a symmetric intransitive game
why: A rarer option is less often countered, raising the value of the option that beats it

text: Touching the same area repeatedly gives diminishing returns, and surface variation and movement speed raise difficulty.
when: Rewarding repeated actions on a surface.

text: Raising the payoff for a favored outcome can turn a losing game into a fair or favorable one, so payoffs are a direct lever on expected value.
when: Tuning rewards in a probabilistic game
why: Expected value scales linearly with each outcome's value.

text: When each player's payoffs differ by side, the equilibrium is a mixed strategy in which both players randomize side choices in specific proportions, and deviating lets the opponent exploit it.
when: two-player simultaneous choices with asymmetric payoffs
why: No pure choice is stable when the opponent can always counter it.

text: Game theorists model a decision as a payoff matrix listing each player's result for every combination of choices.
when: Interactions where each player's result depends on what the others choose

text: Reasons to build asymmetry include simulation, exploration, personalization, leveling the playing field, interesting situations, and customizable handicaps.

A true dilemma requires the payoff order Temptation for defection, then Reward for mutual cooperation, then Punishment for mutual defection, then Sucker's payoff for unreciprocated cooperation; exact values do not matter.
when: Designing a choice where cooperation and betrayal both feel tempting
why: Only this ordering makes individually optimal play always pay less than cooperation

text: Matching pennies is the design pattern for asymmetrical interactions without a pure equilibrium: one side wants a match, the other wants a mismatch.
when: Asymmetrical two-sided interactions, such as attacker versus defender battles
why: Each side's goal directly opposes the other's, so neither can hold a fixed choice without being countered.

text: A penalty kick is a matching pennies game with unequal payoffs: the goalkeeper wants to match the kicker's side, and the kicker wants a mismatch.
when: analyzing one-shot side-choice duels
why: Both players choose sides simultaneously without knowing the other's choice.

text: The equal-payoff theorem applies only to strategies actually used, so dominated options should be removed before applying it.
when: Applying equal-payoff reasoning to an intransitive game
why: A dominated option has a lower payoff and is never chosen

text: Dilemmas disconnected from the game's main objective make choices less interesting.
why: Choices only engage the mind if they change how the game proceeds, so tangential dilemmas carry no weight.

text: Tuning exact payoff values while ignoring whether their order holds can silently destroy a dilemma.
why: When one choice is always best, players converge on it and the game repeats the same way each time.

text: 1) Write the payoff matrix for the interaction. 2) Find the probability mix where every option yields the same average payoff. 3) Play that mix to remove exploitable bias.
when: Interactions with no pure equilibrium.

text: 1) Break the choice into simple moves. 2) List each player's options. 3) Diagram outcomes in a payoff matrix. 4) Check whether one option is clearly best.
when: When studying the choices players face in any game
why: Simple move structures expose the potential outcomes of each strategy for each player.

text: 1) Defuzzify to a single number. 2) Give each enumeration value a non-overlapping numeric range. 3) Map the number to the enumeration whose range contains it.
when: Output options form an ordered series, such as ranked belts by skill
why: Ordering lets a single numeric result select a meaningful rank.

text: 1) List developments that are likely to happen. 2) Treat them as foundations for less certain forecasts. 3) Discuss your predictions with others and revise them.
when: forecasting future game technology
why: Likely developments give a sound base for speculative predictions.

text: 1) Compare every pair of rows and every pair of columns. 2) Remove any option that is never better than another. 3) Repeat the comparison on the reduced table until no dominated options remain.
when: before solving a payoff table for mixed strategies

text: 1) List each option and its payoff when the other player cooperates or defects. 2) Check that mutual cooperation gives the best joint outcome. 3) Check that cooperating alone gives the worst result for the cooperator. 4) Tie the dilemma to the main objective.
when: When the payoffs for defecting alone, mutual cooperation, mutual defection and lone cooperation rank in that order.

text: Enforce binding deals by blocking the forbidden action for the deal's full term.
when: When players make trades or treaties with obligations that extend into the future.
why: The game stores the agreed terms so it can check later actions against them.

text: Watch continuously for loopholes and remove each one when found; ignoring them lets griefers keep finding new ways to disrupt play.
Combine many microdecisions into one macrodecision, such as choosing a route instead of directing each step of a deployment.
when: When players find a mechanic too repetitive or tiresome, as fresh playtesters report.
why: Combined strategic impact still matters, yet every single choice costs more effort than it returns.

text: Remove pure equilibria from a strategy interaction entirely, so that anticipating and deceiving the opponent always pays.
when: When a strategy interaction would otherwise settle into one fixed outcome.
why: In a configuration with no pure equilibrium, one side always gains by switching.

text: A game is an observable artifact that enables an experience, while the experience itself is private to each player and is what designers are actually judged on.
why: Designers never see the experience directly; they only build artifacts likely to produce it.

text: Games differ from productivity tools: they entertain, are enjoyed, and are an art form meant to evoke emotion.
The immersive fallacy is the belief that a game's meaning comes entirely from fiction and that players lose track of the game; no player forgets they are playing a game.
Games can combine text, images, video, sound, and music, and any other medium can be placed inside a game.
Games offer players far fewer verbs than books or films do, because stories are authored in advance while game actions must be simulated during play.
Games serve as a vehicle for crafting experiences; because life consists of experiences, games can meaningfully influence how people live.
Games are argued to be a medium that will eventually subsume all other media.
Games can move people beyond what traditional media achieves.
A good game is not necessarily a successful one; success also depends on understanding the game's purpose and its market position.
Games are enjoyed for their own sake, and immersion in a game resembles its play equivalent of immersion in an artwork.
Game spaces act as self-contained immersive systems, but they depend on players, which makes them systems for metacommunication.
Games are assemblies of designed parts like machines, but game mechanics interact in specific complex ways, while machine parts move in intricate but fixed patterns.
1) Ask what the player's role is. 2) Ask what goal the player has. 3) Ask what obstacles stand in the way. 4) Ask what resources the player has.
when: When defining core gameplay from game verbs
why: The formal structure follows from the player-experience vision, so the core questions should be answered from that vision.

text: Gamification means applying game-design elements and principles in non-game contexts.
Common gamification frameworks, including self-determination theory, the MDA framework, HCI principles, and player taxonomies, are mostly not empirically validated.
Attaching points and badges to an activity to gamify it can backfire by draining the enjoyment players already had.
when: when adding rewards to a fun activity
why: Extrinsic rewards can displace intrinsic motivation.

text: In practice gamification often reduces to adding extrinsic rewards and progression metaphors to boring activities.
A rush is an early attack launched before any military units are built.
A rhythm game requires players to input actions in time with a track. Rhythm games evolved from earlier call-and-response toys that asked players to repeat sequences.
Rhythm means elements or movements recurring at set intervals, a principle that organizes games, buildings, and music alike.
Real-time strategy is a small share of total game sales but one of the strongest genres on PC.
More rugged and mobile technology is likely to make games for outdoor playground play feasible.
why: Feasibility, not demand, has kept the industry away from this venue.

text: Rhythm supplies structure to games and buildings through pacing, column spacing, and beats, and it shapes people's cognitive responses to them.
A shared item that works only if both players buy it creates a cooperation dilemma, since buying alone can cost more than it saves.
why: Lone buyers gain nothing and pay extra

text: Judging a design only by what happens on screen misses the emotion created by possibilities that were never realized.
why: Emotion comes from possible futures the player's unconscious perceives, even when none of them happen.

text: Designing around one input system gives strong quality on that platform but makes the game hard to port to others.
when: Quality on one chosen platform matters more than reaching many input systems
why: Input systems differ so much in the experience they produce that a design fitted to one rarely ports.

text: Some games, such as many massively multiplayer worlds, simulations, and certain ranked card game versions, have no winner, no scoring and no end state, so groups may play for hours.
Goals give individual moves meaning; without clear goals, players cannot judge whether actions are useful, so they cannot become absorbed in the task.
when: Designing the goal structure of a game
why: Goals trickle down to make moment-to-moment actions meaningful

text: Games reach goals through indirect routes, such as knocking out an opponent or finishing under par, and these routes look inefficient outside the game.
why: the value of the goal inside the game makes roundabout methods worth playing

text: Players who can pause and resume quests at any time spread a single quest across many sessions and paths.
when: the game lets players leave and return to quests freely
why: players split play around their own schedules

text: Clear experience goals focus the creative process from the start.
A game's basic purpose is to deliver enjoyment.
A termination set defines how a game ends, such as when all sprites of one type disappear or when two particular sprites collide.
A reward system can only pay for achievements it can detect; open-ended or procedural systems make player-invented solutions hard to detect.
Every design decision is shaped by the purpose a game is made to serve, such as profit, art, or self-expression.
Missing goals indicate a game design issue, unclear goal expression a usability issue, and goals that lack meaning an engageability issue.
when: when players are not motivated by goals

text: Balance short-term and long-term goals so players know what to do now and believe they will eventually achieve something significant.
when: Structuring a sequence of goals
why: Near goals give immediate direction, while distant goals give a sense of purpose.

text: Subgoals along the way keep players engaged through long games, as well as a single final goal.
when: long games
why: Intermediate targets give recurring progress

text: When simplifying, keep the founding goal, what the player should feel, as the test for which elements stay.
when: When optimization and bug fixing threaten the production schedule.
why: Because the design was grounded in the intended feeling, simplifying could keep the game's essence.

text: Goals a scoring system cannot detect, such as racing, copying a sequence or maximizing damage, need special modes with their own win conditions.
when: Players pursue goals outside the standard score
why: Standard scoring cannot measure these goals, so separate modes give them alignment.

text: Goals allow success, failure, partial failure and improvement over earlier attempts, which shapes how players judge their own skill.
The nature of a goal sets player focus: precise, specific goals demand precise movement, while broad goals allow broad movement.
Pairing an explicit goal, an implicit goal such as speed, and a fail-state constraint can turn a basic input into a precise, twitchy tool.
why: Touching the wall ends the attempt at once, so every small cursor movement carries consequence while speed is pursued.

text: In a ticking clock, a weak defender holds out for a set time while a strong attacker must eliminate all defenders before time expires.
when: Asymmetric objectives
why: Time limits offset the attacker's strength against the defender's need only to survive.

text: Moving objective objects in a capture-the-flag level changes the centre of all action, so repositioning them alters the feel of the level.
when: when designing a level with objective objects
why: Each objective area becomes the focus of play, so location decides where fighting and movement concentrate

text: A first objective that requires crossing the whole environment previews later challenges, and later visits go faster because players already know the layout.
when: When players will revisit the same world over several visits.
why: Challenges and layout seen on the first pass are remembered, so later visits need less searching.

text: The paths-and-goals pattern, a network of paths linked to goals, draws players through a space and suits guiding them through a level.
when: When planning movement routes through a level
why: Paths linked to goals guide players naturally

text: Goals can be layered in three tiers: short-term (win the next match, catch a creature), mid-term (beat gym leaders, level up), and long-term (complete the collection, defeat the final challenge).
why: Reaching nearer goals more often gives a steadier sense of progress than waiting on distant ones.

text: Games set goals at three timescales: a long-term objective, short-term tasks along the way, and goals players set for themselves.
when: Games of substantial complexity or length
why: A single end goal would leave long stretches of play without purpose and frustrate players.

text: Without a goal, the pleasure of control wears thin quickly and players explore only a small part of the possibility space.
why: Goals give control inputs a meaning to compare against outcomes, which keeps exploration purposeful.

text: Chasing too many goals can leave a product mediocre, without a compelling experience at any level.
why: Each added feature or goal draws resources and focus from the others, so none becomes compelling.

text: 1) Draw a tartan diagram of a game's goal structure. 2) Note how short-term and long-term goals are spaced.
1) State the high-level goal. 2) Break it into sub-goals. 3) Keep breaking them down until each piece maps to a real-time control action.
why: Players act only through real-time controls, so an abstract goal guides play only once it is split into those actions.

text: 1) Ask whether players can state their short-, mid-, and long-range objectives. 2) Check whether they see how a given item will raise their competence.
when: when reviewing whether goals motivate players
why: Goals reached more often make players feel they advance faster and more steadily than distant ones.

text: 1) State the goal sequence explicitly. 2) Explain how each goal relates to the others. 3) Confirm players can see the path from current to final goal.
when: Presenting a series of goals
why: Clear relationships between goals keep players oriented.

text: 1) Count the qualifying events. 2) Compare the count with a threshold. 3) Reset the count when a time window expires. 4) Announce the state as ready when the threshold is met.
when: A special state should unlock after repeated actions in a short time

text: Set goals at three horizons, immediate, mid-range and extended, each with a meaningful reward attached.
Present overarching goals early and short-term goals throughout play.
when: Designing goal structure and onboarding.
why: Players need to know both long-term direction and immediate next steps.

text: Establish short-term and medium-term goals that players reach more frequently than long-term goals, so progress feels faster.
when: When the long-term goal feels too distant for players to sense progress toward it
why: Progress toward a far-off goal feels too slow, so nearer goals reached more often make advancement noticeable.

text: Stop a helping move from carrying a piece directly into the goal, so it cannot bypass the main route to the goal.
Aim for powerful player experiences as the design goal, rather than personal artistic expression.
why: Designers exist to craft experiences for others, not to satisfy a creator's own need for expression.

text: Make goals clear, meaningfully related, concrete, achievable and rewarding, balance short- and long-term goals, and let players choose some goals for themselves.
when: when designing a game's goal structure

text: State the game's goal simply and clearly, since it is the most important rule.
why: Every other rule rests on the object of the game, making it the base of the whole rule set.

text: Set the intended drama and feel of combat first, then engineer code, art, audio and numbers to deliver it.
when: designing or tuning combat
why: A clear target gives tuning a goal and avoids slow number-first trial and error.

text: Have players apply the curriculum to goals they find interesting and meaningful within the game.
when: when designing educational games
why: Learning gained inside a game may not carry over to new situations, so applying curriculum to goals players care about targets that gap.

text: Loosely enforced goal order gives players freedom to choose or bypass goals, at the cost of firm control over progression.
why: With no time limit, players can roam freely and pick the order in which they pursue goals.

text: Game information falls into three categories: privileged, known to one player or a subset; common, known to all players; hidden, known only to the game or to no player.
when: when examining a game's knowledge structure
why: Players make decisions based on information, so who knows what shapes the choices they can make.

text: Hidden information, such as an unknown card mix, keeps players alert and makes the game feel vast and open-ended.
when: When players cannot see which cards or elements will appear in a duel
why: Not knowing the mix forces players to stay on their toes, so surprises keep recurring.

text: When the full set of actions is hidden, players discover them by experimenting, and solving a puzzle may depend on guessing an unusual action.
when: The available action set is unclear to the player
why: Players must guess the interface's vocabulary, so discovery itself becomes part of play.

text: Learning that a game secretly fudges results to make players feel skillful can change how players view that game's skill.
when: Players discover hidden result manipulation
why: Discovered manipulation undermines trust in the feeling of mastery.

text: Players fill hidden information with assumptions about unseen opponents, teammates and the population's skill, then revise those assumptions as events occur.
when: competitive games with hidden positions
why: Partial knowledge forces players to infer the likely state of the world.

text: Players guess hidden enemy positions by judging which team arrangements are unlikely, such as a whole team travelling one route together.
when: enemy positions are hidden
why: Unusual team behavior is treated as less likely.

text: When lethal damage is fast, the decisive choices happen before players see each other, relying on sound, tracking and attack paths as the only information.
when: Games where a kill takes one or two shots.
why: Whoever attacks from behind usually wins before the target can respond.

text: Information starvation: players lack information needed to predict outcomes, so the game is unplayable for anyone who does not already know it, even when its systems are consistent.
An open information structure lets players see the full game state, which favors calculation-based strategy.
A mixed information structure reveals some information while keeping other information hidden, changing as the game progresses.
Variables are the numbers that define game objects and settings, and changing one often forces changes to others.
Information balancing is designing what the player is shown or hidden so a decision is comprehensible but not obvious.
Players gather information from the scoreboard, the kill announcement feed, gunshots, and the equipment teammates carry.
Under time pressure, relevant information can be present yet effectively hidden, because searching for a missing detail costs time the player does not have.
when: split-second decisions

text: More information generally improves decisions, such as knowing which of two identical enemies is weakened, so the player knows which to attack first.
One game often mixes all three information categories, such as a player knowing their deck's contents but not its card order.
In the diamond layout of the elements, technology is least visible to players, aesthetics most visible, and mechanics and story fall between; other layouts are equally valid.
Many games hold internal state that the game knows but no player does, such as hidden pieces, a game master's notes, or most computer game variables.
when: Designing information that players must not see
why: Such state is hidden from every player by design.

text: Card games and guessing games such as poker or Battleship are built around hidden attributes that players must infer or conceal.
when: Choosing a genre structure
why: Hidden attributes are their central play.

text: Game state can include information not visible on the board, such as castling eligibility and whether a pawn just moved two squares in chess.
when: Designing or analyzing games where hidden flags affect legal actions.

text: Isometric view is a 3D space without linear perspective that gives a god's-eye view, common in strategy, construction, and role-playing games.
Knowing the limits of your understanding is valued above learning more, because it reveals how much lies beyond what you know.
why: it keeps designers alert to unknown risks

text: Use open structures to reward careful calculation; use hidden or mixed structures when guessing, bluffing, or reading opponents should matter; use dynamic structures when information should change as players act.
when: When guessing, bluffing, or deceiving should be central to play
why: Hiding data shifts strategy toward social cues and deception rather than calculation.

text: Isometric view suits games where the player must track many units or much information at once, since it gives a god's-eye view.
why: Its lack of linear perspective in a 3D space shows a wide area at once.

text: The same decision is incomprehensible with too little information, engaging with the right amount, and trivial with too much; balance fails through starvation (too little) or glut (too much).
Making enemies threaten a visibly valued resource, such as stealing treasure, raises the perceived importance of defeating them.
why: Players connect the enemy's action to a loss they can see

text: The clearer players can see and anticipate consequences, the more meaningful their choices, especially for larger decisions.
when: designing choices with significant outcomes
why: Players can only weigh decisions whose effects they can foresee.

text: Once player counts exceed what people can model, the mind-game element fades and play becomes mostly mechanical.
when: large-scale multiplayer design
why: Players cannot track enough opponents to predict them.

text: Yomi rests on three basic tools: seeking information, denying information, and planting false information; layered deception emerges from combining them.
when: designing or analyzing competitive information games
why: Each tool changes what opponents believe and can be combined.

text: Yomi layers model counters within counters: a dominant strategy needs about three layers of counter-strategies during play, and one fewer at the metagame level.
when: Designing strategy balance in competitive games.
why: Each layer lets players counter the previous one, keeping options balanced.

text: A Venn-style model maps which knowers hold each piece of information: fate or randomness, the game itself, and each player. Overlaps show shared or hidden knowledge.
when: Designing hidden-information rules
why: It clarifies who knows what before rules are written.

text: Vague rules about what players may say about specific cards leave the line to players and can feel like an unclear kludge rather than a core mechanic.
when: When restricting talk about private information

text: A creature free to wander may meet a predator before the player arrives, so the player finds the flock already eaten.
when: Creatures roam freely while the player is away.
why: Random roaming can leave a creature beside a hunter when the player shows up, so the flock is already gone.

text: Judgment that players do not trust or care about will not drive improvement.
Viewing artwork only through labels hides the detail that makes a world feel unique.
why: Brains filter visual detail to stay efficient, so a name for an object replaces actually seeing it.

text: Vague forecasts that name no time frame or reason give no basis for planning.
Assuming that a game with all information visible has no meaningful decisions overlooks hidden future, internal, and perceptual information.
why: A visible board shows the present, while consequences several moves ahead stay hidden behind chains of interaction.

text: Classify a game's information structure as open, hidden, mixed, or dynamic; if the game is unfamiliar, substitute a known game.
Yomi needs strategy interactions without pure equilibria plus a system with interesting fuzzy edges around them.
when: designing competitive depth
why: Without no pure equilibrium, one dominant choice removes prediction; without fuzzy edges, the game stays a solved abstraction.

text: Provide tools for seeking information, such as scans, sensors, or listening cues, and tools for denying it, such as smoke, jamming, or killing scouts.
when: designing competitive games with fog or hidden state
why: Both sides of information control create decisions about what to reveal or hide.

text: Spending deck or resource budget on gaining information competes with spending it on direct attack or defense.
when: When building a deck in a collectible card game with cards that let players peek at others' cards.

text: Less information means less-informed choices, a weaker sense of control, more chance, and more room for misinformation or deception.
Open information lets players calculate ahead for deep planning, while limited visibility such as fog of war adds tension and forces decisions on partial, quickly outdated data.
when: choosing how much game state to reveal
why: Full visibility rewards calculation; partial visibility rewards anticipation under uncertainty.

text: A dynamic information structure changes what players can see during play, for example when a fog of war reveals areas only while a unit occupies them.
When each player holds vital information that only others can act on, players must communicate constantly to succeed.
when: When designing cooperative multiplayer gameplay
why: Information that only others can use creates a constant need for communication.

text: Dynamic information structures shift the balance between knowledge-based and cunning-based strategy, and have been practical mainly in digital games that can manage complex information exchange.
why: Computers handle intricate exchanges among multiple participants, which a shifting information state depends on.

text: Hide something, then reveal it: fog of war teases that something new exists without revealing it, luring players toward unforeseen areas and sustaining curiosity.
why: Signaling that something exists without revealing it gives players a concrete reason to keep exploring.

text: Few players read rulebooks, since nonlinear play resists text, yet they read even minor item, codex or ability text closely, so well-written small text gets noticed.
when: A game ships with a rulebook or documentation; a game has item, codex or ability text
why: Play details are nonlinear and resist textual description.

text: With hidden trade contents, players treat opponents' trading behavior as evidence of what those opponents hold.
when: Trading with concealed offers over several exchanges.

text: Players who like a game write their own walkthroughs and post them online, revealing what they enjoy, which sections feel too hard, and which feel too easy.
Players read physical feedback through their mind's model of cause and effect, so feedback should support that model rather than talk over it.
when: when designing audiovisual feedback
why: Players interpret physics through an internal model that noisy feedback disrupts.

text: Reading an opponent's hidden plans and perceived weaknesses is among the most satisfying forms of victory, so hidden internal state adds real depth.
In playtests, players dropped their current activity to deal with an enemy as soon as its distinctive sound was heard.
when: a learned enemy sound signals high danger
why: The sound signaled a high-priority threat.

text: Players must mentally project multi-turn consequences because the board shows only the immediate result, and working this out takes real mental effort.
when: In complete-information games like chess.
why: Future states are not visible.

text: A fruitful void is a designed space, the intersection of rules and player personalities, that leaves room for them to interact and produce memorable, emergent play.
A hidden information structure withholds some data about opponents, so players know only partial information such as card counts or betting behavior.
Information can be public to everyone, shared by a subset of players, private to one player, known only to the game, or known only to randomness.
when: Classifying a piece of game state
why: Each category implies different player knowledge and strategy.

text: Uncertainty is when a player has no idea what to expect, so outcomes cannot be predicted from available information.
when: when describing unknown outcomes in a game

text: As competitive play grows, player-made proof of an advantage increasingly decides who wins.
when: Competitive scenes with growing stakes.

text: Like perception and memory, attention is shaped by what a person already knows.
The most important cost of a mechanic is player attention: players have to read directions, err, fail and try again.
A deterministic game can still feel non-deterministic to a player when the opponent's move is unknown until it happens.
Motion can be relative to the avatar, relative to the camera, or relative to another point in the world.
Real degenerate strategies are rarely obvious; they hide in emergent interactions among tools and mechanics.
Real games have fuzzy edges: outcomes cannot be counted precisely, actions blend, and players lack full information or perfect randomness.
when: comparing real games with game-theory models
why: Messy boundaries let players slightly shift payoffs and learn more or less about opponents.

text: Use fractal interest curves: each long peak can contain a smaller copy of the overall pattern, repeating across as many layers as needed, since such curves carry echoes.
when: For experiences lasting hundreds of hours, such as long multiplayer games.

text: Ration information in a structured way, since tension can be generated through revealing or withholding when real value changes are hard to keep producing.
when: When value changes are hard to sustain.
why: Denying and revealing information creates the same emotional shifts as changes.

text: Concealing ratings and reserving them for pairing lowers the stakes, since nothing visible is at risk of loss.
why: players with nothing visible to lose play more freely

text: Treat dice as distinguishable, like one red and one blue, when counting combinations of multiple dice.
when: Counting multi-die outcomes.
why: Prevents undercounting or double counting rolls.

text: In games with hidden skill, managing the opponent's perception of your skill is part of strategy, so design for players reasoning about each other's ability as well as odds.
why: Odds of success depend on how accurately a player estimates the opponent's skill, which is itself a skill.

text: When a symptom such as excessive player damage appears, consider all contributing causes, such as few healing items, slow enemy kills, weak weapons, or slow level gains, rather than assuming one.
when: Diagnosing a balance symptom.
why: Several causes can produce the same symptom, and any one or several may be responsible.

text: Withheld information, through hidden traitor allegiance or privileged knowledge, stops one player dominating co-op decisions, because others lack the shared knowledge to direct.
when: When designing co-op games against the commander problem; when a co-op game has a hidden opposing player
why: Hidden allegiance discourages sharing information that could be exploited; decisions need shared knowledge that privileged information withholds.

text: Players naturally filter, prioritize, and interpret incoming information, and noise appears when this natural process fails.
why: Unusable signals leave players unable to grasp events, which blocks any thoughtful reaction.

text: Hiding what each side offers or receives turns a trade into a contest of guessing and bluffing rather than a comparison of known values.
when: Trades where one or both sides' contents are concealed.
why: Players cannot evaluate the exchange directly, so they rely on inference and deception.

text: Restricting communication so players cannot tell each other what to do forces each player to decide alone, though it can make players feel less like a team.
when: When designing co-op games against the commander problem
why: Players must act on their own when they cannot direct one another

text: If players cannot see who leads, they cannot choose a target, so hidden scoring can stop coordinated takedowns of the leader.
when: In games with hidden scoring
why: A vague sense of who is ahead does not give players enough confidence to commit to ganging up on one target.

text: In games that end, the possibility space shrinks as play proceeds until a winner is declared.
when: Finite games with a win condition.
why: Each move eliminates reachable states.

text: Hidden opponent information supplies much of a game's luck, and revealing it would remove bluffing and much of the game's interest.
when: Deciding whether to hide a game's state
why: Concealment creates the uncertainty that bluffing and inference depend on.

text: Locking bets before the random reveal, with no later raise or fold, leaves players little chance to respond, so the result is mostly luck.
when: When bets are placed before any cards are revealed and cannot be raised or folded afterward

text: When one side knows the full game state while the other must deduce it from clues, unilateral play combines information imbalance with teamwork.
when: In asymmetric one-versus-many games where one player sees the full game state
why: The lone player's full view is offset because the others must pool clues into a shared deduction.

text: A procedural model can represent uncertainty in a system by letting players choose among actions whose outcomes vary, such as randomized assignments and optional evasion.
when: When simulating a real-world system whose true effectiveness is uncertain

text: Removing information can create a decision where none existed, while a constant, complete display of threats removes tension and cat-and-mouse play.
when: When a constant, complete display of enemy positions would otherwise be shown
why: With every position known, players never have to guess at movement, so the cat-and-mouse play collapses into reaction.

text: Fully unpredictable outcomes make planning impossible and reduce play to fast reaction, while fully predictable outcomes remove thinking and leave only picking the best known option.
why: Without any prediction, planning is impossible; with total prediction, there is no mental work left to find a path to a good result.

text: Players may be aware of the current iteration, foresight into the loop's outcome, near and far future loops, anchoring goals, and exits such as leaving for another system or quitting.
Decision-relevant information can stay hidden in complete-information games in three ways: in future consequences, in an opponent's internal state, and through the speed of perception.
when: In complete-information games where both players can see the whole board
why: Visible present positions do not reveal where chains of play lead or what an opponent plans next.

text: Unflagged unreliability or hidden random adjustments breed distrust when discovered: players distrust all information and cannot plan around what they do not know exists.
when: Designing information that can be wrong; using concealed random adjustments in a game
why: Players who later discover unreliability distrust all information, not only the faulty piece; players cannot use information they do not know exists.

text: Hidden or unclear rules make beginners expect a gotcha, so they distrust the game.
when: In games with unclear rules
why: Players assume concealed traps exist

text: Traitor mechanics can make players suspicious of one another, so bad luck and sabotage become hard to tell apart.
when: In traitor games
why: Restricted sharing leaves a bad outcome unexplained, so players cannot tell misfortune from sabotage.

text: Action games that seem to test quick reactions may actually demand puzzle solving and memorization of enemy timing, which can feel more tedious than designers expect.
when: Designing a game around reflexes
why: Unlisted skills can dominate how players experience the game.

text: Making players track too many pieces or statistics confuses and overwhelms them.
State-dependent input meanings only add many responses if the player can clearly perceive which state applies.
when: When the states that change an input's meaning are clear to the player

text: Revealing a new area can delight engaged players while losing others who cannot see long-term goals.
when: When a surprise reveals a whole new area of the game
why: Players who have not identified long-term goals may drop away at such a reveal.

text: Hidden information only creates tension when players understand the limited visibility as a condition of the game.
when: introducing fog of war or hidden state
why: Players who don't understand the limit feel the outcome is arbitrary.

text: Glut does not announce itself and rarely draws complaints, since smooth play hides it from testers, so designers must actively look for it.
why: Smooth play masks the problem, so testers and players seldom notice or complain about it.

text: Showing enough cards that winning options become obvious tips information into glut and removes the decision.
when: When visible cards reveal who holds the strongest hand
why: Once the winner is obvious, betting offers no real choice to weigh, because the answer is given away.

text: 1) Decide whether the space is discrete or continuous. 2) Count its dimensions. 3) Identify its boundaries. 4) Identify subspaces and how they connect. 5) Consider whether more than one abstract model fits.
when: Judging a game's layout without aesthetic assumptions
why: Stripping aesthetics first reveals the structure that actually governs play.

text: Think about space in functional, abstract terms; this is an essential designer skill.
when: When a game seems to have trivial or no physical space
why: Every game's state must exist somewhere, so an abstract model of its space exposes where that state sits and how it moves.

text: Avoid random deviations that the player cannot see or account for when they have clearly aimed well.
when: Adding random elements to aimed actions
why: Unseen deviation makes correct play feel punished.

text: Public state reduces guessing and gives clear calculation but less room for bluffing; hidden state creates inference and bluffing but raises guesswork and frustration.
when: Deciding the visibility of game state; choosing what players can see
why: Each visibility level changes the kind of thinking players do; visibility determines which strategies are possible.

text: Revealing hidden random results after each round builds trust against AI opponents, but against human opponents it can expose bluffing patterns and strategy.
why: Against human opponents, revealed results would expose their bluffing patterns.

text: Successful studios often shift to defensive cash-cow milking, stretching an initial hit indefinitely, which leaves them vulnerable to newcomers with bold ideas.
when: an established studio's flagship product stops evolving
why: Complacency replaces the risk-taking that produced the original success.

text: Derivative games reuse the action set of earlier games, while innovative games introduce new basic or strategic actions.
A market value is a facet of a game that draws a particular audience in a particular way.
Innovation areas are unique mechanics beyond existing genres, reaching non-hardcore players, emotionally rich gameplay, games and learning, and what games are and do.
A prototype can fail as a game yet still teach something, so judge it by what it reveals rather than whether it is fun.
why: A prototype that is not fun can still produce a novel feeling that informs later design decisions.

text: Judge interest by experiencing the work with your whole self, combining analytical and intuitive skills.
why: Interest has no absolute units, so judging relative changes requires felt experience rather than measurement.

text: Keep far-fetched ideas rather than discarding them, and learn when to stand by an odd concept; that judgment is part of the craft.
when: when an unusual concept seems unlikely to work
why: Combining unrelated elements can produce a creative spark that appeals to a broad audience.

text: Innovation sells best when placed on top of a proven genre, which balances the risk of the new element.
when: When an innovative game is pitched to a publisher who funds by market data
why: Publishers fund what they can sell, so building novelty on a proven base offsets its risk.

text: Innovation often thrives at the edges of an industry rather than in its established center.
when: When developers self-produce and distribute games outside the established industry
why: Self-production gives freedom to try original concepts, change ideas midstream, and keep ownership of what is made.

text: Success adds shareholder expectations, larger staff, entrenched habits and bureaucracy, which can drain a studio's willingness to keep innovating.
when: a small studio becomes successful
why: Pressures from success make risky creative choices harder to sustain.

text: Changing story details and core ideas too often teaches developers that nothing is stable, so they stop investing themselves and creative vibrancy fades.
when: When core ideas change frequently during development.
why: Developers withdraw commitment when they cannot rely on the direction of the work.

text: Innovation is judged by three overlapping criteria: feasibility (what production allows), viability (a self-sustaining business), and desirability (what audiences value).
Underinvesting in input, whose benefit is unseen, can undermine the whole game without anyone identifying the cause; input investment is almost always worth its cost.
when: Under tight budgets or deadlines.
why: Input affects every moment of play, but teams cut it first since it is invisible.

text: Judging a feature only by its own certainty overstates its chance of survival, since its foundations also carry uncertainty.
when: Assessing how stable a planned feature is
why: Dependencies multiply the risk beyond the feature's own design.

text: Games with too many pieces, too many rules, or extraneous components are not feasible to produce and get rejected.
when: When an inventor submits a game with many pieces or complex components to a publisher
why: Extra pieces and rules add manufacturing complexity that a publisher may be unable to produce cheaply.

text: Judging a decision only by its design effects misses costs that appear in schedules, relationships and team morale.
when: When evaluating a design decision.
why: Delays in one area cascade through dependent work, so a decision's true cost includes effects beyond the design itself.

text: An innovative idea can fail the business filter, so novelty does not guarantee commercial viability.
when: When a novel game concept is checked against market, cost and business-model questions
why: High production cost or a weak business model can make a novel idea unprofitable regardless of its originality.

text: 1) Identify what the game judges about its players. 2) Examine how the game communicates that judgment. 3) Check whether players find it fair. 4) Check whether players care about it. 5) Check whether it makes players want to improve.
when: when evaluating whether a game judges players well

text: Know the game inside and out, and locate its faults by watching it being played, as a mechanic finds faults by listening to an engine.
when: Evaluating a game in development
why: Problems show up in how the game is actually played.

text: Do not judge a prototype by its visual polish or technical performance; judge the fundamental mechanics.
when: When evaluating an early prototype.
why: Polish and optimization are not meaningful until the core mechanics are proven.

text: Ask whether the game contains something players have not seen before, since novelty is subjective but important.
when: If you are designing a new game

text: Invent new gameplay by recombining formal elements and considering new ways to combine them.
why: Understanding how elements work together enables new designs.

text: Pursuing breakthrough player experiences risks time and money; internalizing a playcentric method is presented as the way to balance both.
when: When seeking breakthroughs while keeping exposure to time and money limited
why: Involving players throughout development lets experimental ideas mature instead of being judged at their first spark.

text: Incumbent leaders must choose between abandoning the flagship product to keep innovating or holding on and waiting for someone else to innovate.
when: judging a large competitor's response to a challenger
why: Both options carry costs, and the choice often determines whether the incumbent is displaced.

text: Mapping is wiring an input signal to a game parameter.
Input hardware largely defines a VR or AR experience, more than most other choices; gamepads, motion-tracked hand controllers and empty-hand tracking each create very different experiences.
A backward somersault can grab a ledge only if the character is facing it.
when: Ledge grab after a backward jump
why: Backward motion relative to facing means the grab depends on orientation

text: Restrictions can cap jump distance, room height, cast size, resource quantity, dialogue length, inventory capacity and vehicle size.
