When a design list grows beyond about ten items, regroup the ideas, since the list may still be incomplete.
Each new iteration of a series tends to pair a new input design with a more sophisticated simulation.
when: With each new installment of a series that changes its input devices

text: Let the interface and controls follow from the game's formal elements and purpose, rather than borrowing them from a successful game.
when: designing an original game's interface
why: Borrowed interfaces yield clones, while purpose-driven ones suit the concept.

text: The physical input to world mapping sets run speed, acceleration, deceleration, and whether a double-tap triggers a dash.
When a thumbstick controls turn rate, a partial push turns slowly and a full push turns quickly, so deflection scales speed rather than setting a position.
when: When the input modifies a rate or magnitude rather than a position

text: Releasing the jump button sets upward speed to a low value that continues for a fixed delay under gravity before the apex.
An input can map to avatar position, rotation, spawned entities, animation playback or simulation variables, possibly several at once; assuming it only controls position overlooks these.
The control path runs from device signal, through optional filtering, into a simulation layer, and out as a response; a raw signal may skip the simulation and map directly to output.
why: Mapping raw signals straight to output forgoes the chance to tune how the input feels.

text: Moves map from input through four kinds of condition: basic presses, multi-button chords, time-sensitive inputs and state-sensitive inputs; each adds forces to a simple simulation.
Input interpretation gives one input different meanings depending on time, space or avatar state: time-based, spatial and state-based interpretation.
Chasing realistic input removes amplification, and direct mapping alone does not guarantee play unless the input connects to a rich system.
when: When an input mapping does not connect to a rich underlying system
why: Realistic mapping removes the amplification that makes controlling a game enjoyable.

text: 1) Pick the control scheme you intend to employ. 2) Shape the game around that scheme's strengths and limits.
when: Starting a VR or AR project
why: A game designed around one input system is strong on that platform

text: Resolve jump, ground pound and backflip inputs with deterministic priority so the same input sequence always produces the same result.
when: Multiple actions share overlapping button combinations
why: Consistent outcomes preserve player control and trust

text: Keep provided operations high-level, and move code duplicated across subclasses into a new base operation.
when: Several subclasses repeat the same sequence of calls.
why: Higher-level operations reduce duplication and keep subclass code short.

text: Mark provided operations protected, and usually non-virtual, to show they exist for subclasses to call.
when: Designing the base class interface for subclasses.
why: The access level and lack of overriding communicate the intended use.

text: Restricting control creates challenge: turn-based games limit options, and that constraint shapes difficulty, while high freedom and real-time movement suit spontaneous action.
when: Give high freedom when spontaneous action is the appeal; restrict control when challenge should come from constrained options.
why: Limiting options blocks the simplest route, so difficulty comes from the constraint itself.

text: Ignoring the interface reaches more buyers but tends to yield dull play; building the core around a platform's unique qualities can justify dropping other platforms.
when: When the core interaction is a unique type of play tied to one physical interface.
why: A distinctive interaction draws enough attention to offset the audience lost by dropping other platforms.

text: Input randomness adds replayability while keeping strategy meaningful, but without other depth, optimal strategies become evident and the game can be solved at the table.
when: Using only starting-setup randomness in a game
why: Varied setups add replay, but limited decisions let strategy become obvious.

text: Low input with low response gives stiff, grid-like control; low input with high response feels organic and smooth; high input with low response is natural but lacks a sense of mass; high input with high response rewards mastery.
why: Responses that never react make the object act like an oversized cursor, with no mass to feel.

text: A high-sensitivity input with low-sensitivity response, or a low-sensitivity input with high-sensitivity response, can each yield expressive control, so the balance between them varies by game.
Responsiveness offers the greatest potential for improving game feel, since games can simulate complex phenomena such as fluids, gases and flocks.
why: Simulating fluids, gases, flocks, springs and weights opens many novel ways to control objects.

text: Linear media maps creator output fairly directly onto audience experience, whereas interactive games widen the gap between the artifact and the experience players have.
why: Player control over pacing and sequence, plus random events, make experiences less predictable.

text: Interactivity is often modeled as turn-taking conversation, a metaphor that fits real-time control poorly.
1) Player forms an intent. 2) Player sends input. 3) Computer reconciles input with its internal model. 4) Player perceives the result. 5) Player acts again.
why: Each result is weighed against the original intent, and that comparison drives the next input.

text: Games give players control over pacing and sequence and add random events, which makes the experience harder to predict but enables feelings like choice, freedom, responsibility, and accomplishment.
why: Those feelings are rarely available in linear media, so designers accept the loss of predictability.

text: Transitive balance: if A beats B and B beats C, A beats C; options rank clearly and stronger ones cost more or carry drawbacks. Intransitive balance drops this ranking.
Intransitive balance: no option beats all others; each beats some and loses to others, so strength depends on the opponent's choice.
A transitive mechanic is a system where better items, actions or rewards cost more or demand more effort, so cost and benefit rise together.
Triangularity is balanced asymmetric risk, where a safe small reward competes with a dangerous large reward.
why: The tension between the two options creates meaningful choice.

text: In three-player rock-paper-scissors, one player's two opponents can be merged into a single combined opponent for analysis.
A relation is transitive if A relates to B and B relates to C the same way, so A relates to C; equality and less-than both behave this way.
Rock-paper-scissors is intransitive: rock beats scissors and scissors beats paper, yet rock does not beat paper.
RPG power is mostly transitive: higher character level, costlier items, or higher player level usually means more power.
Fighting-game matchups are often intransitive, and civilization games are intransitive in their civilization powers but transitive in unit cost and strength.

Intransitive relationships appear in fighting games, RTS unit counters, layered counter systems, vehicle and weapon matchups, RPG class matchups, trading card counter-decks, and combat with first strike or bluffing under hidden information.
Combat genres use a counter loop: block beats strike, grab beats block, strike beats grab; strategy genres use spearmen beating cavalry, archers beating spearmen, cavalry beating archers.
In an intransitive game like Rock-Paper-Scissors, the best long-term approach is to play each option equally, a 1:1:1 ratio, because favoring any one lets an opponent exploit it.
when: Intransitive games with a counter for each option.
why: A predictable bias gives an opponent a winning counter strategy.

text: When two choices give equal win chances, no choice is optimal and the decision becomes a matter of player psychology rather than odds.
when: switch and stay odds are equal
why: no mathematically better option remains

text: Use intransitive design when outcomes of player strategies are hard to predict or balance changes will be hard to make after release.
when: Predicting or patching a balanced game is difficult
why: Intransitive relationships act as an emergency brake against runaway dominant strategies, even without knowing the game's balance.

text: Intransitivity does not change the actual possibility space, but it makes the right choice harder to see, so the perceived space of options feels larger.
why: Players must work out relative strengths, which makes the options feel more varied.

text: Three mutually countering options give more strategic variety than one dominant strategy, and players can adapt their choices during play, sometimes in real time.
when: When an intransitive mechanic sits inside a larger game where players can switch strategies mid-match.
why: Each option has a counter, so no single choice dominates and play varies more.

text: Game properties, objects, systems or mechanics can be classed as transitive, intransitive, or mixed.
Games occupy different triangle positions; a position indicates how much physical accuracy the game must deliver, not its artistic quality.
when: when using triangle placement to plan a game's physics
why: Position determines which behaviors must be physically accurate

text: Matching pennies is rarely named, so designers may build it without recognizing the mind game they have created.
when: In asymmetrical games where one side seeks a match against hidden choices.

text: Kingmaking can happen directly through trades or negotiation, or indirectly when a required move clearly helps one player over another.
when: When a trailing player's move or trade decides between two leading players.

text: Kingmaking happens when a player who cannot win decides which of the other players wins.
Kingmaking is usually undesirable because the winner seems to have won by favor rather than skill.
Kingmaking needs three conditions: a player recognizes they cannot win, the losing player recognizes they can support any leader, and the losing player chooses a leader to help.
when: In player-versus-player games where a trailing player can influence who wins.
why: The chain of events breaks if any one condition fails, so each is needed.

text: Cap daily trades, or block trades once a player is eliminated, so eliminated players cannot hand resources to favorites.
Children discovered geometry rules by trial and error when programming a turtle to draw things they cared about.
when: when learners program toward personally meaningful goals
why: Wanting a personal outcome motivates testing and refining rules.

text: Edutainment combines learning with entertainment across reading, writing, arithmetic, problem solving, and how-to topics, serving children and adults building skills.
Play-based education has been proposed as the best preparation for children in the twenty-first century.
Only a few educational games have been scientifically tested with measured learning gains; most commercial games labeled educational lack such evidence because the label is uncertified.
why: No certification process exists for the educational label.

text: Exergames, which require physical interaction, can encourage exercise.
Play lets the brain experiment with new and complex situations, so it functions as learning, and it matters most in childhood because young brains are more malleable.
Spread teaching over time rather than massing it, pacing how many elements are introduced at once based on complexity and early UX tests.
when: Planning how many elements to introduce
why: Distributed learning beats massed learning

text: Decide what players already know before writing a tutorial, using target audience and game references, then verify those assumptions through playtesting rather than trusting them.
when: During tutorial planning and early design
why: Wrong assumptions about prior knowledge waste time teaching known skills or leave players lost

text: A playful learning environment built around meaningful activities works better than adding rewards to a boring task.
when: when designing educational or gamified products
why: Learning tied to meaningful activity is more effective than rewards alone.

text: Dismissing fixed-answer challenges as non-games leads to excluding many acclaimed adventure games.
when: When judging challenges whose response to a given input never varies.
why: Fixed input-to-output mapping describes many well-regarded games

text: Make rules discoverable through play rather than requiring players to memorize them.
when: In complex videogames whose rules players cannot take in at once.
why: Players who must memorize rules get overwhelmed and confused before forming any idea of how the game works.

text: Do not accept claims that a single brain hack produces large effects with little effort; prefer complex, evidence-based explanations.
when: judging design advice or persuasion claims
why: Real cognitive effects are small, context-dependent, and rarely produced by one easy trick.

text: Open-world creatures can change with the day/night cycle and weather, which makes the world feel reactive over time.
when: open worlds with day/night or weather systems

text: A dungeon is a maze-like space of connected challenges, rewards and puzzles, paced so the player moves through it in sequence.
The environment can either facilitate or obstruct learning.
Between a dungeon's entrance and exit sit treasure, monsters, rescued characters and traps.
A dungeon crawler's core needs a character, a dungeon, a hero, monsters, and leveling up.
Judge a game's setting by how it makes the player feel, since environment can carry much of the game's emotional impact beyond its combat or roleplay systems.
why: Humans are drawn to landscapes that once signaled a place to thrive, and learned preferences add to the effect.

text: Weather, light and terrain shape emotion: enclosed darkness that opens into bright light can mark progress and produce a strong emotional payoff.
why: Contrast between confinement and open light is felt as freedom and accomplishment.

text: Give players several ways out of bad situations, such as healing, teleporting dangerous enemies away, protecting against deadly status effects, and scouting traps and monsters before entering danger.
why: Players can see the odds and have several exits, so bad luck never feels unfair.

text: Games should support good environmental practices or at least avoid promoting harmful ones.
Let players choose among dungeon paths while keeping pacing strict, so no challenge exceeds the player's current skill level.
when: In dungeon-style levels, as opposed to open worlds or sandbox cities
why: Confined backtracking space in dungeons keeps players from reaching areas beyond their current skill.

text: The magic circle is the temporary space set apart from ordinary life where a game's rules apply; inside it, thoughts, feelings, and values differ from outside.
when: A player accepts the game's rules or is invited to play.
why: The agreement separates play from everyday life, so the game is temporary and players can leave it; the rules gain their power inside.

text: The magic circle is the closed internal problem-solving system a game creates, which works well even though its mechanism is poorly understood.
Playing suspends everyday rules in favor of the game's rules, and finishing returns the player to ordinary life.
In competitive multiplayer, group players of similar skill into lobbies or ranks.
when: In competitive multiplayer matchmaking.
why: Being destroyed quickly or winning too easily is not fun; matching similar skill keeps outcomes driven by play rather than experience gaps.

text: When players choose their own opponents, they tend to pick the most favorable matches, which distorts rating gains.
when: Unmatched, player-chosen challenges in rated play.
why: Each player gains from a match the other would prefer to decline.

text: When players with different input precision or speed share a server, the faster or more precise group can dominate and the game is perceived as unbalanced.
when: multiplayer games mixing platforms or skill levels
why: Advantages in speed or precision compound in direct competition.

text: A character can look dominant among beginners yet fall to mid-pack at higher skill, because skilled players learn to counter its most-used moves.
when: Win rate is compared across rating bands.
why: Experienced players recognize and counter predictable tactics.

text: A strategy degenerate for experts can be a mystery to novices, who have not discovered it or cannot execute it.
when: When players differ widely in skill.
why: Access to strategies depends on skill.

text: An if-clause is a match object whose matching method takes the database and a bindings list; the list starts empty and is filled during matching.
Match Making Rating (MMR) is an internal skill rating per player, usually updated like Elo or TrueSkill, used to pair players of similar skill.
A ladder ranks players by their results in challenges, where players gain rank by beating those above them, making rank a separate system from rating.
Each matching behavior has an opposite that moves the character as far from matching as possible, such as avoid being the opposite of catch.
Some MMOGs have little AI, with only animals or occasional monsters, while players control other characters.
Most MMOGs add AI-based challenges similar to those in first or third person adventure games.
Matchmaking that pairs players of similar skill and racing-opponent adjustment are common uses of game AI.
Implicit difficulty selection through strategic options works in competitive multiplayer, where explicit difficulty selection does not.
Skill is hard to measure alone because performance mixes power and skill; playtesting and analytics such as death frequency, failure locations and first-encounter completion time reveal it.
A starting rating has no fixed meaning; it matters only relative to the ratings of other players.
Players are assumed to have skill within a range, so a balanced game does not present challenges far outside that range.
when: When setting difficulty for a target audience

text: Rating systems built for two players must be extended for multiplayer games, and the designer chooses how individual or team ratings predict outcomes.
when: Free-for-all or team games.
why: Two-player formulas do not cover multiple competitors.

text: MMOG AI uses largely the same technologies as shooters, but its implementation must handle many characters in a much larger world.
when: Scaling shooter AI to MMOGs
why: Simple pathfinding copes with a shooter level's 5–50 characters, so MMOG-scale counts need reworked implementations.

text: Testers who are unusually good at playing to win are very valuable for balance testing.
when: When playtesting for general balance to find overly strong or weak strategies or objects

text: Player skill rarely stays fixed, so designers must keep supplying challenges that match the player's growing skill.
when: As players' skill increases during play
why: Boredom or frustration at a fixed challenge level drives players to seek growth.

text: Free lobbies without ratings suit games played among friends, where rating integrity matters less.
when: Unrated games.
why: No ratings means no incentive to exploit matchups.

text: Ask whether one strong player can carry a weak team and whether one weak player can sink a strong team, then choose weighting accordingly.
when: Designing team rating weights.
why: Answers determine how members should be weighted.

text: Skilled opponents and traders tend to target a player who has bought a strong deck, which offsets purchasing power.
when: In a trading card game where skill is strong enough to beat purchased decks
why: Skilled traders and duelists can exploit a buyer's strong deck, eroding the purchase advantage.

text: Split metrics by player rating before judging balance, since results can look different across skill levels.
when: Assessing character or strategy balance in a competitive online ranked multiplayer title.

text: Judge balance by how close matches are: blowouts suggest one unit is much stronger, while wins with almost no health left suggest evenly matched units.
when: When playtesting designed characters through randomized one-on-one tournament pairings

text: When outcomes depend on skill, performance-contingent rewards and skill-based ratings such as star rankings convey real growth and signal progress.
when: Performance or outcomes depend on skill rather than luck.
why: Rewards and ratings reflect the player's own improvement, showing competence growth.

text: Mixed messages from player feedback often cause sudden, dramatic worsening, and behavior may plateau or regress even while players expect improvement.
when: Players give inconsistent feedback to a learning creature.
why: The network generalizes from conflicting lessons.

text: Matchmaking tracks each player's experience level and win rate and pairs players with similar records; the concept is simple but building it well is a major engineering challenge.
when: online competitive games
why: Pairing similar players reduces skill differentials.

text: Matchmaking that pairs players of similar relative skill reduces the effect of initial-condition differences.
when: In multiplayer PvP games where turn order or starting position varies randomly

text: In an adjacent-challenge ladder, games alternate so a player challenges upward in one game and downward in the next.
when: In a ladder where players challenge only the player immediately above or below them

text: Once spending has occurred, rating-based or power-based pairing usually puts heavy payers against one another, cancelling what they bought.
when: In free-to-play games where paid power is matched by win/loss or power-level pairing
why: Money sorts players by spending, so rating-based pairing groups high spenders together.

text: Without a luck term, underdogs win more often than the rating predicts, so skilled players lose more points against weaker players than they gain.
when: Rating systems applied to games with chance.
why: Ratings overestimate skill gaps when luck is ignored.

text: Teammates who have played together often may beat stronger teams of strangers.
when: Team games where players repeatedly team up.
why: Familiarity improves coordination beyond individual skill.

text: Pairing each strength with a weakness, such as fast but fragile or strong uphill but poor in corners, keeps options competitive.
when: Designing unit or vehicle traits
why: Each option's edge over one rival is offset by a weakness to another, so no single option dominates.

text: Greater player skill can amplify an existing imbalance, because skilled players exploit it, rather than reducing it.
when: games with a built-in imbalance
why: Skilled players find and exploit the imbalance.

text: Skills that scale with an attribute, such as damage equal to twice Magic, give players reason to invest in that attribute above others.
when: Linking skill power to attribute scores
why: Scaling creates an incentive to raise the linked attribute.

text: The size of a TrueSkill rating change depends on the ratio of the players' σ values, so a high-σ player gains more from a match against a low-σ opponent.
when: When a high-uncertainty player faces a low-uncertainty opponent in TrueSkill-rated matches
why: High-uncertainty players gain more information from such a match.

text: TrueSkill rating changes also depend on the difference in μ, so an upset moves ratings more than an expected win.
A team's rating change is split among members by their σ, so more uncertain players change more.
when: team matches
why: An uncertain player gains more information from a result than a certain one does, so their rating moves more.

text: With several players racing to a finish, the game ends when the first finisher arrives, so it tends to end sooner than a single player's typical finish time.
when: Multiple players race on the same track and the first finisher ends the game.
why: The minimum of several independent finish times is earlier than a typical single finish.

text: Rushes are easy for novices to execute and hard for them to stop, while skilled defenders can stop them, so rushes become rare at high skill levels.
when: In a real-time strategy game at high skill levels where defenders know rush counters
why: The defender's advantage grows with skill.

text: In one-on-one fights, a win rate above 50% means above average and below 50% means below average.
when: In one-on-one fighting-game matchups

text: TrueSkill models each player's skill as a bell curve with a mean (μ) and an uncertainty (σ), and was one of the first rating systems to handle multiplayer matches directly.
Online learning can produce a bug that cannot be replicated without replaying the same play history.
when: When learning algorithms adapt during play rather than offline between levels

text: A ladder has only one top spot and requires constant play to hold a position, so it can feel like a treadmill.
when: In a single-track ranked ladder where only one player occupies the top rank

text: Climbing past the halfway point of a ladder is hard for most players, which can discourage them from trying.
Relying on matchmaking to rescue new players from difficult early matches does not solve their bad first experience.
when: Onboarding new players in multiplayer or free-to-play games.

text: Scenarios designed for one player count often do not scale; a balanced three-player scenario can be heavily unbalanced with six players.
when: Games supporting varied player counts.
why: Balance depends on player count and no automatic scaling exists.

text: A large number of mediocre rated games can outscore a few wins by a strong player, so the total reflects experience as much as skill.
Most masterpoint systems ignore opponent strength, so a win over a novice earns the same as a win over an expert, favoring players who face weaker opponents.
1) Check whether the prototype has skill levels. 2) If it does, describe how they work and how they were balanced. 3) If not, decide whether to add them and predict how they would change play.
when: Reviewing a prototype's difficulty

text: 1) Have each strategy play many simulated games against the others. 2) Compare win rates. 3) Discuss why the winning strategies outperformed the rest.
when: evaluating competing decision formulas

text: 1) Take a recording of dense play. 2) Replay it at reduced speed. 3) Examine the decisions second by second.
when: decision density is too high to analyze at normal speed
why: Normal speed hides too many decisions to examine

text: 1) Determine the player's average damage output and how much damage the player can take. 2) Derive the character level from total XP of all enemies placed so far, using the level curve, plus other XP sources. 3) Use this power to set how many hits kill an enemy, enemy weapon power and expected survival time.
when: In progression games where the character improves over time
why: Encounter strength must match the character's current power

text: 1) Rank players by final standing. 2) Treat each player as having played one one-on-one game against every other player, N−1 games in total. 3) Count the better-ranked player as the winner of each such game.
when: free-for-all matches with N players
why: Earlier rating systems had no explicit way to handle multiplayer matches.

text: Mitigate mixed-feedback problems in learning creatures by combining learning with built-in instincts, since no general procedure solves them.
when: Designing player-taught creatures.
why: The problem is partly a weakness of the approach.

text: Use MMR when even matchups are the goal and matchmaking speed matters; automated queues are the usual approach.
when: Online competitive games where the goal is evenly matched opponents.
why: Games between similar-skill players are the most exciting; mismatches are predictable and frustrating for both sides.

text: To compare players without spreadsheets, have each play for the same set time and rank them by how far they progress.
when: comparing players in a live idle game
why: Progress over a fixed time reveals relative performance without needing the game's cost and benefit formulas.

text: Give strong players only small, temporary bonuses from single successes.
when: Rewarding player success
why: A reinforcing loop keeps paying the leader more, cutting the match short with the leader winning.

text: When players of different skill levels play together, design deliberately for what keeps the game challenging and interesting for each of them.
when: players of different skill levels play together

text: In TrueSkill, a win always raises the player's mean μ and a loss always lowers it.
Results that are close enough may count as a draw, with the threshold set per game; racing games may disallow draws entirely.
Each team acts as one player; its rating may be the mean or weighted toward some members, whereas TrueSkill sums members' μ and σ.
when: Team-based multiplayer rating.
why: Team strength depends on how members combine; TrueSkill uses the sum.

text: Tighter matchmaking gives closer matches but longer waits; looser matching shortens queues but allows more mismatched games.
when: Designing automated matchmaking.
why: Match quality and queue time compete.

text: Skill-dominated games need opponents of similar skill; a small player base may leave some players without viable matches, while a large audience can be matched easily.
when: Choosing how skill-heavy a competitive game should be
why: Skill gaps make matches unenjoyable, and small audiences cannot supply evenly matched opponents.

text: A mechanic is one complete loop from player input, through the programmed response, back to the player.
Converting turn-based moves to simultaneous moves requires extra rules for handling collisions.
Some board games use sand timers to limit turns, and some blend turn-based play with real-time minigames.
The most common form of time manipulation in games is rewinding, where dying returns the player to an earlier checkpoint.
Simple objects have few properties, and those properties stay fixed during play; for example, a piece's color never changes.
A mechanic can interact with itself, as when arrangements of identical pieces create different structures that claim territory.
In a linear progression, a player at a given level has usually mastered the skills taught in earlier levels.
The best-feeling games often have their mechanic and spatial context created at the same time.
A small game with rich object interactions is better than a large one with weak interactions.
why: Weak interactions break presence, whereas richly responsive objects delight players who like combining items.

text: The order of existing content can matter as much as its quality, and reordering alone can change how an audience responds.
why: Audience interest built gradually toward a climax when the strongest material came last.

text: Change a curated option list often so that offerings do not go stale.
when: Options are offered repeatedly

text: Describe mechanics as verbs by asking what the player is able to do.
Objects give motion meaning: movement abilities like wall kicks or long jumps lose their meaning without objects to interact with, and motion is hard to perceive without a backdrop.
when: When the game world has no backdrop or objects for the avatar to pass or interact with.
why: A moving avatar needs things to pass or bump into.

text: When non-binding plans are revealed simultaneously, betrayal becomes nearly required for strong play.
Changing a single core action can produce a completely different game.
why: Actions largely define a game's mechanics, so games sharing an action set tend to feel alike.

text: When both sides act at the same time, neither can react to the other's choice, even if one acts a few milliseconds earlier.
when: Simultaneous-move designs.
why: Each side's action is hidden until resolution.

text: In a game the player perceives the game state, compares it to an internal ideal and acts to close the gap, on the same roughly 240 ms cycle.
when: Real-time control in games.
why: Game control reuses the same perception-thought-action loop as physical movement.

text: Simultaneously active mechanics can combine into more than the sum of their parts.
when: Several distinct mechanics running concurrently and overlapping within one game

text: Feel can emerge from seemingly arbitrary but interdependent relationships among variables, such as gravity roughly doubling at a jump's apex, creating a self-consistent physical world.
when: Tuning a physics-based character controller
why: Consistent internal logic makes odd rules feel natural

text: Once controls are mastered, sensitive controls enable improvisation, with fluid new motion combinations that react to the environment.
why: Improvised motion that reacts to the environment without forethought is intensely pleasurable, a flow experience.

text: Threats and challenges in mechanics produce raw arousal, especially when play is fast, decisions are tough, and stakes are high.
when: When designing core mechanics meant to excite.
why: Fast, high-stakes decisions generate arousal in the player.

text: Very different games share underlying elements that make them feel like games; comparing them reveals common requirements and forms a basis for studying game design.
when: Comparing two games that seem completely dissimilar
why: Shared underlying elements are what let us recognize an experience as a game, even across very different types.

text: 1) Select: each player places one card face down. 2) Reveal: cards flip and each player loses health equal to Cost. 3) Battle: the lower Strength card is discarded; ties keep both in play. 4) Damage: cards in play deal Damage to the opponent. 5) Cleanup: discard cards in play; each player draws one if the deck is not empty.
when: Each round of a simultaneous-reveal card duel.

text: 1) Open with a strong, attention-grabbing piece. 2) Follow with a smaller, calmer piece. 3) Build to a grand finale.
why: An attention-grabbing opener wins the audience, and a calmer piece lets them settle in before the build.

text: In a light-touch game, keep contact on the surface without breaking it, without stopping, and without a discernible pattern.
when: Designing a continuous light-touch mechanic.
why: The somatosensory system predicts patterned input so neurons anticipate it; unpredictable contact is more stimulating.

text: Make interfaces resemble familiar things; use familiar symbols and controls from other games, real life, or cultural archetypes, giving players a shortcut to meaning.
why: Players already know these conventions, which cuts comprehension effort; creating new ones costs players too.

text: A metaphor misleads when its extra associations conflict with how the system works, or when the features that matter are not conceptually similar to the borrowed object.
An interface metaphor is a visual symbol that helps players navigate a system, such as a desktop with folders and trash cans, or a backpack for carried items.
A metaphor gives a new thing the appearance of a familiar thing so people grasp it quickly.
Removing representation and treatment leaves core systems functional but weakens the game's identity, so metaphor affects identity rather than mechanics.
when: when testing how much a game depends on its metaphor
why: Core functionality is independent of presentation

text: Many PCG systems fit more than one metaphor, but few show all of them equally.
Need not represent the real world to be meaningful and fun; explore iconic, surreal or abstract concepts via metaphor, like controlling a fluid or giant worm, not just visuals.
why: Meaning, interesting interactions and strong game feel do not depend on representing the real world.

text: Metaphors need not simulate perfectly; games omit many borrowed-object properties, like cars never needing oil changes or food never spoiling, so closeness suffices for meaning to come across.
why: An implicit agreement lets players accept that only some borrowed properties are implemented, so they won't object.

text: Aim for interfaces that feel magical, not merely intuitive, since players respond strongly to that feeling.
why: Players expect new systems to lead somewhere better, and lose faith when they stop caring.

text: Simple, iconic visuals set few expectations about how an object should behave, giving designers freedom in its motion.
when: choosing the visual metaphor for a game object
why: Fewer realistic expectations leave room for stylised movement.

text: A metaphor works when the new thing's structure resembles the familiar one, even if the materials or substance differ.
when: Choosing a familiar object to represent an unfamiliar system.
why: The familiar word conveys most of what players need, since shared structure matters more than the substance.

text: Metaphor fit is a soft metric: it measures how response, context and polish align with expectations the metaphor creates, not objective reality.
when: when evaluating whether a game's feel matches its metaphor
why: Players perceive according to their expectations

text: Game metaphors draw on three sources: real-world objects, cultural archetypes, and game conventions or clichés.
why: Metaphor draws on players' stored common knowledge, so any recognizable source can serve.

text: Inconsistent conventions force players to relearn rules in different parts of the game.
1) Identify what each object represents to the player. 2) Determine expected behaviors, effects, animations, motion, interactions and sounds, since visuals alone miss these channels.
when: when auditing or measuring a game's metaphor
why: Expected behavior is the basis for judging feel; expectations come from all sensory and behavioral channels.

text: 1) Check whether the interface already borrows from a familiar real-world object or idea. 2) If it does, judge whether the borrowing clarifies or gets in the way. 3) If it does not, ask whether a familiar metaphor would make it more intuitive.
when: reviewing how easily players will understand an interface
why: Borrowed interface metaphors can either aid understanding or confuse players, so each must be checked.

text: 1) List candidate metaphors for the interface, such as a farm, road map, shopping mall, or railroad. 2) Free-associate on each for about five minutes. 3) Keep the metaphor whose associations match the game's procedures, rules, and boundaries.
when: choosing an interface metaphor
why: Associations that match the system communicate it; mismatched ones confuse players.

text: 1) List what each game object represents. 2) Place its visual treatment on the realistic-iconic-abstract spectrum. 3) List the behaviors, animations, sounds and interactions the player should expect. 4) Check whether actual behavior matches those expectations; if not, adjust the metaphor or the element.
when: during design reviews once each object has a clear representation and treatment
why: Metaphor mismatches make game feel dissonant

text: When a custom physical interface is impossible, use a metaphor that links physical inputs to the game world.
Teach players to read fictional cues, and establish a consistent metaphor vocabulary in each game so players can tell which elements are mechanical.
when: When a game's fiction shows interactive-looking details that may not be simulated
why: Consistency lets players learn which cues are real.

text: Established input conventions and technical limits keep designers from exploring a device's full input space, but trying new mappings carries risk.
when: when choosing control schemes
why: Technical limits and entrenched input conventions narrow what designers try, and new mappings carry real risk.

text: Detailed resource diagrams capture every resource and interaction but grow complex, while abstract diagrams stay simple and hide detail.
when: modeling a game's resource flow as a diagram

text: Players may solve puzzles by using an input device's physical features in unanticipated ways, and they enjoy the discovery rather than treating it as an error.
Input rules that look messy in code are acceptable because their complexity costs designers and programmers, not players, when the interface disappears.
when: When the rules stay invisible and serve control feel.
why: Players cannot sense the rules, so they add no burden to play.

text: A trigger's cylinder shows its collision radius, and the player can interact with it only inside that cylinder. Collision Height and Collision Radius are set in the trigger's cylinder component.
A ground pound gives landing precision that air steering cannot, though very small targets remain fiddly to hit.
A time-insensitive jump arc stays predictable, so players judge landings reliably. Ranking a jump second-highest and second-longest among moves creates clear tiers.
why: Fixed arcs make landings easy to judge.

text: Unconventional controlled roles such as weather, fear, a disease or a city can be used in games, with physical interaction represented within a world not bound by natural law.
Gesture-based core mechanics can replace point-and-click and drag as a game's central interaction.
A tactile control can map input strength to finger curl and position to a mouse, or use a small pressure window that the mouse keeps light.
when: Mapping pressure-sensitive touch to devices.
why: Separating the pressure input from the movement pattern lets one mouse cover both jobs.

text: Input responses tend to evolve step by step by adding states, time-sensitive moves and chords rather than changing the underlying approach.
Each added degree of failure headroom and success legroom spares another group of players from either a frustrating failure or a boring ceiling.
why: Partial setbacks keep play going instead of forcing a win or loss, so the spectrum can stretch in both directions.

text: Physics-driven locomotion is high-risk because it is hard to implement and hard for both AI agents and players to handle.
A loop where players gather valuables while evading a threat creates tension between reward and risk.
when: In a mode where players grab items while evading a pursuing horde.
why: Item spawners sit in cramped areas, so lingering there exposes players longer while they grab loot.

text: Without a speed cap or drag, a character driven by seek accelerates indefinitely.
when: When the steering output is an acceleration rather than a velocity.
why: Seek applies its full output as acceleration toward the target, and nothing in the behavior caps speed.

text: A hard-to-control scheme frustrates players even when it is novel, especially when it is bolted onto a mini-game with awkward constraints.

1) State the ideal behavior you want from players. 2) Test constraints, goals, interface, visual design, characters, and music or sound in turn. 3) If none fit, find another method that steers without reducing freedom. 4) Check the design does not induce unwanted desires.
when: Planning how to get a behavior without forcing it
why: Routing the desired behavior through many levers keeps players acting by their own choice.

text: 1) While thrust is held, grow thrust speed by thrust acceleration each frame, up to max thrust speed. 2) Build a thrust vector along the heading using thrust speed. 3) Add that vector to ship velocity.
when: thrust input is held
why: Ramping thrust over time and adding it as a vector along the facing direction gives gradual, direction-independent acceleration.

text: 1) Cancel horizontal momentum in the air. 2) Freeze briefly. 3) Drop under stronger gravity. 4) On impact, shake the screen and spawn particle effects.
when: When the character is airborne and the dedicated button is pressed.
why: A fixed, predictable motion keeps the outcome of an input easy to anticipate.

text: Designers should understand and control how the illusion forms in the player's mind, since a well-made experience can feel as real as reality or more real.
why: The player's perceived experience is the product.

text: Steer players toward chosen actions indirectly, through breadcrumb rewards, rather than telling them what to do.
when: when guiding player behavior among many possible actions
why: Indirect guidance keeps choice meaningful

text: Trigger a Triple Jump only when moving faster than about half of top speed, at the walk-to-run animation switch; below that the third press produces a basic jump.
when: Third jump input during a jump chain

text: Games can emphasize physical dexterity or thinking; many blend both or alternate between them, and the right mix depends on the target market.
when: When deciding how much of a game demands physical skill versus thought
why: Audiences differ in whether they want dexterity or puzzle-solving

text: Limit antisocial play in online multiplayer games: show a code of conduct players commit to before play, enforce it, and design so antisocial acts are unrewarded or impossible.
why: Harassment makes the game a bad experience for victims, so it is treated as a high-priority usability issue.

text: Speaking aloud can make some players more careful, so their behavior no longer reflects natural play.
when: during think-aloud sessions

text: Players carry habits from other games into a new community, and a design can override them by shaping the expected tone.
when: When players move between online games with different social norms.
why: Environment and available communication tools guide conduct more than prior habits.

text: When one player is clearly ahead, others gang up on them, and players often overshoot by destroying the leader completely, which makes doing well feel punished.
when: In multiplayer games with a clear leader.
why: Negative feedback from opponents is useful but tends to be overapplied.

text: Players enjoy acting out social roles: top players enjoy power, underdogs enjoy the fight, and upsets feel gratifying.
when: Games with visible ranking and social hierarchy.
why: Roles give players emotional stakes beyond winning.

text: Open trading and at-will challenges let player reputations form around strong play, lucky wins and bluffing.
when: When players can trade cards between games and challenge others at will, beyond one duel.

text: Players who organize their own parties or play with friends tend to treat cutscene waits as a shared experience and tolerate them.
when: self-organized or friend groups
why: Shared goals and social bonds make waiting acceptable.

text: A player who leaves a multiplayer game is pursuing a divergent goal, since they want something else while remaining players want to continue.
when: In tightly structured, finely balanced multiplayer games where roles are precisely assigned.
why: Goals affect everyone in a group, so one player's divergent goal disrupts the whole team.

text: Girls in group play socialized more, shouting warnings and suggestions and holding face-to-face huddles to divide responsibilities.
when: cooperative group play in a shared space

text: Leading players cannot relax, since a strong item might hit them at any moment.
when: a race uses catch-up item distribution
why: strong items can be aimed at the leader

text: Theft of items attracts griefers because items give players power, and victims feel violated.
when: In games where possessions grant users substantial strength.
why: Items confer power, so robbing a player takes something valuable and feels like a violation to the victim.

text: In click-based social games, losing progress is nearly impossible and skill only speeds progress.
when: In early-generation click-driven social games with straightforward progression.
why: Progress is almost never lost and power accrues steadily, so nothing punishes weak play.

text: In social deduction games, players gather information by asking questions and reading other players' faces, which adds a social layer to logic.
when: when deduction happens among several players
why: Asking questions and reading faces add information channels beyond pure logic.

text: Most players in persistent online worlds dislike malicious attacks on other players, while a minority sees them as adding richness.
when: Persistent multiplayer worlds that allow player-on-player attacks.
why: Attacks let evil characters play evil roles, which some players value as added richness.

text: Players read coordinated tactics such as ambushes into enemies that each run simple independent rules, though no coordination is coded.
Crowds watching together seem to sense one another's reactions, which deepens their shared feeling.
when: a crowd watches the same event together
why: Audience members may pick up on how others around them are reacting, and that unspoken awareness steers and strengthens their own emotional response.

text: Adults aged 25 to 35 are mostly casual players whose time is scarce, while hardcore players in this group buy many games and influence their social network's purchases.
when: Designing for adults aged 25 to 35
why: Family formation makes time precious, and heavy buyers shape purchases in their social circles

text: Multiplayer play draws players more strongly than solo play because it meets basic social needs.
when: comparing multiplayer with single-player games
why: Social belonging sits lower in the hierarchy than self-esteem, so meeting it exerts a stronger pull.

text: Judging whether an action will succeed depends heavily on how skilled players think their opponent is.
Players may perceive a program's hidden knowledge, such as knowing every card, as cheating even when it never uses that knowledge.
when: A program holds information the player cannot see
why: Players judge fairness by what the program could know, not only by what it does.

text: Games give players a socially safe way to see how others act under stress, which is part of why people like to play together.
when: Players play with others
why: Competition and cooperation affect survival, so people test them in play to learn who is skilled at what and how to team up.

text: Games give people something to share and focus on, so they can gather and spend time together without needing awkward conversation.
why: A shared activity gives people a neutral focus that won't make anyone uncomfortable, so they don't have to force conversation.

text: People need to feel part of something, and this social need is a powerful motivator for continued play.
why: Community membership fills a social need, and such needs are strong enough to keep people coming back.

text: Most people prefer playing with family and friends rather than alone, yet many such relationships, like couples or remote grandparents, remain underserved by games.
Players taking opposing sides of a conflict simulation often first think a few simple moves will resolve it, then find pressure on both sides makes it far harder.
when: a simulation of a conflict played from both sides
why: Experiencing both sides' pressures exposes complexity hidden from a single view.

text: When new players have a safe starting zone, hostile players can wait just outside it to attack newcomers.
when: open multiplayer worlds with safe zones
why: The safe-zone boundary becomes a predictable ambush point for opponents.

text: A player can be near the top of a local list even when only one player is number one worldwide, so local scopes can make players feel highly ranked.
when: when a game offers local rank lists
why: smaller comparison groups make standing look better

text: In multiplayer, the same action can carry very different social meaning depending on the state of the target player.
when: When one player performs an action toward another, such as a melee attack.
why: The target's state and context give the action its social message.

text: Repeatedly attacking a defeated player's body reads as insulting and belittling, while attacking a living opponent reads as ordinary play.
when: When a defeated player's body remains visible before respawn.
why: The defeated player watches from the body's viewpoint until respawn, so the repetition feels personal.

text: Witnesses are about twice as likely to misidentify an out-group member as a perpetrator, regardless of the witness's own group.
when: When identifying a suspect in a simulated or real crime
why: Group membership biases identification

text: The individuals-versus-game pattern suits noncompetitive, social players and gambling-style games.
when: when players want a social, low-pressure experience
why: Players act alongside others without needing to interact with them directly, so no direct interaction is required for the experience.

text: Players differ widely in outside knowledge, and most fall somewhere between the most and least informed players.
why: Outside knowledge of designer habits and genre conventions lets players predict events, which reduces tension and weakens immersion.

text: Winning a strategic exchange comes from predicting the opponent and misleading them about one's own intentions.
when: When an opponent is actively reasoning about the player's moves in return
why: Each player must predict the other's decision process, including what the other believes about them, so the contest becomes one of minds.

text: Stable player groups build shared histories and meet in hubs such as towns, taverns, chat rooms, and forums.
why: Consistent player groups accumulate shared gameplay events, and familiar members can protect and introduce one another.

text: In asymmetric two-sided games, one side may score early, the other build defenses mid-game, and the first break through late, so each side's strengths peak at different phases.
when: in asymmetric games with distinct sides
why: each side's goals peak at different times

text: Top-rated players in Elo-style systems sometimes skip matches to guard their standing, particularly when they suspect their rating is inflated.
when: when a visible rating is high
why: losing a high rating feels costly

text: A listener who sees the game as their own defends it to others; ownership is the ideal outcome of a pitch.
when: Pitching to a decision-maker
why: People defend ideas they feel invested in.

text: In open player-versus-player worlds, players tend to form protective groups that hunt those outside them.
when: Combat is allowed anywhere in the world
why: Group members protect each other from other players

text: Gift giving pleasure is the enjoyment of making someone else happy through a surprise.

Playing a game often signals something beyond play, such as adulthood, fearlessness or romantic interest.
Public interaction, even passing contact, yields social and economic benefit that reinforces safety and builds relationships.

Adding a player changes both strategies and the social dynamics of a game.

Any multiplayer feature added to a game, including to a generated or procedural one, inherits the same trust concerns about cheating.

New kinds of online communities may become permanent elements of human culture.
Community property need not be tangible; a shared status, such as a guild's reputation, can serve the same community-building role.

Unilateral competition, which mixes cooperation and competition, is underused and promising for digital game development.

text: When designing for a group you once belonged to, recall how you reasoned, what you enjoyed, and how things felt at that age.

why: Memories of past experience give direct insight into the audience, though people tend to forget how things really felt

text: Eye contact, natural gestures and movement in a shared space make a remote person and place feel real.
why: The brain is specialized for reading faces and gestures, so eye contact and shared movement create a sense of presence.

text: Showing the players immediately above and below a player in global rank lets them see their nearest competitors.
when: when displaying global leaderboards

text: Creatures high in a food chain should not work in coordinated groups; they may appear in groups but should act as individuals.
when: Designing upper-tier predators.
why: Group coordination makes behavior more complicated.

text: Choose a conflict that both children and adults can relate to, so players of different ages can play together.
when: Games meant for mixed-age groups
why: A shared conflict gives each age group a reason to engage

text: Alternate cooperative and competitive phases to add variety and to reveal whether a partner prefers cooperation or competition.

text: In online worlds, buddy lists, guilds, and recurring shared locations let players see each other repeatedly and find time to talk, which builds community.

why: Repeated contact with the same players turns strangers into a community.

text: With more than two players, treat all other players as one combined opponent; each added player raises equation degree: quadratics for three players, cubics for four, quartics for five.

text: Design multiplayer actions with the target's state in mind, since one action can read as friendly or hostile depending on that state.

text: Link a physical artifact to an online leaderboard so players gain a place in a wider community.

text: Title odds depend on each player's full path, so seeding, not only match odds, strongly shapes who wins a single-elimination bracket, since small per-match skill edges compound across rounds.

text: Friends lists drive engagement in online social games for many women, because playing with real friends builds real relationships.

text: A negative loop runs from sociopathy to griefing, which brings negative attention.

why: Shared stakes require ongoing coordination and friendliness.

text: Relationships formed around a game create an emergent layer that can keep players engaged even after official support ends.

text: Social experiences succeed when they move a relationship's status, such as stranger to friend or low to high standing.

why: Actions gain meaning and tension because they strengthen or damage the trust and reputation others observe.

text: When a visible player's mistakes can damage reputation in front of teammates, the moment becomes tense; skilled play builds reputation while errors erode it.

text: Disruptive behavior that goes without consequences is tolerated and tends to spread through the community.
when: In multiplayer games where some players deliberately harass others.
why: Without consequences, others see the behavior as acceptable.

text: A shared objective alongside individual goals produces shifting alliances, since players must cooperate on the common aim while competing for their own.
when: Multiplayer games with shared and private victory goals
why: Players must block rivals' private goals while guarding the shared one, so both cooperation and betrayal pay.

text: A large player count dilutes the effect of divergent goals, since one goofing-off player matters far more on a team of two than on a team of twelve.
when: When comparing a two-player team with a twelve-player team.
why: One player's goofing off or quitting weighs far less when many others carry the team.

text: When two throws match and one differs, the lone thrower gains 1 point per opponent it beats and loses 1 per opponent beating it; the matching pair get the reverse.
when: two throws match and one differs

text: Player choices, such as where a piece is moved, change relationships among objects, so the same setup can evolve in different ways.
when: In games where players' moves can shift how pieces relate to each other.

text: Placing trainers and vendors for many classes in one place encourages players to mingle.

text: In a 2015 survey, 57% of teenagers had met a new friend online and 52% spent time with friends playing games.

text: Social progression loops are expression leading to cosmetics, connection leading to guilds, superiority leading to leaderboards, and community value leading to an influence loop.

text: A disruptive persuasive game can make players and bystanders uncomfortable, since its strangeness is part of its effect.

text: Deterministic match outcomes, where skill always yields the same kill count, can make a multiplayer mode feel predictable and dull even when skill matters.

text: 1) Identify the social roles players want, such as competitors, collaborators, helpers, or teammates. 2) Determine whether they want quick chats or long-term relationships. 3) Offer low-pressure ways for strangers to meet. 4) Provide channels and shared content for conversation. 5) Support the point where strangers become friends. 6) Give friends lists and guilds for reconnecting.

text: 1) Use a rating system to measure player skill. 2) Pair players with similar ratings. 3) Rely on pairing rather than handicaps to keep matches balanced.

text: 1) Define a shared goal for players to pursue. 2) Announce the goal to the player base, for example through a mass email. 3) Let players work toward it together.

text: Genius loci (spirit of place) is the aim of giving a space a memorable identifiable emotional character, understood through its own elements and direct sensory experience rather than prior knowledge.

text: Under the material metaphor, generation is a new medium that a designer manipulates and sculpts, much as a sculptor works stone or clay.

text: Mechanics versus motif contrasts designs that begin from core mechanics with designs that begin from a story or visual theme.

text: Player expression is a frequently neglected area of multiplayer design, so it is worth revisiting during reviews.

text: Subthemes for a playful game can include having fun with friends, escaping from reality, and simplicity combined with transcendence.

Relationships between objects can be expressed through location, through hierarchy such as ranked values, or through other means.

text: Choose a fantasy with clear appeal, since players either are drawn to a fantasy or are not.

text: Modern settings work unusually well only when the player gains extraordinary power over ordinary life.

text: Touch, distance, facing direction and eye contact are underused design material for expressing intimacy and interpersonal relations in games.

text: Games with unifying, resonant themes produce much stronger experiences than games with weak themes or none.

text: The strongest themes connect to desires players already have, such as wanting freedom from obligations and worries.

text: Not every game needs a resonant theme, but a resonant theme, once found, is worth using fully across the design.

text: Once the theme is settled, keep an element if it reinforces the theme and remove it if it does not.

text: Limit invented words to about one per line, applying the same limit to character names even when they are English, since overloaded names make speech hard to follow.
when: Sci-fi or fantasy dialogue
why: Dense made-up names become unintelligible to listeners and actors, especially when a line is spoken aloud.

text: Exaggerated fictional rules, such as a hazard that spawns giant creatures, can justify content that a realistic model would not allow.
when: When a game's fictional premise is deliberately absurd rather than modeled on reality.
why: Absurdity gives the fiction license, so content a realistic model would forbid stays plausible to players.

text: Mechanics that yield vivid storytelling or social moments can stay in the design even when they permit degenerate strategies.
when: In a game not centered on skill, where high-skill balance is not required.
why: Testing needs no long study or dedicated players, and a found exploit does not ruin a game that isn't about skill.

text: Use symbols with real-world associations, such as wood and pickaxes, so players carry prior knowledge into their choices.
why: Players bring prior knowledge of real objects, so they can predict how a new item will be used.

text: When a story's spatial logic matches the camera or view angle, the threat or drama reads more strongly to the player.
why: Shooting upward at descending enemies makes an approaching threat feel like imminent doom for the player's own ground.

text: Showing a desirable item or ability before players can obtain it stimulates curiosity and motivates them to grow toward it.
when: When other players visibly use an item or ability they have earned in the game.
why: Curiosity is an intrinsically motivating factor.

text: When story moments hinder gameplay, players abort them one after another; when story makes a moment important without hindering play, gameplay and story merge.
when: When a cutscene would interrupt an intensive, central activity such as a boss fight.
why: Most players come to play, not watch, so story that blocks the active activity gets skipped.

text: In interactive experiences the guest can be the main character and change the story world directly, which makes projection especially strong.
why: Events happen to the guest directly, and the guest can manipulate the world, merging perception with imagination.

text: Repeatedly pairing a motif with a character builds firm expectation, so sounding the motif without the character, or danger without its warning, produces shock.
why: Once a pairing is learned, the listener expects it, so breaking that expectation induces tension or surprise.

text: When mechanics actually enforce a fiction's harshness, such as scarce resources and little chance of survival, players feel that harshness directly and become immersed.
when: the fiction implies scarcity, danger or entrapment
why: Players experience the fiction's conditions through play rather than being told about them

text: Deception can be layered, where one player makes the opponent believe something false about what the first player knows; multilayered deception is hard to design directly and emerges from combining basic tools.
when: designing deep information games
why: Combining basic tools creates nested beliefs that designers cannot easily script.

text: When every element reinforces a truth-based theme, the experience becomes powerful. Realistic presentation can make players feel the theme's consequences personally.
why: A single theme reinforced by every element gives the work more emotional force than polish alone.

text: Without a dramatic premise, many games stay too abstract for players to invest emotionally in the outcome.
when: When a game's interaction is presented as raw data rather than a setting.
why: abstract rules give players no concrete stakes

text: Persistent weather and night settings can add a melancholy undertone to a game's events, such as loss or crime.
when: A game whose story of loss or crime plays out under persistent gloomy weather or night
why: Sustained gloomy environment colors how players feel about the story.

text: Graphics, sound and fiction let players pretend mechanics are more than rules, and a mechanic framed as a thematic event can add emotional echo beyond its rule.
when: Mechanics are presented with graphics, sounds and fiction rather than abstract shapes
why: Framing gives abstract rules human meaning such as hunger, grief or desire.

text: Pairing violent excitement with mournful tone, such as combat set in ruins of a beautiful civilization, creates an unsettling contrast that deepens emotion.
when: Violent gameplay is paired with a mournful setting, theme or soundtrack
why: Clashing feelings reinforce each other when placed together.

text: When a setting is grounded in an established fiction, designers cannot freely change its basic rules, such as physics, to balance a challenge, so the mechanics suffer.
when: fiction-first design with a realistic or established world
why: fiction constraints block the parameter changes balancing needs

text: Offering several possible futures at each moment makes play feel decision-rich, while a single future at a time leaves play emotionally empty.
when: At any moment the player's world offers many possible routes or actions, as in an open world
why: Players keep weighing alternative futures and feel pulled toward them, which a single fixed path does not provide.

text: Wrapping abstract mechanics in a setting such as a growing city or an ancient war makes them easier to learn, because the fiction shows how relationships connect.
when: A system of intricate mechanics would be hard to learn if shown only as abstract shapes
why: A familiar setting conveys how elements relate using understanding players already have, so learning is faster.

text: Narrative space by medium: a novel for hours, a feature film about 120 minutes, a TV episode about 45 minutes, a sitcom about 25 minutes.
The story stack has five layers from least to most flexible: fantasy, action, economy, world, and story, and designs should be built bottom up starting from a strong fantasy.
why: Lower layers constrain the higher ones, so the base must be fixed first.

text: A game can be viewed as a machine that generates sequences of events; the less story is prescribed in advance, the more varied and memorable the stories players produce.
why: Systems generate unplanned events that players retell, while heavy prescripting leaves little room for such events.

text: A narrative designer needs knowledge of content design (level, asset and audio production) and systems design (game mechanics).
why: Narrative content must be implemented and communicated through game devices, so systems knowledge is required alongside writing.

text: Story criteria for judging a generated experience are characterization, a climax that is unpredictable yet inevitable, smooth invisible exposition, and overall structure such as three-act.
when: A mechanics-generated experience is evaluated as an emergent story
why: Reframing the experience as story prompts different questions than judging it only by accessibility and depth.

text: Fiction suggests many actions a game may not support, and players cannot tell which fictional ideas are real mechanics, nor assume everything in the fiction is mechanical.
when: a mechanic's imagery implies interactions the systems do not simulate
why: Fiction carries no reliable information about which interactions are mechanically supported; treating it as mechanical would be wrong most of the time.

text: Placing a story stake first forces an inflexible fantasy to be dragged to that spot.
why: Fantasy is inflexible, so a story point fixed early forces the fantasy to be bent to fit it.

text: Gathering more research does not produce a theme on its own; a shift in thinking about what the subject is really about is needed.
why: Accumulated details give no clear point of view until the designer reframes what the subject is really about.

text: Rejecting theme because players will never consciously notice it discards a benefit that works below conscious awareness.
why: Theme works at a subconscious level, so players feel it through reinforcing elements even when they cannot name it.

text: Treating theme as a puzzle of hidden symbols that players must decode misreads what theme is for.
why: A theme's job is to focus all elements on one experience, not to hide a message that players must decode.

text: Working without a defined theme leaves the game's elements pulling in different directions.
why: Elements aiming at a common goal reinforce one another, and a settled theme gives a test for what belongs.

text: A subtheme on its own is not enough; without a central conflict it lacks the power to unify the game.
why: A theme without an opposing force lacks bite; a natural opponent supplies the conflict that unifies the game.

text: Treating a rejected idea as bad is a mistake; it may simply not be useful to that listener now.
when: after a rejection
why: Ideas are judged by how useful they are to the listener right now, not by their overall merit.

text: A thin game layer over exercises is not enough; many educational games are neither truly educational nor fun.
when: When an educational product is built by adding game elements to drills.
why: Learners disengage when the activity itself is not engaging.

text: Relying on a popular theme attached to a traditional game, without real design work, gets submissions rejected.
when: Pitching to a market that buys games on gameplay rather than theme
why: Some markets treat gameplay as the main selling point, so a popular theme on a traditional game does not carry a submission.

text: Scripted storytelling modes borrowed from other media often break down when applied to games.
why: Designers design mechanics that generate events rather than the events themselves, a layer of indirection other media lack.

text: Adding a fiction on top of finished mechanics rarely works; fiction and mechanics must be designed together so they integrate.
why: Fiction and mechanics threaded together enhance each other in ways neither can do alone.

text: Puzzles that rely on fictionally plausible solutions leave players guessing among many reasonable answers, because only the implemented one works.
when: When a rule or puzzle outcome is communicated through fiction rather than through mechanics

text: The machine's facilities do not uniquely determine the choice of representation, which is often difficult.

1) Decide the game's theme, the idea that ties the whole game together. 2) Use every available means to reinforce it, applying it to nearly every element, including hardware, sound and rules such as invulnerability, not only the story, especially in clever, unexpected ways.
when: Early in design, before other choices are made
why: A settled theme guides every later decision; unexpected details can carry a theme as strongly as obvious ones.

text: 1) Find a powerful but inflexible fantasy. 2) Build the other design elements around it. 3) Craft a story that explains why the stake sits where it does.
why: A story stake placed first forces an inflexible fantasy to fit, whereas a fantasy chosen first lets story explain its position afterward.

text: 1) Ask what about the design feels powerful and special. 2) Note which ideas excite people most when you describe it. 3) Imagine the game without constraints. 4) Examine what drives your instincts about how it should be.
when: When searching for a game's hidden power or resonant core.
why: Resonance often shows up in your own reactions and in other people's.

text: Let story serve the game experience rather than master it.
why: Story can justify nearly any situation, so left unchecked it tends to dictate the whole design process.

text: Keep subthemes, such as teamwork, only where they serve the main theme.
why: Subthemes that drift from the main theme dilute it

text: Music should inform game design rather than be added on, with music systems tuned to the game's circumstances.
when: Planning music for a game
why: Music added late cannot shape play as designed music can.

text: Keep story and characters important but secondary until formal elements are settled.
when: Early in design
why: Dramatic elements pull attention away from gameplay if they are considered before the core formal elements are set.

text: Thread fiction and mechanics into a single system of emotion instead of giving either one primacy.
why: the strongest games unify both rather than balancing one against the other

text: Choices with no stat or path effects can rely on fiction alone; once a choice changes mechanics, it needs unambiguous mechanical information.
when: moral or narrative choices
why: Players can only act reliably on mechanical effects they can read.

text: Connect narrative development, cultural ideas, and usable gamespace so that a layout carries meaning as well as function.
when: Designing any layout that must convey meaning
why: Level design already communicates with players, and design can carry cultural and narrative meaning alongside its function.

text: Design play so people can roam the setting and discover who their avatar is, with decisions that carry weight and suit the persona.
when: In games where players build their own player character through character creation
why: Self-defined characters need a solid world and developed NPCs to supply the material players use to define themselves.

text: Ludologists hold that a game's most important qualities lie in its mechanical systems, while narratologists hold that mechanics scaffold a story, which is the main source of value.
why: Story details restrict which mechanical fixes are allowed, so fiction and mechanics seem to pull against each other.

text: Expanding the story or adding mechanics both tend to be expensive, while trimming either side is possible but hard when plot and mechanics are strong.
when: when story and mechanics are out of step
why: each fix has a different cost

text: Heavily prescripted design gives authors control of the plot but yields fewer player stories; systems that generate events yield more varied stories.
when: Deciding how much story to script in advance
why: Prescripting reduces the variety of stories players produce

text: Keep controls and outcomes predictable; add occasional novelty via mountains of varied content, mechanics introduced over time, and more sophisticated physics simulation. Too much novelty at once overwhelms, exhausting attention.
when: After players have mastered the setting, inputs, and rules.
why: Too many new stimuli at once compete for attention and tire the player.

text: The first games using new technology gain an emotional rise from some players simply because the technology is new.
when: For the first few games using a newly introduced graphics, animation, or physics technology
why: novelty itself excites, but only temporarily

text: New technologies create new accidental harms, not only the harms that existed before.
Newer controllers such as dance footpads, handheld touch screens, and motion remotes have expanded game audiences beyond traditional players.
Networked multiplayer remains manageable when rapid-fire machine guns are avoided.
when: when designing weapons for networked multiplayer

text: Successful games combine novel elements with familiar ones, so players have anchors while still encountering something new.
why: Wholly unfamiliar titles have flopped by arriving before audiences were ready, so familiar parts keep them accessible.

text: Early sales come from novelty, yet a game lacking solid play loses its players just as rapidly.
why: Novelty draws initial attention, but without solid underlying play nothing holds players past the first draw.

text: Chasing what technology can do can distract designers from their real goal, a great game; engineers are especially prone to this.
when: When pressure for novelty and attractive new technology is strong
why: Novelty can replace the purpose of the game

text: When meeting a new technology, ask how it could become foundational to your game instead of only polishing an existing design.
when: evaluating a new technology
why: Decorative use leaves the core experience unchanged, while foundational use enables mechanics that could not otherwise exist.

text: Narrative goals give actions flavor, while gameplay goals such as high scores or access items shape how play feels.
Obstacles are physical, such as hazards or bumpers, or mental, such as puzzles.
