Objective categories group game goals by what players do: capture, chase, race, forbidden act, construction, exploration, solution, and outwit.
An objective gives players something to strive for and defines what they are trying to accomplish within the game's rules.
Partial objectives, or miniobjectives, are smaller goals that help players reach the main objective.
No single algorithm beats all others on every problem; an algorithm outperforms others only by specializing in a narrow set of problems.
Restarting from a random state every iteration is optimal only when all states and actions are equally likely.
Specialised game AI fails on rules it did not know in advance, so general game-playing research needs games whose rules are unknown beforehand.
Some stealth and action games let players finish without entering combat, offering a route that avoids fights entirely.
Films and books give objectives only to their characters, not to the audience, whereas games hand the objective directly to the player.
Obstacles matter most in single-player games.
Different players can have different objectives, players can choose among several, or they can form their own goals.
Pair each desired behavior with a suitable algorithm, since the obvious choice is often not the right one.
when: when choosing the technique for a character behavior
why: Complex AI does not guarantee convincing behavior, so matching technique to behavior matters more than sophistication.

text: Use achievements with measurable physics thresholds, such as holding balance for ten seconds or throwing an object a set distance, to give long-term goals.
why: Specific measurable targets give players concrete goals that prompt repeat playthroughs.

text: Offering several paths to victory makes players reweigh their choices, which increases replayability.
when: Designing goals for replayable games
why: Different routes change which options players consider worthwhile

text: Rewards align easily with goals that are easy to measure, such as completion time in a timed challenge.
when: When a player's goal is easy to detect as achieved, such as in racing
why: Rewarding only what players already want to do keeps rewards from damaging the core experience.

text: When the goal can be reached in many ways, it is unclear which player is furthest along, which weakens targeting of the leader.
why: Even coordinated players cannot agree on a target when they cannot tell who is ahead.

text: When a goal can be reached only one way, players will not look for unusual interactions. Offering several routes to the same goal encourages players to explore unexpected ways of solving it.
when: Designing goals such as boss defeats
why: A single route gives players no reason to search for alternatives.

text: The chosen objective sets a game's tone; a goal of capturing an opponent feels very different from a goal of spelling longer words.
Goals can nest: a short-term task, such as retrieving a required item, unlocks a mid-term objective, which contributes to the longest goal.
when: In games where the final goal requires collecting several items
why: Each small task gates access to the next stage, so finishing it advances the larger aim it serves.

text: 1) Decide whether objectives must be explicit. 2) Decide whether players can determine them. 3) Define how multiple objectives interact.
Give everything players must do or learn a clear meaning, including purpose, value and visible impact.
when: During onboarding, for the mechanics that form the core experience
why: Meaning attached to tasks and lessons addresses the intrinsic drives for competence, autonomy and relatedness.

text: Set objectives that feel challenging yet achievable.
Games often mix objective categories, which can split player focus; real-time strategy blends war and construction and appeals to different player types.
why: Blending goals spreads attention across them, drawing players who would dislike either goal taken alone.

text: Objects are game mechanics' nouns (characters, props, tokens, scoreboards); properties are attributes describing them, each holding a state, often several values such as rank, color, location.
The museum venue is any place where people examine unfamiliar things for variety, knowledge, and a fresh view of daily life.
Object complexity is measured by the number of an object's properties and how much those properties vary.
A game level combines a mission, which lists what the player can or must do to finish it, and a space, which is the geometric layout where those actions happen.
The museum venue covers zoos, aquariums, city sightseeing, and browsing unusual shops.
A single portable device can serve several venues, from the hearth and reading nook to the gaming table and anywhere else.
In open spaces such as fields or streets, player behavior is hard to predict unless other control methods are added.
Giving each object many possible interactions creates expressivity, which players experience as freedom and personal style.
when: Designing objects the player can act on in traversal or combat
why: Multiple valid ways to use one object let players express individual play styles.

text: Use the museum venue for experiences that present a range of things to examine and compare, rather than one sustained session.
why: Browsing many varied items gives variety, widens knowledge and renews perspective on familiar things.

text: Do not force an activity into a single venue when it clearly spans several.
when: When an activity's venue is ambiguous, such as pinball in a restaurant or a casino
why: Venues have stable properties while games and platforms keep changing, so venue fit matters more than the product.

text: Large objects that move slowly are easy to predict, while small objects that move quickly are much harder to dodge.
when: when mixing object sizes and speeds in a hazard field
why: Speed and size together determine how readable a threat is

text: A space with no nearby obstacles offers no challenge and nothing to measure skill against, however good movement feels.
why: Challenge comes from limiting space, so with no nearby obstacles, movement speed and turning have nothing to be judged against.

text: 1) Give each object type a small set of behaviors. 2) Define rules for how objects interact. 3) Let encounters emerge from these interactions instead of scripting each one.
when: Designing interactive worlds with many objects
why: Emergent interactions often produce creative and unusual results

text: Define each game object's purpose before setting its numbers, such as whether a class deals damage, protects allies, or boosts loot.
when: when starting content creation
why: gives the numbers a target to aim at

text: Define each game object's nature, complexity, evolution, and availability timing so players can learn how it behaves.
when: When underlying numbers are visible but players learn objects through experience instead of calculating
why: Players build intuitive knowledge of units through play rather than computing their variables, so the learning path matters.

text: Build worlds from modular, richly interactive assets, varying them as a communicative system players learn to read.
when: players must learn a system of meaning quickly
why: Reusing a contained set of assets lets players learn their symbolism, and variations signal mechanics they then recognize.

text: A season is a league in which a new one begins as soon as the previous one ends.
Questioning the convention that each play session stands alone can produce a design with persistent consequences.
Online seasons are usually treated independently, though winners may receive a small starting bonus in the next season.
Seasonal play is common in online player-versus-player games.
Many social and mobile games are built for sessions of ten to twenty minutes, so a long cutscene could take up an entire session.
The right match or session length depends on the experience the designer intends, not on a fixed number.
Match the mix of decision scopes to the intended pace: many twitch decisions suit frenetic action, while profound choices suit slow strategy.
A sharp transition appears when a discrete change, such as regions with different scoring or rounds with distinct feels, marks the phase boundary.
why: Discrete rule changes between regions or rounds give each phase its own feel, so players sense the boundary.

text: A seasonal reset puts everyone back on equal footing, so each new season gives every player a similar chance to rise.
when: when a ranked system resets each season
why: Because rank can be a separate system from lifetime rating, it can be reset without erasing the rating.

text: Decision scope and decision pace are independent: a large decision that takes long fills the timeline smoothly, while a large decision made in an instant produces a sharp spike.
why: Ample time lets a weighty decision occupy the timeline without leaving an empty gap in flow.

text: Let sessions start quickly, support different playing styles, and help players form an emotional connection with the world and character.
when: Designing session entry and overall player experience.
why: Quick starts reduce friction and varied styles broaden the audience.

text: Sound and music affect player mood and emotional responses to the gamespace, so deeper involvement of audio specialists can noticeably improve the player experience.
when: When sound design is integrated from the start rather than added near completion
why: Audio reaches players emotionally, so supporting gameplay across the project shapes how the experience feels.

text: Confirm player input with sound when the controller has no physical response, since the mind maps sound to touch and sound stands in for tactile feedback.
when: when the controller has no rumble or physical response
why: Virtual interfaces give little touch feedback; many controllers lack haptic feedback.

text: Changing only a weapon's sound, not its stats, can make players feel the weapon was fixed.
when: Responding to players finding a weapon weak
why: Players perceive value through audio feedback.

text: Players follow a distinctive 3D sound toward its source to discover hidden areas or learn new actions.
when: early in a level, when a sound marks a new area
why: 3D sound grows louder as the player nears its source, so it draws attention to one specific spot.

text: Noise is any signal that adds no meaningful information to a player's mental model, not only static or random interference.
Poetry of presentation is the aesthetic quality of an experience, arising from artistry in writing, music, dance, acting, comedy, cinematography, and graphic design.
Synchresis is the brain fusing an object's look and sound into one event, so layered sounds can give a new character while seeming to come from the object.
Effects that let players view others' hands or decks give limited access to information that is normally hidden or privileged.
For VR and AR, the feeling of presence rooted in proprioception matters more than the 3D images themselves.
Overhead view looks straight down, a somewhat unnatural angle, and is used for level maps and board-style games.
Separating sounds is usually harder than separating visual elements, and stereo sound can make it harder still.
Future interfaces are expected to use tactile feedback more, but sound is the best option until then.
Sound can draw player movement, set the atmosphere of play, reward achievements, and set the pacing of action.
Make positive and negative feedback sounds slight variations of a few source sounds, so they form a recognizable family.
when: When designing menu navigation sounds for forward, backward, accept or decline
why: Variations of shared sources read as one family rather than unrelated sounds.

text: When many effects fire at once, rank visual and audio feedback by importance and cut lower-priority cues, giving top priority to effects showing the player is being hurt.
when: busy combat, especially multiplayer
why: Showing every effect for every element becomes incomprehensible.

text: Tune relationships for what players perceive rather than strict realism; exaggerated motion, like squash and stretch in animation, reads more clearly.
why: Small cues let players deduce general rules about the world, and later confirmations make that world feel coherent.

text: Changing a game's point of view changes how the experience feels and what players can perceive, so view choice should be considered as a design decision.
when: Evaluating or choosing a camera or perspective
why: Viewpoint controls what players see and how they relate to the game world.

text: Let a threat be heard before it is seen so it feels like a constant presence and builds anticipation.
when: when the threat is meant to feel omnipresent
why: Sound signals presence before sight confirms it, so players stay alert.

text: Enemies whose attacks greatly weaken the player are worth giving a recognizable warning sound.
why: Sound can warn players of danger before contact, and distinct sounds add tension to encounters with powerful enemies.

text: Sound can carry atmosphere when graphics are too limited to do so, letting simple visuals still feel tense.
when: when graphics are simple
why: sound conveys mood the visuals cannot

text: When a signal becomes noise, the player does not understand the event and cannot think about or respond to it.
when: When players fail to filter and interpret information from a signal channel.

text: Showing enemies only in periodic pulses forces players to infer movement between updates, and skilled players learn to move away from the last pulse.
why: Players who know they are tracked can move away from displayed positions, adding a strategic layer.

text: Sound is closely tied to touch, so the mind uses hearing to help locate the body and judge the surrounding world.
when: When a game aims to create a sense of presence in a virtual world.
why: Missing sounds for physical actions remind the player the world is fake, breaking presence.

text: Adding a sound to an attack can supply weight and violence that the animation lacks, so the animation does not need reworking.
when: An attack feels lacking in impact
why: Sound carries the impression of force that the visuals fail to convey.

text: Playing an impact sound when two objects cross can make them appear to bounce apart instead of passing through each other.
when: Objects that visually overlap without physical response
why: The sound supplies the missing collision cue.

text: Sound and shadow can make a space seem larger than the area around the avatar, suggesting movement beyond what is visible.
why: Awareness that a threat may be off-screen makes the unseen space feel like it extends beyond what is visible.

text: Ambient sound that turns into threatening voices as a horde approaches tells players how much time remains without a timer.
when: In levels where players have only limited time before a large enemy group arrives.

text: Sound effects provide feedback for mechanics and serve as rewards for completing important tasks.
why: Players learn which actions produce which sounds, which teaches them how to play properly.

text: A jarring audio burst that plays when a threat comes into view signals players to avoid its sight.
when: When avoiding detection by a threat is a central mechanic.
why: The burst gives immediate notice of being seen, which matters when avoiding sight is the core task.

text: Pairing realistic visuals with generic or cartoonish responses breaks the player's belief in the world; choose a consistent level of fidelity across visuals, sound and motion.
when: when a realistic-looking object has unrealistic reactions
why: Mismatched fidelity creates dissonance

text: Check a VR or AR design by asking: Is the player feeling presence, and could it be stronger? What diminishes presence? What builds it? Repeat these questions as the design changes.
when: reviewing any VR or AR design
why: keeps the designer aware of where the player's mind and body really are

text: Present mechanical facts such as exact damage values directly when the fiction cannot convey them.
when: Mechanics have no in-fiction representation
why: Exact numbers have no equivalent in the story, so without direct delivery players would never learn them.

text: Pair each colored input area with a light and a tone, so every press gives matching audio and visual feedback.
when: when designing a set of input areas for a memory game

text: In stealth games, make the player feel their actions can be heard, so they adopt sound-aware strategies.
when: When enemy AI shows awareness of sound.
why: Players only plan around noise if they believe enemies can hear it.

text: When a player delays a needed action, have the guiding voice nudge them with a timed prompt.
when: a required action is delayed

text: Introduce sound-linked enemies first in isolated or easy encounters, so players can see the effect and hear the warning before facing harder threats.
when: When a sound-linked enemy type is met for the first time.
why: players learn the link safely

text: Perceptual-shift puzzles offer either a large reward or nothing, since players either have the insight or get no partial progress.
when: Use sparingly in videogames, where players expect steady progress
why: Such puzzles give no gradual difficulty ramp and leave non-insight solvers stuck

text: Digital play limits perception with fog-of-war or view-distance features, while a physical design can block the view directly.
why: Virtual space has no inherent edges, whereas physical reality imposes hard barriers that can simply obstruct sight.

text: Orientation is the direction a character faces; rotation is the active process of changing orientation.
A physics game is one where the player mainly engages with the rules of a sophisticated simulation, built on a full model rather than only the parameters a mechanic needs.
Boards, dice, chips, and health meters are physical or visual ways of tracking foundational game state.
Physical skills include strength, dexterity, coordination, and endurance; their demands vary with the input method, from a controller to full-body motion tracking.
A new physical board feature can enable previously impossible mechanics, such as taking an opposing counter by pushing it over the rim.
Every game world needs a believable physical reality, where events feel credible, feedback reflects player actions, and objects and AI react to the world, each other, and the player.
Board and card games can gain similar expressive depth from physical components such as cards, dice, and tokens.
Decide whether players want mindless action or intellectual challenge, and check whether success can come from dexterity or from clever strategy needing little physical skill.
when: Positioning a game on the physical-to-mental spectrum
why: Matching the mix of dexterity and thinking to the audience keeps the challenge suited to them

text: A physics-driven character's response to player input can become the core of puzzle design rather than only a visual effect.
when: a companion character responds to every player movement

text: Physical constraints shape procedures, so seek creative, elegant solutions that are intuitive and easy to remember.
when: When designing procedures for a game played in a nondigital setting or on fixed devices.
why: Environmental limits such as input devices and viewing distance directly affect how procedures can be accessed and remembered.

text: Give players a physical artifact, such as a printed score with initials, to take home from the experience.
why: Gives a tangible takeaway and a structured way to end the experience after play is finished.

text: Physical laws built into a game can implicitly limit actions, so the rules need not state every restriction, as gravity limits where pieces can be placed in Connect Four.
when: In nondigital games where the physical world already enforces a constraint.
why: Built-in constraints compress the amount of explicit rule text needed.

text: Making every physical interaction perfect can remove the skill players are meant to learn and master.
when: Tuning physics-driven movement systems
why: When technology handles the difficulty, the physics no longer offers a skill to master.

text: 1) Build a general, robust physics simulation. 2) Play within it to find interactions that are enjoyable. 3) Emphasise those interactions as the core gameplay.
why: Starting with a broad simulation shapes the feel and gameplay that emerge, unlike simulating only what is needed.

text: Minimise physical load, meaning the gestures and button presses required, unless physical effort is the core challenge.
when: Designing input for games that are not built around physical activity.
why: Excess physical demand causes discomfort and reduces accessibility.

text: The arena is a specialized, usually large, outdoor and public field for competitive play, where winners and losers are a matter of public record.
Play space design is the practice of shaping the space where play happens, and it falls under the broader umbrella of experience design.
A platform experience hosts many different stories, so the designer cannot know in advance which content will be played.
Arenas, card tables, stages, and courts of justice are examples of playgrounds set apart from ordinary space by special rules.
Anywhere venue games, such as paper puzzles and smartphone games, fit into spare moments, are interruptible, have simple interfaces and stories, and are played in short bites.
when: Designing for spare-minute play.
why: Players use these games in brief, interruptible sessions.

text: The playground is any open space for children's improvised outdoor play, such as backyards, streets, vacant lots, or caves, and this venue has been largely ignored by the games industry.
why: Building games for it has not been feasible with past technology.

text: Some activities, such as pinball in a restaurant, bowling, or casino play, fit several venues at once and are hard to place.
A portable collectible card game built on a video game's core rules, sold cheaply, appeals especially to children and suits trading with peers.
A platform that was mainstream can become fringe within a year after a rival platform becomes good enough.
Pocket-carried devices, such as smartphones, tend to converge many technologies into one for convenience.
why: Carrying one device is more convenient than carrying several.

text: A platformer can work without jumping, with a grappling arm as its main way of moving through the level.
In 2021 a major PC game storefront banned games that allowed exchanging cryptocurrencies or NFTs.
Platform levels share free space, walls, collectibles, enemies and traps with dungeons, but gravity limits movement, so platforms and gaps become the core vocabulary.
Building a game's core design around a platform's distinctive hardware strength, such as very fast scrolling, can make the game feel new.
when: the platform has a distinctive hardware capability
why: Fast scrolling was a hardware edge over rival consoles, and players had not experienced such speed before, so the novelty made the games feel exciting.

text: A platform network can thrive by dominating a venue that rival platform owners leave unfocused.
when: rival platform owners focus on other venues

text: An arena tends to attract a surrounding theater of spectators, so one place hosts two venues at once.
when: Competitive games held in a public place where outcomes are visible to onlookers.
why: Outcomes are a public matter and watching is exciting, so onlookers gather around the field.

text: Debates about the best platform often overlook that successful technologies do not last forever.
why: Human nature leads people to assume that present success will last indefinitely.

text: An action card's power requirement may name specific types, generic power, or both. Specific types are covered first, and any other power fills the generic part.
Choose the venue by considering setting (classroom, on the go, reading nook), whether players are alone or with others, time limits, and whether a helper is present.
when: before finalizing the design
why: Context strongly affects whether transformational goals are met.

text: Players may sacrifice a winning position to help a weaker player, a nurturing style that appears in group play.
when: competitive games with uneven skill
why: Nurturing tendencies, seen in caring for younger children and pets, lead some players to help a weaker opponent over winning.

text: In a prisoner's dilemma, players facing a stranger in a single round usually defect, while expecting repeated rounds with one partner raises collaboration, especially early.
when: when players meet a partner once versus repeatedly
why: Repeated contact creates a shared future that makes trust worthwhile.

text: Players know an activity is a game yet still care about it as if it mattered greatly.
when: while playing any game
why: Motivation overrides the knowledge that the activity is trivial.

text: Once a player judges an experience too intense, awareness that it is only pretend returns and works against the presence the designer builds.
when: A player feels an experience has become excessive
why: The mind reasserts that the threat is not real

text: Play is manipulation that indulges curiosity.
Play is free movement inside a more rigid structure, like the slack a steering wheel has before the wheels turn, existing only because the system does.
Toys are manipulable like puzzles but have no fixed goal, while stories involve fantasy play but cannot be changed by the player.
A toy is any physical object meant to be played with.
A good toy is fun to play with; being played with alone does not make something a toy, since nearly anything can be played with.
Primal actions are so intuitive that animals were performing them hundreds of millions of years ago.
It is unknown whether group play tendencies are innate or learned, but understanding them helps designers include more players.
Play is the clearest intrinsically motivating activity because it is autotelic, done for its own sake.
Play lets people experiment with situations more complex than everyday life, and it contributes to building culture.
Play is especially important in childhood, when the brain is more malleable.
Frequent players spent longer on optional puzzles than infrequent players, even though they could skip them.
why: This correlational result does not show that games cause perseverance.

text: Humans also respond emotionally to music, philosophical ideas, humor, wit, and many forms of art.
Game rules create play only as players enact them, so play must be discovered through testing rather than predicted.
Tournament and league play with a fixed rule set is a traditional game, even though free-form play resembles role-playing.
Solving participatory play for large audiences would likely require very clever use of technology.
Defining play as manipulation that indulges curiosity also covers artists playing with color and scientists testing ideas, not only games.
Primal play includes gathering, fighting threats, finding one's way through unfamiliar terrain, and overcoming obstacles to reach a mate.
Persuasive games present the designer's subjective model of the world, and players compare it with their own to see where the two converge and diverge.
Video games with physical and skill demands cluster lower left; board and turn-based games cluster upper left; gambling games cluster upper right; games for very young children cluster lower right.
Play matrix placements are not absolute; differing placements are acceptable and the matrix serves as a discussion tool.
Physical play builds motor skills, pretend play builds language, and rule-based board games with numbers build math skills.
When gameplay is built on the most fun parts of a toy, the toy's fun and the game's fun support each other.
When designing a good puzzle, build a satisfying toy first, so players enjoy manipulating it before they solve it.
why: A toy offers manipulation without a fixed goal, so enjoyment does not depend on solving it.

text: Build a good toy first, with obvious manipulations that draw players to handle it, then turn it into a puzzle.
when: Physical or mechanical manipulation is the main appeal
why: Players who want to touch and play engage with the object even without intending to solve it

text: Let the player experience story through play rather than exposition: play, don't tell, the game counterpart of show, don't tell.
when: Designing how story reaches players
why: Gameplay usually takes priority in design decisions, so the story must be carried by how players act.

text: Minimal or abstract representation leaves gaps that the player's mind fills, so the more abstract the representation, the more room there is for personal interpretation.
why: the imagination builds details that explicit visuals or sound would otherwise supply

text: A survey of 1,178 U.S. youngsters, ages 8 to 18, found about 8% with pathological play patterns, and these children had poorer grades.
Caillois's four types of play are competitive (agôn), chance-based (alea), make-believe (mimicry), and vertigo (ilinx).
The play matrix plots games on two continua: skill versus chance horizontally, and mental calculation versus physical dexterity vertically.
why: These two axes capture fundamental features of any interactive experience, so every game can be placed on them.

text: Labeling passionate play as pathological fuels moral panic and encourages unnecessary, costly treatment.
why: Problematic play may be a coping response to depression or anxiety rather than a distinct addiction needing special treatment.

text: Designers often forget the toy perspective, focusing on goals before the underlying interaction is fun.
A set of small puzzles with no final goal lacks a point that holds them together.
why: Each puzzle stands alone rather than advancing a shared aim

text: 1) Build an enjoyable interactive toy first. 2) Confirm it is fun on its own. 3) Design a game on top of it, adding goals and problem solving.
why: Playing the toy can suggest unexpected game ideas.

text: 1) Ask whether the interaction is fun with no goal. 2) Ask whether people want to start interacting before they know what to do. 3) Change whatever makes the answer no.
when: when evaluating an existing game or inventing new interactions
why: Toylike qualities make a game more approachable and enjoyable to manipulate.

text: Set explicit play values before prototyping, such as broad audience appeal, low technology barriers, easy to learn but deep, intrinsically social, and fit with the platform's tone.
when: at the start of a new game's design
why: Play values give concrete targets for judging later design decisions

text: Check which forms of play your game offers, and decide whether to add play types or deepen existing ones, since players differ widely.
why: Players seek many different forms of play, since there are as many play types as players.

text: Players pick dialogue or scripted options to roleplay values, such as refusing payment for a good deed or being good or evil, or to guess designer habits for best payoff.
when: A dialogue offers choices with moral or personal weight.
why: Predefined dialogue choices are made from fictional or sentimental values rather than by reasoning through game systems.

text: A decision carries weight when it genuinely alters subsequent events and the ending, and presents multiple workable options.
when: Judging if a choice is significant
why: Options that shift results grant players a sense of control.

text: Agency is the player's ability to make decisions and meaningful actions, and their belief that these drive the story; it threatens authored stories since players can contradict or skip content.
At the challenge ramp, players choose among staying and monetizing, grinding through skill, or leaving the game.
when: challenge outpaces player resources
why: Pressure rises past the difficulty curve while resources stay fixed, leaving players no way to keep pace.

text: Players feel their actions drive the story when events would have clearly gone differently without them.
when: Story is designed around player interaction

text: Poorly managed railroading makes players feel hampered or angry, and frequent railroading can make them stop playing.
when: When forced choices or situations are frequent or poorly handled.
why: Forced outcomes override the player's abilities and decisions.

text: Players act out of character to explore simulation limits, consume content, acquire items, meet goals, impress others, or watch spectacle.
when: the fiction offers actions the character would not take
why: player goals sit outside the character's motives

text: Players may react strongly to endings that break a world's internal logic, because the illusion of reality can matter more than the story's quality.
when: An ending or event contradicts the world's established logic

text: In participatory performances, performers follow scripts while audience members choose which scenes to follow, so no single participant sees the whole story.
when: audiences move freely through a staged story
why: each participant's path is different

text: A choice is not meaningful when one option is obviously best, when options cannot be evaluated, or when options produce the same result; balance options so none is obviously best.
A player is a voluntary participant who makes decisions, is invested in the outcome, and can win.
Felt freedom is the player's sense of having freedom of action, and it can matter more than real freedom.
A hollow decision has no real consequences whichever option the player picks.
An obvious decision looks life-and-death but has one clearly best option, so it is not a real choice.
Immediate decisions have impact right away, while long-term decisions have impact felt later in play.
Decision scope measures how much deliberation a choice demands: choices with many variables are large, while those with one or two are small.
Nondecisions are answers so obvious they are done by habit; they keep the hands busy but do not sustain flow.
Impossible decisions exceed the player's understanding, so the player chooses randomly and flow does not occur.
Decisions are the basic units of interactivity and the emotional trigger unique to games.
A decision is a process of inferring the right answer from available information, so if the answer is stated outright, no thinking occurs.
Agency is the character's practical role as the player's stand-in, while empathy is the player's emotional attachment to the character and shared goals.
Railroading occurs when the game forces a narrative choice or situation that conflicts with the player's earlier choices or abilities.
A task is any goal the player must reach through gameplay; missions and quests are both kinds of task, and each may involve several tasks.
A task is what the player is asked to accomplish, while an obstacle stands in the way and must be overcome using the available actions.
A predefined decision is an authored branch whose options each lead to a scripted outcome chosen by the designer rather than resolved by systems.
Every successful videogame combines something familiar with something novel.
Meaning runs through the competence, autonomy, and relatedness needs and is a key concept to keep in mind throughout design.
Scripting lets players create their own behaviors, which extends a PC game's shelf life well beyond typical titles, and most triple-A titles include scripting.
Communication originally meant an exchange of ideas, which depends on listening, but now often means only talking.
Some designers aspire to let players attempt any verb they can imagine within a game.
Making interesting decisions is itself a mental skill, so nearly every game involves some mental skill.
A designer who could make a game do good but chooses not to may be as at fault as one who makes a harmful game.
The number and type of participants determine what must be directed and drive decisions about timing, pacing and volume.
Open-ended games still provide moments of resolution and measurable achievement.
Decisions can be classified into eight types: hollow, obvious, uninformed, informed, dramatic, weighted, immediate, and long-term.
Twitch shooting, tactical movement and team strategy are different flavors of decision, and each contributes to the pacing of play.
Decisions are clearly separated in some games, such as fold-or-call choices, but overlap heavily in fast real-time games, where they still exist.
Collusion-style simulation of goal-driven characters may become central to the future of interactive storytelling.
Narrative agency problems fall into two categories: player-character motivation alignment and the human interaction problem.
Games differ from other media because players have agency over a story instead of passively absorbing it.
Aim for a decisive advantage to form near the actual end, so the final stretch does not drag while the result can no longer change.
when: when tuning the ending of a game
why: a dragging finish with no way to change the outcome frustrates players

text: Letting players influence when phase transitions happen adds interest to the game.
Players decide from the information they have, so the attributes that change during play and what changes them form the core of a game's mechanics.
why: Players make decisions from the information available, so the attributes that change during play and their triggers are central to mechanics.

text: Few choices can be best when each option is interesting, while some players want many choices, such as a detailed item-shopping interface.
when: Deciding how many options to offer
why: The right count depends on whether players want variety or simplicity in that context.

text: For each choice offered, ask whether it is meaningful, how many options exist, and whether more options would empower the player or fewer would clarify the game.
when: Auditing a game's decision points
why: Choice count and meaning shape whether players feel their actions matter

text: Offer repeated pairs of safe and risky options within a game, such as a low-risk path versus a high-risk path with more rewards.
when: Building the decision structure of a racing or action game.
why: Repeated risk choices keep players making meaningful decisions throughout play.

text: Balance decisions across types rather than relying on a single type.
Give players a goal and freedom to choose how to reach it, since meaningful choice and self-expression are more motivating.
why: Self-determination theory holds that activities satisfying needs for skill, self-direction, and social connection feel intrinsically motivating.

text: Favor emergent systems when breadth matters more than input count, since players learn fewer controls to master.
when: aiming for variety with minimal input learning
why: Combining simple mechanics multiplies their experiences into many new emergent possibilities rather than merely adding them.

text: Keep rules few and stable so players can practice them and plan routes through challenges.
why: A consistent, comprehensible system lets a player, with practice, foresee which moves succeed and which dangers await.

text: Let players choose their starting point along a moving path, which gives them control over how they begin.
why: Spawn spots close to the action let a respawning player rejoin quickly, while sheltered areas let players recharge and plan.

text: When an experience lacks a coherent story, the player's own imagination can supply the story if the other elements support the theme.

Start worldbuilding at the macro level, deciding world size and locations, for open worlds that encourage exploration; start at a fixed protagonist's origin when the protagonist has a defined backstory.
when: choosing where worldbuilding begins
why: The genre and character type determine which scope the world needs first.

text: Personal experience input is most useful when research alone feels abstract.
when: the world needs emotional texture

text: Check agency at every planning stage and ask whether a small change could increase it.
when: During story planning.
why: The more complex the narrative, the more past player choices must be honored to make agency feel convincing.

text: The strongest fix for players acting against the story is making them want what their character wants, so the urge to deviate never arises.
when: players are likely to take actions the story cannot absorb
why: a shared goal removes the motive for deviation instead of forbidding it

text: Incorporate an unwanted player action as narrative content when it honestly expresses a motivation the designer is willing to support.
when: When the player's motivations point in a different direction from the character's.
why: When player and character motivations diverge, players take actions the character would never take, breaking the narrative.

text: When player choices become permanent, each change makes the idea that actions alter the world visible across sessions.
when: Campaign games where results carry from one session to the next
why: Persistent consequences reinforce the theme through play

text: Special jumps with fixed upward trajectories regardless of button hold time let players judge only whether a platform is reachable.
when: Designing jump types for precise platforming
why: Predictable arcs reduce the judgement players must make

text: A meaningful reason often leads to another feature; needing a weapon implies finding ingredients, which makes scavenging meaningful.
why: Each feature needed to reach a goal creates requirements for the next, so the chain of needs makes new features meaningful.

text: Fixed relationships, such as ranked hierarchies or a linear sequence of spaces, constrain play by keeping the order of objects unchanged throughout.
As a player learns, the same decision can move from impossible to profound, then tactical, then twitch, and finally to a nondecision.
why: A choice a novice must deliberate over may need no thought from an expert, so skill reshapes each decision's weight.

text: Because the player is the protagonist, a supporting character's win or loss feels personal, so players can feel beaten when a villain succeeds.
why: Game characters can stir players emotionally in ways other media cannot, and the protagonist's ego is at stake, unlike a movie viewer.

text: Skill gating keeps content technically available from the start but requires skill, upgrades, or allies first, so players experience content in rough order along a progression.
why: Players lack the skill, upgrades, or allies to survive far from their start, so they naturally follow a sequence.

text: Adding a fourth option to each of the four original properties gives 256 cards, about three times the base complexity, which is already difficult for players.
A two-minute round in a fast competitive shooter can contain about 100 decisions.
Decision scope falls into five groups: non-decisions, reflex-level choices, tactical choices, deep strategic choices, and impossible choices.
Decisions vary in importance, difficulty, amount of information, certainty, speed and spacing, and each combination creates a different emotional flavor.
If a game rewards not interacting, players turtle, which removes the interaction that is usually the fun part of the game.
when: When attacking leaves an attacker weaker than players who avoid fights

text: Novelty that appears only at the start will not sustain long-term play.
Autonomy that has no effect on gameplay adds personality but not challenge.
why: The character's own actions, separate from player control, establish a distinct identity for it.

text: A long run of same-scoped decisions at the same rate creates plodding flow that quickly becomes monotonous.
when: When a long sequence of same-scoped decisions arrives at an unchanging rate

text: Designing decisions as fixed, individually authored items tends to destroy them.
Adding choices is easy to create and measure but is not inherently valuable and often adds complexity without benefit.
when: When at least two viable strategies already exist for the player
why: Beyond two viable strategies, added options don't improve the experience unless they make decisions more nuanced.

text: If a VR scene never establishes the player's identity, the player keeps being reminded they are not really there.
Interactions whose emotional effect depends on built-up attachment and specific context are hard to translate into interactive form.
when: Adapting a non-interactive scene into a game.
why: The scene relies on context the game may not supply.

text: Weak agency is a frequent reason individual scenes or entire games feel flat.
when: When a later mission ignores what the player's earlier actions achieved

text: A single player action that falls out of step with the story can topple the whole structure the author built, since authored stories depend on each part supporting later events.
when: When players can make choices that contradict or skip story pieces
why: Each story part is built to support later events, so one break cascades through the chain.

text: 1) Watch playtests for overflow. 2) Reduce decision pressure where overflow appears. 3) Choose a minimum skill level deliberately and design around it.
when: When playtests show overwhelmed players with lesser skill
why: Designing for everyone can leave the core experience unclear.

text: 1) What actions exist? 2) How do actions group into goals and states? 3) What triggers a behavior change and what information does it need? 4) Is look-ahead planning needed? 5) Should responses depend on memory or on learning from the player?

1) Mark moments of freedom and check whether players feel free there. 2) Mark constrained moments and check whether they feel constrained. 3) Find where freedom can expand or is overwhelming. 4) Pick indirect control methods that create felt freedom where real freedom is limited.
when: Auditing a level or sequence for pacing and freedom
why: Players respond to the feeling of freedom, so perceived freedom can stand in for real choice.

text: 1) List the decisions in your gameplay diagram. 2) Place each on a consequence scale. 3) Rework low-consequence decisions to carry more weight.
when: after the core loop exists
why: Shows which decisions players actually make

text: 1) List the decisions players make. 2) Classify each by decision type. 3) Flag hollow, obvious, and uninformed decisions. 4) Redesign flagged decisions so they carry consequences and information.
when: When auditing a game you have already designed
why: Nondecisions and hollow choices waste player time without engaging the mind.

text: 1) Look for spots where the player-character feels passive or is upstaged by NPCs, in dialogue or gameplay. 2) Restructure the scene so the player is in command.
when: When the player-character feels passive or upstaged by NPCs in dialogue or gameplay

text: 1) Anticipate which choices a participant is likely to make. 2) Subtly limit those choices through the environment or framing, not by overt restriction.
when: when designing interactive stories with some control over player choice
why: preserves the feeling of freedom while keeping the story coherent

text: Put the player on the defensive with reactive moments in which events happen to the character that the player did not start.
when: Keeping agency in a linear story
why: Players need to feel they are in the driver's seat even when outcomes are fixed.

text: 1) Recall memorable scenes you loved or hated. 2) Note how strongly each made you feel. 3) Compare: favorite scenes keep the character central and make the player feel important, while disliked ones upstage or invalidate the character. 4) Redesign a disliked scene to give the player more agency.
when: Warm-up before designing a linear sequence
why: Scenes that keep the character central make players feel important, while upstaging ones invalidate them.

text: If players do not feel they strongly influence outcomes, change the design so their actions matter more.
why: Meaningful control is essential for immersive interactivity.

text: Build features such as guilds and easy, meaningful ways to friend strangers to favor cooperation.
why: People favor in-group members, and trust and help come more easily to those they know.

text: Do not force play by threatening loss of progress or loot.
when: when designing retention mechanics
why: Threatening loss exploits loss aversion and fear of missing out, pressuring players who cannot play every day; children and teens are most exposed.

text: Define what happens when a player has no legal option, such as losing the turn, so play never stalls.
Withhold a special option when it has no meaningful target, such as when a player has only one piece or all pieces share one space.
when: When a player's only movable unit is alone or every unit sits on one shared tile.

text: Support different play styles so each has a role, such as close-range and cover-based approaches.
why: Players with different styles stay engaged when their approach is viable.

text: Leave success open-ended when players should define what winning means, as construction games often do.
when: players should define their own success conditions
why: Player-interpreted success suits construction play.

text: Use non-zero-sum outcomes when graded rewards, statistics, or several objectives are wanted rather than one winner.
when: graded rewards or multiple objectives are wanted
why: Non-zero-sum outcomes allow finer gradations and measurable results without forcing a single final winner.

text: Choose a range or variable player count when group size should flex with the social situation.
when: group size should adapt to the social setting

text: Rework decisions that carry little consequence so they matter, and remove those that cannot be made to matter.
when: When many of a game's decisions seem minor or tangential to the main objective.
why: Inconsequential choices hurt the experience

text: Simple decisions are acceptable if they are not hollow, obvious, or uninformed; purely creative or exploratory choices also have value.
when: When a choice is meant to be creative, expressive, or exploratory rather than strategic.

text: Support autonomy by letting players express themselves and choose how to overcome obstacles, such as through appearance or movement options.
when: When a game offers cosmetic or movement options that players find meaningful.
why: autonomy is one of three intrinsic motivation needs

text: A decision needs at least two viable strategies that could reasonably lead to a good outcome; with only one, the decision is degenerate.
why: Without a second workable path, there is no real tradeoff to weigh, so the choice empties out.

text: Aim to create a rich internal thought process in players, with epiphanies, doubts and dilemmas, even for skilled players, by making the decision process more nuanced.
when: Once a decision already has two viable strategies.
why: Depth of reasoning comes from nuance in weighing viable options, not from how many there are.

text: Narrative should not hamper gameplay or take away player control; favor narrative built into gameplay.
why: Long non-interactive sequences are costly to produce and reduce how engaging the game feels.

text: A choice only matters when its consequences are visible in the game, so consequences must be shown rather than left implicit.
when: In branching narratives where player choices drive the story.
why: Respecting a player's sense of agency means the design must honor choices, showing their effects.

text: Let the player have the great idea instead of an NPC, and use cutscenes that reward player actions rather than interrupting them.
when: When a scene or cutscene gives weak agency.
why: Complex stories demand tracking many past choices, since players need to feel their actions drive the plot.

text: Let an 'I'm not interested' option rarely end a quest outright; have the NPC plead or invite the player to return.
when: A player declines a quest.

text: Never include in a cutscene a moment that allows player agency or interactivity, because removing control turns a reward into an annoyance.
why: Stripping control from a moment that could have been interactive makes it feel like a nuisance instead of a payoff.

text: When a needed change is impossible because content is finished or locked, add an in-game artifact, such as a document or letter, to patch the gap.
when: a narrative problem cannot be fixed at its source

text: Use standard game verbs such as moving, collecting, pushing, jumping, and shooting to express social interaction and drive plot branches.
when: the game needs player interaction without a separate dialogue interface
why: the controls stay the same and the player's control rhythm is preserved

text: Use predefined choices when the player should influence narrative content that no system can simulate, such as a full human mind or an entire story world.
when: narrative content beyond what systems can simulate
why: Systems cannot simulate a full human mind or an entire narrative world.

text: Strengthening the effect of decisions widens the gap between viable and optimal builds but makes character choices matter more.
when: When every character build is viable yet they all play alike and choices seem not to matter.

text: Interactivity gives players control, but full control is expensive and can be boring. Removing freedom for a key scene can make it more exciting while players still feel free elsewhere.
when: When deciding where players should act freely and where the designer directs the experience
why: A game can be more interesting than real life, so cutting tedious or unnecessary decisions is acceptable

text: Indirection between mechanics and events is the fundamental difference of games from other media; it is both their greatest opportunity and their toughest challenge.
why: Events emerge from play with mechanics and never recur identically, so they can't be authored like scenes in other media.

text: Tragedy requires inevitability, while interactivity grants freedom; gaining one costs the other, so solutions must be carefully crafted.
when: designing tragic interactive stories
why: Freedom and destiny are opposites

text: Combining agency and empathy is hard because their sources of drama differ.
when: Designing a game where story matters
why: Empathy draws drama from watching characters struggle, while agency draws it from the player's own effort, so the two pull design in different directions.

text: Characters who run and shoot tell emergent stories more easily than characters who stand and talk, which avoids the difficulty of human interaction.
when: Designing emergent narrative in a combat-heavy game.
why: A postapocalyptic setting makes desperate people turn violent, so run-and-shoot characters fit the world and let the game avoid long conversational scenes.

text: Techniques from mind-influencing genres may spread to more games, or similar AI algorithms may be applied directly to mainstream genres.
Offer ways to show status within a group, and reward prosocial acts such as gifting and tagging items for teammates, since these can prompt others to try.
when: Designing social progression or cooperation
why: Visible status confirms competence socially and teases others into pursuing it

text: Relying exclusively on metagame correction as the only balance tool is poor design.
When players do not use a system as intended, add restrictions and affordances that steer them toward the intended play.
when: Players exploit an unintended strategy.
why: Players who exploit a system are chasing quick results rather than fun, and unremoved degenerate strategies get found and used anyway.

text: Define intended player feeling, such as compassion or moral dilemma, and what is fun; keep these as the guide and use psychology knowledge to identify variables producing the feeling.
when: Conception phase or early design
why: Stakeholders without design expertise need a clear statement of the core pillars, and a shared target feeling helps explain the plan.

text: Adding a visible change to a familiar enemy signals a threat that is both known and unknown, prompting players to investigate.
when: enemy variants
why: Familiar forms lower the cost of learning while the change keeps interest.

text: An experience-based theme aims to deliver a specific essential experience matching players' fantasies and desires; most game themes are experience based.
Satisfaction is how pleasant players find the product to use.
Experience points are awarded for completing game tasks, with the amount set in game data by designers, and experience levels are gained when a set total is accumulated.
Deep seeing covers an object's shape, color, proportion, shadow, reflection, texture, relation to its environment and users, function and meaning, not just its name.
Experience pillars are the core activities a game is built around, each challenging particular player skills such as attention, reflexes, coordination, or planning.

A UX mindset means thinking about humans first throughout development, aiming for games that are usable, accessible, safe, inclusive, and fun, using human factors psychology and the scientific method.
Depth means providing meaningful play at high skill levels, where players can keep making consequential choices.
Design thinking, UX research and analytics are tools for refining the UX approach to a specific game.
At the Self-referential stage, barriers are time, budget, and resources; user research on small projects or subtasks is the main tool, because it can show quick wins.
Games rely on a fixed menu of animations, such as walk, run, fight and open door; animations outside that menu, such as a kiss, are very expensive to create.
The reading nook is a quiet, comfortable, lean-back spot away from the TV, where calm, simple tablet games fit well.
why: Reading and similar relaxed activities suit this lean-back posture.

text: UX designers often use Plutchik's model to explore the range of human emotions.
The usability pillars are a practical framework rather than an exhaustive list, and emotions elicited by interaction are handled separately under engageability.
Presentation quality raises the perceived value of an identical item.
Player experience is shaped by marketing, onboarding, matchmaking, sound design, level design, music and community management.
Board and card games extend invitations socially, while digital games usually use a start button or entry screen.
A real experience cannot be copied perfectly in a game, and a good game does not need to copy it; the essence can take a very different form.
Games are autotelic, so engagement is their purpose, and the real design question is when engagement becomes excessive.
Alternating repetition, such as a level-then-boss cycle or a tense-then-release pattern, gives play a rhythm.
Classic arcade games were designer-led and were designed to last about three minutes per play session.
UX pillars overlap heavily, so strict categorization of a design issue into one pillar is difficult.
when: Classifying UX problems
why: Many elements affect several pillars at once

text: Borderline play forms include solitaire, trivia, dexterity challenges, chance-based puzzles, and poll-based questions, which blur the lines between puzzles, games, and toys.
Curiosity alone does not make play; play also requires willful action that touches or changes something, and curiosity means seeking answers freely rather than from obligation.
In a game world, player intent comes from the designer, who creates goals that motivate action, rather than being fully innate.
why: Real-world motivation is hard to explain, so game intent must be built.

text: Perceptual illusions in art are acceptable when the illusion itself is the specific intent of the design.
Successful games can deliver very different numbers of core pleasures; one with few pleasures can still be highly addictive, so element count does not predict fun.
when: auditing a prototype's pleasures
why: Fun depends on the right combination of pleasures, not their quantity.

text: Game experiences vary widely in length, from about a minute in a fighting game to a hundred hours in an open-world role-playing game.
Games with layered, interacting lessons support lifelong learning, while games with few lessons are shallow.
Start with a grid for ease of implementation and debugging, and experiment with other representations once the core code is robust.
Keep UX feedback brief and direct, since busy developers need straight-to-the-point findings to make quick decisions.
when: Production deadlines
why: Developers are swamped while trying to ship on time, so they cannot spend hours reading long reports and need brief, actionable findings.

text: Auto-save writes backups in the background, and its frequency balances losing work against wearing out storage with constant saves.
when: Designing periodic saving for user-created data
why: Frequent saves reduce loss but add write load, and infrequent saves risk losing work

text: Readability matters most when players choose between classes, abilities, skills or gear, especially when the choices are strategic rather than cosmetic.
when: Presenting options that affect strategy.
why: Players choosing among strategic options need the key advantages readable at a glance, which matters more than narrative flavor for their decisions.

text: Deliver an intended feeling through artwork, sound, or game rules, choosing the mechanism that conveys it best.
when: designing for a specific emotional quality
why: A feeling does not have to be reproduced literally; its essential elements can be carried by stand-in artwork, sound, or rules.

text: When a mapping feels good but play is aimless, add goals and constraints to focus the player's movement.
when: the mapping feels good but play is unfocused
why: A goal gives control meaning by letting players compare intent with outcome, turning the pleasure of movement into a skill that can succeed or fail.

text: Making the link between each player action and the turn outcome clear is often the hardest design problem, needing many revisions guided by tester feedback.
when: designing turn-based feedback
why: Every turn's result depends on all players' choices, so early versions felt arbitrary until the outcome was clearly tied to what happened.

text: Give players details that their imagination can use and that spark fantasy; a single evocative detail can lead players to build much more themselves.
when: When adding flavor or identity to game elements
why: Concrete role-suggesting details help players grasp how elements work and invite imaginative play

text: Deep, well-balanced interaction can carry a game's success even when its presentation is primitive.
when: Deciding how much effort to put into visuals versus game systems
why: Years of balancing made the interactions rich and engaging, which carried the game even though its graphics were very limited.

text: Mastering a graded technique, such as consecutive hits without taking damage, gives players lasting feelings of power and control that carry into the rest of the game.
when: when designing skill training within a game
why: Practiced skills carry forward into later challenges, preparing the player for success and sustaining a feeling of control.

text: In a crowded market, a small usability problem in the purchase flow can meaningfully reduce revenue.
when: When players can easily choose among many competing games on the market.
why: Buyers can spend their time and money on other titles, so a friction point in the store can cost a sale.

text: Products designed with UX in mind tend to be more satisfying, which can make them more popular and raise revenue.
Absolute clocks cap play by measured time, such as a sand timer, a game clock, or the fixed duration of an in-game action.
Six mappings connect player, interface, and world: input to world, world to output, input to virtual interface, virtual interface to world, world to virtual interface, virtual interface to output.
One playability model lists four components: gameplay, story, mechanics and usability.
In an adjacent-challenge ladder, each player challenges only the player just above or below; a lower-ranked winner swaps places, and otherwise standings stay the same.
Assuming an interface element is obvious because developers understand it leads to missed usability problems.
when: When developers watch newcomers to the game do something the developers find odd during testing.
why: Knowledge developers have is invisible to newcomers.

text: Overconfidence and cognitive dissonance lead developers to avoid uncomfortable user experience problems.
when: When past shipped success makes developers confident they already know what players will enjoy.
why: Knowing the game intimately makes it hard to foresee how a new player will perceive it.

text: Small glitches such as a character's foot clipping through a stair break immersion, because real-world perception never shows such errors.
why: Everyday perceptual skill, built up since birth, makes any small inconsistency stand out to players.

text: Defining play by pleasure, exhilaration, power and self-initiative is too broad, since an executive closing a contract can feel the same without playing.
why: The listed feelings also occur in non-play work, such as an executive chasing a deal, so they do not isolate play.

text: Adding stimulation to a flat section can reduce the impact of the moments that follow it.
when: When the stimulation added to a flat section is set too high
why: Overly intense filler raises the baseline, so the moments that follow feel less interesting by comparison.

text: A loop that blocks while waiting for input cannot advance the game on its own, so the world freezes between player actions.
when: Game loop waits for player commands
why: Nothing updates while the loop is blocked on input.

text: A mechanic with utility is not necessarily good design, since one that teleports the player to the exit could trivialise the game.
when: when accepting generated mechanics based on solvability alone
why: Solvability measures function but not quality or player experience.

text: When flow breaks, the rest of the experience falls apart, so many problems with bad games trace back to broken flow.
why: Flow underpins most good games, so when it collapses, every other part of the experience collapses with it.

text: Time spent eliminated between rounds can exceed the time the strategy decision needs, creating a long dull flow gap.
when: When a player is eliminated and waiting for the next round

text: Menu transitions, movement animations and dialogue that block action create flow gaps, and attractive presentation weakens the decisions around them.
why: Presentation elements that block action serve the fiction and look good, but they weaken the mechanical decision stream.

text: Very large decisions make players sit and deliberate for long periods, stalling the game.
when: In turn-based games where a single decision has a very large scope
why: Turn-based play lets players set their own pace, so a big decision simply takes a longer turn.

text: Assuming the experience starts exactly where the designer defines it causes problems, because audiences arrive with context that spills in.
why: Experiences have no hard cutoff in practice.

text: 1) Search for the layout that makes your AI take the most turns. 2) Use that layout to test other AIs.
when: stress testing a guessing AI
why: worst-case layouts can reveal weaknesses that average-case tests miss

text: 1) Split the game into its parts: controls, reaction, situational framing, finishing touches, symbolic imagery, and mechanics. 2) Notice what feels wrong and try implementations until the feel improves. 3) Record the small decisions and the principles behind them.
when: when studying a game's feel in order to understand or recreate it
why: Feel emerges from numerous minor implementation choices, not one single technique.

text: 1) Form hypotheses about possible solutions. 2) Verify them through UX research. 3) Repeat the cycle iteratively.

1) Pick questions from the four affordance types: clickability, perceived feedback, item function from shape, enemy behavior from design, and next goal from environment. 2) Ask testers targeted questions, such as naming each HUD element from a screenshot. 3) Repeat during each testing phase.
when: during the iterative testing phase, before engine implementation when possible
why: Targeted questions find critical problems faster than open-ended testing, and early changes are cheaper.

text: Designing for personality types: 1) Map your own personality type first. 2) Map three theoretical personality types. 3) For each, describe a game you would design for it, covering mechanics, theme, depth, and other design elements.
when: designing games for different player types
why: self-mapping and varied types expose design assumptions

text: 1) Identify what makes a game challenging for you. 2) State the game's premise. 3) Identify a story that moved you and why, or explain why no game story affected you.
when: studying what makes a game engaging
why: Links challenge, premise, and story to emotional response

text: 1) Describe how players start or join the game. 2) List the social, procedural, and technical steps involved. 3) Compare entry steps across games to find similarities.
1) Decide what players should feel, see, and hear. 2) Choose the means that produce that drama. 3) Direct the drama with numbers.
when: Designing combat encounters
why: Players come for this drama, so it should be deliberately crafted rather than left to emerge by chance.

text: 1) Consider extrinsic rewards first. 2) Then add intrinsic motivation through competence, autonomy, and relatedness. 3) Then examine how the two interact.
when: making a game more engaging
why: the layers build on each other in order

text: 1) List the challenges players face in the prototype. 2) List the ways players express themselves through fantasy or play. 3) Describe how these elements interact to make the game fun. 4) Identify weak links to improve.
when: auditing a prototype before adding more content
why: Seeing which pleasures are supported exposes gaps and overlaps.

text: 1) List the established rules. 2) Ask what would happen if players broke a rule to gain an advantage. 3) Note the dynamics that emerge.
when: Designing mechanics before playtesting
why: Players invent dynamics designers did not plan

text: Design rules and pieces that produce emotional responses and a potential experience rather than controlling every outcome, since designers cannot create the experience directly.
why: Players' actions determine the actual experience.

text: Use UX practice to realize designers' intended vision, including hardcore difficulty goals and other deliberate intents, rather than diluting it into something easier or more standard.
when: When the target audience is hardcore gamers and the designer wants them to struggle
why: UX work exists to help the designer realize their goals, not to flatten the intended challenge.

text: Separate the sensory feel of a digital game from its core system and leave its refinement for later development.
when: In the early stages of developing a digital game
why: Sensory feel is only one part of engagement, so the core system can be assessed separately from it.

text: Prioritize feedback that can be applied now over comments on features that will be redone soon.
when: When a feature will be redone soon and the team is short on time
why: Overloaded developers can only act on brief, usable points, not on long reports.

text: When a feature returns for rework, retrieve earlier UX findings so the same mistakes are not repeated.
when: Feature reworked
why: Earlier findings record problems already found, so the next iteration can avoid repeating them.

text: Avoid the usability police role; keep UX concepts fun and do not report to management as an enforcer.
why: Developers resist UX when it feels like policing, so it must be offered as a service to their goals.

text: Refine audience-focused or technology-driven challenges into player experience goals before brainstorming on them.
why: Only a player experience goal specifies the gameplay potential to create, while audience or technology challenges do not address it.

text: Show the effect of a choice on secondary attributes and affected skills before the player locks it in, such as when a level-up adds to an attribute.
when: Players make irreversible or hard-to-undo character choices
why: Players who see effects only after committing may choose differently with full information.

text: Use and polish affordances to make the game more intuitive; the form-follows-function usability pillar relates to cognitive affordances.
Define clear player experience goals and test against the intended audience.
when: When testing a game for fun and challenge
why: Fun and challenge mean different things to each player, so only the intended audience reveals them.

text: Build around the style of play your audience will enjoy.
Before choosing technology, test each part of the AI model against a set of questions about how characters should move, decide and coordinate.
why: Late AI requests force rework, and tangled code is harder to fix than slow code is to speed up.

text: Stay vigilant about violent content as technology enables more extreme play, since psychology cannot yet give a definitive answer.
when: When technology makes more extreme violent play possible
why: Research on the effects of violent games is inconclusive, especially for newly emerging forms.

text: Design around specific player types and skill bands rather than one average player, since a large player base contains many kinds of players.
when: Designing or tuning for a large, varied audience.
why: An average player does not exist in a diverse population.

text: Let the intended player experience drive the formal structure, so the result may include familiar elements but still feels new.
when: When defining a new game's formal structure
why: Established genres have already resolved many gameplay problems, so fresh experiences need new questions.

text: Use player knowledge to entertain, never to exploit human limits for profit; keep player interest and well-being at the center even when profitability matters.
when: When business goals pull against player interest and well-being
why: Using knowledge of human attention to exploit people is the opposite of a UX mindset, and studios still need profit.

text: Give goal-free systems learnable, nonobvious properties, because players will build their own goals from them.
when: designing sandbox or toy-like systems
why: self-made goals only sustain interest if the underlying system has depth

text: Consider what players will consider doing and what they expect the game to do in response, not only what actually happens on screen.
why: Imagined outcomes that never happen still shape a player's emotions and decisions.

text: Designing the user experience of a scripting tool is real work, and the resulting behavior must still be translated into lower-level bytecode for efficient execution.
when: Building a visual scripting tool on top of a VM
why: The friendly front end and the efficient runtime form are separate representations.

text: Designed frustration from a deliberate challenge can support flow, while frustration from usability problems prevents it; removing the first or keeping the second both damage play.
when: Evaluating player frustration in playtests
why: Only deliberate challenge is part of the experience; usability friction blocks it

text: Focusing only on experience shows how something feels but not why or how to improve it. Focusing only on structure can yield designs that look sound but play poorly.
why: Feel alone cannot reveal its causes, and structure alone can look right on paper yet fail in play.

text: Expression is the pleasure of creating and self-expression, such as custom characters or shared levels, and it was long neglected in design.
Expressive design means that architecture, products, and games express stories, emotions, and cultural ideas through their form and mechanics, not only their function.
Expression features may not advance a game's core goals, so justify them against the game's aims before adding them.
why: Many expression features don't help players reach goals, though some players play for them.

text: Review expression together with beauty and status, since these overlap with it.
why: Expression overlaps with beauty and status, so reviewing them together gives fuller coverage.

text: Expressive behavior emerges from recombining simple rules rather than being explicitly defined, so global rules should leave room for player improvisation.
when: When a game has global rules about object interaction
why: Simple rules interacting create unscripted options that the designer never specified.

text: 1) List the channels, such as avatars, chat styling, items and creative play, that let players express themselves. 2) Look for overlooked outlets, including those in offline games. 3) Check whether players display their identity with pride; if not, ask why.
when: reviewing a multiplayer design
why: Self-expression boosts players' sense of vitality, pride, importance and belonging.

text: 1) List the explicit problems the game asks players to solve. 2) Identify hidden problems that arise during play. 3) Check how new problems appear over time to draw players back.
when: when reviewing a game's problem structure
why: New problems appearing over time give players reasons to return.

text: 1) State the problem and a clear goal. 2) Set boundaries, problem space and allowed methods as rules. 3) Build a simplified internal model with only needed relationships, which can be manipulated. 4) Pursue the goal through conflict. 5) Absorb attention so the outside world fades. 6) Give objects importance when they advance the goal. 7) Win by defeating the problem or lose to it.
why: Problem solving proceeds through a simplified internal version of reality that holds only the needed relationships.

text: 1) State the problem the game must solve. 2) List assumptions about the game that are unrelated to that purpose. 3) Check whether a game is truly the best solution, and why. 4) Define how you will know the problem is solved.
why: Stating constraints and goals as a problem gives a quicker route to a clear design.

text: State a design problem as a goal plus constraints, and check whether each constraint is truly needed.
when: when framing a design problem
why: unneeded constraints can rule out good solutions; a clear problem statement lets design proceed much faster

text: Craft a satisfying resolution, usually measurable and unequal, since players invest emotion in the outcome.
why: Players stop when outcomes are predictable, and tension depends on uncertainty they emotionally invest in.

text: If the real problem becomes clear only after exploring ideas, go back and restate the problem clearly.
when: after exploring ideas reveals the true issue
why: A clear statement lets ideas be measured and keeps collaborators on the same problem.
