text: A design X must work as a feature filter (razor) and as a memorable slogan; a slogan that cannot guide feature decisions is weak.
when: When writing the core statement of a game.
why: A vague slogan like a generic achievement phrase cannot decide which features belong.

text: A problem stated too narrowly rules out clever solutions, while one stated too broadly yields designs that miss the real goal.
when: when wording a design problem
why: scope determines which solutions remain possible

text: Use existing or new games as tools for specific lessons or learning and health goals, not as complete replacements for a course.
when: planning educational use of games
why: Games work best as tools within education rather than as full systems

text: Any game with a goal presents a problem for players to solve, such as beating opponents or completing a level.
Games offer concrete situations and problems to solve, which makes them useful for creating teachable moments.
The claim that complex games improve players' problem-solving ability remains unproven.
Games can teach players patience, perseverance and resilience.
when: After a player fails at a challenge

text: Games can let players manipulate things impossible in real life, such as time or space, to teach concepts.
why: Immediate feedback lets players adjust at their own pace while handling elements unavailable in reality.

text: Game engineering faces four recurring challenges that make patterns especially useful: time and sequencing, compressed iteration with many programmers, tangled behavior from many interacting parts, and critical performance.
when: designing game architecture
why: These pressures recur in game code more intensely than in typical business software.

text: Playing games with simpler models lets players practice digesting and experimenting, preparing them for more complex models later.
when: when a game is used to build skills for complex situations
why: Practice on simple systems transfers to harder ones.

text: Games are predigested models with simple rules that are easy to absorb and manipulate, which is why they feel relaxing compared with reality.
why: Simple rules lower the effort needed to understand the system.

text: Use games for practice where learners must combine several skills and techniques in an integrated way.
when: training skills that must work together
why: Games demand integrated application of skills

text: Procedural rhetoric: a game's rules form a communication system that persuades through how it works, especially when a claim depends on system behavior under varied conditions.
Procedures are the actions and methods of play rules allow players to pursue objectives, such as dealing cards or walking and shooting, guiding behavior into interactions unlikely outside the game.
Procedurality is a computer's ability to execute rule-based behavior, and video games are a form of procedural representation.
A video game models the behavior of a source system, such as traffic or football, by writing code that simulates the behavior the designer wants to focus on.
why: Code models a range of possible outcomes, unlike prose, photos, or video.

text: Most games share four procedure types: starting actions that put play into motion, progression actions that are ongoing, special actions available only under certain conditions, and resolving actions that close play.
Players who reason directly toward the goal will find some required procedures inefficient, and that friction is intended by the rules.

1) Identify the starting action that puts the game into play. 2) Identify the progression of ongoing actions. 3) Identify special actions available only under certain conditions. 4) Identify the resolving action that brings play to a close.
when: Analyzing how a game's procedures are structured, board or digital
why: Comparing procedure lists across games reveals differences in special actions and in whether the system or players resolve the game.

text: 1) Ask who can use the procedure: one, some, or all players. 2) Ask what exactly the player does. 3) Ask where it occurs and whether location limits it. 4) Ask when it occurs and whether turns, time, or game state limit it. 5) Ask how players access it: physical, indirect controller, or verbal command.
when: Describing or designing a game's procedures
why: Answering these five questions makes each procedure's scope and access explicit.

text: Layer short-, medium- and long-term goals, each tied to a meaningful reward, so players always have a nearby objective and a distant one.
why: Keeps players motivated across stages of play.

text: A level cap stops character growth at a set point, keeping experience needs in line with content and preventing indefinite grinding.
Inventory is a general term for collected objects that are neither power-ups nor units, such as armor and weapons.
A loadout is the specific set of equipment chosen for a build.
Item restrictions often bar trading achievement rewards, flagged untradeable items, and progression values such as experience, levels, or stats.
A hardware link between two devices can let game items or creatures travel between players' copies of a game.
Linear story-driven RPGs are the narrowest case of character progression, so designers must supply variety and challenge throughout.
Use intermittent rewards to enrich gameplay; the same scheme may not raise engagement in unrelated settings such as paid work.
when: enriching gameplay

text: Use item-based growth, such as permanent stat boosts, when a level cap or the absence of an experience system fits the design better.
when: When the game has a level cap or no experience system.
why: Unbounded experience let standing track playing time, with no catch-up for players ahead.

text: Use a level cap when the game needs a defined endpoint or when content must stay ahead of progression, and avoid an open-ended cap when standing should depend on skill.
why: Each level gain brings stronger stats and skills, which then need matching challenge content.

text: Intermediate rating tiers reward partial success, so the top tier can stay demanding without being the only reward.
when: a task has a hard perfect-performance goal
why: Without partial tiers, most players face an out-of-reach goal.

text: Repetitive actions can mask real progress, so players feel no movement.
when: When players are forced to repeat the same battle type over and over.

text: Classify items by how they behave in play, not by how they look, since a quest item can resemble a permanent item or a consumable.
Every skill or gear piece should support at least one workable or best-in-class build where it shines, linked to a playstyle.
when: For equipment loadouts and skill trees, where characters pick from a larger pool.
why: Characters pick only a subset from a larger pool, so a piece need only suit some builds.

text: Puzzles occur in every genre, such as counter-strategy choices in fighting games, turbo timing in racing and enemy ordering in shooters; many games with other objectives mix in puzzle elements.
why: Any moment that makes the player stop and think is a puzzle

text: Puzzles requiring navigation of 3D spaces intrigue males but can frustrate females, and studies suggest males generally have stronger spatial reasoning.
A puzzle is something fun with a right answer, separating it from games and toys; forms include abstract, word, action, story and simulation.
A riddle demands a single answer with right-or-wrong feedback; a puzzle demands an answer reached by manipulating something that brings the player closer step by step.
why: Incremental manipulation supplies a sense of progress that pure guessing lacks

text: A puzzle is a miniature game with a dominant strategy, whose goal is to discover that strategy.
why: Once the dominant strategy is known, the challenge disappears, explaining low replayability

text: Text adventures supported dozens to hundreds of verbs, but players could not tell which existed; frustration with unresponsive verb sets may have helped cause their decline.
Verbal puzzle audiences, such as crossword and word-game players, skew heavily female.
Puzzles span word, visual, and math types and can be graded from very easy to very hard.
Puzzles usually have little replay value because their goal is to find a single solution.
Adding a code position to a deduction puzzle multiplies the possibilities exponentially, while adding a symbol is a smaller but still significant change.
Side-scrollers offer a narrow range of outcomes: the player either completes the challenge or is stuck.
Action platform games often alternate running and jumping with short puzzles, and boss fights frequently combine puzzle-solving with quick, precise movement.
when: When structuring a game that mixes dexterity and thought
why: Alternation gives variety and pairs thinking with physical challenge

text: The move from explicit to integrated puzzles came mainly from designers maturing and developing more fluid, continuous control schemes, not from changing audience tastes.
why: Better control schemes made environmental puzzles practical.

text: A hundred-puzzle set of increasing difficulty with hidden goals admired by puzzle fans sold poorly with general audiences.
why: Little guidance and differing goals per puzzle deter non-specialists

text: Single-player design, lack of interactivity and fixed outcomes are weak grounds for excluding puzzles from the category of games.
why: Puzzles respond to the player and have conflict between player and system

text: Ten puzzle design principles are: clear goal, easy start, sense of progress, solvability, gradual difficulty, parallelism, pyramid structure, hints, giving the answer, and perceptual shifts.
why: They form a strong foundation though not an exhaustive list

text: Alignment games are often puzzle-like, requiring solutions to spatial or organizational problems.
Puzzle games come in four kinds: story-driven, action, strategy, and construction. Puzzle mechanics are common in casual design.
Mechanics such as long jump, triple jump and wall kick depend on physical interaction with environmental objects.
Integrated puzzles use natural parts of the environment, making solving them a direct goal of the avatar rather than a separate interruption.
why: Puzzles that belong to the world avoid breaking the flow of play.

text: Interactive features in intimate space sit within reach of inherent abilities, a reach that shifts as abilities expand, such as with a high jump.
Draw puzzle ideas from beyond other computer games, such as puzzle books, mysteries, physical puzzles, science and mathematics, since imitating only seen puzzles limits invention.
why: Puzzle forms can vary as widely as songs, films or tales, so the pool of possible puzzles is effectively unlimited.

text: A puzzle that starts solved and is scrambled by a short sequence the player can reverse is obviously solvable.
why: reversing the sequence restores the solved state

text: Provide an in-game way to reveal answers for players who are truly stuck, rather than making them leave the game to search online.
when: Genuinely stuck players, not as a default
why: Answers are widely posted online anyway, so an in-game option keeps players in the experience

text: Look for puzzle moments in action genres that designers do not label as puzzles, since they add mental variety to action play.
when: Auditing action-based games
why: Brief decisions that require thought function as puzzles

text: Side view suits puzzle-heavy play, because limiting control to two planes keeps the challenge cognitive rather than mechanical.
when: designing puzzle-focused games
why: Fewer movement planes free attention for solving complex puzzles rather than handling controls.

text: In multiplayer games, competition can supply conflict, so puzzles are less necessary there.
when: Designing multiplayer games
why: Competition with human or computer players can supply the conflict that puzzles otherwise provide.

text: Check that scale matches across sizes, speeds, health, distances, money, energy, resources, time, and character counts.
why: Mismatched scales force tedious conversions and rounding, which break the natural interactions between quantities.

text: Let players fully master a system's physics on a single screen before expanding the play space around it.
Keep each puzzle within one screen so the whole puzzle stays readable at a glance.
why: A one-screen scope keeps abstract visuals manageable for players and gives designers an achievable goal.

text: Tie puzzle elements such as switches, found items, and enemies to the same space so puzzles belong to the level's structure.
when: Designing dungeons or levels with puzzles.
why: Puzzles integrated into the space feel like part of the level rather than an add-on.

text: Recurring layouts such as a deep pit, a wide canyon, or tilted wall panels can signal which mechanic a room requires.
when: when designing rooms that require a specific mechanic
why: Players learn to read the shape of a space as a cue for its puzzle type.

text: Switching to another related puzzle and returning later renews energy for the stuck one.
when: a player is stuck on one puzzle
why: the change of task acts like rest

text: Changing how elements are arranged changes results, with effects ranging from barely noticeable to catastrophic.
Puzzles create tension and give meaning to surrounding choices, since searching a chest gains meaning when it hunts for a key.
when: In single-player games, where puzzles are a key source of conflict.
why: Solving a puzzle carries innate tension, and puzzles make surrounding choices meaningful by framing them as moving closer to or further from the answer.

text: When measures share a scale, resources can convert into one another in almost every direction, creating many interactions without fiddly math.
In strong puzzle games, players learn how each piece moves and relates to the others before understanding the solution, and may struggle for twenty minutes or more.
Abilities that interact with geometry, such as hiding, leaning, or upgrades, turn a space into pieces the player can use in strategy.
A pyramid puzzle is a series of small puzzles, each yielding a clue to a larger puzzle, which supplies short-term goals inside one long-term goal.
when: Building a sequence of puzzles that must cohere
why: Gradual difficulty and a single meaningful final goal hold the set together

text: Players who suspect a puzzle is unsolvable feel their time is wasted and quit, and when the outcome seems uncontrollable the playful challenge vanishes, leaving a mere activity.
when: a puzzle's solvability is in doubt
why: they perceive wasted effort; without a solvable problem, the playful challenge disappears

text: Parallel challenges that are too similar to each other give a stuck player little benefit.
Wraparound projectiles can let players hit targets from positions where they are safe, so wraparound needs exploit testing.
Scripting every encounter separately produces a predictable world that players quickly learn to anticipate.
Explicit puzzles that clash with the game world break the flow of play.
when: Designing puzzles that sit apart from the game world.
why: Players lose immersion when a puzzle feels unrelated to its surroundings.

text: 1) Offer an attractive goal. 2) Teach rules seamlessly. 3) Give feedback during play. 4) Provide appropriate rewards at the end.
why: These elements keep players in flow during puzzle play.

text: 1) List every puzzle in the game. 2) Decide whether the puzzle count should rise or fall, and why. 3) Check which puzzle principles apply to each puzzle. 4) Flag puzzles that feel incongruous and integrate them better.
when: Reviewing the overall puzzle content of a whole game, not a single puzzle
why: A full-set audit reveals count, fit and principle gaps that single-puzzle review misses

text: 1) Make the goal clear. 2) Make the first move visible and obvious. 3) Let the player start manipulating without needing the full solution.
when: Designing any puzzle that depends on manipulation
why: A clear goal alone does not help if no starting move is visible

text: 1) Generate a random sequence of inputs. 2) Replay the sequence to the player. 3) Compare the player's presses in order against it. 4) Grow the sequence as the player succeeds.
when: when building a memory-based sequence game

text: Define exactly what counts as valid, such as shape, typeface and rules, since shapes readable as several answers let players dispute the intended answer.
when: designing a puzzle with a right answer
why: Ambiguous terms let players justify other answers

text: Place readable signs at chamber entrances naming the mechanics used; players who see a sign then play the room learn which symbol matches which mechanic.
when: designing puzzle chambers
why: Players can plan before entering rather than discovering the mechanic by trial; repeated pairing of cue and outcome teaches the association.

text: Build player confidence that a puzzle is solvable by showing visible progress or by stating outright that a solution exists.
when: When players are working through a difficult puzzle
why: Players who suspect a puzzle has no answer fear their effort is wasted and quit in frustration.

text: Make each puzzle's goal obvious to players.
when: General audiences; hide the goal only when discovering it is the intended fun for puzzle-focused players
why: Players unsure of the goal quickly lose interest

text: Attach rewards for solving and punishments for failure to turn a puzzle into a dramatic element.
why: Linking actions to progress toward or away from a solution gives ordinary choices meaning and creates tension.

text: Weave puzzles into progress; if a puzzle does not enable progress, redo or remove it, though a puzzle can also reveal plot.
when: Designing puzzles inside a game
why: Puzzles that do not advance progress become distractions

text: Build puzzles from well-understood mechanics that behave in obvious, consistent ways, so the player's decision is about choosing a path rather than guessing what the system allows.
when: designing puzzles
why: Players can only reason about systems they can predict.

text: Create risk by placing communicative symbols, which offer certainty, against new ambiguous challenges such as a dark cave or a hallway with unknown enemies.
when: when designing risky encounters
why: Known symbols give players enough information to reason about an unfamiliar space.

text: A large code space makes a logic puzzle hard, while a smaller puzzle space combined with chance, movement, and story makes deduction more accessible.
why: Many possible combinations make pure deduction harder, while extra ways to gather information and added chance let players progress.

text: Hints reduce the sense of solving a puzzle unaided, but a hinted solution is still more satisfying than quitting or copying an answer.
when: Designing hint systems
why: Some autonomy is traded for keeping the player engaged

text: Because people want to control fate, chance-driven games can feel like skill, and players keep engaging with no real choices, treating influence over outcomes as a puzzle.
when: Games where results are predetermined or driven by chance
why: Players perceive a puzzle in whether they can influence fate.

text: Random group members have low tolerance for delay, since they may have joined for loot or an achievement or may have already seen the scene.
when: random matchmaking groups
why: Members have unrelated goals and little shared investment.

text: Players optimize payoff relative to risk rather than fun, seeking the best reward-to-risk option they can find.
when: Players facing a set of available actions in combat.
why: Their main goal in combat is defeating enemies, so they pick the most efficient option over the enjoyable one.

text: Players may experience an outcome as random even when it is not truly random.
when: when a system's causes are not visible to players

text: Randomness creates excitement and challenge while players still feel in control, but produces hopelessness and lost control when they do not.
when: when random outcomes affect play
why: Players' sense of control determines how randomness feels.

text: Players often do not know the true chances of an action and form their own estimates, usually through trial and error.
when: the real odds are hidden or unclear
why: Without stated odds, a few unlucky tries can convince players that an action is worthless.

text: Players rarely notice a change to a random range, but they readily notice a change to base damage.
when: adjusting numbers that players see in play
why: Random ranges are hard for players to perceive.

text: Players perceive a game as chance-based when none of their decisions changes the odds, even if the operator profits over time.
when: games with no meaningful player decisions
why: players judge skill by their own influence on results

text: Players accept an improbable win as normal but resist an improbable loss, so self-serving bias works only in the player's favor.
when: When players lack hard statistics on their own results
why: Wins are remembered far more vividly than losses, so people inflate their own win rates.

text: Casual players usually accept random results that are close enough to ideal rather than checking for bias.
when: casual play
why: Checking for bias would take more effort than a casual game warrants, so close-enough results are accepted.

text: A sound, animation or effect that nearly matches a realistic representation but falls short is more distracting than one that is fully abstract or fully stylized.
when: when an object is styled realistically but its reactions are not
why: Partial realism breaks the player's belief in the world

text: A randomly generated line spoken during a dramatic moment can feel like an emotional exchange, though no system models its meaning.
when: a dying character speaks during combat
why: the player's mind supplies the emotional context

text: Random outcomes that let a lucky break reverse a defeat keep players starting new matches, since any match might bring a streak.
when: competitive modes with random swings
why: A single match can bring a large lucky result

text: Pure randomness makes outcomes feel like unfair losses or lucky wins, while predictable patterns let players plan.
when: enemy or hazard timing and damage
why: Players can only attribute outcomes to skill when they can anticipate threats.

text: A deterministic mechanic always produces the same output for the same input, while a non-deterministic one adds randomness so identical actions can yield different outcomes.
A straight is five consecutive ranks; aces count only as high cards, so a run from ace down to four is not a straight.
Two pair means exactly two pairs of different ranks, so four of a kind is not two pair; a full house is three cards of one rank plus a pair of another.
Input randomness shapes the starting setup before a choice, while output randomness is triggered by a player action and resolves its result.
when: Classifying a game's random elements
why: The two differ in when randomness acts relative to the player's decision.

text: Predictable results means a player's input yields the response they expect, with no interference between intent and outcome. Controls may be complex yet still predictable.
Reproducible is not the same as predictable. A predictable result should also hint at possibilities the player has not yet tried.
Real randomizers such as dice, coins, cards and spinners are not perfectly random and carry small physical biases that shift outcomes away from ideal probabilities.
Perceived odds can diverge from true odds through player psychology or through the computer's implementation of randomness.
Machines are fundamentally deterministic, but networking, clock reads, and thread timing can make a program non-deterministic.
True randomness needs special hardware that measures chaotic physical processes, which is outside typical computer use.
Third-party services can supply truly random numbers, but they are usually impractical for standard game use.
A single-pass swap shuffle of n elements needs n random numbers and n swaps, so its cost grows linearly with list size.
when: estimating runtime of a shuffle
why: the loop runs once per element

text: A shuffled sequence of two outcome types can be encoded as a bit string, and the probability of a long run of one bit is a finite counting problem.
when: analysing streaks in random sequences
why: reducing the sequence to bits makes the counting uniform

text: With three sequences, a perfect initial distribution has run counts equal to two consecutive Fibonacci numbers.
when: polyphase sort with three sequences
why: Perfect counts let merge passes finish without wasted partial passes.

text: Performance varies along a distribution, so extraordinary runs of success occur by chance and do not signal a lasting change in ability.
Random outcomes such as dice rolls and card draws can make games exciting and are widely used.
Calling a game deterministic is a description, not a judgment; deterministic games can stay popular for thousands of years.
Randomness makes games accessible and social because their emotional triggers are not decision-based, which is why many gambling and board games are starved on purpose.
Deterministic games can be memorized and played perfectly, while adding randomness to a system stops memorized patterns from working and forces players to respond to new ones.
In die-based combat, randomness appears in to-hit and damage rolls, spell or skill failure, saving throws against area attacks, and random stat gains on level-up.
Pips cut into a die's faces make the 1 face heavier than the 6 face, which can tilt results toward 6s.
Rounded corners or an oblong shape make some faces land more often; oblong d20s land on their flatter part more frequently.
Playing uniformly at random in Rock-Paper-Scissors yields equal wins, losses and draws, for a net expected score of zero.
Three pitfalls make results seem random: control ambiguity, state overwhelm and staging.
Identical events can carry different emotional weight depending on game state, such as losing a minor piece early versus the piece guarding a king late.
why: The value at stake changes with circumstances.

text: Analyze luck and skill directly rather than placing games on one continuum; do not assume casual games are luck-based while core games are skill-based.
when: Classifying a game's luck and skill balance
why: Games mix luck and skill in varied ways, so a single line or genre label misrepresents them.

text: Judge a random system's fairness by player perception as well as mathematics, since players may call sound mechanics unfair and perception drives trust.
when: Designing random outcomes
why: Perceived fairness can differ from underlying odds, and game balance depends on players perceiving the game as fair.

text: People judge probability by how easily examples come to mind, which is usually reasonable when common events are the most memorable ones.
Random bullet deviation on a precise aim feels like arbitrary punishment, so avoid it in skill-based shooters.
when: Designing a skill-based shooter with aimed shots
why: Players who aimed well feel the game stole a skillful kill.

text: When a game mixes randomness with choices, skill dominates only if players gain benefit from anticipating and reacting to the random elements; otherwise luck dominates.
when: When a game has both randomness and meaningful choices
why: Over many repetitions luck averages out, leaving the player's handling of probabilities to decide results.

text: Use random events with major, game-altering consequences very carefully, since players react strongly to them and trust can be badly damaged.
Treat ideal fair randomness as a target to approach, not a guarantee, when designing random systems.
why: Ideal fair randomness never appears in real dice or pseudorandom generators, which have physical imperfections and implementation limits.

text: Acceptable randomness depends on context: casual play, high-stakes competition and regulated gambling each tolerate different levels of deviation.
why: Perfect randomness is an ideal, so designers must settle for close enough, with the acceptable level set by the stakes.

text: When balancing possibility against predictability, lean toward more possibility, scaled to the game's ambition.
when: Designing open worlds or replayable games
why: Predictable structures reduce replayability

text: Make decision outcomes partly predictable, neither unknowable nor inevitable, so players can plan while still facing real uncertainty.
why: Players can only weigh options when they can foresee some of what follows; with no foresight, planning collapses and decisions lose meaning.

text: Repeated random rolls pull results toward expected value, so single luck events matter less and the more skilled player wins over many games, though any player can win one game.
when: Evaluating a competitive game that mixes luck and skill, or considering adding rolls
why: Law of Large Numbers; luck adds variance per game, so skill advantage shows mainly across many games.

text: The same seed produces exactly the same sequence, so testers can reproduce a result precisely.
why: Because the generator is deterministic, a fixed starting value regenerates the same numbers each run, letting testers rerun an outcome identically.

text: Results that land close to a win but miss, produced more often than chance predicts, raise excitement and keep players playing.
when: reward displays in chance-based games
why: Near misses feel like almost winning and encourage another attempt

text: A single player overwhelmed by an endless sea of enemies can be used deliberately to create a sense of futility.
when: Enemy numbers are intentionally unbeatable
why: Because the hopelessness is plainly visible to the player, the staged impossibility reads as amusing rather than unfair.

text: Removing randomness from outcomes makes results fully predictable, which lowers strategic value and player engagement.
when: When combat damage is fixed at maximum rather than varying randomly
why: Players can compute exactly how many attacks a kill takes, so each encounter's uncertainty and the strategic choices built on it disappear.

text: In dice or card games, randomness usually sits in the roll or draw, while movement after the roll is deterministic.
when: In board or card games where a random roll or draw drives movement
why: After the random draw, applying movement rules is fixed, so an identical roll always produces the identical result.

text: Allowing limited rerolls of non-target dice lets players chase or avoid a bad result, producing repeated reversals of fortune within a turn.
when: dice games with a risky result that players can influence by rerolling
why: Players hope to avoid a costly outcome or add one more beneficial one.

text: When odds are known, players can make informed decisions, as in dice games where outcomes near the middle of a sum range come up more often than extremes.
when: Designing randomness meant to inform strategy
why: Known probabilities let players weigh options against likely results.

text: A six-identical-outcome streak has about a 1 in 32 chance, so among 3.2 million players about 100,000 would see one in their very first game.
when: When a game built on many repeated coin flips is played by a large audience
why: Flips are independent, so across a large audience rare streaks are statistically certain to appear for someone's first game, even though they look unlikely.

text: Probability design raises three questions: whether it is a professional ethics matter; where to draw the line between player wishes and accurate simulation; whether actual or perceived mechanics matter more.
For conversational hidden-information games, model the hidden item in one party's mind, the accumulated knowledge in the other's, and the conversation as the channel carrying information.
when: A game built on questions and answers with a secret
why: Every game holds some state, and in a question-and-answer game that state is split between the secret-holder, the guesser's reasoning, and the exchanged dialogue.

text: Shuffles are not perfectly random: 52-card orders far exceed any 64-bit seed space, and machine bit width limits distinct orderings, so most permutations never occur.
when: a shuffle must cover every possible permutation
why: The number of permutations of a large list can exceed what the seed and word size can represent.

text: Players who believe they control chance can misjudge the real odds, so their perceived probabilities diverge from actual ones.
When the same input seems to give different results, players stop practicing and disengage, even if the controls are complex.
when: When controls are complex or difficult, as long as each input yields the same result
why: Random-seeming controls make practice pointless.

text: Adding randomness does not automatically make a game more accessible or better, especially if players lose meaningful choices.
when: Considering whether to add randomness to improve a game
why: Randomness removes player agency when it overrides decisions.

text: Equating random outcomes with luck-dominated play is a mistake when probabilities are exposed and escape options exist.
Random events that favor the player are generally fine, but random destruction causes confusion, a sense that play is pointless, and accusations of cheating.
when: When a random event can drastically change the outcome of a player's strategy
why: Players who lose to a bad roll wonder what they did wrong, feel their plan was nullified, or assume the AI cheated.

text: If the RNG is re-seeded on every reload, a player can save before a risky roll and reload on failure until it succeeds.
when: save-anywhere systems
why: Each reload becomes a fresh attempt.

text: 1) Take a tiny deck, such as three cards. 2) List every sequence of random choices the shuffle can make. 3) Count the resulting orders. 4) Compare them with all possible orders to see whether each is reached equally often.
when: When checking whether a shuffle algorithm produces every order equally often
why: Small decks have a finite number of orderings, so every possible random path can be enumerated and compared exactly.

text: 1) Start with an ordered deck. 2) For each position i from the last down to the second, pick random r from 0 to i inclusive. 3) Swap the elements at i and r.
when: producing a randomized ordering of a list
why: one random draw and one swap per element gives a fair shuffle cheaply

text: 1) Define each state as the remaining counts of each card type plus the current streak length. 2) Assign probabilities as remaining count divided by remaining deck size for each draw. 3) Multiply probabilities along each path to a target state. 4) Sum the probabilities of all final states meeting the streak condition.
when: computing the probability of a streak in a deck drawn without replacement
why: tracking remaining cards makes draw probabilities depend on history

text: 1) Number rows 1 to 52 in one column. 2) Build item names in an adjacent column by joining rank and suit lists with CONCAT. 3) Place shuffled random ranks in another column. 4) Use VLOOKUP on each rank to return its name.
when: Shuffling a set of named items from a numbered list.
why: Joining the parts with a concatenation function builds each full name, and a lookup then returns the right name for each shuffled number.

text: 1) List the 52 card names in A1:A52. 2) Enter =RAND() in B1:B52. 3) In C1, enter INDEX over A1:A52 using RANK of B1 within B1:B52 as the row and 1 as the column. 4) Fill C1 down to row 52.
why: Random numbers ranked against each other give each item a distinct position, and INDEX then fetches the name at that position.

text: 1) Count results satisfying the condition. 2) Count all equally likely results. 3) Divide the first count by the second.
when: Single random event with equally likely results.
why: Ratio of favorable to total outcomes gives probability.

text: 1) Watch players' betting patterns for signs of tracking the deck. 2) Deal from a multi-deck shoe so the remaining composition changes more slowly.
when: Casino-style games where hidden deck information can be exploited.
why: Makes tracking the remaining cards harder and less rewarding.

text: 1) Choose a game with fairly simple rules. 2) Revise its rules so outcomes no longer depend on chance. 3) Describe how the change affects gameplay.
when: when studying how chance shapes play
why: Working through the change builds a deeper grasp of how gameplay is structured.

text: Do not leave seed-based replay enabled by accident in the final release.
when: When the game ships, as opposed to during testing
why: A fixed seed reproduces results exactly, which suits testing but would be unwanted by accident in a shipped build.

text: For networked games that cannot tolerate out-of-sync states, generate random results on a server so there is one authoritative game state.
when: networked games needing a consistent state
why: If one client draws a number the other never sees, their generators drift apart and later rolls disagree.

text: Give the house no independent choices; house actions should follow strict fixed rules.
when: Games where a house or dealer acts against players.
why: Fixed rules keep outcomes predictable and the odds measurable.

text: Avoid expecting convergence into a single device by default; the exception is hardware people carry in a pocket.
when: predicting how devices will evolve
why: Each technology progresses on its own timeline, so separate devices let each be upgraded alone; pocket items converge for convenience.

text: Any pairing system can be modified so no pair meets twice and no player receives two byes.
Lower luck by narrowing result ranges, using fewer die faces, rolling more dice, turning random events into choices, and limiting each event's impact; reverse these to raise luck.
Set-aside dice return to play only when every die rolled on a turn shows a 1; ignoring this changes the state transitions.
when: modeling dice games where dice are set aside after rolling 1s
why: the return condition alters which dice count carries into the next state

text: Make events credible rather than realistic: signs, feedback, and form-follows-function still apply.
when: Any game with a physical world, whether realistic or cartoony
why: Players have strong intuitive expectations about physical events, so the world must behave in ways they find plausible.

text: Warn players in advance that catastrophic random events may occur, without stating timing or severity, and give them ways to mitigate the damage.
when: designing high-impact random events
why: Warned players feel in control rather than cheated.

text: Balance surprise against player choice so that choices stay dominant; if every choice yields random effects, players feel their choices are meaningless.
when: Adding randomness to player decisions

text: Skilled players can exploit opponents' predictable random-generation biases, such as detecting a target mix that is actually played at a different rate.
when: competitive games with mixed or random choices
why: Human approximations of equilibrium deviate in detectable ways.

text: Choosing a random alternative spawn when the spawn is blocked reduces the reason to camp, but adds an element of luck.
when: When the spawn cell is taken by a wall or by another participant
why: Spawn location is no longer predictable, so there is no fixed point to wait at.

text: Random attribute rolls force players to make the best of what they get, while point-buy lets players shape a character by spending a fixed pool of points.
when: choosing how players assign attributes
why: Random rolls remove player control; point-buy gives it.

text: Output randomness adds excitement and quicker play and rewards risk assessment, but it can let luck dominate and make players blame dice for cheap losses.
when: Using action-triggered randomness in a game
why: Unpredictable results speed play and reward risk judgment, yet bad rolls can overshadow good decisions.

text: Exposing random statistics lets players verify fairness, while hiding how the system works lets the community solve it through shared data, suiting community-focused games.
when: choosing between transparency and concealment for a random system
why: Visible statistics let players check the odds themselves, reducing doubt that the outcomes are unfair.

text: Rolling at rates different from those displayed can match players' expectations, but it teaches them something false and conflicts with honesty.
why: Lowering the chance of each repeated failure shortens streaks, so felt results sit closer to displayed odds.

text: In some professional sports, rankings are subjective, assigned by expert judge panels who may use their own systems.
In star-based ranking, each win adds a star, and filling a rank's required stars advances the player to the next rank.
Losses remove a star only below a threshold rank, and streak bonuses add stars only for wins, so a loss costs at most one star per game.
when: When a player's rank is below the protected top ranks of a star ladder

text: A source system never exists in pure form, and a procedural model reflects the designer's subjective choices rather than a neutral copy; each person's view of it is subjective.
why: Many different procedural models can represent one system, each emphasizing different aspects.

text: A game's effective skill range can shift as its player base changes, so a game feels easy when most players are new and hard when most have years of practice.
when: When the player population's experience changes over time.
why: Newcomers versus veterans set the perceived difficulty.

text: Real-time combat unfolds as it happens; it is standard in shooters, many strategy games and some RPGs.
A rescue or escape objective requires moving a defined unit or units to safety.
Include places where players can relax their thinking and simply play, and add puzzle elements where more intellectual engagement would help.
when: Pacing a game's mix of mental effort and rest
why: Alternating demanding and easy moments keeps engagement without exhaustion

text: Exaggerate distinctive props or silhouette elements so a character stays recognizable from the back of a large audience.
when: Staging a character for a live performance or a distant audience
why: Distinct props stay identifiable at long distances, like seats far from a stage.

text: Real-time mechanics leave no time for one player to make everyone's decisions, so each player must act on their own.
when: When designing co-op games against the commander problem
why: Time pressure removes the opportunity for one player to direct all moves

text: A unit removed by a shot returns at a spawn point its player chooses at the start of the next round.
Each fire input creates one projectile that moves at a constant, predetermined speed in the facing direction.
Ranged attacks enable cover use, elevated firing positions, and support roles, while short-range attacks cannot use cover.
why: Being close to targets means it cannot hide behind cover.

text: A slow power cycle, such as a weapon that fires only every few seconds, creates a flow gap whenever the player has no other meaningful action to take in between.
why: Cooldown delays are added for balance, leaving the player nothing to decide during the wait.

text: A two-by-two grid crosses real versus simulated with here versus there: AR brings simulation to the body's location, VR sends the body to the simulation.
Respawn speed affects how often kills happen, so it is part of the design and can change scoring outcomes.
when: when designing free-for-all scoring

text: In a melee-focused game, ranged tools must feel rewarding without becoming a degenerate strategy that removes the fun of melee.
when: When adding ranged tools to a melee game
why: Degenerate ranged play undermines the core mode

text: Grant respawned players a short invisibility window, about two to three seconds, so they can fight back.
when: When players are being spawn camped at their spawn point
why: Being unseen right after spawning lets a player move and shoot before campers can react.

text: Judge real-time control by whether the player steers continuously rather than issuing discrete commands; turn-based play does not qualify.
when: classifying a game's control
why: Input is a flow of small corrections the player perceives as immediate, rather than discrete exchanges.

text: Real-time and turn-based designs differ in how turn length is set, and changing between them alters the whole feel of the game.
when: When deciding turn structure.
why: Real-world decision time is separate from in-game time, so turn length sets the pacing the player feels.

text: Aim for a wide skill range when a game should offer years of learning. A narrow range can suit a short experience that relies on art and narrative.
when: When deciding target range width.
why: Long-lived games need depth; short story-driven games do not.

text: A real skill is an ability the player must actually possess and exercise, such as pressing the right buttons at the right time.
Aim for a balance of real and virtual skills rather than relying on either alone.
Realistic characters pushed toward human appearance without matching motion and detail can fall deep into the uncanny valley.
when: Realistic or mimetic game characters
why: Imperfect human likeness in motion looks wrong even when single frames look natural

text: A game whose visuals look realistic must deliver realistic physics; if visuals promise more than physics deliver, players lose faith in the world's fidelity.
when: when a game's visual realism exceeds its physical behavior
why: Broken visual promises erode player trust

text: Make sure player choices are real and the player is not railroaded; when unsure, ask what the player knows or wants right now.
when: reviewing choice points

text: Skill tests must include real failure, and that failure must not destroy the experience when it happens.
Realism works against amplification, while a game can offer a clean, simple-to-learn version of a complex system.
why: Controlling a complex system through simple inputs gives players a satisfying sense of amplified power that realistic controls would lose.

text: Tuning becomes very difficult as a system's relationships grow into the hundreds or thousands.
Larger possibility spaces come from adding objects with defined relationships, as in life simulations, real-time strategy titles, and massively multiplayer worlds.
Remove a hero or unit whose role is already covered by another faction's existing unit, since the overlap adds nothing to the roster.
when: trimming a roster of heroes or units
why: Redundancy dilutes the distinct identity each faction needs.

text: 1) Alter up to three rules of a pure-luck game: insert, delete, or modify. 2) Remove as much luck as possible. 3) Add as much skill depth as possible.
when: converting a pure-luck game into a skill game
why: The starting game has zero decisions for players, so skill depth has to be introduced.

text: If a design feels wrong, consider removals alongside additions, and look for single-purpose elements that could be combined.
when: a design does not feel right
why: Elements that serve only one purpose add weight, while elements serving several purposes make a design more elegant.

text: Remove inner contradictions in a design instead of tolerating them or making excuses, such as a simplifying device that is hard to use or a fun game that is boring.
when: A design has elements that work against its own purpose
why: Inner contradictions are the core source of bad design

text: Remove options that appear in no intransitive loop before solving, since they are strictly inferior and cannot be in the optimal mix.
when: When balancing a game with intransitive mechanics.

text: Larger possibility spaces generally add replayability and unpredictability, but more outcomes do not always improve a game; constrained spaces can sustain challenge if difficulty matches and grows with player ability.
when: Comparing replayability across games, or deciding how many outcomes to allow.
why: For players of constrained games, navigating a defined set of possibilities is itself the challenge.

text: When players repeat the same task, they feel stuck; varying action types and showing how each action advances toward victory helps.
when: When players are forced to repeat the same type of action over and over.
why: Repetition masks real progress, so players feel stalled even while advancing toward their goal.

text: The possibility space is the set of motions a player can perform, not the motions they will perform; each reachable motion has its own aesthetic character.
The possibility space is the set of all game states that could ever arise in a game, and is usually a theoretical concept because listing them all is impractical.
A possibility space offers compelling problems within a narrative, creative options for solving them, and responses to player choices with meaningful consequences.
An endless stream of simple, repeated events offers scant space for intrinsic appeal or artistry of presentation.
The size of a possibility space depends on scope: all possible games, a match between two chosen decks, and a match 15 minutes in each form a progressively smaller space.
when: Defining what set of states is being analyzed.

text: In games, replay is common while redo is uncommon.
Use expected recurrence as a quick elegance check, since repetition does not guarantee elegance but elegance is impossible without it.
when: choosing between candidate features
why: Recurrence is easier to judge than the nuance of a mechanic's interactions.

text: Small pauses that seem harmless still cause boredom and frustration when they repeat across a session.
when: When many small delays accumulate across a single play session.
why: Players feel boredom even from a one-second gap, and enough gaps turn smooth flow into stop-start frustration.

text: Craft the possibility space as carefully as possible, then playtest it rigorously, since outcomes cannot be fully predicted in advance.
why: How object properties and relationships shape system dynamics is hard to generalize, so outcomes must be tested.

text: Forbid moves that recreate an earlier state to prevent endless loops of play, as Go does with repeated board positions.
when: When a game's moves could otherwise cycle back to an earlier board state.
why: Without this limit, play can cycle indefinitely.

text: Seasonal resets provide progression and a fresh chance for players who felt they had peaked, while a stable lifetime rating can stagnate.
when: when choosing between permanent and seasonal ranks
why: Replaying to recover a former standing gives players a reason to come back after they felt they had peaked.

text: Loosely connected objects matter to an agent according to its current needs; a hungry character finds food sources interesting while a satiated one does not.
when: when relationships depend on proximity or the agent's current needs
why: the agent's current state changes which objects it relates to

text: Progression is the rate at which a player moves through a game's power, difficulty, gameplay, or narrative ramp.
Progression feels well-paced when players are neither stalled nor hurried.
Gameplay progression is the player's wish to see something new, such as a mechanic, level, item, or enemy.

Progression systems can include experience points, experience levels, faction standing, skill levels, and ranks, and games without experience points may show growth through items, story, or abilities.
An access reward grants limited forward movement, typically through a single-use key or resource.
when: When designing rewards that unlock progress
why: Access rewards control where and when players can go

text: Progression is an exchange in which the player gives time or effort in return for advancement in the game.
Active skills let a player take an action they otherwise could not take; passive skills apply constantly or trigger automatically in the right situations.
A skill tree starts the player with a small selection and unlocks more skills as earlier ones are taken, forming a directed acyclic graph rather than a true tree.
Player progression means skill improves while the game's content stays the same; it is typical of most shooters and classic board and card games.
A progression arc moves from one point to another once, while a progression loop repeats a cycle of challenges.
As a design tool, progression mainly serves to conclude the game within a reasonable time.
A permanent rank is usually a direct function of a lifetime rating, so it follows the rating across the player's whole history.
Non-contingent rewards are given regardless of behavior, such as an unexpected bonus; they are considered less controlling.
Most game design targets the player level, where players understand the game and are immersed in mastering it.
Removing levels that players already earned is less acceptable to players than a cap set in advance.
Reaching new audiences requires new player experiences, as shown by demand for novel hardware and rhythm-based music games.
Reward-driven gamification is often shallow, but rewards work well when combined with other teaching models.
when: When using rewards to motivate learning
why: Rewards alone rarely produce deep learning

text: Each new thing a player sees can serve as a reward in itself.
Progression-based games usually make older weapons obsolete by design.
Progression is only one small part of game design and may or may not suit a given game as a core or auxiliary system.
Adventure games usually do not let the character grow in wealth, status, or experience as role-playing games do, relying on inventory and puzzles instead.
Monetary rewards activate reward circuitry more strongly than verbal rewards, and higher monetary pay raises effort on simple tasks.
why: Students offered four dollars outperformed those offered ten cents on a repetitive dragging task, and brain-reward activity was stronger for money than for verbal reward.

text: A resource list can be skipped for genres whose resource relationships are so standard that the balance patterns are well established.
when: Genre has well-known balance patterns, such as RPGs with experience, levels, HP and gold.
why: Standard relationships are already known.

text: Unlock new content on a win or a death in games with much randomness or a harsh curve, so failed runs still feel like progress.
when: Runs are often lost and progress would otherwise feel futile
why: Visible unlocks give a sense of advancement even when the run itself is lost.

text: Rewarding returning players more for longer breaks is a way to encourage players to disconnect.
when: When the game targets a young audience or is widely played by children.
why: Young players find it harder to resist attention-economy pressures, and sleep and varied play matter for their development.

text: Each loop should carry several motivators at once rather than relying on a single one.
why: Reliance on one motivator leaves players without reason to continue if that motivator weakens.

text: Color-coding points by event prestige and requiring a minimum of high-prestige points for invitational events gates access by proven achievement.
when: when designing invitational event eligibility
why: Points are weighted by event prestige, so eligibility reflects the kinds of events a player has actually competed in.

text: Measure progress in several ways at once rather than relying on one system.
why: Several indicators give players a clearer sense of achievement, much as a visible path does across a long campaign.

text: Skill levels rise the more a player uses that skill, and players can often spend points on skills when they gain a character level.
When progression stops mattering, after a level cap, full skill unlocks, or maxed stats, the player enters an elder game with a different goal.
when: Progression has no further meaningful gains
why: Once the progression reward runs out, the player needs a new motivation to keep playing.

text: Skill gating slows skill growth by offering progressively harder challenges with little teaching, so each completed challenge signals readiness for the next.
when: When the designer wants to slow skill progression rather than speed it up.

text: A reward space that advances a piece extra spaces can carry it straight into the goal, so one lucky roll can finish a piece.
when: When a piece lands on a reward space through a direct throw.
why: Entering the goal does not require an exact count, so the bonus spaces can carry the piece all the way in.

text: Gating levels behind rare, powerful collectibles turns progress into a countable path, where each collected item is a measurable step toward the final goal.
why: Rarity and power give each item meaning, and each one counts as a visible, quantifiable advance toward the main objective.

text: Progression tied to weapon choice, with weapon energy earned from enemies and lost when hit, forces players to switch weapons and plan usage order.
when: when designing weapon upgrade or resource systems
why: Coupling energy gain and loss to combat makes choices matter at every fight

text: Procedures that offer inefficient routes to the objective force players to use particular skills.
In team shooters that use a ticket count, completing objectives drains the opposing team's tickets.
when: When designing objective-based modes with a ticket system

text: A fixed ratio above one-to-one pays a batch of rewards on every Nth action, so most actions earn nothing.
When rewards match intrinsic desires exactly, extrinsic and intrinsic motivation add up rather than competing.
why: Rewards that reward only what players already wish to do avoid undermining the play they came for.

text: Tools that unlock harder resources widen a sandbox, and the player's goal shifts from fixed survival tasks to self-defined aims.
why: Better tools open richer resources, so survival pressure fades and players set their own aims.

text: Random reward systems can feel like progress through near misses and hidden drops, even when each outcome is independent.
when: Designing random loot or chance-based rewards
why: Players perceive each failure as a step closer to the useful outcome.

text: Progression has four kinds: power, difficulty, gameplay, and narrative.
Every progression system has a motivator, then an arc or loop, then a reward that satisfies the motivator.
Individual arcs are accomplishment and discovery; individual loops are difficulty, complexity, power and cosmetic content.
Rewards not tied to clear goals are less likely to motivate players.
Repeating the same core tasks for small gains feels grindy.
why: Rewards must feel worth the time invested, otherwise repeated core tasks feel like unbalanced drudgery.

text: Free rewards for trivial actions, such as a first-login trophy, water down later achievements and suggest the game needs no effort.
when: Adding early or easy rewards
why: Arbitrary rewards reduce the sense of accomplishment that genuine achievements provide.

text: Using progression gates or loss threats to hold players in place when core gameplay is weak breeds resentment rather than engagement.
when: Core interactions are missing their goals.
why: Artificial rewards or threats do not raise enjoyment when the core is weak.

text: Customization that players rarely see, such as avatar appearance in a first-person game, feels wasted and adds little value.
when: Camera hides the customized element
why: Players cannot enjoy or notice what they cannot see

text: A game cannot simply promise a need; it must deliver fulfillment, or players who expect it will move to a game that does.
why: Some games fulfill needs far better than others, so players compare and move toward the ones that deliver.

text: A dip in interest that is not followed by renewed rising interest can lead players to leave.
why: Dips are meant to build anticipation for a later rise, so a drop with no rise after it defeats that purpose.

text: Protected saves erase the save on reload and may penalize resets, so honest players can be punished, for example when a power outage counts as a loss.
why: The system cannot tell a reset from an outage or crash, so honest players lose progress too.

text: Many possible actions without worthwhile payoff feel tedious, and collectibles lose individual meaning when they are scattered without clear reward.
when: when designing many collectibles or optional actions
why: Actions without payoff lose the player's motivation

text: Unadvertised milestones leave players unsure what they are striving for.
why: Players enjoy advancing, and that enjoyment depends on seeing a target they are working toward.

text: Tuning a game for motivation alone can produce a game whose players feel only regret for the time and money they spent.
why: A design centered only on motivation ignores whether play fulfills, leaving players regretful about time and money spent.

text: A missing reward can feel like punishment; if a crowd ignores a heroic act, players feel disappointed.
why: Rewards are feedback about mastery, so a missing reward reads as negative feedback.

text: A reward players do not understand feels like no reward at all.
when: Designing reward feedback
why: Players cannot value a reward whose meaning is unclear to them

text: The perceived value of each scored action shifts as players gain experience, so reward balance is a moving target that needs continued checking.
1) Identify a hard progression cap in a game. 2) Consider why the cap exists. 3) Imagine removing it. 4) List problems the removal would fix. 5) List new problems the removal would create.
when: Evaluating whether a hard progression limit is justified
why: Removing a cap reveals the purpose it serves and the costs it carries.

text: 1) State the design goals. 2) For each progression system, check whether it improves engagement or only blocks access to the game's best systems.

1) For higher-rated, lower-rated, and equal-rated opponents, compute expected rating gain or loss using assumed win probabilities. 2) Compare the expected values to see whether players are pushed toward similarly rated opponents.
when: when checking whether a point scheme creates the intended matchmaking incentive
why: Stakes shrink as the rating gap grows, so expected gains against each tier show whether players are drawn to close matches.

text: Grinding for growth is acceptable only while content keeps pace with rising experience needs and the core loop is enjoyable in itself.
when: Games where characters must grind experience points to advance toward a level cap.
why: Extra time spent on an enjoyable core loop is hardly felt as punishment.

text: Avoid extrinsic rewards in freedom, creativity, or exploration games, as they reduce intended play; for creative, exploratory, or social systems with undetectable achievements, use no reward system.
when: Creative, exploratory, or social game systems whose achievements the game cannot detect.
why: Extrinsic rewards reduce the play those games are meant to produce.

text: Digital explicit-future systems may need tools that log deals and flag them resolved, since players otherwise must recall promises.
when: Games where promised future trades are made explicit in the rules.
why: Without a log, players must memorize promises, which adds complexity during play.

text: Never let players lose progress without saving, warn about checkpoint distance, and warn players about the consequences of abandoning a multiplayer match.
when: Designing save systems, checkpoints and multiplayer quitting.
why: Players lose trust and motivation when progress disappears unexpectedly, including when they quit by closing the console or window.

text: Allow players to reset skill-tree points so they can recover from a later-regretted decision.
when: Designing skill trees or build systems.
why: Permanent choices with no reset increase frustration when players regret them.

text: Well-designed skill trees offer both competence and autonomy by showing progression toward clear goals and meaningful specialisation.
List the skills your game demands; most games require a blend of several, so a single-skill view is incomplete.
when: When designing a game, to catalogue what the player must exercise.
why: Most games blend several abilities, so a one-skill view misses parts of the challenge.

text: Verify that participants understand their next step and feel motivated to take it.
when: Reviewing advancement systems

text: Do not add rewards to every experience hoping for an easy motivation boost.
why: Rewards can make players treat play as work, which removes the desire to do it unprompted.

text: An open-ended level system lets players keep growing indefinitely, but in competitive games it can let time played decide standing instead of skill.
why: Each new level needs more repetitive grinding, so accumulated play time drives growth.

text: Allowing a player to misrepresent one card in a trade makes every trade carry risk, because any offer may hide a bluff.
when: Trades where a player may lie about one item.
why: Trading is necessary for progress, yet a hidden card means each offer exposes the initiator to loss.

text: Keeping all progression after a loss reduces the sting of death, but makes victories depend on time invested rather than skill.
when: Deciding whether a defeat keeps experience, levels, and loot
why: Persistence-based progress can make overcoming a challenge feel meaningless.

text: Scoring a partial winner from game state can reward a player who builds a lead and then logs off before the opponent can answer.
when: in two-player games
why: Players can exploit it: take an early lead, then quit before the rival catches up.

text: Giving all skills at once maximizes choice but can overwhelm new players, while linear unlocking gives designers control and easier balancing but reduces player ownership.
when: Deciding when players gain skills
why: A fixed unlock order eases balancing and designer control, yet the player owns the character less.

text: Tree branches create trade-offs between a strong skill that dead-ends and a mediocre skill that leads to a great one later.
when: Designing skill tree branches
why: Designers can hold powerful skills back for later while still offering a manageable set of early options.

text: Character progression narrows the possibility space because players meet only the content provided, while player progression keeps it open through skill.
when: choosing a progression type
why: Players keep needing stronger opponents, and those can be found endlessly in competitive play.

text: Removing monster rewards faces a dilemma: monsters that do not respawn empty the world quickly, while respawning monsters without rewards stop being fought.
when: In games where players gain loot from killing monsters.
why: Finite monsters get wiped out quickly, while unrewarded respawns give players no incentive to fight them.

text: Performance-contingent rewards are most controlling but give competence feedback that offsets control when progress is visible; completion rewards feel less controlling but give no sense of growing competence.
when: When rewards tied to performance standards sit alongside visible progression.
why: Performance rewards double as feedback on skill, which can offset their controlling feel.

text: Without a central plot, players judge larger quests as more important, and repeatable small tasks can feed a bigger goal.
when: multiplayer quests lacking a central plot
why: Small repeatable tasks add up over time, so each one still feeds a larger goal.

text: Facility rewards add a new capability, such as a new weapon or ability, expanding the player's moveset; they may or may not open new areas.
Glory rewards are the sense of achievement from overcoming a challenge or winning, and they are not always part of the mechanics.
Sustenance rewards keep the avatar going by restoring health, ammunition, or magic.
Access rewards unlock previously blocked areas, often as one-use items such as keys, and can also be narrative items or out-of-game extras.
Avoid stacking a level transition, plot advancement and power increase at the same moment; reserve such overlap for major dramatic moments.
when: Scheduling different reward types
why: Players perceive different reward types similarly, so simultaneous rewards blur together.

text: Reward reinforces behavior more effectively than punishment, so prefer rewards to punishments where possible.
when: When choosing how to shape player behavior
why: Rewards encourage repeated behavior without the frustration punishment creates

text: Occasionally offering a hard, risky, high-reward target makes each appearance a difficult choice and keeps repetitive play engaging.
when: Designing a repeated core action that risks becoming tedious.
why: Rare high-risk options break monotony and create tension.

text: Check reward systems against actual fun, because rewards can drive behavior that players do not enjoy.
when: when designing loot, kill counts or other reward systems
why: Reward-driven behavior can persist without enjoyment

text: Use reward anticipation when players must persist through difficulty to reach triumph, social connection, or artistic satisfaction.
when: When games create moments of displeasure or failure that players must push through.
why: Anticipating a reward triggers a motivation surge that drives pursuit of the goal.

text: Most games fall between easily measured and hard-to-detect goals, so reward design is a craft of detecting and rewarding what players already want.
when: Games whose goals sit between easily detected and hard-to-detect player motivations.
why: A game can only reward what it can detect, so rewards must track what players already want.

text: A chain of rewards leading to a major payoff steers players toward chosen actions and makes the skills they require feel valuable.
when: when wanting players to practise a specific set of skills
why: Rewards make the target actions worth repeating

text: Attaching a rule that some instances of a repetitive action yield rewards can make the action engaging even when the action itself gives little feedback.
when: when the core action offers little physical satisfaction, such as cutting grass with no resistance
why: The reward gives the action meaning and keeps the player repeating it

text: A reward gained earlier can change the strategy needed in later levels, keeping challenge fresh.
why: New strategies from earlier rewards raise challenge without simply tightening obstacles.

text: Designs encourage behaviors by rewarding them and discourage others by punishing them, so unanticipated antisocial behavior can emerge and should be monitored.
when: When unplanned antisocial behavior can occur in games that were not designed to control it.
why: Rewards and punishments are the mechanisms that steer what players do, so no design is neutral.

text: 1) State what the player will feel rewarded for. 2) Confirm the player can influence the outcome. 3) Confirm the reward follows a deliberate action.
when: Designing a new goal or achievement
why: Outcomes the player cannot influence leave them frustrated after losses, since effort does not improve their chances.

text: When removing an item that serves as a quest reward, supply a replacement reward for that quest.
when: an item used as a quest reward is removed
why: otherwise the quest loses its payoff

text: Make rewards deepen immersion by increasing capabilities or expanding customisation.
when: Designing progression rewards.
why: Meaningful rewards extend engagement beyond the immediate reward.

text: Ask why each mechanic exists and why one moment of play stands out while another does not.
when: when reviewing play experiences

text: Make sure players always know what a quest will give them; advancing the story is a reward, and experience or money makes it more attractive.
when: Quest-based narratives where players must work to complete a task for a quest-giver
why: Players invest effort in solving the task, so they need to see the payoff for that effort in advance.

text: Pair the removal of rewards for harmful play with rewards for the cooperation you want, so the desired behavior becomes the better option.
when: when designing player-to-player interaction
why: players repeat rewarded actions

text: Make the time players invest return real value, since games cost players time rather than money and taking time creates an obligation to give something back.
Reward only activities the player already wants to do, because this leaves the core experience least damaged.
why: Rewarding wanted activities does not displace intrinsic motivation

text: Rewards alignment is how closely the activities a reward system encourages match those the player would pursue without it.
Risk is uncertainty where the player knows what kind of unknown lies ahead, giving incomplete information that can be used to infer what to do.
when: when describing uncertainty that players can reason about
why: Partial knowledge lets players make informed decisions despite the gap.

text: Progression rewards can be power gains, access to new areas or levels, or story advancement.
Games with near-identical mechanics but public versus hidden scoring differ sharply: with hidden victory points players disagree about standings and coordinated attacks on leaders are much rarer.
Games use ten reward types: praise, points, prolonged play, gateway, spectacle, expression, powers, resources, status, and completion.
why: Each type fulfills a different player desire, and most games combine several of them.

text: No scoring system is perfect or balanced in an absolute sense; changing it alters emphasis and does not make the game wrong.
Rewarding many metrics attracts a broader audience than rewarding only the most competitive players.
when: PvP games that have cooperative or team features
why: Celebrating only the top killer leaves support and other players without recognition; varied metrics give each role a way to matter.

text: A simple scoring rule that gives +1 per opponent beaten and -1 per opponent lost to matches more complex rules in plain multiplayer rock-paper-scissors, but diverges once outcomes are weighted unequally.
when: Scoring a multiplayer intransitive game
why: Unequal weights change net scores in mixed rounds

text: Award points for damage the player's own vehicle takes, so hitting obstacles feels rewarding instead of penalized.
why: Collisions then carry no penalty, so the player's feeling about impacts stays positive whether or not they hit something.

text: Non-zero-sum games often use subtler gradations of reward and loss, such as ranking systems, player statistics, or multiple objectives.
why: Measurable results can be produced without a finite win-or-lose verdict.

text: When points come only in a few rounds and later rounds are worth more, the mid-game leader is not necessarily in control.
why: Later rounds are worth more, so an early lead is only a minor advantage.

text: A high-skill option can yield greater benefit than a simple option when used well, but penalizes poor execution.
when: Choosing between a demanding control scheme and an automatic one.
why: Higher reward for skilled use rewards mastery while keeping the simpler option viable.

text: Game systems can attach auxiliary rewards to dull, repetitive factual material, carrying learners through drilling.
when: content is inherently repetitive, such as times tables or state capitals
why: Rewards make repetition worth doing

text: Granular scoring always leaves a reachable small improvement, so players at every skill level have a next goal.
why: Scores scale upward with skill, so a small gain stays available at any level.

text: Good tutorials mix reward types (glory, access, narrative, sustenance), even within short stretches; giving every reward one type, such as prizes for the right action, limits motivation.
when: When designing reward structure for early play, or when every tutorial reward has the same form
why: Mixing reward types keeps early play satisfying and tied to mechanics; a single reward type gives players only one kind of motivation

text: Treating skill as one score hides how games differ in kind and in skill cap.
when: Rating or comparing game skill
why: A single number merges unlike skills.

text: Rewarding an immoral act while making the virtuous alternative impossible raises ethical concerns, especially when the act echoes real-world violence.
when: When the game offers no virtuous alternative to the rewarded immoral act
why: Rewards and punishments define what the game sanctions, so the only route that pays well becomes the harmful one.

text: Haphazardly applied rewards can corrupt, warp, and ruin the central essence of play, leaving behavior without the feeling it should carry.
why: Extrinsic rewards separate from the activity can displace the satisfaction the activity already gives.

text: Place fixed level transitions first, then scatter power-based rewards through the stretches between them.
when: Planning reward timing across a game
why: Fixed transitions are easy to plan, while power rewards can fill the gaps.

text: Avoid hidden achievements, since players cannot demonstrate the rewarded skill without outside hints.
when: Designing achievements that reward skill
why: Players who never learn the condition must rely on a guide or FAQ.

text: Reward attacking by tying income, card draws and bonuses to conquest, so that holding territory and winning fights pays off.
when: in territory or conquest games
why: gives players a reason to act instead of hiding

text: Celebrate civil players by letting others express sympathy toward them or by offering benevolent teammates a desirable ranking status.
Rewarding perseverance and thanking players for engagement, such as with a daily chest, is an acceptable retention approach.
when: When the reward thanks players for engaging and does not punish them for stepping away.

text: Use rewards as feedback on performance and progression, not as the main source of engagement.
why: Extrinsic rewards that are withdrawn can take the drive to continue an activity along with them.

text: Describe scoring and win conditions separately for single player, multiplayer, and each competitive mode.
Role-playing games centre on creating and growing characters within rich, quest-driven stories.
Role-playing games offer roles such as healers, fighters, and magic wielders that define basic abilities, and players often create several characters to try different roles.
Traditional RPGs are expected to offer a vast realm to explore.
To push an object toward its role, raise the stats that serve that role and lower the stats that work against it; a glass cannon maximizes damage and minimizes damage-soaking.
when: once the object's role is defined
why: Stats are chosen to serve the intended function, so the role determines which numbers to set.

text: Changing which role the player controls can transform a familiar game concept into a new kind of game and unlock new gameplay areas.
