when: when rethinking a game concept
why: Switching the controlled role changes what the game is about, opening gameplay areas never considered.

text: Roguelikes combine character leveling with arcade-style punishment, so power resets each run while player skill accumulates across runs.
when: Games with permadeath, where death deletes the character and the player restarts from scratch.
why: Deaths teach the player, so skill grows across runs even as the character's power is lost.

text: An attribute that boosts only one role becomes a god stat for that role and a dump stat for the others, breaking role balance.
when: Designing attributes for distinct team roles.

text: 1) Give each character exactly three attributes. 2) Ensure every attribute has some value to all three roles. 3) Describe each attribute's general effect, not exact numbers.
when: Designing attributes for a multi-role team game.
why: Every attribute stays meaningful across roles.

text: 1) Take a familiar game concept. 2) Ask what would happen if the player controlled a different entity in it. 3) Define that entity's goal. 4) Test whether the new role yields new play.
Rules can be enforced by players' fair play, other players, an impartial referee, or code; traditional games rely on players or a referee, while computer games enforce rules themselves.
Players try hard to solve games but resent the designer once solved, since solved games lack uncertainty, victory, or defeat; play becomes following fixed steps to a guaranteed result.
when: When a game has a known winning method that guarantees the result
why: Players value gaining new skill, and a solved game leaves nothing further to learn or risk.

text: Rough, unpolished games often draw more honest player feedback than finished-looking ones.
when: When testing early prototypes with caveats given up front.
why: Players feel free to criticize work that is visibly unfinished.

text: Players exploit any rule that rewards them, so friendly fire invites trolling, body blocking lets players trap others, and loot for last hits encourages credit stealing.
when: Designing multiplayer rules, rewards, or social channels
why: Many players min-max, seeking maximum gain for minimum effort, sometimes at others' expense

text: Players who learn of a shortcut past a low-interest stretch tend to prefer it, as it seems more fun.
when: when a dull stretch has an available shortcut
why: the shortcut seems more fun than the dull stretch

text: Players do not expect perfect accuracy, and loopholes often prompt questions about why the real world differs, which can lead to deep insight.
when: when a simulation departs from reality
why: Loopholes provoke questions about real-world differences, and those questions can lead to deep insight.

text: Players who exploit save and reload follow the systems as designed but do not play the game as intended.
when: save and reload exploitation
why: The systems permit the behavior.

text: Sparse spacing with no gameplay function can lull players into a zoned-out state and lead to disengagement.
when: Objects are far apart and movement has no gameplay purpose.
why: Long stretches of purposeless movement remove the demand for attention.

text: Safe settlements let new players assess their options before entering dangerous areas.
when: A new player arrives in a hostile open world
why: Protection removes the pressure to act immediately

text: Players expect fair resource spacing from design conventions and predict when supplies appear, so fiction implying long scarcity gaps often fails to create tension.
when: fiction implies scarcity
why: Players trust genre conventions over the fiction's logic.

text: Rules are arbitrary relationships between abstract variables, such as a coin's value; out of context a rule makes little sense, but it gives objects and actions purpose within its system.
why: Objects have no value outside their game system; meaning comes from relationships within it.

text: Within a game, rules are the rigid structure and play is the player's freedom to act inside them, which is the source of emergent experience.
Game feel as a skill covers the progression from clumsiness with unfamiliar controls to triumph over challenge and the joy of mastery.

Situational reinvention begins once manual skills are mostly unconscious, and players then decide whom to target, when to act, and how to counter patterns; most players and most design sit at this level.
Serendipity is the positive form of an unknown unknown, such as players loving a minor character, inventing a new tactic, or finding emotion in an overlooked part of the game.
Most games are closed, formal systems that clearly separate in-game elements from outside forces; outcomes, including simulated destruction, have no real consequences outside them.
Rules alone do not explain a game's immersive effect; it comes from the human mind responding to the rules.
Medium- and high-level rules that assign meaning to objects and interactions can make everyday actions more rewarding throughout a game.
Rules and territorial limits act as boundaries, and a game without rules does not function as a game.
Rule design is usually harder than level design, and reusable rule sets can generate thousands of puzzles while some rule sets yield only one.
Rule authority rests on players' implicit agreement to submit to the experience; a player who ignores the rules is no longer playing the game.
A rule-based system has the same three parts as a blackboard: a database playing the blackboard role, rules acting as experts, and an arbiter.
Rules define a game's space, timing, objects, actions, consequences, constraints, and goals; the goals supply its purpose.
Rules change how players perceive objects, define challenges and modify the sensation of control; they are independent of the other metrics but reinforced by them.
Point-and-click adventure games lack a mechanical core because their experience is driven by content, making them exceptions to the core approach.
Consider spectator modes when designing play, since many people enjoy watching others play.
why: Players can gain equal enjoyment without taking the same active role, so watching often satisfies people.

text: Don't introduce two demanding mechanics back to back in the tutorial.
when: ordering the tutorial sequence
why: Each hard feature demands learning effort, and fewer features can be taught alongside it.

text: If players must decide how the rules apply, the system is probably not internally complete.
Technical limits can sharpen design focus, and some of the most inventive computer games were made on primitive systems.
when: When the platform's technical capabilities are very limited
why: Restricting yourself to basics helps ideas become clearer and more focused.

text: Economic rules shape how a game feels: scarce resources and winner-take-all auctions make play cutthroat, while constant trading and negotiation make play collaborative.
when: In games that have an in-game economy of resources and trades
why: Rules change which actions are attractive, and those actions set the play style.

text: Identical mechanics can take different emotional labels depending on the fiction, such as terror in a zombie horror game or gritty determination in a military game.
when: When pairing mechanics with a theme.
why: The fiction determines how the same arousal is interpreted.

text: Letting players watch a hazard from a safe distance, without interacting with it, lets them learn the threat before facing it.
when: when a hazard could disorient or harm the player if met first
why: observation teaches the threat at no cost

text: A game rule that forces a response to a felt state, such as putting on gloves when hands get too cold, builds that feeling into play.
when: When a particular sensation is central to the game's experience
why: Rules can deliver a felt experience even when the real-world event never happened, so it becomes part of play.

text: Constraints remove motions from the possibility space rather than emphasizing others, shifting which skills the challenge requires.
when: When exploring a new control mapping for a prototype

text: When each basic action changes which spaces are threatened or enterable, the effective game space shifts with every move, making new strategic actions likely to appear.
when: Designing basic actions
why: Changed constraints alter what other actions are possible.

text: Changing a single rule, such as a reward for collecting items, can alter game feel in subtle but measurable ways, including how collecting and steering through a level feels.
when: When a reward or incentive is attached to an action like collecting items
why: Rules shape the purpose and intent behind player actions

text: When one option wins short fights and another wins long ones, players must forecast fight length, which makes the choice an emotionally meaningful judgment.
when: When a choice between options is decided by the expected duration of the encounter
why: Each option's advantage depends on the condition.

text: Three rule levels combine to convey overall feel: high-level rules give objects meaning, medium-level rules give actions special meaning, low-level rules define physical properties such as mass and toughness.
when: when analysing or designing how rules shape play and feel
why: Each level shapes the play experience in a different way.

text: Conditional rules follow the pattern: if a specified circumstance occurs, a defined result follows.
Treat play boundaries as two sets: limits set by the design within the play space, and limits physical reality places on that space.
when: In digital games with unbounded virtual space
why: Virtual space lacks set limits, so physical reality is the only hard boundary the design must respect.

text: Difficulty is multi-dimensional: one game may be hard for one player through reaction speed, for another through spatial navigation, and for a third through story comprehension.
when: When adapting a game to players with unbalanced skill sets
why: Players' skill sets are unbalanced, so one game can challenge each player along different dimensions.

text: Adding rules to fix a balance problem can substitute for understanding why the problem exists.
when: When tempted to add rules to force a desired behavior
why: Forced rules bypass the effect that would arise naturally from the game's interactions.

text: Breaking rules the designer has set damages the player's sense of the world more than having few rules at all.
when: When a game portrays objects as having certain physical properties
why: Players build expectations from the rules and feel betrayed when they fail.

text: Unclosed loopholes let players exploit rules, so a rule may be needed to block an action that would otherwise defeat the game's intent.
when: When players could exploit an unstated gap in a rule
why: Without the explicit rule, a player could argue that an intended penalty becomes a reward.

text: A designer system must create a game's rules, not only its content, which makes autonomous design harder.
when: When procedural generation moves from producing content toward fully autonomous design

text: Changing rules constantly makes prediction impossible, so players cannot learn from earlier outcomes.
when: When players are meant to make decisions whose outcomes matter
why: Without some foresight players cannot plan, so the thinking that makes a choice meaningful disappears and play becomes simple reaction.

text: 1) Note any house rules or laws forming during development. 2) Check whether modes simplify or complicate the game. 3) Identify who enforces each rule. 4) If players are confused, decide whether to change the rule or explain it better.
when: when reviewing a game's rule structure

text: 1) Define high-level rules that gate new areas and story to drive progression. 2) Define medium-level rules linking resources and combat choices. 3) Define low-level rules setting damage and health numbers.
when: when layering a game's rules from progression down to numbers
why: Layers work together to shape which skills players develop

text: Enforce rules through the design of space, objects, and actions so that forbidden moves simply cannot happen.
why: Players then need not memorize prohibitions, because a forbidden move is simply unavailable, so the rule works as a physical limit of the world.

text: Offer a short curated list of options that still lets players choose, rather than an open field or a long catalogue.
when: Players may be overwhelmed or the designer needs predictable choices
why: Short lists still feel like choice and steer players toward chosen outcomes

text: Rules must be clear to players, or in digital games intuitively grasped, so the game feels fair.
when: In digital games where the system adjudicates rules for players, so rules are grasped through play
why: Players then perceive outcomes as fair and as responding sensibly to what they did.

text: Forbid actions that cause a player to lose by accident, such as moving one's king into check in chess.
why: Accidental self-defeat is unlikely to be the intended outcome of play.

text: Build designs by adding and removing constraints rather than editing raw geometry, so that edits stay consistent across the design.
why: A change made to a shared original automatically flows through every drawing or design that uses it, keeping them consistent.

text: A constrained possibility space offers mastery of a defined path, while a larger space offers more choice, creative solutions, and replayability that appeal to certain player types.
when: choose based on whether the appeal is mastery or creative exploration
why: Some players find satisfaction in mastering a fixed set of outcomes, while adding interacting objects widens choice, creativity and replayability.

text: Subclass Sandbox is closely related to Update Method and Template Method, and to Facade; Template Method reverses which class holds the composing method.
Give the base class protected getters for the state a sandbox method needs, so the method can branch on game state.
when: Subclass behavior depends on current state such as position.
why: Getters let the composed method use real control flow instead of only fixed data.

text: Subclass Sandbox has a base class define one abstract protected sandbox method plus protected provided operations, so derived classes implement behavior using only those operations.
why: The pattern concentrates coupling to outside systems inside the base class.

text: Modeling each variant as a subclass with hard-coded stats forces a code change and recompile for every number tweak and makes designers dependent on programmers.
when: Variants differ mostly by numeric data and are each a separate class.
why: Stats are compiled into code, so every balance change needs a programmer.

text: Serious games are games designed to educate, train, or persuade, using game elements to engage players with weighty real-world themes.
An indie game jam is a short shared weekend in which designers and programmers rapidly build experimental games on a common engine, offering a break from long, conservative commercial schedules.
A game is a system of knowledge, so the core design work is inventing and refining that knowledge, while implementation is secondary.
Game programming stresses speed, borrows heavily from other disciplines, and modifies borrowed techniques substantially.

A game curriculum should cover seven areas: game design and programming; visual and audio design; interactive storytelling; production; the games business; critical game studies; and games in society.
Later jams added artists, sound designers, game theorists, and educators alongside designers and programmers.
Licensed projects offer a safe setting in which to learn production and narrative design.
Game development generates very large amounts of knowledge constantly, including tacit skill that practitioners cannot fully explain.
War games and simulations are central to military education because they make abstract concepts concrete.
Simulations act as final exams in emergency services, earth science, building design, and administration.
A meta-analysis found serious games produced a small but positive gain in science learning versus conventional teaching.
Write game-specific questions rather than relying on generic ones.
when: When collecting playtester feedback on a specific game
why: Questions aimed at the areas where the designer needs input produce more useful answers than generic ones.

text: Before adopting learning, estimate total effort including data preparation and validation, not just the algorithm itself.
when: Deciding whether to use a learning approach.
why: Hand-holding costs can make the project more expensive rather than cheaper.

text: An internship or apprenticeship shows real industry pressure and builds teamwork, communication, and professionalism.
when: Evaluating a game program
why: Working under real industry pressure shows students what the job demands and lets them practice teamwork, communication and professionalism.

text: Use a short jam to generate and test ideas quickly when research time or budget is limited.
when: Research time or budget is limited
why: A jam compresses exploration into a short window, letting people quickly try out new ideas and see what works.

text: Include a short concrete gameplay example, such as a scene with a choice, to show how mechanics and story combine.
when: Writing a game design document
why: A concrete scene makes abstract systems easier to grasp

text: The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends infants avoid screen media other than video chat until 18 months, with about one hour per day of high-quality content for ages 2 to 5.
when: when advising parents on children's screen use
why: Toddlers under two struggle to relate video content to real life and learn more from adults in person, and screen time displaces that human interaction.

text: Schooling mirrors game structure: students are players, assignments are goals, due dates are time limits, and grades are scores.
In schools, escalating challenges act as level progression, the final exam acts as a boss, and the honor roll acts as a leaderboard.
why: The final exam can be passed only by mastering every skill taught, so it works as a gate that requires full mastery of the earlier challenges.

text: A weekend is usually too short to build deep, engrossing games, and many participants must return to their day jobs.
why: Participants have limited technical skills, tools and time, and many must return to day jobs before finishing.

text: Assuming a serious game or gamification label guarantees both learning and fun is a mistake; some measured educational games are not fun enough to be called games.
why: Decorating dull content with animations and badges appeals to extrinsic motives but does not make it engaging, and engaging games are hard to build.

text: 1) Record a meaningful play moment in detail. 2) Note what you thought, felt and did. 3) Identify which rules and systems produced that moment.
when: when keeping a designer's game journal
why: Writing about meaningful moments builds a designer's own way of thinking about games, much as sketching builds an artist's skill.

text: 1) Play games you know. 2) Analyze each using its formal elements. 3) Record the analysis in a journal to build understanding of gameplay.
when: when beginning as a designer
why: The journal builds the ability to articulate complex game concepts.

text: 1) Play a game with a group. 2) Write a formal, dramatic, and dynamic analysis of it. 3) Watch a group that has never played it learn without explanation. 4) Note how they learn and what impressions they form.
why: Board game mechanics are visible on the surface rather than hidden in code, so they can be observed and taken apart.

text: 1) Prepare a formal presentation of a game's elements. 2) Back it with a detailed walkthrough. 3) Present to an audience. 4) Lead a public discussion.
when: When critically analyzing a game with peers
why: Public debate sharpens critical skills and generates new ideas.

text: Teach preproduction skills through short hands-on workshops rather than lectures, because teams need practice and success to form lasting habits.
why: Teams already understand their problems; lasting habits come from practicing techniques and succeeding with them, which handouts and lectures do not supply.

text: Analyze games by their underlying systems, breaking each into formal, dramatic, and dynamic elements, rather than listing top-level features or judging how cool they seem.
when: When keeping a game journal or critiquing games
why: Surface-level feature review yields little design insight.

text: Match a game program to your target role: programmers need strong programming courses, and visual designers need many visual design courses.
when: Choosing an academic game program
why: Role-specific coursework builds the skills that role uses

text: Look for programs offering teamwork, rapid prototyping and iteration, serious student responsibilities, cross-discipline collaboration, and teaching that handles multidisciplinary work.
why: Productions increasingly rely on many kinds of media professionals whom a designer must direct and support, so the program should prepare collaboration across fields.

text: Combine a contextual review, practitioner experience, and a sample of games across platforms and genres when studying game environments.
When combat makes sketching impossible, keep a gameplay journal and write notes right after each session or level.
when: during intense play
why: Notes written soon after play stay accurate.

text: Serious games must be engaging and must enable transfer of learning, not only deliver rewards.
when: Serious games aimed at learning, health, or behaviour change
why: Bolting rewards onto a dull task does not make it engaging enough.

text: A rotation can be represented as a 3D vector whose direction is the rotation axis and whose length is the angular speed in radians per second.
The ship simulation is driven by rotation, position, velocity, thrust speed, thrust acceleration, thrust velocity and max thrust speed, with thrust velocity added to velocity while thrust is held.
when: building a thrust-driven ship simulation
why: Separating these named values lets rotation, thrust and velocity be tuned independently.

text: Simulation and building games manage resources to grow a company, city, or other system, focusing on growth rather than conquest.
A simulation's construction determines which tunings are possible; tuning values alone cannot produce a different structure.
Simulated inertia, where thrust adds force along facing and turning sets orientation directly, gives a ship a flowing feel that can outsell simpler designs.
Holding the run button does not raise top running speed in this design; speed is set by the simulation rather than button duration.
The side somersault reaches about five times the character's height and keeps the character airborne for more than one second.
Mario-style games simulate Newtonian forces only to the extent their mechanics need, which is top-down design rather than physics-game design.
A football game can model movement mechanics, play strategy, and individual athletes' performance, while a city simulator can model residents, workers, the economy, crime, and pollution.
Simple Boolean buttons with a clear mapping to movement are satisfying and easy to follow, and using several inputs at once keeps players engaged.
when: designing a control scheme for a small set of actions
why: Clear one-to-one mappings are easy to learn, and multi-finger coordination adds challenge.

text: In physics-driven games, most of the feel comes from the underlying simulation, so tune it before adding content.
Simulating muscles rather than arbitrary forces is an unexplored option for building complex physical responses in games.
Learners may adopt a technique that works only inside the simulation and fail when applying it in reality.
when: simulation used without debrief
why: Simulation flaws can make a technique look valid.

text: Choose one key transformation and execute it especially well rather than spreading effort across many goals.
when: When tempted to make one game replace an entire curriculum

text: Aim simulation at an interesting, self-consistent and stable result that serves entertainment, not at realism for its own sake.
why: Players judge realism by consistency and stability, and reality itself is rarely fun.

text: Visual-only simulation changes how a game looks, while mechanic-linked simulation changes play; simulate detail only where it affects play, since non-gameplay destructible scenery adds little.
when: when deciding how much physics a game needs or scoping physics simulation
why: Only mechanic-linked simulation alters decisions and outcomes.

text: A simple, internally consistent model works better than a detailed model whose rules conflict with each other.
when: When choosing how much detail a game world simulates.
why: Inconsistent detail breaks trust in the rules.

text: Movement actions are larger requests such as running for cover or chasing a target, staged into primitive actions like applying a force that physics or an animation controller executes.
when: Classifying AI actions
why: High-level movement goals decompose into low-level primitives executed by other systems.

text: Mental skills include memory, observation, and puzzle solving.
Use fine-grained interaction when you want players to outdo each other in precise knowledge rather than memorized counters, since this raises the skill ceiling.
when: designing games meant to deepen with mastery
why: Precise, continuous choices reward understanding over memorization.

text: 1) Should characters be individuals or only group effects? 2) Must movement look realistic, or can characters be placed directly? 3) Is physical simulation needed? 4) Must they plan routes, or only wander, follow paths or chase? 5) Do they need formations or coordination?
when: When designing movement and behaviour for AI-controlled characters in a game.

text: Muscle-based control is a largely unexplored model because it is hard to design for and hard to play, which limits its adoption.
A game's skill range is the span of skill levels at which it offers meaningful challenge, often through twitch, tactical or profound decisions.
A skill-only arcade challenge gives no power gain, so the goal is to survive as long as possible rather than to finish.
The skill ceiling is the highest level of performance a player can reach, beyond which no way to improve exists.
Skill challenge requires new ways of playing, such as smarter enemy AI, new challenge types, or puzzles that combine several skills.
why: New skill demands raise difficulty beyond raw power.

text: A game's skill ceiling is set by the scope of its largest decisions.
Chess is probably limitlessly deep, since human-computer teams beat human grandmasters, while tic-tac-toe has a low ceiling because perfect play is easy to learn.
Skill ranges can be stretched by reinvention, elastic challenges, training, emotional life support, and difficulty modification.

1) Identify the lower skill limit, below which the game becomes frustrating. 2) Identify the ceiling past which play turns tedious. 3) Decide whether and how to widen these limits to include more players.
when: When analyzing a game's target audience.
why: Flow-friendly challenge sits between frustration and boredom, and that band shifts from player to player.

text: 1) Let players practice solo before group play. 2) Ensure newcomers never hold critical group roles early. 3) Offer single-player modes where failure harms no one.
when: games with group roles or skill-sensitive team play
why: Players learn where failure hurts no one before facing skilled peers.

text: Aim for a skill that is intuitive and easy to learn yet deep, expressive and fresh across many challenges.
why: Actions with predictable results, clear goals and immediate feedback read as challenge rather than arbitrary noise.

text: A deliberate skill plateau suits games meant to be learned fast or dropped after learning, while a rising skill curve suits games meant to be mastered.
why: Deep, interacting mechanics keep a loop of mastery desire pushing complexity and player skill upward.

text: A character may lack a skill entirely, while every character has a score in every attribute.
Skill and luck are often inversely correlated across games, but not always.
Casual, luck-based games tend to be shorter, while deep strategic games can sustain longer play.
when: when setting game length
why: depth of skill gives play more room to extend

text: Balance skill and chance for the target audience, and replace tedious or overly random parts with skill or strategy so players feel in control.
when: Tuning how much outcomes depend on skill versus luck
why: Players feel more in control when outcomes depend on skill, and chance can liven tedious sections

text: The skills that make a design entertaining can equally be used to exploit players.
why: the same techniques serve delight or manipulation

text: When success depends on player skill, the player works out how to defeat the challenge, producing a sense of personal accomplishment.
why: The player, not a character, resolves the built-up tension, so the accomplishment is theirs.

text: Although thousands of skills exist, they group into three categories: physical, mental, and social.
Skill and luck are two independent axes, not opposite ends of one line; a game can have much or little of each.
Too much chance negates the effect of player skill, and too much skill negates the role of chance.
why: Each force weakens the other when either dominates.

text: 1) List the skills the game requires. 2) Check for missing skill categories. 3) Identify dominant skills. 4) Check whether skill gaps make the game feel unfair. 5) Check that players can improve and reach mastery at a suitable challenge level.
when: when reviewing a game's skill demands
why: Exercising a skill stays enjoyable only when the skill is rewarding and challenge needs to fall in a band that is neither dull nor overwhelming.

text: Games of skill feel like contests that identify the best player, while games of chance feel relaxed because fate decides much of the outcome.
when: Choosing the balance between player skill and randomness.
why: Each emphasis creates a different experience and suits different players.

text: A game is solvable when one best action is knowable in every state, even if it does not always succeed; deterministic, perfect-information, transitive games are at least theoretically solvable.
Solvability does not require an action to always succeed; a game is solved when one action succeeds more often than any alternative, and the solution may state that probability.
when: Non-deterministic games.

text: A solution objective rewards solving a problem or puzzle faster than competitors.
Tic-tac-toe has a very small game tree: with optimal play, the first player can always win or tie, and the second player always can at least tie.
Turn-based strategy games often exceed what tree search handles alone, so they need supplementary techniques.

Games are trivially solvable (a human can solve them in play or by memorizing best moves), theoretically solvable (a human could in principle, but time or space size prevents it), or computationally solvable (only a computer can).
when: Classifying a game's solvability before judging its balance.
why: The type determines which balance evaluation methods are feasible.

text: Once a dominant strategy is found, players stop making real decisions and the game's puzzle is solved.
when: A dominant option goes unaddressed
why: Removing the need to decide ends engagement

text: Defining games by strict closure excludes open-ended designs, so a game definition should allow for them.
when: when defining or categorizing game designs
why: Not every game has strict closure.

text: 1) Assign each option its own fuzzy set. 2) Compute each set's membership. 3) Output the option whose set has the highest membership.
when: Output options are unrelated categories, such as eat, sleep or watch
why: Unordered options have no numeric scale, so comparing memberships directly picks the strongest choice.

text: 1) Build the payoff table. 2) Remove dominated rows and columns by pairwise comparison until none remain. 3) Find intransitive loops by following best responses and drop options outside loops. 4) Write payoff equations, setting payoffs equal for each player and summing probabilities to 1. 5) Solve for every unknown. 6) Keep probabilities between 0 and 1 that are uniquely determined as the optimal mix. 7) Sum player values to classify the game as zero-sum, positive-sum, or negative-sum.
when: Solving a finite intransitive game with a payoff table

text: 1) Write one payoff equation per throw. 2) Eliminate one probability using the sum-to-one constraint. 3) Substitute into the remaining equations to get a single-variable polynomial. 4) Solve it and reject any root that gives a negative probability.
when: When a rock-paper-scissors-style mix leaves three equations in two unknowns.
why: probabilities cannot be negative

text: A discrete game space has only certain positions that matter, while a continuous space has meaningful positions throughout its area.
Discrete game time advances in turns with no meaningful time between them, while continuous time is measured by real clock time.
Moving from 2D to 3D expands movement and camera options, so a few variable changes can yield very different experiences; treating the shift as minor underestimates its design impact.
when: When a game's player character moves from 2D to 3D

text: 1) Check inventory breadth: does the player have several options? 2) Check cover: can the player block, hide, or retreat? 3) Check movement: can they reach cover quickly without lag? 4) Check each enemy has a counter or protection. 5) Check options exist at close and long range. 6) Check threats are predictable enough to plan against.
when: grid-based or discrete-space games
why: These checks catch missing counters in turn-based and tile-based combat.

text: Longer matches create stronger special pieces: four in a line, five in a T or L shape, and five in a straight line each yield a different special piece.
Special-piece explosions often scale with the number of pieces they clear, so setups that clear more pieces are rewarded.
Patching a problem with special-case rules to protect a favored idea produces inelegant design.
when: When a favored concept turns out unbalanced in testing and cannot be tuned
why: Layered special cases hide imbalance in a pet concept instead of fixing its underlying design.

text: Projects with special purposes need extra filters; an educational game must also check that it actually teaches what it is meant to teach.
when: projects with goals beyond entertainment
why: A design is only finished when it passes every applicable filter, so goals beyond fun add checks that cannot be skipped.

text: A force field around each spawn blocks entry and destroys lingerers, making spawns safe, but several campers can still wait nearby.
Sports games simulate real sports, usually following real rules, and often include team, season, and tournament modes.
Sports games cover a wide range, from large franchises to simulators of single sports such as pool.
Competitive play has used specialized fields for thousands of years, including chariot racing, boxing, team sports, and courtrooms.
Newer sports games take more creative liberty with real rules and formats.
Traditional sports can contain degenerate strategies too, not only games designed for play.
Switching a turn-based or sequential contest to real time makes reaction speed decide the result.
A stripped-down mode that keeps only one core element can remain popular, suggesting the core itself can carry the game's appeal.
A multiplayer game that a single player can master alone diminishes the value of community.
when: When a multiplayer game lets individuals succeed without others
why: Community needs situations where success depends on others, and a game that is solo-masterable removes that dependence.

text: Each combat mode should feel fulfilling on its own, so a player who never switches still has a satisfying experience.
when: When designing a game with melee and ranged combat

text: A dump stat can be safely ignored, so investing points in it is wasted.
Static attributes never change during play, while dynamic attributes change during play and matter most to design.
Slots take many forms: RPG gear such as weapons, armor, and magic items, FPS main weapons, sidearms, and gear or grenade slots, and limited equipped skills from a larger pool.
Stat setters that take a target index and a value, for health, wisdom and agility, cover a surprisingly wide range of magical effects.
when: Designing spell effects that modify character stats
why: Few primitives can express many distinct effects when combined with varying values.

text: Different design details produce different valid dependency stacks for the same game.
The dependency stack method can be applied to one system or subsystem, not only to a whole game.
In a creature set, power plus toughness often equaled total mana cost plus a fixed constant, with a few exceptions.
when: creature sets with a consistent design pattern

text: In CRPGs, player power rises faster than player skill.
Leave players unable to max every stat; aim for one or two exceptional stats, several high, most mid-level, and one low, so choices stay meaningful.
why: Maxing every stat removes the meaning of choosing between them.

text: A dull skill can be made engaging by framing it as a virtual skill and giving it the right challenge.
when: when a required skill feels tedious
why: Exercising skills is joyful only when the skills are interesting, rewarding, and set at a balanced challenge level.

text: Successful small games usually concentrate on one or two values that rise sharply above competitors, forming tall narrow spikes on a value curve.
when: When evaluating a design's value profile
why: A spike shows a clear, superior reason to play; flat profiles offer none.

text: Use the dependency stack to decide what to build now and what to postpone, as a practical decision tool rather than an academic exercise.
when: When a design has too many interdependent elements to analyze completely
why: Ignoring the weakest dependencies avoids analysis paralysis and keeps focus on the strongest, most dangerous ones.

text: As a starting point, set single-class power at 1.5× dual-class power, then tune through playtesting.
when: versatility is valuable but not certain
why: Dual-class value falls between the no-foreknowledge and full-foreknowledge extremes, so a 1.5 ratio is a reasonable starting point.

text: Stacking several triggers that drive the same feeling pushes the experience toward one emotional peak that no single trigger could reach alone.
when: When designing for a single dominant emotion.
why: Each trigger adds to the same emotional direction, compounding intensity.

text: Personality labels earned from events, such as marriage or winning battles, can grant bonuses and weaknesses, tying flavor directly to the systems.
when: When named characters have individual histories tracked by the game
why: Tracking individual records lets players read their own stories into events, tying flavor to the systems.

text: Dual-class power per class ranges from half of single-class power, with no foreknowledge, to equal power, with complete foreknowledge; real cases fall between.
when: When judging how much players know about the challenges they will face
why: Players with no foreknowledge need coverage from both classes, while players with full foreknowledge need only one.

text: If one attribute is clearly stronger than the rest, players concentrate their points in it, so the relative power of attributes must be checked.
when: In a point-buy attribute system where players spend points to raise attributes
why: Players optimize toward the strongest option.

text: Every character has every stat, so each stat should be meaningful for all viable builds.
when: For core stats that every character possesses
why: Every character has each stat by definition, so each stat always shapes every build's decisions.

text: Keep variant stats out of compiled code so numbers can change without recompiling the game.
when: Designers tune numeric values for many variants.
why: Recompiling for each change makes programmers a bottleneck.

text: The commander problem, also called the alpha player problem, occurs when one player takes over decisions and directs others by rote in a multiplayer co-op PvE game.
A complex strategy is a set of contingencies, with a planned response for each reaction an opponent might make.
Chess is negative sum: it has no reinforcements, captures are the only way pieces leave the board, and equal trades give a mild edge to the side ahead.
Each chess unit has a color, rank, location, and set of behaviors, and every move changes unit locations so relationships between units change constantly.
The commander problem only arises when every player knows the same game-state information, because private information leaves no one able to decide for others.
when: When designing co-op games with shared state
why: Shared knowledge lets one player direct others

text: Competition for status combined with complex strategies leads players to share and discuss tactics, so rivalry can deepen community.
when: when a game pairs competitive ranking with deep strategy
why: Complex strategies give competitors reasons to exchange tactics, so rivalry turns into shared discussion.

text: Each race should keep only units that are meaningful and distinct, rather than filling it with 20 to 30 units; races can share some unit types but should differ in how they use them.
when: designing multiple playable factions or races
why: Too many similar units dilute each race's identity and make balance harder to control.

text: Three mechanical fixes for the commander problem are real-time play, privileged information and restricted communication, and they can be used alone or together.
when: When one player dominates decisions in a co-op game
why: Restricted communication forces each player to decide for themselves, making what is shared a scarce, critical choice.

text: Strategic actions are specific plans built from basic actions toward a goal; they range from simple to complex and are meaningful only within the larger picture of play.
Strategy games centre on tactics, planning, and managing units and resources, often with themes of conquest, exploration, or trade.
Most turn-based strategy titles hold imperfect information because actions involve skill checks or combat randomness.
A game's list of strategic actions is usually longer than its list of basic actions.
Strategies learned in playful contexts were more likely to transfer to other contexts than strategies learned in formal instruction.
When strategies can be mixed in fine increments, the strategy space becomes nearly continuous, and each blend requires a precisely fitted response that only experts can find.
when: games with fine-grained unit or resource counts
why: Fine increments make the number of possible strategies nearly infinite.

text: Comparing strategic moves against routine moves gives a loose, judgment-based gauge of how much emergent play exists.
why: Strategic actions arise from interactions rather than written rules, so counting them gauges how much emergence the game has.

text: The number of strategic actions scales roughly with subjects, verbs, and objects multiplied together, so growing any of the three multiplies the emergent possibilities.
when: Estimating a game's strategic depth
why: Each combination of subject, verb, and object can yield a distinct action.

text: Simple patterns like rock-paper-scissors and matching pennies form a skeleton, while yomi adds the deceptive prediction layer that makes the game feel alive.
when: analyzing competitive game depth
why: Abstract structure alone does not produce mind games.

text: Requiring every version of every strategy to be equally strong is a mistake; viability is judged between strategies played well.
when: In PvP titles built to allow several approaches and routes to winning.
why: Strategies are compared at equal player skill, so a loose, unfocused build is not a fair test of its strategy.

text: Stun effects appear across many genres, from fantasy spells and nonlethal grenades to webs and physical blows, and they vary combat pace and enable follow-up attacks.
Stun must be meaningful, and the stunned player's flow must survive it; fully disabling input creates a gap players resent even when the stun is fair and fictionally sensible.
when: When designing stun or disable effects.
why: Stunned players cannot decide anything, which breaks their flow.

text: Let enemy abilities respond to situation, such as healing when health is low.
why: Situational abilities reward players who read the state of the fight.

text: A surprise outcome can reinvest players, such as an unexpected companion that proves more valuable than the promised reward.
when: When an unexpected result follows a choice the player made.
why: People enjoy surprise most when the event feels foreseeable in hindsight, and an unexpected payoff can outweigh the reward that was promised.

text: Games often encode the hot-hand idea by giving players on a streak temporary performance boosts and visual effects.
Lengthen the middle phase and shorten the final phase by tuning feedback loops or the total power in play.
when: when the end game drags
why: loops and total power shift where phases transition

text: Frame resources that enemies drop as content the player will need later, so sustenance rewards gain meaning.
when: When introducing collectible resources early
why: Explaining future use gives the reward a purpose now

text: Generating new problems over time, rather than offering only fixed goals, is what keeps players returning to a game.
why: Fresh problems give players reasons to continue

text: Break an established rule in a way that keeps the game's logic coherent while offering discovery.
when: When players probe the edges of a game world and find nothing for it.
why: Hidden surprises beyond established boundaries give a sense of discovery to players who would otherwise explore without reward.

text: Stagnation has four patterns: repetition, balance of power, loops, and no progress, each with a remedy.
when: Diagnosing why players feel stuck
why: Repeating the same kind of action masks real advancement, so the game feels at a standstill even when players are progressing.

text: Tying rewards to win streaks can make the eventual end of a streak feel like a setback that taints the whole streak experience.
when: When outcomes vary randomly and a player rides an uncharacteristically good stretch.
why: Self-serving bias makes players credit a temporary high to skill, so the later return to normal results feels like failure.

text: Rewarding only rare special targets, such as floating hoops, makes players ignore everything else and drains life from the core action system.
when: Adding bonus objectives to a core action system
why: Players optimize for the only rewarded goal and neglect the rest of the mechanics.

text: 1) Check story, rules, artwork and technology for unexpected elements. 2) Check whether the rules let players surprise each other. 3) Check whether the rules let players surprise themselves.
when: when reviewing a game for surprise
why: The brain is wired to enjoy surprise; random sprays felt more pleasurable than a fixed pattern delivering the same amount of sugar.

text: Alternate suspenseful slow planning with short bursts of rapid choice, and add enforced breaks between rounds, to sustain interest.
when: the design needs both tense, slow planning and bursts of rapid choice
why: Varied pace sustains interest across a play session

text: Systems are used to control a significant group of related gameplay toward a specific outcome, which is what makes them the unit for balance work.
A system needs all its elements; if removing a component leaves function unchanged, the set is merely a collection.
In that definition, system means interrelated elements, formal means clearly defined by rules, and closed means the system has boundaries.
Emergence is crucial to how game systems become meaningful, since complex systems let things happen that designers did not expect.
Understanding a game as a system, rather than a single story, lets designers predict how a change will affect other experiences.
when: When a designer has observed many playtests covering the game's different possible paths.
why: Each playtest reveals one branch, and only the full set of branches shows how elements interrelate and how changes will spread.

text: Game elements are interdependent, so one change can ripple through many other elements and alter the whole system.
when: When changes are made in the final phases of development.
why: Games are fragile systems.

text: When studying any activity, look beneath the surface for its objectives, rules, procedures, resources, conflict, and skills to learn.
when: When looking for game system ideas in everyday activities, hobbies, or reading.
why: Everyday pursuits already contain structured parts, such as goals, rules, and resources, that a designer can borrow as game systems.

text: Systems range from precise and predictable, with one or two outcomes, to varied and unpredictable, with countless outcomes. The designer chooses where a game sits on this range.
when: when setting how many outcomes a game can produce
why: more possible outcomes add variety but reduce predictability

text: Focusing play on a separate handheld screen visible to only one player keeps play away from the shared room and weakens group appeal at the hearth.
when: Designing hardware or features for shared home play.
why: Shared rooms need action that others can see and join.

text: A herding game moves a group of characters through a usually hostile world.
The theater venue gathers a crowd to share one sequence of events, such as plays, films, concerts, sporting events, or planetarium shows.
Graphical-logic games are built from 2D elements that move, collide, appear, and disappear, typically with a player-controlled avatar.

Extending miniature battles into character-based play created paper and digital RPG lineage; character systems, card rules and persistent worlds from tabletop design shaped digital RPGs and collectible games.
Pen-and-paper RPGs often tie each turn to in-game time, so one choice may represent a fixed span of game-world seconds regardless of real time taken.
Future trades are more common in tabletop games than in digital games.
Simple herding simulators have existed since the 1980s, and a few newer games have advanced the technique.
Real herding competitions require years of training, so a game should not demand that level of skill from players.
when: Designing herding difficulty.

text: The gaming table is a face-to-face venue for intense small-group play with board, card, and dice games, and upright digital screens are the main reason digital games have rarely settled there.
when: Designing for face-to-face small-group play.
why: Vertical screens do not suit a shared table.

text: Cheaper large touch screens and augmented reality glasses could bring digital games to the gaming table venue.
why: These technologies remove the vertical-screen barrier.

text: The hearth is the shared living-room venue where games suit groups, either because they allow shared play or because they are fun to watch.
when: Designing for group or spectated play at home.
why: Television has taken over the role of the family fireplace in this venue.

text: Physically active games that are entertaining to watch, and singing and dancing games, suit the hearth venue.
why: They engage several people in the shared room.

text: Predictions that new technology will end the shared hearth are overstated, since the hearth has persisted since the dawn of humanity.
why: Shared home gathering places have endured across technological change.

text: Actual museums increasingly add gameplay to explain what visitors are viewing.
Processing power, audio delivery and other hardware factors differ widely between VR systems.
Riddles, crosswords, chess, poker, tag, and soccer predate computers, and most new designs recombine well-known game elements.
Early adventure games were text-driven, using rich descriptions in place of graphics; later graphic adventures and modern titles blend in action.
Graphical-logic games differ from board games in near-continuous positions, short time steps, several moving NPCs at once, hidden state, and physics that keeps running when the player is idle.
A generated grid game runs for a fixed count of time steps; the player wins by reaching a set score threshold.
Games entertaining several people at the hearth work through shared play or by being watchable, while designs that cut off most of the room from the action fit poorly.
when: Designing for shared living-room play.
why: Privacy supports immersion, but the hearth is a shared social space.

text: Take a medium's power seriously and use it deliberately to nurture its audience rather than merely to entertain or dismiss it.
Virtual content placed in ordinary real-world locations can make everyday surroundings feel like a game.
when: Blending virtual and real space.

text: Strong feature concepts can combine elements from several existing genres or media, such as a game, a talent show, and a video-sharing site.
when: When pitching a new feature for an existing game

text: A hazard that holds a piece until its owner's next turn cancels the advantage of a high roll that lands there.
when: When a boat lands on the sandbar space.

text: A special piece that is harder to create but easier to use, and that clears scattered pieces, makes further chain reactions more likely.
why: The wildcard piece can match anything at any time, while the other special piece may be left unmatched when the game ends.

text: Herding games often set up species within a predator-prey web, with the player working to keep one or more prey species safe.
A text adventure's core is a loop that reads a command, handles it, and repeats, doing nothing while it waits for the next command.
when: Structuring an input-driven game
why: The program must wait for each player command, taking turns like a conversation, so it idles until the next input arrives.

text: Teach mechanics through environment art and object placement, not just decoration, since many players skip manuals; show cause-and-effect procedures and let placements explain the world.
why: Players are conditioned to pick up items they see on the ground, so placing unusable items in the world can teach what cannot be used.

text: Obvious tutorials, text messages, hints, or the game talking at the player pull players out of the game and make them feel controlled and powerless.
why: Training that is noticeable interferes with the rest of the experience, so the most effective training goes unnoticed.

text: Do not interrupt play to explain; teach a mechanic when players need it to progress or earn a reward, since no designer will be present.
when: When players must learn a new action to advance or gain something.
why: buyers will not have a designer present

text: Plan dedicated tutorial tasks for mechanics that depart from genre conventions; familiar mechanics need little teaching, as teaching intuitive skills wastes time and removes discovery pacing.
when: designing onboarding for a game mixing familiar and unfamiliar mechanics
why: Players lack existing schemas for new mechanics, so teaching effort belongs where expectations are violated.

text: Avoid squeezing all tutorials into the game's beginning, which is inefficient and goes unappreciated; teach mechanics in the first short levels instead of long tutorials.
why: Each task taught and reinforced in its own short level lets correct actions be rewarded as the player performs them, instead of all at once.

text: Many female players prefer clear step-by-step examples that show exactly what to do before attempting a task, rather than learning by trial and error.
when: designing tutorials and early instruction

text: Loading-screen hints convey information through text, a weaker route than hands-on experience, so they suit reinforcing or reminding players about a feature.
when: During loading waits, provided the tips are not relied on too heavily.
why: Text is a weaker teaching route than acting, and dense tips may go unread or be quickly forgotten, though they keep waiting players occupied.

text: Players die often early in an open tutorial, yet a compelling space keeps them engaged despite repeated failure.
when: In an open tutorial area where failure is possible.
why: Learning through failing and retrying is part of constructivist learning, so failure in an open space still supports learning and engagement.

text: In extreme cases, players may reveal their decks and skip the match.
when: metagames where deck matchup largely decides results
why: Once dominant and counter strategies are strong enough, deck choice settles the outcome, so actually playing the match adds little and focus shifts to the metagame.

text: Players may quit when early progress feels unrewarding and no longer-term goal is visible, though encouragement from others can keep them playing.
when: Early game progression

text: Teachers who were told certain randomly chosen students were gifted saw those students improve, showing that believed potential drives actual performance.
when: When leaders or teachers hold a stated belief about a person's ability.
why: Expectations held by authority figures influence how people develop.

text: When new players meet an encounter, they may invent unexpected strategies, snipe from distance, charge past enemies, fall through floor holes, get flanked, or miss obvious hazards.
when: first playthroughs of a fight by unfamiliar players
why: Newcomers do not share the designer's assumed approach

text: Transfer of learning is applying skills or knowledge from one context to another; it rarely happens easily, and far transfer to very different real-life situations is the main educational goal.
Learnability is how easily players accomplish basic tasks on first contact with a game.
Titles, marketing messages, interviews and word of mouth set player expectations, which shape how the game is experienced.
A good learning curve makes a game easy to learn and difficult to master, a maxim often quoted in design circles.
Players learn games through embedded guides, websites, and printed handbooks.
Early computer games lacked social, verbal, and emotional elements, had steep learning curves, and offered unlimited virtual destruction, mostly attracting male players.
when: affordable early home computers

text: Games have been proposed as tools to help people imagine career success, leave abusive relationships, break addictions, or become better volunteers.
Interactive tutorials teach through play and work well, but they take many iterations and can only be finished once the game reaches its near-final state.
Traditional education often lacks surprise, projection, pleasure, and community, and its interest curve is poor.
Standardized networked tablets for students and teachers may make teacher-guided multiplayer simulations practical.
Learning by doing beats reading tutorial text and explanation: acting needs deeper processing, improving retention and interest; its advantage depends on task complexity.
when: teaching new or complex mechanics and essential features
why: Performing a task forces deeper working-memory processing than reading does, which aids retention.

text: Teach key mechanics where attention already is and remove distractions: prompts shown during a focal task or NPC speech go unnoticed unless the NPC says the same.
when: timing tutorial prompts alongside other tasks or dialogue
why: Divided attention blocks salient prompts; players attend to the speaker rather than overlaid text.

text: Large environmental text can lead players along a path they are meant to leave, and this is a deliberate narrative device.
when: When the text is a deliberate narrative device that players are meant to deviate from.
why: It parodies how games direct players along paths, so deviating from the text is itself the point.

text: Teach on smaller board sizes and reserve the full board for skilled players, so learners master the rules before full complexity.
when: When learners progress toward using the full playing space as they master the game.

text: Make a new skill the means to a goal the player already wants, such as reaching loot on a high platform, so practicing it feels worthwhile.
when: Introducing a new mechanic
why: Without a worthwhile goal, on-screen instructions give players little motivation to practice

text: Tutorials are most effective when they are both contextual, built into a mission, and meaningful, tied to the player's current goal and sparking curiosity.
when: Designing onboarding for any mechanic
why: Each property alone leaves players either unmotivated or unable to learn while playing

text: New players often remove the color property, leaving a 27-card deck where sets are easier to find.
when: when learning Set
why: fewer properties make sets easier to spot

text: Small changes in who knows which facts can make a game much better or much worse, so knowledge distribution is a design variable.
why: Decisions depend on information, so knowledge shapes play.

text: Teach complex interacting systems through play, because linear media like lectures, readings and videos struggle to convey them.
when: the subject is a system of interacting parts
why: Such systems must be experimented with to be grasped.

text: Pair a simulation with a live instructor who points out where the model departs from reality, especially when the subject is serious.
when: serious subjects where misapplied lessons could be costly
why: Learners may otherwise carry over techniques valid only inside the simulation.

text: Give learning by doing to high-priority and difficult elements. Teach simple or low-priority elements with cheaper methods such as tutorial text or dynamic tips shown only when a player fails to act.
when: assigning teaching resources
why: Learning by doing cannot cover everything, so costly methods are reserved for the features that need them.

text: Learning should be contextual, meaningful, and distributed over time, drawing on behavioral, cognitive, and constructivist principles.
why: Educators already apply these learning principles, so game UX can draw on the same ideas.

text: Begin with few actions, such as movement, jumping and punching, plus one forced early goal, such as building shelter before nightfall.
when: sandbox or survival openings
why: Punching any block reveals that blocks break, can be collected and placed, while the nightfall deadline pushes quick resource gathering.

text: Keep each new task just ahead of what the player has learned so lessons stay engaging.
why: Introducing the next step as soon as one is learned keeps lessons from stalling on skills the player has already mastered.

text: Model a demonstration room on a familiar real-world layout, such as a lecture room, so players recognize the social context and do not rush through.
when: When a tutorial needs to halt the player for a showcase.
why: The familiar social setting signals that a presentation is taking place, so players do not rush through it.

text: Place tutorial mechanisms against normal geometry within a small space so they stand out.
when: When introducing a new interactive object
why: Contrast with ordinary geometry draws attention to the new element

text: In tutorials, thresholds should first teach, showing scannable objects, goals behind barriers not yet crossable, and how locks change as they are worked, rather than offering deep strategy.
when: When designing thresholds for early play
why: Early players need instruction before strategic depth

text: Teach core interactions in an enemy-free opening area with accessible platforms and no pits, where each interactive object is visible and can be tried without risk.
when: at the start of a game or level
why: Players can infer object use safely before threats appear.

text: Teach players how to use their avatar through clear, easily understood cues, since levels act as an indirect conversation with players.
why: Levels communicate with players indirectly, so teaching has to be readable without explicit instruction.

text: Deliver story and tutorial information during play, such as through voiceover or interface cues, so nothing stops the action to explain controls.
why: interruptions break flow and annoy experienced players

text: Teach through gameplay by making successes trigger large visual effects, offering things to experiment with, and reloading failed levels quickly.
why: rewarding feedback and fast retries let players learn by doing

text: When assessment is the goal, designers can assume players already have some experience with the skill being tested.
why: Assessment tests whether a subject has been learned, so the player is already expected to have some experience with it.

text: Build lessons from reusable blocks, each teaching a different mechanic, so a variety of mechanics can be taught.
why: Repeated symbolic assets build strong associations that shape how players interact with the lesson.

text: When giving hints is a limited, deliberate action, choosing what to share and when becomes the central decision for each player.
when: When designing cooperative information sharing
why: Scarcity turns sharing into a meaningful choice

text: A tutorial that appears inside a mission, and only when the player is stuck, teaches a mechanic better than a text block that pauses play before any action.
when: Teaching a mechanic such as jumping in a platformer
why: Players learn while doing, and instructions tied to a goal feel like help rather than a list to endure

text: Learners absorb knowledge most readily when they are ready, so that certain information suddenly seems useful and important.
when: a learner is in a state of readiness
why: Readiness makes knowledge feel relevant

text: A limited asset set with clear limits defines the possibility space, making it learnable and easier on player memory.
why: Modular assets make the world's possibilities easy to understand and reduce the memory load on players.

text: A guide who leads the player and scolds straying enforces a limited lesson plan within an open area.
when: Tutorial section of a game whose selling point is a large open world
why: A straight path keeps actions narrow until the player has gained the full skill set.

text: When a rule restricts the player but not enemies, placing the item enemies use in the environment explains where enemies get it.
why: Players reflexively try to pick up ground items because they have been taught to loot, so the restriction must be shown visibly.

text: Players have little time to be captivated; if they don't sense achievement and direction within the opening minutes, they quit.

Three learning paradigms guide game learning: behavioral (stimulus-response, rewards and thoughtful punishments), cognitive (mental processes and limits), and constructivist (knowledge built through interaction).
why: Each paradigm targets a different aspect of learning, so none has replaced the others.

text: Three teaching models for levels are operant conditioning, the Montessori Method, and constructivism; use them together as lenses on one design task.
The instructor can act as a dungeon master who runs a scenario with difficult problems for students.
when: teacher-guided game scenarios
why: The teacher keeps control of the scenario, and the tool amplifies abilities the instructor already has.

text: Levels can be nested like lessons: one puzzle is one problem, a level is a lesson of several problems on one concept, and the whole game is a subject unit.
when: content must be taught in ordered concepts
why: Scaling from problem to lesson to course keeps teaching sequenced.

text: Teaching many moderate or difficult features at once overloads players and makes them stop learning; dying while still learning feels unfair.
when: onboarding with many new elements, especially when sorted by difficulty
why: Concentrated load exceeds what players can absorb; overload and unfair deaths both increase frustration.

text: Assuming completed tutorials guarantee lasting retention is a mistake; unreinforced information fades according to the forgetting curve.
why: Retention falls off exponentially over time, and memories are rebuilt on recall rather than replayed, so they drift.

text: The first-time user experience decides whether a game is worth players' time and money; treating tutorials as trivial is a mistake, since newest elements are learned there.
when: designing tutorials and onboarding
why: The brain can tolerate only so much workload, so onboarding effort should go to core challenges rather than menus and controls.

text: Assuming players learned something because they dismissed a tutorial text with a button press, which requires only shallow processing.
why: Shallow processing like a button press yields weak retention, while acting on information requires deeper processing that encodes it better.

text: Many players quit during early play below the skill barrier, before they experience the game as intended.
when: When early play requires skill the player does not yet have.
why: Early play that feels like a chore drives players away.

text: Writing the story first can force onboarding to fit it, hurting the learning curve.
why: Ordering the onboarding first lets the narrative wrap around the teaching, rather than forcing the teaching into a finished plot.

text: Mandatory exposition in action games is often skipped by players.
when: Games dominated by fast action gameplay with short combat-driven pacing
why: Non-interactive dialogue makes players passive observers, and short attention spans lead them to skip it.

text: 1) List everything players must learn. 2) Sort the list by importance. 3) Reserve deep teaching and reminders for the top items.
why: Players will forget some information regardless of onboarding effort, so the plan must budget for reminders and deep teaching of top items.

text: 1) Let players skip training voluntarily. 2) Test players to decide which training they need. 3) Detect missing knowledge and teach it at the moment it is needed.
when: designing training for varied player knowledge
why: The least intrusive training is training never needed; targeted training avoids forcing unnecessary lessons.

text: Testing a non-interrupting tutorial: 1) Have a player learn a popular game with such a tutorial. 2) Observe how quickly they master its mechanics. 3) If they are slow, ask afterward how and why they got stuck.
when: evaluating a tutorial that does not interrupt play
why: observed struggle reveals teaching gaps

text: 1) Write one interface control on each index card. 2) Sort the cards into groups. 3) Repeat with several other people. 4) Compare the groupings to find natural clusters.
when: deciding how to group interface features
why: Independent sorts reveal groupings that match how people think about the features.

text: 1) Give each interactive action a distinct environmental cue. 2) Introduce the cue in a spot where it is the only route forward. 3) Reuse the identical cue in every later area.
when: A game has several interactive actions that the environment could leave ambiguous.
why: Players learn cues by necessity and recognize them later without labels.

text: 1) Break a large task into smaller steps. 2) Reinforce each correct step as the player completes it.
when: teaching a multi-step skill
why: Rewarding correct steps as they occur shapes the proper method, since the skill is built one piece at a time.

text: 1) Introduce a capability in a safe area where players can experiment. 2) Give a simple area that uses it. 3) Give a harder challenge combining it with existing abilities.
when: Teaching a new mechanic.
why: Ordered teaching ramps skill quickly.

text: 1) Put the player somewhere that acquiring or mastering the system feels worthwhile. 2) Introduce the system, mechanic, or item within that setting.
when: Introducing a new system, mechanic, or item
why: Players understand a system's value when they first meet it in a meaningful context

text: 1) Identify the core pillars of the game. 2) Decide where players should be challenged and where friction should be removed. 3) Apply learning principles to teach the core elements efficiently.
why: Core pillars show what players must master, so challenge is placed there while routine parts like menus are kept frictionless.

text: 1) Teach each action alone, rewarding simple steps first. 2) Add the next action as each one is learned. 3) Combine learned actions into complex sequences.
why: Each action mastered in isolation becomes the base for the next, keeping the next task just ahead of the learner.

text: Designing a tutorial: 1) Write a lesson plan for each level listing the mechanics to teach and any graphic or symbol associations. 2) Build each level on earlier lessons. 3) List the concepts at a lesson's start, showing what will and will not be covered.
when: designing a tutorial or level sequence
why: planned lessons ramp difficulty and information gradually

text: 1) Make learning spaces destinations with their own identity, such as a dojo or a special realm. 2) Or make the practice space itself the reward, placing it at the end of a path that leads to a rewarding encounter.
when: When designing how tutorial material is framed within a level
why: Framing gives learning spaces purpose, so players are drawn through them

text: 1) Give a reminder soon after first exposure to a complex mechanic. 2) Introduce a second feature while the first is still being reinforced. 3) Repeat both across different contexts.
when: teaching a complex mechanic
why: spaced reinforcement strengthens memory

text: 1) Open with noninteractive art and story that raises questions. 2) Grant movement alone in a safe space with no threats. 3) Add one tool at a time. 4) Combine tools into puzzles and fights.
when: designing an opening for a game with many systems
why: Players learn controls and systems without noticing the training.

text: 1) Introduce the concept in a safe place to practice. 2) Develop it with a more complex iteration. 3) Add a twist on the concept. 4) Test mastery in a final challenge.
when: introducing a new mechanic players must practice before combining it with others
why: Staged practice builds mastery before the challenge.

text: Keep loading screen tips to no more than three simple, brief bullets, since players skip or forget long text.
when: Loading screens used for reminders or low-importance tips
why: Learning from reading is shallower than learning by doing, so text packed onto one screen is poorly retained.

text: Teach mechanics through level design that spreads learning by doing across play, using clear signs, affordances and immediate feedback, not text tutorials.
when: designing onboarding and complex mechanics
why: Text-only teaching fails for core loops and feels patronizing; players retain mechanics better through practice.

text: Do not make players hold tutorial text in mind across a pause, follow a story while learning a new mechanic, or read many messages packed into one pause.
when: During onboarding, while a new mechanic is being introduced
why: These demand attention and inhibition of distractions; players cannot remember packed messages.

text: Design onboarding around limited working memory: new tasks need more resources than familiar ones, so keep focus on the core mechanic being practised.
when: during onboarding
why: The mind has limited capacity; tutorials carry high cognitive load.

text: Do not base tutorial design on a supposed learning style or on a personality or style test label, since these are unsupported bases.
why: Learning preferences are hard to measure, and the classification schemes used to label them are inconsistent with one another.

text: Establish why players should care about each feature at the moment it is introduced, before teaching how to become competent, since this affects retention.
when: introducing a feature in a tutorial
why: Players engage with features they see a reason to care about; motivation affects whether they stay.

text: Let players practise new actions without punishment or severe consequences, and discover story through play rather than large text blocks.
when: designing onboarding and narrative delivery
why: Safe practice builds skill and keeps players engaged; punishment during learning disrupts acquisition.

text: Offer help when players need it; games should not require manuals, and gathering tooltips in one place helps players.
Teach rules, threats, and abilities early through onboarding; do not leave tutorials until the last minute.
why: Without understanding rules, threats, or the right abilities, players cannot feel growing mastery and tend to churn.

text: Distribute tutorial teaching over time and avoid massed learning, where too much is taught at once.
why: Players forget much of what they are taught, so spreading lessons over time counters that loss.

text: On resume, remind players of mechanics and controls, and recap the story, especially when the game requires their input.
when: players return after a break
why: forgotten controls create skill mismatch

text: Teach rules through tutorials that feel like part of the game, so players learn the rules and how to succeed.
when: When onboarding new players.
why: Players must understand the rules to reach a state of flow, and integrated tutorials let them become competent quickly while keeping immersion.

text: Before adding an indicator, check whether a part should be learned before another part that is less visible, and swap visibilities to match the learning order.
when: adding a new HUD indicator
why: Players should notice the next most important item as skill grows, without being overwhelmed or coddled.

text: Helper objects such as triggers, colliders and volumes must be easy to show and hide, or placement errors are missed until late.
when: evaluating editor visibility tools
why: Hidden helper objects like triggers and colliders are not visible in the final game, so placement errors go unnoticed.

text: Build tutorial text into the environment's graphic design and give it a narrative voice, instead of pop-ups, when the budget is small and style would suffer.
when: when voice acting or pop-ups are unaffordable or break the game's aesthetic
why: integrated text keeps the aesthetic intact

text: Show typical players how to have fun with the game rather than assuming they will discover it.
when: designing for casual or typical players
why: Typical players may never discover the fun on their own.

text: Decide during design how players will learn the game; players who cannot work out how to play will not keep playing.
