Offer hints that escalate from vague to specific, with a small point cost, so stuck players can continue without copying the answer.
when: Hard puzzles where frustration could cause quitting
why: A timely hint revives hope and curiosity and beats no solution

text: Show a working version or a slideshow of what playing feels like rather than describing it, especially when the game is early.
when: Presenting an early-stage game
why: Players and listeners understand play better from direct experience.

text: Shift challenge toward Discovery and Mastery and shorten Learning to reduce the feeling of endless difficulty.
when: designing challenge pacing
why: A long Learning phase with no visible progress feels endless.

text: Limited saves need guidance on average save spacing and danger locations, since otherwise players feel the game expects psychic knowledge.
when: limited saves are used
why: Without guidance, players must know the best save spots in advance, which they cannot, so they replay long stretches.

text: Support learning with helpers: tutorials, auto aim, dynamic difficulty adjustment and rubber-banding rules.
Make multiplayer onboarding efficient so new players are not crushed in their first matches.
when: Designing multiplayer games with PvP.
why: Unskilled players beaten early have a bad experience, and balanced matchmaking alone cannot fix this.

text: Check whether players understand how to play the level; if not, add a clearer introduction or more teaching moments before the repeated mechanic.
when: observing a playtest
why: confusion blocks learning the mechanic

text: Use playtest observations to write a tutorial lesson plan based on what players actually need to learn.
when: designing a tutorial after playtests
why: observed needs are more reliable than assumed ones

text: Do not place an early level that uses every object in the game; it overwhelms players, so move it later and add preparatory levels first.
when: an early level uses many objects at once
why: players need preparation before combining everything

text: Plan onboarding across levels and treat tutorials as part of level design.
why: Planning onboarding early avoids cramming all tutorials into the opening, which is inefficient and disliked by players.

text: Strong first levels let players use mechanics safely, offer tension or reward, keep tutorial content unobtrusive or optional, and introduce ideas that return later.
A good tutorial excites players and teaches mechanics in a fun, nonintrusive way, preparing players to use them without being pushed through instructions.
Make the first screen introduce the symbols, an enemy and a power-up, along with the rules that recur later.
why: A single opening screen can give an overview that teaches the larger world before the player reaches it.

text: Summarize the player's task in a short task list or journal entry, and state the underlying problem in quest text or dialogue.
when: In quest-based narrative games.
why: Interactive storytelling should focus on the essentials, so players learn only the core problem.

text: Keep tutorials very streamlined and get players into the core game as quickly as possible, especially on free-to-play platforms.
when: Free-to-play and mobile games.
why: Each extra click can cost players who would otherwise continue.

text: Start with critical mechanics needed in the first hours, but importance alone does not justify early teaching; complex key components can wait while players enjoy easier systems first.
when: ordering the onboarding sequence
why: Priority measures importance, not readiness to learn.

text: Learn-then-do tutorials front-load instructions before play, while learn-by-doing spreads teaching into play, distributing learning but requiring tasks that carry meaning.
why: Weakly communicated meaning lowers motivation and attention, which weakens memory for the lesson.

text: Treating technology as the goal, not the play it serves, is a pitfall; building mainly around new technology can fail as both the imitated medium and as a game.
why: early full-motion video games on CD-ROM were among the worst ever made

text: Technology is any material or interaction that makes a game possible, from paper and pencil to lasers, and it enables some things while preventing others.
For a game designer, technology is the physical medium a game is made of, such as a board and dice or a computer and screen, not only electronics.
A true metaverse is a shared 3D world that is persistent, decentralized, interoperable, and built on user-generated content.
In build-up strategy games, a large technology lead lets the more advanced side's units attack the rival's older units when armies first meet.
when: armies first meet after a long build-up

text: Telepresence, where the body goes to a real distant place, is rarely used in games.
Much of the near future of technology and games can be guessed by reasoning carefully, even though fast change discourages many predictors.
Technologies tend to diverge into separate devices over time rather than merge into one device.
Technology is the most volatile tetrad element; many new physical media appear within one career, and many can support new kinds of games.
The shape of future games follows from technology combined with human psychology, so forecasts should consider both.
Look for technologies on the verge of breaking through; designing for them can yield unexpected success if they are foundational to the game.
when: choosing which emerging technology to design around
why: A technology that has just become good enough can suddenly reshape the market, as a motion controller nearly took over consoles.

text: Custom hardware built for a game can make mechanics possible that a standard platform would not easily support.
why: The advancing-army mechanic depended on a motherboard built specifically for that game.

text: Technology can remove creative pressure: a game that needs nothing more to excite players becomes a technology demo that works only for a while.
why: Developers have not yet learned how best to use new technology, which temporarily lowers design quality.

text: Novelty wears off fast, so a game depending on new technology looks poor within a few years.
why: The early excitement comes from the technology itself rather than the design, so it fades.

text: 1) State how the technology will look in two years and why. 2) State how it will look in four years and why. 3) State how it will look in ten years and why.
when: planning around a technology's likely state at future dates
why: Reasons build instinct for how technology fits the human mind.

text: 1) List the technologies that will deliver the experience you want. 2) Check whether each is used foundationally or decoratively. 3) If a technology is not foundational, question whether to use it at all. 4) Ask whether it is as impressive as you think and whether a disruptive alternative fits better.
when: selecting technologies before committing to them
why: Keeps the choice tied to the experience rather than to excitement.

text: New technologies open up new forms of play, so designers should grasp both the constraints and the capabilities of each tool.
when: Designing with new or existing technology
why: Innovation depends on knowing what a technology can and cannot do.

text: Use new technology to unlock new interactions; it can enable design leaps but cannot produce them by itself.
why: Trusting technology alone to carry a game led to failures, while lasting hits used it to create new experiences.

text: A league groups players who compete regularly across an extended stretch, usually between one month and one year.
McMahon gives each player starting points based on rating, as if they had already won some games, so stronger players meet earlier.
when: swiss events, as used in some Go tournaments

text: A Swiss tournament pairs players each round against opponents of similar standing, so everyone plays the same number of games without elimination.
when: large or long events

text: Triple or higher elimination formats add more loser brackets but are rare because their bookkeeping becomes unwieldy.
A two-player single-elimination event with N entrants needs about log2 N rounds: four entrants take two, eight take three, sixteen take four.
when: two-player games

text: An N-player Swiss event with log2 N rounds lasts as long as a single-elimination bracket, and N−1 rounds makes it effectively a round robin.
when: choosing the number of swiss rounds

text: Swiss-system tournaments typically award 1 point for victory, 0.5 for tie, 0 for defeat, though any running total, including in-game points, works.
Player elimination is a problem mainly when it happens early in a long game; very short games or late eliminations are less of a concern.
when: Players eliminated early while the rest of a long match continues.
why: Eliminated players must sit and wait while others play, and sitting out is usually not fun.

text: Leagues can use most tournament formats, but elimination is usually avoided because players are meant to play many games.
when: When a league's players should each play many games
why: Elimination would cut players out early, limiting how many games each one plays.

text: Use leagues or seasons when players should compete across a long period rather than on a single event day.
when: Competition runs regularly over one month up to a year, rather than a single short event.

text: A bye in a late round is worth more than a bye in round one, because it skips what is likely a strong opponent.
when: In elimination brackets, after many players have been knocked out.

text: Alliances can form when a leader wants to finish off a weakened opponent while others want to keep that opponent in play.
when: When players can help each other and one player nears elimination.

text: In double elimination, a main-bracket player must lose twice to be out, while a loser's-bracket player is out after one more loss.
when: In games with some chance, where a good player may be knocked out by bad luck.
why: Lets a strong player absorb one loss, so bad luck alone does not end their run.

text: At the end of a league period, players are ranked by overall performance and the winner is chosen from that total.
when: At the conclusion of a league's time period.

text: Swiss qualifying gives each entrant many games and results that help determine seeding for the final bracket.
when: When an elimination tournament will follow a Swiss stage.
why: So the final winners must beat opponents rather than win on a tiebreaker.

text: In Swiss, removing a departed player from rankings and future pairings has little effect on others, but it can change who receives byes later.
when: a player leaves a swiss event early

text: When a Rock win counts double, a three-way round is no longer a draw; Rock gains a net point while Scissors loses one, so Scissors looks riskier and Rock safer.
when: Scoring multiplayer rock-paper-scissors with a double-weighted Rock win
why: Weighted wins change the net score of mixed rounds

text: In a best-of-three round structure, only the first round lacks elimination stakes; after it, a fighter faces elimination, which focuses the player on each motion and control.
when: when structuring a multi-round match
why: Elimination stakes raise attention to every input

text: In a round robin with N players, each player plays N − 1 games.
Single elimination pairs players and removes each player after a loss, so the field narrows until one winner remains.
Masterpoint-style schemes reward participation yet treat accumulated experience as if it were skill, which weakens pairing.
when: When a rating system never lets a rating decline.

text: McMahon's rating-based starting points can look like an unfair advantage to some players.
when: In seeded Swiss-style tournaments where players begin with points derived from their rating.
why: Skilled players meet early, instead of weaker players facing the best right away.

text: Other Swiss round counts usually leave several players tied at the top, so a tiebreaker decides the winner, which feels anticlimactic.
when: When a Swiss tournament runs fewer or more rounds than log2 N.
why: Swiss lacks the final head-to-head showdown that elimination provides, so ties go to tiebreakers.

text: Swiss pairings must be recalculated after every round, which makes the system complex to run.

1) Run the main bracket as in single elimination. 2) Each round, fill the loser's bracket with players who lost in the main bracket. 3) Keep playing both brackets until one player remains in each. 4) Those two players meet for the title.
when: In games with chance, where one unlucky loss should not end a player's run.

text: 1) Rank players by win/loss record. 2) For tied players, first use games between the tied players. 3) If still tied, or three or more are tied, compare results against the top-ranked opponent, then the second-ranked, and so on. 4) Otherwise use a playoff or shared standing.
when: when players have identical records

text: 1) Group players by cumulative score. 2) Rank players within each group. 3) Pair the top half of each group with the bottom half in matching order, so rank 1 meets rank n/2+1.
when: swiss events where strict score-group pairing is wanted

text: 1) Play a set number of Swiss rounds. 2) Take the top four, eight, or sixteen players by standing. 3) Seed them into an elimination bracket by Swiss rank and play it to a winner.
when: events needing broad participation and an exciting climax
why: Swiss alone often lacks the exciting climax that an elimination final provides.

text: 1) Pair round one randomly or by seeding. 2) After each round, rank players by record, using tiebreakers for equal records. 3) Pair each player with a close-ranked opponent. 4) Repeat for the chosen rounds; the best final rank wins.
Reward players for eliminating opponents only when they are strong enough to win outright.
when: When knocked-out competitors must sit idle for an extended period.
why: Otherwise elimination becomes a shortcut that distorts play.

text: In a fixed-round tournament where byes earn points, set enough rounds that a player starting at zero could still win the event by winning every game.
when: choosing the number of rounds for a bye-points tournament
why: Without enough rounds, a player who starts at zero from early losses has no realistic route to the top.

text: With an odd-sized field, one player receives a bye each round; the organizer must decide who gets it and how it counts toward ranking.
when: odd-sized swiss fields
why: Bye counting affects standings, which are built from a cumulative win/loss record.

text: When a round-robin player leaves early, either nullify their games or keep their earlier results as information for tiebreakers.
when: In a round-robin tournament of sufficient size where a player leaves before it ends.
why: Results against a departed player still carry information that can settle ties.

text: Swiss tiebreakers that examine opponents' results must define how to treat opponents who left early.
Define the dropout rule for each tournament format before the event starts, since every format needs one.
when: In a tournament of sufficient size where players may leave early.
why: Departures are likely in large events, and each format needs a stated way to handle them.

text: Do not reward win streaks; downplay them so players may not even notice, avoiding hot-hand letdowns when a streak ends.
why: It addresses the hot-hand fallacy, the belief that a winning streak will carry on.

text: Double elimination softens one bad result, so strong players are less often knocked out by chance, but everyone plays at least one more game, lengthening events relative to single elimination.
when: choosing double elimination, especially in games with a meaningful element of chance
why: Luck can knock out a strong player after one bad game, so a single loss is tolerated.

text: Round robin is the fairest format but only practical for small fields, because game count grows quickly with each added player.
when: when choosing a tournament format
why: Full round robin needs more games than an all-day event suits, prompting compromise formats.

text: Single elimination finishes quickly but removes half the field each round, so players who need many games get few.
when: events that must end fast versus events where players need many games
why: Half the field is eliminated every round, so most entrants stop after only a few games.

text: Pick the method that yields strong early pairings when those matter; pick Dutch when strict score-group pairing is preferred.
when: choosing between a strong-early-pairing method and Dutch pairing

text: Swiss gives many games per player without the length of a full round robin, but it is a poor fit when a dramatic final between the top two players matters.
when: choosing an event format

text: Training sequences can double as elastic challenges that reward speed or skill, so novices learn the lessons while experts treat them as a challenge.
when: When designing a training sequence.
why: One activity serves both learning and skill expression.

text: A realistic treatment implies physical behavior, an iconic treatment allows cartoon physics, and a non-iconic treatment leaves expected behavior open.
when: when choosing where an object sits on the triangle
why: Each position sets different expectations of motion

text: Undo is costly unless core; add targeted undo for common regrets, like a recent shop purchase or sale, and include undo in turn-based games where players may roll back moves.
when: Deciding whether to add undo to a system.
why: Undo deeply integrated into state is costly, but targeted undo covers common regrets cheaply.

text: Beyond game length, time shapes turn timing, time to level, action points, effect timers, build times, and movement speed, each affecting how gameplay feels and interacts with other resources.
Turn-based combat runs in rounds: everyone acts in initiative order, usually set by a speed or agility stat, and the round ends when all have acted.
Turn-based strategy games are usually adversarial and military-themed, with players managing resources and moving units across a board.
Timed effects such as poison, sleep, and invincibility last for a designed duration.
Game drama depends on uncertainty renewed in every play, whereas a familiar film's outcome is already known to a repeat viewer.
Changing turn structure, such as requiring two placements per turn in different columns, alters strategy and can change balance.
Time can matter without a clock, since very long play can exhaust participants.
Some games make manipulating time their central mechanic rather than an occasional feature.
Turn-based board games advance time in discrete alternating turns, and play consists of moving pieces around the board.
Alternate intense moments with breathers, which let players appreciate accomplishments and anticipate what comes next.
why: Peaks lose effect without valleys

text: Long deliberation on big decisions suits chess-like games but can kill the experience in many-player or fast-paced games.
when: In multiplayer games or games meant to be fast.
why: Waiting for slow deliberation hurts pace.

text: Pacing depends on time pressure, not the label: turn timers, including idle-advancing ones, add pressure to each decision and make turn play intense; real-time matches can be pre-planned.
when: When a turn-based game sets a time limit on each turn.
why: Per-turn time limits can make turn-based decisions feel as intense as real-time play.

text: Restricting communication to set times, such as for alibis or accusations, limits discussion so a single player cannot direct the whole group.
when: When a hidden-role game needs controlled talk
why: Scheduled talk prevents one player controlling discussion

text: Pickups that add or subtract seconds from a timer make collection a choice between rewards and penalties to remaining time.
when: when pickups change a countdown

text: Time-based interpretation changes an input's meaning according to its timing, as in combos and timed jumps.
A timed threat, such as an approaching horde, forces players to finish gathering before it arrives, adding urgency to exploration.
when: In a looting mode where players must leave before a horde arrives.

text: Effect wording such as opponent loses next turn can be misread as a far stronger effect than intended.
when: When card text states when an effect applies, such as skipping a turn.
why: Ambiguous timing words make a card's power easy to misjudge.

text: Sources use 'move' inconsistently: some mean a full round, while strategy games usually mean a single turn.
when: reading AI or game design sources
why: terminology differs between fields

text: 1) Draw phase: draw two cards. 2) Power phase: play one Power card, otherwise discard one card. 3) Action phase: play one Action card whose power requirement is satisfied, otherwise discard one card. 4) Alternate turns until one player loses.

1) Identify what sets the length of each activity. 2) Check whether players are frustrated by early endings or bored by long ones. 3) Test whether clocks, races, or time limits would help or irritate.
when: Reviewing the pacing of gameplay
why: Each check targets a common cause of poor pacing.

text: Turn-based time makes real-time pacing irrelevant to the rules, while continuous time makes timing part of the mechanics.
when: Deciding whether a game's clock should affect its rules
why: In turn-based play the game treats each turn as a discrete unit, so elapsed clock time carries no rule meaning.

text: The workbench is the quiet, private, often messy work area of the home, such as a desk, workshop, or sewing corner, rarely seen by guests.
A venue is a persistent place where people use devices to play, and is a framework for understanding what gameplay fits where.
As of 2019, head-mounted VR displays, which favor intensity and privacy, seemed better suited to the workshop than to the living room.
when: as of 2019

text: The venue system has gaps and overlaps but has repeatedly proven useful for deciding which gameplay works best in which setting.
Venues change very little, while games and technologies change constantly.
Few VR experiences port easily to other input systems.
VR and AR aim to deceive proprioception as well as vision, so the body feels present inside the simulation.
Under age 2, children have trouble relating video content to the real world, the video deficit, and learn better from adults.
Use the workbench for challenging, long-session games played alone or with dedicated online peers; avoid it for casual family or group play.
when: choosing a venue for a game

text: Learn venues and their properties, not just games and platforms, to see past current technology.
why: Games and technologies shift quickly, while the kinds of places where play happens stay stable over time.

text: 1) Identify which venue best suits the game. 2) Identify any special properties of that venue that will shape the game. 3) List which game elements harmonize with the venue and which do not.
when: Checking that a design responds to where it will be played.
why: Places people play strongly influence what works in game design.

text: A video pitch follows the same rules as a live pitch: get to the point, seem organized, and show rather than tell.
when: Making a video pitch
why: The audience judges a video by the same standards as a live presentation.

text: Concept art explores potential looks, palettes and styles, and shows intended look and feel before building; art alone does not convey story, so pair it with design documents.
Contour drawing traces the edges of forms to show where objects sit in space, and it is useful for quick field documentation.
Art direction, including menu and UI presentation, has a non-negligible effect on players' overall appreciation of a game.
Better storage and scanning let game landscapes move from block pixels to detailed digitised paintings, raising visual quality in the 1990s.
Digital art programs add colour, lighting and atmosphere to level plans, sections and perspectives, and layers let designers show or hide notes.
Game designs are abstract while illustrations are concrete, so concept art can ground a design at the very start of a project.
Concept art can supply a unifying vision of the experience.
Players accept cartoon physics, such as exaggerated jiggly collisions, in iconic games when volume is maintained through principles of animation.
when: when designing iconic or cartoon-styled motion
why: Stylized motion is acceptable if it still reads as coherent

text: Colors carry learned associations, such as black for death or blue for cold, which metaphors can imitate to communicate meaning.
Players perceive whole objects by filling in gaps, so negative space can work in both art and game design.
when: Designing shapes, icons or art with gaps
why: The mind completes partially drawn forms.

text: Show a character in close-up at the start, then reduce it to a small sprite for the rest of the game.
when: Presenting a character with limited on-screen detail
why: The early close-up lets players imagine the character's detail later.

text: A composition should keep the eye moving rather than settle on one image.
why: Elements at the edges pull attention outward, so viewers keep searching for more instead of settling on the center.

text: Choose a noise-minimizing art style early when many entities must be read quickly at once.
when: Starting art direction for a fast multi-entity game
why: Style decisions made late are costly to change and affect readability across the whole project.

text: Three adjacent colors on the wheel form an analogous group that creates a harmonious mood, such as cool, somber tones.
when: setting a calm or somber mood

text: Complementary colors, opposite each other on the wheel, make contrasting elements stand out.
Stylized, cartoony characters generate empathy easily and avoid the uncanny valley more reliably than attempted realism.
when: Choosing a visual style for characters, especially when realism is not achievable
why: Stylized forms stay on the safe side of the empathy curve

text: Animation placed over an unchanged random process makes outcomes appear more legitimate to players without altering the underlying odds.
when: When a computer generates the random outcome, such as a dice roll or card draw, and players may doubt it.
why: Players distrust computer randomness because they miss the tactile feel of physical dice and cards, and animation restores that feeling.

text: Designers create four kinds of reality: logical (cause and effect), spatial (movement through space), proprioceptive (where the body feels it is) and social (how people interact).
In a facade variation, the base class hides the entire game engine from its subclasses, so subclasses reach engine services only through it.
when: Base class is designed to shield subclasses from engine internals.
why: A facade puts one simplified interface in front of many subsystems, and the base class plays that role for the engine.

text: LOD based only on distance can misallocate detail, since distant hills may deserve more detail than flat ground beside the player.
when: When applying level-of-detail to terrain, where distant hills may be more prominent than flat ground near the player.
why: Noticeability matters more than distance alone.

text: Fictional cues about physical properties, such as whether a material stops bullets, are read as mechanics, so they mislead players unless the game enforces them.
when: When fiction implies what objects can do physically, such as whether a material blocks bullets or breaks.
why: Fiction supports many plausible readings, so players cannot tell which cues are real rules unless the game enforces them.

text: 1) Draw a reference square. 2) Add horizontal and vertical midlines. 3) Draw arcs between the midpoints of the square's sides to form the circle.
when: sketching circles by hand
why: The square and midlines give the arcs accurate reference points.

text: Make sure visual beauty does not hide features; players must be able to find what they need.
when: When artists reshape a screen or layout to look better and may remove or condense features.
why: Players judge a screen by whether they can find what they need, not by how attractive it looks.

text: Overshoot line ends slightly past corners so that lines meeting at a corner cross, producing clean, closed joins in level sketches.
when: drawing straight strokes in architectural or level sketches
why: Overshoot makes corners read as deliberately joined rather than gapped or fuzzy.

text: Use full-color renderings when the game's true feel must be shown.
when: a rough sketch cannot convey the game's feel

text: Keep assets consistent so players learn which surfaces are solid, which harm or slip them, and which items, gates and puzzle elements matter.
why: Consistent visuals let players build familiarity with the rules, which is the basis for understanding how the game works.

text: Familiar physics costs nothing to learn, while invented physics, such as gravity that repels, allows novelty but is much harder for players to understand.
when: Choosing between conventional and invented physical rules.
why: Unconventional rules would be extremely hard for players to understand, even though they could unlock new kinds of play.

text: Zero-sum game: one player's gain is exactly the other's loss; payoffs are negatives summing to zero, so one value X describes both sides and winning equals opponent losing.
Even a game with no board and no movement can be modeled as a space, because its information must reside somewhere, so a single point can serve as one.
Several players can reach an objective, yet the outcome still singles out one winner, with the rules handling special cases such as ties.
Keep the win condition separate from intermediate warning states, treating warnings as signals of danger rather than as the goal itself.
when: when a game has warning states such as threats or alerts

text: Over many rounds, winners are the players who gain most from their wins and lose least from their losses, not those who win single rounds.
when: games where one round is mostly luck
why: round-level luck is mostly averaged out across many rounds

text: Systems check at defined intervals whether a winning state has been reached; if a winner is found, the game resolves.
when: In games with a predetermined win condition, rather than open-ended games that have no set end.

text: In a zero-sum win-loss scheme, a win counts as +1 and a loss as -1, so all outcomes sum to zero.
Losing for an entire game is frustrating, so hide standings or add other systems that keep trailing players engaged.
when: when a positive feedback slide decides the game early
why: a visible hopeless position drives players away

text: 1) Pick two zero-sum examples and two non-zero-sum examples. 2) Identify the main difference in outcomes between the two groups. 3) Explain how that difference affects gameplay.
when: when comparing game outcome types
why: Comparing contrasting outcome types sharpens understanding of gameplay and the ability to describe complex game ideas.

text: A game should appear winnable to all players while never being truly winnable, so continuing motivation is sustained.
when: When designing a continuing challenge
why: Perceived winnability keeps players trying, while true winnability ends the challenge

text: Change the victory condition so players focus on scoring rather than elimination, for example a race to a set number of victory points.
when: When multiple victory paths make it unclear which player is furthest ahead.

text: Keep ratings zero sum: features that add points from nowhere, like a minimum rating or bonuses for specific modes, invite farming.
when: when designing a competitive rating
why: points created from nothing can be exploited

text: Use a zero-sum outcome when a single winner must be decided by a finite judgment.
when: a single winner must be decided
why: A zero-sum outcome gives a finite verdict on who wins, whereas rankings or statistics produce graded results without that verdict.

text: Treating a multiplayer game as zero-sum simplifies analysis but ignores that its outcomes need not balance.
when: analyzing a game with more than two players

text: Floor polygons are usually identified by a designated floor material, and per-polygon data can flag floors manually.
Before committing to full 3D, check whether the situation can be forced into 2.5D, since that executes faster.
when: Choosing between 2.5D and full 3D steering.
why: 2.5D executes faster.

text: Treating characters as points for everything ignores their extent, which breaks collision and obstacle avoidance.
when: When collision or obstacle avoidance depends on the character's physical size

text: Using a left-handed convention without flipping the x sign of the facing vector produces the wrong facing direction.
when: Converting orientation in a left-handed coordinate system
why: The sine-cosine vector formula assumes right-handed axes, so a left-handed setup must negate the x component.

text: The Command pattern wraps a method call in an object, so the call can be stored, delayed or moved between code locations.
The Command pattern can be seen as a way to emulate closures in languages that lack them.
In Chain of Responsibility, an object in a hierarchy either handles a command itself or passes it on to a subordinate.
Arbitration lets one or more steering behaviors take complete control of the character.
An action combination executes all its sub-actions simultaneously, for example playing an animation while changing a value.
An action sequence runs its sub-actions one after another, waiting for each to complete before starting the next.
A hierarchical machine reports its current states as a list from highest to lowest level; a plain state lists itself, and a composite state lists itself first, then its active child's list.
An AI action runs another AI routine, such as steering toward a set target, searching for firing targets, or planning a route.
Action prediction estimates which option from a limited set a player will choose next.

A concrete action is an object carrying world-state changes, prerequisites, timing and animations, associated with level objects; an action's meaning is the goals it achieves and the goals it compromises.
Nodes are waypoints marking where a character can perform an action, such as using a computer; being near a node tells it which actions are available.
Action Description Language extends STRIPS with open-world semantics, richer goals, conditional effects, equality tests, and typed variables.
The same idea appears under other names: callbacks, first-class functions, function pointers, closures and partially applied functions.
Delegated behaviors can serve as the base for other delegated behaviors, for example arrive forms the base of pursue.
Action combinations and sequences can contain each other, and nesting can go to any depth.
The common arbiter asks each expert for a numeric insistence value, picks the highest, and breaks ties randomly.
Internal actions are built into each algorithm, while external actions can take one uniform form shared by all algorithms.
Some actions are compound sequences of smaller steps that run together as one action.
The active list can report the priority of its highest-priority action, which is its first item, and the manager uses this to decide whether a queued action may interrupt.
In many games every action is always available, but in others the available set depends on location, held objects or earlier actions.
Route all character actions through one central action handler; this makes capabilities explicit and makes debugging, logging and reporting simple.
when: Designing character action systems, especially when AI behaviour is hard to trace across many decision makers or action types are expected to change often.
why: Debugging is the strongest reason to centralize: each action can carry its origin, queue time and completion state for inspection; explicit capabilities let action types be added or removed easily.

text: Use action scripts freely in game AI: they often achieve desired results more cheaply and reliably than research-heavy techniques such as neural networks or cognitive models.
when: When several characters must perform actions at the same time.
why: They are easy to implement and offer practical value.

text: Use the Command pattern to untangle complicated code in games and other large programs.
when: complicated control flow in large programs
why: Turning a request into an object lets code hold, delay, record, or reverse it.

text: In languages with real closures, closures are a good way to write commands.
when: languages that support closures well
why: Command classes stand in for closures where a language lacks them, so native closures replace that scaffolding.

text: Use copy-down when breed attributes are fixed after creation and speed matters; use dynamic delegation when breeds may be modified at runtime.
when: selecting how breed inheritance is resolved
why: Copy-down favors fast reads and dynamic delegation favors runtime flexibility.

text: When effects must happen together, have one decision return a compound action of several atomic actions that execute simultaneously, rather than coordinating separate decision routines.
when: Coordinated simultaneous effects, such as a small attack alongside a flanking assault
why: Coordinating separate decision routines to produce simultaneous effects is difficult

text: Have AI code emit commands through the same interface as player input, so AI modules can drive any actor or control the player in demo mode.
when: several sources should drive the same actors
why: Commands are objects, so the choosing AI and the executing actor share no direct calls, and any source can drive any actor.

text: An action structure, created when a character acts, holds an action type plus optional object and indirect object; structures can add fields such as a required location for certain actions.
why: Action types differ in which object slots they need, so each type records whether it requires an object or indirect object.

text: An action sequence keeps an index of its current sub-action, starting at the first, and executing it runs that sub-action and advances the index once it completes.
why: Only one sub-action runs at a time, so the sequence must remember which one is current and move on when it finishes.

text: Objects appear to act together though they run one after another within each frame; each frame is one complete turn of the simulation.
when: When many independent entities must run inside one shared game loop.
why: Each entity encapsulates its behavior behind a common update method, so the loop needs no knowledge of their concrete types.

text: With nu at zero, the learner keeps chaining actions from each resulting state, which lets it follow action sequences that may reach success.
when: When the length-of-walk parameter is set to zero.
why: Each iteration begins where the last one ended, so the learner can trace chains of actions toward a rewarding outcome.

text: Action manager memory use grows linearly with the maximum number of queued actions, not counting sub-actions.
Per-update time cost is proportional to the number of active actions times the number of queued actions, with sub-actions counted in both.
when: When many actions sit in both the queue and the active set.
why: Compatibility checks try pairings between queued and active actions.

text: All actions share a base interface: expiry time limiting queue wait before discard, priority deciding precedence, interrupt check, pairwise compatibility check, completion check, and execute.
why: Sharing the base interface lets compounds be subclasses, so they can wrap other actions at arbitrary nesting levels.

text: The action manager holds a queue of pending actions from any source until they can run, a list of actively executing actions, and a counter for the current time.
why: Actions wait in the queue until they are allowed to run, and the active set tracks what is running now.

text: Decision making selects what to do while movement AI and animation handle how; some decisions need movement, some only animation, some only state change with no visible feedback.
Commands can flow through a queue or stream from producers, such as input or AI, to consumers, such as a dispatcher or an actor.
why: A queue between producer and consumer means neither side needs a direct reference to the other.

text: A complete AI structure has an alarm mechanism updated every frame and a decision maker, both feeding an action queue that drives execution.
when: designing sophisticated game characters
why: Emergencies can be scheduled each frame, while the decision maker runs only when the queue has nothing to do.

text: Collaborative action primitives are state change, animation, AI, compound, sequence, signal, and wait. Compound runs a group simultaneously; sequence runs a group in series.
why: Signals and waits let characters coordinate, via shared identifiers, when to act together.

text: Enqueuing messages without caring which code processes them resembles a service locator, which hides who handles the work.
when: When queued messages are requests meant for one specific service.
why: If other code takes messages off the queue, the intended handler never receives them, so the approach only works with one expected listener.

text: Choosing the action before considering tactical information can prove foolish when no safe spot exists nearby.
when: Decision systems that pick actions before seeking cover
why: Commitment to an action ignores whether a suitable location is available

text: A simple 'can be pushed' flag is not enough for goal-oriented behavior, since the same action can achieve very different goals depending on the object.
when: When a character chooses actions to advance a goal.
why: A flag only says an action is possible, not what it changes, so the character cannot pick actions that advance its goal.

text: 1) Add logging to each action class's execute method. 2) Record the decision maker, queue entry time and completion status on each action. 3) Output this data at run time.
when: Debugging AI actions during play.
why: Run-time records reveal which decision produced each action and when.

text: 1) Update the alarm mechanism each frame, queuing emergency actions when needed. 2) Call the decision maker only when the action queue is empty. 3) Send a valid action at the queue head for execution.
when: each frame of an AI action manager

text: Choose among valid behaviours with one of four rules: 1) any available, found by binary search on range midpoints then checking neighbours, which is most efficient; 2) first available in a priority-ordered list; 3) the most central behaviour, which keeps it longest; 4) the smallest range, which prefers the most specific behaviour.
when: When more than one behaviour is valid at the same moment and one must be chosen.

text: A full AI action has four classes: state change (game state), animation, movement and AI request; animation goes to an animation controller, movement to movement algorithms, AI requests to another decision maker.
when: Designing AI action classes or executing non-state-change AI actions
why: Each flavor requires different handling by a different game system, and is best executed by the system that specializes in it.

text: Store action types in a database recording whether each needs an object or indirect object: some need none, some an object only, others an object plus optional indirect object.
why: Actions differ in how many targets they accept: some take none, some need a required object, others an optional second one, so each type must record its needs.

text: Store each potential blackboard action with agreement flags and execute it only after every expert able to object has approved it; experts with no possible objection need not agree.
when: When an expert posts an action that has not yet been fully thought through.
why: Without approvals, an unvetted action could run before the other experts had weighed in on it.

text: Action timing is travel time to the location plus time to perform the action; each action should report total completion time so planning can weigh quick gains against long ones.
when: Planning with timed actions
why: A step toward a larger goal can look almost instant while the goal as a whole takes far longer, so the reported time must cover the whole chain.

text: An action combination can interrupt if any sub-action can, can run alongside another action only if all its sub-actions can, is complete when all sub-actions are complete, and executes every sub-action.
Store the action queue and active action set as priority heaps, since heaps keep their contents in priority order.
when: Implementing a decision-making action manager
why: Heaps maintain priority ordering so the highest-priority action is always accessible.

text: Pass the target actor into execute as a parameter rather than looking it up through global functions, so one command can act on any actor.
why: A hardwired lookup of one fixed object restricts each command to a single character, which limits how far it can be reused.

text: Consider Chain of Responsibility when the object model is hierarchical and the target is not fixed in advance.
when: When the object model is hierarchical and it is unclear in advance which object should handle a command.

text: Let higher-importance decisions interrupt actions in progress, and make the action manager support this.
when: Running multiple timed actions for a character.
why: An action that was sensible at start may become foolish later.

text: Scheduling an action should only append it to the queue; interruption, promotion, expiry and execution all happen in the per-frame execute step.
For compound actions, emit signals for specific actions, such as 'I can cook raw food', rather than for motives, so characters follow signals for what they can actually do.
when: When an action needs several steps or items.
why: Characters can weigh the actions they detect nearby against their own goals, instead of tracking a signal tied to a single motive.

text: While a unit is mid-action, such as moving, exclude new action choices for it until that action finishes.
when: a unit's action takes time to complete
why: Choosing a new action mid-motion has no defined meaning in the game.

text: Objects must describe not only the actions they support but what those actions achieve, because goal-oriented planning chooses actions by their effects.
when: In people simulation games where characters have broad competencies and can use objects in many ways.

text: Take available actions from an object database rather than simulating recognition of objects.
when: When a character in curious mode needs to know which actions are available.
why: Simulating sight and recognition is unnecessary because the game already holds a list of the objects it can interact with.

text: The full action manager is flexible and suits sophisticated characters, but may be overkill for simple subsidiary characters; its flexibility helps as character behaviour grows more complex.
when: choosing an AI structure for a character
why: Character needs tend to grow over development

text: Action-based signals support many actions and are easy to extend, but they lose the elegance of following one smell per motive.
Decision making picks the most appropriate behavior for a character at each moment from its options, such as attacking, standing still, hiding, exploring, or patrolling.
Strategy AI coordinates a group of characters through a shared approach, while each member keeps its own decision making and movement shaped by that group plan.
Early game AI was a small program written per character, while modern games keep general AI routines in a shared engine and assemble characters from them.
AI is branchy, running different code at different times, and self-referential, feeding results back into earlier operations, so it fits pipelined rendering poorly.
The line between bottom-up and top-down AI is hazy: level-of-detail techniques tend to be top-down, while most character AI is bottom-up.
Dynamic AI behavior is easier to understand by running it than from screenshots or static diagrams, because motion shows timing and interaction.
when: Studying movement-based or behavioral AI

text: Most action-based 3D games use only movement and decision making, without a strategy layer.
Most elaborate AI that looked bad never shipped.
Deciding when game AI should be complex and when it should stay simple is its hardest part.
Steering pipelines are designed specifically for steering, unlike general decision trees or blackboard architectures.
Decision making is the middle part of the game AI model and is often a small share of total AI effort.
Most games use very simple decision making, mainly state machines and decision trees, while rule-based systems are rarer but important.
Decision techniques apply both to intra-character decisions, a single character's choices, and inter-character decisions, coordination between characters.
Some fuzzy decision maker implementations require the membership degrees of one input's states to sum to 1.
Studios typically keep processor-heavy AI tasks, such as pathfinding, in engine code rather than in scripts.
Fully bottom-up control is closer to emergent cooperation than to what developers usually mean by multi-tier AI.
Upper tiers use decision making and tactical tools, while lower tiers use pathfinding and movement to carry out orders.
People simulation games are leading the move toward characters with broad competencies, such as using gadgets and everyday objects.
RTS AI architecture varies more between games than in earlier genres, depending on which gameplay elements are used, so the model is only a starting point.
Each side-level need is handled by its own AI component, and the complexity of these components varies widely between games.
Context-free decision making lets the same module serve either the player or an enemy side.
Even with AI-friendly design choices, turn-based AI eventually needs substantial execution management.
Common AI needs in games include locomotion, route finding, choice logic, tactical and strategic planning, learning, and procedural content generation.
Game AI cannot assume days of processing or gigabytes of memory; a fixed speed and memory budget clarifies algorithm choice and optimization targets, unless cut late in production.
when: When the AI runs within a fixed time and memory allowance.
why: A fixed budget tells developers which algorithms can fit and gives them a concrete target for optimization.

text: Simple rule-based selection suffices when a character needs only a few reactions; complex enemies that chain several actions need more elaborate tactical decision systems.
when: When a character needs only a few simple reactions, such as animals that move away when approached.

text: Scripting does not remove the need to choose a sound AI architecture; a script-based system still needs deliberate character architecture design.
when: When character behaviour is written in a scripting language rather than in code.
why: Several developers assumed scripting removes the need for architecture design and fell into this trap.

text: Adding context sensitivity to tactical waypoints greatly improves AI competence when simple labels produce odd behavior.
when: Tactical waypoint behavior looks odd
why: Context lets the same label mean different things in different situations

text: Managers with very specific functions, such as telling soldiers when to clock off, are hard to fold into a general broadcasting manager alongside other event kinds.
when: When an event manager has a very specific function, such as notifying characters at a set game time.

text: The decision-making architecture is the hardest choice, since most techniques can do what the others do; choose by fit to requirements rather than capability.
when: When choosing a decision architecture and no specific required behaviour rules out state machines.
why: Most techniques can achieve the same behaviours, so capability alone does not separate them and fit to the requirements decides.

text: Replacing several Boolean flags with one state enum makes invalid flag combinations impossible.
A director system estimates player stress from variables such as health, skill mastery, and location, then adjusts enemy spawns and item drops.
why: Presented as a more efficient way to control pacing than fixed visual punishments such as blood splatter across the screen.

text: Feedback scheduling measures how long each behaviour actually takes and adjusts its bias, so a behaviour that always overruns receives less time.
when: When the scheduler distributes frame time among behaviours by bias weights

text: A generic bottom-up physics system, where many objects collide with any part of the world, produces emergent physical behaviours and exploits that were not explicitly designed.
when: When a generic physics system is built for objects moving under forces, not only what is needed
why: Predictable simulated rules combine into unplanned interactions.

text: AI memory budgets are about 1 MB on a 32 MB console and 8 MB on a 512 MB machine, enough for heavy algorithms like pathfinding.
why: Most AI algorithms need little memory, so a modest share covers even heavy methods.

text: AI's share of processor time has grown over five years to about 20 percent in many games and over 50 percent in some.
For each case that genuinely requires a sophisticated algorithm, expect five or more where a quick heuristic suffices.
The pipeline runs in O(c·n) time, with c denoting constraint steps and n denoting constraints; constraint checking dominates the cost.

Top-down control has one system decide for a whole population rather than each character deciding: the highest level decides and passes instructions down, each level interpreting and deciding in turn.
when: When one system simulates a whole population rather than each character deciding
why: Each level interprets the instruction it receives and passes on a refined version.

text: AI infrastructure connects AI algorithms to the game: it turns movement requests into visible action, supplies game information to the AI, and manages processor time and memory.
A general AI engine needs behavior management, a world interface, standard movement and animation interfaces, and a standard behavior structure linking decisions to actions.
why: Every algorithm must plug into shared management, information and action mechanisms.

text: Specialist roles can be layered onto a squad with individual state machines: a grenadier fires on enemies behind light cover, a medic treats fallen comrades, and a radio operator calls air strikes.
when: adding specialist squad roles
why: Individual state machines can add team specialties without any higher-level coordinating layer.

text: Most modern game AI addresses three needs: moving characters, deciding where to move, and thinking tactically or strategically.

Game AI is organized as movement and decision making per character, strategy per team, surrounded by infrastructure: animation, physics, scripting, world interfacing, execution management and content creation.
why: The model shows how techniques fit together and which ones are alternatives to each other.

text: The top tier is often strategic reasoning built from expert systems, state machines, tactical analyses, or waypoint tactics, deciding where to move, take cover, or stay hidden.
why: Its outputs are orders for lower levels to carry out, not actions the character schedules itself.

text: In bottom-up control, individuals decide autonomously and higher algorithms only supply information about the game state.
Tactical and strategic AI, the third layer of the AI model, covers inferring the situation from sketchy information, deciding with that situation, and coordinating several characters.
why: Single-character decision techniques cannot predict the whole situation or coordinate characters, so a higher layer is needed.

text: A typical RTS architecture also includes execution management, tactical analysis, pathfinding, and kinematic steering.
when: In real-time strategy games

text: Each creature combines a simple decision framework, such as a finite state machine or decision tree, that controls a portfolio of steering behaviors.
when: When decisions only need a very simple reaction to the environment.
why: Simple steering behaviours combine without complex arbitration in open areas with few constraints.

text: Treating the layer model as a rigid framework; it is a general model to guide design, not a straitjacket.
why: Dividing lines blur, since many techniques fill roles in more than one category.

text: Assuming that more complex AI makes characters look better to players is a fallacy; matching behavior to technique matters more.
A fixed chain of AI modules only passes information forward, so downstream results cannot change upstream decisions without special-case backward messages.
why: Targeting must wait for route planning to find a firing position, which a forward-only chain cannot signal back.

text: Choosing an action only for the top goal ignores side effects; an action may relieve one need while pushing another need to the top.
why: Drinking a soda lowers the hunger goal yet pushes the bathroom goal to the top, so the chosen action worsens another need.

text: Flat identifiers for deeply nested facts force many candidate lookups, which becomes unwieldy as nesting depth grows.
when: Facts are nested several levels deep
why: Each possible nesting path needs its own identifier, so checking every candidate name multiplies lookups as depth increases.

text: Fixed scripts fail when the player interferes, because they cannot react, which is why they are mostly limited to cutscenes.
when: the player can disrupt the sequence
why: A fixed sequence cannot respond when the player blocks it, so the character keeps running the script regardless of the obstacle.

text: A learner may never reach its specific stage, leaving only the general behaviors in play.
why: Fine-grained rules take a long time to learn, so general rules are used early even though they will often be wrong.

text: 1) Create AI data in modeling, level or AI tools and package it with the level. 2) On level load, create behaviors from level data and register them with the AI engine. 3) Each frame, the game calls the engine, which updates behaviors using world information and internal state. 4) Apply the results back to game data.
Plan the engine structure before much AI code is written; new behaviors can then be developed while the game runs and replace placeholders once ready.
when: Early in AI development, before much behavior code is written
why: A shared behavior structure lets new behaviors be built while the game runs and swapped in for placeholders.

text: Provide tool support for visualizing and editing AI geometry.
when: For very complex level geometries
why: Automatically widened geometry can create tiny polygons in corners and crevices that trap characters.

text: Represent context as parameter values or as discrete facts similar to the action representation.
when: Encoding context for learning characters.
why: Large amounts of context slow learning, and players expect visible improvement within a short time.

text: Central control is powerful but hinges on how good the top-level choice is, and a unit that cannot follow an order is left unable to advance; emergent control avoids this single point of failure.
when: choosing squad control style
why: Central orders are only as good as the top decision, and a unit that cannot carry out an order stalls, whereas characters watching each other avoid that single failure point.

text: A steering pipeline handles cooperation but slows as scenes grow complex, while simple blending is cheaper but occasionally makes foolish moves.
Adding context to steering behaviors increases their complexity and reduces their independence from one another.
why: Each behavior must now account for what the others are doing, so it can no longer act selfishly on its own.

text: The steering pipeline suits tight passages and pathfinding integration with lightweight steering, but few developers had used it when it was written.
when: Choosing a steering architecture
why: It is designed to let steering behaviors interact constructively, which performs well in situations that are normally problematic.

text: Always overwrite replaces the stored entry whenever a clashing entry is stored. It is easy to implement and often sufficient.
when: Simplicity matters more than tuning

text: Algorithms can be studied analytically and reused across games, which makes them the basis of an AI engine.
Bindings can be stored as a list of identifier and item pairs or as a hash table indexed by identifier.
Array-based Q-value storage uses memory proportional to states times actions, so growth in the state count quickly exhausts memory.
when: Q-values are held in arrays
why: Memory scales with the number of states and actions, so the state count quickly becomes the limiting factor.

text: AI, a term coined in 1956, aims to make computers perform thinking tasks that humans and animals manage, creating machines that think or act like humans.
Make computer characters make mistakes, since perfect driving or aim is not fun; game AI need not be perfect, only interesting, aiming for less artificial.
why: Game AI only has to be interesting, so flawless play is unnecessary.

text: Many developers do not treat actions as a separate concept, so each decision technique's output is just a code snippet that calls functions or changes state directly.
when: Building AI without an action layer.
why: Ad hoc output hides what the character can do.

text: Behaviorism judges a thing by its observable behavior rather than by the nature of its inner mind.
The actor serves as the exploration strategy, controlling which actions are selected.
Satisficing means optimising for a satisfactory result rather than the best possible one; its exact meaning varies between writers.
The game itself is a separate entity that does not play but makes the decisions that enable play to happen.
First-person shooter bots have attracted more academic research than any other game genre.
Once a problem is solved comprehensively, it is no longer regarded as AI, so unsolved tasks remain the core of the field.
The best AI techniques depend on genre, and most useful characters combine several techniques rather than one.
Hacks and heuristics can make characters seem as alive as the most complicated algorithm.
Game AI takes a behaviorist stance and cares how characters appear, not how their minds work.
Most advanced game AI techniques suit current-generation handhelds, which face the same constraints as any console.
Processing time and memory costs are among the main reasons new AI techniques fail to reach common use.
Ordinary wildcards match independently, so separate wildcard tests within one pattern may bind to different entities.
Hard-coded state machines remain important but are less common now that level designers control state logic.
Newer designs require AI to infer player intent from actions and support it without explicit orders.
AI teammates can exchange exact plans through messages, but a player signals only through actions the AI must interpret, making intent harder to detect.
The basic event mechanism is enough to handle cooperative message passing between characters.
Advanced techniques like neural networks, genetic algorithms and GOAP are rarely used commercially, partly because their character-specific code is hard to fit into level editors.
Most AI design tools focus on finite state machines, movement and pathfinding, since these use simple processes and data designers can adjust.
Futuristic racing games are built on the same racing AI technology as driving games.
In adventure games, enemies are treated as another puzzle for the player to solve.
Most side-level decisions rely on lightweight methods like finite-state machines and decision trees.
Simple driving games often have escaping cars follow a fixed path and chasing cars use a simple homing algorithm.
Most games use rule-based AI, while developers experiment with machine learning for level generation, adaptive challenge scaling, and non-player character behavior.
Narrow AI for specific tasks is the practical goal today, while strong AI (artificial general intelligence) remains far off.
Believable AI for both player-controlled and nonplayer characters is widely considered a central goal of game design.
Even enemies with simple AI can serve as powerful spatial tools that shape how a space is used.
A very simple technique applied well can create an illusion of complexity, which is preferable to complicated systems that may fail visibly.
why: Complicated AI systems have often shipped looking stupid, while simple techniques used well can look right.

text: Simple emergent rules include moving toward other characters to keep the group together; more complex rules include choosing a teammate to protect and keeping them covered.
when: designing squad behavior
why: Each member reacts to the others' state, so the team coheres without a higher-level controller.

text: Use simple state-based AI when the genre's needs are met by it; many genres still rely on decades-old techniques because nothing more is needed.
when: In genres where simple AI is all the gameplay needs
why: The genre's needs are already fully covered, so extra complexity adds nothing.

text: Game developers mainly need engineering: algorithms that make characters appear human or animal-like, aiming for believable behavior rather than a faithful model of cognition.
when: building AI for a shipped product
why: The goal is characters that look right to players, not an accurate model of the mind.

text: When a learning system cannot handle basic tasks late in development, falling back to simpler algorithms usually saves the release.
when: late in production
why: A learning AI that still fails basic tasks cannot ship, so simpler algorithms take its place.

text: Start from the desired character behavior and apply the most relevant, cheapest tool, rather than inventing an algorithm and searching for a use.
why: Good in-game AI starts from the wanted behavior, so the tool serves the character rather than the reverse.

text: Simple scripted actions, such as sideswiping rivals or gesturing at enemies, convey character attitude without any AI infrastructure.
why: Attitude reads through the animation the player sees, so the visible act carries the meaning without underlying decision logic.

text: On extremely constrained devices, capacity may not allow a full execution management layer, so the AI algorithm itself must be fast.
when: On very low-spec devices where there is not enough processing for an execution management layer.

text: Use a simple positional rule mixed with randomness when the goal is an impression of intelligence rather than real planning.
when: the goal is perceived intelligence

text: Use simple blending when simplicity matters more than avoiding every foolish movement.
why: Satisfying every constraint may be impossible and can loop endlessly, so the system must eventually give up.

text: Many genres do not need tactical AI; in 2D shooters and platformers, where players expect predictable behavior, it can frustrate them.
when: Where players expect predictable behavior, such as in 2D shooters or platform games.

text: A predictive AI can challenge players more by anticipating which passage, weapon, route, or cover point they will pick.
when: When the player chooses one option among alternatives such as passage, weapon, route, or cover point.
why: People cannot randomize their choices, so their past behavior reveals what they will pick next.

text: An AI can place walls using influence maps and spatial reasoning, putting them between economic buildings and likely enemy positions.
when: When the AI, rather than the level designer, is responsible for building walls in a real-time strategy game.

text: Biased inputs produce biased decisions, and the bias is often hard to identify in the output.
why: The model's output looks objective even when its inputs are skewed.

text: A system needs only enough agent-like behavior for players to read it as an intelligent agent, not a realistic simulation of a mind.
when: designing characters or agents that should feel intelligent
why: the player's mind supplies the rest

text: In mechanics-driven games, design AI first as a mechanic, since the fiction serves the mechanics rather than defining them.
when: games where mechanics drive the player's experience
why: Fiction exists to support the mechanics

text: Non-player characters powered by AI methods can generate distinctive, sometimes striking replies to what the player does, rather than fixed scripted reactions.
when: When story is meant to emerge from gameplay rather than follow a predetermined structure.

text: Characters that act on their own can conflict with what the player wants, creating tension between player intent and character intent.
when: When a character controlled by AI rather than by the player has its own autonomy.

text: The more complex an AI's decision-making becomes, the less predictable it is, and the less the player can plan several steps ahead.
when: Where the AI is built as a layered simulated mind rather than a predictable mechanic.
why: Players can only plan around behavior they can anticipate

text: Agent-based AI builds autonomous characters bottom-up: each character takes in game information, decides what to do, and acts, so overall game behavior emerges from these individual behaviors.
Game AI blends three approaches: hacks (improvised fixes and clever tricks), heuristics (rules of thumb that work in most cases), and algorithms (formal, analyzable methods).
when: Most character behaviors, where a simpler hack or heuristic will handle the job.
why: Hacks and heuristics alone force reinventing the wheel, while reusable algorithms are analyzable and shared across games.

text: The AI model has six parts: movement, decision making, tactical and strategic AI, world interface, execution management, and content creation.
why: The parts cover where AI gets its information, where its output becomes on-screen action, and related technologies, serving as a planning checklist.

text: Visitor AI has four modes: scared (recover), curious (examine and explore), social (stay with group, console others), and bored (leave for a refund).

The example's technology suite has six parts: kinematic movement, A* over a waypoint graph, a four-state finite state machine, sense management, a pathfinding planner pool, and a random number generator.
when: Small simulation-style AI

text: Letting AI difficulty vary with hardware can be rejected by QA and publishers.
when: When targeting PCs from casual to hard-core, where weaker machines give the AI less processing time.
why: Reducing AI work on slow machines makes the AI effectively dumber and shifts difficulty, unlike graphics scaling that leaves gameplay unchanged.

text: Blending a behavior that always returns maximal acceleration, such as seek, dilutes collision avoidance: at equal weights avoidance has at most half the influence.
why: Requested accelerations are summed and then cropped to a maximum, so a full-strength seek output competes for the same limited budget.

text: Adding debugging output to a hard-coded state machine is harder than doing so in a flexible implementation.
Genre-specific names for influence mapping and terrain analysis can hide that they share the same underlying technique.
when: In some genres such as shooters, where constraints make both approaches produce the same structure.
why: Their general theory is remarkably similar, with the technical differences mainly coming from the genre.

text: The more elaborate the AI, the slower it is to yield a result, so without anytime behaviour the character is more likely to look foolish.
why: Anytime algorithms can be queried at any moment for their current best answer, so a rough early result is acceptable and gets refined as time allows.

text: Getting the AI to interact correctly with the game environment is among the hardest parts of AI development.
why: Events must be acted on correctly, agents must know what is happening to themselves and others, and some algorithms need the world in a specific representation.

text: Military-rank names for AI tiers are common but loosely agreed, which causes confusion; define what each tier means explicitly.
when: When AI hierarchy levels are labelled with military ranks such as general, colonel or lieutenant.
why: different readers assume different meanings for the same level name

text: Attractive exotic techniques can pull a design away from its requirements; a few impressive behaviors matter less than making the rest of the AI work reliably.
when: When tempted to use an exotic technique for a behaviour that state machines could likely achieve.
why: Simpler systems like state machines have proven their flexibility, and novelty alone is not enough reason to risk the rest of the AI working reliably.

text: 1) Keep the character tracking the player. 2) When the player comes near, trigger the chase behavior. 3) The character then appears to have been unable to see the player earlier.
when: When the character's knowledge should appear limited even though it actually tracks the player.
why: Hiding full knowledge behind a trigger creates the appearance of limited perception and a sense of mystery for the player.

text: 1) Build a simple AI. 2) Observe what playtesters find easy or strange. 3) Add rules to prevent those cases. 4) Repeat.
when: Developing AI that must feel believable
why: Playtesting reveals which behaviours break immersion or make the AI too easy, so fixes can target those specific cases.

text: Ideal opponents meet three criteria: player actions that beat them are fun, several effective counter-strategies exist, and visible behavior gives clues to the best counterplay.
when: When designing enemy AI
why: Each enemy implicitly defines the player behaviour that beats it, so its design should make that response enjoyable, varied and discoverable.

text: An opponent should be challenging but not a cakewalk, and players should win more often than they lose in real life so they keep playing.
when: When tuning enemy difficulty
why: Players need regular wins to stay motivated

text: Write glue code that translates game data into the representation each algorithm needs, which eases integration.
when: When an AI algorithm needs game state in a representation the game does not already provide.
why: A translation layer lets the algorithm work with the form it expects while the game keeps its own data.

text: Borrow academic AI methods where they help get the job done, and survey academic work to find which ones may be worth adapting.
when: When an academic method directly helps a game character appear human or animal-like.
why: Games developers are concerned with the engineering side, building algorithms that make characters look lifelike, so research is useful where it serves that.

text: Judge goal-oriented behaviour by whether the character looks goal-driven to players, not by the internal mechanism that controls it.
when: In genres such as people simulation, where few characters are on-screen with changing emotional and physical parameters.
why: Players only perceive the behaviour, so what controls the character internally is irrelevant if it looks right.

text: Give flavour characters fixed routines and central story characters more varied behaviour, while keeping quest information easy to find.
when: For background characters that most players will barely observe.
why: Routines on minor characters are almost never noticed, while a story character repeating the same circuit would be obvious to most players.

text: Build a formal world interface when characters must interact with the world or with each other; self-contained behavior can skip communication infrastructure.
when: characters must interact
why: Communication lets the right AI know the right facts at the right time, which becomes essential when characters must coordinate.

text: Add more detailed AI geometry as obstacle density grows, rather than keeping coarse shapes in cluttered spaces.
when: rooms with many obstacles
why: Raw polygon geometry is slow to search for obstacles, and more complex environments tighten the constraints on movement.

text: Game AI should challenge without cheating: it should fight well, lose believably, and offer players the same opportunities the AI has.
when: When the AI is an opponent meant to challenge the player.
why: Making the player feel clever and skillful is what usually makes the experience compelling, which requires the AI to be beatable.

text: Have an agent visibly respond to world changes, such as a builder rushing to an upgraded building and working on it with matching sounds.
when: When something changes in the world, such as a player action or a time-of-day shift.

text: Characters that ignore the world, such as patrolling guards, are easy to build but cannot interact with others.
why: Such characters do not sense events or colleagues, so they need no world interface but cannot respond to others.

text: Some medical sensors have systematically overestimated blood oxygen for non-white patients, so device bias can cause real harm.
Marginalized populations are underrepresented in training data unless the model is deliberately designed for inclusion.
when: When data is collected without a deliberate inclusion effort.
why: Models learn mainly from data where these groups are scarce, so their patterns receive little weight.

text: LLM-driven NPCs can be persuaded through player conversation into offensive or hateful output.
when: When an unfiltered language model speaks as a game character.
why: LLMs can be readily persuaded through conversation, so unfiltered output can drift into offensive content.

text: When using advanced AI, keep inclusivity and users' best interests in mind.
why: Predictive AI can automate wrong decisions that harm individuals, and generative AI gives plausible but not necessarily accurate answers.

text: If processing time runs out before an action is queued, the AI system returns having done nothing for that frame.
when: limited per-frame AI processing time

text: AI level of detail gives processing time to characters that matter most to the player or are most sensitive to visible error, expressed as one importance number per character.
An anytime algorithm always has a best current answer available and improves it the longer it runs.
Each behaviour record stores a behaviour, minimum and maximum importance, and optional entry and exit routines; the record is valid when importance lies within its range.
Movement and pathfinding are the most common anytime uses; other candidates include turn-based AI, learning, scripting interpreters and tactical analysis.
