why: Movement and pathfinding are usually the most time-consuming AI processes.

text: Behaviours consume memory as well as time, and many characters cannot all keep every behaviour's data loaded at once.
AI load is uneven across frames: route planning can take much time, route following very little, and some frames may need almost no AI work.
Behaviours differ in whether they must run regularly, can be split into small pieces, or benefit from spare time, and one priority number cannot capture all of these.
Under severe memory and processing limits, AI choices narrow to simple state machines and chase-the-player behavior.
when: On simple devices with very tight memory and processing limits, where a full execution management layer will not fit.
why: With almost no spare capacity, the AI algorithm itself must be fast, which rules out heavier techniques.

text: Ambient characters such as pedestrians, crowds and bird flocks can scale freely, using more characters when spare time is available.
when: When spare processor time is available on the machine.
why: Its cost can be dialed up or down by changing the character count, unlike typical AI whose time stays fixed.

text: The first-available selection rule costs O(1) memory and O(n) time, and linear scanning is acceptable with about four LODs per character.
when: When each character has only a handful of behaviours to choose between, around four.
why: Scan time grows with the number of behaviours, so a small count keeps the linear search affordable.

text: Each importance range maps to a behaviour, so a character can run expensive behaviours when important and cheap or no behaviours when peripheral.
Behaviour compression passes useful data from the outgoing behaviour to the incoming one, such as a planned destination kept as the next target.
when: When switching from a complex planner to a simpler behaviour.
why: Outgoing data is normally discarded at switch-off, so passing useful state across reduces the noticeable seam between behaviours.

text: 1) If there is no current behaviour or it is no longer valid, scan the records in order. 2) Select the first record whose importance range contains the current importance. 3) Call the outgoing behaviour's exit routine and the incoming one's entry routine if set. 4) Store the new behaviour as current and run it.
when: Each frame, for each character.
why: Holding every behaviour's data for every character in memory at once is impossible, so memory and time must stay low.

text: Act on the best current guess while planning refines it; anytime behaviour fits an existing frame scheduler if that guess is always available before returning control.
when: When planning spans multiple frames.
why: People tolerate rough early moves better than visible stalls.

text: Manage the AI budget by dividing execution time among AI needing it, running algorithms incrementally over several frames, and favouring important characters when resources are scarce.
when: When AI demand is uneven, with bursts of heavy work such as pathfinding alongside long quiet stretches.
why: Three things are needed for an effective AI system.

text: Give each behaviour an overlapping range of importance values, and keep the current behaviour while importance stays within its range.
When AI gets less time, it either does less work and becomes effectively stupider, changing difficulty, or takes longer, lowering frame rate or slowing decisions.
when: on weaker hardware
why: Less AI work changes difficulty and gameplay, unlike graphics cuts, and QA and publishers won't accept a much easier game on weak machines.

text: Avoiding overlap between the outgoing and incoming behaviours prevents memory spikes, at the cost of a brief moment when neither is fully set up.
why: Enter-before-exit would keep both behaviours' memory active together, which can cause memory spikes.

text: Predicting movement is most often needed for aiming firearms, which requires solving ballistic equations for a firing solution.
With quadratic drag no simple closed-form firing solution exists, so an iterative simulation is needed; dropping the quadratic term leaves a model that can be solved exactly.
when: When computing firing solutions with drag

text: Homing behavior can be extended with traversal actions, such as grabbing and climbing blocks, to reach the player.
when: Enemies that must reach a player on raised terrain

text: With drag, the elevation needed to reach a target is higher than a drag-free solution suggests.
when: Aiming a projectile with drag
why: Drag slows the projectile, so it drops short without extra elevation

text: A drag-free model is often an acceptable, simpler approximation to try first; but in physics-driven games, where engines usually include drag, drag-free solutions can be inaccurate at long range.
when: When predicting projectile hits for AI aiming; the drag-free model suits short range, while long range in a physics-driven game calls for drag
why: Physics engines include drag for numerical stability, so a drag-free model is simpler but can miss at long distances.

text: Discontentment is a score computed from all goal insistence values, rising as insistence grows; the character minimizes it. Some search literature calls it an energy metric.
Model-free learning does not model how the world works; it tracks only visited states and actions, which makes it much simpler to implement.
Machine learning relies on algorithms that detect regularities in datasets, adapt from them, and improve performance without hand-written rules.
Specificity depends only on rule structure, so the priority order can be computed before the system runs.
Developers are increasingly experimenting with replacing traditional decision-making techniques with learning systems.
Learning mode most commonly applies backpropagation, which works backward from the output layer to adjust weights.
SSS* and DUAL* were both shown to be special cases of MTD, which also removed the complex special-case code that earlier MTD versions needed.
Learning techniques range from simple number tweaking to complex neural networks, each with quirks; use one in a game only when you understand its quirks and have realistic behavior expectations.
when: Choosing or considering learning for game AI.
why: Unfamiliar techniques can behave unexpectedly in live play.

text: Expect published game AI implementations to differ from textbook versions, since developers modify borrowed algorithms heavily for their own game's needs.
when: Comparing game AI implementations with textbook algorithms
why: Speed and game-specific needs drive modification

text: If a human cannot reliably learn or implement a technique, a generic learning algorithm is unlikely to find it easily.
when: When a method is hard for people to solve and implement.
why: Learners struggle with tasks that are hard for humans, such as cornering at the limit of tire grip.

text: Movement systems, decision tools, behavior suites and high-level decision making are easier to implement directly, with intra-behavior tuning added afterward.
when: When building the base systems, before learned tuning is layered on top.
why: Learning every part is doubtful to be economical, so learning is best confined to tuning parameters.

text: Specific rules let characters act with high competence and capture how small circumstance changes, such as an object's material, change its tactical use.
when: When characters must perform at a high level of competency in specific situations.
why: Human actions shift sharply with small circumstance changes, so detailed rules are needed to match that sensitivity.

text: Discontentment selection takes O(nm) time for n goals and m actions, and O(1) memory.
Choosing an AI technique because it is new or complex, rather than because it suits the behavior, produces characters that look foolish.
Simulating light bouncing around corners can cost more than its noticeable gameplay effect justifies.
1) For each action, add its change to each goal's current value. 2) Sum each goal's discontentment at its new value. 3) Keep the action whose predicted total discontentment is lowest.
when: When a character chooses among possible actions that affect several goals at once.
why: Squaring goal values lets high-valued goals dominate, so medium values cannot swamp one important goal.

text: 1) List each required behavior. 2) Map each to the technology that directly provides it, such as A* for pathfinding or a formation motion system for group movement.
when: After the required behaviours have already been identified.

text: Do not consider an action that raises discontentment compared with the previous depth; discard that branch and move on.
when: Depth-first GOAP planning
why: It cuts the number of branches searched

text: Use standard game-tree algorithms directly only when the game has no hidden randomness and all moves are known; otherwise adapt them.
when: Game has no hidden randomness and all moves are known

text: Developers using machine learning in games must account for known AI limits and keep players safe.
when: when applying machine learning to game systems
why: Learned models only reflect patterns in historical data, so without human oversight they can lock in mistaken choices that hurt people.

text: Decision making, movement, tactics and board game AI trade speed against accuracy; when accuracy is sacrificed, a heuristic usually replaces the search for the correct answer.
when: Decision making, movement, tactical or board game AI where full reasoning would be too slow
why: Working out every consequence is costly, so agents fall back on rules of thumb that have worked before.

text: Discontentment pruning avoids mid-plan trouble but misses plans that accept short-term discomfort for a later gain.
Discontentment selection is much slower than simple selection on large sets, but its per-goal calculations can run in parallel on SIMD hardware.
when: Large numbers of actions and goals
why: The algorithm suits SIMD optimization, so its calculations can be vectorized and run in parallel.

text: The more flexible the learning, the less control the designer has over gameplay.
when: Choosing how broadly a learner can change behavior.
why: Whatever lets a character learn useful changes also lets it learn harmful ones, and replaying its experiences to fix bugs is often impossible.

text: A move-to parameter can be set in the staging tool beforehand or by a trigger during play; richer staging needs an AI design tool that can change decision making and internal state on triggers.
when: When level staging needs more than a movement destination set by triggers
why: Richer staging needs more complex decision sets, which only a fuller design tool that can modify decision making supports.

text: A negative decay constant with inverse square falloff creates attraction, pulling characters toward others within a radius. This is rarely useful.
Basins of attraction can depend on direction or orientation, which makes them hard to visualize.
Real games have attractor states that many action sequences lead to, and walking keeps the learner near them longer, which is useful.
Movement driven only by attractors and repulsors is full of traps and leaves characters stuck.
when: When many attractors and repulsors in a level drive character movement mostly on their own

text: Often no expert or only one expert wants control, so the arbiter has little work to do.
why: Choosing among experts is only needed when several signal interest, since the arbiter hands control to one at a time.

text: In a blackboard architecture, each steering behavior reads what other behaviors intend before deciding its own output.
A balanced decision tree has roughly equal leaf counts under each branch, keeping the average path to any behavior short.
A wildcard lets one rule match any database entity that satisfies a condition, such as anyone with health below a threshold.
A world model is a changeable representation of game state that a planner can modify freely without altering the real game state.
A behavior differs qualitatively as a mode of action, such as laying an ambush, rather than a parameter tweak within one mode.
Binary trees are easier to optimize, and some tree learning algorithms require binary splits.
Any multi-branch decision tree can be expressed as a binary tree.
Blackboard content depends on the application: steering uses locations, maneuvers, or animations, while decision making uses game state, positions of enemies or resources, and character state.
The value store interface must read a Q-value, write a Q-value, and return the best action for a given state.
Add a strategy layer when a team must coordinate its behavior to reach a goal; otherwise movement and decision making are often enough.
when: designing a group of characters
why: Strategy operates above individual characters, shaping each one's decisions toward a shared group approach.

text: Use cooperative arbitration when simple blending or priorities produce believable-looking failures in tight situations.
when: When two steering behaviors, such as pursuit and wall avoidance, conflict near an obstacle
why: A context-sensitive behavior accounts for the other behavior's goal, so its effect is not diluted into sluggish, tangential movement.

text: In a chain of binary checks, order the tests so the most likely outcomes come first to reduce wasted work, though repeated checks remain.
when: When a chain of binary tests re-checks the same value several times
why: Common outcomes are reached sooner, so typical cases walk less of the tree, but duplicate checks still occur.

text: Write fuzzy rules directly in block format when possible; conversion tools mainly help translate a rule set that already exists.
when: When authoring a fuzzy rule set from scratch for a game rather than converting an existing one
why: Block format is a complete direct representation, while conversion tools only pay off for rules that already exist.

text: Use a rule-based system when characters must reason about situations the designer cannot anticipate well enough to encode in a decision tree.
when: behavior depends on unpredictable world states
why: Rules that examine a knowledge database can derive responses to situations no one encoded in advance.

text: Prefer scripted teamwork when tactics are recorded as step-by-step sequences instead of open-ended layered or emergent AI.
when: When the tactics to implement exist as documented sequences of steps
why: A scripted approach matches how such tactics are laid out, as ordered sequences of events toward an objective.

text: Use Action Description Language instead of simple STRIPS when a planning problem needs quantified goals, conditional effects, or other features the simple form cannot express.
when: a planning problem is too complex for simple STRIPS
why: the extended form adds the needed expressiveness

text: A blackboard lets each AI module communicate freely with others without explicitly setting up a separate channel for every pair.
when: When AI modules need to share information in more than one direction
why: Shared information lives in one common store that modules read and write, instead of wiring up every pair.

text: A positive-level transition exits the current state, does nothing else at that level, and returns its exit action with the transition, reducing its level by one at each step up.
when: A transition must be handled by an ancestor level
why: Each higher machine in the hierarchy handles the transition in turn, so the exit is passed upward one level at a time.

text: Propagating value along a sequence needs several iterations in the same region, and following known good actions speeds this up.
when: Learning long action sequences.
why: Repeated updates in one region pass value backward along the chain.

text: Information not supplied to a learning character is effectively ignored, so conditions that make an action inappropriate must be represented.
when: Designing context for learned behavior.
why: A learner can only use inputs it is given, so it disregards anything left out of its context.

text: In a hierarchical state machine, a substate that does not handle an event passes it up to its superstate.
when: When several states need the same handling for events, such as jumping and ducking
why: Shared handling sits in a parent state, avoiding duplicated code across the children without inheritance's tight coupling.

text: AND nodes run sub-behaviours in sequence, and OR nodes offer alternative ways to achieve a behaviour, like if-then-else logic.
why: Sequence nodes chain steps in order while alternative nodes choose among methods, together matching if-then-else logic.

text: Applicability criteria prune subtrees that the current world state does not support.
when: Selecting behaviours in a reactive script

text: With eight equally likely behaviors, a balanced decision tree always takes three decisions, while an unbalanced one averages a little under four and a half.
when: eight behaviors, equally likely
why: Balance splits the leaves evenly at each decision, which keeps lookup logarithmic.

text: Organizing thousands of rules into switchable sets reduced the number of active rules at any time to about a hundred.
when: Large rule-based systems with thousands of rules where the matching algorithm itself lags.
why: Only enabled sets are evaluated

text: A blackboard system has three parts: experts, a shared blackboard that any expert can read and write, and an arbiter.
The utility-based GOB model has two inputs: goals, each with an insistence value, and actions that promise to change those insistence values.
World interfacing uses two techniques: event passing, extended to simulated perception, and polling.
Behavior-combination tools let programmers expose prebuilt behaviors and let designers combine them, usually into finite state machines, with decision logic based on game state.
why: Scripting is hard for non-technical level designers, so prebuilt behaviours let designers avoid writing code.

text: Blackboard actions run after the iteration ends, possibly before other experts check them; without agreement flags, they run even if not properly thought through.
when: When an expert posts an action and the iteration ends before other experts have checked it.

text: 1) Experts indicate interest. 2) The arbiter selects one expert. 3) That expert works, possibly changing the board. 4) The expert releases control.
why: The arbiter gives control to one expert at a time, so experts take turns.

text: 1) Return the exit action of the sub-state holding the pending transition. 2) Honor the transition at the level where it lands, returning exit actions of states left on the way. 3) Return the transition's action, then the target's entry action.
when: A sub-state transitions to a state at a higher level

text: When a wildcard identifier matches, record the matched database item as a binding.
when: pattern matching with wildcards
why: Bindings let later rules refer to the matched items

text: Build an opening book only when it is useful for the game, and use other techniques after the opening phase.
when: In games where expert play has established known good opening move sequences.
why: The computer can pick moves from a stored sequence instead of searching with minimaxing.

text: Rule databases should hold true game state, since beliefs there make rule actions likelier to fail; a planner's world model should hold the character's beliefs, so unaware characters lack hazards.
when: choosing what a rule database or planner world model stores
why: An action can fail in many ways, so the database should record only actual game state.

text: Use a blackboard when AI modules need feedback in both directions, so a downstream result can revise an upstream decision.
when: modules need two-way feedback
why: a plain chain cannot express backward messages

text: Under broadcasting, a character can begin reacting to a new event type without re-registration, because the data is already delivered to all listeners.
when: scripts or late design changes need new reactions
why: Listeners already receive every event

text: Fixed numeric priorities give the same result as first-applicable arbitration, because sorting by priority and firing the first triggered rule is equivalent.
In a layered design, pursuing an enemy can be split into a pathfinder, a path follower and an animation scheduler.
Leaving a composite state for a state outside it returns the composite's exit action, and the composite keeps its record of the last sub-state.
when: A transition exits a composite state with history enabled

text: Regular state machines can also use inactivity transitions, though numeric state machines use them more often.
First-applicable arbitration suits rule sets already ordered by priority, especially where repeated firing is intended, such as a rule that always reports current state.
when: When the rules are already arranged in order of priority.

text: Use running mode to obtain decisions from a trained network, and switch to learning mode only when adjusting weights.
when: operating a neural network in a game

text: When a character's importance drops, it is often better to switch its behaviour entirely than only reduce its scheduling.
Use instincts to mitigate poor learned behavior, since instincts perform fairly well by default.
when: Creatures whose learned behavior may go wrong.
why: Built-in fallback behaviours that work reasonably well by default limit damage from poor learning.

text: When characters switch modes, one change can force another, and the chain can cycle into oscillation; hysteresis helps only a little.
when: characters switch behavior modes based on each other
why: Each mode change triggers the next, creating feedback loops.

text: A queued action may interrupt running actions only if its priority is higher than theirs; if it does, it enters the active set.
when: When a queued action wants to interrupt currently running actions.

text: First-applicable arbitration fires the first triggered rule in a fixed ordered list and ignores the rest, giving earlier rules strict precedence.
when: When the rules are already arranged in order of priority.

text: The queue and active set always hold actions sorted from highest to lowest priority, so the top action is first and easy to retrieve.
If the player reinforces an instinct, it becomes part of the learned behavior and is carried out much more often.
when: Learning creatures with built-in instincts.

text: In collusion each character has two goals: to challenge the player and to lead the player to interesting places.
when: Designing enemy or companion behavior
why: Characters act as an indirect control channel, combining goals, character behaviour and visual design so the designer can shape the pacing of play.

text: Narrative directive behaviours are tied to event templates and control many characters at once like a stage manager, while local autonomous behaviours are tied to NPC types and run when an NPC is not in an event.
when: Running a planner-generated story inside an open-ended game world.
why: Autonomous behaviours give NPCs an apparent inner life between events.

text: Dynamic priority arbitration is the slowest arbiter, since all triggered rules must be found and each priority request may search the database.
A rule that fires without changing the database, with no external change, will fire again on every run and can loop endlessly.
when: When rules are chosen by fixed-order, first-applicable arbitration.

text: 1) Collect every triggered rule. 2) Request a priority from each rule, computed at run time from its current importance. 3) Fire the rule with the highest value.
when: When rules should rise in importance gradually instead of jumping to top priority.

text: 1) Arrange behaviors into groups, each blending its members with weights. 2) Order the groups by priority. 3) Consider each group in turn and skip any whose total magnitude is below a small epsilon. 4) Steer with the first group that exceeds epsilon.
when: When some behaviors must always override others, such as avoidance over pursuit
why: Higher-priority urgent behaviors take control without blending with lower ones

text: 1) Ask the top set for one triggered rule. 2) Search that set's own rules, then delegate to contained sets. 3) Each set may use its own arbitration method, such as most-specific.
when: selecting a rule from a hierarchy of rule sets
why: Grouping rules into sets by weapon, power-up or enemy presence lets each group choose its own arbitration.

text: Arrive has no leave counterpart; to leave a target, use flee at full acceleration as the practical opposite.
Fallback behaviours with ranges covering all importance values should run only when nothing else applies; with the smallest-range rule a fallback is always overruled.
Behaviours must save all the data they need before returning control, and only that data.
when: writing behaviours for a cooperative scheduler
why: The scheduler cannot forcibly interrupt a task, so it depends on tasks yielding control in good order, sparing it switch-time clean-up.

text: Select mode from fear level: crossing a threshold means scared; near a scared character means social; very low fear means bored; otherwise curious.
why: Fear levels shift with what characters see, hear or smell, and each stimulus carries an oddness intensity.

text: Implement an interrupting behavior that can occur in any state by pushing its state onto the stack, then popping it when finished to resume the prior state.
when: A behavior such as firing can interrupt any state and must return to the state that was active.
why: The stack records the prior state, so no return transitions need to be hardcoded.

text: Most game characters behave the same regardless of who is present, so they seem less alive than characters that adjust to the status of others.
when: When designing non-player character responses
why: Characters that track their own and others' status appear more responsive.

text: Static character state is a 2D position plus one orientation value, with no velocity. Algorithms using only this data are called static because nothing describes motion.
Only a few actions are usually active at once, so compatibility checks rarely cost much in practice.
Typical external context data include distance to the nearest enemy, distance to safety, time of day, number of observers, and other game-specific quantities.
when: Choosing context for learning characters.

text: Give incidental characters just two behaviors: a standard action and an action the player happens to spot.
when: characters the player will only glimpse
why: Players notice shifts in what a character does far more than steady behaviour, and such shifts mostly happen when the player is close or has been seen.

text: Straight-line sensing assumes characters are stationary, so a fast-moving listener near a sound hears it earlier than a slow one at the same distance.
why: Sound arrival is computed from distance alone, so a listener's changing position never enters the calculation.

text: To suggest emotion, trigger emotion animations at the right moments instead of modeling an emotional state.
when: When characters should seem emotional and modelling their emotional state would be too complicated.
why: A simple animation triggered at the right point gives the illusion of intelligence without any AI infrastructure.

text: Offer a toggle to switch an automated behavior on or off so players can avoid the cases where it fails.
when: When an automated behaviour sometimes works against players in certain cases.
why: Some players were frustrated when automated moves pulled their defensive structures out of position, so letting them choose avoids that.

text: The point of closest approach differs from the point where paths cross, because characters may reach that point at different times.
Games with heavy collisions, such as ice hockey, pool and snooker, may need to predict the results of impacts.
when: Designing movement for collision-heavy games.

text: The squared-time acceleration term in full integration is tiny at high frame rates, so it is usually dropped.
Collision geometry is usually a simplified version of render geometry and is a common basis for AI obstacle data.
A sprite set defines each sprite type's movement, such as static, patrolling, or chasing, and physics may be grid-based or continuous, with or without gravity.
Make context-sensitive avoidance consider the pursuit target so the combined acceleration avoids sharp stalls.
when: When a character pursues a target while also avoiding walls.
why: Blended behaviours that each ignore the others produce glitches, so cooperation between them is needed to avoid stalls.

text: A repulsion force pushes apart characters that come too close, so they avoid each other.
when: When the level is dynamic and other characters move about along the route.
why: Route-following alone cannot react to other moving characters, so a simple push-apart force handles the interaction.

text: The cone threshold is the cosine of the cone's half-angle.
Time of closest approach equals the dot product of relative position and relative velocity divided by the squared length of relative velocity.
why: Positions at a single instant can't reveal whether two paths intersect, so the nearest-approach moment must be found instead.

text: Closest-approach avoidance uses constant memory and time linear in the number of candidate targets.
Assuming any requested acceleration can be applied ignores physical limits, so the requested change may be unattainable.
when: steering a physics-based character
why: Force and motion constraints limit achievable accelerations.

text: Cone-based evasion reacts to proximity and can panic even when the two characters' paths will never meet.
when: When avoidance is triggered by proximity alone, without predicting whether paths will meet.

text: Two characters on a collision course can each sit outside the other's cone until contact, so neither evades.
why: The forward cone only registers the other character at contact, so no evasive trigger fires in time.

text: A constant-velocity forecast fails when the target is about to change direction or speed, such as when approaching a wall.
when: Target is about to turn or change speed.
why: The forecast assumes the current velocity continues unchanged.

text: Collision information is often not in an AI-friendly format, so obtaining it can cost far more than the steering math. Anticipating motion with ray casts or trial movement can be expensive.
when: When collision avoidance must anticipate a character's motion through level geometry.

text: 1) Compare the character's facing vector with the direction to the other character using a dot product. 2) If the result exceeds the cone threshold, evade.
when: In urban areas where many characters' trajectories cross.

text: 1) For each candidate target, compute time to collision and minimum separation. 2) Skip targets whose separation exceeds the radii sum. 3) Keep the earliest positive time. 4) Steer along the normalized relative position at that time, scaled to maximum acceleration.
when: Avoiding groups of characters, where averaging positions and velocities performs poorly.
why: Only the imminent closest approach should drive steering first; later threats are handled once it is cleared.

text: 1) Model each obstacle as a sphere with a center and radius. 2) Test whether any path segment passes within the radius of a center. 3) On violation, project the closest path point outward so the path clears the sphere by a margin greater than the radius. 4) If the path passes exactly through the center, use a point at right angles to the segment.
when: When avoiding circular obstacles with a path-based steering pipeline
why: Sphere tests are cheap and the projected point gives a valid new goal

text: Whether giving or receiving fire, an AI should predict the likely trajectory of the weapon involved.
why: Straight-line aim misses once physics simulation bends projectile paths, so shots fall short.

text: Characters already colliding should act immediately; head-on center-to-center paths should evade current positions and sidestep in different directions.
when: When the character and target are already overlapping.
why: Skipping the future-collision calculation lets action happen immediately.

text: A successful jump needs the right speed, the right direction, and the jump triggered at the right moment, not too late.
when: Designing or implementing character jumps
why: Any of the three can cause the jump to fail

text: Square each goal's insistence before summing discontentment, so one high goal outweighs several medium goals.
when: Combining several goals' insistence values
why: Raw sums let medium goals swamp a high goal, and squaring was found sufficient

text: Give braking overtakes a second designer-defined racing line, which lets the car brake later and take the corner exit.
when: Overtaking under braking at corners
why: Positioning on this line keeps braking later possible, so the car can seize the corner's exit.

text: Spheres suit small obstacles, but a large object's sphere can fill a room and walls cannot be spheres; for isolated objects, a whole-object sphere is often enough.
when: Choosing obstacle representation.
why: Large spheres would block room a character needs, and walls have no sphere form; complex contours matter little when avoiding an object wholly.

text: Post-processing checks let characters exploit quirks, such as a cover point that protects only against attacks from one walkway.
when: Choosing among cover points with live checks
why: Live checks reveal which directions a cover point actually protects

text: In bounding overwatch, some squad members stay in cover watching for enemies, ready to return fire, while others move to the next cover point.
Cover points are usually placed by designers by hand as part of the level data, or computed from the level layout.
For a reasonably sized level, billions of candidate locations may need checking, taking minutes or hours.
when: automatic tactical waypoint generation

text: For cover, the post-processing check is usually a line-of-sight test against the actual enemies.
when: Validating cover waypoints
why: Cover is only useful if it blocks sight from current enemy positions

text: A sense system can account for cover broken by foliage such as bushes, so passing through them can expose a unit.
Four directions, two stances, and five weapon types give 40 states for one cover waypoint.
when: When very high-quality tactics demand many precomputed cover states per waypoint.
why: Precomputed states avoid tactical calculation at run time, but the combinations multiply quickly.

text: 1) Select the cover points closest to the anchor, one per slot. 2) Map each slot to one selected point. 3) When a point leaves the nearest set, the entering point takes the ID of the slot whose point left. 4) Points remaining in the set keep their IDs; a character whose point left steers toward the point now holding its ID.
when: Formation cover points that drop out of the set nearest the anchor point.
why: Reusing the vacated slot ID keeps each assigned character pointed at a valid target.

text: Set the start radius far enough to make the attack non-trivial but not so far that attacks come from another room; keep the random radius below radius times sine of the angle step so positions cover every angle; shrink the angle step as iterations increase.
when: tuning ray-sampled cover estimation
why: Parameter ranges keep samples meaningful and complete.

text: Widen or drop coherence after another behavior moves the character far across the level, so the follower need not rejoin its previous section.
when: Character was relocated by another behavior.
why: Previous parameter no longer near the character.

text: Remove cover points near the leader from the set of available slots, so squad members do not compete for the leader's own cover.
when: Assigning cover slots around a moving leader
why: Otherwise followers try to share the leader's cover.

text: Add ordinary pathfinding waypoints to tactical waypoints, because tactical locations are otherwise unreachable from one another.
when: When tactical waypoints must be connected into a pathfinding graph.
why: Tactical points sit apart with peculiar properties, so none connect easily to the rest.

text: Boolean inputs store one membership value for true and one for false. Enumerated inputs store a fixed membership value for each possible value.
A Boolean fact can be stored as an identifier alone, where the identifier's presence means true and its absence means false.
Child data can nest to any depth, but each node holds only one value.
Datum values can be any type the game supports, including structures or function pointers, and the database treats them as opaque.
Observable game data is vast while actions are limited, so learners can encode very specific rules, but learning every nuance takes a long time.
A Boolean flag can replace a full state machine when the second aspect has only two states.
when: When a secondary aspect of a character has only two possible states.

text: Continuous tactical values let characters rank equally reachable options, preferring the one with the higher value.
when: When a character seeks cover and several waypoints are equally achievable.
why: The numeric value measures how much of a property each waypoint offers, so options can be ranked.

text: Every decision technique takes a character's knowledge as input and produces an action request as output, giving one shared interface for comparing techniques.
when: Comparing decision techniques
why: The input and output interface stays the same across techniques

text: A decision script is a short sequence of primitive actions, such as moving to a point, playing an animation or shooting, that a decision maker requests as a single action.
Decision scripts reportedly delivered most of the desired effect in major commercial games at a fraction of the cost of advanced techniques.
If a decision script is blocked mid-run, the decision maker can choose a different action.
when: the character's path or action is obstructed during a script
why: A scripted sequence submitted as one action can be dropped mid-run, so decision logic reselects instead of being locked in.

text: A bot scripting system runs game-specific script, sometimes JIT compiled, that polls perception functions and requests actions such as animation, movement and pathfinding.
why: Perception functions poll the live game state, letting scripts query what the character can see.

text: 1) Write short lower-level scripts for each action: move into position, throw grenade, move into corner, flank doorway. 2) Write a top-level script that picks the two corners nearest the door, excluding those too close for defense. 3) Reuse the lower scripts for squads of different sizes.
when: Building coordinated squad behaviors from reusable scripts
why: Small reusable scripts compose into larger operations and adapt to casualties

text: Early in learning ID4 rebuilds the tree often with each new example, but as data grows changes become rarer and speed holds up.
when: Early in learning, when few examples have arrived so far.
why: larger example sets stabilize the best attributes

text: A decision tree maps many inputs onto few actions: walking from the root, each branch tests a game-world aspect until an action leaf runs.
Polymorphism lets one algorithm work with many implementations; a chase behavior needs only the target's location, not its type.
Characters usually perform several actions at once, such as gesturing while moving, pursuing an enemy and using a health pack, so actions are layered.
External actions change the game world, such as throwing a switch or moving, while internal actions change the character's own state, such as its emotion or goal.
Information gain is the parent's entropy minus the sum, over child nodes, of each child's share of examples times its entropy.
Not every game needs every layer: board-style games may need only strategy, while purely reactive platform games may have no strategy layer.
Layer boundaries are not sharp: pathfinding can serve both movement and decision making, and tactical analysis can drive one character or a whole team.
Arbitration may return blending weights rather than a single behavior, so the two approaches can be nested.
Multi-branch decisions usually compile down to chains of binary tests, so their implementation speed is often similar to binary trees.
In a decision tree, only the decisions along the path taken are evaluated on a run, so cost is far below the total node count.
Decisions do not combine Boolean operators internally, so compound logic must be expressed through the structure of the tree.
Many utility-based games avoid action-ordering conflicts by design, shaping levels and actions so conflicts rarely arise.
Large rule sets accumulate over releases from new features, player feedback and bug fixes, and can become too slow for the rule engine alone.
Extra children in a database group are ignored, so a pattern matches a record that has more fields than the pattern lists.
A floating-point decision test returns the true child if the value lies between a minimum and maximum, and the false child otherwise.
Because only nearby pairs are compared, the first comparison is usually the strongest waypoint against its weakest close neighbor.
Visibility comes from terrain analysis, security from an influence map, and distance from other towers from an influence-like map of distance to the nearest tower.
Lower behaviors often combine several algorithms: a guard order may use formation steering, while an explore order may use pathfinding plus tactical analysis.
ID3 is simple and relatively efficient, but industry has largely moved to its optimized successors C4, C4.5 and C5.
ID3 works directly on discrete attributes; continuous attributes need a separate extension.
Information gain is a heuristic estimate of a branch's usefulness and may not be the best split criterion.
Use a decision tree when inputs are many, outputs are few, and simple tests are enough to separate the cases.
when: Many inputs must map onto a small set of simple outputs
why: A tree groups many inputs under one action while still letting significant inputs drive the output.

text: Specify each set's characteristic value directly instead of deriving it from membership functions, then blend using normalized degrees to save computation.
when: Speed matters more than deriving values from membership functions
why: Skipping representative-point calculation per fuzzy set cuts computation, while the weighted blend still works.

text: Running a learned decision tree is cheap in game AI, so elaborate split methods are rarely worth their effort over simple ID3 optimizations.
why: Gains from fancier splits are highly domain-specific, while real speedups come from incremental update methods.

text: Decision making driven by messages beats per-frame polling: a character stands still until told it can see danger, instead of checking every frame.
when: When what counts as danger is a game-wide property of objects rather than the character.
why: Polling every frame costs run-time processing.

text: Nest substates inside a complex state, such as scanning, pursuing, and moving through terrain within a chase state, to organize intelligent character behavior.
when: Behavior of an intelligent character is complex and easy to confuse
why: Complicated diagrams are hard to manage flat, so related states are grouped under a parent state.

text: A multi-branch decision holds many daughters and a test value; its branch method reads the value once, selects one daughter, and the walk recurses into it, replacing repeated binary tests.
when: A single value has many discrete outcomes
why: One lookup replaces a chain of binary tests

text: ID4 stores all examples per node, rebuilds a subtree only when its best attribute changes, and always matches ID3's tree on the same examples, though the tree may keep changing.
when: examples arrive online
why: avoids full retraining while staying equivalent to ID3; some regard the continual change as unstable learning

text: An expert can object to a flagged action by deleting it or by posting a new action, such as moving into position, and the original stays pending until that action completes.
why: The action stays on the blackboard so the objecting expert can hold off agreeing until the matter is resolved.

text: Each state fires only its first triggered transition per iteration, so several transitions can fire in one iteration when several states are active.
when: A fuzzy state machine where a character may be in several states at once.
why: Every active state gets to check its transitions each iteration, and only its first triggered one fires.

text: A fuzzy trigger may return a partial confidence that serves as the transition degree, so a condition met at 0.5 produces roughly half the normal effect.
when: When a transition's condition uses fuzzy logic that yields a partial membership value.
why: The transition's degree exposes the fuzzy result, scaling how much of its effect applies.

text: After an upward exit, a machine may have no active state, so its next update enters the initial state first.
when: A transition has exited the machine's composite state upward

text: Assigning the same decision to several true or false child slots merges branches, turning a decision tree into a directed acyclic graph that the existing walk still handles.
why: The walk needs no change, since a shared decision is just reached by more than one path.

text: A decision node's branch method runs its test and returns the chosen child; its walk method calls branch and then recurses into that child. Action nodes return themselves.
ID3 memory is about a log_v(n) and time is about a v n log_v(n), where a is attributes, v is values per attribute and n is examples.
Give each action layer its own simple decision maker, and let a manager collect single-form actions and decide which of them can be layered together.
when: Several simultaneous actions are chosen by separate concerns
why: Each routine emits a single simple action, so coordinating them directly is hard and the manager must sort out layering.

text: Transition decision trees reuse ordinary decision nodes, replacing action leaves with target-state leaves that may also hold actions.
why: Decision trees already sort through chains of conditions quickly, which carries over to choosing transitions.

text: A decision tree is made of decision nodes and action nodes under a common base node that declares a walk method; the walk starts at the root and recurses through decisions to an action.
Multi-tier AI places behaviors at several levels: individual characters, squads, and optionally groups of squads or whole teams.
why: Shared tactical logic sees the wider situation and drives large-scale choices, while individuals refine specifics.

text: Multi-tier AI needs a communication mechanism to pass orders down and a hierarchical scheduler to run the right behavior at the right time.
A combat decision tree checks ammo, enemy visibility and nearby cover in turn, leading to reload, attack, hunt or take-cover actions.
Strategy AI can be multi-tier: a top-level board game AI chooses strategies, and a lower-level AI carries them out through around 20 atomic actions.
when: When the number of possible moves per turn is too large for full minimax search.
why: Grouping moves into broader strategies cuts the options per turn, so the search is manageable.

text: Cycles in child references, such as a merge pointing back to an earlier node on its path, make the walk loop forever without reaching a leaf; keep the structure acyclic.
when: adding merged references to a decision graph
why: A cycle sends the walk round without ever reaching a leaf.

text: If filtering removes everything, a stationary character stays immobile until the target moves or numerical error breaks the deadlock.
when: Stationary character with fully filtered request.
why: No part of the request remains doable, so filtering leaves nothing to act on and the character stalls.

text: Extra programming effort and reduced flexibility may outweigh the small speed gain of multi-branch decisions.
why: Multi-branch code typically reduces to binary tests, so its implementation speed barely differs.

text: Reordering decision tests changes how many decisions run, so the most likely paths should be checked first.
why: A value may be re-tested several times, so testing likely outcomes first cuts repeated work.

text: Large hard-coded state machines become tangled, unclear code that is hard to read and maintain.
when: The machine has many states and transitions

text: Designer-assigned unit influence values strongly shape AI behavior, so tuning is almost always needed.
A state object storing fields specific to one machine cannot be shared this way.
when: When sharing state objects in a State pattern implementation
why: Shared state would mix data from different machines.

text: Every task needs a decomposition schema; if no schema applies to a task, the hierarchical planner fails.
Some example orderings force ID4 to rebuild at almost every step, which can make it slower than running ID3 on each new example.
1) Store daughters in a hash table keyed by discrete values, or in an array searched by binary search for numeric values. 2) Look up the daughter matching the test value. 3) Recurse into it.
when: Choosing among many daughters

text: Lower levels choose the weapon and range for an attack, then use pathfinding and steering to carry it out.
when: executing an explicit order
why: The player only specifies a goal such as attacking a location, so lower levels must work out how to achieve it.

text: 1) Remove every steering component the character cannot perform. 2) Apply the remaining request. 3) Rerun the filter every frame so the motion builds up gradually.
when: Character has movement constraints such as a car's inability to slide sideways.
why: The car cannot accelerate sideways or turn without moving forward, so unachievable components are stripped out each frame, letting motion build up gradually.

text: 1) Offline, sort rules by clause count, most clauses first. 2) At run time, apply first-applicable matching to the sorted list.

1) To AND two decisions, place them in series so the second is tested only if the first passes, with the both-true action at the end and the fallback elsewhere. 2) To OR two decisions, place them in series and swap the actions: action 1 runs if either passes, action 2 runs only if both fail.
when: When a decision needs a Boolean combination of two tests
why: Each decision makes only one simple test, so series placement and swapped actions encode the combined logic.

text: 1) Start with a simple tree. 2) Add decisions while testing in the game to trap special cases or add behaviors.
when: While testing the AI inside the game
why: Decision trees are easy to assemble and can grow incrementally, one stage at a time.

text: 1) If the node is null or a target-state leaf, return it. 2) Otherwise run the node's test. 3) Continue into the true or false child according to the result.
1) Start at the root decision. 2) Evaluate its true-or-false question. 3) Follow the branch that the answer selects. 4) Repeat until a final action is reached.
when: When you want to observe how a decision tree reaches its action
why: tracing shows how the tree reaches its action

text: 1) Give the entity one state reference per machine. 2) Pass each input to every machine. 3) Let each machine respond, spawn behavior and change state independently.
when: Two mostly unrelated sets of states
why: Keeps state counts additive

text: 1) Start with one leaf holding all examples. 2) Split by the attribute with highest information gain. 3) Give each child its subset. 4) Recurse until every example in a node shares one action.
why: The split with the highest information gain tends to produce the most efficient tree.

text: 1) Walk the new example to a leaf. 2) If the leaf action matches, store the example. 3) If not, make the leaf a decision and choose its split with ID3. 4) At a decision node, recompute the best attribute with the new example. 5) If unchanged, pass the example to its matching child. 6) If changed, delete the subtree and run ID3 on the node's examples plus the new one.
when: When each new example arrives during incremental learning

text: 1) At each node, check whether the existing decision still gives the best gain. 2) If it does, pass the example to its matching child. 3) If not, discard the subtree and rebuild it with ID3 on all examples.
why: Changing a decision would invalidate every subtree beneath it.

text: Process waypoints from strongest to weakest, comparing each against its nearby neighbors from weakest to strongest.
when: When condensing waypoints separately for each tactical property
why: Reduces dependence on processing order; without a fixed order, condensation can keep different waypoint sets from the same level, since each removal changes which later pairs compete.

text: Design the engine's AI structure to make sense across multiple genres, not just one.
when: When the same engine is reused for games of different genres
why: Core engine functions are shared by all games, with only a genre-specific layer added on top.

text: Shape decision trees by balancing them, making common branches shorter than rare ones, and placing the most expensive decisions late in the tree.
when: When some decisions are much costlier to run than others
why: Common outcomes then need fewer decisions, and expensive tests run only when absolutely necessary.

text: For characters with many parameterized actions, present a suite of actions and choose the one that best meets immediate needs, rather than building a huge decision tree.
when: When a character has hundreds of parameterized actions to choose from
why: A decision tree over that many actions would become huge, so ranking actions by immediate need avoids this.

text: Check each new merge to ensure it does not create a cycle before accepting it.
when: building merged decision structures
why: Cycles prevent the walk from reaching a leaf

text: Use fixed scripts for cutscenes, and use decision scripts where the environment may change during execution.
when: choosing how to script a character action
why: A fixed script cannot react if the player disrupts the action, so it suits only cutscenes.

text: Before comparing two waypoints, check that a character can move easily between them, usually with a line-of-sight test allowing slight deviations; pairs that fail never compete.
why: Otherwise a good point behind a wall could be lost to a point on the other side.

text: Discard the lower-valued waypoint of a pair when the quality difference exceeds a weighted distance between them.
when: When a movement check between the two waypoints succeeds.

text: Middle tiers should combine current game state with the order from above to judge whether an action is sensible now.
why: Orders from above may not suit the current situation, so the tier checks them against live game state.

text: Pass decisions down as orders to lower tiers rather than scheduling them directly on individual characters.
Store search depth with each table value and do not use shallow entries for deep searches, since a shallow search value is inaccurate for a deeper one.
when: Reusing table entries in a search
why: Shallow values miss consequences that deeper search would reveal

text: Default to state machines for decision making, reserving other methods for behaviors that state machines cannot express.
why: Their adaptability has repeatedly proven valuable.

text: Decision components should return a quick result first, then refine it with extra processing if time is available.
when: In a turn-based game

text: Keep context narrow: the character's internal state plus a handful of important external data.
when: Designing context for learning characters.
why: Large context can improve performance but dramatically reduces learning speed.

text: Decision tests can use ints, floats, Booleans or game types and read game data directly, avoiding duplicate representations but tying the tree to the game's data structure.
when: Decision tests use the game's own types
why: Direct reads need no translation layer, but changes to the game's structure during development can break tests that rely on it.

text: Output filtering is fast, easy and surprisingly effective for most cases, but poor where steering must be followed closely, such as high-speed driving, tight spaces, matching animations or jumping.
when: Choosing an actuation method.
why: Those cases need the steering request honored closely, and a small margin of error in steering breaks filtering.

text: A lower distance weight makes quality differences dominate and leaves fewer waypoints; a higher weight keeps more waypoints. The weight is tuned by hand per level.
when: When tuning the weight for a specific level's size, geometry and quality spread.
why: No fixed rule exists, since the best weight depends on level size, geometry and quality spread; the right output count is judged by eye.

text: Scoring locations by a numeric quality that balances distance against quality stops the character crossing the whole map for a slightly safer spot.
when: Choosing tactical locations by score rather than nearest match
why: Pure nearest selection ignores how much better a farther spot would be

text: Decision trees classify known examples accurately but generalize poorly into gaps between examples, while neural networks generalize more smoothly but may misclassify some training examples.
when: Choosing a classifier for game situations.
why: Hard decisions in trees versus smooth interpolation in networks.

text: Independent AI modules are simpler to build but act without coordination; a central AI can steer them toward one plan, such as favouring offensive construction, training and command.
why: Independent modules only react to their own inputs, so they do not plan ahead for one another.

text: ID4 costs at worst as much as ID3 and at best as much as the naive update; in practice it is much faster than rerunning ID3 and yields flatter trees than the naive update.
when: When the example set is sensible and realistic.
why: Data tends to stabilize quickly, so costly subtree rebuilding rarely happens.

text: Quinlan's gain ratio is an alternative split criterion, but it is more complex mathematically and its results are often domain-specific.
A Dirichlet domain, or Voronoi region, is the set of positions closer to a node's characteristic point than to any other node's point.
Dirichlet domains are widely used because they are easy to program and to edit in a level editor without changing level geometry.
Edge areas of adjacent corridors can be assigned to the wrong node, and routes passing over one another vertically cause similar misclassification; the character then plans a wrong path.
why: A character in the misclassified region believes it is in a different area, so its planned path is wrong.

text: Interlinked rule sets and interacting mechanics produce semirealistic behavior and unauthored events, such as an ally dying, a betrayal, or a character killing others after unmet needs.
when: When simulated entities interact through shared systems.
why: Events arise from combinations of mechanics rather than from scripts.

text: Fire team state machines of this kind work well up to about six or seven characters before group behavior becomes hard to manage.
when: scaling emergent squads
why: Past a complexity threshold, group behavior becomes difficult to control; the threshold depends on individual behavior complexity.

text: In a large emergent group, gaps between V arms are filled by smaller V shapes, and the arrowhead effect stays clear whatever the group size.
when: large groups using emergent formations
why: The shape emerges from each character's local follow rules rather than a fixed geometry.

text: A relatively large number of characters with simple individual behaviors produces larger-scale emergent patterns.
Emergent groups look coordinated without a central planner or leader, as each character accounts for teammates; having one member not position itself relative to another helps.
when: designing squad behavior without a central planner
why: Coordinated shape arises from each character's own steering rules, as flocking does.

text: Each emergent member avoids obstacles and collisions individually, so turning and wall avoidance need not account for the group's size.
when: As long as each character has avoidance behaviors in its steering system.
why: Local avoidance keeps group logic independent of group size.

text: Emergent formations have no formation geometry; each character runs arrive toward a target chosen from other members' positions, so the group shape arises from local rules.

Emergent groups show unintended, annoying behavior that looks unintelligent to players and rarely disappears by tweaking individuals; designers try variations until group behavior is reasonable, then tune it.
when: emergent group design or tuning
why: Group-level dynamics are hard to predict from individual rules.

text: Emergent formations are hard to debug and often produce controlled disorder rather than formation motion, limiting their use where precise group movement is required.
why: The resulting shape hinges on each character's target choices, and unlucky choices break the intended formation.

text: 1) Pick a character ahead as the leader target. 2) Choose a steering point trailing it, off to one side. 3) If another character claims that point or a nearby spot is already targeted, keep searching. 4) Each frame, recompute the point from the chosen character's position and facing. 5) If unreachable, pick a new point.
Emergent formations are simple and effective but hard to tune for exact shapes; members may jostle in the V center or form a single diagonal line from poor target choices.
when: When formations arise from each member's individual steering rules rather than explicit positioning.
why: Each member's target choice shapes the overall result, so small poor choices can produce a different shape entirely.

text: When a player's shields drop and they take cover, enemies that back off give the player time to recover, rather than flushing them out of cover.
when: When the player is weakened and sheltered
why: Letting players recover keeps pressure fair after a risky moment

text: Enemies can use waypoints to occupy defensive positions that surround the player when possible.
when: when the player is in an open area with enough enemies

text: Enemies that are harmless alone can become dangerous in groups, because they flank the player.
when: enemies appear in numbers
why: Group behavior adds spatial pressure that individual enemies lack.

text: Varying the encounter mix changes which builds feel strong, so a playthrough built around one stat type feels different from one built around another.
when: encounters vary in their difficulty for different builds
why: different encounters make different stats easy or hard to rely on

text: Enemies can act as player-sized alternative architecture, shaping routes and behavior like walls; plan them as design elements of the space, not separate additions.
Enemy AI can be framed as negative space: every tactic given to an enemy implies the player behaviors that would defeat it, and the designer shapes those behaviors.
when: When designing enemy tactics
why: Enemy behavior defines which player strategies succeed

text: AI staging lets designers coordinate movement-based events: triggers switch characters on or off, and high-level actions, mostly parametric move-to commands, are assigned to groups.
Enemies can run, fire and aim at once: running and firing are animation channels, while aiming is procedural, driven by where the character looks.
Games need far more distinct entity behaviors than ordinary software, since a typical role-playing game has many inhabitants, items and quests.
Enemies already placed up to a given point determine the expected character level, so the strength of later enemies can be derived from the XP budget before them.
when: When placing enemies in a progression level

text: Reuse a small set of enemy variants with consistent tactics so players learn each enemy's habits.
when: when designing a set of enemies across a game
why: Recognizable and consistent behavior lets players predict and counter enemies.

text: Enemies need little meaning beyond their function, which is to present danger and dominate space.
when: designing enemies in a stylised game
why: Functional clarity matters more than narrative depth for hazards.

text: Distant characters are processed as a group behaviour rather than individually, since thousands cannot all run individual behaviour and switching them off is easily noticed.
when: Large populations away from the player.
why: Group processing keeps a living community at much lower cost.

text: Enemies moving at about the player's walking speed create regions where the player must time movement carefully.
when: tuning enemy speed against player movement
why: Matching the player's speed makes timing the central challenge.

text: Enemies that threaten damage can block a passage the way walls do, so the player must weigh the risk of passing or fighting.
when: when enemies occupy routes in a level
why: Players cannot pass through enemies without risk, so they function as spatial barriers.

text: The approach to a narrative stage can signal its presence by having no enemies, which is readable in games with random encounters.
when: when random encounters occur while walking

text: Gauge encounter danger by counting how many such fights a party survives before a wipe, compared with fights between full heals, and how many wins bring significant progression.
when: evaluating difficulty and progression pacing
why: Survivable fight counts set against full-heal opportunities reveal whether the party can sustain the danger.

text: When the designer knows typical encounters, set defensive and offensive stat costs to match the expected mix, or adjust the mix so that being outnumbered occurs about as often as outnumbering.
when: the designer knows the encounter composition ahead of time
why: equal frequency of advantage and disadvantage makes the two stat types equally valuable

text: Fear rises when agents see, hear, or smell odd things; each stimulus has an oddness intensity for each of the three senses.
when: When a character perceives a spook or trick through sight, sound, or smell.
why: The fear level decides which behavior a character enters, so each odd stimulus shifts what the character does.

text: Allies and enemies that track area knowledge and their own fear can retreat when outnumbered, making encounters more exciting and replayable.
when: When allies or enemies are outnumbered and afraid.
why: fear-based retreat makes outcomes less scripted

text: Strong or hard-to-kill enemies in real time can herd the player toward the location the designer intends.
when: designer needs to steer the player to a specific place
why: Advancing enemies take over previously safe ground, pushing the player onward.

text: Fixed enemy placements, recognizable enemy types and weapons, and generous checkpoints let players build strategies that carry across repeated attempts.
when: when players retry the same encounter many times
why: Predictable elements let players learn from each attempt and refine their approach.

text: In stealth levels, enemies act as architectural elements, so the level becomes a spatial puzzle about their placement.
when: When level design uses prospect and refuge gameplay to move players between hidden spots.
why: Players must find refuges that reveal guard positions, so enemy placement shapes the route through the level.

text: Enemy health sets a hierarchy of power: the weakest enemies die in one shot from any weapon, while larger enemies take many shots from the basic weapon.
when: Designing enemy health tiers against a fixed set of weapons
why: Shot counts give the player a clear measure of how strong each enemy and weapon is.

text: Average time between new enemies equals total playtime divided by the number of distinct enemies, which allows comparing enemy variety across games.
when: comparing content pacing across games

text: Areas where players go too long without encounters are boring, too long with too much health are too easy, and too long with too little health are too hard.
when: Analyzing aggregated session data per area.
why: Gap length and health levels signal pacing and difficulty problems.

text: Typical platform and adventure enemy AI has two states: player spotted, and normal behavior, often standing with animations or following fixed patrols.
when: When enemies do not pathfind and move only locally.
why: Most games use only local movement, so the simplest decision techniques remain the standard.

text: When enemy colour matches the warning signal colour, competitive players can lose reaction time.
when: Especially for novice players, or players who just trained on the other team's colour.
why: Players trained to react to one colour may take longer to detect enemies of the other colour.

text: Testing a layout without its enemies misses that an easy exit can become blocked once a horde arrives.
when: In a mode where players must leave before a zombie horde arrives.
why: Where the player meets an enemy can drastically change how the encounter feels, which an empty layout hides.

text: 1) Show the new enemy in a cutscene 2) face it alone 3) face it with stronger enemies or in disadvantageous spaces 4) pit it against a newly gained weapon.
when: When introducing a new enemy type in a shooter and building up its combinations.
why: Mining one mechanic for many interactions yields varied play without needing many assets.

text: 1) Set total playtime and the share spent in combat. 2) Set the target length of an average combat. 3) Divide combat time by average combat length to get encounters. 4) Divide encounters by enemy variants needed, allowing for reuse, to get the required enemy count.
when: sizing enemy content for a game
why: Expected combat length depends on the expectations the game and its genre set for the player.

text: Vary enemy attack range and approach: give some enemies both ranged and close-range attacks, and have some hang back at range while others tank and rush the player.
why: Range and approach variety forces players to change position, and different styles demand different responses.

text: Every action an enemy can take should have at least one counter the player can use, so players feel empowered to make winning decisions.
why: Players who have a counter blame themselves for failure rather than blaming an unfair or unbalanced game.

text: Give each enemy one to five distinct traits, such as range, abilities, vulnerabilities, or squad behavior, and give more traits to rare, important enemies.
why: Varied traits force players to learn several counters instead of one.

text: Give enemies vulnerabilities the player can exploit, such as silencing spellcasters, dispelling magical beings, or outrunning slow creatures.
why: Exploitable weaknesses give players a reason to identify and use the right counter.

text: Vary enemy strength, speed, and damage range, where damage may depend on armor, to create distinct threats.
why: Multiple variables give enemies different roles in play.

text: Position enemy spawners so enemies appear to emerge from natural features such as woods, so their origin feels explained.
when: enemies should seem to come from the environment
why: Environment art can suggest what happened to characters, so spawn points placed in matching scenery work as narrative clues.

text: Make action-game spawns defensible and isolated from main nodes, yet close enough that players can rejoin a fight quickly.
when: In action-oriented multiplayer shooters where spawns must not hold players back.

text: A stable equilibrium pulls a nudged character back, and its basin of attraction determines how likely the character is to get trapped.
Conflicting steering behaviors can create equilibria in which the character stops and does nothing.
when: when behaviors pull in opposing directions
why: Blending combines the outputs of conflicting behaviors, so opposing demands can settle into a balance point where the character stays put.

text: Priority steering cannot escape a large stable equilibrium: the fallback moves the character out, but if it stays inside the basin, it oscillates back.
when: When a character sits in a large stable equilibrium of its behaviors
why: The fallback's movement is too weak to leave the basin

text: 1) Store each random decision's last result with the frame number it was made. 2) If tested on the next frame, reuse the stored result. 3) Otherwise, redraw and store a new result; a skipped frame discards the stored choice.
when: When random choices in a decision tree must persist across consecutive frames.
why: If a tree skips a frame because another branch was taken, the world has changed, so discarding the stored choice is intended.

text: External knowledge is what a character can observe of the game world: enemy and character positions, level layout, switch and door states, sound directions, available power-ups, surviving squad mates.
An expert system is the purest symbolic form: a large knowledge base of rules applied to derive new facts.
Explainable AI is a research field aiming to make models more transparent and accountable.
A state change action alters game state, often invisibly to the player, such as switching a weapon's fire mode or using a health pack, without requiring character activity.
when: Classifying AI actions
why: State changes modify data rather than producing direct visual output.

text: An entry action runs whenever a state is entered, regardless of where the transition came from. An exit action runs just before the state is left.
A representation converts game information into a form an AI algorithm can process efficiently, usually discarding irrelevant detail.
A hard-coded state machine stores its current state as an enumerated value and writes transition rules directly in game code, usually as conditionals in an update function.
A history state, marked H*, returns a composite state to its last active sub-state on re-entry, and uses the initial sub-state on first entry.
when: A composite state is re-entered after being left

text: A hierarchical transition carries a level offset: zero stays at the current level, positive moves up, and negative moves down.
A transition triggers when its conditions are met, and fires when the character is moved along it to the target state.
A hierarchical state machine lets a state have a superstate, so shared behavior is written once and inherited by its substates.
A pushdown automaton is a state machine that stores its states on a stack, with the current state on top.
A state machine is a diagram of states (circles) and labeled transitions (arrows) that starts in an initial state and may have final states; it models random processes and deterministic game AI.
A state is a condition a system can be in, not a physical location.
UML does not distinguish decisions from transitions and usually leaves decision nodes unlabelled; labelling each decision with its test makes the tree clearer.
when: Documenting decision-tree transitions in UML
why: Unlabelled decisions hide which condition is being tested.

text: Most FSM run time is spent inside the state and transition methods it calls rather than in the update loop itself.
when: Profiling a state machine
why: Optimizing the user-defined methods has more impact than optimizing the loop.

text: A sub-machine state routes action queries to its state part and updates to its machine part, and places itself first in its hierarchy list.
Method-call overhead is usually not the bottleneck for hierarchical state machines, but with thousands of states, cache efficiency can become one.
State machines implicitly use first-applicable arbitration, where the first triggered transition fires; other arbitration schemes are possible but rarely used.
Transition checks are ordinary game functions, such as testing whether a character can see the player, that read the current game state.
Re-entering a composite state through its history record may skip the restored sub-state's entry action, a design choice the implementer can change.
when: A composite state is re-entered with history

text: In game AI, finite state machine (FSM) refers to a character decision structure, whereas in computer science FSM often means a simpler text-parsing automaton.
Running mode is fast, involves no learning, and gives the same output for the same input in a feedforward network.
Finite state machines come from automata theory, the same family that includes the Turing machine.
A finite state machine is not Turing complete, meaning it cannot implement a Turing machine.
Simple state machines and pushdown automata are limited for complex AI, and game AI trends favor behavior trees and planning systems.
With the Gang of Four State pattern, class inheritance implements the hierarchy, with the superstate as base class and substates deriving from it.
Define state machines in data files loaded at run time, using generic transitions that trigger when a data value lies in a given range.
when: Designers need to edit AI behavior without code changes
why: Range-based generic transitions let whole machines be built from data.

text: Keep a flag per piece of state and do work only for pieces whose flags are set, especially where objects stay idle for long stretches.
when: Objects remain idle for long periods and only occasionally need processing.
why: Skipping idle state avoids processing data that has not changed.

text: Use a state machine when characters act in a limited set of ways and change behavior only when an event or influence occurs; decision trees suit choosing among many actions.
when: When selecting a decision structure for a character.
why: State machines hold internal state alongside world input, which suits behavior that persists until an event changes it.

text: Use a finite state machine when behavior depends on internal state with few distinct options and the entity responds to inputs over time.
why: Ad hoc branching on mutable fields is error-prone and grows buggy as moves are added, so explicit states help.

text: Finite state machines suit user input handling, menus, text parsing, network protocols and other asynchronous behavior.
why: Input meaning depends on the current action, and tracking that state blocks invalid repeats such as air jumping.

text: Prefer a stack over many nearly identical states with hardcoded return transitions when an interrupt must resume whatever state was active.
when: Several states need the same interrupt that returns to the previous state.
why: Hardcoded returns multiply states and transitions that differ only in where they return.

text: Use a state machine to describe how a system moves between conditions, especially when each change depends on a rule or a probability.
