Changing avatar state, such as ground versus air, changes how the same button and directional input is interpreted, expanding control without adding buttons.
when: When an avatar has distinct movement states, such as on the ground versus in the air.
why: Each state changes the avatar's physical properties and assigns new meanings to the same inputs.

text: A generic FSM stores only the current state and any triggered transition, so its extra memory use is constant.
when: Estimating memory for a generic state machine
why: The machine tracks only the active state and the transition being taken.

text: Coding transitions as a state machine automatically forbids illegal moves between states, which cuts down on puzzling bugs.
when: When designing complex behaviors with many possible transitions for a game object.
why: Drawing every state and trigger forces the designer to confront every possible change before coding.

text: Queuing the inputs of a finite state machine makes it respond asynchronously, and state machines with per-machine input queues called mailboxes form the actor model of computation.
when: When a state machine must react to inputs asynchronously rather than immediately.
why: A state machine needs a stream of inputs, so a queue turns it into an asynchronous responder.

text: Enemies that switch to a temporary revenge state after a power-up give the player a clear, visible shift in threat.
when: When an enemy AI has a normal mode and a retaliatory mode triggered by a player power-up.

text: A sequence records which sub-action is currently active and updates that record as each sub-action completes.
A transition's trigger check runs the decision from the root and stores the resulting target, so the transition fires only when that target is not null.
why: A branch with no result ends at a null leaf, which means there is no target state to move to.

text: State identifiers start at zero and are contiguous, so they index arrays directly. Each rule stores its input state identifiers and one conclusion identifier.
why: Degrees of membership can be stored directly in an array when state identifiers are contiguous and start at zero.

text: A transition may give each target its own transition degree, and each target's degree is then updated using only its own value.
when: When a character can belong to several states at once, as in grey-area situations.
why: Each state holds its own membership value, so several states can be active together without a single current state.

text: When one source has several transition degrees, the source is reduced by one minus the largest of them, combined with its current degree by minimum.
Unlike state machine transitions, rules react to the contents of the database rather than only switching between states.
when: comparing rules with state machines
why: Rules fire from whatever the knowledge store currently holds, and their outcomes aren't limited to switching states.

text: Hysteresis uses different switching boundaries depending on whether importance is rising or falling, so overlapping ranges prevent flicker.
when: When a value hovers near a switching threshold and flips behaviors repeatedly.
why: Rapid toggling stands out to the player and can starve anytime algorithms or repeat costly entry and exit steps.

text: Transitions in a four-state finite state machine depend only on the agent's own fear level and on others visible in its line of sight.

A stealth guard can be modeled as states Patrolling, Searching and Attacking: noise moves patrol to search, sighting the player moves either to attack, losing the player for 30 seconds moves attack to search, and 30 seconds of finding nothing returns search to patrol.
when: designing deterministic enemy behavior with alert levels
why: each change is triggered by a specific condition, so the states describe behavior clearly

text: If no transition in the current state matches the incoming input, the machine ignores that input.
Pushing a state keeps the previous state directly beneath it. Popping removes the top state, so the one beneath becomes current again.
when: When a temporary state, such as firing, should hand control back to the prior state.
why: Leaving the earlier state in place on the stack lets it be restored when the temporary one ends.

text: Changing an input's mapping by state can make a low-sensitivity input more expressive without feeling jarring, provided the state change is clearly perceptible.
when: Input mapping changes with game state.
why: The player perceives that the character is in a different state.

text: The cost of one FSM update grows linearly with m, the number of transitions per state.
when: Estimating per-frame state machine cost
why: Each update checks the current state's transitions in turn.

text: Hierarchical state machine memory is linear in the number of layers, and time is linear in layers times transitions per state; recursion adds only linear cost.
why: Actions must be buffered while the search descends and ascends through the layers.

text: A hard-coded state machine needs no extra memory, and its time grows linearly with the number of states plus the transitions per state.
why: Actions run directly in code rather than being returned to another routine, so nothing is buffered.

text: A practical Q-learning scale is about 100,000 states with 10 actions each.
when: When learning must finish in a few minutes using about 10 MB of memory.
why: Experimentation showed about five million iterations remain workable and affordable at this size.

text: A sheep-like creature's FSM has four states: grazing, flocking, separating and fleeing; transitions depend on predator proximity, distance from other creatures, or whether it is calm or nervous.
when: Simple creatures in an outdoor herding game with few spatial constraints.
why: Steering can act locally and combine without complex arbitration, so the creature rarely needs sophisticated AI.

text: For Q-learning, a game is modelled as a state machine of states linked by actions; the game maps its situation to a single state number, and the learner never maps back.
why: The learner is model-free and treats the world purely as states, so it only needs a number per state.

text: The reference hierarchical state machine implementation has five parts: a shared base class, a hierarchical machine, a plain state, a levelled transition, and a sub-machine state.
Early game enemies were often state machines: each switched between states such as chasing or fleeing, choosing routes at junctions with state-dependent probabilities.
A state machine holds one state at a time; each state has outgoing transitions with a target state and conditions, and only the current state's transitions are considered.
A finite state machine is a restricted blackboard: the single current state replaces the board, and transitions act as experts that rewrite the state.
why: Finite state machines are a special case of rule-based systems, which are themselves a subset of blackboard architectures.

text: Do not rely on a plain finite state machine for complex game AI: its constrained structure, its greatest virtue, becomes its greatest flaw as behavior grows.
when: When many new behaviors keep being added to a simple state machine.
why: Branching and changing fields are error-prone, so each added behavior tends to break existing ones.

text: The trigger test is the hardest part to generalize, because each transition needs its own conditions.
when: Making a generic transition class
why: Conditions vary too much across transitions to share a single fixed test.

text: Only the first triggered transition is taken, so the order in which a state's transitions are listed determines which one wins.
when: Writing multiple transitions out of one state
why: Later transitions are never tested once an earlier one triggers.

text: Replacing virtual methods with one large type switch quickly becomes messy and hard to extend.
when: Type-specific behavior is replaced by a central switch statement
why: Every new type edits the same switch, so the code grows tangled

text: Changing how a tested value is stored, for instance from a single angle to a four-component quaternion, can silently break decisions that read it.
when: The data layout changes during development
why: Decision trees read game state directly with no translation layer, so a changed representation silently breaks them.

text: Decisions that are rarely executed can fail for a long time without anyone noticing, which makes their bugs hard to find.
Pursuing high tactical quality with fixed states can make the state count grow very large and quickly become unmanageable.
why: Each combination of facing, posture and weapon needs its own state, so the count multiplies.

text: Handling each new move by adding flags to a state machine tends to create bugs as branching and mutable state grow.
why: Every edit to a tangle of branches and changing fields tends to break existing moves.

text: A plain finite state machine has no memory of previous states, so returning to an earlier state needs many duplicated states.
why: A plain machine keeps only its current state, so returning requires a fixed transition built into each duplicate state.

text: The stack in a pushdown automaton stores history, while the stack in a hierarchical state machine manages nesting. The two serve different purposes and should not be confused.
When a state machine cannot express a behavior, the cause is rarely arbitration; the usual fix is a more capable technique.
why: Machines are built for simplicity and take the first valid transition, so a missing behavior usually reflects their structure rather than the choice among transitions.

text: 1) Walk the current state's transitions in order and find the first that triggers. 2) If one triggered, collect the old state's exit action, the transition's action, and the new state's entry action. 3) Move to the target state and return the combined list. 4) If none triggered, return the current state's action.
when: Running a generic state machine each frame
why: Taking the first triggered transition gives a deterministic outcome and bundles all work for the change.

text: 1) If no state is active, enter the initial state. 2) Otherwise, check for a triggered transition. 3) Recurse into the current state's update.
when: Each update of a hierarchical machine

text: 1) Recurse up to the transition's target level. 2) On the way back down, exit active states and enter each next state.
when: A transition with a negative level is applied
why: The target sits in another branch, so each intermediate ancestor must exit and re-enter while descending toward the destination.

text: 1) Branch on the current state value. 2) Check that state's transitions in order. 3) Change state when a transition applies. 4) Map the resulting state to its actions, or perform the actions directly.
when: Each frame of a hard-coded state machine update

text: 1) A plain state returns its action. 2) A sub-machine calls its own update. 3) Any pending transition it returns is honored or passed upward according to its level.
when: No transition triggers at the current level
why: The parent only queries a sub-machine when it has no triggered transition of its own, and a transition belonging to the sub-machine's own level is resolved inside it.

text: 1) For each attribute, list its states. 2) Draw arrows between states. 3) Label each arrow with the event that triggers it. 4) Mark the start state with a double circle.
when: An object has an attribute that changes over time
why: Writing out every state and trigger makes the designer think through everything that can happen to the object.

text: 1) Keep the current state chain as a stack, top being the current state. 2) Start at the top and walk down until a state handles the event. 3) If none handle it, ignore the event.
when: Hierarchical state machine implemented without the State pattern
why: A sub-state that does not handle an input defers it to its superstate, so the nearest ancestor that handles it supplies the behaviour.

text: 1) List the objects in the game. 2) List each object's attributes. 3) List each attribute's possible states. 4) List what triggers each state change.
when: when analyzing a game's mechanics
why: Gameplay is decision making based on information, so the states and triggers that change information are central to the design.

text: Keep trigger testing separate from firing: isTriggered tests firing, getTargetState gives the destination, and getAction gives work done on firing, such as a sound or reset.
when: Designing transitions that do work on state change
why: Separating the trigger test from the fired action keeps each concern isolated and lets transitions perform side effects without changing state logic.

text: Visualize state machines in a debugger or design tool to step through them, view and set character states, and inject events into the event system.
when: a state machine editor is available
why: Inspecting memory cannot reveal how a complex state machine responds, while a tool attached to the running game can read and write its state.

text: Make state changes clearly perceptible, since unclear transitions make results unpredictable, inputs feel random and players resort to random button mashing.
when: One input does different things across states.
why: Unperceived state changes make inputs feel random.

text: Apply state change actions directly to the game state.
when: Executing AI state change actions
why: State changes modify game data and need no intermediary system.

text: Implement most states with one shared class that stores its entry, active and exit action lists and its transition list as data.
when: Building a generic state machine
why: A single data-driven class avoids writing a new state class for every state.

text: Define a representation by the interface an algorithm queries, so decision code works unchanged whichever implementation sits behind it.
when: When a value such as character health could be computed in several different ways.
why: Implementations can then be swapped freely.

text: Any state a pattern must check, such as which entity holds an item, has to be stored as a database fact, otherwise the rule cannot test it.
when: In rule-based systems whose conditions are matched against a database of facts.
why: Rule conditions are checked against the database, so a condition can only succeed on information recorded there.

text: Transitions at higher levels take priority: a sub-state's transitions are checked only if no super-state transition triggers.
when: A composite state has both its own and a sub-state's transitions

text: Reduce the state count by dividing the level into areas, quantising health and ammo into a few levels, and approximating movement with discrete actions.
when: When Q-learning must represent game positions or values that are continuous.
why: Q-learning's memory needs grow with the number of states and actions, and continuous values create effectively unlimited states.

text: Include in the state every factor that affects decisions, such as health, because anything left out of the state cannot be learned.
when: designing the state for Q-learning
why: unrepresented factors cannot influence learned values

text: Write transition routines for each pair of behaviours likely to follow one another, unless importance is guaranteed to change slowly.
when: When the importance of behaviours may change rapidly.

text: A generic FSM built for maximum flexibility is unnecessarily inefficient when only a small part of that flexibility is used.
when: Choosing between generic and specialized state machine designs
why: Unused generality adds overhead without benefit.

text: Multiple inheritance merges the machine and state roles, while encapsulation avoids that; making a machine a state subclass forces the top level to always return its active action.
when: Designing the class structure of a hierarchical state machine
why: A sub-machine must look like a state to its parent while also running its own states, so it combines both roles.

text: Passing private base state through constructors guarantees it exists after construction, but every derived constructor must forward it and expose it.
when: Base class needs a dependency it should keep hidden from subclasses.
why: Forwarding forces derived classes to know about state the base wants private, and adding state requires editing every derived constructor.

text: Polymorphic calls make transition trees flexible but add overhead that may be unacceptable when many transitions or decisions are checked.
when: Many transitions or decisions are evaluated each update

text: Storing only primitive qualities saves memory and avoids cluttering levels with rarely used waypoint data, but querying compound tactics costs extra processing time.
when: Choosing what to store in tactical waypoint data
why: Derived queries run each time they are needed, while stored compounds use memory

text: Finite state machines are the dominant decision process and offer more flexibility, while decision trees have had some success but are less favored.
when: When level designers combine a palette of AI behaviours in an authoring tool.

text: Flocking, modeling bird flocks as boids, is a weighted blend of separation, alignment (velocity matching) and cohesion, applied within a neighborhood to produce group motion.
Flocking suits herds, swarms or crowds that should move together while avoiding each other.
Equal weights may suffice for flocking; separation is typically most important, then cohesion, then alignment.
when: tuning flocking weights

text: Flocking is often misused to mean any steering behavior, since it is only the best-known one; alignment and cohesion weights are sometimes reversed in implementations.
why: Flocking is so widely known that its name gets applied to all steering behaviours.

text: 1) Separation: steer away from neighbors that are crowded. 2) Alignment: match the velocity and direction of the flock. 3) Cohesion: compute the flock's center of mass and pass it as a target to arrive.

Flocking considers only neighbors within a neighborhood, usually a radius cut-off (angular also possible); separation uses nearby boids, cohesion and alignment use neighbors' position, facing and velocity.
why: Ignoring the neighborhood makes every boid respond to the whole group, which is slow and unnatural.

text: If a fire team member is removed, the remaining members still keep themselves safe and can supply offensive capability.
when: a squad member is lost
why: Each member's rules are self-contained.

text: Enemies that coordinate to surround the player, with one taking a flanking position, make combat feel tactically intelligent.
when: enemies are grouped under a shared strategy
why: Coordinated positioning reads as planned rather than random.

text: A formation's structure often depends on its member count: a defensive circle with 20 defenders is wider than one with 5, and with around 100 it may use several concentric rings.
when: When designing formations whose size varies
why: Slot spacing and ring count must grow to fit more members

text: While the anchor moves below full speed, members have room to deviate from their slots around obstacles and the formation shape stays visible.
when: Formation moving through obstacles
why: Members keep slack to take account of their surroundings while the leader is below full speed, so each still holds its slot.

text: Most RTS games move groups as formations: fixed slot patterns defined for a fixed set of units, kept while the group moves as a whole.
Cooperative arbitration makes steering behaviors aware of each other's goals so that context-sensitive behaviors account for them.
A defensive circle places characters evenly around a circle, all facing outward.
Dynamic slots are formation slots whose positions move relative to the anchor as a function of elapsed time, so a formation can change shape while moving or while stationary.
Formation motion moves a group of characters so they keep group organization once the decision to move together has been made.
Soft roles replace yes-or-no role eligibility with a slot cost per character and slot, measuring how hard that character finds the role. Assignment minimizes total cost.
why: A formation still fills sensibly when ideal characters are missing.

text: Compound tactics are assembled by combining primitive qualities, such as a sniper location with both cover and a wide view of the enemy.
A defensive circle has no fixed upper limit on slot count, though very large circles may look silly.
With sequential assignment the slot count equals the number of assignments; the general version finds the highest used slot number and adds one, at some speed cost.
Dynamic slots underpin set plays in sports games and provide the basis for tactical movement.
Formations range from fixed geometric patterns, such as a V or line abreast, to patterns that make use of the environment.
Formation movement appears in team sports, squad titles, real-time strategy genres, and a rising number of first-person shooters, racing titles, and action adventures.

Military and RPG formations often give each member a set job, such as riflemen, grenadiers, machine gunners, and leaders in fixed positions, or magicians and missile users in the middle with melee fighters around them.
Some games reorganize a formation's slot distribution when new ships join, and use more complex movement algorithms than simple formation examples.
With no member holding a special role, a dead member does not require a replacement leader.
when: Formation uses an invisible anchor

text: A waypoint's tactical value often depends on the character's stance, the enemy's direction, or the weapon in use.
AI cooperation ranges from a whole side in an RTS to squads or pairs in shooters.
Formation steering is multi-tiered: squad-level steering moves the group, while individuals keep formation and avoid local obstacles.
A military chain of command is close to top-down, with information also flowing upward to moderate decisions.
A team's state count is roughly the product of each unit's state count times the shared flags, so it grows quickly as units are added.
when: designing the state for a group of learning units
why: Each unit multiplies the combinations the learner must cover.

text: Treat slot costs as high-is-bad, suiting assignment algorithms and cost-based design: zero is ideal, and a very large, effectively infinite cost makes a slot impossible.
Capping formation speed at about half the characters' maximum is a rough fix, but in complex levels it is often not enough.
Use formation motion when a group should stay organized and the decision to move together has already been made.
when: Group movement after a group decision
why: Formation motion is simple, flexible, quick to write, and more stable than collaborative tactical decision making

text: Cost variation matters little for moving formations but can be significant for defensive ones.
why: Units differ in how far they will move to reach a position, and that difference bites mainly when choosing defensive cover.

text: Indoors the anchor's steering must avoid walls, because a formation driven into a wall strands all its members.
when: Formation moves in an enclosed space
why: All members are tied to the anchor's path.

text: Extending formations into three dimensions can suggest space flight, and keeping a clear up and down direction keeps the formation readable.
when: space units
why: a clear vertical axis preserves orientation

text: Choose the formation from the terrain: beside a wall, units line up behind cover; in open ground, they can form a wedge.
when: units moving through varied terrain
why: the formation shape should fit the available cover and space

text: The anchor's target lies just ahead, so arrive slows each character, lowering average speed and formation speed until the formation halts.
when: anchor moderation is applied
why: Slower members pull the anchor back, forming a feedback loop.

text: When the AI detects a particular play, such as a double play in baseball, it can switch each fielder from a fixed slot to a dynamic pattern whose slots follow the play's paths.
when: when a recognized situation calls for a coordinated movement
why: Dynamic slots move along the play's paths, bringing each fielder into place in the sequence of the play.

text: If the anchor is not at the average position of occupied slots, the formation moves each frame and drifts across the level even when it should be stationary.
when: When a formation that should stay stationary resets its anchor to the slot average each frame
why: Shifting slots to the new anchor moves the average again, so the anchor keeps sliding and the formation keeps drifting.

text: Using distance as slot cost makes a character in a spread-out formation prefer a nearby slot over a distant one.
when: Formation is spread out

text: Each squad gets its own narrowcast manager, which routes data fast to the intended members and stops squads mixing up messages.
Formations set only final positions, so units move independently during the move and can be ordered to cover each other.
when: When a cover request is made during movement

text: Formations can nest: a slot holds a character or sub-formation with its own anchor steered by a higher formation, to any depth if both expose the same interface.
why: A shared interface lets the formation system accept either an individual or a sub-formation in any slot.

text: A formation pattern's slot-location query takes the time elapsed since the formation began, letting slots follow timed paths or jump to new positions.
when: When a formation's shape must change over the course of a play
why: Time-dependent queries let one pattern express plays that change shape.

text: A fixed formation is a set of slots defined relative to the leader's slot, and the leader serves as the origin of the pattern.
A formation manager holds a list of slot assignments (character plus slot number), a drift offset, and a formation pattern, and writes each slot's world target to its character on every update.

A formation pattern reports its slot count (possibly fixed), returns the drift offset for a set of assignments, returns a slot's location by number, and says whether it can support a given slot count.
Hard slot roles restrict which characters may fill which slots, so a character occupies a slot only if it can fulfil that slot's role.
Set play slots can be anchored to the field, as in baseball, or to the line of scrimmage, as in football. A fixed anchor means two-level steering and drift correction are unnecessary.
when: Anchor is fixed

text: Coordination approaches include multi-tier AI, emergent cooperation, scripted group actions, and military tactics, which can be used alone or combined.
Territory assignment has three complications: sources differ in strength, each source's region must be contiguous, and each source has a maximum radius set by its strength.
A squad-based shooter example has four layers: rule-based strategy, tactical analysis, group planning and movement, and individual movement for each squad member.

Compound tactics can combine one location's qualities or span two nearby locations, for example a cover point with a fire point within a sideways-roll distance, or an ambush point as an exposed point beside a cover-and-shadow point.
when: Designing tactical waypoint data
why: Derived tactics need not be stored separately

text: Set play pattern books extend the opening book idea to board regions and later game stages, using pattern matching because exact whole-board matches are rare.
Individual-competition sports like one-on-one tennis leave out the coordinated movement layer that team sports AI relies on.
when: In non-team sports such as singles play, where a player competes alone
why: With no team, the team-coordination layer has nothing to direct.

text: A party whose members cannot fill every role cannot fill the slots for the missing roles, so a party of only melee fighters cannot fill missile or magic slots.
when: Hard roles with fixed party composition
why: A hard role admits a character into a slot only when that character can perform the slot's role.

text: Compute drift offset from occupied slots only: 1) average their positions and subtract that centroid from each slot's coordinates. 2) Average their orientations as unit vectors, normalize, convert to an angle in minus pi to pi, and subtract it from each slot's orientation.
when: When an occupied slot empties, such as when a character is killed, shifting the center of mass
why: Otherwise the formation drifts or spins on the spot.

text: 1) Slot angle equals its share of the total slots times a full turn. 2) Radius equals character radius divided by the sine of half the angle between neighboring slots, so shoulders just touch. 3) Position is radius times the cosine and sine of the slot angle, in the horizontal plane. 4) Orientation faces outward at the slot angle.
1) Let slots jump to new positions and have arrive move characters there. 2) For complex plays, have slots follow indirect routes that characters weave along.
when: For simple plays where slots need no travel path, or for complex plays with indirect routes

text: 1) Place the pattern so the leader sits in its slot facing the correct way. 2) For each slot, rotate its offset by the leader's orientation and add the leader's position to get its world position. 3) Set its orientation to the leader's orientation plus the slot's relative orientation. 4) Place each follower directly at its slot.
when: When followers have their position and orientation set directly rather than steered.
why: Followers need no steering of their own when placed this way.

text: 1) Get the anchor point and build its orientation matrix. 2) For each assignment, get the slot location relative to the anchor. 3) Transform it by the anchor's position and orientation. 4) Subtract the drift offset. 5) Pass the result to the character as its steering target.
when: Each update of a formation manager
why: Keeps every character tracking its slot as the group moves

text: 1) To add a character, check the pattern supports one more slot; if so, append an assignment and renumber slots, otherwise report failure. 2) To remove a character, find its assignment, delete it, and renumber slots.
when: Membership of a formation changes
why: Slot numbers must stay contiguous so every occupied slot has a valid location

text: The manager asks each character, through a method, how costly it would be to occupy a given slot.
why: The assignment algorithm only needs a cost value per slot, so where that cost comes from does not matter.

text: 1) Steer the formation anchor along the pattern path. 2) For each member, arrive at its assigned slot. 3) Add collision avoidance or other steering each member needs.
when: Moving a formation of characters
why: Steering each member toward a target slot lets it adjust to its surroundings while the leader's pace stays below maximum.

text: 1) Store a 0-to-1 membership value for each tactical property at each waypoint. 2) Define the compound tactic as a combination of those properties. 3) Compute its value as the minimum of the clause values for AND.
why: Treating values as fuzzy membership degrees lets complex multi-clause definitions reduce to one dependable value.

text: 1) Interpret the player's action, such as assuming they keep moving down a corridor. 2) Choose a squad strategy supporting it, such as covering their back, covering side passages, or securing room flanks and exits. 3) Let individuals pick movement that carries out the strategy.
when: When the squad must back up the player's intended action with a shared plan.
why: The squad-level plan sets the aim, and each member then picks movement that serves it.

text: After casualties, reuse the same lower scripts in smaller top-level scripts: a three-person version keeps one soldier at the door, a two-person version leaves the door unoccupied.
when: Squad size drops during a coordinated operation
why: Lower scripts stay valid, and only the top-level assignment changes

text: 1) List each member's weight per category. 2) Take the worst value per category. 3) Use those values as the squad's weights.
when: Computing a squad's movement weights from mixed members
why: Taking the maximum cost per category keeps the squad within every member's limits

text: Define slot locations as a function of total member count, computed at runtime with no stored slot list, so any number of units can fill the formation.
when: groups whose size changes at runtime
why: A fixed slot count cannot absorb extra units; computed slot positions adapt automatically as members are added or removed.

text: Give the formation's steering a very high maximum acceleration and velocity, since the characters hold it back and it never reaches them.
Limit the leader's turning rate so outlying members do not sweep around at implausible speeds, and account for the whole formation's size in collision and obstacle avoidance.
when: When the formation leader pulls its followers along.

text: In defensive formations, characters should take the best cover first and partial cover only when no better slot is free.
when: Defensive formation using cover

text: Players should not follow their formation blindly; they must still react to what happens on the field.
why: Making slot positions dynamic only moves the burden of sensible movement into another routine.

text: Exclude corners too close to the door when selecting positions, since they do not allow a defensive position.
when: Choosing corner positions for a room-clearing team
why: Close corners leave no room to defend against entry

text: Cooperative AI needs each character to know what its teammates are doing and intend to do.
when: characters that cover exits or wait for teammates
why: Reading teammates' internal state or polling them is fast but error-prone and needs rewriting whenever the AI changes; events avoid that.

text: Store adjusted slot coordinates and recalculate only when occupied slots change; but for dynamic slots, recompute drift correction every frame since slots move over time.
when: When the slots of a dynamic formation move over time.
why: Occupied combinations vary, so offline precomputation is often impossible; moving dynamic slots need per-frame correction.

text: Fixed formations suit simple requirements such as small strategy-game squads, but leader movement constraints make them hard to extend beyond very simple patterns.
when: When formation requirements are very simple, such as small squads in a large-unit strategy game.
why: The leader's turning limits and whole-formation collision constraints make larger patterns hard to move.

text: Separate formations for each party composition are optimal but may need hundreds of designs; generating formations from role counts in code is powerful but complex.
when: Supporting varied party compositions
why: Each party mix moves differently, so a formation designed for one mix suits it best.

text: Frequencies can be dropped entirely, so each behaviour receives a share of AI time according to its priority alone.
Rendering, physics and input must run every frame, whereas AI decisions often change slowly and can run at lower rates.
The lowest level of a group LOD hierarchy can add a priority LOD that favours individuals closest to the player.
Re-requesting an action every frame forces extra transition states, and the number of such states grows quickly as the number of states increases.
when: When actions involve animation or movement that takes time to finish.
why: Most actions take time to finish, so they cannot be completed in a single request.

text: Checking each goal's change on every GOB run costs O(n) for n goals and does not noticeably slow the algorithm.
Both the learning rate and the discount rate should lie between zero and one.
why: Above one, Q-values can grow without limit, so learning never settles on the best solution.

text: The priority scheduler runs in O(n) time and O(m) memory, excluding the work done by the behaviours themselves, matching the load-balancing scheduler.
In request-based scheduling each behaviour asks for a certain amount of time; requests exceeding available time wait for a later frame, usually under a precedence order.
1) Sort queued actions by decreasing priority. 2) Move each one into the active set if it can run alongside the actions already active. 3) Stop when nothing more fits.
why: Priority ranks queued actions, and each action reports whether it can run alongside those already active.

text: 1) Each frame, find the behaviours due to run using their frequency and phase. 2) Sum their priorities. 3) Give each due behaviour remaining time equal to its priority divided by that sum. 4) After each behaviour, recalculate remaining time so overruns shrink later shares.
1) Place the player in a queue. 2) Look for opponents with close MMR. 3) Accept larger MMR gaps as the wait grows. 4) Stop when a match is found.
when: When finding a close-skill opponent takes a long time

text: Cap the action queue when actions come from untrusted sources such as user scripts, and drop the lowest-priority action when the queue is full.
when: actions come from untrusted sources
why: Unbounded input can flood the queue.

text: Developers have been slow to adopt fuzzy logic and neural networks for decision making because they are hard to get working correctly, despite interest in them.
why: They are difficult to make function correctly, so developers avoid them.

text: Fuzzy AND takes the minimum of two degrees, so compound tactics take their value from component properties; fuzzy OR takes the maximum, NOT one minus the degree.
Blending runs every steering behavior and merges their outputs using weights or priorities.
Blends of minimums, maximums and averages are named Smallest or Left of Maximum, Largest or Right of Maximum, and Mean of Maximum (MoM).
Fuzzification converts ordinary game data, such as numbers, Booleans and enumerations, into degrees of membership in fuzzy sets.
A degree of membership is a number from 0 to 1 stating how far an item belongs to a fuzzy set, where 1 means full membership and 0 means none.
In a fuzzy state machine each state has a degree of membership. A state with degree above zero is active, so a character can be in several states at once.
Insistence is a goal's pull on behavior: higher values pull harder, and zero means the goal is fully satisfied.
The IEEE fuzzy control method also called center of gravity does not crop membership functions; each function has a fixed point, so it fits the blended points approach instead.
when: Comparing defuzzification methods with the same name
why: Methods sharing a name can differ, so the correct one must be identified.

text: With crisp (0 or 1) transition degrees a fuzzy state machine behaves like an ordinary one; intermediate degrees express grey areas between fully entering one state or another.
Blending and arbitration are two ends of a continuum rather than exclusive choices.
A fuzzy decision maker produces sensible conclusions, not optimal ones.
Fuzzy NOR is one minus the maximum, NAND is one minus the minimum, and XOR is built from ANDs with NOTs so that exactly one input is true.
Classical logic identities still hold for fuzzy operators; for example, A OR B equals NOT(NOT A AND NOT B).
Restricting degrees to 0 and 1 recovers classical set logic, so all classical logic rules still hold in that case.
An item can belong to several fuzzy sets at once; mutually exclusive classical groups become membership values that ideally sum to 1.
Most implementations do not enforce that memberships sum to 1. Fuzzification is relied on to roughly achieve it, and small deviations matter little.
A fuzzy transition's trigger test can reuse ordinary state machine conditions, including decision trees or fuzzy logic evaluations.
Some modalities always pass their extra check, while others, such as sight, apply a real test.
Center of gravity defuzzification cannot be precomputed offline because its cropping level depends on runtime memberships, so it is often evaluated numerically and is slower.
when: Planning fuzzy control in real-time games
why: The integral depends on input-dependent cropping values known only at runtime.

text: Set each tactical threshold low so many locations pass, because a poor-cover spot may be the best in a room with almost no cover.
when: Rooms offering almost no cover, where weak cover could be the top option
why: Keeps marginally good locations from being discarded early by setting thresholds loosely.

text: Use blending when the behavior set is small and fixed, so its linear cost is negligible.
When a fuzzy set matches a Boolean directly, use membership 0 for false and 1 for true.
when: the fuzzy set is the Boolean condition itself

text: Use a fuzzy decision maker when actions can apply by degree, extremes are easy to decide, and intermediate actions are hard, such as how hard to brake into a corner.
when: Actions where extremes are clear but in-between amounts, such as braking force in a corner, are grey areas
why: Simple either/or methods can only switch, so they cannot represent in-between degrees.

text: Use fuzzy states and terms when behaviour should shift gradually across a range rather than flip between two options.
when: When a character should grow gradually bolder rather than jump between two modes
why: Fuzzy membership blends the two states, so no abrupt switch occurs.

text: Linear falloff is reasonable in practice and cheaper to compute than the alternative falloff curves.
why: Practical results are good and processing is quicker than with alternative curves.

text: Character importance combines story role, which often sets how likely the player is to watch a character, with noticeability such as distance.
why: Players are likelier to watch some characters depending on the role they play in the story.

text: Good designs blend knowledge routes, keeping internal knowledge always available while external knowledge comes through any route.
when: Games that already use sophisticated sense management

text: Blending weights each set's characteristic point by its membership degree, giving smoother output than choosing the set with the highest membership.
Each fuzzy set has its own membership function that maps a numeric input to a degree. One input can feed many functions, and their outputs need not sum to 1.
why: Memberships need only roughly total one, since small deviations barely affect results.

text: In a fuzzy rule 'if A and B then C', the degree of C is the minimum of the degrees of A and B, so a conclusion is no stronger than its weakest condition.
A transition raises its target's degree to the larger of the target's old degree and the smaller of the source degree and the transition degree.
A transition lowers its source's degree to the smaller of its current value and one minus the transition degree.
why: The source keeps only the share not transferred, which is the complement of the transition degree.

text: Linear falloff computes influence as base influence divided by (1 + distance), so doubling the distance halves the influence.
why: Influence shrinks as distance grows and eventually becomes too small to matter.

text: Fuzzy state machine memory is O(n) for n active states, and time is O(nm) for n active states with m transitions per state.
why: Each active state needs its own temporary storage, and every transition of each active state is examined.

text: Location quality values serve as degrees of membership in fuzzy tactical rules, so the strongest applicable tactic wins when actions are mutually exclusive.
when: choosing between tactics that depend on location quality
why: Graded values let the AI rank options rather than only test existence.

text: Every sensory channel carries an attenuation factor, a range limit, and an inverse transmission speed; zero inverse speed means instant perception.
Fuzzy tactical rules are a simple extension with powerful results, yet most games do not use them and rely on simpler tactical information.
Blending within a group dilutes its members' contributions, so a strong member can be cancelled by weaker opposing members.
when: When grouping behaviors with regular weights
why: Each behavior's requested acceleration is scaled by its share of the weights, so opposing requests cancel out its effect.

text: LM abbreviates two different blending methods, and some references use these names only for the single-function case.
when: When defuzzification involves only one membership function, as in some reference texts.

text: Do not read a degree of membership as a probability or percentage, since fuzzy results rarely match probabilistic methods.
why: Membership numbers only carry meaning inside the fuzzy framework, so they are not chances or percentages.

text: Highest-membership defuzzification is coarse: inputs 0, 0, 1 and 0.33, 0.33, 0.34 produce the same output, so small membership differences are ignored.
when: Using the highest-membership method
why: The output changes only in steps, discarding information in the other memberships.

text: 1) Give each action a fuzzy rule of tactical conditions. 2) Combine multiple conditions with AND by taking the minimum membership. 3) Pick the action with the highest resulting membership.
when: rules combine several conditions
why: Tactical scores can enter the rules directly as membership degrees, so the rule evaluation itself does the comparison.

text: 1) Map each crisp input to fuzzy state degrees with membership functions. 2) For each rule, take the minimum of its input degrees. 3) Give each output state the maximum over rules that conclude it. 4) Defuzzify the output states to choose an action.
why: Clauses are joined by AND, so a rule's strength is set by its least-satisfied input.

text: 1) Copy the active-state list and sort the copy by decreasing degree. 2) For each state, test its transitions; on a trigger, read its degree, update targets and add new active targets. 3) Reduce the source degree by one minus the transition degree. 4) Remove the source if its degree reaches zero and skip its other transitions.
when: each iteration of the update
why: Working on a sorted copy keeps the live active list from changing mid-iteration.

text: Start with importance based on distance alone to get the system running, then add other factors later.

1) Tie each character's scheduling frequency or priority to its importance. 2) Map importance to frequency by a function (higher importance, lower frequency value) or by categories. 3) Apply the mapping to priorities too.
when: When a priority-based scheduler is in use, alongside a frequency-based one.
why: Scheduling gives an LOD effect with no extra machinery

text: 1) Crop each membership function at its set's degree. 2) Integrate each cropped region to find its center of mass. 3) Combine the cropped shapes and take the centroid of the result as the output.
when: Accuracy across all memberships matters more than speed
why: Using every membership gives a smooth output that reflects all contributing sets.

text: 1) Find the set with the highest membership degree. 2) Output a characteristic point of that set.
when: Speed and simplicity matter more than precision
why: Only one set and one point are needed, so it is very fast and easy to implement.

text: Normalize membership degrees so the blend weights sum to 1; without it, the output can exceed the value of the fastest set.
when: Blending fuzzy set outputs

text: Recalculate a membership only when its input changes, and reuse the stored degree while the input stays the same.
For systems with many inputs, use a small set of general rules or Combs method, whose rule count grows linearly with the number of input states.
when: When a system has so many input variables that a complete rule set becomes infeasible.
why: Complete rule sets explode combinatorially as inputs grow, which these alternatives avoid.

text: Use the standard min, max and complement operators unless an alternative definition is explicitly stated, because different definitions give different results.
why: These are the most widely used definitions, so they are a safe default.

text: Keep actions out of fuzzy states. Let an external defuzzification step choose which action to perform from the state degrees.
when: When actions are tied to defuzzified values that combine several fuzzy states.
why: A defuzzified value depends on several states together, so no single state can own the action request.

text: Blending weighs all concerns at once but struggles under many movement constraints and tight, constrained layouts; arbitration gives one behavior full control to handle constraints.
when: When a character faces many constraints on how it can move.
why: Blending combines all behaviors' outputs, so constraints can be diluted, while arbitration gives one behavior full control.

text: Center of gravity uses all memberships: more accurate but costlier and harder to extend; blended characteristic points are much quicker and simpler, similar in the reported comparison.
when: Choosing a defuzzification method
why: Accuracy and implementation simplicity pull in opposite directions.

text: A datum is an identifier paired with either one value or a list of child data, and the identifier gives its value meaning.
A hierarchical datum structure gives a matching algorithm more flexibility than flat identifiers do.
Before the mid-1990s, game AI rarely simulated perception and at most used a ray cast to test line of sight.
Goal-oriented action planning was one of the first full planning systems in game AI.
Early turn-based strategy games were simplified board-game variants, and their AI used minimax search.
Games use several different matrices, each tied to a game event, rather than repeatedly applying a single matrix.
when: When the state is updated by distinct in-game events, such as a shot being taken.
why: Each event produces a different state change, so each needs its own transition.

text: Raw frequency prediction suits single choices or counts gathered from many players, where it estimates where a new player is likely to go.
when: When each player makes a choice only once, or when counts are pooled from many players.
why: A single choice offers no sequence to learn from, and pooled counts reflect typical behavior that can hint at a new player's choice.

text: Early choices in a sequence often predict later choices, so predictors that use history outperform raw frequency counts.
when: choices occur in a series
why: Earlier choices in a series carry predictive information that a single overall count does not use.

text: Use history string prediction for choices a player repeats many times, such as cover points or weapon picks during enemy attacks.
when: a choice is repeated many times in similar situations
why: Repetition gives the history enough matching patterns to predict from.

text: The first guess controls MTD speed: a guess closer to the true minimax value needs fewer test iterations and finishes faster.
Targeting probability drops for squares near misses and rises sharply for squares near hits, so a probability-based guesser naturally follows up on found pieces.
when: during play after feedback
why: each result removes or adds consistent layouts

text: Keeping a complete history for data that changes every frame can consume substantial memory and may be impractical.
when: Per-frame data is tracked over long play sessions
why: Every frame adds a new value to the record, so the history keeps growing with play time.

text: 1) Run N-gram windows of increasing size on the same data. 2) Register each sequence in every window, using the most recent sub-sequence that fits. 3) To predict, try the largest window first. 4) If it has enough samples, use it; otherwise drop to next smaller. 5) If no level qualifies, return no prediction or a random one.
when: Running a hierarchical N-gram predictor, especially in online learning where early data must still produce decisions.
why: Large windows are slow to fill, so smaller ones give early predictions.

text: 1) Try a candidate action in simulation. 2) Measure how near it gets to the goal. 3) Adjust and repeat until the result is close enough.
when: Predicting the outcome of impacts such as shots.
why: Running trial simulations is time-consuming, so it is reserved for cases where simpler methods give poor results.

text: 1) Compute where the projectile will land. 2) Test whether its path touches the target character.
when: When predicting whether a projectile will hit a character
why: Landing point and path intersection are separate questions

text: 1) Keep a count for each option. 2) Divide each count by the total to get its predicted probability. 3) Predict the most frequently chosen option.
when: When predicting a player's choice from tallies of that player's past picks.
why: Tallied frequencies serve as a raw estimate of how likely the player is to repeat each option.

text: 1) Store the player's choices as a sequence of symbols, which can be numbers or objects. 2) Take the last k choices as the window. 3) Find earlier occurrences of that window in the history. 4) Predict the choice that most often followed them.
when: predicting a repeated player choice

text: Group related facts about one entity under a shared parent identifier rather than under separate flat keys.
when: Storing several facts about the same character or object

text: Reducing frequency for low-importance characters makes decisions stale and causes overshooting or late collision reactions; reducing priority causes poor routes and unchecked paths.
when: scaling AI detail by character importance
why: Less processing time per update means pathing cannot finish a good search and avoidance checks get skipped.

text: Minimax assumes each player always picks the move best for themselves and the opponent always picks the move worst for the searcher, maximizing their minimum guaranteed result in two-player zero-sum games.
With timing considered, a character with an urgent need prefers a quick partial fix over a long complete one.
when: A need is urgent and actions vary in length
why: Shorter completion time carries more weight in the choice

text: A learner may settle on a small reward it can collect repeatedly instead of heading for the main goal, producing a sub-optimal strategy.
when: Extra small rewards are added to a reinforcement learner.
why: Repeatable small rewards can look more valuable than the distant goal.

text: In late game, edge pattern scores matter less because the last 10 to 15 moves can often be searched fully, so no evaluation is needed.
when: Late game with few remaining moves
why: Full search replaces evaluation near the end

text: A null leaf in a transition decision tree means that the branch leads to no result.
Negamax negates every child's score and keeps the largest at each level, giving the same result as minimax using a single code path.
when: two-player zero-sum games

text: Principal Variation Search repeats a failed scout pass with a standard alpha-beta negamax call rather than a wider scout search.
Each transposition table bucket holds one entry, so when two positions map to the same bucket a replacement rule decides which entry to keep.
Prefer-later-moves replacement keeps the stored entry unless the new clashing position comes from a later move, on the idea that later positions stay useful longer.
why: Later positions remain relevant for longer in the search

text: The static evaluation function is a heuristic that scores a board from one player's point of view. It holds all strategic knowledge, since search algorithms contain none themselves.
The simplest bot state machine has two states: has seen the player, and has not seen the player.
A mixed Nash equilibrium occurs when each player randomizes among moves with set probabilities, and every option yields the same average payoff so no player gains by deviating.
A transposition table is a fixed-size hash table keyed by a world model's hash that records states already reached during search.
Each transposition table slot holds one entry recording the number of actions used to reach that state.
AB negamax is negamax extended with alpha-beta bounds, the practical baseline search for two-player zero-sum games.
Alpha-beta pruning skips branches that cannot change the final decision, so it returns the same move as plain negamax, only faster.
Alpha is the best score the mover can already guarantee; it is a lower limit, and any line scoring below it is never chosen.
Beta is the most the opponent will allow; it is an upper limit, and any line scoring above it will never be reached.
Minimax and MTD are tree-search algorithms for turn-based games, and both require the game to be represented as a special tree.
when: turn-based games

text: The branching factor is the number of moves available at each node of the game tree.
Depth is the maximum number of turns a game can last, and it bounds how far down the game tree a search can go.
The history heuristic orders moves for a deeper search using the results of a shallower iteration.
A transposition table stores board positions and their search results, letting search reuse stored values instead of repeating work; it also serves as working memory for other algorithms.
A transposition is a board position reached by different sequences of moves, and in many games the same position can also recur within a single game.
The horizon effect occurs when a fixed-depth sequence looks excellent but one more move reveals it is terrible, such as capturing a piece only to be checkmated next move.

Normal minimax cannot search even one turn in complex turn-based strategy games, since per-turn move options from many units and cities combine multiplicatively, pushing AI toward real-time techniques.
when: Complex turn-based strategy games with many units and cities
why: Move combinations grow multiplicatively

text: The strict optimal termination condition matches the classic shortest-path algorithm's termination and explores roughly as many nodes as that algorithm does.
Pruning speeds up planning but does not change its scaling with depth, goals, or actions.
Orders can carry strategy, individual targets, areas to avoid because other characters are there, and sometimes complete routes.
No general formula can confirm that a solution found by parameter search is the best possible.
Minimax-style tree search has limited use in real-time games, occasionally appearing as a strategic layer for long-term decisions.
when: real-time games

text: Complex games may use tens of separate scoring mechanisms to judge a position.
Evaluation weights can be adjusted automatically from game experience with a simple learning method, rather than set entirely by hand.
Chess has endgame databases, called tablebases, that record how to force mate with each combination of remaining material.
Minimax works for any two-player perfect information game, from small grid games to chess, needing only a small board interface.
MTD can start from infinity (MT-SSS), from a static evaluation guess (MTD-f), or from guesses carried between iterative deepening searches.
MTD(f) competes with aspiration-window NegaScout for the title of quickest tree search, frequently proving markedly faster in trials, though researchers still argue about additional tuning.
Most top programs still use negascout, but modern game AI increasingly relies on an MTD core.
MTD started from positive infinity reproduces SSS* behavior, and MTD started from negative infinity reproduces DUAL* behavior.
MTD-f, which uses a guess from a previous search, is the most powerful general MTD variant.
Developers often say minimax when they mean a negamax-based version, most commonly alpha-beta negamax.
Principal Variation Search's other differences from negamax are minor, and negascout generally performs better in practice.
Commercial opening database scores come from long histories of expert games and are unlikely to be wrong overall.
Larger chess opening databases, and most databases for less popular games, are generated by a strong program playing itself and recording its most favourable lines.
Expert players accumulate opening knowledge over many years, and for popular games such as chess this knowledge is captured in large databases.
Negascout never examines more boards than alpha-beta negamax on the same tree.
Aspiration negascout wraps negascout in an aspiration driver and is used in leading Chess, Checkers and Reversi programs as a strong game search.
The best move is stored in a table entry because it is the move whose resulting board has the highest inverted score.
Most tree-search methods assume two players, zero-sum outcomes and full information, so many of their strongest speedups do not carry over to broader strategy games.
Rock-paper-scissors has no pure equilibrium but one mixed equilibrium: each throw is chosen one third of the time.
AB negamax is much faster than plain negamax in almost all cases; only when move ordering allows no pruning does it add comparisons without benefit.
AB negamax is the simplest practical board-game AI search and the foundation for further optimizations.
The basic tree-search algorithms are shared and can be applied to any board game, while the strongest versions add per-game tuning.
Minimax is the most famous game search algorithm and dominated turn-based game AI for a long time.
Lookup and store each take constant time, and the table's memory grows linearly with its number of entries.
Terminal positions have no further moves and carry final scores, such as plus one for a win, minus one for a loss, or zero for a draw.
A fixed-depth minimax search does not guarantee finishing before the move deadline, and a large branching factor makes even a few plies slow.
MTD-f combined with iterative deepening is described as the fastest general-purpose game search algorithm.
The MTD family of search algorithms is designed with transpositions in mind.
Swapping the roles of the two sides in the input reverses which side the stable marriage search favours.
Use multi-branch decisions when one value has many distinct outcomes; prefer binary decisions when the tree will be optimized or learned from data.
when: When a decision tree will be optimized or fed to a learning algorithm.
why: Binary trees are easier to optimize, and some learning algorithms only accept binary splits.

text: Feature weights often shift across the game, so a feature that matters in the opening may be weighted differently in the endgame.
when: games whose strategy changes by stage
why: which features matter changes as the board develops

text: Search the likely best moves first, so the alpha-beta window contracts early and later weaker moves are more likely to be pruned.
why: The chance of pruning rises as the window narrows, so anything narrowing it faster yields more cuts.

text: Order moves using results from earlier searches, such as previous depths in iterative deepening or searches on previous turns, which gives better ordering.
why: Calling the evaluation function again and again slows the search, while earlier minimax results rank moves more effectively.

text: In mid-game, the static evaluation should estimate how likely a player is to win from a position, so a clear advantage scores close to the winning value.
when: When the balance of winning or losing is unclear, as in mid-game positions.
why: Search algorithms carry no strategy, so strategic preferences must be encoded in the static evaluation.

text: Give each option a rough score and try the highest-scoring option first; even an inaccurate score beats trying options at random.
when: When several options are open and each can be given a rough score.
why: Trying high-scored options first still front-loads the likely good ones, even when individual scores are poor.

text: The previous search's score is a good aspiration estimate for the next search, since scores usually change little between consecutive searches.
when: consecutive searches of a similar position
why: scores tend to stay close from one search to the next

text: Size the table from the game's branching factor and maximum search depth, since searching many positions needs a large table.
when: When sizing a transposition table for a search with known branching factor and maximum depth.
why: Many checked positions must be stored, so table capacity has to scale with the search.

text: If the table rarely returns useful entries, it is probably too small or its replacement strategy is wrong.
when: Debugging a transposition table whose lookups rarely hit useful stored entries.

text: The optimal root of a subtree lies between the optimal roots of the two subtrees one key narrower, which restricts the root search.
why: This is Knuth's observation.

text: Use a growing search tree when the set of keys expands over time and a fixed array would not suit the data.
when: Choosing a structure for dynamic key sets
why: Insertion adds keys without reallocating or resizing a fixed structure

text: A severely unbalanced tree of eight behaviors can need eight decisions to reach its deepest behavior versus three when balanced, making worst-case lookup linear rather than logarithmic.
when: When comparing a severely unbalanced decision tree with a balanced one holding the same behaviors.
why: Lookup cost equals the path length from root to leaf, which a balanced split keeps near the minimum.

text: In complex games, the tree of possible outcomes becomes too large to map beyond the first few moves, so players and programs rely on pattern recognition.
when: When the range of possible situations is too large to map beyond the opening moves.
why: Recalling solutions from past play avoids plotting an optimal line for every move.

text: Shot transition matrices reduce the total of the state vector each time they are applied, so the total is not conserved and repeated shots eventually leave no safe position.
when: When the same shot matrix form is applied repeatedly to the safety values.

text: Predicting the start of a player's move sequence lets the AI select a counter before the sequence finishes.
when: combo-based melee combat

text: The best-action lookup serves two purposes: choosing which action to take and supplying the maximum next-state term in the update.
The maximum next-state term passes value backwards, so a state gains value when its successor states are good.
Reading a transposition table lets the search jump to promising moves, which plain recursion cannot do.
when: In memory-enhanced test searches that depend on an efficient transposition table.
why: Plain negamax recursion works only by climbing back up and descending again, so it cannot leap to other positions.

text: Negascout's scout passes depend on the first move's score, so good move ordering makes that score accurate and reduces scout failures.
why: A wide-window first-move search gives a reliable estimate, so fewer scout passes fail and need re-search.

text: Positions reached by different move orders share one entry, so looking up the current board returns every playable recommended move.
when: When the opening book is stored as a hash table keyed by board position.
why: Positions can lie on many opening lines, so one board entry can hold several recommended moves.

text: Combined with search extensions, quiescence pruning concentrates most search effort on the parts of the tree most critical for good play.
when: When the position has calmed and leadership on the board has stabilised
why: A branch whose heuristic value barely changes across successive depths is likely accurate, so deeper search there adds little.

text: A smaller alpha-beta window prunes more branches, since only moves scoring inside the current window are of interest. The window starts infinite and should narrow as fast as possible.
why: Better-ordered moves contract the window sooner, so weaker later moves fall outside it and get pruned.

text: Alpha-beta pruning discards scores outside its window, so stored scores may be exact, fail-low (alpha-pruned) or fail-high (beta-pruned) bounds rather than exact values.
when: When a stored transposition-table result came from a search that pruned branches
why: Scores outside the window are ignored rather than computed exactly, so a pruned search only gives bounds.

text: When one reply to a move already scores worse than the best alternative found so far, the move's remaining replies need not be checked.
when: searching a move whose first reply is already refuted
why: The opponent would never allow a score above beta, and we would never pick one below alpha, so the refuted branch sits outside the window.

text: A narrow search window around a good estimate causes many more cutoffs than a full window, so the search finishes much faster.
when: a reliable estimate of the score exists
why: tighter bounds let alpha-beta prune more branches

text: Memory-based search algorithms, such as those using transposition tables, improve dramatically when the best moves are examined first.
when: When a search keeps results in memory such as a transposition table
why: better ordering produces more prunes

text: Before searching a position, the algorithm checks whether it is already stored and reuses the stored value if so, avoiding repeated search.
when: When the same board position recurs through different move orders or repeated play
why: The table records positions with their search results, so earlier work is reused instead of repeated.

text: Per-room delivery relies on denial rather than distribution: information never given to a manager cannot be gained by its listeners.
when: When characters are told about sounds through a manager rather than polling for data.

text: Knuth-Morris-Pratt and Boyer-Moore improve the worst case by using information gathered during the scan, which straight search does not use.
With ascending keys each new key becomes the right child of its predecessor; with descending keys it becomes the left child, forming a chain.
when: When keys are inserted in sorted order, all rising or all falling
why: Each new key lands beside its predecessor with no branching, so the structure ends up as a single chain of nodes.

text: In one test at depth four with about fifty actions per stage, discontentment pruning gave roughly a hundredfold speedup.
Minimax time grows as n to the power d, where n is moves per position and d is maximum depth, while memory grows only with d.
MTD runs in O(n^d) time like negascout, and its memory is O(s), with s being the transposition table entry count.
Table size depends on branching factor, search depth, and hash quality; deep chess searches commonly use tens of megabytes, a few million entries.
when: When searches are deep, as in chess-playing AI; smaller searches or simpler games need far less.
why: Collisions overwrite entries and degrade MTD, and the needed size grows with branching factor and depth.

text: Alpha-beta pruning without move ordering can be about ten times faster than plain minimax, and with excellent ordering it can be roughly 100 times faster than minimax.
Chess scores use plus or minus 1000 for a win or loss, with a pawn worth 10 points, allowing strategic scoring down to a tenth of a pawn.
About 1000 entries was suggested for ten actions at depth ten; the right table size should be tuned by profiling.
when: Choosing transposition table size
why: Speed and memory trade off, so the size is set by experiment and profiling rather than fixed in advance.

text: Transposition-table IDA* uses O(t) memory for t entries and O(nd) time, where n is actions per state and d is depth.
If twice the noise range is smaller than the score gap, the best neighbour always wins; larger noise lets worse neighbours win sometimes.
A starting learning rate of 0.3 is a reasonable guess, though it needs tuning for each problem.
when: Setting alpha for Q-learning.
why: The rate sets how strongly new feedback overrides stored values; a good starting point still needs tuning.

text: AB negamax has time complexity O(n^d) and memory O(d), the same order as plain negamax.
Extensions of 10 to 20 moves have been reported on a base search depth of 8 or 9.
when: If high branching blocks deep search and the horizon effect is noticeable
why: Only the most likely moves are considered at each turn, so promising lines can be searched many levels deeper.

text: In a degenerate search tree the average search takes n/2 comparisons, so cost grows linearly with n.
when: Keys arrive already sorted in one direction, ascending or descending
why: Each new key lands beside its predecessor, so the tree degenerates into a linear chain.

text: A minimax board must provide five operations: list legal moves, apply a move to produce a new board, evaluate for a player, report the current player, and report whether the game is over.
why: Move generation and move application are delegated to the board, keeping the search itself game-independent.

text: A turn-based game is drawn as a tree where nodes are board positions, branches are moves, and players move at alternating levels.
why: Each move changes the board only once, so every branch links one position to the next.

text: Because move sequences can merge as well as split, the game tree is really a graph rather than a strict tree.
when: When different move orders can produce the same board position

text: Tuning decision tree shape to extremes is rarely worth the effort, since trees are already fast; extra branches slow running only slightly, rarely noticeably.
why: Running a decision tree is very fast, so extra branches add only a small cost.

text: The basic top-level match returns on the first matching item, so it reports one set of bindings per pattern rather than all possible bindings.
Choosing the move with the highest possible outcome can be a mistake, because the opponent's best reply may leave a lower guaranteed result than another move.
why: The opponent's replies are assumed worst-case, so a move's value is what remains after their best answer.

text: Numerical instability can stop MTD from converging, so an iteration limit should normally be applied.
why: Instabilities can stop the guess from ever matching the gamma value, so the loop may never end.

text: MTD needs a large transposition table; when positions collide and overwrite needed entries, performance drops badly and the search may fail to return a result.
when: Deep searches with high branching factors that need large transposition tables
why: Different positions mapped to one entry overwrite needed results, which can stop the search returning anything.

text: Negamax is invalid when one player's gain is not exactly the other's loss; non-zero-sum games need the general minimax form.
when: Games that are not two-player zero-sum
why: Sign-flipping of scores is valid only when the opponent's score is exactly the negation of the player's.

text: The name Principal Variation Search is often used incorrectly to mean negascout.
A line strong on paper may lead to a tight position that suits human players but exposes the program to horizon effects, so expert scores may not fit it.
when: When an expert-rated opening leads into a tight strategic position that the program handles poorly
why: each AI has different characteristics

text: Techniques designed for perfect information often perform noticeably worse on imperfect information games unless they are adapted.
when: In imperfect information games, such as those with dice rolls or hidden opponent moves

text: A position's stored value can change within one search because entries are overwritten, so a later lookup may miss and re-search the position with a different result.
when: When transposition table entries are overwritten during the same search
why: A later lookup may miss and force a fresh search that returns a different value.

text: In rare cases a position's score oscillates between two values, which can make some re-searching algorithms loop forever, though basic negascout is not affected.
when: Re-searching algorithms with transposition tables
why: Re-searching can return a value that differs from the stored one, so values may keep alternating.

text: Training on a biased sample leads to a biased outcome, because the model reproduces the skew in its data.
when: When the training sample under-represents some groups or cases.
why: The model reproduces the skew in its training data, and as a black box the bias is hard to find.

text: A single very large maximin connection value can block a direct route, forcing a much longer detour, here a cost of 25 against an optimal 12.
when: group costs use maximin
why: one inflated link value dominates the group cost

text: A high alpha kept throughout training can overwrite hard-won Q-values when transitions are noisy.
when: Alpha stays high and transitions vary.
why: Early learning benefits from fast updates, while a lower rate later protects Q-values already learned from noise.

text: A pruned result is fail-soft: the returned value is a bound rather than the exact score, so storing it requires care.
A failed aspiration search returns no usable best move, so it must be repeated, and the wasted effort grows when the estimate is far off.
when: the estimate is far from the true score
why: a score outside the window cannot be trusted

text: A one-ply search rarely speeds up the overall search on its own.
Extensions rely heavily on the static evaluation function, so a poor evaluation can lead the search to extend along useless options.
when: When search extensions are used in high-branching games with a noticeable horizon effect.
why: Extension choices are driven by the static evaluation, so an inaccurate score steers deepening toward unhelpful lines.

text: Setting the payoff vector to all zeros yields only the all-zero solution, which is not a useful probability distribution.
when: When the payoffs of a zero-sum game are all zero.

text: Without a look-ahead element, the end of a run cannot be recognized on a sequential file.
when: Implementing run detection on sequential input.
why: Spotting a run's end means comparing neighboring keys, yet a file exposes just one element at a time.

text: Keeping a list ordered gives no search gain when lookups of all keys occur equally often.
when: When every word in the text occurs with equal frequency.

text: 1) Search a branch at successive depths. 2) If its heuristic value stays steady across those depths, stop searching it; steady values are probably, not certainly, accurate. 3) Spend the saved effort on other branches or extensions of the most promising lines.
when: Lead changes quickly in early search but later settles into a stable position
why: A stable value is probably accurate, so deeper search adds little information there

text: 1) Generate each legal move and apply it to get a new board. 2) Recurse on each resulting position, increasing depth by one. 3) At game end or maximum depth, return the static evaluation. 4) Keep the highest score on the searcher's turns and the lowest otherwise. 5) At depth zero, record the move giving the best score.
when: searching a two-player perfect information game
