text: 1) Set gamma to the current guess. 2) Run the test on the root at gamma minus a small offset. 3) If the returned value equals gamma, stop and return its move. 4) Otherwise use the result as the new guess and repeat, up to an iteration limit.
1) Keep several transposition tables, each using a different replacement strategy. 2) On lookup, check each table in turn for a matching entry.
when: When no replacement strategy is agreed to be best for a given game.
why: Each strategy's weakness is offset by the others

text: 1) Fully search the first move from each position with a wide window. 2) Scout each later move with a zero-width window based on the first move's score. 3) If a scout fails, re-search that move with a full-width window.
why: A wide window on the first move's pass prevents failure, giving a reliable score to base later scout windows on.

text: 1) Add a Zobrist key that counts repetitions of the position. 2) Each repetition then gets a different hash and is recorded separately.
when: Game scoring depends on repeated positions
why: Tables score every repeat identically, which can make the program give up a won position when it repeats moves.

text: 1) Set the node's best score to negative infinity. 2) For each legal move, apply it and recurse with negated bounds: child beta is the negated maximum of alpha and best, child alpha is the negated beta. 3) Negate the child's score; if it exceeds best, store it with its move. 4) If best reaches beta, return immediately.
when: implementing AB negamax search
why: As the alpha and beta bounds converge, the window narrows, which constrains how much of the tree gets searched.

text: A complete transposition table is a fixed-size array. 1) Compute the index as hash modulo table size. 2) Lookup: return the entry there only if its stored hash matches, otherwise report nothing found. 3) Store: always overwrite the entry at that index.

1) Set alpha and beta to the estimate minus and plus the window size. 2) Run alpha-beta. 3) If the score is at or below alpha, set alpha to a very large negative value and repeat; if at or above beta, set beta very large positive and repeat. 4) Return the score once it lies strictly inside the window.
when: When the board was scored in an earlier search and the player later reaches it.
why: A window around a good estimate allows more branches to be pruned, speeding the search.

text: 1) Start with a guess of zero. 2) For each depth from two up to the maximum, run the MTD search using the previous result as the guess. 3) Check the time limit after each depth.
when: When a move must be chosen within a fixed time limit.
why: Completed shallower searches supply a fallback move, so the program is never left without one when time expires.

text: 1) During the opponent's turn, search the move the computer would make in reply. 2) Store the results in the transposition table. 3) On the computer's own turn, reuse the stored results to search faster.
when: When the computer can predict the human player's likely move.
why: Otherwise the computer sits idle during the human's thinking time.

text: 1) Count valid placements for each piece, including both orientations. 2) If pieces may overlap, multiply the per-piece counts to get the total number of configurations.
when: counting legal layouts on a grid when pieces can overlap
why: without an overlap constraint, each piece's placement is independent of the others

text: 1) Pick a starting option for one player. 2) Alternate best responses between players, following each tie as a separate branch. 3) Stop when the chain cycles. 4) Repeat from every starting option and keep only options that lie on some cycle.
when: reducing a large payoff table before solving
why: Different starting points can reach different loops.

text: Repair a threat, a step that could undo a causal link, by adding an ordering constraint that places it outside the link, or a binding constraint that separates it from the linked steps.
when: A step could undo an established causal link

text: Terminal positions receive the final game score; non-terminal scores must stay strictly below win and loss scores, since a near-win above an actual win makes the AI avoid winning.
when: When scoring boards in the middle of the game rather than terminal ones.

text: For an optimal path, keep searching until the smallest open cost-so-far exceeds the cost of the path found to the goal.
when: an optimal path is required
why: Open nodes with smaller accumulated cost could still lead to a shorter route, so none can be ruled out yet.

text: Experts should run for a short time and then release control so other experts can act.
why: Relinquishing control after a short time lets other experts take a turn on the shared blackboard.

text: Test at a value slightly below gamma, with an offset smaller than the smallest evaluation increment, rather than testing equality, to avoid asymmetry when signs flip during recursion.
when: calling the test from the MTD driver
why: equality checks cause asymmetry under negation

text: Write the static evaluation from the viewpoint of the player to move, so it needs no player argument and checks whose turn it is.
when: When the evaluation runs inside a negamax search where the viewpoint alternates each move.
why: the viewpoint alternates each turn

text: Use negamax for two-player zero-sum games, since it is simpler and faster to execute than minimax.
when: two-player zero-sum games
why: A player's gain is the opponent's loss, so one maximum over negated scores replaces separate min and max.

text: Pair negascout with a transposition table, because its re-searches of parts of the tree gain greatly from recalling earlier results.
when: When scout passes fail and parts of the tree must be re-searched.
why: Re-searches revisit positions already examined, so recalled results save repeated work.

text: Include the opening book in the static evaluation: weight its advice heavily while the position appears in a recorded line, and ignore that term once the game leaves the book.
when: When the opening book is used inside a general-purpose search rather than as a separate tool

text: Play the next move from a stored line without searching when that line ends in a position favorable to the AI.
when: at the start of a game
why: skips minimax entirely

text: Match the agent's skill to the evaluation goal: use a goal-finishing agent to test playability and a human-imitating agent to estimate player experience.
when: When content is judged for playability, such as whether a start-to-end path exists in a maze

text: Because IDA* keeps no open or closed lists, detect repeated states with a transposition table to avoid duplicated work.
why: Without open and closed lists, IDA* cannot notice a revisited world state, so repeated action sequences go unchecked.

text: When minimizing a score in annealing, treat lower values as better, reversing the usual hill-climbing comparison.
when: When the annealing search is treated as minimizing a function value
why: Annealing methods are conventionally framed around energy landscapes, where minimizing is the goal.

text: Start the root search with alpha at negative infinity and beta at positive infinity, then return the best move found.
The aspiration window size should depend on the range of scores the evaluation function can return.
For transposition tables, prefer one entry per bucket because lookup speed matters more than keeping every entry, and rarely recurring positions need not be stored.
when: transposition table design
why: lookup speed matters more than full storage

text: Extend minimax-based search with a transposition table so that each merged position is searched only once.
when: When the game tree contains merging branches.
why: The same position can be reached through different move orders, so the tree merges and repeats work unless results are stored.

text: A good state hash spreads likely positions widely across its range, and a small board change should produce a very different hash.
when: In games where successive boards differ only slightly from move to move
why: Most possible boards never occur, so spread avoids collisions among real positions.

text: In basic linear search, check the index bound before comparing the element, because the order of the two factors in the compound test matters.
when: writing the basic version without a sentinel

text: A search for one solution stops at the first complete placement and reports it, without exploring the remaining candidates.
when: Only one solution is needed.
why: Stopping at the first complete placement makes the program simpler than enumerating every solution.

text: Record each move by writing its move number into the board matrix, where zero means unvisited, and clear the square back to zero to undo it.
when: Backtracking over board squares.
why: Keeping a history of successive occupations lets each move be identified by its sequence number.

text: Basic turn-based search assumes two players; extending minimax to more players uses the same code, maximizing on the searcher's turns and minimizing on others' turns, but makes its optimizations harder to apply.
when: more than two players
why: Most algorithms and optimizations were designed around two players, so extra players make the optimizations harder to apply.

text: Entries store hash, best move, depth and score; alpha-beta needs a score-type flag for exact or bound values, while MTD's min and max scores make the flag unnecessary.
when: When alpha-beta search stores results in a transposition table from branches it pruned
why: Pruning can leave stored scores as bounds rather than exact values, so each entry must say which kind it holds.

text: Deep decision trees make decisions from fine detail, while shallow trees produce broad, general behavior.
when: Designing decision tree structure for AI.
why: More branch points capture finer distinctions.

text: MTD-best returns the best move without accurate scores for each position; it is slightly faster than MTD-f but more complex, does not indicate how good moves are, and is less common in most turn-based games.
why: Most turn-based games need to know how good each move is, which MTD-best does not provide.

text: Move ordering trades knowledge against search: perfect knowledge of the best moves would remove the need to search, while ordering with the static evaluation costs time when that evaluation is called repeatedly.
why: Ordering well requires knowing the better moves, which is what the search itself is supposed to determine.

text: Fail-soft alpha-beta returns the best result found when it fails, while plain alpha-beta returns only alpha or beta, giving no sense of how far to move the guess.
why: Returning the best value found lets the caller adjust the guess and re-search with a sensible window.

text: Simple turn-based strategy games can use tree search directly, with research, construction and troop movement forming the moves while the board is static during a turn; complex ones usually need real-time-style techniques.
when: Simple turn-based strategy games versus complex ones.
why: Complex strategy games bog down search before it reaches a sensible decision, so they rely on other techniques.

text: Deeper search counters the horizon effect, but high branching can make it impossible, so extensions are used instead.
when: When the horizon effect is noticeable and branching prevents full deep search.
why: Deeper search lets the computer see a refutation that lies just beyond its horizon before committing to a move.

text: Generative NPCs let developers define a character's background, attitude, and personality, while a language model handles player conversation.
Generative AI produces plausible answers that are not necessarily accurate, and can fabricate misinformation, discriminate, or generate hate speech.
Decomposers run in series and order matters. Early decomposers do broad coarse planning, such as pathfinding, and later ones refine sub-goals in detail.
when: When a steering pipeline chains several decomposers, passing each sub-goal along
why: Later stages only decompose the sub-goal, so they need not consider the full route and can work in more detail.

text: GOAP extends utility-based decision making to action sequences that best fulfil goals overall; depth-first GOAP judges each sequence by the discontentment it leaves after its last action.
Dijkstra's loop is a multibranch WHILE loop with its own guard for each branch, which makes braided loops easier to write correctly.
Goal-oriented behaviour makes a character pursue internal goals or desires rather than only reacting to inputs.
A hierarchical task network represents a plan as a hierarchy in which abstract operators are decomposed through schemas until only primitive operators remain.
Complex AI usually runs on the CPU, which on earlier consoles had budgets like those of 5- or 10-year-old PCs.
Evaluation functions usually return a signed integer, since many algorithms need integers and integer arithmetic is faster than floating point on most machines.
Most toolchains are data driven, letting users add data to an object's definition for use in decision making.
Guaranteed intelligent movement requires full motion planning, which is slower than pipeline steering.
Goal-oriented behaviour covers a simple goal-seeking framework, utility-based decision making, and goal-oriented action planning, which plans sequences of actions.
Planning action sequences is hard for two reasons: combinations grow quickly, with naive cost O(nmk) for k steps, and actions enable or disable other actions.
Recalculating only changed goals may approach O(nm) cost in some cases, though it gave little practical gain.
Depth-first GOAP planning is brute force, and no better general solution is known for this form of GOAP.
A multi-step action reports the total time to reach its goal, including every internal step such as preparation.
A character can hold any number of goals, also called motives, and some games allow hundreds of possible goals.
Goals are either fully satisfiable, dropping to zero when met, or permanent, staying low when met, like a stay-healthy goal.
Goals and motives can be treated as the same thing, so a belief layer that derives goals from motives is unnecessary.
Several different actions can fulfil the same goal, and each action lists the goals it can achieve.
Store the goal in the heuristic at construction so one general implementation can estimate distances between any nodes for any goal.
why: Writing a separate estimator for every goal in the world is cumbersome, so the goal is passed in as a parameter.

text: Goal-oriented behaviour suits genres where characters have many needs and many possible actions, such as people simulations.
when: Characters with many internal needs and a very large set of parameterized actions
why: A decision tree over that many actions would become very large, so ranking actions by how well they meet current needs is more manageable.

text: The quartic can yield up to two real arcs; no real root means the target is unreachable at that muzzle speed, and one root means it is at the absolute range limit.
when: solving for a fixed muzzle speed

text: Recording geometric constraints, such as perpendicular edges, lets a sketch update consistently: changing one element propagates to every diagram that uses it.
Different orders of the same actions often produce the same world state, so a depth-first planner revisits identical states.
when: In GOAP applications where different orderings of the same actions reach one result
why: Without OPEN and CLOSED lists, the search cannot tell that a world state was already reached by another path.

text: A character periodically re-evaluates its goals and selects the most relevant one, which keeps control until another goal is chosen.
when: When each character has a pre-determined set of goals that influence its behaviour

text: Continuous planning needs O(1) memory beyond temporary storage; running time scales linearly with n, the count of nearby vehicles nearer than the front car in this lane.
Depth-first GOAP planning uses O(k) memory and O(nmk) time, for depth k, n goals, and m average actions per stage.
Flattening alarm behaviors into one state machine doubles the state count for each alarm level added.
when: Multiple alarm levels interrupt the same agent
why: Each interrupt must remember the behaviour it displaced so it can resume it afterward, which multiplies the states.

text: Goals hold a value and a discontentment method; actions hold a goal change method that returns their effect on each goal.
why: Letting each goal compute its own discontentment allows different curves, such as cubing insistence for very important goals.

text: Hybrid goal-based AI gives each character predefined goals, each controlled by its own finite state machine.
Goal-oriented action planning replaces pre-built state machines with a planner that chains available actions to satisfy a goal.
An algorithm that looks compelling in a simple demo can bring a full production game to a standstill through its cost.
when: When a demo-proven algorithm is moved into a production game with fixed time and memory budgets
why: Game AI works within limited processor time and memory, which a simple demo does not have to respect.

text: Time-aware utility works poorly for on/off goals, such as in shooter-style games, because those goals have no internal state that changes over time.
when: Goals are binary rather than continuous quantities
why: Without a changing value, there is no natural rate of change to predict

text: 1) Replace a state's transitions with a decision tree whose leaves are target states. 2) Test shared conditions once near the root. 3) Route each path to the state it selects.
when: Several transitions share tests, especially expensive ones
why: Shared tests run once instead of being repeated across flat transition conditions.

text: 1) Allocate world models one more than the maximum depth, the first holding the current state. 2) At maximum depth, score discontentment and keep the best. 3) Otherwise take the next untried action, copy the model to the next level, apply it there, and go deeper. 4) When no actions remain, go up one level. 5) Stop when depth returns to zero. Execute the first action of the best sequence.

1) Start from an abstract root operator. 2) Pick an abstract operator to expand. 3) Select a decomposition schema whose preconditions hold. 4) Replace the operator with its subtasks. 5) Repeat until no abstract operators remain and all preconditions hold; fail if no schema applies.
Give actions their own algorithm for managing and running them, called a general action manager, when actions are treated as a distinct concept.
when: Designing action execution for characters.
why: A separate manager is needed to schedule and run distinct actions.

text: Require simultaneous actions to be embedded in explicit combinations rather than combined ad hoc in the active list; this makes time cost linear in queue size.
when: When there are many actions both in the queue and in the active set
why: Pairwise compatibility checks between queued and active actions are avoided.

text: Give each goal its own discontentment method; squaring is the default, higher powers suit critical goals, and minor goals should contribute little.
when: Tuning goal weights
why: Each goal needs a different response curve in practice

text: Use discontentment-based choice when one action affects several goals and side effects matter.
when: When an action's side effects on other goals matter for the choice
why: Maximising one goal alone can ignore risks; minimising total discontentment across all goals accounts for side effects.

text: Use a goal's designed rate of change directly when designers set it, since the game already updates the goal at that rate.
when: The rate is set by game design
why: The game already updates each motive at that rate, so the value is directly available to the planner.

text: Stopping at first goal reach or smallest open estimate is faster but may return a non-shortest path; the strict condition is optimal but loses much of A*'s speed.
when: When the heuristic is tuned to allow sub-optimal results in exchange for speed
why: Closed nodes may later improve, so early stopping can miss the shortest path.

text: Searching every action sequence to a fixed depth finds the best plan within that depth, but search time grows with the number of sequences.
Large-scale movement means moving whole characters around the level, not limbs or faces, which belongs to animation.
Light units may accept travelling farther for a slot than heavy units, so mobility should enter the slot cost.
when: Units differ in mobility

text: Most platform and adventure enemies use purely local movement; only a few use pathfinding, typically over a navigation mesh.
If the anchor leader moves at full speed, followers have no time to reach cover and appear to trail it; slowing the leader lets them take cover around it.
when: Squad uses a leader character as the overwatch anchor
why: Followers need time to reach cover slots before the anchor moves on.

text: Ordinary avoidance can choose a maneuver a skidding vehicle cannot execute well, when accelerating forward would avoid impact.
when: when the character's current motion limits its options
why: Vehicles favor forward travel toward their goal, so an avoidance result that requires reversing and steering fits them poorly.

text: A large squad may be unable to pass a narrow area that its members pass individually, which needs dedicated rules such as code, a decision tree, or an expert system.
when: Squads moving through narrow areas
why: Group size creates constraints that individual pathfinding does not capture

text: Have each character announce its intentions to others as events rather than having others read or poll them.
when: When characters in a coordinated action must know what teammates are doing and intend to do next.
why: Event-based sharing is more robust than reading internal state

text: Pursue builds a seek target from another character's motion, collision avoidance builds a flee target from obstacle proximity, and wander creates its own meandering target.
Role suitability varies by degree; a mage may find melee slots very costly and missile slots only somewhat costly.
Group behaviors first summarize many targets, either by averaging a property such as center of mass, or by ordering and searching for the nearest or colliding targets.

Simplify each character's rules for large numbers of identical enemies, where challenge comes from numbers; for more characters generally, use a multi-tier design where each squad is an emergent unit obeying group orders.
when: scaling enemy group size
why: Simpler individuals scale better; tiers keep group behavior manageable.

text: Top-down, flow-based simulation suits large populations that need individual detail only where the player can see them.
when: Large crowds such as traffic or pedestrians where most members are off-screen
why: Simulating unseen members individually wastes processing time

text: Combine fixed motions for some roles with responsive roles for others. In a corner kick, three players run fixed motions while the rest respond to the defense.
when: Team plays with both scripted and reactive roles
why: Fixed roles give teammates a predictable anchor, such as where the ball will be placed, while responsive roles adapt to the defense.

text: Use kinematic seek toward visible targets for social movement, rather than planned paths.
when: Agents moving toward others they can see

text: Use a hierarchical state machine when several states share the same responses, such as jumping and ducking while on the ground.
when: When several character states share the same input responses, such as standing, walking, running and sliding on the ground.
why: Avoids duplicating shared behavior across states

text: Agents can record visited and interesting places and share interesting ones with peers, spreading knowledge through the group.
when: Groups of agents that remember and exchange experiences
why: Models how word of good experiences spreads.

text: Group coordination comes either from complementary individual decisions, or from a group decision (e.g., a shared response to threat) that members then carry out individually.
when: When a squad-level decision, such as taking cover under fire, must be carried out by each member individually.
why: The group sets intent and members handle execution.

text: Sensors and detectors tested only on one user group can fail for others, such as skin tones or faces absent from testing.
when: When validation covers only a narrow set of users.
why: Blind spots stay hidden because the failing group was never tested.

text: With many targets, react only to the first imminent collision, because averaging over targets works poorly.
when: When a character must avoid several other characters at once.
why: The algorithm must find the character whose closest approach comes first and react only to it, since averaging over several fails.

text: Use the same decision tools for groups as for individuals, with outputs issued as orders to lower tiers; no special group algorithm is needed.
when: In top-down multi-tier AI where higher levels issue orders to lower tiers.
why: Group decision tools take world input and produce an action, the same as individual decision tools do.

text: A state object with no fields specific to one state machine can be shared as a flyweight and reused by several machines at once.
when: The state's behavior does not depend on which machine runs it.
why: Without machine-specific data, one instance serves every machine.

text: Intent orders (defend, all-out assault) are flexible but need hard, often unconvincing AI intent interpretation; prefer explicit orders when inferring intent is too hard or the squad feels poor.
when: offering orders in a shooter squad
why: Intent identification is difficult for the AI; explicit orders remove the need to infer intent.

text: Fixed slot patterns suit rigid, well-practiced plays, while a coordinating routine suits play where characters must respond to opponents. Pure scripts and fully free improvisation both fail in different ways.
when: Designing team movement
why: Fully dynamic slot placement only moves the hard question of sensible movement into other code, so an intermediate approach is practical.

text: Decision trees often read the global game state directly rather than a character's model of what it knows.
In a hierarchical machine, a lower machine is considered only when the higher machine does not respond to its alarm, so the highest active state always controls behavior and priority is unambiguous.
when: Each alarm level has its own machine
why: A lower machine is consulted only when the higher one ignores its alarm, so priority is fixed by level.

text: Hierarchical state machines are difficult to coordinate when they are implemented in hard-coded style.
why: Hard-coded machines must be rewritten and recompiled for every behavior change, and nested structures are hard to coordinate this way.

text: Reserve costly responses such as ambushes for predictions whose probability is high, and use lower-cost responses otherwise.
when: acting on an N-gram prediction
why: A wrong prediction then wastes less of the AI's effort.

text: Consolidate interrupt behavior duplicated across several states into a hierarchical state machine rather than repeating it in each state.
when: When a shared action such as firing can be started from many states and must return to the prior state afterward.
why: A plain state machine forgets the prior state, so returning to it would need a near-duplicate state for every combination.

text: A sharpening filter does the opposite of a blur: it concentrates values in regions that already hold the most, helping locate the central hub of an influence.
A sharpening matrix has a positive center value surrounded by negative values, and larger matrices follow the same principle.
when: Designing influence map filters

text: Influence map sharpening is typically run just a few passes and seldom iterated until it converges.
when: Applying sharpening to influence maps
why: Many passes concentrate influence onto unit locations, reducing usefulness.

text: Encoding actions as discrete data lets a character imitate observed actions and vary them slightly.
To imitate echoes with a model that has none, emit fresh sounds every few frames.
when: when the sound model lacks echoes
why: Sounds fade and vanish in this model, so repeated fresh emissions are needed to keep an echo-like effect present.

text: Influence mapping, pioneered for real-time strategy games, scores map areas by which side controls them and has since spread to squad shooters and massively multiplayer games.
A frag-map is a per-location map learned from combat: locations where the AI was hit or killed get negative values, and locations where it scored hits get positive values.
why: It lets the AI learn dangerous and advantageous locations from experience.

text: An influence map records, for each location, which side controls it and by how much, computed by summing each unit's influence, which decays with distance from the unit.
Map flooding is a Dijkstra-style expansion from several source locations that assigns each location to the source giving it the strongest influence.
A convolution filter replaces each tile's value with a weighted sum of its neighborhood, using an odd-sized square weight matrix whose center element refers to the updated tile.
Building a detailed frag-map requires many combat experiences per location; filtering can extend known values to nearby unexplored locations.
Influence maps reveal very secure areas, areas to avoid, and weak border points where the influence difference is small, which can guide attack placement and movement.
An influence map outputs, per location, the controlling side, the degree of control, and optionally the degree of security.
For a withdrawal point, the check can use an influence map to test whether the location is under enemy control.
when: Validating retreat waypoints
why: Influence maps show where enemies dominate the map

text: With a fixed number of height checks per location, terrain analysis takes constant time per location.
Record where agents became frightened on a tactical waypoint map, built like a fragmap, to guide avoidance.
A non-conservative transition matrix lets the state total rise or fall over successive updates.
The same technique is called a kernel filter or impulse response filter in other fields.
Convolution-based influence starts with spikes at unit positions and repeatedly blurs them outward across the map.
Map flooding needs only a function returning each location's neighbors, and sources must expose their location and strength; grid neighbor lookup can be inlined for speed.
Negative frag-map areas are dangerous to linger in, while positive areas are good for picking off enemies.
when: When a character observes kills and hits happening around it and builds the map from those observations.
why: Only observable kills and hits are used, since using hidden hit-point totals would give the AI information players lack.

text: Support both general and separable convolution in a tactical analysis server, because most convolution matrices are not separable.
when: When writing a tactical analysis server meant to be reused as widely as possible.
why: Most convolution matrices are not separable, so the general algorithm is needed alongside the faster separable one.

text: Spread influence calculation across many frames; one full pass every ten seconds often gives data recent enough for sensible character AI.
when: When the balance of power on a level changes slowly from frame to frame.
why: The calculation can be interrupted and spread over frames, and slightly stale data still lets character AI look sensible.

text: The combining formula is designer-chosen and needs tuning; showing each layer and the combined result as a debug overlay helps.
when: When combining several influence analyses into one score for a location.
why: No inherent rule makes one way of combining the layers better, so the developer must choose and tune the formula by hand.

text: Combining frequency and priority helps: frequent running avoids overshooting while longer running improves decisions, though collision avoidance remains costly.
when: When AI scheduling is reduced by level of detail for characters of differing importance.
why: Frequent runs stop a character committing to stale plans, while longer runs return better-reasoned results.

text: Online frag-map learning multiplies all values toward zero before each new event, unlearning old information so the AI adapts to the player's style.
when: online learning
why: Old combat results lose weight as new ones arrive.

text: With direct lighting and static lightmaps, shadow checks for hiding can be spread over several frames to fit the performance budget.
when: stealth titles using static lightmaps
why: Lighting is baked into static maps, so runtime shadow checks need no costly global illumination and can be spread across frames.

text: Map flooding gives each location the strongest single-unit influence reaching it, runs in about O(min[nr, m]) time and O(m) memory, and can incorporate terrain.
when: When influence must account for terrain while spreading out from each unit.
why: It propagates influence outward from each unit with a shortest-path style expansion, which keeps it fast.

text: Decaying by 0.9 per new frag, a spot hit from two directions stops being used after about five frags, versus ten frags without decay; five may still feel slow.
when: two attack directions, online decay of 0.9
why: Each new frag multiplies every stored value first, so older kills shrink in weight and the AI gradually forgets the ambush spot.

text: A 3x3 blur takes nine multiply-add operations per location directly but six when separated; for size 3 in the larger example the counts are 25 and 10.
when: When the convolution filter is the outer product of two vectors.

text: Combined quality can be security × visibility × distance, with security set to zero wherever an enemy controls the location.
Replacing distance with tower influence gives quality = security × visibility ÷ tower influence; tower influence must never be zero.
when: When tower influence replaces distance from the nearest tower as the third factor.
why: The influence value sits in the denominator of the quality formula.

text: Spreading influence across an n-by-n map may need up to n passes, or about half that when sources are central.
when: repeated convolution passes
why: Each pass spreads influence only to neighboring locations, so repeated passes are needed to reach every location.

text: A convolution pass over a w-by-h map with filter size s takes O(whs²) time and O(wh) memory for the copy.
why: Memory grows with the map because a full copy of the source data is needed to write updated values.

text: Naive influence computation costs O(nm) time and O(m) memory for n units and m locations; 1,000 units over a million locations means about a billion calculations.
why: Each unit must be considered for each location in the level, so cost multiplies units by locations.

text: Map flooding runs in O(nm) time, where n counts locations inside a source's region and m is neighbors per location, and uses O(n) memory since distant locations are ignored.
why: Locations outside the influence range are never stored, so memory only covers the influenced region.

text: Starting with high values for weak locations can make the AI repeat an obviously failing tactic for a long time.
when: When precompiled starting values for hot locations are set too high.
why: Many failures are needed to drain inflated values, so the AI keeps repeating the failing tactic.

text: Cropping after summing lets large opposing requests cancel and hide a strong individual request.
when: When the summed acceleration exceeds the character's maximum acceleration.

text: Convolution can be slower than naive computation when a map has far more locations than units.
when: When the map has significantly fewer units than locations.
why: Filtering updates every map location and repeats the whole update, so its work scales with the map, not the units.

text: Map flooding assumes one strong unit can overpower many weak ones, which is a dangerous assumption.
when: When many weaker units cover the same location as one strong unit.
why: Each location takes only the largest single unit contribution, so additional units add no influence.

text: Subtracting tactical benefits can push a connection's cost below its physical distance, breaking the guarantee that Euclidean distance never overestimates.
when: When connection costs use tactical quality instead of plain distance.
why: Euclidean estimates stay valid only when real path costs are at least the straight-line distance.

text: 1) Start every location at zero. 2) When any character is hit, subtract a value from the victim's location, proportional to hit points lost or fixed per kill. 3) When the AI sees a character hit another, add a value to the attacker's location.
when: When the AI observes hits on characters, including itself.
why: Fixed values are common because the AI should not know other characters' hit points.

text: 1) For each location, sum the influence of every unit on each side. 2) The side with the highest total controls the location. 3) Degree of control is the gap between the winner and the runner-up. 4) A very large gap means the location is secure.
why: Summing each side's unit influence per location allows control to be compared directly.

text: 1) Compute an influence map. 2) Apply a sharpening filter a few times. 3) Read the strongest region as the central hub, such as a site for a base.
when: Locating where influence is concentrated on a map
why: Sharpening concentrates values toward existing hubs

text: 1) Put every source on an open list carrying its source and strength. 2) Take the largest-strength location. 3) For each neighbor, compute the strength this source gives it via an arbitrary function. 4) Skip neighbors below a threshold. 5) Keep the stronger claim on conflicts. 6) Close the processed location; updated neighbors reopen.
why: The strongest location lies nearest a source, so expanding it first moves outward from the sources.

text: Normalize filter weights to sum to one so values stop growing and repeated passes settle; add each unit's influence every pass while subtracting an equal total bias.
when: repeated blurring of influence maps
why: Normalization prevents runaway growth; balanced add and subtract keeps total influence stable.

text: Read from an old copy and write to a new copy, swapping roles each iteration, plus an integer category copy; in-place updates make results depend on scan order.
when: When running a cellular automaton over a tactical analysis map.
why: In-place updates are rarely acceptable.

text: A combined tactical analysis takes the update category of the fastest-changing input it uses.
when: When any base analysis changes during play.
why: A changing input forces the combined value to be recalculated, so it takes the category of the fastest-changing input.

text: Combining base terrain cost and gradient by weighted sum or product equals running two analyses and layering their results.
Whether something counts as dangerous belongs to the whole game's design, so designers can add new hazards without new AI programming.
when: In games using message passing rather than polling the world each frame.
why: Danger is a property of objects set by level design, so new hazards need no AI code.

text: Track occupied rows and diagonals in Boolean arrays rather than a board matrix, so each safety check becomes a few array lookups.
why: A board matrix makes each safety check costly to compute.

text: Dividing by the square root of (1 + distance) drops influence fast at first but reaches farther; dividing by the square of (1 + distance) stays flat, then tails off steeply.
Shrinking the matrix at edges, using nine variants, is most correct but blocks SIMD optimization, making it 1.5 to 5 times slower than the regular fast algorithm.
why: Switching between matrices stops the convolution from being easily vectorized across locations, costing speed.

text: A fixed border of values that are never updated is fast but leaves a pale halo near edges; a wider border updated normally makes the artifact less visible.
why: Fixed border values feed constant contributions into edge cells, pulling nearby influence down, so a visible pale band forms near the boundary.

text: When a character follows a pathfinding route, it recognizes labelled jump connections automatically from the route it has been given.
when: Character follows a pathfinding network route
why: Labelled connections carry the jump data

text: Computed jump velocity accounts for the character's own capabilities, so a heavily loaded character needs higher speed to make the same jump.
when: Computing jumps for characters with different loads
why: Maximum speed limits the reachable horizontal speed

text: Local steering without pathfinding has to detect upcoming jumps with its own lookahead.
when: No pathfinding network in use

text: A jump commits the character to a trajectory, so small disturbances such as clipping an obstacle, gun recoil or explosion blast can make it miss the landing.
when: Jumping during combat or physics interaction
why: A jump cannot be corrected once airborne, unlike steering

text: The computed jump model assumes gravity and the jump both act vertically and that there is no drag.
when: Using the computed jump velocity model

text: Use the jump detector approach when the landing area is large and failure is unlikely, such as a wide chasm.
when: Choosing a jump method

text: The margin for deciding a character is close enough to the jump target should scale with speed and character size.
when: Triggering a computed jump
why: Faster or larger characters cover more distance per frame

text: A pathfinding network can tag a connection spanning a gap as requiring a jump, handled at run time much as a takeoff point paired with a landing point.
when: Game already has a pathfinding network
why: Jump data is stored on existing connections rather than as separate entities

text: A single jump point cannot describe the approach needed for thin walkways, narrow ledges or pedestals, which require exact direction or speed.
when: Narrow or thin landing surfaces
why: Those jumps depend on tight direction and speed constraints a point does not capture

text: Jump difficulty depends on approach direction, so a point marked for one side may be easy from there and hard from the other side.
when: Jump points used from multiple sides
why: Difficulty is directional but a point stores only one placement

text: Jump points cannot record how severe a failed jump is, such as landing in shallow water versus falling into lava.
when: Failed jumps have different consequences
why: A point has no field for failure cost

text: Hand-placed jump data is error-prone and hard to tune, and bugs can stay hidden because testing rarely tries the wrong approach.
when: Many manually placed jump points
why: Testers usually follow the intended approach

text: 1) Decide to jump and select the jump point. 2) Velocity-match into the point. 3) Launch the character when it touches the point. No separate jump-timing logic is needed.
when: Jumps are limited in number and failures are forgiving
why: Jump timing is fixed by the placed point rather than computed at run time

text: 1) Fill gaps with invisible jumpable-gap volumes whose edges stop jumps from the far wall. 2) Let the character steer normally, with a jump detector treating gap volumes differently from walls. 3) Move the character toward the gap at full speed. 4) Jump at the collision point, the last moment on the ledge.
when: Character must cross a chasm or gap
why: Characters can leap from any point along the gap without paired jump points

text: 1) Velocity-match toward the computed target. 2) When position and velocity are close enough to the target, schedule the jump and stop steering.
when: Executing a computed jump
why: Launch happens only once the approach matches the solution

text: When characters move at varying speeds, store a minimum velocity on each jump point, as a full target velocity or as a minimum component toward the far side.
when: Characters differ in speed
why: A fixed point cannot launch correctly from every approach speed otherwise

text: If a computed jump trajectory is infeasible, the jump behaviour should request no acceleration.
when: Computed jump has no valid solution
why: No trajectory can reach the target

text: The jump behaviour needs full control of the character, since blending with avoidance can skew the trajectory and make it miss the take-off or land wrongly.
when: Executing a computed jump
why: Blended steering alters the intended trajectory

text: Limiting jump placement to safe jumps avoids unrecoverable failures but restricts level layouts.
when: Designing jump-based levels with a safety rule
why: Only safe jumps are allowed, so layout options shrink

text: A justification record stores, for each database item, the rule that added or changed it, the matched items and their values, and a timestamp.
Expert systems use justification trails to explain decisions; in games they mainly serve testing and debugging, since players are not shown the explanations.
Use deep learning only when it meaningfully supports gameplay, since developers want control over most system elements.
when: When a learning system would add real value to what players experience and gameplay can carry it.
why: Games are treated as an artistic medium, and developers prefer controlling most system parts rather than handing them to learned behavior.

text: Machine learning models are black boxes: inputs and outputs can be observed, but their reasoning is hard to understand.
why: Its behavior comes from patterns learned from data rather than authored rules, so the internal reasoning is not readable.

text: 1) Query an item's justification trail. 2) Recursively query each matched item in that trail. 3) Stop at items supplied by game code or initial data.
when: Explaining why a decision or item exists
why: Each derived item stores the rule and matched items that produced it, so following those links reconstructs where it came from.

text: Abrupt velocity changes from kinematic output can be smoothed over several frames.
when: Kinematic output changes velocity suddenly
why: Direct velocity jumps look unnatural

text: Kinematic movement sets velocity directly from position and orientation alone, ignoring acceleration and slowing, and can change it instantly; dynamic movement also uses current velocity and outputs forces or accelerations.
Kinematic algorithms use only position and orientation, with no velocities, and output a desired velocity that is often simply full speed or stationary with a direction.
A kinematic character record stores position, orientation, linear velocity and angular velocity (rotation).
If drag is proportional to velocity alone, the equation of motion has an exact closed-form solution giving position at any time.
when: Drag depends only on velocity, not its square
why: Linear drag yields a solvable linear differential equation

text: With linear drag, acceleration equals gravity minus k times velocity.
when: Projectile subject to viscous drag

text: Blend weights are unconstrained and need not sum to one, so a weighted blend is a weighted linear sum, not a weighted mean.
Blend weights are usually chosen by trial and error; genetic algorithms and neural networks have been tried for this with poor results.
For a given force, the resulting acceleration falls as inertia rises; linear inertia is mass and angular inertia is the moment of inertia (inertia tensor in 3D).
when: a force is applied to a physics-driven body
why: Acceleration equals force divided by inertia.

text: When blended behaviors conflict, the character can settle into stable or unstable equilibria where it stops or creeps.
when: strongly conflicting blended goals
why: Opposing steering outputs are summed into a net that can settle where the forces balance, leaving the character stuck.

text: Blended steering uses constant memory beyond temporaries and time linear in the number of behaviors.
why: Each behavior's output is added into one accumulator in a single pass over the list.

text: Kinematic seek and flee run in constant time and constant memory.
why: Each call only computes one direction vector and scales it to a fixed speed.

text: That split allows free motion but can produce jarring movement and animation combinations; a richer animation palette helps counter this.
when: When movement decisions are separated from the code that turns them into animations.
why: Movement and animation are chosen independently, so some pairings look wrong; a larger animation set makes a plausible pairing easier to find.

text: Blended steering: 1) Hold behavior-weight pairs plus maximum linear acceleration and maximum rotation. 2) Create an empty accumulator. 3) For each pair, request its steering and add it scaled by its weight. 4) Crop the linear and angular totals to their maxima. 5) Return the result.

1) Compute the vector to the target; if its length is inside the satisfaction radius, stop and return nothing. 2) Divide the vector by the time to target to get desired speed. 3) Clip that speed to maximum speed along its direction. 4) Set orientation from velocity and output zero rotation.
when: Character must stop at a fixed point
why: Slowing near the target avoids overshoot and wiggle

text: 1) Compute the vector from character to target. 2) Normalize it. 3) Scale it by maximum speed to get desired velocity. 4) Set orientation from velocity. Output zero rotation.
when: Character must pursue a target
why: Orientation follows the movement direction, so no separate rotation output is needed.

text: Flee uses the seek steps with the vector reversed, running from the target to the character.
when: Character must run from a threat

text: 1) Set velocity to maximum speed along the facing direction. 2) Set rotation to a random binomial value times a maximum rotation below the physical limit. 3) Move forward each frame in the facing direction.
when: Character must roam with a meandering path
why: Small random turns keep the heading most of the time

text: 1) Pick one characteristic point per set, using its minimum, maximum, average or bisector. 2) Normalize the membership degrees so they sum to 1. 3) Output the weighted sum of the points.
why: Normalized membership degrees weight each set's value, so the output blends between them.

text: Train taught creatures using a mix of heavy guidance drawn from watching demonstrations and light guidance from player feedback.
when: Designing training for taught creatures.

text: Internal knowledge is a character's own state, such as health, equipment, state of mind, ultimate goals, movement and recent activity; characters should have unrestricted access to it.
The broader claim that the knowledge-search trade-off explains all intelligent behavior is largely discredited, though the trade-off itself is real and theoretically proved.
External knowledge can usually drive any decision algorithm, while each algorithm determines which kinds of internal knowledge it can use.
Choose the format and quantity of character knowledge to meet the game's requirements.
Wrapping all game-state access in an interface layer usually insulates decision logic from changes in data structure.
when: Decisions must survive changes to game data layouts
why: Direct reads tie decisions to the current data layout, so routine structural changes during development break them.

text: External knowledge reaches characters via direct access, selected notification through event managers or polling stations, or simulated perception through sense managers.
why: Gating knowledge through events or polling limits characters to what someone embodied in the world could plausibly know.

text: Hidden information can be modeled across entities: each player knows its own hand, while the game algorithm knows all hands and the deck.
Conversion to a representation discards information by design, so discarding the wrong detail can leave the AI unable to make correct decisions.
why: Dropping detail is the intended purpose of the conversion, yet the cut may accidentally remove data the decision needs.

text: Knowledge representation is closely tied to most decision algorithms, which makes a fully general representation hard to build.
More built-in knowledge means less search, since reasoning often consists of searching possibilities; faster search can compensate for less knowledge.
when: Symbolic reasoning systems where answers are found by trying out possibilities.
why: Search and knowledge are intrinsically linked, an unavoidable engineering fact.

text: A single steering ray can miss a wall the character will graze; splaying several rays like whiskers avoids this.
when: When implementing wall avoidance with rays

text: Waypoint sets with topological information already include connections, while regular waypoints and most tactical analyses do not.
Timing and intensity of visual signals are taken from the connections between nodes rather than computed separately.
Some implementations derive the sight graph from the rendering engine's potentially visible set, a feature common in modern engines.
The sight modality adds a sight-cone test, followed by a ray-cast line-of-sight test, to the standard checks.
Rendering, physics and AI can each use a different geometry suited to its own purpose.
Even when viewing distance is uncapped, use a distance threshold for noticing small objects.
why: Resolving an object requires it to appear large enough, and being able to resolve something differs from actually noticing it.

text: A signal's initial strength can be set in proportion to light on its emitter, so characters in shadow send weaker signals that high-threshold characters may miss.
when: Stealth where characters hide in shadow from sensors that use intensity thresholds.
why: Dimmer emitters send weaker signals, which can fall below a sensor's high detection threshold.

text: Sight tests can pass through partly transparent objects to the target, then continue past it to find the next thing hit.
when: When sight checks must judge camouflage against the background behind a character.
why: The background beyond the target is needed to judge whether its camouflage blends in.

text: Visual notification delay is computed from the 3D Euclidean distance between signal and sensor; if sight is instantaneous, sensors are notified immediately.
Connections may link rooms where only a small corner of one room is visible, so line-of-sight tests must still do the real filtering.
why: Connections are created whenever any part of the destination is visible, so most destination points stay hidden and only per-point tests reject them.

text: Shadow-based hiding that ignores background contrast makes a backlit character a visible silhouette, so designers must avoid such setups.
when: characters hide in shadows near bright areas
why: Visibility depends on contrast with the background, so a dark figure against bright light stands out whatever the shadow.

text: 1) Sample lightness at several points spread across a character-sized volume. 2) Take the maximum lightness as the character's exposure.
when: judging whether a hider is visible
why: a hider is seen through its most visible part, not its average

text: Signals spread one connection step to sensors in the source node and directly connected nodes. Give every line-of-sight node pair a direct connection, since sight is not relayed onward.
when: graph-based sensing; building the sight graph

text: Similar states and actions tend to have similar quality, so heading toward known high-value pairs is a good way to find other good pairs.
when: Searching for good actions in Q-learning.
why: Value generalizes across similar situations.

text: When agents share experiences, others may come to copy or debunk them.
when: Agents exchanging experiences about a stimulus

text: Online learning adapts during play, consuming data as the game generates it; offline learning processes collected game data between levels or at the studio, storing it and loading it whole later.
Credit assignment is deciding how much each earlier action deserves credit for a later rewarded event, such as a kill, and which actions in a series helped and which did not.

Weak supervision gives no answer set; a monitor or developer scores actions, penalizing outcomes such as being shot and rewarding success. Output-layer error is computed from such outcomes, not example answers.
Natural computing is AI drawing on biology or other natural systems, including neural networks (biologically inspired), genetic algorithms and simulated annealing.
A perceptron stores its list of input records, its current state, and its current error; each input record holds a source neuron reference and a weight.
Decision learning lets an AI choose one behavior from a fixed set by associating observed game values with decisions.
Hebbian learning is unsupervised: it strengthens connections between neighboring nodes that share a state, weakens those that differ, and needs neither examples nor error values.
Statistical confidence measures how unlikely an observed pattern is to have arisen by chance; it is high when that chance is low.
Off-policy learning keeps the action-selection policy outside the algorithm, so it can be replaced while the algorithm stays valid if all states are eventually visited.
On-policy learning builds its exploration strategy into the learning itself, so the action-selection policy is part of the algorithm.
Over-fitting, or over-learning, means a learner memorizes the responses to experiences it has had instead of generalizing to new situations.
A perceptron multiplies each input by its weight, adds a bias weight for an always-one input, and outputs zero if the sum is below zero, otherwise one.
A radial basis function outputs near one inside a bounded range of inputs and near zero outside it.
Strong supervision gives a learner a set of correct decisions, each paired with the observations at that moment, often recorded from a human player.
Context lets a character associate an action with the circumstances in which it is appropriate, such as eating being good but not while under attack.
when: Designing learning characters.

text: Deep learning is a subset of machine learning based on neural networks with many layers.
Connectionist AI learns patterns from data through networks of simple interconnected processing units, and covers most machine learning and deep learning.
Defuzzification converts membership values back into a single output value that approximates an output which would produce those memberships, since an exact match often does not exist.
when: Turning fuzzy results into game values
why: Fuzzy memberships can imply combinations no single output can reproduce exactly.

text: Alpha is the learning rate, between zero and one, that sets how strongly new feedback overrides a stored Q-value; zero learns nothing and one uses only the latest experience.
In a feedforward network the leftmost input layer is set by the programmer and the rightmost output layer gives the final result, with values passing in one direction.
Neurons are designed to compute in parallel; on machines without suitable parallel hardware, each neuron is computed in turn.
Neural networks were proposed in 1943, before the symbolic era, so the later shift to natural computing was partly a change of fashion.
Natural computing implementations need largely unbiological optimizations before they give sensible results.
For many characters or very complex conditions, compound qualities can be computed offline and stored, removing designer effort but not runtime memory use.
when: Complex tactical conditions across many characters
why: Precomputation trades designer work and runtime query time for stored data

text: The critic is usually a basic temporal-difference learner, though Q-learning also suits it.
The target output is one for the desired action and zero for all other output neurons.
Each perceptron only needs to know which perceptrons feed it, so the network architecture is not fixed.
Decision tree learning is the most practicable of three learning techniques for game AI, with reinforcement learning and neural networks as larger fields with potential.
when: Choosing a learned decision maker for games.
why: Decision trees are simpler to apply in practice.

text: Game AI typically uses variants of Quinlan's ID3 to build decision trees, and such algorithms exist for classification, prediction and statistical analysis.
Uncorrelated neighboring nodes average out to no net change in Hebbian weights.
The neural network family is large and varied, so few general truths apply to all members and little of its theory transfers to games.
The multi-layer perceptron trained with backpropagation is the most common form of neural network.
Online learning is rare in shipped games.
Shipped games use offline learning for multiplayer map tactics, pathfinding and movement data, and bootstrapping physics interaction.
Different learning algorithms are susceptible to over-fitting to different degrees, and neural networks over-fit when misparameterized or oversized.
A sigmoid neuron splits its input into high and low categories around a dividing point, and its bias weight moves that point away from zero.
A sigmoid network can respond to a range using two neurons, one for each bound, at the cost of extra neurons.
Adjusting weights, including the bias, lets a radial basis neuron learn any minimum and maximum of a range.
In weakly supervised learning, hidden-layer error terms and weight updates are computed the same way as in the standard algorithm.
Outcome-based training can produce varied character behavior without a large hand-written behavior library, and can learn behaviors the developer did not foresee.
Most negamax optimizations transfer to strict minimax.
Internet text contains hate speech and toxic content, and it does not represent the world's population. About 80% of global Wikipedia editors identify as men.
why: Learned models absorb whatever skew their training data contains.

text: Deep learning is rare in games because black boxes are hard to debug, unpredictability can ruin the experience, and models demand processing power on players' hardware.
Supervised learning trains on labeled data and is commonly used for image recognition.
when: When labeled examples of the target outputs are available.

text: Unsupervised learning draws inferences from unlabeled data, such as clustering users into groups for customized experiences or targeted ads.
when: When no labels are available.

text: Convolutional networks suit visual pattern detection, and recurrent networks suit processing certain sequences.
Deep learning has driven advances in speech recognition, language processing, and image generation, and it underlies large language models and generative image tools.
Neural-network methods, including machine-learning and deep-learning models, can mirror human biases in opaque, hard-to-debug ways.
CPPNs are very similar to ordinary neural networks, so the same evolution algorithm applies to both.
Traditional neural networks typically use a sigmoid activation with a slope constant.
Standard neural networks are mainly used for control or classification, and their behaviour depends on architecture and weights.
The decision tree walk uses no working memory, so its cost depends only on the number of nodes it visits.
As the search space grows, finding any particular solution generally becomes harder.
Use online learning when the best parameter values shift as player behavior changes, such as when scores drift or are noisy.
when: choosing a learning mode
why: Scores drift or are noisy, and the best parameter value changes with player behavior.

text: Use a per-neuron structure for a clear, flexible implementation, and expect production code to use a different memory layout.
when: implementing a neural network for study or prototyping
why: Clarity and flexibility matter more than speed early on.

text: Scale the filtered request back to the original magnitude so the character does not move slower just because its request was filtered.
when: Filtered request is much smaller than the original.
why: Restoring the original magnitude keeps a character's speed from dropping merely because part of its request was filtered out.

text: Choose neural networks when smooth generalization matters more than exact match to examples; choose decision trees when accuracy on known cases is the priority.
when: Selecting a classifier for AI behavior.
why: Accuracy and generalization trade off against each other.

text: During online play use an exploration rate of 0.1 or less so behavior looks sensible to the player.
when: Learning happens while the player is playing.
why: A high rate would make decisions look random to the player.

text: During offline training use a higher exploration rate, around 0.2 as a starting value, to learn as much as possible within the trade-off.
when: Learning happens offline before release.
why: Players do not see the training behavior.

text: Constrain learning to one task whose output can be visualized and checked by eye, such as choosing cover points.
when: Adding learning to a game.
why: Narrow, inspectable tasks are easier to reproduce, debug and verify.

text: Use neural networks mainly as classifiers; they have been over-hyped as general controllers for large-scale game behavior.
when: choosing an AI technique for a game
why: Developers who applied them to large-scale behavior control reported disappointing results.

text: Watch closely for over-fitting when the learner has few experiences and the model is large.
when: training a learner from limited encounters
why: A learner can memorize responses to the exact situations it saw instead of generalizing, and an oversized network makes this more likely.

text: Reinforcement learning fits when the best action depends on circumstances that cannot be anticipated at design time.
when: Games where the right action depends on player behavior or randomly generated maps.
why: Action quality only becomes clear much later, after a long chain of actions, so the learner must work out which earlier actions mattered.

text: Tune the steepness h for each network, because the best value tends to fall as layer size and weight magnitude grow.
when: Neural networks using the sigmoid threshold function.

text: Use outcome-based training when the correct action is hard to specify but bad outcomes are easy to recognize.
why: The error term comes from how badly the character was punished, so no explicit correct answer is needed.

text: The most promising deep learning uses in games are dynamic difficulty adjustment, believable NPC behavior and conversation, and procedural content generation.
Use incremental learning such as ID4 when examples arrive during play and the tree must adapt; plain ID3 suffices for a complete offline example set.
why: Batch learning can process a complete example set once, while online examples keep arriving and the tree must change over time.

text: A multilayer perceptron's hidden layer usually matches or exceeds the input layer in size, and is frequently far bigger.
when: Planning a network with three layers.

text: Feedforward structures suit mapping a set of inputs to an output, such as a multi-layer perceptron.
when: The task maps inputs to outputs.

text: Smooth activations such as sigmoid act like a step far from zero but give intermediate outputs near the threshold, so small weight changes produce graded output changes, which learning needs.
when: When a multi-layer perceptron's weights must be trained by learning.
why: A hard step gives no graded output, so there is nothing to adjust weights against.

text: Tactic weights can change during play; a damaged unit can raise its enemy-proximity weight so its route home becomes more conservative.
when: When an infantry unit is damaged.

text: The critic receives reward feedback, learns values, and sends a critique signal that guides the actor's simpler learning.
A negative error weakens the inputs that contributed to a bad result, a positive error strengthens them, and a near-zero error changes weights very little.
Rewards for the same state-action pair may differ between attempts; the update averages them, so the Q-value tracks the action's overall success.
when: When identical state-action pairs receive different rewards because of context absent from the state.

text: In a radial basis neuron the bias sets the range's position, while larger overall weights narrow the range and smaller weights widen it.
Raising the steepness parameter h pushes the sigmoid toward a hard step, while lower values give a smoother, more graded curve.
Most network outputs are illegal because the action, object, or indirect object may be unavailable; only legal outputs are carried out.
when: Choosing actions from a neural network controller.
why: Actions depend on what is available at that moment.

text: A single training pass changes behavior very little, while many iterations can make a network forget behaviors it already learned.
when: Choosing how many training passes to run.
why: Learning speed and forgetting speed must be balanced.

text: NEAT grows a flower network's hidden structure over time, so generated flowers become more complex.
when: evolving CPPN-generated content
why: Added hidden nodes increase the expressiveness of the generator.

text: Fewer tokens per coastline agent mean more agents and finer coastline detail.
when: When coastline is generated by agents that each have a fixed token budget.

text: A hidden neuron's error equals its output times one minus its output, times the sum over the next layer of connecting weight times that neuron's error; it reflects the neuron's share of downstream error.
Memory use is O(nw), where n is the neuron count and w the inputs per neuron, and feedforward and backpropagation each take O(nw) time.
An output neuron's error equals its output times one minus its output, times the difference between target and output.
Offline training on a dedicated machine may extend the practical state scale by about an order of magnitude.
when: training runs offline on dedicated hardware

text: Sigmoid output equals 1 divided by (1 plus e raised to the negative of h times the weighted input sum), where h sets the steepness of the curve.
For small game networks, steepness values up to about 10 work well, though many texts start from h equal to 1.
when: choosing a starting steepness for a small network
why: The ideal steepness depends on layer width and weight size, and those factors tend to pull it downward.

text: Offline, a nu of roughly 0.1 yields streaks averaging around nine consecutive actions.
when: learning offline with a simulator

text: With two choices, windows beyond about 10 actions predicted worse than random guessing, even on a very predictable sequence.
Multi-layer analysis merges several base per-location analyses into one score, such as choosing tower sites by visibility, security, and distance from other towers.
A generic multi-layer perceptron network holds three collections of perceptrons: input, hidden, and output.
A decision learner has a fixed set of behavior options and observable game values, such as distance to nearest enemy, ammo left, or relative army size.

A taught creature's controller is a multi-layer perceptron: inputs are world context including internal parameters; outputs are action type, object, indirect object, and any other data needed for an action.
when: Building a learning creature controller.

text: In player-taught creature games, a character replicates observed actions, then the player gives positive or negative feedback, such as tickles or slaps, to encourage or discourage repeating them.
when: Designing player-taught characters.

text: A Hopfield network places neurons on a grid and connects each neuron to its neighboring points.

Assuming natural computing is the future or always superior is a pitfall: it has not scaled better than symbolic methods and often fails to beat simpler approaches, though some suit particular domains.
why: The no-free-lunch result shows no approach beats the others over all problems.

text: Thresholds set too high discard locations that are significant but only marginally so.
when: When filtering candidate locations by per-property tactical thresholds during condensation.

text: Steering demos in sparse open areas hide failures that appear in indoor or urban levels.
when: In realistic indoor or urban settings rather than sparse outdoor demos.
why: In realistic settings characters often get stuck in ways that are hard to debug.

text: Running sharpening many times makes influence collapse onto unit positions, giving an uninspiring result.
when: Applying sharpening to influence maps repeatedly
why: Repeated concentration removes the spread that gives useful terrain information

text: Multiple hills (multi-modal problems) and many reward points make hill climbing fail, the situation most likely to fail under Q-learning.
when: Games with many goals or reward points.
why: Learners get stuck on local peaks.

text: A Hebbian network may take a while to settle into a stable pattern.
when: Running a Hebbian grid to estimate hidden areas.
why: Only the unseen neurons update, via their normal sum-and-threshold rule, while visible states stay clamped.

text: In on-policy learning, changing the action-selection policy can stop the algorithm from reaching a reasonable solution.
when: When the learning algorithm is on-policy, so its exploration strategy is part of learning.
why: The policy is intrinsically tied to how learning operates.

text: Outcome-based networks can learn dull, predictable play, or actions the developer can see are wrong.
why: Learning only from results can favor safe, self-preserving actions over interesting ones.

text: Behaviors such as last stands may not emerge from outcome feedback alone when the alternative is punished less, so designers must shape the feedback to steer them.
why: Feedback based only on outcomes would reward running away over a last stand.

text: A physics-driven car knocked off its racing line keeps trying to regain it and tends to overshoot the next corner and leave the track.
when: When a physics-driven AI car is nudged off its defined racing line.
why: Because the line is not a rail, the car cannot always reach it and keeps trying to regain it.

text: Oscillations involving several species are hard to debug and can look artificial.
when: cycles appear only when several species are together
why: Such cycles emerge only from interactions among several groups, so they are hard to isolate and tweak.

text: Generalization can turn a specific punishment into avoidance of an entire behavior, such as a creature starving because it avoids eating altogether.
when: Punishing a specific action in a learning creature.
why: Learning generalizes across inputs, so punishing one food-eating action spreads to eating in general.

text: The token count and the agent count are linked, so changing one silently changes the other.
Many references describe different algorithms under the same defuzzification name, so the specific algorithm must be checked before implementing.
when: Reading fuzzy logic references
why: Identically named methods may behave differently.

text: 1) Set the input layer from the input values. 2) For each hidden neuron, sum weighted inputs, apply the threshold, and store the result as its state. 3) Repeat for each output neuron. 4) Read the result from the output layer.
when: evaluating a neural network for a game decision
why: Each layer needs the states of the layer before it, so layers must be computed in order from inputs to outputs.

text: Estimate a goal's rate at runtime when it depends on events, such as health lost to hits: 1) On each GOB run, compute each goal's change since last run. 2) Divide by elapsed time for observed rate. 3) Update stored rate as 0.95 times old plus 0.05 times new sample; weights may be any pair summing to one.
when: The rate depends on events
why: Checking each goal costs only linear time, so sampling each run barely affects execution time.

text: 1) For each input, multiply the source neuron's state by its weight. 2) Sum these products. 3) Apply the threshold and store the result as the new state.
1) Take the current error. 2) For each input, add gain times error times source state to its weight. 3) Store the error so upstream layers can use it.
why: Upstream layers require the stored error, so it must be kept for them.

text: 1) Record observation-action examples where each example carries its correct action. 2) Build the tree automatically from these examples. 3) Execute the learned tree like any hand-made tree during play.
when: A labeled set of observation-action examples exists.
why: Learning replaces manual tree authoring.

text: 1) Train on many games, each with full safe and dangerous maps per turn from influence mapping. 2) Apply the Hebbian rule to neighboring grid nodes. 3) In play, fix visible tiles at known values and let the rest of the network settle to estimate hidden areas.
when: Estimating unseen map information, such as fog-of-war safety in an RTS.
why: Hidden tiles are inferred from learned correlations with neighbors.

text: 1) Record each creature's recent input-output pairs over at least several seconds. 2) When player feedback arrives, train the network to strengthen or weaken every pair in that window. 3) Reduce the feedback's influence for pairs further back in time.
when: When player feedback arrives and the specific action it judges is unknown.
why: Players cannot say which action they judge, so the feedback is assumed to cover a window of recent actions.

text: 1) Find a representation for the observed action. 2) Find a representation for the current context. 3) Train the network on that input-output pattern.
when: A character learns by observing other characters or the player.

text: 1) Start with a high gain near 0.7 (a reasonable starting gain is 0.3) to bring weights roughly into the right region. 2) Lower the gain to about 0.1 to refine weights and keep learning stable.
when: Setting gain for neural network weight training, especially when initial weights are far from good values.
why: High gain moves weights quickly early on, and low gain protects the refinement from single-example noise.

text: 1) Start with minimal networks that have no hidden nodes. 2) Add nodes and connections by mutation over generations. 3) Let topology grow automatically, so the designer does not fix neuron count.
when: evolving neural networks or CPPNs
why: Growing complexity lets evolved content become more elaborate over time.
