text: 1) Sort examples on the attribute. 2) Place the first in category A and the rest in B. 3) Compute gain. 4) Move the lowest-valued example from B to A and recompute. 5) Repeat until all splits are tried. 6) Keep the split with highest gain.
when: When a continuous attribute must be split into two categories by one threshold.

text: 1) Collect 20 to 100 scenarios pairing inputs with desired outputs. 2) Split them into a training set and a testing set, with at least ten of each and ideally fifty of each. 3) After training, run feedforward on the test set to check results.
when: Preparing and validating a neural network for game behavior.
why: A separate test set reveals whether learning generalises.

text: Limit online Q-learning to problems with fewer than about 100 states.
when: learning happens during play
why: Live play visits states too slowly for the learner to gather enough experience on each one.

text: Give credit to the actions leading up to a rewarded event, even though no feedback arrived while they were performed.
when: rewards are sparse and delayed
why: The rewarded action is only one link in a long chain, so earlier actions must inherit credit from it.

text: Use a sigmoid rather than a hard step wherever learning needs graded outputs.
why: Graded outputs give learning something to adjust against.

text: During online play, set nu to zero, because the game controls the current state and random jumps are impossible.
when: learning while the game controls the state
why: During play the game dictates the current state, so the learner cannot start from arbitrary states.

text: Use threshold splitting only when a continuous attribute needs just a binary decision at a node.
Skipping zero values saves memory but requires a reliable way to record each value together with its meaning.
when: Large outdoor worlds, such as strategy or massively multiplayer games, where memory is a real constraint.
why: Without zeros stored by position, each saved value needs an explicit label to keep its meaning.

text: Online learning gives a more consistent challenge by adapting to the player's style, but makes behavior unpredictable and bugs harder to reproduce.
when: designing adaptive game AI
why: A constantly changing game is hard to test and replay.

text: Radial basis neurons are more complex because each needs an extra weighting parameter, but they cover a range with fewer neurons than sigmoid neurons.
when: a neuron must respond to a band of values and neuron count matters
why: A sigmoid needs separate neurons for each bound, while a radial basis neuron sets its own range through its weights.

text: Strong supervision is easier to get right but needs someone to define correct and incorrect actions; weak supervision can discover these itself but is much harder to make work.
when: choosing how a learner gets feedback
why: Strong supervision gets explicit correct answers from a person, while weak supervision only scores the choices the learner made.

text: Penalizing illegal outputs through a weakly supervised step yields near-term gains but may produce pathological states later.
when: Training a network whose outputs are often illegal.

text: A high learning gain learns quickly but lets a single input-output example cause large weight changes. Keeping it high throughout training makes the network unstable.
when: Gain is set high or stays high throughout training.
why: Each example moves the weights strongly, so noisy or unusual examples have outsized effect.

text: Deep learning needs large amounts of data and computing resources, which consumes a lot of energy.
why: Without data the learning process has nothing to fit, and heavy computation is what drives the energy use.

text: NEAT lets network size emerge from evolution rather than be fixed by hand, which suits interactive settings that need speed.
when: choosing how to evolve network topology
why: Automatic growth removes manual topology design, and NEAT is fast enough for real-time games.

text: A Markov state vector holds one number per state, and it may contain zeros, any values and any total, with the total equal to 1 when it represents a distribution.
A transition matrix is square, and entry (i, j) gives the proportion of old value i that flows into new value j.
A Markov state machine maintains a set of numeric values per state that are updated over time without fuzzy interpretation, and its mathematics is a Markov process.
when: decisions need priorities or scores such as safety or ranking

text: In mathematical Markov processes, state vector entries give probabilities over possible outcomes, and the transition matrix supplies the probabilities for the next trial.
In AI, Markov chains predict the future from the present, as in speech recognition predicting the next word to tell similar-sounding words apart.
Learning algorithms can estimate transition matrix values, letting a system adapt to a particular user.
Transitions belong to the whole machine rather than to states, so actions come only from transitions; states carry no actions.
why: There is no single current state

text: The state vector is stored as a plain list of numbers that the rest of the game can read as needed.
A first-order Markov process uses one matrix and depends only on the current vector, while higher-order processes also use earlier vectors.
No consensus exists for naming this algorithm; some call it a fuzzy state machine, though fuzzy logic is a separate technique.
Each iteration without a fired transition counts down the timer; a fired transition resets it to the reset time. At zero, the default transition matrix applies and the timer resets.
when: a state machine should drift back to a baseline after inactivity
why: The default should only fire after a quiet period, so the clock must reset whenever another transition fires.

text: One Markov iteration is ordinary matrix multiplication, so every new value draws contributions from every old value.
why: Each matrix entry moves a share of one old value into one new value, and normal multiplication sums those shares.

text: Mathematical Markov values are probabilities, but a game's Markov state machine places no such constraint on its values.
when: When several game events each trigger a different matrix that reshapes the stored values.

text: Matrix values are usually set by hand and are difficult to tune, so the acceptable tolerance depends on how the values are used.
when: When no known probability distributions exist to derive the matrix values from.

text: 1) Check transitions in list order. 2) If a transition's trigger holds, multiply the state vector by its matrix and return its action list. 3) If none fires, return no actions.
when: each iteration of a Markov state machine

text: Separate code must convert the state vector into an action, such as choosing the position whose value is largest.
when: a Markov state machine drives a choice
why: The machine occupies no single state, so states have no action to hand back and values need interpreting.

text: A time-based transition in the ordinary list would need to watch every other transition, duplicating effort, so building the timer into the machine avoids this.
N in an N-gram is one greater than the window size, so a 3-gram uses a window of two recent actions.
The most widespread use of N-gram prediction is in combo-based melee games, where timed move sequences are predicted.
Use a small sample threshold, such as 3 or 4, for online game AI, since more possible actions need more examples and game AI can take more risks.
when: Setting the enough-samples threshold for N-gram prediction.
why: Early decisions matter more than statistical certainty in online play.

text: 1) Each time an action occurs, take the last N actions. 2) Use the first N-1 as the key and the last as the value. 3) Increment the value's count and the key record's total.
1) Take the most recent N-1 actions as the window. 2) Look up its record. 3) Return the follow-on with the highest count, or nothing if the window is unseen.
when: When the game needs to predict the next action from recent history.

text: Here graph means a mathematical structure of nodes and connections, not a chart.
A connection's cost can represent distance for shortest paths, time for quickest paths, or any blend of concerns such as danger.
In a directed graph each connection is one-way, and a connection is an ordered pair of nodes plus a cost.
A* and Dijkstra cannot operate directly on level geometry, so the level must first be simplified into a graph.
Each graph element can be created separately with different techniques, or the whole graph can be built in one pass.
Dynamic graph methods such as D* are efficient only when the graph changes infrequently.
Distance and travel time differ: running 10 feet can be quicker than climbing a 10-foot ladder, so time-based costs can differ from distance-based costs.
when: choosing costs for quickest paths

text: The major pathfinding algorithms support directed graphs.
Pathfinding literature uses graph to mean a directed graph with non-negative weights.
A connection's stored distance need not equal its geometric length, which allows long-range links.
Over a sort, each item travels about n/3 places on average.
Index cells or rooms by a coordinate key in a fixed-size hash array to check in near-constant time whether a grid position is occupied.
when: a generator needs fast occupancy queries on a fixed grid
why: A key maps straight to an array slot, so no dynamic allocation is needed and lookup only verifies the match.

text: Dynamically moving edge nodes is overkill; a fixed graph combined with path smoothing usually gives adequate results.
when: Deciding whether navmesh edge nodes should move
why: Smoothing already provides the flexibility that moving nodes would add at higher cost

text: Matching player-watching quality through condensation needs a grid about every 10 centimeters of game space for human-sized characters.
when: When generating tactical waypoints by condensing a grid instead of recording human play
why: Testing nearly every location, rather than anticipating good ones, only approximates watched-player quality when the candidate set is extremely dense.

text: A typical level's dense graph can hold roughly 10–99 million nodes and 100–999 million links, demanding substantial time and memory.
when: Building the initial full-level grid graph before it is simplified
why: Nodes placed every half-meter across all playable space make node and connection counts grow very large.

text: A pathfinding graph needs three elements: node placement with localization information, connections between nodes, and connection costs.
Keeping only a global top 50 of waypoint candidates can cluster waypoints in one part of the level and leave tight areas with none.
when: selecting waypoints from scored candidates
why: Top scores tend to come from one region, while tight areas, which matter more, have few high-scoring candidates.

text: A poor simplification discards useful information and yields poor paths.
why: Pathfinders can only search the simplified graph, so the resulting path is only as good as what the simplification kept.

text: Stopping as soon as the goal is first discovered is faster but can return a route somewhat longer than the optimal one.
When goals are far apart, a heuristic favouring the nearest goal can make the search explore widely, possibly the whole level, if that goal is blocked.
when: Open goal search with widely separated goals
why: A low heuristic near a blocked goal pulls the search toward areas that lead the wrong way

text: 1) For each pair of candidate locations, run a movement check or line-of-sight check. 2) Record a connection for each pair the character can move between directly.
when: When waypoints or tactical map locations have no stored connections between them
why: Pairs a character can walk between directly are the usable links a planned route can rely on.

text: 1) Connect each grid cell to its adjacent cells. 2) Remove connections whose gradient exceeds a threshold. 3) Remove connections into cells occupied by obstacles.
when: RTS grid graphs
why: Grid adjacency yields links for free, and gradient and obstacle tests then prune links a unit could not actually use.

text: Place graph nodes by hand where level structure and movement patterns matter, and compute connections and costs automatically.
why: Level structure and likely movement patterns are judged better by a human, while connections and costs can be computed reliably by an algorithm.

text: Average minimum does not help when only one route connects two rooms, because averaging cannot fix a single connection's cost.
Placing nodes on shared edges with connections across each polygon face suits portal rendering, and needs no line-of-sight tests because every edge of a convex polygon sees every other.
when: Choosing navmesh node placement
why: Edge nodes give visibility for free inside convex polygons, unlike polygon-centre nodes

text: Scripted team coordination can look uncanny, with characters moving like a well-drilled team performing intertimed actions.
when: When multiple characters execute scripted tactics together
why: Tightly timed coordinated actions read as drilled, unnatural teamwork

text: Scripted AI usually means preprogrammed actions carried out in a fixed order without decisions.
Drive NPC behavior with three inputs: perception via sound, sight and touch; remembered world state like enemy sightings and weapon spots; and emotion, such as fear rising under attack.
Scripts commonly use macro commands such as moving to a path node or playing an animation.
Character behaviour over time can be generated with decomposition schemas that choose activities from current needs such as fatigue or hunger, which can also generate story.
Friendly NPCs and enemies can populate worlds, enhance spatial types, and direct player action.
Have an NPC perform the desired action, since players tend to copy observed NPC behavior, which teaches the behavior without explanation.
when: A behavior should be taught to the player.
why: Players learn through example more readily than through explanation.

text: Heavily promoted AI may deliver little visible behavior; a much-hyped system can mostly make characters walk back and forth, so judge AI by what players observe.
Rejecting action scripts because scripted AI has a bad reputation causes teams to miss their practical value.
when: When teams weigh decision scripts against neural networks or emotional and cognitive models
why: Scripts give most of the visible effect with less technical risk and far lower cost than research-heavy alternatives, which rarely convince yet.

text: Scripts for characters that must coordinate depend on timing, so a sequence can succeed once and fail the next time.
when: When several characters must cooperate through per-character scripts
why: Each character's script runs independently, so relative timing between them varies from run to run.

text: A creature that navigates too autonomously becomes too smart to manipulate, which undermines the point of the game.
when: When designing creatures in a herding game where the player must steer them

text: 1) Script each stage of an operation as its own behavior. 2) Write a higher-level script that coordinates those stages. 3) Feed execution feedback back in so scripted behavior stays sensible.
when: When a team of characters must carry out a multi-stage operation together
why: Scripted behaviors must stay sensible while they run, so execution results need to feed back into the script.

text: Generative NPCs need guardrails and safety filters before release, since their output is hard to fully control.
when: When a language model drives NPC dialogue.
why: Generated dialogue can carry model biases and may produce hate speech or unsafe content.

text: Adding branches, loops, or calculations to scripts raises implementation difficulty and authoring burden, while signals and waits suffice for simple collaborative sequences.
when: When only simple collaborative action sequences between multiple characters are needed
why: Full logic constructs would raise implementation difficulty and content authoring burden, while signals and waits cover coordination.

text: The curve drawing uses a pen primitive that moves the pen a given length in a direction indexed by an integer, with directions 45 degrees apart.
Looking-where-you're-going suits aerial vehicles such as helicopters and hovercraft, and human characters that can sidestep if sidestep animations exist.
when: Choosing a facing behavior for a character.

text: Vehicle display orientation can be faked from velocity and turn rate by assuming roll is faster than pitch and pitch faster than yaw, so roll and pitch are visually made to produce yaw.
when: when visual believability matters more than physical accuracy
why: Physical roll, pitch and yaw simulation is costly and usually unnecessary for enemies.

text: Facing can be decoupled from movement, so a character can aim at a target while moving elsewhere.
when: Characters need to aim while moving
why: Movement and orientation are independent outputs

text: Face the travel direction by computing a target orientation from velocity via arctangent, keeping current orientation at zero velocity, and delegating turning to align.
when: Character faces its travel direction
why: Zero velocity has no direction to face; gradual angular acceleration looks more natural than directly setting orientation.

text: Reversing the roll sign makes a vehicle lean outward in turns, which can simulate soggy suspension.
when: When applying this to the chassis of a driving car

text: When an agent cannot turn in place or has a large turning circle, graph nodes must encode orientation as well as location, creating separate nodes for each facing.
when: Agents whose facing constrains reachable neighbours
why: A neighbouring tile may be reachable only from a specific orientation

text: Align runs in O(1) time and memory.
Four procedures, one per orientation, call each other for their sub-curves and draw the connecting lines between them.
when: When a curve of a given order is built from four half-size copies of the previous order
why: Three connecting lines join the four sub-curves, and the base order is just straight lines, so drawing can recurse down to it.

text: Subtracting orientations directly fails near the 2π boundary, producing a near-full turn when a small one exists.
why: Orientations repeat every 2π radians, so a raw difference can take the long way around instead of the short one.

text: Recursive drawing procedures keep their state in the pen position, so calls must occur in the order the scheme prescribes.
why: The Draw module retains the current pen position, so each line depends on where earlier calls left it.

text: 1) Subtract the character's orientation from the target's. 2) Map the difference into the range minus π to π by adding or subtracting multiples of 2π. 3) Take the sign as the turn direction and the absolute value as its size.
why: Wrapping the difference into (−π,π) makes its sign the true turning direction.

text: 1) Compute tilt as the arcsine of vertical velocity divided by speed. 2) Compute roll as the arctangent of rotation rate divided by a lean constant; roll approaches but never reaches pi. 3) Combine yaw about the up axis, then pitch, then roll to get the display orientation.
why: The arctangent of a finite ratio is bounded, so roll cannot reach the limit however fast the rotation.

text: 1) Take the orientation angle. 2) Set the vector's x component to its sine and z component to its cosine. 3) In a left-handed system, negate the x component.
when: Converting between angle and facing vector

text: 1) Compute the rotation as the inverse of the current orientation times the target orientation. 2) For a unit quaternion, invert by conjugation: negate the vector part and keep the scalar. 3) Recover the angle as twice the arccosine of the scalar part, and the axis as the vector part divided by the sine of the angle.
when: aligning a 3D orientation to a target
why: Undoing a rotation means the same axis at the opposite angle, which for unit quaternions is the conjugate.

text: 1) Run the 2D align algorithm on the angle, as if starting from zero orientation, to get a rotation speed. 2) Combine that speed with the axis using the rotation-vector formula.
why: The 3D case reduces to 2D because the axis is fixed and only the angle's speed remains to choose.

text: 1) Cross the base orientation's local z direction with the target vector. 2) Set the angle to the arcsine of the cross product's length and the axis to the normalized cross product. 3) Build a quaternion from axis and angle. 4) Multiply the inverse of the base orientation by that quaternion to get the target orientation.
when: a character should face a 3D direction without its roll being fixed by that direction alone
why: The minimal rotation that points the local z axis at the target is given by the cross product's direction and sine.

text: 1) Quantize both position and orientation when defining nodes. 2) Connect nodes with translations, such as moving forward. 3) Connect nodes with rotations, such as turning 90 degrees.
when: Planning for agents with constrained turning
why: Plans then mix moves and rotations within one graph

text: To face away from a target orientation, add π to it and align to the result, because there is no true opposite orientation.
why: Fleeing an orientation by negating it returns the character to where it started.

text: The kinematic orientation drives steering, while the faked orientation is calculated only for display.
why: Being a post-processing step, it reacts immediately and leaves the steering system unloaded.

text: Below a speed threshold, blend the faked orientation with the kinematic orientation; at zero speed use the kinematic orientation alone. Skip the blend for vehicles that never stop, such as aircraft that cannot hover.
when: When the application never has stationary vehicles, such as aircraft that cannot hover.
why: Blending stops the orientation from jumping as the vehicle slows, since motion gives no usable heading at zero speed.

text: Most characters should face their direction of motion, so orientation usually has to be set from the direction of travel.
when: Characters that look where they move
why: Visual facing otherwise contradicts motion

text: If the base z direction equals the target, return the base orientation; if opposite, return its negation, since the cross product is zero in both cases.
why: The axis is the normalized cross product divided by sin θ, which breaks down when sin θ is zero.

text: Faked orientation trades physical accuracy for constant-time, believable visuals, while full actuator-level roll modeling is complex and usually overkill for enemies.
when: When the AI is not controlling a physically modelled aircraft.
why: Enemies only need to look right, so full actuator-level modelling is overkill for most cases.

text: Turning through angular acceleration looks more natural than setting orientation directly as kinematic movement does.
when: Choosing how a character should rotate to its heading.
why: Direct orientation setting produces abrupt snapping.

text: Minimum distance is very optimistic because it assumes no cost for moving within a group, while maximin is pessimistic because it always uses a large value.
when: choosing a hierarchical connection cost
why: Minimum ignores internal traversal cost; maximin takes the worst-case link.

text: Coarse node spacing produces swerves that look arbitrary: some look death-defying while others miss clear gaps in traffic.
when: fast traffic with coarse graph nodes
why: Few nodes are placed at useful times.

text: A combined search and pathfinding step yields a route the character can follow while continually reconsidering its tactical situation.
when: Characters moving to tactical locations during combat
why: The route and the tactical choice are produced together, so it can be updated as the situation changes

text: In some games the apparent leader changes rapidly every turn, making the horizon effect very pronounced, though these swings are often temporary and settle into positions with a clear leader.
when: Search is shallow in games with rapidly changing leads
why: Limited search depth sees only partial consequences of moves

text: Because all nodes in a cluster share one estimate, A* tends to fill an entire cluster before moving on to other clusters.
when: When clusters are large rather than small.
why: Nodes within a cluster receive identical heuristic values.

text: Routes that detour through unrelated areas look unintelligent to players, while short sensible routes look purposeful.
when: Characters moving to a destination in view of the player
why: Players judge character intelligence by the apparent sense of the route

text: Routes recur across many characters, especially with hierarchical pathfinding, because high-level plan components are shared by many requests.
when: Hierarchical pathfinding in a populated world.
why: Many requests share the same high-level route segments.

text: A* takes a directed graph with non-negative costs, a start node, a goal node and a heuristic object; it returns a least-cost connection list (any minimal path is accepted), or nothing if no path exists.
IDA* is depth-first search over action sequences with a cost cutoff and heuristic, finding lowest-cost plan for one goal; suits large action sets, keeps memory bounded, eases adding depth limits.
when: Single-goal GOAP planning
why: Memory stays small even when the action set is large

text: Three ways to derive a cost between two node groups from low-level links are minimum distance (cheapest link), maximin (largest of per-link minimum distances plus outgoing cost), and average minimum (average of those per-link values instead of the largest).
when: planning on a hierarchical graph

text: A monotonic path parameter increases steadily along the path, like distance traveled, and both line segments and splines can be parameterized this way.
Coherence means searching only path parameters near the previous value, since the character cannot move far in one frame.
when: Following a path during normal motion.
why: Limits the search to nearby sections.

text: A pathfinding heuristic exposes one operation, estimate(node), which returns the estimated remaining cost from that node to the goal.
A* keeps an open list of nodes found but not yet processed and a closed list of nodes already processed.
Estimated-total-cost is a node's cost-so-far plus the heuristic estimate of its remaining distance to the goal.
Unlike Dijkstra, which finds shortest paths to all nodes, A* aims to find one least-cost route between a start node and a goal node.
A pathfinding graph has nodes and connections; in its basic form, a connection is an unordered pair of nodes.
In pathfinding a node usually represents a region such as a room, corridor section, platform or outdoor patch, and a connection links two regions.
A path is a sequence of zero or more connections: zero when start and goal coincide, one when they are directly linked.
Condensation drops weaker tactical waypoints that sit near stronger ones, keeping those of very high quality or those isolated, distant from every other waypoint of their kind.
The base cost, such as distance or time, keeps characters from choosing exceptionally long routes.
Node array A* is a specialized A* storing node data in an array indexed by sequential node numbers; it suits graphs up to about 100,000 nodes, roughly 2 MB.
A navigation mesh uses artist-defined floor polygons as nodes, with connections between polygons sharing an edge, giving a graph with little artist effort.
when: Ground movement or representing walkable areas for pathfinding
why: Polygon adjacency gives a graph with little artist effort

text: Two tactical waypoints link up if one is directly reachable from the other; obstacles such as walls sever those links.
Pathfinding graph links can be marked with the action needed to cross them, such as vaulting, opening a door, breaking a barrier, or rappelling down a wall.
A domain model is a library of plan operator templates that encodes the knowledge of a story world, and planners use it to choose actions.
The cluster heuristic groups highly connected regions of a graph into clusters and precomputes shortest path lengths between cluster pairs to estimate remaining path cost.
The open list holds reached nodes not yet processed, and the closed list holds processed nodes; initially open holds only the start and closed is empty.
Fill is the number of nodes a search considers that never become part of the final route; each costs processing time, so less fill is better.
Open goal pathfinding lets the search accept any node in a goal set as the destination, so the goal test asks whether a node belongs to the goals.
when: Several locations can satisfy the task
why: The character only needs one of several valid destinations

text: Pathfinding computes a sensible, short route through a level from a character's current position to its goal, and sits between decision making and movement in game AI.
when: Characters must reach destinations
why: Movement needs a route that connects decisions to physical motion

text: Random search samples random points in the search space.
Searching finds the element of a fixed collection of N array items whose key equals a given argument, returning its index so other fields can be reached.
when: the collection is fixed during the search

text: In a topological ordering of subroutines, a callee is placed before its caller.
Topological sorting embeds a partial order in a linear order in which every item comes after its predecessors. It is possible exactly when the relation contains no loops.
The path length of a node is the number of edges from the root to it, and the internal path length of a tree is the sum of these over all nodes.
In games a direct path usually exists, so Dijkstra is rarely the main pathfinder, though it matters for tactical analysis and a few other game AI uses.
The vertical quadratic has zero, one or two solutions: zero means the projectile stays below the height, one means it touches it at its peak, two means it crosses on the way up and down.
Precomputed heuristic lookup tables are possible in some cases but usually too large, since the number of node combinations is high.
Each reached node stores its cost-so-far, the connection it arrived by, and its estimated-total-cost.
Most game pathfinding systems use A* or a variant of it, and the algorithm also applies to problems beyond pathfinding.
The A* loop mirrors the classic shortest-path algorithm but orders the open list by estimated-total-cost and calls the heuristic for newly found nodes.
Dijkstra never needs to reopen closed nodes, but A* may, because an earlier estimate can have been too optimistic.
If the open list empties before the goal is reached, no path exists between the start and goal.
Continuous graphs rarely revisit a node with the same position and time, so they behave like trees and storing many nodes gains little.
The choice of pathfinder is independent of how the graph is implemented.
In discrete pathfinding, direction changes can occur only at graph nodes, whose placement is fixed by the graph builder, which fails for fast vehicles in predictable traffic.
Localising a position in a domain graph returns the characteristic point of the node whose domain contains it.
Connections join bordering domains; they can come from a Delaunay triangulation, designer specification, or ray casts between points.
Together the regions partition the whole level into connected pieces.
A null heuristic always returns zero, so the search reduces to the plain uniform-cost shortest-path algorithm.
Group pathfinding is typically no harder than individual pathfinding, because most corridors are wide enough for several characters.
when: Pathfinding for squads of characters
why: Most corridors accommodate several characters side by side

text: Precomputed connection costs need a separate stored set for each set of tactic weights.
A separate base-cost weight is not strictly needed, since scaling all tactic weights by a factor matches scaling the base cost by its inverse.
Tactical waypoints and tactical analyses are often treated separately, yet their general theory is very similar.
Locations alone are not enough for tactical pathfinding; a record of connections between them must also exist.
The base pathfinding graph supplies easy movement between different parts of the level.
The pathfinding list needs add, remove, smallest-element by cost-so-far, find-by-node, and contains tests; finding the smallest and lookup are most worth optimizing.
Automatic node placement, split into geometric analysis and data mining, gives mixed results; people judge level structure and likely movement better, so supervision is usually needed.
Navigation meshes are overwhelmingly popular, have a reputation for reliability, and suit characters that climb walls or cross ceilings.
when: Choosing a pathfinding representation
why: Polygon surfaces can be defined on walls and ceilings as well as floors

text: A full-featured route planner may need tens of milliseconds per character, and on a large graph that can exceed the frame budget at 30 or 60 fps.
Euclidean distance to the goal never overestimates when connection costs equal distances between region points; it ignores walls, so it is exact without obstructions and underestimates with them.
when: connection costs are distances between region points

text: Waypoint connections can be taken from the pathfinding graph or from a separate set of tactical waypoints.
Energy landscapes are minimized to find valleys, and fitness landscapes are maximized to find peaks; the search techniques are the same.
An original turn-based game has no existing opening database, so its opening book must be produced manually.
Dirichlet domain waypoint graphs are the most common representation and are used across driving, shooter and strategy games.
Connections and costs can be computed algorithmically from line of sight and level geometry.
Polygon floor meshes represent 3D movement poorly and make jumping awkward; these limits cannot be fixed at the tool stage.
Movement that must match realistic physics is usually much harder to build than tuning the physics to suit AI characters.
Alternative overtaking racing lines are usually created by hand rather than generated by AI.
A graph search such as Dijkstra can find the best route from already-known technologies to a goal technology.
Open city driving games have no fixed track, so their vehicles need pathfinding and tactical analysis to catch or avoid other cars.
Waypoints are now nearly universal in shooter games, used for both navigation and tactics.
The cluster heuristic is related to hierarchical pathfinding, which uses similar clustering.
The result of a graph search is a list of connections rather than nodes, because two nodes can be joined by several connections with different costs.
Multiple connections between the same node pair matter when costs change over time or differ between characters; many games allow only one connection per pair.
In open outdoor tile levels, Euclidean distance gives minimal fill and good performance.
Euclidean distance has very low computational cost and is the simplest common heuristic.
Game pathfinding has no agreed terminology; writers use many names, such as dots, locations, arcs, links and lines.
In indoor tile levels, fill ranks from highest to lowest: zero heuristic, Euclidean distance, then a tailored cluster heuristic.
when: indoor tile levels

text: Heuristics generated automatically from graph structure have been researched but are not yet convincing.
Perfect heuristics are rarely practical, since computing one requires solving the problem itself.
Animation-based movement planning was not in production use when first described, though its author expected it to appear in games within about five years.
Ray-cast path smoothing does not test all possible smoothed paths, so it may miss the optimal smoothing.
when: Evaluating smoothed path quality
why: It makes greedy local choices rather than a global search

text: In 2D, shortest paths bend only at convex vertices of obstacles, and in 3D only at convex polygon edges or vertices.
when: Building graphs from level geometry
why: Optimal routes wrap around convex corners and never bend elsewhere

text: On a rectangular grid, tile connections normally go to the eight surrounding tiles.
when: Building a square tile graph.
why: Eight-way adjacency includes the diagonals.

text: Euclidean distance is a valid heuristic for distance costs because any real path is at least as long as the straight-line distance.
when: connection costs are plain distance

text: Tile graphs need almost no hand-authored AI data, because the layout is fixed and movement costs derive from tile and terrain properties.
when: levels on a fixed grid, such as RTS maps

text: Tile graphs persist in pathfinding-heavy games because they need no extra infrastructure, even after graphics moved away from sprite tiles.
In early RTS games pathfinding was the main technical challenge, since large grid levels can hold tens of thousands of tiles.
Indoor levels can be modeled using comparatively compact navigation graphs that are quick to search.
Navigation meshes are widespread in shooters, and some developers are returning to waypoints to combine pathfinding with tactical analysis.
Outdoor games often use grid-based pathfinding graphs.
A natural mountain profile is S-shaped: it rises slowly, then steepens, then levels off at a rounded peak.
Searching has three variants: linear search for unordered data, binary search for ordered data, and table search for structured keys such as strings.

Use minimum distance when rooms are roughly the same size, maximin when routes pass through many rooms, and average minimum often otherwise, except for long thin corridor-like rooms or sparse room connections.
when: choosing a hierarchical connection cost
why: Each method suits different room layouts.

text: Treat automatic tactical waypoints as an initial guess and refine them with level design tools.
why: Tactical value can flip with a small positional error, so generated spots need checking.

text: Automatic generation pays off for huge, tactically complex levels; with only a few tens of waypoints per kind, manual placement is likely better.
when: choosing waypoint placement for a level
why: Automation only pays off if the implementation effort is repaid by saved level-design time.

text: Routing toward the target's current position at each decision point gives enough apparent competence, even when the route is long or fruitless.
when: When the route to the target may be complex, double back, or end up fruitless as the target moves.
why: A simple rule of thumb gives apparent competence without finding the true route.

text: With a small set of options, simulate each maneuver and compare the resulting situations to pick the best.
when: when the character has only a few discrete actions
why: Checking each option is practical only with a small set of maneuvers; otherwise the options are nearly unbounded.

text: Tree walks are usually fast enough, so the cost of individual tests matters more than the cost of the walk itself.
why: A balanced tree is walked in logarithmic steps, so one costly decision node dominates the total time.

text: Derive a connection's tactical value by averaging its two endpoint location values, which suits most games when character time splits reasonably between them.
when: character time is split reasonably between the two endpoint regions
why: Tactical values are stored per location, not per connection.

text: Look ahead at opponent replies and beyond, even a couple of moves, since static evaluations are narrow and rarely perfect; shallow search already plays much better than the heuristic alone.
when: the static evaluation is imperfect
why: evaluations cannot judge a position accurately on their own

text: Real-time games can use the same abstraction by viewing the ebb and flow of play from an overview rather than particular moves.
when: When a top-level action needs many atomic actions from a lower-level AI.
why: Abstracting away individual moves keeps the search at strategy level, where the full problem is otherwise huge.

text: Unless enemies always rush the player, a pathfinding layer is usually needed beneath the tactical waypoint layer.
Use Euclidean distance when connection costs equal distances between region points, which is common when every route is equally possible.
when: connection costs are distances between region points

text: For a tile-based main graph, merge world and instance logic rather than layering implicit graphs.
when: main graph is tile-based

text: Use distance to the goal as the heuristic for movement planning; include velocity in the heuristic when the movement involves a jump.
when: A* over an animation-based movement graph
why: Distance usually suffices, but jumps depend on velocity as well as position

text: The bisector can be computed by integrating the membership area once and stored, so it adds no runtime cost during play.
when: Using the bisector as a characteristic point
why: The area split is fixed per set, so it can be calculated offline.

text: Pathfinding speed becomes critical when many units may be sent across a large map.
when: large maps with many units
why: every unit needs its own route

text: Making one side of a chasm lower means the character can jump only from the high side, creating a one-way jump.
when: Designing one-way traversal

text: Accurate estimates narrow the search toward the goal, while poor estimates can make A* slower than Dijkstra.
why: Nodes nearer the goal get expanded first, concentrating the search in the most promising region.

text: A large negative tactic weight applied to a connection with a small base cost and a high tactic value can produce a negative total cost.
when: Tactic weights combined with base connection costs
why: The negative weight term can exceed the base cost

text: Waypoint tactics that already mark room corners and door positions let the same script work for many building shapes.
when: Coordinated squad scripts in varied building layouts
why: Scripts query tagged waypoints rather than hard-coded geometry

text: Dynamic connection costs run the cost function on every request, and caching results lets repeated queries within one frame reuse them.
when: tactical situation changes during play
why: Precomputed costs cannot reflect shifting military influence or enemy cover, which only a live calculation captures.

text: Marking nodes with tactical information lets one graph serve both simple tactical decisions and full tactical pathfinding.
why: Tactical nodes hook into the regular graph, which supplies travel between areas that tactical spots cannot reach from one another.

text: Some games score a position depending on how it was reached, such as Chess draws after three repetitions, so reusing a cached value can ignore repetition history.
when: Game rules depend on move history such as repetition
why: Caching stores one score per position, so repeated positions get identical scores whether it is their first or last repeat.

text: Waypoint-based state machines that respond to nearby characters and the tactical situation, with small randomness, vary play and look cooperative without squad AI.
when: When designers want emergent behavior that differs on each playthrough.
why: Small randomness in decisions makes each run differ, and reacting to nearby characters gives the look of teamwork without squad logic.

text: The difficulty of a found path can influence AI decisions.
when: RTS AI choosing between routes

text: When a character reaches a marked link, it changes behavior so it appears to know the terrain; developers called this embedded navigation.
when: Pathfinding links marked with the action needed to traverse them, such as vaulting or opening a door.

text: The cluster heuristic captures long real routes through corridors that a short straight-line distance through a wall would hide.
when: convoluted indoor layouts
why: Straight-line distance underestimates the true route when walls separate nearby points.

text: A* assumes connection cost does not depend on how the start node was reached; when costs depend on arrival time, A* family algorithms cannot work directly on the graph.
when: connection availability changes with arrival time
why: Arriving earlier or later can open or close a traffic gap.

text: Games with a small branching factor and a deep tree are easier for computers to search than games with a shallow tree and a huge branching factor.
Total signal travel time depends on the total distance covered and the speed of the modality.
Methods that move items one place per elementary step need order n² steps, so faster methods must move items over longer distances in single leaps.
why: Items must travel about a third of the list on average, so one-place steps need order n-squared moves.

text: Checking every character's trajectory against all others for 100 characters requires 10,000 checks.
when: predicting collisions among many characters
why: Individual checks are fast, but sheer numbers of pairwise queries make the total grow quickly.

text: The getParam lookup runs in O(1) for some paths but O(n) in the number of segments for others, and then dominates performance.
when: Path has many segments.

text: A perfect heuristic lets A* reach the goal in O(p) time for a path of p steps.
why: More accurate heuristics leave less wasted exploration, so the search runs faster.

text: If the largest overestimate over all nodes is x, the final path is at most x longer than the optimal path.
Path smoothing by ray casting runs in time linear in the number of path nodes, with most time spent on ray casts and constant extra memory beyond temporary storage.
when: Estimating smoothing cost
why: Each node is visited a bounded number of times

text: Tile movement cost combines distance and gradient terms, and gradient cost can be computed directly from height values.
The POP heuristic estimates the length of the best complete plan from the number of steps and the number of flaws in a partial plan.
when: Ranking partial plans during search
why: Ranking partial plans by estimated completion steers search through a space that otherwise grows exponentially with plan length.

text: Subtree path length p_ij equals w_ij plus the minimum over candidate roots k of p_i,k-1 plus p_kj.
A path interface maps a position plus the last parameter to a path parameter, and maps a parameter back to a position.
when: A steering behavior that must follow a predefined path

text: A pathfinding graph is a directed graph of nodes, connections and costs, a level summary shaped for the search algorithm; tactical waypoint AI uses similar structures.
A character plans an abstract route first, then plans each stage at finer levels down to actual movement. Only the next section is planned when the previous one completes.
when: Route planning for a long journey split into nested stages of increasing detail
why: spreads planning work over time and across levels of detail

text: Movement planning models a character as a graph whose nodes hold position, velocity and the animations allowed next, and whose connections are animations leading to the state reached when they finish.
when: Planning detailed, constrained local movement with animations
why: Animations move characters by fixed amounts, so the state after each one must be tracked explicitly

text: Each floor triangle is a node with up to three links, one per edge; link two floor triangles sharing two vertices when both are marked floor.
Running full pathfinding for every candidate action or waypoint adds significant overhead, especially with thousands of actions in large levels.
when: Searching many candidates each decision
why: Pathfinding is expensive per call, so repeated calls multiply cost.

text: Minimum cost can make the planner prefer a route through fewer rooms over a much more direct one, while maximin can block a direct route with one large cost.
when: planning on a hierarchical graph
why: The chosen cost method changes which paths are returned.

text: Even with limited connections, a movement state graph can become very large and planning time grows accordingly.
when: movement planning over many states

text: A heuristic that works most of the time can still frustrate players in the cases it fails, such as units stepping out of position.
why: The rule pulls units out of defensive positions, which players disliked when enemies approached.

text: Without a target velocity or landing notion, a character cannot compute a take-off that avoids missing a small landing spot.
when: Small landing targets

text: A failed jump may be impossible to recover from and, at the limit, can kill the character.
when: Jumps with lethal falls
why: A committed jump offers no mid-air correction

text: Without coherence, a path follower can latch onto a nearby but unrelated section of path where lines are close together.
when: Path sections run close together.
why: Global search may pick the wrong section.

text: The heuristic runs in the innermost search loop, so an expensive estimate can dominate total search time.
when: When the heuristic estimate involves a complex algorithmic process.
why: It is evaluated at the innermost point of the loop, so its cost is paid on every iteration.

text: Failing to reopen closed nodes leaves downstream costs stale and can produce incorrect routes.
when: When a later route reaches an already-closed node with lower cost-so-far.
why: Unlike Dijkstra, A* can later find a cheaper route to a node it has already closed.

text: IDA* is unsuitable when getting outgoing connections is expensive, because it regenerates the same nodes on every iteration.
Node placement is the hardest part of a continuous planner to debug.
Intricate domain shapes can make travel between two connected domains cross an impassable third domain, making the graph invalid.
when: When node placement uses Dirichlet domains that form intricate shapes.

text: Pruning helps greatly, but when no valid plan exists the search approaches an exhaustive search.
when: Planning with an unreachable goal

text: Every waypoint stores a full set of values, so five properties mean five numbers per waypoint even when most are zero.
when: When tactical properties are stored as numeric values per waypoint rather than membership sets.
why: Membership sets record only qualifying waypoints, so no storage entries are wasted.

text: Dynamic cost evaluation sits in the innermost pathfinding loop, so its expense is usually noticeable in search time.
when: When connection costs must reflect dynamic tactical factors, such as enemy influence or cover.
why: The cost is evaluated in the lowest loop, so its expense is repeated on each connection lookup.

text: Endpoint averaging can make an exposed connection look acceptable when both endpoints are safe, hiding a longer detour that would be better.
when: connection crosses dangerous ground between safe locations
why: It assumes the character spends half its time in each endpoint's region, which can misjudge the connection.

text: Counting exits can mislead in dense areas, because several exits may lead to the same vicinity, so the count favors a spot in the middle of the room.
when: ranking positions by number of exits
why: exits may converge on the same region

text: Topological results are very sensitive to waypoint density, so changing how densely waypoints are placed can change tactical rankings.
Without connection data, nearby waypoints cannot be classified as real exit routes or as points separated by a wall.
when: When topological analysis is run on tactical waypoints.
why: Topology is judged from how waypoints connect, beyond their positions and qualities.

text: Automatic widening leaves very small polygons in corners and crevices, and these can trap characters.
when: When AI collision geometry is generated automatically by shifting walls out by the character radius.

text: Manually built graphs must be rebuilt whenever level geometry changes, which motivates automating graph creation.
why: Manual creation is time-consuming, so developers have experimented with automatic generation of such graphs.

text: A decorative patch wrongly flagged as non-floor can cut off an entire room from navigation.
when: When ornamental textures lie over the center of a floor area
why: Floor status comes from the material applied to each polygon, so a wrong material removes that area from navigation.

text: Scanning the whole open list for its smallest node every iteration is slow.
why: Finding the smallest element is among the operations typically most worth optimizing.

text: In indoor tile levels with large obstructions, Euclidean distance produces large fill and poor performance.
when: In indoor tile-based levels where walls block direct routes
why: Going around walls only ever adds distance, so a straight-line estimate becomes an underestimate.

text: With a minimum cost of 1 on every room link, the planner prefers the route with fewest rooms over a much more direct one, producing a path of cost 25 where the optimal is 9.
when: group costs use minimum distance in room-based layouts
why: fewer rooms beats direct routes when each link looks cheap

text: A character in the air is quantized to the first polygon below it, which can be wrong when walkways lie above a room.
when: Localizing airborne characters on a navigation mesh
why: The nearest polygon below may belong to a different level than the character's position

text: Using the geometric centre for localization works reliably for triangles but only for concave polygons among larger shapes.
when: Localizing on navigation meshes with larger polygons
why: The centre of a convex polygon may fall outside it or in a misleading place

text: Direct moves between connected triangles can collide with walls, so connections alone do not guarantee clear movement.
when: Using navmesh connections for direct movement
why: Adjacent polygons may still have obstacles between their interior paths

text: Graph simplification often discards information a person would consider obvious, so the result usually needs review and adjustment.
why: Automatic simplification removes structure a person would notice, so the result needs review.

text: Straight search repeats comparisons already made at earlier start positions, which makes its worst-case cost quadratic in the input sizes.

1) Lay a dense grid over every floor area. 2) Discard cells a character cannot occupy, such as those too close to walls or under obstacles. 3) Score each valid location with real-valued tactical qualities. 4) Drop locations that fail every threshold. 5) Condense the rest into the best few per property per area, covering the whole level.
when: selecting waypoints from scored candidates
why: Testing nearly every location avoids having to guess the best spots in advance.

text: Because movement graphs are generated on demand, use a basic two-list A* rather than an optimized variant that requires the node count in advance.
when: the state graph is built during search
why: Optimized A* needs the total node count beforehand.

text: 1) Log each agent's location once per frame or every few frames. 2) Flag a spot when a character stays near it for several consecutive samples. 3) Flag spots that many characters reuse over the game. 4) Score flagged spots for tactical quality and keep those that pass.
when: the engine can record character actions during play
why: where characters linger or gather often marks useful tactical positions

text: 1) Move straight until reaching a junction. 2) At the junction, take the route toward the player's offset location with the enemy's own probability, otherwise take a random route.
when: grid-style enemies choosing routes
why: Per-enemy probabilities make each enemy's personality differ, and no pathfinding is needed.

text: Very small gap volumes can act as 3D jump points when labelled with a target velocity.
when: Precise jump points needed
why: The jump detector fires automatically when the character steers toward the gap, so one object covers both sides.

text: 1) Find the character's nearest point on the path. 2) Move along the path by a fixed offset to get the target. 3) Delegate to seek. Arrive is unnecessary because the target keeps moving.
when: Character should follow a path.
why: A continuously advancing target means the character never settles, so slowing to stop is pointless.

text: 1) Check each segment of the line path. 2) Find the segment nearest the character. 3) Take the nearest point on that segment.
when: Path is made of line segments.
why: Straight segments make converting a position into a path parameter simple, unlike curved splines.

text: Split pathfinding work across frames when decomposers run expensive pathfinding and many goals are distant, so a single frame does not stall.
when: When pathfinding decomposers are slow and many characters need goals
why: Pathfinding inside a decomposer can take long enough to cause frame spikes

text: 1) Put a start record with cost 0, no connection, and estimate equal to heuristic(start) on open. 2) While open is non-empty, take the lowest estimated-total record; if it is the goal, stop. 3) Process each outgoing connection. 4) Move the current node from open to closed.

1) Compute the tentative cost-so-far as current cost plus connection cost. 2) If the neighbour already has an equal or lower cost, skip it. 3) If it is unvisited, create its record and call the heuristic once; otherwise reuse its stored heuristic. 4) Store cost, connection and estimated total; put it on open, removing it from closed if needed.
why: Reusing a node's stored heuristic avoids calling the possibly expensive heuristic function again.

text: 1) Start at the goal node. 2) Follow each node's stored connection back toward the start, collecting connections. 3) Reverse the collected connections to get the path.
1) Plan the nearby route continuously at the lowest level. 2) Plan the remaining route intersection by intersection at a higher level.
when: long driving routes
why: Continuous planning is too costly over long distances.

text: 1) Set the initial cutoff from the heuristic at the start model. 2) Run a depth-first search; prune branches whose cost so far plus heuristic exceeds the cutoff, and return the plan on reaching the goal. 3) If no plan is found, raise the cutoff to the smallest pruned total that exceeded it and repeat; stop when no plan is possible.

1) Query a spatial structure for suitable waypoints near the character. 2) Sort candidates by distance. 3) For each candidate, measure path length with a pathfinding step. 4) Stop once the path exceeds the nearest candidate found so far.
when: Finding tactical waypoints near a character in levels with walls or complex layouts
why: Straight-line distance can pick points behind walls; path length gives the true travel cost and the early stop limits pathfinding work

text: 1) Extract each board edge. 2) Look up each edge in a database of edge configurations, each with a strength score. 3) Weight those scores highly in the static evaluation during the middle game.
when: Board game where edge play matters, such as Reversi
why: Full board positions rarely repeat exactly, so looking up sections such as edges is more practical.

text: 1) Choose a target room. 2) Plan a route with A* over a room waypoint graph. 3) Follow the route with path following.
when: Agents heading to a room
why: A room-level waypoint graph lets movement fit with the tactical and strategic AI.

text: 1) Partition the graph into clusters, by a graph clustering algorithm, manual design, or level structure. 2) Offline, run many pathfinding trials between every pair of clusters. 3) Store the minimum lengths in a lookup table.

1) Start at the goal. 2) Take the connection used to arrive at the current node. 3) Move to that connection's start node. 4) Repeat until the start node is reached. 5) Reverse the collected connections.
1) Group low-level locations into clusters. 2) Make each cluster one node at the next level. 3) Store a mapping from each node to its group. 4) Repeat upward to form the hierarchy.
when: When many low-level points in a room can be treated as one for higher-level plans
why: each level becomes an ordinary graph the standard search can use

text: 1) Start at the highest level where start and goal fall in different nodes. 2) Run A* on that level and refine the first stage of the plan. 3) At each lower level, keep the current start and set the goal to the end of the first higher-level move. 4) Skip levels where start and goal share a node.
when: When pathfinding over a hierarchical graph where start and goal share a node at upper levels
why: higher-level results limit the work needed below

text: 1) Run A* one iteration at a time. 2) Pause after any iteration, keeping the open and closed lists. 3) Resume on a later frame until the path completes.
when: a single planning call would exceed the frame budget
why: spreads planning across several frames

text: 1) Define the goal as a region of acceptable positions rather than one exact position and orientation. 2) Run the search. 3) Use the resulting animation list as the plan.
when: Animation-based movement planning
why: An exact position and orientation may be unreachable, causing the search to fail after exhausting the graph

text: 1) Create a record for every node up front, indexed by node number. 2) Store each record's category as unvisited, open or closed. 3) Use a separate priority queue for the open list.
when: Implementing A* on a graph with known, indexed nodes
why: Constant-time lookup replaces searching the open and closed lists, and the category answers membership without a separate closed list

text: 1) Choose one goal with a decision step. 2) Run ordinary pathfinding to that single goal.
when: Goals are widely separated
why: Avoids the wide search caused by heuristics that guess the wrong goal

text: 1) Start the output with the first node. 2) Ray cast from the last output node to successive input nodes, starting at the third node. 3) When a ray fails, add the node before the failing one to the output and restart casting from the next node. 4) Append the end node.
when: Smoothing a path whose adjacent nodes are connected by clear routes
why: Removes unnecessary intermediate nodes in linear time

text: 1) Find the floor polygon containing the character's position. 2) Check the previous node and its neighbours first, relying on coherence between frames. 3) Use the geometric centre of the polygon for localization.
when: Locating a character on a navigation mesh
why: Coherence makes the check fast, and the centre gives a reliable test point for triangles

text: 1) Trim floor polygons inward by the agent's size. 2) Recompute connections, checking doorways especially.
when: Preparing a navigation mesh for agents of a given size
why: Size changes which polygon edges remain passable, often at narrow doorways

text: 1) List the connections along the route. 2) Sum their costs. The result is the route's total path cost.
when: Computing the cost of a candidate route.
why: Route cost is additive over connections.

text: 1) Clear the board matrix. 2) Mark the start square as move 1. 3) Call the recursive try procedure from that square.
1) Pick any item with no remaining predecessor. 2) Place it at the head of the result and remove it. 3) Repeat on the remaining set until it is empty.
when: When items form a partial ordering with no loops and must be laid out in a linear sequence.
why: Without loops, some item must lack a remaining predecessor, so the choice can always be made.

text: 1) For each pair x before y, find or insert leaders for x and y, add a trailer for y to x's list, and raise y's predecessor count. 2) Gather leaders with zero count into a zero chain. 3) Repeatedly take a leader from the zero chain, output its key, lower each successor's count, and add any successor reaching zero to the chain.
when: Sorting items under partial order constraints
why: Items with no unmet predecessors can be emitted safely

text: Characters can use different cost functions weighing visibility, speed or terrain by role; dynamic evaluation lets each apply its own weights at runtime, giving distinct personalities.
when: When costs depend on changing tactical conditions such as enemy cover or military influence.
why: Precomputed costs cannot reflect changing conditions, so the cost function must be evaluated when requested, which slows pathfinding.

text: Add an assertion or debug message when a connection gets negative cost; otherwise such bugs appear as pathfinding that never returns or subtler faults.
when: Developing tactical pathfinding or pathfinding with negative edge costs
why: Negative-cost bugs are hard to track down; the search cannot terminate correctly with negative costs.

text: Generate many more waypoint candidates than will be used, so that quality assessment has enough weak candidates to filter out.
when: When candidate waypoints are gathered from logged positions of players or characters.
why: filtering needs a surplus to select the strongest positions

text: Add pathfinding to steering to overcome the horizon problem, since adding more steering behaviors cannot fully fix it.
when: When obstacles or corners lie beyond what a local steering behavior can sense ahead.
why: Steering reacts only to immediate surroundings, and no tweak to steering can see past its horizon; only looking ahead through pathfinding can.

text: Look where you're going uses the same procedure as face, with the normalized velocity as the target direction.
Reverse the direction of travel along a path by negating the offset.
when: Character must traverse a path backward.

text: Prefer basic path following where a path must be completed fully, such as a patrol route.
when: Patrol routes or paths that must not be skipped.
why: Predictive following can skip sections.

text: Process the open node with the smallest estimated-total-cost next, not the one with the smallest cost-so-far.
The heuristic must never return a negative value, because graph connection costs are non-negative.
Compare candidate routes on cost-so-far rather than estimated-total-cost, since estimates include heuristic error.
when: When a newly found route reaches a node already on the open or closed list and its recorded values must be revised.
why: Cost-so-far contains no guessed component, so it is the only reliable value for comparing routes.

text: If an improved node is still open, update it in place; if it is closed, move it back to open so it is processed again.
when: When a node receives a lower cost-so-far after it has already been processed.
why: Its successors were computed from the old value, so they must be rechecked to propagate the improvement.

text: Use a memory-bounded A* variant for large continuous graphs that rarely revisit nodes.
when: When pathfinding graphs are huge and continuous, and the search seldom returns to a visited node.
why: Memory savings matter and storing many nodes gains little.

text: Place nodes where the vehicle will be at that time, not where other vehicles are now, so traffic must be predicted for each arrival time.
when: When traffic differs over time, so the same place costs differently at different arrival times.
why: Other vehicles move, so their positions change with time.

text: Connection costs are usually travel time, but penalties such as for close calls with other motorists can be added.
when: When risky maneuvers near other motorists should be weighed against the time they save.
why: Elapsed time is the normal measure because the goal is speed of travel, with other penalties added on top.

text: Add danger-related costs, such as exposure to enemy fire or dangerous terrain, so the chosen path has the lowest danger.
when: tactical pathfinding in RTS games
why: Exposed or dangerous connections are given higher costs, so the search steers away from them.

text: Before linking neighbouring domains, check for walls between them, since adjacency alone does not guarantee passage.
when: When neighbouring domains touch but a wall may lie between them.

text: Back up domain graph travel with a fallback such as an avoid-walls steering behaviour.
when: When the domain graph's validity cannot be guaranteed, such as with intricate Dirichlet domain shapes.
why: A path between linked domains can cross a third domain the pathfinder excluded, leading characters into obstacles.

text: IDA* planning needs three inputs: an action cost, which may equal duration; a goal fulfilment test; and a heuristic estimate method.
when: When planning goal-directed actions over a huge number of possible actions with limited memory.
why: The heuristic lets the search prefer actions near the goal, and every A* variant needs one.

text: When a suitable location is found during decision making, store it so movement goes straight there without another search.
when: When decision making searches for a suitable location, such as cover, and movement will then head there.
why: Repeating the search after the decision duplicates effort.

text: Use D*, dynamic A* that replans only the part of an existing plan affected by new information, when environment is uncertain or changes and replanning from scratch is too expensive.
when: When the level keeps changing, so repeated full replanning never finishes.
why: Only the parts of a plan that may have changed are recalculated, avoiding repeated full replans.

text: Add other factors, such as equipment wear in harsh deserts, to terrain analysis when the game supports equipment breakdown.
when: the game supports equipment breakdown

text: For very complex level geometry, first simplify the collision shape before generating the offset AI geometry.
when: very complex level geometry
why: Automatically widened geometry can produce tiny polygons in corners and crevices, which can trap a character.

text: Visualize the floor flags so misclassified polygons are caught before they break navigation.
when: When level editors must tag which polygons count as walkable floor, via materials or manual flags.
why: Mislabeled decorative surfaces inside a room can make the whole room impassable, and such errors show up at a glance when flags are drawn.

text: Profile before optimizing search; in some observed cases over 80% of execution time went to heuristic evaluation.
why: The heuristic runs in the innermost loop, so an expensive estimate can take most of the search time.

text: When start and goal share a cluster, estimate with Euclidean distance or another fallback; otherwise look up the stored cluster-pair length.
when: at runtime
why: Stored values only cover distinct cluster pairs.

text: When a reached node is already open or closed, update its cost and connection only if the new cost-so-far is lower; if it is closed, reopen it and remove it from closed.
when: When a node reached during search is already on the open or closed list.
why: A lower-cost route found later must replace the old record, or a better route is lost.

text: Opaque, non-numeric node types need translation operations in place of adding and subtracting an offset.
when: node types are not numeric

text: Pair interruptible pathfinding with D* or LPA* when the character moves or the world changes during planning, so the search does not restart from scratch.
when: the character moves or the world changes during planning
why: Planning spread over several frames gives the character time to move, and incremental algorithms reuse prior search work instead of restarting.

text: Use animation-based planning for detailed local movement, not for whole-level routes.
when: Choosing a planning scale
why: Its graph grows quickly, so it suits short constrained sequences

text: Use only non-negative connection costs with Dijkstra and A*, because these algorithms are invalid with negative weights.
when: Choosing edge costs for a pathfinding graph.
why: Negative weights can create cycles with no shortest path, so most such searches loop forever.

text: Prefer exact methods when they are practical, and use Monte Carlo only as a check or when no exact method is feasible.
when: When estimating odds of an event such as a rare item drop from a loot table.
why: Monte Carlo results are approximate and vary between runs.

text: Model stations as nodes and direct links as weighted edges, then search for the minimum time between departure and destination, since not all pairs are directly linked.
Dynamic costs yield better tactical routes but add planning time; precomputed costs plan faster but ignore changing conditions, so precompute only when tactical features are static.
when: choosing how to evaluate tactical connection costs
why: Stored costs cannot reflect changes in the tactical situation; the choice depends on whether extra planning time is acceptable.

text: Player-watching gives better tactical waypoints than condensing a grid, but needs action-logging infrastructure and a lot of tester time.
when: placing tactical waypoints
why: Matching that quality through condensation requires starting from an extremely dense grid of candidate points.

text: Predictive following is smoother on complex paths but can jump to another section where two path sections are close, cutting corners and skipping path.
when: Choosing a path following variant.
why: Predicted point may land on a nearby unrelated section.

text: Straight segment paths suit characters that turn quickly, while maneuver paths such as constant-radius turns suit vehicles; maneuver paths are harder to check for violations because of curved sections.
when: When choosing path representation for a character or vehicle
why: Fast-turning characters can follow sharp segments, while vehicles cannot turn instantly

text: Caching connections would fix IDA*'s speed problem but undermines its memory goal.
why: IDA* re-expands the same nodes on every iteration, and each connection lookup is costly, so caching would reintroduce the storage IDA* avoids.

text: Finer node spacing is needed for fast traffic, but most fine nodes are unreachable because vehicles block them.
when: When the pathfinding task changes rapidly but predictably, such as with fast-moving vehicles.

text: Computing transition level offsets at run time by searching the hierarchy is flexible but slow, whereas computing them offline gives a fast hybrid.
why: Searching at run time means stored level values never need to be trusted, but each transition then costs a full search.

text: Path-length search handles walls and complex layouts, while plain Euclidean distance is enough for simple levels.
when: Choosing the distance measure for waypoint search
why: Path search is more accurate but costs more than a straight-line check

text: Clamping costs to a positive minimum is a safety net, but it adds processing time and can make many connections share the same cost, losing ranking information.
when: When weights cannot be guaranteed non-negative
why: Clamping hides the weight problem and flattens differences between routes

text: A single shared waypoint system can serve pathfinding and tactics, but a separate tactical point set is often more efficient, since cover and sniping points are generally poor path nodes.
why: Tactical locations such as cover and sniping spots are not good pathfinding graph nodes.

text: Overestimating heuristics reach the goal faster but may miss the best route; large overestimates make A* perform worse quickly, and in games believable results can matter more than optimality.
when: When an overestimating heuristic is only slightly off, or is consistently close to perfect.
why: Slight overestimates often yield the same path as the best one, so the loss of path quality is rarely significant.

text: A general A* handles any cost type, node data type, and graph size but runs slower than specialized versions tailored to graph assumptions.
when: When the graph has a modest number of nodes that can be numbered with sequential integers.
why: Assuming a small, integer-numbered node set lets the search use array indexing instead of general-purpose list operations.

text: Balance among the pathfinding list's four operations determines speed, and the best balance differs between games.
why: The open and closed lists' four operations are critical and directly determine performance, so their balance decides speed.

text: D* saves planning time at the cost of storing intermediate data that may be needed later, which can be large.
why: D* replans only the portions that might have changed, so it must keep intermediate results from earlier planning.

text: Cluster heuristics greatly reduce fill indoors but do not help outdoors and can reduce performance there.
when: When the map has large obstructions, as in indoor levels.
why: Straight-line distance is a poor estimate of real travel distance around large obstructions, while on open outdoor maps it is far more accurate.

text: A* variants that reduce memory use usually cost some speed, so the trade-off should be measured in the target game.
Path-following steering already smooths paths somewhat, so smoothing is worth adding only after testing; for some games it is essential.
when: Deciding whether to add path smoothing
why: Steering may already hide erratic turns, making smoothing redundant in some games

text: LPA* stores data about small plan sections, which are reusable across varied tasks, but its storage cost is high and suits small graphs.
when: Choosing a replanning algorithm for a level.
why: Storage grows with graph size, so large open levels are where speed matters most yet storage is least practical.

text: The time-indexed road graph is effectively infinite, so it is generated only where needed and constrained by changing lanes as soon as possible and travelling to each lane change as fast as possible.
when: Generating continuous road planning graphs.
why: Full generation is impossible, and the speed assumption can miss optimal timing such as passing gaps at lower speed.

text: Pre-computed routes for common paths speed up static levels, but deformable terrain makes pre-computation impossible, so routes must be searched live.
when: Games whose terrain can be deformed during play

text: The variant that ignores equality until the end has simpler termination and finds the least-index match, at the cost of a few extra comparisons, which the per-step gain outweighs.
why: Each step's efficiency gain outweighs the few extra comparisons, and the number of steps stays logarithmic.

text: A naive matcher tries every possibility on each iteration, so it is adequate only for very simple systems; larger systems need a more efficient matcher such as Rete.
when: Rule count and database size grow
why: Repeated full testing of all rules is wasteful

text: Goals need a name and a value, and actions need a function that returns their goal change for a given goal.
The ideal AI scheduler controls total execution time, guarantees that every behaviour runs, and reports statistics on how each behaviour uses its share of time.
