Communication between tiers can be simple, while scheduling is the harder part to get right.
Machinery for scheduling AI has also been repurposed for incremental level loading, texture handling, gameplay rules, sound timing and physics updates.
Beyond proportional priority, a scheduler can grant requested time, run every behaviour each frame, or adjust biases from measured overruns.

Most games need no complex scheduling unless they have complex AI; a simple frequency scheduler suffices. Switch to priority policies when behaviours differ widely in interruptibility or required run rate.
when: choosing an AI scheduling approach
why: Priority-based systems introduce subtle problems

text: Use separate matchers for each kinematic element and merge them later with combination techniques, rather than one general matcher accepting any element combination.
when: Several elements may need matching simultaneously
why: Matching several elements can conflict, for example matching velocity rules out getting closer, and merging resolves such conflicts.

text: Heavier units usually give large positive weights to difficult terrain, enemy proximity and visibility, while lighter units weight these much less.
why: Heavy artillery cannot cope with rough ground, fights poorly at close range, and is a prime target when exposed.

text: A polling station's cache recalculates data at most once per frame, and only if it is actually requested in that frame.
when: When polling is the best approach but each check is time consuming
why: A shared cache lets several characters reuse one expensive check instead of each repeating it.

text: A naive nearest-point search over n domains costs O(n) per query.
why: Finding the closest point means checking every point in turn, so the cost grows with the number of points.

text: In a sleep and on-guard example, two states need four states in total under per-frame re-requests, and five states would need 40 additional transition states.
when: When states must repeat timed actions every frame.
why: Each re-requested action needs its own intermediate state, so the number of transitions multiplies as states are added.

text: Investing heavily in incidental characters that most players never study wastes effort, and reviewers may still judge the result sloppy.
when: Incidental characters that players observe only briefly
why: Players read unexplained actions as poor implementation, and only the rare dedicated player sees the intent behind them.

text: A producer that adds an action every frame can flood the queue; expiry times help but may be too slow, so producers must be kept under control.
when: When the manager accepts actions from user scripts or other sources it cannot control
why: Expiry times clear the queue too slowly to stop a flood, so a size cap that evicts the lowest priority action is used.

text: Changing hard-coded behavior requires programmers to edit and recompile the game, which is costly when builds take minutes or hours.
when: Large projects with long build times
why: Every behaviour edit forces a rebuild, and rebuilds in large projects can take a very long time.

text: Drawing a new random choice every frame causes visible jitter, so the choice must be held stable until it is redrawn.
when: Decision logic that runs every frame and includes random branches
why: Redrawing the random choice each frame makes the character flicker between behaviours, which looks odd to the player.

text: Global illumination is very slow, so combining it with runtime shadow calculation is problematic.
when: For games with dynamic lighting
why: Global illumination is slow and best computed offline; interactive-rate versions are only just emerging.

text: Suspending a character when it leaves the screen and resuming it in the same spot looks odd, so AI should not depend only on on-screen status.
when: When AI activity depends on whether a character is currently visible
why: Characters are expected to keep acting, so one frozen mid-action and then found in the same spot looks wrong.

text: Under high load, finding a workable time-allocation strategy can require considerable tuning.
when: Under high load
why: Behaviours differ in how often they must run and whether they can be split, so no single priority scheme fits all.

text: When each call site fetches data where it needs it, information flows through many places and becomes hard to trace and debug.
when: When each character queries the world for its own information
why: Information reaches many scattered call sites, making data flow hard to trace and debug.

text: 1) Add velocity times elapsed time to position, and rotation times elapsed time to orientation. 2) Add acceleration times elapsed time to velocity, and angular acceleration times elapsed time to rotation.
when: When updating a character's position and orientation each frame without a physics layer
why: Simplified Newton-Euler-1 integration is accurate enough at typical frame rates

text: 1) Advance the time counter. 2) Scan the queue for interrupters, stopping when priority is no higher than the top active priority; if one can interrupt, clear the active list and keep only it. 3) Discard expired queued actions. 4) Move queued actions compatible with all active actions into the active list. 5) Remove completed active actions and execute the rest.

1) For each rule in fixed order, create an empty bindings list and test its if-clause against the database. 2) Run the action of the first rule that matches, passing the bindings. 3) End the iteration. 4) If none match, run a fallback or do nothing.
when: Simple rule-based systems

text: A behaviour scheduled at frequency 1 is called every frame; if each call does a little more work, it eventually completes.
when: When a behaviour does a short slice of work per call and then returns
why: The scheduler needs no thread-switch housekeeping because the task saves its own data before returning.

text: Each frame, convert inputs to degrees and then compute rule minima, keeping the degrees of inputs that did not change since the last frame.
Game-specific optimizations designed for one scenario, such as many chess-specific techniques, are of limited value unless your game matches that scenario.
when: Your game does not match the scenario the optimization was designed for
why: Such optimizations only pay off in the few scenarios they were built for.

text: Agents must react to world events, to each other and to the player, and track what happens to themselves, colleagues and enemies, so they feel alive rather than scripted.
why: Ignoring world events makes characters follow fixed routines that appear oblivious to what is happening around them.

text: Players notice distant characters less, so distant characters can ignore precise rules, such as passing through one another or taking longer to decide.
when: When a character is far from the player's view.
why: Errors on distant characters are unlikely to be seen.

text: When the player is not nearby, creatures typically sleep or stand around.
when: No player is near a group of creatures.
why: Free-roaming creatures could wander into predators or be eaten before the player reaches them, which would spoil the encounter.

text: An enemy that appears at varying distances and advances when the player looks away makes the player's movement feel slow.
when: When the enemy's whole environment is dark, open space it can hide in

text: Enemies that cannot see but have sharp hearing make players move slowly and quietly around them.
why: Because such enemies locate players by sound, players must limit their speed to avoid being heard.

text: The finite element approach replaces continuous space with a directed graph of regions across which signals pass; it gives believable perception only if the regions are chosen carefully.
Perception is what information a character knows; it covers every interface between the game world and the AI, not only simulated sight and hearing.
An alarm behavior interrupts normal activity to handle an urgent condition, then lets the interrupted activity resume.
when: An agent must respond to urgent events regardless of its current task

text: A signal carries an identifier and is delivered to any interested AI behavior, optionally through an event or sense system for finer control.
The memory-enhanced test is a zero-width alpha-beta negamax backed by a transposition table, taking one guess called gamma instead of separate alpha and beta bounds.
Smell is propagated iteratively because it lingers and diffuses; unlike sound, each node stores a smell intensity and the time it was last updated.
why: Smell lingers and diffuses

text: Sound is modelled as a wave spreading outward through nodes from its source, losing intensity across connections until it falls below a minimum.
Proxy data is a substitute variable, such as zip code or language pattern, used when objective data is missing. It can encode discrimination.
when: When the objective measure is unavailable to the model.
why: Proxies correlate with sensitive attributes and carry their bias into decisions.

text: Quantization converts a game position into a graph node, and localization converts a graph node back into a game location a character can move to.
when: Connecting game worlds to pathfinding graphs.
why: Pathfinders work only on nodes, so both conversions are needed.

text: A sense graph node is a region where signals pass unhindered, storing an attenuation per unit distance for every modality and, for smell-capable nodes, a dissipation value.
A sense graph connection joins two nodes through which one or more modalities can pass, storing attenuation and distance per modality and 3D positions at both ends.
Smell spreads by gas diffusion, which is slow and limited in distance, is much more noticeable downwind, and ordinary sources such as a person's scent carry only a few tens of feet.
Concentrated chemicals carry smell farther than ordinary sources, and animals with a good sense of smell can detect people at much greater distances in suitable wind.
Most games do not model smell; hunting games are the typical exception.
A decision tree can combine several perception and position tests, such as visibility, distance, audibility and flanking, to choose between actions.
Most decision tests take constant time, but some, such as checking for a visible enemy with ray casts through geometry, are expensive.
Shadow quality depends on the lighting model: global illumination is commonly baked offline into lightmaps, while stealth games may use direct lighting with static lightmaps.
Culling skips locations that cannot possibly be seen; indoor levels allow more culling than outdoor levels.
Visiting nodes in distance order matches arrival time when sound speed is constant.
when: sound propagation with constant speed

text: The sound model does not linger and does not simulate echoes.
Deep, low-frequency sounds reach farther and diffract around obstacles more readily than high-pitched sounds.
Many games make characters omniscient, for example by letting them always track the player's location.
Checks involving level geometry, such as line of sight blocked by movable objects, can be expensive to compute.
Crowd and military simulations use detailed perception models, even when their underlying AI is simple.
Vision cannot bend around corners; it requires a direct, unobstructed straight line.
Light-emitting events, such as muzzle flashes, can be seen around dark corners, unlike unlit objects.
In open scenes, humans have no inherent distance limit; atmosphere and the curve of the earth impose the practical limit.
Communication lets AI agents hold the correct information at the proper moment; it is essential even for simple AI and matters most when characters coordinate.
Early shooters faked perception with a radius around each enemy, and the enemy activated when the player entered that radius.
A cone-of-sight check is a common way to model a guard's vision.
In one shooter, AI decisions ran on roughly 30-second timescales and mission scripts on roughly 3-minute timescales, with the combat loop bridging them.
Under open-world semantics, a condition that a state description does not mention is unknown rather than false.
The finite element sense manager is a state-of-the-art approach but is complex, and its sense graphs need dedicated level tools.
Model vision as instantaneous: light travels about 300 million meters per second, so it crosses a game level within one frame.
when: When the game does not involve very large distances through space
why: Light travel time is negligible at game scale.

text: With several characters in the cone, evade either their average position and speed or only the closest one; both suit only a handful.
when: When several characters are inside the detection cone

text: Estimate visibility by testing a random subset of locations, provided enough samples are used for a good estimate.
when: full testing is too slow
why: Testing every location pair is very slow on large levels, while enough random samples still approximate the true result.

text: Sample important locations, such as strategic points from an influence map or enemy positions, instead of random ones; this is usually done during online play.
when: visibility must be estimated at runtime

text: Give characters different hearing thresholds to model keen hearing or temporary deafness, such as deafness after a nearby explosion.
why: Sound fades uniformly with distance until it drops below a threshold, so per-character thresholds change how far each one can hear.

text: Model normal attention with a cone of around 60 degrees.
when: modeling everyday attention
why: people consciously monitor only a few degrees at a time

text: Cap the distance at which enemies notice the player, so enemies do not surprise the player from across an open area.
why: Without a distance cap, enemies across a clearing would spot the player at every corner and attack by surprise.

text: Creatures in herding games rarely need sophisticated AI, even predators.
why: Outdoor settings with few spatial constraints let simple steering behaviors act locally and combine without complex arbitration.

text: In less realistic genres, a regional sense manager or a plain event manager is often better than full sense simulation.
when: sensing is not central to the game
why: Full sense simulation is complex and needs dedicated tooling, so it only pays off when sensing is a feature of the game.

text: Enemies that track smell can follow a trail of increasing intensity to locate the player.
why: Smell spreads outward from its source, so moving toward stronger concentrations leads to the source.

text: If objects emit signals only when the particular character can use them now, a character carrying raw food is drawn to the oven and one without it to a fridge, greatly reducing planning.
why: Filtering signals to those usable right now means the character has far fewer steps to plan toward a goal.

text: Signal diffusion respects level geometry, taking time around corners and not passing through walls, and intensity falls with distance, so characters naturally favor close options.
why: Diffusion through the level's geometry removes the need to pathfind to each option, since the nearest source gives the strongest signal.

text: Sources can emit signals of different intensities, so a weak source of a motive is less attractive than a strong one, which keeps characters choosing balanced options.
why: Scaling the strength each source emits lets a convenient but weak source be outweighed by a stronger one.

text: Scores bubble up from leaves: on the searcher's turns the highest child score passes upward, on opponent turns the lowest, so each level alternates goals.
when: When two opponents alternate turns in a game tree
why: Each side is assumed to pick its own best option, so the opponent's reply is treated as the worst case for the searcher.

text: Each sense manager run spreads smell to neighboring nodes according to the transmission and distance of the connections between them.
why: Capping spread by the simulated time keeps the smell from outrunning plausible diffusion timing.

text: Each node's smell intensity fades at that node's dissipation rate.
Sound is not stored in nodes, so a sensor perceives it only while the wave passes through its node.
why: Sound is a transient wave that fades to nothing at its minimum limit, so a node holds no lingering value to perceive.

text: Intensity falls evenly as distance grows, and sound is lost once it dips under a character's hearing threshold.
why: Frequency-dependent effects are too subtle to matter for game AI, so all sounds share one falloff.

text: A loud noise may be heard nearby but not across a level or behind soundproof glass, because distance and barriers limit what a character perceives.
A camouflage check compares a unit's camouflage id with the pattern id of its background material, so matching patterns hide it.
Sound carries within the current room up to a radius that depends on its volume.
A looping delay that resets a counter lets a patient player fire again undetected, so alert state decays over time.
when: Stealth alert system with repeated events
why: A timed reset zeroes the shot counter that drives the alert, so only shots fired in quick succession count.

text: A character in green camouflage gets an extra attenuation of 0.1 against foliage but 1.5 against sky, showing camouflage effects depend on background material.
Signal intensity at distance d equals source strength multiplied by the attenuation factor raised to the power d.
Wall avoidance itself runs in O(1), but the ray cast depends on environment complexity and dominates running time.
why: Ray casts against level geometry are expensive and scale with environment complexity, unlike the constant-time steering logic.

text: Halo's AI does not change difficulty in a fixed way. It waits to see how hard the player pushes, then pushes back at a resistance suited to how the player plays.
when: When enemies should respond to the player's style
why: Resistance matched to play style keeps challenge proportional to what the player does

text: Smelly GOB represents each motive as a signal that diffuses through the level from objects that affect it, and characters follow the strongest signal to the source for their most pressing motive.
why: Following a diffusing signal avoids running a pathfinder to compare the cost of each possible source.

text: Fantasy senses reuse existing modalities with altered parameters: aura or magic as modified vision, telepathy as modified hearing, and fear, reputation or charm as modified smell.
why: Changing a modality's parameters yields a different sense built on the same machinery.

text: An expensive test placed in a decision tree can dominate the tree's total runtime, so it should be reached as rarely as possible.
when: When a decision node runs a costly check such as ray-cast visibility.
why: Tree runtime grows with the number of nodes visited, so a slow decision adds cost on every visit.

text: A simple object signal such as 'I can provide food' misleads characters when the object's action needs extra steps they cannot yet perform, such as an oven without raw food.
when: When an object's action requires several preconditions.
why: The object's signal advertises the action without revealing unmet requirements, so characters must still work out what they can do.

text: In several games, tactical line-of-sight checks consumed over 30% of total processor time, which may be unacceptable for fast-reacting characters.
when: Fast-reacting characters using live tactical checks
why: Line-of-sight tests are expensive, especially across many candidates

text: Averaging lightness over a character's body favors spots where the body is dark but the lit head still exposes the character.
when: When rating a hiding spot by sampling light across a character-sized volume.
why: An average would favor spots where the body is dark but a lit head still gives the character away.

text: Testing line of sight from every location to every other location can take many minutes on very large levels and is too slow.
when: On very large levels with exhaustive pairwise visibility checks.

text: Smell passing repeatedly between neighboring nodes can greatly increase the number of calculations needed.
when: When smell is added to the graph-based sense manager.
why: Smells spreading back and forth between nodes need much more stored state, multiplying calculations.

text: Straight-line sensing lets a character behind a thick insulating barrier hear a sound produced near the source, a serious error.
why: Sound transmission is distance-based and ignores level geometry except for line-of-sight tests.

text: Concealment that ignores the background lets a dark figure in a bright area go unseen, so levels must be designed to make this rarely noticeable.
when: When one player character is checked against shadows and hiding effects.
why: Concealment is computed from the player's own lighting and hiding effects, not the surrounding background.

text: Static sound zones become more damaging when enemy AI reacts to sound, since mismatched audio then also misleads enemy behaviour.
when: Enemy AI responds to sound and the environment can change.
why: Enemies act on audio that no longer reflects the actual barriers.

text: Triggering enemy music on distance alone ignores orientation, so it fires for enemies that are facing away from the player.
when: When music is tied to an enemy's distance from the player.
why: Distance ignores orientation and visibility, so music can start for enemies that cannot see the player.

text: 1) Cover noisy surfaces with trigger volumes that each increment a counter. 2) Reset the counter on a repeating one-second delay loop. 3) Alert the guard when the counter reaches two within one second. Scripted hearing only imitates perception and is often simpler than real AI hearing.
when: Faking enemy hearing with a scripted counter instead of real AI hearing.
why: A simple timed counter is often easier to build than full sound-based AI perception.

text: 1) Compute the time to impact. 2) Compare it with the grenade's fuse length. 3) Choose to run away or to catch based on that comparison.
when: Character reacts to a thrown grenade
why: Time left before detonation decides the response

text: Use signals and waits so the team waits for the grenade to explode, then moves while maintaining cover.
when: Sequencing dependent team actions
why: Waits hold the team until the preceding event completes

text: 1) From a location, cast rays at fixed angular intervals. 2) Measure how far each ray travels. 3) Use the average length as the visibility score.
when: Indoor level layouts.
why: works well for indoor layouts

text: 1) If a stored entry is deep enough and its bounds decide against gamma, return it. 2) Else create an unbounded entry. 3) At terminal or maximum depth, set both bounds to the evaluation. 4) Else recurse on moves with negated gamma. 5) A best score below gamma updates the max bound; otherwise the min bound.
why: Stored bounds let the search jump to promising moves, which plain recursive negamax cannot do.

text: 1) After a line-of-sight ray succeeds, cast further rays beyond the character. 2) Record the material each ray hits first. 3) Compute an extra attenuation from those materials and the character's camouflage. 4) Multiply signal strength by it. 5) Pass the signal on only if it stays above the character's threshold.
1) Gather sensors from every node whose smell intensity is above the minimum. 2) Run the usual testing step on those sensors. 3) Send notifications for sensors that pass.
when: each smell iteration

text: 1) Collect sensors in the source node and mark it visited. 2) Move along sound-carrying connections, reducing intensity by each connection's attenuation. 3) Skip visited nodes. 4) Visit nodes in distance order. 5) At each node, gather candidate sensors and stop when intensity falls below the minimum. 6) Test each sensor's threshold and queue passing notifications.
why: Distance order matches time order when the sound's speed is constant.

text: 1) Aggregate sensors within the modality's maximum range. 2) Test each sensor's threshold and any modality-specific checks. 3) Queue passing sensors with delivery time equal to now plus distance times inverse speed. 4) Each frame, deliver queued notifications whose time has passed.
why: Inverse speed lets infinite-speed senses like vision be handled, which an un-inverted speed cannot.

text: 1) Compute a concealment level from shadows, mist and other hiding effects. 2) If it is below a threshold, the AI spots the player.
when: single player character with AI observers
why: With only one player character to track, each enemy can just test whether it is visible.

text: 1) Guess randomly until a hit. 2) Probe neighboring squares in each direction to find the piece's ends.
when: a simple human-like baseline for hidden-piece guessing
why: a common, easy-to-implement comparison strategy

text: Give characters information only through their senses; wanting information does not acquire it, and perception works as an input process, not a search that fails for most requests.
why: Game worlds simulate physics, so a character learns about its surroundings only by sensing them.

text: When teaching, use the character's own context; when observing, use the observed character's context. Observer context creates wrong associations, like learning that eating means not being hungry.
when: Pairing observed actions with context during observational learning.
why: An observer cannot know another's internal state.

text: Match the AI effort spent on a character to how long and how closely the player will watch it.
why: Most players give minor characters little attention, so extra AI pays off only for the rare attentive player.

text: Use tactical waypoints as the location set in indoor levels or in games without tactical analyses.
Do not propagate smell across a connection when either endpoint's intensity sits under the minimum.
Limit smell travel to the simulated time, usually the gap between manager calls, so smell never spreads faster through the graph than through the level.
why: Time-capped spread keeps smell from outrunning how fast a signal would cross the actual level.

text: Update a node only when its stored time lags the current time, so each node changes at most once per iteration.
why: Timestamps stop a node from being updated more than once in a single pass.

text: For AI hearing, let sound pass around corners regardless of its pitch.
why: Pitch-dependent differences in how sound bends are too subtle to model in game AI.

text: In stealth games, let contact or proximity within a small fixed distance alert a character regardless of whether it can see or hear the player.
when: stealth games
why: Touch needs direct contact, so collision detection can notify the character directly.

text: Give every creature a well-defined radius for noticing things, so players can predict which creatures react and when.
when: Designing creature perception in a complex ecosystem.
why: Players need to plan strategy around predictable reactions.

text: Decide whether an enemy's music should start when the enemy cannot see the player, or when the player cannot see the enemy.
why: Music can warn the player of an approaching enemy or of being spotted.

text: Let enemy spawn or movement logic respond to where the player is looking.
why: Enemies that move only when unseen make the player feel watched from beyond their view.

text: For enemy herding to work, foes should arrive in large crowds, strike hard, or take a long time to defeat.
why: Advancing foes take over safe ground, pushing the player where the designer wants.

text: Large-scale pathfinding and perception need scalable implementations, such as pooled planners, hierarchical pathfinding, or instanced geometry.
when: Large worlds with many characters
why: A simple pathfinder that handles a shooter level stalls when a thousand characters plan across a continent-sized world.

text: A shared accurate map never underestimates opponents but feels like cheating and can make AI seem oblivious to hidden threats; predicting hidden forces is fairer but hard to get accurate.
when: fog of war
why: The shared map uses information a human would lack; prediction must infer hidden units.

text: Broadcasting avoids registering interests and allows late designer-driven reactions, but most delivered data is useless and wasteful; narrowcasting is faster but needs explicit interest registration, so choose by event volume.
when: event system design
why: Precise registration of listener interests is hard to make general, so sending everything is simpler.

text: A wider ray fan angle reduces the corner trap but blocks narrow passages; fan angles near π make side-ray hits come too late, so walls are still grazed.
when: When choosing the fan angle for wall avoidance rays
why: Narrow fans let the character enter small gaps; near-π fans detect side collisions too late to react.

text: Character-specific signals require a separate sensory simulation for each character, which is practical for a handful of slow characters but impractical for larger or faster simulations.
when: When deciding between shared and per-character signals.
why: Characters rarely share identical carried objects or actions, so each needs its own simulation.

text: Signal diffusion avoids costly per-option pathfinding when several sources compete, and yields realistic behavior, but it needs modification before a game can rely on it.
when: When several sources compete for a character's attention.
why: Fading signals naturally draw the character toward whichever source is easiest to reach.

text: Radial ray casting suits indoor levels, but outdoors it needs very many rays to cope with hills and valleys.
when: Terrain analysis that casts rays outward from a test location at fixed angles, in an indoor level versus outdoors
why: Outdoor elevation changes are hard to model with rays, so the ray count would have to grow very large.

text: Firm sensory and movement limits trade some believability for playability; realistic sense simulation is usually not appropriate for such games.
when: Choosing how realistic creature senses should be.
why: Emergent herding behavior cannot be predicted until the game is built and tested.

text: Use a limited radius when units have a natural maximum reach; use map flooding when speed matters more than exact accumulation of influence.
why: Computing every unit's influence at every location is O(nm) work, which is huge for all but the smallest levels.

text: Ray-cast vision becomes expensive as many characters look at many targets, eventually requiring dedicated sense code.
when: When many characters each try to see many different targets with line-of-sight checks

text: Playtesters discover unplanned uses of physics objects, such as letting enemies grab explosive barrels, which designers may then adopt as level content.
when: a level contains physics objects and enemies that interact with them
why: Players experiment with the rules and find actions the designers did not script.

text: Movement with variable frame rates requires an explicit elapsed time: a character moving at 1 m/s over a 20 ms frame advances 20 mm.
when: When frame durations vary

text: Spin-induced lift and time-varying wind affect some projectiles in flight; predicting them is often best done by running the simulation itself, possibly at coarse resolution.
when: When projectiles are spinning or wind varies during flight

text: Include action timing when action lengths vary widely or game time is compressed.
when: In games where game time is extremely compressed
why: Decisions can only weigh quick actions against long ones when each action reports how long it takes.

text: The delay between a character's staggered updates can stand in for its reaction time.
when: Staggered update schedules
why: Characters act slowly and do not need full AI every frame, so refreshing only a few per frame costs little.

text: Unfiltered chatbots may encourage harmful behavior or disclose sensitive data.
when: When NPCs converse freely with players through an LLM without safety filtering
why: People can bond deeply with chatbots, which makes any sensitive information they reveal more problematic.

text: 1) Place a trigger and a toggleable ambient sound. 2) In the visual scripting editor, create a Used event on the trigger. 3) Connect Used to a Toggle action. 4) Set the Toggle target to the sound actor. 5) Set Max Trigger Count to 0 and untick Aim to Interact if interaction is hard.
Combining state factors in one machine multiplies counts (n×m) rather than adding them (n+m), so few small factors yield an enormous state space; separate machines need only n+m.
when: a state is built from several factors, or an entity has two mostly independent aspects of behavior
why: each combination of factor values is a separate state; product versus sum of state counts

text: During long planning, such as seconds of route calculation spread across frames, a character appears to stand still and seems unintelligent.
when: When planning takes many frames.
why: Nothing visible happens while the plan is incomplete.

text: A primitive action is a single effect, such as a state change, animation, movement or AI request, that carries out its own work directly.
A plan's cost can be its number of actions, its total duration, or a combined value that includes resources such as magic, money, or ammo.
A planning heuristic estimates the remaining cost from a world model to goal fulfilment; building a good one can be hard, and progress may appear absent.
A planner finds a route from a starting state to a goal, and the actions along that route can be read as a story.
Plan-space search explores candidate plans as a whole, while state-space search builds a plan step by step by adding parts in sequence.
A partial plan is reusable because the shortest route from an intermediate node to the goal is the tail of the shortest route through it.
when: Storing and reusing plans on the same graph.
why: Subpaths of shortest paths are themselves shortest paths.

text: Parallel rewriting builds a new string entirely from the previous string, replacing every symbol at once, while sequential rewriting updates the string as it is read.
why: The two orders can produce very different results, so the order must match the intended model.

text: A partial-order plan orders only the steps that threats require, leaving other orderings open, whereas a total-order plan fixes every ordering.
A planning problem has an initial state and a goal state; a solution is a plan, a sequence of actions, that is sound if executing it from the initial state reaches the goal.
Domain knowledge for a planner is a library of operators, each with preconditions and effects.

A partial order gives precedence relations between some pairs of items but not all. It must be transitive, asymmetric and irreflexive, which together ensure the relation's directed graph contains no loops.
Continuous planning is complex, hard to debug (especially node placement), and not fast relative to other pathfinders, even when working correctly.
Even depth two changes character behavior noticeably, while deeper plans add diminishing gains in believability.
The problem interface must supply a random start state, list the available actions for a state, and apply an action to return a reward and a new state.
Strong human players often plan 20 to 30 opening moves in advance.
Computers have fully solved checkers and four-in-a-row, while chess and Go remain unsolved, so their AIs rely on heuristics.
Conditional effects apply only when their stated condition holds, so one action can yield different outcomes in different states.
STRIPS and ADL are widely used formal languages for describing states, actions, and goals with classical planners.
The plan a planner selects depends on the agent's capabilities, the available facilities, its preferences, and its current circumstances.
Planning algorithms aim to find plans that maximise goals under given conditions, constraints, and preferences.
Storing partner arrays for both sides is redundant but speeds up lookups.
Partial orders occur in word definitions in a glossary, subtasks in a project, prerequisite courses in a curriculum, and procedure calls in a program.
For large numbers of simple agents, simple blending may suffice; reserve pipelines or planning for key agents.
when: Simulating a large number of characters

text: Choose the formal planning language so that it expresses the problem domain well, since the choice shapes what the planner can represent.
From a set of items, handle first the one with the fewest valid options, such as a target that only one weapon can hurt.
when: Picking which enemy to attack when only a rare weapon can penetrate one of them
why: it is the most likely to be left with no valid option

text: Fixed patrol routes are simple but can be fooled by moved objects, and free wandering can look aimless and get stuck; runtime routes suit goals unknown in advance.
when: Choosing how characters move through a level
why: Fixed routes cannot adapt to changes, and unconstrained wandering lacks purpose

text: A continuous planner stores each connection's driving action on the connection, so the vehicle executes it without recalculating.
when: When a pathfinder returns a final path that a driving AI must execute
why: The driving sequence was already computed during pathfinding, so recalculating it would be redundant.

text: Interactive evolution searches for the optimum in the human's preference space, so the target exists only in the user's judgment.
when: Evolving artifacts where a human user selects which individuals reproduce

text: Swapping input and output file roles only requires resetting file positions, since no data is copied.
when: In each pass of a balanced merge over files
why: Access goes through riders, which can be repositioned to point at different files.

text: Hundreds of visits per state may be needed before Q-values settle in practical Q-learning runs.
when: practical Q-learning runs
why: Q-learning is only proven to converge in the limit, so practical runs must try each action repeatedly at each state.

text: Direct-access frequency scheduling takes O(f·p) time, where f is the number of distinct frequencies and p the behaviours per phase, and O(f·F·p) storage, where F is the average frequency.
when: Fixed set of frequencies known in advance.
why: Time falls to O(m) when phase slots are full, but memory grows with frequencies used.

text: With text length N and pattern length M, feasible start positions run from 0 to N minus M, inclusive.
Forward chaining starts from the current database and repeatedly fires rules that change it, directly or through character actions; it is the form used in game rule systems.
when: Building rule-based game logic
why: Starting from known data and applying rules until no more change is a natural fit for game state updates.

text: In plan-space search, the root is the problem, internal nodes are partial plans with flaws, and leaves are complete plans or partial plans that cannot be refined further.
Searching without a depth limit lets an unreachable goal run forever while memory keeps growing.
when: Action planning where a goal may be unreachable and actions are always available, unlike pathfinding
why: The planner cannot tell an unreachable goal apart without trying every possible combination of actions.

text: Without failure feedback from movement, a high-level target that movement cannot reach leads to a stalemate in decision making.
when: When a high-level AI picks a location that the movement algorithms cannot reach

text: Wide and deep game trees make minimax very slow, because the number of positions grows exponentially with search depth.
when: When the game tree is very deep
why: motivates later optimizations

text: A refined result can reveal something missed, forcing a change of direction, which must be handled gracefully.
when: When an incremental plan is refined after the agent has already started acting
why: Early rough solutions are usually close enough that a late correction is seldom disruptive.

text: Plan-space search is computationally expensive, so it is uncommon in large practical applications.
why: Its search space grows exponentially with plan length, which makes it costly to run.

text: 1) Quantize start and goal positions to graph nodes. 2) If the start and goal nodes differ, run A* between them. 3) Return the first node of the resulting path as the sub-goal.
when: When a decomposer must route a character across a navigation graph
why: Converts a distant goal into a nearby sub-goal the actuator can steer toward

text: 1) Add a lane-change node per adjacent empty lane, costed at current speed. 2) Add a boundary node trailing the nearest car ahead, matching its speed; skip if a crash is unavoidable. 3) Add safe opportunity nodes just past each adjacent-lane car, assuming collision avoidance. 4) Add unsafe opportunity nodes at those same spots, assuming top speed without avoidance.
when: when expanding a node in a continuous traffic graph
why: Unsafe nodes matter because braking for a car ahead is pointless if the plan is to swerve.

text: 1) Use the current position and time as a new start node. 2) Repeat successor generation using traffic predicted for each time.
when: each planning call
why: A time-stamped start node lets the planner forecast where traffic will be at each future step.

text: 1) Give each available research advance a numeric score. 2) Pick the highest-scoring advance.

1) Parse the plan for NPCs. 2) Instantiate each NPC where it first takes part in an event. 3) Let each NPC adapt its behaviour at run time, since world geometry and prior events are unknown in advance.
when: Populating a world from a story plan
why: Events extend over time, so NPCs must elaborate them across whichever earlier events and terrain occur.

text: 1) Create a column holding MONTH() of each row's due date. 2) Use COUNTIF() to count cells in that column matching MONTH(TODAY()).
when: Counting tasks due in the current month

text: 1) Start with a root node describing the problem. 2) Select a non-terminal node by heuristic value. 3) Select a flaw in it. 4) If no flaw remains, return the node as the solution. 5) Otherwise repair the flaw and repeat.
when: Searching plan space with POP
why: Internal nodes are partial plans with flaws, so search refines them by fixing flaws until none remain.

text: Repair an open precondition either by linking it to an existing step that establishes it, or by adding a new step whose effects imply it.
when: A precondition no earlier step establishes

text: Update a node's values only when the newly calculated cost-so-far is lower than its stored value.
when: When the search reaches a node already in the open or closed set.
why: Only cost-so-far is a reliable measure, unlike estimates that rely on heuristics.

text: Use continuous planning only for small planning sections, since in practice it covered about 100 yards of route.
why: Its cost and complexity grow quickly with route length.

text: To return a whole plan rather than only its first action, the best-result record must store the full action sequence.
Consider planning when actions share resources or when one action unlocks another.
Plain A* on huge graphs returns more detail than often needed. Coarse routes planned first and refined later avoid wasted work on distant irrelevant detail.
when: Long-distance travel across a very large environment, such as between cities in an MMOG.
why: Fine detail about distant obstacles is irrelevant to the early route but still costs time and memory.

text: Use open goal pathfinding when goals are close together, not when they are far apart.
when: Choosing between open goal search and a single chosen goal
why: Close goals make the heuristic's guess about the chosen goal rarely badly wrong

text: Use final-state statistics only when the chain has a final state, since a chain that bounces indefinitely has none to measure.
when: When the process has a final state and we want the time needed to reach it.

text: Rerunning full search on each new observation may leave no plan finishing before the next begins when the level changes constantly; plain replanning suffices only when it changes occasionally.
when: When the game level changes constantly and triggers repeated replanning.
why: The pathfinder restarts before finishing each plan, so it never completes one.

text: Removing an old goal during a rewrite keeps the data simple, while keeping it lets the AI resume that goal later.
when: A rewrite replaces an active goal that may be needed again

text: Storing complete plans is cheap and ready to use for exact repeats, but partial plans are more often reusable across varied tasks.
when: Deciding what search results to cache.
why: Identical tasks rarely recur, while route sections recur more often.

text: Direct-access frequency scheduling is a good fit for few shared frequencies, but with many frequencies and phases memory use grows and speedup shrinks, so a hierarchical scheduler is preferred.
when: Many distinct frequencies and phases.
why: Sparse phase slots waste memory on empty arrays.

text: Neural-network creature brains produced complex behavior that often looked stupid to players, so technical sophistication does not guarantee believable behavior.
when: Using learning-based brains for game characters
why: Complex learned behavior can be hard to read as intelligent

text: Learners can learn the wrong thing; the capacity for dramatic behavior change also implies the capacity for dramatically poor behavior.
when: Learning is unconstrained.
why: Learning optimizes whatever signal it receives, including bad outcomes.

text: Players often accept AI behavior they do not understand if it matches their expectations, and their mental model of AI is shaped by what they expect in early playtests.
when: Players observe AI actions
why: Matching expectations makes behavior seem intelligent even when it is random.

text: Players imitate other players' strategies in multiplayer and imitate NPCs' actions in single-player, often without realizing it.
when: Players observe other agents performing actions.
why: Learning by imitation is a basic human tendency.

text: Intra-behavior learning tunes a small, bounded part of a character's existing behavior without changing its overall mode of action, and it is easy to control and test.
when: One bounded aspect of a behavior needs tuning and can be checked easily.

text: An active research direction uses learned models of player behavior to control a character during network lag.
Action recognition for the player can be rule-based, and the squad strategy layer can be a state machine or decision tree.
Learned decision making is probabilistic, so every possible action keeps some chance of being chosen, however small.
Learning how to act entirely from scratch is currently considered almost pure fantasy in game AI.
The main obstacles to using learning in games are reproducibility and quality control rather than technical complexity.
Reinforcement learning can learn a player's play style and imitate it, which is one option for a dynamic demo mode.
An assistive module must estimate the player's strategy, which is very difficult to infer from observation, and few games have attempted it.
Players can take as long as they like on a turn, so turn-based AI still needs timing control when optimizing many simultaneous decisions.
Some learning combinations leave a creature largely incapable of sensible behavior, a state called learned impotence.
when: Creatures trained by player feedback with neural networks.
why: This outcome seems an inevitable consequence of the AI approach.

text: Game characters can learn behavior from player rewards and punishments, shaping how they respond over time.
Designers can tag generated patterns as liked or unliked for each beat to steer later generation.
Against fixed-pattern opponents, an AI that uses the observed history of past plays and scores can adapt and beat each fixed strategy.
when: opponents follow repeatable patterns

text: Keeping players in flow is comparable to keeping learners in their zone of proximal development, and machine learning can adjust difficulty to each learner's performance.
when: When designing adaptive learning or difficulty for individual players.
why: Both need challenge matched to current skill.

text: A character whose estimated damage rate is rising expects actions to cost more health and acts defensively; one doing well grows bolder.
when: Goal rates adapt to recent events
why: Recent changes weigh more than older ones

text: An AI director that adjusts pacing and difficulty to player behavior and performance can keep a game engaging.
Enemies that learn from player interactions can adjust their behavior and develop grudges, making opponents feel personal and persistent.
An AI director that watches player performance and adjusts enemy and resource placement keeps a handmade level varied across play sessions.
when: Handmade levels that must feel different each session
why: Fixed layouts stay the same, so changing enemy and resource placement alters each run.

text: Pairing generation with player models lets content be tailored to each player's enjoyment, learning, or engagement, using models of how that player responds to game elements.
why: A model learned from measured responses to individual elements guides which content to generate for each player.

text: Encounter selection is random or constrained by mood variables, so a volcano level favours fire creatures and a crypt favours undead.
when: populating themed dungeons from an encounter database
why: Mood constraints keep encounters consistent with the setting.

text: User selections reweight a multi-dimensional aesthetic fitness: patterns in chosen items are reinforced and patterns in unchosen items are reduced.
Intra-behavior learning only tunes details of the existing mode of action, so it cannot switch to a better strategy; a run-and-jump character never discovers stairs to reach a high ledge.
when: A better alternative strategy exists outside the current behavior, or a fundamentally different approach is needed.
why: Learning is confined to tuning within the existing behavior's mode of action, so it cannot reveal a different one.

text: Multi-tier AI handles the player poorly: the player's choices can silently undermine higher-layer decisions, making teammates look poor.
when: When a player-controlled character is part of a squad driven by multi-tier AI
why: Teammates act on their guess of the player's wishes rather than the higher layer's intent, and cannot read the player perfectly.

text: A learned state can depend on a unique history, so a bug may appear only after particular learning and be hard to reproduce or verify as fixed.
when: Learning has run over varied play sessions.
why: Each learner's accumulated state differs, so the same bug may not recur on a fresh run.

text: Multiple modular learners can coexist but may interact harmfully, such as targeting that keeps hitting cover another learner selected, so they need checking together.
when: Running several learners in one game.
why: Each learner's output affects the inputs or conditions of the others.

text: Chasing realistic character minds in game AI can erase the planning that makes the mechanics meaningful.
when: When the player must plan an approach around enemy behaviour
why: Smarter AI is often unpredictable, while simple behaviours can be predicted and planned around.

text: 1) Give each evolved item (e.g., weapon) a fitness equal to how often the player uses it, a cheap proxy for preference. 2) Evolve new items, favouring high-fitness items as parents. 3) Spawn the new items into play for the player to pick up. 4) Repeat during play so items become personalised to that player.
when: game items or weapons that should adapt to each player, or evolving content from player behaviour data
why: Usage frequency is a cheap proxy for player preference.

text: 1) Generate an output from the input pattern. 2) Run backpropagation against the desired output.
1) Implement the atomic behaviors by hand. 2) Learn only which behavior to choose among a fixed set, possibly parameterized.
why: Learning everything is uneconomical, and basic movement, decision tools and high-level choices are faster to build directly.

text: 1) Search the action tree depth-first. 2) Backtrack when an action sequence fails to finish the level. 3) Use action priorities and domain rules to prune branches.

1) Evolve a neural network controller to drive like a specific player. 2) Score each candidate level by letting that controller play it in place of the player. 3) Keep candidates whose performance statistics fit that player.
when: When content should suit one individual player.
why: An imitation agent stands in for the player, so its performance measures how well the content fits that player.

text: 1) Build a player experience model from a gameplay feature dataset using a chosen machine learning or data-mining technique. 2) Use the model to recognise a new player's playing style. 3) Adjust content when the player's experience changes.
1) Record the player's style while a level is played. 2) Score each candidate design by fitness from that behaviour and the design's content features. 3) Show the best individual as the next level.
when: When personalisation runs online while the level is being played
why: Playing style is assumed to persist across consecutive sessions, so earlier play predicts how the player will handle the next level.

text: RTS players sit atop the AI hierarchy, giving units explicit orders with no character; place no higher layer above them so their team decisions take precedence moment to moment.
when: designing unit control in strategy games
why: Inferring player intent is very difficult, so explicit orders avoid guessing what the player wants.

text: Learn lines that recur across many thousands of games by averaging their results and win likelihood, and record those values in the book.
when: a program can play thousands of games
why: Expert database scores may not suit a computer's own characteristics, such as horizon effects, so its own recorded results can serve it better.

text: Let the player choose the destination while the AI chooses the formation that fits the terrain.
when: When squad formations should adapt to the walls and open ground around them
why: the player directs intent while the AI handles positioning

text: Give the learning mechanism to only a small number of characters in the game.
when: Designing player-taught creature games.

text: Let players choose starting points or equipment rather than generating them randomly, as a direct lever for balancing generated content against player agency.
when: designing procedural content
why: Choice gives players agency that random generation removes.

text: A polling station is a hub all polling requests pass through, a shared cache for costly checks and relay from AI to game level, compromising between polling and events.
Polling means an AI character directly queries the game state whenever it needs to know something, getting the answer immediately.
Most polls return nothing useful: a siren is off more often than on, and a character rarely collides with more than one other per frame.
No single communication approach is fastest in every case; the better choice between polling and events depends on the application and is hard to predict in advance.
Prefer polling over event passing for a single occasional check, such as one object checking whether a siren is sounding.
when: a single occasional check is needed
why: Querying the state directly is quick and needs no extra machinery, and the answer arrives exactly when it is needed.

text: Use polling for checks needed only occasionally, such as while in a particular state, since sending state as events every frame is wasteful.
when: checks are needed only occasionally
why: polling is often faster for such checks

text: Avoid polling when each agent repeats the same expensive check; an event system could compute it once.
when: many characters need the same information every frame
why: Pairwise checks for 100 characters need 10,000 calculations, so repeated per-character cost multiplies quickly.

text: A counter that is never reset and counts all events can trigger a late-game consequence at a fixed threshold.
when: Tracking cumulative player actions

text: The load-balancing cost figures exclude scheduler overhead, which holds only when the scheduled work dominates the cost.
Route all polling requests through one station so they are easy to monitor and debug.
when: When polling is the best approach but each check is time consuming
why: Requests routed through one shared point can be monitored and debugged, and a shared cache serves many characters at once.

text: Polling is fast and needs no extra infrastructure, but scales poorly as characters and checks grow; event passing needs extra code and is overkill for simple situations.
when: As the number of characters and checks to monitor grows
why: Most checks return negative results, so most processing time goes to checks that find nothing.

text: Polling returns information exactly when it is needed, while event passing adds delay and extra message handling.
when: When each character's check cannot be shared between characters
why: Events are stored until the character reaches the relevant code, adding processing and delay that direct polling avoids.

text: A lead history records, at each turn, the difference between the estimated strengths of the eventual winner's and loser's positions.
Many game AI behaviors depend on predicting how other objects will move under physics, not only on the character's own motion, such as intercepting a ball or leading a teammate's throw.
Earth's gravity is about 9.81 m/s² downward, but games often use roughly double that, since true gravity can make projectiles look floaty.
when: When tuning projectile gravity for a game
why: Stronger gravity makes shots read as more natural in play

text: Gravity keeps most characters on the ground, so their movement is effectively two-dimensional and most classic movement algorithms are defined only in two dimensions.
Players often face harder physics than AI cars, though many games now give AI cars the same task as the player.
Sports AI often must predict a fast-moving ball's motion, either to intercept it or to work out the effect of a strike.
Projectile prediction methods, including firing solutions used for firearms, carry over directly to predicting ball motion in sports games.
Evade predicted positions at closest-approach time so the correction starts immediately.
when: When the predicted closest approach lies in the future

text: N-gram prediction can be applied beyond combat, for example to predict where players will be, which weapons they will use, and how they will attack.
Model all sounds alike in AI hearing, because pitch differences in propagation are too subtle to matter for character behavior.
when: designing AI hearing
why: Pitch-dependent propagation differences are too subtle to be worth representing in a game's AI.

text: Weapons that home in need only approximate targeting, not a full firing solution.
when: Racing AI that fires homing weapons
why: The weapon steers itself toward its target.

text: Confidence in a follow-on rises as its observations accumulate and other follow-ons stay rare; a near-even split of outcomes gives almost none.
when: counting follow-on outcomes for a window
why: Random variation easily explains small or evenly split samples.

text: A collision is predicted when the separation at closest approach is less than the sum of the two radii.
when: When characters are assumed to keep their current velocities.
why: Cone-based avoidance misses collisions where neither character sees the other before impact.

text: Under gravity alone, a projectile's position at time t equals the firing point plus the firing direction times muzzle speed times t, plus half of gravity times t squared.
when: When predicting projectile position without air resistance
why: The parabolic arc follows directly from constant gravitational acceleration

text: Aiming along a straight line at a projectile affected by gravity makes shots fall short, landing at the target's feet.
when: When projectiles follow physics-simulated trajectories rather than straight lines.
why: A straight line only approximates a fast projectile's path over small distances.

text: Near a ledge, a projectile can miss the character's height entirely and fall into the gap behind it.
when: Projectile impact near ledges or walkways
why: The simple height test does not check whether the impact is valid

text: Predictive AI can draw wrong conclusions from past data, so it needs human supervision before automating decisions that affect people.
when: When automating decisions that may harm individuals.
why: It finds patterns in past data, which can lead it to wrong conclusions.

text: To pursue a target assumed to keep its velocity, aim ahead to cut it off. 1) Compute prediction time as distance divided by current speed, using a maximum time if speed is too small. 2) Cap the prediction time at a maximum. 3) Set a surrogate target at the target position plus its velocity times prediction time. 4) Seek that surrogate.
when: Chasing a target with steady motion, or a moving target that keeps roughly its current velocity
why: Aiming at the predicted position avoids seeking the target's stale location

text: 1) Treat firing point, target, muzzle speed and gravity as known. 2) Add the normalized-direction constraint to get four equations in four unknowns. 3) Eliminate the direction to get a quartic in time with no odd powers. 4) Solve as a quadratic in time squared, take square roots, and discard negative times.
when: muzzle speed is known and constant and drag is negligible
why: Eliminating direction yields a closed-form solution in constant time and memory.

text: 1) Solve the vertical position equation for the time the projectile reaches the target height. 2) Use the larger time value; if it is negative, the projectile will not return. 3) Substitute that time into the full position equation to get the horizontal impact point.
when: Predicting where a projectile lands on a known height
why: The descending crossing determines the landing point

text: 1) Compute the horizontal impact point. 2) Use its terrain height as the new target height. 3) Recompute until the horizontal values stabilize.
when: Projectile lands on rapidly changing terrain
why: Terrain height at the impact point changes the solution

text: 1) Predict the character's position a short time ahead from its velocity. 2) Find the nearest path point to that predicted position. 3) Offset forward from it to get the target.
when: Path has complex sudden turns.
why: Prediction smooths following on sharp direction changes.

text: Prefer the lower arc when hitting a target, because it leaves the enemy less reaction time and avoids ceilings and obstacles; use the higher arc to fire over walls.
when: two valid firing arcs exist
why: The lower arc is faster to reach the target and clears fewer obstacles; the higher arc clears walls.

text: Reduce a prediction-based AI's competence so the player retains a fair chance of winning.
when: tuning a prediction-based combat AI
why: Full competence makes the AI effectively unbeatable.

text: Run the physics when ball dynamics are complex and central, as in pool or golf; predict the trajectory directly when dynamics are simpler, as in baseball or soccer.
when: When the ball's behaviour is intricate and central to gameplay.

text: Pursuers heading to an interception point should use tactical pathfinding that avoids crossing the player's path.
when: when intercepting a moving player
why: the interception is not given away

text: Aim assistance should act indirectly rather than pulling the crosshair straight onto the target, because direct snapping feels obvious and breaks the illusion of player skill.
when: Implementing aim assist for thumbstick shooters
why: Overt snapping is noticed, while indirect adjustments are accepted as the player's own aim.

text: Pure homing is easy for players to predict, while pure randomness feels dull; blending the two gives better gameplay.
why: Each extreme alone gives predictable movement or movement with no direction toward the player.

text: Proper confidence weighs the chance that a smaller window captured the real pattern against the chance that a larger window was fooled by random variation.
Tracked vehicles accelerate much slower than cars and turn at any speed, rapidly at rest; decision arcs touch at zero speed, so they can brake to nothing and turn sharply.
when: Tracked vehicle movement and steering decisions
why: Tracks allow turning without forward motion, removing the car's minimum-speed constraint.

text: A racing line is usually stored as a spline, a mathematical curve that can also carry data such as speed.
A race objective requires reaching a physical or conceptual goal before other players do.
A tank can turn in place, and a human can accelerate in any direction, with different top speeds forward, sideways and backward.
when: Modeling tank or human movement.

text: Driving game AI centers on movement tasks; goal seeking, tactical reasoning and route finding may appear but are not core.
Extreme sports racing games use the same racing-line AI as driving games at their core, with a tricks sub-game layered on top.
A designer defines the racing line, and a car following it reaches optimal speed along the track.
Many background cars in open-world games use the spline racing-line approach.
In a hybrid water-and-air racing game, one playtested layout used about 60% underwater, 20% airborne, and 20% near-surface level space.
when: when splitting level space across environments

text: Estimate travel time as proportional to straight-line distance, or compute it with pathfinding.
when: When the journey to an action's location is needed.
why: Action duration does not include getting to the location, so a separate figure is required.

text: Judge driving AI mainly by how well it drives the car, since players evaluate it that way.
when: Testing or tuning driving AI
why: Players judge driving AI by driving quality.

text: A racing AI vehicle can slow down to let an enemy overtake it, then target that enemy.
when: Racing AI with weapons
why: So it can then target that enemy.

text: When game time is compressed, travel time can outweigh the action itself, so a long walk before a short action dominates the choice.
when: Compressed game time
why: Walking across a level can take longer than the action it leads to, so journey time dominates.

text: Recent racing AI applies control inputs to the physics simulation, so cars behave realistically rather than being moved along a path.
why: The car follows the racing line by driving, rather than having the line act as a rail.

text: In race games the board path is the route players travel, so the layout directly defines which moves are available.
Races have no fixed time limit; players pressure each other to go faster, so relative competition sets the pace.
when: When players are judged by beating each other rather than a clock.

text: Races can be decided by dexterity, by chance, or by a mix of strategy and chance, depending on the design.
Continuous road planning nodes combine lane, distance along the section and time, so each node's outgoing costs are fixed and A* works without tracking the path taken.
when: Planning car or vehicle movement on roads with timing.
why: Including time makes connection costs independent of the route that reached the node.

text: Racing AI architecture has four parts: a state machine selecting the driving line, a Markov or fuzzy state machine generating steering, capability-sensitive steering, and marked-up track data.
when: Racing games
why: The crucial tasks centre on movement, and players judge the AI by how it drives.

text: Spline-following cars cannot easily overtake, will not avoid crashes ahead, tend to drive into a crashed car in a stream, and are not deflected when hit by the player.
when: When computer cars simply drive a predefined spline path.
why: Speed-tagged curves supply position and speed directly, leaving no reaction to other cars.

text: 1) Wait for a long straight. 2) Pull out to pass the slower car.
when: Overtaking slower cars
why: Mirrors a common real-world overtaking ploy used with medium and low-powered cars.

text: Record which specific data items a rule triggered on, and suspend it until those items change.
when: When a rule's trigger data stays stable while other database content changes every frame.
why: Clearing suspension on any database change lets the same situation recur.

text: When a spline-following car is knocked out of position, engage simple steering that returns it to the line.
why: Otherwise the car keeps chasing an unreachable line, overshoots the next corner and ends in the gravel.

text: Give each race a clearly distinct role, such as sneaky, micromanagement, heavy ground, versatile, or magic, so that races can be contrasted in competitive play.
when: designing playable races for multiplayer
why: Distinct roles let players compare and fight races meaningfully on ranked or online play.

text: A random branch chosen fresh every frame makes a character flicker between options, such as standing still and patrolling.
when: When a random choice is evaluated in a per-frame decision tree.
why: Each frame draws a new random result, so consecutive frames disagree.

text: randomBinomial returns a value between minus one and one that is most likely near zero, built as the difference of two uniform random numbers from zero to one.
when: Generating small random turn values
why: Differencing two uniforms concentrates values near zero

text: Nu is the chance per iteration that the learner jumps to a random state instead of continuing from the state its last action reached.
A decision tree can replace some true-or-false tests with random or timed choices, making its behavior vary between runs.
Random outcomes such as dice rolls are private information to every entity until they are revealed.
A random number generator is not an AI technique itself, but applied judiciously it produces apparent intelligence in many situations.
When choosing among many behaviors requires complicated weighing, pick one at random using chosen probabilities; players often do not notice the difference.
why: Players may not notice the difference, so a random pick is good enough.

text: Vary the timeout, for example with a random stop time or by switching behavior when the timeout occurs, so an agent does not stand still several times in a row.
when: Using timed random decisions

text: When enemy behavior is random, no fixed pattern reliably works, so play rewards quick reactions over memorization.
when: enemy behavior includes randomness
why: Players cannot memorize a sequence that reliably beats enemies whose moves vary, so the challenge becomes responding quickly as things happen.

text: Choosing a fully random direction each frame gives jerky linear motion, and randomly changing orientation directly gives twitchy rotation.
when: Simple random roaming
why: The random value drives movement or heading directly, with no intermediate layer to smooth how it changes, so each new value shows up as a jolt.

text: Predator-prey chases can oscillate: the prey stop when out of range, the predator closes in after a delay, and the prey resume moving, repeating the cycle.
when: Groups of different creatures that each trigger behavior changes in another group, where individual hysteresis is not enough.
why: delayed responses create a repeating loop

text: Homing enemies without randomness are easy to predict, and enemies with randomness but no direction are just noise.
why: Each enemy picks the player-directed route with its own likelihood, and otherwise picks a random route.

text: 1) Check every rule and collect all triggered rules. 2) Pick one of them at random and fire it.
when: When more than one rule's conditions are triggered at the same time.

text: 1) Choose an available action at random. 2) Remember the object used. 3) Exclude remembered objects from later choices.
when: Agents choosing among repeatable actions

text: Keep each random component change below the square root of 3 to avoid producing a zero vector, and keep the random rate below about 0.577.
when: Perturbing a 3D wander target
why: Overly large changes can make the vector zero, which breaks normalization.

text: Random arbitration cannot stop at the first match, so it must search all rules and is less efficient than first-match methods.
why: It must collect a full list of triggered rules, while earlier schemes stop at the first triggered one.

text: The common exploration policy is mostly greedy, picking the highest-Q action for the current state, with occasional random actions controlled by a parameter.
when: Q-learning action selection.

text: In a first-order Markov process, tomorrow's state depends solely on today's, and repeated use of a transition matrix forms a Markov chain of probabilities.
Rho sets how often the learner tries a random action instead of the best known one; zero means pure exploitation and one means pure exploration.
An experience tuple of start state, action, reinforcement and resulting state is the unit of Q-learning.
Reinforcement learning lets a game character improve its action choices from experience instead of hand-written rules.
A neural network's architecture, or topology, is the pattern of connections between its simple neurons, each of which runs the same basic algorithm.
The exploration policy is not part of Q-learning itself. Q-learning is off-policy, so it can pair with different exploration strategies, each with its own strengths and weaknesses.
Learning AI promises adaptive opponents, believable characters and less hand-written AI, but reinforcement learning has seen little game use and its practical payoff lags its hype.
why: Learning is hard to deliver in practice despite considerable effort.

text: Describing games in a common formal rule language lets general game-playing agents play unseen games, including generated ones, and lets competitions test agents on them.
Q-values converge only when the problem and rewards stay stable; random game events in rewards keep shifting them, and once converged further iterations change nothing.
when: Q-learning on a fixed problem with consistent rewards; reward signals include random game events.
why: Changing rewards keep shifting the values.

text: A recency-weighted average of goal rates gives simple adaptive learning with very little implementation effort.
Several developers have proposed actor-critic for games, yet its practical benefit over simpler methods is often judged marginal.
Backpropagation is the learning rule for multi-layer perceptrons trained on labelled examples.
Following rising Q-values is a form of hill climbing, which works reliably only when the problem has a single hill (unimodal).
when: Reinforcement learning value landscapes.

text: Hash tables store only action combinations that actually occur, and the implementation works for any window size and number of actions.
Q-learning convergence is proven only in the limit of infinitely many iterations, so practical runs depend on tuning rather than guarantees.
Keeping part of the old Q-value preserves previously learned information instead of overwriting it with each new outcome.

Applications include tactic selection, bootstrapping simple character AI, limited movement control, multiplayer social interaction, timing actions such as jumping or firing, board position evaluation, and strategy setting in turn-based games.
The global optimum is usually unknown, and a good parameter set found by search cannot be recognised as the best possible.
Temporal Difference methods handle random state transitions less well than Q-learning, which tolerates much greater randomness in outcomes.
The temporal difference update rule closely resembles Q-learning's, and its tuning parameters respond to adjustment in much the same way.
Temporal Difference style learning has produced strong game play, including a backgammon program that reached international-level play.
Reinforcement learning has produced game-playing systems that defeated world champions in complex strategy games.
Few developers have reported successfully combining neural networks with Q-learning in games, though the success of TD-Gammon suggests the complexity can be managed.
Use state machines to forbid actions outright, such as firing without ammo, since learners only make them unlikely; use learning to choose among permitted options.
when: Enforcing rules that must never be broken.
why: Learned choices are probabilistic and cannot reliably guarantee a prohibition.

text: Keep a single solution with a single reward, and add extra rewards only when learning is too slow or gives poor results.
when: Designing reinforcement learning rewards for a game.
why: Extra rewards can speed learning but add risk of unintended behavior.

text: Reinforcement learning suits offline learning problems with many interacting components, such as groups of characters or order-dependent action sequences.
when: Problems with many different interacting components, such as coordinating a group of characters.
why: Its strength in handling uncertainty means the states fed to it can be simplified and need not capture everything.

text: Train against a simple scripted opponent model in a simulation without rendering, which runs far faster than playing the full game.
when: early training of a learning agent
why: Rendering costs time that learning does not need.

text: For online learning, learn broad general rules first, even if they are often wrong, and add specifics as data accumulates.
when: learning online during play
why: Broad rules that look sensible can be deployed quickly, while nuance takes much longer to learn.

text: Before enough game statistics exist, score an opening line by search instead of relying on learned results.
when: early in learning
why: Opening lines only recur often across many thousands of games, so learned scores take time to accumulate.

text: Bots slightly better than players can serve as useful training tools.
With a single solving action given a large reward and all others zero, rising Q-values form a trail leading to that action after enough iterations.
when: Reinforcement learning with one goal solution.
why: Values propagate backward from the reward through repeated updates.

text: Q-learning memory and training effort grow rapidly with the number of states and actions, so state must be grouped and discretised aggressively.
why: Memory needs are highly sensitive to the number of states and actions, and raw game state can be effectively unbounded.

text: A penalty tied to a terminal event teaches the learner which situations are dangerous, even when the cause, such as the enemy's position, is not in the state.
when: the state omits some factor that drives the bad outcome
