why: The learner still associates the states that lead to the penalty with lower value.

text: Negative outcomes produce output error in proportion to their severity, so a full team wipe yields far larger error than a couple of hits.
when: When it is hard to say what the right action would have been but easy to say the chosen action was wrong.
why: The error is computed from how badly the AI was punished, rather than from a worked-out correct answer.

text: Reinforcement learning trains agents with rewards and punishments, applying operant conditioning principles from behavioral psychology.
A neural network can replace the Q-value table, which lowers memory limits and lets learned values generalise across similar situations.
when: State or action space is too large to store in a table.
why: The network estimates values for unseen situations from similar ones.

text: A weight's new value equals its old value plus the gain times the receiving neuron's error times the sending neuron's state.
why: A neuron that feeds an erroneous neuron shares responsibility for that error, so its weight shifts in proportion to its contribution.

text: A starting gamma of 0.75 is suggested; with it, a reward of 1 adds about 0.05 to an action ten steps earlier in the chain.
when: Initial setting for Q-learning discount rate.
why: It balances speed and sequence length: higher values favor longer action sequences but learn more slowly, while lower values stabilize faster but favor short sequences.

text: Around 5,000,000 iterations and about 10 MB of memory give workable results in a few minutes at the practical scale.
when: at roughly 100,000 states with 10 actions each
why: Guaranteed convergence may need many hundreds of visits per state, so a practical run settles for a rougher but usable result.

text: Updated Q-value equals (1 minus learning rate) times the old value, plus learning rate times (reward plus discount rate times the highest Q-value among actions available in the next state).
why: It mixes the observed reward with how good the next state looks, so each value reflects both immediate and later outcomes.

text: Reinforcement is commonly kept between minus one and one, with zero used when there is no clear signal.
when: When feedback gives no clear indication of how good an action was.

text: Actor-critic keeps two structures: a critic that learns values from reward, and an actor that holds the action policy.
why: The actor's policy gets its training feedback from the critic's signal, which is in turn driven by rewards.

text: Q-learning code is built on two interfaces: a problem interface that supplies states, actions and outcomes, and a value store that holds Q-values.
why: The learning loop must query the current state, the legal actions, and each action's outcome, while values are indexed by state and action.

text: Reinforcement learning has three parts: an exploration strategy that tries actions, a reward function that scores them, and an update rule connecting both.
why: An action's quality is often unclear when it is chosen and feedback comes rarely, so the learning rule must carry credit back to earlier actions.

text: A multi-layer perceptron arranges neurons in layers, with each neuron connected to every neuron in the layers immediately before and after it.
A discount rate above one makes Q-values grow without bound, so the algorithm never converges to a best solution.
when: Setting the discount rate in Q-learning.
why: Values compound each update instead of converging.

text: Toy problems converge in a few thousand iterations; real games with many states need far more, so learned values are usually used before learning settles.
when: Deploying Q-learning in a game.
why: Real problems need far more iterations than practical.

text: With a hash table, a state whose visited actions all have negative Q-values can make the best-action lookup pick a visited negative action over an unvisited action whose implicit value is zero.
when: hash table Q-value storage
why: Missing entries read as zero, so they can outrank negative values.

text: Spreading feedback across many actions can reinforce actions the player did not mean to judge.
A neural network does not return the same value it was given, so Q-values fluctuate during learning even when they are not being updated, and Q-learning may not reach a sensible result.
when: Q-values are stored in a neural network.
why: Weight changes from other updates shift outputs for all inputs.

text: Adopting a neural net for storage makes the issue more multi-modal, and such issues often yield suboptimal behavior.
when: Q-learning stores its values in a neural net.
why: Multi-modal problems tend to yield suboptimal behavior, and neural-net Q-values drift even when not being updated, so convergence is not guaranteed.

text: 1) For each output neuron, compute its error from its state and target, then adjust its weights. 2) For each hidden neuron, compute its error as the weighted sum of output errors scaled by its state factor, then adjust its weights.
when: Once the inputs are fed in and the forward pass has completed
why: output errors must exist before hidden errors can be computed

text: 1) With a set probability, jump to a random state; otherwise stay in the current state. 2) List the available actions. 3) With another set probability, pick one at random; otherwise pick the best-valued action. 4) Take the action and observe the reward and new state. 5) Update the Q-value and move to the new state.
when: each iteration of Q-learning

text: 1) Encode the game state as logical facts such as position, speed and direction. 2) Link components with rules that infer possible next actions. 3) Send the chosen action to a physics simulator.
why: Facts encoded from the game state are what the reasoning agent uses to infer the possible next actions.

text: 1) Initialize all weights to small random values. 2) Repeatedly take one training example in turn, looping back to the start. 3) For each example, run feedforward to produce a guess. 4) Run backpropagation to correct the weights. 5) Repeat for hundreds or thousands of iterations.
when: Training a multi-layer perceptron.
why: Backpropagation needs both the network's guess and the true output to measure the error it corrects.

text: Use a hash table for Q-values only when iterations are far fewer than actions times states, since each lookup costs more execution time.
when: When the iteration count is far below the number of actions times states
why: Array memory scales with actions times states, while a hash table only stores visited pairs.

text: Compare group output against a small epsilon rather than zero, because numerical error can prevent exact zeros.
when: When a priority-based steering system checks whether a group's blended output is negligible

text: Store a world model as differences from the real game state, checking the difference list first and falling back to game data for absent items.
when: Planning for many characters
why: Copying all data for each character is wasteful

text: Group continuous quantities, such as 3D positions, into discrete states before learning, because they otherwise create effectively infinite states.
when: continuous values appear in the state
why: infinite states cannot be stored or learned

text: Make practical Q-learning usable by tuning the learning rate, adding intermediate rewards, and limiting the number of iterations.
when: When the state count is large, up to roughly 100,000 states with about 10 actions
why: full convergence needs more visits than a game can afford

text: Avoid reinforcement learning when solution quality is easy to judge directly, since planning fits those problems better.
when: solution closeness can be measured easily

text: Avoid reinforcement learning when successful strategies change over time, because it needs a fairly stable environment.
Decision tree learning is the first choice, with RL and neural networks as overviews unless large investment is possible; Q-learning is an alternative start for game AI.
when: Choosing a first learning technique.
why: RL and neural networks are large fields needing substantial effort; Q-learning is simple, widely tested outside games and tunable without deep theory.

text: Q-values can be stored in a hash table keyed by state-action pair, which saves memory when few pairs are visited, or in a dense array indexed by state then action, which gives immediate lookups.
when: When choosing storage: brief or online runs suit a hash, runs revisiting all pairs several times suit arrays
why: Arrays suit runs that visit every state and action several times.

text: Higher gamma values favour longer action sequences but learn more slowly, while lower values stabilise faster but support only short sequences.
when: Setting the discount rate in Q-learning.
why: Long-horizon credit assignment costs learning speed.

text: Trying unknown actions may find better options but often costs more, while exploiting learned knowledge gives safer, known results.
when: Choosing an exploration rate.
why: Classic trade-off between unknown and known actions.

text: Per-state values use much less memory than per-state-action values when states have many actions, but they assume each action leads to a definite next state.
when: choosing a value representation
why: Q-learning tolerates more randomness in outcomes because it stores actions alongside states.

text: A pattern with wildcards passes down every set of bindings, while a pattern without wildcards needs only one match to proceed.
Without unification, an AND join outputs once both inputs have matched; other Boolean operators can be join nodes or built into network structure as in decision trees.
Each node in a Rete network stores all database facts that match its pattern.
Each path through a Rete network covers all patterns of one rule.
Rule nodes are often left out of descriptions of Rete, but an implementation needs them to mark rules that can fire.
Rete is not the fastest known matching algorithm, but commercial expert systems commonly use it and it provides a base for further optimization.
Removed items move to a deleted list with their trail, changed values keep the old value, and edits made by game code are marked as external.
when: Items are removed, modified, or set directly by game code
why: Auditing must separate changes fired by rules from direct edits made by the game.

text: A removal request goes to all pattern nodes; a node holding the fact deletes its match and forwards the request, a join node deletes entries using the fact, and a rule node deletes trigger records containing it. Nodes without the fact ignore it.
when: A fact is removed from the database
why: A modified fact is removed and re-added with its new value, so its old matches must be cleared.

text: An added fact is stored by matching pattern nodes, which notify downstream; join nodes create new non-clashing combinations using the fact, and rule nodes add trigger records, while unaffected nodes stop propagation.
when: A fact is added to the database

text: Facts enter at the top of a Rete network; pattern nodes pass matching facts with their variable bindings downward, and a join node outputs only combinations whose shared variable bindings agree.
Each rule node reached holds trigger records containing its matched facts and bindings, and arbitration then selects one to fire.
A clause used by several rules is stored once and matched once, which avoids duplicated matching work and is a key speed feature of Rete.
when: several rules contain the same clause
why: matching effort is not repeated per rule

text: Unifying variable bindings in join nodes can dominate matching time when many wildcard matches are possible, though this is usually a minor concern.
when: many possible wildcard matches exist
why: Each join must unify bindings across many candidate wildcard matches, and that unification work grows with their count.

text: A join node that receives a match on one input but no valid partner on the other produces no output, so propagation of an added fact can stop early.
when: an added fact completes only part of a rule

text: When a rule node loses its last valid match, its rule is removed from the triggered set.
when: a removal invalidates a rule's match

text: Rete matching time is roughly proportional to the number of rules, times clauses per rule, times facts in the database.
when: estimating matching cost

text: Rete memory use is roughly proportional to the number of rules, times clauses per rule, times distinct wildcard matches per pattern.
when: estimating memory cost

text: Rete stores rules in one directed acyclic network: pattern nodes at top represent clauses, join nodes combine inputs with AND, rule nodes at bottom represent fireable rules; common patterns shared.
Published matching algorithms can still be patented, so implementing Rete may require a licence; consult an intellectual property lawyer when unsure.
when: When implementing a published algorithm, even if the code is written from scratch.
why: patent claims can restrict implementation

text: 1) Treat each changed value as old fact removal plus new fact addition. 2) Process removals first, clearing their matches from pattern, join and rule nodes to prevent stale triggers. 3) Then process additions, pushing matches down; a join node passes a match only with a valid input combination. 4) Triggered list holds every possible rule; arbiter picks one.
when: Facts change between iterations
why: removals first prevents stale triggers from firing

text: Rete keeps stored matches between iterations for fast incremental updates, but uses significantly more memory than a naive rule matcher, the price of that speed.
why: retained matches let updates touch only changed facts

text: Strategic decisions in RTS AI are typically handled by a rule-based system or custom code.
Per-character behavior in RTS AI typically uses a finite state machine.
Most complex decisions happen at the whole-side level: collecting resources, guiding research, scheduling construction, training units and marshalling forces.
Real-time strategy AI has four core needs: pathfinding, group movement, tactical and strategic AI, and decision making.
RTS AI works at several tiers: individual units, formations or groups, and the whole side.
why: Decisions occur at several levels, with each tier passing its choices down to the one below.

text: Rule-based systems are often regarded as inefficient and hard to build, yet they keep behavior predictable and simplify implementation and debugging.
A database rewriting rule changes the AI's stored data directly, such as replacing a patrol goal with an attack goal when an enemy is sighted.
A rule's condition is a pattern matched against database facts, assembled from facts, numeric ranges, and logical connectives like AND, OR, and NOT.
Block format is a set of AND-only fuzzy rules that stores outputs in plain arrays, so decisions can be made by direct array lookup.
A rule-based system pairs a database of knowledge with a set of if-then rules.
A rule becomes eligible once the fact base meets its condition; an eligible rule may be chosen to execute its action portion.
An arbiter chooses which of several triggered rules fires; many rule-based systems include one.
when: more than one rule is triggered

text: A reactive script can be modeled as an AND-OR tree: internal nodes are abstract behaviours that may be shared among characters, and leaves are primitive behaviours such as animations.
Game AI tends to rely more on condition-action rules than on database rewrites, unlike many industrial AI systems.
Any consistent set of general fuzzy rules can be converted to block format, whatever operators or clause counts it uses, because a complete AND-rule table can express any truth table.
The rule count grows exponentially with the number of inputs, so block-format decision making only suits small systems.
Rule conditions compare values for absolute equality; numeric values may also use less-than, greater-than, or within-range tests.
A hard step function jumps directly from zero to one, though many other threshold functions are used in practice.
Bot scripting languages can be exposed to players or modders to change AI or create new autonomous characters.
Most video game AI is rule-based, with developers defining exactly how the game and its characters behave.
Reactive scripting technologies include behaviour trees, hierarchical finite state machines, HTN planners such as SHOP2, and the ABL planner.
Prefer rules with harder-to-meet conditions, since they match the current situation precisely; in Boolean-combined conditions, more clauses signal greater specificity.
when: When several rules are triggered and the arbiter must pick one to fire.
why: Rules with easy conditions are likely general.

text: If one behavior is chosen most of the time, placing it near the root can beat a balanced layout.
when: one behavior dominates
why: A frequent outcome placed near the root is reached in fewer decisions, lowering the average number of checks.

text: Test a numeric range, such as health below a threshold, rather than one exact value, when the condition allows it.
when: The condition is a numeric state that can vary
why: A range test matches any qualifying value, giving the rule more flexibility than one exact value.

text: Rule sets can be switched by game code or by the then-part of another rule, such as switching movement sets from enemy information already in the database.
Use region-level patterns, such as board edges, rather than full-board matching, since full-board matches are unlikely to succeed.
when: In games whose board positions are too numerous for any exact position to recur.
why: The number of possible full-board positions is so large that an exact full-board match rarely occurs.

text: Rules in disabled sets never get the chance to trigger, so switching sets on and off limits which rules are evaluated.
when: When a rule set grows so large that even Rete matching becomes too slow.
why: Only active sets are matched, so the rules evaluated per iteration drop from thousands to about a hundred.

text: The database can change between iterations, both through the action of a fired rule and through game code, so each iteration must re-evaluate the rules against current data.
when: When the database changes between iterations through fired rules or other game code.
why: Each iteration's matching checks the rule's IF-clause against the database as it currently stands.

text: A rule pairs an if-clause with an action function that receives the variable bindings and may change the database.
Decomposing AND rules breaks down when several rules share a conclusion, since split rules can conflict for the same input state.
why: Decomposed single-state rules that share a conclusion can contradict each other, because the correct response depends on context they cannot see.

text: Ten inputs with five states each would need nearly ten million block-format rules, far too many to author by hand.
why: Block format needs one rule per combination of input states, so the rule count multiplies across inputs.

text: Hand-written rule sets become difficult to maintain as the number of interacting conditions grows.
when: Building AI decision rules with many interacting inputs.
why: Interactions multiply and become hard to manage by hand.

text: Reading other agents' internal state or polling their intentions is fast but error-prone, and both must be rewritten whenever a character's AI changes.
when: When characters must understand what cooperating characters are doing or intend to do.
why: Reading internals or polling ties each character to others' AI, so every AI change forces rewrites.

text: A model trained on past hiring decisions learned to penalize résumés likely from women, reproducing past discrimination in its own decisions.
when: When training labels come from historical human decisions.
why: Past outcomes encode past bias, which the model learns as a pattern to follow.

text: Split a rule 'a1 AND ... AND an THEN c' into n single-input rules, one per input state, so rule count grows linearly rather than exponentially.
when: fuzzy rule sets with many inputs
why: ten inputs with five states give 50 rules, not about ten million

text: 1) Group rules into sets that can be switched on and off. 2) Place sets in a hierarchy under an always-enabled top set. 3) Let higher-level sets hold only rules that enable or disable their children, and lowest-level sets hold working rules.
when: a rule system has grown too large to evaluate fully

text: 1) Loop over top-level database items and stop at the first that matches. 2) A datum matches when type, identifier (or wildcard) and value bounds agree. 3) A group matches when type and identifier agree and every pattern child matches some database child.
when: matching a pattern against a hierarchical database

text: Support then-parts that change game state, request game actions, rewrite the database, or run arbitrary code when a rule fires.
why: Rules must both request game actions and change the database, and arbitrary code adds flexibility beyond those fixed effects.

text: Let a condition-action rule only request an action, and let the game decide whether it succeeds and update the stored state when it does.
when: The action takes place in the game world and may fail, such as an item out of reach
why: Only the game knows whether the action actually succeeded

text: Use direct database rewrites for AI-internal data, such as goals, that has no meaning to the rest of the game.
when: When the data concerns AI-internal state, such as goals, with no meaning to the rest of the game.
why: The game code only handles game-state changes, so AI-only data can be rewritten directly without scheduling an action.

text: A block-format rule set must cover every state of each input and include a rule for every combination of those input states.
Use rule-based logic when decisions must be transparent and predictable.
why: Explicit if-then criteria can be read directly to explain how a decision was reached.

text: Combs format has no general transformation from block format and cannot express every truth table, but designing rules directly in it makes tuning easier at the cost of sophistication.
why: Single-state rules cannot represent every truth table, so no general conversion from block rules exists.

text: General rules that are parsed at run time may be faster than block format for many inputs, but they give up block format's fixed array structure.
Ruggedness is the steepness of a location; for a height-field cell it can be estimated by comparing its height with its neighbors' heights.
A sentinel value larger than any possible evaluation is used as the initial best score, so the search always records a move even when every move scores poorly.
when: initializing the best score at the root

text: Momentum, adaptive resolution and multiple trials usually find better solutions faster than simple hill climbing, but none guarantees the best one.
Core game-search algorithms are each simple yet admit many optimizations; alpha-beta cutoffs and transposition caches are vital for speed, while other tweaks squeeze out extra gains.
Other sequence-dependent games need more complex hashing or special search code to handle move history.
A learner trained on a small set of encounters may perform well only on those and fail against new player behavior.
when: When a learning AI is trained on a limited number of experiences.
why: It memorized responses instead of generalizing.

text: 1) Generate a few trial successors. 2) Rate them with the heuristic. 3) Generate more trials around the best ones. 4) Repeat until the best successors are found with confidence.
when: movement planning on an infinite state graph
why: Concentrates search effort on promising successors.

text: 1) For a large area, take a fixed number of random height samples inside it. 2) Use the highest minus lowest sample as ruggedness; sample variance is an alternative.
when: the area is too large to check every cell
why: A fixed number of samples per location keeps the cost of each location constant.

text: Wrap the recursive search in a function that starts at depth zero and returns only the chosen move.
why: Best moves are recorded only at depth zero, so the top-level call is what yields the chosen move.

text: Implement both negascout and MTD and profile them, since the faster algorithm depends on the game; they can share the table, alpha-beta function, and game class.
when: choosing a tree search for a specific game
why: relative speed is game-dependent

text: Sampling successors is slow and very sensitive to heuristic quality, while discretizing animation ranges into a few values is the more common choice.
when: choosing how to handle continuous animation parameters
why: Sampling successors is slow and heuristic-sensitive, and discrete values avoid adapting A* to infinite graphs.

text: Fixed action sequences can make characters seem spiteful, reckless or secretive without any AI effort.
when: characters follow a fixed action sequence
why: the scripted order itself reveals apparent motives

text: A visibility map scores each location by how much of the level it can see from that location.
A sensor registers its position, its orientation, and a threshold for each modality it can sense.
A signal resembles an event but also carries its modality, its source intensity, and its source position.
Sense management checks whether a character can physically perceive game events, simulating how senses such as sight and hearing deliver knowledge.
Complex sense simulation is expected to become standard in first- and third-person action games and spread to real-time strategy and platformer games.
Visibility and cover are not strict opposites; a position can offer strong cover while still giving some view, like peering through a gap.
The most advanced knowledge delivery uses sense managers that distribute information from a physical simulation of the world.
Many stealth and action games build their core gameplay on AI sensing.
Modeling light bouncing off surfaces or mirrors requires extending a framework that assumes vision travels only in straight lines.
Touch requires direct physical contact and is best implemented with collision detection rather than the sense manager.
Visibility does not prove navigability: no simple test confirms movement between two locations, and complex action sequences are hard to anticipate geometrically.
A level's sightlines affect how movement input feels, so generated layouts should account for the camera views they create.
Early designed architecture used sight lines and alignments to direct occupant attention, making attention-directing one of the oldest spatial design concerns.
when: Understanding the history of spatial design
why: Early builders shaped occupant attention through form before other spatial concerns.

text: Reconnaissance favors locations that see far, while stealth favors locations that are hard to see from elsewhere.
when: choosing positions for scouting or hiding
why: A reconnaissance unit needs locations that can see a long way.

text: Event-based delivery is preferred for sensory perception only; ordinary information requests can still use polling.
why: Polling sensory checks would mostly fail, wasting performance, since perception is an input process.

text: Straight-line sensing suits open-air levels and indoor levels whose walls are thicker than a signal can travel.
when: open-air levels or thick-walled indoor levels

text: Use measured jump limits, such as a four-tile platform height gap, five-tile maximum and two-to-six-tile pits, as hard bounds when generating traversable layouts.
A generator that outputs only a 2D layout will not capture height-based connections such as ramps, bridges and drops.
when: generating 3D levels
why: Plan-only output lacks vertical transitions.

text: Dividing spaces with doorways, windows, trellises, and screens instead of solid walls lets players see rewards or goals before reaching them.
when: In isometric-view games where players scavenge locations for loot
why: Visible but blocked rewards let players weigh the risk of exploring against the value of what lies inside.

text: Simulated senses let characters notice allies and their deaths, which makes stealth and alertness playable as design elements.
A sensor perceives a signal only when the attenuated intensity at its location reaches its threshold for that modality.
why: Each step of range multiplies intensity by an attenuation factor, so strength falls off with distance.

text: An enemy that kills instantly when startled forces players to move slowly and carefully through the area around it.
why: Its attack is triggered by loud movement, so players avoid noise to stay safe.

text: Minimising a count of vertical parent links as a soft preference biases generated mazes against vertical links.
When snipers punish players peeking from open cover, a large blocking object is needed to hide sightlines, and cheap props such as crates are the fastest way to provide one.
when: open areas with long sightlines and peeking
why: Blocking sightlines protects players from being killed as they look out.

text: A visibility analysis yields either a count of visible locations or, for the ray method, an average ray length.
A sense management system, such as a region sense manager, reports sights, smells, and sounds to the AI.
when: When characters need information about unusual sights, smells, and sounds

text: A single line-of-sight ray can be fooled by a thin structure that blocks it, giving a false result; one ray is faster but less reliable.
when: evaluating cover with a time budget; line-of-sight tests through level geometry
why: One ray may miss a thin obstacle or pass through a gap

text: Visibility-based links err both ways: distant regions can falsely connect via doorways, obtuse corners or inclines, and dense areas around a corner can wrongly appear unconnected.
why: A few sight checks can pass through gaps between distant regions, creating links that should not exist.

text: Building an influence map from only visible units tends to underestimate the enemy under fog of war.
when: fog of war
why: Each side sees only some units, so the map can wrongly show control of much of the level.

text: Thin walls confuse simple distance checks, so designers should avoid them where possible.
when: Placing walls in levels that use distance-based waypoint search
why: Thin walls let straight-line checks see through to the wrong side

text: In action games with thin walls and close quarters, straight-line sensing produces unpleasant artifacts that developers patch with extra tests, special cases and heuristics.
when: first- and third-person action games
why: The basic model is only good where walls are thicker than the signal's reach, which these environments lack.

text: 1) Cast rays outward from the character's eye position at the waypoint. 2) Measure how far each ray travels before hitting geometry. 3) Average the lengths to score visibility.
when: When analysing indoor levels with ray casting from a waypoint
why: average ray length approximates how much of the level the position can see; no random offset is needed

text: 1) Check that the sensor is interested in visual stimuli. 2) Check the signal's intensity against the sensor's threshold. 3) Check the sight cone. 4) Check line of sight. 5) Optionally check background conditions.
when: testing sensors for visual signals after gathering candidates

text: 1) Add a trigger and resize its collision. 2) In the visual scripting editor, create a Touch event on the trigger with Max Trigger Count set to 0. 3) Connect Touched to a Toggle action. 4) Set the Toggle target to a toggleable ambient sound actor.
why: A zero trigger count lets the trigger fire repeatedly without being exhausted.

text: Use ray casting for indoor levels, and use culling or sampling for large outdoor levels.
Deliver external knowledge through event managers or polling stations so characters get only what a real person in the environment might know.
why: Omniscient access lets characters always know the player's position, undermining any appearance of mystery.

text: Let shots that miss pass where the player can watch them, so misses read as believable rather than as cheating.
why: visible misses make high accuracy feel fair

text: Model virtual opponents as individual entities with their own knowledge, just as human players are modeled.
when: Reasoning about what an opponent knows
why: An opponent that knows hidden state, like cards in the deck, appears to cheat.

text: Let players see the goal and possible paths from a room's entrance so they can judge the space before committing.
when: rooms with patrolling enemies
why: Players can then plan their approach.

text: Usually make any location visible on the map reachable.
when: open world with a visible map
why: Players who see a place expect to reach it, which sustains the open, exploratory feeling.

text: Sniper positions need a view of the main competition area, even if reaching them requires a long route through corridors.
when: placing ranged vantage points in shooter levels
why: A vantage point must see the contested area to be useful.

text: More comprehensive sensing solutions handle these errors better, but greater sophistication raises processing cost.
World objects can supply their own actions, offered only when the current game state allows them.
why: Each object checks the current state, such as whether a character carries raw food, before offering its action.

text: Embedding simple rules in both characters and objects, where an object's value attracts characters whose needs match it, produces emergent behavior, as when a sleepy character is drawn to a bed.
when: When a character nears an item
why: The character's need rules and the item's value rules interact, so a sleepy character is pulled toward a bed.

text: In object-oriented engines, a decision can call an instance method and apply a simple test to its return value, leaving heavy computation in compiled code.
Give each object at most one action, such as toggling a light switch or opening a door.
Companion characters that move through, solve, or use abilities in a level guide players, who imitate them without noticing.
when: A companion acts alongside the player in a level.
why: Players copy what companion characters do because social imitation makes them follow visible actions without conscious awareness.

text: Collusion means computer characters pursue their own goals while also serving the designer's goal of an optimal player experience.
Conversation trees remain a common way to handle complex character interaction in RPGs, though they offer limited responsiveness.
Breaking a deal lowers other parties' willingness to trade with the breaker.
Squadmates with personal agendas grow satisfied or unsatisfied depending on whether the player cooperates with them, making the player's choices affect the group.
when: Companions have their own goals
why: Goals beyond points and forward progress create interpersonal conflict, which games rarely model apart from violent conflict.

text: A cumulative points total that cannot fall is a poor tool for matchmaking or predicting outcomes, because it no longer tracks current skill.
1) Implement each strategy as explicit purchase rules. 2) Run every strategy over the same fixed simulated time. 3) Compare final income. 4) Analyze each strategy's strengths and weaknesses.
when: comparing automated or hand-made idle game strategies

text: Complex AI minds are worth their unpredictability when emotional triggers depend on nuanced interaction among AI characters, so simple predictability must be given up.
when: the design centers on emotional interplay between AI characters
why: Emotional triggers depend on nuanced interaction among AI characters

text: Least-recently-used arbitration spreads firing opportunities across all rules, directly reducing endless repetition of a single rule.
when: When one rule keeps repeating and firing should be shared across the rule set.
why: Each fired rule moves to the back of the list, so recently used rules lose priority over the others.

text: Reusing a target member name in a derived class shadows the superclass member; this works in most languages but breaks in some, such as Python, which needs different names.
when: When implementing a derived steering behavior in an OOP language
why: Most languages create two separate members for the same name, so the derived target does not overwrite the base one.

text: Iterate over copies of the queue and active list when removing items, because removing items from a list during iteration breaks the loop.
when: When a scheduler loop removes actions from the queue or active set while iterating over it.
why: Items are removed while the lists are being iterated.

text: 1) Scan the ordered rule list and fire the first triggered rule. 2) Move that rule to the end of the list. Over many firings, the first triggered rule is the least recently used one.
when: When one rule would otherwise keep firing over and over.
why: It is meant to counter the looping issue of a single rule firing repeatedly.

text: 1) Let one machine claim an input. 2) Have other machines ignore claimed inputs. 3) Without this, several machines may respond to the same input.
when: Parallel machines receive the same input
why: Prevents conflicting responses

text: Measure before choosing a steering pipeline, since it can add execution cost in complex scenes.
when: When deciding whether a complex steering pipeline is needed over straight-line paths.
why: Its running time grows with the number of constraint steps, which rises as more constraints are added.

text: Inheriting from seek keeps code reuse, while inlining the seek code is faster but duplicates code.
when: When implementing pursue on top of seek
why: Polymorphic calls cost performance, so removing inheritance speeds things up.

text: Mixing polling and events is often fastest, but information then travels along several paths, making it harder to see what happens where.
when: When a game uses some polling and some event passing together.

text: Inheritance in a state hierarchy couples classes tightly; it is powerful reuse but a strong form of coupling.
when: When states are arranged as a hierarchy of superstates and substates.

text: Offset AI geometry is level geometry pushed outward from every wall by the character's radius, assuming a sphere or cylinder.
Multiple checks against level geometry from a character's left and right extremes can cause steering problems and stuck characters.
why: Steering treats characters as widthless particles, yet they must behave as solid bodies.

text: Bounding spheres of many nearby obstacles can overlap and block routes that are actually passable.
when: cluttered rooms
why: Spheres are coarser than real object shapes, so neighbouring spheres can overlap and exclude passable routes.

text: Avoid searching detailed render polygons for obstacles; use simplified collision-level shapes instead, since polygon searches are slow and perform poorly.
when: When level geometry is very complex.
why: Searching raw polygons for obstacles takes a long time and yields poor results.

text: In team sports, a character must react to a situation while accounting for what the rest of the team is doing.
why: Strong team patterns in sports like baseball mean each player's position must fit the team's overall movement.

text: Sports and driving games face open AI problems, such as computing the fastest route around a race track dynamically.
Sports games have a large body of readily available expert strategy, but encoding that knowledge into AI is often difficult.
Some team sports have strong set patterns: a double play always follows the same overall movement, while fielder positions depend on where the ball is struck.
Some characters work well together, so a team can perform better than the sum of its individual members.
when: Evaluating team compositions.
why: Complementary abilities multiply value.

text: Team sports AI has three tiers: a high-level strategy layer, a coordinated motion layer that triggers set movement patterns when match events occur, and individual player AI that varies behavior within the strategy.
when: team sports
why: The middle layer only coordinates teammates, so it has no role for solo sports.

text: 1) Compute each team's MMR as a plain mean of member MMRs or a weighted form such as using only the highest-rated player. 2) Compare team values against other teams' values.
when: Games where one strongest player dominates play and teammates contribute little
why: When teammates add little, the top-rated player alone largely determines the team's strength, so only that rating matters.

text: The high-level strategy layer of a team sports game often uses learning so that the challenge stays fair.
when: team sports
why: Parameter or action learning is the technique used to calibrate strategic choices against the player.

text: Broadcasting sends many kinds of events to many listeners, and each listener filters out what it does not need.
A finite state machine has a fixed set of states, exactly one current at a time, and transitions that move between states when inputs arrive.
Event-based transitions can run in a handler that game code calls when an event occurs, instead of the machine polling for the condition every frame.
when: A transition is triggered by something discrete, such as a loud noise

text: Often AI generates too few events for broadcasting to be noticeably slow.
Players came to expect enemies to perceive events around them; at minimum, characters should receive messages about nearby events.
A finite state machine keeps no record of prior states, so it cannot easily return to whichever state it was in before.
Use fixed per-waypoint states when the relevant states are obvious, such as cover directions or firing arcs; they fit poorly for withdrawal points.
when: Tactical points whose possible states are clear-cut, such as cover directions or firing arcs
why: Context like enemy-controlled territory has no clear set of states to enumerate, so one state per point fails there.

text: Simple event codes can represent any interest, and a manager matches an event's code against a listener's code without knowing what the codes mean.
why: Codes that are cheap to compare let developers filter events quickly, which suits typical implementations.

text: Use event-based intention sharing when team behavior changes often and characters must stay in step.
why: Letting characters read each other's internal state or poll intentions is error-prone and needs rewriting on every AI change.

text: Use event passing when many similar characters all need the same piece of information.
when: many similar characters share one information need
why: events are often faster in that case

text: Four-character fire team states are Disengaged, In cover, In motion and Suppression attack; transitions depend on enemy sightings, team movement, arrival, and whether the highest-ranked unit reached its cover.
when: Squad-based games where each character decides for itself while considering teammates
why: Mutual cover and a coherent look emerge from the states and transitions alone, with no higher-level coordinator.

text: Improving a closed node reaches its downstream nodes only when it is reprocessed, because nodes depending on its old cost must be re-examined.
when: When a search reaches a closed node with a lower cost-so-far than the recorded value
why: Cost-so-far is the only dependable value for comparing nodes, unlike estimates, which may be inaccurate.

text: Fixed states cannot exploit environmental quirks, such as a structure that gives cover from one specific walkway only.

1) Find the target's ancestor level, by run-time search or from precomputed offsets. 2) Walk down from that ancestor to the target. 3) At each level, exit the active child and enter the next, collecting actions.
when: A transition with a negative level is applied

text: 1) When a behaviour starts, call its entry routine; when it stops, call its exit routine. 2) If the same behaviour continues, call neither. 3) Let the exiting behaviour pass useful data forward and clear its own memory.
why: Entry and exit routines handle setup, cleanup and handover.

text: 1) Broadcast events during development to ease behaviour tuning. 2) If the event system proves slow, replace it with several narrowcasting managers before release.
when: While the game is still in development
why: Broadcasting eases tuning of character behaviour, and AI events are rarely numerous enough to slow it.

text: Simple exit counting is cheap but crude; checking where each connection leads is more accurate but becomes very complicated.
why: Counting exits ignores where they lead, so a room centre with several exits to one area can look better than it is.

text: Event-based sensing pushes game knowledge to capable characters, whereas polling runs a perception test on each request and most requests fail, wasting performance.
when: implementing character perception
why: Polling would make most requests fail, wasting performance, whereas perception works as information arriving at characters.

text: A character near a fixed distance threshold may switch back and forth as the player moves, which is noticeable and can stop an anytime algorithm from finishing.
when: Behaviour switches at a single fixed boundary.
why: Each switch costs setup and cleanup time.

text: A composite state contains a sub-machine, so an agent can be in several states at once, one per hierarchy level.
Hysteresis within individual behaviors cannot solve oscillations between different species, which need separate handling.
When parallel machines must interact, use conditional checks on the other machine's state, such as forbidding firing while jumping.
when: Two machines' states must constrain each other
why: Less elegant than input consumption but practical

text: A transition that leaves a sub-machine discards its record, so returning to it restarts from the initial sub-state unless history is kept.
when: A transition jumps out of a composite state to another level
why: A history node stores the last sub-state, so re-entering a composite state can resume where it left off.

text: A finite state machine with crisp states makes a character jump abruptly between behaviours, which looks unnatural.
why: Two crisp states switch at one threshold, so the change appears in a single step rather than gradually.

text: A committed character may get stuck, since games rarely let AI reverse a decision.
when: Tactical movement with committed actions
why: Without reversal, a poor choice persists even when conditions change

text: Dynamic arrive accelerates toward the target, then accelerates the other way so speed reaches zero exactly at the destination.
when: Character must stop precisely using acceleration
why: Braking through acceleration reaches zero speed at the goal

text: Evade uses the same prediction as pursue but delegates to flee, moving away from the predicted position.
An action may promise a goal only after several hidden steps, so its effect on that goal is delayed.
Discretize an animation's playback range into a few sampled values, for example exposing only a few frame rates from a 15 to 30 fps animation.
when: movement planning with continuous animation parameters
why: A small set of states keeps the graph finite and tractable.

text: Send units toward the enemy's likely location rather than to random points on the map.
when: Real-time strategy games where the AI moves troops across the map

text: Changing behavior weights over time, based on game or character state, shifts which steering concern dominates.
why: Blending and arbitration sit at opposite ends of a continuum, so weights changing over time can move between them.

text: Repeated filtering lets a car speed up over frames, which then permits turning, so its path emerges from the repeated process.
when: Vehicle steering is filtered each frame.
why: Turning requires speed.

text: Because the target stays ahead, the car starts turning well before a corner, and steers more heavily for a severe corner.
when: In rally games where an invisible target leads the car along the racing line
why: Keeping the target ahead of the car makes it begin turning first, so steering starts at the right point.

text: Enemies that attack and then flee draw players along a route, and timing an enemy's defeat to a chosen location brings players there.
when: Enemies the player pursues through a level
why: Players fixed on destroying enemies will chase fleeing ships, so the chase carries them to chosen spots.

text: 1) Detect a zero filtered result. 2) Switch to another method, such as driving forward and turning hard.
when: Filtered steering output is zero.
why: When every component of the request is blocked, filtering alone leaves the car stuck until the target moves.

text: When steering behaviors are blended, combined through a blackboard, run in a state machine or chained in a pipeline, delay actuation to one final step.
when: Several steering concerns are active at the same time
why: Each behavior that accounts for physical limits gives poor results when combined, so the combined output should be actuated once at the end.

text: Dynamic steering suits characters that must accelerate and stop precisely, while kinematic output may suffice where abrupt velocity changes are acceptable.
when: Choosing movement type for arrival
why: Dynamic arrival needs acceleration and smooth braking, which kinematic output lacks

text: Steering tolerates small errors because it re-decides every frame, so a slightly wrong estimate is corrected at the next update.
when: Continuous steering movement
why: Each frame's decision is simple and constantly revised

text: Kinematic seek moves at constant full speed and never stops, so it keeps pursuing a target it never reaches.
when: Seek is used without arrival logic
why: Seek always outputs full speed toward the target

text: Movement direction and facing are not linked by default, so a character can face one way while travelling another.
when: Character movement is not tied to orientation
why: Position and orientation update independently unless coupled

text: Seek against a moving target makes the character orbit rather than close in directly. With drag, the orbit becomes an inward spiral that, given enough drag, looks like direct approach.
when: Target is moving
why: Seek aims at the current position, so the character keeps turning around the target.

text: Units sharing the same tactical data move in distinct styles when each uses its own weight set; scouts can seek exposure while artillery avoid it.
when: units need different routing priorities from shared analysis data
why: Distinct preferences come from the weights applied to the same data.

text: Players notice sudden changes in motion more than smooth motion, so dropping collision for distant pedestrians is less noticeable than frequent pinball-style collisions.
when: Peripheral characters far from the main action, such as strollers on a faraway path or figures glimpsed while crossing a bridge
why: The eye picks up abrupt shifts in movement far more readily than steady movement, so characters passing through each other goes unnoticed.

text: Grazing can be implemented as a slow wander that pauses to eat from time to time.
Creatures flock with their own kind, especially when in danger, and respond to the player by fleeing as if it were a predator or by following.
Steering behaviours alone may handle highly constrained characters poorly, such as vehicles needing maneuvering room or characters that cannot turn on the spot.
when: Characters with limited turning ability
why: Steering assumes free motion, while constrained characters need exact combinations of moves and turns

text: The movement layer, the lowest layer of game AI beneath decision making and strategy, turns AI decisions into motion, from homing in on targets to avoiding obstacles and navigating rooms.
Align turns a character to match a target orientation using only angular acceleration, ignoring position and velocity.
Arrive is a steering behavior that slows a character so it stops at its target instead of overshooting it.
Capability-sensitive steering selects among the maneuvers a character can actually perform, choosing the one that best serves its goal.
Steering behaviors is the term for dynamic movement algorithms, introduced by one researcher.
Actuation, or motor control, converts steering movement requests into motion a physical character can actually perform.
when: Steering requests exceed what the character can do.

text: Separation pushes a character away from nearby characters within a threshold distance, with strength falling off with distance. Its contributions are summed and clipped.
Constraints are avoidance behaviors for moving or static obstacles that check the actuator's planned path.
Orientation can be stored as a scalar angle from the positive z axis or as a unit-length vector pointing in the facing direction, and the two convert using sine and cosine.
Velocity matching accelerates a character so its velocity equals the target's velocity; alone it is rarely useful but serves as a building block for behaviors such as flocking.
Cars cannot turn while stationary or move sideways, turn less sharply at speed due to tire grip, brake harder than they accelerate, and reverse more slowly than they drive forward.
when: Modeling car or wheeled vehicle movement
why: Vehicle physics limit steering options.

text: Movement planning handles short sequences, such as crossing a room with obstacles, and fills in detail for the next part of a route rather than the whole level.
A final actuator receives one combined request with no knowledge of the behaviors behind it, so it cannot compare alternative routes.
Rotation values do not wrap, so a large rotation value simply means fast turning.
Arrive produces no angular output and runs in constant time and memory.
Steering is nearsighted: it reacts only to immediate surroundings and cannot foresee problems beyond its horizon.
The steering pipeline is a cooperative arbitration mechanism tailored to steering rather than a general decision tool.
Decision trees, state machines and blackboards have all been used to control steering, and no single approach is yet standard for games.
Only seek, align, and velocity matching are fundamental steering behaviors; rotation matching exists by analogy but has no known application.
A formation character needs only a method that sets a steering target from a position and orientation.
Humans can move in any direction but are much faster forward, so sideways and backward movement is rarely chosen unless the target is very close.
Dynamic movement is growing but remains a minority in games, which still rely heavily on kinematic movement.
Steering behaviours output a linear acceleration vector and an angular acceleration value.
Physics simulation now drives movement almost universally in driving games, is used for flying characters, and is spreading into human character physics.
Inputs always include the character's position; velocity is optional and needed only by some algorithms. Others include other characters' positions, special locations, paths and level geometry.
The most common movement output is a desired velocity, while older games often output only a direction for stationary, walking or running states.
Some games use only movement algorithms with no higher-level decision making and still appear convincing.
Resource management and turn-based games often skip movement logic, because the chosen destination can simply be set.
when: Game is resource management or turn-based.

text: Full 3D steering suits characters that scurry along roofs or walls, airborne vehicles that tilt and roll, and gun mounts that spin freely in any direction.
when: Characters or vehicles are not limited by gravity.

text: Projected volumes are the only complete solution to wall avoidance and are used by physics engines, but they are slow to query and hard to interpret; no widely trusted steering method exists yet.
Separation alone is not useful: characters jiggle out of range and stop. It is designed to combine with other behaviors.

Ten of fourteen 2D steering behaviors are purely linear and carry over unchanged to 3D: pursue, seek, evade, flee, arrive, path following, velocity matching, separation, collision avoidance and obstacle avoidance.
when: Converting 2D steering to 3D

text: Align, face and look where you're going are purely angular and need new orientation math in 3D. Wander is handled separately because its orientation drives its linear motion.
when: Converting 2D steering to 3D

text: Steering behaviors extend basic movement by outputting acceleration and rotation rather than only velocity. They are widely used in PC and console games and dominate some genres such as driving games.
Jumping, ledge drops and elevators still move grounded characters through the third dimension even in 2½D.
Motorbikes cannot travel backward, so their rear decision arc is zero.
In 3D wander the offset and maximum acceleration become vectors, typically with only the forward z component non-zero, and angular motion is delegated to 3D face.
Steering and path smoothing soften discrete graph limits but do not handle rapidly changing yet predictable situations.
Hard-coded state machines are usually faster than flexible implementations, except for very large machines with thousands of states.
Steering behaviors treat characters as zero-width particles, yet characters must behave as solid objects.
An open research direction is a wanderer that uses earlier logs to target poorly covered areas with novel move combinations.
Selected actions are often little more than steering behaviors, which is enough for most character behavior.
Inverse kinematics or other constraints can limit which movements an animated character can perform.
Creatures that move along walls and ceilings cannot be represented with a strictly 2.5D model.
Non-grazing creature states are either a basic goal-seeking behavior, such as fleeing, or a sum of goal-seeking behaviors, such as flocking.
Creatures flee threats and handle simple movement steering and obstacle avoidance.
Grid object movement patterns can be standing still, random moves with frequent or infrequent direction changes, or clockwise or counterclockwise motion along walls.
A facing vector does not determine a unique 3D orientation, since infinitely many orientations look down the same vector.
Stop steering once the character is within a small arrival radius of its target.
when: When the target is fixed
why: Otherwise small positional errors keep the character moving.

text: With a nearly continuous range of speeds or turn angles, use a set of heuristics to pick the action from the current state and target.
when: when the action space is effectively continuous
why: Checking every maneuver in turn is infeasible when the options are almost unlimited, so heuristics must choose the action.

text: Use cone-based evasion for a few characters where simplicity matters most, not for crowds.
Arrive can be split into computing a velocity target and then applying velocity matching, and this split is a common pattern in delegated behaviors.
why: Seek, align, and velocity matching form the basic set, so other steering behaviors reduce to producing a target for one of these.

text: Pairing slowing with a satisfaction radius allows a much smaller radius without wiggle or an instant stop.
when: Arrive behaviour needs precise stopping
why: Slowing removes the abrupt stop that a small radius would otherwise cause

text: Use seek to chase a constantly moving target at full speed. To stop on a target, use arrive instead.
when: Choosing a chase or stopping behavior

text: Separation suits crowds heading in roughly the same direction. It works poorly when characters cross paths, where collision avoidance fits better.
when: Crowd movement

text: A cover-based overwatch squad needs its anchor movement switched off, and the anchor should move slowly relative to the members, since bounding overwatch is not a fast maneuver.
when: Squad moves between cover points using a shared anchor
why: A stationary squad's center of mass never changes, so the anchor never advances to new cover.

text: Movement algorithms usually treat a character as a single point at its center of mass, mirroring physics engines, while collision and obstacle avoidance still need the character's size.
when: Designing movement logic for a character with volume
why: Movement can ignore extent, but avoidance and collision depend on it.

text: A good hit-and-run position combines a clear view of the target area with several exit routes.
when: choosing a spot to attack and withdraw from
why: Good visibility of the room lets the attacker strike, and several exits let it withdraw afterward.

text: Use kinematic movement for autonomous agents that need no realistic physics; add pathfinding when they must head for destinations such as an exit.
when: Agents moving through a game world
why: Full physics is unnecessary, so kinematic movement suffices; a specific destination such as an exit still needs navigation.

text: A simple algorithm can make pursuers try to surround the player.
If a character is too fast to stop in time, the target velocity is smaller than its current velocity, so acceleration points backward and brakes it.
when: when speed exceeds what the remaining distance allows
why: Velocity cannot change instantly, so the acceleration is set by reaching the target velocity within a fixed time.

text: Both decision arcs shrink as speed rises, at a rate set by tire grip and found by tuning.
when: Vehicle decision arcs at varying speed
why: Higher speed reduces the grip available for turning.

text: With offset geometry, collision detection and prediction can test point locations, which is cheaper than testing the character's extent.
when: When a character must act as a solid body rather than a point
why: Offsetting walls by the character's radius lets collision be tested on points, which makes prediction cheaper than checking its extent.

text: Staging assigns high-level actions in response to triggers, mainly for many characters in a scene; a decision state executes a move-to-location behavior with the location as its parameter.
when: Many characters are in the scene.

text: Crowd instability appears as sudden behavior changes, caused by decisions propagating through the group and being amplified at each step.
when: When group decision making and steering are made more sophisticated

text: The cost of entering a group can depend on the group you came from, so one link cost can be cheap from one side and expensive from another. Good grouping reduces this effect but cannot remove it.
when: When a path enters a group from different neighboring groups

text: Priority steering uses constant extra memory and time linear in the total number of behaviors across all groups.
why: Only a temporary acceleration value is stored while the behaviors run, so extra memory stays constant.

text: A time-to-target constant of 0.1 is used for align.
Relative position is the target's position minus the character's; relative velocity is the target's velocity minus the character's.
The sidestep radius, the very-slow movement threshold, and the forward arc size must be tuned to the scale of the character's animations.
why: Animation clips naturally cap how much turning can be added before motion looks wrong, so thresholds must match them.

text: Pursue runs in O(1) time and memory.

Linear falloff strength equals max acceleration times (threshold minus distance), divided by threshold. Inverse square strength equals the smaller of a constant times distance squared and max acceleration.
when: When a nearby character is inside the separation threshold distance.

text: Velocity matching runs in constant time and memory, O(1).
Updating formation targets takes O(n) time for n occupied slots and O(1) extra memory beyond the output assignments.
Adding a character costs O(1) time and memory; removing one costs O(log n) time and O(1) memory with a suitable hashed lookup structure.
when: Hashed structure used for finding members
why: Removal must first locate the character in the assignments list, and hashing makes that lookup cheap.

text: The velocity-facing behavior runs in O(1) time and memory.
2½D keeps a full 3D position with one scalar orientation about the up axis, giving four degrees of freedom; it suits most grounded game characters.
when: Default choice for most game AI; movement is planar with vertical freedom
why: Grounded characters are effectively two-dimensional, so one orientation angle suffices.

text: Two actuation approaches exist: output filtering and capability-sensitive steering.
when: When an actuator's physical limits must shape steering outputs, not just execute them.
why: Steering outputs are only requests, and physics-driven motion means a motor layer must work out how to execute them.

text: Every movement algorithm reads geometric data about its character and the world, then returns a geometric description of the movement it wants.
Most steering behaviors take the moving character's kinematic data plus target information, then output steering. The target input varies: another character, collision geometry, or a path.
Many steering behaviors are variants of one or two themes, and many have an opposite formed by a small change, such as seek and flee. A child behavior can be seen as extending its parent.

The steering pipeline is a cooperative arbitration design with four ordered stages: targeters set the goal, decomposers split it into sub-goals, constraints limit movement, and one actuator produces the path and motor output.
when: When steering must handle tight passages or integrate with pathfinding.
why: Its ordered stages refine goals into sub-goals and check constraints before the actuator commits a path.

text: Vehicles use a forward arc for targets reachable by turning without braking and a rear arc for targets reached by reversing, with the rear arc usually capped by a maximum reversing distance.
when: Vehicle steering decisions
why: Vehicles are slower in reverse, and the cap prevents long reversing trips to targets behind them.

text: Urban driving AI has four parts: pathfinding, a destination selection layer (state machine, rule system, or script), kinematic steering, and explicit traffic and pedestrian simulation.
when: Urban driving games
why: Different routes and shared roads with ambient traffic require destination choice and traffic handling beyond driving.

text: A common split: the AI chooses where to move, and separate code turns that movement into animation.
why: Decoupling gives the AI complete freedom of motion, with animation handled separately afterward.

text: Near walls, wall avoidance with pursuit can push a character the wrong way, since independent behaviors ignore context and avoidance may give only tangential acceleration, making a pursuer slow sharply.
when: When a pursuer approaches a wall
why: Basic steering behaviors act only on their immediate surroundings and cannot anticipate outcomes, so they pick wrong courses.

text: Moving at full speed toward a fixed point causes overshoot and back-and-forth wiggle around the target; seek never slows down, so use arrive when the character must stop at a spot.
when: Character approaches a fixed target or must stop exactly at a location
why: Full speed cannot brake in time to stop on the point.

text: Conflicting constraints can cause the goal-revision loop to cycle without reaching a compromise, and the step limit then forces the deadlock fallback.
when: multiple constraints compete in a complex environment
why: Fixing one constraint can break another, so the revision loop must iterate toward a compromise.

text: Neglecting basic movement and collision handling makes characters snag on scenery or stick permanently, which players notice at once and resent.
why: When movement is the entire gameplay, poor movement directly drives player frustration.

text: If each behavior applies its own physical limits, the blended result of several behaviors is unlikely to make sense.
when: When several steering behaviors are active at once and their outputs are blended.
why: Each behavior's independent capability limits conflict once combined, so actuation has to be handled globally.

text: Removing the arrival radius rarely shows at normal frame rates but can cause instability at low frame rates, high maximum speeds, or low accelerations.
when: Arrive without a target radius, when updates are infrequent or characters are fast but weakly accelerating.
why: Slowing into the target makes overshoot oscillation unlikely under normal conditions.

text: A roll-only steering behavior lags behind the turn, which looks odd when the behavior runs only a few times per second.
when: When a roll-only behavior updates only a few times per second rather than every frame.
why: Roll is set from the measured rotation rate, so it responds after the turn has begun, causing lag.

text: Snapping facing directly to the direction of motion causes visible sudden turns.
when: Orientation is set instantly from velocity
why: Turns happen in one frame with no transition

text: Shoehorning a problem into 2.5D eventually takes longer than doing the 3D math, so past some point switching to 3D is worthwhile.
when: A problem strongly resists the 2.5D constraint.
why: Workarounds accumulate cost.

text: When the chaser is faster than its target, seek oscillates around the target; replacing the delegate with arrive avoids this.
when: When a faster pursuer uses seek against a target
why: Seek overshoots the target and reverses, while arrive slows down near it

text: At low speed the arcs must touch, since a gap makes the vehicle brake to a stop where it cannot turn, while touching at too high a speed causes a skid on a sharp turn.
when: Tuning vehicle decision arcs
why: A stopped car cannot steer, so a gap would strand targets there; at high speed a sharp turn risks skidding.

text: Straight-line distance ignores level geometry: it can pick a waypoint in an adjacent room behind a wall, or let a farther listener hear a sound first around an angled corridor.
when: Levels with thin walls, corridors close to other rooms, or angled corridors
why: Euclidean distance ignores obstacles that lengthen the actual route

text: A walk can get trapped in a small set of states, or need rarely chosen low-value action sequences to escape.
when: When the walk length is set to zero, so each iteration starts from the previous state.
why: Continuing from the last state reached keeps the walk in a small region with no exit or only low-value exits.

text: Enemies that are few, weak, or easy to kill will not herd the player, so herding with them fails.
when: When enemies are deployed to herd the player toward a designer-chosen area.

text: 1) Take the desired velocity change from the steering output. 2) Find the combination of applicable forces that gets as close to it as possible. 3) The simplest version multiplies the desired acceleration by inertia to get a force.
when: steering outputs accelerations for a physics-based character
why: A character may be unable to apply every requested acceleration.

text: 1) Update targeter goal channels in order. 2) Run decomposers in strict order, each possibly replacing the goal with a sub-goal. 3) Up to a fixed step limit, ask the actuator for a path to the goal and check constraints against it. 4) On the first violation, ask the constraint for a new goal and restart. 5) If no violation, return the actuator output; if the limit runs out, return the deadlock behavior output.
when: a valid path is needed without a full planner
why: Bounded looping with a fallback keeps behavior predictable when constraints conflict.

text: 1) Iterate groups in priority order. 2) Compute each group's blended steering. 3) Return the first result whose linear or angular magnitude exceeds epsilon. 4) If none exceed epsilon, return the final group's output. Use squared magnitude for the linear test and scale epsilon to match.
when: the number of groups is small and behavior evaluation is cheap
why: Returning the first sufficiently large result avoids evaluating lower-priority groups.

text: 1) Stop inside the target radius. 2) Outside the slowing radius, use maximum rotation; inside it, scale target rotation down linearly with the sign. 3) Set angular acceleration to target rotation minus current rotation, divided by the time-to-target constant, clipped to the maximum.

1) Measure distance to the target. 2) Desired speed equals maximum speed outside the slowing radius, zero at the target, and scales with distance between. 3) Target velocity is the unit direction to the target times desired speed. 4) Acceleration is (target velocity minus current velocity) divided by time-to-target. 5) Clip acceleration to the maximum.
why: Velocity cannot change instantly, so the acceleration is spread over a fixed time window.

text: 1) Compute the direction from the character to its target. 2) If the direction has zero length, make no change. 3) Otherwise pass the direction to the 3D align-to-vector procedure to get a target orientation.

1) Compute the direction as target position minus character position. 2) If the direction has zero length, make no change. 3) Compute the orientation from the direction components with an arctangent. 4) Store it as the align target. 5) Let align perform the steering.

1) If the character is stationary or very slow and the target is very close, step directly to it, even backward or sideways. 2) If stationary with a farther target, turn to face it, then move forward. 3) If moving with the target inside a speed-dependent forward arc, keep moving and add rotation limited by the straight-line animation. 4) If the target is outside that arc, stop, turn on the spot, and set off again.
when: Steering a human-like character to a target
why: Matches how people actually move at different speeds

text: Each frame, rotate a fixed fraction of the remaining angle toward the target heading, smoothing the change over several frames; the example rotates halfway each frame.
when: Smoothing a character's turn
why: Repeated partial turns spread the change over frames

text: 1) Know start point, end point, gravity and vertical jump velocity. 2) Solve the three position equations for flight time with the quadratic formula. 3) Take the smaller time, or the larger if its horizontal speed exceeds maximum. 4) Set horizontal velocity to horizontal displacement divided by flight time.
when: Jump onto a landing pad with vertical jump motion
why: Launch velocity is derived from the target landing point

text: 1) Cast a short ray along velocity with length set by a lookahead. 2) If no collision, return no steering. 3) Otherwise target the hit point plus wall normal times avoid distance, and seek it.
when: Character must avoid walls while moving.

text: 1) For each neighbor, compute the offset vector. 2) If distance is below the threshold, compute repulsion strength. 3) Add a unit vector pointing away, scaled by that strength. 4) Clip the summed result to maximum acceleration.

1) If stationary, accelerate. 2) If moving with the target between the arcs, brake while turning at the maximum non-skidding rate. 3) If the target is in the forward arc, accelerate toward its direction up to desired speed. 4) If in the rear arc, accelerate backward and steer toward it.
when: Choosing a vehicle action toward a target
why: Turning at the non-skid rate avoids skidding, and the target will eventually enter the forward arc, letting the car accelerate.

text: 1) Compute the target velocity minus the character velocity. 2) Divide by a time-to-target constant, 0.1 in the sample. 3) If the magnitude exceeds maximum acceleration, normalize and scale it to the maximum. 4) Set angular output to zero.
when: Implementing velocity matching

text: 1) Keep the target as a unit vector on a sphere. 2) Add a small random amount to each component and renormalize. 3) Transform by the character orientation and scale by the wander radius. 4) Offset it forward by the wander offset.
when: Wandering in three dimensions
why: Representing the target as a unit vector makes small random nudges easy, unlike quaternions which need heavy math.

text: 1) Query each steering behavior as if it were the only active one. 2) Multiply each requested acceleration by its behavior's weight and sum them. 3) Trim the sum to the character's maximum acceleration.
why: The summed acceleration may exceed what the character can deliver, so it is capped.

text: 1) Move an invisible target along the racing line using direct position updates. 2) Steer the car toward the target, for example with an arrive behavior.
when: racing or rally-style AI cars
why: The target stays ahead of the car, so steering begins early.

text: 1) Move the entity by its speed times elapsed time in its current direction. 2) If it passes a patrol bound, flip its direction. 3) Reflect its position back across that bound by the overshoot.
when: patrolling between two bounds with time-scaled movement
why: Reflection keeps the overshoot instead of discarding it when a large time slice carries the entity past a bound.

text: Without wind, search only elevation since bearing is correct. With crosswind, alternate between adjusting elevation and bearing.
when: Iterative shot targeting with or without wind
why: Elevation controls distance but not sideways landing, so a crosswind also requires correcting the bearing.

text: 1) If the current pile is lower than its right neighbor, move to the next destination. 2) If the current pile is empty, raise the level, recompute the goal, and return to the first destination. 3) Consume one dummy from the chosen destination.
when: choosing where each real run goes

text: Apply forces directly to physics-controlled characters only when forces are the sole control channel, as with vehicles; human characters are usually not force-controlled.
when: controlling a physics-based character
why: Vehicles are controlled only through drive and steering forces, while steering algorithms usually output accelerations.

text: Constraints may supply only some goal channels; channels a constraint does not specify keep their current values.
when: a constraint suggests a new goal

text: Use movement AI only when a character must travel to reach an action's target; play actions performed on the spot through animation alone.
A final actuator's heuristics must produce roughly sensible movement for any input, working from that single request alone.
when: When steering behaviors are blended or combined into a pipeline, with actuation delayed to the last step.
why: The final stage has no access to the internals of the behaviors that produced the request.

text: Steering output types must support componentwise addition and scalar multiplication for blending to work.
A general steering system should combine elements of both blending and arbitration.
when: When a moving character needs more than one steering behavior at the same time.
