why: The two methods sit at opposite ends of one spectrum rather than being mutually exclusive options.

text: When the closest-approach time is negative, the characters are already moving apart and no avoidance action is needed.
why: Negative time means the relative motion is already carrying the character away from the target.

text: When velocity is zero, do not change orientation, since there is no preferred facing.
when: Character is stationary while using velocity-based facing.
why: Velocity direction is undefined at zero speed.

text: Set the avoid distance greater than the character's radius.
when: Configuring wall avoidance.
why: Keeps the target clear of the character's body.

text: The candidate target must move forward along the path; if it is not farther along than the previous frame, push it forward.
when: Using path following targets.
why: Prevents the target from moving backward and stalling.

text: Store velocities as distance per second instead of per frame, and multiply by elapsed time when integrating.
why: Per-frame velocities break when frame rate varies

text: Combine steering behaviors rather than relying only on attractors and repulsors placed in the level.
when: Designing movement for characters in a level
why: Stuck characters cost more to fix than a more complex steering algorithm.

text: Keep each steering behavior to one job and give it only the input it needs. Build complex behaviors by combining simpler ones with a separate algorithm.
Targeters choose a single goal, so an away-from behavior such as running away must select a point to run to.
when: Designing flee-like behaviors in a pipeline
why: A flee goal names a threat to avoid rather than a place, so the pipeline still needs a concrete location for the targeter to supply.

text: Use strict 2D for fully flat worlds without vertical movement, full 3D for flight and space games where all orientations matter, and 2½D for most other cases.
when: Choosing a movement model
why: Restricting rotation to the up axis simplifies the math, and that gain is worth the lost flexibility in most cases.

text: Lower-level movement should report failure upward, such as with a stuck message, so high-level plans do not stall.
when: When a high-level plan targets a location the movement layer cannot reach from where the character stands.
why: Without feedback, the decision layer may wait on a goal that movement can never reach, causing a stalemate.

text: Flying enemies in platform games need 2.5D or 3D movement algorithms.
when: Platform games that add flying enemies.

text: Give individual behaviors hysteresis: a band of distances in which a creature does not react, so it moves only when neighbors move far away.
when: In groups where one creature's reaction to a neighbor triggers reactions in other neighbors.
why: it prevents chain reactions in the group

text: Give each direction of a link its own cost, since traversal cost can differ greatly by direction.
when: When moving one way between two nodes is cheap but the return trip is costly, as with a drop versus a climb.
why: Each connection stores its own cost, so the two directions can hold different values.

text: Use weighted blending when all concerns must always be considered at once, as in crowds and flocks; avoid it when strong constraints create conflicting goals that can stall the character.
when: Group steering with several concurrent concerns
why: Flocking and formation motion need several behaviors active simultaneously, and blending keeps all of them running together.

text: Arrive time-to-target: about 0.1 s suits a starting value, while about 0.25 s is a default; larger values brake more gently and smaller values brake abruptly.
when: Choosing or tuning arrive's time-to-target
why: Time to target sets how quickly desired speed falls near the goal.

text: Central ray with short whiskers blocks tight passages; a single ray grazes convex obstacles; parallel side rays handle obtuse corners but are prone to the corner trap.
when: When choosing a ray layout for wall avoidance
why: Each layout fails in a different geometry

text: Setting AI grip at the limit of player grip keeps AI driving realistic but means AI cars never skid, so games wanting wheel spin or handbrake turns must retune these parameters.
when: Tuning AI vehicle grip
why: The AI, not the physics, limits the car, so it stays believable and fair.

text: Commercial turn-based strategy games rarely use tree search as main AI; developers abandon minimax look-ahead and rely on heuristics alone.
when: Strategy game trees remain too large after grouping moves
why: Search cost grows too fast to reach useful decisions; search cannot cover the reduced tree.

text: Game theory analyzes moves and countermoves among players who must anticipate each other; in design it applies to individual strategy interactions, not whole games.

Turn-based and real-time strategy AI share architecture and difficulties, covering terrain analysis, influence mapping, scripted strategies, high-level planning, pathfinding, choice logic, and layered tactical and strategic levels.
Real-time strategy AI has reused much technology from military training simulators.
Turn-on-the-spot animation is usually available only to stationary or very slow characters; at walking or running speed, turning happens along a curve.
Traditionally, players give orders, and lower-level AI decides how to execute them.
Turn-based games with free movement can have almost unlimited move options per turn, even though each move is discrete.
Turn-based AI needs less execution management because fewer time-intensive tasks run at once, and its processes can run over several seconds.
For huge turn-based strategy trees, group individual moves into high-level nodes such as attack, regroup, retreat, counterattack, research or attacking a neighbouring nation, and search there.
when: Individual moves are too numerous to search
why: Strategic groupings let the top level choose among fewer options each turn, while lower levels carry out the atomic actions.

text: Strategy AI heuristics include territory controlled, proximity to enemy forces, technological superiority and population contentedness.
when: In strategy games where the game tree remains too large even after aggressive decomposition.
why: Full look-ahead is often abandoned, so heuristics must steer the search instead.

text: Turn-based games rarely need sophisticated movement algorithms; kinematic movement or direct position updates are usually enough.
A turn in a complex strategy game with 5 cities, 30 troops and side-wide choices can have around 10 to the power of 90 possible move combinations.
when: In a world-building strategy game with about five cities and thirty troop units.
why: Each city, unit and national choice multiplies the options

text: Symbolic AI, also called GOFAI, represents knowledge explicitly and makes decisions with conditional if-then rules organized in decision trees.
Criticism of symbolic AI had two sources: simple successes failed to scale to hard problems, and symbolic methods were not biologically plausible.
Practical natural-computing engineering often still relies on symbolic knowledge, such as known formulae and dictionary and grammar rules in speech recognition.
Common AI techniques for games include blackboard architectures, route planning, decision trees, state machines, and steering algorithms.
Symbolic AI was the dominant AI paradigm until the 1980s.
A symbolic system splits into a body of knowledge held as symbols and a reasoning algorithm that combines those symbols to find solutions or new knowledge.
Symbolic AI is easy to explain because its rules are explicit, while connectionist AI learns from data but is harder to explain.
why: Symbolic rules are written out explicitly, whereas connectionist systems learn patterns from data without explicit programmed rules.

text: Characters whose friends have died and who face overwhelming enemy firepower usually flee; otherwise they remain and fight.
when: after allies fall and enemy firepower overwhelms them
why: emotion and state impulses weigh against staying

text: Tactical pathfinding uses blended connection costs that include tactical concerns such as danger or visibility.
Tactical analysis stores per-location values, such as military influence, terrain difficulty or visibility, that AI decisions can query.
Waypoints can carry tactical data beyond pathfinding, so a character standing at one gains that tactical feature.
Tactical pathfinding is not inherently more complex than regular pathfinding; it uses the same algorithms and graph representation, such as A*, and only the connection cost changes.
A simple post-processing step can reduce a dense visibility graph to a usable form, though AI programmers often worry about its performance.
Hand-placing a few hundred cover points is manageable, but context-sensitive or continuous tactical values are hard for designers and need visualization tools.
Each tactic type needs its own property calculation: cover uses simulated attacks, visibility uses rays cast from the eyes, and shadow uses lighting samples.
Fully automatic tactical waypoint generation is not reliably used without some human supervision.
The formation anchor can come from a leader character, a center-of-mass estimate, or an invisible steered anchor.
when: Choosing the reference point of a formation

text: Static tactical properties such as terrain, topology, and constant lighting can be computed offline before play.
Games increasingly need groups of AI characters to cooperate, including with the player, sometimes without explicit orders.
Documented tactical topics include urban operations, wilderness movement, sniping, heavy weapons, room and building clearing, and defensive camp setup.
Base analyses output different values: an influence map gives a side, strength, and optional security; a shadow analysis gives one intensity; a gradient analysis gives one difficulty value.
Influence maps and tactical analyses naturally supply the locations for a tactical pathfinding graph, especially in outdoor levels.

Common tactical location kinds include cover, sniper, shadow, fire, power-up respawn, reconnaissance, and quick exit points, plus negative ones such as ambush hotspots, exposed areas, and sinking sand.
Platform and adventure enemy AI has not been found to use goal-oriented behavior, rule-based systems, or waypoint tactics.
So far, tactical and strategic analysis has mostly guided pathfinding, such as letting units weigh terrain complexity when routing.
Compute tactical properties offline as the usual approach; runtime computation reflects the current game context but costs more, especially with many waypoints.
when: When tactical behavior must reflect the current game context rather than fixed, precomputed properties.
why: Runtime evaluation has a significant performance cost, especially when many waypoints must be considered.

text: Automatic tactical property generation is worthwhile when designers cannot set every property by hand, or when the level is built from tiles or prefabs.
when: Levels whose tactical locations come from a tile grid or prefabricated sections, where hand-setting properties is burdensome
why: Entering numeric context values by hand is a heavy burden, while the locations already exist from the level structure but lack known properties.

text: For attack planning, strike the enemy-controlled border location with the smallest security; chains of weak points often mark a weak area, and flanks usually appear as weak spots.
when: When an AI decides to attack enemy territory and scans enemy-controlled border points on an influence map
why: Low-security border points mark thin defenses, and flank routes tend to appear among them.

text: Most shooters can afford a full set of tactical values per waypoint, whereas large outdoor RTS or massively multiplayer maps may need to economize.
when: Storing numeric tactical values per waypoint in shooters versus large outdoor RTS or massively multiplayer worlds
why: Numbers stored for every property at every waypoint add memory that grows with world size, so large outdoor worlds may need to save memory.

text: Tactical decisions need not run every frame, so the processing cost of derived tactical queries is usually acceptable.
when: Scheduling character tactical decisions
why: Decisions change less often than frames, spreading the query cost

text: Frightened agents avoid places known to be scary, while agents seeking excitement avoid boring areas.
when: When a character is trying to recover its wits after a fright

text: Military command can hold off attacking until enough forces are gathered.
Tactical analysis benefits especially from spending longer on its calculations.
when: In strategy games where AI analysis can run in background threads over several seconds
why: Players may take unlimited time to consider moves, so the AI needs deeper calculation to keep pace.

text: Storing several states per waypoint lets a situation be looked up at decision time, so no tactical calculation runs during play.
when: When fast decision making is prioritized over memory use and per-situation calculation quality

text: A positive tactic weight makes a character avoid that property, while a negative weight makes it seek the property; larger magnitude means a stronger preference.
Adding tactical terms to connection costs lets characters stay in cover and avoid enemy firing angles and typical ambush spots.
when: When characters move through levels where cover, enemy lines of fire, and ambush points matter
why: Regular pathfinding algorithms run unchanged on the same graph; only the cost function gains tactical terms.

text: Tactical analysis of the direction a player is moving can find likely escape routes, which pursuers can then block.
when: In open-world chase games where pursuers must intercept a fleeing player across a wider simulated area
why: Routing around the player's path keeps the pursuers' approach from revealing the interception.

text: Connection cost equals base cost plus, for each supported tactic, that tactic's weight multiplied by its quality for the connection.
why: Base cost alone would allow exceptionally long routes, while tactical quality alone ignores distance or time.

text: A tactical analysis server has four parts: a common API for plug-in analysis modules, weighted-sum combination defined in data files, update scheduling, and a debugging overlay.
when: When a game relies heavily on many different tactical analyses
why: A shared interface for analysis modules speeds adding new tactical concerns and makes tactic problems easier to debug.

text: Tactical analyses fall into three categories by how fast they change: static properties, slowly changing properties, and rapidly changing properties, which determines whether they are computed offline, spread across frames, or on demand.
Tactical waypoints describe very small areas, so small placement errors or short distances can change their quality sharply, such as losing cover, unlike tactical analysis maps.
when: When waypoints are generated automatically by testing candidate locations for tactical properties
why: A spot only slightly offset from a pillar can lose its cover entirely, because the tactical property covers so little area.

text: An expert cannot assume the board is unchanged between its interest check and its turn, since another expert may have removed the item it wanted.
when: When several experts share a blackboard and take turns under an arbiter that grants control
why: Control passes between experts one at a time, so other experts can change the board in the meantime.

text: Online frag-map learning depends on generalizing from known locations to unknown ones; without it, unvisited locations stay uninformed.
why: A location needs several combat experiences before its value is reasonable, so filtering must estimate the rest.

text: A formation anchor that ignores small obstacles and other characters lets members fall far behind the formation.
Approaching a narrow doorway at an acute angle can make obstacle avoidance miss the doorway entirely.
when: Characters moving at acute angles through narrow doorways in constrained indoor areas
why: Obstacle avoidance steering takes over near the walls and can push the character past the opening.

text: Basic slot schemes let any character fill any slot, so a rifle team could take a squad leader's slot or two leaders could occupy one squad.
why: Nothing constrains slot roles.

text: At an acute convex corner, the left ray turns the character left and the right ray then turns it right, so it appears to home straight into the corner.
when: When using side rays for wall avoidance near acute corners
why: Alternating ray hits cancel and the character is steered into the corner

text: Precomputed connection costs cannot reflect dynamic factors such as shifting military influence or cover from known enemies.
when: When tactical factors are dynamic, such as shifting military influence or cover from known enemies, rather than static terrain
why: Precomputed costs are stored once per set of tactic weights, so they cannot track a changing situation.

text: Terrain results computed offline become invalid if the terrain can change during play.
when: When the terrain can change during play

text: 1) Each frame, set the anchor's position, orientation, velocity and rotation to the averages of those values over its occupied slot characters.
when: formation with an anchor and slot characters
why: Slowing the formation lets slot characters catch up when they are struggling to reach their targets, instead of slowing the whole game for rare cases.

text: 1) Update a second-level analysis gradually from slow-changing data to approximate rapid data. 2) Use it to pick candidate locations. 3) Run the detailed, current check only on those candidates.
when: When a rapidly changing check is too costly to run everywhere.
why: Rapidly changing properties would force nearly the whole level to be updated each frame, which is too time-consuming, so a cheap slow analysis narrows the candidates.

text: 1) If only a few locations are needed, compute values on demand. 2) If the AI must search all locations, compute values in the background across many frames.
when: When choosing when to compute tactical values.
why: Computing every location on demand for a whole-graph search may take too long, so spreading the work across frames avoids that cost.

text: 1) Find points with cover and shadow. 2) Check nearby exposed points within the required radius of each. 3) Keep matches as ambush points.
when: Searching for ambush locations from stored primitives
why: Compound tactics are derived from primitive qualities at query time

text: 1) Start with simple tactical labels. 2) If behavior looks odd, add context sensitivity. 3) Add continuous tactical values so characters choose by waypoint quality. 4) For highly tactical games, add compound fuzzy-logic tactics.
when: Increasing tactical waypoint sophistication
why: Most games need only the early stages; later stages add effort that only tactical-focused games repay

text: 1) Choose an action such as reloading. 2) If the action needs cover, query nearby waypoints. 3) Keep waypoints that provide cover. 4) Apply post-processing checks. 5) Move to the nearest one that passes.
when: Squad-based AI seeking cover before an action
why: Nearby tactical points keep movement short while checks confirm suitability

text: 1) Overlay tactical waypoints onto a regular pathfinding graph. 2) Link each tactical location to its adjacent pathfinding nodes.
when: When tactical locations cannot easily be reached from one another
why: The regular graph lets a character travel easily between tactical spots that would otherwise be isolated from each other.

text: At decision-tree level, use tactical availability as a yes-or-no condition, such as whether any cover point exists, rather than weighing location quality.
when: When a decision node or state transition only needs to know whether a qualifying tactical location exists
why: Prevents choosing an action that has no available target.

text: Provide a debugging interface that shows any registered tactical analysis as an overlay on the level.
why: Without it, tactic problems are hard to diagnose.

text: For directional cover, count hits separately for each attack direction; during play, use real enemy positions with random offsets instead of random angles.
when: evaluating cover against specific directions
why: Pooling all hits together would hide which direction a threat comes from, and during play random directions add nothing when real enemy positions are known.

text: Trigger an attack's animation and damage only after movement has brought the character into range of its target.
when: When an attacker must first travel to its target before it can strike

text: Place the anchor a fixed distance ahead of the formation's center of mass, along its velocity, using a tuning constant.
why: Without an offset, slot targets sit so close that slot speeds drop, and the averaged formation speed sinks until the formation halts.

text: Store each tactical property per waypoint as a value, typically from 0 to 1; integers from 0 to 255 suit platforms without fast floating point.
when: When the target is short on memory or has no fast floating point unit

text: Offline learning builds the map during testing and fixes the values in the final game; online learning usually starts from a pre-learned map and keeps adapting during play.
why: Learning during testing gives a good approximation of a level's potential, and starting from pre-learned values avoids relearning obvious facts.

text: Sophisticated enemy tactics cost much effort and may matter less than enemy behavior that shapes where players go.
when: Deciding where to invest AI effort

text: Primitive tactics are basic stored waypoint qualities such as cover, visibility, shadow, and exposure.
Rally points are tactical locations used as fixed, safe retreat points for a fight that is going badly.
A playbook is a set of movement patterns a team uses in a given circumstance, covering either the whole team or a smaller group such as two players.
Rapidly changing tactical properties, such as dynamic shadows or danger, cannot be recomputed for the whole level every frame.
The minimum-based combination extends to compound tactics with many clauses and still gives a dependable value.
Proximity-based influence maps, which depend mainly on nearby enemy units and bases, make up an estimated 90% of game influence mapping, since other factors like weather usually have small effects.
Public military training manuals written for regular forces document proven tactics that can inform game behavior.
Military tactics suit any genre or setting, from historical conflicts to science fiction or medieval fantasy.
Military deployment is often hard-coded if-then logic that depends on results from a tactical analysis engine.
For rapidly changing properties, recalculate only the areas the AI plans to use, such as locations near its characters, since quality may change before the AI arrives.
when: When computing a rapidly changing tactical property.
why: Quality of distant spots may change before the AI reaches them, leaving a chosen target invalid by the time it arrives.

text: Post-processing checks suit characters that can take a couple of seconds to weigh options, and benefit squad-based shooters most.
when: Deciding whether live tactical checks are affordable
why: Slower decision cycles absorb the check cost

text: A strong tactical AI keeps units outside enemy missile range, then attacks from several flanks at once.
when: When enemy units carry missile weapons

text: An invisible anchor point that no character occupies avoids the lurching that a visible leader's dodges cause in followers, since the anchor ignores small obstacles and terrain.
when: Formation with a moving pattern
why: Followers mimic a visible leader's sideways dodges, making all slots lurch.

text: Each waypoint stores one tactical value, and a check against the current game state runs before the location is used.
when: Selecting tactical waypoints in combat
why: Live state can reveal whether a stored value still holds

text: Playbook execution combines coordinated movement, which sets the correct timing for each character, with formation motion, which makes team members move in visually realistic patterns.
Jumping to the most complex tactical waypoint stage without need adds effort that most games will not repay.
when: Planning tactical waypoint systems
why: Simple stages already suffice for most games

text: Model the decisions a sensible human would make about when each action is useful, since no single general algorithm exists.
when: For capability-sensitive steering, where each vehicle's possible actions must be chosen
why: A vehicle prefers moving forward, so weighing its available actions as a person would picks the route that avoids the obstacle.

text: Mark actions that need several characters so each participant knows it is performing them jointly.
when: When an action in a sequence needs more than one character to take part
why: Marking the action lets each participant know it is performing the action jointly, rather than acting alone.

text: Linking tactical points to the pathfinding graph is usually unnecessary, though it can be powerful in special cases.
Characters may wander far to reach sniping points, and players usually do not mind this.
when: Characters seeking sniper positions
why: Players tolerate long movement when it fits a sniper's role

text: Enemies may make a risky run past the player to reach a flanking position.
when: when a flanking position is available
why: flanking is valued enough to accept danger

text: A chase targeter sets the goal ahead of the victim's position by the victim's velocity multiplied by a lookahead parameter.
Muzzle speed is the scalar speed at which a projectile leaves the weapon; it has no direction, which is supplied separately by the firing direction.
Shooter enemies are either bots with physical abilities like the player's, or cannon fodder that is simpler and more numerous.
Assistive AI lets the player hand decision tasks to the AI, which uses the same decision infrastructure as enemy forces.
when: turn-based games

text: Shooting AI has two requirements: firing accurately and responding to incoming fire.
Straight-line aiming tests work reasonably well for fast projectiles over short distances.
when: fast projectiles over short distances

text: With physics-simulated projectiles, trajectory prediction is a core part of shooter AI.
Target-state and action accessors read the stored target and return nothing when no decision has been made.
Slowly changing tactical properties, such as RTS influence or city fire and police coverage, can be updated gradually, reconsidering only a handful of locations each frame.
For a sniper point, Boolean flags can record whether enemies have fired toward the location, a rough sign that the enemy knows it is there.
when: Validating sniper waypoints
why: Enemy fire toward a location suggests the position has been discovered

text: Shooters viewed from first or third person are the most commercially significant genre, and their AI centers on movement and firing.
Pathfinding is needed for complex enemies or bots, while tactical AI handles safe positions, ambushes and advanced tactics.
Movement and firing are key in every shooter; later needs become expected in sophisticated shooters and support good critical reception.
Supporting shooter AI systems include line-of-sight checks, waypoint tactics or frag-maps, a scripting language, kinematic movement, and an animation controller.
Thumbstick aiming was long thought to make console shooters inferior to mouse-controlled PC shooters until aim assist showed that console aiming could be made playable.
when: Designing aiming for thumbstick-controlled shooters
why: Indirect assistance proved that console controls could be competitive with mouse aiming.

text: Assistance types include jump assist for safe landings, attack assist for clean hits, driving assist to avoid spinning out, and movement assist for ledges and obstacles.
when: Designing assistance beyond aiming
why: Assistance can help many actions, not only aiming, and each form should help without misjudging intent.

text: Narrow an enemy's aiming window as the score rises, so accuracy grows with player progress.
when: Shooter-style games where enemies aim at the player.
why: A perfectly accurate enemy would be unenjoyable, so limiting its shots to a range of possibilities keeps the challenge fair.

text: When a character intends to catch an object, aim the target height near chest level, otherwise the object appears to drop at its feet.
when: Predicting a catch point
why: Catching at the feet looks unnatural

text: Start with a window of about 4 actions for typical use, then tune it by trial and error.
when: choosing a window size for a new predictor
why: Formal models for choosing the window need input statistics that are hard to obtain, and games rarely use them.

text: Platform game enemies use obvious, learnable patterns that players can exploit.
when: Designing platform game enemies
why: Platform games target a younger audience, so patterns are kept obvious.

text: Enemies can lower their defenses for a few seconds after attacking, giving the player a window to strike back.
when: Designing enemy attack timing
why: Designers want enemies that are interesting yet predictable, so observing them and exploiting their weaknesses pays off for the player.

text: Use an influence map of controlled areas to find a safe spot for an important building.
when: When picking a location for an important building in an RTS game.
why: The map records which areas are controlled, so a safe site can be read off directly.

text: Enemies that respond to player style produce low risk for careful play, such as picking enemies off, and strong pushback for reckless charging, which is likely fatal.
when: When enemy response is tied to player behavior
why: Pressure scales with how aggressively the player acts

text: Widening an enemy's firing window makes it easier to survive; narrowing it makes it harder, so the window works as a tunable difficulty variable.
why: Random shots within a bounded window miss more often as the window widens and hit more often as it narrows.

text: Slowing incoming projectiles lets the player see them and dodge, which keeps high enemy accuracy from overwhelming the player.
when: When enemy shots are so accurate that the player cannot react to them.
why: Visible, slower shots give the player time to see them coming and move out of the way.

text: Aim assist strength depends on target distance, angular offset, other nearby targets, difficulty setting, and weapon.
when: Tuning aim assist strength
why: Each factor changes how much correction the player needs and how noticeable it becomes.

text: Shooter AI has four key needs: movement, firing, decision making (usually simple state machines), and perception of whom to shoot and where they are.
when: In first and third person shooters.

text: Shooter AI architecture combines decision making, movement, tactical and strategic AI, and pathfinding.
Testing cover only at a single point height misses cover that protects against low attacks but not high ones.
when: evaluating cover

text: Making an enemy simply smarter and tougher can produce an opponent players cannot beat in a satisfying way, and an opponent that keeps getting tougher becomes one players almost never win.
when: When raising enemy difficulty
why: Unbeatable opponents stop being fun

text: Enemy fire that is too accurate overwhelms the player and reads as unfair.
when: shooters with fast projectiles
why: the player has no realistic chance to react

text: 1) Fire rays from numerous attacker spots arranged on a ring around the candidate point, adding random offsets and a constant angle increment. 2) Throw out spots lying beyond the room's boundary. 3) Point each ray at a random location inside a volume sized like a human. 4) Dividing successful hits by total iterations yields the cover score.
when: measuring cover quality when accuracy outweighs runtime cost
why: Testing many attack angles catches cover that one sight-line check would overlook.

text: 1) Use a narrow fan while moving freely. 2) On a collision, widen the fan. 3) If collisions continue on successive frames, keep widening. 4) When trapped, pick one ray as the winner and ignore other rays' collisions for a while.
when: When wall avoidance rays must handle both passages and corner traps
why: Adjusting the fan to the situation balances passage blocking against corner trapping

text: Use a transition matrix for each shot that sets the fired-from value low and raises the others slightly, then apply a recovery matrix over quiet time to restore values.
when: tuning position safety for a sniper
why: Shooting alerts the enemy to one position, lowering its safety, while the enemy's focus moves away from the others.

text: 1) Assemble outside the doorway. 2) Throw a grenade, stun if non-combatants may be present, lethal otherwise. 3) Move the first member along the near wall to a corner. 4) Move the second member to the adjacent corner. 5) Others cover the room center. Every member fires at visible targets while moving.
when: Squad clearing a room through a door
why: Corner positions give cover while the team enters and covers the interior

text: 1) Assume every legal layout consistent with prior results is equally likely. 2) For each square, count layouts covering it. 3) Divide by total layouts. 4) Shoot at the highest-probability square, breaking ties arbitrarily.
when: building a hidden-information guessing AI
why: picks the square most likely to hit given results so far

text: 1) Track moving targets by replacing part of the stick input with motion matching the target. 2) On stick release over a target, slide the crosshair onto it during deceleration. 3) When a sweep would pass a target, bend its direction slightly, not its speed.
when: Building aim assist for console shooters
why: Each subsystem acts in moments the player cannot detect, so assistance stays hidden.

text: Assistive modules should rely minimally on player strategy, which is hard to infer; lacking it, they may pick safe options conflicting with the player's long-term plan.
when: designing assistive decision modules
why: the player's strategy is hard to infer by observation

text: Each targeter sets one channel (position, orientation, velocity or rotation), and only one targeter may set each channel. Unset channels are don't-care.
when: Designing steering pipeline targeters
why: The steering algorithm does not check for overwrites, so it depends on targeters cooperating.

text: Terrain difficulty combines a base cost for each terrain type with a ruggedness value estimated from height samples.
Terrain analysis is the military simulation and game AI term for a very similar technique, but it covers only one kind of tactical analysis.
Terrain types such as rivers, swamp, grassland, mountains and forest have difficulty that varies by unit; their type value can be used directly without analysis.
Terrain difficulty suits movement costs in pathfinding; because it is cheap, it needs little optimization when terrain is static.
when: terrain is static

text: Use automatic topological analysis only for the simplest tactical queries; for richer needs, have level designers specify tactical locations.
why: automated analysis is hard to get right

text: A time cell that increases by 1 each iteration, with other values updating from game state, models time-dependent effects within one run.
when: Modeling time-dependent behavior in a spreadsheet via iterative calculation
why: Iterative calculation lets a circular reference resolve over a capped number of passes instead of raising an error.

text: A task scheduler decides which tasks run on which frame, handling tasks with different execution frequencies and durations, so the workload stays smooth without large peaks.
Timing errors from moving listeners are rarely noticed for sound but can matter greatly for smell.
Each of the two instability checks is a single linear scan over part of a preference list.
Integer counts can replace probabilities when computing search tree cost, since only the relative sizes of the weights matter.
Among actions with equal priority, order by increasing expiry time so actions nearest to expiring sit at the front, which gives a marginal performance gain.
when: Priorities tie
why: Equal-priority order is otherwise undefined

text: Schedule the most difficult task early, because its constraints narrow the options left for the remaining tasks.
No group cost method is correct everywhere. The best trade-off for a game usually comes from tweaking the costs and testing the resulting paths.
why: Every candidate method has failure cases that cannot be eliminated, so the best choice comes from evaluating its errors.

text: Find a frequency's set by hashing, or by direct array indexing when every frequency up to a maximum has a set.
when: When a set exists for every frequency up to a maximum value.

text: For many agents at one frequency, assigning each a distinct phase, even beyond the frequency, is less error-prone than fixed phases.
when: Many agents sharing a frequency.
why: Changing the frequency alone will not stop a behaviour from running.

text: A timed random decision stores its choice with the frame it was made, redraws the choice when the stored choice is stale or a timeout passes, so a behavior varies over time instead of persisting forever.
when: A behavior should vary over time
why: Prevents an agent staying in one state indefinitely

text: A counter that resets every second lets a slow player cross one noisy surface safely, while two noisy steps within one second trigger an alert.
when: Scripted noise detection with a one-second reset.
why: The reset window defines how much noise is tolerated per second.

text: Hierarchical search takes O(plm) time for p levels, with l and m as defined in the source, and O(1) memory beyond A*. Good hierarchies can make search about two orders of magnitude faster on graphs of tens of thousands of nodes.
when: For large graphs of tens of thousands of nodes.
why: Each level runs a much smaller search than one raw search, so practical performance is far higher.

text: The basic frequency scheduler needs constant O(1) memory and linear O(n) time, with n denoting the count of behaviours.
A hierarchical partition splits space into a few regions and recursively subdivides any region holding more than a maximum number of objects, typically into two, four, or eight parts.
when: When a region still holds more objects than a set maximum.

text: A behaviour repeatedly interrupted before returning a result, e.g. by thread synchronisation, may leave its character standing still; tiny processing changes can trigger this and it is hard to debug.
when: Interruptible processes that never get enough time.
why: Thread switches can keep cutting the behaviour off before any output is produced, so nothing updates the character.

text: Clearing suspension on any database change fails when game code writes to the database every frame, because suspension is constantly lifted while the triggering data stays stable.
when: When world data is written to the database every frame while the data that triggers the rule stays stable
why: Any write counts as a change, so unrelated constant churn keeps lifting suspension for a rule whose trigger data never moves.

text: Assigning each character in turn its lowest-cost slot can leave some character until last with no sensible slot left.
when: Naive greedy assignment
why: Early choices consume slots that later characters need

text: With very frequent changes, even incremental replanning can overwhelm the pathfinder.
when: When the environment changes unpredictably or its information is incomplete

text: Hierarchical search locks in the high-level route, so a shortcut visible only at a lower level is never found. The error comes from the single link cost chosen per group.
why: No single value can represent every route through a node group, so it is wrong for some routes.

text: Ignoring the time dimension in continuous planning reintroduces path-dependent costs that A* cannot handle.
when: Planning with timing-sensitive connections.
why: Costs then depend on the path taken to reach a node.

text: Frequencies sharing divisors, such as 2, 4 and 8, run together, leaving some frames empty and others overloaded.
when: When behavior frequencies share a common divisor under frame-count modulo scheduling
why: Coinciding runs cluster work onto the same frames.

text: Changing access statistics can change the optimal tree, because its shape depends on the frequencies.
1) Request the wake-up action when leaving the sleep state. 2) Request the go-to-sleep action when entering it. 3) Wait for the animation to finish without continual processing.
when: When states involve timed animations or movement.
why: Continual per-frame requests force extra transition states that multiply rapidly as more states are added.

text: 1) Place markers at predefined points on the racing line. 2) When the character reaches a marker, schedule a trick of a given duration.
when: Scheduling animated tricks during jumps

text: 1) Predict the likely airtime of the jump. 2) Schedule a trick whose duration fits that airtime.
when: Scheduling tricks without fixed markers

text: 1) Fix start and end locations at every level. 2) Restrict each lower-level search to nodes inside the groups of the high-level plan. 3) Run the search over only those nodes.
when: the complete detailed plan is needed up front
why: the restriction shrinks the search dramatically

text: 1) Increment the frame count on each call. 2) For each behaviour, run it when the frame count plus its phase is divisible by its frequency, using modulo on integers.
why: Integer modulo is very fast on current hardware, keeping the check cheap.

text: 1) Build a top-level graph of indoor sectors linked by portals. 2) Plan long routes between sectors. 3) Compute a navigation mesh route inside each sector.
when: Games set primarily indoors whose levels are divided into sectors separated by portals
why: fine routes are only needed within the sectors on the long route

text: Suspend a rule as soon as it fires, and lift the suspension when the database changes.
when: For rules that must not keep firing endlessly while the database is unchanged
why: Stops a rule from firing repeatedly without changes.

text: Give actions that involve animation or movement a duration, rather than having the decision maker re-request them every frame.
when: When an action takes time to complete.
why: Re-requesting the action every frame keeps the decision system constantly processed, making it more complex than needed.

text: A hierarchical scheduler must run the right behavior in the right order, and only when that behavior is required.
when: When multi-tier AI has layers that pass orders downward

text: Include an object only if the total weight stays within the limit; otherwise abandon extending the current selection.
when: When selecting objects to maximise total value within a limit on total weight
why: The unpruned search has 2^n candidate sets, so acceptability checks cut the candidates drastically.

text: The basic frequency scheduler suits tens or hundreds of behaviours at small frequencies, but wastes checks when many behaviours always run together.
when: With tens or hundreds of behaviors at fairly small frequencies

text: Different party compositions give different total costs, so one formation can handle a wide range of characters.
Simple gameplay can still demand varied AI behavior, since agents react differently to the same frights.
Individual units make small tactical choices, such as a ranged unit deciding whether to hold position or advance to engage.
Using tactical analysis to find weak points and strike them with the whole army is widely discussed but seldom built into games.
Position, orientation and velocity matching are simple steering behaviors that each match one kinematic element of a target, taking the character and target kinematics as input.
when: When a steering behavior must match more than one kinematic element of a target at once
why: Matching several elements at once can make them conflict, since matching velocity stops the character closing distance.

text: Each unit has one designer-set military influence value, which can differ from its offensive or defensive strength; a reconnaissance unit may have high influence with little combat power.
1) Start evolution from weapons that shoot straight lines. 2) Let NEAT add nodes with functions such as Gaussian and sine. 3) Get more varied particle movement over generations.
when: evolving particle weapons with NEAT
why: Added nodes diversify motion from simple starting behaviour.

text: Make units obey orders exactly, immediately and the same way each time so players can build complex strategies on them.
when: strategy games where players direct groups of units
why: Consistent responses let the player, rather than the AI, determine outcomes

text: Giving units an unpredictable inner life makes battles swing randomly and shifts outcomes from the player to the AI, while automaton-like units keep planning meaningful.
when: In real-time strategy games where players plan around predictable unit behaviour
why: Complex internal AI would make identical battles swing randomly, letting the AI rather than the player decide outcomes.

text: Minimizing predicted total discontentment can pick an action that does not touch the highest goal when it avoids creating a larger new need.
when: An action has side effects on other goals
why: Total discontentment counts every goal's predicted value

text: Blended weights let a squad cross modestly rough ground that is fairly far from enemies when constraints are preferences.
when: Squad movement with soft terrain preferences
why: Soft constraints allow compromise where risk is low

text: The predicted change in insistence serves as a heuristic estimate of action utility; the selection inverts it so the most reducing action has the highest utility.
Situation classification groups game inputs, such as enemy distance, friend health and ammo, into behavior categories learned from examples.
The same action can sit at several leaves, so many different input combinations can produce one behavior.
Physical and emotional parameters, such as hunger, can serve directly as goal insistence values.
Each available action is rated against every goal, and one action can reduce one goal's insistence while raising another's.
Simple GOB selection makes two maximum-style passes, one over goals and one over actions.
Simple selection gives surprisingly sensible results in games with few actions, such as shooters, third-person action, adventure, and RPGs.
Single-character decision making serves one character and does not predict the whole situation from what it knows.
A single dividing point cannot treat a band of values differently from values above and below that band.
Human actions influence each other over short spans, so longer sequences mostly arise from shorter ones and add randomness rather than signal.
In a zero-sum game, a board's score for one player is exactly the negative of its score for the opponent.
No general agreement exists on the best transposition table replacement strategy; different games probably need different strategies, so experimentation is needed.
Probabilistic methods such as Markov models are more common in RTS AI than in most other genres.
Show the reason for an action, such as a broken switch or a waiting colleague, because a short glimpse rarely gives enough context.
when: When a player only glimpses an AI character briefly
why: A brief glimpse does not give enough time to see the character's context, so its actions look faulty.

text: Balancing matters most for large trees or equally likely outcomes; otherwise shape the tree around outcome frequency and decision cost.
when: When all behaviors are equally likely
why: Balanced branches keep the number of decisions needed to reach any behavior small and uniform.

text: The simplest time-aware method makes the discontentment calculation return lower values for shorter actions, all else being equal.
when: When pathfinding to time every candidate action is impractical
why: Exact timing for each candidate would need costly pathfinding, so a heuristic stands in for it.

text: A tree whose root is a single action always returns that action, which is useful for prototyping.
when: Prototyping an agent

text: Prefer decision trees or state machines when they can produce the required behavior, which is almost always possible; rule systems are more than most games need.
when: designing character decision making
why: simpler structures are easier to build and debug

text: Increasing a point's weight enlarges its domain, so weighted domains let designers set region size.
why: A higher weight steepens the cone's slope, so the cone's share of the map grows.

text: A single rule whose priority scales with a value, such as health, rises gradually, whereas separate rules for ranges switch suddenly at their boundaries.
when: When a rule's importance depends on a continuously varying value such as health
why: Separate range rules would each carry a fixed priority, so the top rule would change abruptly at each boundary.

text: Counting drift during an action's duration can reverse choices: a short action fixing an urgent need may beat a long action that lets another need rise sharply meanwhile.
when: Goals rise on their own at different rates and actions take different times
why: A long action lets unrelated needs grow, and the prediction reflects that growth

text: Characters built from standard AI goals and sensor-triggered behaviors can carry a story forward while their choices follow a designer-encoded tension curve.
when: Building a dialogue-driven simulation
why: Choices are checked against a designer-encoded tension timeline, so the story keeps its pacing while goals are pursued.

text: Simple GOB selection takes O(n + m) time for n goals and m actions, and O(1) memory.
why: It runs two separate max-style scans, one over goals and one over actions, using only temporary storage.

text: Predicted goal value equals current goal value plus the action's direct change plus the goal's natural rate of change multiplied by the action's duration.
when: Scoring actions in a utility system where goals change over time
why: Natural drift during an action changes the state the action leaves behind

text: Time-aware utility needs O(1) extra memory and O(nm) time, and stays SIMD-friendly with a couple of extra operations.
when: Goal values are stored in arrays
why: Stored-value lookups map well onto SIMD hardware, though they add a couple of operations over the basic form.

text: A matrix with 1.0 on the diagonal and 0.1 elsewhere, applied once per minute without gunfire, makes safety values increase over time.
when: In a game where safety should recover while no shots are fired
why: A realistic model would keep every location unsafe, which a game may not want.

text: A single decision can test whether a Boolean is true, match one value of an enumeration, check that a number lies in a range, or check that a vector's length lies in a range.
why: Different data types need different comparison logic, so separate decision forms exist for each type.

text: A complex evaluation runs many scoring mechanisms, each detecting one feature, and combines their results into one score, most simply as a weighted sum with fixed weights.
Changing weights can make a distant domain bulge into a wrong area, so display the domains to check for overlaps.
when: When weighted Dirichlet domains are assigned by hand
why: Altered slopes can let a cone spill into another point's area, which complicates pathfinding debugging.

text: Small changes in one input can decide between a sensible and a foolish action, so tests should target the values that matter.
why: A method grouping many inputs under one action must let only the significant values change the output.

text: Choosing the best single action at each step can fail when actions consume shared resources, because the greedy pick can block a better combination.
when: Actions share limited resources
why: Greedy choice ignores what later actions need

text: Simple selection ignores the side effects an action has on other goals.
Simple selection has no timing information, so it cannot tell short actions from long ones.
Time spent choosing which behaviour to run must be deducted from the time passed to the behaviour; the basic version omits this.
why: Otherwise the frame budget is overrun.

text: 1) For each attacker, measure the largest free angle among opponents within its shot cone. 2) Score each attacker by that angle. 3) Choose the highest-scoring target.
when: Choosing a passing or shooting target

text: 1) Find the goal with the largest insistence. 2) Among available actions, choose the one that fully fulfils that goal or gives the largest drop in its insistence. 3) Break ties at random or by taking the first action found.
why: The promised drop in insistence is a heuristic estimate of an action's utility to the character.

text: 1) For each legal move, apply it to get the resulting position. 2) Score that position. 3) Choose the move with the highest score.
when: only with a perfect evaluation
why: a perfect evaluation makes lookahead unnecessary

text: 1) Compute a stop threshold from your score and the opponent's score. 2) Keep rolling while the turn total is below the threshold. 3) Stop once the turn total reaches or exceeds it.
when: deciding when to end a turn in the dice game Pig

text: Score tactical qualities as real values, since a Boolean yes-or-no will not support condensation.
when: When a condensation step filters candidate locations by tactical quality
why: Discarding locations by threshold needs graded values, which a yes-or-no judgement cannot provide.

text: Rely on tested, reusable methods for movement, decision making and tactics instead of reinventing them for each game.
why: Relying on hacks alone forces each game to rebuild the same solutions from scratch.

text: A weight of zero effectively switches a steering behavior off.
when: When steering behaviors are combined by weighted blending

text: Even a simple first-in first-out action queue provides the debugging benefit of centralizing actions.
when: Centralizing actions without a full manager.
why: A single entry point is enough to log all actions.

text: With one goal, every plan must fully fulfil that goal, and the planner should select the plan with the lowest total cost.
when: Planning for a single goal
why: A single goal plus one cost value to minimise lets the A* search be used to drive the planner.

text: Use SIMD-friendly discontentment evaluation for small goal and action sets; use simple selection for large sets.
when: With small numbers of actions and goals, and suitable optimisations applied
why: The calculation suits SIMD hardware, which speeds it up; without that, large sets make it slower.

text: Adopting time-aware prediction requires goals to provide a rate-of-change method and actions to provide a duration method; only the discontentment calculation changes.
when: Upgrading an existing utility-based decision system
why: Goals drift at their own rate, so the expected value after an action adds that rate multiplied by the action's duration.

text: Run condensation separately for each tactical property, so a waypoint is not removed because a waypoint for a different tactic is nearby.
The weakest-member rule (take each category's worst value) suits hard constraints that must never be violated; blended weights suit soft preferences that can be traded off.
when: Choosing how to combine squad member concerns
why: No single member has the blended concerns, so the worst value gives a safe approximation; hard constraints must never be violated, while soft preferences can be traded off.

text: Modelling shared resources as extra motives can fix ordering conflicts, but many permanent effects such as doors, traps, and alerts would need thousands of extra motives.
when: In a game with many hundreds of permanent effects such as doors, traps, and alerts

text: Sequences run their elements strictly in order, whereas compound actions can mix parallel and sequential parts; allowing compound actions inside sequences combines both at any depth.
when: structuring character actions

text: A weighted sum can combine layers instead of multiplying them, but it must avoid placing value on another side's territory.
when: When combining several analysis layers into one value for a location

text: Tilting the base orientation with turn rate can make a character lean into its turns.
when: When the character's rotation rate is high

text: A physics-driven car follows its defined racing line by driving, so it may fail to reach the line after being nudged by another car.
when: Especially when the car has been nudged by another car
why: The racing line is not a rail, so the car must reach it through physics inputs, which can fail after a nudge.

text: An open-world game can simulate only the area near the player and inject vehicles at suitable positions when pursuers are needed.
when: In a sandbox driving game where police or enemy pursuers must home in on the player
why: simulating the whole world is costly

text: A large satisfaction radius alone can make the stop look abrupt; pair it with slowing.
when: Arrive uses a large radius without slowing
why: The character halts from speed when entering the radius

text: 1) Measure the track's free extent ahead to the left and right. 2) Measure nearby vehicles. 3) Feed both to a hand-written Markov state machine that chooses the next action.
when: Racing AI using fuzzy decision making instead of racing lines
why: Players judge driving AI by how well the car is driven, so movement quality matters more than goal or route reasoning.

text: Because small random turn values dominate, a wandering character usually keeps its direction, and sharp direction changes remain possible but rare.
when: Kinematic wander running
why: Near-zero rotation values are most likely

text: Wander keeps a character roaming without a destination by placing a target on a circle ahead of it and seeking that target.
when: Character should roam without a fixed goal
why: The orientation is kept between calls, so it changes smoothly even though the target jitters around the circle.

text: A wait carries an identifier and halts its script until a signal with the matching identifier arrives.
Place a wander behavior in the lowest-priority group to provide a fallback that can break unstable equilibria.
when: When characters can get stuck in equilibria between behaviors
why: Wander moves the character out of positions where higher-priority behaviors cancel

text: Use a smaller radius for the vertical component than for horizontal ones so the wanderer turns up and down more slowly, suiting flying creatures.
when: Wandering flying creatures with an up axis along y
why: A smaller vertical radius limits how fast the target moves up and down.

text: Targets near the circle's edges make the character turn quickly, so it spends more time turning in either direction.
when: Wander target placement on the circle
why: The angle subtended by the circle edges sets turning speed.

text: Wander is controlled by four parameters: wander offset, wander radius, wander rate and maximum acceleration, and costs O(1) time and memory.
Setting maximum rotation near the physical maximum produces twitchy turning rather than a leisurely meander.
when: Tuning wander turn rate
why: Large rotation per frame makes turns abrupt

text: 1) Place a circle ahead of the character at the wander offset along its facing. 2) Each frame, change the wander orientation by a random binomial value scaled by the wander rate. 3) Set the target as the circle center plus the radius along the target orientation. 4) Face the target. 5) Accelerate at maximum along the current facing.
when: Implementing wander steering

text: 1) Wander until the protagonist is spotted. 2) Home in on it using seek or pursue.
when: Enemies that wander freely until they notice the player

text: While a script waits for a signal, run a waiting action such as an idle behavior so the character does not freeze.
when: While a script is blocked on a wait element
why: A wait halts the script until a matching signal arrives, so without a fallback action the character would sit still.

text: Window size is the number of most recent choices used to match against the stored history when predicting the next choice.
A zero-width alpha-beta window tests whether the true score equals a guessed value. It prunes almost all branches, so it is very fast but loses useful branches if the guess is wrong.
Raw probability prediction is equivalent to an N-gram predictor with a zero-length window.
With more choices, the minimum useful window grows, and with five choices a 3-action window was noticeably weaker than a 4-action window.
Each likely window needs several visits before its prediction is reliable, so longer windows can look poor for a long time.
Mathematical models can estimate the best window size, but game practice commonly tunes it by trial and error.
In a two-choice experiment with 1000 trials, predictive power peaked at a window of 5, but a window of 3 captured most of it with fewer samples.
when: In a two-option guessing game with a sequence of about 1000 trials
why: A smaller window keeps most of the predictive power while needing far fewer training samples.

text: Each extra window action multiplies the probabilities to store by the number of choices, doubling them with two choices and tripling them with three.
In the air, horizontal acceleration uses separate values, the run modifier has no effect, and steering is reduced while running speed can carry through a jump.
when: a character is airborne with horizontal momentum
why: Airborne control is intentionally limited, and existing speed persists.

text: A character can be clumsy on the ground yet expressive in the air, letting airborne traversal carry most of the feel.
Slower air movement with retained control gives precise adjustment for landing on small platforms.
when: A character moves differently on ground and in the air
why: Reduced air speed with some steering lets players aim landings without full mobility

text: Near the apex, raise gravity to roughly three times normal to shorten the hang time of the jump.
when: When the jump arc has completed, after the apex
why: Strong downward pull cuts the time the player has reduced control, and makes the fall feel weightier.

text: Horizontal and vertical motion form two mostly separate subsystems, and their interplay produces much of the expressive feel.
Use stronger gravity whenever the character moves downward, including at the jump peak, after walking off a ledge, and after a ceiling hit.
why: Using the same gravity for rising and falling makes jumps last too long and feel light and out of control.

text: Trigger slow motion when a vehicle rises above a set height, so airborne stunts are emphasized.
when: When a vehicle flies a set height above the environment in a stunt.

text: An animation action plays an animation and updates game state; it is often the only primitive several characters can perform together, tagged with unique identifiers showing joint versus parallel action.
Second-order motion is motion produced by the player's action beyond the direct input, such as a tool head swinging widely from a small wrist turn.
Movement requests become visible action through animation or physics simulation, and animation is normally part of the graphics engine rather than AI code.
Characters have sets of animations, such as walk, run, sprint, and turns made while walking, on the spot, or crouched.
Each animation suits only a range of velocities; a walk cycle needs a matching travel rate or the feet appear to slide.
The range of believable combinations of position and orientation is much smaller than the range of believable velocities.
Procedurally generating animations to fill gaps is an open problem, so most developers rely on a modest set of authored animations.
Momentum in many games exists only within animations rather than as a simulated property.
Most natural actions follow an arc or slightly circular path, like a swinging pendulum, including arm movement, head turns and eye movement.
Hybrid models let animation drive ragdolls and ragdolls drive animation, so colliding characters can transition into believable active ragdolls.
when: for humanoid collisions

text: Organic, complex, fluid motion following curved arcing paths rather than rigid straight lines tends to feel more appealing than simple, uniform motion.
why: Natural bodies move along arcs like pendulums, which makes curved paths read as more natural.

text: Convey much of a character's behavior through animation rather than complex cognition.
why: Triggering an animation at the right moment needs no cognitive model, unlike expressing emotion through actions.

text: Adventure game AI relies more on animation than on other cues to show what a character is doing.
when: Adventure game enemies

text: When the scales tip late in a game, let the win be dramatic and wrap it up quickly.
when: Outcome becomes clear late in play
why: A decisive finish satisfies the winner and spares the loser a prolonged, drawn-out defeat.

text: Make object motion consistent and predictable first, since motion carries more weight than other cues in building a convincing physical world.
why: Motion has the strongest effect on perceived physicality.

text: In emergencies, cut a full animation short for a rapid turn and blend a couple of frames into the new animation to avoid a visible jump.
when: Interrupting character animations abruptly.
why: Abrupt animation switches look jarring without blending.

text: Animation should enhance and emphasise the simulation rather than drive it.
when: designing character animation for physics-based movement
why: Keeping the simulation authoritative prevents animation from breaking the feel of motion.

text: Use a few key poses to set both the path a body moves along and its shape, so slowing, reversal and return read with very few frames.
why: Each pose fixes both where the body sits and how it is shaped, so the motion reads from few frames.

text: Animating a simulated object, including the body's response to a heavy attached object, conveys weight and presence the simulation lacks; the player perceives that weight as part of the motion.
when: When a visual animation layers over a simulated object that drives its movement.
why: The animated visual becomes the object in the player's mind.

text: Identical animation repeated many times becomes tiresome and erodes control even when quality is high, because real motion is never exactly repeated and recurrence without subtle variation looks wrong.
why: Perception expects real motion never to repeat exactly, so recurrence without variation looks wrong.

text: Continuous distances and speeds from animations create a state graph with infinitely many connections, since each distinct value is a separate state.
when: movement planning uses animation-driven transitions
why: Animation plays across a span of distances and speeds, letting it transition to many neighbouring states.

text: Animation can impose speed ranges, such as walk at 0.8 to 1.2 m/s and jog at 2.0 to 4.0 m/s, with no speeds available between them.
when: Character movement is driven by discrete animations.
why: Only the animated speed bands are reachable.

text: Playing an animation faster covers slightly faster motion, but beyond a point the movement looks unbelievable.
when: scaling playback rate of a locomotion animation
why: Each animation is authored for a particular speed range.

text: A walk can change into a run only at suitable points, so transition timing constraints give each movement a natural length.
why: Transitions fire only at a matching point in a cycle, and stopping mid-animation can look wrong.

text: At 60 fps, fast-moving on-screen motion visibly breaks into discrete positions instead of looking smooth.
when: When fast-moving content is displayed at a refresh rate of about 60 fps.

text: Keyframe animation governs perception until a stronger force, such as a tackle, hands control to the physics simulation, as in ragdoll solutions.
when: Blending keyframed animation with physical simulation.
why: Whichever source is driving the motion determines what the player perceives.

text: Changing animation alters perceived speed without changing actual velocity, so slow-feeling backward movement can be fixed through animation.
when: When players report that backward movement in a third-person camera game feels too slow.

text: Vivid animation of small-scale actions, such as a unit consuming a target, makes early scenes satisfying and gives them strong game feel.
when: In the introductory levels that teach a game's systems.

text: A mechanic that locks input for about 900 ms while an animation plays fails the real-time control response threshold.
when: When further input is locked until a single animation finishes.
why: Input locked during playback breaks the continuity that real-time control needs.

text: A character's standing-to-full-run transition can take about 900 milliseconds when driven by animation, which players feel as sluggish.
when: animation-driven movement
why: Input-to-movement lag is felt as awkward, and the animation itself is what delays the start.

text: Animation principles such as squash and stretch and overlapping action are broadly applicable standards for conveying physical interaction.
why: They let animators directly shape how viewers perceive an object's physical nature.

text: Smooth animation, metaphor and input mapping can hide short control breaks, but a game may look fluid while failing real-time control tests because it masks unresponsive control.
why: Real-time control is judged by the player's perception, so masking a break can preserve their sense of control.

text: Acrobatic enemy movement is hard to keep synchronized with animation.
when: Enemies with many acrobatic moves such as cartwheels, vaults and leaps
why: Many simultaneous movement abilities multiply the animation states that must stay matched, making basic travel hard to sync.

text: A single canned failure animation that plays back identically every time quickly loses its appeal.
when: Crashes and failure states, which players encounter frequently
why: Players spend much of their time in failure states, so repeated identical results there are quickly noticed.

text: Suggest eased pendulum-like motion with predetermined frames spaced closer at the apex, easing out there and reversing with a snappy turn, instead of simulating physics, to convey weight.
when: After a hook connects and the character enters a swinging state
why: Spacing frames closer at the arc's end signals speed change without tracking acceleration or velocity.

text: Emphasize good motions by attaching goals to them and remove bad motions with constraints.
when: Exploring a new control mapping.
why: Goals reward good motion while constraints prune poor ones.

text: Make second-order motion produced by player actions powerful and interesting to watch and to control.
Model the avatar as a non-rotating rectangle moving freely on a 2D plane, so its local and global movement are identical.
why: With no rotation, the avatar's local axes already match the world axes.

text: Make dropped pickups bounce on decaying parabolic arcs that slow at the top, so they read as physical objects.
when: When destroying certain enemies spawns pickups
why: Decaying bounces that lose momentum match how real dropped objects behave.

text: When a single frame's direction change exceeds about 90 degrees, stop the character briefly, play a foot plant, then move in the new direction.
when: Sharp reversal while running
why: A plant sells the weight of a hard turn

text: Let a jump press during a foot plant convert it into a special somersault move.
when: Character is in a foot plant state

text: Sync character animation to speed, jumps and landings, with leaning into turns and planting feet, so motion reads as a physical body.
Animate a near-opposite input with a planted foot and slight slide before reversing, while the underlying motion stays unchanged.
when: near-opposite directional input
why: Animation supplies physical weight without changing the simulation.

text: Layer baked-on animation, such as squash and stretch, and secondary effects like dust onto simple movement to increase its appeal.
when: Simple movement that feels bland without added animation
why: The added layer makes simple underlying motion read as organic and complex.

text: Long easing or release phases are acceptable only after an immediate initial visible reaction to the input.
why: The largest visible reaction arrives early, so a long tail still feels immediate.

text: Scaling playback to simulated speed conveys speed without changing physics and prevents foot slip, but dynamic matching can cause skating when playback and ground movement fall out of sync.
when: Locomotion animation driven by object speed.
why: Players read footing against the ground, so mismatched playback looks wrong.

text: In third person, visual character design and interface hints can signal abilities, so players need little exposition.
when: when the camera shows the player-character
why: The character is seen directly, so visual cues carry the information.

text: The camera often stops at the moment the grapple attaches, which reinforces the sense that the grapple anchors the avatar.
when: Grapple connects to a surface
why: Stillness at attachment ties the camera's motion to the anchor point.

text: This camera view uses three-point perspective, with edges meeting at horizontal vanishing points and one vertical vanishing point below the level.
The camera supports both a detailed 3D environment and reveals of hidden information the character cannot see.
Third-person cameras keep the full 3D spatial toolkit of first person, including complete environments and sight lines.
Many engines offer view-angle options that can produce warped, stylized perspectives.
Digital games commonly use five viewpoints: side, overhead, third person, isometric, and first person. Each trades how much of the world the player sees against how close they feel to the character.
A fast object seen from a great distance appears slow, so distance reduces apparent speed.
The camera is indirectly controlled: it follows the avatar and scrolls farther than in comparable platformers, supporting a sense of unbounded motion.
why: Extended scrolling distance makes the level feel larger than the visible screen.

text: Placing a small character at the bottom of the frame conveys insignificance, and first-person views can produce a similar feel.
when: Choosing camera framing to convey scale
why: Framing position affects how small or large the character appears.

text: Rapid, repeated camera scrolling is a likely cause of motion discomfort, so keep the camera steady during frequent vertical movement.
when: Games where the camera follows frequent jumping and vertical movement
why: Theories point to a mismatch between perceived motion and the body's sensed stillness.

text: Settle camera placement by testing it in the real engine rather than relying on design documents alone.
when: choosing camera placement
why: Playing in the actual view reveals navigation and selection problems that documents miss.

text: Use third-person views for acrobatic platforming and brawler-style melee that moves in and out of enemy groups.
when: Games with acrobatic platforming or brawler melee moving in and out of enemy groups
why: Third person lets players line up with obstacles and weave among enemies, which is hard in first person.

text: Measure jumps and distances in the character's own height, which keeps the unit consistent on screen regardless of camera position.
when: Designing jump and distance values
why: The character stays on screen and its height does not change with camera position.

text: In first-person games, lens effects, blur, shake, movement bob, crosshairs, and visual cues matter more because the player tracks their own view.
when: Designing first-person camera feedback
why: The player's view is the only aiming reference.

text: While the avatar moves right past the dead zone, the camera scrolls at its speed, holding it at the same screen position, locking the view to forward motion.
when: Avatar has moved beyond the horizontal dead zone edge
why: Tracking at matched speed keeps the avatar's screen position constant while the world scrolls.

text: A camera that collides with walls and surfaces stops its motion in that direction.
Pushing toward a camera while directly beneath it makes the character run in circles under camera-relative control.
when: Camera-relative movement with the player positioned directly beneath the camera
why: Input toward the camera always pulls the character toward it, so directly beneath it the motion loops.

text: Changing a sport's viewpoint or dropping one of its rules shifts the core challenge to a different skill.
when: Adapting a sport to a side-on display
why: Display limits forced the sport's rules to be simplified.

text: Camera position and how it moves relative to the avatar together shape the player's impression of speed.
Effects applied to the camera, such as shake, view-angle change, motion blur and slowdown, change perceived force and speed without altering the objects themselves.
when: When conveying concussive force or increasing perceived speed
why: The camera is the player's view of the world, so its effects shape how players read the objects they see.

text: Inside the slow zone, the camera speeds up gradually as the avatar accelerates from a standstill, giving a progressive response.
when: When the character is inside a slow zone near the screen edge
why: Reduced scroll speed inside the zone lets the camera's speed build with the character's acceleration.

text: A horizontal dead zone covering about one-third of the screen, centred, keeps the camera still while the avatar moves inside it, and only horizontal camera motion is affected.
when: Camera tracks a side-scrolling avatar in running state
why: The camera stays steady near centre and only pans once the avatar crosses the threshold.

text: A very narrow field of view with a tilted horizon can make players feel claustrophobic, which suits horror survival games but not relaxed exploration.
when: When choosing a camera for tension-filled horror survival rather than relaxed exploration
why: A narrow view with a hidden horizon closes in the space around the player.

text: Well-designed control and camera build physical presence, and strong spatial design such as VR supports it.
when: In VR games, when the 3D spatial immersion is executed well
