why: Control and camera together address many presence components, since the controlled avatar comes to feel like part of the player's own body.

text: Third-person cameras come in rotating, behind, and over-the-shoulder forms; behind cameras hold a fixed point behind the player.
why: A behind camera is parented to the player object, so it keeps a set spot relative to the character.

text: A camera avatar follows the character beyond a radius, pulls back slowly when the character runs toward it, and freezes at close range while tracking from a fixed position.
when: Designing a follow camera for a third-person character

text: Camera problems are most noticeable in open terrain, while following the character around a tall spire or pillar keeps the camera reliable.
when: Designing a third-person camera for level geometry
why: Prominent landmarks give an instant point of reference, improving camera behavior around them.

text: A virtual camera that moves while the player's eyes and head stay still creates the visual-vestibular mismatch that drives sickness.
Expecting players focused on the screen center to grasp animated elements in their peripheral vision.
when: When players mostly gaze at the screen center while animated elements appear in their periphery
why: Visual acuity is sharp only at the gaze center and drops quickly with distance, so peripheral motion needs an eye movement to perceive.

text: Camera AI is hard to code well, and cameras that work against the player are a common problem.
Jarring camera motion or sudden frame-rate drops can cause nausea and make the game feel awful, as visuals seem to break down.
when: For a player sitting stationary in a room, playing on an unmoving screen
why: Sickness arises when inner-ear and eye signals disagree; a seated player's screen must carry the perceived motion, so stutters feel like the world breaking.

text: Relying on Doppler shift or screen blur for core speed feel misses the layout and visual cues that actually carry it, since both are polish that leaves the simulation unchanged.
why: Speed is perceived from object size, relative motion and sound changes, while blur and Doppler are layered on top without changing the simulation.

text: A camera that stops when the player moves left can feel oppressive and abrupt.
when: When a side-scrolling camera can only advance and never move back
why: A one-way camera cramps the screen and pushes the player into constant forward motion.

text: A camera that tracks the avatar at all times during pendulum motion causes nausea and can make the game nearly unplayable.
when: Avatar is swinging on the grapple
why: Constant lively camera movement during pendulum swings induces motion sickness.

text: A camera stuck in geometry makes players feel unskilled.
when: When the character stands close to a wall in third- or first-person view
why: Awkward or unsettling angles from walls distract from the action and weaken the sense of control.

text: Camera shake can disturb players and cause sickness, especially in VR; shaking the UI instead is one alternative.
when: When camera shake is used for effects like an explosion, especially in VR

text: 1) Decide how much game state the player must access. 2) Decide how close the player should feel to the character and other objects. 3) Choose the viewpoint that matches both, and explain its effect on formal and dramatic elements.
when: choosing a viewpoint for any game
why: A deliberate choice matches information access and drama to the design.

text: 1) Move the camera no more than necessary. 2) When it must move, move it smoothly. 3) Give the player control when programmed camera behavior fails to produce a good result.
when: designing camera behavior
why: Unneeded or jerky camera motion comes between the player's intent and the result, making controls feel less intuitive, and can cause nausea.

text: Hold the camera still while the target stays near screen center, and pan only when it nears an edge.
when: When the tracked character sits near screen center, not yet near an edge
why: Frequent rapid panning was the most probable source of discomfort, so the camera holds back until it is actually needed.

text: Map stick input relative to camera orientation, so a push moves the character relative to the view rather than a fixed world axis.
Choose the camera view, whether it is still or scrolling, how it follows the character, and its field of view deliberately.
why: The camera defines the player's perspective on the game world, which makes its view and motion critical.

text: Choose the viewpoint by first deciding what information the player should have, not by habit.
when: selecting a camera viewpoint
why: Habitual choices often mismatch what the player needs to know.

text: Keep the horizon level and avoid virtual rotation where the camera turns apart from the player's head; let players look around with real rotation.
why: Inner-ear canals detect rotation very well, so virtual rotation separate from the head triggers motion sickness.

text: The camera should show the player the target, reticle, and tracked enemy, and should be judged by where it looks, how it moves, and whether the player can still act.
why: Players need the information required to act, so the view must reveal the reticle and tracked enemy.

text: Keep camera shake subtle: use small roll and small field-of-view bumps, and move the camera while the aiming point stays where the player wants it.
when: Adding camera shake
why: Strong shake disrupts aiming.

text: Widen the view progressively or on a turbo boost to suggest speeds faster than the display can show, when the feel of speed matters more than accuracy.
when: Boost or high-speed moments.
why: A widened view creates a sense of speed beyond what is displayed.

text: Rotate the camera on sideways movement without moving it, first tracking the exact position then gradually leading ahead of the character.
when: Character moves sideways relative to camera

text: At rest, slowly orient the camera toward the character's facing direction, and let manual camera pushes drift back slowly.
when: Character stopped or camera manually adjusted
why: Rapid, repeated scrolling is most likely to cause discomfort, so camera motion is slowed.

text: Make camera control removal easy for players to anticipate, otherwise they feel controlled and lose autonomy.
when: When temporarily removing camera control so players can see a particular object in the world.

text: Views sharing the character's movement and limited knowledge heighten tension and closeness; views showing more of the world, even close outside ones, reveal environment and clues but feel less close.
when: choosing a camera viewpoint
why: Viewpoint controls both what the player knows and how near they feel to the character.

text: Set tire sideways friction well above forward friction to get a carving turn rather than a floaty, sliding one.
when: When a wheeled vehicle starts to turn
why: Low forward grip relative to sideways grip makes the vehicle bite into the ground and arc instead of pivoting in place.

text: Spurted movement gives creatures a furtive, nervous air, which may suit the game.
when: Choosing creature movement style.

text: Traits should show in movement and animation as well as in dialogue, for example a sneaky character's jump or a depressed character's walk.
when: When animating characters
why: Movement reveals character as much as speech does.

text: Add small weight-shift cues, such as raising a back foot to counterbalance a launch and planting it on attachment, so the body feels solid.
why: The body's balance change makes the grapple's launch and attachment visible, so the character reads as heavy and solid.

text: Squash and stretch can make a soft object read as soft rather than rigid, like stone, with no change to its behavior.
why: Perception is active, so polish alone can change how players read an object's properties even when its behavior is identical.

text: Short cables play the same animation frames as long ones, but horizontal distance between frames shrinks in proportion to cable length, so a short swing takes the same time and covers less ground.
when: Grapple attaches to a nearby connection point
why: Fixed animation timing with scaled spatial distance preserves rhythm while changing arc size.

text: Weight-shift cues can be tiny, around three pixels of movement, and still read as physical weight.
1) Make creatures move in small spurts with pauses. 2) Use spurts rather than reduced speed so chased creatures can still run continuously.
when: Slowing creature movement for player control.
why: Pauses give the player time to circle creatures, and uniform slowdown looks artificial.

text: Most racing games use a near-frictionless collision response, so a vehicle that hits a barrier deflects off it and keeps moving.
Bounce is conveyed only by objects given explicit bounce behavior; other surfaces read as hard and slick.
Make hits feel like personal injury and grabs feel like reaching into the game, and use polish and simulation to make these interactions precise.
when: designing interactions with objects or enemies
why: Real-time control makes players identify with their avatar, so impacts register as bodily harm and grabs as direct reach.

text: Collision feel can be described and compared by matching it to everyday objects, such as soft springy objects or rigid solid ones.
Deformation polish alone can change an object's perceived substance without any change to its physics.
Collision response is part of context: an object the player passes through does not change the feel, however many such objects there are.
Collisions that return energy with rebound and visible reaction make a space feel interactive, while dead collisions with no rebound make it feel empty.
why: Without returned energy, contact produces no visible reaction, so players have little reason to notice their surroundings.

text: On the ground every tile is solid, including connectable tiles, but in the air collision loosens so a swing can carry the avatar partway into a tile.
when: Avatar is on the ground versus in the air
why: Air collision is relaxed, enabling penetration of connectable tiles during swings.

text: Matching collision code to another game does not reproduce its feel; movement tuning drives the result.
when: Porting a platformer's collision to a new game
why: Identical collision logic can produce different movement depending on tuning.

text: Head-on collisions still stop the character, and blocky hard-edged geometry does not produce the same edge-sliding flow as rounded or angular passages.
when: Designing collision shapes and level geometry
why: Side friction is absent, so only a head-on contact stops motion; glancing contacts are resolved by redirecting along the edge.

text: Clipping, and objects flying off on slight touches, erode the sense of a cohesive world, and frequent occurrences may drive players to quit.

Near-frictionless contact keeps driving precise; high friction makes vehicles stick, roll or crumple and disrupts control, yet zero friction leaves jump force unslowed against walls, feeling loose and slippery.
when: In precision-focused racing or driving games where vehicles hit barriers
why: Contact friction decides whether a hit snags the vehicle or lets it carry on; with no friction, nothing slows movement against surfaces.

text: The player chooses swing arc size by timing when to fire the grapple between connections, so firing at the wrong moment gives a swing too small or large for the next target.
when: Player fires grapple between connection points
why: Arc size depends on fire timing, not on a separate control.

text: Releasing from the grapple lets gravity take hold gradually, so the release feels organic and the flight follows a graceful arc.
when: Avatar releases a swing
why: Gradual gravity build-up after release reads as natural motion.

text: A weapon's sound set can include fire, alt fire, raise, lower, equip, put-down and pickup cues, which weapon scripts reference through separate properties.
Instant-hit weapon impact sounds belong in attachment scripts, projectile impacts in projectile scripts, and handling sounds in weapon scripts.
Let weapon sound convey condition, such as a fire sound that changes as the clip runs low, wear from overuse, or a clip-ejection sound when empty.
when: During combat, when the player needs weapon condition without checking the HUD
why: Players in combat rarely watch the HUD ammo counter.

text: Give powerful enemies, or enemies placed in key spots, unique sounds to add tension to encounters.
why: Sound can warn players of danger before it arrives and interrupt their play.

text: Mirror attack and release times, so slowing to zero takes as long as reaching top speed; this soft release keeps the loose feel.
why: Without a release phase, stopping feels abrupt; a release keeps motion easing out after input ends.

text: When ramming targets is the goal, make contact carry the target along the vehicle and into nearby objects, so the hit feels physical and satisfying.
Superficial visual damage such as dents on panels, paired with strong sound, can stand in for full deformation when deformation is not modeled.
when: no full deformation model
why: Cheap cues can carry much of the impact feel

text: An avatar with no attack and no release moves at constant speed as soon as input activates.
A long attack feels floaty or loose, and players can enjoy this in motion meant to feel floaty.
when: When the motion is meant to feel floaty, as with a thruster

text: A long attack that begins with a rapid initial rise gives an immediate response while keeping a loose, organic feel.
when: When a long attack phase would otherwise show no immediate response to input
why: A perceptible initial change prevents the game feeling unresponsive, since imperceptible change reads as lag.

text: A short attack feels tight and responsive, and a curved rather than straight short attack keeps an organic feel.
why: A nonlinear curve keeps motion fluid while making the initial response seem immediate.

text: A very short, purely linear attack from off to on feels twitchy, and can feel stiff.
Control with no release feels abrupt when the input ends.
why: Release time mirrors attack time, so motion slows gradually rather than halting at once.

text: Weapon swings convey their character through arc size, pre-swing pause, follow-through and sound: huge ponderous arcs read heavy, while quick swings with blur read light.
when: Designing melee weapon feel
why: Each timing and visual choice signals mass and speed to the player.

text: A very short attack ramp smooths rotation input so full rotation speed is reached over about a third of a second, which reads as slight inertia before the ship turns.
when: rotation input passes through an attack curve
why: The brief ramp softens the start of turning without adding the looseness of acceleration.

text: A layered visual reaction, such as a brief jiggle, can show impact without moving the object's position, and contrasting reactions for different sizes convey relative mass.
when: a solid object is struck by a character
why: Visual contrast signals strength while leaving the simulated world unchanged.

text: Without an early-release clamp, even short hops rise high because full force still applies for a time, which narrows the range of jump heights.
when: jump height depends on hold duration
why: Clamping upward velocity on release is what makes short taps noticeably lower than full holds.

text: Attaching the grapple and starting a swing greatly enlarges the horizontal dead zone, so the avatar can swing almost to the screen edge before the camera moves.
when: Grapple attaches and a swing begins
why: A larger dead zone lets the swing play out without constant camera motion.

text: Collision is turned off while swinging; a horizontal arc entering an impassable tile bounces the avatar into a state where the grapple cannot fire until he touches solid ground.
when: Avatar swings into an impassable tile
why: Disabling collision during swings means impassable geometry must be handled by a bounce state.

text: A short attack that includes a small forward lunge adds emphasis to the hit.
Targets with no health, knocked out by one hit, make the attacking vehicle feel much more massive than its targets.
when: In a vehicle game where objects have no health, so a single hit decides the outcome.
why: A single hit shows the attacker overwhelming the target.

text: A full swing cycle can be animated with about ten frames, and combined with attachment to any point this carried the game's feel.
when: When controls have low sensitivity, such as a basic gamepad with limited analog input.
why: Ten frames read as a fluid arc to the eye, a perception that carries strong impact.

text: A minimal combat prototype needs a player, one or two weapons, a space and an enemy.
Relying on visuals alone to convey weight or power fails, since people judge these mostly from sound.
when: When communicating a weapon's relative weight and power to players.
why: The brain fuses what is seen and heard into one event, and sound carries cues about material and nature.

text: Leaving button presses unconfirmed leaves players unsure whether their input registered.
when: When the physical controller offers little tactile feedback, such as having no rumble.
why: Audio substitutes for the touch feedback that physical buttons normally provide.

text: Impact that undersells the action weakens the whole combat loop.
why: Players feel the hit only through its feedback, so weak feedback reads as weak combat.

text: Vertical and horizontal hooks feel plain, rigid and dull, so the diagonal swing must carry the expressive feel of the movement.
when: Designing grapple firing modes
why: Non-swing hooks lack the varied motion that makes swinging engaging.

text: Choose a weapon sound system based on the weapon's nature: single shot, retriggered, looping for speed, looping for consistency, or another approach.
when: Starting weapon sound design

text: Decide whether the weapon should give the player audible feedback before choosing its sound layers.
Treat weapon fire, flybys, impacts and ricochets as one related sound system rather than as separate assets.
when: In a shooter game with real-time acoustic processing available.

text: Each weapon needs a crisp, distinct sound, especially in its first microseconds, since sound shapes how powerful a weapon feels.
when: Designing weapon audio
why: Players judge weapon value partly by sound.

text: Make weapon sounds convey force and kind, so shots bang, rockets explode, and blades ring out.
Check that a weapon's look and sound match its gameplay purpose and the situations where it is best used.
when: evaluating or designing a weapon
why: A mismatch weakens players' reading of what the weapon does.

text: Exaggerate weapon carry and recoil animation, and pair it with recoil effects and crisp audio, so weapons feel heavy.
when: When players want to see themselves carrying heavy guns that feel badass.
why: Visible and audible weight makes the weapon feel powerful to the player.

text: Show the path of shots, such as with tracers, so players can see where their attack went.
why: Visible trajectories confirm player agency and aiming accuracy.

text: Celebrate player victories through audio and animation, from a weapon flourish to a victory dance.
when: Once a combat encounter has ended.
why: Positive feedback after combat reinforces the player's sense of accomplishment.

text: Tracers confirm shot paths for the player but can reveal the shooter's position to opponents in multiplayer.
when: multiplayer shooters
why: Feedback meant for the shooter also gives information to enemies.

text: Contact behaviors such as sliding versus sticky surfaces and instant versus delayed explosions change how a game feels.
Context is the simulated space, including object layout, collision code and level design, which gives meaning to avatar motion and real-time control and shapes game feel.
why: Avatar motion and control have little meaning without a space to act against.

text: Judge context by player impressions rather than hard measurements, since its effect depends on subjective perception.
when: Assessing the feel of a game's space or spacing.
why: Context has no finite numeric measure that captures how space feels.

text: An uninterrupted correction cycle is a repeated loop of perceiving, thinking and acting, lasting about 240 ms, letting people track and hit goals beyond one action; central to game feel.
Aesthetic sensation of control is the pleasure of tinkering in empty space and seeing things react to button presses, before any challenge, regardless of context.
In a game, frames are states generated in response to input rather than a fixed sequence played back in order.
Crossover sensation is whether separate mechanics seem to obey the same physics and belong to one world; a mechanic that breaks this, like floaty swimming, feels out of place.
when: Designing multiple movement states such as running, swimming and flying

text: Control feel describes the instant-to-instant sense of conveying intent through an interface.
when: Designing responsiveness of player input
why: It describes how input translates to felt action during play.

text: Control latency is the lag from the moment a game takes in a player's input until the resulting change appears on screen.
Real-time control breaks from frame rate drops, delays between computer and display, and an overloaded processor.
Control feel techniques are many and varied and appear across racing, fighting, action and shooter genres.
when: Designing control feel for any genre
why: Different genres rely on the same family of hidden input adjustments.

text: Each pass of the correction cycle improves precision, and the cycles needed depend on distance and target size.
Game control amplifies space: small real movements of the thumbs produce large reactions in the game.
when: When manipulating objects in purely invented digital space via a mouse, thumbstick or motion controller.
why: Proprioception stays active, so thumbs sense their position and button resistance, and tiny motion yields big virtual effects.

text: Releasing on a fixed apex frame gives every launch the same slightly upward horizontal trajectory.
when: When the swing release is tied to one fixed frame of the swing animation.

text: A steering response that turns faster the larger the angle between the target direction and current facing gives an immediate, visible reaction to input.
when: When a player redirects a steered object toward a new direction.
why: A large angle produces a fast initial turn, so the reaction is instantly visible.

text: Keep the computer's response within one perceptual cycle of about 50 ms; beyond it players notice lag, and beyond a full correction cycle real-time control breaks.
when: When judging whether a game's response is perceived as immediate.
why: The round trip from input to changed pixels and sounds must close before the player's perception completes one cycle, or the sense of control breaks.

text: Real-time control needs at least 10 fps; about 20 fps gives smooth motion, about 30 fps looks pleasingly smooth, and most games aim for 30 fps or more.
why: Images shown at these rates fuse into motion.

text: The correction cycle has three processors in a closed loop: perception tracks the target, thought compares position to goal and plans a correction, and motor execution carries it out.
when: When an action demands precise, continuing coordination of muscles over time.
why: Each action changes the world, which is then sensed again and compared to the goal, so corrections repeat continuously.

text: The computer accepts input, processes it and returns changes through output devices such as monitors, speakers and rumble motors, and this response must feel instantaneous to close the loop.
why: The loop only completes when the player's senses take in the changed state, which must happen within a fraction of a second.

text: A wind-up animation lasting a quarter to half a second before a jump delays the visible response and frustrates players.
when: Animation anticipation precedes an action that must feel responsive.
why: Players sense a fault when an interface lags past a tenth of a second, and a wind-up runs longer than that.

text: 1) List which inputs change which parameters. 2) Describe how those parameters relate to one another. 3) Judge feel from those relationships rather than individual mappings.
when: Analysing or designing the control feel of a mechanic
why: Feel emerges from relationships between parameters

text: 1) Measure frame rate, response time and continuity. 2) Compare each against the thresholds of 10 fps, 240 ms and 100 ms. 3) Use the results as a baseline classification of real-time control.
why: Known cycle times let a game be classified, leaving player perception as the remaining variable.

text: Check whether controls feel good to you and to friends, and whether they fit the game idea.
when: Early in prototyping, before ideas are polished.
why: Like an experiment, an idea must be checked against results, so untested assumptions can waste implementation time.

text: A release clamp may look like a hack on paper, but it should be chosen for feel rather than physical accuracy.
when: a gameplay mechanic departs from physical realism to improve control
why: Players judge jumps by how they feel, not by how closely they match physics.

text: A designer may lock control for a long time on a chosen, powerful move; players tolerate the loss of control when they chose the move and it suits the character.
when: Heavy moves that exceed the correction cycle threshold.
why: The player accepts the risk-reward exchange, so the lock feels earned rather than broken.

text: Characters that barely react to being shot make the player perceive them as bulky, reinforcing their sense of mass.
when: Enemies or characters that are meant to feel heavy
why: Lack of visible reaction signals high mass and toughness.

text: Enemies that die in one or two hits feel fragile and insubstantial next to a boss that needs three hits.
when: enemies shown alongside bosses
why: Hit-count contrast sets perceived weight.

text: Enemy interaction rules can signal a hierarchy of mass and power, such as enemies that leave a shell suggesting more mass than those that vanish.
when: designing enemies with different weights or defeat methods
why: Differing outcomes communicate relative size and strength to players.

text: Enemies that take several hits should make a different sound when struck, adding a sense of mass and solidity.
when: Enemy requires multiple hits to defeat
why: Distinct impact sounds communicate toughness and weight to the player.

text: Make boss hits feel heavy by delivering them through the environment, such as launching the enemy into hazards.
when: When bosses must read as far heavier than basic enemies.

text: Carrying an object slows movement, and a weighed-down animation signals the object's mass.
when: When the player character grabs or picks up an object.
why: Movement and animation changes on the carrier make the held object's heft felt through control.

text: Tune herding steering to be less fluid than animation steering, so the player can react to flocks that start to separate.
when: Designing creature movement for player herding.
why: Fluid animation-style steering is too fast for a player to react to.

text: Increase creatures' desire to form cohesive groups to support herding.
when: Designing flock behavior the player herds.
why: Pauses give the player room to loop around the group and steer it; smooth flocking would undermine that control.

text: Polish the player causes through their own actions is more powerful than passive effects they only watch.
why: Effects the player triggers are felt through their own senses, while passive effects are only watched, as in film.

text: Animation and trail effects that point to different physical properties make a character feel unclear: a floating trail with foot slides that look like swimming undermines a sense of weight.
when: A character has a trail effect plus stylized locomotion
why: Clashing effects convey something other than the intended impression.

text: A continuous feedback loop has input and response flowing without breaks, allowing ongoing correction cycles.
Decay occurs when speed just after an input change is higher than the sustain level, so the value drops toward it.
Most games use visual feedback as the core channel, adding sound and rumble as polish.
Make every effect push toward the same impression, such as heavy mass, high friction, or sturdy form, so visuals, sound, motion, simulation and rules support one cohesive, unique physical reality.
when: Designing a character's feedback
why: Consistent cues make the object read as one coherent physical thing.

text: Feedback such as particle effects, screen shake, and sound makes actions feel satisfying and reinforces the play they reward.
when: When rewarding a correct player action
why: Sensory feedback signals success and encourages repetition

text: Without polish, collisions still convey physical interaction, but much of the game's appeal is lost.
when: control and simulation present, polish absent
why: polish carries much of the appeal

text: When decay is present, the player must keep pressing to hold top speed, which fatigues the hands and is almost never desirable.
when: When speed just after an input change is faster than sustained speed.

text: Give continuous feedback for every player action, and if it is missing, identify why.
when: When evaluating whether an interface feels juicy or dry.
why: Interfaces with continuous feedback engage the player immediately, while those lacking it are called dry.

text: Acknowledge each input immediately, even if the full result takes longer, so players feel informed and in control.
when: When the full result of an input takes longer than the immediate reply.
why: Without an immediate sign, players doubt their input and feel uncertain and not in control.

text: When a result is hard to perceive because it is fast or buried in motion, give clear immediate feedback, often exaggerated with particle effects.
when: Result is fast or visually buried.
why: Players must tell what their input did to repeat it at will.

text: Game feel is the satisfaction of interacting with the game system, shaping players' emotions; it covers the camera, controls and characters, called the three Cs.
Polishing visuals, art and audio before the core action is proven wastes effort; it gives short-term emotional lift but recurring rework whenever mechanics change.
when: early prototyping; polish added to an unfinished design before the next tests need it
why: The art's emotional lift fades quickly, while each mechanic change forces reworking the art, so the cost recurs.

text: Rigid, slow-steering motion confined to one screen edge feels stiff compared with a ship with flowing inertial motion.
when: when comparing constrained movement with inertial movement
why: Limited range and slow steering reduce the sense of flow

text: Recasting sword fights as contests of insults and comebacks, rather than pure combat, can make a mechanic one of a game's most popular features.
when: When designing duel mechanics in a comedic adventure game
why: Film sources suggested swordplay could be about talk more than fighting.

text: Players describe game feel with vague words such as floaty, loose, tight and responsive.
when: Gathering player feedback on control
why: Feel is perceived subjectively and has no standard vocabulary

text: Input sensitivity and tactile feel affect player feel mostly subconsciously.
when: Evaluating input device feel
why: Players sense these qualities without consciously noticing them

text: Small, easy interactions that give a continuous flow of visible reward make even a plain tool feel playful and satisfying to use.
when: when a system is juicy
why: Continuous reward follows from little effort.

text: Good physical feel can arise from polish effects alone, even with an invisible avatar, if the camera keeps tracking the avatar and stops to show collisions.
when: Avatar is hidden or absent.
why: Players read camera motion and collision stops as physical contact.

text: Game feel is an impression formed in the player's mind, mainly a property of their perception of movement, so improvements must be judged by how they are perceived.

Polish is non-simulated, layered-on effects that enhance impression of physical reality, making objects seem solid, heavy or elastic, such as squash, particles, sound and rumble, without changing simulation.
why: A rebound between solid objects is simulation, while the sparks and dust around it are polish.

text: A game has game feel only when real-time control, simulated space and polish all meet; lacking any one places it outside the definition.
Sensation is pleasure from the senses, delivered mostly by aesthetics.
Classifying a game by feel describes the medium only; it is not a judgment of quality, so games outside true game feel can still be excellent.
when: classifying a game by its feel
why: classification measures the conditions of the medium, not how good the game is

text: Metaphor is how representation and treatment shape player expectations about objects.
A system is juicy when it shows much second-order motion that is easy to control and gives players power and rewards.
Juiciness is the intensity of sensory feedback, such as music, sound, particles, screen shake, glow, and flash, that signals progression.
why: Feedback shapes how large players perceive a gain to be.

text: Game feel is the sense of responsive, real-time manipulation of digital objects in a simulated space, enhanced by polish.
Treatment is how the art is executed, and it sets player expectations about how objects behave.
Low-level context is the intimate, tactile interaction between objects, mainly collision detection and collision response.
Game feel is the composite aesthetic experience of how a control scheme and simulation respond, built from many small, interacting decisions.
Representation is what an object appears to be, and treatment is how its art is executed, ranging from highly realistic to highly iconic or abstract.
Game feel is the real-time handling of digital objects in a virtual environment, with polish making each interaction stand out.

Polish includes feet particles, impact sounds, camera shake on heavy hits and keyframed squash and stretch; impact polish can combine debris, sparks, smoke, skid marks, positional audio and controller rumble.
Feel comes from many trivial-seeming decisions adding up; no formula produces the right control feel, so designers make hundreds of small decisions and judge the result aesthetically.
No agreed definition of game feel exists; designers rely on informal vocabulary, and attempts to define it unravel into lists of best practices and personal experience.
Polish is hard to measure: player perception is relative and hard to aggregate across players, so polish metrics are approximate.
One full cycle of the game feel loop takes about 240 ms, so it repeats four to five times per second.
The game feel loop can be used to tell games that have game feel apart from games that lack it.
Sensory pleasure cannot rescue a poor game but can noticeably improve a good one.
The seven principles of game feel are: reliable outcomes, immediate reaction, accessible yet deep, novelty, appealing feedback, organic motion, and harmony.
Input and response suit hard, data-driven metrics, while metaphor sits on the softer, impression-based side.
when: Choosing how to measure a game feel element

text: No settled thresholds separate real-time control or simulated space; games with heavy clicking and indirect collisions remain hard to classify.
Collisions feed back into the simulation, while polish is separate and only enhances how an interaction looks, sounds or feels.
Designers' accounts of game feel name four facets: intuitive controls and learnability, physical impact and timing, realism or immersion, and aesthetic appeal from layered effects.
The hard problem is unity: how separate facets of game feel combine into one experience.
Game feel has no standard measures, so a shared vocabulary of measurable elements is needed to compare the feel of different games.
Games that look alike on the surface can feel very different, and measuring feel helps explain why.
Every game uses its own units, so a stated speed value does not correlate across games, even within one genre.
Polish grounds players in unfamiliar game spaces and physics, helping them understand how unfamiliar topologies and objects behave.
A realistic visual metaphor combined with unrealistic collisions causes dissonance, even when other systems are well executed.
when: A game aims for realistic physics
why: Players judge the whole interaction against the realism promised by the visuals.

text: Game feel covers the sense of skill or awkwardness in control, the physical-feeling connection to objects, and how the avatar moves, how other characters behave, and the ambience and art direction.
Postpone a costly design decision when a wrong choice would be expensive and the current information is thin.
when: the cost of a wrong choice is high and information is limited
why: waiting gathers information before committing

text: Make opposites strongly contrasted, such as opponents, controllable versus uncontrollable factors, and reward versus punishment; sharp contrast makes play feel more meaningful and powerful.
A game that is too perfect loses character; leave handmade touches, such as player-made house rules, so the game feels alive.
Make character roles recognisable by silhouette alone, so teammates can coordinate roles at a glance.
when: Designing character classes in team-based games.
why: Distinct silhouettes communicate role without reading or inspection.

text: Designers should be prepared to argue for no music, because silence can be as powerful as sound.
when: Deciding whether a game needs music
why: Absence of music can carry emotional weight equal to its presence.

text: Treat the seven game feel principles as a starting checklist rather than a complete specification, since the list may be incomplete.
why: The principles resemble well-proven animation principles but are not guaranteed exhaustive.

text: Use scaffolding to raise difficulty gradually, and juicing when asset budgets are small and mechanics need many uses.
when: When a game needs rich play from a concise set of assets.
why: Finding multiple interactions for each mechanic yields richer play without adding new assets.

text: Tune feel for each skill level by knowing which skills the player has mastered, which they focus on, and which they have not yet met.
when: When a player's skill can be inferred from current level, inventory, or multiplayer playtesting
why: Knowing which skills are reflexive, which was learned last, and which are unseen lets feel be shaped over time.

text: Stylized representations, such as exaggerated cartoon deformation, can be equally believable and have more leeway in behavior than photorealistic ones.
when: When the art is cartoonish and iconic rather than photorealistic
why: Players carry preconceived expectations about how things move, and the art treatment shapes those expectations.

text: Consider tactile feel when players report that cross-platform versions of a game feel different despite identical game logic.
when: cross-platform versions feel different with identical logic
why: Spring quality and construction of buttons and joysticks change perceived responsiveness, subtly affecting how players handle virtual objects.

text: Emulating reality is not the most efficient route to perception; stylized squash and stretch can make an object look more physical than a rigid, realistic one.
when: Designing how an object's contact and motion look.
why: Stylized deformation communicates weight and elasticity more clearly.

text: Effects should be simple, cohesive and self-consistent, and matched to the processing power available.
when: choosing visual or audio effects under hardware limits
why: Cohesive simple effects read clearly and fit performance budgets.

text: Feel-driven hacks, such as setting jump velocity mid-jump, can beat a strict physical simulation when players find them better.
why: Feel is an impression in the player's perception, so any part of the system may be changed if it improves how the game feels.

text: Removing all polish leaves gameplay and functionality unchanged, but makes the experience less convincing and appealing, altering how players perceive objects' physical reality.
why: Polish is nonessential to function yet carries perceptual clues.

text: Slowing the world during a turn lets a turn-based player react in real time, such as dodging, which adds drama.
when: At chosen dramatic moments within turn-based combat

text: Combat feel comes from repeated playthroughs in which the designer tweaks and tests changes.
why: Each playthrough tests one change and judges how it fits with everything else.

text: With an auction time limit, the highest bid when time runs out wins, which makes exact value calculation harder and adds last-minute tension.
when: An auction has a fixed end time

text: Intense feedback at level-ups, chests, or new zones makes the gain feel larger, especially when it follows smaller gains.
when: rewarding progression moments
why: Contrast with smaller gains amplifies perceived size.

text: Polish cues convey material properties such as heavy, light, soft, sticky, metallic or rubber, shaping how players judge what an object is made of.
Changing only the represented object, while keeping structure and tuning identical, can change how control feels.
why: The represented object sets player expectations.

text: Polish changes how solid, heavy or elastic objects seem without changing the game's rules or functionality.
The overall structure of a space sets a general feel of open or closed, which can be catalogued but not measured in finite numbers.
As more processing power goes to polish, effects can support increasingly advanced simulations and better game feel.
when: as hardware budgets grow

text: Roughly 70% of a game's quality comes from the last 10% of development.
when: When the alpha build is being refined into the shipped product in the final development stage
why: Attributed to an industry producer's estimate.

text: The three computer thresholds for real-time control are motion above 10 fps, response within 240 ms, and continuity at 100 ms or less.
when: When judging whether a computer game supports real-time control
why: Player perception is the unknown variable, so measured frame rate and latency serve only as a baseline.

text: The game feel model is a cycle that combines the building blocks of game feel, the five experiences of game feel, and the three human processors.
The game feel loop has seven elements: the human processor, muscles, input device, computer, game world, output devices and senses.
why: Every element is needed to keep the cycle running.

text: Game feel is analysed through six metrics: input, response, context, polish, metaphor and rules. Input is the physical device carrying player intent; response is how the system processes that input in real time; context is the effect of simulated space, including collision and level design, on control; polish is effects that artificially enhance an impression of physical reality; metaphor is how representation shapes expectations about object behaviour; rules define relationships between variables.
Game feel can be analysed through seven aspects: input, response, simulation, context, polish, metaphor and rules, with separated thrust and rotation as the core of a loose feel.
when: analysing why a game's controls feel the way they do
why: Checking each aspect shows which layer produces a given sensation.

text: Game feel can be analyzed in layers: input device, what each input modulates, simulation over time and space, spatial context, polish effects, metaphor and rules.
when: Analyzing why a movement system feels good
why: Each layer contributes to the overall feel

text: Six designer-controlled elements of game feel are input, response, context, polish, metaphor and rules.
when: Analysing the computer side of the Game Feel Model
why: These are the parts of game feel a designer can change directly

text: A feel prototype needs three foundations: mapping inputs to motion, a basic layout giving motion a frame of reference, and camera behavior.
why: without all three, feel cannot be reliably tested

text: Three blocks combine into seven kinds: true game feel (all three); raw (control, simulation); aesthetic control (control, polish); vicarious (simulation, polish); naked control; naked simulation; naked polish.
Game feel is placed on a three-part diagram: real-time control, simulated space and polish, each checked on its own.
Context has three levels: high (space, speed, motion and size), medium (immediate space and object avoidance), and low (tactile collision between objects).
Avoidance feel is tuned with two sets of knobs: the programmed response to input and the spacing of objects, with feel tuned mainly where they meet.

Polish analysis has three angles: 1) individual free-standing effects, judged by motion, size, shape and nature; 2) groups of effects that convey general perceptions; 3) physical properties such as mass, material and texture inferred from those perceptions.
when: Analyzing or designing polish
why: A particle burst's timing and intensity can change how heavy a collision looks even when the simulation is unchanged.

text: Game feel has six components: input, response, context, polish, metaphor, and rules; input, response, and context are the core focus.
why: Game feel problems are intertwined with overall design, so splitting it into parts makes them more manageable.

text: Making a prototype look like a finished game defeats its purpose, since the goal is answering a question, not presentation.
why: Only the functional elements are needed, and polishing beyond that spends effort the prototype should use to test design.

text: Tuning fun while the game is still incomplete or unbalanced splits focus and slows progress.
when: During the formal details stage.

text: Polishing the parts of a game you feel confident about, while ignoring potential problems, delays discovery of the game's real risks.
when: When assessing a game in development for its biggest risks.
why: Confronting the endangered parts early allows more iteration loops, and those loops are more useful, yielding a better game.

text: Balancing before core mechanics are settled wastes effort, because mechanic changes discard much of the earlier balance work.
when: While the game's core mechanics are still changing.

text: Polish can become a development rabbit hole because there is always another effect to add, so focus on the overall perception being built.
when: Adding polish effects during development.
why: Endless effects waste time without strengthening the target feel.

text: Testing too early produces feedback that is not needed.
when: When content has not reached a suitable development state for testing.
why: UX testing carries real costs, so it should only run once content is developed enough to produce useful feedback.

text: Starting the outline and text too early skips the step that forces the team to think through the full player experience.
when: Before several prototyping iterations have been completed.
why: Sketching flow and screens surfaces inconsistencies before any art or programming work begins.

text: Adding branches before a solid core story exists increases scope without improving the narrative.
when: When starting a story from scratch for a newly conceived product.
why: Complex structures risk scope creep.

text: Copying a successful design tends to produce only timid, incremental improvements.
when: Designing mechanics from an existing successful game
why: Imitation limits exploration of the underlying feel principles

text: Designers often overlook juiciness, even though it strongly affects how fun a system feels.
why: Small, easily controlled actions that produce many simultaneous rewards keep the player continuously rewarded and engaged.

text: A dry, painful interface placed before a fun game undermines the game, so the interface itself should be rewarding.
when: When the interface is the first thing players meet before the fun gameplay.
why: It contradicts the game's fun promise, making the experience undercut itself from the start.

text: Juice cannot be tuned by adjusting numbers in a spreadsheet and must be judged by feel.
when: tuning feedback
why: Sensory intensity has no direct numeric equivalent.

text: Polish alone gives only indirect perceptions of interaction, so it cannot replace a simulated space.
why: Polish only adds cues on top of an interaction, while real-time perception needs literal space to be simulated.

text: Meeting the numeric thresholds does not guarantee good feel: 10 fps motion can look stilted and 200 ms response can feel sluggish.
when: When classifying real-time control by measuring fps, response latency and input continuity.
why: Thresholds are a baseline, and the player's impression is the final judge.

text: Polish is often dismissed as cosmetic, but it strongly affects whether the game world feels convincing and consistent.
why: Players read effects against past experience, so polish cues set expectations for how objects should behave.

text: Assuming a simple-looking game has simple feel leads to overlooking the many details that shape its movement.
why: Feel emerges from many small choices in simulation and input response that are invisible at a glance.

text: Adding gloss to every interaction distracts from the physical sensation being conveyed and makes it hard for players to understand what is happening physically.
when: When nearly every interaction is covered in particles and animated flourishes.
why: Excess effects compete with the physical cues the player needs to read.

text: When visuals approach photorealism but behaviour does not, the mismatch creates an uncanny valley of game feel.
when: When visuals approach photorealism but object behaviour and interaction do not.
why: Players bring real-world knowledge that the behaviour fails to match.

text: Game feel is often overlooked as an emotional concept, even though it strongly affects engageability.

1) Play the game and note each observed effect, treating each animation as its own. 2) Sort each effect into animation, visual, sound, cinematic or tactile. 3) Group effects into perceptions such as weight, speed, material or friction. 4) Infer the physical properties behind each perception, such as mass, gravity, friction, material, shape.
when: Analyzing how a game's polish builds its feel or communicates its physics.
why: Sorting and grouping reveals which perceptions the polish builds; combining clues reveals the physical model players perceive.

text: 1) The human processor produces motor instructions. 2) Muscles execute them. 3) The input device converts movement into signals a machine can interpret. 4) The computer integrates input with game state. 5) Output devices turn the updated state into perceivable signals. 6) The senses take in sight, sound, touch and proprioception, closing the loop.
why: Every stage is required, so the loop from player intent to perceived response only keeps running if all stages function.

text: 1) Ask how you want players to feel in combat. 2) List the mechanics, space, audio and pacing that produce that feeling. 3) Change or cut anything that works against it.

1) Populate a test space with many different objects. 2) Space the objects at varied intervals and try a range of shapes and configurations. 3) Tune the mechanic against all configurations, not one test case.
why: Feel comes from how space and motion interact, so tuning has to cover varied spatial layouts rather than one test case.

text: 1) List the game's mechanics as player verbs. 2) Test each against the real-time control thresholds. 3) Check the whole system sustains them together. 4) Check simulated space. 5) Check polish.
why: Judging the whole game at once makes the thresholds hard to apply.

text: 1) List each individual effect. 2) Sort it by the physical impression it supports, such as weight or mass. 3) Check whether any effects contradict each other or the intended impression.
when: An intended impression such as size or weight is not coming across
why: Clashing effects convey something other than the designer intended.

text: 1) Decide which physical sense the game should convey. 2) Check that it fits the metaphor. 3) Check that it matches the simulation. 4) Build effects around that sense.
why: Every effect supports one impression of physicality, so effects that contradict the simulation or metaphor break believability.

text: Design game feel from first principles and compare games by criteria, not copying; identify feel system parts and their relationships to build by understanding, not emulation.
when: Building or evaluating a game's feel, or recreating a classic feel in a new design
why: Criteria let designers compare and reason about feel; understanding structure supports original design instead of imitation.

text: Add polish to emphasize physical interactions and appeal only after the underlying simulation exists; without it, sounds and particles suggest physical reality that motion fails to match, creating dissonance.
when: designing feedback for interactions
why: Polish only adds cues on top of an existing simulation without changing it, so it has nothing to enhance without one.

text: Do not restructure data for cache locality in advance. Apply it only to measured hot paths where cache misses cause the slowdown.
when: Code is rarely executed or is slow for reasons other than cache misses
why: Optimizing unneeded code adds complexity and reduces flexibility

text: Use the six game feel elements as a checklist when analysing a mechanic or a game's feel system.
when: Analysing a mechanic's feel
why: The checklist covers every designer-controlled source of feel

text: Measure game feel with both soft and hard metrics, and aim for general principles rather than guessing or copying another game's tuning.
when: Evaluating game feel
why: General principles transfer to new designs, while copied tuning does not

text: Build a game-feel palette suited to interaction rather than copying film or animation; borrow film or animation conventions only where they fit how the player interacts.
why: Film and animation conventions often do not match interactive control.

text: Design games that feel good in their own right, instead of imitating real-world things that feel good.
why: The designer substitutes a game world for physical reality, so the feel forms its own unique physical reality.

text: Mechanics change during play, so evaluate those that are gained, upgraded or removed later, not only the starting set.
Aim game feel at simplification rather than simulation, and design the software and the input device together.
why: Treating feel as an artistic whole rather than literal simulation aims at fun games that feel good to play.

text: Be ready to change any part of a movement system to improve feel, not only to make its physics more accurate.
why: Feel comes from many small decisions that combine, so any part of the movement can change perception.

text: Choose camera, controls and character behavior deliberately to match the emotional tone the game intends.
why: Control and camera drive physical presence, character design drives narrative presence, and together they build emotional presence.

text: If inexperienced decision-makers must be involved in graybox review, premature production may be needed despite its cost.
when: When experienced graybox evaluators are unavailable
why: Higher-fidelity art can prevent the halo effect from distorting judgment, at higher expense.

text: Photorealism requires every detail to behave realistically under scrutiny, while an iconic, cartoony style lowers expectations and makes harmony easier to achieve.
when: When visuals aim for realism and players manipulate objects in unpredictable ways.
why: A cartoony treatment lowers expectations of realistic behavior, and consistent abstraction across visuals, sound and motion keeps the game in harmony.

text: When traversal relies on a grapple, swinging feels expressive and liberating, while ground movement feels rigid and heavy.
when: when a grapple is the main traversal method
why: Swinging is a continual act of staving off a fall, while ground movement feels clumsy and lacks inertia.

text: Once released from a swing, the player can attach immediately to the next connection point.
when: Avatar is airborne after a release

text: Without a jump, a grapple fired vertically, horizontally, or diagonally gives all the avatar's upward movement; only the diagonal shot starts a swing, which drives the swing feel.
when: Avatar has no jump and relies on a grappling launcher
why: Firing direction determines whether the movement is a pull, a hook, or a swing.

text: The cable length equals the distance to the connection point, so far connection points give a large sweeping swing arc.
when: Avatar swings on a grapple cable
why: Longer cable radius produces a larger arc.

text: A grapple swing continually works against gravity, with the player timing each release at the last possible moment to keep momentum.
Adding many avoidable objects during a focus-demanding movement adds load, since the movement already takes much of the player's attention.
when: swinging or similar demanding movement
why: The movement already absorbs much of the player's focus, so extra objects to dodge are unnecessary and crowd out improvisation.

text: Players rarely treat physical actions as input until a game uses them, and when a game does, players often find the interaction refreshing.
when: when a game uses an unusual physical input
why: Unusual physical actions expose how narrowly players think about input devices, so they had never seen such actions as meaningful input.

text: A distinctive physical component can make buyers pick up a game before they know how it plays.
when: When a game is first seen on a shelf or in a showcase.

text: Players perceive a heavier, more solid controller as higher quality, and that can make the actions it drives feel weightier and more satisfying.
when: when choosing or tuning a physical controller

text: Surface materials shape how players feel about the controller and, through that, about the game they play with it.
Snapping an airborne pickup to the attachment point after a proximity check makes the grab feel tactile, like catching a dropped ball.
when: grabbing items in the air with an attachment
why: The attachment acts as a surrogate hand.

text: Force feedback applies active resistance to pushing, pulling or rotating a controller, on top of the springs that hold it neutral.
Visual effects appear briefly at points of interaction and seem caused by an object without being that object, such as sparks from a scrape or splinters from a crate.
why: They emphasize motion at the moment of interaction.

text: A player experience model takes three input kinds: gameplay behaviour, objective bodily measures, and game context, which must be combined because any one alone can mislead.
A controller gives no proprioceptive feedback from the avatar's body, but the player's thumbs and hands still receive proprioceptive feedback from the controller.
Current controllers mostly use rumble from weight-loaded motors, which is always rotational and therefore somewhat blunt.
why: The motor spins an off-center weight, which limits the kinds of sensation it can produce.

text: Controller shape, weight and texture affect how good the input device feels in the hand.
Input conventions differ by platform, so a hold-button action common on consoles may be unfamiliar on PC.
when: Porting or designing input prompts across platforms
why: Players carry platform-specific expectations about input.

text: Passing objects back and forth between two people adds further presence.
why: Shared gaze and body language with a person nearby make both the place and that person feel real.

text: Feedback that spreads a gradient glow from the contact point shows the player exactly which area they have touched.
when: Showing touch locations.

text: Multidirectional vibration can let players sense textures by moving a hand across objects, which could serve as a core mechanic.
when: when advanced rumble hardware is available
why: Many combinations of vibration patterns would give far richer tactile signals than current motors.

text: Muscles execute motor commands and also send touch and position-sense signals back to the perceptual processor, closing the hand's part of the loop.
A trigger wired to a toggleable ambient sound lets the player press E to switch the sound on, and press E again to switch it off.
when: player interacts with a trigger that controls a sound

text: Tactile artifacts such as dust puffs or star sprays on collision convey an object's weight and mass.
Constant low rumble during grinding correlates the feel of the interaction with a third sense, touch, when used judiciously.
when: Sustained contact in a game
why: Tactile cues tied to an action reinforce the sense of that interaction.

text: Tying a sound to an action that can repeat binds the two tightly in the player's perception, strengthening agency and game feel.
why: Repeated pairing of a sound with one specific game event tightly links the two in the mind.

text: Avoid particles on contact without a clear physical reason: they add clutter and suggest stored energy that serves no purpose. Where simulation conveys an interaction, let physics carry feedback.
why: Excess polish is hard to read, so it obscures the physical sensation being conveyed.

text: Advanced multidirectional haptic hardware is still too expensive or fragile for mass production.
Strong visuals cannot compensate for thin sound and implausible, inconsistent prop motion, which breaks the impression of physicality.
why: Visuals that promise physical detail clash with contradictory sound and motion, undermining the sense of solidity.

text: A controller that is too light feels cheap, and one that is too heavy is also a problem for feel.
why: Players judge heavier, more solid controllers as higher quality, which carries into how weighty actions feel.

text: 1) Link each sound's Finished output back to its Play input. 2) Optionally add a randomized Delay to control retriggering timing.
when: Keeping a looping sound layer playing continuously
why: Finished events fire the sound again when it ends

text: Shake the controller in the direction of a directional impact on the avatar so the vibration matches what happened in the game.
when: when the avatar receives an impact with a clear direction

text: Give levers and heavy doors sounds that convey their weight, since satisfying feedback makes these interactions feel substantial.
why: Sound played in response to player actions makes it seem they have strongly changed the space around them.

text: Haptic feedback strengthens the sense of a physical object but adds fatigue to the arms, wrists and hands, which is one reason it has not caught on.
when: Choosing between haptics and simpler rumble
why: The sensation gain is offset by physical strain on the player.

text: Grooves snap a stick toward eight directions, easing cardinal aiming but lowering precision between grooves and feeling jarring when rolled in circles.
when: choosing analog stick housing design
why: Detents guide input at the cost of fine control.

text: Rumble works best when tied to a metaphor, and gun recoil is a strong match.
when: Designing controller feedback for an action
why: A clear physical metaphor makes the vibration read as meaningful.

text: Give constant rumble for continuous actions such as sustained fire and a single rumble for discrete actions such as a single shot.
when: Mapping rumble to firing or repeated actions
why: Matching the rumble pattern to the action's timing keeps it legible.

text: Use rumble judiciously, because rumble applied everywhere loses its meaning.
Map a player's health to audio or haptic intensity, such as heartbeat volume or loop speed, to convey health without a HUD.
when: Designing health feedback that supports or replaces a visual readout.
why: Players can monitor an audio rhythm that tracks health continuously.

text: A health-damage warning that repeats faster and faster as the player stays in a hazard signals rising danger without stating it, letting the player read their state from the sound alone.
when: Player is in a continuous damage area and needs to know their health is falling.
why: Accelerating repetition conveys increasing urgency through rhythm, which the player perceives directly.

text: Small rewarding interactions, such as a block jiggling or a coin popping out, cushion early failure and make playing badly feel acceptable.
when: early play with unfamiliar controls
why: reward offsets frustration from errors

text: Leave a usable escape window between the final warning cue and lethal damage; warnings with too little time to react arrive too late to change the outcome.
when: Designing escalating hazard feedback that ends in damage or death.
why: Without a reaction window, the warning informs the player only after the outcome is already decided.

text: When giving a reward, deliver it through several channels at once, such as a visual reward object with a celebratory fanfare, and add more channels where possible.
why: Rewards are often multimodal.

text: Add dust particles, lens distortion, screen shake and strong sound to events to build a compelling sense of physicality.
A pause of roughly 20 milliseconds on a hit emphasizes its severity.
when: Strong hits in action games

text: Layer sound, particles, a ragdoll-style reaction and slow motion on hits and long jumps, so the impact itself reads as satisfying feedback.
why: Slow-motion camera work during impacts and long jumps highlights how physical the interactions are.

text: Removing debris from destroyed objects makes them simply vanish, which makes smashing feel unsatisfying.
why: Debris is one of the few cues a player has about how physical the world is.

text: Moment-to-moment game feel is the lowest-order feedback loop; if it does not feel good intuitively, players stop playing.
why: Players have very little time to hook in, so they need to feel capable and grounded within roughly the first two minutes.

text: ADSR envelope: four phases after an input: attack (rest to peak time), decay (peak down to sustain level), sustain (level held while input active), release (return to rest).
1) Add small detail particles for immediate feedback. 2) Add larger, longer-lasting volumes for weight. 3) Play fast impact effects at double or triple the normal rate so they feel instant.
when: designing hit effects
why: Layering short and long effects gives both immediacy and substance.

text: Make hit effects meet or exceed what players imagine the weapon does.
why: Players judge a weapon by the impact they expect from it, and undersized feedback weakens the loop.

text: Save the most intense feedback for rare, significant milestones such as major puzzles or the hardest areas cleared.
when: When progression lands on an uncommon yet important point, like cracking a key riddle or conquering the toughest zone.
why: Reserved feedback keeps milestones feeling significant.

text: Show impact damage as deformation, such as compression or mushing, while the object keeps moving, so visible damage does not stop motion.
when: A near-frictionless collision response is in use.
why: Deformation conveys impact without adding friction that disturbs control.

text: Give impacts three tiers, light, medium and hard, each with its own animation, visual effect and sound, scaled up with impact force.
why: Matching animation, visual and sound tiers to impact strength makes the character and world seem physically believable.

text: Show ground contact with dust puffs on slides and foot reversals, and an expanding dust wave on heavy ground impacts.
why: Dust kicked up at contact conveys that friction was defeated.

text: Play slow motion and zoom the camera toward the point of impact when the vehicle hits a character, emphasizing the collision.
Show physical impact consequences, such as gradual cracking then breaking with particles, and visible damage to objects after collisions.
why: People hold strong intuitive expectations about how physical objects behave, so breakage and damage must look believable.

text: Effects should explain physical cause and effect, e.g. a slide puff; but on high-speed collisions, spray particles may lack physical basis because violent motion conveys force.
when: when designing feedback for a physical action
why: Readable cause-and-effect aids understanding; violent motion can justify stylized effects.

text: A visible result or perceived response delayed beyond about 100 ms after input feels unresponsive and bad, so players sense something is wrong.
Unintended ambiguities, such as unexpected responses, make players feel the game is not responding to their input.
why: What matters is whether the player blames their own skill or the game's response, so an odd outcome shifts blame onto the game.

text: When input gets no immediate feedback, players repeat or hold presses and watch for results anxiously.
when: A delayed response gives no acknowledgment.
why: The player cannot tell whether the press registered, so they repeat or hold the press to be safe.

text: Longer input latency demands more player skill and makes the game feel less synchronized.
why: The response arrives after the target has moved on, so the player must act before the aim visibly lines up.

text: Input is the hardware design of the apparatus by which player intent gets to the system.
Response is how the system processes and modulates input in real time.
A button returns a binary signal, a trigger or paddle returns one float, and a thumbstick or mouse returns two floats.
when: Comparing input devices

text: A button and trigger have two hard boundaries, a paddle two hard rotational limits, a thumbstick one round boundary, and a mouse four soft boundaries.
when: Comparing input devices

text: Button, trigger and paddle move along one axis, while thumbstick and mouse move in two; buttons, triggers and thumbsticks sense force against spring resistance, the paddle senses torque, and the mouse senses position change.
when: Comparing input devices

text: A button has two states on one axis, a trigger has hundreds of discrete states, and a thumbstick moves on two axes within its casing.
Inputs can be scaled by a multiplier, divided, added to, or multiplied by themselves to produce a different value range.
A stiff, long thumbstick on an older console can need roughly twice the force to displace compared with sticks on later consoles.
Laggy or unintuitive controls can make a strong game feel unplayable, much as a fuzzy picture ruins a good film.
Ramp the input scale over the first milliseconds to give a responsive control a slightly soft attack, changing the input without altering the simulation.
when: A responsive control should feel slightly soft.
why: Ramping the value lets light taps make fine adjustments while the response still begins immediately.

text: A short input lockout is tolerable if a continuously controllable mechanic remains available alongside it.
when: A brief lockout such as an attack animation.
why: The continuous mechanic keeps real-time control available.

text: Transform raw input before it drives a response; mapping it directly gives up control over game feel and is rarely done.
why: Scaling or filtering input is where game feel is tuned, so passing raw input directly removes that control.

text: Judge responsiveness by the perceived delay to the first visible result, not by the total length of an action, which may last several seconds.
why: Long easing delays the first visible change, which makes the game feel sluggish and unresponsive.

text: With a fixed per-frame turn amount, a brief tap makes small adjustments while a sustained hold reaches full turn speed.
why: The turn amount is applied each frame while the input is held, so press duration sets how far the ship rotates.

text: Because pushing a stick outward takes time, a character appears to speed up slightly as the stick travels from center.
when: When rate-based movement is driven by an analog stick
why: Pushing a stick from center always takes some time, so the speed briefly rises as it travels outward.

text: A simple input device can feel very sensitive when the system responds with nuanced real-time reactions such as gradual acceleration, variable jump height, and different behavior on ground versus air.
when: tuning movement feel
why: Nuanced responses convey control even from a low-resolution input.

text: Respond to input with a visible result within roughly 70 to 100 ms, inside one perceptual cycle, so the player senses causality even if full motion lasts longer.
why: The player senses causality when the response falls inside one perceptual cycle.

text: The game must update faster than the player's perceptual processor; slower updates skip perceptual frames, letting perception separate input from result and breaking the feeling of control.
A response within about 50 ms feels instantaneous, a lag above 100 ms is noticeable but ignorable, and a response at 200 ms feels sluggish.
Response lag between trigger and feedback of 50 to 100 ms feels tight and responsive, and controls grow gradually sluggish above that range.
why: The range fits inside one human perception cycle, so the delay blends into the action.

text: At 30 fps with four frames of pipeline lag and 50 ms of display lag, total input latency is about 183 ms.
why: Input latency adds frame delays and display delay together, so the total is the sum of both.

text: Each input is described by its number of states, its degrees of freedom and whether its range is bounded.
A game that responds only some of the time breaks the flow of control, even when its average response figures look acceptable.
why: Players link an action to its effect only when the response lands inside one perception window; inconsistent response breaks that link.

text: Even at 60 fps a delay of about three frames is nearly unavoidable in a game, unlike in physical reality where response is continuous.
why: Game output is generated in discrete frames, while physical objects respond continuously.

text: A mechanic can respond instantly yet lack real-time control if input is locked out after one press or cut off until an animation ends.
when: when a button press starts a fixed animation that blocks further input
why: The player cannot adjust the action after it starts, so the sustained correction loop is broken.

text: Rapidly alternating between two directional inputs can create an attack overshoot above the sustain limit, letting players exceed intended top speed.
when: when rapidly switching between sideways and forward movement at one particular angle

text: 1) For each input, record dimensions, movement types, position or force sensing, direct or indirect action, boundaries, and signal format. 2) Count the device's inputs and their combinations. 3) Record resistance, springiness and overall tactile feel.
when: Measuring an input device before comparing two devices or versions
why: Hard metrics are countable and soft metrics are felt, and both shape feel

text: 1) Add small dead zones to remove noisy input. 2) Smooth inputs over a few frames. 3) Buffer early presses briefly and use them when the action becomes possible, discarding them if another press arrives first.
when: Improving input responsiveness
why: Each step makes input feel more intentional without the player noticing the processing.

text: 1) Count the frames of pipeline latency and multiply by frame length. 2) Add display lag. 3) Fire that total time before the target reaches the crosshair.
when: Aiming at moving targets in games with input lag.
why: Firing when the target appears aligned lands after it has moved past.

text: Accept player input at all times, not only when the player is actively giving it, so the game never ignores an input the player is already making.
why: The player's processors run concurrently and may change input at any moment.

text: Choose which inputs the game uses, such as thumbsticks, buttons or both, because that choice sets the sensations of control available.
when: The designer usually cannot choose the device itself.
why: Valid inputs determine which control sensations the game can offer.

text: Make input feedback immediate, since a slow response feels sloppy.
why: Players sense control only when their input visibly takes effect at once; delay undermines that feeling.

text: Harder pressing has no effect on jump height, yet a short release window can make jumps feel responsive to emphasis.
why: Height depends only on how long the button is held, so the emphasis feeling comes from the hold-and-release setup.

text: A platformer with no jump button can still have excellent game feel when its core traversal is a grappling swing.
Horizontal control while airborne is weaker than control on the ground.
Tune platformer movement through inertia, ground friction, and whether air control is allowed.
when: platformers

text: Jumps following predetermined positions feel crisper and more precise than jumps produced by a simple simulation.
why: A fixed sequence of positions is defined exactly rather than computed from physics.

text: Pressing jump sets upward velocity to a high value at once, and gravity then reduces it each frame, so the rise is an arc from a limited impulse.
why: Gravity erodes the initial burst every frame, so no further lift remains after it.

text: Gravity can be low during ascent and roughly triple after the apex, so the jump floats up and then falls quickly.
why: A changing gravity curve gives a jump a responsive, weighty arc.

text: A jump started while running is higher than one started from standstill, because the horizontal speed carries into the jump's height.
Buffer a jump press for a few frames before landing so the jump fires the instant the character touches down.
when: A player presses jump slightly before landing.
why: Forgiving timing makes the jump feel responsive even when the press is early.

text: Gestural input and animation playback can smooth the player's impression of motion and response when raw numbers fall short.
when: when frame rate or response time falls below perception thresholds such as 10 fps or 200 ms
why: Game feel is an impression in the player's mind, so perceived smoothness can be adjusted apart from raw figures.

text: Easing in too slowly makes controls feel unresponsive, even when the final motion is correct.
when: when the delay between player input and visible motion exceeds about 100 ms
why: Response time carries more weight in games, so a slow start reads as sluggish.
