text: Treat the sustain level as a true hard limit on the modulated value, such as a top speed, so attack overshoot cannot exceed it.
why: Overshoot above sustain gave some players an unfair speed edge, so the cap must hold.

text: Teleport sparingly in VR.
when: designing VR locomotion
why: teleportation drains presence

text: After turning to a new heading, a velocity-based ship can take nearly three seconds for its velocity to align with its facing direction.
when: thrust is additive and the ship has built up velocity in another direction
why: Existing velocity persists, so the new thrust direction gradually bends the motion.

text: A run feels fast only in contrast with the walk, so the gap between walk and run settings drives the sense of running.
when: when tuning walk and run speeds
why: running reads as fast only against a slower walk

text: A run button that can be pressed partially lets players reach many speeds between standing, walking and running.
why: the button can be pressed at any moment, so players can feather it

text: Max speed sets the sustain level of an envelope: the constant speed reached after the attack phase.
Changing a character's movement speed may require new animations when the animation system cannot stretch existing ones, which raises production cost.
when: movement speed is tied to animation
why: existing animations cannot be scaled to the new speed

text: Grid, tile and hexagonal movement use space abstractly and do not count as literal simulated space.
The envelope idea comes from sound design but applies equally to how game control changes over time.
An envelope can come from the simulation or from filtering the input before it arrives, and both shape how control feels.
Absolute speed and turn-rate values carry no meaning until they are tied to a layout of curves and obstacles.
Remove movement exploits that give skilled players an overwhelming advantage, since they break the intended speed limit.
when: When a movement quirk lets veteran players run well above the designed speed

text: Instant horizontal movement cannot carry a game alone and works only in combination with other movement types.
when: Designing a game around instant horizontal movement
why: Stiff horizontal motion lacks the variety needed to sustain play by itself.

text: Adding acceleration to velocity each frame gives static inertia: speed persists unless another force acts; drag after release gives smooth attack and release.
when: When the object should keep drifting after input stops, like a spacecraft
why: Momentum is conserved between inputs, so the object keeps moving without thrust.

text: Movement speed affects both game feel and gameplay, and timing in action games can make or break the experience.
when: In action games where movement rate is treated as a resource

text: If an envelope drives avatar motion, its shape determines how players experience control.
when: When the modulated parameter feeds the real-time motion of an avatar

text: Very low damping lets an accelerated ship keep moving for several seconds before coming to rest, producing a frictionless, spacelike feel.
when: ship velocity decays with little or no friction
why: Minimal drag means momentum persists, and players associate this with space.

text: Separating thrust from rotation lets the ship turn freely regardless of its velocity, creating a loose, floaty feel.
when: a ship can thrust in its facing direction while moving another way
why: Velocity and heading are independent, so turning does not disrupt momentum.

text: Reversing direction emerges from opposing acceleration that counteracts velocity until the object stops and moves the other way, without a separate canned animation.
when: a physics-driven character is pushed opposite to its movement
why: Letting physics produce the reversal keeps motion consistent with the simulation.

text: Replacing single-speed movement with stopped, walking and running states, plus a slide to a halt, gives a character inertia and a fluid feel.
when: When movement is binary, only full speed or stopped
why: Gradual acceleration lets quick taps make fine position nudges, and a slide on release adds momentum.

text: Ducking switches state as soon as the button press registers, with a short standing-to-ducking transition of about a tenth of a second.
when: Duck button pressed
why: Immediate response keeps input feeling responsive

text: Ducking while running above a certain speed makes the character slide rather than stop.
when: Character ducks during a run
why: Speed and the duck input are tied by an arbitrary variable relationship rather than real physics.

text: Pushing a control to its maximum can switch it into an acceleration mode where input passes beyond its usual range.
when: Designing input ranges for racing or shooter controls
why: Extending input beyond its normal range gives extra response at full deflection.

text: A slide started at full running speed lasts just over one second.
when: slide started at full running speed
why: A large per-frame friction term decelerates the character until it halts on flat ground.

text: Movement feel is built from thumbstick mapping (direction and rate), terrain incline and friction updating ground sense, and button-driven state switches such as ducking and jumping.
when: Analyzing a character movement system
why: Incline and friction keep reshaping how the character feels in contact with the ground, while stick input sets direction and rate.

text: Overwriting velocity directly with thrust makes a ship carve circles with perfect grip, losing the floaty feel and resembling a remote-controlled car.
when: thrust sets velocity to the facing direction instead of adding to it
why: Direct overwriting removes inertia, so the ship no longer drifts.

text: Omitting deceleration leaves a character sliding indefinitely once it has moved, because it can never come to a stop.
when: horizontal movement stops when input is released
why: Without a stopping value, velocity never returns to zero.

text: Stepping off a ledge that sets fall speed high at once feels strange, because the avatar falls at a speed that should have built up over time.
when: Avatar walks off a platform edge
why: Skipping the build-up from zero makes the fall read as unnatural.

text: 1) Each frame, add acceleration in the held direction to velocity. 2) Clamp velocity to a max speed for each direction. 3) Update position from velocity. 4) When no direction is held, reduce velocity using a separate deceleration value.
when: a character moves horizontally under gradual acceleration
why: Separate acceleration, speed cap and deceleration let speed ramp up, stay bounded and stop cleanly.

text: A held run button raises both acceleration and max speed, including from a standstill, producing a faster run state.
when: a run button changes horizontal movement
why: Scaling both values together makes running feel faster in the same way.

text: Scale walk and run values together, keeping their ratio, to preserve the feel when units or overall speed change.
when: When both walk and run speeds are raised or lowered together
why: Perceived speed comes from the contrast between the two values, not their absolute size.

text: Do not set velocity directly to the desired value on landing. Let tire friction close the gap so the vehicle catches as it touches down.
when: vehicle lands with a gap between desired and actual speed
why: Snapping velocity directly feels artificial to players

text: Low creature inertia is easier for players to control and lets creatures stop and redirect, though less believable than high inertia.
when: Choosing creature inertia for herding the player must redirect.
why: High inertia spreads one decision across many frames and the whole group.

text: Zero acceleration and deceleration give instant start and stop, easing precise per-pixel positioning but producing a stiff, robotic feel unlike physical motion.
when: Choosing horizontal movement tuning for a character positioned by set position per frame.
why: Instant starts and stops are unlike physical motion, so players read the movement as mechanical; zero acceleration makes exact positioning easy.

text: Slow, precise crawling with looser direction control and no foot plant trades speed for precision, letting players take risky thin paths over drops as a risk-reward choice against faster running.
when: Low-speed movement while ducked
why: The crawl is slow but nearly guaranteed safe, so players weigh its safety against faster, riskier running.

text: 1) Start the jump with full initial upward velocity. 2) While jump is held, keep applying upward force for a limited time, up to a maximum height. 3) If jump is released while upward velocity exceeds a threshold, set velocity to a fixed low value close to zero but not zero.
when: jump height should depend on how long the button is held, with minimum and maximum heights
why: The early-release clamp gives a range of heights while keeping every jump's descent shape the same.

text: Cap falling speed at a hard-coded terminal velocity; once reached, effective gravity is zero, so the falling character stops accelerating.
why: Without a clamp, falls from height would keep accelerating and reach dangerous speeds.

text: Releasing upward inside a thick connectable platform and reconnecting higher lets the avatar climb through it; detaching at a high enough point snaps him onto the nearest valid ground above.
when: Swing carries avatar partway into a thick connectable platform
why: Connectable-only tiles can be penetrated in the air, enabling reattachment above them.

text: Time between encounters serves two purposes: building anticipation for the next combat and letting players recover from the last one. Both can happen together, so empty space can serve both.
when: Designing space between encounters

text: An existential foothold is a point of attachment that lets people dwell in a place; players need one in a level to feel attached and return to it.
A slide starts from ducking at speed, sliding back down a too-steep hill, or running onto a steep downhill.
Even basic running speed and turning have no meaning without a real setting for the player to move through.
Sparse environments convey vast openness, while densely packed ones make objects seem to rush at the player.
Chunks about one screen in size are common in procedural platformers, where they carry the core mechanics.
Elements such as columns, stairs, shadows, doorways, and terraces generate movement and a sense of continuity.
A single jump button can produce rich control feel when press length, non-constant gravity, and forgiving input rules are combined.
why: Each rule is small, but together they make controls satisfying.

text: Tune horizontal movement with separate acceleration, max speed and deceleration values for each direction, and separate values for running and air, since states change how responsive input feels.
when: setting up a character's horizontal feel, especially when it moves in several states like ground and air
why: Separate parameters allow each aspect of movement to be tuned independently.

text: Size a gap to a specific jump tier: if a gap looks exactly right for the longest jump, it almost always is meant for that jump.
when: platformer gap design
why: Players learn to judge horizontal distances by eye, so a gap matching a jump tier signals that jump.

text: Harder challenge usually comes from longer, more precise horizontal jumps.
Give a presence-triggered platform a return path so players can get back across.
when: When a moving platform starts automatically once the player stands on it

text: Stretch platforms horizontally to absorb overshoot, since the jump is imprecise.
why: Jumps land imprecisely, so extra platform width gives players room to overshoot.

text: Use fixed platform spacing when movement speed is predictable and the design aims at continuous forward play.
when: When the top speed is known in advance and levels are built around it
why: At top speed jumps and obstacles are easier, and the camera blocks the path back.

text: Let the environment's physics stop the player so the limit feels self-caused, a victimless blame shift that signals good level design.
when: Designing a barrier or limit
why: Players accept blame they can understand

text: Precise landings on small targets are hard in 3D, so avoid stomp challenges or add a ground shadow to help players judge landing position.
when: 3D platforming
why: Depth makes exact landings hard to judge.

text: Whether movement stores acceleration and velocity or only updates position changes how the movement feels.
A frictionless tile system suits a loose feel; add friction only where grip matters, such as vehicles that turn.
when: When a car or bike should carve satisfying turns
why: Without simulated friction, a tile-based body slides loosely and never catches on surfaces.

text: Pressing the action button at full run speed triggers a slide that adds forward force, damages enemies it touches, and can be cancelled with a small hop.
when: When the attack button is pressed while moving at full speed in a direction
why: The slide counts as an attack state, so anything it touches takes damage.

text: Releasing movement input halts a character immediately, so accidental falls off open platforms are rare and running feels safe.
when: relative to running speed
why: Instant stopping keeps running within the character's control.

text: Keeping core controls constant while changing ledges, cover and open arenas yields very different challenges from the same mechanics.
when: When the same core controls face enemies in rooms with varied ledges, cover or open arenas
why: Terrain features change the problem the same controls must solve.

text: A jump taken while moving faster than walking speed receives a small extra initial velocity, a binary boost that depends on whether the threshold is exceeded at takeoff.
when: jump initial velocity should reward running speed
why: A binary threshold rewards running speed without scaling jump height continuously.

text: Without a speed cap, velocity grows without bound under constant acceleration, so a maximum speed is needed.
when: a character accelerates under held input with no speed limit
why: Constant added acceleration keeps increasing velocity until it is clamped.

text: A narrow vertical dead zone governs the camera only while the avatar moves vertically; he falls through the zone with the camera still, then tracking begins at the zone edge at his speed.
when: Avatar falls or swings vertically
why: Vertical movement needs a separate, much narrower threshold than horizontal movement.

text: A vertical hook that latches pulls the avatar straight up along a predetermined animation, which the player starts but does not control.
when: Grapple fires straight up and latches
why: Fixed animation makes the vertical pull rigid and predictable.

text: A small hop cancels a slide, and a slow stand-up animation after landing makes the landing feel like a crash.
why: Lets players escape the long lockout of control after the slide, reducing a sense of unresponsiveness.

text: High friction ends a slide quickly on flat ground, so low-speed slides are brief and return the character to crawling.
when: When a slide starts at very low speed.

text: When sideways friction is much higher than forward friction, the vehicle arcs through turns instead of spinning on its axis.
Space platforms about four tiles apart vertically, under the five-tile maximum jump height, so landings occur on the shallow part of the arc.
when: When target platforms sit just below the avatar's maximum jump height.
why: Targets at this height let the avatar touch down near the flattest part of its arc, which is easier to hit.

text: Pit widths of two to six tiles cover the usable range, and a six-tile pit already feels quite risky.
A full-speed run can clear about 10 tiles, but levels rarely demand it because it is so hard to execute.
why: Executing the longest run jump is very hard, so designers avoid requiring it.

text: Landing targets narrower than about five avatar widths are rarely enjoyable, so avoid them.
why: Smaller targets feel too hard to enjoy.

text: Keep gaps narrower than the avatar's full jump distance; a gap wider than that requires an intermediate platform.
why: Otherwise players cannot cross the gap.

text: Special jumps are triggered by button combinations, button sequences, wall contact, or speed after a landing, and keep steering at the reduced air rate relative to takeoff facing.
when: When a jump is triggered by button combinations, button sequences, wall contact, or landing speed.

text: Ledges fall into three tiers: reachable by a basic jump, reachable only by a special jump, or out of reach without another route.
why: Players learn the predictable heights of each jump, so ledge reachability becomes readable by walking around.

text: Use both horizontal and vertical planes: vertical forces act as landmarks, horizontal forces lead across the ground, and diagonal forces lead upward and outward from the view.
why: Directing the player's eye through the scene matters, and these planes steer where views point.

text: A velocity diagram plots linear against angular velocity, with regions for stand still, creep, walk, run, shuffle turn, and turn on the spot.
why: Animations only look correct at matching movement rates, and speeding them too far looks unbelievable.

text: Leaps of faith that hide the far side force players to jump without seeing where they will land.
when: side-scrolling levels
why: Side-scrolling levels keep needed information within one screen, so hidden landings remove what the player needs to judge the jump.

text: In games, separating zones or forcing long trips between them isolates players, for example through distant ammunition or chore-like routes between shops, quests, and training.
when: When interactive elements sit far apart with wide empty gaps between them.
why: Long empty travel makes the space feel isolated and tedious.

text: Rotation with no attack ramp feels stiff and inorganic, even when the rest of the simulation is correct.
when: direct heading changes with instant full speed
why: Instant rotation lacks the slight inertia that makes motion feel natural.

text: A fixed jump arc and a single movement speed make a platformer feel stiff.
why: Without gradual acceleration or air control, the character's motion cannot respond to the player's input.

text: A jump input during a slide should emphasize horizontal distance with added vertical and horizontal force, have no timing window, and stay air-steerable.
when: When the A-button is pressed during a slide.
why: Rewards committed slides with distance without precise timing.

text: An attack input during a slide should add horizontal force, bounce the character up and down twice, count as an attack, and be cancelable by a small hop.
when: When the B button is pressed from the sliding state.

text: Include a few areas with less safe ground that demand exact footing to raise challenge within otherwise open layouts.
when: In levels where running elsewhere is open and safe.
why: Unsafe ground contrasts with easy running elsewhere, so exact footing demands focused attention.

text: Place gaps only where ample take-off and landing space surround them, so the approach's weaknesses are not exposed.
when: Designing gaps for jump detection
why: Without a target velocity, the approach cannot compute a takeoff that clears the gap and reaches a landing spot.

text: Tune gap sizes so jumps are easier at maximum speed, rewarding bold, fast play.
why: A predictable maximum speed lets designers align obstacle sizes to it.

text: Size and space platforms and objects to fit the height and distance of avatar jumps, so every challenge matches what the avatar can do.
Set basic-tier ledges below the apex of a basic jump so many jumps can land on them.
Some velocity combinations have no matching animation and should be used only briefly.
why: Animations cannot switch mid-cycle and must reach a transition point first, so unmatched speeds cannot be sustained.

text: A low terminal velocity feels like an artificial clamp the player notices, while a high one makes falls from height feel wrong.
Controlling a moving thing has an intrinsic, aimless pleasure, and players describe the result as smooth, floaty or stiff.
why: Immediate response to the player's inputs gives a physical enjoyment of motion.

text: Real-time control is continuous, uninterrupted avatar control where input and result feel simultaneous; numeric thresholds are necessary, but overall player impression decides if it feels real.
Intuitive controls translate player intent into game outcome with near-perfect fidelity, so the avatar feels like an extension of the body.
Establishing real-time control is the largest part of game feel analysis; the remaining checks are simulated space and polish.
Real-time control rests on a human correction cycle of about 240 ms, and the computer must meet three thresholds: motion, instantaneous response and continuity.
why: Thresholds are tied to human correction timing and human information processing, so machine timing is judged against human limits.

text: 1) Build a real-time avatar prototype in a space with varied objects. 2) Ask questions the space provokes, such as reaching, flying or jumping. 3) Let skills and challenges emerge from exploration. 4) Keep the best-feeling motions. 5) Constrain motions that feel bad.
when: Early development, when the desired control feel is not yet known.
why: The answer to a good feel often emerges through experimentation.

text: Kinesthesia, often used interchangeably with proprioception, is the subconscious sense of body position in space, weight, and movement of muscles, tendons and joints.
Kinesthetics are the feel of a game: how its controls respond and how the interface feels to the player.
The screen, speakers and controller extend the player's senses, so the player perceives the game world only through them.
Immersive graphics, sound, and motion or other controllers add to a game's fun through sensory stimulation.
The inner ear senses changes in speed rather than steady velocity, so accelerating virtual motion causes discomfort.
when: When the on-screen camera whips around while the player's body stays still.
why: A mismatch between what the eye sees and what the inner ear senses can cause nausea.

text: Players judge object size and distance mainly from visual cues, while sound and rumble signal contact with objects.
when: moving near objects of varying size
why: vision is the primary perceptual channel

text: Spatial reference during play comes only from impassable tiles, enemies and enemy projectiles.
A large slow or distant object reads massive, a small fast one reads small; motion speed carries most size impression, sound, particles and screen shake only support it.
when: When a large object is seen at a distance and its movement must convey scale.
why: Size and motion are perceived together, so motion signals scale.

text: For a large object, keep the camera aligned along the line from the avatar to the object and widen the view angle to exaggerate distance and reinforce its height.
when: Conveying the scale of a giant or large object.
why: Aligned framing and a wider angle make the object seem to tower over the player.

text: Balancing a character's size against its speed defines much of a fighting game's feel.
when: Designing character stats in fighting games
why: Larger characters are easier to hit but move differently than smaller, faster ones

text: Players who see movement faster than they have seen before perceive the game as new and exciting.
when: a game delivers an unfamiliar speed of movement
why: Unfamiliar speed is novel, and novelty drives excitement.

text: Staging means presenting an input's result so clearly that the player understands it and can reproduce it on purpose.
why: Results that happen too fast or are lost among other motion look random.

text: Staging principles depend on controlled camera behavior, so they transfer to games less directly than other animation principles.
Falling reads as faster than any other movement, and at long grapple length horizontal swing reads faster than vertical pull.
In third-person games, a lock-on feature keeps a target tracked, without which players must consciously manage their aim.
when: Designing third-person combat targeting
why: Lock-on removes the burden of manual tracking.

text: Speed is perceived relative to surrounding objects: an empty stretch removes the sense of speed, and fast apparent motion of richly textured static background objects carries most of it.
why: Without nearby objects to move against, motion has no reference point and so no sense of speed.

text: Speed is conveyed through view-angle changes (suggesting increasing speed), motion blur (conveying speed as a real camera would), sound and fast-moving nearby objects.
Peripheral visual cues strongly affect the sense of motion, so removing side cues from a display can change how much a player feels movement.
when: When blinders or framing block the player's side view of the display.
why: Blocking side vision removes the cues that convey movement, weakening the feeling of motion.

text: Camera distance, viewing angle, object size and relative object speeds change perceived speed, regardless of the simulated speed.
why: Perspective alters how fast motion appears to the player.

text: Widening the view angle beyond 90 degrees exaggerates the distance travelled and the perceived speed.
when: Applying a wider view to suggest speed.
why: The enlarged angle stretches apparent motion.

text: A slowed-scroll zone runs from about 25 percent of screen width, measured from the left edge, to the centre.
Real-world cues that build the impression of speed are object size, relative motion against nearby objects, and changes in sound.
why: The audiovisual system judges motion from these clues, so reproducing them makes motion seem to occur.

text: Motion, sound and particles must all agree on a large object's scale; scaling up size without scaling motion makes it feel small, and polish cannot fix it.
when: Making a creature or object appear larger or massive.
why: Speed of motion carries most of the sense of size; if one channel conveys smaller size, the object feels smaller despite its simulated mass.

text: Judge a game's speed by comparison with nearby objects and real-world analogues rather than by the speed value stored in code.
when: Tuning how fast movement feels.
why: The player's impression, not the internal value, determines perceived speed.

text: Vignette the edges during intense focus on a destination to limit peripheral motion cues, but a vignette at the wrong moment distracts and breaks presence.
when: the player concentrates on reaching a specific destination
why: limits peripheral motion cues that trigger discomfort

text: Holding a direction during a swing can feel like nudging the arc, though input only counts on the two apex frames.
when: while swinging on a predetermined arc
why: Each swing frame stores position for collision and damage, so the arc looks continuous while input is checked only at the apex.

text: Dust particles kicked up under moving wheels show that the vehicle is in motion and in contact with the ground.
Use a non-linear stick steering curve that raises the steering ratio as deflection grows, giving small turns at small deflection, sharper turns at full deflection, and less twitchiness.
when: When a thumbstick returns a continuous range of deflection values.
why: A constant ratio makes small stick movements produce jumpy turns, which a rising ratio damps.

text: Tune vehicle forward speed, turning, sliding and friction slip only with a track and surrounding terrain present.
why: Handling values only gain meaning against the curves and slopes the car must negotiate.

text: With physics simulated, the rear of the car slides out slightly, producing a power slide naturally.
when: In rally games where the AI steers early and heavily into a severe corner.

text: A direction change snaps instantly at zero speed, but at nonzero speed the heading blends toward the desired direction each frame, producing a carving turn whose rate depends on speed.
when: Character turning from a stick input
why: Frame-based blending avoids a stiff, robotic feel

text: A large gap between desired and actual velocity makes the tires break loose and slide, like a peel-out. This also applies when a vehicle lands sideways while spinning.
when: large velocity gap
why: The difference overwhelms tire friction, so the tires lose grip

text: Moment-to-moment steering corrections occur about every 240 ms, nested under higher goals.
why: Higher intentions split into many sub-goals, and each one is handled inside the same repeating correction cycle.

text: A realistic vehicle in a stylized world creates a visual disconnect that a playful tone can help offset.
when: When a realistic vehicle is placed in a fantastical world with stylized creatures.
why: Setting the expectation that handling won't match full simulation lets the mismatch hold together.

text: When direction input changes quickly, let the character arc toward it with a slight lag rather than tracking the input one-to-one.
when: rapid direction changes
why: An arc reads as a physical body turning.

text: Spawn a ground tire mark when the friction on a wheel exceeds a set threshold during a hard turn.
Drive passenger animation from gameplay parameters such as steering and reversing, so the character reacts to vehicle state without bespoke clips.
A realistic driving model rewards precise control but makes unrealistic crash reactions conspicuous, while a stylized model with a special slide button keeps control accessible and forgiving.
when: Choosing the handling model for a racing game
why: Each approach sets different player expectations for handling and collisions.

text: A particle is a 2D textured plane placed in 3D space that billboards to face the camera, and it usually ignores lighting and forces.
Many polish effects are camera-facing particle sprites played with randomized frames.
Motion matters more than texture for effects: fading, blasting particles feel satisfying even when their color or form makes no physical sense.
when: Designing particle effects for power
why: Players perceive power through motion, not realism.

text: A full simulation can be shown by visualizing only object interactions, letting the player build a picture of the world through contact.
when: World is simulated but visually sparse.

text: A volume such as a smoke column can be built from many planes with painted depth, and because they are never seen at an angle they blend into one pillar.
when: Building volumetric-looking effects cheaply
why: Viewing angles that would reveal the flat planes are never shown.

text: A sectional axonometric also shows the extruded interior geometry of a form.
Semi-planned axonometrics may not follow the plan exactly and can show 3D gameplay concepts.
when: planning vertical gameplay ideas rather than exact geometry

text: A section cuts a space vertically and is used with plans to describe three-dimensional space.
Sections help map multilevel puzzles, multiplayer battle positions, side-scrolling pacing, and height transitions such as ramps, overhead bridges and cliffs to drop from.
when: designing vertical or multilevel gameplay

text: Nesting is a practical way to represent a complex world simply, since each interior connects to the outside only through its gateway.
when: when a world is too complex to model as one continuous space
why: People mentally treat an indoor space separately, paying little thought to how it connects to the outdoors.

text: Design one hierarchically important view for a key moment, rather than a set of equally weighted three-dimensional views.
Spaces designed as a planned sequence of views, with previews and choices along the route, let visitors anticipate a destination and make decisions before reaching it.
when: Designing the route into a major landmark or destination
why: Staged previews build anticipation and turn approach paths into a series of meaningful decisions.

text: Assign one graph-paper square a set unit, such as one yard, to make quick sketches that stay accurately proportioned.
when: sketching level layouts to scale
why: Many engines already measure space in grid units, so a scaled sketch lets the designer judge proportions.

text: Before building a level, sketch one area for each step of the sequence so the teaching order is planned.
when: laying out a hand-built teaching level

text: A more complex level representation yields fewer, more homogeneous regions, trading implementation simplicity for fewer analysis cells.
when: Level geometry is not built from tiles.

text: A parti is a measurement-free spatial sketch of a level's layout, used early to explore which gameplay ideas and orientations are worth pursuing, not for final planning.
when: Exploring level concepts before committing to measurements
why: Partis are fast to make but lack the precision needed for construction.

text: Architectural types are building forms linked to a function, formed when same-use buildings share a form over time; proportion-based architectural orders formed a shared vocabulary of recognizable forms.
Divided space carves an irregular space into sections, like a real map.
Architecture mainly shapes the experience people have inside a structure, not its outer look, and game designers share this goal of building spaces that produce experiences.
A ziggurat is a temple set atop a man-made hill, frequently constructed from kiln-fired brick.
Figure-ground arranges solid masses as figures within open negative space, and the spaces framed between figures become positive space that matters as much as the figures.
Form-void is a three-dimensional extension of figure-ground in which spaces are carved from solid masses or created by adding masses, suited to non-top-down views.
Intimate space is neither confining nor oversized; everything in it is reachable with the character's inherent abilities and fits its size and movement.
A labyrinth is a unicursal structure with one winding path that loops around and reaches an endpoint, serving as the model for linear gamespaces.
Contradiction in space means one place can feel both good and bad at once, such as safe yet threatening.
A bad space is a space designed to place players in specific, exhilarating danger.
Architectural rhythms of columns, arcades, tiles, and shadows guide people's movement and regulate how quickly they pass through a space.
Historic designers consistently composed buildings for visitor experience, including sight lines, movement sequences, form communicating meaning, storytelling through space and social play.
when: Learning spatial design from architecture
why: Architects designed how people moved through and perceived buildings, and each era shaped this, which transfers to levels.

text: Game worlds can treat architecture as navigable space with circulation and activity areas, or treat it as scenery with no navigable role.
Architecture offers practical theory on how people perceive space and provides precedents for emotionally evocative levels.
when: Seeking spatial principles for level design
why: Architecture has long shaped perception and emotion through space.

text: Monumental forms and materials can express a ruler's connection to the divine, and placing chambers with symbolic meaning reinforces that message.
when: Designing a space that conveys status or belief
why: Form, materials and placement communicate meaning to everyone who experiences the space.

text: Industrial materials allowed taller and wider buildings, and this provoked a backlash that favored handcrafted, natural materials.
when: Understanding how material technology shapes spatial taste
why: New capability prompted a return to honest, crafted materials.

text: Relief sculpture and mosaics can pass biblical narratives to audiences who cannot read.
when: audience largely illiterate

text: Buildings that change hands can gain narrative layers their original builders never intended.
Raising a sacred structure on a mound was understood to bring it closer to the gods and to recall the mountains of origin.
Supporting spaces attached to a playing area, such as a bullpen, can carry their own rules.
Renaissance architecture revived classical arches, domes, and column orders, and added symmetry and centralised floor plans.
Roman architecture contributed mainly engineering and structural innovation layered onto Greek architectural language.
Refinements of the arch, vault, and dome made large interior spaces possible.
Lintels, posts, column orders, domes, arches, and vaults are structural forms that make a gamespace feel believable.
Seeing architecture means processing its spatial, formal, contextual and historical elements, not only what the eyes detect.
Game levels do not have to obey physical, environmental or regulatory constraints, so game spaces can use experimental or freeform layouts that real buildings cannot.
In games, interior and exterior are mostly labels derived from the visual style applied to a gamespace.
Labyrinth floor patterns in medieval churches were used for meditative walking.
Buildings offering healing and curse removal can be marked by religious symbols and plan features such as a narthex or apse.
Pattern languages with explanations were written so non-experts could design their own spaces, such as houses.
Pattern language ideas have influenced building codes, urban planning, web development and computer science.
Later urban planning favoring walkable, mixed-use neighborhoods builds on these diversity ideas.
Standardize a few recognizable forms, reusing them with consistent building types and signage to form a shared visual language that makes a whole environment readable.
when: Building a consistent visual language across many spaces
why: Recognizable repeated forms make an environment easier to read and to navigate.

text: Reuse the same sprite or model for service buildings across towns, and keep consistent functional props such as anvils, stoves or counters, so players recognize function everywhere.
Use figure-ground for plan-view layouts, placing figures to mark out rooms, corridors and meeting areas by reading the spaces they frame; use form-void when the view is not top-down.
when: Choosing a spatial method for a level
why: Framed spaces, not just solid figures, define how areas are used; figure-ground suits plan views while form-void handles 3D views.

text: Combine several uses of a mechanic rather than in isolation; place systems side by side or stacked for satisfying complexity. Contrasts add drama to space and mechanics.
when: When systems sit next to each other or are layered over one another.
why: Combined uses make mechanics and systems more interesting to players.

text: Urban planning theory can guide the design of augmented reality, alternate reality, and large-scale physical games.
when: Planning spatial design for location-based games
why: Urban theory addresses how people move through and use shared spaces.

text: Divided space fits games that replicate a real map.
when: Choosing divided space organization

text: Use terraces and colonnades to move visitors through a sequence of scenes, letting the space reveal a narrative step by step.
when: Designing a route that tells a story or shows a sequence of scenes
why: Stepped progression paces the reveal and guides the visitor through each scene.

text: Place the entrance on a short side of a long room so the room reads as long and the visitor walks toward a focal point at the far end.
when: Designing a linear room that leads to a goal
why: Entering the short side makes the length of the room the dominant experience.

text: Show structural and handcrafted materials honestly rather than hiding them, so the space communicates how it is made.
when: Choosing finishes and materials for a space
why: Honest materials make a space's construction legible and credible.

text: Zone multi-storey buildings by floor: a taller, plainer ground floor for business and a shorter upper floor with more elaborate windows for guests.
when: multi-storey buildings with public and private functions
why: Upper floors signal status and host visitors.

text: Articulate public and private areas and align landmarks on an axis to move visitors through a public space.
when: Public areas where visitors should be guided along a route.

text: Spaces with little distinct character work as circulation that carries players toward the next destination, offering rest or building suspense.
when: When a space has little or no distinct character.

text: Repeating a few building or room types helps players locate their next objective from a single viewpoint.
when: in large open worlds
why: Recognizable repeated structures reduce navigation effort.

text: Adding contradictory features that both strengthen and threaten the player's sneaking lets one space serve several functions at once.
when: when a level space feels flat or single-purpose
why: The same space works as an asset or a liability depending on the player's strategy and choices.

text: Arcs can apply at multiple scales: to a whole story, each book, each chapter, or each world, with each world following its own arc.
when: Structuring games with many levels or worlds

text: Use facades or balconies to summarize a space's contents or to hint at areas beyond what the player can enter.
when: When secrets lie beyond the player's current location.
why: Showing unseen possibilities draws players to explore a place to find them.

text: Focus multiplayer space design on interaction, leaving open room where memorable player events can occur, not only on working mechanics.
A dense grid of columns beneath a heavy roof produces a sense of vast, dim, ethereal space that feels both enclosed and expansive.
when: Designing a large interior meant to feel awe-inspiring or otherwise
why: Repeated supports and low light create depth and mood.

text: Heavy, closely spaced supports feel weighty and assertive, while slender, raised supports feel light and lifted, so support form sets a space's emotional tone.
when: Choosing the visual character of supports in a space
why: Proportion and spacing of supports convey weight and lightness.

text: An axial layout that leads visitors toward a focal point structures their movement and can express a hierarchy between leader and congregation.
why: Such layouts evoke the kingdom of heaven.

text: Minimising interior structural stone lets large stained-glass windows grow and filter light, making visitors feel closer to the divine.
A required daily ritual can fix building orientation and add a functional element, such as a tower for a call to prayer.
when: When worshippers must pray facing a fixed direction several times a day.

text: A concealed backstage structure lets unseen voices and costume changes occur out of the audience's view.
With compartmentalisation declining, players can cross mountains, forests, and underwater caves without progressing through structured levels.
when: In modern 3D game environments where players can move freely along all three axes.

text: A visual pattern can take on new meaning across levels as mechanics grow, such as a shield pattern later marking explosive puzzle pieces.
when: when a game reuses a visual pattern across levels
why: Players relearn the pattern's role in each new context.

text: An arcade can separate a shaded space beneath it from a bright open courtyard, so one open area feels like two distinct spaces.
When housing is cut off from the rest of a city, public social life can shrink to whatever connecting passages remain.
why: Residents had no other public venue inside the complex, so activity spilled into its elevated walkways.

text: Walkers entrain to large repeating floor patterns, so shrinking the pattern at a destination slows them as they approach.
when: large floor pattern leading to a shop entrance
why: walkers match their pace to the pattern

text: Oku layouts wind streets and passages like onion layers, hiding gathering spaces found only by explorers, combining Zen views of other layers, layered walls, non-90-degree corners and access-denying passages.
A Greek theater had three parts: a circular orchestra, a skene building serving as backdrop and backstage, and a proskenion where the performance took place.
Amphitheater arenas combined tunnels, scenery, elevators, and trap doors to bring animals in for hunts and staged recreations.
A modernist open-plan model has five points: piloti, free façade, ribbon windows, open floor plan, and roof terrace.
why: Because the columns carry the structure, the façade and interior walls are free of load-bearing duty.

text: Four generators of city diversity are multiuse districts with constant activity, short blocks, buildings of varying age, and high population density.
A tartan interleaves structural members and surface elements at several levels of hierarchy, from large to small. Game tartans combine large prospect rhythms with intimate ones.
why: Layering large-scale events over individual challenges makes gameplay richer than planning only from the outside.

text: A support that could not plausibly carry its load is noticed by players, and that can break engagement.
Copying decorative motifs without their underlying design logic produces a theme-park feel that reads as artificial.
1) Clarify the functional space first and use it as the skeleton. 2) Choose an organizing principle: linear, grid, web, points in space, or divided space. 3) Combine principles where needed.
when: Starting to lay out a game space
why: A clear organizing principle gives the layout a skeleton

text: 1) Enter from a transitional entry space. 2) Pass through the main long interior. 3) Reach the focal point at the far end, with an optional rear room behind it.
when: Designing a room sequence that builds toward a focal point
why: A clear progression from entry to goal organizes movement and builds anticipation.

text: 1) Study the architectural style you want. 2) Define the game's look from it. 3) Build fictional structures from that style's real forms.
why: Allusions to real architectural styles can theme a gamespace and give it an epic, otherworldly feel.

text: 1) Learn why the space was built and what it serves now. 2) Look up while walking, noting forms, layering and materials. 3) Sense size, shape, light, sound and adjacent spaces. 4) Understand how structure holds the space up. 5) Judge whether materials work in compression or tension and whether they feel heavy or light. 6) Determine construction and materials. 7) Examine historical precedents. 8) Analyze composition, proportion and rhythm. 9) Observe fit with the setting. 10) Analyze what makes it special.
when: when analyzing an existing space as a designer

text: Record a lobby- or courtyard-sized space, real or in a game, by drawing at least three of plan, section, elevation, axonometric or perspective, plus notes or diagrams.
when: studying how spaces are represented

text: 1) Ask why the level is built the way it is 2) ask what gameplay experience it creates 3) ask what precedents it draws on 4) ask how its space is composed.
when: when analyzing a level you played

text: Build spaces either by placing geometric forms into open space or by carving them out of a solid mass, using Boolean-style combination of models.
when: when constructing 3D gamespaces in an engine or art tool
why: Both methods create the same spatial relationships in different ways.

text: Use meeting spaces only when a tutorial must truly stop the player for a demonstration.
Use a labyrinthine structure when a narrative, theme or argument must reach the player in a fixed order, or for linear navigation of one level.
why: Labyrinth-like twists, turns and challenges add interest even when the pathway is straightforward and linear.

text: Give starting settlements trainers for every class and introductory quests tied to the player's background.
when: In MMOs and online worlds where players enter a centralized town or beginner's area.
why: Trainers and starter quests let players sample the available character types before they commit.

text: Zoning functions into separate areas simplifies layout but prevents chance meetings; mixed-use spaces let players of different skills, styles and types meet.
Many players are surprised at how real a space feels once they explore it by looking around.
when: Players examine a detailed VR space
why: Turning the head lets the brain assemble a three-dimensional mental map of the surroundings, which strengthens the feeling of being there.

text: Notice the feelings you have while exploring in real life, then recreate them in the game.
when: designing exploration

text: Arrange simple features so they evoke a remembered landscape; a gnarled tree placed among rocks suggests craggy mountains.
why: Natural-looking arrangements act as a symbolic language that signals a landscape type to viewers.

text: When environment surfaces respond physically, such as squishy versus solid, the avatar's motion feel changes accordingly.
when: Designing terrain or surfaces that the avatar interacts with physically
why: Surface response shapes how movement is felt, so surface quality is part of control feel.

text: A seasonal change can alter how the same landscape plays, so one space offers different experiences over time without changing its geometry.
when: when the same layout is revisited across a game's time cycle
why: Seasonal changes let designers link the environment's appearance to gameplay, giving players an alternative version of the same place.

text: 1) Decide the intended feel of each space, such as restful, tense or meditative, before detailing its content. 2) Shape it with lighting, shadows, spatial organization and size. 3) Reinforce it with environmental art and sound.
when: when planning a space

text: 1) Set most content in the domain that embodies the theme. 2) Stage the climax in the opposing domain, so the contrast reinforces the central theme.
when: Choosing settings and level structure for a theme
why: Setting and contrast reinforce the central theme

text: Level design should carry meaning as well as mechanics, using architecture, vernacular, and art assets to convey narrative.
Classic axonometric games from the early 1980s created an impression of 3D space with 2D art and no perspective distortion.
Show as much information on screen as possible in axonometric views, unless the world is expansive enough to resemble a top-down game.
when: in axonometric views
why: Downward cameras limit sight lines, so visible information matters more.

text: Players struggle to orient in axonometric space because cardinal directions are unavailable and sight lines are limited by the downward camera.
when: in axonometric views
why: The downward-facing camera restricts visible directions and distance.

text: Mark vantage points, sniping spots and spatial puzzles over a visual backdrop in an axonometric diagram to plan three-dimensional gameplay.
when: planning gameplay in three dimensions
why: Axon-style diagrams make verticality and sight lines readable at a glance.

text: Show vertical relationships between surfaces very clearly in axonometric views; poorly drawn views cause optical illusions that disorient players and misread height and position.
when: When a game uses an axonometric view without perspective distortion.
why: Without perspective depth cues, height and position are easy to misread.

text: A blockage halts progress until a condition is met; examples include a locked door needing a key, a guard wanting a favor, or a camera requiring the lights to be off.
Combine a newly introduced hazard with terrain from earlier mechanisms, so the player must apply both skills at once.
when: late in a level sequence
why: Introducing a mechanic safely, then layering it into harder challenges, lets players build skills in steps.

text: A blockage guarantees that whatever happens while meeting its condition occurs before whatever lies beyond it.
Enemies that sweep beams across the screen can remove connection points in the places the player wants to reach.
when: Placing enemies over areas that hold connection points
why: Hazards that cover anchors cancel the player's chosen routes.

text: Dense obstacle placement makes a vehicle harder to drive, so spacing must be wide enough for its speed and turn rate.
why: Steering precision depends on turn amount relative to forward speed, which governs how accurately a moving target can be chased.

text: Mark each barrier with a visible symbol matching the tool that breaks it; a barrier lacking a visible tool or cue leaves players no clear path back.
when: When the player is expected to return with a newly found power to open earlier barriers.
why: so players can plan backtracking

text: Environmental mechanisms should be usable in many different ways to be valuable.
when: Designing environmental mechanisms
why: A mechanism with one use adds little variety over repeated play.

text: Place hazards such as enemy spawns that must be cleared, so clearing them makes an area passable.
why: Clearing threats is paired with in-game rewards such as items, reinforcing the behavior the way conditioning does.

text: Players who can move forward tend to look forward and seldom look around unless the design holds them in place.
when: Players are free to move in a VR scene
why: Early low-frame-rate VR taught players to hold their heads motionless to prevent nausea.

text: Players read screen shake that follows a short delay as a shockwave, and a jarring shake on an impact as a force of enormous size.
when: Impacts and blasts shown with camera shake
why: Players learn this shake vocabulary from film and recognize it as a sign of concussive force even without everyday analogues.

text: A Zen view is a brief, deliberate glimpse of a reward, such as a vista or narrative stage, along the route, making players strive to reach that space.
Graphical perspective is the viewpoint a camera provides, like first or third person, shaping which actions players believe are available.
A modern isometric 3D camera is angled above and behind the character, aims downward, and uses perspective projection.
Level of detail allocates the most computation to what the player is likely to notice, rather than simply to what is nearest.
The 'ant farm' view abstracts three-dimensional space into a simplified overview, a representation that later shaped depictions of real and fictional 3D space.
In 3D engines the camera is an object whose placement determines what the player sees of the gamespace, so point of view depends on camera placement.
Some areas switch to a fixed view from a preset vantage point rather than following the character.
Mode 7 on 16-bit consoles simulated three-dimensional depth, extending the ant-farm perspective of environments.
In perspective, circles become ellipses.
when: drawing circular forms in a perspective view

text: Making things look good from far away is easy; making them hold up up close is the hard part.
In first-person views the camera sits at eye level inside the avatar's head region, if the game uses a body model at all.
Pathfinding and orientation methods from 3D games are largely unusable in side-scrolling levels.
Top-down views suit expansive exploration, interaction with non-player characters, and aligning the character with targets for shooting, sword fighting, or basic jumping.
Mixing direct and indirect camera control can feel clumsy, and level layout plus fixed views can offset the problems.
why: Fixed vantage points plug specific gaps, and large open layouts with landmarks reduce the problems.

text: Enemies near the player should appear large, central and identifiable, while distant enemies appear smaller, because distance tracks relevance in 3D space.
Over-the-shoulder cameras sit close behind the character and let players swing the view toward where it looks, blending first- and third-person perspectives.
The bigger the group, the more a cutscene should be avoided or carefully placed, because members differ in interest and tolerance for waiting.
when: MMO group content
why: Random groups mix players who want loot or achievements and skip story, and they have little patience for waiting.

text: A centered focal point draws the eye to the middle first, while interest placed at the edges pushes the eye outward.
when: Composing a view or framing a space
why: Objects on the edges pull attention outward, as viewers want to explore beyond the frame.

text: Good level design lets visual cues guide players through a space, so they sense agency over their route.
why: Routes pulled by the eye let players feel their path was freely chosen, sustaining both control and immersion.

text: Build large areas around tall, rounded structures, where the free camera is rarely obstructed and objectives stay visible.
when: designing large open 3D areas
why: Clear sightlines keep objectives visible.

text: Use porticos to let inhabitants look out onto vistas, and keep room-size ratios consistent across the space.
why: Basing spatial proportions on human scale grounds the layout in how people actually move and interact.

text: When screen space is limited, split a large world into framed views and compose each with painting techniques.
when: limited screen space
why: Splitting the world into screen-sized pieces mirrors how traditional landscape art is framed, borrowing painting methods within fragmented 2D space.

text: Test visual effects and foreground content to find how much clutter players can track before they lose their avatar.
when: When experimenting in dedicated test levels before building playable levels

text: Choose the camera to suit the point of view the player will have.
Because the player controls where to look in first person, use lines of sight and other architectural tricks to direct attention to details and guide movement.
when: in first-person levels
why: The player, not the designer, chooses the view direction.

text: Careful drawing of level geometry and backgrounds can deliver rewarding vistas in top-down games.
Vertical elements such as columns, trees, or doorframes are effective framing tools.
when: when framing a path or view in a level
why: Vertical shapes clearly bound the view around the focal point.

text: Negative space works best when a visible prospect implies a beyond extending past what the player can see.
why: Players unaware of what surrounds them feel anxiety, which strengthens the effect of a visible prospect.

text: A narrow opening that reveals a reward for a moment on the way to a goal can be built into the route to that goal.
why: Openings in the route serve progression while also showing the player their destination.

text: Treat each view as a film shot and plan what sits in the frame, especially for scenes meant to fit a single frame.
when: When a whole scene must fit within one frame
why: Framing a view strongly shapes how players understand what they are supposed to do.

text: A camera is well designed when players do not notice it.
why: Good camera work is judged by the absence of comments about it, which signals it moves correctly.

text: Use a one-way camera that never scrolls back to discourage backtracking and keep the player moving forward.
why: Going left against a frozen camera feels abrupt and unyielding, so the one-way view makes backtracking feel bad.

text: 2D and top-down views can show information beyond the character's line of sight, which most 3D games hide, since top-down games rely less on reaction-based action.
Framing choices change what viewers notice and how they respond; camera framing can convey story, and wide horizontal panoramic formats can suit simulating field experience.
when: when framing a shot to convey story or simulate field experience

text: Visual processing separates objects in a scene below awareness and draws boundaries, so a line drawing arrives already sorted and needs less effort to understand.
when: when deciding how much visual detail to render
why: Preprocessing removes work the brain would otherwise do.

text: Players move toward whatever draws their attention first, so controlling where they look controls where they go.
when: When designers want players steered without being told where to go
why: Food is the most attention-grabbing thing for a dog, so a held-out treat steers its gaze.

text: Framed openings and widening spaces can foreshadow or heighten the player's arrival at a location, turning transitions into guideposts.
when: when designing transitions between areas
why: The framing hints at what lies ahead and builds anticipation.

text: Off-center placement of a character and landmarks steers the player's gaze toward the landmark rather than holding it at center.
when: when a landmark should draw the player's attention
why: The eye is pulled along the off-center offset toward the focal element.

text: Vertical elements like windows and columns converge through perspective, drawing the gaze downward into a drop.
when: when a space has a drop or pit
why: Converging lines heighten the sense of height, so the fall feels more intense.

text: Showing information beyond the avatar's view lets designers hint at secrets before the player can reach them.
why: Without the character's viewpoint limiting the frame, designers can reveal places the player cannot yet reach.

text: A small amount of game reaction smooths jerky mouse input in first-person aiming.
when: When input sensitivity is high but game reaction sensitivity is low, as in mouse-driven aiming
why: Directly tied mouse motion feels snappy and jerky, which a small game response softens.

text: The main view families are first-person, third-person, 2D side-scrolling, 2D top-down, and axonometric or isometric.
Top-down gamespaces are viewed from above like a building plan, giving few sight lines but strong orientation.
why: Many top-down spaces read as a plan, so players can orient by cardinal directions and landmarks.

text: Miniature spaces are either vantage-point gardens viewed from a fixed spot or stroll spaces walked through; large worlds often mix both.
A camera set too low gives a disorienting pseudo-third-person view, which hurts both navigation and unit selection in a strategy game.
when: choosing camera placement for strategy games
why: A low angle hides the battlefield and makes selecting units difficult.

text: Scenery placed near the player's route is ignored when it does not match their current goals.
why: Players fixed on a goal focus their attention on the chase, not on nearby sights.

text: Making everything obvious from the start reduces the reasons players have to look around.
why: Controls that do nothing prompt players to explore, which builds a sense of presence.

text: Early pseudo-3D methods such as isometric and prerendered 3D lowered landscape quality for a time because designers had not yet learned the new tools.
when: when adopting a new rendering technique before mastering it
why: unfamiliar tools cause weaker results until skills develop

text: In first-person views players can drift away from narrative events, and without exterior views they may not understand the shape of the surrounding space.
when: in first-person levels
why: Nothing keeps players near events, and the exterior contours of the space are hidden.

text: 1) Place cutscenes before major encounters to give the group a final moment to prepare and to introduce the boss. 2) Place cutscenes after major battles, when timing matters less.
when: Cutscenes in multiplayer groups, where some members may not want story content
why: Random group members have mixed motives and low tolerance for delays, so cutscene timing must avoid stalling them.

text: 1) Select a city-level LOD: one economic behaviour for the whole city, or a block-by-block simulation. 2) Give each block its own LOD: block behaviour, or per-citizen behaviour for the block containing the player. 3) Run individual behaviours only at the lowest level.
when: Large simulated cities with a player present.
why: Each level of detail is scheduled by the level above.

text: Allow participants enough time and clarity to react to dangers and openings, and do not let them easily become stuck or disoriented.
when: Designing wayfinding and hazard display.
why: Those short on data or time experience unjust strain and lose interest.

text: Limit movement while players are visually cut off, to reduce injury from real-world objects.
when: In VR games where players cannot see their real surroundings

text: Judge confined, dungeon-like spaces played in first person from the player's viewpoint.
when: evaluating room size in first-person levels
why: Editor views differ from the player's eye-level perspective, so flaws surface only after building time is spent; an eye-level view catches them sooner.

text: When the camera is central to a game, test camera systems in a toy box.
why: A separate test space lets designers check how mechanics interact before those mechanics are built into the real levels.

text: Scrolling stops at screen edge zones, so the avatar can push against the edge as if it were a solid wall.
when: Avatar reaches a level's screen edge zone
why: Edge zones prevent the camera from revealing areas beyond the boundary.

text: Reserve gentle screen shake for heavy objects, so the camera response signals mass.
Many small vertical lines draw the eye upward, yet players rarely look up, so use verticality for grandeur or direction rather than as a surprise.
when: when designing vertical space in a level
why: players focus on the ground path ahead

text: Fixed cinematic camera angles from below, in front, or close up add drama but reduce player control.
when: For certain dramatic scenes in fixed-perspective third-person games

text: In third-person views, scaling rooms and furniture requires choosing between avatar size, cavernous rooms, sparse layouts, and slightly enlarged furniture spread out; the last counteracts third-person distortion best.
when: Designing interiors for third-person games
why: Players sense their body floating behind the avatar, making normal rooms feel cramped

text: A fixed camera avoids camera collisions in cramped spaces but removes free viewing, which can make those areas feel weaker.
when: confined spaces
why: Free camera movement is obstructed in tight, closed-in caves, so a fixed camera position compensates for that.

text: First-person views suit line-of-sight relationships and aiming and can be very immersive, but they suit platform jumping and melee fighting poorly compared with wider perspectives.
when: when choosing a camera for a game
why: Narrow view limits awareness of surroundings and spatial timing.

text: Foreground elements that surround a focal view, like a picture frame, direct attention to that view and make the arrival at it more dramatic.
when: when designing a view or destination the player should notice
why: Framing isolates the focal point against its surroundings.

text: Place a checkpoint at each scene of a few screens so a failed player restarts close to the problem and can retry quickly with a new approach.
when: levels that teach through failure
why: Constructivist learning relies on repeated failure and retry.

text: Place checkpoints before significant challenges, so a retry starts just before the difficult section rather than at a distant start.
when: when placing checkpoints in a level with hard sections
why: Restarting players at a spot where they can easily try again keeps the learning loop going.

text: Environment art such as banners and stone can hint that valuable items lie ahead of the player.
when: when a path leads to a reward
why: Environmental cues such as banners and stone signal a dungeon's significance, so players sense a reward is ahead without seeing it.

text: Levels that signal upcoming challenges, such as a boss gate with a preceding hallway, build anticipation and give players time to prepare resources.
when: Designing transitions to major challenges
why: Advance cues let players make informed decisions before a threat arrives.

text: Established certainty enables dramatic reveals, such as a threat that suddenly makes a normally safe room dangerous.
when: when a predictable safe space is later made unsafe
why: The violated expectation carries more weight when the player had reason to trust the space.

text: Place characters and clues at strategic spots so stuck players can find the way forward.
when: When a player repeatedly fails at the same obstacle
why: Stuck players keep retrying and may quit, so clues placed by characters help them proceed.

text: Annotate secrets on a map along with how to find them again, so the location can be revisited.
when: mapping areas with hidden content

text: Up to four-versus-four the defender has the edge, since ties go to it; from five-versus-five upward the attacker gains the edge, growing with more armies on the board.
when: Comparing attacker and defender odds in small and large territory battles.
why: Ties favor the defender and small rolls make ties frequent; in larger battles the attacker's extra dice and reserve effects accumulate across exchanges.

text: Aggregated play data shows where players are likely to die, guiding placement of helpful items.
when: Level and item placement.
why: Death clusters reveal where players struggle.

text: A god stat is overpowered or required for an optimal build.
Custom health games have produced measured benefits, including improved visual acuity in amblyopia, fewer emergency visits for diabetes, and better treatment adherence in cancer patients.
Combat adds pressure and cognitive load, while navigation lets players set their own pace unless a time limit applies.
Boss fights are hard to make fair and entertaining without a clear picture of the player's level, gear, spells and skill.
Place high vantage points and clear sight lines, since height gives advantage as occupants look down on opponents, and high refuges offer wide views.
when: In single-player games where the player should hold an advantage over enemies
why: Clear sight lines let the character's abilities give the player an advantage over foes.

text: A game only improves lives if many people play it, so aim for broad appeal combined with a positive effect.
when: designing a game meant to have a positive effect
why: Unplayed games help no one, so reach determines impact.

text: When character speed rises, spread environment objects farther apart to counteract the crowding that high speed causes.
when: Fast-moving characters in densely populated environments
why: Fast movement through dense objects makes the space feel cramped and overwhelming, so wider spacing restores a sense of openness.

text: Keep creatures' independent travel small and bound movement with barriers like fences, doorways, or gates.
when: Building levels with wandering creatures.
why: A smaller hinterland makes the level easier for a designer to build.

text: Alternate challenges with short scenarios and build toward a finale, so the experience keeps changing and interest rises.
when: Structuring a timed encounter or sequence
why: Pairing a challenge goal with a goal of leading players onward keeps them moving through varied places toward a surprise finale.

text: Off-curve enemies that hit hard can create spikes in encounter difficulty, which is acceptable as a reminder that foes can still be powerful.
when: Placing strong enemies in encounter sequences
why: Spikes in difficulty are noticeable to players

text: Later sections can raise challenge by adding more enemies that are faster and less predictable, so no area feels safe.
when: progressing difficulty through a level sequence
why: Unpredictability removes safe zones and keeps tension high.

text: NPCs can block a space until the player completes a task, such as guarding a doorway or sending the player on a quest.
when: when designing progression through a space
why: Blocking until a task is done directs movement without walls.

text: Chain refuges so players move cover to cover in combat or hiding spot to hiding spot in stealth; these sequences create exciting play.
why: Moving between protective spots and exposed open spaces creates the tension players feel as they advance.

text: Obtuse corners can partially reveal rewards, enemies, or events, so what lies around the corner may be a reward or a threat.
why: The brain seeks to complete incomplete information, so partial views draw curiosity and create a sense of risk.

text: Pair large overlook spaces for sniper duels with smaller hiding spaces for ambushes, so one encounter offers both long-range and close-range tension.
when: designing a staged encounter with ranged and close combat
why: Varied sightlines and cover shape how the encounter is played.

text: Give one battle area several uses, such as cliff tops for sniping, low cover for sneaking, and a midway landmark.
why: Several uses for one compact area let varied tactics coexist, which produces emergent play.

text: Similar objects in a game should be proportional in strength, since one super unit makes the rest irrelevant.
Judge an attack's damage against its economy position, target HP, weapon range, target armor, attacker position, and the number of hits the fight should take.
when: tuning damage values
why: A damage number only has meaning relative to target health, armor, range, position, and encounter length.

text: If players are usually outnumbered, cost defensive stats higher because they are more powerful in that setting.
when: players typically face more enemies than they can match
why: defense blunts the pressure of numerical disadvantage

text: When costing area damage, estimate how often enemies cluster and how long they stay clustered during an encounter.
when: When area damage is used against enemy groups whose members fall during the fight
why: Clustering frequency and duration set how much area damage actually hits

text: Make hazards that also launch the character cost more health than ordinary enemy contact, so they feel more physically harmful.
Enemies that take many hits feel solid and imposing, while enemies that die in one hit feel fragile, so hit count communicates perceived strength.
when: Tuning enemy durability or setting enemy health relative to player damage
why: Players read hit count as a sign of the enemy's physical substance.

text: Health and damage systems give meaning to moment-to-moment interactions.
when: Designing combat or hazard interactions
why: Consequences of each interaction depend on health and damage values

text: Letting players heal only others, not themselves, raises the value of healers and encourages nurturing play.
why: Designers wanted the healing appeal to work equally well for males and females, and found healing others very appealing to the players they consulted.

text: For each healing point, the player moves the discard pile's top card below the last card of their draw pile; healing beyond the discard pile's size is ignored.
When each card's cost is paid in the same health that decides the game, every cost is a direct loss toward defeat.
when: Card duels where costs are paid in the win-deciding resource.

text: Walkable spaces with meaningful destinations and dead-end paths limit through-traffic, so the same people keep meeting and become familiar with one another.
when: designing social spaces or neighborhoods
why: Repeated sightings build acquaintance, which is a precondition for community.

text: Moving enemies turn a space into a hazard, so even small enclosures can become dangerous and nearby terrain feels different.
when: enemies patrol near platforms or stairs
why: Enemy motion covers and reshapes the area around them, not only their location.

text: Boss fights usually introduce a new mechanic and need a specially designed area; whether they are built depends on dramatic effect, budget, and staff availability.
when: Planning boss encounters

text: A story area that needs new environment art is cut if no artists are available to build it.
when: Scheduling narrative-driven areas
why: Production capacity limits what can be built

text: Narrative beats that seal off regions players could previously enter reduce the playable space.
Defense and Attack both act like HP, since each lets a character survive more enemy encounters, and higher Attack shortens fights so enemies get fewer attacks.
when: balancing combat stats in an RPG
why: Both reduce the damage a character takes over a fight.

text: A Strength 1 card can never eliminate an opposing card, so it survives only against an equal Strength 1 card, a 20% chance.
when: Uniform 1-to-5 Strength distribution.
why: Any higher-Strength opposing card eliminates it, so only a tie out of five equally likely values leaves it in play.

text: Attacking is worth more when a character is stronger than the opponent, and defending is worth more when the character is weaker.
when: comparing offensive and defensive stat values in a combat system
why: the advantaged side benefits from converting strength into damage, while the weaker side benefits from avoiding it

text: Doubling an opponent's damage per hit doubles the value of armor class relative to attack bonus, because avoiding each hit becomes more important.
Once a hit chance reaches 100% or falls to 0%, further bonuses to that stat add nothing.
when: a bonus pushes hit chance past its limit

text: A damage multiplier adds no value against targets that a normal hit already defeats, since the outcome does not change.
When enemy health varies, area damage kills weaker targets over time, so total area output shrinks as the group dwindles.
when: Enemies in a group have unequal health
why: Low-health targets die first and stop contributing

text: Changing unit costs or damage values shifts the optimal unit mix, so rebalancing requires re-solving the payoff table.
When being hit drains both health and a weapon's energy, players must switch weapons quickly and plan order for high-health enemies, assuming weapon levels will drop.
when: when damage also reduces resources
why: Compounded losses shape tactical decisions

text: Expected DPS equals average damage per projectile, times projectiles per shot, times shots per second, times the chance each projectile hits.
when: Comparing the effective output of weapons.

text: Adjacent hexes hit with 100 percent chance, and the chance falls by 10 percent per hex of distance; resolve with a ten-sided die.
Units start with five hit points; every hit they take removes one.
Deathtouch is worth about 2 points, reflecting its strength in combat.
A card's expected damage is (Strength/5) × Damage, and each point counts as one opponent health only if the card survives.
when: Estimating a card's offensive value.
why: A card with lower Strength gets discarded by higher-Strength opposing cards, so its Damage only lands if it survives.

text: Doubling the contagion period can roughly multiply the number of people who adopt the game about tenfold, according to the epidemic model.
when: modeling word-of-mouth growth
why: Small changes in how long players keep talking strongly affect total sales.

text: An item's chance to critically hit can double its value relative to an otherwise identical item.
