when: Pricing a crit-enabled item

text: Enemy contact or enemy projectile costs one health container, spikes cost three, and falling into pits costs more than enemy contact.
why: The amount of damage an interaction inflicts signals how dangerous that interaction feels to the player.

text: Bosses take three powerful hits, while basic enemies die in one or two.
why: The damage system is used mainly to make bosses feel clearly distinct from basic enemies.

text: In this design, health has eight slices and each coin restores one empty slice.
why: Coin pickups restore health directly, which makes coins attractive to collect whenever health is missing.

text: Balance heroes for typical battle size; in one hero-driven strategy game armies were about 12 to 15 units, with 24 close to the maximum.
when: tuning hero power against army size
why: A hero tuned for large battles overwhelms small fights.

text: Projectile drag is modeled as a linear term in velocity with coefficient k and a quadratic term in speed with coefficient c; the quadratic term couples the axes.
when: When simulating projectile flight with air resistance
why: Quadratic drag makes the drag on one axis depend on motion along the others

text: Presenting a small base value followed by many bonuses leads players to underestimate their total damage or output.
when: An RPG where a small base damage value is followed by bonuses added later.
why: Players anchor on the small starting figure and fail to add the later bonuses into their estimate.

text: Placing intense encounters in quick succession turns a level into a relentless slog with no recovery.
why: Quieter stretches for movement, exploration, or recovery give high-action moments the contrast that makes them feel exciting.

text: Treating damage over time as equal to burst damage makes sustained effects look too strong; discounting future damage corrects this.
when: When modeling spells that deal damage over time alongside instant-damage spells

text: Expected DPS for spread or splash weapons assumes every projectile hits, so it overstates real output at range.
Halving damage does not halve its value when enemies have flat armor, because a fixed reduction can cut a small hit to zero.
when: When enemies have flat armor that subtracts a fixed amount from each hit

text: Assuming other factors are equal rarely holds, so the simple target-count multiplier alone tends to overvalue area damage.
why: Enemy offense and health changes alter value during the fight

text: 1) Fix a typical enemy HP. 2) For each damage value, count the hits needed to defeat it. 3) Price each damage value by the usefulness of that hit count, not by its raw number.
when: pricing weapon damage against a fixed enemy HP
why: With fixed hit points, extra damage adds value only at hit-count thresholds, so cost should track real combat usefulness.

text: 1) Wrap the target object in a dynamic trigger volume, which is easier to set up for weapon damage than a standard trigger volume. 2) Set the object's collision to block weapons and enable block-rigid-body and block-complex-collision-trace flags. 3) Create a take-damage event on the volume and set its damage threshold to 1.0.
when: Setting up a shootable object that should trigger a game event when damaged by a weapon
why: Damage events fire only when the object's collision and trigger setup allow weapon hits to register

text: To estimate effective HP from a healing spell, multiply MP by the healing ratio and add it to current HP, when that spell is the only healing and the only use of MP.
when: a single healing spell is the sole use of MP
why: Without other MP uses, MP converts to HP at a fixed rate.

text: To balance a heal against an attack spell, compare the extra damage taken without the attack spell against the HP the heal restores.
when: comparing healing and damage-dealing spells
why: Both are valued by how much HP they keep the character from losing.

text: To balance an Attack item against a Defense item, compare the HP saved by fewer enemy attacks with the HP saved by reduced damage per hit.
when: comparing attack and defense items
why: Both effects are measured in HP preserved over a fight.

text: 1) Value each effect on one scale where benefits are positive and costs negative. 2) Sum the values. 3) Classify the effect as a benefit if the net is positive, and as a cost if it is negative. 4) Keep all values positive by adding costs and benefits, never subtracting.
when: Effects that combine benefits and costs
why: A single signed scale makes net value easy to read

text: 1) Pick a realistic combat where party power fits. 2) Define party stats and inventory. 3) Gather monster stats and the game's hit and damage formulas. 4) Simulate the fight in a spreadsheet. 5) Compare worst-case, best-case, and average outcomes using probability or Monte Carlo simulation, and recheck if they disagree.
when: judging how dangerous an encounter is
why: Comparing how likely the extreme outcomes are against the average shows whether a fight is actually risky.

text: 1) Multiply total hours by the combat share to get total combat time. 2) Divide by average combat length, including longer boss fights, to get encounters. 3) Assume encounters per enemy type and divide to get distinct enemies. 4) State every assumption not given.
when: budgeting enemy assets for a long game

text: 1) Write the expected value as the immediate payoff plus the continuation probability times the expected value of the next state. 2) If all states are identical, set the value equal to itself. 3) Solve the resulting linear equation.
when: A repeated chance process where each continuation is identical to the start.
why: Identical states collapse the recursion into one equation with one unknown.

text: 1) Estimate the expected number of targets hit per attack. 2) Multiply the single-target attack's benefit by that number to get the area attack's value.
when: Targets are clustered and roughly equal in health

text: 1) Compute basic damage minus target armor, plus piercing damage, as maximum damage. 2) Roll a random amount from 50 to 100 percent of that maximum per attack.
when: when designing combat where rules set a range and chance picks the outcome
why: Rolling within a band injects randomness into how one unit's attacks affect another.

text: Decide the hit count a creature should take to die before tuning raw hit points; any hit point scale that produces that count works.
when: When players hold expectations about how long fights should take
why: Players judge fights by hit counts, mainly perceiving the hit count.

text: For an average enemy, character and weapon, count hits to kill; use that average as the starting metric and midpoint when adjusting weapon damage and creature health.
when: When choosing a starting point for hits-to-kill with an average enemy, character and weapon
why: Players already carry expectations about how long fights should take, which the count must match.

text: Place quiet, empty space before and after large encounters, and structure combat into waves or segments separated by quiet periods, even in shooters, to create rhythm and tension.
when: Designing encounter pacing
why: Quiet space builds tension and allows recovery.

text: Balance each enemy's damage needs per weapon and upgrade level so enemies feel made of one material; keep each enemy type's shot count constant so weapon power stays readable.
when: Tuning damage across weapons and upgrade levels, or setting enemy health values
why: Consistent relative damage makes the world feel coherent, and consistent shot counts make weapon strength readable across encounters.

text: A player whose health drops to zero or below loses; if both players reach that threshold together, the match is drawn.
when: Card duels where health reaching zero ends the game.

text: A unit that stands on a first aid hex for a full round restores its hit points to the starting amount.
A fight lasting 10 minutes or more with few enemies needs other content to fill the time, or enemies with many hit points or stages.
when: encounters with few enemies
why: Otherwise the fight drags or feels thin.

text: When analyzing a combat level, record whether the player is armed, which enemies are hostile, how enemies limit the path, and how enemies act as level elements.
when: When playing a game whose level design you want to learn from
why: Notes taken right after play keep memories of the gameplay that would otherwise fade.

text: When objects conflict, decide which sits above or below the curve using expert game knowledge or strategy analysis.
when: When one object is clearly better than another, so they cannot share a balance curve
why: Raw cost-curve math cannot say which object sits above, so outside game knowledge fills the gap.

text: Decide the number of combatants by weighing growth over time, performance limits, player cognitive load, and team hours and budget.
Before choosing enemy counts, set how long an average enemy should take to kill and how long a typical combat should last.
Vary damage and enemy hit points within ranges, and vary enemy counts at a location within a range.
when: When fixed damage and fixed enemy health would let players calculate every outcome exactly
why: Ranges keep outcomes uncertain while staying within designed limits.

text: In Risk-style combat, one army must stay behind, so only armies beyond the first can attack; attackers roll up to three dice and defenders up to two.
when: Resolving a territory battle with dice.
why: The rules cap dice and reserve one army in the territory.

text: To hit in a d20 system, roll a twenty-sided die, add the attack bonus, and succeed if the total equals or exceeds the defender's armor class.
when: In a d20 system where attacks add a bonus and compare against armor class

text: Set damage so that heavy, slow actions do more damage than light, quick ones, matching the player's perception of each move's physical nature.
when: when assigning damage to attacks of different weight or speed
why: Damage that matches perceived physicality feels right even though the mapping is arbitrary

text: Regeneration gives even, immediate pacing without resource searching but weakens hidden-item rewards and low-health drama; managed resources give drama and exploration but uneven pacing.
when: when choosing a core health system

text: Keeping the player in close quarters forces melee but can feel constraining, while enemies that rush the player either force melee or make the player back up.
when: When using environment or enemy behavior to steer combat mode
why: Neither environment nor enemies settle the mode choice alone

text: Ammo-free melee weapons offer unlimited use but only at short range, while ranged ammo weapons reach farther but depend on a finite supply.
why: Without an ammo count, melee attacks never draw down a supply that could run out.

text: Elevations show a building's exterior sides from outside; for game levels they only need the surfaces the player sees, so they lean toward concept art.
Concept diagrams express a core abstract idea, such as public versus private density, using hatching, color, arrows and shapes.
For each advertising method, sketch a scene from an existing game that uses it as a teaching device, and annotate where event triggers would go if the scene uses them.
Use arrows for foot traffic, sight lines and design axes, and color to encode function.
when: annotating concept diagrams
why: Arrows encode direction, which suits showing how people move, what they can see and how a layout is organized.

text: An arrival is the moment a player first enters a space, and how that space feels depends on the spaces before it.
Use one embellished entrance to guide visitors into a climactic interior that rewards arrival.
when: When the destination is a climactic interior reached through a single entry.

text: Place arrivals before enemy encounters, item pickups, and story events so they land with more impact.
why: A contrasting space before the arrival makes the new space feel bigger.

text: The space a player arrives from shapes how the next space feels: a high room feels grander after a small one, and a dark room feels scarier after a bright one.
when: When sequencing rooms or areas of contrasting size or lighting
why: Perception of a space depends on the contrast with the previous space

text: Consider an early climactic confrontation in the opening that previews what the game offers.
when: the game needs to hook players at the start
why: An early peak shows players the game's potential before they commit.

text: Players explore a room they expect to hold a reward even when the reward is not immediately accessible.
when: a room is expected to contain a reward
why: expectation drives searching

text: Level design goals mostly cover facility and sustenance rewards, which are largely items such as recharges, keys, and power-ups.
Reward head movement with hidden containers, fine print, falling objects, close-inspection scanners and hazards that players dodge by moving their heads.
when: Positional tracking is available
why: Positional tracking lets the game detect head motion

text: Calm spaces can double as reward vaults when they offer healing, combining meditative and rewarding functions in one space.
when: In games with intense combat or platforming that calm spaces can break up.
why: Healing rewards the visit, while the soft atmosphere gives players a break from high intensity.

text: Exploring with managed resources trades extra risk for possible helpful rewards, making the level far less linear than a regenerating design.
when: In games where resources are managed rather than regenerating.
why: Searching the whole maze risks harm but may yield helpful items, pushing players to explore beyond the direct route.

text: Promise discovery and then deliver it, building anticipation and a fear of getting lost without making exploration feel rote.
Graybox is a low-fidelity placeholder of flat gray boxes and simple geometry for a mechanic, system, or level, letting teams test gameplay goals cheaply before art and audio exist.
Prototyping means writing just enough working code to test whether a gameplay idea works before investing in it.
A graybox can cost about a hundred times less than the finished version to build, so most failed ideas are cheap to discard.
Mechanics tested thoroughly in gray boxes usually keep working after art is added.
when: When the base level was playtested thoroughly in graybox before art was added.
why: Art changes alter how a fight is perceived, not its mechanical structure, which was already proven.

text: Build and test mechanics in graybox before adding art, since a problem can be found, fixed and retested in minutes.
when: Early in design when mechanics are still changing.
why: Gray shapes are cheap to change and carry no visual clutter.

text: Involve artists in graybox design so they help shape the placeholder forms they will later polish, and their work is discarded less often.
why: Artist work is trashed less often when they shape the boxes first.

text: Repeated grayboxing reveals which objects designers use most, which helps prioritize which environmental objects to create first.
when: Planning environment art production
why: Frequently used objects deliver the most value when made first.

text: Simple features stand in for natural forms: rocks for mountains or cliffs, gravel or ponds for water, moss for distant trees or close grass, small pines for forest.
when: When the landscape being conveyed is distant rather than close.
why: These stand-ins suggest natural landscapes within a small, explorable space.

text: Young artists often avoid showing rough work for fear it will make people misjudge their talent.
when: When artists are young or early in their careers and must show rough work.
why: They fear rough quality will lead people to misjudge their talent.

text: Group decisions about grayboxes are especially vulnerable to the halo effect, which is often the biggest problem in graybox review.
when: When a group reviews a graybox
why: Group judgment amplifies a shared negative impression of visuals.

text: Running a graybox playtest: 1) Have a player new to the level, or a partner unfamiliar with a commercial game, play it. 2) Do not interrupt. 3) Take detailed notes on where players get stuck and what is unclear.
when: a graybox level is ready for testing
why: uninterrupted play shows real difficulties

text: 1) Replace cutscenes with still images or text pop-ups. 2) Replace complex interfaces with labeled buttons. 3) Replace sounds with synthesized beeps. 4) Replace dialogue with text-to-speech or on-screen text.
when: when building a graybox of a game with these elements
why: Placeholders still show what is happening, so the game stays playable and testable.

text: 1) Build a rough space from simple geometry. 2) Playtest it. 3) Edit the geometry. 4) When edits shift from major spaces to small details, begin environment art.
when: Developing a level before art production
why: Edits shrinking to details signal the layout is stable enough for art.

text: 1) Sketch the gameplay as spatial diagrams. 2) Use large masses for major areas, thin zones for connecting paths, and small shapes for secondary areas. 3) Test which uses of each mechanism are worth pursuing.
when: Exploring a level concept early
why: Diagrams reveal the spatial relationships gameplay depends on.

text: Represent gameplay spaces such as boss rooms, sniping spots or finish lines as bubbles sized by type, with line type showing priority and connection kind.
when: planning adjacency of gameplay spaces
why: Bubble size indicates a space's required size, a convention borrowed from building proximity diagrams.

text: Vary hatch orientation to distinguish zones, and mark shared spaces with intersecting hatches.
when: diagramming zones that differ in use
why: Varied hatch directions can carry distinct meanings, so zones and mixed-use areas stay readable.

text: Only evaluators experienced with many grayboxes should judge early graybox design quality or approve designs, since inexperienced reviewers cannot separate design quality from missing art.
when: When judging or approving an early graybox design
why: Inexperienced evaluators reject good designs for their appearance.

text: Lock down movement mechanics in graybox before animating characters, because animation built on a changing movement system must be redone.
why: Design parts are interdependent, so a change to one forces every element that depends on it to change.

text: Judge a 3D game space by how it feels to the player inside it, not by whether it works as a realistic 2D blueprint.
when: Evaluating game layouts that are physically unusual
why: Players experience space from inside and rarely check realistic plans

text: Use different hatch patterns to indicate the material of a cut form.
when: annotating cut forms in drawings

text: Graybox testing suits mechanics-driven games, while experiences that depend on audiovisual emotional triggers lose most of their impact in graybox.
when: when deciding whether graybox testing will reveal the game's real appeal
why: Mechanics-driven play survives crude visuals; emotional audiovisual impact does not.

text: Grid space divides the play area into repeated cells, which can be squares, rectangles, hexagons, or triangles.
Hexagonal grids let units move diagonally, which a square grid does not allow.
Tabletop map makers rely on grid paper, and many game engines measure space in grid-based units.
Encounter fixes range from small changes, such as better enemy lighting, to structural changes, such as rebuilding a flanking route.
when: After a playtest reveals a list of encounter problems.

text: For levels not built on tiles, impose a grid over the geometry and analyze that grid.
why: Tactical analysis methods already run on tile grids, so imposing a grid on geometry lets them apply.

text: Grid layouts suit games where players need easy understanding, alignment, and consistent proportion, and where computers must handle the space easily.
when: Choosing grid organization
why: Regular cells are easy to read and compute

text: Base level measurements on human-scale metrics of interaction, which underpin how spaces are sized and felt.
why: Renaissance proportion systems were based on human-body geometry.

text: A first-person camera set above about seven feet or below about five feet distorts the view, because players judge scale using an eye level close to their own.
when: Setting first-person camera height
why: Players judge scale from their own body height

text: Levels built without regard to the player character may not fit it; some doors can be too small for the character to pass through.
why: Geometry sized without the character's metrics can block movement.

text: Comparing grid types: build one 3D level on a non-orthogonal grid and one on an orthogonal grid, then observe whether sightlines to points of interest change exploration.
when: choosing a grid for 3D level layout
why: sightlines can steer where players go

text: Use the Top and Perspective views together when judging layout and height.
Snap geometry to the grid to avoid leaks that stop a level from compiling; some editors snap to power-of-two units such as 16, 32, 64 and 128.
when: building geometry in editors that compile levels
why: Off-grid gaps can leak and block compilation.

text: Rewards that mismatch their context feel arbitrary or unrealistic: a story reward in a dull area with no earning behavior, or a valuable reward for a trivial chore.
when: when placing story progression between fixed milestones (for the story-reward case)
why: No player behavior seems to earn the reward in that context; mismatched reward and task breaks believability.

text: A narrow maze with hidden enemies is stressful for a low-health player but only risky for a healthy one.
when: In games where player states shift quickly, such as those managing survival resources
why: Low-health players are most vulnerable entering a space that disadvantages them, while healthy players must keep their state through danger.

text: Small content is often given to new writers; it is not critical-path dialogue, yet the game still needs it.
Place secret rooms above and below a main scrolling space to reward curious players.
Players can see items placed inside solid terrain that the character could not logically perceive.
when: In side-view 2D games that reveal areas beyond the character's sight

text: Hiding spaces such as lockers, vents and crawl spaces restrict both the character's mobility and the player's view.
when: In stealth games with lockers, vents, or crawl spaces
why: Such spaces reinforce that the player character is weaker than its enemies in these games.

text: Hide optional items in obscure alcoves and cantilevered ledges so exploring players find refuges that reward looking.
when: in exploration-focused levels

text: Meditative spaces can be kept off the main path and hinted at through partial reveals.
why: Incomplete information makes the brain seek verification, which draws players toward the hidden space.

text: Reused assets such as textures, existing geometry and recycled characters can make memorable secrets when a studio lacks resources for full side quests.
when: the studio has limited production resources
why: Reused assets are fast to produce and place, and can still create memorable rewards.

text: Showing a threat the character cannot see creates suspense, because players know danger is near while the character remains unaware.
why: Gap between player knowledge and character knowledge

text: Hiding the exit or placing large obstacles that conceal enemies makes a room frustrating, especially in single-player play.
why: Visible goals and routes let players plan around enemies from a safe vantage point.

text: Triggers are hidden by default and invisible during play; unhide one while testing to see where it sits.
when: When testing a trigger's action in the level editor
why: Without seeing the trigger's position, the designer cannot verify where it sits or whether it works.

text: Hidden lethal danger with no clues can feel unfair and bring players back less often.
when: when a hazard can kill without any prior hint
why: Players cannot anticipate or prepare for the danger, so deaths feel arbitrary.

text: Dark alcoves are hard to see from a lit area, so enemies hidden in them can ambush the player who looks into the light.
when: when the player moves from light into the surrounding dark
why: shadow hides danger from a viewer in the light

text: 1) Place the reward in view but out of reach. 2) Route the path through other rooms, or behind walls that hint at it through windows or cracks.
why: Making the player locate the path turns the route into a puzzle they solve.

text: A hub is an intimate lobby connecting to levels, called spokes, through portals or doors; it is a central point to return to and jump between gamespaces, and is semi-rhizomatic.
Hub spaces are typically non-threatening, letting players explore within the abilities their character already has.
Place casual gathering areas along routes players pass regularly for important tasks, so socializing happens naturally during play.
when: designing hubs in online games
why: Players gather where they already travel, not in places they must go out of their way to reach.

text: Hub settlements can grow from vendors and trainers to include inns, auction houses, banks and guild spaces.
when: When a multiplayer settlement grows from a town into a larger city
why: Extra functions in cities push players toward social interaction.

text: Hub-based quests should push players outward, with many requiring travel to other hubs, so they form tours of the game's possibilities.
when: As players gain power and travel between hubs becomes easier
why: Quests that send players onward from each hub build a tour of the game's possibilities.

text: Players remember one detail per hub, the last one stated, so end each hub on the concrete problem.
when: Writing any player-facing hub.
why: The final words of a hub are what players still hold in mind when choosing replies.

text: Word order in a hub often affects player understanding more than writers expect, so place key information deliberately.
when: Before the player faces their own dialogue choices in a hub
why: The final words are what players carry into their choices, so they must anchor the problem.

text: A hub can supply a story justification for characters heading to thematic realms, such as frozen, volcanic or jungle settings.
when: When characters would otherwise have no logical reason to travel to a themed world

text: Interactive hotspots can simulate depth within a 2D space.
when: When large environments are broken into smaller screen spaces in 2D games
why: Borrowed painting techniques applied within fragmented screen space create the impression of depth.

text: A hub journey is linear like a ladder, while the player largely decides how to overcome each rung.
why: The general level order is fixed, while players choose missions, backtracking and exploration pace.

text: In a hub-and-spoke structure, players complete a set of stages in any order, and after all are done the story becomes linear toward a finale.
when: a set of stages can reasonably be done in any order
why: free ordering gives choice, and a linear finale gives a climax

text: Hub-and-spoke dialogue returns to a root topic list after each topic resolves: the root list is the hub, and each topic branch is a spoke.
why: Looping back to the root list avoids infinite story branching.

text: In the hub and spokes structure, each spoke is a self-contained content nugget independent of the others.
Non-decision hub: 1) Offer one correct guess about the NPC's next line. 2) Offer one incorrect guess. 3) Offer one 'Tell me more' option. This lets players characterize themselves.
when: The NPC will continue speaking regardless of the player's choice.

text: Use a hub when levels should load separately and the game is built around a central lobby; avoid it when a seamless large world is the goal.
why: Levels load one at a time instead of all at once, which keeps the performance cost low.

text: Make quest hubs larger and slower-paced than spawn points, so they invite exploration and interaction.
why: Such spaces are meant to be carefully explored and are packed with things to do, which encourages interaction between players.

text: Each middle hub must show the NPC reacting to the player's choice, with a distinct response for each option.
when: Within a dialogue that has several middle hubs, before splitting it into two encounters.
why: Otherwise the conversation feels scripted and the player's choice seems inconsequential.

text: Loading levels separately is efficient, but it loses the seamless feel of a large sandbox world.
why: Only one level loads at a time, which lowers the performance load, but the separation through portals or doors breaks the continuous world.

text: Level design arranges architecture, props, and challenges to make play fun and interesting, translating mechanics into spaces players can inhabit; it is game design applied in detail.
Single-tile platforms make players approach slowly and carefully, so many of them turn a run into a plodding sequence.
when: Platforming levels with many one-tile-wide blocks and wide pits.
why: Very little margin for error makes players avoid the full-speed long jump the level could allow.

text: Early levels with many connection points relative to the player's goals give a large expressive range, so each approach to an enemy can differ.
when: Area has many connectable platforms and no impassable ones
why: Many valid attachment options let the player choose varied routes.

text: A player who lingers in one spot of a level for several minutes may signal frustration and weak level design.
why: Behavioural playing patterns map directly to content quality, offering an alternate measure that avoids the biases of self-reports.

text: Arcade players read more distinct screens as a sign of a more advanced game, while home buyers value expansive worlds as more content.
when: arcade versus home console
why: Home games must justify the buyer's purchase with expansive gamespace, whereas short arcade sessions suit a single screen.

text: In coordinate-addressed worlds, commerce concentrated on points along the axes and centre diagonal, which became busy thoroughfares.
when: coordinate-addressed virtual worlds
why: Such points are easy to travel to and remember, so they become busy thoroughfares.

text: Smaller floor patterns near high-value items make people slow down and browse, since the denser rhythm sets a slower pace.
when: spaces near valuable goods
why: denser rhythms slow walking pace

text: Spatial transposition gives an input combination or position a different meaning via chording (simultaneous inputs) or context sensitivity, where object locations relative to the avatar change the input's meaning.
A toy box is a developer-only test level for building and testing mechanisms, their interactions, and how the character interacts with geometry, before they go into playable levels.
Points in space is a sparse layout of locations that suits wandering with returns to a safe oasis, or games where players define the space themselves.
when: Choosing points-in-space organization

text: Level design workflow covers how a level moves from idea to implementation and where production should start, which affects development schedules.
A level is a medium of communication between designers and players, which is why designers bring players in to test it.
why: the level's message is only known through player reactions

text: The void is a deep, open center surrounded by clutter; placing a major encounter in a large hollow space shows this quality.
A symmetric level mirrors one part of the level onto another; asymmetric levels leave most areas unmirrored.
Linear space has the player moving forward and possibly back along a line, which may have two ends or loop back.
A level designer uses a level editor or toolkit to build missions, scenarios, or quests, and lays out components that fit the game's theme.
Edges are boundaries not formed by paths, such as walls, rows of buildings, vegetation changes or genius loci changes, that mark a change in character.
Paths are channels of travel that connect important gamespaces, often intimately scaled with few aesthetic features.
Nodes are intersections that serve as navigation references, gathering places, and strategic decision points.
A node is a play area containing hostile meetings, collectible drops, spawn locations, or chances for action.
A tour is a linear opening level that teaches mechanics while previewing later content.
Good space has qualities such as completeness, comfort and egolessness, which resemble refuges where people feel safe.
Tactical level splitting matches pathfinding splitting, so methods like Dirichlet domains and floor polygons apply; some developers use Dirichlet domains for tactics, though less often than grids.
Whether a narrative designer must also work as a level designer depends on the team.
Several expressive rule-based games incorporate spatial interaction directly into their rules, and they use rules to make statements about the human condition.
In 3D game space, y points up against gravity and x and z lie in the ground plane. Movement uses x and z.
Adjacency between discrete positions gives a space its structure; without it, the positions are just disconnected points.
Medium-level rules reward spatial mastery, and collecting a valuable object often feels more satisfying than skilfully avoiding a hazard.
when: when comparing object-based rules with pure hazard-avoidance challenges

text: Boundaries can be physical, like an arena edge or board, or abstract, like a shared social contract to play.
Spatial configurations channel how people move and act, a psychological method shared by buildings and game levels.
why: layout shapes behavior in both architecture and games

text: Multiple floors give players prospect and refuge advantages over one another.
Level schedules do two jobs: they list the pieces that make up each environment, and they support art direction.
In dungeon exploration a party must arrange its roles so magicians and missile users are protected in the middle.
Dirichlet domains are hard to apply to tile-based levels, but map flooding computes equivalent regions on tile maps.
Country-scale strategy games need characters with distinct identities, which calls for group LOD methods, and those methods were later adapted in several real-time strategy games.
Screen-based media trains people to sit still and face forward, and low frame rates in early VR taught players to keep their heads still.
Level designers implement level designs, propose level concepts, and test levels, working with the designer to improve gameplay.
An initial level-design plan needs only the number and kind of each environment, such as wilderness, city or dungeon; the levels need not be built or mapped yet.
A story plan alone does not give a playable experience; it needs a spatial environment in which each plan event maps to a location.
Axial routes combined with nodes, such as plazas or focal buildings, form a planning model that has been reused across cities and capitals.
when: Planning the overall structure of a large urban area
why: The model gives clear orientation and organizes movement across many destinations.

text: Unlike 3D art, level design has no single accepted method, so spatial knowledge must be learned from several sources and applied across tools.
when: Planning how to learn level design
why: No standard procedure exists, so principles must be drawn from varied theory and practice.

text: Text output alone can create large imaginary worlds with no graphics.
The dungeon graph method applies to 2D and 3D action adventures, role-playing games, point-and-click adventures and Metroidvania-style games.
Arcade-style games with short levels and few mechanics need no extensive teaching levels, since their complexity comes from level mechanisms, enemies, and items.
Side-scrolling levels, viewed from the side like a building section, are among the most spatially limiting level types.
Architecture, landscape architecture and garden design develop spaces through the orientation of features and materials, and their methods can be adapted to digital games.
Patterns differ in how many spatial forms they allow: some admit few, while fluid patterns admit many implementations.
Capture-the-flag maps are typically symmetrical, with team bases at opposite ends of a wide battle space.
Choose a space model by the design question: 2D continuous for boundary changes, 3D continuous for height changes, discrete zones for analyzing which play happens where.
when: Changing a game's space or analyzing its play areas
why: Each model exposes different interrelationships. No hard rule fixes whether a space is 2D or 3D, or discrete or continuous; the model is a thinking tool, so use whichever is most useful at the moment.

text: Draw the curve to find the exact location of a flat section before choosing a fix for it.
when: after drawing an interest curve
why: The drawn curve made the flat stretch visibly obvious as the real problem, while the fix stayed unclear.

text: Pairing simplicity with godlike power to create and destroy makes abstract worlds compelling.
Give layout and story a strong center; a strong avatar at the center of the game world is generally preferred.
Architecture helps designers understand how people relate to spaces, which matters when designing game worlds and cities.
when: Designing environments
why: Spatial design depends on human relationships with space.

text: Altering a game's boundaries is an interesting design exercise for exploring new play.
why: Boundaries define a game's identity, so changing them alters the strategy and the play experience.

text: When unsure how to structure a game world, consult a catalog of spatial patterns; matching patterns to the world can make the structure seem obvious.
when: stuck on world structure
why: The catalog's detailed patterns change how a designer views everyday spaces, so the world's structure becomes easier to see.

text: Custom levels built in an editor show how a level is assembled from a game's formal elements, a practical reference for designing level structure.
why: Editors expose the same formal building blocks, such as grids, rooms and objects, that underlie level structure.

text: A board with a linear path can act as an interactive diagram that shows designers and players the intent of a linear experience.
why: A path with minimal forks makes the emphasis on scripted story beats over player choice visible at a glance.

text: Design in one-screen increments so each moment of play shows the core mechanics clearly.
Withhold weapons and tools in a tutorial's opening area and use a strict path to focus player actions on the lesson.
why: Denying the tools that enable combat keeps the player's actions on the lesson rather than on other mechanics.

text: Natural features such as cliffs, valleys, caves, trees, bluffs, and high points can serve as thresholds, and a viewpoint on arrival can stage landmarks visited later.
when: When creating entry points or overview points without artificial barriers
why: Natural features let players survey the world without interrupting immersion

text: Avoid layouts with adjacent navigable regions, since thin walls, walkways through rooms and heavy vertical movement fit Dirichlet domains poorly.
why: Such layouts make the automatic region division misclassify locations, which is costly to diagnose through playtesting.

text: A dungeon can be built as its own separate space, reached through a gateway from a larger map.
when: when designing a dungeon entered from a larger map

text: Decide deliberately where players should feel constrained and where they should feel free when sequencing rooms and paths.
when: Arranging generated or designed rooms and paths
why: A sense of control lets players project their imaginations into the world, so the feeling of freedom matters more than true freedom.

text: A few well-placed details can make a game world seem deep, so spend detail where it matters most.
when: you cannot detail everything
why: Close-up detail that exceeds the impression from afar makes viewers feel the place is deep, beautiful and real.

text: Challenge is often built by pairing hazards with wide, precise jumps made in quick succession, usually leaving one optimal full-speed path that the player learns to master.
when: designing a sequence of jumps with enemies
why: A single best route turns the section into a course that players can master through repetition.

text: Favor rounded or angular passages over blocky hard-edged geometry so the character's collider keeps flowing along edges instead of catching.
when: Laying out traversal spaces for a capsule-shaped character
why: Rounded edges preserve the edge-sliding flow that makes steering forgiving

text: Subtrees of a partition tree can serve as themed zones with one entrance that can be locked, decorated or given a shared difficulty.
when: when a partition of the dungeon is connected to the rest of it by only one corridor
why: One entrance isolates the group, so it can be locked, dimmed or stocked with harder monsters as a unit.

text: Adapt a space's layout to its specific site and terrain so the environment feels native to its location.
when: Designing a space tied to a specific natural setting
why: Responding to the existing site creates a sense of place, a principle often called genius loci.

text: Place large open plazas where routes converge so they can hold the crowds that the connecting paths bring.
when: Designing the endpoint of multiple converging routes
why: Convergence concentrates visitors, and open space absorbs them without congestion.

text: Restate genre-specific spatial rules as general principles so they apply across genres, such as treating advantageous high positions as a principle for many game types.
when: Extracting reusable lessons from a genre-specific level rule
why: Genre-neutral principles transfer to other games and levels.

text: Many keys before one lock, or one key before many locks, implies open-ended exploration; a graph read this way shows how many choices players have.
when: when judging how open or linear a lock-and-key layout is

text: Keep design player-centric and view a level as a series of scenes, which helps communicate it to players.
Even a straightforward linear path stays interesting when it includes twists, turns and challenges.
when: when a level is navigated along a single linear path

text: Use side-scrolling for mechanics best understood from the side, such as jumping, climbing, flying, and shooting.
when: when the core mechanics are jumping, climbing, flying or shooting
why: Side-scrolling teaches these mechanics well because everything the player needs is within one screen's distance of the avatar.

text: Make narrative staging spaces unique, large, and visible from a distance, using vaulting, arches, domes, and tall structures so they are recognizable as goals.
when: designing a space for a climactic or scripted event
why: Players notice and approach spaces that stand out from their surroundings.

text: Give each node a distinct spatial character, sometimes called genius loci, so every landmark offers a different experience.
when: when a level is a set of landmark nodes linked by transitional edges
why: Nodes host the notable gameplay, while edges only move players between them.

text: Transitions can use different geometry from nodes, such as sloped ramps as edges with corridors or mazes as nodes.
when: when intense gamespaces must be linked by transitional passages
why: Edges carry players between intense nodes, which keeps the contrast between transition and intensity clear.

text: Divide the view into thirds both vertically and horizontally and place key elements along the dividing lines rather than at center.
when: when composing a view or framing a key element
why: Off-center placement keeps the eye moving and makes the composition more interesting.

text: Small left or right offsets along a path create a more interesting route than a straight line.
when: when designing a path through a space
why: Gentle shifts add visual interest and direct movement without full turns.

text: Levels that combine competition with exploration in a large open world must plan both activities together.
when: when a large open world combines multiplayer combat with exploration
why: Resources found through exploration reward searching, whereas regenerating health speeds combat but undercuts that reward.

text: Spaces with several simultaneous functions, such as both-and rather than either-or features, are richer than spaces built on one function.
why: One feature can both aid and threaten the player, such as elevation and hiding spots strengthening or weakening sneaking.

text: Make environments quickly reachable and clearly bounded, abstracted into symbolic assets, so players can take them in at a glance.
when: when a game world's boundaries and assets are kept limited
why: Contained, limited spaces let players learn the symbolic system and interact with it more effectively.

text: Grouping features in a triad, with two shorter ones beside a tall central one, implies stable horizontal movement.
why: Triangular arrangements read as stable, and pieces pointing at one another pull the eye sideways.

text: Give a linear section of context before open areas, rewarding later freedom with new abilities.
when: when previewed open areas are reached only after a required linear passage
why: The linear section gives previewed content context, and later free exploration reads as a reward.

text: Keep interactive areas close together, with routes that pass near other areas, so players and residents meet and interact.
when: laying out towns and multiplayer maps
why: Chance encounters sustain activity and safety.

text: A change in spatial relationship between avatars, such as pairs being unable to fit through spaces a single avatar could pass, can communicate relational meaning.
when: Designing spatial constraints tied to character relationships
why: Altered physical constraints carry emotional or social meaning for the player.

text: Content spread over time is remembered better than content packed into long pauses, since massed learning is hard to retain.
when: when teaching a mechanic to players
why: Tutorial texts stacked one after another overwhelm memory, whereas learning in a motivated situation sticks.

text: Removing a game's boundaries changes the strategy and abilities it demands, because players gain options the rules once excluded.
Rules kept as lists or abstract networks stay intact but can be unplayable, while placing elements on a 2D plane makes them playable through spatial reasoning.
when: Abstract relationships among many elements must be played by a person.
why: Spatial reasoning is a strong human capacity.

text: Removing connection points and usable screen space reduces the player's ability to improvise routes.
when: Later level sections have fewer or smaller connectable areas
why: Fewer attachment choices leave the player fewer ways to approach goals.

text: A story detail, such as a habitual sound, can serve as a search cue, so narrative becomes part of solving a puzzle.
Wraparound, where an exit on one edge reappears on the opposite edge, lets complex strategies fit inside a single screen.
when: when action is confined to a single screen
why: Wrapping an exit to the opposite edge simulates endless space on a small playfield.

text: A large space feels even bigger when it is entered after enclosed spaces.
when: when arriving in a large space from preceding spaces
why: How a space feels depends on the conditions of the spaces that came before it.

text: In narrow space, room becomes a scarce resource, so conflict arises as players or NPCs compete for it.
Coordinate-based travel lets players reach any position by entering its coordinates, so access does not depend on the map's path structure.
when: worlds with coordinate addressing
why: Every point links directly to every other, so typing a destination's address substitutes for any route between places.

text: Contrasting intimate, warm materials with cold, public transitional spaces makes the difference between refuge and passage readable.
when: Designing spaces that should feel private versus public
why: Intimately scaled, comfortably finished rooms read as safe, while cold, open transit spaces read as dangerous.

text: Shaping limits interaction until players are ready, teaching the elements of a space gradually.
when: Spaces offering many interactive possibilities, such as miniature garden worlds.
why: Players can only take in a world's possibilities when they are ready, so the designer holds interaction back until then.

text: Rooms with loops let players place level geometry between themselves and enemies, enabling escape through another exit.
why: A second route lets players escape around level geometry that blocks pursuers.

text: Super-block layouts sized for cars, with vast green space and highway links, leave few chances for residents to run into one another.
when: Cities that separate living, working and government functions into super-blocks linked by highways.
why: Large distances limit casual encounters.

text: A 10-hour RPG reaching level 30 averages about three levels per hour, faster early (around four) and slower later (one or two).
when: As a starting point for a 10-hour RPG; other values may fit other designs.

text: Level quality rests on three non-ranked elements: functional requirements (firmitas), usability (utilitas), and delight (venustas).
when: Evaluating or planning a level's overall quality
why: The three elements cover what a space must do, how easily it is used, and how it engages.

text: Nested spaces place separate spaces inside a larger one, such as interiors entered through gateway icons on a continuous outdoor map.
when: Games with a continuous outdoor map where locations are entered through icons.
why: It is not geographically realistic, but it matches how people mentally model entering a building as a separate space.

text: Game spaces can be organized in five ways: linear, grid, web, points in space, and divided space. Designers often combine them.
when: Planning the structure of a game space
why: Mixing these organizing principles produces new and more interesting kinds of game space.

text: Four spatial relationships guide level building: vertical height, horizontal distance, the X/Z size of walkable platforms, and terrain incline angle.
when: Designing level geometry for a platformer
why: Object sizes and distances are tuned within the same system as jump height and running speed, so they evolve together.

text: Level design relies on contrast, sightlines, routes, dramatic build-ups, and uncertainty about where the path leads.
why: These elements shape the experience of arriving in a space, which is how the level communicates with the player and guides them onward.

text: Molecule design models a level as a graph, where nodes are play spaces and edges are visual or travel links between them.
why: Treating spaces as graph nodes and links lets designers allow or block access between them to shape play.

text: Tools for building tension in spaces are spatial psychology, prospect and refuge, lighting, negative space, and height.
why: Spatial contrasts draw on survival instincts, which designers treat as a key to pleasurable design.

text: Architectural portals such as doors, arches or gaps mark passage to a new opportunity; use them as a model for how game introductions signal what lies ahead.
when: When introducing a player to a new space or first level.
why: A portal symbolically marks passing into a fresh opportunity, the same goal good game introductions aim for.

text: A tile can be split into nine scenes: four empty edge pathways connecting areas, and five gameplay scenes at the four corners and the center.
why: Edge pathways serve travel, while the corners and center suit gameplay patterns.

text: Placing objects without a plan, or building around appealing but untested ideas, often yields levels that are not fun once prototyped.
when: Building a level in an editor
why: Without a stated goal, layout lacks a purpose that play can confirm.

text: Crowding many complex mechanics into one space overwhelms new players.
when: When a single level introduces many new mechanics at once
why: Too much new information at once exceeds what players can process

text: Tightly packed objects relative to movement speed feel clumsy and oppressive and can cause frustration.
why: Object placement is one variable balanced against avatar movement, so spacing relative to motion sets how the game feels.

text: Confining a swing-based traversal mechanic to single-screen rooms leaves no room to swing, making such levels feel claustrophobic and painful.
why: A swing needs open room, and on a single screen nearly every arc runs into a wall.

text: Equating good level design with fun narrows the range of experiences a designer can aim for.
why: Many games aim for playful, visceral or thrilling experiences that go beyond simple fun.

text: Structural methods about compression and tension apply weakly to games, because most game art is not a rigid body under engine physics.
when: when applying architectural analysis to game levels
why: Many game elements are not rigid bodies in the engine, so they do not respond to its physics like real structures.

text: Reading a molecule graph's shape as the level's physical layout is a mistake; the shape shows how spaces interact.
why: The same molecule can yield different level layouts, so the diagram describes how spaces interact rather than their geometry.

text: Locations reachable only by typed coordinates stay hidden from players who do not know those coordinates.
Confusing layouts usually come from poor environment art, such as bland, repetitive spaces or meaningless spatial configurations.
when: when players cannot tell where to go
why: Without distinct visual cues, players cannot read the space.

text: A space built from one idea, such as open ground with cover, tends to feel flat and simplistic.
why: A space that serves several functions at once lets one mechanic be both aided and challenged by the same features.

text: Linear levels with few choices, such as long hallways between cutscenes and encounters, can leave players detached and less likely to finish the game.
when: When a game strips away choices such as customization, job selection or side quests from linear play.
why: Players lose attachment to places where they have little choice or sense of dwelling.

text: Placing trees, rocks and buildings at random makes a scene feel unplanned; plan each position deliberately.
why: Players read a world through where its scenic assets sit, so haphazard placement gives them nothing meaningful to interpret.

text: 1) Sketch the level design. 2) Gray-box it. 3) Playtest the grayboxed level with the target audience.
when: When starting from initial level ideas for a new level

text: 1) Try different data layouts. 2) Measure the speed difference of each. 3) Keep the layout that performs best.
when: When the hot and cold split is unclear.
why: Rarely used data bloats each component, so fewer components fit in a cache line and more misses occur during frequent updates.

text: 1) Identify the game's physical boundaries. 2) Identify its conceptual boundaries. 3) Compare both to see where play separates from everyday life.
when: when analyzing any game's structure

text: Building a toy box level: 1) Create at least three simple mechanisms in a comfortable engine. 2) Find at least two ways their objects combine into new interactions.
when: exploring how mechanisms combine
why: combinations of simple objects produce new play

text: 1) Play an online multiplayer game. 2) Identify spaces that push players toward a distinct strategy or play style. 3) Sketch each space and its layout.

1) Make all puzzle pieces feed one final challenge. 2) Nest small pyramids into a hierarchy of increasingly challenging elements leading to the final challenge. 3) Make the top challenge interesting, compelling, and clear so players want to reach it.
when: A set of puzzles lacks a common goal, or when designing a multi-stage puzzle structure.
why: A shared final goal gives scattered puzzles a purpose and direction.

text: 1) Check whether the ship's position exceeds the screen size on X and on Y separately. 2) If it does, move the position to the opposite edge.
when: objects must stay on a bounded playfield
why: Separate per-axis checks keep the object in play without leaving the screen.

text: 1) Outline all levels and name them. 2) Write a one-paragraph description of each level. 3) Design a map for each level. 4) Populate each map with content.
when: Designing a set of levels
why: Each part of a game system depends on the others, so earlier sections get revised while later ones are written.

text: 1) Ask how players know where to go and what the landmarks are. 2) Ask whether new mechanics such as flight or teleportation are needed. 3) Ask whether existing assets can build it, and whether new assets can be reused. 4) Identify key visual elements. 5) Define governing world rules. 6) Define daily life beyond the hero's story.
why: A believable world gives its inhabitants their own problems rather than existing only to serve the protagonist.

text: 1) Choose a level from a game. 2) Describe how its layout, sight lines and boundaries shape player movement and choices. 3) Note the emotional or narrative effect of the space.
when: Analyzing an existing level to learn spatial design
why: Structured analysis turns observation into transferable spatial knowledge.

text: 1) Draw a straight critical path from entrance to exit. 2) Write the number of locks on the critical path on that path. 3) Branch sub-paths with keys off the critical path. 4) Place puzzles and significant obstacles on the graph, marked as locks but labeled with the obstacle. 5) Count the keys and locks ahead of the player to read linearity.
when: when graphing a dungeon or lock-and-key level
why: A flow-chart style graph gives an objective, shared way to read a dungeon's progression and its blocking obstacles.

text: If another department cannot build a planned scene, find out what they can build that still serves the story.
when: a planned scene is not buildable

text: Decide deliberately where a game's boundaries are defined and whether or when to breach them.
why: Boundaries mark which elements can interact with the game, and most games keep in-game and outside elements from interacting.

text: Remove boundaries between an experience and its physical surroundings by using physical controls and tangible output instead of screens.
when: when the goal is to integrate play with the physical space
why: Screens create a boundary that separates the experience from its environment.

text: Build levels toward three goals: adjusting player behavior, transmitting meaning, and augmenting space with information.
when: Planning a level
why: A clear goal separates deliberate design from an arbitrary arrangement of objects.

text: Extend a space across several scenes only when the pathways between the screens are clear.
why: As enemy numbers grow, players must be able to escape encounters, which requires readable routes between screens.

text: Use sparse spacing where cruising is the intent and dense spacing where demanding navigation is the intent.
when: Choosing spacing for a stretch of play.
why: Spacing sets how much attention the route demands.

text: Size special-tier walls and platform spacing to the specific special jump required to reach them.
why: Spacing and sizes were tuned in the same system as jump height and running speed, so distances match what the jump can cover.

text: Treat learning the game as part of the experience and design it with level design methods.
why: Learning is part of play, not a separate step before it.

text: Lay out each level's design as detailed as possible, since the level layouts are what builders implement.
why: Detailed documents answer the questions teammates would otherwise have to guess at.

text: Pin hand-placed level geometry with positioning constraints so the generator never moves it and minimises the number of position changes it makes elsewhere.
why: Pinned geometry lets the generator respond to designer edits in real time without undoing the designer's placements.

text: Study why bad levels are bad as well as why good ones work, since both teach design lessons.
when: when analyzing level design

text: Keep a separate scene, room, or level file in the engine for building and testing the parts of a level.
why: Being inaccessible to players lets you test geometry and mechanisms without polishing the space.

text: Follow light spaces with dark ones, dangerous spaces with safe ones, and busy areas with sparse ones.
when: When a player arrives in a space from a preceding space in the level sequence
why: The preceding space's conditions shape how the arriving space feels, so an enclosed predecessor makes a large space seem larger.

text: In single-player games, use intimate space for friendly areas or to give the player an advantage.
why: Vantage points and sight lines let the player use their abilities against foes, whereas multiplayer intimate spaces aim for comfort for many players.

text: Use walls or gates for abrupt edges; for gradual ones, use cues such as burned trees or arrows that warn of danger.
when: When entering an area that is the site of an event or the realm of a specific group
why: Landscape rarely changes suddenly, so abrupt borders need architectural marking, while gradual shifts build anticipation for the next zone.

text: Give sandbox worlds distinct districts with unique gameplay; without them, many landmarks can still leave the world feeling empty.
why: Districts hold distinct narrative events and gameplay challenges, which landmarks alone do not supply.

text: In side-scrolling levels, show the far end of any pitfall within one screen width of where the player stands.
why: Players should not have to commit to landings they cannot see, so unseen leaps of faith are avoided.

text: In side-scrolling levels, give enemies and projectiles enough time between entering the screen and reaching the player to be seen and avoided.
Let core mechanics decide node form: place intense uses such as gunfights, sharp turns, boss battles, or hard platforming in dedicated nodes.
why: Intense uses of core mechanics mark which spaces are significant gameplay nodes, which is otherwise hard to tell.

text: Make main-route elements bright or warm and side-passage collectibles cooler or analogous, so the main route stands out.
when: when a level has both a main route and optional side areas
why: Contrast separates the path players should follow from optional spaces.

text: Design spaces that are rich in meaning, not merely clear, by using contrast and ambiguity between safe and dangerous qualities.
why: Games can use danger as a tool, and the emotional release after overcoming it is a source of pleasure.

text: Gate paths between areas with a condition, such as main quest progress or a strength threshold the player can reach.
when: In open-world games where new districts open as the player progresses through the game
why: Skill gates stay closed until the player has learned a district's choices, and mastering its last skill triggers the next opening.

text: Arbitrary bounding shapes are hard to support in editors, so tools usually offer boxes, which may be aligned at any angle.
why: Arbitrary bounds are complex to author and support.

text: Single-screen rooms give a tight, contained feel at the cost of the traversal space a movement mechanic needs.
why: A single-screen room confines the view and space, so free swinging cannot take place inside it.

text: Designers can control how much and what kind of information reaches players by choosing what each room communicates.
when: when deciding what a level should convey
why: Each room sets a bounded load, so information is paced and selected.

text: Pacing is the rhythm of stress and relief, arranged so intense action alternates with quieter moments such as puzzle-solving, exploration, or practicing movement.
Set generated gap width and object spacing against character speed and jump distances so every route stays playable and feels right; verify layouts against movement abilities.
when: Generating platform routes, dungeons or level layouts.
why: Otherwise generated routes may require impossible jumps; spacing is a balance against what movement allows.

text: Fatigue raises perceived difficulty: a hard enemy feels harder right after a long stretch of multitasking.
when: after prolonged multitasking
why: Fatigue reduces the attention available for the challenge.

text: Pacing is the game's tempo, shaped by perceived pressure from stress, cognitive load or sustained attention, time limits, and harsh punishment for mistakes.
An island is an area where story events happen. A bridge is an area between islands where open-ended play happens.
A level schedule is a chart listing modular pieces, their sizes, and their locations, which also serves as a style guide for level art.
A sawtooth difficulty pattern alternates easier encounters with harder ones, creating moments of winning followed by harder moments where players may die repeatedly.
Kishotenketsu is a four-part storytelling structure from Japanese manga that can also sequence how platformer levels introduce mechanics.
Randomly placed level contents, such as enemy locations, are hidden information until the player explores them.
A generated level usually starts as geometry, so the AI needs a representation that converts that geometry into a form suited to its algorithms.
when: AI must act in procedurally generated levels

text: Spatial layout is one of the two sources of context, so generated room and corridor layout shapes the feel of play directly.
Maze and level constraints can cover start points, goals, cell types, and required paths through the level.
A level authoring tool can combine evolutionary generation with a physics-based agent that checks solvability and playtests designer-made levels.
Nonlinear experiences lack one fixed sequence, which makes interest curves harder to apply to them.
Use steady-with-spikes pacing, with tense combat between longer dialogue, exploration and scavenging, since a rising escalation curve breaks apart when play is suspended and resumed.
when: players are expected to leave and return between sessions
why: Steady-with-spikes pacing stays engaging when cut into pieces.

text: The order and content of rooms or encounters in a generated level can carry learning, and can raise difficulty and pressure over time.
why: Game flow covers challenge, pressure and learning-by-doing, which level design is preferred to distribute over time.

text: Design the data a generated level exposes to AI code as deliberately as the generation itself; the interface often dominates AI development effort.
when: Procedurally generated levels that AI characters must read
why: World interfacing is a major share of AI work and debugging

text: Visible wayfinding cues can be applied in generated spaces where navigation is not the intended challenge.
when: When the game's main challenge does not involve careful pathfinding
why: Clear signs reduce cognitive load so players can spend their attention on the core challenges.

text: Layout decisions belong within the wider UX strategy, since level design is one of many elements shaping player experience.
why: Players experience marketing, onboarding, sound and level design together, so a global UX strategy makes the largest difference.

text: Generated level layouts and mission order should be planned with narrative in mind if they must support foreshadowing.
when: when generators build levels for a story
why: Foreshadowing depends on which places and sequence players experience.

text: Free-space measures and A* shortest paths can serve as direct, abstract simulations of unit movement when scoring generated layouts.
why: Shortest-path calculations can be read as abstract simulations of unit behaviour, so they can stand in for simulation.

text: Build the geometry first, then place missions and objects onto it.
when: Generating environments that must serve mission setup
why: Mission placement depends on the terrain's affordances

text: A gated tile type, such as lava traversable only after touching a key tile, is a common dungeon pattern that adds progression constraints.
when: Designing dungeon progression

text: Check that generated layouts, including dungeons, can be completed by an automated agent before they are presented to players.
A hierarchy of time structures, such as several short rounds forming one larger round, can give pacing both quick feedback and a satisfying overall length.
when: Designing the timing of a game
why: Nesting lets short and long rhythms coexist.

text: Interest curves chart an experience's most powerful moments, not every event in it.
why: An experience is a series of moments of uneven power, and the interest curve tracks only the strongest of them.

text: Puzzle difficulty should rise through a chain of intermediate sub-goal actions, each slightly harder than the last, rather than jumping straight to the final challenge.
why: A puzzle is either solved or not, so its difficulty lives in its steps.

text: Balance the time players spend traveling against the time they spend interacting or practicing non-travel mechanics.
when: a level has travel between mechanics
why: excess travel dilutes the experience of the mechanics

text: Start with short levels and let each successive level run slightly longer on average, with some variation.
when: Pacing a sequence of levels or dungeon sections
why: Early short levels feel exciting before players are invested, and longer stretches are easier to tolerate later.

text: Give combat rooms several encounter spots, flanking routes and height variation so the room is interesting to fight in.
why: Several encounter spots, a visible goal and height variation let players plan their approach from a vantage point.

text: Build levels from fixed-size blocks of scenes, focusing design effort on key scenes and using the rest for circulation.
When a literal gate is used, place it right after the first enemy encounter, without needing a key.
when: When using a literal gate as a skill gate early in play
why: Placing it after the first encounter ties the gate to the mechanic just learned

text: A shortcut can let players skip a low-interest stretch while keeping that stretch available for those who want it.
when: When a low-interest section is too costly to cut late in development
why: Players who discover the bypass choose to take it, so the flat section stays optional instead of mandatory.

text: Unusually fast completion times in a tutorial usually indicate a shortcut or exploit, so check the level and play records.
when: completion times far below the rest of the data

text: Long horizontal layouts with few movement limits suit traversal mechanics and tend to feel best to play.
when: levels built around swinging or other traversal
why: Movement needs room to play out.

text: Dungeon groups can be given distinct pacing, playing a role similar to rhythm in platform levels.
when: In dungeon-based games, where the tempo of moving through rooms and hallways matters

text: Alternate intense and calm phases, such as waves of enemies followed by preparation, so that stress is followed by relief.
when: When planning the pacing of a level or encounter sequence.

text: Build levels that vary space size, map complexity, and exit count so they challenge a mode's mechanics in different ways.
Each highlighted gameplay moment, such as an encounter, puzzle or rest stop, can have its own distinct emotional character.
why: Contrasting spatial conditions make key places such as boss rooms or goals stand out from ordinary space.

text: Establish safe zones early through several encounters with no enemies, so players learn them without needing explanation.
when: when a game needs players to recognize safe spaces
why: Repeated safe experiences teach the rule implicitly.

text: Make early exposed crossings narrow enough to force slow movement, so tension builds before the player reaches the reward view.
when: when designing routes over rooftops, ledges or beams
why: Constrained width slows the player and heightens exposure.

text: Alternate safe and dangerous spaces, either between scenes or within one scene, to add gameplay complexity.
why: Placing danger on the route to goals turns reaching them into a thrilling risk.

text: Within individual challenges, the same idea appears as high or low survival moments, depending on the survival mechanics.
when: When a game's survival mechanics set how exposed the player is within a challenge
why: Scene-sized vulnerability can deliver the drama of testing how far players can push their limits.

text: Chaotic background action creates tension while the real threat remains low.
why: The noisy backdrop lets players practise basic functions safely while the scene still feels dangerous.

text: The verbs in a level summary reveal pacing, moving from sneaking to fighting signals a shift in tempo.
when: Writing level summaries to check pacing
why: A verb sequence traces how activity changes across the level, which exposes its tempo.

text: Object construction and spacing, judged against the avatar's speed, shape the sense of motion, so the same speed feels different in different layouts.
when: generating or placing objects in levels
why: Nearby objects act as reference points, so perceived speed depends on what the avatar passes.

text: Spacing is a main challenge lever: wider gaps ease navigation, closer gaps raise difficulty. Tightening spacing later shrinks the steering and jumping margin.
when: Raising difficulty across a game, such as early levels with far-apart, slow obstacles that later levels tighten.
why: Closer objects shrink the margin of error, making steering and jumping harder.

text: Predictable alternations, such as safe rooms before bosses, tell players when to unwind and when to prepare, so they internalize a schedule that pulls them through the game.
when: when a level or game repeats a structure that alternates tension and relief
why: Players learn the rhythm and adjust their expectations and effort; repeated alternation becomes expected.

text: Nested inside a longer total clock, a much shorter clock pushes players to take risks and keeps play interesting.
when: games with a total time limit

text: When players can choose harder or easier levels at any time, confident players progress quickly while timid players power up longer, and failure can drop them back a level.
when: Offering free level selection in a game
why: Self-selection matches challenge to each player's confidence.

text: Empty space after a fight builds anticipation because players do not know whether a surprise waits, and longer walks can increase unease about the next combat.
when: Designing empty corridors between combat
why: Uncertainty about what comes next grows with time spent without knowing.

text: Game rules and match conditions can generate a pacing curve on the fly, following a three-act shape that varies slightly each time.
when: When pacing comes from rules rather than a fixed script.
why: Emergent conditions reproduce the curve's shape while changing details.

text: A shortcut can block progress as an obstacle on the outward trip, then open as a shortcut on the return trip.
when: When the player retraces the route back from higher areas

text: Freytag's five-part arc (exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, dénouement) can structure levels, worlds, and quests so that high and low action alternate.
when: Structuring a level, world, or quest's pacing
why: Alternating high and low action creates good pacing through contrast

text: Levels where every space is always open become predictable; making some spaces available only at certain times restores uncertainty.
why: Time-limited access turns navigation into a puzzle, which is more interesting than static space.

text: A battle space that is quick to cross makes raids fast, keeps fighting nearly constant, and can hold many players and vehicles.
why: Combined size and crossing speed produce emergent play styles.

text: When a housing area is cut off and its more stable residents leave, decay and crime tend to grow.
why: Remaining tenants could not generate the maintenance income the buildings needed.

text: When an enemy can kill instantly, its patrol locations strongly shape the routes players take.
why: Since one hit is fatal, players must route around their positions to avoid them.

text: Tension worsens before it improves, and escalating conflict is what makes drama effective.
when: Once a game's conflict has been set in motion
why: Escalating conflict generates tension, which builds the dramatic arc of a story.

text: Throttle points, where branches rejoin, are where railroading is most noticeable.
Suspense requires something valuable at risk, such as life, victory, or wealth, with both success and failure genuinely possible.
Divide distinct weapons and enemies by playtime hours to get content per hour; overlapping items mean the effective rate is lower than the raw count.
when: checking whether content volume is excessive
why: More content than a good experience needs is wasted effort.

text: Mixed time systems combine turns with a continuous clock, such as a per-player total time limit in turn-based tournament play.
when: When a turn-based game gives each player a continuous clock that limits their total time
why: The turn structure stays discrete while the clock adds real-time pressure.

text: Each level has fresh aesthetics or challenges at its start, a series of rising challenges, and often a boss battle at the end.
why: Interest curves are fractal, so each long peak internally repeats the overall rise-and-climax structure.

text: In a level graph, nodes carry gameplay intent and size, while edges carry the character of the transitions between nodes.
No guaranteed method exists for designing cellular automaton rules that are certain to settle.
why: Rule behavior can be extremely complex, making outcomes impossible to predict accurately.

text: An early prototype that held players for only about two minutes made them question whether there was anything more to do, signalling a flat interest curve.
when: Early playtests of an encounter
why: Battles alone lacked buildup, so interest waned and players wanted more structure.

text: 1) Graybox a level with tightly packed small elements at ground level and large forms beyond. 2) Playtest which rhythm players follow.
why: Playtesting shows whether rhythmic elements change the player's pace and draw them along.

text: 1) Start with an easier opening section. 2) Place a mid-boss. 3) Follow with a harder section. 4) End with a final boss. 5) Give a power reward after each peak.
