when: Building a level or dungeon floor with a repeating difficulty pattern.
why: Repeats the spike-and-reward pattern within a single level.

text: 1) Draw a map of the level. 2) Add call-out boxes for significant gameplay areas. 3) Check their spacing to judge whether pacing works.
when: Reviewing a level's pacing
why: Spacing of key areas reveals rhythm and pacing problems.

text: Plan pacing: 1) draw the whole level at macro scale 2) mark its intense micro-scale encounters 3) spread them evenly across the map 4) fill the gaps with circulation space for movement, exploration or rest.
when: when planning a level layout on paper, before detailed building
why: Quiet space between intense moments keeps high action from blurring into a never-ending slog.

text: 1) Record the player's progression through each campaign section with its underlying numbers and time spent. 2) Note the difficulty, effort and skill each section demands. 3) Compare sections to find the most and least engaging pacing.
when: charting a single-player or cooperative campaign
why: Underlying numbers and time per section reveal where challenge and effort shift, exposing compelling and dull stretches.

text: 1) Hook. 2) Rising action. 3) Build-up. 4) Climax. 5) Denouement.
when: When pacing a sequence or match.
why: This reusable curve holds attention without exhausting the audience.

text: 1) Plot each emotion by intensity and valence. 2) Chart a winding path across the emotional spectrum. 3) Move the player through different flavors, not only up and down.
when: When planning emotional progression through a level or experience.
why: Moving across valence as well as intensity yields richer emotional variety.

text: 1) Identify the gameplay the space supports and its mechanics. 2) Look up and down; check whether contrasting art or reversed verticality creates danger. 3) Sense size, shape, light and sound and how they make the player feel. 4) Analyze pacing: whether the level moves the player quickly or invites exploration, and whether detours are required or bonus. 5) Check whether one play style or several are supported. 6) Ask how the space expresses narrative as backdrop, through exploration or through scripted events. 7) Examine historical and gameplay precedents. 8) Analyze composition, proportions and rhythms of environment art. 9) Compare level geometry with the avatar's movement abilities and check what lies beyond them. 10) Note which art repeats, whether it is interactive and whether it corresponds to a mechanic.
when: when analyzing an existing level or a level being designed
why: Varying how one views a space helps designers notice mechanics, mood and pacing they would otherwise miss.

text: 1) Begin with no opposition or simple waves 2) add a single threat 3) add hazards, puzzles, power-ups, more enemies, and new enemy types one level at a time.
why: Simple starting mechanics make easy configurations easy to distinguish from harder ones.

text: Use molecule and proximity diagrams to pace level elements and study how they interact, and urban design principles to organize large worlds.
when: when planning pacing and organization of a level

text: 1) Place NPCs acting out an event in the player's view. 2) Build lines of sight toward the event. 3) Use spatial size types and landmarks to usher the player toward it.
when: in first-person scenes where narrative events happen
why: Players may wander away from events without spatial cues.

text: 1) Show the challenge simply in the first room. 2) Make the second room more complex. 3) Make the third room hardest, when three rooms guard one reward.
when: when several rooms guard a reward
why: Graduated rooms let players anticipate the puzzle-and-reward rhythm while first learning how the challenge works.

text: 1) Arrive at the level. 2) Overcome smaller obstacles. 3) Overcome a large challenge or enemy. 4) Reach the goal. 5) Emerge victorious.
when: Designing the internal structure of a single level
why: Structuring a level as a dramatic arc makes players feel they accomplished something, and closing beats let them slow down.

text: Set obstacle spacing in generated layouts against avatar speed and turn rate, so the player has room to steer and the challenge is controlled.
when: Generating obstacle courses or avoidance layouts, especially for fast-moving or driven characters.
why: Challenge depends on spacing relative to motion; matching spacing to speed and turn rate keeps layouts drivable.

text: Set the open or closed overall structure of a generated map to control its high-level feel, and use dense, twisting layouts to keep the player focused on nearby space.
when: Generating maps or levels.
why: Overall structure sets the feel, and dense layouts restrict attention to nearby space.

text: When pacing generated levels, avoid long purposeless sparse stretches, and alternate them with dense stretches that add navigation demand.
when: Generating routes or levels.
why: Sparse layouts without purpose lull the player, while dense layouts add demand.

text: Hint at the direction of a hidden reward without making the route of exploration feel rote.
when: generating hidden rewards
why: Discovery's thrill depends on anticipation, which fades when the route to the reward is too obvious.

text: Generated challenges should be deliberate and match the target experience rather than appear at random.
when: when generating dungeons or content
why: unintended friction frustrates players

text: Let skilled players move quickly through easy content, since fixed-length levels for all skill levels bore skilled players.
when: When the game gradually increases difficulty across levels and players vary widely in skill.
why: Players differ in skill, so content one finds boring another finds challenging.

text: To smooth a difficulty spike, reorder content so difficulty rises gradually across the game.
when: a difficulty spike appears in the sequence
why: reordering spreads the challenge into a curve

text: Gate a final, very hard level and new ending behind secret objectives that players must discover.
when: Designing optional endgame content
why: Hidden objectives reward thorough play and extend replayability.

text: Insert breathing spaces after intense sections, such as a calmer cutscene after action or a shift to an activity needing less attention.
when: after intense or high-load sections
why: A challenge right after a long, load-heavy sequence feels harder, since player fatigue builds up.

text: Surround a tutorial area with lethal drops or hazards that have no escape, so players stay within the intended lesson area.
when: Early in an open-world game, before the player's health and stamina have grown.
why: Hazards limit exploration and the player's vulnerability, keeping them inside the lesson area.

text: Split the level into chunks whose properties are roughly uniform for the tactic being analyzed, such as similar illumination for shadow-based tactics.
when: When performing tactical analysis of a level for a property such as illumination.

text: Place weapon and health caches before large battles so players can choose how to approach based on their strengths.
when: In multiplayer or open-world games with large-scale battles where players have differing strengths
why: Caches let players pick their own approach to the upcoming challenge, and also control the pacing of the game.

text: Define the target combat experience at several points in play, such as 5 minutes, 1 hour and 5 hours, to guide balancing.
when: When setting balancing targets for combat early, mid, and late in a long play session
why: Balancing needs a specific goal at each stage of the game.

text: Place dramatic story climaxes at the hardest gameplay moments, with rising tension during rising difficulty.
when: Planning story beats alongside difficulty
why: Aligning the two curves makes the climax feel earned.

text: Wide, regular rhythmic elements move players quickly through large circulation paths, while smaller, denser rhythms slow them to stop and explore.
when: When a large circulation path should keep players moving versus when a zone should make them stop and explore
why: Players entrain to the rhythm of their surroundings, so wide repeating elements carry them forward while dense ones slow them down.

text: A connectable tile can be attached to and is solid on the ground, but can be penetrated in the air.
when: Tile is flagged connectable

text: A design pattern pairs a recurring human problem with a spatial or material configuration that addresses that problem.
CAD drawings are clearer than most hand drafts and take less time to produce, and grid snapping in CAD can be set to real-world units matching engine units.
when: when a drawing must convey more than a single sketch

text: CAD blocks are stored drawings, such as doors or fixtures, that can be inserted at any size, and editing operations avoid redrawing by hand.
Simple interacting objects create new play: water can put out fire, and fire can ignite oil pools that slow players.
why: object interactions multiply options

text: On a small project one person may build every level; on a larger one, a lead typically manages several level builders.
Typical engine primitives include cubes or box shapes, spheres, cylinders, and planes; certain engines add stairs and cones.
Primitives can make most large spatial geometry, since many level editors are robust enough for that.
when: blocking out large spaces

text: Art-style changes, different models, or texture transitions can each create an edge between areas.
Examining a level through many design lenses makes the best layout choices clear.
when: Making layout decisions for a level
why: Each lens exposes different aspects of challenge and choice

text: Characterize the overall open or closed feel of a space before tuning finer detail.
when: Early in designing a world or level.
why: Overall structure frames how every later detail is perceived.

text: Avoid micromanaging level implementation; a strong gameplay system produces combinations and situations the designer did not foresee.
when: When a designer has built a strong gameplay system and hands level layout to a level design team
why: Controlling designers limit what level designers can produce

text: Analyse a single visible landscape rather than a whole game world when the full world is too broad for one study.
when: full world too broad to analyse in one study
why: Narrowing makes it easier to spot dominant or emerging design paradigms.

text: Primitives match engine grid measurements and transfer easily from graph paper or CAD.
when: moving layouts from paper or CAD into an engine
why: Primitives match the engine's grid-based measurements, so layouts sketched on graph paper or in CAD translate directly into the engine.

text: Plan level geometry around measurements so spaces fit the realities of gameplay.
Test chained mechanisms in a toy box, such as an element that neutralizes a hazard while switchable barriers control access to that element.
when: When chaining level mechanisms together before building the actual level

text: Organize arena design as a kit of parts, each piece serving the needs of a particular player type.
when: Designing first-person shooter arenas for mixed player types
why: Arenas built as a set of interchangeable parts can each respond to the needs of a particular player type.

text: Apply the gamespace generators when a multiplayer space should produce unplanned encounters between different player groups.
when: When a multiplayer space should produce unplanned encounters between different player groups
why: Spatial features such as landmarks, paths, and districts naturally bring people together and create interactions the designer did not script.

text: In ordered levels of rising difficulty, skilled players clear easy levels quickly, so skill differences balance themselves without boredom.
when: In games with a sequence of levels that gradually rise in difficulty
why: Skilled players move quickly through easier levels until they reach ones that challenge them, which keeps them from getting bored.

text: Using primitives gives access to engine systems such as particles and lighting, so atmosphere can be tested early.
when: prototyping before final art
why: Primitives give designers access to engine systems like particles and lighting, letting them test gameplay against atmosphere before art exists.

text: Multilevel approaches to a flag let defenders hide below or snipe from above, giving them varied defensive options.
why: Elevated and low positions give defenders different options: hiding below or sniping from above, each with different cover and sightlines.

text: Water built as block volumes placed on the map and detached from the terrain looks crude and offers no player interaction.
when: when water is implemented with limited technology
why: Simulating rivers, lakes and waterfalls was technically unavailable, so water was limited to detached block volumes with no player interaction.

text: Most engines work best with square or rectangular prefabricated pieces, so angled geometry is harder to build.
1) Playtest to find the action players already want in a scene. 2) If all testers want the same thing, script that action. 3) Check that testers do not notice the lost freedom.
when: When considering removing player freedom for a specific scene
why: Players who expect freedom elsewhere accept a scripted moment that matches what they already wanted

text: 1) Note repeated pieces found while sketching. 2) Make each repeated piece a prefabricated asset. 3) List these assets to set artists' production priorities. 4) Assemble levels from them like building blocks.
when: when planning environment production from sketches
why: reusable prefabs avoid building each environment from scratch

text: 1) Draw a map of the level. 2) Highlight significant gameplay areas and measure the distances between them. 3) Assign letters to item, enemy, and obstacle types and check how they are spaced.
1) Play a commercial game and select scenes or rooms. 2) For each, note what makes it effective and what gameplay it creates. 3) Identify the player types or challenge levels each space is built for.
when: Studying level design from existing games
why: Structured analysis turns play experience into reusable design knowledge.

text: 1) List each modular piece in the level. 2) Record its model, quantity, size, and location. 3) Also itemize unscaled elements like flora and shrubbery. 4) Use the list to define the level's style guide.
when: Documenting a measurement-based level
why: A complete list supports consistent construction and art direction.

text: 1) Find bottlenecks where players cannot proceed unless they solve one challenge. 2) Add parallel challenges for when a player is stumped. 3) Make the parallel challenges different enough to be useful. 4) Connect them so progress on one makes the others easier.
when: Designing sequences of challenges where one could block the player.
why: Parallel routes prevent a single challenge from halting progress.

text: 1) Writers supply the area's storyline and its links to neighbouring regions. 2) Designer drafts map layout and quest concept from that background. 3) Designer and writers review each quest's contribution and refine questlines. 4) Designer builds a rough map, iterates until an artist can polish it, then places spawn areas and interactive objects.
1) Design the ideal level that showcases the mechanics 2) work backward, introducing each idea so players are ready when that level arrives.
when: When designing a game's first levels after ideal mid-game levels have been drafted

text: 1) Mark the highlighted gameplay moments. 2) Place them on a macro-scale plan of the whole level, like a map. 3) Detail each space afterwards.
When nodes are placed automatically, give level designers a way to adjust the result.
when: When nodes for a pathfinding graph are placed automatically from level geometry
why: Automatic node placement typically produces mixed results that need human supervision for optimum outcomes.

text: Build the first levels last in production, since tools are refined and engine limits are known by then, while still treating them as the most important levels because they hook players.
when: When a team is building levels in production and tools and engine limits are still being refined

text: Make a weapon's trajectory editable through a learnable parameter, so obstacles can be passed only by applying the taught concept correctly.
when: teaching a math or logic concept through play

text: A maze is a multicursal structure with branching paths and dead ends that leads to an exit.
A labyrinth is unicursal with one defined path, while a maze is multicursal with more than one.
A maze feel can come from ambiguous scenery and darkness rather than from walls.
Maze levels are often paired with powerful enemies or time limits to add pressure.
why: Their branching, dead-end structure already poses uncertain risk-reward choices, and these features turn those choices into tense moments.

text: Use mazes for dramatic gameplay where uncertain choices matter.
why: Branching routes with possible dead ends give a rich risk-reward structure for weighing uncertain options.

text: A metroidvania is a side-scrolling platformer set in large, contiguous mazes, where players progress by expanding their movement abilities.
Metroidvania spaces are maze-like, with branching paths, dead ends, distinct districts and boundaries.
1) Play a game and note how it limits or directs exploration. 2) Note how symbolic assets build associations that suggest next steps. 3) Note how choices encourage exploration.
when: When analyzing how a metroidvania-style game guides exploration
why: These three cues show how a game directs movement without explicit instruction

text: 1) Teach through direction and some uncertainty. 2) Reward exploration. 3) Lock new regions behind earned rewards. 4) Offer multiple equally enticing paths that encourage risk-taking.
when: designing an interconnected world with gated progression
why: Rewards and denied access until earned reinforce exploration and shape how players move through the world.

text: Miniature game spaces act as scale models: a few arranged elements suggest varied natural landscapes and large terrain in a small explorable area, offering many landscapes in a short time.
why: Landscaping features such as rocks and raked gravel stand in for mountains and water, so scale is suggested rather than built.

text: Miniature worlds rely on three elements: clear boundaries, overviews and consistent abstraction.
why: These elements make the small world feel both manageable to navigate and believable to players.

text: Map a world with a miniature garden space by drawing its regions and showing how each reflects a different landscape type.
when: When analyzing how a compact world is divided into regions
why: Mapping regions reveals how varied landscapes organize a space

text: 1) Give players an overview of the space. 2) Offer guided tours through it. 3) Keep boundaries defined but expandable, so new possibility appears over time.
when: designing a bounded play world that should feel open
why: Overview and tours introduce possibility, while expandable boundaries keep it growing.

text: Use movable markers, such as matchsticks standing in for paper arena walls, so layouts can be moved and rearranged quickly during physical prototype tests.
when: physical layout prototypes
why: Quick rearrangement makes the system easy to tweak.

text: Modular pieces are premade, repeatable parts that can be assembled like building blocks, reducing art production and making measurement-based construction practical.
Organic pieces such as landmasses and trees can be scaled and rotated without looking out of place, while non-organic spaces benefit from strict modular tiles.
when: Choosing between organic and modular pieces
why: Organic forms hide scaling and rotation, while rigid geometry shows it.

text: Use modular, repeatable elements such as columns, mats and screens to define interior space, and arrange natural features to guide experience even when they look unplanned.
when: Designing interiors or natural-looking outdoor areas
why: Modular parts make spaces readable, and deliberate arrangement steers attention while preserving a natural look.

text: A slight gap between two modular walls can let a player leave the intended space, so modular pieces must fit together exactly.
when: assembling modular pieces
why: Difficult snapping forces filler geometry, and unnoticed overlaps or gaps are what players can slip through.

text: Build early levels around individual obstacles, then mix and match them in later levels.
when: when designing a progression of puzzles or challenges
why: Familiar parts combined in new ways create variety without new teaching.

text: Modular games reuse elements and reshuffle them in new arrangements, so each room becomes an experiment that players iterate on.
when: when a game is built from reusable parts
why: Recombined familiar elements invite experimentation without new learning.

text: Play a game and sketch the modular objects or tiles that repeat in its environment to see how the level is assembled.
when: analyzing modular level construction
why: Repeated pieces reveal how a level is assembled from reusable units.

text: Build a set of 2D or 3D tiles or environment objects that combine into a level, breaking a level into reusable units.
when: creating level construction kits

text: Meeting spaces, such as courtyards, squares, meeting rooms, and classrooms, are places where people stop and socialize.
Multiplayer and online games use meeting spaces too: spaces before climactic encounters, safe houses at level start and end, and towns or taverns for planning.
Multilateral intimate space appears in corridor shooters and multiplayer arenas that have no significant vantage points above or below.
Open, expansive plans are a common approach in multiplayer shooter maps.
In multiplayer, a prospect with a vantage point above others gives one player a spatial advantage.
In multiplayer, use intimate space to create an even playing field.
when: Multiplayer arenas with level footing and no major raised or lowered positions to exploit.
why: Every part of the space is reachable with the same inherent abilities, so no one holds a spatial edge.

text: 1) Show an obstacle the player cannot yet cross, such as a lock that needs a broken tool, so level geometry signals the needed tool. 2) Then introduce the key, such as resource harvesting, so learning it feels meaningful.
why: An obstacle the tool solves gives players a concrete consequence they can avoid by learning the skill.

text: Teach through narrative and in-world events so players learn unnoticed, but hiding a direct instruction in subtext leaves them unsure; state direct instructions when players must act.
when: When designing tutorials or early instruction
why: Invisible teaching avoids breaking immersion and feeling controlled, while hidden instructions can leave players unsure what to do.

text: Players who enjoy only part of a tutorial reveal which elements work, which is useful information for designing other levels.
when: analyzing which tutorial parts players enjoy
why: Players who linger on an element may be having fun or be confused, so each pattern needs checking before designing further.

text: Scaffolding introduces a concept and applies it in increasingly complex ways across several exercises.
Scripts can define level triggers, such as which keys open which doors, which is the kind of logic a dungeon's content layer needs.
Games teach mechanics either through a dedicated tutorial or through spaces where players discover mechanics on their own.
Levels can add their own mechanic on top of the core mechanic for distinct identity and progression; assuming each level must repeat the core mechanic limits variety.
when: when a level needs its own identity

text: Build each challenge area of an open tutorial around one tool so each area teaches one lesson.
Keep an exit open during a demonstration so the scene persuades rather than forces the player to stay.
Physical props that suggest a use, such as a tool beside an object, can prompt players to examine or climb without written instructions.
when: You want players to act without explicit tutorials
why: The objects' placement implied a purpose, which prompted the visitor to try the action.

text: Use telling details in a room to communicate a character's history and state of mind without dialogue.
when: When generating or designing rooms that should convey a character.
why: Players piece together a character by exploring, rather than being told through heavy-handed exposition.

text: Introduce two or three mechanisms per level, then mix them in new ways in later levels.
why: Each mechanism is introduced early in a safe setting so players can learn it before facing danger.

text: Keep the key elements of a teaching sequence within one screen's view, so the cause and effect are visible together.
when: when introducing a mechanic in early levels
why: Seeing trigger and outcome at once makes the link obvious.

text: Build the opening level so experienced players still enjoy replaying it.
why: It teaches without stopping play, so returning experienced players still get a satisfying run.

text: Keep early learning steps short and rewarding so players reach the full system with each mechanic already learned.
why: New concepts are layered onto familiar ones, so each is practiced alone before the concepts are combined.

text: Opening sequences can teach combat, locks, hazard avoidance, object pushing and lifting, environmental puzzles, stealth and enemy types in sequence.
why: Teaching inside a story scene avoids lecturing the player, instead of having a character explain the rules.

text: Genre and audience set how much instruction is repeated; casual social games often restate instructions in dialogue, gameplay text and hints.
when: Designing instruction text for casual social games
why: Genre and demographics determine how much information the game gives, since RPGs leave more for players to work out.

text: Deliver awkward control instructions through a character's voice in the fiction, so the instruction fits the story.
when: When the budget cannot cover voice acting for a tutorial
why: Instructions spoken as an in-game character seem to come from the world rather than from an outside tutorial.

text: Wider spacing relative to movement speed makes the input-to-response mapping matter less to how the space feels.
when: When the space is largely featureless with few objects to interact with
why: Spacing only matters once two objects can interact, so without interaction the movement mapping is irrelevant.

text: Teaching placed inside a meaningful, low-stress situation, without punishing death, lets players learn mechanics through action rather than pressure.
when: Designing opening sequences and early tutorial situations.
why: Stress and punishment during learning reduce attention available for the lesson.

text: Scenic features, sound such as running water, and movement through a space guide visitors along a route.
why: Scenic features act as a medium that directs what the viewer experiences as they move through a space.

text: Open tutorials limit possibility space in three ways: linear paths, a guide who corrects straying, and danger that discourages leaving the area.
why: Dangerous boundaries keep players inside an area without a physical wall.

text: 1) Introduce each obstacle or ability alone in a safe spot where failure is cheap, especially risky ones such as wall-jumping over a pit. 2) Only then require it in danger or combine abilities in new puzzles.
when: When building a level sequence that teaches multiple abilities, or when an ability's first real use would be dangerous
why: Isolating an ability lets players learn it before stakes rise, and low-cost failure allows practice before pressure.

text: 1) Place an outer trigger that plays a warning sound. 2) Place an inner trigger that applies damage if the player continues. 3) Stop the warning when the player leaves the immediate proximity.
when: A hazard the player can retreat from
why: A warning before harm lets the player choose to retreat.

text: 1) Introduce one mechanic in an early level. 2) Repeat it with increasing precision in varied obstacles. 3) Introduce a second mechanic while the first is reinforced. 4) Combine them later.
when: sequencing mechanics across levels
why: staggered repetition aids retention

text: 1) Place players in a situation that needs the feature 2) Provide the resources to solve it 3) Let them use the feature to escape or progress, teaching it through necessity.
when: teaching medium or difficult features

text: 1) Introduce a mechanism in a safe space 2) use it above a small platform 3) use it above a hazard 4) use it above a hazard with enemies.
when: When a level is built around a single core mechanism
why: Introducing the mechanism away from hazards lets players learn it safely before riskier uses are added.

text: 1) Show the game's identity through a memorable, high-energy moment. 2) Scaffold controls through a few set-pieces: low-resistance practice areas first, then a harder test of the same skills. 3) Deliver information without interrupting play.
when: when designing a first level
why: an opener can teach core skills while dramatizing the game

text: 1) Place a demonstration of the hazard before the player meets it. 2) Set the trigger distance, trigger size, and timing of the triggered event.
when: when building scripted demonstrations
why: trigger parameters control when the demonstration appears

text: Limit each single-screen scene to one new mechanic, and separate teaching scenes with practice scenes rather than placing them back to back.
when: When designing tutorial and introductory levels or sequencing tutorial scenes, especially for new mechanics
why: Players can process only a small amount of information at once, and spacing lets them absorb a mechanic before practicing it.

text: Write the narrative after tutorial order and feature reasons are set, especially the first-time experience, so the story supports the onboarding plan rather than forcing changes to it.
when: When writing the story for a game's onboarding and first-time experience
why: Writing the story after the onboarding order is set avoids struggling to fit teaching into a story already written.

text: Change stages when the player enters a new zone, not when the player gains a level.
when: Tuning when enemy stages advance in a game where players level up
why: Level-triggered changes make monsters shift suddenly during play, which feels wrong.

text: When a level adds a moving object such as a cart, playtest whether passages block it, and widen narrow passages that do not fit it.
when: When a level includes a moving object such as a mine cart that must pass through passages
why: Standard-width passages can stop the object and frustrate players.

text: Introduce a game's world and mechanics by showing them in play rather than explaining them in text.
when: designing opening spaces

text: Turn a new mechanic into a problem by requiring precise use of it to open a locked path, so practice becomes the solving step.
when: When a new mechanic is needed to proceed past a gate
why: Practicing the new mechanic is required to solve the challenge, so learning happens through its use.

text: For multiplayer mode tips, focus on the why (main objective) rather than the how or the what.
when: multiplayer mode tips

text: Sandbox games generate their entire world and most of its content algorithmically, as procedurally generated worlds made of blocks that teachers use for many learning goals.
When the open ground is hazardous, scattered refuges become stepping stones, and players must reach them by movement or a tool.
when: in hazardous open areas
why: Contrasting vulnerable open spaces with safe ones creates linked sequences of safe and unsafe space.

text: Districts are identifiable sections players enter, distinguished by their NPCs, enemies, events or mini-games.

Late-1990s environments were largely confined to a flat x,y plane, and depth on the Z axis was the next differentiator; by 2000–2010, environments became detailed 3D spaces traversable on all three axes.
Role-playing games centre on inventory, world exploration, and accumulating wealth and experience, so a generated dungeon can serve as their exploration space.
Modern environments (2000–2010) used varied and seasonal weather, including fog, dust, complex clouds, whirlwinds and tornados, as part of the environment rather than surface detail.
Procedurally arranged assets range from whole universes down to enemy and item placement in familiar spaces.
A tutorial space can feel open while still following a limited lesson plan.
Action games may have around 200 characters per level, often switched on or off, so a frequency scheduler for active characters is usually sufficient.
City simulations run only a few characters out of thousands, and off-screen characters keep no identity beyond a few story characters.
Functional space is the skeleton of a layout, while the fleshed-out space is what players actually experience.
As hardware improved, designers extended play beyond a single screen through scrolling worlds, distinct screens, and room-by-room structures.
Natural game spaces grew sharply in scale, in some cases spanning several virtual square miles.
A layout can use a large ocean dotted with archipelago islands instead of a single central landmass, which is a different spatial structure.
A newly planned district with separated functions can start out largely empty and still draw few pedestrians.
Players value unpredictable variation, so procedurally generated content can add enjoyment by producing varied outcomes rather than fixed patterns.
when: when designing content generators
why: Variation supplies the surprise players value

text: A generator can apply a sawtooth pattern of easier and harder encounters when placing rooms or enemies.
Include landmark placement rules in procedural world generation so generated worlds keep navigational reference points.
when: When a game's environments are generated by an algorithm
why: Tall visible structures let players see large areas and orient themselves toward their objectives.

text: Scripted travel options let designers build world logic around a fully connected set of locations.
when: generating or designing location networks
why: Scripted access lets locations exist only within the virtual world, through its own coordinate system.

text: Add closed canyons, rock outcroppings and dense tree areas as deliberate contrast to open space.
when: When the overall world is very open
why: Enclosed areas act as contrast, so the surrounding open space reads as wider.

text: Structure an open world as an open area with specific goals rather than a dense city, which supports exploration appeal.
Give small spaces clear boundaries and clearly defined pieces so they stay understandable and easy to shape.
why: Well-bounded possibilities let a newcomer learn the game quickly and reshape the space without confusion.

text: In open levels, emphasize gateways vertically and use environmental cues to guide the player through.
Boundaries that organize space and mark territory can partly reveal what lies beyond, drawing the eye outward while denying access.
A playfield about two kilometers square, measured in the game's own distance unit, reads as a large open valley.
why: Pockets of closed-in terrain provide contrast that keeps the overall space feeling open and wide.

text: Explorable space is judged by counting the paths and keys available before the player meets a lock or item-requiring puzzle.
when: when measuring how much a dungeon offers before a gate
why: Several keys or paths leading to a single lock indicate the player has multiple routes to choose from.

text: Grouping buildings of the same technology type together lets a single attack destroy all of them.
when: RTS base layout

text: Reusing the same landscape chunks produces regularities that are easy to see from high altitude.
when: Large terrains assembled from repeated pieces
why: Repetition becomes visible when the player views a wide area

text: Making a world larger does not convey size if architectural detail that signals scale or proportion is lost.
when: Expanding level or world size
why: Size is perceived through detail, so empty enlargement reads as nothing special.

text: A featureless space can make movement abilities feel pointless.
why: Abilities such as a wall kick need a physical object to act on, so without objects they cannot be used.

text: A fixed world can fail a story plan by missing needed locations, including irrelevant ones, or by needing rearranged locations for a coherent flow.
when: When a fixed game world must host an automatically generated story plan.

text: Players lose track of their location in large open 2D exploration worlds.
when: In large open-world 2D games with side-scrolling views.
why: Side-scrolling layouts leave little room for pathfinding design, so the player's location is hard to read.

text: Separating interactive elements, or leaving large empty space between them, isolates people and reduces the contact that keeps a place lively and safe.
when: designing cities or multiplayer spaces
why: Regular contact between people sustains activity and safety.

text: 1) Place defensive buildings near raw materials. 2) Put basic buildings on spots between two defensive buildings. 3) Put advanced buildings of a different type between two basic buildings. 4) Put very valuable facilities between two advanced buildings.
when: laying out an RTS base with cellular automaton rules
why: Placing buildings by these rules keeps the layout steady and prevents erratic configurations.

text: 1) Identify the scenes or environment chunks that repeat in a PCG game. 2) Note what differs between repeats, such as enemy placement or theming.
1) Start with a large open space. 2) Add elevation changes. 3) Add better vantage points. 4) Add hiding places. 5) Adjust how players arrive so each addition serves both threat and safety.
when: when an open arena feels too simplistic
why: Adding spatial contradictions turned a simplistic space into a nuanced one.

text: 1) Give each district a set of tasks. 2) Unlock the next district when its tasks are completed.
why: Finishing a district's final skill acts as a trigger that opens the path onward.

text: Design each reusable scene to address a player-experience need, since players in constructionist systems will see it many times.
when: Scenes reused by a constructionist generator
why: Players see the same scene repeatedly.

text: Populate the world from a data file or level editor, separating world population from world implementation so designers can place entities without code changes.
why: Entities sit in a collection instead of being hardcoded, so adding or removing them needs no code change.

text: Players in a room with two exits almost always leave through one of them, because doors invite opening.
when: An empty room with a few exits
why: Even two options count as a choice

text: Web space joins several marked points with paths so players can reach destinations in different ways, with travel that is meaningful or instantaneous.
A Steiner point is an added intermediate point, connected to several spaces, that gives the shortest connection among them when they are not directly linked.
Web layouts suit cases where several destinations should be reachable through a number of different routes.
when: Choosing web organization

text: Early areas can offer optional routes using special moves to reach higher ledges sooner.
when: early level progression

text: Gate a zone behind a key found in another zone, and split monster difficulty between the child nodes.
when: Designing locked sections from a partition tree
why: Only one corridor joins the two cells, so that corridor can be locked off to seal the section.

text: Optional dead ends and side branches off a main route can hold treasure or coin caches that reward exploration.
Steiner shortcut spaces can be rewarded with power-ups to encourage players to use them.
when: When players can reach play spaces vertically by climbing or jumping between nodes.
why: Dropping from high ledges onto lower ones saves time, which makes the shortcut worth taking.

text: Offer risky optional routes with extra supplies, so skilled players can take them while others skip them.
Give narrow spaces two exits so players keep an escape route when enemies clog one of them.
when: Narrow spaces in a level where enemies may block one exit
why: Playtesting revealed that a blocked single exit would unfairly kill testers; a second exit removes that trap.

text: Steiner spaces act as shortcuts: players jump or climb from a node to a Steiner space, then to another node, or cross open space to skip long-route parts.
when: Where a level lets players climb or jump vertically between nodes

text: 1) Find a refuge that overlooks the prospect. 2) Read enemy placement and patrol timing from it. 3) Move to a secondary refuge. 4) Wait in refuges until the best moment to advance.
when: in stealth levels with patrolling enemies
why: Refuges let players observe threats before committing to movement.

text: A parti is a simple formal study that isolates the shape a building or level will take; it can be made on paper or as a model.
A plan is a top-down, perspective-free cut of a space, assumed viewed from about 4.5 feet above ground, with cut walls filled solid or hatched.
Blueprints reveal how areas are laid out and connect, serving as level maps for challenge and pacing.
An overview shows the scope of a space from an elevated or omniscient view without granting full access to it.
Outdoor terrain often already uses a grid-based height field, which can serve directly for tactical analysis.
Most people find it difficult to draw an accurate 2D map of a familiar place, even though they know which doors lead to which rooms.
why: Spatial knowledge is relational rather than cartographic

text: Plans are usually an architect's first drawing, so they generate the spatial arrangement of a building.
Plans cannot show the third dimension; multilevel areas need dotted lines or a section.
In 2D games the camera looks from the top or side, and turning off perspective produces an orthographic view.
Sketch many uses of a single mechanism early, including its variants, before working out how each will function.
when: Developing a mechanism for a level
why: Breadth of uses reveals which variants are worth building.

text: Shape a building's plan around occupants' need for light and around household functions that should be close together.
when: Laying out interior rooms
why: Plans organized around use and light serve occupants better.

text: When building exteriors are not shown, plan shape must carry the type; when they are shown, exteriors should resemble familiar forms.
when: When building exteriors are not visible to the player
why: Viewers link a building's use to its form through societal associations, so types help them read their surroundings.

text: Designing solely from a top-down plan yields a largely flat 3D space, offering few spots where players must glance upward or move vertically.
when: When a 3D game's level is laid out using only plan drawings
why: Without vertical design, height adds little to play.

text: Overviews are passive; overusing them or fly-over cutscenes makes pacing stagnant and breaks the sense of discovery.

1) Design a mechanism the player must react to. 2) Sketch three zones for it: safe introduction, slight danger, and high danger. 3) Check that each zone teaches or tests the mechanism at its intended stakes.
when: Planning how a new mechanism is introduced in a level
why: Graded danger lets players learn the mechanism before it is tested under pressure.

text: 1) Gray-box a level that gives a tour or overview. 2) Note what the overview shows. 3) Check how it prepares players to interact with the level.
when: When designing an opening overview or tour of a level
why: An overview orients players before they act

text: 1) Rotate a plan 30 or 45 degrees. 2) Project it upward to create 3D forms.
when: showing three-dimensional form without perspective distortion
why: Plans and sections must be combined to show 3D space, whereas a projected drawing shows three-dimensionality directly from one plan.

text: Sketch a short game-world stretch taking roughly thirty seconds to a minute to cross, noting three or more spots where the layout highlights a particular mechanic.
when: analyzing how a level teaches or emphasizes mechanics

text: 1) List the required functions and spaces of the program. 2) Draw bubbles for spaces, sized by required area. 3) Connect bubbles with lines weighted by how important their adjacency is.
when: analyzing which spaces must sit next to each other

text: Plan maps that blend spaces for different play styles with proximity diagrams, placing related spaces near one another before building.
when: multiplayer map layout

text: Proximity diagrams analyze function and are not final spatial plans.
when: When a building program is translated into spaces, before a spatial layout is drawn

text: Spaces in a separate dimension can be entered by surprise and are hard to telegraph in advance.
Empowering players inside dangerous spaces can create exhilarating experiences rather than only fear.
when: when the player is given strength inside a threatening space
why: Dangerous spaces already evoke fear; turning their threat into player advantage shifts the emotional response.

text: Coupling player agency with environment design shows that meaningful interaction with the world can deepen immersion.
why: Terrain embedded as a gameplay feature, not just decoration, lets player actions reshape the world.

text: Branching paths create a risk-reward structure, because players must weigh uncertain options with different costs and rewards.
when: In maze-like levels whose branches include potential dead ends
why: Dead ends make each branch's outcome uncertain, so choosing one means accepting a gamble.

text: Testing denied rewards: 1) Sketch a level where a reward is visible but access is blocked, so the player must search. 2) Graybox it. 3) Playtest and observe whether the path changes after the player finds the reward.
when: testing whether rewards draw exploration
why: visible but blocked rewards motivate searching

text: Removing choice entirely can make a level less remembered and reduce replay value, while combining unique materials, experiential detail and rule-signalling symbols keeps a space memorable.
when: designing a level's balance between linear structure and player choice
why: Dwelling in a space gives players an existential foothold, and that attachment is what brings them back.

text: Reward explorers with optional content: visual puns, ambient dialogue, lingering sounds, in-jokes, Easter eggs, elaborate side quests, or simple texture-based secrets.
when: When information is optional and not needed for progression
why: Hidden detail gives explorers something to discover without burdening other players.

text: A final challenge that blends previously taught skills works as a final exam for the player.
why: it tests whether earlier lessons were learned

text: Successive gates along a route can express social hierarchy by restricting access to the central space, so that visitors must pass several thresholds to reach the most important area.
when: Designing a hierarchical or restricted central area
why: Each gate signals rank and controls who reaches the innermost space.

text: Graphing a non-dungeon level with major objectives in place of locks shows several objectives that can be completed in any order.
when: when graphing a level without locks

text: Communicating the limits of a game world builds a sense of possibility for players who test those limits.
In this structure the first piece may be found by chance, while later pieces come from progressing through conflicts.
The structure marks progression through both levels and narrative at once.
Plan loot in a generated dungeon as a chain where newer items depreciate older ones.
when: When generating dungeon loot.

text: Build skill gates from environment features such as pits, switches, and boxes instead of keys, so the world feels organic rather than mechanical.
when: When the world should feel natural rather than game-logic driven
why: Environmental gates hide the mechanical nature of progression

text: A small implicit target built into the environment can steer behavior while users keep their feeling of freedom; placing it slightly off-center softens the angle.
when: Designing environmental prompts
why: The etched fly serves as an aim point, so users aim better while still choosing freely.

text: Place goals and well-spaced objects so they reward precise movement and big jumps, such as from launch areas.
why: Goal targets reward a high degree of steering accuracy, so precise control is what earns the reward.

text: Pair a rescue goal with level-based partial objectives to layer progression.
when: when designing a rescue or escape goal
why: Partial objectives add layers of progression on top of one overall goal.

text: Games usually raise challenge as they progress, and integrated games let the story develop alongside that rising challenge.
when: Plotting tension across levels or sessions
why: Challenge usually increases over play, so linking the story to it makes rising action match the formal system.

text: Making travel options available early is a hallmark of modern open-world design.
when: open-world games
why: Instant travel between visited places cuts the time spent crossing large, expansive maps.

text: Layer long-term and short-term goals together rather than planning from the top down alone, because layering produces richer gameplay.
why: nested rhythms at several scales add depth

text: Reward each completed challenge with more story and a new challenge, so story and play advance together.
when: When a finely crafted story is punctuated by periods of interactivity and challenge.
why: Pairing story beats with challenge balances gameplay against storytelling, a combination the source credits as working well.

text: When several products share one world, make each one reinforce the others rather than compete with them.
when: Several products share one world
why: Each product gives audiences another entry point, and interactive versions let them act within the world, which deepens rather than dilutes it.

text: Physical attractions can act as an additional gateway into a world, giving audiences another way to enter it.
when: Extending a world beyond its original medium
why: Offering a physical destination keeps audience interest alive, since visitors re-enter the world through another route.

text: Without a cap, encounters repeat the same enemies because the player has outgrown the content, and expansions start from an uncertain player level.
when: When an RPG has no level cap and its content stops keeping pace with experience gains.
why: Players hit the content ceiling, so encounters repeat, and expansions cannot know where players will start.

text: A stat that controls carrying capacity or heavy-door access can gate treasure rooms, tying that stat to exploration.
when: Dungeons where obstacles or loot depend on a stat.
why: Gives a stat that a class would otherwise avoid practical use, so even specialized characters find it worth investing in.

text: Granting a traversal item that removes the danger lets players leave a limited area safely and ends its restrictions.
A designer-placed trigger switches a character on or off, and the character's AI then acts accordingly.
when: When many AI characters are in the scene, such as a swarm or squad.

text: Designers can use terrain shape to restrict access to parts of an environment, aligning progression with gameplay and narrative.
when: when pacing progression through a space
why: terrain blocks movement, so it controls when areas become reachable

text: When a map extends a mostly linear chain of upgrades, designing from the beginning onward fits the structure.
why: Building in order suits the player experience, since players meet upgrades in sequence.

text: Character abilities such as hiding at walls and peeking around corners turn sharp corners into strategic hiding places.
when: When the player character can hide behind walls and peek around corners.
why: The ability changes how corners work: they stop being plain geometry and become places to hide.

text: When collectibles unlock portals and levels, players choose which missions to take, when to backtrack, and how long to explore.
when: In hub-based games built around collecting resources.

text: Denying access to areas pushes exploration; ability rewards such as jump upgrades, armor or weapons open previously blocked areas.
when: In Metroidvania-style games.
why: Advancement depends on finding rewards, so players are driven to explore blocked areas.

text: After gaining a new power, players return to earlier spaces that now open, which drives backtracking.
when: In Metroidvania-style worlds that grow as the player acquires abilities.
why: Multiple passages with no marked correct one leave players uncertain, which draws them back to check the alternatives.

text: Limiting new players to their starting area until they earn permission and resources gives them a bounded introduction to the wider world.
why: Planned early encounters teach mechanics and shape how players interact and play.

text: Early jobs that tour the first areas and visit social spots can teach the world before rank unlocks deeper systems.
why: Early missions double as tours of early planets and social spots, so players learn the world as they progress.

text: Rewarding a character for reaching the goal it is driven toward communicates its motivation through play.
when: when a mechanic should show a character's drive
why: Scoring tied to the character's desire, like flying, makes the motivation readable through what the player is rewarded for.

text: Layered denial places several barriers between the player and a reward, and the layers can run horizontally or vertically and escalate in difficulty.
when: When a level is structured as layers of challenge leading toward one reward.
why: Layers let players anticipate the rhythm of puzzles and rewards, since each descent brings greater challenge and greater reward.

text: Long-term goals such as boss battles, cutscenes, and story events form a foundation, with shorter goals like stages, tasks, puzzles, and enemy encounters nested inside them.
why: Shorter goals nested inside big events form rhythmic patterns at several scales.

text: Action-adventure designs can cycle through overworld tasks, then a dungeon that usually unlocks a fresh tool and a key story object, forming a repeating loop.
Replays that repeat much of the content, and alternate endings that change little, make players feel replaying is tedious.
when: designing multiple endings
why: Repeated content looks poor on replay

text: Requiring other gateways to follow a story alienates most audiences, though it may intrigue a few; a product that needs another medium to make sense is a warning sign.
when: When a tie-in work only makes sense to players who have already experienced its source material
why: Newcomers who entered through one gateway find the work confusing, so only a small group engages with it.

text: 1) Confine the player to a small territory blocked by obstacles they cannot cross. 2) Let them find enhancements there. 3) Use enhancements to leave or defeat the blockers. 4) Repeat so the world keeps expanding.
when: when the world should grow as the avatar grows stronger
why: It draws on people's innate drive to grow stronger and gain power, so an expanding map rewards that desire.

text: 1) Create a graybox level that directs players to a specific point. 2) Test whether environment art, overviews, tours, and visual forces lead players to the intended goal.
when: When validating that a level guides players to a target
why: Testing confirms that direction cues actually work for players

text: 1) Break the critical-path story into narrative-level missions from the high-level breakdowns. 2) Detail each mission with wireframes where needed. 3) Use the result as a visual reference for level and gameplay teams.
why: Detailed mission diagrams serve as a quick-reference visual for designers building levels and gameplay from the story.

text: 1) List the game's goals from long-term to short-term. 2) Draw major goals with thicker lines and minor goals with thinner lines, according to their importance.
when: when checking how a game's rhythms layer
why: line weight shows how goals nest at different scales

text: Set a trigger event's Max Trigger Count to 0 so it can fire indefinitely; otherwise a Touch event may fire only a limited number of times.
when: events that must repeat, such as entering and leaving an area
why: Repeated content looks poor on replay

text: Give each level a grade or stars; passing unlocks progress, and players who unlock everything can chase top grades on earlier levels.
why: Lets novices advance while giving experienced players a reason to replay earlier levels for a harder goal.

text: Signal growth goals with level-gated areas or zones where stronger enemies quickly defeat players.
why: Seeing the obstacle before getting the tool means players already understand the new item's value once they obtain it.

text: Enforce content order with both scripted triggers and level geometry, such as requiring a route be crossed or an area explored before later content opens.
when: content must be encountered in a specific sequence
why: geometry and scripts together make order feel natural rather than arbitrary

text: A first level should excite the player, introduce the world and core mechanics, and invite further exploration, since it carries more teaching work than any other space.
when: designing the opening level or area of a game
why: Players must want to keep playing while learning how the game works.

text: Information needed to progress should be obvious to every player, while optional detail is placed for those who explore.
when: In action-oriented games, where players may be busy moving and not notice small details
why: Players differ in how much they explore.

text: Keep the critical path simple so its parts can be written separately.
when: On a multi-writer team building a large RPG with many quests
why: Otherwise individual quests end up with critical-path information that feels unrelated or skippable.

text: Make endings rewarding through victory, closure for characters, or legendary loot, and make the journey to them exciting and memorable.
why: No single ending can please everyone, so a fun journey keeps the game memorable even when players dislike the ending.

text: If an NPC rewards the player in the world, put the reward in the dialogue itself, and include success and failure lines that address the player.
when: Writing mission completion and failure dialogue.
why: Keeps reward delivery consistent with the story.

text: Letting players choose step order lets them tackle easy parts first and gain hints for harder ones, but fixed order forces the ramp on everyone.
when: When a puzzle has several steps that can be tackled in any order
why: Players naturally begin with what they can solve, and each solved piece supplies clues for the rest.

text: Players tend to move through prospect spaces and stay still in refuge spaces, so each space type suits a different activity.
why: This draws on early humans who searched open plains for food and returned to sheltered spots to assess threats.

text: A prospect is a large open area that leaves its occupant exposed to attack.
A refuge is a small, sheltered space where an occupant can stay hidden while looking out to assess threats.
Fog, music and shadows can heighten the vulnerability a player feels in a prospect space.
when: In open prospect spaces where players already feel exposed, such as wide multiplayer maps
why: Wide open ground produces an anxiety similar to fear of open space, and atmosphere amplifies that exposure.

text: Pair each prospect with a refuge the player can watch it from, so the player can evaluate threats in the open space.
why: A sheltered spot overlooking open ground lets the player judge danger from a position of safety.

text: Set refuges on a different level: higher for a wide view, or lower for a cloistered hiding place.
why: Lower ceilings make a space feel more protected, while a raised position gives an advantageous view.

text: Place refuges as protrusions overlooking a large circulation prospect, so occupants can watch the flow below.
when: in large atrium or hub spaces
why: Large circulation spaces are uncomfortable to linger in, so a raised refuge gives a static place to watch the flow.

text: Large prospect structures pull players from one battle to the next, while explorable interiors hold richer reward and narrative content.
why: Large-scale rhythms keep battles flowing, while interiors reward players who detour to explore.

text: Prospects and refuges each come in primary and secondary types; primary ones are occupied or looked onto, secondary ones lie in the distance.
Refuge-based spaces use low broad ceilings, natural materials, a central hearth, depressed sitting areas, and large overhangs that conceal occupants.
Set spacing between refuges in generated spaces, since the distance players cover between them controls pace at any scale.
when: when generating arenas or landscapes
why: The travel distance between refuges sets how quickly play moves, at any scale of arena or landscape.

text: The shrinking fortress is a scenario where enemies surround protagonists and progressively capture the safe territory they hold.
The shrinking fortress scenario usually needs a large level space to work well.
Keep scenery and narrative content sparse in PvP maps, since it pulls attention away from opponents the map should keep in focus and players rarely look at it for long.
when: competitive multiplayer maps
why: Few other obstacles keep player attention on opponents rather than on the environment.

text: In competitive deathmatch maps, favor easy navigation with many loops and few dead ends so players meet one another quickly.
when: competitive PvP shooter maps
why: Quick encounters keep matches active.

text: Gradually shrinking the playable area forces surviving players to meet, bounding how long a match can last.
when: Designing last-player-standing matches.
why: A shrinking space removes places to hide and drives encounters.

text: Spectator areas can turn a game into both a game and a performance.
Players perceive a repeated layout as different when enemies or hazards in it change, because encounters shape how a space feels.
when: A layout's geometry repeats across generated levels
why: Enemies and hazards change how a chunk feels.

text: Rhythmic elements can turn a single space into several perceived spaces.
Show a key landmark several times along a route so that players keep orienting toward it and perceive it from multiple angles.
when: Designing routes that lead to a central landmark
why: Repeated views reinforce the landmark as a goal and reward continued movement toward it.

text: Track user views, representation, communication, lighting and materials as recurring spatial elements when analyzing or designing a space.
when: Analyzing or designing a level
why: These elements recur across eras and shape how spaces are experienced.

text: Once the format is clear, spread the elements apart in later iterations to create new challenges.
when: when a mechanic has been taught and players understand it
why: Familiar rules become a basis for harder variations.

text: Repeated rhythmic elements such as columns or openings draw players onward through a space.
why: Partially visible structure triggers a human urge to fill in the missing knowledge by moving through the space.

text: A recognizable landmark on high ground that offers resources and a vantage point is welcomed by players even when it recurs.
when: When the same landmark pattern appears across multiple distinct environments.
why: Landmarks offer resources and a vantage point.

text: Making every area look alike leaves players lost, and making every area look different makes the space monotonous; too much chaos is as monotonous as too much order.
when: Designing repeated or varied areas
why: Both extremes remove the cues players use to orient and remember

text: Repeating whole tiles is noticeable to players, and a shared theme does not fully hide the repetition.
when: When a player encounters the same level theme many times.

text: A reward vault is a room holding items, information, or resources, set apart from ordinary space by lighting, music, and architecture; some also serve as save rooms.
A rewarding vista is an impressive view that gives the player a pause after intense action, usually without gameplay resources, and its value lies in pacing and celebrating a climb.
Reward clues suggest that a reward may exist nearby without showing it directly, so the player is motivated to check.
Spaces themselves can act as rewards, including reward vaults, rewarding vistas, meditative spaces, and narrative stages.
A consistent reward pace, such as one reward every few rooms, keeps players moving forward through a level.
when: When players know that rewards arrive at a consistent pace.
why: regular payoffs maintain expectation

text: Chart a level so it prompts the player to return and search for a required item before a later challenge.
when: planning backtracking in a level
why: Flow charts approximate what the player thinks while playing, exposing where the player must be told to return.

text: Rewards break up tense moments and encourage players to keep exploring.
when: Following stretches of danger or conflict in a level's pacing.

text: Reward vaults are often small and may use high ceilings, vaulting, or arches that celebrate the space, like a church apse.
why: Such features set the reward space apart from ordinary level areas through lighting, sound and form.

text: For reward vaults, show the reward while obscuring the path to it.
when: When the reward sits within the player's line of sight.
why: A visible reward with a hidden route turns the path into a mystery that drives curiosity and exploration.

text: Place rewards such as resource replenishment, a sought-after artifact, or a dramatic escape in the falling action or dénouement, where players can slow down.
when: Placing rewards near the end of a level or quest arc
why: Falling action gives players a pause in which rewards can be appreciated

text: Rewards placed off the direct route draw players onto riskier or less direct paths, much as scenery draws detours; use this to structure exploration and pace play in generated dungeons.
when: when side areas should be explored or when placing rewards in generated dungeons
why: players are drawn toward perceived value even when it costs a detour

text: Placing rewards in narrow areas makes players linger where they are most vulnerable, so reward and danger rise together.
when: In a looting mode where players grab items while avoiding a pursuing horde.
why: Tight spaces are meant to waste player time while the player stays exposed to the threat.

text: Analyzing a game's reward pacing: 1) Identify its reward spaces. 2) Describe how it alternates them. 3) Describe how they pull players forward. 4) Describe how they are spaced.
when: studying how a game paces rewards
why: structured analysis reveals pacing patterns

text: Create reward clues with reusable modular assets, textures, lighting, and prefabricated symbols that recur throughout the game.
when: When a reward should be hinted at rather than shown directly.
why: Recognizable recurring symbols let players learn the signal and pursue it, leaving them a mystery to solve.

text: Give reward rooms their own lighting, sound, or architectural motif so they read as special spaces.
when: in generated or hand-built layouts where rewards must be recognized
why: distinct signals mark a room's function apart from normal play

text: A rhizome is a network in which every point connects directly to every other point, with no fixed entry or exit; mathematically, a complete graph.
In a room-based sensing model, room membership alone can decide what each character can hear.
Rooms map naturally to sense graph nodes, and doors, windows, ducts, and video links map to connections with per-modality rules.
when: designing a sense graph for a dungeon

text: A single route pulls an entire group to one spot, while a branching route spreads players across several destinations.
when: Routing a group of players through a space
why: Forced movement strips players of the freedom they value, so a subtle painted guide line can steer them instead.

text: Showing a world one room at a time lets limited hardware present a large space; later graphical adventures adopted this room model.
when: When hardware cannot draw a full large world at once.
why: Home play needed large worlds to justify the purchase, which single-screen display could not supply.

text: A shared map can be structured with landmarks, districts and nodes, plus architecture for sniping, guerrilla refuge and isolated building.
why: Distinct architecture lets players of different competitive styles find spaces that match how they prefer to play.

text: A sense graph built from ray casts around geometry misses glass windows, ducts, and closed-circuit TV links.
when: the graph is generated from geometry ray casts
why: Ray casts only sample solid level geometry, so they cannot represent effects like glass, ducts or cameras.

text: Upward climbs with fewer connection points and sections of isolated tiles increase falling risk and limit route choice.
when: Designing vertical sections or chains of swings to small anchor areas
why: Higher positions have fewer connection points, so a missed attachment means a fall.

text: Room-based levels place checkpoints naturally and reduce how much must load at once.
Small calm rooms placed between intense sections give players a recovery beat in pacing.
when: when pacing intense sections
why: The quiet space lets the player settle after one challenge and get ready for what comes next.

text: With no threats present, players explore at an unhurried pace, which lets them learn controls comfortably.
when: the player has control but no danger
why: Removing pressure lets the player focus on learning.

text: Stock protected safe rooms with ammunition and health so players can plan before the next stage; make them larger or add caches when the game rewards planning and cooperation.
why: Enemies can barely reach these spaces, so players can stay and plan their next moves.

text: Make settlements safe havens by placing strong non-player guards who prevent player combat inside them.
when: An open player-versus-player world needs safe zones
why: Reduces player fighting in populated areas

text: Virtual worlds lack many real-world scale cues such as lighting, textures, stereo vision, and the body, so players easily misjudge size and feel disoriented.
when: Building a virtual space
why: Missing real-world cues make scale hard to perceive

text: Players feel speed when small nearby objects, such as ground texture, plants and trees, rush past quickly.
when: fast travel through a space with small surface detail
why: Close, fast-passing detail gives strong motion cues

text: Swarms of enemies can make even a large space feel narrow.
when: enemies arrive in large numbers
why: crowding limits where the player can move

text: Moving from narrow, intimate space into open prospect space creates a sudden, dramatic reveal for players.
when: transition from confined to open space
why: Moving from confined to expansive scale shifts gameplay intensity and opens a spatial advantage.

text: Level design works at two scales: macro, which shows a whole level, and micro, which shows one individual gameplay instance.
Narrow space confines its occupant, leaving little more than the character's own size for movement.
Strong open vistas convey a sense of huge space and possibility, and crossing an interesting open space is pleasurable in itself.
when: Designing large open environments

text: Playfield dimensions define a game's challenge, so changing its width alone can make it a very different game.
Race tracks wide enough for several vehicles let racers compete for position.
A few objects with interesting relationships in a small space can be as impactful as a wide space full of hazards.
why: Keeping everything in view makes object interactions easy to read and maximizes the impact of each screen.

text: Frame a large open area with mountains and an apparently endless sea so the space feels vast, with higher and lower levels beyond it.
when: When the game is free-roaming with little constraint on movement.
why: An ocean that seems endless, combined with few movement limits, makes the area feel boundless.

text: Walls placed close together make wall-based movement easy to use.
when: When surfaces sit close together within reach of a wall jump.
why: Close spacing offers a low-risk setting where players can experiment with the movement at their own pace.

text: In player-versus-player play, narrow spaces form bottlenecks for ambushes and traps, and create tight passing moments in racing.
why: Scarce space becomes a prized resource that players fight to control.

text: Place a view at the top of a climb to reward the effort, pairing spatial achievement with a pause.
when: when a route involves a climb
why: the view makes the effort feel rewarded

text: Use vistas in games with near-constant action to create quiet contrast without stopping play.
when: in games with near-constant action
why: a brief pause relieves intensity without slowing pace

text: Reference sizes: player height about 96 units, average room about 1024 by 1024 by 256 units, door about 128 units high.
when: sizing levels and placing objects

text: Narrowness is measured against the player character's size; a passage fitting only two characters side by side is narrow.
Objects can be compared on five dimensions: number of objects, size of objects, nature of objects, layout of objects, and distance between objects.
when: When comparing how avoidance feel differs between games
why: Feel is tuned where input response meets how objects are spaced in the environment.

text: Wide spaces tempt designers to place every switch, hazard and movable wall at once, which crowds the scene.
when: When a level designer is inexperienced, especially new to level design

text: Using units with no real-world meaning makes scale problems hard to diagnose and fix.
when: Defining the unit system of a virtual world
why: Without real-world reference, nobody can tell what size is right

text: Textures that are too large or too small for their real-world counterparts, such as oversized bricks or undersized floor tiles, break the illusion of scale.
when: Applying textures to surfaces
why: Textures carry the scale cues players rely on

text: Scaling walls and furniture together up makes the avatar feel tiny, and normal-sized furniture in an enlarged room creates cavern-like or sparse spaces.
when: Scaling interiors for third-person play
why: Scale changes alter avatar perception and furniture usability

text: Tight or narrow spaces that ignore how avatars and objects move cause player frustration.
why: Comfortable traversal depends on spaces that fit avatar metrics; otherwise players get stuck on obstacles.

text: Without an established norm of scale, gameplay and visuals can mismatch or become unplayable.
when: Before building high-gameplay moments in any project

text: 1) Pick virtual units you know intimately, such as feet or meters. 2) Keep everything in proportion to them. 3) Relate units back to the real world when something seems out of scale.
when: Setting up measurements for a virtual world
why: Real-world units make out-of-scale elements easy to diagnose

text: Check four scale cues: first-person eye height near five to seven feet, people and doorways that fit human size, common man-made objects present, and textures matching real-world scale.
when: Diagnosing a world that looks out of scale despite correct proportions
why: Players assume eye height and doorways match their own body and everyday objects

text: Map each room on graph paper, with each grid square standing for a fixed unit, so the map is to scale.
when: documenting or analyzing a level's layout
why: A fixed unit per square makes room sizes comparable and checkable.

text: Set object size, spacing and nature relative to avatar speed and movement rather than in absolute terms, so the world stays in harmony with how the avatar moves.
when: Comparing or tuning avoidance difficulty; sizing and placing objects
why: The same gap is easy or hard depending on how fast the avatar moves.

text: Widen passages in levels to avoid steering failures in narrow spaces.
when: when designing levels for steered characters
why: Wider passages reduce doorway misses and wall-induced equilibria.

text: Let minimum traversable floor widths override planned narrow dark passages, since technical limits can change the world layout.
when: When implementation limits such as minimum floor widths conflict with the planned layout
why: Level designers implement most content and know the engine's technical limits.

text: For 2D games, map one grid unit to a power-of-two pixel size such as 16, 32 or 64, and proportion assets and spacing to those measurements.
when: when sizing 2D level assets
why: fixed pixel grids keep sprites and spacing consistent

text: Use narrow space for horror and stealth where the character is weaker than its opponents, or for skill-based conflict and tense bottlenecks.
why: Such spaces restrict movement and visibility, making the character feel weaker than enemies.

text: Scale can express insignificance by making the player small relative to the world, or power by making the character large relative to it.
when: Choosing how the player should feel about the world
why: Relative scale carries emotional meaning independent of the actual size of the world.

text: A scene is one screen's worth of designed level space the player sees at one moment, and is the basic unit of pacing.
when: When dividing a level into units for teaching
why: Screen-sized units match what players can process at once.

text: Scanning is the number of looks, such as camera pans and repositioning, a player needs to understand a space.
A scene is a single-screen or room-sized gameplay chunk that feels complete and self-contained, a trait many architectural patterns share.
Block out and playtest levels, and test scoring or level layout, with cheap physical prototypes before committing to full construction.
when: When scoring or level layout needs fast testing
why: Cheap physical prototypes allow fast play-testing and quick multidisciplinary fixes.
