text: Prototype a single room first to focus on enemy movement and character interaction, then add hallways and connected rooms in later iterations.
when: stealth or enclosed-space levels
why: A single room isolates movement and interaction questions before adding complexity.

text: Build levels in order when the game is simple or its progression is linear and upgrade-driven.
when: When the game is simple enough to skip planning extensive teaching levels
why: Each level can add complexity on top of what came before.

text: Spaces are single-scan, understood from one spot with one camera pan, or multi-scan, needing scans, movement around obstacles, and further scans.
1) Graybox a level using rhythmic architecture. 2) Have playtesters report whether it changes their pace and draws them along.
1) Set column widths to match row heights so cells are square. 2) Draw a bordered grid, such as 20 by 20. 3) Fill cells with black to form walls, mazes or dungeon layouts.
when: sketching grid-based levels by hand
why: Square cells let a spreadsheet work as graph paper for sketching layouts.

text: Use the simplest geometry that simulates the colliders of the final level when grayboxing.
when: Building graybox test levels
why: Simple shapes capture physical interaction without wasting effort on art.

text: In 3D, treat rooms, hallways and other architectural sections, along with transitions between them, as scenes.
when: In 3D games that lack the restricted cameras of 2D and isometric games
why: Scenes concept helps structure transitions, which are the connections between spaces.

text: Single-scan spaces give quick understanding for casual players; multi-scan spaces give hiding places and surprises for competitive players.
when: choosing how readable a space should be for a skill level
why: Casual players need quick reads of a space, while competitive play rewards hiding spots for surprise.

text: A skill gate is a section that blocks progress until the player successfully performs a specific in-game action.
when: When designing obstacles that require a mechanic to pass
why: Gating progress behind skill ensures players practice the mechanic

text: Skill gates range from simple, such as an enemy to jump over, to complex, such as using a newly acquired ability to escape the room where it was found.
Short cliffs that the player must jump over can serve as skill gates that require jumping to continue.
when: When gating progress through platforming skill
why: A jump requirement tests the mechanic directly

text: Progressions can be built by choosing each level according to which skills it forces the player to use.
A movement ability that exceeds existing level constraints forces every level to block its unintended side effects with crates, invisible walls and misplaced props.
when: adding a new capability late in development
why: each level must contain the new ability's consequences

text: Setting a clear rule early and then breaking it later creates delight, because players who learned the rule notice the exception and seek hidden routes.
when: After a rule has become part of players' understood logic, such as across a series
why: A broken rule reads as a surprise only once players already expect the rule.

text: Removing the early easy steps of a puzzle makes it hard from the first moment and removes its lasting appeal.
why: Gradually increasing difficulty is what gives a puzzle its lasting appeal.

text: Use environmental changes such as wall colour or texture to signal the player is moving deeper into a large dungeon.
when: Designing large dungeons with multiple depth regions
why: Visual change marks progress and prevents the sense of walking through identical levels.

text: Let progression unlock before every stage is cleared, so stuck players can advance and return to the remainder later.
when: When designing progression gates for a set of levels.
why: Requiring full completion can trap players who are stuck on a few stages.

text: Keep a district border closed until the player has learned all the skills of the previous district.
when: players must master one skill set before facing the next

text: Gated expansion structures are not spatially complex, but they produce achievement and drama as players test their limits.
when: When a game confines the player to a small area until upgrades let them cross or defeat blockers.
why: Overcoming enemies or obstacles that once stopped the player gives a sense of achievement and drama.

text: Separated-use planning divides a space into distinct districts for living, working, and gathering, each serving one function.
Sacred buildings in both traditions separate their interior sacred space sharply from the outside world.
Developers often place species apart in the level or use only a few species at a time to limit unpredictable interactions.
when: When several different creature types can react to one another in the same level.
why: Chain reactions among several species can oscillate and look artificial, and multi-species cycles are hard to debug.

text: Separate circulation and gathering spaces, as larger prospects, from private activities placed in enclosed refuges.
when: when planning area functions
why: Open movement suits open space, while rest suits enclosed space.

text: Plan relationships between spaces with a molecule graph before drawing the level.
why: Diagram proximity and edge styles are defined to carry meaning about views, movement and directness.

text: Public zones support open interaction and movement, while private zones support intimacy and focus; a space's placement along this spectrum shapes what players do in it.
when: Deciding how accessible or secluded each area of a level should be
why: Varying openness changes how players behave, including whether they socialize, hurry, or pause.

text: Teach movement and mechanics through the world, its atmosphere, or narrative events rather than explicit prompts or a separate tutorial, so players act immediately.
why: Weaving lessons into story or atmosphere avoids a lecture from the game, letting players engage the mechanics directly.

text: Teach players what building types do through training and demonstration, so they can later read function from appearance.
Staged skill progression has three stages: teach a basic form, advance that form, then combine it with other skills.
when: teaching a skill across levels
why: each stage builds on the last

text: Introducing a mechanism next to pits or enemies, rather than in a safe space, makes it hard for players to learn.
when: When a mechanism is first introduced in a level.
why: Introducing a concept, then applying it in harder forms, lets players learn it before danger is added.

text: Teaching abilities through obstacles: 1) Introduce each ability alone in an obstacle. 2) Repeat that situation to reinforce it. 3) Later require combining abilities, such as running and jumping into a long jump.
when: a game has several player abilities
why: isolated lessons build up to combined use

text: Design a teaching level for one reactive mechanism: 1) introduce it safely 2) add a little danger 3) twist it 4) end with a final high-danger test; use four or five scenes.
when: when grayboxing a tutorial level

text: 1) Place enemies far from traps so players see they cannot be defeated directly. 2) Place spawn points surrounded by traps so players watch enemies hit traps. 3) Let the player lead enemies into traps, with trap, enemies, and door visible in one view.
when: when teaching a mechanic that combines enemies, traps, and an unlock
why: Each step shows the mechanic in a progressively more active way.

text: 1) Split a complex system into stages. 2) Teach one stage per level. 3) Add a level where players perform the full process. 4) Then let players use the systems freely.
when: a system has many interacting parts that must be learned in order
why: Each stage is learned before players face the whole system.

text: Teach symbols by letting players use them through the avatar's abilities, then repeat them in later levels.
when: when introducing a new symbol or mechanic
why: Hands-on use with repetition makes the symbol's meaning stick.

text: Withholding part of a landscape from view invites players to explore further.
when: In top-down games with expansive worlds where parts of the map stay off-screen.

text: An uncertainty node is a decision point offering a choice between equal options whose contents are unknown.
Risk and randomness arise wherever players meet the unknown, not only in dice or generated numbers.
Raise stakes gradually so that the climax has everything hanging in the balance.
Use a winding, forced approach with staged reveals rather than a straight one to build anticipation.
when: When a player enters a space and must read its layout from what they can see.
why: Controlling what each view reveals steers the viewer's perspective, making successive reveals more satisfying.

text: Tying a game event to a real-world value, such as money or physical punishment, gives small in-game failures much more emotional weight.
when: When in-game outcomes can be tied to real wealth or physical sensation.
why: The stake is felt beyond the screen.

text: Designers of 2D games often underuse showing players what the character cannot see, a source of suspense.
when: top-down or side views
why: Players can be shown threats the character cannot see, so suspense comes from the gap in what each knows.

text: Suspense sags into boredom when nothing is at stake.
when: When a moment has no meaningful consequence.
why: Without stakes, the anticipation that drives suspense has nothing to act on.

text: Building areas players never see adds no freedom and wastes effort that could improve the places they do visit.
when: When a clearly marked fastest route guides players, so they rarely explore side areas.

text: Control how a scene is first revealed using thresholds or entrances that let players pause unseen and survey the space before engaging or entering.
when: When designing the entry to a new area, especially in 3D
why: The first view determines whether the space is readable or confusing

text: Give players things to look into instead of making everything visible from the start.
when: Designing the layout of a VR room
why: Hidden detail gives players reasons to look around

text: Use uncertainty nodes only once the player understands the space well enough to take educated risks.
when: Once the game has shaped players' understanding of its possibility space.
why: Familiarity with the space lets players judge which uncertain paths are worth the risk.

text: Naming unseen places enlarges the perceived world cheaply, but detailing them later when players ask multiplies the content needed.
when: When players might ask for detail about places they never reach in the game.

text: Initial environments were motionless: foliage stayed rigid, vegetation was still, and players couldn't interact with the ground.
By the modern era water was no longer a major technical constraint, so rivers and lakes became common and their transitions to terrain were handled more subtly.
A slight change in terrain, such as adding hills steeper than the tuning space allowed, can make a vehicle bottom out and lose all its momentum.
when: When terrain features are steeper than those the vehicle was tuned on.

text: Editing terrain, such as placing a forest patch, updates AI movement costs behind the scenes, so the designer never sees the AI data.
when: In tile-based games whose level tool calculates AI data behind the scenes.
why: The tile tool calculates movement costs automatically, so no separate pathfinding infrastructure is needed.

text: Tile flag combinations set grapple behaviour: connectable-only tiles can be attached and pass through in air; impassable-only tiles make the grapple ricochet without connecting; both-flagged tiles can be attached to, but swinging upward into them knocks the avatar off.
when: Tile carries one or both traversal flags
why: Each flag combination determines whether the grapple connects, whether the avatar passes through, and whether he bounces off.

text: When the avatar alters terrain, the dug space changes state, so the layout becomes a mechanic rather than backdrop.
when: When the avatar can dig or remove terrain as a movement action.

text: Vertical shadows converging on a vanishing point can make a height feel more dangerous, just as horizontal shadows set rhythm.
when: When the view looks down into a pit or drop.
why: Vertical elements pull the eye down toward the base, intensifying the feeling of depth.

text: Most published tactical methods assume tile-based representations, so their examples may need translating for non-grid levels.
when: When applying tactical analysis to indoor games whose levels are not laid out on a grid
why: Tactical analysis grew out of grid-based RTS games, so its published methods mostly use tiles.

text: Thick connectable platforms let the player move through them, which must be set intentionally in level design.
when: Designing thick connectable platforms
why: Unintended penetration changes traversal and can break intended routes.

text: Draw walls as lines on the grid, and treat them as blocking both movement and shots.
when: When building a physical hex-grid prototype of a first person shooter arena

text: Make platforms at least 2 units wide when players must balance on them with tilt controls, since narrower tiles feel unfairly hard.
when: Designing narrow platforms for tilt-controlled movement
why: Two units is the narrowest width players can balance on without frustration.

text: A level editor is a program for building custom levels, usually with drag-and-drop tools, so no programming is needed.
An impassable tile can never be attached to or penetrated, even by the swinging trick.
when: Tile is flagged impassable

text: Metrics are gameplay-based measurements in engine units, such as character size, jump distance, attack reach, and distance covered over time when running or walking.
Molecule graphs use dotted lines for viewable spaces, solid lines for travel, arrows for one-way links, and thick lines for direct paths.
Hardware limits and short arcade sessions kept much early action confined to a single screen.
An enlarged character sprite in narrow levels makes the space feel more cramped and isolated.
when: narrow levels with large sprites
why: the avatar fills more of the view

text: An architectural weenie is a landmark that draws players toward goals while the world still feels open.
Repeated architectural structure with shadow leads people through a space; repeated arches with shaded lighting in a large hall also create atmospheric ambiguity.
The same building shape can signal different functions in different cultures, so form cues are culturally learned.
Contrast can create landmarks in open worlds and in small spaces such as halls, courtyards, and rooms.
when: when designing landmarks at any scale

text: Hold players in a fixed spot with interesting things to inspect, which gradually leads them to look around the space.
when: Early VR levels where players hesitate to turn their heads
why: Looking around builds presence, because the brain constructs a spatial picture of the room when players scan it.

text: Focus richness on the places players will look at closely.
when: you cannot detail everything
why: Viewers extrapolate the rest of a scene from one fully rendered element, so a few well-placed details can suffice.

text: Familiar archetypal visuals and sounds, like flames and magma for dragons or Gothic-style buildings for undead, signal a theme quickly.
Place telling details so players can choose to learn more; they should not be forced, but also not so subtle that players miss them.
Align architectural elements with specific phenomena, such as solstice light, so the structure directs occupant attention to a chosen moment or view.
when: Designing a space where a focal moment or view should be noticed
why: Deliberate alignment guides where occupants look and when they notice an event.

text: Lifting a dominant structure above surrounding settlements expresses power and ferocity.
Pure design concepts become more useful when contrasted and combined with other concepts rather than used alone.
Landscape features and level geometry should direct players toward places of interest.
Exhaust earlier options so that only one action remains, making the next step obvious.
when: When the player has finished everything in earlier areas before reaching a dead-end
why: Players who know earlier options are used up can infer that the only remaining action is the next step.

text: Clerestory windows set high above viewers bring light from above, making the interior feel ethereal.
A visually dominant marker can hide other scene elements, stopping players from considering other actions.
why: A bright dominant marker crowds out other scene elements, so the ideas those elements would suggest never form.

text: Removing guidance abruptly can leave players at an obstacle with no clue how to proceed.
when: When a guide character who shows the way is killed or removed mid-sequence

text: 1) Make relevant elements stand out. 2) Remove irrelevant load while teaching something important. 3) Do not rely on vision alone for key information; add another channel.
when: Designing UI cues and level signals for important lessons.
why: Focused attention on relevant inputs improves learning.

text: Plan environment colors around cultural and genre associations; color meanings differ across cultures (white signals weddings in some cultures, mourning in others), so avoid assuming one culture's meanings apply everywhere.
when: When the game will reach audiences from diverse cultures with different color meanings

text: Use one consistent visual language, such as shared color or shape, for interactive objects so players can recognize what they can use.
when: Designing interactive objects in a level
why: Consistent signals let players identify usable objects without explanation.

text: Attach a light to the player to create a torch that follows them as they move.
when: When the level's lighting fails partway through, such as a corridor light going out

text: Give each environmental symbol a unique appearance, distinct even from similar environment objects, so players can tell it apart from surrounding scenery.
Repeat each environmental symbol across the level so players learn what it means through repeated exposure.
Let one element serve several functions, including contradictory ones, so it helps in one context and hurts in another, creating tension.
when: when designing interactive controls or terrain
why: Ambiguity makes the same object meaningful in different situations.

text: Place light sources deliberately where they create the dramatic effects you want.
why: Real-time lighting is graphically expensive, so light placement has to be chosen with care, while baked lighting can carry the effect.

text: Placing an opposite quality, such as a bright element among dark ones or a complementary hue against the main color, draws attention to that element and guides players along a route.
when: when a route or important element must stand out in a scene
why: The unusual element breaks the dominant pattern and attracts the eye.

text: Players rarely consciously notice environmental steering such as music, layout or visual cues, even while following them, and believe they chose freely, so steering works best subtle.
when: Ambient or visual cues guide players without explicit instructions
why: Music affects mood, desire and action below conscious awareness.

text: Use tall landmarks, called high weenies, as central route points that hold rewards and offer camera-friendly views of the world from above.
when: Structuring open levels around a focal point
why: Landmarks orient players and create a sense of vastness.

text: Use highly visible cues such as bright paint, large arrows, or visual indicators and landmarks to help players find their way, freeing attention for core challenges.
when: when navigation is not the core challenge, or in strongly handmade levels
why: Clear directions reduce attention spent on pathfinding.

text: Making the best route obvious helps, but forcing players too strongly guarantees arrival at the cost of freedom and a poor experience; a subtle marker guides while keeping freedom.
when: Deciding how strongly to route players
why: Subtle guidance keeps players feeling in control and immersed, whereas strong forcing removes the sense that the choices are their own.

text: Players often do not notice lost freedom in a scene when the scripted action matches what they already wanted and the game has trained them to expect freedom.
when: When a scene removes control but gives the player the outcome they want
why: The scripted outcome satisfies the expectation that drove the player's choices

text: In third-person games, players sense their body floating behind the avatar, so normal-sized interiors feel tight and players blame the room rather than the camera.
when: Playing third-person games indoors
why: Split body awareness distorts perceived space

text: Players sometimes backtrack to power up seldom-used weapons before boss fights, preparing deliberately for known challenges.
when: when a boss or challenge is known to require a specific tool
why: Players invest in preparation when rewards and threats are clear

text: In a symmetric level, knowing one half reveals the other, whereas asymmetric levels keep players guessing.
when: a level with mirrored halves
why: a mirrored layout lets one half predict the other

text: Players lost in a maze mark places they have already visited by dropping items there.
when: Navigating large spaces with no visual landmarks
why: Players need a way to tell visited areas apart

text: Designers cannot create experiences directly; they guide people indirectly through the structure of a space.
when: Shaping how players feel and move through a space
why: Experience emerges from how people use the structure

text: Players remember game spaces relatively, through doors and connections, rather than as accurate absolute layouts, so odd layouts rarely register as strange.
when: Designing space that players must understand
why: The mind stores spaces relatively, not as precise maps

text: From a high vantage above an enemy area, players scout patrol patterns like a plan and can memorize them without being in danger.
when: when a safe elevated view overlooks enemies
why: Distance from enemies removes immediate threat, so players study rather than react.

text: When every match uses the same map, players learn it like a neighborhood and navigate by its landmarks.
when: Maps reused across many matches
why: Repeated shared use builds familiarity.

text: Landmarks are recognizable guideposts, natural features such as volcanoes or built structures such as towers and castles, that help players orient themselves relative to well-known features.
Readability is how easily a player, on entering or approaching a space, can evaluate its elements and understand it at first view.
when: When judging whether a scene can be read on first view
why: Players must evaluate elements quickly on entering a space

text: Desk jumping is a player action the character would never take, because the player's motivations sit outside the fiction.
An Easter egg is a hidden joke or reward placed in a game for players to discover.
Before auto-maps, many players drew their own paper maps resembling graph-paper and architectural plans; such maps capture memories as well as layouts.
A sight-only long-distance connection can model a video link, such as a control room watching another room.
Landmarks help players find where they are and where they are going, and make a space interesting to look at and memorable.
when: Designing any game space
why: Landmarks are what players remember and talk about

text: Objects at the ends of path shifts can act as symbols of specific mechanics.
when: when placing markers along a shifted path

text: Landmarks, boundaries and districts help players plan routes through a space.
Mark map nodes and junctions, which channel player traffic and host large battles, with brighter lighting or distinctive scenery to show players where to go.
why: Light draws the eye toward intended routes.

text: A shortcut is valuable when it removes a penalty-driven obligation, but is worthless for voluntary play with no penalty for skipping.
why: Obligation comes from avoiding a penalty, while voluntary play is pursued for pleasure with no penalty for skipping it.

text: Mark the fastest route clearly and add a few side paths and shortcuts, since players mostly stick to the main route while side paths add freedom.
when: Designing routes through a level
why: Players only travel where they believe it advances their goal, so a clearly marked route holds them, while side streets give a sense of freedom.

text: A single, visually dominant floor marker can guide most players to a target without them consciously noticing it.
when: You need players to reach a specific spot without forcing them
why: A dominant visual element draws attention so strongly that players follow it without consciously registering it, and other details are missed.

text: Place a single striking landmark where players first enter a space so they head toward it.
when: Designing the entry view of an area
why: Arriving visitors could wander the entry area with no sense of direction.

text: A visible, attention-catching object placed at a point of interest can signal the direction players should move toward their next goal.
when: Laying out a space where players must find their way.
why: Players follow salient cues in their visual field.

text: Place a major landmark at a slight angle to the main approach so players experience it three-dimensionally as they move around it, rather than facing it head-on.
when: Positioning a focal structure that players will walk around
why: A straight-on frontal view feels static, while an angled view reveals depth and form during movement.

text: Connect major landmarks with straight, axial routes so visitors can navigate by moving from one visible destination to the next.
when: Designing wayfinding across a large area with several landmarks
why: Visible endpoints along a clear axis help people orient and travel without a map.

text: Light unvisited destinations so they draw players toward them and invite exploration.
why: Bright light stands out against the surrounding colors, so it is easy to spot from high ground.

text: Use contrast and reveals to mark important encounters or goals.
why: Contrasting spatial conditions set the room apart from its surroundings, signaling that it matters.

text: A landmark visible from most areas lets players see how close they are to their goal.
Show distinctive landmarks from an early vantage point so players see destinations they can later pursue.
when: When players reach a junction where they cannot tell which direction is best.
why: Visible goals give players direction in open spaces.

text: Transparent textures or openings let players see a goal at the center of a maze, keeping them aware of the destination.
when: when a maze ends at a goal
why: The visible goal keeps players on task while they deal with enemies and collect treasure.

text: Maze pickups visible from a top-down view motivate players to rush toward them, to escape enemies or gain points.
when: when a maze holds pickups and enemies
why: Knowing where rewards sit lets players plan a rush to them when enemies press or points are needed.

text: Make out-of-reach ledges and doors very visible, and revisit them once a new ability unlocks access.
when: when the player may later gain a new ability
why: prominent targets prompt return visits after progression

text: Augment space with information so that the environment itself communicates where rewards and routes are.
when: When progress depends on collecting rewards hidden in the level.
why: Showing a repeated reward marker teaches players where to search for more.

text: Place a reward within the player's sight line but out of reach, and hide the route to it so the player must search.
when: when players should choose optional routes rather than follow the main path
why: a visible goal with an unknown path creates a mystery the player wants to solve

text: In 3D spaces, vistas from cliffs and high points reveal landmarks and objectives, showing players what to do and where to go.
why: An elevated view lets players survey the world and find out what is possible within it.

text: Use ground patterns such as striped shadows to lead the eye toward doorways and other destinations.
why: Linear marks on the floor carry the eye along their direction, ending at the opening.

text: Terrain between main hubs can hold landmarks such as caves, tombs, and towers that lead to optional side quests.
when: In open-world games where paths run between main quest hubs.
why: Letting players customize their travels, with tasks easy to find from main paths, allows more meaningful emergence.

text: Place special quest items in a designer-set order inside a procedural system to add a storytelling layer to otherwise random placement.
when: In procedurally generated games where event order is otherwise random.
why: Otherwise random generation has no narrative throughline; designer order adds a story component a purely procedural system lacks.

text: In an unfamiliar place the mind must look around to build an internal 3D model of the surroundings.
when: The player enters a new environment
why: Familiar places already have stored details, so the brain fills them in without the player looking.

text: A connection can pass one modality in one direction only, such as sight through one-way glass, with no reverse connection for sound or smell.
when: a barrier passes some senses in one direction
why: Each modality is attenuated separately, so a barrier can block some senses while letting others through.

text: Steep inclines that slip the character back act as invisible limits, redirecting players without visible walls.
when: Restricting access to an area
why: Consistent slide physics makes the limit feel like a consequence rather than an imposed barrier

text: Remains of victims placed on roads and in yards signal a threat in the world and guide players toward the enemies responsible.
when: when placing enemies in a level with a story threat
why: Enemies are usually found near the remains, so world detail doubles as level design

text: Light sources guide players; a dark area with no light can leave players lost.
why: Light sources direct players through areas, and a space with none gives them no guidance.

text: Circuitous room sequences leading to a central hall disorient visitors and heighten the sense of absolute power.
Boundaries and zones marked on a playing field govern possession, so codified sports encode their rules in the space itself.
Instant travel lets players cover large distances quickly, which reduces the time spent crossing a world.
when: In large adventure games that offer an instant transportation function

text: Levels can work as memory palaces, embedding information such as plot, enemy locations, or puzzle components in rooms that players recall.
when: when a level must convey information players need later
why: Players remember information tied to places they moved through.

text: Losing a cohesive, gravity-bound world structure leaves players little chance to map and become familiar with the space.
when: Designing open or non-cohesive level structures
why: Players build spatial familiarity from consistent structure they can learn.

text: Layout and physical setup can create expectations the design never fulfills, which weakens the experience.
Similar-looking props blur which objects matter to play, so players cannot tell which objects they can interact with.
when: In puzzles, after early encounters have taught players what markings mean through gameplay and rewards
why: Players learn what each marking signifies and then search for those markings as cues for their next action.

text: Without an established understanding of the space, unmarked branches read as confusing rather than rewarding.
1) Place a toggleable ambient sound at the objective. 2) Switch it on with a trigger along the approach path. 3) Switch it off and hide the pickup when the player arrives.
when: Steering players toward a pickup or objective
why: Audio placed at the target and switched on by the approach path acts as an attractor that leads players along the route.

text: Use a color-coded key on a map to mark doors, item pickups and other significant objects.
when: annotating a level map

text: 1) Name who the player is helping in the game. 2) Strengthen the player's connection to those characters. 3) Show in the story how reaching goals helps them. 4) Let the helped characters show appreciation.
when: Goals feel abstract and need tying to someone in need
why: People naturally want to help, so tying goals to a character who needs help taps into that impulse.

text: Make navigational symbols, guideposts and landmarks stand out from surrounding environment art through contrasting color so players notice and can read them.
when: when designing navigational symbols, guideposts and landmarks in a level
why: Players cannot use symbols that blend into the surrounding scenery.

text: Make locked obstacles visible early, such as walls needing a tool not yet acquired, so players recognize the tool when they get it.
why: Previewing the lock gives players a clear goal and a sense of progression that sparks interest in the new tool.

text: Limit level navigability rather than trying to improve connection analysis, since teams that succeeded did so this way.
when: Automatic region connection is unreliable.
why: Sight lines do not guarantee traversal, and geometric analysis cannot yet reliably predict complex move sequences.

text: Use level layout, such as a forked road, to steer players toward a story location or offer them a meaningful choice.
when: When story is delivered through environmental narrative rather than cutscenes or interactive dialogue
why: Directional layout leads players to locations where plot points, hints, or foreshadowing await.

text: In open fields, guide players with dirt paths, signposts and rivers so they do not get lost.
when: when paths cross open terrain
why: Open terrain offers no natural channels of travel

text: At junctions, hint at each branch with a distinct clue, so players can make informed choices rather than guessing.
when: when a level splits into multiple paths
why: Clues let players judge which branch is worth taking and avoid needless backtracking.

text: Extended ambient dialogue leaves players as passive observers, so they tend to skip it.
when: during action games with long non-interactive dialogue
why: Players cannot respond to non-interactive speech, so they disengage from it.

text: Ambient dialogue is any talk during gameplay from the player character, AI companions, voiceovers, radio headsets or passersby, triggered by in-game events.
Ambient lines come in two kinds: generic, short situational lines that often hint direction, and customized one-time lines, usually for important missions, giving specific navigation clues.
Ambient dialogue is triggered by entering an area, taking damage, or attempting an action, such as opening a locked chest.
Ambient lines can be ignored, though they often carry useful instructions such as directions.
In first-person shooters and real-time strategy genres, ambient chatter is often the main or sole dialogue form and can carry a compelling narrative.
Barks often need many variant lines to express one simple idea, so they add far more writing than their size suggests.
Companions can follow the player and share information at key points, then thank and reward the player ambiently after objectives, keeping story inside the game world.
why: Story delivered during normal play means the player never stops to take in narrative.

text: Because the player keeps moving during ambient lines, they can absorb world detail without being pulled out of play.
when: When voiced lines play while the player performs normal gameplay tasks
why: Gameplay continues during the dialogue

text: Action-game players have short attention spans of roughly fifteen to twenty seconds, so keep each dialogue exchange brief.
when: in action games
why: Action players are short on attention, and long non-interactive dialogue gets skipped regardless of its quality.

text: Ambient dialogue takes three forms: overheard NPC conversations, local street chatter that teaches about a place, and conversations involving the player's own character with companions or party members.
why: Too many cutscenes badly hurt pacing, so ambient dialogue is a better option.

text: Ambient dialogue must never force the player to stop or pause play, must be supported by the gameplay situation, and its player-character lines offer no choice.
when: When dialogue is prompted by in-game events such as entering an area, taking damage, or attempting an action
why: Voiceover can be heard while players focus on combat, so dialogue can layer over play without pausing it.

text: Keep all other dialogue optional and skippable so it does not slow players who want to act.
when: Dialogue is not required for plot or motivation.
why: Players who want to act should not be slowed.

text: Never place critical narrative information in generic banter, because it is interruptible and players may never hear it.
when: When writing generic banter, which usually occurs in-game and can be interrupted
why: Interrupted banter can be missed entirely.

text: Customized banter may carry mission or narrative information, but coordinate its placement with level design so it doesn't collide with or get interrupted by other encounters.
when: Writing customized banter tied to a level.
why: Otherwise other encounters can overlap or cut the lines off before the mission information lands.

text: Add ambient sequences, such as NPCs walking, chatting or buying goods, or a cat chasing a mouse, to make the world feel alive.
why: Routine activity makes the world more believable, and believability is what makes players care about it.

text: Avoid two-way conversation with the player character by design, using world and emergent tools that do not require it.
when: the story would otherwise need rich dialogue with humanlike characters
why: current technology cannot support it convincingly

text: Shouted ambient lines in fully voiced action games can carry much story, but avoid exposition in intense combat: players rarely listen and audio engines often drop voice under battle noise.
when: Story via shouted lines: fully voiced action games. Exposition: busy or intense combat scenes.
why: Voice lines can be heard without pausing gameplay; players rarely listen while issuing orders, and audio engines often do not prioritize voice over battle noise.

text: Ambient dialogue keeps action uninterrupted but gives players no say; interactive dialogue lets players shape the conversation.
when: Talking that plays during gameplay and is triggered by events such as entering an area or taking damage
why: Gameplay keeps running rather than pausing for the lines, and the player has no say over what the player-character says.

text: Tell completed events through remains or traces, not live scripted scenes, when players should discover them in any order; their authored story stays fixed.
when: the events are already over when the player arrives, and the story is told through remains or traces of a completed event
why: Completed events have no live state for player actions to alter

text: Record game events and present them as a laid-out history, so players can reconstruct their own story without recalling everything.
when: Games that aim to emphasize emergent stories arising from player actions
why: Players cannot remember every event, and a visible record makes the story legible.

text: Scripted live events need tricks or restrictions to force a correct path, whereas fixed past-event clues allow free exploration without forcing an order.
when: Story told through world clues in an explorable space where the player can discover them in any order
why: Scripted events would need forcing tricks or restrictions to ensure the right order, while clues read in any order still convey the story.

text: A sound source large enough that its origin is hard to pinpoint can create unease similar to a rear sound.
when: When listening over a 5.1 or higher surround sound setup
why: Hearing evolved to flag hidden or distant danger, so a source whose location is hard to pinpoint raises perceived threat.

text: An analogue is a fictional element that alludes to a real counterpart found in research, without copying it exactly.
Listeners use timing and filtering differences between the ears to focus on one voice in a crowd, the cocktail party effect.
Sound can evoke empathy, hatred, and love more readily than visuals alone, and higher-quality audio can make visuals seem better.
when: deciding how much investment audio needs
why: Audio strongly shapes emotional response and perceived quality.

text: Analogues feel believable because they echo something real, so players accept their plausibility even without noticing why.
when: designing fictional worldbuilding elements
why: The real counterpart supplies the sense of truth.

text: Prefer consistent, believable game sound over strict realism, because perceptual reality is unachievable in games and players judge sound against everyday listening.
when: Designing sound for immersion, including fantasy settings.
why: Players expect sound to behave as it does in the physical world, and consistency sustains immersion.

text: Prioritize what players believe and enjoy over physical accuracy when shaping a story world.
when: Designing settings, devices or events in a story world
why: Players judge plausibility by credibility and fun, not by strict physics

text: Use analogues for governments, settings, inhabitants, characters, and time periods when the world must feel believable but need not match a real place or event exactly.
when: worldbuilding in realistic or fantastic games
why: Analogues borrow details from things that really exist, so players can sense they are plausible, even without noticing why.

text: In a branching narrative, each choice leads to predetermined changes that alter individual plot and gameplay sections, while the branches rejoin at key points.
Each added choice multiplies outcomes exponentially, so branches cannot be fully authored; modeling every decision naively leaves each player missing most content.
when: designing branching narrative

text: Filming shared scenes with different dialogue but the same information does not relieve the tedium of replay.
In choice-driven stories, leave room for player choice in middles and endings while making players feel in control of outcomes.
when: In story-driven games where player choices lead to distinct branching middles and endings

text: Games without major story decisions still benefit from narrative design, which can reinforce a gameplay feature or convey brief world detail with little or no text.
when: social, mobile and casual games
why: In a crowded market, extra entertainment value helps a game differentiate itself from competitors.

text: Give a game element several narrative links across the world, not only its gameplay uses, so it deepens coherence.
why: The more links an element forms, the more elegant the world feels.

text: Random events built as dilemmas with branching outcomes, dialog and custom art add variety to a travel or journey mode.
In a branching dialogue, the player's politeness in chosen responses determines the outcome, such as an NPC letting the player pass or attacking.
when: Dialogue choices gate progress

text: Branches that converge at pinch points let choices alter sections of the story while the overall plot still moves toward a common climax.
when: In branching narratives where player choices change individual plot sections
why: Pinch points keep each divergent path on the overall story's course toward a shared climax.

text: When player choices physically alter the world, the changes and their harm to affected NPCs become visible in locations.
when: When player decision-making changes the game world

text: Player dialogue choices set conditions that the game later recognizes, changing character reactions or tailored content.
when: In games where players actively select what their character says in dialogue

text: Post-level reports can vary with method, accuracy, kills, and surviving witnesses, so the reported story reflects how the player played.
when: In games that summarize a level's outcome, such as a post-level report
why: Systems that interpret and link events build a coherent account from chaotic play, as a sportscaster does.

text: Twenty opportunities of three choices each, from start to finish, yield over five billion distinct story outcomes.
when: estimating branching scope
why: Counts this large exceed what any writer could author, so storytellers end up fusing outcomes together.

text: Large branching dialogue causes narrative (coherence), asset (file count) and organization (tracking lines) problems, so visually scripting every branch becomes unmanageable.
when: When branching dialogue grows to many lines and sound files across characters and responses

text: Letting players reverse every serious bad outcome removes the sense of destiny and the sorrow of a doomed path.
when: When the story aims for tragedy where a doomed path must feel inevitable
why: Interactive protagonists can undo any serious bad event, so inevitability cannot be sustained.

text: Starting a branching design without understanding its costs can exhaust the budget.
when: When choosing a branching or open narrative structure
why: Branching content requires far more writing and costlier testing of every variant than a linear narrative.

text: If rejoin points are not planned carefully, branches feel disconnected from each other.
why: Pinch points are what keep each branch tied to the overall story path.

text: Repeating the same type of meaningful choice again and again can feel railroaded and dull.
why: A dull, unchanging structure undermines players' engagement with the story, pushing them toward other games.

text: Treating predefined choices as systems-driven decisions confuses their purpose and leads to designing them the wrong way.
why: Systems cannot model a person's thinking or a full story world, so affecting those requires predefined options that players read as designer intent.

text: 1) Telegraph the big choice during build-up so players anticipate it. 2) Let players understand likely consequences before they choose. 3) Show ramifications within about thirty minutes and again at the end of the game.
when: Designing a large, consequential choice
why: Players engage more with choices whose stakes they understand and see paid off.

text: Create the audience's desire to decide, then know when to fulfill it and when to hold it back.
when: when designing story pacing
why: Listeners of any story keep making decisions, so the urge to act already exists even without interactivity.

text: Plan branching carefully, since poor planning produces broken paths.
when: When a story is built with branching paths.
why: Branching paths grow complex and expensive, so every route must be planned carefully to avoid breaking.

text: Make every offered dialogue choice matter to the story, with distinct options and outcomes, so dialogue works as a game system rather than flavor.
when: When the game lets players pick what their character says in conversations.
why: Dialogue picks set conditions the game later reads, so each option needs distinct outcomes.

text: Branching works fully only when nearly all content is generated emergently; with predefined events, limit branches.
when: When predefined events make up a significant share of the story.
why: Possible timelines grow explosively, so a single playthrough reaches only a fraction of the content.

text: Converging branches keeps scope manageable but can make choices feel pointless, so plan convergence deliberately rather than applying it as a late fix.
when: scoping or designing branch convergence
why: Converged choices lead to the same place

text: Branching gives story impact but costs at least twice the linear writing, and testing every variant takes more effort than producing content; use it only when the story justifies that.
when: When considering a branching structure for a story.
why: Branches need at least double the writing of a linear story, plus testing effort for each variant.

text: Branching is easy to build but has limited scope, so restricted choices can feel simplistic and some branches yield uninteresting outcomes.
why: Each choice only routes to predetermined possibilities, so the range of outcomes stays fixed.

text: A player-character represents the player in the world; players project their decisions into it and can become it, experiencing its challenges directly, unlike a film protagonist.
when: Designing characters that players control or judge
why: Interactivity lets players act as the character, not only feel for them.

text: Players need only a small share of a world's detail to feel it is alive, while the team needs a much deeper foundation of knowledge.
when: building a game world
why: Players perceive a world through a few visible details, not its full depth.

text: People often assume a distant group holds special insight, granting its experts a reputation for gifts others lack.
when: Cultures with legendary views of a neighboring group
why: Legendary beliefs about innate ability raise the status of the group's specialists.

text: Players often protect a player-character when that character's past is revealed, and this suggests a subverted stereotype has worked.
when: when a protagonist has a criminal or stigmatized past
why: Players invest in a character they feel responsible for.

text: Players bond emotionally when they empathize with the hurdles and events the lead character faces.
when: Character design

text: Players are more willing to help an NPC who is already trying hard, which makes the quest-giver more sympathetic.
when: When an NPC is visibly engaged in an action before asking for help.
why: Visible effort reads as genuine need.

text: Mobile players often need instructions yet have little game experience, which explains why a helpful NPC speaking directly to the player is a common convention.
when: Mobile and social games with new players.
why: Inexperienced players need guidance that a direct-address helper provides.

text: A character who speaks their own intentions while acting can teach players what to do without interrupting play.
when: the opening sequence of a game
why: Spoken intent paired with visible action explains the step.

text: Interactive dialogue is branching, player-driven conversation that pauses gameplay and offers a list, wheel or other set of responses; it often drives story and progression.
why: Its development and play-time cost makes it a major investment that shapes game structure.

text: Round characters have well-defined, realistic traits or change significantly over the story, while flat characters have few traits, little change, and often serve as stereotypes or foils.
Meaningful conflict keeps players from reaching goals too easily and creates tension about the outcome.
A character profile gives the team the personality, motivations, history, affiliations, relationships, and appearance needed to bring a character to life.
Postures are short animations in which NPCs, creatures or the environment set a scene, and they can be reused across levels.
Player-character alignment means the player and the character pursue the same goal, even when their motivations come from different sources.
Some games let story events permanently change the main character rather than leaving the protagonist unchanged.
Characters in the same group can view one another very differently, because motives such as insecurity, envy, or loyalty shape each character's feelings.
when: Writing relationships within a cast

text: Human faces are highly expressive, and the eyes carry much of that expression, so character faces deserve attention even when animation is simple.
why: A large share of the brain handles facial expression, and humans have visible eye whites.

text: Each medium shapes its characters: novels reveal inner thoughts, films show speech and action, and games center on physical conflict.
why: Each medium's form determines how a character's struggle is shown to the audience.

text: Game characters tend to be more fantastical and less deep than novel or film characters, because game plots and character depth shrink from novels to games.
why: Games center on physical conflict, and the player supplies the thinking.

text: Low-status behaviors include fidgeting, looking away, touching one's face, and tension; high-status behaviors include relaxation, control, strong eye contact, and a still head while speaking.
Status is relative: a character can be high status with one character and low status with another.
A cartoony, surreal world with a physical logic can coexist with more realistic 3D materials when the character stays an iconic, exaggerated figure.
when: Establishing art direction for a stylized 3D game

text: Writing characters for games differs from other media because the player inhabits the protagonist, and NPCs must support that experience.
Game characters are built with techniques shared by all media, such as archetypes, flaws, diversity, and believable villains.
Game character design covers choosing a player-character type, keeping players invested, working with the team, creating nuanced characters, and subverting tropes.
Characters of color are often given racialized roles based on stereotypes, such as serving a white protagonist without agency.
Secondary traits such as love languages or Type A and Type B, and methods like the Frankenstein Method, can enrich a character beyond the basic workflow.
Customizable characters are built by players during character creation, so the developer knows little about the protagonist and the world and NPCs must give players material to define themselves.
Player characters in games without customization have predominantly been heterosexual white males, while NPCs show more diversity.
Postures can reveal how an NPC perceives the world around them.
Buttons, joysticks, and motion sensors cannot express thoughts and feelings to a machine, and machines cannot yet simulate a human mind to respond in kind.
Characters can still appear as insane or quasi-human characters, inhuman AIs, humans talking to each other, or recordings of earlier conversations.
when: the player cannot converse with a character

text: Appearance cues such as facial hair or jaw shape can signal character traits like villainy or bravery, but the mapping depends on the culture.
why: Cultural archetypes are learned associations, not universal ones.

text: Use a fixed protagonist when adapting an existing character whose history player decisions cannot change; most games based on existing properties do so.
when: Adapting an existing character
why: Detailed histories already exist in popular culture.

text: Imagining yourself in another's position helps you judge which moves that individual could make when facing a puzzle.
when: Designing puzzles or situations where players must assess a character's options
why: Taking another's perspective reveals which actions are available to them

text: Let players personalize characters and settings so they care about outcomes and similar playthroughs feel different.
when: When the game lets players customize their characters and surroundings.
why: Personal investment makes outcomes matter

text: If the protagonist cannot change, let a sidekick or villain change instead.
when: The protagonist must remain fixed
why: Some games cannot change the lead, yet sidekicks and villains can still develop, and fixed types make storytelling dull.

text: A cartoon character drawn with a blocky, iconic style sets expectations of weight and presence, and players may expect cartoon physics.
when: Designing a stylised character whose abilities differ from the player's expectations
why: Stylised art implies physical properties that players then apply to the character's movement.

text: Use predesigned characters when a specific story must be told, and customizable avatars when investment in the player's own identity matters.
why: Players invest heavily in avatars they create, which can make them as empathetic as scripted heroes.

text: Give a stereotyped archetype a detailed culture and memorable characters so it becomes distinctive rather than generic.
why: Culture and characters turn a cliché into an iconic figure.

text: Treat mistakes in character writing as lessons and seek feedback, rather than fearing doing it wrong.
when: When writing characters from backgrounds different from one's own.
why: Fear of error stalls writers, while feedback turns errors into improvement.

text: Letting players alter only appearance is a safe customization level, and letting them choose among backgrounds that later affect the game is better still.
when: When the story depends only weakly on the protagonist's background or behavior.
why: Stronger story dependence on a character's background requires more fixed design, leaving players less freedom.

text: Mentoring newer characters can test whether a guarded character can share what they know and stop keeping others at a distance.
when: When the newer characters are still learning a skill the guarded character already has.
why: Mentoring forces the guarded character to open up and depend on others, overcoming fear of exposure.

text: Build characters from experiences, culture and talents, not just identity labels; orientation, gender and race are only some of the factors shaping identity.
why: Past experiences shape how characters view the world, what they want, and how they act.

text: Pair an epic plot with a personal, human motive so players have an emotional anchor.
when: When planning an epic plot.
why: Players connect more with personal motives than with saving the world.

text: An NPC who shares personal details alongside the quest feels more human than one focused only on the task.
One-liners are quick to write and record, so they can be added late to fill dead time or clarify sections that testers found confusing.
when: Late in production, to fill dead screen time or fix problems.
why: Such lines take little time to write and little effort to record.

text: Use interparty dialogue during a natural pause in gameplay, such as while a character picks a lock, and end the conversation when the pause ends.
when: A calm pause in play
why: Players ignore lines that continue after the pause ends

text: Give characters memorable labels or traits, such as a role or a title, so players have material to build stories about them.
why: labels give players' imagination something to construct stories from

text: Design character appearance to signal occupation: grungy work clothes and a simple hairstyle suggest a tinkerer or researcher rather than a salesperson.
why: players read role from clothing

text: A friendly character's request for help can serve as a quest hook, turning a conversation into a concrete goal the player pursues.
Following one character through a fictional world tends to produce ideas for stories set in that world.
when: Searching for fiction ideas.

text: Explore a character through the medium you think in: performers can improvise a skit, and audio-minded people can build a soundscape.
when: Developing a character or world without a purely written approach.
why: Working in one isolated element, such as color alone, shows how a visual and emotional progression unfolds.

text: Persistent characters and settings let returning audiences recognize them, and growing familiarity deepens empathy and projection into the fantasy world, making their events more interesting.
when: Episodic entertainment where characters and settings persist from one experience to the next
why: Empathy grows as characters become familiar.

text: An objective well integrated into the game's premise or story can give the game strong dramatic qualities.
An obstacle that opposes the player's building or progress can signal a rival force's intent, such as its expansion.
When players choose among protagonists with different motives, each choice sets a different starting location and personal reason for pursuing the same goal.
when: Designing selectable protagonists sharing one goal
why: Different starting points and motives create distinct experiences of the same event.

text: A personality-based profile lets team members infer body language, movement, and clothing from the character's outlook.
why: Concept artists take the narrative's character information and turn it into visual signifiers.

text: Pairing merits and flaws within a character creates internal conflict, which makes each character feel unique.
why: Everyone struggles with weaknesses while succeeding at strengths, and that tension is what makes each person unique.

text: When a protagonist knows something the player does not, the character feels less like the player's own, creating a disconnect.
when: When the protagonist must know key world information from the start of the game

text: NPCs can pass on information through ambient dialogue, point players toward places, or behave strangely so players go investigate.
when: When plot must be delivered without cutscenes, animatics, or interactive dialogue
why: Odd NPC behavior prompts players to find out why, which leads them to locations and plot points.

text: As players progress, NPC relationships should evolve and dialogue should reflect that change.
when: Games where the player can alter the world.
why: NPCs naturally react to what players do to their home.

text: Packing objectives, story, instructions, hints and rewards into one dialogue box makes speech unnatural and turns NPCs into signposts.
when: Social and mobile games with tight text space.
why: People do not normally state the exact task and reward aloud.

text: Consistent recurring characters, such as shopkeepers, help community members look after one another and make introductions.
why: Recurring public figures give residents a familiar feeling that lets them protect each other and facilitates introductions.

text: The interpersonal circumplex plots characters on two relative axes, friendliness and dominance, around a chosen reference character placed in the middle.
when: When mapping relationships among a cast
why: Both axes are relative, so every chart needs a reference character.

text: Characters can be read psychologically as a mirror for audience fears and desires, symbolically as an idea, or representatively as a group.

Player-characters come in four types: Cipher, Fixed Character, Customizable Character, and Fixed Background with Customizable Character, placed along a spectrum of how much the player defines the character.
why: A game's protagonist must be inhabited by the player, since player-characters represent the player within the world.

text: A character profile combines demeanor, appearance, a motto, a bio, and a list of emotional states, tying these together into one readable character.
Define a character's view of the world and self, motivations and desires, how they pursue them, bearing, speech, interests, and dress.
why: Players may never learn these details, but considering the experiences that shaped a character helps designers build it.

text: Life factors that shape a character include spiritual beliefs, gender identity, social status, philosophical and political leanings, family relationships, work experience, childhood, and education.
why: The factors help design complex inner conflicts for characters.

text: Empathy can be manipulated, because models can make people feel emotion without a real subject.
when: Using characters or visuals to evoke feeling
why: The brain responds to models as though they were real, so feelings can be engineered

text: Defaulting to traditional role assignments, such as making the princess the hostage, wastes creative options in the cast.
when: When casting characters by listing the functions each role must fill

text: Games often keep characters as fixed types, such as a villain who is always a villain, which makes the storytelling dull.
Games rarely explore their characters' relationships in depth, though deep character-web exploration is how many successful TV dramas build their appeal.
why: Writing down each character's view of every other character exposes how and why they feel about one another.

text: Characters with dull, dead eyes feel lifeless even when the rest of the character is well made.
Inconclusive violence research does not settle concerns about harmful representation, which is a separate question from aggression.
when: When a game's content perpetuates harmful stereotypes about underrepresented groups.
why: Using stereotypes for entertainment without any moral reflection is ethically questionable, regardless of what aggression studies show.

text: Mixing traits and abilities in the first iteration makes the contrast between governing and conflicting elements confusing.
when: When choosing between traits and abilities as the vehicle for a character's conflict in a first pass.
why: Blending both kinds early washes out the contrast, leaving the conflict muddled.

text: A female protagonist whose most notable trait is sex appeal overshadows her actual skills, which can be corrected by redesigning her to emphasize competence.
Players may not identify with a role they did not choose, so the writer must earn that identification through the character's choices.
when: When the player character is fixed, with personality and backstory set by the developers.
why: Players cannot fill in gaps in a fixed character's personality or history themselves, so the writer must define them fully.

text: Heavy eye dialect makes lines a chore to read and can turn a character into a parody or make them seem uneducated.
why: Precise phonetic spelling is hard to parse, slowing reading for players.

text: Options that all trigger the same NPC reaction, or player lines removable without changing the NPC's story, make the player character passive.
when: When writing NPC dialogue trees that offer players response options.
why: If an NPC's story still works with the player's lines removed, the player's choices have no real effect on the exchange.

text: When every NPC is friendly and helpful, they become interchangeable and dull, effectively one character.
when: When all NPCs in a social or mobile game share one friendly, helpful personality.
why: A single trait gives no basis for distinct personalities.

text: Presuming to know what the player's character values produces scenes that contradict earlier choices and break immersion.
when: writing scenes after branching player choices
why: Earlier choices may have established motives the scene ignores.

text: Forcing characters into illogical choices is a mistake, because players spot it quickly.
when: When a plot beat needs characters to act against their motivations just to move the story along.
why: Players quickly notice when a character acts against their nature

text: When most characters are nondescript, players have little to build stories around, and the emergent narrative stays thin.
1) Ask what the character wants. 2) Ask what the character needs. 3) Ask what the audience or player hopes for. 4) Ask what the audience or player fears.
when: Drafting any character who must carry dramatic weight
why: These questions link the character's motives to the audience's emotional investment.

text: 1) Define the character's story function. 2) Choose traits or abilities as the vehicle, picking one type at first. 3) Define exactly one adjective. 4) Pick an MBTI type and/or four-temperaments blend and be able to explain its theory. 5) Select a governing trait or ability that drives actions. 6) Pick a conflicting trait or ability nearly opposite the governing one.
when: When a narrative designer needs to build internal conflict quickly, for any character including minor sidekicks.
why: A fast workflow adds inner conflict when there is no time for full backstories.

text: List characters; write each via template and sample bio, in order: identity (name, gender, age, height, build, ethnicity, complexion, hair, eye color, inspiration, appearance); personality (traits, conflicts, breaking point, introversion/extroversion, dream, fear, humor, sadness, dark secret); society (religion, government attitudes, law, norms, subcultures, education, income, job, love life, family, stranger behavior, food, drink, clothing); story (bio, involvement, development, growth, relationships).
when: When creating a character profile for a game.
why: A fixed field order gives writers, artists, and animators a complete, shared profile.

text: 1) Check how much the story relies on a strong protagonist, a specific background or culture, or other characters expecting certain behavior. 2) Define the protagonist only as far as that dependence requires. 3) Leave other traits to the player.
when: when designing a customizable protagonist
why: Over-defining removes player freedom, while under-defining breaks story dependencies.

text: 1) Let a refusing option lead the NPC to plead. 2) Link the plea back to the same explanation a player who asks for more information receives.
when: Designing refusal branches in a middle hub.
why: Keeps divergent branches connected so the explanation is reused without duplication.

text: Populate the world with NPCs from diverse backgrounds, each with concrete personality, desires, motivations, likes and dislikes, merits and flaws, and a clear relationship with the player.
when: Designing NPCs, even when no player avatar exists
why: Depth makes NPCs distinct and believable.

text: Consider whether characters are predesigned or player-created, whether they have backstories and motivations, and whether they allow customization and growth.
Use direct representation when the game recreates a real place or event players may know and accuracy is a selling point.
when: choosing a real-world setting

text: Design player characters and NPCs carefully, since direct player interaction with the protagonist deepens immersion for every protagonist type.
why: Players view the story through the protagonist, which lets them feel present in the world and its choices.

text: Use life factors to design inner conflicts and to identify what a character values, since those values shape their goals.
Test a character's limits by asking what they will fight for, what they will refuse to fight for, and whether their convictions could make them risk their life for an antagonist.
NPCs must fill the roles the genre and story require while staying consistent and supporting character-centric arcs.
When opportunity allows, give NPCs their own lives, agency and interests rather than making them tools for the protagonist's progress.
why: NPCs used only as tools for the protagonist's progress can leave players disengaged.

text: Keep combat shouts to crucial information, and save longer banter for quiet moments such as walks or cooldowns.
when: When a line plays during active combat versus during cooldowns or walking.
why: Interruptions in combat are seen as fun-killing, and attention for each exchange is short.

text: Use eye dialect sparingly: a couple of non-standard words per line, standard spelling for the rest, and consistent spelling of repeated words for each character.
why: A few altered words already signal an accent, so heavier spelling adds reading effort and risks caricature.

text: Do not have every NPC deliver all the information each time; ask what the character would naturally say.
when: When dialogue boxes have limited text length.

text: Use dialogue when a critical plot juncture cannot be explained any other way; in character-driven games, a crucial character reveal also qualifies.
when: A plot point or character reveal has no other delivery channel.
why: Dialogue exists to move players smoothly and naturally through the game, so it is warranted only when no other channel can carry the information.

text: Begin each conversation as late as possible, with characters cutting straight to the point, since the player's arrival already starts the scene.
why: The player's arrival already opens the exchange, so the scene only gains momentum if the characters skip the greetings themselves.

text: Have characters react little or not at all to a recurring hazard, which signals to the audience that the hazard is routine.
when: writing scenes with repeated danger
why: Muted reactions communicate familiarity without extra exposition.

text: Use sexual signals only when the game and its audience can accept them; for serious or broadly targeted games they are often not worth it.
when: Games that are serious or aimed at a broad audience rather than a niche one.
why: Gratuitous sexual content undermines a serious story's atmosphere and believability and alienates players who don't want it.

text: Let a character perform actions just ahead of the player so they watch the action before doing it themselves.
when: the game has voice or animation budget
why: Watching an action first makes it easier to repeat.

text: Fixed name, background and personality ease writing and story control, but players lose freedom to define the protagonist and must be persuaded to identify.
why: Writers control every decision about the character, but players cannot fill any blanks in the personality or backstory themselves.

text: Direct representations of real cities, events, or figures demand factual accuracy and more research time than analogues, while analogues allow creative license.
when: choosing between real and fictional counterparts
why: Real references are checked against what players know.

text: Simple reflective NPCs suit stories that need little from them; full characters cost more work and should be built when time and scope allow.
why: NPCs with no agency of their own can leave players disengaged, so they suit only roles that need little beyond reflecting the protagonist.

text: Status is a constant, mostly subconscious negotiation over who is in charge of an interaction, and it is a behavior a character performs rather than a fixed property.
when: Whenever two or more characters interact

text: Status can be signaled through slow motion and spatial position, where high-status characters occupy the most important place in a room and low-status characters move where they are unlikely to be noticed.

Villain design faces recurring tensions: making a villain threatening enough to motivate defeat while players keep winning against the villain's forces, and characterizing a villain the player cannot meet until a final showdown.
why: Players expect constant victories and may win too early against a villain without a final confrontation.

text: The stronger the contrast between a governing trait and its conflicting trait, the more interesting the character's inner conflict.
why: Opposed traits pull a character in two directions, and that tension is what makes a villain interesting.

text: Supporting characters should make players feel important without making the world implausible, and villains must threaten enough to motivate defeat while allowing frequent player victories.
when: When the player controls the protagonist that other characters beat or help.
why: A rival's win over the controlled hero registers as a loss to the player, so the character's effect is felt personally.

text: Comedy arises from unexpected status reversals, such as followers mocking a leader or enemies being mocked by those beneath them.
when: When writing comedic character interactions
why: Reversing expected status produces surprise.

text: Making players dislike a villain steers their choices against him.
when: Designing player choices against antagonists
why: Emotional dislike motivates opposition

text: A protagonist whose goal never wavers and has no internal conflict, paired with a threat that never escalates, misses an opportunity to integrate story with gameplay.
why: stakes stay flat so the drama adds little to the mechanics

text: Supporting characters who lack their own motives serve the story rather than making choices that affect the plot.
why: Without motives, they cannot drive events and exist only to support the protagonist.

text: Turning a spurned gay or lesbian character into a vengeful villain repeats a harmful stereotype, whether the story uses it for sympathy or shock.
Assigning stock mechanics to a character can contradict that character's actual abilities and story.
when: Designing character abilities or party roles
why: Story and mechanics can exist separately, so mechanics attached without narrative ties can be swapped without changing the story.

text: 1) List the character's traits. 2) Check that they appear in its words, actions, and appearance. 3) Check that single lines or actions can carry several traits at once.
when: When writing or designing a character
why: Traits left as labels in a design document are not felt by players.

text: 1) When a character receives news, avoid a direct reaction. 2) Do something unexpected that draws attention back to the character. 3) Return to the character's established persona.
when: When writing a dramatic reaction
why: Unexpected reactions regain audience attention.

text: Simple characters doing mainly physical actions are the easy path in games, but deeper characters are possible on a simple gameplay structure.
when: When deciding how much character depth a game needs
why: Players want richer characters, and depth can be built alongside simple mechanics.

text: Presence requires the player to have a sense of who they are within the virtual space.

Personality shorthand models include MBTI, with sixteen types each having a dominant and an inferior function, and the four temperaments, where each person blends two of sanguine, choleric, melancholic, or phlegmatic.
Personal details must still fit the world's logic, or they will feel out of place.
why: Details drawn from real things are easy for players to accept as plausible.

text: Personality typing models such as MBTI are useful shorthand, but their accuracy for real people is contested, so they should not be treated as established fact.
Never base a character's personality solely on race, ethnicity, sexual orientation, or gender; these inform identity but are not the only factors.
why: Characterizations based solely on a stereotype or archetype lack nuance.

text: Phrase a design as a character that is female rather than a female character, and likewise for ethnicity.
why: Framing the trait as one attribute of a whole person avoids making it the defining feature.

text: Optional interactions that differ between characters, such as how each handles a task, reveal their personalities without dialogue.
when: when two or more characters are played or observed
why: Players read character from how each acts in small moments.
