text: A cipher is a blank-slate player character with a name and appearance but little defined personality or agency, letting players feel they are playing themselves.
A character can be an agent through which a dramatic story is told, letting players empathize, or a vessel the player creates and directs.
Major characters strongly affect a story's outcome, while minor characters have little impact on it.
Characterization comes from what a character says, what they do, how they look, and what others say about them.
Character motivations live inside the fiction, while player motivations come from outside it, such as entertainment, social status, and curiosity about mechanics.
Create a fresh character by changing one defining trait of a familiar archetype.
when: Designing characters from a well-known type
why: The familiar base keeps the character readable while the change adds novelty

text: Giving one character two roles can save development cost and create an ironic twist, such as a mentor who turns out to be the final boss.
when: The cast is smaller than the list of roles
why: It avoids developing an extra character while still adding an ironic twist.

text: Reduce a long character profile to a short set of distilled traits that hold across defining situations, and accept that these traits may contradict each other.
when: When designing or writing a character
why: Real people hold contradictory traits, and a small trait set stays usable where a full profile becomes too long to apply.

text: When a protagonist already has a defined backstory, adding an internal motivation that counterpoints the external goal makes the climax more engaging than the external story alone.
when: protagonist has some defined backstory
why: A climax can resolve internal wants as well as external goals, which an external-only motivation cannot provide.

text: Give characters a life outside their quest, such as personal history or bonds, so they feel like people rather than quest dispensers.
Character design uses traits, abilities, merits and flaws: traits are identifying habits, abilities are capacities to act, merits are benefits, and flaws are weaknesses.
A character's growth arc can be built around a fear the story forces them to confront, resolved by learning to open up to and depend on others.
Believable characters need insight into their inner world, what matters to them, and why they respond to conflict the way they do.
A character list separates player-characters, major NPCs, and minor NPCs.
Artificial characters rarely show status behaviors, because creators do not notice they perform these behaviors themselves.
why: Status signaling is a subconscious social language that people use without noticing it.

text: 1) List the roles the game needs. 2) List characters already imagined and existing characters. 3) Match characters to roles, looking past obvious assignments. 4) Check whether one character can fill several roles. 5) Create or add characters for unfilled roles.
when: When planning a game's cast or checking that it covers the game's needs
why: Separating a character's function from its look and personality shows missing jobs and reveals efficient role combinations.

text: 1) List every character. 2) For each character, write how it feels about every other character and the motive behind each view. 3) Check that each feeling is specific and no connection is missing or too similar; make similar ones more distinct.
when: When mapping or deepening relationships across a cast
why: A web reveals interactions that positional or summary views miss; deep character webs drive engagement in ensemble stories, which games rarely explore well.

text: 1) List characters down one side of a grid. 2) List story sections across the top. 3) Mark every point where each character undergoes some change, small or large, temporary or permanent.
when: Reviewing how a cast changes across a story
why: Following each character over time, not only the plot thread, reveals changes a plot-only view misses

text: 1) Ask whether the avatar is an ideal form players will resonate with. 2) Ask whether its iconic qualities let players project themselves into it.
when: When designing the player avatar
why: The avatar is the player's gateway into the game world.

text: 1) Define how each character changes through the game. 2) Communicate those changes clearly to the player. 3) Check that changes are sufficient, surprising, and believable.
when: When planning character arcs
why: People attend to what might change them, so transformation draws players in.

text: 1) Ask what the player character wants. 2) Ask whether the game's mechanics can communicate that want. 3) Ask whether other characters have motivations of their own.
Before writing for a customizable protagonist, answer two questions: what knowledge does the character start with, and why is the character so naive?
when: In RPGs where the protagonist is a customizable character the player shapes.
why: These answers keep the protagonist believable from the start.

text: Build players' care for characters before relying on them to prompt action; players help those they empathize with, and steering fails without that connection.
when: When characters are used to nudge what players choose and how they feel about it.
why: Empathy makes players want to help.

text: Provide alternative paths: several characters in the world should be able to fill the role that starts an arc.
when: When an arc can be started by different characters.
why: Open-world players tend to value gameplay and freedom more than a tightly told story.

text: Check that each character acts according to their motivations, and that no one is forced into nonsensical acts just to move the plot.
when: during revision
why: Players quickly notice when characters act against their motives just to push the plot.

text: Concrete, easy-to-remember goals motivate players better, while abstract goals reach a smaller audience and need a matching budget.
Adding characterization competes with clear gameplay explanation; the balance depends on how much immersion matters compared with how clearly goals are explained.
when: Deciding dialogue depth in social or mobile games.
why: Small mobile and social screens leave little room for text, which limits how deep dialogue can go.

text: Conflict arises when the protagonist's goal is opposed by the environment, an antagonist, or both.
Dramatic elements are a toolset that gives gameplay context and overlays the formal system to make it meaningful and emotionally engaging.
An external want is the goal a character pursues in the plot, while an internal want is a deeper personal need; strong stories give the protagonist both, resolved at the climax.
In many games, the story is only backstory whose progression does not depend on player actions.
Mapping conflict categories to both the premise and the formal system deepens players' relationships with both.
Link a character's present constraint, such as a need to stay hidden, to a specific past event so the constraint reads as caused rather than arbitrary.
when: writing a character background

text: A trusted ally's betrayal can expose a character's own blind spots, forcing them to ask why they missed the warning signs.
when: When a keen observer who reads people well is blindsided by a close friend.
why: Confidence in reading others makes the betrayal expose the character's own weaknesses.

text: Conflicting goals produce unpredictable outcomes, which creates surprise.
when: When another character has a goal that conflicts with the protagonist's.

text: Arguments are interesting because status seesaws back and forth as each side tries to raise its own status or lower the other's.
when: When writing conflict between characters
why: Dramatic change is inherently interesting, and status keeps shifting during arguments.

text: In games, drama comes from the player's own struggle to overcome obstacles (agency), whereas films and novels rely on empathy with characters who struggle.
In games the player controls the protagonist, so the story often gives only an external motivation, such as defeating an enemy.
why: Players direct actions, so internal motivation is harder to deliver.

text: The more intense the conflict, the deeper it reveals a character's true values.
when: When designing character conflict.
why: Pressure forces choices that expose inner nature.

text: A story's core structure has three ingredients: a character with a goal, obstacles that block the goal, and other characters whose goals conflict with it.
why: Obstacles force problem solving, conflicting goals produce surprises, and larger obstacles allow bigger dramatic change.

text: Dramatic conflict takes six forms: character versus character, nature, machine, self, society, and fate.
Game conflict takes four forms: player against player, player against the system, player against multiple players, and team against team.
Basic dramatic elements such as challenge and play appear in all games, while premise, character, and story are more complex and explain abstract systems.
why: Story-level techniques supply context that turns abstract rules into an experience players find meaningful.

text: If story and characters dominate early work, they can obscure the gameplay.
when: During early design

text: Treating every backstory detail as essential to the main story makes the experience slow and unfocused.
why: Only information that directly shapes what players see and do belongs in the main path; other backstory is irrelevant to them.

text: Deliver backstory through environmental narrative and on-demand storytelling rather than adding it to quest text.
when: When quest dialogue would be read by players in groups who have little time for long text.
why: Keeps quest texts short without losing world depth.

text: An adaptation that mirrors a game's quest path and mechanics teaches viewers which strategies to use when they play.
Talk-to and breadcrumb quests can develop deeper storylines and connect characters.
when: When a fast action RPG has no cutscenes and very limited quest text space.
why: Text-only quests can carry deeper story without slowing the fast action pace of the game.

text: Build each critical path quest around one or two big reveals.
why: Without a central reveal, critical-path information feels disconnected from the individual quests and players may skip it.

text: Lines can be combined to save space: dialogue carries the story while the instructions line carries the search location and reward.
when: When screen or text space is tight.
why: Objective, reward and hint text contain no character speech, so they can be combined into fewer lines.

text: An item interaction, such as photographing a marked location, can reveal the next destination and gate progression.
why: Environmental cues can direct players to places and reveal plot points without relying on cutscenes.

text: Many RPGs combine a fixed chain of mandatory quests, the critical path (critpath), with many optional side quests; designers should plan both layers.
when: Designing branching RPG quest structure
why: The fixed chain advances the plot while optional content gives players freedom

text: Contradictions or inconsistencies between gateways break a world's solidity and can reduce the value of every product.
why: Each product is a gateway into one shared world, so inconsistencies between them undermine that world's sense of solidity.

text: 1) Summarize the critical path as a few large events. 2) Check that the summary is simple enough for several writers to build on. 3) Plan information flow, set concrete goals, and keep the main plot visible in side content.
when: several writers share one large critical path
why: Several writers on a large RPG risk the main storyline losing consistency without shared planning.

text: 1) Player meets an NPC with a problem and is asked for help or chooses to get involved. 2) Player visits places, finds clues or talks to characters to learn why the problem exists. 3) Player either solves the problem or decides whether it should be solved.
when: As a starting skeleton for critpath and side quests.
why: The three-step problem, investigation, decision shape gives quests a reusable skeleton, while the overall game plan sets how long each one runs.

text: Make in-game challenges match the protagonist's obstacles; unrelated challenges weaken the experience, while matched ones fuse story and game structure.
when: When the game aims for a tightly integrated story.
why: Alignment joins narrative and mechanics

text: A critpath backbone with optional side content gives wide player freedom, suited to long games; it is costlier to write than a single linear chain.
when: Long games where designers want wide freedom
why: Optional content multiplies writing and integration work

text: In VR, characters who act as if the player is not there make the player feel absent and prompt questions about their role; screen audiences accept an unseen camera.
when: Characters in a VR scene behave as if the player is not there.
why: In VR the viewer is physically placed in the scene, so being ignored stands out.

text: A cutscene is non-interactive, narrative-scripted dialogue outside gameplay that offers no choice, usually sparse, built in-engine and paired with animated sequences filmed outside the gameplay camera.
Animatics are non-interactive still-image sequences edited together with text, narration and soundtrack; they replace cinematics when budget or memory is limited, including handheld and mobile.
when: Budget or storage is limited.
why: Cinematics consume much memory.

text: In principle a cutscene is a payoff that shows the player's achievements rendered cinematically after a stretch of play.
Sequences are brief scenes, at times containing replayable lines, that can repeat without growing wearisome.
Interactive cutscenes are scripted and in-engine like cutscenes, but they let the player choose dialogue options.
Full motion video is a heavily scripted scene where the player has a limited set of inputs, such as pressing buttons at the right time.
Cinematics are entirely pre-rendered films played inside the game, with no player interaction, high production values, and usually the highest budget.
Brief cinematics opening and closing each level, stage, zone or world carry players forward, reveal progress, and can tease rewards for finishing.
Linear stories rarely use interactive dialogue, because there is no way to respect player dialogue choices; they rely on cutscenes and environmental narrative instead.
when: Linear game story delivery
why: Dialogue choices cannot be honored in a fixed storyline

text: Visual novels and adventure games use animatics as a genre convention for their text-heavy sections.
In some games cutscenes are the only way to deliver story beats, whether exciting, intimate or expository.
Win and lose cutscenes can show characters celebrating a win or encourage the player to try again after a loss.
Lower-budget, social and mobile games can use voiced cutscenes, scores, altered storylines and story twists much like traditional games.
Scripted scenes come in seven types: postures, sequences, animatics, cutscenes, interactive cutscenes, full motion video and cinematics.
Cinematic sequences are among the most economical means of adding animated visual storytelling to a game.
Camera position determines which environmental details players see, so framing, focus and layered views can deliver narrative alongside gameplay.
Arrange vehicles and barriers so they look driven through or blocked, implying a panicked escape.
when: suggesting a past flight or chase through the environment
why: Props arranged as traces of past events let players piece together what happened from the environment alone.

text: Cutscenes need extra thought in multiplayer worlds, since they can block the interaction that much of the play depends on.
when: Online multiplayer games where play centers on player interaction.
why: Groups split over whether to watch a scene can frustrate players, who may log off or skip story content.

text: Place cutscenes after about 30 to 40 minutes of gameplay so working memory gets a break.
when: When a game uses cutscenes, rather than at the start of a session.
why: sustained attention fatigues

text: Cutscenes placed after intense action act as breathing space, while cutscenes placed before action cost more to justify.
Use cutscenes for high-impact story moments that benefit from animation and camera control, and keep player choice in interactive dialogue.
when: Planning story moments in a game with interactive dialogue.
why: Cutscenes lack player choice, so choice belongs elsewhere.

text: Place cinematics at the start to set up the story and at the end as the payoff, and consider a midpoint cinematic as a reward if the budget allows.
when: When the project budget allows for cinematics.
why: The opening introduces essential exposition to draw players in, while the ending rewards them with a big moment.

text: Cutscene guidance can be scaled in length, assets and production quality to suit any genre, team or budget.
why: Length, assets and production quality can be adjusted independently, so the advice does not tie to one genre or budget.

text: Keep a cutscene under about thirty seconds where possible; longer scenes need a reward strong enough to hold attention.
when: When a cutscene must run past the usual length limit.
why: Short cutscenes stay impactful, and a longer one must repay the viewer with a strong reward.

text: A cutscene ought to deliver wonder and delight, not interrupt the action.
Shoot cutscenes from the player-character's point of view so the player sees what the character sees, and avoid pulling the player out of that frame.
why: A camera outside the character's frame pulls players away from the perspective they are controlling.

text: Cutscene rules are often broken, but first weigh the payoff against the effect on players; a wider view can be justified when it clearly serves the payoff.
Avoid sequences that play in only one specific situation or that few players will see, because their cost is hard to justify.
when: When weighing whether a sequence justifies its production expense.
why: Few players benefit from a sequence seen only rarely.

text: The more a sequence benefits players and story while staying reusable, the more it is worth building.
when: When a sequence can be used often across the game.
why: Reusing material cuts production time and cost, which weighs on whether building a sequence pays off.

text: Cutscene sounds spatialised from the camera change orientation abruptly on each camera cut, so they appear to jump sides of the screen, producing extreme, disconcerting panning.
when: A sequence switches between cameras with sounds spatialised from the camera, such as in-game cutscene dialogue with camera cuts.
why: Spatialisation is computed relative to the current camera, so each cut changes the apparent direction.

text: Long opening cutscenes are expensive to produce and often damage engageability by breaking game flow early.
when: Opening sequences
why: Long opening footage withholds player control before play begins, hurting engagement early.

text: Because attention goes to the art rather than movement, animatics encourage stylized and detailed art, and can suit a game's style better than motion.
when: On handheld or mobile devices with tight storage, or when a team cannot afford elaborate cinematics.

text: Sequences play without interrupting gameplay, so they suit MMOs, where players can enjoy them whenever they have time.
when: designing story content for MMOs
why: Non-interrupting scenes fit players who log in for varied lengths of time.

text: Leaving cut-scene sound to the automatic 3D sound engine does not produce polished results.
when: Mixing cut-scenes.
why: Automatic spatialisation ignores the deliberate mixing a linear film needs.

text: Starting a cutscene or textbox in the middle of an encounter is one of the worst mistakes, because players cannot absorb it.
when: While an encounter is underway, for example a boss battle in fast action titles.
why: Players are focused on beating the encounter and will not take in text or voice.

text: Wordy lines during combat are treated as obstacles that spoil the fun.
when: during combat
why: Talk that breaks into fights reads as an obstacle, and non-interactive speech gets skipped by action players.

text: Expecting an artist to reproduce your mental image without discussion leads to a mismatch between the intended scene and the result.
when: When a script is passed to storyboard artists or animators for a cinematic.
why: Nobody else sees the scene as the writer imagines it, so the writer must communicate it.

text: Letting a cutscene decide an outcome that the player's earlier choices should have decided undermines agency.
when: In RPGs or games with many dialogue choices, where agency is central.
why: Taking control away from the player turns a moment meant as a reward into a frustration.

text: Long or annoying cutscenes can make players put the game down.
Importing film methods wholesale blinds designers to the central challenges of game story, which are choice and players who depart from the author's plan.
when: When borrowing film techniques for a game's story.
why: Film offers no concept of interactivity, choice, or players who diverge from the author's plan.

text: 1) Mute game sounds with sound modes. 2) Recreate the sounds with sound tracks in the cutscene sequencer. 3) Apply environment reverb to dialogue files in the audio editor.
when: In-game cutscene dialogue
why: Sound tracks are not emitted by objects, so attenuation and reverb do not apply

text: 1) Enable a cinematic mode that blocks player input. 2) Fire an event just before the dialogue. 3) Apply a ducking sound mode. 4) When the sequence completes, reset the mix to default.
when: When cutscene dialogue plays over busy ambient sound in a quiet scene.
why: Lowering competing background sounds keeps players' focus on the spoken lines rather than the surroundings.

text: 1) Have the cinematics team check each cutscene script against budget and tools. 2) Ask animators whether they want exact physical action or only dialogue. 3) If the team is overloaded, add a description of the action.
when: Writing cutscene scripts
why: Animators differ in how much direction they want

text: 1) Add setting notes to the script. 2) Review the scene with writers, animators and leads. 3) Storyboard it with panels showing camera angles, characters, items and expressions, each with a line or two of description. 4) Iterate until everyone is satisfied. 5) Keep talking to animators during production.
why: The writer is the only one who sees the scene as imagined, and animators know their skill limits

text: 1) Write a scene heading whenever location changes, using INT for indoor and EXT for outdoor. 2) Write character names in caps at first appearance and in dialogue headings. 3) Center dialogue under the speaker's name. 4) Put short parentheticals above dialogue.
when: Writing cutscene scripts in screenplay style
why: Consistent format makes scripts readable to the team

text: 1) Let the player encounter recurring clues without explanation. 2) Withhold their purpose. 3) Reveal the meaning of all gathered pieces together at a late point.
when: designing story or puzzle reveals
why: Players gather many clues before understanding them, so the late reveal lands with more force.

text: Identify the main gameplay activity at a story moment; the more gameplay or required interaction it holds, the more you should avoid a cutscene.
when: When planning a cutscene in any genre, including multiplayer games needing group interaction.
why: Pausing for footage interrupts the activity players are already absorbed in, stalling their engagement.

text: Avoid cutscenes that end an activity players want to continue, such as during an intense boss battle.
when: During an intense battle that players are fully engaged in.
why: Halting play that players still want to continue cuts off engagement they have chosen.

text: Avoid cutscenes at the start of a session, when working memory is fresh and can be used to interact with the game.
when: session start
why: fresh working memory is better spent on play

text: Use cutscenes sparingly because of their production cost.
In unvoiced games, place story in the breaks between gameplay tasks rather than during active play.
when: Unvoiced games
why: Players can read text only when not engaged in action

text: Before committing to a cutscene, consider ambient dialogue, voiced conversation the player hears while still playing, and ask first whether the cutscene is necessary.
when: Planning how to deliver story
why: Cutscenes can badly disrupt pacing

text: Test the first instinct to use a cutscene for vital information against other storytelling tools, since a cutscene is not always the best choice.
why: Varied delivery makes the decision more valid and rewarding

text: Know each cutscene's budget before writing, since budget shapes both the dialogue and the animation plan, and confirm with the cinematic department how many cutscenes are planned.
why: The budget sets both how the scene's writing is shaped and what animation work is planned for it.

text: Show in a cutscene only what gameplay cannot deliver with equal impact, and show the rest through the gameplay camera or player actions.
why: Moments that would lose impact under the gameplay camera or player control are better suited to a cutscene.

text: Don't lean on a cinematic as a blatant stopgap for engine constraints; favour spectacle assembled from mechanics the title already supports.
An opening level cutscene should hint at the level's theme, a simple story setup, and likely obstacles, NPCs, abilities and weapons.
when: starting a themed level or world
why: Players get a preview of what the level will ask of them.

text: An ending level cutscene can show the victorious character moving on, defeated enemies, grateful NPCs, or overcome obstacles that remind players of their achievements.
why: Such scenes show players their progress and link one section to the following section.

text: Keep win and lose cutscenes very short, using images or animations players will not tire of, especially where winning or losing happens often.
when: outcomes that repeat frequently
why: Repeated viewing turns long scenes into annoyances.

text: Even short cutscenes help by giving players useful information about the game and adding visual and auditory interest.
when: In social and mobile games with short play sessions, where long cutscenes don't fit.
why: Brief scenes fit within short sessions that cannot spare long cutscenes, yet still convey information.

text: Place short cutscenes at the opening and closing of levels, stages, zones and worlds, at wins and losses, and at the very start and finish of the game.
when: games with short sessions
why: These moments fit brief scenes without consuming a whole session.

text: An opening cutscene in a light-story game should quickly introduce the player character, NPCs, world and gameplay.
when: In games that are light on story
why: Players come for short sessions rather than deep story, so the scene must set up play and story quickly.

text: An ending cutscene should reward finishing by recalling rescued or defeated NPCs, levels beaten, or other feats.
Opening-style scenes that share useful tidbits suit a game's start and the beginning and closing points of each major division such as levels, stages, zones or worlds.
why: Such a scene tells players who they control, what they must do, how, and what opposes them.

text: Keep cutscene dialogue short and reserve cutscenes for visuals players cannot get elsewhere, such as large battles or dramatic arrivals.
when: RPGs and higher-budget games
why: Ambient and interactive dialogue can carry the story instead, so cutscenes should hold visuals unavailable elsewhere.

text: Have each cutscene follow directly from the action the player just took, such as an arrival scene after choosing to be taken to a leader.
why: Scenes the player did not trigger themselves can feel unwelcome and get rejected.

text: Label non-interactive cutscenes clearly in the script and start them only after the preceding gameplay action has settled.
Use a camera pan from an interior view to an exterior shot to reveal the wider state of the world after a focused scene.
Choose the lightest scene type that delivers the story, because cinematics cost the most.
when: planning scripted scenes
why: Cost rises sharply from postures and sequences up to cinematics.

text: An opening cutscene under a minute can establish the player character, their goal, their abilities, the opposition and the first area.
when: designing a short game introduction
why: A brief scene can inform players of all four without long exposition.

text: Cutscene restrictions on player agency matter most in RPGs and games with many dialogue choices, where player decisions shape the narrative.
when: RPGs or games with many dialogue choices
why: Removing control there undermines choice

text: Cutscenes let designers use every film technique but fully disable player interactivity, so overuse creates a jerky stop-start rhythm.
when: When a game places cutscenes frequently between stretches of play.
why: Full loss of control at each transition interrupts the player's flow.

text: Dialogue trees, or hub dialogue, list social actions or option words a player picks, each with a scripted response; designers author both sides, so no simulation is needed.
A gateway is a product that opens onto one part of a shared world, so the world itself is what is being sold.
The primary purpose of game dialogue is to help players progress through the game smoothly and naturally.
why: Other dialogue roles are secondary to player progression.

text: Secondary dialogue roles are characterization, worldbuilding through history and backstory, pacing through breather moments between intense action, and humor that lightens mood or sets up a later surprise.
Generic banter is a short exchange involving two or more characters, optionally the player too, that is situational or character-driven and usually interruptible.
A token is a placeholder, such as @player_name, that the game fills in from player choices like name, gender or faction, letting one line fit many possible heroes.
Toys and games based on a fantasy world give children more ways to enter it and spend more time there.
Writing good game dialogue is a learned skill that takes years of practice rather than innate talent.
Dialogue often carries narrative and instruction with less help from visual storytelling than film has, which makes clumsy writing easy to produce.
Writing dialogue is both art and craft; mastering the structure of ambient and interactive dialogue frees a writer to focus on polished, memorable lines.
Each quest or story segment starts with a quest-giving dialogue, and many mid-plot dialogues also set up the next stage.
Placeholder dialogue is revised repeatedly until it is final.
In visual and auditory media, players judge writing mainly by dialogue, even when plot takes most of the effort.
when: games with spoken or on-screen dialogue
why: Being visual and auditory, the game's spoken and displayed words are what players recognize as writing.

text: Test a line's length by asking how long you would want someone to explain it while you are being hunted and need an escape route.
why: Players have only about fifteen to twenty seconds of attention, so long explanations lose them.

text: Stammered, broken-off words in text suggest anxiety or fear.
why: Plain text lacks a voice, so formatting and context must carry the character's emotional state.

text: A condescending tone in lines can convey a character's contempt for the player.
In limited-space writing, showing what you can say in a small space is more valuable than showing how much space you can fill.
when: Portfolio or short-form dialogue.

text: Linked gateways into one fantasy world reinforce each other: wanting to win a game motivates watching its show, and the show makes the game feel more vivid.
when: A world is reached through several connected products
why: Each product creates a new reason to engage with the others

text: Writing tends to be the first element revised, since rewriting dialogue costs far less than reanimating a scene.
why: Changes ripple down the line through other parts of the project, and text is the easiest element to alter.

text: Looping dialogue back to a shared root reuses a small number of nodes, avoiding a new branch for every possible conversation path.
why: otherwise infinite branching becomes unmanageable

text: A single play session may expose only about ten percent of the recorded dialogue, so each session feels different.
when: Simulations with large recorded dialogue

text: A sample budget allows up to 150 characters of dialogue and 50 characters of instructions per box.
why: Dialogue already tells players what to do, so the instructions can stay a brief restatement.

text: Short side quests may use one middle hub, while longer dialogues can have up to about six; beyond that, split the dialogue into two encounters.
when: When designing quest dialogue length.
why: Hub count bounds how long a conversation can run before it becomes unwieldy.

text: A good quest-giving dialogue has six parts in order: opening hook; first NPC hub stating the problem; first player hub to pursue or leave; further NPC hubs detailing the quest; further player hubs for questions and acceptance or refusal; immediate goal stating the first step.
Dialogue in games divides into three general types: ambient lines, interactive conversation, and cutscenes.
why: These categories cover the varied terms used across genres and companies.

text: Near-identical options, such as three versions of 'yes' or identical greetings in a first hub, give no real choice and make players feel the dialogue is forced.
why: It only confirms that a dialogue has started.

text: Writers whose strength is long, poetic description may not suit games, since game writing has different demands.
why: Play is both seen and heard, and dialogue is what players most readily identify as writing.

text: Perfunctory small content lowers game quality, since players either notice the carelessness or do not care at all.
why: Small content such as log entries and ability text forms a large share of how players experience the game.

text: Simplifying a story for a supposedly unsophisticated audience leads to substandard work; clarity should be matched to genre and audience expectations rather than dumbed down.
when: Being asked to simplify a story
why: Players notice holes in science and lore

text: Writing dialogue that describes placeholder visuals, such as a character saying they are sad, becomes redundant or clumsy once the finished animation arrives.
when: placeholder art or animation
why: Finished art and animation fill the narrative gaps that placeholder visuals leave.

text: Scripting a live scene forces the designer to handle every action a player might take, which multiplies contingencies that past-event storytelling avoids.
when: When a story unfolds in the present tense during interactive play.
why: Past events cannot be disrupted by player actions, so the game need not handle or block interference.

text: 1) Decide which information types each dialogue box holds. 2) Allot each information type a character limit, counting spaces but not words.
when: when designing dialogue box content

text: Quest dialogue self-check: 1) Confirm the objective is clear and restated in the final line. 2) Confirm every path states it before acceptance. 3) Confirm optional lines hold only optional information. 4) Confirm options are distinct. 5) Confirm the NPC reacts to every choice. 6) Confirm options span player types. 7) Confirm lines read well aloud.
when: After drafting a quest conversation.

text: Write speech with slang, hesitations, stumbles and short fragments, breaking exposition into short chunks rather than complete encyclopedic sentences, since formal sentences make NPCs sound like reference material.
Review all dialog as a designer, since one line may conflict with a gameplay rule.
why: Dialog lines can easily conflict with mechanics, and only a designer reviewing them will spot it.

text: Decide how much dialogue or text to use by first deciding which emotion the player should feel.
why: Explaining a major revelation in the moment can dampen the player's own emotional response.

text: Use a fixed box template so each information type always appears in the same place, such as story first, task next, and reward last.
when: When each dialogue interaction must deliver specific information.
why: Fixed placement lets players locate each piece of information at a glance.

text: Use dialogue when the player needs narrative motivation in order to proceed.
when: The player would otherwise lack a reason to continue.
why: Dialogue is mainly paid for to guide players onward smoothly and naturally.

text: Place a player-response hub fairly early, and split important information into separate sections that players can react to.
when: A new piece of information must register with the player.
why: Players who tune out during long exposition learn less than when info is split and they respond.

text: Cut greetings and farewells such as 'Hello,' 'Goodbye' and 'Thank you' when they add nothing to the story.
why: Such lines consume space without moving the plot forward.

text: Give the first NPC hub enough to draw the player in, but not so much that it overwhelms them.
when: When the NPC opens a quest dialogue right after the player enters it.
why: Players tend to retain only one detail from a hub, the final one said.

text: Make the first hub offer at least three distinct options: an eager reply, a refusal, and a curious reply such as 'Tell me more.'
when: The quest is clear to the player.
why: These cover the most likely player sentiments and branch cleanly into the next hub.

text: Always include an eager option that lets players skip the details and go straight to the next action.
Write repeated sequence dialogue so it does not become annoying on the tenth hearing.
when: Repeated sequence dialogue that can replay endlessly
why: Since the sequence replays without limit, any line heard again and again becomes tiresome.

text: Check that dialogue reads well and keeps a consistent tone and style across characters.
when: during revision

text: The player character must never hold a two-way exchange with a sane, conscious, coherent, humanlike character.
why: Keeping sane humanlike characters off the player's conversational path avoids simulating a free two-way exchange, and world and emergent tools do not need one.

text: Branches that are closer to separate stories give distinct experiences, but middle-path players may be left dissatisfied.
when: designing paths between extremes

text: Dialogue trees give designers full control over responses but limit the player to a handful of options rather than open-ended conversation.
when: choosing how to handle player interaction
why: Designers can author every side of each exchange, so nothing needs to be simulated, but the player's choices stay limited.

text: Emergent story is generated during play by mechanics, players, and chance interacting, creating plot, character, and theme in response to player decisions rather than a fixed designer sequence.
Interactivity creates emergent narrative because each player's actions differ, so designers guide experiences rather than fix them.
why: Player choices produce different stories

text: Gameplay snapshots arranged as captioned scrapbooks and shared online let players communicate their emergent stories to others.
Whether emergent story will significantly change games is still open, but designers keep seeking ways to integrate story without diminishing gameplay.
Apophenia underlies nearly all emergent stories, and it is what makes characters and feelings possible in them.
Emergent stories can cross from fiction into real life: a player's own experiences, such as a changing relationship formed through play, become true stories no designer can author.
Emergent story can only contain events the mechanics model, so subjects outside the game's systems, such as mundane everyday routines, cannot emerge.
Use emergent story when player-driven variety matters more than authored narrative control.
when: Where a fixed branching structure would limit player choices and produce dull outcomes
why: Core systems give players elements to build countless stories and share them, so the story arises from play.

text: Insert authored story segments at intervals within a procedurally set sequence of events to keep the plot moving forward.
when: Procedurally generated games that need a continuous narrative thread

text: Story sequences that trigger depending on player actions let narrative respond to play rather than follow a fixed path.
why: Fixed paths restrict choice and can end in dull outcomes, so tying story to what players do avoids that.

text: Spaces with identifiable qualities and interactive features give players reasons to use them in unplanned ways, creating emergent narrative that can outlive the original design.
when: When a space has an identifiable quality and built-in interactive features
why: Players find reasons to return to and act within distinctive spaces.

text: Give small backstory fragments at random after combat or during exploration, and hide optional items such as notes to reward thorough exploration.
when: Delivering lore in gaps between major beats
why: Lore tied to actions the player takes feels earned rather than arbitrary.

text: Designers can use emergent techniques to make game scenarios more believable and unpredictable.
why: From simple starting rules, lifelike patterns can develop, so outcomes are not fully set in advance.

text: Use art, sound, decals, particles and light settings to set tone and atmosphere, reinforcing an area's theme; form and ornament can convey ideas beyond function.
Show environmental facts and story through level layout, art and contents rather than stating them directly, so players piece them together.
when: For background facts that are not needed for gameplay or the plot
why: Players learn setting, characters, and plot by inspecting construction and objects.

text: Players increasingly prefer nature content aligned with their own culture, which shifts depictions away from Western-influenced defaults.
when: nature depictions in games

text: Games without text or dialogue can let players' imagination and emotion carry the story.
when: story is told without words
why: Players fill gaps with their own interpretation and feeling.

text: Players infer past events from object arrangements, reconstructing what happened from abandoned items and traces.
when: a scene conveys story without dialogue or cutscenes
why: players look for causes behind scattered or displaced objects

text: Players assume unfamiliar objects behave like familiar real-world equivalents unless the game shows otherwise.
when: Vehicles or objects shown without explanation
why: Players map new things onto what they already know

text: Audiences keep products that carry a whole world and casually discard products that do not.
why: Audiences value re-entering a world they can visit, reshape and make their own, more than any single story told in it.

text: Players who find fixed clues of a past event in any order can still reconstruct the full story from them.
when: clues of a completed event are scattered and discoverable out of sequence
why: Each clue is fixed and consistent with the same underlying story

text: Embedded narrative is predetermined story that designers make work through mechanics, holding it in architecture through sculpture, calligraphy, or evidence of past use, and deciding what each space reveals.
Levels execute gameplay rules and also express those rules to players, making them the designer's main channel for communicating gameplay.
Environmental storytelling conveys a wordless mini-narrative by arranging prefabricated scene assets, which can establish tone, tension and foreshadowing without dialogue.
Environments reveal a character's social status, values, and development, and can expose an unreliable character.
Environmental narrative is the story told through the game world and the player's exploration of it, using audio, visual, and design techniques.
Environmental narrative delivers plot through ambient NPC dialogue, NPC behavior, and level design instead of cutscenes or interactive dialogue.
Mise-en-scene is the arrangement of leftover traces of past events in a space, so the setting reveals recent history without explicit telling.
Evocative spaces use familiar architectural elements to set mood, establish fiction, or signal positive or negative events, and work because players understand the vernacular.
why: Players read familiar architectural language to infer meaning

text: A staging space is a large, visible space where important gameplay or narrative events happen, working like a theatrical set.
Decoration quoting a sacred text makes the ornament itself carry narrative meaning.
Early game environments used block forms, no lighting, and little or no colour.
when: 1980s game landscapes

text: Visual details missing from the source text, like costume items or props, can become a character's defining icons when adaptations repeat them.
Recurring objects placed in a character's memories can reveal hidden emotional history, such as an affection the character could not express verbally.
when: Memory-based or retrospective narratives

text: Environmental narrative techniques can be audio, visual, design-based, or physical, such as tying mechanics to controller vibration.
Environmental narrative can show the world's state, use settings to guide progress, give insight into characters, and be built into level design or mechanics.
Scenery-based storytelling can guide players toward places, expose plot points, offer hints, and foreshadow later events.
Familiar real-world environments, such as a mountain monastery or an igloo, evoke particular kinds of people and ways of life.
Illustrated symbols work best when paired with behavioral and Montessori teaching approaches.
Vernacular is built through symbol-building, where a space borrows recognizable forms from a real place or era to carry meaning.
Spatial qualities such as size, orientation, lighting and views evoke emotion and keep players returning to a game.
Arrange terrain, locations, creatures and loot so players can build their own stories from them.
when: when designing environments for player-driven narrative
why: Players make emergent stories from the places and objects they find

text: Aim for emotionally resonant levels that may be scary, personal, heartbreaking, funny, or tragic, since that range makes levels strong.
why: Art is judged great when it can unsettle, sadden or move people, not only please them.

text: Because the camera shows the character within its surroundings, designers can use spatial size types dramatically.
when: In isometric games
why: The camera view supports a detailed 3D environment and can reveal what the character cannot see.

text: Narrative rewards can reward required actions and also players who test the boundaries of a game world.
when: Designing rewards for exploration

text: Environmental text such as graffiti should add worldbuilding or revelation rather than restate what the scene already shows.
when: When the scene already makes its emotional impact obvious to the player
why: Text that restates what is shown can break the mood, as on-the-nose dialogue does.

text: Use traces that lead from an event to a focal spot, such as a trail toward a lit doorway, to imply what happened and where the actor went.
why: Clues pointing toward a spot invite players to infer what happened and choose their next move.

text: Strong visual and audio clues that belong to the game and its gameplay work best for conveying small pieces of story.
when: Games with a small screen or a heavy gameplay focus, where space is limited and little text is possible
why: Reinforcing a gameplay feature can convey information with little or no text, adding entertainment value in a limited space.

text: Safe settlements can carry story content that draws newcomers into the world's narrative.
when: Designing safe zones for new players
why: Calm spaces allow players to engage with the story

text: Use a physical method for early brainstorming and a shareable file for review by other departments.
when: Wireframing workflow
why: It keeps the narrative consistent while details change and gives a steady view of the whole body of work.

text: Repeat a core idea through plaques, statues and graffiti to keep it present without exposition.
when: when a society's founding principle must shape the world
why: Repeated visible cues reinforce the idea as players move through the space.

text: Arranged remains signal the kind of event: bound bodies at a wall suggest execution, emaciated bodies in rags suggest genocide, and bodies in royal garb suggest revolution.
why: Players rely on familiar environmental associations to read what kind of event left the arranged remains.

text: Let architecture and visual details convey setting before any dialogue, using decay, cheap shelters, and hand-painted signage to signal extreme poverty.
when: establishing a harsh setting at the start
why: visual cues communicate faster than exposition

text: Players tend to meet nearby content before distant content, so spatial arrangement softly orders what the player experiences.
when: When one piece of content must be consumed before another, such as teaching mechanics in a set sequence

text: A distant feature visible during play can later be reached, turning top-down spatial depth into a storytelling tool.
when: In top-down games, where parallax scrolling makes backgrounds appear far below the gameplay space
why: Independently scrolling distant layers convey height and depth even with primitive graphics, and players can later reach what they saw.

text: With no enemies present, players can drop their combat mindset, rest, and take in the story, even when a battle follows.
when: In narrative stages where no enemies are present
why: Narrative stages create pacing changes that give players a chance to rest before the next challenge.

text: Identical prefabricated assets carry different meanings by arrangement, so arrangement, not asset identity, determines the story; reused assets stay evocative in new arrangements.
when: assets are reused across a level or game
why: interpretation depends on arrangement rather than on asset novelty

text: Players learn a repeated symbol's meaning after several cases where it reliably precedes the same outcome, such as danger or reward, so repeated symbolic assets shape their behavior.
when: When a symbol repeatedly appears before the same outcome, such as danger or reward, across several encounters
why: Repeated pairing of a sign with a consequence builds association.

text: A smell-only connection can carry poison gas from one room to a guard in another room, as through an air duct.
when: When a connection between rooms is a critical puzzle element, such as an air duct
why: Connection distance is processed separately from 3D distance, so connections need not be limited to nearby regions.

text: Naming places, people and events that never appear makes a world seem larger and richer.
Ornament on a structure can both narrate a story to viewers and advertise the builder's authority, so decorative detail carries communicative as well as aesthetic meaning.
when: Designing façades or decorative detail in a monumental space
why: Ornament has long served as a communication channel for narrative and status.

text: Environmental details such as ruins in a city never rebuilt can reveal a past event and a defeated people's inability to recover.
when: designing explorable environments
why: Players infer history from visible traces.

text: Environmental details that contradict a character's account, such as nonsensical signage, can lead players to question that character's mental state or reliability.
when: Unreliable narrator or character design
why: Players notice inconsistencies between the environment and the character's words

text: A guiding entity that leads players to letters, memos, or diaries can deliver objectives and background as players follow it.
when: When a haunting entity is a constant, unpredictable presence in the environment

text: Found documents written by ordinary people can reveal a character's life before the player meets them, establishing that character without direct interaction.
when: a character is absent or not yet encountered
why: documents show the character's life one step ahead of the player

text: When combat leaves every corpse, weapon, and scorch mark where it fell, players can read the remains to reconstruct how the fight unfolded.
when: Battles with many combatants and persistent debris.
why: Arrangements of bodies and scorch marks encode what happened, so the player can interpret them as evidence.

text: In 2D or top-down games, camera framing can show threats or plot objects that the player's character cannot see.
why: The relationship between camera framing and object position directs player attention to elements the designer wants seen.

text: Subtle environmental clues such as abandoned objects or traces of an unseen character reward observant players and build hidden story and foreshadowing.
when: Players look closely at the environment
why: Players who notice details assemble story from them

text: Contrasting architectural vernacular assets, such as urban buildings beside overgrowth, shows decay and elapsed time.
when: Showing how long a place has been abandoned
why: Clashing vernacular styles set side by side let the player infer a place's history from the mismatch.

text: Staging spaces host climactic battles, cutscenes and scripted events, and they can also function as goals or pacing controls that shape the rhythm of play.
why: Their large scale and monumental features signal in advance that important events will occur there.

text: Staged background events can run alongside active play in a linear space, so the world feels alive while the player moves through it.
when: a linear space is used for play
why: Scripted events happen around the moving player, so the space conveys activity without interrupting play.

text: A memory palace, or method of loci, stores information as memorable locations in an imagined space that a person mentally walks through.
when: when designing levels that carry information for players to recall
why: Spatial memory makes ordered information easier to retrieve.

text: A hero's-journey arc can be mirrored spatially, moving from comfort to epic wilderness to a dark, corrupted final area.
why: Surface textures and visuals shift as the hero progresses, matching a recurring pattern across stories.

text: Twine organizes a story into rooms linked in a flow chart called a map, which can be navigated like architecture.
Some players will miss information no matter what, so every player should still be given a real chance to notice core messages.
when: In action-oriented games where players are busy moving through the space
why: Not all players explore, so information needed to progress must be obvious to everyone.

text: Mystery plots make each writer depend on earlier content, so they are harder to split among writers than a simple ancient-evil plot.
when: In a large game split among multiple writers
why: Each writer must know exactly what came before, while separate quests can stay distinct and link only at the end.

text: Choices that lead to the same result reduce dialogue to decoration.
when: In games with interactive dialogue where players choose what their character says
why: Dialogue choices matter only when they set distinct conditions that later change character reactions and content.

text: Spaces lacking identifiable qualities or interactive features give players little reason to return, so emergent narrative does not form.
why: Landmarks and interactive features make players want to use areas beyond simply passing through them.

text: Designers mark objects with AI-relevant flags, often reusing non-AI flags, such as a collectable power-up also serving a guard that defends collectables.
why: The flag is needed for basic game rules anyway, and the AI reads the same marks, so new objects need no extra programming.

text: Tailor an area or room with objects and details so players explore and absorb who the character is, rather than relying on heavy exposition.
why: Room details let players infer a character's state themselves instead of being told through heavy exposition.

text: 1) List locations that matter to the character. 2) Ask how formative places shaped them. 3) Ask what each location says about personality. 4) Check whether it shows change. 5) Identify objects that reveal something.
when: Designing character-revealing environments
why: Places people live in and possessions they keep signal status and priorities, and the setting can expose what unreliable characters conceal.

text: 1) Decide which locations tell the story. 2) Plan how players reach them. 3) Decide what they find there, such as NPCs, items or visual clues. 4) Choose how NPCs communicate without speaking to the player-character.
why: Environmental storytelling can guide players to places and deliver plot points, hints, and foreshadowing.

text: 1) Show the scene's outcome on first visit. 2) Add motive clues, such as documents. 3) Add method clues, such as a weapon. 4) Add relationship evidence and recorded testimony from the participants.
when: designing a scene that rewards return visits
why: World narrative does not reveal everything at once, moving from broad impressions to details, so replays expose motive and method.

text: 1) Choose the emotions the space should convey. 2) Build materials and details that evoke them. 3) Add small sensory cues, such as a subtle sound, that work below conscious awareness.
when: designing a space to carry a specific emotional tone
why: Emotional intent guides the design, and subtle cues deepen the effect without drawing attention.

text: Scatter supplies around abandoned shelters and vehicles to imply that the occupants left in a hurry.
when: suggesting a recent past event through props
why: Props arranged as if people passed through let players infer their fate from traces rather than being told.

text: Place the answer to a puzzle in nearby dialogue the player can overhear, so the clue is found through play.
Any environmental narrative technique, such as interactive objects, NPC behavior, or sound, can be placed in level design.
why: Layering more such techniques raises how invested players become in narrative and play alike.

text: Use asset arrangements to suggest past events when a story must be conveyed without dialogue or cutscenes.
when: story delivery is limited to the environment
why: Arranged props imply a sequence of events that players reconstruct on their own.

text: In action-oriented games, environmental story visuals must be large and noticeable enough to be seen while the player moves past them.
when: action games
why: Players running through the space will otherwise miss them.

text: Introduce a strange item through in-world setup, such as signs or establishing shots, before players need it.
when: An unusual item is essential to both story and mechanics
why: Setup creates anticipation so the item seems natural when it appears

text: In a comedic world, replace costly arbitrary physical outcomes with stylized ones, such as an object shattering instead of being cut into new geometry.
when: Realistic handling would be technically hard, such as cutting objects into arbitrary pieces
why: A stylized outcome avoids the cost while the tone keeps it plausible

text: Leave as few traces as possible in behind-the-scenes material, since fans will dig through anything that ships with the game.
why: Fans will find whatever is in the game regardless of how deeply it is hidden.

text: Confirm that every asset a cutscene's dialogue refers to is in production, since dialogue about nonexistent assets, such as a tank with no tank model, creates a serious problem.
why: Scene visuals beyond the dialogue shape the final product, so referenced assets that never get built break the scene.

text: Show a world state through short animations, such as villagers cowering or hiding, instead of long explanatory text.
when: a village or area has just been affected by an event
why: Visible behavior conveys emotion and situation with fewer words.

text: Use deep focus, keeping foreground and background both sharp, so two narrative events can be shown in one frame.
why: Deep focus shows two narrative events in one frame, conveying story that would otherwise need dialogue.

text: Place a foreground detail that reveals meaning the characters' words do not state.
when: dialogue hides or softens a story point
why: A foreground object can reveal what characters' words leave unstated, adding character detail and raising questions.

text: Show a large background structure as a vista during a pause before a boss, then use it later as a dramatic payoff.
when: When a level has a pause in gameplay before a boss fight.
why: The vista rewards players who reach a level's end and lets them watch the climax during downtime.

text: In 3D games, use lighting, shadows and contrast to highlight embedded objects as the player arrives at them.
when: In first- or third-person 3D games without fixed cameras.

text: Simple objects can be packed densely into one scene, but complex interactive mechanisms need more isolation, so object count per scene should depend on complexity.
when: When deciding how many objects to place in a teaching scene
why: Complex objects demand more processing than simple ones

text: Keep story information shallow and to what players need when attention is short, but extra context usually does not limit improvisation, so explaining more can be safe.
when: deciding how much story context to give players
why: Shallow context suits short attention and avoids unused detail; extra context rarely constrains player-driven stories.

text: Explanatory text or a character commenting on a major event reduces its emotional effect on the player.
when: when players face a major event or revelation
why: The explanation tells players how to respond instead of letting them react on their own.

text: Fluff text is a short line taken from the story world, such as dialogue, that conveys the game's mood and atmosphere.
when: Writing a narrative pitch doc
why: It shows the tone without full exposition

text: Players fill gaps with their own imagination, so decide which details to show and which to leave to the player. Only show what you can render well.
when: When choosing how much detail to put into scenery, sound, characters, animation or effects
why: A detail that looks worse than what players can imagine lowers perceived seriousness

text: The more technical detail a designer explains, the more consistency the designer must maintain across the game.
why: Detailed explanations give players more claims to check, and factual errors get spotted and shared quickly.

text: To disguise a forced acceptance, pair the agreement option with a reward question so players can accept for altruistic or practical reasons.
when: The quest requires the player to accept.
why: The reward question makes the forced choice less visible to the player.

text: Sane characters can speak only remotely, while face-to-face characters are hostile, so attempted interaction turns into attack, which the game can simulate.
when: the fiction can justify the absence of conversation
why: remote or hostile characters explain why the player cannot talk to them

text: Attach fictional labels such as names, personality tags, and biographical events to existing mechanics so players invent stories the systems never simulated.
when: When a game names and tracks individual units or characters that the player can review.
why: players' imagination supplies the story

text: Enemies placed where locked doors would be, and escalating their response on repeated attempts, can convey a world's setting without exposition.
when: when introducing a setting without dialogue
why: Player encounters with hostile forces communicate the world through action.

text: Story exposition can serve as a reward for completing large battles or skill challenges.
Revealing a previously private fact at the right moment can create drama, because the information a player acts on changes during play.
when: when a hidden fact is disclosed mid-game
why: Who knows what can change over the course of play.

text: Flavor text added to functional item text turns dry mechanics into lore by naming the maker and their fate, showing cultural value, or telling a brief story of use.
when: writing item and ability descriptions
why: Lore adds meaning without changing the mechanics.

text: Writers who master every game detail become valuable across disciplines, and quality assurance turns to the narrative team when unsure of a detail.
why: Detail knowledge is needed by other teams, not only by writers.

text: Exposition introduces settings, characters, and concepts the action depends on; traditionally it establishes time, place, characters, relationships, and the prevailing status quo before conflict begins.
Dialogue that only moves the plot forward tells the player nothing about the speakers.
when: When writing character dialogue that carries plot information
why: Plot facts get delivered, but the lines never show who the speakers are, since personality only comes through what characters say and do.

text: Covering poor systems with exposition does not fix them, and players will rightly criticize it.
Exposition delivered in one long block before the player speaks is largely lost, because players tune out and learn less.
when: A conversation opens with extended information and no player response.
why: Each chance to reply raises engagement, so information split into pieces players can react to sticks better than one unbroken stretch they tune out of.

text: Packing too many personal details into a hub buries the core problem.
why: Players carry the closing few words of a hub into their reply choices, so a problem buried earlier in the hub gets lost when they respond.

text: Writers tend to leave out details that seem obvious to them, so the script can be unclear to anyone without their context.
when: When the writer has finished a first revision and a fresh reader from the team has not yet seen the script.
why: Details feel obvious only to the author

text: Showing too much explicit detail can erase the personality or relationship the player was constructing in their imagination.
why: Specific detail leaves less room for the player to supply their own picture, while sparse presentation lets their imagination complete it.

text: 1) Choose how the protagonist can ask questions: use amnesia, make them an outsider to the world, or write dialogue where NPCs imply information. 2) Check that the chosen method fits the protagonist's origin.
when: when the protagonist grew up in the game world
why: A native protagonist asking basic questions sounds unnatural.

text: If an unrealistic detail must stay, explain it instead of ignoring it.
when: An unrealistic detail cannot be removed
why: Unexplained oddities invite doubt

text: Do not rely on imagination for educational content about unfamiliar places; provide far more detail.
when: The purpose is teaching players about a place they have never been
why: Players cannot fill gaps in knowledge they lack.

text: Deliver lore through dialogue that arises naturally in conversation, since a passing remark can reveal a major event or how one class views another.
when: writing NPC dialogue
why: Casual remarks convey history and attitudes without exposition.

text: Tell players about abilities beyond normal human capability before the level requires them.
when: when a solution depends on a non-human ability
why: Without setup, players search only within their own experience and may miss the intended solution.

text: Consider graphical perspective and player attention span whenever possible, even though they are not always treated as narrative design.
when: When the tool does not harm the work of other disciplines.

text: Separate essential from optional content, and check that testers can tell them apart and that the story still makes sense when optional parts are skipped.
when: When writing a testing plan for branching story content.

text: Block unwanted actions through the fiction's logic when the setting makes them naturally impossible; flex the fiction around mechanics when it would block the intended experience.
when: When the story world can credibly justify the restriction.
why: Players accept restrictions that feel honest within the world, but a fixed fiction can prevent the intended experience.

text: Explicit detail in graphics, sound, and dialogue adds clarity and presence, but reduces the room players have to interpret, while minimal representation does the reverse.
when: choosing how explicitly to present characters and events
why: Gaps left unspecified get filled by the mind's own imagining, so specifying more removes that room for the player.

text: Fans may write their own stories set in your world with your characters.
Free interactive-story tools include Twine (branching text), StoryNexus (choose-your-own-adventure), Ren'Py (visual novels), ChoiceScript, inklewriter, and Inform (interactive fiction).
The most devoted fandoms usually surround the strongest transmedia worlds, which typically have a deep core fans want to enter.
when: Judging a world's long-term fan potential
why: Fans seem driven more by wanting to step inside the fantasy than by liking a plot or its characters.

text: Write prompts that state concrete situations and explain the comedy or theme, rather than relying on players to supply background knowledge.
when: humor or theme depends on background context
why: Prompts that assume shared knowledge make the tone confusing.

text: Idioms, jokes, swearing and names may lack direct equivalents in other languages, so writer and translator must agree on adaptations, and names may need changing per release language.
when: Localizing for multiple languages
why: Expressions and names can carry different meanings abroad

text: A language reflects the culture of its speakers, so its sound and tone can express that people's character.
In games, clarity usually matters more than literary quality, so ask how a line's meaning will survive translation.
when: Writing lines that will be localized
why: Players must understand what to do and where to go, so essential instructions cannot rely on subtext.

text: Keep localization notes clear and well organized, and send lines with context, since lines sent without context produce poor translations and waste budget.
why: Disorganized notes and lines sent without context consume much of the localization budget.

text: Explain the meaning of sentences and idioms to translators every time they ask, even when repetitive, because bad translations are traced back to the writer.
when: A translator asks about meaning
why: Translation errors are first attributed to the writer, who has to answer for them.

text: Consider culturalization across territories, since content fine in one place may offend or be misunderstood in another.
when: games distributed in multiple territories
why: Content that is fine in one region may read as insulting in another, or be misunderstood by a different culture.

text: Treat any words drawn into art, such as a sign on a door, as text that must be translated along with the dialogue.
when: When art includes words, such as a sign on a door.
why: New art is expensive and time-consuming, so text baked into it adds costly rework.

text: A premise places a game's action in a setting or metaphor, giving abstract rules a dramatic context.
Game characters mostly use physical verbs such as run, shoot, jump, and climb, while stories rely on communication verbs such as ask, argue, and persuade.
Integrating story with gameplay and building deeper empathy for characters are named hard problems in game design.
Games' emotional impact has not yet reached its potential, so designers should master traditional drama tools and understand good gameplay.
Games needn't include narrative to be enjoyable, yet story can stir emotion.
Game stories range from none at all to sprawling epics, but all of them are interactive, which sets them apart from traditional media.
Game stories fall into three structure categories: linear, branching, and open, each with its own writing requirements.
Most games have stories, either as backstories or as structures that shape play, and these stories can be treated as generated content.
Games can convey social messages about migration, conflict, depression, sustainability, and simple living, presenting them as art that moves players and prompts reflection.
Story-to-play transitions that feel forced break the flow of the experience, as early implementations of this method often did.
when: Joining authored story to play segments

text: Use a gameplay segment to carry the player through the aftermath of a scene, letting them act out its consequences before a closing cutscene.
when: moving from a cinematic into gameplay and back
why: Interactive aftermath keeps the player involved between scripted moments.

text: Film shares moving images, sound, three-act structure and phased development with games, and teaches framing, pacing and visual effects, but not player choice or departures from the author's plan.
why: games do not work like films because players act within the story

text: Film climaxes release tension built through audience empathy, while game climaxes add personal accomplishment on top of sympathy for characters.
when: When the climax requires the player to work out the resolving action.
why: The player figures out the key action after tension builds over many levels, so resolving it adds personal satisfaction.

text: Treating a film as the origin of a world and other products as mere copies misses how a world can grow through the rules of handheld play.
why: Adaptations that mirror a game's mechanics carry its world into other media, while loosely linked adaptations leave the world's rules behind.

text: Swinging through the air like a jungle hero fulfils a fantasy of cheating gravity, which makes the air a natural environment for the character.
when: Character moves primarily through the air on a swing mechanic
why: Gravity-defying movement taps a common childhood power fantasy.

text: A besieged world faces assault from an external power or entities from elsewhere that threaten conquest or ruin.
Fantasy worlds made for children can become shared modern mythology that guides people for the rest of their lives.
Designing for a particular age requires understanding which pastimes and subjects were in vogue during that audience's youth.
when: Designing for a specific age group
why: Play across life links to childhood, so the audience's formative pastimes and subjects shape their expectations

text: Horror games that use asylums and psychiatric settings as shortcuts to fear reinforce stereotypes about mental illness.
when: When horror games use psychiatric settings as emotional shortcuts
why: Designers project society's internalized beliefs into their worlds, so shortcut schemas about mental illness get carried into games.

text: Stereotypes slip under notice because they are so prevalent that even the groups portrayed may not notice them.
when: When media exposure to a stereotype is pervasive
why: Stereotypes are common enough to look normal, and some truths within them make flat characters harder to spot.

text: Every story leaves an implicit message, intended or not; games without a chosen theme tend to end up with 'good will conquer evil against all odds.'
when: Games without a deliberate theme
why: Every story conveys a message whether or not one is chosen, so an unchosen theme defaults to a common message.

text: Culture shapes stereotypes, especially when they are not clearly condemned, and people may absorb them implicitly.
when: Stereotypes appear in media without explicit criticism.
why: Unchallenged portrayals are absorbed without conscious awareness.

text: A licensed IP is a game based on an existing movie, TV show or novel, or a sequel to an existing game.
Image-led advertising portrays a product within an attractive scene instead of enumerating its features.

Screen media may influence players' attitudes, beliefs, and prejudices toward groups, but the evidence is uncertain and effects are not established as causal; state such claims carefully, not overstated.
why: Evidence is mixed, so overstating media effects is a pitfall.

text: Narrative design adds entertainment value in crowded markets and gives players small insights into the game's world.
Instrumental and atonal techniques from 20th-century composers give flexible ambiguity that suits horror music.
when: Scoring horror or tense games
why: Ambiguity lets intensity shift without jarring transitions.

text: Marketing should sell the ultimate purpose or meaningful fantasy, such as becoming a hero who saves the world, rather than only listing actions like shoot, explore or craft.
when: when writing marketing for a game or mode
why: purpose gives players a reason to care about actions

text: Add humor or absurdity to a grim setting to give players emotional relief, so the setting's heaviness does not overwhelm them.
when: the core setting is bleak and survival-focused
why: emotional relief keeps players engaged

text: Avoid promising a specific emotional moment in marketing, because players then watch for it during play and may judge the game by whether it appears.
when: writing marketing copy for a game
why: Promised moments become expectations players actively track.

text: The hero's journey is a shared heroic story structure across myths, staged as call to adventure, trials, a benevolent force, a malevolent force, and a return with a boon.
Draft the story first, then compare it with the hero's journey stages as a diagnostic lens to find missing elements, not to dictate plot.
when: Revising or after drafting a heroic story
why: Comparison reveals gaps without dictating content; shows whether mythic elements would improve the story.

text: Treating the hero's journey as a guaranteed formula for an entertaining story.
when: When a planned gameplay mechanic needs a different story structure than the template
why: Stories are flexible and can be reshaped around the gameplay a team wants, so no fixed template is assured.

text: 1) Ordinary world 2) Call to adventure 3) Refusal 4) Mentor aid 5) Cross threshold 6) Tests, allies, enemies 7) Approach cave, setbacks 8) Ordeal crisis 9) Reward 10) Road back 11) Resurrection, greater crisis 12) Return with elixir.
