The interactive story dream is a fully interactive story that feels like a great film while giving the participant complete freedom of action, thought, and expression.
Digital games now offer emotional characters, richer stories, and play with real friends at convenient times.
The debate between focusing on game mechanics and focusing on story has largely settled into viewing games as rule systems combined with meaningful structures.
Interactive stories are not fundamentally new; traditional storytelling skills apply to them, and the core difference is the participant's ability to act.
Treat the full interactive story dream as a motivation for experiments rather than a near-term target for a project.
when: planning a narrative project
why: No one has yet come close to realizing it

text: Make licensed toys and products interactive, portable, flexible, and social so players can visit a world and reshape it for themselves.
when: Designing products that extend a fantasy world
why: Letting owners visit and alter a world gives them personal ownership, so the world feels more meaningful rather than less.

text: Interactivity makes storytelling harder, because the designer must predict, account for, respond to, and integrate the participant's actions.
when: When the audience can take actions that change the story

text: Narrative progression must hold attention enough that the player wants to continue playing.
Many games gate progress behind collecting a set of items, such as a number of tokens or activated sources.
Levels can carry story and character elements that are important to the game.
Landmarks and interactive elements give players reasons to use a space beyond simply travelling through it.
Level gating restricts access to content beyond a point until the player reaches a required level, letting designers shape the larger story while players choose the pieces.
when: When the story needs some order without a fixed sequence.
why: Players' routes cannot be predicted, so level thresholds become the main way to control which content they reach.

text: Carry narrative and persuasive messages through level rules and geometry, not only through cutscenes and dialog.
when: Designing story content in levels
why: Meaning conveyed through play is absorbed through action rather than passive viewing.

text: A quest is a self-contained storyline in a larger or open-world story, like an anthology story rather than a chapter; order is fixed, but it can start and pause anytime.
Generated levels can carry narrative when layout and contents embed a story, since narrative can be framed as a spatial creation engine.
when: Procedural dungeon or level generation, including levels built from spatial design rather than hand-placed content.
why: Embedded space story applies directly to generated layouts and contents.

text: Players find side quests by exploring and talking to minor characters, and many optional quests will never be discovered by a given player.
when: Optional content in open RPGs
why: Discovery depends on exploration and conversation rather than on any guaranteed prompt

text: Quest hubs are towns or starting areas where players gain supplies, learn mechanics, and receive quests that send them outward.
A quest is a relatively linear story section in which every player action serves one goal; it ends when its goal changes.
A mission is one fixed step of a linear story; missions always play in the same order and can build on each other.
when: Linear story structure

text: A mission is a goal or set of goals for the next map, usually given between maps like a military briefing.
A quest is a task driven by current story state that advances the narrative on completion, e.g. collecting an object, aiding a non-player character, slaying a creature, or hauling freight.
Side quests are optional content beside the main path that players can consume or ignore, and they affect little of the main story.
The order of set pieces affects the player's experience independently of how good each individual piece is.
A story that affects gameplay can have its map generated together with the story, or the map can be generated afterwards to follow the story.
Search and optimisation techniques can map plot points onto physical locations in a game world.
A common linear form is a sequence of pass/fail missions, where failure brings a Game Over screen.
The same story can be split into several quests linked by a larger questline, so quest boundaries are a design choice.
Long RPGs may offer hundreds of quests, most of them optional.
when: Long open-world or RPG games

text: Mission-based narrative is typical for strategy and simulation games, which have much narrative space between missions and little during them.
Most MMOs present dialogue as structured quest text boxes, and some titles use quest texts as their only story tool.
Treat skill gates as blocking elements when generating dungeon progression.
when: a generated dungeon has progression locks
why: gates are the same kind of blocker as locks in progression graphs

text: Enemy placement can be linked to narrative cues, so spawn logic can be driven by story markers placed in the level.
when: when generating or placing enemies in procedurally or manually built levels
why: Narrative cues and spawn logic reinforce each other

text: Use a string-based mission for simple linear games, and a graph-based mission when the level needs optional paths, locks, or several ways to reach the goal.
when: when choosing how to represent a generated level's mission
why: Graphs express branching and lock structure more naturally than strings.

text: Pair generated mechanics with varied themes, since similar mechanics under different fiction can feel distinctly different.
when: When a generator reuses mechanics across levels.
why: Fiction changes how players label the same arousal.

text: A generated path to a goal can be built as stacked challenges of rising difficulty, with environment art signaling that a reward lies at the end.
when: when generating a path to a goal
why: Environmental cues let players sense a payoff ahead, even when the reward itself stays hidden.

text: Designating an enemy-free, distinctively shaped room for story beats gives a generated dungeon a readable pacing shift.
when: when generating dungeon pacing
why: Distinct spaces like these address pacing and sight lines, so their form marks a shift in a level's rhythm.

text: Winding passages that let rewards be seen through other layers can give a generated maze both puzzle structure and visible payoffs.
when: when generating maze layouts
why: Partially visible spaces hint at rewards beyond, so the layout gives puzzle structure while keeping the payoff in sight.

text: Quest hubs encourage exploration and introduce mechanics through introductory quests.
when: In multiplayer game worlds with shared entry spaces
why: Introductory quests teach mechanics in a social space, and hubs send players outward to explore the world.

text: Quests that send players to other hubs give them a tour of the world and self-guided goals.
why: Travel between hubs lets players set their own interactions and goals while seeing the world.

text: Required quests should show escalating conflict between fixed events, while optional quests add flavor around them.
why: The critical path must move the main plot forward, while optional quests add separate side stories that need not do so.

text: Very large quests suit the critical-path backbone, while four or five steps is usually the complexity limit for a side quest.
when: When the quest forms part of the main story path rather than a side quest
why: Side quests reach their complexity ceiling quickly, so longer chains suit the main path.

text: Keep in-mission text and dialogue minimal, with thin motivation, while objectives and opposition still reflect the story.
when: inside a mission
why: Gameplay takes priority during missions.

text: Reduce each quest to its simplest form to reveal exactly which assets the game must build.
Story-to-space generation maps story locations to islands, where story events happen, connected by bridges, where open-ended play happens. Bridges may branch, so some areas need not be visited.
when: Generating a game world from a story plan
why: Separating event areas from connective areas gives story events fixed places while leaving travel open-ended.

text: Spacing side quests and points of interest along a main path can draw players into exploration and lengthen play.
when: open-world or MMO route design

text: Freeing bound hostages can reward players with loot while showing their heroic impact on the world and its people.
why: Direct rescue gives the player a visible role in the townspeople's lives, rather than a loot grab alone.

text: One quest in a large RPG may exceed 70,000 words, covering eight-plus levels and no fewer than four dungeons.
when: When a very large quest is meant to act as a piece of the critical path backbone

text: An average quest chain runs about 25 to 30 minutes, which can guide how much story each part of the game delivers.
In a level-based quest, each piece is the goal of one level, and each level is a string of smaller challenges such as puzzles, enemy encounters, and obstacle courses.
why: A predictable schedule of goals and rewards lets players anticipate what comes next.

text: Quest-based stories map onto TV structure: several quest chains make a season, one chain an episode, one quest an act, and one task a beat.
why: Comparing quests to TV units helps organize the story and decide what to tell when.

text: A quest has five components: an issue, a persona, a set of tasks, obstacles or opposition, and a payoff.
A role-playing game may be built as one large quest divided into smaller quests that alternate gameplay and narrative advancement.
when: Structuring a role-playing game

text: Computer RPG quests are often just lists of milestones, while tabletop quests adapt during play; procedural quest generation aims to restore that flexibility.
when: Designing computer RPG quests
why: Fixed milestone lists cannot respond to player choices the way a game master can.

text: Players may miss a scripted beat, see it from a poor angle, or interfere with it, so the beat must not depend on player attention.
when: Soft-scripted events.
why: Player controls stay live during soft scripting, so the designer cannot dictate what the player sees or does.

text: 1) Build a directed mission graph with a graph grammar. 2) Expand each mission into a node-and-edge network. 3) Convert each network into game space with a shape grammar.
why: Gives gameplay-based control over the layout

text: 1) Take a tile-based world map and select the mission location. 2) Generate terrain with tile grammars and cellular automata driven by vegetation, elevation and building tiles. 3) Analyse terrain into an abstract space graph. 4) Generate mission specifications with a string grammar and plot them onto the graph. 5) Add enemies. 6) Place mission objects on the tile map and combine them with terrain.
when: Generating a mission environment from a world-map tile

text: 1) Apply the start rule once. 2) Apply add-task rules repeatedly. 3) Add a boss once. 4) Define tasks. 5) Move locks as needed.
when: Generating a mission graph with fixed rule sequences
why: Unrestricted rule use lets the number of generated tasks grow without bound, which makes the structure hard to control.

text: 1) Lay out the mission graph with an automatic layout algorithm. 2) Sample the laid-out graph into a tile map.
when: when a generated mission must become a traversable space for action-adventure or narrative games
why: Mission coherence and pacing are kept, though this transition is the hardest of the three strategies.

text: 1) Generate geometry with cellular automata, grammars, evolution, or another method. 2) Analyse the geometry into an abstract graph. 3) Derive missions from that graph.
when: when level geometry must come first, such as strategic games or levels with consistent architecture
why: Geometry-first generation yields spaces with natural mission hooks, though control over the mission is reduced.

text: 1) Parse the story plan for locations. 2) Build an abstract space tree of location types. 3) Realize the tree as graphics.
when: Generating space from a story plan
why: Story events become islands in the generated world, linked by bridges of open play.

text: 1) Play an open-world or MMO game and travel the main path between two story events. 2) Map that route. 3) Mark side quests and points of interest along it. 4) Note how they are spaced.

1) Settle genre: meet expectations with a few surprising twists. 2) Define a concrete villain with enough henchmen to survive many defeats. 3) Agree target length, then compare similar games' cutscene, level and twist counts. 4) Set tone deliberately.
when: When moving from a broad story outline to detailed mission plans.

text: 1) Quest-giver conversation sets goal and reward. 2) Fight, with much gameplay and few story moments. 3) A twist undermines the reason the player came. 4) Offer a new goal, less desirable but higher reward. 5) Player chooses a goal. 6) Complete the chosen goal and its final fight. 7) Return to the matching NPC for the reward.
when: When building a quest with a moral twist.

text: Quest-scene drafting: 1) Write one interactive scene in which the player receives a new objective. 2) Use one to three non-player characters. 3) Keep the scene between two and four player responses, with two or three middle hubs. 4) Prioritize clearly communicating the plot step over stylistic wordplay.
when: Writing a scene that delivers a quest or main-plot objective.
why: A scene that communicates the objective is more useful than one that only shows style.

text: Closing a quest conversation: 1) Remind the player where they are in the overall story. 2) Tie the quest to their larger goals. 3) State the next step in small, clear terms.
when: The player has decided whether to take the quest.
why: Lengthy dialogue pulls the player out of the momentum of the larger story.

text: 1) State the objective in character speech. 2) Tell the player where to look. 3) Warn about the threats. 4) Restate the task and reward in an instructions line. 5) Add a hint a character would not know.
when: Writing a mission's dialogue and supporting text.
why: Each part conveys a different piece of information the player must learn.

text: Tie side quests back to the main plot so the critical path stays alive throughout a long game.
when: When approving a side quest in a role-playing title with a runtime of sixty hours or more
why: After hours of play, players focus on the immediate problem and forget the opening premise.

text: Make each mission flow directly from the player's accomplishments in the previous mission.
why: Preserves the player's sense of control in linear play.

text: Narrative designers must write each quest's own storyline and also ensure all quests join into one coherent overall story.
when: Writing quests for a large game

text: Use 'mission' when order matters and 'quest' when content can be picked up in any order; designers may still restrict some quests to a fixed sequence.
when: Naming and structuring story units
why: Missions build on each other in a linear story and so keep a fixed order, while quests are self-contained and need not affect one another.

text: In mission-based games, place major exposition and story progression between missions, in cutscenes or interactive story spaces.
why: Downtime between maps is where players can absorb story.

text: For each quest, document the quest giver or how it is received, the tasks, each task's obstacles, the gameplay used to pass each obstacle, and the reward.
Work out the complete plan for every branch of a quest that can be completed in several ways before the quest is built into the game.
when: when a quest can be completed in more than one way

text: Keep quest texts short and focused on the NPC's current problem, without background detail that is not needed at the moment the player is asked to act.
when: Writing MMO quest texts.
why: Players in groups have little time to read, and most skip to the summary and rewards.

text: Turning a mission into building instructions makes graph-to-tile conversion easier, but producing multiple paths to the same goal becomes hard.
when: when generating linear platformers or some story-driven levels
why: Instruction-based building follows a fixed sequence, which limits alternative routes.

text: Events that play regardless of player action, such as timed mail, appearing objects, or radio broadcasts, are cheap and powerful but cannot react to the player.
when: When a beat must happen regardless of what the player does.
why: They need no custom semi-interactive design.

text: Some consequences stay hidden until a player replays the game to see alternatives.
Give each moral option real weight and a believable reason, such as reasons to spare or kill a villain, so consequences reinforce why the player chose as they did.
when: Designing right-versus-wrong or good-versus-evil choices where player values are the point of the scene
why: Consequences must reinforce why the player chose as they did.

text: Moving the audience's empathy from one character to another through framing and shot choice steers how they feel about the story.
when: Directing audience attention to particular characters
why: Viewers' empathy follows the character the camera or framing emphasizes

text: Interactive fiction that approaches the full dream should at least keep the potential for tragedy.
when: designing ambitious interactive stories
why: Without any real chance of tragedy, serious harm can always be reversed, so the sense of being pulled toward an inevitable doom disappears.

text: Game narrative can evoke guilt that film or books struggle to produce, because reflective meaning can shape visceral responses through player complicity.
when: when a game's revealed outcome implicates players in a horrific event they took part in
why: Players who take part in a morally troubling action feel complicit.

text: When an injury or disease cannot be cured, care shifts toward relieving suffering, so healers specialize in comfort and palliation.
when: Designing healing practices in a setting with incurable conditions
why: Without a cure, the practical goal becomes reducing pain and improving quality of life.

text: Games that place players in the position of a refugee or an immigrant officer use player choices to convey moral and social perspectives.
when: when designing games with social awareness goals
why: Making players decide within a constrained role builds understanding of that role.

text: Players are moral agents who make choices within game rules, which force particular behaviors through their design.
why: Rules define the options players have, so the moral weight of choices depends on the rules.

text: Story content that does not fit the game's established setting wastes production effort, however well written it is.
when: when story content clashes with the game's established setting
why: The narrative designer must keep the whole project consistent, so material that clashes with the setting is wasted.

text: A late moral choice feels nonsensical when players have already committed many actions that contradict its moral stance.
when: earlier play has rewarded or normalized contradictory actions
why: the choice no longer fits the player's accumulated behavior

text: Never presume a player will pick the ethical option, and never presume your idea of morality matches someone else's.
when: when offering players a moral choice

text: The more complex the narrative, the more past player choices from gameplay and dialogue must be honored before writing new content.
when: In narratives with many branching decisions.
why: Plot points that follow from earlier player successes make players feel their actions drive the story.

text: Deliver lore as optional content players access on demand, placed where combat won't interrupt it, to introduce characters or hint at dangers ahead.
when: Placing audio logs or lore items in a game with a strong core mechanic
why: Uninterrupted lore sets up later encounters, combines anticipation with recovery, and enriches the core without blocking it.

text: Justify restrictions that seem arbitrary, such as the inability to jump, with the fiction; reframing a story element can justify technical limitations and strengthen drama.
when: Introducing an unusual movement restriction or a technical limitation
why: Players read an unexplained limitation as arbitrary.

text: When a world's rules shift, players see it as a broken artifact rather than a living place.
when: Rules change or are bent during the story
why: Inconsistency exposes the construction behind the world

text: Long quest conversations pull players out of the main flow of play, so the closing line must reorient them.
when: A quest conversation runs long.
why: Extended dialogue pulls players away from the main story, so the closing line must reconnect them to it.

text: A raw simulation log lacks pacing, dramatic tension, foreshadowing, and narrative arc unless these arise by accident.
when: Telling stories from simulated world events
why: Simulation records what happened, not what is dramatically worth telling.

text: Story integration explains how the story enters the game and which mechanic carries which story element.
when: Planning how a story reaches players
why: Shows the story is delivered through gameplay systems

text: Ludonarrative dissonance is the conflict between what works best for the story and what is most fun to play.
Designers disagree on how much story to include, whether gameplay should change the story, and whether story should dictate gameplay.
Games can make arguments through cause-and-effect between player actions and rules, a idea called procedural rhetoric.
Interactive story problems have no single fix, and realistic artificial characters or human game masters alone do not solve them.
Story can be integrated by writing text through any tool built for that purpose, or by applying level and game design methods.
Story is often not a core mechanic; it exists to make the game more attractive and enjoyable.
A released game's story rarely matches the writer's original concept, because games are collaborative and must appeal to a broad audience.
Scripted choices involve no system reasoning, unlike a chess move or a fighting-game attack, because their outcomes are authored rather than learned.
Players who master a game's mechanics can use them to tell their own stories.
Game environments often move from natural settings toward harsher materials such as wet stone, lava, and alien metal as play advances.
Let the game's cards define its physics, rather than fixing a world's physics first and building cards around it.
why: Fixed world physics constrains card design and creates problems.

text: Tie a demonstration's presenter to the story, so the lesson feels part of the narrative rather than separate from it.
Story bits work best when they highlight or reinforce the core mechanics, so start the design from gameplay.
when: in games centered on gameplay, where players expect little story development

text: Long timers and collectible items need in-world logic from worldbuilding, and collectibles can tell players about the world and characters.
when: when a mechanic has a long wait or a collectible item
why: Players accept mechanics more readily when the world explains them

text: A character's desire or a world conflict can be conveyed through mechanics, sound and animation rather than through text.
Develop unused material such as languages and cultures, since it deepens the author's understanding even when players never see it.
when: Building a world's depth
why: Background detail keeps the visible content coherent.

text: Story is among the most flexible elements, so narrative can be modified to compensate for last-minute problems or cut levels while keeping the experience smooth.
when: when last-minute problems or late cuts force changes to levels

text: A setting can justify the core mechanics: a desperate, violent world supports constant combat, and a dead world supports very low population density.
when: when the game is set in a postapocalyptic world
why: Justified mechanics let the designer avoid building extra systems and characters.

text: Obstacles that block a goal create problem solving, which people find interesting.
when: when a character's goal is blocked by obstacles, especially if a rival character pursues an opposing aim
why: Solving blocked goals engages the audience

text: Bigger obstacles create greater potential for dramatic change.
A scripted event fired at the same point each time feels unpredictable to a first-time player.
when: Triggered by a significant act such as defeating a hard boss.
why: The player cannot anticipate the trigger timing.

text: Ordinary events gain interest from their relationships in a story arc, since early setups make a later discovery meaningful.
when: when events connect to one another in a story arc

text: Narrative tools improved and players accepted some loss of freedom in exchange for engaging stories, allowing story to be woven into gameplay.
An obstacle is resolved through whatever actions the game's mechanics afford, so combat fights it while stealth sneaks past it.
As unintended actions are blocked level by level, the fictional backdrop thins, the game grows less sensible and its levels weaken.
when: When a movement change, such as higher jumps, lets players reach many places they should not.
why: Each containment fix is an artificial object placed to stop escapes, and the time spent on these fixes is taken from improving the levels.

text: Recorded voices convey emotion and capture conversations or natural events, and hearing a voice early prepares players to recognize that character later.
when: audio logs or recordings are used
why: voice creates an impression that players carry forward

text: When the story climax falls after the hardest fight, or the final boss is trivial after a power upgrade, the ending feels anticlimactic.
when: Aligning story beats with the difficulty curve
why: Story and difficulty curves do not line up, so tension drops at the climax.

text: Too much narrative content placed on the core path can block gameplay, damaging the game's feel and core idea.
when: Adding narrative content to a game with strong core mechanics
why: Story that is not a core mechanic exists only to make the game prettier, so it should leave the designed gameplay untouched.

text: Dialogue players must read during intense gameplay is easy to miss or ignore.
when: Unvoiced games with active play
why: Reading competes with gameplay attention

text: 1) Define the player character's motivation and check whether mechanics can communicate it. 2) Give other characters motivations and show them through play. 3) Decide what is happening in the world. 4) Use sound, animation and visuals to convey character and world.
when: when a game has little or no story yet
why: Story then reinforces the mechanics instead of sitting apart from them

text: Make longer story blocks and backstory optional, placing backstory in lore books or optional dialogue, so players choose how much information they receive and when.
when: When story content is not needed for gameplay or to follow the plot.
why: Players only need what directly affects them and their story; background only the team needs can stay optional for those who seek it.

text: If story cannot be explained through the game's systems, move it to another medium or rewrite it so gameplay tells it; unmatched story may not belong as written.
when: The story cannot be explained through the game's systems or has no matching mechanic
why: Story that lives outside mechanics is weakly connected to play and detached from it.

text: For games built on aiming, shooting and dodging, tell story in fast moment-to-moment beats and save longer story for breaks between action.
when: For a first-person shooter built on aiming, shooting and dodging.
why: Story players can opt into while still fighting enriches the core mechanic without interrupting it.

text: For games built on resource management and base building, use brief event-driven story pieces during play and interactive cutscenes between missions.
when: For real-time strategy games built on resource management, unit building and base building.

text: For games built on questing, exploration and combat, use complex slow-paced plots with deep character arcs, keeping story present throughout.
when: For role-playing games built on questing, exploration and combat.

text: For games built on jumping, pair an overall objective with level-based stories told mostly through the environment.
when: For a platformer built on jumping.

text: For games built on construction, exploration and combining, build the story around the player character's exploration of and interaction with the world.
when: For sandbox games built on constructing, exploration and combining.

text: When an unusual visual detail draws repeated player questions, adjust it to look normal.
when: A visual detail repeatedly prompts player questions
why: Questions stop once visuals match player expectations

text: Reshape the story when it blocks a mechanic or technical approach that works well.
when: A story detail conflicts with a working mechanic or technical approach
why: A story change can give an in-world reason for a visual approach, so the working technique can stay instead of being scrapped.

text: Make mechanics and story support each other: story reflects gameplay, the world expresses the mechanics, and gameplay shows off the world and characters.
Story is valued only as part of the game; well-written content that does not fit the project should be cut.
why: Other disciplines impose limits, such as spoken lines needing fewer words than printed ones, so story must be shaped to fit them.

text: Keep a narrative pitch doc short, but explain the story integration plan clearly.
when: Writing a narrative pitch doc
why: Short docs get read, while the integration plan must be unambiguous

text: When gameplay is complete, write story to fill the gaps between gameplay scenes and connect levels not designed with narrative in mind.
when: When gameplay is entirely complete and levels were built without narrative in mind.
why: With abilities already locked, no scene can show the character doing what play does not allow.

text: Let players react to major moments without telling them how to feel; explain consequences later or have characters discuss events after they process them.
when: When a major event or revelation is about to hit players.
why: Explaining in the moment pre-empts the player's own emotional reaction, which can weaken the event's impact.

text: Design fiction and mechanics together as a unified whole, because the desire must be instilled in the player and mirrored in the character.
when: aligning player and character motivation
why: separately built pieces joined afterward rarely share the same drive

text: Find actions that support the narrative and translate them into mechanics, so story and gameplay reinforce each other rather than existing separately.
when: Designing a game where story should shape play
why: When story and mechanics exist independently, the story becomes a backdrop

text: Keeping an unusual item costs setup effort and may confuse, while replacing it with a conventional one is simpler but may lose the distinctive idea.
when: Deciding whether an unusual item is worth its strangeness

text: Some projects focus on gameplay, some weight story and gameplay equally, and some let gameplay serve the story. Each choice changes how the story is delivered.
when: when setting the balance for a project

text: Free mechanical experimentation supports exploration in mechanics-driven games, but it clashes with the fiction when actions make no sense in character.
when: designing a mechanics-driven experience with a narrative layer
why: the mechanics layer and the fiction layer follow different logic

text: Professional writers often reply to a story overview with proposals that reshape the entire game design.
when: after receiving a story overview

text: The narrative designer is the team's go-to person and primary advocate for the game's story, usually knows it best, and writes most narrative documentation from pitch to post-production.
A narrative designer combines writer and game designer roles, an overlap rather than their sum, aimed at telling story through mechanics; not every writer or designer fills this role.
Narrative designers need command of world-building, plot development and tempo, character design, dialogue, and how narrative draws players in via systems.
Narrative design is the craft of telling a story in a game with its own techniques, combining gameplay with visual and acoustic methods to engage players.
A writer's role can range from writing dialogue where needed to scripting the whole story. If you are not a strong writer, bring one in early and work with them throughout.
Narrative designer duties range from worldbuilding, story concepts and character profiles to dialogue, codex entries, item naming and marketing blurbs.
A narrative designer should understand interactive storytelling and the dynamics of game stories, and be able to implement story through scripting and design.

Writers and narrative designers share some tasks, including overall story development, establishing and maintaining tone, and writing content. Narrative designers also own planning, implementation, scheduling and scope tracking.
when: Dividing narrative work across a team

text: A narrative designer may originate a concept, write a pitch for another person's idea, or present a pitch directly to executives.
when: During the concept phase

text: Narrative designers write backstories and histories and work with artists and animators on character appearance and behavior.
In tabletop roleplaying, a human game master voices every non-player character and can respond to anything players do, because a real person decides each reaction.
Work with colleagues who see that narrative can improve gameplay, since that makes working with narrative staff easier for them.
Writing is usually the easiest game element to change in production.
when: A team must revise content late in development
why: Text changes need less work from other departments than gameplay or art

text: If you cannot get from one story point to another because a middle point is required, try removing that middle point.
when: story progression is blocked by a required scene

text: Changes made elsewhere in a project propagate into narrative content, so story and dialogue are revised constantly during development.
why: Rewriting words is much faster than reanimating a scene, so writing is usually the first thing changed when other parts shift.

text: A narrative designer needs four qualities: organisation and communication, understanding of the intended game experience, an ear for dialogue, and teamwork.
The role designs the world, characters and plotlines, writes dialogue, and stays involved through testing, post-production and dialogue recording.
Narrative designer responsibilities include being the go-to person for story assets, writing, designing and copyediting content, and keeping lore documentation current.
Assuming narrative design equals writing is a mistake: strong writers may lack the design skill to make story work through game rules, and dialogue skill alone does not cover the role.
why: The role combines writing with game design, and writers without design skills cannot bring story to life through game rules.

text: Original creators may lose control of a world's defining features, since adaptations can establish icons the source never intended.
why: New media open new entry points, so audience perception of the world shifts beyond what the creator intended.

text: Assuming interactivity cancels the craft of storytelling leads to poorly told stories.
why: Storytelling mechanics are innate to human communication, so interactivity does not nullify them.

text: Film and novel writers often struggle to move into games, either resisting player-driven story or resisting shared authorship in a multidisciplinary team.
why: Writers from film or novel backgrounds hold to sole authorial control, which conflicts with player agency and team collaboration.

text: Study creative writing, fiction and screenwriting conventions, past storytelling devices and what makes strong story, and keep writing to improve.
why: Much of the job is writing, so the craft rules of fiction apply directly.

text: Identify every way the game already uses storytelling, then plan with the team how to carry each one out.
when: Planning environmental narrative
why: The world speaks to players and gives them feedback, which draws them in.

text: Only players who want the story will stay for it, so story content reaches the audience that values it when dialogue is skippable.
when: When the game lets players skip dialogue.
why: Players cannot be forced to like story by being made to sit through it.

text: Story unfolds over the course of play, whereas a premise need not go anywhere.
A truth-based theme is grounded in an enduring truth about the world, which the whole game expresses through its design.
A story overview is a short document describing a game's important settings, characters and actions.
A story bible sets the rules of the story world, stating what can and cannot happen in it.
A script holds the dialog of non-player characters and may sit in a separate document or as an appendix to the design document.
A game narrative designer champions an interactive story and blends the roles of writer and game designer.
A high concept, also called a one-liner or logline, condenses a game or any single part of it into one or two sentences, giving a clear vision that is easy to communicate and remember.
The narrative pitch doc describes only a game's story, using the same structure as the game pitch doc.
when: Pitching the story of a game
why: Separates story content from the game pitch

text: A game bible, also called a universe or story bible, documents worldbuilding and lore, and may include character development, storylines, and missions or quests.
In a unified story, the problem introduced at the beginning keeps its meaning through to the ending.
Because most story is communication, games remain limited as storytelling media until characters can converse meaningfully.
Dialogue is usually written late in production. Early narrative work is talking, deciding direction, and often discarding the work and restarting.
A script stays only words until someone plans how its elements will be built into the game.
Narrative designers most often produce two kinds of document: a game-level proposal and a story-level proposal.
Games are rarely sold or funded at the pitch stage; a pitch aims to show the project deserves serious consideration and earn a meeting or second look.
when: Writing a game pitch for publishers, developers or investors

text: The game bible serves as a shared reference for level builders, systems engineers, artists, sound designers, and game writers.
Common game bible sections cover setting, timelines, history, magic and technology, cultures and societies, languages, characters, storylines and plot development, and glossary and appendices.
why: The size of the bible depends on the game's needs.

text: A core story is not always built in linear order; the ending may be known first and the rest built toward it.

Screenplay conventions include CONT'D for a speaker resuming after interruption, transitions such as CUT TO, FADE IN and FADE OUT between scenes, and Courier size 12 font; in-house formats override these.
A cinematic script can set scene, tone and dialogue together, so that location, mood and speech reinforce one another.
Story generation can use planning, and map generation can be shaped to fit a generated story.
Plan events are abstract and temporally extended, so the plan omits travel time and incidental play between events.
In narrative games with few mechanics and low challenge, balance matters less than the story, so build the core narrative first and make other elements serve it.
when: Interactive stories with light mechanics and low challenge.
why: Players expect an interactive story rather than a contest.

text: If a fictional choice sends an unwanted message, replacing it with an alternative can keep the mechanics while avoiding controversy and making the design feel novel.
when: When a story choice risks an unwanted reading.
why: The original fiction sent a bad message, and a new theme made the game feel novel.

text: Consider who players can tell their story to, and whether those listeners will actually care about it.
when: designing for player-told stories
why: Stories gain value when shared with interested listeners

text: Thriving worlds usually come from one creator's vision, because a holistic vision gives integrity; large teams rarely succeed at this.
why: A single holistic vision gives the world integrity and strength that large groups struggle to reproduce.

text: Build a transmedia world when you expect it to remain valuable over a long period.
when: Planning a world intended to last
why: Well-managed worlds can earn for decades, and children who grow up with them often pass them on to their own kids.

text: Give a short story overview to contracted writers who work far from the team.
when: writers are outside the core team
why: A short overview gives remote writers the key story elements without constant contact.

text: Unify formal and dramatic elements within the premise so the setting and the mechanics reinforce each other and heighten the experience.
why: Without a dramatic premise, outcomes stay abstract and players do not feel emotionally tied to them.

text: Narrative designers need only basic competence in level design and scripting, since nobody expects perfection in either.
Even an idealized setting needs conflict, which can come from hidden problems beneath its perfect surface.
when: Writing a utopian setting
why: Without tension beneath the surface, the story has nothing to resolve.

text: Characters met early have little emotional impact on players, so a death needs earlier history with the character to matter.
A game bible is needed for story-heavy games with many contributors; a non-story-driven game may need only a small one.
when: Deciding how large a bible to create
why: The bible is a reference for every discipline on the team and documents all worldbuilding and lore.

text: Breaking a standard convention, such as bodies vanishing, can make a late revelation land harder and implicate the player.
when: near a late revelation or emotional decision
why: The lingering consequence reinforces the revelation before a critical choice.

text: Once the first full draft is written, the outline can usually be discarded unless someone keeps it updated; check the logline and game goals instead.
when: after the first words-on-paper draft
why: Outlines left unupdated tie the team to outdated theories rather than the actual player experience.

text: Planning inside the story world matches the places and events the player actually experiences, so it is more straightforward for games than author-level planning alone.
when: Designing story generation for a game
why: Players act inside the story world, not inside the creator's mind, so in-world planning matches their experience.

text: Pick cutscenes or soft scripting by weighing which narrative beat must be conveyed against the core mechanics in play.
why: Cutscenes halt interactivity and break flow, while soft scripting keeps controls active but reduces designer control.

text: Deliberately weak short stories can serve as prompts that spark fiction ideas.
when: Searching for fiction ideas.

text: A game bible keeps details consistent across hundreds of contributors and transmedia spin-offs, making contradictions such as changed dates or eye colors visible.
when: Large teams or multiple games sharing a world
why: Without a central reference, contradictions between games go unnoticed.

text: A central theme such as 'freedom vs. security' can drive most quest design, with each quest offering a choice between the freedom of some and the safety of many.
when: Branching quest design
why: A recurring dilemma gives every choice the same weight

text: Roughly 10 percent of writing and design work is immediately relevant to players, and the remaining 90 percent serves the team and transmedia.
when: During worldbuilding, when a game may also feed other media
why: Only details that shape the player's own story experience matter to players; the rest guides the team and other media.

text: Core narrative design questions: how can story be interactive; how can players shape it; which mechanical obstacles can stand for story obstacles; what story players actually experience.
Narrative designers need working knowledge of level design, systems design, localisation, and the limits of art and animation.
why: Spoken lines need sparser writing than read text, and cutscene dialogue differs from conveyed-by-art scenes, so writers must know these limits.

text: Game content design covers narrative, quest and mission, and level design, while game system design covers mechanic, combat, encounter and rule design.
A story can be represented as a tuple of events, temporal orderings between events, and causal links, where a causal link records that one event establishes a condition needed by a later event.
Clinging to a story detail that conflicts with gameplay or technology.
when: When a story detail is fixed before the other design elements are built
why: Forcing an inflexible fantasy to fit a fixed story point is hard; the story should be crafted afterward to explain the other elements.

text: A premise that is only a thin label can leave the underlying abstraction unchanged for players.
why: A premise's first job is making the abstract formal system concrete and playable for the player.

text: Choosing a worldbuilding approach without checking the project can leave world scope or history mismatched with gameplay.
when: When choosing whether to start worldbuilding from the macro scale or from a fixed protagonist's origin
why: Genre, gameplay features, narrative type and protagonist type determine which starting point fits the project.

text: A logically sound, short plan is not automatically a good story, because soundness does not check character plausibility, such as whether a character has reason to cooperate.
when: Generating stories from logical plans
why: Planners verify causal validity but not motivation.

text: 1) Write a one- or two-paragraph synopsis of the story. 2) Write a complete outline that unfolds as the player progresses through the game.
1) Designer implements quests as empty but functional quest files. 2) Writers then write final quest texts and name creatures and objects in the area.

1) Identify the assets the script needs. 2) Plan their production with other departments. 3) Discuss required features with programmers. 4) Check the script against the overall story experience and rewrite where needed.
why: A script is more than text, so the assets and features it needs must be planned with other departments to work in the game.

text: 1) Open with four one-line items: title, genre, platform, audience; use a placeholder title if none exists. 2) Add a one-liner description, comparison, or both. 3) Add sections for story, gameplay, innovations and key selling points, and a gameplay example. Use paragraphs and bullets to stay brief.
when: Writing a game pitch doc
why: A snapshot lets readers decide quickly whether to continue

text: 1) Gather enough people to voice every character in a scene, mission, or arc. 2) Reserve a meeting room. 3) Assign each person a character. 4) Read the material aloud, working through it line by line.
when: game with voice-over
why: Hearing dialogue read aloud exposes pacing and wording problems and makes the voice actors' work easier.

text: Use in-world simulation when the story must match player actions; add author-level goals on top of world events when the game needs a narrative arc or dramatic structure.
when: Choosing a story generation approach
why: Generating stories within the story world keeps them tied to the locations and events the player actually interacts with.

text: Heroic stories share an internal structure despite different surface forms; use its stages to diagnose stories, not dictate scenes, since not all twelve need appear or in order.
why: Stages describe common patterns rather than required steps.

text: Build a story bible when many team members will propose story changes; it lets engineers, artists and designers integrate suggestions with art, technology and gameplay within shared limits.
when: many team members will propose story changes
why: Everyone can propose story ideas within the same limits, and suggestions then fit the art, technology and gameplay.

text: In the narrative pitch doc, omit genre, platform, audience and gameplay, which the game pitch doc covers; include the one-liner, fluff text, setting and story integration.
when: Writing a narrative pitch doc
why: Avoids duplicating game pitch doc content; the included parts cover story-specific content.

text: Choose a theme early for unified, effective games, especially branching or large writing teams, where it guides many small decisions, keeps coordination under tight deadlines, and avoids endless iteration.
when: Branching games or large writing teams
why: A shared theme guides many small decisions and reduces rework.

text: Use traditional storytelling techniques when writing the story parts of a game, since interactivity does not make them obsolete.
when: writing game narrative
why: Interactive design still depends on desire and emotion

text: Build an onboarding plan early in development that sorts elements by complexity and prioritizes them, so players learn efficiently.
when: Early in the development cycle, as soon as possible

text: Unite the whole team under one story vision and keep it consistent through development, sequels and add-ons.
when: Especially in large development teams
why: Without shared vision, disciplines build clashing settings, such as mismatched art styles and eras

text: Choose a world archetype early to define the core conflict before writing lore.
when: Starting worldbuilding
why: A defined core conflict gives all later lore a consistent direction.

text: Decide early how many clues and red herrings come before a mystery's solution, and what players can do after they have figured it out.
when: When the central storyline is a mystery in a large RPG written by multiple writers
why: Without planning clues early, critical-path information ends up feeling unrelated or skippable.

text: Have QA review narrative plans ahead of time, since early review can prevent months of work and complex retconning later.
when: Before narrative production
why: Plot holes found late are costly to fix

text: Check the franchise's formatting conventions first, since some games disallow bold, italics or all caps.
when: When working on an established franchise
why: Games differ in which emphasis formats they allow, so existing conventions must be respected.

text: Put scene descriptions or general actions longer than four lines before the character name, not in a parenthetical, since parentheticals are only for very short details.
when: Action runs during dialogue
why: Inline stage directions are reserved for very short, dialogue-specific details only.

text: Remember your earlier notes, since an issue you flagged may be resolved in a later scene.
why: A flagged issue may be resolved by a later scene, so it may not be a real problem.

text: Weigh each comment against your view of the whole narrative, since reviewers often see only part of it.
when: triaging feedback

text: Place a visible background threat early so players sense danger before it reaches them.
Consider what the world promotes, ignores, or challenges, since level and NPC design reflect community values and stigma even without conscious intent.
when: Designing worlds and characters
why: Ideologies can enter a design beyond conscious awareness

text: Author-centric generation may ignore plausible character intentions, while character-centric generation keeps characters consistent but rarely yields a tellable story without authorial goals; intent-driven planners combine both.
when: Choosing how story plans are generated
why: A minimum-step plan can be logically valid yet require a character to act with no motive to cooperate.

text: In films and plays the author resolves the audience's uncertainty, while in games the players resolve it, which makes traditional storytelling methods hard to integrate.
Author-oriented planning is harder in games because players act in the game world rather than in the author's head, so planned sequences can conflict with player actions.
when: Planning narrative for a player-driven game
why: Authorial plans assume events the player may not produce.

text: Hybrid tools such as loudspeaker news, dropped pamphlets, town criers, car radios, stock tickers, and overheard conversations convey world state in present tense rather than advance plot.
A narrative tool is any device that forms a piece of story in the player's mind.
Different practitioners use different names for the same narrative tools, so understanding what a tool does matters more than its name.
when: When collaborators or professionals use different terms for the same narrative tool.
why: A tool is identified by what it does, so the same device remains the same whatever label people give it.

text: Narrative design can solve some testing problems, such as supplying a story or worldbuilding explanation for a glitch.
when: When problems surface during testing.

text: Narrative designers also implement content, including scripted prototypes of interactive elements, work with external writers to make material game-relevant, keep story consistent across departments, and support marketing.
Implementation tools include quest-based narrative, mission-based narrative, environmental narrative, graphical perspective, and player attention span.
when: When using a tool does not harm the work of other disciplines.

text: Narrative tools driven by mechanics come in three types: authored plot, environmental storytelling, and emergent story.
Maintain an internal wiki that records what was, what is, and what will be in the game.
when: During development of a game with lore
why: A single record of details keeps the whole team consistent.

text: Designers can convey a pre-created story through a level, or create conditions for players to generate their own stories; leaving room for players to build the story suits the latter.
when: when writing narrative content for a game
why: Players' imagination completes the story.

text: Players build countless stories from a game's formal system elements when the system allows open-ended play, as in life simulation games.
when: Open-ended simulation games
why: Players combine system elements into their own narratives.

text: Because content must make sense in many scenarios, the same content may need to be produced several times with different outcomes or starting conditions.
when: When the project uses an open story structure in which players define their own role.

text: 1) Build the story from small story blocks. 2) Give each block a precondition that triggers it. 3) Make blocks work in almost any order.
when: When players may take the story in an unpredictable order.
why: The designer cannot predict the path a player will take.

text: 1) Let players capture snapshots of simulated characters. 2) Let them arrange the snapshots with captions. 3) Let them share the results as their own narratives.
when: Simulation games with recognizable characters.
why: Players then author stories from simulation output.

text: Open narratives are the most expensive and hardest-to-document story structure, so teams should decide how much freedom players really need before choosing them.
when: When considering an open narrative structure.
why: Every block must make sense in many scenarios.

text: Predefined character arcs play out identically each time and are reliable, while generated arcs emerge from interacting mechanics and vary with each play.
when: When deciding how character stories are produced.
why: Authored arcs are consistent; emergent arcs are unscripted but less controlled.

text: Briefly playing a game with stereotyped enemy characters from a group can increase stereotyping of that group.
when: Players are exposed to a game where a group is portrayed only as enemies.
why: Repeated portrayals can shape attitudes even after short exposure.

text: A stereotype is a cliche that uses a single concept to give a character superficial development and nothing more.
Institutions funded by a central authority can make a region a cultural center whose specialists shape the wider country.
Female characters are often defined by femininity, sexuality, or romantic interest in the player-character, and supporting women often compete for the male lead's attention.
Common female stereotypes include beauty or appearance obsession, seeking a man's affection, nurturing or supportive roles, and being less athletically gifted than men.
Trans female characters appear in games more often than trans male characters.
Reusing a fantasy-style 'tell me about your race' dialogue template for real groups turns it into offensive stereotyping.
when: Writing dialogue about real ethnic or national groups
why: Invented races are fiction, but real groups are not, so the same framing becomes a stereotype.

text: Basing a character's personality or appearance on one identity marker produces stereotypes and flat characters, and this happens to white, male, and heterosexual characters too.
when: When a character's personality or looks rest solely on gender, sexuality, or race.
why: Identity traits are only one part of a whole person, so reducing a character to one of them lacks nuance.

text: Female, minority, gay, and transgender characters are often written as stereotypes that hurt, lack agency, and lack complexity, a problem seen in all media.
Defining strong women mainly through sexuality or appearance, or making them secretly in love with the protagonist, reduces their role to romantic decoration rather than capable characters.
Gay and bisexual characters are often confined to best-friend roles defined by romantic longing for the protagonist, and spurned ones often turn villainous.
Common portrayal pitfalls include reducing trans characters to men in dresses, using shock reveals, mocking or pitying them, and casting them as unstable or villainous.
why: These portrayals ignore the complexity of trans identities.

text: Subject content perpetuating discrimination against women, BIPOC people, LGBTQIA+ people, or people with disabilities requires ethical review.
when: When a game's material reinforces damaging prejudice toward marginalized groups.
why: Stereotypes exist independently of games, so using them for entertainment without moral questioning is the concern.

text: Familiar tropes reassure players about a new IP but risk a generic result; distinctive culture avoids that but takes more worldbuilding effort.
when: When designing a fantastical world for a new property.
why: Familiar elements help players overcome their fear of the unfamiliar so they stay long enough to become invested.

text: A one-note stereotype may be all a project can afford, but a trope used to introduce a multilayered character rewards writer and player more.
when: choosing character depth under limited budget or narrative focus
why: A trope can quickly establish a character so that emotional depth can follow, instead of stopping at a flat type.

text: Gratuitous sexual content damages atmosphere and believability in serious narratives and alienates players who are uninterested in it.
when: In serious or broadly targeted games, rather than niche games made for a specific audience.

text: A university library is the strongest library source for scientific research.
An unsolved real-world case gives a writer creative license to propose their own explanation for events.
Starting research without a clear starting point feels overwhelming and unfocused; applying the six questions first gives direction.
when: Beginning research on an unfamiliar subject
why: Open-ended research without guiding questions stalls progress.

text: 1) List the six questions: who, what, when, where, why, how. 2) Use them to pick initial research topics. 3) Use them to judge whether a source is relevant. 4) Turn answers into narrower follow-up questions. 5) Repeat, moving from general to specific details.
when: Starting worldbuilding research or choosing sources
why: The questions give structure when a starting point is unclear.

text: Cross-check every fact found online, because much of what circulates there is wrong.
A retcon changes existing lore or a game's world or story so it appears planned from the start and stays consistent with what has already been published.
After a contradiction, audiences may find the characters and setting phony from then on.
when: In an episodic series whose returning audience already knows its persistent characters and world.
why: Each episode deepens audience familiarity and the sense that the world is real, so a contradiction undoes that accumulated trust.

text: A retcon that affects too many player decisions angers players and the fan base.
why: Retcons that interfere with players' earlier decisions or impressions of the world undo the agency players already used.

text: Contradictions in setting, such as animals from opposite poles appearing together, are plot holes that a typical player will notice.
when: Writing settings and worldbuilding
why: Players quickly spot logical inconsistencies

text: Weigh every retcon's pros and cons, including fan engagement and likely reaction, before making the change.
when: Considering changes to published lore
why: Retcons can alienate fans even when they fix problems.

text: Use a retcon to add new content to a sequel only when it can be explained without undoing player choices.
when: When new content is needed in a sequel.
why: Explaining new material as hidden lore lets it fit alongside published content rather than contradicting it.

text: Audiences judge whether a device is plausible against the technology they believe exists, so a premise can seem credible in its era and absurd later.
when: Premises set in an earlier or future period
why: Plausibility depends on perceived technological progress at the time

text: A discipline that is both science and divination uses observed patterns to predict events such as famine, disasters and changes in leadership.
Games can create utopias, ideal societies against which people compare other nations and cultures.
Players from a real-world location notice factual errors, and such mistakes are often posted publicly within hours of a game's release.
when: Writing about a real country, city or culture

text: Versions of a long-lived story vary in details, but the element that stays constant across versions often carries a truth to build a theme on.
when: When looking for a truth-based theme in a myth or traditional story
why: Survival across thousands of years suggests the core holds a shared truth

text: Set a fantasy era by analogy to a real historical period, which helps define the world's tone and technology level.
when: Early setting design for a fantasy world
why: A familiar historical reference quickly communicates expected technology and atmosphere.

text: When realistic behavior would bore players, choose the version that feels exciting, even if it is less accurate.
when: Tuning speed or movement in action games
why: Accurate behavior can reduce engagement

text: Trace each fantasy archetype back to its source and examine the assumptions it carries before adopting it into your world.
when: When fantasy races, gods, or place names are borrowed into a new fantasy world.
why: Unexamined assumptions get copied into the new world.

text: Ground future technology in current scientific research and theory, which makes far-fetched ideas easier for players to accept.
when: hard science fiction
why: Established science anchors the speculation.

text: Hard science fiction requires explicit, consistent rules, while science-as-magic settings stay looser but give players less rigorous grounding.
when: When choosing between hard science fiction and fantasy-based settings for magic or technology.
why: Hard sci-fi must be grounded in researched science, while fantasy settings let designers set their own magic and technology rules.

text: Dialogue grows more anxious the longer a character lingers in a hazard, signalling rising stakes and lost hit points; trigger lines at story locations so urgency builds near climactic events.
when: when a character lingers in a hazardous area; when the player nears climactic events at story locations
why: The escalation tells the player the threat is growing and that health is dropping

text: A hard script is scripted content that plays the same way every time, such as fixed character dialogue.
A soft script sets up conditions for an event and lets game systems resolve its outcome, as in combat encounters.
Soft ordering encourages a sequence of content without guaranteeing it, using skill gating, timing, and spatial arrangement.
When players design the protagonist's look, keep key story events fixed, so every version of the character shares the same central losses and stakes.
when: When players customize a protagonist's look and some background, but the plot needs set events.
why: Shared events keep the plot coherent while appearance varies.

text: Enforce a fixed content order when a setup must precede its payoff, when too many plot threads should not run concurrently, or when mechanics should be taught gradually.
when: When a setup must precede its payoff, plot threads should not run together, or mechanics should be taught gradually.
why: Narrative tools generally work better when the order of their use is controlled rather than scattered.

text: A linear backbone of fixed events can still hold meaningful decisions when choices change how an event resolves, such as fighting, dueling, or paying a costly price for peace.
when: When critical-path events are fixed in order but each can resolve in different ways.

text: Even when dialogue is hard-scripted, letting players choose which lines to say makes the same scene play out differently under different choices.
when: When conversation lines are authored in advance but the player selects which ones to say.

text: A story can suffer badly when players derail planned events.
when: In open-narrative games that let players act before the story expects.
why: Open-world players often value gameplay over story, so they accept a disjointed narrative in exchange for freedom.

text: 1) Disable movement during a scripted sequence. 2) Keep shooting or another action enabled. 3) Time the sequence so the player's action matters.
when: Semi-interactive scripted events that must break normal pacing.
why: Removing movement gives the authored sequence a controlled feel, while keeping shooting active keeps the player engaged.

text: Preserve the feeling of freedom for the participant rather than actual unlimited freedom.
why: Players already make decisions constantly while following any story, so the wish to act matters more than unlimited options.

text: Do not offer a build choice and then force a behavior pattern that contradicts it, such as placing a stealth, non-lethal player in situations requiring killing.
when: When character creation offers a playstyle such as stealth or non-lethal play.
why: Players find it hard to identify with a protagonist whose behavior was forced against their build.

text: In first-person games, direct the player's gaze toward important objects using lines, contrasting colors or lighting.
why: Camera framing conveys spatial narrative, so directing attention lets designers show what matters.

text: Soft scripting spans heavy designer control to wide freedom. Active controls let players watch, walk past, run, or interfere; partly or fully limited controls keep scripted events on track.
when: Deciding whether controls stay active during soft-scripted events.
why: Uninterrupted controls protect flow, but the designer gives up control over what the player sees.

text: Granting players more freedom increases their control, but it becomes harder for creators to orchestrate the most dramatic plot beats.
Forcing every player through full backstory tends to simplify the quest, while skippable dialogue lets story-focused players stay and gameplay-focused players reach rewards quickly.
when: Deciding whether dialogue can be skipped.
why: Repeated mandatory explanations wear down quest quality, even for QA staff.

text: Hard scripts give authorial control but cannot adapt to player choices. Soft scripts and emergence give variety but surrender that control.
why: Scripts, systems, and player decisions interact to produce many permutations, so each player's experience differs.

text: Soft scripting protects flow by keeping controls active, but designers lose control of camera angle, visibility, and player interference.
why: Player controls stay live, so the player decides position and reaction, which the designer cannot fix.

text: Demonstrating characters teach through watched action, but voice acting raises file size and cost, and extra animation can add months of work.
when: the production budget is limited
why: Voice and animation are production costs.

text: Narration that directs the player against real choices can suit comedy but undermines tension in serious experiences.
A sportscaster system interprets game events into a coherent narrative with character, tension, climax, and resolution, and can be an advanced form of recordkeeping.
Sports games such as baseball and golf produce thousands of player stories although their designers never planned those stories.
Story play moves the narrative toward a conclusion, while open-ended play, such as exploring, neither advances nor blocks the story.
Analyze dynamically generated situations through a story lens as well as mechanical criteria, since the story lens brings a large set of narrative analysis tools.
when: evaluating dynamically generated situations
why: The story lens brings a large set of narrative analysis tools that a purely mechanical review would miss.

text: Stories can be generated by simulating characters in a world and recounting events, or by planning a narrative sequence from an author's goals; game stories often need a hybrid of both.
why: Recounting simulated events yields a log that lacks the crafted pacing, tension, and arc that make a story interesting.

text: Incorporated actions can expand without limit, since each repeat invites further reactions, so close off the response scope in advance.
when: When players keep repeating a player-driven action that the game answers with reactions.
why: repeated actions demand escalating responses

text: Games find it very hard to systemically interpret the events that matter to people.

1) Pick a sample narrative item. 2) Apply an unreasonable change request, such as changing a character trait, the genre, or the climax type. 3) Revise the affected dialogue and bible sections. 4) List the other effects the change causes.
when: practising adapting under pressure
why: Extreme requests reveal how far one change spreads through narrative work.

text: For management simulations, limit story to short, non-distracting plots on the sidelines.
Simpler interactive stories with limited structure and freedom can still be enjoyable and memorable, even though the full dream has not been achieved.
The main delivery tools for linear stories are cutscenes and environmental narrative, which uses level design, supporting characters, and ambient dialogue.
when: Linear game story delivery

text: Video recordings can play on loops or from projectors, and may come from television, news, propaganda, home video, or security footage.
Use a cipher when the goal is for players to feel they are playing themselves.
why: Blank gaps in the character's background and motives let players supply their own imagination to fill them.

text: Reveal essential world knowledge that the protagonist holds early, before the player bonds with the character, since later the chance to convey it through the protagonist is lost.
when: When the protagonist must already know crucial world information, before players bond with the character.
why: Knowledge the character has but the player lacks creates a disconnect, making the character feel less like the player's own.

text: Assume players have forgotten any information they were never given a chance to comment on.
why: Exposition delivered in one block without chances to respond gets tuned out, so players learn less than from broken-up sections.

text: Keep event interpretations simple so they prompt the player's imagination; complex ones crowd out the player's own story-making.
when: When a system narrates player-caused events for the player in text.
why: Elaborate interpretations occupy the space where players would otherwise build their own story.

text: Do not present story as a separate block delivered to a passive audience; deliver it through gameplay or alongside it as often as possible.
why: Story presented as something told to the player conflicts with interactivity and weakens the player's sense of control.

text: For games built on resource management, unit movement and tactical combat, tell story as events happen, with short cutscenes at the start and end of a map.
Use short cutscenes when a story is present and sessions allow it; skip them in brief-session games without a narrative focus.
when: deciding whether a game needs cutscenes
why: Cutscenes cost session time that story-light games cannot spare.

text: Story is the sequence of events in a game, which may be linear and scripted or branching and emergent.
Storytelling covers setting, pacing, environmental narrative, gameplay and the emotions a game evokes, not only written words.
Surreal elements are common in games and must be integrated smoothly into the world.
Most newcomers find storytelling in games harder than they expect.
Narrative design can be integrated into any game genre.
Small content such as data pad entries, diary pages, ability descriptions, barks and onomatopoeia shapes the overall gameplay experience.
Games use story to different degrees: some only as backstory that sets mood and motivation, others with a narrative arc that structures the whole experience.
One game alone does not by itself change how players perceive their bodies, but cultural objectification of women has some impact on implicit biases.
Tone can vary within a genre or theme; a humorous action-adventure has more absurd situations and banter than a serious military simulation, and grim horror can include dark humor.
when: Choosing tone for a genre or theme

text: Use an unusual story element to explain unusual mechanics, and make sure it does not confuse or alienate the player.
when: unusual mechanics need story support, or the world feels flat
why: Odd story elements can justify unusual mechanics and make the world feel distinctive, but excess oddity confuses players.

text: A war-torn world centers on factional war, while a fallen world centers on hopelessness; a setting may lean toward one emphasis.
when: Deciding how dark a setting's conflict should be
why: Choosing the emphasis clarifies the tone of the world's lore.

text: The same unexpected event breaks presence in a serious world but reinforces the world's rules in a comedy world.
when: An object behaves in an unrealistic way
why: A strange event in a serious setting contrasts with reality and breaks immersion, whereas in comedy it confirms the world's odd rules.

text: Showing a strange item for the first time without setup makes it feel arbitrary.
Piling up many strange story elements makes the story puzzling; remove or merge some of them.
when: several weird elements coexist
why: Accumulated strangeness confuses players

text: Violence as a theme is legitimate; glorifying it or reinforcing discrimination for fun is the line to avoid.
when: When the game rewards an immoral action and offers no virtuous alternative.
why: Rewarding behavior that mirrors real harms to communities, such as violence against women, makes glorification especially problematic.

text: The expanded story breakout should be a beat-by-beat account of the critical path, while side stories go elsewhere.
why: A full breakout can span many pages, so it must stay limited to critical-path content.

text: Cut any content that does not change the story's progression, keeping genre and budget in mind.
why: Removing a non-essential step can make the remaining sequence of events flow more smoothly.

text: When done well, players experience the player story and world story as one narrative in which their actions matter.
when: When the two story layers are well integrated.
why: The designers' invisible thread guides players logically through the world, keeping their personal story coherent.

text: The Rod of Many Parts is a story structure in which a character gathers seven parts of a magical artifact to progress.
A story is a sequence of events that one person relates to another.
Interactive stories contain two stories: the player story, formed by the player's actions and imagination, and the world story, built by designers from environments, enemies, plot and dialogue.
Narrative types describe how a story is told in an interactive setting, specifying the elements that must be added to a story structure so it works in a game.
Convergent narratives present decisions that split the primary plot, but the splits later merge back into one thread.
Story ordering devices are levels, quests, and blockages; each makes one piece of content get consumed before another.
A narrative stage is a space where scripted story events happen, often marked by celebratory architecture or an absence of enemies.
Films with three acts, songs with intro, verses, chorus, bridge and finish, tragedy, comedy's rule of three, and roller coasters share the rising-then-resolving curve shape.
Even short personal anecdotes build tension toward a peak moment and then resolve, showing the curve at a small scale.
Games usually work within established genres such as action, space opera and Tolkienesque fantasy, where cliché is hard to avoid.
Storytelling and emotional attachment to characters are established ways to increase player engagement.
Narrative can trigger emotions that movies or books cannot.
Most story games described as non-linear are actually branching, because fully non-linear play tends to produce a muddled story.
In a linear game every player sees the same events in the same order on every playthrough, though linear does not mean simple.
