Linear games can still contain many plot twists and a strong emotional arc while most players see the same story.
A true story is an ordered sequence with beginning, middle and end, so a truly non-linear story cannot exist; designers instead create a sense of non-linearity.
Living history sites, museums, galleries, ruins, graffiti, and crime scenes are nonlinear stories that visitors explore in their own way.
Whole designs can be labyrinthine, forcing players along a single predetermined sequence of events.
Narrative descriptors, which give mechanics meaning through story, can appear as cutscenes, text, art, or packaging.
Prioritize one story-structure goal: a strong narrative thread favors linear, agency favors branching, and freedom favors open structure.
why: Too much freedom removes designers' ability to script the most impactful storyline.

text: Story pacing should match what a genre's core mechanics demand, since each genre pairs with particular storytelling techniques.
when: When the core mechanic is continuous combat and narrative must not interrupt play.
why: On-demand story lets the core loop gain depth without being halted.

text: Pair a familiar hook with a novel twist so players can enter the game and still find it fresh.
when: Choosing a premise or setting
why: Familiar elements give players a point of entry

text: Meaningful interactive experiences may blend story and game structures in untraditional ways.
why: The goal is players' actual experience, so mixing traditional and unconventional structures serves players better than a story-first focus that neglects how play feels.

text: Encode a tension curve over time that shapes what characters say and do, so the drama stays interesting across play.
when: Authoring characters in an open simulation
why: Characters with goals also weigh whether their lines fit the right tension for the current story moment, not only pursuing their own aims.

text: Knowing the whole story lets the narrative designer judge where each part belongs in the overall game.
why: Content written without the whole game in view can contradict the game's actual setting, so consistency depends on someone holding the big picture.

text: Avoid long, complex storylines spanning several questlines; let each questline tell its own small story nested inside a larger one.
when: Writing quest stories for a fast-paced hack-and-slash action RPG
why: Fast action gameplay and short attention spans favor quick, clear payoffs, so long chained plots would interrupt play and clarity.

text: Use branching when player choices should change specific plot sections but the overall story must still reach a common conclusion.
why: Unrestricted play order would muddle the story, so choices affect local sections while rejoining points keep every route on the same overall arc.

text: Choose a story structure early, based on game length, genre, studio specialty, and intended audience, since the requirements of each differ.
when: Starting a game's story planning
why: The chosen structure sets the writing workload, and it is usually settled before writers join based on length, genre, and audience.

text: If complex structure does not improve the story much and is not required by company culture or audience, enrich a linear structure with complex elements instead.
when: Deciding between linear and complex structure
why: Simpler structures avoid unnecessary cost.

text: Linear structure suits stories whose emotional beats the designer wants to control closely.
why: A fixed sequence of scenes lets a designer reproduce a film-like emotional arc in an interactive form.

text: Choose an open narrative only when the team decides players need to define themselves and find their own role in the world.
why: Open-world players often value freedom over a coherent story, accepting a disjointed narrative in exchange, and every route then needs content prepared.

text: Use the space between missions to introduce characters, conflicts, plotlines, and background.
why: Mid-mission attention belongs to the objective, so exposition is placed in the gaps where the player is not busy with the task.

text: Plan-space search suits story generation because its causal structure supports narrative analysis and resembles how people build a mental model of a story.
when: Generating stories with a planner
why: Its plan structure mirrors the mental model readers form of a story, and its search mirrors human problem solving while exposing causal links for analysis.

text: Combine structures when a single model cannot meet the game's needs; a hybrid can carry an authored start and end around an open middle, softly ordered by skill or level.
when: one structure cannot satisfy the game's needs
why: authored openings and climaxes keep control while the middle stays free

text: Put events on a clock at fixed times to order them, as time-based games do.
Build in order when a linear element such as story is central to the game's enjoyment.
why: The map works as an extension of a mostly linear upgrade chain, and the pleasure of exploring to find new paths depends on that structure.

text: Subverting an expectation set by an earlier moment, such as a familiar planet being revealed as something else, creates surprise in a quest.
when: Planning reveals in a quest
why: Matching an earlier setup and then altering one detail makes the audience's prediction fail, producing surprise.

text: Ending a scene on an escalating threat, such as a structure tilting until characters must flee, or on a sudden collapse or explosion, sets a cliffhanger that drives urgency into the next scene.
In story-driven games, narrative designers become more involved in system design and help develop narrative and other gameplay systems.
when: Story is a central pillar of the game
why: Gameplay still ranks first, but when story matters more its influence reaches the rules, so systems designers need frequent narrative input.

text: Reliable foreknowledge from a respected prediction practice can protect a society from disaster, which makes its practitioners central and revered.
when: Designing institutions built around prediction
why: Avoiding harm earns the practice social authority.

text: Each plot point becomes a gameplay and environment decision: story text specifies fights, loot, bosses and areas that level designers must realize.
when: Handing narrative to level design
why: Each plot element consumes art, design, and budget resources, so a story beat can be cut if the needed staff are unavailable.

text: Writers often structure narrative progression with the three-act structure or the twelve-stage hero's journey.
why: Story progression must keep most players' attention enough that they want to continue, and interest levels vary across players.

text: Also called rivers and lakes, this method alternates noninteractive story segments with bounded stretches of play that have a fixed goal, and is the most common videogame method.
why: Players enjoy the alternation of scripted story and bounded play, despite critics calling it not truly interactive.

text: The dramatic arc has six stages: exposition, conflict, escalation, climax, de-escalation, and dénouement.
why: It is the shared backbone of drama across media, so games adopt it as their basic shape.

text: The point of attack, the moment that disrupts the existing order, introduces the conflict and launches the plot.
why: Framing a formal system interaction as a character's action gives it dramatic meaning beyond its mechanics.

text: Multilevel storytelling lets designers choose how much freedom players get at each moment, combining linear authorship with player freedom.
when: When you want both authored story and player freedom in one game.
why: Every interactive story has a player-driven layer and a designer-built layer, which players experience as a single narrative when the designer does the work well.

text: At the broadest level, narrative types split into word-based forms, such as quest-based or mission-based narrative, and wordless forms, such as environmental narrative.
A well-crafted authored story works like a house of cards, where each nuance and line of dialogue supports later events that build toward the conclusion.
when: a linear or authored narrative
why: removing or contradicting one element can collapse the events built on it

text: In the string of pearls structure, linear arenas are where the player moves freely, joined by one-way transitions; larger arenas feel more open and smaller ones feel pointless.
when: When sizing the arenas in a string of pearls layout.

text: Forcing a story to match a structure such as the hero's journey, especially at the start, bends it and makes it hackneyed and formulaic.
when: applying a story template

text: Adding choices without unity, letting player decisions abandon the central problem, makes branching stories feel watery, weak, and disconnected.
when: When a story offers many branching paths with differing endings.
why: A story built as one unit has a beginning and ending that belong together, and branches that drop the central problem break that fit.

text: A new feature that conflicts with what the audience expects of a world may be rejected even when its creator is famous.
when: When adding a new feature to a long-lived transmedia world.
why: Audiences collectively and informally judge whether a feature fits, and the world adjusts slightly to accommodate it.

text: Assuming a linear story means player choices do not matter breaks the player's sense of agency.
when: When the narrative is linear.
why: Whether or not choices change outcomes, players need to feel they are in control of the story.

text: Linearity can seem to work against interactivity, so the designer must find ways to keep the player involved.
when: When a game's story is built as a linear structure.
why: A linear narrative in a game still differs from a film, so the player's role has to be designed in.

text: Ending a hub on a vague emotional line leaves players unable to connect their responses to the quest.
when: When a hub of NPC dialogue ends just before the player chooses a reply.
why: Players carry the final few words of a hub into their own dialogue choices, so a vague ending gives them no clear problem to respond to.

text: Players can recognize a famous scene without understanding its premise, so familiar references still need explicit context.
when: When players may lack prerequisite knowledge of a famous source.
why: Without knowing the source, players read a parody as an ordinary fantasy, so the prompt must supply the comedic context.

text: When a story feels dull, it usually lacks surprise, emotion, or both. 1) Check the story for emotion. 2) Check it for surprise. 3) Revise whichever is missing.
1) Deliver a noninteractive story segment. 2) Give the player free movement toward one fixed goal. 3) On success, unlock more story and a new challenge. 4) Repeat from step 1.
when: Authoring a story-driven game with set challenges
why: Alternating a crafted story with bursts of challenge makes further story the reward for succeeding.

text: 1) Pick one plot point from the wireframe. 2) Show the player's starting point, coming off the previous plot point. 3) Show every critical-path mission or quest. 4) Mark decision points that cause branching. 5) Show the resulting ending state or states. 6) Show optional side quests available during this plot.
when: Expanding a wireframe into a detailed flowchart

text: 1) Identify the minimum narrative players need to understand the game. 2) Push that content through dialogue or cutscenes. 3) Put optional detail in a pull layer, such as logs or discoverable mechanics.
when: When story supports a game that is not story-centric.

text: 1) Keep the top-level core story linear to serve as a template for later choices. 2) Keep it at the level of general events that drive the story. 3) Name only key characters, and mark planned multiple endings for later work.
when: For the first wireframe pass before choices and details are added.
why: Choices and consequences are designed later on top of the simple core.

text: 1) Set the motivation. 2) Provide the entry. 3) Stage the climactic battle. 4) Resolve with falling action and rewards.
when: when structuring an embedded dungeon story
why: Players anticipate the dungeon rhythm after a few tasks, and the repeated pattern drives them onward.

text: For games mixing exploration and combat, alternate slow and fast parts and add an in-depth personal story for the protagonist.
when: For action-adventure games built on exploration and combat.

text: For games built on combat, questing and item gathering, use fast on-demand storytelling in short pieces, with longer pieces during breaks.
when: For games built on combat, questing, and item gathering.
why: Story pacing is matched to the speed of the gameplay around it.

text: For games built on puzzle solving and exploration, use slow-paced storytelling delivered through puzzles and environment, varying puzzle complexity for depth.
when: For adventure games built on puzzle solving and exploration.
why: Slow pacing lets the puzzles and environment carry the story, and varying puzzle complexity deepens it.

text: Do not prioritize story over balance when players expect a fair fight.
when: Games where players expect competitive fairness.
why: Narrative priority fails when fairness is the expectation.

text: Craft the beginning and ending of a story as a single unit, so the opening problem drives the story to its resolution.
when: writing branching or open-ended narrative
why: Unity gives the story meaning

text: Make each gateway understandable and enjoyable on its own, because any one may be a player's first contact.
when: You cannot predict which gateway players will reach first
why: Any gateway may be a guest's first contact, so each must make sense and be enjoyable on its own.

text: Single-player endings should reward the hours, conflict, and struggle the player invested, built into the story rather than a generic praise animation.
when: Designing the final scenes of a single-player game
why: Generic praise wastes the payoff of long play

text: Create an invisible thread that leads players logically through the world; without it, the player story becomes muddled.
why: Players need logical guidance to make sense of their own path.

text: Make each new plot point follow narratively from what the player has just achieved, so the player feels their success caused it.
when: When designing successive plot points.
why: Causal links create a sense of agency.

text: If the quest is not yet clear, offer sympathetic, curious and dismissive options in the first hub instead.
when: The quest has not yet been explained.

text: Never build a hub from a single line, and do not make players click through a plain 'continue' button.
Open quest dialogue in media res, with the NPC already busy when the player arrives, rather than with a stiff greeting that asks for help outright.
when: Games with voiceover and ambient NPC animation.
why: Makes the quest-giver seem to have existed before the player arrived, so the problem feels believable.

text: Spread the full story across dialogues, books, journals and ambient chatter rather than placing it all in the quest text up front.
when: When players vary in how much story they want and the backstory is optional.
why: Lets players reach the story at their own pace.

text: Never place information the player needs to advance in ambient dialogue, since players can walk away before it ends; put it in a cutscene instead.
when: When the player must learn a piece of information to advance or make sense of the game.
why: Players can walk away from ambient dialogue before it finishes, so they may miss essential lines.

text: Use an opening event, such as the protagonist being separated from home, to establish a clear motivation for the player.
when: When players tend to play in short sessions without wanting to be drawn into a story.
why: One brief opening sequence can deliver the goal, the setting and hints of threats before the player commits time.

text: Start from narrative when the story's key experiences can be translated into actions the player takes.
when: Deciding whether to begin from story
why: Mechanics built from what the character actually does make the story's traits playable, rather than falling back on generic class archetypes.

text: Feedback from people who do not know writing jargon is often vague, and notes from higher-ups tend to be the worst.
when: When the team has no large writing staff, so most reviewers are non-writers.
why: Non-writers may lack writing jargon and miss how small wording changes can improve a line.

text: The first storyboard reveals what others understood and what was forgotten because it seemed obvious to the writer.
when: Reviewing a first storyboard
why: The writer's own mental image hides gaps that seem obvious to them, and others only expose them when they render it.

text: A table read is a session where a group speaks the script aloud, each person taking a character, to reveal awkward dialogue pacing, poor word choices, and clumsy sequences.
Ask how essential the story is at a given moment; consider moving it to another point or leaving it to the player's imagination.
when: When gameplay or player-to-player interaction is prevalent at that point in the game.
why: A cutscene would interrupt an activity players are engaged in and block the flow of play.

text: Restructuring a sequence so the player takes charge can address a vague note even if the commenter never notices the change.
Before investing in story, ask whether the game really needs one and why players would care about it.
when: any game, including abstract ones
why: Story only earns its place when it adds value

text: 1) Set the relative status level of each character. 2) Show status behaviors suited to each level. 3) Check that status conflicts and status changes are interesting. 4) Give the player chances to express status.
when: When making characters react to each other through status
why: People adjust their behavior according to relative status when they interact, so status shapes how characters react to one another.

text: 1) Check whether the premise is compelling and imaginative. 2) Check whether characters are unique. 3) Check whether the story drives gameplay or emerges from it. 4) Check whether players play because of the story or in spite of it. 5) Identify which story and character elements work or fail for players.
when: Evaluating a game's story
why: Premise, character and story-gameplay balance are elements that, when well executed, raise a game's appeal.

text: 1) For each part, ask what players should know afterward. 2) Check whether testers found that information easily. 3) For each section, list the mechanics taught, introduced, or heavily used, and check that testers understood them.
when: building a testing plan
why: Test plans set the quality target and tell QA what kind of feedback to expect, so every branch gets covered.

text: The narrative designer writes story material and keeps all of it consistent with the rest of the game.
why: The narrative designer knows the story best and can judge where each part fits within the whole game.

text: Audiences fill missing details with their own imagination, so suggestive text or simple displays, such as text games using descriptions and directional commands, can feel richer than literal depiction.
when: comparing written or suggestive presentation with literal depiction
why: the audience's imagination adds detail that feels personal; simple displays can still deliver rich narratives because players supply missing detail

text: Presenting text so that passages twist into a spatial map can make the narrative's world function like a memory palace.
When text is the only storytelling tool, decide which stories it can carry and how they fit fast gameplay without interrupting it.
when: When the project has no cutscenes and quest text is capped at a short length.
why: Text-only stories have to fit around quick action so that they do not interrupt play.

text: Using more environmental techniques together increases how much players engage with both the story and gameplay.
why: Interacting with objects and characters in the world reveals personality, tying story to movement and play.

text: Add text only to convey information; skip it when the environment can already explain the event.
when: When players are about to experience a major event or revelation.
why: Explanatory text or dialogue during a revelation can weaken its emotional impact.

text: Use italics for stress, emphasis, urgency, irritation or sarcasm; bold for a raised voice; all caps for shouting; and asterisks for sounds like coughs.
why: Formatting signals how a line is delivered, letting players imagine the tone and manner of speech.

text: Exaggerated movement in dramatic scenes can make players laugh and undercut tone, making balance fixes political; a deliberate comic reveal with an irritated reaction can lighten tense scenes.
when: Unintended exaggerated movement during dramatic scenes versus a deliberate comic reveal paired with an irritated reaction
why: exaggerated motion reads as comic to players

text: The circumplex is not a complete tool, but it is useful for the questions it prompts about relationships.
when: When characterizing relationships relative to one focal character.
why: Friendliness and dominance only make sense relative to another character, so plotting others against one shows relationship patterns.

text: Presence is easier to build in a cartoonish comedy world, because players expect odd rules and discovering them is part of the fun.
when: When the world is a cartoonish comedy, where players do not expect everything to work realistically.
why: Players expect odd rules and enjoy discovering them, so unexpected behavior does not break immersion.

text: Consider a comedic tone when strict realism would be too costly or when the technology cannot meet every expectation.
when: Setting the tone of a VR project with limited technical resources
why: Players in a cartoonish world don't expect everything to function, and discovering its odd rules becomes enjoyable.

text: Controlling the information players receive in a level shapes the emotion the space evokes, turning it into a memory-palace-like experience.
why: Color and contrast help symbols be distinguished from the rest of the level's information.

text: 1) Choose a reference character and place it at the center of a hostile-to-friendly and submissive-to-dominant graph. 2) Plot others relative to it by how friendly and dominant they appear. 3) Examine gaps and extremes for relationship questions, and check whether friends share quadrants.
when: When analyzing relationships in a cast or a character's relationships
why: Friendliness and dominance only mean something relative to one another, so each character is placed against the chosen reference.

text: Transmedia tells multiple stories in one world across fiction, comics or manga, film, animation, prose and games, rather than only in games, deepening the experience for devoted fans.
A transmedia world is a fantasy world reached through many media, for instance books, movies, cartoons, merchandise, and digital play, where each product is a gateway into a different part of it.
Most strong transmedia worlds began as a strong product in one medium and stayed strongest in that original medium.
Tabletop RPG sourcebooks keep a product line alive with backstory, city descriptions and monster ecology, but they mainly serve the game master rather than players.
A story can continue in other media such as novels or comics, and transmedia is a large market.
Focusing on a single medium is usually not enough for a world to succeed.
In tabletop roleplaying, the game master's descriptions and player responses drive the world, so its history depends on what players do.
1) Have technical designers set up tokens early in the design process. 2) Use tokens for forms of address, names, factions, cities and regions where the player's choices vary them.
when: Writing dialogue for games with player-chosen identity.
why: Early setup keeps lines consistent as the dialogue grows.

text: Trope subversion introduces a character with a familiar trope as shorthand, then reverses it to create an unexpected arc or plot twist.
A trope is a widely known concept, recognized by the audience, used as shorthand that sets expectations players can react to quickly.

Stereotyped roles include Middle Eastern characters as terrorists, Black, Asian, and Latino characters as gang members or prostitutes, Black male characters as imposing or tanks, East Asian characters as martial arts masters or tech nerds, and characters defined as exotic.
Cameos and fan-appreciation content reward fans and developers only when used sparingly; frequent use clutters content and lowers the value each one gives fans.
why: Fans notice every inserted detail and will find a reference however deeply it is buried.

text: A protagonist can subvert media stereotypes by giving them a non-stereotypical profession and physique, which makes players question assumptions and grow to care for them.
why: Players who see a character defy expectations tend to empathize more.

text: Before subverting a trope, understand why it is negative and research how the group has been portrayed, since that shows how to challenge those views.
when: When the trope being subverted is negative or problematic.
why: Research shows both why a trope is harmful and how to challenge the views it reinforces.

text: A trope turns into a stereotype when that trope is all the character is, with no inner world or motivations beyond it.
Successful subversion has two keys: a strong understanding of the trope being subverted, and believable characters.
why: Players from any background can relate to a character whose specific desires and goals are clearly drawn.

text: Amnesia answers every question at once but is often met with eye-rolls from players, though it rarely stops them from playing.
when: When the protagonist's past and reason for amnesia are central to the story.
why: Without any history, players can fill in the protagonist's past themselves.

text: Overusing trope subversion turns it into a gimmick.
Templates that rely on gender or other stereotypes are useful for demonstration but should not appear in finished products.
when: When the template is only meant to demonstrate a plot structure, not ship as finished content.
why: Its clichés serve as quick shorthand for showing a structure but would not work as a finished product.

text: 1) Begin with the individual character, not with a question about a demographic. 2) Study how film and other media depict and typecast marginalized populations. 3) Apply those findings to sidestep or undermine clichés.
why: Starting from a demographic tends to produce clichés; examining media representations shows where those clichés originate.

text: Do not portray a nation or ethnic group as villains for plot convenience; include sympathetic members of that group, such as a strong ally or love interest.
when: Writing antagonists tied to a real nation or ethnicity
why: Demonizing a whole group for convenience is unfair and damages credibility.

text: Use subversion only when it serves the story; if there is time to introduce a character properly, do that instead of risking a gimmick.
when: When a trope is being used as shorthand to introduce a character.
why: Overused subversion risks becoming a gimmick instead of supporting the character.

text: Overusing a cliché wears out player interest, but avoiding clichés entirely can leave players unable to relate, since nothing familiar anchors them.
when: Choosing premises or tropes; designing an offbeat setting
why: Repetition stops feeling engaging, while players need something comprehensible to understand the game.

text: Attach scripted tactical hints to enemies, such as preferred positions, and let enemies respond on their own to the player's actions.
why: Enemies still behave believably while steering them toward designer intent.

text: A character who seems to help the player but later deceives them can gain credibility within the setting and create a surprise twist.
Players dislike the hologram or vanishes-in-smoke trick for building conflict.
Open-narrative games may let players kill major villains early, which can disrupt the planned story.
why: Open-world players often value gameplay over story and accept a disjointed narrative as the cost.

text: Foreshadow future enemies in an opening scene by showing them watching from cover before they become active threats.
why: Players want short sessions, so an opening must hint at enemies and set up the story in under a minute.

text: Punish the protagonist through fiction, such as injury, loss, or hardship, rather than punishing the player with loading screens, replays, or grinding.
when: When designing consequences for failure.
why: Strong characterization makes fictional consequences meaningful without wasting player time.

text: Wireframing maps a story's information hierarchy as a flowchart, giving writers and departments a quick shared view of the structure.
Wireframes can cover a whole game's story arcs, a single quest, a multi-branch dialogue, or narrative elements balanced across the timeline.
Wireframes can be built in diagramming applications, note-taking apps, on whiteboards, on corkboards with index cards, with sticky notes, or in free online diagram tools.
1) Wireframe a high-level linear core story for a proposed game. 2) Once the structure is solid, add choices and multiple endings in a second pass.
when: Designing a new game's story structure
why: A solid linear skeleton makes branching and endings easier to add without losing coherence.

text: Use wireframes to pitch ideas, check narrative consistency, and explain structure to other departments working on missions or cinematics.
when: Pitching and coordinating narrative
why: A flowchart is understood at a glance

text: Any wireframing method is acceptable if the work can be walked through with others or shared as an easily distributed PDF.
when: Choosing a wireframing method
why: The output must be reviewable by others

text: Check the original wireframe against the scenes and cinematics currently in production, and confirm with leads whether the outline or the logline and game goals need revising.
when: during revision
why: Outlines lose value after the first draft and, without heavy upkeep, lock the writer into superseded ideas instead of how players actually experience the game.

text: Define the world's rules, including those of invented science, and apply them consistently everywhere, including edge cases; strange rules are acceptable when consistent.
why: Rules that conflict with the game's economy make the whole experience feel hollow and fake to players.

text: Worlds aimed at children can stay profitable across generations, since children often share them with their own children.
when: When child fans of the world grow into adults

text: Players and approvers do not share the same cultural references, so a reference obvious to one person may be unfamiliar to another.
when: Writing pitches that use references from films, comics or books
why: Cultural frameworks differ between readers

text: Players sense whether an analogue or direct representation rings true, and inaccurate details break immersion even when players do not consciously notice them.
when: presenting real-world-inspired content
why: Players judge believability intuitively.

text: People seek a scarce cure for themselves or family, and some hoard it to resell at high prices, which intensifies competition.
when: A life-saving resource is limited in supply
why: Desperation and profit motives both push people to accumulate it.

text: Players infer past events from what a space contains or lacks: a defensive wall suggests threat, and a hidden venue suggests violated social norms.
when: exploring a built environment
why: features imply history through their presence or absence

text: Striking player actions in confined, interactive spaces can become shared community lore that people retell.
when: arenas are tightly confined and contain interactive objects
why: Memorable moments are repeated and passed on among players.

text: Micro worldbuilding is bottom-up, starting from a small event or place (a coronation, election, central city) or a recurring event with a few protagonists, not full history, and expanding outward.
A vision is a mental picture of a desired experience, and it is not a design of the system that produces that experience.
Worldbuilding happens in two ways: crafting the rules of how a world works, and communicating those rules to players through gameplay.
A world is a set of rules, while a story is a series of events, and story sits at the top of the stack to make actions and progress matter.
Treating a game world as a place that exists apart from the game, reachable through a doorway, helps shape its identity.
World building is the deep, intricate design of a fictional world, including maps, histories, cultures, languages, governments, and economies.
Macro worldbuilding is top-down: it starts from broad concepts such as shared cultural history, world scale and world origin, and applies them down to the world.
An awakening world is newly created, with little history and many possibilities, so early player decisions can shape its development.
A changing world sits on the brink of a major change, and the story begins when that change is decided.
A newly discovered world has just been found by one or more races, creating conflict over the unknown.
A war-torn world has two or more factions almost always in conflict, and its lore reflects constant war.
A perfect (utopian) world has reached the best possible outcome, yet still needs a conflict to drive a story.
The setting section covers genre tone, time period, geography, population, and the governing body of the world.
The technology/magic section describes how the world's technology or magic works and what it is used for.
The world-altering events section records major happenings that changed the world.
The cultures/character classes section describes the peoples and classes of the world and their origins.
Lore is the full collection of material that describes and defines a world and its history.
Worldbuilding means defining the setting in which a story takes place; every game has a world, whatever its genre.
why: The setting determines a game's scope and suggests how it should look and sound.

text: World narrative is backstory conveyed through a place's landscape, construction, object placement, junk, loot, corpses and documents, conveying both information and emotion about its past and people.
A coherent fictional world follows its own rules and explores the implications of those rules, with every observable fact fitting every other across historical, physical, and cultural levels.
Worldbuilding creates fictional geography, cultures and histories that give a space meaning; geography works as a stage shaped by the cultures and relationships within it.
War settings suspend normal rules, and powerful weapons make the player a godlike arbiter of who lives and dies.
Visuals and meaningful context in games help players learn and remember facts.
Backstory that players never see still gives a game world solidity.
Adding new gateways to an existing world is difficult, and a fresh perspective on known material is especially valuable.
Well-built transmedia worlds can stay profitable for decades, far longer than most individual products.
A fantasy world can be entered through written tales, verse, music, cinema, correspondence, and in-person meetings with its central figure.
Games with underdeveloped characters or worldbuilding can still do narrative work through short, well-placed details.
Books, codices, journals, and in modern settings emails or text messages can carry lore on geography, culture, history, mythology, art, and personal experience.
The worldbuilding approach applies to any setting, whether high fantasy, space opera, or a suburban community.
Hard sci-fi research sources include journals, news sites, forums, mailing lists, professional blogs, video channels, library books and science fiction novels.
Either macro or micro worldbuilding can be applied to an original IP or a licensed property.
Dedicated wiki specialists are rare, so the narrative team usually maintains the internal wiki and its details.
All writers build a setting, and games of every genre, from action-adventure and RPGs to mobile, indie, and social games, take place in a world.
Retold stories lose the uncertainty, decision, and consequence they had in the moment, so lived experience is the deepest model for interactive story.
The strongest fictional worlds contain large amounts of implied content that is never shown.
Prior research into art and philosophy can shape a game's setting and atmosphere.
why: Deep research provides coherent thematic material.

text: Heroic landscapes are visibly deficient in support or reassurance, such as ruins or open wilderness.
Designers and team members draw characters, locations and storylines from their own lives, since real events read as authentic; frequent moves can give locations a transitory or disorienting feel.
why: Details from real events or observations read as authentic.

text: Upper design layers often change as the foundation solidifies, so a planned element may be replaced by a better one after lower layers are playtested.
when: In risky, potentially breakthrough games where foundational design elements are uncertain
why: Uncertainty compounds across dependent layers: a failure in any foundation forces changes upward, so upper designs rarely survive unchanged.

text: Worlds with intuitive shared rules need little explanation, because audiences assume a consistent universe already exists.
when: Audiences already know the category of world being shown
why: Audiences already carry shared assumptions about the category, so the world needs no explicit description.

text: Judge a world's pull by its core fantasy rather than its plot or characters, since the wish to enter the fantasy drives fans to extremes.
when: Assessing long-term fan engagement
why: The urge to inhabit the fantasy itself, rather than enjoy plot or characters, drives extreme devotion.

text: Pair an iconic, simple character with a richly detailed world; the combination is powerful.
why: A sparse character invites the audience to project itself onto it, while detail in the setting makes the world feel more foreign.

text: World building often begins with maps and histories before extending to cultures, languages, and economies.
Spread lore across the small share of the world players see, placing some in the story and some for devoted fans to find while exploring.
when: placing lore in a game world
why: Most players see only part of the world, so layered placement serves both casual and devoted players.

text: Science fiction novels are useful research sources only if the designer already knows the genre well.
Let a culture's beliefs determine where features sit in the world, such as placing taboo sites outside the city, so the layout feels logical.
Build a rich, historically grounded world, then ask which parts players need now and save the rest.
why: Unused background stays available, since a successful game can mine it again for a sequel.

text: A few research-based details can make a familiar setting feel new and keep players engaged.
when: When a game's setting is one of the familiar archetypal worlds players have seen often
why: Unfamiliar details break the predictable social dynamics and storylines that players have learned to anticipate.

text: A modern military or spy setting is easier for players to grasp than a fantasy world that opens with long histories of invented peoples.
when: Choosing between a realistic and a fantasy setting
why: Familiar contexts need no explanation, so players understand the situation quickly.

text: A micro-level world suits a game built around a single event and fixed protagonists, since the event gives the story a clear focus.
when: Choosing the scope of a game's world
why: A narrow focus keeps the world's content tied to the story.

text: Detailed background lets other writers keep new work consistent with existing lore.
when: Adding writers to an established world
why: Shared background reduces contradictions between contributors.

text: Convey recent changes in the world through NPC dialogue that implies both the shift itself and how things formerly were, rather than stating facts directly.
when: When the characters already know the basic facts the player needs

text: Pair grand, opulent spaces with gore and decay to show a society's past potential and its decline without telling players.
why: Visual contrast lets players infer history by themselves.

text: Sealed settings with unbreakable barriers and hostile residents, or stories with few characters and one restricted tool, naturally remove many unwanted actions.
when: designing a setting that must limit player actions
why: the premise itself makes escape, combat, or conversation impossible

text: Cultural symbols communicate through association: architectural styles evoke ideas such as empire, conquest, wealth, or evil, so choose styles for the meanings they carry.
why: players map styles onto familiar associations

text: Reveal world narrative in layers, from broad facts to fine detail, so a first visit feels complete while return visits add motive and method.
when: replay value matters
why: layers reward exploration without withholding the core story

text: Low population density reduces the character count the team must build and avoids the need for large crowds the technology handles poorly.
when: In a post-apocalyptic setting where the world has died out
why: Sparse population spares building a large cast and explains away crowds the engine handles poorly.

text: Writing an idea down helps the designer develop it, because the work moves out of limited working memory.
why: Writing it down frees limited mental capacity and lets the idea be developed further on the page.

text: A well-built world feels more real to an audience as the audience visits more of its gateways.
when: When the world is well constructed
why: Each medium adds to the audience's mental picture, so the world feels independent of any single product.

text: As new media open new gateways into a world, the world's features or the audience's perception of them adjust to accommodate those gateways.
why: For an imaginary world, audience perception is effectively the world itself, so it can absorb changes introduced by new media.

text: Real countries, cities and landmarks carry existing associations, so they communicate setting and motive to players quickly, without long explanation.
when: Writing a game set in a recognizable real location
why: Players already hold images of real places, which the writer can use instead of building them.

text: When a group is undervalued and lacks time, few members gain specialized training, so specialist skills concentrate in better-funded regions.
when: Designing a society with unequal access to education
why: Economic position and time limit who can pursue demanding skills.

text: When a scarce, time-limited resource lies far away, travelers grow desperate, and anyone carrying it risks robbery and violence.
when: Placing a valuable resource far from the population that needs it
why: Distance and scarcity raise both desperation and the reward for theft.

text: A disease that forces victims to return repeatedly for treatment sustains demand and keeps constant pressure on the affected community.
when: Designing an illness that needs ongoing care
why: Repeated need prevents recovery from becoming a one-time event.

text: Where wealthier areas can afford treatment and rural areas cannot, rural communities lose residents and some settlements die out.
when: Designing unequal access to care across regions
why: Lack of treatment drives population loss, which compounds economic decline.

text: A narrative designer's worldbuilding guides art and sound design by suggesting how the game should look and sound.
A world story continues whether or not any individual player takes part, so players can see events progress without their involvement.
when: MMO and persistent world design
why: Developers fix the events and outcomes in advance and players cannot alter them, so history proceeds regardless of individual participation.

text: Games can combine world story, hard scripts, and soft scripts so that the player's emergent story arises from these layers plus the player's choices, at micro and macro levels.
why: Each layer supplies material without fully scripting the result, so no two players have the same experience.

text: In a world built by many creators without formal authority, features audiences embrace persist while rejected ones disappear, so audiences effectively govern it.
when: Long-lived transmedia worlds with many contributors
why: Audience reception acts as the only selection process

text: Writing serves two audiences: players need only information affecting their experience, while the team needs wider backstory that shapes environments and designs.
when: When deciding which backstory to show players; only what gameplay or the plot requires.
why: Wider backstory shapes how artists and designers build environments, even though players never see it.

text: Licensed lore has three layers: the tip the public sees, the rest of the iceberg of insider lore, and the new stuff that is undefined and open to expansion.
when: When joining a licensed project that already has established lore and internal documentation.
why: Internal material gives the IP a uniform framework, and any expansion must stay consistent with what already exists.

text: Five world archetypes are defined by their position in history: newly created, on the brink of change, very old and ending, newly discovered, and destroyed.
Four world archetypes define the core conflict: war-torn, besieged, fallen, and perfect.
A world overview document is organized into six parts: backdrop, technology and magic, world-changing events, peoples and class types, major landmarks and sites, and conflict summary.
when: Documenting a game's world for the team
why: Each section captures a different layer of the world.

text: Like an iceberg, most worldbuilding stays hidden, and only a small visible part reaches players.
when: Planning how much lore to write
why: Hidden material supports the visible part even though players never see it.

text: Each interactive character's small story combines into a region story, and region stories combine into the overarching world storyline.
when: Designing MMO world narrative
why: Each character needs only its own small thread, so a world with many interactive characters can be built from modest pieces.

text: Contradicting established facts or rules, even through one convenient exception or an off-character episode, can damage the whole story world, since one logical break can ruin it.
when: When a world persists across episodes and returning audiences already know its characters and settings.
why: Suspension of disbelief is fragile, so a single inconsistency pulls the audience out of the experience.

text: Some elements resist theming through hardware, so a designer may need a fallback such as in-character dialogue to carry the theme.
When many independently written subclasses reach directly into engine subsystems, they duplicate code, couple to internals, break on engine changes, and bypass global invariants.
when: A large family of subclasses calls engine services without a shared layer.
why: Each subclass handles sound, effects, physics and entity management itself, so changes and invariants spread across the codebase.

text: Visions picture the best moments and skip the long walks, repeated failures, and downsides of trade-offs, so they give a misleadingly positive picture of a game.
when: When relying on a designer's vision to judge a game
why: The imagined scene selects highlights and omits the everyday experience players will have.

text: A world the designer does not feel is real shows as unimaginative work, and players sense the missing reality.
why: Gaps in grounding appear in the details

text: Fantasy worlds built from borrowed racial archetypes without their own history leave characters with no past and no life beyond the plot.
when: inexperienced designers building fantasy worlds
why: Borrowed archetypes supply traits but no reasons behind them.

text: Presuming all players want to absorb every detail of the world makes them skip dialogue, especially when characters recite long histories on every greeting.
when: When characters repeatedly deliver long world history during routine dialogue such as greetings.
why: Creators who have invested heavily in their lore find it hard to accept that others don't need it, so they overload dialogue.

text: A world made of individually interesting details that do not relate has no depth, and players cannot imagine navigating or changing it.
why: Each detail means only its surface content.

text: 1) Deliberately imagine the worst experiences the game will produce, such as frustrating failures, boring grinds, and unclear interactions. 2) Judge the design against that balanced picture.
when: When evaluating a design vision
why: Imagining the worst outcomes corrects the bias toward highlights and gives a balanced view.

text: 1) Set the rules of the world. 2) Let players explore within them. 3) Add art and writing that give interactive elements narrative context.
when: building a game world around interactive systems
why: Rules come first so that added narrative context matches what players can actually do.

text: 1) Ask what fighting techniques exist and their origins. 2) Ask where the main conflict begins and who is involved. 3) Ask what major prior event occurred and its effect. 4) Ask what makes the main cultures unique. 5) For class-based games, ask how many classes exist and their homelands.
when: before starting worldbuilding research
why: The answers direct which research topics to investigate.

text: 1) Research architecture, clothing, and local flora of the real setting. 2) Use period sources such as vintage clothing, aerial photos, and archival maps for the target era. 3) Study commercial and residential zones of the era.
when: recreating a real place in a historical period
why: Period sources capture how the place actually looked and was lived in.

text: 1) Plan how the world is introduced in the game and its objects. 2) Plan how it is extended through later DLC or transmedia. 3) Use this plan when a world holds more material than one game can show.
when: planning a long-term world
why: Planned staging spreads the world across releases.

text: 1) Research the planned world topics. 2) Write a world overview covering setting, technology or magic, world-altering events, cultures or classes, major locations, and the world's central conflict.
when: documenting a game world after initial research
why: A single overview document keeps the team's world knowledge consistent.

text: 1) Pick the setting's year. 2) Read daily contemporary newspapers across the whole period. 3) Note recurring images and topics on front pages. 4) Tune the setting's tone to what the public saw.
when: When a game's setting is a specific real historical year.
why: Daily front pages show what the public routinely saw, so public reactions reveal how characters would realistically respond.

text: 1) Check internal documentation or wikis and update outdated material. 2) Learn how the lore works from an insider's view. 3) Find undefined gaps that can be expanded, respecting existing canon.
when: When joining a licensed project that already has established lore and internal documentation.
why: Current internal material is the base later work relies on, so new content must stay consistent with canon.

text: 1) Play the existing game. 2) Research its wikis. 3) Read player discussions. Together these reveal the visible lore to build on.
when: When applying for or starting work on an existing licensed property.
why: What the public already sees is easy to reach through play, wikis and player discussion.

text: 1) Define the cultures and societies. 2) Pick locations that show them. 3) Decide whether story or player choices change the world. 4) Choose which locations show those changes and how.
why: Visible traces let players infer what changed without needing explicit explanation.

text: Use world building when a game needs long-term engagement and depth beyond individual levels, since its depth and story potential sustain interest over long periods.
when: When a game aims to hold players over long periods of play.

text: Define how your world offers something better than reality, since that is what makes it worth entering.
when: Designing a world's identity
why: The world is a separate place existing only in players' imaginations, so it must justify being entered.

text: Do not consider worldbuilding final until designers, artists and programmers have all signed off on it.
when: When art or gameplay limitations will force changes to the world vision.
why: Level and art teams build on the backstory and must turn it into buildable content, so practical constraints can force revisions.

text: In voiced games, write only lines actors can say comfortably, and check for tongue-twisters, alliteration, unintended rhymes and other mismatches between page and speech.
when: Writing dialogue for voice actors
why: Performers must speak the lines aloud, and some written patterns are hard to say even when they read fine.

text: Know the game world in depth as a real place, not merely as a plot with characters and rules.
when: After the game's fantasy, core actions and economy are already defined.
why: Rules of a place are a separate layer from plot events; they explain where a game's items and currencies come from.

text: Detailed world planning is rarely necessary, but designers must be able to answer basic questions about world history and character motivation.
when: Developing a game world

text: The imagined world need not be realistic, but must be internally consistent, since one contradiction can break suspension of disbelief and pull the guest out.
why: Immersion boosts projection and interest, and only the world's internal logic keeps the audience inside it.

text: Do not build a world around a single plotline; leave room for future stories and for audiences to imagine their own.
when: When a world must support many stories across multiple media.
why: A world with interconnected solidity beyond any one plot can withstand the pressure of many media gateways.

text: Document backstory for reference, the narrative devices that reveal the story, and subplots tied to both gameplay and the main plot.
why: Non-linear games can weave several smaller stories into the main plot, each needing an explanation of how it ties in.

text: Cover these world topics: overview, key locations, travel, mapping, scale, physical objects, weather, day and night, time, physics, and society or culture.
when: If the game involves creating a world.

text: Name items, objects and encounters so they reflect the different cultures within the game world.
Decide how world information reaches players, such as through codices or dialogue about cultures, since the delivery channel shapes what they perceive.
when: planning world delivery
why: Players experience only what the game chooses to show.

text: Make lore follow believable character behavior, for example keeping forbidden knowledge in a library rather than speaking it aloud.
when: writing characters who hold secret knowledge
why: Characters act in ways consistent with their role and culture.

text: Search every invented name for gods, cities and characters before becoming attached to it, since it may already be a famous title.
why: Even unintentional overlap with an existing famous title can create legal trouble, regardless of intent.

text: Respect existing content and lore above all when writing for a licensed game.
Deliver history through the story, so that dialogue contains only the history relevant to the current plot.
why: In books and film, history arrives through story rather than exposition.

text: Keep unused lore material and use it in a sequel if the game succeeds.
when: if the game succeeds

text: Research a real-world setting thoroughly before writing, because gaps in places, slang or customs are quickly exposed by players who know them.
when: Building a realistic setting
why: Skimped research is visible to knowledgeable players.

text: Derive place names from a local physical detail, such as a creek or a rock formation, to give each location a grounded origin story.
when: Naming settlements and landmarks
why: Names tied to real features feel believable and carry a story.

text: Give concept artists a culture and environment brief before they sketch, so designs avoid generic stereotypes and need fewer revisions.
when: Commissioning character or location concept art
why: Without background, artists fall back on generic and stereotyped designs.

text: Skip the world history section for games that are not story driven.
when: Game is not story driven

text: Each large world storyline should reveal that it is only part of a larger, unfinished arc.
when: Persistent world storytelling
why: Keeps players anticipating what comes next

text: A single shared world gives cohesion but limits strange interactions; a multiverse of distinct worlds permits odd combinations at the cost of one unified setting.
when: When the content pool keeps growing with diverse additions.
why: Building one world jointly by many creators tends to lose cohesion, whereas separate worlds let diverse contributions coexist.

text: In realistic settings, disallowing actions requires arbitrary locked doors and interface limits on communicating with strangers, which feel less honest than fiction-based restrictions.
when: the setting is realistic and open
why: nothing in the world explains the restrictions

text: Mistakes and corrections during generative map-making push the design forward, and the finished map ends up describing the world in detail.
Present very different expansions as different worlds, so a diverse card pool still feels coherent and playable.
when: When expansion sets vary greatly in flavor yet are used together in one game.
why: Presenting them as different universes makes their mixing read as creative interaction while keeping the structure playable.

text: Expansion content can bring players back to a world through supporting characters, fresh locations, or playable tales about events the main game merely alludes to.
when: planning post-release content
why: Returning to a known world builds on existing player familiarity.

text: In large MMOs, faction storylines and quest order shape each player's unique story, while lore events occur regardless of individual players.
when: In large MMOs with faction-based quests.
why: Players' order of play connects otherwise unrelated quests into a personal narrative, even though the quests have little in common.

text: 1) Start with a blank map. 2) Place each feature and give it a name. 3) For each named feature, work out its history, the society that made it, and why it exists.
when: Inventing a fictional world from scratch.
why: Naming and relating each element forces development of depth that a finished map alone would not show.

text: When levels, character models, abilities, or gameplay are finished, the story must fit them and cannot require new environments, appearances, or abilities.
when: when other content is already locked
why: Finished content cannot be changed to suit the plot.

text: Material cut from a story may reappear in places you did not expect.
Lower-budget games can replace full cinematics with animatics (comic panels or static images in sequence) with text or narration; choose formats matching budget and voice-over presence.
when: Small-budget or unvoiced games
why: Without voice-over, a game cannot rely on spoken ambient barks, so simpler visual or text formats must carry the narrative.

text: Forced points are acceptable only when budget cannot support more branching and throttle points are handled carefully.
when: When branching is limited by budget.
why: Extra narrative branches would drive up development costs, so designers constrain agency to keep production affordable.

text: Sequences cost animation time but save text, voice-over and localization work, unless an animation does not suit a culture.
why: Visual content carries meaning without words, so it avoids the writing, recording and translation work that spoken or written lines require.

text: Experience-driven PCG treats game content as the building block of experience, adapting it with learned player-experience models to guide generation, aiming at experience rather than only difficulty.
Adaptive PCG analyses player interaction and creates content from previous behaviour; it is also called personalised or player-centred.
Adaptive PCG can adjust pacing based on the player's emotional intensity to keep them engaged.
Adaptive generation can supply more of the content kind a player seems to enjoy, not only tune difficulty.
when: When the goal is supplying more of the content a player seems to like, not tuning difficulty.

text: Encounters are drawn from opponent, trap and treasure databases scaled by difficulty.
when: populating dungeons with difficulty tiers
why: Scaling lets the same database serve different difficulty layers.

text: 1) Train a model predicting an experience aspect (challenge, frustration, engagement, spatial involvement) from content. 2) Use it as the scoring step in search-driven PCG and in co-creative, human-tool PCG.
when: When generating content tailored to an individual player through search-based or mixed-initiative methods.
why: Player experience is what content is built to shape, so a learned experience predictor can score candidate content.

text: 1) Elicit emotion through varied content types. 2) Integrate content into computational models of user affect. 3) Use the content to adapt the experience.

Effective content adaptation should be tailored to individual players' experience-response patterns, fast, yet not necessarily noticeable, and rich in game context, adjustable elements and player input.
why: Efficient generation guided by player-experience models is what lets the framework meet these needs.

text: A player experience model for level fitness takes content features computed from each generated level and gameplay features estimated from the player's behaviour on a test level.
why: Behavioural features from play let fitness reflect how a specific player will experience each design.

text: Attention is limited, so generated content competes for the small share of focus a player can spare.
why: Listeners attending to one stream retain almost nothing from another, so spare attention is scarce.

text: A generator service can be wrapped in a logging decorator to log its activity on demand, without editing the generator's call sites.
when: When the systems to be logged are exposed as services.
why: Scattered log calls produce too much output mixed across systems, while a wrapper can be enabled selectively.

text: Automatic explorers are run only a couple of game minutes at most because they get stuck.
when: When an automatic character explores a level to build a log.
why: Automatic explorers tend to jam and keep revisiting one small region of the map.

text: Coverage is large in scale: an average level, crossed in about 30 seconds at full speed, may need millions of log points.
when: When the character moves randomly or the level has areas needing fine sequences of jumps.
why: Every region and link must be sampled, which pushes the required movement time up sharply.

text: Combine automatic wandering with player-recorded logs for difficult areas; this hybrid works in practice.
when: Some areas are hard to cover automatically.
why: A player combines moves accurately, so fewer samples are needed where automatic wandering fails.

text: Map each log entry to its node by localization and add a connection where the log shows direct movement between two nodes; points-of-visibility is faster but can miss links around corners.
why: Line-of-sight tests can wrongly rule out a link between nodes that sit around a corner, whereas observed moves reveal it.

text: Characters that can jump or fly must use their full movement range, or the log will miss areas.
when: When the character can jump or fly.
why: Otherwise the log would be incomplete and the pathfinding graph would miss parts of the level.

text: Locator-provided shared logger suits cross-cutting logging in deep generator steps, but hides dependencies, making bad layouts hard to trace. Use locators only for shared facilities, not generator-specific logic.
when: Logging from deeply nested dungeon or level generator steps; debugging a generator through globally reached state.
why: Hidden dependencies complicate reasoning about code, since a function's behaviour depends on state outside its body.

text: A human player combines moves well and needs fewer samples, but exhaustive exploration takes a long time, so hand creation of the graph is faster.
why: Covering every move combination by play is slow, so the graph is quicker to build by hand.

text: Agent-based digging carves corridors and places rooms by moving a digger agent through a dungeon area, producing organic layouts.
Agent-based landscape generation grows terrain through the actions of software agents, allowing finer control than fractal methods.
Beach agent parameters are flattening depth, total steps, working altitude limit, and height range.
Five agent types run concurrently and can sense and change the environment; designers set each type's count and its lifetime measured in actions.
An agent's move style is either a line in one of eight directions with a step size, or a random step.
when: encoding level-generating agents

text: An agent's trigger state can be always, terrain hit, area full or empty, or a probability.
when: encoding level-generating agents

text: An agent's boundary behaviour can be bounce, return to start, or stay within an area.
when: encoding level-generating agents

text: An agent's action type can be a single tile, a rectangle or circle outline, a filled rectangle, a platform, or a cross.
when: encoding level-generating agents

text: Use agent-based methods when designers must shape the output and control how much agents change the environment.
when: When designers must control the generated terrain, which fractal methods do not allow.
why: Agent behaviour allows finer-grained measures of terrain quality, unlike fractal methods judged mainly on efficiency.

text: In city-building games, a building's state can change with its surroundings, so a building surrounded by run-down neighbors may decline.
when: When a building's state depends on the state of its neighbourhood.
why: Cellular automaton rules update each building based on its neighbourhood.

text: Beach agents follow the shoreline in random directions and flatten sandy areas near water, with a narrow height range giving flat beaches and a wide range giving bumpy ones.
when: When the designer specifies the range of height values for beach points.
why: New heights are drawn at random within the bounds the designer sets, so the bounds' width determines flatness.

text: Coastline generation starts with the whole map below sea level, and a single agent may split into many until each covers a small part of the map.
when: In the coastline phase, before agents for other terrain features run.
why: Subdividing agents scale with map size, so each ends up responsible for a small area.

text: Agent numeric parameters include spawn time 0 to 200, period 1 to 5, tokens 10 to 80, and spawn radius 0 to 60.
when: encoding level-generating agents

text: Agent categorical parameters are move style, trigger state, boundary behaviour and action type.
when: encoding level-generating agents

text: 1) Define areas such as squares, industrial, commercial and residential zones. 2) Have agents build the road network. 3) Use extenders to search for unconnected areas. 4) Use connectors to add highways and direct roads.
when: Generating a city with agents

text: 1) Take a seed point on the edge with a direction and a token budget. 2) If the spot is already land, search along the direction for a new start. 3) Generate an attractor and a repulser point. 4) Score candidate points, favouring those nearer the attractor. 5) Raise the top-scoring point above sea level.
when: When several agents generate terrain at the same time on one map.
why: Agents work simultaneously, so a seed spot may already have been raised by another agent.

text: In answer set programming (ASP) you declare constraints and logical relations, and the solver returns every configuration that satisfies them, with each answer set treated as one content artifact.
In AnsProlog, a fact is an atom, either atomic or with parameters, that holds unconditionally.
In AnsProlog a rule has the form head :- body, variables begin with a capital letter, and each rule is implicitly universally quantified over its variables.
Stopping an optimising ASP solver early yields an approximately optimal answer rather than the true optimum.
ASP-based generation can enforce solvability and pacing through constraints, building up from perfect mazes to styled, playable dungeons.
AnsProlog resembles Prolog syntactically but has different semantics, closer to SAT and MAX-SAT.
Quantifier-free conditions over all solutions of a level can express Sigma-2-P problems, which are widely assumed harder than NP.
Use ASP when many desired properties are hard constraints that depend on game mechanics.
why: Hard constraints that rely on mechanics are stated as explicit logic, and the solver returns only content that conforms to them.

text: Game logic for ASP generation has two parts: structure (grid tiles, walls, items) and mechanics (movement, item pickup, breaking barriers).
why: Encoding the game's logic in computational logic lets it guide generation.

text: Optimising solvers emit several answer sets before reaching the optimum, so an optimum must be verified if it is strictly required.
ASP does not specify the order in which answer sets are produced, so results should not be assumed to follow any ordering.
Constraints over all solutions need an extended disjunctive solver and are far more expensive than standard ASP.
when: When a condition must be unavoidable across all alternative solutions to a level.
why: Such conditions reach a complexity class assumed much larger than NP, requiring a disjunctive solver.

text: 1) Write a choice rule that defines the broad design space of possible content. 2) Add integrity constraints, which are rules with an empty head, to reject unwanted choices.
A choice rule can bound how many facts it selects, such as requiring between 5 and 10 walls.
Search-based PCG pairs an encoding with a numeric evaluation function, whereas ASP states game logic and constraints explicitly in a symbolic language and hands them to a solver.
No graphical game generator yet produces novel, high-quality games comparable to the best generated board games.

1) Restructure data so each deal and its outcome sit in a single row. 2) Fill down formulas for as many rows as there are initial deals. 3) List every distinct initial deal, one per row. 4) Sort rows by win probability. 5) Pick the deal(s) whose win probability is nearest 0.5.
when: Designing a deal for a fair two-player card game whose outcomes can be enumerated
why: Each distinct deal is equally likely, so enumerating all deals gives exact win chances and lets a balanced deal be chosen by hand.

text: 1) Encode each complete game as a string read into rules by a compact description language. 2) Play it with a minimax agent whose evaluation function is tuned for that game. 3) Measure game length, draw rate, and rule count. 4) Combine these with a weighted sum whose weights come from successful games.
when: evolving complete game rule sets
why: Weights were derived from empirical study of traits found in successful board games.

text: 1) Specify properties that generated games must have or must avoid. 2) Solve for rule sets that meet those constraints. 3) Refine the constraints iteratively to narrow the space toward interesting regions.
why: Constraints leave a smaller space containing only satisfying games, instead of rating each game individually.

text: A cellular automaton is a grid of cells that update in discrete steps, each cell's next state depending on its own and its neighbours' previous states.
Cellular-automaton caves can be generated fast enough for runtime use, producing nine 50-by-50 rooms in under a millisecond on a modern computer.
Use cellular automata for fast, organic cave layouts generated at runtime without storing a large map, when few intuitive parameters are an advantage.
when: When endless caves must be generated at runtime and should look organic.
why: No storage medium can hold an endless cave, so content must be produced at runtime.

text: Simple neighbor-based cellular automaton rules can produce plausible-looking patterns, useful for smoothing zones, growing buildings, and laying out bases.
A cellular-automaton cave generator has four parameters: rock percentage, number of generations, neighbourhood threshold, and neighbourhood cell count.
Edge locations have fewer neighbors, so unhandled edges make cellular automaton results differ at the map border.
when: When the grid is bounded rather than infinite or toroidal.

text: Cellular automata cannot directly enforce room counts or connectivity, so such dungeon-level constraints need a separate mechanism.
why: Gameplay features are only loosely tied to the control parameters, leaving no direct handle on them.

text: Each cellular-automaton parameter affects several map features at once and links to gameplay loosely, so its effects are found by trial and error.
1) Set each cell to rock with probability r. 2) For n steps, make a cell rock if at least T neighbours are rock, otherwise free space. 3) Label rock cells bordering empty space as walls.
why: Wall cells are functionally rock but drawn differently, a purely aesthetic choice.

text: 1) If no opening connects the largest empty areas, drill a tunnel at the point of least separation. 2) Run two more automaton iterations over all rooms to smooth edges.
when: When generated rooms' exits may fail to line up with adjacent rooms' entrances.
why: Alignment of exits is not guaranteed, so the cave needs a connection between the largest open areas.

text: Decorations are sprites such as grass, trees, buildings, or paving stones, chosen by environment type.
Use chunk assembly when a library of hand-authored pieces should be combined into varied levels.
Assemble tiles from smaller scenes rather than repeating whole tiles to add variation.
why: Testers noticed whole tiles repeating, and smaller recombinable scenes are meant to reduce that.

text: Recombining hand-authored content through a simple system adds replayability while every piece stays authored.
Context-free grammars place chunks without regard to neighbours, so they can collide; conflicts arise when chunks share a height and overlap horizontally, and must be resolved afterward.
when: when chunks are placed by a context-free design grammar
why: Context-free grammars let chunks be placed independently, so they can collide.

text: Chunk assembly needs a minimally interesting chunk library, otherwise the generated levels lack versatility.
why: Library chunks and their occurrence odds act as implicit parameters that set geometry and variety.

text: Chunk assembly can be inefficient, since specific levels may need a lot of manual authoring work.
when: When the designer's mixed-initiative steering is taken too far.
why: Heavy manual steering turns generation into near-manual construction, which erodes the efficiency PCG should offer.

text: Chunk-based generation has inherent weaknesses, and repeated geometry is one of them that enemies and theme must offset.
why: Enemy placement, neighbouring geometry and level theme alter how the same chunk feels.

text: 1) Pick a random potential player location. 2) Select a library chunk compatible with the surrounding context. 3) Integrate it with existing geometry. 4) Repeat. 5) Post-process to place objects such as power-ups.
when: Combining pre-authored chunks into levels

text: Write a custom probability function giving the chance of each decoration at each tile, shaping structure, such as building blocks, streets, and perimeter towers in a town.
when: Placing decorations with designer control
why: Designer-given placement odds at any coordinate let the designer dictate the overall layout pattern.

text: Any pixel on a tile flagged as connectable can serve as an attachment point for the grapple.
when: Tile is flagged connectable
why: Per-pixel attachment makes connectability a data decision that defines valid hook surfaces.

text: Asset granularity ranges from large chunks to single art assets; coarse systems need whole sections authored, fine ones need individual assets with rules.
Constraint-driven generation places assets by designer-defined relationships, such as chairs placed around tables.
Many content generation tasks, such as puzzle levels, can be framed as constraint-solving problems and encoded in Answer Set Programming as logical rules a solver satisfies.
The game engine and non-player character behaviour are excluded from what counts as content.
A constraint solver returns rule sets that satisfy hard constraints, rather than maximising an evaluation score.
A level is rejected if any alternative solution uses the same level-design atoms but fails the concept condition.
When a generator guarantees every output is playable, playtesting can shift from checking reachability to judging fun.
when: when the generator enforces playability constraints

text: 1) Sort chunks by priority, coordinates, and type. 2) When two chunks overlap, keep the higher-priority one and remove the other. 3) Priority order is hills with bill blasters or piranha plants, blank hills, platforms with enemies, blank platforms, then coins and blocks.
when: when post-processing a generated level with overlapping chunks
why: Ordering by priority gives a deterministic way to remove conflicts.

text: Constrain generated rules to forbid unwinnable states, such as losing all objects of one kind while others remain, and to require winnable interactions.
Write theming and consistent design rules into the generator so procedurally placed elements stay architecturally coherent rather than purely random.
why: Purely random placement can break architectural coherence.

text: Constructive generation makes content in one pass, producing one output per run in a fixed, usually short time without evaluating or regenerating the output.
Cellular automata and other constructive algorithms can generate roguelike dungeons and similar 2D navigation levels.
