Constructive dungeon methods form five families: space partitioning, agent-based digging, cellular automata, generative grammars, and separate passes of probabilistic rules.
Constructionist generation pairs well with architectural pattern languages, since both assemble reusable spatial units.
Most constructive methods are simple to implement and can often be adapted from dungeons to other content types.
why: Running in fixed time without scoring output keeps these methods simple.

text: Constructive methods suit roguelikes and certain platformers where predictable, short runtime matters.
why: Output is never scored or regenerated, so runtime stays fixed.

text: Author hand-designed scenes as modular pieces for a constructionist generator to assemble at random into varied levels.

Constructive methods run in predictable, short time but offer limited control, making output hard to steer toward specific design goals, unlike search-based methods that evaluate and regenerate output.
A genotype is the encoding used for search and evaluation; a phenotype is the actual content decoded from it, and it is the phenotype that gets evaluated.
Some representations use a multi-step genotype-to-phenotype mapping, which is itself a procedural generation algorithm.
when: indirect encodings

text: A generated two-dimensional cell array is converted into a valid game map.
A heightmap's matrix width and height correspond to the x and y extents of the rectangular surface it describes.
Restrict the encoding to one genre so the generator can take shared elements as given, which raises the share of playable candidates.
when: when a high share of playable output matters more than variety
why: Genre structure supplies rules the generator would otherwise have to discover.

text: Level representations, from most direct to most indirect, are a level map, an entity list, a pattern repository, desirable properties, and a random seed.
why: Directness sets how much control the evolutionary search has over the output.

text: A candidate map can be encoded as about 100 real numbers: some give base and resource positions, others drive a turtle-style procedure that draws impassable regions.
A grid game encoding has six parts: game length, score threshold, object count per colour, movement pattern per colour, a collision-effect matrix, and a score-change matrix.
A map can be encoded by the positions of all its objects, and constraints then limit which maps are permissible.
Design a game representation so that small mutations reach nearby games, and keep its descriptions compact and readable by humans.
Indirect representations give less control and possibly sparser coverage, but cope better with the curse of dimensionality.

Features may be represented as frequencies, accumulated times, or ordered sequences; the representation shapes which experience dimensions can be captured and the search space and efficiency of content creation.
A CPPN is a pattern-generating neural network mapping position to properties such as intensity, colour, direction or particle property; it is both a content generator and an evolvable representation.
CPPNs are mainly pattern generators rather than controllers, so their terminology and use differ from ordinary networks.
Because a CPPN is a composition of functions, it can be sampled at any resolution.
CPPNs have been applied to generating images, 3D objects, and musical accompaniment.
In a CPPN, a periodic sine gives segmented repeating patterns, a Gaussian gives symmetric patterns, and linear functions give straight lines.
Querying a CPPN over many input coordinates and drawing each output as ink intensity produces an image.
A CPPN maps inputs such as position and distance from the source to outputs such as velocity and colour, and NEAT evolves its structure.
when: when generating evolved projectile or particle properties

text: Choose a CPPN's activation functions deliberately, because the set strongly determines which patterns appear.
Factory Method hides an object's constructor behind an interface that performs the lookup and returns the appropriate instance.
when: Used with lazy flyweight creation.
why: The interface can return an existing shared instance instead of always constructing a new one.

text: Pass a generator's random source or layout cache explicitly rather than reaching it through a singleton, so generation stays reproducible and testable.
when: Building a dungeon or level generator
why: Explicit inputs keep results reproducible and testable

text: Open addressing with quadratic probing can store placed room or tile records in one flat array, resolving position collisions without dynamic allocation.
when: Generating content placed at grid positions
why: Fixed storage avoids allocating a node per placed element

text: A direct-access frequency scheduler groups behaviours into one set per frequency, with one list per phase value, so each frame only the due list is run without testing each behaviour.
why: Lookup by bucket avoids per-behaviour checks, trading memory for speed.

text: 1) When a flyweight is requested, search the pool for an identical existing instance. 2) If found, return it. 3) If not, create it, add it to the pool, and return it.
when: The set of flyweights needed cannot be predicted ahead of time.
why: Creating only what is actually requested avoids building unused shared objects while still sharing identical ones.

text: When a generator accepts a partial map, fixed tiles must stay consistent with every constraint, not only the style rules.
when: Filling a partially specified dungeon

text: Rationing what the player learns about a generated dungeon, such as enemy positions or unexplored room contents, builds suspense.
when: When generating dungeons or levels where the player explores.
why: Withheld information creates anticipation of change.

text: A generated space's perceived options matter as much as its actual outcomes.
why: Engagement comes from the internal decision process, not from on-screen motion; movement without expectation and consequence leaves players disengaged.

text: RPG dungeons need lock-and-key puzzles, bonus objectives, multiple paths, and dead ends with ability-gated areas, which graph structures express more easily than strings.
when: when generating explorative adventure or dungeon levels
why: Explorative games depend on branching and gated progression.

text: Binary space partitioning recursively divides an area into smaller units, then connects them in order to form a dungeon.
Separate-pass generation adds different content types in successive passes, each using simple rules with probabilities.
Space partitioning subdivides a two- or three-dimensional space into disjoint cells, each point in exactly one cell, and applies the subdivision recursively to form a tree.
A space tree is a discrete graph of location types that records the world's size, the number of unique locations, and which locations are adjacent.
Assigning each side different starting abilities, combined with randomized maps and opponents, produces varied matchups.
Indoor visibility is typically easier to cull than outdoor visibility, so visibility analysis of generated indoor layouts is cheaper.
when: generating dungeon-style levels

text: Procedurally varied layouts with no fixed sequence face the same difficulty of shaping interest curves.
Dungeon-based games built on repeated exploration loops depend on generated space to supply new areas to explore.
when: When designing a dungeon generator for an exploration-driven game.
why: Repeated exploration needs a continuing supply of traversable space.

text: A grid dungeon phenotype is a 2D matrix where each cell is free space, wall, start, exit, monster, or treasure.
Besides layout and connectivity, dungeons also contain non-player characters, decor, and gameplay objects.
Dungeons usually consist of rooms joined by hallways, though they may also be caves or man-made structures.
A sketch-based generator with playability checks has been applied to roguelike dungeons as well as strategy maps.
In a dungeon crawler the dungeon is a core element at the base of the dependency stack, so anything that generates it sits low in that stack.
Spaces formed between solid forms can work as rooms, corridors and places to hide or chase, mapping onto room and corridor generation.
when: when generating dungeon rooms and corridors

text: Subtractive operations can produce secret passages and alcoves, while additive placement builds masses inside negative space.
when: when generating hidden spaces in dungeons

text: A dungeon can serve as the teaching level, introducing mechanics before the wider world opens.
A fixed set of same-size tiles can be combined to form maze-like layouts.
when: Generating or assembling maze layouts
why: Uniform tile sizes make the pieces interlock predictably.

text: Generated levels must provide connected spaces that characters can traverse, because movement AI depends on that connectivity to reach targets.
when: Procedurally generated levels with AI characters
why: Movement AI needs routes around obstacles and between rooms, so the level's spaces must link up for characters to reach their targets.

text: A hub with landmarks pointing in several directions sends players outward toward several rooms or corridors.
when: Laying out a central area with multiple exits
why: Visual landmarks draw the eye first and the feet after, so players follow the cues without being told where to go.

text: Room and corridor dimensions relative to avatar speed change the feel of control, so generated layout sizes matter.
when: When generating spaces for an avatar with a set movement speed.
why: Spacing defines the feel of motion; objects packed tightly against the avatar's movement make play feel clumsy and oppressive.

text: A procedural dungeon fills rooms with many monsters, items and encounters, so the variety of behavior these patterns address applies directly.
when: When a game must define many inhabitants, items and quests, each with distinct behaviour.
why: Such games need far more behaviour than typical software, and these patterns let designers define and refine it quickly while keeping it maintainable.

text: Use agent digging when organic, chaotic or cave-like layouts are wanted, or when the player should not easily predict the layout.
when: When organic, chaotic or cave-like layouts are wanted rather than neatly organised rooms.
why: The layout depends on the agent's behaviour parameters, which are hard to predict without trial and error, so results are unpredictable.

text: Use topology-first, two-stage generation when the room layout should be fixed before geometry is produced.
when: When a level's room topology must be fixed before any geometry is produced.

text: Use separate generation passes when content types can each be added with simple probabilistic rules.
Generated spaces feel insubstantial without goals and context, so a generated dungeon may need a quest or story reason for its layout and encounters.
when: Generating dungeons
why: Unanchored generated worlds lack meaning or motivation for the player, so their content becomes insubstantial and tedious.

text: Use required content when the designer must guarantee specific rooms, such as a boss area, inside a generated level.
when: designer needs fixed areas in generated dungeons
why: Required blocks keep key rooms while search fills the rest.

text: Place exits to the next level in the last layer of a breadth-first room traversal.
when: populating a dungeon graph with a multi-level structure
why: The deepest layer is the furthest point from the entrance.

text: Using see-through partitions between rooms lets a generated layout show a goal while still requiring the route to it.
when: when generating room layouts
why: The barrier shows what can be found while still blocking access, so players weigh the risk of extra exploration against better rewards.

text: Hexagonal or obtuse-angled rooms can break the blocky grid that engines and level tools impose, making generated layouts less obviously grid-based.
when: when generating room layouts
why: Non-rectangular pieces hide the square tile structure that engines favour, so the layout reads less like a grid.

text: Place dungeon entries at recurring intervals in an overworld loop, since players learn the spacing and come to anticipate each dungeon.
when: games with overworld task cycles
why: regular spacing becomes a rhythm players learn

text: Weighted nodes enlarge a node's region so that it attracts more volume.
when: When every node in a region layout can carry its own weight.

text: The number of exits a room offers directly shapes where players go next, since they choose among those exits.
when: Generating rooms and their connections
why: A door signals an invitation to open it, and players are curious, so they go through one when little else is available.

text: Forcing unavoidable time in each gameplay state produces hidden rooms off the main path that were not written in directly.
when: when the level must force detours or backtracking

text: Distances between checkpoints are computed with dynamic programming, and the fitness function scores the level using them.
when: fitness based on inter-room distances
why: Shortest-path distances capture navigational structure of the level.

text: In a blind digger, the chance of changing direction starts at 5% per dug tile and rises 5% per step in the same direction; a turn resets it to 0%.
In a blind digger, the chance of placing a room starts at 5% per dug tile and rises 5% per tile without a room; placing one resets it to 0%.
Rooms placed by a blind digger are randomly three to seven tiles wide and long.
Walls covering at least half of the map is a style threshold for dungeon layouts.
when: When discarding undesirable candidate layouts using style rules.
why: Too few wall tiles stop the map reading as a dungeon, so a minimum density filters out weak layouts.

text: A procedural dungeon generator usually has three elements: an abstract topology model, a construction method, and a geometry method, kept separate so each can be tested and changed alone.
A level can be a grid of rooms with start and end rooms, where adjacent rooms are joined by corridors.
Rooms are tile matrices drawn from predefined templates, where marked slot positions are replaced by multi-tile obstacles such as spikes or traps.
The FRP generator builds adventure modules in five stages: designer-required content, map search filling the rest, room detection, room graph construction, and room population.
when: generating pen-and-paper style adventure maps
why: Separating stages lets each be replaced by another method.

text: Digger generation halts when no room or corridor fits without intersecting existing content, even if much of the area remains empty.
when: When every candidate room or corridor would intersect existing content.

text: Agent-digger output gives no guarantee of non-overlapping rooms or full area coverage, and its parameter effects are hard to predict.
why: Parameter effects only show up after many trial runs, so the agent's output is hard to foresee.

text: Blind-digger randomness can suit caves but may make maps unplayable, so parameter balance matters.
why: Loss of control lets caves look organic and less predictable, but the same randomness can leave maps unplayable.

text: When level structure and enemy placement are stored in separate maps, both must be filled consistently or they conflict.
Isolated rooms reached only by breaking walls with limited bombs can be unreachable without that resource, so the supply must be designed for.
when: When some rooms are reachable only by destroying walls with a limited item.

text: 1) For each room, paint outward into all adjacent empty squares until none remain. 2) Record rooms reached as neighbours of the focus room. 3) Erase the paint before the next room.
when: computing room adjacency in a grid map
why: Painting one room at a time avoids wrong adjacencies. Painting all rooms at once can produce wrong adjacencies where empty space touches more than two rooms, because paint from different rooms merges.

text: 1) Generate corridors with a maze method. 2) Carve out rooms from the maze.
when: a non-search baseline for dungeon layout
why: Gives a constructive comparison point for search-based generators.

text: 1) Start at a random tile with a random direction. 2) Turn each dug tile into a corridor. 3) At each dug tile, possibly turn or place a room, decided by probability rules.
1) Start with the whole dungeon area as root. 2) Pick a random leaf and split it on a random vertical or horizontal line. 3) Repeat until cells fall below a minimum size.
1) Give each final cell one room with randomly chosen corners inside the cell. 2) Connect sibling cells bottom-up through the tree until the root's children connect.
1) Lay out rooms from templates with an entrance and exit. 2) Place obstacles with an agent that follows heuristics. 3) Place monsters with a second agent.

1) Fix the grid width and define tiles with an adjacency relation linking tiles one step apart. 2) Place the start tile at (1,1) and the finish tile at the far corner. 3) Let each tile hold at most one of wall, gem, or altar. 4) Require exactly one gem and one altar.
why: Only maps with a single gem and a single altar are wanted, so maps with other counts are rejected by integrity constraints.

text: 1) Start from the rooms containing the entrances. 2) Traverse the room graph breadth-first. 3) Place lesser challenges such as traps and small monsters in the first layer. 4) Place tougher monsters in the next layer. 5) Place treasure not carried by monsters in the layer after that.
when: populating a dungeon graph with encounters
why: Layering by graph distance gives a difficulty progression from entrance inward.

text: 1) Build a solution path from start to the level's end. 2) Add dead-end rooms around the path. 3) Place enemies and hazards after the layout is set.
Avoid narrow corridors and corners in generated dungeon layouts when camera collision is a concern.
when: camera collision is a concern
why: Camera clipping into level geometry undermines the player's sense of skill.

text: Stage generated dungeon content in passes: outline the dungeon, describe it, lay out its map, then fill the map with content.
when: Generating a dungeon

text: Procedural generators should enforce minimum passage widths and place light sources, so generated spaces stay navigable.
why: Light sources guide players through areas, and unlit spaces leave players without guidance.

text: Forbid walls on tiles two steps from an altar, and give each altar four adjacent tiles.
why: Altars are meant to sit in open surroundings, so walls are kept out of the two-step ring.

text: In the positive wall representation, keep maximum wall length small, around 5, since walls near the level diameter rarely give connected levels.
why: Walls near the level's diameter make connected levels unlikely.

text: Once a square is marked as part of a room, it is no longer empty, which keeps rooms disjoint.
when: detecting rooms in a grid map
why: Marking prevents a square from belonging to two rooms.

text: Use vertical elements such as columns or doorframes to frame generated room entrances and exits.
when: when generating room entrances and exits
why: Framing makes openings readable as transitions.

text: Blind digging gives organic, hard-to-predict layouts but can produce dead-end corridors and overlapping rooms.
why: Random digging gives little control, so it can overlap rooms and leave dead-end corridors.

text: Bridge length and branching factor are set by the designer or by a player model, controlling how long and how branched the open-ended travel between islands is.
when: Tuning open-ended travel

text: Each required block entry gives its dimensions and a pattern where 0 or 1 squares are forced, 2 squares are left to the search, and 3 squares are empty checkpoints for distance measurement.
when: designer-specified blocks in a bit-grid dungeon

text: The chromosome holds two integer loci per required object, taken modulo the side length to give candidate corner positions.
when: encoding placement of required blocks

text: Pruning removes almost all false connections, except those without an intermediate navigable region, such as a large vertical gap, which still need hand fixes.
Worth can be a difficulty level for a wandering monster, so the same above-or-below test can sort monsters by difficulty.
why: Worth is the sum of assigned benefits minus assigned costs, so it can also express monster difficulty.

text: Use a consistent reward rhythm in generated dungeons so players have a clear expectation to pursue.
when: generating a dungeon
why: expectation gives direction to exploration

text: Hazard placement logic should consider how a hazard reshapes its nearby area, not only its location.
when: generating or placing moving hazards in a procedural layout
why: A hazard's motion changes the usable space around it, so location alone misrepresents its impact.

text: Layout that produces panic can be intended, so judge a layout element's placement against the emotion the game aims for.
when: when placing obstacles or threats in horror levels
why: Panic is the intended emotion in a horror game, so a struggle caused by placement matches the design.

text: A generator can vary parameters such as a trap's fire delay per placed entity, giving each instance its own tuning.
Check that a room fits without intersecting existing rooms before placing it; this is a direct way to avoid overlaps.
After layout, scan for spots that suit a monster, such as a wall tile with empty space behind it.
A well-designed fitness function keeps encounters in an acceptable difficulty order even in branching levels, which supports replayability.
when: populating branching dungeons
why: Good ordering keeps difficulty sensible across varied layouts.

text: Dungeons that place many chests, enemies and resources across the layout so a reward is always nearby apply overlapping reward schedules and keep players motivated.
when: Generating dungeon layouts with reward placement
why: A nearby reward is always close to its payoff, which covers motivation dips.

text: In single-player games, a prospect can serve as a boss room where abilities give no advantage, forcing a fight against a powerful foe.
Place a strong special enemy in narrow spaces and regular encounters, not only as a finale, so it is harder to avoid throughout the level.
why: In narrow spaces the enemy is harder to avoid, while a large open space lets players move far away.

text: Characters can be spawned as the player moves, based on general area properties and time of day, a basic form of group LOD.
when: Large city simulations where only a few of thousands of characters are active.
why: Off-screen characters have no identity, so only area and time properties need to be used.

text: Nearby weapons, shops, and upgrade options at a spawn point shape a player's early strategy.
why: Spawn location trades gradual gearing in isolated areas against big upgrades that draw other players.

text: Taller building tiers appear where a square borders two, then three, then four buildings one size smaller.
Building a typed encounter database that enforces mood and style is a critical and substantial task.
when: planning a populated dungeon generator
why: Typed content must cover many cases before generation is credible.

text: Tactical locations may come from a tile grid or from prefabricated sections containing tactical points, but each generated location still needs its properties computed.
why: Knowing a location's position does not tell you its tactical properties.

text: 1) Place locks and keys randomly between the entrance and goal, making the first task a key and the last task a lock. 2) Assign lock-and-key relationships, allowing one lock to need several keys and keys to be reused.
when: when generating a dungeon with lock-and-key progression
why: Separating placement from relationship assignment lets two simple grammars cover many variants.

text: Prune obviously unwanted candidates, such as silent audio or meshes with disconnected triangles, before showing them to the user; pruning helps but does not guarantee wanted content.
when: When showing many candidate outputs to a human user in an interactive evolutionary system.
why: Human users are overburdened by many simultaneous on-screen items, so showing fewer candidates limits fatigue.

text: Check that a generator's reward placements provide at least one of four things: resources, access, abilities, or achievement.
when: when designing reward placement for generated dungeons
why: the four reward categories cover what a reward can give the player

text: Place healing opportunities where the player is likely to need them, and keep difficult encounters from appearing before the player is ready.
when: When generating encounters and healing for a dungeon.
why: Hit points are the core resource, and managing them depends on pacing challenges and offering healing.

text: Assign rarer good item drops to stronger encounters, so a generator can use difficulty to set reward quality.
when: Generating item rewards for encounters of varying difficulty.
why: Keeps rewards proportional to challenge.

text: Place a level-one building on empty land bordered by one water neighbor and one tree neighbor.
why: Building growth responds to the neighbouring squares, following a neighbourhood-driven rule like a cellular automaton.

text: In generated layouts, place encounters so that combat amount and spacing are both right, since correct totals with poor placement still cause fatigue.
when: Generating levels with encounters
why: Placement, not only quantity, determines whether players feel fatigue.

text: Set a range for how many enemies spawn at a location, and test the maximum against player survivability.
when: generating encounters
why: Generated sizes must remain within what the player can handle.

text: Set dungeon penalties such as level drain with awareness that they shape how carefully players approach encounters, especially when placing dangerous monsters.
when: placing dangerous encounters in dungeons
why: Penalty severity changes how players treat the same monster.

text: Content a generator places should enrich the core loop rather than obstruct it.
when: Generating content around core mechanics
why: Obstructing the core harms play

text: Necessary content, such as a level's main structure or required items, must always be correct; optional content can be discarded or swapped.
Penalise undesired structures, such as a corridor attached to a room corner, or a room linked to excessive corridors.
After a rare entity spawns, set its spawn probability to zero to guarantee only one per level.
when: Random spawning of unique entities

text: Rejecting every world where the completed predicate fails leaves only playable, styled maps.
why: Only a definition of a valid solution is needed, so the surviving worlds are those where the level can be completed.

text: Protect required content from the search's variation operators so that mutation and crossover cannot remove it.
when: evolutionary generators with fixed content
why: Variation would otherwise destroy designer-specified areas.

text: If required objects overlap, assign the worst possible fitness to that chromosome.
when: placing multiple required blocks
why: Overlap makes the layout invalid, so it is penalised heavily.

text: Tag required content for a special population engine, such as a boss room or a themed area.
when: populating a dungeon with designer-fixed areas
why: Themed rooms need encounters that differ from generic ones.

text: Keep a trigger, its target, and the resulting unlock within one screen in early generated rooms.
when: when generating early rooms that teach a trigger mechanic
why: Players can connect cause and effect when all parts are visible together.

text: Mark spawn points with a distinct token, since units reappear there after being removed.
Place spawn points so players can refresh before energetic battles.
when: In multiplayer game worlds where players enter energetic battles.

text: Spawn size: large intimate spawns let players gather resources before rejoining battles; small spawns near action with few weapons suit fast deathmatch shooters, where players lack time to linger.
when: when sizing spawn points
why: Size sets whether players pause to gather or return to action quickly.

text: Removing every overlap between chunks produces flat, uninteresting levels, so some overlaps such as hills of different heights and coins placed with hills should be deliberately allowed.
when: when designing a generated level's chunk conflict rules
why: Overlaps that create variety in height and placement make levels more interesting.

text: Evolutionary design can produce unexpected yet valid solutions that human designers would not imitate, so it can extend creativity beyond human habits.
Evolved unit logic can produce mechanics that no designer planned, where unit abilities depend on relative positions.

1) Encode strategy games in a description language paired with a playable engine. 2) Use genetic programming to evolve unit damage values toward balanced unit sets. 3) Evolve full unit logic that stays balanced while units differ in function.
when: When generating turn-based strategy games played on a discrete board.
why: A playable engine lets a human or computer play any game written in the description language.

text: A strategy game description language encodes turn-based strategy games, and a companion engine lets a human or a computer play any game written in it.
A video game description language is a compact, Python-like language for arcade-style graphical games, kept separate from its engine, metrics and generator.

A generator's rule set requires the same specification as defining every object, behavior and relationship; designers author the rules that produce rooms and encounters, not the encounters themselves.
why: In games, events arise from mechanics interacting with players during play, rather than being authored directly as in other media.

text: Generating complete games means a generator also creates rules, reward structures and graphical representation, not only levels and characters.
Each ludeme is a discrete piece of game information, and board game rules can be encoded as symbolic expressions assembled from ludemes.
Hand-set costs are rare for geometric graphs because distance is trivial to compute.
Generated rules are mechanics the team controls; the dynamics players build on them cannot be set directly.
when: Procedurally generating rules

text: Generate-and-test can produce a complete playable game design, such as a two-player board game, with no human authoring of the game.
Generators that output graphical-logic game descriptions are still preliminary, and they do not yet produce good games for humans to play.
Generation of graphical games has so far targeted classic arcade games and early home console games.
A generated level needs placement rules for demonstrations and triggers, since hand placement cannot be assumed.
when: when generating levels that use scripted demonstrations
why: generated levels lack hand-placed triggers

text: Changing board conditions each time a mode is entered is generated variation, since the same mode rules yield different spaces each time.
when: When designing one strong central mode instead of many levels with unique mechanisms.
why: Changing the board's condition on each entry creates variation without authoring new unique levels.

text: A gameplay matrix stores statistics from a player test session, such as jumps, running time, items collected and enemies killed, to drive level generation.
when: When a level generator is meant to be fun for specific players.
why: Behaviour recorded during a test level is collected into statistics the generator can use.

text: A video game description has four parts: a level mapping, a sprite set, an interaction set, and a termination set.
Build description languages for other game types, and generators that account for each type's design affordances and challenges.
when: When generating game types beyond classic arcade and early home console games.
why: Existing generation work has mostly targeted classic arcade-style games, leaving other game types largely unexplored.

text: Characters produced by a generator can draw player empathy as readily as hand-made characters.
when: Generating characters procedurally
why: Empathy is triggered by the model of a character, not by whether a designer made it

text: A generated system of interacting entities can produce character stories without a script, so generated inhabitants can carry emergent narratives.
when: When generating populated worlds with autonomous inhabitants.
why: Entity interactions create stories that no one scripted.

text: A generated level can vary emotional valence as well as tension and release, moving the player through different emotional flavors.
when: When generating levels meant to shape emotional progression.
why: Valence adds variety beyond intensity alone.

text: A level judged well in isolation can still fail in a full game, such as walls placed over the player's start point, so combined games need evaluation through automated playouts.
when: when assembling separately generated level components into a game
why: Component quality does not guarantee the components cooperate.

text: A direct evaluation function computes a quality value straight from features extracted from the generated content.
An evaluation function maps a generated artefact to a number indicating its quality, such as playability, intricacy or aesthetic appeal.
Simulation-based evaluation runs AI agents through generated content and scores it using statistics of their behaviour.
Static evaluation keeps agent behaviour fixed during play, while dynamic evaluation uses an agent that adapts as it plays.
An intensity map is a two-dimensional matrix of real numbers where each cell's value sets the brightness of the matching pixel.
A rule set is fit if playing it against itself over many trials produces a non-trivial and interesting contest.
Eight evaluation functions covered base positioning, resource positioning, and routes linking bases.
Fractal methods are usually judged on efficiency because they allow little interaction, while agent methods let designers evaluate aesthetics of the output.
Early systems scored terrain by user preference, while later work used direct fitness functions.
A board game generator can score candidate rule sets by letting computer agents play them many times and measuring how close each side's win rate is to 50/50.
when: when outcomes are hard to predict from rules alone and many playouts are affordable
why: Simulation can stand in for an evaluation function that is too complex to specify directly.

text: Expressivity metrics are domain specific: linearity and leniency suit 2D platformer levels but not weapons for a space shooter.
Top-down evaluation uses expressivity statistics on content, while bottom-up evaluation has players experience content and assess its quality.
Bottom-up assessment of generated content can use user studies, crowd-sourced data, and annotations from designers or experts.
Quality of content can be assessed along axes like originality, practicality, enjoyability, and credibility.
Quality of content may be encoded as a category, a scalar or vector (such as continuous annotation across a level), or as a relative preference.
A crowd-sourced study can supply enough data to machine-learn content evaluation functions.
Producing any content is trivial, while producing valuable content for a given goal is hard, and producing content that is both valuable and novel is harder still.
Evaluating generated content is difficult because players are subjective and diverse, designer intents vary, and algorithmic randomness and human unpredictability both affect quality.
Generators are evaluated to understand their capabilities, confirm guarantees about output, iterate toward the programmer's intent, and compare with other approaches.
Generated content can produce discoveries nobody scripted, as randomly generated dungeon games showed with emergent stories and unplanned reward scheduling.
when: when designing procedurally generated content

text: Playthroughs can show whether procedurally generated levels sustain engagement over a full run, and telemetry paired with them can explain patterns in generated content.
when: When players play through a large part or the entirety of the game.
why: Such runs expose engageability problems, such as stretches that are too easy or too difficult or goals that stop exciting players.

text: A section of a generated dungeon can be tested with about six players at once to check its usability and pacing.
when: When participants play only parts of a game rather than its entirety.
why: Usability tests focus on usability, with engageability issues also examined.

text: Denial-and-reveal tests can be run on generated layouts to check whether players actually find and follow hidden rewards.
when: validating a generated layout
why: generated layouts need the same behavioral checks as hand-built ones

text: A generator that produces challenges the player cannot judge, or responses that arrive late, works against the conditions for flow.
when: generating content for real-time play
why: Enjoyment in flow depends on the difficulty being just right for the player's current skill.

text: Test generated room layouts in gym-style rooms to see how quickly players reach or aim at exits.
when: When checking whether players can complete a specific task in the game.
why: Short task tests measure specific metrics such as completion time and number of errors.

text: Card sorting can show how players group generated items or rooms, helping define those categories.
when: When a feature is still a prototype and nothing is implemented yet.
why: The categories players naturally use to group cards reveal how to organise the system.

text: A required pass proportion of zero is common, so one passing check suffices and the search can stop early; if one check passes, most others usually pass too.
when: When the required pass proportion for connecting two regions is zero

text: Judge a procedurally generated game by how many interesting stories it produces, and improve it as a story generator.
when: Evaluating procedural generation
why: Good games keep producing event sequences so striking that players want to retell them.

text: Randomly generated layouts and placements can coexist with skill-based play when players can see the odds and have ways to respond.
when: designing procedurally generated dungeons
why: Exposed probabilities let players compute their odds, and several escape options mean no situation is unavoidable.

text: Prefer direct evaluation when relevant features can be extracted cheaply from the content; data-driven variants first require player data to build the mapping.
why: Direct functions are fast and simpler to build, while mappings to fitness may depend on models of player style or affect.

text: Measure dungeon quality directly by counting unreachable rooms.
Judge personalised content with several evaluation functions based on the imitation agent's performance statistics, checking challenge and diversity for that player.
when: When content is personalised to one individual player's play style
why: A network trained to imitate the player drives candidate tracks in their place, so performance can be measured.

text: Useful map checks include base fairness between players, room to grow each base, and equal access to nearby resources.
Genre knowledge tells the evaluator what to measure: board games are judged on balance and multiple nontrivial strategies, shooters on pace, wave patterns and difficulty progression.
when: When evaluating generated rules for one specific genre rather than games in general
why: Genre-specific design knowledge is more mature and easier to formalise than criteria for games in general.

text: Keep a human as judge when quality is subjective, unknown in advance, or too hard to formalise, and let the computer produce variants quickly.
why: Algorithms produce some content very well and very fast, but some aspects are still better made by people.

text: Combining top-down statistics with bottom-up player evaluation gives a fuller picture of what a generator does and whether it suits the designer's purpose.
Examine the generator's output distribution to claim variety, and include players to claim that they find the experience more engaging.
Judge a generated dungeon by how often it presents meaningful choices, treating decision density as a design goal for flow-sustaining games.
when: evaluating generated dungeons for flow-sustaining play
why: Flow depends on a steady supply of decisions

text: Evaluate generated spaces by what the player actually sees, treating a visible view as the unit of analysis.
When several players rate the same population, each candidate's fitness is the average of all players' scores, which smooths individual taste.
when: when multiple raters share one population

text: Simulation-based generation starts from a base environment, such as a landmass, and runs processes like erosion and climate to shape its geometry.
Of 1,389 evolved games, only 19 were judged playable and two were of exceptional quality, so most evolved output must be filtered out.
why: Each evolved rule set is screened for correctness, playability, performance and similarity before it counts as a game.

text: Direct evaluation comes in two varieties: theory-driven, built from qualitative theories of player experience and intuition; and data-driven, approximating content-to-affect mappings from questionnaires or physiological measurements.
Evaluation functions fall into three classes: direct, computed from content features; simulation-based, scored by AI agents playing the content; and interactive, with a human in the loop.
Aesthetic measures for generated games fall into three groups: intrinsic (from rules alone), playability (from self-play outcomes), and quality (from trends in play). The system used 57 measures.
Minimal variation yields non-expressive output, while random assembly of components yields senseless, unplayable content.
Automatic generation can yield compelling play while producing content with weak visual appeal.
An accessibility fitness that rewards smooth, vehicle-traversable ground drives evolution toward completely flat maps unless it is balanced by other measures.
why: Counterbalancing terms such as obstacle edge length stop flatness from dominating.

text: Many evolved card game candidates turn out unplayable, so playability must be enforced in the encoding or the evaluation.
when: When evolving card games in a description language that spans several known card games

text: Measures computed from rules alone did not improve agreement with human rankings, because a game's true character appears only in play.
why: A game's true character only emerges during actual play, so rule-only measures fail to track human judgments.

text: Quality estimates from play trends are less reliable than playability measures, so they should not be trusted on their own.
Treating connectivity alone as a sign of level quality is a mistake, since connected levels can still be poor.
when: When random levels are generated sparsely so that nearly all of them are connected
why: Sparse starts yield highly connected levels, and that over-connection makes them weak even though they are connected.

text: Choosing a gameplay metric imports the designer's assumptions into evolution, and different metrics, such as survival time or shots fired, favour different content.
when: When player preference is inferred from in-game actions instead of explicit selection
why: The mapping from actions to preference is ambiguous, so the chosen action measure encodes designer assumptions.

text: Assuming human and computer always have equal say is naive, because initiative is usually distributed unevenly.
when: When humans and software co-create content in a mixed-initiative system
why: Initiative shifts between them: sometimes the human brings the idea and the computer supports, and sometimes the reverse.

text: Distance-based fitness prediction depends on how distance is defined, which biases the search, and long sprints amplify the error.
when: When offline evolution estimates fitness of unseen individuals from user-rated ones by distance
why: Distance assumptions could bias the search, so offline runs are kept to a few generations before new feedback.

text: Using a metric highly correlated with an input parameter, such as difficulty as both input and metric, gives only confirmatory results and a false sense of insight.
when: When a generator takes parameters that could also serve as evaluation metrics
why: Expressive range evaluation aims to reveal emergent properties, which input-correlated metrics can only confirm.

text: A hot spot in an expressive range chart reveals a generator bias, but the designer must still ask why the bias exists.
when: When an expressive range heatmap shows concentrated clusters of output
why: Hot spots reveal biased output, and the designer must then uncover what causes that bias.

text: Implicit quality estimates assume that content which is selected, used, experienced or altered more during play is more valuable, which may not hold.
when: When content quality is inferred from how players select, use, or alter it
why: Direct end-user assessment has a core limitation: players may act as random content evaluators.

text: Use steering behaviors, a wander behavior plus obstacle and wall avoidance, to cover the level automatically, restarting from random locations and running only briefly.
when: Generating log data automatically.
why: Explorers often get stuck and repeatedly cover a small region; restarts reduce stuck errors.

text: 1) Pick a random sequence from a precomputed table. 2) Compute the maximum streak of it and of a human-entered sequence. 3) Guess that the longer-streak sequence is the random one. 4) Break ties arbitrarily.
when: judging whether a human-invented sequence looks random

text: 1) Generate a level that fits a design theory. 2) Let the designer edit it. 3) Let the designer add constraints. 4) Regenerate only the affected portions of the level.
why: Alternating generation and human editing lets the designer modify output and add constraints for regeneration.

text: 1) Generate a candidate. 2) Test it against the criteria. 3) Repeat until a satisfactory solution appears.
1) Run generated code and catch runtime exceptions. 2) Give mechanics that throw errors a zero or low fitness. 3) Test the remaining mechanics on a level that is unsolvable without them.
when: when evaluating automatically generated game code
why: Catching errors lets the search continue past broken mechanics.

text: 1) Pick metrics as axes. 2) Generate many pieces. 3) Score each piece on the chosen metrics. 4) Plot the results as a histogram or heatmap.
when: When a generator can output far more content than a person could review by eye
why: Heatmaps of scored samples expose biases that viewing a handful of outputs would miss.

text: Choose qualities to optimise and how to formulate them; building an evaluation function is hardest, since a poor one makes search optimise the wrong thing or find no good content.
Give generated levels and content a written description that other team members can check against, since level designers use the document to see how each level fits the overall structure.
when: Content is produced by a generator
why: A written design document keeps the overall vision communicated across a large, complex team.

text: Generated content should not look machine-made; aim for believable output.
Measure expressive range by a quality relevant to player experience, not by raw counts of possible configurations.
why: Raw configuration counts ignore how output plays, while player-relevant qualities reflect the experience itself.

text: Evaluate generated rule sets as whole games, using evaluation functions or constraints, rather than judging isolated artefacts.
when: When generating an entire game rather than content for an already existing game

text: Evaluate an evolved content generator using many samples of its output, not a single artefact.
when: evolving generators with highly variable output
why: One sample can miss the generator's real range.

text: Everything a human can produce must also be something the computer can generate alone, so the set of available choices must be meaningful.
when: In mixed-initiative PCG systems where a human co-creates content with the computer.
why: Expressiveness is what lets the system offer a meaningful range of choices to the human collaborator.

text: Include designer constraints, hard or soft, in quality evaluation of generated content.
Expressivity and diversity compete with reliability, since broader output makes consistent quality harder to guarantee, and measuring expressivity is non-trivial.
when: When content must vary without looking like minor variations on one theme.
why: Fully random piece assembly produces nonsensical, unplayable levels, while a fixed output lacks variety.

text: Input-linked metrics only confirm a generator honours its parameters; independent metrics can reveal emergent behaviour but are harder to choose, so pick them as far from inputs as possible.
when: When running an expressive range evaluation to reveal a generator's emergent properties.
why: Metrics that mirror inputs only confirm what was built in, while independent metrics can reveal emergent behaviour.

text: Direct evaluation is fast and often easy to implement, but some aspects of content are hard to express as direct features.
when: When some element of game content resists being captured by a straightforward scoring formula.
why: Direct functions score features extracted from the content itself, so no simulation is needed, but some aspects have no easy direct feature.

text: Some map objectives conflict, so no single map maximises them all, yet certain objective combinations still give interesting, reasonably fair maps.
when: When combining several map evaluation objectives that partially conflict with each other.
why: Some objectives pull in opposite directions, so no single map can satisfy all of them at once.

text: Direct evaluation is fast, simulation-based evaluation needs an AI to play part of the game, and interactive evaluation needs a human in the loop.
A representation must be expressive enough for truly novel games yet searchable, with local neighbourhoods and a density of good games; more expressivity makes search harder.
when: When generating novel games with a game description language.
why: Searching needs nearby representations to behave similarly and enough good games scattered through the space.

text: Expressive range heatmaps support claims about variety, bias, and frequency, but they are aids for understanding and not perfect proofs of variety.
when: When a generator can produce thousands or millions of distinct levels.

text: A generator needs to supply only the details a player cannot reasonably infer from what is already present.
when: when generating content for a player to experience
why: Players fill unstated gaps themselves, so surplus detail is wasted effort.

text: A generator that creates many variants from one base type should keep variant stats in data rather than in a separate subclass per variant.
when: Producing many monster or content variants procedurally.
why: Hard-coded per-variant classes would reproduce the recompile bottleneck at generation scale.

text: When found items supply most of the power, the base values of items a generator places largely set the power curve.
when: generating items for a progression game
why: Generated base values are the main source of power differences.

text: A Gaussian distribution clusters decorations near a location's centre, so neighbouring locations blend into each other.
when: Placing decorations in a location
why: Decorations cluster toward the centre, so decorations from adjacent locations spill over and blend at their borders.

text: 1) Draw the outermost layer first. 2) Draw each inner layer on top, scaled by depth. 3) Use one network for all layers so they share regularities.
when: generating multi-layer shapes with one CPPN
why: Shared network regularities mirror how real layered structures relate.

text: Give each procedurally generated object category a representation and treatment that together imply its behavior, and check each category's behavior against that implication.
when: when a generator produces multiple object categories
why: Each category sets its own expectations; unstated behavioral expectations lead to dissonance.

text: Generated assets should share one stylistic language across visuals and sound so procedural content feels like part of one world.
when: when generating visual and audio assets procedurally
why: Consistent style across senses keeps generated content believable

text: Set a generator's reward density deliberately, because randomly generated spaces with frequent loot drops are a direct source of the acquisition emotion.
when: When generating dungeons or levels with loot.
why: Reward density directly shapes the feeling of acquisition.

text: Give generated interactive objects a look distinct from static walls and props so players can identify them.
when: when generating dungeon or level content

text: A generative grammar is a finite set of recursive production rules that expand an axiom into larger structures until only terminal symbols remain; sampling it yields new instances.
A graph grammar applies generative grammar rules to graphs with graph nodes as terminal symbols; each node on a rule's left side is matched and replaced individually.
A formal grammar consists of rules that rewrite strings beginning at a start symbol; each rule swaps a left-hand side pattern for a right-hand side.

A deterministic grammar has exactly one applicable rule per symbol, while a nondeterministic grammar may have several, so a selection method such as random choice, per-rule probability, or parameters is needed.
An L-system is a grammar that expands all symbols simultaneously, producing strings with repeating structure.
A mission graph grammar alphabet includes a start node as axiom, entrance nodes, task nodes, goal nodes that end the level, lock nodes needing a key, key nodes, and non-terminal task nodes.
An axiom is the seed string from which an L-system begins its rewriting.
Mission grammars were the first grammar approach to give dungeon generation gameplay-based control.
A player-action grammar approach was shown on a single game to produce playable three-dimensional dungeon levels.
Changing rule details or turn angles generates different but still plant-like forms from the same grammar structure.
Evolved L-system plants can be scored by height (phototropism), symmetry, exposed surface area, structural stability, and proportion of branching points.
By convention, uppercase symbols are nonterminals that are rewritten further, and lowercase symbols are terminals that are final.
Graph grammars and space grammars extend grammar-based generation beyond strings to level structures and quest structures.

A grammar-based level generator gives a simple way to describe level structure, open-ended size, exploration beyond designer imagination, built-in domain knowledge, and easy generalisation to other games.
L-systems were introduced by a biologist in 1968 to model the growth of plants and algae.
A two-rule yeast-growth L-system produces strings whose lengths follow the Fibonacci sequence, with each string being the concatenation of the two strings before it.
Even very simple L-system rules yield highly complex yet regular strings, which makes them useful for procedural content generation.
Starting from axiom F, replacing each F with F+F-F-F+F repeatedly and reading the result as turtle commands draws a snowflake-edge fractal curve.
L-system strings grow quickly with each expansion, so the first expansion of the Koch rule already exceeds a dozen symbols.
Patterns are interchangeable spatial solutions to human experience problems, which suits them to procedural assembly.
Generative grammars can capture higher-level dungeon design aspects.
Use grammar generation with gameplay-concept control when designers should steer dungeons through difficulty, fun or player actions rather than geometry alone.
when: When designers want to steer dungeon generation through gameplay concepts instead of geometry alone.

text: Use bracketing when a shape branches and cannot be drawn as one continuous line.
when: When a branch must be finished before the drawing returns to the stem.
why: Bracket symbols act as push and pop on a stack, saving and restoring drawing position and orientation.

text: Use nondeterministic grammars with probabilities when output variation is wanted; use deterministic grammars when output must be fully predictable.
why: Each symbol has a single applicable rule, so no choice is made when rewriting.

text: If existing buildings never degrade on their own, the layout stays fixed until the player removes buildings.
when: building systems with growth but no decay
why: Buildings are not tied to the neighbours that generated them, so removing those neighbours leaves them in place.

text: Bracket symbols act as ordinary symbols during rewriting but as stack operations during drawing: [ saves the turtle's position and heading, and ] restores the most recent saved state.
when: Drawing branching L-system strings with a turtle
why: The stack is last-in, first-out, so branches return to the most recent fork

text: Grammars expand an axiom through production rules to generate plant structures, action-adventure levels, physical structures and missions; the grammars themselves can be evolved.

A design grammar specifying the type, position and properties of items or level components can be evolved with grammatical evolution for a more expressive representation; a readable, editable grammar lets designers adjust generation.
why: Describing each item's type, position and properties gives richer structure than a few fixed parameters.

text: A hierarchical game grammar with options for board layout, movement, capture and win conditions can generate chess-like games by stochastic sampling.
why: Sampling the grammar builds each game directly, and basic checks then filter out unplayable ones.

text: Large patterns break into chunks, and chunks break into components, so generation can work at the matching scale.
why: Knowing how each piece works lets systems be built at different complexity levels, matched to asset granularity.

text: Hand-written, ad hoc grammar rules and parameters must be rewritten for each new game, so they do not transfer easily.
when: Generalizing a hard-coded grammar approach to many games or goals
why: Its rules and parameters are fixed in code, so each new target demands fresh inputs and rules.

text: Applying L-system rules sequentially instead of in parallel gives a different result, so the rewriting order must match the intended model.
when: when expanding an L-system string
why: Sequential updates let newly written symbols be rewritten again in the same pass.

text: A single grammar that generates everything at once is hard to design and nearly impossible to debug and maintain.
when: when generating expressive content with many interacting elements
why: All decisions are tangled together in one rule set.

text: Loosely written constraints can yield locally plausible levels that are nonetheless unplayable.
why: Sample outputs reveal unexpected results, so the desired properties must be revised after seeing them.

text: 1) Designer writes constraints in a vocabulary of player actions. 2) Constraints become a generative graph grammar. 3) Sample a player-action graph. 4) Map it to a dungeon layout. 5) Generate room and hallway geometry.
why: Grammar rules that drive generation are hard for designers to read and control, so designers state constraints in player-action terms.

text: 1) Add symbols that rotate the turtle around its drawing axis. 2) Keep bracket push and pop behaviour unchanged. 3) Draw the expanded string in three dimensions.
when: Extending a bracketed L-system to 3D
why: Rotation symbols about the drawing axis extend the same branching principle to three dimensions.

text: 1) Write an L-system whose rules encode branching structure. 2) Expand it to the desired depth. 3) Interpret the resulting string as drawing instructions.
when: when generating a tree or bush procedurally
why: Drawing instructions turn the symbolic string into visible plant geometry.

text: Design a game description language expressing whole games in a few lines, covering known games and unexplored ones between them, so search reaches new designs.
why: Compact descriptions covering known games implicitly include the designs lying between them, which search can reach.

text: Suggestions can be evolved to maximise balance and exploration objectives, or to diverge from the current sketch through feasible-infeasible novelty search.
Treat how often players choose an option as revealed preference, so usage counts can guide which content evolves.
when: when selecting content from player behaviour
why: Players are assumed to use options they dislike less.

text: Start interactive evolution from a saved good candidate or a small seed network, so the user begins in a good region of the search space.
why: Saved candidates already sit in a good region, so variations from them are more likely meaningful than from random starts.

text: Limit interactive evolution populations to about 10 or 20 individuals to speed convergence and reduce fatigue.
when: When large populations make each generation slow to appear to the user
why: Long idle waits between sets of content add fatigue, and small populations shorten convergence.

text: Prune generated content with selection mechanisms before players see it, since treating players as random evaluators is a limitation.
when: When an automatic generator can output massive amounts of content
why: Judging unfiltered output makes players act as random evaluators, a core limitation of user-based assessment.

text: When powerups change game variables and exact values are evolved, the system can make fine distinctions, such as jump heights of 120 versus 121 pixels.
when: when generating numeric game variables by search
why: Evolving exact values rather than choosing from hand-picked options allows very fine tuning.

text: A computer that speaks is not thereby mixed-initiative; PCG systems give it only speaker initiative, none sharing task or outcome initiative, so humans keep control of problem and solution.
why: Such systems reserve choice of the design topic for the human, so the computer only contributes to the dialogue.

text: Showing only the highest-fitness items in interactive evolution causes stagnation, so display should keep variety.
why: Fitness there comes mostly from user picks, so the top individuals end up nearly identical to earlier ones.

text: 1) Define a base breed with shared attributes. 2) Define variant breeds that inherit unchanged attributes and override only what differs. 3) Edit the base to update the whole family.
when: generating or authoring families of related enemy types
why: Shared tuning lives in one place, so one edit propagates to all variants.

text: 1) Represent tracks as segment lists with smooth curves joined at control points. 2) Let players play and rate a population each generation. 3) Use ratings as fitness and evolve the next generation.
Levels forecast to be more absorbing, irritating or demanding for a given player receive higher fitness when experience predictions feed the fitness function.
when: When generating content tailored to one specific player's predicted experience
why: The predicted emotional state is used directly as fitness, so search climbs toward the predicted experience.

text: Rate generated games by learnability: low if random play wins, high if an evolved learner raises its score; fitness reflects how well and how fast it learns.
when: When machine learnability is taken to stand in for human learnability
why: Since much enjoyment is assumed to come from improving at play, games that random players can win get low scores.

text: A level fitness function can be a weighted sum of two normalised measures: distance of the placed-chunk count from a maximum threshold, and the count of conflicting chunks.
when: when evaluating generated levels with a search-based generator
why: The two measures partly conflict, since adding chunks raises the chance of conflicts.

text: Content encodings range from direct, where genotypes resemble phenotypes, to indirect, where genotypes are much smaller than the outputs they produce.
A tile grammar rule has one left-hand side and one or more right-hand side alternatives, may use wildcards, cannot change the tile count, but can stack tiles instead of replacing them.
A level is a two-dimensional matrix of ASCII characters, and the level mapping says which sprite type each character stands for.
In a neural network, each neuron's activation applies an activation function to the weighted sum of its inputs.
A negative representation starts from a grid of filled squares, and loci define room corners, lengths and heights that are carved out; corridors are rooms with one side of length one.
A binary bit-grid encoding stores each map square as 1 for full or 0 for empty, optionally preceded by loci that place designer-specified blocks.
A positive representation describes walls by start position, direction and maximum length, plus a 0/1 control: 0 stops a wall at the first wall it hits, 1 lets it grow through.
A symmetric bit-grid encoding stores one quarter of the level, with each bit setting four rotationally symmetric squares at once.
when: dungeon with enforced rotational symmetry
why: Encoding only a quarter guarantees symmetry in the full map.

text: The flower CPPN takes polar radius r, angle θ, a layer input L and a bias, and outputs RGB colour plus a maximum-radius value.
when: evolving radially symmetric shapes with CPPNs

text: Non-spatial elements such as enemies are components of procedural systems that add variety to generated levels.
Representation is one of two main problems in search-based PCG: it determines what content can be generated, whether search works at all, and affects search performance and appearance.
why: Search operates on encodings rather than on the content itself.

text: In tile-based worlds, tactical labels can be attached to corresponding tiles, so a grid-based generator can assign them per tile.
Machine learning is a route to procedural content generation, including game levels and music.

Candidate representations for a dungeon include a grid of cells, a list of walls with position, length, and orientation, reusable patterns with their distribution, a list of desired properties, and a random seed.
In a direct level representation, each genotype variable corresponds to one content tile, such as a brick or a question block.
A real-valued vector can be decoded partly as positions and partly as parameters for drawing structures such as walls.
Content can be encoded as typed design elements placed on 2D maps and evolved with a genetic algorithm.
The same set of outputs can be encoded in many different genotype spaces, so the encoding is a design choice.
A multi-wall encoding can generate two paired mazes at once, each tuned for a different player movement ability.
Room adjacency can be stored as neighbour lists or as an edge list.
Separate level tiles can be presented as one continuous overview map, so independent sections read as a single world.
Choose the genome encoding to match the desired visual style, since fitness alone does not set the look; encoding changes shift layouts among mine-, cave- and building-like.
when: designing an evolutionary dungeon generator
why: Style is strongly set by representation, and the encoding biases which layouts the search can easily produce.

text: In a large generated tile grid, measure terrain lookup speed before committing to a pointer-based flyweight design.
when: Choosing between pointer-based terrain references and an enum in a tile grid
why: Large grids magnify any cache-miss cost of indirection.

text: Three-dimensional dungeon generation would likely need a much larger chunk library than two-dimensional platform levels.
why: 2D platform levels overlap heavily in structure, so fewer distinct chunks cover them.

text: Feed the angle into the network as sin(Pθ) rather than raw θ, which makes radial symmetry easier to produce, with P setting the petal count.
when: generating radially symmetric shapes with CPPNs
why: A periodic input repeats the pattern and sets the number of repetitions.

text: The encounter database needs many more entries than any single generated level will use.
when: building an encounter database for generation
why: Repetition across levels is avoided only when the pool is large.

text: A small set of reusable tiles can produce many layouts, so a tile system supports building varied spaces from pieces.
when: when building varied spaces from pieces

text: Tag level elements with both functional need and theme, so generated placement matches the area's requirements and its story.
when: An element's placement depends on both function and theme

text: Variety in chunk-based generation comes from enemies, surrounding geometry and theme, not only from the chunks themselves.
when: When chunks are fixed in advance and an algorithm assembles them into levels
why: The same chunk feels different when enemies, nearby geometry or theme change, even if its layout repeats.

text: Tile grids can store pointers to a few shared terrain or tile objects, such as grass, hill, and river or floor, wall, water, and trap, which carry properties like movement cost.
when: When many object instances repeat identical data such as meshes and textures
why: Properties live in one object, so each tile reaches them through a shared reference.

text: A group of characters can be stored as a count plus a statistical distribution for each value, then regenerated into individuals when a high-importance LOD needs them.
when: Background populations where individual identity does not matter.
why: Keeps the population's overall shape while discarding per-character data.

text: Negative room encodings tend to produce mine-like layouts.
when: dungeon encoded as carved rectangular rooms
why: Carved rooms and corridors from a solid grid resemble mine tunnels.

text: Binary bit-grid encodings tend to produce cave-like systems.
when: dungeon encoded as a per-square bit grid
why: Independent square decisions yield irregular, organic open areas.

text: Positive wall encodings resemble building floor plans, and restricting walls to four directions makes the output look more like buildings.
when: dungeon encoded as growing walls
why: Walls that stop on contact and run axis-aligned mimic architectural plans.

text: Representation affects how well the search explores and biases it toward some regions of the content space over others.
when: search-based content generation
why: Only encoded regions are reachable with ease, so the encoding shapes exploration.

text: The world is a 2D tile grid of screen-sized blocks, with each location spanning a small grid of screens, so world size and location size are set in tiles and screens.
when: Realizing a space tree as tiles

text: Direct representations are not automatically best, since large direct genotypes can be too hard to search because of dimensionality.
1) Compute tileX as floor(x / tileSize). 2) Compute tileZ as floor(z / tileSize). 3) Use the tile's centre as its representative point for localization.
when: Mapping positions to square tile nodes.
why: Floor division gives each position a unique tile index.

text: 1) Make each terrain type an immutable object with const accessors for its properties. 2) Store one instance per type. 3) Point each tile at the shared instance for its type.
when: When every property of a terrain type is intrinsic and context-free, so one shared instance suffices.
why: Replaces scattered switch statements with per-type data.

text: 1) List the objects and mechanics of a game in natural language or bullet points. 2) Encode that list in the game description language. 3) Run the encoded game and compare its behaviour with the list.
when: When the game is a graphical-logic game whose objects and rules fit the VGDL vocabulary.

text: 1) Traverse the space tree depth-first. 2) Place each child next to its parent. 3) Randomize the order of cardinal directions. 4) Backtrack when placement fails. 5) If no mapping exists, discard the space tree and search for the next best one.
when: Mapping a space tree onto a grid
why: Randomized directions avoid a bias toward growing the world one way.

text: 1) Give each non-root tile exactly one parent among its four neighbours (up, down, left, right). 2) Define a recursive linked predicate: the root is linked, and any tile whose parent is linked is also linked. 3) Add an integrity constraint rejecting any unlinked tile.
why: An unlinked tile means the parent directions are inconsistent, so that assignment is invalid and must be rejected.

text: 1) Split each level into tiles about one city block in size. 2) Load the tiles when the mode starts. 3) Load the next tile when the player reaches its exit.
When generating levels from random tiles, each tile's scenes must stay individually interesting and readable, because tiles combine unpredictably.
when: When levels are assembled by loading randomly selected tiles.

text: Choose the content representation so it both defines and limits what can be generated and still allows effective search.
Encode only the mechanics relevant to the content you want to generate.
when: When the content to be generated depends on only part of a game's logic.

text: Change the representation to improve search speed, to obtain useful secondary content properties, or to fit existing computational infrastructure.
when: designing a search-based generator
why: Encoding choice can serve performance, content quality, or integration needs.

text: Very general encodings yield mostly non-games or unrunnable games, very narrow ones too few interesting games; smaller spaces are denser in playable candidates, larger allow more varied designs.
Eager creation of all flyweights up front is simpler; lazy creation needs a lookup, a way to judge two requests identical, and a pool, adding structure.
when: Choosing how to instantiate flyweights.
why: Eager creation avoids the extra machinery but only works when the needed set is known and small.

text: Direct representations keep genotypes close to phenotypes and give more control; indirect representations shrink genotypes far below phenotype size, cope better with dimensionality, but give less control and possibly sparser coverage.
A rigid representation of rules can reflect too many of the designer's own preconceptions, which limits the surprise a generator can produce.
when: when designing a representation for automatic game generation
why: Fixed structures encode the designer's assumptions about what games look like.

text: Direct representations are simpler and usually give higher locality, while indirect representations yield smaller search spaces.
when: choosing a search encoding
why: Direct encodings are easy to map but large; indirect ones compress the space.

text: To-scale mapping lets designers analyze how levels account for character metrics, and generated layouts can be checked against the same kind of to-scale map.
when: testing a generated or hand-built layout against character size
why: Each square represents a fixed unit of measurement, so the map is an accurate, to-scale picture of the level.

text: The most general graph form uses designer-placed bounding regions as nodes; its contents count as one planning node, and it avoids the constraints of Dirichlet domains and floor polygons.
An environment transition graph holds designer beliefs about likely transitions between environment types, with a probability on each edge, and supplies the types used for bridges.
Anchor a setting in a single named place with a clear scale to define a bounded world before building generated content.
when: Defining the scope of a generator's world
why: A bounded world sets limits that generated content must respect.

text: A search agent that must reach the exit from the start works as a simulation-based reachability check for a generated dungeon.
when: When evaluating content for playability, such as whether a path from start to exit exists.

text: Constrained evolution with two populations can keep vital components, such as bases and resources, connected by passable paths.
when: When every generated suggestion must be guaranteed playable, with vital components connected.

text: Most automatic graph costs are distances: point-to-point distance, centers of adjoining triangles for polygon meshes, and center-to-center distance for regions.
why: Pathfinding usually targets short routes, and distances are trivial to compute, so distance is the natural cost.

text: Designers place points, often invisible tagged helper objects, which become graph nodes; each node owns the locations closer to it than to any other point.
A topology graph has rooms as nodes and adjacency as edges; generating it before geometry settles room connectivity first.
when: Generating dungeons in two stages
why: Connectivity is fixed before spatial detail is built

text: Random dungeon generation often lacks an entrance-to-exit path: filling binary-map squares with probability 0.5 almost never connects them, and random carved negative-representation rooms often fail to connect without search.
when: When random binary fills use probability 0.5, or wall lengths approach the level diameter.
why: Random carved rooms often fail to connect.

text: Mapping a player-action graph to a level needed a specialised generator for each game.
Treat generated levels with no exit or entrance as catastrophic failures, unlike cosmetically odd content, which is a minor problem.
why: A missing exit or entrance breaks play itself, whereas a cosmetic oddity leaves the game still playable.

text: 1) Check whether a room fits at the position without intersecting existing rooms; if it fits, place it. 2) If no room fits, dig a corridor of three to seven tiles in a direction that avoids existing geometry.
when: When every possible room size would intersect existing rooms at the current position.

text: In mixed-initiative PCG, a human and software both take initiative and both shape the result, with the human cooperating with the algorithm to produce desired content.
Control is the set of options a designer or adaptive mechanism has to specify output aspects such as handling, mood or shape, together with the effort that steering takes.
A generative space is the set of all games a rule encoding can express, and it can be explored by scoring and evolving games or by carving out a subset.
