Designers can sculpt a generative space by including or excluding games according to explicit criteria, instead of receiving one game rated as best.
A design amplifier is a tool that helps non-expert designers, such as homeowners, produce valid designs with computer support.
In computer-aided design, the human directs the process and the computer acts only when asked and as specified.
Mixed-initiative interaction is dialogue in which either party may ask questions or lead, rather than only the human or only the computer.
A mixed-initiative level tool can complete unfinished designs, suggest modifications unprompted, give quality-metric feedback, enforce constraints and test playability.
Until reliable exploring AI exists, hand optimization is still needed for consistently usable log-based graphs.
Terrain generation with agents has three phases: coastline for the outline, landform for mountains, beaches and lowlands, and erosion for rivers, with one agent per river.
Earlier rule generators output complete rule sets without human input, whereas mixed-initiative rule tools let the human and the system both shape the result.
In an interactive rule-building tool, pressing a consequence button applies its effect immediately.
Creativity support tools aim to augment a human creator, keeping the human in charge while the computer defers to human decisions.
True mixed-initiative interaction, long studied in HCI and AI, has rarely been applied to game content generation.
Mixed-initiative procedural content generation handles just some of the work, requiring more human input during generation than fully automated approaches.
Generators show highly emergent behaviour, so it is hard to predict what a given algorithm will produce.
Other AI uses in UX include synthesizing survey answers, finding behavioral patterns in telemetry, and evaluating prototypes against design and usability guidelines.
Different participants can hold different initiative types at once, such as one raising the problem while another assigns the follow-up work.
A generator's difficulty must keep rising with the player's growing skill, or the player slides out of the flow channel.
when: generating content for a player who improves over time
why: Matching challenge to growing skill prevents boredom in skilled players and the frustration that makes others quit.

text: Derive the number of floors, encounters, and enemy types from a target session length using the same planning arithmetic.
when: When generating dungeon content for a session of set length.

text: Expose effect durations and cooldowns as parameters rather than fixing them, since they are design variables.
when: When generating content that uses timed effects.

text: A generator's random number source is a natural candidate for locator access, since random numbers are needed across most of a game.
when: When a system is needed by almost every part of the codebase.
why: Almost every game area draws on such a service at some point, so it must be reachable everywhere.

text: Tune a generator's environmental details to a documented historical reference so its tone matches a real setting.
when: When the game world is modeled on real-life counterparts or past events.
why: One primary-research detail can set the tone of a whole content layer.

text: Good generator control gives consistent results, such as playable levels, while keeping variety.
Place special content by hand first and let the algorithm fill the rest when key moments must be authored.
when: When special event rooms must be placed by hand before the rest is generated.
why: Designer control and versatility rise while the algorithm still takes manual work off their hands.

text: Apply each graph rule once to one location at a time, and split broad rules into narrower ones, to keep generated missions controllable.
when: When a graph grammar rule can keep adding structure with no upper limit.
why: Indiscriminate application gives no clear stopping point

text: When designing a generator, ask how you would build the level by hand and whether those changes can be captured by transformational grammars.
when: when deciding how to model level generation
why: Modelling manual design steps keeps generated levels close to designer intent.

text: A generated dungeon framework is an outline whose many details depend on the rules system it is joined to.
when: integrating a level generator with a tabletop ruleset
why: Content semantics come from the rules layer, not the layout.

text: Keep designer control through required content and an encounter database, while the generator fills in the rest.
when: generating adventure content
why: Designer-fixed content guarantees key areas and the database controls encounter quality.

text: Keep the occupancy of a fixed grid-indexed table below a chosen threshold so that lookup cost stays bounded during generation.
when: a procedural generator places entities into a fixed hash-indexed grid
why: expected probe count rises as load factor approaches 1

text: If a generator removes rooms or tiles during rework, prefer chaining or a tree structure, because open-addressed deletion is awkward.
when: entities are removed during generation
why: deleting from an open-addressed table breaks probe sequences

text: Local cellular automaton rules can produce global behavior: mutually dependent locations may oscillate, and some rule sets keep changing the whole map endlessly.
when: When two adjacent locations keep flipping their state in response to each other.

text: A constraint satisfaction algorithm can fill in the unspecified parts of a partly drawn level while keeping it playable.
when: When a designer has drawn only part of a 2D level.

text: In interactive sketching of worlds, edits are kept consistent with the world model, so designers can change results without breaking them.
when: When designers manually edit and tune generated landscapes or cityscapes.

text: A feature vector can steer generation toward output that meets stated feature specifications.
Parameters such as average movement complexity let a user shift generated output somewhat, without fully controlling it.
when: When a generator samples stochastically from a rule grammar and offers a few knobs.
why: Output is sampled from a grammar, so knobs only bias what is likely rather than fixing it.

text: Acceptable generation time ranges from milliseconds to months, depending on whether content is generated during play or during development.

Mixed-initiative systems form a sliding scale: computer-aided design has the human leading, interactive evolution the computer leading, and generators where users only set desired properties sit at the far end.
A time-limited, location-based event that disappears if not reached in time is a timing and distance constraint a generator can model.
when: Designing generated content with deadlines
why: Deadline and distance together define a reachable region the generator must respect.

text: Generation can be controlled by a random seed, by parameters along several dimensions, or by a feature vector.
In chunk assembly there are no explicit control parameters; chunk library contents and their probabilities act as the controls.
when: When a chunk-based generator exposes no explicit control parameters.
why: Chunks and their probabilities determine level geometry and versatility, so they steer output implicitly.

text: In mixed-initiative level design, a constraint-based generator keeps levels playable while the human edits geometry and pacing, with generator actions interleaved with designer edits in real time.
when: When a designer edits a level and the generator must react at once.
why: Guaranteed playability lets early playtesting focus on fun rather than reachability.

text: Event weights set by hand must be tuned manually, so the frequencies of gaps, hills and enemies depend on tuning effort.
Pushing mixed-initiative too far turns generation into manual construction and loses the benefits of procedural generation.
why: Much manual placement per level makes generation inefficient, eroding the advantages of procedural methods.

text: Without a reference solution, styled maps can have no path from gem to altar or from entrance to exit.
when: When maps are sampled using only local style constraints.
why: Local style rules yield plausible-looking regions that may not support the intended play.

text: A constraint on touch counts in one solution looks equivalent to a concept requirement but does not force time to be spent, so wandering stays possible.
when: When a touch-count integrity constraint replaces the concept-based construction for forcing time to be spent.
why: Observed wandering in a solution does not show it was required, since the player could simply have chosen to waste time.

text: Every creation tool pushes an agenda, often unintentionally: even a tool that never overrides the human shapes the work through what its generator can produce.
1) Choose input parameter settings to vary. 2) Generate expressive range charts for each setting. 3) Compare the charts to see how the output space shifts.
when: When assessing how far a generator can be steered and how parameter or rule changes affect its output range.
why: Side-by-side charts reveal whether changed settings shift or narrow the range of content the generator can produce.

text: Keep generator parameters in a file read when the program starts so they can be adjusted without changing code.
when: procedural generation tuning

text: Proposals for generated content should describe how the player interacts with that content, since system designers ask this first.
when: Proposing generated content
why: Gameplay usually takes priority over story, and producers want to know how players will interact with the narrative.

text: Generators must respect the intended mechanics, opportunities and limits of the game they serve.
why: This is what separates PCG from generative art and most computer graphics.

text: Express soft preferences with a minimize statement and hard requirements as integrity constraints.
when: When many desired properties are hard constraints, as in logic-based solving.

text: Constrain the whole space of play when the goal concerns how the player experiences a level, not one specific layout.
when: When the goal concerns how the player experiences a level rather than one specific layout.
why: The requirement is quantified over every possible solution, so the experience holds whichever layout is produced.

text: A level authoring tool should offer complete generation, input of full or partial designer designs, automatic playability checks, and optimisation of designs for playability.
Changing L-system fitness weights gives fairly precise control over plant type; but when user choices act only through weights, their link to output is indirect and hard to predict.
when: Evolving L-system plants with weighted fitness
why: Each fitness function measures a concrete shape property of the plant, so weighting them steers the result directly.

text: Grammar-based gameplay control gives designers strong steering, but the graph and shape rules needed are far from intuitive for most designers.
when: When steering dungeon generation through a mission graph followed by a shape grammar.
why: Control is exerted by the individual grammar rules themselves rather than by real control parameters.

text: The Moore neighbourhood, radius one, includes the eight adjacent cells; the von Neumann neighbourhood, radius one, includes only the four orthogonal ones.
A perfect maze is a spanning tree embedded in a grid: every tile is reachable from the root and there are no closed loops.
Region node links are made by hand or by the tool, and costs can be set manually or generated from geometric properties of the node boxes.
Mesh representations need no mining because polygons are the nodes; mining of general bounding regions is an open question.
Limit nodes to at most two children so each node has at most three neighbours, making collisions between placed locations less likely.
when: Mapping a space tree onto a grid
why: Fewer children per node means fewer adjacent grid slots claimed, so two nodes are less likely to land in the same portion.

text: The parent-pointer and linked-reachability pattern can enforce connectivity of rooms in dungeon layouts.
when: When each tile is given a random parent, leaving disconnected components in the maze.
why: Reachability is defined recursively from the root, so only tiles linked back to it satisfy the constraint.

text: Point-based nodes each hold a representative point, and a line-of-sight check between each pair creates a connection when it passes; this can produce vast numbers of connections.
why: A check runs between every pair of representative points, so connections grow with the number of pairs.

text: The number of neighbourhood configurations equals the number of states raised to the power of the neighbourhood cell count.

1) Build the level. 2) Place a character under player or AI control. 3) Log its position continuously. 4) Turn high-density log locations, typically junctions and thoroughfares, into nodes; aggregate nearby points by condensation or by counting points per floor polygon and using its center. Turn logged direct transitions into connections.
when: A pathfinding graph is needed without reachability geometry.
why: The character uses real legal moves, so the log reveals reachable locations.

text: 1) Choose sample points within each pair of regions. 2) Run line-of-sight checks between them. 3) Add a connection when the required proportion of checks passes.
when: Bounded regions must be linked automatically.

text: For Dirichlet domains, place a node at each movement-density peak: set a node count in advance and pick that many peaks that are not too close together.
when: Using Dirichlet domain nodes with logged movement data.
why: Movement-density peaks mark the thoroughfares players actually use, so nodes sit where traffic is heaviest.

text: On irregular grids or at map edges, use the proportion of a larger neighborhood instead of fixed neighbor counts, such as a 25% threshold.
when: When the neighbour count varies by location, as on irregular grids or at map edges.
why: Fixed counts treat edge and irregular locations inconsistently.

text: Traversal behaviour is controlled by a small set of per-tile flags, so changing one flag changes how a whole structure can be used.
when: Generating or authoring tile-based levels with grapple traversal
why: Flags act as a compact control surface over movement across many tiles.

text: A platform level is a grid of cells, each holding either empty space, a coin, a hostile character, or a solid brick block.
Rhythm-based generators expose a general path, rhythm kinds, geometry types and frequencies, coin distribution, and per-group parameters such as jump frequency.

1) Make passes over the level from left to right, adding one element type per pass: ground height and gaps; background hills; static enemies such as pipes and cannons; moving enemies; unconnected horizontal blocks; coins.
when: Generating platform levels in separate content passes
why: Each pass adds one content type using weighted random choices

text: 1) Choose player actions for each small rhythm group. 2) Choose geometry that realises those actions. 3) Combine many candidate levels. 4) Let critics select the best one.
when: Generating platform levels from rhythm groups
why: Level structure is tied to the rhythm of how players act and repeat moves, so actions come first and geometry follows.

text: Constrain vertical positions and heights to jumpable ranges, for example y from 3 to 5 and height 3 to 4, so items stay reachable and a start-to-end path exists.
when: Bounding generated platformer geometry
why: Jumpable limits keep the path from start to end playable

text: Storage limits on early home computers drove many early PCG techniques, as early games generated most content procedurally to fit limited storage, so data-driven content has a long history.
when: when considering content generation approaches
why: storage limits forced compact generation

text: Identical behavior patterns shared by many generated objects, or identical copies of a level pattern shown repeatedly, make the generation visible and the pattern predictable.
when: when many procedurally generated objects use the same motion or reaction
why: Repetition makes the generation visible.

text: A PCG method is an algorithm that produces game content, run by a computer alone or with human help.
A PCG system is a larger system containing a PCG method, such as an adaptive game or an AI-assisted design tool.
Game content spans characters, vehicles, weapons, music, quests, items, stories, textures, rules, maps and levels.
Generic PCG produces content without considering player behaviour; most commercial games work this way.
Deterministic PCG reproduces the same content from the same starting point and method parameters; stochastic PCG usually cannot.
Multi-level, multi-content PCG aims for one generator that produces all of a game's content at high quality, with the pieces fitting together coherently.
Procedural content generation uses algorithms to build parts of a game, including its environments.
In PCG-based game design, PCG is so central that removing it leaves nothing recognisable of the game.
A fluid pattern admits many implementations, such as a moving platform over a pit or an area outside a searchlight's view.

PCG is motivated by cutting development time and content cost, augmenting designers, enabling new kinds of games, supporting player-adaptive play, increasing replayability, sparking creativity, and understanding design.
Procedurally generated levels are an established use of AI-driven generation, producing game worlds rather than hand-authoring each one.
why: Predictable rule-based generation keeps the output within the intended experience.

text: Commercial PCG since the early 1980s has often been peripheral or narrow, while academic research pushes both the scope and quality of generated content.
Ideal PCG solutions are fast, reliable, controllable, expressive and creative, but these properties usually need tradeoffs against each other.
A detailed taxonomy of a PCG solution helps reveal its strengths and weaknesses.
PCG draws on many fields, so its methods are diverse.
Some generators guarantee quality criteria while others produce output without checks; reliability matters most for content whose failure breaks play.
The PCG definition is deliberately fuzzy at its edges, and some people use 'generative methods' for a wider set of methods.
A tool that only places or removes items by hand does not count as PCG, because it generates nothing.
Traditionally, designers mostly tuned algorithm parameters, and the main goal was endless variations of playable content.
PCG taxonomy dimensions are continua rather than binary choices, so a method usually sits between the ends of each one.
The long-range PCG visions are not achievable with current technology and may never be realised exactly as stated, but they expose current limitations.
Card games have a limited vocabulary and small branching factor, which makes them easier to play automatically and attractive for generation research.
Generating playable, interesting, original first-person shooters is an open problem, and which game traits make games easier to generate remains unknown.
Earlier methods generate content, such as levels or weapons, for a fixed game, whereas rule generation treats the game's own rules as the thing generated.
Formalising rules defines the space of candidate rules more precisely than prose descriptions can.
The rule aspects chosen for formalisation determine what a generator can vary and what it treats as worth exploring.
The generator targets small heroic-fantasy adventure modules played with a human referee rather than a computer.
Player experience models serve as measures of content quality, so the game can produce personalised or player-adapted content.
Mixed-initiative game design tools draw on three threads: mixed-initiative interaction, computer-aided design, and creativity support tools.

Most current PCG algorithms seem to show skill but not creativity; exploratory creativity (novel combinations within a constrained space) and transformational creativity (breaking design boundaries) are distinct.
Procedural generation reduces level-design workload and increases replayability.
A generator can hold pedagogical expertise, constraining levels so they meet educational goals.
PCG system is a generic term, and systems differ in how they are used and how they relate to design.
Recurring level patterns have been catalogued across action, strategy, role-playing, adventure and sport games.
Present procedural generation as augmenting designers and artists rather than replacing them, because replacement framing threatens the people whose work it would automate.
when: When selling procedural generation to designers and artists.
why: Replacement framing creates resistance from designers and artists.

text: Keep generation stages and content rules decoupled so that a rule change touches few files.
when: building a procedural dungeon generator whose requirements will change
why: Frequent requirement changes are cheap to absorb when stages are independent.

text: Building generators for narrowly defined tasks is as worthwhile as pursuing the ambitious long-range visions.
Complex level-design properties tend to arise from combining simple rules and constraints.
why: Recursive composition of basic rules yields constraints whose combined effect produces emergent layout properties.

text: Repetition hurts when generated chunks ignore player needs, but it helps when each chunk addresses a player need.
when: When scenes, patterns, or PCG level systems reuse the same chunks.
why: Recognizable repeats remain welcome when they provide valuable resources or a vantage point for players.

text: Decide growth caps or scaling before content runs out, since unbounded growth eventually serves repeated enemies at high player levels.
when: When generating content with unbounded growth.
why: Without a ceiling, players outpace the content and every later encounter just recycles the same enemies.

text: Fix a generator's overall scale before filling in its rooms and paths, since the world's scope is set before its detail.
when: When designing procedural generation for dungeons or levels.
why: Scope set early keeps later detail consistent with the whole.

text: When a fixed world does not fit a story plan, generate the world itself so that it supports the plan's events.
when: a fixed map conflicts with the story plan
why: plan events need matching locations

text: Rising hand-made content cost and growing team sizes make fewer games profitable and reduce studios' willingness to take creative risks.
when: commercial games with large teams
why: Much of the expensive staffing is in design and art roles, not in programming.

text: If content is generated as fast as the player consumes it, the game need not end.
why: Games end when authored content runs out; generation at play speed removes that exhaustion point.

text: Generating several versions of one level improves replayability for players who have already seen the dungeon.
when: players replaying a generated dungeon
why: Different layouts from the same specification feel fresh.

text: As a generator, the designer authors boundaries and tendencies, while the interplay of mechanics, player choices, and chance determines each specific plot at run time.
when: designing systems that produce story content
why: It shifts authorship labor onto game systems and players, and can keep generating stories indefinitely.

text: PCG systems fall into four approaches: simulation-based, constructionist, constraint-driven, and optimization-based.
A PCG system can be framed through four metaphors: as a tool, a material, a designer, or a domain expert.
Four gamespace generators of emergence are multiuse spaces, close proximity of functional spaces, spaces for different styles or factions, and accommodation of player density.
when: When designing multiplayer gamespaces for emergent gameplay.
why: They adapt urban design diversity principles while avoiding the separation of uses found in Modernist planning.

text: Writing each character's AI data by hand gains nothing over writing separate AI code for each character.
why: Character behaviour is data selecting from a shared algorithm pool, so hand-filling that data repeats the same manual work.

text: Judging randomness by which sequence has the longer maximum streak is only a rough guess, not proof that either sequence is random.
1) Store each authored event as a self-contained object with its script and art. 2) Shuffle the events like cards. 3) Spawn them at developer-defined intervals.
why: Shuffling the handmade events gives replayability while each event keeps its own handmade branching and art.

text: 1) Name the problem a level design pattern solves. 2) Judge whether the pattern can be read in many ways or only a few.
Repeated props in a generated dungeon, such as pillars or torches, can be drawn with instanced rendering: one shared model and varying per-instance placement data.
when: Many identical props are placed in a generated level.
why: Shared model data is sent once.

text: Components the designer constrains stay fixed while the system evolves the rest of a complete level.
when: When evolving complete playable levels from a designer-constrained starting design.

text: Define each level design pattern by the negative player experience it fixes.
why: Patterns are understood as answers to design problems instead of as attractive spaces in themselves.

text: Faster generation often costs output quality, so speed and quality are a common tradeoff.
Procedural animation can animate player-created content without hand-animating each creation.
Per-pixel random values look like television static, which is wrong for natural surfaces such as rock.
Embed placement rules in individual assets, such as requiring each lamp to sit across from another, so composed layouts follow the pattern.
Generative material produced in real time stays valid when a designer edits it, because its output is re-derived from its rules each time.
when: When designers sculpt procedurally generated assets by dragging, adding or removing their parts

text: Place procedurally generated visual content deliberately on the realistic-iconic-abstract spectrum, since that position determines the behavior players expect.
when: when generating visual content
why: Placement sets player expectations

text: A pairwise collision effect can be nothing, one or both objects die, or one or both teleport; a parallel matrix sets score changes.
A generator placing encounters can alternate combat rooms, which add pressure, with navigation rooms, which let players set their own pace.
when: when generating dungeon layouts
why: Alternation varies pressure across the play session.

text: Assign one collectible piece per dungeon level in a generated campaign to give players a clear progression marker.
when: generating multi-level campaigns
why: Giving each level one piece as its goal sets a regular rhythm of objectives and rewards.

text: A generated dungeon's layout should create unease, discovery, and choice, using atmospheric cues, branching paths, and side routes that players can explore or skip.
when: when generating dungeon layouts for exploration-driven play
why: Players experience exploration as an uncertain, mysterious space

text: Only a genuinely single resource, such as a file handle, may justify a singleton in a level generator.
when: Building a level or dungeon generator

text: Rewarding a narrow area on the shortest path between two bases creates a choke point that a skilled player could use for defence.
when: When a strategy map generator scores the shortest route between two bases

text: Editing pacing directly as a structural layer, such as adding, removing or lengthening beats on a timeline, can be applied to dungeon sequencing.
A single player plan can hold attention for a long stretch, so generated content should track how each event changes that plan.
when: designing generated encounters that shape player plans
why: Changed circumstances are what raise decision pace

text: Generators should produce situations that create choices rather than script each choice individually.
why: Scripted choices lose their emotional force

text: When generating dungeons, treat each dungeon as one tier in a goal hierarchy that also includes the main quest and smaller item goals.
why: dungeons gain meaning from their place among larger and smaller goals

text: 1) Build the physical structure. 2) Compute candidate positions on platforms. 3) Place each enemy in one candidate position.
when: Adding enemies to a generated platformer level
why: Deriving candidate spots from the generated platforms yields varied enemy placement across levels.

text: A story plan used for space generation must be fully ordered, so its events read as a sequence of locations, each becoming an island with a type from the domain's initial state.
when: Converting a story plan to islands
why: A sequence of locations is needed to place islands in order.

text: Walls cannot be touched, and the finish must be touched in state 3, enforced by an integrity constraint on the completed predicate.
why: Constraints reject layouts where the finish cannot be reached under the rules, so output is always solvable.

text: Plan encounter spots as part of the room layout, since enemy placement is a spatial decision.
when: when generating rooms with enemies
why: Encounter drama depends on blending the space with the player's condition, so layout shapes how fights feel.

text: Puzzle-driven dungeon rewards build discovery and cleverness but offer less power growth; stat-driven rewards build progression but weaken puzzle-driven discovery.
when: when deciding how a generated dungeon should reward progression
why: Adventure-style games center play on puzzle solving rather than accumulating improvements, so rewards stay about discovery.

text: Quantities where most individuals score low and a few score high usually follow a power law, controlled by a single exponent that sets how flat the curve is.
why: Money among people is a typical example.

text: RANDBETWEEN(min,max) returns a whole number from min to max inclusive, so RANDBETWEEN(1,1024) selects one row of a 1024-row table.
Random-number formulas such as RAND() and RANDBETWEEN() re-roll every time the sheet updates, so one roll must be pasted as values to keep it.
when: Generating random content in a spreadsheet
why: Recalculation regenerates random formulas on each update.

text: Players can be served a sequence of games sampled from one constrained space and work out the shared rules behind them.
Random events in a design make the resulting player experience harder to predict, so generated content needs review of the experiences it produces.
when: Designing procedurally generated content.
why: Randomness widens the gap between what is built and what players feel.

text: Randomness in agent start positions and behaviour makes the same generator produce a different level on each run.
when: agent-based level generators
why: Each genome defines a distribution of levels, not a single recipe.

text: Fully random placement of monsters and traps gives variety at the cost of designer control.
Sampling a grammar spreads output across the space rather than searching it, so quality is controlled only implicitly.
why: Generation applies random sampling and basic playability checks only, with no quality testing inside the process.

text: 1) Fill two adjacent columns with pseudorandom numbers for about a thousand rows. 2) Plot each row as an x,y point. 3) Regenerate and see whether clusters move. 4) Judge no visible pattern as passing a quick check.
when: casual check that a generator shows no obvious structure, or relying on a visual check of generator output
why: a scatter plot exposes gross patterns cheaply but cannot establish the exact level of randomness, since subtle statistical biases are invisible in it

text: For finite generators, count all variations; for infinite ones, increase the sample size until the charts match the previous smaller sample.
when: When a generator can produce infinite variety rather than a countable set
why: Viewing every output is infeasible at thousands or millions of levels, so charts stand in for review.

text: Roguelike games procedurally generate dungeons at runtime, randomizing layout, monster and treasure placement, so each game start yields new levels and high replayability.
Online generation happens during play, giving endless variation, high replayability and room for player-adapted content.
Offline generation happens during development or before a session and suits complex content such as environments and maps.
Letting players enter their own seed lets them share or replay a specific generated layout.
A single pass with one random draw per element is cheap enough to produce randomized orderings at runtime.
when: generating randomized sequences during play
why: linear cost with one draw per item keeps per-frame work low

text: Generate and display alternatives in real time from a population seeded by the user's sketch, so the sketch's integrity is preserved.
when: When a designer works from a coarse map sketch in a level-design tool
why: Alternatives evolve from a population seeded by the sketch, so they keep its layout.

text: Size rooms, doors and gaps to the character's measured size and jump distance, and leave enough horizontal and vertical space for movement; a room one screen wide can break traversal.
when: generating or sizing rooms, doors and gaps; procedurally generated rooms with movement-heavy mechanics
why: Measured character metrics give a fixed baseline for fit; movement mechanics need horizontal and vertical space to function.

text: Binary space partitioning splits space into two parts per step, quadtrees split 2D space into four quadrants, and octrees split 3D space into eight octants.
Portal-based engines often assign one cluster per room, which suits room-based dungeon layouts.
Room-and-portal layouts can serve as a coarse top-level planning graph, with finer routes computed inside each area.
when: When a level is set primarily indoors and divided by portals
why: Portal-separated sectors already partition the space, so they can serve as a route graph for long trips.

text: Use space partitioning when rooms must not overlap and the layout should look structured and orderly.
why: Following partition rules strictly yields symmetric, square dungeons, giving an ordered look.

text: Breaking a level into reusable modular units is the same kind of decomposition a dungeon generator uses when assembling layouts.
when: designing layouts for procedural assembly

text: Recombining the same prefabricated pieces into different arrangements produces different implied stories, so modular layouts can yield varied narrative content.
when: generating levels from modular prefab pieces
why: Arrangement of reused props implies past events, so players read a story even from familiar assets.

text: Joining sibling cells bottom-up means siblings connect before their parents, so corridors follow a natural order through the tree.
when: When connecting rooms generated from a binary space partition tree
why: Once two siblings are joined they count as one group, so the parent's connection comes later.

text: Stop splitting cells once they fall below about a quarter of the area's width and height.
when: Stochastic BSP partitioning of a dungeon area

text: Randomly chosen quadtree splits can produce highly symmetric square dungeons unless the leaf rule is relaxed.
when: Dungeon from a randomly split quadtree whose leaf quadrants must be uniform

text: Required-content rooms that do not satisfy the room-detection definition will be missed as rooms.
when: combining required blocks with room detection
why: Detection uses an implicit definition that custom blocks must meet.

text: 1) Create rooms first. 2) Connect them with corridors.
when: a non-search baseline for dungeon layout
why: Gives a constructive comparison point for search-based generators.

text: 1) Randomly choose quadrants to split. 2) Mark each final quadrant as empty or as a room. 3) Connect all rooms.
1) Place one room of any size, smaller than its quadrant, in each leaf quadrant. 2) Connect the rooms afterwards without using the tree.
when: Avoiding symmetric quadtree layouts
why: Rooms of varied size, connected without consulting the tree, add randomness beyond the tree's grid, though layouts stay fairly orderly.

text: 1) Find room-sized open spaces, including required rooms. 2) Number each room. 3) Save the numbered map for the referee.
when: after map generation in a room-based generator
why: Numbered rooms let a referee and later stages refer to each area.

text: 1) Treat each room as a vertex. 2) Connect rooms that are adjacent into an adjacency graph. 3) Pass the graph to the population stage.
when: after rooms are detected
why: Population needs room connectivity to decide placement order.

text: 1) Start a room counter at zero and scan the map in reading order. 2) When an empty 3x3 block is found, mark it as the next room. 3) Repeatedly absorb empty squares with three neighbours inside the room. 4) Increment the counter.
when: turning a bit-grid map into rooms
why: Growing from seed blocks yields disjoint room regions.

text: Introduce each obstacle alone in early generated rooms, then combine obstacles in later rooms.
when: when generating rooms with a difficulty progression
why: Isolated introduction lets players learn each obstacle before combinations appear.

text: Repeat a small set of room and building types so generated spaces stay readable at large scale.
when: Large open-world map with many similar-looking structures visible on screen
why: Recognisable building types let players spot their next goal among many structures on screen.

text: Partitioning lets the root control the whole layout, but its neatly ordered results can look predictable.
why: Added randomness on top of a tree still leaves dungeons fairly orderly.

text: Symbolic rule expressions can be stored as trees, which makes standard crossover and mutation directly applicable to rule sets.
A formal rule encoding defines a space of possible games and records what its designer considers interesting.
Because each update depends only on the previous iteration's values, locations can be updated in any order.
Code models a set of potential outcomes that all follow the same general rules, so one rule set yields many outcomes.
Formal description languages such as the Video Game Description Language let algorithms generate game rules, not only content.
Simple movement and collision primitives still support a large range of games, making this domain a natural target for automatic rule generation.
N-in-a-row win conditions dominated evolved rule sets and appeared in the strongest ones.
High-level rule descriptions can be recognised without learning the system, and rule sets can be edited as conceptual units, as humans think about games.
Judging rule quality is harder than judging other generated content, because it must measure game-theoretic and aesthetic properties beyond correctness.
Search-based and constraint-satisfaction methods, including answer set programming, have been used to generate board and arcade game rules.
Prefer a single neighbor-count threshold over a band of counts; bands behave unpredictably, while a single threshold tends to fill or settle the map.
when: designing cellular automaton rules

text: Simple cellular automaton rules are often enough in games, because changing game state already supplies dynamism.
when: Cellular automaton running in a game where player actions keep changing the game state
why: Changing game state supplies the dynamism, so the automaton rules need not be complex.

text: Test core generation rules in a prototype before building content pipelines around them.
when: Building a procedural dungeon or level generator.
why: Early testing exposes flaws before dependent content work is built.

text: A generated mechanic has utility if it makes a previously unsolvable test level solvable, offering an affordance the player lacked.
when: when screening generated mechanics by simulation
why: A pass-or-fail solvability test gives the search a usable signal in an unpredictable state space.

text: A state-based touch model is a reusable template for checking solvability of levels with keys, items, and exits.
when: When generated level maps must be guaranteed playable
why: A valid reference solution is a proof by existence that the level can be solved.

text: Within a state the player may touch any adjacent tile; touching the gem advances to state 2 and touching the altar in state 2 advances to state 3.
Adding or removing rules from a rule-based generator changes the shape of its generative space.
A touch(Tile, State) predicate traces a player path through three states: before the gem, after taking the gem, and after placing it in the altar.
why: Numbered states encode the required order of actions, so only worlds completing that sequence pass.

text: Current rule generation is simplistic, so generating complete games remains far from solved.
An unconstrained add-task rule can produce anywhere from one task upward without limit, since it stops growing only when the start node is removed.
when: Applying growth rules to mission graphs without control
why: Growth halts only when the entry point disappears, leaving no other cap on task count.

text: 1) Record every consequence-button press along with the history of actions. 2) Learn why each press was made. 3) Infer the game the player is building. 4) Induce that game's rules.
when: When rules should be generated interactively from a player's choices rather than fully automatically
why: Machine learning over the history of actions is how the system infers the intended game.

text: 1) Choose a rule representation first. 2) Search that representation for good rule sets. 3) Evaluate candidates on game-theoretic and aesthetic qualities, not only on correctness.
For specific patterns with few spatial forms, vary materials, assets or themes so repeats feel fresh; use rule-based components for fluid patterns that combine into many forms.
when: Specific patterns with few spatial forms
why: Few spatial forms leave little room for variety, so surface treatment is what makes repeats feel different.

text: Increment a location's category when two or more neighbors are higher, and decrement it when no neighbor is as high.
when: Map locations already labelled with one discrete category from a set

text: Require each wall to have at least two wall neighbours and each gem to have at least three wall neighbours.
why: Walls avoid isolated rocks and spurs, and gems stay embedded within a larger wall.

text: Two simple grammar steps can produce many relationship variants, whereas explicit rules for each variant would need many more rules that are harder to maintain.
when: when a generator must support many structural variants
why: Rule count grows much faster than the number of variants a composed approach covers.

text: A rule representation trades expressivity against density of feasible rules and against compactness and readability; gaining one can cost another.
Solver-based approaches, such as Answer Set Programming, specify logical conditions that content must satisfy.
Search-based PCG treats content creation as search: a stochastic optimiser repeatedly modifies candidate artefacts and keeps changes that raise an evaluation score.
Optimization-based generation uses end-user input, such as play or ratings, to decide what to generate next.
Search-based PCG is popular in academia, and a few complete games have shipped using it.
Choosing both the target variable and its value from all variables in the game code, via reflection, lets a generator produce mechanics that a hand-built representation would not offer.
when: when a generator is given access to the engine's code
why: Open access removes the designer's preconceptions from the representation.

text: In multiplayer, the usage rates of all players together determine which content evolves.
Use search-based terrain generation when terrain must satisfy explicit constraints or gameplay requirements such as traversability.
when: Terrain must meet explicit constraints, gameplay requirements or traversability requirements.
why: Noise and fractal methods struggle to express explicit properties, whereas search can directly target them.

text: Use exhaustive search when the search space is very small and generation time is not a constraint.
when: The search space is tiny, or there is ample time available for producing content.

text: Use random search when good content is easy to find and variety matters more than optimising.
when: Good solutions are easy to find and output diversity matters more than quality.

text: Simple evolutionary algorithms often work well enough as the search engine in search-based content generation.
Restrict the candidate space to a size that allows exhaustive search when every candidate must be evaluated by simulation.
when: when each candidate needs a full simulated evaluation

text: Stronger local search, such as Monte Carlo tree search over rule choices, is a proposed way to find nearby good designs that mutation misses.
when: An evolved design is a single change away from a strong design that search has not reached.

text: Use ASP when you want the generator's declarative specification kept separate from the search algorithm.
Evolving content such as weapons from a player's earlier use and preferences yields items tailored to each player.
when: Generation is player-centred, with a player's interaction analysed to create content.

text: A representation with few parameters limits generation to the range those parameters allow; looser structures impose fewer constraints and give a wider range.
why: A fixed-dimension vector only controls those dimensions, while a grammar with fewer constraints lets the generator reach more structures.

text: Searching over grammar rule choices for ones that match target difficulty, fun and size steers the generated topology toward those goals without generating geometry.
when: Topology is generated by a graph grammar
why: A high-level topological representation lets parameters like difficulty, fun and size control generation.

text: Search-based terrain generation gains controllability because constraints can be written as objectives that the search optimises.
why: Other terrain methods make explicit properties hard to express, a gap that search-based approaches fill.

text: A map search fills unspecified space so that distances between designer-required objects match the designer's specification.
when: designer places required blocks in a generated level
why: Fitness measures inter-object distances, pushing the fill toward the specified layout.

text: With similar fitness, different encodings can yield very different dungeons.
when: comparing evolutionary dungeon generators
why: Fitness does not fix the structure of the output; encoding does.

text: Search-based PCG has three core parts: a search algorithm, a content representation that can be sampled effectively, and evaluation functions that separate good content from bad.
Feasible-infeasible two-population search keeps infeasible candidates that fail rendering, physics or balance constraints out of the user's view while pushing them toward feasibility.
when: when generated content has hard validity constraints
why: Infeasible candidates are optimised toward feasibility in their own population, so the shown set holds only valid content.

text: Evolution may miss a nearby strong design when the needed change is one specific mutation that is never tried, and one unhelpful attribute can ruin an otherwise good rule set.
when: When the needed change is one specific mutation that is never tried.
why: A single extra attribute can wreck an otherwise strong rule set.

text: Without a reachability rule, random parent choices produce disconnected components and parents outside the grid.
when: Tiles are each given a random parent with no connectivity enforcement.
why: Without enforcing that the root is reachable from each tile, parent links are unconstrained.

text: A parameter change that looks harmless can drastically alter a generator's output space in some configurations, so check the full set of configurations rather than a few.
when: When rules, priorities or input parameters of a generator are adjusted.
why: Some configurations yield drastically different output spaces even when the change looks minor.

text: 1) Generate a highly randomised graph. 2) Restructure it into something that fits the game. Each step acts as one stage of a design process.
when: when generation must yield coherent, expressive structures
why: Simple steps are easier to design, debug, and reuse than one large grammar.

text: Search space trees with any optimisation algorithm, scoring on bridge length, bridge branching factor, side-path length, and how closely adjacent transitions match the transition graph's probabilities.
when: Fitting a space tree to designer parameters

text: Evaluate generated content offline using logical operations, constraint satisfaction and simulated AI agents, without player input.
when: When content is generated in massive amounts and must be pruned before players see it.
why: Player annotation can treat subjects as random evaluators, a limitation offline evaluation avoids.

text: Initialise random dungeon populations with a filled-square probability of 0.2 (20% ones, 80% zeros) so most starting levels are connected; crossover and mutation raise the fraction of ones.
when: when starting evolution of random dungeon populations or a bit-grid dungeon
why: Sparse starts keep early maps open and let search add walls gradually.

text: Sparse starts give mostly connected levels, but these are overly connected and poor in quality, so search must improve them.
when: Random levels are initialised so they stay mostly connected.
why: Dense random fills almost never connect entrance and exit, so sparse fills are needed to get connectivity.

text: A procedurally generated world seed is one instance within the space of every world that could be created, and stores block states, items, structures, and entity data.
when: Procedurally generated worlds with saved changes.

text: Seeding can come from entry ratings or rankings, from preliminary rounds, or from random assignment when no performance data exists.
Save points suited early games with limited storage, because storing a few locations keeps save files small.
A seeded generator lets you rebuild the exact same generated run when testing or debugging.
why: The generator is deterministic, so a fixed starting number reproduces the same sequence of outputs.

text: If a generated layout is tied to a saved seed, the layout becomes predictable after every reload.
when: Seed stored in the save file, and a reload follows an unlucky roll.
why: Restoring the stored seed replays the identical random sequence, so the same roll outcome returns.

text: Storing a seed number and regenerating content from it lets a small program produce a very large set of worlds without storing them.
when: When content storage is too limited to hold every generated item.
why: Only the seed must be stored, not the generated content.

text: Once the seed is saved, the game becomes fully deterministic, so a player who knows exactly how an enemy acts can optimize every choice.
when: When a player can learn in advance how an enemy will act.
why: Knowing outcomes ahead lets each decision be tuned to them.

text: Saving the seed blocks simple rerolls, but it is a weak barrier: other random actions such as random-heal items, tiny wagers or changing action order still allow rerolls.
when: the seed is saved with the save file
why: Random side actions produce new outcome variance, letting the player retry until a combination works.

text: A player can manipulate the past by rerolling or the future by foreknowledge; no fully deterministic save design avoids both.
when: When pseudorandom numbers are part of the game's rolls.
why: Any save-and-reload either allows retrying a past roll or reveals future outcomes beforehand.

text: 1) Take a gameplay matrix and a difficulty value. 2) Use a random seed for variation. 3) Scale the number, frequency and types of obstacles and enemies. 4) Output the level structure and enemy placement.
why: Gives infinite, tunable variation

text: 1) Show individuals only every 5 or 10 generations. 2) Predict unseen individuals' fitness from the closest seen neighbour, scaled down with distance. 3) Run short offline evolutionary sprints between shown generations.
when: Interactive evolution where a user must rate every shown individual.
why: Reduces the number of user selections needed.

text: With save-anywhere, limit exploitable payoffs such as high-payoff gambling, or block saving in a radius around such areas.
when: save-anywhere is kept
why: Otherwise a player saves before a high-stakes random roll and reloads until it succeeds.

text: Placing a save just before a very hard challenge invites seed exploitation, while placing it far back makes repeated failure frustrating.
when: When the seed is saved and a save point sits just before a very hard fight.
why: Nearby saves make rerolls cheap; distant saves make each retry replay long stretches.

text: Full guidance on save spacing and dangers removes surprise and can make the game feel too easy, while less guidance leaves players guessing.
why: Full information removes the thrill of the unknown, while missing hints leave players feeling the game expects guessing.

text: Turtle graphics reads an L-system string as drawing commands: a turtle moves across a plane holding a pen and traces its path, so expanded strings become geometric patterns.
Self-similarity means natural variation at small scales resembles variation at larger scales, and it is the basis of fractal terrain.
A map sketch tool can test playability, display navigable paths, evaluate gameplay properties, and convert sketches into playable levels.
Sketch-based 3D world builders let non-specialists create complete virtual worlds by sketching, with surroundings adjusted automatically as each feature is added.
Favouring symmetry produces organism-like structures, and favouring bilateral symmetry produces animal-like forms.
when: Weighting symmetry in evolved L-system plants

text: A two-mode sketch world builder has a landscape mode, where a 2D brush grid encodes elevation and soil materials, and a feature mode, where specific features such as cities and rivers are added.
Turtle interpretation without branching only traces figures drawn in one continuous line; branching shapes require bracket symbols.
when: when interpreting L-system strings as drawings
why: Without brackets the turtle cannot save and restore its position and heading.

text: 1) For each angle, query the network at radius zero to get the maximum radius. 2) Query every polar coordinate from zero to that maximum to get colour values.
when: generating radially symmetric outlines and surfaces with a CPPN
why: Separating outline from colour lets one network define both shape and surface.

text: Enforce symmetry by encoding one side's rules and mirroring them to the other player, so any rule change applies to both sides.
when: When the generated two-player game must be symmetric for both sides.
why: Only one rule set is encoded, so any change applies to both sides automatically.

text: Let users sketch a coarse abstraction of a level and render it at high resolution, since a coarse sketch reduces user fatigue and the cost of evaluating candidates.
why: A coarse abstraction lowers user fatigue and cheapens automatic evaluation of candidates.

text: Terrain can be a visual backdrop with little mechanical effect, as in flight simulators, or a constraint on movement and course of action, as in shooters.
when: Deciding how much gameplay weight terrain should carry
why: The genre sets whether terrain mainly serves realism and scale or guides player choices

text: A heightmap is a two-dimensional matrix of real numbers where each cell stores one number giving the terrain height above a baseline at that point.
1/f noise sums noise at frequency f, plus half of the noise at 2f, a quarter at 4f, and so on.
Fractional Brownian motion is a random walk with specified statistics, used as the underlying concept for fractal terrain, and practical methods approximate it.
why: Exact random walks are too expensive to compute directly.

text: Genetic terrain programming evolves an expression tree that maps each map coordinate to a height value.
Gradient noise assigns random slopes rather than random heights to lattice points, and derives heights from those slopes.
Noise adds small variations to a surface, such as cloud cover, settled dust, water, fire, or skin and fur colouring.

Fractal and noise methods are fairly random and expose few global, unintuitive parameters, and fractal and agent methods struggle to encode constraints such as maximum altitude variation or reachability.
A bell-curve quantity is described by its mean, which gives the peak, and its standard deviation, which gives the spread.
Drawing tiles from a bag, dealing face-down tiles onto a board, and drawing colored balls without replacement all follow the same dependent-probability model as a shuffled deck.
when: Analyzing odds for tile, token, or urn-based draws
why: Each draw removes an unseen item, so later draw odds depend on earlier ones.

text: All sequences of ten Heads/Tails flips form a table of 1024 rows, since each flip has two outcomes.
Fractal and noise algorithms generate terrain, and can also drive search-based and agent-based landscapes.
2D platform roguelikes can vary their levels automatically between runs.
Procedural terrain and texture generation can make each replay of a simple mobile 2D game look different.
Fractal landscapes can also serve as generative material for designers.
Real-valued vectors can be read as control points of B-splines, which are chains of Bézier curves, giving smooth candidate shapes for evolution to search.
Mountain shape is controlled by slope limits, maximum altitude, width, slope, agent count, steps, and foothill length and frequency.
Hill agents resemble mountain agents but work at lower altitude, use smaller ranges, and build no foothills.
Fractal terrain methods fall into five categories, and all of them are implementations of fractional Brownian motion.
The genotype is an evolved expression tree and the phenotype is a heightmap, so this indirect encoding is compact.
Typical function sets include arithmetic, trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions, and terminals include x and y coordinates, Perlin noise and distance from the map centre.
Terrain phenotypes can include resource and base locations, and conflicting goals such as map symmetry can be optimised together by a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm.
Real elevation is statistically correlated across nearby points, so a point near a peak is likely high and a point on a plain is likely low.
Almost every three-dimensional game has ground to stand or drive on, often with vegetation and elevation variety.
Minor topological variations of the ground can be treated as noise, linking terrain generation with noise generation.
Plants are self-similar, with the same shape recurring in their sub-branches, as seen in ferns and Romanesco broccoli.
Procedural vegetation is regarded as a success story of PCG, and a well-known commercial foliage tool is cited as used in dozens of AAA games.
Terrain-editing decisions affect a space's usability as well as its appearance.
Use layered fractal noise when terrain must look natural at several scales rather than repeat a single frequency.
when: Terrain must look natural at several scales.
why: Real landscapes show similar variation at every zoom level, which layered self-similar noise reproduces.

text: Use gradient noise when terrain should look organic without rectangular grid patterns while keeping the efficiency of lattice-based generation.
when: Terrain must look organic without grid patterns.
why: Smoothing the rate of change and placing peaks from slopes avoids the grid-aligned artifacts that value interpolation creates.

text: Because noise and terrain share the matrix representation, a noise technique can usually generate terrain and the reverse also holds, though not equally well.
why: Both are stored as 2D matrices of real numbers, so one technique maps onto the other.

text: Use bilinear interpolation when speed and simplicity matter more than natural slopes, and avoid it when straight-edged stylised terrain is unwanted.
when: When a stylised, straight-edged terrain look is wanted.
why: Straight lines drawn between sampled peaks and valleys produce sharp, angular slopes.

text: Treat a landscape as a natural pattern interpreted as 3D elevation, so the same solutions used for 2D textures apply.
why: Independent random values look like static, while natural patterns need structured variation that landscapes also need.

text: Interpolating between sampled height values greatly improves terrain quality, though methods differ in quality and computation time.
why: Random unrelated heights look unnatural, while blending between samples smooths them.

text: Terrain with detail at only one frequency looks artificial; generating heights at several scales looks more natural, as in diamond-square.
why: Natural landscapes vary at many sizes, and zooming in reveals similar variation at smaller scales.

text: Larger roughness values produce rougher terrain and smaller values produce smoother terrain, because roughness sets the magnitude of the random offsets.
why: Roughness scales every random value added in the diamond and square steps.

text: Mountain agents act only on terrain above a threshold, raising V-shaped ridges along random paths that turn within 45 degrees, producing zigzag ridgelines.
when: Map regions above a set altitude, which beach agents leave untouched.
why: Occasional random turns of up to 45 degrees from the current heading bend the agent's path into a zigzag.

text: Mountain agents also build perpendicular foothills off their ridges.
Fractal terrain sums noise layers at increasing frequency, and layers at larger scales get larger amplitude.
why: Large features such as mountains rise more than small features such as boulders.

text: An expression-based terrain can be enlarged or zoomed by querying the program at new coordinates, with no change to the program.
when: When the map resolution is increased or the map is expanded.
why: Each cell is computed by querying the program with its own coordinates, so the output scales with no change to the program.

text: Peaks and valleys emerge from rising and falling slopes rather than sitting on lattice points, so gradient noise looks more organic and shows no grid pattern.
why: Peaks and valleys come from changing slopes between lattice points, so they are not tied to the grid spacing.

text: Smoothing the rate of change of gradient noise gives an extra level of smoothness compared with smoothing heights directly.
why: Interpolating slopes rather than heights means the rate of change is what gets smoothed, so slopes change gradually.

text: Bilinear interpolation produces straight-line slopes and sharp peaks and valleys, which look like a child's drawing of mountains.
why: Each slope is a straight segment joining neighbouring random peaks and valleys, so no curvature appears.

text: Mountains bound traversable space and block line of sight, so terrain shapes where players can go and what they can see.
when: Open-world terrain with both aesthetic and mechanical roles
why: Elevation features act as walls and occluders

text: Each added feature triggers a local adaptation step that blends it with its surroundings, such as clearing trees off a generated road route or laying a connecting road for a generated bridge.
when: Whenever a user adds a new feature such as a city or river.
why: Sketched edits appear live in 3D, so each addition must be merged into neighbouring terrain.

text: A lattice value's weight equals one minus the cell's fractional distance to that lattice point, so a cell one tenth of the way gets 0.9 and 0.1.
when: Lattice spacing is ten cells.

text: Terrain generation has two remedies: make terrain smooth by construction, or define a smoothness criterion and optimise the terrain against it.

Terrain generation methods include gradient-based (slopes first, then heights), fractal or noise-based (heights at several scales), agent-based (multiple feature types), and search-based (constraint satisfaction).
when: Agent-based for multi-feature environments; search-based when gameplay constraints such as traversability apply.

text: Filling each heightmap cell with an independent random value produces random spikes, not terrain, because neighbouring values must be related; randomised heights alone look unnatural.
why: Real elevations correlate with nearby points, while independent random draws ignore that correlation.

text: Sharp peaks and valleys from bilinear interpolation make collision detection unreliable, and characters can get stuck on them.
when: In games, particularly where characters traverse the terrain.
why: Sharp discontinuities at peaks and valleys disrupt collision detection, so characters catch on them.

text: 1) Apply the vertical filter vector to each column, storing results in a temporary array. 2) Apply the horizontal filter vector to the temporary array to produce the output.
when: filter is separable, such as a Gaussian
why: Reduces work per location from O(whs²) to O(whs).

text: 1) Generate mountain ridges with mountain agents. 2) Apply a smoothing step to blend the ridges. 3) Add noise to recover the detail lost in smoothing.
why: The noise pass restores fine detail that smoothing erased.

text: 1) Start a river at a coastline point and a ridge point. 2) Climb toward the mountain by following the gradient. 3) Descend to the sea, digging a widening wedge as it goes.
why: Following the terrain gradient and widening the cut mimics how natural rivers form.

text: 1) Wander randomly across the map. 2) Revisit the starting point a set number of times. 3) At each visited cell, set its height to a weighted average of nearby heights.
why: Repeated averaging over neighbouring heights removes sudden elevation jumps, and more revisits smooth a wider area.

text: 1) Loop over every heightmap cell. 2) Query the evolved program with the cell's x and y values. 3) Store the returned value as that cell's height.
why: Heights come from coordinate queries to a compact program, not from a stored grid.

text: 1) Assign a random two-dimensional gradient to each lattice point and set lattice heights to zero. 2) For a point between lattice points, compute each surrounding lattice point's gradient dot its offset vector. 3) Interpolate the four contributions bilinearly or bicubically.
why: Each gradient's contribution equals its slope times the distance moved along it, the dot product of gradient and offset.

text: 1) Generate random values on a coarser lattice of peaks and valleys. 2) Fill the in-between heights by interpolating so they connect the lattice values smoothly.
why: Random values at every point produce spiky terrain, while generating fewer values and smoothly connecting them yields gentler slopes.

text: 1) Take a weighted average of the surrounding lattice values along one axis. 2) Take a weighted average along the other axis. The order of the two passes does not change the result.
Convert terrain into a graph by separating walkable, impassable and water areas, with each graph node covering a fixed block of tiles that is referenced for object placement.
when: Building a navigable abstract graph from tile terrain
why: Objects can then be placed in the correct region

text: A cell turns secure when four or more of its eight neighbors already are, or when half of its neighbors are secure at map edges.
when: smoothing irregular zones on a grid
why: It turns irregular zones into more convex shapes, which suits an attacking side.

text: Quantize real-valued data into categories before applying a cellular automaton, using enumerated types or by binning numbers.
when: When map values are real numbers rather than already-discrete types.
why: Update rules compare discrete labels at each location, so continuous values must first be assigned to a category.

text: Enforce a minimum river length: retry river placement several times, and abandon the river if the length requirement is still not met.
when: When designers set a shortest allowed river length.

text: Generated plants must be similar yet recognisably varied, because copy-pasted trees are easy for players to spot.
when: when populating a game world with many plants
why: Repeated identical instances break the illusion of a natural environment.

text: Heightmaps store one elevation per point and are cheap, while voxel grids can represent caves and overhangs but need much more storage.
when: Use a heightmap when no caves or overhangs are needed; use a voxel grid when they are required and the storage is acceptable.
why: Heightmaps hold one elevation per location, so they cannot represent overhangs, which 3D voxel cells can.

text: Terrain that must satisfy gameplay needs requires high controllability, while terrain with little mechanical role is judged mainly by visual realism and scale.
when: Terrain must support mechanics such as traversal, line of sight or roads
why: Mechanical constraints must be enforced by the generator, whereas a backdrop only needs to look believable

text: Procedurally generated worlds can feel meaningless to players unless relevant story is generated along with them.
when: Generating worlds procedurally
why: Players look for purpose in space, and without story the space seems arbitrary.

text: Location tracking may be less necessary when levels are procedurally generated.
when: when levels are procedurally generated

text: Generators can determine a map plus the kinds, counts and locations of items and monsters.
Later city systems added agents for main roads and small streets.
Reusable building-type assets let generated towns communicate function, and generated buildings read as their type when they include consistent functional props such as anvils or counters.
why: A shared model lets a building type carry its meaning across towns, and functional props let players read its purpose from its look.

text: To differentiate generated areas, assign each a theme signalled through archetypal visuals, sound and lighting.
Vary the size, shape, cover, lighting, and angles of enemy approach across locations.
when: designing or generating combat spaces
why: Varied spaces change how the same enemies must be fought.

text: Short, repeatable matches with a stake can be replayed compulsively, with players repeating until they grow bored.
when: a simple two-player format with an ante
why: easy repetition with stakes keeps players returning

text: Tweens and teenagers are particularly vulnerable to streak mechanics, because friendship matters to them, they dislike breaking long streaks, and their brains are still developing.
when: streak-based engagement features
why: Friendships matter a lot to them, breaking a long run feels bad, and their brains are still maturing.

text: Players expect streaks to end or continue more or less than probability allows.
when: When random outcomes are shown to players with a stated probability.
why: gambler's and hot-hand fallacies

text: Substance addictions involve physical dependence and tolerance, while behavioral addictions, such as to sex, shopping or sports, do not involve a substance.
The main clinical diagnostic manual recognizes only gambling disorder as a behavioral addiction; internet gaming disorder is listed as needing more research.
Players are drawn to different aspects of persistent games, and outside life problems can also drive compulsive play, so causes vary by player.
when: analyzing why a player plays compulsively
why: Individual motives and circumstances differ

text: In real play the streak effect is minor and slightly reversed: the more consecutive hits a player scores, the less likely a further consecutive hit becomes.
Knowing cognitive science and behavioral psychology does not by itself prove that UX professionals exploit users.
Teenagers may feel pressure to keep buying until they get a fashionable item, and peer pressure and bullying can occur around virtual goods.
Among people who play, more than two in three report no gaming disorder symptoms.
why: Playing a lot is not by itself enough to count as a pathological pattern.

text: Problematic gaming can reflect underlying depression or anxiety that gaming helps manage; players likeliest to show disorder symptoms are those whose needs gaming meets but real life does not.
when: When gaming satisfies needs for competence, autonomy, or relatedness that real life does not.
why: Activities meeting these needs are intrinsically motivating, and gaming disorder has been linked to a lack of need satisfaction in daily life.

text: Treating variable rewards as automatically addictive ignores that personality and life circumstances shape how players respond.
why: The effect of variable rewards depends on context and on the individual's personality and circumstances.

text: Streaks that exploit loss aversion or fear of missing out are dark patterns, especially harmful for children and teenagers.
when: When the players are children or teenagers.
why: Threatening lost progression or loot to force play punishes stepping away, unlike rewarding persistence.

text: Gaming detox camps may distract from underlying causes such as child neglect or anxiety.
why: Focusing on gaming itself may hide root problems such as neglect or anxiety, and such programs can be costly.

text: To tell whether outcomes depend on earlier ones, examine statistics across many trials, since single sequences cannot separate skill, confidence or chance.
when: judging whether success streaks change later odds
why: Short sequences cannot reveal whether streaks change later success rates

text: Sports game players expect human-level competence from the AI.
Players cannot tell simulation from polish; both are experienced as the object's physical behavior.
why: Polish supplies sound and animation cues that signal weight and material, so the interaction feels physical.

text: In a restricted, controlled environment, AR players can focus more fully on the task, as with training simulations.
when: When AR is integrated into a controlled space such as a training room.
why: Fewer real-world hazards let attention stay on the virtual task.

text: Shared VR and AR experiences are expected to become common once connected headsets pass ten million.
Sequence mining finds the most frequent event sequences across input modalities and game context, and uses them as features for player models.
why: Hand-picked statistical features tend to limit player-experience modelling, while frequent patterns across inputs can supply more meaningful features.

text: Confusing better performance on a game-like test with general intelligence or smartness overstates what training shows.
why: Correlational findings cannot show whether gaming builds the skill or skilled people simply play more, so causal gains are uncertain.

text: The cocktail party effect is the ability to tune in one conversation among many talking at once, filtering out the others.
when: noisy environments with several sources
why: focused attention selects one source

text: Attention strongly affects working memory and learning, so unattended information is poorly learned, and motivation and emotion in turn shape attention.
when: During onboarding or when players must learn an important mechanic or system.
why: Working memory depends on attentional resources.

text: Fitts's law predicts time to reach a target from its distance from the start point and its size; larger, closer targets are faster to hit.
when: Placing buttons, cursor targets and touch controls.
why: Movement cost grows with distance and shrinks with target size.

text: Dividing attention across several tasks (multitasking) lowers performance on each and hurts learning, since attention is a finite, scarce resource.
when: When trying to do several tasks at once, especially during onboarding and when teaching important content.
why: Attention is limited and must be shared among tasks.

text: Adding detailed art to a working graybox level can make puzzles unreadable, routes hard to find and enemies hard to spot, even though the mechanics are unchanged.
when: When replacing gray shapes with final art.
why: Art adds shapes and colors with no mechanical meaning, which the player must mentally filter out.

text: A distinct alert sound can trigger a rise in awareness and a fight-or-flight reaction in players.
when: A game signals that an enemy has noticed the player.
why: The sound is learned as a threat cue through repeated pairing.

text: Players must inhibit a trained reflex to shoot red targets when red elements such as teammates appear, a Stroop-like effect that may slow detection of enemies.
when: red-coded allies and enemies share a colour
why: Trained shooting reflexes conflict with the colour cue.

text: Players give more attention and cognitive resources to things they care about once they understand why those things matter.
when: Presenting goals or challenges
why: Understanding value directs attention and working memory

text: Players of multiplayer shooters at home keep their attention in the arena, so these games function as arena play despite the home setting.
when: multiplayer first-person shooters played at home
why: Attention is focused on the competitive arena.

text: Audiences assume characters from the same franchise share one world, even when creators never planned that connection.
when: Multiple characters appear under one franchise
why: Viewers treat a shared setting as common knowledge, so the connection is inferred even when it is never stated.

text: All five experiences are present to some degree at any moment, and one may come to the forefront, such as frustration or a well-timed satisfying hit.
when: during play

text: Players think in terms of their avatar's abilities and constraints, so a new ability changes which parts of the world are reachable while the world itself stays the same.
when: When a game lets the avatar's abilities or tools change over time.
why: Spatial awareness is shaped by what a body can do, mirroring how players engage with game worlds through their avatar's capabilities.

text: Players at very low health treat a nearby health pack as the top priority, and their attention narrows so that every motion of the game feels more heightened.
when: when the player's health is very low and a health pickup is nearby
why: Leaving the pickup to an opponent costs the player a valuable resource, so everything else matters less until it is collected
