text: A player carrying a flag avoids fights and heads straight for their base, and movement feels slower and more urgent.
when: when a player holds an objective object that must be returned to a base
why: Carrying the object makes it the focus of all action in the space

text: Distraction usually erases a briefly held code, such as an eight-digit two-factor code, except perhaps its first and last digits.
when: a player must hold information while distracted
why: distraction disrupts short-term storage

text: People counting a target action often miss an unexpected figure walking through the scene; about half of viewers did in one study.
when: attention focused on counting a target
why: focused attention filters out unexpected events

text: AR players must divide attention between the real environment and virtual elements at once, which raises cognitive load.
when: When AR content is shown while players move through the real world.
why: Multitasking between real and virtual information costs attention.

text: When tasks are demanding or new, dividing attention takes longer and produces more errors.
when: When multitasking on demanding or unfamiliar tasks.
why: Working memory cannot handle the switching load.

text: Players following an established plan keep decision pace low, but a change in circumstances sharply raises it as they re-plan.
when: an event invalidates or redirects the plan the player is following
why: A changed circumstance forces new decisions into a short interval

text: Skill raises how much information a player can absorb, so one information density bores experts while overwhelming novices.
when: setting the information density of a game for a mixed audience
why: Experts process a game much faster than novices.

text: Anger, fear, and intense focus inhibit creative association, so creative breakthroughs need relaxation.
when: When seeking insight on a design problem.
why: Stress and focus reduce the flow of associative thinking.

text: The Gulf of Execution is the gap between what a user intends and the physical action an input device requires.
Memorability is how easily players regain proficiency after a break from the game.
Diverse redundancy delivers the same information through different forms or channels, such as dialogue, animation, level visuals and HUD markers, rather than repeating one form.
The attention economy is the competition among companies for users' time across streaming, social media, games and media outlets, made constant by smartphones.
Focus is selective attention that ignores some inputs and concentrates on others, and it leads to the flow state.
The corpus callosum is a large nerve pathway connecting the two brain hemispheres so they can share information.
Sensation is the physical stage where sensory receptors respond to energy emitted or reflected by objects.
Cognition gives access to semantics, the meaning attached to what is perceived.
Active attention is top-down and controlled, aimed deliberately at a goal.
Passive attention is bottom-up, captured by an environmental stimulus that triggers a response.
Focused attention works like a spotlight that selects one element and leaves the rest largely unprocessed.
Divided attention, often called multitasking, means simultaneously processing several items.
Cognitive psychology (the cognitive paradigm) studies the mind's inner processes, including perception, attention, memory, motivation and emotion.
Attention picks out a small share of incoming signals for further processing, leaving most other input largely unprocessed.
Active (top-down) attention is deliberately directed by the person toward a goal, such as reading carefully.
Passive (bottom-up) attention is pulled toward something by the environment, such as a sudden question or noise.
Selective attention filters out irrelevant input so that one stream, such as one speaker in a noisy room, can be followed.
Cognitive load is the mental effort demanded when information is excessive or a task is highly demanding.
Sensation is the raw input received by receptor cells.
Behaviorism studies observable behavior rather than inner states.
Attentional resources are scarce and very restricted, performance is best when full attention goes to one task, and people are mostly unaware of those limits.
The brain reorganizes itself, as when learning an instrument or recovering from injury; this is real learning potential, not a hidden reserve of unused capacity.
Hick-Hyman reaction time for a decision grows logarithmically with the number of displayed options.
Noise arises from layers of aesthetic detail, signals that demand too much skill to read, and signals packed too closely together.
Attention is focused or divided, filters inputs, can cause inattentional blindness, and runs on finite resources.
Attention cannot efficiently cover several elements at once, which is the main limit on what players can take in.
Behaviorism ignores unobservable factors such as attention and memory and overlooks side effects.
Human minds did not evolve to grasp this kind of complexity.
why: cognition evolved for simpler environments

text: What a person focuses on at any moment is a blend of unconscious desires and conscious will.
Perception is subjective, memory fades, and attentional resources are scarce.

Behaviorism studied only measurable behavior with repeatable experiments and won the early psychology split, while introspection examining experience as it occurs could not be reliably measured, leaving psychology to avoid subjective experience.
why: Scientific verification standards push psychology away from the nature of experience.

text: Gameplay rests on four mental abilities: modeling, focus, imagination, and empathy.
why: These are the working tools a player brings to any game.

text: Most of what happens in the brain is hidden from conscious awareness, yet it steers much of what people perceive, say, and do.
why: Game experiences happen largely in this hidden layer.

text: Recent studies show health benefits of mental exercise, especially for older adults.
Attention has never been especially strong and varies with task complexity, familiarity, motivation and the environment; it is not notably worse today than before.
why: Survival logic makes attention shift to threats and important cues.

text: The brain is not pre-wired; it is plastic, and experiences such as games, language, discussions and sports shape it throughout life, with plasticity decreasing with age.
why: Learning changes synaptic connections, so every experience leaves an effect.

text: The brain uses about 20% of the body's energy while being about 2% of body weight, and it can tolerate only a limited workload.
why: Limited capacity makes unnecessary mental effort costly for players.

text: Describing the brain as processing information is a simplification, because the brain does not work like a computer.
Although the hemispheres differ in some specializations, for any given activity both cooperate rather than one doing the work alone.
The left hemisphere is relatively better at generating words and applying grammar, while the right is relatively better at analyzing speech intonation.
No scientific evidence shows that either brain hemisphere specializes in creative or logical processing.
No scientific evidence shows that women multitask better than men.
Neurological differences cannot be reliably linked to cognitive or behavioral differences.
The dual-system approach is criticized for lacking nuance.
People recognize a word faster when a semantically related word was just shown, as in lexical decision tasks.
Masked priming, where the prime is too brief to be consciously seen, is the best-validated subliminal effect but has very limited influence.
Attention is essential for noticing changes but is not always sufficient.
Attention is tied to engagement, a central concept in video game design.
Running a language task alongside another task can cut its brain activation by more than half.
Some situations require inhibiting automatic emotional responses, since an instant reaction can create new danger.
when: an automatic reaction would cause harm elsewhere

text: The brain does not literally process, encode, or store information the way a computer does; the computer metaphor is useful but inaccurate.
The brain is malleable, so every interaction with the environment can rewire it, not only interactions with games.
The left-brain versus right-brain split is wrong, since both hemispheres collaborate on nearly any activity.
Adolescent media multitasking is linked to poorer working memory, weaker achievement, and reduced growth mindset.
Bare skin, attractive faces and alluring expressions capture attention, since human biology is tuned to notice them.
Games that are limitlessly deep often become multiplayer because a person can learn any game system but can never fully understand another human mind.
Players rarely miss signals because they are too quiet; they miss them because overall signal density overwhelms their perception.
when: a player fails to notice important information
why: Perception capacity is limited, so extra signals become noise.

text: Reduce chaos by presenting new enemies clearly and keeping enemy behavior simple and easy to read.
when: Combat has many combatants or offscreen causes
why: Under pressure players' focus narrows, making cause and effect hard to track, and offscreen actors in multiplayer add further causes.

text: Let players perceive their immediate next goal from the environment rather than relying on walls of text.
why: Players perceive environmental cues directly, while text is a weak substitute.

text: Detail that looks strong in a still image often blurs into noise in fast play with many entities, so artists and designers should balance detail against the cues needed to read the scene.
when: Designing art for crowded, fast-moving scenes
why: Still renders show detail that players cannot resolve during motion.

text: Keep both mind and hands engaged; unthinking menial tasks let attention wander, and idle thinking makes hands fidget.
when: When building an activity meant to put players into a flow state.
why: Distraction pulls focus from the task, so an activity must occupy both thinking and physical action to hold attention.

text: Silence notifications and other distractions when a task needs sustained attention, since distraction reduces work quality.
when: tasks requiring concentration
why: Every incoming stimulus can pull focus away, and a demanding task suffers when that focus drifts.

text: Use biological explanations for fast, automatic responses such as fight-or-flight arousal, not for complex deliberate decisions.
when: explaining player reactions
why: biology explains automatic responses far better than complex choices

text: Automatic emotional responses help in immediate danger but can be wrong when the threat is a false alarm.
when: immediate danger is perceived
why: speed is valued over accuracy in automatic responses

text: Learning is hindered when task demands, or the attention they require, exceed working memory limits, so onboarding must be designed carefully.
when: Designing tutorials and onboarding.
why: Working memory is limited, so overloaded learners retain less.

text: Attention determines what is perceived and how deeply it is processed, and the attention paid to a stimulus largely sets how strong its later memory is.
why: Attention sets how much processing an input receives, and depth of processing drives long-term retention.

text: Attention and emotion during processing set learning quality; environmental factors such as noise and information organization affect them, and attention's impact on learning makes it key to user experience.
why: Attention is very restricted in the brain, creating many limits that user experience design must account for.

text: AR raises cognitive load because users must attend to the digital overlay and the real world at the same time.
when: When a player must split focus between a digital overlay and the physical surroundings at once.
why: Splitting focus across two information sources draws on the same limited attention pool.

text: Cognitive load theory predicts that heavy load hinders learning, unfamiliar tasks need more resources, and people multitask poorly while mostly unaware of it.
why: Attention is finite and scarce, so a task that consumes most of it leaves too little for learning.

text: The processors run concurrently and feed one another, so new input can be perceived while earlier input is still being acted on.
A sensory substitution device helps the user perceive only when the user controls its input, and passive exposure gives no useful perception.
why: Active control turns the device's signal into meaningful information.

text: Two stimuli falling within the same perceptual cycle are fused, much as animation frames fuse into continuous motion.
why: Perception runs in discrete cycles of roughly 50 to 200 ms, so near-simultaneous inputs merge into one frame.

text: When attention is divided between two language-based tasks, people switch back and forth between sources and fill gaps, creating a processing bottleneck.
when: When one must follow two spoken streams of information at the same time.
why: Both language tasks compete for the same verbal processing channel, forcing rapid switching between them.

text: The heavier a task loads working memory, the more attention it needs, and the more disruptive distraction becomes.
why: Working memory has limited capacity, so a demanding task leaves little room to absorb distraction.

text: Multitasking costs more than the sum of its separate tasks, because executive control is needed to coordinate them; this is called underadditivity.
when: When attention is split across several tasks at once rather than one demanding task.
why: Coordinating several tasks needs executive control on top of each task's own resources, adding a cost.

text: Higher working memory load increases inattentional blindness; more inputs and complex information leave less attention for new or surprising events.
when: When a player is deeply focused on a demanding task, such as combat.

text: A new skill takes nearly all attentional resources, so doing anything else at the same time becomes very difficult.
when: while a skill is still new
why: Until a process becomes automatic, it needs attention and executive control, leaving little for other work.

text: With enough practice a task becomes automatic, handled by fast intuitive processing that needs little attention and almost no executive control.
when: After a task has been practiced long enough.

text: Executive control must inhibit the automatic response to a word before the target feature, such as ink color, can be detected and named.
when: conflicting distractor present
why: automatic reading competes with the task

text: Multitasking is mostly rapid task switching that works only for automatic, undemanding tasks; efficient multitasking is largely a myth, and lost efficiency often goes unnoticed.
when: When the tasks combined are both undemanding and largely automatic.
why: Attention mostly shifts back and forth between tasks instead of covering both, and the lost efficiency goes unnoticed.

text: Signals flow from the amygdala to the cortex more strongly than the reverse, so fear can persist even when the threat is known to be fictional.
The limbic system regulates cortical areas, changing how broadly attention spreads and where it is directed.
Attention filters inputs, selecting some and dropping others, so players can miss important elements that are outside their focus, a effect called inattentional blindness.
Overly complex or poorly understood rules demand more from players and reduce meaningful choice and the sense of control.
why: Complex rules raise comprehension demands; rules players cannot grasp, rationally or intuitively, cannot support informed choices.

text: Familiar, automatic activities need fewer attentional resources, freeing capacity for other tasks such as navigation.
when: Once a skill has become automatic.
why: Attention is a heavily limited pool; skills practised into routine free up capacity that can be redirected to other tasks.

text: The amygdala and hippocampus identify a situation, compare it to stored events, and help store the new experience.
when: In a fight-or-flight situation, such as when danger is present.
why: Storing the event lets a person avoid the same danger more efficiently later.

text: Ten one-hour sessions over ten days of action shooter play improved visual attention, such as tracking multiple moving elements, compared with a puzzle-game control group.
when: adult non-gamers

text: Fifty hours over nine weeks of action games improved contrast sensitivity compared with a control group playing a life simulation game.
In one study, 63% of participants primed with rude words interrupted a conversation, against 17% primed with polite words.
why: Several minutes of exposure to a concept's words primes behavior aligned with that concept.

text: Executive control is subtracted from resources first, then the remainder is split between tasks, so split attention is slower than sequence when one task is demanding; undemanding pairs are fine.
when: when at least one task is demanding
why: both tasks compete for limited working memory resources

text: A user's mental model is their picture of how a system works, while the system image is how it actually behaves; usability errors arise when these differ.
why: The mental model frames interaction and sets expectations of results, so a mismatch makes outcomes surprise the user.

text: The Model Human Processor splits human interaction into perceptual, cognitive and motor processors, each with a cycle time.
why: The model is a collected result of many studies of human reaction and response time, with cycle times given as ranges.

text: Signal Detection Theory treats player decisions as made under uncertainty, with the relevant cue hidden among noise; designers can tune how easily cues are detected.
why: Reasoning and decision-making always occur with some uncertainty present.

text: Information processing starts with perceiving an input and ends with a change in memory through synaptic modifications.
The dual-process model has two modes: System 1 is fast, instinctive and emotional; System 2 is slow, deliberate, logical and handles effortful work.
Attention varies along two axes: active or passive, driven by a goal or by the environment; and focused on one element or divided across several.
The brain turns sensory input into stored memories via perception, working memory, attention, motivation and emotion; it is a simplified map.
why: The brain is still largely unexplained, so the map is simplified, not literal architecture.

text: Assuming players reliably perceive, remember and retain every game element or lesson, even when well designed, ignores known limits of attention and memory.
why: Memory fades quickly for material with no meaning or reinforcement, so retention cannot be assumed.

text: Many game menus and HUDs ignore proximity, which adds friction when players first encounter them.
when: Designing menus and HUDs
why: Players rely on grouping cues to parse unfamiliar layouts.

text: Flooding players with information, such as too many tips on a loading screen, overwhelms them and reduces retention.
when: Presenting tips and instructions
why: Excess information competes for limited attention.

text: A mental model alone is rigid and misses the player's emotional relationship to the world, such as a feeling of open space or loneliness.
why: What matters to the player is the feeling the world evokes, such as openness and possibility, which a system picture does not capture.

text: Assuming developer intent, implementation and player experience line up overlooks that the gap between them can be large.
why: The experience is crafted through many minds and implemented under system and production constraints, so intent and outcome diverge.

text: Exploiting users' cognitive limits to maximize revenue at their expense is the opposite of the UX purpose.
If the computer behaves in ways that do not match the designer's mental model of the system, the designer may become frustrated or confused.
when: In mixed-initiative procedural content generation, where a human designs alongside a computer
why: If designer and computer cannot explain their reasoning to each other, the collaboration becomes hard to carry out.

text: Making one signal louder in an already crowded scene overloads the player further rather than helping them notice it.
when: a key signal is being missed in a busy scene
why: Added volume increases total density, adding to the overload.

text: Assuming players who share a space will mingle; if they cannot find people they want to talk to, they quickly leave.
when: In social games where players share a space and want to meet specific kinds of people
why: Desired contacts vary by age and play style, so mixing alone does not satisfy players who cannot find those they want.

text: Treat 240 ms as a typical value, not a fixed limit, since the ranges around each processor's time are wide.
why: The 240 ms figure combines perceiving, thinking and acting, each with its own wide range, so it is an average.

text: People often cannot accurately explain why they feel as they do, so introspective survey answers are unreliable.
when: Interpreting survey answers about motives
why: Self-reported reasons may not match actual causes.

text: Constant internal questioning during an experience is the most common cause of disrupting it, so observation should avoid long analysis.
when: Self-observing during play.
why: Too many questions in the mind spoil the experience being observed.

text: Trying to boost creativity by stimulating one hemisphere is practically impossible in healthy people and would not help anyway.
when: In healthy people, not split-brain patients with a severed corpus callosum
why: Research finds no proof that hemispheres specialize in creative or logical functions, so the approach would not help.

text: Romanticizing or dismissing a person based on a left-brained or right-brained label has no scientific basis.
why: Research does not support the idea that each brain half specializes in creative or logical thinking.

text: Assuming deliberate thinking always catches intuitive errors made by fast thinking.
why: System 1 makes automatic intuitive errors, and System 2 may not notice that those errors are happening.

text: People assume they multitask well and are often unaware of how poorly they do it.
why: Attention is limited and drives how well information is processed and retained, while people underestimate how much divided attention costs.

text: Overloaded players may feel overwhelmed and also fail to learn the mechanics and systems being taught.
when: During tutorials and onboarding, when new tasks demand more attention than familiar ones
why: Once cognitive load exceeds working memory limits, players cannot learn the mechanics being taught.

text: Automatic skill does not make players immune to distraction; reactions to unexpected events slow when attention is elsewhere.
when: When attention is focused on another task
why: Attention works like a spotlight that filters out whatever is not its focus, so unexpected events can go unnoticed.

text: Assuming that what players learn in a game will transfer automatically to other contexts.
when: In gamified activities that rely on points, badges or rewards to change behavior
why: Rewards change behavior within one context, and the skills do not carry over once the rewards stop.

text: Respect brain capabilities and limits and system limits; plan onboarding, feedback and interface load around perception, memory and attention limits.
when: When designing a game whose vision must fit both engine limits and player capabilities
why: Acknowledging cognitive limitations is the first step to overcoming them in design and decision making; UX guidelines rest on these capabilities.

text: Direct players to the information that matters while keeping their cognitive load low.
when: When teaching unfamiliar, important information, such as during onboarding
why: Attention filters input and its resources are finite, and unfamiliar tasks need far more of them than familiar ones.

text: Reduce cognitive load for anything not meant to be challenging, so irrelevant information does not demand attention or memory.
when: Designing HUD, menus and secondary information.
why: Limited working memory and attention are wasted on irrelevant demands, hindering learning and flow.

text: Reduce player memory load with relevant, contextual information in the HUD and interface, so the game does not depend on recall.
why: Memories are fallible reconstructions, and players forget much of what matters, so recall cannot be assumed.

text: Manage cognitive load and verify, via a player action, that key details were noticed, rather than blaming players for missing something merely shown on screen.
why: Cognitive overload obstructs learning, and multitasking adds executive control demands on top of each task's attention.

text: Plan for players to miss signals by sending important messages several times rather than forcing attention through camera control or interrupting dialogue.
when: In games where players can look anywhere and get distracted during play
why: Forced observation breaks flow and immersion and creates new problems.

text: Where possible, direct the limited attentional resource to a single task rather than splitting it.
why: Focusing on one task is the ideal condition for performance.

text: Avoid multitasking during tasks that need undivided attention, such as operating a vehicle.
when: When engaged in an activity that requires undivided attention, such as driving
why: Divided attention in such activities could lead to severe consequences.

text: Keep teaching within the player's cognitive load, the mental effort needed to understand something, so players are not asked to learn too much at once.
why: Information reaches long-term memory only when teaching stays within the effort a player can spend understanding it.

text: Fast-paced games are feared to weaken attention, yet robust training studies show action games, mostly shooters, lastingly improve visual acuity, visual attention and spatial cognition, mostly via near transfer.
when: When evaluating action games, such as shooters, in training studies
why: Benefits appear on tasks similar to what was trained, while distant domains show no such gain.

text: Well-made sound feedback makes players enjoy an interface, but they often cannot say exactly why.
when: Sound is used well as a stand-in for touch.
why: Sound can simulate touch, a sense interfaces otherwise lack, so the interface feels tangible and enjoyable.

text: Room tone makes an environment feel more real and can set the mood of a place.
when: a looping background sound fills a space
why: constant sound grounds the player in the space

text: Spectacular failures attract observers, who become tempted to play.
when: When failures are visually entertaining to watch.
why: Watching an impressive failure creates curiosity about playing.

text: Players learn to anticipate repeated rhythms, and with practice may feel the game is playing them rather than the reverse.
when: rhythms repeat over play
why: learned timing builds expectation

text: Big visual spectacle gives a quick emotional rise but a shallow payoff.
why: Spectacle needs only a big event, while other emotional sources depend on interlinked mechanics or characters, so its payoff stays thin.

text: 1) Stop interacting. 2) Wait in the game's space. 3) Notice the emotional background that remains.
when: When checking whether a game has atmosphere.
why: Atmosphere is felt in the background, so pausing reveals it.

text: Reserve spectacle for moments that amplify relief or pride the player has already earned, like a blast after a hard fight is won.
why: It amplifies relief and accomplishment the player already feels, so it builds on existing emotion rather than creating it.

text: An avatar is the character a player controls, entering the game world through it; it is the player's instrument for both perception and expression, and all perception passes through it.
Player identity with an avatar is malleable, shifting between feeling like the character and feeling detached, so players claim credit for good outcomes and blame the avatar for falls.
when: after outcomes of play
why: identity transfer is unstable

text: Player criticism often means the player imagines a different game than the one being built.
Players who care about computer-controlled characters want to obey, protect, help, or destroy them, which gives designers a strong tool for steering choices.
when: Players have built an emotional connection to characters
why: Care motivates players to act on characters' behalf

text: Audiences invest effort imagining a fictional world only if it satisfies a deep, important desire.
why: Imagining a fantasy takes effort

text: Players of a visible avatar wince when it is hurt and sigh with relief when it escapes harm, as if its injuries were their own.
when: A visible avatar in danger
why: Player and avatar identity merge during play

text: Players value visible faces, and an avatar's face shown on screen, tied to its health, lets players sense injury through peripheral vision.
when: When an avatar's face is normally hidden from the player
why: Players can read a small face image without focusing on it, so it conveys state while they look at the action.

text: Beyond their play style, players want to express who they are, so games that offer direct identity expression tend to be more appealing.
when: In multiplayer games
why: Strategy shows how players play, but identity needs its own outlet.

text: Observing enough interactions lets players assemble a coherent picture of a world's physical traits, such as heavy, sticky, soft or sharp.
why: Senses extended into the game let players perceive virtual objects through handling, as with real things.

text: Players can feel as much or more empathy for customized avatars they create as for story-driven predesigned characters.
when: Games offering character customization and identity investment
why: Investment in one's own created identity builds emotional attachment.

text: Players relate to specific personal details even without sharing the designer's background, because the details reflect common human experiences.
why: Lived details feel as believable as historical ones, and most players can recognize something in them.

text: Players become possessive of a protagonist they built and object to dialogue or plot moments that force an attitude or decision.
when: When writing for a customizable protagonist.
why: Players see the character as their own identity, so out-of-character content feels like a violation.

text: Players care about characters when they share history with them, so attachment to a character often depends on established history rather than on the character alone.
Players tend to engage less with NPCs introduced purely as reflections of the player character.
when: an NPC exists only to mirror the protagonist
why: Such NPCs act only as progression tools with no life of their own, so players disengage.

text: Players who care about a specific person work hard to protect that person, even when the wider world is saved or destroyed by accident.
when: When a character is tied to a personal stake.
why: Players will do everything to protect someone they care about, so world-scale results follow.

text: A directly controlled avatar lets the player feel they are the character, adding an interpretive layer and sense of identity that board games lack.
when: when a game has a player-controlled avatar
why: Direct control makes the player embody the character rather than move pieces.

text: Players viewing crude symbols can build vivid scenes and relationships, such as characters sharing a quiet moment, that detailed graphics would replace.
when: the display uses abstract symbols or minimal graphics
why: the player's mind supplies the emotional detail

text: A vulnerable avatar becomes relatable because the player must protect it, making its safety a personal concern.
when: When the avatar can be harmed or fail during play
why: Vulnerability taps into the player's own survival instincts and need to protect themselves from danger.

text: Imagination is the everyday capacity to fill in gaps and reason with mental pictures, used for communication and problem solving.
Actors are the objects that drive game events, such as triggers, lights and static meshes.
Primary attributes are bought directly with points, while secondary attributes are calculated from primaries plus bonuses and cannot be bought directly.
Pregenerated character selection lets players choose one of several fixed characters, each built around a role or play style, instead of creating one.
Identity transfer to an avatar cannot be forced directly by design.
The brief moment of half-sleep is short and unpredictable, yet can still be enough for the mind to be refreshed.
Imagination serves two functions in play: communication, especially storytelling, and problem solving.
Imagination matters as much as empathy, since every experience builds a small world in the guest's mind.
Power comes in four types: Bio, Gear, Magic, and Science.
An object's position is a common attribute, and the play space is usually treated as distinct from objects.
The new element of VR and AR is letting the player's body enter the simulated world.
Expressive multiplayer avatars created in childhood may remain part of people's personal and professional lives for decades.
why: Multiplayer worlds offer the most expressive online identity.

text: Pregenerated characters are common in team arena games, fighting and melee games, driving-race games, and cooperative board games, and serve as quickstarts in longer RPGs.
A game can pair a directly controlled character with an indirectly controlled avatar, such as a camera operator, which the player can override.
Players enjoy characters who surprise them, so each character should be designed with surprises to discover, as a toy is designed.
when: When designing characters for play
why: Fun is pleasure with surprises.

text: Use real players as narrative characters mainly in face-to-face groups where participants know and respond to one another.
why: social pressure encourages good-faith participation

text: Time spent imagining oneself in a world increases projection into it.
when: When the world is consistent and compelling enough to fill the imagination
why: Repeated familiar characters and settings make the fantasy world feel more real with each visit.

text: Letting players customize a personal place, through relationships or surroundings, fosters a sense of belonging.
why: Custom homes give players reasons to visit and exchange gifts, pulling them into socializing.

text: A meter that grows through in-character actions, in place of a standard stat, reinforces a character's persona.
The controlled object in a game works as a surrogate body, and the player learns its properties through handling it, as with a new physical object.
when: When the player is handling an unfamiliar virtual object or world
why: Feedback returns through the controlled object to the senses, so the player builds perception of it.

text: The five-factor trait model covers neuroticism, agreeableness, extraversion, conscientiousness and openness to experience.
Avatar archetypes: an ideal form that players wish to be, and an iconic blank slate with little detail anyone can fill; many successful avatars combine both.
why: Simple, nonthreatening avatars with little detail make it easy for players to project themselves.

text: Avatar motion can be described by six criteria: type (linear or rotation), dimensions (axes moved or rotated along), frame of reference, position versus rate, direct versus indirect control, and integrated versus separate dimensions.
Annoyance, tedium, or unclear links between what a player intends and what happens can disrupt identity transfer to the avatar.
Treating the avatar purely as a tool limits how deeply players project into it; projection is stronger when players relate to the character.
why: Players project onto anything they control, often subconsciously, as bowlers do with body English on a ball.

text: Letting players insert their own photo into an avatar seems appealing but does not last, because players prefer an aspirational self over their actual appearance.
Overlapping abilities or units across races blur each race's identity, so overlaps should be cut even though removing content may upset fans.
when: finalizing race and hero kits
why: Redundant kits make races feel interchangeable.

text: Closeness alone can create intimacy without contact, provided the proximity is welcome and the other party is not a stranger or unwanted.
when: Designing interpersonal or sensual interactions.
why: Moving into another's personal space heightens physical intimacy on its own, even without any touching.

text: Build systems that stop players seizing things not rightfully theirs; this makes griefing harder.
why: Policing griefing forces designers to judge intent, which is costly, so systems that don't enable griefing avoid that burden.

text: Build ownership by combining many states with high-utility objects spaced so that transitions between any two are easy.
why: Easy transitions between any two objects from any direction let players improvise, so their combinations rarely repeat.

text: Pregenerated characters suit short play that needs fast entry, while attribute and skill systems suit games where the character is central and used in many ways.
when: choosing a character creation approach
why: Pregenerated picks let players start at once, without the lengthy attribute screens that deep character creation requires.

text: Players blame themselves when the cause is visible (such as an unused counter), but blame the game or controls when cause is missing, though their skill may be at fault.
when: a failure occurs
why: Without a visible cause, players attribute failure to the system.

text: Players attribute random setbacks to luck rather than their own choices; weaker competitors who lose blame luck, cheating, glitches or poor balance.
when: random setbacks occur or competitive losses happen
why: attribution bias

text: A single puzzle that blocks progress can make players quit the game entirely.
when: progress depends on one puzzle
why: a stuck player has nothing else to do

text: When reloads are fast and death is framed as learning, players cycle through dying and retrying calmly.
when: Games where each checkpoint restarts the player quickly after a failure.
why: Short restarts from nearby checkpoints make each failure cheap, so retrying feels calm rather than punishing.

text: Players who struggle without guidance often blame the game and quit in anger.
when: Players lack guidance on a difficult task.
why: Missing guidance makes failure feel like the game's fault.

text: Blaming the avatar for a failure releases frustration and keeps the player engaged, returning them quickly to the pleasure of control.
when: after a failure

text: Blaming technology for a supposed collapse in attention overlooks how attention normally works and that people may simply face more distractions.
why: Attention limits are the same for every generation, so changed behavior reflects different expectations and distractions rather than weaker focus.

text: Prefrontal cortex, linked to the limbic system, regulates emotion including automatic responses and helps control impulses; it matures until about age 25, so children and teenagers find self-control harder.
Children aged 4 to 6 first show interest in games, which must be very simple, and parents often bend the rules to keep play enjoyable.
when: Designing games for children aged 4 to 6
why: Young children need simple rules, and parent-led play adjusts rules to keep it fun

text: Players keep trusting that a puzzle is solvable even when solving it takes far more moves than the scramble.
when: the puzzle was scrambled from a known solved state
why: the known solvability sustains confidence

text: Players roll dice a certain way, carry lucky charms, or follow rituals to influence fate.
when: When outcomes are pure chance and players have no way to control them.
why: people seek cause and effect and want to feel they influence outcomes

text: Fans of physical skill sports track statistics and bet on single-play outcomes, treating them much like random events.
when: watching or betting on skill-based sports
why: individual plays are uncertain, so fans reason about them probabilistically

text: Skilled players in random games estimate their odds, factor in opponents' likely reactions, and size their actions to match.
when: randomized games where players can respond with bets or choices
why: Players are rewarded for predicting and responding to randomness, so their grasp of probability directly affects results.

text: When a few recipients receive only correct predictions over repeated rounds, they assume a working system exists, since chance successes look like skill.
when: repeated predictions sent to split groups
why: Coincidental hits are mistaken for genuine ability

text: Highly skilled people may assume tasks are easy for everyone, so they underrate their own abilities.
Skilled estimators and other players form very different perceived probabilities for the same event.
Showing players the actual odds can prevent misjudgments of chance.
why: Enumerating the outcomes reveals that combined rolls are not equally likely, which intuition often misses.

text: Use emotional triggers that work regardless of skill, such as art, characters, music, shared humor, and tech demos, to keep new players engaged early.
when: During early play, before players can handle skill-based activities like puzzles, creation, or combat.
why: Such triggers engage players who lack the skill needed for the core activities.

text: Children aged 10 to 13 often become passionately absorbed in particular interests, often games for boys, as rapid neurological growth supports deeper and more nuanced thinking.
when: Designing for tweens aged 10 to 13
why: Rapid neurological growth supports deeper thinking, and the intense absorption is sometimes called the age of obsession

text: Teens aged 13 to 18 prepare for adulthood, male and female interests diverge significantly, and all teens eagerly seek new experiences that gameplay can provide.
when: Designing for teens aged 13 to 18
why: Preparing for adulthood drives experimentation, and interests split by gender

text: Most adults separate game fantasy from reality and focus on mechanics and skill rather than on violence.
why: Players focus on skill, puzzles and goals rather than the violent theme, and can tell fantasy from reality.

text: Children and teenagers face higher risk of harm in online games than adults.
when: online games
why: limited self-regulation and susceptibility to peer pressure

text: Children regulate their emotions less well than adults, and they are especially vulnerable to time pressure and peer pressure.
when: Designing for players under 18
why: The prefrontal cortex that regulates emotion is not fully mature until about age 25

text: Adult age groups are separated mainly by family and career transitions, and time, money, and responsibilities shape how much and what adults play.
Children aged 0 to 3 find abstract interfaces such as gamepads beyond them, while direct interfaces such as touch screens fascinate them.
when: Designing games for children aged 0 to 3
why: Direct manipulation matches their developing motor and cognitive abilities

text: Video games can support cognitive development, as long as children also have diverse kinds of play.
Parents should check content rating systems before letting children play a game.
when: choosing games for children
why: Rating sites exist specifically to help parents make informed choices, since the research on aggression effects is mixed.

text: Designers who know a game well or are highly skilled assume familiar features are obvious, so they stop noticing barriers and miss where first-time players get stuck.
when: evaluating onboarding and interface clarity
why: Familiarity and skill hide the difficulty newcomers face.

text: Assuming players think and perceive things the way the designer does is a pitfall, since perception is constructed individually; teams without user research tend to make this assumption.
when: teams without user research
why: Perception is a subjective construct the brain builds from sensation, so designers' views are not shared by default.

text: Designers who play constantly or know their game too well have biased difficulty judgment and cannot see when it is too hard; empathy with the player is needed.
when: judging difficulty as the designer
why: Familiarity hides the newcomer's experience.

text: Designers lose objectivity about their work as development goes on, and especially when they built the features they test, since personal investment dulls critical judgment.
when: late in long development, or when the designer builds the features they test
why: Prolonged involvement and personal investment dull critical judgment.

text: Designers often fear players will dislike work they invested heavily in, and may avoid playtests by delaying them, missing them, or drifting off during them.
why: Criticism of heavily invested work is painful, so the fear of hearing it drives designers to avoid tests.

text: Experts lose their feel for what a new player expects, so watching a first-time player shows whether the opening is too hard or well judged.
when: When the designer has played the game many times.
why: Long familiarity with a game hides the experience of newcomers.

text: Designer confidence must be rebuilt at every stage: novices doubt their ability, practitioners fear past success was luck, and veterans fear they have lost their touch.
when: Working through each career stage
why: Each stage brings different doubts about skill and success.

text: People underestimate common everyday risks and overestimate rare dramatic ones, and the distortion seems to follow their fears.
when: estimating how likely different events are
why: estimates are shaped by fear rather than frequency

text: Players who believe the first mover has an edge may perform worse as the second mover, a possible psychological cause of the advantage.
when: top-level play when the second player holds this belief
why: Belief in an edge can lower the second player's performance.

text: Players often refuse bets with positive expected profit when stakes are high or wins are very rare, because expected value does not match how the bet feels.
when: offered favorable gambles with large stakes or rare wins
why: Felt risk and rarity outweigh the calculated edge

text: When an action and its response fall within the same perceptual cycle, the player reads the response as caused by the action.
when: Computer responses arriving within about 100 ms of the player's input.
why: Shared perceptual cycles bind cause and effect in perception.

text: When response does not harmonize with the metaphor, players experience dissonance and frustration and may disengage; when everything harmonizes, designer and player both benefit.
when: when a game's elements disagree in fidelity
why: Dissonance undermines immersion and engagement

text: People reduce dissonance by changing a belief, such as deciding an unreachable goal is not worth having or that a risky habit is worth its cost.
why: Holding inconsistent beliefs causes discomfort, which motivates reconciling them.

text: Adding a third, dominated option steers choices toward a target option; removing the decoy shifts choices toward the cheaper alternative.
when: when players compare several priced options
why: relative comparison makes the target look like the best value

text: People rarely change default settings, so defaults strongly shape outcomes and deserve careful design.
when: when designing default options
why: status quo bias keeps people with preset choices

text: In an otherwise even contest, consumers favor familiar titles, so an already popular game beats an unknown one.
when: two games of similar quality compete
why: Familiarity lowers perceived risk for consumers.

text: The curse of knowledge is the difficulty of ignoring what you already know, so designers who understand a system cannot easily perceive or predict how new players will perceive it.
why: Familiarity hides what is confusing to newcomers.

text: Anchoring is overweighting the first number seen, so all later numbers are judged relative to it.
Dunning–Kruger effect: people with low skill overestimate their ability, because judging competence depends on the competence being judged.
Cognitive biases, also called cognitive illusions, are systematic patterns of thought that distort judgment and decision making, arising from intuitive shortcuts called heuristics.
why: Heuristics produce predictable reasoning errors.

text: Cognitive dissonance is the discomfort of holding inconsistent beliefs, which motivates people to reduce the inconsistency.
Gambling operators, politicians, marketers and scammers exploit the same cognitive biases designers face, so recognizing these mechanisms helps designers avoid misusing them.
People believe their decisions are rational, but research shows strong biases in judgment; designers must account for their own biases as well as players' biases.
why: Decision making is systematically influenced by biases that people do not perceive.

text: Developers suffer from the curse of knowledge, so they cannot see the game as a new player does; researchers help by observing how the target audience discovers it.
why: Designers who know the game cannot judge its clarity for newcomers.

text: Check whether your intuitions about the interest curve match what players actually show.
why: Players differ, so designers' intuitions about interest can diverge from what players actually show.

text: Designers are inevitably wrong about how systems will play out, so plans should be treated as hypotheses to be tested.
when: When writing a plan that predicts player experience
why: Emergent system behavior is hard to predict from the design document alone.

text: When a designer feels 90% sure a design will work, its real chance of success is closer to 30%.
when: when judging how likely a new design is to succeed
why: Overconfidence from optimism bias.

text: Appearing weaker can lure an opponent into risky actions that succeed only against a weak player.
when: In games where a player can conceal or misrepresent their skill level from opponents.
why: An opponent who underrates the player misses subtle plans and takes gambles that only pay off against a weak player.

text: If the designer does not believe enough to champion the game in person, others are unlikely to believe in it either.
when: When seeking funding, publication or distribution for a game.
why: The designer knows the game better than anyone, so their visible conviction signals to others whether it is worth backing.

text: Cognitive biases mostly arise because System 1 runs automatically and produces intuitive errors.
why: The slower deliberative system often fails to notice the errors made by the fast, intuitive one.

text: Assuming your own enjoyment predicts your audience's enjoyment fails: designers have unusual tastes, teammates may disagree, and many audiences are shut out.
when: When the intended audience's tastes differ from the designer's own tastes.
why: Personal enjoyment does not predict other people's enjoyment.

text: Believing awareness of a bias makes you immune is a mistake: biases are mostly implicit and persist after you know they exist, like optical illusions.
why: They do not disappear through knowledge alone.

text: A designer who knows an encounter too well cannot play as a real player would, so self-testing stops revealing new problems.
when: After the designer has repeatedly self-tested a feature until it feels finished to them.
why: Familiarity hides how newcomers approach the challenge

text: Players are more creative than designers expect, so the designer's own testing will not catch every loophole.
when: In complex games with many interacting rules that behave differently under varied conditions.
why: Players act in ways designers did not anticipate, and rule gaps that look fine on paper appear only once implemented.

text: Creators focused on individual parts may fail to notice that the overall sequence has a poor shape.
Assuming the designer's intended reading of a visual element matches the player's reading of it.
why: Perception is a personal mental interpretation, shaped by a player's prior knowledge and expectations.

text: What designers, programmers or artists perceive may differ from the audience, because culture, gaming references and generation shape perception.
when: When the audience's background, familiarity with games, or age group differs from the creators'.
why: Perception is shaped by a person's experience, expectations and sometimes culture, so creators read signs differently than players.

text: Let developers see their own progress directly, such as a designer watching their playtests or a programmer seeing tests pass, rather than only through reviewers.
when: When organizing feedback for creative staff.
why: Progress that only a reviewer sees may not register with the person who made it.

text: Include the lusory attitude in the psychological state a designer considers when designing for players.
when: playcentric design
why: Players voluntarily accept the rules as constraints on reaching the goal, and that acceptance becomes part of their psychological state.

text: Loss aversion is acceptable when the loss is known, consented gameplay, but charging a fee to avoid that loss is exploitative.
when: When the loss is part of gameplay that players knowingly accept, rather than a route to payment.
why: The pressure shapes the experience for informed players and does not push them into paying to escape the loss.

text: In cooperative play, all players form one team against the game system itself rather than competing with each other.
The commander problem usually appears when player skill differs a lot, such as an expert teaching beginners.
when: When players have uneven skill in co-op play
why: Skill gaps make experts' directions accepted by others

text: Collaboration declines as the end of a play session approaches.
when: near the end of a session
why: Players expect fewer future interactions with their partners.

text: Players often start a game for its gameplay but stay for the community around it.
why: The group's social rewards keep players returning long after the game's own pleasures have begun to fade.

text: Players with known friends can make shared plans and respond to each other's intentions, which reduces the guesswork needed about teammates.
why: Communication and familiarity reveal intent.

text: Highly committed designers keep thinking about their project during everyday life, carry notebooks, research solutions and work at odd hours.
when: When a developer has self-identified commitment to the work.
why: The work has become part of their identity, so it occupies them off the clock.

text: Sharing an activity or place with the same people does not by itself create community, while strangers who share an obscure interest may feel a strong one.
A community is a collection of people bound by a common interest, aim, or objective who grow more familiar with one another over time.
The period of contagion is the time a player talks constantly about a game; interest spreads through people during this window, modeled like an epidemic.
Cognitive socialization is the knowledge and cognitive skills a society expects its members to have, which play helps build.
Community property is an asset owned by several players rather than one, such as a ship no single player can afford.
Children's games target ages 2 to 12, where entertainment is the primary goal and education is only a possible component.
Cooperation reflects that a team with many eyes, hands, and abilities is more powerful than one person.
Player-made wikis dissecting all components of a game reveal how communities uncover information designers keep hidden.
Designing for community serves three goals: meeting players' social needs, extending the period in which they recommend the game, and keeping them playing for many more hours.
Cooperative play has received more attention in children's board games than in games for adults.
Role-playing games often place cooperative quests inside a competitive overall structure.
Cooperative games can be non-zero-sum because one player's gain does not necessarily mean another's loss.
Cooperative players of a protein-folding puzzle game identified a monkey virus crystal structure within weeks, far faster than researchers who had worked on it for years.
why: Human pattern recognition in puzzle form can solve structural problems quickly.

text: Designed social experiences include building and breaking trust, joking, beating opponents, rescuing companions, and finishing a task together.
Cooperative play often engages players more than competition, so competitive games benefit from adding cooperative modes.
why: Players are social, and cooperation usually engages them more deeply than competition does.

text: A cooperative game should provide communication opportunities, suit both friends and strangers, create synergy rather than antergy, assign roles where useful, and include tasks no one can finish alone or that force communication.
when: Designing or reviewing cooperative play
why: Communication, roles and interdependent tasks make teamwork produce more than the sum of its members

text: Audiences are delighted more by the care put into planning for their reaction than by the object alone.
A code of ethics matters most for large studios and popular games, especially those played by under-18s.
when: In large studios and in popular games, particularly those played by children under 18.
why: Human interests should take priority over business considerations, since exploitative designs serve the company at users' expense.

text: Community keeps players talking about a game longer, because the game becomes part of their daily life and gives them things to discuss.
why: Once a game becomes part of players' daily lives, they keep discussing it, which keeps their enthusiasm spreading to others.

text: A game that creates community can stay in play for a long time even when its other qualities are weak, such as simple rules with few decisions.
why: Social interaction alone can hold a group together for hours.

text: Players who assist each other toward a shared objective show reduced negative effects from violent games compared with solo players.
when: violent games played with teammates
why: Cooperative play builds group cohesion and trust, and that trust carries over into cooperation after the game ends.

text: Cooperative play increases later cooperation with a partner compared with solo play.
when: Players who cooperate as teammates on a shared goal, compared with playing solo.
why: Team play builds cohesion, which activates trust norms that carry over into later cooperation.

text: Guilds joined in childhood can shape social networks for life, much as sports team loyalty does today.
why: Early online identities are kept for decades, so the social ties tied to them can persist too.

text: When pieces move, capture, or otherwise interact, their relationships to the board and to each other shift, so the system's state keeps changing.
Coupling a mechanic's roles, such as restricting movement while an action is used, creates new tactical choices for the player.
when: When one mechanic can serve several roles at once, such as offensive, defensive, and tactical.

text: Unrestricted PvP can make the whole community feel unsafe, not only the players who are attacked.
when: When PvP has no limits and is not the core activity of the game.
why: Players who are betrayed after building trust stop trusting strangers, eroding community trust overall.

text: 1) Identify a player who dominates discussion and ruins fun. 2) Treat the problem as a player issue rather than a game flaw. 3) Remove that player from the group, as tabletop RPG groups sometimes do.
when: When one player consistently ruins the group's fun
why: Social problems may be better solved socially than by redesigning the game

text: 1) Identify whether the core conflict pits players against each other, against the game, or both. 2) Check whether the world layout and gathering places bring players together again. 3) Confirm newbies, players and elders each have suitable experiences. 4) Schedule regular community events. 5) Give players real reasons to cooperate and stay in contact.
when: when checking whether a game fosters a strong community
why: Community depends on how these areas interact, so review them together.

text: Give competitive social games a quick, built-in way to resolve disputes so that group play does not stall.
when: In informal, unstructured competitive group play where disputes arise between players.
why: Disputes that cannot be settled quickly halt the whole group, while quick resolution lets play continue.

text: Design situations where players must communicate and cooperate to succeed, rather than letting a single player master the game alone, so that community gains real value.
when: When designing multiplayer systems
why: Mandatory interaction makes community meaningful; solo mastery reduces its value.

text: When a game supports social loops formally, design their progression and integrate it with other arcs and loops.
why: Social loops only carry meaning through player interaction, and formal support lets their progression be designed explicitly.

text: In team-based PvP, celebrate actions that help the team and its objectives, and value support roles as much as offensive roles.
when: team-based PvP
why: Recognizing only kills rewards the top shooters, whereas valuing team-helping actions motivates a wider audience.

text: Define what counts as inappropriate behavior and require players to read and accept a code of conduct.
when: When some players are expected to deliberately harass others.
why: Behavior aimed at strangers is felt as harassment or unfairness, and neither feeling motivates players.

text: Treat protecting game communities, especially minors, as an ethical responsibility of developers.
Give each cooperating player a specific role and a way to clearly contribute to the team's success.
why: Relatedness is met when each cooperating player's contribution to the team is noticeable and meaningful.

text: Design for friendship deliberately rather than leaving it to chance, since people love to play with friends.
why: Friendships form only with chances to talk, icebreakers, and tools to keep them going.

text: Define participants explicitly: PvP or PvE, single-player or multiplayer, team or solo, AI or humans, and squad or single character.
Design casual games for everyone by avoiding twitch play, violence, and complex rules, so players of any gender and age can pick them up.
when: when aiming for the broadest possible audience
why: Those elements exclude many potential players

text: Girls rarely start large spontaneous games because disputes stop play and are hard to resolve, whereas boys argue, resolve the dispute, and continue.
when: unstructured group play with competition
why: Disputes draw most girls to sides and resolve slowly, so the game halts and may not resume.

text: Males enjoy competing to prove they are best, while many females find the bad feelings of losing, or of causing another's loss, outweigh the pleasure of winning.
Competitive players model a game's balance to find items or strategies furthest above or below the curve, gaining an edge.
when: Competitive play in an established game.
why: Outlier items reveal balance weaknesses or strengths that opponents can exploit.

text: Players who choose their opponents may collude with friends to throw games, and may run second accounts that feed easy wins or swap losses.
when: when players can pick opponents
why: control over pairing enables coordinated losses

text: Competition produces losers, and losing is frustrating, especially when the game feels unfair or humiliation is possible.
why: Competition always has losers, and only one player can top the scoreboard, leaving the rest demoralized.

text: Constant conflict between characters pulls players into taking sides, making them invested in the drama.
when: Characters argue in front of the player
why: Each character pushes the player to side with them, turning the player into a party to the argument.

text: Conflict against other players lets people show they are better than others, creating status-driven rivalry.
why: Opposing players give people a way to show superiority over others, which drives status rivalry.

text: Players compete fiercely inside a game's boundaries and then part amicably, because the conflict stays within the play space.
when: after a competitive game ends
why: Boundaries keep conflict from spilling into relationships.

text: Intense skill-based competition absorbs all attention, so it conflicts with relaxed social enjoyment such as laughing with friends.
when: When high-skill competitive play occurs alongside social play.
why: Full attention on competition leaves no room for relaxation.

text: Competition helps individuals establish their status among others.
The conflict effect also appears with shapes: naming one shape while ignoring a word that names another slows responses.
Conflict is central to communities. Conflict against other players, or against the game resolved through cooperation, builds community, because cooperating on game conflict builds shared ties.
why: Groups bond through shared struggles, like rivals or a common cause, while solitary conflict creates no community.

text: Being the best clearly expresses competence, but only one player can hold the top spot, so others may feel demoralised.
when: Competitive games with winners and losers, especially when the game may feel unfair or humiliation is possible

text: Competence is feeling in control and skillful, with growing mastery, desire to be challenged, impact, and progression via positive feedback; without visible progress, motivation drops.
Players modulate held continuous inputs in small, quick increments over time, below conscious thought, like a driver steering; this works only if the game keeps responding consistently.
why: Sustained real-time control needs the computer side to refresh within about 100 ms, the continuity threshold.

text: Letting players choose powers that suit their skills makes them feel powerful and shapes the game around their preferred style.
Players satisfy their need for certainty either through control, such as improving drop rates, or by accepting randomness and grinding until luck delivers.
when: Players face random drops
why: Both control and randomness provide certainty about eventual success.

text: Players feel competent when their actions have impact, accomplishments are celebrated, they learn how to improve after failure, and they can see progress toward goals.
when: When players improve on personal metrics or overcome difficult challenges

text: Adding more customization options, such as avatar looks, emotes, or base names, generally increases players' sense of autonomy.
when: Designing player-facing customization
why: Choosing among options gives players control over how they present themselves

text: Players who feel in control also tend to feel powerful, so both feelings should be checked and increased together.
Players describe responsive control with words such as floaty, smooth or loose, which name how controlled objects respond.
when: describing how controls feel

text: Ongoing action, perception and contemplation of one object produce control fusion, the feeling of controlling something external to oneself.
why: Action and its response perceived within one perceptual frame bias the player to see the result as caused by their action.

text: New players may need hours of practice to map on-screen movement onto controller inputs.
when: a game uses complex control mappings
why: Translating screen motion into input takes time before play feels natural.

text: The shared aim of the game feel principles is a sense of control and mastery strong enough that players use it as a tool for self-expression.
Hand designs with closed cards and small text discourage showing cards, and a theme that reinforces personal decisions encourages each player to make their own choices.
when: When a co-op game faces one player dominating
why: Expectations set by the theme and components shape player behavior

text: PC gamers are generally older than console players and split more evenly between men and women.
when: When choosing a platform for a target audience.

text: Demographics such as age, gender, income, and ethnicity are external; grouping by them is a proxy for finding what people find pleasurable.
Games set in familiar real-world settings may require cultural knowledge, such as the meaning of everyday rooms, objects, and social events, before players can interpret in-game events.
when: the game depicts a familiar real-world culture
why: players read events through their own cultural knowledge

text: Ask whether the intended audience, such as an age bracket or niche interest group, will like the game enough.
Players who cannot explain a loss blame the game, so even a fair game feels unfair; visible counters keep blame on their own choices.
when: losing players lack an explanation
why: Losers who cannot see why they lost may think the game is unfair even when it is fair.

text: Hidden randomness lets players suspect secret result alteration, since computers could do so; unexplained losses draw the strongest complaints because they invite cheating suspicion.
when: number generation is not visible

text: If players believe designers inflate power on purpose to drive purchases, they may leave the game.
when: players perceive inflation as deliberate

text: Players who lack an equal chance to reach the goals feel cheated and lose interest.
when: a built-in advantage favors some players

text: When players blame control flaws or game flaws, or believe success requires superhuman performance, they see the game as unfair and reject it.
when: When players fail a challenge
why: Perceived unfairness ends engagement

text: When cheating is possible and cheaters cannot be identified, fair players may quit, fearing they cannot win without cheating or that they will lose to a cheater.
when: in competitive games where cheaters are hard to spot
why: Players cannot trust the outcome of matches.

text: Players may report too much combat when total combat is reasonable, because spacing or variety is wrong, such as a large fight followed directly by a small one.
when: Players complain about combat volume
why: Back-to-back strong encounters cause fatigue without recovery time.

text: Repeated setbacks make players call a game unfair, and heavily invested players may accuse others of cheating.
when: repeated losses, high stakes
why: losses are blamed on external causes

text: Players tend to trust computer random generators less than physical dice, cards and tokens, perhaps because they cannot physically handle the randomizer.
when: Video games generating random results with no visible physical randomizer such as dice or cards
why: Lacking tactile involvement may reduce perceived legitimacy

text: Stuck players may press every control at random for minutes, and mounting frustration can lead them to quit quickly.
when: unresolved obstacles

text: Players may struggle far longer than designers expect with a step that looks trivial, and watching this makes the problem hard to dismiss.
when: a step the designer expected to take seconds
why: Watching testers struggle in person is hard to dismiss, while written summaries invite being waved off as unrepresentative.

text: Tuning for a hardcore audience was common in early 1980s games but is not always in fashion.
when: Choosing a difficulty target for a game's audience.

text: Players who must trust that a leap is survivable without seeing the outcome can experience emotionally interesting moments of blind trust.
when: when a level withholds visibility of a safe landing
why: Forced trust heightens tension and makes the choice feel meaningful.

text: When turn results depend on several players' simultaneous choices and are not explained, players perceive outcomes as arbitrary and lose trust in the game.
when: simultaneous-choice games with unclear feedback
why: Players cannot see how their actions connected to results

text: Trial and error can mislead: repeated misses on a 20% attack can convince a player it never hits, so they value it at zero.
Dopamine is released slowly when people are motivated and spikes on unexpected rewards, not expected ones, signalling the gap between predicted and actual outcomes.
why: Dopamine has many roles, such as being critical to movement.

text: Measured dopamine rises: about 100% during video game play, about 65% in meditation, 150–300% from food or sex, and over 1000% from methamphetamine.
when: Measurements taken in a 1998 study of older video games; no recent studies exist.

text: Dopamine supports learning, motor control and motivation, and its low levels accompany Parkinson's disease.
No recent studies have measured dopamine during modern video games, so current evidence on games and dopamine is lacking.
Without motivation there is no behavior; disrupting dopamine in animals can stop them seeking food.
Dopamine rises before a reward arrives and marks motivation, wanting, rather than pleasure in the moment of receiving it.
when: interpreting reward and motivation in players
why: Anticipation drives seeking, separately from enjoyment.

text: The brain's reward center normally releases dopamine in response to everyday stimuli such as food, money, or an attractive mate.
Dopamine fasting advice is misleading, since lowering dopamine is harmful rather than healthy.
why: Dopamine governs learning and movement, and low levels are linked to Parkinson's disease, so lowering it harms.

text: Judging addiction risk by dopamine increases is a pitfall, since dopamine level does not predict how many people become addicted or how severe addiction is.
why: The roles of dopamine and related chemicals in addiction are still poorly understood.

text: Emotional engagement is built through formal elements such as challenge, premise and story, plus responsive AI creating presence, great music and physical believability rather than photo-realism.
Meeting a new enemy type excites players, because they expect repeated defeats may yield a useful ability.
when: when a new creature is encountered
why: Players anticipate the reward from repeated kills.

text: When intensity becomes overwhelming, players want to remove the headset and their presence collapses.
when: Bodily threats are pushed beyond the level players find thrilling
why: Once a threat feels too real, the player's inner awareness that it is pretend pushes back against the sense of presence.

text: Fast or physically active games let players release anger and frustration on opponents in a safe setting.
when: a player feels anger or frustration
why: Safe outlets allow emotional release

text: Whimsical games with funny situations take the player's mind off troubles and show that fun is still possible.
when: a player is distressed
why: Humor shifts attention away from worries

text: Being rescued by an unseen fighter produces relief and gratitude, even though the rescuer's motive is never modeled.
when: the player is pinned down and then saved
why: players attribute intent to unexplained actions

text: Identical physical situations produce different emotion when the perceived consequence differs, since emotion tracks the anticipated outcome.
when: the same physical event carries different perceived danger
why: Emotion follows the anticipated consequence

text: Pride in accomplishment is the lasting satisfaction of an achievement, called naches in Yiddish when it concerns children.
Thrill is fun that combines terror with a sense of safety.
Triumph over adversity is the satisfaction of winning against long odds, called fiero in Italian.
Wonder is awe and amazement that lead to curiosity.
Discovery is the pleasure of finding something new, such as world areas, secret features, or clever strategies.
Dramatic decisions engage the player's emotional state, while weighted decisions carry consequences on both options.
An experience is the full arc of emotions, thoughts, and decisions a game creates from start to finish, and it changes as it moves from setup to payoff.
Surprise underlies humor, strategy and problem solving, and the brain enjoys surprises; brain scans show even unpleasant surprises activate the brain's pleasure centers.
Reading player emotion from faces is a skill that improves with practice.
Perception and cognition can induce and shape emotion, not only follow from it.

Objective input includes ECG, photoplethysmography, galvanic skin response, respiration, EEG and electromyography, plus motion tracking of posture, facial expression and head pose, and verbal cues in social games.
Primal threats include filth and rotten food (revulsion), venomous creatures (recoil), visibly diseased people (avoidance) and ghastly wounds (adrenaline).
why: people are genetically wired to react to these cues

text: In everyday life people set their own goals and need not reach every one to count as successful.
A game's value comes from the experience it creates when played; without play, the physical or digital artifact is worth nothing.
Conscious experience is all a person can know as real, since senses and minds filter the world, so experiences designed through games can feel as real and meaningful as everyday ones.
why: Experience is the only reality accessible to us.

text: Some mechanics exist to entertain rather than to solve level challenges, so utility-based evaluation can miss them.
Classic action arcade titles maximize thrill by layering rapid-tempo soundtracks, perilous scenarios, brutal fictional content, and head-to-head social rivalry.
A game's resulting experience can last minutes, days or years.
Emotional weight grows with the importance of the value and the size of its shift.
Other media provoke emotion through spectacle, character or music, while games alone provoke emotion through decision.
Upheaval, or merely the prospect of it, is always engaging and sustains attention, so key shifts should be made more dramatic.
why: Drama combines anticipation with uncertainty, so the possibility of change keeps attention even before it arrives.

text: When feeling nervous, recall a time of supreme confidence and deliberately return to that state.
when: Feeling nervous before or during a pitch
why: Recalling a confident memory can restore a steadier bodily and vocal state.
