text: Ask whether a psychological pressure serves gameplay and is transparent to players, or mainly serves retention and conversion metrics.
when: when judging any pressure mechanic
why: separates legitimate design from exploitation

text: Refinement should look for ways to add emotional pull that keeps players returning to the game.
when: During the refinement stage of design

text: Define one key emotional experience early and build gameplay, story, and art around it, since it can drive the whole game.
when: when starting a new game concept
why: a single emotional anchor gives the design a consistent direction

text: Drawing practice trains perception, and better seeing improves drawing; the two skills reinforce each other.
why: The brain attaches category labels to familiar objects for efficiency, hiding detail that a more visual way of looking can perceive.

text: Shape player expectations indirectly through control mapping, metaphorical representation and art treatment rather than relying on raw button-to-event mapping.
when: When designing a real-time control system whose results players must anticipate
why: Players press imprecisely and their intent is ambiguous, so simple mapping is not enough.

text: Letting units grow stronger over time and risking their permanent loss can make players more emotionally invested in them.
when: When adding progression to units in strategy games
why: Players attach more feeling to units they have invested in and could lose.

text: Vary the experience over time, since a single sustained emotion becomes tiring and loses power.
when: When designing experiences longer than a brief moment.
why: Sustained emotion exhausts attention, so variation keeps it powerful.

text: Ask where the experience starts and ends, and what constraints physical reality provides, before shaping the play space.
why: Limits run in both directions: the design's own edges and the constraints real life places on it both shape the play space.

text: Tiredness, pain, stress and hunger reduce learning efficiency.
Hours of practice build an emotional unconscious that signals which option feels better, and players act on that signal alongside conscious thought.
when: When a player has no time to deliberate over options
why: Decisions merge awareness and instinct, so a trained gut feeling steers choice when deliberation is impossible.

text: People make decisions by imagining a scene and judging the feeling it produces, a process called prefeeling.
when: When choosing between imagined options
why: Imagined feelings guide choices even when they misrepresent what the experience will be like.

text: An experience cycles from thought to emotion, emotion to idea, idea to reaction, and reaction back as feedback.
why: Each stage prompts the next, so the experience feeds itself.

text: Game experience forms in order: designers create mechanics, mechanics are wrapped in fiction, interaction produces a long event sequence, events trigger unconscious emotions, and emotions merge into one experience.
Plutchik's Wheel of Emotions has eight primary emotions arranged as polar pairs: joy-sadness, anger-fear, trust-disgust and surprise-anticipation, with intensity varying within each primary.
Emotions vary along two dimensions: intensity and valence, the flavor of the feeling, so high-intensity emotions can differ as fury, grief, or terror.
when: When plotting or comparing emotional states.
why: Two separate axes describe emotions more fully than intensity alone.

text: Two-factor theory holds that emotion combines physiological arousal with a cognitive label explaining its cause; the label decides which emotion is felt.
Eight primary game pleasures are sensation, fantasy, narrative, challenge, fellowship, discovery, expression, and submission.
Experience bleed is the spillover of context across an experience's edges: the audience's life carries into play, and the designed context carries into their life afterward.
why: Designed experiences lack hard edges, and the player's surrounding context begins shaping play as soon as they decide to engage.

text: Repeated gore, creatures or spectacle numbs players, who then tune triggers out or laugh at them; spectacle not tied to earned effort deadens players, especially without a prior challenge.
when: When gore or spectacle recurs often, or lands with no preceding challenge
why: long overuse dulls the reflex

text: Reading through abusive comments in search of useful points wastes effort and damages wellbeing.
when: When feedback contains personal attacks or insulting remarks
why: Such material is demoralizing and can harm mental health, which no one should have to risk for their job.

text: Inferring player feelings from faces is hazardous without carefully designed measurement, since expression is culturally variable and universality is doubted.
when: Game development relies on facial reading without a measurement protocol.
why: Expressions vary across people and cultures, and the universal nature of expressions has been questioned.

text: Claims that players can be hooked by releasing oxytocin or delivering dopamine shots are oversimplified or neuromyths; how these chemicals work is poorly understood.
when: When a claim about brain chemicals is offered as a way to hook players
why: they are released in many situations, but their mechanisms are not well understood

text: Physiological signals without game context may yield erroneous experience states, since a rise in galvanic skin response can mean frustration or excitement depending on the cause.
when: When physiological signals are read without the game's real-time state
why: The same physiological rise can signal opposite high-arousal states, so the cause must be known to interpret it.

text: Building elaborate logic to support a feeling that seems obviously true.
why: Introspective feelings do not reliably match reality, so a sense of obvious truth is weak support for conclusions.

text: Interpret emotional expressions within the person's own evaluation of the event.
why: Emotion arises from each person's appraisal of an event, so the same expression can reflect different evaluations across people.

text: Read frustration scores as a balance question rather than a simple negative when checking whether players reach flow.
when: when using the observation grid to check flow

text: Design play to produce positive emotion, and avoid negative emotion not tied to gameplay, such as usability problems or bugs.
why: Emotion steers behavior, so people gravitate toward pleasant experiences and avoid unpleasant ones.

text: Identify small emotions individually, such as a brief flash of anger, a dash of disgust or a surge of triumph, as a chef distinguishes single flavors.
when: analyzing or designing play experience
why: Subtle emotions are what the game is ultimately built to produce, so designers must detect them.

text: Build discovery and surprise into the game as part of its emotional experience.
Approach games first through experience design, with technology supporting the intended experience rather than driving the design.
Be deliberate about which expectations your cues, labels and presentation set, because they shape how players judge a mechanic before experiencing it.
when: when presenting a mechanic or item to players
why: Pre-experience expectations can outweigh actual response

text: An event provokes emotion only when it signals a meaningful change in a human value, so design events as shifts between value states.
why: Emotion depends on change, not on the event alone.

text: The limbic system (hypothalamus, hippocampus, amygdala) is generally regarded as the emotion system, though it is loosely defined and some researchers doubt it exists as a unit.
why: Researchers have not reached agreement on which brain structures belong to it.

text: Players can enjoy manipulating a system even without knowing its goal, as with rotating blocks in falling-block puzzles.
why: Manipulating a system is a more basic layer of play that can be enjoyable before the player grasps any objective.

text: Players often like a game without knowing why, usually because its elements all reinforce something that interests them.
why: Theme works subconsciously, so players sense the attraction without being able to name the connecting idea.

text: Audiences want fictional worlds to be real and believe they might someday be reachable, so these worlds feel more real than their defining media.
why: Audiences want the world to feel real, and each consistent product visited strengthens it in their imagination.

text: Players feel tense when health is low and lives are scarce, because a final loss would send them back to the start.
when: low health with few lives and no saves
why: A full restart makes each loss costly.

text: Feeling humiliated, or believing the game is unfair, does more damage to players than losing itself.
when: when players lose a match
why: Players judge the game by their perception, which is shaped by the brain, so unfairness feelings count even when the system is fair.

text: Players can express dissatisfaction with a game by plotting games they enjoy in other quadrants.
Narrow hallways paired with tank-style controls intensify claustrophobia, and removing those controls changes the feel of the same space.
why: Narrowing space near the limits of player movement makes them feel unable to act as they otherwise could, evoking vulnerability.

text: Cognitive reappraisal changes how a situation is evaluated, which in turn changes the emotion the situation produces.
Pleasure depends on context: dancing can delight at a party yet embarrass at a job interview.
The brain empathizes with mental models, so people can feel emotion toward drawings, photos, or characters that have no real subject.
when: Designing characters and images meant to evoke emotion
why: Empathy responds to representations as well as to real beings

text: Combat can produce shock, panic, closure, tension, chaos, anticipation, struggle, and the realization of mastery.

Discrete emotions serve different functions: interest supports selective attention, joy opens social interaction, sadness slows activity to scrutinize trouble, anger mobilizes energy, and fear drives escape.
Cognition influences emotion, so how players interpret events changes how they feel about them.
People can attribute physiological arousal from a frightening situation to an unrelated cause, such as attraction to someone they meet there.
why: Emotions do not reliably report their true causes; arousal is interpreted in context.

text: Common emotional triggers include physical danger, changes in social status, learning, acquiring possessions, sexual opportunity, family and safety, and certain natural environments.
Prototypes can be used to discover which mechanics evoke a target feeling, such as relaxation or freedom.
why: Prototypes make a rough idea concrete enough for the team to understand and evaluate.

text: Use intense bodily threats for thrill, but stop short of the point where players want the experience to end.
when: Designing fear or danger for a VR experience
why: Such threats feel like real bodily danger, so beyond a threshold they overwhelm players and drive them to quit.

text: To horrify modern audiences, threats must disturb at a deeper level than the basic reflex the trigger produces.
when: designing horror
why: Basic reflex triggers have been overused, so audiences tune them out or laugh at them.

text: When one source of arousal can stand in for another, the character's fear and the player's excitement merge into one feeling.
when: When the character's threat and the player's mechanical challenge coincide.
why: Substitutable sources of arousal blend into a single emotion.

text: Humans mirror the emotions they see in others, which is why watching characters in conflict is compelling.
why: Mirroring makes observed emotion feel shared.

text: Games can use danger directly because failure risk is built in; players enjoy the release that follows overcoming it.
why: Architecture aims for safety, so buildings rarely use danger this directly.

text: Listener mood can be scored across eight dimensions (tension, vigor, caring, hostility, mental clarity, fatigue, relaxation, sadness) using a 45-item questionnaire.
1) Identify a negative emotion that follows from gameplay, such as losing a match. 2) Help players reinterpret it, such as by pointing out what they did well.
when: negative emotion is tied to gameplay and cannot be avoided
why: reappraising an event changes its emotional weight

text: 1) Check whether players understood what to do. 2) Check whether they felt free to make decisions. 3) Check whether any character depictions were uncomfortable or biased. 4) Check whether they expected polish not yet in place.
when: finding the cause of a negative reaction

text: Put reactions into concrete words, since feelings are abstract and designers need concrete words to describe the experiences they want to create.
when: Describing target experiences
why: Concrete language makes experiences designable.

text: Emotion and cognition influence each other both ways: emotion can precede, occur without, or be shaped by cognition; perception and cognition can induce emotion; emotion guides behavior.
Logical explanations players give for a game are often rationalizations; the underlying feelings are what shape how the game is experienced.
when: interpreting player feedback
why: people justify feelings after the fact

text: When players choose, emotion drives the decision far more than logic, although they explain it afterward in logical terms.
when: players face a decision
why: A purely rational decision is a myth; explanations are logical but choices are emotional

text: Panicked players attack prematurely and greedy players chase expensive targets, distorting their payoff evaluation.
when: high-pressure competitive decisions
why: Emotion overrides careful assessment of payoffs.

text: An emotional trigger is anything in a situation that causes emotion, because the unconscious mind evaluates situations automatically and produces a feeling.
Emotions are automatic and do not report their causes; the mind attaches plausible reasons to a feeling, often incorrectly, usually crediting the most noticeable thing in view.
Emotions reward and motivate learning, and all games teach.
Events matter to players only when they provoke emotion, so design each event around the feeling it should create.
Emotion influences perception, cognition and behavior; it can enhance or impair reasoning and push choices toward good or poor outcomes, so its role is not black or white.
why: The limbic system regulates cortical areas, changing how widely attention spreads and where it is directed.

text: Strong emotional cues draw player attention; a dangerous hazard draws more attention than an ordinary environment.
why: Emotion focuses attention on what the player must notice.

text: Emotionally charged choices are easier to decide than neutral ones, because strong feelings about the outcomes make the options clear.
why: Reasoning can weigh what two paths would bring, yet cannot select between them; feelings supply that final step.

text: Negative emotions can drive repetitive, cautious play, while positive emotions can support creative problem solving.
Blaming all irrational decisions on emotion is too simple; many systematic reasoning errors come from how cognition itself is built.
Explicit (declarative) memory holds facts and events a person can consciously recall and describe. It has two forms: semantic memory for facts and episodic memory for events.
Leading wording can implant false memories of details that never appeared, and these persist about a week later.
when: When a leading question is asked and recall is tested after a delay
why: Distorted information is reconstructed into memory

text: An encoding deficit occurs when information is stored superficially because attention was low or processing was shallow.
Emotions are the foundation of memorable experience.
Eyewitness testimony is a major contributor to wrongful convictions.
Players forget much of what they learn, and their recall is a fallible reconstruction rather than an accurate copy.
Better recall of emotional events is correlated with greater amygdala activity during the event.
Flashbulb memories are overstated: people recall one or two central details accurately but feel highly confident about the whole memory, which is often as distorted as ordinary memory.
Eyewitness memory is not fully reliable.
Many design mistakes come from believing we understand things that we do not.
when: When a game combines many interacting mechanics, technologies and human player behaviors.
why: overconfidence hides gaps in knowledge

text: Counter encoding deficits by drawing attention to important information and making players process it deeply.
when: When players must remember critical information such as controls, mechanics, or objectives.
why: Encoding quality shapes later storage, so shallow processing from low attention or depth causes memory lapses.

text: People misattribute arousal to a nearby person or stimulus, such as reading fear as attraction, and this is hard to avoid because arousal is difficult to distinguish from its actual source.
when: arousal occurs near a person or stimulus, such as a frightening moment coinciding with a social encounter
why: the nearby source receives the blame for the arousal

text: Players expect to win far more often than displayed odds imply; at a shown 75–80% chance, many expect wins around 95% of the time.
when: When a displayed chance of winning is high but short of certain.
why: Self-serving bias

text: Fear can trigger quick automatic reactions, and reacting to a possible threat is safer than ignoring it.
when: a threat is possible but uncertain
why: a false alarm costs less than a missed threat

text: People given unexplained arousal adopt the emotion suggested by surrounding cues, and people told the true cause of their arousal report no emotion.
when: unexplained physiological arousal
why: Arousal is interpreted through a label; a known cause removes the need for one.

text: A player in a quiet turn-based duel can cycle through strain, relief, dominance and suspense within minutes, while observers see only calm moves.
when: turn-based competitive play
why: emotions pulse with every move while the visible actions look unchanged

text: Decision emotions respond to what might happen, whereas most emotional triggers respond to something happening in the present.
when: the player faces a choice with an uncertain outcome
why: Decisions concern possible futures rather than current events

text: Players are more willing to pass layered barriers when they know a reward waits at the end, even if the reward is not shown.
when: When players know a reward waits at the end of a sequence of challenges.
why: Layered spaces let players anticipate the rhythm of challenge and reward.

text: Appraisal theory holds that emotion depends on how a person evaluates a situation, so the same event can trigger different emotions in different people.
Bottom-up emotion arises from perception and attention; top-down emotion arises from prior knowledge, expectation, and appraisal.
Galvanic skin response measures sweat-based arousal but not whether an emotion is positive or negative; it is costly and slow to analyze, so it suits short sessions or a trailer climax.
when: Considering biometric measures
why: Arousal alone does not identify valence, and analysis is expensive.

text: The hypothalamus controls the pituitary gland, which in turn regulates other endocrine glands.
How biochemicals shape complex decisions is still poorly understood.
Game content forms the link between content and experience, covering the game environment and its effect on spatial and affective involvement.
Gaming activates reward patterns involving dopamine, similar to gambling, drugs, and food.
Electrically stimulating human reward centers has produced overwhelming euphoria, strong enough to make people repeat the stimulation.
An under-used brain feels restless, and games engaging eyes, ears, hands, and mind together leave no spare restlessness.
when: only part of the mind is occupied
why: Idle attention produces restless behavior such as fidgeting

text: Believed bodily feedback can change how strongly people rate a stimulus, even when their actual arousal has not changed.
when: a stimulus is rated while the person receives false feedback
why: people use perceived arousal as evidence for their feelings

text: Once aroused, people extend that arousal to the whole experience, not only to the element that caused it.
Cognition shapes emotional experience: the same item feels better in a setting with a strong reputation than in a plain one.
why: Appraisal changes how an experience feels.

text: In a biofeedback game, calm breathing makes the in-game light shine brightly while stress dims it, so physiological state directly drives game feedback.
when: when designing biofeedback-driven games for anxiety
why: Real-time feedback lets players learn to regulate their own arousal.

text: Basic emotion theory holds that a small set of emotions is innate and universal, rooted in evolutionary psychology and linked to universal facial expressions.
why: Darwin's view that facial expressions are innate and universal grounds the theory.

text: An affective game framework has four areas: narrative, interface (usability and appeal), avatars (player identification), and NPCs (believability).
why: Emotion sits at the heart of a player's level of engagement.

text: Over-promising rewards creates disappointment when they arrive, which discourages players from returning.
when: Advertising or building up a reward
why: A reward that falls short of expectations reduces motivation to continue.

text: Treating biochemistry as fully determining behavior ignores impulse control and social rules, which also shape conduct.
why: Humans can control impulses, and societal rules constrain conduct in a social species.

text: Watching players' faces reveals how they feel, which surveys and postgame interviews often miss.
A large part of the brain processes human faces and gestures, so seeing another person matters greatly for social experience.
The mapping from content features to fitness may depend on a model of a player's playing style, preferences, or affective state.
Chosen features differ for each reported emotional state, so each emotion (engagement, frustration, challenge) needs its own feature subset and network topology.

Traditional extraction techniques include principal component analysis and linear discriminant projection; traditional selection techniques include forward sequential selection and evolutionary-search-driven selection.
1) Name the emotions the player should feel and why. 2) Identify the emotions players, including the designer, actually feel while playing and why. 3) Plan changes that close the gap between the two.
when: Reviewing whether a design produces its intended emotions.
why: Comparing target and actual emotion reveals where the design falls short.

text: While playing, record your emotional cycles, such as frustration, exhilaration, confidence, uncertainty, pride, tension, and curiosity, because they are hard to recall later.
when: When keeping a game journal
why: Emotional states fade quickly from memory.

text: Emotion is a state of physiological arousal, such as a faster heartbeat or sweaty palms, that may or may not include cognition about it, which people experience as a feeling.
For many female players, emotion is the goal of play itself rather than an add-on, so emotional storylines and relationships can drive engagement.
when: designing for broad audiences

text: Events happening to the player feel more interesting than events happening to others, and projection closes this gap.
when: when comparing events involving the player with events involving others
why: projection lets the guest place themselves in the event

text: Schadenfreude is delight when an unjust person gets their comeuppance, important in competitive games.
Six core emotions are recognized across cultures from facial configurations: fear, anger, disgust, sadness, happiness, surprise; contempt was later added as a seventh.
Later emotion research expanded the taxonomy to over twenty emotional states.
Emotion theories fall into three loosely bounded families, appraisal, basic emotion and dimensional, which disagree on many points.
why: No consensus exists on what emotions are, and the family boundaries are fuzzy.

text: A feeling of influence over chance is part of what makes gambling exciting; removing it from a pure chance game drains much of its fun.
VR can simulate bodily fears such as falling from a height, drowning, swarming insects, and creatures touching the player.
Emotion's core function is to motivate behavior that supports survival and reproduction.
Conscious feelings are only the visible part of emotion; several physiological systems, evolved for different purposes, generate it.
Emotion steers conduct: humans pursue whatever feels good and shun whatever feels unpleasant or painful.
Three views on emotion and motivation: emotion drives motivation; motivation comes first and emotion gives feedback; or motivation has primacy and emotion serves it.
why: the order is debated

text: Players' faces can display seven measurable emotions: rage, dread, revulsion, joy, grief, astonishment, and curiosity.
Emotion supports survival but can also drive irrational choices.
Emotion mostly arrives as many small pulses that climb and drop with each stimulus, not merely as extreme states like rage or grief.
Fiction relabels raw arousal as a specific emotion, and without fiction arousal remains generalized excitement.
when: When mechanics produce arousal that should carry a specific feeling.
why: The label gives the arousal a particular emotional meaning.

text: Russell's circumplex places emotions on a plane defined by valence, running from negative to positive, and arousal, running from deactivated to activated.
An emotional response has five components: expression, action tendency, bodily reaction, feeling, and appraisal.
when: Analyzing or designing for an emotional response.
why: All three theory families describe emotion as multi-component, though they emphasize different parts.

text: Emotions play five roles in games: providing sensation, focusing attention, aiding decisions, affecting performance, and motivating learning.
Pleasure categories overlap and most people combine several, so labeling a player with a single category oversimplifies them.
Everyone has some innate ability for empathy, and practice improves it.
People take on others' emotions and matching facial expressions without meaning to, and empathy can shift between people quickly and extends to animals.
when: Staging emotional interaction between characters or people
why: Empathy is triggered automatically by visible emotional cues

text: Empathy is projecting oneself into another person and sharing their thoughts and feelings.
In immersion, the player's experience mirrors the character's: the player perceives what the character perceives, and also thinks and feels as the character does.

1) Think of people you know in the target demographic and imagine being them. 2) Spend time with the audience, talking with them and observing them. 3) Imagine their experience from the inside. Mentally taking on many player types reveals needs a narrow viewpoint misses.
when: Designing for an audience outside your own experience; expanding a game's audience beyond your own
why: Empathy with people you have not been can be built through direct contact and imagination, and it widens the players your designs reach

text: Heightened expectations boost appreciation unless the experience noticeably betrays them; overinflated promotion-driven expectations make it feel less interesting.
when: when promotion or hype raises expectations above what the experience delivers
why: Betrayed expectations reverse the boost, and the gap between anticipated and actual interest lowers perceived interest.

text: Pre-play labels, branding, marketing or reviews set expectations, so players judge the same item more favorably and read play as confirming them.
when: when players form judgments from labels, presentation or prior opinions
why: Expectations set before experience shape perceived quality, and confirmation bias shapes how experiences are perceived.

text: Players infer unshown details, so not every detail must be shown; a simple name or label can suggest unsimulated emotions like grief or family affection.
when: when deciding how much detail to render or simulate
why: Players fill gaps with their own mental pictures and apophenia.

text: Priming temporarily activates related thoughts that shape behavior for several minutes, and is a main source of short-term effects in lab studies.
when: Right after a player is exposed to a related stimulus, such as an ad or an image
why: A person always has something on their mind that affects what they do next.

text: Use priming to direct attention or shift choices among options the player already has, not to manipulate players or force behavior the game cannot support.
when: when designing how to influence player decisions
why: Priming changes the balance among existing options but cannot invent motivation.

text: Players arrive with conventions such as WASD movement assumed; control layouts differing from familiar ones surprise them and can leave them stuck on basic actions.
when: When a new game's controls differ from the conventions players learned in other games
why: Players judge new controls against habits from other games, and gamers absorb conventions that others do not know.

text: Players expect a represented object to handle, sound and react like its real counterpart, based on generalized experience, rewarding met expectations and are thrown off when they are not.
when: when controlling or interacting with an object the game represents
why: Expectations form from generalized experience, and players map visual cues onto behavior they already know.

text: A title that signals an untested, probably unbalanced game leads players to accept the imbalance, while a title promising balance would likely be criticized.
when: Games whose imbalance is intentional or unavoidable.
why: Expectations set by the title frame how players judge fairness.

text: People reason intuitively by weighing prior experience alongside new evidence, which resembles Bayesian updating.
when: judging uncertain outcomes
why: A frequentist search uses only the current signal, while people also fold in where the object usually turns up.

text: A clever action that differs from what the player expected can still look stupid to the player.
when: Learning creatures act in ways players did not anticipate.
why: Player expectations shape how behavior is judged.

text: Players typically hold a vague picture of a game as a story world, a set of rules, and hidden software that runs it. This is enough for playing.
when: When players only need to play the game, not build, fix, or diagnose it
why: Playing requires only a surface understanding.

text: Real life is hard to act in because its rules are unclear, so people work to learn them without knowing whether they are acting correctly.
when: when comparing real situations with game systems
why: Unclear rules make every action uncertain.

text: Repeating a related word beforehand biases a person's answer to a later question toward that word, even though they are unaware of the influence.
when: when a player has just been exposed to a word, phrase or concept
why: Subconscious priming shifts responses below awareness.

text: Visual illusions can expose the brain's internal model, such as dots that appear to change color as the eyes move while staying the same.
when: when a visual stimulus conflicts with the perceptual model
why: The perceptual model produces an output that differs from the physical stimulus.

text: Results that conflict with an audience's models produce surprise, which is visible as a collective gasp at the moment the models are broken.
when: when an outcome violates what the audience expected
why: Surprise marks the breakdown of the mental model.

text: When advancement is tied to elapsed time, players develop timing expectations and feel progress is stalled when it arrives late.
when: progression paced against playtime
why: Pairings of progression type and time create learned pacing expectations that become embedded in genre conventions.

text: Players assume a new system works like systems in similar games, so an unusual design such as a dump stat that matters must be clearly signaled.
when: A game departs from genre conventions
why: Players rely on prior expectations to choose, and unsignaled differences lead to misjudged choices.

text: Players shown a large, prominent figure first overestimate their chance of winning.
when: reward or jackpot figures are displayed prominently
why: anchoring on the first large number

text: Absurd creatures set few behavioral expectations, so detailed physical interactions stand out against them.
when: Surreal settings populated with fantastical characters
why: Surreal visuals promise little about behavior, so detailed physical interaction exceeds expectations and feels more compelling.

text: A realistic-looking vehicle leads players to expect it to handle like a real car.
when: vehicle rendered with realistic appearance
why: Visual realism signals physical realism

text: Players differ in expectations and mental models of a product according to their prior experience with similar games, regardless of age.
when: anticipating how players approach a new game
why: Players of shooters and players of sandbox building titles approach a game differently because of their genre experience.

text: When players act in ways developers find weird or irrational, the behavior often reflects missing knowledge about where to look or what matters rather than irrationality.
when: interpreting playtest failures
why: Something is obvious only to those who already know where to direct attention and which information matters.

text: People expect machines to be more objective than fallible humans, so biased automated decisions are noticed and questioned less often.
when: When decisions are made or assisted by automated systems.
why: Trust in machine objectivity lowers scrutiny of its outputs.

text: When a game world is archetypal, players can predict its storylines, character types, social dynamics and the choices they will face.
when: When a game is set in a familiar, genre-standard world such as a medieval, urban, or dystopian setting
why: Familiar settings follow well-known patterns.

text: Players expect a spatial environment containing all relevant locations, characters, and the player character.
when: when playing a story-driven game
why: a spatial world is part of what players expect from a game

text: Players predict outcomes by applying mental models of systems such as physics, psychology, economics and game mechanics.
why: Understanding a system's rules lets the mind run its likely responses ahead of time, before an action is taken.

text: When each agent must act before seeing others' choices, reasoning about what others know and think they know can loop endlessly without a decisive answer.
when: Simultaneous choices under uncertainty, such as a standoff.
why: Each agent must predict others' predictions, creating recursive uncertainty.

text: Skilled players reason through branching trees of predictions about the opponent's predictions in real time, not only the immediate move.
when: Fast-paced multiplayer combat.
why: Deadly, accurate weapons make the decisive moves happen before opponents see each other, so the reasoning done out of sight is what matters.

text: Players lacking background knowledge often read a humorous or thematic premise as straightforward and misunderstand how its pieces fit together.
when: content depends on source material players may not know
why: Players fill gaps with a default genre reading.

text: The mind uses simplified models rather than reality, since reality is too complex to handle directly, and mistakes these internal simulations for the world itself.
Mechanics are partly explicit rules and partly mental, describing the largely subconscious mental models players form about a game.
Metaphor is the player's past experience, from life, film and cartoons, of how an object should move and react.
Priming occurs when exposure to one stimulus influences the response to a following stimulus.
A mental model is the set of associations a player brings to a game, which a metaphor draws on to communicate how the system works.
Player modelling builds computational models of a player's behaviour, preferences or skills so that content can be tailored to that player.

Player experience modelling (PEM) is user modelling within games covering behaviour, cognition and affect, and it consists of signal processing and feature extraction for input, experience annotation for output, and machine learning to map between them.

Game designers borrow communication methods (hotkeys, tooltips, slow motion, vignettes, voiceover, a small X closing windows, fades to black) from software UI and filmmaking, adapting them to game needs.
when: when choosing communication techniques for games
why: Borrowed methods must be adapted because games have different demands than software or film.

text: Diversity and inclusion in games remain at an early stage and still need substantial progress.
Perception is subjective, relative and general, so people describe game physics with words such as pointy or springy rather than measured values.
why: Judgments are made by comparison with other things, as with tea and ice water.

text: Expectancy-value theory is mostly applied in education and educational games.
Intuition improves with experience because it draws on past reasoning and past emotional outcomes, so experienced people often outperform novices.
Mental reinvention, maintaining concentration and psychological play, is reached only by expert competitive players, since emotional upset or distraction can cause defeat.
Experienced players choose mixed strategies with close to the mathematically correct frequencies, even without computing them.
when: repeated real-world randomized choices
why: Practice and intuition approximate equilibrium play.

text: Players can model one or two opponents well; tracking three is near the limit, and beyond four players the mind game becomes impossible.
when: designing competitive player counts
why: Human attention cannot model many minds at once.

text: Players are primed before play by a game's title, cover art, and others' opinions of it.
Where doubt is low, hand knowledge directly to characters instead of simulating how a signal physically travels to them.
when: the result is not in doubt
why: physical simulation of sound propagation is unnecessary

text: Understanding players better than they understand themselves is the key to a game they will enjoy.
when: Designing a game meant to be enjoyed
why: Players cannot always articulate what will please them, so designers must infer it

text: Metaphor primes players with preconceptions about how an object should behave, and treatment sets how accurate they expect its nature and motion to be.
when: when an object's look suggests a level of physical accuracy
why: Players judge behavior against the expectations the presentation creates

text: Predictable results let players infer game structure early, such as learning that falling into a hole costs a life.
when: During the first couple minutes of a game
why: Consistent outcomes let players extrapolate the whole structure from a few instances, reducing disorientation when learning mechanics.

text: Players who believe they can accomplish an objective are more motivated to complete it.
why: expectancy-value: motivation depends on both belief in success and value

text: Because players supply input to run a model, they form ideas about both the model and the source system it represents.
when: When the player must provide input to make a procedural model run
why: Their input is what makes the model run, so the player is directly exposed to how the model and its source behave.

text: Gaps between a designer's model and players' preconceptions make games expressive, because players test and reconcile their views against the model.
when: When players' existing understanding of a simulated system differs from the designer's model
why: Reconciling their own understanding against the model forces players to interrogate how the world works.

text: A review describing a game as challenging makes an unfair loss feel intended, while the same loss after a review calling it unfair is judged a flaw.
when: the same game event is framed by prior descriptions
why: Prior framing changes how identical experiences are judged.

text: People tend to live up to how they are treated: treating people as capable encourages capable work, while treating them poorly produces anger and helplessness.
when: When people are treated as capable and special, or as incompetent and ordinary, by those around them
why: Expectations communicated by others act as a self-fulfilling prophecy on effort and output.

text: Expectancy-value theory holds that choice, persistence and performance depend on expected success and task value, which are the best predictors of effort, performance and persistence.
when: When motivation is studied in achievement settings such as education or educational games

text: Designers work from their own mental model, which must be adjusted to system limits, while players build a separate model from the system image and prior expectations.
when: When an interactive product such as a PC game is designed and implemented.
why: Players can only form their model from the part of the system they interact with and perceive.

text: Copying genre rules of thumb without checking them against the game's players can make controls fail for those players.
when: When copying interface conventions that recur across a game genre

text: Treating motivation as easy to predict from design intent alone ignores how unpredictably it directs behavior.
1) Ask what users already know. 2) Identify what is unknown to them. 3) Borrow familiar patterns from apps and games they use. 4) Verify the choice with a UX test on early prototypes.
when: when designing a new interaction
why: Users already trained on familiar gestures and apps are likely to carry that learning over to a similar new action.

text: 1) Record gameplay sessions and extract features as indicators of affect, performance and play style. 2) Select features with sequential forward selection, scoring candidates by how well simple perceptron or MLP models predict emotional states. 3) Grow network size by adding hidden nodes and layers, monitoring performance at each step.
when: When building a player experience model from recorded gameplay data.
why: A large candidate feature set and a complex mapping from gameplay to reported experience make selecting features a critical step.

text: Set difficulty expectations up front, especially when higher levels cheat; a clearly labeled cheating level avoids player resentment.
when: When higher difficulty levels secretly manipulate the numbers to cheat the player.
why: Discovering after the fact that a supposedly fair opponent was secretly rigged breeds resentment.

text: Choose defaults for the mainstream audience and follow industry standards, such as subtitles on by default.
when: Setting defaults for options and accessibility features.
why: Most players want the common default, and most never change it.

text: Keep cues, responses, input schemes, screens, navigation paths, and world logic consistent so players never have to relearn how things work.
Extrinsic rewards can distort, displace or destroy intrinsic motivation, mainly by undermining competence, autonomy or relatedness; a reward signaling growing mastery reinforces competence instead.
why: The reward is also felt as feedback on growing mastery, which supports rather than curbs competence.

text: Extrinsic motivation is doing something to obtain a reward separate from the task itself, such as money, a badge or loot.
Extrinsic rewards sit outside an activity, like gold for a defeated enemy, while intrinsic rewards are inseparable from it, like satisfaction in a good fight.
Extrinsic rewards give useful immediate feedback, but motivation can vanish when they are removed, and skills transfer poorly to other contexts.
why: Motivation is tied to the external reward itself, so it disappears when that reward is taken away.

text: Motivation depends on the reward value of a behavior and the probability of obtaining that reward, and players learn which behaviors lead to pleasant outcomes.
when: Designing reward systems
why: Learned needs form from noticing which actions produce pleasant or negative results

text: Cute animations and extrinsic badges added to dull exercises do not make them fun; extrinsic rewards alone do not sustain engagement, so games also need intrinsic motivation.
when: when designing educational games
why: Motivation driven by external rewards fades once the rewards stop.

text: Treating the intrinsic or extrinsic label of an event as fixed ignores that it depends on how the player perceives it.
why: Designers shape the environment but not the player's perception, so one event can register as either kind.

text: A reward loop without fulfilling content can keep players returning, which can be exploited as an abusive pattern.
when: designing timed-reward or retention mechanics
why: Returning behavior does not imply enjoyment.

text: Extrinsic rewards can enhance performance and creativity when instrumentally important and valuable to the player's goals, but tend to undermine creativity in tasks that require creativity.
when: Enhancing when rewards serve valued player goals; undermining when the task requires creativity

text: Where players expect a fair fight, imbalance reduces enjoyment; where they expect progression or an unfair setup, imbalance is accepted.
when: Competitive versus progression-focused play.
why: Player expectations set the tolerance for imbalance.

text: People resent unfair judgment rather than judgment itself, and when dissatisfied with their judgment they work harder until judged favorably.
when: when players receive a poor evaluation from a game
why: Judgment perceived as fair motivates improvement.

text: Even with exposed true odds and a fair generator, players may complain because their flawed probability model makes the game feel wrong.
when: When true odds are shown to players and the random generator is fair.
why: Players' flawed probability judgments, such as anchoring and gambler's or hot-hand fallacies, make a fair game feel wrong.

text: Players expect random sequences to look balanced and assume a losing or winning streak must end soon, even though each trial is independent.
when: watching independent random trials
why: Intuition expects short sequences to mirror the long-run proportion

text: Players accept losses as legitimate only in fair games; in an unfair game a win reveals nothing and the loser blames the game.
when: In competitive games between players.
why: Unequal starting advantages make the result meaningless as a measure of skill, so the loser can blame the setup.

text: Coins, spinners, wheels, and teetotums with equally likely outcomes behave like dice with the same number of outcomes, so the same probability methods apply.
when: Modeling odds for coins, spinners, wheels, or teetotums
why: Each device produces independent, equally weighted outcomes, so balance reasoning can treat them identically.

text: Assume a die is fair in probability problems unless the problem states otherwise.
why: A die is defined as a generator giving each integer from 1 to n equal probability, so equal sides is the baseline.

text: Too many surprises alienate players.
Relying only on enforcement against antisocial play is less efficient than designing out the rewards that encourage it.
why: Behaviour that gets rewarded tends to recur, so removing the reward cuts off its reinforcement.

text: Assuming the two remaining options are equally likely after a reveal is wrong; the reveal shifts probability toward the unopened option.
Standard probability calculations assume the shuffle is fair and the deck is unmarked, so every unseen face-down card is equally likely to be any card not yet seen.
when: Computing odds from a shuffled or face-down set
why: Equal likelihood of unseen cards is the premise of the standard calculations.

text: A balanced deal set by hand leaves only play choices to supply luck, while a random deal adds input luck to every game.
when: Choosing whether a card game's starting setup should be randomized or fixed
why: Manual placement removes deal luck, so outcomes depend on decisions during play.

text: Players act out fantasies in games, living aspirational roles and striving to become what they secretly wished to be, including scenarios they would avoid in real life.
when: a game lets players take on an idealized role
why: Strong underlying desires for freedom and adventure make idealized roles compelling to act out.

text: Strong transmedia worlds become a personal utopia that fans fantasize about visiting, a brief escape for some and a lifelong draw for others.
when: A world with a strong fantasy core
why: Fans are drawn by the wish to enter the fantasy

text: Once an enemy looks human, its attacks seem angry, its retreats seem afraid and its pursuits seem like desire, even though the underlying behavior is code.
when: enemies or characters given human appearance
why: Players project emotional intent onto behavior that their appearance suggests.

text: People instantly fill in unstated details of a short story with invented specifics, and revise those details when new information arrives.
why: Ordinary mental gap-filling, not creative fantasy, operates on any story or scene.

text: Escapism comes mainly from flow and mechanics rather than from an appealing fictional protagonist.
why: Flow comes from moment-to-moment decision timing inside the mechanics, which a fictional wrapper does not supply.

text: Players with ongoing group obligations keep showing up to avoid low status and the shame of letting teammates down, since broken commitments lower others' opinions.
when: When players have ongoing obligations to a group that depends on them
why: People dislike being judged negatively and avoid social pain; broken commitments damage standing.

text: Vivid, well-publicized rare events can be used to stir fear of unlikely dangers, because people overweight outcomes they can easily picture.
when: When unlikely dangers are heavily publicized, such as terrorism or natural disasters.

text: When sensory input signals threat, the hypothalamus triggers hormones such as epinephrine, norepinephrine, or cortisol, which raise heart rate and focus attention.
when: a threat is perceived
why: hormones prepare the body for rapid action

text: Pattern detection is very fast because quick recognition of threats mattered for survival.
Anger and fear make people hold back risks and ideas, and observers quietly adjust their own risk taking, so the team's creativity declines even when pressure looks effective.
when: When a leader uses anger or harsh criticism on a team.
why: Fear makes people avoid exposure, and the effect spreads beyond the person targeted.

text: 1) Senses relay input to cortical and subcortical areas. 2) The thalamus relays it to the hypothalamus and amygdala. 3) The hypothalamus triggers adrenaline, noradrenaline and cortisol release, raising heart rate, dilating pupils, raising glucose and blood pressure, and tensing muscles. 4) The amygdala and hippocampus identify the input, compare it with stored memories, and store the event.
when: During a fight-or-flight response.

text: Flow is energized, enjoyable, absorbed focus in which lost self-consciousness, distorted time and real-world distractions fall away, as the mind engages through action, reaction, decision and outcome.
when: when challenge is close to current ability

text: Flow is engagement from challenge matched to skill, lying in the channel between boredom and anxiety: too hard causes confusion and anxiety, too easy causes boredom, just-above-skill challenge engages.
when: When challenge stays constant while the player keeps improving over a long game.
why: Either extreme pulls attention toward a more rewarding activity, so the challenge must stay within a narrow band.

text: Flow is total, concentrated, intrinsically motivating immersion in meaningful voluntary effort that stretches mind or body; it is central to happiness and must be worked for.
An autotelic activity is done for its own sake, unlike exotelic ones done for outside goals; games, typically autotelic, need pleasurable use as well as ease of use.
The flow zone is the challenge range where players stay engaged; it rises with ability and shifts with expertise, fatigue and perception. Too much causes frustration, too little boredom.
when: As the game progresses and the player's ability grows over time
why: Enjoyment comes from keeping challenge balanced against a growing ability.

text: Flow is supported by four components: clear goals, no distractions or limited stimulus field, direct immediate feedback, and continuous challenge.
when: When creating an activity meant to put a player into a flow state
why: Focus is required for flow, and these features keep attention on the task and show whether each action works.

text: Game flow is an engageability pillar with three parts: difficulty curve for balanced challenge, pacing of pressure and relief over time, and learning curve (onboarding) for distributed learning by doing.
Game feel mixes five experiences: aesthetic enjoyment of control, satisfaction of mastering a skill, sensory extension, identity extension, and interaction with a distinctive physical world.
Distractions and fear of failure break concentration and self-absorption; remove distractions before players reach flow, since external events can pull them out once inside.
when: Before the player reaches the flow zone
why: Full concentration is needed to enter flow, and once inside it is easier to stay focused unless an outside event intrudes.

text: Check that a design has: 1) a completable challenge requiring skill, 2) merged action and awareness, 3) clear goals, 4) immediate, unambiguous feedback, 5) concentration on relevant stimuli, 6) a real sense of control over an uncertain outcome, 7) loss of self-consciousness, 8) transformed time, 9) an autotelic experience, 10) personal meaning.
when: Judging whether a design supports absorption.
why: Each condition supports sustained absorption in an activity.

text: Vary pacing: avoid sustained tension, which exhausts players, and sustained relaxation, which bores them; alternate them for variety and anticipation.
why: Oscillating between tension and calm gives players both excitement and rest, plus the pleasure of variety and anticipation.

text: Players in flow withdraw quietly: solo players mutter and react slowly or irritably to interruption, while multiplayer players chat cheerfully yet stay focused.
when: observing play sessions
why: Intense absorption in the game makes players slow to answer or irritated when interrupted, so their reactions are muted.

text: A far-off aspirational goal can feel out of reach, so progress toward it feels slow.
when: When a long-term aspirational goal feels distant enough that progress toward it is hard to see
why: Players sense progression only when they can perceive advancement toward specific nearer goals.

text: When a player's skill matches the game's difficulty, the player stays in the flow channel.
Players enjoy bounded challenges alternating with authored story, even though critics say the method is not truly interactive.
why: Succeeding at a challenge unlocks further story and new challenges, so rewards pair narrative with interactive play.

text: Casual players may play several times a week just to kill time, and they spend less per person.
when: When the player does not self-identify as a gamer
why: Content that matters a lot to self-identified gamers drives high spending, which non-identifying players lack.

text: Players complain about confusion more readily than they praise a challenge they enjoyed.
when: Interpreting playtest feedback
why: Negative feedback about confusion is more frequent than positive feedback about challenge.

text: Players in flow lose track of time, so a short session can run far longer than expected.
when: absorbed play
why: Total absorption removes awareness of elapsed time.

text: Flow works as escapism because it pushes everyday worries about money, bills and relationships out of the mind.
when: absorbed play
why: Full attention on the activity crowds out other concerns.

text: Players in flow accept strange fiction, rough graphics and unclear interactions.
when: the player is in flow
why: Absorption in play outweighs surface flaws

text: Flow is the zone where meaningful, clear-goal challenge is neither too easy nor too hard for the player; a well-designed game keeps players there, and it is intrinsically motivating.
A divergent goal is a player pursuing aims the designer did not intend, which can harm other players as well as the player who holds it.
Flow arises in goal-directed, rule-bounded activities that require skills; a task without needed skills feels meaningless, while one with skills but uncertain outcome feels challenging.
Flow describes optimal absorption under constant but not unassailable challenge; it covers only challenge, one dimension of experience.
A flow gap is any period when the player's mind has nothing to process, and it can last from a second to an hour.
Fellowship is the pleasure of friendship, cooperation, and community, and it is the main draw for some players.
Intense pacing leaves players few breathers; methodical pacing has players weigh many circumstances before each action.
Juicing extracts many interactions from one mechanic, yielding rich play from a small asset set.
Pleasures beyond standard lists include anticipation, completion, schadenfreude, gift giving, humor, possibility, pride in accomplishment, surprise, thrill, triumph over adversity, and wonder.
Games demand active participation, unlike music or theatre, where the audience is the primary consumer.
Experiences are hard to analyze because they cannot be seen or touched, and each person's experience of the same thing is unique.
Flow can be uncomfortable during the effort that comes before a skill is mastered.
People who experience flow often are happier, and they report being happiest when they experience it frequently.
Flow occurs at every intensity level and emotional tone, including action games, contemplative puzzlers and humorous social games.
Flow breaks in two ways: when stimulation runs out, leaving the mind underused, and when it overflows, leaving the player overwhelmed.
Explicit goals are named, while implicit goals such as health are always present but rarely named until they are threatened.
Fluid intelligence means solving problems in unfamiliar situations, and it depends on working memory capacity.
Slow movement can be expressive, conveying massive scale, and forcing slow movement is a deliberate feel choice.
Game feel, including the 3Cs, presence and physical reality, supports the emotional experience of play.
Each of the five experiences traces to one or more of the three building blocks: real-time control, simulated space, or polish.
Flow is hard to see in short sessions, and a game that induces flow early may become boring or frustrating later, so check over longer play.
when: When testing whether a game keeps players in flow
why: Early engagement can mask later boredom or frustration, which only shows up in extended play.

text: Choose explicit feedback when accuracy matters more than uninterrupted play, and implicit feedback when the session must not be interrupted.
why: Explicit answers are reliable and accurate but break the session, while implicit signals are noisy and rely on assumptions.

text: Combining behaviour with physiological signals such as eye gaze or skin conductance helps when any single signal is too unreliable.
why: Collecting data across multiple modalities offsets the drawbacks that each single method has.

text: Fun is one pleasurable emotion among many; many gripping games are not fun in the everyday sense yet still hold players strongly.
when: setting emotional goals for a game
why: Fun became the default term because games began as folk culture, but today's varied player emotional appetites call for more terms.

text: Many apparent design problems are really flow breaks, so diagnose them by asking what interrupts the player's engagement.
when: When a design problem seems to arise in another area of the design
why: Without flow, players notice and complain about every annoyance; in flow they tolerate otherwise odd content.

text: When time is limited, focus on the most distinctive part of a design and drop secondary details.
when: Scope must be cut to fit available time
why: The distinctive mechanic is what players remember.

text: A game built on rules from a different genre can fail to capture the excitement of its source; choose mechanics that produce the desired feel.
when: Designing a game for a genre with a distinct feel
why: Rules from one genre can drain the excitement of another.

text: Resonance cannot be reached by logic alone; it must be felt, which requires listening to your own reactions.
when: When deciding which theme to build a game around
why: Logic alone cannot reveal which themes will resonate; only feeling the resonance internally shows it.

text: In a game that cannot be failed, use a fixed round timer as the main source of challenge.
when: game has no fail state
why: Time pressure replaces the risk of losing

text: Shape feel at several levels by pairing expressive controls with rules such as goals and challenges, and with context such as spatial layout.
when: When a game seems to lack depth
why: Expressive interactions need rules and spatial context to shape feel at several levels, which adds depth.

text: Design for free-form play by letting players choose their own approaches within a game's systems rather than forcing one path.
when: when designing systems-driven or immersive games

text: Pace play in mini-arcs of about one hour, ending each with a memorable moment that brings players back.
when: Structuring long games across play sessions
why: One hour matches how long an average player sits at a game

text: Treat pacing as part of the design target, so generated paths keep challenges matched to the player's progress.
when: When a level offers free exploration but progression must stay tightly controlled
why: Exploration is bound to designed progression, so players can choose paths without meeting unreachable challenges.

text: Treat flow as the baseline goal for nearly any game, since most games must sustain it to work.
why: A broken flow makes every other part of the experience collapse, so many weak games trace back to interrupted flow.

text: When a choice must be made, favor sustained flow over elaborate transitions, because flow keeps paying off during play while visual polish impresses only once.
why: Visual transitions and dialogue halt the player's ability to act, which weakens the mechanical decision-making even while they enrich the fiction.

text: Extrinsic rewards suit repetitive or chore-like tasks, since there is no intrinsic interest for them to displace.
Exact distances and speeds matter less to players than the felt quality of a space; a slightly slower traversal can change whether a world feels lonely.
when: When tuning travel speed in open environments.
why: Players judge the feeling of a space, not its measured size.

text: Set up player expectations with metaphor and treatment, then exceed them through the game's interactions.
Create flow mostly in mechanics by matching the challenge to the player's skill.
when: When tuning core mechanics for immersion.
why: A matched challenge keeps attention absorbed.

text: Autoplay recommendations can stretch a short session well past what the player intended.
when: when content plays automatically after the previous item

text: Flow is not a stable point: boredom or frustration returns and the cycle repeats at higher complexity, which drives growth and discovery.
Clear goals and immediate feedback let players know what to do and how well they are doing.
Player confidence strengthens goal-directed steering: confident players follow their own instincts, while confused or doubtful players second-guess and steer weakly.
when: Players pursuing goals in a world

text: Improvisation produces a flow experience when the player's skill matches the challenge.
why: Responsive controls, once mastered, let players combine actions fluidly in real time without deliberating, keeping attention absorbed.

text: Flow must come first for immersion, because stray real-world thoughts break the mirroring between player and character.
when: When building immersion through mechanics.
why: Distracting thoughts about outside concerns prevent the player from absorbing the character's state.

text: Flow feels enjoyable because it rests on an unbroken string of minor achievements.
Overlapping progression loops that stay open, staggered so the player is always close to completing another goal, keep players hooked.
when: When designing long-term engagement in a strategy game
why: Open tasks create lasting cognitive load and near-completion draws players on

text: Fear of being caught makes stealth tense even when the player succeeds.
when: Designing stealth gameplay
why: A penalty that is only threatened still produces dramatic tension, and that tension gives weight to even trivial choices.

text: Very short character lifespans with near-instant respawns keep flow unbroken, so players stay motivated to avoid death and feel gratified when they do.
when: Games built around frequent deaths.
why: Near-instant respawn prevents death from interrupting play.

text: Full action, perception and response loop takes under half a second; nominal processor values add to about 240 ms, the player's correction cycle and basic real-time control unit.
why: Human perception and reaction time is fixed, so the machine's response speed is the part that can be tuned to keep control.

text: The game flow model equates player enjoyment, the main goal of games, with Csikszentmihalyi's psychological concept of flow, and combines usability heuristics into an enjoyment evaluation.
A full game structure has an opening, a sequence of levels of increasing interest, and a climactic finale where the player beats the final challenge.
Flow is easy to miss without practice in recognizing its signs.
when: When observing players during playtests
why: Flow only emerges over long stretches of play, so brief observation cannot reveal it.

text: Unfair or misunderstood deaths and failures, lost control, losing hard-won possessions, and overly harsh punishment or insurmountable obstacles all break players' flow.
when: Designing challenge, punishment, or control loss
why: These frictions are intense enough to break suspension of disbelief and pull players out of flow

text: A clumsy statement of the goal can drive players away at the start, because they cannot act with confidence without knowing what their actions are for.
when: when players first learn a game

text: Measuring flow only with coarse averages of skill and challenge misses the moment-to-moment decision rhythm that actually sustains it.
why: Decisions enter the player's mind and get worked on within moments, so flow depends on the timing of each one rather than on averages.

text: A harder post-game eventually tires veterans too, so plan what comes after it.
when: When veteran players have mastered a very difficult endgame.
why: Even an extremely hard challenge can eventually be exhausted by veteran players.

text: Because time is invisible and cannot be stopped, designers easily overlook it as a design factor and should examine it deliberately.
A timed scenario can end at its fixed time whether or not the player meets the objective, so the player's sense of control can be misleading.
Overwhelming pacing comes from mismatched PvP players, missing matchmaking, or AI that gives players no time to think or recover.
when: When combat moves too fast for players to consider options or form a response.
why: Players who cannot form a response grow frustrated and hopeless, and then quit.

text: Missing juice makes a major moment feel anticlimactic.
when: When a major milestone, such as cracking a hard puzzle, receives little sensory feedback.
why: Players judge the importance of a moment partly by its sensory feedback.

text: 1) Are goals clear, and if not, how can they be clarified? 2) Do players pursue the intended goals? 3) Which parts pull players off their goal? 4) Is challenge a steady stream, neither too easy nor too hard?
1) Identify each phase. 2) Plot the power curve inside each phase. 3) Contrast how long each phase lasts. 4) Adjust any phase that feels dull or drags.
when: when tuning pacing in a PvP game
why: measurement shows which phase is out of proportion

text: Sustain flow with a gradual ramp of ever-greater challenges matching growing player skill, avoiding both boredom and frustration.
when: when pacing difficulty over a game
why: Challenge that tracks skill avoids both boredom and frustration.

text: Reduce distractions that pull players from their goals, or tie those distractions to the goals.
when: When parts of the game distract players enough that they forget their goal.

text: Pick two or three words that describe combat pacing, such as intense, methodical or pre-planned, or a mix of them.
when: Before starting combat design and balance.

text: If a game has phases, make each phase an appropriate length relative to the whole game.
when: when a game is divided into phases

text: Visual style and movement should match, since realistic visuals paired with surreal movement make the mismatch obvious.
when: a character's art style and its movement rules are chosen
why: Mismatched realism between look and motion is immediately noticeable to players.

text: Design for the player's perception of what happened, not for the computer's millisecond-level input timing, since perception is far softer than hardware precision.
when: When designing real-time controls that map button presses to game events.
why: Controls designed only around computer precision feel unresponsive.

text: Keep friction that is designed in, such as challenges to motor skill, perception, memory or emotion, and remove only frustrations that are not intended.
If a delay cannot be removed, fill it with a meaningful decision, such as letting the player use another action while a recharge completes.
when: When a design choice must trade fancy menu transitions or animations against player flow.
why: Visual polish impresses only at first, whereas decision flow keeps paying off with repeated play.

text: Opponents stop challenging a clearly strong deck for ante unless a handicap applies.
when: a deck is clearly stronger than its opponents' decks
why: challenging it for ante is unattractive

text: In an arcade, players move from game to game, try each, and settle on the ones they like best.
Expert players tend toward optimal builds, while most players end up with viable builds.
Chaos grows with the number of combatants, and multiplayer adds causes that happen offscreen.
when: Designing large or multiplayer combat
why: Pressure narrows player focus, so extra combatants and unseen actors make cause and effect harder to follow.

text: Players avoid repeating their last choice, so countering their previous move wins more than chance in repeated rounds, and the advantage grows as rounds accumulate.
when: head-to-head choice games with repeated rounds

text: Players use the basic punch more than specialty moves when encounters, such as boss fights, require it.
when: encounters that demand the basic attack
why: Encounter design dictates which attacks players rely on.

text: Beating a human feels different from beating a computer, even with identical play, because the social meaning adds a layer to the win.
when: competitive play with the same mechanics against people or AI
why: social meaning adds emotional weight

text: 1) Equip agents with computer-based representations of thought, conduct, and feeling. 2) Ground them in theoretical frameworks such as OCC so the player feels absorbed.
when: when agents must immerse the player emotionally
why: Agents need rich, emotional interaction with the player to produce meaningful experience.

text: When filter workarounds take more effort, they become less fun for griefers, so fewer of them keep trying.
why: Griefers treat obscenity as a game, so withholding feedback on whether a filter worked removes its appeal.

text: Words can conflict with body language, such as saying 'I'm fine' while frowning and avoiding eye contact, which signals a need to discuss a serious problem.
when: Talking with players or teammates
why: Tone and body language carry meaning that words hide.

text: Workbench games are often difficult and demand hours at a time, usually without family, though online players who share the same commitment may join.
when: playing games at the workbench
why: Both work and play at a computer are intense and solitary, so they gravitated to workbench spaces.

text: Workbench play is a leaning-forward activity, in contrast to the relaxed posture of reading.
Skillful control can lead to a zone state in which self-consciousness drops away and time passes unnoticed.
when: control is fluent and well matched to skill
why: attention shifts fully to acting

text: Writers attached to their stories often miss the flaws in them.
when: after long work on the story
why: Deep attachment hides problems from the person who wrote them.

text: Yomi refers to the psychological contest of anticipating, misleading and outmaneuvering an opponent beyond what game-theoretic calculation captures; the word comes from Japanese for reading.
when: competitive games with imperfect information
why: It labels the psychological layer that equilibrium analysis misses.

text: A solid, impressive-looking world makes players take the game more seriously and raises the value they assign to it.
Players' brains substitute game stimuli such as sights, sounds, rumble, button push-back and finger position for the physical-world cues they normally use.
when: while playing a game
why: A game's world is a reduced subset of reality.

text: Game skills and real-world skills are learned the same way, though game skills use smaller, more focused movements and are not bound by physics.
Debate persists over whether games leave lasting effects on the mind, with views ranging from no effect, to harm, to a cornerstone of education.
Games are unlikely to make players smarter in general, just as music and chess training do not.
In one study, children who played video games scored higher on creativity measures than children who did not play.
Long-term studies of over 1,000 children linked game and TV exposure to teacher-reported attention problems, without separating game types.
In an experiment with 64 boys aged 6 to 9, immediate console access produced worse reading and writing post-tests than access delayed by four months.
The General Aggression Model predicts violent play increases aggressive cognition, affect and conduct over the short run.
when: When the aggression studied is mild, prank-level behavior, as in experimental studies.

text: Treating correlational evidence of game persistence as proof that games cause perseverance overstates what the data shows.
why: Transfer of perseverance beyond games is still unproven.

text: The General Aggression Model has drawn significant criticism, and some studies have found no support for it.
why: Reanalysing the same body of experiments found their support weaker than originally presented.

text: Evaluate games for enjoyment as well as task completion, since games are meant to be enjoyed rather than used to accomplish a task.
Players who recognize a classic game reference need less explanation, because the reference signals skills they already have.
when: When a game borrows gameplay or naming from a well-known classic
why: Familiar genre conventions carry prior knowledge that players bring in

text: Many players find game worlds appealing because they offer simple logic and clear rewards for effort.
when: Playing a game world with defined rules.
why: Simple logic makes effort-to-reward relations easy to read.

text: Players do not expect much story in every genre, so brief story details are often enough to add meaning.
when: in genres where story is not central
why: Expectations of story depth vary by genre

text: Historical scenarios are often unfair because the real events were unfair, and players want to explore history rather than compete.
when: Historical war games where players prefer exploring history over competitive play.

text: Hidden-object games are popular with women; the popularity is well established even though evolutionary explanations for it are disputed.
Narrative space by game genre: sandbox hours to days, single-player RPG hours, RTS and MMO minutes, action RPG and FPS seconds, each contracting and expanding during play.
Visible progress, such as completed work or leveling up, feels satisfying, makes advancement clear and motivates players and learners.
when: a task's progress is otherwise invisible, or a learner works through a long activity
why: visible results give a sense of accomplishment; clear progress signals achievement

text: In unstructured play, players largely set their own goals, so trading and deck building often matter more than individual duels.
when: unstructured, free-form play
why: Players define their own objectives.

text: Completing a visible portion of a large task makes the remainder feel reachable, which keeps players engaged.
when: Multi-part manipulation puzzles
why: Perceived nearness to completion sustains effort

text: Players feel motivated by contribution when they can clearly see their own impact on a shared goal.
when: players contribute to a collective goal
why: visible impact makes effort feel meaningful

text: Most people stop once they meet standards, beat competitors or earn approval, doing only what is needed to reach that goal.
why: External rewards are the only motive, so nothing remains to pull the person forward after they win.

text: Recording and displaying how long an action takes sets a benchmark on the first run, and later gains become harder, pushing players toward new strategies.
when: Simple control sets where the completion time of an action is tracked.
why: Early runs teach the player, but each later improvement requires more, so the player must vary strategy.

text: Artificial gating through cheap psychological tricks can make players feel their time was wasted.
