when: When core gameplay misses its goals and progression rewards are used to patch it.
why: Forced tasks with rewards not worth the time breed resentment, so players leave bitter instead of wanting sequels.

text: 1) Define what progress means in the challenge. 2) Check whether there are enough interim steps of success, adding more if not. 3) Identify which progress is hidden and reveal it to the player where possible.
when: Any extended challenge where players must solve a difficult problem over time.
why: Players must see they are advancing through a difficult problem to feel it is worth continuing.

text: Some players find tormenting others more enjoyable than the game itself and gain higher status by spoiling games others care about, especially with tricks victims don't know.
when: Multiplayer games with player-versus-player or shared spaces; exploits unknown to victims.
why: Spoiling others' fun gives them a feeling of power over the community.

text: When a likely winner appears, other players cooperate to stop them, a common social negative loop.
when: In multiplayer games where players can interact to hinder others.
why: Players act together to prevent a leader from winning.

text: Negative behaviors such as griefing usually emerge from systems that accidentally enable them rather than from deliberate design.
when: Analysing toxic player behavior
why: Unintended system affordances let players exploit or harass others.

text: Griefing is deliberately destroying other players' experiences for one's own amusement.
Harassment of strangers is perceived as either harassment or unfairness, and both feelings demotivate players.
when: Multiplayer communities
why: Negative social experiences reduce willingness to keep playing

text: Play tendencies described for a group are averages that do not describe every individual in that group, so apply them with care.
when: designing for mixed audiences
why: Group patterns describe tendencies, so speaking of them as universal excludes individuals who deviate.

text: In family playtests, boys played offensively, hunting every enemy target while communicating and focusing on skillful destruction of enemies.
when: mixed-skill family audiences playing a combat game together

text: People favor and help those close to them in their social circles, a tendency called ingroup bias.
when: Designing social features
why: Trust and willingness to help are higher toward known people

text: Affiliation with a group such as a guild, clan, or faction makes players feel their actions matter beyond themselves.
when: players belong to a group with a shared identity
why: belonging gives actions a larger purpose

text: Many MMO participants cite duty toward their guild as a top reason for logging in regularly, driven partly by seeking high status and partly by avoiding low status.
when: When players belong to a persistent guild or group

text: Groups are either short-term, formed for one challenge, or long-term, such as guilds or clans; long-term ties encourage members to care for one another.
Pressure from a group, such as guild members demanding more play, can turn voluntary play into an obligation.
when: Social games where guild or group members are pressured to play more.
why: Players shift from pleasure-seeking to pain-avoidance motives, so they keep playing without enjoying it.

text: Group discussion pushes attitudes toward more extreme positions, which can distort measurements taken from focus groups.
when: When using group discussion to gauge player opinion
why: Members who feel alone in disagreeing stay silent, and pauses make consensus look real.

text: Under real-time control, senses extend into the avatar as an extended body acting on and perceiving the world; self flows into it: success brings pride, crashes separate self from it.
why: An avatar acts as both a tool for acting on and perceiving the world, so game feedback overwrites the senses.

text: People come to feel a vehicle or tool they control as part of their body, extending their sense of self to it.
when: using a controlled object or tool
why: Proprioceptive feedback from the hands stays active, and small motions produce large reactions, amplifying body sense.

text: Culture and social presence affect how much people mask negative facial expressions, so faces are an unreliable readout of feeling.
when: Observing players' faces to infer emotion, especially when others are present.
why: Participants masked negative expressions when an experimenter entered, and some people are less expressive than others.

text: Players feel cared for when a game helps them become better people, because it shows that someone cares what they become.
when: a game is designed to build positive qualities in players
why: Players value being cared for.

text: Players can feel free while having few or no real choices, which lets the designer keep control of the interest curve and events.
when: Real freedom is limited
why: Feeling of freedom satisfies the player while the designer retains control of pacing and events.

text: Familiar conventions, such as mechanics borrowed from a known game or recognizable races and situations, help players learn quickly and overcome wariness of a new IP.
when: the audience knows the source game; when launching a new IP
why: familiar conventions transfer; recognizable elements lower fear of the unfamiliar.

text: Players set aside everyday rules when entering a game's bounded space and resume ordinary rules when they leave it.
when: starting and finishing a game session
why: The bounded space marks a temporary shift in rules

text: Immersed players describe their actions as things done in the game world, such as running and swinging a sword, rather than as button presses.
when: During immersive play.
why: The interface has become second nature to them.

text: In the first seconds of an encounter, players absorb information, make assumptions, and prepare to fight or flee.
The five experiences of game feel can surface within seconds of picking up a controller and blend together into one feel.
when: first moments of play

text: Players who feel they are really there experience senses extended into the game, with game feedback overriding direct sensory input.
when: immersive real-time play
why: feedback from the game becomes the dominant sensation

text: Players' choices are shaped by the environment and by which options are shown, so choice telemetry needs that context.
when: when analyzing player choices
why: presented options and surroundings steer decisions

text: In first person, players assume they can only do what a real person could do in a similar situation.
when: in first-person games
why: Players judge options against their real-world experience.

text: A scene triggered by someone else's action rather than the player's own may be rejected by the player.
when: RPG cutscenes tied to player choices
why: The player feels the scene does not reflect what they did.

text: Players plan their next steps only as far as they can read the space from the entry point.
when: when a player enters a new space
why: Sight lines from the entry determine how much of the space is readable.

text: Players offer opinions, advice or warnings to one another during play, which counts as positive experience bleed.
when: when an experience is played in a shared physical space
why: Shared physical output lets bystanders and players interact around the experience.

text: Audiences carry worries, stresses and plans into an experience, so they take time to settle in and lose functional play time after entering.
when: when a timed experience begins with a live audience
why: Incoming personal context competes with attention at the start.

text: First-person shooters already show that players can perceive physical presence when the avatar itself is never seen.
why: Feel can be produced by feedback alone, without a simulated or visible avatar.

text: Immersion objectively gauges how well a system shuts out the physical world; presence describes the felt sense of inhabiting that space. Interchangeable use blurs platform properties with player experience.
Immersion arises as the psychological boundary separating real identity from the character blurs, making avatar events feel personally significant.
Immersion is a state in which the player's mind forgets it is being entertained and accepts what it perceives as reality.
Extended reality (XR) is an umbrella term for technologies that alter reality or generate a virtual one, including AR, VR, and mixed reality.
Embodiment occurs when players perceive their virtual body's movement as their own movement.
A first-person view does not make sound subjective by itself, because listeners choose what to attend to.
Every experience, such as watching a film, practicing an instrument or reading, changes neural connections, so claims that one technology uniquely rewires the brain are overstated.
Player experience models may target enjoyment, challenge, difficulty, or frustration; content is then tuned to the chosen target.
Every experience, including playing a game, reading or conversing, happens in the mind, which is a product of the brain and body.
Graphical fidelity, believable fiction, relatable protagonists and dim lighting do not reliably produce immersion; some games have them without immersion and some immersive games lack them.
Players can be objectively immersed without feeling present, for example when a technical fault breaks the virtual interaction.
Familiar places such as a car interior, fast food counter or basketball court need only a few relevant details, as the brain fills in the rest without looking.
when: Depicting a place players already know, such as a city street or house interior, or the player is in a setting they already know
why: players already know what such places are like and imagine the rest.

text: Use the right amount of familiarity, especially in the player's immediate surroundings, to produce unexpectedly strong presence.
when: Designing the starting environment of a VR scene
why: Familiar detail lets the brain build the space quickly

text: Full immersion makes people lose track of time and disregard hunger, thirst or sleep, and full concentration can enhance learning.
when: When the challenge is neither too easy nor too hard.
why: Deep absorption in a challenge sized to the player's ability causes them to disregard time and bodily needs.

text: Immersion is built in three steps: flow strips the real world from the mind, raw arousal is produced by mechanics, and fiction labels that arousal to match the character's feelings.
when: When the goal is for players to share a character's feelings.
why: Each step supplies a layer needed for the player to mirror the character.

text: The avatar acts more as a perceptual substitute than a tool: it has its own bodily space, and the world is reachable only through its actions.
why: Perception is extended one step removed from the player's body.

text: Immersion has four measurable dimensions: inclusiveness (real world cut off), extensiveness (senses served), surrounding (field of view), and vividness (fidelity).
Removing the HUD to increase immersion can make the experience less immersive, because it adds memory load and menu trips.
when: When the HUD is removed entirely with no information offered within the game world
why: Information missing from the screen forces players to open menus, which pulls them out of the game world.

text: Focusing only on graphics or fiction misses the internal mirroring between player and character that is missing in most failed attempts at immersion.
why: Games with strong graphics and fiction can still fail to be immersive, because immersion depends on the player's experience mirroring the character's.

text: Designing for total immersion can ignore that players bring outside knowledge and personality into the game and knowingly play within its frame.
why: Players arrive with outside knowledge and personality, which conflicts with pure immersion.

text: Judge spatial interaction by whether the player feels it directly, not by whether the computer simulates it.
when: assessing whether a game has simulated space
why: Collisions can exist in the simulation while the player's control is mediated, so the interaction is perceived only indirectly.

text: Give characters physical personality through animation, such as distinctive running poses, so movement expresses who they are.
Solvers who cannot make a required conceptual leap stare and strain for inspiration rather than making incremental headway.
when: Puzzles needing a sudden change in assumptions
why: No partial progress is available to them

text: Players sense clues before insight, fail to interpret them, and interpret them afterward, producing a feeling of having missed something obvious.
Insight makes players believe they can predict similar surprises next time, which is why it feels valuable.
why: Players expect that recognizing the same clues later could let them anticipate a repeat, which makes the surprise worth something.

text: Insight occurs when one new piece of information triggers a chain reaction that makes many earlier clues suddenly make sense.
Operators who trust an incorrect automated warning act on it far more often than those using a checklist, with errors of 75% versus 25% in one simulation.
when: When an automated alert conflicts with the correct action.
why: Reliance on automation lowers attention to errors.

text: Non-binding promises can be broken, causing frustration and mistrust that can damage friendships.
when: When trades in the game are non-binding, so a player can refuse to honor their side
why: Nothing enforces a non-binding deal, so the other player can refuse to deliver after agreeing.

text: Telling people to avoid a concept can make it more available, so they produce more of the behavior the instruction forbids.
why: Keeping the forbidden idea in mind in order to suppress it primes it, raising how readily it comes to mind.

text: 1) Identify each critical action. 2) Show an on-screen instruction at the moment the action matters. 3) Let novices play imperfectly without total confusion.
when: teaching action-based games with critical moments
why: Prompts guide novices through key decisions as they occur.

text: A player who alone makes every decision and whose success depends on their performance feels intense projection, even with repetitive content.
when: when content is simple and repetitive
why: the player's own decisions and outcomes carry the stakes

text: Players act on virtual objects with their bodies even while knowing intellectually that the objects are not real.
when: playing VR
why: proprioception responds to the body's experience regardless of belief

text: Hooking almost any point gives players a sense of improvisation and freedom to use the environment.
why: Being able to attach to nearly anything lets players use the environment as they choose.

text: Heading and speed changes made in the air appear on touchdown, which matches what players expect airborne control to do.
when: player steers or accelerates while airborne
why: Players expect airborne input to take effect when the vehicle lands

text: Controls driven by the player's body, such as shadows or arm movement, can make play physical, with players bumping, blocking, and wrestling.
when: Input is tied to the player's physical movement
why: Each player's shadow acts as an obstacle to the other, so blocking an opponent is done with the body.

text: Players readily attribute personality, fear, or desire to inanimate objects that merely move or respond.
when: objects move or respond in ways that look purposeful
why: the mind is especially eager to find personality and intent

text: Large open prospect space creates agoraphobia, the opposite of the claustrophobia that narrow space creates.
why: Open areas leave the player exposed with no cover, much as open ground exposes people to predators and weather.

text: Lower ceilings create a stronger feeling of protection than high ones.
Bodily space exists through degrees of freedom and skilled use; learning a skill changes it, and clothing, tools and prostheses also change it.
why: Bodily space is set by what the subject can potentially do, so anything that alters those potentials alters the space.

text: In modern 3D games, players generally know every action available to them, so action discovery is not a source of play.
when: In modern 3D games with a limited, visible range of basic actions
why: Visible action sets remove the need to guess the interface's vocabulary.

text: Players often ignore the interface unless it becomes confusing.
when: The interface works smoothly.
why: Players project their consciousness into the controlled character, so the interface drops out of awareness.

text: When an object is controlled as a large cursor with no simulated response, players orient easily but perceive no mass, weight or presence.
when: input maps directly to object position
why: no simulated response adds inertia

text: Players reach maximum jump height by holding the button for most of the jump.
why: Holding the button keeps accelerating upward against gravity, while releasing cuts upward velocity to a low value.

text: Players notice crosshairs moving on their own but not a few pixels of early stopping or slight direction bending, because surrounding motion masks these small changes.
when: Adjusting aim without player awareness
why: Motion around the small correction hides it from perception.

text: Design situations where players need help and can easily ask for it, because helping others is satisfying and others will come to aid when asked, even though players often hesitate to offer help.
when: When designing cooperative assistance
why: Players hesitate to offer help unprompted, but respond when a clear need is visible and easy to voice.

text: Intuitive interfaces produce a sense of control, so judge how easy or hard the interface is to master.
why: Meaningful control is essential for immersive interactivity.

text: Check whether the interface has become invisible by listing how players describe their actions; world-based wording signals success.
when: During playtesting.
why: A poorly designed virtual interface walls players off from the world, while a good one amplifies their control.

text: Judging control by intuition alone misleads, because the same scheme feels different to a novice and to a practiced player.
when: evaluating control schemes
why: feel depends on skill level

text: Players expect a button press to act immediately; when a control gives no feedback or an unseen delay, they keep pressing or think it is broken and may reject the scheme.
when: when a control gives no feedback or has a delay players cannot see
why: Players expect immediate response to input.

text: Under negative feedback, players try to avoid being mid-decline when the game finishes.
when: when a turn or time limit is near
why: ending on a down-swing loses the declared lead

text: Earlier games often made AI activation visible to the player, such as characters waking as the player approaches; modern practice hides it better.
Changes to visible mechanics, such as platformer physics, are more obvious to players than changes to hidden formulas.
when: When choosing between changing visible mechanics like movement physics and changing hidden formulas
why: Players perceive only the outcomes of random rolls, not their range, so hidden-math tweaks take many results to notice.

text: Frustration from poor framerate, long loading times, or ad pop-ups may be blamed on the gameplay itself.
when: players experience technical friction
why: players misattribute the source of their frustration

text: When one action triggers both a musical flourish and a visual change, players experience several sensory effects at once, a synesthesia-like response.
when: actions that produce matching sound and visuals
why: one input drives multiple senses

text: A storage deficit occurs when information is encoded correctly but weakens over time, following the forgetting curve.
Both thinking systems are active whenever a person is awake, and they influence each other.
What ultimately matters is the player's perception, understanding, behavior, and emotion.
A character that should change behavior but does not looks wrong, breaking the sense that it is aware, such as when a companion is removed or the player appears.
when: When a nearby character is removed, or when the player comes close or gets seen.
why: Behavior changes stand out far more than steady behavior, so a missing reaction breaks the sense of awareness.

text: Pick one word for how players should feel as they approach and enter combat, such as scared, tense, coordinated or hopeful.
Counter storage deficits by reconsolidating information through repetition across different contexts.
when: When players learned information correctly but it fades over time before it is needed
why: Memory traces weaken after encoding, and repeating the content across varied settings strengthens them again.

text: Identical values framed as penalties below an average or as losses weigh more than when framed as base plus increments or gains, even though the math is identical.
when: presenting stat-based values, or options framed as losses versus gains
why: Players respond to framing, not only to numbers; framing changes the emotional weight of the same numbers.

text: Polished visuals bias judgment of underlying design via a halo effect: players forgive rough mechanics, and inexperienced reviewers may reject an excellent graybox for looking unfinished.
when: when a game has rough mechanics but polished visuals; when reviewing a graybox
why: The halo effect makes visual quality distort judgment of the underlying design.

text: Friends and family tend to be either too harsh or too forgiving, depending on their habits with the designer.
when: Once the game is playable with a clearly defined set of rules, and testing moves past the early stages
why: Close personal relationships with the designer make confidants either too harsh or too forgiving, which clouds their objectivity.

text: Players work hard to avoid the embarrassment of imagined judgment, such as an in-game evaluator scoring their creations.
when: A game scores or judges the player's creations
why: Imagined judgment feels embarrassing

text: Identical odds or payouts feel different depending on framing: a larger-looking first number can make an equal trade seem enticing or unacceptable.
when: presenting odds, payouts or prices
why: anchoring on the first number

text: After an outcome is known, people recall their earlier predictions as more accurate, remembering confidence in correct guesses and doubt in wrong ones.
when: when reviewing past predictions after results are known
why: Memory is edited to make past events look more predictable than they were.

text: Anthropology views people holistically, covering physical, mental, and cultural aspects, and compares peoples across places and history.
Honest probability does not automatically drive players away; some games remain popular and profitable while punishing any flaw in probabilistic thinking.
Humility helps designers notice unexpected opportunities and counters the bias of judging from only the information at hand.
why: it makes designers more observant and thoughtful

text: People rate a product more highly when they took part in creating it, so players tend to value elements they helped build or design.
when: Players build or design game elements
why: A known cognitive bias, often called the self-built effect, raises perceived value of self-made items

text: Gut feelings come from bodily signals that steer focus and working memory inside the prefrontal cortex.
when: When choosing between morally consequential options, or between options of similar cost and benefit
why: Limited attention and working memory make full analysis impractical, so bodily signals guide choices instead.

text: Each in-game impression primes related ideas for a few minutes, so what the player sees and hears shapes what they are inclined to do next.
when: During play, whenever players see or hear something in the game
why: Exposure makes related ideas more available, so they bias what players are inclined to do next.

text: Implicit (procedural) memory holds skills and conditioned responses performed without being able to describe them, such as motor skills and fighting-game combos; it is usually more durable than explicit memory.
Constructionism holds that learners discover rules more efficiently by actively building knowledge while exploring in meaningful contexts toward goals they care about, such as programming.
The classic forgetting curve loses about 40% of memorized material after 20 minutes and nearly 70% after one day; it is a worst case because it uses meaningless content.
when: meaningless material with no purpose and no mnemonic aids
why: worst-case baseline

text: Studying a detailed pattern catalog trains people to notice the same qualities in everyday surroundings they previously overlooked.
when: after studying a detailed pattern catalog

text: The forgetting curve plots how memorized material is lost over time, with the steepest loss occurring soon after learning.
A growth mindset treats intelligence as a process that effort can develop, so success or failure reflects effort rather than fixed ability.

Cognitive science examines how minds perceive, recall, focus, acquire skills, infer and solve puzzles, which players rely on during play; neuroscience instead investigates the nervous system as a separate discipline.
The Montessori method learns through the senses first, then applies intellect to practical problems.
when: when designing how players learn a game's mechanics
why: Sensory absorption builds the base that later problem solving depends on.

text: Implicit learning is often considered more robust than explicit learning and tends to last longer, though it can still be forgotten.
When people judge word meaning rather than letter case, without expecting a memory test, their later recognition of those words is far higher.
when: incidental learning conditions
why: meaning-based judgment forces deep processing

text: Most memory-based rhythm games use fixed repeating patterns rather than randomly generated sequences.
A custom-designed driving game reduced multitasking costs in adults aged 60 to 85 compared with controls, with gains lasting six months.
Players of research games can contribute scientific results; over two million people played a spatial navigation game whose data helped study early signs of Alzheimer's disease.
Grading learning can undermine its intrinsic reward, because the learner's reason for engaging shifts to the external grade.
when: learning is intrinsically rewarding for the learner
why: external grades replace internal interest

text: Purposeful learning, often achieved through play, works better than forced teaching.
when: When learners explore and experiment with immediate feedback on their successes and failures
why: learners engage more when the learning has meaning

text: Newer approaches have not replaced these paradigms; each explains a different facet of learning, so they can be used together.
why: Each paradigm concentrates on a different facet of learning, so none makes the others obsolete.

text: Childhood play is a rich source of design material, since children learn social order and group dynamics through play.
why: Children work out social order and group behavior while making and playing games.

text: Design non-obvious properties that reveal lessons in sequence, because the subtler and less visible an insight is, the more satisfying it feels to learn.
when: When a game is meant to offer lasting learning rather than shallow play
why: Obvious lessons give little satisfaction.

text: A repeated stimulus gradually loses its interest and attention (habituation), and attention returns when the stimulus changes (dishabituation).
Each challenge passes through four phases: Discovery, Learning, Mastery, and Fluency.
when: When a challenge forms one discrete unit of content in a progression system
why: The phases describe how players move from unknown problem to internalized skill.

text: The General Learning Model holds that any stimulus, including games, can have short- and long-term effects through learning mechanisms.
why: People acquire behaviors and beliefs by watching others, a route the model applies to any stimulus.

text: Cognitive science supplies knowledge of how the mind takes in, handles and stores information, while UX supplies the methodology and procedures for applying it.
Design learning around human limits in perception, attention, memory, motivation, and emotion.
Player feedback mostly concerns an action from about a second earlier.
when: when players give feedback on a creature's action
why: players need time to position the cursor

text: When events come faster than players can consider them, players cannot form a response, become frustrated and quit.
when: combat outpaces decision time

text: When combat is too slow, players have already decided their moves and grow bored waiting for the outcome.
when: combat pacing is slow

text: In Fluency, the player internalizes the lesson and applies it to similar problems with little friction.
when: After a player has succeeded at a challenge, in the final stage of learning a problem
why: Learned solutions become reusable, so later problems cost less effort.

text: People who see ability as fixed tend to prefer performance goals, while those who see it as malleable prefer learning goals.
when: choosing goals for a task
why: beliefs about ability shape goal preference

text: Players read a teammate's loadout as a signal of intended play, such as long-range rifles suggesting aggressive engagement.
when: On a public team server where teammates' intentions cannot be discussed beforehand
why: Equipment is visible while intentions are hidden, so the chosen weapon is read as a hint of planned engagement range.

text: Players assume the designer uses metaphor to teach and that not every property is simulated, so they must work out which fictional elements are real mechanics.
when: A game's fiction suggests actions that the mechanics may not support.
why: Metaphors promise more than the game simulates.

text: Listeners are the game characters interested in events, and events can represent sight, radio messages, specific times, or any other game data.
Three main factors shape learning quality: attention, motivation and emotion.
System 2 may be unaware that System 1 errors are happening.
Whether far transfer can be reliably achieved is still debated in psychology research.
Players learn challenges through a cycle: attempt an obstacle, reflect on the outcome, form a strategy, then test the new strategy in a fresh attempt.
when: when a player faces a challenge that requires repeated tries
why: Freedom to experiment combined with feedback on outcomes lets players build understanding from concrete experience.

text: Treating seven as a fixed limit for everyday processing, where people also process information while holding it.
when: When a task requires holding information while manipulating it, such as mental arithmetic
why: Working memory is severely limited and must both store and manipulate the items at once.

text: 1) New players feel clumsy and accept frustration, trusting that effort will be rewarded. 2) The pleasure of control soothes frustration until the first success. 3) Skills become automatic. 4) The player breaks through, and the next challenge restarts the cycle.
when: When a new player first picks up a game and is still learning its basic tasks
why: Players accept the awkward start as the cost of entry, expecting the designer to pay off the learning later.

text: Explicit feedback is accurate and reliable but can interrupt play; implicit feedback from behaviour is unobtrusive but noisy and depends on assumptions about what behaviour means.
when: When measuring player experience during gameplay sessions

text: Deeper processing of material improves retention more than shallow passive exposure.
when: When learners can explore freely and get instant feedback on what works
why: Acting on material, rather than just reading it, engages it more deeply in working memory.

text: Curious learners teach themselves more and retain what they learn, because they pursue knowledge by choice.
when: learners pursue topics they choose
why: Self-chosen learning feels owned and is remembered

text: Exposure to a concept, such as conflict or care, makes behavior matching that concept more likely for several minutes afterward.
when: A person has recently encountered a concept.
why: The activated concept influences behavior without conscious intent.

text: Priming a concept also activates behaviors linked to it in memory, such as walking more slowly after age-related words are primed.
when: When players are exposed to cues before play begins, such as a game's title or cover art
why: A primed idea also spreads activation to linked concepts, which then shape the behavior they connect to.

text: Constructivism holds that people actively build knowledge through interaction with their environment rather than receiving it passively.
Distributed learning, with teaching spread over time, works better than massed learning, where material is concentrated in one block.
Strategies that learners develop in discovery settings can transfer to other contexts.
Deep learning recognises patterns across multiple signals, produces complex spatio-temporal attributes, and can fuse data from several players or from player input combined with game content.
Twelve hours of non-violent action mini-games improved visual attention and reading speed in children with dyslexia, compared with a control group, with benefits lasting two months.
Constructivism is a strong single account of how players learn games, because it combines freedom with feedback.
Structure challenges, feedback, and setbacks so players are motivated to iterate toward mastery.
Game time displaces homework and other learning activities, since time spent on one activity is not spent on another.
when: When children have a game console available as a new activity alongside schoolwork

text: Deep processing costs more time and cognitive resources than shallow processing, but it produces stronger long-term retention.
when: When the task is complex enough to demand real engagement, not simple acknowledgment

text: People learn by observing others as well as through direct interaction with their environment.
Most human knowledge is learned from others rather than firsthand, and relying on others is an adaptive necessity since learning everything firsthand would often be fatal.
Repeat important information over time using the spacing effect, rather than presenting it once.
when: any feature players must learn and remember
why: spaced repetition strengthens memory

text: Explaining content in your own words is a way to process it more deeply and so improve retention.
when: When trying to learn or remember material.

text: Operant conditioning reinforces actions, Montessori sequencing orders challenges, and constructivism structures iterative problem solving; each does a distinct job.
Make the learning process itself rewarding for newbies.
when: When new players are challenged mainly by learning how to play, not by the game's content
why: newbies overwhelmed by learning quit before engaging, shrinking the audience

text: A learning pyramid ranks being able to do at its top, so game-based learning focuses almost entirely on doing.
Matching instruction to a preferred learning style, such as visual or verbal, has no solid scientific support as a way to improve learning.
Preferred learning styles are hard to measure, and the criteria used to classify them are inconsistent.
Order puzzles so players can deduce solutions from recognizable elements, even when those elements are used in new ways.
when: When a level or puzzle series is built from reusable modular assets
why: Recognizable assets let players carry prior understanding into new situations.

text: Applying the learning-styles concept to instruction can sometimes be damaging to learners.
when: When tailoring teaching to a presumed learning-style preference
why: No evidence shows matching instruction to a preferred style improves learning; some studies contradict that idea.

text: Scalar ratings or class labels suit regression and classification learners such as deep nets, Bayesian models, trees, SVMs and linear regression.
when: When recorded data is a scalar rating or annotated class labels of user states
why: Ranked annotations would turn the problem into preference learning, which standard supervised methods do not cover.

text: Projection is stronger when a guest watches a risky act in person, because they can imagine the danger falling on them.
when: when a guest watches a risky act live
why: the guest can imagine the danger happening to them

text: Fear of losing progress makes players cautious, and if pushed too far it can make them quit.
when: games with progress loss
why: Loss aversion shapes risk-taking and motivation.

text: Players who regret purchases leave unhappy and return less often, shrinking the future audience for games from the same and other studios.
when: Players feel pressured into spending
why: Regret reduces trust and return visits

text: Ladder challengers rarely lose standing if they fail, so many ladder games feel risk-free and climbing gives a sense of progression.
when: ladder play with challenge matches
why: a failed challenge does not drop the challenger's rank

text: Gamers tend to reload a checkpoint after a severe loss, yet usually shrug off minor ones.
when: Games offering manual saves

text: People often post-rationalize decisions or failures to avoid the discomfort of inconsistency.
when: When a person's action or failure conflicts with what they already know or believe
why: Holding inconsistent beliefs causes discomfort, which motivates reconciling them.

text: Players facing repeated hurdles and failures may stop playing and conclude the game is not worth playing.
when: repeated failure
why: dissonance between effort and failure

text: Players may repeat the same obstacle because of missing information, a missed opportunity, or a lack of experience or intuition.
when: When an obstacle seems impossible to a portion of players, even if it is solvable

text: People accept or reject the same option differently depending on whether it is framed as a payment or as a possible loss.
when: When an option is framed as a possible loss rather than as a cost.
why: Losses weigh more heavily than equal gains, which is loss aversion.

text: Loss aversion is the tendency for losses to weigh more heavily than gains of comparable value.
Player's remorse is the regret a player feels after spending time on a game that motivated them but did not fulfill them.
Limited saves let players save anywhere but cap the total number of saves.
Losing hard-won possessions is a strong flow breaker because loss aversion is a strong psychological effect.
when: Designing item loss or permanent penalties
why: Losses weigh more heavily than equivalent gains

text: Prospect space recalls open ground early humans crossed for food and water, exposed to predators and weather.
Games with no failure, no time pressure, and freely leaving at any time reduce stress and suit relaxing experiences.
Use cognitive reappraisal to reframe unavoidable losses, emphasising what the player did well or improved on personal metrics, so they accept losses they understand.
when: after a loss; when the negative outcome cannot be avoided
why: Reappraisal regulates negative emotions tied to losing; reframing helps players accept losses they understand.

text: Combine limited carrying capacity, limited combat, quick running, and a timer before hostiles fill the map to create tension in a looting mode.
An extra losing condition, such as forming a line of three first, can create forcing moves where one player dictates the other's reply, producing rewarding sequences.
why: Forcing moves let one side dictate the opponent's replies, enabling clever forced sequences that players find compelling.

text: When a kill takes many shots, the first shot loses importance and play becomes mostly aim and dodge with little hidden information.
when: Low-lethality weapons.
why: Hidden pre-contact maneuvering only pays off when one hit matters, so with weak guns aim and dodge become the real contest.

text: Predictable outcomes lead players to concede or quit early, as chess players resign once they calculate a certain loss.
Reframing cannot make an unfair or unbalanced outcome feel fair, since it only supports players who understand their loss.
why: Players who cannot see why they lost feel the game is unfair even when it is fair, since perception outweighs the design's actual fairness.

text: A player instantly loses the game once their hand or draw pile has no cards left.
A player whose Cost is at least their remaining health loses at reveal, before battle or damage resolve.
when: Card duels where cost is paid in health.
why: Cost is deducted from health at reveal, so a cost at or above remaining health drops it to zero before battle.

text: Invented coin flips switch outcomes after a repeat about 60% of the time and rarely contain runs of four, which real flips produce regularly.
when: people generating random-looking sequences from memory or without a physical randomizer
why: Invented sequences avoid long runs that seem non-random, so people are poor at producing random sequences from imagination.

text: After several wins, players tend to expect that another win is likely.
why: Humans seek patterns and often perceive them where only chance operates, so a streak reads as predictive.

text: Card games such as Poker mix luck of the draw with skill in reading opponents and knowing odds, and the balance between them is a design question to weigh.
Young children tolerate luck-only games because they are learning turn-taking and counting, while most adults find them dull due to few decisions.
when: Designing luck-only games for different age groups
why: Children value the social and counting practice, whereas adults need meaningful choices to stay engaged.

text: Players who lose two even-odds contests in a row often suspect foul play, although such losing runs are expected in fair random games.
when: short sessions of even-odds random bets
why: Short runs are mistaken for evidence of manipulation

text: Judging skill from randomness is misleading: identical randomness feels different across games, heavily random games can still seem skillful, and games without randomness can lack followings.
Low-skill players are more likely to quit, which tends to push a rating system toward inflation.
why: Players who do poorly feel frustrated and leave, and a departing below-average player takes rating points out, inflating the rest.

text: As a player gains mastery, a task that once engaged them stops engaging, so challenge must keep rising with skill.
when: Players improve over time with a fixed task
why: Skill growth shrinks the gap between ability and challenge.

text: Males often enjoy mastering challenging things even when the mastery serves no practical purpose, while many females want mastery to serve a meaningful purpose.
Players who die from misused abilities, missed dangers, or misunderstood rules feel no growing mastery and are likely to quit or grow hostile.
when: when deaths come from misunderstood rules, threats, or abilities
why: Players do not perceive their competence growing.

text: Skill-based games can yield deep mastery, and competitive players often exploit unintended mechanics such as movement tricks.
when: games with high skill ceilings
why: Competitive players probe beyond the designed rules, turning code bugs into advantages that deepen mastery.

text: When combos are linked across event types, players keep seeking the next target and care less about incidental collisions.
when: linked combo systems
why: Continuing chains reward chasing the next event.

text: Winning a competitive match raises appreciation of the game more than losing lowers it.
when: players finish a player-versus-player match
why: the outcome colors the whole experience

text: A masterpoint system awards points for taking part in organized events and for performance, and a player's rating is the lifetime sum of those points, so points only accumulate.
Metagame information is outside knowledge, such as expected length from genre, difficulty from friends, plot predictions from clichés or studio habits, technical limits, and trailers.
Midway through Mastery the downward trend in difficulty becomes visible, while completion is often closer than it appears.
why: The late-stage trend becomes apparent only after enough progress has been made.

text: Practicing isolated sub-skills such as aiming and tracking before full play is a way to build the base skills a game requires.
why: Compelling challenges make isolated practice feel worthwhile, since the sub-skills transfer to full play.

text: A skill is joyful when it is interesting and rewarding and its challenge sits between too easy and too hard.
when: when tuning skill challenge

text: A lighthearted failure state that costs little time and resource loss keeps players trying again, while still making them feel setbacks.
when: Designing how players recover from losing a fight.
why: Low-stakes recovery keeps frustration down so players return to play quickly.

text: Successful outcomes from a player's own choices create a sense of mastery and control, which can counter a run of real-life failures.
when: a player faces repeated real-life setbacks
why: Success from own choices restores a sense of control

text: In Mastery, understanding reaches critical mass and the pieces fall together, so solving speeds up until the problem is complete.
when: Once the player has already learned the problem and pushed at its boundaries.
why: Accumulated understanding compounds once enough pieces connect.

text: In games where players steadily lose power, the player may feel ground down for the whole game.
when: when power declines throughout play
why: Continuous loss without relief produces a sense of punishment.

text: A winning run may take dozens of hours and many deaths, a steep barrier for new players.
when: In permadeath roguelikes, where death erases the save and restarts the character.
why: Skill to win is built across many deaths, each of which restarts progress from scratch.

text: Treating every player struggle as a defect removes deliberate tension; a struggle that produces the intended emotion is a design success.
when: When the game's intent is to elicit a specific emotion such as panic, as in horror.
why: Panic is desirable in horror, so the struggle is by design rather than a usability defect.

text: Players form expectations about how long a kill should take and complain when fights drag or end too quickly.
when: fights that run much longer or shorter than expected
why: Their sense of fair fight length depends on expected kill time.

text: Internet access may widen the gap between curious people, who become experts in their interests, and incurious people.
when: people have wide internet access
why: Curious people use available information to pursue their interests

text: Concern about new media, including games, has followed earlier media such as comic books, rock music, and radio once they became popular.
Longitudinal studies have been used to argue that violent games are a causal risk factor for long-term harm.
Judge game effects by specific game and play context, since video games as one category are too broad for a single verdict.
why: The video games category is not homogeneous, and play context such as motivation and social setting shapes effects.

text: The General Aggression Model also predicts long-term effects: aggressive attitudes and desensitization to aggression.
why: Learning from observed behavior shapes attitudes, grounded in the social learning theory the model draws from.

text: Lab studies mostly measure mild, prank-level aggression rather than fighting or pushing, so they say little about serious violence.
Games played by under-18s need stricter enforcement of all commitments, plus guardrails against child sexual exploitation.
when: games played by under-18s
why: minors are more vulnerable

text: Children have specific rights, so studios targeting minors carry extra ethical responsibility.
when: When a game is played by or aimed at children
why: Children hold specially protected entitlements under a UN human rights treaty, so studios owe them added ethical care.

text: Teach children and parents media literacy, since offline problems such as bullying and sexting now appear online.

Sudden insight, an aha moment, occurs when reframing makes a solution clear at once, making previously random components' purpose visible and pleasurable; payoff depends on earlier gathered information.
when: When a puzzle's solution depends on an unnoticed property of the controls or world.
why: A reframed understanding restructures the perceptual field at once.

text: Working memory is short-term, lasting a few minutes at most, and holds and processes information at once, replacing the older short-term store and being more relevant to video game play.
No known limits govern how long or how much long-term memory holds; the brain need not delete older memories to acquire new ones, though forgetting still happens.
Memory is reconstructive: it is encoded, decoded and re-encoded at each recall, introducing errors and biases, so people can recall events that never happened.
why: cognition distorts recollection just as it distorts perception

text: Adults can hold roughly three to four items at once in working memory; children have even less capacity, and capacity can be lower for some people.
when: When a person is under stress or anxiety, or is a child

text: Players memorize winning patterns against deterministic enemy behavior, because the same positions always produce the same responses.
when: enemy AI depends only on current positions
why: identical states always yield identical responses

text: When a new fact arrives, people reshape their mental picture and change earlier answers they gave about it.
when: when a game reveals information that contradicts or refines an earlier impression
why: Mental models are flexible and get rebuilt around new evidence.

text: The pleasure of an insight is triggered by seeing the answer, and a mind that has seriously considered a problem gets a strong rush from it.
when: Players who see a solution after genuine effort
why: Prior consideration primes the mind to enjoy the revealed answer

text: Players overestimate how likely memorable, rare events are, because such events stand out in memory.
when: When rare, dramatic events are widely publicized and vivid
why: selection bias

text: Players remember dramatic wins far better than humiliating losses, so without tracked statistics they overestimate their win rate and skill.
why: Memory favors vivid wins, a self-flattering bias that makes players feel good about themselves.

text: Players infer broad world rules from tiny cues, and later interactions that confirm those rules make the world feel real and consistent.
when: interactions reveal physical behavior over time
why: Players generalize from small evidence and then test that generalization.

text: Replays and other artifacts generated from player input become valuable to players and help them identify with the game and their achievements.
when: When the game produces artifacts such as replays from the player's own inputs
why: Owned expression produces artifacts players want to show others.

text: A single leading word in a question can change later recall, raising estimates and producing false memories of details that never occurred.
when: When people are asked about a past event with suggestive wording.
why: Memory is rebuilt at each recall and can absorb the question's framing.

text: Creative people, and children with weak associative barriers, readily link unrelated pictures into a coherent story.
when: given randomly chosen picture prompts
why: weak barriers between unrelated ideas ease story making

text: Responsive input keeps players delighted across a game's whole length, while unresponsive or mushy input turns simple actions into frustrating chores.
why: Input is felt constantly, so its quality shapes the entire experience.

text: Sensory memory briefly holds raw sensory input, for under a second to a few seconds, and fades unless attended; it is usually considered part of perception.
A recall deficit occurs when information is stored but temporarily inaccessible, as in the tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon.
Short-term memory holds a limited number of items for under about a minute, and its capacity at any moment is limited.
An item is the largest meaningful unit, such as a word, number, or date, so grouping information into meaningful chunks increases what can be held.
The zone of proximal development is the range between what a child can do alone and what they cannot yet do even with help.

Long-term explicit (declarative) memory stores knowledge and implicit (procedural, conditioning) memory stores how to do things, using different brain regions; both are subject to the forgetting curve.
The Zeigarnik effect is that people remember incomplete tasks better than completed ones, so open tasks create lasting cognitive load and completing them brings relief.
People with hippocampal damage can learn new motor skills while being unable to recall the sessions in which they learned them.
The decline of long-term memory is commonly described as exponential.
Remembering requires encoding, storing, and retrieving information, so memory is more than storage alone.
Iconic memory stores visual input and echoic memory stores auditory input. Other sensory stores exist but have received less research.
Thirteen unrelated digits are hard to hold, while three meaningful numbers are manageable.
why: meaningful grouping reduces the number of items

text: Working memory limits also constrain attention and long-term retention, not only immediate task performance.
Manipulating the environment helps learners think and learn; perception alone teaches object properties, but active manipulation still matters.
Human memory consists of three parts: short-lived sensory stores belonging to perception, working memory, and long-term memory.
Tasks needing many items at once, such as multiplying two three-digit numbers mentally, overload working memory.
Information processed more deeply in working memory is retained better over the long term than information processed shallowly.
why: deeper processing creates more durable memory traces

text: Recall favors the first items in a list (primacy effect) and the last items (recency effect).
when: When recalling a sequence of items after encoding them in order
why: Items at the start and end of a sequence get processed differently during encoding, so they are remembered better.

text: Stress, anxiety and young age all reduce working memory capacity.
Processing ends in changes to memory through synaptic modifications, such as forming new connections between neurons.
Working memory controls attention for executive functions, such as reasoning, deciding and completing complex tasks.
Short-term span is about seven items (plus or minus two) recalled error-free after rote encoding, a limit mainly applicable to rote memorization without other processing, uncommon in daily life.
when: rote memorization right after encoding

text: After studying a list of about 20 words for one minute, people typically recall roughly 5 to 9 words.
Working memory holds about three items and lasts a few minutes, and it demands heavy attention.
For meaningless syllables, about 40% is forgotten after 20 minutes and close to 70% after a day.
when: When learning content that has no meaning, as a worst case.
why: Later studies replicated this forgetting pattern.

text: Memory lapses come from three sources: encoding deficits, storage deficits, and recall deficits. They often occur in combination.
Working memory has a central executive that supervises a phonological loop for language and a visuospatial sketchpad for visual and spatial information.
The mind is a leaky cup: decisions are the water, and flow requires them to drain in steadily without overflowing.
when: When designing flow at the level of moment-to-moment decisions, not overall skill-challenge balance
why: Each decision occupies the mind as it enters and clears over moments, so incoming decisions must not exceed what drains.

text: Assuming all players of a generation share one mental model leads to wrong expectations about how they will read a game.
why: Brains work alike across eras, so generational differences come from accumulated experience with products, which shapes expectations and mental models.

text: Treating perception, attention, memory, motivation and emotion as independent sequential stages misrepresents how they interact in the brain.
why: Separate chapters are a teaching simplification; in the brain, attention and emotion shape learning quality, so the processes blend together.

text: Reading the multi-store model as a strict serial pipeline in which information always passes through each store in order.
why: Memory components are functional rather than separate physical areas and overlap, so information does not always move through them in a fixed order.

text: Interruptions can make a person forget an ongoing step in a process.
Do not rely on players remembering what they were taught; counter recall deficits with frequent reminders so players need not retrieve information unaided.
when: When information is stored in memory but momentarily cannot be retrieved, such as on the tip of the tongue.
why: Memory is a fallible reconstruction, so players will forget important details and should not be relied on to retrieve them unaided.

text: Use only the playing style from the most recent level when personalising during play, because learning effects change behaviour across a series of levels.
when: during a series of consecutive levels
why: learning during play makes older behaviour a poor predictor of the player

text: Subjective rankings can be contested by fans, especially when used for tournament seeding.
when: when subjective rankings determine tournament seeding
why: Expert panels rank by their own systems, personal opinions and whims, so fans who disagree have grounds to contest the results.

text: One hypothesis holds that the brain treats sensory mismatch like poisoning, which would explain why the response includes vomiting.
The claim that people use only ten percent of their brain is false; people use essentially all of it.
Entrainment is the process by which a living thing aligns its own timing with an outside rhythm or with other organisms.
Landscape, weather, time of day and season each evoke different feelings, from depression to giddy triumph, so environment can be tuned to accentuate a target emotion.
why: People have evolved preferences for fertile, moderately open landscapes and also prefer scenery they grew up with, so matching settings evoke ease.

text: Triggers include real motion (boats, cars, roller coasters, spinning rides), apparent motion (large-format films, VR racing) and reading in a moving car.
Motion sickness occurs when the inner ear and eyes disagree about motion: hair cells in the inner ear detect acceleration and rotation, and conflict with vision can trigger nausea.
when: When the body perceives motion, or its visual appearance, that it does not expect, such as on a boat or in VR.
why: Nausea may be a poison-defense response, since toxins can scramble brain processing so inner-ear and visual signals no longer match.

text: Motion sickness drugs block the response but tend to make people drowsy and disconnected from the experience.
when: A player takes medication to prevent nausea
why: Medication acts broadly on the nausea circuit rather than precisely, so drowsiness and disconnection come along as side effects.

text: Self-determination theory holds that competence (feeling good at something), autonomy and relatedness are innate needs; satisfying them makes games engaging and intrinsically motivating, while thwarting them undermines intrinsic motivation.
why: Psychological needs are as real as physical ones, so when they go unmet a person's mental health suffers.

text: Maslow's hierarchy ranks five need levels as a pyramid: physiological (food, shelter, warmth), safety, belonging, esteem, and self-actualization (pursuing one's talents).
why: When a lower need is unmet, attention drops back down to that base level, so higher aspirations wait until basic needs are satisfied.

text: Unmet lower needs pull attention down, so meet them before higher needs motivate; but the order is not strict, and players may pursue higher needs while lower ones stay unmet.
when: when reasoning about the order of player needs
why: Needs are ordered, so lower needs take priority; critics find fixed hierarchies too rigid.

text: Relatedness is the need to feel affiliated, connected and belonging with others, through reciprocal care, such as being part of a supportive team.

Motivation drives all behavior, but no unified theory explains all human behavior; theories address particular aspects, like intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, so no framework predicts every player choice.
The intrinsic/extrinsic split is imperfect, unstable and hard to separate cleanly since they often co-occur, yet developers use it widely.
Players given too much open freedom feel frustrated; short lists are easier to decide from. Autonomy must be guided, since confused players feel neither autonomous nor competent.
when: when offering open-ended options to players
why: Open freedom forces hard imaginative work.

text: Rewards added to enjoyed activities may weaken intrinsic motivation (overjustification effect); this is strongest when rewards feel external or are later removed, which reduces future play and misattributes motives.
when: when rewards are added to or removed from activities players already enjoy
why: External rewards displace the internal reason for the behavior, reframing it as external.

text: Players who set their own goals or subgoals feel accomplishment beyond in-game rewards, even when the main goal is out of reach, since success they define feels earned.
when: games offering open-ended personal goals or when the main goal is out of reach
why: Self-made targets still give progress.

text: When conscious and subconscious motivations align, a creator works with more passion, focus, and intensity.
when: after identifying a personal theme
why: Conscious and subconscious drives point the same way.

text: Telling players their goal steers their attention and can make them miss details, such as hunting for a named villain.
when: at the start of a playtest
why: A named target draws players to search for it, so they overlook other details they would otherwise have noticed.

text: Players may ignore objectives and chase kills when kills are tracked persistently and feel more rewarding than objective progress.
when: objective modes that track individual kills
why: Kills are more gratifying to watch than the team score

text: Players who want to look after a group will take a station that offers the best view, control of pace, and turn-sharing, then invest in using it well.
when: group play where one station can steer or direct the others
why: The role gives them a stake in how the group's experience goes

text: Motivation is driven by wanting, and liking can sustain it, with liking often occurring unconsciously without a conscious feeling of pleasure.
why: Brain reward circuitry drives both desire and enjoyment, mostly without awareness, so enjoyment can happen without a conscious sense of pleasure.

text: People differ in implicit drives such as power, achievement, and affiliation, which change how strongly they want to dominate, improve, or connect.
when: Designing for varied players
why: Designer motives can bias a game toward some players and away from others

text: Puzzles are fun when they are novel, neither too easy nor too hard, and require a shift in perception.
why: Puzzles that feel easy disappoint and ones that feel too hard discourage, while a perceived modest difficulty keeps players interested.

text: Uncertainty about the result is a key motivator that keeps players engaged.
why: If the result can be foreseen, players have no remaining reason to keep playing.

text: Players invent their own goals, such as racing to finish a stage within a time limit, and compete with others over them.
why: Mechanics that offer measurable outcomes let players invent personal challenges, such as finishing a stage within a time limit.

text: People visit museum-like venues to escape daily routine, see exotic things, expand knowledge, and return with a new perspective.
why: People seek variety away from routine, want to learn about the wider world, and return with a fresh view of familiar things.

text: Score-chasing motivation tends to appear only after players finish all content, and very difficult games rarely let players reach it.
when: After players have completed all the levels and have no remaining goal to finish.
why: While finishing levels is the dominant aim, a higher score does nothing for it, so collectibles lack inherent value.

text: Many players say they enjoy games because they like solving problems, a strength humans may have evolved for survival.
when: when players explain why they enjoy a game
why: Human problem solving is a strong capacity, possibly shaped by survival

text: A repetitive task can feel like play when the worker pursues a personal goal, such as beating their own best time.
when: when a worker performs monotonous, repeated tasks
why: A self-set goal changes the reason for acting, from pay alone to a personal challenge

text: Once a simple goal is set in a player's mind, it gives strong motivation to pursue it.
when: after the goal is clear to players
why: A simply stated goal is easier to visualize.

text: People who act out high or low status behaviors soon feel superior or inferior and unconsciously adopt matching behaviors.
when: During role-played status exchanges
why: Body behavior feeds back into how a person feels about their own standing.

text: Owning most of a set of linked items increases demand for the remaining items in that set.
when: Items award bonuses for grouping
why: Completing a set becomes more valuable as the group nears completion.

text: A slow player who sees their pace speeding up stays motivated, while a fast player who sees pace slowing must decide whether to continue or switch loops.
when: when progress velocity changes during play
why: Rising acceleration reinforces effort, while falling pace prompts reassessment of the current activity.

text: People with a strong achievement motive tend to prefer challenging tasks.
when: choosing between tasks of different difficulty
why: their drive is to improve, which challenge supports

text: Learners engage deeply when they do real, meaningful work such as a collaborative scientific study, rather than earning rewards for a chore.
when: when choosing between real work and reward-driven tasks
why: Meaningful work sustains engagement better than extrinsic rewards.

text: When characters choose their own actions without instructions, players feel both responsibility for and surprise at the results.
when: a free-will option lets characters act unprompted
why: players cause the situation but do not fully control its outcome

text: The more freedom players have had during a game, the more likely they are to reject a narrow final outcome.
when: Player has had extensive agency
why: Players who had wide freedom expect the ending to honor that open potential, so a narrow conclusion feels like a letdown.

text: Play becomes extrinsic when it is done for pay or to please someone else.
when: When play is done for money as a profession or to satisfy someone else.
why: Games are autotelic, so their purpose lies within the play itself; an external payoff moves the purpose outside the activity.

text: Friends often agree to play casually, lowering skill intensity so the social experience can take priority.
when: When a group wants social enjoyment over competitive intensity.
why: Lower skill intensity makes room for the social experience they want.

text: Players enjoy repeating actions such as building, defeating enemies, or decorating, because each repetition produces a new outcome shaped by their decisions.
when: a mechanic recurs many times
why: The same tool yields different experiences as the player's choices and the situation change.

text: Players of goal-free games invent their own objectives, such as maximizing a resource or pushing a physical skill further, and treat those objectives as the game.
when: a game has no official win or lose conditions
why: players seek challenge and visible progress, so they create it when the game does not supply it

text: Players feel pleasure when well-honed tactical skill lets them foresee outcomes.
when: In fast-paced situations where information is hidden by speed and outcomes are uncertain.
why: Projecting possible futures from prior knowledge exercises trained judgment, even when the results stay uncertain.

text: Player-defined tasks, such as buying a round of drinks for others, can yield social rewards.
Autonomy is the sense of meaningful choice, volition, self-expression venues, and control over how a task is done, with clear systems letting players feel in control of their fate.
Meaning is a sense of purpose, value and impact, extending beyond the self, behind player actions; players engage when they understand why something matters, which enhances motivation.
Achievers want to win and build the most powerful character possible, collecting rare loot and topping player-versus-player rankings.
Socializers play for other players through conversation or role-play and may care more about appearance than stats.
Possibility is the pleasure of many choices, as at shopping or buffet tables.
The lusory attitude is a player's voluntary acceptance of rules that require less efficient means to reach an end.
Ludus is rule-based play and paida is free-form improvisational play; they modify the four play types.
Motivation is the mechanism that makes trivial game activities feel important to players, even though they never forget the activity is only a game.
Pleasure seeking drives play through rewards such as collecting or scoring, while pain avoidance drives play through escaping enemies or avoiding failure.
A 'hafta' activity is done to avoid penalties such as fines, while a 'wanna' activity is done voluntarily with no penalty for skipping it.
Implicit motivation consists of spontaneous physiological processes, such as hormone release, that maintain homeostasis and cannot be directly controlled.
The power motive is an implicit drive to dominate or influence others.
The affiliation motive is an implicit drive toward close, harmonious relationships with others.
The achievement motive is an implicit drive to improve at a task.
Hunger is the belief that work can always be better, paired with a drive to keep improving regardless of outside standards or expectations.
Player experience goals describe the situations and feelings players should have, rather than the features that create them.
Motivation survey questions cover whether players look forward to goals, understand rewards, feel progress, have meaningful choices, and find the game more fun with others.
when: once critical systems exist

text: Adults often seek people who share their problems, teenagers often want different or more interesting peers, and children usually prefer friends from real life.
when: Designing social features for different age groups.

text: The OCEAN model helps capture individual needs.
Ten player types, adapted from Bartle's basic types, describe different motivations: competitor, explorer, collector, achiever, joker, artist, director, storyteller, performer, and craftsman.
No unified theory of motivation exists; motivation types include implicit, intrinsic, and extrinsic, linked to biological, learned, cognitive, and individual needs.
Self-Determination Theory is a common intrinsic motivation framework in game development, often applied superficially and rarely questioned.
A platformer with rising difficulty leans on competence, while a creative open-world sandbox leans on autonomy.
Relatedness is often served by multiplayer features, and meaningful non-playable characters can also satisfy it.
Motivation directs behavior in complex, hard-to-predict ways, and focusing on meaningful activities is central to it.
Puzzle design shares game design's goal of keeping the player in a pleasurably challenging flow state.
Fun is hard to define, yet most players ask for it and recognize it when they experience it.
Motivations build on one another and lie on a continuum, so extrinsic motivation is not automatically low-value.
why: Motivation grows from the person's true self to varying degrees.

text: A single game can address the whole hierarchy: a survival fantasy meets lower needs, while social play, mastery, and creation meet upper ones.
Pleasure seeking and pain avoidance are separate motivational circuits, not opposite ends of one scale.
Mental needs are more than desires; when they go unmet, they harm psychological health.
Games commonly satisfy all three mental needs by offering mastery, freedom in how to play, and social connection.
Self-attributed motives can be consciously controlled, whereas implicit motives run as body events that cannot be chosen directly.
Shared mammalian drives include hunger, thirst, sleep, pain avoidance, and sex, regulated mainly by the hypothalamus in the limbic system.
Play has intrinsic incentives, so simply playing is often the main motivator for players.
Meaning supports the needs for competence, autonomy, and relatedness.
Some theorists distinguish autonomous from controlled motivation rather than intrinsic from extrinsic motivation.
Motivation is the core engageability pillar, because no behavior or engagement happens without it, and emotion and game flow support it.
Behavior requires motivation; motivated people tend to focus more closely, handle challenges more capably and memorize material more effectively.
Some emotional triggers are fixed by genes, others are learned, and most involve interactions between conditioning and human nature.
Creative game developers are mostly motivated by wanting their output to matter to the world, and this drive comes from within rather than being purchased.
Game development is full of hard challenges, so designers need a strong drive to overcome them, and that drive is easy to misdirect toward work that does not help the game.
In the needs hierarchy, physiological and safety needs rank above self-actualization needs.
In platform-style games, short-term goals include defeating foes, gathering boosts, collecting coins and bonus lives, and reaching each stage's exit.
Player time is the most basic resource in any game; most games add currency, items, hit points, and mana on top of it.
Players are moral agents, but their choices are bounded by what the game rules allow.
Letting players express creativity, such as building a character, adds another dimension of fun.
Performance still matters in games, unlike most software, because players favor the game that pushes the hardware furthest.
why: Faster hardware has made performance a non-issue for most other software.

text: Players pursue their own goals, such as fun or exploration, and may ignore scripted goals; consider their true motivation, not only the goal the game sets.
when: A scripted goal conflicts with what players want to do
why: Players act on the reason they want a goal, so when that reason differs from the scripted objective, they skip the scripted step to pursue their own aim.

text: Check that your motivation comes from your own purpose rather than habit or outside pressure.
when: Early in developing a game, while the designer's own personal theme is still undefined.
why: When personal conviction and subconscious drive align, the work gains passion, focus and intensity.

text: Achievement and mastery in games correspond to the self-esteem level of the hierarchy, which many game activities provide.
why: Lower needs must be met before people pursue esteem-building goals, so mastery sits above safety and belonging in the hierarchy.

text: Activities that connect players with others serve the belonging level, while letting players build and express themselves serves the higher levels.
when: analyzing which needs a game's activities meet
why: Social connection satisfies the belonging need, while building and expressing oneself corresponds to the upper tiers of the needs hierarchy.

text: Psychological research on motivation closely matches what game designers need, so it is a valuable complement to design instinct.
why: Designers mostly build motivation through trial and gut feel, so evidence-based psychology fills a gap in their understanding.

text: Match fantasy powers to the emotional needs of the target audience, such as power over others for players who feel misunderstood.
when: Designing a power fantasy for a specific audience
why: Powers that address a felt need attract that audience

text: Satisfying the needs for competence, autonomy and relatedness makes tasks feel intrinsically rewarding, per self-determination theory.
The strongest novelty changes how players see a familiar world, rather than only adding new content to it.
why: Reinterpreting a familiar space through a new kind of interaction stretches thinking, which is rewarding.

text: Forced activity with weak rewards extends play briefly but causes resentment, and players who feel held hostage leave bitter and lose interest in sequels.
when: When the reward for forced, unwanted activity seems small relative to the time spent.
why: Players sense manipulation that wastes their time, so they leave resentful rather than anticipating a sequel.

text: The more an incentive controls a person, the more it tends to undermine intrinsic motivation.
why: Incentives that regulate behavior pressure people, which frustrates a basic psychological need and weakens inner drive.

text: Clear goals and rewards let players plan a strategy, such as building strength before attempting a harder challenge.
why: Defined goals with linked rewards give players a basis for planning ahead.

text: Insulting people to push them harder produces anger, which destroys creative capacity, and continued mistreatment produces helplessness that stops emotional investment in good work.
when: When leaders use insults or harsh treatment to drive output.
why: Anger and helplessness consume the energy and openness creative work needs.

text: Motivation depends on the reward value of a behavior for a need and on the probability of obtaining that reward.
when: Estimating how strongly a player will pursue a reward-producing action.
