why: Hull's 1943 account ties motivation to both value and probability.

text: Four interacting motivation types: implicit biology-based drives, environment-shaped learned drives, intrinsic cognitive-need drives, and personality-based individual needs, which together shape motivation.
why: No single theory covers all human behavior, so splitting motivation into interacting types gives a workable framework.

text: The Gamer Motivation Model, built from over 250,000 gamers, has six clusters: Action, Social, Mastery, Achievement, Immersion and Creativity, containing 12 distinct motivations.
why: Survey data from a large gamer sample grouped motivations into clusters.

text: The PENS model of player motivation is based on self-determination theory.

Each intrinsic motivator pairs with a matching loop and reward: agency with stat gain, mastery with difficulty, curiosity with discovery, closure with accomplishment, expression with cosmetics, connection with guilds, superiority with leaderboards, community with influence.
when: Designing progression around player motivations
why: Linking each motivator to a fitting loop keeps progression tied to what players already enjoy.

text: Motivations can be plotted on a matrix with internal versus external on one axis and 'hafta' versus 'wanna' on the other.
The motivation pillar blends inner drives such as mastery, self-direction and social connection with outer incentives: clear goals on short, medium and long timescales that carry meaningful rewards.
why: Because play is done for its own pleasure rather than as a means to something else, usability alone does not make a game worth playing.

text: The same contest is skill-based for participants and random for spectators, so whether it is luck depends on the observer's role.
when: Judging whether an activity is luck or skill
why: Participants control outcomes while spectators do not, so each sees different uncertainty.

text: Player ethics commitments cover inclusion, dark patterns, safety, children, localization, environment, and AI transparency.
Taking players' stated requests at face value can miss what would actually satisfy them.
when: Interpreting player feedback about what they want
why: Audiences often ask for one thing while seeking another, and hidden desires may go unnoticed

text: Obligations added gradually can slowly turn an activity players want to do into one they feel they have to do.
why: Players gradually shift from seeking enjoyment to avoiding the pain of losing something they have invested in.

text: Assuming all players want open-ended goals; some find them too loose and need clearer direction.
why: Some players find open-ended systems too loose to engage with, so preference varies across the audience.

text: With anonymous strangers or in competitive games, players' motivations rarely align with the narrative, so sustained rich roleplay is hard to arrange.
why: Getting each participant to commit to a role is very hard, while friends' social pressure encourages good-faith participation.

text: Treating fun as pleasure fails, since a meal or basking in sunshine is pleasurable yet rarely described as fun.
Assumptions about an audience can drive design choices, such as content that signals a narrow demographic, that deter other players from joining.
when: when designing for a presumed demographic
why: the design signals exclusion to players outside the assumed group

text: 1) List every motivation players have for playing the game. 2) Sort motivations by how internal or external they are. 3) Separate pleasure-seeking motivations from pain-avoiding ones. 4) Identify motivations that reinforce each other. 5) Identify motivations that conflict.
when: when analyzing what drives players in a game

text: 1) Choose a target player type and genre. 2) Answer the world-construction questions: how many interesting things to see; whether challenges are immediate or need practice; what action obstacles call for; whether other players are allies or obstacles; whether actions affect a larger narrative; what rules discourage bad behavior. 3) Use the answers as layout guidelines.
when: When laying out a multiplayer game space for a chosen player type and genre.
why: Player-profile domains map onto world-construction factors, so answers about the player indicate how to lay out the space.

text: 1) List the pleasures your game gives players and judge whether each can be improved. 2) List pleasures it lacks, find why, and decide whether to add them. 3) Check known pleasure lists against the game. 4) Look for unique, unclassified pleasures that could make the game stand out.
when: Evaluating a game's pleasure design
why: Comparing against known pleasures reveals gaps, and unclassified pleasures can give the game its distinct quality

text: Write survey and interview questions carefully and neutrally, since leading questions bias answers.
when: When writing questions for playtest surveys or interviews.
why: Word choice in a question can shift both estimates and recall, so a leading phrasing contaminates the data.

text: Meet basic needs such as food, safety, and healthy relationships before creative work, and curb dangerous appetites rather than feeding them.
when: when creative work stalls due to strong cravings or personal troubles
why: strong appetites and troubles make the subconscious obsess and block creative work; fed appetites grow

text: Show players their wins, losses and win percentage at the start of each game, so they see an accurate picture of their performance.
why: Without tracked stats players overestimate their win percentage, so showing actual figures corrects that perception.

text: Extrinsic rewards are effective when they contribute to competence, autonomy, and relatedness.
why: Satisfying those three psychological needs helps people find the task intrinsically rewarding.

text: In games, make the protagonist's goal the player's goal so it drives movement through the content.
when: When a game aims for a tightly integrated story with its challenges.
why: A shared goal gives the player a reason to progress

text: Recurring daily or weekly tasks paying out in-game currency can nudge players to log in regularly.
Prioritize players' best interests, including respect for their time and money, and define ethical lines for design.
Aim for a combination of core pleasures that complement each other and are clearly apparent to players, rather than including every type of challenge or play.
when: selecting which pleasures a game should offer
why: Cramming many pleasures dilutes each one and muddles the experience.

text: Pair motivation mechanisms with fulfilling experiences, since motivation alone can keep players playing without giving them anything they enjoy.
when: designing reward and retention systems
why: Motivation without fulfillment risks compulsive engagement without satisfaction.

text: Pleasure theory says people pursue what feels good, with dopamine carrying pleasure; but wanting and liking can split, so players may want what they do not enjoy.
when: analyzing why players keep playing
why: Motivation and enjoyment are distinct systems.

text: Awarding points for merely participating encourages attendance, but it weakens the link between points and performance.
when: when designing a points system for events
why: Counting attendance as points conflates experience with skill, so frequent but weak players can look like strong ones.

text: Pitch confidence means knowing all details, staying steady under hard questions, and believing the team suits the game. It is separate from passion.
when: Presenting a game to a publisher or funder
why: Confidence signals that the team can deliver, which listeners need to trust.

text: Music can comment on player actions positively to reward them, or negatively to punish them and steer their behavior.
Events falling within one perceptual cycle of about 100 ms are seen as a single moving object rather than separate static images.
Visual, aural, tactile and proprioceptive input combine into one sensation, so controller rumble and finger position both contribute to the game experience.
Visual, aural and tactile clues let players build a detailed mental model of how virtual objects behave.
Player experience can be modelled from three data sources: subjective self-reports, objective head movements from video, and gameplay features from logged actions.
Human decisions use information about one tenth of a second old, so events happening within roughly that window are effectively hidden from the decider.
why: Perception and processing take time, so the newest information has not yet entered the decision.

text: Per-room delivery cannot capture that a loud noise may be heard down a corridor while a gentle noise is inaudible a meter away.
when: sounds vary in loudness across distance
why: room membership ignores loudness and distance

text: Teach tutorial information through several senses used together and repeated, rather than through a single text channel.
when: When audio is available for delivering the tutorial.
why: Multimedia learning works by using multiple senses repeatedly.

text: Diegetic music feels closer to reality and can carry cultural meaning about time, place and listeners.
when: Choosing diegetic music for a game
why: Music sourced from the world ties it to the setting.

text: Deep listening goes beyond hearing words to attend to body language, facial expression, tone of voice, and gestures, and to what people mean beneath what they say.
Designer music increased caring, relaxation, clarity, and vigor, while lowering hostility, fatigue, sadness, and tension.
Presence depends on game feel, the look and feel of an experience, which developers often call immersion.
Players resent cutscenes that interrupt progress, feeling the designer takes control, and tolerate them more readily at natural breaks such as loading a level or opening a door.
when: when a cutscene interrupts play or when deciding when a cutscene should start
why: It removes the player's control at a moment they expected to act; interrupting action breaks the player's focus.

text: Griefers bar a path so others cannot reach their destination, a simple move that annoys other players.
why: A narrow passage can be fully obstructed by one player, which is why doorways are widened.

text: In free-form play, players treat each deck as a character with its own personality and quirks, and often give decks names.
when: during free-form, unstructured play

text: Players perceive an underlying goal when simple reactive rules combine, such as hunting enemies while retreating at low health.
when: simple behaviours respond to different needs at once
why: Combined reactions to different needs read as a single aim.

text: Some adult fans revisit a world only as an occasional mental break, using a physical object such as a display toy as a quick gateway back.
when: A fan who wants a short mental escape
why: The object works as a convenient cue that lets them step into the fictional world briefly.

text: Some devoted fans engage with a world every day, to the point of adopting its identity in their own lives.
Large persistent worlds with social obligations and multiyear goals can draw some players into self-destructive patterns.
when: a game has social obligations and long goals
why: Social ties and long-term goals make leaving costly

text: Players read NPC reactions to violence as a signal of how normal it is, so curious onlookers make events feel commonplace.
Many players in open narratives prefer gameplay over story and accept a disjointed narrative for total freedom.
why: Freedom is valued as a reward that outweighs narrative coherence for these players.

text: Players want to act on the world rather than passively watch or read, so time for text and non-interactive story is limited in many genres.
when: In genres where the narrative space for text and cutscenes is limited.
why: Players prefer interaction to passive consumption.

text: Overly long cutscenes cause players to disengage from the story.
With managed survival resources, the same space plays differently depending on the player's current health and supplies.
when: Games where game states change quickly, such as managing survival resources
why: A low-health player feels most vulnerable entering a space at a disadvantage, while a healthy player experiences the same space very differently.

text: In fast-paced games players tend to run toward the next fight, but an interesting visual asset or animation makes them stop.
when: in games with near-constant action
why: players are pulled forward by action unless something visual holds their attention

text: Narrative space is the amount of player time and attention available for story, which differs by genre and expands or contracts during play.
Presence is a felt sense of belonging inside a virtual environment, experienced subjectively.
An experience whose appeal rests mainly on presentation quality becomes dull when its performance is poor.
Presence in VR and AR is invisible, ephemeral and fragile, so it can be lost quietly as the design changes.
Presence can be measured with questionnaires, and presence has been linked to enjoyment.
Games that satisfy players' motivational needs allow better presence.
Non-player characters with social and emotional behaviour can trigger desired player experiences.
Players differ in preferred atmospheres, such as scary, intense or contemplative, so adaptation should not target difficulty alone.
Real head movement in VR stays comfortable and is a unique strength of the medium.
Narrative presence can occur without sensory immersion when player choices visibly change the story, as in some mobile games.
Combining objective observation with empathetic introspection reveals insights that a detached viewpoint cannot.
when: Understanding what an audience will enjoy
why: Feeling the experience from inside exposes what outside observation misses.

text: Narrative presence is strongest when player choices have real consequences.
Control and camera build physical presence, character design builds narrative presence, and all three together build emotional presence.
Because players experience the game through the player character, they feel more immersed in the setting, the narrative, and the decisions they face.
Narrative space contracts during intense moments, leaving little time for text or voice, and expands again after the fight ends.
when: during and after intense encounters
why: Players have little attention to spare mid-fight and more afterward.

text: Physical presence grows as the virtual body matches the player's real movements.
when: In VR with a first-person camera that tracks real head and body movement

text: A single reference to something outside the imagined world can destroy the player's immersion in it.
When players recognize a game's systems too well, they may dismiss areas built to create atmosphere.
why: Observant players notice that the vent rules contradict the threat, and that contradiction breaks the atmosphere the area was built to create.

text: Players take default options, so switching a default from opt-in to opt-out sharply raises participation; nudging changes defaults and presentation without removing choices.
when: When designers want players to take a certain action without being told exactly what to do
why: Least-resistance behavior makes defaults and obvious routes dominant; default bias keeps people with the preset option.

text: People expect a new technology to be life-changing, reject it when it is not, then use it for what it does well.
when: a new technology is announced
why: Inflated expectations are followed by disappointment before realistic use.

text: Players buy games partly because they are new, which creates constant pressure on designers to offer novelty.
why: Newness is a strong purchase motive

text: Players become more willing to pay for the last few units when they are close to a goal.
when: Players near completing an upgrade or set
why: Proximity to the goal raises the value of the remaining units.

text: Promising something new just ahead, such as on the next level, gives players a strong reason to keep going.
why: Players are natural explorers who are drawn to what is new, so an anticipated novelty pulls them onward.

text: Making a game too novel can alienate players who need familiar anchors to understand and enjoy it.
why: Successful games blend novelty with familiarity, and overly novel ones have often failed by arriving before players could follow.

text: Relying only on novelty can slow presence in the player's immediate space.
why: Familiar places let the brain fill in surrounding details without looking around, so presence builds quickly there.

text: Player-to-player commitments such as agreed meetups and repaid favors drive regular play, but imposed obligations feel like work and can cause avoidance-driven return and abandonment.
when: Designing player-to-player commitment systems favors commitments; obligations such as return deadlines or friend invitations added after pleasure-based rewards in free-to-play designs, or any required activity, shift players toward pain avoidance.
why: People feel obligated to honor promises and return favors, which strengthens community; play depends on freedom of choice, so felt obligation feels like work; avoidance keeps players returning after enjoyment fades.

text: Games demanding many parallel tasks at once, such as life and farm simulations, attract majority-female audiences.
why: The link rests on a stereotype that women keep many parallel tasks going without dropping any, which is what these games demand.

text: Observing an experience while it happens changes it, so activities such as watching yourself enjoy a movie or play a game tend to fade or falter.
when: Observing your own experience during play.
why: Attention on the activity itself disrupts it, a version of the Heisenberg problem.

text: Visible, noisy physical output invites onlookers even though reading over someone's shoulder is socially taboo.
when: when a device prints or displays output in a shared space
why: Printed paper and its noise attract attention that private screens do not.

text: Incidental characters may be on screen for seconds, while significant enemies can be visible for minutes.
Watching real players predicts their enjoyment better than imagining them, and the more you watch, the more accurate the prediction becomes.
why: Watching real play shows actual reactions that imagining a player cannot, and each additional observation sharpens the prediction.

text: Optional link-cable trading in a handheld game is used only occasionally, because most players mainly play alone.
when: A single-player handheld game with optional link trading

text: Small physical customizations, like marks players add to their character cards, prompt them to invent stories about how their characters got that way.
when: tabletop or offline games
why: Visible personal touches invite narrative and social conversation.

text: Once a game is on a major console storefront, many owners are likely to buy it.
when: when a game reaches a console storefront

text: Named units that survive while their squadmates die lead players to imagine bonds between them, making later orders to sacrifice one feel dreadful.
when: a named unit is ordered into a risky task
why: names make individual units feel personal

text: Players tear off and keep physical artifacts from play, and later share them with others, extending the experience beyond the session.
when: when an experience produces a tangible take-home object
why: A physical artifact carries the experience into the player's life.

text: Ownership is the personal investment that keeps players playing after they have mastered a mechanic; the industry often calls it replayability.
When players can express themselves meaningfully through a game, ownership forms; they then take pride in achievements and want to share them.
why: Expression through input produces identification with the game and its results.

text: Customizable homes, shops, and towns give players a sense of ownership and belonging, which encourages repeat visits and social exchange.
when: In games whose main mechanic is socializing, where players build homes that others can visit
why: Visiting one another's built spaces gives socializing a reason to happen and lets subcultures form around shared activities.

text: Perception is the brain's subjective construction that organizes raw sensory input into meaningful shapes, groups and patterns.
Inattentional blindness is failing to notice an unexpected but visible event while attention is focused elsewhere, including on one intensely concentrated task.
when: While concentrating intensely on one task.
why: Limited attention is consumed by the focused task.

text: Human senses extend beyond sight, hearing, touch, smell and taste to include temperature, pain, balance and the position of the body in space.
The brain is a fast, strong pattern recognizer that accepts false positives, sometimes perceiving patterns that are not there; this is why perceptual illusions exist.
When visuals conflict with motion and sound, players trust motion and sound and revise their belief about what the object is.
when: visuals contradict motion or sound
why: Motion outweighs the other cues in creating a sense of physicality.

text: Players notice a change of behavior more than the behavior itself, so characters should switch only when the situation clearly calls for it.
when: designing character behavior
why: A switch draws attention.

text: Players believe homing enemies with random sidesteps anticipate their shots, although the enemies do not always do so.
when: enemies that home in but sidestep at random intervals
why: Occasional unpredictable moves read as deliberate choice.

text: Camouflage hides a unit only against backgrounds it matches; the same colors become conspicuous against a contrasting background.
when: a camouflaged unit moves between different backgrounds
why: visibility depends on contrast with the background

text: Whether an activity feels like a 'wanna' or a 'hafta' depends on the person's attitude and penalties, not on the activity itself.
when: when some people enjoy an activity that others dread
why: Attitude and penalties determine whether the activity feels voluntary or obligatory.

text: Once clear, achievable goals exist, players mostly move toward places where they believe those goals can be met, so the world can be shaped around them.
when: Goals are clear and achievable
why: Players only go where they expect progress toward their goal, so the layout can steer them without explicit signposting.

text: Viewers who first see a rich, animated, colored version of a simple sprite-based character carry that image back and map it onto the small original.
when: After watching a high-fidelity adaptation of a low-fidelity game
why: The detailed mental image replaces the crude visuals, so the original's graphics matter less

text: Less visual detail lets audiences project into a character, while added detail makes alien, foreign, or frightening characters seem other.
when: Designing an avatar's appearance
why: Projection needs room to fill in, and detail signals difference

text: Playing a different role in a new reality with new rules often lets players see systems and relationships from a new perspective.
when: games that place players in another role or world
why: Games create realities with their own rules, so the player takes on a different viewpoint.

text: Listeners notice interrupted rhythms, unresolved chords and hanging melodies, so music that avoids these expectations makes intensity changes less noticeable.
when: Music that changes intensity during play
why: Clear pulse and tonality set expectations whose breaking draws attention to the change.

text: Players perceive space actively when exploring it through real-time control, and passively when only watching the same interactions.
A small object that hits hard feels heavy, and players are surprised when apparent size and impact contradict each other.
when: objects whose size and heft disagree

text: People perceive a situation against all of their prior experience, including attitudes, expectations and misconceptions, not only the immediate stimulus.
Inconsistency across senses stands out immediately, such as a character passing through a wall, because real perception never produces such mismatches.
when: When the player can freely explore every action and response in a game world
why: Players' perceptual skill is honed from birth, so even small mismatches stand out clearly.

text: Collisions with smooth response but no rebound or visible reaction leave players feeling the world is barren and empty at the tactile level.
when: collisions lack rebound and visible reaction
why: no tactile feedback is returned

text: An identifiably human figure lets players read states such as running, jumping or swimming, so reduced air control is accepted when the state change is visible.
when: a character's state changes affect control
why: Recognisable body language communicates the state, so players accept the change.

text: Players notice small inconsistencies in how objects look, sound or behave, because active perception is far more acute than passive perception.
when: When players actively interact with objects in the game world.
why: Active engagement makes players scrutinize how objects respond.

text: Prior exposure determines whether people recognize a familiar figure hidden in an ambiguous abstract image.
when: When viewing an ambiguous abstract image
why: Exposure primes the viewer to recognize the familiar form

text: Surrounding context sets expectations that change how an ambiguous glyph is read.
when: When a symbol is ambiguous and shown among other lines or shapes
why: Expectation from context selects one interpretation

text: People overestimate their ability to detect changes, a tendency called change blindness blindness.
when: When the element that changes is not the focus of attention

text: Players focused on a screen can miss real hazards, because attention filters what is perceived and inattentional blindness can occur.
when: When AR play happens in open, hazardous spaces such as traffic.
why: Attention is limited, so screen focus can hide the real environment.

text: Players accustomed to one genre's or platform's control and interface conventions expect the same conventions elsewhere, so perception is not universal.
when: when players move between genres or platforms
why: learned conventions shape expectations

text: An accidental event involving a visually distinctive character is read as deliberate, because the distinctive trait gives the character a recognizable identity.
when: a distinctive character causes an unplanned outcome
why: identity leads players to assign motive

text: Players use metagame knowledge in their decisions even though it is part of neither the mechanics nor the fiction.
The brain expects repeated experiences, and confirmed expectations feel pleasurable, so implied figures reinforce the player's mental model.
when: when a level implies forms through structural markers or echoing negative space
why: Confirmed expectations produce pleasure, according to one established account.

text: Looking down on the character from above can create a sense of vertigo.
when: When the camera looks down on a character in an open space with rhythmic vertical elements

text: A high place feels comfortable and advantageous when architecture stands between the occupant and the fall, and perilous when nothing does.
when: when a player stands at elevation
why: Physical barriers signal protection from falling.

text: The perceptual field is the player's constructed model of reality, built from experience, skills, concepts, misconceptions, system image, thoughts, feelings and generalizations, and updated as new experience arrives.
Apophenia is the human tendency to perceive patterns, and often intent, emotion or meaning, in complex, random or unmodeled data or events.
The perception window is the no-win situation where a sensible character action looks faulty to a brief observer who lacks the context behind it.
Contrast detectors respond to edges, lines and patches of change in the visual field.
The binocular effect: a close-up seen early is stored in memory, so imagination fills in distant figures afterward.
why: Viewers reuse a stored detailed image to interpret less detailed views.

text: People who lose proprioception can still move by watching their bodies and using subtle cues, and players do something similar with virtual objects.
Objects must be large enough to be resolved; a person can be resolved beyond half a mile but is unlikely to be noticed unless searched for.
Some wavelengths are not perceived because perceiving them would be useless or harmful, such as infrared, which the eye's own glow would blind us to.
why: Perception is shaped by usefulness, not by completeness.

text: Color categories are an artifact of the retina: the spectrum is a smooth gradient, yet people perceive distinct colors because that grouping is useful.
Mental models leave out things rarely needed, such as microscopic life, so people are unaware of much around them.
why: Models only include what matters for everyday action.

text: The five experiences describe what players feel, not the physiological and psychological processes behind them, which require studying human perception.
Perception is partly learned, and people build new distinctions and skills throughout life.
Perception is active: people learn to perceive largely by moving and exploring, not by passively receiving stimuli.
why: Kitten studies showed passive subjects failed to develop normal perception despite identical stimulation.

text: Players judge physical properties such as mass, friction and material by perception, not by measured physics values, so a very heavy object moving like a light one reads as light.
why: Perception is what the player experiences, and most physics properties cannot be perceived by sight, sound or touch.

text: Haptic feedback originated in aircraft to restore the tactile sense that servo-controlled flight controls removed from pilots.
Colorblindness, influenced by DNA, affects about 8% of cisgender men and 0.5% of cisgender women.
The multi-store model's components are functional rather than fixed brain regions, and they are not always cleanly separated.
Persistence of vision, which makes about 24 images per second look like continuous motion, reflects iconic memory.
Mind wandering and divided attention raise the risk of missing hazards, as in driving and in mixed reality interfaces that split attention.
Humans, even infants, expect solid objects not to pass through each other and objects not to fit into containers that are too small.
Because contrast sensitivity is a clinical vision measure, such gains could in principle help eyesight.
Later multimedia learning research holds that audio and video work better in tandem than either alone.
A game's internal state is more precise and mathematical than the world the player experiences, and the system is designed to produce an experience in the player's mind.
Context supplies meaning and a reference for scale, speed and weight, but appeal must be judged separately from that context.
Use the multi-store model as a coarse framework for locating where information is lost between perception and recall.
why: Its components are functional rather than physical and not strictly independent or serial, so it is a simplification.

text: Briefly flash a cue near where an enemy will appear to draw attention and prepare players to react quickly.
when: before an expected enemy appearance
why: attention is directed to the likely location

text: Partially revealed visuals draw players to explore: the brain completes partial visual information and seeks verification, creating curiosity.
when: when only part of a space is visible
why: the brain fills in partial images, driving curiosity

text: Objects are hard to see mainly because they lack contrast with their background, not because too little light reaches the eye.
when: When viewing objects in dim light or against a matching background
why: Camouflage removes contrast change between an object's edge and its background, so the object is not seen.

text: Distance from real-world problems through play helps players return and see those problems as smaller.
when: a player returns to real problems after play
why: Time away reduces the apparent size of problems

text: People construct information when they perceive and encode it, and reconstruct it when they remember it, so recall is not a faithful replay.
Access to knowledge lets people name what they perceive, which turns a raw pattern into a recognized thing.
why: Perception is often top-down, so a viewer's existing knowledge shapes how the input is interpreted.

text: Each new fact removes some options and reshapes which plans still make sense, so a death can invalidate a plan even when it was expected.
One polish effect can support several perceptions at once, such as overlapping armor motion suggesting both weight and material.
Image perception cycles take roughly 50 to 200 ms, varying with the person and circumstances.
A person with a still head has a sight cone of about 120 degrees vertically and 220 degrees horizontally; eye and neck movement can cover 360 degrees.
Alternating an image with an altered copy separated by a blank flicker of about 80 ms makes the change hard to spot without attention.
when: the changing element is not attended
why: the flicker masks the transient motion cue

text: During a brief occlusion, about half of people fail to notice a major change such as their conversation partner being swapped.
when: When a change occurs during a brief interruption, even to an element being attended to
why: attention is not on the changed element

text: Perception biases that distort players' view of randomness include selection, self-serving, attribution, Dunning–Kruger, anchoring, gambler's, and hot-hand effects.
The multi-store model divides memory into three components: sensory stores, a short-term store, and a long-term store.
Norman's three design levels are visceral (automatic emotional response), behavioral (pleasure and ease of use), and reflective (meaning, values, self-image and memories).
Five perception implications explain game feel: perception requires action; perception is whole-body; senses fuse effortlessly; perception is ongoing skill-building; and perception extends to tools.
Avoiding uncomfortable information, the ostrich effect, distorts decisions by hiding evidence that contradicts what you want to believe.
Assuming people see the world as it physically is, rather than a mental representation shaped by experience.
why: Sensory input is organized into meaningful shapes by pattern matching, which sometimes misfires and produces errors.

text: When players do not feel their contribution matters, their motivation drops.
when: contributions have no visible effect
why: effort without perceived impact feels pointless

text: Treating processing stages as separate compartments or as strict sequences oversimplifies how the brain works.
why: The stages interact, and the brain does not process information like a computer.

text: Drawing attention to the opposite area before an event is likely to slow the player's reaction.
when: Right before an enemy enters the scene, when a cue appears in the opposite corner of the screen
why: A cue placed elsewhere pulls attention away from where the event will occur, so players are not prepared to react.

text: 1) Adopt the player's physical viewpoint, such as crouching to see at a child's eye height. 2) Adopt the player's mental viewpoint, trying to see, hear, and think as the player does. 3) Repeat this regularly during design.
when: Designing for a target audience
why: Designers drift toward their own high-level viewpoint, so projection into the player's perspective must be actively maintained

text: Treat perception as a subjective construct of the mind and plan around it as the main limitation in game design.
why: Players' prior knowledge and expectations shape what they perceive, so designers must anticipate those differences.

text: Account for visual imagery effects such as mental rotation and for the Weber-Fechner bias when designing.
Measure context effects by comparing the feel of the same game across different contexts.
why: The effect is a general impression of space that cannot be quantified directly.

text: Before tuning, identify the preconceptions about movement that the chosen representation brings with it.
why: The representation shapes what players expect an object's movement and interactions to be.

text: Proprioception is the mind's sense of where the body is in space and how it is positioned, letting a person touch their nose with eyes closed.
A character's perceived speed depends on the speed of other characters on screen, so a slow character seems ponderous next to a faster one.
when: Characters with different movement speeds appear together.
why: Perceived speed is relative to nearby moving objects.

text: The processors are abstractions, not literal brain structures, but they let designers attach numbers to an interactivity diagram.
Touching is primal behavior animals have practiced for hundreds of millions of years, while tool use is relatively recent and relies on higher brain function.
No scientific evidence shows that either sex is prewired for language or for math and spatial tasks.
The more a game engages primal brain functions, the more intuitive and powerful it tends to feel.
why: Older brain layers handle touch-like activity directly, while tool use relies on higher neocortical processing.

text: To judge whether an activity is primal, ask whether animals can do it; this is a practical substitute for brain-region research.
when: When brain-imaging research on an activity is not available to the designer
why: Activities animals can perform tend to rely on low-level, primal brain processing, so they serve as a rough proxy.

text: Proprioception lets players reconcile hand position with on-screen results, so they ease off an input when movement proves too fast.
why: The physical position of the hand on the input device gives feedback that players compare against on-screen motion.

text: Spray timing and intensity can change perceived mass while the underlying collision simulation stays the same.
when: Adjusting the feel of a collision
why: Polish cues are read as evidence of mass, independent of the simulation.

text: Nominal cycle times: perceptual about 100 ms (range 50–200), cognitive about 70 ms (range 30–100), motor about 70 ms (range 25–170).
why: The values are aggregated from many separate studies of human reaction and response.

text: Play is driven by curious questions, such as what a control does, whether a team can win, or what lies past the end of a level.
why: Players act to answer questions they care about

text: Discovery encourages audiences to visit a world through many different gateways.
when: A world offers new parts to discover
why: A world built around discovery invites entry points from many different directions.

text: In Discovery, the player learns that a problem exists and how large its scope is.
when: At the start of each individual challenge or puzzle in a progression system
why: Players must recognize a problem before they can invest effort in it.

text: Discovery brings pleasure, and that pleasure motivates players to behave efficiently.
Designers can shape the environment to stimulate intrinsic motivation and use feedback, rewards, and punishments, but cannot control biology, mood, or personal needs.
One event can be both intrinsic and extrinsic: gaining a skill point can signal growing competence and can also be spent.
Curiosity is useful to consider when judging inherent interest.
A curious mind may become one of the most valuable personal assets in coming decades.
It is unknown whether curiosity is innate or can be taught and strengthened; if it can be nurtured, it should be a top educational priority.
when: planning education
why: Curiosity may drive learning outcomes

text: Pleasure seeking and pain avoidance are both valid and can work well when used together in one game.
Most people want to be helpful, so framing player goals as helping someone channels their behavior into engaging play.
Games create displeasure through failed challenges and lost resources, so they need motivation to keep players from quitting at the first setback.
why: Anticipated rewards drive players past setbacks; without that drive, a single failure would end play.

text: Players expect a designer to lead them toward a better world; when they stop caring about new games, they have lost faith that the designer knows the way.
why: Players expect new games to deliver worlds better than this one, so disengagement signals lost trust.

text: Players' perception of fairness matters more than the design's actual fairness, so design for how fair the game feels.
why: perception is a construct of the brain

text: Four MMO player types, originally proposed for multi-user dungeon games: achievers seek challenge in reaching goals; explorers seek discovery of breadth; socializers seek fellowship; killers seek competition and defeating others.
Explorers are curious, enjoy adventuring, want to see everything, map the world, experiment with mechanics, and seek the outer boundaries of the game world, physical or mental.
Use group-level player models to widen supported motivations, not to sort players into rigid boxes; account for individual differences in needs and implicit motives.
when: When the game is not deliberately aimed at one narrow population with specific motives.
why: generalizations can exclude people if applied rigidly

text: 1) Interview players and learn as much as possible about them. 2) Place yourself in their position and imagine how the experience feels, including what they feel while choosing and what they will later tell friends about the high points.
when: Designing for a particular audience or when setting experience goals
why: Combining player accounts with imagined perspective reveals insights a detached view misses.

text: Players approach the same level in very different ways, such as stealthy, fast, or exploratory, so one adaptive music system may not suit all of them.
when: When a level supports multiple play approaches.
why: Each style produces different time spent, pacing, and exposure to the music.

text: Very fast tutorial finishers may have found a shortcut or exploit, or skipped dialogue and missed core mechanics.
when: Tutorial completion timing with a few very quick players.
why: Skipping content shortens time without learning the game.

text: In the same playtests, many girls defended their own ship against invaders rather than hunting targets, and enjoyed the game without any assumed interest in battle.
when: combat games played by mixed audiences

text: Men played much like boys but more reservedly, often carefully working out the optimal approach before acting.
when: combat games played by mixed audiences

text: Adults tend to seek friends with similar interests, while children prefer to play with real-life friends.
when: choosing play partners
why: Adults want partners who can understand their problems, while children have little interest in strangers and prefer friends they already know.

text: Masocore games, which are punishing and built around repeated failure, rose in response to accessible designs, showing that players also seek deliberately hard challenge.
when: When accessibility has become the norm in a market
why: Swings in preference push designers toward the opposite extreme

text: Its severity depends on personality: some experts want to win even if others lose out, some timid players want a trusted leader, and some players prefer to take only their own turn.
when: When assessing commander problem risk in a group
why: Player temperament shapes whether someone takes over or defers

text: Players of masocore games expect to fail early and often and succeed rarely, only after mastering the game's details.
when: Designing a masocore game with heavy difficulty
why: Heavy difficulty is the core appeal for this audience.

text: Even when rules reward attacks, players still turtle in defensible areas, but they must eventually expand or fall behind.
when: when a safe, defensible region exists
why: defensible spots feel safe until rules penalize waiting

text: Even experienced players in a genre misjudge unfamiliar rules and keep dying to the same hidden threat.
when: when a game's rules differ from familiar genre conventions

text: Experienced players may cling to set habits and miss innovative strategies.
when: When playtesters are experienced with the game and have fixed ideas about its units.
why: Set opinions about how units should be used keep them from noticing new ways of playing.

text: A model learned from one player's choice habits can improve play against a different player, because human choice habits share common traits.
when: When an opponent needs to guess which passage, weapon, route or cover point a player will pick.
why: People cannot randomize their choices well, and deep shared traits let one player's habits be predicted without watching that same player.

text: Adults aged 35 to 50 are mostly casual players dominated by career and family, and they often make expensive purchases seeking games the whole family can enjoy together.
when: Designing for adults aged 35 to 50
why: Career and family demands dominate, and this group controls large purchases for shared household play

text: Adults aged 50 and older suddenly gain free time as children leave and retirement approaches, and they favor social experiences and return to games from their youth.
when: Designing for players aged 50 and older
why: Children leaving and retirement free up time, and this group values social play

text: Around age seven, children start school, read, solve harder problems, and begin choosing their own toys and games instead of accepting parental choices.
when: Designing games for children around age seven and older
why: Reading and harder problem solving open up more complex play, and children gain autonomy over their choices

text: People are natural explorers drawn to what is new, which is why novel products often attract more attention than familiar ones.
why: Classics get shelved while new releases sell, showing that newness outweighs proven quality in drawing interest.

text: Players perceive skill-based games as more serious than chance-based games.
when: Judging the tone a game's mechanics convey
why: Skill signals judgment and seriousness while chance signals casual risk-taking

text: The same content can be engaging to one player type and dull to another, so interest curves differ by player type.
when: when a game serves several player types

text: Sickness triggers vary greatly between people, and one bad experience can create an aversion that keeps a player away from a game for years.
Playing reveals how people solve problems, decide under stress, show mercy or betray others, and whom to trust, while conversation tends to be filtered toward what listeners want to hear.
when: When people play a game together rather than just talking with each other.
why: Actions in play are less filtered than spoken words.

text: Playing also reveals players to themselves: whether they let others win or crush them, how they handle public defeat, whom they pick as teammates, and whom they imitate.
when: When players are with others rather than playing alone.

text: Players find probing an unfamiliar virtual world with a virtual instrument very pleasurable.
when: When a player explores an unfamiliar virtual world governed by different rules and physics.
why: Active exploration engages perception more than passive viewing.

text: First-time fighting game players often mash buttons randomly until patterns emerge.
when: Players unfamiliar with a complex input scheme.
why: Results are not yet predictable.

text: Experienced players can more easily follow a relevant threat amid heavy effects and sound than occasional players.
when: busy scenes with explosions and sound effects
why: experience improves filtering of irrelevant input

text: Players usually have a primary play style and switch to other styles only when it suits them.
when: When a switch to another play style would serve the player's purposes.

text: Nonconformist responses in a group may reflect attitudes toward the social setting rather than toward the idea itself.
when: When interpreting dissenting focus group responses
why: Group discussion pushes attitudes toward extremes, so a dissenting voice may reflect the group dynamic instead of the content under discussion.

text: Players rotate between playstyles within a single session.
when: In games that offer several of the four fun types within a session.

text: Players keep playing as they age; about 40% of PC gamers are over 36.
why: Generations who grew up with digital games kept playing into adulthood.

text: Feeling competent may lead people with strong visuo-spatial skills to play action games more, an alternative explanation for correlations.
when: when interpreting correlations between game play and skill
why: Skill can drive play choices, not only result from play.

text: Experts use every degree of a continuous input to optimize results, while novices succeed using only the extremes.
when: a mechanic offers a continuous input range
why: Skilled players extract precision from the full range; casual players need only coarse control.

text: Personality labels with backstory can lead players to blame a loss on a leader's personal attachments rather than on his stats.
when: a leader with a personality label loses a battle
why: the label offers a personal explanation for the outcome

text: Performance on a hard test dropped for a group when they were primed with a negative stereotype about their group, and recovered when told the group performs equally.
when: Evaluating people on demanding tasks where a group stereotype exists.
why: Expectations about one's group shape how well one performs under pressure.

text: Killers, often called griefers today, enjoy ruining other players' experiences through attacks, looting bodies or abusive chat.
A competitor plays to beat other players, regardless of the game.
A collector acquires items, trophies, or knowledge and enjoys building sets and organizing history.
An achiever plays for levels of achievement; ladders and levels reward this type.
A joker plays for fun and does not take the game too seriously; jokers can annoy serious players but can also make a game more social than competitive.
An artist is driven by creativity, creation, and design.
A director likes to be in charge and to direct the play.
A storyteller loves to create or live in fantasy worlds.
A performer enjoys entertaining audiences.
A craftsman wants to build, engineer, or puzzle things out.
Player personality mapping classifies players by personality type and links each type to design choices.
why: types guide what a game should offer

text: Psychographics group players by how they think and what they enjoy, rather than by external traits.
Lifestyle psychographics tie players to concrete activities or identities, such as a dog lover or a hardcore shooter player.
Pleasure-based psychographics classify the kinds of pleasure people seek, since much human action traces back to pleasure seeking.
Play is best recognized by the attitude of doing an activity for its own sake, which matters more than the activity itself.
why: People play because they like to

text: Hardcore and casual labels hinge on whether someone considers themselves a gamer rather than on hours played, and the line between them is fuzzy.
The perceptual self is a person's self-image within their perceptual field, and actions that do not serve the body can still strengthen it.
Serious Fun is play with a purpose, such as changing behavior or doing real work; People Fun comes from cooperating, competing, and communicating with others.
Newbie ambition is an over-scoped proposal whose features exceed what the schedule and budget allow; it is a common reason outside ideas are dismissed.
OCEAN predicts behavior imperfectly and does not explain all personality; MBTI is not scientifically validated and should not guide important decisions such as hiring.
The Big Five (OCEAN), found by factor analysis and tested across populations and decades, is the most robust personality model: useful for understanding differences, not predicting behavior.
when: Thinking about personality differences
why: It is useful for understanding differences but not for prediction

text: A survey of over 140,000 gamers found three clusters: Action-Social, loosely linked to extraversion; Mastery-Achievement, to conscientiousness; Immersion-Creativity, to openness; neuroticism and agreeableness showed no link.
when: Interpreting exploratory gamer clusters
why: These mappings are exploratory, not predictive

text: Average brain imaging differences between sexes exist, but overlap is large: variation within each sex is usually larger than the difference between the sexes.
Expert players often need more challenge than casual players to stay within their flow zone.
Many questionnaires claim to measure player traits or motivations, yet little evidence shows that they measure what they claim.
No current player model reliably predicts how a given type of player will behave in a specific game.
Men and women now play digital games in roughly equal numbers.
Playfulness is a state of mind, so even serious subjects can be approached playfully.
Self-esteem is the level of Maslow's hierarchy most closely connected to games, since people deeply need to know how they stack up against others.
Generational labels such as digital natives do not imply cognitive or behavioral differences; all humans share the same attention limitations, and Millennials are not better at multitasking.
why: Different environments produce slightly different wiring, not generation-level cognitive gaps.

text: Genetics and epigenetics, meaning how experience changes gene expression, influence how people process information.
People differ in aptitudes, but tailoring teaching to a learning style does not enhance learning.
Individuals perceive the same input differently because of prior knowledge, expectations, culture, genetics and environment.
The dark tetrad traits (Machiavellianism, narcissism, psychopathy, sadism) were linked to the competition motive in gamers, with sadism possibly indirectly tied to problematic gaming.
Differences between people reflect how well their competence, autonomy, and relatedness needs are satisfied or thwarted.
Rank-based questionnaires reduce self-report bias but do not remove it, so physiological, behavioural and implicit measures can triangulate player reports.
Even games with no goals need a minimum skill level, such as reading, mouse control, and understanding interface windows and buttons, before players can engage meaningfully.
Combat can occupy a minority of play, such as a third of the game, while management systems take the rest.
Community seniors showed improvement in subsyndromal depression after three months of playing a motion-based sports game.
Designers should know players better than they know themselves, through deep listening to thoughts, emotions, fears and desires, since unhappy players mean the game has failed.
when: Designing for a target audience
why: Players often cannot state what they will enjoy, and the game must satisfy the people who play it.

text: In random groups, assume all four Bartle player types are present with no shared preference for narrative.
when: random groups
why: Random members are not selected for shared tastes.

text: Examining the pleasures of each play type helps set player experience goals for a system, and choosing which types to emphasize shapes the kind of pleasure a game offers.
when: When setting player experience goals for a game system.
why: Naming the specific pleasures tied to each type of play lets designers talk precisely about the experience a system should deliver.

text: Exact ordinal ranks are most useful for the top few percent of players, for whom being ranked by number is itself a milestone.
when: when a player is among the top few percent
why: Being given an exact place is itself an achievement for elite players, and a bare rank reveals little about the total size of the player pool.

text: Online personalisation assumes a player's style largely persists across consecutive sessions, so the previous level's behaviour predicts the next.
when: When generating a player's next level online from the playing style recorded during the previous level.

text: Personality elements connect to domains of play through concerns: openness to entering a game, task approach, solo versus group play, narrative interest, and event sensitivity.
The outcome of gaming depends on the player's motivation to play and on the social and economic setting.
Player types differ in what they act on: achievers act on the world, explorers interact with the world, socializers interact with players, and killers act on players.
Five commonly observed male play tendencies are mastery, competition, destruction, spatial puzzles, and trial and error.
Designers effectively create three games for newbies, players and elders, and each level needs its own kind of support.

Big Five (OCEAN) traits are openness (inventive versus practical), conscientiousness (organized versus spontaneous), extraversion (outgoing versus reserved), agreeableness (trusting versus suspicious), and neuroticism (anxious versus stable).
Extended player-type models use five personality traits and five play domains (novelty, challenge, stimulation, harmony and threat), with threat scored separately to form a 4 × 4 grid.
The killer category is loosely defined and does not map cleanly onto other player-type taxonomies; it also covers players who mainly want to help others.
why: Its members seek a mix of competitive and destructive pleasures, which another taxonomy's categories do not capture.

text: Predicting a player's behavior from a fixed type label can cause teams to overlook players the model does not describe.
when: When using player-type models to predict behaviour or sort players, rather than to inspire design.
why: No current motivation model reliably predicts how a given player type will act in a specific game.

text: The same controls can feel excellent to an expert and terrible to a novice, so feel disputes may be unresolvable because each side is correct about its own experience.
Many people with minor gifts achieve little because they lack the major gift; relying on innate talent alone rarely leads to great work.
when: Assessing your own potential
why: Without love of the work, practice is not sustained.

text: Assuming the games you personally like best match what the broader market likes is a common mistake.
when: judging market potential from personal taste
why: Personal preferences are not representative of most players

text: The overconfidence effect can still impair expert judgment even when intuition is well trained.
Treating girls' games as one fashion, shopping, and makeup genre for ages 6 to 10 misreads a broad and diverse market.
why: Weak sales of a few clone titles were generalised into a belief that girls don't play games.

text: Popular brain-labeled articles and neuro-branded products often present false or grossly simplified claims, which can seem convincing because they are easier to accept than complex explanations.
when: evaluating brain-related claims about games or marketing
why: Simple narratives promise effortless results and are more appealing than evidence-based explanations.

text: 1) Choose an MMO with distinct classes and list each class's role, play style and optimization strategies. 2) For each class, decide which player types it appeals to and why. 3) If none fit, name the player type it does suit.
when: When analysing an MMO that has distinct character classes.

text: Do not rely on surface changes like pink packaging to attract female players; design from research into what that audience wants, since today's female audience is discerning and technically savvy.
when: When developing a title aimed at the female market.
why: Discerning players reject titles that miss what they want

text: Understand who players are, what they are familiar with, what they expect, and the limits of the human body and mind.
why: Designing around the people who will use the product means solving their actual problems, which requires knowing them.

text: Make players of the target audience feel welcome, defining that audience by the games they already like.

when: repeated choices with win or loss feedback
why: Recent outcomes bias the perceived value of options.

text: Players assume a newly found item works like a familiar one that was introduced through the same reward pattern.
when: after an interaction has been learned and rewarded
why: Players generalize from a known interaction to similar new objects.

text: Repetition builds player expectations, so a rhythm can be taught as well as felt.
Through repeated play, players map each action to its sound, and that mapping teaches them how to play.
when: When enemies or events each have a distinct, recognizable sound effect.
why: Event-driven sound is repeatable, so repeating an action brings back the same audio cue.

text: Overflow is a state in which the player is overwhelmed by decisions, while flow gaps cause boredom.
Skill is an acquired, coordinated motor pattern that turns intent into results; measuring skill means measuring how efficiently intent becomes results.
An instinct is a built-in fixed behavior, such as eating or sleeping, that acts as a fixed input-output pair and can never be completely forgotten.
when: Designing creatures that learn from the player.

text: Skill is the mechanic that concerns what the player must be able to do, so it shifts the focus onto the player.
Player skill is the real ability to make good decisions, and more of it makes challenges feel easier.
why: Decision quality is the player's own contribution to difficulty.

text: The skill barrier is the minimum skill needed before a game becomes playable.
Manual reinvention is moment-to-moment mechanical skill, such as aiming, placing pieces, or moving units, and every game starts here.
Procedural literacy is a player's familiarity with a game's rules and how they work within an established possibility space.
In the slope of enlightenment, people and businesses work out where the technology is actually useful.
Tacit skill built through years of practice cannot be fully transferred to a leader through instructions.
Objectively, skill always improves, but subjectively controls alternate between clumsy and intuitive depending on the challenge at hand.
Games can help people transform into their ideal selves in mind, body and spirit; this is difficult to deliver, yet demand for it is strong.
A clear majority of people rate themselves as above average at common everyday skills, such as driving.
Differences in science or language performance are more likely due to practice, cultural environment, stereotypes and social pressure than to brain wiring.
Practice strongly improves both multitasking and single-task performance.
Training on a falling-block puzzle game improved spatial ability, such as mental rotation speed, in late adolescents and young adults.
Skill is not a single quantity: games reward strategic thinking, reaction speed, pattern execution, or social reading, and each kind has its own skill cap.
when: Evaluating the skill demands of a game
why: Different skill kinds cannot be scored on one scale.

text: Expertise can be formal, such as what makes a rule set elegant, or about players, such as what they find challenging, fun or boring.
Distribute learning over time, and repeat important information with reminders, because compressing learning into one session ignores the spacing effect.
when: Designing teaching and onboarding schedules.
why: Spaced repetition strengthens long-term retention.

text: Build skills through repeated practice rather than explanation, since skills are stored implicitly and tend to persist.
when: when players must acquire a skill
why: implicit learning is more durable than explicit learning

text: When options have about equal cost and benefit, people follow instinct rather than calculate.
when: when options are roughly equal in cost and benefit
why: calculation is costly given limited attention and working memory

text: Advanced AI techniques work like a spice: useful in small amounts and harmful when overused.
when: When a design stacks many exotic AI techniques such as neural networks, sense management, steering pipelines, or expert systems
why: Simple techniques carry most of the work, so exotic ones only help when kept to a few targeted uses.

text: Learning perceives a stimulus and ends in a brain-plasticity synaptic change storing memory; attention strength largely sets memory strength, and motivation and emotion also affect learning.
Skills grow through practice like muscles, so a person with the major gift can eventually match or exceed someone who has only the minor gift.
when: Comparing talent with sustained practice
why: Practice compounds, while innate ease does not grow by itself.

text: Permadeath erases the save, so each death teaches what to avoid and the player reaches a little further next time.
when: In permadeath games where a death deletes the save and the player restarts from scratch
why: Each death exposes the exact way the player failed, so they reflect on it and avoid that mistake next time.

text: When a player's skill rises, the same challenge becomes boring, and flow returns only if the challenge is raised or the player quits.
when: When a practiced player's skill outgrows a fixed challenge they once found right
why: Boredom and anxiety are unpleasant, which pushes the player to seek flow again.

text: Deep, layered mechanics keep skill rising, with jumps when players grasp a new way of thinking.
when: When a game's mechanics are deep and layered, with many interacting strategies
why: Mastering the basics unlocks more abstract views of the game, so skill keeps climbing with occasional jumps.

text: Shallow games or games with heavy luck show a short skill rise followed by a plateau.
when: In a shallow game or one with a significant luck component
why: Little depth to master, so skill stops growing quickly.

text: Repeated reward, punishment and memory of an experience form learned drives that shape behavior efficiently through implicit systems.
when: A player repeatedly experiences rewarding or aversive outcomes from the same activity.
why: The amygdala and hippocampus store whether a stimulus was rewarding or aversive, so it is approached or avoided on later encounters.

text: A broad range of possibilities keeps a game challenging long after players master its rules.
when: In a game whose simple objects keep changing relationships and produce a very varied possibility set
why: The combination of simple behaviors and shifting relationships keeps the space of possibilities large.

text: Practice moves an action from effortful, conscious movement to automatic, concrete movement, freeing attention for other things.
when: When an action is repeated in practice until it becomes familiar
why: Repeated practice moves neural pathways toward automatic processing, away from conscious thought.

text: Forgotten mechanics, controls, or objectives open a gap between player skill and challenge, which can make players feel less capable.
when: When players return to a game after time away from it
why: Memory fades during the break, so skill and the challenge level drift apart.

text: Play can extend a learner's zone of proximal development, so the skills a child can reach with support expand over time.
when: When play is designed around a child's current challenge range.
why: Play is a means of extending the zone of proximal development, so children develop skills beyond what they reach unaided.

text: Programming and debugging a computer encourages learners to think about their own thinking and to discover rules through trial and error.
why: Iterative trial and error while pursuing goals makes learners reflect on their own reasoning.

text: Learning feels good because lessons tied to human values, such as survival or reproduction, are inherently rewarding.
when: When a lesson is important to a human value such as survival or reproduction
why: Play practices skills that helped ancestors survive and reproduce.

text: When a player's largest decisions become nondecisions, nothing new enters the mind, flow becomes impossible, and the player tends to leave.
when: When a player's largest decisions become nondecisions for them
why: With no fresh input for the mind to take in, the player's flow breaks down.

text: Once a symbol is established as a reward marker, players learn to look for it wherever it appears.
when: after the symbol has been repeatedly associated with rewards
why: players learn the association and search for the marker

text: Once players learn a symbol's meaning, they can interpret small variations of it.
when: After players have been taught how game symbols, sounds, or objects correspond to gameplay
why: Internalized symbolic systems let players decode variations of patterns they already recognize.

text: Asymmetry can equalize challenge when opponents differ greatly in skill, such as a human facing computer-controlled opponents.
when: When opponents differ greatly in skill, especially when they are computer-controlled
why: Adding more computer opponents offsets a human's edge at outwitting a single AI opponent.

text: Games built only on mastery lose novelty over time, so they need new weapons, enemies or levels, or players grow bored.
when: When the game is built only around mastery of its gameplay
why: Mastery alone has an endpoint, after which novelty must come from new content or players tire.

text: Final margins carry skill information: a decisive win, such as ending well ahead, reflects more skill than a narrow win, so margins can inform ratings and point spreads.
when: Measuring match results beyond win or loss.
why: Larger margins show a larger skill gap.

text: Games that do not let players feel growing mastery may foster antisocial behavior.
when: designing progression systems
why: Feeling incompetent, according to self-determination theory, is linked to more aggressive thinking and conduct.

text: Art paired with procedural behavior lets players build strong associations, so objects act as symbols of their mechanics rather than decoration.
when: when art and scripted behavior are consistently matched
why: Consistent pairing turns visual cues into predictions about what the object does.

text: Perceived challenge equals (virtual challenge plus skill challenge) minus (virtual skill plus player skill); plotting it over a playthrough gives the difficulty curve.
when: analyzing difficulty across a playthrough
why: The formula captures how challenge and capability combine to set felt difficulty.

text: Model-based approaches rely on a theoretical framework mapping game context and responses to experience; model-free approaches learn an unknown function without assuming its structure; hybrids lie between the two ends.
Solo developers find it hard to see their own weaknesses, so evaluating your own project alone is unreliable.
when: When handing a design plan out for outside feedback
why: Comparing your own strengths and weaknesses with an open-minded reviewer's assessment shows what you missed.

text: Learned impotence leaves players with unpredictable and tedious recovery gameplay, since they cannot know the real effect of their feedback.
when: A taught creature has become incapable of sensible behavior.
why: Players cannot foresee how their feedback will change the creature, making recovery unpredictable and tedious.

text: Assuming a learned skill is never forgotten. Implicit skills fade with disuse, so returning players must retrain their muscle memory.
Expecting players to master a hard skill after a short tutorial; mastery takes time and repeated trials.
Many brain training and educational games only improve performance on the exercises themselves, which is not transfer.
when: when evaluating brain training or educational games
why: Improvement on the trained task does not show skill carried to new tasks.

text: Adding more symbols to a rock-paper-scissors structure, such as lizard and an extra gesture, adds no new equilibrium structure or decision interest, only fiction and learning burden.
why: The interest comes from predicting an opponent's choices, which extra symbols do not add to.

text: 1) Talk while keeping your head still. 2) Talk while turning your head often. 3) Compare how each version feels.
when: When learning to recognize status through body language
why: Status is relative to the other people in a scene rather than fixed to one individual, so small body behaviours shift it.

text: 1) Listen and write down every sound you hear. 2) Compare the list with someone else's. 3) Map each sound on a diagram, with circle size showing relative volume. 4) Record the sounds for reference.
when: training sound design listening skill
why: builds awareness of the layers of real environments

text: Check whether player skill grows at the intended rate, and change what drives growth if it does not.
Reduce cognitive load on tasks where the designer does not want to challenge players.
when: When tasks are not meant to challenge players, or when players must learn an important mechanic or system
why: Attention is scarce and divided attention works poorly, so extra load overwhelms players and hampers learning.

text: Listening is the most important designer skill; creativity ranks second, ahead of critical thinking, logic, and communication.
when: Prioritizing skills to develop
why: Designers must understand people before making things for them.

text: Game designers need to grasp the essence of how people experience play, beyond only the tangible components.
when: Designing any game
why: Creating experiences is the core task of game design.

text: Once players learn how a trainable creature works, they can manipulate it, but the feeling of teaching a real creature is lost.
when: after players learn the creature's internal workings
why: Understanding how the creature works lets the player manipulate it directly, which removes the feeling of teaching a real creature.

text: Model-based approaches build components ad hoc without machine learning, while model-free approaches learn the mapping; optimising model-based parameters through empirical studies moves them toward model-free.
why: Tuning model parameters requires empirical data, and that data-driven step is what moves a model-based approach toward model-free.

text: Enthusiast players perceive differences in flavor, texture and feel between driving games that casual players often miss.
when: When comparing driving games for feel, mechanics, or handling
why: People have a lot of real-world experience of cars to compare against, which makes them sensitive to driving feel.

text: Fans of a licensed property often know its source material better than developers do, and they will notice nearly any detail placed in the game.
when: licensed or established-fanbase properties
why: Fans are more engaged and remember every detail.

text: Event passing is the natural choice when a character's perception must be simulated in more detail.
Extraversion may correlate with social play in games, though this association needs replication.
Fan conclusions about hidden content may be wrong, yet any content placed in the game can be found, even when deeply buried.
Supporting only meeting and early friendship lets bonds fade, because players cannot find each other again.
when: When players must keep friendships going after their first meetings
why: Without community support for the later phases of a friendship, players drift away from the game.

text: Players who believe others can cheat feel like chumps, and many stop playing even if no one cheats.
when: a game is perceived as cheatable
why: they feel like chumps

text: People form strong emotional bonds with chatbots and disclose sensitive information to them, even simple early ones.
when: When people converse with a chatbot.
why: Conversational interfaces invite personal disclosure.

text: Antisocial behavior in online multiplayer games includes discrimination, trash talk, bullying, and trolling.
when: online multiplayer play

text: A simple audio phone call also creates a sense of being in a social space with another person.
A game's communication system can change how players treat each other; a menu-based chat with mostly supportive phrases encouraged polite, cooperative behavior.
when: Online games where chat is restricted to predefined options.
why: Limiting expressible phrases steers social conduct, even reducing trash talk common in competitive communities.

text: Cheating against or among other players breaches the social contract and draws shaming from others, while cheating alone mainly harms only the cheater.
when: in multiplayer or competitive games
why: Other players are affected and expect fair play.

text: Antisocial behavior reduces player engagement and makes online games feel toxic.
why: Players targeted by it find it distressing, and it has been linked to lower engagement with the game.

text: Help players find people they might like, then offer a low-pressure way to show a little of who they are.
when: When designing how strangers first meet and begin to interact
why: First meetings are awkward, so low-pressure ways to show personality help people open up.

text: Games can foster compassion, feeling and bonding via decisions and flow, social play, physical movement, and remote connection between players.
Players assemble a mental model of a virtual space from whatever cues exist; when visuals, sound, touch and motion agree, the illusion feels seamless.
when: On first encountering a virtual space
why: People subconsciously apply real-world physics knowledge to limited cues to build a mental model of the space.

text: Players build a mental map of an avatar-driven world, forming a general feel first and then learning landmarks and detail.
when: When exploring a new game world.
why: Learning a new physical place follows the same order: overall impression, then specifics.

text: People prefer landscapes they grew up in, and no group of people wanted to live in a desert or rainforest they had not known.
why: Acquired familiarity shapes landscape preference alongside innate taste.

text: Players who can see other layers of a maze can observe enemies, gather information about challenges, and find rewards before entering.
when: when a maze has see-through layers
why: Observing the other layers gives players advantages, such as spotting enemies, learning about challenges, and finding rewards early.
