text: When players learn that enemies never attack in a space, they feel safe there and the space's tension deflates.
when: tense spaces where enemies rarely attack
why: Once players work out the system's rule, a threat that never acts no longer feels real, so the tension drains away.

text: Mental rotation time grows with the angle to be rotated; a 180-degree rotation takes nearly twice as long as a 90-degree one.
Humans have innate landscape preferences: the ideal habitat combines open grassland, patches of woods and running water, neither too hot nor too cold, and neither too open nor overgrown.
why: Such habitats were fertile and safe for early humans.

text: A visible enemy can still go unseen when the lights are out or the character faces away from it.
when: low light or facing away from the enemy
why: sight depends on both illumination and orientation

text: An enemy that moves mostly predictably but has random vertical motion and fires more often when the player is close creates pressure that rises with proximity.
when: when designing an enemy that shoots back at a nearby player
why: Proximity-weighted firing makes close range the most dangerous

text: Sustained attention fatigues quickly, and its capacity varies with motivation, task complexity and individual differences.
why: Working memory becomes fatigued quite rapidly, so sustained attention cannot last indefinitely.

text: Under stress, anxiety narrows attention into tunnel vision, focusing a person on the most urgent cues in the environment.
when: under acute stress or threat
why: arousal narrows attention to the information needed for immediate action

text: Under immediate threat, a player may have to choose between staying safe and taking a risk within a moment.
when: the player is under fire with a risky alternative available
why: Threat leaves little time, so the decision is compressed

text: A threat that spawns at random around the player, with unknown location, feels present everywhere and raises anxiety.
when: during pursuit or search
why: Unknown location keeps the player from ever feeling safe.

text: Mixed friendly, hostile and neutral cues leave players unsure whether a room is safe.
when: in spaces with mixed atmosphere cues
why: Conflicting indicators remove a reliable sense of safety.

text: Stress and emotional pressure that suits adults can overwhelm younger players, so intensity should be calibrated to the target audience's emotional development.
when: Designing for teen or younger audiences.
why: Emotion-regulating brain regions mature around age 25.

text: Two tasks that draw on the same working memory subsystem compete strongly, while tasks using different subsystems, such as language and vision, split more easily.
why: Two language tasks both draw on the phonological loop and overload it, while language plus visuo-motor tasks use separate subsystems.

text: In danger, the hypothalamus regulates hormones such as adrenaline and cortisol, raising awareness and tensing muscles.
when: When a situation is perceived as dangerous.
why: The hypothalamus releases hormones such as adrenaline and cortisol, which heighten awareness and tense the muscles.

text: Withholding a threat and showing only its point of view can make it seem to be the environment itself.
why: An unseen threat that only shows its point of view can come to feel like the surrounding environment itself.

text: Excessive cognitive load can impair learning even when the learner is unaware of it.
when: When information or task demands are too high.
why: Attention is limited, and splitting that finite capacity across competing tasks makes processing less efficient.

text: When two audio streams differ enough, listeners can repeat the attended one but usually retain little or nothing of the unattended stream.
when: dichotic listening with headphones, one voice per ear
why: Attention filters what reaches conscious memory

text: Players often sense a game's theme without being able to name it, because theme works at a subconscious level.
when: When a work emotionally moves its audience.
why: Theme operates subconsciously, and elements reinforcing one theme create a pull players feel but cannot explain.

text: Players unconsciously simulate possible futures, including winning, losing, living and dying, even when those outcomes never occur.
why: Emotion is driven by the outcomes the mind imagines, not only by those that actually happen.

text: Subconscious processing anticipates what comes next and shapes speech and reactions, often without reasoning the person can report.
How subconscious mental processes work is still largely unknown, though psychology is slowly making progress.
Emotion arises from anticipating future change, so suspense depends on how much remains in the balance.
when: When one minor event could swing the whole match's result.
why: The emotional unconscious looks ahead for threats and opportunities and signals them with emotion.

text: Overstating subliminal priming's influence on player behavior is a pitfall: it is too weak to stealthily control behavior, so persuaders tend to exploit cognitive biases instead.
Watching others play forms virtual theaters: esports tournaments draw millions and recorded streams spread online. Spectating has existed for thousands of years, but only for games worth watching.
when: When who wins and loses is visible to onlookers.
why: Onlookers get excited watching public contests, so a crowd of spectators gathers around them.

text: Experienced players often enjoy giving hints to struggling newcomers, so mixed-skill play can help both groups.
when: newcomers and veterans play in the same activity
why: Veterans take pleasure in teaching, much like skilled people in other pursuits.

text: Veteran players leave a leveling game once it stops offering new discoveries, unless given a different game to play.
when: after progression runs out
why: the novelty that held them is gone

text: In unrestricted PvP, players feel they are never safe and become wary of talking to strangers.
when: unrestricted PvP
why: any player may attack without warning

text: Some griefers befriend a player, build trust, then unexpectedly kill them and take their inventory, gaining no game advantage.
when: open PvP games
why: they do it to torment others

text: When a game does not formally support social loops, players often form their own groups.
when: Games without official guilds or social systems.
why: Players build their own scaffolding for social progression.

text: Players are more likely to troll or exploit random teammates they will never meet again.
when: when teammates are anonymous and one-off
why: No trust relationship needs to be maintained.

text: Players often shift from strangers to friends after a shared play experience.
In multiplayer elimination games, players may team up to eliminate a rival, while two-player games lack this option.
when: when three or more players compete
why: Coalitions form against a leading player, but cannot form in a duel.

text: When many states and transitions are available, no two runs match, and players chain long sequences and share recordings of them.
when: When a system offers many states and easy transitions between them.
why: Flexible recombination makes each run distinct and worth sharing.

text: Team play attracts fans as well as players, and clans or guilds form quickly around multiplayer games.
when: in multiplayer games with team play
why: Team competition appears to meet a need that players answer by organizing into groups, and it also draws spectators.

text: In public matches, players assume teammates are skilled enough to take good routes and shots, but know little else about their plans.
when: unknown teammates on public servers
why: Only general skill can be assumed without communication.

text: In team competition, two or more groups compete against each other.
Older games were largely communal, meaning people gathered physically and played together face to face.
Team competition blends competition and cooperation, is common in athletics, and has grown with networked gaming.
In team games, distinct positions together make up the full team, and every position must be filled.
The team fully controls mechanics, but cannot directly control the dynamics players invent with them.
No single recipe makes a compelling game; each team should find its own mix of design ingredients for its specific audience.
when: When targeting one specific audience.
why: The right mix depends on the audience, so teams must find it through empathy and a scientific approach.

text: Strong game teams build a sense of eliteness through camaraderie around a shared symbol or idea that sets them apart from others.
when: When trying to motivate a team, especially one in a plain or impersonal organization.
why: A set-apart identity gives people a precedent to live up to.

text: A small group of uncivil players can spoil the game for the majority, reducing retention and revenue.
Team play raises cohesion, which activates trust norms, which in turn increases cooperative behavior.
when: When teammates cooperate toward a shared goal rather than playing alone.

text: DPS deals large damage; Tank draws enemy attacks away from DPS; Support keeps Tanks alive and/or buffs DPS damage.
when: Team-based games with three roles.
why: Each role protects or boosts the others, raising the team's overall effectiveness.

text: Team love for a game can break down in three ways: members who cannot love any game, members who love a different kind of game, and passionate members who hold different visions of the same game.
On a team, a single disconnect can unjustly punish all teammates.
when: in team games
why: Team results are shared, so one member's failure determines the outcome for everyone.

text: A team must eventually settle on a decision everyone accepts, even when individuals still disagree, and must not leave differences unresolved.
when: Disagreement persists after debate
why: Unresolved disagreement eventually shows up in the game

text: Rubber-banding, where trailing AI gets impossible speed boosts, is disliked because it feels unfair compared with real competition.
when: Racing or competitive games with catch-up mechanics.
why: Players notice artificial help that breaks the expectation of a real contest.

text: Players in multiplayer shooters camp near spawn points to shoot opponents right after they respawn, which victims often feel is unfair despite following the rules.
when: Multiplayer shooters with fixed spawn points and more than two players.
why: Rules can be clear and complete while the system still permits a tactic that feels unfair to victims.

text: Solo players in open player-versus-player worlds may struggle to survive because they lack group protection.
when: A new player has no group in an open combat world
why: Groups hunt and protect their own members

text: In group play, mistakes turn into friendly ribbing that keeps players engaged, while the same activity played alone can feel like studying.
when: Playing games with others versus alone, especially early on.
why: Social interaction makes errors entertaining rather than tedious.

text: In individuals versus game, several players face the system in each other's company without acting on one another.
A human value is anything important to people that moves through positive, neutral and negative states, such as life/death, victory/defeat, wealth/poverty and freedom/slavery.
Social interaction influences player experience but is excluded from elicitors in this framework because it poses a hard problem for AI, signal processing and experience-driven PCG.
why: it is a hard problem for AI, signal processing and experience-driven PCG

text: Common griefer loopholes include disconnecting mid-battle to deny a reward, crashing the server through an exploitable spot, arranging public objects to spell obscenities, and stealing resources.
Gifting between players drove much of the viral spread of social games on Facebook.
when: When designing social or social-network games

text: Most games throughout history were designed to be played with or against others, and solo games such as solitaire were rare before computers.
Group-owned property has been a major factor in the sustained success of some large online games.
The individuals-versus-game pattern is rare in digital games despite its social appeal.
Outwit games that use in-game knowledge create social dynamics that are largely unexplored in digital games.
Solve griefing that entertains the griefer but destroys others' play; ignore low-severity cases like passive play rather than distorting core design, since they fade without reaction.
when: the behavior is unwanted but does not break the game
why: Ignored behavior stops once it earns no interesting response, and players feel less controlled than under prohibitions or punishments.

text: Conflict that players face alone, such as in solitaire, will not produce community no matter how engaging it is.
why: Community is built on conflict shared between groups, and solo conflict involves no rival group.

text: Showing a player stuck at the bottom of global rank with no change can drive them to quit.
when: When a player sits low on a global leaderboard and their position never moves.

text: Rewarding players for recruiting friends in pyramid fashion, or impersonating players to recruit, exploits social obligation and standing.

1) Before adding a feature, review its griefing potential for cheap ways to spoil others' play, especially player-versus-player combat, item transfer, theft, trading, chat and movement blocking. 2) Make disruption dull: limit PvP to special areas, withhold feedback from abusers, prevent item seizure. 3) Hunt loopholes such as disconnect tricks, server-stressing actions and vandalism of shared spaces.
when: Adding features to a multiplayer game, or protecting a game from griefing.
why: Griefing leaves players feeling under constant threat, so they stop trusting strangers and the community suffers.

text: 1) Align player goals with sensible objectives such as conquest, exploration, communication and impact, as first defense against griefing. 2) Use large player counts to dilute divergent goals. 3) Fix severe griefing directly, such as letting players pass through each other or adding safe zones. 4) Add policing systems such as voting or moderators when the design cannot protect the game from within.
why: Getting every player's goals to match at the same moment is almost unattainable, so extra safeguards are required.

text: 1) Anticipate how the game may affect social behavior. 2) Set a code of conduct. 3) Enforce it, for example with temporary bans after warnings. 4) Reward fair play.
when: When design choices such as allowing friendly fire could shape how players treat one another.
why: Unaddressed antisocial conduct that goes unanticipated can persist and spread once it has surfaced.

text: Human interests should take priority over business considerations when they conflict.
why: No design is neutral, so ethics has to be weighed during development.

text: Abstract or cartoonish violence draws little concern, even after a real school shooting, because it feels remote; visible gore draws the most parental concern.
when: Shortly after a real school shooting, when showing cartoon cannon violence to families.
why: Stylized settings feel detached from real life.

text: Males enjoy destroying things, and games can offer virtual destruction far beyond what is possible in reality.
why: Boys often find tearing down what was built to be the thrill, and games can scale that far past reality.

text: Games without blood can still draw protest when they reward harming people, especially when the framing of the victims is not believed.
when: When a game rewards harming figures and the claim that they are not really people fails to convince.
why: Parents may find rewards for harm disturbing even without gore if the victims look human.

text: At close range, players can mash fire and get responses about as fast as the button can be pressed.
when: targets one or two tiles away
why: Shots leave quickly, freeing slots for new ones.

text: Players can find harming others more dramatic and rewarding than cooperating, so cooperation often needs deliberate reward to stand out.
when: in early playtests of player-to-player interaction
why: harmful actions can feel more exciting than cooperative ones

text: If a game has only combat before a social encounter, players tend to attack non-combatants on sight.
when: A social scene follows a stretch of play that is entirely combat.
why: Combat priming makes violent action the most available response.

text: Video games are neither good nor bad; there is no single effect, since effects depend on which games, how played, and context, as with books, film and TV.
Feeling pulled to return to a game is different from a game damaging a person's life.
when: assessing a player's habits
why: Strong engagement is not the same as harm

text: The core concern about violent play is that it may desensitize players or make violence seem fun, and evidence on this remains unclear.
Children are a greater concern than adults for violent game content, though some violent play is natural and healthy for development.
The medium a person is immersed in while young shapes how they think for the rest of their life.
Decades of research found no evidence that violent video games are linked to aggression in teenagers, including vulnerable groups.
A 2018 global estimate found about one in three women has experienced violence at least once.
After 30 minutes, players of non-violent games showed less aggression than players of violent games and less than a no-game group.
Violent games show the most downsides of the game types examined.
A meta-analysis of correlational, experimental, and longitudinal studies linked violent games to aggression, desensitization, low empathy, and low prosocial behavior.
A re-analysis of the same dataset judged experimental support weaker and attributed short-term effects to priming.
A study of over 1,000 teenagers aged 14 and 15 found no observable link between violent games and aggressive behavior.
A two-month longitudinal study of adults found no relevant negative effects from playing a violent game.
An expert review found violent games a risk factor for adverse outcomes, but evidence on delinquency or criminal behavior was insufficient.
A 2020 professional resolution said real-life violence should not be attributed to violent game use, though one of its divisions disagreed.
Grunge-style rock raised hostility, fatigue, sadness, and tension, while lowering caring, relaxation, clarity, and vigor.
Ask which specific games produce which effects rather than asking about games in general.
Lack of felt competence is linked to more aggressive thoughts, feelings, and behavior in players.
Under the General Learning Model, prosocial games increase prosocial behavior and violent games increase aggressive behavior.
why: Under this model, a game can shape behavior in both brief and lasting ways through various learning routes.

text: The catalyst model attributes aggression to genetic predispositions, harsh early environments, and current stress.
why: Its proponents regard media as too remote and feeble to meaningfully shape aggression.

text: Treating correlational or lab findings on violent games as proof of real-world violence is a mistake.
why: Lab studies mostly capture mild aggression, and the methods of some such studies have been challenged.

text: Most action games contain violence, so most action-game studies involve adults; when studying children, use non-violent action titles.
when: When studying children with action-game interventions.
why: Most commercial action titles are unsuitable for young players, which limits child studies.

text: Do not punish disengagement; players should not feel pressured to play.
why: Losing a reward upon returning feels punishing and can erode intrinsic motivation.

text: Provide content warnings so players can make informed choices about what they play.
why: informed choice respects players

text: Excessive play that displaces homework, physical activity, or sleep is harmful even before it becomes pathological.
Avoid long sessions of violent play before bed, since they can cut sleep.
when: When a violent game is played in long sessions just before bedtime.
why: Long evening sessions cut into total sleep, whereas short ones have only a mild effect.

text: People recall where items sit on a wall far better than the contents of a list, so posted ideas help them find connections.
when: Reviewing posted brainstorm ideas
why: Spatial memory is stronger than list memory

text: Trailing players stay attentive because a game-changing item could appear at any moment.
when: a race uses catch-up item distribution
why: the chance of a strong item keeps them watching

text: People respond faster under intense focus and slower when relaxed or in poor conditions such as dim light.
when: When circumstances are heightened versus relaxed or dim, poorly lit conditions.
why: Individual physiology and surrounding circumstances make each processing stage's timing shift.

text: Players judge an AI as unintelligent when it fails to react to slow projectiles, though fast ones leave too little time to react.
when: slow projectile weapons are fired at the player
why: Slow shots give visible time for a reaction.

text: People often miss objects they are not looking for, even when those objects are in plain view.
when: attention is occupied by another task
why: perception is directed by what the viewer is searching for

text: Large open spaces invite players to look outward and feel small, while tight, constrained spaces focus attention on the immediate surroundings and prompt introspection.
why: Expansive space prompts pondering one's own smallness, while tight space narrows attention to the immediate surroundings.

text: A fast speed value feels slow on empty ground, and adds no sense of speed without nearby objects or surface texture to measure motion against.
when: Moving through a space with no visual reference.
why: Impressions of speed need a frame of reference.

text: Players' impressions of speed vary little between people, since everyone constantly judges moving objects.
why: Judging moving objects is a constant everyday activity.

text: Players keep a running model of game physics, and interactions that contradict it stand out and shape later expectations.
why: Surprising interactions become part of the backdrop players use to predict behavior.

text: Players associate low friction with space because of cultural exposure to astronaut footage and space films, so frictionless motion reads as believable.
when: a space setting uses low-friction movement
why: Familiar space imagery sets expectations that make drifting motion feel correct.

text: Pilots in light aircraft feel an approaching stall through the control stick, and jetliners artificially reproduce that shaking as angle of attack nears the stall angle.
why: Tactile warning conveys a state that the player would otherwise miss.

text: Trained listeners follow a target melody better than untrained listeners when distractor notes are added.
when: noisy input with distractors
why: training improves selective attention

text: Players tend to see a malformed plant as an odd visual detail rather than a gameplay problem, because vegetation usually carries little functional significance.
when: when generating non-interactive scenery such as plants
why: Scenery rarely affects play outcomes, so flaws mostly affect appearance.

text: Vertical elements arranged in rhythm across a large open space can evoke epic hugeness.
when: in open prospect spaces
why: The three-point perspective of wide prospect spaces lets repeated vertical forms read at a grand scale.

text: Players encounter recurring symbols near helpful items or breaks in long action, so the symbol becomes linked with reward or relief.
when: a symbol appears in staged game spaces
why: Position near outcomes shapes the meaning players attach.

text: Sounds of wading through swamps can unsettle players by making them aware of what their avatar is moving through.
when: In games where the player cannot physically touch the terrain their avatar crosses.
why: audible material raises awareness of the environment

text: Randomized variations in repeated sounds, such as gunshots or footsteps, still give players the impression that their actions have effect.
when: Where sound design relies on randomized variations of repeated sounds.
why: Sounds act as symbolic signals, so players read even varied audio as a response to their own input.

text: Well-designed spaces can strongly direct player behavior yet leave room for players to improvise their own actions within the system's mechanics.
when: Designing gamespaces
why: Spatial configuration directs behavior, as architecture has long done for building occupants.

text: Players mentally treat an interior as a separate place, paying little attention to how it relates to the space outside.
when: when a player is inside an interior
why: Indoor thinking focuses on the interior itself.

text: Players perceive a world as open when a fixed-perspective side view scrolls freely across a long level, even though only one screen is visible at a time.
when: long horizontal levels with free scrolling
why: Continuous scrolling suggests the world continues beyond the visible screen.

text: Letting players fix a distant point and travel toward it creates a different kind of openness than scrolling does.
Parallax scrolling moves sprite layers at different speeds as the screen scrolls, so a side-scrolling 2D scene reads as having 3D depth.
Subjective sound presents the soundscape as the character hears it, rather than as a neutral 3D picture.
The Stroop effect is slower, more error-prone naming when an irrelevant word conflicts with the feature being named, such as a color word printed in a different ink.
why: automatic word reading must be inhibited

text: Mimicry spaces are built to stage performance, anticipating choreography, lighting, orchestra pits, and scenery.
Landscape is the environment as perceived, especially visually.
One-point perspectives suit elevation-like views, two-point perspectives match typical eye level, and three-point perspectives suit tall buildings seen from above or below.
when: choosing a perspective type for a level view

text: Negative space in level design is what the player cannot see or know, such as surroundings hidden from view.
Perceived intensity change is logarithmic: stronger stimuli need a larger increase before the difference becomes noticeable.
Visible light is a narrow slice of one continuous range of electromagnetic radiation that includes infrared, ultraviolet and microwaves.
Perceiving motion relative to one's own body matters more to learning perception than the stimulus alone.
why: Subjects who could move freely developed normal perception; passive subjects did not.

text: Visual acuity is sharpest at the fovea and drops quickly with distance from it.
Gamespace architecture applies spatial arrangements from architecture and classic structures to game levels, hubs, sandboxes and camera views.
why: Spatial arrangements shape the player's experience of a level.

text: Designers plan all four prospect and refuge types, but players mainly perceive relations among refuges, prospects, and secondary refuges.
Square corners hide what is around them, while obtuse corners reveal part of the next room, so occupants must move around the corner to see it fully.
Occupant anxiety rises on higher floors, so limiting how many stories a space occupies is a spatial response to that experience.
Use tactile materials such as modeling clay to shape ideas physically.
when: When brainstorming ways to solve a problem.
why: Handling physical material engages creativity tactilely as well as visually, which can spark new ideas.

text: Read the design documents before spotting, since sound implementation often starts before mechanics and scripting exist.
when: Beginning sound work on a project.
why: Design documents reveal intended feel before features are built.

text: Record the map coordinates of events such as player deaths and plot them as a heat map to reveal the most dangerous areas.
when: Analyzing where events happen on a map
why: Color intensity maps event counts onto locations, so concentrations of deaths stand out.

text: Alternate large open areas with small enclosed spaces that demand precise obstacle avoidance, so the level varies what it asks of the player.
why: Dense objects in tight areas make the vehicle seem to zip quickly between them, adding a sense of speed.

text: Pair large open areas for circulation with covered, columned areas for lingering and stationary activity, so each space type supports the action it suits.
when: Zoning a hub where players move through and also gather or pause
why: Open space supports movement, while enclosed or covered space invites people to stay.

text: Use freeform layouts driven by player movement, narrative events or mechanics rather than believable building plans.
when: when the layout should serve gameplay rather than realism
why: Gamespaces need not follow physical or regulatory constraints.

text: In top-down games, parallax backgrounds can suggest terrain lying far below the gameplay space.
why: Layers scrolling at different speeds make elements read as existing at different depths.

text: Scrolling distant layers independently of nearby geometry can convey great height even when the playable level is blocky.
why: Distant layers scrolling apart from nearby geometry imply vertical distance the level itself does not contain.

text: Perception is a subjective construction, often top-down: prior knowledge, input context and expectations shape what is perceived, not only the reverse.
why: Using stored knowledge to interpret input speeds recognition, which mattered for reacting quickly to threats like predators.

text: Without a blank flicker, a changed element stands out as the only moving part and becomes easy to notice.
when: When two near-identical images alternate on screen.
why: Without flicker, the eye does not rely on fleeting sensory memory to compare images, so the lone moving element is noticed.

text: Constant exposure to a view makes it lose its power, while a view withheld and glimpsed briefly stays striking.
when: when designing reward visibility
why: scarcity of a view preserves its impact

text: Moving through layers of 2D environments, forward and backward, adds a z-axis to side-scrolling levels.
why: Standard orientation cues fail in side scrollers, so layered movement supplies a depth axis for navigation.

text: Vision has two functional systems: a fast object-identifying 'what' system and a slower action-guiding 'how' system that handles tasks like grabbing or catching.
Perception unfolds in three levels: sensation, perception and cognition, each adding organization or meaning to sensory input.
why: Pattern recognition turns raw input into meaningful shapes, so organization and meaning are added at each level.

text: Tutorial levels alternate positive spaces, where players learn new mechanics, with negative spaces, where they practice them; people pass through negative spaces and dwell in positive ones.
when: When structuring a tutorial level's sequence of learning and practice
why: Alternating the two space types keeps the dwelling and moving experiences distinct

text: Gamespace is assembled from small-scale additive and subtractive volumes plus larger forms like open sandboxes, hub areas and traditional gamespaces, sized by spatial size types.
why: Sizing gamespace by spatial size types matches each space to the gameplay experience it houses.

text: 1) Place a middle-height feature to set the base height. 2) Place the tallest feature beside it.
why: A mid-height piece gives the arrangement a reference level, so the tallest one reads against it.

text: Artists should specify the shadows and textures they want, and engineers should match that vision rather than adopting whatever technique is fashionable.
why: Artists have trained for years to define integrated visions, so they should set the target engineers work toward.

text: Design for how players perceive gamespace through points of view and cameras, and make levels support navigation.
Disable rendering of foreground objects that block the character so the player does not lose the character behind structures.
when: in axonometric views
why: Downward-facing cameras place structures between the camera and the character.

text: Players in a presence-filled VR world expect objects to support varied, multi-purpose interactions, not only single-purpose uses.
when: VR environments
why: Real-world objects are used in many ways, so narrow interactions break expectation.

text: Players' sense of closeness to their avatar varies: sometimes they feel distant from it, and at other times their own state merges with it.
when: During play with a controllable character
why: Players readily project themselves into anything they control, so their mental state can fuse with the avatar.

text: A sudden force on an otherwise inert wheel makes it seem to come alive and can distract the player.
when: when force feedback fires abruptly
why: Unlike steady cues such as engine pitch that players adapt to, an abrupt force has no lead-in, so it reads as something arriving from nowhere.

text: Cybersickness, simulation sickness and motion sickness share symptoms such as nausea, dizziness, disorientation and cold sweats; VR is well known for inducing cybersickness.
The headspace no-no zone is the area too close to the eyes for content to be comfortable, so virtual elements should not breach a set minimum distance.
The choice of avatar decides who the player relates to and implicitly limits what the player will try, since different avatars invite different actions.
when: Choosing a player avatar

text: AR currently causes less sickness because it gives less false information to peripheral vision, which the brain uses to sense motion.
when: Compared with fully virtual displays
why: Peripheral vision carries motion cues that AR leaves mostly accurate

text: Rich avatar creation and chat features that convey emotion or let players choose text colors and styles are popular with online players.
AR shares VR's physical fatigue, such as headset weight or arm strain from holding a phone, and visual fatigue from refocusing between near and far.
VR can produce far stronger thrill and fear than screens because it can activate the brain's system that tracks objects approaching the body.
why: Traditional screen games cannot activate this system, while VR and AR can

text: Virtual embodiment, letting people inhabit a virtual body, may reduce pain perception, aid stroke rehabilitation and let players experience a different body.
VR is more likely than mobile, PC, or console games to elicit presence, especially physical presence in a 3D space.
Presence weakens when the virtual body differs from the real body in posture, scale, position or appearance, or when virtual objects pass through it; strong alignment increases presence.
why: The mind keeps an internal model of the real body, so a visible body that conflicts with it, or objects intruding on it, makes the illusion fail.

text: HUDs and 2D overlays in VR cause visual fatigue because the eyes must keep refocusing between near and far elements.
when: When players must repeatedly refocus between nearby interface elements and distant scenery in VR.

text: Empathy for characters rises as they look more human, then drops sharply when they look nearly human but not quite, creating a dip called the uncanny valley.
when: Designing characters that aim for human or realistic appearance
why: Near-human figures are perceived as diseased or dangerous, provoking revulsion

text: VR and AR communication can feel more natural than a screen video call because the other person seems physically present.
why: The brain is specialized for reading faces and gestures, so seeing a remote person's eye contact and movement registers as their real presence.

text: Through practice, a tool's effortful use becomes automatic and part of the user's perceptual field, extending their reach.
why: The tool returns orienting feedback that the user reads as if it came from their own hand, so attention passes through the tool to the world.

text: Varying speed and pattern of contact prevents the nervous system from predicting input, which is why people cannot tickle themselves.
when: Designing touch sensations.
why: Predicted input is attenuated in perception.

text: Combined visual, aural and tactile feedback creates a virtual proprioception that players experience as real.
why: Combined visual, aural and tactile feedback produces a sensation beyond what any single channel provides, and the senses accept it as real.

text: In positionally tracked VR, the player's avatar keeps their real height, unlike fixed-size avatars in most games.
why: If the player's real feet sit above or below the virtual floor, they feel buried or floating, so the camera height must follow real height.

text: Arm fatigue, called the gorilla arm effect, can begin after about 10 seconds of holding hands in front above the waist.
when: When players hold their hands out in front above the waist while using VR.
why: Headsets are heavy and arms are unsupported.

text: Treat 60 fps as the absolute minimum frame rate for VR and aim for 90 fps or more.
when: designing or tuning VR
why: Quick head and eye motion makes stepped frame updates noticeable, and the brain registers the error when rates fall well below the high targets.

text: Presence has three kinds: physical (feeling of being in the world), emotional (events feel like they happen to the player), and narrative (players care about believable, relatable characters and story).
Players often misjudge distances when grabbing objects by hand, so grabbing needs careful feedback.
Short VR players may not feel heroic or powerful, especially when shorter than all the NPCs around them.
when: tracked VR with variable player height
why: Avatar height follows the player's real height, so the feeling of a towering hero is undercut when surrounded by taller characters.

text: Very tall VR users can exceed trigger volumes and break scripting that assumes a fixed player size.
when: tracked VR with variable player height
why: Avatar height varies with each player in tracked VR, so trigger volumes and scripts sized for one fixed height can be exceeded.

text: Show no avatar body rather than a visible body that sits out of place with the player's real body.
when: Choosing whether to display the player's avatar
why: Misaligned visible bodies fall into the uncanny valley of VR avatars

text: Use teleport instead of walking, limit head movements, and provide a stable rest frame to reduce cybersickness.
when: when players move through large 3D spaces
why: These reduce the conflict between visual motion and the stationary body.

text: Avoid virtual camera movement that the inner ear does not match.
when: When the in-game camera moves quickly while the player's body stays still.
why: A mismatch between what the eyes see and what the inner ear senses can trigger nausea.

text: If the camera must move in VR, keep the motion linear and avoid acceleration.
when: virtual camera movement is unavoidable
why: the inner ear senses speed changes

text: Teleportation avoids motion sickness but weakens presence, because the mind builds a model only of spaces it has actually looked at.
when: choosing locomotion in VR

text: Children and teens find it harder than adults to stop enjoyable activities or resist pressure to keep playing, as the impulse-controlling prefrontal cortex matures only around age 25.
when: when an enjoyable activity could be stopped
why: Impulse control is still developing in young players.

text: Children and teenagers often struggle to regulate emotion, showing tantrums and risk-seeking.
when: during emotional arousal
why: the prefrontal cortex that regulates emotion is not yet mature

text: Do not design for children as small adults; account for their different experience, attention, memory, and emotional regulation, and consult child development experts.
when: The audience includes players under 18
why: Children differ from adults in perception, attention, working memory, and emotion regulation

text: Packaging agents can help developers win deals they might not get alone, or command a premium in budget or royalty rates.
Packaging agents secure content, attach a developer and talent such as writers and designers, and shop the package to publishers or financiers.
Passive Hollywood-style agents representing film clients typically earn a 10% fee.
when: When an agent only represents a film client's interests, such as securing likeness or voice rights for a publisher.

text: Packaging agents usually do not do development work, so don't confuse them with producers; they earn a share of the license fee and developer compensation, not a producer's fee.
The Agile Manifesto was written in 2001 by software engineers and sets out values and principles for building software.
Over 80% of videogame developers report using some version of agile.
Agile is a philosophy rather than a prescribed method, so implementations vary between teams.
Agile development is the most successful descendant of the spiral model.
Most backlog ideas will never be implemented, so ideas that do get used are likely strong.

A software statement ranks four pairs: responding to change over following a plan, customer collaboration over contract negotiation, working software over documentation, and interactions between individuals over processes and tools.
why: Satisfying the customer through early, continuous delivery of valuable software is the top priority these values serve.

text: Agile teams use a prioritized backlog, short sprints ending in working deliverables, daily scrums, demo days, and retrospectives.
Agile is a modular, adaptive, people-centered framework for software development.
1) Once the foundation is solid, choose an idea from the backlog. 2) Place it on top of the stack. 3) Repeat after each layer solidifies.
when: When the current design layer is solid and near-certain.
why: Choices from the backlog rest on known foundations, so the designer knows what the new piece depends on.

text: Keep backlog ideas unconnected; do not fix them into a plan, since that implies certainty the designer does not have.
when: When an idea is not scheduled for near-term work.
why: Fixing unscheduled ideas into a plan would claim confidence the designer lacks, since their upstream choices remain uncertain.

text: Character AI data may include scripts that drive the algorithms in the pool.
Behaviors with many conditions need complicated matching rules, which in tools often look like program code and are hard for designers to author.
when: When a behavior must check many special cases inside an authoring tool.
why: A programming language is the most natural notation for such matching rules, so they take on code form.

text: 1) Count the avatar's states. 2) Record how each state changes the interpretation of every input.
when: cataloging a game's control
why: Letting one input mean different things by avatar state yields many distinct responses from few buttons, giving the player wide expressive range.

text: 1) Pick three compelling characters from games you know. 2) For each, decide whether it is rounded or flat. 3) For each, decide whether it is dynamic or static.
when: when analyzing character depth
why: Judging characters by depth and change helps build them with more believability and dramatic weight.

text: Fewer AI plug-ins are built now because development has shifted toward separate level editing tools, whose functions match the AI plug-in candidates.
In the UX process, AI can analyze user data, automate routine tasks, and support design evaluation.
AI with many tunable parameters, such as movement algorithms, nearly requires an in-game tweaking system on consoles.
when: When AI has many tunable parameters and the target is a console.
why: Console builds and round trips are slow, so tuning values in-game avoids repeated full rebuilds.

text: 1) Start from the behaviors in the design document. 2) Find the simplest technologies that deliver them. 3) Check each AI model part against those behaviors. 4) Choose technologies and a basic integration approach. 5) Build the layer connecting the AI to the game engine.
when: Planning game AI from a design
why: Understanding the requirements the behaviors impose lets the designer choose techniques that implement them.

text: 1) Generate many random legal layouts. 2) Play the AI against each until all pieces are sunk. 3) Record turns to win. 4) Report mean and median, and compare with baseline strategies.
when: comparing guessing strategies
why: simulation gives reliable performance statistics

text: Analytics can show causes and effects that explain why metrics move, but telemetry alone shows what players do, not why; pair it with qualitative research.
why: Behavioral logs show what players do but not their motives, and typical metrics miss enjoyment and burnout.

text: Once a UX finding is explained it seems obvious due to hindsight bias; recognizing this is the first step toward compensating when reviewing past predictions.
when: when reviewing UX findings after they are revealed
why: People forget the uncertainty they felt before learning it; hindsight bias makes people feel they knew the answer all along.

text: Game analytics collects and interprets player telemetry to show what players do at scale, such as where they die, get stuck or ignore features, to inform decisions within business intelligence.
An A/B test randomly divides players into two groups, changes the game for only one, and compares metrics to verify causality, such as which button color yields higher conversion.
Analyzing an experience while it happens is hard because the analytic part of the mind is busy with the experience itself.
when: Trying to analyze play as it happens
why: Attention is divided between experiencing and analyzing.

text: People avoid heavy cognitive work and therefore reach quick, less nuanced conclusions from data.
when: when interpreting charts or dashboards
why: cognitive effort is costly, so people economize on it

text: Analytics collects quantitative data from large player samples at home, outside the lab, showing what is happening, such as many players dying at one point; it complements lab methods.
when: Planning post-launch or large-scale data collection
why: It captures behavior at a scale and setting labs cannot reach.

text: Data hooks are instrumentation built into the game engine that record player movement and actions.
Frequentism estimates probabilities from expected values and significance tests on observed outcomes.
Hard metrics are finite, quantifiable measurements such as timings, scores and play durations.
Soft metrics capture impressions of fun, such as silent strategic thought, raucous laughter or relief after a hard day.
Discrete values are one of several distinct options, such as a character chosen in a fighting game. Time counted in months is also discrete.
Continuous values can be any number within a range, such as a timestamp.
A heat map shows spatial values through color intensity, so brighter areas mark higher counts.
Analytics asks what players and systems are up to, what follows from those actions, and how effective each one is.
DAU is the number of unique players active on a given day. MAU is the number of unique players who played at least once in a month.
Analytics is balance assessment built on data from real games, turning soft human aspects of design into quantitative analysis, complementing playtesting and mathematical models.
Telemetry is remote data gathering from players' devices, showing live behavior at scale, such as play frequency, session length and events that cause churn.
Four 11-point sets can share nearly identical means, spreads and correlation yet show a noisy trend, a parabola, a near-perfect line and a vertical stack, two of them outlier-pulled.
Analysis is only as good as the data it is built on.
Data hooks show where players progress as expected and where they slow down or get stuck.
Automatic data collection gathers more data than manual notes, making the data more useful for analysis.
when: When choosing how to record playtest or live data

text: Playtest data quality depends on programmers implementing the collection code that designers request.
Probability has built-in sanity checks, such as results that must lie between 0 and 1, but statistics often lacks a known expected answer.
Hard metrics can be compared across playtests, but assigning them meaning is a design judgment.
Useful sources for analyzing a game include strategy guides, FAQs or wikis, reviews, developer interviews or talks, and Let's Play videos; keep a list of them.
Analytics gains statistical power as the player base grows, and it requires a playable game with a large number of players, so it usually comes late in development.
when: Planning when to rely on analytics in a development cycle.
why: Reliable patterns need many players and a playable build.

text: Ratings predict match outcomes only partly, and other factors such as chosen objects, team synergy, familiarity and margins can refine them.
True ratings are unknown in live play, so a rating system is validated by comparing predicted and observed win rates across players to find over- and underestimates.
when: Checking a rating system against live match data.
why: The true skill of each player cannot be measured directly.

text: Randomly splitting one identical process into two groups yields slightly different means and standard deviations.
when: comparing two random groups from the same process
why: Random sampling produces variation even when nothing has changed.

text: Analytics often sits in the business intelligence team, whose findings feed marketing and publishing decisions.
Studios gather more telemetry each year, but the main bottleneck is making sense of it, which requires data analysts and data scientists.
Perception is shaped by prior knowledge and expectations, so people can misread charts; visualization design needs deliberate care.
Gameplay metrics are game-specific. Examples: deaths, deaths by type (bullet, melee, fall), progression events at mission start and completion, weapon accuracy and weapon power.
Data shows what is happening, not why; external context such as competing releases, sports events, server issues or collection bugs must be investigated separately.
Massive datasets alone don't ensure success; worth emerges when information pairs with leadership, engineering and analytical capability.
Telemetry can expose missions where players fail massively and paths players take that designers did not intend, guiding targeted fixes.
Data mining in companies is more often aimed at retention and conversion than at user experience, and it usually requires working closely with busy data scientists.
When mean and median are close, the data has no strong extremes or its extremes balance on both sides.
why: A few extreme values pull the mean away from the median, so a close pair suggests outliers are not distorting the data.

text: Analytics can show which repeated causes of defeat correlate most strongly with quitting, so check those causes first.
when: when reviewing data from a live game
why: The defeat cause players repeat most often tracks closely with churn, so it points to the biggest driver of quitting.

text: When decomposing a design problem, expect some pieces to connect in non-obvious ways.
when: When dividing a prototype's design problem into smaller pieces to test.
why: Building everything at once cannot reach a conclusion, and hidden links between pieces can cause failures later.

text: Choose measures by the problem: time each procedure for a clunky, slow start, and use qualitative questions for a game that feels undramatic.
why: Different problems call for different evidence, so the measure should follow the question being answered.

text: A retrospective split should be framed as a hypothetical A/B test; if it cannot be, causal conclusions may not be meaningful.
when: when analysing data without a planned experiment
why: Causal claims need a comparison of comparable groups.

text: Compare discrete values side by side with bars, and use a pie chart to highlight the largest or smallest value.
when: Comparing two values where one or both are discrete
why: Bars make side-by-side comparison easy, while pie slices draw the eye to the largest or smallest share.

text: An extremely long session usually means the game was paused or left idle rather than played.
when: a single session far longer than the rest
why: A lone very long session most likely reflects a paused or abandoned game rather than actual play.

text: A genuine problem hidden inside abusive feedback is usually noticed and raised constructively by others.
when: When feedback is laced with personal attacks or insulting commentary.
why: Others tend to notice and raise any real problem hidden in abusive wording, so it is not lost.

text: Measure preference through activities players already perform, such as shooting, trading or surviving, rather than asking them to rate content.
when: When preference can be inferred from actions players already take in the game.
why: Explicit evaluation requires repeated effort, which causes fatigue.

text: A design change alters player behavior, which then alters the metric, so a metric can move without revealing the reason.
why: The change shifts player behavior, which moves the metric, so the metric shows an effect without revealing its cause.

text: Concentration is scored from 0 to 4, from attention on the environment (0) to attention fully absorbed in the activity (4).
when: when using the observation grid
why: The scale separates attention on surroundings from full absorption, indicating how intense the flow state is.

text: Frustration is scored from 0 to 3, from no signs (0) to exclamations or swearing during or after play (3).
when: when using the observation grid
why: Vocal outbursts are observable and can be scored directly, so an observer can measure frustration.

text: A solo session rate can reach 200 lines per hour with an experienced actor and fall to 50 for complex emotional scenes.
when: Adjusting session plans for actor skill and scene difficulty
why: Experience speeds delivery while emotional complexity slows it

text: COUNT tallies cells containing numbers, so comparing that tally with total rows shows how many records are complete.
when: checking how many playtest rows produced usable data
why: Counting only numeric cells skips blanks from incomplete sessions or crashes, so the gap from total rows shows unusable records.

text: Four analytics investigation types: building intuition by finding unknown correlations, finding general problems by comparing play to the ideal, answering specific suspicions, and monitoring past changes.
Analytics claims, from weakest to strongest, are: observation, correlation, plausible causality, verified causality and statistical model.
when: Judging how much evidence a finding supports.
why: Each level supports different decisions with different certainty.

text: Self-serve exploration by people with basic statistics but little bias awareness turns noise into apparent patterns, and a self-serve culture without fallacy training can cause harmful changes.
when: when self-serve exploring data
why: unchecked biases turn noise into apparent findings

text: People use the word average for either mean or median, so confirm which measure is meant before comparing numbers.
why: A few extreme values can pull the mean far from the median, so the two figures can describe very different things.

text: Choosing which data set serves as the baseline changes the z test result.
when: comparing two data sets

text: Assuming hard, fact-based data is automatically better than observed enjoyment is a mistake.
why: Soft metrics capture the nebulous, evolving sense of what playing the game is like, which hard metrics cannot quantify.

text: Hasty interpretation by observers or developers behind the mirror can contaminate the whole analysis.
when: Analyzing UX test results
why: Early conclusions shape how later evidence is read.

text: The hardest part of a sense simulation is the source data, so designers need tools to mark where each modality can pass.
why: Accurate sense graphs need dedicated tool support, since rough approximations from level geometry are limited.

text: Charts, formulas and level maps pile up quickly, so keep analysis material manageable.
why: A full campaign analysis produces many charts, formulas and level maps to review.

text: Aggregating metrics across several patches can hide the effect of any single patch, because the largest and most recent periods dominate the totals.
when: Summarizing data that spans multiple updates.
why: Periods with more players carry more weight in combined totals.

text: Results are biased when the protocol does not isolate the variable being tested.
Media headlines often drop the caveats researchers attach to their findings, distorting public understanding.
when: When a study is reported in the media before its results have been checked for replication.
why: Click-bait headlines strip out the caveats researchers attach, and failed replication then adds to public confusion.

text: Two groups can share the same average while their spreads differ widely, so compare variance before treating a difference in means as meaningful.
when: when comparing group averages
why: large within-group variation can make a difference random

text: Hasty conclusions can cost more time, and possibly money, than careful analysis.
when: When monitoring the health of a beta or live game under pressure.
why: Without solid hypotheses, panic drives reactive changes that can harm the user experience and revenue.

text: Acting on cache-profiler numbers without understanding them can lead to restructuring that does not address the real bottleneck.
when: Reading cache miss reports for the first time
why: Profiler figures are complex and easy to misread

text: Explaining away an odd result to protect the current design can hide the most valuable discovery.
when: When a test produces an unexpected outcome
why: A worldview held too tightly filters out signs of value.

text: Recorded data can show that an event occurred without revealing how players experienced it.
why: Logged variables do not capture perceived effects.

text: 1) Spread per-location updates over many frames. 2) Compute static values offline or at level load. 3) Compute rarely needed values only when requested.
when: When a game relies heavily on tactical analyses.

text: 1) Use a dynamic trigger volume to detect the event. 2) Route each event to a sound playback object. 3) Assign the appropriate cue to each playback object.
when: sounds trigger from gameplay events

text: 1) Start from a design whose information is fully visible to all players. 2) Add an element of hidden information, adding new concepts if needed. 3) Playtest the modified design. 4) Note how strategy changes and why.
when: When converting a game with an open, perfect-information structure into one with hidden information.
why: Hidden information shifts strategy from calculation toward social cues and deception, which appeals to a different type of player.

text: 1) Schedule actions with varied priorities, expiry times and interrupt abilities. 2) Observe how the queue and active set respond.
when: Learning how an action manager behaves.
why: Watching queue changes reveals how settings interact.

text: Show each node's region in the editor so designers can spot and diagnose misassigned areas faster.
when: When node regions are assigned by Dirichlet domains in a level's path graph.
why: Misclassified regions otherwise take extensive playtesting to discover, which is slow and frustrating for designers.

text: 1) Restate each key question in quantitative terms the data can answer. 2) Query the data for a smaller relevant set. 3) Check whether a meaningful pattern exists or the result is noise; if questions cannot be answered, revisit earlier steps. 4) Ask why repeatedly, listing all plausible root causes and drilling down until the core cause is found. 5) Present findings through visuals, narrative and key metrics, and keep a record. 6) Change the game to fix problems, or make no change if none are found.
when: when analysing game data to inform design
why: A structured path turns data into justified design decisions.

text: 1) Designer sets key questions 2) Analyst chooses metrics that answer them 3) Gameplay programmer adds tracking hooks 4) Database programmer plans storage for easy access 5) Ship updates and collect data over time 6) Clean data before analysis
when: Planning game balance analytics

text: 1) List each unknown that affects outcomes, such as how much luck matters. 2) Express each as a variable in the rating formula. 3) Give each variable an initial guess. 4) Use analytics to estimate its true value.
when: designing a rating system with missing information

text: 1) List each distinct value with its probability. 2) Mean = sum of value × probability. 3) Median from cumulative probability. 4) Standard deviation = square root of probability-weighted squared deviations from the mean.
when: Finding statistics for a value drawn at random from a weighted set

text: 1) Remove redundant data. 2) Interpret what remains. 3) Discard noise.
why: Information comes from stripping redundancy out of raw data, and only what remains useful for a decision yields insight.

text: 1) Read the Intent section to find a pattern matching your current problem. 2) Study Motivation and the distilled Pattern. 3) Check When to Use It and Keep in Mind. 4) Read Design Decisions before implementing.
when: choosing and applying a pattern from a pattern catalog
why: Each use of a pattern differs, so the options must be weighed before coding.

text: 1) Take screenshots and notes during play 2) turn them into analysis sketches afterward.
when: When intense play makes sketching during the session impractical.
why: A journal kept alongside play helps players retain their memories of what happened.

text: Find and clean collected data: fix or remove collection bugs, corrupt values, outliers and gaps, since uncleaned errors distort every later result.
why: Fixing collection bugs in the code means the data does not need to be scrubbed the same way every time.

text: Design analytics hooks early, choosing which data to record and store, and add them during beta so data can be analyzed before release and inform balance decisions.
when: Preparing a game for beta testing.
why: Early data lets designers refine systems before launch.

text: Raw records are not knowledge, and knowledge is not insight; genuine analytics needs statistical analysis and predictive modeling, not merely gathering numbers.
why: The value of collected data comes only when it is paired with managerial, engineering and analytic skill.

text: Analysis needs clear objectives and critical interpretation; check qualitative feedback before acting on a quantitative pattern rather than treating it as a complete diagnosis.
why: Studies are artificial setups, so they cannot deliver simple universal answers to complex issues, and results need critical review before action.

text: Combine primitive tactical analyses only with weighted linear sums, so a simple data file can describe how compound values are formed.
Rely on analytics only when the game can gather live data and be patched after release.
why: Offline or physical games cannot upload play data to servers, and their imbalances are harder to patch.

text: Look at raw collected data to check whether it makes sense before drawing conclusions from it.
when: Telemetry gathered by software that may contain bugs
why: bugs can corrupt data silently

text: Graph or otherwise visualize raw data before trusting statistics derived from it.
why: plots reveal shapes that numbers hide

text: Anchor each dashboard panel to one central value, such as DAU, and draw each series as its own line graph against it.
when: Many values must be compared at once
why: A shared anchor keeps each series readable, while extra encodings like color or 3D quickly become unwieldy.

text: Show MAU as a rolling 30-day average and the DAU/MAU ratio, each as a line graph over time.
Split every metric by player rating so that averages can be read in context and changes can target the right skill level.
when: A game has player accounts and a matchmaking rating system.
why: Averages across all skill levels can hide opposite trends for different players.

text: Check each update, such as new characters, maps or core mechanic changes, against the metrics that motivated it.
when: Evaluating whether an update achieved its goal.
why: Linking updates to their motivating metrics shows whether they worked.

text: Use forward Markov steps to find the likely state after many repetitions; use recursion when a complex event reduces to simpler events with easier probabilities.
when: Deciding how to analyze a repeated random process.
why: Each method fits a different shape of question.

text: Use UX methods to find the root cause of a problem, since problems must be discovered rather than assumed to be obvious.
why: UX work applies knowledge of human cognition and a rigorous method to catch issues developers did not intend, testing hypotheses through standardized protocols.

text: Use analytics only after understanding its limits and human biases, and guide it with a strong UX strategy.
why: Analytics shows what players do, while explaining why they do it requires qualitative research.

text: Tracking an ability requires logging its use, timing and context; for complex rules, capture the full situation at the key event, such as a death.
when: when a hypothesis depends on an ability or a rule
why: use alone cannot explain outcomes

text: Validate telemetry hooks; bad data is worse than no data, because broken events can silently inflate metrics.
when: When analytics instrumentation was never built or verified, or the data collection pipeline has a defect
why: silent failures look like real results

text: Near the end of production, define analytics hypotheses and questions so telemetry hooks can be scheduled for gameplay and business intelligence.
when: End of production

text: From alpha onward, have the analytics pipeline ready and reliable, since marketing and publishing become more involved.
when: Alpha and later
why: Marketing and publishing start weighing in more heavily from alpha.

text: Analytics hooks compete with gameplay work for programmer time, and collected data costs bandwidth, storage and framerate; in high-action games, recording everything can hurt performance, so choose the most important data.
when: Planning to use analytics to inform game balance decisions later
why: Hook programming takes time from building the game itself, and recording everything can drop framerate.

text: Data collection code competes with feature work for limited programming time, so the team must weigh one against the other.
when: planning development tasks
why: programmer hours are finite

text: Frequentist methods are simpler but ignore prior knowledge, while Bayesian methods need heavier math yet can give more realistic estimates.
when: choosing an estimation method

text: An exact full-state transition matrix is accurate but grows explosively with player count, while sampling per-player finish times scales easily but gives an estimate that improves with trial count.
when: Modeling a multi-player race where the joint state space is too large to store.
why: Exact joint states are infeasible beyond small cases, so sampling trades exactness for tractability.

text: Data-driven decisions can mean reacting passively to numbers; data-informed decisions keep decision makers in control while using data.
1) Ask what each sound contributes to the experience. 2) Ask how the player should feel at that point. 3) Use the answers to decide each sound, rather than matching assets to a checklist.
when: Spotting sound for a level with designers.
why: Function-driven choices focus sound on player experience rather than on literal asset coverage.

text: 1) Identify useful elements first. 2) Work out what the artist intended. 3) Open with a positive point before raising problems.
Ignore artwork in early prototypes, since polished visuals slow iteration and make designers reluctant to change things.
when: Early drafts of a physical prototype
why: Spending time on artwork slows the process, and attachment to polished work makes change counterproductive during iteration.

text: Gathering art and music with personal meaning often produces stronger game ideas than brainstorming alone.
when: when generating early concepts for a prototype
why: personal material evokes mood and a clear core idea

text: An animatic is an animated mock-up built without real game technology, so it cannot convey kinesthetic feel.
Iteration loops grow to several days once art is involved, because art is slow to produce.
when: After art is added to a level

text: When art and technology are out of balance, the game feels split down the middle; when balanced, it can be striking.
An art bible may hold character sheets, environment examples, color usage, interface mockups, or any other material that establishes how game elements look.
Making art keeps the hands working while ideas are recorded, pulls people into flow, reducing inhibitions, and puts thoughts on paper that words cannot express.
Modular, reusable art assets save production time and also support teaching methods.
Covering design faults with art hides the mechanical core, so fixing the weakness later means tearing the art off.
when: after a failed playtest
why: Art built around weak mechanics locks them in, since changing them means reworking the art.

text: 1) Prove mechanics on gray boxes. 2) Replace gray shapes with real art. 3) Retest the loop, since art changes how players perceive the encounter. 4) Widen the loop to dialogue, audio, writing, and bug-fix testing before shipping.
when: When gray-box mechanics are replaced with real art assets
why: Art changes how players perceive the encounter even when its mechanical shape stays the same.

text: 1) Build an abstract prototype. 2) Let it suggest how the game should look. 3) Let the art suggest how it should play. 4) Build a new prototype from those insights. 5) Repeat until art and gameplay complement each other.
when: early in a project, while the design is still abstract
why: each cycle grounds the design in both visuals and play

text: 1) Explain your vision to the lead artist or art director. 2) Listen to their response. 3) Review references together, naming what you like and dislike about each.
why: Artists usually have studied more visual references than the designer and can take initial concepts further than the designer could alone.

text: Create an art bible, a guideline document giving several artists shared rules for one consistent look, when they work on one title.
when: Several artists work on one title

text: Attach concrete references such as images, sound files and sketches when briefing other teams.
why: Words alone let collaborators read different meanings into a description, so concrete examples are needed to pin down what is intended.

text: Check whether the design feels right to the designer; team gut feelings also count, and other filters balance their errors.
List every asset to be produced, grouped into categories fitted to the game, such as interface, environments, characters, animation, music, and sound effects.
why: A detailed up-front list with naming conventions prevents confusion when assets are later produced and tracked.

text: Give off-site artists reference material early, since narrative designers need time to find the references they require.
when: when art is outsourced to off-site artists
why: finding references takes time and delays the art

text: Colleagues often underrate sound and music because they do not know what these can do, which is a gap in knowledge rather than intelligence.
when: Audio is often underrepresented in team decisions
why: Others lack knowledge of sound and music's capabilities

text: Audio director, audio manager, audio lead, sound designer, audio designer, technical sound designer, audio engineer, audio programmer, audio integrator, audio implementer, voice director, note tracker, music transcriber, composer, music director.
Junior writers frequently aren't brought in during a project's earliest conception or planning, especially on writing teams. This is normal.
The only reliable way to judge an interactive music solution is to test it in the game it belongs to.
why: Music's time-based structure collides with game events that can occur at any moment, so problems only surface in actual play.

text: Plan branching dialogue carefully before recording, since its line count grows fast enough to make late changes costly.
why: Each line must be recorded in several versions, one per character and per gender choice, so the total line count multiplies quickly.

text: Keep actors' voices fresh with plain water, avoid milk, tea and coffee which build phlegm, and offer gum or green apples to stimulate saliva.
when: Running long voice recording sessions
why: Some drinks and dryness impair vocal clarity and comfort

text: Start new stories with a linear core concept, which shows whether a more complex structure would actually improve the story.
when: Developing any new story
why: A linear draft tests whether added complexity pays off.

text: A story reaches its potential only when it is integrated into game production, so teamwork is essential.
why: Story is delivered through the work of other disciplines, so an isolated narrative effort cannot succeed on its own.

text: Audio job titles are used inconsistently across studios. One studio's audio engineer may run recording sessions while another's audio engineer is an audio programmer.
why: Titles do not reliably indicate duties, so role descriptions must be read closely.

text: 1) Pick colleagues who know nothing about the feature and fit the target audience. 2) Test the feature with each one. 3) Tweak the design and retest with another colleague.
when: Studios that cannot recruit external participants
why: Internal testing gives quick feedback when external recruiting is impossible.

text: 1) Write the script early. 2) Have voice actors record and improvise lines. 3) Revise lines and design characters around the performances. 4) Repeat recording sessions as the project evolves.
when: Developing narrative-heavy games where emotional performance matters
why: Iterative recording lets performance drive character design and produces stronger emotional impact

text: 1) Open the Content Browser. 2) Use the package tree to find the sound's group. 3) Search by name, or filter by object type such as Sounds. 4) Double-click a sound name to hear it.
Track ambient lines in a spreadsheet or similar tool, since they are numerous, separate and disconnected from one another.
when: A project contains many ambient lines.
why: Such tools easily track many separate single lines, which are quick to write and record, so late additions stay manageable.

text: Repetition check: 1) Ask QA testers to log how often each ambient line plays. 2) Add variants for lines that repeat too often.
when: Testing ambient or bark audio before release.
why: Hearing the same line repeated quickly irritates players, so the frequency of each line has to be watched.

text: 1) Show the evaluator ten sample levels per generator. 2) Let them play one level. 3) Show an estimated playability from simulation. 4) Show a cloud overlay of levels to reveal shared patterns.
when: judging generators whose output varies
why: Multiple samples reveal the generator's real range, not one artefact.

text: Name audio packages with the prefix A_, for example A_TutorialTestpackage.
when: creating a package for imported sounds
why: follows the engine's naming convention

text: Attend voice-over sessions when possible to clarify unclear notes and advise the voice director on delivery.
when: When the writer is given the chance to attend voice-over sessions.
why: Actors record out of sequence without full context, so attending lets the writer resolve unclear notes directly.

text: Matching paper totals don't guarantee balance; play is the final judge of fairness, and workable values like grid size, hex size or wall density can only be learned by playing.
why: Numeric models are untested theories, and only play reveals whether the resulting gameplay actually feels fair.

text: Patches typically fix pervasive problems that escaped testing: feature problems, incompatibility issues, and medium- and high-severity bugs.
when: After a game has shipped and can be updated online.

text: On a 1-5 pacing scale: 1 is slow grind (very hard on first encounter, roadblocks, oversized or artificially slow), 3 is average, and 5 is fast and easy (overleveled or overprepared, little resistance).
when: Rating sections of a game's progression.

text: Check whether a fix overshot its target, since monitoring can reveal that a correction went too far.
when: Monitoring a change meant to fix slow progression or difficulty
why: A change made to fix a problem may fall short or overshoot, so its actual effect has to be measured.

text: Pacing ratings: 2 is slight grind, a little slower than normal without standing out as frustrating; 4 is slightly easy, a little faster than normal but not instantly blasted through.
when: Refining the 1-5 pacing scale for sections near average.

text: Learning by doing takes more time, so those players meet fewer enemies and die less, which can make a tutorial look better because of pacing rather than teaching.
when: comparing tutorial methods by death counts
why: Time spent and encounter rate differ between groups and drive the outcome.

text: 1) Track hit points and actions on paper or a whiteboard. 2) Add or remove rules. 3) Repeat until the rules feel ready to code.
when: when balancing turn-based combat before coding
why: Paper versions are fast to make yet capture much of the same play, so flaws surface before any code is written.

text: Give content creators a path to add plays, because programmers rarely know every play and do not want to test every combination.
Expect to balance the game from the start, and build systems that make the values you will need to change easy to change.
when: Early in production, while you can still choose how values are stored and exposed.
why: Balancing is continuous, so values must be adjustable without rewriting code.

text: Finance is not beyond you: learn enough business to think and talk with producers, executives, and marketers, without mastering every detail, to be a valuable team member, not a specialist.
why: Business decisions are bets on human psychology, a field designers already know, so financial reasoning is within reach.
