text: Overhead covers nonlabor costs needed to run the business, such as rent, utilities, supplies, and insurance; an accountant should calculate the true overhead percentage from real costs.
Markup is the percentage charged above costs, letting a developer earn money on a production if it is managed closely and meets expectations.
The budget is often one of the first documents made, because it helps secure funding.
A company prospectus works as a studio résumé, listing location, project history, technologies, staff by department and shipped titles.
Pitches can be made more concrete than text through one-page design, prototyping, or journeys, each making the idea experienceable rather than only described.
when: Presenting a game idea to an audience

text: Business skill matters as much as design skill for transformational games, since sustainable business models for them are hard to find.
why: A game cannot change anyone if its makers cannot afford to build it or deliver it.

text: Treat every business interaction as a chance to learn, since the relationships built with businesspeople make a designer better at the craft.
why: Showing respect for the business process builds better ties with the businesspeople who fund and publish your game.

text: Designers who understand players, the market, and how deals are structured make better commercial decisions about a design.
Arguing against a funder who is fully caught up in inflated expectations rarely changes their mind.
when: When pitching to a funder caught up in inflated expectations about a technology
why: Their backing rests on a belief about a technology's profit potential rather than the design's merits.

text: Aggregators provide no production funds, so the developer must finance the game.
Calculating overhead incorrectly causes developers to underprice their work and lose money.
1) Collaborate tightly with all departments to estimate tasks. 2) Keep the budget evolving to stay within allocation.
when: Estimating and tracking game cost
why: The producer alone cannot estimate accurately

text: Treat memory budgeting as part of the creative process, because RAM is limited and costs money.
when: Planning sound design scope
why: Memory limits shape which sounds can be made

text: Learn the goals of every party involved, including publishers, console makers, and retailers, and understand the contract and deal structure for your own game.
why: Knowing each party's needs helps get original ideas produced and published

text: Choose tactic weights so that no connection's total cost can become negative, since standard algorithms such as A* do not support negative costs.
when: Setting weights for tactical pathfinding
why: A* assumes non-negative costs; negative costs break the search

text: Even a basic cost/power sheet needs two subtotal columns, one summing costs and one summing benefits.

Common playtest failure sources are unblinded testers with expectations, group tests creating social competition, think-aloud requests changing behavior, biased tester selection, and small samples with high variance.
Free open-source bug trackers are recommended for tracking bugs, though paid bug databases also exist.
Scripting debug tools may never ship in the final game but are needed to ship it, and in a moddable game they ship too.
Treat a bug report about your design as a chance to fix the problem before players see it.
when: When QA lists a design feature as a bug
why: QA is the last check before release, so flagged problems can be fixed before players meet them.

text: Dismissing a game as just polished underrates how polish sells interaction, and how it supports game feel and the player's sense of discovery.
when: Evaluating or discussing a game's feel
why: Polish creates the feeling of a physical reality, letting players infer possible interactions and feel discovery.

text: Apparent common-sense usability problems still ship, due to the curse of knowledge, habituation, or competing priorities.
why: Developers know the game too well, stop noticing familiar issues, or face other priorities.

text: Getting defensive about bug reports on your features undermines the working relationship with QA.
when: When QA lists your design feature as a bug
why: A bug report on a feature is QA helping confirm the design works, not criticism of the design.

text: Cosmetic and low-severity issues are usually not patched, so players may keep complaining about them after launch.
when: When a game is patched after launch
why: Post-launch patches are kept small and aimed at pervasive problems, while minor bugs are judged unobtrusive and shipped.

text: 1) Check the design document or rule sheet first. 2) Plug each hole so the rules make sense. 3) Expect fixes to affect other parts of the game and plan several testing sessions.
when: Fixing rule gaps found in testing
why: Rules that look clear on paper often hide gaps, and filling one gap can ripple into other systems.

text: 1) Owner fixes the bug and the fix is tied to a build. 2) The bug returns to QA. 3) QA retests it. 4) QA marks it resolved only when satisfied.
why: Assigning each bug to an owner and tying fixes to a numbered build keeps a record of who fixed what, and where.

text: 1) Hold a triage meeting to assess the current code state. 2) Prioritize bugs. 3) Work through the database starting from the highest priority.
why: Console titles can carry several thousand bugs, more than can be fixed at once.

text: Separate the playability checker from the generator and run it as a machine playtester to flag flaws in hand-made levels.
when: Validating levels with automated checks
why: The checker was first built to reject generated levels, so the same logic can point out flaws in hand-made ones.

text: Judge completeness only after the game is functional.
why: Gaps in rules and win conditions only show once a newcomer can play through unaided.

text: Include player state, such as tutorial or progression position, and platform details like version and memory in feedback, because this information helps find bugs.
when: When collecting bug reports from players
why: Progression state and platform specs narrow down where a bug occurs.

text: Fix problems under pressure with small, controlled, iterative changes, because a rushed fix can unbalance the game and create new problems.
when: when schedule or crisis pressure invites a quick fix
why: Interdependent systems let one rushed change spread side effects.

text: Observe QA going through the game element by element, since experienced testers can offer insights no one else has.
why: Testers' experience gives them a view no one else on the team has.

text: Each bug record should hold a description, exact steps to reproduce, severity, and the name of the tester who found it.
Assign each bug to a specific owner, such as sending a database bug to the database programmer, so fixes can be tracked by build.
why: It makes the repair history traceable to the responsible person and to a specific version of the project.

text: Near the end of production, a producer may defer remaining minor bugs, such as small non-gameplay cosmetic errors, since nearly every game ships with some.
when: near the end of production
why: Nearly every shipped game has some remaining minor bugs.

text: Testing late, whether playtests, usability tests or core mechanics, leaves too little time to fix flaws; essential elements can no longer change and critical UX issues become costlier to fix.
when: When new features are first tested by researchers only after they have been built

text: Involve artists and sound designers early to avoid late catch-up and visual-driven design change; add art and audio as late as possible so they still yield useful test data.
when: Scheduling art and audio work
why: Early involvement avoids late catch-up and design change; late addition keeps test data useful.

text: Once a feature is committed, teams resist drastic change; late changes cost more because they ripple through production and force rework of art, animation and code.
why: Accepting that a committed feature needs drastic change is hard, and any such change propagates through all dependent production.

text: Waiting for beta or content lock to playtest lets critical flaws survive into costly late development, leaving core problems unfixable and only top-level features changeable.
when: Planning playtest schedule for a large project
why: Late discovery leaves little room to redesign dependent content.

text: Deferring analytics, balance work or marketing input to late development leaves too little time to act on what they reveal.
when: When balance or analytics work is postponed to the final stretch of production
why: Late involvement removes time to act on that insight.

text: Story changes are cheap, gameplay changes can take weeks of balancing, and technology changes can take months of reprogramming.
Standardized content pipelines with run-time tools integrated into development tools are considered essential for large games and are spreading to smaller studios.
The last UX maturity stages are much harder to reach than the early ones, especially the final stage.
Games are built in approved stages, each ending at a milestone, and developers are usually paid a fixed amount when each milestone is reached.
why: Publisher contracts tie payment to milestones.

text: Close to shipping, story problems such as plot holes may be marked Will Not Fix, since only crash-level changes are accepted that late.
when: near release

text: Apply controlled-change techniques at every revision stage, most of all when fine-tuning a game that works marginally well, so earlier work is preserved.
when: Revising any stage of the game
why: Changing many things at once can spiral out of control and discard earlier work that already functioned.

text: As production proceeds, core design and software become harder to change, since the goal is an eventual release; early prototyping prevents costly mistakes.
why: Software design grows rigid once production starts, so prototyping before then catches mistakes while they can still be avoided.

text: Stretch goals, such as an added feature at a higher total, give backers a free reason to promote the campaign.
when: Designing a crowdfunding campaign with stretch goals
why: Backers gain from the added content and so spread the word at no cost.

text: Late changes to a console game are costly and can delay the release date, causing a team to miss its market window.
when: When the console maker tests and reviews the game before its release
why: The console maker holds final approval and can return a game with significant flaws, so changes there can delay release.

text: A sprint lasts a few weeks and ends with a concrete working deliverable.
when: When a team uses agile development rather than pursuing one long, multimonth goal

text: Testing only at beta, after assets are finished, is too late to fix basic design problems, so playtest level ideas at every production stage.
when: When evaluating level ideas during design, before asset production is finished

text: Leaving compound actions out of an AI design until late forces a rewrite of the decision tool, including save and load formats, engine links and scripting bindings.
when: When the AI's decision output must run several actions at once
why: Separate decision routines struggle to coordinate actions that must execute together.

text: Cutting content late in development to save the schedule is a common cause of games that are dead on arrival.
when: late production with schedule pressure
why: Time runs out, leaving known mistakes unfixed and the remaining game patched by amputations.

text: Focus tests often aim to sell a game rather than improve it, and they often happen too late to change much.
Adding research topics midway, especially near deadlines, makes completing the research harder and slows progress.
when: running worldbuilding research under a schedule
why: Late additions compete with work already due.

text: Environmental storytelling cannot patch plot holes found late in production; planning late leaves writers filling gaps with desperate text.
when: Late-stage narrative production
why: Environment and mechanics need lead time

text: Building an area that exists only after a player choice is expensive, and few players will see it, so the team must agree early.
when: When a player choice opens an entirely new area in the world
why: Such content is hard to add at the end of development.

text: Treating game UX as a late task or as only interface design misses its role; it should guide every development step.
Finished content can be destroyed by a late change to something it depends on.
why: Animations built for one movement speed must be redone when that speed changes.

text: Develop a system through successive spiral iterations, starting from the middle and cycling through four quadrants: 1) Create a basic design. 2) Identify the greatest risks. 3) Build prototypes that mitigate them. 4) Test the prototypes. 5) Produce a more detailed design from what was learned. 6) Return to the risk step. Repeat until the system is done.
when: Developing a system through successive iterations
why: Each iteration addresses the greatest remaining risks while refining the design, converting test results into a more detailed design and new risk assessment.

text: 1) List concerns about gameplay, aesthetics, kinesthetics and technology. 2) Rank them and mark any that would kill the game if they failed. 3) Focus the first digital prototype on the top concern. 4) Propose a simple solution, starting with something like controls or interface. 5) Build the prototype and test it.
when: When a game concept has open concerns that could make it fail
why: Prototypes validate or refute ideas rather than generate them, so each one should test a clear claim.

text: 1) Everyone experiences what the sprint produced at a demo day. 2) The team performs risk analysis. 3) The team plans the next sprint. 4) The team holds a retrospective on what works, what fails, and how to adjust.
when: at the end of each sprint
why: Demos give a shared baseline for planning, and retrospectives review how the team works, not the product.

text: 1) Record each publisher approval and decision in writing. 2) Log every requested change as a change request. 3) Use these records to justify extra budget for added features.
when: When a publisher requests design changes during production
why: Written records of approvals and decisions give the producer grounds to negotiate a bigger budget.

text: 1) Put the point of contact first, even if it is not you. 2) Give a short high-level summary with only critical data. 3) Add a bullet list, one sentence per point. 4) Organise sections by discipline or topic. 5) Link in-depth material. 6) Edit repeatedly, with an editor if available, and update the document.
when: when writing emails, documents or wiki pages for the team
why: Team readers have heavy workloads and skip walls of text

text: Change one thing at a time in response to playtest notes, because batch changes make it hard to tell which change caused which effect.
when: Revising a prototype from playtest feedback
why: With several variables altered together, the effect of each one cannot be separated out.

text: Once a game is functional, complete, and balanced, test whether its fun essence survived rather than whether the core idea is fun.
when: Late testing stage
why: Building out a game can change it, so its original appeal must be confirmed rather than assumed.

text: After alpha, additions to core design usually need a formal Change Request process.
when: Post-alpha production.
why: Locked design makes unplanned changes costly.

text: Change a game system only to serve a chosen player experience goal, not for its own sake.
Make prototype changes based on problems observed in play, not on problems imagined in advance.
when: Iterating a prototype
why: Observed failures are real; imagined ones may never occur in play.

text: When scope exceeds capacity, cut anything that does not enhance the game's core actions.
when: When the team cannot change the amount of planned content it must build
why: A core loop that is not fun leaves nothing worth shipping, so peripheral work has to go.

text: Designers can only steer the broad strokes of a creative process; no loop or schedule can direct its details.
why: Knowledge arises from many unscheduled sources.

text: New animations close to content lock are expensive and risk breaking other systems, while removing an existing upgrade is cheap but can disrupt economy balance.
when: Choosing between a new feature and removing an existing one late in development
why: Each option carries different cost and risk profiles.

text: Scatter plots, area charts and radar charts exist beyond bars, pies and lines; most of them can be made in a spreadsheet.
Engineers should prepare the pipeline overview for artists, keeping it as simple as possible.
why: Integrating art assets is hard, and artists need explicit rules for their content to display correctly.

text: Developing a consistent personal spreadsheet style, like a programmer's coding style, keeps sheets readable across projects.
when: Maintaining many spreadsheets over time.
why: Consistency lets you and collaborators read a sheet quickly.

text: A shared game overview helps separate teams, including strike teams, coordinate work and break down silos.
why: Developers absorbed in one task can lose track of how their feature fits the whole game.

text: Adding too many series to one graph, or switching to 3D, makes it unwieldy and harder to read.
when: When comparing many values on one graph
why: Charts hold only so much density, and extra encodings such as color or depth quickly become unwieldy.

text: Near the end of pre-production, print a large poster showing gameplay loops, systems, key features, and how players progress toward goals.
when: late pre-production
why: Stepping back from narrow task focus restores a view of the experience as a whole.

text: Share the game overview with support teams such as marketing and analytics so they keep the intended experience in view.
why: Non-development teams gain a shared reference point for the intended direction when they can see the overview.

text: Update the overview poster whenever prototyping reveals new information or the game changes direction.
when: When prototyping turns up discoveries or the game must change direction
why: keeps the big picture accurate

text: 1) List a game's cheats or hidden debug features. 2) For each one, infer how testers would use it to reach or check content. 3) Relate the set to how it makes testing more efficient.
When a short-deadline brief arrives, build the new concept on earlier prototypes that already embody the core idea.
why: Earlier designs can be turned into a concept within days.

text: Rebuilding a simple commercial game on paper reveals how its system is built.
when: When first practicing analysis of existing game systems
why: Repeated practice of system analysis deepens understanding of mechanic types and sharpens design skill.

text: Reuse, fake, or adapt existing code in prototypes rather than writing production-quality software.
why: Prototypes exist to test ideas roughly and quickly, so their code need not be production quality.

text: Reusing existing animation saves time and money, which can decide whether a sequence is worth creating.
why: Animations reused across areas and scenes lower the cost of each use of a sequence.

text: Read the licence terms of any sample code before reusing it, even when the licence is liberal.
Save a package after importing into it; an unsaved package is marked with an asterisk, so check for one before testing.
when: After importing new assets into a package, before using them
why: An unsaved package carries an asterisk, making the unsaved state visible before testing.

text: The community manager role combines three functions: nurturing, listening, and encouraging.
Depending on staff to catch cheaters increases support workload and hands enforcement to customer service teams.
when: In competitive online games where winning brings prizes or status
why: Community staff are meant to provide service, so punishing players conflicts with that role.

text: Community does not appear by chance; provide communication and organization tools so players can connect and coordinate with each other.
Community managers should plant seeds and respond to specific needs they observe, rather than creating the community directly.
On unreliable hardware, compatibility work costs much development time, but a reputation for guaranteed reliability can sway buyers more than extra content.
when: the platform's hardware is unreliable
why: Buyers of a new, unreliable hardware format sought out the one title known to run dependably on it, so reliability became the selling point.

text: Direct download sells games straight to consumers over an internet connection, removing publisher, retailer, platform holder, and disc manufacturer; developer keeps roughly 70% of price.
when: self-publishing via storefronts
why: Fewer intermediaries take a share of each sale, so more of the price reaches the developer.

text: Console developers know the exact target machine, so AI budgets can be fixed in milliseconds and algorithms judged against a known limit.
Console technical requirements fix standards such as frame rate, which can differ by region.
Faster processors help, but they do not solve the core problem of slow algorithms.
Some consoles and many handheld devices lack the general networking that remote AI debugging requires.
State the distribution method, such as DVD, internet, or wireless, and the requirements that method imposes on the game.
Games written for one known machine could assume its CPU speed, so their pacing depended only on how much work each frame did.
when: fixed console or home computer with known hardware
why: The developer knew the exact hardware, so timing could be tuned to it.

text: Consoles require a demo mode that runs automatically when the player is idle at the main menu, to prevent screen burn-in and suit store kiosks.
when: Shipping a game on consoles or kiosk displays.
why: Static menus can burn in screens, and kiosks need attract-mode play.

text: Config-driven locating mattered less for standardized consoles, but matters more now that games target many different mobile devices.
Early 3D games used vector worlds and perspective projections, and first-person shooters became practical 3D gamespaces once they could present interactive worlds convincingly.
when: Tracing the history of 3D game spaces
why: Technical limits shaped what kinds of 3D spaces early games could offer.

text: Licence-driven publishers can focus heavily on consoles; one publisher's releases were 69% console, 22% handheld, and 9% computer.
Digital games hold far more data than tabletop games, so working backward from their numbers is harder.
Console publishers owe the hardware maker a per-unit license fee, typically $3 to $10, in addition to retail margin, marketing, freight, operating expenses, and creation costs.
Consoles account for roughly two thirds of video game sales, and the hardware market has historically been dominated by one or two companies.
New console hardware arrives every three to five years.
A new console with a high price and few games sells slowly; price cuts and a growing game library are needed to lift adoption.
when: when launching a console with a small library at a high price
why: Buyers need affordable hardware and a large selection before they commit

text: High-end console development costs have risen since the 1980s and now typically run $13 to $30 million, while launch prices stayed at about $50.
when: Producing a high-end console title for newer hardware generations.
why: Players expect more and better media that uses the capabilities of newer hardware, and media capacity has grown enormously.

text: Early commercial games were tiny, ranging from roughly 4 to 28 kilobytes including all art and sound.
when: Describing commercial digital games from the 1970s and early 1980s.
why: Early machines had little capacity, so titles stayed small enough for one person to build.

text: Console frame rates impose fixed deadlines: processing must finish within about 33 ms at 30 Hz, 20 ms at 50 Hz, and 16 ms at 60 Hz.
when: targeting 30, 50 or 60 Hz frame rates
why: Consoles require steady frame rates

text: A typical console title has several thousand bugs in its database.
Downloadable console games typically sell for $5 to $15.

Console licensing splits the work: the publisher handles concept, development, testing, marketing, and distribution; the console maker approves the concept, tests, approves the final version, and manufactures.
when: Third-party publishers developing a game under a console licensing deal.
why: Approval rights let the maker confirm a title functions in every circumstance and clears its quality bar.

text: On consoles with a separate SIMD unit, communication and synchronization can outweigh the speed gain for short code sections.
when: short sections on a console with a separate SIMD unit
why: transfer and sync overhead

text: List all the software and hardware needed to produce the game.
Expect the console maker to hold final approval, able to block release or return a game with significant flaws until they are fixed.
when: When the console maker finds flaws it considers significant during testing.
why: Its quality standards must be met, and serious flaws it finds can be sent back for repair before release.

text: Console releases pay per-unit royalties to platform holders, while computer releases avoid them but reach a smaller market.
An observed correlation can have four explanations: X causes Y, Y causes X, a hidden third factor such as player expertise drives both, or chance produces it.
when: Interpreting a correlation, such as two behaviors moving together.
why: Two linked variables may be driven by one another, a hidden shared factor, or chance, and the correlation alone cannot tell these apart.

text: A confounding variable is a hidden third factor that changes with the tested variable and drives both measured variables, producing a correlation or difference instead of the design change.
why: Such a factor makes the two variables correlate without either causing the other.

text: Acting on a correlation as if it were an actionable cause without further evidence can lead to changes that do not work or do nothing.
why: A correlation alone cannot separate a true cause from a hidden factor or chance, so the change may target the wrong variable.

text: Correlation describes whether two data sets move together (direct, positive) or in opposite directions (inverse, negative).
CORREL pairs two equally sized ranges cell by cell and returns a correlation coefficient describing how the two move together.
When many unrelated variables are compared, some strong correlations appear by chance, and small samples make such chance results more likely.
Correlations describe general trends rather than absolutes; random variance can occasionally reverse them, so strong real correlations rarely reach exactly ±1.
why: Noise shifts observed coefficients away from the extremes

text: Correlated variables can have several distinct root causes, so list alternative explanations before acting on a correlation.
when: When two variables are noticed to be correlated.
why: One observed relationship can arise from a direct cause, reverse cause, shared factor, or chance.

text: Correlational findings suggest leads, but usually need further research before a causal conclusion is drawn.
when: When findings rest on correlational studies.
why: A relationship between two variables does not by itself reveal whether one causes the other.

text: The correlation coefficient ranges from -1 to 1: 1 means perfect direct correlation, -1 perfect inverse correlation, and 0 no correlation.
Treating a correlation as proof of cause is a common mistake: co-movement does not show which variable causes the other or whether a third factor drives both.
when: Interpreting two metrics or behaviors that move together.
why: Two variables can move together without one causing the other; the coefficient only measures that co-movement.

text: Treating a correlation between gaming and a problem as proof that gaming caused it.
when: reading negative-impact studies
why: many such studies are correlational

text: When computing a correlation, use two ranges of identical dimensions with each value aligned to its matching value in the other range.
when: Computing a correlation coefficient in a spreadsheet or script.
why: Mismatched pairs or differently sized ranges produce a meaningless coefficient.

text: Correlational studies alone cannot show whether a game built a skill or whether already-skilled people chose the game.
when: when evaluating claims that games improve skills
why: Self-selection and reverse causation confound correlations.

text: Cognitive biases distort how analysts read data and how players behave, so telemetry must be interpreted in context. Named types include survivorship, self-fulfilling prophecy, confirmation and decoy effects.
Candor means forming your own opinions and stating them clearly, even when disagreeing with a superior or a group is uncomfortable.
Completeness is partly objective and partly subjective, and any game can be called complete until someone finds a flaw.
Being honest with yourself and with players about results tends to yield the most useful insight.
when: When playtesting an early prototype or game idea.
why: Owners who explain away feedback or feel an idea is not ready lose ideas that could have been fixed.

text: Before dismissing criticism, check your own sensitivity, whether the criticism is truly harmful, and how other testers react to it.
when: When a playtester's critical comments make you feel offended.
why: Feedback is meant to be learned from, and one skewed tester can distort results, so reactions need checking first.

text: When a disagreement stalls, ask whether you might be wrong.
when: When teammates reject an idea you are attached to and the debate stalls.
why: Strong attachment to a sudden inspiration makes it hard to judge an idea objectively during disputes.

text: Check whether a motivational tactic points people toward the game or toward personal rewards before using it.
when: When choosing how to motivate a team.
why: Tactics aimed at personal rewards can pull effort away from the game.

text: Common sense only holds what is already established, so it cannot anticipate undiscovered usability issues; assuming it suffices to skip iteration is a fallacy.
when: When people argue a design should succeed on its first pass without iteration.
why: Common sense only covers what is already known, so it cannot reveal problems no one has yet encountered.

text: Pressure to confirm a hypothesis can introduce unconscious bias, and in extreme cases fraud. People seek data supporting existing beliefs and ignore contrary evidence, which social media feeds amplify.
Treating sound spotting as a checklist of assets, such as hearing a shaft because it is seen, misses what each sound is for.
when: When starting sound implementation before game mechanics or scripting are in place.
why: Each sound should serve a purpose tied to what players feel and what happens in gameplay or story; matching assets to visible objects misses that.

text: 1) Assess each applicant alone and as a fit for the group. 2) Review their past work record. 3) Consult former collaborators about personal output and how they behave within a group.
why: Talent alone is not enough; someone who cannot work productively with teammates can cost the group more than they contribute.

text: Tell testers you need help finding problems, since they avoid hurting feelings, especially if they think you made the game.
when: When playtesters know or believe you helped make the game.
why: Testers soften criticism to spare the feelings of someone they believe built the game.

text: Recompute worked numerical examples from the stated formula before using them as test cases, since printed figures may not follow the formula.
when: Using example numbers from design documents or books as expected values
why: Printed arithmetic can contain errors

text: Read the whole text carefully before commenting, since skimming produces weak notes.
when: When reviewing a colleague's document and giving feedback on it.

text: Designers tend to treat their own discipline's element as primary: designers favor mechanics, artists favor aesthetics, engineers favor technology and writers favor story.
when: when a team discusses which element matters most
why: Each discipline sees the game through its own element

text: Designers tell narrative staff about changes only when they feel comfortable doing so, so building good working relationships with them matters.
when: cross-discipline projects
why: comfort determines whether changes get communicated

text: Narrative designers work with programming, game design, level design, art and sound to integrate story with the available mechanics, designs and assets.
Understanding how your ideas affect other teams' work makes you more useful and welcome on a team.
when: On large AAA productions where many specialist teams depend on each other.
why: Upstream teams supply your tools and go-ahead, while downstream teams wait on your finished output.

text: Consult domain experts, such as geologists for terrain, to ground an environment in realistic natural processes.
Relying on other people for knowledge raises process burden, because every task then needs spec writing and discussion.
why: Specs and discussion can take longer than the actual implementation, so overhead dominates each task.

text: Confer with every discipline while writing the design document, since the writing process itself creates communication across the team.
why: Without a shared document, team members interpret the game their own way, so art, tech and gameplay drift apart at integration.

text: 1) Involve sound, design, and art teams early so they take ownership. 2) Explain how each team can contribute, with examples. 3) Make narrative decisions early. 4) For each element, state its purpose and what mechanics or levels can say.
when: Planning environmental narrative with teams
why: Each narrative use adds time to another department's schedule

text: Learn the language of other disciplines so you can understand their problems and find solutions that serve both sides.
why: Grasping other disciplines' problems from their viewpoint lets you reach joint solutions that serve both sides.

text: Communicate with other disciplines at all times and keep iterating on narrative content.
Balance narrative needs against interdependent departments, and know when to put others' needs ahead of your own work.
If a change affects another discipline, clear it by email first and get agreement from everyone involved.
when: When feedback would lead to changes that affect other disciplines.

text: Asking for a larger amount does not seem to make backers give more.
when: Choosing a crowdfunding target
why: Backer generosity does not scale with the ask.

text: Set the lowest workable funding target, since missing an all-or-nothing target means receiving nothing; raise more later if the campaign succeeds.
when: Planning a crowdfunding campaign with all-or-nothing rules
why: A reachable target protects the campaign from total failure.

text: Keep rewards simple. Early release at a good price is the main draw, while extra items add mailing work and little funding.
when: Designing crowdfunding reward tiers
why: Many tiers overwhelm backers and extra merchandise changes funding little.

text: Plan about one month to design the page and video, one month to run the campaign, and one month to fulfill rewards, totaling two to three months.
when: Scheduling a crowdfunding campaign
why: Campaign preparation and fulfillment take substantial time away from building the game.

text: Crowdfunding works as a preorder system, not an investment or charity; backers want something special, early access, and a good price.
when: Framing a crowdfunding campaign
why: Backers pay to get the product early, not for a financial return.

text: Treating crowdfunding as easy money or as a shortcut that skips pitching leads to poor results.
when: Planning funding strategy
why: Crowdfunding still requires a compelling pitch and substantial work.

text: Crowdfunding fits physical products or games priced at about twenty dollars or more; free-to-play games struggle because little reason exists to pay before trying.
when: Deciding whether crowdfunding suits a game
why: Backers need a reason to pay upfront before playing.

text: Crunch and lack of inclusivity harm staff health and creativity, which in turn lowers game quality.
why: Overtime and exclusion erode staff well-being and creativity, which lowers the quality of the games released.

text: In a 2023 developer survey, 28% of developers said their job involved crunch time; 63% of those had crunched more than twice in two years.
Do not encourage crunch; use measures that avoid overtime as much as possible.
Give too much information in briefs rather than too little, and invite questions, especially the first time documents are shared with a team.
when: When sharing a document with a team for the first time, or with a team you have not worked with before.
why: Team members differ in writing and speaking styles.

text: A design document shaped by the game's own needs, not by a template, is the result of recording what must be remembered and communicated.
why: Noting open questions and their resolved answers, with reasons, lets the structure grow out of the project itself.

text: A description that is too general hides the unique idea.
when: Writing a one-liner description
why: Vague wording removes what makes the idea distinct

text: Each game needs its own memory and communication documents, discovered for that game; no magic or industry-standard template exists, or ever will, so shape structure around the game.
why: Each game's memory and communication needs differ, so no single format fits all.

text: The game designer is the primary author of the living design document or game bible, keeping it current throughout production as the team makes decisions.
when: When a game is complex and the team is large, not when the team is very small or working alone.
why: Writing down the overall vision and a detailed plan makes sure every team member receives the same communication.

text: The detailed design document is often the thickest yet seldom kept current, and often abandoned midway because the running game holds the details; keep it small enough to be useful.
when: Mid-project in development
why: The running game becomes the authoritative record of details

text: Faced with a list of use cases, programmers tend to code each case separately because it is the least effortful approach.
when: when a problem arrives as a list of use cases
why: Handling each case separately requires the least upfront effort.

text: A detailed design document may be weighed more than it is read, and a clear presentation of why the game will sell is even better.
when: When pitching a game to win a publishing or funding deal.
why: Reviewers need proof the game will be fun and profitable, not just the creator's belief that it will be.

text: A design document covers overview and vision, target audience, platform and marketing, gameplay, interfaces, controls, levels, and media list, plus characters, story and world where the game has them.
A technical design document covers systems such as screen rendering and network data, and helps new team members understand how the system is meant to work.
A system limitations document records hard limits such as polygons on screen, update messages per second, or simultaneous explosions.
Tech artists keep visuals working inside the limits set by the engine and code.
A game is functional but incomplete when its rules have gaps, even if its core systems run.
when: Reviewing a prototype

text: An internally complete game lets players operate it without any point where gameplay or functionality is compromised.
Laws are explicit clarifications of rules, written once competitive play becomes serious enough to need records of sportsmanship or rule interpretation. Over time they can merge into official rules.
when: A game has a competitive scene
why: Competitive play exposes ambiguities that require written answers.

text: Advisory rules are tips for playing better and are not mechanics in the strict sense.
when: Distinguishing strategy advice from game rules
why: They guide play without changing how the game works.

text: The design overview is a brief, high-level document of a few pages that explains what the title is and its target audience, without deep detail.
Intent is the purpose behind work: what a piece of content is for, which goals it serves, and what role a system plays in the overall design.
The detailed design document describes all game mechanics and interfaces, serving designers' memory and helping engineers and artists.
The game design document is the written plan that communicates a game's vision and how to execute it to everyone on the team.
A technical design document rarely stays current past the midpoint, yet writing it is often essential to architecting systems and starting code.
A technical design overview states the engine, tools, hardware, code history and middleware in terms non-engineers can follow.
Story content is implemented with level and quest editors, spreadsheets or scripting languages, often needing level design, art production and programming help.
Novel questions may require custom protocols, such as for elderly players, new data analysis for unusual economies, or new brainstorming formats for teams across continents.
The detailed design document is seldom seen by outsiders and is often messy, with just enough detail to spark discussion.
A design document is out of date as soon as it is written.
Game documents serve exactly two purposes: memory and communication, and their form should follow from what the team must remember and share.
A project plan covers goals, deliverables, schedule, and budget, showing the team has thought them through.
A developer's project plan is arguably the top deliverable, and once approved it is typically attached to the contract.

Each discipline uses the document differently: artists lay out interfaces, programmers define modules, level designers place levels in the story arc, producers build budgets and schedules, and QA writes test plans.
Large teams and complex games make written documentation essential, and most publishers expect a design document before production starts.
A design document typically takes about a dozen passes to complete, and it keeps needing updates as development changes the design.
Co-authored by the whole team, a living design document becomes a shared platform that unites everyone and helps them understand the evolving game; solo-written documents are less valuable.
why: Collaboration engages the team and focuses it on the current project.

text: Break the game into modules when many systems interact and changes keep causing surprise side effects.
when: During revisions of a game built from several interrelated subsystems
why: Dividing the design into separate functional parts makes visible how each part's mechanics connect to the others.

text: Number lists of ideas, since numbering lets items be referred to easily in discussion and makes them seem more important.
Label every element in a flow diagram so that each one clearly represents something specific.
Consistent formatting makes data easier to find and reduces errors when editing or adding entries to a spreadsheet.
when: a spreadsheet is edited or extended by others
why: Because collaborators read spreadsheets directly rather than compiling them, layout works like a coding style aimed at the people using the sheet.

text: Answer basic questions such as victory conditions, screen density, and time pressure by trying options in play.
when: While prototyping a core mechanic, when open questions about win/loss rules and pacing come up
why: Play gives answers that speculation cannot

text: A strong design document can be brief, around 50 to 100 pages, as long as it holds the essential information for building the game.
why: Busy executives and programmers can then find their sections quickly.

text: Write the document in repeated passes, filling sections as they become clear and revising earlier sections after later ones, since each design aspect depends on the others.
when: While drafting a design document, filling each section once its content firms up
why: Finishing the document in a single pass is a pitfall.

text: Writing that neither draws on other disciplines nor enhances them will not reach its potential.
when: When a writer's narrative must mesh with gameplay, level layout and environment design
why: The emotional effect of a game comes from combining story, setting, pacing and gameplay into one whole, so isolated writing loses it.

text: No fixed recipe exists for diagram symbols, so designers should develop a consistent personal grammar.
when: creating a diagram language
why: Consistency lets a reader decode symbols.

text: A game design contains thousands of decisions, and people forget many of them within weeks.
when: Over a long project as design decisions pile up across weeks
why: Logging decisions outside memory prevents re-solving old problems and helps the designer develop ideas on paper.

text: A written decision invites discussion, and someone will find a flaw or propose an improvement, which strengthens the design.
when: When a design decision must be shared with many team members
why: Committing a decision to paper gives colleagues something concrete to challenge, turning communication into a back-and-forth dialog.

text: Writing a document makes people think differently than they do alone, allowing diagrams, references, and logical chains that reveal details impromptu thinking misses.
when: For deep analysis of a complex design, which can take weeks, rather than quick idea generation
why: Written form forces structure and exposes gaps.

text: A design document expresses the author's current theories about what will make a game good, and only practice shows whether those theories hold.

Spreadsheet cells can be classed into five roles: data (hardcoded values), inputs (hand-tuned values), calculations (intermediate formulas), controls (choose between alternatives), outputs (final results).
A game design document's opening sections cover the vision, target audience, platform and system requirements, competitor analysis, sales expectations, and legal obligations.
A game design overview covers story, mechanics, level outline, controls, interfaces, art and music style, feature list, milestone schedule and team bios.
when: When pitching the game to a publisher, who may only skim the materials
why: A publisher needs proof the whole project is thought through, without needing every detail.

text: A one-page game design sample covers: one-liner comparison, setting, target audience, genre, key features, gameplay summary, story, platforms and a gameplay example.
when: Writing a one-page game design document
why: Gives a complete overview on a single page

text: Treating design documents as specifications, scripts, blueprints or fixed plans to follow without question causes confusion, since they are theories that practice must test.
Sentimental attachment to a design makes it hard to abandon even when it is clearly failing.
when: When a committed design decision starts failing in play

text: Google Sheets comments look like cell notes but behave differently, so the two should not be treated as interchangeable.
when: Using notes or comments in a shared sheet.
why: Their names, reply threads and resolution behave differently.

text: Treating the design document as an end in itself, rather than as a means of communication, undermines its value.
Assuming everyone has read and understood the written vision after it is published; documentation does not replace meetings and in-person discussion.
why: Writing gives the team a shared reference point, but readers may not have absorbed the vision.

text: Design documents tend to grow very large, especially on collaborative wikis where content expands easily.
when: Writing a design document on a collaborative wiki
why: Shared online editing makes it effortless for content to keep expanding.

text: Writing documents for yourself produces material the team will not read, since the team is the real audience.
why: The team has a full workload of documents to read

text: Complicated phrasing confuses readers, so a description should communicate rather than puzzle.
when: Writing a one-liner description
why: Readers who are confused cannot judge the idea

text: Niche jargon confuses readers whose background is unknown, so use everyday terms instead.
when: The reader's background is unknown
why: Unfamiliar terms block understanding

text: Trusting inherited formulas and reference data without testing them can lock in errors.
Beginners often describe features instead of the experiences they should create, and seeing past features to player experience is hard.
when: Beginner designers setting player experience goals for a game

text: Analyzing an open design decision: 1) Hold a brainstorm. 2) Run targeted research. 3) Write each candidate idea on a card. 4) Allow time for unconscious rumination before deciding.
when: a design decision is undecided and costly
why: each step adds information or fresh perspective

text: Test written movement rules: 1) build a paper prototype of a level 2) write movement rules 3) have a player read and execute them, noting what was clear and what was wrong 4) read the rules aloud and see if performance changes 5) reword and retest.
1) Ask what must be remembered while making the game. 2) Ask what must be communicated. 3) Create documents that serve those needs and skip those that serve neither. 4) Repeat as the project changes.
when: Before creating any new document or when an existing one goes stale
why: Memory and communication needs shift over the project

text: 1) Identify who needs to see the document. 2) Decide what it should contain based on those readers.
when: Before deciding a document's contents
why: Decisions must reach many team members, and documents let more people review them sooner.

text: 1) Ask why you are doing this work. 2) Look past surface reasons to your underlying purpose. 3) Check that your current work serves that purpose.
when: before starting a new game or major phase, or when work feels unfocused or lacks energy
why: Knowing the deeper purpose behind the work lets you judge whether it deserves your time.

text: To explore an intransitive game, ask which option is best against a new opponent, how much of the outcome comes from luck versus skill, and how a new option changes the optimal strategy, then judge whether it belongs in the core game.
when: Evaluating a proposed change to an intransitive game

text: 1) List everything you can think of on a topic. 2) Make lists of variations on that topic. Writing items down supports free association and organization together.
when: When brainstorming a topic

text: 1) Write gameplay and technical goals. 2) List every deliverable and check it with the team. 3) Build a detailed schedule with all tasks specified and dependencies marked. 4) Draft a budget from a sample, using best guesses. 5) Cut the budget by a set percentage, revising goals first, then deliverables, schedule, and budget.
when: Building a project plan for a game idea.
why: Practices how the pieces of a plan fit together; accuracy matters less.

text: 1) Set goals, covering gameplay aims, technical aims, target platform, and launch date. 2) Derive deliverables grouped by the stage that creates them. 3) Give media deliverables concrete counts and durations. 4) Allocate budget and a schedule slot to each deliverable.
why: Goals shape deliverables, which set schedule and budget.

text: 1) Put all essential information on exactly one page, printed as large as possible. 2) Use visuals wherever possible. 3) Place the main mockup at the center and explain it through callouts.
when: Giving a quick visual overview of a character, location or idea
why: Keeping all essential information on one large, visual page makes a quick overview easy to grasp.

text: 1) Collect the concept summary, the sales pitch, the Game Design Document, the world or universe bible, the narrative bible, and any art or prototypes. 2) Check them with later playtesting in mind.
when: When reviewing a client's existing documentation for narrative work
why: Documentation lets both the client and developers understand the project, so it is worth reviewing.

text: Technical details may sit in the design document or a separate technical specification, usually by the technical director or lead engineer, covering technology, risks, tools, delivery, engine and specific systems.
Write a technical design document when more than one engineer works on the code.
when: More than one engineer works on the code
why: Records how the non-game technical systems are meant to work for people who join later.

text: Internal development tools have a user experience; tools programmers should understand UX because poor tools waste time.
Technical analysis should identify new technology, major software tasks such as building versus licensing or reusing an engine, risks, lower-risk alternatives, and resources needed.
List and describe system parameters such as maximum players, servers, customization, persistence, saving, and loading.
When briefing audio or art teams, state the specific intent, not just a label: say whether a sigh is exasperated, bored or weary.
when: Briefing audio or art teams, especially a team you have not worked with before
why: Vague labels lead to assets that miss the goal.

text: Test card wording with fresh readers, since they may interpret effects differently from the designer.
why: Designers cannot easily see second readings of their own wording.

text: Keep between-level learning short, keep its bugs replicable, and store game data in a format that is easy to extract.
when: learning runs between levels
why: Load times are part of acceptance criteria, and replicability and data extraction are needed for debugging and analysis.

text: Every central mechanic should be fully playable by the midpoint of the schedule.
when: when planning a production schedule
why: Leaves time for the loops that make the game great, even when problems occur.

text: Tailor each design document to the team: a common core can stay consistent, but structure and style change with each game.
when: Writing design documents for a new game
why: The document must act as the team's go-to reference for information and clarity.

text: Write down decisions you may later forget or that others must act on.
why: Memory fades across weeks of decisions, so recorded choices spare the team from re-solving old problems; writing also sharpens thinking.

text: Use a design-notes text column for notes covering a whole row or group, and attach a note to a cell when the comment targets that specific cell.
when: Documenting a spreadsheet's formulas or layout.
why: Placement tells readers exactly which data a note explains.

text: Explain what cells do with cell comments, or with notes in headers or a notes field.
why: Readers cannot otherwise tell what a cell does, and brief notes supply that meaning right in the sheet.

text: Do not rest on proven genres; ask how an idea might break new ground artistically.
when: When deciding whether to keep an idea that only repeats established genre conventions.
why: A designer must stretch artistically, and ideas that merely echo proven work fail to do that.

text: Create a subdocument for any area that needs more detail as production moves forward, especially areas expected to expand during production.
when: An area grows during production
why: Keeps the main document short enough that busy readers can locate what concerns them.

text: Organize the design document in modules from the start so it stays manageable as it grows.
when: When a design document is a living document that will be revised many times.

text: On a wiki, create a separate page for each area, with subpages for deeper detail, images, and charts.
when: The document lives on a wiki
why: A wiki enforces modularity naturally.

text: Keep a design history listing each version and its major changes in word-processor documents; on a wiki, rely on the edit history instead.
when: Tracking document versions
why: Teammates rarely reread the whole document, so flagged changes tell them what to review.

text: A gameplay synopsis should cover what makes the game unique, its core mechanics, its setting, and its look and feel.
Be the team's go-to person for documentation, and express ideas concisely, since colleagues often prefer not to read long material.
why: Team members often avoid long reading, so concise writing is what gets absorbed.

text: Make a game bible easy to navigate: include a table of contents listing every section, subsections and page numbers.
when: For any bible that more than one person edits or reads.
why: Anyone must find information quickly in a reference.

text: Show the version and date on the cover page of each bible update, and keep a change history recording what was added or removed and why.
when: For any bible that more than one person edits or reads.
why: Readers can confirm they hold the latest version and see what changed since their last copy.

text: In linked web archives, create cross-linked pages; in word-processing files, avoid bloat by moving ancillary material to separate documents.
when: When a word-processing document grows so bloated that readers avoid it.
why: Bloated documents scare readers off, so moving ancillary material out keeps the core text readable.

text: When a document is missing, explain to the client and developers why it matters.
when: When the client lacks some standard design documents.
why: The client and the developers building the game both rely on these documents, so their purpose must be understood.

text: If you can write a missing document, offer to do it and negotiate a fee as part of your scope.
when: When the missing document falls within the writer's own expertise.

text: Designers should play widely and learn unrelated fields such as economics or history, since any field can supply analogies for a solution.
when: When seeking a creative solution to a design problem.
why: Humans think by analogy, so broader knowledge gives more material.

text: Omit the characters, story, world, or media list section of the design document when the game does not need it.
when: Writing the design document outline
why: Each of these sections applies only to some games.

text: When asked to simplify a pitch, clarify whether the request means making it clearer or dumbing it down.
when: Receiving feedback to simplify
why: Dumbing down underestimates the audience, while clarity is justified when matched to genre and audience expectations.

text: If the client can only pay for documentation, make sure they can explain the narrative design and every document themselves.
when: client budget covers only documents
why: Without the designer present later, the client must carry the design to other team members and QA.

text: Use tabs in one document for related data that must cross-reference; use separate files when the data groups are completely independent.
when: Deciding how to split game data across spreadsheets
why: Cross-referencing within one file is simpler than linking to another file

text: Cutting a flat section removes its problem but wastes invested work; keeping it means finding a fix such as a shortcut.
when: late in development with work already invested
why: Removing a section discards labor already sunk into it, which weighs heavily late in production.

text: Early in a project, many small documents covering separate subsystems are usually better than one giant document.
when: Early project stage
why: One huge document tends to go stale and be abandoned midway, while small ones stay focused.

text: Strong vision keeps design directed, but loosening control to explore possibilities and seize emerging value captures serendipity; the two must be balanced.
when: When balancing a clear vision against exploration
why: A vision held too tightly blinds the designer to what players actually do.

text: Architectural drawing must be more precise than artistic sketching because it exists to communicate spatial relationships.
when: drawing spaces for planning rather than expression
why: Such drawings must convey shapes, masses and how objects relate in space, so they need clean lines.

text: Emergent story hands much authorship to systems and players, yielding near-endless story variety at the cost of the designer's direct control over outcomes.
why: Authorship shifts to systems and players, since the plot emerges from mechanics, choices and chance rather than scripted events.

text: Criticizing ideas early breaks the flow of idea generation.
when: During brainstorming, while ideas are still being generated.

text: Reusing engines across titles has reduced programming effort.
Working in an engine's level editor, which exposes grids, rooms, units, and objects, helps you learn a genre's formal elements.
why: The editor exposes the same structural building blocks a prototype uses, so hands-on use builds a feel for the genre's form.

text: Keep formation patterns and roles out of code, defining them with separate tools.
when: Authoring formation content
why: Most developers prefer this separation

text: Displaying or recording the events delivered to each character makes complex decision making easier to debug.
when: decision making is complex
why: delivered events show what each character reacted to

text: Draw the interest curve even when opinions on ideal shapes differ, since skipping it risks missing the big picture.
why: Charting interest across the whole experience reveals its overall shape, which detail-focused views hide.

text: Deferring work moves its cost to a later point, often the moment the result is needed; if that work is slow, the player sees a pause.
when: Batched or postponed computation is needed right when requested
why: The deferred cost lands at the moment of use rather than being spread out

text: The engine holds a central pool of AI algorithms, and each character's data names which techniques it uses, how they are parameterized, and how they are combined.
why: Describing each character as data rather than compiled code lets one shared algorithm pool serve many characters.

text: A dirty flag can be cleaned on demand, at checkpoints, or in the background; each option trades responsiveness, timing control, and redundant work.
when: Choosing when to process flagged data.
why: Work hidden behind a loading screen or cutscene costs nothing visible, but deferred work can wait far longer than planned if the player gets lost.

text: Re-sorting groups by dynamic priority every frame adds time for little gain; a cooperative arbitration system may be a better choice.
when: group priorities change dynamically
why: Requesting and sorting dynamic priorities every frame costs time for little practical gain, so a full arbitration system is the better step.

text: 1) Hold Ctrl and drag with the left mouse button to move an actor along X. 2) Hold Ctrl and drag with the right button for Y. 3) Hold Ctrl with both buttons for Z.
Right-click an actor and choose Go to Actor, or press Home, to make all viewports focus on it. Then fine-tune the position.
when: when navigating a large level
why: Home jumps to a rough area quickly

text: Use an engine when a quick, working prototype matters more than engine-independent design.
why: Engine prototyping saves considerable time and resources.

text: Design AI for the lowest common denominator, the minimum specification in the technical design document; faster machines simply use less of their AI budget.
why: Letting AI quality or speed vary by hardware would make difficulty differ across machines, which QA and publishers find unacceptable.

text: Prefer simple, parameterized behaviors when designers must author AI through a tool.
when: designers author AI through a tool
why: Simple behaviors parameterize easily by physical capabilities and are shared across characters, while condition-heavy ones need complex matching rules that are hard to author.

text: Buffer shared per-frame state so every actor reads the previous frame's values, and write new values separately, then commit them together after all actors have updated.
when: Multiple actors react to each other's state within one update pass
why: Keeps results independent of update order so actors appear to act simultaneously.

text: Store game behavior in data files loaded and executed by the engine so designers and patches can change logic without recompiling.
when: Designers, patches, or mods need to change behavior often
why: Hard-coded behavior forces an engineer and a full recompile into every tuning cycle.

text: An engine saves time and resources, but its capabilities can push design toward what it does well; letting engine features determine the game instead of design goals distorts design.
why: The engine's existing feature set pulls decisions toward what it can already do, so the tool can drive choices instead of design goals.

text: Data binding automates updating a UI element whenever a bound value changes, while keeping imperative code; it suits UI and non-critical areas but is probably too slow and complex for a core engine.
when: Choosing an update mechanism for a game's UI.
why: It removes repetitive update code without building the whole program around a dataflow graph.

text: Time and cost estimates reflect large console and boxed titles; PC, phone, and online projects or teams with different experience differ, and mobile makes single-person teams feasible though costs rise.
An 80/20 plan (working game, then polish) lets overruns eat polish time, shipping a late, weak game; too little refinement time ships a noticeably weaker game.
when: When unplanned problems arise during development and the schedule has no slack left for polish.
why: Overruns usually eat the time reserved for polish first.

text: Professional estimators are overconfident: fewer than one percent got nine of ten ranges right, over ninety percent got five or fewer; optimism bias makes 90%-confident estimates act like 30%-confident ones.
when: when estimating software or project work
why: Optimism bias drives the overconfidence.

text: Consumers expect RPGs to feel epic in length, so development tends to add content rather than remove it.
when: When designing RPGs where story and gameplay both set how long the game runs.
why: players equate length with value

text: Once programmers and artists are in place, changing core gameplay becomes very hard.
Schedule and budget often prevent full completion work, so released games still hide flaws.
when: Planning production

text: On a medium or large game, keeping the schedule current can be a full-time job, and it changes weekly at least.
when: Medium or large game production

text: At the peak of inflated expectations, far more people talk about a technology than have used it.
How high the plateau of productivity sits depends on the breadth of a technology's usefulness.
Schedules are commonly drawn as Gantt charts using project-management software, spreadsheets, or a paper calendar.
A thorough study of an intricate design can take weeks and draw on broad research and formal statistical or mathematical methods, yielding knowledge guessing cannot.
when: Complex design questions.

text: Make schedules realistic, since listeners lose confidence quickly in unrealistic timelines, and expect to be held to any fastest-finish answer.
when: Estimating development time
why: Overpromising damages credibility once a listener checks it.

text: A demo for a major showcase creates a real deadline that forces the game to be self-contained, stable, and comparable to other titles on its platform.
when: When preparing a demo for a showcase event with a fixed submission date.
why: A deadline with no slack means the demo cannot depend on unfinished parts and must stand on its own.

text: Expect understanding the existing code to take longer than writing the change; once the problem is clear, the typing is often trivial.
when: estimating how long a code change will take
why: Comprehension of the affected code usually dominates programming time.

text: Willingness to write whatever a project needs can open the way to critical-path work and pitching.
when: When a junior writer is on a team with varied writing assignments.
why: Taking on any writing and giving feedback builds knowledge that prepares you for higher-level work.

text: Match the effort spent on a decision to its importance: fast individual judgment for small choices, full deliberation for major ones.
when: When deciding how much process a design choice deserves.
why: Deliberation has its own cost in time and research, which is wasteful on minor choices.

text: Total project cost cannot be known until the transition point is reached, so predictability arrives as early as is realistically possible.
when: Before development reaches the point where the game's design is settled enough to schedule the remaining work.
why: Costs can only be predicted once the core design is fixed, which takes spending a set share of budget first.

text: Fixing usability issues early leaves more time later for systemic and game-balancing problems.
when: When paper or interactive prototypes exist before features are built in the engine.
why: Fixes are cheaper before implementation and art polish, freeing later time for systemic and balance problems.

text: If reaching the preproduction end point costs one million dollars, the remainder of the project will probably cost about 2.3 million dollars.
when: when estimating total cost from early spending
why: Two finished levels mark when the design is settled enough that remaining cost can be planned.

text: Keep preproduction exercises to 15 to 20 minutes so teams must collaborate immediately.
when: When the exercises address a team's real, current game problems rather than classroom tasks.
why: Tight time limits cut off over-deliberation about why a task can't be done, so everyone contributes at once.

text: Each design change can be assessed across design effects, implementation cost, immaturity burden, critical failure risk, economy risk, political effects, and uncertainty, since one option often shifts all of them at once.
when: Weighing a difficult design change
why: Listing all effect types exposes hidden costs that a single view misses.

text: Plans that create false certainty drive overplanning; precision that ignores real-world uncertainty becomes ridiculous and wastes effort.
when: When a team feels anxious about an uncertain future.
why: Unexpected factors invalidate detailed plans.

text: Developers overestimate the challenge players need, partly because of the curse of knowledge, and QA testers are especially prone to this.
when: When testers or designers have played the game repeatedly and know its systems well.

text: Underestimating the time needed for optimization and bug fixing can consume a large part of the schedule.
when: When a build must be shippable and self-contained by a hard external deadline.

text: 1) Play many games in the target genre. 2) Or run user research to learn how players respond to difficulty. 3) Use the result as the baseline for the market average.
when: Before setting a game's difficulty target
why: What counts as average is subjective and shifts with genre, monetization model, and the decade's style.

text: 1) Write the design document. 2) Build a first playable. 3) Reach first alpha, then second alpha. 4) Reach beta and launch. 5) Plan post-launch update frequency.
when: Presenting a development schedule
why: Named milestones show the team understands how the project progresses.

text: 1) Count headcount and duration. 2) Add other expenses. 3) Compare the total with the revenue range.
when: Estimating a game's budget
why: A complete cost basis is needed to judge profitability.

text: 1) At the start of production, review the full design with the producer. 2) Producer builds schedule and budget from that scope. 3) Designer checks every line item against the design vision and raises issues early.
when: Start of any production
why: Realistic schedules and budgets need a clear scope

text: When behind schedule, the producer may cut ambitious low-priority features rather than delay the milestone.
when: Production is behind schedule.
why: Alpha means all features must be complete, so unfinished low-priority features are removed to hit that milestone.

text: 1) Break each deliverable into tasks. 2) Assign team members and estimate each task's duration in days. 3) Set a start date for each task. 4) Mark dependencies to find parallel and sequential tasks. 5) Balance each person's workload. 6) Output a timeline and resource list that becomes the budget basis.
why: Some tasks run in parallel while others must wait for prerequisites, so dependencies set the order of work.

text: The schedule should respect that one person should not work more than forty hours per week and that some tasks depend on others.
In early content work, aim numbers at playability and tone rather than final balance.
when: before core systems are stable
why: Early numbers only need to set tone and reach a playable version fast so playtesting can judge fun.

text: Do not treat a first cost estimate as final once playtesting or analytics data becomes available; revise it from observed use.
when: After a built game produces play data
why: Early estimates are educated guesses made before real data exists

text: Plan sequences carefully with the art and animation departments to tell more with less.
why: Visual sequences let players grasp situations by observation, so less text is needed for explanation.

text: Ask the team which content might be cut or changed, and assess how each change affects the narrative and writing.
why: Story or worldbuilding can explain glitches, so narrative design can help solve problems found in testing.

text: Early design should favor flexibility over raw speed: code can be optimized later, but flexible behavior is hard to add to rigid code late.
when: Early AI architecture decisions
why: Quick placeholder code tends to get patched so heavily that later rewriting becomes nearly impossible.

text: A restriction's benefits are immediate and concentrated, while its costs spread over years and fall mainly on other team members.
why: The gain shows up quickly in prototypes and playtests, while the burden lands later on other staff.

text: Marketing and business staff often request design decisions earlier than the dependency order allows.
when: The game is still early and its details are unstable.
why: Highly detailed early decisions are likely to be reshaped by cascading changes, so their value rarely outweighs the cost.

text: The executive producer oversees the whole project and carries final responsibility for it.
Executive management includes the CEO, president, CFO, COO, vice presidents, and directors, who run the company and oversee departments.
Developer executives are often founders or former core designers, while publisher executives often come from business, marketing, other industries, or hobbyist gaming.
Outside parties such as advertisers, marketers, investors, hiring managers, and retailers need product information months ahead, so underplanning also harms them.
when: When scheduling a game's release and external commitments
why: Advertising, marketing, hiring, and distribution all run on long lead times.

text: Do not expect executives to play your prototype unless they are already excited, since they may embarrass themselves or crash it.
when: when showing a prototype to executives
why: Unenthusiastic viewers may fumble or crash the build, which reflects badly on the presenter.

text: Before dismissing an executive's input, learn which games they have worked on and what their expertise was.
why: Executives may have real development experience and market knowledge that their track record reveals.

text: Before blaming management, check whether they had a clear view of the game, since they may not have read the design documents or played a recent build.
when: When executive decisions feel like they are ruining the game.
why: Designers are responsible for communicating the vision upward, so they may share blame for misdirection.

text: Incorporating executive suggestions that improve gameplay helps the publisher back the game when it ships.
why: Executives want authorship of the game, so seeing their ideas improve it builds their backing.

text: When criticism reflects a different imagined game, fix the presentation so the intended game is clear, or change the game itself.
why: Players judge the game against an ideal version in their heads, so their own suggested fix is rarely the real solution.

text: Executives need to understand both the value and the limits of a player-centered approach.
why: Clear proof of value for management often only comes after launch, when metrics link UX issues to retention or revenue.

text: A control situation forces testers into a specific part of the game, such as the ending, a rare event, or a new feature, instead of waiting for it by chance.
Combining methods can reveal differences: individual forms after a group discussion yield different responses than group discussion alone.
Pick a user research method by development stage, research question, and available resources. No single method answers every question, so combine several.
when: Planning which UX research method to use at a given stage
why: Each method answers a different kind of question and fits different constraints.

text: Changing one rule variable often reveals the need to change other variables, so test those connected changes next.
Control situations matter most when time is limited, because some games take days to reach their later states.
why: Controlled setups push players straight into a specific part of the mechanics instead of waiting for it to arise.

text: Changing two or more variables together makes it hard to separate their individual effects on the system.

Before attributing a measured difference to a design change: 1) Write the experimental hypothesis and its null hypothesis. 2) List every variable that differs between test groups, such as time spent or encounter count. 3) Control or measure those variables. 4) Run significance testing. 5) Attribute the effect only if no confound explains it.
why: A significant result can still come from a hidden variable.

text: 1) For each condition, compute the mean and standard deviation of the metric. 2) Compare the difference against a chosen confidence interval. 3) State the threshold used so the uncertainty is known.
