when: Comparing two designs or settings on a measured metric
why: Confidence intervals show how much of a difference could be noise.

text: 1) List which inputs map to which parameters. 2) Count controlled objects and avatars. 3) Classify each avatar's motion type, dimensions, frame and directness. 4) Quantify each input's modulation as an ADSR envelope. 5) Infer whether filtering, simulation or both produced it.
when: when analyzing how a game's control feels
why: to identify the tuned variables and their relationships

text: 1) Define three control situations for the prototype. 2) For each, state its purpose and function. 3) Run each and record observations.
when: planning prototype test sessions
why: Rare events may never occur by chance in a session, so forcing them into play makes them observable under varied conditions.

text: 1) Generate random combinations of themes and conditions 2) playtest each combination 3) keep the ones that feel intuitive and drop those that feel overwhelming.
Use control groups for comparison; to learn what engaged players like, also survey less-engaged players.
when: when interpreting differences between player groups
why: without a comparison group, group differences cannot be attributed

text: Test controls with players, because first control attempts are rarely as intuitive as designers expect.
Choose control targets among the game's end, rare random events, special situations, particular levels, and new features.
when: planning control tests
why: Each target lets a specific portion of the mechanics be tested independently of the others.

text: Control testing aims to see what happens under every condition, not to make testers comfortable or the game fair.
when: In the foundation prototyping stage, when only basic functionality is under test.

text: A strong feature concept can serve as a portfolio piece, since designers at established companies often receive feature work early in their careers.
Cut features once systems take shape, ideally at end of pre-production before the core experience settles, since teams tend to add features; more features do not guarantee success.
when: late pre-production when systems are forming
why: Because the iterative cycle can reshape whole systems, leftover elements that don't serve the intended experience must be removed.

text: Cramming features in quickly accumulates hacks and inconsistencies that steadily drain future productivity.
when: under pressure to finish current work
why: Shortcuts left in code slow every later change.

text: Journal entries that only review features miss the point; entries should discuss experience and the reasons behind it.

1) Write a one-page description of the feature: why it matters, how it works and all its possible states. 2) List every state. 3) Derive the signs and feedback needed for each state. 4) Share the list early so UI, art and sound teams can prepare assets.
when: As soon as a feature, mechanic or behaviour is defined.
why: Late sign and feedback planning makes it hard to produce assets in time, and unlisted states ship without signals.

text: 1) Time how long players take to reach a point with the feature and without it. 2) Ask players how they feel about the feature.
when: When you suspect a specific feature is causing a problem in the game.

text: 1) Take a teammate's idea. 2) Reshape it so it fits the overall framework from a systems perspective. 3) Work with the teammate rather than arguing against the idea.
when: A team idea does not fit the framework
why: Collaboration builds trust.

text: 1) Design the feature 2) Prototype or implement it 3) Test it 4) Analyze results 5) Define changes 6) Repeat.
1) Choose a favorite game. 2) Pick a feature you would add. 3) Ignore technical difficulty. 4) Illustrate how it works with words and storyboards.
when: When proposing a feature for an existing game
why: Feasibility is set aside so the concept can be explored and communicated first.

text: After playtesting, remove features that do not support the core experience, such as weather, cycles, or terrain, when they distract from it.
when: an emotional prototype is losing focus
why: Playtester responses show which features help the core feel.

text: Critique only after understanding the team's intentions, constraints and challenges, or critique is uninformed; nitpicking without clearly stated intent yields confused work, so leaders must state intent first.
why: A worker who does not understand the intent cannot fulfill it, so later criticism misses the mark.

text: Customers judge an immature new technology as not good enough, but do not treat that verdict as final; it keeps improving in the background.
when: a new technology is still immature
why: Customers judge against current needs; ignoring a new technology while improving the old one misses its progress.

text: Developers become more receptive to UX findings when they feel the UX team is not always there to criticize their work.
why: Relaxed people accept input more readily, so it lands better when criticism is not always expected.

text: Good editors work at both word level, catching errors such as typos that change meaning, and story level, catching missing steps in dialogue and plot pacing.
Strong QA testers have played widely, are practised at spotting plot holes, and reason more like a typical player than any other teammate.
when: Choosing narrative reviewers
why: Repeated exposure to many games builds habits for spotting plot holes.

text: Feedback forms with standard questions produce quantitative data, which survey tools or spreadsheets can collect.
At the Distributed stage, UX sits at the same level as finance, production, and marketing, which requires senior executive buy-in.
The long-term aim of UX practice is a distributed UX culture across the whole studio.
Online developer communities, including engine and software forums and mod communities, are places to find reviewers.
Game development work is hard to judge from outside: contributions are intertwined and uncertain, so good work can end in failure while shirking can look fine.
when: When assessing individual contributions to a game project.
why: Outcomes are shaped by uncertainty and mixed contributions, not just individual effort.

text: Critics argue the hero's journey is over-formulaic and forces many different stories into one pattern.
Value feedback by its form: a complaint flags a problem, a complaint with a reason gives its cause, and a suggested change needs probing because the real fix often differs.
why: A suggestion names a presumed fix, so the real problem must be uncovered before a solution can be chosen.

text: Defining design terms is worthwhile even if the definitions stay imperfect, because the effort sharpens analytic thinking.
why: Clear terms help others think and express ideas more precisely, and strong ones spread.

text: Client opinions range from wise to foolish or hypocritical, so designers must learn to handle both kinds well.
A live demonstration can overcome a skeptic's doubt more effectively than argument alone.
When UX feedback clashes with team goals, the cause is usually mismatched priorities or poor communication, not UX itself.
when: When the development team's goals differ from the publishing or executive team's goals.
why: UX feedback weighs business objectives alongside design objectives, so it can echo goals the team rejects.

text: Frequent questions from an editor about intent signal that the draft is not yet ready, and the writer should offer to take it back for revision.
when: An editor repeatedly asks what a writer meant
why: What is clear in the writer's head may not work on the page

text: Treat a reviewer's reported feelings as valid, but treat their suggested fixes with more caution, since suggesters often know the material less well.
why: Suggesters know the material far less well than the designer, so their fixes are suspect, while reported feelings are self-reports.

text: Fix feedback that takes under about five minutes first, unless it sits in a section likely to be cut anyway.
when: triaging feedback

text: A percentage in a note usually signals a local problem that does not need a complete rewrite.
when: When a non-writer's review note asks for a change expressed as a percentage.
why: Non-writers may lack writing jargon, so a percentage is how they signal the problem's scope.

text: Playtest feedback is not capped by a leader's understanding, so developers can keep improving, while a leader's judgment caps the achievement it grants.
when: When a designer is motivated by playtest outcomes rather than by a boss's judgment.
why: Results are real outcomes rather than rewards one person designs to steer you, so they don't feel controlling.

text: Only a complete game released to real players gives feedback strong enough to change a designer's planning beliefs; friendly testers and unfinished prototypes soften the lesson.
when: When deciding whether feedback will change a designer's habits
why: Players with no reason to be kind reveal a game's true worth.

text: Verbal playtest reports are distorted by memory editing, mixed-in design suggestions, and feelings about the designer or studio.
when: When you need to learn what happened in a playtester's mind, beyond what watching the session shows.
why: Memories are edited or invented, reports mix in design suggestions, and feelings about the designer cloud judgment, often without the tester intending it.

text: Censoring ideas early can block good ones, which often appear only after the poor ideas are out.
when: When starting a creative problem and tempted to wait for a brilliant idea before writing anything.
why: Poor ideas must be expelled before good ones emerge, and a stupid idea can spark a strong one.

text: Designers who cannot cope with strong client opinions tend to become unhappy in the role.
when: When a paying client has firm views on the game's visuals, behavior, and gameplay.
why: The client is paying, and if they are unhappy with the direction, the project can end.

text: Designers invested in their games may dismiss audience feedback to ease their own internal conflict.
UX feedback on work that will be redone within a month wastes effort.
when: When the feature under review is scheduled to be redone within about a month.
why: The team is swamped and needs immediately applicable, decision-ready feedback, so comments on soon-replaced work are wasted.

text: Getting defensive when testers say they did not have fun blocks learning why the experience fell short; listen instead of defending the plan.
when: When a tester reports that they did not have fun with the game.
why: Testers stand in for part of the audience, and audiences leave if the game isn't enjoyable, however much effort went into it.

text: Dismissing criticism because one comment was positive is a mistake; use positive remarks as a gut check and double-check the criticism instead.
when: deciding whether to act on criticism
why: A positive remark can check your instincts, but a single compliment doesn't cancel out criticism that deserves a second look.

text: Undirected media intake that matches peers' consumption yields the same ideas as peers, producing homogeneous designs.
when: When a designer consumes media without any direction, just following what peers play and watch.
why: Shared references lead to similar games across the industry.

text: 1) Build a storyboard following a player who succeeds with the feature. 2) Show the progression from beginner to success. 3) Present it to peers for critique.
when: When testing how a feature communicates to others
why: The exercise is communication: moving the idea from your mind into another person's mind.

text: Developers sit closer to the game, so their opinions are distorted; test with them anyway but take their feedback with a grain of salt.
when: When playtesting with developers who work on the game.
why: They are closer to the game than any real player will be, which distorts their views, yet they play a lot and give thoughtful feedback.

text: State precisely what you like or dislike, why, and how it could improve; a vague verdict like 'it was just bad' gives no direction.
when: Analyzing any experience or evaluating a design
why: Specific reactions point to specific changes; judgments by feel alone do not show how to improve.

text: Distinguish expertise from preference when weighing feedback, even from non-designers; test, review and data findings count as evidence, most neutral when practitioners understand design and business goals.
when: When feedback arrives via usability sessions, expert critiques, or metrics, and reviewers grasp the design and business aims.
why: Test, review, and data results are measured evidence rather than personal taste, so they tend to be less biased than opinions.

text: State your design opinions directly, including flaws in a superior's idea; hedging a position until it is vague weakens its value.
when: When a superior's idea has a flaw you can see, or the room is about to agree with something you think is wrong.
why: Candor requires moral courage and effort in expression, not just mental effort in forming ideas.

text: Match feedback to the development stage: early playtests address gameplay and art, while late playtests focus on bugs.
when: collecting playtest feedback
why: each stage has different open questions

text: Ask participants for blunt feedback and a short reason for each reaction, since participants tend to be too polite.
when: Collecting feedback in a UX test
why: Politeness bias softens honest reactions.

text: Accept editor notes, and learn from recurring mistakes and frequently misspelled words, since clear-seeming text may be unclear to others.
when: When an editor finds that dialogue isn't ready to edit.
why: What is clear in your head may not read clearly to others, and editors reveal recurring mistakes you can learn from.

text: Critique the work, never the person, and avoid personal attacks or derisive language.
Ask the writer what kind of feedback they want, and tailor your notes to that focus.
Explain why you are raising an issue, so the writer has something concrete to act on.
Point out what works as well as what needs improvement.
Sort each feedback comment into one of three groups: Useful, Not Sure, or Will Not Use (WNU).
when: reviewing a pile of feedback
why: Testers' comments reflect their interest and knowledge, which do not always coincide, so feedback quality varies widely.

text: Fix glitches and trim content with QA feedback until the core of the story comes across clearly.
when: time remains before release
why: Testers unfamiliar with the story reveal what gets across and what does not, and problems left unfixed resurface later as public complaints.

text: Use underscores instead of spaces in every filename, including sound and music files.
when: naming any asset file
why: game software does not handle spaces in filenames well

text: Set a file naming convention at the start of production to prevent confusion later.
when: At the start of a project
why: Setting the scheme early prevents later confusion across the many media assets.

text: High frame rates make motion feel smooth and responsive, while low frame rates make motion look jerky like stop-motion.
when: Players watch the game at different frame rates
why: Fewer rendered updates per second leave visible gaps between positions.

text: Frames per second measures how often the game loop cycles in real time.
When the loop runs as fast as possible, frame rate is set by the work done per frame and by the platform's speed.
when: Loop is not capped and runs flat out
why: More per-frame work or slower hardware reduces how many cycles fit in each second.

text: Game time and real time differ, since the world advances only when the loop cycles, so slow frames slow the world down.
when: Frame rate drops under load
why: Game progression is tied to loop cycles rather than wall-clock time.

text: 1) Count the frames between input and feedback. 2) Divide the frame count by the frame rate. 3) Multiply by 1000 to get milliseconds. Three frames at 60 fps is about 50 ms.
why: Delay between a player's input and visible feedback is what makes a game feel unresponsive.

text: 1) Record frame start time. 2) Process input, update, and render. 3) Sleep for the frame length minus the time elapsed since the start. 4) Repeat.
when: Capping frame rate to a steady target
why: Sleeping pads fast frames so the loop does not run faster than the target.

text: 1) Fix the match format, such as elimination type, round count, and timer. 2) Set fair-play rules, such as equipment policy. 3) Ban any option whose power makes choosing it almost guarantee a win.
when: Running a competitive tournament
why: Each setting shapes fairness and match outcomes.

text: Track entries used over time, number of overwrites, and misses on previously stored positions, since these show whether the table is well parameterized.
when: When implementing a transposition table for a game-tree search.
why: Rarely finding useful entries signals poor sizing, such as too few buckets, so the table is not performing well.

text: Rank tournament winners by individual record, not unit record, so players try to win even when playing someone else's unit.
when: In a tournament where players pilot randomly assigned characters rather than their own.
why: Players are scored on their own results, so the goal of winning stays with them rather than with the character.

text: Each mechanic demands design labor to build, adjust and verify, and draws on computing resources that other features could use.
Win rates by object, character or strategy can be factored into expected outcomes, though most rating systems do not do this.
when: Refining a rating system's predictions.
why: Object strength affects results beyond player rating.

text: Build a version of a system with every parameter set to zero, then tune each parameter upward to learn its effect on feel.
when: when learning how a feel system's parameters behave
why: A zeroed baseline isolates the contribution of each parameter

text: 1) Playtest the combined combat repeatedly. 2) Iterate on the balance. 3) Study successful games with the same genre, difficulty and camera view for reference.
when: When balancing melee and ranged combat with no ready-made fix
why: No off-the-shelf solution exists

text: 1) Select matches with extreme skill mismatches. 2) Measure how often the weaker player wins. 3) Double that percentage to estimate the luck factor.
when: Estimating how much randomness affects outcomes.
why: Luck favors the expected winner half the time, so the weaker player's upset rate is half the luck share.

text: 1) Randomly set up the hidden state. 2) Apply one strategy. 3) Record the result. 4) Repeat thousands of times. 5) Compare win rates across strategies.
when: verifying a counterintuitive probability result
why: large simulated runs reveal true rates without manual counting

text: Some world editors can change map size and nearly every facet of a game, not just individual levels.
Designers who move along the zoom axis with greater range and speed usually produce better design, whatever is being designed.
Weapon accuracy equals hits divided by shots; weapon power equals kills divided by hits.
when: when measuring weapon performance from gameplay events

text: Design work moves along a vertical axis running from vision through organization to execution, with designers shifting back and forth between goals and constraints.
1) Tune spread, recoil, and trace. 2) Add client-side prediction so input responds immediately. 3) Iterate until the weapon feels natural enough that players stop noticing it.
when: tuning shooter weapons
why: Responsive, natural-feeling weapons let players focus on the game rather than the controls.

text: 1) Playtest a navigation section with the cue. 2) Playtest it without the cue. 3) Compare where players struggle to find the way.
when: For navigation sections where the designer does not want players challenged.
why: A visible cue that stands out against a busy environment directs attention, freeing players' attention for core challenges.

text: Modeling a whole level suits decoration and uses less memory on weak devices, but testing is slow because it needs export and import; modular tiles assembled in the engine allow faster iteration.
when: when choosing how to build level geometry from 3D modeling
why: Importing one model is easier to render on weak hardware, but the non-interactive modeling tool makes testing slow.

text: Some feel decisions look counterintuitive, such as deliberately altering gravity at a jump's apex.
Designers can apply flow questions to their own working time, since flow is when the most work gets done.
Playtests can also ask whether players want to play again and which strategies they discover on their own.
Rules are discovered gradually through experimentation; write them down late, once the game is playable.
when: during early development
why: Rules arrive gradually and experimentally.

text: 1) Play several games under the baseline rules and note how long each takes. 2) Change one variable, such as grid size, win length, turn structure, or player count, and play several games. 3) Compare play time, interest, strategy changes, balance, and social effects, and whether the change suggests other variables to change.
when: when changing a rule variable such as turn structure or player count

text: 1) Score each option's attributes on an ordinal scale, low 1, medium 2, high 3, and total them. 2) Compare totals with observed play results. 3) If they disagree, raise or lower one attribute's weight, rescore, and recheck. 4) Playtest the revised model and repeat until the options feel fair.
when: balancing a set of options rated on several attributes
why: The scoring is only a theory, so play results are what confirm whether the model is correct.

text: 1) Propose a wording fix. 2) Judge whether it is too complicated. 3) If so, simplify it and repeat until the wording is simple.
1) Slow down before changing anything. 2) Think broadly about wider implications and implicit goals. 3) Let emotions fade. 4) Then decide on the change.
when: A playtest reveals an apparent imbalance
why: Quick fixes often create hidden side effects, so a change helps only if it causes fewer new problems than it solves.

text: 1) Write down a game's rules as you did its procedures. 2) Play the game using only that written version. 3) Note any rules you forgot and how their absence changed play.
when: Checking whether a rule set is complete and clear
why: Forgotten or missing rules reveal gaps in written documentation.

text: 1) Give a stranger only the rulebook. 2) Watch them learn and play without help. 3) Cut rules that do not serve the fun.
when: testing whether rules are unclear or hard to learn

text: An asset tracker records what has been created and its state, covering code, levels, art, sound, music, and design documents.
Designing and refining tools for building knowledge is a core part of game design work.
Several engines are designed for beginners, with tutorials and low prices for students and independent developers.
Toolset quality is a major factor in publisher funding decisions.
A cross-sheet reference with dollar signs, such as =Sheet!$B$5, stays fixed when copied, while a relative one shifts with each copied cell.
Interfaces of real complexity require modes.

Left mouse button pans and moves forward and back; right mouse button gives mouse look; holding both moves left/right and up/down; holding right button with W, A, S, D flies, with Q and E for up and down.
Use a graphical authoring interface, such as dragging blocks or menus, for authors who are not highly technical.
when: Authors are non-programmers or not highly technical
why: Text syntax errors constantly frustrate people without programming experience.

text: Choose tools that fit the project's workflow and scale; lightweight tools suit small projects, and a feature-rich 3D engine may be overkill.
when: when selecting level design tools

text: Spend the most effort on what will be noticed, and on what cannot be approximated easily, such as a motorbike headlight whose round shape exposes corners.
why: Viewers readily detect flaws on simple curved shapes.

text: After a pointer swap, the buffer being read holds data from two frames ago, so any technique reusing old data must account for an extra frame of age.
when: Buffers alternate with pointer swaps and old data is reused
why: Each buffer is only rewritten every other frame, so its contents lag by one extra frame.

text: If lighting results require compiling or rendering, lighting quality suffers because iteration is too slow to compare options.
when: evaluating lighting workflows
why: Long waits for compiling make designers forget earlier versions and avoid comparing options back and forth.

text: Text baked into art is much harder to localize than dialogue; plan for this early in multi-language releases.
when: When a game ships in multiple languages and has text embedded in its world art.
why: Changing art for each language is costly.

text: The reasons for bytecode describe much of a typical game, so they alone do not justify the pattern and it should be adopted deliberately.
when: Evaluating whether to introduce a bytecode VM
why: Bytecode adds significant complexity, so broad reasons are not enough on their own.

text: Producing axonometrics takes time that could go toward prototyping the level in an engine.
when: deciding how much diagramming to do before building
why: Axonometrics are derived from existing drawings, so their effort competes with building level prototypes in the engine.

text: 1) Right-click the cell and choose Insert Note. 2) A corner marker appears and the text shows on hover. 3) Reopen Insert Note to edit, or use Clear Notes to remove it.
when: Explaining one specific cell's formula or value.
why: A note attached to the cell avoids ambiguity about what a comment refers to when a text column is impractical.

text: 1) On the first change, launch a fixed-length countdown. 2) When it expires, process all accumulated changes. The lag between input and response is called hysteresis, and the countdown length tunes how often work happens.
when: Processing changes while the player keeps playing.
why: Batching on a timer gives fine control over processing timing so the game can absorb the work smoothly.

text: 1) Whoever breaks the build fixes it. 2) They receive a visible symbolic token, such as a rubber chicken. 3) The token passes on when someone else breaks the build, with no confrontation needed.
when: Teams where broken builds happen often
why: Breaking the build costs the whole team, so individuals have little reason to avoid it on their own.

text: 1) Open the Content Browser's Scene tab. 2) Select Persistent level to list all actors in the level. 3) Select an actor and press F to focus the viewports on it. Tick Auto Focus to focus on every selection.
1) Switch to the Top view. 2) Hold the middle mouse button and drag. 3) Read the distance from the readout.
when: When judging a distance such as an ambient sound's radius in the editor.
why: Helps set radii and other distances.

text: The editor has four viewports: Front, Side, Top and Perspective. Change a viewport's type from its Viewport Options menu, or cycle with the P button. Use Maximize Viewport to restore the four-view layout.
when: If the editor starts with one full-screen viewport.

text: Choose a language and tools you already know so you can change things quickly.
Track approvals for every asset, recording whether the right people have approved it, not only the finished ones.
Understanding a tool means knowing its basic concepts and limits, not being an expert in using it.
when: When a career path, such as narrative design, requires level-design or content tools.
why: Tool familiarity lets content integrate quickly and eases moving into another role later.

text: When programmers build narrative tools, ask whether they can think of a scenario that fits the gameplay.
why: Colleagues who see narrative adding to gameplay will consult the writer sooner, making their work easier and better.

text: Record each branch choice as a quest state condition, such as flag true or false, so testers can confirm that both outcomes are tracked.
when: testing a branching quest

text: If a complex feature must stay, make its representation clear or introduce it after players understand the core systems.
when: When a complex feature provides depth that cannot be cut from the game.
why: Confusion breeds frustration and a sense of lost control, which can drive players away.

text: Handle user mistakes gracefully in creative authoring tools, for example by providing undo.
when: Designing an authoring tool for creative work
why: Mistakes are normal in creative work.

text: Design creativity tools to be intuitive, powerful and expressive, giving instant creative results that beat what users make alone while preserving their original intent.
why: Built-in computational support lets a novice produce better work than they could unaided.

text: An asset browser should show names, scale, 3D previews and usage, since relying on memory limits the palette and leaves good assets unused.
when: evaluating asset management in editors
why: Nobody can memorize thousands of asset names, so assets go unused when people rely on recall.

text: Use a camera that matches the player's first-person view, since orbit controls in confined spaces misrepresent what the player sees.
when: judging room size and navigation during building
why: Orbit views in confined spaces hide how the player will perceive the room in first person.

text: Each abstraction layer or extension point costs time to develop, debug, and maintain, and pays off only if the flexibility is actually needed later.
when: deciding whether to add an extension point
why: Predicting future needs is unreliable, so speculative flexibility often goes unused.

text: Modes add variety to a game, but each one is something players must learn and understand.
why: Players can misread the rules when a mode change goes unnoticed, and more modes raise that chance.

text: Showing many object types at once clutters the editor view and can slow the editor; use default visibility settings unless a specific type is needed.
when: When many actors and other objects crowd the editor viewport.
why: Each displayed object type adds to what the editor must draw.

text: A graphical authoring tool can stop mistakes as they happen, while a text tool sees nothing until a whole file is submitted; the graphical tool requires building a user interface.
why: Stepwise interactive building lets the tool see each change, while text tools only see content in a full file.

text: Concepts that are hard to explain verbally should be shown as a playable build, since players grasp them by playing.
why: Hands-on play let executives judge the charm and simplicity that a verbal or storyboard pitch of an unclassifiable idea could not convey.

text: Avoid hiding rows and columns in a spreadsheet when you can, since hidden data is easy to overlook.
when: building or editing a spreadsheet
why: hidden cells are easily forgotten

text: Small hobby programs stay manageable for one person, but become hard to hold in one's head as they grow past that size, prompting a search for organization guidance.
when: a personal project grows beyond what its author can track mentally
why: Working memory cannot hold all interactions once a codebase exceeds a modest size.

text: House rules are changes players make to operational rules after noticing a deficiency over several rounds of play.
when: Players are modifying a game for their group
why: Repeated experience reveals problems that the written rules leave open.

text: Hobby tabletop games are very complex, such as role-playing games, miniature-figure battle games, and trading card games.
Hobby shops are typically small, privately owned stores run by enthusiasts.
Generating ideas on demand, a learnable skill, gets faster and better with practice; expert brainstormers build on teammates' contributions as a team activity.

Software design patterns descend from an architecture pattern language, adapted to software; game researchers adapted pattern languages to catalogue recurring game elements and the player problems they solve.
Unrelated subjects, such as a simulation economy from another game, a biological system from microbiology, or high-brow with low-brow knowledge, can spark mechanics and original designs.
why: Cross-domain analogy transfers structures into new systems; unlikely combinations produce ideas existing designs lack.

text: Aim for dozens of ideas per brainstorm and about 100 ideas per hour, welcoming wild ideas.
1) Record yourself speaking freely about the topic for about five minutes. 2) Transcribe the recording afterward. 3) Mine the transcript for valuable ideas.
when: When brainstorming ideas aloud
why: Spoken, unedited ideas feel more real and often contain useful concepts hidden among rambling.

text: While generating ideas, do not self-censor when working alone; in a team, do not censor, dismiss or criticize others' ideas before they are developed.
when: during idea generation
why: Criticizing ideas too early breaks the flow of open thinking and collaborative extension that brainstorming depends on.

text: Record ideas constantly in a notebook, handheld device, cheap voice recorder or app, and transcribe periodically before they fade.
when: throughout the creative process
why: Human memory is poor, and unrecorded ideas keep occupying mental energy until recorded, freeing the mind to relax.

text: Look for design inspiration outside games and outside your own genre; cultivate unusual interests to escape the echo chamber and gain distinct design material.
why: Unusual sources supply ideas peers do not share.

text: Designers feel a strong sense of accomplishment when a mechanic finally works, and searching for starvation threatens that feeling, so they may avoid testing.
Playing a real, even crude, build produces concrete ideas that come while inspiration is fresh, which thinking on paper rarely yields.
when: Early prototyping of a concept
why: Concrete play experience exposes problems and possibilities imagination cannot reach.

text: An odd idea can be explored by extending it until it becomes a distinct concept, even if it is later rejected.
when: when a strange idea surfaces during brainstorming
why: exploration turns a random thought into a usable concept

text: Most people who offer design ideas want to be heard, not to take control of the design.
why: Their motive is caring about the outcome, which is why being heard satisfies them rather than taking over.

text: People tend to jump to solutions before they have clearly defined the problem.
why: Rapid mental processing favors immediate fixes over careful problem framing.

text: Unconscious rumination keeps working on a problem after conscious effort stops, so surprising insights can arrive during idle time with unpredictable timing.
when: Taking a break from direct testing of a problem.
why: The mind continues connecting ideas during unrelated activity.

text: Rereading your own script after a break often surprises you with your earlier choices, and this reaction is normal.
when: rereading a script after a break
why: Distance from the writing process

text: Quick, low-effort handling of unimportant decisions can look like laziness but is rational indifference, since the decision barely affects the game.
when: When a minor design decision has no significant effect.
why: Spending heavy effort on trivial choices wastes time better used elsewhere.

text: Going along with the group takes little thought and avoids social risk, but flaws go unnoticed and spread through the design.
why: Constant agreement signals laziness or fear, so no one is left to flag inconsistencies.

text: Procedural literacy covers knowing how machines operate, how code is organized, and the broad principles of game programming.
A blue sky project assumes a technology is possible even though it cannot be built today, so ideas are not limited by current capability.
Incubation is a period when ideas churn below conscious awareness; it can last years or only a few hours.
Insight is the 'aha' moment when separate pieces come together into an idea.
Brainstorming is a semiformal group process for quickly producing large numbers of diverse ideas.
The nameless quality is a hard-to-name trait of well-designed things that makes them feel alive, whole, comfortable, free, and free from inner contradictions; people recognize it by experience.
when: Evaluating whether a design feels special or lifeless
why: It resists verbal definition but is recognized in well-made places and objects

text: Across playtest versions, core rules can stay largely stable while the card mix, player count and art change.
Dreams can deliver solutions to hard problems, since the subconscious communicates through images.
Good concept art makes the idea clear to the team, helps people imagine entering the world, excites players and workers, and can help secure funding.
Suitable games for balance work include TCGs, LCGs, deckbuilding games, miniatures games, tabletop RPGs with combat rules, and TBS or RTS computer games with mod tools.
when: choosing a game

text: In games, macro-level ideas come from a studio, a prototype group, or a game jam, and micro-level UX work asks what problems players meet with a specific system.
Conception outlines game pillars, gameplay loops, progression, features, design and artistic intents, target audience, and business goals.
Many chance-based idea methods come from surrealist and dadaist artists, who used chance to draw on the unconscious mind.
Most ideas build on earlier ideas, so no idea may be truly original.
Good game ideas grow through successive layers and iterations that refine an original concept rather than appearing in a single flash.
For teams, whiteboards gave better mind-mapping results than software tools.
The concept/contract stage ends with a signed agreement covering rights, deliverables, and payment schedules; the opening checkpoint is executing the contract and approving the project plan.
Many revolutionary designs are stumbled upon, and famous games changed fundamentally during production; their best qualities often could not have been planned on paper.
Game companies usually have more of their own ideas than they can produce.
Relaxation is a second ingredient of rumination, since new ideas often arrive during relaxed activities such as showering or commuting.
Harsh, fear-based standards suit procedural work with clearly visible mistakes, such as following defined cooking steps, but fail creative game development.
when: Choosing a management style for a team's work.
why: Creative work needs risk taking and failure, which fear suppresses.

text: A catalog of 253 architectural patterns, from town-scale layouts to window-scale details, influenced game design and the software design-patterns movement.
Practitioners in music, architecture, writing, film, product, web, visual design and choreography all hold principles about human experience.
Combining entries from different idea lists produces concepts that feel complete and unexpected, each with its own life.
Some elements are not beautiful alone but become beautiful in combination, so composition is part of presentation.
People matter more than ideas: a good idea given to a mediocre team gets ruined, while a mediocre idea given to a good team gets fixed.
Speech recognition, artificial intelligence and brainwave sensing are technologies that many designers currently ignore despite their potential.
Pillars are decided non-linearly, with each decision informing the others.
No reliable formula for game success exists; design can only draw on ingredients from cognitive science and development best practices.
Every design shapes user behavior, so no design is neutral.
The next few decades of designers will decide whether games live up to the medium's promise.
The game pattern catalog has thirteen patterns in four categories: sequencing, behavioral, decoupling, and optimization.
A single game can have several possible cores, and each choice yields a functional but different game.
Architectural pattern theory can bridge handmade and procedural design, letting both coexist.
Do the groundwork yourself and rely heavily on the subconscious silent partner, which supplies inspiration when its work is respected.
when: When brainstorming or creative tasks, especially about games.
why: Division of labor keeps the partnership productive.

text: Begin variant design with very simple games, since minor tweaks to a finely tuned setup may produce major effects.
Add AI editor support and level-editor markers for tactical locations and areas, so designers can place them without code.
why: Manually made AI data is no better than hand-writing AI each time, so toolchains should let content enter the game without manual steps.

text: Keep asking questions while listening: Is that right? Why is it this way? Is this how they really feel? What does this now imply?
when: Listening to feedback or observations
why: Questions turn what you hear into understanding.

text: Change your physical viewpoint and location, such as standing on a chair or working in a bus, on a beach, in a mall, or in a toy store.
when: Brainstorming when ideas feel stuck
why: New viewpoints and places generate new perspectives

text: Use partners or small groups for narrow problems rather than broad, open-ended ones.
when: when choosing a brainstorming format
why: groups work better on narrow problems

text: Committing quickly to one seed idea is more productive than waiting for a perfect option, provided you stay ready to drop it when it fails.
when: when a long list of ideas leaves you stuck in indecision
why: Committing makes an idea's flaws and benefits visible, which indecision hides.

text: Phrase alternatives as questions, such as asking what would happen if the team did B instead of A, so everyone weighs both options neutrally.
when: when comparing competing design options
why: Questions keep the debate from becoming a contest of positions.

text: Random combinations of category options work for brainstorming and can force a creative constraint on a short project such as a game jam.
Game ideas only have value once someone executes them, so speculative concepts should be prototyped rather than only discussed.
why: Ideas amplify execution rather than carrying value alone.

text: Identify the right problem before reacting, since identifying it matters more than reacting quickly.
when: Live operation issues
why: Without solid hypotheses, panic drives reactive changes that can harm user experience and revenue.

text: Use brainstorming when an idea must be produced on a schedule rather than waiting for inspiration to arrive.
when: When a creative professional has no time to wait for inspiration to strike.
why: It is frequently required by business needs and lets each teammate share authorship of the design.

text: Creative stages recur rather than run in order, so reaching insight may take several loops through the stages.
why: The loop count scales with how deep and wide the problem is, so insight can take many passes.

text: Spend a significant part of each day on non-game inputs such as reading, film, music, sketching, exercise, or volunteering to keep a steady supply of ideas.
when: when a steady supply of raw design ideas is needed
why: ideas depend on rich input

text: A source topic may inspire a systemic mechanic that looks nothing like the topic itself.
Most good ideas arise when the subconscious combines dissimilar things in new ways.
when: When generating new game ideas

text: Expect iteration in every phase and keep alternative plans ready; treat concept-phase plans as iterative drafts, since production constraints will change them.
when: Concept and pitch phases
why: No plan survives production unchanged.

text: Many fiction clichés persist because they justify good mechanics; changing one can damage mechanics players depend on, so check the mechanical need first.
why: Clichés cleanly justify mechanics, so altering a fictional element can leave a needed mechanical function unsupported.

text: Systems designers need frequent narrative input and feedback on the systems they design when story is central.
when: Story-driven game development

text: Derivative designs, clones, and ports can be planned almost completely because they rely on established knowledge.
when: when the design reuses a proven core
why: Earlier games in a genre show how a new one will behave, so its outcomes can be predicted in advance.

text: Parti studies are cheap and noncommittal, usually skipping measurement so designers focus on spatial and formal ideas.
when: exploring overall level shape early
why: Skipping measurement keeps early exploration fast and focused on form.

text: Meaningful complexity should grow out of a simple system rather than being stacked on top of it through added explicit rules.
when: When a designer adds rules to force a desired balance outcome in a game.
why: A desired effect arising from interactions is natural balancing, while piled-on rules are artificial.

text: Roughly 20% of features drive about 80% of usage, so prioritise the core features in the default experience.
when: Deciding which features to surface by default.
why: The Pareto principle says a minority of variables drive most results.

text: Study patterns of use rather than hardware to gain insight into the past, present, and future of gameplay.
when: deciding what kind of game suits a setting
why: Hardware is ephemeral, while the places people use it persist and reveal lasting usage patterns.

text: While playing, observe your own experience and reason at the same time about the elements causing it. This combined skill takes practice.
when: When analyzing or revising a game.
why: Experience and structure reveal their causal link only when assessed together.

text: Emergent strategies are fragile, so interesting ones should be noticed and nurtured, much as a garden is tended.
when: When interesting strategic actions begin appearing in a game under development.
why: Emergent play follows its own course yet can be easily destroyed.

text: The brain handles concrete examples better than abstract principles, so manipulable systems that show concepts aid learning.
when: teaching a concept
why: Concrete instances are easier to process and remember

text: While playing, notice the numbers behind decisions, since even simple games contain many design choices that affect gameplay.
why: Even the simplest games hide many decisions where altered numbers change gameplay, which builds analytical intuition.

text: Designers combine deterministic and non-deterministic mechanics to shape the player experience rather than using only one kind.
why: Deterministic patterns can be memorized, while randomness stops patterns from being reliably memorized.

text: Examine a game both as separate elements and as a whole in play, since each view reveals different things.
why: Some qualities only emerge from the interaction of all elements once the system runs, so separate inspection cannot predict them.

text: Real originality changes fundamentals rather than surface details, and unique content can still use familiar symbols to communicate.
when: When a designer considers introducing unique content or new conventions.
why: Unfamiliar conventions take extra effort to understand, whereas familiar symbols communicate unique content quickly.

text: A change in one part of a game system can alter how players perceive other parts, so fixes produce ripple effects.
when: Changing one element of an interrelated system
why: Game systems are interrelated

text: Silly prompts loosen thinking and reveal new perspectives, and new perspectives tend to produce strong ideas.
when: Stuck or rigid brainstorming sessions
why: Playful framing breaks habitual thinking

text: Crunch, tiredness and stress all reduce performance.
Rumination forms new connections between old ideas, so a larger store of knowledge yields more possible connections.
when: When seeking a creative solution to a design problem.
why: Creative association draws on existing material.

text: A group's output is shaped more by how its structure, culture and hierarchy route knowledge, power and resources than by the personalities of its members.
when: When a team's structure routes knowledge, power and resources in a poor direction.
why: Capable individuals in a badly routed organization can collectively act foolishly.

text: Ants find food through random wandering, then lay pheromone trails on the return trip; other ants follow, and each successful trip reinforces the trail, making rich sources' paths straighter and stronger.
when: When the path ends at an abundant food source.
why: Followers reinforce what earlier successes marked, so trail quality compounds without any central control.

text: Before speaking up, people weigh credit and learning against wasted time and public rejection; a good climate tips this toward sharing ideas, and a fearful one tips it toward silence.
when: When a person decides whether to share an idea with colleagues.
why: People tally expected credit and learning against time wasted and public rejection before deciding to speak.

text: Open-ended creation without set goals, and focused on building rather than destroying, can become a breakout genre with a broad audience.
when: When a game centers on creating things without set goals.
why: Players are drawn to making things on their own terms.

text: Letting outside elements into a game, such as real money or extra cards, turns it into a different game.
when: When outside elements such as real money or added cards enter the game's boundary.
why: Game boundaries are what define the game, so outside elements that cross them change it intrinsically.

text: Because interactions multiply, a small rule set can generate endless different games, from long struggles to quick sweeps.
why: Interactions among simple mechanics multiply into a large number of possible play experiences.

text: Limit a brainstorm session to about an hour, because group energy drops after that.
when: When running a brainstorming session.
why: Brainstorming is high-energy, so the session naturally fades after roughly sixty minutes.

text: Mini-expansion sizes: card game 5–10 new cards; strategy game 5–10 new units; miniatures game units for one faction or a new mini-faction; tabletop RPG abilities, feats, or a class.
when: When designing an expansion to showcase a new mechanic.

text: Creativity is described as five stages: preparation, incubation, insight, evaluation, and elaboration.
why: Insight timing cannot be predicted, so preparation and incubation need constant attention.

text: Adding more visual or sound work than the question needs wastes valuable prototyping time.
when: When a prototype is meant to test mechanics rather than aesthetic questions.
why: Surplus aesthetic work takes time away from prototyping that is scarce and valuable.

text: Being paranoid about idea theft is counterproductive; an estimated 99.99% of people have no intention of stealing ideas.
Fighting for one's own ideas against the team damages trust and slows the project.
when: Working in a design team
why: The designer's role is to hold the game's overall vision rather than to win every idea contest, so fighting for personal ideas works against that role.

text: Doubts about past luck, narrow skills, or a changing field can stop you from attempting design work.
when: Deciding whether to start a design project
why: Doubt replaces action and so prevents learning.

text: Nagging or looming over the creative process slows it down, and straining for an immediate answer blocks the answer from surfacing.
when: When a designer is straining for an answer to a creative problem that has not yet surfaced.
why: The subconscious keeps working on an unsolved problem in the background, and watching or pressuring it does not hasten the result.

text: Partners who poke holes in every idea, or who have very narrow tastes, make poor brainstorming partners.
when: when choosing a brainstorming partner

text: Letting engineers choose whatever shadow algorithm is trendy can produce a look that does not match the artistic vision.
when: When engineers are choosing rendering techniques such as shadows or textures for a game with an established artistic vision.
why: Artists are trained over long periods to form integrated visions, so they should set the aesthetic direction while engineers recommend how to reach it.

text: Assuming creative people are excused from being organized undermines trust with listeners.
when: Preparing a pitch as a creative professional
why: Disorganization reads as unreliability to decision-makers.

text: Each change in metric-driven design is a guess in a huge design space, so trial and error can be slow and unfocused.
when: When a designer tunes a live game by changing features and watching engagement or revenue numbers.
why: Each change alters player behavior in ways that feed back into the metrics, so correlations appear while the underlying cause stays unknown.

text: Worrying about losing control of a brainstorm is itself a sign that control is already slipping.
Unsolicited game ideas are usually ignored, deleted, or returned unread, because a later dispute over a similar idea would be costly.
when: When sending a game idea to a company that has not asked to see it.
why: Legal risk from ownership disputes.

text: Sending a game unasked, showing up at a publisher's office, or using wacky demos to impress is not recommended.
when: When approaching a publisher with a game it has not requested.

text: Assuming an idea alone has value is a pitfall; hard work and contribution to a company's goals are what get things done.
Developers in the same codebase often reinvent solutions that already exist elsewhere in it, because proven patterns go undocumented and undiscovered.
when: large teams sharing a codebase without a shared pattern vocabulary
why: Good solutions stay buried in code and are not written down for others to find.

text: Studios often give ethics little careful consideration during development.
Early enthusiasm in blue-sky meetings does not show a project is on track.
when: Early in a project, during blue-sky meetings that lack a shared, concrete plan.
why: Excitement about ideas hides the lack of a shared, concrete plan.

text: Intense focus on a problem can block the insight you need, so pushing harder is not always productive.
when: Stuck on a design problem.
why: Focus suppresses the associative thinking that produces insight.

text: Teams often pour effort into the component that is established and easy to fund, even when it is not the real bottleneck to the goal.
why: Established components have known designs and budgets, so effort is easy to direct there.

text: A trivial code change can cost days when other people are blocked waiting for it, and problems in immature systems can stay hidden for months.
when: When making small changes in a shared pipeline or immature system.
why: Blocked dependents turn a small fix into a large schedule cost.

text: Political thinking can lead a designer to avoid good ideas, which signals organizational deficiencies but may still be the best choice for the process.
when: When a feature would be politically costly to cut later because others would become invested in it.
why: Once others are invested, a failing feature would be hard to remove, so the designer may avoid pushing it.

text: Treating a fixed, certain stance as strength closes off better ideas.
Designers often focus on the physical level of rules and overlook assigning meaning to objects, wasting a major design asset.
when: When designers are captivated by how objects physically move, steer, or respond to the player.
why: Assigning meaning to objects through higher-level rules is one of a game's strongest design resources, and tactile focus pulls attention away from it.

text: Important resonant ideas are often buried in a designer's thinking and can be hard to notice at first.
when: When a designer is trying to identify what the core appeal of their own game is.
why: Resonant ideas sit buried in a designer's instincts and feelings, so they are hard to notice without deliberate probing.

text: Open-ended puzzles with little feedback about whether the player is on track frustrate most players.
when: When puzzles are aimed at a general audience rather than dedicated puzzle enthusiasts.
why: Without feedback players cannot tell if they are making progress

text: Self-expression is important but easy to forget during design; keep it in mind as a deliberate lens to avoid leaving it out.
Trying to replace an entire curriculum usually produces a game that does everything poorly.
when: When a transformational game is conceived as a replacement for an entire curriculum.

text: Playing many games does not by itself confer design expertise; design knowledge has to be studied explicitly.

1) Gather random words and images from a printed page, web searches, or a dictionary, or write one idea per index card. 2) Cut out or draw two to four pieces at random. 3) Combine them into a game concept; wilder pieces yield richer combinations.
when: When needing outside stimulation during brainstorming
why: Random pairing of unrelated pieces creates novel concepts.

text: 1) Score leading ideas on technical feasibility, market opportunity, artistic merit, and cost or scope, fitting the team's scope. 2) Trim to about three ideas. 3) Brainstorm features for those ideas. 4) Write one-page descriptions and test them with an informal feedback group.
when: When choosing which of several game ideas to pursue, before committing to one.
why: Scoring against four qualities filters out ideas the team cannot build, sell, or scope.

text: 1) Invent a computer puzzle inspired by a news headline. 2) Define its rules precisely. 3) Create an easy and a hard level. 4) Build a paper prototype. 5) Test with others and record enjoyment and confusion points. 6) Revise rules based on feedback.
when: Designing a puzzle game where the solution must be exactly defined
why: Precise rules and iterative testing reveal where players enjoy, get stuck, or get confused.

text: Add rules and procedures incrementally so people without your full vision can play, and playtest after each addition.
when: Building structure in a prototype
why: Incremental additions keep faults traceable to the latest change

text: Check whether the foundation survives real players, the game has beginning, middle, and end, players can reach the objective, they engage with the designed conflict, and they enjoy it.
when: Evaluating a structured prototype
why: Only real players, lacking the designer's full vision, can show whether the underlying intuition and foundation actually hold.

text: 1) Sit upright in a firm chair with head tilted back and arms relaxed. 2) Hold a heavy key loosely over an upturned plate on the floor. 3) Relax into drowsiness. 4) When the grip loosens and the key drops, its noise wakes you to note the idea.
when: when seeking ideas during a brief rest
why: the falling key's noise wakes you at the moment of half-sleep, when the mind is refreshed

text: 1) State the problem clearly. 2) Make its importance clear. 3) Leave it alone so it incubates. Answers may arrive quickly, slowly, or not at all.
when: when stuck on a creative problem
why: straining for an answer slows the process

text: 1) Each person brainstorms independently first. 2) The group then shares, mixes, and solves problems together.
when: when running a team brainstorm
why: a group that gathers cold to brainstorm wastes time

text: Use the ten puzzle principles as a review checklist when evaluating any puzzle design.
when: Evaluating a puzzle design
why: A checklist catches common puzzle design failures

text: 1) Draw a large, detailed pencil sketch of the whole. 2) Pick one key element. 3) Render that element fully with color, clean lines and shading. Viewers then see the scope of the whole and the quality of finished detail.
when: presenting concept art
why: viewers can imagine the whole finished at that same level

text: 1) Have art and design teams work together. 2) Produce concept images showing how elements will look within the game design. 3) Spread these images across design overview, detailed design document, and technical documents.
when: When many team members need to see the intended look before the game is built.
why: Technical documents use concept images to show the look technology should aim for

text: 1) Note topics the listener raises during the pitch. 2) Reuse those topics in later examples. 3) Adapt examples on the fly to include their ideas.
when: Delivering a live pitch
why: Reflecting the listener's contributions makes them feel ownership of the game.

text: 1) Compute the exact win probability for each side and for a tie. 2) Confirm the three sum to 1. 3) Verify with a simulation of a few thousand games.
when: race-to-damage games with multiple outcomes
why: An independent simulation cross-checks the exact math, so any mismatch exposes an error in one of them.

text: 1) Create one column per category, such as genre, setting or theme, or platform. 2) Fill each column with several options. 3) Pick one item per column at random with INDIRECT. 4) Join the picks into one string.
when: generating brainstorming prompts

text: 1) Pick five games you have played. 2) Write each game's premise. 3) Describe how each premise enhances the play experience.
when: when studying how premises support gameplay

text: 1) Pick a subject, such as a character or role. 2) Identify what about it would be engaging to control. 3) Decide how it reacts and whether it acts freely. 4) Design its controls, allowing unusual functions. 5) Generate as many ideas as possible.
1) Pick a book, article, or hobby. 2) List its systematic elements. 3) Repeat several times a week using different subjects.
when: When practicing a designer's way of seeing everyday subjects and hobbies.
why: Structures beneath everyday activities contain intrinsic systems that yield game-system ideas a surface view misses.

text: 1) Write continuously about the game for about 10 minutes without editing for coherence, spelling, or punctuation. 2) Stop and read back the output.
when: When brainstorming ideas
why: Unedited writing avoids self-criticism and can surface better ideas than polished work.

text: 1) Pick something apparently unrelated to a stuck problem. 2) Look for links between it and the problem. 3) Develop those links into a concept.
when: When stuck on a design problem
why: Unrelated input breaks fixation on existing solutions.

text: 1) List concrete alternatives. 2) Survey each person individually. 3) Ask them to choose or rank items. 4) Frame choices as realistic trade-offs.
when: When deciding between alternative ideas or features.
why: Individual ranked choices among real options produce clearer, more actionable answers than open group discussion.

text: 1) Place the core idea at the center. 2) Radiate related ideas outward with linked lines. 3) Add the verbs the player performs and the feelings tied to those actions.
when: When generating or structuring ideas for a game concept.
why: Mind mapping structures nonlinear thinking, and mapping player verbs and feelings gives the team shared vocabulary.

text: 1) Brainstorm widely and generate far more race and hero ideas than can fit. 2) Cut, modify, or keep each idea as a cornerstone. 3) Repeat narrowing until the set fits the game's roles.
when: early design of factions and heroes
why: Early abundance gives options, but a focused final set keeps each faction clear.

text: 1) Hold an open brainstorm with the team. 2) Invite executives so they can offer advice. 3) Let them see implementation issues firsthand.
when: Design disagreements with management
why: Shared discussion turns conflict into shared ownership of decisions

text: 1) Pitch high concepts for favorite games with teammates. 2) Study high concepts from films and other games.
when: Learning to write one-liners
why: Compressing a game into one or two sentences signals a clear vision and is easy for others to grasp and recall.

text: 1) Notice strange behavior or nonsensical results in a system you understand. 2) Investigate the hint instead of dismissing it. 3) Reorganize your thinking around the observation rather than forcing it to fit your worldview.
when: When a system behaves unexpectedly during design or testing
why: Valuable opportunities appear as anomalies inside well-understood systems.

text: 1) Keep a notebook at hand. 2) Record ideas the moment they arrive, including during easy tasks. 3) Review the notes later.
when: Harvesting results of unconscious rumination.
why: Ideas arrive unpredictably and fade if not captured.

text: 1) Ask what the protagonist's goal is and why they care about it. 2) List the obstacles between them and the goal. 3) Identify any antagonist and their relationship to the protagonist. 4) Check that obstacles gradually increase in difficulty. 5) Check that obstacles are big enough, and could they be bigger. 6) Ask how the protagonist transforms to overcome them.
when: After setting a goal, to confirm obstacles give the goal meaning.
why: A goal with no meaningful obstacle is not worth pursuing.

text: 1) List alternative points of view on a broad subject, such as documentary, conflict, quest, or antagonist. 2) Gather research from history, existing works, original builders, staff, and players. 3) Ask what the subject is fundamentally about, and commit to one theme drawn from that.
when: When a topic is too broad to guide design.
why: A specific point of view gives design a direction.

text: 1) Make a separate idea list for each tetrad element. 2) Write a dozen or more entries per list. 3) Combine entries across lists into complete concepts. 4) Create new categories whenever you need them.
why: Mixing entries from separate lists lets complete concepts emerge that no one would have predicted.

text: 1) Ask whether the design feels alive and which parts feel dead. 2) Identify which of Alexander's fifteen qualities the design already has. 3) Find ways to add more of those qualities.
when: Reviewing a design that feels mechanical
why: Checking for organic qualities reveals lifeless parts

text: 1) Set small milestones along the way to the grand goal. 2) Advertise each milestone to the player. 3) Reward each accomplishment.
when: Designing progression for campaigns or long games
why: Players enjoy visible progress, and small payoffs can feel sweeter than the final victory

text: Write down everything related to the problem, including silly ideas, since a silly idea can inspire a good one; memory is poor and combining ideas requires paper.
why: Writing also clears the mind of crowded ideas.

text: Use several brainstorming structures and vary them from project to project, letting leaders try unfamiliar ones and inviting members to suggest and lead sessions, and develop your own.
when: when the usual structure stops producing ideas
why: Each designer and game needs a different process, since fixed processes tend to produce the same results.

text: State the emotional response you want each asset to produce, not only what it depicts.
when: When coordinating with other teams on environmental narrative assets.

text: Start designing games now instead of waiting for permission to become a designer.
when: Deciding how to begin a career in game design
why: Designers become designers by doing the work, not by waiting for approval.

text: Immerse yourself in the problem: observe your audience in real settings, learn your technology deeply, study adaptations of your story, and play games with and without your core mechanic.
when: Preparing for brainstorming on a game concept
why: Deep exposure supplies material for new ideas

text: Use the rational mind for planning, taking precautions, and practical matters such as paying taxes.
when: When planning, taking precautions, or handling practical matters instead of brainstorming.
why: The rational side is needed to plan and set things straight, which the impulsive subconscious cannot do alone.

text: After brainstorming, narrow the broad list of ideas and develop the best ones into something useful.
when: After a brainstorming session has produced a long list of raw ideas.

text: Take odd thoughts, feelings, and dreams seriously and reflect on them briefly, since the subconscious offers more when its ideas are valued.
when: during brainstorming or idle moments
why: serious consideration encourages the subconscious to keep contributing

text: Limit brainstorming groups to four people or fewer, since adding more people does not necessarily help.
when: when forming a brainstorming session

text: Maximize the work not done, and have the team regularly reflect and adjust its behavior.
when: when planning and running development
why: Regular reflection lets the team become more effective and adjust its behavior over time.

text: Before choosing a seed idea, consider what it must grow into to survive later evaluation.
when: when selecting a seed idea

text: Judge ideas by how well they solve the stated problem rather than by personal preference, using the problem statement as the anchor.
when: When team members discuss and evaluate design ideas.
why: Without a problem anchor, discussion becomes a contest of opinions and gut feelings rather than of solutions.

text: Refer to ideas by their content rather than their owner, so the whole team takes ownership of them.
Before brainstorming, state a precise challenge, ideally as a player experience goal, and set aside solutions you already have in mind.
when: at the start of each session
why: Paring a challenge down to its core frees the mind from solutions already in view.

text: Open contributions with an affirming 'yes, and' response so that each idea builds on the previous one.
when: During a group brainstorm, while colleagues' ideas are still undeveloped
why: Criticism of half-formed ideas breaks the momentum and makes people hold back, which stifles creative output.

text: Hold brainstorms in a neutral space away from normal desks, and use simple playful objects to help people relax.
when: When the usual desk-and-screen work area makes it hard to think creatively
why: Familiar work settings resist free thinking, while playful distractions help the group relax and think more openly.

text: Post ideas on whiteboards or large taped paper so the whole group can see and build on them; this gets people standing and talking.
why: Ideas the whole group can see spark further ideas and support collaboration.

text: Number each idea so the group can cross-reference during a session and track output.
when: When developing a big concept with many linked ideas
why: Numbers let the group cross-reference ideas by shorthand without losing the larger line of thought, and they track output.

text: Develop ideas left over from a brainstorm in the following days rather than extending the session.
when: When a brainstorming session has gone on for about an hour
why: Brainstorming is high-energy, so mental and physical fatigue sets in after roughly an hour of focused work.

text: When an idea cannot be built yet, brainstorm workarounds or keep it for when technology catches up.
when: When an idea is not technically possible yet
why: Technology may advance later and make the idea feasible, so it is worth keeping rather than discarding.

text: Cut ideas that are too expensive or ambitious unless they can be scaled down, and keep them on a list for a future larger project.
when: When an idea exceeds the team's time or budget and cannot be scaled down
why: Keeping cut ideas on a list preserves them for a later, larger project with more resources.

text: Discuss the top five to ten ideas in a positive tone, weighing each idea's merits rather than bashing it.
when: when choosing among shortlisted ideas

text: Begin an open-ended list of proposals, accepting that some will never be adopted.
why: Keeping suggestions open to everyone avoids cliques and can surface good ideas a closed process would miss.

text: Run brainstorming sessions that anyone may join during design, from production assistants to QA staff.
when: During the design phase.
why: Excluding staff from design fosters cliques and can cost the team good ideas.

text: Designers should understand the stage structure and work with a producer on it, even if they never manage a project.
why: Knowing expected outcomes at each stage helps design ideas succeed.

text: If you want no payment or lawsuits, state in writing that the company may use the idea with no strings attached.
when: you do not want money or legal claims

text: Do not count on an unsolicited idea reaching decision makers.
when: When sending an idea to a game company without being asked
why: Companies generally prefer their own internal ideas, so outside pitches are often not heard.

text: Before moving to production, the core of the project must be clear and communicable, the team must understand the key design concepts it depends on, and one sentence must expand into a full pitch document.
when: Finishing the concept phase
why: Production builds on a clear, shared core

text: Assess how developed a concept is, for example whether it has concept art or a prototype, before estimating the narrative work it needs.
when: When a client's concept ranges from a vague premise to one that already has illustrations and a playable prototype.

text: Work on several problems in alternation so the unconscious can process one while you attend to another.
when: Hard problems that focused effort has not solved.
why: Background processing continues on the unattended problem.

text: Offer several ways to overcome a challenge, and story changes, so choices feel meaningful.
why: Choices whose effects players cannot perceive leave them without a sense of meaning or agency.

text: Keep inspiration concrete and grounded in real life so it can guide concrete design decisions.
Ask what a number emphasizes, not only whether it is balanced, because designers also change numbers to encourage particular play.
when: When adjusting numbers for reasons other than balance
why: Changing numbers can shift which style of play is emphasized, a separate effect from whether the game is balanced.

text: Acting enthusiastic may slowly create real enthusiasm when other options fail, but faked enthusiasm shows in the finished game; aim to restore real feeling.
when: When real enthusiasm is absent for a dreary task and other options have failed.
why: Faked enthusiasm makes the finished game mediocre at best.

text: Brainstorming with many developers quickly generates many unproven ideas, while high-skill balance testing slowly explores the nuances of an existing design.
Brainstorming yields volume but refines poorly with uneven quality, while written analysis yields depth but can take weeks.
when: Brainstorm when generating options; use written analysis when a question needs depth.
why: Each method suits a different stage of thinking.

text: Rumination is slow and cannot be scheduled, so it suits hard problems but cannot guarantee timely answers.
when: Hard, unsolved problems.
why: Insight timing is unpredictable.

text: Fear gives fast, obvious results but is a weak fuel for creativity, while love and appreciation work slowly, indirectly and quietly, and need patience before they pay off.
when: Deciding how to motivate a creative team.
why: Speed of results trades against the durability of creative output.

text: When rules allow only one-to-one requests, each request risks losing the turn and reveals to others that the asker holds that rank.
when: card games requiring indirect requests
why: Indirect routes trade speed for information exposure

text: Observer gives looser coupling and lets you reason about a subject alone, but makes communication flow harder to trace than an explicit call, since targets exist only at runtime.
when: When studying one subject's behavior without unrelated observers cluttering the view
why: Observer targets are determined dynamically, unlike a statically findable call.

text: An indie aggregator distributes and markets independent games on the developer's behalf, handling online distribution, marketing, and sales.
An independent publisher is not owned by a platform company.
Independent production means a developer self-funds and produces a game, keeping ownership and creative control while accepting long odds of success.
Independent developers fund projects through other jobs, work-for-hire, credit cards, or loans from friends and family.
Choose independent production only with a truly original idea and the passion and resources to finish it.
when: deciding whether to self-produce a game
why: Self-production is a long shot that often stalls before release, so it is worth it mainly for the freedom and ownership it grants.

text: Independent developers can publish through five routes, ranked easiest to hardest to enter: a personal website, user-generated game hubs, indie aggregators, casual publishers and portals, and downloadable console games.
Underestimating the effort to finish and distribute a game leads many independent projects to stall or never reach a release channel.
when: When an independent team is self-funding a long production run
why: Self-funded teams must survive months of production through other jobs, work for hire, or borrowed money.

text: If no publisher picks up an independent game, sell it directly online or use it as a demo to win a publishing deal for another game.
when: no publisher deal is offered

text: Independent production keeps full ownership of the idea and its implementation and allows mid-project changes, at the cost of high financial and completion risk.
Iterative design is repeated cycles of prototyping, testing, analyzing and refining, in which the design is shaped by how players experience it.

Cloning the biggest hit with rushed, budget-cut copies saturates the niche and lowers production values; adding features without removing anything leaves no value above competitors and predictable market failure.
when: When building a clone of a successful game
why: A copy cannot be the original, so every other version looks weaker beside it, and lower sales push studios to cut costs further.

text: 1) Observe players. 2) Generate ideas. 3) Prototype and try it out. 4) Test and revise. 5) Repeat until the design is satisfying, or good enough.
Iterative gains climb toward good-enough solutions, but can trap a design on a low hill; reaching a higher peak needs large untested jumps, taken only when refinement stalls.
when: when deciding whether small iterative refinements will reach a good design
why: Small steps cannot cross the valley between a low hill and a higher mountain.

text: Designers focus on current problems and ignore potential ones, because existing problems carry emotional weight while potential problems stay abstract.
why: Current problems are cognitively easier to think about than the many new problems a fix might cause.
