text: Design churn comes less from uncertainty in individual pieces than from change shockwaves propagating through dependencies, so concepts can persist while specifics change repeatedly.
when: Explaining repeated redesign of upper-layer features
why: Changes in foundations force revisions upward through every dependent system.

text: Players expect novelty and careful balance, so designers must iterate constantly, and waiting on engineers or slow recompiles breaks creative flow.
when: Planning production workflows for designer-facing behavior
why: Constant iteration means long turnaround on each change interrupts design momentum.

text: Designers often understand the case for iteration intellectually but only come to believe it emotionally after painful planning failures on a complete, significant game.
when: When a designer has read about iteration but still plans deeply
why: Belief depends on felt consequences, not on abstract argument.

text: Strong designers signal uncertainty with phrases such as 'my gut says' or 'the way I see it', which keeps discussion open.
when: When a designer proposes ideas in a team discussion that could turn into disagreement
why: Such phrasing reflects that all knowledge is uncertain and leaves room for others' better ideas.

text: A game is functional when a person who knows nothing about it can play from start to finish without the designer's help; it may still be clunky and unsatisfying.
RITE, Rapid Iterative Testing and Evaluation, tests a narrow element with one participant at a time and fixes discovered issues before the next participant tests the revised version.
when: Iterating quickly on one feature
why: Fast fixes between sessions speed up improvement.

text: Design thinking finds the right problem, weighs several solutions, and chooses the most suitable one, which is often imperfect.
Evaluation asks whether an insight is valuable and original.
Elaboration is usually the longest and hardest stage, and much of invention is sustained effort rather than inspiration.
Development means financing a team and managing it to deliver a high-quality game on time and within budget.
Therapeutic planning is planning mainly to feel better about an uncertain future rather than to coordinate work.
Debate exists to find flaws in ideas, exposing hidden assumptions and logical fallacies.
The designer owns the player experience from start to finish, making sure mechanics function at every level and working with almost every team member.
why: Gameplay depends on how it is programmed, visualized, and supported by sound and voice.

text: Explicit futures let players trade a future favor for a present resource.
Finishing means reaching the single stated long-term goal, while completing means finishing all tasks, including optional quests and locations.
Foundational technology enables an experience that was not possible before; decorational technology enhances one that already exists.
A transformation check asks how a game can change players for better or worse, since games change people through the experiences they create.
Transformational games aim to change players in a specific way, and the term is preferred over serious games, which implies seriousness matters more than fun.
A design knob is a tunable number on a game object that can be changed to adjust how the object plays.
A transition is an arrow between states, labeled with the condition, such as a die roll or fixed requirement, that allows the change.
Feature design is proposing a focused addition to an existing game rather than a whole new game.
The creative core, or X, is a concise concept that serves as both a razor for cutting features and a slogan that conveys the game.
Game development is deciding which appealing features can be built within limited time and limited cash.
Under the tool metaphor, PCG is an instrument that extends a designer's capabilities by adding a generative component to the workflow.
The crazy method calls the player's bluff by being unfair, arbitrary, or beyond technical norms, showing that the designer's rules do not follow convention.
Design effects are how a decision changes what players experience, and predicting them is the main work of game design.
Flow charts map the decisions a player faces as abstract nodes and branches, approximating what the player is thinking rather than physical level geometry.
Degenerative design breaks a game's established rules to surprise players, and designers can plan such breaks so the game's logic stays intact.
Game design is at once an individual craft and a shared, collaborative conversation between designers and players.
Iterative design comes from human-computer interface design and resembles the scientific method, repeatedly testing a hypothesis.
The usability and engageability framework can guide collaboration across teams, iterative design, user research and analytics.
The formal details stage can make or break a game.
Iteration loops vary by project: narrative games iterate story beats first, and loops may involve one person or ten over weeks.
In the trough of disillusionment a technology fails to meet its hype and can become unfashionable or despised.
Expansions may introduce entirely new mechanics, and their development follows a process similar to the original game's, usually on a shorter timeline.
Many structures and ideas from one driving implementation generalize to other driving mechanics, even when specific implementations differ.
The game UX framework was built from team-level practice and has not yet been tested academically.
Fun rating scales are not a good predictor of a game's later success or enjoyment.
User research helps teams identify early which problems to solve, rank their severity, and find solutions.
A game degree helps but is not required; many successful developers never earned one.
Understanding, changing and cleaning up code is an ongoing loop that never truly ends.
Revision checks cover the outline, wireframe, cuts, character consistency, and player agency, and should be repeated after each revision pass.
when: during any revision

text: A design framework lists fifteen properties shared by things that feel alive; the first five are levels of scale, strong centers, boundaries, alternating repetition and positive space.
No standard notation exists for foundational rules, so designers usually write them down only as needed.
Games have different target lengths, ranging from about 3 minutes for an arcade game to about 100 hours for a CRPG, and progression can be tuned to keep play within that range.
A designer's plan becomes an interactive experience only when players take part, much as a blueprint or script waits for use.
Good design comes from understanding what you have built and improving it step by step over months or years, not from a single flash of brilliance.
why: Listening to playtesters shows what the mechanics actually do, not what the designer wants or imagines they should do.

text: The iteration loop is a good basic approach but is not sufficient on its own.
why: Design knowledge comes from several methods with different costs, and the team must react to changing project conditions.

text: If playtests show a mechanic works better reversed, change the story to support the reversed version.
why: A story change can make a mechanic believable, so the team does not have to discard a mechanic that playtests favoured.

text: Do not agonize over the first iteration of numbers; every designer's first numbers will be off.
when: Early numeric design.
why: Balance is an ongoing process and player preferences shift, so hitting the target on the first attempt is unlikely.

text: Time to figure out a task is more informative than success or failure, since think-aloud changes how long players take to understand.
when: Measuring think-aloud results
why: Speaking changes the task, so duration reveals more than outcome.

text: Keep adding, testing and removing optional rules, since each addition can spark new design ideas.
Early definitions can be revised later, but they give the team a framework that prevents aimless trial and error during production.
when: Early in development, before a production team is launched
why: Physical prototyping forces the designer to define each element and how the elements interact before any digital build exists.

text: Minimize the time to a prototype's first failure, meaning its first rejected hypothesis, and be willing to stop early once it occurs.
why: Checking a prototype against its hypothesis is scientific practice, and an early failure avoids building ideas the designer does not actually have.

text: Single-change discipline matters most in late fine-tuning, when many playtester requests arrive at once and tempt batching.
when: Late fine-tuning.
why: Changing many things at once can make balancing uncontrollable and lose parts of the design that already worked.

text: Each design loop sharpens the problem statement, and early prototypes expose serious problems while they are cheap to fix.
why: Even a little playtesting reveals requirements such as networked play and which visual effects are too costly.

text: The number of loops needed to resolve a design cannot be planned in advance.
Simple card or board games can be built and tweaked repeatedly rather than following a strict loop-count plan.
when: when the game is cheap to build and change
why: A simple game can be prototyped in an hour or two, so repeated trial and error costs little.

text: Loop as fast as possible by building many rough prototypes rather than polished ones.
when: Iterating on design questions during development
why: Rough prototypes are cheap, so more loops fit into the available time

text: With online distribution, the iteration loop continues long after launch, so balancing never fully ends.
when: Games distributed online and updated after release.
why: Patches and value changes can be delivered after the game ships.

text: If you feel pulled toward work that connects to no purpose you can name, question whether to pursue it.
why: Only the designer can identify the personal purpose that makes the work worth doing.

text: Some inconsistencies are unavoidable in production, and awareness of them helps reduce their impact.
why: Each feel element shapes how players perceive the game's physical reality, so awareness lets you anticipate where small annoyances will show.

text: Rank issues by severity to players and by importance of the feature affected; a core-pillar issue can outrank a more severe minor one.
why: Priority depends on how badly players are hurt and how central the affected feature is, so a mild hit to a pillar can matter more.

text: Iterative design should include checking whether players are actually having fun.
why: Fun is hard to assess and personal to each player, so testing is how you confirm it is actually there.

text: Shared frameworks keep discussions about fun productive and prevent endless debate when fun is subjective.
Ideas are cheap; execution matters more, and a well-matured average idea can beat a poorly implemented great one.
why: What matters is how the end user experiences the product, not what the creators had in mind.

text: Discussing high-level goals while facing constraints, and staying concrete while dreaming, unifies design work and keeps it deliverable.
when: When moving between high-level vision and real-world production constraints.
why: Dreams must accept limits to be produced, so keeping both levels in view ties vision to what can actually ship.

text: Make training fun, since fun both drives productivity and reflects it.
when: When running short workshops that teach teams new tools.
why: Fun makes people more creative, receptive and productive, and it may both cause and reflect productivity.

text: Speeding up a fun game is simpler than making a fast game entertaining.
when: prioritizing early game development
why: Gameplay design is harder to retrofit onto optimized code than performance is to add later.

text: Give level editors undo, because designers become frustrated when they cannot reverse edits.
when: building game levels with an editor tool

text: Step away from the script for a day, a weekend, or a week before a full revision, to gain distance and spot mistakes you could not see while writing.
when: before a full revision
why: Being immersed mid-draft hides errors, and time away lets the writer evaluate the work with fresh eyes.

text: Each repeated revision pass usually needs fewer rewrites than the pass before it.
when: repeating revision cycles
why: Rewriting a scene restarts it as a first draft, so keeping existing work keeps each draft tight.

text: Use the interaction-count check early as a rule of thumb; this judgment improves with experience and is not a substitute for testing.
when: evaluating designs before implementation
why: Heavy testing takes a lot of time, so designers need ways to spot elegance on paper first.

text: Expect progress in small increments over years rather than a single breakthrough; no one moment marks the work as complete.
why: Each iteration fixed the feeblest parts, drew lessons from breakdowns, and built on what worked.

text: Make future deals explicit when players strike many complex, ongoing deals; skip it when deals are simple enough to remember.
when: When the game encourages many complex ongoing deals between players.
why: Players forget the details of many complex deals, so the game should record them; simple deals are remembered by players.

text: When player-written FAQs make a game noticeably better, the game is likely starved of information.
why: Without understanding a choice's implications, players cannot plan, so the game's value stays hidden until they learn it.

text: Each outside field supports a design task: economics informs in-game resource economies, and mathematics covers probability, risk, and scoring systems.
when: Choosing which outside knowledge to study
why: Matching fields to concrete tasks shows where they are useful.

text: To test for the major gift, start designing and notice whether the work makes you happy; early confidence does not settle it.
when: Deciding whether design suits you
why: Enjoyment shows only once you actually design.

text: A mechanics taxonomy should aim to produce great games rather than philosophical completeness, accepting some gray areas for practical use.
when: when classifying a game's mechanics
why: Designers need knowledge that serves making great games, and philosophically watertight analysis is less useful to them.

text: In a fair seeding, each lower rank has a lower title chance than the rank above it; if a lower seed has an easier path, the seeding is unfair.
when: when comparing candidate bracket seedings
why: A lower seed's path can contain more stronger opponents than a higher seed's path, changing its title chance.

text: Higher visual realism demands more detailed control, simulation and effects, since players notice inconsistencies more.
when: Increasing rendering realism
why: A realistic treatment creates expectations about behavior, while an iconic, absurd one sets few, so the detail must match.

text: A fascination with a subject, such as social insects, seen as a system to study and deconstruct, can generate original game concepts.
when: when seeking original concepts from the world
why: Viewing a subject as a system with rules and competition gives designers organized structure to turn into play.

text: Modifying existing genre mechanics attracts core genre players because it appeals to their taste for novelty while keeping familiar play.
when: When your idea fits an established genre and its audience
why: Core genre players receive novelty layered onto the play they already know, so they are likely to engage.

text: The future of game design depends more on serving deeper play and interaction than on immersive devices.
why: Immersive technology matters only insofar as it serves deeper play, which is what lets games move people beyond traditional media.

text: The greatest competitive win is a value no other game offers, since such a value attracts players who have nowhere else to go.
when: When looking for a distinctive design position
why: Players seeking an unserved experience have no alternatives and must choose the game.

text: Flow charts suit branching stories and complex systems, and also work for mapping key gameplay points in a level.
when: choosing a diagram for branching or systemic design
why: They model the sequence of decisions a player moves through, mirroring the player's reasoning rather than the physical layout of space.

text: Define the core experience first, then extend the design beyond its edges so important content is not lost at the boundaries.
when: when planning the scope of an experience with no hard cutoff
why: Audience context blurs where the experience starts and ends, so content placed exactly at the edge gets cut.

text: As production advances, playtest-revise cycles tighten, so the issues found and the changes made become smaller.
why: Because the game must eventually ship, late iterations are kept to small fixes rather than fundamental redesign.

text: When a disruptive technology becomes good enough, being faster, better and cheaper, customers can switch to it almost overnight.
when: the disruptive technology reaches a good-enough threshold
why: Buyers judge the newcomer against today's standards and stay put until it clears a threshold, while it keeps improving unnoticed.

text: Short iterations followed by review force strong team communication and build bonds among members.
when: Small cross-functional teams working in short, reviewed iterations.

text: Going into detail forces the team to think the game through from high-level vision down to file types and font sizes, exposing gaps early.
when: When writing a design document that covers the whole game in detail.
why: Conferring on details across text, visuals and specs makes each member check the whole game, catching mismatches before separate work is integrated.

text: Demanding perfection at every stage stretches each loop through overanalysis, which means fewer cycles and a weaker final game.
when: when each stage is held to near-final quality
why: Game quality depends most on how many iteration loops occur, and perfectionism lengthens each loop and reduces how many fit in.

text: Iterative processes avoid long-range assumptions and run constant reality checks, so disasters tend to surface early.
why: Frequent checks against reality surface unforeseen problems early, and not committing to distant-future assumptions lets the team redirect quickly.

text: The main cost of a critical failure is the disruption it causes to other processes, not the fix itself, and damage is worst when it hits during a time-critical event.
when: When a hidden flaw surfaces late in development.
why: Failures cascade into blocked work for everyone depending on the broken part.

text: Design has four steps: foundations, where the core idea is tested for fun; structure, where enough rules exist for people without your vision to play; formal details; refinement.
Playtesting follows a continuous loop of playtest, evaluate and revise, repeated from the first moment of design onward.
why: Testing late leaves no room for fundamental change, and a weak core mechanic cannot be fixed at that point.

text: The formal details stage has three goals: make the game functional, make it internally complete, and make it balanced.
when: Once a promising core idea needs a fully working version built out.

text: Design thinking manages creativity through repeated cycles of generating ideas, prototyping, testing, and iterating until the design satisfies from a UX standpoint.
Design thinking runs in three stages: understand users, explore through ideas and prototypes, and materialize through testing and iteration.
Three levels: vision (why: concepts, purpose), organization (how: systems, links, org and flow charts), execution (what: breakdowns, asset lists, technical, legal and human constraints).
why: The top level sets goals, the middle defines the means to reach them, and the bottom accepts real-world limits so the work can actually be produced.

text: Development has five stages: concept, preproduction, production, QA/polish, and maintenance.
A complete game design covers four tetrad elements: technology, mechanics, story, and aesthetics.
Iteration is a loop of short-range planning, implementation, and testing, where each test checks assumptions against reality and informs the next cycle.
why: Planning need only extend to the end of the current loop, since each test supplies reliable knowledge for planning the next one.

text: Real knowledge creation is organic: many activities overlap, testing is unscheduled, and the approach adapts daily, so no fixed loop fully describes it.
why: Invention is an ever-changing frontier rather than an assembly line.

text: Decisions have eight kinds of effects: design, implementation cost, immaturity burden, critical failure risk, process burden, political, cultural, and decision cost.
when: When evaluating a design decision beyond its effect on the game.
why: Good decisions require considering effects on processes, people, businesses and markets, not just the game itself.

text: Play can be structured in three levels: newbies, who get a separate, low-stakes challenge; players, who face the main challenge; and elders, who create challenges for others.
when: When designing a game community.
why: Newbies are challenged by learning the game itself, so that learning process must be rewarding or they will quit before engaging.

text: Each card has three stats: Cost is paid in health at reveal, Strength decides battles, and Damage is dealt if the card stays in play.
when: Simultaneous-reveal card duels.

text: A designer must listen to five targets: team, audience, game, client, and self. The five are interconnected.
why: Design decisions are linked to each other, so listening to one group feeds into what the others need.

text: Five technology bets most likely to lead toward a better world: magical interfaces, fair payment, less artificial AI, play with family and friends, and self-transformation.
why: Players who lose interest in new games have lost faith that designers know the way.

text: Skill mastery in games passes through three reinventions: the manual level of mechanical interface skill, the situational level of reading and deciding, and the mental level of concentration and psychological play.
when: As players progress up a game's skill range.

text: Many games are not thoroughly prototyped, so they fail to reach their full potential.
when: When core mechanics go untested until late in production.
why: Flaws surface late, when they may be too costly or impossible to fix.

text: Letting the design get ahead of iterative research removes room for change, and some assumptions will prove wrong.
why: Assumptions are often wrong, so the design needs room to change based on playtest learning.

text: Iterating in any order other than dependency order wastes much of the benefit of iteration.
why: Each change sends ripples through dependencies, so iteration must follow those links.

text: Designing AI around a fixed set of game inputs leads to rework late in the project.
Small incremental steps can trap a designer on a local maximum that only a larger redesign would escape.
why: Incremental changes can only reach nearby improvements, while a better design may need a fundamental change.

text: No save design is perfect; if the designer does not decide, the gameplay programmer will decide by what is easiest to code.
why: Leaving it unchosen means the implementer picks whatever is simplest to build, not what suits play.

text: Depth cannot be reliably predicted during design, so it must be tested with players rather than assumed.
why: Which element combinations produce depth cannot be foreseen in advance.

text: Assuming any single enjoyment or fun framework is empirically proven leads to overconfidence in its predictions.
why: Many fun frameworks are hard to unify, and some lack empirical validation.

text: Designers too close to their work may fix one problem while creating several others, and keep changing the game until it loses its appeal.
when: Especially harmful in a project's final development phases.
why: Lack of outside perspective and repeated unchecked changes.

text: Starting a prototype without a stated purpose produces results that answer nothing specific.
Expecting high-level work early is unrealistic. It is not the norm, though it can happen.
when: When someone starts a writing career at entry level on a team.
why: Core creative work is usually reserved for leads and executives, so juniors rarely get it.

text: A design document specifying everything in advance can contradict real play; building strictly from it wastes effort, and trusting it over observed play leads to ignoring discoveries or discarding it.
when: when a full design document is treated as fixed and observed play contradicts it
why: The document fixes every piece in advance, so pieces are placed as predetermined rather than as play reveals.

text: Early negative focus-group results and executive doubt can wrongly kill an unconventional concept, so a skunkworks effort can keep it alive until it proves itself.
when: When testing an unfamiliar concept with a small group
why: Unfamiliar concepts often test badly because audiences and executives judge them against familiar categories.

text: Treating the current best standard as the ceiling on what is achievable limits progress.
why: People do only what a goal requires, so once they top the standard, they stop.

text: Using existing games as the main reference from the start makes the new design derivative.
when: When a design is described without first physically prototyping it.
why: Without physical prototyping, the design description leans on existing games, binding it to them.

text: Decorative technology cannot rescue a boring game; a novel feature added to weak core gameplay will still flop.
why: Novel features do not compensate for weak core play; they cannot carry a game that is dull at its center.

text: Accepting a professional obligation without thinking it through is risky, because a commitment like this is hard to set aside once made.
when: When deciding whether to accept the responsibilities of a game designer.
why: The obligation is meant to be lifelong, serving as a constant reminder of responsibility.

text: Many submitted games are rejected because they are not fun to play.
when: When submitting a game concept to publishers.

text: 1) Make the game functional. 2) Make it internally complete and balanced. 3) Refine it only after that, restoring and strengthening the originally envisioned fun.
when: ordering design work

text: Run prototypes concurrently by discipline: engineers test technology, artists test art, and designers test gameplay at once, using many small independent prototypes.
when: Multiple team members are available and several questions are open at once.
why: Parallel independent prototypes answer more questions in less elapsed time than a single sequential prototype, multiplying the design loops completed in a given time.

text: Discover deep object interactions by repeated playtesting, since they rarely appear in design documents.
why: Unhandled object uses break presence and remind players they are playing a game, so these interactions matter.

text: 1) Build an analytics plan listing key questions and what good answers look like. 2) Run the playtest. 3) Note each problem. 4) Modify game objects or fix the cost curve and its math. 5) Repeat as time allows.
when: balancing a game through repeated playtests
why: The goal is balance as close to perfect as time allows.

text: 1) Observe players during the session. 2) Ask them questions. 3) Adjust the design based on what you saw. 4) Test again.
when: after each playtest session
why: Player experience cannot be fully predicted, so decisions must rest on how the prototype actually plays for testers.

text: 1) Modify one element of a working prototype, such as its board, units, goal or play procedures. 2) Change one aspect at a time so its effect is identifiable. 3) Play the variant with a partner. 4) Describe the change's effect on play in writing. 5) Note any new system that emerges and consider spinning it off.
why: Manipulating the structure of a prototype invariably sparks new ideas, and entirely new systems can emerge from it.

text: Iterative design cycle: 1) Produce a prototype. 2) Test whether a user can interact with it properly. 3) Evaluate the results. 4) Change the design. 5) Test again.
when: during any stage of development
why: each loop tightens the design against real use

text: 1) Test the design against all eight filters. 2) If any filter fails, change the design. 3) Rerun all eight filters on the revised design.
when: After a design revision made to fix a failed filter
why: Fixing one failed filter can break a filter the design already passed, so the full set must be rechecked.

text: 1) Test the narrow element with one participant. 2) Fix the issues found. 3) Test the revised prototype with the next participant. 4) Repeat.
when: Running RITE on a single feature
why: Each session tests the latest fixes.

text: 1) Analyze the formal system: part sizes and counts, starting positions, and purpose of special areas. 2) Decide whether skill or chance decides outcomes. 3) Set a player experience goal. 4) Brainstorm several goals before changing anything. 5) Choose a metaphor matching the goal. 6) Modify or rebuild the prototype. 7) Playtest and check whether the goal was met.
when: When modifying an existing prototype's system
why: Changes should serve a chosen experience goal rather than change for its own sake.

text: 1) Find a loophole or dead end. 2) Tweak the system. 3) Playtest again. 4) Repeat until no critical deficiencies remain.
when: Fixing loopholes and dead ends
why: Each fix can take days or weeks.

text: 1) Write several original solutions to a design problem. 2) List the pros and cons of each solution.
1) Run the game. 2) Navigate to the test spot. 3) Test. 4) Write or change code while the game keeps running. 5) Return to testing without restarting.
when: when the scripting system supports code changes during play
why: Avoids the compile, link, and restart cost of each cycle, allowing more loops per day.

text: 1) Write code. 2) Compile and link. 3) Run the game. 4) Navigate to the test spot. 5) Test. 6) Restart the cycle if the result is bad.
when: when changes require a full rebuild before testing

text: 1) State the problem. 2) Brainstorm possible solutions. 3) Choose a solution. 4) List the risks of that solution. 5) Build prototypes to mitigate those risks. 6) Test the prototypes; stop if good enough. 7) State the new problems and return to step 2.
when: when iterating on a design problem
why: Each round makes the problem statement more specific.

text: 1) If results show a fundamentally flawed idea, return to step one. 2) If results point to improvements, modify and retest. 3) If positive, the loop is complete. Without funding at step three, return to step one.
when: after each playtest in the playcentric process

text: 1) Each person writes an article and an adjective, folds the paper, and passes it on. 2) Each then adds a noun, a verb, an article and adjective, and a noun. 3) Unfold the paper and read the sentences aloud.
why: Chance combined with the unconscious mind produces unexpected ideas that deliberate brainstorming tends to miss.

text: 1) Give each team a key feature to test. 2) Allow 20 minutes to build a physical prototype of it. 3) Play and compare results with the team.
when: Run as a short exercise when teams rarely build physical prototypes
why: Time limits force quick, cheap builds whose results are often surprising.

text: 1) Pick one challenge. 2) Set a 60-minute limit. 3) Aim for 100 ideas. 4) Number ideas as they are written. 5) Keep energy high throughout.
when: When running a rapid brainstorm
why: A high quantity target pushes past obvious ideas.

text: 1) Finish every revision step. 2) Take a break. 3) Run the whole checklist again. 4) Repeat until the script is polished enough for the lead, editor, or producer to review.
when: after each full pass
why: Each repeated pass tends to need fewer rewrites than the one before, so the script converges.

text: 1) Sketch and prototype designs guided by HCI principles. 2) Gather user feedback on the prototype. 3) Redefine the design from that feedback. 4) Test again, repeating until the target is met or time or budget runs out.
why: Perception is subjective, and the experience lives in people's minds rather than in the design itself.

text: 1) Fix the number of loops in advance, or 2) loop until quality is acceptable or budget runs out.
when: when deciding how long to keep iterating
why: Each test checks assumptions against reality, so long-range plans beyond the current loop are unnecessary.

text: 1) State the design problem. 2) Generate an initial idea. 3) Push the idea through all eight filters, revising until it passes.
when: When a design fails one of the eight filters during revision
why: Fixing one failed filter can break a filter the design already passed, so the full set must be rechecked.

text: 1) Propose a definition. 2) Find fun things that lack pleasure. 3) Find pleasurable things with surprises that are not fun. 4) Revise the definition to fit both kinds of case.
when: when defining a design term
why: Counterexamples expose cases a proposed definition misses, showing where it needs revising.

text: 1) State your theme clearly enough to guide decisions. 2) Check whether every available means reinforces that theme. 3) Separate the elements with the elemental tetrad and test each against the theme.
when: When checking whether a game's parts serve one central theme.

text: 1) List ten favorite games. 2) Name each game's objective. 3) Look for shared objective types. 4) Define the kinds of games that appeal to you.
why: Seeing which objectives you like or dislike shows which objective types to use in your own ideas.

text: Before keeping a task, check that it is necessary and that its decision is neither obvious, hollow, nor uninformed.
why: Tasks that are unnecessary or have obvious, hollow, or uninformed decisions can kill the fun of the original concept.

text: Fail early and often, learning from each failure, so that success arrives sooner.
when: Iterating on design and prototypes.
why: Failures before large investment pay off, and rapid failure yields information faster than extended planning.

text: At foundation, playtest alone to confirm the core idea is fun; defer loopholes, dead ends, and questions like movement range, interaction, and conflict resolution.
when: Testing a bare core-mechanic prototype during foundation prototyping.
why: Answering every question early slows progress; answers emerge through play.

text: Use the framework's pillars to structure team discussions and to organize research and analytics questions.
why: A single shared framework gives teams a common structure across design, research, and analytics work.

text: Divide the design problem into small, manageable pieces, since building every system at once amounts to building the full game and tends to fail.
why: Building every system at once prevents fast work and reaching any clear conclusion, so the prototype fails.

text: The foundation stage goal is to make the game work, even as a rough approximation.
when: Early prototype work, while experimenting with the fundamental concepts of the system

text: Begin formal detailing only after the foundation shows promise and the structure lets others play the game.
why: A foundation-only build only tests the designer's own intuition, so others need enough structure to play it.

text: Make only one change per iteration and retest the whole system afterward to gauge its effects.
why: A single change touches one aspect of gameplay, so balancing becomes a methodical process rather than guesswork.

text: Check each refinement change against the experience originally intended, since changes can drift from the vision.
The highest priority is keeping clients happy by shipping useful software early and on an ongoing basis.
when: when planning a development project

text: Treat ideas as cheap and disposable, and reverse an early decision as soon as evidence shows it is not working.
when: when an early choice starts failing
why: Attachment to a decision keeps teams committed to designs that are clearly failing.

text: Make every design loop count and loop as fast as possible, because loops are expensive for large games.
when: when a game needs long test-and-improve cycles
why: Large computer games can afford few loops, so each one must produce useful information.

text: No decision is final until the whole team agrees it is final.
when: When a meeting participant seems unconvinced despite verbally agreeing
why: Unresolved doubt can turn into quiet dissent, and the team loses contributions that person would have made.

text: Do not wait for a template before starting to design; begin recording ideas now.
when: Before a design template is available

text: Know the design thoroughly and have at least a reasoned guess for unsettled parts, including play hours, time to finish a level, and how multiplayer works.
when: Preparing for a pitch
why: Listeners probe design details, and gaps reduce confidence.

text: Do important self-reflection now rather than postponing it, since time runs out without warning.
why: Life and career are short.

text: Identify your personal theme as early as possible in a project or career.
why: Knowing your personal purpose triggers a significant shift in how your creative thinking works.

text: Discuss ideas as a conversation rather than an argument.
when: Disagreeing with team members about design
why: Teams working long hours depend on members who communicate and get along, which matter more than tool skills that change often.

text: In the earliest development stages, make core moment-to-moment gameplay fun first, since balance is not yet meaningful while mechanics keep shifting.
when: earliest development stages
why: Mechanics shift constantly at this stage.

text: Enrich the game UX framework with academic research and the game UX community's work rather than treating it as fixed.
why: The framework grew from industry practice and has not been tested academically, so it stays open to revision.

text: Draw the design document's table of contents from the prototype, flowchart, and wireframes.
why: Writing from the game's own artifacts lets the document unfold in stages, rather than requiring the whole game to be worked out at once.

text: Decide early who will engage with the product, what they will spend on it, and why, and choose the target market, since casual and hardcore markets need quite different approaches.
why: Hardcore players spend more on games they care about, while casual players are hard to get noticed by.

text: A design is finished only when it passes all eight filters without further change; filters may be adjusted when constraints demand, such as retargeting a different demographic.
when: when reviewing a design before committing time, or when project constraints force change
why: A fix that passes one filter can break another, so every change must be rechecked against all the filters.

text: Before revising, duplicate the source document as a fresh draft labeled with its filename and date, enabling reversion to the prior version.
when: before starting a revision pass
why: Allows reversing edits that fail to pan out.

when: looking for edge cases or unusual play
why: Outliers are where edge cases and unexpected behavior appear.

text: Discarding outliers suits typical-play analysis since they reflect unusual sessions; but dropping them without investigation can hide exploits or player confusion.
when: analyzing normal play patterns
why: Outliers reflect unusual sessions rather than typical behavior.

text: Most tabletop companies find it cheaper to buy or license designs from independent inventors than to employ inventors.
Three routes get an outside idea made: ask the company first under a nondisclosure agreement, get a job inside a studio, or build a team and working demo.
Outsiders often misjudge technology limits, development time, finances and scheduling when pitching game ideas.
why: Outsiders lack basic knowledge of how games are built, so pitches overlook real production constraints.

text: A pattern-based design method resembles game playtesting and iteration.
Some sounds can stream from disk, but sounds that must play instantly need to reside in RAM, which competes with graphics assets.
when: Deciding where sounds are stored
why: Disk access is too slow for instant playback

text: Some older memory-limited consoles avoided double buffering by synchronizing drawing directly to the video refresh.
Because rendering sits outside the inner update loop, a slow machine drops visual smoothness rather than slowing the simulation.
when: Using a lag accumulator with fixed updates
why: Rendering is not repeated per update, so simulation stays correct while the display becomes choppier.

text: 1) Record the screen and the controller together with an inexpensive camera at 60 fps. 2) Count frames between the input and the on-screen response. 3) Convert the frame count to milliseconds.
when: When measuring the delay between a controller input and its visible on-screen response.
why: Filming both sides gives an objective measure of delay.

text: In a game, balance search time against solution quality, then commit to the best result found rather than searching indefinitely.
why: No formula can prove a solution is optimal, so searching can never be certain it has finished.

text: Reducing per-frame work to hit the budget lowers quality for every player, including those on fast machines.
when: Frames regularly overrun the budget
why: The reduction is applied globally rather than only to slow hardware.

text: Favor images over words, such as concept art, to make the idea concrete, and focus on what is unique, why it beats competitors, and why it suits this listener.
when: Building pitch slides or presenting a game idea to a game company
why: Visuals communicate faster, and many game company executives came up through art.

text: 1) Within a few days of the pitch, or if no reply comes within 7 to 10 days, send a follow-up with a real reason, such as answering a question the listener asked. 2) Follow up at most one email and one phone call per week. Demanding an answer or following up too often damages goodwill and invites a quick no.
when: After a pitch without response
why: A useful reason keeps contact warm; pressure makes listeners decline rather than deliberate.

text: Slick visuals are hard for teams and funders to resist, so polish alone can strongly sway decisions about a concept.
A rejected game can open a better opportunity when the rejecter is willing to hear a different idea from the same designer.
when: A publisher rejects a specific concept but remains open
why: Rejection of one proposal can prompt a request for a different, more fitting one.

text: Silence after a pitch rarely means rejection; listeners often thank the presenter and promise a reply, then get busy.
when: No response follows a pitch
why: Busy decision-makers delay replies without rejecting the idea.

text: Elegant designs are hard to spot early because they lack gimmicks, so evaluators favor more exciting-sounding concepts.
when: reviewing or pitching game concepts
why: pitches emphasize surface hooks over underlying depth

text: A pitch is the presentation to a publisher, and it must show the strength of the team, the plan, and the idea together.
A pitch is a negotiation in which you seek what you want while showing the listener that your game helps them get what they want.
Power is the ability to get what you want, made of two parts: the ability to get, and knowing what you want.
The summary of conflict states the central tension in the world.
A publisher may return months after a pitch, so impatience about timing is usually misplaced.
when: Waiting for a publisher's answer
why: Decision timing depends on the listener's schedule, not the presenter's.

text: Pitches occur throughout development, from rough concepts and prototype approval to publisher, crowdfunding, change, and post-release press pitches.
Pitch size varies from multimillion-dollar funding requests to small changes, and both part-time indies and large studio staff pitch heavily.
Gaps in row numbers or column letters, and small arrows in headers, are the visual signs that adjacent rows or columns are hidden.
A pitch usually reaches business and legal first, which then builds consensus among the other groups, and those groups may compete with each other.
A sell sheet is a short document giving title, genre, player count, platform, ship date, a two-paragraph description, feature bullets and art.
A presentation deck of key visuals and points lets a pitch carry on when the presenter is not in the room.
A full pitch document is usually produced by a team of professionals from several game design and development areas, not by one writer alone.
A pitch document is the basis for the later Game Design Document, which records the design team's intentions.
Pitching an interactive experience requires basic game-design vocabulary, such as mechanic, core mechanic and dynamic.
Serious games often aim for transformational play as a primary goal, teaching players through direct experience.
The concept phase is where a new game, game part, or story first takes shape, and the central idea everything else is built on is formed.
Refine the opening speech over several sessions until it is clear and efficient, since it can become the basis of the in-game tutorial.
when: Repeated playtest sessions run one after another with the same introductory script.

text: Let skeptics play a prototype, since experiencing an unusual idea can convince them where descriptions fail.
why: Playing a concept lets people judge it directly; a pitch that failed to win interest for an odd idea succeeded after play.

text: A rough playable build that mimics the intended control feel can sell a concept quickly to decision makers.
why: Players judge feel by using controls, which words and static visuals cannot convey.

text: Write on one side of each sheet in large letters so sheets can be laid out side by side and read from a distance.
when: During brainstorming sessions
why: Spreading every sheet across a table or floor lets the whole set be scanned at once.

text: The venue can affect a pitch's impact, so choose a setting that reinforces the game's theme when practical.
when: Choosing where to pitch
why: A thematically fitting setting can make the idea more persuasive.

text: Organized presenters seem lower risk to publishers, so planning logistics signals seriousness and builds trust.
when: Preparing any pitch from internal meetings to publisher presentations
why: Publishers judge reliability partly by how well a pitch is prepared.

text: A one-line design brief can be enough for a small, short project when the core concept is specific and concrete.
when: small team on a short schedule
why: A concrete concept keeps the build focused

text: Pitch reviewers judge the team first, creative materials second and the project plan third.
Pitch to a publisher after you have industry experience, a strong idea and a solid project plan, since publishers favor experienced teams.
when: After gaining industry experience, when you want to submit personal original concepts to a publisher.

text: Name a clear intended audience in a pitch, since it makes the pitch's appeal concrete.
when: Writing any game pitch
why: A named audience shows who the appeal is for

text: Evoke the feel of works the audience loved earlier, or invoke fans' nostalgia for a known series, to make a pitch resonate.
when: Pitching to an audience with shared past favorites
why: Familiar feelings create interest quickly

text: Use humor, such as a surprising contrast or a cartoon showing a market need, to make a pitch feel fun.
when: Presenting a pitch
why: Humor keeps the audience engaged

text: Put a single defining idea in one sentence on the first page, since many readers will not read beyond it.
when: writing a game pitch document
why: The first page must carry the idea on its own.

text: Open with an early spike of interest, a hook, to grab attention, such as a striking opening number, sound, or early playable moment.
why: The early spike carries attention through the less engaging stretch that comes after it.

text: Beautiful presentation of inherently interesting events is the best case.
why: Artistry in presentation raises how interesting guests find an experience, and inherent interest gives that artistry more to work with.

text: Learn about the listener beforehand. If the game does not fit the listener's needs, do not pitch it.
when: Before scheduling or delivering a pitch
why: A pitch aimed at a mismatched listener wastes both sides' time.

text: Get to the point quickly, skip points that bore the listener, and let them ask for details.
when: Pitching to busy listeners who have heard many pitches
why: Busy listeners have seen hundreds of pitches and tune out long setups.

text: Plan for a listener who loves the pitch but must persuade colleagues, and make that persuasion easy for them.
when: Preparing materials for a decision-making listener
why: The listener may need to sell the game to others without you present.

text: Know precisely what you want from a pitch, since without that focus you keep grasping and are never satisfied.
why: Power is the ability to get something, so the desired outcome is half of what defines it.

text: A combat system is a formal exchange between data sets, and a premise gives that same exchange emotional meaning.
why: Described in raw system terms the exchange sounds abstract and dull; the premise supplies a concrete frame.

text: Give the gist of the idea in a pitch rather than too much detail.
when: Writing a short pitch document

text: A well-written one-liner shows the creator has a clear vision and can serve as the core vision during development.
when: Writing a high concept
why: Compressing the whole project into a sentence or two makes it easy to communicate and remember.

text: Pitch a new IP as a known genre formula plus one distinctive twist, such as a familiar fantasy setup with one inverted social rule.
why: New properties carry risk because players favor sequels to known titles, and familiar elements ease their wariness of the unfamiliar.

text: Presenting progress to the whole team often reveals new problems and sparks fresh brainstorming, which begins the next round of the design cycle.
when: After the core design team has reached consensus on a design.

text: Premise, character, and story give formal elements context and emotional meaning: premise sets context and involves players emotionally, character gives an agent or vessel, story unfolds during play.
why: Context helps players understand their choices.

text: A pitch package has nine parts: sell sheet, playable demo, gameplay video, game design overview, company prospectus, storyboards, presentation deck, technical design overview, competitive analysis.
when: When preparing a pitch package to submit to a publisher.
why: Several different people at a publisher assess the project, so the package must build confidence across those audiences.

text: A pitch interest curve has four stages: a hook, a build, tension and release, and a climax.
when: Structuring a pitch
why: Pacing the pitch like a story keeps listeners engaged to the end.

text: A premise can frame abstract points as concrete rewards, such as treasure, turning scoring into a meaningful goal.
why: A generic point total gives players no reason to act, while a tangible in-world object does.

text: Pushy, sales-first presentations put listeners off; the pitch should serve the listener's problems.
when: Delivering a pitch
why: Listeners respond to relevance to their needs, not to pressure.

text: Overly long pitch documents are often skimmed or missed by executives, so keep each item brief.
why: Executives often skim pitch materials and will not read every detail of a long document.

text: Pitching before the package is complete leaves reviewers without the materials they need to judge the project.
why: Reviewers may be away from a computer or present the idea to others without you, so they need complete materials.

text: Discussing specific scenes or abilities lets participants fixate on one detail and lose the overall concept.
when: Presenting a pitch with many details
why: Attention narrows onto vivid specifics

text: Opening with a long backstory or saving the game's identity for later weakens the pitch, since story quality does not predict game quality.
when: Structuring the opening of a pitch
why: Listeners judge the game by its concrete identity, and backstory alone does not show it.

text: Expecting the released game to match your original concept exactly sets you up for frustration, since compromises are normal.
why: Development is collaborative and must serve a broad audience, so the finished product drifts from the first vision.

text: 1) Plan each moment, including when teammates join and when the prototype appears; planning does not drain energy and frees attention for the listener. 2) Keep the plan loose enough to deviate when needed.
when: Preparing a live pitch
why: Planning removes uncertainty about timing and keeps room to adapt.

text: 1) Name the biggest project risks briefly across technical, gameplay, aesthetic, marketing, financial and legal areas. 2) Plan how to manage each risk. 3) Predict the questions listeners will ask and prepare strong answers.
when: When preparing a project pitch

text: 1) Ask why this game is being pitched to this specific listener. 2) Define what success looks like for you. 3) Identify what the listener gains by saying yes. 4) Identify what the listener must learn about the game.
when: Preparing a pitch before delivering it
why: Answering these questions focuses the pitch on purpose and the listener's benefit.

text: 1) Confirm the date and time of the meeting. 2) Bring enough printed handouts that are easy to reach. 3) Bring all needed cables. 4) Arrive early and test projectors, computers, and internet connection.
when: Preparing for a pitch meeting
why: Testing in advance prevents technical failures from disrupting the pitch.

text: 1) Compose a headline line that hooks purchasers. 2) Draft highlight captions for the three or four headline features. 3) Pick visuals like screenshots, characters or bespoke art, labeling which aspects each depicts. 4) Run an informal focus session with testers on the packaging, then revise the pitch based on their input.
when: Presenting a game to buyers

text: 1) Find and read two sample design documents. 2) Note each one's strengths and weaknesses. 3) Decide whether you could execute the described design. 4) List the questions you would ask its designers.
when: Learning design document practice

text: 1) Assemble the pitch materials with your team, including the prototype, design document and project plan. 2) Build a target list of companies from your contacts and research. 3) Find a contact inside each company. 4) Arrange a pitch with each.
why: Even without a sale, pitching builds industry contacts and can lead to meeting people and getting a job.

text: 1) Lead the audience through the interactive experience across slides. 2) Mix traditional presentation with choose-your-own-adventure style interactivity.
when: Pitching an interactive experience

text: 1) Confirm every approver knows the referenced sources. 2) Informally share the gist of the idea. 3) Send the formal document only afterward.
when: Before submitting a formal pitch
why: Not everyone at the publisher knows the referenced film, book or genre, so the gist should be shared first.

text: 1) State the basic concept. 2) Name the genre. 3) Add the protagonist and story. 4) Add an appeal hint and a clear audience. 5) Trim the whole pitch to under forty words.
when: Building a short game pitch from a basic concept
why: Covers genre, concept, protagonist and story in one brief statement

text: 1) End the presentation on the initial pitch. 2) If questions arise, restate the pitch before leaving.
when: Concluding a pitch meeting
why: People remember the last thing they hear

text: 1) Start the experience before the room, such as theming the entry area. 2) Have the host perform rather than read. 3) Send reminder messages tied to the narrative before arrival.
when: when audiences need to be focused and ready at the start
why: Pre-start cues move the audience's attention into the experience early.

text: 1) Describe the player characters. 2) Describe important NPCs. 3) Describe the main storyline and conflict. Narrative-driven games need more detail here.
when: Writing the story section of a pitch

text: Describe a challenge, what the player might do, and how gameplay and story combine in that scenario.
when: Writing the gameplay example of a pitch

text: Before leaving a pitch meeting, ask when to expect a preliminary response.
when: at the end of a pitch meeting
why: It sets shared expectations for when a response comes and for the follow-up both sides intend.

text: Do not pitch while playing; have a colleague play while you talk and answer questions, since pitching while playing wastes time and sounds unfocused.
when: When a demo is shown during a pitch.
why: Narrating during play makes the presenter seem impaired and burns limited meeting time.

text: Write the opening speech in advance and deliver the same introduction to every tester.
why: A few misplaced words before play can spoil the test by steering players toward certain things.

text: Rehearse the pitch by memorizing the chain of ideas rather than exact wording, so it sounds natural.
why: Repeated practice builds comfort, which makes delivery feel natural.

text: Rehearse on anyone willing to listen, and rehearse any demo you plan to show.
why: Each practice run builds comfort, making the pitch flow more naturally.

text: Back a prototype with evidence of design, market, and monetization thinking, since a prototype alone is not enough.
why: Publishers judge how serious a developer is about building the game from documents they weigh rather than read.

text: Know your market's top sellers before pitching, since funders will know them.
when: preparing a pitch to funders
why: Funders judge your market understanding by the top games

text: Wrap a sheet name containing spaces in single quotes before the exclamation point, such as ='Sheet Name'!A3.
Frame a pitch around the company's needs, for example by asking which kinds of games it wants to review.
why: Publishers screen out overconfident developers, so showing you fit their needs signals legitimacy and talent.

text: Send a short thank-you email right after a pitch, with any materials the publisher requested during the meeting.
why: Prompt follow-up is valued, but excessive eagerness wears on the publisher.

text: Build a playable demo that lets the publisher judge gameplay; it may vary in completeness but must show how the game plays.
when: preparing a pitch
why: Most publishers surveyed considered a playable demo indispensable when judging a pitch.

text: Pitch with a gameplay video or storyboards as a fallback when no playable demo can be built.
when: no playable demo is possible
why: A video built from actual game code is more credible than one made from storyboards.

text: Pitch in person when possible, dressed professionally but not necessarily in a suit.
Keep a checklist or spreadsheet of every publisher and contact, since one publisher may have several evaluators to track.
After writing a clear comparison, add a hint of what will be enjoyable in the finished game.
when: Writing a pitch that already follows the clear template
why: Clarity alone rarely excites anyone

text: Choose well-known reference games, since audiences recognize them more quickly than obscure ones.
when: Adding an optional reference game to a comparison
why: Recognition speeds up understanding

text: Use the reference game to convey how the final product will feel, not as a showy description of that game.
when: Adding an optional reference game to a comparison
why: The reference should set expectations about play feel

text: For a sequel, explain clearly how the project differs from the original.
when: Pitching a sequel
why: Listeners need to see why the sequel is new

text: Stay relaxed during a pitch, since stiffness makes the audience uncomfortable in informal game companies.
when: Presenting a pitch in person
why: Informal settings favor a relaxed presenter

text: Keep a pitch to its high points: what the game is, how it feels to play, what the player accomplishes, and which audience need no other game meets.
when: Presenting a pitch in limited time
why: These points carry the concept

text: Keep pitch documents visual with many pictures, state technical information only in broad strokes, and mark and cite any material that is not your own.
when: writing a game pitch document
why: Visuals convey the idea quickly, and unattributed material creates legal risk.

text: A designer who wants a specific feeling must plan how to deliver it, since emergent play rarely produces it reliably.
Explain the game plainly, avoid jargon, and test the explanation on people unfamiliar with the idea.
when: Preparing any pitch
why: The listener has never seen the game and must understand it quickly.

text: Open by stating platform, audience, and genre. Hiding these makes listeners fixate on guessing what the game is.
when: Opening any game pitch
why: Unstated basics force the listener to guess and distract from the idea.

text: Design the pitch as an experience with the same care as the game, applying the same design lenses.
when: Preparing a pitch
why: A pitch that is accessible and surprising holds listeners better.

text: Add showmanship such as detailed animation, unexpected sound, humorous images, or physical props to make the pitch memorable.
when: Staging a pitch
why: Vivid sensory moments make the pitch stick in memory.

text: Only pitch a game you are genuinely excited about, since ambivalence fails to excite listeners.
when: Choosing which game to pitch
why: Presenter ambivalence transfers to the audience.

text: Use the negotiation framing before any pitch to decide what to ask for and who should hear it.
when: before any pitch
why: Getting what you want requires knowing what you want first; without a clear aim, effort keeps chasing and never lands.

text: A premise can be minimal and still create tension; elaborate backstory is not required for emotional engagement.
why: The threat is visible on screen, so players feel tension from the approaching danger without needing any story.

text: Narrative designers are usually expected to write pitches that are clear, well written and easy to communicate.
when: Writing a concept pitch
why: The concept phase forms the initial idea everything else is built around, and the pitch must sell it to the team and executives.

text: Sources disagree on pitch length: two to five pages including cover, never over eight, versus one page plus cover, single-spaced, no longer than a page and a paragraph.
when: writing a game pitch document
why: A pitch is a marketing document meant to be read quickly, not a novel.

text: Selling from your own site or a user-generated site gives full creative control and direct access to players, but offers little money or marketing support and makes traffic hard to earn.
when: Budget for marketing is small.
why: Full control comes at the cost of no production or marketing help, so single-game sites struggle to draw traffic.

text: Conversion rate is the percentage of free players who start paying, counting any amount however small.
DAU (daily active users) is the number of unique users active per day, counted over the last 24 hours with no minimum play time.
why: Counting daily unique players is the simplest engagement fact to measure, so it draws much attention.

text: People treat their first experience of a game as the whole game, so a single playtest can be mistaken for the entire design.
when: judging a design after one session
why: The WYSIATI effect favors what has been seen and ignores what has not

text: Some player desires are so hidden that players are not consciously aware of them, and these are often the most important.
when: Analyzing what drives player enjoyment
why: Unconscious desires shape enjoyment without being reported, so they go unstated

text: Few players finish games; in one popular title only 10 percent reached the final mission.
when: Even for critically acclaimed, wildly popular games
why: Players often leave before the ending, so the journey carries much of the experience.

text: Exploratory analyses include clustering players by behavior, engagement and spending, and factor analysis to find what drives retention, such as what early churners do or skip.
Analytics means gathering and examining big volumes of gameplay telemetry from actual players.
Experienced designers can predict the effect of a balance change with a high degree of accuracy.
Flow can be measured by self-report questionnaires, physiological measures such as electroencephalography, or direct observation of players.
The Flow-State Scale is the most popular self-report questionnaire for flow and can be applied to games.
when: when players rate their own flow during or after an activity

text: The player experience spans trailers, website, downloading, menus, gameplay, customer service, community management and the online platform.
Engageability pillars are unvalidated guidelines for video games, used to reveal engagement strengths and weaknesses, fix issues early, and interpret telemetry after Beta.
Average Day-1 retention for mobile games is reported below 30%, so the first 10 minutes on mobile and the first hour on PC and console are critical for keeping players.
when: free-to-play and mobile games
why: Players who quit early never reach later content.

text: Other exploratory questions cover paths players take, items they unlock, missions they play, and heroes they pick.
Game user research demands strong grounding in ergonomics, human-machine interaction, and cognitive psychology.
Gameplay input covers player actions and real-time preferences; game metrics include generic measures such as performance and time on task, and game-specific measures such as items picked and used.
Living games such as MMOs and games earning ad or free-to-play revenue test balance mainly through analytics, since the only way to test balance success is to let players in and analyze their data.
when: When balancing live games with large player populations
why: Live ecosystems can only be validated by real players in the wild.

text: Dates matter for game balance mainly through timestamped analytics collected from a game server.
In beta and live, analytics are read together with UX test insights, and focus shifts to difficulty, progression balancing, and monetization.
when: Beta and live operation

text: When only a small share of players uses an important feature, investigate why rather than assuming the feature is unwanted.
when: Analytics shows low adoption of a key feature
why: The feature matters to enjoyment, so a low share of use signals a possible problem worth tracing down.

text: Near-duplicate data entries that repeat stats such as health and resistances should inherit from a common entry, since otherwise every balance change must be applied to each copy.
when: when many game entries share most of their values
why: duplicated values are error-prone to keep in sync

text: Enjoyment is scored from 0 to 3, from no expressed enjoyment (0) to exclamations of enjoyment during or after play (3).
when: when using the observation grid

text: Engagement cannot be measured objectively in a simple way, and self-reported fun is biased.
A 2019 industry report found that 73% of U.S. residents age 2 and up play video games.
The DAU-to-MAU ratio is a high-level engagement indicator showing the share of monthly players who engage on an average day.
The Flow Observational Grid is an observer-scored model with three dimensions: concentration, enjoyment, and frustration.
when: when an observer watches players in play

text: Two complementary methods analyze repeated random state transitions: stepping a Markov chain forward to track state probabilities, and working backward by recursion, splitting a complex event into simpler events.
when: Analyzing a chance game's length or outcome, or choosing decisions under uncertainty.
why: Each method answers different questions about the same process.

text: Facial expressions are unreliable indicators of player appreciation or emotion; webcam footage needs advanced micro-expression analysis before it can reveal feelings.
when: Using facial expressions or webcam footage to read player emotion or appreciation
why: Surface expressions do not reliably reveal feelings.

text: Eyetracking shows where players look, not necessarily what they attend to; heatmaps suit still HUD elements, trailers, or cutscenes.
when: Interpreting eyetracking data
why: Gaze does not always equal attention.

text: Treating a positive test result as near-certain disease is a mistake when the condition is rare, even if the test is highly sensitive and specific.
when: the condition being detected is rare
why: false positives from the large healthy group can outnumber true positives

text: Assuming hours played defines the casual or hardcore category is a mistake, since some casual players play long stretches and some hardcore fans play briefly.
when: When deciding whether a game targets hardcore or casual players.
why: Playtime overlaps across groups: a casual player can log long sessions while a dedicated fan may play briefly.

text: 1) Observe players and note the moment that pulls them out of flow. 2) Remove or change that moment in the next prototype.
when: Once a player is noticed entering flow during play
why: Flow does not last, so the disruptive moment must be found and removed before the next prototype.

text: 1) Plot the curve the designer expects. 2) Plot the observed curve from playtests. 3) Compare the two to find gaps. 4) Plot separate curves per player group.
when: before release, to find trouble spots
why: Charting expected interest makes trouble spots visible, and different groups can find the same experience great or boring.

text: 1) Break each hit into its features. 2) Run statistics comparing feature presence with sales. 3) Keep the features that correlate with success.
when: analyzing a dataset of commercial games
why: Statistics show which features drive success

text: 1) Compute the standard error for each group. 2) Plot error bars for each group. 3) If the bars do not overlap, the groups are probably distinct.
when: Quick visual check of whether two groups differ.
why: Non-overlapping error bars suggest a real difference between groups.

text: 1) Plan a target emotion profile at the start of design. 2) Choose mechanics intended to produce each target emotion. 3) Test whether those mechanics actually produce the emotions.
when: designing for specific player emotions
why: Experience can't be built directly; designers must set rules that trigger the emotions players feel.

text: Testing for hidden assumptions: 1) Have a non-gamer play a game with a tutorial. 2) Note what they find hard to learn. 3) List the assumptions the game makes about the player's background.
when: checking whether a game assumes gaming knowledge
why: non-gamers reveal conventions that gamers take for granted

text: 1) Collect play statistics such as win rates by matchup and map. 2) Check whether a suspected imbalance appears in the data. 3) If the problem is only perceived, wait before changing anything. 4) Combine the data with designer judgment before adjusting.
when: Investigating a suspected imbalance
why: Some perceived problems are not real.

text: If design decisions depend on statistical feedback, push for data collection to be built early in development.
when: design relies on playtest metrics
why: late data leaves no time to act

text: Make a game easy to learn by iterating until its basic skills are simple to pick up.
why: Mappings players already know from everyday life mean nothing new has to be learned.

text: Analytics-driven balance suits games that can be patched and monitored, but is much harder for tabletop trading card games, since home games cannot be uploaded and printed cards are harder to patch.
when: When choosing balance methods for a game type
why: Patchability and data upload determine whether analytics is feasible.

text: Playtest results are natural consequences of real play rather than rewards set up by one person to manage another, so they do not feel controlling.
Rely on personal judgment early and daily, and use playtesting to check audience reactions once there is something playable to test.
when: Early in development, before there is a playable game to test
why: Playtesting happens only occasionally while design decisions are needed daily, and testers may reject unfinished ideas before seeing them complete.

text: Players expect games to be updated based on their feedback, so keep an ongoing feedback loop between designers and players.
Treat playtesters as guides who reveal design problems below the surface of the game.
when: When designers have grown too close to their own work and lost perspective.
why: Outside players bring a fresh perspective that reveals issues the designer no longer sees.

text: When playtest feedback piles up, sort it into a prioritized list of changes and address one phase at a time.
when: Playtest comments overwhelm the designer
why: Breaking testing into phases focused on specific design aspects moves the game step by step from core prototype to complete model.

text: When a matchup looks unusual, gather replays from top-level players to see how they actually play it.
when: Competitive games with suspected imbalances
why: Expert play reveals the strategies that matter.

text: Responding to player complaints about a disruptive problem is a form of playtesting and can close the problem.
Interacting with players throughout design gives experimental ideas time to mature into workable experiences.
when: when developing unusual or experimental ideas
why: Innovation tends to grow through long-term development and experimentation rather than from a first spark.

text: Complaints left unaddressed at the testing stage can resurface after release as forum posts or memes.
when: During testing, while problems can still be fixed before release.
why: Problems left unfixed before launch get aired publicly by players afterwards.

text: Hoping a community forms on its own is not a plan; without tools and management it may never develop.
why: Organizers may appear unprompted, but tools help self-appointed leaders keep groups running.

text: An unfinished version released online shapes first impressions, so the player base may need restricting.
why: First impressions carry weight, and a broadly open online audience is hard to keep secret or control.

text: Teammates rarely reread the whole design document at each release, so significant changes go unnoticed unless they are announced.
when: When a new version of the design document is released.
why: Teammates lack time to reread the full document with every release.

text: Presenting personal preference as if it were a problem with the work makes notes hard to act on.
User-generated game sites accept free uploads, let players rate games, and feature top-rated titles; they offer high traffic but face heavy competition and provide no development budgets.
why: Open uploads and public ratings invite fierce rivalry, meaning merely a sliver of titles earn notice.

text: The creative subconscious communicates through imagery and emotion rather than words, acts on impulse, feels intensely, and is playful and irrational.
Even involuntary signals like sighing or eye-rolling make people go easy on a boss's bad ideas, reducing debate usefulness.
when: A boss debating subordinates.
why: People read subtle reactions as punishment.

text: Many of the best creative ideas come from below conscious awareness rather than from logical argument.
The subconscious draws on experience more directly than the conscious mind does.
Use light, occasional, nonserious social signals, not money or threats, to encourage a specific action; money penalties breed anger and paranoia, and confrontation damages team climate.
when: When one action needs encouraging in a team.
why: Social signals motivate without the side effects of economic rewards or punishment; light symbolic penalties keep people careful without making them paranoid.

text: Examine your own motivations as well as external feedback, because subconscious drives can shape your design choices without your knowing why.
when: making creative decisions on a project
why: Subconscious forces operate below awareness.

text: Frequency of small wins matters more than their size: a solved problem, a finished asset or a playtester understanding a detail all count.
when: When planning tasks for developers.
why: Frequent small wins sustain daily engagement better than rare large milestones.

text: Treat the creative subconscious as a separate, playful partner that supplies ideas, so you can interact with it as with a person.
why: Anthropomorphizing gives a familiar model for interaction

text: 1) Sit apart from your own engaged mind as an observer. 2) Silently watch your thoughts and feelings as they arise. 3) Keep the observing mind separate from the engaged one.
when: Observing experience continuously during play.
why: Two minds, one engaged and one observing, allow monitoring without spoiling the experience.

text: Playcentric design is an iterative method building mechanics from the ground up around player experience, inviting early feedback and playtesting prototypes until gameplay delights testers and meets experience goals.
A persona is a named, human-like profile of a hypothetical user, built from market research and interviews, used to guide design decisions.
when: Defining target players for design
why: A concrete profile helps teams make consistent decisions.

text: Human-centered design, called player-centric design in games, means considering the user experience throughout development.
Personas are often reused as generic player types across games; a persona is not a real person, so teams may design for a stereotype unless the data stays accurate and current.
when: Using personas over the life of a project
why: Stale or stereotyped profiles mislead design decisions.

text: 1) Conduct field research on the target audience. 2) Distill it into a profile of goals, preferences, expectations and behaviors. 3) Share that profile across development, marketing and publishing.
when: Aligning a team on its core player
why: A shared concrete profile replaces abstract market segments and keeps the audience in view.
