text: Playtests should reveal what players experience, not just collect suggestions, because designers are too close to the game to feel what another player feels.
why: Designers lack the outside perspective needed to feel what another player feels, so watching testers play reveals it.

text: Observe many sessions to map the experiences a game can produce, including its branch points and how they interact.
when: When a game offers many possible paths and playtesters take different threads through it.
why: A single path cannot reveal interactions between branches

text: Stop running playtests when testers repeatedly show the same experiences, since the designer then understands enough to decide.
why: Once testers repeat experiences, the designer can predict how changes will affect the game as a system.

text: Avoid leading questions such as asking whether a player noticed a specific object, because players answer yes to appear perceptive or to please the interviewer.
when: When checking whether a player perceived a particular element of the game.
why: The question itself hands the tester information, so they answer yes to seem perceptive or to please the interviewer.

text: When players genuinely need information the game lacks, deliver it through a method planned in advance as part of the test protocol.
why: Unplanned hints from the designer would contaminate the test by revealing knowledge testers should not hold.

text: Playtest at every development stage, not only at beta, because waiting leaves fundamental design issues too late to fix.
when: When the game is still before its beta stage, while assets are not yet complete.
why: late discovery of core problems is costly

text: Choose non-digital or digital test forms according to the development stage.
when: choosing how to test a design
why: early stages can be tested before digital work exists

text: Prepare focused questions or a paper survey before a playtest, and record extra comments while holding to the test's goals.
when: planning a playtest
why: focus keeps results useful

text: Vet enthusiastic player suggestions against the game's core vision, and dismiss them kindly if they do not fit.
when: players offer design suggestions
why: a coherent vision matters more than any single idea

text: Match each tester group to the questions you need answered, and use a mix of expert and fresh testers at different times, since most games need both.
when: When planning playtest sessions
why: Each tester group reveals different kinds of problems.

text: Log important game events during each session, such as time spent in character creation, hits needed to defeat a boss, average score, and most-used weapons.
when: When evaluating player behavior during playtests or live play
why: Logged events reveal how players actually play.

text: Phrase suggestions as options for the team to weigh rather than as orders, since the researcher clarifies problems and does not take control of design.
when: Writing fix suggestions in a UX report
why: Directive wording makes the report feel bossy and reduces its usefulness.

text: Play the build first and prepare an observation sheet with specific objectives; give feedback on features ready for testing, not unfinished ones.
when: Preparing for a UX test
why: Developers dislike feedback on incomplete work, and objectives focus observation.

text: Participants must not watch each other play, to avoid peer pressure and copying.
when: Running group or sequential sessions
why: Watching others changes how a participant behaves.

text: Tell participants the game is being tested rather than their skill, that mild confusion is worth reporting, and that researchers do not work on the game so harsh feedback will not hurt anyone.
when: Briefing participants before a test
why: Framing reduces politeness bias and encourages honest criticism.

text: Participants sign an NDA, and recording devices are stored in a locker whose key the participant keeps.
when: Running a UX test with external participants
why: Protects confidentiality and recordings.

text: Run task analysis sessions one-on-one, with one participant observed by one researcher.
Build a studio-wide UX strategy so that user experience becomes everyone's concern.
why: A shared framework gives separate teams one set of player-experience criteria to guide iteration, research, and analytics.

text: Do not answer criticism; write it down and listen carefully.
why: Designers are attached to what they made and tend to get defensive, which shuts down useful feedback.

text: Aim playtests to discover what players dislike or misunderstand, not to collect praise.
why: Praise reveals nothing about what needs fixing, so the goal is to surface what testers dislike or misunderstand.

text: Set ground rules at the start of group sessions: everyone respects opinions, everyone gets a chance to speak, and no one criticizes another tester's ideas.
when: When several testers are questioned together in one group session.
why: A particularly vocal tester can sway the others, so clear etiquette keeps each person's opinions independent.

text: Observe testers from behind one-way glass, through a video feed, or quietly from inside the room.
when: Running a playtest session of a game that is still in development
why: Quietly watching testers yields more learning about how they actually play than guiding them does.

text: Observe confidant testers without asking leading questions.
when: Testing a prototype with friends or family

text: Playtest your own prototype and record your thoughts in a playtesting notebook.
when: Early prototype stage, when the goal is making the game work at rough quality
why: Self-play is how core mechanics are found and glaring problems get solved at this stage.

text: For most tests, recruit new testers for fresh input; later, bring back articulate testers to see progress and whether removed features were missed.
when: Later in the design process, when checking how the game has progressed
why: Returning testers can point out whether removed or changed features no longer work as well.

text: Test regularly with target-audience participants who know nothing about the game, not friends or family, who please the team with soft feedback; developers cannot see their own knowledge gaps.
when: Regularly during development, with testers from the target audience who know nothing about the game
why: Developers cannot perceive their own knowledge gaps; biased testers distort conclusions.

text: Before building a complex choice, check with QA testers whether a simpler one looks the same to players.
When humor derails a group discussion, the facilitator must steer it back to the topic.
when: Brainstorming sessions that include jokes
why: Unchecked jokes can take over the session

text: Log every playtest fix in writing, because an unrecorded patch tends to resurface later.
when: during playtesting

text: Test interface sounds with other people to check that each one reads as its intended meaning.
when: Choosing UI feedback sounds such as forward, back, positive, or negative cues

text: Do not graph a single value, whether discrete or continuous; state the number directly.
when: Presenting one analytics value at a single point in time

text: Plot each metric as a time series and mark significant patch dates on the graph.
when: Tracking a live game's metrics across updates.
why: Averages hide change, while time plots reveal when shifts happened.

text: Build a small representative set of content for playtesting, such as three roles or one baseline character, rather than full content.
when: early in content creation
why: keeps early builds playable and cheap to change

text: When a group is underrepresented, each candidate cause implies a different fix, so test the causes separately before choosing an intervention.
when: investigating a gap in applicants or hires
why: Different causes such as outreach, wording, bias, offers or chance require different responses.

text: Test reward strategies with players, since predicting which rewards will hamper intrinsic motivation is difficult.
when: choosing rewards
why: intuition about reward effects is often wrong

text: Use standardized protocols to test hypotheses, because biases affect developers and players alike.
why: Biases affect developers and players alike, and without standard procedures it is easy to miss or misread what happens.

text: Write test questions that match the specific feedback you need.
when: When content is ready for testing and you know what feedback you need
why: Premature content or unfocused questions produce random feedback you do not need.

text: Test against predefined UX goals, pillars, and metrics, and guard analysis against cognitive biases.
when: During the testing step of an iterative development cycle
why: Cognitive biases and hasty conclusions distort analysis unless they are controlled for.

text: Test VR with a wide range of physical attributes, not only typical player segments, since body size and mobility issues are missed otherwise.
when: Developing VR experiences where the player's avatar matches their real-world height
why: Body size changes how experience design works, so typical player segments miss edge cases and feelings of power.

text: Do not treat a single small test as proof that a design change works.
when: interpreting playtest results
why: Single studies can be wrong or later discredited.

text: With a dedicated UX team, use an integrated UX process to plan what needs testing and when.
when: Dedicated UX team exists

text: Hold editing sessions on different days from brainstorming so ideas mature; mixing the two reduces the productivity of both.
why: Letting time pass between phases keeps evaluation from blurring into brainstorming, which lowers brainstorming's output.

text: Use focus groups to generate ideas, not to judge the quality or popularity of an idea.
when: Running a focus group where attendees are invited to talk openly and push back.
why: Group dynamics distort judgments of ideas.

text: Accessibility testers must belong to the target market, be objective rather than friends or relatives, and have never played the game; earlier playtesters are disqualified.
when: recruiting accessibility testers
why: Prior exposure or personal ties bias what testers notice and tolerate.

text: Treat participant struggles as valid evidence; a designer's opinion that a feature is obvious does not outweigh observed confusion.
when: interpreting accessibility test results
why: Observed confusion reflects the actual experience of new players.

text: Give remote playtesters a channel to talk to each other so social and competitive exchange can still surface.
when: remote playtests
why: Room cues are lost when testers are apart

text: Test whether an audience wants freedom to set its own goals before adding open-ended personal goal setting.
when: Deciding whether to add open-ended personal goal setting for an audience that may find open systems too open-ended
why: Players set private subgoals within systems they cannot win, seeking a sense of accomplishment anyway.

text: Route requests through the lead or technical director rather than going around them, because bypassing them undercuts their authority.
when: Working in a team with a programming hierarchy, whether large or small

text: Send change requests to the owner of the decision, such as the art director rather than the person who would carry it out, and consult the technical director before changing the database or interface.
when: When a change needs to touch the database or part of the interface

text: Use geopolitical review to catch cultural problems before release; handling sensitive themes is a judgment about audience and region, not censorship.
when: Large games whose sensitive themes must suit the intended audience and region of distribution
why: Deep localization reveals regional taboos and how in-game context can strengthen or soften a message's meaning for players.

text: Agree with the client on what player experience to measure in beta testing and which questions to ask beta testers.
Ask reviewers to sign a non-disclosure agreement to protect your ideas, since industry people are used to signing them.
when: you worry about idea theft
why: A confidentiality commitment deters outside reviewers from taking shared concepts for their own use.

text: Discuss how reviewers' ideas could improve the design, but make the final decision yourself.
Thank every reviewer, whether or not you plan to use their comment.
In each test row, note what key information the step conveys, how it fits the story, and any design concerns such as weak side quests or overly hard encounters.
when: recording test results

text: In a party-based RPG, test party compositions that lack key abilities, such as no lockpicker or no healing magic, and teams made only of one class.
when: testing a party-based RPG

text: Validate designs with real users instead of assuming they work, because perception is subjective.
why: The player's experience forms in their minds rather than being contained in the design, so the designer's intent alone cannot reveal how it lands.

text: After each match, highlight one standout moment and show personal statistics compared with the player's past performance, so players feel good even on a losing team.
when: After a match that the player's team does not win.
why: positive feedback on individual performance offsets team loss

text: Study other games' cost curves for insight rather than copying their math.
when: Researching balance in comparable games.
why: Each game's systems differ, so numbers borrowed from another game will probably misfit this design.

text: To test whether a balance model finds the most broken objects, pick clearly overpowered, clearly underpowered and well-balanced objects, focusing on extremes rather than slightly off ones.
Simplifying a simulation by removing player choices, such as fixed buying policies, limits what it can reveal about the game's balance.
when: when building a simulation for balance analysis
why: Fixed policies remove the decisions that shape real outcomes.

text: Repeat a shuffle simulation many times and average the results, because a single trial gives no meaningful average.
Balance with structured, systematic approaches, because haphazard changes make the game swing between imbalanced states.
why: Mechanics are linked through many strategies, so each fix to one ripples into new imbalances elsewhere.

text: Interrupting players with questions reveals insight but disturbs natural play, and constant questioning can ruin the session; waiting until the end risks players forgetting the moment.
when: When a player does something surprising that the designer cannot explain.
why: Interrupting can disrupt natural play, while waiting until the end means the player may no longer recall the moment.

text: A studio is convenient and lets the whole team watch real players, but unfamiliar surroundings can make testers uneasy.
why: Testers in an unfamiliar workplace with colleagues watching may hold back noise, fun, and candid opinions.

text: Public venues such as malls, campus events, games festivals, or street tables are cheap and reach many testers, but finding the right demographic and avoiding distraction are harder.
why: Competing activities at a public venue pull testers' attention away from the session.

text: Testing at the playtester's home shows natural play and social interaction, but few observers fit and hardware may need carrying.
why: Home play mirrors how buyers will actually use the game, including social settings.

text: Online testing reaches many machine configurations and suits stress and massively multiplayer questions, but gives less insight and makes secrecy harder.
when: When the questions concern stress testing or massively multiplayer play.
why: Many testers on varied hardware play at once, but without observers the insight into their behavior is thinner.

text: Multi-day lab sessions give deep data but are hard to recruit for, while remote tools are easier to run but make observation harder.
Group testing generates ideas well but evaluates them poorly, while one-on-one testing is better suited to evaluating ideas.
Strangers give objective, fresh perspectives that close contacts cannot, so use strangers when objectivity matters most.
when: Choosing between friends and strangers as testers
why: Close contacts bring familiarity and bias that blur judgment

text: Developers can watch from a one-way mirror, which keeps them out of the room, or together in a room, which sparks useful discussion.
when: Arranging observer seating for a test
why: Separate viewing reduces interference, while shared viewing aids discussion.

text: Use eyetracking or biometrics only when budget justifies them and for short, specific moments; efficient observation is usually better otherwise.
when: Choosing lab instruments
why: Expensive instruments cost more than their insight in most tests.

text: Observation suits small groups and early prototypes; analytics needs large samples, so near launch beta-scale play data guides balance once observers are impractical to recruit.
when: Choosing a balance method based on player scale.
why: Large player counts make observation-based playtesting impractical.

text: Programmers supplying navigation data directly means every new level needs new data, which hurts reuse across games and makes simple level changes difficult.
when: When the game level changes.
why: The AI's knowledge of the environment comes from programmer-supplied data tied to each layout, so it cannot be carried over.

text: Ensemble recording makes dialogue flow naturally and builds chemistry, but adds pressure, ego conflicts, misunderstandings and retakes; solo sessions are easier to plan.
when: Choosing how to record a dialogue scene
why: Actors reacting to each other sound more natural but cost more time and coordination

text: Lab research reveals causes in depth but struggles to predict how much a lab-observed behavior matters across a larger audience.
when: when deciding whether a lab finding needs scale validation
why: small samples cannot estimate how common a behavior is

text: An imagined real-time walkthrough is less accurate than playtesting but far cheaper and easier, and it is better than no pacing analysis.
when: before playtesting is possible
why: The imagined run tends to skip ahead to exciting moments and hide flow gaps, so every second must be walked through in order.

text: Signals such as a key system failing or playtesters becoming attached to a minor character can indicate that the game's broad structure needs changing.
when: Reviewing playtest or team results
why: Leaders iterate on level progressions, plot structures and market positioning, so failures and attachments that point to broad structural flaws are the lessons they need.

text: A feature shared by most winners may be a symptom of winning rather than its cause.
when: analyzing what winners have in common
why: winning may drive the feature's adoption

text: Before acting on a suspected problem, check whether it is real or just a vocal minority.
when: When the player community complains about a particular aspect of the game

text: Use user testing to find stuck points, since a designer's sense of an obvious task may not match players' experience.
When stuck on a design issue, present it to coworkers as a creative challenge to draw out their ideas.
when: When the team is stuck on a design issue during the design phase

text: 1) Find where the prototype stagnates. 2) Decide whether a balancing loop or balance of power causes it. 3) Design a way to break the cycle.
when: Auditing a prototype for stagnation

text: Gold code means all bugs are resolved.
Implementation supplies narrative delivery tools, production supplies the teamwork to build them, and neither works without the other.
Hindsight bias makes past development look smooth and predictable, which leads teams to believe the future can be planned in detail and so to overplan again.
when: when post-project reviews are used to set future plans
why: Erased mistakes and tangents make past development seem controllable.

text: The planning horizon usually lengthens over a project, moving from wild exploration early to detailed scheduling near the end.
when: across the stages of a project
why: Early on, assumptions are untested and keep shifting, while late in a project the structure is set and only small details remain.

text: Designing gameplay without considering the controls of the final platform leads to a game that does not feel right.
when: When conceiving gameplay for a game with a specific target platform
why: Different input devices give very different feel, so gameplay conceived without the final controls can end up feeling wrong.

text: Features implemented without design, prototyping, or testing, especially under crunch, lead to costly problems.
when: Under tight deadlines or a weak production process, such as crunch
why: Once a feature is implemented or polished, people grow attached and resist removing it even when it fails.

text: 1) Assemble the relevant stakeholders. 2) Hold several rounds of discussion. 3) Produce written reports, studies and analyses before deciding.
when: When a design decision has major consequences.
why: For important decisions, a better outcome is worth the cost of a careful process.

text: Beta is the content-complete, bug-focused stage, entered when all features are complete and no priority 1 bugs remain; it is the final chance to tune balance, especially individual numbers.
Alpha is usually the feature-complete point where all mechanics are in and the engine works, no new features are added, and content and bugs remain; core design is largely locked.
when: Production milestone.
why: Marks the transition from building features to producing and balancing content.

text: Before sharing an unpublished game idea with a company, ask whether it wants to hear it and offer to sign a nondisclosure agreement, since companies usually require one to view unpublished material.
when: before sharing a game idea with a company
why: Companies generally prefer their own ideas and rarely accept outside pitches, so asking first avoids wasted effort.

text: Have another team member, or each group lead, review the production plan, even in a two-person studio, to estimate its cost and duration.
when: When a plan is made by more than one person, such as at a two-person studio
why: Approval makes the plan binding.

text: People often do not see why a seemingly small change is costly to implement, so feedback may ignore coding cost.
when: when stakeholders request small-looking changes
why: Implementation effort is often invisible outside engineering.

text: People find uncertainty unpleasant and judge uncertain people as ineffective, so they plan to soothe their anxiety rather than to coordinate work.
when: when facing an uncertain future
why: Plans offer a false sense of certainty that relieves the anxiety of uncertainty, even though they do not coordinate work.

text: A nondisclosure agreement is a simple promise not to reveal a product before release.
A prioritized backlog is a sorted feature list where new ideas are added and reprioritized each sprint, with the top item taken next.
Preproduction lasts until two publishable levels are fully finished with all necessary features, at which point the core design is known well enough to schedule the rest.
The project schedule lists tasks, durations, deadlines, and assignees, and is usually the most frequently updated document.
Preparation means immersing yourself in a domain and its open problems.
Unknown unknowns are mistakes and assumptions that designers do not realize they are making, and they often matter more than known unknowns.
Process burden is the time cost of coordinating work, including notes, specs, meetings, production staff, bug tracking and design wikis.
Many studios build mid-game levels first, leaving opening levels for last; teams also start mid-game early for trailer footage, a demo level, and budget and staffing reasons.
Beta spaces on distribution services help control player expectations.
Production or build time is the wait before an upgrade or item is ready to use.
In a mass-market game, programming is a small share of effort; most time goes to models, textures, environments, sound, music, animation and detailed level design.
Publisher milestones often demand early functionality, so temporary code is written and later replaced.
Some risks, such as an outside request to retheme the game, cannot be solved by prototypes and need management decisions or contingency plans.
The waterfall model became widely adopted in the 1970s as a seven-step process, often pushed by nontechnical management, and was taught in universities and corporations.
A full production cycle, from conception through post-release, has distinct balance concerns at each stage.
Modern expectations include cinematic effects, music, voice acting, animation, performances by well-known actors, and live orchestras.
At the end of preproduction the publisher either funds full production or cancels the project, and a cancelled developer keeps the preproduction milestone payment.
Production, roughly months 7 to 22, is the longest and most expensive stage; its goal is to build all features and reach alpha, when feature work stops.
Production covers how narrative design works with upstream and downstream teams, cinematics, and quality assurance.
Non-developer clients commission games to build brand loyalty, reach new customers, earn mobile or social revenue, or teach skills to employees or children.
Online games need constant content updates, and meeting that need often forces development teams into regular overtime.
Planning is taught from childhood and has enabled major projects with precise designs, but game design's uncertainty makes the same habit mislead developers into overplanning.
when: When applying general planning habits to game development
why: Game discoveries can change the core of the product, unlike fixed-spec construction.

text: In game design, overplanning harms more projects than underplanning does.
Setbacks in hard invention include designs that fail basic function, wrong reference data, missing components that must be invented, and no off-the-shelf part light enough.
A large study of creative workers found that those most interested in money were not the most creative.
To notice surprises, first write predictions about how players will behave.
when: When running playtests of the game
why: A surprise only registers against an expectation you already held, so predictions must be written down first.

text: Iterate when player experience cannot be predicted from paper alone, which is always true to some degree.
why: Player experience can never be fully forecast, so decisions must rest on what players actually experience during iteration.

text: Welcome changing requirements, even late in development, and treat them as a competitive advantage.
when: when requirements shift during production
why: Agile values responding to change over sticking to a fixed plan.

text: Measure progress primarily by working software, and maintain a sustainable pace.
when: when assessing project progress
why: Agile processes aim for a pace that sponsors, developers and users can sustain indefinitely.

text: Build one representative unit of a large content set to measure its production time before committing to the full set.
when: when content scope may exceed the schedule
why: a single sample reveals the real cost per unit

text: Specify deliverables concretely, including format, length, and deadline, since vague promises invite confusion.
when: assigning design work
why: Specific requirements leave less room for misreading.

text: Rare risks still matter at scale: a one-in-a-million event happens about five times among five million players.
when: large player populations
why: With enough players, a one-in-a-million event becomes a near-certain recurring occurrence.

text: New art, custom animation and recorded dialogue usually cost more time and money than writers expect, so plan them early.
when: When content depends on new art, custom animation or recorded dialogue
why: Content that needs art or artists nobody has time to make may be cut from the plot.

text: Trivial, small exercises are too simple to tempt designers into deep planning, so they rarely produce the conviction that iteration matters.
when: When designing a learning project about iteration
why: Deep planning tempts only when the project has enough scope to need it.

text: Avoid overplanning by tolerating the stress of uncertainty and reevaluating constantly, rather than locking decisions away.
when: when a team feels pressure to fix decisions early
why: Fixed decisions create a false sense of certainty, and reckless forecasting is more harmful than living with uncertainty.

text: Elements above the solid foundation are usually too uncertain to implement; at paper stage their certainty may fall below 50%.
when: Until the foundation elements have been implemented and playtested
why: Elements built above an untested base inherit its uncertainty, which compounds as more layers are stacked on top.

text: Plan several moves ahead on political effects, and drop an idea early if it could not be cut later, since others would become too invested in it.
when: When proposing ideas in group design.
why: Early abandonment avoids entrenched investment that is costly to reverse.

text: Build a library of level precedents from notes and screenshots, and draw on it when designing your own levels.
when: when designing a new level
why: Studying existing levels supplies reusable ideas.

text: Build mid-game first when players control complex mechanics, so designers quickly learn what players already understand.
when: When players operate complex mechanics and designers must learn quickly what players understand

text: Each new gameplay element needs more balancing time, so add balancing time when adding new elements.
why: Schedules that run out before the game works leave too little time to balance it before release.

text: Record how long key milestones take to reach, then scale the progression curves so the game ends within a target length range.
why: Hard time limits can be a lazy substitute, signaling insufficient playtesting of how long play actually takes.

text: Approve developer work against milestones, since each publisher-approved stage triggers a milestone payment to the developer.
Without a clear scope, producers fall back on canned numbers or rough estimates, making schedule and budget inaccurate, possibly insufficient, and stressful.
when: At the start of any production, when the producer builds the schedule and budget

text: Once approved, the project plan becomes an addendum to the signed contract, legally binding the developer to it.
Work done without a plan is often discarded because it turns out to be superfluous or gets overtaken by later progress.
when: When starting tasks without a plan
why: A plan reveals the minimum steps needed and removes unneeded work before it is done.

text: Without shared planning, performance budgets get consumed by parallel work, funding becomes hard to secure, and design drifts across genres, forcing late cuts and crunch.
when: When many people build content separately from a shared design vision
why: Unaligned content and systems accumulate cost that surfaces near release.

text: Nonfatal bugs and unstable balance slow down everyone working with them, and an unfinished story adds uncertainty that makes level polishing harder.
when: When a team builds on unfinished tools, mechanics or narrative.
why: Dependents must work around instability, which costs them time.

text: Coordination cost and complexity grow as teams get larger, so the share of time spent on tracking and scheduling work rises with team size.
why: Large teams need dedicated production staff, bug trackers and wikis to coordinate, which consumes time.

text: Design changes requested mid-production increase cost, so documented approvals and change requests are needed to justify added budget.
when: Publisher requests changes during production.
why: Written approval records give the producer grounds to negotiate a bigger budget for added features.

text: Milestone payments for development act as an advance on royalties, so the publisher keeps all revenue until sales repay the advance and the developer earns royalties afterward.
when: in a standard publisher-developer deal

text: The transition from preproduction to production typically occurs after about 30% of the necessary budget is spent.
why: Once two complete levels exist, the design is known well enough to schedule the rest of development safely.

text: A vision statement should run about 500 words, opening with a one-sentence logline, followed by a gameplay synopsis of no more than a couple of pages.
A 90% confidence estimate range should contain the true value about nine times in ten; most people's ranges capture only two to four of ten answers.
when: when judging whether estimates are well calibrated
why: Most people are overconfident in their numerical estimates.

text: In one solo level-design case, process burden was about 4 percent of total work time; in a large studio case it was about 50 percent.
why: Specs and discussion meetings in large studios consume time that a solo worker never needs.

text: The V-model shows that creative flexibility is broad early and narrows as production advances, so changes are cheap early and costly late.
when: Approaching the testing stage of a project
why: Late changes force rework of art, animation, and code; only variables built to be flexible adjust cheaply.

text: Overplanning consumes time, makes cutting plans costly, and creates false certainty; planning too far ahead also defeats iteration because plans age before they can be tested.
when: When deciding how much detail to write into a design plan
why: Written plans feel certain even though they are built on untested assumptions.

text: Building upper layers on an untested foundation exposes them to excessive cascading change when lower elements are revised.
when: Designing risky, potentially breakthrough games where per-system certainty is low
why: A failure in any foundational element forces upper layers to change, and uncertainties compound multiplicatively.

text: Starting a large unfinished project before proving its core ideas with small prototypes is the real failure mode.
why: Large projects built without prototypes often die unfinished.

text: Milestone code that is patched until it cannot be removed often ships as the final AI.
when: When publisher milestones demand functionality early in the development cycle

text: The linear waterfall process, with each step finished before the next starts and no return to earlier steps, ignores the iteration that real development needs.
when: Choosing a development process for software or games
why: Complex software reveals problems late, and forbidding a return to earlier steps makes those problems costly to fix

text: Underestimating the effort needed to debug and balance multiplayer games is a common mistake.
when: When developing a multiplayer online game
why: Multiplayer games are much harder to debug and balance than similar single-player ones.

text: Repeatedly offering options without asking about purpose frustrates both the designer and the client.
when: When a client cannot say what they want and keeps rejecting offered options
why: Helping the client clarify their wants is a core designer job; guessing options only repeats the cycle.

text: An excellent transformational game without a funding or distribution plan may never reach the people it is meant to help.
when: Designing games meant to change players' behavior or outlook

text: Each added variable multiplies the relationships to track, so physics-heavy games can become spreadsheet-like and need visualization tools.
when: A vehicle physics simulation exposing many separate tuning values for suspension and friction

text: Warning signs of weak preproduction include unclear game design, unclear key roles and processes, low urgency, and panic late in preproduction.
Each added element, such as more player characters, a new dimension, or an unfinished platform, multiplies control and design problems during production.
when: Adding more player characters, a new dimension, or a platform still in development during production
why: Controls are already hard to design for one character, so each extra one compounds the problem.

text: Self-publishing without a production or marketing budget makes traffic very hard to build, and user-generated sites are intensely competitive.
when: Self-publishing a game with no production or marketing budget

text: Funding an independent game with debts you cannot repay, such as loans or credit, risks serious financial harm.
when: When an independent developer self-funds a game through loans, credit cards, or similar debt

text: Starting production with only a brief kickoff lets each discipline build its own version of the game, producing an incoherent product that struggles to ship.
when: When a team begins production right after a brief kickoff discussion of concepts
why: Disciplines lack a shared picture of the final game, so their work diverges.

text: Overly serious or explicit penalties make people paranoid and degrade team climate.
when: When deciding how to punish a team member whose change breaks the shared build
why: Harsh consequences make people over-guard their own work and damage working relationships.

text: Reactive decisions made in a panic during live operations can damage both player experience and revenue.
when: Live operation
why: Without solid hypotheses to test, panic rather than evidence drives reactive decisions.

text: Developers who overspend during concept and preproduction, expecting the upcoming milestone check to cover the shortfall, risk going out of business.
when: When concept and preproduction spending exceeds plan, betting on the next milestone payment

text: 1) Set the expected game length. 2) Derive the target level for that length. 3) Divide levels by hours for a levels-per-hour rate. 4) Derive stages, enemy configurations, and stat gains from those targets.
when: Before production, for any game with a fixed or expected length.
why: Targets derived from length keep content volume matched to play time.

text: 1) List what could keep the game from being great. 2) List how to stop each of those from happening. 3) Solve the most dangerous problems first.
when: when deciding what to prototype or work on next
why: Working on riskiest parts first yields more useful loops than polishing comfortable parts.

text: 1) Hold a team review listing everything that might jeopardize the project. 2) For each risk, choose a mitigation. 3) Reduce each risk early, usually with a small prototype.
when: before committing to full production
why: Avoids discovering fatal problems months into development.

text: 1) Before committing time to a game, ask whether making it is worth your time. 2) Answer by consulting what matters to you, not only the market, team, or client.
when: choosing among projects or deciding whether to continue a time-consuming game
why: Keeps effort focused on important work.

text: 1) Build and tune the core simulation until basic interactions feel satisfying. 2) Build the larger world. 3) Reward every physical interaction with scoring events. 4) Layer a combo system on top.
when: building a physics-driven game
why: Each layer rests on the feel established below it.

text: 1) Confirm the ultimate goal is clear. 2) Check that players always move toward it. 3) Check that milestones exist. 4) Describe how the system motivates the final goal.
when: Auditing a prototype's goal structure

text: Number each build so bugs can be traced to the build where they first appeared.
when: When programmers periodically assemble versions of the project during development

text: Send the alpha build to the publisher's QA; if approved, the publisher pays the milestone and the team moves into QA/polish.
when: When a developer reaches alpha and submits a build to publisher QA

text: 1) Revise goals first. 2) Shorten deliverables to match the revised goals. 3) Shorten the schedule to match. 4) Lower the budget to match. Work item by item from goals down.
when: The first budget is far above the publisher's advance or a requested cut.
why: Changing numbers while keeping goals risks overpromising and underbudgeting.

text: 1) Accumulate elapsed time. 2) Run fixed updates while accumulated time exceeds the step. 3) Cap the number of updates per frame. 4) Accept slowdown instead of freezing when the cap is reached.
when: Running a fixed-step simulation that must survive slow frames
why: The cap prevents an unbounded catch-up loop that would lock the game up on slow hardware.

text: 1) Decide what the sequence should tell. 2) Work out how a character would move or stand there. 3) Check what looks believable. 4) See whether existing animation can be reused. 5) Estimate how often it can play.
when: before building a sequence
why: These questions decide whether a sequence is worth its cost.

text: 1) Choose the audience: professional designers or players with no design experience. 2) Choose which content aspects users can manipulate, guided by generator priorities. 3) Balance direct manipulation against computer suggestions. 4) Decide how conflicting desires are handled. 5) Ensure the computer can generate everything the human can produce. 6) Plan how the computer explains its actions.
when: when scoping a new mixed-initiative design tool
why: The generator's underlying priorities make some design aspects easy to expose for direct user editing.

text: 1) List tasks on a wall. 2) Keep each task small enough that two or three can be finished per day. 3) Cross off each completed task in a visible color.
when: When a team or individual needs visible daily progress.
why: Completed tasks give a mood boost and make progress observable.

text: Treat predicted playtest problems as hypotheses, and confirm them through prototyping and playtesting before changing the design.
when: When early guesses predict where a design may fail with particular audience groups

text: Rate issue severity by how much it blocks players, how much frustration it causes, and which feature it affects; raise severity for issues affecting a core pillar or monetization even when players find a workaround.
when: Assigning severity to UX issues
why: Blocking, frustration, and core-feature impact determine how much an issue harms the game.

text: Add visual or sound work to a prototype only when it clarifies a mechanic or answers an aesthetic question early.
when: When a prototype's mechanics are hard to read, or an aesthetic question must be tested early
why: Excess aesthetic polish wastes time, while a little visual or sound work helps convey how mechanics work.

text: Apply the same safe-environment rules to production meetings so team members speak freely without personal attacks.
why: People share candid input only when they feel safe, which leads to a motivated, invested team.

text: Consult an intellectual property lawyer before committing to an open source scripting language for a distributed product.
when: When a distributed product relies on any third-party scripting language, open source or not
why: Licence and liability obligations can be hidden

text: Design so that if half the budget were removed, a shippable game would still remain.
when: when scoping a project
why: Forces simple systems and guarantees a shippable result when cuts are needed.

text: Treat unexpected extra development time as an opportunity to run more iteration loops, discarding what failed and refining what worked.
when: Schedule slips or platform changes unexpectedly give the team extra time
why: Additional loops let the team improve what works and cut what does not, as happened with Halo's platform moves

text: Check the target platform's audio RAM budget before designing any sound, since sounds that cannot fit in memory will not play, however good they sound.
when: Starting any game audio project
why: Most sounds must reside in RAM to play instantly

text: Sort beta bugs into three groups: those blocking testing, those to fix before release, and those that can wait.
when: beta testing
why: Bugs that stop further testing halt everyone else's work, so they take priority.

text: During beta, designers answer whether behavior is working as intended and tune numbers, while programmers handle bugs.
when: During beta, once the game is both feature complete and content complete
why: Mechanics and content are finished, so designers check intent and tune numbers while programmers fix bugs.

text: Plan UX tests well in advance for each milestone, since milestones are usually when the build is most stable.
when: When a production schedule must fit UX testing around each milestone
why: Advance planning keeps UX testing from adding pressure to an already busy team.

text: Have each team leave with a rough preproduction schedule built on a movable board, such as a whiteboard with repositionable notes, so it can be revised.
when: In a multi-day interdisciplinary preproduction workshop where teams work through short, time-limited exercises.

text: Get legal and project management approval before discussing NDA-protected material with anyone outside the company.
when: sharing project information with consultants
why: Outside disclosure can breach confidentiality obligations.

text: Plan far ahead when plans are likely to work and only a short distance when plans are uncertain.
when: when setting how far ahead to plan before testing
why: Long horizons on uncertain plans waste effort on problems that never appear and hide faulty assumptions, while short loops waste time and fail to get developers coordinated.

text: Identify the missing capability that limits the whole goal and focus on it, even when little knowledge or industry supply exists for it.
when: When a needed capability has no industry or supplier from which it could be bought.
why: With no one available to sell or research it, the team has to develop the missing capability itself.

text: Link into the official plan only the elements that will be worked on soon.
why: Fixing distant, uncertain elements into a plan claims a certainty the team lacks, so keeping them in an unordered pool preserves flexibility.

text: When an outside group requests a very detailed high-stack decision, negotiate a compromise instead of committing to it immediately.
when: When marketing or business asks for a very detailed decision high in the dependency stack, long before the game needs it.
why: Detailed decisions near the top are likely to be reshaped by downstream changes, so early lock-in can cost more than it gains.

text: Plan a level before building it rather than placing objects freely in an editor, and answer layout questions with non-digital sketches first.
when: when starting a level
why: sketches answer layout questions without consuming production time

text: The waterfall model's one good quality is encouraging more planning and design before coding, at the cost of rigid sequencing that blocks iteration.
when: Evaluating upfront planning against iteration
why: Heavy upfront planning helps, but a fixed linear sequence cannot absorb what is learned later

text: Clean architecture, fast runtime performance, and quick delivery of current features pull against each other, so each decision must weigh all three rather than follow one universal rule.
when: making a development decision
why: Optimizing for one goal usually costs another.

text: Deep planning can reveal distant design peaks, but planned leaps may land on foothills; tight iteration refines a known direction more reliably.
when: when choosing between a conceptual leap and refining a known direction
why: Iteration climbs the nearest peak of the design space, so it refines a known direction rather than jumping to a different one.

text: Too little planning causes parts of the team and game to work against each other, while too much detailed planning breaks on contact with reality.
why: Both extremes carry harm, so planning must balance structure against uncertainty.

text: Playtest core mechanics with paper or interactive prototypes early, before engine and art polish, since design problems surface fastest and cheapest; jumping straight into full production skips this stage.
when: before committing to full production
why: Early prototypes expose design problems at the cheapest stage. Problems found late cost far more to fix.

text: 1) Start with paper prototypes, building a working nonelectronic version quickly. 2) Play and analyze it to test mechanics. 3) Refine the design. 4) Move to interactive prototypes. 5) Implement in the engine only after that.
when: when testing mechanics early or working alone
why: Traditional prototypes avoid digital technical limits and reveal design issues faster.

text: Build a playable version as fast as possible and playtest it as much as possible; without an early one, months may pass before testing, leaving core problems late.
when: Early development of a new game or long project.
why: Late testing leaves little time to fix core problems.

text: Start every prototype with a clearly stated question, such as how to control a school of fish with a mouse, or it becomes a time-wasting project.
why: Without a clearly stated question, a prototype drifts into costly work that does not inform any decision.

text: Build a playable demo to pitch an interactive idea: games are visual and playable, so a demo is easier to judge than a document or verbal pitch.
when: Pitching an interactive idea, if you can program or prototype, or when the team must feel the idea rather than read about it; a modifiable existing product or paper-and-dice analog version works.
why: Playing communicates the idea better than description, and a demo shows seriousness.

text: Build prototypes and iterations quickly, and do not hold early work to final-quality standards, since the number of iteration loops is the most important factor in quality.
when: During early iteration, where work is expected to be revised and rebuilt many times before reaching final quality.
why: Quick iterations let the team test many versions in a short time.

text: Developers are available for long sessions and give thoughtful feedback with no NDA, since they know the material; but their playtests are unrepresentative, being more skilled and knowing internals.
when: When developers are the first people to try the game, before outside players see it.
why: Insider knowledge and game skill make developers play faster and differently than the target audience, skewing what their feedback reveals.

text: Carry forward ideas, not prototype code, since prototypes show intended behaviour, not implementation; but evolving code directly into the final game is practical for a team using one language.
when: For a small team that uses a single language for both the prototype and the final game.
why: A dedicated programmer would implement the systems at a lower level.

text: A designer who can sketch is perceived as having a clear creative vision.
when: When presenting an abstract game design to others at the very start of a project.
why: Designs are abstract while illustrations are concrete, so a sketch makes the designer's vision visible to others.

text: Showing the effect of each sketch stroke in the 3D world immediately lets designers specify procedural operations, see their results, and build worlds iteratively.
when: When a designer sketches terrain or features that a tool turns into a 3D world.
why: Seeing each procedural operation's effect directly lets designers evaluate and refine the world step by step.

text: A first emotional target can shape a whole game even when the final prototype changes tone and music.
when: when a prototype departs from its initial mood
why: the original emotional idea persists as the seed of the design

text: Designers often discover a game's strongest direction by playing prototypes, such as a camera moving closer, rather than by following the initial concept.
when: When a prototype shows unexpected appeal
why: Playing a working system reveals qualities that a written concept cannot predict.

text: A prototype answers a question, and a playtest is a prototype of the game experience.
A hypothesis is a specific idea being tested in a prototype, more precise than the question it answers.
A prototype formalizes an idea or isolates an issue so the team can learn what works before committing to the final design.
A storyboard is a rough sketch of a visual sequence, useful for planning cutscenes and mapping potential play within a level.
Technology prototypes test the software a game needs, such as graphics, AI, physics, game-specific problems, and the content pipeline.
Rapid prototyping builds many small, fast, throwaway projects, each posing one question about gameplay.
Brownboxing mocks up a VR scene with cardboard boxes and playtests it physically, with a person acting as game master.
when: Early in VR prototyping, before any digital work starts

text: Constructionism holds that learners build knowledge most effectively when they create something meaningful with material, and learning is driven by making rather than being taught.
Early prototypes should be judged by four qualities: fast, cheap, public, and physical.
A storyboard visualizes a feature as a sequence of incrementally changed images, often built from edited screenshots.
A prototype is a rough, playable working model of a design idea, built to test feasibility and find improvements by isolating a few core mechanics.
Early playtesting is inexpensive: no professional test lab is needed, just the designer's time and some volunteers, and designers can run the methods alone.
Prototypes need no game engine or standalone program; a rough build or spreadsheet can serve as a gameplay prototype.
Paper prototypes allow quick iteration on the fly, and the same testing and revising process applies across digital prototype revisions.
Degenerate strategies usually surface in playtesting, and visual polish does not remove them.
Many teams skip physical prototypes, moving from concept to write-up to implementation.
Building a paper version makes abstract rules concrete, so a designer can see how the mechanics fit together.
Major game concepts can grow from small prototypes kept in a studio archive.
Physical prototypes can be built from paper, cardboard, drawn-on markings, miniatures, or parts taken from other games.
Prototypes come in physical, visual, video and software forms, and a project may need several, each answering a different question.
Paper prototypes cannot replace play of real-time or 3D games, but they still greatly help a game's overall system in early development.
Some prototyping tools, such as multimedia animation software, are useful for prototypes but are not full game engines.
Prototypes validate or refute ideas but do not generate them.
A first rough prototype is expected to be poor, with placeholder geometry, badly scaled objects, and sometimes missing weapons.
when: Building the first version of a fight
why: Rough builds are for testing the idea, not for judging polish.

text: Professional game designers commonly work through this idea-test-revise loop, so it is standard practice rather than an amateur habit.
Well-known genres like falling-block puzzlers and first-person shooters can be mocked up on paper in minutes using cardboard cutouts, graph paper, and counters.
when: Testing core concepts before any code is written
why: Paper versions require minimal production work, so they can be assembled and evaluated right away.

text: Brownboxing reveals how players want to use their hands and what they can reach.
Creating simple, rough but useful sketches is a skill that needs practice.
A working prototype is now expected in a pitch; sketches and descriptions that once sufficed for a publisher deal no longer do.
Common early prototype types include paper setups with playing cards and dice, three-dimensional physical models, and basic software prototypes.
Physical prototyping lets a team focus on mechanics without production or programming distractions, and saves time because everyone understands the game.
A digital prototype tests the essence of a game in the format it will ship in and extends the physical prototype rather than replacing it with a fresh start.
when: a game will ship on a digital platform
why: Physical prototypes have limits that digital testing can overcome.

text: A technology and art prototype proves the engine and asset pipeline, and differs from a block-based gameplay prototype.
when: early project planning
why: Each prototype type answers different questions.

text: Swapping buffers by pointer is the most common double-buffering approach for graphics.
Interface prototypes may take the form of static boards or animated mock-ups, and may begin on paper before going digital.
At first playable, testing targets engagement, core mechanics, and fit with the designer's vision; expect many problems and repeat the fix-and-test cycle.
when: first playable stage
why: Early builds are expected to differ greatly from the designer's vision, so testing exposes fundamental gaps that must be fixed.

text: Start icon testing early, since it needs minimal effort, and repeat it as the build matures to confirm players read icons as intended.
when: When checking whether HUD and UI icons are perceived correctly, early in development.
why: A survey asking what icons depict is cheap to run, so it adds little effort.

text: Sketch the game's physical places early, since drawing a place prompts questions about its inhabitants, their occupations and motives, shaping the story.
when: Story ideas have not yet formed

text: Test features with cheap paper prototypes before investing in software, since this helps justify software spending.
when: when a feature would be costly to implement in code
why: Paper tests show whether a costly feature works at low cost, which makes committing software resources easier to justify.

text: A paper prototype can have the designer act as the game program, processing each turn and tracking scores by hand, to test rules cheaply.
when: When a game's basic turn-based rules are first being tested on paper, before any digital version exists.
why: Processing turns by hand produces a playable test without writing any code.

text: Core rules proven in a text-only, turn-by-turn version can often be carried into a graphical version with little alteration.
when: moving a tested design to a fuller presentation
why: Logic validated early needs little redesign

text: Judge a paper prototype by whether its rules let someone grasp the game and give feedback, not by its crude artwork.
why: Playable rules alone can convey the mechanics, so artwork does not determine whether testers can give useful feedback.

text: Make many rough sketches or experiments before committing to a finished version, as artists do before a finished piece.
when: Before committing to a major undertaking.
why: Early variants reveal which ideas work.

text: A working paper system can be adapted to other modes, such as capture the flag, cooperative missions, or deathmatch, to test its range.
Make prototypes fun and exciting; when the designer and peers feel compelled, players usually feel that way too.
why: The designer's and colleagues' enthusiasm is a proxy for how players will react to the prototype.

text: Use physical prototypes to test board games and turn-based systems, and to rough out the structure of any game.
why: Paper rules can be altered and retested at once, so many design iterations fit into a short time.

text: Physical prototypes suit many cheap experiments in a short time, since they need little cost or resources.
why: Paper versions cost little and need few resources, so experiments can be broad and deep.

text: A playable prototype conveys a complex system to newcomers better than a written spec, though a written treatment also helps.
when: explaining a design to team members unfamiliar with it
why: Team members who have never seen the concept can grasp it by playing, and get something tangible to build on.

text: Begin digital prototyping with the core mechanic and add features only after it works.
when: When a gameplay question cannot easily be modeled on paper.
why: Keeping the early build focused on one question avoids tangling unrelated questions together; integration can come later.

text: A rough prototype can explain a concept to the team and then be refined into a fuller version that shapes much of the gameplay.
why: A rough build that already feels close to the final game persuades decision makers quickly.

text: In the foundation stage, the designer is the best tester, trying out core mechanics and fundamental concepts.
when: foundation stage
why: Early on the designer is the only tester available, and experimenting with fundamentals reveals core mechanics and obvious flaws.

text: Early loops can run in minutes and typically test three to eight large concept changes; within a few hours a working concept emerges, after which loops lengthen to two or three hours and changes shrink to adjusting walls and pillars.
when: Early concept prototyping
why: Early loops test broad ideas while later loops refine details.

text: Playtest demonstration scenes several times before settling on the room layout.
when: When a tutorial must stop the player for a demonstration scene.

text: Start with placeholder behaviors and flesh them out once the AI infrastructure works.
when: Early AI development
why: Full behaviors are built only after the integration infrastructure exists, so placeholders come first.

text: Sketch even if you cannot draw, since drawings trigger new ideas.
Test a technical limit with a throwaway prototype that isolates only that limit, such as the number of on-screen items.
when: when unsure whether an engine can handle a planned scale
why: isolating the limit answers the question cheaply

text: Prototypes need not be digital or interactive; board games, paper versions, and animated sketches can capture gameplay and reveal problems sooner.
when: When a videogame idea can be tested with a simple board game or paper version.
why: They are quick to make and can test the same gameplay.

text: Having other people help run a paper prototype is the best approach.
when: when running a paper prototype

text: Noninteractive animations and sketches can answer gameplay questions before interactive systems are built, letting the team plan how to build them.
when: when a movement or animation system is hard to specify

text: Mechanics can be abstracted into simple shapes and playtested before art exists, technical limits can be tested with a prototype that only counts on-screen items, and content cost can be measured by timing one sample asset.
when: when reducing technical, art, or mechanics risk
why: Discovering limits before art is produced avoids costly late surprises; a cheap sample reveals whether the schedule is feasible.

text: Every game should be explainable on a poster diagram showing how the whole game fits together.
why: A one-picture summary gives management and every team member the big picture without detail.

text: Build prototypes of music systems to learn how they behave in play, so you can describe a desired effect precisely to a programmer.
when: Designing interactive music.
why: Knowing the behaviour lets a programmer implement it efficiently.

text: Review wireframes with the QA manager and usability test them before building the game, since interface changes are still cheap then.
when: When interface wireframes exist and implementation has not started.
why: Design problems are caught before implementation.

text: Avoid games with long histories and very large card pools, since an original mechanic is hard to fit and cards take long to sort.
when: choosing a game to expand
why: Original mechanics are hard to fit into long-established games, and huge card pools take too long to model.

text: Simple mechanics make a game easy to learn and modify, so they suit a first prototype better than large trading card games.
when: choosing a first prototype
why: Simple rules are easy to learn and change, while large card games take a long time to get right.

text: Use analytics to catch objects or strategies never used, always used or used suboptimally, and players not learning or not winning enough.
why: Numbers reveal problems that would destroy balance or play experience, so they can be caught early.

text: Physical prototypes are underrated: they engage the whole brain and help teams find their blind spots.
Use a paper and dice prototype to work out a game's metagame and scoring systems before building software.
when: When testing scoring or metagame structure
why: Paper, card and dice versions are quick and inexpensive to build and change, so scoring can be tested early.

text: A playable, fun prototype is not finished; a good game is not necessarily a brilliant one, so keep improving it before moving on.
when: When a prototype already works.
why: Further iteration can turn a good design into a great one.

text: For games aiming at an emotional experience rather than conflict, build the prototype around the core feeling and cut features that playtesters find distracting.
when: designing a relaxation or wonder-focused game
why: Extra features can dilute the core experience players care about.

text: Use a nonvisual tool to handle accounting in a prototype, keeping visuals on paper, and make values editable at runtime rather than hard-coded.
when: building a software tool for a prototype
why: Editable values let designers tune during playtests without recompiling.

text: Choose a simple concept as an early commercial project when its prototype has already solved many design problems, lowering the risk.
when: For a team's first commercial title that must ship within about a year.
why: The simple project leaves room for the inevitable early mistakes of a first commercial release.

text: Build ideas quickly in garage-style programming, trying them immediately to see what happens rather than deliberating at length first.
when: Generating and testing new game ideas
why: Short deadlines and a supportive shared setting free people to experiment with ideas.

text: A technical executive asking for technical details during publisher review is a good sign.
when: When other internal groups have liked the pitch and escalate it to a technical executive.

text: Good packaging matches a developer's technology to a suitable property, since both technology and property count as content.
why: At high per-game prices, matching technology with a property determines whether buyers feel their money was well spent.

text: Storyboards help reviewers who are away from a computer by giving a visual walkthrough and character profiles.
when: reviewers cannot play the game

text: Test whether a game idea is fun before polishing its code, because polishing time is lost if the idea gets cut.
when: early exploration of a new game idea
why: Polish spent on an idea that gets cut is wasted.

text: Write a prototype in a different language from the game so it must be rewritten before it can enter the real project.
when: when you want to stop throwaway code from being kept
why: Forced rewriting prevents prototype code from slipping into production unchanged.

text: Some computer science knowledge helps narrative designers communicate with programmers.
why: Narrative designers script story elements into the game, so they must coordinate closely with programmers.

text: Building a paper prototype forces the designer to work out how game elements interact and to define each one precisely.
when: early in development

text: To test a mechanic, ask how one added rule or piece of information changes a familiar activity, then build a rough version to see.
Use the feel of an early prototype as the guide for later design decisions, since it solidifies the core concept and keeps the design coherent.
why: Knowing what the player should feel gives a reference for resolving later design and production trade-offs.

text: Prototypes are cheaper to change than engine implementations, and teams become attached to implemented or polished features, making later change harder.
A cheap prototype can be thrown away or radically changed, and cheapness removes the need to ask permission to build it.
when: When a team is picking among its favourite brainstormed ideas.
why: Teams hesitate to try ideas that require approval or large investment.

text: When testing is cheap, a shorter planning horizon is appropriate, and good tools make risky experiments practical by lowering the cost of failure.
when: when deciding how far ahead to plan
why: Building and testing an idea quickly makes deliberating about it first less worthwhile.

text: Sketching drives discovery: a shape suggests another, a mistake is covered by a new object, and each change forces further changes until something new emerges.
why: Physical marks and mistakes push the artist toward ideas hard to put into words.

text: A prototype that covers design, build, testing and revision should take two days to two weeks; longer is a warning sign.
when: When building a prototype to validate a specific core gameplay idea.
why: Long prototypes tend to drift into engine work that does not test the core idea.

text: In one survey of publishers, 77 percent of respondents called a playable demo essential to a pitch.
Laying out screens on a 32-pixel cell grid gives a 1280 by 960 pixel screen a 40 by 30 cell layout.
when: mocking up screens in a spreadsheet

text: Aesthetic prototyping methods include comic-strip sequences, visual design sketches, motion previews, screen mockups, and sound sketches.
when: When an aesthetic question, such as how animation fits combat, must be tested early.
why: Small amounts of visual and sound detail help make mechanics understandable.

text: Digital prototyping has four areas: game mechanics, aesthetics, kinesthetics (the feel of play), and technology.
A playable graybox reveals nearly as much as a screenplay, while a design document reveals far less, since it specifies mechanics but not the events they produce.
why: Mentally simulating every mechanic and player choice from a document is impractical.

text: Attachment to a prototype's look or rules makes designers resist iteration changes; paper prototypes ease changes because no code has been invested.
when: when prototyping on paper instead of in code
why: Paper avoids the attachment teams develop to their code.

text: A developer's own appraisal of players' faces can cause anxiety that the evidence does not support.
when: When a developer watches playtesters' faces during a playtest and reads their expressions as a verdict on the game
why: Each observer's own interpretation of a neutral face shapes the emotion it triggers, and expressions are poor indicators of enjoyment.

text: Starting code before the mechanics are understood, because a game seems safe as a variation on standard mechanics, leaves the design unproven.
when: When designers skip a physical prototype and go straight to implementation for a game built on standard mechanics
why: Standard mechanics give designers confidence the idea works, so they code before testing it.

text: Prototyping in a different language from the final game, such as Java for a C++ game, discourages reuse of the prototype code.
when: When the prototype's language differs from the language the final game will be written in
why: Code in another language cannot be used directly, so only abstract ideas carry over.

text: Unreliable hardware makes software fail in many ways, so testing across configurations can be a major development cost.
when: target hardware varies widely and is unreliable
why: Many manufacturers and drivers multiply the ways software can fail, so testing every configuration becomes costly.

text: Not everything can be tested with prototypes; some systems can only be tested efficiently in closed beta, so some issues appear late.
when: When a game system can only be tested efficiently in closed beta

text: Beginning designers often abandon a workable concept too early when a prototype feels flawed.
when: When a playable prototype has balance or flow problems.
why: Problems are often isolable and fixable rather than fatal.

text: Prototype code that works on screen is tempting to ship, yet it usually lacks tests, documentation and stable structure.
when: When prototype code is written only to answer a design question, quickly and with minimal polish
why: Its value depends on being discarded, so keeping it means inheriting code never built for production.

text: A prototype that feels good conceals what its restrictions cost, and the real price is usually higher than anticipated.
why: Each limit yields a small immediate gain, but many limits together can choke the game.

text: Rejecting rough early iterations because they are imperfect reduces the number of loops and produces inferior work.
when: When judging rough work in the early iterations of a game
why: Iteration count drives game quality more than anything else, and perfectionism stretches each cycle.

text: Blacking out unimportant elements can make them look more important than the subject, pulling attention away from it.
when: When sketching to establish visual hierarchy in a drawing
why: Dark values attract the eye regardless of importance.

text: Chicken-scratch lines and hurried shapes distract from a drawing's meaning.
when: When drawing architectural sketches meant to communicate spaces to others
why: The drawing's purpose is communicating spatial forms, so messy marks obscure its meaning.

text: 1) Draw the play area on paper. 2) Represent moving elements with cutouts or tokens. 3) Have one person control each element. 4) Advance with a fixed timer or slow shared clock, such as a metronome, so players can think through decisions and notice map size, room shapes, weapon properties, and spatial details fast play hides.
when: Prototyping real-time or action games on paper at a slow tempo
why: Slowed play leaves room to reflect on what works and what fails, exposing details that fast play hides.

text: 1) Take the set of pre-built decks. 2) Have every deck play every other deck once, giving a minimum of six matches for four decks. 3) Note which deck and which mechanic seem most and least powerful.
when: Building intuition about balance across a set of competing decks.
why: Round-robin matches reveal relative strength of each option quickly.

text: 1) Build a cheap, playable model of the core mechanics using paper, index cards or acting out. 2) Play it with friends. 3) Refine it before programmers, producers or artists join. 4) Check whether player experience goals are met.
when: right after brainstorming, before production
why: Instant feedback shows whether player experience goals are met before costly production begins.

text: 1) Draw a grid and give each player a distinct marker. 2) Decide who moves first. 3) On each turn, a player drops a marker into a column, where it stacks on the lowest free cell. 4) Time each session. 5) Write questions and a session script before testing. 6) Recruit testers, introduce the game, and let them begin.
1) Identify elements that depend on nothing. 2) Iterate and playtest them until reliable. 3) Build the next layer on that solid base. 4) Repeat upward one layer at a time.
when: designs containing original, unproven elements
why: Building in dependency order limits cascading change from lower layers

text: Prototyping a level: 1) Build a paper version using pieces whose movement roughly mimics the game's movement style. 2) Write rules for the other core mechanics. 3) Graybox the level in an engine around one mechanic.
when: a level idea is being tested before digital work
why: cheap prototypes reveal problems early

text: 1) Start with a cheap paper prototype where the designer resolves turns by hand. 2) Move to a text-only version to test core logic. 3) Build the graphical version, reusing proven logic, and playtest at each stage.
when: developing a new multiplayer game
why: Each stage tests the design cheaply before more production is invested

text: 1) Diagram the idea on paper. 2) Work out as many details as possible before writing code. 3) Write the prototype code.
why: unfinished thinking leads to implementing ideas that are not fully formed; diagramming also speeds up coding

text: 1) Give each player a concealed placement grid and a separate guess grid, each 10x10 with rows A-J and columns 1-10. 2) Keep the placement grid hidden from the opponent. 3) Place five straight, non-diagonal pieces of lengths 5, 4, 3, 3 and 2.
when: Designing two-player hidden-information grid games.
why: Separating concealed placements from recorded guesses keeps each player's information clear.

text: 1) On a turn, call a coordinate such as B5. 2) The opponent answers hit or miss. 3) When every segment of a ship is hit, announce it sunk. 4) Record hits and misses on the Target Grid, for example with an H. 5) The first player to sink all five opposing ships wins.

1) Build the paper system exactly as specified, logging every problem and open question. 2) Add each feature, noting how it changes play. 3) Test unusual additions too, since they can reveal unexpected designs.
why: Odd additions may surface design possibilities nobody planned.

text: 1) Cut paper into equal-sized pieces. 2) Line them up as a track. 3) Mark special sections on specific pieces. 4) Make an end card with numbered goal slots across its top.

1) State what the prototype is for. 2) Identify who will use it. 3) Identify what matters, such as look, feel, load time, or persuasion. 4) Build only enough programming, art, and interface to test that.
why: Doing too much at once stops progress, so prototypes must stay small to move quickly.

text: 1) Decide whether the prototype is symmetrical or asymmetrical. 2) Describe how and why the sides differ or match.
when: Reviewing a prototype's structure

text: 1) Create a variant of the prototype with asymmetrical objectives. 2) If single player, offer a choice of objectives. 3) Note how the gameplay changes.
when: Testing objective asymmetry

text: 1) Build a rough version of a basic fight within an hour. 2) Play it immediately. 3) Note what fails. 4) Remove failing elements and rearrange cover, weapons, and enemies. 5) Repeat.
when: Early in concept exploration, when testing broad ideas
why: Playing a crude version surfaces concrete ideas that imagination alone cannot reach.

text: 1) Turn the design brief into a list of risks. 2) For each risk, build a small prototype or measurement that tests it early. 3) Use results to cut, reuse, or redirect content.
when: when a project is long and risks remain untested
why: early playable builds reveal problems before much of the schedule is spent

text: 1) Rank prototypes by the biggest risks they address. 2) Put first any prototype whose result could make other prototypes pointless. 3) Build the top-ranked prototype first.
when: Planning which prototypes to build when many questions are open
