why: Facing the largest risks first avoids wasting effort on work that a single early answer could invalidate

text: 1) Build the VR scene from cardboard boxes. 2) Playtest it with a game master who describes what happens when the player touches, picks up or manipulates each object. 3) Iterate on the brownbox. 4) Measure it and pass the measurements to a modeler to create a first whiteboxed digital prototype.
when: VR or AR projects with many unknowns that need experimentation.
why: Simulating a virtual scene is itself a real-world task, so physical stand-ins reveal reach and hand interaction quickly.

text: 1) Brainstorm with as much of the team as possible. 2) Core members design independently. 3) Core members discuss and work toward consensus. 4) Core team presents progress to the whole team and invites criticism.
when: When design discussions are too detailed for the whole team to run together.
why: Staging limits debate to a small group while keeping the whole team informed and involved.

text: 1) Save a copy of the project first, with a name that includes the date and version. 2) Save later changes under a new version number.
when: before changing a project
why: keeps earlier working states recoverable

text: 1) Break or misuse existing tools to test a sound idea quickly. 2) If the idea is accepted, have programmers implement it properly.
why: Misusing tools illustrates the point, so the idea can be judged before engineers build it properly.

text: 1) Plan the layout on paper. 2) Implement findings and prototype digitally in an engine. 3) Playtest it against the original design goals. 4) Iterate until the experience matches the goals, keeping layouts aligned with the intended player experience.
when: when building a level
why: Playtesting checks whether the level fulfills its design goals.

text: 1) Cut out printed card sheets, or hand-make cards from index cards, which can be larger and easier to handle. 2) Mark each card's deck label on its bottom edge. 3) Separate the cards into labeled decks.
when: building a physical card prototype

text: 1) Build a test level with near-final character, animations and moves, plus many interactive objects. 2) Tune jump heights and running speed alongside object spacing. 3) Adjust spacing and mechanics together rather than sequentially.
when: Developing movement mechanics alongside levels
why: Object size, spacing, jump height and speed form one interdependent system

text: 1) Describe what the control would feel like. 2) Prototype that feel first. 3) Only then add goals, constraints and mini-game rules.
when: Designing a new control scheme.
why: Starting from imposed constraints can ask the wrong design questions and produce frustrating controls.

text: 1) Devise dramatic elements for a simple game, such as backstory, distinct piece looks, or special areas. 2) Play it with others. 3) Note their reactions.
when: Testing whether added drama changes player engagement
why: Player reactions show whether the added elements work.

text: 1) Take screenshots of the existing game. 2) Edit them to show the feature's start and interface changes. 3) Add a series of slightly different stills. 4) Assemble them in slides with minimal text. 5) Rehearse the presentation flow.
when: When visualizing a new feature
why: Showing successive small changes simulates play and makes the feature understandable.

text: 1) Build the core gameplay with cheap materials such as cardboard, paper, glue, and pens. 2) Draw a rough board or map. 3) Create basic objects such as setting, units, and resources, plus the key repeated action cycles. 4) Play the core alone.
when: When starting a physical prototype of a new concept.
why: A foundation prototype reveals whether the concept is worth pursuing before details are added.

text: 1) Carry core mechanics, map, and objects over from the physical prototype. 2) Replace card or turn systems with real-time logic. 3) Create a control map for the target input device. 4) Design the visual display for the target screen.
when: When moving a validated physical prototype into software.
why: Core mechanics stay valid across media, while input and display must be redesigned for the platform.

text: 1) Name the purpose: answer design or technical questions, prove a production pipeline, or communicate the vision to a team or publisher. 2) Build models only of the systems whose questions matter, such as logic, physics, environments, or levels.
when: before starting a digital prototype
why: A stated purpose prevents prototypes that answer nothing specific.

text: 1) Ask whether the tool is really needed. 2) Define its requirements. 3) Choose the quickest build. 4) Confirm it will be flexible enough for changes.
when: before building a software prototype tool
why: Planning keeps the tool small and useful for answering the design question.

text: Build the first prototype around the core mechanic, testing only that interaction before adding any content.
when: start of prototyping

text: 1) Keep the team small. 2) Build one playable level or environment that proves the differentiating features and risky technology. 3) Refine design, technology, staffing, schedule, and deliverables. 4) Write a thorough design brief and engineering spec or wiki. 5) Present the prototype, progress, documents, and plan for funding.
when: Preproduction, roughly months 2 to 6.
why: Proves feasibility before the full team is hired.

text: 1) Build a playable prototype first. 2) Flowchart the entire game. 3) Sketch a wireframe for every screen, showing all features the interface needs. 4) Add callouts explaining each feature, supported by bullet points.
when: Before drafting the design document text
why: Inconsistencies surface while changes are still cheap.

text: 1) Add abstraction only when confident it is needed. 2) Plan for performance throughout, delaying lock-in optimizations. 3) Explore the design space quickly without leaving a mess. 4) Discard prototype code without polishing it when it will be thrown away.
when: moving through prototyping, mid-development, and pre-ship stages
why: Each step balances flexibility, performance, and exploration against lasting code quality.

text: 1) Lock all reads and writes to both buffers. 2) Exchange the two buffer pointers. 3) Release the lock. Keep this step as fast as possible.
when: Swapping double buffers by pointer
why: Pointer exchange takes a few assignments regardless of buffer size, minimizing the locked interval.

text: 1) Build a paper prototype of a mixed-initiative tool. 2) Have a partner play the designer while you act as the AI. 3) Limit your responses to what a real AI system could do.
1) Make paper or cardboard mockups of buttons and menus. 2) Have people act out playing the game using those mockups. 3) Observe where they struggle and what they intend at each moment.
when: Building interface prototypes well before the game is complete.
why: Interfaces cannot be assumed clear, empowering or fun until real people try them.

text: In 2D engines without primitives, use placeholder art such as squares, circles and triangles, often called programmer art.
when: blocking out 2D levels before final art
why: Simple placeholder shapes let gameplay be tested before final art is imported.

text: Prototype a level with physical materials: 1) pick a scale, macro for a whole game layout or micro for one room 2) represent walls, enemies and props with tokens 3) write simple movement rules 4) play and rearrange pieces.
when: early in development, before digital work
why: Movable tokens such as matchsticks let designers quickly try different spatial layouts.

text: Test mechanics and aesthetics with analog methods first, but kinesthetics can only be prototyped digitally and must be tested in a playable build.
Do not stake your career on technology you have not seen work; test it before relying on it in a pitch, since trusting untested technology risks a failed presentation.
when: When a funder or team is caught up in inflated expectations about a new technology.
why: Equipment and connections often fail unexpectedly.

text: Prototype rules without computers first, because non-digital tests quickly reveal how a game works.
when: early game design
why: Fast tests cost less than building software.

text: If one test cannot cover every question, run several minitests.
Test difficulty with a small sample of the target audience, and add telemetry once the game reaches beta.
when: Before the Beta stage, when a large audience cannot yet be tracked.
why: Telemetry from a large audience is needed for reliable difficulty balance, which small playtests cannot provide.

text: Replace unbuilt features with paper materials, such as a tutorial printed on sheets, and stay honest about what those substitutes cannot show.
when: when a feature is not yet implemented

text: Stay completely silent during over-the-shoulder tests, with no talking, laughing, groaning or signaling. If asked, reply neutrally.
why: Any reaction can steer the tester and corrupt results

text: Document what worked and what should change after each prototype test.
when: after each prototype test
why: records guide the next iteration

text: Build prototypes that are fast, cheap, public and physical, since they get the team talking.
when: Early preproduction, before production takes off and the team is coding and drawing.
why: Core gameplay becomes very hard to change once production is underway, so cheap early tests matter.

text: When testing movement values such as jump height, attack specifications, or run speed, use primitive shapes and prioritize function over style.
why: Function-first prototypes save time for animators, designers and programmers alike.

text: Keep each prototype focused on one open question instead of combining several questions into one early prototype.
Build a digital gameplay prototype when a mechanic is hard to model physically, since paper cannot model it well.
Build a kinesthetic prototype when the game's appeal depends on how its controls feel.
when: the appeal depends on control feel

text: Use technology prototypes to test and debug tools and workflow, not to do full software engineering.
Effective quick prototypes state something testable and yield learning you can act on.
why: Prototypes do not create ideas. They only check existing ones, so a testable claim is what makes them useful.

text: A physical prototype needs a full set of written rules; a software prototype needs a working interface or written rules, so testers can play with little designer help.
why: Independent testers uncover gaps the designer has not considered, which designer-guided play would hide.

text: Build prototypes rough and fast, caring only whether they answer the question, because polish hides problems and creates false confidence.
when: When building early concept sketches meant to be thrown away
why: Rough work invites testers to point out flaws.

text: Expect to throw many prototypes away, keep the pieces that work, and combine them.
why: Planning to discard the first version is standard practice.

text: Draw interface ideas to check whether they are possible before committing to them.
why: Designs are abstract while drawings are concrete, so a drawing exposes whether an idea can actually be shown.

text: Prototype a proposed change of combat time model before rejecting it, since switching between real-time and turn-based can transform a game.
when: considering a major change to combat timing

text: Request a dedicated test space when research grows, so the test environment can be controlled better.
when: Developers want more user research

text: Test a nudge's consequences on a small scale before rolling it out widely.
when: before wide rollout of any nudge
why: Hurried users skim fine print and click prominent buttons, so a nudge can produce unintended outcomes.

text: Let the whole team see and experience prototypes together; shared play can beat isolated work on a large design document.
Add a rule to a physical prototype only when it is absolutely necessary for playability, and keep the core mechanic to as few rules as possible.
when: During early physical prototyping.
why: Extra rules added early obscure whether the core mechanic works.

text: Do not polish a digital prototype like a finished game, since minimal art and sound are enough to answer questions.
when: building a digital prototype
why: Polish consumes time without advancing the purpose of the prototype.

text: Build a software prototype only when paper cannot test the game well, such as when accounting overwhelms players; otherwise use a cheaper paper playtest.
when: choosing between paper and software prototyping
why: Software adds build cost and can grow more complex than the problem it solves.

text: If no prototype was built during concept, build and playtest one during preproduction before committing to full production.
why: Major problems surface before art or code is produced, so they are caught before that work is invested.

text: If prototype code might end up in the product, write it defensively and well enough to survive being kept.
when: prototype code with a real chance of being kept
why: Code that looks like it works often gets kept despite being unmaintainable, so it should be written to survive that.

text: Use a small graph-paper booklet as a portable sketchbook for level design notes and idea collection.
when: When doing non-digital level design and collecting ideas
why: A portable book lets you capture ideas wherever you encounter levels.

text: Show the designer's sketch beside generated suggestions so the designer can compare them directly.
A paper arena tests weapon balance, territorial control and layout cheaply, but cannot show the feel of running, aiming and shooting in 3D.
when: When prototyping a first person shooter on paper
why: Paper captures tactical and strategic questions but not the moment-to-moment motion of the player in 3D.

text: Inventing toys before deciding on games can uncover ideas you would not otherwise find, but it is risky when a schedule is fixed.
when: when developing new ideas under a deadline

text: Brownboxing cannot test everything, but it teaches interaction design quickly before any digital production begins.
when: For VR or AR projects with many open unknowns
why: Simulating a reality-based experience means building it in physical form, which quickly reveals how players want to interact.

text: Quick throwaway code is cheap to write but unmaintainable; clean architecture costs more up front but pays off for long-lived code.
when: deciding how much structure to build
why: Clean architecture takes careful thought and sustained effort, which only pays off for code lived in over a long period.

text: A pencil can serve as viewfinder and straightedge: hold the thumb halfway up the shaft to measure and lower down to read angles.
when: measuring proportions from life

text: Non-digital prototypes are cheap and quick to rearrange, but give an abstracted trial that cannot fully test a specific environment's gameplay; use digital prototypes for that.
when: When gameplay depends on testing a particular detailed environment layout
why: A paper version only abstracts spatial play, so it cannot fully test how gameplay plays out inside a specific environment.

text: Most physical games stay on shelves three to six months; unsold copies are returned, leaving publishers holding stock, so sold-in and sold-through figures differ greatly; only sold-through matters.
Developers may attend playtests only if they stay objective and police their own behavior, and must not interact with participants, since contact inflates hype and biases feedback.
when: When a developer cannot stay objective and police their own behavior during the session
why: Developer presence or contact biases testers' expectations and feedback.

text: Publishers favor top developers or projects built on known content.
when: evaluating developers or projects for a deal
why: Publishers are risk averse.

text: Retailers work on thin margins, so they cut every corner they can, which keeps their share of a sale high.
when: evaluating retailer shares of revenue
why: Low margins force high percentage cuts

text: Publishers may cancel weaker products mid-development to save money for titles they expect to sell.
when: when a product looks unlikely to sell well
why: Cutting losses frees budget for likely hits

text: The publisher's producer is the publisher-side project leader, the main link to the developer one step removed from daily production, owning schedule and budget and tracking, allocating and forecasting resources.
In a publisher-developer arrangement, the developer builds the product while the publisher finances and distributes it.
Publishing takes a game from concept to store shelves through four elements: development, licensing, marketing, and distribution.
American specialty is a catchall category for abstract strategy games, war games, and physical play, usually released in small print runs by small publishers.
A red ocean is a crowded market flooded with suppliers, where competition erodes profit.
Profit funds the game industry, so designers should keep profit in view while designing, and people who enjoy managing money are needed for it.
Most game deals reportedly start with a mutual friend making an introduction.
when: Seeking a publishing deal
why: Personal introductions are a common path to deals.

text: The split varies: a developer may handle everything except marketing and sales, or a publisher may develop titles entirely in-house.
A publisher-owned studio still has a publisher-developer relationship with its parent, so it must manage its own cash flow, profit and loss, schedule, and staffing.
Casual publishers fund games they believe will earn money, manage production through completion, check quality, and market the game to over 500 casual game sites worldwide.
Publishers examine each area's leaders, how the team operates, obstacles it has overcome, and its history with previous publishers.
Some aggregators seek quirky, innovative, offbeat titles that mainstream retail would be unlikely to stock.
Some aggregators publish anthologies of indie games on physical discs sold through retailers and accept submissions through a web site.
Some aggregators do not publish casual games.
Publisher rejection does not prove weak demand; a self-published niche title can still sell strongly.
PC and Mac games form a smaller market than console games, split between the two dominant operating systems.
Some platform-focused publishers invest heavily in original ideas, with about 45% of one publisher's releases being new intellectual properties.
Publishers are the main source of game funding.
Crossover appeal can bring players of one hobby into another product line, which is why licensed products are common.
Large publishers can sell directly to big chains, while small publishers depend on distributors.
Mail order, auction sites, company websites, educational distributors, and sporting goods stores are other channels, though none match the traditional markets' sales.
American specialty is the easiest tabletop category for a new inventor to enter.
After weighing risks, publishers prepare a return-on-investment analysis of a title's profit potential.
Publishers are expected to rely on agents and independent producers to supply packages.
Proactive Hollywood-style agents package developers with film projects and earn a share of the package budget.
A publisher picking up an independent game usually offers better ownership and royalty terms, and a finished product lowers the publisher's advance risk.
Console makers and app stores impose strict quality rules, and a single crash bug can block a release.
when: Planning release risk for platform-certified games
why: Platform certification makes stability a gate that hard-coded changes must pass.

text: A finite property market with currency and auctions lets market value emerge from player competition after purchase.
A publisher controls card release quantities and rarity but not how cards are traded or priced.
Publishers coordinate many parties and absorb losses from failed titles, including buying back unsold copies, so they take a large share.
when: a title sells poorly
why: Publishers carry the financial risk of unsold stock

text: Public beta tests help find loopholes, especially in massively multiplayer games, because large player bases expose flaws that small groups miss.
when: Planning late-stage testing
why: Internal testing cannot find every loophole before release, so a wider public test catches the remaining ones.

text: The idea itself matters least to publishers, who rely on market data about which genres audiences will buy.
why: Publishers judge pitches by what they can sell rather than design merit, so they lean on market data.

text: Publishers weigh a team's track record most heavily, then its project plan, when deciding whether to fund a concept.
when: When a publisher hears a game pitch
why: Production is expensive, complex and risky, so a proven team lowers the publisher's risk the most.

text: A developer with many PC titles may be judged riskier for a console game than one with a single console hit.
Consider a PC or Mac release when the target audience is older or more gender-balanced.
when: When the target audience skews older or is more evenly split by gender

text: Build acceptance triggers a payment to the developer, so a build must pass publisher QA and its strict technical requirements before payment follows.
why: Publisher QA decides whether to accept the build as a deliverable, and acceptance is what pays the developer.

text: When a resource economy only adds resources and rarely removes them, average production per turn rises over time, causing inflation.
when: Turn-based economies where production outpaces removal.
why: Growing builds raise future production.

text: Publishers recoup their investment before paying developer royalties.
A data entry with a prototype field inherits every property it lacks from the named entry, so it lists only what differs.
when: when authoring monster or item data as property bags
why: shared values are defined once and changes propagate to all inheriting entries

text: A publisher's portfolio can be split between new concepts, sequels, and licensed properties, for example 41%, 50%, and 10%.
when: Comparing publisher strategies.

text: A single mass-market chain accounted for 19% of US tabletop sales.
when: US tabletop sales in the surveyed period.

text: Fewer than 4 percent of the thousands of submissions publishers receive each year get published, and only one or two of those become hits.
why: Many submissions are rejected immediately, often for inadequate submission materials.

text: Publishers reject games for ten reasons: poor gameplay, unoriginal mechanics, wrong category, theme over gameplay, missing legal forms, narrow appeal, infeasible production, license dependency, unclear rules, cannibalization.
Publisher teams fall into three divisions: marketing and sales, production, and business and legal affairs.
Publishers weigh seven risks in a pitch: time to market, design, technology, team, platform, marketing, and cost.
Assuming your audience reads cues the way you do, or relying on abstract market segmentation instead of a concrete user profile, leads to unnoticed usability problems.
when: Planning audience analysis
why: Designers' own reading of cues differs from players', and segments lack concrete behavior.

text: Showing content publicly before beta makes later cuts visible and controversial, so reveal material only once the set is largely settled.
when: deciding when to publicize unfinished content
why: Players react strongly to content they saw and then lost.

text: Developers working with casual publishers usually give up creative control and do not own the intellectual property.
Comparing game revenue directly to box office is imprecise, since films also earn from DVD, broadcast, cable, and foreign rights.
why: Film revenue comes largely from home video and licensing channels beyond the box office, so box office is not an equal baseline.

text: Publishers reject games that compete with an existing hit from the same company, a problem called cannibalization.
when: When the new game targets the same consumer segment as a company's existing hit
why: A new product may pull customers away from the current hit as much as it attracts new players.

text: Open Science practices include transparency and pre-registration, where peer review happens before data collection so publication does not depend on the result.
when: planning a study whose result you could be tempted to over-interpret
why: Publication decisions then rest on question and protocol quality rather than whether results confirm the hypothesis.

text: 1) Survey the target audience. 2) Interview its members. 3) Observe them in play study groups. 4) Design the product from these findings.
when: Before designing a game for a specific audience.
why: Design grounded in audience evidence rather than assumptions or copied hits.

text: 1) Check the publisher's attitude toward external developers. 2) Check the genres and trends it follows. 3) Review its recent products. 4) Frame your pitch around its focus.
when: Before approaching a publisher with a game.
why: A well-matched pitch is more likely to be accepted.

text: 1) Buy games from publishers. 2) Warehouse them. 3) Mark them up about 50%. 4) Send retailers a catalog to order from.
when: When selling to small publishers or independent retailers outside chains
why: Small publishers cannot directly serve the many independent stores, so distributors bridge that gap.

text: 1) Invent a game for one consumer type and fix problems strangers reveal. 2) Research publishers whose lines target that consumer. 3) Contact them by cold call, email, convention, or agent. 4) If interested, send a prototype or video demo. 5) Wait for the decision. 6) If declined, get feedback and keep trying with several games. 7) If accepted, negotiate a contract.
1) Find the publisher's website or main switchboard. 2) Ask for the contact who handles third-party product acquisitions.
why: Pitching starts with reaching whoever screens outside submissions, so that person is the entry point.

text: 1) Take the wholesale price as about 64% of retail. 2) Subtract goods (about $5), co-op advertising (15% of wholesale), marketing (8%), and return reserve (12%). 3) The remainder is the publisher's net, about 32% of retail.
when: physical retail distribution of a console game

text: Assign one designated contact on each side for communication; veteran developers want a single publisher-side person who can approve work and authorize payments.
Build AI in a PC project, where changes compile and test without a full console build; mini-applications and shared libraries help.
when: When AI has parameter values needing heavy tweaking on a console-targeted project.
why: Each console round-trip adds time, whereas PC changes can be assessed rapidly as code is added.

text: Ask instructors what problems they need solved, and make the game a tool for them rather than a replacement.
when: When an instructor is the one using the game to transform someone.
why: A game cannot match an instructor's accumulated experience, and trying to replace them alienates the instructor.

text: Understand the audience's prior knowledge and expectations before designing inputs they must read.
why: Players may perceive the same input differently.

text: Pitch to casual publishers with a playable demo, which is generally expected; relationships with company staff also help.
when: When pitching a lighter game to a casual publisher that distributes online.
why: Publishers weigh a playable demo heavily, and prior relationships with staff greatly raise the odds of a deal.

text: Choose a publisher whose focus, market, and past games match your game, rather than defaulting to the largest or best-known.
why: Knowing a publisher's focus and trends lets you frame your game within their goals and plans.

text: Research a publisher's product lines before submitting, since publishers reject games for lines they do not produce.
why: Many rejections happen because the inventor did not research the publisher.

text: Be courteous and persistent in following up with publishers, because calls and emails often go unreturned.
when: When calls to a publisher go unreturned.

text: Define the target audience with an age range and an interest group.
when: Writing a game design document
why: Specific audiences make design choices clearer

text: Do not advertise a detailed high-stack feature until it has been iterated, since changes below it are likely to alter it.
when: When a high-level design decision is highly detailed and marketing needs it early.
why: Changes lower in the dependency stack cascade upward and likely reshape a detailed high-level feature.

text: Ask where the money goes in the business model and why, what production, marketing, distribution and maintenance cost, how much it will earn and on what reasoning, and what barriers to entry exist.
when: while designing a game
why: Profit is what keeps game companies operating, so costs and earnings must be understood.

text: Publishers may decide within about six weeks at most, yet reviews can take 4 to 16 weeks, depending largely on how aggressively you follow up.
when: after submitting a game to a publisher

text: Publishing on your own web site gives full creative and marketing control, but provides no budget and little help.
Each distribution route trades creative control, funding, marketing, and IP ownership differently, so choose based on which factor matters most for your project.
when: when selecting how to publish an independent game

text: Developers aim for the highest quality within their resources, while publishers aim for a bestseller with low cost and risk. These goals overlap but conflict over time and money.
why: Publishers aim to limit risk through low costs, so spending on quality becomes a point of disagreement.

text: Retail leaves publishers about 32% of the price after costs and returns, while digital delivery lets them keep the full sale price, lowering risk and encouraging innovation.
why: Retailers can return unsold stock, and games often sell on shelves for only three to six months.

text: QA may want to play the game before hearing your input, in order to stay objective.
when: Early in testing, when QA receives design information.
why: Testers want to form independent impressions.

text: QA testing is performed by dedicated testers to find technical bugs and is essential in any video game production process.
QA tests levels and plot points, reports most bugs, and verifies that changes do not break the game or narrative flow.
Developer and publisher teams both employ QA engineers; publisher QA tests before accepting code delivery, knows the game less than developer QA, and decides whether to accept the build.
why: Publisher QA does not work alongside production.

text: Quantitative feedback from forms reveals trends and helps prioritize how severe issues are.
QA engineers are also called testers, and many people start in QA before moving into producer, programmer, or designer roles. QA lead and QA manager are advanced positions.
The QA/polish stage, roughly months 23 to 24, shifts focus from new features to correctness and polish, refining the alpha build into the shipping product.
QA feedback shows how someone unfamiliar with the story perceives it, revealing what testers understood and what they missed.
1) Build a test plan from the design and technical specifications. 2) Execute the plan. 3) Record unexpected behavior. 4) Categorize and prioritize issues. 5) Retest after fixes.

1) List the areas and features of the product. 2) Specify the conditions under which each will be tested, based on the design document or wiki. 3) Run tests against the current build. 4) Log each deviation from the specification as a bug.
1) Meet the QA lead to share your testing requests. 2) Ask when feedback will arrive. 3) Ask to review QA's final plan before testing starts.
when: working with QA
why: QA writes its own final plan but should welcome input on what matters

text: Test narrative material before release so players are not the first to report that they do not understand what is happening.
why: Setbacks found during internal testing cost far less than problems the public discovers after launch.

text: UX research follows the hypothetico-deductive scientific method: state a hypothesis, measure a predicted effect with a standardized protocol defined beforehand, then confirm or reject; iterative, like design thinking.
why: Reduces bias from gut feelings and subjective memory.

text: Choose methods by question and stage, reacting as conditions shift, since no algorithm picks them; when none fit, return to first principles and invent one.
when: When the ideal test setup is unavailable because of prototype or environment limits.
why: No fixed procedure picks the right knowledge method, so choices must adapt as project conditions shift.

text: Test insights against predetermined hypotheses and combine quantitative analytics with qualitative user research before deciding, since quantitative data alone lacks context.
why: Numbers show what players do, often away from the lab, but they cannot explain why.

text: Rigorous scientific testing by skilled researchers is the ideal proof but costs time and money, so game teams must balance rigor against time and resources.
when: a project needs strong proof
why: Rigorous studies demand substantial time and budget, so teams must weigh rigour against available resources.

text: Knowledge emerges constantly from designers' thoughts, artists examining scenes, and programmers running the game briefly to check a widget.
when: Larger teams in production.
why: Many small observations accumulate into design knowledge.

text: A player whose view is whited out but whose controls still work relies on remembered position and listened-for sounds to keep acting.
when: When perception is blocked but control is kept.
why: Memory and audio cues stay usable when sight is removed.

text: Semirandom research is study without a specific question, building a store of ideas that feeds rumination; it is the counterpart to targeted research.
Bayesianism treats a probability as itself uncertain and combines prior knowledge with new evidence to update it.
A natural experiment is a retrospective study in which chance divides players as an A/B test would, without designer intervention.
A gameplay hypothesis links an early player behavior or understanding to later engagement or retention, such as disengagement from unclear features.
Targeted research is study done to answer a specific question the project currently has, such as how a historical setting looked or how a mechanic works in other games.
Knowledge-creation methods include mathematical calculation, field testing, lab testing, rumination, argument and debate, and research and study.
The behavioral paradigm focuses on environment, stimuli and observable responses, and on how rewards and punishments shape behavior.
Measurable options include time to read rules, clicks to perform a function, speed of level progression, and 1-to-10 ratings of features.
Gut feelings are unreliable because perception is subjective, attention is scarce, and memory is fallible.
Anecdotes of clear behavior change inspire and sell well but do not prove a game's effectiveness.
when: evidence is based on stories
why: Individual stories cannot show the cause of change

text: Replication means repeating an experiment and getting the same outcome; it shows the method was sound and the effect was not due to chance, while failure to replicate is a warning sign.
Knowledge creation includes inventing, refining, testing, debating, and linking ideas, not only generating them.
A small team with little money can beat a larger, well-funded rival by mastering how it creates knowledge, not by relying on connections or budget.
Experience annotations take three formats: ratings on scaled items, class judgements such as yes or no, and preference comparisons between sessions or variants.
Treat small experiments, including failed or unusual ones, as studies: failures show which ideas to pursue, and silly-seeming interactions can lead to later successes.
why: Small experiments build design skill and inform larger projects.

text: Designers build intuition for soft metrics by staying attuned to them across many projects.
why: Soft metrics blend into an evolving sense of what playing the game feels like for everyone.

text: Good listening accepts being upset or having your assumptions contradicted, rather than holding a fixed position.
when: Receiving criticism of a design
why: Staying off balance lets new information change your view.

text: Designers may combine behavioral experiments with introspection and use whatever seems true in subjective experience, since they are not bound by scientific rigor.
when: Gathering evidence about player experience.
why: Designers need practical truth about experience rather than verifiable proof.

text: Partner with subject matter experts, who are often eager to share detail and help get the content right.
when: When the game's subject matter lies outside the team's own expertise.
why: Specialists have devoted careers to the topic and are keen to make sure every detail is correct.

text: Plausible causality, backed by reasoning about game systems and confounders, may be enough to act; verify the causal link when more certainty is needed.
when: Deciding whether to change a game based on a suspected cause.
why: Acting on a weak cause risks wasted or harmful changes.

text: Clear hypotheses save implementation and testing time and help anticipate the effects of behaviors and of their absence.
why: Building telemetry takes effort, so ranking hypotheses in advance focuses that work on what matters most.

text: Anger from hypersensitive testers flags imbalances and rough spots that disturb the flow of play, even when such testers are unpleasant to be around.
when: When a hypersensitive tester starts raging at the game during play.
why: Such testers react strongly to anything disrupting their experience, so they expose rough spots others miss.

text: Task analysis answers specific-task questions with time and error metrics; usability tests cover section-level usability with several participants; think-aloud shows first reactions one participant at a time.
when: Choosing among observational test methods
why: Each method captures a different level of player behavior.

text: Playthroughs assess engageability across a whole game and benefit from larger samples; surveys suit closed beta or testing with many respondents.
when: Choosing methods for run-level or large-audience feedback
why: Whole-game engagement and broad sampling need different scale than section tests.

text: Heuristic evaluation suits rough builds or when tests cannot be run; RITE suits rapid iteration on one narrow feature; personas suit conception and preproduction for team alignment.
when: Choosing methods for early or constrained stages
why: These methods work without full target-audience testing.

text: Lowering prevalence or raising the false-positive rate lowers the chance that a positive result is correct.
why: fewer true cases or more false alarms shift positives toward wrong results

text: Knowledge creation uses a deck of methods, including playtesting, brainstorming, discussion, debate and daydreaming, each with its own effect and resource cost.
when: As conditions of the project keep shifting, requiring continuous reaction.
why: Each method yields different outcomes and draws on different resources, so they trade off against each other.

text: Accepting the first plausible explanation of playtest data without checking other explanations.
why: Several explanations can fit the same numbers, so more data is needed to separate root causes.

text: A badly run playtest is worse than none, because it creates false knowledge, and its flaws often look smooth and are hard to notice.
why: Flawed protocols make sessions feel smooth and produce plausible-looking results, hiding the error.

text: Relying on one method alone misses what others reveal: analytics shows what happened, while tests explain why it happened.
when: Designing a research plan
why: Telemetry and observation answer different questions.

text: Omitting positive findings and fixed issues makes a UX report feel one-sided.
when: Writing a UX report
why: Balanced reporting keeps the team's trust and tracks progress.

text: Relying on gut instinct alone to find a structure that enables the intended experience leans heavily on luck.
when: Searching for a mechanic that produces a target feel
why: Without method, finding a working structure depends on chance.

text: Sloppy studies with loose protocols and small samples damage trust in the results.
why: Results from loose methods often fail to replicate, which signals weak methods and erodes public trust.

text: Falling in love with the game introduces bias into observation and interpretation.
when: When user researchers are embedded in the team building the game.
why: Attachment to the game can distort how researchers observe and interpret player behaviour.

text: Surveying only engaged beta testers misses players who left, so feedback can wrongly suggest that features like competition are unneeded.
when: when sampling only active or engaged players
why: players who churned are absent from the sample

text: Describing an idea as 'X mixed with Y' can signal that the idea has already been made.
when: Writing a one-liner description
why: Blended references suggest an existing product

text: Assuming a leader can capture and direct the team's knowledge through instructions alone leads to waste in creative work.
Useful signals are hard to extract from raw player telemetry, and improvised statistical feature crafting frequently degrades player-experience model performance.
when: When player-experience models take multi-modal inputs such as behaviour, physiology and game context.
why: Signals arrive as complex spatio-temporal patterns across modalities, which makes useful features hard to locate.

text: Few experimental studies exist, so the causal link between play and sleep remains unclear.
why: Observed associations are correlational, so the direction and mechanism of the effect remain uncertain.

text: 1) Define who the target players are. 2) Identify their skills and needs. 3) Build a process for recruiting them into playtesting. 4) Balance the game for them.
when: Before tuning a game for a specific audience
why: Balancing without a clear target produces a mismatched difficulty.

text: 1) Float the idea informally with the affected stakeholder to gauge reaction. 2) Ask a knowledgeable team member how feasible the change is. 3) Seek several outside opinions. 4) Decide once the knowledge gap has narrowed.
when: Uncertainty is high and premature commitment would be costly
why: Information gathered cheaply reduces the risk of a costly wrong decision.

text: 1) Set aside mechanics and ask which basic human needs the game serves. 2) Identify which Maslow levels it operates on. 3) Check whether it fills competence, autonomy and relatedness needs. 4) Ask how it could fill more basic needs. 5) For served needs, ask how to fill them better.
when: when evaluating a game's fit with player needs
why: Everything people do tries to meet basic needs, so a game must actually satisfy them rather than merely promise to.

text: 1) Pick a convenient population size. 2) Apply prevalence to get the affected group. 3) Apply sensitivity to find true positives. 4) Apply the false-positive rate to the unaffected group. 5) Divide true positives by all positives.
when: estimating what a positive result means
why: counting people avoids confusing conditional probabilities

text: 1) Review general theories and literature. 2) Make broad observations and define questions. 3) Form hypotheses. 4) Design a standardized experimental protocol. 5) Run the test. 6) Analyze results. 7) Confirm, reject, or refine the hypothesis, then return to theory.
why: Standardized measurement and analysis are meant to keep bias out of judging whether a proposed explanation holds.

text: 1) Define gameplay and business hypotheses and exploratory questions. 2) Map each to events to track. 3) Assign each question to user research or analytics. 4) Pick visualizations such as heatmaps, histograms or lines to fit each hypothesis.
why: Without predefined questions, searching a large body of data for a relevant pattern is nearly hopeless.

text: 1) Use analytics to locate problem spots at scale. 2) Use user research to explain why they occur.
why: User research alone cannot easily predict how much a lab-observed behavior matters for a larger audience; combining methods connects the two.

text: 1) Learn what the target audience already plays. 2) Observe them interacting with existing games and with each other. 3) Ask what they feel is missing.
when: When designing for a specific audience.
why: Observing real play grounds design in actual behavior and reveals unmet needs, unlike a focus group.

text: 1) Decide all research topics before production begins. 2) Split topics among team members, including non-writers such as artists. 3) Narrow research over time from general to specific subjects.
when: planning worldbuilding research
why: Assigning topics early keeps the research on schedule.

text: 1) Before sharing, write down your own perceived strengths and weaknesses, and keep the list private. 2) Share the work with reviewers without stating your view. 3) Compare their findings with your list and ask about anything they did not mention.
when: Before handing a design plan to reviewers for feedback
why: Stating your view first can influence reviewers.

text: 1) Check whether the study is correlational or experimental. 2) Note the number of participants and their ages. 3) Identify which game was used. 4) Identify what was measured.
when: when reading news reports of game research
why: A correlational design cannot establish causality, and missing details about design, sample, game and measures leave a study's conclusions unclear.

text: 1) Name the design question, such as which mechanics made a genre succeed. 2) Choose existing games in that genre. 3) Play them, noting which mechanics worked and why.
when: A specific design question needs answers from outside sources.

text: 1) Note how the experience made you feel. 2) Note what it made you think. 3) Note what it made you do.
when: Playing your own or others' games
why: These three responses break an experience into analyzable parts.

text: Playtest with people from the intended audience, such as buyers of similar games, not only the designer or friends, since they give more relevant and detailed feedback.
when: Balancing difficulty, pacing, or choice quality for a specific group
why: Insiders misjudge difficulty for players outside their circle.

text: User research and analytics both apply the scientific method with different tools; pair a researcher with a data analyst, or embed hybrid-skill researchers, so both drive decisions together.
why: Analytics supplies quantitative data from large samples playing in natural conditions, which complements the other method.

text: Treat a prototype as a hypothesis and accept results that contradict it, even when they are unwelcome.
why: Ideas fail when creators dismiss or rationalize unwelcome feedback, so validation must stay open to contrary results.

text: For a game built around an activity, study closely the preferences of players who already love that activity.
when: designing a game themed on a specific hobby or activity

text: Write down assumptions and purpose, then design the measurement to affirm or deny a stated hypothesis.
why: Statistics gathered without stated objectives are hard to read, so their value depends on knowing what is being tested.

text: The whole team should agree on the level of evidence rigor required before the project starts.
when: planning assessment of a transformational game
why: Different projects need different levels of proof

text: Researchers should give objective analysis based on data and scientific knowledge, not personal opinions or an agenda, so developers can decide.
why: Opinions or an agenda can bias findings and turn research into persuasion rather than reliable knowledge.

text: Keep the researcher embedded in the team for trust, but keep emotional distance from the game.
why: Growing attachment to the game could introduce bias, so the researcher must stay emotionally detached even while embedded.

text: Collect data tied to gameplay and business hypotheses; without hypotheses, finding a meaningful pattern is like searching for a needle in a haystack.
when: before deciding what to track
why: unfocused data hides the patterns that matter

text: Form strong hypotheses before reading live data, so results can be checked against predictions.
when: Live operation analytics

text: Research UX challenges of a new technology in scholarly databases and HCI papers, not only in LLM answers, which can be biased or misinformed.
when: when learning the UX challenges of a new technology
why: Generative models produce plausible-sounding answers that may be inaccurate or invented, so they are unreliable sources for UX research.

text: Study a topic thoroughly, gain hands-on experience with the mechanics you intend to simulate, and check whether any discovery could inspire a game idea.
when: Looking for game concepts rooted in real-world activity.
why: Firsthand knowledge reveals which details matter and which to drop, even if the final game is not meant to be realistic.

text: Frame user research as studying the product, not the people who use it.
why: The term suggests people are studied, but what is tested is the product, using a representative small sample.

text: Specify which game, genre, mode and play style a study examines, since video games are not one category.
when: when reporting or comparing game research
why: games vary widely in genre, mode and competitive or cooperative play

text: Playful learning experiences, where the learner makes something meaningful, are preferred over gamification and serious games that use the computer mainly to deliver lessons.
when: Deciding how to frame an educational or onboarding activity.
why: Learners who teach the system retain more meaningful understanding.

text: Rewards tied to output create perverse incentives: politics, gossip, hidden work, risk avoidance, and competition that suppresses idea sharing.
when: When rewards are linked to measured performance in a team.
why: People optimize for the reward rather than for the shared goal.

text: Critical failure risks are fatal flaws hidden in a project, such as severe bugs, unpredicted dominant strategies or narrative holes, that surface later like time bombs.
Common development disasters include a hard-to-fix degenerate strategy, an interface newcomers cannot understand, a sudden publisher change of direction, and the loss of a key programmer.
Use a clear dependency stack to limit how much of a project relies on immature designs, though it cannot remove immaturity burden entirely.
when: When organizing a project with interdependent work.
why: Reducing dependence on unfinished parts lowers exposure to their instability.

text: Each design element may change; a feature's odds of surviving unchanged roughly equal its own certainty times each foundation's certainty, so high-layer features rarely survive unchanged.
when: Planning features built on other systems; stacked designs with several dependency layers
why: A feature's survival depends on every foundation beneath it; each uncertain layer multiplies the risk, so odds fall quickly with depth.

text: Dismissing a risk because its chance per player is tiny can be a mistake when the player base is large.
when: When a game lets strangers communicate and its player base could reach millions.
why: Rare per-player events still occur many times over across a very large population, so tiny odds can produce real harm.

text: Dependency-based caution can look wasteful or irresponsible to colleagues who do not yet understand the dependency risk.
when: When marketing or business needs a detailed design decision very early in the dependency stack.
why: Early detailed decisions get reshaped by cascading changes, so locking them in early risks rework.

text: Small samples make significance hard to reach and conclusions unreliable; three testers make timing statistics nearly meaningless, while a few thousand make them much more reliable.
Logging input and system state every frame turns a vague complaint about controls into millisecond-level data on input and system output.
UX lab samples are rarely large enough for reliable statistics, so comparing conditions in a lab is difficult.
when: Analyzing results from small playtest groups
why: Few participants give wide uncertainty.

text: Use a line graph to compare two continuous values, or discrete values with a clear order such as months in sequence.
why: At this scale, a difference of one unit is negligible, so integer counts ordered in time behave as continuous.

text: Real innovation usually comes from long-term development and experimentation, not from the first spark of an idea.
why: Ongoing contact with players lets experimental ideas grow into playable forms instead of being judged in their earliest rough form.

text: Larger samples make groups match more closely, but they never match exactly and never remove the chance of a false difference.
why: Sampling randomness means no finite sample can rule out an extreme chance outcome entirely.

text: Working in isolation misses valuable context held by other teams.
when: When analysts work without coordinating with user research, the game team, or marketing

text: 1) Measure completion times and compute mean, median and standard deviation. 2) Compare mean with median to infer skew. 3) Inspect very fast and very slow outliers. 4) Generate several candidate explanations. 5) Test them in follow-up playtests.
when: Analyzing playtest completion times.
why: Statistics point to questions, not causes.

text: 1) Compute the probability of the observed streak. 2) If it is very small, check the random number generator for a fault before blaming chance.
when: evaluating a suspiciously long run of failures

text: 1) For each player, draw a finish turn from the single-player finish distribution. 2) Sort the draws to rank finishers. 3) Repeat many trials and average the placements.
when: Estimating multiplayer race outcomes from single-player finish distributions.
why: Independent per-player draws reproduce the race without storing the joint state.

text: 1) Give a standardized pre-test of the target skill. 2) Train the experimental group on the target game and the control group on another game. 3) Give a post-test to both groups.
when: when testing whether a game changes skills
why: Comparing change against a control shows whether training caused the gain.

text: Add testers when a result is suggestive but not significant; more data points shrink the standard error, so the same difference becomes more statistically significant.
when: After a small playtest shows a time gain that could be random noise
why: Larger samples narrow the standard error and improve significance.

text: Surveys, closed beta telemetry, and A/B tests with larger samples need a defined acceptable uncertainty level before analysis.
when: Analyzing results from large samples
why: Without a set threshold, conclusions become arbitrary.

text: For hundreds or thousands of respondents use seven-point Likert scales; for smaller samples five points are enough.
when: Choosing Likert scale length
why: Larger samples support finer distinctions.

text: Check whether a sample is representative; a closed beta group is often self-selected and more extreme than the mainstream audience.
when: when generalizing from a beta or small sample
why: self-selection skews opinions and behavior

text: A 15-participant task test gives stronger evidence but is slow for quick prototypes; a smaller sample is faster but gives weaker evidence.
when: when prototyping quickly
why: Game development's tight schedules, especially on time, stop teams from recruiting large enough samples for every quick test.

text: Without a shared reference, team members interpret the game in their own ways, so their work may fail to integrate, such as art built to unusable specs.
when: Team members lack a common design document
why: Each discipline fills gaps with its own assumptions.

text: Shared online documents have become the usual way to draft and revise game design documents.
Teams and studios use the usability and engageability framework to create a common language across roles.
Broad design pillars rather than exhaustive lists help design teams share a common language.
When everyone shares an understanding of the design, small implementation decisions by programmers, artists, and executives reinforce it and unify the project.
when: When much of production work involves small unplanned choices made by non-designers

text: Shared documents let more people examine the design sooner, so weaknesses are found and fixed faster.
when: As soon as a design decision is written down for others to review

text: Trusting a friend not to repeat details of unreleased work is a mistake, because leaks can happen by accident and the writer who shared it is responsible.
when: sharing an unreleased script outside the team
why: Even well-meaning readers can slip up without meaning to, and sending the script outside the company already breaches the NDA.

text: Share ideas with the rest of the team as soon as the core team reaches consensus, rather than waiting for a later milestone.
Within a studio, agree on shared production terms so that the same term means the same thing to everyone.
why: Shared vocabulary lets communication flow horizontally across teams and studios.

text: Describe the game as shared work by saying 'we' rather than 'I' when you speak.
Software can reveal emergent behavior that is hard to see when tracking many interacting systems by hand.
when: a game has many interacting systems
why: Computers track bookkeeping that overwhelms manual tracking.

text: Stable toolchains let artists and designers create content and insert it into the game without manual help from engineers.
Because all checks run in one location, it is easy to log every check and its result.
Building effective concatenation systems is complex, so better synthesis and processing tools are needed to reduce repetitive recording work.
Developers often keep cheat codes in final releases so players can experiment with situations that would otherwise be impossible.
Larger storage media raised player expectations for graphics, sound, and gameplay, which raised production costs.
why: Buyers expect content that uses newer hardware's features, and larger storage makes that content costlier to build.

text: Waiting for full console builds to test each AI change greatly slows iteration.
when: When developing AI on consoles that have long turnaround times
why: Each console round trip adds time, whereas a PC setup can compile and test tweaks without a full game build.

text: Character-specific code slows level creation and limits how much AI code can be reused between projects.
when: When using advanced AI techniques that need character-specific programming
why: These techniques are hard to map into level editing tools, which favor letting designers change data over code.

text: Outside code holding a persistent pointer into an alternating buffer can silently refer to the other buffer after a swap.
when: Buffers are swapped by pointer and alternate each frame
why: Pointers still refer to the buffer's old address, which now holds the other frame's data.

text: Sleeping only pads frames that finish early; a frame that overruns its budget produces negative sleep time and the game slows down.
when: A frame takes longer than its time budget
why: Sleeping cannot shorten work already done.

text: 1) Add input fields for character and monster stats, formatted so users see they can change them. 2) Add output fields showing the combat outcome. 3) Run the simulator at points flagged as very fast or very slow and compare with prior intuition.
when: When testing combat pacing at spots earlier marked as unusually quick or unusually slow

text: 1) Make a significant change to the properties, behaviors, or relationships of core objects. 2) Play and check whether balance changed and the game is still playable. 3) If playable, repeat with another change. 4) When unplayable, identify the crucial change that broke it and explain why.
when: Stress-testing a game's rule system
why: Stepwise changes isolate which rule carries the system's balance.

text: 1) Write a script that covers the most needed words. 2) Record those words in the least recording time.
when: Planning a concatenation recording session

text: 1) Choose a meaningful goal for the learner. 2) Break the goal into a sub-task the learner must first solve. 3) Let the learner program that sub-task through trial and error. 4) Reuse the solved sub-task to reach the larger goal.
when: Designing learning activities where a complex result is built from simpler verified parts.
why: Building up from solved parts makes the underlying principles, such as the geometry of a square, discoverable through mistakes and successes.

text: 1) Load the relevant existing code into your head. 2) Decide on a solution. 3) Write the code. 4) Clean up. Then repeat for the next change.
when: each code change
why: The existing code's behavior must be understood before any change, and gathering that context is often the slowest step.

text: 1) Measure the code with timers to find slow sections. 2) Profile those sections for cache misses with a cache-aware profiler. 3) Restructure data only if misses are confirmed as the bottleneck.
when: Deciding whether to apply data locality changes
why: Timers show slowness but not cause, and restructuring without evidence adds complexity

text: Run the game in demo mode continuously for days to expose creeping fragmentation or leaks, which commonly cause long-run failures.
when: Validating long-running stability before release.
why: Long-run failures appear only after extended operation.

text: Build cheat codes that disable hidden systems or grant extreme resources to test specific situations, such as monitoring AI behind fog of war.
when: prototyping and testing
why: They isolate systems that are hard to observe under normal play.

text: Give QA the information a complete test plan needs, because a design document alone does not give them full understanding of the game.
when: When handing a design to QA so they can write a test plan

text: Copy the next buffer into the current buffer when state is small and outside code holds pointers that must stay valid.
when: State is small and pointers into it must remain valid
why: Copying a small value costs little and keeps the current buffer no more than one frame old.

text: When no reliable instrument exists for measuring what you need, build your own test apparatus.
when: When no supplier or existing research offers the control tools needed
why: Full-size trial and error was expensive, so a cheaper test rig was built to gather data.

text: Processing dirty data at natural checkpoints, such as docking or loading screens, hides the work and gives timing control, but checkpoints can be missed if the player never reaches them.
when: The game has natural pauses where work can be hidden.
why: Missed checkpoints defer work longer than planned.

text: Scientific management, or Taylorism, concentrates all planning in a few minds and trains workers to execute prescribed methods exactly.
Winston Royce's foundational paper on software development emphasized iteration and returning to earlier steps, and it never used the word waterfall.
Scrum suits game development because fluid change helps solve hard design problems.
Scrum organizes work into small cross-functional teams that set priorities every day and iterate in short cycles.
A tool can introduce design problems the designer does not notice, and skill can offset a weak tool but a poorly designed tool still holds back strong designers.
In a cost-curve sheet, any column that is not a core stat is a mechanic, such as keywords, unit classes, unit abilities or feats.
Google Sheets Insert Comment records the author's name, has a Resolve button and supports threaded replies, so teams can discuss a cell in a shared sheet.
when: Collaborating on a shared online spreadsheet.
why: Comments are built for team questions rather than static notes.

text: Spreadsheets are often both code and user interface and are shared directly as the deliverable, so format them clearly for readers, since clear presentation saves considerable time.
when: When a spreadsheet is shared with others who read it directly rather than running it
why: They exist to communicate calculation results to the author or team.

text: Prefer offline learning when results must be tested exhaustively or when reproducibility matters.
when: choosing a learning mode
why: Processing recorded data before release lets risky learning methods be checked thoroughly, whereas behavior that keeps changing during play is hard to reproduce.

text: Generate balance tables in a spreadsheet and enter manual inputs in separate marked cells to reduce input errors.
when: Building numeric tables
why: Generated values stay consistent when inputs change.

text: Build heat maps with a custom tool connected to the game engine, since spreadsheets handle them poorly.
when: Showing where events occur across a level map

text: Split complex formulas into simpler intermediate calculation cells, which makes the sheet easier to troubleshoot.
why: Also makes the logic easier for another person to follow.

text: A 10-hour, 30-level game needs about 15 stages, since adjacent stages overlap to give about 29 effective challenge stages, and at least 45 enemy configurations, about three per stage.
when: As a starting point for a 10-hour, 30-level RPG.
why: Adjacent stages overlap, so fewer stages are needed.

text: Hiding rows and columns can conceal content without making it obvious that anything is hidden.
when: Managing large design spreadsheets
why: Hidden data is easy to forget and hard to notice

text: Hand calculation mistakes happen even when the code is bug-free, and wrong statistics can look plausible.
when: When computing statistics by hand instead of through code
why: statistics offers few built-in sanity checks

text: Offline pipelines that need long post-processing of huge log files are impractical.
why: Offline learning depends on game data being readily available in a usable format, which digging through huge logs does not provide.

text: Copying, pasting, or referencing ranges that cross unnoticed hidden rows or columns can give unexpected results and errors that are hard to trace.
why: Hidden rows or columns are easy to overlook, since only tiny arrows and a gap in lettering reveal them.

text: 1) Lay out the spreadsheet with the technical team so it mirrors the game's systems. 2) Give each subsystem, such as combat, economy, or social systems, its own interconnecting tables. 3) Apply purity of purpose and modularity to each table. 4) Use the sheet to start the design and to refine and perfect gameplay.
when: Organizing design data
why: A mirrored layout eases communication with programmers.

text: To reference a cell on another sheet, write the sheet name, an exclamation point and the cell address, such as =Weapons!B5. Or: 1) Type = in the target cell. 2) Click the other sheet's tab. 3) Click the source cell. 4) Press Enter.
when: When cells must draw on another worksheet in the same file rather than a separate file
why: Referencing within one file is much easier than linking to a separate document.

text: 1) Create one worksheet per purpose, such as stats, weapons, armor, or level curve. 2) Rename each tab to describe its contents. 3) Keep related groups in one document so cells can reference each other.
when: Organizing game design data that has several related but distinct tables
why: Separate tabs are easier to navigate than hidden rows and columns, which can conceal content unnoticed

text: 1) Watch one playtester on one level. 2) Count the events of interest by hand, such as deaths. 3) Compare the manual count with the count the software reports.
when: validating analytics output
why: reveals collection errors

text: 1) Create the audio package and add subgroups to organise assets. 2) Import sounds. 3) Store the package via the context-menu Save option or with Ctrl+S before using the sounds.

1) Give each line a row with character, line ID, actor, location, context, inflection, effect, filename, take number and keeper flag. 2) Tag lines by mission, area and character, using generic for ambient lines. 3) Mark good takes as keepers during the session.
when: Tracking dialogue through recording and integration
why: A structured record makes lines searchable and avoids searching raw takes later

text: 1) Make a time column in seconds starting at zero. 2) Add gold, unit count, income and next-cost columns. 3) Set each row's gold and counts from the previous row and its purchases. 4) Fill rows down to the horizon.
when: simulating an idle game in a spreadsheet

text: 1) Write a solver or simulation that picks moves randomly weighted by a candidate strategy and current state. 2) Have candidate strategies play many thousands of games against each other. 3) Compare results and discuss why winners won.
when: Testing candidate strategies for an intransitive game
why: Simulated play exposes which strategies outperform others

text: 1) Click the row or column headings to select them. 2) Right-click the selection. 3) Choose Hide Rows or Hide Columns. 4) To reveal hidden cells, click the small arrow in the header.
when: When a shared sheet shows a final result while helper data columns sit beside it
why: Helper data beside a final result could confuse a reader, so hiding it keeps the view clean.

text: 1) Select the cells holding formulas. 2) Copy them. 3) Paste Special, then Values, into the same cells. 4) Recalculate. The cells keep their current numbers and no longer change.
when: you need a fixed snapshot of generated or random data
why: Formulas recalculate and pasted values do not, so frozen data stays stable

text: Test number-heavy mechanics in a spreadsheet that embeds the game logic, so many rule permutations can be checked quickly.
when: the question is mostly arithmetic and rule permutations

text: Generate AI knowledge offline from raw level information when levels change often and the run-time processing budget is limited.
when: Levels change often and run-time processing budget is limited.
why: Run-time processing is scarce, and generating the knowledge automatically avoids hand-supplied data that hampers reuse and quick level edits.

text: Keep purchase amounts in their own input columns, so different buying strategies can be tested without rewriting the simulation formulas.
when: building a spreadsheet simulation to compare strategies

text: Plot several discrete series on one line graph, with one line per series, to show their differences or similarities.
when: When categorical values are arranged on a scale with an obvious sequence, such as time order

text: If data must be hidden, move intermediate values to a separate worksheet and reference them from formulas instead.
when: hidden data cannot be avoided
why: keeps working values out of view while formulas still reach them

text: Remove noise, meaning unnecessary elements, to focus on core pillars and improve usability.
why: Excess features can erode a player's sense of agency, which may drive them away from the game.

text: Perform the buffer swap at the end of a display refresh, so the whole frame appears at once.
when: Presenting double-buffered graphics on a refreshing display
why: Swapping mid-refresh shows part of the old frame and part of the new, causing tearing.

text: Connecting the editor over a network to the running game gives direct manipulation and instant testing, but takes significant effort and some platforms make it harder.
when: When AI with many tunable parameters needs heavy tweaking on a console build

text: Cleaning a dirty flag on demand avoids unused calculation but may cause a noticeable pause when the work is slow.
when: Deciding to process flagged data only when its result is used.
why: Work happens at use time, so slow work lands on the user-facing path.

text: Harder tools require cross-disciplinary knowledge, but learning them builds new skills and respect for colleagues' work.
when: When making a first game in tools that demand cross-disciplinary knowledge

text: Even when clients expect designers to be the experts, they typically have firm views on how the title ought to look, behave and play.
when: When an outside client pays for the game rather than it being a hobby project.
why: Clients fund the project, so they feel entitled to shape how it looks, behaves and plays.

text: Clients do not always tell the truth about their motives, so asking is only a starting point for understanding what they want.
why: People carry layered desires, from what they say to what they think and feel deep down, so stated answers can miss the real want.

text: Designers often must satisfy a client, such as a publisher, rights holder or non-expert buyer, as well as their team and players.
How a designer handles the client affects the client relationship, the designer's reputation, the designer's happiness, and the quality of the game.
Clients offer more than funding, including connections, business expertise and insight into the audience.
A client who knew exactly what they wanted would already have the design, so clarifying their wishes is part of the designer's job.
Competing demands are common: publishing may want monetization events, researchers may flag retention problems, and developers may want more features before a deadline.
One company can act as both publisher and developer, which makes the publisher-developer relationship easy to confuse.
A publisher's success can rest on one flagship franchise developed in-house.
Non-developer clients may not know specialized roles such as systems designer or character rigger.
Clients often want ownership of the work; giving them a real creative role keeps them supportive of the project.
why: A client who helped shape the work will defend it when others criticize it.

text: When a client's concern comes from how the work looks to them, letting them help adjust it can satisfy them more than explaining the technical reason.
when: When a client objects to how the work looks from where they stand.
why: Their stated complaint may hide deeper desires, so a lesson on the technical cause would not address them.

text: Designers should come to know the client better than the client knows themselves, much as they know their audience.
why: If the client already knew exactly what they wanted, the design would already exist, so helping them find it is part of the job.

text: Learn a client's real goals by asking whether they want quick money or a reputation, whether the market is new or existing, and what they think makes a good game.
Designers benefit from understanding the concerns of executives and marketing staff, even when they are not in negotiations.
when: When the designer is not part of the deal-making process.
why: Knowing business constraints lets a designer speak clearly to executives and marketing and see how deals shape design.

text: Early involvement in development builds the knowledge needed later to write pitches for missions and quests.
when: When a junior writer is not yet trusted with high-level pitch work.
why: Giving feedback on early concepts builds the skills needed when the writer's own pitch turn arrives.

text: Removing a feature that fans already anticipate, or that appears in tie-in media, meets resistance from fans and stakeholders.
when: a feature is publicly known or promoted
why: audience expectations and existing material make removal costly

text: Relying on email alone can mean messages never get read, so decisions and questions go unanswered.
why: Talking in person lets you clarify questions and check understanding, which a message alone may not achieve.

text: When a client cannot say what they want, help them discover it rather than offering endless guesses. 1) Ask what kind of result they want. 2) Ask what it will be used for. 3) Use that purpose to choose a strong candidate and check it with the client.
when: When the client is unsure of the specifics or cannot describe the result they want
why: Helping the client work out what they need is design work in itself, and it educates the client at the same time.

text: 1) Note what the client says they want. 2) Note what they think they want. 3) Work out what they really want deep down.
when: Before proposing a new idea to a client, or when making a game for someone else

text: 1) Ask the report readers what information they need and what they do not need yet. 2) Involve stakeholders in preparing the test, which builds relevance and trust.
when: before running a user research test
why: The more stakeholders take part in preparing the test, the more relevant the feedback becomes and the more trust is built.

text: Clients fund the project and may take work elsewhere or end it if their wishes go unmet, so listen deeply to learn what they really want.
when: Working with a paying client
why: Stated requests can hide the real need.

text: Align business and design goals before giving UX recommendations, because developers, publishers and executives may hold different targets.
when: when stakeholders have different goals, such as a hardcore title versus a mainstream freemium title
why: Recommendations must account for both business and design goals.

text: Define exactly what you need before contractors start, because time spent working out their task wastes paid hours.
when: When hiring short-term contract specialists who bill by the hour or day.

text: Make stakeholders understand that prototype code which looks like it works may still be unmaintainable and need rewriting.
when: When throwaway prototype code is requested and may later be kept.
why: Stakeholders may treat a prototype as finished once it appears to work.

text: Keep cold contact with consultants short, to the point, and respectful of their time, and thank them again if they decline or do not reply.
when: approaching outside experts
why: Experts are often willing to help but value their time.

text: Pay consultants appropriately through in-game credits, a copy of the game, or actual payment, and never take advantage of consultants who help for free.
when: engaging subject-matter consultants
why: Fair treatment keeps experts willing to help.

text: Consult the client directly and early, even when they already work with a development team, since you may be their first narrative contact.
