when: When a non-developer client hires a narrative designer at any point in development.
why: Narrative designers often wear several hats, so they may be the client's first point of contact.

text: Prepare the client for testing early, because you may not be present when QA begins.
When several stakeholders request work that cannot all fit before a deadline, a shared UX strategy ranks tasks by their impact on the whole experience.
when: Several stakeholders request work before a deadline
why: Shared awareness of tradeoffs, with tasks ranked by their effect on the overall player experience, gets the most value from limited time.

text: Consistent wrong answers on the test set suggest too few training examples or examples that are not varied enough.
when: Network is evaluated on held-out scenarios.
why: Matching outputs on unseen examples signal genuine learning, so persistent misses point to gaps in what the network was trained on.

text: The mean is the sum of all values divided by the number of values, and it approaches the expected value with many samples.
Standard deviation measures how spread out data is around its mean; larger values mean the data is more scattered.
Metrics are measurements, often called KPIs, that report what changed in a game.
Verified causality changes the suspected root cause and watches the correlate, either prospectively by changing then observing, or retrospectively by checking past events.
when: Confirming a suspected cause of a metric change.
why: Only a deliberate change or historical check separates cause from correlation.

text: Statistical significance is the minimum confidence required before concluding that two data sets truly differ.
A null hypothesis states that the tested variable has no impact on the outcome.
About half of the values in a data set fall below the median and half above it.
Validated engagement questionnaires include PXI, FSS, GEQ, IEQ, and PENS; GEQ, IEQ, and PENS converge considerably.
when: Choosing an existing questionnaire
why: Validated instruments avoid designing unreliable items from scratch.

text: Confidence in a finding grows with a sustained trend, a longer observation period, a larger data set and a larger effect.
when: Deciding how much to trust an observed pattern.
why: More data and longer duration reduce the chance the pattern is random.

text: Standard error shrinks as the amount of data grows.
Statistical conclusions carry a built-in chance of error that more data reduces but never eliminates.
A null result can itself be a scientific achievement.
Keeping 30% of users active on day two is regarded as an excellent result in mobile games.
Dividing a follow-on's count by the window total gives a probability that can estimate how accurate a prediction is likely to be.
Strong agreement between the model's ranking and real play increases confidence that the cost curve is reasonably accurate.
when: When comparing a card cost model against real-world play, tier lists, tournament decks and prices.

text: When the median exceeds the mean, most players take longer than the mean suggests, and the level probably runs long.
when: Completion-time distributions.
why: A few fast finishers pull the mean below the typical time.

text: Playtesting and metrics can reveal the effects of small changes on player feeling, but the inner mechanism causing the feeling stays hidden.
why: Emotional triggers are automatic and unconscious, so players cannot report which cause produced a feeling.

text: A very small effect, such as a win-rate shift of a few thousandths of a percent, is probably noise and smaller than the system's random variation.
when: Judging whether a measured change matters.
why: Tiny differences are usually within normal random fluctuation.

text: A Z test is a good starting point for statistical significance but not always the right test; chi-squared and ANOVA are other common choices, each suited to different data.
when: Choosing a significance test for game metrics.
why: Different tests fit different data types and assumptions.

text: Aim for heuristic estimates close to the true cost but slightly below it.
Use a random comparand or the median of a small sample, such as three keys, to greatly improve the worst case while barely changing the average.
when: Choosing a quicksort comparand.
why: Sampling makes consistently bad splits unlikely.

text: A few extreme values pull the mean toward them while the median barely moves, so a large gap between mean and median signals skew or outliers.
when: reading a data set's shape
why: Extreme points exert a much stronger pull on the arithmetic average than on the middle value, so a gap between the two signals them.

text: Large-scale play data surfaces rare degenerate strategies that small internal playtests miss, since one player in a million produces a visible spike.
when: Public betas or large player populations.
why: Rare behavior is statistically invisible in small samples.

text: A common significance standard requires about 95% confidence that a change is not random variation, accepting at most a 5% chance of a wrong conclusion.
when: setting a significance bar
why: A lower bar produces false trends, while a higher bar throws away real ones.

text: In roughly bell-shaped data, about two-thirds of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean and well over 90% within two.
when: data is roughly normal

text: A 95% confidence interval is the usual research minimum; an 80% interval can justify an internal default despite not passing research standards.
when: Deciding how strict a comparison must be
why: Looser thresholds suit fast internal decisions where some uncertainty is acceptable.

text: MAU/DAU equals MAU divided by the mean of the month's DAU values. It ranges from 1, when everyone logs in daily, to about 28–31, when each player logs in once in the month.
when: Measuring how often the average player returns.
why: It shows typical login frequency in a single number.

text: The null hypothesis is rejected when significance tests show results are unlikely under it, typically at 95% confidence or higher.
when: After results are analyzed and significance tests show the findings are unlikely under the null.
why: Results that would be very improbable if the variable had no effect give grounds to drop the no-effect claim.

text: A confidence interval shows how much uncertainty the data contains around an estimate.
when: Comparing averages of two groups whose members vary widely within each group.

text: A Markov process is conservative when every row of its transition matrix sums to 1.
With 1000 random pairs the correlation is usually under about 0.05, while with 10 pairs its size can exceed 0.8.
when: Random independent data in a spreadsheet.

text: A visible improvement in a mean is not enough on its own; sample size determines whether it is statistically significant.
when: When comparing a new sample's mean against an established prior mean.
why: Small samples can show differences that are just random variation.

text: Relying only on mean, median and standard deviation can hide very different data shapes, including curves and outliers.
when: When a data set is curved or contains outliers and only summary numbers are checked.
why: Distinct data sets can share the same means, spreads and correlation, so summary numbers cannot tell them apart.

text: Assuming the most obvious causal link without additional evidence leads to wrong conclusions.
when: When a strong correlation is found between two measured things.
why: Statistics alone cannot reveal direction or cause, and reverse or third-factor explanations fit the same numbers.

text: A result not significant at 95% does not prove no difference; the sample may simply be too small to detect one.
when: Interpreting small-sample comparisons
why: Lack of significance reflects limited data, not confirmed equality.

text: Statistics can mislead, so designer judgment is still needed when interpreting measured results.
when: When a large volume of quantitative gameplay data has been collected.
why: Without knowing how to read the figures, measurements deliver little value, so tests should target defined questions.

text: Noise can look like a meaningful pattern, so a critical check for statistical significance must precede any design decision.
when: when interpreting analytics results
why: Random variation can produce apparent trends that do not reflect real player behavior.

text: Focusing on money ignores whether players enjoy the game, whether it enriches or harms their lives, and whether they are burning out.
when: When relying on revenue and download metrics to guide design.
why: Revenue-style figures cannot reveal whether players enjoy the game or whether it harms them.

text: Treating a tiny sample's average as a trend is a mistake; if only a couple of players out of millions do something, their average says little.
when: Reading results from very few data points.
why: Small samples are dominated by outliers and chance.

text: Probability answers can feel intuitively right and still be wrong, so verify them with explicit calculation or simulation.
when: When reasoning about probabilities in games with random mechanics.
why: Randomness is counterintuitive, so a confident probability answer can still be wrong.

text: Using cumulative probability directly as the per-transition figure gives wrong results; subtract the previous value first.
when: When reading cumulative probabilities of reaching a final state across turns.
why: The cumulative figure includes mass that arrived in earlier steps, so that earlier mass must be removed.

text: 1) Compute standard error by taking the spread and dividing it by sqrt(n). 2) Compute z as sample mean minus established mean, divided by standard error. 3) Convert z to a probability using a normal table or cumulative distribution function.
when: Comparing a small playtest mean against a large baseline or established mean.
why: The z test shows whether an observed difference is likely real.

text: 1) Compile and analyze notes from all sessions. 2) Compare each variant with the original design. 3) Record how each change affected the player experience. 4) Decide which changes to make based on the sessions. 5) Check whether the notes support firm conclusions.
when: When comparing rule variants of a game through playtest sessions.
why: Changes to system variables directly shape play, and only playtesting reveals how.

text: 1) Sort the values from smallest to largest. 2) Take the middle value. 3) If the count is even, average the two middle values.
why: Half of the values fall on each side of the middle value, so it marks the midpoint of the ranking.

text: 1) Compute the mean. 2) Subtract it from each value and square the result. 3) Average the squared differences. 4) Take the square root of that average.
when: When two data sets share a mean but differ in how spread out their values are.
why: Averages alone cannot tell tight clustering from wide scatter.

text: 1) Make a design change 2) Watch a chosen metric 3) Keep the change if the metric improves 4) Undo it if the metric worsens 5) Repeat the cycle
when: Tuning a game by metric response
why: Metrics respond to player behavior that a change causes only indirectly, so the reason for a movement stays unknown.

text: 1) Compute the analytic answer. 2) Check it with a Monte Carlo simulation. 3) Investigate any disagreement.
when: When an exact probability for a game of chance is calculated by hand.
why: Double-counting is an easy error in hand-calculated probabilities.

text: 1) Add one rule with input randomness and one with output randomness triggered by player moves. 2) Play a matched series: unmodified, each rule alone, and both. 3) Rank which variant is most interesting, most skill-based and most luck-based, and explain why.
when: testing how randomness types affect perceived skill

text: 1) Compute an expected value with a Markov chain. 2) Check it with a Monte Carlo simulation. 3) Confirm it with an algebraic solution of the recursion.
when: Validating a probability or expected-value result from a chain model.
why: Three independent methods agreeing gives confidence in the result.

text: 1) Code each category outcome as 1 or 0. 2) Compute the sample mean, which equals the proportion, and the standard deviation. 3) Apply a Z test against the reference proportion.
when: comparing a category share, such as gender, against a known benchmark
why: Z tests need numeric data, and 0/1 coding turns a category into a proportion.

text: 1) Compute the probability that the observed difference arises by chance. 2) Set a confidence bar. 3) Declare a difference only if its confidence clears that bar.
when: deciding whether a playtest or analytics change is real
why: Random variation can always make distinct data sets look similar, so the analysis always carries some chance of being wrong.

text: 1) Record events such as position, health, time, and key actions. 2) Aggregate many sessions. 3) Graph results to find problem areas.
when: Tuning balance and pacing with play data.
why: Aggregated graphs reveal patterns single sessions hide.

text: Verify statistical results with several independent methods rather than trusting a single calculation.
when: When the expected answer of a statistical analysis is not known in advance
why: Probability has built-in sanity checks, such as values outside 0 to 1, but statistics offers no such signal for wrong answers.

text: The z test needs an established mean from prior data; when comparing two data sets, treat one as the baseline and the other as the new sample.
when: When a z test compares a new sample against a mean that must already exist
why: The z-score measures how far the new sample's mean deviates from the reference mean, relative to standard error, so a reference is required.

text: Use the z test only for roughly normal data and avoid it for strongly non-normal distributions, such as flat single-die roll results.
when: When the underlying data is roughly bell-curve shaped, as most real-world behavior tends to be
why: The z test assumes the data comes from a normal distribution, so results are unreliable when that assumption fails.

text: Use hard metrics to compare timing and performance between playtests, and soft metrics to judge whether players are actually enjoying themselves.
why: Soft metrics combine into an evolving, shared sense of what playing the game is like for players, which hard numbers do not capture.

text: Do not substitute trial-and-error metric chasing for understanding the system behind the numbers.
why: Blind metric chasing makes each change a guess, reveals nothing about the system, and incremental tweaks can trap the design at a local maximum.

text: Before relying on a spreadsheet method, rebuild a known published result with it and confirm the numbers match.
why: Matching a trusted result confirms the method works before using it on new problems

text: A confidence bar set too low produces many false trends, while a bar set too high discards genuine trends.
when: choosing a confidence threshold

text: Demanding higher confidence requires much larger samples, which many developers cannot collect, so 95% is a practical balance.
when: planning playtest or analytics sample sizes

text: Specialized media contractors include writers, sound designers, musicians, motion-capture operators, martial arts instructors, and dialogue coaches.
Studios often kept AI techniques secret, and developers adapt the same algorithm differently, so implementations are hard to recognize across studios.
Most studios start as small groups of friends who worked or studied together, and many never move past the concept stage.
Few teams win a production deal and fewer still produce a hit; small studios with only one or two games often close after a dry spell.
why: They lack a financial cushion for unexpected costs

text: Talent from a closed developer often reappears at another company under a new name, and a successful developer may be bought outright by a publisher.
Have studio leaders co-lead training so that local leaders can carry the practice forward.
when: When a team must form new long-standing working habits
why: Habits come from engaging hands-on sessions that fit the local culture, not from handouts and lectures.

text: Presentation tips apply to small internal pitches as well as formal presentations.
when: Presenting to a small internal group
why: The same listening patterns apply

text: Committing money you expect from a deal before it is paid is risky.
when: While a publisher deal is still pending and no final contract has been signed
why: The publisher may still cancel the project at the final contract stage for internal reasons.

text: Define the studio's creative vision along with its impact on user experience.
Assess the game's environmental impact and work to reduce carbon emissions, using external sustainability initiatives for guidance.
Studios with no budget may rely on internal testers, which accepts higher bias in exchange for feedback.
when: Studios lacking budget for external testing
why: Internal testers are cheaper but see the game differently from players.

text: 1) Measure the share of follow-up hits landed on stunned opponents. 2) Count stuns per matchup. 3) Measure how often each move starts a combo. 4) Compare these against win rate before changing values.
when: Suspecting a stun-and-combo pattern is causing a play-experience problem.
why: These checks confirm whether the pattern, not raw strength, drives the problem.

text: Keep surveys short and wording simple, and show a progress bar, since people tune out near the end.
when: Designing a player survey
why: Short, clear surveys reduce drop-off and confusion.

text: Use precise, objective survey questions without leading wording, since leading questions bias answers.
when: When writing player surveys
why: Leading wording skews responses.

text: Players probe a game world thoroughly, testing every action and response, so rules must hold up under free exploration rather than a fixed path.
when: In a game where players can freely explore every action and response in the world
why: People are highly skilled at perceiving their surroundings, so any tiny inconsistency becomes glaring to them.

text: The wording of a question about an event changes the details people report, such as estimates that differ between two verbs.
when: When asking people to report details of an event they witnessed
why: Wording pushes the answer toward the implied framing

text: Player experience can be elicited by many game parts through short- and long-term interaction with core elements, including game content, mechanics, narrative, rewards, audiovisuals, camera and effects.
Free or cheap online survey tools are easy to set up for playtest surveys.
A small number of user selections is enough to capture a user's taste in an adaptive aesthetic model, which reduces fatigue.
Player questionnaires can include tick boxes or multiple choice, free-text answers, player experience instruments such as the Game Experience Questionnaire, demographics, and personality traits.
Lower the selection burden in interactive evolution by using a five-star or like/dislike scale or pairwise rankings instead of detailed ratings.
when: When interactive evolution uses large populations that leave the user waiting long stretches
why: Fewer rating levels reduce the cognitive load of each evaluation, so the user can rate content more easily.

text: Prefer a five-level scale with explicit wording like awful, poor, mediocre, fine, and superb over a one-through-ten numeric rating.
why: Each point on a clearly labeled five-point scale is explicit, which yields more consistent responses than an open one-to-ten range.

text: The effort a player puts toward a game's objective is a measure of how involved that player is.
why: Without an objective the experience loses its structure, so the effort a player directs toward it reflects how involved they are.

text: Interactive evolution fitness can come from a like/dislike choice or a 1-to-5 star rating.
why: The player's feedback on each generated item is used directly as the fitness that drives the evolutionary search.

text: Survey data is not truly scientific, and testers tend to make up answers when unsure, so do not treat it as gospel.
Survey respondents may let a chatbot write open-ended answers, which undermines research into how players actually feel.
when: When collecting open-ended player feedback.
why: Chatbots can be prompted to write survey answers, so open-ended responses may be machine-generated rather than the player's own feelings.

text: Analysing rating-based questionnaire data after the fact is unreliable because the data carries several critical biases.
Ask for the top three favorite and least favorite things, and ask how the player would describe the game to a friend.
when: Ending a player survey
why: These prompts surface priorities and framing in players' own words.

text: 1) Match survey answers to gameplay data. 2) Keep respondent identity confidential. 3) Read which players do what and what they liked or found confusing.
when: where confidentiality allows
why: Pairing stated reactions with logged actions lets designers connect each player's comments to what that player actually did.

text: 1) What do your players generally like? 2) What do they dislike, and why? 3) What do they expect in a game? 4) If you stood in their place, what would you want to see? 5) What would they like or dislike about your game?
why: Designers should keep the player in view and advocate for them, so questions probe the player's perspective.

text: Use pictures of game elements or scenes in surveys so players know exactly what you mean.
when: When questions refer to specific game components or in-game locations.
why: A picture pins down the referent so respondents interpret the question as the designer intended.

text: Hand out the survey right after play, while the experience is fresh.
why: Players' memory of the session is fresher then, so their answers reflect the experience itself.

text: Have someone available to answer testers' clarifying questions during the survey.
Record each tester's age and gender so you can check whether they relate to opinions.
Ask one question at a time and avoid combined items such as clear and powerful, and avoid leading questions by using open-ended prompts.
when: Writing survey items for UX research
why: Combined or leading items produce ambiguous answers.

text: Ask why as well as whether, and ask objective questions such as what a tutorial taught rather than whether it was clear.
when: Designing survey questions about experience
why: Reasons and objective recall are more informative than yes-or-no ratings.

text: Build survey items from the engageability pillars, covering compulsion, mastery, control, meaningful choices, and perceived progress.
when: Writing engagement survey items
why: Pillar-based items measure the experience the design targets.

text: Design each test to answer one specific question, and invent new test methods or apparatus when existing ones cannot answer it.
when: Solving a hard problem through experiments.
why: Many targeted tests, each answering one question, let the early aviation pioneers succeed where far better-funded attempts failed.

text: Do not take a player's stated reason for a feeling at face value, since the reason is often an automatic addition.
when: when interpreting playtest feedback
why: The raw feeling is real, but the attributed cause may be wrong.

text: Ranked preference annotations require preference learning methods, such as neuro-evolutionary preference learning, rank-based support vector machines or linear discriminant analysis, since standard supervised learning does not apply.
when: When player experience is annotated as a ranking rather than as ratings or class labels.

text: Tabletop publishers accept games for three reasons: a strong hook, crossover appeal to new players, or gameplay staff want to replay.
Tabletop retail has two traditional categories, mass-market chains and hobby stores, with online stores an emerging third.
People will work hard for small symbolic tokens, as a famous commander observed of soldiers and colored ribbons.
Get multiple takes of each line and track them, since post-production cannot rescue a flat performance.
when: When recording voice performances in a studio session.

text: The tabletop market has four categories: mass market, hobby, American specialty, and European. Each is defined by its typical consumer, distribution methods, and product expectations.
why: Knowing a game's category helps an inventor choose the right publisher.

text: 1) Start with a germ of an idea and play with it. 2) Build a working prototype. 3) Test it with many players and collect feedback. 4) Revise repeatedly. 5) Pitch the finished game to publishers.
Shutting out team or tester input drains the team's love for the game, misses chances to improve, and predictably produces a design that pleases no one.
why: Designers who feel threatened by others' ideas build alone and crush contributions.

text: Colleagues tend to respect people who stand behind their ideas, even when they disagree with those ideas.
why: Standing behind an idea signals courage and sincerity, which respected colleagues value even when they reject the idea.

text: Designs that satisfy a client's stated request, private plans and personal motives together, such as using their ideas or giving them credit, can earn lasting loyalty.
when: When a stakeholder's stated request may mask a personal motive.
why: Taking a stated request at face value can produce resistance; meeting the unspoken motive channels the person's energy into the project.

text: Ideas tend to fail when owners are overprotective, judge work unready, dismiss feedback, explain away responses, or trust only their own opinion.
Assuming the publisher or its lawyers will keep harmful content out of a game is risky; confirm the content yourself.
Closed studios and audio's underdog status can encourage a siege mentality, which damages collaboration with the rest of the team.
when: When audio staff work in closed-off studios or feel like the team's underdog.

text: Treat teammates as you want to be treated: do not cut them off or roll your eyes, be polite and patient, find something positive to say, and look for common ground.
why: People who feel respected share ideas openly and honestly, which the team needs.

text: When someone seems not to buy in despite saying they agree, stop and find out why.
when: A member agrees verbally but acts otherwise
why: A member who secretly disagrees can quietly lose love for the project and their contributions are lost

text: Show legitimacy and talent in a submission, since publishers screen out overconfident pitches before they reach a reviewer.
when: When pitching an invented game to a publisher.
why: Many people in the industry overrate their own talent, forcing publishers to filter out weak candidates first.

text: Debaters must respect each other and separate personal feelings from the logical process.
when: During debate, where the purpose is finding flaws in ideas.
why: Otherwise debate damages relationships and becomes counterproductive.

text: A reputation for dishonesty in any area makes others afraid to speak candidly with you.
why: Trust depends on honesty, and candid talk depends on trust.

text: Designers often want executives to fund a game and then leave them alone, which creates friction.
when: Developer and executive relations
why: Designers tend to expect autonomy once funded

text: People with different knowledge, experiences, and assumptions spot weaknesses in others' ideas that they cannot find in their own.
why: Blind spots differ across people with different backgrounds.

text: Arrogation springs from leaders who do not trust their subordinates and fear others will ruin important decisions.
why: Leaders cannot see what they have never encountered, so they believe their grasp is complete.

text: In a productive climate people feel energized and safe, take risks, ask questions and stay focused on work; in a fearful climate they feel angry and afraid and spend energy dodging blame.
why: Climate sets whether people weigh the cost of speaking up.

text: A braintrust is a recurring group that meets every few months to assess each project in production.
Arrogation is a leader claiming decisions that belong to someone else with natural authority over them, often through micromanagement.
Political effects are shifts in influence and relationships among developers caused by a design decision, and group design works like trading favors.
Cultural effects are changes to a team's shared expectations, assumptions and habits, which shape its long-term health.
Skill at building compromises that delight both designer and client strongly predicts a designer's long-term job happiness.
Some professions, such as engineering, mark graduation with a ritual that reminds practitioners of their lifelong duty to society.
Onboarding continues for as long as players keep learning new gameplay, not only at the start.
At the Unintentional UX stage, UX emerges from necessity; the usual barrier is unawareness or rejection rooted in misconceptions, addressed by training and explaining what UX is and is not.
At the Centralized stage, UX roles are spread across teams and research is consistent, but scalability is limited and UX is treated as an internal service.
Shared authorship aims for every team member to take pride in having contributed to the game.
Distributing authority does not mean each person works alone; decisions drawing on many people's knowledge still require communication.
Results once considered extraordinary, such as early Olympic times, often become ordinary as later performers surpass them through training and expectation changes.
why: Expectations held people back; with enough effort, earlier limits were beatable.

text: Shared love for the game and its audience, not mutual liking, lets members set differences aside to make the game as good as possible; mutual liking helps but is optional.
when: teams with mixed disciplines
why: Common affection for the work outweighs disagreements about approach.

text: When designers control their own marketing, they can set productive givens about who their players are.
when: designers run their own marketing
why: marketing shapes player expectations

text: Do not judge whether a task is possible before attempting it; some major innovations came from people unaware the task was considered impossible.
when: Facing a design task that seems too hard
why: Assumed impossibility can stop attempts that would have worked.

text: Team members who are hungry, thirsty, or overtired communicate poorly, so make sure basic physical needs are met before important discussions.
why: Physical discomfort degrades communication quality.

text: Talk one-on-one with each team member, since people share painful truths and pride-laden concerns more easily in private, and these talks build trust in a self-reinforcing cycle.
when: When the honest message is painful or the person's ego is invested in the work.
why: Privacy lowers the risk of sharing candidly, and candor deepens trust.

text: Schedule relaxed shared time with developers, since watching players struggle in UX tests is painful for the team.
when: After UX sessions
why: Shared enjoyment gives the team something besides problems to solve together.

text: Explaining core design pillars of a systemic game to outside partners such as publishers may need UX support.
when: Pitching to publishers

text: Use a UX maturity model to evaluate the studio's current level and identify tools to move forward.
Cut ideas the team is not passionate about, since a lack of passion at the start makes a project feel worse after months of work.
when: When the team is not passionate about an idea at project start.
why: Lukewarm enthusiasm at the start turns into dissatisfaction after months or years of work.

text: Credit where an idea came from, because failing to do so causes confusion and awkward disputes.
when: When an idea is borrowed or adapted from another source

text: If a relationship with an executive stays difficult, note the behavior that frustrates you and avoid repeating it with your own team.
when: When tension with a senior manager persists after you have studied their past work.

text: Give artists freedom beyond your initial concept, since shared authorship builds their investment in the result.
when: When the creator cannot produce the art personally.
why: Working openly with the art director yields ownership of final art even when it departs from the original concept.

text: Assign each team member a role within a larger system so collective intelligence emerges from local actions rather than from one person's grasp of everything.
when: Teams where the work exceeds any single person's understanding
why: Game development is too complex for one mind to hold.

text: Protect team culture even at the cost of short-term gains, since culture drives every action each person takes.
when: When a choice trades short-term results against team climate.
why: Culture shapes the long-term output of all team members.

text: Trust builds over time through the quantity of communication, especially face-to-face, because people read trust through subtle cues.
why: Face-to-face nuance lets people make subconscious trust judgments that digital channels miss.

text: Quick wins from iterative cycles build trust in UX quickly.
when: Once a basis of trust exists with the team.

text: Pairing free camera zoom with free movement can resolve both interface clarity and emotional immersion problems in a 3D game.
when: prototyping a 3D exploration game
why: Players can choose the scale at which they view the world.

text: Debate is productive only when debaters are skilled and hold diverse perspectives; weak debaters waste time attacking strong points or missing fallacies.
why: Skill and diversity determine whether flaws are found efficiently.

text: Self-identified commitment, where a developer sees the work as part of who they are, is the strongest motivator; money carrots and dehumanizing environments kill it before it grows.
when: When trying to motivate developers over the long term.
why: Identity-based commitment is internal, so external pay or control undermines it.

text: In a 2015 developer survey, 62% of developers reported experiencing overtime.
why: Insufficient time, money, or people pushes developers into overtime to meet deadlines.

text: Team health has six parts to check: right team for the project, objective communication, clear communication, comfort with each other, trust and respect, and ability to unify around decisions.
why: Everyone touching a game shapes its design, so the whole team must work together.

text: Meaningful work has eight qualities: a creative outlet, fitting difficulty, pride, acknowledgment, ownership, belonging, accountability, and freedom.
when: When designing or assigning work for a team.
why: Motivation comes from inside when people want work that makes a real difference.

text: Blaming individuals for a bad outcome misses the real cause, often a poor structure or a communication gap between disciplines; blaming the worker is usually wrong.
when: When a bad decision traces back to relevant knowledge that never reached the person deciding
why: Structure controls how knowledge flows, so the decision suffers when the needed information never reaches the decider.

text: Teams working long hours can forget the player and drift away from what players need.
when: Long development crunch
why: Long hours narrow perspective and familiarity replaces fresh player viewpoints

text: Designers often talk too much and reveal plans; a script and an objective facilitator help prevent this.
when: When a designer is running their own playtest sessions
why: A written script keeps the facilitator on task and reminds them they are there to observe, not to explain.

text: Passion can mislead because it is an emotion, so take it seriously without relying on it alone.
when: At the end of every sprint, while reviewing prototypes and planning next steps
why: Passion signals the subconscious's excitement; though irrational, it is the force that gets projects past obstacles.

text: Blaming a client for not knowing what they want, instead of helping them find out, damages the working relationship.
when: When a client cannot articulate what they want from the game
why: A client who already knew their wants would not need the design work; clarifying them is the designer's role.

text: Being caught unprepared by a predictable question can undermine an otherwise strong pitch.
when: When a question the presenter could foresee comes up during a pitch

text: Presenting ideas without a prototype or evidence signals low commitment, and enthusiasm alone does not prove fun or profitability.
when: When pitching a game to a publisher or funding panel
why: A panel reads an unbuilt idea as low commitment; a working prototype and market thinking show the developer is serious.

text: Dismissing business people as beneath you is a mistake, since they are essential to the industry.
why: Profit sustains the industry, so people who are skilled at managing money are needed to run it.

text: Obscurity can let designers slip out of personal responsibility for what they ship, because nobody asks them to answer for their work.
when: When working in relative obscurity under a publisher's name
why: Companies bear legal duties but no ethical ones, since only individual people can hold moral responsibility.

text: Interpreting test failures as player irrationality rather than as a teaching gap hides the real design problem.
when: When watching playtesters act in ways the designer finds irrational
why: Designers already know where to look and what matters, while new players lack that knowledge, so the behavior reflects missing teaching.

text: UX without its own budget at the Centralized stage is often treated as a service rather than a strategic area.
when: Centralized stage
why: Scaling UX needs dedicated people and skills, which are missing when it lacks its own funding alongside departments like production or marketing.

text: Using scientific findings against developers, or reporting their mistakes upward, damages trust.
when: When UX staff work alongside developers inside a studio
why: Using findings against developers or reporting their mistakes upward makes UX feel like policing, which erodes trust.

text: Arriving unprepared wastes the time of everyone else in the room.
when: When setting up or joining a team meeting
why: Without a goal known beforehand, attendees cannot prepare and the meeting accomplishes little.

text: Assigning one team member several parallel tasks makes the schedule unrealistic, since they finish far fewer than planned.
If a narrative designer cannot work well with other disciplines, narrative delivery suffers on both large and small teams.
why: Narrative is delivered through the team's shared decisions, so collaboration across departments is as central to it as the storytelling itself.

text: Guarding decisions against people you judge less capable than yourself only hobbles the team.
when: When a design leader oversees people they consider less capable
why: A leader cannot understand every decision across the studio, so defending against others' work leaves decisions worse.

text: Treating skilled people as incompetent is among the most demotivating things a leader can do.
why: Being treated as incompetent breeds anger that drains creative capacity, while expectations shape what people believe they can do.

text: 1) Build trust around UX practices. 2) Demonstrate quick wins. 3) Establish a common language and common UX processes. 4) Build a studio-level UX culture.
when: When a studio is building its UX practice and maturity
why: Each step rests on the previous one: trust enables quick wins, which enable a shared language and a studio-wide culture.

text: 1) Find one element you can be proud of, such as a moment, mechanic, or interface. 2) If you are not in the target audience, think of the game as a gift for its intended players. 3) As a last resort, act enthusiastic until real feeling returns.
when: when a designer has stopped loving the project
why: Each step restores motivation with increasing effort.

text: 1) Count the games each player has played with each teammate. 2) Treat frequent partners as effectively higher-rated.
when: Adjusting team ratings for familiarity.
why: Familiar teams coordinate better than strangers.

text: 1) Set the Tutorial order values. 2) Filter the table by Tutorial order. 3) Read the result as the chronological teaching plan.
when: When planning which game features to teach and in what sequence
why: Unique order numbers let sorting arrange the tagged elements into an exact teaching sequence.

text: 1) Run a brainstorming session. 2) Have each team member contribute personal experiences. 3) Turn those details into characters, locations and storylines.
when: When inventing characters, locations or storylines for a game
why: Details drawn from lived experience feel as credible as ones borrowed from real history.

text: 1) Establish that disagreement will not be punished. 2) Prove evenhandedness through consistent behavior. 3) Only then debate subordinates' ideas.
when: A manager debating with direct reports.
why: Subordinates soften critique of a boss's ideas if they fear punishment.

text: 1) Subordinates send condensed summaries of newly gained knowledge upward. 2) Leaders use these to iterate on broad structure such as level progression, plot and market positioning. 3) Leaders receive results of decisions, not moment-to-moment detail.
when: Coordinating a team with distributed decisions
why: Leaders can guide the whole without being everywhere.

text: 1) Set the target you need. 2) Reframe it as a bigger aim beyond that target. 3) Let the team reach the original target as a natural result.
when: When a team needs to hit a demanding goal.
why: A more ambitious framing makes the real target feel reachable.

text: Answer tough questions with a firm affirmative backed by evidence; hedged yes or probably signals uncertainty, and absolutely without evidence sounds empty.
when: Answering a challenging question in a pitch
why: Evidence makes the answer credible; unsupported certainty is quickly exposed by follow-up questions.

text: Treat UX as a mindset for the whole product team, ideally the whole company, not as a single role, deliverable or step.
why: UX is an iterative, science-based mindset rather than a single pipeline step, so the whole team must carry it.

text: Consult players with disabilities throughout development.
Provide a quiet space at a comfortable temperature, with enough chairs and a large writing surface for design discussions.
why: Comfortable people get distracted less and speak more openly.

text: If you offend someone, apologize sincerely rather than defending what you said.
Team members must always feel they are getting the truth from you, even when politics tempts you to stretch it.
why: Without confidence in the candor of the person leading, teammates' exchanges get strained.

text: When a team wants a game built around an unproven technology, explain the Hype Cycle before committing to that direction.
when: a team proposes a game built around an untested technology
why: Explaining the cycle can prevent a dangerous decision made in the grip of hype.

text: Do not immediately explain why a client's suggestion is bad; this usually backfires, so seek the client's reasoning first.
when: A client offers an idea the designer believes is weak.
why: Immediate rejection tends to alienate the client

text: Pursue a game's positive effect quietly within the design rather than pitching social improvement as the goal to management.
when: management may read the goal as misaligned priorities
why: A stated social goal can be seen as conflicting with commercial aims.

text: Attend as many team meetings as you can and take part in the wider team, not only your own discipline.
why: Grasping the vocabulary of other disciplines sharpens communication and reveals other viewpoints, helping teams find shared solutions.

text: Rehearse arguments beforehand and present them calmly and reasonably, avoiding irritability.
when: Raising a disagreement with colleagues

text: Include business and economic constraints in a UX strategy, but keep the approach human-centered rather than business-centered.
why: UX's goal is improving people's lives through technology, not serving business metrics.

text: A UX culture needs clearly established values, a commitment to inclusion, and accessibility.
when: When a studio aims to fully reach a UX culture.

text: To advance from the Centralized stage, link UX metrics to business KPIs, such as tying UX issues to retention drops.
when: UX operates as an internal service
why: Tying UX to business figures makes its effect visible to the business side.

text: Coordinate UX at the project, production, and studio levels.
why: No single discipline or department can define UX alone, so it needs coordination across roles.

text: Celebrate small UX victories together with the development team.
Question and test UX theories, including ones drawn from practice, because the scientific method depends on challenging every idea.
why: The framework itself has not been empirically validated, so its ideas need testing.

text: Share the goal and agenda in advance so attendees can gather what they need, such as research for brainstorming or a workload review for status meetings.
why: Meetings without a clear agenda waste attendees' time and accomplish little.

text: Discard abusive or insulting feedback, because no one should risk their mental health for their job.
when: reviewing feedback from playtesters or colleagues
why: Personal attacks harm the receiver and carry no actionable design content.

text: Do not be possessive of reassigned work or take frustration out on the new writer; resolve any issues with your lead.
when: When work is reassigned only once, not repeatedly.
why: The incoming writer depends on your help to get up to speed.

text: Check company policy before working on personal projects, since some employers require approval and may take intellectual property rights.
when: At employers whose policies restrict outside personal projects.

text: Participants must feel no dread toward each other, since those holding less authority won't argue candidly out of fear of reprisal.
when: Any debate involving unequal power, such as a manager and subordinates.
why: Power imbalance corrupts honest critique.

text: Choose people you can count on and then fully trust them, because no leader can cover others' mistakes or understand every decision across a large team.
when: When a team generates more decisions than one leader can track.
why: A leader lacking full knowledge of the process makes worse decisions when overriding others.

text: Assign a decision to the person who holds the most relevant knowledge about it, not to the person with the most seniority.
why: Those nearest a problem can apply their full judgment and local knowledge, which a distant boss lacks.

text: A producer owns schedule and budget while a designer argues for more time and money on gameplay, making the designer-producer combination the sharpest role conflict.
when: Designer and producer roles combined

text: Prestigious schools offer industry connections, while small community college programs may suit a budget or location better.
Small teams keep process burden naturally low, which gives them a major advantage over large teams.
why: Coordination cost and complexity rise as team size grows, so small teams carry less tracking and scheduling overhead.

text: Climate is the daily emotional tone of work, shaped by expectations about how failure and questioning are received.
Frequent checking of email and chat, open offices and instant messaging add distraction, even though multitasking is often praised at work.
Game development is collaborative, and development teams keep growing larger and more complex.
Talent has limits, and the right mix of talent and personality matters even more than talent alone.
Specialization in programming and art has created new job categories, increasing the number of distinct roles on a team.
On small teams the narrative designer may also implement story content, handle in-game text, and take on game design and level design.
when: when the team is small

text: Writers are usually not narrative designers, but narrative designers can also write, and on small teams one person may cover both roles.
Great games need committed teams, and commitment hinges on working habits, company ethos, inner drive, and how the organization is arranged.
Even with good communication, some knowledge stays tacit or too voluminous to share, so the person with natural authority usually makes the final call.
Steering behaviors are easy to expose to designers because they are simple, parameterized by physical capabilities, and identical across characters.
When a discussion stalls over whether something is a game, have each side state its own working definition and continue the discussion.
when: when people disagree about what counts as a game
why: Stated definitions let the debate move forward without a standard vocabulary

text: Keep a concrete worst-case scenario, such as a headline about a child abduction caused by missing safeguards, in mind within the team, without showing it outside.
when: designing safety features
why: Concrete worst cases make abstract safety risks harder to dismiss.

text: Build a team environment where everyone can contribute at their fullest.
why: Team results depend on members contributing fully

text: After a strong idea, building the right team is the most critical step toward producing a great game.
why: Team structure and working environment determine whether talent succeeds, so talent alone is not enough.

text: A team that has shipped together is a lower risk to publishers than a talented group that has never worked together.
when: When a publisher decides whether to fund a development team's project.
why: Publishers judge whether a team can deliver on budget and schedule, and past shipped work is the best indicator.

text: Learn each team's culture, choose which battles are worth fighting, know your allies and protect your energy. Reassess when changing team.
when: when joining or changing a company or team
why: Each company and team has its own culture

text: Pitches may be work in progress, since aspects change during development and readers do not expect a finished product.
when: Writing an early pitch
why: Game aspects keep changing before and during development, so readers do not expect a finished description.

text: Use centralized, prescribed-method management only when a job involves little knowledge, since a central manager can then hold all relevant knowledge.
when: Organizing simple, repetitive jobs
why: With few decisions to make, one manager can track every worker's activity and decide for them.

text: Small teams especially need visible progress, since they lack group momentum, and detailed to-do lists help sustain motivation.
when: When managing small development teams.
why: Without a crowd's momentum, individual visible wins carry more of the motivation.

text: Richer art, audio, and production values require large specialized teams drawn from many backgrounds, ranging from database engineers to UI designers and 3D artists.
when: When a game's production values approach those of television and film.
why: Content volume now exceeds code size, and many specialist disciplines are needed to create it.

text: Repeated silence in a fearful climate leaves ideas unspoken, so the game becomes bland and unoriginal, and the cause is hard to notice.
when: When team members fear being torn apart or losing social standing for voicing ideas.
why: The harm is an absence of ideas and debates, which teams rarely see.

text: Each workshop team should include six to ten leads from the major disciplines, and three to ten teams can attend one session.
why: Lasting preproduction habits form through practice and early success, not through lectures or handouts.

text: Commitments toward studio staff cover inclusion, UX priority, limits on crunch, protection from community abuse, and environmental responsibility.
Team structure diagrams show vertical reporting lines to the producer and horizontal lines that let groups interact directly with each other.
why: Lateral links let groups coordinate directly while the producer and leads still keep overall hierarchy.

text: A team runs at full creative capacity when three conditions hold: the right people hold authority in the right places, knowledge flows to where it is needed, and members trust one another.
why: Investing heart is delicate and depends on a combination of work practices, culture, motivation, and structure.

text: Silencing critics defeats the purpose of playtesting.
why: Explaining the game to testers erases their natural first impression, which the test is meant to capture.

text: Rewarding only flashy, visible presentations breeds resentment toward unseen technical work and makes people perform for the reward instead of improving the game.
when: When rewards are tied to demonstrations or showcases.
why: Unrewarded invisible work feels devalued, and visible performance is favored over real progress.

text: 1) Hand over your work in an organized, clear and concise way. 2) Answer the new writer's questions. 3) Be ready to move on to your next task.
when: When a writer's work is reassigned to another writer to finish.
why: Work gets handed off for many reasons, so the original writer must still enable the next person to complete it.

text: Use confidants once the prototype is playable with defined rules, and stop relying on them as the game matures.
when: When the game matures beyond early prototype testing.
why: Friends and family have personal ties that bias their feedback, making them too harsh or too forgiving.

text: Have business people and developers work together daily, and build projects around motivated, trusted individuals.
when: when organizing a project team
why: Face-to-face conversation is the most efficient and effective way to convey information within a team.

text: State the confidence level whenever drawing balance conclusions from playtest or analytics data.
when: reporting balance findings
why: Statistics can mislead even under ideal conditions.

text: Non-specialists should work with data analysts to extract and interpret meaningful information.
when: When non-specialists lack adequate training in statistics and data analysis.
why: Raw data is not information, and untrained users with little awareness of cognitive bias can misread it.

text: Walking away over a design decision should be a last resort, since your vision may not have been communicated clearly.
when: When executive design decisions seem to be ruining the game and other options have failed.
why: Executives may never have read the design documents, so the designer's vision may not have been communicated.

text: Schedule a standing weekly gathering of department heads to review project status, so information moves across teams.
why: Structured communication with department heads ensures everyone's input is heard, supporting shared authorship.

text: Fund your own project through work-for-hire while you develop it, as many independent developers do.
when: you need income during independent development
why: Self-produced games are hard to fund, so paid side work covers costs while the game is built.

text: Ask colleagues for low-budget creative solutions, since troubleshooting narrative problems is a team effort.
when: When a narrative fix is blocked because the content is already finished or approved.

text: Spread decision authority across the team; removing decisions from workers prevents the distributed intelligence that complex development needs.
why: Too much happens in development for one mind to hold, so collective judgment must emerge from local decisions.

text: Organizations should keep providing work that has the qualities of meaningful work, because that is their central task in motivating developers.
when: When managing a creative team.
why: Developers stay engaged when the work continuously offers those qualities.

text: Involving the whole team costs time and energy, and it pays off in the long run only if the team can communicate well.
why: Presenting to the whole team surfaces new problems and restarts the iterative cycle.

text: When reviewing work, limit comments to general deficiencies and offers of help rather than prescribing specific fixes.
when: Reviewing a teammate's work
why: Specific orders block the worker from using knowledge the leader lacks.

text: Repeated wrong confident predictions normally teach a group to stop listening to the predictor, which corrects overconfidence.
when: When cause and effect is clear and results show quickly, so failed predictions are visible.
why: Visible failures erode trust in the confident voice

text: Relaxed, friendly interaction makes colleagues more likely to listen to UX critique.
why: Colleagues who do not see the critic only as a fault-finder are less defensive about criticism.

text: Game design hides cause and effect, so results arrive years later and blur, and overconfident predictions persist, letting confident leaders gain more followers than accurate ones.
when: long development cycles with delayed results
why: The correction that normally exposes bad predictions is broken

text: A stakeholder's past unpredictability on changes adds uncertainty that the stakeholder may not recognize, so their likely reaction should be checked rather than assumed.
when: Proposing a change that affects a stakeholder's work
why: Hidden uncertainty makes outcomes harder to predict.

text: Ignoring the subconscious's suggestions causes it to stop making them.
why: The subconscious is handled like a partner, and partners stop offering ideas once their input is dismissed.

text: Taking a client's words at face value and ignoring their real motives tends to cause resistance and erratic behavior later in the project.
why: Clients hold unstated goals beneath their stated request, which later surface as pushback.

text: Ignoring topics the listener raised earlier makes them feel unheard and weakens ownership.
when: Delivering a pitch
why: Listeners want to see their input acknowledged.

text: Harsh comments make team members hold back their ideas, which damages the group's creativity.
when: When criticizing ideas during brainstorming, before they are fully developed.
why: Criticizing half-formed ideas breaks the momentum of members adding onto one another's contributions.

text: Letting the wish for team harmony replace honest criticism allows design flaws to persist.
why: Without someone to point out flaws, inconsistencies go unnoticed and multiply until the game ships.

text: Respond to curveballs such as a hostile listener, a shortened meeting, or a rejection with composure, because walking out insulted closes the door on later opportunities.
when: A pitch goes off plan or is rejected
why: The goal is publishing games in general, so one rejected concept need not end the relationship; leaving badly ends the chance to offer something else.

text: Open discussion after play can be one-on-one or group, and can be free-form or guided by specific questions.
The caller usually acts as discussion leader, may hand parts of the meeting to others, and keeps the group moving toward the goal.
Differences of opinion help solve problems, so approach a topic from several angles.
when: When a team meeting is working to resolve a problem.

text: Without a clear agenda, meetings waste time and accomplish little.
when: When you are the one calling a meeting.
why: Without a goal everyone knows beforehand, people cannot prepare, and the meeting accomplishes little.

text: 1) Warn anyone who makes personal attacks, and ask them to leave if it continues. 2) Before closing, review decisions and assigned action items. 3) Schedule any needed follow-up early enough for preparation. 4) Send notes of decisions and assignments to participants and key absent members.
Assign someone in every design meeting to take notes the whole team can read; on many teams this is the producer's job.
why: Spoken words fade and get misremembered, while written records can be checked by anyone later.

text: Join team discussions at the highest level you can, come prepared, and keep your input focused on the meeting's goal.
A meeting should have one clear goal that is completed by its end, and the person calling it sets the agenda.
Do not leave anyone out on purpose, and do not criticize speakers.
Everyone who touches the game affects its design, even if not everyone shapes it, so respect every suggestion and pull together for the shared vision reaching the final game.
Learn what other disciplines need, who teammates are, and what they enjoy; communicate with them and make sure they know your own role.
why: Narrative only reaches its potential when integrated with the practical details of production, which requires knowing teammates.

text: Groups follow confident leaders over rationally uncertain experts, even when the confident leader is less accurate.
when: group planning under uncertainty
why: People are drawn to those who seem to see the future clearly

text: Team members who love the game look forward to finishing it, eager for release in the way children anticipate a holiday.
why: Shared affection for the game and its audience sets disagreements aside in favor of making it well.

text: A designer seen as objective receives more honest feedback from the team and can calm tense debates between others.
when: When design debates turn tense and some participants are not being objective.
why: Impartiality makes people trust the designer's judgment.

text: Artists put more enthusiasm into projects that match their interests, so a poor style match can reduce their effort.
when: when a project's style does not suit an artist
why: Effort follows personal interest.

text: The producer is the project leader on the developer team, responsible for delivering the game to the publisher as promised.
A technical artist has an artist's eye and a programmer's mind, bridging both teams and building tools so artists feel in command of technology and engineers feel in command of art.
Programmers are everyone who technically implements the game: coders working at both upper and lower layers, network and systems engineers, database developers, and hardware support.
The lead designer owns the creative vision for narrative and gameplay, and the lead artist owns the game's visual look.
Natural authority is a developer's right to make any decision that they understand better than anyone else on the team.
why: Local knowledge is hard to relay to a distant leader.

text: Immaturity burden is the steady cost imposed on people whose work depends on buggy tools, half-made mechanics or a shifting story.
Some companies have no dedicated designer, and programmers, artists, executives, or producers take on design work.
Producers sit on both publisher and developer teams and act as a single point of contact that keeps both sides on the same assumptions.
The producer's office often becomes the place where team members air grievances and concerns.
Producers interact with publisher contacts more than anyone else and may represent the team at conferences or to the press.
Artists and engineers are both empowered and restrained by technology.
Modern game teams mix artistic, technical, design, and business people who often have different backgrounds and priorities.
Related roles include studio engineer, location audio recorder, orchestrator, score copyist, editor of music, editor of dialogue, voice-over director, and casting and localization staff.
Advanced programmer titles include senior programmer, lead programmer, technical director, and CTO. Studios also name specialists such as tools, engine, graphics, and database programmers.

Typical programmer duties include drafting technical specifications, building prototypes, tools, modules, engines, and data structures, managing communication, documenting code, and working with QA on bugs.
The publisher's producer coordinates with internal executives, marketing, and QA, spending less time with production and more time with marketing.
A producer has a stake in market success and can sometimes judge a game's potential more objectively than its designer.
Hiring talented people is not enough on its own, since team structure and working environment largely determine whether they succeed.
Lateral communication does not remove hierarchy: the producer and department leads still set the big-picture vision and each group's daily tasks.
Team sizes, budgets, and development timelines for A-list console titles have grown steadily, and A-list PC games have grown similarly.
In the 1970s, one person with solid programming knowledge could produce a complete commercial game, acting as designer, producer, programmer, artist, and sound designer.
Senior art positions are lead animator, art director, and senior art director; some studios add creative directors who keep one consistent look across the product line.
Artists come from varied backgrounds, and a degree is not required; some learned traditional tools before moving to computer tools.

In production, programmers write game code, artists build art and animation, sound designers make effects and music, writers produce dialogue and in-game text, QA engineers do light testing, and the producer manages communication, schedule, and resources.
Working inside a studio greatly improves the chance your ideas get noticed, since most legal concerns fall away.
Game companies rarely hire people for ideas alone; progress comes from hands-on contribution.
Industry terms are not standardised. Mechanics may be called systems, so underlying principles matter more than the labels.
Job titles such as writer, game writer, narrative designer and quest designer vary between studios, so the role is best defined by its functions.
Teamwork is part of game design rather than a separate discipline, and a strong story reaches its potential only when integrated into production.
Freelance narrative designers often wear several hats, acting as both game designer and game writer.
Work is reassigned for varied reasons, such as a teammate preferring certain missions, a junior's task becoming an emergency for a senior writer, or tasks being shuffled.
Hunger is not talent: a driven designer may be no more able than peers but is not bound by the standards around them.

Employers often value flexibility, fast learning, and being easy to work with and communicating well above mastery of specific software or knowledge, since tools change and studios use in-house tools.
why: Tools change and studios use in-house tools

text: Combine design with another role only when the project is small and the individual's skill allows it.
when: Staffing a project with combined roles
why: Effect of combining roles depends on scope and skill

text: Run individual answer sessions after related group questions, so participants can go deeper on their own.
when: When combining focus groups with individual interviews
why: Individuals can expand on group discussion without social pressure.

text: Let nontechnical team members contribute to paper prototypes, widening the range of perspectives at a high level.
when: When prototyping a design with physical materials rather than software
why: Giving input requires no programming expertise, so non-programmers can engage directly in the design.

text: Hiring people who already run fan communities or statistics sites can supply valuable analysis skills and game knowledge.
when: Staffing a game team
why: Enthusiasts bring domain knowledge and tooling.

text: The lead designer acts as holder of the game's vision and conduit for team ideas, rather than the main idea generator.
when: Leading a design team
why: The designer's position lets them add many design elements, so channeling everyone's ideas serves the team better than fighting for their own.

text: No designer masters every field, so growth comes from working beyond your current limits.
when: Building design skill over time
why: Stretching into unfamiliar fields expands what you can design.

text: Listening to yourself is often the hardest kind of listening, but mastering it makes it a powerful tool and a source of creativity.
when: Developing personal creative judgment
why: Self-awareness drives creative work.

text: Choose a small core design team from people who both enjoy and are productive at detailed design debate, since not everyone can sustain hours of argument over fine details.
when: When detailed design debates run for hours on fine points of a feature
why: Not everyone can sustain long detailed debates, so membership should depend on who enjoys and is productive at them.

text: Leave some detailed design open, especially in areas you are unsure about, so the developers closest to that feature can work out details and feel ownership.
when: For parts of the game the designer is unsure about
why: Those who shape a feature feel pride when it ships.

text: Open offices help build trust because constant face-to-face contact about anything strengthens relationships.
why: High-bandwidth communication about anything builds trust, and constant face-to-face contact supplies that communication.

text: Decision-makers who control schedule and budget listen most to people they know, like, and trust, so build those relationships before the pitch.
when: Pitching inside an organization
why: Trust makes busy decision-makers receptive to proposals.

text: An inside advocate already sold on the concept can defend it to colleagues in the room.
when: Pitching to a group with decision-makers
why: Peers trust a fellow insider's endorsement.

text: Be willing to lose a small argument if it helps you win the larger goal.
Having one person own both mechanic design and level design, at least initially, keeps the two tightly tuned together.
when: Staffing a movement-driven game
why: Level spacing is built around the avatar's movement, so one person owning both keeps them tuned together.

text: Listen to teammates and compromise; ideas you do not use may spark ones you do, and involving teammates gives them authorship.
why: Ideas you don't use can spark ones you do, and involving teammates gives them authorship that reinvests them in the project.

text: When presenting a design visually, clarity matters more than artistic polish; simple imagery is enough.
when: When creating storyboards or concept visuals
why: The goal is communicating the idea rather than polished graphics, so simple imagery serves better.

text: Fresh playtesters detect micromanagement best, and complaints of too much work are a warning sign.
when: When deciding how much control to give players and whether tasks have become tedious
why: Fresh playtesters give the most certain signal of whether tasks have become repetitive or tedious.

text: No single method structures a team; treat team rules as a starting point and adapt them to your project and people.
why: Each project and group of people differs, so the right structure has to be found for them rather than copied.

text: The best executive combines game development experience, deep market understanding, and a hands-on approach.
Aim for a programming team that actively joins iterative improvement, for example by asking when the next playtest is.
why: Working through the technical lead respects their authority, while going around them creates an adversary.

text: Hire artists for specific tasks such as 3D modeling, animation, texture mapping, or interface design, since skill in one area does not carry over to another.
when: When staffing an art team for a production with distinct required skills
why: Artists strong at cityscapes may be unable to animate characters.

text: Agents look for established developers with proven technology, or new developers with strong talent and capable management.
why: Publishers hire developers on the strength of proven technology or top talent with capable management.

text: Hiring in-house business development staff can cost no more than hunting agents charge, so large developers may prefer it.
when: large developers deciding how to find deals
why: Employing in-house staff to secure and sell projects typically costs no more than what hunting agents charge.

text: A single reassignment is usually routine, but repeated reassignment is a sign to discuss with your lead why the work is moving.
when: When the same work keeps being moved away from you, not just once
why: Repeated reassignment signals that the team may see you as nonessential, a warning sign to raise with your lead.

text: Use centralized control only for simple, repetitive work; for complex creative work a central manager overloads, ignores details, oversimplifies and wastes effort.
when: Choosing how to organize a task
why: Knowledge volume and tacit skill then exceed what one mind can hold.

text: Climate affects how people relate, think and act every moment, so it is among the strongest factors in game quality.
why: Climate shapes how people relate, think, and act at every moment, and poor climate silently stops good things from happening.

text: Compare how much time coordination consumes against production time to judge how much process machinery a project truly needs.
when: when deciding whether to add coordination tools or roles to a project
why: Coordination cost rises as teams grow, while small teams naturally carry little of this burden.

text: One member who does not buy in slows the whole team and can eventually split it apart, like a single misfiring cylinder in an engine.
when: A team member does not accept the team's direction
why: Their reluctance to accept the chosen direction shows up in the finished game and drags down everyone's output.

text: Tight control over each worker's actions does not produce careful work; people do attentive, quality work only when they are committed.
why: Attention and care cannot be enforced through direction alone.

text: A strong trail draws specialized roles such as obstacle clearers, patrollers and bridge-builders, so colony-level behavior emerges without any individual understanding the overall strategy.
when: When a foraging trail among ants grows stronger
why: Individuals act on simple local rules, and their combined behavior forms a distributed collective intelligence.

text: When intent flows down and summaries flow up, leaders iterate on broad strokes and workers iterate on details, so outstanding games do not require genius developers.
why: Combined knowledge is applied efficiently.

text: Producer responsibilities include delivery planning, schedule and budget, resource tracking and allocation, forecasting needs, team leadership and motivation, solving production problems, and publisher liaison.
Large productions can organize Scrum teams around game features, letting many creative people work without heavy top-down management.
when: Large productions
why: Game design problems are hard to solve, and the team must be able to change its approach fluidly.

text: Large AAA teams usually include executive producers, lead designers, lead artists, level and systems designers, animators, artists, programmers and QA testers. Titles differ between studios.
Leaders who command low-level specifics that subordinates understand better degrade decisions by overriding the people closest to the work, who often have the long iteration and testing leaders lack.
why: Leaders lack the hands-on iteration and testing hours that the people doing the work have.

text: Hubris causes overplanning, overconfident quick judgments of others' work, and too little playtesting, which misses serious design flaws.
when: a designer is overconfident
why: overconfidence skips testing and checking

text: Designers who try to replace skilled teachers insult them and ignore their experience.
when: When a transformational game is used alongside an instructor who guides the learner.
why: A game is unlikely to match an instructor's accumulated experience, and replacing them disrespects it.

text: A director who cannot decide what they want upsets actors more than almost anything else.
when: When a director is guiding actors through a recording session.

text: A separate UX team alone will not have enough impact; the whole studio has to adopt UX methods.
why: UX spans art, design, marketing, business and executive goals, so it depends on coordination across all of them.

text: Teams that lack shared key vocabulary, or use the same words to mean different things, struggle to align on a design.
Going directly to a database engineer for a quick change, bypassing the technical director, turns the technical director into an adversary.
when: When requesting a quick change from an engineer on a team with a reporting hierarchy
why: Going around the supervisor weakens their authority and invites open hostility.

text: Dismissing producers and executives as people who do not understand creative teams makes collaboration harder, since few people enter the industry to make bad games.
why: Being away from daily production lets them assess what the game could become with less bias.

text: Excluding people from the design process breeds cliques and can cost you good ideas.
Brilliant people who cannot interact productively with teammates can cost more trouble than their contribution is worth.
when: When assembling a team and choosing who to hire
why: Talent alone does not guarantee a team's success; personality fit determines how well people work together.

text: Team members making decisions with the other company without producers involved risks inconsistent outcomes.
why: Decisions need one accountable channel per side to stay consistent.

text: Assuming you must be an expert scripter or level designer before becoming a narrative designer is a mistake. Some strong narrative designers cannot script.
why: Narrative design centers on telling the story, so tool knowledge only needs to be useful, not expert-level.

text: Do not assign a task to a specific role from a table layout whose markings are unclear; verify ownership against the original source before deciding.
when: A task table's columns or marks are ambiguous
why: Misread marks lead to wrong role ownership

text: Without a shared plan, team members cannot see how their work fits the whole, causing technical incompatibilities such as non-standard models or memory-hungry subsystems, and creative clashes in story, design, and art style.
when: When a team grows beyond a couple of developers
why: Coordination across people requires a shared view of the whole product.

text: Clean post-project stories hide the messy false predictions where the real lessons lie, so teams lose the lessons they most need.
when: when writing up a finished project
why: Hindsight bias makes past events seem more predictable, so teams believe they can plan deeper next time.
