text: Designers who protect a beloved, costly plan may discard surprises that would have improved the game.
when: when a detailed plan is attached to a large investment
why: Serendipity is among iteration's greatest benefits, so rigidly keeping a plan forfeits it.

text: Teams that hire people who think like themselves lose the diversity that makes debate useful.
why: People naturally hire similar thinkers, so diversity must be deliberately fostered.

text: The best people are the hardest to motivate, so generic incentive approaches tend to fail them.
when: When designing motivation for a studio's most capable staff.
why: Top performers respond to meaningful, identity-based work rather than standard incentives.

text: 1) List every skill the game demands, both general and specific. 2) Include physical skills, resource management, and memorization. 3) Compare the list with the skills you intended to test.
when: Reviewing a game design before or during playtesting
why: Designers often overlook the skills that dominate the experience.

text: 1) Agree beforehand on who answers which questions. 2) Answer as a group, not individually. 3) Keep the team's answers consistent.
when: Presenting as a team
why: Clear roles make the team look unified and prepared.

text: 1) Compare matches where one team is all strangers against matches where the other team has played together many times. 2) Measure the win-rate difference to estimate the effect of team experience.
when: Measuring how much prior teamwork affects team games.
why: Contrasting experienced and unfamiliar teams isolates the familiarity effect.

text: 1) Map the usual team roles onto your prototype. 2) Identify the positions you cannot fill yourself. 3) Recruit for them through local bulletin boards or websites, since many people want to work on game projects.
when: Prototype needs collaborators

text: 1) Narrative design supplies profile and psychology. 2) Concept art creates distinctive visual signifiers. 3) Character modeling builds the model from concept art and narrative cues. 4) Animation creates tailored animations reflecting psychology. 5) Cinematics combines all departments' work to place characters in settings.
why: Personality and outlook shape body language, movement and clothing, so many departments must contribute to bring characters alive.

text: 1) Leader states the purpose and goals of the work. 2) Worker chooses the detailed methods to reach them. 3) Team iterates on methods during development instead of returning to the leader for each detail.
when: Delegating creative or design work
why: The worker holds the detailed knowledge and can find problems and solutions the leader did not anticipate.

text: 1) Picture a future self with more skills, knowledge, emotional range and work discipline. 2) Take a step toward that self every day.
why: Small daily efforts accumulate over years into large gains.

text: Call tests of a team's own features internal design reviews rather than playtests.
when: When developers themselves play the build to discuss features, not outside testers.
why: Playtests require outside participants unfamiliar with the game; team-run checks lack that, so they are reviews.

text: A producer must make tough calls, such as hiring and firing and refusing excessive resource or spending requests.
when: When the team must meet the delivery schedule during production.
why: Hitting the delivery schedule requires hard decisions on staffing and spending.

text: Listen deeply to the team and communicate for real, so that key decisions are made together and the team acts as one unit.
when: Making key design decisions
why: Shared listening lets people act as if they shared the same skills.

text: Listen with an open, childlike stance: assume nothing, observe everything, and withhold judgment and rebuke.
when: Gathering input from any source
why: Assumptions and judgment filter out what people actually say.

text: A designer without drawing talent should find an artistic partner with whom communication is good, rather than relying on their own sketches.
when: the designer lacks drawing skill
why: a vague concept can turn into a firm visual target quickly

text: Let artists set the artistic destination, while engineers navigate, recommending routes, shortcuts and improvements to reach it.
when: When the team can let artists lead the aesthetic direction.
why: artists have trained for years to define integrated artistic visions

text: Check that others understand you, illustrate ideas when possible, and never pretend to understand; keep asking until you do.
why: Unclear messages create confusion, and a team only communicates meaningfully when everyone shares the same understanding.

text: When emailing about design, include the whole team so no one is left out or feels left out.
Design every polish clue together across designer, artist and programmer, since perception is multisensory and draws on past experience.
when: When a polish effect involves design, art and programming at once.

text: Consider human capabilities, performance and limits throughout development and after launch, while still checking viability and profitability.
Disruptive or antisocial behavior between colleagues should not be tolerated.
Protect and support staff who interact with players on platforms or social media, and cover respect for them in the code of conduct.
If no game program is available, build your own curriculum from existing courses at your school, covering the same game-related areas.
when: No game program is offered locally

text: Hold one-on-one creative talks with key team members.
Before hiring artists, decide what the game needs, such as predominantly 3D art, animation, or an interface aimed at a specific market.
why: Individual artists often excel at some skills but not others, so skills must be matched to tasks.

text: Beginners should first join an established developer or publisher and build a track record before pitching their own projects.
when: when new to the industry
why: New teams must establish credibility before winning funding.

text: Act as an information nexus: know the answer, find it with the time and work needed, or know who holds it.
Juniors can ask for pitch and concept documents once ready, and giving feedback on them is an effective way to learn.
Learn the mechanics of colleagues' jobs and general game design, plus your own project's design, so you share their language and can support them.
Avoid potentially insulting terms in pitches, since the reader may be the executive who approves the deal.
when: Writing any pitch for outside decision makers
why: Offense can end a deal before the idea is judged

text: Understand what teammates rely on you for, what you rely on them for, and which techniques make narrative come alive.
why: Without working well with other disciplines, narrative delivery suffers and the story reaches the audience less well.

text: Ask reviewers from several disciplines, including narrative, programming, art, sound, game design and marketing, since each spots different strengths, weaknesses and technical limits.
when: When working alone and judging your own design work
why: Solo authors miss some blind spots, and other disciplines judge strengths, weaknesses and technical limits from viewpoints the author lacks.

text: Pursue improvement for the pleasure of doing the work better, rather than for external rewards or approval.
why: External goals end once met, while intrinsic pleasure in the work keeps driving improvement.

text: Treat music as collaborative work between composer and developer, so the score is shaped alongside the design.
why: Music shifts listeners' emotions, and empathetic scoring supplies the feeling expected for what is shown on screen.

text: Community managers must balance a hands-on approach against a hands-off approach, and each carries its own costs.
when: managing online communities
why: Managers cannot build community themselves; they seed it and nurture its growth by observing members' needs.

text: On a team assigned by a large company, you either adapt your vision to the team's skills or communicate ideas clearly enough for them to implement.
when: when a large company assigns you an art team
why: Artists engage more eagerly with work mirroring their own interests, so a mismatch forces a choice.

text: Large word budgets justify hiring an editor, or bringing one on contract once most writing is done, and editors can make cost-saving arguments that appeal to management.
when: The project has a large dialogue or script word budget
why: Writing that seems clear to its author may be unintelligible to others, so an outside polisher helps.

text: Small teams can cope with design through frequent conversation, while larger teams have a much harder time.
why: Readers treat design documents as plans, theories or blueprints, and only conversation reconciles that difference.

text: The team shrinks in QA/polish because most production artists and outside talent are no longer needed.
when: In the final months of production, during QA and polish
why: Work shifts from building new features to verifying and polishing what already exists.

text: The large-team process assumes a specialist for each role, while smaller studios often use generalists who handle more aspects themselves.
A smaller team may need to cut ideas that a larger team could build.
when: When a smaller or less experienced team assesses its idea pool
why: Feasibility depends on the team's capacity, so ideas buildable by larger teams can be unbuildable here.

text: Larger teams and longer schedules increase professional and personal stress, which must be managed.
when: As team sizes grow and production schedules lengthen

text: For team sessions, use large sticky sheets of about 2 by 2.5 feet, or butcher paper taped to walls.
when: Team brainstorming sessions
why: Large surfaces let teams reposition and reuse ideas

text: Web games cost less to produce, so experimental designs carry less financial risk than boxed products.
A method that reproduces known results is more trustworthy for new cases than one checked only on its own output.
A packaging-style agent suits a team that has technology but needs a desirable property to pitch.
why: They combine technology and property into a packaged pitch that publishers might not spot alone.

text: Consider bytecode when the host language is too low-level for the task, compile times slow iteration, or behavior must be sandboxed because it is untrusted.
when: Deciding whether a game system should use a bytecode VM
why: These conditions make scripted behavior worth its added complexity.

text: Use memory-based analysis when in-the-moment analysis would spoil the experience.
when: Experience would be disrupted by analysis
why: Preserving the experience matters more than immediate notes.

text: Add abstraction only when confident the code needs that flexibility; resist speculative design, following the principle that you aren't going to need it.
when: designing new code
why: Unused flexibility adds cost without benefit.

text: Think-aloud is a method in which players or participants narrate their thoughts, actions and reasoning continuously during a task, revealing first reactions and expectations about an interface.
when: Understanding first contact with an interface
why: Narration exposes the mental model behind actions.

text: Think-aloud commentary reveals players' expectations and choices, but many people need help getting started with it.
when: Running think-aloud playtests
why: Speaking aloud while acting is unfamiliar to many, so they need prompting to begin.

text: Some players find thinking aloud natural; identify them, or train repeat testers to do it.
why: Speaking can change how some players act, and others freeze or go silent under stress.

text: Run think-aloud tests one on one with about six participants.
when: Planning a think-aloud study
why: Individual sessions avoid peer influence.

text: 1) Ask testers to think aloud about their choices and uncertainties. 2) If they fall silent, prompt them with a question about what they are thinking.
when: When playtesters stop narrating their choices during play
why: A running monologue exposes expectations that silent clicking would hide.

text: 1) Ask testers to narrate their goals aloud during play. 2) Compare their stated goals with the planned goals. 3) Note any drift onto tangents.
why: Shows whether players pursue intended goals

text: Ask participants to speak as they think and tell them no way is wrong; say the software is being tested, not the participant.
when: Briefing participants for think-aloud
why: Clear framing reduces anxiety and keeps feedback honest.

text: Transfer of learning means a skill trained in one context improves performance in another context.
Subject matter experts come in two kinds: those who hold the facts and those who know the best ways to teach them, and designers benefit from both.
Training studies are fewer than correlational studies, so the evidence base for game-based skill training is thinner.
Months of testing condition combinations can yield a teaching curriculum that becomes the basis for a first-level tutorial.
Keep presentations to about 15 minutes and devote most of the session to team practice.
why: Short time pressure filters out mental blocks that stop teams from trying.

text: Five evidence levels for transformation, weakest to strongest: feeling it works, anecdotes, expert approval, informal surveys and in-play assessment, scientific testing.
when: checking whether a transformational game works
why: Evidence strength rises with rigor

text: Have teams work on their current game during training rather than on classroom exercises, so the work is real.
why: Practice on real problems forms lasting habits, which handouts and lectures fail to create.

text: Learning level design through a specific tool builds software skill but can miss what makes spaces memorable, while learning through theory builds understanding but can ignore playability; both are needed.
when: Choosing how to develop level design skill
why: Tool mastery and spatial theory each cover what the other lacks.

text: Stick to the comparison formula, since people expect it and it keeps discussion on the idea rather than the presentation.
when: Writing a pitch comparison
why: Familiar structure reduces distraction

text: A first tutorial level should take about 5 minutes for players to complete.
when: When timing playtesters through the first tutorial level

text: 1) Ask players objective questions about an item's purpose or a mission's goal. 2) Avoid asking whether the game was clear.
when: Testing onboarding with players
why: Objective questions reveal actual understanding, while asking about clarity gives vague opinions

text: 1) Download the engine and the companion tutorial files. 2) Unzip the package and read its README. 3) Note the engine install folder, whose exact name changes with each version. 4) Open the tutorial level from the File menu and start it with the Start this level on PC icon.
1) Expand the concept description into a three to five page treatment. 2) Ask formal and dramatic questions while writing. 3) Treat the document as a draft that will change.
when: After outlining the formal system

text: 1) Use playtesting to find what players must learn. 2) Build the tutorial as short scenes that teach basic mechanics and introduce the story.
Design details change until the last minute, so tutorial and manual text drifts from implementation; assign someone to verify it against the implementation.
when: Late in development
why: Text written against an earlier design can easily contradict a gameplay rule the team has since changed.

text: An onboarding plan is a spreadsheet listing every element players must learn, grouped by system, with priority, timing, order, difficulty, rationale, teaching method, and narrative support.
Observing players as they use a tutorial, through playtesting, reveals how they internalize skills.
Use marquee selection in the Top view, where a selection box is easiest to draw.
when: selecting several actors by box
why: a flat top-down view makes the box easy to place

text: Invest in lowering skill barriers, since a large community of potential players would enjoy the game with lower entry costs.
why: Expert designers stop noticing barriers they have already mastered, so they undervalue accessibility.

text: Without a shared UX strategy, each group pushes its own priorities and the team loses sight of the overall experience.
why: Development is a series of tradeoffs, and a shared experience goal guides which choices fit.

text: 1) Hold Ctrl and click to select several actors. 2) Hold Ctrl and Alt and drag a marquee in any non-Perspective view to select everything inside the box.

1) List the main elements players must be taught. 2) Estimate how hard each is to learn, rating original mechanics as harder than familiar ones. 3) Prioritize the list. 4) Plan onboarding early and schedule its production with the team.
when: Early production when time and budget are limited.
why: Teams rarely have time to give every lesson its own quest or map.

text: 1) List the elements to learn in WHAT. 2) Assign each to a Category. 3) Set Priority 0-3. 4) Give approximate WHEN timing. 5) Assign unique decimal Tutorial order values such as 1.1, 1.2, 2.1. 6) Rate Difficulty as Difficult, Moderate, or Simple. 7) Add WHY, HOW, Narrative wrapper, and UX feedback.
why: Unique decimal order values let the table be sorted into a chronological teaching sequence.

text: Set onboarding priority from the UX view of what players must learn, not from the production schedule. Use a 0 to 3 scale from must-learn to ok-if-never-learned.
why: Priority should reflect what players need, not what is convenient to build first.

text: Fill in the WHY column, the player's reason to learn, for every feature that is not simple to learn.
when: building the onboarding plan, early in development
why: Skipping WHY for complex features loses the meaning of teaching them.

text: Story audiences constantly ask what happens next, what the hero should do, and where something went, making decisions even in noninteractive stories.
why: the desire to decide exists in noninteractive stories too

text: Once testers are told how a game works, their natural first impression can no longer be observed.
Nervous manner suggests the presenter does not believe what they say, so listeners discount the message.
when: Presenting a pitch
why: Listeners read body language and hesitation as doubt about the content.

text: Players may interpret cues differently than developers intended, and even experienced players can get stuck when a hold-button prompt reads like a loading message.
when: Designing unfamiliar input prompts or start screens
why: Designers' familiarity with a cue does not mean the audience shares their reading.

text: Strong artwork draws in players who would otherwise pass over a game.
when: when deciding whether a game gets noticed or tried
why: Artwork that makes a world feel solid and real leads players to treat the game with more seriousness.

text: Faked enthusiasm reads as phony, while genuine excitement is contagious and draws the audience in.
when: Presenting a game
why: Audiences detect insincerity and respond to real energy.

text: Audiences often prefer particular play-matrix quadrants, and young children tend to prefer physical and chance play, moving toward mental and chance play as they age.
The unconscious can reach a feeling through inferences the person cannot consciously trace, as in a detective's hunch.
when: When a feeling arises without a clear conscious reason.
why: Emotional evaluation can combine cues the conscious mind does not register.

text: A designer cannot control the audience once they join an experience, but can control the context they bring in, which gives the most leverage.
when: when designing an experience with a live audience
why: Audience members' prior circumstances shape how they engage from the start.

text: A love deficit is a team condition where shared enthusiasm for the game is missing, and experienced members recognize it readily.
Correlation means two variables rise and fall together, but it does not show which one, if either, causes the other.
Good quality and usability are necessary for an enjoyable game but not sufficient on their own.
Postgame interviews handle questions too complex for surveys and reveal how players really felt.
Post-play surveys collect quantifiable answers after a session.
Postgame questions can cover general impressions, formal elements, dramatic elements, procedures and controls, and end-of-session appeal.
Professional usability labs tend to produce superior results, and their methods can be adapted for in-house sessions.
Recorded facial expressions can be coded into emotional categories to quantify enjoyment, though designers rarely do this.
Postgame question themes include first impression, frustration, pacing, satisfaction, most exciting moment, and whether the game felt too long or short.
UX research labs were part of production at some AAA studios in the 2000s, and a few UX experts such as usability specialists worked in games during that period.
At the Expert stage, a small dedicated team or one person does UX, but the process is not yet deep or consistent; quantifying research and comparing tested and untested projects advances it.
Clear proof of UX value for upper management often appears only after launch, when business metrics can be linked to UX issues.
An earlier UX maturity model has eight stages, from hostility toward usability at stage 1 to a user-driven corporation at stage 8.
During production, usability and game feel are tested first, and engageability follows as systems start to mesh.
Studies report casual game audiences are 60 to 70% female, making casual design an easier route to female-friendly titles.
Treat team love for the project as a necessity rather than a luxury, since a great game is unlikely without it.
Look for curious developers within the game team; they will try a few UX methods on their own.
when: Building UX adoption

text: When research requests keep increasing, propose a dedicated UX team.
when: When requests for user research from teams are steadily rising.

text: Game studios can progress quickly through early UX maturity stages by building trust and delivering quick wins developers can own.
when: Early UX maturity stages
why: The game industry lets the early UX stages move quickly, unlike the later stages, which are much harder to reach.

text: Prefer ranking annotation schemes over rating scales, because ratings showed order-of-play effects, inconsistent answers and lower inter-rater agreement.
when: when collecting experience annotations for player models
why: rating scales show order-of-play effects and inconsistent answers

text: Lead creative teams through inspiration, collaboration and appreciation, and set people up to look smart, rather than through fear.
when: Leading creative game development teams.
why: Love and appreciation encourage voluntary risk taking that fear cannot produce.

text: Prior player knowledge changes how much cognitive load a mechanic introduces, so know the target audience before introducing it.
why: Cognitive load depends on the learner's expertise, so the same situation affects players with different prior knowledge differently.

text: Check a design against the list of player types to see whether it appeals to a range of motivations or serves only a few.
when: Evaluating whether a game's appeal is too narrow
why: Different motivations need different rewards; a list reveals neglected audiences.

text: The same scene can demand different attention from different players, so judge how much a scene can carry against the intended audience.
why: Processing two sources of information at once is extremely difficult for people.

text: Audience comprehension drives enjoyment, so creative leads should imagine the game from the audience's view.
A negative reaction may come from someone outside the target audience; you can set it aside, but still ask why the reviewer reacted that way.
when: the reviewer is not in the target audience
why: Outsiders are less familiar with the material, so their proposed fixes are suspect, yet their reactions expose hidden team assumptions.

text: A usability facility with observation glass and an adjacent viewing room lets developers watch sessions as they happen and discuss them.
when: After teams become keen on running more user studies and a dedicated test space is approved.

text: The earlier UX issues are identified, the less they cost to fix.
Usability testing run throughout development can substantially raise sales when a game is designed to reach a wider audience.
why: Fixes from repeated testing make the game accessible to more players.

text: Asking 20 or more questions in a row exhausts testers and degrades their answers.
why: Tired testers stop answering accurately, so answer quality matters more than question count.

text: Lost play time on entry can reach about five minutes, which is over 8% of a sixty-minute experience.
when: when a timed experience has a fixed duration
why: Functional play only starts after players enter the room, even though their experience of the game begins earlier.

text: Treating correlation as proof of causation, e.g., assuming games improve player skills or cause attention problems, ignores that struggling students may play more.
Long, exhaustive UX reports sent to a busy team are likely to be ignored.
when: when the development team is swamped and under pressure to ship on time
why: They cannot spend hours reading long reports and need concise feedback they can act on quickly.

text: Forgetting earlier UX findings when a feature returns for rework can repeat old mistakes.
why: Retrieving earlier feedback prevents the team from repeating mistakes already identified.

text: Inventing answers on the spot to look competent misleads the team. Find the right answer or point people to whoever has it.
Judging an audience by cheap lookalike products can create a lasting stereotype and the false conclusion that it does not buy games.
why: The industry files the audience under one product genre rather than seeing it as a market.

text: Show concept art and storyboards to the target audience to test whether characters, story, and audience appeal work before the game exists.
when: when appeal of characters, story, or audience is uncertain or being validated
why: Appeal cannot be discovered late, so the test must happen before characters and story are built into the game.

text: 1) Categorize each issue by type, such as UI, learning curve, or metagame. 2) Rate its severity as critical, medium, or low. 3) Give each issue a short headline and a detailed description with screenshots or clips. 4) Suggest options tied to developers' goals. 5) List what worked well and issues fixed since the last build.
when: Writing a report after a UX test
why: A consistent structure makes findings traceable and shows progress.

text: 1) Pose hypotheses with the game team. 2) Design a standardized protocol. 3) Collect and analyze data. 4) Remove human biases where possible.
why: Personal perception, limited attention and unreliable memory can lead to expensive setbacks.

text: 1) Ask whether you love the project; if not, find how to change that. 2) Ask whether everyone on the team loves it; if not, find how to change that.
when: enthusiasm seems to be fading
why: Team love is a predictor of project success.

text: 1) Write a detailed UX report to keep research rigor. 2) Send a short email listing the top five issues needing immediate attention.
when: Production teams with little time
why: Balances rigor with brevity.

text: 1) Form hypotheses about users. 2) Generate ideas. 3) Build prototypes. 4) Test with users. 5) Iterate on the findings.
when: same loop applies to PC, VR, AR, and AI-based products
why: The UX mindset gives a framework that reaches product goals more efficiently, whichever platform is used.

text: 1) Observe your own experience of games. 2) Observe others playing. 3) Imagine yourself in their place. 4) Build a picture of how their experiences differ from yours. 5) Predict which experiences they will and will not enjoy.
when: When playtesting happens only occasionally while design decisions are needed every day.

text: 1) Define the target market before development starts. 2) Research what that audience does in its spare time, what it plays now, and what it likes and dislikes. 3) Design from those answers, not assumptions.
when: when targeting a specific audience such as women
why: Guessing what an audience wants is risky; only research into their spare time and tastes shows what fits.

text: Plan UX within the iteration pipeline early in development, following development's rhythm and constraints rather than running on a separate schedule.
when: early in development
why: Issues found on prototypes are cheaper and quicker to fix than after features are built into the engine.

text: Prepare a question script with space for answers and for notes on unexpected turns.
when: When interviewing players after play, for topics too intricate for a simple survey form.
why: Conversations often take unexpected turns, so room for notes captures what the script did not anticipate.

text: Interview players privately when possible, since people speak more honestly without others listening.
why: Testers are less candid when people they know can overhear.

text: During playtester interviews, do not defend the game; focus only on how the tester feels and why, using neutral prompts such as 'What don't you like about it?' or 'Can you tell me more about that?'
when: When interviewing playtesters
why: Defending the game biases answers and hides the real reaction.

text: Code observed behavior literally, such as stayed a long time on the naming screen, and do not infer intent until notes, performance, and survey data are combined.
when: Coding observations during analysis
why: Early intent guesses can contaminate the analysis.

text: Run UX testing only once content is mature enough to produce useful feedback.
why: Testing unready content produces random feedback that is not needed.

text: Expect to iterate on UX findings, since identifying the right problem is often not easy.
why: Each game and audience varies, so the correct problem is not always known upfront.

text: Build lasting UX influence with neutral, data-driven insight grounded in science and cognitive science.
why: Trust builds slowly because UX wins show mainly through live metrics, and many factors make it hard to tie UX changes to revenue.

text: Appeal to a broad population unless deliberately targeting a specific group, because designers with strong power motives may build games that favor dominant players.
when: Setting the target audience
why: Designers' own drives can alienate other players

text: Fit puzzle design to the audience's interests and skills, since enjoyment varies from person to person.
Learn the target audience's prior knowledge, familiarity and expectations before designing visual communication.
why: People build what they see from what they already know, so players with different backgrounds read the same visuals differently.

text: Context-free modelling is desirable but less studied than context-aware modelling; objective measures require sensors and recordings, so gameplay input is more readily available.
why: Objective measures need sensors and recordings, whereas game metrics are derived from interaction patterns the game already produces.

text: Visual artist is a catch-all term for everyone designing a game's visuals, including character creators, illustrators, animators, UI designers and 3D modelers.
Concept art explores characterization, mood, or a space; storyboards fix framing, coloring, and sequencing; previsualizations explore ways to communicate an idea.
Some middleware shows complex Boolean conditions and state machines graphically, so designers can author them without writing code.
Each editor viewport has its own perspective, so moving an actor looks different in each one.
Visual artists design characters, worlds and world objects, interfaces, animations, and cutscenes.
Choose a cheaper actor who understands games over a famous name, and budget for experienced voice actors.
why: Well-known actors are not shown to increase game sales

text: Communicate design through a mix of text, wireframes, concept art, and flowcharts, because game developers tend to be visual thinkers.
why: Writing the details forces the team to think through the whole game, from top-level vision down to low-level specifications.

text: Use visual references such as other games, magazines, art books, captured video of real motion, and motion textbooks when briefing artists.
Finalize voice-recorded dialogue well in advance so actors can be booked, cast and recorded, and translations can follow.
when: When voice recording and translated versions of a game's dialogue are planned.
why: Booking, casting, recording and translation steps all depend on settled decisions, so later changes disrupt each of them.

text: Schedule time for a voice-over comment pass in the production plan, because rushed comments can hurt performances.
why: Poorly written voice notes can degrade how actors deliver the lines, and rushed passes leave no time to fix them.

text: Scripts-first production lets voice shape characters and performance, while voice-last production suits volatile scripts but makes voice acting weaker and costlier to revise.
when: Deciding when to record voice in development
why: Late script changes are cheap for voice-last but building characters around voice is expensive

text: A blackboard entry needs three components: a value, a type identifier giving its format, and a semantic identifier giving its meaning.
why: independent experts must interpret shared data

text: A blackboard is a coordination mechanism, not a decision technique, that lets several decision makers share information and take turns acting on it.
An AI request occurs when a high-level decider chooses which lower-level decider to use, such as one AI choosing to build while another chooses which building.
when: Layered AI decision making
why: Hierarchical deciders delegate choices down to specialized deciders.

text: Behavioral rules are unstated norms of good sportsmanship that players follow without being written down, such as not stalling or distracting an opponent.
Behaviors are the potential actions an object can perform in its current state.
Behavior management decides which behavior runs when, and every algorithm must work with both it and the world interface.
Optional metadata on blackboard entries can support execution control, performance measurement, debugging, or an audit trail of which expert wrote each entry and when.
Unless there are very many experts or they scan large linear lists, the experts' run functions determine overall efficiency.
Rete performs unification while also speeding up matching, so it is often used instead of standalone unification algorithms in rule systems.
Connection weights in a perceptron start at small random values.
Looking up the weight from a given neuron searches the input list and returns zero when no connection exists; this search is slow for large networks.
The learning gain is a single global value shared by the whole network.
A general-purpose AI needs infrastructure that delivers the right information to the right code at the right time.
In a special-purpose AI built for one game, the boundary between world interface and AI code may disappear.
Sense management can run incrementally every frame, spreading its work across frames.
Fully defining behavior as data can be done with the Interpreter or Bytecode patterns.
when: type behavior must be fully data-defined
why: These patterns let behavior be expressed as interpreted data rather than compiled code.

text: Standard game AI techniques are separate components that must be combined to make a complete character AI; they do not form a full game AI on their own.
Some games make AI itself the core mechanic, so character behavior is the gameplay rather than support for it.
Blackboard experts can be built with any decision technique, such as decision trees, expert systems, or neural networks.
A blackboard generalizes rule-based systems by allowing any trigger and any rule, so rules can be hosted as experts inside a blackboard.
Top board-game AIs for chess, draughts, backgammon and reversi use dedicated hardware or game-specific optimizations and can compete with top human players.
If every build is viable yet play feels identical, first confirm attribute effects are actually implemented in code, since some have gone unimplemented in shipped games.
when: When every character build is viable yet all of them play the same.
why: Programmers may have skipped implementing some attributes' effects, so the choices change nothing in play.

text: When a list of use cases shares an underlying structure, look for one general solution covering them all instead of coding each case.
when: use case lists with a shared hidden order
why: Piecemeal conditional code for each use case fails on inputs slightly different from the examples the coder considered.

text: Level geometry that is easy to analyze, a research tree that is easy to search, and short turns all ease the turn-based AI's workload.
when: designing turn-based games
why: they keep the search and movement options manageable

text: Each added behavior generally adds player choice and makes outcomes less predictable.
A blackboard has two parts: a main entry list the arbiter ignores, and a separate list of ready-to-execute actions.
why: Working only through the actions list is faster than searching the main blackboard for confirmed actions.

text: Basic range conditions can be combined: AND and OR conditions hold two sub-conditions, and NOT holds one and inverts its result, so conditions nest to any depth.
when: Building complex transition logic from simple tests
why: Combining simple tests supports arbitrarily complex rules.

text: Three patterns define large amounts of behavior: Type Object groups behaviors into categories, Subclass Sandbox offers safe primitives to compose behaviors, and Bytecode moves behavior into data.
why: Games demand far more distinct behaviors than typical software, such as many inhabitants, items, and quests.

text: AI action output falls into four flavors: state changes, animations, movement, and AI requests. Most real actions combine at least two of these flavors.
when: Classifying what an AI decision produces
why: Separating action types lets each be executed by the appropriate system.

text: Simplified lookup and removal helpers in formation sample code must be adapted to a real game's character data, since engines usually differ.
when: Porting formation code into a real engine
why: Implementation depends on the other character data a game tracks, which the simplified sample does not cover.

text: Changing the board inside an insistence check can leave the expert with nothing to do once it is given control.
when: When insistence checks are run for every expert in turn.
why: Another expert may remove the items an expert found, leaving it with nothing to do once given control.

text: With a lookahead shorter than the least common multiple, load spikes can still occur in theory.
when: When the scheduler's lookahead window is smaller than the least common multiple of the frequencies.

text: Software bugs and botched implementations can make a shuffle or die roll less random than intended.
why: Pseudorandom numbers have natural limits on randomness, and software bugs or botched implementations can reduce it further.

text: 1) Define a struct holding an identifier, a type, and a value. 2) Store the board as a list of such entries.
why: A type code tells an expert the data's format, but a separate semantic identifier is needed to know what the value means.

text: 1) Compute node entropy and stop if zero. 2) For each attribute, split examples and compute weighted subset entropy. 3) Keep the attribute with largest gain as the node test. 4) Remove it from the list passed down. 5) Create one child per attribute value and recurse on its subset.

1) Select one fuzzy set and a cut-off value. 2) If its membership is below the cut-off, output false; otherwise output true. 3) If several sets contribute, first merge them into one set with a fuzzy rule.
when: Converting fuzzy membership into a Boolean game decision
why: A single comparison against a cut-off gives a clean yes/no output from fuzzy inputs.

text: Build AI as reusable, combinable tools in a shared engine; each new game usually needs only one or two new algorithms, so this structure speeds development.
when: developing AI for multiple games or characters
why: Level designers and technical artists can then assemble characters from components.

text: Divide complex AI into bite-size components that run across multiple frames, which can make an otherwise too-slow algorithm practical.
when: when an algorithm is too expensive to run in one frame
why: Many algorithms take too long to finish in one frame, so their work must be distributed; a single-frame run would not fit the budget.

text: An expert's insistence function returns a value above zero when the expert can contribute and must not change the board, because it is called for every expert.
why: it runs for all experts each iteration

text: Keep the insistence function fast; an expert that cannot decide quickly can insist and work out details when it gets control.
when: When an expert's check for whether it is useful takes a long time.
why: The expert can defer detailed work until it has control, so the quick check need not do it.

text: The blackboard language must support whatever rule-style matching you intend to perform.
when: When a game requires blackboard architecture alongside rule-driven logic.
why: Blackboard architectures generalize rule-based systems, so the blackboard can manage rules as experts.

text: Keep all behaviors available and switch between them without frame-rate blips or sprawling special-case code.
when: When lower-level behaviors run several different algorithms depending on the orders they receive.

text: Expose formations and synchronized motion to content authors so they can define movement patterns themselves.
when: When the programmer cannot know all the movement patterns that will ship, as in sports games.
why: Programmers cannot anticipate every play and would otherwise have to test every combination themselves.

text: Type identifiers can be type codes, a polymorphic base class with subclasses, or subclasses carrying a type identifier.
when: When stored blackboard data can be of several types, such as integers and vectors.
why: Because data of varied types must be read correctly, the identifier tells an expert how to interpret it.

text: Allowing only same-level transitions removes recursion and simplifies implementation, and runs about as fast when all levels are zero, but cross-level transitions become unavailable.
when: Cross-level transitions are not needed
why: Recursion is only used for cross-level transitions, so same-level transitions bypass it and pay no hierarchy cost.

text: Existing phases are never changed, so the overall schedule is not guaranteed optimal, though the dry-run method works very well in practice.
when: When phase values are chosen as behaviors are added incrementally.
why: Greedy placement never revisits earlier choices.

text: Letting an AI bot take over and the result stand is harder to abuse, but it needs a competent AI; a weak AI makes a disconnect nearly equal to a loss.
when: in two-player games
why: The bot keeps playing for the disconnected player, so a forced disconnect does not hand the attacker an easy win.

text: Blackboards offer flexibility in expert techniques, but that freedom often makes blackboard systems large and cumbersome.
when: When individual experts may use any decision technique, from decision trees to neural networks.
why: Coordinating experts built with any technique requires extra management code and complicated data structures.

text: A blackboard suits mixed expert types, while a dedicated rule system with Rete matching suits stable rule sets where performance matters, since blackboards cannot use rule-specific optimizations.
when: When the rule set is fairly stable and matched with the Rete algorithm.
why: Rete is a rule-specific optimization

text: Major 3D modelling packages expose SDKs, typically C or C++ libraries, plus scripting languages, so developers can write plug-ins that capture AI data.
All engine assets are stored in packages, and an asset's full name begins with its package name, the text before the first full stop.
A tool that translates a higher-level authoring format into bytecode is essentially a compiler.
An imported sound file becomes a SoundNodeWave asset. The terms sound, wav, and SoundNodeWave refer to the same thing.
When reverb volumes overlap, the volume with the higher Priority value supplies the reverb settings for the shared space.
when: Nested or overlapping reverb volumes, such as a small room inside a large area
why: The engine resolves overlap by priority, so the smaller volume overrides the larger one where they intersect

text: The sample array-based file implementation has a fixed maximum of 4096 elements, so a file cannot grow beyond that limit.
when: using the sample implementation
why: Storage is a fixed-size array declared with a constant bound, so it cannot grow past that limit.

text: Editing game scripts to change sounds alters behavior for every player on that game version, not just testers.
when: When sound references are changed in a game's script file.
why: Script changes are compiled into the game version, so they reach every player of that version, not only testers.

text: Randomized parameter values take effect only when a sound is triggered again, so sounds must be retriggered to hear the change.
when: Varying a playing sound's parameters at runtime
why: Parameters are read when playback starts

text: A nested IF places one IF inside a parameter of another IF, chaining tests so that a later result depends on an earlier test.
The fundamental operators are the equality test, which yields TRUE or FALSE, and assignment, which makes one variable equal to another.
OR(...) returns false only when all its parameters are false.
NOT(x) takes a single argument and returns the opposite of its truth value.
A procedure that calls itself only behind a condition is equivalent to a loop, and a recursive type whose recursive part sits behind a condition is equivalent to a sequence.
An optimizing compiler uses knowledge about the program to drop branches whose outcome it can determine, producing shorter and faster code.
when: a variable's value is known at a test
why: Knowing the value a variable must hold lets the compiler evaluate the test ahead of time, so the branch is not needed.

text: Conjunction and disjunction are conditional: p & q is FALSE when p is FALSE, and p OR q is TRUE when p is TRUE, so the right operand is not needed and may be undefined.
when: When the left operand of a conjunction is FALSE.
why: The result is already fixed by the left operand, so the right operand's value is never consulted.

text: A transition holds a condition object whose test method is called when checking whether the transition triggers, enabling composable trigger logic.
when: Designing state machine transition triggers
why: A plain state machine struggles to express combined tests such as far away AND low health.

text: Each condition test is a method call; in C++ polymorphic calls slow evaluation and can disrupt the processor pipeline, which matters when many characters check every transition every frame.
when: Evaluating many transitions per frame
why: Virtual dispatch adds overhead on every test.

text: Writing a separate conditional for each use case is fragile: it breaks when inputs differ slightly from the examples considered.
when: When a problem arrives as a list of separate use cases with different required outcomes.
why: Case-by-case logic only covers the cases its author anticipated.

text: 1) Push the current value of each input onto the stack. 2) Apply the operators in grouping order, popping operands and pushing results. 3) Recall the saved value and combine it with the result. 4) Store the final result into its target.
when: Translating a nested arithmetic expression into bytecode for a stack VM
why: Each remember maps to a push and each recall to a pop, so the translation is mechanical and grouping needs no explicit instruction.

text: Double buffering makes a series of sequential updates appear simultaneous to observers, so update order is irrelevant because every object reads the previous frame's state.

Buffering collects a stream of data in memory and transfers it in blocks, letting producer and block-oriented device run concurrently; sequential access allows this, using secondary storage far more effectively.
why: Devices such as tapes need fixed-rate data in large blocks.

text: A buffered class keeps a current buffer and a next buffer of its state. Reads come from current, writes go to next, and a swap publishes finished changes at once.
A circular buffer is a finite array used as a first-in-first-out queue with write and read indices that wrap around, plus a count n with 0 ≤ n ≤ N.
why: Fetched slots are no longer needed, so the array can be reused.

text: Double buffering works at the implementation level, so most of the rest of the codebase is unaware that it is used.
The swap is often as cheap as assigning a pointer.
Graphics APIs provide buffer swapping to avoid tearing: OpenGL uses swapBuffers(), Direct3D uses swap chains, and XNA swaps framebuffers inside endDraw().
The full output sequence of a 64-bit generator cannot fit in typical memory, so seed candidates must be narrowed first.
Let the nature of the data decide buffer granularity: use one monolithic buffer for a single block of state and distributed buffers when each object owns its data.
why: Swapping a monolithic buffer takes one pointer swap, while distributed buffers require telling every object to swap.

text: A buffer decouples producer and consumer, so a slow consumer can catch up later; decoupling grows with buffer size and helps only when average rates match but fluctuate.
when: Producer and consumer rates are about equal on average but fluctuate.
why: The buffer holds the surplus data meanwhile, so a slow consumer can catch up later.

text: 1) Apply each incremental edit to the next buffer. 2) When edits are complete, swap the buffers so the old current buffer becomes the next buffer and is reused.
when: When state is modified incrementally, may be read mid-edit, and readers must not wait or see work in progress.
why: Writes go to the next buffer and a swap publishes them at once, so readers see only completed states.

text: 1) Choose buffer size N as a common multiple of producer block size Np and consumer block size Nc. 2) Track empty slots ne and filled slots nf separately. 3) Producer waits when ne becomes negative; consumer waits when nf becomes negative.
when: Producer deposits blocks of Np elements and consumer fetches blocks of Nc elements.
why: Separate counters make the symmetry between fetching and depositing visible, replacing one shared counter.

text: 1) Copy the cells. 2) Right-click the target cell and choose Paste Special. 3) Choose Paste Values Only.
when: A random or formula result must stop recalculating
why: Pasting values stores each cell's current result as a plain value, so it no longer recalculates when its inputs change.

text: 1) Start with an array. 2) When it is full, double its size and copy the items over. 3) Enqueue then has constant amortized cost.
when: Capacity may exceed a fixed bound.
why: Doubling spreads the copy cost across many enqueues.

text: The buffer swap must be atomic: no code may access either buffer while the swap happens.
when: When double buffering, at the swap step after the state has been modified

text: Fetch requires n > 0 and deposit requires n < N; in single-agent use, violating fetch's condition is a programming error and violating deposit's means the buffer is too small.
when: When only one agent activates deposit and fetch

text: A monolithic buffer swaps with a couple of pointer assignments. Distributed buffers require visiting every object to swap, so the cost grows with the object count.
when: When many objects each hold a piece of the buffered data

text: Double buffering always needs twice the memory because two copies of the state exist. On memory-constrained devices, look for other ways to keep state from being accessed during modification.
A primitive type can be defined by listing its values, and its values are then the enumerated constants of that type.
A type is the set of values that a constant may hold, a variable may assume, an expression may yield, or a function may produce.
Explicit pointers let programmers state exactly where storage is shared, and allow general structures, including infinite, circular and shared ones, that implicit storage allocation cannot express.
C++ types are not generally first-class values, so passing a class itself as a runtime value needs extra work.
Since C++11, a function-local static is initialized only once even under concurrent calls, so an accessor returning one is thread-safe for initialization.
A compiler can sometimes remove a virtual call once it knows the concrete type, and this happens more often within JIT compilers.
when: The concrete type is known at compile or JIT time
why: Knowing the target lets the compiler replace the indirect call with a direct one

text: New types are usually defined from previously defined types, and values of a structured type combine component values.
Keep an object's type fixed after creation where possible, because a fixed type simplifies code, understanding, and debugging.
when: deciding whether types may change at runtime
why: Changing types adds state that must be validated and makes behavior harder to follow.

text: Use explicit pointers when the number of components is unknown in advance or when sharing and selective updating are needed; fixed small structures do not need them.
when: When structures must be shared or be circular or graph-like
why: Explicit references allow circular or graph structures and dictated sharing, which purely recursive data definitions cannot express.

text: Without inheritance, designers end up tuning the same value in many places.
when: many types share attributes and no inheritance exists
why: Shared values must be edited separately in each type, so changes are error-prone.

text: Have the depth-first search return an action and the next cutoff, passing the cutoff by reference so the caller receives the updated value.
when: Implementing IDA* in C++
why: The caller must see the smallest exceeded cutoff

text: Treat the attribute list as fixed in advance; if it is not, an extra application-specific algorithm is needed to choose attributes.
when: When attributes are consistent across examples and known beforehand

text: Fix a maximum string length when storing strings, so that no dynamic storage allocation is needed.
when: When a bounded maximum length still gives enough flexibility for the application
why: Each value's length is capped at a maximum, so storage can be fixed rather than dynamically allocated.

text: Explicit class fields make a command's data clear to readers, while closures capture state so implicitly that it is hard to see.
when: When the command has multiple operations, such as undo support, even in languages with closures
why: Automatic capture of state by closures hides what data they hold; a class with fields states it outright.

text: Encapsulated type objects hide the pattern from the rest of the codebase and let the typed object override type behavior; exposed type objects allow use without a typed object but widen the API.
when: designing a type object system
why: Encapsulation limits what callers depend on, while exposure gives simpler access at the cost of a larger public interface.

text: A trigger is an invisible area that starts scripted events, such as audio playback, when the player enters it.
A level can be stored as a grid of typed tiles, such as sky, brick or pipe, each addressed by two numbers with tile (0,0) at the upper left.
when: When building the level of a 2D game
why: A typed list of tiles makes each tile's relation to others easy to find, without detailed per-object positions.

text: 1) From current velocity, predict the next-frame position. 2) If it falls inside a solid tile, place the character on top of it or flush against it. 3) Set vertical velocity to zero on any collision, from above or below.
when: When gravity constantly acts on a character standing on solid tiles
why: Gravity would otherwise keep pushing the character through solid objects, so the snap-back must repeat each frame.

text: Keeping confirmed actions in their own list lets execution run faster, since no search of the main board is needed.
why: Confirmed entries are already gathered, so execution never has to filter the full blackboard.

text: History cells that refer to themselves are only retained when iterative calculation is enabled; without it the recorded history is lost.
when: Building a move log with self-referencing cells

text: 1) Use the general source code of an action manager. 2) Modify it to nest compound actions more deeply than its interface allows.
when: Extending an action manager to deeper hierarchies.
why: The source is general, so structural changes are possible beyond the UI.

text: 1) Keep a list of executed commands and a pointer to the current one. 2) Executing appends the command and moves the pointer. 3) Undo moves the pointer back and undoes that command. 4) Redo moves the pointer forward and executes its command. 5) A new command after undos discards the commands past the pointer.
why: A list with a movable current reference generalises single-step undo to several levels.

text: 1) Create a global timer cell that increments by 1 each iteration. 2) Place numbered slots in a separate range. 3) In each slot, return the current move if the timer matches the slot number, otherwise keep the slot's previous value.
when: Logging which action was chosen at each time step using iteration
why: Records which move was chosen at each time step, so the choices persist across iterations.

text: Run every action through a common execute method so the manager can process any action type uniformly.
when: Implementing AI action dispatch
why: A shared interface lets new action types plug in without changing the manager.

text: Map each input to one clear action with its own timing, so every control has a predictable effect.
when: when designing the input-to-action mapping for a ship or character
why: Distinct actions with distinct timing make control legible

text: Create a new undo-capable command object for each player action, since each one records a specific change at a specific time.
why: Each command keeps a reference to the state from before it ran, so undo can return to it.

text: Placing a queen marks its row and both diagonals occupied; removing it marks them free again, so backtracking restores the state.
why: A queen checks every piece in its column, row and diagonals, so those lines cannot hold another queen.

text: Hiding behavior behind an opaque execute method keeps decision makers from running arbitrary code, at the cost of making action behavior less visible.
when: Designing action execution for AI systems
why: Restricting what actions can do makes behavior safer but harder to inspect.

text: Snapshotting a whole object for undo wastes memory when a command changes only a small part; storing just the changed fields is cheaper.
when: a command touches a small part of an object

text: Pointing a command at a different actor lets the player control that actor, though this is uncommon in practice.
Serializable commands can be sent over a network and replayed, which supports networked multiplayer.
Request and command are alternative names for a message.
An interface with a single method that returns nothing often indicates the Command pattern is in use.
Siblings that communicate only through shared message values remain decoupled from one another.
when: components exchange notifications through a container
why: Each component depends only on the message format, not on other components.

text: Keep communication simple: use a few message types stored where lower behaviors can read them, such as an in-tray per behavior that higher layers write orders into.
when: Multitiered AI where only a handful of distinct messages pass between layers.

text: Have the subject pass itself to the observer so that an observer watching several subjects can tell which one sent the notification.
when: when one observer watches multiple subjects
why: the notification alone does not identify the sender

text: Do not use a queue when the sender needs a response, because a queued sender has no way to receive one.
when: When the sender needs a response to the request it makes.
why: Queues take control from the sender, which can only enqueue a request and cannot follow up.

text: A queue gives the receiver control to delay, aggregate or discard requests, while the sender loses control and can only enqueue and hope for the best.
why: The buffer sits between push and pull, so timing decisions move to the receiver.

text: Coupled code means understanding one piece requires the other; decoupling lets each be reasoned about alone, and a change to one usually does not force a change to the other.
why: Decoupling is the main tool for making change easier, since the fewer places a change touches, the easier it is to make.

text: The container acts as a Mediator, passing messages along without knowing what they mean.
when: a container routes component messages
why: Routing without interpreting messages keeps the container generic.

text: Dependency injection means outside code passes a dependency into the object that needs it, rather than that object or a locator constructing the instance itself.
Connection getCost and getToNode normally return stored values, so the connection class is rarely a bottleneck.

Three patterns decouple code in different ways: Component separates domains within an entity, Event Queue decouples communicating objects in space and time, and Service Locator decouples code from the provider of a facility.
when: choosing a decoupling pattern
why: Each pattern decouples along a different axis.

text: Shared facilities such as memory management, logging and random numbers are needed almost everywhere in a game.
Before using a global, consider passing the object as a function parameter; this is simple, makes coupling obvious, and covers most needs.
when: The object is core to the function's job, such as a rendering context.
why: Keeps dependencies visible in the signature.

text: Avoid wrapping an outside call in an operation that only forwards to it, since the outside method can be called directly.
when: An operation's only job is to pass the call to an outside system.
why: Pure forwarding adds little value; the exception is when it keeps a base class field, such as an engine reference, hidden from subclasses.

text: Direct component references suit closely related domains such as animation and rendering, input and AI, or physics and collision.
when: choosing a communication method between components
why: Tightly related domains already depend on each other, so the coupling is acceptable.

text: Use coupling when the pool serves one known object type and memory matters; use decoupling for a generic pool holding arbitrary types.
when: When pooled objects already carry state that shows whether they are in use.
why: Using the object's own state avoids storing extra in-use flags, saving memory.

text: The most common service locator design registers providers from outside code; the locator knows only the abstract interface while outside code constructs the concrete provider and registers it.
why: Outside code builds the concrete provider, so it can pass in details like a remote player's address that the locator cannot know.

text: A configuration file names the provider class, and reflection instantiates that class by name at runtime, so the service needs no compile-time reference.
why: Reflection creates the named class at runtime, so no compile-time reference to the service is needed.

text: Disabling a service this way saves its memory and CPU and stops its side effects, such as sounds playing while a debugger is paused.
why: Unregistered services stop consuming memory and CPU, and stop sounds that would fire while debugging.

text: Passing cross-cutting services such as logging or memory management as parameters clutters function signatures and a module's public API, where they do not belong.
when: Shared services used by many functions.
why: Such concerns are unrelated to the module's core parameters, such as rendering parameters for rendering code.

text: Direct calls from many gameplay areas scatter feature logic, such as achievements, through unrelated code like collision resolution.
when: When achievement unlocks are called directly from many gameplay areas across the codebase.
why: Each trigger site must know about the feature.

text: Conditions that mix several domains, such as collision, visibility, and sound, in one check make a change in one domain break others without warning.
when: One class contains logic spanning physics, rendering, and audio.
why: Each domain depends on the others' internals.

text: Deferring the connection between two code pieces to runtime adds flexibility but makes their dependencies harder to see by reading the code.
why: Wiring happens at runtime, so the code alone does not reveal which pieces connect.

text: 1) Create the object with its parameterless constructor. 2) Call its init method with the remaining data. 3) Return the initialized object, so callers cannot skip initialization.
when: Two-stage initialization is used and half-built objects must be prevented.
why: Wrapping creation in one function makes the init step unskippable.

text: 1) Give a component a pointer to its matching peer at construction. 2) Call the peer's methods directly when the state is needed.
when: wiring components that belong to the same domain pair
why: Construction-time wiring makes the dependency explicit and avoids lookups at runtime.

text: Make callers, including entities, depend only on abstract interfaces rather than concrete classes, so providers can change without touching them.
when: Components or services are supplied from outside.
why: Hides concrete types behind interfaces, supporting encapsulation.

text: Skip registering a system's provider so a null service takes its place; wrapping that null service in a logger still logs the calls it would have handled.
when: Disabling a system temporarily.
why: Callers always receive a valid object, so they never need to check for null.

text: Isolate and abstract modules from each other, giving each clear inputs and outputs, like objects with defined interfaces.
when: In large-scale game projects with many interacting subsystems.
why: Defined inputs and outputs make it possible to trace how a change elsewhere propagates.

text: Read pattern samples for the idea they express, not as models of production style, since sample code may avoid modern language idioms.
when: studying pattern sample code
why: Samples are written to teach ideas, not to demonstrate best practice in the language.

text: Aim for decoupling where it lets one part of the code be understood or changed without the other, since less coupling means smaller ripple from each change.
when: structuring game code modules
why: Lower coupling reduces the knowledge needed before making progress.

text: Share code between classes by having each own an instance of a shared class rather than inheriting from a parent.
when: Two unrelated classes need the same behavior.
why: Composition avoids the hierarchy problems that inheritance creates.

text: Do not expose a class that is valid only in one phase or context, such as simulation but not rendering, through a global locator.
when: When a class is only valid in one phase or context, such as simulation without rendering.
why: Other code could call it at the wrong time.

text: Config-driven locating lets designers swap services without source changes and lets one codebase run several configurations, but the infrastructure is heavy to build and maintain.
when: When designers need to toggle features without touching source code.
why: Location moves out of the codebase, so one codebase can run several configurations.

text: A plain decision tree is predictable and players can learn to exploit it; a timed random element adds apparent life for little implementation cost.
when: Players might learn an agent's pattern
why: Fixed responses are exploitable

text: Automated tests are feasible for much of game code and are a natural part of the change workflow.
Adding justification tracing to an AI system greatly improves debugging of its behavior.
Drawing the influence map as an in-game overlay confirms that areas under a unit's influence are actually picked up.
when: When tuning unit influence values that affect the AI considerably.
why: Designers set influence values, and the overlay shows whether tactical analysis actually picks up each area.

text: A small change to a decision probability can produce a very different play style, which makes such parameters good learning targets.
when: When no formula predicts a parameter's suitability and it must be tried in play.

text: Ad hoc script code can become as hard to debug as C++, and sometimes harder, especially when scripting tools are immature.
when: When character behavior is written as ad hoc code in scripts.
why: Scripting languages often have less mature debugging tools than general-purpose languages.

text: Agreement across many trials does not prove a parameter set is optimal, so treating a converged result as the global best is unjustified.
why: Starting guesses that miss the slope can climb a smaller peak than the true optimum.

text: Copying a large buffer during the swap takes significant time and blocks all reads and writes to both buffers for that duration.
when: Buffers are large, such as full framebuffers
why: The lock held during the copy stalls all access until it finishes.

text: Deferred saves can be lost entirely if the program crashes or loses power before the deferred write runs.
when: Saving state to persistent storage only on close or exit
why: Unsaved changes exist only in memory until the deferred write happens

text: Gaps between walls may be invisible in the editor and hard to find without many testers.
when: When snapping geometry or modular assets together is difficult in the level tools.

text: 1) Find a sudden spike or drop that later returns to normal. 2) Isolate the most extreme time slice. 3) Investigate what changed during that slice.
when: A metric spikes or drops sharply and then recovers.
why: The extreme slice reveals the event behind the anomaly.

text: 1) Strip the game to its core mechanics. 2) Reintroduce removed rules one at a time. 3) Watch how each rule changes the system. 4) Repeat until the broken part is identified.
when: When a prototype is slow, unbalanced, disjointed, or has conflicting rules.
why: Seemingly minor rules can unbalance the system through non-obvious interactions, so isolating them one at a time finds the cause.

text: 1) Track previous time and lag starting at zero. 2) Each frame, add elapsed real time to lag. 3) Process input once. 4) While lag is at least the step, update and subtract the step from lag. 5) Render once.
when: Running a fixed-step simulation decoupled from rendering
why: Updates advance game time in constant steps while rendering happens once per frame.

text: Debug steering by visualizing each behavior's inputs and outputs separately, including when behaviors are blended.
when: When steering behaviors are blended, especially in realistic indoor or urban levels.
why: Blended steering is hard to debug from the final result alone.

text: When anything unusual occurs, whether beneficial or harmful, look into its cause.
when: When anything out of the ordinary happens during playtesting, good or bad.
why: Only someone with expectations can recognize an outcome as surprising.

text: Digital games can track more complex game states than nondigital games because software can store and update many variables.
When an algorithm touches scattered data, each cache miss stalls the CPU for a few hundred cycles while main memory is fetched; a cache hit reads quickly.
why: The processor cannot run the next instruction until the missing data arrives, so it sits idle while the fetch completes.

text: A dirty flag marks derived data as out of date after its primary data changes, and is also called a dirty bit.
when: Caching derived values such as world transforms
why: The flag tells later code whether a costly recomputation is needed

text: A processor can work only on data in cache, and operating-system address translation can add constraints such as aliasing failures between addresses.
On 32-bit PCs, data structures larger than about a megabyte are hard to manage for cache performance.
A full implementation would need several cache classes, one for each data type.
Cache levels L1, L2 and L3 grow larger and slower with each step outward from the CPU.
Cache-hostile memory access can make identical computation about fifty times slower than cache-friendly access.
A cache line-sized block, for example around fifty items, is fetched per miss, and only one block fits in the fast store at a time.
when: Explaining why sequential access beats scattered access
why: Neighbors arrive together, so reading them in order costs one fetch per block

text: Cachegrind is a free profiler that runs a program on a simulated CPU and cache hierarchy, reporting all cache interactions.
when: Measuring cache misses without commercial tools
why: Simulation reports misses per location without requiring specific hardware counters

text: The dirty flag pattern applies to calculation work, such as transform math, and to synchronization work, such as writing data to disk or sending it over the network.
Web frameworks and physics engines use dirty flags to mark data needing processing, letting unchanged data be skipped.
Cache a topic when it is requested repeatedly within a frame.
why: The stored result is refreshed only when its frame stamp lags the current frame, so repeat requests within one frame reuse it.

text: Caching world transforms pays off when many objects are static; eager refresh is acceptable when few objects change and each change is independent.
when: Choosing between caching and eager refresh of world transforms.
why: Static objects keep a valid cached transform indefinitely, so recomputing their unchanged transforms every frame is wasted work.

text: Cache derived data behind a dirty flag for slow calculations when memory is cheap; compute on demand when time is plentiful and memory is scarce.
when: Deciding between caching and on-demand computation.
why: Stored results let later requests skip the calculation, while discarding them saves memory but repeats the work each time.

text: On a cache miss, the CPU loads a contiguous cache line, typically 64 to 128 bytes, so memory adjacent to recently accessed memory is reached faster than arbitrary memory.
when: When the next byte needed sits inside the chunk that was just fetched.
why: Neighboring data arrives with the requested byte.

text: Pointer-based traversal adds an indirection per access; contiguous arrays keep needed data adjacent in memory, improving cache use and speeding up loops.
when: When a per-frame update loop walks many components in sequence.
why: Walking contiguous arrays in order streams adjacent bytes to the CPU instead of following pointers to scattered locations.

text: Dirty-flag batching computes each affected derived value once per batch of changes, and skips objects whose inputs never changed or were removed before use.
when: Many primary changes occur between uses of the derived data, such as once per frame before rendering
why: Chained changes collapse into one recalculation, and unused results are never computed

text: Caching world transforms with a dirty flag passed down the traversal lets a render pass recompute only changed world transforms, since a node is dirty if any ancestor was dirty.
when: Scene graph rendering where the world transform is read only by the render pass.
why: Ancestor changes reach descendants through the traversal flag, so no per-child marking is needed during the update.

text: Refreshing world transforms immediately on each local change repeats work when several ancestors change in the same frame, since a world transform can depend on several changed local transforms.
when: Multiple ancestors of an object change within one frame.
why: Each immediate refresh is thrown away when the next ancestor changes.

text: Each supported polling topic costs constant time and memory to access, excluding the cost of the underlying polling query.
why: Each topic stores only one value and one frame stamp, a fixed amount of data regardless of game state.

text: A concrete polling station keeps, for each cached boolean topic, a value and the frame when it was last refreshed, in slots keyed by group and topic.
why: The frame stamp is what lets the station tell whether a stored value has gone stale.

text: Cache setups differ across PCs, consoles and mobile devices, so performance measurements taken on one machine may not hold on others.
why: Cache hardware differs between machines and platforms, so timings taken on one are not guaranteed on another.

text: The dirty-flag traversal is only safe when render is the sole reader of the cached world transform; other readers need a different approach.
when: Caching world transforms alongside a dirty-flag render pass.
why: Other readers would not trigger the recomputation and could read stale values.

text: 1) If the stored frame is older than the current frame, call the game query. 2) Save its result as the new value. 3) Store the current frame number. 4) Return the stored value.
why: Skipping the query when the stored frame is current avoids repeated lookups of the game state within a frame.

text: 1) On changing primary data, set the dirty flag only, with no computation. 2) When the derived value is needed, check the flag. 3) If set, recompute and clear the flag; otherwise reuse the cached value.
when: Derived data is costly to compute and read less often than primary data changes
why: Deferring recomputation to the point of use collapses many changes into one calculation

text: Use dirty flags only when primary data changes more often than derived data is read; skip them when derived data is read after nearly every change.
when: Considering a dirty flag for derived data that is hard to update incrementally.
