why: Frequent changes relative to reads clear flags only after data is stale again, and a flag set on every read skips no computation.

text: Cache or pass back the evaluated score so identical parameters are not evaluated twice by the driver and the step function.
when: score evaluation is expensive
why: recomputing wastes time

text: Store the hash in the board object and update it inside the move-making routine, so the hash is not recalculated from scratch on each request.
when: When tens or hundreds of pieces are in play at once.
why: full recalculation is costly

text: Every code path that modifies primary data must set the dirty flag, because a missed path leaves stale derived data that causes hard-to-track bugs.
when: Caching derived data behind a dirty flag.
why: Derived data is a cache, and invalidation is the hardest part of caching.

text: Skipping clean-node math saves computation, but the new conditional branch can cause mispredictions and pipeline stalls that offset the savings.
when: Adding dirty-flag branching to a hot render loop on modern CPUs.
why: Branch mispredictions cost cycles, so the saving is not guaranteed.

text: Fine-grained dirty flags process only changed data but cost more memory and per-chunk overhead; coarse-grained flags save memory and overhead but may process unchanged data.
when: Choosing the size of the unit tracked by a dirty flag.
why: Flag count drives memory and metadata cost, while unit size drives redundant processing.

text: Keeping derived data in memory speeds reuse but uses memory; computing it on demand and discarding it saves memory at the cost of repeated computation.
when: Choosing whether to store derived data behind a dirty flag.
why: Memory and computation trade against each other.

text: Execution management keeps AI within appropriate processor time and memory budgets; it resembles per-area level-of-detail schemes used in rendering but uses its own techniques.
An elegant solution is a small, general piece of logic that correctly covers a large space of cases, found by spotting the hidden order behind examples.
Determinism means the same inputs always yield the same outputs, so failures can be replayed and debugged reliably.
An engine owns the loop and invokes your code; with a library, your code controls the flow and calls the library.
Simple code means less total code to hold in mind before a change, which makes changes easier to reason about.
Classic object-oriented design patterns stay relevant longer than frameworks and methodologies, because object-oriented design changes more slowly.
Dataflow and functional reactive programming have succeeded mainly in narrow domains such as audio processing and chip design.
Modern game codebases can be enormous, with some reaching millions of lines of C++.
when: Assessing the cost of changing hard-coded behavior
why: Large codebases make every behavior change expensive to build and verify.

text: Many games assign each domain its own thread, such as audio, rendering and AI.
Engines with strong level editors mainly import decorations and specialty items, where scale matters less than when whole rooms are imported.
Keep code flexible while design is still being explored, and delay low-level optimizations that lock in assumptions until the design settles.
when: early and mid development
why: Locked-in assumptions make later design changes costly.

text: Get the data structures right first, then the algorithms, then build the rest of the program on top of them.
when: when starting to design a solution

text: Refine a solution by distilling it down to less code, not by accumulating more code on top of it.
why: Less code is easier to hold in mind when changing it, and simple code carries less overhead.

text: Many manager classes are unnecessary; moving their behavior into the class that uses it is often enough.
why: Such caretaker classes often just reflect a weak grasp of object-oriented design rather than a real need.

text: A first bytecode version can fix all parameters, such as always targeting the player, to get a working prototype quickly.
when: Starting a bytecode VM prototype
why: Fixed parameters remove operand decoding, so the core loop can be validated first.

text: If a shared test is costly, such as a line-of-sight check, a decision tree runs it once and is significantly faster than flat transitions that each repeat it.
when: Transitions depend on an expensive sensing test
why: Eliminating repeated evaluation of costly tests saves most of the cost.

text: The closer a language abstraction is to a real computer, the easier representation choice is for the implementor, and one choice usually suits almost all uses.
Update Method, Game Loop and Component together often form the core, or nucleus, of a game engine.
Bundling single instantiation into the class forces that limit on code that only wanted convenient access, and it becomes entrenched at every call site.
In deterministic games that keep players in sync, reading state outside the synchronized set can cause hard-to-find non-determinism bugs.
when: Game logic depends on lockstep or deterministic simulation for network sync.
why: Values outside the synchronized state can differ between machines, so simulations diverge.

text: Exposing a type object makes it part of the typed object's public API, which widens what must be maintained.
when: choosing to expose a type object
why: Callers may come to depend on the type, so changing it becomes costly.

text: 1) Trigger the hazard volume on entry. 2) After a fixed delay, start a looping timer. 3) On each loop, subtract a fixed step from the delay to speed up the repeat. 4) When the delay passes a threshold, play the final cue and apply lethal damage.
when: Building a hazard that escalates while the player stays inside it.
why: Decreasing the loop interval gives a smooth, predictable acceleration toward the threshold.

text: 1) Right-click the sound cue in the content browser. 2) Choose the option to list objects that reference it, to see which scripts use it.
Each expert adds its actions to the action list only once they are confirmed, and keeps unconfirmed actions off it.
why: Because the list holds only agreed actions, execution can run straight through it without checking each entry.

text: Keep the run function short; a long calculation can pause and claim high insistence next iteration, spreading work across frames.
when: When an expert's calculation takes a long time.
why: Returning high insistence guarantees the expert regains control on the next cycle to resume its calculation.

text: Record system limits early, before designers and artists commit to content the platform cannot handle.
when: Before content production starts
why: Designers and artists often don't know what the platform can handle, so they can commit to assets it cannot run.

text: Use a fixed seed during testing, where exact reproduction of results is valuable.
when: testing
why: The same seed yields an identical sequence, so a test's outcome can be rerun and reproduced exactly.

text: For direct device-to-device play, designate one device to resolve random events and broadcast the correct state.
when: direct device-to-device play
why: With no server to hold authoritative state, one device must resolve the logic and send every player the same result.

text: Specify the engine's design, features, and details, including collision detection.
Understand only the parts of the program relevant to your problem, not the whole codebase.
when: before making a change

text: Virtual dispatch and interfaces cost runtime speed and cause cache misses, while locality-driven optimizations lock in assumptions and give up flexibility, inheritance and interface benefits.
when: Choosing between generic and specialized code, or designing core data structures for performance
why: Dispatch deferred to runtime costs overhead, and each pointer hop or vtable lookup crosses memory; assumptions locked into code resist change.

text: Custom data-driven level editors store behavior data per object, so AI markup such as 'to be avoided' or 'to be collected' fits naturally, but they cost a major project.
when: When a studio plans to reuse one custom-built level editor across all its games.
why: Building such an editor is a major project unsuitable for small studios or hobbyists.

text: Moving types into data gains flexibility but loses compiler management of class data and makes type-specific behavior harder to express.
when: choosing a data-driven type object design
why: The compiler no longer tracks type lifetimes and behavior must be modeled manually.

text: With open-source engines a team can change the engine to fit a new idea; other engines permit only scripting within existing features.
why: Engines can steer design toward what they already support, so modifiable source lets a team keep its original ideas.

text: Open source scripting languages are free and modifiable, but some licences require releasing your own product or modifications as open source, and without a vendor nobody takes responsibility for faults or patent and copyright claims.
when: Considering a free scripting language for a commercial product
why: Copyleft-style licences force a product to be published openly, which conflicts with selling a closed commercial game.

text: A class that holds input, motion, collision, animation, rendering, and sound grows into a huge file only a few experts dare to edit, and collects bugs faster than features.
when: One class contains all of a character's behavior.
why: Many behaviors in one place make even small changes far-reaching.

text: The same thing can be modeled as several objects or as attributes of one object; pick whichever representation makes reasoning clearest at the moment.

1) Read input and adjust velocity. 2) Add velocity to position and resolve collision. 3) Choose a sprite from velocity sign and draw it. Doing all three in one routine grows unmanageable as features are added.
when: A single entity update handles input, motion, and rendering together.
why: Each added feature enlarges the same method.

text: Store timers and other per-instance state as fields of each entity, so adding instances needs no new shared variables.
Fetching components from a container adds indirection, which can slow performance-critical inner loops, although components can improve cache coherence.
when: Tight inner loops access components through pointers.
why: Each access must first look up the component.

text: Data Locality arranges data so that data processed together is contiguous in memory in processing order, keeping the CPU cache full as the loop runs over same-type objects.

Component pattern lets one entity span several domains without coupling them: the entity owns components, each handling one domain (input, physics, graphics, sound, AI) and delegates its work to them.
when: one entity must cover several game domains; structuring an entity with the Component pattern
why: Isolated domain classes keep input, physics, graphics, sound, and AI from depending on one another; the entity delegates domain work instead of implementing it.

text: Data-oriented design arranges data in memory for cache-friendly access, treating data layout as a key part of performance design.
when: Performance-critical code touches large amounts of data
why: Access patterns, not object abstractions, determine most of the cost

text: Components stored in flat arrays can keep their own data and methods, so encapsulation is largely preserved.
The base state's update returns a result holding actions, a pending transition and a level, and by default returns the state's own action.
Component is the common game-industry name for this pattern, and it is also the name of an unrelated business-software pattern.
when: searching for or discussing the pattern
why: The shared name can cause confusion when reading other sources.

text: Unity's core GameObject is built around components, Delta3D's GameActor uses an ActorComponent base, and XNA's Game class owns GameComponent objects that apply the pattern to the whole game.
when: Looking for production examples of the component pattern.
why: Several major engines adopt it.

text: CPU speed has grown much faster than RAM access speed since 1980, so programs often wait on memory rather than computing.
when: Judging whether data-heavy code is limited by compute or memory
why: Processor gains outpace memory latency improvements

text: Large class hierarchies are hard to manage, so engines often model entities with Component and Type Object patterns instead of one class per kind.
when: when a game has many entity kinds
why: composition avoids deep hierarchies

text: Entities that are off-screen or not yet unlocked, such as guards, can be moved out of the active list until they are needed.
A plain array of entity pointers with a count suits a small sketch; production code should use a proper collection class.
when: In illustrative sample code where the goal is explaining a pattern, not shipping production code.

text: Data locality can speed up looping over many entities or components each frame, and is worth considering once profiling shows cache misses.
when: Per-frame loops over many entities or components where cache performance matters.

text: Updating entities one domain at a time, such as all AI then all physics, makes it easy to slice components into cache-friendly groups.
when: Entity components are processed in separate passes each frame
why: Each pass touches one kind of data, so the working set stays small

text: Entity variants such as decorations, zones, and props can be built from one GameObject class plus optional physics and graphics components, avoiding subclasses and duplicated code.
when: Designing game entities that differ only by which capabilities they have.
why: Each entity plugs in only the parts it needs, so no class combinations must be hand-written.

text: Larger component structs fit fewer per cache line, so unused cold fields dragged into every frame reduce the useful data a loop gets from each cache line.
when: When a component holds fields used only once in an entity's lifetime but is looped every frame.

text: An entity is just a numeric ID binding components stored in separate collections; components know their entity's ID and find siblings by it, so adding components needs no entity change.
when: Entities need open-ended component sets.
why: The entity has no fixed structure to modify.

text: An abstract entity declares a pure virtual update(), and a world holds pointers to entities and calls update() on each once per frame.
1) Allocate one large contiguous array per component type, sized for the maximum entity count. 2) Store components by value in those arrays, not as pointers. 3) Loop by indexing each array directly.
when: performance-critical update loops
why: Contiguous arrays let the loop read components in sequence without chasing pointers to each one.

text: 1) Move the input-reading code into a component whose update takes the owning entity. 2) Expose position and velocity on the entity so components can read and write them. 3) Have the entity hold the component and call its update first.
when: Splitting input handling out of an entity's update.
why: Components hold no position data, so they must receive the entity.

text: 1) Move motion and collision into a physics component that owns the collision volume. 2) Move sprite selection and drawing into a graphics component. 3) Keep shared position and velocity on the entity and call components in their original order.
when: Completing the split of an entity's update into components.
why: Shared state stays with the entity, and order preserves correct results.

text: Apply the component pattern when a class touches domains that must stay decoupled, when a class has grown massive, or when inheritance cannot precisely select reusable parts.
when: Deciding whether a class should be split into components.
why: Each signal indicates the monolithic design is costing more than it gains.

text: 1) Store an abstract ID per component in the entity. 2) Resolve the ID through a component manager using a linear search for a stored unique ID or a hash table mapping IDs to current indices.
when: When components must move in memory.
why: Raw pointers would break when components move in memory, whereas an ID resolved through a lookup stays valid.

text: 1) If component size s is not a whole number of words, round it up to S. 2) Leave S minus s words unused per component. This unused space is padding.
why: Hardware transfers whole words at once, and a whole-number component size keeps address arithmetic simple.

text: Keep data that different threads modify on separate cache lines, since modifying nearby data across threads causes costly cache synchronization.
when: Multithreaded code.

text: Flat component arrays speed hot loops but make entity handling less direct; a retained entity wrapper pointing into the arrays keeps non-performance code simple.
why: Walking entity-to-component pointers in a loop costs a cache miss at each hop, which flat arrays avoid.

text: Putting update() on the entity class is simplest but scales poorly as entity kinds grow; putting it on components lets parts like rendering, physics and AI update independently.
when: When the game has only a few kinds of entities
why: Subclassing per new behavior becomes brittle, and shared code may not fit a single inheritance chain.

text: Components holding direct references to a peer and calling its methods is simple and fast, but tightly couples that pair while keeping coupling limited to the pair.
when: two closely related components must communicate
why: Direct calls are cheap, but each component depends on the other's interface.

text: Components add complexity: each object becomes a cluster of instances that must be created, initialized, and wired together, and communication and memory layout become harder to manage.
when: Deciding whether to adopt components.
why: The pattern trades simplicity for decoupling and reuse.

text: Entities holding raw component pointers give one-hop access and ignore component placement, but break when components move; entities holding component IDs resolved by a manager allow packing and moving at the cost of lookup speed and complexity.
why: The ID resolves through a lookup to the component's current index, which costs time and bookkeeping memory.

text: 1) Write a free function per monster type that returns a newly constructed instance, not a copy of existing state. 2) Give a single Spawner a callback of type taking no arguments and returning a monster pointer. 3) Pass the desired spawn function to the Spawner constructor. 4) spawnMonster invokes the stored callback.
when: Monster types already have their own classes and a spawner class per type would be redundant boilerplate
why: A plain function pointer avoids a spawner class per monster while keeping the monster classes intact; unlike a prototype-based spawner, it builds fresh instances rather than copying an existing object's state

text: Cache the object count before the update loop so objects spawned during the loop do not update in their spawn frame.

1) Let each listener declare a filter for events, such as mouse events or events in a UI region. 2) Before notifying, compare each event with every listener's filter; invoke only matching handlers and drop non-matching events.
when: A broadcast queue has many listeners.
why: Filtering limits the handlers invoked per event.

text: An event queue is an asynchronous Observer, also called message queue, publish/subscribe, or actor-model mailbox; it stores notifications FIFO so senders enqueue and return while processors handle items later.
Coarse interest means registering for one event code, such as all explosion events.
Fine interest is a focused description of wanted events, such as grenade explosions within a set distance of the listener.
An event notifies that something already occurred, such as a monster dying; it works like an asynchronous Observer and usually has many listeners.
why: The event is in the past, so the sender usually does not care who receives it.

text: Temporal coupling is the root issue behind unregistered-service crashes: code must execute in a required sequence for the software to function.
A basic event needs only a code field that identifies the event type.
In practice, many developers pair plain event codes with narrowcasting to cut unwanted notifications.
C# events register delegates, which are method references, and JavaScript event listeners are usually plain functions, showing that languages commonly use function references for observers.
when: when comparing observer implementations across languages

text: For smell and slow sound, only notifications for the immediate future are generated, whereas sound handled in one pass may queue notifications several milliseconds or seconds ahead.
Use fine-grained interests only when the savings in unwanted events outweigh the extra complexity.
why: Checking every game state for any listener's interest may be too much work; tracking interests avoids this.

text: If nothing listens to a notification, its sending code can be removed; the flexibility matters during development rather than permanently.
when: When a removed listener was the last one receiving a sender's notifications
why: Unused notification code adds no value.

text: A doubly linked list allows constant-time observer removal, while a tail pointer or walk is needed to add at the tail.
when: when observer removal must be fast
why: removal needs the predecessor, which a doubly linked list provides directly

text: In event systems, listener processing usually dominates total cost rather than the manager's own bookkeeping.
Specialized managers that check only one type of information, such as collisions, sound, or switch states, are a normal design.
when: When the things checked are each verified by a different method
why: Each kind of information needs its own checking method, so one manager per type fits each method.

text: Track live merge sources with an index map of live files rather than a Boolean active array, because selection runs most often.
when: When the selection step runs far more often than any other step
why: It tracks which sources are still in use, giving a more efficient selection procedure than a Boolean array.

text: Buffered event flags are seen only in the following frame, so outcomes no longer depend on update order, but designs needing same-frame response must accept that one-frame delay.
why: Reads come from the current state while writes go to a next state, which is copied in only after every actor has updated.

text: When an event in one component triggers a second event that the first component listens for, synchronous dispatch overflows the stack and crashes quickly, while queues unwind the stack so the loop keeps circulating unnoticed.
Synchronous notification blocks the subject until every observer returns, so one slow observer delays the subject.
when: when an observer performs slow work during notification
why: the subject calls observers directly and waits for each to finish

text: In a broadcast queue every listener sees every event, and events with no listeners are discarded.
Event managers that track each character's interests deliver only useful events to that character.
A per-room event manager notifies sounds made in a room only to characters registered with that room's manager.
when: When there is doubt about whether knowledge reaches characters
why: Information never supplied to the event manager cannot reach its listeners.

text: Total attenuation over a multi-node signal path is the product of the attenuation of the source node, each connection, and the sensor's node.
when: When a stimulus travels across several nodes and connections

text: Notifications wait in a time-ordered queue until they are due, so the region manager dispatches them in time order.
why: Distance determines when the sensor needs to be notified, so the notification is queued until then.

text: A smell dissipation value of 0.5 halves a smell's intensity each second.
A simple locator returns NULL when no provider is registered, so callers that skip the check or fetch the service before registration will crash.
when: When code may request the service before any provider has been registered
why: The locator depends on outside code registering a provider first, so lookups before that return nothing.

text: Assuming the current world state matches the state at the time an event was raised causes bugs, and feedback loops can go unnoticed while the game keeps running.
why: Shared state writable from anywhere in the codebase creates hidden interdependencies.

text: With fast signals, the pending count stays near the total signal count, so memory can approach O(m).
when: signals travel quickly
why: most signals remain pending

text: Skipping a common spawner base class forces every piece of generic code that uses spawners to take a template parameter as well.
when: Designing spawners as templates in C++
why: A non-template base lets code that doesn't care about the monster type use spawners without the type parameter.

text: Direct component references allow any method the peer supports, which can make the design drift back toward a monolithic class.
when: components use direct references without limits
why: Unrestricted calls tighten coupling until the components behave like one class.

text: Callers holding pointers to pooled objects may keep referring to an object that was reclaimed and reused.
Most division schemes do not enforce validity, and a small layout change can turn a tolerable invalidity into a fatal one.
when: Building or editing a pathfinding graph.
why: Invalidity comes in degrees that are hard to predict.

text: Polling characters can bypass per-room event delivery unless access to each polling station is filtered.
when: characters poll stations directly
why: polling reads information outside the room's manager

text: When sound is handled in one frame, fast characters can be notified at the wrong time; iterative handling fixes this at the cost of memory and time.
when: fast characters hear sound handled in one frame

text: Pasted values no longer follow their source cells, so later upstream changes do not appear in the pasted copies.
when: Values were pasted to freeze a result
why: Only the computed results are carried over, leaving out the formulas that linked each cell to its source.

text: 1) Aggregate and test sensors for the new signal. 2) Queue the resulting notifications. 3) Flush any notifications that are already due.
when: On every frame, including frames in which no new signals arrived.
why: Queued notifications waiting for their due time are released only by this flush step.

text: 1) Before destroying a subject, send a final notification to its observers. 2) Let each observer react as it sees fit.
when: when observers may still expect notifications from a subject being destroyed
why: observers otherwise keep believing they are attached to a live subject

text: 1) During each object's update, read its current flag and write the new value to its next flag. 2) After every object has updated, swap each object by copying next into current and clearing next.
when: Objects send events to one another within a frame and results must not depend on update order.
why: Reads come from state that stays fixed until every object has updated, so update order cannot change what an object observes.

text: 1) Extend the base event with type-specific fields. 2) Give each event type its own distinct code value. 3) Use subclassed events in object-oriented languages.

1) Measure the 3D distance from source to the start of the connection. 2) Use the stored connection distance along the connection. 3) Measure from the connection's end to the sensor or next connection.
when: a signal crosses several sense-graph nodes
why: Only the two end legs need fresh 3D distance measurement, since the length along the connection is already stored.

text: 1) Compute the total attenuated intensity. 2) Compare it with the sensor's threshold. 3) Notify the sensor if the threshold is met.
when: Only for sensors in nodes whose intensity exceeds the minimum value.

text: Avoid sending events from code that is handling an event, and use debug logging in the event system to catch loops.
A script should remove its own signals before it runs.
when: Scripts that may run more than once
why: Clears leftover identifiers that would satisfy waits falsely

text: Leave a topic uncached when it should always query the game, such as line of sight.
In production, send touch events through the sense manager so that all sense information arrives by one route.
when: production systems

text: Bind a Null Object command, whose execute does nothing, to buttons with no action so no null checks are needed.
when: For buttons intended to do nothing when pressed.
why: Otherwise an unbound button would fail when its command is called.

text: Have the base observer class track every subject it watches and unregister from all of them on destruction.
when: when the safest protection against dangling links is needed
why: it removes the need for each observer to remember to unregister, at the cost of two-way pointers and added complexity

text: When maintaining a separate active collection, add and remove objects in both collections on creation and destruction, but not on temporary deactivation.
In C-based event systems, put a generic data pointer in the event structure so it can reference any other data structure.
when: event system is written in C
why: C lacks subclassing for carrying type-specific data

text: Use immediate dispatch in simple event managers that do not need storage.
when: the manager is simple and events need no storage
why: It needs no queue management code, so the manager stays simple.

text: When designing insert and delete procedures for a tree structure, first state its invariants, then check that each update preserves them.
A central event bus lets senders and listeners avoid direct knowledge of one another, but behaves like a global variable and carries the same hidden interdependencies.
when: Systems must communicate without referencing each other.
why: Senders and listeners need no direct knowledge of one another.

text: Fine-grained registration narrows searches and cuts unwanted events, at the cost of slower decisions and more intricate code.
when: When many listeners ignore most events of a kind they receive, such as per-frame time announcements.

text: Event-only designs are easier to change, upgrade and debug, for example by printing events or firing them with special key presses.
when: flexibility, debugging and easy change matter more than raw speed
why: Mixing polling with events spreads information flow across several channels, making it hard to tell where things happen.

text: Synchronous observer notification is simple but blocks and risks deadlock, while asynchronous event queues decouple senders from receivers and suit highly threaded engines.
when: when choosing a messaging style for a multithreaded engine
why: queued messages let the sender continue without waiting for receivers

text: Immediate dispatch needs no storage or queue management but spreads AI load unevenly across frames, while queued dispatch smooths frame cost at the price of complexity.
when: When many events reach many characters and notifications cannot be spread across frames.
why: Dispatch waits for spare AI processing budget, so no single frame takes a disproportionate share of the load.

text: Smell and iterative propagation add state and calculation cost, so they should be implemented only when the game needs them.
why: Stimuli that spread between nodes are passed back and forth over repeated passes, multiplying the calculations performed.

text: A rider is an object attached to a file that holds the current position and an end-of-file flag.
Create files by appending elements, since writing at arbitrary positions is often complex.
when: When generating a new file whose elements are added in order.

text: Reading to the end raises the rider's eof flag; a failed write raises it too, so both Read and Write require the flag to be clear.
when: When reading a sequence element by element with a rider.
why: The flag records that a preceding read reached the end, so the reading loop knows when to stop.

text: Reading text with fixed-type read calls is unreliable when the type of the next item is not known in advance.
when: reading mixed text input
why: The reader wants to take the next element whatever its kind, rather than assuming a kind in advance.

text: 1) Open the file with Old for an existing file or New for a new empty file. 2) Attach a rider with Set at position 0. 3) Read or Write at the rider. 4) Close, which flushes buffers to persistent storage.
why: Each rider carries its own position, so reads and writes advance through the sequence from that place.

text: Flyweight shares one instance among several owners at the same time; Object Pool reuses an object's memory over time after its owner is done, with no sharing during its life.
Flyweight splits object data into intrinsic state, which is shared, context-free, and identical for every use, and extrinsic state, unique to each instance such as position, scale, or tint.
why: Sharing the intrinsic part lets many objects reference one copy.

text: In the source tests, flyweight pointers showed no penalty compared with an enum and were noticeably faster, though results depend on memory layout.
why: Measured results vary with how other data is laid out in memory.

text: Keep position and velocity on the entity when almost every component uses them, which gives components a simple communication channel without coupling.
when: Several components read the same state.
why: Shared data on the entity avoids direct component-to-component links.

text: Converting a singleton to a non-singleton later still requires touching every call site when callers use the instance() form.
when: After a singleton has been hard-wired throughout a large codebase.
why: Global visibility lets any file pull in the instance, tying new code to it without anyone intending that.

text: Share stateless command instances with the Flyweight pattern instead of creating a copy for each use.
when: commands hold no state
why: Duplicate stateless instances waste memory.

text: Keep shared flyweight objects immutable, for example with const methods, because a change would appear in every place that uses the object.
why: A single shared object affects all of its users at once.

text: Use flyweight when there are too many objects, either from memory use or from the processing cost of each one.
when: When a scene holds very many repeated objects, each with large meshes and textures.
why: Sharing reduces the number of distinct objects that must be stored or handled.

text: Flyweight can replace an enum with many switch statements while keeping an object-oriented style without creating a huge number of objects.
why: Shared objects give behavior and data in one place.

text: Store shared flyweight instances directly in their owning object rather than dynamically allocating them, which keeps lifetimes simple.
when: When one shared instance is referenced from many places, such as tiles of a world grid.
why: Owned members have predictable lifetimes.

text: Flyweight shares data purely for memory efficiency, and the shared data may not match any conceptual type; Type Object defines types, and sharing can accompany either.
when: Choosing between flyweight and type object.
why: They solve different problems even though both may share objects; flyweight's goal is memory efficiency, not modeling what an object is.

text: Besides processing each frame, the game loop must decouple progression from input and processor speed so the world advances at a consistent rate across hardware.
Fixed time steps advance the world by one unit per update; variable time steps pass elapsed time into update(), so each frame simulates the previous frame's duration.
The update time step is the fixed granularity at which the game is simulated, which is separate from the visible frame rate.
A game loop is a continuously running cycle that processes input without blocking, advances the game state, renders the result, and tracks time.
One cycle of the game loop is called a tick or a frame, and each cycle advances the game state by some amount.
Some platforms, such as web browsers, cannot be opted out of: their event loop is embedded in how programs run, so a classic game loop is practically unworkable there.
Traditional AI debugging adds code that reports internal state on screen or to a log file for later analysis.
Many game worlds run on their own sense of time, so the programmer must invent that time and build the machinery that drives it.
Drawing a scene piece by piece breaks the illusion of a coherent world, so each displayed frame must appear whole.
A monitor draws the screen row by row from top left to bottom right, then returns to the top left, repeating this about sixty times a second.
A game on a platform with a graphical event loop has its own application loop, and the two loops must cooperate.
Updates fire at fixed steps, but renders occur at arbitrary times, so frames often land between two updates.
Fixed step without sync runs as fast as hardware allows; adding one delay or sync point at loop end caps the speed.
Production loops commonly sync with the display, for example by double-buffering frames and timing the buffer swap to the monitor's refresh.
Several game engines use the per-object update structure in their main base classes, such as the core game and sprite classes.
Storing deferred requests in an array processed by an update method is known as the Update Method pattern, and update may run on the main loop or a dedicated audio thread.
A 60 fps game has about a third of the processing power per frame of a 30 fps game.
Almost every game uses a game loop, though relatively few non-game programs do.
Scripts should yield at natural pauses so a scheduler can grant them more time when it is available.
when: scripts run across several frames
why: A natural lull is a clean break point, so the scheduler can resume the script later or spend the time elsewhere.

text: Use manual scheduling when many behaviours run at once and reserve threads for a small number of long-lived tasks; a few dozen threads may suit a PC, but one per character's pathfinding is excessive.
when: Many simultaneous AI behaviours.
why: Thread switching cost grows with thread count.

text: Fixed per-check methods are simpler while the set of checks stays small.
when: the number of polling checks is small
why: A central request method must first work out which check is wanted, an extra step that dedicated methods avoid.

text: Improve how each step of the design loop is done rather than replacing the loop itself.
why: Refining ideas by trying and changing them is already how professional designers work, so gains come from doing each stage better.

text: Without timing control, speed follows hardware and scene cost: fast machines blur, slow ones crawl, heavy AI or physics slows; tuning work to one PC shifts pace elsewhere.
when: When a game must run on hardware the developer cannot know in advance.
why: Frame work sets speed directly, so each frame takes as long as its work and the machine sets the pace.

text: When objects update sequentially and share state, update order silently changes behavior, since each reads whatever value was last written, such as a shared flag or previous frame position.
when: components or actors read shared state written by others in the same frame or pass
why: Reading and writing the same state within one pass makes results depend on update order, breaking the appearance of simultaneity.

text: A pending transition at level zero is handled at this level, a positive level exits the current state and reduces the level, and a negative level passes to the parent's downward routine.
when: A transition returned from a state update
why: The level counts remaining steps up the hierarchy, dropping by one at each exit until it reaches zero.

text: A manual scheduler relies on each behaviour returning control after a short bout of processing, so no thread housekeeping is needed.
when: When many behaviours must run at once and a thread for each would be too costly.
why: Hardware thread switches flush caches and add housekeeping, which a cooperative hand-off avoids.

text: Storing polling tasks in a hash table keyed by task code lets a request be served by looking up the task and returning its cached value.
when: When pollable topics must be added without changing the polling station's interface.
why: All tasks share one cache rule, so a lookup only needs the matching task's stored value.

text: Digital systems run calculations behind the scenes that tabletop players would perform with dice, so the program produces random outcomes and results without the player doing the math.
when: Role-playing combat resolution
why: The program can run more calculations faster than a person with dice.

text: A fixed-step loop cannot skip work to catch up, so a frame that overruns its time budget makes the whole game run slower.
when: When each frame's work varies with hardware or scene complexity.

text: Fixed update with variable rendering keeps simulation at a fixed step and skips rendering frames to catch up, so it does not fall behind.
when: While the game can keep its fixed updates running in real time.
why: A fixed simulation step keeps physics and networking deterministic, which variable steps make much harder.

text: Staggered update interval equals characters divided by characters updated per frame, divided by frame rate; 50 characters, 5 per frame, 30 fps gives 0.33 s.
when: Updating many agents in groups
why: Characters act slowly, so they need not all process their AI every frame; a simple rotation suffices.

text: Virtual reality titles need a minimum of 90 frames per second, as lower rates invite simulator-induced nausea.
Each pluggable polling task holds a task code, stored value and last-updated frame; it refreshes only when stale versus the current frame, using one caching rule for all tasks.
why: A frame counter lets each cache tell whether its stored value predates the current frame.

text: Schedulers can run as behaviours inside other schedulers, forming a tree that divides time from the whole game down to individual character subtasks.
when: When a character is made of several behaviours that each need scheduled time.
why: Each character's AI can be upgraded without unbalancing the rest of the game.

text: Game time machinery uses three patterns: a Game Loop that drives the world's clock, Update Methods that let objects respond to each tick, and Double Buffer that makes sequential updates look simultaneous.
Game loop ownership has three options: use the platform's event loop, use an engine's loop, or write your own loop.
The Update Method simulates independent objects by giving each an update() that advances it one frame; the game loop calls update() on every object once per frame.
why: The loop only needs an abstract interface rather than concrete types, which keeps each entity's behavior separate from the loop and from other entities.

text: Resuming a re-entrant script after a rapidly changing event can make it act on outdated information.
when: a script pauses across a fast-changing event
why: Continuing from an earlier point risks acting on information that has since become incorrect.

text: A desync can stay hidden for several turns until a random event resolves differently on each machine, and both players then suspect cheating.
when: When one client draws a pseudorandom number without telling the opponent, due to a bug

text: Loops that update and render together in one fixed step slow down sooner than loops that separate updating from rendering.
when: When combined updating and drawing in a frame overruns the frame time

text: Poorly written game code can push input lag to five, six, seven or more frames, so programmers must actively prevent lag beyond the hardware floor.
when: When code errors add input delay beyond what the hardware pipeline imposes
why: Hardware that keeps the CPU and GPU busy imposes a minimum of roughly three to four frames of input lag.

text: Treating the three-part iteration loop as the whole process misses the overlapping, unscheduled knowledge creation that drives progress.
when: When the design process runs without a fixed schedule, with overlapping actions interacting.
why: The loop omits how knowledge bubbles up continuously in every developer.

text: 1) Process input without waiting. 2) Update the simulation, including AI and physics. 3) Render the frame. 4) Repeat continuously.
when: Structuring a real-time game loop
why: Each pass advances the world and draws it, so the game keeps moving when the player is idle.

text: 1) Split planning into a setup routine and a single-iteration method. 2) Schedule iterations across frames so planning does not hurt frame rate.
when: Real-time games
why: Protects frame rate

text: 1) Split the character's decision logic into stages. 2) Run stages until the frame's time budget is used up. 3) Yield between stages and resume at the next stage on a later frame.
when: a decision takes longer than one frame's budget
why: Spreading the AI work over several frames keeps any single frame within its time budget.

text: 1) When adding a behaviour with frequency f, dry-run the scheduler over a fixed number of future frames, counting running behaviours without executing them. 2) Find the frame with the fewest running behaviours. 3) Set the new phase to that frame's offset from now.
why: Places the new behaviour where it adds least clumping.

text: 1) Record the commands each entity executed in each frame, instead of full state. 2) To replay, run the normal simulation and execute the recorded commands.
why: Storing the full state each frame would consume too much memory, so only the commands are kept.

text: 1) In the main function, start the game loop. 2) Each pass, handle pending OS messages with a non-blocking poll, such as PeekMessage. 3) Update and render the game. 4) Repeat.
when: native Windows application
why: A non-blocking poll keeps the loop running when no input arrives.

text: 1) Choose a cap, often 30 or 60 FPS on mobile. 2) Run the frame's work. 3) If it finished early, sleep for the rest of the frame's time slice. 4) Start the next frame.
when: battery-powered devices
why: Sleeping instead of doing extra work conserves battery once the cap is reached.

text: 1) Set high-level experience goals during brainstorming, before choosing features. 2) Brainstorm features that meet those goals. 3) Playtest to verify the goals are actually met.
why: Stating the experience up front focuses creative work, since features are then judged against it.

text: Choose a fixed update step small enough for high-end hardware, yet longer than one update takes on the slowest supported hardware so low-end machines keep up.
when: When the game must run on the slowest supported hardware
why: A step shorter than the update cost means the game can never catch up with real time.

text: Compile justification tracing out of shipped builds to avoid its memory overhead.
when: Tracing is used during development but not needed by players
why: Full trails can use substantial memory

text: The stability method needs a frame counter that increments once per tree call; if the tree is not run every frame, advance the counter each time it is called.
when: When implementing stable random decisions.
why: Storing the frame of each decision avoids having to clear stale values for unused decisions.

text: Every schedulable item exposes one run method that accepts a time value, and schedulers implement the same interface so they can be composed.
when: When scheduling is hierarchical, with schedulers at multiple levels
why: Shared interface lets schedulers nest inside each other.

text: Route the polling that an event-based design still needs through a dedicated polling station, which gains speed and easier debugging.
when: When an event-driven design still requires some polling for the AI's inputs
why: some polling is usually needed to avoid awkward workarounds

text: Run the flush every frame, even when no new signals arrive, so cached notifications are dispatched on time.
when: When no new signals arrive in a given frame
why: cached notifications would otherwise be delivered late

text: In a browser, drive the game loop with requestAnimationFrame, letting the browser call your code back each frame.
when: web browser target
why: The browser's event loop runs the program, so the game must hook into it.

text: Pass the normalized lag fraction to rendering instead of raw lag, so the renderer can ignore the update rate.
why: Dividing by the step size makes the fraction range from 0 to just under 1 whatever the step length.

text: Turn-based games need a loop too, since animation and audio stay active during player waits.
when: turn-based game
why: Visual and audible state keeps changing between turns.

text: Keep the game loop lean, since it runs every frame and small inefficiencies accumulate across every frame.
why: The loop is among the small share of code where most run time is spent, so inefficiency there costs the most.

text: Decide which class owns update(): the entity itself, a component, or a delegate such as a State or Type Object.
when: designing per-frame behavior for entities
why: A single inheritance hierarchy reuses code poorly, while components or delegates let parts of an entity update independently.

text: Using an engine's loop saves writing and optimizing a loop but loses control when your needs fit the engine poorly; usually rely on it when building on an established engine.
when: building on an established engine
why: Avoids authoring and tuning the core loop yourself, but the engine decides when your code runs.

text: Binary search for nearby cars costs O(log2 m) for m cars in a lane; caching search results brings practical cost back to O(n).
when: Speed-critical lookup of nearby vehicles in the innermost pathfinding loop, where a binary search is used.
why: Stored results mean each neighbor lookup is paid once, leaving cost proportional to nearby vehicles.

text: Using the platform's event loop gives simplicity, platform friendliness, and no input plumbing, but costs timing control and often yields a slow, choppy loop.
when: When the host platform's event model rules out writing a classic game loop.
why: Most application event loops were not built for games, so their scheduling tends to be slow and uneven.

text: Writing your own loop gives total control over timing, but you must periodically hand control back to the platform so its framework does not hang.
why: The host still needs slices of execution to handle its own event queue.

text: An uncapped frame rate gives the smoothest play and most detail but draws the most power; clamping saves battery at the cost of peak frame rate.
when: Mobile games where battery use matters more than maximum detail.
why: Idling the processor once a frame's work is finished avoids burning spare cycles on extra frames.

text: Variable time steps track real elapsed time when frame rates vary but complicate update logic; fixed steps are simpler to write and reason about.
when: When frame durations vary and each update must advance by the real elapsed slice.
why: Each update must receive the elapsed time, since the length of each step changes from frame to frame.

text: Two-stage initialization uses a parameterless constructor and a separate init call, which keeps derived constructors simple but risks half-built objects if init is skipped.
when: Base state is supplied after construction.
why: Callers can forget the init call, leaving the object in an unusable state.

text: A shorter update step gives higher-fidelity simulation on fast machines but requires more processing to catch up, while a longer step makes gameplay choppier.
when: Choosing a fixed update step size
why: Smaller steps cost more computation per unit of game time.

text: Fragmentation is a serious risk on consoles and mobile devices, where memory is scarce and compacting managers are rare.
As objects are allocated and freed over time, heap memory becomes increasingly disordered, so the placement of objects cannot be predicted.
when: Entities are created and destroyed repeatedly during play
why: Freed gaps are reused unpredictably, scattering related objects

text: Free heap memory split into small separate pieces can fail a request even when total free memory is enough, because the largest contiguous block may be too small.
when: Allocating from a heap with scattered in-use memory.
why: Allocation needs one contiguous block, not total free space.

text: Even infrequent fragmentation can gradually turn a heap into scattered holes, eventually crashing a game that runs for long periods.
when: A game runs for days and creates and destroys objects while running.
why: Small holes accumulate over time until large allocations fail.

text: The database can be a tree, because group nodes hold child nodes inside an overall list of nodes.
A flat scene graph is a list of objects, while most scene graphs are hierarchical, where a child's transform is relative to its parent's.
Dynamic structures such as lists, rings, trees and graphs are created at run time.
Database nodes come in three kinds: a base node with an identifier, a group holding children, and a datum holding a value.
why: Groups may hold either further groups or values, so the whole database forms a tree.

text: Equality tests and assignments on large, highly structured values can cost substantial computation.
when: When the compared or assigned values are large and highly structured.

text: Traversing a cyclic pointer structure without stopping at the cycle never terminates.
When grouping examples by attribute value in a structure used as both dictionary and list, initialize each new key to an empty list before insertion.
when: When adding an example under a key that has not been used before.
why: insertion fails otherwise

text: Complex data can be stored as flat values or as a hierarchy; a hierarchy lets an expert find an item without knowing its current location or state.
why: Experts can read parts of a structured entry without being hard-coded to its type.

text: A class that grows too large and too coupled discourages editing, so programmers add workaround hacks elsewhere instead of changing it.
when: A monolithic entity class has grown very large.
why: Editing it is risky and costly, so the codebase accumulates hacks.

text: A base type is a structured type whose components all share one type.
Prototype-based languages can support multiple parents and let parents change at runtime, a capability called dynamic inheritance.
when: when designing reuse in a prototype-based language
why: parents are ordinary objects that can be reassigned

text: Inheritance has a poor reputation largely because base classes accumulate code over time.
Use a class rather than a closure when a command needs several named operations, such as execute plus undo.
when: When a command has multiple operations, such as undoable commands.
why: A single function maps poorly onto multiple operations.

text: When a base class becomes a tangle of unrelated code, move some of its provided operations into separate classes that it delegates to.
when: A sandbox base class grows unrelated responsibilities
why: Extracted responsibilities keep the base manageable.

text: Prefer data-driven types when variation is mostly numbers and strings; subclassing keeps its advantage when type-specific behavior is complex.
when: choosing between data-driven types and subclasses
why: Data suits simple variation, while complex behavior is easier to express through subclassing.

text: Restructuring the class hierarchy around a shared base to avoid duplicated lookups is usually more trouble than it is worth.
when: When unrelated classes both need a service restricted to one branch of the class tree.

text: Copy-down delegation copies inherited attributes into the child at construction, so lookups are plain field reads and no parent pointer is needed; children never see later parent changes.
when: breed attributes are fixed after creation and lookup speed matters
why: Resolving inheritance once trades flexibility for faster access; it becomes incorrect if parent attributes change after child construction.

text: Cloning copies both class and state, so a variant spawner needs only a differently configured prototype rather than a new class.
when: when spawning several variants of one type
why: the prototype carries its configuration into every copy

text: When a lookup fails on an object, it is retried on that object's parent, then the parent's parent, continuing up the chain.
when: when resolving a property or method in a prototype-based language
why: delegation is how reuse works without classes

text: With a delegate, the main class's update() is non-virtual and forwards to the delegated object, so changing the delegate changes the entity's behavior.
when: entity already uses State or Type Object

text: Subclasses reach the rest of the game only through their base class, so the base class becomes coupled to every system any subclass needs, and changing it can break many subclasses.
when: Using a base class as the sole gateway to outside systems
why: Every subclass is tied to the base class, forming a coupling web.

text: Changes inside a helper class do not disturb the base class, since the base is coupled only to the helper's interface.
when: Operations are moved into a helper object
why: The helper encapsulates its own dependencies on the underlying system.

text: Dynamic delegation checks overrides at every lookup and walks the parent chain, so runtime changes to breeds take effect, but it costs memory for the parent pointer and time per lookup.
when: breeds may be modified at runtime
why: Resolving the chain on each access reflects current values at the price of extra work.

text: Many higher-level steering behaviors compute a surrogate target (position or orientation) and delegate the actual steering to a fundamental behavior such as seek, align, or velocity matching.
why: Reusing primitives this way builds complex behaviors from simple ones.

text: Face is implemented as a subclass of align that overrides its target member, using the same shadowing approach as pursue.
Fine-grained interest descriptions are usually game specific, which reduces reuse between games.
when: When characters register narrowly focused interests rather than a single event code.
why: The events worth filtering on tend to change from one project to the next, so narrow filters are hard to reuse.

text: A correct clone requires deciding between deep and shallow copying, such as whether cloning an object also clones the objects it owns.
when: when implementing clone for objects that hold references to other objects
why: copy depth changes whether copies share mutable state

text: Encapsulated type objects need forwarding methods for every exposed type method, which becomes tedious for large type classes.
when: a type class has many methods
why: Each method must be duplicated on the typed object and forwarded to its type.

text: Creating typed objects with a direct constructor call bypasses the factory and therefore skips its memory management scheme.
when: the type provides a factory
why: Direct construction does not go through the allocation logic the factory applies.

text: Multiple inheritance creates the Deadly Diamond when two inheritance paths lead to the same base class, causing shared-base ambiguity and duplicated state.
when: Combining collision and rendering behaviors through inheritance.
why: Two paths reach one base, so the hierarchy becomes tangled.

text: 1) Copy the existing scripts (weapon, attachment and projectile scripts, or three vehicle scripts) into your own mod class folder and clear read-only flags. 2) Rename each file to the new name. 3) Update every internal reference to the old names. 4) Replace sound cue references. 5) Compile and check for errors.
when: when creating a custom weapon or vehicle from an existing one

text: 1) Clone a base object. 2) Add fields and methods to the clone. 3) Clone that object as needed to create family members.
when: when building a family of similar objects without classes
why: each clone inherits the configuration of its parent

text: 1) Define a spawner template parameterized by monster class. 2) Its spawn method returns a new instance of that type. 3) Derive it from a shared abstract Spawner base so generic code can hold any spawner through a Monster-typed interface.
when: C++ is used and one spawner implementation must serve any monster type
why: A common base avoids forcing every consumer of spawners to be templated too

text: 1) Give a base class protected accessors to a shared object. 2) Derived classes call those accessors. 3) The object stays unexposed globally.
when: Many leaf classes in a shallow hierarchy share one dependency
why: Gives shared access without making the object global

text: 1) Give each breed an optional parent, with null meaning none. 2) Treat a non-zero health as an override. 3) Treat a non-null attack string as an override. 4) Otherwise inherit the parent's value.
when: implementing single inheritance for breed data
why: Each attribute resolves to the child's own value when set, and to the parent's value otherwise.

text: 1) Define abstract interfaces for each component domain. 2) Make the entity store pointers to these interfaces, receive them in its constructor, and call them in order in its update. 3) Write factory functions that build an entity by choosing concrete components.
when: Building many entity types from interchangeable parts.
why: The entity stays generic while factories control its composition.

text: 1) Create a wrapper implementing the service's interface and holding a reference to the current provider. 2) Log each call in the wrapper. 3) Forward the call to the wrapped provider. 4) Register the wrapper in place of the original.
when: When the services to log are exposed behind an interface.
why: Logging can be enabled for only the services of interest and removed entirely from final release builds.

text: Store per-instance state on each object, and attach shared behavior to the prototype object so all instances of a type use it.
when: when defining constructor-based types
why: shared methods on the prototype avoid duplicating them per instance

text: Let each object encapsulate its own behavior so the game loop only iterates and calls update(); new entity types can then be added without changing the loop.
when: When the game loop has grown to contain logic for several entity types together.
why: The loop needs only the shared update contract, so each object's behavior stays separate from the loop and other objects.

text: Restrict direct references between components to pairs that truly must exchange information, rather than letting every component reach every other.
when: Components are split along domain boundaries and some interaction remains.
why: Limited links keep components independently changeable.

text: Keep unrelated domains such as AI, physics, rendering, and sound isolated so they do not know about each other.
when: Designing game systems.
why: Isolation keeps edits in one domain from breaking others.

text: Delegating via polymorphism (subclasses override the target and call the parent's steering method) avoids copying character data and parameters into each delegate, whereas holding primitives as members requires keeping that data synchronized across all of them.
when: When a steering behavior extends another by computing a different target for it
why: Subclassing removes duplicated state that must otherwise be kept in sync.

text: A hierarchy lets a character swap its active behaviour without the top scheduler knowing; a flat design must remove and register behaviours on every change, risking leaks and run-time errors.
when: Level-of-detail selection changes behaviours at run time.
why: Flat registration is prone to hard-to-trace bugs.

text: The caller can construct the typed object and pass in its type, or call a factory on the type object so the type controls allocation.
when: creating typed objects
why: Caller control and type control of allocation each suit different ownership and memory-management needs.

text: Reassigning the type of an existing object avoids re-creating it but requires validating the object's state against the new type, since old invariants may no longer hold.
when: an object's type must change during play
why: A new type may assume values, such as current health below the new starting health, that the object no longer satisfies.

text: Replacing an overridden method with a member variable makes type-specific data easy to vary but type-specific behavior hard to vary.
when: deciding what should vary per type
why: Data can be set per type, while behavior needs code or selection mechanisms.

text: Inheriting one behavior and duplicating the other's code avoids multiple inheritance but copies logic; putting all behavior in one base wastes memory on unused data.
when: Entity types need overlapping but different capabilities.
why: Each shortcut costs either duplicated code or unnecessary per-object data.

text: A gesture is a pattern recognized across time in input signals, detected by a layer between raw input and the simulation.
Gravity is the speed, in units per second, at which an input axis returns to neutral when no key is held.
Sensitivity is the speed, in units per second, at which an input axis moves toward its target value when a key is pressed.
Snap, when enabled, resets an input axis to zero when the opposite direction is pressed.
Keyboard matrix wiring limits how many keys can be read at once.
The game loop typically calls handleInput once per frame.
A binary key sends only on or off signals, so keyboard-only controls need axis smoothing to turn it into a gradually changing signal rather than abrupt values.
when: control scheme uses only keyboard keys, or binary inputs drive a continuous simulation
why: Keys cannot express intermediate amounts of input, and gradual signal changes avoid abrupt force jumps

text: Throttle changes made in the air raise desired speed but not actual speed, so the vehicle keeps its old speed until a force acts on it.
when: vehicle airborne while input changes
why: No ground friction or other force acts on the body while airborne

text: Example starting values for keyboard driving axes: steering gravity 3, dead zone 0.001, sensitivity 2. Throttle gravity 3, dead zone 0.001, sensitivity 3.
when: tuning keyboard-driven vehicle axes
why: Throttle responds faster than steering in this setup

text: Each added control-feel rule can make code look like poor design because it adds complexity the player never sees.
when: Implementing control feel rules
why: Invisible adjustments add code complexity without visible benefit to the player.

text: 1) Route keypad button events into a chain of gates. 2) Each correct input opens the next gate. 3) The final gate triggers the door animation.
when: When a keypad puzzle requires entering a code in a fixed order

text: 1) Check whether an incoming input is the first part of a known pattern. 2) If so, wait for the next part within a short time window. 3) If it does not arrive in time, reset the sequence. 4) When the full pattern matches, send a special signal to the simulation, such as an animation, unlock or added force.
why: A sequence is not built into raw input signals, so the game must add that sensitivity itself.

text: 1) Input handler selects and returns a command without running it. 2) The caller executes that command on the target actor, such as the player's actor.
when: the input handler does not know which actor to target
why: The handler lacks the target, so the caller supplies it.

text: 1) Define a base Command class with a pure virtual execute and a virtual destructor. 2) Subclass it once per game action, each calling that action. 3) Have the input handler store one command pointer per button and delegate handleInput to it.
when: When the action tied to a button must be swappable
why: Wrapping each action in an object gives the handler something it can reassign instead of fixed direct calls.

text: Object.create, which creates an object delegating to an existing one, arrived with ECMAScript 5, years after JavaScript's first release.
when: when targeting prototype-style creation in JavaScript

text: 1) Call the constructor with new to create an empty object. 2) Link it to the constructor's prototype. 3) Run the constructor body to set fields. 4) Return the object.
when: when instantiating objects with constructor functions in JavaScript

text: Prototype-style code is possible in JavaScript without cloning, but its constructor and new syntax pushes code toward a class-based approach.
when: when writing JavaScript with prototypes
why: the language's syntax favors class-like structure

text: Avoid lazy initialization for systems whose startup cost must be scheduled, such as audio or memory-sensitive systems.
Lazy creation saves memory and CPU when the instance is never used, and lets it read runtime data and depend on other singletons.
Lazy initialization can run an expensive setup, such as audio startup, mid-gameplay, stalling frames and fragmenting the heap.

Internal initialization hides objects from callers and keeps them safe from reuse, but the pool needs a create method for every init signature; external initialization keeps the pool interface small but must handle a full-pool null return.
when: When an object pool of fixed size may have no free slot when requested
why: Callers can call whichever init overload they need on the returned object directly.

text: Visual resource-flow tools can run in a browser, save and share diagrams, and simulate the diagram in real time.
Reuse an existing codebase as a host for new experiments to speed up testing ideas.
Limits are often not clear-cut, but writing them down saves time later and encourages creative workarounds.
when: When designers and artists may not know what the platform can handle

text: With single-level undo, after the last command is undone, executing that same command again acts as redo.
when: When only the most recent command is kept for undo

text: Log calls scattered through the code produce too much output and mix messages from different systems, making each system's messages hard to read.
why: Every system writes to one shared stream, so each team must filter out others' messages.

text: 1) Play an example game and write down its rules. 2) Read its definition file and compare it with your notes. 3) Replay with the rules in mind. 4) Repeat until you can explain how the encoded rules produce the observed play.
when: When studying an example game in a VGDL-based framework

text: Have execute record the prior value of anything it changes, because the target object does not remember it and undo needs it.
when: When a command must support undo

text: Store resume state in fields, since execution position is lost when update() returns; the State pattern often helps organize it.
when: behavior spans several frames
why: Execution position is lost on return.

text: Enable logging per system on demand and keep no logging in the final build.
when: When developers need logs from only some systems at once

text: Lua is a small procedural language designed for embedding in host programs; it is the most widely used game scripting language and runs on a compact register-based bytecode VM.
Kismet is UDK's graphical, object-oriented visual scripting system, in which objects perform actions and wires between them build game systems.
Kismet contains actions, conditions, variables, and events. Actions, conditions, and events are shown in brackets and variables in italics.
Lua works with C and C++ with little interface code, and its behavior can be adjusted, not only extended with new functions and types.
Userdata holds generic values with a tag and is commonly used to store C++ instance pointers, reducing interface code.
Lua's simple execution model is fast in practice, and its C-like syntax is moderately easy for non-programmers to learn.
Graphical scripting tools built into game editors, such as node-based visual systems, are an example of combining an editor with behavior scripting.
Graphical-logic games can be described in a restricted description language, and existing interpreters can simulate such descriptions. The language covers a set of games rather than all games.
Indentation-based syntax is readable and easy for non-programmers such as level designers and artists to learn.
why: Without brackets to forget or indentation habits to unlearn, newcomers pick it up more easily.

text: Registered tag routines on events such as addition, function calls, table queries and garbage collection change Lua's default behavior, enabling rudimentary object orientation and exposing C++ types.
Some ways of converting a level into a graph prevent a simple index lookup table, which can make pathfinding much slower.
why: The lookup runs inside the inner loop, so any extra processing there costs a lot.

text: Lua has weaker documentation than other major languages and debugging scripts can be difficult.

1) Open the visual scripting editor by clicking its K icon, or press Ctrl+K with a referenced actor selected. 2) Press K to show linked actors, and press K again to hide them. 3) Right-click empty space to list available objects.
Include help, the player manual, and setup or installation routines in the technical specification.
Lua's small core library is easy to learn and flexible, which suits games that mostly need maths and logic.
when: choosing a scripting language for a game
why: Games rarely need a large standard library in scripts

text: Separate Lua state objects give some re-entrancy but cost extra memory and cannot communicate with one another.
when: running several independent Lua contexts

text: A factory on the type object can route allocation through custom allocators or an object pool before initializing the new object.
when: managing memory for many typed objects
why: Centralized creation gives a single point to control how memory is obtained.

text: Recursive structures vary in size, so they cannot receive fixed storage at translation time. Each component is allocated at run time and linked through pointers.
why: Only a fixed-size address slot is reserved at compile time, while the component itself is stored elsewhere.

text: Exceeding a fixed-capacity file implementation's limit reflects the implementation's shortfall, not a mistake in the calling program.
when: When a file module is implemented with a fixed maximal file length.

text: 1) Reify each request as a small struct holding its id and parameters. 2) Store pending requests in a fixed-size array sized for the worst case. 3) Sender asserts room, appends the request and increments a count. 4) An update method plays every pending request in one pass, then resets the count to zero.
when: Every pending request can be handled in a single update call.
why: A plain array needs no dynamic allocation and its contiguous memory is cache-friendly.

text: Defer removals by marking objects dead, skipping them, and sweeping later, so no object is skipped while the list is being iterated.
Keeping inactive objects in one collection wastes time checking flags and can hurt cache use; a separate active-only collection saves that cost but costs memory and must stay in sync.
when: many objects are dormant

text: Reference counting frees memory eagerly at a CPU cost on every change, simple garbage collection defers work but causes pauses, and deferred ref-counting or incremental GC fall between them.
when: Choosing a memory reclamation strategy
why: Eager work spreads cost across operations, while deferred work concentrates it into pauses

text: Coupled pooled objects store their own in-use state and can restrict creation to the pool, which is simpler and cheaper; decoupled pools can hold any type but track in-use state separately.
why: Objects can signal availability through state they already hold, so the pool needs no separate in-use flags.

text: Fetching data from RAM takes far longer than processing it, often hundreds of CPU cycles on current hardware, so processors rely on cache, which holds streamed copies of memory.
when: Estimating the cost of a cache miss
why: Main memory latency is far larger than register or cache access time.

text: An array whose elements are arrays forms a matrix. Ten outer slots, each holding a four-slot REAL array, can be written ARRAY 10, 4 OF REAL, with M[i,j] selecting row i, column j.
Sequential access reads by stepping from an element to its successor and writes by appending at the end; only the current element is directly reachable.
Simpler devices such as non-game mobile phones, set-top boxes and low-end PDAs have severely limited memory and processing.
Standard library hash containers are far more efficient than hand-written bucket code, which is mainly useful for illustration.
Hot and cold parts stored in parallel arrays indexed the same way can remove the pointer between them.
RAM is called random access because any address was once about equally cheap, but access order now strongly affects cost.
when: Reasoning about memory access patterns
why: Caches and prefetching make sequential access far cheaper than scattered access

text: In synchronization cases, derived data often lives on disk or elsewhere, so the memory cost of caching it rarely applies.
when: Caching derived data for synchronization work.

text: Most languages give programmers no control over representation; one proposed notation prefixes ARRAY or RECORD with PACKED to request packing.
Structures may be nested to any depth, but their ultimate components are atomic.
Computer storage is a homogeneous mass of bits. Types supply the abstract structure that gives those bits meaning.
Program constructs correspond to data types: assignment to scalar, enumeration to record, for to array, conditional to variant record, while or repeat to sequence, and procedure to recursive type.

Split a pool into size-specific pools when object sizes vary widely, since large slots holding small objects waste memory. Speed-efficient memory managers keep several block sizes and allocate each request from the matching pool.
when: object sizes vary widely
why: Large slots holding small objects waste memory.

text: Pool objects that are created and destroyed often, are similar in size, are slow or fragmentation-prone to allocate, or wrap expensive resources such as connections.
when: When a burst can spawn hundreds of short-lived objects that must be created quickly.
why: Reusing a fixed set avoids the fragmentation that repeated allocation and freeing would cause.

text: Skip creating new effects like particles when the pool is full, but kill the quietest existing sound when a new important sound needs a slot.
when: the pool is full
