why: A missing new particle goes unnoticed, while a silent important sound is more noticeable than a cut-off one.

text: Pack array components only when several fit in a word, especially when the storage saved is a factor of two or more.
why: Padding wastes storage, yet avoiding it forces partial-word access that can make compiled code grow.

text: Choose an array-to-store mapping that keeps address computation simple and efficient. The simplest case is a component size of one word.
why: Words are the smallest transferable unit, so a whole-word component size keeps the linear address formula exact.

text: Prefer recursive types and sequences for well-structured data, and reserve pointer graphs for cases that need the extra flexibility.
when: When data must form circular, infinite, or shared structures.
why: Recursive definitions let storage be allocated automatically on first reference, hiding pointer handling.

text: Persistent data structures return a new object on each change while sharing data with the old one, so keeping the old version is cheap and undo just switches back to it.
when: When undoable commands change only a small part of an object's state.
why: Unchanged parts stay shared between versions, so keeping the old one costs little compared to a full copy.

text: Memory is fetched in blocks, so after one access nearby data is cheap to reach; this is locality of reference, and a miss costs a slow fetch of a new block.
when: Successive accesses fall in nearby addresses
why: Hardware loads neighboring data with each request, so sequential access reuses it

text: Knowing a variable's range of values lets the compiler allocate storage statically, avoiding dynamic allocation, which is often key to efficiency.
why: Storage size is fixed from the value range, so the compiler reserves it without run-time allocation.

text: With n components of size s packed per word, utilization is u = n*s divided by n*s rounded up to whole words. With one component per slot, u = s/S, where S is s rounded up to whole words; u exceeds 0.5 whenever s exceeds 0.5.
why: Rounding each component up to whole words leaves unused space, lowering utilization below one.

text: For component index i with n components per word, the word index is i DIV n and the position within the word is i MOD n.
why: Access needs both the word that holds a component and the slot inside that word.

text: Arrays and records are random-access structures for primary store, while sequences serve secondary stores such as disks and tapes, since tapes and each disk track allow only sequential access.
why: Secondary stores such as disks and tapes are sequential-access, so sequences fit them.

text: In the memory hierarchy, registers hold the data a CPU works on directly, RAM is the large slower store, and the cache sits between them as a small faster on-chip SRAM buffer.
why: The cache is small because it must fit on the chip and its fast memory is costly.

text: Memory is modeled as an array of bytes, each 8 bits, addressed by index. A word is the unit a machine transfers at once.
why: Hardware transfers small groups of contiguous bytes in parallel, which sets the unit of transfer.

text: Scattering per-object data across memory causes cache misses in tight loops, slowing the algorithm.
when: When an algorithm's data is spread around memory.
why: The processor must fetch a fresh block into cache for only a couple of instructions, which is costly.

text: Skipping cleanup after a change leaves rough spots that the next developer must work around.
why: Leftover rough edges from a quick change are left in the source for whoever works on the code next, so reorganizing it afterward matters.

text: The hard part of observer cleanup is remembering to unregister, not writing the unregistration code itself.
when: when designing observer cleanup
why: forgotten unregistrations are the usual source of dangling observers

text: If swapping takes longer than modifying the state, double buffering gives no benefit.
A large time slice can make a moving object overshoot its bounds, such as a patrol range, so boundary handling must clamp or reflect the position.
when: variable time step

text: Data used by only a few components wastes memory on every configuration when placed on the shared container.
when: storing component-specific data on a shared container
why: Every entity pays the memory cost even when no component reads the data.

text: A raw component pointer silently breaks when its component is moved in memory, unless the entity's pointer is updated at the same time.
when: When components are moved to keep active ones packed.
why: A pointer does not know where its target lives, so moving the component leaves the entity pointing at stale memory unless it is also updated.

text: A heap can have enough total free memory and still fail allocations, so checking total free space alone does not show an allocation will succeed.
when: Checking whether memory is sufficient for an allocation.
why: Fragmentation leaves no contiguous block large enough.

text: A reused pooled object keeps old field values, and since it has the same type, missing reinitialization can look almost correct and cause subtle bugs.
why: A reused object has the same type as its old contents, so the leftover values can hide a missed initialization and look nearly correct.

text: Every access to a packed component must compute its word and position, and partial-word access costs time.
why: Accessing part of a word is a cumbersome, inefficient process, so each packed access carries extra computation and cost.

text: 1) Keep a count of active particles. 2) Activate by swapping the particle with the first inactive one past the active block, then incrementing the count. 3) Deactivate by decrementing the count, then swapping the particle with the last active one. Only activation and deactivation break active-first ordering, so no per-frame sort is needed.
when: Pools where most slots are inactive and the update loop is hot.
why: The update loop touches only live data and needs no active flag.

text: Route every modification of primary data through a single narrow interface that sets the dirty flag, so no path can skip it.
when: Implementing dirty flags across a codebase.
why: A single entry point prevents a missed flag.

text: In production code, store neural network weights in arrays indexed by neuron number rather than searching input lists for a weight.
when: Implementing a neural network for production use.
why: Searching lists for weights is slow.

text: For data processed in sequence, store the actual values contiguously one after another rather than as pointers to scattered objects.
when: Single-threaded loops over many items.
why: Neighboring items are already in the loaded cache line when needed.

text: When pooled types vary, check object size against the slot size, since an oversized object in a small slot corrupts adjacent memory.
when: When a pool holds objects of different types or subclasses that add fields
why: Each slot must be sized for the largest object, otherwise a bigger object overwrites its neighbour and corrupts memory.

text: Object-oriented per-character layouts aid clarity, but storing all character positions in one array may be far more cache-friendly.
why: Per-object layouts are clear, but jumping between scattered objects causes cache misses, so one shared array suits algorithms that touch many objects' positions at once.

text: Storing connections with fixed costs is simple; computing a cost only when needed uses the current level state but is more complex.
Parallel component arrays indexed by entity ID must stay in sync, which blocks sorting or packing each array by a different criterion, such as disabled physics and invisible rendering.
Keeping particles packed by active state couples the particle to its system, which must handle activation, but moving bytes can beat following pointers when it keeps the cache full.
why: Profiling should confirm the choice.

text: Packing record fields costs much less access efficiency than packing array components, since the compiler still computes each packed field's fixed offset.
when: choosing between packed records and packed arrays
why: Each packed field's offset is fixed and known at compile time, so access stays cheap compared with packed array elements that need runtime offset calculation.

text: Padding lowers storage utilization, but omitting it may require slower partial-word access that enlarges compiled code, so compilers normally pad automatically.
Empty a player's inventory before granting a weapon, so the player receives only the intended item.
when: When the player is about to reach a weapon's locker in a level

text: Clear references held by a pooled object when it is released, so dead objects do not keep others alive in garbage-collected systems.
when: When a pooled object is released and the environment uses garbage collection
why: A pool keeps released objects in memory, so any references they still hold stop the collector from reclaiming the objects they point to.

text: Compression saves space at the cost of processing time to decompress.
A message is a request for a future action, such as playing a sound; it works like an asynchronous service API and usually has a single listener.
why: If other code could take messages, the queue would lose its value.

text: Event queues need not be global; they are useful inside a single class or domain as well.
Event queues may pair one sender with one receiver, one with many, many with one, or many with many. Fan-in is the many-to-one case; fan-out is the one-to-many case.
Garbage-collected languages keep a message in memory while it is needed, whereas in C or C++ the programmer must ensure the object lives long enough.
Shared ownership keeps a message alive while any reference exists and frees it when forgotten; in C++ shared_ptr provides this.
When the queue owns messages, the sender requests a fresh message from the queue, fills it in, and the receiver processes the same stored message; this backing store is an object pool.
Message queue usually names a system that communicates between applications, event queues live inside one application, and publish/subscribe usually names large distributed systems.
Queue readers come in three kinds: single-cast, where one owner pulls from the queue; broadcast, where every listener sees every event; and work queue, where each item goes to exactly one listener.
Keep the narrowcast hierarchy simple, since a tangled network of unrelated managers may cost more effort than it is worth.
Use narrowcasting when in-game speed matters more than the effort of setting up registrations.

Real designs mix communication methods: shared state for basic data such as position, direct references for closely related pairs, and messages for less important notifications; start simple and add paths as needed.
when: designing communication between components
why: Each method suits a different kind of data and coupling.

text: Narrowcasting uses many specialized managers, with listeners explicitly registered to those likely to want most of their events, so nearly every delivered event is wanted.
Narrowcasting wastes few events and keeps no per-listener interest records, so runtime is faster when listeners want nearly everything they receive.
when: When listeners want nearly everything they receive
why: Targeted delivery wastes few events and needs no per-listener interest records, so events are processed without filtering overhead.

text: A queue decouples sender from receiver both statically, meaning who they are, and in time, meaning when work happens.
why: The sender only places the request into a first-in, first-out store and returns, while a processor handles it later.

text: With one writer the sender is implicit, since only one object can add to the queue, and one writer usually comes with multiple readers.
why: Only one object can add to the queue, so any listener can safely assume that object is the sender.

text: Narrowcast managers form a hierarchy: one per small group such as a team, a shared manager across groups such as a battalion, and one manager per side for global information.
when: RTS-style games with many groups
why: With one manager per group, events reach only the correct individuals, so few events are wasted.

text: Characters changing groups during play require re-registration, which is hard when a group has been largely destroyed.
A sender receives its own broadcast, so message feedback loops are possible.
when: a container broadcasts messages to all components, including the sender
why: Broadcast delivery includes the origin of the message.

text: Queued work runs after the sending call has returned, so the sender cannot count on an immediate result.
why: The call returns as soon as the request is enqueued, and a processor picks it up at a later time.

text: 1) Give every component a receive method that accepts a message. 2) Have the container send a message by looping over its components and calling receive on each. 3) Let components send messages to the container.
when: components must notify each other without referencing one another
why: A container routing messages keeps siblings decoupled from each other.

text: Queued events must carry full details, since by handling time entities may be deallocated and nearby objects moved; the receiver cannot safely inspect the world.
when: when designing events for a queue, or when events are processed later than they were raised
why: The world may have changed since the event was raised.

text: Use per-squad messaging to avoid ambiguity when the same script runs for multiple squads.
when: Concurrent copies of a script for different squads
why: Separate message channels keep each squad's signals distinct

text: Use a queue only when a push-style sender and a pull-style receiver must meet through a buffer; the queue supplies that buffer.
when: Choosing between a queue and simpler decoupling patterns like Observer or Command.
why: Queues are complex and reshape architecture, so simpler patterns are preferred unless time decoupling is needed.

text: Decide who owns a queued message, since it outlives the enqueuing call; options are passing ownership to the queue, sharing ownership, or letting the queue own pooled messages.
when: Messages are queued rather than processed synchronously.
why: A queued message outlives its sender's call, unlike a synchronous notification on the stack.

text: Narrowcasting setup needs substantial code to decide how listeners attach to the managers.
when: When there are hundreds of event managers
why: Managers keep no record of listener interests to gain speed, which moves the wiring work into setup code.

text: Single-cast keeps the queue an implementation detail, is more encapsulated, and avoids contention between listeners, but the sender only sees the methods the owner exposes.
when: The queue is part of a class's API.
why: One owner pulls the queue, so no other listener competes for items.

text: MMOGs need far more storage, and their servers run on dedicated hardware separate from clients, with much more RAM and processing.
Networked games share one seed across machines; if one player draws a random number without informing the others, their generators fall out of sync.
when: Online games where random numbers are generated on the players' machines rather than a server
why: Both machines must generate every number to keep their seeds in step, so an uninformed draw breaks that.

text: In peer-to-peer play, it is hard to tell who dropped, and dropping just before a result is submitted lets a player manipulate the outcome.
when: when games connect players directly
why: attribution is unclear and reporting can be manipulated

text: 1) Predict a delayed character's position with the keep-going assumption. 2) When the prediction proves wrong, correct it gradually for massively multiplayer games or snap it for shooters.
when: Multiplayer updates are delayed.
why: Simple prediction keeps network play responsive during lag.

text: Pair players using past disconnect frequency as a stability measure, and use ping as a criterion in games spread across several servers.
when: Automated matchmaking; ping-based pairing in large games with servers spread around the world
why: stable players are less likely to drop mid-match

text: Specify networking requirements for LAN, internet, or wireless play.
when: When the game requires internet, LAN, or wireless networks

text: Remote debugging connects a diagnostic tool to a live game so AI state can be inspected and altered, useful for faults that never appear in isolated tests.
Routing play through the game's servers makes it easier to identify who dropped and keeps each player's IP address hidden from the others.
On a PC, debugging tools attach directly to the running game; on consoles, a development PC connects remotely to the test hardware.
Grouping players with close latency cuts unfair edges and lowers the odds of dropping.
Building a tactical analysis server pays off only when the game relies heavily on tactical analyses; lighter projects can skip it.
when: When the game relies heavily on tactical analyses
why: Implementation effort should match how much the game depends on tactics.

text: Network delay in remote debugging can make the displayed game state already out of date.
A brief grace period to rejoin keeps a single lost packet from settling the outcome.
why: Players get time to reconnect, so one dropped packet does not decide the match for them.

text: The Null Object pattern returns a special object implementing the same interface, doing nothing, wherever NULL would otherwise be returned.
NIL is a value added to every pointer type and marks an absent component of a record.
Have the null service print debug output whenever it is used, so a missing registration does not stay hidden.
when: When a real service was not registered and a null service is returned instead
why: A null substitute gives no error, so the misbehavior must be traced back to the missing registration.

text: A locator defaulting to a null service always returns a valid object, so callers never handle a missing real service.
why: Initialization sets the null provider as default, so the lookup always finds some provider to return.

text: Using NIL for absent components removes the need for a tag field, so finite variant-like structures can be built from plain pointer records.
when: Recursive record types in which one variant case has no further components

text: When lookup fails, a locator can return NULL for callers to check, assert and halt the game, or return a null service so the game keeps running.
When outside code supplies components, someone can forget to wire the right ones, which breaks the object.
when: An entity receives its components from external code.
why: Nothing enforces that every required part is supplied.

text: A record type may admit meaningless field combinations, such as an impossible calendar date. The programmer must ensure such values never arise.
when: when fields are independent of one another
why: the record type itself admits the invalid combinations

text: Use a null service on large teams where waiting on other systems or disabling buggy ones is common.
when: On large teams where a feature depends on a system not yet in place
why: It saves downtime and gives an easy way to turn off a faulty service.

text: Returning NULL needs checks at every call site, and one missed check crashes the game; asserting removes call-site checks but stops the game until the problem is fixed.
A null service keeps the game running when a dependency is not ready, but an accidentally missing service becomes harder to trace because the game silently misbehaves.
when: On large teams where a feature depends on a system not yet in place
why: A null substitute gives no error, so the wrong behavior has to be traced back to the missing registration.

text: Moving the null check from every access into the provide step saves a branch per access, but the locator must be initialized early for the null default to be set.
why: Dropping the conditional from the accessor means each service lookup skips a comparison, so every lookup stays cheaper.

text: ORD(ch) gives the ordinal number of a character and CHR(i) gives the character with ordinal i; they are inverses, so ORD(CHR(i)) = i and CHR(ORD(c)) = c.
Implementations often store membership as integers, such as 0 to 255, because integer arithmetic is faster and can be more accurate.
A number format changes only how a value appears; the stored value used in calculations stays unchanged.
Portable code can assume 26 capital letters, 26 lower-case letters, 10 decimal digits and punctuation marks.
Compilers can turn DIV and MOD by a power of two into a fast shift or mask.
Code that assumes a particular numeric encoding of characters is not system independent.
why: No single character encoding is used on every computer, so the numeric codes assigned to characters differ from machine to machine.

text: DIV rounds toward negative infinity, so -31 DIV 10 gives -4, not -3, and -31 MOD 10 gives 9.
when: When the divisor is positive
why: The remainder must lie between zero and the divisor minus one, which pushes the quotient down toward negative infinity.

text: ENTIER(x) returns the integral part of x.
A linear trendline is the straight line that minimizes the total distance to every data point.
REAL values approximate real numbers with round-off error, so results may be inexact and should not be expected to match exactly as INTEGER results do.
why: Round-off error makes REAL results approximate; this is why INTEGER and REAL are distinct types.

text: A scalar can be normalized to its sign by dividing by its absolute value, or by flipping the sign bit where bit patterns are accessible.
A float range condition passes when its watched value lies between a minimum and maximum, inclusive.
when: Implementing numeric transition triggers
why: Range checks are the simplest building block for composable conditions.

text: The perceptron threshold is a sigmoid whose sharpness is set by a width parameter, and it can be replaced by another function such as a radial basis function.
ROUNDDOWN, ROUNDUP, and ROUND behave like FLOOR, CEILING, and MROUND but take a digit count instead of a significance value.
Game code favors explicit character classes and labeled rosters of enemies, items, and skills over one-of-a-kind creatures.
when: when modeling game content types
why: well-defined kinds are easier to design, balance, and maintain

text: The Java Virtual Machine and the .NET Common Language Runtime use single-byte opcodes, though some VMs use multi-byte instructions with complex decoding.
when: Choosing an opcode width for a bytecode VM
why: Single-byte opcodes keep decoding simple, which is sufficient for many VMs.

text: In Unity, one unit equals one meter, which helps designers reason about distances characters must cover.
when: sizing level geometry in Unity

text: Unlike conditional boolean operators, the sum x + y is undefined if either operand is undefined.
WriteInt and ReadInt are specified abstractly, while their binary representation is left platform dependent.
An INTEGER value may be assigned to a REAL variable, but a REAL value needs truncation or rounding before it can go into an INTEGER variable.
The standard primitive types are INTEGER, REAL, BOOLEAN, CHAR and SET.
The slash gives a REAL quotient, while DIV gives an INTEGER quotient.
Standard primitive types come with arithmetic and logical operators.
An integer is an optional minus sign followed by digits.
Integer output can be padded with blanks to a minimum width.
Type checking catches errors such as assigning a Boolean to an arithmetic variable before the program runs, a key advantage of high-level over assembly code.
Using a zero base orientation keeps a character upright when the target lies in the x-z plane.
Three row operations keep a matrix system valid: reorder rows, multiply a whole row by a constant, and add two rows together.
Some five-card hands match none of the standard categories, so summing all category counts gives less than the total number of five-card hands.
Game systems such as physics, collisions, distance-based audio volume, and proximity-limited chat depend on a sense of space.
When cancelling entries, prefer whole-number row multipliers over fractions, since fractions are harder to manipulate by hand.
If goals are indexed by integers, the goal-change lookup becomes an array access that takes constant time.
when: When the complete set of goals is established before the game runs
why: Looking up a value by integer index is a single array access, taking the same time regardless of how many goals exist.

text: Logical operations on a machine word act on all its bits at once, so set operations on small bit strings are very fast.
when: When set elements fit within a small, fixed number of machine words
why: Machine logic instructions act on every bit of a word in parallel, so one operation handles many set members at once.

text: Integer arithmetic is treated as exact, and a result outside the representable range is an overflow that interrupts computation.
why: The integer type is a bounded slice of whole numbers, so a result beyond its limits cannot be stored exactly.

text: Removing the separating key from the parent can underflow the parent, so balancing or merging propagates upward, possibly up to the root.
when: When removing a key leaves an ancestor page below its minimum size
why: Each merge takes a separator out of the parent, which can leave that parent too small and trigger the same repair one level higher.

text: Seconds elapsed in the day equal the day fraction multiplied by 86400, which is 24 × 60 × 60.
Rounding a real number x to the nearest integer is obtained as ENTIER(x + 0.5).
why: The integral-part function discards the fraction, so adding one half before truncating rounds values at or above a half upward.

text: With n-bit two's complement, INTEGER values run from -2^(n-1) up to 2^(n-1) - 1.
when: When INTEGER values are stored in n-bit two's complement notation

text: For positive n, q = m DIV n and r = m MOD n satisfy q*n + r = m, with 0 <= r < n.
when: n is positive

text: FLOOR(RAND()*faces+1,1) returns an integer die roll from 1 to the number of faces.
when: Custom integer rolls where RANDBETWEEN is not used.
why: Flooring is required because the scaled value never reaches the top of the range.

text: A 100 × 100 grid encoded as a vector has 10,000 variables, a length that many search algorithms struggle with.
Display rounding can hide the stored value: a cell showing 1 for 1.4 gives 14 when multiplied by 10.
when: a cell uses a whole-number format
why: Formatting changes only how a value is displayed; calculations still use the underlying unrounded number.

text: Single-byte literals limit the range of values a script can use, so the encoding must cover the full numeric range before shipping.
when: Designing literal encoding in bytecode
why: A one-byte operand can represent only 256 distinct values.

text: When zero means inherit, a breed that truly has zero starting health cannot be expressed.
when: using zero as the sentinel for inherited health
why: The sentinel value is indistinguishable from a legitimate zero.

text: An overflow assertion may be compiled out in release builds, so the fixed array must be sized with margin rather than relying on the check.
why: Overflow is caught only in debug builds.

text: The axis is undefined when the sine of the angle is zero, so that case needs special handling.
As printed, the inverse square formula multiplies the constant by distance squared, so strength grows with distance, contradicting the decay. Verify the formula against its source before use.
when: When separation strength follows an inverse square law decay

text: Typing decimals in place of exact fractions introduces rounding errors that accumulate through iterations.
when: When entering fractions such as one third as spreadsheet cell values
why: A typed decimal is only an approximation, while a fraction formula keeps the exact value.

text: 1) Process digits from position 1 onward. 2) Form carry r = 10*r + digit. 3) Store r DIV 2 as the new digit. 4) Keep r MOD 2 as the carry into the next position.
when: Fraction stored as an array of decimal digits.
why: Carry-style division halves the value digit by digit.

text: 1) Scan the character sequence from its start. 2) At each word position, compare the text with each word A_i. 3) On a match, write its counterpart B_i in place.
when: text held as a character sequence, with word pairs whose words have a small fixed maximum length

text: 1) Fetch a neighbouring page. 2) If it has spare items, redistribute the items of both pages evenly. 3) Otherwise merge both pages with the separating key from the parent and discard the neighbour.
when: a page has underflowed after deletion
why: Fetching a neighbouring page is a costly operation, so moving several items per fetch is worth it.

text: Distances use integers, while volume and radius values use floats; objects that expect one type fail when given the other.
when: entering property values and visual-script variables
why: Wrong number types stop objects from working.

text: Model at a standard unit, such as one grid square equals one engine unit, and if imported objects arrive at one-twentieth size, scale them by twenty.
when: when moving assets between a 3D modeling program and a game engine
why: consistent scale keeps imported level pieces in proportion

text: Declare types before use, since a computer offers only one typeface and types cannot be shown by notation.
when: writing programs
why: the compiler needs types to check the program and allocate storage

text: If a character has no open valid slot, report the error, for example to the player.
when: Greedy assignment fails for a character

text: Mark a node terminal when one of its flaws cannot be repaired, and stop the search with failure once the graph exceeds a preset maximum node count.
when: Plan-space search with a node limit

text: Real-valued insistence costs no more than on/off values, but for thousands of characters on/off goals save storage.
when: Many characters and goals
why: Algorithms using real-valued goal weights are no more complex than ones using flags, so the only trade-off is storage.

text: A terminator character marks the end of a variable-length string. A stored length is directly available but caps string length at the character-set size, such as 256 for ASCII.
when: storing variable-length strings
why: The length is kept in one leading character, so its value cannot exceed what that character set can encode.

text: An object pool is a store that tracks a set of instantiated objects so they can be found and reused.
when: Holding lazily created flyweights.
why: A pool gives a natural place to keep existing shared instances.

text: Object Pool keeps a fixed collection of reusable objects allocated up front, handing them out and reclaiming them instead of allocating and freeing each one individually.
why: Trades flexibility for fewer allocations and less fragmentation.

text: Object pools suit game entities, visual effects, and less visible structures such as the list of currently playing sounds.
Pools are less common in garbage-collected systems but still help avoid allocation cost on slower mobile CPUs.
Tune pool size deliberately: keep it no larger than expected peak use, since extra slots waste memory; undersized pools usually surface as crashes.
why: Too small a pool shows up quickly as a crash, while an oversized pool locks up memory other features could use.

text: Object Pool management lets objects be added and removed in a contiguous array over time, which locality-focused designs usually rely on.
when: Objects are created and destroyed often in performance-critical code
why: Reusing slots keeps the array packed without repeated heap allocation

text: Spawned room contents such as enemies or items are good pooling candidates because they need reliable slots.
when: generating or spawning dungeon room contents

text: Pooled pathfinding benefits most in persistent worlds where levels stay active for long periods, and less in RTS games, though it is worth trying when pathfinding is a bottleneck.
when: Choosing whether to pool pathfinders.
why: Persistent levels keep reusable stored data valid for longer.

text: When each path is short and computed in one go, use a small pool of planners with a request queue.
when: Pathfinding with short paths
why: Each request gets its complete path in one computation, so no anytime algorithm is needed.

text: Infer in-use status from existing state, not a stored flag: a particle is in use while its lifetime counter exceeds zero; a coupled object may be unused when offscreen.
when: Pooled objects that have a limited lifetime, such as particles.
why: The existing lifetime counter already shows whether the object is live, so no separate flag needs storing.

text: Serving pathfinding requests from a shared pool of pathfinders fed by one queue, instead of one planner per character, reduces total memory use.
when: Many characters request routes at once, such as in RTS or MMORPG servers.
why: Per-character planners hold large data that may exceed cache, while a fixed pool reuses stored data across requests.

text: Particle systems store particles in one contiguous pool, but most slots are often inactive. Skipping inactive entries by testing a flag still pulls unused data into the cache.
when: Pool is sized for a maximum count and many slots are unused at any moment
why: Checking the flag loads the whole particle block, so inactive entries waste cache bandwidth

text: Pool allocates one block at startup and does not free it during play; each object tracks an in-use state, and reclaiming it just resets that state, so the memory manager stays out of the loop.
when: Many short-lived objects spawned in bursts that must be created very quickly.
why: Avoids repeated allocation and freeing cost.

text: Faster planning lets fewer pathfinders serve the same load, so total memory can fall even though each pathfinder stores more data.
when: Pooled pathfinding with reusable stored results.
why: Fewer active pathfinders means less total stored data.

text: Type objects must be managed manually, and new typed objects without a valid type reference will break.
when: using type objects without compiler support
why: Nothing enforces that each typed object refers to a live, valid type.

text: Free list pointers must be updated correctly on every create and destroy, and creating from an empty list must be guarded, or the list breaks.
when: Implementing a free-list object pool.

text: Because a pool's limit is hard, a burst of activity can exhaust it, so full-pool strategies must be decided in advance.
Implicit allocation hides where storage sharing is intended, which causes problems when records are updated selectively.
when: When selective updating of records is permitted.
why: Hidden handling forces shared ancestor records to be stored twice, so sharing cannot be expressed.

text: 1) Preallocate a pool of identically sized nodes at startup. 2) Take nodes from the pool when observers register. 3) Return nodes to the pool on removal instead of calling the allocator.
when: when observer registration must avoid dynamic allocation
why: reusing fixed-size nodes avoids allocator calls during gameplay

text: 1) Keep a static flag. 2) Set it in the constructor and clear it in the destructor. 3) Assert in the constructor that the flag is not already set.
when: A class must stay limited to one instance without global access

text: 1) Keep a head pointer to the first available object. 2) Have each unused object point to the next available one, with the last pointing to nothing. 3) Store the pointer in a union shared with live state. 4) Chain all objects together in the constructor.
when: Implementing an object pool for particles or similar short-lived objects.
why: Chaining reuses dead objects' memory, so no extra array is needed.

text: 1) To create, take the head object off the list and initialize it, which takes constant time. 2) When an object dies, push it onto the front of the list.
when: Using a free-list object pool.
why: Pushing and popping the list head only swaps a few links, with no searching for a free slot.

text: 1) Scan slots from the start for the first unused object. 2) Initialize it with the new state. 3) Return it. 4) If no slot is free, drop the request.

Choose a full-pool strategy by comparing: 1) size the pool to never overflow, 2) skip creating the new object, 3) forcibly kill an existing object, 4) grow the pool at runtime or add an overflow pool.
when: the pool has no free slot
why: The right choice depends on how noticeable a missing new object is versus a disappearing existing one.

text: Partition memory into separate pools per object type, since a fixed limit caps one type so a flood (explosions) cannot exhaust memory for others (new enemies).
when: one object type could crowd out others

text: Set every field when reinitializing a reused object, and clear the slot in debug mode on reclaim, since reuse skips the memory manager's debug fill that catches uninitialized memory.
when: Reusing a pooled object instead of allocating a fresh one.
why: Reuse bypasses the memory manager's debug fill, and leftover old data looks almost valid, hiding forgotten fields.

text: Call the pool's update once per frame, looping over every slot and updating each object, with inactive objects doing nothing.
A single pool with mixed object sizes must make each slot fit the largest object, and an undersized object write can overwrite its neighbor.
when: objects of different types or subclasses share one pool
why: A larger object placed in a smaller slot spills over into the memory of the next slot.

text: Pooling adds bookkeeping and fixed capacity, so it is wasteful when allocation is rare or cheap.
when: allocation is rare or cheap

text: Splitting pathfinding over frames to share a pool lengthens queue waiting time as the number of characters grows.
when: Many characters requesting paths through a shared queue.
why: Requests wait longer while the fixed pool works through the queue.

text: The notification queue must stay sorted by time, so it is implemented as a priority queue.
Observer lets you observe the object that did something interesting, while an event object lets you observe an object representing what happened.
The observer pattern has two roles: an observer interface with one notification method, and a subject that keeps a list of observers, offers public add and remove methods, and notifies each in turn.
when: when implementing observer-based communication

text: Indirect calls usually carry a far higher cost than direct ones, chiefly via pipeline stalls and cache effects rather than extra load.
Plain function pointers hold no state, so a command that needs stored data requires a class or functor.
when: in languages where function pointers lack closures

text: Observer notification walks a list and makes virtual calls, with no message objects or queues, so it is slower than a direct call but negligible outside hot code.
when: when judging observer overhead
why: virtual dispatch costs little unless it runs in tight loops

text: Indirect call overhead matters little when the work is spread across frames, since the overhead is spread too.
when: work is spread across frames
why: Spreading the algorithm across frames spreads the added call cost too, so each frame barely notices it.

text: If understanding one side of a communication requires understanding the other, use an explicit call instead of an observer.
when: When understanding a program part requires reasoning about both sides of a communication link at once.
why: Observer hides the link between the two sides.

text: Use observers for communication outside performance-critical loops, where the cost of dynamic dispatch is affordable.
when: when deciding where observers belong
why: hot code paths are sensitive to per-call overhead

text: Register functions or closures as observers instead of implementing a full observer interface, which feels heavyweight when only one notification is needed.
when: when the language supports first-class functions
why: a single class cannot easily use different notification methods for different subjects

text: A registry records each listener's interests so the checker searches only relevant items and the dispatcher delivers only matching events.
when: When a listener cares only about specific events, such as one particular time, not everything the manager produces.
why: Limiting what gets looked for and sent avoids wasted checks and wasted messages.

text: Nearly every gameplay change requires code changes, and modular design limits how far a single change spreads through the codebase.
when: Throughout a game's production cycle, when gameplay changes are requested.

text: With observer, listeners can be changed or removed without editing the subject, which keeps sending notifications that nothing receives.
why: The subject does not depend on any particular listener.

text: Deleting an observer that a subject still references leaves the subject notifying freed memory; deleting a subject leaves observers waiting for notifications that never arrive.
when: when observers or subjects are destroyed while registered
why: registration links are one-directional bookkeeping that the destroyed object cannot clean up on its own

text: In an intrusive linked list, observers themselves carry next pointers and the subject keeps a head pointer, so registration and notification need no dynamic allocation.
when: when avoiding allocation for observer registration
why: the list nodes are the observers, so no separate node objects are needed

text: When one observer watches several subjects, each subject's list uses separate node objects that point at observers, so one observer can sit in multiple lists at once.
when: when an observer must watch several subjects
why: each node carries its own next pointer, freeing the observer from a single link

text: In a GUI, the operating system queues user input and the app's loop pulls the oldest event and routes it to a handler, unlike interrupts that force a jump at any moment.
why: The app chooses when to pull events.

text: Observers that add or remove observers during notification can corrupt the subject's list, so notification must prevent or handle concurrent modification.
when: when notifying a list that observers may modify
why: the notify loop walks the list while observers change it

text: Observers should not depend on notification order, since depending on it signals hidden coupling between them.
when: when observers are notified in list order
why: list order is an implementation detail that can change

text: An observer that tries to acquire a lock held by the notifying subject can deadlock the game.
when: when observers and explicit locks are mixed
why: the subject waits on the observer while the observer waits on the subject's lock

text: Observer is often confused with events and messaging, which are distinct patterns, and the confusion makes communication harder to reason about.
when: when naming or choosing a communication pattern
why: the patterns differ in coupling and timing

text: 1) Take notifications from the front of the time-sorted queue. 2) Deliver each one whose time has passed. 3) Stop at the first notification scheduled in the future.
when: When signals take time to travel, so each queued message carries a scheduled delivery time.

text: 1) Place a reference to the sender inside the event object. 2) Listeners read that reference when they need to know who sent the event.
when: A listener needs to know the sender.
why: Multi-writer queues do not otherwise reveal the origin of an event.

text: Unregister observers when no longer needed; a subject keeps references to them, so garbage collection cannot reclaim them and they keep receiving notifications (lapsed listener problem).
when: Observers are created and abandoned without unregistering.
why: Subjects retain their listeners; the subject's reference keeps the observer alive.

text: Use observer to decouple mostly unrelated subsystems or a feature reacting to events from several unrelated domains; avoid it inside one cohesive feature.
why: Observer suits decoupling, not tightly coupled logic; the subject announces events without knowing its listeners.

text: Register a listener for a specific trigger, such as a set time, rather than for repeated updates it would ignore each frame.
when: When a listener needs one specific moment, like a set time, and other events are useless to it.
why: Receiving every per-frame update would flood the listener with messages it has no use for.

text: Have each observer unregister itself from its subjects in its destructor.
when: when the observer knows which subjects it watches
why: the simplest way to prevent dangling observer pointers

text: Give the observer interface a virtual destructor and one pure virtual notification method that receives the sending entity and an event identifier.
when: when defining an observer interface in C++
why: the virtual destructor keeps polymorphic deletion safe

text: A concrete observer should switch on the event identifier and act only on the events it cares about.
when: when one notification method serves many event kinds
why: ignoring unrelated events keeps each observer focused

text: Keep observer handlers fast: return quickly and move slow work to another thread or a work queue.
when: when an observer must do expensive work
why: blocking the notifying thread stalls the subject and the game

text: Making a class observable by inheriting from Subject exposes notify only to the class itself, but composing a separate event object keeps the class hierarchy free of the base class.
when: Making an engine or system observable.
why: Production code usually prefers composition over inheritance.

text: Keeping observers in a collection, not one slot, keeps them independent, because one registration cannot silently unhook another.
when: when a subject can have several observers
why: one slot means a new registration can replace an existing one

text: Using one array per concrete type allows non-virtual calls on tightly packed objects, but adds collection-management overhead and requires the code to know every type.
when: The number of types is small and manageable
why: Separate collections must be maintained and code loses decoupling from open-ended type sets

text: SIMD applies one instruction to several data items at once, usually four at a time on current hardware.
PC hardware varies widely; graphics APIs hide hardware differences but do not remove the need to detect features and adjust.
Early power concerns were minor for mains-fed devices and handhelds, but phones and laptops made battery use central.
Hardware pipelining imposes a floor of about three frames of input lag; input arriving mid-frame adds up to about four frame lengths.
when: Standard multistage rendering pipeline.

text: Running every expensive AI algorithm for every character each frame becomes impossible when a game has thousands of characters, as in real-time strategy.
Online incremental algorithms give the largest speedups, and heuristics such as those in SITI can improve them further.
Unpredictable flag tests in hot loops cause branch mispredictions that flush the pipeline, so developers avoid per-item branches in performance-critical inner loops.
when: Condition changes unpredictably between iterations of a loop running over many items every frame
why: Branch predictors guess wrong on irregular patterns, each misprediction flushes the pipeline, and mispredictions and cache effects of branches add up across the loop.

text: Check whether an optimized AI technique depends on C++-specific features before porting it, since such optimizations may not transfer to other languages.
when: Porting optimized AI code to another language
why: The optimization relies on language-specific features that other languages may lack.

text: SIMD and multi-core parallelism speed up AI only when the data and code are structured for them.
when: On platforms where parallel AI must be designed in from the start, not just enabled by a setup call.

text: Distance-to-nearest-enemy and flee-direction calculations suit SIMD well, and steering algorithms gain the most.
when: When many characters each run the same distance or direction calculation.
why: One instruction operating on several characters' data at once fits these per-character calculations.

text: Profile before abandoning flyweight for performance reasons, since its cost is often unclear without measurement.
why: Pointer indirection's cost depends on memory layout and may be negligible.

text: Keeping neuron states and weights in separate arrays lets SIMD instructions process four neurons at once and keeps relevant data in cache, giving large speed gains on big networks.
when: Network is large and runs in production.
why: Contiguous data allows parallel arithmetic and better cache use.

text: The load-balancing scheduler takes O(n) time and O(m) memory, where n is all behaviours and m the number due, and its two loops cannot be merged.
when: When a load-balancing scheduler divides frame time among only the behaviours due to run.
why: The share depends on the due count, so counting must precede running.

text: Game performance work spans three layers: low-level hardware tuning, mid-level patterns, and algorithm research.
Reference AI code omits platform-specific optimizations, which need machine-specific assembly and would obscure core algorithms, so profile it in your own game before shipping.
when: Reusing sample or library code in a shipped game
why: Code written for clarity carries little optimization.

text: A single expensive behaviour, such as pathfinding, can cause a frame spike on its own, so long processes should be spread over several frames.
when: When one piece of code is so costly that it spikes a frame by itself.
why: Frame time is capped, so one large job alone can exhaust a frame's budget.

text: Iterating a contiguous array and skipping inactive items does not restore locality when useful items are scattered among inactive ones.
when: Active items are a small or interleaved fraction of the pool
why: Skips jump across memory and the cache keeps reloading unused blocks

text: Conversion routines that ignore arithmetic overflow may produce wrong values for numbers too large for the integer type.
Operation-count formulas ignore loop control and other overhead, and their coefficients depend on the system, so they cannot alone rank real run times.
when: When choosing between algorithms by practical run time, beyond asymptotic classification.
why: Formulas count only comparisons and moves, skipping loop control, and the constants vary by machine.

text: 1) Collect the behaviours due this frame using the frequency modulo test. 2) Count them. 3) Give each an equal share of remaining frame time and pass the share in. 4) After each run, subtract elapsed time from the remaining time before computing the next share.
when: Frame has a fixed time allowance.
why: Overruns reduce later shares, keeping the total within the allowance.

text: Do not route a hot loop through an entity object when it needs only component data; the entity adds an extra hop without useful state.
when: When a hot loop only needs component data and the entity holds no useful state.
why: Going through the entity adds an extra pointer hop with nothing useful gained.

text: Profile to reveal cache misses, then keep each algorithm's data together, since this often brings dramatic speed-ups.
when: When an algorithm's data is spread around memory and profiling shows cache misses.
why: Scattered data rarely stays in cache, so the processor refetches memory blocks for only a few instructions each.

text: Clip velocity in the update step: if speed exceeds the maximum, normalize velocity and scale it to the maximum. Keep this out of the steering behavior itself.
when: Acceleration-based movement with no other speed control
why: Acceleration alone lets speed grow without limit.

text: Keep slot costs well below the data type's maximum, since several costs are added together.
when: When a slot-assignment algorithm sums several slot costs for one character
why: Summed costs can overflow.

text: Cap the number of moves in any simulation or unbounded loop, for example at 500, and treat reaching the cap as the end, and keep the same safeguard in shipped code.
when: running simulations or generators that could run indefinitely
why: rare endless games or loops can hang the process, and small probability changes can make them common

text: Design a game that does not depend on special platform features from the start, especially if the team lacks time to learn that platform.
when: when the team is unfamiliar with a target platform
why: Unfamiliar platform features can consume scarce time.

text: SIMD needs many characters performing the same operation with their data stored together, which restructures code and lowers readability.
when: many characters run identical operations
why: SIMD units can only fetch a group's data efficiently when it is stored contiguously, unlike the usual per-character layout.

text: SIMD hardware can evaluate rules in parallel, but this drops the early-exit shortcut, since heavy branching parallelises poorly.
when: When the rule evaluation is implemented on SIMD hardware such as PC SSE extensions

text: Bookkeeping structures use extra memory, so the pattern is a poor choice when memory is tighter than CPU time.
when: memory is the scarcer resource
why: The structure is a memory-for-speed trade, so it works against a tight memory budget.

text: Tally strokes make addition very simple but are poor for large numbers, while Arabic positional numerals make addition of large numbers, multiplication and division easier.
when: When the main workload is adding numbers rather than multiplying or dividing
why: Positional weight of digits lets large sums, products and quotients break into simpler, systematic steps.

text: Without an animated body, a movement capsule does not read as arcing or turning, and moves like ground pounds look odd.
when: a physics body is shown without its character animation
why: Players read motion from the visible body.

text: Slope-dependent friction and clear slip thresholds give players a constant sense of surface texture and where footing will fail.
when: traversing varied slopes
why: Changes in grip reveal the surface.

text: A collider makes an object interact physically as a simple shape, such as a box, regardless of its visible art.
Game feel fakes Newtonian physics: players infer an object's properties from how it moves and interacts with other things.
Ragdoll physics produces lifelike, unscripted movement for characters in real time, with limbs reacting to forces without hand-made animation.
Simulated space is a physical world in which the avatar collides with and responds to objects, and the player perceives that world directly.
Interaction with a unique physical reality is the fifth experience: players assemble a self-contained physical universe with designer-created laws from how objects respond.
The ideal lookahead equals the least common multiple of all frequencies, but that is often large, so a manually tuned window is usually used.
Offset AI geometry is usually generated automatically by a geometric algorithm.
Motion-controller gestures use the same principle, with more complex pattern seeking over accelerometer and pointer data.
Real-time control of fluids, fog, smoke and flocks using Boids-style flocking are further options for responsive simulation.
Most game feel arises from the interplay between space and motion, so space is the other half of tuning.
Mass and gravity can be perceived independently: a heavy-feeling character can have very high gravity and no vertical jump, while a light-feeling one can have very low gravity.
why: Each property is conveyed by different movement cues.

text: Simulation can be hooked into particles so their movement responds to forces.
Tune behaviour through the underlying generic system first, then layer specific case adjustments on top.
why: Generic physics applied to many objects produces a wider range of results, including unplanned exploits.

text: Simulating a fluid-like material with particles and a Lennard-Jones force model can give it a viscous, mercury-like feel, and thousands of particles can run in real time.
when: building a soft, cohesive material from particles
why: The force model keeps particles clustered and flowing together.

text: Richer physics lets players use objects in unplanned ways, such as stacking objects against a door, expanding the set of solutions available.
Clamp the frame rate on battery devices where good-enough smoothness matters more than maximum detail; run uncapped when power is not a concern.
when: On mobile-type games focused on gameplay quality over maximum detail
why: Running uncapped spends every spare cycle on frame rate or fidelity, drawing maximum power and heating the device.

text: Adding spatial motion to VR raises the risk of discomfort, so it needs extra comfort work.
when: adding spatial motion to a VR game
why: Motion the eyes perceive but the inner ear does not feel creates a disconnect that can cause nausea.

text: Cartoon physics fits a stylized metaphor when players do not expect real-world behavior, so exaggerated collisions read as intended.
when: A game uses non-realistic vehicles or characters
why: Expectations match the stylized treatment.

text: Build movement on sound physics, then add extra rules so the character can do things physics alone would not allow.
when: Designing an action character beyond realistic physics
why: Consistent base interactions reinforce one another, so the world reads as having its own coherent laws.

text: Games aiming for real-world fidelity are prone to failure, because players bring real-world experience to every interaction and notice any departure.
when: when setting a realism target

text: Drag slows a character every frame, capping top speed without an explicit clip check.
when: Physics engines that apply drag

text: Aiming an area-damage explosive at the player's own feet pushes the player farther when combined with physics, enabling unplanned movement.
when: Area damage and knockback physics coexist
why: Blast force and physics push add up on the player's body.

text: Turning while jumping can convert angular velocity into forward speed, producing movement faster than normal.
when: Air control and turning physics coexist
why: A physics interaction adds the turn's momentum to forward motion.

text: Sideways friction makes a vehicle grip and carve; without it, turning feels floaty, as if driving on ice.
when: When building the feel of carving through turns in a driving game
why: Sideways tire friction lets the tires dig in and resist sliding during turns, as a real car does.

text: High ground friction keeps a standing or moving character from slipping on flat ground.
when: When a character is in contact with the ground

text: A chained move can override a collision animation already in progress, even after that animation's particles have started.
A vehicle's center of gravity moves depending on whether its tow chain is extended and whether a heavy object is attached.
when: When the tow chain is extended or an object is hooked to it
why: The chain and any attached load change the rig's mass and balance, shifting where its weight sits.

text: A physics engine applies general rules to resolve any interaction between any objects, and greater sophistication makes object interactions more detailed and the world feel more physically real.
when: When a game's simulation becomes more sophisticated
why: General rules resolve any object interaction, instead of tuning each case separately.

text: Physics engines tune approximations and damping to one step size, so a different step can make them unstable and launch objects with wrong velocities.
when: When the simulation step size changes from the value it was tuned for
why: Damping stops approximations from blowing up, but it is only balanced for the step it was tuned to.

text: With a variable time step, the distance a moving object covers grows in proportion to the elapsed time passed into update().
when: When the game loop's time slice varies with the previous frame's duration
why: Each update must know the elapsed slice, since the slice differs from frame to frame.

text: Physics engines mark resting bodies as idle, so they need no processing until an impulse touches them, and the moving bit acts as a dirty flag.
when: Simulating many bodies where most are at rest.
why: Resting bodies stay unchanged until a force acts on them, so skipping them saves work.

text: A game substitutes its own world for physical reality at the point where a player's action would normally reach the world.
Varying mass between colliding objects adds variety to interactions, while uniform mass makes collisions feel less varied.
when: Designing collisions between many objects
why: Different masses produce different outcomes when objects collide.

text: Gravity is the only simulated parameter in grapple-based platformers: ground running and swinging use fixed values, while falling uses velocity, acceleration and position up to a terminal velocity.
when: Designing movement with a grapple and no jump
why: Only falling needs physics simulation, so other states can use tuned constants.

text: Side contacts with objects are nearly frictionless, redirecting the character along the object's edge so it slides past rather than sticking, which makes near-misses steer forgivingly.
when: Non-head-on collisions with a character capsule
why: Low side friction stops players from being caught on every object

text: Combining and chaining moves built on a simple physics system with a few key relationships (forward speed, vertical thrust, air steering) yields expressive variety.
when: Designing a movement set
why: Predictable responses from a few physics relationships let a player combine and steer triggered moves in many ways.

text: A physics system that resolves input differences finer than the player can perceive makes every run different, even when the player repeats an action.
when: In physics games whose simulation reacts more finely than the player can perceive.
why: Parameters react identically to each input, yet players cannot sense the tiny differences between their own inputs.

text: Spatial constraints give motion meaning: crowded space makes motion feel oppressive, while sparse space makes tuning pointless.
when: designing level spacing for movement
why: Constraints create the frame in which speed and distance matter.

text: Tires can be massless raycasts pointing down from each wheel well, not colliding wheels, so suspension forces come from ray hits on a rigidbody body.
why: Tire position and push force come from ray distance, so the vehicle looks normal even when no ground is hit.

text: Each tire keeps its own velocity and two friction values, sideways and forward, that act against that velocity. All vehicle motion comes from the tires.
why: Velocity held by the tires persists through airtime, so changes made in the air show up on landing.

text: In active ragdoll control, the player's inputs act through internal springs that change size like muscles, instead of applying external forces to the object.
A full physics simulation gives every object properties such as force, velocity, shape, gravity, friction and drag, so gameplay can emerge from their interaction.
when: when building a physics-based game
why: A broad simulation with many built-in properties opens gameplay types that a minimal, top-down simulation cannot reach.

text: Simulated space has two parts: collision detection and response between the avatar and objects, and object placement and spacing relative to the avatar's speed.
why: Without collisions and spacing that respond to movement, the player gets no physical sense of the world.

text: Physical properties behind polish perceptions include mass, velocity, momentum, friction, gravity, shape, elasticity and plasticity.
If the physics engine applies drag, ignoring it in the firing solution makes long-range shots miss.
when: the engine simulates drag
why: The analytic solution assumes drag is negligible.

text: Rotation formulas assume angular speed in radians per second; using degrees per second requires different math.
when: When computing a rotation vector from a rotation axis and an angular velocity

text: Small inconsistencies, such as a character's feet clipping through stairs, can appear even in well-made games.
why: A feedback cue that contradicts the others disrupts the player's mental model of the space.

text: Physics-driven motion can look wrong on some kinds of terrain.
when: When physics-driven bodies, such as hit NPCs, land on certain terrain types.

text: Relying on a detailed simulation the player only observes indirectly produces no tactile sense of interaction, however complete the simulation is.
when: When the player only sets destinations and the computer handles steering and aiming.
why: The actions that produce tactile feel are automated, so the player only observes the simulation from outside.

text: Sticky collisions with scenery can remove all momentum, even at top speed with a boost, which feels negative to players.
when: When collisions are made stickier to favor ramming other vehicles.

text: Motion that ignores surfaces, such as a character running in place against a wall, breaks the illusion of a physical world.
when: When a running character can be pushed into a wall.

text: Visual realism that outpaces the underlying physics creates a mismatch the player notices.

1) Reset the best expert to none and the highest insistence to zero. 2) Ask each expert for insistence and keep the largest. 3) If an expert was found, run it on the board. 4) Return the passed actions.
1) Make the floor a physics-simulated actor driven by an animation track. 2) On player entry to a trigger volume, switch its physics to falling. 3) It drops until it hits the surface below.

1) Cast a ray down from each wheel well. 2) If nothing is hit, place the tire at a set maximum distance below the body. 3) If ground is hit, apply upward force that grows as the hit gets closer to the start. 4) Interpolate the visible tire toward the hit point.
why: With no ground hit, the tire stays at a set maximum distance, keeping the vehicle looking normal.

text: 1) Identify only the forces and state the game needs. 2) Choose the simplest model that works. 3) Let hardware limits shape the approach. 4) Build outward only as needed.
when: when hardware is limited
why: Limited hardware forced the simplest model, and that minimal simulation still gave a distinct, good feel.

text: 1) Query the CPPN for each particle every animation frame. 2) Move each particle to its new position. 3) Query the network again for the next frame.
when: CPPN-driven particle motion
why: Repeated querying produces continuous per-frame particle behaviour.

text: 1) Group the perceptions of each game into physical properties: mass, velocity, momentum, materials, friction, gravity, shape, elasticity, plasticity. 2) Compare the two sets side by side.
when: Comparing the physical feel of two games
why: A shared property list makes differences in perceived physics explicit.

text: Keep desired velocity, a motor-speed target set by throttle input, separate from actual velocity, which the physics engine computes for the body.
when: Vehicle with throttle input and physics-driven motion; airborne input must take effect on contact, or wheel slip must be simulated.
why: Keeping them separate lets input and physical motion evolve independently.

text: Objects should not pass through one another or move bizarrely and unpredictably, and heavy objects should not react to slight contact; players notice these violations immediately.
when: When an object is visually portrayed as large, heavy or massive.
why: Real perception never produces such behaviour, so it disturbs players and undermines physical reality.

text: Limit player projectiles with a timed firing delay and a maximum on-screen count, and make each projectile inherit the shooter's velocity.
when: when designing a ship or character's projectile weapon
why: Delay and cap prevent spam, and inherited velocity keeps shots tied to motion

text: Apply movement and turning forces relative to the vehicle's own facing. Drive along its forward axis and turn by rotating around its vertical axis.
why: Forces then follow the vehicle's orientation as it turns

text: Place a vehicle's center of gravity backward and low so it stays controllable across all combinations of extended chain and attached load.
why: Without shifting the mass backward and down, the vehicle becomes squirrely and hard to steer once a load hangs off the tow.

text: Set a breakable link's stress threshold so heavy-load acceleration never breaks it, while wrapping it around an obstacle should almost always break it.
when: Tuning a tow link tested by accelerating while loaded and by wrapping it around an obstacle.

text: Build failure animations from a ragdoll rig with joint constraints and separate limb masses, so each crash produces different, organic results.
when: When players spend much of their time in failure states such as crashes.
why: A physics rig with joints and per-limb masses yields varied, lively outcomes, which makes failure fun and eases learning.

text: A physical-to-virtual movement link needs accurate position and rotation tracking, since without it the one-to-one illusion breaks.
when: Mapping real device movement to in-game movement.
why: Sensitive sensors reading small position and rotation shifts let the on-screen view track the device at a matching rate, so it reads as a window.

text: Do not make geometric objects primitive types in a general-purpose language when their future operations are unknown.
when: designing a general-purpose language
why: Their best representation depends heavily on operations the language designer cannot foresee.

text: Apply gravity every frame, including while the character stands on ground.
Store a collision position per animation frame when the animation also drives damage and collision checks.
Set the handling fidelity you intend to deliver, so players do not expect simulation-grade accuracy the vehicle cannot match.
when: When a vehicle looks close to photorealistic but the surrounding game is silly or fantastical.
why: Absurd elements such as silly sounds and flying feathers soften the expectation that the vehicle handles like a real one.

text: Keep one consistent level of abstraction across visuals, sound, motion, simulation and rules.
when: When an object must look, sound and move properly while players manipulate it unpredictably.
why: Player expectations about how objects behave are malleable and are shaped by how the object is treated.

text: Turn surface contact into a mechanic, such as taking cover, and back it with matching sound, particles and animation.
when: When a running character can be pushed into walls and other surfaces.
why: Otherwise a character can keep running into a wall unharmed, which undermines the impression of a tough character.

text: Each polish effect should support one clear impression of physicality that fits both the game's metaphor and its simulation.
when: when adding effects to a game
why: Effects that share one impression read as coherent rather than noisy.

text: Setting position directly each frame gives precise, responsive control that stops at once on release but can feel rigid and stilted, while velocity-based simulation gives smooth, gradual acceleration.
when: When a challenge needs precise positioning and accurate jumping.
why: A separate velocity that forces modify builds motion gradually, instead of snapping the position each frame.

text: Altering projectile velocity, damping and lifespan makes projectiles bounce and last longer than defaults, changing how the player builds sound.
when: Tuning weapons whose projectiles must bounce
why: Default projectile motion ends bounces too quickly for layered musical play.

text: A rearward, low center of gravity off the body keeps driving stable but makes airborne spinning look strange; stable driving was judged worth that cost.
why: The center of mass sits outside the chassis, which is what makes mid-air rotation look unnatural.

text: Sticky collisions suit games that reward hitting targets. Slide-away collisions suit games where the player must avoid obstacles and keep moving.
when: choosing collision response for a vehicle
why: Each style reinforces a different player goal

text: A pointer type is declared as pointing to a given element type, and this binding fixes what the pointer may refer to.
A pointer is typically no larger than an enum, so the memory overhead of pointing to a shared object is almost nothing.
Passing ownership means the queue claims the message on enqueue and the receiver deallocates it after processing; in C++ unique_ptr provides these semantics.
Consider a polymorphic value interface only for an open-ended set of value types that lies outside performance-critical VM code.
when: Value types must be extensible by code outside the core VM
why: Implementing a base interface lets new types be added without changing the core.

text: Reading a property through a pointer follows the pointer to the shared object, and this indirection can cause cache misses and slow access.
when: Replacing a value with a pointer to a shared object.
why: The extra memory hop may not be in the cache.

text: Storing entities and their components behind pointers, then updating them in passes, makes each step a likely cache miss, and the cost repeats every frame.
when: Entities and components are allocated individually on the heap and updated in several passes
why: Each pointer hop lands on a scattered heap address, so the CPU waits on memory for every component

text: Base-class pointer arrays keep polymorphism and variable object sizes, but each element's pointer hop hurts cache locality; avoid them in tight per-frame loops over many objects.
when: Acceptable when code is not performance-critical and flexibility matters more than speed; avoid when a tight loop processes many objects per frame.
why: Each element is reached through an indirection, so the extra pointer hop per element causes repeated cache misses.

text: Polymorphic match classes are clear but may run slower, while merging their data fields into one structure can be more efficient.
Representing VM values as a class hierarchy with virtual type tests and conversions is open-ended and clean, but verbose, heap-heavy, and slow for a VM core.
when: Choosing how to represent VM values in an object-oriented language
why: Each value is a heap object reached through pointers, and every access is a virtual call.

text: Packed arrays need uniform element size, so polymorphic subclassing conflicts with them. Avoid virtual dispatch in cache-critical code, or keep one homogeneous array per concrete type.
when: Optimizing data-heavy code where object types vary
why: Virtual calls and variable object sizes break contiguous, uniform storage

text: In a prototype-based object model, an object delegates failed property lookups to another object called its prototype.
when: when working with prototype-based languages
why: delegation provides reuse without classes

text: Very little production code is written in a fully prototypal style, and such code is harder to follow.
when: when deciding whether to adopt a prototype-only style
why: most programmers find class structure easier to read

text: The text found no case where Prototype was the best answer for its contrived example, and it assumes one class per monster, a practice most engines have moved away from.
when: when judging Prototype for game entities
why: modern engines avoid a class per monster type

text: Write prototype code for implementation speed rather than runtime efficiency when the goal is rapid experimentation.
when: When the goal is rapid experimentation with rules and features.
why: Implementation speed, not runtime performance, is what limits how quickly ideas can be tried.

text: The Prototype pattern creates new objects by cloning a stored example object, so the object itself acts as a template for further copies.
when: when many objects share a configuration that is costly to build from scratch
why: cloning avoids a separate factory or class for each kind

text: A pure prototype language shifts structural work to the user, who must rebuild the organization that classes would otherwise provide.
when: when choosing a prototype-only language for large code
why: without class structure, programmers must invent conventions

text: 1) Give each monster class an abstract clone method returning an identical object. 2) Create one generic spawner holding a configured prototype. 3) Have the spawner call the prototype's clone to produce new objects.
when: when one spawner per monster type would duplicate code
why: a single spawner can serve every type by swapping the prototype

text: Treat prototype code as disposable and do not try to reuse it.
when: When the game's elements are not yet clearly defined.
why: Early reusable code locks in decisions before the design is settled.

text: The Prototype pattern removes per-type spawner classes but requires a clone method in every class, which can be about as much code as the spawners it replaced.
when: when weighing Prototype against per-type spawners
why: clone methods add per-class code in exchange for removing spawner classes

text: A vector is rotated by a quaternion q as q times v times the conjugate of q, and the vector part of the result is the rotated vector.
Orientation is a single angle in radians, measured counterclockwise from the positive z axis. With zero orientation a character faces down the z axis.
Numerical error gradually pushes quaternions away from unit length, so math libraries normalize them periodically.
when: Quaternions are updated repeatedly over many frames
why: Accumulated floating-point error.

text: Combining detailed position simulation with direct rotation gives both precise control and flowing expressiveness.
when: when implementing a ship that moves by thrust and turns by direct rotation
why: Tracked velocity and acceleration give motion depth while direct turning keeps aiming responsive

text: Quaternion multiplication is not commutative, so multiplication order changes the result. It is also not element-wise, so use the math library's routines rather than multiplying four-element arrays by hand.
when: When multiplying quaternions or multiplying position vectors by them.
why: Element-wise arithmetic produces incorrect rotations.

text: Implementations differ on quaternion component ordering, as the scalar part may come first or last.
when: Exchanging quaternions between libraries

text: 1) Take the rotation axis and angle. 2) Scale the axis by the sine of half the angle for the vector part. 3) Use the cosine of half the angle as the scalar part.
