when: Building a quaternion from an axis and angle
why: Any orientation can be reached as a single rotation about one fixed axis from a reference orientation.

text: Store full 3D orientation as a unit quaternion with four components, which has three degrees of freedom, rather than a three-value vector or a nine-element matrix.
when: Full 3D orientation is needed
why: Quaternions keep three degrees of freedom with a single constraint, unit length, that is easy to maintain.

text: A record joins components of possibly different types into one compound value, forming the Cartesian product of its field types.
A recursive record type refers to itself through pointer fields, and an extra NONE value can mark where such a structure ends.
A recursive data type has components of its own type, just as a recursive procedure calls itself, and suits nested structures such as arithmetic expressions and family pedigrees.
After a scan, the item's value is available in the field matching its class, together with the character that immediately follows the item.
Because record field names are fixed, the compiler knows every field offset in advance, which makes record field access efficient.
A record field's offset is the sum of the sizes in words of all preceding fields, so the first field has offset zero.
The number of possible values of a record equals the product of the number of possible values of each field.
why: Each possible record is one choice from every field's set, so the total count multiplies across fields.

text: Duplicating a shared record instead of pointing to it means an update through one path is not seen through the other.
when: When records representing shared relatives can be selectively updated.
why: Read-only access cannot distinguish duplicated records from one shared record, but an update reaches only the copy it targets.

text: Select record fields by fixed field name using a dot, and chain selectors for nested fields. Array components are selected by computed index instead.
Every recursive data type needs a variant (conditional) component so that its values are finite, just as a recursive procedure needs a conditional to terminate.
Records allow fields of differing types but select each by its fixed identifier, with no computed selection; arrays hold uniform components selected by computed indices.
why: Mixed field sizes rule out a single linear offset formula, so record fields are picked by fixed names that let the compiler fix each position beforehand.

text: Reflection lets code inspect the type system at runtime, finding a class by name, locating its constructor and invoking it.
Lisp, Smalltalk and Python support reflection natively, and C# and Java support it too.
Time cost is O(n*m), with n sensors and m signals.
Memory consumption grows as O(p), with p denoting the quantity of signals still waiting.
why: Only signals not yet delivered are retained, so storage scales with that pending count.

text: Region sense manager uses three interfaces: modality (range, attenuation, inverse speed, extra check), sensor (position, orientation, detection test, notify) and signal (strength, position, modality).
Players usually do not notice corrections to extrapolated positions, which are less noticeable than the stutter caused by drawing without extrapolation.
when: A rendered prediction is corrected on the next update
why: Brief position corrections blend into motion, while stutter is a sustained visible defect.

text: Instanced rendering is a GPU feature that sends one shared model plus a list of per-instance parameters, then draws all copies in a single draw call.
why: The common mesh and textures are sent to the GPU only once.

text: A framebuffer is a byte array in RAM holding pixel colors. Current consoles typically use 32 bits per pixel: eight each for red, green, blue, and other purposes.
Tearing is a partly drawn image on screen, caused when the display reads pixels the program has not yet written or reads them while writing is still in progress.
when: The program writes to the framebuffer while the display is scanning it out.

text: A scene graph holds every object in a world, each with a model and a transform.
A local transform is relative to the parent, while a world transform is absolute and is what the renderer needs; children inherit parent movement automatically.
when: Working with hierarchical scene graphs.
why: Parent-relative transforms make moving a parent move its children.

text: Light baking is done in content tools: the environment's color texture is rendered with its lighting already included.
Light mapping stores lighting data in a texture and cuts the number of real-time lights in areas whose lighting barely changes.
Older consoles were optimized for graphics, which made running AI efficiently hard.
Graphics LOD uses fewer polygons for distant objects, lower-resolution texture mipmaps for distant surfaces, and reduced or removed effects and animation at distance.
Direct3D and OpenGL both support instanced rendering, which is hardware-level support for the Flyweight pattern.
Every graphics algorithm ultimately works by setting byte values in the framebuffer.
A transform is usually a 4x4 matrix, and two transforms can be merged into one by multiplying their matrices.
Graphics can be reduced on weaker machines, such as with simpler shadows or texture mapping, without changing gameplay.
when: When a PC game must run on low-specification machines.
why: Rendering detail is separate from what the game decides, whereas AI given less time must change how it responds.

text: Use a buffered class when state changes incrementally, may be read mid-update, and readers must neither see work in progress nor wait while it is written.
when: When state is modified incrementally, may be read mid-update, and readers must neither see work in progress nor wait.
why: Readers always use a stable copy while writes go to a separate copy, and a swap makes the finished result visible at once.

text: Use double buffering when observers must never see the partial results of a multi-step update.
why: Watching a sequential build-up would break the illusion of a coherent world, so each displayed frame must be complete.

text: Rendering hardware is a pipeline where data enters, passes simple programs and exits for display; data cannot easily pass back, and the return amount is small.
Recomputing a world transform means combining transforms from root to object, so per-frame recalculation of static objects wastes CPU, and caching the derived world transform avoids it.
when: Rendering a scene graph where many objects do not move each frame.
why: Static objects produce identical world transforms, so traversal every frame is redundant.

text: Modern games use a multistage pipeline in which several frames are in different stages at once, raising throughput but adding frames of input lag.
when: Modern computer systems that use a multistage rendering pipeline.
why: Overlapping stages keeps CPU and GPU busy, but each stage adds a frame of delay before input reaches the screen.

text: Standard application event loops block until input arrives, so idle events suffice for cursors and progress bars but not for games that must keep moving.
when: Choosing an event loop for an interactive graphical program
why: Games must advance animation, effects, and AI without waiting for input.

text: Milliseconds per frame equals 1000 divided by frames per second, so 60 FPS allows about 16 ms per frame.
when: Setting a target frame rate
why: A steady rate holds only while processing and rendering fit inside that per-frame time budget.

text: Double buffering works like two stages with separate lights: the audience watches one while the crew sets up the other, and toggling the lights changes scenes instantly.
when: Explaining double buffering
why: Separating display from work area lets preparation overlap with presentation without visible gaps.

text: Underestimating world interfacing work leads to underestimated AI effort, because it often takes the largest share of an AI programmer's time and debugging.
why: Interfacing covers all links between the game world and the AI, far more than sensing, so it absorbs much work and debugging.

text: Without frozen headings, matching a distant row to its column names requires repeated scrolling, and you can lose track of which column holds which value.
Without buffering, a system that reads state mid-update can show visible artifacts such as tearing or behave incorrectly.
when: When state is modified incrementally and may be accessed in the middle of that modification.
why: Readers then see work in progress rather than one atomic change, so the result looks wrong or behaves incorrectly.

text: Drawing only the most recent update state yields jerky motion whenever a frame lands between updates.
when: When a frame is rendered between fixed-interval updates rather than at an update point.
why: The renderer uses the last updated state and ignores how far the render time falls between updates.

text: 1) Clear the back buffer, so stale pixels from earlier frames do not persist, then draw every scene element into it. 2) Display the front buffer. 3) When drawing finishes, swap buffers so the finished frame becomes front. 4) Reuse the old front buffer as the next work area.
when: A scene is redrawn every frame and a display driver reads a recycled buffer that alternates each frame.
why: Presentation and drawing overlap, so the viewer always sees a complete frame.

text: 1) Accumulate real elapsed time as lag. 2) Run fixed-size updates while lag covers a full step, reducing lag by one step each time. 3) Divide remaining lag by the step for a fraction from 0 up to just under 1. 4) Draw each object at its position plus velocity times that fraction.
when: fixed-step updates with variable-rate rendering
why: Drawing partway ahead of the last update smooths motion between steps.

text: Replace the simple rendering and maths helpers in sample programs with your engine's own libraries, since those helpers are not structured for performance.
when: When the game already has its own engine with math and rendering libraries.
why: The sample helpers were written for simplicity and transparency, not structured for performance or commercial use.

text: Copy world models on assignment rather than sharing references, because shared references make all levels share data and break the algorithm.
when: When a search stores a world model per depth level and assigns one level's model to the next.
why: Applying an action at one depth would also alter the state seen at other depths, breaking the search.

text: Adjust in-game camera height to match each user's real height so their feet sit correctly on the virtual floor.
when: tracked VR experiences
why: If real feet sit above or below the virtual floor, the player feels buried in or floating above the geometry.

text: Describe lighting modes, models, and light sources, and detail 2D or 3D rendering and camera operation as thoroughly as possible.
why: Lighting often makes up a large share of how a game looks and plays.

text: Use instanced rendering when drawing thousands of copies of the same mesh, such as a forest of trees.
when: When many copies of one model vary only by position, color, and scale.
why: One draw call replaces many separate draws.

text: A local transform setter should assign the new value and set the node's dirty flag, without recursively marking children dirty.
when: Updating a node's local transform in a cached scene graph.
why: Recursive marking is slow; the render traversal propagates dirtiness to descendants instead.

text: Use baked or mapped lighting in areas where light will not change significantly, to save real-time lighting cost.
when: in static environments
why: Real-time lights cost performance that static lighting avoids.

text: Do not swap framebuffers by pointer when the video driver expects the framebuffer to stay at a fixed memory address.
when: Video driver requires a fixed framebuffer address
why: A pointer swap changes which memory the framebuffer occupies, violating the driver's expectation.

text: Real-time lighting can change during play but has a graphical cost; baked or mapped lighting is cheap to render but cannot change.
when: When a scene's lighting is largely static and changes little over time.
why: Lighting is baked into textures ahead of time, so the engine skips computing it at runtime.

text: Copying buffer contents avoids redirecting outside pointers but costs time proportional to buffer size, while swapping pointers costs a constant few assignments.
when: Choosing how to exchange current and next state buffers
why: Copying keeps outside pointers valid; swapping is fast but invalidates them.

text: Rendering extrapolated positions keeps motion smooth between updates, but a collision or speed change can make the drawn position wrong until the next update corrects it.
when: Drawing objects between simulation updates
why: The next state is unknown until the full update runs, so the prediction can be invalid.

text: A tree walk must identify each node's kind and call the matching test, which object-oriented languages usually handle with run-time type information and polymorphism.
Storing all tree nodes in one contiguous memory block avoids the cache misses that scattered nodes cause, which slow the walk.
why: Nodes scattered across memory are fetched from different places, thrashing the cache.

text: Without buffering, a display driver can read between draw calls, so an element missing from the partial frame flickers for one frame.
when: When the display driver may read the drawing buffer at any moment mid-frame.
why: Pixels read partway through a frame capture an incomplete image.

text: 1) Receive the parent's world transform. 2) Combine it with the node's local transform. 3) Draw the mesh if present. 4) Recurse into children, passing this node's world transform. Start by calling render on the root with the identity transform.
when: Rendering a hierarchical scene graph without caching.
why: Passing transforms downward avoids walking the parent chain for each node.

text: Nodes need no special data type; a unique number, usually an integer, is enough to identify them.
When run-time type information or virtual functions are unavailable, give each node class a numeric code that identifies its kind and selects its test.
when: The engine disables run-time type information or virtual dispatch for performance
why: Many C++ games disable run-time type info and virtual calls for speed, so a manual code must pick the test.

text: Lex generates tokenizers and Yacc generates parsers from descriptions of a language's tokens and grammar; both output C code.
A tokenizer splits the character stream into tokens such as names, operators, numbers, whitespace and end-of-statement markers, without working out how they fit together.
A scanner reads the next item of text, reports its class (integer, real, name, string or special character), and gives its value.
Lex and Yacc are usually included with UNIX distributions and are available on other platforms; Flex and Bison are common Linux variants.
Both Lex and Yacc allow custom C code to be attached to tokenizing or parsing actions.
Lisp-style syntax is easy to parse, so compilation can be efficient, and the fastest Scheme versions can match other scripting languages.
A parser may build a symbol table of variable and function names; this is optional, since some languages look names up at run time.
Syntax errors are detected during parsing, because no tree can be built from invalid input.
Apps where several matching rules can stack need fewer rules for overlapping conditions than apps that apply only the first match.
Yacc-generated parsers are as good as or better than hand-written ones unless the writer is an experienced parser author, and can be tuned further where speed matters.
when: choosing between generated and manual parsers

text: Independent unification clauses are searched separately, each at most linear in database size, so m clauses cost at worst about n times m for n items.
when: When each clause of a pattern can be checked against the database on its own.
why: Each clause needs its own scan of the database, and the scans add up.

text: Lisp-style bracketed syntax is hard for programmers used to C-style languages, so an editor that checks bracket matching becomes essential.
when: For serious development in a Lisp-style language with deeply nested brackets.
why: Almost every construct is a bracketed call, so nesting grows deep and hard to read.

text: Hand-translating nested expressions into bytecode is error-prone, so real content needs a compiler-like tool to emit the bytecode.
when: Writing bytecode for non-trivial expressions by hand
why: Each step must be sequenced and tracked on the stack, and manual errors accumulate quickly.

text: A recursive definition without a terminating alternative has infinitely many instances, which makes its values unbounded.
why: Each instance requires another instance of itself, so with no end case the structure never terminates.

text: 1) Describe each token's pattern in Lex, such as what forms a number. 2) Generate C code that converts a text stream into token codes and token data.
when: building a tokenizer for a scripting language
why: Lex turns token patterns into a C scanner

text: 1) Write the grammar in Yacc, stating which tokens combine and which larger structures are built from smaller ones. 2) Generate C code that parses the token stream.
when: building a parser for a scripting language
why: Yacc turns grammar rules into a C parser

text: Language notation trades familiar mathematical abstractions against efficient compilation; overly machine-oriented notations and fully representation-open notations both fall short.
why: A general-purpose designer cannot know which operations matter, so any representation choice may suit some uses poorly.

text: Scripted or data-defined behavior runs slower than compiled code, but the cost is small compared with the gains from extra iterations and faster designer authoring.
when: Choosing between a scripting layer and low-level code for gameplay, or adding scripted or data-defined behavior to types
why: Interpreted behavior is faster for designers to write and change.

text: Embedding means the scripting language is built into the game, which decides which scripts run and tells the scripting system to process them.
A re-entrant script runs until its time budget is used up, then pauses and resumes later.
A parser takes tokens, works out each one's role, and builds a hierarchical parse tree, also called a syntax tree or abstract syntax tree.
Desired properties of moddable behavior are sandboxing from the core game, easy modification, easy reloading, and separation from the executable.
A type is ordered, or scalar, when its values have an ordering. Enumerated values are then ordered by their listing sequence.
Pseudo-code can be converted into any programming language and is about half the length of equivalent C++ source.
Middleware now offers on-target debugging tools for consoles.
Interpreting conditions in a homegrown scripting language is only slightly faster than polymorphic calls, unless compiled to machine code; for complex code it costs at least as much.
when: Choosing a condition implementation for designer-editable logic
why: Interpretation overhead offsets the benefit unless the script is compiled.

text: Ruby is elegant and object-oriented, easier to integrate with C than Python, can manipulate its own code, but is weakly re-entrant from C++ and has thin documentation.
Scheme is a LISP descendant with hundreds of versions, which differ widely in speed and memory use.
Very small Scheme implementations can fit in under 2500 lines of C but omit some advanced features.
A non-optimizing compiler translates a parse tree literally into byte code, so even a trivial test produces a full compare and jump sequence.
The four script processing stages need not run in sequence; tokenizing, parsing and compiling can run offline, with interpretation done later.
Scripts run inside the main game loop, so slow scripts take time away from rendering, physics and audio.
The most common script authoring format is a text file with a primitive for each action, plus signals and waits, read by a parser.
when: Designers authoring coordinated AI scripts
why: Text data separates designer authoring from engine code

text: In dynamically typed languages such as JavaScript, Python and Ruby, classes are ordinary objects, so a monster's class can be passed directly to a spawner.
Implementing the parser is comparatively easy; parser generators or a hand-written recursive descent parser both work.
Narrative working tools can range from simple, such as writing dialogue in a spreadsheet, to complex, such as a custom engine and dialogue toolset.
A name starts with a letter and may continue with letters or digits.
The type of an expression can be derived from its form or declaration without executing the program.
Each operator or function expects fixed argument types and yields a fixed result type. Overloaded operators such as plus are resolved by language rules.
Many engines with scripting provide script editing, debugging and stepping through code.
How much scripting or level editing a writer must learn depends on how the studio defines the role. A writer-only role does not require it.
Scripts are usually compiled outside play, so small compiler inefficiencies are usually acceptable.
when: When compilation runs outside of active play sessions.
why: Compilation does not run during gameplay

text: Calling Foo::bar() directly is simpler than Foo::instance().bar() and makes static memory use explicit.
why: Singletons hide global state and couple unrelated code, costs that grow over time.

text: Simple bytecode can be debugged without much tooling, but as content grows, invest in tools that show what the bytecode is doing.
when: Custom bytecode content is growing
why: Bytecode errors are hard to diagnose without source mapping and inspection features.

text: A call pushes the current instruction index onto a return stack and jumps; a return pops that index and jumps back.
when: Adding callable procedures to a bytecode VM
why: A separate return stack lets procedures nest and return to their caller.

text: Instructions push values onto an operand stack and pop their parameters off the top, so values pass between instructions only through the stack.
when: Designing data flow between bytecode instructions
why: Instructions need not know where their inputs came from, keeping each one small.

text: Script processing has four stages: tokenizing, parsing, compiling and interpretation, each converting its input into a form that is easier to handle.
A team can keep Python's syntax but write its own language to solve Python's speed and size problems.
when: Python's syntax is wanted but its runtime is too slow or large
why: Python's runtime was too slow and too large for the team's needs.

text: Two concurrent copies of a script, such as for two squads in different places, need further identifier disambiguation to avoid ambiguity.
when: Running the same script for several groups at once
why: Shared identifiers let one group's signal satisfy another group's wait

text: Plug-ins are constrained by the host's undo system, user interface and internal data format, and SDKs differ so knowledge rarely transfers between packages.
when: When building plug-ins for content creation tools with their own SDKs.

text: If the engine is not set up to use custom scripts, your script edits will not appear in the game.
when: When the engine is not configured to load custom scripts.
why: All weapon systems are scripted, so custom scripts must be loaded before edits show up.

text: A VM without external primitives can only burn CPU cycles and has no visible effect on the game.
when: Designing a bytecode instruction set
why: Only external primitives reach outside the VM to change the game world.

text: Some consoles and iOS forbid running machine code generated at runtime, which rules out just-in-time compilation on those platforms.
when: Targeting consoles or iOS with scripted or generated code
why: Platform policy blocks executing code that is produced or loaded at runtime.

text: Set-pieces need their own planning and scripting, especially for unique elements such as giant monsters, vehicles, and moving environment parts.
when: When a level chains several set-pieces that each carry a separate goal.
why: Each set-piece teaches a different skill toward its own goal, so planning cannot be shared.

text: Scripting languages are programming languages, so non-technical designers struggle to build complex character control scripts.
when: When non-technical level designers must write complex character AI control scripts.

text: 1) List the engine operations that scripts need to call. 2) Express each as a plain function with explicit parameters. 3) Only then design the bytecode instruction set from that API.
when: Building a scripting or bytecode system on top of a game engine
why: The instruction set should expose what the game needs, so the API comes first.

text: 1) Define each engine operation as a one-byte opcode in an enum. 2) Read each byte in a loop. 3) Switch on the opcode and call the matching engine method.
when: Building the core interpreter loop of a bytecode VM
why: One-byte opcodes make a script a plain byte array, and a switch maps each byte to its operation.

text: Home-grown scripting languages start tiny and grow ad hoc into full languages; allow growth only by deliberate decision, otherwise restrict what bytecode can express.
when: Maintaining or developing a home-grown scripting system or language
why: Each small addition seems cheap, so scope creeps; unplanned feature growth produces an unwieldy system.

text: Build a syntax tree from the parser for later processing instead of emitting byte code directly from grammar rules.
when: professional compiler work for games
why: Direct byte code emission makes optimizing compilers very hard to write

text: Before designing your own scripting language, study Scheme and read a couple of simple implementations.
when: building a custom scripting language
why: Scheme treats code and data alike, so scripts can be passed around, altered and run later; simple implementations reveal how approachable language building is.

text: Compile scripts offline and ship only the byte code, so the parser and compiler stay out of the shipped game.
when: preparing scripts for release
why: Parsing and compiling modules are bulky, so keeping them out of the shipped build avoids their overhead.

text: Design the scripting system so programmers can expose new game functions or classes to scripts on request.
when: When the game functions scripts need cannot be known when the scripting language is chosen.
why: The needed game functions are rarely known in advance, so new ones must be easy to expose later.

text: Keep custom scripts in your own mod class folder rather than the original engine packages, and compile them before testing.
Once code stabilizes, move tunable values into a text file read at launch so they can be refined without changing the program.
when: after code solidifies
why: Designers can tune numbers and levels independently while programmers keep building the remaining code.

text: Sources conflict on scripting's origin: it was the first way for designers to develop AI, or it first handled level logic like door triggers before being extended to character AI.
why: Scripts can be edited without recompiling and tested quickly.

text: Interpreted languages such as Python or Ruby are too slow for a production AI core but suit scripting.

An off-the-shelf scripting language gives robustness, optimization, community support and modder familiarity; a custom language gives only the features needed, game-specific features, and staff who can fix bugs quickly.
when: Choosing a scripting language for a game
why: Mature languages carry other developers' debugging and optimization work, while a self-built one is understood in-house and fixable quickly.

text: Python is readable, object-oriented, easy to embed and supports re-entrant functions via generators from version 2.2, but its speed and size are poor for games, since many operations use string-keyed hash lookups.
when: Considering Python for game scripting
why: Core operations such as function calls and variable access rely on string-keyed hash lookups, which add substantial overhead.

text: Fixed-parameter opcodes are simple but cannot target other entities, lower stats, or play multiple effects, so they lack expressiveness.
when: Deciding how much to parameterize early opcodes
why: Simplicity of decoding trades against the range of behavior scripts can express.

text: Providing more operations in a sandbox base class reduces subclass coupling to outside systems but increases the base class's coupling and size.
when: Deciding how many operations the sandbox base class exposes
why: Coupling moves between subclasses and the base as operations are added or removed.

text: A sandbox base can provide no operations, so subclasses call outside systems directly, or provide all operations, so subclasses need only the base header; middle ground mixes both.
when: Choosing the scope of a sandbox base class
why: Each extreme shifts coupling to a different place.

text: High-level procedural rule concepts are readable and recombine meaningfully, but every rule must be predefined; general logic languages are broader but low-level.
Subclass Sandbox: many command classes share a concrete base class offering high-level helper methods, which derived commands compose inside their execute methods.
when: when writing many similar command classes

text: Subclass Sandbox gives instances access to shared state without making that state globally available.
A standard debugger steps through the VM itself, not the intent of the bytecode, and cannot map bytecode back to the high-level source it came from.
when: Debugging behavior written in custom bytecode
why: The debugger sees VM instructions, not the designer's source.

text: A VM with few instructions and a bounded stack is a safe sandbox, because bytecode can reach the engine only through a small set of defined primitives.
when: Running untrusted or modder-written behavior
why: Limited instructions keep bytecode away from unexpected engine parts.

text: 1) Bound the stack size and check for overflow on every push. 2) Count executed instructions and stop when a threshold is passed.
when: Running untrusted bytecode in a VM
why: Capping memory and execution time keeps bad behavior contained.

text: Using third-party scripting code costs some control over the codebase, which usually is outweighed by its benefits but is essential to keep for some projects.
when: Projects where keeping control of the codebase is non-negotiable.
why: Third-party code is code you cannot fully govern, so some control is ceded whenever it is included.

text: Letting users supply native machine code is unsafe, so a sandboxed bytecode VM trades raw speed for control over every instruction.
when: Deciding whether user-defined behavior should run as native code
why: A game-controlled VM handles every instruction, so it can be sandboxed.

text: Subclass sandboxing isolates derived classes from the rest of the world, so most behavior lives in them and the codebase is easier to maintain, at the cost of a bloated, brittle base class.
when: Applying the subclass sandbox pattern
why: Isolation of behavior is paid for with coupling concentrated in the base.

text: A sequence is a homogeneous structure of variable length whose elements are accessed one at a time, with its length changing during execution.
A sequence is complete when its index moves past the last sub-action.
Sorting treats numeric cells by value and date cells by calendar date.
Input sequences are not inherent in the raw signals; the game listens for patterns among them.
A sequence's declaration is separate from its access mechanism, so several access points can work on one sequence at different positions.
Because a sequence grows and shrinks, storage must be allocated dynamically as it grows and reclaimed as it shrinks.
why: No fixed storage amount can cover a length that is open-ended and varies during execution.

text: Reading beyond the current end of a sequence is a programming error and should not be handled silently.

1) Create a subsequence with an external variable as input. 2) Compare the value to an inner and outer range with integer comparisons. 3) Combine both results in a comparison that fires only when both hold. 4) Finish the subsequence to return control to the parent, which plays the matching sound.
when: Selecting one sound out of several by value range in a visual scripting graph.
why: Subsequences keep graphs readable when many connections would otherwise tangle.

text: 1) Give each object two value slots in an array. 2) Keep one shared static index marking the current slot. 3) Read from the current slot and write to the other. 4) Flip the shared index once to swap all objects together.
when: Distributed state must swap without visiting each object and old values need not be touched.
why: Keeping the index shared means one flip swaps every object's state, so no per-object visit is needed.

text: A sequence's interrupt check depends only on its first sub-action, but its compatibility check must require every sub-action to be compatible.
why: checking only the first sub-action lets a sequence become incompatible partway through

text: Use sequences for large persistent data or data moved between media. Avoid them when elements must be reached by index in arbitrary order.
when: When data is transferred between memory and persistent storage.
why: Sequential access lets data stream in buffered chunks, making secondary storage use far more effective.

text: Service Locator is a dedicated class giving global access to a service via an abstract interface; unlike Singleton, it decouples callers from the concrete class and from its source.
Singleton restricts a class to one instance and provides a global access point to it.
Script compilation can happen when a level loads or, more commonly, before the game ships.
A map with hundreds of teams can need hundreds of narrowcast managers arranged in a hierarchy.
Exposing an audio system through a service locator works best with an abstract interface that declares play, stop and stop-all operations and is implemented by a concrete provider.
why: The interface decouples callers from any particular audio implementation.

text: In enterprise software, a service locator usually searches for its implementation at runtime.
Service Locator is a sibling of Singleton, and engine component lookup methods combine it with the Component pattern.

A service locator does not require the service interface to know it is accessed through a locator, so it can be applied to existing classes not designed for it, unlike Singleton which shapes the class itself.
Use the Singleton pattern only when a class truly cannot work correctly with more than one instance, and use it sparingly.
why: Singleton is applied more often than it deserves, and reaching for it by default is a mistake; it is often misused as a convenience for global access.

text: Bind services at compile time when the choice is fixed per build and speed and guaranteed availability matter more than runtime swapping.
when: The service must not change while the game runs.

text: Restrict a service to a class when it serves one game domain, such as a network service used only by online classes; make it global when widely used, such as logging.
when: When a service serves only one domain of the game.
why: Scoping a service to one branch of the class hierarchy keeps systems that should stay decoupled apart.

text: Use a service locator sparingly, since globally accessible objects invite the same problems as Singleton.
when: When passing the object as a parameter would be gratuitous or make the code harder to read.
why: Global access hides coupling, whereas passing the object in keeps every dependency visible.

text: Choose internal initialization when objects must stay hidden; choose external when objects have many init variants and a simple pool interface is preferred.
when: When pooled objects can be kept completely internal to the pool.
why: Internal reinitialization stops other code from holding references to objects that could be reused unexpectedly.

text: Global state makes code harder to reason about, because a function reading it depends on code far away from it.
why: Without global state, a function's body alone can be understood; touching global data forces tracing that state through the whole codebase.

text: A compile-time locator holds one static service whose type is chosen by preprocessor conditionals, such as a debug or release flag, so the choice is fixed per build.
Because the service is chosen at build time, a successful compile guarantees it exists, and the accessor is usually inlined, leaving minimal runtime cost.
why: Build-time selection leaves no runtime work, so the compiler can inline the accessor, and a successful build ensures availability.

text: Because the registering code builds the provider, it can supply runtime data the locator cannot know, such as a remote address for a networked service.
why: The locator knows only the abstract interface, so it cannot supply constructor data like a remote player's address; the registering code can.

text: Registered providers can be replaced while the game runs, so a null service can temporarily disable a system such as sound during testing.
when: During development and testing, though the final game may not use it.
why: The locator depends only on an abstract interface, so swapping one provider for another, such as a null one, does not affect callers.

text: Global scope encourages all code to share one service, so no code has a reason to create its own provider.
when: When the locator grants access to the whole codebase, rather than only a base class's descendants.
why: Most services are meant to be singular, and a shared lookup stops other code from instantiating duplicate providers because the real one is reachable.

text: A simple service locator stores a pointer to a service in a static member, exposes a static accessor to fetch it, and a static provide operation so outside code can register an implementation.
Service locator implementations vary on three questions: how the service is located, what happens when it cannot be found, and whether its scope is global or class-restricted.
The pattern has three roles: a service interface defining operations, concrete providers implementing it, and a locator that finds and hands out an appropriate provider.
A singleton is global state in a class, carrying hidden dependencies and coupling; global access lets any code include a header and reach objects the architecture meant to keep separate.
why: Global visibility means any file that includes the header can reach the instance, pulling unrelated code into a coupling.

text: A singleton's restriction on instance count spreads to every call site, so splitting the class later, such as a Log split into per-domain loggers, is costly.
If providers are not registered before anything uses them, the game crashes or a service silently misbehaves; registration order creates initialization dependencies.
why: Any code that accesses the service assumes some earlier code has registered it, so a missing registration breaks that assumption.

text: Unlike a singleton or static class, a locator lookup can fail, so callers may receive no service and must handle that case.
why: Singletons and static classes always supply an instance, but a locator defers wiring to runtime, so a lookup may come back empty.

text: 1) Group related operations into a helper class. 2) Keep a private instance of it in the base class. 3) Expose it to subclasses through a protected getter, so only derived classes can use it.
when: A base class has several operations for one outside system
why: One getter replaces several base methods and limits base coupling to the helper.

text: 1) Make the constructor private. 2) Hold a static instance pointer. 3) Provide a public static accessor that creates the instance on first call and returns it.
1) At startup, construct the concrete service implementation. 2) Register it with the locator. 3) Let all other code fetch the service through the abstract interface.
when: At game startup, ahead of any code that fetches the service.
why: Only the startup code then knows the concrete class, so the locator stays decoupled from the provider.

text: In a game engine, use a single central world interface for stability and reuse.
when: In a game engine that includes AI, rather than a single-purpose game AI.

text: An abstract service interface should have a virtual destructor and pure virtual operations, with no implementation of its own.
when: Defining a service that concrete providers implement.
why: Keeping the interface free of implementation lets providers be swapped freely.

text: Let callers find a service by name through one central lookup, so the service owner controls how it is found and replaced.
why: Changes then touch one place instead of every caller.

text: Any code can request a globally located service, so it must behave correctly in every calling context.
Treat a failed service lookup as a fatal bug and assert when it should never happen.
when: Failing to find the service is a fatal bug.
why: Asserting makes a missing service the locator's bug and halts the game before later code uses a null service.

text: Reserve a service locator for singular, ambient facilities such as audio devices or display systems, and for cross-cutting concerns such as logging.
when: When passing the object as a parameter would clutter code or thread through many layers.
why: Keeps non-domain concerns and single shared facilities out of every interface, avoiding passing them through many layers of calls.

text: Making the component manager a singleton is an easy fix, but it inherits Singleton's problems, so read about Singleton before adopting it.
when: When entities are just IDs and components must be found through a registry

text: Routing all requests through one method keyed by a request code lets new checks be added without changing the interface, and makes all activity loggable, at the cost of an extra lookup step.
when: When the polling interface has grown large and is hard to extend
why: Every poll passes through one entry point, so debugging tools can observe all of them.

text: A runtime flag check catches duplicate construction only when it runs, whereas Singleton's guarantee is enforced at compile time.
A single global Game object exposing systems through getters reduces the number of separate globals but couples all code to the Game object.
when: Reducing the number of global objects is the priority

text: A service locator lets a base operation fetch its dependency at call time, so outside code need not supply it, but initialization burden moves into the base class mechanics.
when: Base operations need a shared service that callers should not have to pass in.
why: Callers are relieved of supplying state, but the base now depends on the locator to find it.

text: An object that builds its own components always has everything it needs but is harder to reconfigure, while injected components make it a reusable container that can change behavior by swapping parts.
when: Deciding who creates an entity's components.
why: Self-building guarantees completeness; injection gives flexibility.

text: Compile-time binding gives speed and guaranteed availability, but changing the service requires recompiling and restarting the game.
Global scope makes one shared service easy to reach but gives up control over where and when it is used; class scope keeps coupling controlled at the cost of repeated lookup code.
when: When a service is meant to exist as a single shared instance

text: A locator is a more flexible and configurable cousin of Singleton that adds flexibility with little runtime cost, but used poorly it carries all of Singleton's baggage and worse runtime performance.
when: When the facility is fundamentally singular, like an audio device or display

text: SET denotes sets of small integers, typically from 0 to 31 or 0 to 63, with operators for union, intersection, difference, symmetric difference and membership.
Set literals are a singleton such as {5}, a range {x, y..z} holding x up to z, and the empty set {}.
Set operators are * for intersection, + for union, - for difference, / for symmetric difference, and IN for membership.
A test x IN {c1..cn} runs much faster as a bit-set membership test than as a chain of equality tests joined by OR.
when: When the set is held as a bit string in a small fixed number of machine words
why: one shift and a sign test replace many comparisons

text: Union, intersection and difference of bit-string sets become OR, AND, and AND combined with the negated second set, applied to all bits together.
when: When sets are stored as characteristic bit arrays
why: Logical instructions act on every bit of a word at once, so all elements are handled together.

text: A set of small integers is stored as a characteristic bit string with one bit per possible element, set to 1 when that element is present.
when: When the set's elements are small integers
why: Representing the set this way lets union, intersection and difference become elementary logical operations.

text: 1) Shift the set's word so the tested element's bit lands in the sign position. 2) Test the sign bit, which is set when the element is present.
when: When the set is held in a fixed word that supports shifting

text: Represent sets as bit strings only when elements are small integers. The largest usable element is the machine word length minus one.
why: Elements must fit within the fixed number of words used to hold the set.

text: Store a bit-string set in a small, fixed number of words that support logical operations and shifts.
when: When basic set operations must run efficiently
why: efficient set operations need these primitives

text: In SET expressions, * and / bind tighter than + and -, which bind tighter than IN, so x IN s + t reads as x IN (s + t).
why: Membership is classed as a relational operator, which ranks below the set operators.

text: Reifying a concept means making it first-class: turning it into a piece of data you can store in a variable or pass to a function.
Listeners of a specialized manager, such as a collision manager, may want anything it can generate.
Simple code often runs faster due to less overhead, but this is not guaranteed, since dense loops or recursion can still be slow.
Simple code is not necessarily quicker to write than messy code.
Six classic object-oriented patterns are Command, Flyweight, Observer, Prototype, Singleton and State.
Certain limits arise from design consequences; others exist to keep frame rate acceptable.
Representation decisions form a chain: early choices such as coordinate system depend on the problem, while later choices such as number format depend more on the tool and its technology.
Production code can drop polymorphic flexibility where it is not needed, which can speed up hot code such as pathfinding.
when: When the object types used at runtime are known in advance, especially in pathfinding
why: Removing polymorphism eliminates indirect function calls, which carry overhead.

text: Centralize a dependency in the base class when many derived classes share it, accepting a larger base class that becomes harder to maintain as it grows.
when: Several subclasses need the same outside system
why: One shared access point avoids repeating the dependency in every subclass.

text: Calling a method that does not modify state is a safer form of coupling than calling one that changes state, so read-only calls are better candidates for shared access.
when: Choosing which outside calls a base class should expose to subclasses.
why: A read-only call cannot break the game, while state-changing calls tie subclasses more deeply to the underlying code.

text: Private constructors and friend classes can restrict object creation to a factory function.
when: Two-stage initialization needs to force creation through one path.
why: Callers outside the factory are unable to construct the object directly.

text: Keep heavy abstractions where performance matters little, and apply locality-focused layout only to bulk data processing paths.
when: Choosing how widely to apply data-oriented layout in a codebase
why: Locality has costs in flexibility, so it pays off only where data is processed in bulk

text: Hide a data structure's representation behind an interface so clients cannot break its invariants directly.
when: designing a module that exposes a structure with an invariant
why: Clients can then change the structure only through operations that keep the invariant.

text: Design programs by reasoning with numbers, sets, sequences and repetitions rather than bits, storage units and jumps, which makes the design more reliable.
when: When the language treats numbers as elementary objects
why: Programmers avoid number representation questions, and familiar abstractions are easier to design with reliably.

text: Overzealous interfaces, base classes, and virtual layers slow tracing of real behavior and fill the developer's working memory with scaffolding.
when: code has many layers of indirection
why: Each layer must be traversed and held in mind to find actual behavior.

text: In a shared library used by several games, changing a global design means coordinating changes across several teams.
Relying on the right operand of & or OR being evaluated is wrong, because it is skipped when the left operand decides the result.

1) Identify each domain's code in the monolithic class. 2) Move each domain into its own component class. 3) Have the main entity hold an instance of each component. 4) Reduce the entity to a minimal wrapper that links the components together.
when: A class mixes several domains such as input, physics, and graphics.
why: Separated components can change independently.

text: Use numeric constants rather than strings for semantic identifiers in games, because string comparisons are slow.
when: game blackboards
why: string comparison costs runtime

text: Before building complex routing and filtering for queued communication, check whether a simpler design is enough.
when: When a game's communication runs through event or message queues
why: Elaborate routing adds cost that simple designs avoid.

text: A spreadsheet formula starts with an equals sign and can combine numbers, the operators +, -, *, and /, and cell references.
A cell reference combines a column letter and a row number, and a formula that uses it takes the value currently stored in that cell.
A relative reference stores its position relative to the formula's cell, so copying the formula shifts the referenced cell by the same offset.
An absolute reference places dollar signs before the row and column, like $C$2, so it stays fixed when the formula is copied or filled.
when: Applying one shared constant to a whole column of formulas.

text: Conditional formatting styles only the cells that satisfy a chosen rule, using a fill or a text style.
Freezing pins chosen top rows or left columns in place so they stay visible while the rest of the sheet scrolls.
A tiebreaker sort column orders rows only where all earlier sort criteria are equal.
The mean equals the total of all values divided by their count.
MEDIAN returns the middle value, MODE the most frequent value, MAX and MIN the largest and smallest values, and STDEV the standard deviation.
COUNTIF tallies the matching cells within a range for a given criterion, while SUMIF totals their values using the same parameters.
IF(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false) returns one of two results depending on whether a Boolean test holds.
FLOOR(number, significance) rounds a number down to the nearest multiple of the significance value.
A spreadsheet function call is written as its name, an open parenthesis, its parameters if any, and a closing parenthesis.
SUM() accepts any number of parameters, each a single cell or a cell range, and returns their total.
A range is written as two corner cells joined by a colon and covers every cell in the rectangle between them.
MATCH(key, range, type) returns the position of a key within a single row or column, counting from 1 at the top or left.
MATCH's third argument sets the search mode: 1 assumes ascending order and returns the closest value not exceeding the key, -1 assumes descending order, and 0 requires an exact match.
INDEX(range, row, column) returns the cell content at the given row and column inside the range.
INDIRECT builds a cell reference from a text string, so a random number joined into the string can select which cell's content is returned.
A named range is a name assigned to a single cell or a range of cells, which formulas can use in place of cell addresses.
COUNTA(range) returns a tally of non-empty entries within the given span.
COUNTBLANK(range) returns the number of empty cells in the range.
ISBLANK(cell) returns TRUE if the cell is empty and FALSE if it holds anything, and works as the condition inside IF().
SPARKLINE() places a small chart inside a single cell, letting many rows each show a trend without large charts covering the sheet.
A solver add-on takes input cells, a target output cell and a desired value, then searches for input values that reach the target or come as close as possible.
BOOLEAN has values TRUE and FALSE, with conjunction &, disjunction OR and negation ~; comparisons yield BOOLEAN results that can be assigned or used as operands.
CAP(ch) returns the capital letter for a lower-case letter and leaves a capital letter unchanged.
An AND match succeeds only when both sub-matches succeed, while a NOT match tests its sub-match with a fresh bindings list and so records nothing.
A computer can simulate a dN for nearly any N, so virtual dice are not limited by physical manufacturing.
Fill Up and Fill Left have no keyboard shortcuts; instead, drag the small square at the bottom-right of the selection in any direction.
Freezing rows and freezing columns are separate choices, so you can freeze headers, a name column, or both.
AVERAGE accepts any mix of cells and ranges and skips blanks, text and other non-numeric entries.
Summing a column of IF results that return 1 or 0 gives the number of rows that meet the condition.
Comparing a cell to an empty pair of quotation marks returns true when that cell is blank.
AND(...) returns true only when all its parameters are true, so a lower and upper bound check combined inside IF tests a range.
CEILING rounds a number up to the next multiple of a significance value, and MROUND rounds it to the nearest multiple.
Functions can stand alone or combine with numbers and cell references in arithmetic, and a parameter can itself be another function.
Omitting one side of a range selects an entire row or column.
Forced recalculation shortcuts differ between spreadsheet programs, so search the program's help for recalculate to find the right command.
VLOOKUP searches only the leftmost column of its table, and its column index counts from the left, with 1 meaning the leftmost column.
CONCAT joins its inputs as text, so it can insert separator words between parts of a name.
INDEX and MATCH together look up values at any position, not only in the leftmost column.
The & operator joins text strings in all major spreadsheet programs without needing a special function.
A named range is an absolute reference, so copying, pasting, or filling formulas does not change which cells it points to.
HOUR returns 0 to 23, while MINUTE and SECOND each return 0 to 59.
In a popular browser-based spreadsheet, Ctrl+R forces a recalculation.
A spreadsheet can be configured to refresh each minute or each hour, though not each second or never.
Painting a selected group of cells applies the group's formatting as one unit rather than cell by cell.
Write derived column formulas that reference inputs in the same row, so each row computes its result independently.
when: building calculated columns from input columns

text: Freeze header rows and the name column in any sheet larger than one screen, so each value stays labeled while you scroll.
when: the sheet has more rows or columns than fit on screen

text: Rotate long column headings so they remain readable and a wide sheet stays compact.
when: column headings are long and the sheet is wide

text: Text aligns left and numbers align right by default; centering column headings often makes them easier to read.
when: When labelling column headings in a spreadsheet

text: Merge cells mainly for presentation, such as a category heading spanning a group of column headings, rather than for storing data.
when: When grouping several column headings under a shared category label
why: Resizing a row or column changes every cell in it, while merging changes only one block.

text: Use IF to flag rows that meet a criterion, or to assign values to every item that has a given attribute.
when: Setting stats for all entities sharing an affiliation, or marking rows matching a test.

text: For simple done versus not-done tallies, blank checks are easier to use than COUNTIF.
when: When completion is marked by typing a simple symbol like an x into a cell
why: Any entry marks completion, so checking blank versus non-blank needs no specific value to match.

text: Date formulas suit organizing personal work, such as deadlines and countdowns.
when: For smaller projects or personal organization, where the designer builds their own schedule

text: TODAY, NOW, RAND and RANDBETWEEN keep their values until the sheet changes or a recalculation is forced, since any edit triggers recalculation of random-based cells.
Inserting or deleting rows and columns, and cutting and pasting cells, automatically updates every formula that refers to the affected cells.
When a formula is copied or filled, its cell references shift to match each new position, so every copy refers to its own row or column.
A formula that references other cells updates its result automatically whenever a referenced value changes.
why: The reference reads whatever is currently stored in the named cell, so the result follows that cell's contents.

text: When computing a cell, the spreadsheet first evaluates each parameter, then applies the function to those computed values.
Adding a fraction of a day to a date-time value shifts it by that share of a day, so adding 0.25 moves it forward six hours.
Dates behave as numbers: subtracting two dates gives the days between them, and adding a number gives the date that many days later.
Each lookup costs CPU, and the first use of a service pauses while it is found, so caching the result avoids repeated delays.
when: When a service is located at runtime through a configuration system

text: A datum match stores an identifier with minimum and maximum values; equality is a zero-width range, and one-sided tests use an infinite bound.
why: A range can serve as the most general match, so one structure covers exact, less-than and greater-than tests.

text: Numeric cells not matching a value equal COUNT over the range minus COUNTIF for that value over the same range.
In some spreadsheet apps, once a rule matches, its formatting applies and later rules are skipped, so an earlier match blocks later rules and rule order decides the visible formatting.
when: rules are applied with first-match-only behavior

text: If the test value falls outside the mapped set of daughters, the lookup finds no daughter, so the node must handle that case explicitly.
In a recursive odds grid, a formula that points to the wrong cell gives wrong results silently, so check several cells against hand-calculated base cases.
when: Building a recursive spreadsheet table for game odds.
why: Mis-referenced cells propagate errors through every dependent cell.

text: Resizing a row or column alters every cell in it, making it a clumsy way to adjust a single cell.
when: When one cell needs to look like a larger rectangular block for appearance

text: A merged block keeps its value only in its top-left cell, so referencing any other cell in the block returns no value.
when: When a formula must read the value inside a merged block

text: Including header rows in a sort risks pushing headings into the data rows.
when: When the sort selection includes a header row

text: Dates and times are stored as numbers, so SUM or AVERAGE over them gives meaningless results, although COUNT still tallies them.
SPARKLINE syntax is harder to write than basic chart tools because its many options make it versatile but intricate.
when: When placing a small chart inside one cell

text: Pasting only formatting is a separate action from pasting the full block, so confirm which paste option you selected.
when: When a copied block should carry over only its results, not its formulas

text: The ArrayFormula function is specific to one spreadsheet app; other apps use curly braces, so exported array formulas may need manual fixing.
when: When exporting a cloud-spreadsheet array formula into another spreadsheet program.
why: Other programs mark array formulas with curly braces instead of a function name.

text: Spreadsheet matrix work is harder to build and check than ordinary formulas, so expect more effort.

1) Compare the deadline cell with TODAY(). 2) Inside IF(), show a blank if the task is complete, OVERDUE if incomplete and deadline earlier than today. 3) Otherwise show days remaining until the deadline.
when: tracking deadlines in a task list or marking items whose deadline has passed
why: Dates behave as numbers, so subtracting TODAY() from a deadline gives the days remaining.

text: 1) Select the formula cell and the cells below or beside it. 2) Press Fill Down (Ctrl+D) or Fill Right (Ctrl+R) to copy the formula across the range.
when: copying one formula across a row or column

text: To fill a formula across a rectangle, select the whole area, apply Fill Right, then apply Fill Down.
To verify a filled formula, select any cell in the range and read the formula shown in the formula bar.
when: After a formula has been filled across a range
why: The formula bar displays the actual formula stored in any selected cell.

text: 1) Enter a starting value in the first row. 2) In each following row, add a fixed increment to the cell directly above. 3) Repeat down the column.
when: building a column that grows by a constant step

text: 1) Place the shared constant in a fixed cell. 2) Reference it with dollar signs in the formula. 3) Fill Down the formula. Changing the constant then updates every row.
when: Using one tunable value across a filled column.
why: The absolute reference keeps every filled formula pointing at the same cell.

text: 1) Select the cells. 2) Open conditional formatting and set the condition, such as less than 0. 3) Choose a style, such as a background color. 4) Add another rule for each further condition.
1) Select the cells. 2) Click Merge and choose Merge All. 3) To reverse it, select the merged cell and choose Unmerge.
when: When grouping several column headings under one shared category name

text: 1) Select the rows to sort, leaving out the header row. 2) Choose Sort Range. 3) Pick a column and ascending or descending order. 4) Add tiebreaker columns. 5) Click Sort.
when: When many rows share the same value in the first sort column

text: 1) Open the Data menu. 2) Choose Named Ranges. 3) In the side panel, select the cell or range and enter its name.
why: Names read more clearly than cell addresses, though addresses show where the data lives.

text: 1) Give the data range as the first argument. 2) Give options as the second argument inside curly braces. 3) Write each option as its name, a comma, then its value. 4) Separate multiple options with semicolons. Chart type options include line and column.

1) Copy a block of cells. 2) Right-click the target and choose Paste Special. 3) Choose Paste Transpose. The block's rows and columns swap, so a 3 by 4 block becomes 4 by 3, keeping its data and formulas.
when: chart data is laid out sideways

text: 1) Highlight a source cell. 2) Click the format painter button. 3) Click a target cell, a row or column heading, or drag across a range to apply its formatting.
when: When a new area should match the formatting of an existing one
why: Reselecting borders, fills and text colours one at a time takes too long.

text: 1) Select an empty, unformatted cell. 2) Click the format painter. 3) Click the top-left corner of the sheet to strip special formatting from the whole sheet.
1) Loop over every element of the array. 2) For each record, test the conditions on its fields. 3) Increment a counter when all conditions hold.
Avoid connected-wildcard searches on large databases: two connected clauses take O(n²) time, and more connected clauses cost considerably more than independent ones.
when: When the rule database is large, or clauses share wildcards.
why: Each candidate from the first clause must be tried against the second.

text: When results look wrong, read the true value of the selected cell in the formula bar instead of trusting the displayed number.
why: Number formatting changes only how a value looks, while the stored value still feeds later formulas, so the displayed figure can mislead.

text: Resize a row or column by dragging its heading border, or enter an exact size from the heading's right-click menu.
Shade computed subtotal columns in a distinct color so they are not typed over by hand.
Reference a whole column, such as C:C, in statistics formulas so that new rows are included without editing the formula; text headers are skipped.
when: the column has a header row and its data keeps growing
why: AVERAGE counts only numeric cells and skips blanks and text, so a whole-column reference needs no edits when rows are appended.

text: Give a bare value for an exact match, and write a comparison as one quoted criterion such as '>=14' with the operator inside the quotes.
Set MATCH's third argument to 0 for unsorted data so it returns only exact matches.
when: the lookup list is unsorted
why: the approximate modes assume sorted data

text: Use MATCH to find a key's position when it sits in an arbitrary place, such as an item in a loot table.
Place summary cells above a task list that count incomplete tasks and overdue tasks.
Anchor matrix references with absolute row or column markers and leave vector references relative, so one formula fills correctly down and across.
when: When one formula must be filled both down and across a matrix-times-vector calculation.
why: Each matrix row fixes its columns while the row index advances, and each vector fixes its rows while its column advances, so each reference anchors the axis that must not shift.

text: Names make formulas read clearly at a glance, while cell addresses show exactly where the referenced data lives.
when: choosing how formulas reference data

text: Spreadsheet matrix work keeps data in one tool and avoids exporting, but dedicated matrix software suits large or unwieldy work better.
when: choosing where to compute matrix operations
why: Keeping data in place saves transfers, while large matrices strain spreadsheets

text: Stateless commands behave identically in every instance, so keeping many copies of one wastes memory.
The State, Strategy, and Type Object patterns have similar structure. They differ mainly in intent.
Use the State pattern when a conditional on state is complex enough to justify dynamic dispatch. A simple if is often all a small branch needs.
when: When a state-dependent switch is complex enough that dynamic dispatch fits better than an if.
why: Each state-dependent behavior becomes a virtual method, so the owner no longer branches on state itself.

text: A stateless state with only one method can be replaced by a plain function, with the state field holding a function pointer instead.
when: When a state has no data fields and exactly one virtual method.
why: With no machine-specific data, one shared instance serves every state machine, so a plain function pointer suffices.

text: Visiting every object to swap distributed state is acceptable when each object's state must be touched every frame anyway.
when: Every piece of distributed state is cleared or rewritten each frame.
why: The visit cost is already paid by the per-frame work.

text: Add jumps and procedures only once scripts need conditionals, repeated code, or reusable fragments.
when: Growing a bytecode instruction set incrementally
why: Simple scripts run fine without control flow, so adding it early adds complexity without benefit.

text: The component pattern fits large codebases; in small projects it risks over-engineering a problem that does not yet exist.
when: Choosing an architecture for a project of a given size.
why: Decoupling and reuse only repay their overhead at scale.

text: Assigning the owner's state pointer to a different state object changes how the owner responds to every delegated call.
A state interface has four methods: getAction runs while active, getEntryAction on entry, getExitAction on exit, and getTransitions lists outgoing transitions.
when: Designing a generic state machine
why: Separating entry, active and exit actions lets each run at the correct moment.

text: The State pattern has a state interface with a virtual method for each state-dependent behavior, one class per state implementing it, and an owner holding a pointer to its current state.

Strategies are usually stateless and define how an object behaves, while components often hold state that defines what the object is; a stateless component can be shared and then behaves like a strategy.
when: Distinguishing the Strategy pattern from the Component pattern.
why: State is the main difference between the two delegation forms.

text: Undo only works if every data change goes through a command, which requires discipline across the codebase.
Allocating a new state object on every transition can fragment memory. An object pool can reduce the problem.
Subclassing for every new behavior eventually produces hierarchies in which code cannot be reused cleanly.
when: When there are many different kinds of entities that each need their own behavior.
why: Shared code often cannot map onto a single inheritance tree, so reusing it across behaviors becomes awkward.

text: 1) Define a state interface with a virtual method for each state-dependent behavior. 2) Create one class per state, moving that state's switch cases into it. 3) Move state-specific data into the state class that uses it. 4) Have the owner hold a pointer to its current state and delegate calls to it.
when: A switch on state keeps growing or state data is only meaningful in one state.

text: 1) Define a fixed set of predefined behaviors. 2) Store in each type which behavior it uses, such as a function pointer for AI. 3) Select the behavior from type data at runtime.
when: type-specific behavior must vary without full scripting
why: A fixed set keeps behavior manageable while type data picks among options.

text: 1) Make the input component an abstract base with a pure virtual update. 2) Implement a player input class and a demo input class against it. 3) Pass the chosen implementation to the entity through its constructor.
when: An entity's control source must change, such as to an AI-driven demo.
why: Physics and graphics stay unchanged because they never see which input is used.

text: Add an undo method next to execute in the command interface, and have undo reverse the state that execute changed.
why: The changed object forgets its prior values, so the command must record them itself before execute changes them.

text: Have a state's transition method return the next state so the owner swaps it in after the method returns. Never delete the current state from inside its own method.
why: Deleting an object while its own method is still running is unsafe.

text: A state that holds data specific to one object must be newly created on each transition, and the owner deletes the old state after swapping.
Recording full game state each frame makes replay simple but uses too much memory; recording per-frame commands is compact but needs re-simulation.
why: Storing whole snapshots for every frame grows too large in memory, so logging the actions taken each frame is preferred.

text: The cardinality of a type is its number of distinct values, which measures the storage needed to hold it.
Type Object, Prototype, and Flyweight all share data among objects, but differ in purpose; Type Object focuses on organization and flexibility rather than memory savings.
when: comparing type object to related sharing patterns
why: Each pattern shares data for a different primary reason.

text: A C++ vtable is essentially a type object, and an object's vtable pointer is its reference to that type.
when: understanding type objects through language features
why: The type object pattern mirrors the mechanism language compilers already use.

text: Prefer a static class for single-instance behavior when only one instance is needed and neither lazy initialization nor polymorphism is needed.
A state with no per-object data needs only one instance, which can be shared by many state machines and avoids allocation on each transition.
when: When a state class has no fields beyond its method table pointer.
why: Copies would match exactly, so creating more of them gains nothing.

text: Single inheritance is usually the best balance of power and simplicity for type data; multiple inheritance gives little duplication savings but is hard to reason about.
when: choosing inheritance for type objects in games
why: Single inheritance is simple to understand, which matters because non-programmers must work with the system.

text: The owner of a service can publish a stand-in object instead of the real one, keeping the actual implementation hidden from callers.
why: Callers reach a stand-in through one lookup point, so the real implementation's type stays hidden from them.

text: Old class names left inside any script break the link between renamed weapon files.
A log stored as a static member of a base class is held by nothing outside that base class, but every derived class can reach it.
Storing per-object data in a static state breaks as soon as two objects are in that state at once.
when: When several state machines occupy the same state at the same time.
why: A static instance can only be shared safely when it holds nothing specific to one machine.

text: Calling a service through a static class or singleton ties every call site to the concrete class and its access method, so later changes force edits everywhere.
why: Each caller names the concrete class and its access mechanism, so changing either forces edits at every call site.

text: 1) Keep a static flag. 2) Have the constructor check that the flag is clear and set it. 3) Clear the flag in the destructor.
when: A class must be non-static but limited to one instance
why: Used as a fallback when a static class cannot provide the single instance.

text: 1) Store shared attributes such as starting health and attack text in the type object. 2) Give the type a factory method that creates typed objects. 3) Copy starting values from the type into each new object. 4) Keep a reference to the type for lookups it forwards.
when: implementing a type object with a factory
why: The factory centralizes creation, and forwarding keeps shared data in one place.

text: 1) Take the cardinalities of the base types. 2) A record's cardinality is the product of its field cardinalities. 3) Repeat this combination upward through nested types.
Type Object delegates invariant identity data, while State delegates current configuration; a type object doubles as State only when its type may change at runtime.
when: deciding whether delegated data is a type or a state
why: Invariant identity and current configuration are different kinds of data; changing type over time makes delegated data behave like current configuration.

text: A static-instance singleton avoids lazy setup but loses polymorphism, requires static-time construction, and cannot free its memory.
Shared static states avoid allocation but cannot hold per-object data. Instantiated states hold separate data per object but cost an allocation on each transition.
when: When a state class has no fields beyond its method table pointer.
why: Nothing machine-specific is stored, so one shared copy behaves identically for every state machine.

text: A base class can hold shared state such as a particle system as a private static member set once by a static init, which saves per-instance memory and initializes once.
when: All instances of the base class share one resource.
why: Static state avoids storing a copy per object, but it carries many singleton problems, since all instances share one object that makes reasoning harder.

text: Formatting converts data between its internal binary form and readable text notation, because standard input and output carry readable text.
Character scripts must query game state, such as what the character can see, and return an intended action; the functions they need are rarely known in advance.
Wrap resizes a cell's height to fit its text; without it, long text spills into neighboring cells or is cut off.
Text files are universal and simple compilers are portable; only line endings and encodings cause trouble.
No single character set is standard on every system, so portable algorithms should rely only on minimal character properties; ASCII is the most widely accepted set.
ASCII has 95 printable symbols and 33 non-printing codes; most of the latter handle data transmission and printer control.
A real number has digits, a decimal point and more digits, with an optional exponent marker E or D and an optional sign.
A string is enclosed in double quotes.
Special characters are taken from a fixed list of punctuation and operator symbols.
Items in text input are separated by blanks or line breaks.
A standard text module provides a text type, readers and writers for texts, and procedures to read and write characters, integers, cardinals and strings.
Text compared inside IF without quotation marks is not treated as the intended text, so the formula returns wrong results.
why: Quotation marks mark the value as text rather than a number or cell reference.

text: Use shared wildcards when a pattern must relate several unknown entities, such as the same person appearing in two clauses.
when: When writing rule patterns over multiple unknown entities.
why: The first clause's results bind the variable used in the second, so the clauses cannot be evaluated separately.

text: Letters and digits form ordered contiguous subsets, so range tests such as "A" ≤ x ≤ "Z" identify capitals, and similar tests work for lower-case letters and digits.
Monolithic classes whose methods must run on different threads, such as sound and rendering, make deadlocks and other concurrency bugs likely.
when: Domains run on separate cores in a multi-threaded game.
