why: One class forces unrelated domains to share state across threads.

text: Software threads are lightweight behaviours that process briefly and then return control to the scheduler, letting many behaviours run cooperatively.
A monitor keeps shared variables local to a module whose procedures run under mutual exclusion, so at most one process actively executes a procedure while others are delayed.
why: Mutual exclusion is sufficient, though not always necessary.

text: Handheld consoles usually trail full-sized consoles and PCs in technology by about 5 to 10 years.
On a console with parallelized rendering, synchronization and communication became hard, and several developers shipped very simple AI as a result.
Multi-core processors in later consoles made fast AI much easier to achieve.
Some platforms need only an extra setup call to run AI in parallel threads, while others require AI designed for parallelism from the start.
Branch-free update functions can run in parallel on a GPU or vector unit, whereas heavily branched rules usually run serially on the CPU.
Operating system threads pause and resume code through preemptive multitasking, saving and restoring processor state, but each switch flushes caches and adds significant time.
Modern CPUs run several pipelines and multi-core machines contain multiple full processors, so work can be split across them, but many threads still incur switching costs.
Micro-threads drop operating-system features such as error tracking and advanced memory management, reducing switching overhead.
Threading and multi-core hardware reduce sequencing problems, but only a few operations run concurrently, so sequencing still matters.
In Go, the language's native channel construct functions mainly as a queue carrying events or messages.
Straight-line single-threaded code uses only one core at a time, so threading is needed to make full use of the processor.
A process waiting in a wait statement does not count as actively executing within a monitor.
Assignment is rare, so it can be split across several frames without the player noticing.
when: When the operation runs only on rare player actions, such as picking a new formation.
why: A few frames of lag before the change takes effect is hard for a player to notice.

text: Where possible, spread scripted reasoning over several frames as an anytime algorithm, though some problems need a complete solution at once.
when: a script's computation is expensive
why: Slow scripts running in the main loop consume time needed for rendering, physics and audio.

text: Different levels of a scheduler hierarchy may use different scheduler types, such as a frequency scheduler for the whole game and priority schedulers for individual characters.
when: When schedulers are arranged hierarchically, with one scheduler nested within another.

text: Shared mutable state is very difficult to manage correctly, so keep it minimal.
when: components write to shared container state
why: Changes from many writers are hard to trace and reason about.

text: Use signals and monitors when several processes share one buffer and must not busy-wait.
when: Several processes share a buffer.
why: Polling a shared variable keeps the store busy, so a waiting process blocks the partner that needs that same memory.

text: Hyper-threading gives each thread its own pipeline of a super-scalar processor so pipelines run simultaneously; multi-core systems give each processor its own thread.
when: On processors and operating systems that support hyper-threading
why: Switching threads on a single pipeline is slow and wastes cycles, so each pipeline keeps its own thread.

text: Moving graphics work onto the GPU frees CPU time, which has let AI, physics and environmental audio take larger shares of processor time.
why: Animation and collision detection are typically processor-bound, so offloading them relieves the CPU's load.

text: On multi-core processors, AI for different characters can run in separate threads on different cores, giving parallel speed-ups.
why: Cores share fewer dependencies than hyper-threaded pipelines do, so speed-ups can be larger.

text: A signal records its identifier in a central store when it runs, and a wait checks the store each frame and completes once the identifier is present.
when: Synchronizing coordinated script actions
why: The store makes signal delivery visible to waiting actions

text: Adding a local input delay equal to the network delay keeps games in sync across machines in synchronous multiplayer play.
when: in synchronous multiplayer games across machines
why: The artificial delay matches the unavoidable travel time of a network message, so commands reach each machine equally.

text: Making an object globally visible shares its memory across threads, which can lead to deadlocks and race conditions.
why: Any thread can read or write it with no awareness of competing accesses.

text: In sequential updates, an object updated later sees earlier objects' new state, while an object updated earlier sees later objects' previous state.
A signal is tied to a guard: Wait delays the caller until the guard holds, and Send announces that the guard has been established, so the guard acts as a postcondition of Wait.
when: When one process must be delayed until another process establishes a condition.
why: A process sends the signal only after establishing the guard, so a returned Wait implies the guard holds.

text: Schedule quality is measured by sampling many random times and recording the minimum, maximum, average and distribution of behaviours running per frame; a good schedule has a narrow distribution with extremes close to the average.
why: The sampled statistics expose how behaviours clump together within frames.

text: Reading state mid-modification gives inconsistent or bogus values, from another thread's unsynchronized writes or from code reading its own changes, as physics and AI entities often do.
when: Reading shared state in a multithreaded engine.
why: Reads and writes overlap without synchronization, so the reader can see partially updated data.

text: If a script runs again, old signals remain in the store, so waits may complete without actually waiting.
when: Re-running scripts that use signals and waits
why: Leftover identifiers satisfy waits immediately

text: Leaving a severe performance problem, such as running at one frame per second, until shortly before shipping is risky.
when: nearing release with unresolved slowdowns
why: Late fixes may require restructuring code that has already hardened around the slow design.

text: Thread-safe initialization of a singleton does not make the singleton's own methods thread-safe.
With multiple writers any code can enqueue, which makes it easy to enqueue mid-event and raises the chance of feedback loops.
when: Many systems write to one shared queue or bus.
why: Any handler can add new events while the queue is being processed.

text: Expecting faster CPUs alone to speed up data-heavy code is misleading, because memory waits can dominate runtime.
when: Planning performance for data-heavy code on newer hardware
why: Memory latency improves much more slowly than processor speed

text: The simple circular buffer is only safe with one depositor and one fetcher; concurrent callers need guard violations turned into delays.
when: When deposit and fetch are called by concurrent processes instead of a single producer and consumer.

text: Busy waiting, where a process polls a shared counter, should be avoided because it hinders the partner process that needs the shared store.
when: When two processes run on separate processors and share the same counter.
why: The idling process holds access that its partner needs, since only one process can use the store at a time.

text: Unprotected updates to a shared counter can interleave, yielding n+1 or n-1 instead of n, so such interference must be prevented.
when: When a producer and consumer, or two peers, fetch the counter at the same moment.
why: Both processes read the counter before either writes, so the final value depends on timing.

text: 1) Make the request method and the update method thread-safe so the queue is never modified concurrently. 2) Lock briefly in the request method. 3) Have the update method wait on a condition variable so it uses no CPU until a request arrives.
when: Moving queue processing onto a separate thread.
why: Brief locks keep callers unblocked, and waiting avoids spinning.

text: 1) Deposit waits while the buffer is full and sends not-empty when the count becomes 1. 2) Fetch waits while empty and sends not-full when the count drops to N-1.
when: Concurrent buffer with not-full and not-empty signals.
why: Waiting on a signal avoids polling the shared counter and hides the synchronization details.

text: The scheduler runs every frame and manages many tasks, so its own code must be fast.
when: When the scheduler runs every frame over many tasks.
why: Any cost inside the scheduler repeats constantly, so overhead would accumulate across many tasks.

text: Design the game to adapt to a range of devices, because developers rarely know the exact hardware players will use.
when: targeting modern PCs, consoles, or phones
why: Code that does a fixed amount of work per tick speeds up or slows down on different hardware.

text: Use a queue when you need to decouple in time, not just decouple who receives a message; if only the receiver needs decoupling, Observer or Command is enough.
when: Choosing a communication pattern between systems.
why: Simpler patterns suffice when time decoupling is not needed.

text: Keep the work done while holding a queue lock minimal, since heavy work inside the lock blocks callers for longer.
when: A request method holds a lock while enqueuing.
why: Other threads wait for the lock to be released.

text: Micro-threads are very fast but difficult to develop and debug, so they suit only a small number of critical systems.
why: Trimmed thread overhead gives speed, but code must know how switching works, making bugs hard to trace.

text: Splitting behavior into single-frame slices is complex; threads, coroutines, fibers or bytecode let code stay straight-line at the cost of extra machinery.
when: When the language offers generators, coroutines, or fibers for lightweight concurrency.
why: Pausing and resuming mid-behaviour lets code avoid returning each frame and read as ordinary imperative logic.

text: Sequential updating keeps the world valid after each change and serializes moves for online play, but parallel updates create ambiguous conflicts, such as two pieces entering one empty square.
Components communicating through state on a shared container stay decoupled but push data upward and make behavior depend on update order.
when: components need to share data without referencing each other
why: Decoupling is gained at the cost of implicit, order-dependent communication.

text: A work queue gives each item to one listener that parcels jobs to a thread pool, and must schedule them using policies from round robin and random to more complex prioritization.
when: Items must be handled by exactly one worker.
why: Each job goes to a single consumer, so the queue needs a scheduling choice.

text: Background dirty processing needs asynchronous support such as threading and state safe for concurrent modification, and it can repeat work on mostly unchanged data.
when: Choosing background processing for dirty data.
why: Concurrent access needs safety, and small changes in large state can trigger redundant processing.

text: Executing a tree of small pointer-linked objects with virtual calls is slow to load, heavy in memory, and hurts both data and instruction caches.
when: Choosing an execution model for a scripting language
why: Many small heap objects, pointer chasing and virtual dispatch each add runtime cost.

text: A small arithmetic expression as an object tree needs about 68 bytes on a 32-bit machine, excluding padding, once vtable pointers are counted.
when: Estimating memory cost of an object-tree expression representation
why: Each node carries object overhead, including a vtable pointer.

text: An abstract syntax tree combined with an interpreter forms roughly half of a compiler.
when: Relating interpreters to compilers
why: The tree captures parsed structure, and the interpreter supplies execution, the rest being code generation.

text: 1) Give every expression node a common evaluate operation. 2) Literals return their wrapped value. 3) Operators recursively evaluate their operands, then combine the results.
when: Implementing a tree-based expression interpreter
why: Recursion through the tree computes the final value without a separate execution engine.

text: Unification makes wildcards that share a name refer to the same entity, letting one rule express relationships between unknown items.
why: Without it, many separate rules would be needed to cover each combination.

text: Wildcards use a reserved identifier value, so the matcher can distinguish a don't-care from a real identifier.
A wildcard flag can be packed into a single bit of an identifier.
With shared wildcards, a rule for an injured person holding the radio fires only when the radio holder is the injured person, whereas separate wildcards could match different soldiers.
when: When a rule relates several unknown entities.

text: Comparing two floating-point health values without unification would need a little under 2^32 rules, which is impractical.
when: Matching a rule that compares two floating-point values from facts, without unification
why: Explicit rules would have to enumerate every possible pair of float values, which is far beyond practical limits.

text: Each iteration can represent one unit of game time, such as one second, so the time granularity should match what is meaningful for the game.
when: Setting up a time-based simulation

text: Timer-driven simulation suits player-versus-player and time-based genres such as fighting, brawling, MMO and MOBA games, as well as idle games.
Experienced game developers often advise against variable time steps for simulation.
An expert with zero insistence is never run, so when no expert insists, no work is done.
when: When every expert returns zero insistence on the blackboard
why: The arbiter only hands control to a selected expert, and selection requires insistence above zero, so nothing runs otherwise.

text: A variable step copes with play that is too slow or too fast: bigger steps let simulation time catch up to real time.
when: When the game cannot keep up with real time because frames take too long

text: On faster hardware a variable step draws more frames for the same total movement, so gameplay looks smoother at the same pace.
why: Many small steps spread the same total movement across more frames on fast hardware.

text: Sampling interval is about half a second for slow simple shots, and a tenth or hundredth of a second for fast shots with wind, lift and drag.
when: When tracing a projectile's flight to find its closest approach to a target
why: Checking only at intervals speeds the search, and fast, complex flights need finer intervals.

text: A constant referenced without dollar signs drifts to other cells when filled down, silently producing wrong results in every row after the first.
when: Filling formulas that depend on a fixed constant.
why: Relative references shift as the formula moves.

text: A simulation that uses the same model as the rating system cannot reveal flaws in that model's assumptions.
when: when validating a rating system by simulation
why: The simulation must reuse the rating model, so it cannot test whether that model's assumptions match reality.

text: 1) Record the previous frame's time. 2) Each frame, work out elapsed time by subtracting the recorded time from now. 3) Pass elapsed time to update. 4) Store the current time as the new recorded time.
why: The update must advance the game world by the real time that passed since the last frame.

text: 1) Place a reset cell that, when non-blank, blanks the timer and the log. 2) Have the timer and log formulas run only when the reset cell is blank. 3) Clear the reset cell to restart.
when: A self-running iterative simulation needs manual restart
why: Formulas depending on the reset cell go blank while it is set, letting the user restart the board.

text: Behaviours must honour the time they are given, because the scheduler trusts them to return on time.
when: When a load-balancing scheduler passes timing data to software-threaded behaviors
why: Nothing stops a behavior from overrunning, so the scheduler must rely on it to return on time.

text: Scale per-frame movement by elapsed time, so an object covers the same distance per real second regardless of frame rate.
why: Multiplying velocity by real elapsed time makes distance per second independent of how many frames run.

text: Variable time step keeps pace with real time but breaks determinism; fixed update with variable rendering stays deterministic at the cost of more complexity.
when: When physics or networking must run on a variable time step
why: Faster machines run more physics updates for the same real time, so rounding errors accumulate differently and identical events diverge.

text: A weapon CPPN takes four inputs, the particle's relative position px and py, and its distance dc from the firing point, and outputs velocity components and RGB colour.
when: evolving particle weapons

text: A vehicle is built from three scripts: a behaviour script, a content script for effects and sound cues, and a factory script that spawns the vehicle actor in game.
Weapon behaviour and sound references are defined in scripts, so changing a weapon's sound often begins as a code edit.
Use the highest available muzzle speed to minimize flight time; with obstacle-heavy indoor layouts, fixed speeds may need trial and error.
when: weapon muzzle speed can vary
why: Higher speed shortens flight time, reducing the window for the target to move.

text: Storing speed on the spline lets the game look up any car's exact position and speed at any time, so cars can be rendered directly.
when: When computer-controlled cars simply follow a predefined racing line defined as a spline
why: Because the spline carries speed data, a car's exact position and speed at any time can be read directly.

text: Thrust that adds force along the facing direction up to a maximum builds up over seconds and releases slowly, making the ship feel floaty.
when: when tuning thrust acceleration and deceleration
why: Slow ramp and slow release create inertia that the player must anticipate

text: In the slide state friction drops sharply, so the character slides along the slope at a rate set by its steepness, with slight steering at reduced force.
when: When the incline is steep enough, around 75 degrees, that forward force cannot overcome the opposing force
why: Much less friction applies in this state, so the slide follows the incline's angle and direction.

text: Without dampening, a raycast suspension rocks with growing force and can launch the body. Dampening reduces each upward force as the suspension settles toward equilibrium.
when: When a raycast-suspended vehicle is dropped onto terrain without damping
why: Dampening lowers each upward push as the suspension approaches equilibrium, preventing the growing oscillation.

text: As a tire turns, its velocity direction changes, and the friction forces applied to it change with that direction.
why: Each tire's side and forward friction counteract its own velocity, so both are affected when that velocity changes.

text: As a tow chain unfurls, it switches from a non-simulated object to a physically simulated one, and a simulated attached door swings outward at the same moment.
why: Making the chain's deployment a physical process looked convincing, so it was kept even though not strictly required.

text: A vehicle rig jiggles in response to changes in its mass and balance, so attaching or deploying parts produces visible physical reaction.
when: When the tow chain is deployed or a raptor is attached to it
why: The vehicle's center of gravity shifts when the chain is out or a raptor is attached, so the rig reacts.

text: Dynamic flora can move by linking plant motion physics to wind speed, so vegetation responds continuously to the environment's wind state.
Read and Write each act at the rider's position and then advance the rider by one element.
why: Each rider holds its own position, so reads and writes proceed element by element through a sequence.

text: Uphill slopes beyond about 45 degrees apply an opposing force that scales with incline, slowing the character, which can still climb up to about 60 degrees.
Past about 75 degrees of incline, forward force cannot beat the slope force, so the character enters the slide state.
Character movement is built top-down: gravity pulls a capsule until it rests on the ground, each input-driven parameter has its own rule, and collision is the only broadly shared code.
why: Each relationship is hard-coded narrowly, so motion and its simulation can be discussed as one piece.

text: A vehicle physics model tracks suspension compression, each tire's forward and sideways grip, motor speed, travel speed, mass, air drag and rotational damping.
Raycast suspension is tuned with global gravity, body mass, extra vehicle-only gravity, and per-wheel maximum distance, minimum distance, suspension force and dampening.
why: Lacking damping, suspension pushes can make the vehicle spin wildly.

text: Failing to zero vertical velocity on contact stores hidden energy: ledges send the character plummeting and ceilings make it stick.
when: When the character lands on a tile or hits a tile above during a jump
why: Collision keeps the character from sinking in, so the unzeroed vertical velocity accumulates unseen as force.

text: Rapid height changes such as curbs can make visible tires snap. Interpolation reduces this but cannot remove every odd case.

1) Each frame, measure the difference between desired and actual velocity. 2) When the difference exceeds a threshold, adjust front and side tire friction along a response curve. 3) Apply the adjustment gradually over frames.
why: Gradual friction changes close the gap without abrupt snapping

text: Make every internal reference in copied vehicle scripts match the new name, because mismatched references stop the copied vehicle from working.
Change an internally simulated velocity with forces, rather than assigning position, to produce flowing, organic motion.
why: Setting positions directly yields straight, stiff paths, while accumulating force over time curves the path.

text: Virtual and interface method calls are indirect: they load the target from a lookup table before jumping, disrupting branch prediction and caching, so they run slightly slower than direct calls.
A virtual machine emulates a machine that does not exist in hardware; its instructions are chosen by the designer and can be high-level, such as converting data into game coordinates.
An interpreter reads script text line by line, works out each line's meaning and performs the action.
A classless prototype language stores both state and behavior in each object, and lookups start on the object itself rather than in a class.
when: when comparing classless and class-based languages
why: removing classes merges state and behavior into one object

text: An instruction set has external primitives that affect the game, internal primitives that manipulate VM values, and control flow and abstraction features.
when: Designing a bytecode instruction set
why: Each category has a distinct role in what scripts can express and do.

text: The Interpreter pattern represents a language as a tree of objects built from its grammar and executes it by having each node evaluate itself recursively.
when: Understanding tree-based language execution
why: Each grammar rule becomes an object whose evaluate operation recurses into its operands.

text: A programming language is an abstract computer whose built-in notions hide machine representation details from the programmer.
C++ has long been the de facto standard for PC and console games, and C# may eventually displace it.
Game AI is most often coded in C++, then C; scripting frequently uses Python, Lua, Lisp, Java, Lingo or ActionScript.
Lisp-style languages do not separate code from data, so scripts can be passed around, modified and executed later.
Byte code instructions include load, set value, get value, compare, conditional jump and return.
Byte code is sequential binary data, typically much more compact than the source text.
Just-in-time compilation converts byte code to machine code just before execution, and it is uncommon in game scripting.
A thin layer between script and program makes manipulating game data easy.
Most common game scripting languages are byte-compiled.
Inspecting memory and variables is hard for complex state machines and cannot explain how a neural network performs.
Machine code is dense, linear, built from minimal instructions that compose into behavior, and fast because hardware executes it directly.
when: Comparing bytecode to native machine code
why: These traits are what a bytecode VM imitates while remaining under game control.

text: In language circles, virtual machine and interpreter are used interchangeably, while the Interpreter pattern refers specifically to the tree-based design.
when: Reading language implementation literature
why: The terms overlap in common usage, so the pattern name is kept distinct.

text: A bytecode generator often holds an internal object tree, which a compiler can walk recursively like an interpreter, emitting bytecode instead of executing behavior immediately.
when: Building a tool that compiles behavior to bytecode
why: The tree structure is the same one the Interpreter pattern expects.

text: The Java Virtual Machine verifies bytecode when it loads a program because hand-crafted bytecode can skip the compiler's guarantees.
The four basic structuring methods are array, record, set and sequence. They are mathematically equivalent and differ in the operators used to select components.
The GOTO statement corresponds to a general graph built from pointers. Pointers allow any data pattern, including rings, just as GOTO allows any program pattern, including loops.
Start with a stack-based VM rather than a register-based one: it matches how nested expressions evaluate, keeps instructions small, and is simpler to generate code for.
when: Beginning a new bytecode VM or choosing an intermediate value model
why: Stack evaluation follows the nesting order of expressions naturally.

text: Add read and arithmetic instructions once designers need rules that depend on values, not only on constants.
when: Scripted behavior only sets fixed values
why: Without reads and arithmetic a spell cannot scale with a wizard's current state.

text: In a stack-based VM, operand order encodes operator grouping, so nested arithmetic needs no parenthesis or grouping instructions.
when: Compiling or designing instructions for arithmetic in a stack-based VM
why: Pushing operands in evaluation order lets each operation consume the correct stack values.

text: Shipping only compiled scripts stops players from writing their own scripts.
when: the game should not support player-written scripts
why: Players have no route to turn text into bytecode once the compiler is left out of the release.

text: Scripting systems that allow code changes during play increase loops per day and raise game quality.
why: More iterations per day give more chances to find and fix problems.

text: The scope of an instruction set defines what behavior bytecode can express and strongly affects VM speed.
when: Choosing how many instructions a bytecode VM supports
why: Scope determines both expressiveness and the work the dispatch loop performs.

text: A jump sets the instruction index to a target, acting like a goto, and higher-level conditionals and loops are built on it.
when: Adding control flow to a bytecode VM
why: Branching and looping reduce to changing the instruction pointer.

text: A literal instruction reads the byte after it as a number and pushes that value, so constants sit directly in the bytecode stream.
when: Encoding constant values in a bytecode VM
why: Embedding constants in the byte stream avoids needing another source for values.

text: A set-health instruction pops the amount and then the wizard index, so values pushed earlier are consumed in reverse order.
when: Executing a stat setter that takes arguments from the stack
why: The stack is last-in-first-out, so the most recently pushed argument is popped first.

text: Each value access in a polymorphic value design becomes a virtual call, and small values such as booleans and integers still incur heap allocation, so costs add up in the VM core.
when: VM core executes many value operations
why: Heap allocation and indirect dispatch per value erode the speed bytecode is meant to provide.

text: Instructions that pop a wizard index and push that wizard's current stat let spells depend on present game state instead of fixed constants.
when: A VM must express rules that depend on in-game values
why: Reading live state lets behavior scale with what the game currently holds.

text: Without loop or jump instructions, total bytecode size bounds execution time, which also makes the bytecode not Turing-complete.
when: Designing a VM instruction set for sandboxed behavior
why: Straight-line code runs each instruction at most once.

text: A typical virtual machine is a large switch over byte codes, with a short snippet of code for each one.
The bytecode pattern encodes behavior as bytes that a VM executes through an instruction set and a stack, with complex behavior built from simple instructions.
when: Understanding the bytecode pattern as a whole
why: Combining simple instructions on a stack yields complex behavior from a small core.

text: Assuming virtual calls are slow without profiling the game first can blame a design that causes no real bottleneck.
Writing an efficient compiler is a large task, and many home-built scripting languages end up with poor compilers.
When looping over hidden neurons, index the hidden list; taking the neuron from the output list by index is an error.
A fixed-size stack must be checked on every push and pop, or a bad program can overflow or underflow it.
when: Implementing a bytecode operand stack
why: Unchecked stack access lets malformed bytecode corrupt memory or crash the VM.

text: Shipping compiled-in behavior means fixes or new content require patching the executable, and user-written code mods need a full toolchain and could crash other players.
when: Behavior is compiled into the game executable
why: Code-level mods run with full access to the game process.

text: Assuming a register-based VM is faster without measuring your own instruction set can be wrong.
when: Choosing between stack and register VM designs for speed
why: Speed depends on the instruction set and other details.

text: Untagged unions are compact and fast, but bad bytecode can misread a number as a pointer and crash the game or breach security.
when: Bytecode may be hand-crafted or untrusted
why: Nothing is checked at runtime, so types are only known to the programmer.

text: Once looping instructions exist, the size bound on execution time no longer holds, so an instruction budget becomes necessary.
when: Adding loop or jump instructions to a sandboxed VM
why: Loops can run arbitrarily long without a counter.

text: 1) Push the first operand to the top of the stack. 2) Push the second operand. 3) Apply the operation to the top two values. 4) Store the result into its destination.
when: Computing a = b + c on a stack-based VM
why: Each operand must be moved to the top before the operation runs.

text: Prefer a single value type where possible, otherwise a tagged union, over a polymorphic class hierarchy for VM values, as nearly all language interpreters do.
when: Designing value representation for a performance-sensitive VM core
why: Polymorphic values are verbose, heap-heavy and slow in the core loop; single types avoid tagging costs, and tagged unions allow safe runtime dispatch.

text: Choose an off-the-shelf language when mature tooling and a modding community matter more than fine-grained control; build a custom one when control over the code is required or game-specific features are needed.
why: Other developers have already invested debugging and optimization effort, and a community keeps fixing it.

text: Avoid fully compiled scripting languages that link machine code into the game unless you have a proven run-time linking system, since they defeat the purpose of scripting.
when: choosing a scripting language
why: linking machine code removes the benefit of a separate script layer

text: After a change works, reorganize the new code so it fits the rest of the program and leaves no sign of when it was added.
when: When the change is more than minor
why: Leftover traces of quick additions would confuse the next developer who edits that code.

text: Do not have designers write raw bytecode, which is as hard as assembly; provide a higher-level authoring format instead.
why: Assembly-style authoring is no easier to use than the low-level code it would replace.

text: Adopt bytecode only if you can build, or commit to building, the authoring translation tool; shipping bytecode without one defeats its purpose.
why: Authors prefer a higher-level format, which only becomes usable bytecode through a translator.

text: Tcl, Java, JavaScript and Ruby each have significant in-game drawbacks, such as slow string-based execution, large memory footprint, or difficult integration, and none is known to have commercial in-game use.
when: Considering these languages for game scripting

text: Byte-compiling converts scripts to compact internal byte code, trading a longer start-up for faster execution than interpreting text.
when: When the costly compile step can run while a level loads
why: Byte code is laid out for execution, so it runs faster than parsing text each time

text: Bytecode is worth its cost when iteration speed and sandboxing matter more than the convenience of the host language.
when: Deciding whether behavior should be scripted in bytecode
why: Scripted behavior loads without recompiling but adds an extra layer and a slower execution path.

text: Bytecode runs slower than native code, so it is a poor fit for performance-critical engine code.
when: Choosing where to place bytecode in an engine
why: Interpreting each instruction adds overhead that native code avoids.

text: Stack-based VMs use tiny, operand-free instructions that are simple to generate but need more instructions, while register-based VMs use larger instructions and fewer total instructions.
when: Choosing an instruction format for a bytecode VM
why: Stack operands are implicit, while register operands are encoded in each instruction.

text: Single-type, tagged, and untagged value representations trade simplicity and runtime safety against memory use and speed.
when: Choosing how the VM stores values
why: Tags cost memory, while untagged bits are compact but unchecked.

text: A Zobrist key is a table of fixed-length random bit patterns, one for each possible state of each board location.
Checkers fits in 32-bit keys, while a complex game may need 128-bit keys.
Chess needs 64 squares times 2 colors times 6 piece types, giving 768 key entries; a 64-bit key is better than 32 bits for chess.
when: Chess-sized games.
why: Key length must cover the number of distinct states.

text: Update a Zobrist hash by XORing a piece's key in when it is added and again when it is removed. For a move: 1) XOR the moving piece's origin-square key out of the hash. 2) XOR its destination-square key into the hash.
when: When a move takes a piece from one square and places it on another
why: XOR is reversible, so a second XOR cancels the first

text: 1) For each occupied location, look up the random key for its state. 2) Combine all looked-up values with XOR to get the board hash.
Add extra keys for state outside the board, such as a doubling cube or repetition and move-count rules; some implementations drop these rare keys and accept occasional ambiguity.
when: When the game has state beyond piece placement.
why: Dropping them speeds hashing, since the extra state is rarely needed and occasional clashes are tolerated

text: Initialize Zobrist keys with random values from a good generator, since the C rand function has known quality problems.
why: Generator quality flaws are hard to debug, showing up only as hard-to-trace slowdowns

text: Design for all players, including disabled players, so games are inclusive and accessible and do not add unnecessary barriers.
Do not rely on colour alone to convey meaning; add text labels or notes so the information survives printing and colour-blind viewing; about 8% of males are colour blind.
when: Using colours to mark categories, cell roles or colour-coded information.
why: Colour is not the only way to convey information, and a significant share of male players cannot reliably distinguish certain colours.

text: Let users tailor the interface: offer full control remapping, subtitles and colour-blind modes so players face no unnecessary barriers.
Accessibility means a game works on its own, letting players understand and play it without the designer present to explain the rules.
Frequent eye movements between screen areas can be physically tiring, especially in first- and third-person action games.
when: In first- and third-person action games
why: Repeated saccades cost physical effort

text: Even without a retro reference, the core audience suggests what skills players will bring to the game.
when: When no classic reference exists
why: Audience expectations still predict baseline skills

text: Most players want several market values at once, so audience segments overlap heavily and one game can serve many of them.
The more customisable a game is, such as in control mapping, font size and colours, the more accessible it is to varied players.
when: Designing options for controls, text and visuals.
why: Customisation lets players adapt the game to their own abilities and needs.

text: A larger font for emphasis works best when columns are widened or rows are made taller to fit it.
when: emphasizing a heading or key value

text: Very young children cannot sustain attention through long games, while busy adults may prefer quick, short-burst sessions.
when: when choosing a target game length
why: attention and available time vary by audience

text: Familiarity with many kinds of games, from simple party games to large commercial titles, supplies raw material for new designs.
when: Generating new design ideas
why: Wide exposure gives more patterns to recombine.

text: Including everyone brings more ideas to choose from, quickly weeds out flawed ideas, exposes the game to many perspectives, and gives everyone a sense of ownership.
when: Whenever the team can be involved in design rather than one designer's vision alone

text: Each added seat dilutes every person's interactivity, leading to either tiring play or a theater too small to be profitable.
when: participatory play for a large crowd
why: Interactivity gets diluted in proportion to audience size, since each person gets a smaller share

text: Movement time depends on device start/stop time a, device speed b, distance D to the target, and target width W along the axis of motion.
when: Predicting how fast a hand or device reaches a target of given size and distance

text: Fixed controls, fonts and colors exclude players with specific needs.
An interface can silently rule out activities the designer did not mean to exclude, and players often do not notice those activities are missing.
when: When the physical interface shapes what players think they can do
why: Players stop thinking about the interface and form expectations from it, so hidden limits go unnoticed

text: Force that fights the player makes the device an obstacle rather than an amplifier, and actuated devices cause fatigue that limits how long players use them.
when: When a force-feedback controller pushes against the player's input
why: When a device fights the player's intention, the gulf of execution widens and frustration grows

text: Oversensitive inputs frustrate players, because small unintended movements produce large effects.
1) Define screening criteria such as no prior retail game experience and basic computer operation. 2) Recruit testers matching those criteria. 3) Observe them complete the tutorial and play.
when: recruiting testers for a game meant for nongamers

text: 1) Pick critical areas such as starting the game and key choices. 2) Write a short script leading testers through those tasks. 3) Recruit 3 to 5 objective, never-played testers per market segment, eight preferred. 4) Test one-on-one and have a note-taker sit outside the participant's view or record. 5) Revise and retest until most target players complete the critical tasks.
when: checking whether new players can understand and reach the core of a game
why: Designers who know the game cannot easily predict where newcomers get stuck.

text: 1) Ask how players will know how to begin. 2) Check whether it needs explaining or is self-evident. 3) Check whether it resembles something players already know, and if so highlight the similarity; if not, help players understand it. 4) Check whether it invites players to touch and manipulate it, and if not, change it to do so.
when: Early design of any puzzle or game, and when reviewing how it opens.
why: Clear first steps and familiar behavior let players start without help.

text: Make colour indicators perceivable to colour-blind players through accessible palettes or options-menu display modes, since otherwise they are left without cues.
Prefer sans serif fonts, use at most three fonts and colours, avoid long all-caps text except for short headings, and place text over a contrasted overlay rather than bare game world.
when: Designing in-game text and interface typography.
why: Creative fonts are hard to read and difficult to verify as readable.

text: Account for motor differences such as left-handedness, temporary injury, permanent conditions and situational limits like holding a baby.
when: Designing input schemes.
why: Players differ in physical ability, both permanently and temporarily.

text: Treat accessibility as critical as the other design goals, since a fun game that players cannot access may go unplayed.
when: During the refinement stage, when testing the game without its designer present

text: Games aimed at young audiences should encourage breaks and varied play, since good sleep matters for them.
why: Child development depends on varied play and good sleep, so pushing extended play is unethical

text: Make sure players perceive signs and feedback as the developers intended, and test key elements with the target audience.
when: When verifying how the most important elements are perceived by the intended audience.
why: to avoid confusion

text: An affordance is the relationship between an object's properties and an agent's capabilities, such as a handle affording a grip, so its form can communicate how it should be used.
when: Designing interface and object forms

text: A clarity failure means players do not perceive an element's form; a metaphor failure means they perceive the form but misread its function.
Informative signs describe what is happening, and inviting signs encourage a specific action.
Iconic visuals abstract reality through simplification while still conveying meaning, whereas non-iconic abstraction uses shapes, colors and lines that represent nothing.
when: when classifying a visual style
why: Iconic and non-iconic styles set different expectations

text: Cultural affordances are learned conventions, like a ladder signaling a vertical path; defined affordances are explicit markers, like strong paint in complex 3D spaces.
An affordance lets people perceive how an object can be used; the signifier is its perceivable part, and it should be polished so players perceive it correctly.
Signs must be perceptible before they can be read, since a low-contrast sign is simply missed.
Well-designed signs teach rules without tutorial text, which reduces localisation work and helps players return after a long break.
Doorframe colours show direction: green leads forward, red leads back, blue leads forward into annex rooms, and yellow leads back from annex rooms.
After flat design, interfaces returned to shadows and gradients that signal which areas are interactive.
Avoid figure/ground ambiguity and multistable images in icons unless the ambiguity is intentional, because players may misread them.
when: Designing icons and UI graphics
why: Ambiguous images can be read in unintended ways, and once seen that reading is hard to undo.

text: A good metaphor explains a mechanic, gives immediate feedback, and reinforces the game's theme all at once.
An informative sign turns inviting when its state needs immediate attention, such as a low health bar that turns red and flashes.
when: state needs immediate attention
why: The urgent state is meant to prompt the player toward a corrective action.

text: Intuitive affordances need less learning and memory, and so less attention, which reduces the explanation needed and improves usability and flow.
Real-world textures and shadows help users understand early touch interfaces, and the cue can be dropped once users know the medium.
when: early touch interfaces
why: A major mobile OS moved to flat design in 2013 because users had grown familiar with touch.

text: Visual representation sits on a triangle with three corners: realism, iconic simplification and non-iconic abstraction. Written language marks the most abstract corner that still conveys meaning.
when: when placing an object's visual treatment
why: Position signals which behaviors players will expect

text: Hartson's framework defines four affordance types: physical, cognitive, sensory, and functional.
Icons, objects or signs whose look or meaning suggests a different function than intended cause player confusion.
False affordances, where elements look interactive or reachable but are not, such as invisible walls, unclimbable ladders or unreachable map areas, frustrate players and break trust in game signals.
when: Elements that look interactive but are not.
why: Players act on the visual promise and are blocked, which breaks trust in the game's signals.

text: Using one look or control for two different functions confuses players, such as a close button later reused to delete items.
Icons based on obsolete objects, such as a floppy disk for saving, carry no meaning for players who never used them, so their function must be learned.
when: When the target audience is from a different generation or culture than the designers.
why: Icon meaning comes from prior experience with the real object, so players who never used it lack that link.

text: Sending visual or audio cues is not enough, because a deeply focused player may never perceive them.
when: When the player is absorbed in a taxing activity such as combat.
why: Higher working memory load raises inattentional blindness, so more simultaneous inputs make cues easier to miss.

text: Ads imitating system elements, like fake hair on a screen, trick users into unintended swipes that lead to advertisers.
why: users act on familiar interface cues

text: A cue that changes its appearance between areas undoes the vocabulary and forces players to relearn it.
1) Select the important HUD and UI icons. 2) Ask players what each icon depicts. 3) Ask players what function each icon performs.
when: Very early in development, to catch perception issues in HUD and UI icons.
why: The survey needs minimal effort and reveals how players read the icons.

text: Make an item's or icon's appearance accurately convey its function, designing for affordance so form follows function and its purpose is apparent.
If most players misread an icon's function, replace it with a different metaphor.
when: When players perceive an icon's form correctly but misread its function.
why: A correctly seen form that is misread shows the metaphor itself is the failing part.

text: Use language and metaphors familiar to players, such as presenting inventory as a backpack.
why: Familiar real-world concepts help players grasp how the system works without explanation.

text: Place informative signs such as health bars, ammo counts, cooldowns and minimaps where they are easy to perceive without distracting from the main action, usually in peripheral vision on the HUD.
Make inviting signs, which persuade players to act, salient against the game world, such as a yellow exclamation mark above an NPC.
when: In most cases, except when deliberate subtlety supports one of the game's pillars.

text: Use defined affordances such as strong visible markers when a realistic, complex 3D environment becomes too hard for players to read.
when: complex realistic 3D environments
why: players can be overwhelmed

text: Use button labels, icon shapes, and metaphors so players can learn and decide what to do.
Support tasks with functional aids such as inventory sorting, item comparison, filtering, and pinning a crafting recipe to the HUD.
Make similar signs and feedback behave alike, and make elements that cannot be used look different from usable ones.
why: Players generalize from one element to its look-alikes, so they expect those to behave identically.

text: In environment-heavy games, separate gameplay symbols from pure scenery so players can tell which elements matter for play.
when: when environment art is dense or detailed
why: Players cannot read functional symbols if they blend into decoration.

text: Explicit indicators make mechanics clear, but constant overlays obscure the fiction and become tiring for players.
when: Deciding how to mark interactive elements.
why: Fiction often includes details that do nothing mechanically, so players cannot assume every visible cue works and need a signal to tell which do.

text: Audio and visuals should share one stylistic language; a stylized look paired with realistic sound, or the reverse, creates mismatch that weakens the player's sense of the world.
when: when choosing sound and art direction for a game
why: Mismatched sensory styles break expectations the visuals set

text: 1) Open the UI movie. 2) Fire interface events that play sounds, or 3) attach sounds to interface elements through a sound theme.
when: When players press buttons or navigate menus in the interface.
why: Audio confirmation tells the player an input registered and makes the interface more satisfying to use.

text: Build interface sounds from the game world, such as armour and sword sounds for fantasy and electronic sounds for sci-fi.
when: When the game has a defined setting, such as a fantasy or sci-fi world.
why: Sounds drawn from a shared source read as one related family rather than a set of unrelated sounds, adding coherence.

text: Error bars show the standard error on each data point, indicating how reliable that value is.
A scatter plot shows (x, y) pairs with no required order, while a line graph connects points in succession along the x-axis.
Number formats can display cell values as currency, percentages, decimals with a chosen number of places, or dates and times.
Use simple, pre-sorted visuals when the goal is to make content quick to absorb.
when: when speed of comprehension matters most
why: Pre-sorted visuals require less processing effort.

text: Reinforce one fact by changing several dimensions of a channel together, so the meaning still reads if the player misses one dimension.
when: when a fact is important or must be read quickly

text: Encode different facts on different dimensions of one channel, such as allegiance on color and remaining health on size, so one channel carries several meanings.
Overlapping error bars generally suggest two data points are not significantly different, though this is a rough guide rather than a formal test.
when: Comparing two data points on a chart with error bars

text: Small error bars indicate reliable data, while large error ranges mean reality may differ substantially, so the data should not be trusted much.
when: Judging confidence in a chart's data
why: Error bars display standard error, a measure of how reliable the data is; wide ranges mean the true value may differ.

text: Use a line graph to track change over time or against level, and a bar graph to compare several data sets point by point at each x value.
when: Choosing a chart type for game metrics
why: Lines emphasize the trend across the x variable, while bars give each x value its own height for direct comparison.

text: Multiple rank lists are beneficial but can confuse players about which list is official.
when: When a game displays several ranking lists at once, such as guild, friends, or server rankings.
why: Narrower lists let players rank near the top when only one player can be first worldwide, but players may not know which list is official.

text: Default chart axis ranges may not fit the data, so set them manually; data ranging from 0 to 1 may otherwise get an axis running to 1.2.
when: Charts whose default scaling looks wrong

text: 1) Open the chart editor from the chart's Edit option. 2) Select the series to modify, or add a new series. 3) Set the cell range the series draws from.
when: Chart shows wrong data or needs an added series

text: 1) Choose the chart type. 2) Open the chart's Series customization. 3) Add error bars, either as a percentage of each value, a constant, or another option. Works for line and column charts.
when: Showing data reliability on a chart
why: Error bars make the standard error visible, showing how reliable each value is.

text: 1) Compute the standard error. 2) Enter it as a constant error bar value.
when: The standard error is already known

text: 1) Highlight the data in one row or column. 2) Choose Chart from the Insert menu. 3) Select the line graph type.
when: Plotting a single data series over time or level
why: Connecting points in order lets the reader track one value rising or falling as another changes.

text: 1) Include a header row or left column holding the x values alongside the data. 2) Mark that row or column as headers or labels when creating the chart.
when: Charting data that needs labeled x values
why: A plain series lacks meaningful x-axis labels; labeling the x-axis with values such as dates makes the chart readable.

text: 1) Arrange every series as a separate row or column. 2) Highlight all of them together when creating the chart.
when: Plotting several data sets on one chart

text: Give every chart a title and label each axis with its quantity. For charts with several curves, name each curve in the legend or remove the default legend.
why: Labels let readers identify what each curve and axis represents, and a chart copied elsewhere loses its surrounding context.

text: To compare curve shapes, chart one column at a time and leave out text label columns, since labels would be the horizontal axis entries.
when: Comparing the growth shape of several numeric columns.
why: Plotting one series at a time keeps the shape readable and avoids a cluttered axis.

text: High granularity shows an exact position, clarifying standing, while low granularity shows broad tiers, creating a general sense of progress.
when: when choosing how precisely to display rank
why: Exact ranks at the top are a milestone and need not reveal player counts; broad tiers hide exact numbers.

text: Sparklines give a compact view of many rows but lack titles, axis labels and error bars, which full charts provide.
when: you need a bird's-eye view of many rows versus a detailed chart
why: Sparklines are small by design, so they omit labelling features

text: Simple, familiar visual patterns match the brain's internal models, so they feel natural at first glance and look wrong only on reflection.
when: when designing characters or icons with exaggerated or abstract features
why: Familiar patterns match stored models before analysis begins.

text: A visual cue showing an enemy is unaffected by one action steers players toward the alternative action.
when: two actions can defeat an enemy
why: the cue removes the ineffective option

text: A channel conveys a stream of information to the player through attributes like digits, hue, scale, and typeface, each carrying part of the message.
Legibility is the organization that lets observers understand a space, and it is the goal for sandbox gamespaces.
Red is the traditional colour for danger and damage, so it often signals damage taken or a threat and stands out when contrast is high.
Assigning information to channels relies on instinct and experience, but mostly on trial and error through many sketches that get reworked.
The text color tool changes a cell's font color, which can draw attention to a value or help distinguish groups of cells.
Rendered plans and sections can show atmosphere and its progression across a level, which perspectives alone cannot convey.
The additive model mixes red, green, and blue light, which combine into white; each screen pixel uses these three elements.
The subtractive model uses RYB or CMY; combining these forms black, with CMY common in printing and RYB giving the familiar color wheel.
Games reuse color associations, such as red or green for health items and blue for magic or mana.
Reserve red for immediate threats, being hurt, or low health, and use orange for enemy markers such as outlines or health bars.
why: Orange marks enemies without causing red overload.

text: Colored translucent overlays can add color cheaply when screen zones match the layout, with one color assigned to each functional area.
when: When a fixed-layout display has zones that map to gameplay roles.
why: The display could not produce color, so colored translucent strips added color cheaply without changing the hardware.

text: Allocate display space in proportion to importance; the most critical status element can take a large share, such as close to a third of the dashboard.
when: When a status element is critical to gameplay and must stay visible at all times

text: Color theory, contrast, and related principles help symbols stand out from other information in a level.
Red, red-orange, and orange together create a warm or hot feeling.
why: Hues carry culturally learned metaphorical associations, and this warm group is tied to the feeling of heat.

text: Hazardous shortcuts that give faster times to players who master them reward skill and create optional risk.
when: Designing track or level routes
why: Skilled players gain an advantage that others can pursue.

text: Green often marks alien creatures or monsters, through links to toxic materials or swamps.
why: Green evokes radioactive substances and marshland, which people link to creatures of that kind.

text: Use distinct color for hazards, such as red explosive barrels versus silver strong enemies, so players can judge risk before engaging.
when: when planning encounters with varied threats
why: Visual contrast lets players assess danger at a glance.

text: When many irrelevant elements are red, a new red warning becomes harder to detect because the red noise competes with the signal.
when: many game elements are red
why: Irrelevant red elements hide the relevant red signal.

text: Different shades of one color can create distinct characters while still signaling the same category, such as friendliness.
when: when a color code must distinguish several entities in one category
why: The shared hue preserves the category while the shade differentiates members.

text: Grunge textures showing wear and damage mark areas that were once safe and are now corrupted, contrasting with clean, inviting spaces.
when: Showing that a formerly safe area has become corrupted
why: Dirty, worn surfaces contrast with the neat, welcoming look of safe zones.

text: Setting text color and background color to the same value makes the text invisible.
Subverting a visual convention can mislead players, but it gives them choices that depend on whether scenarios match the game's visual language.
when: when a game's visual language is established
why: players trust conventions and subversion tests that trust

text: 1) Identify what data must travel to and from the player. 2) Rank which data matter most. 3) List the channels that can carry it and which suit which data. 4) List each channel's dimensions and decide how to use them.
when: when laying out an interface

text: 1) Teach players a symbol's meaning through demonstration and reinforcement. 2) Keep showing the symbol while adding obstacles between it and its payoff, or subvert its convention.
when: when designing symbol-based communication in games
why: learned symbols can be varied once players understand them

text: When two modes conflict on one input, move one mode to a separate input, such as a second thumbstick, if the interface offers one.
when: The physical interface has a spare input channel.
why: Overlapping modes on one stick could run at once and fight each other for control, which can be disastrous.

text: Apply a strict color code, such as making one color always mean friendly, so players can read abstract shapes reliably.
when: when a game uses abstract or minimal art
why: Consistent color meaning makes abstract shapes readable as game information.

text: In indoor levels, mark pathfinding nodes with tactical information during node placement, using Dirichlet domains for quantization.
why: Tactical waypoints are not easily reachable from one another, so a basic graph is needed to connect them.

text: Decide which scenery is a gameplay symbol and which is only environment art before styling objects.
when: during level art planning
why: Unclear roles make it hard to apply distinct styling correctly.

text: A noise-minimizing art style, such as cartoon look with simple textures inside exaggerated silhouettes, aids readability and gives a distinctive look, but it constrains realism.
when: Choosing an art direction where many entities must be read quickly
why: Simple shapes and textures reduce visual noise and solve several problems at once.

text: Natural mapping means on-screen motion matches the physical input controlling it, such as a thumbstick moving an on-screen ship in the same direction.
when: designing control mapping
why: Matching motion makes the control feel direct and intuitive.

text: Control layouts that differ across platforms or machine variants force players to readjust, causing errors even among highly trained operators.
when: when a game ships on several platforms or machine variants
why: Readjustment increases player errors.

text: Copying a physical interface, or porting a prototype to a new platform without fresh design, is a common trap, since input and access differ by device.
when: when copying a physical interface or porting a prototype to a new platform
why: Controls and interface need fresh design rather than reuse, because the physical interface does not carry over.

text: Keep controls and menu navigation behaving the same throughout the game and across its states, mapping similar functions to the same button.
when: Across game states whose controls change, such as driving, flying or riding
why: Players build procedural memory for control mappings, which is hard to unlearn and frustrates them when it changes; similar controls reduce wrong actions in new states.

text: When two actions must be performed at once with the same hand, players struggle if the controls force an awkward grip; a comfortable input layout must be found and then practiced.
when: Mapping several frequent actions to one controller
why: Awkward physical demands add a skill players must learn separately from the game's logic.

text: First person limits what the player knows, which allows tension and surprise, while also creating immediacy and empathy with the character.
Control ambiguity: near-simultaneous inputs resolve in an order the player cannot perceive, making press order a hidden variable, so outcomes look random and cannot be learned.
when: when multiple buttons, such as jump-related ones, are combined or pressed closely together
why: Ambiguous input resolution breaks the player's sense of control.

text: Direct control means acting on the element itself, while indirect control means influencing elements one step removed, such as changing prices or ride design to attract guests.
Natural mapping links a display to a familiar physical pattern, so players read its meaning from cultural expectations about direction or rising bars.
Control exclusivity describes physical relationships between controls and which combinations can be used at the same time.
when: Mapping controls on a gamepad or device
why: Physical layout determines which inputs a player can press together.

text: Control mapping is the relationship between physical controls and the actions they trigger; good mapping lets players predict an action from the control used.
Indirect control steers player behavior by arranging information in ordinary ways so players take the intended path without noticing the guidance.
Controls are the means by which players invoke a game's procedures, so a digital version needs controls for each allowed action.
Friction is the resistance between the player and the reward, and it mixes player skill, luck, and time investment.
why: Friction is the basis of progression, since without it no progression system exists.

text: Flight and other simulations recreate real activities such as flying or operating vehicles, demanding mastery of realistic controls rather than twitch play.
An input device defines a possibility space, and its physical construction partly determines which actions a player can perform and expects to perform.

Control follows physical design: board and card games manipulate pieces directly, computers use keyboard, mouse, or joystick, consoles use proprietary controllers, and arcades use game-specific controls.
Mapping game information onto channels and dimensions is the heart of interface design.
Target platforms differ widely, including touch, motion, mouse and keyboard, gamepad, and mixed reality headsets, each with different input qualities.
The Enter key's effect varies by program: some move the cursor down one cell, while others keep it on the current cell.
A mouse is an indirect device whose desk movement maps to scaled on-screen movement set by the control-display ratio, while touch screens have control-display unity.

Controllers range from keyboards, mice, and gamepads to steering wheels, plastic guns, guitars, touch screens, motion sensors, data gloves, and VR headsets, though many are impractical for general play.
Realism is not automatically better than abstraction; what matters is whether the control fits the intended experience.
Frame or label an item and show the button that activates it, so players are reminded which input controls that item.
when: when items are controlled by buttons

text: Custom physical interfaces are often judged infeasible, but specially crafted ones can give old gameplay new life.
why: The marketplace rewards experimentation and novelty, which custom hardware can offer.

text: Keep a control scheme small for average players, and add detail or custom options mainly for expert players.
when: designing controls for a broad audience
why: Average players are frustrated by many options, while experts want depth.

text: Use the full range of an input only where skilled players gain value from fine control, and let novices safely ignore most of it.
when: designing mechanics on continuous or multi-state inputs
why: Expressive range rewards mastery without forcing beginners to manage it.

text: Use 60 fps for shooters, racing and fighting games, which need rapid input; 30 fps suits art- or narrative-focused games and skill games without rapid input.
when: When high-skill players use systems that demand rapid-response input
why: Rapid input genres punish added latency most.

text: Input mapping and polish effects change how responsive a control feels, so timing thresholds serve as a baseline rather than a final verdict.
why: Mapping and polish alter how input lag is perceived, so the point of tight-to-sluggish has no fixed cutoff.

text: Tune console shooters through acceleration between targets and aim stickiness.
when: console shooters

text: Each mapping transforms data rather than passing it through unchanged, so each can be designed and tuned separately.
Displayed values' placement, color, font, and effects such as pulsing or sound when very low determine how state is conveyed.
Placing inputs far apart on a physical controller turns control into a two-handed task, which can make play demanding yet engaging.
when: when designing a physical control layout
why: Spacing forces both hands to participate

text: A ship faster than its hazards, with screen wrap applying to both, makes every hazard feel unsettling because the ship can reach danger quickly and hazards can reappear close by.
when: when the player's craft is faster than the hazards around it
why: Wrapping space keeps all objects close and unpredictable

text: When a hazard breaks into smaller pieces that inherit the parent's velocity and receive extra random force, the pieces usually move faster and the field becomes more cluttered.
when: when designing hazards that split when destroyed
why: Inherited velocity plus random kick raises average speed with each split

text: A continuous jump stays time-sensitive: releasing the button early cuts it short, and it shares the apex and release gravity changes of the basic jump.
when: Continuous jump is airborne
why: Its higher starting upward speed reaches greater height, and only holding the button reaches the maximum.

text: Well-chosen mapping relations yield graceful, lyrical motion, while poor ones yield jarring or nauseating motion.
why: Expressive potential lies in the relationships between input and motion, so the pairing shapes the sensation of control.

text: Changing one parameter or movement speed affects the character's interaction with the space on many levels at once.
why: Context supplies the reference against which speed is perceived, so a change ripples into how the avatar relates to its space.

text: Response is the mapping connecting input signals to game parameters and defining how those parameters change over time.
Control can be compared with three hard metrics (controlled object count, per-avatar motion dimensions, type and frame, and per-input ADSR envelope) and one soft metric, overall sensitivity.
when: Measuring the sensation of control across games
why: For measurement, the underlying simulation matters little; the output envelope and overall sensitivity are what count.

text: Indirect control has three methods: nudging, priming and social imitation.
when: When a designer wants players to take certain actions without being explicitly instructed.
why: Arranging information straightforwardly lets behavior flow naturally, so players are guided without noticing.

text: Control mapping involves four relations: response gradual or immediate; movement relative to screen or avatar; rotation or translation; forward speed versus turning speed.
Light guidance on core controls can make a game look broken to newcomers, even when the audience is expected to be experienced.
when: a game gives little control guidance
why: newcomers lack the assumed knowledge

text: Mapping exclusive controls to nonexclusive actions forces players to stop moving to change tools when both controls sit under the same thumb.
when: Assigning movement and action controls on one hand
why: Conflicting physical reach prevents combining actions the game allows together.

text: Defining play as free movement within a rigid structure is so open that it covers light on a wall and a child scrubbing a floor.
Treating cursor clicking as real-time control mistakes a transparent interface to choices, closer to browsing a page, for continuous steering.
why: The cursor is meant to pass through to choices, so its use resembles reading a webpage rather than steering.

text: A fast-turning ship still cannot escape an incoming hazard unless the player plans ahead, so the feel of quick turning can mislead players about reaction time.
when: when a craft turns quickly but must still be steered with foresight
why: Turn speed does not replace positional planning

text: Accepting a default viewpoint without asking what the player needs to know can misalign information access with the design.
1) Start with a motionless rectangle centred on screen, all parameters at zero. 2) Add horizontal motion. 3) Add vertical motion, keeping the two systems mostly separate.
when: when building a platformer character controller from scratch
why: The expressive, fluid feel arises from the interplay of horizontal and vertical systems, which stay mostly separate in the simulation.

text: 1) Measure the input space of one device. 2) Compare it meaningfully with another device. 3) Examine how the physical construction of each device affects feel.
why: Measuring and comparing input spaces reveals how far the physical device defines the possibility space of the controlled object.

text: 1) Hold up a hand. 2) Treat each finger as an axis of motion. 3) Compare how the input moves with how the controlled object moves, to judge whether the mapping feels natural.
1) List the interface elements that show game state. 2) For each, identify a familiar physical pattern it could mirror. 3) Sketch how the element would change as the state changes.
when: auditing an interface for natural mapping
why: Players must read status at a glance mid-game, and familiar physical patterns cue meaning through cultural expectation.

text: 1) Classify each control method as direct or indirect. 2) Classify it as real time or turn based. 3) Note any cases where these distinctions are mixed.
1) Check hindsight: does the player learn from a hit? 2) Check threats are predictable with enough lead time to react. 3) Check evasion is possible for each threat.
when: continuous-movement games such as platformers and bullet hell
why: Real-time games punish unreadable or unavoidable threats more harshly than turn-based ones.

text: 1) List the procedures from the physical prototype, such as moving, turning, firing, and changing weapons. 2) Map each procedure to a control. 3) Group detailed controls under a menu or visual device reachable by one control or a small set. 4) Record each control and its procedure in a table with one column per control and one for the procedure.
when: translating a physical prototype into a digital control set
why: The table confirms that no procedure is missed and no control is unused.

text: Support both WASD and arrow-key movement, because many players will try either scheme.
when: designing keyboard movement
why: players bring different habits

text: Consider mapping both mouse buttons to the same action in any game needing only one button, especially for young players.
when: players may click the wrong button
why: small hands often press the wrong button

text: On PC and console, offer full control remapping and a reset button; on mobile, offer as many control schemes as possible.
when: Designing control options by platform.
why: Remapping lets players fit controls to their hands and needs.

text: Follow platform and genre conventions, such as a magnifying glass meaning search or a circular back button on a console.
why: Familiar conventions help users understand the system without learning new meanings.

text: Map controls to the things they affect so each control's position or motion matches the result, as with a stove knob lined up with its burner.
why: Natural mapping makes the correct action obvious.

text: Make actions that users are expected to want easy to reach using Fitts's law.
when: Designing interface controls.
why: The screen edge halts the pointer, so the target acts as unbounded in one direction and cannot be overshot.

text: Keep input-output predictable and feedback clear and immediate; build gym levels to test this with task analysis.
why: Controls give players agency, so unpredictable input-output undermines that agency.

text: Document controls and their procedures with tables, flowcharts, and written descriptions together.
If a game fits an established genre, use the genre-standard control scheme.
when: the game belongs to a known genre
why: Players already know the genre's controls, so they start with lower learning cost.

text: Map exclusive controls to actions that are also exclusive in the game, and if the mapping cannot change, add a game restriction that mirrors the physical one.
when: Assigning actions to controls with physical conflicts
why: Matching exclusivity avoids awkward input and makes the restriction feel natural.

text: Make each control resemble its effect, using spatial, shape, color or motion similarity, so the mapping works as a built-in memory aid.
when: Designing input layouts or button assignments.
why: Similarity lets players infer the link without memorizing abstract symbol-to-action pairs.

text: Use a clear snapping system, since it prevents overlap and sliver bugs and shows art at its best.
when: choosing or evaluating an editor's snapping
why: Imprecise joins let players slip through gaps into the void and hide overlaps, while precise snapping avoids both.

text: Design so players exercise a skill, take risks, and work a strategy at all times, since any risk-taking involves chance.
when: When the game is designed to be addictive
why: Constant engagement of skill and strategy keeps decisions meaningful.

text: Allow a second jump press shortly after landing to trigger a continuous jump with higher initial thrust, a taller stretched animation and a higher, longer arc, at any speed.
when: Within a short window after landing
why: Rewards rhythmic re-jumping with extra height

text: Set sensible default values, leave only the most important decisions to players, and automate chores like resource management.
when: When a strategic action splits into many minor per-unit choices that make each one not worth the effort
why: Each minor choice costs players more effort than it is worth, so bundling them keeps attention on the choices that matter.

text: Giving hardcore players fine control over details can burden or alienate average players, so balance must be found through heavy playtesting.
when: When a game gives fine-grained control over minute details to both hardcore and average players
why: Detailed control adds chores that average players find unwanted and tedious.

text: Giving a key role to less action-oriented players needs intuitive controls; the cost is that they may steer poorly, but more players can take part.
when: When steering or a core control must be handled by players who rarely play action games
why: Including a key part of the audience is worth the cost of weaker steering by less experienced players.

text: Letting players customize controls can help or hurt, so its effect should be tested rather than assumed.
