Very close motion-based mapping attracts casual players but costs much more in hardware than conventional button controls.
when: Choosing between motion controllers and standard controllers.
why: Close mapping of movement to in-game actions appeals to casual and inexperienced players, which justifies the expensive hardware.

text: A first-person view with no visible avatar is argued to maximize projection, while a visible avatar lets players feel its injuries and relief directly.
when: Choosing a camera and avatar presentation
why: Players project their identity into anything they control, so a visible avatar can feel like their own body.

text: A fused all-in-one device forces replacement of the whole device for each new feature, while separate devices let you mix, match and adopt new features independently.
when: choosing between one combined device and several separate devices
why: Technologies advance at different rates.

text: Choosing a frame rate trades graphical richness against responsiveness: higher frame rates reduce latency but leave less processing time per frame.
when: After removing avoidable code lag, when hardware latency is already fixed
why: Hardware sets a minimum latency in frames, so changing frame length is the remaining way to reduce delay.

text: A dark pattern is a deceptive interface or product design that tricks users into actions benefiting a business at their expense, frequently on purpose, usually to maximize profit.
Dark patterns exploit limited attention and cognitive limits, so users miss the costs they incur and business goals are favored over users; intent is not strictly required.
when: When a costly option is hidden behind a prominent call-to-action button in a checkout flow
why: Hurried users miss hidden costs in a prominent button, so the business gains from their inattention.

text: Players who learn a predictable dynamic difficulty system may play poorly to stay behind, then exploit the benefits of trailing to win late.
when: When DDA is predictable and players understand it.
why: Players optimize against the rule rather than the intended challenge.

text: Few players compute the effective per-unit price of in-game currency, and fewer compare bulk purchases or sale events.
when: players buying currency bundles with real money
why: Irregular bundle sizes and conversion rates make the math tedious.

text: The attention economy describes products that use bottomless scrolling, autoplay, and push notifications to keep people engaged beyond their original intent.
why: Attention is scarce and valuable to these platforms.

text: A nudge is a well-intended design that guides people to choices benefiting their health, money, or society.
Associative advertising shows an appealing context and leaves the product use to the viewer.
Demonstrative advertising shows a product in use and how it helps, and game versions show features in a list.
The term dark pattern was coined in 2010; a catalogue of 16 types, from fake scarcity to trick wording, has been compiled.
Scams, false advertising, and possibly propaganda also count as dark patterns, not only interface tricks.
Dark patterns are incompatible with the UX mindset because they exploit users for the company's benefit.
Regulators are increasing scrutiny; deceptive designs that cause unintended purchases have led to very large fines.
Some dark patterns are subtle, such as the decoy effect in pricing.
An unclear element is better than a misleading one, because players who hold a wrong belief become more frustrated than puzzled.
when: When most of the audience reads an icon as meaning something other than its real function
why: Players who wrongly believe they understand an element become more frustrated than players who are merely puzzled.

text: An item on a dark-pattern list is not automatically a dark pattern; context and audience decide, and the list is not exhaustive.
When business goals outrank human goals, the UX mindset disappears and practices like dark patterns can take over.
why: Design cannot be neutral, so the same persuasive skills used for good can be turned to exploit users.

text: Players can plant false information using normal mechanics, such as an action that suggests one plan while the real plan differs, not only through explicit lying tools.
when: games with readable actions and hidden intent
why: Opponents read actions as evidence about intent, so misleading actions shape their beliefs.

text: Four categories of game dark patterns: temporal (wasting time), monetary (overspending), social-capital (exploiting obligation or standing), and shades of gray (cognitive-bias tricks).
Forbidding cash trades only through terms of service is weak, because tracking and banning violators costs support effort and banned players often cause public backlash.
when: When designers do not want players trading in-game goods for real money
why: Tracking and banning violators consumes support time, and banned players create public backlash.

text: Some engagement techniques are unethical and may count as dark patterns, and it is not always easy to tell when a feature has moved from good UX into a dark pattern.
why: Teens and tweens are especially susceptible, since social connection matters greatly to them and their brains are still immature.

text: Tracking alone does not create hand presence, because interactions must also feel meaningful.
when: Hand tracking is added without meaningful object manipulation

text: Pre-ticked opt-out boxes, such as newsletter sign-ups, are dark patterns because they favor the company over users who never noticed.
why: People tend to leave default settings unchanged, so pre-ticked boxes capture consent that users never actually gave.

text: Assuming users will adopt a new interaction without verifying it through testing.
when: When a new interaction is modeled on a gesture users know from elsewhere and prototypes are ready
why: Familiarity with a similar gesture suggests adoption, but that remains an assumption until users test it.

text: Treating a current design trend as permanent, since interface trends come and go.
why: Design trends fade over time, as earlier popular styles such as realistic-texture interfaces did.

text: Treating a UX framework as scientifically validated overstates its evidence, since its own author states it has not been empirically tested.
why: The framework was never empirically tested and blends in concepts with less research behind them.

text: A large primary button with a tiny opt-out link, plus hard-to-find cancellation, can trap users in unwanted recurring memberships.
why: Such designs trick users into actions that cost them while benefiting the company behind them.

text: Ads disguised as debris on the screen can open a store when users try to swipe them away.
why: Users mistake the ad for real clutter, so their dismissal gesture unknowingly opens the sponsor's store.

text: Dark patterns rely on users not noticing them, so they are hard to spot without deliberate review.
Users may buy a product twice when the interface does not clearly show that the first purchase succeeded.
when: Bad UX that is confusing but not intentionally deceptive.
why: Missing success feedback leaves users unsure whether the action worked.

text: Designers often cannot tell a missed message from a deliberately ignored one, so failure-triggered backups can feel like nagging to players who chose to ignore the first prompt.
when: When backup prompts trigger only after the first prompt goes unheeded.

text: 1) Stress that the team can win the next round. 2) Highlight what the player did better than the winning team. 3) Point out personal improvement on a metric compared with earlier play.
when: showing a loss to a player
why: reframing around progress softens negative emotion

text: Print dots on number tokens equal to each outcome's expected count in 36 rolls, letting players compare odds at a glance.
when: tokens representing dice-sum outcomes
why: Dot counts equal expected occurrences over 36 two-dice rolls, so players can read the odds directly.

text: Do not reframe negative emotion caused by bugs or usability problems; remove the cause instead.
when: negative emotion comes from a bug or usability problem
why: reframing hides a problem that should be fixed

text: Make an element hard to perceive only when difficulty perceiving it is the intended challenge; otherwise it damages usability.
when: When making an element hard to perceive is the deliberate challenge of the design.
why: Otherwise the hidden element works against the core task, since locating it is not the challenge.

text: Restrictive nudges need public debate and inclusive design, since they can exclude users with mobility limits, temporary injuries, or heavy loads.
when: When a design restricts some personal freedom for the wellbeing of the wider population.
why: Citizens must understand the design's intent and be able to debate it, and it must not exclude people with disabilities.

text: Game studios that respect their audience should not use dark patterns.
why: Dark patterns are deceitful designs that serve the company at the expense of its players.

text: Top-down design saves time and feels familiar but risks a clone look; small changes accumulate until the interface looks distinct.
when: When designing an interface for a well-established game genre.

text: Ask for confirmation before harmful or irreversible actions, such as salvaging or destroying rare items, and offer undo so players can recover from regret.
when: Before a potentially harmful action, such as closing unsaved work or destroying a rare item.
why: Mistakes are inevitable, so prevention targets errors outside the challenge and recovery helps after one happens.

text: Give invalid actions plain-language feedback explaining why and a fix, e.g. 'Out of ammo!', not just a negative sound; or a short sound, flashing cooldown icon and pop-up.
when: When players press an input that has no effect in the current context.
why: Without feedback, players keep pressing the control, unsure whether it is invalid.

text: When a natural action fails, give feedback that acknowledges the attempt and guides the player onward, rather than failing silently.
when: VR, a natural action is not supported
why: Acknowledgment softens immersion loss, though it is only a mild fix.

text: Give clear negative feedback on a failed action, such as a missed jump, and let the player recover and retry locally rather than restarting the level.
when: during onboarding
why: Harsh non-physical punishments cause stress that can hinder learning, so failures should allow local retries.

text: Design out predictable errors unless the error is part of the challenge, by spacing opposite controls apart and avoiding accidental triggers.
when: Placing opposing actions such as confirm and cancel.
why: Close opposite controls raise the chance of accidental clicks, following Fitts's law.

text: Signs should explain why an action failed, since otherwise players are left guessing.
Anticipate likely player errors and prevent them for non-core tasks.
when: When a task sits outside the game's central experience.

text: Let players undo or recover from mistakes wherever applicable.
Restrict each outcome entry cell with data validation so it accepts only Heads, Tails, H or T, using rejection or a dropdown.
when: spreadsheet cells where players enter outcomes

text: Handle syntax and semantic errors well, since users make errors constantly and the tool must guide them back; this is among the most important and difficult parts.
when: When the interface is a typed-text parser that players write commands into.
why: Parsers only see unexpected input, so guiding users back to valid input is hard to do.

text: Do not use emotional pressure such as guilt in confirmation steps, because that turns helpful friction into a dark pattern.
why: Emotional manipulation serves the company rather than preventing the user's mistake.

text: Give every player action immediate feedback confirming it was accepted, with different responses for different outcomes, such as different impact effects for a damaging blow and a parried one.
why: Delayed feedback lets attention drift and makes focus hard to maintain.

text: Players look away, get distracted or control the camera, so they miss signals; testing must confirm they understand the game.
when: When the player, not the designer, controls the camera or view direction
why: Players control their view and attention in interactive play, unlike in a film where everything important is on screen.

text: Player information travels as signals across channels such as screen regions, the avatar, sound effects, music, the screen border, a character's body, speech bubbles, and haptic feedback.
Send critical information through several channels, with at least one visual and one audio cue; different forms get through under pressure better than repetition, and this aids accessibility.
when: Designing tutorial or alert cues; critical instructions where delivery matters more than economy of signals.
why: Relying on one channel leaves players who miss it without information; each channel can be missed independently, so more channels lower the chance of total miss.

text: Confirm dramatic or irreversible actions, such as deleting a long-invested character; use undo for less precious items.
when: Actions such as deleting a character or selling items; actions with serious consequences that cannot easily be undone.
why: Confirmation adds physical load, so reserve it for costly errors; the extra step prevents accidental loss, matching the error prevention guideline.

text: Show progress made, what remains (e.g. quest items left) and goals close to completion; let players compare results and avoid unnecessary memorisation.
when: Designing progression displays and results screens.
why: Clear progress information is critical to feeling competent; visible progress and comparison motivate players and reduce memory load; counts of remaining goals let players learn the game's rhythmic system.

text: Menu sounds should signal forward or backward movement, accept or decline choices, and each button gaining focus should have a distinct sound.
when: When creating sounds for menu navigation and other UI feedback

text: Give every feature state and interaction its own sign, since unsignalled ones leave players unguided; yet not every state change needs showing, only crucial ones must be communicated.
when: Feature states and interactions versus general state changes.
why: Unsignalled feature states and interactions leave players unguided.

text: Visual scale and appearance signal threat: a larger enemy suggests danger and length, and visible effects hint at abilities.
when: enemy design
why: Players infer behavior from appearance before they test it.

text: Waiting feels shorter when a progress bar is animated, accelerates rather than slowing and stalling, and players have something to do.
when: loading or waiting screens
why: Waiting is painful, and perceived duration depends on what the screen shows during the wait.

text: Signs are visual, audio or haptic cues informing players about game state or inviting action; feedback is a sign reporting the system's reaction to a player action.
Feedback is information the game returns to the player, and its quality strongly affects understanding and enjoyment.
Signs and feedback are all stimuli players perceive, including the responses a game gives to their input.
Well-designed feedback helps ensure clarity, challenge, and reward in play.
Use visual feedback for precise information such as exact resource levels or unit locations, since sound alone leaves players guessing.
when: presenting exact status information
why: Visual channels convey exact values that sound cannot.

text: Feedback can support play without changing the rules, for example by making a scored event visible and audible to all observers.
why: Clear feedback makes outcomes legible without altering mechanics.

text: Player confusion signals unclear design; respond by stacking several cues, such as particles, sound, and character flashes.
when: players misread a game signal
why: one cue is easy to miss

text: Keep the core status display visible on every screen and in every mode so players always see essential information.
when: when the game has multiple screens or modes

text: Trigger dynamic tutorial tips when a required action goes unused for a while, since they work better as reminders than first teaching.
when: a required action is neglected
why: Between sessions players forget mechanics and controls, and an interactive game only advances when players act.

text: The computer should appear intelligent and ideally explain its actions; meta-level communication about design tasks and outcomes remains largely unexplored.
when: When a computer tool collaborates with a human designer on creating content
why: A collaborator that keeps acting against the designer's mental model causes frustration and confusion.

text: Use lighting, floor lines and prominent button cues to draw players toward the intended path or action.
when: When you want to encourage a player action without telling players exactly what to do
why: Cheap visual cues guide choices without restricting options or changing incentives.

text: Show secondary and tertiary messages only when the primary message fails to achieve its goal, such as a timed action the player missed.
when: The cost of extra messages is high and success of the primary action can be checked.
why: Backups stay dormant unless needed, which avoids clutter.

text: Detail and dark values draw the eye, so background areas can be simplified using loose scribbles or coarse outlines.
when: composing a sketch so attention goes to key elements
why: Viewers are drawn to the most detailed and darkest areas.

text: Complex, striking art buries mechanical cues such as facing, movement and held items, plus nuanced sound and animation, making the game state harder to read.
when: When visual richness competes with gameplay readability.
why: Excess visual intensity hides needed information; in a gray world every shape has mechanical meaning, so no mental sorting is needed.

text: If mockup geometry is hard to texture, players cannot tell rocks, grass, water or lava apart in playtesting; varied solid colors can serve instead.
when: mockup and playtest stages
why: Testers must quickly recognize what each surface represents, and untextured geometry hides that information.

text: Slow or awkward texture scaling limits what gets built.
when: evaluating editor texturing tools
why: Textures that are hard to change or scale cap what the tool makes possible, so creators build less.

text: Design redundancy so that a player who misses about half the content still receives the critical parts.
when: When players will predictably miss some signals because they look away or get distracted
why: Repeating a signal in several forms lets critical parts still get through when players miss much of the content.

text: A visual hierarchy shows all information at once but assigns each item visibility matching its importance, so players notice the most important items first.
when: ordering information in a dense interface
why: Humans unconsciously ignore the least visible parts of an overloaded signal, and bigger, closer, brighter and faster items are noticed first.

text: Silent failure of a natural player action is a strong immersion breaker in VR.
when: VR with natural actions
why: The player receives no feedback, so presence breaks.

text: Play lacking feedback frustrates and confuses players.
Over-communicating is a common trap, but leaving players to die without any indication of why is equally harmful.
when: Designing feedback on failure
why: Unclear or inconsistent failure makes players focus on finding the cause instead of the challenge itself.

text: Status cues that players do not share, such as unfamiliar symbols, fail because natural mapping depends on shared expectations.
when: When a status display relies on conventional symbols such as gauges or bars
why: Natural mapping only reads correctly when players share the cultural expectations behind the cue.

text: Assistance the player can detect may feel unfair or misjudge intent, so assistance must stay hidden to work.
when: Implementing any assistance system
why: Visible help breaks the sense of player skill and can act against what the player meant to do.

text: 1) Identify the player's goal at this moment. 2) Choose feedback that helps them reach it. 3) Decide what players should feel now and how feedback can create that feeling.
when: At every moment of the game, since feedback is continuous but must differ by situation
why: Checking goal and intended feeling at each moment keeps the feedback loop aimed at the intended experience.

text: 1) Display the randomizer on screen, such as dice or a deck. 2) Animate the roll or shuffle. 3) Animate the drawn result moving to the player's hand or board.
when: when a game generates random results by computer
why: Computer randomness lacks the tactile sensation of physical randomness, so players trust it less.

text: 1) Determine what the player must learn from feedback. 2) Choose a channel for each item: aural, visual, or tactile. 3) Match the channel to the kind of information.
when: planning feedback for a game
why: Matching channel to information type keeps status clear.

text: Prefer diverse redundancy over plain repetition, which can grate; use simple repetition only when the game cannot know whether a message was received.
when: Announcements or messages with no feedback on receipt.
why: Without a way to confirm receipt, repeating the message is the only assurance, though repetition grates.

text: Match visuals to behavior: similarly acting objects should share an appearance, and visually different objects should behave differently unless their sameness is intended.
when: When an object's dynamic state changes affect play and must be communicated to the player
why: Players assume looks signal differences in speed, scoring or other properties.

text: Avoid autoplay, and make replaying a match an opt-in choice.
why: Self-control is still developing in children, making it harder for them to resist attention-economy pressure.

text: Turn voice and text chat off by default and let players opt in.
when: Designing multiplayer communication settings.
why: Enabled-by-default chat can expose players to hate speech and toxic behaviour.

text: Show players which inputs a crafting or combining action requires, so they avoid mistakes.
when: Designing crafting, equipping or combining systems.
why: Visible requirements prevent players from attempting invalid combinations.

text: Tell players that customisation options exist, since most players do not explore menus before starting the game.
when: Designing first-launch experience.
why: Players who never see options cannot use them.

text: Make an unavoidable input delay visible as a process, such as a signal traveling from control to target with a matching sound, so the wait reads as cause rather than fault.
when: When an unavoidable delay separates a player's command from its visible effect
why: Players expect button presses to act immediately, so an unexplained delay reads as a fault.

text: Reassess feedback continuously during play, asking what players need, want, and feel at that moment.
why: Feedback needs differ across situations.

text: Units should telegraph what they can do through distinct visual signatures, and key attributes such as health and max health should always be visible.
why: On-screen information must support player decisions and faithfully reflect what just happened.

text: Give players feedback that tells them whether they did it right or have room to improve, so they can learn.
Show an accurate progress indicator wherever the challenge allows it.
when: challenges where progress can be measured
why: A visible measure of progress corrects players' linear-progress assumption.

text: Show a visible cue when a character changes state so the changed response does not feel jarring.
when: a character enters a state with different response rules
why: Players who see the cue can understand why controls changed.

text: Make teaching meaningful and repeat it across different contexts and activities.
Draw attention explicitly to important changes, for example by blinking the element or adding a sound effect.
when: a change matters to the player
why: players may miss it otherwise

text: Warn players about what could hurt them in the next few turns, so the system reflects the reason behind actions.
when: turn-based strategy
why: In complex strategy games, the consequences of actions are not felt right away, so warnings reveal upcoming threats.

text: Use surface finishes as material cues, so players can tell which surfaces accept an interaction and which do not.
when: when an interaction works on some surfaces but not others
why: A consistent finish lets players predict whether an interaction will succeed.

text: Show interface pop-ups only when context requires them, and let allies or objects in the world signal the next action instead.
why: Characters demonstrating moves just ahead show players what to do without interrupting play.

text: Visual and audio form should reveal function: icons, characters and items look like what they do, e.g. drop shadows signal pressability, green cross suggests health, threatening look signals harm.
when: Designing interface elements, objects and visual elements representing gameplay functions.
why: Players read affordances from form, so visual style also determines usability; intuitive forms need no learning, reducing cognitive load and tutorial text.

text: Tools shape how people create, so the physical constraints of the medium appear in the finished work.
The shape of a thumbstick's housing changes its feel; square or grooved casings feel different from round ones.
why: The casing sets the physical limit of stick travel, so its shape alters the motion players feel.

text: 1) Show one element per page in randomised order. 2) Ask a representative sample what they see. 3) Ask what the element does. 4) Compare answers to locate where the design fails.
when: when testing icons or other visual elements
why: Comparing what players perceive with what they think the element does reveals whether the metaphor carries the function.

text: A form signals function only if the form is clearly identifiable and accurately conveys the function.
when: Evaluating whether a visual element communicates its function.
why: Ambiguous or misleading forms fail to communicate.

text: Game AI needs environment knowledge, and where it is produced determines run-time cost and reuse. In a toolchain approach, the content team supplies it, often via offline processing of raw level data.
why: Environment knowledge saves run-time processing, a scarce resource in games with many tracked things.

text: Events and generated rooms matter only if players perceive and understand them; an event never communicated effectively has not happened for the player, so generated content needs clear communication.
when: Designing game events and feedback; generating rooms or events procedurally
why: Emotional impact depends entirely on what the player can perceive; unperceived content contributes nothing to the player's experience.

text: Game UX applies the UX mindset to games, putting the player's actual experience, perception and interaction first from development through post-launch.
A game's experience happens in players' minds, so teams can design for it but cannot design it directly; many developers craft it under system and production constraints.
A practical game UX framework has two pillars: usability, meaning ease of use, and engageability, meaning how enjoyable, captivating and emotionally resonant the experience is.
why: Players are self-motivated by the play itself, so enjoyment is required, not optional.

text: Game studios balance fast turnaround against scientific rigor, so research is often run to a looser standard that is still better than deciding without data.
when: Studios working under deadlines
why: Deadlines limit the time and participants available for rigorous studies.

text: A heuristic evaluation has one or more UX experts assess usability and engageability against rules of thumb, then report findings to the team.
when: Evaluating a game without player testing
why: Expert review gives fast feedback when participants are unavailable.

text: Game user research evaluates a game's ease of use and its ability to engage players, finding usability and engageability issues with fix suggestions while respecting design intent and business goals.
Game UX covers usability plus emotion, motivation, immersion, fun and flow.
Homogenous redundancy repeats the same message in the same form, and can be hidden, such as an audio log placed in several locations that stops appearing once heard.
The core purpose of game user research is to verify that the intended experience is the one players actually have, and if not, to understand why and find ways to fix it.
Many user research methods exist, and the right one depends on the development cycle stage and the research question.
Game UX is gaining traction in the video game industry but is not yet well formalized, and no clear definition of its roles and responsibilities exists.
Some game UX models list four experience factors: ease of use, fun, challenge and pace.
Use heuristic evaluation early, when a game is too rough for participants or testing is not possible.
when: Early development stages
why: Rough builds may not be ready for real players.

text: Hiring UX people for interface work is useful, but a global UX strategy for the game and studio has the biggest impact.
why: Players' experience is shaped by everything they perceive, so a UI-only focus leaves most of it unaddressed.

text: A highly innovative game can survive usability problems because players accept extra effort, but this should not be relied on.
when: When a game is innovative enough that players might push through friction.
why: Buzz or friends' participation can motivate extra effort, but such cases are rare.

text: Rule gaps cause arguments in board games and loopholes, dead ends, or system breakdowns in software.
why: Complex systems act unexpectedly in varied conditions, so rules that look complete on paper leave gaps once implemented.

text: Because games are interactive, art that conflicts with perception principles or usability principles can keep players from fully experiencing it.
when: When art direction conflicts with HCI laws or usability principles.
why: Players must provide input to reveal a game's content, so unusable art blocks that experience.

text: Good UX respects users and avoids major friction, so satisfied users make the product profitable in a win-win.
Game UX rests on four pillars: human-centered, grounded in science, collaborative, and benevolent.
Game user research combines two tools: knowledge of cognitive science, HCI, human factors, and heuristics, and the scientific method as methodology.
why: Using the scientific method limits human bias in judging whether players experience the intended design.

text: Game UX evaluates the experience players will have, how they sense and act in the game, and which feelings and involvement follow, measured against design intent.
Heuristic evaluation cannot replace user testing, since most real usability issues only appear when the target audience tries to work out the game.
when: Deciding whether expert review is enough
why: Experts evaluate against rules, while players reveal actual confusion.

text: Assuming a learner will save work without counting the hand-holding can make the project more expensive, not less.
when: Planning a project that relies on learning.
why: Data preparation, validation and testing add effort.

text: 1) Identify information players must remember across activities. 2) Check whether it is visible only in a distant mode or screen. 3) Move it to an always-accessible log or menu.
when: Players fail to act on requirements they were shown earlier.
why: Requirements shown only in a distant mode force players to hold them in memory across other tasks, causing overload.

text: Gamified, educational, health, and social change games need the same UX mindset and framework as entertainment games.
why: Serious games need usability and engageability like any interactive product, or they fail to teach or retain players.

text: When existing references miss the target look, gather your own real-world material, such as physical samples, to build the palette.
Players notice a peripheral element as something popping in but cannot identify it until they move their gaze to fixate on it.
when: When an important element appears in the periphery during play
why: Peripheral vision lacks the resolution to identify detail, so a saccade is needed

text: Third-person views let players see where the character will land, and a shadow under the character helps in 3D platforming.
when: Platform jumping in a third-person 3D game
why: The character's own body stays visible, so the landing point can be judged; a ground shadow gives further guidance.

text: Mixed-initiative dialogue has two properties: context, so questions stay relevant to the discussion so far, and relevancy, so answers contain only information relevant to the question.
Interface elements connect players to in-game data such as ammo counts and enemy information.
At any moment the player's attention roams over a small area of the level, which deserves the most effort.
Game state can be displayed on in-world objects, such as a weapon, instead of only in standard interface areas.
To remain equally legible in peripheral vision, elements must grow larger with distance from the fovea.
Screens and speakers are narrow output channels, and a game usually has more happening than they can carry at once, so designers must structure and sequence information.
when: Presenting multiple simultaneous events
why: Limited output bandwidth forces prioritization of what reaches the player.

text: Obscure HUD functions are acceptable if players can learn them and they do not mislead.
when: When a function is hard to express, such as a very specific ability shown by a tiny icon

text: Menu items anchored to a screen edge are effectively very large and quick to reach, needing few correction cycles.
With first- or third-person cameras, prefer an egocentric minimap, because a fixed map forces players to mentally rotate and adds cognitive load.
when: Designing minimaps for first- or third-person games
why: Mental rotation adds effort and slows navigation.

text: Group items that share a display format, such as short numeric counters, so players read them as one set.
when: when laying out a status display
why: Items needing the same number of digits are grouped even when their functions differ.

text: Tiers suit players outside the top group, giving them something to work toward without making them feel weak.
when: when displaying rank to most players
why: Coarse tiers hide exact standing, so lower players sense progress without feeling like they are at the bottom.

text: Bold outputs and use conditional formatting to recolor them by value, such as red for an item far off a cost curve.
when: When output values can be judged against an expected cost or power curve
why: draws the viewer's attention to results

text: Avoid on-screen information that conflicts with the task being performed, since conflicting distractors add workload and slow or degrade performance.
when: When players must handle a second, unrelated task at the same time
why: Attention is finite, and coordinating two tasks consumes part of it, leaving less for each.

text: A minimal display can mirror the layout of the physical input it pairs with, keeping the interface readable at a glance.
Shooter HUD elements can be tuned to their importance: health and ammo grow more visible as they become critical and quiet down when the state recovers.
when: designing shooter HUD indicators
why: Visibility matched to current criticality keeps the signal meaningful without constant clutter.

text: An allocentric map keeps a fixed orientation, usually north up, while an egocentric map rotates so the player's facing direction points up.
when: With a camera that follows the avatar from behind or within its eyes, instead of looking down from above.
why: Players must mentally turn a fixed-orientation map to match their facing, which costs time.

text: Designers tend to write too much item text, and dedicated UX writers are rare in the industry.
when: When item descriptions appear in interfaces where players make important choices
why: Readability matters most where players must decide, so surplus text can hinder those decisions.

text: Removing the HUD entirely increases friction and memory load, because players must open menus to find information, pulling them out of the game world.
why: The HUD exists to stop players from remembering or searching for key information, so removing it forces trips into menus.

text: Dense but complete information, such as long skill descriptions or small percentage modifiers on wide damage ranges, may be ignored entirely by players.
when: Presenting numeric or descriptive detail to players
why: Completeness does not guarantee that players read or process the information.

text: Displaying important gameplay information in small or cluttered peripheral positions.
when: When important gameplay information is shown outside central vision
why: Visual acuity falls away from the center of gaze, so peripheral details may be missed or force eye movements.

text: Relying on one sensory modality, such as vision, to convey important information makes it easy to miss.
Reducing UX to interface work or aesthetics ignores most of what the experience is.
why: UX spans the whole customer journey, from first hearing about a product to support, not only the look of the interface.

text: 1) List all information the player needs. 2) Sort it into three groups: needed every moment, glanced at from time to time, and needed only occasionally. 3) Keep frequent items on top and put rare items behind secondary controls before building layers.
when: At the start of designing an information display.
why: Not all information is equally important, so sorting by how often it is needed decides what stays visible.

text: 1) Present the main advantages of an item as bullet points. 2) Keep text short, since most players skip long sentences. 3) Organize items so they can be compared side by side. 4) Show strengths and weaknesses as infographic bars.
when: When item descriptions inform strategic decisions rather than cosmetic ones
why: Most players skip long sentences, and side-by-side comparison helps them decide.

text: Remove irrelevant information, especially from the HUD and home screen, and avoid HUD clutter and overload, for example by making HUD elements context-sensitive.
why: Showing elements only when relevant avoids a clunky, overwhelming HUD while keeping needed information reachable.

text: Show control mappings or contextual action prompts persistently on the HUD when players would otherwise have to memorise them, so attention stays on movement and play.
when: Designing complex control schemes with many actions; remembering is not the challenge.
why: Removing the need to remember mappings frees attention for the activity itself; players never need to memorize them.

text: Keep the default interface lean, displaying just the controls players require right when they require them; advanced users can attach extra panels and extensions.
when: Designing default HUD and interface layouts.
why: A minimal default serves most players, while optional additions serve power users.

text: Make a cue salient against the environment when players must attend to it, so it is not missed.
when: players must notice the cue
why: A critical sign that blends into the environment will be missed.

text: At critical health, avoid visual effects that intensify danger and punish players already in trouble; encourage narrow escapes instead.
when: When player health is critical
why: Intensifying effects such as reduced vision punish a player already in trouble, while narrow escapes feel satisfying.

text: Layer the interface with modes and submodes so rarely used functions sit behind a secondary control, keeping the main interface simple.
when: When many options compete with the need for a simple main interface
why: Rarely used functions sit one press away, so the main screen stays simple while options remain available.

text: Present stat effects as base values plus bonuses rather than as penalties below an average, so equivalent options are not avoided.
when: designing how stat values appear
why: Framing changes perceived value.

text: Give players the information they need to act, and show accurately what just happened; decision-relevant info should be visible or within easy reach such as a hover.
when: When players must have data to make a choice.
why: Players can only act on information they can see or reach quickly, such as through a hover.

text: When sizing a score display, plan for top-end outliers, since leaderboard analysis is dominated by the highest scores.
when: deciding how many digits a score display needs
why: Extreme top scores set the maximum width required.

text: Keep peripheral cues simple and easily distinguishable, especially when they affect gameplay.
when: When peripheral cues affect gameplay
why: Peripheral vision cannot resolve fine detail, so small or unclear elements may be missed or force repeated eye movements that tire players.

text: UI icons are often too small to be accessible, so enlarge them, though not every HUD element must grow.
Display the relevant interaction prompt when a player approaches an interactable object.
when: When a player comes near an object that can be searched or interacted with

text: Place key information at the start and end of a sequence, where recall is strongest, such as in marketing trailers.
when: When a sequence of items must be remembered after brief encoding, such as a memorized word list
why: primacy and recency effects

text: Place complicated features less prominently in the UI so only more committed players find them, following the 80-20 Pareto principle.
when: When a complex feature must stay because the added depth is essential to play.
why: Confusion from complex features can frustrate newcomers, making them feel out of control and more likely to quit.

text: Give items and abilities functional text stating how they are used, required skills, damage dealt, or health restored.
when: writing item and ability descriptions
why: Players need functional information to make choices.

text: Only relative visibility matters: assign each element visibility proportional to its importance, since players perceive items roughly in that order as skill rises.
when: deciding visibility levels across interface elements
why: Players perceive items in roughly the order their visibility implies.

text: Egocentric minimaps rotate with the player's facing direction and avoid mental rotation, while allocentric maps fixed to the world suit large maps.
when: Choosing minimap orientation.
why: Egocentric views reduce mental work for immediate navigation, whereas allocentric views give global overview.

text: Ammo can be shown at increasing loudness: small corner text, bullet icons nearer center, crosshair display, half-screen flashing icons, then a spoken count after each shot.
when: choosing how prominently to show ammo
why: Each step trades attention cost against how quickly the player can read the value.

text: People interpret icons and symbols through their knowledge, expectations and culture, so a symbol may be meaningless to people without that background.
when: When designing icons or symbols for varied audiences.
why: Perception is top-down, shaped by prior experience.

text: The system image is what players perceive and interact with; it shows how clearly the system conveys its meaning and use, forming players' mental models.
Reference information a player must recall should be placed where it can be accessed on demand rather than only in a distant location, because players forget it during other activities.
when: Information needed for a later action is only visible in a separate mode or place.
why: Players must hold it in working memory while doing other tasks, and overload causes them to forget it.

text: Too many modes confuse players.
when: When a game switches between modes whose rules change so much they feel like separate games

text: Make every state of a feature distinguishable to players, and verify with usability tests that players read each sign as intended.
when: Designing state indicators for features such as skills or weapons.
why: Players must tell states apart, and testing reveals confusion between them.

text: Human-computer interaction emerged in the 1980s as computers entered homes and has established principles for interfaces.
HCI focuses on usable, pleasurable interfaces rather than the full product journey, so the broader term user experience was introduced in the 1990s.

Ergonomics has three areas: physical ergonomics (anatomy, fatigue), cognitive ergonomics (mental processes, limits of perception, attention and memory), and organizational ergonomics (process optimization).
Human-centered design puts people at the core of the design process; UX studies end users' interactions and the emotions and behaviors they produce.
Human factors psychology and ergonomics designs machines around human capabilities, performance and limits, drawing on disciplines such as psychology and physiology.
A technology can exist for decades and still be dismissed as too expensive or unreliable until a design makes it good enough.
Human factors and ergonomics was firmly established during World War II, when psychologists were hired to reduce machine-related errors in military equipment.
Human-centered design began after wartime aircraft errors, when designers shifted to shaping machines around human bodies and minds rather than the reverse.
HCI principles also apply to digital products like websites and games, improving how easy and enjoyable interfaces are to use.
Put people before business goals, and treat ethics as a critical part of the approach.
If firing requires releasing the accelerator, players lose momentum while shooting, so a fire action that interrupts a core action gives rivals an advantage.
when: Binding a secondary action to a button used for a primary action
why: Interrupting the primary action has a real cost.

text: Critics dismiss a new input technology that merely imitates an old control scheme, and opinion shifts once games are designed to need it.
when: a new input technology copies an existing control scheme
why: Imitation hides what the technology can add that old controls cannot.

text: Players can feather or flick a thumbstick, which makes it a highly sensitive input.
why: Free two-axis deflection with continuously varying readings gives far more distinguishable positions than a button can.

text: Players hold a trigger partway down, at about a quarter, half or three-quarters, without pushing it to either extreme.
why: Its travel has hard stops at both ends, leaving a sensitive middle zone where many distinct positions can be held.

text: Large, springy buttons that give a clear click and sit near flush with the surface make pressing feel satisfying.
when: when designing physical buttons for an arcade-style controller
why: Tactile cues confirm each press

text: Reading a button's binary signal over time gives four states or signals: up, pressed, down and released.
Discrete inputs, such as keys and buttons, send momentary signals; continuous inputs, such as joysticks, mice and steering wheels, send ongoing signals.
Sensitivity is roughly the number of states an input can occupy, a soft metric; signal format is a hard, exact metric.
A paddle is a bounded, one-axis rotary input turned by a knob, returning a signed float from -1.00 to 1.00 with 0.00 at centre.
A standard button moves along one linear axis between two hard stops and has exactly two states, ON or OFF.
A thumbstick moves on two linear axes at once, is spring-loaded back to centre, and is bounded by a circular housing.
A trigger moves along one linear axis with a graded zone between its ends, returning a float from 0.00 to 1.00 under spring return.
Rate-based analog control maps stick displacement to movement speed rather than to acceleration.
Standard mapping relies on conventions players already expect, like a wheel turning a vehicle, a pointer driven by a mouse, or WASD keys moving an avatar.
The goal of input design is synchronization between a player's intent and the resulting in-game action.
The input device is the player's organ of expression: every intent passes through it, and its affordances, constraints and physical feel shape the experience.
The control-display ratio sets on-screen movement per unit of physical movement, applied as simple multiplication, such as two units on screen per unit of hand movement.
A handheld portal is a device whose screen shows a first-person view that moves one-to-one with the device's physical movement, so the device acts as a window into the game world.
Input is how the player expresses intent, and the physical properties of the device set its sensitivity, from a two-state button to an unbounded mouse.
On a classic pad, each button signal is discrete: one moment, on or off, no intermediate states, so each button has low sensitivity.
Two-state buttons send ON, OFF and HELD signals rather than continuous values, giving Boolean input values and making discrete state changes easy to detect.
when: Reading input from digital buttons

text: A paddle has hundreds of distinct states between its two hard stops, which are set by a catch at each end of rotation.
Paddle controllers have largely fallen out of use in modern games.
Keyboard keys, mouse buttons and controller shoulder buttons share standard button behaviour, though shoulder buttons travel only a tiny distance.
A thumbstick's positions are effectively infinite, so counting discrete states is not meaningful; players experience fluid, accurate positioning.
A controller trigger has roughly four or five usable states, including fully off and fully on.
A directional pad plus two action buttons on a simple pad can still cover six low-sensitivity inputs used in active play.
This classic home console controller has fourteen discrete inputs: A, B, four C-buttons, four directional-pad directions, Z, left and right shoulder buttons, and Start.
A spring-loaded stick measures force rather than position, making it an indirect control unlike a touchscreen where the user touches the target directly.
when: Choosing between stick and touch control schemes
why: Indirect control changes how players map input to motion

text: Force feedback pushes back against player controls and is common in simulation hardware, but is usually used as a blunt special effect rather than to convey subtle ongoing state.
All control over virtual objects is mediated by an input device, which makes input the starting point of game feel.
Output bandwidth from computer to user is typically much greater than input bandwidth from user to computer.
Existing devices can sense inputs that games rarely use, such as swapping controller ports, opening a DS lid, or the thumbstick's sensitivity.
Analog inputs can read exact stick angle and graded trigger depth, not just on or off, and a single button can act on press, release, or hold.
Players express intent via key presses, thumbsticks, controller pads, touch surfaces and motion detectors; no one of these suits every task equally well.
when: Choosing input devices for a game
why: Each input type suits certain tasks more naturally, so a single device rarely serves all intent well.

text: On a typical gamepad, the shoulder bumper and trigger sit beside each index finger, so pressing them together is awkward.
when: Assigning inputs on a standard gamepad
why: Index finger reach restricts pressing bumper and trigger at the same time.

text: Input devices differ widely in sensitivity: a button has two states, a trigger four to five, a paddle hundreds, a thumbstick thousands and a mouse millions.
when: Comparing input devices
why: Sensitivity determines how finely a device's input can be read

text: Button, trigger, paddle, thumbstick and mouse are all indirect inputs, since the player does not touch the screen.
when: Classifying input devices
why: Direct input, such as touch screens, lets the player touch the screen itself

text: Feel depends heavily on available inputs, so the same game can feel very different on keyboard and mouse than on a motion-controlled device.
A discrete input such as a single strum responds quickly but lacks continuity, while a continuous input such as a bar that varies a value gives ongoing control.
A device's layout, materials, weight and spring strength all affect how it feels to use.
Ranked by expressiveness, a thumbstick is more expressive than a trigger, which is more expressive than a standard button.
A mouse tracks movement on two axes, making it far more sensitive than a single button.
A fluid swing can be delivered on low-sensitivity controllers, so input precision is not the only source of movement feel.
The controller has ten standard buttons, a directional pad and one thumbstick.
Shoulder buttons and the bottom button reach their pressed state faster than the front face buttons on the same controller.
Under the Weber-Fechner law, the input change needed to notice a difference on an analog stick scales with the intensity already applied.
Use a rotational one-axis control when the in-game action is a turn or sweep along a single dimension.
when: the action is a turn or sweep along one dimension
why: Its rotation is bounded by stops, so a single axis yields a continuous value with hundreds of distinguishable states.

text: Use a button for a simple yes-or-no event such as fire or jump, not for expressive continuous control.
why: Its travel is a single linear axis between two hard stops, so it can only sit fully on or fully off.

text: Use a thumbstick for proportional movement or aiming, where smooth direction and magnitude both matter.
why: Two-axis movement with spring return to center gives smooth and highly accurate positioning.

text: Use a trigger when a graded amount of force matters, such as acceleration or throttle.
why: The trigger reports a continuous value across its travel, so partial pull amounts are readable.

text: Relying on button states rather than chords suits simple pads, as platformer input often does.
when: On a simple pad with few low-sensitivity buttons

text: Accept roughly away-from-wall stick input and a jump press close in time to it, so chained moves stay forgiving.
when: When a move needs a stick flick and a button press completed close together
why: The completion window is wide, so loosely timed inputs still register as the chained move.

text: Map a wall jump to pulling away from the wall toward the desired direction plus a button press, a mapping that feels natural.
why: The stick direction matches the escape motion and the button keeps its usual jump meaning.

text: Motion hardware tuned to the movement the theme implies, such as a rocking vessel, makes the physical experience feel more authentic.
when: In a simulation whose theme implies a specific bodily motion, such as sailing
why: Peripheral vision strongly shapes how motion is felt, so blocking it weakened the sailing feel.

text: Prototype feel with a well-built controller rather than a keyboard, since build quality changes perceived feel.
when: When judging control feel during prototyping.
why: Build quality affects feel, all other factors being equal.

text: Spring tension and mechanical travel determine whether a press feels tight or loose, quick or sluggish, so small differences can make the same game feel different across platforms.
when: When a game is ported across platforms with the same engine and a close button layout
why: Mechanical differences in spring tension and travel change how a press feels, which players read as one controller being better.

text: Adding side-to-side, forward-back and up-down weight movement alongside spinning lets rumble convey direction, not just intensity and rhythm.
when: when the controller uses multiple actuators or moving weights

text: A device's total sensitivity depends on how its inputs combine and are laid out, not only on each input alone; combinations can give a low-sensitivity device more range than its parts.
Mutually exclusive directional inputs, where opposing directions cannot be pressed together, reduce a device's sensitivity.
Button combinations laid out for use by both thumbs multiply possible input states, raising a device's sensitivity above what any single button offers.
Spring resistance on a paddle's rotation gives it a force-based feel and high sensitivity along its single axis.
A thumbstick returns two float values, one per axis, updated continuously as the stick moves.
A thumbstick often maps directly or nearly directly onto in-game motion, so how far and how fast it is pushed sets the motion's character.
when: When a thumbstick acts as a direct or semi-direct substitute for in-game movement
why: Position is read as continuous and finely graded rather than stepping through discrete states.

text: A game may register inputs to the millisecond and know their exact order, while players perceive no consistent order between them.
when: When two buttons pressed at nearly the same time trigger different responses

text: Lower control sensitivity weakens attachment to the avatar, while direct one-to-one mapping of input to rotation leaves almost no barrier.
when: When control is not too frustrating and lacks crippling control ambiguity

text: While a rotate button is held, a fixed small amount is added to the ship's heading every frame, with no acceleration or damping, so it turns only while held.
when: ship rotation controlled by a held button
why: Fixed per-frame increments make turning direct and precise, with rotation stopping immediately on release.

text: A stiffer, longer spring makes the stick need more force to move, giving players physical resistance that helps them sense positions between fully pressed and fully released.
when: analog stick input with spring return
why: Resistance gives proprioceptive feedback for fine control.

text: Small differences in input, such as a slightly different angle, can produce noticeably different outcomes, which adds expressiveness.
The first measurable property of a device is its number of separate inputs; a modern gamepad may have around fifteen.
An ideal motion controller tracks absolute position and rotation in three dimensions and can reduce to two or one dimension when needed.
when: when designing motion input hardware
why: Relative sensing limits how precisely a gesture maps to a position.

text: From the exact centre of the screen, the avatar can move about one-sixth of the total screen width before the camera begins panning.
when: Horizontal dead zone is one-third of screen width, centred
why: Half of the one-third zone lies on each side of centre, giving one-sixth of screen distance of free movement.

text: Controller rumble can be extended along three adjustable dimensions: rapidity of shake, motion type, and softness, combining into many distinct sensations.
when: If the varied rumble hardware is affordable and sturdy enough for mass production
why: Current rotating-weight rumble is essentially on or off at a set rhythm, so it offers little expressive range.

text: Input devices can be measured at three levels: micro (individual inputs), macro (whole device, layout and implied actions), and tactile (how construction affects feel).
why: Lets game feel be compared across devices.

text: Continuous inputs can be classed by motion type (linear or rotational), sensitivity type (position or force), dimensions of motion, direct or indirect input, and boundaries on motion.
The analog thumbstick is the only continuous input, sending two float values on X and Z axes, each from -1 to 1 by displacement from center.
when: Reading analog stick input
why: Buttons send only binary signals, while the thumbstick streams a value that changes with how far it is displaced from center.

text: Directional pads often cannot register opposite directions together, unlike keyboard keys, so games feel different; a direction may combine with A or B and one other direction, not its opposite.
Tiny screens or complex fine motor control frustrate players aged 50 and older, because eyes and hands decline with age.
when: Designing interfaces for older players
why: Declining vision and dexterity make small targets and intricate inputs hard to use

text: Promising a broad set of actions that responds to few inputs frustrates players, since each supported action implies many rejected ones.
why: Players expect the stated freedom and feel cheated when most inputs fail.

text: A two-state button conveys very little on its own, so nuance must come from how the game responds to each press.
Tight, multi-input timing windows can be demanding enough to strain players' hands.
High input sensitivity paired with few response animations makes precise gestures earn nothing and play feel like imprecise flailing.
when: when mapping fine motion to actions
why: Motion precision is discarded when only a few prerecorded animations are triggered, so the player's intent is obscured.

text: Some motions suit an input device better than others, so ignoring a device's constraints distorts the perceived feel of the controls.
why: Player intent is filtered through the device's affordances and constraints before the system interprets it.

text: Guiding an avatar indirectly through a pointer or stylus lacks real-time control, even when every stroke responds instantly.
when: When the player steers an avatar by drawing lines it follows on a touch screen.
why: The player corrects the line while drawing it, so the avatar's path is fixed in advance rather than steered live.

text: A stick that feels loose at rest and gritty in travel undermines confidence in precise input.
when: When precise partial stick deflection matters, such as sneaking past sleeping enemies.
why: Firmer spring resistance gives the hand feedback, letting players judge partial deflection more accurately.

text: 1) For digital games, identify the input and output devices, such as a keyboard and mouse or a proprietary controller. 2) Design procedures that suit those devices before finalizing them.
when: when designing digital game procedures
why: Device limits such as keyboard versus controller and screen distance constrain which procedures players can actually use.

text: Count a part as an input only if it can physically move and send a signal to the computer.
why: Each input's motion produces a signal the computer can interpret and answer through output devices.

text: Let players hold a button to sustain an action, such as sprinting or galloping, instead of requiring repeated presses.
when: Designing continuous actions.
why: Holding a button reduces repeated physical input.

text: In fast-paced games, make frequent actions such as grenades, weapon swaps and equipping take as few inputs as possible.
when: Designing actions performed often during combat.
why: Each extra input on a frequent action adds up to significant physical and attention load.

text: Bind steering and throttle to separate keys, each mapped to its own input axis, rather than one combined control.
when: When controlling a vehicle whose movement is relative to its own facing direction.

text: Identify unintended input ambiguities, especially simultaneous or near-simultaneous combinations, and resolve them so that input feels consistent.
when: When simultaneous or near-simultaneous presses trigger different actions.
why: The game orders inputs by milliseconds, an order players cannot perceive, so outcomes look random.

text: A force-feedback device should be holdable like a controller while still pushing back, rather than using a thick grip that feels unnatural.
when: When a force-feedback device is aimed at the general game-playing public, not enthusiasts.
why: Thick or awkward grips weaken the illusion of touching something.

text: Describe the controls tools and their function, flagging any unusual input device that needs special programming.
when: When the game plans to support an unusual input device needing specialized programming.

text: Add sensitivity between input and response so that subtle, nuanced control becomes possible.
when: If the game seems to lack depth.

text: Command-bound buttons let players remap controls by swapping commands, while hardwired input checks are simpler and fine when mappings never change.
when: When players must be able to remap their button controls.
why: Actions stored as swappable objects can be reassigned to different buttons, unlike direct hard-wired calls.

text: A trigger is more graded than a button but far less sensitive than a thumbstick or mouse, so it suits coarse analogue control over precise positioning.
A few-button pad limits wrong presses and keeps each thumb's task small, while a keyboard allows opposite directions and multi-finger input, changing control feel.
when: When a game is controlled by keyboard instead of a few-button pad.

text: Under stress, players fumble controls and miss crucial information when the interface is hard to use.
when: when the interface is hard to use under pressure

text: The interface is the narrow boundary where player and game world meet; its job is giving players a sense of command over their experience.
why: Failure of the interface loses the experience of interacting with the game

text: An interface mode is a change in one of the six input-output mappings, so the same input produces a different effect.
Top-down interface design starts from a successful genre interface and adapts it to the game's unique features, saving design time and feeling familiar.
HSB describes a color by hue, saturation (purity), and brightness (how much black or white it contains).
Event designs of this kind mirror the mouse, window, and key press messages used by many windowing toolkits.
Many states multiplied by per-button actions and chorded inputs can map dozens of moves onto each button.
Use a color gradient when the size of a deviation matters, not just whether a value is above or below a target, so larger deviations show deeper colors.
when: Highlighting how far values sit from an expected curve.
why: A gradient shows magnitude, which a binary highlight cannot.

text: Group related interface features together, such as several health meters or all combat controls, so players know where to look.
when: laying out a game interface
why: Players scan for related information in a predictable place.

text: Combine an automated chat filter with a way for players to report rude behavior; this combination works best.
why: Human players detect abuse patterns better than any automated filter can.

text: Pressing inputs together can yield a response that neither produces alone, letting a few buttons map to many actions.
when: When the game reads sequences of inputs over time, as in fighting-game moves.
why: Pattern recognition adds a processing layer between input and response, enlarging the input space.

text: Holding a modifier button to change what the directional pad does creates a chorded input that adds actions without new buttons.
When modes look identical and give no feedback, players cannot tell what their inputs will do and trigger wrong commands.
when: Modes share visuals and the game gives no indication of the current mode.
why: Keys that act differently per mode give no hint about the current mode, so players cannot predict results.

text: Changing a working convention without good reason adds learning cost for players with no payoff.
why: Unique conventions take extra effort to understand, so players pay a cost that must be justified.

text: Copying a successful game's interface and controls while only changing the theme produces a clone with little originality.
1) Draw the interface as a flowchart with rough sketches. 2) Test the screen flow in a lightweight prototype. 3) Implement only after the flow works.
why: Problems found in a lightweight prototype save implementation time later.

text: 1) Group players into rating ranges or percentiles. 2) Assign each group a tier label for low-granularity display.
when: When a low-granularity rank is needed instead of a full ordering of players.

text: 1) Identify what is special about the core concept. 2) List the properties of the core conflict and its elements. 3) Assign properties to elements and let them interact. 4) Let the interface evolve from these needs rather than designing it first.
when: developing an original game's controls and interface
why: The interface then expresses the game's tension instead of generic conventions.

text: Design the interface so players stop noticing it; good input leaves players attending only to the game, not the controls. An interface that buries the game communicates nothing.
when: Designing UI and HUD.
why: Visible interface draws attention away from the game events it should convey.

text: Keep interface design uniform within a title and across a series, use plain vocabulary, and block errors that don't stem from the gameplay itself.
when: Designing interface language and layout.
why: Uniform wording and layout lower confusion and slip-ups.

text: Place waypoints on the map and show them on the radar to reduce the need to remember routes.
when: Designing navigation aids for objectives.
why: Waypoints offload route memory to the interface.

text: Design the interface to be robust, powerful and as invisible as possible; treat looks and smooth motion as welcome but secondary to feeling in control.
why: Player control, not aesthetics, is the core function of the interface

text: Check that the interface does what players expect when they use it, and if it does not, find out why.
why: Meaningful control is essential for immersive interactivity.

text: Theme interface artwork to match the rest of the game and review it for visual consistency, even when a different artist creates it.
Keep each interface element in the same place across screens and areas, and do not move features when the screen changes.
when: designing multi-screen interfaces
why: Moved controls cause frustration and confusion.

text: Provide a wireframe for every interface artists must build, describe each feature's function, and detail every interface state.
when: When documenting the controls and interfaces that artists must build.
why: Artists need a functional view of each interface's features to build it.

text: Design text syntax as user interface: a grammar easy for a parser is easy to write, but one suited to users is hard to design.
when: When the game defines a text-based language for players to write.
why: Parser-friendly grammars are easy to define, but user-friendly ones are hard, and text limits the interface.

text: Encode weapon category in preview shape: long thin parallel lines for long range, a short wide cone for short range, and a circle for area effect.
when: Designing weapon or ability previews that share one visual style.
why: A shared visual treatment with shape-coded categories lets players identify the category at a glance.

text: In conception, use UX to develop personas and help the core team explain its plan to stakeholders.
when: Conception phase
why: Explaining the core pillars of a deeply systemic game to stakeholders can be tricky.

text: Platform-native UI frameworks are often tied to one operating system, while cross-platform toolkits can feel foreign on every platform.
when: When choosing which UI framework to build an interface with.
why: Many native frameworks are tied to one OS, which limits portability.

text: Hatching uses parallel lines where closer lines give darker tones; crosshatching adds a second crossed set for still darker tones.
when: shading sketches

text: Gestalt principles describe how the mind organizes visual input, including figure/ground, multistability, closure, symmetry and similarity.

The mind stores far more detail about heads and faces than other body parts because they carry most emotional information, so exaggerated heads are accepted while small heads with large feet look absurd.
why: Faces are the main source of emotional information.

text: Board game procedures appear in the rule sheet, while digital game procedures usually appear in the manual's controls section because players access them through controls.
Unlike true axonometric views, this perspective camera makes changes in height easy to perceive.
Apply Gestalt grouping laws such as proximity to organize UI elements and icons, and avoid ambiguous iconography (multistability) unless the ambiguity is part of the challenge.
when: Organizing interface elements and icons.
why: Ambiguous icons confuse players unless ambiguity is intended.

text: Players group elements that share color or shape, and group matched symmetric pairs such as brackets, so use these cues to organize UI.
when: Organizing UI and map icons
why: The mind groups similar and symmetric elements automatically.

text: Use Gestalt principles, affordances, and iconography to shape how inputs are read, applying each where it fits the situation.
why: Perception is biased by prior knowledge, context and expectations, so people read the same input differently.

text: Apply the Hick-Hyman law to reduce interface complexity, since decision time grows with the number of options.
when: Designing menus and choices.
why: Decision reaction time grows logarithmically with the number of displayed options.

text: Elements placed closer together are perceived as one group, and added empty space separates them into distinct groups.
when: Laying out menus or interface elements
why: Proximity is a strong grouping cue that can replace lines or arrows.

text: Interface patterns such as hamburger menus and swipe gestures become user expectations once smartphones and apps popularize them.
why: Repeated exposure turns a pattern into a learned expectation.

text: Placing skill nodes so that vertical proximity suggests a different unlock direction than the actual rule adds friction; spacing and shape changes can correct it without extra space.
when: Designing skill trees or progression menus
why: Proximity cues override small arrows, which players may not notice.

text: 1) List every problem users have with the existing way of doing a task, including unstated ones. 2) Design a new solution for that list rather than only refining the existing tool.
when: When an existing tool or way of doing a task is being redesigned.

text: 1) Take a screenshot of an existing game screen. 2) Use a painting program to find the pixel ranges of each element. 3) Rebuild the layout in grid cells using color, text and borders.
when: When recreating an existing game screen layout as a study exercise.

text: Keep options and information visible in the UI instead of requiring players to remember them, e.g. breadcrumb trails or a controller image highlighting the required button.
when: Whenever players would otherwise have to remember information.
why: Working memory is small and easily overwhelmed.

text: In nondigital games, make procedures easy for players to remember.
when: when players have no digital reminders
why: Players cannot rely on software to recall procedures.

text: Use the thickest lines on outer edges that touch no other object, and very light lines where objects meet.
when: inking sketches to communicate spatial distance
why: Line weight conveys which edges are in front and which sit against other forms.

text: Pair pop-up text with voice, animation or in-world presentation carrying the same information when the information is complex.
when: the taught information is complex
why: Learners process information through several channels, and information taught effectively moves into long-term memory.

text: Players want many options while designers want a simple interface, so the two must be balanced rather than maximized.
why: The two desires conflict, so both cannot be maximized at once.

text: Input latency between a player's action and in-game feedback is a major contributor to cybersickness, so performance problems raise the risk.
Immersion can overwhelm an already limited attention system, making attention management harder than in traditional games.
when: When the player fully controls the camera, as with head-tracked VR.
why: Because the designer does not control the camera, players may miss cues they do not look at.

text: Ignoring hardware limits such as controller type or viewing distance makes procedures harder for players to access.
when: When the input devices or viewing distance of the play setting are fixed.
why: Procedures are shaped by physical constraints, so they must stay intuitive and easy to remember.

text: A button that switches a thumbstick from moving an avatar to aiming a tool changes the mapping from physical input to the game world.
Organize modes as one main mode with several submodes.
when: When a game has several distinct modes to organize.
why: Too many modes confuse players, while one main mode with submodes keeps a clear hierarchy.

text: A button can switch to a secondary display area with its own dashboard, moving rarely needed information out of the main view.
when: when the main view must stay uncluttered

text: 1) Decide which modes the game needs and why. 2) Collapse or combine modes where possible. 3) Give overlapping modes different input channels. 4) Communicate each mode change in more than one way.
when: when reviewing an interface with modes
why: The questions exist to keep players from getting confused or overwhelmed by the interface's modes.

text: Make each mode visibly distinct so players can identify their current mode at any moment, especially after dramatic mode changes.
why: Players cannot act correctly in a mode they cannot identify.

text: Distinguish modes by changing a large visible on-screen element, the avatar's action, on-screen data, or the camera perspective.
why: Modes that look identical are impossible to tell apart, so even experienced users get confused.

text: Packing several facts into one channel is efficient and elegant, but players must learn what each dimension means, and some will struggle to remember it.
Free-to-play players who have invested no money may quit within minutes or seconds over small frustrations, and confusing purchase flows can reduce revenue.
when: Free-to-play games
why: Players have no sunk investment holding them in the session.

text: Intuitive displays of odds let players judge fairness and make decisions without statistical training.
Showing only a rank, not the total player count, keeps the population size private.
when: When the developer wants exact player counts kept secret.
why: Ordinal rank reveals a position without disclosing the size of the whole population.
