text: A hidden rule that repeatedly punishes players, such as an undisclosed damage trigger, can become a major cause of quitting.
why: Players who did not understand the trigger kept dying and were the most likely to churn.

text: Making the unwanted option large and prominent while the real path is small and text-like leads users into paid subscriptions they did not intend.
when: checkout and sign-up flows
why: attention goes to the prominent button

text: Social mechanics whose events combine in many ways are hard to show: text cannot cover every case, and arbitrary symbols must be learned by rote.
when: designing social or multi-factor mechanics for a camera view
why: events combine too many ways to script, and symbols rarely make intuitive sense

text: 1) Identify the tiles adjacent to a candidate site. 2) Add their dot counts. 3) Compare the totals across candidate sites to judge which is likely to produce most.
when: comparing placement options using printed odds
why: Dot counts equal expected rolls out of 36, so summing adjacent dots gives relative expected yield.

text: A mouse reports displacement on two axes each frame, not absolute position; lifting and replacing it leaves the cursor where it was.
A mouse has no spring return and no physical boundary; its effective limits are the desk surface, rarely reached, and software-enforced screen edges.
In PC mouse games the left button is the main button, and the right button should do nothing unless the game is in a special mode.
Poor snapping forces filler to cover gaps, causes hidden overlaps, and leaves slivers that let players walk through walls into the void.
when: editor snapping is weak
why: Hard-to-align pieces leave gaps that go unnoticed, and a slight gap can let players slip through geometry.

text: Players who misread a targeting input may conclude the game is broken and warn others away, so target-based actions need clear cues.
when: attacks require clicking a specific target
why: a misreading can spread to other players

text: Small targets and deeply nested submenus need more correction cycles to hit, slowing how fast users acquire them.
why: Each correction cycle takes roughly 240 ms, and precision improves across cycles depending on distance and target size.

text: Use relative pointer input when precise pointing across a large space matters.
A cell address combines a column letter, lettered across the top, with a row number, numbered down the side.
The fill handle is the small square at a selected cell's bottom-right corner. Dragging it continues the pattern of the selected cells.
Some spreadsheet formula bars have X (cancel), check mark (commit without moving cursor) and fx (functions) buttons; some web-based programs omit the X and check mark.
While typing, the entry shows up in the cell and also in the formula bar above the grid.
Arrow keys move the cursor one cell at a time, clicking jumps to a cell, Tab moves right, and Shift+Tab moves left.
Deleting a column shifts all content to its right one column to the left.
The Edit menu can also delete the row or column where the cursor currently sits.
Row and column insertion always affects the entire row or column, never only part of one.
Some spreadsheet programs have a simpler Insert Row or Insert Column command that inserts at the selected position and pushes other content down or right.

Selection methods: Shift with arrow keys or click-drag selects a rectangle; Shift+click selects non-adjacent cells; heading clicks select rows or columns; corner click or Ctrl+A selects the whole sheet.
With cells selected, Ctrl+C copies, Ctrl+X cuts, and Ctrl+V pastes; the same commands appear in the Edit and right-click menus.
Shift+clicking an already selected cell removes it from the selection.
when: a cell was selected by mistake

text: Ctrl+B bolds, Ctrl+I italicizes, Ctrl+U underlines, and Alt+Shift+5 strikes through the selected cells' content.
Formatting applied to selected cells affects every selected cell and the entire contents of each.
Cell background colors are cosmetic and have no effect on how formulas calculate.
Shift with an arrow key extends the selection one cell at a time, which is useful for copying, pasting or deleting.
The midpoint of a three-color scale can be any value chosen to match the curve, not necessarily the mean or median of the column.
when: Setting up a three-color scale for deviations from a target.

text: Holding Alt while pressing Enter inserts a paragraph break inside a cell in Excel.
Cell formatting covers number format, font and size, text styles, text and background colors, alignment and wrapping, and borders.
On large sheets, the row and column headings of the active cell are highlighted, which helps you locate your position quickly.
when: working on a large sheet
why: Highlighted headings let the user locate their position quickly on large sheets.

text: Practice moving between cells and entering text before attempting formulas or complex operations, especially if you are new to spreadsheets.
when: new to spreadsheets or returning after a break
why: basic navigation underpins later skills

text: To insert many rows at once, select as many row headings as you need first, then insert; the number inserted equals the number selected.
when: adding a large number of rows
why: inserting one at a time is tedious

text: Shade entire rows or columns to cluster related categories: for instance, use one tint for expenses and restrictions, another for advantages and strengths.
when: A sheet holds several categories of related entries.
why: Grouping by color makes categories visible without restructuring the data.

text: Data validation can also check a calculated field that must stay in a known range, such as a probability between 0 and 1.
when: When troubleshooting and a calculation is known to fall within a given range.

text: Large cells holding documentation or rules text are best read with word wrap and wider columns.
when: cells containing long documentation or rules text
why: Word wrap grows the row height so the full text stays visible.

text: Ctrl with an arrow key from a blank cell jumps to the next non-blank cell in that direction, or to the sheet edge if no data remains.
when: Navigating long sheets with gaps between data.
why: Stepping through thousands of cells one press at a time is slow, so jumping saves effort.

text: Ctrl with an arrow key from a non-empty cell moves to the last non-empty cell in that direction, reaching the edge of the current data block.
when: Locating the boundary of a contiguous block of data.
why: Blank gaps between data stop the jump early, making navigation less efficient.

text: A graphical script editor can disable invalid options or supply defaults so that programs stay valid at all times.
when: Authoring scripts through a visual interface
why: Constraining input at the interface makes invalid programs impossible to create.

text: Restricting the view through a physical scope makes the display a deliberate boundary that controls what the player perceives.
why: The scope lets the designer control exactly where the visible area cuts off.

text: A 1,600 by 1,200 screen offers roughly 1.9 million cursor positions, though small targets cannot be reliably hit.
why: Mouse sensitivity resolves far more positions than a person can accurately point at.

text: Clicking another cell while still editing inserts that cell into your entry as a reference; press the cancel button to undo it.
when: editing a cell and clicking elsewhere
why: While a cell is being edited, a click inserts that cell's reference into the entry instead of simply moving the selection.

text: Committing an entry overwrites whatever content the cell previously held.
Blank spacer rows or columns added for visual spacing break Ctrl-arrow jumps and slow navigation on long sheets.
when: Laying out data on large sheets.
why: Blank cells stop the jumps, unlike whitespace in a text document.

text: Retyping the same formula many times risks one mistyped copy, which can throw off every value below it.
when: Building long columns by hand.
why: A single mistyped copy propagates into every value calculated below it.

text: Very long wrapped text can make a row taller than the screen, and widening the column usually reduces that height.
when: Wrapped cell holding a very long text string
why: Word Wrap makes the row grow to fit all the text, and more column width gives the text more horizontal room.

text: Unsorted x values produce a tangled line, since the chart connects points in the order they appear; sort by the x values or force ordering with the aggregate option.
when: Building a line graph from unordered data
why: Connecting points in input order scrambles the line.

text: A parser that only knows it hit unexpected punctuation gives poor feedback to the user.
when: When the user interface is a typed string of characters, as in a text-based language.

text: 1) Insert a top row and merge cells to group categories. 2) Color-code each group. 3) Put object names in column A and freeze column A and the header rows. 4) Format numeric columns as integers, fractions, decimals or percentages. 5) Apply tiers or a gradient to the balance column. 6) Sort by the balance column without sorting header rows.
when: Building a cost/power spreadsheet for game balance.
why: Grouping and highlighting make off-curve objects easy to spot.

text: 1) Select a cell. 2) Type its content. 3) Press Enter or Tab to commit; Tab also moves the cursor one cell to the right.
1) Select the row. 2) Right-click its row heading. 3) Choose delete, which sits just below insert. Rows beneath it shift upward.
when: When a row should be removed and the rows beneath it should move up.
why: Clearing contents with Delete does not move other cells, so shifting needs the row-delete action.

text: 1) Right-click a row heading. 2) Choose to insert a row above or below it. Column insertion works the same way from column headings, and the Insert menu offers the same actions.
when: When a list is missing an entry in the middle.
why: Avoids retyping the entries that follow the missing one.

text: 1) Double-click the cell to edit its text. 2) Select the words to change. 3) Apply the formatting to that selection.
when: only part of a cell's text should be emphasized
why: Formatting applied to a cell changes all of its text, so mixed styling requires editing the text itself.

text: 1) Place the cursor in one corner of the block. 2) Press Shift and Ctrl with the arrow keys to extend the selection to the opposite corner.
when: Selecting a large rectangular block quickly.
why: Keyboard extension is faster than dragging across thousands of rows.

text: 1) Type the starting number in a cell. 2) In the cell below, enter a formula adding 1 to the cell above. 3) Fill Down from there to build the sequence.
when: Filling a column with consecutive numbers such as 1 to 20.
why: A formula avoids typing each value and reduces mistypes.

text: 1) Copy a formula cell. 2) Select the blank cells below it. 3) Paste. Each pasted cell updates its references as Fill Down does.
when: Filling a column with a formula without using the fill handle.

text: 1) In the conditional formatting panel, choose a color scale. 2) Pick two or three colors. 3) Set each anchor as a fixed number, the range minimum or maximum, or a percentile.
when: Shading cells by their value across a range.
why: A fixed number can serve as a meaningful midpoint, such as 0, even when it is not the average of the column.

text: 1) Select the cells. 2) Open Data > Data Validation, or right-click the cell and choose it. 3) Set the criterion, such as a number range or a list. 4) Choose a warning or outright rejection for invalid entries. 5) Save.
1) Choose the list criterion. 2) Enter comma-separated items, or point to a range of cells in the sheet. 3) Check the in-cell dropdown option so the cell shows an arrow.
when: Input cells with only a few options to choose from.
why: Restricts the user to the listed choices so they cannot type a wrong value.

text: 1) Merge the cells that will hold the word. 2) Turn on word wrap. 3) Insert a line break after each letter so the word stacks vertically.
To show all text in a cell, widen its column, merge it with neighboring cells, or turn on word wrap so the row grows tall enough.
when: a cell's text is cut off by a neighboring value
why: The text stays in the cell even when cut off, so the fix is a display change.

text: Format computed cells distinctly from tunable inputs and treat computed cells as read-only; use one such color scheme across all sheets.
when: Designing spreadsheets that others or future you will tune.
why: A consistent scheme shows at a glance which cells to change; treating computed cells as read-only prevents accidental modification.

text: Use right-side borders between adjacent columns and thick outlines to isolate blocks; the border tool outlines selections or draws a divider along one side of a row or column.
when: When cells need grouping or separation without being merged, like several charts on one sheet.
why: Borders set regions apart visually while leaving each cell unmerged.

text: Insert whole rows or columns only when the entire line must move; to move part of a row, select those cells and use copy and paste.
when: only some cells in a row need to move
why: Insert Row adds a full row, so moving only some cells needs copy and paste.

text: Format whole cells when all their text should look the same; edit the cell's text when only part of it should be emphasized.
Use the fill handle for quick simple lists, and use formulas when the sequence follows a rule the fill handle cannot infer.
when: Choosing how to generate a list of values.
why: The fill handle can misread complicated patterns.

text: Use borders instead of merged cells to separate regions of a sheet, since borders keep each cell distinct and its structure intact.
when: Several tables or regions share one worksheet and must look distinct.
why: Merging can break formulas and sorting that depend on individual cells.

text: Shade formula cells in pale grey and use charcoal lettering to signal they should not be edited.
when: For calculation fields that viewers should not change.
why: Matches the grayed-out look of unselectable menu options, signaling the field is not to be changed.

text: Style input cells with bright yellow or a thick border so they stand out as fields meant to be edited.
when: For fields the viewer is expected to edit in a sheet.
why: Distinct color or border makes editable fields stand out from calculation fields.

text: Divide a sheet into functional sections with shading and borders, using shades of one color for related groups.
when: When a sheet has several functional sections, such as cost and benefit columns.
why: Shades of one color show groups are distinct yet related.

text: Apply data validation to input cells that have a few valid options or a reasonable range, to prevent typing mistakes.
when: Input cells with a few valid options or a range of acceptable numbers.

text: Fill every cell in a decorative area with a background color so the gridlines no longer show.
when: building a decorative spreadsheet layout

text: Clearing empties cells and leaves others in place; deleting removes cells and shifts remaining cells up or left to close the gap, changing other cells' positions.
when: choose clear for blank cells in place, delete to close the gap
why: Clearing only removes the contents of the selected cells, so no neighbouring cell gets repositioned.

text: A square grid pushes designers toward boxy, right-angled buildings because those are easiest to make; hard off-grid editing discourages interesting shapes.
when: choosing grid or free placement in an editor
why: Right-angled forms are the least effortful to construct on a grid, and awkward off-grid editing lowers the urge to try varied shapes.

text: A transparent interface gives players the right information at the right time without getting in the way, keeping their imagination inside the game world; it does not require removing the HUD.
An interface feels transparent when players read information effortlessly, and becomes noticeable only when it is hard to use.
when: When players can find and read the information they need without struggling
why: Attention goes to the player's goal, so an interface that supports it goes unnoticed until it gets in the way.

text: Players form expectations about what they can do from the interface without questioning it, because they expect interfaces to be transparent.
A compact top dashboard can carry seven kinds of information: counters, keys, health, distant surroundings, equipped weapon, equipped item, and consumables.
Stale observers of closed UI screens keep updating hidden elements and may trigger sounds, wasting CPU time and producing visibly wrong behavior.
when: A UI screen is closed without unregistering its observers.
why: Each reopening adds another live observer to the subject's list.

text: States that were never listed tend to ship without any signal, leaving players confused about what is happening.
when: Features with several states, such as locked, available, owned or overheating.
why: Without an enumerated state list, no team member is assigned to communicate it.

text: Assuming players will notice a new menu promotion or a newly unlocked HUD element.
why: Detecting a change requires attention, and people tend to overrate how well they notice changes.

text: Show which actions are possible through signifiers, and give fast feedback, such as a pressed button lighting up or a Play button showing that loading has started.
when: After a user interacts with the system and no error occurs
why: Without acknowledgment, users cannot tell whether their input registered and may repeat it out of uncertainty.

text: Test that players can do what they want, use the interface without thinking after practice, find it intuitive as newcomers, and stay immersed while using it.
why: An invisible interface lets players stay absorbed in the game world rather than in the controls.

text: Show status the player checks often in a form readable at a glance, using cues the player already knows.
when: displaying quantitative game state during play
why: Players process quantitative information quickly during play.

text: Use leftover space on a secondary screen to show instructions for using its contents.
when: when a secondary screen has unused room

text: Choose a text authoring language when users are programmers comfortable with text and command-line tools; non-technical users often find strict text off-putting.
why: Plain text that programmers find flexible reads to non-programmers as rigid and punishing.

text: On small screens and in gameplay-heavy games, plan for a finite space and fit short bits of story into it rather than building a full world.
when: small screens or gameplay-heavy games
why: Such games have a bounded space to fill, so the designer thinks of a finite area rather than an open world.

text: Text longer than its cell spills into blank cells to its right; once a neighboring cell holds data, the display is cut off but the full text remains stored.
when: When the cells to the right of a long text cell are empty
why: Overflow is only a display effect; the full content remains stored in the original cell.

text: Relying only on interface pop-ups reduces complex information to simple labels, so players are underserved on how the system actually works.
when: When pop-ups are used exclusively, not alongside other multimedia such as voice lines
why: Pairing pop-ups with sound or voice delivers the information to more senses, which works better.

text: If the engine forces timed pop-up text, require players to acknowledge it with a button press rather than letting it disappear automatically.
when: Displaying important timed pop-up text
why: Auto-dismissed text is easily missed.

text: Make subtitles legible and ideally on by default, since they help deaf players, players with sound off and non-native speakers.
when: Designing subtitle options.
why: Subtitles serve several player groups who cannot rely on audio.

text: Consider viewing distance and resolution: a screen seen up close and one seen several feet away support different procedures.
when: When players sit close to a high-resolution screen versus several feet from a low-resolution one
why: Procedures must suit the limits of the environment, such as input devices and display quality.

text: The virtual interface can be almost nonexistent or very dense with buttons, sliders, displays, and menus.
Skillful use of a touch interface can be a major factor in a mobile game's commercial success.
Exact combination counts are rarely useful; rough sensitivity gaps between devices, such as a six-button pad versus a mouse, suffice to guide design decisions.
when: choosing intended feel for a target device
why: Exact counts add effort without changing design choices.

text: Use Fitts's Law to judge how quickly users can reach controls and to compare how target size and distance affect pointing speed.
why: The model has been reproduced and verified in many studies, so its predictions are reliable.

text: Place interactive targets far enough apart that a small pointing error does not hit the wrong one, because close targets raise mis-click risk.
when: Designing button layouts.
why: Pointing error is common, so close targets are easily confused.

text: Virtual cursor speed does not match physical movement, so cursors need full-deflection speed boosts and sticky target areas.
when: Designing thumbstick or gamepad cursors and cursor-based menus in games.
why: Mismatch between hand motion and cursor motion makes precise targeting tiring.

text: World changes such as score or energy changes appear in the interface, and can trigger pop-ups or mode changes.
A target at a screen edge is easier to hit because the cursor stops at the edge, so the target effectively extends without limit in that direction.
when: When a cursor is used to aim at a button placed at a screen edge or corner
why: The cursor cannot overshoot the edge, so users need not slow down near it.

text: The virtual interface sits between physical input and output and the world, holding input elements such as menu choices and output elements such as score displays and floating numbers.
Very high pointing sensitivity is not fully usable: targets below a certain size cannot be reliably hit.
when: designing clickable targets
why: Precision limits the usable part of the input space.

text: Virtual elements add abstraction, which tends to weaken the emotional connection to content, so the virtual layer needs careful handling.
why: Each layer of abstraction between player and content dampens how strongly they feel about it.

text: Weak virtual interfaces turn into a barrier that separates players from the game world.

1) Identify information the player needs that is not obvious from the world. 2) Decide when it is needed: constantly, occasionally, or at certain points. 3) Deliver it without blocking world interaction. 4) Check whether some world elements are easier to act on through a virtual element.
why: Poorly designed interfaces wall off the world, while good ones amplify the player's control over it.

text: Consider how players hold the device and which thumb reaches which area: place frequent controls within easy thumb reach and rarely used controls, such as settings, in hard-to-reach corners.
when: Designing mobile control and menu layouts.
why: Grip and thumb reach determine ease of use; buttons far from the thumb take more time and effort to reach.

text: Place frequent or costly actions close to the expected cursor or thumb path, and use larger targets for them.
when: Designing menus, cursor-driven interfaces and touch layouts.
why: Distant or small targets add time and effort to every use.

text: Match the virtual interface style to the physical input device, since some styles, such as pop-up menus, suit a gamepad poorly.
Players who struggle with simple tasks may quit, and severe usability problems can make a game unplayable.
why: Struggling with basic tasks creates obstacles strong enough to push players away.

text: Usability covers how players perceive, understand and interact with a game, and how well they attain set targets, judged by effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction within a given context.
UX concerns usability, meaning ease of use, and pleasure of use, which is called emotional design.
Ctrl+Z undoes the last change, and Ctrl+Y redoes a change that was undone.
Human capabilities and limitations change slowly, so core UX principles stay constant even as products and technologies change.
Mixed initiative is often described as turn-taking, but speakers can interrupt or speak twice in a row.
Game-specific usability heuristics have been published since the early 1980s and proliferated in the 2000s, covering controls, goals, feedback, pacing and consistency.
Usability heuristics help teams interpret what user researchers report about a game.
when: when reading researcher reports
why: Heuristics name likely causes of friction, so teams can map what researchers observed onto specific design problems.

text: Solving problems users never state, including missing progress feedback, can turn a dull chore into an enjoyable activity.
why: Designs that fix problems users would never voice produce psychological appeal beyond practical benefits.

text: Keep subgames short enough that players can still recall their goal in the main game.
Usability error assessment covers how many errors occur, how severe they are, and how easily players recover from them.
A compelling game user experience needs two components: usability (ease of use) and engageability (ability to engage).
Usability has seven pillars: status cues and responses, legibility, form matching purpose, uniformity, minimum workload, error prevention and recovery, and flexibility and accessibility.
Usability has five components that can be assessed separately: learnability, efficiency, memorability, errors, and satisfaction.
Flow-based heuristics break the experience into eight groups: focus, difficulty level, skill capability, sense of control, explicit goals, responsive feedback, absorption, and social interaction.
when: Evaluating game flow in design
why: Researchers adapted flow-theory components to games.

text: Motivation often fails because goals and progress are unclear in the UI and game world, not because goals are missing.
when: Designing goal and progress display
why: Players cannot pursue goals they cannot read

text: Friction from poor usability rather than meaningful challenge makes a game frustrating, while pushing input toward maximum naturalness can erase the challenge that makes play rewarding.
when: When input is pushed toward natural gestures in place of simple controls.
why: Simple inputs with little bandwidth give players the joy of manipulating a complex system, which natural gestures can undercut.

text: Frustration caused by poor usability is often blamed on gameplay, and in the worst case it leads to rage-quitting.
Usability frustrations produce negative emotion and should be avoided.
why: Emotion shapes perception, cognition and behaviour, and can impair reasoning.

text: Once unintended friction is found, fix it without dumbing the game down, since left unfixed it becomes a dark pattern; intentional challenge should be kept.
when: When a design is unintentionally frustrating and the team leaves that friction unfixed.
why: Usability targets friction that ignores perception, cognition and motivation, not designed difficulty.

text: Let players undo actions and change their minds.
why: Players make mistakes and change their minds, as shoppers do when they edit a cart.

text: Usability design should account for human limits in memory, perception and attention, anticipate likely player errors, and match players' expectations and abilities.
why: Players are people, so their capabilities and limits decide whether the game is usable.

text: Implement stuns by impairing precision, perception, or control mapping, such as slowed turning, screen whiteout, or scrambled inputs, rather than removing the player's ability to act.
when: When a stun should hurt without freezing play.
why: The impaired player still decides and acts.

text: Designing for every skill level dilutes the core experience, while choosing a minimum skill level deliberately keeps it clear, though some overflow is then accepted.
why: Some players are so unskilled they cannot play at all, so a fixed minimum is unavoidable.

text: Usability testing, borrowed from software design, has realistic users attempt key tasks on the interface and controls, checking they understand core concepts; it returns interface knowledge, not play-experience knowledge.

Usability in games stands on seven principles: signposting and feedback, clarity, form that follows function, consistency, low effort for body and mind, mistake avoidance with recovery, and adaptability plus access.
Minimize cognitive load (attention, memory) and physical load (button presses) for non-core tasks; show information when needed and let common actions take few inputs.
when: especially during onboarding
why: Attention is scarce, so reducing load on non-core tasks frees attention for the challenge.

text: Males often prefer learning by experimenting over reading directions, so interfaces that reward experimentation suit them, linking to the pleasure of mastery.
why: Learning by experimenting connects with the satisfaction of gaining mastery.

text: Players cannot enjoy a game they cannot understand, so the wording of tutorials and manuals matters.
why: Videogames are complex, and players learn them through in-game tutorials, web pages and manuals, so that text decides how well they understand.

text: Observers that receive a state change often just update a UI element to match, repeating the same update pattern.
when: Observers feeding display elements.
why: Each display needs the same mirror-the-value code.

text: A usability test has players play parts of a game to check usability and engageability, usually with about six participants playing at the same time.
A pipeline overview lists the do's and don'ts artists must follow for their assets to display correctly in the game.
UX researchers help a team decide by analyzing player experience, not by offering subjective opinions or designing the game in the team's place.
A UX framework's main purpose is communication and collaboration between team members, respecting the capabilities and limits of both player and designer brains.
Fitts's Law was first formulated for arm reach, later shown to apply to moving a mouse cursor to on-screen objects, and is a well-studied HCI model verified across many studies.
Nielsen's ten usability heuristics are rules of thumb that help evaluators spot friction, anticipate common problems and fix them faster, not design standards or replacements for detailed guidance.
Professional usability labs record controls, facial reactions and spoken thoughts; HCI usability methods are well established in software, and the games industry has adopted them more slowly.
Usability testing focuses on interface and controls, while playtesting focuses on core gameplay; the two are separate activities.
Many studios hire third-party usability firms for a series of late tests, while some publishers run in-house usability labs integrated from start to finish.
Usability sessions produce data from video, audio, task success or failure, and questionnaires, which specialists analyze before recommending changes.

Game usability is organised into seven high-level pillars that give a studio a shared vocabulary for improving player experience; usability means intuitive, effective, efficient and satisfying play for the target audience.
Card sorting is a common method for designing website category structures.
Early testing of a mixed-initiative rule-building system showed it was far from easy to use.
Design can be treated as a reflective conversation between designer and medium, in which computer support can join as a participant.
Test usability early, since it is mostly tested in early development; test engageability once critical systems exist, since it is harder to measure.
when: Early development stages, before critical systems are implemented

text: Test the interface in all situations, including high speed and tight corners, since it may confuse players in some cases.
When players are confused, identify which of the six input-output mappings the confusion occurs on to locate the problem.
when: When something about the interface confuses players during testing

text: When users repeatedly err, check the design for inconsistency before blaming the user.
when: when users keep making the same mistake
why: Errors often come from inconsistent design rather than user failure.

text: Learn how players navigate the interface and struggle with controls, since this observation improves your design judgment.
Start to Crate (StC) measures seconds from game start until the first crate appears; across 26 games, only five took over 10 seconds and ten showed one at zero seconds.
why: Quantifies how quickly games fall back on cheap fiction shortcuts.

text: Usability observation draws on three sources: playthrough playtests, expert usability evaluations by HCI specialists, and broader general user research.
why: Players often cannot pinpoint what causes a usability problem, so their observed behaviour is more reliable than their complaints.

text: Bringing in a usability expert does not make a game more fun by itself.
when: When stakeholders expect usability work alone to make the game enjoyable
why: Usability testing only checks whether the interface and systems are intuitive, while enjoyment depends on other kinds of testing.

text: Some designers wrongly treat usability testing as focus testing or marketing, which hides its real purpose.
Judging the clarity of your own game by your own impression misses how newcomers will actually read its icons and interface.
why: Perception biases depend on what an audience already knows, so the designer's own reading of icons is not representative.

text: Improving business metrics at users' expense is not the purpose of UX.
why: Satisfying experiences lead to popularity and revenue as a side effect, so satisfaction is the target rather than metrics.

text: 1) Run usability tests. 2) Record common errors. 3) Treat repeated errors as a sign that the design encourages them and revise it.
when: Evaluating a playable build.
why: Repeated player errors indicate design problems rather than player fault.

text: 1) Observe players for errors. 2) Check what players understand about the game and its objectives, using established human factors principles.
when: Assessing usability
why: Ease of use can be checked against established human factors principles and observed errors, making its quality fairly predictable.

text: 1) Record the participant's hands on controls and facial reactions with separate cameras. 2) Have the participant think aloud over the game audio. 3) Run a detailed test script while observers watch behind one-way glass. 4) Have participants complete tasks. 5) Record task success and rate each finding's severity in a report.
when: Testing a game's usability with professional methods
why: Combined recordings reveal both behavior and reasoning

text: Testing an interrupting tutorial: 1) Observe player reactions to tutorial interruptions. 2) After play, ask how the player felt about the interruptions.
when: evaluating a tutorial that pauses play
why: reactions reveal whether interruptions help or annoy

text: 1) Write each item on a paper card. 2) Have players group the cards into categories. 3) Review the groups to reveal players' intuitive structure before building the feature.
when: before implementation, when organizing categories
why: matches the team's organization to players' thinking

text: 1) Build a rapid paper or interactive prototype. 2) Test it internally, or with the target audience when possible.
when: Pre-production
why: Prototypes let the team evaluate early ideas and explain systemic designs to stakeholders who lack design expertise.

text: 1) Run task analyses as features arrive. 2) Run short usability tests in gray box and gym levels. 3) Tune game feel and the 3Cs from results.
when: Feature implementation

text: 1) Watch or take part in a third-party usability test session. 2) Note the tasks subjects were asked to complete. 3) Record whether each task succeeded and identify why or why not. 4) Consider how the findings help the software's designer.
when: When a third-party usability lab permits observation or participation
why: Sessions teach designers how to break down play, navigation, and control problems, improving their craft.

text: Test iconography and HUD configuration early, for example with surveys, to confirm players perceive what the designer intended.
when: While features are being implemented, in parallel with task analyses and short usability tests
why: form follows function

text: Test with real people who are not industry professionals, not only experts, to produce a game almost anyone can pick up.
when: aiming for accessibility to new players
why: Industry testers do not represent the broad audience.

text: Test interfaces with real people as early and as often as possible, since no interface is clear, empowering, and fun on the first try.
why: New games need new interfaces that cannot be assumed to work.

text: Make controls customisable with industry-standard defaults, give immediate feedback, and apply pacing pressure without frustrating the player.
when: Evaluating game usability.
why: These are established usability heuristics for games.

text: Praise small achievements with specific feedback that informs skill, such as 'Perfect move!' rather than 'well done!'.
when: for small achievements
why: Specific praise tells players what they did well.

text: Remove points of confusion so that the game is easier to learn and more intuitive.
when: During the first-time user experience, when players decide whether to keep playing
why: Understanding how learning works reveals where players get stuck.

text: Do not use AI as a replacement for usability testing with real users, including users with disabilities.
why: AI cannot reveal how real and diverse users actually experience a design.

text: Integrate explicit questioning into play so it does not pause the session or break immersion.
when: When collecting explicit player feedback during a gameplay session
why: Explicit responses give a more reliable estimate of player experience than noisy implicit data.

text: Check five qualities in research: usability, pleasure, accessibility, inclusion and safety; when one fails, find its cause and fix it efficiently.
when: When an experience is found not to be usable, pleasurable, accessible, inclusive, or safe
why: Knowing the cause of a problem, not just its existence, is what allows an efficient fix.

text: The main goal of user experience design is to make the player's mental model match the developers' intended model.
why: Players bring prior knowledge and expectations and form their own model by interacting with the part of the system they perceive, which can diverge from the design.

text: Anyone on a team can hold a UX mindset, and UX is everyone's concern in a team and company, while UX practitioners supply the tools and process.

Four design groups: dark pattern (deceives for company gain), nudge, bad UX (confuses without intent), good UX (respects users, serves business). Grouping depends on intent and consequences, not design alone.
why: Intent decides the group: unintended friction is bad UX, but if left unfixed it turns into a dark pattern.

text: UX, introduced in the 1990s, covers the whole journey, from first hearing of it: discovering it, forming expectations, buying or installing, using it, and getting customer support or community help.
why: HCI focuses on usability and not the full journey (discovery, purchase, support), so UX was introduced to cover all of it.

text: Judge the product from the target audience's perspective, not the makers', aiming for the best experience across the whole journey.
why: Makers' view of their own product is subjective and necessarily biased, so the audience's viewpoint is needed.

text: UX practitioners rely heavily on cognitive science and the scientific method to anticipate issues developers did not intend, rather than offering opinions.
User research uses qualitative data from small observed lab sessions; its strength is showing why behavior happens, such as players failing because a required item is hard to find.
The UX manager's main goal is to support production and help the team reach business goals with the right tools, at the right time, for the right people.
UX is a mindset that serves both player experience and business results by reducing friction and reaching a broader audience.
User researchers study the product with a small, representative sample of the target audience, during development and after launch.
User experience is not a fixed property of a product; it is relative to end users, so teams must verify what those users actually experience.
UX broadly means how it feels to interact with software and how engaging that interaction is.
The goal of UX is to improve people's lives with technology, including games.
Efficiency is how fast players perform tasks once they already know the product.
UX design draws on human factors and ergonomics, improving products and services through repeated scientific iteration on how people experience them.
Bad UX is unintended friction in a product.
UX is a philosophy rather than a discipline: shifting from an ego-centered to a player-centered view using empathy, generosity, and a scientific approach.

Initiative has three components: task initiative (choosing topic and problem), speaker initiative (deciding when each party speaks), and outcome initiative (deciding how to solve the problem and who does which task).
UX designers shape interactions and information architecture, such as how a purchase flow works and where information appears.
UX tests estimate attention from three sources: eye tracking, behavioral data such as speed and success, and survey answers.
UX practitioners work with developers to define the intended experience, with marketing and consumer insights to understand users, and with publishing to understand business goals.
Built from over ten years of collective practice across organizations; its visual form clarifies benefits and barriers at each level.
UX return on investment can be estimated, but it is not easy to calculate.
Usability specialist duties include heuristic evaluation of interfaces, writing user scenarios, recruiting target-market subjects, conducting sessions, and reporting findings with recommendations.
Some companies provide visual tools that let designers assemble scripts from visual components instead of text.
when: Designers authoring coordinated AI scripts
why: Visual assembly lowers the barrier for non-programmers

text: Core user-experience positions include interface behavior planner, information structure architect, and usability researcher.
A practical UX framework can combine brain and behavior research, usability heuristics, and less-studied concepts like game feel, without being empirically validated.
Conflicting user desires can be handled by showing an error, picking one at random, or offering several plausible answers; most tools keep the user's final say.
Early visions of human-computer symbiosis criticized systems where the human supplied all initiative, direction, integration and criteria, and proposed sharing initiative with the computer.
The gap between the intended level and the built level is largely set by the tools used, and this holds for other disciplines too.
Plan player-facing decisions with UX goals in mind, treating UX strategy as central to development.
why: UX strategy shapes how players experience the game from the start.

text: Hiring UX designers can make the design process more efficient.
No game has perfect UX, so tradeoffs between usability and other goals should be decided by the intended experience.
why: Games that remain faithful to their intended experience tend to be more fun and engaging.

text: Designing with usability guidelines from the start gives a better starting point for later usability tests.
why: Guidelines let teams catch pitfalls early, anticipate problems, and understand what researchers report about friction.

text: The core mechanic is the action players repeat most; if it is hard, unintuitive, or unenjoyable, players may quit.
why: The core action is repeated throughout play, so its quality shapes the experience of the whole game.

text: Bottom-up design is necessary for novel gameplay and can reveal new ways to play even with conventional gameplay.
when: When the gameplay is novel.
why: Building the interface from scratch forces examination of the problem instead of copying what already sells, which can reveal new play.

text: Use AI to flag common usability issues or to speed up iterations on prototypes.
when: Early or frequent design iteration where fast feedback helps.

text: The interface and underlying technology depend heavily on whether users are professional designers or players with no design experience.
when: When designing a mixed-initiative level-editing tool for a given audience.

text: Reaching stage 7 of the eight-stage UX maturity model was estimated to take about 20 years, and stage 8 about another 20.
when: Organizational UX maturity
why: Organizations must pass through successive stages of adoption, which takes a long time.

text: A five-stage UX maturity model: Unintentional, Self-referential, Expert, Centralized, Distributed. Each stage has a typical barrier and a main advancing tool.
when: When discussing UX strategy with upper management.
why: Locates a studio's current UX level and picks the next tools.

text: UX can expand in steps: dedicated test space, UX lab with one-way mirrors, hiring UX designers, dedicated UX team, integrated UX process, analytics coordination, and a voice at upper management.

AI in UX has three uses: analyzing user data to predict behavior and personalize; automating routine design tasks with real-time optimization; supporting usability evaluation via video analysis and automated feedback.
AI and UX have a two-way relationship: AI can improve user experience, and UX quality affects how effective the AI is.
why: Without a UX framework in their design process, AI tools struggle to be effective and useful.

text: Two core UX questions: can users reach their goals with ease, and is the experience enjoyable?
Treating UX as only UI leaves out many elements that shape the player experience; many game UX jobs titled UX/UI reinforce this front-end view.
why: Labelling the job UX/UI narrows the discipline to front-end visuals, hiding that its core is solving user problems.

text: Expecting upper management to fund UX before any live evidence exists leads to disappointment.
1) Listen to developers' needs, challenges, and problems. 2) Only then introduce UX processes.
when: Starting as a lone UX practitioner

text: 1) List the information the player needs. 2) List the input and output channels. 3) List the dimensions involved. 4) Design the interface from these lists.
1) Test a design element such as icons with players. 2) Highlight usability issues so the designer can iterate. 3) Retest the revised version.
when: Working alongside developers

text: UX manager should bridge analytics, game and publishing/BI teams to keep the player central, not only business goals; coordinate UX with analytics and other UX-focused teams to improve studio communication.
why: Analytics shows what players do while user research explains why, so the teams need to connect their findings.

text: A similar group can assess games in development and live games, with members concerned about user experience.
Explain what UX is and debunk misconceptions by letting developers experience the limits of their own perception.
when: Building UX understanding

text: Present UX as helping the team reach its goals with science, not as designing the game for the team.
why: Presenting UX as an ally keeps it from being seen as policing that reports misconduct to management.

text: Set up a UX plan for individual projects, covering the production workflow, and another for the whole studio.
why: Strategy at both project and studio levels is needed to deliver strong player experiences across the whole pipeline.

text: Start any product by understanding users: their problems, their needs, and what they already know.
Bring usability specialists in early in development, not only at the end, so findings can still change the design.
when: during development
why: Changes are still possible early, before shipping.

text: When a user's mental model does not match the system's behavior, fix the design so the system behaves as the user expects, rather than blaming the user.
when: When players make errors even though the system works as it was built
why: The design model is at fault when it diverges from the model users form of the system.

text: Prioritize users' best interests, with inclusion, accessibility and ethics as central concerns.
UX professionals should have a seat in AI product decisions, since they are often left out of them.
when: When AI features are planned or built for users.
why: Human-centered AI needs UX expertise to shape outcomes.

text: Use a UX framework as a starting point and adapt it to your own challenges, not as a fixed rulebook.
why: The framework is not empirically validated, and the scientific method requires testing theories, including those drawn from practice.

text: Automating routine design work frees time for ideation, but it also encourages automation bias, which lowers the detection of errors.
when: When routine design or evaluation tasks are handed to automated tools.
why: People reduce their own checking when a tool handles the task.

text: A seated player in a walking-based VR game perceives the scene as fake because the body and the experience disagree.
when: Player posture differs from the posture the game assumes
why: Proprioception is the body's sense of its position, and sitting while walking virtually conflicts with it, so presence breaks.

text: Physical input is how the player touches a device to change the game world, such as a controller, keyboard, mouse, or moved board pieces.
Physical output is how the player perceives the game world, through a screen, audio, or other sensory output.
Proprioception is the body sense of where the body is and how it is posed, such as sitting, standing or crossing a leg.
In games, natural input means relationships that feel instinctive, not input that copies real-world physical interaction.
Augmented reality overlays virtual elements on the real world, spanning a continuum from assisted reality to mixed reality, on phones, headsets, or glasses.
A 3D underlay is a simple 3D scene painted over in an image program, letting an artist produce many looks from one scene.
Seeing and meaningfully using one's own hands strongly builds presence in VR and makes the virtual world feel solid and stable.
Augmented reality overlays digital information on real places by recognizing images and pairing them with data, and waypoints can guide players to social locations.
when: Designing location-based games

text: A wider field of view on AR displays could change how much sickness AR causes.
Screen games largely ignore proprioception, but VR depends on it, so a mismatch in posture breaks presence.
Looking at a world differs greatly from reaching out and touching it.
As foot and full-body tracking become standard, body alignment will matter more and can produce stronger presence.
First-person views are better suited to aiming and to some line-of-sight relationships than third-person views.
A familiar gesture, such as pinch-to-zoom, may make its VR equivalent easier to adopt, but that assumption must be tested.
when: when moving a known interaction to a new platform
why: Users' existing familiarity with a gesture from touch screens may carry over, but that carry-over is an assumption to be tested.

text: Physical actions such as one unit attacking another are clear and need no interpretive symbols, so mechanics built on them are easy to learn and read.
when: choosing core interactions for readability
why: this clarity explains why violence recurs across many games

text: A controller or prop built for one task invites only that task, while a generic controller invites wider guesses about what else is possible.
when: Choosing physical controllers or props
why: Players set expectations about what is possible from the interface, so a physical prop silently limits what they try.

text: When virtual head height does not match the player's real posture, the player feels they float or that the world has shrunk.
when: A seated player is given a standing-height viewpoint
why: The mind knows the virtual scale is impossible for the real body

text: The strongest hand presence comes from natural, meaningful manipulation of the environment, not from hand visibility alone.
why: Hands are humans' main means of acting on the world, so manipulating things with them builds presence.

text: VR cybersickness arises when visual and auditory cues show body motion while the vestibular and proprioceptive systems sense a stationary body.
why: Visual and auditory motion cues conflict with the body's balance and position senses, and that conflict is the main cause.

text: Gesture that merely substitutes for a button wastes sensing detail, feels unsatisfying, and removes the skill that gives mastery its value.
when: mapping an action to a motion gesture
why: Mapping subtle, high-sensitivity motion onto one fixed, prerecorded result discards the precision that gives skill its reward.

text: Letting virtual objects pass through the player's body disconcerts players and eventually breaks presence, because bodies resist being penetrated.
when: Player walks through a virtual table or similar object
why: Players feel subconscious fear when a virtual object enters their body, and that fear quickly breaks presence.

text: Visible hands or feet that are not where the real ones are break presence faster than any other avatar error.
when: Avatar limbs are shown in VR
why: A visible limb out of position conflicts with the body's felt position, so the mind treats the scene as unreal.

text: Overlaying AR on the open real world without considering hazards has been linked to large numbers of traffic accidents and deaths.
when: When AR is overlaid onto the open real world rather than a restricted environment
why: Distraction from screens in public spaces causes measurable real-world harm.

text: Use gesture recognition when measured detail such as rotation and speed can shape the response, layering subtle measures; avoid it when the result collapses into a single binary outcome.
when: the device reports detailed motion data
why: Shaping outcomes with measured detail makes results more satisfying than binary responses.

text: Make the physical objects players touch more pleasing, and make the mapping from physical actions to world actions as direct as possible.
when: When the player has a physical interaction with the game through a physical interface

text: Consider whether a physical output device would make the game world feel more real to the player.
Hide the player's hands while they hold a tool, since attention shifts to the tool tip and most players do not notice.
when: A tool is held in VR
why: The mind focuses on the tool tip rather than the hands

text: Design scenarios such as a desk or a car interior for seated players when the player will be seated during play.
when: The player sits during play
why: The body's posture matches the virtual setting

text: Place frequently used objects where a real person naturally reaches, such as over the shoulder for arrows stored in a back quiver.
when: Players must retrieve items repeatedly
why: The movement matches natural body motion

text: Make physical actions easy: use large buttons for cursor or finger input and place common commands near the thumb on mobile, as Fitts's law supports.
when: When players point at targets with a cursor or finger, including on mobile screens
why: Physical affordances help users physically act, and large, reachable targets make pointing and thumb reach comfortable.

text: Make signs and feedback noticeable, discernible, legible, and audible, for example with legible font sizes.
Use AR in restricted, controlled environments and avoid requiring screen focus in open, hazardous spaces such as busy streets.
when: When designing where and how AR play takes place.
why: Minimizing cognitive load and keeping players safe depends on the environment.

text: For VR sessions longer than roughly 15 to 20 minutes, allow seated play with arms on the lap and use a physical controller instead of gestures.
when: When a VR game session runs longer than roughly fifteen to twenty minutes
why: Headsets stay heavy and raised arms quickly tire, so resting arms and using a controller reduces physical strain.

text: At minimum, give 2D UI in VR depth and place it inside the 3D environment.
why: Content placed too close to the eyes is uncomfortable to view, so UI needs a comfortable depth.
